questions.question: Two adults of same weight and height show different health risks: one has 83% lean body mass, the other has 65%. Which body composition principle explains their risk difference?
questions.explanation: Health risk from body composition is determined by the proportion of lean body mass to stored fat rather than total body weight. The individual with 65% lean mass has 35% body fat, far exceeding the health-associated threshold, while 83% lean mass reflects a favorable composition. Fat cells do not contribute to ATP production and represent metabolically inactive mass that costs the body additional energy to carry.

questions.question: A muscular bodybuilder has a BMI of 31. What does this BMI classification most likely misrepresent about his health status?
questions.explanation: BMI cannot differentiate between fat mass and lean muscle mass, leading to misclassification of highly muscular individuals as obese when their excess weight is actually hypertrophied muscle tissue. A muscular bodybuilder with a BMI of 31 likely has normal or low body fat percentage. Additional body composition assessment tools such as waist circumference or DEXA are needed to accurately classify such individuals.

questions.question: A patient reports doing rapid bouncing stretches at end range. Which complication is the patient most at risk for?
questions.explanation: Ballistic bouncing at end-range stretching triggers the myotatic stretch reflex, causing protective muscle contraction that opposes the stretch and risks tissue injury. Static stretching allows the stretch reflex to subside, enabling safer tissue lengthening. The patient should be retaught static stretching technique to avoid reflexive resistance and potential tissue damage.

questions.question: A physiotherapist applies FITT principles to prescribe exercise for a deconditioned adult. Which component of FITT directly addresses the category of physical activity selected for the programme?
questions.explanation: The Type component of the FITT principle specifies the category of physical activity prescribed, such as aerobic exercise, resistance training, or flexibility work. This selection determines which physiological systems are stressed and what adaptations will result. The other FITT components quantify how often, how hard, and how long exercise is performed.

Weight reduction in obese hypertensive patients significantly reduces cardiac workload and blood pressure by decreasing total peripheral resistance and venous return to the heart. This makes exercise-induced weight loss one of the most potent non-pharmacological treatments for hypertension.

A patient underwent hydrostatic weighing for body composition analysis. Which characteristic most directly accounts for this method's superior accuracy over field techniques?
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic weighing is considered a criterion standard for body composition assessment against which field methods are validated for accuracy. It uses Archimedes' principle to estimate body density and calculate fat versus lean mass with high precision. Despite its superior accuracy, its complexity, expense, and equipment requirements limit its use to research settings.

questions.question: A postmenopausal woman presents with significantly increased waist circumference compared to pre-menopausal measurements. Which hormonal mechanism is most directly responsible?
questions.explanation: Decreased estrogen levels after menopause promote central or abdominal fat accumulation by altering fat distribution patterns from gynoid to android distribution. Estrogen normally promotes peripheral fat deposition, and its absence shifts adipose tissue to visceral depots. This hormonal change explains why obesity becomes more prevalent in women after menopause and increases their cardiometabolic risk.

questions.question: A patient finds normal breathing difficult during static stretching. The physiotherapist corrects this by emphasizing relaxed breathing. Why does normal breathing specifically enhance stretching effectiveness?

This dual cardiovascular and relaxation benefit makes normal breathing an essential component of safe and effective stretching technique.

• IUD: a small T-shaped plastic and copper device inserted into the uterus via the vagina; copper IUD (hormone-free, 5-10 years) or hormonal IUD (progestogen: Mirena, Jaydess).
• Before: assess vagina and womb for position, size and infection; give broad-spectrum antibiotics if infected; explain procedure, relieve anxiety, obtain consent; give prescribed analgesic (e.g. PCM).
• During: dorsal lithotomy position; speculum inserted and cervix swabbed with disinfectant; tenaculum steadies cervix; uterine sound measures depth; IUD pushed into applicator and inserted, applicator removed leaving the thread; thread trimmed; removal with ring forceps pulling the thread.
• After: teach that cramps, bleeding, long or heavy periods may occur and resolve.
(b)
• Contraindications: pelvic infection (STI or PID), uterine structural abnormality, unexplained vaginal bleeding, gestational trophoblastic disease, cervical or endometrial cancer, pregnancy; levonorgestrel IUD: breast cancer or allergy; copper IUD: Wilson disease or allergy to copper.
• Danger signs: foul-smelling vaginal discharge, raised temperature, pruritus; risks: pelvic infection if infection contracted, rejection or displacement, ectopic pregnancy if it fails.
(c)
• Return for check 3-6 weeks after insertion and yearly pelvic examination; good personal and sex hygiene; teach how to feel the threads.
• Advantages to teach: works straight away, 5-10 years protection, safe in lactation, fertility returns on removal; does not protect against STIs.

• Pulmonary embolism: occlusion of pulmonary arteries by thrombi from elsewhere, typically deep veins of the legs or pelvis. Risk factors: pregnancy or birth within six weeks, oral contraceptives/HRT, DVT, heart failure/stroke history, prolonged inactivity, BMI >25/obesity.
• Pathophysiology: deep thrombi detach and embolise; vascular occlusion impairs gas exchange and circulation; lower lobes more often affected.
(b)
Signs: tachycardia, tachypnoea, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea; less common cough and haemoptysis; massive emboli: hypotension, presyncope, syncope, cardiac arrest. Extremities assessed for warmth, redness, inflammation. Tests: Doppler ultrasound, helical CT, chest X-ray, echocardiography, pulmonary angiogram, V/Q scan.
(c)
Impaired gas exchange; Ineffective peripheral tissue perfusion; Acute pain; Anxiety.
(d)
• Monitor vitals and oxygen saturation, oxygen therapy, head of bed elevated, deep breathing, position changes; elevate affected leg, compression stockings, warm moist heat, hydration, analgesics; teach anticoagulant use.
• Medical: LMWH is the treatment of choice and warfarin is avoided in pregnancy; prophylactic LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg once daily) for women with previous PE or thrombophilia until 6 weeks postpartum; thrombectomy for severe DVT.
(e)

questions.answerText:
(a)
• DMPA (Depo-Provera): deep intramuscular injection into the arm or buttock; slowly absorbed to give contraception for 1-3 months; Noristerat (200 mg) is another progestogen-only type.
• When to start: first seven days after menstrual bleeding starts; six weeks after childbirth or any time once menses return; immediately or on day seven after childbirth if not breastfeeding; after miscarriage or abortion; immediately after stopping another method.
• Mechanism: prevents ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, thins the endometrium.
(b)
• Specific contraindications listed include severe liver impairment, severe arterial disease and pregnancy.
• Side effects: menstrual disturbance, weight gain, headache, dizziness, hair loss, acne, loss of sexual feeling; delayed return to fertility averaging four months to one year; no protection against STIs.
(c)
Advantages to teach: private, long acting, does not interfere with intercourse, suitable for breastfeeding women, reversible, reduces seizures in epilepsy.

questions.question:
A woman at more than 20 weeks' gestation has new-onset hypertension with a systolic blood pressure of 160 mmHg or more and/or diastolic of 110 mmHg or more. She has no proteinuria and no recorded pre-pregnancy blood pressure. She is a nullipara.
(a) Identify the likely condition or stage from the findings.
(b) Interpret the blood pressure, proteinuria and gestational age.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ signs = gestational hypertension; with BP at or above 160/110 mmHg she is managed as preeclampsia with severe features; proteinuria would upgrade the diagnosis to preeclampsia.
(b)
• Preeclampsia = new hypertension with proteinuria or significant end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive woman (may develop postpartum); hypertension before 20 weeks is usually chronic hypertension.
• BP normally falls from 6 weeks, nadir at 16-20 weeks, then rises to pre-pregnancy level by term, so pre-existing hypertension may appear new; preeclampsia is more common in nulliparas.
• Some 10-25% of gestational hypertension progresses to preeclampsia; it usually resolves by 12 weeks postpartum; persistence beyond 12 weeks = chronic hypertension; resolution without preeclampsia = transient hypertension of pregnancy.
(c)
• Differentials: chronic hypertension (proteinuria normal or under 1 g/day; urate not elevated); superimposed preeclampsia (new or sudden increase in proteinuria, worsening hypertension); CKD exacerbation (active urine sediment, creatinine above 1.2 mg/dL without marked hypertension).
• Others: HELLP (haemolysis, raised liver enzymes, low platelets); eclampsia (grand mal seizure); pheochromocytoma (sweating, palpitations, tremor, pallor); hyperthyroidism (hypertension with tachycardia); drug-induced hypertension (cocaine, amphetamines, withdrawal of clonidine or beta blockers).
(d)
It is safer to assume new-onset hypertension in pregnancy is preeclampsia, since it may progress quickly to eclampsia or severe forms; accurate diagnosis guides timing of delivery and need for antiseizure prophylaxis.

(a)
• Chorioamnionitis (intraamniotic infection):.
• Acute inflammation of the membranes and chorion, typically due to ascending polymicrobial bacterial infection after membrane rupture.
• Signs: fever, uterine fundal tenderness, maternal tachycardia (>100/min), fetal tachycardia (>160/min), purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid, diaphoresis.
• Common organisms: Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma hominis, Gardnerella, Bacteroides, GBS, E. coli.
(b)
• Diagnosis: CBC (leucocytosis >12,000 or >15,000/mm3), CRP, amniotic fluid culture (most reliable, results up to 3 days), placental pathology.
• Management: IV ampicillin every 6 hours and gentamicin every 8-24 hours until delivery; clindamycin or metronidazole if caesarean; antipyretics.
(c)
• Vulnerable: longer membrane rupture, prolonged labour, nulliparity, internal monitoring, multiple vaginal examinations, meconium-stained fluid, smoking, alcohol or drugs, immune-compromised states, epidural, GBS, bacterial vaginosis, STIs.
• Risk rises after three or more vaginal examinations and five-fold after eight.
(d)
• Mastitis: inflammation of breast tissue, mainly lactation mastitis, affecting about 10% of breastfeeding mothers; symptoms: breast tenderness, swelling, redness, fever.
• Both are inflammatory processes with similar symptoms, but chorioamnionitis leads to more complications and can cause death of the mother or baby.
• Mastitis complications: recurrence, abscess, sepsis; chorioamnionitis: neonatal sepsis, cerebral palsy, maternal bacteraemia, septic shock.
• Mastitis is treated with 10 days of antibiotics and continued breastfeeding; chorioamnionitis with IV antibiotics until delivery.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Endometriosis is an endometrial disease in which endometrial tissue grows outside the uterus; associated with hormonal imbalance, especially excess oestrogen, causing inflammation and pain.
• Cause unknown: retrograde menstruation, high oestrogen and genetic factors.
• Signs: dysmenorrhoea, pelvic pain and cramping before and after periods, heavy or irregular periods, pain with bowel movements, pain with intercourse, fatigue.
(b)
• Diagnosis: history of menstrual symptoms and chronic pelvic pain; laparoscopy with histological verification.
• Medical management: NSAIDs/analgesics; progestin-based contraceptives (POPs, implant, injection, IUD) because high oestrogen worsens disease; Laparoscopic removal of lesions, adhesions and scar tissue.
(c)
• Vulnerability: women with high oestrogen levels, a genetic predisposition, and retrograde flow of menstrual blood through the fallopian tubes.
• Complications: scarring, adhesions, blocked tubes, cysts from trapped blood, possible infertility.
• Nursing: counsel women wanting children not to postpone childbearing.
(d)
• Endometritis: inflammation of the endometrium from bacterial infection (STIs, TB, vaginal bacteria) with fever, pelvic pain, bleeding or discharge.
• Endometriosis: pieces of uterine lining develop in places other than the uterus (ovaries, fallopian tubes).
• Risk factors of endometritis: D&C, D&E, biopsy, hysteroscopy, childbirth with prolonged membrane rupture, IUD; complications: infertility, pelvic abscess, septicaemia.

(a) State the assessment findings.

(c) Describe the medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hyperemesis gravidarum: excessive vomiting before 20 weeks, leading to dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, weight loss and anorexia. Findings: persistent severe nausea and vomiting, weakness, dehydration, emaciation, rapid pulse, low BP, sunken eyes, dry skin, scanty urine with acetone, furred tongue, dry cracked lips.
• Severe cases: hypotension, proteinuria, jaundice, delirium, coma and death. Predisposing factors: psychological factors, rising oestrogen and HCG, multiple pregnancy, hydatidiform mole, acute hydramnios, hepatitis, pyelonephritis.
(b)
• Complete bed rest, daily bed bath, oral care and pressure-area care; strict intake and output chart; test urine daily for protein, acetone, bile, chloride and specific gravity; monitor and report vital signs.
• Weigh on admission and on alternate days; mild laxative if constipated on prescription; involve the husband in care.
• Oral diet when vomiting has stopped for 24 hours: easily digestible food in attractive form, small frequent portions, avoid fried and oily foods, give fruit juice.
(c)
• Admit; history and examination to rule out hepatitis, hydatidiform mole, UTI; IV rehydration and correction of electrolyte imbalance and hypoglycaemia.
• Suspend oral fluids about 24 hours; antiemetics (largactil 25 mg or avomine 25 mg) used with care because of possible effects on the embryo; multivitamins, iron and daraprim; keep fluid balance record and a separate record of vomitus.

(a)
• Tubal (ectopic) pregnancy: the fertilised ovum embeds outside the uterine cavity, commonly in the fallopian tube (also abdomen, cervix; rarely ovary).
• Signs: history of amenorrhoea, mild or acute lower abdominal pain, sharp stabbing localised pain, nausea, brownish discharge, dizziness, shoulder pain (bleeding into peritoneum), other pregnancy signs may be absent, shock may be present.
(b)
• Predisposing: congenital tube abnormality, previous infection, tubal surgery, IUCD, assisted reproduction; ectopic is somewhat more common with the mini pill.
• Pathophysiology: the blastocyst erodes the tubal epithelium and attaches to the muscle layer.
(c)
• Outcomes near the distal end: tubal abortion, tubal mole, tubal rupture (gradual or sudden), abdominal pregnancy.
• Ultrasound may assist diagnosis.
questions.question:
A woman with amenorrhoea presents with acute lower abdominal pain, sharp stabbing localised pain, nausea, a brownish vaginal discharge, dizziness and shoulder pain. She has a history of tubal infection and an IUCD.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State the possible outcomes.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The period from the birth of the baby to complete expulsion of the placenta and membranes.
• It involves the relationship of mother, baby and father, separation, descent and expulsion of the placenta and membranes, control of haemorrhage from the placental site, and sometimes the start of breastfeeding.
(b)
• After the placenta is delivered check that the uterus is well contracted and fresh blood loss minimal.
• Inspect the perineum and lower vagina with a strong light, as gently as possible, to assess trauma before repair.
• Active management (AMTSL): routine prophylactic uterotonic (IV, IM or occasionally oral) with early cord clamping, regardless of obstetric risk, to reduce PPH.
• Higher-risk women (e.g. multiple birth) may get a prophylactic infusion of larger uterotonic doses over several hours.
• Examine placenta and membranes for completeness; controlled cord traction and fundal massage form part of management of the third stage.
(c)
• Deviations: retained placental fragments, incomplete separation, atonic uterus and trauma lead to PPH (the 4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin).
• Causes of atony: prolonged or precipitate labour, full bladder, multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, macrosomia, oxytocin induction, fibroid, anaemia, mismanagement of the third stage.
(d)
• Atonic uterus fails to contract and retract so torn vessels keep bleeding (placental site blood flow about 500-800 ml/min).
• PPH of 500 ml or more: signs are visible bleeding, boggy uterus, pallor, tachycardia, hypotension and collapse; obstetric haemorrhage is a leading cause of maternal mortality.
• Maternal collapse is a sign of severe PPH.
questions.question:
Describe the third stage of labour.
(a) Define it and state what it involves.
(b) Describe completion of the stage and active management.
(c) State how deviations relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how a complication may progress and its effects on the mother.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• WHO: exclusive breastfeeding for six months, then complementary foods with breastfeeding until at least 2 years; weaning begins at six months.
• Starting before four months raises risk of allergies, diarrhoea and choking; delaying beyond eight months may cause malnutrition and iron-deficiency anaemia.
• Readiness signs: sitting unsupported, reaching for food, chewing motions, losing the tongue-thrust reflex, interest in family meals.
(b)
• Principles: gradual; one new food every 3-5 days; thin purees then mashed by about eight months, finger foods at 9-12 months; nutrient-dense; hygienic; responsive feeding.
• Frequency: 2-3 meals/day at 6-8 months; 3-4 meals plus snacks at 9-24 months. Foods:.
• Pap/ogi, rice cereal, millet, beans, vegetables, fruits, egg yolk, fish, yoghurt or cheese; no added salt, sugar or strong spices.
• Methods: spoon feeding, baby-led weaning, or a mixed approach.
(c)
• Breast milk alone no longer gives adequate energy, iron, zinc and vitamins after six months; weaning gives a balanced diet and boosts immunity.
• Problems to prevent: diarrhoea (poor hygiene), food refusal, allergy, choking, malnutrition.
(d)
• Nurse educates on timing, safe preparation and textures, demonstrates preparation, addresses myths, monitors weight, length and head circumference.
• Promote continued breastfeeding; encourage safe cultural practices and gently correct harmful ones such as herbal mixtures or restricting nutrient-dense foods.
• Introduce allergenic foods (cow's milk, eggs, nuts) one at a time and watch for rash, vomiting or breathing difficulty.
questions.question:
Describe weaning as a child nutrition measure.
(a) Define it and state the recommended timing and readiness signs.
(b) State its principles, foods, methods and schedule.
(c) Explain its role in reducing child malnutrition and illness.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and health education.

A child aged 18 months is brought with cough and diarrhoea. The mother reports the diarrhoea has lasted several days without blood. The nurse counts 40 breaths per minute in a calm child, finds no general danger signs, no chest in-drawing and no stridor. The child's eyes are sunken, the child is restless and irritable, drinks eagerly, and the skin pinch goes back slowly.
(a) Identify and classify the conditions from the findings.
(b) Interpret the findings and state the treatment for each classification.
(c) State the differential classifications and when referral is needed.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and follow-up.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Breathing: fast breathing is 40 breaths/min or more at 12 months to 5 years, so this classifies as PNEUMONIA (no danger sign, chest in-drawing or stridor).
• Diarrhoea: two of sunken eyes, restless/irritable, drinking eagerly, skin pinch slow = SOME DEHYDRATION.
(b)
• Pneumonia: oral antibiotic for 3 days; if wheezing, inhaled bronchodilator for 5 days; soothe throat and relieve cough with a safe remedy; follow up in 2 days.
• Some dehydration: give fluid, zinc and food (Plan B); advise mother when to return immediately; follow up in 5 days if not improving.
(c)
• Severe pneumonia or very severe disease = any general danger sign, chest in-drawing or stridor in a calm child: first dose antibiotic and refer urgently. Cough or cold = no pneumonia signs. Cough over 3 weeks or recurrent wheezing: refer for TB or asthma assessment.
• Severe dehydration = two of lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, not able to drink, skin pinch very slow (Plan C); no dehydration (Plan A); persistent diarrhoea (14 days or more) and dysentery (blood in stool: ciprofloxacin for 3 days, follow up in 2 days).
• If dehydration coexists with another severe classification: refer urgently with ORS and advise continued breastfeeding.
(d)
Check general danger signs first (unable to drink/breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic/unconscious); counsel the mother on feeding and fluids and when to return immediately.

questions.question:
A woman presents after the 24th week of pregnancy with vaginal bleeding before the onset of labour. A sanitary pad is partially soaked with blood and a clot has been passed. The bleeding is painless, the fetal head has failed to engage, and there are signs of fetal distress.
(a) State the assessment findings and investigations the nurse should carry out or anticipate.
(b) Identify three priority nursing diagnoses.
(c) Outline the immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Describe the medical management.
(e) State the expected outcomes of care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Bleeding after 24 weeks before labour = APH; painless bleeding suggests placenta praevia (pain suggests abruption); failed engagement/malpresentation and fetal distress may occur; shock if severe. Investigations: vital signs, FBC, clotting studies, urgent ultrasound (cannot exclude abruption), Kleihauer test and anti-D if rhesus-negative, CTG.
(b)
Deficient fluid volume related to excessive blood loss; Anxiety related to perceived threat of death of self and fetus; Deficient knowledge related to unfamiliarity with condition.
(c)
Assess mother and resuscitate if in shock; assess fetus (FHR), emergency delivery if viable but distressed; monitor vital signs; give prescribed IV fluids (Ringer's lactate, normal saline); left lateral position on bed rest; encourage verbalisation of feelings, coping strategies and counselling referral.
(d)
• Admit even for small bleeding (concealed loss possible); estimate blood loss (minor <50 ml, major 50-1000 ml, massive >1000 ml and/or shock); mother's life takes priority; fetal distress = urgent delivery irrespective of gestational age; bleeding arrested by delivery of the fetus.
• No vaginal or rectal examination until placenta praevia is excluded by ultrasound; gentle abdominal palpation; corticosteroids offered at 24-35 weeks if preterm birth risk.
(e)
Outcome: frequent monitoring and prompt management greatly reduce the risk of neonatal death.

(a)
• Hyperemesis: excessive vomiting before 20 weeks that becomes serious when the woman vomits all day until the stomach is empty; vomitus may contain bile.
• Effects: dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, weight loss, anorexia, malnutrition and metabolic disturbance.
• Causes unknown; psychological factors, endocrine (rising oestrogen and HCG, progesterone relaxing the cardiac sphincter).
• Signs: persistent severe vomiting, weakness, dehydration, rapid pulse, low BP, sunken eyes, dry skin, acetone urine and breath, furred tongue; later proteinuria, jaundice, delirium, coma.
(b)
• Admit; history and examination to exclude hepatitis, hydatidiform mole, UTI; urine tested daily for protein, acetone, bile, chloride and specific gravity.
• IV rehydration, electrolyte and hypoglycaemia correction; oral fluids suspended about 24 hours; antiemetics (largactil 25 mg, avomine 25 mg); multivitamins, iron, daraprim.
(c)
• Vulnerable: unwanted pregnancy, women seeking sympathy or attention, educated and nervous women; Multiple pregnancy, hydatidiform mole, acute hydramnios, infective hepatitis, pyelonephritis.
• Twin pregnancy is associated with more severe nausea and hyperemesis.
(d)
• Morning sickness: begins at 4-8 weeks and usually subsides by 14-16 weeks; correlates with rising HCG, progesterone and smooth muscle relaxation.
• Hyperemesis: severe, persistent, with dehydration, ketonuria and weight loss, needing admission.
• Hyperemesis nursing: complete bed rest, strict intake and output, weigh on alternate days, small frequent meals.
questions.question:
Discuss nausea and vomiting in pregnancy.
(a) Define hyperemesis gravidarum and state its causes and signs.
(b) State the investigations and medical management.
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable.
(d) Distinguish between hyperemesis gravidarum and normal morning sickness.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Procedure: clamping and cutting of the umbilical cord. Before: sterile instruments are used to prevent infection; dry the baby and place skin-to-skin on the mother's abdomen or chest; assess breathing and crying (begin resuscitation within 30 seconds if not breathing).
• During: if stable, delay clamping for at least 60 seconds (delayed clamping is 30 seconds to 3 minutes; it raises iron stores, improves circulatory stability and in preterm infants lowers risk of IVH and necrotising enterocolitis); clamp in two places 2-3 cm apart and cut between with sterile scissors; immediate clamping (15-30 seconds) only for resuscitation or urgent maternal bleeding.
• After: a plastic clamp or tie remains about 2-3 cm from the abdominal wall; keep the stump clean and dry, fold the diaper below it, give sponge baths, do not pull it off (falls off in 7-14 days; normal range 5-15 days, up to 3 weeks); apply nothing unless prescribed (chlorhexidine gel 7.1% in high-risk areas).
(b)
• Cord structures: two umbilical arteries and one vein within a sheath of amnion, protected by Wharton's jelly; about 55-60 cm long.
• Danger signs: foul-smelling or pus-like discharge, redness spreading more than 1 cm, swelling or warmth, non-stopping bleeding, tenderness, fever above 38 degrees C, irritability when touched, cord not off after two weeks (omphalitis).
• Risk factors for omphalitis: unclean delivery, unsterile tools, dirty hands, ash/herbs/cow dung, tight dirty covering, low birth weight or premature babies.
(c)
Teach handwashing before touching baby or cord, dry cord care, no harmful substances, when to seek help; include cord care in antenatal and postnatal classes; use community leaders and TBAs, cord care kits with chlorhexidine, and respectful integration of cultural practices.
questions.question:
A term baby has just been born and is to have the umbilical cord clamped and cut. The baby is stable and the mother is bleeding normally.
(a) Name the procedure and state the nursing responsibilities before, during and after it.
(b) State the danger signs of cord infection and the structures of the cord involved.
(c) Outline the health education and discharge plan for the mother.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• GDM = carbohydrate intolerance first recognised in pregnancy. Early screening criteria: marked obesity, prior GDM, strong family history, previous infant over 4000 g, unexplained stillbirth, poor obstetric history, two positive clean-catch glycosuria tests. Screen at 26-28 weeks.
• Glucose challenge test (50 g oral load, blood draw at 1 hour): above 140 mg/dL (or 130 mg/dL) needs a 3-hour OGTT; above 200 mg/dL diagnoses GDM without further testing. Fundal height above dates suggests macrosomia or polyhydramnios.
(b)
• Careful abdominal palpation at every visit; ultrasound for fetal size and amniotic fluid index if fundal height exceeds dates; keep the woman informed of results; fetal movement counting from 34-36 weeks for diet-controlled GDM.
• Encourage balanced diet and moderate exercise.
(c)
• Goal: maintain a normal fasting blood sugar; most women control GDM with diet and exercise; pregestational diabetics need insulin.
• At 40 weeks biophysical profile twice weekly until delivery; await spontaneous labour if fetus appropriately grown and no hypertension; consider induction at 40 weeks for macrosomia, preeclampsia or term stillbirth history.
• Labour: manage as for other women; no glucose mixture in IV fluids; suspect shoulder dystocia; inform the paediatrician; monitor baby's glucose and start early feeding to prevent hypoglycaemia.
(d)
Good glucose control aims to reduce congenital malformations and low birth weight.
questions.question:
A woman at 27 weeks' gestation is found to have carbohydrate intolerance first recognised in pregnancy. She has a history of gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy, and recurrent glycosuria. Her fundal height is greater than dates.
(a) State the assessment findings and screening/diagnostic tests.
(b) Outline the immediate nursing interventions.
(c) Describe the medical management through to labour.
(d) State the expected outcomes.

Describe barrier methods as a family planning service.
(a) Define them and state the types.
(b) State advantages, disadvantages and eligible users.
(c) Explain their role in reducing STI and unintended pregnancy.
(d) State the health education the nurse should give.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Barrier methods block sperm from reaching the uterus and egg; two types: mechanical (condom, diaphragm, cervical cap, sponge) and chemical (spermicides, pH regulatory gel).
• Condoms made of latex, polyisoprene, polyurethane, silicone rubber or lamb intestine; Male and female types; lamb-intestine condoms are impenetrable to sperm but not to many viruses.
(b)
• Advantages: safe in breastfeeding; no hormones so safe for smokers and women with heart disease or clots; No effect on cycle; fertility returns at once; cheaper; some need no prescription.
• Disadvantages: less effective than IUDs or hormonal methods; must be used at every intercourse; diaphragm and cap need prescription; Cap and sponge work less well after vaginal birth; cannot be used in latex allergy or toxic shock history; cap not during menses.
• The male condom and diaphragm are the most effective barrier methods.
(c)
• Condoms are the only method that may protect against STIs such as HIV/AIDS and herpes.
• Spermicide nonoxynol-9 is minimally effective alone and gives no HIV protection; it destroys sperm and works better with a barrier.
(d)
Teach: insert spermicide high in the vagina and remain supine; use each time; correct condom use.

questions.question:
Describe the physiological changes of pregnancy.
(a) State the factors driving the changes and the endocrine and reproductive changes.
(b) Describe the cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and renal changes.
(c) State how these changes relate to common problems of pregnancy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Changes respond to hormones, increased blood volume, weight gain and fetal growth; they affect musculoskeletal, endocrine, reproductive, cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, urinary, GI, immune systems, skin and breasts.
• HCG is the first placental hormone, maintains progesterone (pregnancy test); progesterone maintains pregnancy and relaxes smooth muscle; Oestrogen grows the uterus and breasts; relaxin relaxes pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix.
• Uterus ascends into the abdomen, becomes about five times bigger; cervix forms the operculum plug; vagina thickens and is prone to thrush.
(b)
• Cardiac output rises 30-50% in the third trimester, blood volume 40-50%, heart rate not above 100, systemic vascular resistance falls 20%; supine hypotension due to vena caval compression.
• Respiratory: diaphragm elevated about 4 cm, tidal volume up 30-50%, oxygen consumption up 30%; women are more prone to hypoxia and dyspnoea.
• GI: progesterone slows motility and lowers LES tone causing reflux; morning sickness starts at 4-8 weeks, subsides by 14-16; constipation and haemorrhoids occur.
• Renal: GFR rises, sodium retention causes oedema, frequent urination in the third trimester, stress and urge incontinence.
(c)
• Common problems listed: rib pain, nerve compression (carpal tunnel:.
• Fluid retention compresses nerves causing pain, numbness, weakness in the hand), pelvic floor dysfunction, oedema, pre-eclampsia, back pain, muscle cramps, symphysis pubis dysfunction, morning sickness.
• Posture changes (centre of gravity shifts, altered spinal curves) and lax joints/pelvic girdle muscles relate to back and pelvic problems; symptoms may persist 8 weeks after delivery.

(a)
• Infertility: a male or female cannot conceive because of a problem with the reproductive system of either partner; Also women who get pregnant but cannot stay pregnant (miscarriage before 20 weeks, stillbirth after).
• Causes: about one third female, one third male, one third both or undetermined.
• Male causes: low sperm count, motility or abnormal shape, testicular overheating, ejaculation disorders, hypogonadism, Klinefelter syndrome, mumps, hypospadias, cystic fibrosis, radiation or chemotherapy, drugs.
• Female causes: ovulation problems (about 25%), blocked tubes, endometriosis, fibroids, PCOS, primary ovarian insufficiency, poor egg quality, surgery scarring, tubal ligation.
(b)
• Women: hormone tests, ovarian reserve, TSH and prolactin, HSG, transvaginal ultrasound, sonohysterogram, hysteroscopy, laparoscopy; men: semen analysis, hormone and genetic tests, testicular biopsy, imaging.
• Treatment: pharmacotherapy (clomifene, tamoxifen, metformin, gonadotrophins), tubal surgery, assisted conception (IUI, IVF).
(c)
• Vulnerable: age over 35 (women) or over 40 (men), diabetes, eating disorders, alcohol, toxins, over-exercise, radiation, STIs, smoking, stress, substance abuse, obesity/underweight.
• Female: PID, past ectopic pregnancy, sickle cell anaemia, thyroid disease, celiac or kidney disease; male: varicocele, undescended testicles, tight clothes, hot tubs, steroids, scrotal injury.
(d)
• Primary: no pregnancy after at least 1 year of unprotected sex.
• Secondary: pregnancy achieved at least once but now unable.
questions.question:
Discuss infertility.
(a) Define it and state the types and causes.
(b) State the investigations and treatment.
(c) Explain why some men and women are more vulnerable.
(d) Distinguish between primary and secondary infertility.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Visible severe wasting or oedema of both feet = SEVERE MALNUTRITION; severe palmar pallor = SEVERE ANAEMIA.
(b)
Very low weight for age without these signs = VERY LOW WEIGHT; not very low weight = NOT VERY LOW WEIGHT.
(c)
Anaemia: severe palmar pallor (severe), some palmar pallor (anaemia), no palmar pallor (no anaemia).
(d)
• Severe malnutrition: treat to prevent low sugar and refer urgently to hospital.
• Severe anaemia: refer urgently to hospital.
• Anaemia: give iron, oral antimalarial if high malaria risk, mebendazole if 1 year or older and no dose in the previous six months; advise when to return; follow up in 14 days.
• Very low weight: assess feeding and counsel on feeding recommendations; follow up in 30 days; if feeding problem, follow up in 5 days (child under 2 years).
• Not very low weight: advise when to return immediately; counsel on feeding if under 2 years.
questions.question:
A child aged 14 months is brought with severe palmar pallor, visible severe wasting and oedema of both feet. The child has a very low weight for age.
(a) Identify the conditions.
(b) Interpret the findings.
(c) State the differential classifications.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning, treatment and referral.

Describe the nursing care of a woman at risk of or with atonic postpartum haemorrhage.
(a) State the prevention and assessment in the third stage.
(b) State the drugs used (oxytocin, ergometrine, syntometrine) and their indications.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities for these drugs.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Active management of the third stage routinely gives a prophylactic uterotonic (IV, IM or occasionally orally) with early cord clamping regardless of risk; Higher-risk women (e.g. multiple birth) may get a larger-dose infusion over several hours.
• After the placenta: check the uterus is well contracted and fresh blood loss minimal; inspect perineum and lower vagina under strong light; examine placenta and membranes for completeness.
(b)
• Oxytocin (Syntocinon 5 units/ml): augments labour in inertia, prevents and treats PPH, induces labour; 10 units in 1 L RL or 5% dextrose by controlled IV infusion.
• Ergometrine acts directly on the myometrium to stop atonic bleeding; 0.2 mg IM for active management; for atonic PPH 1 ampoule slowly over 60 seconds, repeated after 2 hours; Syntometrine (oxytocin 5 units + ergometrine 0.5 mg) IM only.
• Ergometrine only after delivery of the anterior shoulder or the baby; not for induction or abortion.
(c)
• Oxytocin nursing: assess intake/output, contractions, BP, pulse, respiration; give IV infusion with crash cart available; notify the physician of contractions lasting over one minute or absent contractions.
• Oxytocin contraindications: grand multipara, contracted pelvis, previous caesarean or hysterectomy, malpresentation, obstructed labour, incoordinate uterine action, hypovolaemia, cardiac disease; Adverse effects: hypertonic uterus, fetal distress, uterine rupture, water intoxication, neonatal jaundice.
• Ergometrine contraindications: suspected plural pregnancy, organic cardiac disease, severe preeclampsia and eclampsia; adverse effects: rise of BP (vasoconstriction), gangrene of toes with prolonged use.
(d)
Rationale: prophylactic uterotonics reduce PPH risk; ergometrine's tetanic contraction could trap a second twin; bladder emptying aids contraction.

questions.question:
Describe the first stage of labour.
(a) State when labour occurs and what defines the first stage.
(b) Describe the latent, active and transitional phases, effacement and the care given.
(c) State how deviations relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how a complication may progress and its effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, with labour usually between 37 and 42 weeks.
• The first stage is recognised by regular contractions, effacement and at least 4 cm cervical dilatation, ending at full dilatation.
(b)
• Latent phase: may last 6-8 hours in primigravidae as the cervix dilates 0 to 4 cm; allowing it to pass without intervention can prevent a later diagnosis of poor progress.
• Active phase: begins at 4 cm with rhythmic contractions and progresses to 10 cm; usually completed within 6-12 hours; bloodstained mucoid show may accompany contractions.
• Transitional phase: about 8 cm until full dilatation or expulsive contractions; brief lull in uterine activity; many women feel the urge to push.
• Effacement: the cervical canal is taken up into the lower uterine segment; in nulliparous women dilatation follows effacement, in multiparous women they occur together.
• Care: assess progress, abdominal and vaginal examination; record contractions' frequency, length and strength on the partogram at 30-minute intervals.
(c)
• Labour length is influenced by parity, birth interval, psychological state, fetal presentation and position, pelvic shape and size, and contraction character.
• Malposition (any position other than occipito-anterior) and malpresentations are associated with difficult labour and increased operative intervention.
(d)
• Occipitoposterior position (10-30% of labours): long labour; needs close monitoring, fluids, often an epidural; avoid pushing before full dilatation; forceps or caesarean may be needed.
• Face presentation complications: obstructed labour, cord prolapse, facial bruising, maternal trauma.

(a)
• Drugs given in pregnancy: labetalol (alpha and beta blocker), nifedipine (calcium channel blocker), methyldopa (alpha blocker), hydralazine (vasodilator).
• Avoid ACE inhibitors, minoxidil, sodium nitroprusside, diltiazem, atenolol and propranolol: they may cause poor fetal renal function, malformation or IUGR.
(b)
• Labetalol: reduces peripheral resistance by alpha and beta blockade; contraindicated in bronchial asthma, hepatic or heart failure, severe bradycardia.
• Nifedipine: inhibits calcium ion flow in cardiac and smooth muscle and dilates arteries; contraindicated in heart failure and hypotension.
• Methyldopa: inhibits the central vasomotor centre; contraindicated in hepatic disease and lactating mothers; 250 mg BD or TDS, max 2 g daily.
• Hydralazine: direct peripheral vasodilator; 5 mg diluted in 10 ml NS slow IV at 15-20 minute intervals; contraindicated in coronary artery disease, stroke, severe renal impairment.
(c)
• Labetalol: remain supine 3 hours after infusion, monitor BP and glucose in diabetics, rise slowly.
• Nifedipine: monitor BP and heart rate, avoid grapefruit juice, watch for heart failure signs.
• Methyldopa: monitor BP and Coombs test, report involuntary movements, daily weight (report gain of 2 pounds or more in a week); hydralazine: monitor BP, pulse, weight, report muscle and joint pain, fever or sore throat, take after food.
• Furosemide (diuretic): used for PIH with massive oedema, eclampsia with pulmonary oedema, severe anaemia with heart failure and before transfusion; monitor weight, BP, pulse, intake and output; watch for hypokalaemia; take in the morning; avoid sunlight.
(d)
Rationale: orthostatic hypotension is minimised by slow position changes; diuretics risk fetal compromise and hyponatraemia, so monitoring is vital.
questions.question:
Describe the nursing care of a pregnant woman receiving antihypertensive drugs.
(a) State the drugs of choice and those to avoid.
(b) State the actions and indications of labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa and hydralazine.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities for these drugs and for furosemide.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions.

A child aged 3 years in a high malaria-risk area has had fever for 3 days. The child feels hot. There is no stiff neck and no general danger sign, but there is a generalised rash with runny nose and red eyes, and pus draining from the eye.
(a) Identify the conditions or stage.
(b) Interpret the findings.
(c) State the differential classifications.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and referral.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fever classified by malaria risk: high or low; ask duration, daily fever beyond 7 days, measles in the last 3 months.
• Signs of measles: generalised rash plus cough, runny nose or red eyes; pus draining from the eye or mouth ulcers = MEASLES with eye or mouth complications.
(b)
• Look for stiff neck, runny nose, measles signs, deep extensive mouth ulcers, pus from the eye, clouding of the cornea.
• Fever is recorded by history, by feeling hot or by measured temperature.
(c)
• Any general danger sign or stiff neck = very severe febrile disease; clouding cornea or deep extensive mouth ulcers = severe complicated measles; malaria; fever with malaria unlikely.
• Very severe febrile disease: first dose of ACT/quinine for severe malaria, first dose antibiotic, treat to prevent low blood sugar, paracetamol for fever above 38.5 degrees C, refer urgently.
(d)
• Malaria: oral co-artemether or recommended antimalarial; paracetamol for fever above 38.5; advise when to return; follow up in 2 days if fever persists; refer if fever every day for more than 7 days.
• Referral reasoning: complete assessment and pre-referral treatment immediately so referral is not delayed; counsel the caregiver.

(a)
• Implant: inserted subdermally with an applicator, usually in the inner side of the non-dominant upper arm by a gynaecologist or nurse.
• Site: over the triceps about 8-10 cm above the medial epicondyle of the humerus and 3-5 cm below the sulcus between biceps and triceps; best in the first days of the cycle, otherwise an additional method for the first two weeks.
• Before: explain procedure; position dorsal with non-dominant arm straight out or flexed at the elbow, externally rotated and the hand near the head; identify the site; carry out insertion.
• After insertion: ask the woman to palpate the area; keep area dry for 4-7 days; soreness, swelling and bruising are normal; give reminder card (type, date of insertion, month and year for removal).
• Removal: explain procedure, same position, small incision, implant removed with tweezers; place sterile dressing; show all rods to the woman.
(b)
Complications (uncommon): infection at the site within the first 2 months, difficult removal, expulsion within the first 4 months. implant can be felt through the skin and located by X-ray if needed.
(c)
• Etonogestrel levels undetectable within one week after removal and fertility returns promptly.
• Follow-up: remove or replace at the date on the card.
questions.question:
A woman chooses a subdermal contraceptive implant.
(a) Name the procedure and state the nursing responsibilities before, during and after insertion and removal.
(b) State the danger signs and the structures at risk.
(c) Outline the health education and follow-up plan.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Menstruation is the cyclic, orderly sloughing of the uterine lining in response to hormones from the hypothalamus, pituitary and ovaries, caused by a rapid decline in ovarian progesterone.
• Cycle length is counted from the first day of bleeding to the next onset of menses; median 28 days (normal range 24 to 38 days).
(b)
• The cycle has three phases: follicular (pre-ovulatory), ovulatory and luteal (post-ovulatory).
• Follicular phase: begins on day 1 of menses and lasts until ovulation; lower basal body temperature and development of ovarian follicles; FSH rises as corpus luteum steroid production and inhibin A fall.
• Ovulatory phase: ovulation occurs about 10-12 hours after the LH peak; estradiol peaks and progesterone begins to rise; the LH surge lasts 36 to 48 hours.
• Luteal phase: the dominant follicle becomes the corpus luteum; this phase is the most constant, averaging 14 days.
• The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone, peaking at about 25 mg/day 6 to 8 days after ovulation, which develops the secretory endometrium needed for implantation.
• High estradiol, progesterone and inhibin lower LH and FSH; without pregnancy, hormone levels fall and the corpus luteum degenerates.
(c)
Fertilisation requires fusion of spermatozoon and ovum to form a zygote; interruption of any step will almost certainly cause fertilisation failure.
questions.question:
Describe the menstrual cycle.
(a) Define menstruation and state the normal cycle length.
(b) Describe the three phases of the cycle and the hormonal events in each.
(c) State how disturbances of the cycle or its hormonal events relate to common problems.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hepatitis B is spread by blood, blood products, contaminated needles, saliva, vaginal secretions and semen. At risk: multiple sex partners or STI, IV drug users, household contacts of carriers, health workers, dialysis patients, infants of carrier mothers.
• Signs: nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, enlarged tender liver, fever, chills, weakness, headache; HBsAg and HBeAg appear 1-10 weeks after exposure.
(b)
• Maternal: chronic or carrier state, chronic active hepatitis, chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma.
• Neonatal: transfer at delivery or close contact regardless of route; HBsAg/HBeAg-positive mothers have a 90% chance of transmitting; 90% of infected infants become carriers; 25% die of liver failure.
(c)
• Screen all pregnant women for HBsAg; vaccinate HBsAb-negative women (pregnancy is not a contraindication for vaccine or HBIG).
• Infants of infectious mothers receive HBIG within 12 hours of birth and the first of three vaccine doses before discharge; this reduces transmission to under 3%.
• Vaccine schedule: birth, 1-4 months, 6-18 months (not before 6 months); breastfeeding is not contraindicated with HBIG and first vaccine.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis Be antigen. She has nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant pain and an enlarged tender liver.
(a) State the risk factors and route of transmission.
(b) Outline the maternal and neonatal complications.
(c) Justify the prevention and management measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Abortion is bleeding or expulsion of the fetus before the 24th week or less than 500 g (WHO); may be spontaneous or induced.
• About 15% of pregnancies abort spontaneously, peak at 6-10 weeks (about 65% then, linked to low progesterone); 80% in the first trimester; bleeding in the 2nd and 3rd trimester carries greater risk as the placenta is firmly attached.
• Types: threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed, habitual, septic; induced types are therapeutic and criminal.
(b)
• Fetal causes: in about 60% chromosomal abnormalities; mal-development; defective implantation.
• Maternal: infection (acute fevers, rubella, syphilis, chronic nephritis, thyroid dysfunction), drugs, cigarettes, alcohol, ABO incompatibility, high blood lead, diabetes, hormonal imbalance, high parity, retroverted or bicornuate uterus, cervical incompetence, stress.
• Local: anaemia, trauma, fibroid tumours; social: teenage pregnancy, unmet needs, failed family planning, rape conception.
(c)
Vulnerable: women with the above risks; in habitual abortion, an incompetent cervix, fibroid, uterine displacement, diabetes, nephritis or TB.
(d)
• Threatened: bleeding in the first 20 weeks, os closed, slight contractions, membranes intact; 70-80% continue.
• Inevitable: severe bleeding with contractions and cervical dilatation, membranes may bulge, shock may be present; pregnancy cannot continue.
• Treatment: threatened = admit, reassure, no vaginal examination, sedation; Inevitable = ergometrine/syntometrine, analgesia, oxytocin drip or prostaglandin E2 after 16 weeks, evacuation under general anaesthesia.
questions.question:
Discuss abortion.
(a) Define abortion and state its incidence and types.
(b) State the causes (fetal, maternal, local, social).
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable.
(d) Distinguish between threatened and inevitable abortion.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Extra-uterine pregnancy: the fertilised ovum embeds outside the uterine cavity, commonly in the fallopian tube, also the abdominal cavity, cervix, and rarely the ovary.
• Tubal causes: congenital tube abnormality, previous infection, tubal surgery, IUCD, assisted reproduction.
• The blastocyst rapidly erodes the tubal epithelium and attaches to the muscle layer.
(b)
• Signs: amenorrhoea, lower abdominal discomfort or acute pain, sharp localised stabbing pain, nausea, brownish discharge, dizziness, shoulder pain, shock; other pregnancy signs may be absent.
• Outcomes near the distal end: tubal abortion, tubal mole, tubal rupture (gradual or sudden), abdominal pregnancy; ultrasound may assist diagnosis.
(c)
• Vulnerable: women with tubal abnormality, previous infection or surgery, an IUCD or assisted conception; ectopic is somewhat more common with the mini pill.
• Tubal ligation failure and IUD failure carry a risk of ectopic pregnancy.
(d)
• Tubal: the embryo is in the tube, may abort, form a mole or rupture.
• Abdominal: rare; fetus develops outside the uterus after abortion or rupture; placenta attaches to neighbouring organs; Majority do not survive; lie abnormal and fetal parts readily felt; delivery by laparotomy.
• Complications of abdominal pregnancy: abscess, peritonitis, septicaemia; baby may have compression deformities from oligohydramnios.
• Early abdominal pregnancy is re-absorbed.
questions.question:
Discuss extra-uterine pregnancy.
(a) Define it and state its sites and causes.
(b) State the signs, outcomes and diagnosis.
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable.
(d) Distinguish between tubal and abdominal pregnancy.

A woman at 12 weeks has slight vaginal bleeding with mild uterine contractions, mild abdominal cramping and backache. On speculum examination the cervix is closed and the membranes are intact.
(a) State the assessment findings and investigations.
(b) State the immediate nursing interventions.
(c) Describe the medical management.
(d) State the expected outcomes and discharge advice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Threatened abortion: vaginal bleeding in the first 20 weeks, with or without contractions; differs from implantation bleeding, which is bright red and stops quickly. Findings: slight bleeding, os closed without effacement, slight contractions, cramping and backache.
• Investigations: ultrasound scan, grouping and cross-matching, Hb, Rh factor, plasma human placental lactogen (low level suggests the pregnancy will terminate), pregnancy test, fetal heart by sonicaid, speculum examination to exclude local lesion.
(b)
• Admit to hospital; reassure; assess history and vital signs; routine observation twice daily or 4-hourly; no vaginal examination and no enema; save all discharges, pads, soiled clothing and linen.
• Allow up after bleeding has stopped for 3 days; nutritious diet and personal hygiene.
(c)
Drugs: Valium 5 mg tds, amylobarbitone sodium 200 mg at night, pethidine 50-100 mg for uterine contraction pain, morphine 15 mg.
(d)
• Prognosis: 70-80% continue the pregnancy; if bleeding changes from bright red to brownish only about 10% abort; if brown becomes red 66% abort; severe contractions raise the likelihood of abortion.
• Discharge advice: rest, less activity, no lifting or coitus for 2-3 weeks, report any bleeding.

(a)
• Early life (birth to 5) is a crucial period of rapid development in gross motor, fine motor, language, cognition and social/emotional growth.
• Motor development depends on familial patterns and environment; Children walk at about 12 months, climb stairs holding on at 18 months, run well at 2 years, with wide variation; it cannot be significantly accelerated by training.
(b)
• Language: understanding precedes speech; cooing then syllables; "Dada" and "Mama" by 12 months, several words by 18 months, 2-3 word phrases by 2 years; conversation by 3; simple stories by 4; recite the alphabet by 5.
• Cognition: appropriate attachment and nurturing are critical; at 2 years time understood broadly; By 4 years the day is understood as divided into morning, afternoon and night; by 7 more than one aspect can be considered.
• Emotional: crying peaks at about 3 hours/day at 6 weeks; separation anxiety about 8 months; gender identity at 18 months to 2 years; limit-testing at 2-3 years; fantasy play at 3-5 years.
(c)
• Principles: growth is sequential (cephalocaudal, proximodistal), variable between children, has critical periods (first 1,000 days), and physical growth is interdependent with development.
• Inadequate growth can accompany delayed speech, poor social interaction or missed milestones; head circumference detects hydrocephalus or microcephaly.
(d)
• Causes of poor growth: inadequate intake, recurrent infections (malaria, diarrhoea, pneumonia), poor maternal care, unsafe water, poor feeding practices.
• Nutritional and health insults in the first 1,000 days have long-lasting consequences; malnutrition is a leading cause of under-five death.
• Stunting reflects long-term deprivation, wasting acute malnutrition; Z-score below -3 is severe malnutrition.
questions.question:
Describe growth and development in early childhood (birth to five years).
(a) State the developmental domains and motor milestones.
(b) State language, cognitive and emotional development.
(c) State how deviations relate to common problems.
(d) Explain how poor growth may progress and its effects on the child.

Describe the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy.
(a) State its rationale, components and the children it covers.
(b) Describe the case management process and colour-coded classification.
(c) Explain its role in reducing child morbidity and mortality.
(d) State the counselling the nurse should give caregivers.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Rationale: more than 10 million children die before age five in developing countries; about 70% of deaths are linked to five preventable, treatable conditions.
• Core: integrated case management of common childhood problems at a first-level facility; components:.
• Better case-management skills of staff, improved health system, improved family and community practice.
• Two categories: sick child aged 2 months up to 5 years, and sick young infant up to 2 months.
(b)
• Process: check danger signs, assess main symptoms (cough/difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, ear problem, malnutrition, anaemia), nutrition, immunisation and feeding status, then classify and identify treatment.
• Colour triage: red = urgent pre-referral treatment and referral; yellow = specific medical treatment and advice; green = simple home-management advice; each illness is classified separately.
• General danger signs (cannot drink/breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic/unconscious) need urgent referral.
(c)
• IMCI determines whether a child needs urgent referral, treatment at the first-level facility (oral antibiotic, antimalarial, ORS) or safe home management.
• Children referred get first-dose/pre-referral treatment; follow-up visits reassess the child (e.g. pneumonia in 2 days; dysentery in 2 days; anaemia in 14 days; malnutrition in 30 days).
• Severe malnutrition (visible wasting or oedema of both feet) and severe anaemia (severe palmar pallor) are classified for urgent referral.
(d)
• Counsel on how to give oral drugs, feed and give fluids during illness, treat local infection at home, recognise danger signs and return immediately; solve feeding problems.
• Give the first dose of drugs in the clinic and immunise if due.

(a)
• Lactation mastitis: inflammation of breast tissue that sometimes involves infection; affects about 10% of breast-feeding mothers (range to 33%); often within 3 months of birth but up to 2 years.
• Symptoms appear suddenly: tenderness, warmth, swelling, lump, burning pain, wedge-shaped redness, fever 101 F (38.3 C) or more, flu-like symptoms, chills, fatigue, aches.
(b)
• Cause: inadequate milk drainage plus bacteria; poor drainage from infrequent feeding, oversupply, rapid weaning, illness or clogged duct; stagnant milk breeds organisms; bacteria from the baby's mouth or skin enter through cracked nipples.
• Risk factors: previous mastitis, sore or cracked nipples, tight bra or pressure on breast, improper technique, tiredness or stress, poor nutrition, smoking.
(c)
• Medical: 10-day antibiotic course (complete it); acetaminophen or ibuprofen; continue breast-feeding (it helps clear infection; abrupt weaning worsens it); mammogram or ultrasound if not breastfeeding to exclude breast cancer.
• Feeding care: avoid overfilling, ensure correct latch, hand-express a little milk first, massage toward the nipple, warm moist heat before feeding, feed from affected side first, vary positions.
• Home care: ice pack for swelling, NSAIDs, lymphatic drainage, reverse pressure softening, supportive non-tight bra; do not massage aggressively, use massaging devices, soak breast or apply heat.
• Complications: recurrence, breast abscess (usually surgical drainage), septicaemia. Prevention: drain breasts fully, empty one breast before the other, change positions, good latch, stop smoking.
questions.question:
A breast-feeding mother in the first three months after delivery has a tender, warm, swollen breast with wedge-shaped skin redness, a breast lump, burning pain during feeds, fever of 38.3 degrees C or more, chills and malaise. She has cracked nipples and wears a tight bra.
(a) State the diagnosis and how common it is.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management, complications and prevention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Occipitoposterior (OP) position: the most common occiput malposition, in 10-30% of labours but only 5% of births; persistent OP results from failure of internal rotation (malrotation).
• Causes: exact cause often unknown; an abnormally shaped pelvis; in an android pelvis the occiput prefers the larger hind pelvis; an anthropoid pelvis favours direct OP.
(b)
• Long labour; perineal tears or extension of an episiotomy; need for forceps or caesarean section; a labour with malposition is long, tedious and painful.
• Increased risk of operative intervention in malposition and malpresentation.
(c)
• Women should be assured that internal rotation to anterior is common; close maternal and fetal monitoring; epidural frequently recommended; adequate fluids.
• Avoid pushing before full dilatation; vaginal delivery possible if the head is face-to-pubis and the pelvis is adequate; otherwise forceps or caesarean section.
• Encourage comfortable postures, mobility and coping mechanisms; avoid demoralising language; report any sign of fetal or maternal distress or delay.
• Occipito-transverse position: head engages but fails to rotate; manual rotation with Kielland's forceps or vacuum extraction (not if fetal acidosis, because of risk of cerebral haemorrhage); caesarean immediately if forceps fail.
questions.question:
A primigravida in labour has a long, slow first stage with backache. The fetal head engaged but has not rotated, and the woman feels an urge to push before full dilatation. She has an android pelvis.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors.
(b) State the maternal and fetal complications.
(c) Justify the management options.

A woman with a 28-day cycle records a basal body temperature chart and observes mucus that is transparent, stretchy like raw egg white and leaves a wet, slippery sensation. She wants to avoid pregnancy and to identify her fertile days.
(a) Identify the cycle stage and condition.
(b) Interpret the findings.
(c) State the differential methods.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and counselling.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Type 4 mucus (high fertility): transparent like raw egg white, stretchy, liquid, wet and slippery sensation.
• Types: type 1 lowest fertility (dry); type 2 low (damp); type 3 intermediate (thick, creamy, sticky, damp).
(b)
• BBT is the lowest temperature at rest, measured on waking before activity; the follicular phase has lower temperatures; mucus change reflects rising oestrogen.
• Standard Days Method: days 1-7 infertile, days 8-19 fertile (unsafe for unprotected intercourse), day 20 to end infertile.
(c)
Other methods: rhythm (Knaus-Ogino: 18 is subtracted from the shortest cycle to find the end of the pre-ovulatory infertile phase, and 11 to find the start of the post-ovulatory infertile phase), ovulation (Billings) method, cervical palpation, symptothermal method; situational methods: coitus interruptus, douching, abstinence, spermicide.
(d)
• FAMs are 77-98% effective (2-23 pregnancies per 100 couples per year); no physical side effects, no literacy needed; but typical use gives high failure rates and conceptions from ageing gametes may have fetal abnormality risk.
• Counsel with questions: children soon, health conditions, frequency of sex, partners, need for HIV/STD protection, effectiveness, side effects, ability to use correctly every time.

questions.question:
A woman presents after childbirth with fever, pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding or discharge and a general unwell feeling; her labour involved prolonged rupture of membranes.
(a) Identify the condition and state its causes and risk factors.
(b) List the complications and the related infections that may follow.
(c) Justify the medical management and the diagnostic tests.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Endometritis: inflammation of the endometrium caused by bacterial infection; symptoms also include constipation/pain with bowel movements and abdominal swelling.
• Causes: STIs, tuberculosis, or vaginal bacteria that change after birth or a procedure. Risk factors: D&C, D&E, endometrial biopsy, hysteroscopy, childbirth (infection in labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, Group B strep), IUD placement.
(b)
• Complications: infertility, pelvic infection, pelvic or uterine abscess, septicaemia. Related puerperal infections: myometritis, parametritis (pelvic cellulitis, spread to broad ligament).
• Parametritis risk factors: prolonged membrane rupture, retained placental fragments, PPH, pre-existing anaemia, prolonged difficult labour with forceps, intrauterine manipulation; symptoms can appear days after discharge.
(c)
• Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are used because the causative bacteria are unknown; switch to oral antibiotics on discharge (Augmentin; doxycycline plus metronidazole; levofloxacin plus metronidazole).
• Tests: vaginal fluid testing for bacteria/STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea), biopsy, laparoscopy, WBC and ESR, microscopy of vaginal fluid.
• Endometritis differs from endometriosis, where uterine lining develops outside the uterus (e.g. ovaries, fallopian tubes).

(a)
• Puerperium: from expulsion of the placenta until the reproductive organs return to the pre-pregnant state; lasts 6 weeks.
• Features: reproductive organs return to non-pregnant state (involution), lactation starts, mother recovers and assumes care of her infant.
• Care principles: physical well-being of mother and baby, sound infant feeding and mother-child relationship, supporting the mother's confidence.
(b)
• Uterus involutes by ischaemia, autolysis and shedding of the lining; uterus weight falls from 900 g at end of labour to 450 g (1 week), 200 g (2 weeks) and 60 g (6 weeks).
• Lochia: rubra (red, 1-4 days), serosa (pink, 5-9 days), alba (creamish, 9-12 days); alkaline, which favours growth of organisms.
• Vagina regains tone in days and rugae return by the 3rd week; torn hymen heals leaving myrtiform caruncles. Colostrum is rich in protein, sodium, chloride, vitamin A and antibodies (IgA, IgG, IgM, lactoferrin), and has a laxative action on meconium.
• Blood volume, cardiac output and BP normalise in 24-48 hours; oxytocin maintains uterine contraction; pelvic joints return to normal in about 3 months; mood lability is common.
(c)
• Persistent red lochia indicates retained products; complications: severe haemorrhage in the immediate postnatal period, hypertensive complications and infections, thrombosis/embolism, problems from pre-existing disease such as cardiac disease.
• Delayed uterine atony occurs 24 h to 12 weeks postpartum, causes: placental and ovarian remnants, placental polyps, endomyometritis.
(d)
• Delayed atony is potentially life-threatening, especially as women have often left hospital.
• Ambulation and postnatal exercises lessen venous thrombosis and hypostatic pneumonia; nurse advises, reassures and answers questions.
questions.question:
Describe the puerperium.
(a) Define it and state its features and the principles governing care.
(b) Describe the changes in the uterus, lochia, vagina, breasts and other systems.
(c) State how deviations relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how a complication may progress and its effects on the mother.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Eclamptic fit (stages: premonitory 10-30 s; tonic about 30 s; clonic 1-2 min; coma). Warning signs: sudden sharp rise in BP, increased proteinuria, diminished urine, severe frontal headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, vomiting, drowsiness; fulminating eclampsia occurs without warning.
• Emergency aims: unobstructed airway (keynote of survival), prevent injury, prevent further fits, urgent hospital admission.
(b)
• During: do not move her unless in danger; turn to semi-prone side position; remove false teeth/foreign bodies; place a padded wedge between back teeth if jaws allow; wipe saliva and vomit; do not forcibly restrain; keep onlookers quiet; mouth gag and tongue forceps are obsolete.
• After: clean mouth and nostrils, oxygen for at least five minutes; give the best available sedation (e.g. pethidine 100 mg IM with chlorpromazine 50 mg, diazepam 10 mg IV, phenobarbitone 200 mg IM); record time and amount; remain with the patient.
• Record BP, pulse and respirations every half hour and temperature hourly after sedation; avoid noise, bright light and disturbance; never leave her alone; suction at bedside; turn two-hourly; catheter with hourly urine output; IV fluids only.
(c)
• Report: sharp rise or fall in BP; sedation not working; raised pulse/temperature (infection or cerebral haemorrhage); slow respiration; moist respiration (pulmonary oedema); oliguria or anuria (renal failure); jaundice (liver damage); frequent fits; cyanosis needs oxygen.
• Structures at risk: airway (asphyxia), tongue (biting), lungs (pneumonia, pulmonary oedema), kidneys, liver, brain; monitor fetal heart every 2-3 hours and watch for onset of labour.
(d)
Every suspected preeclampsia must be referred to hospital; the community midwife must convince the patient, who feels well, to attend; bed rest at home is not satisfactory; arrange domestic plans to reduce anxiety; prepare delivery bag and record and accompany her; intensive care continues at least 48 hours after delivery.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman with preeclampsia in a rural community suddenly has a fit: her body becomes rigid, respiration stops and she turns cyanosed, then her muscles convulse with frothy saliva before she lapses into coma. She had earlier complained of severe frontal headache, blurred vision and epigastric pain.
(a) State the diagnosis and warning signs, and name the emergency intervention.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities during and after the fit.
(c) State the danger signs to report and the structures at risk.
(d) Outline the health education and referral plan.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fibroids: noncancerous growths of the uterus appearing during reproductive years, from seedlings to bulky masses; single or multiple.
• Types: intramural, submucosal, subserosal.
• Cause unknown; contributing: genetics, oestrogen and progesterone, growth factors, extracellular matrix.
• Signs: heavy bleeding, periods over a week, pelvic pressure or pain, frequent urination, difficulty emptying bladder, constipation, backache or leg pains.
(b)
• Investigations: FBC, MRI, hysterosonography, hysterosalpingography, hysteroscopy.
• Management: GnRH agonists, progestin IUD, oral contraceptives, NSAIDs, double dose of vitamins and iron; nursing aims to minimise bleeding and prevent acute anaemia, dehydration and pain crisis.
(c)
• Vulnerability: hormonal (oestrogen/progesterone) and genetic factors; fibroids do not prevent pregnancy but raise risk of placental abruption, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and pregnancy loss.
• Fibroids may be associated with atonic uterus and postpartum haemorrhage.
(d)
• Fibroid: growth in the uterine muscle; heavy bleeding, pressure symptoms; NSAIDs do not reduce bleeding; progestin IUD does not shrink it.
• Endometriosis: endometrial tissue outside the uterus; painful periods, pain with intercourse and bowel movements; retrograde menstruation and high oestrogen.
• Both involve oestrogen; endometriosis is managed with NSAIDs, progestin contraceptives and laparoscopic surgery.
• Both may be associated with infertility.
questions.question:
Discuss uterine fibroids.
(a) Define them and state the types, causes and signs.
(b) State the investigations and management.
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable and the effect on pregnancy.
(d) Distinguish between fibroids and endometriosis.

A married man with children requests permanent contraception and is scheduled for a vasectomy.
(a) Name the procedure and state the nursing responsibilities before, during and after it.
(b) State the danger signs and the structures involved.
(c) Outline the health education and follow-up plan.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Vasectomy (vasoligation): outpatient procedure under local anaesthesia that cuts and seals the vas deferens; types: conventional, no-scalpel, open-ended, closed-ended, vasclip.
• Before: obtain health, sexual, family and social history; discuss reasons and other male options; obtain signed informed consent and schedule date; instruct to shave the scrotal area; reassure; give prescribed anxiolytics.
• During: local anaesthetic; small scrotal opening; vas exposed, a 1 cm segment removed; ends cauterised and sealed with titanium clips; dissolvable stitch; takes less than 20 minutes.
• After: ice pack for pain and swelling, supportive undergarments, acetaminophen or ibuprofen; bed rest for 24 hours; limit activity and aggressive sexual activity for 3-5 days; bathing allowed but avoid submerging the scrotal area.
(b)
• Danger signs: severe abdominal pain, significant bleeding from the site, unresolved swelling after a few days.
• Structures: testes (sperm production), vas deferens (transport), scrotum, ejaculatory duct.
(c)
• Continue contraception until a post-vasectomy semen analysis confirms no sperm; sperm continue to be produced but are re-absorbed; ejaculate looks the same; clearance can take several months.
• Reversal (vasovasotomy 90-95% success, vasoepididymostomy 65-70%) is possible; first semen analysis at 6 weeks.

(a)
• Antenatal care: advice, supervision and attention to a pregnant woman from confirmation of pregnancy until labour begins; a part of preventive medicine conducted by midwife and doctor.
• Aims: promote physical and mental health through education on nutrition and hygiene; build trusting relationships; Monitor progress for maternal health and normal fetal development; reduce maternal and perinatal mortality; recognise deviations and manage or refer promptly.
• Further aims: ensure a live, mature, healthy baby; support infant feeding and breastfeeding; give parenthood advice; provide holistic care.
(b)
• Booking: start as soon as pregnancy is suspected or menses are missed for two months, to confirm pregnancy and record baseline BP, blood values, urinalysis and fetal development.
• History: social, family (diabetes, sickle cell, hypertension, twins, TB), medical, surgical (previous caesarean, D&C), obstetric (menstrual, previous pregnancies, labour, puerperium), baby's history, and current pregnancy (LMP for EDD).
• Visits: every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly until labour; more often with complications.
• Each visit: general examination for anaemia, oedema, varicose veins, urinalysis, BP and weight.
(c)
• Antenatal care detects deviations early (e.g. hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, multiple pregnancy), allowing prompt treatment or referral and a healthy mother and baby.
• Screening at 26-28 weeks detects gestational diabetes; routine HBsAg screening identifies hepatitis B carriers.
(d)
• Mothercraft talks given simply: hygiene (regular bathing, clean clothing, clean surroundings), fresh air and sunshine, nutrition and rest.
• Report any vaginal bleeding; signs of APH to look out for; breastfeeding preparation.
questions.question:
Describe antenatal care as a maternal health service.
(a) Define it and state its aims.
(b) State its components, schedule and the history taken at booking.
(c) Explain its role in reducing maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality.
(d) State the health education the nurse should give.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Procedure: routine immunisation at 6 weeks (window 4-8 weeks). Before: verify immunisation history; check cold chain storage temperature (+2 to +8 degrees C); confirm no contraindication.
• During: correct route and site: Pentavalent-1 intramuscular in the left anterolateral thigh (0.5 ml); PCV-1 intramuscular in the right anterolateral thigh (0.5 ml); OPV-1 oral (2 drops); Rotavirus-1 oral (1.5 ml).
• After: observe for 15-30 minutes for adverse reactions; document all doses in the clinic record and the mother's card.
(b)
• Contraindications: severe illness with fever; known hypersensitivity to vaccine components; immunocompromise (for live vaccines); severe diarrhoea or vomiting (for oral vaccines).
• Expected mild reactions: fever, pain at the injection site, diarrhoea with rotavirus.
(c)
• Educate caregivers on expected mild reactions and when to return; explain the benefits, safety and schedule of vaccines; address myths and hesitancy.
• Next doses: 10 weeks (Penta-2, PCV-2, OPV-2, Rota-2) and 14 weeks (Penta-3, PCV-3, OPV-3, IPV); 6 months vitamin A; 9 months measles and yellow fever.
• Missed doses: delay leaves the child unprotected and may require restarting a series; reminders by SMS or health records help.
questions.question:
A baby aged 6 weeks is brought to the clinic for the first routine immunisation contact and is to receive Pentavalent-1, PCV-1, OPV-1 and Rotavirus-1.
(a) Name the procedure and state the nursing responsibilities before, during and after vaccination.
(b) State the contraindications and danger signs to watch for.
(c) Outline the health education and follow-up plan for the caregiver.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Two phases: latent (descent and rotation) and active (descent with the urge to push; active bearing down).
• In the latent phase full dilatation is recorded but the presenting part may not have reached the outlet, so no strong urge to push.
• For healthy women and babies it can last up to about three hours before the risk of maternal or fetal compromise increases.
(b)
• Observe four factors: uterine contractions; descent, rotation and flexion of the presenting part; fetal condition and heart changes; maternal condition.
• Prepare a warm room with a spotlight, a clean area to receive the baby, waterproof covers, sterile cord clamps, clean apron, sterile gloves and gowns, and an oxytocic ready.
• Principles of birth: observation of progress, prevention of infection, emotional and physical comfort, anticipation and support of normal events, recognition of abnormal developments.
• Primigravid women have little urgency; multigravid women may progress very rapidly.
(c)
• Epidural analgesia relaxes the pelvic floor, so the presenting part meets less resistance to rotate; second stage is prolonged, especially in nulliparous women.
• Malposition (not occipito-anterior) and malpresentation make labour long, tedious and painful with more operative intervention.
(d)
• Occipitoposterior malrotation: long labour, perineal tears or extended episiotomy, forceps or caesarean; Face presentation: obstructed labour, cord prolapse, bruising, maternal trauma.
• Second stage beyond about three hours raises risk of maternal and fetal compromise.
questions.question:
Describe the second stage of labour.
(a) State its phases and duration.
(b) State the observations and preparation for the birth, and the principles of care.
(c) State how deviations relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how a complication may progress and its effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
