• Uterine fibroids: noncancerous growths of the uterus in reproductive years; single or multiple; classified by location: intramural (within muscular wall), submucosal (bulge into cavity), subserosal (project outside).
• Signs: heavy bleeding, periods over a week, pelvic pressure or pain, frequent urination, difficulty emptying bladder, constipation, backache or leg pains.
(b)
• Cause unknown; contributory: genetic changes, oestrogen and progesterone, growth factors (e.g. insulin-like), and extracellular matrix, which is increased in fibroids and makes them fibrous.
• Growth varies: slow, rapid, static, or some shrink on their own; multiple fibroids may expand the uterus to the rib cage.
(c)
• Investigations: FBC (bleeding disorders, anaemia from chronic loss), MRI, hysterosonography (saline infusion sonogram), hysterosalpingography, hysteroscopy.
• Nursing goals: minimise bleeding and prevent acute anaemia, dehydration and pain crisis; teach when to seek help; identify support systems; explain the treatment plan; therapeutic relationship; emotional support and coping strategies to prevent depression.
• Medical: GnRH agonists (block oestrogen and progesterone, stop menstruation, shrink fibroids, improve anaemia); progestin IUD (relieves bleeding, does not shrink fibroids); oral contraceptives (control bleeding); NSAIDs (pain, not bleeding); double dose of vitamins and iron.
• Pregnancy: fibroids do not stop conception but raise risk of placental abruption, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and pregnancy loss.
questions.question:
A woman of reproductive age presents with heavy menstrual bleeding lasting more than a week, pelvic pressure, frequent urination, difficulty emptying the bladder, constipation and backache.
(a) State the diagnosis and its classification.
(b) State the contributory factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management, investigations and effects on pregnancy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Assessment: persistent vomiting, weakness, dehydration, rapid pulse, low BP, sunken eyes, dry skin, scanty acetone-smelling urine, furred tongue; weigh on admission.
(b)
• Admit; complete bed rest, daily bed bath, oral care and pressure-area care.
• Strict intake and output chart; test urine daily for protein, acetone, bile, chloride and specific gravity and record.
• Monitor and record vital signs; report any deviation; weigh on alternate days.
• Mild laxative (e.g. magnesium chloride) only under doctor's prescription; involve the husband.
• Oral diet when vomiting stops for 24 hours: easily digestible, attractive, small frequent, avoid fried and oily foods, give fruit juice.
(c)
• IV infusion corrects dehydration, electrolytes and hypoglycaemia; oral fluids suspended about 24 hours.
• Antiemetics (largactil 25 mg, avomine 25 mg) given with care because of possible effects on the embryo; multivitamins, iron and daraprim given.
• Keep a fluid balance record and a separate record of vomitus; history and examination exclude hepatitis, hydatidiform mole and UTI.
(d)
Rationale: daily urine tests and weights detect dehydration and ketosis; resting the stomach reduces vomiting.
questions.question:
Describe the nursing care of a woman with hyperemesis gravidarum.
(a) State the assessment.
(b) State the nursing interventions.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities for IV therapy, antiemetics and investigations.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions.

Describe the nursing care of a pregnant woman with anaemia.
(a) Define anaemia and state the assessment findings and history.
(b) State the management and the nursing responsibilities for iron and folic acid.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities for related investigations.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anaemia: reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood (fewer red cells, low haemoglobin or both); in pregnancy Hb below 10 g/dL (below 12 g/dL non-pregnant); iron deficiency is about 95% of anaemia in pregnancy.
• Signs: fatigue, drowsiness, malaise, dizziness, weakness, headache, sore tongue, pallor, pale conjunctivae and nail beds, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting.
• History: iron deficiency anaemia, sickle cell disease, family history of thalassaemia, bleeding disorders, HELLP, HIV, chemotherapy.
(b)
• Management is based on the cause; encourage a balanced diet; Iron (ferrous fumarate): 30 mg orally daily; injection (iron sucrose) 15 mg/kg or max 1000 mg; adverse effects: metallic taste, nausea, GI irritation, black stools; contraindicated in primary haemolytic anaemia, peptic ulcer, ulcerative colitis, repeated transfusions.
• Iron nursing: avoid taking with milk or antacids; do not substitute one iron salt for another (elemental iron varies); report constipation or stool colour change.
• Folic acid: 0.4 mg orally daily (0.4-0.8 mg IM or subcutaneous); for megaloblastic anaemia and prevention of neural tube defects; contraindicated in untreated B12 deficiency; adverse effects: cramps, diarrhoea, rash, irritability.
• Folic acid nursing: women with previous neural tube defect increase intake 1 month before and 3 months after conception; malabsorption may need parenteral route.
(c)
• Initial lab evaluation determines red cell size (microcytic, normocytic, macrocytic), then specific tests (e.g. folate or B12 deficiency).
• Diuretics are used before transfusion in severe anaemia and in severe anaemia with heart failure.
(d)
Rationale: blood volume rises mainly by plasma, so red cells are disproportionately low, greatest in the second trimester, raising iron need with fetal demand.

questions.question:
Describe fertility awareness methods as a family planning service.
(a) Define fertility awareness and state the methods.
(b) State the components and eligible users, advantages and disadvantages.
(c) Explain their role in birth spacing and reducing morbidity.
(d) State the health education the nurse should give.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fertility awareness: a woman identifies when the fertile time of her cycle starts and ends and so when she can become pregnant; Also called natural family planning; uses cycle length and signs of ovulation (cervical secretions, BBT).
• Methods: basal body temperature (lowest resting temperature, taken on waking), calendar methods (rhythm, standard days), ovulation (Billings) method, cervical palpation, symptothermal method.
(b)
• Standard days: days 1-7 infertile, 8-19 fertile, day 20 onward infertile (CycleBeads).
• Mucus types 1-4: type 1 dry (lowest fertility) to type 4 clear stretchy wet (highest fertility).
• Situational methods: coitus interruptus, douching (ineffective, may push sperm up), abstinence (primary or secondary), spermicide (nonoxynol-9).
• Advantages: no physical side effects, acceptable to many religions and cultures, no literacy needed, help women learn about their bodies, effective if used consistently.
• Disadvantages: high failure rates in typical use, conflict and frustration, risk of fetal abnormality from ageing gametes.
(c)
77-98% effective (2-23 pregnancies per 100 couples per year); better when methods are combined; hormonal changes take 12 weeks to settle postpartum.
(d)
• Ask before choosing: wish for children, health conditions, frequency of sex, partners, need for HIV/STI protection, effectiveness, side effects, correct use.
• Spermicide N-9 offers no protection against HIV and is minimally effective alone.

questions.question:
Describe growth monitoring in children as a child health service.
(a) Define it and state its components, tools and schedule.
(b) State the parameters and Z-score interpretation.
(c) Explain its role in reducing child morbidity and mortality.
(d) State the health education the nurse should give.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Routine measurement of weight, length/height, MUAC and head circumference compared against WHO growth standards; It is continuous, comparative and preventive.
• Tools: weighing scales (including Salter-type), length boards and stadiometers, MUAC tapes, measuring tape, WHO growth charts (Z-scores or percentiles), child health cards.
• Schedule: monthly 0-12 months; every 2-3 months at 12-24 months; every 3-6 months at 2-5 years; annually or as needed for school-age children.
(b)
• Weight-for-age (overall growth); length-for-age (stunting); Weight-for-height (wasting/overweight); MUAC (green/yellow/red); head circumference under 2 years.
• Z-scores: -1 to +2 normal; below -2 moderate malnutrition; below -3 severe; above +2 overweight/obesity.
(c)
• Early detection of stunting, wasting, underweight and obesity allows referral and treatment; malnutrition is a leading cause of under-five deaths.
• It evaluates feeding, immunisation, deworming and maternal care interventions and gives community surveillance data for targeting high-risk communities.
• Principles: growth is sequential (cephalocaudal, proximodistal), variable, has critical periods (first 1,000 days) and is interdependent with development.
(d)
• Involve parents in monitoring and explain the growth trajectory to build understanding and responsibility for healthier practices at home.
• Nutrition counselling, maternal education and behaviour-change communication are delivered at monitoring visits.

(a)
• Endometriosis: endometrial tissue grows outside the uterus, causing inflammation and pain; tissue is not cancerous but may cause scarring, adhesions, blocked fallopian tubes and cysts from trapped blood.
• Signs: dysmenorrhoea, pelvic pain, heavy or irregular periods, pain with bowel movements during menses or constipation, pain with intercourse, fatigue or low energy.
(b)
• Cause unknown: retrograde menstruation (menstrual blood with endometrial cells flows back through the tubes into the pelvis and deposits grow); high oestrogen increases inflammation and pain; genetic factors also implicated.
• Diagnosis: history of menstrual symptoms and chronic pelvic pain; laparoscopic visualisation and histological verification show extent of lesions, adhesions and scar tissue.
(c)
• Nursing: encourage patient and partner to verbalise feelings; develop coping strategies (exercise increases circulation); monitor for anaemia and haemoglobin if heavy bleeding; explain procedures and clarify misconceptions including fertility.
• Counsel patient wanting children not to postpone childbearing (infertility is possible); recommend annual pelvic examination; teach adverse effects of drugs; monitor response to therapy.
• Medical: NSAIDs and analgesics (ibuprofen, naproxen); progestin-based contraceptives (POPs, implant, injection, IUD) because high oestrogen worsens disease; laparoscopic surgery through a small incision near the navel to remove lesions, adhesions and scar tissue.
questions.question:
A woman has painful periods with pelvic pain and cramping that starts before menstruation and lasts several days after, heavy or irregular periods, pain with intercourse and fatigue.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Immunisation is the process by which a person becomes protected against a disease, usually by a vaccine that stimulates the immune system; Active (vaccines stimulate own antibodies) and passive (antibodies from another person or animal; immediate but short-term).
• Nigeria adopted the WHO Expanded Programme on Immunisation in 1979 (BCG, OPV, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, measles); NPI created in 1996 and merged into NPHCDA in 2007.
(b)
• NPI protects children under two from six killer diseases: polio, measles, diphtheria, pertussis, TB and yellow fever; aims at 90% national coverage and 80% in every LGA; eliminate neonatal tetanus; interrupt polio transmission; control measles.
• Target population: infants, toddlers, pre-schoolers, school-aged children, adolescents and high-risk groups; pregnant women receive tetanus toxoid (5 doses).
• Schedule: birth BCG, hepatitis B, OPV-0; 6, 10 and 14 weeks Pentavalent, PCV, OPV and rotavirus (IPV at 14 weeks); 6 months vitamin A; 9 months measles and yellow fever; 12-15 months vitamin A, measles 2, meningococcal conjugate; HPV at 9-14 years.
(c)
• Goal: reduce morbidity and mortality from vaccine-preventable diseases and achieve eradication, elimination or control of polio, neonatal tetanus and measles.
• Polio: last wild case 2016; Nigeria declared polio-free in August 2020; herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated.
• Vaccines are kept potent by the cold chain (ice-lined refrigerator, deep freezer, cold box, vaccine carrier, thermometer).
(d)
• Educate caregivers on benefits, safety and schedule; combat misinformation and hesitancy; work with community leaders.
• Keep immunisation records; remind caregivers of due dates; barriers named include low awareness, insecurity and traditional beliefs.
questions.question:
Describe child immunisation as a preventive programme in Nigeria.
(a) Define immunisation and state the types.
(b) State the programme's objectives, target groups and the routine schedule.
(c) Explain its role in reducing child morbidity and mortality.
(d) State the health education the nurse should give.

A pregnant woman has wheezy respiration and breathlessness with reduced pulmonary function; she has a history of asthma.
(a) State the diagnosis and its prevalence and course in pregnancy.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of dyspnoea in pregnancy.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management and effects on pregnancy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Asthma: most common pre-existing medical disorder in pregnancy, affecting about 8-12%; a third improve, a third stay stable, a third worsen.
• Diagnosis as in the non-pregnant state: history, clinical examination (wheeze, breathlessness), reduced pulmonary function.
(b)
• Pregnancy changes: hormones cause mucosal hyperaemia, oedema and friability; thoracic diameters increase; ventilation rises through deeper breathing; FRC falls with diaphragmatic elevation; shortness of breath is common in the third trimester.
• Biggest danger to mother and fetus is poorly controlled or undertreated disease.
(c)
• Multidisciplinary care; objective assessment of pulmonary function and fetal well-being; teach inhaler use and reassure on medication safety; avoid triggers; prevent exacerbations.
• Inhalers preferred over systemic corticosteroids (cleft lip/palate, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes); use beta-2 agonists, inhaled corticosteroids and amoxicillin or augmentin; monitor vital signs if admitted.
• Effects: meconium-stained liquor with fetal distress, preterm labour or delivery, oligohydramnios, pregnancy-induced hypertension, possible link with PPROM; encourage fluids, fruit and a balanced diet.

(a)
• Multiple pregnancy: development of more than one fetus in the uterus at once; twins commonest, then triplets, quadruplets, quintuplets, sextuplets.
• Incidence 5 to 46 per 1000 births worldwide; highest in Nigeria (1 in 20 pregnancies), lowest in far eastern countries (1 in 200); monozygotic 1 in 250.
• Causes: assisted reproduction and ovulation induction, high parity, black race, maternal family history, maternal age 30-35; dizygotic twins may arise spontaneously from two eggs.
(b)
• Classified by number of fetuses, fertilised eggs, placentas (chorionicity) and amniotic cavities.
• Dizygotic (two-thirds): two ova fertilised by two sperms, always two placentas and two amniotic cavities, same or different sex.
• Monozygotic (one-third): single ovum splits, same sex, genes and blood groups.
• Monozygotic timing: up to 3 days two placentas and sacs; days 4-7 diamniotic monochorionic (most common); days 8-12 monoamniotic monochorionic; after day 13 conjoined twins.
(c)
• High-risk: significant numbers of preterm, low birth weight and growth-restricted infants, higher risk of long-term handicap; vulnerable women have risk factors above.
• Monochorionic twins risk cord entanglement and twin-twin transfusion syndrome (one twin gets less blood and produces less urine; the other may develop heart failure).
(d)
• Monozygotic: 1 ovum + 1 sperm, same sex, identical features, single or double placenta, same genetic features (DNA the same).
• Dizygotic: 2 ova + 2 sperm, same or opposite sex, fraternal resemblance, different genetic features (DNA different).
• Effects on pregnancy: premature labour, preeclampsia, polyhydramnios, severe anaemia, hyperemesis.
questions.question:
Discuss multiple pregnancy.
(a) Define it and state the incidence and causes/risk factors.
(b) State the classification and varieties of twin pregnancy.
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable and why the pregnancy is high risk.
(d) Distinguish between monozygotic and dizygotic twins.

A woman in prolonged labour, with prolonged rupture of membranes and multiple vaginal examinations, develops fever, uterine fundal tenderness, maternal tachycardia (>100/min), fetal tachycardia (>160/min) and purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid.
(a) Name the condition and state its risk factors.
(b) Outline the maternal and fetal/neonatal complications.
(c) Justify the priority medical and nursing actions, including nursing diagnoses.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Chorioamnionitis (intraamniotic infection): acute inflammation of the membranes and chorion, typically from ascending polymicrobial infection after membrane rupture.
• Risk factors: longer membrane rupture, prolonged labour, nulliparity, internal monitoring, multiple vaginal exams, meconium-stained liquor, smoking/alcohol/drug abuse, immune-compromised states, epidural anaesthesia, GBS colonisation, bacterial vaginosis, STIs, Ureaplasma colonisation.
(b)
• Maternal: increased caesarean risk, endomyometritis, pelvic abscess, bacteraemia, PPH; rarely septic shock, DIC, ARDS, maternal death.
• Fetal/neonatal: neonatal sepsis, asphyxia, septic shock, pneumonia, IVH, cerebral white matter damage, cerebral palsy/long-term disability, death.
(c)
• Prompt IV antibiotics (ampicillin every 6 h plus gentamicin every 8-24 h until delivery; clindamycin or metronidazole added if caesarean; one extra dose after delivery) to prevent maternal and fetal complications; caesarean is not needed just to expedite delivery; antipyretics (acetaminophen) prevent neonatal encephalopathy and fetal tachycardia.
• Nursing: admit, history and examination, monitor vitals, vaginal/high vaginal swabs, limit vaginal exams (risk rises after 3 and five-fold after 8), perineal hygiene, emotional support, prepare for caesarean if necessary.
• Nursing diagnoses: Hyperthermia related to inflammatory process; Fear related to unfamiliarity with disease process; Risk for shock; Risk for bleeding.

(a)
• Community midwife: a registered midwife who provides antenatal and postnatal care in a community setting.
• TBAs (Agbebi in Yoruba land): skills gained through inheritance or spiritual means, not formal education; Usually elderly women aged 40-55 of good character, married with children; sometimes men.
• Their practice is rooted in beliefs about birth, rituals, taboos, charms and incantations.
(b)
• Advantages: respected, share customs and psychological needs of clients, committed to community safety, community confidence.
• Good practices: preparation for motherhood (e.g. fattening room), well feeding in pregnancy, 40 days indoors after delivery with nutritious diet and rest.
• Harmful practices: chewing sticks to stimulate contractions (ruptured uterus), food taboos, cow's urine or putting convulsing children in fire, FGM/FGC (scarring, difficult coitus and deliveries), force-feeding (choking, aspiration pneumonia), failure to admit limits.
• Kit contents: hand towel, nail brush, razor blade, cord ligature, Dettol/Savlon, soap case, exercise book, biro, kidney dishes.
(c)
• Community midwives study TBA practices, commend strengths and correct weaknesses; seminars on hygiene and early referral reduce deaths; promote safe motherhood and healthy children.
• Government sustains TBA interest through training, supplies, remuneration and supervision.
(d)
• Teach TBAs record keeping, hygiene, recognising limitations and referring patients in good time.
• Counsel mothers on food taboos, FGM and harmful child practices.
questions.question:
Describe the role of the community midwife in relation to traditional birth attendants (TBAs).
(a) Define the community midwife and TBAs and the TBA's background.
(b) State the roles, practices, advantages and disadvantages of TBAs.
(c) Explain their role in reducing maternal and child morbidity and mortality.
(d) State the health education the community midwife should give.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Lactation is synthesis, secretion and ejection of milk by alveoli and ducts in the breasts.
• Secretion: after the placenta is born, progesterone and oestrogen fall and prolactin from the anterior pituitary triggers milk production.
• Ejection: suckling releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which contracts alveolar cells; more suckling gives more milk (supply and demand).
(b)
• Poor latch results from poor alignment and positioning; teach feeding cues (hand to mouth, sucking, rooting) and feed when the baby is quiet and alert, not crying (a late hunger sign).
• Teach positions (cradle, side lying, football); sore nipples result from incorrect latch-on.
• Engorgement: swelling and overfilling of breast and areola, firm areolae, flattened nipples; Explain beforehand, supportive non-underwire bra, frequent feeding 15-20 minutes each breast with gentle massage, warm compresses.
• Pain: breastfeeding should not be painful; assess causes (e.g. engorgement); refer to a lactation consultant (IBCLC) if pain persists.
(c)
• Teach expressing into a sterile cup, boiling and sterilising equipment, hand hygiene, washing breasts with warm water (no soaps or oils).
• Refrigerated milk is thawed in warm water, not at room temperature; discard leftover milk; never refreeze thawed milk.
(d)
Rationale: proper positioning facilitates let-down; feeding when alert eases latching; frequent feeding reduces milk stasis; tight bras obstruct flow.
questions.question:
Describe the nursing care of a mother with breastfeeding problems.
(a) State the physiology of lactation.
(b) Describe the problems (latch, sore nipples, engorgement, pain, prematurity/employed mothers) and nursing counselling.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities for expressing and storing breast milk.
(d) Explain the rationale behind the key actions.

Describe the fetal skull and moulding as a physiological process of labour.
(a) State what moulding is and its protective function.
(b) State the diameters of the fetal skull given.
(c) State how deviations relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how excessive moulding may progress and its effects on the baby.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Moulding: change in shape of the fetal head during passage through the birth canal; the vault bones bend slightly.
• It is protective, preventing compression of the fetal brain provided it is not excessive, too rapid or in an unfavourable direction.
• The skull of the preterm infant is softer with wider sutures than that of the term infant.
(b)
• Subparietal-supraparietal 9 cm: engagement diameter in asynclitism.
• Bitemporal 8 cm (between anterior ends of the temporal sutures); bimastoid 7.5 cm (between the tips of the two mastoid processes).
• Mentovertical 13.5 cm is the presenting diameter in brow presentation.
(c)
• Excessive moulding occurs in prolonged labour, cephalopelvic disproportion and prematurity.
• Upward moulding occurs in occipitoposterior (face-to-pubis) position and after-coming head of the breech.
• Rapid moulding occurs in precipitate labour: rapid compression and decompression.
(d)
• Venous sinuses lie close to the intracranial membranes; tears of membranes from excessive moulding or precipitate labour risk bleeding.
• A tear of the tentorium cerebelli may cause bleeding from the great cerebral vein; rapid moulding may rupture cerebral membranes.
• Pelvic contraction can cause malposition or malpresentation; Preterm babies are at risk of cerebral palsy, developmental delay, hearing and vision problems.

(a)
• Preterm: live birth before 37 weeks; extremely preterm (<28 weeks), very preterm (28-32), moderate to late preterm (32-37).
• Risk factors: diabetes, high blood pressure, multiple gestation, obesity or underweight, tobacco smoking, psychological stress.
• Signs: four or more contractions in one hour with cervical dilatation and effacement (true labour), third-trimester vaginal bleeding, heavy pelvic pressure, abdominal or back pain, watery discharge (premature rupture of membranes).
(b)
• Treatment: corticosteroids, kangaroo mother care; bed rest, sedation and tocolytics to inhibit contractions; Prevention: preconception folic acid, avoid smoking, reduce strenuous activity, healthy lifestyle.
• Premature infants have greater risk of cerebral palsy, developmental delay, hearing and vision problems.
(c)
• Isoxsuprine: IV drip 100 mg in 5% dextrose, continue 2 hours after contractions cease, then 10 mg IM 6-hourly for 24 hours; monitor BP lying and standing, contractions and FHR; change position slowly.
• Ritodrine: IV drip 100 mg in 5% dextrose at 0.1 mg/min increased by 0.05 mg/min, continue 2 hours after contractions cease; Contraindicated in eclampsia, hypertension, dysrhythmias; monitor maternal and fetal heart tones, contractions and fluid intake (stop if overload).
• Ritodrine positioning: left lateral recumbent position; bed rest during infusion; side effects include hyperglycaemia, palpitations, headache, sweating, nausea.
(d)
Rationale: left lateral position reduces hypotension and raises renal blood flow; fluid monitoring prevents overload; tocolytics prolong pregnancy.
questions.question:
Describe the nursing care of a woman in preterm labour.
(a) Define preterm birth and state the risk factors and signs.
(b) State the treatment and prevention.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities for tocolytic drugs (isoxsuprine and ritodrine).
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hydatidiform mole: gross malformation of the trophoblast; chorionic villi proliferate into vesicles like a bunch of English grapes.
• Risk higher in a woman who has had it before (1 in 50) and under age 20 or above 40. Types: complete (no embryo, cord or membrane) and incomplete (evidence of embryo, fetus or amniotic sac).
(b)
Signs: exaggerated pregnancy symptoms by 6-8 weeks, bleeding or blood-stained discharge after amenorrhoea, slight pink or brown discharge, passage of vesicles, anaemia, high chorionic gonadotrophin level, early preeclampsia, uterus larger than dates and doughy.
(c)
• Oxytocin is indicated to expedite expulsion of a hydatidiform mole.
• Ergometrine is used for bleeding after expulsion of a mole.
• Hyperemesis is among conditions that may accompany a mole; check for it.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman at 8 weeks has exaggerated pregnancy symptoms, bleeding with passage of grape-like vesicles, and a uterus larger than dates that feels doughy. She had a similar condition in the past.
(a) Identify the condition and its risk factors.
(b) State the signs.
(c) Justify the management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• PHC (WHO 1978): essential care based on practical, scientifically sound, socially acceptable methods, made universally accessible through full community participation at a cost the community and country can afford; First level of contact with the national health system.
• Aims: services accessible to everyone; tackle problems causing highest mortality and morbidity at affordable cost; technology the community can use and maintain; full community involvement.
• Principles: equitable distribution, manpower development, community participation (most essential), appropriate technology (e.g.
• ORT, weaning foods), intersectoral coordination, availability and affordability, proximity, health promotion and disease prevention.
(b)
• Components: health education, food and nutrition, safe motherhood and family planning, environmental health, immunisation (NPI), control of endemic diseases, essential drugs, treatment of common diseases and injuries, mental and dental health.
• Newer components: accident prevention, occupational health, IMCI, mectizan distribution, malaria elimination, monitoring and evaluation, eye programme.
• Organisation: federal (policy, finance, standards, vaccines), state (state policy, training schools), local government (delivers services; head is the medical officer or community health officer).
(c)
• PHC brings services to the doorstep, includes immunisation, safe motherhood, family planning, nutrition and IMCI, so reducing maternal and child deaths.
• It can be run by community health extension workers, village health workers and TBAs, and is less expensive.
(d)
• Education: health education is a component; mothers educated on immunisation, nutrition and hygiene.
• Limitations: wrong assumption that rural areas lack disease, inadequate records, unqualified personnel, lack of equipment and transport, no supervision, poor roads.
questions.question:
Describe primary health care (PHC) as a service in Nigeria.
(a) Define it and state its aims and principles.
(b) State its components and organisation.
(c) Explain its role in reducing maternal, newborn and child morbidity and mortality.
(d) State the health education and limitations.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• In pregnancy rising oestrogen and progesterone enlarge the breast, darken the primary areola, develop Montgomery's tubercles; Colostrum can be expressed by 16 weeks; secondary areola appears.
• Milk production: prolactin from the anterior pituitary; its action is blocked in pregnancy by placental hormones.
• Milk passage: back pressure from new milk globules and the neurohormonal let-down reflex, in which sucking stimulates the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin.
(b)
Breast milk has less contamination risk, lower neonatal infection and gastroenteritis incidence, protective factors (immunoglobulins, lactoferrin, lysozyme, bifidus factor, antitrypsin factor) against allergy, correct food balance, and saves time and money.
(c)
• Complications: engorgement, painful/cracked/sore nipple, retracted nipple, breast cancer, mastitis, abscess, candidiasis of the breast, lactation failure, failure of let-down reflex.
• Baby-related feeding difficulties: cleft lip, cleft palate (expressed milk by cup and spoon or Haberman feeder), illness, surgery, blocked nose, Down syndrome, prematurity, tongue tie.
(d)
• Mastitis arises from poor milk drainage plus bacteria entering through cracked nipples; engorgement with poor latch reduces emptying.
• Untreated mastitis: recurrence, abscess needing surgical drainage, septicaemia or sepsis.
• Stopping feeding abruptly worsens mastitis; continued feeding helps clear infection.
• Prevention: drain the breast fully, good latch, vary positions.
questions.question:
Describe the physiology of lactation.
(a) State the breast changes in pregnancy and the hormones that produce and release milk.
(b) State the advantages of breast milk over artificial milk.
(c) State how deviations relate to common breast complications in the puerperium.
(d) Explain how a complication may progress and its effects on mother and baby.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Risk factors: positive family or past history of TB; residence in an area of high TB prevalence.
• Treatment as in the non-pregnant state: rest, hospitalisation and chemotherapy; isoniazid and ethambutol in the first trimester, rifampicin after; drug therapy likely continues 9 months; early treatment makes sputum negative by delivery.
• Streptomycin is contraindicated as it may cause vestibular defects in the fetus.
• Admit for rest in the last two weeks; isolate if still infectious; consider social and domestic situation (social worker for financial or housing difficulties); encourage a balanced diet.
(b)
• Labour: episiotomy may speed delivery and reduce second-stage strain; monitor fetomaternal condition, respiration and SpO2; oxygen readily available.
• Postnatal: separation of baby from family is not always necessary except if a family member has isoniazid-resistant TB.
(c)
• Baby: isoniazid-resistant BCG vaccine, plus isoniazid syrup 25 mg/kg/day prophylaxis as the vaccine takes 3-6 weeks to become effective.
• Family planning advice after delivery: avoid further pregnancy until cured and symptom-free for at least two years; avoid oral contraceptives with rifampicin as it reduces their effectiveness.
(d)
• Rationale: isolation limits spread while infectious; streptomycin avoided to protect the fetus; prophylaxis protects baby while BCG becomes effective.
• Pneumonia in pregnancy: avoid quinolones and tetracycline; chest X-ray with abdominal shield.
• Oxygen is made readily available in labour in case of need.
questions.question:
Describe the nursing care of a pregnant woman with tuberculosis.
(a) State the risk factors, treatment and antenatal care.
(b) State the care in labour and postnatally.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities regarding the baby's prophylaxis and the woman's family planning.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions.

A woman aged 38 with four children requests female sterilisation by tubal ligation.
(a) Name the procedure and state the nursing responsibilities before, during and after it.
(b) State the danger signs and the structures involved.
(c) Outline the health education and discharge plan.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tubal ligation: same-day laparoscopic surgery in which the fallopian tubes are coagulated, sutured (Pomeroy), ligated or clipped; methods include postpartum, interval, bipolar and monopolar coagulation, tubal clip and tubal ring.
• Before: health history; educate on the procedure, benefits, risks and body changes; emotional support to client and family; effective contraception for at least a month before; signed written consent in a right state of mind; sterile environment; blood available; any IUD is removed.
• After: assess regularly for complications and infection; monitor and document vital signs.
(b)
• Complications: heavy bleeding, damage to bowel, bladder or major vessels, improper wound healing, abdominal pain; risk higher with diabetes, previous abdominal or pelvic surgery, obesity.
• A woman who misses a period should be tested for pregnancy (ectopic or intrauterine pregnancy is rare but possible).
• Contraindicated in women who desire future pregnancy.
(c)
• Education: keep incision clean, dry and covered; no baths, hot tubs or swimming until healed; avoid heavy exercise for several days; sexual intercourse when ready and pain-free.
• Nursing diagnoses: pre-op anxiety and deficient knowledge; post-op acute pain and risk for infection.

questions.question:
A woman with a maternal family history of twins and a history of ovulation-inducing drugs presents with hyperemesis, palpitations and shortness of breath, swollen legs, varicose veins and excessive abdominal enlargement. The fundus is higher than expected for the known date of her last normal period, the uterus is broad and round, and three fetal poles or two fetal heads are felt. A fetal head seems small for the size of the uterus.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Interpret the findings.
(c) State the differential considerations.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning, management of labour and referral.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Multiple pregnancy (probably twins, the commonest); confirm by ultrasound scan; where unavailable, X-ray after the 30th week.
(b)
• Fundus higher than period of gestation, broad round uterus, fetal movements over a wide area, two heads or backs or multiple parts on palpation, small head relative to uterus; exaggerated symptoms and cardiorespiratory embarrassment support it; risk factors include ovulation-inducing drugs/IVF, high parity, black race, family history, maternal age 30-35.
• Polyhydramnios should alert one to multiple pregnancy; early preeclampsia or sudden unexplained anaemia may also be a response to it.
(c)
Differential: where the date of the last period is uncertain or the abdomen is obese or firm, diagnosis may be delayed until after delivery of the first baby; if the uterus stays large afterwards, palpation confirms a second fetus (ergometrine or syntometrine must not be given before this is excluded).
(d)
• Effects: premature labour, preeclampsia, polyhydramnios, more severe anaemia, pressure symptoms, hyperemesis, backache; in labour: early membrane rupture, malpresentation, uterine inertia, problems with second twin, PPH, maternal exhaustion.
• Deliver in a well-equipped unit with blood transfusion, anaesthesia and special care facilities for premature babies; cross-match blood; admit at 36 weeks if transport is difficult; have two cots, paediatrician and obstetrician ready; label Twin I; palpate to find the lie of the second baby; deliver second twin without delay and seek medical help if not born within minutes.

(a)
• Diabetes is a disorder of metabolism from absent or inadequate insulin from the pancreatic beta cells. GDM: carbohydrate intolerance with onset or first recognition in pregnancy.
• Classification: pregestational (Type I or II) if diabetes antedated pregnancy; gestational if first diagnosed in pregnancy.
(b)
• Type I: absence of insulin, fat and protein breakdown forms ketones, acidosis may cause coma; Type II: insulin present but cells resistant; GDM resembles Type II.
• Human placental lactogen increases insulin resistance, peaking at 26-28 weeks (screening time); before 20 weeks cells are more responsive and glucose may be lower.
• Fetal effects: macrosomia (hyperplasia and hypertrophy), later obesity and diabetes risk; Congenital anomalies (cardiac, CNS, caudal regression), spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, IUGR, neonatal hypoglycaemia; maternal hypertension/preeclampsia.
• Macrosomia raises risk of protracted labour, shoulder dystocia and operative delivery.
(c)
• Vulnerable: marked obesity, prior GDM, strong family history, previous infant over 4000 g, unexplained stillbirth, poor obstetric history, recurrent glycosuria; Type II usually begins after 40 and women are generally overweight.
• Women with prior GDM are at increased risk for abnormal carbohydrate metabolism in future pregnancies; balanced diet and moderate exercise may minimise risk.
(d)
• Pregestational: congenital anomaly risk with poor early control, all need insulin (oral agents such as tolbutamide possibly teratogenic, prolonged neonatal hypoglycaemia); Type I usually diagnosed before pregnancy.
• GDM: early pregnancy glucose usually not elevated so anomaly risk equals the general population; hyperglycaemia rises as insulin demand rises; most are controlled by diet and exercise.
questions.question:
Describe diabetes in pregnancy.
(a) Define diabetes and gestational diabetes and state the classification.
(b) Describe the physiology and its effects on mother and baby.
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable.
(d) Distinguish between gestational diabetes and pregestational (Type I/II) diabetes.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Four disorders: preeclampsia/eclampsia/HELLP; gestational hypertension; chronic hypertension; preeclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension.
• Preeclampsia: new hypertension with proteinuria or significant end-organ dysfunction, typically after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive woman (ACOG 2013 removed proteinuria as essential).
• Eclampsia: grand mal seizure in a woman with preeclampsia without another neurological cause.
• HELLP: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets, probably a subtype of preeclampsia with severe features; 82-88% have hypertension, 86-100% have proteinuria.
(b)
• Chronic hypertension: present before pregnancy, or on two occasions before 20 weeks, or persisting beyond 12 weeks postpartum; may be primary or secondary to kidney disease, adrenal tumours or renovascular hypertension.
• Gestational hypertension: hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ signs. Superimposed preeclampsia:.
• Worsening or resistant hypertension, new or sudden rise of proteinuria, or new end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks in chronic hypertension.
(c)
• Preeclampsia is more common in nulliparas and uncommon in multiparas with previously normotensive pregnancies.
• It is more common in older (over 40) than younger nulliparas; older women are also more likely to have chronic hypertension; women with chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of superimposed preeclampsia.
• Burden: of nearly four million deliveries, 11% had a hypertension-related diagnosis (4.7% preeclampsia, 3.8% gestational hypertension, 1.7% chronic hypertension).
(d)
• Gestational vs chronic: gestational develops after 20 weeks and resolves by 12 weeks postpartum; chronic antecedes pregnancy or occurs before 20 weeks and persists beyond 12 weeks postpartum.
• HELLP vs severe preeclampsia: in HELLP, haemolysis, liver enzymes and thrombocytopenia predominate and BP may not match liver dysfunction; in severe preeclampsia severe hypertension is usual and platelet/liver abnormalities are less marked.
questions.question:
Describe the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
(a) List the four major disorders and define preeclampsia, eclampsia and HELLP syndrome.
(b) State the diagnostic criteria for chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension and superimposed preeclampsia.
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable.
(d) Distinguish between gestational hypertension and chronic hypertension, and between HELLP and preeclampsia with severe features.

At a routine child health visit, a child's weight, length, mid-upper arm circumference and head circumference are measured and plotted on WHO growth charts. The child's Z-score is below -3, the MUAC tape reads red and the plotted trend is stagnating.
(a) Identify the condition and interpret the findings.
(b) State the causes and risk factors to be assessed.
(c) Name the differential conditions the indicators distinguish.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning, follow-up and referral.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Z below -3 = severe malnutrition (below -2 = moderate; -1 to +2 normal; above +2 overweight/obesity); red MUAC = severe acute malnutrition (yellow moderate, green normal; used for ages 6 months to 5 years).
• Declining trends or stagnation on WHO growth charts require prompt intervention; stagnation may indicate a problem with diet, infection or caregiving.
(b)
Immediate causes: inadequate dietary intake (quantity and quality) and recurrent infections (malaria, diarrhoea, pneumonia). Underlying causes: inadequate maternal care, poor sanitation and unsafe water, lack of education on feeding practices.
(c)
Low height-for-age = stunting (long-term deprivation); low weight-for-height = wasting (acute malnutrition); low weight-for-age = underweight; high weight-for-height = overweight/obesity; head circumference (under 2 years) detects hydrocephalus or microcephaly.
(d)
• Early detection allows early referral, treatment and nutritional intervention, preventing complications such as cognitive impairment; malnutrition is a leading cause of under-five mortality.
• Schedule: monthly 0-12 months, every 2-3 months at 12-24 months, every 3-6 months at 2-5 years; integrate in immunisation clinics, postnatal checks, under-five clinics and outreach.
• Involve caregivers, give nutrition counselling and use the child health card to record growth history.

(a)
PPH = blood loss of 500 ml or more after delivery (uterus, cervix, vagina, perineum); signs: visible bleeding, boggy uterus, collapse, pallor, tachycardia, hypotension, restlessness/drowsiness. Investigations: grouping and cross-matching, PCV/Hb, FBC, coagulation test, high vaginal swab, blood culture, ultrasound.
(b)
Deficient fluid volume related to excessive bleeding evidenced by hypotension; Acute pain related to tissue damage; Anxiety related to perceived threat of death; Deficient knowledge.
(c)
Assess vitals (BP baseline), shock, uterus and bleeding; save and weigh pads; side-lying, legs elevated 20-30 degrees; assess lochia frequently; empty bladder (catheter/bedpan) before fundal palpation; gently massage fundus; vaginal examination for tears; manual removal if placenta in situ; IV fluids.
(d)
• Four Ts: Tone (atony): bimanual compression, Syntocinon/ergometrine/carboprost/misoprostol, balloon tamponade, B-Lynch, artery ligation, hysterectomy last resort. Trauma: explore and repair, laparotomy/hysterectomy for rupture. Tissue: IV oxytocin, manual removal, prophylactic antibiotics. Thrombin: correct with blood products.
• Catheterise bladder; IV fluids and blood transfusion to maintain homeostasis.
(e)
Care-plan objectives: BP of at least 100/60 mm Hg within 30-40 minutes; pain reduction within 15-30 minutes; reduced anxiety within 30-40 minutes; client verbalises the pathophysiology in simple terms.
questions.question:
A woman has bled 500 ml or more after delivery of her baby. Her uterus is boggy; she is pale, tachycardic, hypotensive, restless and drowsy, with visible bleeding.
(a) Identify the assessment findings and investigations.
(b) State the priority nursing diagnoses.
(c) Describe the immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Describe the medical management by cause.
(e) State the evaluation criteria for nursing care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Primary infertility: no pregnancy after at least 1 year of intercourse without birth control; secondary infertility: pregnancy achieved before but now unable.
• Risk factors: age over 35 (women) or over 40 (men), diabetes, eating disorders, alcohol, toxins, over-exercise, radiation, STIs, smoking, stress, substance abuse, obesity or underweight.
(b)
• Causes: about 1 in 3 female problems, 1 in 3 male problems, 1 in 3 both or undetermined.
• Male: sperm count below 15 million, low motility, abnormal shape; overheated testicles (varicocele, undescended testicle, hot tubs, tight clothes); ejaculation disorders; hypogonadism; mumps; Klinefelter syndrome; drugs such as sulfasalazine and anabolic steroids.
• Female: ovulation disorders (about 25%): hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid problems, PCOS; tubal blockage, endometriosis, fibroids, primary ovarian insufficiency, age-related egg decline, pelvic surgery.
(c)
• Women: hormone tests, morning temperature, FSH/clomid challenge, HSG, pelvic or transvaginal ultrasound, hysteroscopy, laparoscopy, LH urine test, thyroid tests; men: semen analysis, hormone and genetic tests, testicular biopsy.
• Treatment: pharmacotherapy (clomifene, tamoxifen, metformin for PCOS, gonadotrophins; side effects nausea, vomiting, headaches, hot flushes), surgery (fallopian tube repair), and assisted conception (IUI, IVF).
questions.question:
A couple has been unable to conceive after more than a year of unprotected intercourse. The woman is 37 and obese; the man has a low sperm count and wears tight clothing.
(a) Identify the condition and its risk factors.
(b) State the causes and complications.
(c) Justify the investigations and management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Face presentation: the head is fully extended with the face visible; incidence approximately 1:500.
• Most occur during labour from vertex presentations with the occiput posterior (secondary face presentation); less commonly the face presents before labour.
(b)
• Anterior obliquity of the uterus (multigravida with pendulous abdomen): contraction force is directed towards the chin rather than the occiput, causing head extension.
• Contracted pelvis: in a flat pelvis the parietal eminences may be held up in the obstetrical conjugate, extending the head.
• Polyhydramnios: rush of amniotic fluid after membrane rupture may extend the head as it sinks into the lower uterine segment.
• Congenital malformation: anencephaly; rarely a fetal neck tumour.
(c)
• Nursing: regular clinical examination of progress, effective communication and record keeping, inform and support woman and partner, empathy, comfort and hydration, mobility and comfortable positions, avoid demoralising language, report any sign of fetal/maternal distress or delay.
• Malpresentation is associated with difficult labour and increased operative intervention.
• Complications: obstructed labour, cord prolapse, facial bruising, maternal trauma.
questions.question:
A woman with a pendulous abdomen and slack abdominal muscles in labour has a fetus whose head is fully extended, with the face presenting and the occiput in contact with its spine.
(a) State the diagnosis and its incidence.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management, and the complications.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Incomplete abortion: the fetus is expelled but parts of the placenta and membranes are retained in the uterus; heavy lochia, possibly profuse bleeding, pain may or may not be present, os partly closed, cervix patulous, sub-involution.
(b)
• In the district: send for medical aid; resuscitate if in shock; pethidine 100 mg for pain; accompany to hospital and give post-abortion care.
• If in shock: warm bed, foot of bed elevated; observe pulse every 5 minutes and BP every 30 minutes.
(c)
• Syntometrine 1 ml or ergometrine 0.5 mg IM, repeated after 5-10 minutes if bleeding is profuse; oxytocin 5-10 units in 5% glucose.
• In hospital: syntometrine or ergometrine 0.5 mg; blood for grouping and cross-matching; high vaginal swab; evacuation of the uterus.
• If in shock: ergometrine IV; infusion of 5% dextrose with Ringer's lactate, syntocinon 10 units may be added; evacuate under general anaesthesia when improved.
• Treat anaemia if present; antibiotic cover.
(d)
Discharge on the 5th day.
questions.question:
A woman at 10 weeks has passed the fetus but bleeds heavily; lochia is profuse, the os is partly closed and the cervix is patulous. She appears pale and shocked.
(a) State the assessment findings.
(b) State the immediate nursing interventions.
(c) Describe the medical management.
(d) State the expected outcomes.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The placenta supplies oxygen and nutrition and removes waste; other structures are the ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus and hypogastric arteries (which become the umbilical arteries).
• Oxygenated blood travels in the umbilical vein, which divides: one branch supplies the portal vein, the other joins the inferior vena cava via the ductus venosus.
• Most oxygenated blood entering the right atrium crosses the foramen ovale to the left atrium, then left ventricle and aorta; the head and upper limbs receive about 50%.
• Blood from the superior vena cava passes to the right ventricle; most of it goes through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta and returns to the placenta via the internal iliac arteries.
(b)
• Newborn is assessed with the Apgar scale at one and five minutes (0 to 10) for heart rate, breathing effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability and skin tone.
• After cord blood flow ceases and the first breath is taken, pulmonary blood flow rises, left atrial pressure increases and the foramen ovale closes mechanically; pulmonary vascular resistance falls by about 80%.
• Rising oxygen tension makes the ductus arteriosus constrict, usually within 24 hours, though it may remain patent for a few days.
• Resulting structures: umbilical vein to ligamentum teres; ductus venosus to ligamentum venosum; ductus arteriosus to ligamentum arteriosum; Foramen ovale to fossa ovalis; hypogastric arteries to obliterated hypogastric arteries (first few centimetres remain as superior vesical arteries).
• Adaptation also includes establishing breastfeeding, renal and GI elimination, portal and liver circulation, temperature control and parent-baby communication.
questions.question:
Describe fetal circulation and the newborn's adaptation to extrauterine life.
(a) Name the structures that enable fetal circulation and the course of blood.
(b) Describe the changes that occur after birth and the structures that result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Habitual abortion: spontaneous abortion on at least three consecutive occasions; occurs in about 1% of pregnancies; risk of further abortion is high.
• Causes: mostly unknown, more with incompetent cervix; local causes: fibroid, displacement of the uterus; medical: diabetes mellitus, nephritis, tuberculosis.
(b)
• If the pregnancy continues to mid-trimester there is risk of threatened abortion or premature labour.
• General causes of abortion also include chromosomal abnormalities (about 60%), infection, drugs, smoking, alcohol, ABO incompatibility and hormonal imbalance.
(c)
• Early booking, no coitus, hospitalisation may be imperative.
• Shirodkar stitch (cervical cerclage) at about 14-16 weeks with complete bed rest.
• Ventolin tablets 2-4 mg twice daily.
questions.question:
A woman with three consecutive spontaneous abortions presents in early pregnancy. She has diabetes and an incompetent cervix.
(a) Identify the condition and its risk factors.
(b) State the complications.
(c) Justify the management options.

Describe the nursing care of a woman requesting emergency contraception.
(a) State the types and how they work.
(b) State the method of use, contraindications and side effects.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities including the copper IUD.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• ECP: taken after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure (split condom, missed pill); 98% success within four days for average weight.
• Types: levonorgestrel (Levonelle, Plan B, Postinor-2) and ulipristal acetate (ellaOne).
• Action: stops or delays release of an egg, changes sperm movement; does not work once the egg is fertilised and does not harm an embryo.
(b)
• Levonelle must be taken within 72 hours; ellaOne within 120 hours (5 days); take the first dose as soon as possible and the second 12 hours later where two doses are used.
• Vomiting within 2 hours: repeat dose; two different pills must not be used within 5 days of each other.
• Contraindications: pregnancy, hypersensitivity, undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; ellaOne not with epilepsy, HIV or TB medicines.
• Side effects: headache, stomach pain, earlier, later or more painful next period; no serious long-term effects.
(c)
• ECP is less effective above 70 kg; a copper IUD is then an option, nearly 100% effective if inserted within 5 days.
• Levonelle is safe while breastfeeding; with ellaOne the manufacturer advises not breastfeeding for one week.
• Advise that the pill gives no continued protection against pregnancy from later unprotected sex.
(d)
Rationale: ECP delays ovulation until sperm are no longer active; copper IUD prevents implantation.

(a)
• Abdominal pregnancy: a rare condition in which the fetus develops outside the uterine cavity following abortion or rupture.
• Diagnosis: on palpation the lie is abnormal and fetal parts are readily felt.
(b)
• The placenta attaches to neighbouring organs; the majority do not survive; if early, the product is re-absorbed; it rarely proceeds to term.
• Preceding event: tubal pregnancy may end in abdominal pregnancy.
(c)
• Delivery is by laparotomy; the placenta may or may not be removed, leaving it is safer; prophylactic antibiotic is given.
• Complications: infection leading to abscess, peritonitis or septicaemia; baby may have compression deformities due to oligohydramnios.
questions.question:
A woman with a history of tubal rupture presents with an abnormal fetal lie and fetal parts that are readily felt on palpation.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State the management and complications.

A woman with known cardiac disease becomes pregnant and is obese and a smoker. She is admitted in labour.
(a) State the risk factors and how risk is determined.
(b) State the complications for mother and baby.
(c) Justify the priority medical and nursing actions before and during labour.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk depends on the cardiac lesion, baseline functional compromise and possibility of complications in pregnancy; risk factors include obesity, smoking and unhealthy lifestyle. Pregnancy raises cardiac output 40% and blood volume 35%, peaking at about 30 weeks.
(b)
• Some lesions carry very high maternal mortality (pulmonary hypertension, dilated cardiomyopathy, uncorrectable lesions in functional class III or IV), so termination may be advised; women are prone to PPH, pulmonary oedema and endocarditis.
• Hypertensive disorders may occur; watch for placental abruption.
(c)
• Preconception planning with cardiologist and obstetrician; genetic counselling may be indicated; expect multiple hospital visits; antenatally rest, reduced salt, methyldopa or nifedipine, hydralazine injection for emergency, admission near end of third trimester.
• Labour: notify anaesthetist and cardiologist on admission; cross-match blood; oxygen and resuscitation equipment ready; pulse and respiration every 15 minutes; ECG monitoring; report breathlessness and tachycardia immediately.
• Antibiotic prophylaxis against endocarditis in labour and 48 hours after delivery; avoid lithotomy position (sudden venous return); avoid indiscriminate IV fluids (pulmonary oedema) and record intake and output.
• Pain relief: coping techniques; epidural reduces cardiac output and heart rate and prevents pulmonary oedema; caesarean may be best; vaginal trial if BP controlled, under close monitoring.

(a)
• First baby: umbilical granuloma, a small moist red or pink fleshy bump at the base of the umbilicus after the cord falls off, usually harmless, not painful but may be sensitive, may stain the diaper.
• Second baby: omphalitis (umbilical cord sepsis), a bacterial infection of the stump.
(b)
• Normal healing: stump falls off in 5-15 days (up to 3 weeks); changes from yellowish-white and moist to brown, then black, dry and shrivelled; minimal clear or yellowish discharge; very slight redness that does not spread.
• Infection signs: foul or pus-like discharge, redness spreading beyond 1 cm, swelling or warmth, non-stopping bleeding, tenderness, fever above 38 degrees C, cord not off after two weeks.
(c)
• The midwife must differentiate umbilical granuloma from umbilical hernia (soft bulge near the navel, prominent with crying, painless) and from omphalitis; each needs different management.
• Single umbilical artery is another cord abnormality.
(d)
• Nursing: keep clean and dry; clean with clean water if soiled; do not apply ash, powder, herbs or ointments; do not pull the stump; chlorhexidine gel 7.1% in high-risk areas; handwashing.
• Seek medical help for infection signs; low birth weight or premature babies are at higher risk.
questions.question:
A newborn aged 5 days has a small, raised, moist, pink mass at the base of the umbilicus after the cord fell off, with a little yellowish discharge. A second newborn has redness spreading from the cord base, foul-smelling pus, fever and irritability.
(a) Identify the conditions.
(b) Interpret the findings against normal healing.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and referral.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Omphalitis: bacterial infection of the umbilical stump; risk factors:.
• Unclean delivery, unsterile cord cutting tools, dirty hands, harmful substances, tight dirty covering, low birth weight or premature babies.
• Early signs: redness or swelling at stump base, foul discharge or pus, fever or illness, irritability on touch, cord not off after two weeks.
(b)
• Keep the stump dry and let it fall off naturally; do not pull; avoid powder, oil or herbs; avoid tight diapers or cloths; handwashing before touching baby or cord.
• If soiled, clean gently with clean water and pat dry with sterile gauze; fold the diaper below the stump; give sponge baths.
• Seek medical help for foul or green discharge, spreading redness over 1 cm, swelling, bleeding, tenderness or fever above 38 degrees C.
(c)
• Clamp cord in two places 2-3 cm apart and cut between with sterile scissors; Delayed clamping 30 seconds to 3 minutes (at least 60 seconds if stable); immediate clamping only for resuscitation or urgent maternal bleeding.
• Chlorhexidine gel 7.1% may be advised in high-risk areas; distribute cord care kits.
(d)
• Traditional substances (ash, soil, cow dung, animal fat, herbal mixtures, oils or ghee) can cause infection, sepsis, tetanus or delayed healing.
• Cultural beliefs (spiritual significance, disposal rituals, delayed separation) may delay treatment; educate through leaders, elders and TBAs.
questions.question:
Describe the nursing care of a newborn with or at risk of omphalitis.
(a) State the assessment and risk factors.
(b) State the nursing interventions and prevention.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities regarding cord clamping and chlorhexidine.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key actions and cultural practices.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Inevitable abortion: bleeding with uterine contractions, severe bleeding and dilatation of the cervix, so the pregnancy cannot continue; it may end complete or incomplete.
• Signs: slight or severe bleeding, increased painful contractions, cervical dilatation, membranes ruptured or bulging, shock may be present, products may protrude through the os or into the vagina.
(b)
• Treat as threatened abortion until the doctor arrives; keep all blood loss for the doctor's inspection.
• Admit, reassure, record vital signs, no vaginal examination or enema, save all discharges (as for threatened abortion).
(c)
• If bleeding is severe: ergometrine 0.5 mg or syntometrine 1 ml.
• Analgesics: pethidine 100 mg or morphine 15 mg.
• Oxytocin drip, or prostaglandin E2 if after 16 weeks; evacuate the uterus under general anaesthesia; blood transfusion if necessary.
questions.question:
A woman at 14 weeks has severe vaginal bleeding, painful uterine contractions and a dilated cervix; the membranes are bulging through the os and products protrude into the vagina. She shows signs of shock.
(a) State the assessment findings.
(b) State the immediate nursing interventions.
(c) Describe the medical management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Septic abortion: the most common complication of induced or incomplete abortion.
• Signs: anaemia, signs of miscarriage, feeling unwell, lower abdominal pain, headache, vomiting, pyrexia, rapid pulse, profuse and offensive lochia.
(b)
• Cause: ascending infection; it may be localised or generalised septicaemia with peritonitis.
• Induced abortion may be therapeutic or criminal.
(c)
• Intravenous antibiotics for a start, followed by broad-spectrum antibiotics effective against anaerobic infection.
• Post-abortion care includes treatment of incomplete or unsafe abortion complications, counselling, family planning, and community partnership.
• Midwife prepares the manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) room and gives pre- and post-procedure care.
questions.question:
A woman who had an induced abortion has fever, rapid pulse, lower abdominal pain, headache, vomiting, anaemia and profuse offensive lochia.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State the nursing and medical management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• COCP: ethinylestradiol 20-35 micrograms plus a progestogen; mechanism: ovulation inhibition, thickened cervical mucus, thin endometrium.
• POP (minipill): very low-dose progestin, no oestrogen; usable throughout breastfeeding; no delay in return of fertility.
• Injectables: DMPA and Noristerat (progestogen-only, 1-3 months), Mesigyna (combined, one month); implant: etonogestrel rods; combined vaginal ring and patch also described.
(b)
• POP eligible: women who cannot use oestrogen and lactating women; contraindications: pregnancy, undiagnosed genital bleeding, severe arterial disease, active liver disease, recurrent follicular cysts.
• POP side effects: bleeding changes, headaches, dizziness, mood changes, breast tenderness, abdominal pain, nausea; take daily at the same hour.
• POP missed pill: if more than 3 hours late take it and use extra contraception for 48 hours; vomiting within 2 hours repeat dose.
• DMPA side effects: menstrual disturbance, weight gain, headache, delayed return of fertility; Mesigyna: irregular menses in first 3-6 months, breast tenderness, weight gain.
• Vaginal ring: kept in three weeks then out one week; perfect use over 99% effective, typical use about 91%.
(c)
Methods are reversible, long-acting and effective, preventing unwanted pregnancy and supporting birth spacing; DMPA suits those wanting reliability without daily vigilance.
(d)
• Start POP on day 1 (no extra cover) or after day 5 (48 hours extra); after delivery on day 21; after miscarriage on the day.
• Hormonal methods do not protect against STIs; rifampicin reduces effectiveness of oral contraceptives; implants and injectables need follow-up as scheduled.
questions.question:
Describe hormonal contraception as a family planning service.
(a) Define the methods (COC, POP, injectables, implants, ring).
(b) State mechanism, eligible users, side effects and contraindications.
(c) Explain their role in birth spacing and reducing unintended pregnancy.
(d) State the health education the nurse should give.
