Accurate identification of the subtype and severity guides appropriate goal-setting and selection of the most suitable therapeutic approach.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with cerebral palsy and observes that when the child's head turns to one side, the arm on the face side extends while the arm on the occiput side flexes. This reflex pattern is characteristic of which reflex?

options: Claw hand affecting all four fingers equally
Monkey hand affecting the ulnar-innervated fingers
Wrist drop from radial nerve injury
Benediction sign from high median injury
Ape hand from median nerve injury
questions.question: A patient presents with claw hand affecting only the ring and little fingers after an ulnar nerve injury at the wrist. What term describes this presentation?
questions.explanation: A low ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist classically produces a clawed posture of the ring and little fingers due to unopposed action of the extensor digitorum combined with paralysis of the lumbricals supplied by the ulnar nerve, sometimes described using terms specific to ulnar nerve presentations. This differs from the ape hand seen in median nerve palsy or the benediction sign seen with higher median nerve lesions affecting different fingers. Correctly identifying the affected fingers helps localize the specific nerve and lesion level.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing an infant for early signs of cerebral palsy and notes persistent fisting of the hands beyond four months of age along with asymmetric hand use. What is the clinical significance of this finding?
options: It may represent an early red flag warranting further neurological evaluation for cerebral palsy
It confirms a diagnosis of Down syndrome specifically
It should be ignored until the child reaches school age
It is a completely normal finding at any age with no clinical significance
It indicates the infant has normal, symmetric motor development
questions.explanation: Persistent hand fisting beyond four months and asymmetric hand use are recognized early red flags for cerebral palsy, warranting further neurological evaluation and early referral, as early intervention is associated with improved developmental outcomes. Accurate identification of the subtype and severity guides appropriate goal-setting and selection of the most suitable therapeutic approach. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.

options: Prolonged ice application for tone reduction
Passive range of motion exercises alone
questions.explanation: In the late recovery stage, tone has largely normalized but timing and coordination deficits persist, making PNF techniques particularly useful. Positioning and passive range of motion are instead emphasized during the earlier flaccid stage of recovery. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: Which stroke rehabilitation protocol component specifically addresses timing and coordination deficits typically seen in the late recovery stage?

A physiotherapist wants to inhibit spasticity in a patient's hamstrings before a stretching session using a PNF-based technique that relies on the stretched muscle's own tension receptors. Which technique should be selected?
questions.explanation: The contract-relax technique uses autogenic inhibition, in which isometric or isotonic contraction of the target muscle stimulates its own Golgi tendon organs, producing reflexive relaxation that allows a deeper subsequent stretch, distinct from reciprocal inhibition-based techniques. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

Stereotaxic surgery for Parkinson's disease involves creating destructive lesions in the basal ganglia or thalamus using cryosurgery or chemosurgery, primarily to decrease or abolish tremor and reduce rigidity. Selective dorsal rhizotomy, by contrast, is used in cerebral palsy to treat severe lower limb spasticity. For the MRTB-standard physiotherapist, correctly classifying the presentation directly shapes the choice of handling technique, equipment, and family education.
questions.question: Which surgical intervention for Parkinson's disease involves producing destructive lesions in the basal ganglia or thalamus to decrease tremor and rigidity?

questions.explanation: TMS studies demonstrate an increase in the size of the ipsilateral motor cortex region representing the affected hand muscles following CIMT. Functional neuroimaging also shows increased cortical activation and significant interhemispheric inhibition of the contralesional hemisphere. These neural changes correlate strongly with improvements in motor function following CIMT intervention.
questions.question: After completing CIMT, transcranial magnetic stimulation of a stroke patient reveals enlarged cortical representation of the affected hand. Which neuroplastic change does this finding reflect?

options: Right motor loss and right pain/temperature loss
Right motor intact; right pain loss only
Right motor loss; left pain/temperature loss
Left motor loss; right vibration/proprioception loss
Bilateral motor loss; preserved sensation below
questions.question: A physiotherapist assesses a patient with suspected Brown-Sequard syndrome from a right T6 stab wound. On the RIGHT side ipsilateral to the lesion, which combination is EXPECTED?
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome from right-sided hemisection produces ipsilateral (right) motor weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception via uncrossed corticospinal and dorsal column pathways, with contralateral (left) loss of pain and temperature sensation as the spinothalamic tract crosses within 1-2 segments of entry. This crossed sensory and motor pattern is pathognomonic of spinal cord hemisection and guides physiotherapy strength training and sensory substitution interventions accordingly.

Kabat's PNF approach uses skillfully applied sensory stimuli including touch and pressure, traction and compression, stretch, and resistance to motion, along with auditory and visual cues, to facilitate movement patterns and muscle group activation. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. Accurate identification of the subtype and severity guides appropriate goal-setting and selection of the most suitable therapeutic approach.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is applying Kabat's proprioceptive facilitation approach with a child with cerebral palsy. Which type of sensory stimuli would be used to facilitate movement according to this method?
options: Only auditory stimuli with no tactile input
Touch and pressure, traction and compression, stretch
Complete sensory deprivation with no stimuli
Only visual stimuli with no proprioceptive input

questions.question: A physiotherapist treats a patient with suspected carpal tunnel syndrome presenting with nocturnal hand numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Which test supports this?
options: A positive Lachman's test of the knee
A positive Tinel's sign over the carpal tunnel
A positive Trendelenburg test of the hip
A positive Spurling's test of the neck
A positive straight leg raise test
questions.explanation: Tinel's sign, eliciting tingling in the median nerve distribution by tapping over the carpal tunnel, supports a diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome by reproducing the characteristic sensory symptoms through mechanical irritation of the compressed median nerve at the wrist. The other listed tests assess unrelated structures such as the lumbar spine, cervical spine, hip, or knee and would not be relevant to this wrist-level median nerve compression. Selecting the appropriate provocative test based on the suspected anatomical site of compression is essential for accurate clinical diagnosis.

options: Immediately begin intensive visual tracking exercises without medical referral
Refer for medical evaluation of possible optic neuritis
Assume this represents a permanent, untreatable complication
Ignore the symptom as unrelated to MS
questions.question: A physiotherapist working with an MS patient notices new-onset blurred vision and pain on eye movement. What should the physiotherapist do?
questions.explanation: New visual disturbance with pain on eye movement in an MS patient suggests optic neuritis, a recognized early or relapse feature requiring prompt medical evaluation, since acute relapses are often managed with corticosteroids before physiotherapy progresses further. This distinction is important for tailoring physiotherapy intensity and precautions to the patient's current disease phase. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

options: Activity limitations, participation, and environmental factors
questions.question: A post-stroke patient with right hemiplegia living alone with one step into the home is being discharged to the community. Which ICF domains MUST be addressed in the discharge plan?
questions.explanation: A comprehensive ICF-informed discharge plan must address activity limitations (functional mobility, ADL independence), participation restrictions (social roles, community access), and environmental factors (home modifications including the step entry requiring a ramp or handrail). The ICF biopsychosocial model ensures discharge planning encompasses all dimensions affecting return to meaningful community living, not only physiological impairments. The single step entry presents a specific environmental barrier requiring targeted modification recommendations.

options: Exercises performed exclusively with eyes closed
Vestibular habituation exercises as the primary focus
Strength training targeting only the lower trunk
Passive range of motion exercises alone
Balance and coordination exercises with visual feedback
questions.question: A physiotherapist teaches balance retraining to a patient with sensory ataxia from posterior column loss. Which strategy is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Because sensory ataxia from posterior column damage results from loss of proprioceptive feedback, training that incorporates visual feedback allows the patient to compensate for the lost proprioceptive channel and improve functional balance and coordination. Practicing exclusively with eyes closed would remove the very compensatory strategy the patient relies on and increase fall risk. Visual-based retraining is therefore the appropriate initial approach for this specific type of ataxia.

questions.question: A child presents with rapid, chaotic eye movements, multifocal muscle jerks, gait ataxia, and irritability, associated with an underlying neuroblastoma. This presentation is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Opsoclonus myoclonus ataxia syndrome is an autoimmune, often paraneoplastic disorder associated with neuroblastoma, presenting with chaotic conjugate eye movements (opsoclonus), multifocal muscle jerks (myoclonus), ataxia, and behavioural disturbances. It is frequently initially misdiagnosed as acute cerebellar ataxia or Guillain-Barre syndrome. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

questions.question: A physiotherapist screens a patient with suspected spinal cord injury. The patient has complete motor loss below the neurological level but has sacral sensation at S4-S5. Which ASIA grade does this represent?
questions.explanation: ASIA Grade B (sensory incomplete) is classified when there is no motor function below the neurological level but sensory function is preserved at sacral segments S4-S5, including light touch, pin prick, or deep anal pressure. This sacral sparing indicates incomplete injury and carries a better prognosis for some motor recovery compared to Grade A. The distinction is clinically critical as sacral sparing significantly influences rehabilitation potential and functional prognosis planning.

A grade of 0 indicates an absent reflex, often reflecting lower motor neuron or peripheral nerve pathology such as neuropathy, in contrast to hyperactive reflexes with clonus (grade 4+), which instead suggest upper motor neuron involvement. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.
options: Absent reflex response, consistent with lower motor neuron or peripheral nerve involvement
A finding unrelated to any neurological pathology
A completely normal reflex finding requiring no further action
An upper motor neuron lesion exclusively
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing deep tendon reflexes documents a grade of 0 for the ankle jerk reflex bilaterally in a patient with suspected peripheral neuropathy. What does this finding most likely indicate?
Which structure is primarily responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid that later drains through the shunt system used to treat hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus, a vascular tissue lining the ventricles, is primarily responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid then circulates through the ventricular system before being absorbed by the arachnoid villi. This knowledge underpins safe, well-coordinated physiotherapy care alongside the neurosurgical and paediatric medical team.

options: Supervision by family members only, with no professional oversight
Close, hands-on supervision with clear safety instructions during all mobility tasks
No supervision needed since strength has returned to normal
Supervision only during seated activities, with unsupervised standing
Complete discontinuation of all mobility training
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient recovering from severe TBI who demonstrates impaired judgment and impulsivity affecting safety awareness during gait training. Which supervision level is most appropriate initially?
questions.explanation: Impaired judgment and impulsivity following TBI create significant safety risks during mobility tasks, warranting close, hands-on supervision with clear safety instructions during gait training until safety awareness improves, rather than assuming physical strength recovery alone ensures safety. This understanding is critical for safe, stage-appropriate physiotherapy planning following traumatic brain injury. Recognizing this feature supports timely escalation of care and appropriate interdisciplinary collaboration in TBI management.

Because the trapezius muscle, innervated by the accessory nerve, plays a key role in scapular upward rotation during overhead arm elevation, its weakness commonly produces difficulty and altered scapulohumeral rhythm during overhead reaching tasks. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. This clinical reasoning helps the physiotherapist correctly localize the lesion during a systematic cranial nerve examination.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient's cranial nerve XI function post-neck surgery and finds weakness on the shoulder shrug test with visible trapezius wasting. Which additional functional limitation would the physiotherapist expect to find?
options: Loss of taste sensation on the tongue
Difficulty with overhead arm elevation due to impaired scapular upward rotation
Loss of facial expression on the same side
Complete loss of elbow flexion strength

questions.question: A patient with suspected trochlear nerve palsy reports worsening double vision when reading and descending stairs. Which clinical test should the physiotherapist perform to help confirm this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The Bielschowsky head tilt test is specific for trochlear nerve palsy, worsening hypertropia when the head tilts toward the affected side and improving it when tilted away. Rinne and Weber tests instead evaluate hearing, not extraocular muscle function. This clinical reasoning helps the physiotherapist correctly localize the lesion during a systematic cranial nerve examination.

questions.question: A physiotherapist applies resistance during a PNF technique. What principle should guide the amount used?
questions.explanation: The principle of optimal resistance in PNF means applying an amount of resistance that allows the patient to achieve a maximal but smooth, coordinated contraction, rather than an amount so great that it causes substitution patterns, breakdown of movement quality, or inability to complete the motion. Always using absolute maximum resistance disregards this important qualitative consideration. Adjusting resistance to the individual's current capability supports both effective facilitation and movement quality.
options: Minimal resistance is always preferred regardless of goal
Resistance amount has no relevance to treatment outcome
Always use the absolute maximum resistance possible
Resistance should never be modified during treatment
Optimal resistance for maximal contraction, not defeat

questions.explanation: The early flaccid stage of stroke recovery emphasizes positioning, gentle range of motion exercises, electrical or sensory stimulation, and early mobilization, reserving higher-level activities like stair climbing and constraint-induced therapy for later recovery stages. Recognizing this feature helps the physiotherapist tailor the stage-appropriate rehabilitation protocol and set realistic functional goals. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is designing an early-stage (acute flaccid) stroke rehabilitation session. Which combination of interventions is most appropriate for this stage?
options: Constraint-induced movement therapy for eight hours daily
Stair climbing and community ambulation training
Positioning, gentle ROM exercises, and sensory stimulation
Aggressive resisted strengthening against maximal resistance

questions.explanation: Astereognosis refers to the inability to recognize objects placed in the hand purely by touch, despite intact peripheral sensation, typically indicating a lesion in the sensory cortex of the parietal lobe rather than a dorsal column pathway problem. This finding directly guides the physiotherapist's clinical reasoning and subsequent management planning. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A patient is asked to close their eyes and identify a coin placed in their hand. Inability to do so, despite intact peripheral sensation, is termed:
Mirror neurons account for what percentage of all neurons present in the human brain?
questions.explanation: Mirror neurons account for approximately 20% of all neurons present in the human brain. These neurons are responsible for laterality reconstruction, the ability to differentiate between left and right sides. When using mirror therapy, these mirror neurons become activated and facilitate recovery of affected body parts through the mirror neuron system.

questions.question: Loss of neurons in which brain structure primarily accounts for the dopamine deficiency underlying Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease results primarily from progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra. Most patients have lost 60 to 80 percent of these cells by the time motor symptoms become clinically apparent. This understanding directly informs the physiotherapist's choice of assessment tools and stage-appropriate exercise strategies.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a myasthenia gravis patient and wants to differentiate ocular myasthenia from generalized disease. Which finding over a three-year period would suggest continued ocular-restricted disease?
questions.explanation: If myasthenia gravis symptoms remain confined to the extraocular muscles for three years without progression to limb or bulbar involvement, the disease is likely to remain purely ocular rather than becoming generalized, which the physiotherapist should factor into long-term prognosis discussions. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. This understanding is essential for structuring exercise dosage and activity pacing around the disease's fatigable nature.
options: Rapid progression to generalized weakness within weeks
New onset of proximal limb weakness within the first year
Appearance of bulbar symptoms within the first month
Weakness remaining confined to the extraocular muscles without limb involvement
Development of severe respiratory failure within six months

questions.explanation: Uncal herniation classically presents with acute loss of consciousness, ipsilateral pupillary dilation from oculomotor nerve (CN III) compression, and contralateral hemiparesis, reflecting increased intracranial pressure overwhelming the brain's compensatory capacity. This understanding is essential for safe, evidence-based clinical decision-making throughout the stroke rehabilitation pathway. Recognizing this feature helps the physiotherapist tailor the stage-appropriate rehabilitation protocol and set realistic functional goals.
questions.question: Which cranial nerve assessment finding, including acute loss of consciousness with ipsilateral pupillary dilation and contralateral hemiparesis, indicates uncal herniation?
Which physiotherapy intervention is specifically used in neurocutaneous syndrome management to promote use of a hemiparetic limb and prevent neglect?
questions.explanation: Constraint-induced movement therapy is used in neurocutaneous syndrome patients with hemiparesis to promote active use of the affected limb and prevent developmental neglect, alongside muscle strengthening and spasticity management with orthoses. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. For the MRTB-standard physiotherapist, correctly classifying the presentation directly shapes the choice of handling technique, equipment, and family education.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack and reduce postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, impairing effective neuromuscular transmission. This produces the fatigable muscle weakness characteristic of the disease. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.
questions.question: Myasthenia gravis primarily results from antibody-mediated destruction of which structure at the neuromuscular junction?

questions.explanation: Festinating gait, characterized by progressively rapid, small shuffling steps, is a hallmark feature of Parkinson's disease resulting from postural instability and impaired gait initiation, distinct from the wide-based, unsteady gait of cerebellar ataxia. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. Accurate cranial nerve localization is essential for guiding both further diagnostic workup and targeted physiotherapy management.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is comparing gait patterns and notes a patient with festinating, progressively rapid small steps that gradually increase in speed while decreasing in stride length. This gait pattern is most characteristic of:
A physiotherapist applies a quick stretch immediately before resisted movement during a PNF technique. What is the PRIMARY purpose?
options: To assess passive range of motion only
Quick stretch triggers contraction via stretch reflex
To eliminate the need for any further resistance
To completely fatigue the muscle before resistance
To passively lengthen the muscle permanently
questions.explanation: A quick stretch applied just before resisted movement activates the muscle spindle stretch reflex, eliciting a facilitatory effect that helps initiate or enhance the subsequent voluntary contraction, particularly useful in patients with weak or difficult-to-initiate muscle activity. This is a deliberate neurophysiological facilitation strategy rather than a method for permanent lengthening or fatigue induction. Understanding this mechanism supports its correct and purposeful clinical application.

NDT uses hands-on facilitated movements to promote guided movement as a form of treatment. It is characterized by tactile facilitation and guided movement that establishes stronger connections in the body's tactile, vestibular, and somatosensory receptors. This hands-on problem-solving approach allows precise facilitation and feedback throughout the therapeutic session.
questions.question: NDT is categorized as which type of therapeutic approach for children with neurological disorders?
A physiotherapist observes a Parkinson's disease patient suddenly stop mid-stride, unable to initiate the next step. This gait abnormality is termed:
questions.explanation: Freezing phenomenon describes the sudden inability to initiate or continue walking, common in Parkinson's disease due to impaired motor planning. Festinating gait, by contrast, refers to progressively rapid, shuffling small steps rather than a complete stop. Recognizing this feature is central to designing a safe, functionally focused Parkinson's disease rehabilitation program.

Mirror therapy is applicable in conditions such as phantom limb pain, stroke, or CRPS1 where neuropathic processes cause pain issues. The therapy exploits the brain's preference to prioritize visual feedback over somatosensory feedback, offering potential relief specifically from neuropathic pain. The visual override mechanism is most relevant when sensory mismatches contribute to the pain experience.
questions.question: A patient with CRPS1 is referred for mirror therapy. Which neurological condition must be present for mirror therapy to be applicable in CRPS1?

options: Exercise programs should never be modified regardless of cardiac status
All children with Down syndrome have normal cardiac function by definition
Congenital heart disease is common in Down syndrome and may affect exercise tolerance
Down syndrome has no association with cardiac abnormalities
Cardiac screening is irrelevant to physiotherapy exercise prescription
questions.explanation: Approximately one in three children with Down syndrome has an associated congenital heart defect, making cardiac screening and appropriate exercise intensity modification an important safety consideration before initiating a physiotherapy exercise program in this population. Recognizing this feature supports safe exercise prescription tailored to the specific needs of this population. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a child with Down syndrome for a congenital heart defect prior to initiating a moderate-intensity exercise program. Why is this screening particularly important in this population?
Which receptor is primarily responsible for preventing muscles and tendons from tearing under excessive tension by causing reflexive relaxation?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs continuously monitor muscle tension and, when excessive, trigger reflexive relaxation and lengthening of the muscle to protect against damaging overstretch, opposite in effect to the muscle spindle-mediated stretch reflex. Understanding this reflex pathway supports accurate neurological examination and localization of the level of dysfunction. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

During CIMT task practice, encouragement is given on an infrequent basis specifically every 5 minutes, with performance feedback provided at the end of the task. This contrasts with shaping, which requires constant therapist involvement throughout each set. Task practice involves repetitive practice of functional tasks for roughly 15 to 20 minutes with rest as required.
options: Only at the start of sessions
At the end of each task
questions.question: During CIMT task practice sessions, how frequently is encouragement provided to the patient?

questions.explanation: Toxic parkinsonism results from exposure to industrial chemicals such as manganese, carbon monoxide, or cyanide, representing an occupational hazard particularly for miners. Idiopathic parkinsonism, by contrast, has no identifiable external cause and is the most common form. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: Which secondary parkinsonism cause results from occupational exposure to industrial poisons such as manganese?

options: Isolated foot deformity with no cranial findings
Normal head circumference growth curve with no other findings
A rapidly increasing head circumference or bulging fontanel
questions.question: A physiotherapist is evaluating a newborn with a lumbar myelomeningocele. Which finding would most strongly suggest an associated need for hydrocephalus screening?
questions.explanation: Because hydrocephalus frequently coexists with neural tube defects such as myelomeningocele, monitoring head circumference and fontanel tension is essential; rapid head growth or fontanel bulging should prompt urgent screening for hydrocephalus. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.

options: A purely visual field deficit with no motor component
Complete absence of any cognitive involvement
Isolated peripheral nerve injury unrelated to the stroke
Motor planning deficits (apraxia) commonly associated with left hemisphere lesions
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with left CVA who has difficulty planning and sequencing a multi-step motor task despite adequate strength. Which associated impairment should the physiotherapist consider?
questions.explanation: Left CVA is classically associated with aphasia and motor planning deficits such as apraxia, in which patients struggle to sequence and execute purposeful motor tasks despite having adequate strength, distinct from right CVA which more commonly produces spatial neglect. This understanding is essential for safe, evidence-based clinical decision-making throughout the stroke rehabilitation pathway. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

Rhythmic stabilization uses isometric contraction of the agonist followed by isometric contraction of the antagonist to produce joint stability. Rhythmic initiation, by contrast, progresses through passive, active-assistive, and active movement to teach initiation of motion. Correct application of this principle underpins effective, evidence-based use of PNF techniques in neurological rehabilitation.
questions.question: Which PNF technique uses alternating isometric contractions of agonist followed by antagonist muscles to produce stability without movement through range?
A post-stroke patient undergoes body-weight supported treadmill training (BWSTT). At what body weight support percentage should training IDEALLY begin to enable functional stepping?
questions.explanation: BWSTT typically begins at 20-40% body weight support, providing enough assistance to enable rhythmic stepping while maintaining appropriate proprioceptive loading and lower limb muscle activation. Excessive unloading above 40% reduces proprioceptive input and hampers recruitment of key stance and swing phase muscles. Support is progressively reduced as gait quality and endurance improve, with training speed typically at 2-3 mph.

ALS progression typically spreads in a contiguous manner within spinal cord segments or regions such as bulbar, cervical, thoracic, or lumbosacral, before extending to other regions, an important point for patient education and goal-setting. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. This knowledge guides the physiotherapist's prioritization of restorative versus compensatory strategies across the disease course.
options: Symptoms are expected to fully reverse within six months
Symptoms typically spread locally within a body region before moving to other regions
Symptoms appear simultaneously and equally throughout the entire body from onset
Symptoms remain confined only to one single muscle indefinitely
Symptoms always begin with respiratory failure first
questions.question: A patient recently diagnosed with ALS asks the physiotherapist about the expected disease course. Based on known pathophysiology, how should the physiotherapist explain symptom progression?

options: Isolated upper limb strengthening with no pelvic floor component
Complete avoidance of any physiotherapy involvement in bladder issues
Aerobic exercise alone with no targeted intervention
Immediate surgical referral as the only management option
Pelvic floor muscle strengthening and bladder training education
questions.question: A physiotherapist is managing a patient with confirmed multiple sclerosis who has new bladder urgency and incontinence. Which physiotherapy intervention is most directly indicated?
questions.explanation: Bladder dysfunction in MS is addressed through targeted pelvic floor muscle strengthening and bladder training education, which physiotherapists can provide as part of a symptom-specific management approach alongside the broader neurological rehabilitation program. Recognizing this feature helps the physiotherapist balance symptom management with safe, sustainable exercise prescription. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

options: Only once surgery has been ruled out entirely
Only after complete spontaneous recovery occurs
Never, since it has no clinical benefit
Delayed until at least one year has passed
As soon as possible, inhibiting substitution patterns
questions.question: A physiotherapist explains the optimal timing for functional electrical stimulation after nerve injury with expected reinnervation. What should be stated?
questions.explanation: Functional electrical stimulation is generally most beneficial when initiated early after nerve injury, as it can help maintain muscle bulk and inhibit the development of unwanted substitution movement patterns that might otherwise become habitual while awaiting reinnervation. Waiting for complete spontaneous recovery or delaying for a year would forfeit this early window of benefit. Early, appropriately timed intervention supports better long-term functional outcomes.

Anencephaly results from failure of the neural tube to close at its cranial (top) end during the third week of gestation, leading to absence of major portions of the brain and skull. Spina bifida, the other common neural tube defect, instead involves incomplete closure of the spinal column. Timely recognition of this pattern is critical, since delayed identification can allow preventable neurological deterioration.
questions.question: Anencephaly, one of the two most common neural tube defects, results from failure of the neural tube to close at which anatomical level?
options: The top (cranial end) of the neural tube

questions.question: A child with thoracic-level myelomeningocele at T8 is being fitted for orthoses. Which orthotic device is MOST appropriate for household ambulation at this level?
questions.explanation: T8-level myelomeningocele results in complete loss of lower limb motor function and sensation below the level, requiring hip-knee-ankle-foot orthoses (HKAFO) and a walker for household ambulation to stabilize all lower limb joints during upright movement. High-thoracic-level lesions demand this level of support, and a reciprocating gait orthosis is an alternative for some patients. Most T8 patients eventually prefer wheelchair mobility for community distances due to the very high energy cost of HKAFO ambulation.

questions.question: A neonate presents with tight muscle tone in both legs that is more pronounced than in the arms, with scissoring on vertical suspension. This pattern is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Spastic diplegia primarily affects the lower limbs more than the upper limbs, often producing a scissoring gait pattern from adductor spasticity. This contrasts with hemiplegia, which is unilateral, and ataxic CP, which involves incoordination rather than spasticity. For the MRTB-standard physiotherapist, correctly classifying the presentation directly shapes the choice of handling technique, equipment, and family education.

Oculomotor nerve palsy causes ptosis from levator palpebrae superioris weakness, mydriasis from loss of parasympathetic pupillary constriction, and a down-and-out eye position from unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique action. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A patient presents with ptosis, a dilated pupil, and the affected eye positioned 'down and out'. This clinical picture localizes to which cranial nerve?
During the middle recovery (spastic) stage of stroke rehabilitation, which physiotherapy goal takes priority?
options: Discharging the patient from further balance training
Minimizing spasticity while promoting functional use of the hemiplegic side
Avoiding all weight-bearing activities on the affected side
Initiating passive positioning only, with no active participation
questions.explanation: The spastic stage of stroke recovery focuses on reducing spasticity while encouraging functional use of the hemiplegic side, improving postural control, and progressing bed mobility and transfers. This differs from the early flaccid stage, which emphasizes positioning and tone-abnormality prevention. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.

options: Gentle positioning and prevention of joint stiffness
questions.question: Which physiotherapy precaution is emphasized during the acute relapse phase of multiple sclerosis rather than the stable remission phase?
questions.explanation: During acute MS relapses, physiotherapy emphasizes gentle positioning, prevention of joint stiffness, maintaining circulation, and assisting with bed mobility, reserving strengthening, aerobic conditioning, and balance training for the stable remission phase. Recognizing this feature helps the physiotherapist balance symptom management with safe, sustainable exercise prescription. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

EMG biofeedback provides real-time visual or auditory feedback of muscle electrical activity, helping patients consciously enhance voluntary muscle activation and supporting motor relearning as part of the neurophysiological approach to stroke rehabilitation. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. Recognizing this feature helps the physiotherapist tailor the stage-appropriate rehabilitation protocol and set realistic functional goals.
options: Delivering a therapeutic electrical shock to induce muscle fatigue
Measuring blood pressure response to exercise
Replacing the need for any active patient participation
Providing visual or auditory feedback of muscle activity to enhance motor relearning
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a stroke patient using electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback as part of the neurophysiological rehabilitation approach. What is the primary purpose of this modality?

questions.explanation: In advanced ALS with FVC at 35% and loss of ambulation, physiotherapy shifts entirely to palliative and comfort-focused care including optimal positioning for comfort and symptom relief, secretion management using mechanical insufflation-exsufflation, caregiver training in safe handling, wheelchair seating optimization, and communication aid support. Intensive rehabilitation exercises increase energy consumption and respiratory demand in a critically limited system and are therefore inappropriate and potentially harmful at this advanced stage.
questions.question: A patient with advanced ALS can no longer ambulate and has a FVC of 35%. The patient wishes to remain at home. What should be the MOST appropriate physiotherapy focus?

questions.explanation: The olfactory bulb, located above the ethmoid bone below the frontal lobe, acts as the relay station transmitting impulses from the olfactory nerve to the olfactory tract and then to the cerebral cortex. The optic chiasm instead relates to visual pathway crossing. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.
questions.question: Which structure serves as the relay center transmitting olfactory impulses from the nasal epithelium to the olfactory cortex?
A physiotherapist uses mirror therapy in stroke rehabilitation primarily to achieve which therapeutic effect?
options: Providing visual stimulation of the affected limb to enhance recovery
Delivering electrical stimulation to spastic muscles
questions.explanation: Mirror therapy uses a mirror to reflect the unaffected limb, creating the visual illusion of normal affected-limb movement, which enhances recovery and is also used in phantom limb pain management. This differs mechanistically from constraint-induced therapy, which restrains the unaffected limb. This understanding is essential for safe, evidence-based clinical decision-making throughout the stroke rehabilitation pathway.

options: Mixed cerebral palsy with combined spastic and dyskinetic features
questions.explanation: When a child exhibits features of more than one CP subtype, such as spastic legs alongside dyskinetic facial muscle control, this is classified as mixed cerebral palsy, requiring an individualized treatment approach addressing both tone patterns. For the MRTB-standard physiotherapist, correctly classifying the presentation directly shapes the choice of handling technique, equipment, and family education. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a child with mixed cerebral palsy who has both spastic legs and dyskinetic facial muscle control. Which classification term best describes this presentation?
What specific constraint device is NOT listed as a standard restraint option in CIMT protocols?
questions.explanation: Common restraints for CIMT include slings, plaster casts, triangular bandages, splints, slings combined with resting hand splints, half gloves, and mitts. Elastic bandage wraps are not specifically listed as standard CIMT restraint options. The chosen restraint must effectively limit use of the unaffected limb while ensuring patient safety during the constraint period.

The edrophonium or Tensilon test involves administering a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, which transiently increases acetylcholine availability and produces rapid, brief improvement in muscle strength in myasthenia gravis patients. This understanding is essential for structuring exercise dosage and activity pacing around the disease's fatigable nature. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: Which diagnostic test for myasthenia gravis involves administering a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor to observe rapid but transient improvement in muscle strength?

questions.explanation: When coordination testing accuracy is worse with eyes closed than eyes open, this suggests a proprioceptive (sensory) deficit that the patient was compensating for using vision, rather than a pure cerebellar lesion, in which impairment typically persists regardless of visual input. Accurate cranial nerve localization is essential for guiding both further diagnostic workup and targeted physiotherapy management. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.
options: A proprioceptive deficit being compensated for by vision
Complete loss of all sensory modalities
A pure motor weakness with no sensory component
A pure cerebellar lesion unaffected by visual input
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient's coordination using the finger-to-nose test and observes normal accuracy with eyes open but increased inaccuracy with eyes closed. What does this specifically suggest?

questions.explanation: Research in individuals with cerebral palsy found inappropriate sequencing of muscle activity and poor anticipatory regulation during postural control, with stability frequently interrupted by destabilizing synergistic or antagonistic muscle activity, informing targeted balance intervention. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. Accurate identification of the subtype and severity guides appropriate goal-setting and selection of the most suitable therapeutic approach.
options: Inappropriate sequencing of muscle activity during postural control
Complete absence of any muscle activation
questions.question: Which cerebral palsy balance research finding, described by Nashir and colleagues, highlights poor anticipatory regulation of muscle activity during postural control?

questions.explanation: Extradural (epidural) haematoma classically results from bleeding of the middle meningeal vessels, often following a temporal bone fracture, distinguishing it from subdural haematoma, which typically results from rupture of superficial bridging veins. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a TBI patient with extradural haematoma who underwent emergency surgical evacuation. Which vessel source is most classically associated with this type of haematoma?

questions.explanation: A wet or gurgly voice quality immediately after swallowing is the strongest bedside indicator of laryngeal penetration or aspiration, reflecting pooling of material above or below the vocal cords. This sign has the highest sensitivity among bedside swallowing assessment items and mandates referral for videofluoroscopic or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing. Silent aspiration occurs in up to 40% of stroke patients with dysphagia, further underscoring the importance of formal instrumental assessment.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assesses swallowing in a stroke patient before commencing oral feeding. Which bedside clinical observation is the STRONGEST indicator of aspiration risk?
options: Wet or gurgly voice quality after swallowing
Slow eating speed and mild drooling
Reluctance to eat and reduced appetite
Coughing only at the end of a meal
Reduced oral manipulation of food bolus

questions.question: Which structure found in the neuromuscular junction, when its receptors are damaged by autoimmune attack, produces the characteristic muscle weakness of myasthenia gravis?
questions.explanation: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic muscle membrane are the primary target of autoimmune attack in myasthenia gravis. Their destruction impairs effective binding of acetylcholine, weakening neuromuscular transmission and producing fatigable muscle weakness. This understanding is essential for structuring exercise dosage and activity pacing around the disease's fatigable nature.
options: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
Myelin sheath of the motor axon

questions.explanation: Micrographia and hypophonia reflect the underlying bradykinesia and reduced movement amplitude characteristic of Parkinson's disease; amplitude-focused training approaches emphasizing larger, higher-effort movements across functional tasks can help counter this global movement pattern. This understanding directly informs the physiotherapist's choice of assessment tools and stage-appropriate exercise strategies. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.
options: Only addressing gait, excluding all other motor symptoms
Addressing bradykinesia through amplitude-focused, high-effort movement strategies across tasks
Reducing all movement practice to avoid overexertion
Ignoring these symptoms as unrelated to physiotherapy scope
Assuming these symptoms indicate a different diagnosis entirely
questions.question: A physiotherapist is working with a Parkinson's disease patient whose handwriting has become progressively smaller (micrographia) and speech has become quieter. Which broader physiotherapy consideration should guide the overall treatment approach?

questions.explanation: PNF techniques are particularly suited to the late recovery stage, where tone has largely normalized but timing and coordination deficits remain the primary functional limitation, unlike tone-reduction techniques reserved for the earlier spastic stage. Accurate identification of the subtype and severity guides appropriate goal-setting and selection of the most suitable therapeutic approach. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A patient in the late recovery stage of stroke rehabilitation has regained most movement but struggles with timing and coordination during reaching tasks. Which technique would the physiotherapist most appropriately incorporate?
options: Complete bed rest to prevent overexertion
Avoidance of all functional task practice
Prolonged ice application for tone reduction
Blocked practice for early skill acquisition
Challenge point hypothesis for optimal learning
questions.explanation: Placing the target just beyond the patient's current maximum reach applies the challenge point hypothesis, which posits that optimal motor learning occurs when task difficulty is calibrated to the individual's current skill level, producing meaningful errors without overwhelming capacity. Appropriate challenge generates error-correction learning, drives neuroplastic adaptation, and promotes skill acquisition and retention better than tasks that are either too easy or too difficult. This principle underpins progressive task difficulty design in neurological rehabilitation programs.
questions.question: A physiotherapist targets a reaching task just beyond the patient's current maximum reach during task-oriented training of the paretic arm post-stroke. Which motor learning principle does this SPECIFICALLY apply?

A physiotherapist is treating a patient with suspected uncal herniation showing acute loss of consciousness, ipsilateral pupillary dilation, and contralateral hemiparesis. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: The combination of acute loss of consciousness, ipsilateral pupillary dilation, and contralateral hemiparesis are cardinal signs of uncal herniation, a life-threatening neurosurgical emergency requiring immediate medical escalation rather than continued routine physiotherapy assessment. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. This understanding is essential for safe, evidence-based clinical decision-making throughout the stroke rehabilitation pathway.
options: Recognize this as a neurological emergency and ensure immediate medical/neurosurgical referral
Continue routine physiotherapy assessment as scheduled
Apply passive stretching to the hemiparetic limb first
Delay any escalation of care until the next working day
Attribute the findings to normal fatigue and proceed with exercise

questions.question: A 58-year-old male with confirmed stroke presents to the physiotherapy unit 6 weeks post-ictus. Which finding at 1 week post-stroke BEST predicts eventual functional hand recovery?
questions.explanation: At least 10 degrees of active finger and thumb extension within the first week post-stroke is the strongest predictor of functional hand recovery, indicating sufficient cortical connectivity for voluntary motor output. Absence of this sign early on predicts poor upper extremity functional outcomes and guides rehabilitation goal-setting. Sensation, motivation, and absence of subluxation are important but are not as strongly predictive as early voluntary motor return.

Stage III of the Hoehn-Yahr scale is characterized by impaired righting reflexes and unsteadiness with turning or rising, though the patient can still live independently and maintain some employment. Stage IV instead requires assistance for standing and walking. This understanding directly informs the physiotherapist's choice of assessment tools and stage-appropriate exercise strategies.
questions.question: According to the Hoehn-Yahr scale, a Parkinson's patient with impaired righting reflexes and unsteadiness when turning, who can still live independently, is at which stage?

options: Heat impairs conduction along demyelinated axons
This represents a true disease relapse each time
This reflects an unrelated cardiac condition
This indicates permanent new axonal damage
This always indicates a urinary tract infection
questions.explanation: Uhthoff's phenomenon describes the temporary worsening of multiple sclerosis symptoms with increased body temperature, such as from heat exposure or exercise, due to impaired conduction along partially demyelinated axons rather than new structural damage or true relapse. This transient worsening reverses once body temperature normalizes. Educating patients about this phenomenon helps differentiate it from genuine disease progression or relapse.
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis reports symptoms consistently worsen after a hot shower or strenuous exercise. What is the underlying mechanism?

options: 10 degrees wrist and 10 degrees finger extension
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) to a stroke patient with Fugl-Meyer upper extremity score of 28/66. What minimum voluntary movement criterion must the patient meet for CIMT eligibility?
questions.explanation: Standard CIMT eligibility requires a minimum of 10 degrees of active wrist extension and 10 degrees of active finger or thumb extension in the affected hand, ensuring sufficient residual voluntary motor function for meaningful task-specific practice during constrained hours. This threshold guarantees that motor learning through task practice can occur. Modified CIMT protocols with shorter constraint periods apply to patients with less voluntary movement who do not meet this criterion.

Retropulsion in PSP results from abnormal postural set favoring backward center of mass displacement due to axial rigidity and impaired righting reflexes. Forward weight-shifting cues (tactile cues at the pelvis directing weight anteriorly, visual floor targets placed forward) counteract the backward lean and retropulsion tendency. Anti-gravity cueing combined with wide-base stable gait practice, high-back wheelchairs with tipping prevention devices, and safe fall environments are essential PSP physiotherapy management components.
questions.question: A patient with progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) has repeated falls backward. Which cueing strategy is MOST appropriate given the pathophysiology of retropulsion in PSP?
options: Apply forward weight-shifting cues and visual floor targets
Instruct patient to lean backward while walking
Use backward walking training as a primary strategy
Increase walking speed to overcome retropulsion
Train patient in backward fall techniques only
Manual contact placement has no effect on motor output
Stability training should avoid all manual contact
Resistance should always be applied at the farthest point
Distal resistance always improves proximal stability
Proximal stabilization supports controlled distal movement
questions.explanation: Applying manual contacts and resistance proximally can help facilitate postural stability at the trunk and proximal joints, providing a stable base from which more controlled distal movement can occur, which is particularly useful in patients with poor proximal control such as in ataxia. This contrasts with an assumption that distal resistance alone would improve proximal stability, which does not reflect the proximal-to-distal control principle. Thoughtful placement of manual contacts is therefore an important clinical skill in facilitation techniques.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies manual contacts proximally on a limb to encourage stability in a patient with ataxia. What technique principle is MOST relevant?

options: Begin an aggressive strengthening program immediately
Recommend delaying any medical evaluation for six months
Refer urgently for medical/neurosurgical evaluation for suspected hydrocephalus
Reassure the family that this is a normal developmental variant
questions.explanation: These findings are classic signs of hydrocephalus in an infant and require urgent medical and neurosurgical evaluation, since untreated hydrocephalus can rapidly progress to significant brain damage. Physiotherapy has a role only after appropriate medical management, such as shunt placement, has been established. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: An infant is brought in with a rapidly increasing head circumference, bulging fontanel, and downward eye deviation. The physiotherapist's most appropriate immediate action is to:
A physiotherapist is implementing goal attainment scaling (GAS) for a patient with severe TBI. What is the PRIMARY advantage of GAS over standardized outcome measures in this context?
options: Requires no collaboration with the patient
Individualizes outcome measurement to patient goals
questions.explanation: Goal Attainment Scaling (GAS) individualizes outcome measurement by setting patient-specific goals with expected, better-than-expected, and worse-than-expected levels, allowing meaningful measurement of progress toward individualized rehabilitation targets not captured by standardized measures. It is particularly valuable in TBI where heterogeneous deficits mean that standardized measures may not reflect the patient's most clinically important changes. GAS also promotes patient-centered goal-setting and shared decision-making in rehabilitation.

questions.question: Which TBI rehabilitation technology enhances recovery outcomes primarily by enabling greater repetition of stepping movements to promote neuroplasticity?
questions.explanation: Robot-assisted gait training enables a higher number of repetitive stepping movements than conventional therapy, which enhances neuroplastic change and recovery outcomes. This differs from static splinting, which primarily prevents contracture rather than promoting active neural reorganization. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.

Vomiting, lethargy, and irritability in a shunted child can indicate shunt malfunction and rising intracranial pressure, a medical emergency requiring the session to stop and urgent referral for reassessment rather than continuing therapy. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A child with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for hydrocephalus is referred for physiotherapy. During a session, the child develops vomiting, lethargy, and irritability. What should the physiotherapist do?
options: Stop the session and refer urgently for medical assessment of possible shunt malfunction
Apply deep massage to the abdomen where the shunt tubing lies
Increase exercise intensity to improve alertness
Continue the session as planned since these symptoms are expected
Discharge the child from the physiotherapy program permanently

questions.explanation: The hypothesis was that every time the patient attempted to move the paralyzed phantom limb, they received sensory feedback through vision and proprioception that the limb did not move. This repeated negative feedback created learned paralysis in the phantom limb. Mirror therapy aimed to resolve this by providing visual feedback of movement from the intact limb's reflection.
questions.question: What hypothesis explained the development of learned paralysis in patients with phantom limb pain prior to mirror therapy?
options: Motor cortex inhibition from pain signals

questions.question: A physiotherapist examines a patient with progressive weakness, fasciculations, and hyperreflexia together in the same limb. Which condition is MOST consistent?
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis characteristically presents with a combination of lower motor neuron signs, such as fasciculations and wasting, occurring together with upper motor neuron signs, such as hyperreflexia and spasticity, within the same anatomical region. A pure upper or lower motor neuron lesion alone would not explain this mixed presentation. Recognizing this combined pattern is central to clinically suspecting motor neuron disease.
options: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with mixed neuron involvement
An isolated lower motor neuron lesion
An isolated upper motor neuron lesion
Checking pupillary response to light exclusively
Observing symmetrical soft palate elevation while the child says 'ah'
Asking the child to smell coffee and vanilla
Testing gag reflex first, before any other cranial nerve test
questions.explanation: CN IX and X are conventionally assessed together by observing symmetrical, midline elevation of the soft palate as the patient says 'ah'. The gag reflex is reserved only for cases of suspected bulbar impairment due to patient discomfort, not as a first-line test. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is examining an infant for cranial nerve integrity and wants to test the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves together. Which assessment technique should be used?

questions.explanation: Sparing of forehead movement with lower facial weakness reflects an upper motor neuron lesion, since the forehead muscles receive bilateral cortical innervation that provides some preserved function even when one corticobulbar pathway, such as from a stroke, is damaged, unlike the lower face which receives predominantly contralateral innervation. This pattern differs from a peripheral facial nerve lesion like Bell's palsy, which affects the entire side of the face equally because the lesion occurs after this innervation has already diverged. Recognizing this distinction is essential for accurately localizing facial weakness to central versus peripheral causes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist finds facial weakness that spares forehead wrinkling but affects the lower face on one side. What does this localization suggest?
options: A neuromuscular junction disorder such as myasthenia
A lower motor neuron lesion such as Bell's palsy
A primary muscular dystrophy affecting facial muscles
An upper motor neuron lesion such as stroke
A peripheral neuropathy affecting multiple nerves
Spinal orthosis fitting and wearing only
questions.explanation: FES-assisted trunk muscle activation directly addresses the underlying biomechanical cause of post-SCI scoliosis by electrically activating paralyzed trunk stabilizer muscles below the injury level, restoring active symmetric trunk muscle balance and reducing asymmetric spinal loading. Passive orthoses provide external support but do not address the underlying muscle imbalance causing scoliosis progression. FES-induced active muscle loading generates the mechanical forces needed to influence spinal alignment and slow progressive curve development.
questions.question: A patient with chronic incomplete thoracic SCI is developing progressive scoliosis from asymmetrical trunk muscle weakness. Which physiotherapy intervention is MOST specific for addressing the underlying biomechanical cause?

options: Begin only when the child can cooperate
Start as soon as diagnosis is confirmed
questions.explanation: Early physiotherapy intervention should begin as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed or strongly suspected, capitalizing on maximum neuroplastic potential during the first years of life when the brain's capacity for reorganization is greatest. Early intervention also prevents secondary musculoskeletal complications including contractures, hip displacement, and scoliosis. Family-centered early intervention programs demonstrating superior outcomes in CP management further support immediate initiation upon diagnosis.
questions.question: The parents of a 3-year-old child with newly diagnosed spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy ask when physiotherapy should begin. Which statement BEST reflects current evidence?

questions.explanation: Shaping is the predominant behavioral technique in CIMT, where motor tasks are gradually made more difficult as the patient progresses through successive sets of trials. CIMT has been defined as a behavioral approach to neurorehabilitation using simple behavioral techniques. This systematic progression maintains achievable challenges while driving continuous motor improvement.
questions.question: Which behavioral technique is identified as the predominant method within CIMT for progressively challenging motor tasks?
A physiotherapist selects diagonal movement patterns rather than single-plane exercises during PNF treatment. What is the PRIMARY rationale?
options: Single-plane movements provide superior functional carryover
Diagonal patterns are always easier to perform
Diagonal patterns eliminate the need for resistance
Diagonal patterns crossing the midline mimic function
Single-plane exercises better replicate natural movement
questions.explanation: PNF diagonal patterns intentionally incorporate spiral and diagonal components that cross the body's midline, more closely replicating the multi-planar nature of normal functional movement compared to isolated single-plane exercises. This functional relevance is the key rationale for their use rather than any inherent simplicity or reduced resistance requirement. Selecting movement patterns that mirror real-world function supports more effective transfer to daily activities.

questions.question: Progressive degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons in the brain, brainstem, and spinal cord, producing a mix of spasticity and muscle wasting, describes:
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis involves progressive loss of both upper motor neurons in the cortex and corticospinal tracts and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord, producing a combination of spasticity, hyperreflexia, muscle wasting, and fasciculations. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning. Accurate identification of the subtype and severity guides appropriate goal-setting and selection of the most suitable therapeutic approach.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is managing a patient with early Parkinson's disease who reports difficulty initiating movement from a seated position. Which specific strategy would most directly help this functional limitation?
options: Using rhythmic movement cues and rocking to initiate the sit-to-stand transition
Recommending permanent use of a hoist for all transfers
Instructing the patient to remain seated indefinitely
questions.explanation: Rhythmic cueing and rocking movements can help overcome the akinesia and difficulty with movement initiation seen in Parkinson's disease, facilitating a more successful sit-to-stand transition as part of functional mobility training. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. This understanding directly informs the physiotherapist's choice of assessment tools and stage-appropriate exercise strategies.

questions.question: Which percentage range of adult hereditary ALS cases results from mutations in the SOD1 gene?
questions.explanation: Of hereditary adult ALS cases, approximately 20 percent result from one of more than 100 mutations in the SOD1 gene, which encodes copper-zinc superoxide dismutase. Most adult ALS cases, however, are sporadic without a family history. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.

A TUG score of 20 seconds in a patient with Parkinson's disease indicates high fall risk; scores above 13.5 seconds are associated with increased falls in PD populations and above 15 seconds in general elderly populations. This finding mandates a comprehensive fall prevention program including balance and gait training, cueing strategies, home hazard assessment, and medication review. Serial TUG testing also serves as an objective measure of response to physiotherapy intervention over time.
questions.question: A physiotherapist treats a 72-year-old with Parkinson's disease and a falls history. The Timed Up and Go test takes 20 seconds. What is the CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE of this result?
options: Normal for age; no intervention indicated
High fall risk; targeted intervention required
Moderate risk; only stair rails required
Familiar tasks require less cortical effort
Personal tasks have fewer error patterns
questions.question: Which learning principle from task-specific training best explains why rehabilitation activities should be personally meaningful to the patient?
questions.explanation: Tasks should be relevant to the individual's needs and goals because meaningful activities make patients more likely to be motivated and fully engage in the training. The training involves goal-directed practice of specific activities that are personally meaningful to the person. This engagement and motivation is critical for achieving the high repetition volumes required for neuroplastic change.

questions.question: A physiotherapist notes a patient with suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome shows ascending, symmetric weakness with hyporeflexia. Which key feature would help distinguish this from acute stroke presentation?
options: Identical reflex findings in both conditions
Sudden onset unilateral facial droop identical to stroke
Complete absence of any weakness in both conditions
Cognitive impairment identical to stroke presentation
Symmetric, ascending, bilateral weakness rather than sudden unilateral hemiparesis
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barre syndrome typically presents with symmetric, ascending weakness and hyporeflexia affecting both sides of the body progressively, in clear contrast to the sudden, typically unilateral hemiparesis characteristic of acute stroke. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. Recognizing this feature helps the physiotherapist tailor the stage-appropriate rehabilitation protocol and set realistic functional goals.

Nerve root lesions produce symptoms following a dermatomal distribution because the spinal nerve supplies a specific segmental area of skin and a myotomal group of muscles. A peripheral nerve lesion instead follows the specific territory of that single nerve, which usually does not match a dermatome. Recognizing this distribution pattern is key to distinguishing radicular from peripheral nerve pathology on clinical examination.
options: Pain limited strictly to the joint line
Weakness confined to one muscle belly only
Weakness in a single peripheral nerve territory
Pain or sensory change in a dermatomal pattern
questions.question: A patient presents with weakness, sensory loss, and pain following nerve root compression. Which finding suggests this rather than a peripheral nerve lesion?

A patient overshoots when reaching for a target and demonstrates loss of rhythm during rapid alternating movements. These findings, termed dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia respectively, indicate dysfunction of which system?
questions.explanation: Dysmetria (overshooting a target) and dysdiadochokinesia (loss of speed and rhythm during rapid alternating movements) are hallmark features of cerebellar ataxia, reflecting disturbed rate, regularity, and force of movement coordination. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. This clinical reasoning helps the physiotherapist correctly localize the lesion during a systematic cranial nerve examination.

questions.question: Which structure does the accessory nerve pass through to enter the cranial cavity from its spinal root origin at C1 to C5/C6?
questions.explanation: The spinal root of the accessory nerve originates from the upper cervical spinal cord segments and ascends into the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum before exiting again, along with the cranial root, via the jugular foramen. This clinical reasoning helps the physiotherapist correctly localize the lesion during a systematic cranial nerve examination. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.

Postural control and balance disturbances, including asymmetrical weight bearing and increased sway, are primary motor impairments directly resulting from the cerebrovascular lesion. Secondary complications such as contractures instead develop later from prolonged abnormal positioning. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.
options: A primary motor impairment affecting postural control and balance
A secondary complication unrelated to the stroke
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices asymmetrical body weight distribution and increased postural sway in a hemiplegic patient during standing. This is best categorized as which type of impairment?
During gait analysis of a hemiplegic patient, the physiotherapist observes circumduction of the lower limb during swing phase. The PRIMARY impairment being compensated for is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Circumduction during swing phase is a compensatory gait strategy used to achieve toe clearance when ankle dorsiflexors are weak or paralyzed, resulting in foot drop. The patient abducts the hip in a semicircular arc to swing the limb through without toe drag. This abnormal energy-costly pattern significantly increases the metabolic cost of walking in hemiplegia and is the primary indication for ankle-foot orthosis prescription.

questions.question: Which balance and mobility assessment tool used in stroke rehabilitation times how long a patient takes to rise from a chair, walk a short distance, turn, and sit back down?
questions.explanation: The Timed Up and Go test measures the time taken for a patient to rise from a chair, walk a set distance, turn, return, and sit down again, providing a quick functional mobility and fall-risk assessment distinct from the static Functional Reach Test. This understanding is essential for safe, evidence-based clinical decision-making throughout the stroke rehabilitation pathway. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice.

During a typical NDT session, children are given neurodevelopmental therapy exercises to perform for approximately 5 to 10 minutes. The therapist or caregiver helps guide the child through movements in each session and records progress at regular intervals. These techniques are typically practiced daily unless otherwise instructed by the treating therapist.
questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy receives NDT sessions. How long does a typical NDT exercise session last?
A physiotherapist assesses a post-stroke patient using the Modified Ashworth Scale and scores elbow flexors at grade 3. Which clinical finding JUSTIFIES this specific score?
questions.explanation: Modified Ashworth Scale grade 3 indicates a marked increase in muscle tone making passive movement difficult throughout most of the range of motion. Grade 1 is a slight increase catching at end range, grade 1+ catches in the middle third, grade 2 is a moderate increase through most of range, and grade 4 is complete rigidity. Correct grading directly informs appropriate spasticity management decisions including botulinum toxin dosing thresholds.
options: Slight increase in tone catching at end range
Moderate tone increase through full range
Marked increase; passive movement is difficult
Affected part is rigid in full flexion
Normal tone with no increase detected

questions.explanation: A mirror size of 25 by 20 inches for the upper limb is recommended as large enough for everyday therapeutic usage. The dimension should be sufficient to cover the entire affected limb and allow patients to see all major movements. Mirrors can be made from different materials including glass, foil, or acrylic glass, allowing flexible implementation across clinical settings.
questions.question: What minimum recommended mirror size is appropriate for upper limb mirror therapy?

options: C6 and C7 nerve roots via the radial nerve
S1 and S2 nerve roots via the tibial nerve
L4 and L5 nerve roots via the femoral nerve
T1 nerve root via the ulnar nerve
C5 and C6 nerve roots via the musculocutaneous nerve
questions.question: A physiotherapist assesses a patient's finger abduction strength by asking them to fan out their fingers against resistance, noting significant weakness on one side. Which nerve root and peripheral nerve does this primarily test?
questions.explanation: Finger abduction (fanning of the fingers) is mediated by the T1 nerve root via the ulnar nerve. This differs from elbow flexion (biceps, C5-C6 via musculocutaneous nerve) and elbow extension (triceps, C6-C7 via radial nerve). Mastery of this clinical test is fundamental to accurate neurological assessment at the MRTB standard.

Iniencephaly results from improper neural tube closure causing extreme retroflexion of the head, absence of the neck, and direct connection of facial skin to chest skin due to severe spinal deformity. This differs from encephalocele, which features a sac-like protrusion of brain tissue through the skull. This knowledge underpins safe, well-coordinated physiotherapy care alongside the neurosurgical and paediatric medical team.
questions.question: A newborn presents with severe backward bending of the head, an absent neck, and skin of the face directly connected to the chest. This rare defect is termed:
