questions.explanation: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis is defined by continuous, gradual worsening of neurological function from disease onset, without the discrete attacks and remissions characteristic of relapsing-remitting disease. This course is less common and tends to affect a different demographic and respond differently to treatment than relapsing forms. Correct classification of disease course directly affects treatment selection and rehabilitation expectations.
options: Primary progressive MS with no remissions

questions.question: At what developmental age do children typically begin cooperative play with rules and structured games with peers?
questions.explanation: Cooperative play with rules occurs at approximately 5 years, normally coinciding with when children start school. The child plays structured games with other children, taking turns and using rules. Rules for games become very important at this developmental stage and mark a significant transition in social play capacity.

options: Strengthening the weakened dorsiflexor muscles directly
Replacing the need for any further physiotherapy assessment
Eliminating the need for any future mobility aids
Preventing the toes from dragging during the swing phase of gait
Completely curing the underlying motor neuron degeneration
questions.question: A physiotherapist is fitting an ankle-foot orthosis for an ALS patient with foot drop. What is the primary functional benefit of this intervention?
questions.explanation: An ankle-foot orthosis stabilizes the ankle and prevents the toes from dragging during the swing phase of gait in patients with foot drop from dorsiflexor weakness, improving safety and efficiency of ambulation, though it does not reverse the underlying neurodegeneration. Understanding this feature supports realistic goal-setting and timely introduction of adaptive equipment in ALS care. This understanding supports accurate clinical reasoning and appropriate physiotherapy management planning.

This presentation is classic autonomic dysreflexia (AD), a medical emergency in SCI above T6, characterized by severe hypertension, pounding headache, profuse sweating, and flushing above the lesion triggered by a noxious stimulus below. Immediate management is sitting the patient upright to induce orthostatic blood pressure reduction, then systematically finding and removing the triggering noxious stimulus (most commonly a distended bladder). Failure to act immediately risks hypertensive crisis, stroke, and death.
questions.question: A patient with T10 complete SCI reports sudden onset severe headache, profuse sweating above T10, facial flushing, and bradycardia. What is the IMMEDIATE physiotherapy management?
options: Apply ice pack to forehead; contact physician
Sit patient upright; find and remove noxious stimulus
Lay patient supine; monitor blood pressure

questions.question: A stroke patient scores 18/66 on the Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity assessment at 4 weeks post-stroke. What motor recovery stage does this score indicate?
options: Full voluntary movement in all planes
questions.explanation: A Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity score of 18/66 falls within the range indicating movement predominantly occurring within obligatory synergy patterns (corresponding to Brunnstrom Stages 2-3), with limited ability to perform isolated joint movements outside the mass flexion or extension synergies. Scores of 0-20 typically indicate severe impairment dominated by synergistic movement. Treatment should focus on synergy-breaking task-specific activities and positioning to facilitate emergence of isolated joint control.

questions.question: A physiotherapist selects materials for sensory stimulation during a mirror therapy session. Which material is NOT recommended in mirror therapy sensory input protocols?
questions.explanation: Recommended materials for sensory input during mirror therapy include plastic bowls filled with sand or peas, hedgehog balls, temperature stimuli, different brushes, washing up gloves, and sandpaper. Petroleum-based products are not mentioned as recommended materials and are excluded from the protocol. These sensory materials are especially useful for patients with impairments in body perception.

Aids for daily living encompass devices such as adapted utensils, grab bars, and nonslip surfaces that enhance performance of activities of daily living including eating, dressing, and hygiene, distinct from mobility technology which addresses transportation needs. Recognizing this distinction is important for safe, evidence-based neurological physiotherapy practice. Recognizing this feature supports timely escalation of care and appropriate interdisciplinary collaboration in TBI management.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating the family of a TBI patient about assistive technology categories. The family asks about devices that help with eating, dressing, and hygiene. Which category should the physiotherapist describe?

questions.explanation: Syringomyelia produces a suspended dissociated sensory loss characterized by impaired pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution across the upper limbs and chest, corresponding to crossing spinothalamic fibers disrupted by the expanding syrinx, while vibration and proprioception are preserved as dorsal columns remain intact. This pattern is pathognomonic and necessitates burn and pressure injury prevention education, adapted thermal assessments, and careful handling during physiotherapy sessions.
options: Suspended dissociated sensory loss in cape distribution
All sensory modalities lost below the lesion
Pain and temperature loss confined to one dermatome
Pain and temperature loss in both legs only
questions.question: A patient with syringomyelia presents with the clinical triad. Which pattern of sensory loss MOST specifically reflects syrinx involvement and guides safe physiotherapy assessment?
NDT handling techniques aim to normalize which two primary musculoskeletal parameters throughout the body?
questions.explanation: NDT handling techniques are designed to normalize muscle tone and obtain postural alignment throughout the entire body. They also prepare upper and lower extremities for weight bearing, weight shifting, and function. This whole-body approach addresses the interconnected nature of movement and posture, recognizing that tone and alignment affect all subsequent motor activities.

questions.question: A child presents with light brown café-au-lait skin patches and benign neurofibromas along peripheral nerves, with a family history of an autosomal dominant condition. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 classically presents with café-au-lait spots and benign neurofibromas, and follows autosomal dominant inheritance from a gene on chromosome 17. NF2, by contrast, is characterized by bilateral acoustic neuromas rather than prominent skin lesions. Because these syndromes are lifelong and multisystem, this distinction supports coordinated, interdisciplinary management planning.

Schwannomatosis is genetically distinct from NF1 and NF2, producing multiple painful schwannomas on peripheral nerves throughout the body while notably sparing the vestibular nerve. This vestibular sparing is the key distinguishing feature from NF2. Recognizing this feature helps differentiate between the neurocutaneous syndromes for accurate diagnosis and targeted care.
questions.question: Which neurocutaneous syndrome is distinguished from NF1 and NF2 by growth of multiple schwannomas throughout the body while sparing the vestibular nerve?

questions.explanation: During unmodified CIMT, only toileting, hygiene, and bathing activities are permitted while the unaffected extremity is constrained for 90% of waking hours. All other functional activities must be performed with the affected limb. This strict protocol is designed to maximally force use of the impaired limb and overcome learned non-use.
questions.question: An unmodified CIMT protocol requires the patient to restrain the unaffected limb for 90% of waking hours. Which activities are exclusively permitted during the constraint period?

courses.title: Geriatric Nursing II
courses.objectives:
Concepts of Ageing, Geriatric Assessment, Care Settings and Palliative Care: Q1–9
Age-Related Changes and Their Clinical Effects: Q10–19
Pharmacology, Immunisation and Health Screening: Q20–25
Chronic and Infectious Diseases in Older Adults: Q26–33
Falls, Dementia, Musculoskeletal Disorders and Pressure Injury: Q34–40

questions.question:
A person aged 60 years or older has persistently high blood pressure, with systolic pressure of 140 mmHg or above and/or diastolic pressure of 90 mmHg or above. The person has morning headaches, dizziness, shortness of breath on exertion, blurred vision, fatigue and palpitations. The person is obese, inactive, eats a high-sodium diet, smokes, drinks alcohol and often misses antihypertensive doses.
(a) State the assessment findings and risk factors.
(b) State the nursing problems (nursing diagnosis).
(c) List prioritised nursing interventions with the rationale for each.
(d) State how the outcomes of care will be evaluated.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Findings: persistently raised blood pressure (systolic 140 mmHg or above and/or diastolic 90 mmHg or above), morning headaches, dizziness, breathlessness on exertion, chest discomfort, blurred vision, fatigue and palpitations; early disease is often silent.
• Modifiable risk factors present: obesity, inactivity, high sodium intake, smoking, excessive alcohol and poor medication adherence. Non-modifiable: age, genetics, gender and ethnicity.

(b)
Nursing problems: uncontrolled hypertension with risk of stroke, heart failure, kidney damage, retinal damage and aneurysms, and poor medication adherence.

(c)
• Monitor blood pressure regularly and assess for orthostatic hypotension after starting or adjusting medicines; rationale: shows treatment effectiveness and detects changes.
• Teach medication adherence, how to take medicines and side effects; rationale: failure to take medicines leaves blood pressure uncontrolled. Medicines include diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and alpha-blockers.
• Lifestyle: low-sodium DASH diet, weight loss, walking, smoking cessation, less alcohol and caffeine, and stress management (yoga, meditation, deep breathing); rationale: each removes a modifiable risk factor.
• Assess for stroke, heart failure and kidney disease, manage comorbid conditions such as diabetes or heart disease, and give emotional support for chronic illness stress.

(d)
Evaluation: arrange follow-up care to evaluate treatment effectiveness and adjust medicines, with regular check-ups and kidney function tests to monitor organ damage.

(a)
Rheumatoid arthritis: a chronic, systemic inflammatory disease of connective tissue affecting the hands, wrists, knees and feet; joint deformities appear in advanced stages.

(b)
Predisposing factors: it is an autoimmune disease; reduced immune regulation and accumulated autoreactive immune cells with ageing; it is 2 to 3 times more common in women than men, and onset is most common between 20 and 50 but can occur at any age.

(c)
The immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing chronic inflammation; over time this leads to joint damage and deformities, and systemic features such as fatigue, fever and weight loss.

(d)
• Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biologics to slow progression; NSAIDs for pain relief.
• Physical therapy to maintain joint function, with a safe exercise program and rehabilitation to reduce pain and stiffness and improve joint mobility.
• Fall prevention, and assistive devices for reduced mobility.
questions.question:
An older adult has persistent joint pain and swelling in the hands, wrists, knees and feet, with morning stiffness lasting more than an hour. The person is tired, has fever and weight loss.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
NCDs are chronic conditions not caused by infectious agents and not transmitted between people; they progress slowly, persist for years and are largely preventable and manageable through lifestyle change, early detection and consistent care.

(b)
Characteristics: chronic nature, multifactorial origins (genetic, physiological, environmental, behavioural) and global prevalence (over 70% of global deaths).

(c)
Examples: hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke, diabetes mellitus, COPD, asthma and cancers. Risk factors: age, poor diet, inactivity, smoking, alcohol, genetics, pollution and comorbidities.

(d)
Impact: reduced mobility and independence, depression and anxiety, long-term care and strain on health systems, caregiver financial and emotional stress, and lost national productivity.

(e)
Ageing brings reduced organ function, diminished immune responses and weakened immune systems.

(f)
Older adults carry cumulative exposure to risk factors such as poor diet, inactivity, smoking and alcohol over time.

(g)
A family history of hypertension or diabetes and environmental or occupational exposures increase susceptibility.

(h)
NCDs coexist with depression, arthritis, dementia, obesity or hypertension, complicating treatment and requiring holistic care.

(i)
Ischemic stroke is caused by a blocked artery, often by a clot; hemorrhagic stroke results from a ruptured vessel bleeding within or around the brain.

(j)
Hypertension promotes clot formation in narrowed arteries (ischemic) and raises the risk of vessel rupture (hemorrhagic); it doubles the lifetime risk of stroke.

(k)
Ischemic stroke is the most common type in older adults.

(l)
Ischemic: intravenous alteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Hemorrhagic: blood pressure control and surgery if necessary.
questions.question:
Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) in older adults.
Describe NCDs under the following headings:
(a) Definition
(b) Characteristics
(c) Examples and risk factors
(d) Impact on the individual, health system and economy
Explain why older adults are more vulnerable:
(e) Age-related physiological changes
(f) Cumulative exposure to risk factors
(g) Genetic and environmental influences
(h) Coexisting conditions
Distinguish between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke in older adults with hypertension:
(i) Cause
(j) Role of hypertension
(k) Frequency in older adults
(l) Acute management

Health screening tests for older adults.
Describe the principles of screening:
(a) Definition and purpose
(b) Characteristics of a good screening test and disease
(c) Common screening tests and their methods
(d) Screening in older age
State the safe nursing practice and precautions:
(e) Follow-up of screening results
(f) Preparation for blood tests
(g) Continuing screening beyond the usual age
(h) Explaining the benefits and harms
Explain the rationale for the adverse outcomes of screening:
(i) False-positive results
(j) False-negative results
(k) Overdiagnosis
(l) Physical discomfort and radiation
questions.answerText:
(a)
A screening test is done on an asymptomatic population to assess the likelihood of a disease, with the goal of preventing illness or death from it.

(b)
The disease should be prevalent with significant morbidity and mortality and have an asymptomatic period where treatment helps; the test should be highly sensitive and specific, inexpensive, available, safe and easy, with effective treatment affordable.

(c)
Tests: blood pressure (ambulatory monitoring), lipid profile, fasting glucose, oral glucose tolerance and HbA1c, colorectal tests (stool blood test, sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, CT colonography, stool DNA), mammography, cervical tests (HPV test, Pap test, cotest) and prostate-specific antigen.

(d)
Colorectal screening is advised from 50 to 75, and after 75 the benefit-risk balance shifts; mammography is effective at 50 to 74; cervical screening at 30 to 65 is followed by a provider's decision after 65.

(e)
When a screening test is ordered, it is important to follow up.

(f)
Cholesterol blood tests are usually taken in the morning after an overnight fast, with the site cleaned with antiseptic; fasting glucose needs at least 8 hours of fasting.

(g)
Cervical screening continues after 65 if screening was irregular, or with HIV, a weakened immune system, prenatal diethylstilbestrol exposure, a recent abnormal result or past cervical cancer.

(h)
Explain both the advantages (early detection, less treatment, better survival) and the disadvantages (false positives, overdiagnosis, discomfort).

(i)
False positives cause unnecessary anxiety and further invasive procedures.

(j)
False negatives falsely reassure the person; no test is 100% sensitive and specific.

(k)
Slow-growing disease that may never cause symptoms can be found and treated unnecessarily (for example prostate-specific antigen and cervical screening).

(l)
Pap and HPV testing may be uncomfortable, especially with vaginal dryness, and mammography exposes the breast to low-dose radiation.

(a)
Respite care gives primary caregivers temporary relief so they can rest and recharge; adult day care gives seniors support and enrichment outside the home while giving family caregivers a break.

(b)
Respite takes place in the caregiver's home, at day-care centres or at residential or nursing facilities with overnight stays. Adult day care is social day care, adult day health care, or Alzheimer's and dementia day care.

(c)
Services include social activities, nutrition, personal care, health services, transportation, and caregiver support groups, training programmes and financial aid resources.

(d)
Nurses give information on service options and refer to social workers and case managers; they educate caregivers on managing stress and giving appropriate care and support caregivers who feel overwhelmed.

(e)
Training and respite are needed for caregivers managing dementia or advanced cancer, to prevent burnout and maintain quality care.

(f)
Overwhelmed caregivers may resort to neglect or abuse when caregiving demands are high.

(g)
Family members of people with dementia have more depression and anxiety.

(h)
Adult day care stimulates older adults and reduces loneliness and improves access to health care.

(i)
Caregiving is a demanding, unceasing commitment.

(j)
Without relief, caregivers burn out and may neglect or abuse, which shows as malnutrition, dehydration, untreated conditions and unsafe living.

(k)
Dementia causes progressive loss of independence, so care demands grow.

(l)
Older adults who live alone or lack social interaction are less likely to prepare or consume balanced meals, and loneliness worsens distress.
questions.question:
Respite care and adult day care as support for caregivers of older adults.
Describe the service model:
(a) Aims
(b) Settings and types
(c) Services offered
(d) Role of nurses and other workers
State how it relates to common complications and pathologies:
(e) Dementia and advanced cancer care
(f) Caregiver burden and abuse risk
(g) Caregiver mental health
(h) Loneliness in the older adult
Explain why the problem may progress or lead to wider functional decline:
(i) Continuous caregiving demands
(j) Overwhelmed caregivers
(k) Progressive dependence of the older adult
(l) Isolation

An older adult who is obese and inactive, with a family history of diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidemia, presents with tiredness, weight loss and recurrent infections. There is frequent urination, excessive thirst and increased appetite.
(a) Identify the risk factors for diabetes mellitus in this person.
(b) State the complications to watch for.
(c) List the nursing management and preventive options, and justify one of them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Age-related decline in insulin secretion and rising insulin resistance; obesity and physical inactivity with poor diet; genetic predisposition and family history; comorbid hypertension, dyslipidemia and cardiovascular disease.

(b)
Neuropathy: peripheral (pain, tingling, numbness) and autonomic (gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension). Retinopathy with vision loss or blindness. Cardiovascular disease (heart attack, stroke, hypertension). Diabetic nephropathy and chronic kidney disease. Cognitive decline with higher dementia risk.

(c)
• Lifestyle: balanced diet with controlled carbohydrate, high fibre and low saturated fat; moderate exercise such as walking or swimming; weight management.
• Medicines: metformin, sulfonylureas (glimepiride, glipizide, glyburide), DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, linagliptin); insulin for severe hyperglycemia or failure of oral drugs, using simple regimens such as basal insulin.
• Monitoring and education: blood glucose checks, adherence, recognising hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, and regular screening for retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.
• Justification: metformin lowers glucose without causing hypoglycemia, which suits frail older adults; renal function needs periodic monitoring. Sulfonylureas carry a high hypoglycemia risk with irregular meals, so they are less suitable.

(a)
Medical problems: insulin-treated diabetes, long-term steroid use, chronic renal failure, necrotising fasciitis with debridement and skin grafting, prolonged bed rest and repeated antibiotics. Functional problems: reduced mobility, partial sight and an Abbreviated Mental Test of 8/10; washing, dressing, transfer and kitchen practice need further assessment.

(b)
Age-related changes: reduced organ reserve and homeostenosis (inability to restore homeostasis); by age 75 kidney filtration is about 70% of that at 30; loss of subcutaneous fat and blood supply raises pressure sore risk; sarcopenia is a leading cause of falls.

(c)
Geriatric syndromes: falls and injury, new incontinence, delirium, reduced mobility and iatrogenic events. Frailty conditions: impaired vision, impaired hearing, reduced mobility, cognition problems, depression, malnutrition, urinary incontinence and iatrogenic illness.

(d)
• Priority 1: preventing functional decline, since function indicates quality of life; work to restore function and independence. Urgency clues present: living alone, polypharmacy and recent functional decline.
• Priority 2: a multidisciplinary CGA across physical, functional, psychological, social and environmental domains, with medication review and optimised medical care.
• Priority 3: rehabilitation (home-based, day hospital or in-patient), home set-up and services, discharge planning, caregiver (daughter) partnership, and follow-up.
questions.question:
An 83-year-old woman with insulin-treated diabetes mellitus, long-term steroid treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica and chronic renal failure developed necrotising fasciitis in the right groin. She had extensive surgical debridement and skin grafting, about one month of bed rest and multiple courses of antibiotics. Her Abbreviated Mental Test score is 8/10. She is partially sighted and walks 20 metres with a wheeled Zimmer frame. She previously lived alone in a bungalow and her daughter helped with shopping and housework.
(a) Identify the medical and nursing problems evident.
(b) State the age-related changes involved.
(c) State the related geriatric syndromes and conditions to consider.
(d) Give your nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.

An older adult with several chronic conditions takes many medicines with different dosing schedules. The person has poor vision and arthritis that make opening bottles difficult, sometimes forgets doses, stops medicines when feeling well, fears side effects and cannot afford some prescriptions.
(a) Identify the problem and the contributing factors.
(b) Name the assessment and monitoring procedures.
(c) State the key steps and safety considerations.
(d) State the education for the patient and caregiver.
(e) State the follow-up and team involvement.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Poor drug compliance (non-adherence) with polypharmacy. Contributing factors: complex regimens, sensory decline, physical limitations (arthritis), beliefs that medicines are unneeded when well, fear of side effects, financial constraints, social isolation, side effects, and large pills or difficult formulations.

(b)
Review each drug for necessity and effectiveness; monitor for toxicity, adverse drug reactions, and drug-drug and drug-disease interactions; monitor creatinine clearance for renally cleared drugs.

(c)
• Simplify the regimen by reducing daily doses and consolidating medicines; use pill organizers, electronic reminders or medication apps; choose appropriate formulations; deprescribe unnecessary drugs.
• Safety: adjust doses for age-related changes, be cautious with benzodiazepines and antihypertensives, and take particular care with narrow-therapeutic-window drugs such as digoxin and certain antibiotics.

(d)
Face-to-face counselling on why adherence matters, side effects and treatment benefits, and involve family and caregivers in medication management.

(e)
Regular medication reviews; the pharmacist reviews medicines, compliance and formulations; the social worker assesses finances and social provision; a personalised medication plan is essential.

questions.question:
Immunosenescence in older adults.
Describe immunosenescence under the following headings:
(a) Definition and overall effect on the immune system
(b) Changes in innate immunity
(c) Changes in adaptive immunity
(d) Inflammaging and its consequences
Explain why older adults are more vulnerable:
(e) To infections
(f) To poor vaccine response
(g) To autoimmune disease
(h) To delayed healing and failure to control virus-infected and cancerous cells
Distinguish between innate and adaptive immunity in older adults:
(i) Role
(j) Components affected
(k) Age-related change in each
(l) Practical consequence of each
questions.answerText:
(a)
Immunosenescence is the gradual decline in immune efficiency with age, weakening the ability to respond to infections, vaccines and injuries.

(b)
Innate immunity: reduced skin and mucosal barrier function, reduced phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils, and diminished natural killer cell cytotoxic activity.

(c)
Adaptive immunity: thymic involution reduces naive T-cell production, existing T-cells respond less, and B-cells decrease in number and efficiency.

(d)
Inflammaging is chronic low-grade inflammation with overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, worsened by oxidative stress; it contributes to atherosclerosis, diabetes and Alzheimer's disease.

(e)
Respiratory and urinary tract infections are more likely, and influenza and pneumonia are more severe, often needing hospitalisation with higher mortality.

(f)
Reduced T-cell and B-cell activity and reduced long-term immune memory make vaccines less effective (for example influenza); high-dose vaccines and adjuvants are being developed.

(g)
Reduced immune regulation and accumulation of autoreactive immune cells raise the risk of autoimmune disease.

(h)
Impaired phagocytosis delays healing, and reduced natural killer cell activity weakens the response to virus-infected and cancerous cells.

(i)
Innate immunity is the body's first line of defence; adaptive immunity gives specific and long-lasting responses.

(j)
Innate: skin and mucosal barriers, macrophages, neutrophils, natural killer cells. Adaptive: T-cells and B-cells.

(k)
Innate: weaker barriers, phagocytosis and natural killer activity. Adaptive: thymic shrinkage, less responsive T-cells, fewer and less efficient B-cells.

(l)
Innate: invasion by pathogens is easier, the initial response is impaired and healing is delayed. Adaptive: poor response to new antigens and reduced immune memory, so vaccines work less well.

(a)
Dysphagia (difficulty or discomfort swallowing, from mild discomfort to severe pain): common in the elderly, it complicates eating and drinking and raises the risk of both malnutrition and dehydration. Contributing age changes: weaker esophageal peristalsis, dental problems and cognitive impairment.

(b)
The most common diagnostic examination is the barium swallow.

(c)
• Give small, frequent meals of softer foods that are high in nutritional value; keep the person sitting upright while eating; offer soft or modified-consistency foods and track daily food and fluid intake.
• Surgery may be needed to decrease obstruction, though it is not always necessary.

(d)
Teach caregivers to recognise early signs of malnutrition and dehydration, to prepare balanced nutrient-dense meals and to give fluids effectively; finger foods, adaptive utensils and good lighting ease mealtimes.

(e)
• Arrange dental consultations for chewing and swallowing difficulties, work with the dietitian on meal plans, and refer to the doctor if obstruction needs treatment.
• Evaluate nutrition and hydration strategies regularly and adjust meal plans or seek further medical evaluation.
questions.question:
An older adult with cognitive impairment has difficulty and discomfort when swallowing, choking when being fed, reduced food intake and weight loss.
(a) Identify the problem and why older adults are prone to it.
(b) Name the diagnostic examination.

Immunization of older adults.
Describe the principles of the vaccines:
(a) Influenza vaccine
(b) Pneumococcal vaccine
(c) Shingles vaccine
(d) Tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis vaccine
State the safe nursing practice and precautions:
(e) Timing of influenza vaccination
(f) Pneumococcal schedule and unknown history
(g) Shingles vaccine schedule
(h) Booster intervals
Explain the rationale for the outcomes or adverse effects:
(i) Why influenza vaccination matters
(j) Why pneumococcal vaccination matters
(k) Why shingles vaccination matters and its side effects
(l) Safety of the influenza vaccine and limits of protection
questions.answerText:
(a)
Influenza vaccines are trivalent or quadrivalent, with or without adjuvant (an MF59 adjuvanted trivalent vaccine is licensed for age 65 and over); most are given in the deltoid muscle.

(b)
Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15 or PCV20) is for all adults 65 or older with no prior conjugate vaccine or unknown history; PCV15 is followed by PPSV23, and PCV20 needs no PPSV23.

(c)
Shingles vaccine (Shingrix) protects against the varicella zoster virus that causes a painful blistering rash.

(d)
Tdap or Td protects against tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis (whooping cough).

(e)
Vaccinate before the influenza season, before activity begins in the population.

(f)
Give PPSV23 one year after PCV15 (minimum 8 weeks in immunocompromised people or those with a cochlear implant or cerebrospinal fluid leak).

(g)
Healthy adults aged 50 and over get two Shingrix doses two to six months apart; there is no approved booster.

(h)
Adults need a Tdap or Td booster every 10 years.

(i)
Influenza is a serious concern in the elderly, and related mortality rises sharply after age 65.

(j)
Invasive pneumococcal disease (pneumonia, bacteremia, meningitis) causes high morbidity and mortality in adults over 65.

(k)
Older adults are at higher risk of shingles; 10% to 18% develop long-term nerve pain (postherpetic neuralgia). Side effects: sore arm, redness and swelling, fatigue, headache, body aches, stomach pain or nausea.

(l)
Influenza vaccine is well tolerated, serious adverse events are rare and most resolve within 3 days; protection duration is unclear and vaccines are less effective with immunosenescence.

(a)
Ageing is the period when bodily functions begin to decline; onset varies with genetic and environmental factors, and response depends on social history, home, family, work and opportunities to sustain health.

(b)
Characteristics: inability to meet life's demands, insecurity, loss of status, uncertainty and fear about health, complaining about food, sleep and bowels, difficulty adjusting to a sedentary life, and memory loss for recent events.

(c)
Problems: poverty, poor nutrition, loneliness, mental confusion, dental problems, poor hygiene, physical handicap, poor housing, boredom and risk of home accidents.

(d)
Health problems: heart disease, cancer, pneumonia, accidents, liver cirrhosis, hypothermia, cerebral haemorrhage from chronic hypertension, loss of senses, and arthritis with weak bones, muscles and ligaments.

(e)
The elderly are a vulnerable group: most are physically weak, financially poor, socially withdrawn and lacking political power.

(f)
Skin cannot regulate temperature, causing hypothermia.

(g)
Lack of judgement, weak muscles and bones and poor sight lead to injuries and accidental death.

(h)
Loss of ability to work and compete brings poverty, which with lack of energy to cook, poor teeth and poor appetite worsens nutrition; loss of a spouse or children causes loneliness.

(i)
The elderly are people aged 60 years and above (retirement age in Nigeria), also called senior citizens; the 60 to 69 age group.

(j)
The aged are those aged 70 years and above.

(k)
The standard for defining the age of the elderly is 65 years.

(l)
Older adults are also grouped as young old (60 to 74), middle old (75 to 84) and old old (85 and older).

An older man has urinary frequency, urgency and difficulty starting and stopping the flow of urine. His prostate gland is enlarged and partially blocks the urethra.
(a) Identify the risk factors for this condition.
(b) State the complications to watch for.
(c) List the nursing management and preventive options, and justify one of them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Changes in the prostate gland with ageing.

(b)
Urinary tract infections are more likely; if the bladder is not fully drained, urine can back up into the kidneys (vesicoureteral reflux) and, untreated, cause kidney failure; prostatitis may occur; urinary retention can lead to infections.

(c)
• There is no cure but treatment is available: medicines that relax prostate muscle (tamsulosin, terazosin, doxazosin, alfuzosin, silodosin) and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.
• Bladder training, timed voiding and double voiding to empty the bladder fully; avoid caffeine, alcohol and spicy foods; stay hydrated to prevent infection; prevent constipation.
• Catheters for retention or severe incontinence; prostate surgery if other treatments are ineffective.
• Justification (alpha-blockers): they relax the prostate muscle and reduce tension on the urethra, which eases the blockage causing frequency, urgency and difficulty starting and stopping the flow.
• Justification (double voiding): it helps ensure the bladder is fully drained, which prevents the backflow and infections that can lead to kidney failure.

(a)
• Malnutrition findings: unintentional weight loss of more than 5% of body weight within 6 to 12 months, muscle weakness, fatigue, poor wound healing, memory problems with confusion and difficulty concentrating, depression and irritability.
• Dehydration findings: dry sticky mouth and dry skin, reduced and dark-coloured urine, dizziness and confusion, sunken eyes, low blood pressure on standing with fainting spells, rapid heart rate. Risk factors present: missing teeth or ill-fitting dentures, reduced taste and smell with reduced thirst perception, social isolation and loneliness.

(b)
Nursing problems: malnutrition (imbalance between nutrients taken in and body requirements) and dehydration (inadequate water for normal function).

(c)
• Screen and monitor first: Mini Nutritional Assessment or hydration status scales, daily food and fluid intake record, urine colour chart, skin turgor checks. Rationale: close and consistent contact lets nurses detect subtle changes early.
• Hydration: fluid schedule and reminders, small frequent sips, a variety of drinks (water, herbal teas, soups). Rationale: thirst perception is reduced in older adults; severe cases need IV rehydration under medical supervision.
• Nutrition: individualised plan with the dietitian, small frequent meals rich in fibre, protein, vitamins (B12, D) and minerals (calcium, potassium), oral nutrition supplements when prescribed after assessment. Rationale: appetite is reduced and specific needs are increased.
• Treat underlying causes: arrange dental consultation, provide well-fitting dentures, offer soft or modified-consistency foods, report medication side effects such as dry mouth and appetite loss, and help manage chronic illness. Rationale: these factors reduce intake.
• Psychosocial and environmental support: social dining and community meal programmes, adaptive utensils, good lighting, finger foods, home-delivered meals, and caregiver education on early signs. Rationale: loneliness and isolation reduce appetite.

(d)
Evaluation: regularly review the effectiveness of nutrition and hydration strategies and adjust by changing meal plans, increasing fluid intake or seeking additional medical evaluation.
questions.question:
An older adult who lives alone has lost more than 5% of body weight over 6 to 12 months without trying. The person is constantly tired, has muscle weakness, heals slowly after injuries, has memory problems with confusion, and is irritable. The person also has a dry, sticky mouth, dry skin, dark urine passed less often, sunken eyes, dizziness on standing with fainting spells and a rapid heart rate. The person has missing teeth and a reduced sense of taste and smell.
(a) State the assessment findings and the contributing risk factors.
(b) State the nursing problems (nursing diagnosis).
(c) List prioritised nursing interventions with the rationale for each.
(d) State how the outcomes of care will be evaluated.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Dementia is a syndrome caused by progressive, irreversible brain disorders, with deterioration of memory, thinking, behaviour and the ability to do everyday activities.

(b)
Types: Alzheimer's disease (60% to 70%), vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia and frontotemporal dementia.

(c)
Risk factors: age, genes such as APOE e4, midlife hypertension, diabetes and obesity, smoking, excessive alcohol, inactivity, low education and limited mental stimulation.

(d)
Features: memory loss, poor problem-solving and reasoning, agitation, depression, apathy and psychosis, inability to manage finances, cooking or hygiene, and difficulty finding words or understanding speech.

(e)
Risk roughly doubles every five years after age 65.

(f)
Hypertension, diabetes and obesity in midlife are linked to higher risk.

(g)
Ageing brings brain tissue atrophy, altered neurotransmitters and accumulated cellular damage, with progressive cognitive decline.

(h)
Inactivity, smoking and alcohol add risk, lower cognitive reserve increases it, and affected adults become more vulnerable to physical and emotional abuse.

(i)
Dementia is a term for a syndrome, not a single disease; it includes several disorders.

(j)
Alzheimer's disease is marked by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, with brain shrinkage and cell death.

(k)
Alzheimer's disease accounts for 60% to 70% of dementia cases, making it the most common cause.

(l)
Other forms include vascular dementia (reduced blood flow; impaired judgement and slowed thinking early), Lewy body dementia (visual hallucinations, sleep disturbance, Parkinson-like motor symptoms) and frontotemporal dementia (personality, behaviour and language change).

Dementia in older adults.
Describe dementia under the following headings:
(a) Definition
(b) Types
(c) Risk factors
(d) Clinical features
Explain why older adults are more vulnerable:
(e) Age
(f) Cardiovascular health
(g) Brain changes of ageing
(h) Lifestyle, education and abuse risk
Distinguish between dementia and Alzheimer's disease:
(i) Nature of the term
(j) Underlying pathology of Alzheimer's disease
(k) Share of dementia cases
(l) Other forms of dementia

Age-related changes of the urinary system.
Describe the age-related changes in:
(a) The bladder
(b) The micturition reflex
(c) The kidneys
(d) Common urinary problems
State the safe nursing practice and precautions:
(e) Bladder training methods
(f) Pelvic floor exercises
(g) Diet, fluids and medicines
(h) Devices and skin care
Explain the rationale for the outcomes or adverse effects that can follow:
(i) Small capacity and residual urine
(j) Delayed reflex
(k) Reduced filtration and drug handling
(l) Incomplete emptying and prostate enlargement
questions.answerText:
(a)
Bladder capacity falls to less than half (about 250 ml against 600 ml in young adults) and often holds up to 100 ml of residual urine.

(b)
The micturition reflex is delayed, triggered only when the bladder is nearly full rather than half full.

(c)
Glomerular filtration rate, renal blood flow and tubular secretion decline; kidney filtration is about 70% of its level at age 30 by age 75.

(d)
Common problems: incontinence, urinary tract infections, benign prostatic hyperplasia, overactive bladder, underactive bladder, nocturia and urinary retention.

(e)
Use bladder training (gradually lengthening time between toilet trips), timed voiding and double voiding.

(f)
Teach Kegel exercises to strengthen the muscles that control urine flow, with biofeedback therapy if needed.

(g)
Avoid caffeine, alcohol and spicy foods, increase fibre to prevent constipation, stay hydrated, and monitor creatinine clearance to adjust renally cleared drugs.

(h)
Use absorbent pads or catheters for retention or severe incontinence; change adult diapers promptly, since urine or stool contact can break down skin.

(i)
Reduced capacity and residual urine cause frequent urination.

(j)
The delayed reflex gives a sudden urge to reach the toilet.

(k)
Reduced filtration causes drug accumulation and toxicity, especially with narrow therapeutic windows.

(l)
An enlarged prostate partially blocks the urethra, raising infection risk; undrained urine can back up to the kidneys and, untreated, cause kidney failure.

questions.question:
An 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia is frail and entirely dependent for daily activities. She sits in a chair or lies in bed most of the time, is incontinent of bowel and bladder, and has developed multiple small stage 2 pressure ulcers on her buttocks. Her married daughter cares for her at home.
(a) Identify the problem.
(b) Name the assessment procedure and what it looks for.
(c) State the key care steps and safety considerations.
(d) State the education for the patient and caregiver.
(e) State the referral and community follow-up.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pressure injuries (decubitus ulcers or bed sores): injury to skin or underlying tissue from sustained pressure, shear and other factors, ranging from intact skin with nonblanching erythema to full-thickness loss; impaired mobility and contact of stool or urine with skin add risk.

(b)
Skin assessment of high-risk areas at least daily for nonblanching redness or discoloration, skin breakdown, edema, change in tissue consistency or pain; check skin under and around medical devices at least twice a day.

(c)
• Make regular small position shifts and avoid lying on the injury; use air-filled or high-specification foam mattresses, off-loading devices and special seat cushions.
• Cleanse and protect skin promptly after incontinence and avoid adult diapers where possible; at dressing changes use normal saline or potable water, pat dry and apply the recommended dressing; wash hands before and after; trim nails.

(d)
Teach the caregiver daily skin checks, repositioning, incontinence care, regular bathing and moisturising; protein, hydration and vitamins A and C support skin integrity and healing.

(e)
Contact the health care provider promptly for assessment of any skin impairment; home health care services provide wound care and medication help, and an advanced, frail condition needs a higher level of care such as palliative and end-of-life services.

questions.question:
An older woman reports bleeding after intercourse and between periods, with an unusual watery, bloody, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She has had no regular Pap smear or HPV screening, smokes, and has HIV/AIDS.
(a) Identify the risk factors for the suspected cancer in this woman.
(b) State the complications to watch for.
(c) List the nursing management and preventive options, and justify one of them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Viral: persistent infection with high-risk HPV types, especially HPV-16 and HPV-18. Behavioural: early sexual activity, multiple partners, inconsistent condom use and smoking. Medical: immunosuppression such as HIV/AIDS, long-term oral contraceptive use (over 5 years), multiple pregnancies and poor access to screening. Socioeconomic: limited healthcare access and low awareness.

(b)
Advanced disease: pelvic or lower back pain, pain during intercourse, leg swelling or pain from lymphatic obstruction, and difficulty urinating or defecating; treatment causes physical and emotional side effects, and the cancer can recur.

(c)
• Prevention: HPV vaccination (Gardasil, Cervarix) and regular Pap smear and HPV testing to detect precancerous lesions; screening for ages 30 to 65 by HPV test or cotest every 5 years or Pap every 3 years.
• Treatment: conization or hysterectomy early; pelvic exenteration rarely; radiation; chemotherapy (chemoradiation or palliative); targeted therapy (bevacizumab) and immunotherapy. Screening may continue after 65 with HIV or a weakened immune system.
• Justification (screening): it finds precancerous changes that can be treated to stop cancer developing, and early detection improves treatment outcomes and survival. It is especially apt here because she has no regular screening and is HIV positive.

questions.question:
A postmenopausal woman has lost height over time and has a stooped posture. She was unaware of any bone problem until she sustained a fracture after a minor fall.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteoporosis: weakened bones from reduced bone density and mass that fracture easily; the spine, hips and wrists are most affected, and it is often silent until a fracture.

(b)
Predisposing factors: ageing, oestrogen loss after menopause (and reduced testosterone in men, or hormone treatment for prostate cancer), inactivity, inadequate calcium, vitamin D and protein, reduced calcium and vitamin D absorption with age, smoking, and chronic illness.

(c)
• Bone mineral density begins to fall in the mid-30s and loss accelerates after menopause; resorption by osteoclasts outpaces formation by osteoblasts, leaving thinner, weaker bones (osteopenia progressing to osteoporosis).
• Vertebral compression fractures cause height loss, kyphosis, hip and knee flexion and chronic back pain, harming mobility, balance and internal organ function.

(d)
• Diet: high calcium (amounts given differ between sources, 1,200 mg and 1,500 mg per day) with vitamin D; dairy and dark green vegetables; low-phosphorus diet; avoid red meats, cola and processed foods; cut caffeine and alcohol.
• Activity and lifestyle: weight-bearing exercise, stopping smoking, fall prevention, and bone density tests for early detection.
• Medicines: bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate), selective estrogen receptor modulators (raloxifene), hormone replacement therapy in selected cases, and denosumab or teriparatide for high fracture risk.

questions.question:
Fall prevention and management for older adults.
Describe the care model:
(a) Definition of a fall and the aims of care
(b) Prevention components
(c) Management after a fall
(d) Team roles
State how it relates to common complications and pathologies:
(e) Musculoskeletal conditions and fractures
(f) Immobility-related complications and head injury
(g) Intrinsic conditions and medications
(h) Psychological effects
Explain why falls may progress to wider functional decline:
(i) Fear of falling
(j) Activity restriction
(k) Loss of independence
(l) Social and economic burden
questions.answerText:
(a)
A fall is unintentionally coming to rest on the ground, floor or lower level, excluding intentional movements or major medical events; care aims to prevent falls and injury and preserve independence and quality of life.

(b)
Prevention: home modification (grab bars, non-slip mats, no loose rugs, good lighting, clear walkways), balance and mobility training (tai chi, yoga, physiotherapy, canes or walkers), eye examinations, glasses or cataract surgery, medication review, calcium and vitamin D, exercise and bone density checks.

(c)
After a fall: fracture management, head injury monitoring for concussion or internal bleeding, pain relief, wound care, a comprehensive health check-up, medication review, treatment of chronic conditions, and rehabilitation with physiotherapy.

(d)
Team: physicians, physiotherapists (restore mobility, strength and range of motion), occupational therapists (safe daily-activity techniques) and social workers give multidisciplinary care.

(e)
Osteoporosis, osteoarthritis and sarcopenia raise fall risk; falls cause hip, vertebral and wrist fractures, and hip fractures carry high first-year mortality.

(f)
Fractures can lead to prolonged immobility with pressure ulcers and pneumonia; falls also cause head trauma.

(g)
Intrinsic factors: dementia, diabetic neuropathy, arthritis, Parkinson's disease, cardiovascular disease, low blood pressure, vision and hearing loss, gait disorders, and sedatives, antidepressants or antihypertensives causing dizziness or hypotension.

(h)
Anxiety and depression are common among fall survivors.

(i)
A single fall can cause a fear of falling.

(j)
Fear leads to activity restriction, which causes muscle weakness and impaired balance.

(k)
Even without severe injury, falls reduce functional independence and increase the need for caregivers, assistive devices or long-term care.

(l)
Falls cause healthcare costs, caregiver burden, reduced social engagement and higher mortality.

(a)
Presbyopia is loss of clear close-up vision as the eye's lens becomes less flexible; presbycusis is gradual age-related hearing loss.

(b)
Presbyopia: age-related changes stop the lens changing shape to focus (accommodation) so light cannot land clearly on the retina. Presbycusis: develops gradually with age.

(c)
Presbyopia: need for more light, blurred vision at reading distance, holding reading material at arm's length, headaches and eye strain. Presbycusis: cannot hear high-pitched sounds, turns up volume, tinnitus and trouble in noisy places.

(d)
Presbyopia: correction with glasses, contacts, eye drops or surgery. Presbycusis: hearing aids amplify sound but cannot cure or restore lost hearing.

(e)
The lens, soft and flexible early in life, loses its ability to change shape for near focus.

(f)
Cataracts or macular degeneration hinder depth perception and contrast sensitivity, and hearing loss affects spatial orientation, raising fall risk.

(g)
Loss of touch, sight, hearing, smell and skin feeling is among the common health problems of older adults; reduced taste and smell lower appetite.

(h)
Hearing screening every 10 years, and comprehensive eye examination every 1 to 2 years (yearly with diabetes).

(i)
Presbyopia affects the eye's lens; presbycusis affects hearing.

(j)
Presbyopia usually starts around age 40 and worsens until the mid-60s; presbycusis affects 2 out of 3 people aged 70 or older and is the most common cause of hearing loss worldwide.

(k)
Presbyopia: trouble seeing close up. Presbycusis: trouble hearing high pitches and understanding speech in crowds.

(l)
Presbyopia is a refractive error correctable by lenses or surgery; presbycusis treatment is hearing aids, which do not cure it.

questions.answerText:
(a)
CGA is a multidisciplinary diagnostic and treatment process that identifies the medical, psychosocial and functional limitations of a frail older person to build a coordinated plan; the chief aim is to restore healthy function and independence, or slow functional decline.

(b)
Domains: physical and medical, functional (ADLs, activity, gait and balance), psychological (cognition, mood and depression), social, and environmental (home safety, assistive devices).

(c)
Team: senior physician, coordinating specialist nurse, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, social worker, dietician, speech and language therapist and pharmacist, each with assessment, rehabilitation, nursing, diet, medication or social-care functions.

(d)
Those who benefit: people with difficulty in ADLs, impaired mobility or multiple comorbidities; those who do not: functionally independent, advanced dementia and terminally ill people. Benefits include better diagnosis, shorter hospital stay, less readmission and delayed institutional care.

(e)
Geriatric syndromes predispose to an adverse event needing only a precipitant: falls and injury, new incontinence, delirium, reduced mobility and iatrogenic events.

(f)
Assessment seeks impaired vision, impaired hearing, reduced mobility and falls, cognition problems, depression, malnutrition, urinary incontinence and iatrogenic illness.

(g)
Hospitalised patients also need delirium prevention and treatment, falls prevention, improved physical function, discharge planning and nutritional support.

(h)
Urgency clues: extreme age, living alone, new features of illness, polypharmacy, recent functional decline and worsening confusion.

(i)
In chronic, progressive, usually incurable disease functional status becomes an increasingly important indicator of quality of life.

(j)
Preventing functional decline has highest priority.

(k)
Fragmented care, recent onset of impairment and caregiver strain put people in transition at risk.

(l)
A small improvement across a large population can shift thresholds for falls, carer stress and institutional risk.

An older adult has frequent urination, sudden intense urges to urinate with leakage, frequent nighttime awakenings to pass urine, and difficulty starting urination and emptying the bladder fully.
(a) State the assessment findings and contributing causes.
(b) State the nursing problems (nursing diagnosis).
(c) List prioritised nursing interventions with the rationale for each.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Findings match incontinence, overactive bladder, nocturia, underactive bladder and urinary retention (urinary tract infections and benign prostatic hyperplasia also occur). Age changes: bladder capacity under 250 ml (600 ml in young adults), about 100 ml residual urine, and a delayed micturition reflex.
• Causes: muscle weakness with ageing, hormonal changes, prostate enlargement or cancer, neurological conditions (Parkinson's disease, stroke), medicines (some antidepressants, antihistamines), constipation, and surgery or radiation.

(b)
Nursing problems: loss of bladder control, urgency, frequency, nocturia with disturbed sleep, and incomplete emptying with a risk of infection.

(c)
• Bladder training, timed voiding and double voiding; rationale: they strengthen bladder muscles and help ensure complete emptying.
• Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises and biofeedback therapy; rationale: they strengthen the muscles that control urine flow and build awareness of bladder function.
• Diet and lifestyle: avoid caffeine, alcohol and spicy foods that irritate the bladder, increase fibre to prevent constipation, stay hydrated to prevent infection, exercise, control weight, stop smoking.
• Medicines (alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, anticholinergics, beta-3 agonists, antibiotics); pads or catheters for retention or severe incontinence; surgery only if other treatments fail.

(a)
Osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease): pain, swelling and stiffness, most often in the knees, hips, hands and spine; the most common joint disorder in older adults.

(b)
Predisposing factors: ageing (cartilage deteriorates progressively, and is found in everyone past 70), wear and tear from repeated mechanical stress, reduced repair mechanisms, reduced synovial fluid, inflammation and oxidative stress, and weight-bearing joints; the exact cause is not known.

(c)
Cartilage that cushions the bone ends gradually wears away and thins, leaving rough bone ends exposed, so bone contacts bone; internal ligaments may be damaged, causing pain, swelling, reduced range of motion and deformity.

(d)
• Weight management to reduce joint stress; a safe exercise program and physical therapy (heat, electrotherapy, ultrasound, laser) to reduce pain and stiffness and to build flexibility, strength and endurance.
• Medicines: pain relievers such as acetaminophen, NSAIDs or anti-inflammatories, and arthritis creams; surgery in severe cases (osteotomy, arthroscopy, joint replacement).
• Assistive devices where walking is impaired, and fall prevention.
questions.question:
An older adult has joint pain in the knees and hips after activity or prolonged use, with swelling, loss of flexibility and morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Activity theory (Havighurst and Albrecht): ageing has more positive outcomes when adults stay active and socially engaged; criticised because choices are limited by physical capacity, finances and social resources.

(b)
Continuity theory (Maddox, Atchley): older adults keep the same activities, relationships and coping strategies, preserving internal structures (personality, beliefs) and external structures (relationships, roles); criticised for its notion of "normal" ageing.

(c)
Disengagement theory (Cumming and Henry, 1961): it is natural and rational for older adults to withdraw from active life as death approaches; it is set out in nine postulates.

(d)
Terror management theory (1986): awareness of death raises anxiety that is handled through proximal defences (denial, repression, distraction, rationalisation) and distal defences (symbolic immortality, cultural worldview, self-esteem, identification with something larger).

(e)
Meeting older people raises awareness of one's own mortality and ageing anxiety, prompting defensive attitudes and behaviours toward them.

(f)
Myths and stereotypes lead to ageism, reduced health services, segregation from society and difficulty recruiting nurses for older adults.

(g)
Increased age is a risk factor for social withdrawal because of physical decline and retirement.

(h)
Reduced network complexity is linked to cognitive decline; social engagement is protective.

(i)
Activity theory: staying occupied and involved is necessary for late-life satisfaction. Disengagement theory: ageing means accepting and desiring withdrawal from active life.

(j)
Activity: Havighurst and Albrecht (1953 study, published 1963). Disengagement: Cumming and Henry, in Growing Old (1961).

(k)
Activity: successful ageing comes from remaining socially active. Disengagement: successful ageing means withdrawing.

(l)
Activity theory's central theme is supported by most researchers; disengagement theory lacks empirical support and is largely dismissed, and nurses should promote participation and socialisation to achieve successful ageing.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Findings: xerosis (dry skin) with a fine powdery scale, accentuated creases on the palms and soles, itching (localised or generalised), scaling, cracking, sleep disturbance and excoriation from scratching.
• Contributing factors: thinner subcutaneous layer, reduced sweating, diminished sebaceous gland function, harsh soaps and powders, low humidity, and heaters.

(b)
Nursing problems: dry, cracked, excoriated skin that lets bacteria penetrate and risks infection, and sleep interrupted by itching.

(c)
• Limit warm baths to three times a week and restrict soap to the axilla, groin, scalp and soles; rationale: frequent harsh soaps and products dry the skin and cause itching.
• Apply an emollient (petrolatum, shea butter or cocoa butter cream or ointment) while skin is still moist; rationale: it holds in moisture. Take extra care because emollients are slippery and can cause a fall.
• Use a humidifier to moisten room air; rationale: low humidity, heaters and fireplaces dry the skin.
• Support skin health with protein, adequate hydration and vitamins A and C (fruits and yellow vegetables); keep nails trimmed and filed to prevent scratching damage.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Aims: symptom management and better quality of life for serious illness, dignity and comfort, advance care planning and respect for the person's wishes.

(b)
Components: pain and symptom management, advance care planning (advance directives, living wills, healthcare proxies), family involvement, spiritual and emotional support, comfort care over curative treatment, hospice care, respect for autonomy and cultural sensitivity.

(c)
Rights: informed consent, refusing treatment, pain and symptom relief, dignity and respect, psychosocial and spiritual support, advance care planning, access to palliative services and family involvement.

(d)
Hospice gives medical care, therapy, social support and bereavement counselling around the clock, seven days a week; nurses advocate, educate and support patients and families.

(e)
It is needed for advanced NCDs such as cancer and dementia, and for any terminally ill person with a qualifying prognosis.

(f)
In advanced Alzheimer's disease, severe loss of brain function can cause dehydration, malnutrition or infection, which can result in death.

(g)
Marked weight loss, feeding difficulty, immobility, incontinence and pressure ulcers in frail advanced dementia point to palliative and end-of-life care.

(h)
Older adults in this care may have pain, physical distress, isolation, anxiety, fear or grief needing relief.

(i)
Care becomes necessary when traditional treatments are no longer effective, symptoms worsen and the patient's needs increase.

(j)
Patients can become entirely dependent for daily activities and lose independence.

(k)
Many families wait until the final days and weeks to call hospice, missing months of specialised care.

(l)
Families and caregivers carry a heavy burden and need help to cope with grief.

questions.question:
An older adult has had a cough for more than 3 weeks with chest pain and coughing up blood. There are night sweats, chills, fever, loss of appetite, constant tiredness and breathlessness.
(a) Identify the most likely condition.
(b) State the age-related respiratory changes involved.
(c) State the differential conditions and their distinguishing features.
(d) Give your nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tuberculosis, a bacterial infection that most often affects the lungs and can be fatal if untreated; risk is higher with HIV/AIDS or a weakened immune system.

(b)
Airways and tissues become less elastic and more rigid; lung capacity falls from reduced alveolar elasticity and thoracic muscle mass; osteoporosis may alter chest shape; weaker respiratory and abdominal muscles hinder diaphragmatic movement (maximal breathing capacity is 43% at 75 compared with 30).

(c)
• Asthma: breathlessness, chest tightness, wheeze on breathing out, trigger exposure. COPD: much mucus, wheeze, breathlessness, tight chest, smoking the leading cause.
• Pulmonary fibrosis: breathlessness worse with exercise, dry cough, fast shallow breathing. Pulmonary hypertension: fatigue, lightheadedness or fainting, chest pain, palpitations, foot edema.

(d)
• Priority 1: assess difficulty breathing, rate and depth of respirations, accessory muscle use and abnormal breath sounds; maintain airway patency and assist gas exchange.
• Priority 2: enhance nutritional intake, prevent complications and slow progression, and give information on the disease process, prognosis and treatment.

(a)
Pharmacodynamics is the body's biological response to drugs, including receptor binding, post-receptor effects, chemical interactions, potency, efficacy and therapeutic index.

(b)
Older adults show increased sensitivity to central nervous system depressants such as benzodiazepines and decreased responsiveness of beta-adrenergic receptors to beta-agonists.

(c)
Baroreceptor sensitivity is impaired, reducing blood pressure regulation on standing.

(d)
Renal and cardiac reserve are reduced, altering responses to many medications.

(e)
Use cautious dosing and vigilant monitoring of CNS depressants such as benzodiazepines.

(f)
Monitor carefully and adjust doses of antihypertensives because of the risk of orthostatic hypotension.

(g)
Use individualised dosing regimens and comprehensive monitoring; adjust therapeutic strategy when beta-agonists are less effective.

(h)
Educate on side effects, advocate deprescribing, and review medicines regularly to reduce polypharmacy and interactions.

(i)
Heightened sensitivity to CNS depressants causes sedation, cognitive impairment and falls.

(j)
Impaired baroreceptor reflex with antihypertensives causes orthostatic hypotension.

(k)
Reduced renal function prolongs the effects of renally excreted drugs, and reduced cardiac reserve affects the distribution and efficacy of cardiovascular drugs.

(l)
Enhanced sensitivity to anticoagulants raises bleeding risk, and decreased responsiveness to some drugs causes suboptimal therapeutic outcomes and adverse drug reactions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Aims: maintain airway patency, facilitate gas exchange, enhance nutritional intake, prevent complications and slow progression, and inform the person about the disease, prognosis and treatment.

(b)
Bronchodilators and corticosteroids (by puffer), expectorants, oxygen therapy, antibiotics and vaccines for chest infections, pulmonary rehabilitation (about eight weeks of assessment, supervised exercise and education, then reassessment and referral to a maintenance program) and, in a few, lung volume reduction surgery or endobronchial valves.

(c)
Assess difficulty breathing, rate and depth of respirations, use of accessory muscles, and abnormal breath sounds (wheezes, rhonchi, crackles).

(d)
Prevention: avoid smoking, keep a healthy weight, eat well, stay active, limit alcohol, avoid environmental hazards such as air pollution, and take vaccinations.

(e)
Airway diseases (asthma, COPD) and lung tissue disease (pulmonary fibrosis) make breathing or oxygen diffusion difficult; asthma and COPD have no cure, and smoking is the leading cause of COPD.

(f)
Pulmonary hypertension damages stiff, narrowed lung vessels so the heart pumps harder, with fatigue, fainting, chest pain, palpitations and foot edema.

(g)
Tuberculosis most often affects the lungs; cough over 3 weeks, chest pain, coughing blood, night sweats and fever; risk is higher with HIV or a weakened immune system.

(h)
Airways and tissues become less elastic, lung capacity falls, osteoporosis can alter chest shape, and respiratory muscles weaken.

(i)
Asthma and COPD are chronic with no cure, and pulmonary fibrosis scars the lungs.

(j)
Long-term low oxygen can damage vital organs; home oxygen therapy returns levels to normal, prolongs life and may improve quality of life.

(k)
Pulmonary fibrosis causes breathlessness that worsens with exercise, dry cough and tiredness; pulmonary hypertension causes fatigue and lightheadedness.

(l)
Chest infections are treated with antibiotics and prevented with pneumonia and flu vaccines.

questions.question:
Senescence (biological ageing).
Describe senescence under the following headings:
(a) Definition
(b) Distinguishing characteristics
(c) Reduced organ reserve
(d) Examples of physiological decline at age 75 compared with age 30
Explain why older adults are more vulnerable:
(e) Post-maturational changes
(f) Reduced organ reserve
(g) Stiffening of connective tissue
(h) Variation between individuals
Distinguish between homeostasis and homeostenosis:
(i) Homeostasis
(j) Homeostenosis
(k) Link to ageing
(l) Modifiable influences on decline
questions.answerText:
(a)
Senescence is the decline in fitness components of an individual with increasing age owing to internal deterioration, covering all post-maturational changes and the increasing vulnerability that results.

(b)
Characteristics: universal, arising from within the individual, gradual, and harmful to the individual.

(c)
Reduced organ reserve with ageing means a reduced ability to maintain body equilibrium.

(d)
At 75, compared with 30, the average person has 92% of brain weight, 84% of basal metabolism, 70% of kidney filtration rate and 43% of maximal breathing capacity.

(e)
Senescence causes a group of effects that decrease expectation of life with increasing age.

(f)
Less organ reserve leaves little capacity to cope with stress.

(g)
Stiffer connective tissue makes organs, blood vessels and airways more rigid, and tissues struggle to obtain oxygen and nutrients and remove carbon dioxide and wastes.

(h)
All people age, but not at the same rate.

(i)
Homeostasis is maintenance of body equilibrium: the body's ability to regulate its inner environment so it stays stable against outside fluctuations.

(j)
Homeostenosis is a decreased ability to maintain homeostasis: inability to restore homeostasis after environmental changes.

(k)
Homeostenosis is often associated with ageing.

(l)
Some ageing changes are plastic (modifiable and can be slowed); 70% of physical decline is related to modifiable risk factors: smoking, poor nutrition, physical inactivity and failure to use screening services.

(a)
Influenza: an acute, highly contagious viral respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses.

(b)
Immunosenescence: reduced skin and mucosal barriers, weaker phagocytosis, and fewer and less efficient T-cells and B-cells, so infections are more severe, often need hospitalisation and carry higher mortality; vaccines also work less well.

(c)
Pneumococcal disease: pneumonia, sinus and ear infection, bacteremia or meningitis. Tuberculosis: cough over 3 weeks, night sweats, coughing blood. Asthma and COPD: symptoms worsened by a respiratory virus such as a cold or the flu.

(d)
• Priority 1: influenza is a serious health concern in older adults and related mortality rises sharply after 65, so assess breathing (rate and depth, accessory muscle use, breath sounds), maintain airway patency and assist gas exchange.
• Priority 2: prevent complications, enhance nutritional intake and give information on the disease process and treatment.
• Priority 3: prevention, with influenza vaccine before the season and pneumococcal vaccine for those over 65.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia (60% to 70% of cases): a gradual, progressive decline in memory, thinking, behaviour and social skills that affects functioning.

(b)
Predisposing factors: increasing age (risk roughly doubles every five years after 65), APOE e4 gene mutations, midlife hypertension, diabetes and obesity, smoking, excessive alcohol, physical inactivity, and low education with limited mental stimulation.

(c)
Pathophysiology: the brain shrinks and brain cells die; amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are present, and cell-to-cell communication falls as a chemical messenger is depleted.

(d)
• Medical: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine patch) first; memantine for moderate to severe disease; lecanemab IV every two weeks for early disease; antidepressants for behavioural symptoms. There is no cure.
• Nursing: regular assessment of cognition, behaviour and physical status; individualised care plans; memory aids (calendars, reminders, memory books); validation, redirection and distraction for behaviour.
• Nursing: help with bathing, dressing and eating; accurate medication management; safety and fall prevention; emotional support; education of patient and caregivers; teamwork with other professionals.
• Also: structured daily routine with gentle exercise and cognitive activities, good sleep hygiene, individualised reminiscing (favourite music, old photos, tactile crafts), and an environment with minimal failure and maximal use of retained abilities.
questions.question:

The person has trouble managing bills, cannot do more than one task at a time, wears clothes unsuited to the weather and does not know how to handle food burning on the stove.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the medical and nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Heart diseases are often an accumulation of risk factors from lifestyle choices, family history and ageing; the risk rises with age, and 30% to 40% of people hospitalised with heart attacks are aged 75 and older.
• Age-related changes occur in the heart and blood vessels: resting heart rate usually does not change, but the heart cannot beat as fast as in youth during stress or physical activity.

(b)
Manifestations of coronary heart disease: hypertension, heart failure, atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction (heart attack).

(c)
• Options: control blood pressure, manage cholesterol, eat heart-healthy foods, avoid or limit alcohol and smoking, exercise, maintain a healthy weight and manage stress.
• Medications: statins, aspirin, nitroglycerin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers; surgery and cardiac rehabilitation are also options.
• Justification (lifestyle risk reduction): risk factors accumulate from lifestyle choices, so avoiding smoking and alcohol limits, eating heart-healthy foods, exercising and keeping a healthy weight act on the causes that build up over time.
• Justification (blood pressure control): hypertension is itself a manifestation of coronary heart disease, so controlling blood pressure addresses this person's existing problem directly.
questions.question:
An older adult with high blood pressure and a family history of heart disease smokes, drinks alcohol, eats an unhealthy diet and is physically inactive.
(a) Identify the risk factors for coronary heart disease in this person, including age-related changes in the heart.
(b) State the manifestations and complications of coronary heart disease to watch for.
(c) List the nursing management and preventive options, and justify one of them.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Elder abuse: a single or repeated act, or lack of appropriate action, in a relationship of trust that causes harm or distress. This is neglect, the failure to provide essential care: malnutrition, dehydration, untreated conditions, poor hygiene, unsafe environment. Emotional distress fits emotional abuse (depression, anxiety, withdrawal).

(b)
• Elder Abuse Suspicion Index (EASI): unexplained injuries, patient feelings about the caregiver, poor hygiene or neglect, used in routine encounters.
• Hwalek-Sengstock Elder Abuse Screening Test: risk factors such as dependency, isolation and financial exploitation. Indicators checklist: physical signs, behavioural cues and caregiver-patient interactions, used with clinical judgement.

(c)
• Immediate intervention: ensure a safe environment and give emergency care; start a nutritional plan and wound care for the ulcers; psychologist counselling for anxiety and feelings of abandonment.
• Comprehensive physical and psychosocial evaluation with a multidisciplinary team (doctors, social workers, legal professionals); accurate, detailed and objective records of observations, injuries and statements.

(d)
Educate the son and his wife on elder care and the legal implications of neglect; recommend a caregiver support group, respite care and counselling; teach stress management.

(e)
• Report to Adult Protective Services or local authorities; the social worker works with police and community services; legal professionals assist with restraining orders, guardianship or restitution.
• Temporary residential care with discussion of long-term care with extended family; regular monitoring and long-term care plans and support services to keep her safe.
questions.question:

(a) Identify the problem and the type of abuse, with the indicators.
(b) Name the screening tools and state what each assesses.
(c) State the key management steps and safety considerations.
(d) State the education and support to give the caregivers.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Epidermis and dermis thin with reduced cell turnover and collagen synthesis; collagen and elastin break down, causing wrinkles and sagging; subcutaneous fat is lost.

(b)
Sweat glands atrophy, sebaceous and sweat gland activity falls, nails thicken from calcium deposits, body and head hair are lost, pigment-producing cells fall (graying) and remaining cells enlarge (age spots).

(c)
Reduced fibroblast activity and less vascularisation slow healing; dermal vessel walls become fragile, giving telangiectasia and easy bruising.

(d)
Seborrheic keratosis, actinic keratosis, and basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma are more likely, worsened by sun exposure and impaired immune surveillance.

(e)
Limit warm baths to three times a week and restrict soap to the axilla, groin, scalp and soles of the feet.

(f)
Apply emollients while skin is moist, take extra care because they are slippery and can cause a fall, and use a humidifier.

(g)
Position carefully, avoid adhesives, have at-risk people wear long sleeves and trousers, moisturise and keep the environment safe. For a tear, press with a dry clean cloth to stop bleeding, clean with saline or warm water, realign the flap and apply a nonadherent dressing taped to itself.

(h)
Assess high-risk skin daily, reposition regularly, use support surfaces, trim nails, and refer thick toenails to a podiatrist.

(i)
Less subcutaneous fat, reduced blood flow and fewer sweat glands mean less insulation against cold and heat, risking hypothermia and overheating.

(j)
Reduced fat and blood supply make pressure sores more likely.

(k)
Dry skin itches, scales and cracks, lets bacteria in, interrupts sleep and can lead to infection.

(l)
Thin fragile skin tears, bleeds and bruises painfully, and the weakened barrier raises infection risk and delays healing.

(b) The esophagus
