questions.explanation: RNA polymerase synthesizes mRNA complementary to the DNA template strand. This enzyme adds ribonucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction. RNA polymerase II specifically transcribes protein-coding genes in eukaryotes.

questions.question: Which drug demonstrates enhanced activation in CYP2C1917 carriers?
questions.explanation: Clopidogrel, a prodrug, shows enhanced activation to its active metabolite in CYP2C1917 carriers. These ultra-rapid metabolizers achieve better platelet inhibition than extensive metabolizers. Conversely, poor metabolizers experience reduced clopidogrel efficacy.

The highly polymorphic CYP2D6 gene resides on chromosome 22q13.1 and consists of nine exons and eight introns. Over 100 genetic variants have been identified, resulting from various mutations including duplications and deletions. This gene's extensive polymorphism significantly affects the metabolism of approximately 20-25% of all administered drugs.
questions.question: The CYP2D6 gene is located on which chromosome?
Which CYP3A4 variant demonstrates no enzyme function?
questions.explanation: CYP3A44, 5, and 6 variants exhibit complete loss of enzyme function. These null alleles are relatively rare compared to reduced-function variants. Poor metabolizers experience elevated drug concentrations and toxicity risk.

questions.question: Which chromosomal location harbors the NAT2 gene, relevant to genotyping panels used for acetylator status determination?
questions.explanation: The NAT2 gene is located on chromosome 8p21 and encodes the enzyme responsible for acetylation of numerous arylamine and hydrazine drugs. Polymorphisms at this locus determine an individual's acetylator status, which strongly influences drug clearance and toxicity risk. This chromosomal location is a standard reference point in pharmacogenetic testing panels.

Ultra-rapid metabolizers clear CYP2D6 substrates unusually quickly because of extra functional gene copies, lowering steady-state drug concentrations. Achieving therapeutic effect in these patients often requires doses well above the population average. This contrasts with poor metabolizers, who require reduced doses to avoid toxicity.
questions.question: Which CYP2D6-related finding would most directly explain a patient requiring markedly higher-than-average doses of a CYP2D6 substrate to achieve therapeutic effect?

questions.explanation: The -1639A allele reduces VKORC1 gene transcription, resulting in lower baseline levels of the target enzyme that warfarin inhibits. With less enzyme available, a smaller warfarin dose is needed to achieve the desired anticoagulant effect. Failure to lower the dose in these patients raises the risk of excessive anticoagulation.
options: Lower warfarin dose is typically needed
Only intravenous vitamin K is required
Higher warfarin dose is typically needed
Warfarin has no effect in this genotype
questions.question: A patient starting warfarin carries the VKORC1 -1639A allele, associated with reduced enzyme expression. What dosing implication follows from this genotype?

questions.explanation: Steady-state drug concentrations are typically reached after approximately four to five half-lives of consistent dosing, when the rate of drug administration equals the rate of elimination. Assessing therapeutic effect before this point may lead to premature and inaccurate dose adjustments. This principle applies broadly across drugs with varying elimination half-lives.
options: Time required for renal filtration alone
Time required for complete drug elimination
Time required for first-pass metabolism only
Time required for oral absorption completion
Time required to reach steady state
questions.question: A patient begins a new fixed-dose medication and clinicians wait several half-lives before assessing full therapeutic effect. What pharmacokinetic principle underlies this waiting period?

questions.explanation: PolyA polymerase adds approximately 200 adenine nucleotides to the 3' end of eukaryotic mRNA. This tail enhances mRNA stability and translation efficiency. The polyA tail also serves as a quality control marker indicating complete mRNA processing.
questions.question: What is the approximate number of adenine nucleotides in the polyA tail?
A patient with two non-functional CYP2D6 alleles is started on tramadol and reports no analgesic benefit despite escalating doses. What is the pharmacologic basis for this treatment failure?
questions.explanation: Tramadol requires CYP2D6-mediated activation to its more potent opioid metabolite for full analgesic effect. Patients with two null alleles cannot perform this bioactivation, so therapeutic response is markedly reduced. Poor metabolizers of prodrug opioids often require alternative non-prodrug analgesics.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of enzyme induction?
questions.explanation: Enzyme induction primarily increases transcription through nuclear receptor activation. Ligand-activated receptors bind response elements, recruiting transcriptional machinery. This process requires hours to days for effect.

questions.question: Which CYP2C19 variant is most common in Asian populations?
questions.explanation: CYP2C192 exhibits particularly high frequency in Asian populations, causing poor metabolizer phenotype. This variant significantly affects clopidogrel and PPI therapy. Population-specific allele frequencies necessitate ethnic consideration.

courses.title: Thermotherapy II
courses.objectives:
Principles, Physiological Effects and Indications of Heat Therapy: Q1–6
Hydrocollator Pack and Paraffin Wax Bath: Q7–14
Fluidotherapy, Whirlpool and Contrast Bath: Q15–21
Deep Heating: Ultrasound, Phonophoresis and Microwave Diathermy: Q22–31
Cryotherapy and the Comparison of Heat and Cold: Q32–40

questions.question:
A patient recovering from hand surgery presents with pain, oedema and reduced range of motion of the fingers in the subacute stage, and desensitisation is also required.
(i) State the stage of the condition for which fluidotherapy is used.
(ii) State the modality and rationale.
(iii) State the dosage/duration and method of application.
(iv) State the expected therapeutic effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Stage:
- Fluidotherapy is indicated for subacute and chronic conditions, including postoperative rehabilitation of the distal extremities.
(ii) Modality/rationale:
- Fluidotherapy: the fluidised cellulose particles act like a low-viscosity fluid, allowing the limb to be suspended/float and permitting active/resistive exercise without getting wet, while providing warmth, circulation and a desensitisation effect.
(iii) Dosage/method:
- Temperature about 38-45 degrees C for 15-20 minutes; part undressed, jewellery removed, skin sensation checked, open wounds covered with a plastic sheet.
- Part extended through the portal, sleeve closed; patient exercises the part inside the cabinet; therapist may perform passive movement through additional entry ports.
(iv) Expected effects:
- Decreased pain, increased ROM, decreased swelling, decreased spasm, desensitisation of hypersensitive tissue; mild erythema is a normal finding after treatment.

questions.question:
A patient with tendonitis is being considered for phonophoresis using a topical anti-inflammatory medication.
(i) State the indications for phonophoresis.
(ii) State the general ultrasound contraindications/precautions relevant to this treatment.
(iii) State the precautions specific to the phonophoresis technique.
(iv) Justify the choice of phonophoresis over plain topical medication alone.
questions.answerText:
(i) Indications:
- Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), tendonitis, bursitis, adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), arthritis.
(ii) Ultrasound contraindications/precautions:
- Ischaemic/circulatory-impaired areas, over cancerous tumours, sites of active infection, and other general ultrasound contraindications apply, unless thermal effects of ultrasound are otherwise contraindicated.
(iii) Technique-specific precautions:
- Use only approved ultrasound transmission media; direct coupling is recommended, as bladder-method efficacy has not been established; ensure skin is well moistened, avoiding dry skin.
- Position the extremity to encourage circulation; use continuous output to maximise effect unless thermal effects are contraindicated; cover remaining medication with an occlusive dressing after treatment.
(iv) Justification:
- Thermal and non-thermal characteristics of high-frequency sound waves enhance diffusion of the topical drug; heating increases kinetic energy of drug/cell-membrane molecules and dilates entry points such as hair follicles and sweat glands.
- This enhances drug delivery deeper into tissue compared with topical medication alone, while avoiding the risks and inconvenience of intravenous therapy.

(A) Equipment: Stainless steel or enamelled bath of molten wax (melting point 54-55 degrees C), mixed with mineral/paraffin oil (about 7:1) to stay liquid at 40-44 degrees C.
- Thermostatically controlled with a thermometer to read wax temperature.
(B) Technique: Equipment prepared (temperature regulated to about 49 degrees C); patient skin checked and sensation-tested.
- Methods include dip and wrap, dip and leave-in, dip and leave-in with IRR, dip and wrap with elevation, pouring-on, brushing-on, wrap-on.
(C) Dosage: Dip and wrap uses 6-12 dips to build a 2-3 mm wax coating; dip and leave-in keeps the part immersed 15-20 minutes.
- Bath is usually maintained between 42-52 degrees C.
(D) Indications: General heat indications; particularly useful for poor heat tolerance, dry scaly skin, and stretching scars/adhesions before mobilisation.
(E) Contraindications: Open wounds, skin infection, defective thermal sensation, deficient cutaneous circulation, cancer, tuberculosis, gross oedema, deep x-ray therapy areas, liniments, strong analgesic drugs.
(F) Precautions: Fire precautions (no naked flame, no smoking); fire blanket/foam extinguisher available; never pour water on overheated wax.
- Thermal sensation testing is essential; deal with spillage promptly as it makes floors slippery.
(ii) Clinical basis: Low specific heat (does not feel as hot as water though it holds about six times the heat) and slower heat conduction reduce burn risk.
- Self-insulation from the first wax layer and trapped sweat allow safe, mouldable, even heating of small contoured areas.
questions.question:
Describe the paraffin wax bath under the following headings: (A) equipment, (B) technique of application, (C) dosage, (D) indications, (E) contraindications, (F) precautions.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for its use.

questions.answerText:
(i) Problem(s):
- Chronic low back pain and chronic muscle spasm, both listed as general indications for heat use.
(ii) Category/example:
- Superficial heat; example: hydrocollator (hot) pack, which heats by conduction.
(iii) Physiological effects:
- Vasodilatation and increased blood flow; relaxation of muscle spasm; pain relief via the gate-control mechanism and reduced ischaemia; increased elasticity of connective tissue; reduced joint stiffness.
(iv) Technique of application:
- The heated agent is wrapped with adequate insulation (e.g. towelling) to prevent burns and applied over the low back for about 15-20 minutes (up to 20-30 minutes for a hydrocollator pack).
- Patient positioned comfortably and monitored for excessive redness or discomfort during treatment; can be combined with exercise or manual therapy for optimal outcomes.
questions.question:
A patient with chronic low back pain and muscle spasm is treated with a superficial conductive heating modality.
(i) Identify the problem(s) making this patient suitable for superficial heat.
(ii) State which category (superficial heat, deep heat, or cryotherapy) this modality belongs to and give an example.
(iii) State the physiological effects relevant to the patient's problem.
(iv) Describe the general technique of application.

A patient presenting with a superficial trigger point requiring localised, concentrated deep heating is to be treated with microwave diathermy.
(i) State the modality selected and why.
(ii) Describe the preparation of the patient and the equipment.
(iii) Describe the step-by-step technique of application.
(iv) State the precautions to be observed during treatment.
(v) State the possible adverse effects/dangers and how they are managed.
questions.answerText:
(i) Modality selected:
- Microwave diathermy (MWD), preferred where more concentrated, localised heating of a superficial target such as a trigger point, fibromyositis or epicondylitis is required.
(ii) Preparation:
- Patient positioned suitably on a wooden plinth or chair for easy access; part exposed and rest of body draped; skin cleaned and inspected for cuts, lesions or bruises.
- Applicator (small circular, large circular or rectangular) selected according to the shape of the target area.
(iii) Technique:
- Microwave energy is emitted as a divergent field; a compact fluorescent tube (CFL) may be used to detect the concentrated area of focus, glowing brightest there and fading toward the periphery.
- Intensity is governed by the inverse square law (intensity falls with distance from the source); the patient should experience a sensation of comfortable warmth.
(iv) Precautions:
- Avoid exposure over the genitals, eyes or a gravid uterus.
(v) Adverse effects/dangers and management:
- Strictly contraindicated with a pacemaker or a thermal sensation deficit, so these are excluded first; since MWD is absorbed mainly by superficial fat, monitor for excessive warmth and adjust distance/intensity to avoid overheating.

questions.question:
Describe cryotherapy under the following headings: (A) equipment/forms of application, (B) technique/dosage, (C) indications, (D) contraindications, (E) precautions.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for its use.
questions.answerText:
(A) Equipment/forms: Ice bags (crushed or cubed), commercial ice packs, ice cups (ice cube massage), cold water baths (immersion or whirlpool).
- Also ice towels, vapo-coolant sprays, cold gel, cryocuff/controlled cold therapy units.
(B) Technique/dosage: Usually applied for 20-30 minutes for maximum cooling of superficial and deep tissues.
- The way ice is applied varies with the required effect (ice towels, ice packs, immersion, ice cube massage, excitatory quick ice, ice spray, cold gel).
(C) Indications: Acute or chronic pain, acute or chronic muscle spasm/guarding, acute inflammation or injury, postsurgical pain and oedema.
- Also superficial first-degree burn, muscle spasticity, and use with exercise to facilitate mobilisation and relieve pain.
(D) Contraindications: Cold sensitivity/hypersensitivity, nerve palsy, cold allergy, circulatory or sensory impairment.
- Also hypertension, Raynaud's disease or cold urticaria, uncovered open wounds, cardiac or respiratory disorders.
(E) Precautions: Monitor the sensory response through the cold, aching/stinging, pain/burning and numbness stages.
- Document subjective complaints, agent used, area of exposure, treatment time and patient response.
(ii) Clinical basis: Cold reduces muscle spindle firing rate, cell membrane permeability, tissue metabolism, nerve conduction velocity, pain perception and joint fluid viscosity.
- This underlies its use for pain, spasm, spasticity, swelling and accelerating repair (e.g. ice massage for pressure sores).

questions.question:
(i) Define thermotherapy.
(ii) Classify thermotherapy modalities as superficial or deep heating, giving examples of each and their depth of penetration.
(iii) State the principal modes of heat transfer used by these modalities.
(iv) Describe the physiological effects of heat.
questions.answerText:
(i) Definition:
- Thermotherapy and cryotherapy, the application of therapeutic heat and cold, are referred to as conductive modalities.
- Thermotherapy can involve the use of superficial or deep tissue thermal energy to induce a specific biological response.
(ii) Classification:
- Superficial heating: warm whirlpool, warm hydrocollator packs, paraffin baths, sauna, infrared radiation, fluidotherapy; penetration up to about 1 cm or less (up to 1-2 cm).
- Deep tissue heating: ultrasound, radiowave, microwave and Tecar diathermies.
(iii) Modes of heat transfer:
- Conduction (direct contact, e.g. hot packs, paraffin bath); convection (fluid circulation over the body, e.g. fluidotherapy); radiation/conversion (changing one energy form into another, e.g. ultrasound, radiant heat).
(iv) Physiological effects of heat:
- Vasodilation and increased blood flow; increased metabolic rate; relaxation of muscle spasm.
- Pain relief via the gate-control mechanism and reduced ischaemia; increased elasticity of connective tissue.
- Stimulation of fibroblast proliferation, accelerated endothelial cell proliferation and improved phagocytic activity of inflammatory cells.

(i) Indications:
- General heat indications (subacute/chronic conditions); useful for patients with poor heat tolerance, dry scaly skin, and for stretching scars/adhesions before mobilisation.
(ii) Contraindications:
- Open wounds, skin infections, defective thermal sensation, deficient cutaneous circulation (e.g. recently healed skin grafts), cancer, tuberculosis, gross oedema, deep x-ray therapy area, liniments, strong analgesic (narcotic) drugs.
(iii) Precautions:
- Wax is highly inflammable; never bring near naked lights; smoking prohibited in the wax room; must not be heated over an open flame; keep a fire blanket or foam extinguisher available.
- Never pour water on overheated wax; it renders the floor slippery if spilt and spillage must be dealt with properly; thermal skin sensation test is essential as patients can be burnt easily.
(iv) Justification:
- Low specific heat so it does not feel as hot as water yet provides about six times the heat of water; conducts heat more slowly so tissue heats up more slowly, decreasing burn risk.
- Self-insulating (thin layer of air trapped by first wax layer, non-evaporating sweat); moulds round the bony contours of hands and feet giving even heating.
- Leaves skin moist, soft and pliable, suiting the small, irregular hand joints better than a flat hydrocollator pack.
questions.question:
A patient with chronic hand osteoarthritis is being considered for paraffin wax bath treatment.
(i) State the indications for paraffin wax therapy.
(ii) State the contraindications to paraffin wax therapy.
(iii) State the precautions to be observed.
(iv) Justify the choice of paraffin wax over a hydrocollator pack for this patient.

questions.answerText:
(i) Therapeutic effects:
- Decreases in inflammation, pain, and muscle guarding (only if the patient is receptive to the use of ice).
- Decreased muscle spindle firing rate, cell membrane permeability, tissue metabolism, nerve conduction velocity, pain perception, joint fluid viscosity, muscle strength and endurance; cold reduces spasticity and spasm.
(ii) Mechanism:
- Reflex vasoconstriction via sympathetic fibres and direct effects on blood vessels; the Lewis hunting reaction is a marked increase in blood flow that occurs to maintain tissue temperature and prevent tissue damage.
- Cold reduces spasticity/spasm probably through reduced velocity of nerve conduction and depressed sensitivity of receptors such as the muscle spindle.
- Reduced metabolic rate of cooled tissue allows cooled muscle to contract more times before fatigue and limits further injury by helping the tissue survive post-injury cellular hypoxia.
(iii) Dangers:
- Tissue death, frostbite, nerve damage, freezing of tissue.
(iv) Prevention:
- Observe contraindications (cold sensitivity/allergy, Raynaud's disease/cold urticaria, circulatory or sensory impairment, cardiac/respiratory disorders, nerve palsy, uncovered open wounds, hypertension) before treatment.
- Keep to the recommended application time (usually 20-30 minutes) and monitor the sensory cold-aching-burning-numbness sequence, stopping if adverse signs occur.
questions.question:
(i) State the therapeutic (local) effects of cold.
(ii) Explain the physiological mechanism by which cold produces these effects, including the Lewis hunting reaction.
(iii) State the dangers/adverse effects of cold application.
(iv) State how these dangers are prevented.

(i) Define therapeutic ultrasound and classify it among thermotherapy modalities.
(ii) State its principle of production (how the sound energy is generated).
(iii) Describe its thermal physiological effects.
(iv) Describe its non-thermal physiological effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Definition/classification:
- A deep-penetrating modality producing thermal and non-thermal effects, classified as a deep heating modality; therapeutic frequency about 0.75-3 MHz, depth of penetration up to about 5 cm.
(ii) Principle of production:
- Produced by an alternating current flowing through a piezoelectric crystal in the transducer.
- As the current reverses polarity the crystal expands and contracts (reverse piezoelectric effect), generating high-frequency sound waves transmitted to the tissue.
(iii) Thermal effects (continuous mode, 0.5-3 W/cm2), from a 40-45 degrees C tissue temperature rise:
- 1 degree C increases metabolic rate; 2-3 degrees C reduces pain and spasm and increases blood flow; 4 degrees C increases tissue extensibility and decreases joint stiffness.
- Also increased enzyme activity, increased tissue perfusion, decreased nerve conduction velocity.
(iv) Non-thermal effects (pulsed mode/low intensity continuous):
- Stable cavitation - oscillation and contraction/expansion of gas bubbles allowing fluid movement and membrane transport.
- Acoustic (micro)streaming - fluid movement along cell membranes increasing membrane permeability.
- Micromassage - compression/rarefaction of cells affecting interstitial fluid movement, producing sclerolytic effects and release of contracture/adhesion.

questions.question:
(i) Define cryotherapy.
(ii) State the temperature range and depth of penetration used therapeutically.
(iii) State the principal modes of heat transfer involved in cold application.
(iv) Describe the physiological effects of cold on the tissues.
questions.answerText:
(i) Definition:
- Cryotherapy, or ice therapy, is the application of cold to the body tissues (locally or generally) for therapeutic purposes.
(ii) Temperature range and penetration:
- Therapeutic cold ranges from about 0 to 18.3 degrees C (32-65 degrees F); marked decreases in localised blood flow occur at about 12.83-15 degrees C (55-59 degrees F).
- Skin temperature is often reduced to about 10 degrees C; depth of cold penetration can reach about 5 cm.
(iii) Modes of heat transfer:
- The most common modes of heat transfer with cold application are conduction and evaporation.
(iv) Physiological effects:
- Decreased muscle spindle firing rate, decreased cell membrane permeability, decreased tissue metabolism.
- Decreased nerve conduction velocity, decreased pain perception, decreased joint fluid viscosity, decreased muscle strength and endurance.
- Cold also produces the Lewis hunting reaction, a reflex vasoconstriction followed by a compensatory increase in blood flow.
- The magnitude of temperature change depends on the cooling agent, temperature difference, subcutaneous fat, thermal conductivity of the area, limb circumference and duration of application.

(i) Local effects:
- Increased blood flow, enhancing nutrient delivery and waste removal; increased tissue extensibility, improving joint range of motion.
- Reduction of muscle spasm and muscle relaxation; accelerated healing by promoting cellular activity in subacute/chronic conditions.
(ii) Mechanism:
- Heat stimulates cutaneous thermoreceptors connected to blood vessels, causing release of bradykinin, which along with prostaglandins and histamine mediates vasodilation by relaxing arteriolar smooth muscle.
- Pain relief also occurs via the gate-control theory: large-diameter thermoreceptor/A-beta afferent activation produces presynaptic inhibition of small-diameter nociceptive traffic at the substantia gelatinosa, closing the gate to pain.
(iii) Dangers:
- Burns, particularly over bony prominences or with reduced subcutaneous fat; increased blood flow from heat can induce oedema and exacerbate acute inflammation.
- Superficial heat is contraindicated in acute inflammation, impaired sensation or cognition, areas of impaired circulation, malignancy, and open wounds (for certain modalities).
(iv) Prevention:
- Check sensation and skin integrity before treatment; use adequate insulation (e.g. towels with hot packs); monitor skin colour and patient feedback during treatment.
- Inspect the skin and evaluate symptom change after treatment; avoid heat over bony prominences, acute inflammation, impaired circulation/sensation and malignancy.
questions.question:
(i) State the local physiological effects of superficial heat.
(ii) Explain the mechanism involving bradykinin and the gate-control theory by which superficial heat relieves pain.
(iii) State the dangers of superficial heat application.
(iv) State how these dangers are prevented.

questions.answerText:
(i) Distinction:
- Paraffin wax has a low specific heat and low thermal conductivity, so does not feel as hot as water though it provides about six times the heat of water, and is typically used on small, irregular areas such as the hands and feet.
- The hydrocollator pack's silica gel/bentonite gives high heat retention (about 30 minutes) and is typically applied to larger, flatter body areas.
(ii) Advantages of paraffin wax:
- Moulds round bony contours of hands and feet for even heating, comfortable for patients with poor heat tolerance, leaves skin moist, soft and pliable; 2 or 3 patients can be treated at a time.
- Low specific heat and low thermal conductivity reduce burn risk while still delivering about six times the heat of water.
(iii) Advantages of the hydrocollator pack:
- Easy to apply, sedative effect, saves clinician time, readily available for home use, relatively inexpensive, variety of sizes/shapes, moist comfortable heat with deeper penetration than dry heat, covers moderate to large areas.
- Low level of skill needed for application and it is generally a safe modality.
(iv) Limitations:
- Paraffin wax requires fire precautions; sedimentation/contamination of the bath must be managed and it must be cleaned regularly.
- The hydrocollator pack does not maintain good contact with small/contoured areas, does not allow active motion during treatment, has no temperature control, gel packs could leak, and heat retention lasts no more than about 30 minutes.
questions.question:
(i) Distinguish between paraffin wax bath and hydrocollator pack in terms of specific heat/heat retention and typical areas treated.
(ii) State the advantages of paraffin wax.
(iii) State the advantages of the hydrocollator pack.
(iv) State the limitations of each.

(i) Distinguish between continuous and pulsed ultrasound in terms of duty cycle and effect produced.
(ii) State the advantages of continuous (thermal) ultrasound.
(iii) State the advantages of pulsed (non-thermal) ultrasound.
(iv) State the limitations of each.
questions.answerText:
(i) Distinction:
- Continuous ultrasound: intensity remains constant throughout treatment, inducing a thermal effect, used for chronic conditions (100% duty cycle).
- Pulsed ultrasound: interrupted emission, no energy during the off period, inducing a non-thermal effect, used for acute/subacute conditions with a low duty cycle (e.g. 20-25%, or ratios such as 1:1, 1:4).
(ii) Advantages of continuous/thermal ultrasound:
- Produces measurable temperature rises (1-4 degrees C) that increase metabolic rate, reduce pain and spasm, increase blood flow, and increase tissue extensibility and decrease joint stiffness.
- At 100% duty cycle, 1 MHz output (1.75 W/cm2) needs about 4 minutes and 3 MHz output (1.5 W/cm2) needs about 10 minutes to raise tissue temperature by 4 degrees C.
(iii) Advantages of pulsed/non-thermal ultrasound:
- The inter-pulse duration allows significant dissipation of thermal heat, minimising thermal effect, producing cavitation, acoustic microstreaming and micromassage that aid soft tissue healing without excess heating.
- Non-thermal effects are obtained using a pulsed duty cycle of about 20-25% or a continuous mode below 0.5 W/cm2.
(iv) Limitations:
- Continuous ultrasound is unsuitable for acute injuries, listed as a contraindication at a 100% duty cycle.
- Pulsed ultrasound produces minimal thermal effect, so it is less suited to conditions requiring the specific thermal benefits (e.g. increased tissue extensibility) obtained with continuous mode.

(i) Distinction:
- 1 MHz gives deeper penetration with less attenuation, used on tissues greater than about 3 cm deep (deep lesions, 3-5 cm).
- 3 MHz gives greater attenuation, used on more superficial tissues (about 1-2 cm, or superficial lesions of 2-3 cm).
(ii) Advantages of 1 MHz:
- Effective for deeper lesions such as rotator cuff, vastus intermedius, or gastrocnemius, reaching deep (about 5 cm) tissues.
- The half value depth of 1 MHz is greater than that of 3 MHz in fat, muscle and bone, giving more even heating of deeper structures.
(iii) Advantages of 3 MHz:
- Appropriate for superficial lesions such as patellar tendon, medial collateral ligament, or brachialis, absorbed more superficially with a shorter vigorous-heating treatment time (about 3-4 minutes versus 10-12 minutes at 1 MHz).
- 3 MHz is appropriate for superficial lesions of about 2-3 cm, being absorbed superficially at 1-2 cm.
(iv) Limitations (reflection at interfaces):
- At a soft tissue/bone interface (periosteum-bone), 15-70% of energy is reflected, creating a potential hot spot regardless of frequency.
- The soft-tissue/air interface reflects about 99.9% of energy, so a coupling medium is essential; 3 MHz cannot reach deep tissue while 1 MHz is less efficient for very superficial lesions.
questions.question:
(i) Distinguish between 1 MHz and 3 MHz ultrasound in terms of depth of penetration and typical clinical use.
(ii) State the advantages of 1 MHz ultrasound.
(iii) State the advantages of 3 MHz ultrasound.
(iv) State the limitations of each, with reference to reflection at tissue interfaces.

A patient requires deep heating close to an area with active growing epiphyseal plates, and osteoporosis is also suspected at the site.
(i) State the suitability of deep heat modalities for this patient.
(ii) State the modalities to avoid and why.
(iii) State a safe alternative modality.
(iv) State the patient advice and follow-up.
questions.answerText:
(i) Suitability:
- Not straightforwardly suitable for ultrasound over the area; caution is required when applying ultrasound over epiphyseal plates of growing bone, and ultrasound is contraindicated over stress fracture sites or sites of osteoporosis.
(ii) Modalities to avoid and why:
- Avoid ultrasound directly over the epiphyseal plate/osteoporotic site because of these listed contraindications/precautions; also avoid an incompletely healed fracture site, a listed contraindication.
(iii) Safe alternative:
- A superficial heating modality applied away from the epiphyseal/osteoporotic area, or the lowest possible ultrasound intensity with careful monitoring elsewhere on the limb, keeping the applicator constantly moving to avoid standing waves.
(iv) Advice/follow-up:
- Explain the reason for caution near the growth plate; advise reporting of any pain or unusual sensation; continually evaluate the effectiveness and safety of any treatment given.

questions.question:
(i) State the effects of heat and of cold on pain, muscle spasm and spasticity.
(ii) Explain the physiological mechanism of these effects.
(iii) State the dangers associated with using heat or cold inappropriately for spasm/spasticity management.
(iv) State how these dangers are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i) Effects:
- Heat reduces pain and muscle spasm and produces muscle relaxation.
- Cold reduces pain, spasticity and muscle spasm, but reduction of muscle guarding by cold applies only if the patient is receptive to the use of ice.
(ii) Mechanism:
- Heat: increased temperature decreases type II/gamma efferent firing while increasing Golgi tendon organ (Ib) firing, reducing alpha motor neuron activity and causing muscle relaxation; pain threshold rises via spinal gating and improved circulation.
- Cold: spasticity/spasm reduction is probably due to reduced velocity of nerve conduction and depressed sensitivity of receptors such as the muscle spindle; spasticity is increased tone from upper motor neuron damage with increased anterior horn cell firing.
(iii) Dangers:
- Applying heat to active acute inflammation can worsen swelling and pain.
- Applying cold to a patient not receptive to ice, or with a contraindication such as cold sensitivity, may fail to reduce or may worsen muscle guarding; inappropriate use risks burns (heat) or frostbite/nerve damage (cold).
- Excessive, sustained muscle spasm can itself become a source of further pain and further spasm if not properly managed.
(iv) Prevention:
- Assess whether acute inflammation is still active before choosing heat or cold; check patient receptiveness and contraindications to ice before using cold for spasm; monitor response and skin condition throughout treatment.

questions.question:
A patient with a subacute hand condition presenting with pain, oedema and stiffness of the distal extremity is being treated with fluidotherapy.
(i) State the stage of the condition for which fluidotherapy is indicated.
(ii) State the modality and the rationale for its selection.
(iii) State the dosage/duration and method of application.
(iv) State the expected therapeutic effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Stage:
- Subacute and chronic conditions of the distal extremities, including postoperative rehabilitation.
(ii) Modality/rationale:
- Fluidotherapy, a dry heating agent transferring heat by convection through heated air circulated over fine cellulose particles in a cabinet.
- Combines thermal and mechanical (massaging) stimuli and allows active exercise of the part while heated, useful for pain, oedema and stiffness.
(iii) Dosage/method:
- Temperature range about 38-45 degrees C; treatment time 15-20 minutes.
- Part undressed, jewellery removed, skin sensation checked; open wounds covered with a plastic sheet; part extended through the portal with sleeve closed; patient exercises the part inside the cabinet.
(iv) Expected effects:
- Decreased pain, increased range of motion, decreased swelling, decreased spasm, desensitisation of hypersensitive tissue.
- A mild erythema of the skin is a normal post-treatment finding.

(i) Distinction:
- Superficial heat raises skin/subcutaneous temperature up to about 1-2 cm deep (hot packs, paraffin wax, infrared, warm whirlpool, fluidotherapy, electric heating pads).
- Deep heat modalities (ultrasound, radiowave/microwave, Tecar diathermy) heat tissue to a greater degree at greater depth; ultrasound can penetrate up to about 5 cm.
(ii) Advantages of superficial heat:
- Easy to apply, generally safe, low level of skill needed, relatively inexpensive, readily available for home use, can cover moderate to large areas.
- Moist heat (e.g. hydrocollator pack) penetrates deeper into tissue than dry heat.
(iii) Advantages of deep heat:
- Ultrasound can heat deeper structures to a greater degree and in less time than superficial heating modalities, without excessively heating the overlying superficial structures.
- Frequency selection (1 MHz versus 3 MHz) allows the depth of heating to be matched to a deeper or more superficial lesion.
(iv) Limitations:
- Superficial heat cannot adequately heat deeper tissue because achieving deep penetration by conduction/convection/radiation alone would injure the skin.
- Deep heat such as ultrasound heats only a limited area (treatment area limited to 2-3 times the ERA) and carries the risk of standing waves/hot spots at tissue interfaces.
questions.question:
(i) Distinguish between superficial heat and deep heat in terms of depth of penetration and example modalities.
(ii) State the advantages of superficial heat.
(iii) State the advantages of deep heat.
(iv) State the limitations of each.

questions.answerText:
(i) Modality:
- Cryotherapy (ice therapy), indicated for acute inflammation or injury, acute pain and acute muscle spasm/guarding.
(ii) Preparation:
- Check for contraindications: cold sensitivity/allergy, Raynaud's disease/cold urticaria, circulatory or sensory impairment, cardiac or respiratory disorders, nerve palsy, uncovered open wounds.
- Prepare the chosen cold agent, e.g. ice bag (crushed or cubed), commercial ice pack, cold gel, or a cold water bath.
(iii) Technique:
- Apply the cold agent over the ankle, usually for about 20-30 minutes for maximum cooling of superficial and deep tissues; the patient will experience the cold-aching/stinging, pain/burning, then numbness sequence.
(iv) Precautions:
- Monitor the patient throughout and document the subjective complaints, agent used, area of exposure, treatment time and response, as recommended for cryotherapy and all physical agents.
(v) Adverse effects/dangers and management:
- Possible adverse effects: tissue death, frostbite, nerve damage, freezing of tissue; treatment is modified or discontinued if any of these signs develop or the patient reports excessive pain.
questions.question:
A patient with an acute ankle sprain presenting with pain and swelling is treated with cryotherapy.
(i) State the modality selected.
(ii) Describe the preparation of the patient and equipment.
(iii) Describe the step-by-step application technique.
(iv) State the precautions during treatment.
(v) State the possible adverse effects/dangers and how to manage them.

questions.answerText:
(A) Equipment: A cabinet of finely ground cellulose particles (from corn cob).
- Thermostatically controlled heated air circulated over and through the particles by an electric fan inside a lid-covered steel cabinet.
(B) Technique: Part undressed, jewellery removed, skin sensation checked; open wounds covered with a plastic sheet.
- Part extended through the portal, sleeve closed; patient exercises the part; therapist may perform passive movement through additional entry ports.
(C) Dosage: Temperature about 38-45 degrees C; treatment time about 15-20 minutes.
(D) Indications: Distal extremities - decrease pain, increase ROM, decrease swelling, decrease spasm, reduce inflammation, postoperative rehabilitation, subacute/chronic conditions.
(E) Contraindications: Fever, anaesthetic area, severe circulatory disorder, haemorrhage, heat-sensitive patients.
(F) Advantages: Easy to use, agitation controllable, most areas treatable, allows active exercise, dry comfortable heat, useful for desensitisation.
- Disadvantages: expensive, closed-in feeling disliked by some, particle intolerance, dependent limb position may be needed.
(ii) Clinical basis: Heat is transferred by convection; the air stream creates air pockets/bubbles giving a massaging action.
- The low-viscosity fluidised particles allow the limb to float, enabling exercise with warmth and circulation.
- This underlies reduced pain and stiffness with active exercise.
questions.question:
Describe fluidotherapy under the following headings: (A) equipment, (B) technique of application, (C) dosage, (D) indications, (E) contraindications, (F) advantages/disadvantages.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for its use.

A patient has a chronic musculoskeletal lesion suitable for continuous-mode therapeutic ultrasound.
(i) Identify the problem in this patient that indicates use of continuous ultrasound.
(ii) State which category of thermotherapy modality therapeutic ultrasound belongs to.
(iii) State the physiological (thermal) effects of continuous ultrasound relevant to this patient.
(iv) Describe the technique of application.
questions.answerText:
(i) Problem:
- A chronic lesion is less sensitive and requires a greater intensity/continuous, thermal-effect ultrasound to produce a physiological response; continuous mode (100% duty cycle) is used for chronic conditions.
(ii) Category:
- Deep heating modality.
(iii) Thermal effects (temperature rise 40-45 degrees C):
- 1 degree C increases metabolic rate; 2-3 degrees C reduces pain and spasm and increases blood flow; 4 degrees C increases tissue extensibility and decreases joint stiffness.
- Also increased pain threshold, increased blood flow, increased collagen extensibility/deposition, increased enzyme activity, increased tissue perfusion, decreased nerve conduction velocity.
(iv) Technique of application:
- Coupling gel applied over an area 2-3 times the ERA; sound head kept moving continuously in slow overlapping circular or longitudinal strokes at about 4 cm/second, begun before turning up intensity.
- Lowest intensity producing the desired effect used; intensity reduced or treatment discontinued if pain is reported.

questions.question:
A patient with Sudeck's atrophy requires prolonged elevated heating of the hand using paraffin wax.
(i) State the stage/condition for which this wax technique is used.
(ii) State the modality/technique and the rationale.
(iii) State the dosage/duration and method of application.
(iv) State the expected therapeutic effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Condition:
- This combined technique is used for treatment of Sudeck's atrophy.
(ii) Modality/technique and rationale:
- Dip and leave-in method combined with infrared radiation (IRR) and elevation; rationale is to achieve prolonged higher temperature with elevation.
(iii) Dosage/method:
- Dip and leave-in method: part kept immersed in the wax bath for 15-20 minutes to form a thin glove.
- To achieve prolonged higher temperature with elevation, the part is secured with a bandage around the ankle or wrist, placed under the IRR lamp, and may be combined with active exercise while the limb is elevated.
(iv) Expected effects:
- Heat production, circulatory effect (vasodilatation), analgesic effect, sedative effect, stretching effect.
- Leaves the skin moist, soft and pliable.

(i) Definition/classification:
- A deep heating modality using electromagnetic energy with a frequency of 2450 Hz and a wavelength range of 10-12 cm.
(ii) Principle/dosage law:
- High-frequency electromagnetic force produced by a composite oscillator called a magnetron; energy directed via a co-axial cable to the applicator antenna and then to the tissue; no tuning needed as the tissue is not part of the circuit.
- Dosage is governed by the inverse square law: the greater the distance from the source, the lower the intensity.
(iii) Determining factor:
- Clinical heating depends on absorption of energy rather than linear penetration, and absorption depends on the relative densities of the tissues; MWD is absorbed better by fat than most other tissues.
- The penetration of MWD, like other electromagnetic energy, is directly proportional to its frequency, though heat production clinically depends more on absorption than on linear penetration.
(iv) Physiological/clinical effects:
- Because fat is very superficial, the direct thermal effect of MWD is largely restricted to superficial tissue; any deeper effect is mainly due to heat transfer from the heated superficial fat layer.
- Clinically the patient should experience a sensation of comfortable warmth; preferred for concentrated, localised heating of superficial targets such as trigger points, fibromyositis and epicondylitis.
- Broad clinical indication of MWD is similar to shortwave diathermy (SWD).
questions.question:
(i) Define microwave diathermy and classify it among thermotherapy modalities.
(ii) State its principle of production and the law governing its dosage.
(iii) State the factor that determines the extent/type of its clinical heating effect.
(iv) State its physiological/clinical effects.

(i) Describe how cold affects spasticity and muscle spasm.
(ii) Explain the physiological mechanism responsible for these effects.
(iii) State the dangers of using cold to manage spasticity/spasm inappropriately.
(iv) State how these dangers are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i) Effects:
- Cold reduces spasticity and reduces muscle spasm; spasticity is a pathological state of increased muscle tone from damage to the upper motor neurons, with the anterior horn cell firing spontaneously at an increased rate, increasing tone in extrafusal muscle fibres.
- Spasm is a normal response to injury or pain, an increase in muscle tone aimed at limiting movement and further damage, but excessive sustained contraction can itself produce more pain and further spasm.
(ii) Mechanism:
- The mechanisms by which cold reduces spasticity and spasm are probably the reduced velocity of nerve conduction and the depressed sensitivity of receptors such as the muscle spindle.
(iii) Dangers:
- Cold applied without regard to the patient's receptiveness or to listed contraindications (cold sensitivity, nerve palsy, circulatory/sensory impairment) may fail to relieve muscle guarding.
- Inappropriate cold application could cause tissue death, frostbite or nerve damage.
- Unmanaged, sustained muscle spasm can itself become a further source of pain.
(iv) Prevention:
- Reduction of muscle guarding by cold applies only if the patient is receptive to the use of ice, so patient response should be assessed.
- Contraindications should be checked before treatment, and the recommended duration and monitoring of the cold-aching-burning-numbness sequence should be followed.

questions.question:
A patient has subacute muscle spasm, joint stiffness and pain that make superficial heat with a hydrocollator (hot) pack appropriate.
(i) Identify the patient's problem(s) that indicate this treatment.
(ii) State which category the hydrocollator pack belongs to: superficial heat, deep heat, or cryotherapy.
(iii) State the physiological effects of this modality that address the problem.
(iv) Describe the technique of application of the hydrocollator pack.
questions.answerText:
(i) Problem(s):
- Subacute/chronic muscle spasm, decreased range of motion, subacute/chronic pain, joint stiffness.
(ii) Category:
- Superficial heating modality.
(iii) Physiological effects:
- Vasodilatation with increased blood flow; increased venous and lymphatic drainage removing waste and re-absorbing oedema.
- Increased cell metabolic rate and tissue extensibility; sedative/soothing effect reducing pain and spasm; increased range of joint motion.
(iv) Technique of application:
- Pack heated in hydrocollator unit (water 70-80 degrees C, about 2 hours to fully heat from cold).
- Pack removed and wrapped in a towel folded into 4-8 layers between pack and skin for thermal insulation so skin temperature does not rise above about 42-44 degrees C.
- Check for contraindications and do a skin sensation test first; apply for 20-30 minutes.
- Check the skin after the initial period for excessive redness or blistering.

questions.question:
A patient with a subacute lower extremity condition is prescribed a warm whirlpool bath.
(i) State the modality selected.
(ii) Describe the preparation of the patient and equipment.
(iii) Describe the step-by-step application technique, including temperature and duration.
(iv) State the precautions during treatment.
(v) State possible adverse effects/dangers and how to manage them.
questions.answerText:
(i) Modality:
- Warm whirlpool, a superficial heating modality providing heat and mild mechanical stimulation, immersion of the body part in agitated warm water.
(ii) Preparation:
- Check for contraindications (impaired circulation or sensation, open wounds, malignancy); check skin integrity; position/prepare the part for immersion in the bath.
(iii) Technique:
- Lower extremity water temperature range 98-104 degrees F; the limb is immersed in the agitated water; treatment time 15-20 minutes.
(iv) Precautions:
- Monitor skin colour and patient feedback throughout; use caution with impaired circulation/sensation or cardiovascular problems, monitoring systemic response.
(v) Adverse effects/dangers and management:
- Risk of burn increases with decreased subcutaneous fat (fat serves as an insulator); adjust temperature/duration accordingly and inspect the skin for excessive redness, blistering or generalised sweating, modifying or discontinuing treatment if these occur.

(i) Problem(s):
- Chronic joint stiffness of the hands and dry scaly skin; paraffin gives comfortable moist heat to dry scaly skin (esp. after plaster-of-Paris removal) and moulds round the bony contours of the hands for even heating.
(ii) Category:
- Superficial heating modality.
(iii) Physiological effects:
- Heat production, circulatory effect (vasodilatation), analgesic effect, sedative effect, stretching effect; leaves the skin moist, soft and pliable, useful before mobilisation of stiff joints.
(iv) Technique of application:
- Wax bath temperature regulated to about 49 degrees C, then switched off; skin inspected, sensation-tested, jewellery removed.
- Dip and wrap method for the hand: part immersed for a second, withdrawn, cooled 2-3 seconds, re-immersed, repeated 6-12 times to build a wax coating 2-3 mm thick; hand then placed in a plastic bag and wrapped in a blanket or towel to limit heat loss.
questions.question:
A patient with chronic arthritic stiffness of the hands and dry, scaly skin is being treated with paraffin wax.
(i) Identify the problem(s) that make this patient suitable for paraffin wax therapy.
(ii) State which category of thermotherapy modality paraffin wax belongs to.
(iii) State the physiological effects relevant to this patient's problem.
(iv) Describe the technique of application.

Describe the hydrocollator pack under the following headings: (A) equipment, (B) technique of application, (C) dosage, (D) indications, (E) contraindications, (F) precautions.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for its use.
questions.answerText:
(A) Equipment: Fabric envelope containing silica gel or bentonite crystals that absorb many times their own volume of water and store heat.
- Heated in a thermostatically controlled hydrocollator unit at 70-80 degrees C.
(B) Technique: Pack removed from unit, placed on a towel, another towel folded into 4-8 layers wrapped over it before application.
- Keeps skin temperature below about 42-44 degrees C.
(C) Dosage: Applied for about 20-30 minutes (moist heat delivered for up to 30-40 minutes of pack heat retention).
(D) Indications: Subacute/chronic pain, muscle spasm, joint stiffness, reduction of joint contractures.
(E) Contraindications: Acute injury, impaired circulation, poor thermal regulation, anaesthetic areas, neoplasms, thrombophlebitis.
(F) Precautions: Check contraindications and skin sensation before use; ensure adequate towel insulation.
- Check skin after the first few minutes for excessive redness or blistering.
(ii) Clinical basis: The silica gel/bentonite stores heat energy transferred by conduction, producing vasodilatation and a sedative effect.
- Removes metabolic waste through increased blood flow.
- This is the basis for its use in pain, spasm and stiffness.

questions.question:
A patient with subacute swelling of the hand, in whom acute inflammation is no longer active, is prescribed a contrast bath.
(i) State the stage of the condition for which contrast bath is indicated.
(ii) State the modality and rationale for its use.
(iii) State the dosage/duration and method of application.
(iv) State the expected therapeutic effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Stage:
- Subacute or chronic conditions, once the acute inflammatory process is no longer active (area not warm, not sensitive to light/moderate touch, swelling not continuing to increase, pain not limiting ROM).
(ii) Modality/rationale:
- Contrast bath - alternating hot and cold water immersion; produces marked hyperaemia of the skin and considerable sensory stimulation by alternately activating cutaneous hot and cold receptors, used as a transition from cold to heat.
(iii) Method:
- Hot bath 40-45 degrees C, cold bath 15-20 degrees C (also stated as hot 104-106 degrees F and cold 50-60 degrees F, 3:1 or 4:1 heat:cold ratios).
- Immerse in hot water 3-4 minutes, then cold water 1 minute, starting and finishing in hot; cycle repeated 3-4 times, total treatment 15-20 minutes; top up baths and check temperature with a thermometer.
(iv) Expected effects:
- Hyperaemia and sensory/vascular stimulation ('pumping') of alternating hot and cold; this does not, however, reduce oedema through a pumping action as sometimes suggested.

(i) Indications:
- Acute and post-acute conditions where non-thermal effects are wanted: soft tissue healing and repair, reduction of muscle spasm, pain modulation, increased protein synthesis, tissue regeneration.
(ii) Contraindications:
- Ischaemic/impaired circulation areas (incl. arterial disease), over deep vein thrombosis, anaesthetic areas, over cancerous tumours, sites of active infection/sepsis, spinal cord/large nerve plexus in high doses.
- Exposed metal penetrating the skin; areas around eyes, heart, skull or genitals; thorax with implanted pacemaker; pregnancy over pelvic/lumbar area; incompletely healed fracture, stress fracture or osteoporosis sites; pelvic/lumbar area in menstruating women.
(iii) Precautions:
- Symptoms may increase after the first treatments; caution around the spinal cord (especially post-laminectomy) and epiphyseal plates of growing bone; keep the sound head moving.
- Use only the lowest intensity producing the desired response and move the applicator constantly to avoid standing waves; if in doubt, do not irradiate.
(iv) Justification:
- Pulsed mode is an interrupted emission inducing a non-thermal effect; the inter-pulse duration allows dissipation of heat, so it is used for acute and subacute conditions, unlike continuous (thermal) mode which suits chronic conditions.
- As this patient has an acute injury, pulsed ultrasound with a low duty cycle (e.g. 20-25%) is the appropriate choice.
questions.question:
A patient has an acute soft tissue injury being considered for pulsed ultrasound.
(i) State the indications for pulsed ultrasound in this patient.
(ii) State the contraindications to ultrasound.
(iii) State the precautions to be taken.
(iv) Justify the choice of pulsed over continuous ultrasound for this patient.

A patient with a pressure sore requiring acceleration of tissue repair is treated with ice cube massage.
(i) State the modality selected.
(ii) Describe the preparation of the patient and equipment.
(iii) Describe the step-by-step application technique.
(iv) State the precautions during treatment.
(v) State the possible adverse effects/dangers and how to manage them.
questions.answerText:
(i) Modality:
- Ice therapy applied as ice cube massage, which may be used to accelerate the rate of repair of pressure sores.
(ii) Preparation:
- Check for contraindications: cold sensitivity/allergy, Raynaud's disease/cold urticaria, circulatory or sensory impairment, cardiac or respiratory disorders, uncovered open wounds.
(iii) Technique:
- Ice is applied usually for 20-30 minutes for maximum cooling of superficial and deep tissue, applied as a massage over the area.
- The patient passes through the sensory stages: cold (1-3 min), aching/stinging/discomfort, pain/burning (2-7 min), then numbness (5-15 min).
(iv) Precautions:
- Monitor for excessive discomfort or intolerance; document subjective complaints, agent used, area of exposure, treatment time and patient response, as recommended for cryotherapy and all physical agents.
(v) Adverse effects/dangers and management:
- Possible adverse effects: tissue death, frostbite, nerve damage, freezing of tissue; treatment should be stopped or adjusted if such signs develop or a contraindication is present.

(i) Suitability:
- Not suitable for deep heating modalities using electromagnetic energy or high-frequency current over or near the pacemaker; impaired sensation is a general contraindication to thermal treatment.
(ii) Modalities to avoid and why:
- Microwave diathermy, strictly contraindicated with pacemakers or a thermal sensation deficit.
- Ultrasound over the thorax with an implanted pacemaker and over anaesthetic (impaired sensation) areas, both listed contraindications.
(iii) Safe alternative:
- A superficial conductive modality (hydrocollator pack or paraffin wax) over an unaffected, sensate area away from the pacemaker, since these transfer heat by conduction rather than electromagnetic energy.
(iv) Advice/follow-up:
- Explain to the patient why deep heating cannot be used near the pacemaker or over the insensate area; advise reporting of any unusual sensation.
- Inspect the skin/area during and after any substituted treatment.
questions.question:
A patient has an implanted cardiac pacemaker and impaired sensation over the area requiring deep heating.
(i) State the suitability of deep heating modalities for this patient.
(ii) State the modalities to avoid and why.
(iii) State a safe alternative modality.
(iv) State the patient advice and follow-up.

(i) State the local and general (systemic) therapeutic effects of heat.
(ii) Explain the underlying physiological mechanism of these effects.
(iii) State the dangers/adverse effects of heat application.
(iv) State how these dangers are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i) Local and general effects:
- Local: vasodilation, increased cell metabolic rate, increased leukocyte delivery, increased capillary permeability, increased venous/lymphatic drainage, removal of metabolic wastes, increased elasticity of ligaments, capsules and muscle.
- General (systemic, whole-body exposure): increased body temperature, increased pulse rate, increased respiratory rate, decreased blood pressure.
(ii) Mechanism:
- Heat stimulates cutaneous thermoreceptors, causing release of bradykinin (with prostaglandins and histamine) which relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, causing vasodilation.
- Raised temperature increases nerve conduction velocity; at about 42 degrees C muscle temperature, decreased type II/gamma efferent firing and increased Golgi tendon organ (Ib) firing reduce alpha motor neuron activity, producing muscle relaxation.
- Pain threshold rises via direct spinal gating of A-beta input and indirectly via improved oxygen/nutrient supply and waste removal.
(iii) Dangers:
- Burns (risk increases with decreased subcutaneous fat, which normally insulates); fainting/dizziness (vaso-vagal response); bleeding over open wounds; increased blood flow can induce oedema and exacerbate acute inflammation.
(iv) Prevention:
- Test sensory integrity before treatment; wrap heating pads/packs in 6-8 layers of towelling; check the patient after the first 5 minutes for excessive redness, blistering or generalised sweating.
- Avoid the patient lying on top of hot packs (pressure compromises the vasodilator response); avoid heat in contraindicated conditions (acute injury, impaired circulation/sensation, malignancy, haemorrhagic conditions).

questions.question:
Describe the whirlpool and contrast bath under the following headings: (A) equipment/temperature parameters, (B) technique of application, (C) dosage, (D) indications, (E) contraindications, (F) precautions.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for their use.
questions.answerText:
(A) Equipment/parameters: Whirlpool - agitated water bath; upper extremity 98-110 degrees F, lower extremity 98-104 degrees F, full body 98-102 degrees F.
- Contrast bath - hot bath 40-45 degrees C (104-106 degrees F), cold bath 15-20 degrees C (50-60 degrees F).
(B) Technique: Whirlpool - limb (or body) immersed in agitated water.
- Contrast bath - hot immersion 3-4 minutes, cold immersion 1 minute, starting/finishing in hot, 3:1 or 4:1 heat:cold ratios, baths topped up and checked with a thermometer.
(C) Dosage: Whirlpool 15-20 minutes; contrast bath cycle repeated 3-4 times, total treatment 15-20 minutes.
(D) Indications: Subacute swelling; whirlpool also gives heat and mild mechanical stimulation for subacute/chronic musculoskeletal conditions.
(E) Contraindications: As with other heat modalities - acute injury/inflammation, impaired circulation, impaired sensation, malignancy.
(F) Precautions: Monitor skin colour and patient feedback during treatment.
- Use caution in patients with cardiovascular problems, monitoring systemic response.
(ii) Clinical basis: Alternating hot and cold immersion produces marked hyperaemia and considerable sensory stimulation.
- Cutaneous hot and cold receptors are alternately activated, a 'pumping' stimulation.
- Used as a transition from cold to heat in subacute/chronic swelling.

questions.question:
(i) Define hydrotherapy-based thermal modalities such as whirlpool and contrast bath.
(ii) Classify them as superficial or deep heating.
(iii) State their principal mode of heat transfer.
(iv) State their physiological effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Definition:
- Warm whirlpool is immersion of a body part in agitated warm water providing both heat and mild mechanical stimulation.
- Contrast bath is alternate immersion in hot and cold water.
(ii) Classification:
- Both are among the conductive modalities, with a maximum depth of penetration of about 1 cm or less (superficial heating; contrast bath alternates superficial heating/cooling).
(iii) Mode of heat transfer:
- Convection - transfer of heat by fluid circulation over the surface of the body.
(iv) Physiological effects:
- Whirlpool provides heat and mild mechanical stimulation to the immersed part.
- Contrast bath produces marked hyperaemia of the skin and considerable sensory stimulation through alternate activation of cutaneous hot and cold receptors.
- The alternating stimulation is described as creating a 'pumping' sensory/vascular stimulation to encourage blood flow.
- Contrast bath is most commonly used in subacute or chronic conditions.

(i) Distinction:
- Heat increases tissue temperature and cell metabolic rate (metabolic rate increases two- to three-fold for each 10 degrees C rise in skin temperature up to 45 degrees C), increases blood flow via vasodilation, and increases nerve conduction velocity.
- Cold decreases tissue metabolism, decreases blood flow initially via vasoconstriction (followed by the Lewis hunting reaction), and decreases nerve conduction velocity.
(ii) Advantages of heat:
- Pain relief, increased range of joint motion via increased tissue extensibility, muscle relaxation and reduced spasm, promotion of healing through increased oxygen/nutrient delivery and waste removal.
- Heat also increases capillary pressure and permeability, aiding venous and lymphatic drainage of oedema and metabolic waste.
(iii) Advantages of cold:
- Reduces pain, inflammation, spasticity and muscle spasm/guarding; reduces oedema/swelling; allows cooled muscle to contract more times before fatigue due to reduced metabolic rate; useful for acute conditions, postsurgical pain and oedema.
- At joint temperatures of 30 degrees C or lower, activity of cartilage-degrading enzymes such as collagenase, elastase, hyaluronidase and protease is inhibited.
(iv) Limitations:
- Heat is contraindicated in acute injury/inflammation as it increases blood flow and can worsen oedema.
- Cold is contraindicated with cold sensitivity, Raynaud's disease, circulatory or sensory impairment and cardiac/respiratory disorders; excessive cold risks tissue death, frostbite or nerve damage.
questions.question:
(i) Distinguish between the effects of heat and cold on tissue metabolism, blood flow and nerve conduction velocity.
(ii) State the advantages of using heat.
(iii) State the advantages of using cold.
(iv) State the limitations of each.

questions.answerText:
(i) Suitability:
- Not suitable for heat or contrast bath at this stage; the assessment questions indicate that if the area feels warm, remains sensitive to light/moderate touch, and swelling continues to increase with joint motion, the acute inflammatory process is still active and cold should be used.
(ii) Modalities to avoid and why:
- Avoid heat modalities (hydrocollator pack, paraffin wax, fluidotherapy, whirlpool, contrast bath), because heat is contraindicated in acute inflammation/injury and can increase blood flow, worsening oedema and inflammation.
(iii) Safe alternative:
- Cryotherapy (e.g. ice pack or ice bag), indicated for acute inflammation or injury, acute pain and postsurgical pain and oedema.
(iv) Advice/follow-up:
- Continue monitoring the same assessment questions (warmth, sensitivity, swelling behaviour, pain limiting ROM, continued improvement with cold) at each session.
- Heat/contrast bathing can be safely introduced only once the answers to these questions are 'no', indicating the acute inflammatory process is no longer active.
questions.question:
On assessment, a patient's injured area still feels warm to the touch, remains sensitive to light touch, and swelling continues to increase with joint motion.
(i) State the suitability of heat/contrast bath for this patient at this stage.
(ii) State the modalities to avoid and why.
(iii) State a safe alternative modality.
(iv) State the patient advice and follow-up.

A patient is assessed for cryotherapy and found to have cold sensitivity, impaired circulation and an uncovered open wound over the area to be treated.
(i) State the suitability of this patient for cryotherapy.
(ii) State the modalities/forms to avoid and why.
(iii) State a safe alternative modality.
(iv) State the patient advice and follow-up to be given.
questions.answerText:
(i) Suitability:
- Not suitable for direct cryotherapy over the area; cold sensitivity/allergy, circulatory or sensory impairment and uncovered open wounds are listed contraindications to ice treatment/cryotherapy.
(ii) Modalities to avoid and why:
- Ice bags, ice packs, cold water immersion, ice massage or vapo-coolant sprays over the area, because of the listed contraindications; cold on circulatory-impaired or hypersensitive tissue risks tissue death, frostbite or nerve damage.
(iii) Safe alternative:
- If the condition is otherwise subacute/chronic, a superficial heat modality (hydrocollator pack, paraffin wax, or fluidotherapy) may be considered, provided heat contraindications (impaired circulation, impaired sensation) are also excluded first.
(iv) Advice/follow-up:
- Explain to the patient why cold cannot be used over the area; advise reporting of any adverse, unusual or painful sensation with any modality used.
- Inspect the skin/area during and after any treatment given, for excessive redness, blistering or other signs, before continuing.

questions.question:
A clinician is choosing between a hydrocollator pack and paraffin wax bath for a patient with chronic hand joint pain.
(i) State the indications relevant to each modality.
(ii) State the contraindications common to both modalities.
(iii) State the precautions to be taken with each.
(iv) Justify which modality would be chosen for the small, irregularly shaped joints of the hand.
questions.answerText:
(i) Indications:
- Both used for subacute/chronic pain, stiffness and muscle spasm; paraffin additionally for stretching scars/adhesions and for patients with poor heat tolerance or dry scaly skin.
(ii) Common contraindications:
- Open wounds, skin infection, defective/impaired thermal sensation, deficient cutaneous circulation, malignancy, gross oedema (paraffin); general heat contraindications applicable to both include acute injury, impaired circulation, poor thermal regulation, anaesthetic areas, neoplasms.
(iii) Precautions:
- Hydrocollator pack: adequate towelling insulation (4-8 layers) so skin does not overheat; check skin after the first minutes for redness.
- Paraffin wax: fire precautions (no naked flame, no smoking); thermal sensation test essential as patients can be burnt easily; wax renders the floor slippery if spilt.
(iv) Justification:
- Paraffin wax is preferable for the small, irregular hand contours because it moulds round bony contours for even heating, suits poor heat tolerance, and its low specific heat/slower conduction reduce burn risk compared with a flat hydrocollator pack, which does not maintain good contact with small or contoured areas.
