Hepatic failure with reduced lactate clearance and metabolism
High-dose epinephrine causing aerobic lactate production in muscle
Metformin accumulation inhibiting mitochondrial complex I activity
questions.question: A patient in the ICU has serum lactate of 8.2 mmol/L, pH 7.18, and adequate tissue perfusion on vasopressors. Mixed venous oxygen saturation is 75%. The most likely cause of type B lactic acidosis here is:
questions.explanation: Type B lactic acidosis occurs without tissue hypoperfusion (normal perfusion, normal mixed venous O2 saturation). Metformin causes type B lactic acidosis by inhibiting mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and forcing pyruvate through anaerobic glycolysis to lactate. Risk is greatest in AKI (metformin accumulates from reduced renal clearance), hepatic failure (reduced lactate clearance), and older adults. Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min. Treatment is cessation of metformin and hemodialysis to remove metformin and lactate in severe cases.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is the most common symptomatic primary antibody deficiency, characterised by: late-onset hypogammaglobulinaemia (IgG <7 g/L plus low IgA and/or IgM), normal or near-normal B-cell numbers but absent plasma cells (B cells cannot differentiate to immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cells), and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Unlike XLA, CVID affects both sexes and presents in adolescence to early adulthood. Associated complications include autoimmune disease (ITP, AIHA), granulomatous disease, enteropathy, and lymphoma risk.
options: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia from BTK gene mutation
Selective IgA deficiency as most common immunodeficiency
Hyper-IgM syndrome from class-switching enzyme deficiency
Common variable immunodeficiency from B-cell differentiation defect
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome from WASp protein deficiency
questions.question: A 20-year-old woman has recurrent sinopulmonary infections and low serum IgG. She has normal B-cell counts but absent plasma cells on biopsy. What is the diagnosis?
A patient with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria is started on an ACE inhibitor. What is the primary renal benefit expected from this treatment?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, slowing the progression of diabetic nephropathy. While they do not reverse existing structural damage, early use in microalbuminuria has been shown to reduce the rate of further renal decline.

questions.question: Which laboratory finding indicates diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis requires: hyperglycemia (usually >250 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15 mEq/L), and ketonemia/ketonuria. Results from absolute/relative insulin deficiency causing lipolysis, ketogenesis (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate), and hyperglycemia. Additional findings: elevated anion gap (>12), hyperosmolality, electrolyte abnormalities (potassium, sodium, phosphate), and increased BUN/creatinine (prerenal azotemia). Treatment requires insulin, fluid replacement, electrolyte correction, and addressing precipitating cause.

questions.question: A 70-year-old patient on lithium for bipolar disorder develops polyuria producing 8 liters of dilute urine per day. Serum sodium is 148 mmol/L. The mechanism of lithium-induced diabetes insipidus is:
options: Hypothalamic destruction impairing ADH synthesis and release
Osmoreceptor desensitization from chronic hypernatremia exposure
Renal medullary washout from massive diuresis eliminating gradient
Lithium blocking ADH receptor coupling to adenylyl cyclase
Lithium downregulating aquaporin-2 water channels in collecting duct
questions.explanation: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by downregulating aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels in the principal cells of the collecting duct. Lithium enters principal cells through ENaC and inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3), disrupting the cAMP-PKA pathway that normally inserts AQP2 channels into the apical membrane in response to ADH. Even with high circulating ADH, the tubule cannot concentrate urine. Amiloride (which blocks ENaC) reduces lithium entry into principal cells and partially improves AQP2 expression, providing therapeutic benefit in lithium-induced NDI.

questions.question: What gestational age is optimal for amniocentesis?
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis is optimally performed at 15-20 weeks gestation when adequate amniotic fluid volume permits safe sampling with lowest complication risk. Earlier amniocentesis (

questions.question: A patient with methanol poisoning has pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, PaCO2 20 mmHg, and anion gap 28 mmol/L. The toxic metabolite causing the anion gap metabolic acidosis is:
options: Methanol itself causing direct renal tubular acidosis
Formaldehyde causing lactic acid overproduction in tissues
Methanol metabolized to acetaldehyde causing ketoacidosis
Oxalic acid crystals from methanol renal excretion products
Formic acid from methanol metabolism impairing cytochrome oxidase
questions.explanation: Methanol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase first to formaldehyde and then to formic acid (formate). Formate is the primary toxic metabolite responsible for the severe anion gap metabolic acidosis and optic nerve toxicity in methanol poisoning. Formate inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), causing histotoxic hypoxia and lactic acidosis. The visual toxicity (snowfield vision, blindness) results from selective optic nerve susceptibility to formate-induced cytochrome oxidase inhibition. Treatment includes fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor), sodium bicarbonate, folate (to enhance formate metabolism), and dialysis for severe cases.

Cystatin C is produced at a constant rate by all nucleated cells regardless of muscle mass, making it a more reliable marker of renal function than creatinine in individuals with unusually high or low muscle bulk, where creatinine generation differs from the general population.
questions.question: A bodybuilder with very high muscle mass has a serum creatinine at the upper limit of normal despite a measured GFR within the normal range. What renal marker would better reflect his true kidney function?
What genetic mutation underlies medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN syndromes?
questions.explanation: RET proto-oncogene mutations underlie familial medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN IIA, MEN IIB, and familial MTC syndromes. Almost all individuals with germline RET mutations develop MTC. Genetic screening enables prophylactic thyroidectomy in mutation carriers.

Primary biliary cirrhosis characteristically shows markedly elevated ALP and GGT (cholestatic pattern) with pruritus (from bile acid deposition) preceding jaundice by months/years. Associated findings include elevated IgM, anti-mitochondrial antibodies (>90%), and predominantly middle-aged women affected. Pruritus may be the sole presenting symptom with minimal biochemical abnormalities initially.
questions.question: What liver disease shows markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with pruritus?

questions.explanation: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III hyperlipoproteinemia) results from apo E2/E2 genotype causing defective remnant clearance. IDL and chylomicron remnants accumulate (β-VLDL on electrophoresis), elevating both cholesterol and triglycerides equally (300-600 mg/dL each). Clinical features include palmar xanthomas (pathognomonic), tuberous xanthomas, and premature atherosclerosis. Treatment requires fibrates or statins.
questions.question: Which lipoprotein abnormality characterizes familial dysbetalipoproteinemia?
Which protein is elevated in acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: C-reactive protein (CRP) is a major acute-phase reactant, increasing >1000-fold within 6-8 hours of inflammation onset. Synthesized in liver responding to IL-6 stimulation, CRP activates complement, enhances phagocytosis, and modulates immune responses. Useful for monitoring inflammation severity, infection, and treatment response. High-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) predicts cardiovascular risk. Levels >10 mg/L suggest significant inflammation; >100 mg/L often indicates bacterial infection.

Type II hypersensitivity is mediated by IgG and IgM antibodies directed against cell surface or extracellular matrix antigens. Antibody binding activates complement or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, causing cell destruction. Examples include hemolytic transfusion reactions and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
questions.question: Which immunoglobulin mediates Type II hypersensitivity?
Which condition is diagnosed by detecting Kayser-Fleischer rings and low ceruloplasmin?
questions.explanation: Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is characterized by Kayser-Fleischer rings in the cornea, low ceruloplasmin (<200 mg/L in >90% of cases), low plasma copper, and high tissue/urinary copper. This autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism causes liver disease in 40% and neuropsychiatric manifestations in others. Treatment involves penicillamine chelation therapy.

questions.question: What tumor marker is elevated in 70% of non-seminomatous testicular tumors?
questions.explanation: Approximately 70% of non-seminomatous testicular tumors secrete hCG, making it a valuable marker alongside AFP. Pure seminomas may show mild hCG elevation but not AFP. Combined AFP and hCG measurement provides optimal sensitivity for germ cell tumor diagnosis, staging, and monitoring.

HbA1c =6.5% (48 mmol/mol) confirms diabetes mellitus diagnosis, reflecting average glucose control over the preceding 8-12 weeks. This criterion was added to diagnostic criteria in 2010 due to standardization and convenience (no fasting required). Values 5.7-6.4% indicate prediabetes with increased diabetes risk. The test should be confirmed on a separate occasion.
questions.question: What HbA1c level is diagnostic for diabetes mellitus?

questions.explanation: Reverse T3 (3,3',5'-triiodothyronine) is biologically inactive, produced by inner ring deiodination of T4. Increased rT3 occurs in non-thyroidal illness as an adaptive response. The compound competes with T3 for receptor binding without activating transcription.
questions.question: What iodothyronine is biologically inactive?
Which lipoprotein receptor is increased by thyroid hormones?
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones stimulate formation and activity of hepatic LDL receptors, enhancing cholesterol clearance from circulation. This mechanism explains why hypothyroidism causes hypercholesterolemia. T3 regulates LDL receptor gene transcription directly.

questions.question: What D-dimer level effectively excludes pulmonary embolism?
questions.explanation: D-dimer

questions.question: A forensic pathologist is asked to determine whether a death resulted from alcohol intoxication for a coroner's inquest. Which toxicology subspecialty is primarily responsible for this analysis?
questions.explanation: Forensic toxicology addresses the medicolegal consequences of toxin exposure, including determining cause of death for legal proceedings. It requires strict chain-of-custody procedures to ensure specimen integrity, distinguishing it from clinical toxicology, which focuses on patient diagnosis and treatment.

questions.question: What HER-2/neu status predicts response to trastuzumab?
questions.explanation: HER-2/neu overexpression (3+ by immunohistochemistry) or gene amplification (by FISH/ISH) predicts trastuzumab (Herceptin) response in breast cancer. Only strongly positive cases (3+ or amplified) benefit from anti-HER2 therapy. Equivocal results (2+) require gene amplification testing for treatment decisions.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of action of propylthiouracil?
questions.explanation: Propylthiouracil (PTU) inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking iodine organification and coupling reactions in thyroid hormone synthesis. PTU additionally inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion. The drug is preferred in first-trimester pregnancy due to lower teratogenic potential than methimazole.

options: T4 followed by TSH if low
TSH followed by T4 if high
questions.question: What screening strategy is used for congenital hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: Newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism typically measures total T4 first, with reflex TSH measurement if T4 is low. Some programs use primary TSH screening. Blood collected on filter paper from heel prick within first week enables early diagnosis and treatment initiation.

options: Avoiding need for any future monitoring
questions.explanation: Identifying haemochromatosis before organ damage occurs allows treatment with phlebotomy to begin early, preventing the development of cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and arthropathy that result from progressive iron accumulation if left untreated.
questions.question: A patient newly diagnosed with haemochromatosis through family screening has no symptoms and normal liver enzymes. What is the main benefit of identifying the condition at this stage?

questions.explanation: High-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) provides prognostic information post-ACS, with each standard deviation increase associated with 45% increased relative risk of non-fatal MI or sudden cardiac death over 2 years. However, once necrosis occurs, CRP rises (acute phase response), attenuating prognostic value. For primary prevention: <1 mg/L low risk, 1-3 mg/L intermediate, >3 mg/L high risk.
questions.question: Which cardiac biomarker provides prognostic information post-acute coronary syndrome?
What percentage of cardiac CK is CK-MB isoenzyme?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle contains 20-30% CK-MB with 70-80% CK-MM, while skeletal muscle has <2% CK-MB (98% CK-MM). Plasma normally contains >95% CK-MM. CK-MB >5% of total CK supports myocardial origin. Though largely replaced by troponin, CK-MB remains useful where troponin is unavailable or for detecting reinfarction.

DiGeorge syndrome presents with thymic aplasia or hypoplasia, manifesting as absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray. The condition results from 22q11.2 deletion affecting third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development. Associated features include cardiac defects, hypoparathyroidism, and characteristic facial features.
questions.question: Which immunodeficiency shows absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray?
At what pH does urate become relatively insoluble in body fluids?
questions.explanation: At pH below 7.0, urate becomes relatively insoluble and precipitates as monosodium urate crystals. Normal body pH of 7.35-7.45 keeps urate in its ionized, soluble form. Acidic conditions promote crystal formation in joints and tissues.

Myoglobin has the shortest half-life (10-30 minutes) among cardiac biomarkers, rising within 1-4 hours of myocardial injury and returning to baseline by 18-24 hours. This rapid clearance enables early MI detection but lacks cardiac specificity. Serial measurements detect early reinfarction better than troponins.
questions.question: Which cardiac biomarker has the shortest half-life?

questions.explanation: AST/ALT ratio >2.1 is pathognomonic of alcoholic liver disease, while non-alcoholic fatty liver typically shows ALT>AST. This pattern reflects preferential mitochondrial damage and AST release in alcohol-related injury. The ratio helps distinguish alcoholic from non-alcoholic causes when imaging shows fatty infiltration.
questions.question: Which enzyme pattern best differentiates alcoholic from non-alcoholic fatty liver disease?

questions.explanation: Para-aminohippurate (PAH) clearance measures effective renal plasma flow (ERPF), not GFR, as PAH is both filtered and secreted (nearly completely cleared in single pass). Filtration fraction = GFR/ERPF (normally ~20%). PAH clearance is used in research but not routine clinical practice. GFR is measured by clearance of substances that are only filtered (inulin, iothalamate, EDTA, DTPA).
questions.question: Which GFR measurement method measures renal plasma flow rather than filtration?

questions.explanation: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) monitors unfractionated heparin therapy, with therapeutic range typically 1.5-2.5 times control. Low molecular weight heparins don't require routine monitoring except in specific populations (renal failure, obesity, pregnancy), where anti-Xa levels guide dosing. Platelet counts monitor for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
questions.question: Which laboratory test monitors heparin therapy?

options: PTH-independent renal calcium wasting in tubular hypercalciuria
Medullary sponge kidney causing calcium phosphate deposition
Dietary calcium excess causing absorptive hypercalciuria type 3
Absorptive hypercalciuria type 1 from intestinal calcium overabsorption
Resorptive hypercalciuria from subclinical primary hyperparathyroidism
questions.explanation: Absorptive hypercalciuria type 1 is the most common cause of idiopathic hypercalciuria and results from primary intestinal calcium hyperabsorption (likely from increased intestinal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 responsiveness) with suppressed PTH and normal calcium. Excess absorbed calcium is filtered and excreted in urine (greater than 7.5 mmol/day). Treatment includes thiazide diuretics (reducing tubular calcium excretion), dietary sodium restriction (reducing calciuria), and moderate dietary calcium restriction. Excess dietary calcium (type 3) also raises urinary calcium but normalizes with calcium restriction. Renal calcium wasting (type 2) shows hypercalciuria even during fasting.
questions.question: A 50-year-old with recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis has normal serum calcium, elevated 24-hour urine calcium of 9 mmol/day, and normal PTH. The most common cause of hypercalciuria in this setting is:

questions.explanation: Low complement levels (C3, C4) in systemic lupus erythematosus indicate active immune complex-mediated disease with complement consumption. Type III hypersensitivity drives SLE pathology through immune complex deposition in kidneys, joints, and blood vessels. Serial complement monitoring assesses disease activity and treatment response.
questions.question: Which laboratory finding indicates immune complex deposition in SLE?
Which chromatography type separates molecules by size?
questions.explanation: Gel filtration (size exclusion) chromatography separates molecules based on size using porous gel beads. Large molecules excluded from pores elute first; small molecules enter pores, delayed elution. Medium-sized molecules partially penetrate pores, intermediate elution. Used for desalting, buffer exchange, molecular weight estimation, and protein purification. Pore size is manufacturer-controlled for specific molecular weight ranges.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman has a history of SLE and anti-Ro antibodies. She has a daughter with neonatal lupus. What investigation should be performed on future pregnancies?
questions.explanation: Women with anti-Ro (SSA) and/or anti-La (SSB) antibodies are at risk of having children with neonatal lupus, including congenital heart block (CHB). The cardiac conduction tissue is most vulnerable between 16-28 weeks gestation. Fetal echocardiography monitoring from 16 weeks (weekly or fortnightly surveillance) can detect prolonged PR intervals (1st degree), 2nd degree, or 3rd degree (complete) heart block before clinical compromise. First or second-degree heart block may be reversible with dexamethasone (a fluorinated steroid crossing the placenta). Complete CHB typically requires pacemaker implantation after delivery and may cause hydrops fetalis in severe cases.
options: Weekly maternal anti-dsDNA titres during pregnancy
Fetal echocardiography from 16 to 28 weeks gestation
Fortnightly maternal blood pressure monitoring only
Biweekly maternal serum IgG level measurement
Monthly maternal complement C3 and C4 monitoring

questions.question: Which finding suggests rickets of prematurity?
questions.explanation: Rickets of prematurity presents with alkaline phosphatase >6× upper adult reference limit, usually low-normal calcium, low phosphate, and radiological osteopenia. Results from calcium/phosphate depletion in rapidly growing premature infants with limited stores. Risk factors include prolonged parenteral nutrition, vitamin D deficiency, and medications (furosemide). Treatment requires calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D supplementation.

questions.question: A neonate develops worsening unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia exceeding 350 µmol/L with no response to phototherapy and a family history of severe jaundice. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I results from complete absence of UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity, causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that responds poorly to phototherapy and carries a high risk of kernicterus, unlike the partial enzyme deficiency seen in type II or Gilbert's syndrome.

questions.question: Which classification describes toxicity from extended exposure over organism's lifetime?
questions.explanation: Chronic toxicity describes harmful effects over extended periods (usually repeated/continuous exposure), sometimes lasting the organism's entire lifetime. This contrasts with acute toxicity (single/short-term exposure) and subchronic toxicity (>1 year but less than lifetime). Chronic effects often differ qualitatively from acute effects (e.g., carcinogenesis, organ damage).

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) shows elevated fasting gastrin (often >1000 pg/mL) with increased basal acid output (often >15 mEq/h, BAO/MAO ratio >0.6). Secretin provocative test shows paradoxical gastrin rise (>200 pg/mL increase). Other causes of hypergastrinemia have low/normal acid (pernicious anemia, atrophic gastritis, PPI use). Gastrinomas are often malignant, may be part of MEN-1 syndrome.
questions.question: Which condition shows increased fasting serum gastrin with increased acid output?
A patient with severe hyponatremia of 108 mmol/L has been treated with 3% saline for 6 hours. Sodium is now 118 mmol/L. What immediate intervention is needed to prevent osmotic demyelination?
options: Continue 3% saline infusion at the same rate indefinitely
Switch to oral fluid restriction to allow gradual further correction
Administer furosemide to enhance free water excretion safely
Perform urgent renal replacement therapy to control sodium precisely
Administer desmopressin to halt further inadvertent rapid sodium rise
questions.explanation: Once the initial symptomatic target (5 mmol/L rise or cessation of symptoms) is reached, subsequent correction should not exceed 8-10 mmol/L in any 24-hour period to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). If sodium has already risen 10 mmol/L in the first 6-8 hours (from 108 to 118 = 10 mmol/L), further unsupervised correction risks ODS. Desmopressin (DDAVP) 2-4 mcg IV is administered to stop the antidiuresis, clamp further sodium rise from ongoing 3% saline or mobilization of retained fluid, and prevent overcorrection. This 'brake' strategy with DDAVP is now standard in many protocols for preventing ODS in high-risk patients.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is most abundant in serum?
questions.explanation: IgG constitutes approximately 75% of total immunoglobulins (800-1600 mg/dL), comprising four subclasses (IgG1-4). It's the primary secondary immune response antibody, crosses placenta providing neonatal immunity, activates complement, and opsonizes pathogens. IgG has longest half-life (23 days) among immunoglobulins. Deficiency increases bacterial infection susceptibility. Monoclonal IgG elevation occurs in multiple myeloma.

questions.question: Which value depends on disease prevalence?
questions.explanation: Positive predictive value (PPV) = probability of disease given positive test = TP/(TP + FP), varies with disease prevalence. Higher prevalence increases PPV; lower prevalence decreases PPV. Example: test with 95% sensitivity/specificity has PPV 50% at 1% prevalence but 95% at 50% prevalence. Sensitivity/specificity are test characteristics, independent of prevalence. Pretest probability (prevalence) determines PPV/NPV. Important when applying test results to individual patients: same test has different predictive values in different populations.

questions.question: A 45-year-old with type 2 diabetes on SGLT2 inhibitor therapy presents with pH 7.25, HCO3 12 mmol/L, glucose 9.8 mmol/L, and high anion gap of 22 mmol/L. Serum ketones are strongly positive. The diagnosis is:
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis from insulin deficiency with hyperglycemia
Lactic acidosis from SGLT2 inhibitor mitochondrial complex I effect
Mixed DKA and metabolic alkalosis from diuretic use together
Euglycemic ketoacidosis from SGLT2 inhibitor mechanism of action
Starvation ketosis from recent fasting with coincidental glucose
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) presents with significant ketoacidosis (high anion gap, low HCO3, positive ketones) but near-normal or only mildly elevated blood glucose (euglycemic or minimally hyperglycemic). SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose (by glycosuria), shift energy metabolism toward fat oxidation (promoting ketogenesis), and may increase glucagon relative to insulin. The glucose appears near-normal or only mildly elevated despite significant ketoacidosis, making the diagnosis less obvious than classic DKA. SGLT2 inhibitors should be held perioperatively or during any prolonged fast. Treatment follows DKA protocols with glucose co-administration to avoid hypoglycemia.

questions.question: Which albuminuria category indicates severely increased cardiovascular risk?
questions.explanation: Albuminuria category A3 (>300 mg/g or >30 mg/mmol, previously called macroalbuminuria) indicates severely increased risk of CKD progression and cardiovascular events. Combined with low GFR (especially G3b-G5), risk is highest (red zone on KDIGO heat map requiring frequent monitoring). Albuminuria is both a marker of kidney damage and independent cardiovascular risk factor.

hCG has the shortest half-life (12-20 hours) among major tumor markers, enabling rapid assessment of treatment response in gestational trophoblastic disease and germ cell tumors. Slower-than-expected decline suggests residual disease. AFP (5 days) and PSA (2-3 days) have longer half-lives.
questions.question: Which tumor marker has the shortest half-life?

questions.explanation: Gastric mucus forms a protective barrier against HCl and pepsin, maintaining neutral pH at the epithelial surface despite luminal acidity. Bicarbonate secretion by surface epithelial cells into the mucus layer provides additional buffering. Prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion while inhibiting acid production. NSAIDs damage this defense by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
questions.question: What is the primary buffer in gastric juice?

questions.explanation: Estrogen therapy is contraindicated in severe hypertriglyceridemia as it increases hepatic VLDL production, potentially precipitating pancreatitis. Oral contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy can markedly worsen hypertriglyceridemia in susceptible individuals. Transdermal estrogen has less effect on triglycerides than oral preparations.
questions.question: Which medication is contraindicated in severe hypertriglyceridemia?

questions.explanation: Hemodialysis adequacy is monitored using urea kinetic modeling calculating Kt/V (K=urea clearance mL/min, t=dialysis time min, V=total body water L). Ideal Kt/V is >1.0, ensuring adequate waste removal. This quantifies dialysis dose and guides treatment adjustments. Peritoneal dialysis uses different adequacy measures including peritoneal equilibration test and weekly Kt/V targets.
questions.question: Which renal replacement therapy monitoring uses urea kinetic modeling?
Which cardiac troponin subunit has no cardiac-specific isoform²
questions.explanation: Troponin C has only two isoforms: one in slow-twitch skeletal and cardiac muscle, and one in fast-twitch muscle, with no cardiac-specific form. In contrast, cardiac-specific isoforms of troponin T and I exist and can be measured, making them the cornerstone of MI diagnosis. The troponin complex regulates actin-myosin interaction.

Serum sickness is the classic example of Type III hypersensitivity, resulting from immune complex formation following large protein antigen administration (historically, heterologous antisera). Circulating complexes deposit in tissues, causing vasculitis, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, and fever. Symptoms develop 7-14 days post-exposure.
questions.question: Which disease exemplifies Type III hypersensitivity?

questions.explanation: Liver biopsy allows direct histological assessment of inflammation and fibrosis staging, distinguishing degrees of chronic liver damage that cannot be reliably determined from biochemical tests alone, which are only suggestive of disease activity and severity.
questions.question: A patient with chronic hepatitis undergoes liver biopsy to assess disease severity. What specific information does biopsy provide that biochemical tests cannot?

options: Type III Arthus reaction from immune complex deposition
Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity from T cells
Type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction
questions.question: A child has seasonal rhinitis and conjunctivitis triggered by grass pollen. Skin prick testing shows a wheal-and-flare response to grass pollen extract. What type of reaction is this?
questions.explanation: Allergic rhinitis is a Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. Skin prick testing introduces allergen into the skin, causing mast cell degranulation in sensitised individuals (those with allergen-specific IgE bound to skin mast cells). The resulting wheal (oedema from histamine-induced capillary leak) and flare (erythema from vasodilation) typically appear within 15-20 minutes and represent the hallmark of immediate hypersensitivity. This confirms sensitisation, meaning prior antigen exposure led to IgE production.

Primary fibrinolysis shows elevated D-dimer with decreased fibrinogen but normal or mildly decreased platelets, distinguishing it from DIC which shows thrombocytopenia. PT and aPTT may be prolonged. Causes include thrombolytic therapy, prostate surgery, and certain malignancies. Antifibrinolytic therapy may be beneficial.
options: High D-dimer, low fibrinogen, normal platelets
questions.question: What laboratory pattern indicates primary fibrinolysis?

questions.explanation: Liddle syndrome (pseudohyperaldosteronism) results from gain-of-function mutations in the beta or gamma subunits of ENaC (epithelial sodium channel) in the collecting duct principal cells. Constitutively active ENaC causes sodium retention (hypertension), potassium wasting (hypokalemia), and H secretion (metabolic alkalosis) independent of aldosterone or renin. Both aldosterone and renin are suppressed. Treatment is amiloride or triamterene (ENaC blockers), not spironolactone (which blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor and is ineffective when the defect is downstream of the receptor). Genetic testing confirming SCNN1B or SCNN1G mutation confirms the diagnosis.
options: Primary hyperaldosteronism from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
Cushing syndrome with cortisol-driven mineralocorticoid excess
Liddle syndrome from ENaC gain-of-function mutation in kidney
Secondary hyperaldosteronism from renin-secreting juxtaglomerular tumor
questions.question: A 25-year-old presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, low aldosterone, and low renin. Serum cortisol is normal. The diagnosis explaining this combination is:
Which kidney function marker increases before creatinine in dehydration?
questions.explanation: In pre-renal renal failure (fluid depletion, dehydration), urea rises before creatinine due to increased reabsorption at low urine flow rates (~90% reabsorbed when dehydrated). This creates urea:creatinine ratio >100:1. Urea is flow-dependent and affected by protein intake/catabolism, making it inferior to creatinine for assessing GFR but useful for detecting pre-renal azotemia.

Ion-selective electrodes measure electrical potential difference between reference electrode and measuring electrode separated by ion-selective membrane. Potential varies with ion activity (approximates concentration) according to Nernst equation. Membrane selectivity for specific ions (Na+, K+, Cl-, Ca2+) depends on membrane composition (glass, polymer, crystal). Direct ISE measures undiluted samples; indirect ISE requires dilution.
questions.question: What principle underlies ion-selective electrode measurements?
Which investigation definitively diagnoses the type of chronic hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Liver biopsy with histological examination definitively distinguishes chronic aggressive from chronic persistent hepatitis and assesses fibrosis/cirrhosis. Biochemical tests (transaminases, gamma-globulin) are suggestive but not definitive. Viral serology identifies etiology but not severity. Biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing and staging chronic liver disease.

questions.question: A patient with acute kidney injury is found to have muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy. What underlying renal pathology does this finding suggest?
questions.explanation: Muddy brown granular casts represent sloughed tubular epithelial cells and are characteristic of acute tubular necrosis, helping distinguish this structural renal injury from functional causes of renal failure such as hepatorenal syndrome, which shows normal urinary sediment.

options: NSAIDs inhibiting tubular secretion of ACE inhibitor causing toxicity
NSAIDs blocking prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriole dilation plus ACE inhibitor blockade of angiotensin II-dependent efferent constriction
ACE inhibitors increasing renal sensitivity to NSAID prostaglandin blockade
ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs both causing tubular protein binding nephrotoxicity
NSAID reducing aldosterone preventing ACE inhibitor potassium-sparing benefit
questions.explanation: In states of reduced renal perfusion (elderly, heart failure, dehydration), the kidney maintains GFR by two mechanisms: afferent arteriole dilation via prostaglandins (predominantly PGE2, PGI2) and efferent arteriole constriction via angiotensin II. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, removing afferent dilation. ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II, removing efferent constriction. The combination eliminates both regulatory mechanisms, causing unopposed reduction in glomerular filtration pressure and acute pre-renal AKI. This combination is particularly dangerous in vulnerable elderly patients and those with pre-existing reduced renal reserve or volume depletion.
questions.question: A 70-year-old on ACE inhibitor and NSAID therapy develops acute kidney injury. The mechanism of NSAID-ACE inhibitor interaction causing AKI is:
Which hypersensitivity type causes contact dermatitis?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells responding to haptens like nickel or poison ivy antigens. The reaction develops 48-72 hours after exposure. Sensitization requires initial exposure; subsequent contacts trigger the delayed inflammatory response.

questions.question: What stimulates gastric parietal cells to secrete acid?
questions.explanation: Gastric acid secretion involves three pathways converging on parietal cells: (1) vagal acetylcholine (direct and via gastrin release), (2) gastrin from G-cells (stimulates histamine release from ECL cells), (3) histamine binding H2 receptors on parietal cells. Histamine is the final common pathway; H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine) effectively block acid secretion regardless of stimulus. Proton pump inhibitors directly block H+/K+-ATPase.

questions.question: What invasive test diagnoses fetal chromosomal abnormalities definitively?
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis with fetal karyotyping provides definitive diagnosis of chromosomal abnormalities. Performed at 15-20 weeks, it has ~0.3% miscarriage risk. Chromosomal microarray analysis detects additional submicroscopic deletions/duplications. Chorionic villus sampling (10-13 weeks) offers earlier diagnosis with slightly higher complication rates.

questions.question: Which receptor mediates LDL uptake in peripheral tissues?
questions.explanation: The LDL receptor (LDLR) mediates cellular LDL uptake through recognition of apolipoprotein B-100. Receptor-mediated endocytosis delivers cholesterol for membrane synthesis, steroid hormone production, and bile acid formation. Familial hypercholesterolemia results from LDLR mutations causing defective LDL clearance.

questions.question: Which test confirms amenorrhea due to hypothalamic dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Preserved or exaggerated FSH and LH responses to GnRH stimulation indicate hypothalamic dysfunction with intact pituitary function. Absence of response suggests pituitary lesion. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea from stress, exercise, or eating disorders shows this pattern. Treatment addresses underlying cause.

questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency causes hemolytic anemia following primaquine administration?
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency predisposes red blood cells to oxidative stress-induced hemolysis when exposed to antimalarials like primaquine. This X-linked disorder is common in malaria-endemic regions and also causes favism after fava bean consumption. The enzyme is crucial for maintaining glutathione in its reduced form.

questions.question: What PSA level suggests prostate cancer over benign prostatic hyperplasia?
questions.explanation: PSA

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) affects both cellular and humoral immune responses, impairing T and B lymphocytes simultaneously. Patients experience repeated infections from bacterial, fungal, viral, and parasitic organisms. Bone marrow transplantation is the definitive treatment.
questions.question: Which immunodeficiency syndrome affects both T and B lymphocytes?
Which enzyme deficiency is primarily responsible for Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
questions.explanation: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome results from deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), leading to hyperuricemia, mental retardation, and aggressive behavior. This X-linked recessive disorder affects male children predominantly. The deficiency causes accumulation of purine metabolites and impaired recycling pathways.

Thiazide diuretics cause hyperuricemia by blocking tubular secretion of uric acid, reducing renal excretion. Volume contraction from diuresis enhances proximal tubular reabsorption of urate. Thiazide-induced hyperuricemia often necessitates diuretic discontinuation or addition of urate-lowering therapy in gout-prone individuals.
questions.question: Which thiazide diuretic effect contributes to hyperuricemia?
What CK-MB pattern suggests acute MI?
questions.explanation: Acute MI produces characteristic CK-MB pattern: rise within 4-6 hours, peak at 12-24 hours, return to baseline by 48-72 hours. This temporal pattern distinguishes acute from chronic injury. Prolonged elevation suggests ongoing injury or reinfarction. Troponins show similar but more prolonged kinetics.

questions.question: A 30-year-old diabetic patient presents in ketoacidosis. ABG: pH 7.22, PaCO2 20 mmHg, HCO3 8 mmol/L. The expected PaCO2 using Winter's formula (PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 +/- 2) is:
options: Between 14 and 20 mmHg indicating respiratory alkalosis also
Between 20 and 24 mmHg indicating appropriate compensation
Between 18 and 22 mmHg indicating appropriate compensation
Between 24 and 28 mmHg indicating inadequate compensation
Between 12 and 16 mmHg indicating hyperventilation present
questions.explanation: Winter's formula: PaCO2 = (1.5 x 8) + 8 = 12 + 8 = 20 +/- 2, so expected range is 18-22 mmHg. The measured PaCO2 of 20 mmHg falls within this range, confirming appropriate respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing) for the metabolic acidosis without a concurrent primary respiratory disturbance. If PaCO2 were higher than expected, concurrent respiratory acidosis or inadequate compensation would be present; if lower, a concurrent primary respiratory alkalosis would exist.

questions.question: What time frame characterizes delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions?
questions.explanation: Delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) reactions characteristically develop 24-72 hours after antigen exposure, distinguishing them from immediate hypersensitivity. The delay reflects time required for T cell recruitment, activation, and cytokine-mediated inflammation. Peak reactions typically occur at 48-72 hours.

During the last trimester of pregnancy, maternal IgG (but not IgM or IgA) is actively transported across the placenta via neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn). At birth, neonates have maternal IgG levels equal to or slightly higher than maternal levels. This passively transferred IgG provides protection against the encapsulated bacteria and viruses for which the mother has IgG antibodies. As maternal IgG is catabolised (half-life approximately 21 days), protection wanes over 3-6 months. SCID infants typically present with recurrent infections as maternal IgG falls, often at 3-6 months of age.
options: SCID only manifests after 6 months when infections begin
Infants produce their own IgM protecting against infections
Maternally transferred IgG provides passive protection initially
Breastfeeding provides cellular immunity via T cells in milk
Innate immunity compensates completely for the first 3 months
questions.question: A 2-month-old infant with SCID has no rash, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. Why are infants with SCID generally healthy in the first 2-3 months of life?

questions.explanation: Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith (Sm) antibodies are highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus among ANAs. Anti-dsDNA correlates with disease activity and renal involvement. Anti-Sm is highly specific but less sensitive. Antinuclear antibody screening is sensitive but requires specific antibody identification.
questions.question: What autoantibody pattern indicates systemic lupus erythematosus?
What kidney protein is freely filtered and completely reabsorbed normally?
questions.explanation: Beta-2-microglobulin (low molecular weight, 11,800 Da) is freely filtered at the glomerulus and normally completely reabsorbed and metabolized by proximal tubules, with minimal urinary excretion. Elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin indicates tubular dysfunction. Albumin is partially filtered (negatively charged, 69,000 Da). Tamm-Horsfall protein is normally present in urine (produced by tubules).

questions.question: Which liver synthetic function marker has longest half-life?
questions.explanation: Albumin has the longest half-life (16-24 days, average 20 days) among commonly measured liver synthetic markers, making it useful for chronic but not acute liver disease assessment. Coagulation factors have much shorter half-lives (prothrombin 6-16 hours, factor VII 4-6 hours), making PT/INR sensitive for acute hepatic dysfunction. Albumin production is 10-12g daily exclusively by hepatocytes.

ACR >30 mg/mmol (or >300 mg/g) indicates severely increased albuminuria (A3 category, previously macroalbuminuria), associated with high risk of CKD progression and cardiovascular events. This level may indicate nephrotic syndrome (ACR >220 mg/mmol or >2000 mg/g plus hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia). Requires investigation for underlying cause (diabetes, glomerulonephritis, amyloidosis) and aggressive treatment.
questions.question: What albumin:creatinine ratio indicates severely increased proteinuria?
A 55-year-old man has serum calcium of 3.0 mmol/L, PTH of 8.5 pmol/L (elevated, normal less than 6.5), and 24-hour urine calcium of 7.5 mmol/day (normal less than 7.5). The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in outpatients and is characterized by hypercalcemia with inappropriately elevated or unsuppressed PTH. In hypercalcemia from any other cause, PTH should be suppressed. Elevated PTH of 8.5 pmol/L in the context of hypercalcemia confirms autonomous PTH secretion from a parathyroid adenoma (80%), hyperplasia, or carcinoma. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) also shows elevated PTH but features very low urine calcium (less than 2 mmol/day); urine calcium of 7.5 mmol/day here is not suppressed, supporting PHPT rather than FHH.
options: Hypercalcemia of malignancy from PTHrP secretion by tumor
Secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia from CaSR mutation
Sarcoidosis from calcitriol overproduction by macrophages

questions.explanation: Rapid CKD progression is defined as sustained decline in eGFR >5 mL/min/1.73 m²/year, requiring investigation for reversible causes and nephrology referral. Progression confidence increases with more measurements and longer follow-up. Small fluctuations in GFR are common and not necessarily indicative of progression. CKD progression also defined by GFR category decline plus ≥25% eGFR drop.
questions.question: What percentage of GFR decline annually is considered rapid progression?
What defines a mixed acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation: Mixed acid-base disorders involve =2 simultaneous primary disturbances. Identified when: (1) compensation inappropriate for primary disorder (calculate expected compensation; significant difference suggests mixed), (2) pH normal despite abnormal PCO2/HCO3- (body never overcompensates), or (3) ΔAG/ΔHCO3- ratio outside expected range. Example: diabetic with vomiting has DKA (high AG metabolic acidosis) + metabolic alkalosis. Recognition crucial for proper treatment addressing all components.

options: Blocking intestinal calcium absorption through vitamin D antagonism
Enhancing renal calcium excretion by blocking tubular reabsorption
Inhibiting PTH synthesis in chief cells through nuclear receptor action
Activating calcium-sensing receptors to suppress PTH secretion acutely
Directly chelating serum calcium to reduce measured ionized calcium
questions.question: A 70-year-old presents with serum calcium of 1.6 mmol/L, elevated PTH, and low vitamin D (15 nmol/L). He also takes cinacalcet. After reviewing his medications, cinacalcet is identified as a potential cause. The mechanism by which cinacalcet lowers calcium is:
questions.explanation: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that allosterically activates the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells, making the receptor more sensitive to ambient calcium and suppressing PTH secretion. This reduces PTH-mediated bone resorption and renal tubular calcium reabsorption, lowering serum calcium and phosphate. It is used in secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD and parathyroid carcinoma. If given to a patient with already low vitamin D and hypocalcemia, cinacalcet can worsen hypocalcemia by further suppressing PTH below the level needed to maintain calcium. Dose adjustment or discontinuation and vitamin D supplementation corrects this iatrogenic hypocalcemia.

Fetal macrosomia (birth weight >4 kg) results from maternal hyperglycemia causing fetal hyperinsulinemia and excessive growth. This increases risks of shoulder dystocia, birth trauma, and cesarean delivery. Other GDM complications include polyhydramnios, intrauterine death, neonatal hypoglycemia, and respiratory distress syndrome. Maternal complications include preeclampsia and increased future diabetes risk.
questions.question: What complication is unique to gestational diabetes during pregnancy?

questions.explanation: Secretory IgA predominates in external secretions (tears, saliva, breast milk, respiratory and gastrointestinal mucus), providing mucosal immunity. The dimeric form is transported across epithelium with secretory component protecting against proteolysis. Selective IgA deficiency increases mucosal infection susceptibility.
questions.question: What is the predominant immunoglobulin in external secretions?

options: Antagonizing V2 vasopressin receptors to promote electrolyte-free water excretion
Blocking ENaC in collecting duct to promote sodium and water excretion
Inhibiting Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop to promote aquaresis
Stimulating atrial natriuretic peptide receptors in collecting duct
Inhibiting aldosterone binding to mineralocorticoid receptors in distal tubule
questions.explanation: Tolvaptan (and conivaptan) are selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonists (vaptans) that competitively block the V2 receptor in collecting duct principal cells, preventing ADH-stimulated cAMP production and AQP2 insertion. This causes electrolyte-free water excretion (aquaresis) without significant electrolyte loss - correcting dilutional hyponatremia by removing excess free water. Unlike conventional diuretics, tolvaptan does not cause hypokalemia or volume depletion from sodium loss, making it suitable for euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia (SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis). The rate of sodium correction must be monitored closely to avoid exceeding 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours.
questions.question: A 65-year-old with decompensated heart failure has serum sodium of 130 mmol/L despite diuretic therapy. Tolvaptan is prescribed. The mechanism of action of tolvaptan is:
Which cardiac condition shows elevated troponin persisting weeks after event?
questions.explanation: Myocarditis causes troponin elevation that may persist for weeks due to ongoing myocardial inflammation and necrosis, unlike typical MI pattern (elevation for 7-10 days). Chronic troponin elevation also occurs in end-stage renal disease, severe heart failure, and chronic myocardial injury. Clinical context is essential for interpretation; persistently elevated troponin doesn't always indicate acute coronary syndrome.

questions.question: A patient presents with plasma osmolality of 320 mOsm/kg and calculated osmolarity of 285 mOsm/kg. What is the osmolar gap?
questions.explanation: The osmolar gap is calculated by subtracting calculated osmolarity from measured osmolality (320-285=35). Normal osmolar gap ranges from 10-19 mOsm/kg; values exceeding this suggest presence of unmeasured osmotically active substances like methanol, ethylene glycol, or alcohol. This elevated gap indicates potential toxic ingestion requiring immediate investigation.

questions.question: A patient with acute anaphylaxis is transported to hospital. The emergency physician uses serum tryptase measurement 1-3 hours after the reaction. What does elevated tryptase confirm?
questions.explanation: Serum tryptase (a neutral serine protease stored in mast cell secretory granules) rises within 1-2 hours of mast cell degranulation, peaks at 1-3 hours, and returns to baseline by 6-24 hours. Elevated serum tryptase (above 11.4 ng/mL, or more than baseline + 1.2 ng/mL x baseline) confirms mast cell degranulation as the mechanism, helping distinguish anaphylaxis (IgE-mediated or anaphylactoid) from other causes of collapse. It does not identify the specific allergen (skin testing or specific IgE testing is needed later). Normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis (especially in food-triggered or hypotensive anaphylaxis).
options: The specific allergen responsible for the anaphylactic reaction
Mast cell degranulation confirming anaphylaxis occurred
IgE-mediated sensitisation to the causative allergen
Type III immune complex-mediated reaction occurred
The severity of the anaphylactic reaction by tryptase level

questions.explanation: Rate-pressure product (RPP = heart rate × systolic blood pressure) correlates with myocardial oxygen consumption (MVO₂), used during exercise testing to assess cardiac workload. Though not a biomarker, understanding determinants of myocardial oxygen demand helps interpret cardiac ischemia and biomarker elevation. High RPP with symptoms/ECG changes suggests ischemia; biomarker elevation depends on whether demand exceeds supply sufficiently to cause necrosis.
questions.question: What cardiac measurement indicates myocardial oxygen consumption?

questions.explanation: Appropriate laboratory test use requires: (1) clear clinical question, (2) understanding how results will affect management, (3) considering pretest probability, (4) knowledge of test characteristics (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values), (5) avoiding unnecessary repetition. Clinical decision support tools (guidelines, algorithms, computerized alerts) improve utilization. Inappropriate testing wastes resources, may harm patients (false positives leading to unnecessary procedures, incidental findings). Evidence-based guidelines and laboratory stewardship programs promote appropriate testing.
questions.question: What indicates appropriate use of laboratory tests?
Which vitamin deficiency results from intrinsic factor absence?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, binds vitamin B12 (cobalamin), facilitating absorption in terminal ileum through specific receptors. Absence causes pernicious anemia with megaloblastic changes and neurological complications from demyelination. Causes include autoimmune gastritis (anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies), gastrectomy, or Helicobacter pylori infection.

questions.question: What cardiac chamber releases BNP primarily in heart failure?
questions.explanation: B-type natriuretic peptide is primarily released from left ventricular myocardium (though also from right ventricle) in response to wall stress and volume overload. ANP is predominantly atrial in origin, released with increased atrial wall tension. BNP causes natriuresis and vasodilation, providing counter-regulatory effects in heart failure. Normal BNP virtually excludes CHF.

questions.question: A patient with gout requires urate-lowering therapy. His GFR is 25 mL/min/1.73m². Which urate-lowering agent is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol is the preferred urate-lowering agent in patients with renal impairment. It is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that works regardless of renal function (reduces production rather than increasing excretion). However, its active metabolite oxypurinol is renally excreted, accumulating in renal impairment and increasing the risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS). Dose reduction is required: for GFR 10-30 mL/min, start at 50-100 mg/day. Uricosuric agents (probenecid, benzbromarone) are ineffective and potentially harmful in significant renal impairment as they require adequate GFR for effect.
options: Probenecid at full dose as uricosuric therapy
Benzbromarone with caution for hepatotoxicity risk
Rasburicase as the safest agent in renal impairment
Probenecid at reduced dose for this GFR level
Allopurinol at a reduced dose adjusted for renal function

questions.explanation: Hepatic iron concentration exceeds 40 µmol/g dry liver weight in hemochromatosis patients (reference up to 20 µmol/g). Perl's stain on liver biopsy provides semiquantitative assessment, showing iron predominantly in Kupffer cells and hepatocytes. Treatment by weekly phlebotomy continues until iron deficiency develops and ferritin normalizes, preventing progressive liver damage.
questions.question: What is the hepatic iron concentration in hereditary hemochromatosis patients?
What is the mechanism causing ascites in advanced liver cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: The primary mechanism in ascites is sodium retention (possibly secondary to hyperaldosteronism), compounded by hypoalbuminemia and localized to the peritoneal cavity by portal hypertension. Urine may be sodium-free; as long as sodium intake exceeds output, fluid accumulates. Excess water retention leads to hyponatremia, attributed to increased ADH.

questions.question: What characterizes Type III hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type III hypersensitivity involves immune complex formation and deposition in tissues, activating complement and recruiting neutrophils. Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in blood vessels, kidneys, joints, and skin, causing inflammatory tissue damage. Serum sickness, Arthus reaction, and lupus nephritis exemplify this mechanism.

Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency requires phenotyping, since serum AAT concentration can be falsely normal or elevated during acute phase responses. Phenotyping identifies the specific genetic variant, such as the PiZZ phenotype, which carries the highest risk of liver and lung disease.
questions.question: A patient with cirrhosis and emphysema at a young age is found to have absent alpha-1 globulin on serum protein electrophoresis. What further test is required for definitive diagnosis?

questions.explanation: ADH (vasopressin) acts on the collecting ducts to promote water reabsorption by increasing aquaporin-2 channels in the tubular membrane. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in plasma osmolality and trigger ADH release when osmolality exceeds 295 mOsm/kg. Low ADH levels produce dilute urine while high levels concentrate urine.
questions.question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for regulating water reabsorption in the collecting ducts?
What specimen type is optimal for rapid cardiac troponin point-of-care testing?
questions.explanation: Whole blood or plasma is optimal for rapid processing and point-of-care testing (POCT) of cardiac troponins, though serum can also be used. Different sample types should not be used during an individual's workup when serial timed samples rule in/out MI. Immunoassay is the technique of choice for measuring troponins.

CK-MB peaks 12-24 hours after acute MI onset, rising within 4-6 hours and returning to baseline by 48-72 hours. This earlier normalization compared to troponin makes CK-MB potentially useful for detecting early reinfarction. However, troponins have largely replaced CK-MB for MI diagnosis.
questions.question: What is the peak time for CK-MB after acute MI?

questions.explanation: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity allergic reactions by binding mast cells and basophils via high-affinity Fc receptors. Cross-linking IgE by allergen triggers degranulation and mediator release. IgE also plays a role in parasitic immunity. Elevated total IgE suggests atopy, parasitic infection, or hyper-IgE syndrome.
questions.question: What immunoglobulin mediates allergic reactions?
Which investigation is most specific for detecting prostatic carcinoma currently?
questions.explanation: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is more specific and sensitive than acid phosphatase for diagnosing and monitoring prostatic carcinoma. Serum acid phosphatase estimation is gradually being replaced by PSA measurement, though acid phosphatase remains useful for monitoring treatment of known disseminated disease. PSA is a protein derived from the prostate.

questions.question: Which disease is associated with anti-centromere antibodies?
questions.explanation: Anti-centromere antibodies are highly specific for limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). These antibodies target centromere proteins, showing discrete speckled nuclear pattern on immunofluorescence. The condition has better prognosis than diffuse systemic sclerosis.

options: Primary disease progression before engraftment occurs
Failure of engraftment from immune rejection of graft
Graft-versus-host disease from donor T-cell activity
questions.explanation: In SCID patients undergoing HSCT, the immediate critical risk during the pre-engraftment period (before donor cells engraft and reconstitute immunity) is overwhelming opportunistic infection. SCID patients already lack functional adaptive immunity before transplant, and the conditioning regimens used before transplantation (if used — some SCID patients require no conditioning due to absent immune rejection capability) further compromise innate immunity. Viral infections (CMV, adenovirus, EBV), fungal infections (Aspergillus, Candida), and bacterial infections are all major threats requiring prophylaxis.
questions.question: A child with SCID undergoes unmatched allogeneic bone marrow transplantation. Before engraftment, what is the most important immediate risk?

questions.explanation: Discordant response to ART (undetectable viral load but persistently low CD4 count) occurs in approximately 15-25% of patients. Possible mechanisms include: irreversible immune damage from prolonged HIV infection before ART initiation, impaired thymic output of new naive T cells (especially in older patients or those with prolonged immunosuppression), increased T-cell apoptosis, co-infections suppressing CD4 recovery, and immunosenescence. It is more common in patients who start ART with very low CD4 counts. These patients remain at increased risk of opportunistic infections despite viral suppression and require continued close monitoring.
options: Drug resistance allowing viral replication despite undetectable load
Malnutrition impairing CD4 T-cell synthesis and maturation
Immune reconstitution failure or discordant immune response
ART non-adherence causing intermittent viral blips
A new opportunistic infection suppressing CD4 T cells
questions.question: A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy has undetectable viral load but CD4 count of 190 cells/µL after 2 years of treatment. What is the most likely explanation?

questions.explanation: Prinzmetal's angina results from coronary artery vasospasm rather than fixed atherosclerotic obstruction, producing transient ST elevation typically at rest, often in the early morning, which resolves as the spasm relieves, usually without significant troponin elevation.
questions.question: A patient presents with chest pain and transient ST elevation that resolves spontaneously at rest, typically in the early morning, with normal coronary arteries on angiography. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Alcohol abstinence dramatically lowers triglycerides in susceptible individuals, as ethanol increases hepatic VLDL synthesis and impairs lipoprotein lipase activity. Even moderate alcohol consumption raises triglycerides in hypertriglyceridemic patients. Complete abstinence is recommended when triglycerides exceed 500 mg/dL to prevent pancreatitis.
questions.question: What lifestyle factor most significantly lowers triglycerides?
What percentage of filtered sodium is reabsorbed by the proximal tubule?
questions.explanation: The proximal tubule reabsorbs approximately 65-80% of filtered sodium, water, and bicarbonate through Na+/H+ exchange (NHE3) and Na+/K+-ATPase on the basolateral membrane. Additional reabsorption occurs in loop of Henle (25%) and distal tubule/collecting duct (5-10%, aldosterone-regulated). Immature tubular function in neonates, especially premature infants, causes increased sodium losses.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman is found to have serum phosphate of 0.45 mmol/L (normal 0.8-1.5 mmol/L) after admission for hip fracture. She is on antacids chronically. The mechanism of hypophosphatemia from chronic antacid use is:
questions.explanation: Aluminum hydroxide and magnesium hydroxide antacids bind dietary phosphate in the intestinal lumen, forming insoluble aluminum or magnesium phosphate salts that cannot be absorbed and are excreted in stool. Chronic use depletes phosphate stores, causing symptomatic hypophosphatemia with muscle weakness, bone pain, and in severe cases hemolytic anemia and rhabdomyolysis. The hip fracture risk is compounded by antacid-induced osteomalacia from phosphate depletion. Phosphate-binding antacids are now deliberately exploited in CKD patients to control hyperphosphatemia, but incidental phosphate depletion from antacid overuse is a preventable complication.
options: Antacids causing renal phosphate wasting via PTH stimulation
Antacids inhibiting vitamin D activation impairing Ca-P absorption
Antacids reducing gastric acid impairing phosphate solubility
Aluminum or magnesium in antacids binding intestinal phosphate
Antacids causing metabolic alkalosis shifting phosphate into cells

questions.explanation: AST/ALT ratio >2.1 is pathognomonic of alcoholic liver disease, while non-alcoholic fatty liver typically shows ALT>AST (ratio <1). This, combined with elevated GGT (especially with normal ALP), hypertriglyceridemia, macrocytosis, and elevated IgA/CDT, suggests alcohol etiology. However, liver biopsy provides definitive diagnosis and staging of both alcoholic and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.
questions.question: What investigation distinguishes alcoholic from non-alcoholic steatohepatitis?
What non-lipid cardiovascular risk factor is modified by fibrates?
questions.explanation: Fibrates improve glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity through PPAR-alpha activation, potentially reducing diabetes incidence. However, fenofibrate in diabetics showed no cardiovascular benefit in major trials despite improving dyslipidemia. Other pleiotropic effects include reducing inflammation and improving endothelial function.

questions.question: Which electrocardiographic change is the earliest manifestation of hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Peaked, narrow-based T waves appear when serum potassium reaches 6-7 mmol/L, representing the earliest ECG manifestation of hyperkalemia. Progressive elevation causes P wave flattening, PR prolongation, QRS widening, and eventually sine wave pattern leading to ventricular fibrillation. These changes reflect altered myocardial depolarization and repolarization from elevated extracellular potassium.

options: Excessive dietary potassium intake from high-protein CKD diet
Aldosterone resistance developing in the distal nephron in CKD
Reduced distal sodium delivery impairing potassium secretion in CKD
Acidosis-driven transcellular potassium shift out of cells into ECF
Reduced GFR decreasing filtered potassium load reaching distal nephron
questions.question: A 55-year-old with chronic kidney disease has serum potassium of 6.5 mmol/L despite dietary restriction. The mechanism of hyperkalemia in CKD is best explained by:
questions.explanation: As GFR falls in CKD, the filtered potassium load reaching the distal nephron (where potassium secretion occurs) decreases. Although remaining nephrons compensate by increasing fractional excretion of potassium per nephron (through aldosterone and flow-mediated mechanisms), this compensation is eventually insufficient to maintain potassium balance below GFR of 15-20 mL/min. Metabolic acidosis coexisting in CKD exacerbates hyperkalemia by driving H-K exchange across cell membranes, releasing intracellular potassium extracellularly. The combination of reduced tubular secretion capacity and acidosis-driven transcellular shift makes CKD hyperkalemia challenging to control.

questions.question: A patient on long-term phenytoin has persistently elevated GGT with normal ALP and no symptoms of liver disease. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: GGT is an inducible enzyme that rises with exposure to enzyme-inducing drugs such as anticonvulsants and barbiturates, independent of true hepatobiliary disease. This limits its specificity, particularly when ALP and other liver tests remain normal.
Markedly elevated maternal serum AFP (
questions.question: What AFP level suggests multiple pregnancy?

questions.explanation: IgG is the only immunoglobulin class actively transported across the placenta via Fc receptors, providing passive immunity to the fetus/newborn. IgG levels gradually increase during gestation, reaching adult concentrations at term. After birth, maternal IgG is catabolized with endogenous synthesis beginning; adult levels reach by 3-5 years. Elevated cord IgM (>20 mg/dL) indicates intrauterine infection.
questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is transferred across the placenta?
A 55-year-old man has a calculated eGFR of 52 mL/min/1.73m² on two occasions three months apart, with no proteinuria. What CKD category does this represent?
questions.explanation: An eGFR of 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73m² sustained for over three months defines CKD stage 3a, representing mildly to moderately decreased kidney function requiring at least annual monitoring of GFR and albuminuria in patients otherwise at low risk.

questions.question: What cystatin C property makes it superior to creatinine for GFR estimation?
questions.explanation: Cystatin C is produced at a constant rate by all nucleated cells, unaffected by muscle mass, diet, or gender, unlike creatinine. This low molecular weight (13,250 kD) cysteine proteinase inhibitor is freely filtered, reabsorbed, and metabolized by proximal tubules. However, thyroid dysfunction and corticosteroids affect levels, limiting specificity.

questions.question: Which drug inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption?
questions.explanation: Ezetimibe selectively inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption by blocking the NPC1L1 transporter. The drug reduces LDL cholesterol approximately 18-20% as monotherapy and provides additive benefit with statins. Ezetimibe also lowers plant sterols and decreases intestinal cholesterol delivery to liver.

options: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals embedded in fibrous tissue
Monosodium urate crystals with surrounding granulomatous inflammation
Necrotic tissue surrounded by multinucleated giant cells alone
Calcium hydroxyapatite deposits in subcutaneous tissue
Calcium oxalate crystals from hyperoxaluria deposition
questions.explanation: A tophus is a pathological deposit of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals surrounded by a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response. Histologically, tophi show: a central core of MSU crystals (which dissolve in routine H&E processing, leaving empty 'ghost' spaces); surrounded by a foreign body granulomatous reaction with epithelioid macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes, and fibroblasts; and an outer fibrous capsule. Tophi can form at any site but preferentially develop at cooler peripheral areas (ears, elbows, Achilles tendons, toes) where lower temperature favours urate crystallisation from supersaturated tissue fluid.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man with chronic tophaceous gout has subcutaneous tophi around his elbows and Achilles tendons. What is the microscopic composition of a tophus?
Which urine crystals appear in alkaline urine?
questions.explanation: Triple phosphate (magnesium ammonium phosphate) crystals form rectangular or coffin-lid shapes in neutral/alkaline urine. Calcium phosphate (amorphous or granular) and calcium carbonate (small dumbbell or star-shaped) also form in alkaline urine. Acid urine contains uric acid (rhomboid, rosettes), calcium oxalate (envelope-shaped), and calcium sulfate crystals. Crystal identification helps determine urolithiasis type and guide prevention strategies.

questions.question: What metabolic pathway generates the most ATP per glucose molecule?
questions.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation generates approximately 28-30 ATP molecules per glucose through electron transport chain coupling to ATP synthase. Glycolysis produces only 2 ATP per glucose. The citric acid cycle generates GTP (equivalent to ATP) plus reducing equivalents that fuel oxidative phosphorylation.

Apolipoprotein A-I constitutes approximately 70% of HDL protein mass, activates LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase), and participates in reverse cholesterol transport. Low apo A-I levels correlate with increased cardiovascular risk, while high levels are protective. Genetic apo A-I deficiency causes very low HDL-cholesterol, corneal opacities, and premature coronary disease.
questions.question: Which apolipoprotein is the major protein component of HDL?
A patient taking allopurinol for gout is started on azathioprine for Crohn's disease. Which dangerous interaction must be anticipated?
questions.explanation: Azathioprine is metabolised to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), which is further inactivated by xanthine oxidase to thiouric acid. Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, preventing 6-MP inactivation. This causes accumulation of the active thioguanine nucleotide metabolites, leading to severe myelosuppression (pancytopenia) and hepatotoxicity. When allopurinol and azathioprine must be co-prescribed, azathioprine dose must be reduced by 75% (to 25% of the usual dose) and full blood counts monitored closely.
options: Allopurinol reduces azathioprine absorption from the gut
Both drugs cause hepatotoxicity via the same cytochrome P450
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase increasing azathioprine toxicity
Both drugs compete for the same protein binding sites
Allopurinol inhibits renal clearance of azathioprine

questions.question: What advantage do high-sensitivity troponin assays provide?
questions.explanation: High-sensitivity troponin assays detect myocardial injury earlier through improved analytical sensitivity, enabling MI diagnosis within 1-3 hours versus 3-6 hours with conventional assays. Earlier detection facilitates rapid rule-in/rule-out protocols. However, increased sensitivity reduces specificity for MI, detecting more non-MI cardiac injury.

Pruritus in cholestatic liver disease results from bile acid deposition in skin, not bilirubin. Bile acids irritate cutaneous nerve endings. Pruritus may precede jaundice by months/years (e.g., primary biliary cirrhosis). Cholestyramine (bile acid sequestrant) may provide symptomatic relief. Elevated bile acids are characteristic of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
questions.question: What mechanism causes pruritus in cholestatic liver disease?
What lipid abnormality is characteristic of diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation: Diabetic dyslipidemia characteristically features elevated triglycerides, reduced HDL cholesterol, and increased small dense LDL particles. Insulin resistance and deficiency increase hepatic VLDL production while decreasing lipoprotein lipase activity. LDL cholesterol may be normal but particle quality is more atherogenic.

questions.question: What laboratory finding suggests respiratory acidosis compensation?
questions.explanation: Chronic respiratory acidosis (>24-48 hours) shows renal compensation: increased renal H+ excretion and HCO3- regeneration elevate serum bicarbonate, partially correcting pH. Acute respiratory acidosis shows minimal HCO3- increase (1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg PaCO2 rise from tissue buffering). Chronic shows 3.5 mEq/L HCO3- increase per 10 mmHg PaCO2 rise. If observed HCO3- differs significantly from expected, consider mixed disorder.

questions.question: A patient with ethylene glycol ingestion has serum calcium of 1.6 mmol/L, HCO3 10 mmol/L, anion gap 26 mmol/L, and urine showing calcium oxalate crystals. The mechanism of hypocalcemia is:
options: Ethylene glycol metabolites chelating ionized calcium as oxalate
Ethylene glycol inhibiting parathyroid hormone synthesis acutely
Ethylene glycol reducing renal calcium reabsorption directly
Magnesium deficiency from ethylene glycol causing PTH resistance
Vitamin D conversion impaired by ethylene glycol metabolites
questions.explanation: Ethylene glycol is metabolized to oxalic acid (glycolate then oxalate), which precipitates with ionized calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals deposited in renal tubules, brain, and other tissues. This chelation of ionized calcium by oxalate produces symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, QT prolongation). The combination of anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypocalcemia, and urine calcium oxalate crystals is pathognomonic for ethylene glycol poisoning. Fluorescence of urine under Wood's lamp (if antifreeze-derived ethylene glycol, which contains fluorescein) may be positive. Treatment includes fomepizole and urgent dialysis.

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) shows severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL, often >1000 mg/dL), hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), severe dehydration, and minimal/no ketosis. Occurs predominantly in Type 2 diabetes (sufficient insulin to prevent lipolysis). Presents with altered mental status, severe dehydration, hypotension. Mortality ~10-20% (higher than DKA). Precipitants: infection, stroke, MI, medications. Treatment: aggressive fluid replacement, insulin, electrolyte correction, addressing precipitant.
questions.question: What characterizes hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

questions.explanation: AMI results from imbalance between oxygen supply and demand in myocardium, causing tissue injury and myocyte necrosis. Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with thrombosis (Type 1 MI) is the commonest cause, reducing supply. Restoration of coronary blood flow within 60-90 minutes maximizes myocardial salvage through thrombolysis or PCI.
questions.question: What is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism in acute myocardial infarction?
A 25-year-old presents to the emergency department with hyperventilation and tingling of the lips and hands. ABG: pH 7.54, PaCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L. The most likely cause is:
questions.explanation: Respiratory alkalosis from anxiety-driven hyperventilation presents with circumoral tingling, paresthesias of extremities, carpopedal spasm, and lightheadedness. These symptoms result from the reduction in ionized calcium caused by acute alkalosis (alkalosis increases albumin binding of calcium, reducing ionized fraction). pH of 7.54, low PaCO2 (24 mmHg), and slightly reduced HCO3 (20 mmol/L, representing early renal compensation or normal range) are characteristic. Reassurance, breathing into a paper bag, or controlled breathing exercises to raise PaCO2 are effective. If PE or other organic cause is suspected, further workup is warranted.
options: Anxiety or panic attack causing voluntary hyperventilation
Salicylate toxicity causing central respiratory center stimulation
Sepsis causing early respiratory alkalosis from fever stimulus

questions.question: What is the mechanism by which hydroxychloroquine provides benefit in systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is an aminoquinoline that accumulates in lysosomes and endosomes, raising their pH. This inhibits Toll-like receptor (TLR) signalling (particularly TLR7 and TLR9), which are located in endosomes and respond to self-nucleic acids (ssRNA and dsDNA respectively) in SLE. By blocking TLR7/9 signalling, HCQ reduces innate immune activation by self-nuclear material, reduces type I interferon production (central to SLE pathogenesis), suppresses dendritic cell activation, and decreases autoantibody production. HCQ reduces lupus flares, prevents organ damage accumulation, reduces cardiovascular risk, prevents lupus nephritis, and improves survival in SLE.
options: Inhibition of TNF-alpha production from activated macrophages
Blockade of B-cell CD20 reducing autoantibody production
Inhibition of calcineurin reducing T-cell activation
Inhibition of Toll-like receptor signalling in endosomes
Direct anti-inflammatory effect on neutrophil recruitment

questions.explanation: LDL normally carries approximately 70% of total plasma cholesterol, making it the major cholesterol transport lipoprotein. HDL contains 20-30%, VLDL about 10-15%, with minimal amounts in chylomicrons (fasting state). Elevated LDL-cholesterol strongly correlates with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk, making it the primary target for lipid-lowering therapy.
questions.question: What percentage of total plasma cholesterol does LDL normally carry?
