questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis results from mutations in RBC membrane cytoskeletal proteins such as spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, and protein 4.1. These proteins normally maintain the biconcave disc shape. Deficiency causes the cell to round up into a sphere, increasing osmotic fragility. Spherocytes are less deformable and are trapped and destroyed in the spleen, causing haemolytic anaemia.
options: Glucose metabolism in the Embden-Meyerhof pathway

questions.explanation: Central diabetes insipidus (DI) = ADH deficiency (hypothalamic/pituitary damage); Nephrogenic DI = renal insensitivity to ADH (ADH receptor or AQP2 mutations). Without ADH, collecting ducts are impermeable to water, producing 5–20 L/day of hypotonic urine. Unlike DM, blood glucose is normal. Central DI responds to desmopressin (synthetic ADH analogue).
questions.question: Diabetes insipidus results from deficiency of:

options: Positively charged relative to the exterior
Electrically neutral relative to the exterior
Negatively charged relative to the exterior
Positively charged only in cardiac muscle cells
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is electrically polarised with the inside being negative relative to the outside (resting membrane potential approximately ˜ 70 mV in neurons). This is maintained by Na+/K+-ATPase and the selective K+ permeability via leak channels. This polarity is essential for action potential generation, hormone signalling, and secondary active transport.
questions.question: The resting membrane potential is maintained with the cell interior being:

options: Facilitated diffusion through specific carrier proteins
Solute movement with bulk water flow
questions.question: Solvent drag in renal tubule refers to:
questions.explanation: Solvent drag is passive co-movement of solutes carried along with bulk water flow during reabsorption. As large volumes of water are osmotically reabsorbed in the PCT, dissolved solutes (K+, Cl-, Ca2+, Mg2+) are carried along ? accounting for a significant portion of their reabsorption without specific membrane transporters. It is particularly important for K+ and Cl- in the PCT.

questions.question: Red blood cells assume a SICKLE SHAPE in sickle cell disease PRIMARILY during:
questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, deoxygenation causes HbS molecules to polymerise into long fibrous aggregates, deforming the red cell into the characteristic sickle shape. Oxygenated HbS remains soluble. Triggers for sickling include hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration, and cold, all of which promote HbS polymerisation and vaso-occlusive crises.

questions.question: Aldosterone acts on collecting duct principal cells to increase expression of:
questions.explanation: Aldosterone (a mineralocorticoid) acts via nuclear receptors in principal cells, genomically upregulating ENaC (apical Na+ entry channel) and Na+/K+-ATPase (basolateral Na+ exit pump). This increases Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion. This is the mechanism by which aldosterone expands ECF volume and lowers serum K+. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptors, preventing these effects.

options: Gastric acid reducing ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous (Fe2+) iron
Iron deficiency increasing duodenal absorptive capacity
Ferrous form of iron (Fe2+) at the duodenal mucosa
questions.explanation: Tannins (polyphenols) in tea, coffee, and red wine chelate dietary iron in the intestinal lumen, forming insoluble complexes that cannot be absorbed, thereby INHIBITING iron absorption. Vitamin C reduces Fe3+ to the more soluble Fe2+, enhancing absorption. Gastric acid and iron deficiency state also promote absorption. Phytates in grains and calcium similarly inhibit iron absorption.
questions.question: Iron absorption from the gut is ENHANCED by all of the following EXCEPT:
What comprises the solid matter of feces?
questions.explanation: Fecal solids contain approximately 30% dead bacteria, 10-20% fat, 10-20% inorganic matter, 2-3% protein, and 30% undigested roughage plus sloughed epithelial cells and dried digestive juice constituents. Composition varies with diet.

ADP released from platelet granules upon activation causes nearby platelets to become sticky and aggregate. This positive feedback cycle rapidly amplifies platelet plug formation, with each activated platelet recruiting additional platelets to the injury site.
questions.question: Which chemical promotes platelet aggregation?
Daily glomerular filtrate production in healthy adults is approximately:
questions.explanation: GFR ˜ 125 mL/min ˜ 1440 min/day = 180 L/day. Of this, 99% (178.8 L) is reabsorbed by tubules; only 1.2 L is excreted as urine/day. This enormous filtration-reabsorption turnover allows precise regulation of plasma composition and volume. GFR decreases with age (~1 mL/min/year after 40) and in renal disease.

options: Pain perceived at location other than source
questions.question: Referred pain occurs when:
questions.explanation: Referred pain is perceived at a location distant from the actual source, typically when visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal neurons. Classic example: cardiac pain referred to left shoulder/arm. This reflects embryological development.

questions.question: A healthy 70 kg man produces approximately how much metabolic water per day?
questions.explanation: Oxidative (metabolic) water produced during cellular respiration contributes approximately 200 mL per day to total daily water intake. Total daily water intake is roughly 2300 mL, of which 2100 mL comes from ingestion and 200 mL from metabolism.

RhoGAM (anti-Rh antibodies) administered to Rh-negative mothers during and after Rh-positive pregnancies binds fetal Rh antigens entering maternal circulation, preventing maternal immune system sensitization. This prevents hemolytic disease in subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies.
questions.question: What prevents maternal sensitization to Rh-positive fetus?
Neutrophils constitute what percentage of white blood cells?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils comprise about 60% of circulating white blood cells and are primary bacteria killers. These phagocytic cells rapidly migrate to infection sites, engulfing and destroying bacteria. Their abundance reflects their critical role as first responders to bacterial infections.

Simple columnar epithelium lines regions specialized for secretion and absorption in the GIT. This single-layered structure facilitates efficient nutrient absorption and secretion. The stratified squamous epithelium is reserved for protective regions like the esophagus and oral cavity.
questions.question: What type of epithelium lines the absorptive regions of the GIT?
What is a reticulocyte?
questions.explanation: Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells that recently lost their nucleus but retain ribosomal RNA networks. They circulate 1-2 days before maturing into erythrocytes. Reticulocyte counts assess bone marrow erythropoietic activity, elevated in hemolytic anemia or hemorrhage.

questions.question: The normal inspiratory capacity (IC) equals:
questions.explanation: IC = TV + IRV (tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume). IC can also be expressed as IC = VC × ERV or IC = TLC × FRC. It represents the maximum volume inhaled from FRC (resting end-expiratory position). Normal IC ˜ 3.8 L in males. IC is reduced in restrictive disease and normal in pure obstructive disease.

questions.question: The periovulatory period involves:
questions.explanation: The periovulatory period features rapidly rising estrogen from the dominant follicle creating positive feedback, triggering the LH surge. This brief positive feedback period (late follicular phase) contrasts with negative feedback during most of the cycle.

questions.question: What anchors AV valve cusps?
questions.explanation: Chordae tendineae (tendinous cords) connect AV valve cusps to papillary muscles in ventricular walls. During ventricular contraction, papillary muscles tense these cords, preventing valve prolapse (inversion into atria) despite high ventricular pressure.

options: Varying hormone doses mimicking natural cycle
questions.question: Sequential oral contraceptive pills provide:
questions.explanation: Sequential pills vary hormone doses throughout the cycle, more closely mimicking natural hormonal patterns. Earlier pills may have lower progestin, with increasing doses later. Modern formulations are less common than monophasic or triphasic combined pills.

questions.question: Estrogen affects uterine sensitivity to oxytocin by:
questions.explanation: Estrogen increases uterine oxytocin receptor expression, enhancing responsiveness near term. Progesterone decreases sensitivity. The changing estrogen/progesterone ratio prepares the uterus for oxytocin-induced labor.

questions.question: What is hypertension's primary danger?
questions.explanation: Chronic hypertension damages target organs (heart, kidneys, brain, eyes, blood vessels) through sustained elevated pressure. Complications include left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, renal failure, stroke, and retinopathy, making blood pressure control essential.

Hemophilia management involves transfusions of fresh plasma or purified specific clotting factors. Modern recombinant factors reduce infection risks from blood products. Treatment provides temporary relief (several days) but requires repeated administration due to factor degradation.
questions.question: What treatment helps hemophilia patients?
Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis typically follows which event?
questions.explanation: Subacute thyroiditis typically follows viral URI, causing painful thyroid enlargement with transient hyperthyroidism (from follicle disruption releasing stored hormone), then hypothyroidism, then recovery. It's self-limited. ESR is markedly elevated.

Insensible water loss totals approximately 700 mL/day: evaporation from the skin accounts for 300–400 mL/day and from the lungs another 300–400 mL/day. This loss occurs continuously and cannot be voluntarily regulated, unlike renal and sweat losses which are controllable.
questions.question: The insensible water loss per day from the skin and lungs combined is approximately:

questions.explanation: The median eminence lacks a blood-brain barrier due to fenestrated capillaries, allowing hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones to enter portal blood reaching the anterior pituitary. This specialized vasculature enables neuroendocrine communication. Hypophysiotropic hormones require this access.
questions.question: The fenestrated capillaries of the median eminence allow:
What condition results from excessive aldosterone secretion?
questions.explanation: Aldosteronism (hyperaldosteronism) results from excessive aldosterone production, causing hypertension and edema through sodium retention. Primary aldosteronism often results from adrenal adenomas, while secondary forms involve renin-angiotensin system activation. The condition leads to characteristic electrolyte abnormalities including hypokalemia.

questions.question: The phrenic nerve supplying the diaphragm arises from spinal levels:
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4, C5 (mnemonic: 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'). It provides motor innervation to the diaphragm ? the principal muscle of inspiration. High cervical cord injuries above C5 cause bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis requiring mechanical ventilation. Each hemidiaphragm is supplied by an ipsilateral phrenic nerve.

The enteric nervous system (ENS), with ~100 million neurons in the gut wall, coordinates GI motility and secretion, functioning independently though influenced by autonomic input. Includes myenteric (motility) and submucosal (secretion) plexuses. Called the "brain of the gut."
questions.question: What is the primary function of the enteric nervous system?
What is the "first-pass effect"?
options: Nutrients go to liver before systemic circulation
questions.explanation: The first-pass effect means absorbed nutrients travel via portal vein to the liver before entering systemic circulation. The liver processes, stores, or modifies substances before general distribution. This allows metabolic regulation and detoxification. Oral drugs also undergo first-pass metabolism.

questions.question: The kidney GENERATES new bicarbonate (rather than merely reabsorbing filtered HCO3-) PRIMARILY through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: New bicarbonate generation occurs in the kidney via ammoniagenesis: glutamine is metabolised in PCT cells to NH3 and alpha-ketoglutarate; alpha-ketoglutarate is further metabolised, generating HCO3- that enters the blood. The NH3 combines with secreted H+ in the tubular lumen to form NH4+, which is excreted in urine (carrying the acid load). This process dramatically increases during chronic metabolic acidosis.
options: Direct synthesis of HCO3- from chloride in the collecting duct
Ammoniagenesis producing HCO3? as NH4? is excreted
Passive diffusion of atmospheric CO2 into renal tubular cells
Active secretion of H2CO3 from peritubular capillaries into tubular fluid
Phospholipid catabolism releasing bicarbonate in the loop of Henle

questions.question: What is the optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes function optimally at mildly alkaline pH (7.8-8.3), which is why pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is essential to neutralize acidic gastric chyme. Pancreatic enzymes are inactivated by low pH. Bicarbonate creates optimal conditions.

questions.question: What is normal resting cardiac output?
questions.explanation: Normal resting cardiac output averages approximately 5-5.5 L/min (calculated as 70 beats/min × 75 mL/beat). This pumps the body's entire blood volume each minute, with substantial reserve capacity for increased demands during exercise or stress.

Loss of estrogen's protective effects on lipid profiles and vascular function increases cardiovascular disease risk. Premenopausal women have lower cardiovascular risk than age-matched men. After menopause, risks equalize. This transition emphasizes the importance of cardiovascular risk factor management.
questions.question: Cardiovascular disease risk increases postmenopausally because:

questions.explanation: The macula densa is arbitrarily designated as the point where the loop of Henle (specifically the thick ascending limb) ends and the distal convoluted tubule begins. Macula densa cells sense NaCl concentration in tubular fluid, mediating tubuloglomerular feedback and signalling renin secretion from adjacent JG cells, connecting tubular Na+ delivery to glomerular filtration and renin-angiotensin regulation.
questions.question: The macula densa is designated as the beginning of which nephron segment?
Which physical feature is characteristic of Cushing's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Moon facies (rounded face) results from facial fat redistribution caused by chronic cortisol excess. Other features include central obesity, buffalo hump, and abdominal striae. These changes reflect cortisol's effects on fat metabolism and redistribution.

Cardiomyopathy refers to primary heart muscle disorders causing impaired contractility. Types include dilated (enlarged, weak ventricles), hypertrophic (thickened, stiff walls), and restrictive (rigid ventricles). All can progress to heart failure despite different mechanisms.
questions.question: What is cardiomyopathy?

questions.explanation: The pronormoblast (proerythroblast) is the earliest recognizable cell committed to erythrocyte lineage. This large cell with basophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleus undergoes progressive maturation through normoblast stages, eventually losing its nucleus to become a reticulocyte.
questions.question: What cell is the erythrocyte precursor?

questions.explanation: MEN syndromes are hereditary cancer syndromes affecting multiple endocrine glands. MEN1 involves parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreas. MEN2 involves thyroid C cells, parathyroid, and adrenal medulla. Genetic testing identifies at-risk family members.
questions.question: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are characterized by:
PAH clearance measures effective renal plasma flow because PAH is:
questions.explanation: PAH is freely filtered AND secreted by proximal tubular cells, resulting in approximately 91% removal from renal plasma in a single pass (extraction ratio 0.91). PAH clearance = ERPF ˜ 625 mL/min. Actual RPF ˜ 693 mL/min (PAH clearance/extraction ratio = 625/0.91). This property makes PAH the standard marker for measuring renal plasma flow.

Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via specific sodium-dependent bile salt transporters. This enterohepatic circulation conserves bile salts (95% reabsorbed), recycling them 6-8 times daily. Ileal disease causes bile salt deficiency.
questions.question: Where are bile salts actively reabsorbed?
In Hirschsprung disease, which structure always lacks enteric innervation?
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease always involves loss of enteric nervous system in the distal colon and internal anal sphincter. The aganglionic segment cannot generate peristaltic waves or relax normally. This causes severe constipation and colonic dilation proximal to the affected segment.

Angiotensinogen (453 amino acid protein) is synthesised and released by the liver into the bloodstream. Renin from JG cells cleaves it to Angiotensin I (10 AA). ACE in pulmonary endothelium then converts Ang I to Ang II (8 AA). The liver thus provides the substrate for the RAAS. Hepatic production of angiotensinogen is increased by glucocorticoids and oestrogen.
questions.question: Angiotensinogen is primarily synthesised in the:

options: Is dark red/purplish and has lower oxygen affinity
Lacks the globin portion required for oxygen transport
Carries carbon dioxide instead of oxygen
Bright red, with O2 bound to haem iron
questions.question: Oxyhaemoglobin differs from deoxyhaemoglobin in that oxyhaemoglobin:
questions.explanation: Oxyhaemoglobin (HbO2) is bright red in colour and forms when oxygen binds reversibly to the ferrous iron (Fe2+) in the haem groups of haemoglobin. Deoxyhaemoglobin is dark red/purplish. The transition between oxygenated and deoxygenated forms accounts for the difference in colour between arterial blood (bright red) and venous blood (dark red), which is clinically visible as cyanosis.

Endomysium is delicate connective tissue lining each individual muscle fiber, containing capillaries and nerve fibers. This intimate contact allows metabolic exchange and innervation. The endomysium contributes to the muscle's mechanical properties and organization.
questions.question: Endomysium functions to:

questions.explanation: Type IIb fast glycolytic fibers are anaerobic, glycolytic, and "white" with less myoglobin and mitochondria. They contract rapidly with great force but fatigue quickly. These fibers are ideal for brief, powerful movements like sprinting or jumping, not endurance activities.
questions.question: Type IIb muscle fibers are best suited for:

options: Thickening cervical mucus blocking sperm entry
questions.question: Progestin-releasing IUCDs additionally work by:
questions.explanation: Progestin-releasing IUCDs (like levonorgestrel systems) thicken cervical mucus, impeding sperm entry beyond the mechanical effects. They also thin the endometrium and may suppress ovulation in some users. These multiple mechanisms provide high efficacy with lighter menses.
Lysosomal proteases digest thyroglobulin, releasing free T3, T4, MIT, and DIT. The active hormones then exit into the bloodstream. Lysosomal enzyme deficiency can cause hypothyroidism.
questions.question: After thyroglobulin internalization, which organelles release enzymes for hormone liberation?

questions.explanation: Normal plasma and whole blood osmolarity is 280–300 mOsm/L, reflecting the combined contributions of electrolytes, glucose, urea, and proteins. Values below 280 mOsm/L indicate hypo-osmolarity, and above 300 mOsm/L indicate hyperosmolarity, both of which trigger regulatory responses.
questions.question: The approximate osmolarity of whole blood is:
Maximal cardiac output in females is approximately what percentage less than in males?
questions.explanation: Maximal cardiac output is approximately 25% less in females than males. This difference reflects smaller cardiac size, lower haemoglobin concentration (reducing O2-carrying capacity), and smaller stroke volumes in women. These physiological differences are relevant when prescribing exercise intensity and interpreting cardiopulmonary exercise test results.

Adrenal sex steroids, along with gonadal hormones, drive the adolescent growth spurt by promoting skeletal growth before epiphyseal closure. These hormones work synergistically with growth hormone and IGF-1. Eventually, sex steroids promote growth plate fusion, ending linear growth.
questions.question: What role do adrenal androgens and estrogens play in skeletal development?
What causes gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)?
questions.explanation: GERD results from incompetent LES allowing gastric acid reflux into the esophagus, causing heartburn and potential esophagitis. Chronic GERD can cause Barrett's esophagus (metaplasia) with adenocarcinoma risk. Treatment includes PPIs, H2 blockers, lifestyle modifications.

questions.question: Insulin affects adipose tissue by increasing production of:
questions.explanation: Insulin increases a-glycerol phosphate production in adipocytes, providing the glycerol backbone for triglyceride synthesis. This effect, combined with increased fatty acid uptake, promotes fat storage. Insulin-stimulated glucose metabolism supplies glycerol-3-phosphate.

Normal diastolic blood pressure (lowest pressure during ventricular relaxation) is approximately 80 mmHg. Diastolic pressures consistently above 90 mmHg indicate hypertension requiring treatment to prevent end-organ damage (heart, kidneys, brain, eyes).
questions.question: What is normal diastolic blood pressure?

options: Stimulating insulin secretion from beta cells
Reducing glucagon secretion from alpha cells
questions.question: The SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins) reduce blood glucose in T2DM by:
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) block the Na-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) on the luminal surface of PCT cells, preventing glucose reabsorption. This causes glycosuria, reducing plasma glucose levels. Additional benefits include diuresis (osmotic), weight loss, and cardiovascular/renal protection independent of glucose lowering ? mechanisms including reduced preload/afterload and reduced intraglomerular pressure.
GH excess before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism with extreme height but proportionate features. After closure, the same excess causes acromegaly. Both typically result from pituitary adenomas.
questions.question: Excessive growth hormone in children causes:

questions.explanation: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ion channel-linked (ionotropic) receptors ? four transmembrane domain receptors directly coupled to ligand-gated ion channels. Binding of ACh opens the channel allowing Na+ and Ca2+ entry and depolarisation. Other examples include ionotropic glutamate receptors and GABA-A receptors.
questions.question: Ion channel-linked (ionotropic) receptors include which of the following?
The window of implantation occurs:
questions.explanation: The implantation window is a limited period during the mid-secretory phase (approximately days 20-24) when the endometrium is receptive to embryo implantation. Molecular markers of receptivity appear only during this window. Timing embryo transfer to this window is critical for IVF success.

questions.question: Mucous membranes protect against infection by:
questions.explanation: Mucous membranes provide mechanical barriers in respiratory, gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts. Mucus secreted by specialized cells traps particles and microbes. Ciliated cells in respiratory tract beat rhythmically, sweeping trapped materials out for elimination.
options: Providing mechanical barrier and trapping particles

questions.question: Hypermetabolic hypoxia would MOST likely occur in:
questions.explanation: Hypermetabolic hypoxia: O2 demand exceeds delivery due to greatly increased metabolic rate. Extensive burns (2–3× increase in metabolic rate) and certain cancers require supplemental O2 or increased FiO2. CO poisoning = anaemic; cyanide = histotoxic; heart failure = circulatory; pulmonary embolism = hypoxaemic (dead space). Correct classification guides treatment strategy.
options: Carbon monoxide poisoning reducing Hb O2 carriage
Left heart failure reducing cardiac output
Extensive burns with dramatically increased O2 demand

questions.question: Radial glia primarily function during:
questions.explanation: Radial glia serve as scaffolding for neuronal migration during embryonic CNS development. They guide neurons to proper locations. Some radial glia persist as neural stem cells in adults.

Severe diarrhoea causes massive loss of water, sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate, leading to isotonic dehydration, hypovolaemia, reduced cardiac output, and ultimately cardiovascular collapse/shock. It is a leading cause of mortality in children globally, particularly from cholera and rotavirus. Rapid oral or intravenous rehydration with electrolyte solutions is life-saving.
questions.question: During severe diarrhoea, the IMMEDIATE life-threatening consequence of electrolyte and fluid loss is:

options: Elevated due to overventilation relative to perfusion
Reduced due to underperfusion relative to ventilation
Near zero due to collapsed alveoli
questions.explanation: In the upright position, gravity reduces blood flow to the apex (less hydrostatic pressure) more than ventilation, resulting in overventilation relative to perfusion (elevated V/Q). PAO2 rises and PACO2 falls at the apex. At the base, the opposite occurs (low V/Q ? underperfused relative to ventilation). These regional V/Q inequalities are one reason normal lungs cannot fully saturate mixed venous blood.
questions.question: At the apex of an upright lung, the V/Q ratio is:

questions.explanation: The frontal lobe, particularly the prefrontal cortex, contains most dopamine-sensitive neurons. These mediate attention, reward, planning, and motivation. Dopamine dysfunction contributes to schizophrenia and ADHD.
questions.question: The frontal lobe contains the majority of which neurotransmitter-sensitive neurons?

questions.explanation: Blood velocity is slowest in capillaries despite their tiny individual diameter, because total cross-sectional area is greatest due to their vast numbers. Slow flow (approximately 0.03 cm/sec) allows adequate time for nutrient, gas, and waste exchange between blood and tissues.
questions.question: Where is blood velocity slowest?
Lecithin (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) is the major component of:
questions.explanation: Lecithin (DPPC) constitutes approximately 70% of pulmonary surfactant produced by Type II pneumocytes. Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse. Deficiency of surfactant in premature infants causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS). Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate lung maturation and surfactant synthesis.

Detumescence results from sympathetic stimulation constricting internal pudendal arteries and contracting trabecular muscles. This reduces arterial inflow and squeezes blood from erectile tissue. The penis becomes flaccid, and a refractory period follows before re-arousal is possible.
questions.question: Detumescence occurs because:

questions.explanation: Receptive relaxation is initiated by swallowing through a vagovagal reflex mediated by inhibitory neurons. This anticipatory relaxation occurs before food enters the stomach. Neurotransmitters like VIP and NO mediate the smooth muscle relaxation.
questions.question: What initiates receptive relaxation of the stomach?
What are ketone bodies produced from?
questions.explanation: Ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) are produced from acetyl-CoA during excessive fatty acid oxidation (fasting, low-carb diets, diabetes). They provide alternative fuel for brain and muscles when glucose is scarce. Excessive production causes ketoacidosis.

questions.question: Which blood type has both A and B antibodies?
questions.explanation: Type O individuals lack both A and B antigens on their RBCs but naturally possess both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in their plasma. These preformed antibodies develop within months after birth without prior exposure to foreign antigens.

questions.question: What makes type O blood universal donor?
questions.explanation: Type O red blood cells lack A and B antigens, preventing reaction with recipient antibodies regardless of recipient blood type. However, O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B antibodies, so only packed red cells (plasma removed) truly qualify as universal donor blood.

Horizontal positioning eliminates hydrostatic pressure effects, but mean arterial pressure remains relatively stable through baroreceptor reflexes. However, venous return increases, potentially raising cardiac output and causing slight pressure increase unless compensatory mechanisms adjust.
questions.question: What happens to blood pressure when lying down?
Glucose entry into pancreatic beta cells occurs via which transporter?
questions.explanation: GLUT2, a high-Km glucose transporter, allows glucose entry into beta cells proportional to blood glucose concentration. This transporter acts as a glucose sensor. GLUT2's kinetics make beta cells responsive to physiological glucose fluctuations.

Medical abortion uses medications (typically mifepristone blocking progesterone plus misoprostol causing contractions) to terminate early pregnancy. This method is effective in early pregnancy with appropriate medical supervision. Surgical abortion remains an alternative method.
questions.question: Medical termination of pregnancy involves:
options: Medications inducing uterine contractions and tissue passage
Complete safety with no possible complications

questions.question: MIT and DIT released during thyroglobulin digestion are:
questions.explanation: Intrathyroidal deiodinase rapidly removes iodine from MIT and DIT, allowing iodide recycling for new hormone synthesis. This conservation mechanism is crucial in iodine-deficient states. Congenital deiodinase deficiency causes iodine loss and hypothyroidism.

In HbS, there is a point mutation in the beta-globin gene resulting in substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta chain. The alpha chains are normal. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises, causing the characteristic sickling of red cells, haemolysis, vaso-occlusion, and organ damage.
options: Abnormal alpha chains with normal beta chains
Abnormal beta chains with normal alpha chains
Complete absence of all polypeptide chains
Substitution of iron in the haem group
questions.question: In sickle cell anaemia, the molecular abnormality in haemoglobin S (HbS) is:
Obstructive ventilatory defects are characterised by a limitation of:
questions.explanation: Obstructive ventilatory defects are defined by limitation of expiratory airflow, characterised by reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (< 0.79). Examples: asthma, COPD, emphysema, cystic fibrosis. FVC may be normal or reduced; TLC is normal or elevated (air trapping). Restrictive defects reduce lung volumes (TLC, FVC) with preserved or elevated FEV1/FVC ratio.

questions.question: The countercurrent multiplier system of the loop of Henle primarily serves to:
options: Reabsorb glucose from dilute tubular fluid
Deliver bicarbonate to the collecting duct
questions.explanation: The countercurrent multiplier creates the medullary hyperosmotic gradient (up to 1200 mOsm/L at the papilla): the descending limb reabsorbs water (without solutes), and the ascending TAL reabsorbs NaCl (without water). This creates the gradient that allows ADH-stimulated collecting ducts to reabsorb water and produce concentrated urine (up to 1200 mOsm/L).

Ductal epithelial cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach. Acinar cells produce digestive enzymes. Ductal secretion creates the high pH (7.8-8.3) of pancreatic juice.
questions.question: Which cells in the pancreas secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid?
The glomerular filtration membrane consists of all layers EXCEPT:
options: Juxtaglomerular granular cells of afferent arteriole
questions.explanation: The glomerular filtration membrane has 3 layers: (1) fenestrated capillary endothelium (70–90 nm pores), (2) basement membrane/basal lamina (main molecular sieve), (3) podocyte filtration slits (25 nm). Mesangial cells (contractile) are between capillary loops and regulate filtration area. JG granular cells are located in the afferent arteriole wall ? not in the filtration membrane.

Hemolytic disease occurs when Rh-negative mothers sensitized by previous Rh-positive pregnancies produce anti-Rh antibodies that cross the placenta, destroying fetal red blood cells. First pregnancies are usually safe, but subsequent ones risk severe fetal anemia and jaundice.
questions.question: What causes hemolytic disease of the newborn?
Proteins in the plasma are responsible for approximately what percentage of plasma osmolarity?
questions.explanation: Despite their large molecular weight and biological importance, plasma proteins contribute less than 1% to total plasma osmolarity (roughly 1-2 mOsm/L out of 290 mOsm/L total). However, because proteins are retained within the capillary unlike small solutes that equilibrate across the wall, their oncotic contribution of about 25 mmHg is disproportionately important for fluid balance between plasma and interstitium.

Loss of Na+, K+, and water into the stool creates an osmotic gradient that further draws water into the bowel lumen from extracellular fluid. This leads to dehydration, hypovolaemia, and ultimately shock. The osmotic effect is the immediate physico-chemical driver of fluid loss during diarrhoea.
options: Increased water absorption from the stool
questions.question: During diarrhoea, the IMMEDIATE osmotic consequence of electrolyte loss into the stool is:

questions.explanation: Renin is secreted by juxtaglomerular (granular) cells ? specialised smooth muscle cells mainly in the afferent arteriole walls. Renin cleaves liver-produced angiotensinogen to Ang I. Release is stimulated by reduced renal perfusion pressure (baroreceptor mechanism), reduced NaCl delivery to macula densa, and a-1 adrenergic stimulation (sympathetic activation).
questions.question: Renin is secreted by which cells of the JGA?

questions.explanation: Dalton's law: total pressure of a gas mixture = sum of partial pressures of all component gases (P = p1 + p2 + p3 + ... + pn). Atmospheric pressure (760 mmHg) is the sum of partial pressures of N2, O2, CO2, H2O vapour, and inert gases. This principle is used to calculate alveolar gas partial pressures using the alveolar gas equation.
options: The product of all partial pressures
The highest partial pressure of components
The partial pressure of oxygen only
Sum of all individual partial pressures
The average of component gas pressures
questions.question: Dalton's law states that total gas pressure equals:

questions.explanation: SIADH: excess ADH causes inappropriate water retention (increased collecting duct AQP2 permeability), diluting plasma sodium ? hyponatraemia. Despite hypo-osmolality, the kidney continues to concentrate urine (high urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/L). Causes include ectopic ADH production (small cell lung cancer), CNS disorders, drugs (carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide). Treatment: fluid restriction, hypertonic saline, or vaptan (ADH receptor antagonist).
options: Normal serum sodium with massive polyuria
questions.question: The SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH) causes:

questions.explanation: Transcellular transport refers to movement of solutes and water THROUGH cells, crossing both the apical (luminal) and basolateral membranes via specific transporters. Paracellular transport refers to movement BETWEEN cells through tight junctions. The PCT uses both pathways; tighter junctions in the collecting duct limit paracellular transport, allowing greater hormonal fine-tuning.
questions.question: In renal tubules, transcellular transport refers to movement:
Carbon monoxide poisoning causes toxicity PRIMARILY because CO:
options: Binds irreversibly to haem iron in myoglobin only
Competes with O2 for haem with higher affinity
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to the haem iron of haemoglobin with approximately 200–250 times greater affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) which cannot carry oxygen. This causes functional anaemia. Treatment with hyperbaric oxygen (100% O2 at high pressure) displaces CO from haemoglobin by mass action.

questions.question: HIV causes immunodeficiency PRIMARILY by destroying which cell type?
questions.explanation: HIV specifically targets and destroys CD4+ T helper (Th) lymphocytes by using CD4 as its primary receptor and CCR5/CXCR4 as co-receptors. Progressive CD4+ T cell depletion below 200 cells per microlitre defines AIDS, impairing both cellular and humoral immunity. This makes patients susceptible to opportunistic infections like Pneumocystis pneumonia and malignancies like Kaposi sarcoma.

Humoral immunity involves B-cells producing antibodies that circulate in body fluids (humors). These antibodies recognize specific antigens, neutralizing toxins and pathogens. Humoral immunity is particularly effective against extracellular pathogens.
questions.question: Humoral immunity is mediated by:

questions.explanation: The descending limb reabsorbs approximately 25% of filtered water. It is water-permeable (AQP1 channels) but impermeable to NaCl. As tubular fluid descends into the hypertonic medulla, water exits osmotically, concentrating the tubular fluid (increasing osmolality from 290 to 1200 mOsm/L at the hairpin turn). This is the first step of countercurrent multiplication.
questions.question: The descending limb of the loop of Henle reabsorbs approximately what percentage of filtered water?

questions.explanation: Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation at approximately 157 mEq/L of intracellular water. Sodium at 143 mEq/L is the main extracellular cation. Chloride and bicarbonate are the dominant extracellular anions, and neither is a principal intracellular cation.
questions.question: The PRINCIPAL intracellular cation and its approximate concentration in intracellular fluid is:

questions.explanation: Bile salt deficiency causes steatorrhea (fat in stools) due to impaired fat emulsification and micelle formation, leading to fat malabsorption. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are also poorly absorbed. Ileal disease or resection can cause bile salt deficiency.
questions.question: What is the consequence of bile salt deficiency?
Which substance in pancreatic juice prevents premature trypsin activation?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor is secreted with pancreatic enzymes to prevent premature trypsin activation within the pancreas, protecting against autodigestion. If trypsinogen is accidentally activated, this inhibitor inactivates it. Loss of this protection causes pancreatitis.

questions.question: In METABOLIC ALKALOSIS, the respiratory compensation is:
options: Hyperventilation to blow off CO2 and lower pH
No respiratory compensation occurs in metabolic alkalosis
Increased renal bicarbonate excretion immediately without respiratory change
Stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors causing tachypnoea
Hypoventilation retaining CO2 to lower pH
questions.explanation: The respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis is hypoventilation (reduced respiratory rate), which retains CO2 (raises PaCO2). The increased CO2 lowers pH back toward normal, partially offsetting the alkalosis. However, this compensation is limited because hypoventilation also reduces arterial PO2, and hypoxia eventually stimulates breathing, preventing PaCO2 from rising beyond approximately 55-60 mmHg.
Glucagon activates hepatic glycogen phosphorylase, promoting glycogen breakdown to glucose. This effect rapidly mobilizes glucose stores. Glycogenolysis can sustain blood glucose for several hours.
questions.question: Glucagon promotes which hepatic metabolic pathway?

options: Enhanced FSH sensitivity and local factors
questions.explanation: Follicle selection involves enhanced FSH sensitivity, increased FSH receptor expression, and local growth factor production. The dominant follicle can continue growing despite falling FSH levels. It also secretes factors suppressing other developing follicles.
questions.question: The dominant follicle is selected by:
Epimysium is the connective tissue layer:
questions.explanation: Epimysium is the dense connective tissue sheath surrounding entire muscles. It provides protection, separates muscles, and may blend with tendons at muscle ends. This outer covering completes the hierarchical organization of muscle connective tissue.

Gastric venous blood becomes alkaline after meals due to bicarbonate secretion from parietal cells into blood (exchanged for chloride). This is called the post-prandial alkaline tide. The bicarbonate is a byproduct of acid secretion.
questions.question: What happens to gastric venous blood pH after eating?
Thyroid hormone resistance syndromes result from mutations in:
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone resistance results from mutations in thyroid hormone receptor genes (primarily TRß), causing reduced tissue responsiveness. Patients may have elevated thyroid hormones with non-suppressed TSH. Clinical presentation varies depending on affected tissues.

Central precocious puberty involves early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with normal pubertal sequence but premature timing. Causes include CNS lesions or idiopathic activation. Treatment may include GnRH analogs to suppress the axis until appropriate age.
questions.question: Central precocious puberty results from:

questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle contractions compress veins, forcing blood toward the heart through one-way valves. This "muscle pump" is crucial for venous return from legs, explaining why prolonged standing without movement causes venous pooling and potential fainting.
questions.question: What aids venous return against gravity?
The osmolarity of the renal cortical interstitium is approximately:
questions.explanation: The osmolarity of the renal cortical interstitium is approximately 300 mOsm/L, similar to that of plasma. Moving from the cortex toward the inner medullary papilla, osmolarity progressively increases to 1200 mOsm/L. This medullary gradient is generated by the countercurrent multiplier system and maintained by the countercurrent exchanger (vasa recta).

questions.question: The primary mechanism of cardiovascular response before exercise even begins is:
questions.explanation: Anticipatory (feed-forward) central command from the motor cortex initiates cardiovascular changes at the onset of (and before) exercise, including increased heart rate and cardiac output. This occurs before any metabolic changes develop in exercising muscles. It explains the immediate cardiovascular response at exercise onset, preparing circulation in advance of metabolic demand.
options: Baroreceptor reflex resetting in the medulla
Mechanical effect of the muscle pump on veins
Anticipatory central command from motor cortex

questions.question: What prevents continuous defecation between bowel movements?
questions.explanation: The internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, involuntary) maintains tonic contraction preventing continuous defecation. Defecation reflex causes IAS relaxation. The external anal sphincter (skeletal muscle, voluntary) provides additional conscious control. IAS damage causes fecal incontinence.
options: Internal anal sphincter smooth muscle tone

questions.question: What volume of chyme enters the colon daily?
questions.explanation: Approximately 1500 ml of chyme passes through the ileocecal valve into the colon daily. Most water and electrolytes are absorbed, leaving less than 100 ml in feces. The colon absorbs 5-8 liters total daily (including secretions).

Estrogen increases oxytocin receptor numbers in uterine muscle, enhancing responsiveness to oxytocin. It also promotes gap junction formation for coordinated contractions and stimulates prostaglandin production. These multiple actions of estrogen are essential for transforming the quiescent pregnant uterus into one capable of effective labor.
questions.question: Estrogen's role in labor initiation includes:
options: Reducing gap junction formation between cells

questions.explanation: Coronary blood flow, particularly in the left coronary circulation, occurs predominantly during ventricular diastole. During systole, the strong contraction of the ventricular myocardium compresses the intramuscular coronary vessels, especially in the left ventricle, markedly reducing blood flow. The right coronary artery is less affected due to lower right ventricular pressure.
questions.question: Coronary blood flow occurs PREDOMINANTLY during which phase of the cardiac cycle?
Testosterone during male puberty causes:
questions.explanation: Testosterone stimulates muscle development, voice deepening, facial and body hair growth, genital development, and libido. These androgenic effects produce male secondary sexual characteristics. Testosterone also affects bone growth, body composition, and behavior during male puberty.

questions.question: Which macronutrient is the body's preferred energy source?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the preferred energy source, especially for the brain (glucose-dependent) and during high-intensity exercise. Glucose provides rapid ATP production. Fats are used during rest and low-intensity activity. Proteins are spared for structural functions.

In histotoxic hypoxia, arterial PO2 is NORMAL because oxygen delivery to tissues is adequate. The defect is tissue inability to utilise oxygen (e.g., cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase; sulphide poisoning). Venous PO2 is paradoxically elevated as tissues cannot extract O2. Treatment includes antidotes (hydroxocobalamin for cyanide) plus supplemental oxygen.
questions.question: In histotoxic hypoxia, arterial PO2 is:
What distinguishes L-amino acids from D-amino acids?
questions.explanation: L-amino acids (naturally occurring in proteins) are actively absorbed via sodium cotransport, while D-amino acids are absorbed by facilitated diffusion. Only L-amino acids are used for protein synthesis. D-amino acids are rare in nature.

questions.question: Where is the heart located?
questions.explanation: The heart lies in the mediastinum between the lungs, posterior to and slightly left of the sternum, anterior to the vertebral column, and superior to the diaphragm. This protected position shields it from direct trauma.

An action potential at the neuromuscular junction triggers release of 200-300 synaptic vesicles. Each vesicle contains thousands of acetylcholine molecules ensuring adequate postsynaptic stimulation. This multivesicular release provides a safety factor for reliable neuromuscular transmission.
questions.question: How many synaptic vesicles typically release during a single action potential at the motor end plate?
Integrins function primarily as receptors for:
questions.explanation: Integrins are heterodimeric transmembrane glycoproteins (alpha and beta subunits) that act as receptors for extracellular matrix molecules. They structurally and functionally integrate the ECM with the intracellular cytoskeleton, playing roles in cell migration, differentiation, and bidirectional signal transduction. They are crucial in wound healing, embryogenesis, and tumour invasion.

An embolus is a thrombus fragment that breaks free and travels through the bloodstream until lodging in a vessel too narrow to pass. Pulmonary emboli (trapped in lung vessels) and cerebral emboli (causing strokes) are particularly dangerous complications.
questions.question: What is an embolus?

questions.explanation: The endocardium, composed of epithelium and underlying connective tissue, forms a protective inner lining of chambers and valves. It contains blood vessels and specialized conduction system fibers, continuous with vessel endothelium throughout the circulatory system.
questions.question: What lines the heart's internal chambers?
Which lipid requires special protein for absorption?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol esters must be hydrolyzed by pancreatic cholesterol esterase before absorption as free cholesterol. Free cholesterol is then reesterified in enterocytes. Other lipids don't require this specific processing. Cholesterol is incorporated into chylomicrons.

questions.question: What supplies blood to the heart muscle?
questions.explanation: Coronary arteries, branching from the ascending aorta immediately above the aortic valve, supply the myocardium with oxygenated blood. Despite the heart pumping vast blood quantities, the myocardium requires its own dedicated blood supply for adequate oxygen and nutrients.

Paneth cells located at the base of crypts secrete defensins, which are antimicrobial peptides. These cytokines provide innate immunity by killing bacteria and other pathogens. Paneth cells play a crucial role in maintaining the intestinal barrier function.
questions.question: Which cells in the crypts of Lieberkühn secrete defensins?

questions.explanation: Nipple stimulation sends neural signals to the hypothalamus, triggering oxytocin release (milk ejection reflex). This conditioned reflex can be triggered by infant crying or visual cues. Stress can inhibit the reflex.
questions.question: Suckling triggers oxytocin release through which mechanism?
Pulsatile gonadotropin secretion during late puberty:
questions.explanation: Late pubertal pulsatile gonadotropin secretion stimulates rising sex steroids from gonads. Testosterone from testes and estradiol from ovaries produce secondary sexual characteristics. This hormonal maturation enables reproductive capability and completes physical sexual development.

Congestive heart failure occurs when the heart cannot pump sufficient blood to meet body needs. Causes include coronary disease, hypertension, valve disorders, or cardiomyopathy. Compensatory mechanisms (sympathetic activation, ventricular hypertrophy) eventually fail, worsening the condition.
questions.question: What is congestive heart failure?

options: Decreasing human chorionic gonadotropin and increasing relaxin
questions.question: Which hormonal change increases uterine excitability near term?
questions.explanation: Increasing estrogen with decreasing progesterone enhances uterine excitability approaching term. Progesterone inhibits uterine contractility throughout pregnancy, while estrogen promotes it by increasing gap junctions, prostaglandin production, and oxytocin receptors. This hormonal shift is crucial for initiating labor contractions.

questions.question: Which ion channels open during the depolarization phase of an action potential?
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open during depolarization allowing rapid sodium influx. This inward sodium current changes membrane potential from -70 mV to +40 mV. The opening of these channels is triggered when threshold potential is reached.

At birth, each oocyte is surrounded by a single layer of granulosa cells, forming a primordial follicle. These remain dormant until puberty when cyclic gonadotropin secretion begins. Primordial follicles represent the "resting" pool from which developing follicles are recruited each cycle.
questions.question: Primordial follicles consist of:
options: Mature oocyte surrounded by cumulus cells
Oocyte with single layer of granulosa cells

questions.question: Which cells produce calcitonin in response to hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation: Thyroid parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin when calcium is elevated, though calcitonin's physiological role in humans is limited. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclastic bone resorption. Medullary thyroid cancer produces excess calcitonin.

questions.question: What is the primary stimulus for pancreatic enzyme secretion?
questions.explanation: Cholecystokinin (CCK), released by duodenal I-cells in response to fats and proteins, is the primary stimulus for pancreatic enzyme secretion from acinar cells. Secretin primarily stimulates bicarbonate secretion. CCK acts on CCK receptors on acinar cells.

Interstitial cells of Cajal function as pacemakers generating slow waves in the GIT. These specialized cells are located between muscle layers and create rhythmic electrical activity. Their slow waves determine the maximum frequency of contractions in each GIT segment.
questions.question: Which cells are responsible for generating slow waves in the GIT?
At rest, what percentage of cardiac output does the kidney receive?
questions.explanation: The kidneys receive approximately 20% of cardiac output at rest, despite representing only 0.5% of body weight. This represents approximately 400 mL/min/100g of tissue ? the highest per-gram flow of any organ. This high perfusion is necessary to filter 180 L of plasma per day (GFR 125 mL/min) for precise regulation of plasma composition.

questions.question: The ovarian cycle includes which phases?
questions.explanation: The ovarian cycle consists of follicular phase (follicle development), ovulation (oocyte release), and luteal phase (corpus luteum formation). These ovarian events drive corresponding uterine changes. Understanding ovarian phases is essential for comprehending menstrual cycle regulation.

questions.question: Prostacyclin (PGI2) from vascular endothelium causes:
questions.explanation: Prostacyclin (PGI2), synthesised from arachidonic acid in endothelial cells, is a potent vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation via cAMP. It balances the vasoconstrictive and pro-aggregatory effects of thromboxane A2 from platelets. Disruption of this balance (e.g., by COX-2 inhibitors sparing platelet TXA2) contributes to thrombotic cardiovascular events.

The muscularis mucosae is a thin smooth muscle layer that creates numerous small folds in the mucosa. These folds significantly increase the absorptive surface area of the gastrointestinal tract. Contraction of this layer also aids in expelling secretions from glands.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the muscularis mucosae?
Which of the following bleeding disorders is inherited as an X-LINKED RECESSIVE condition?
questions.explanation: Haemophilia A (and haemophilia B) are X-linked recessive disorders. The gene encoding Factor VIII (and Factor IX for haemophilia B) is located on the X chromosome. Therefore, males (XY) have only one copy and are affected if mutated; females (XX) are usually carriers (one normal copy compensates). Approximately 1 in 5000 male births is affected by haemophilia A globally.

A one-year-old has approximately 100 billion (10^11) neurons. No new neurons are formed after age one, and approximately 200,000 are lost daily (2-5% loss by age 50). Maximum brain weight is achieved around age 21.
questions.question: How many neurons does a one-year-old human have?

questions.explanation: Astrocytes support neurons by anchoring them to blood vessels, regulating local ion concentrations, recycling neurotransmitters, and forming the blood-brain barrier. They also provide metabolic support. Astrocytes respond to injury with gliosis.
questions.question: Astrocytes primarily function to:
Which chamber pumps blood to the lungs?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which divides into pulmonary arteries carrying blood to the lungs for oxygenation.

Receptor-mediated endocytosis begins with specific ligand binding to receptors clustered in clathrin-coated pits. Pits invaginate to form coated vesicles that lose their clathrin coat, fuse to form early endosomes, and receptors are recycled. Examples include LDL-cholesterol and iron-transferrin uptake. It is highly specific and more efficient than pinocytosis.
questions.question: Receptor-mediated endocytosis is characterised by:

questions.explanation: Acromegaly causes frontal bossing (bulging forehead), prognathism (protruding jaw), enlarged nose, and coarse facial features. These changes develop gradually over years. Comparison with old photographs helps diagnosis.
questions.question: Characteristic facial features of acromegaly include:
In achalasia, which structure fails to relax properly?
questions.explanation: In achalasia, the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax due to loss of enteric nervous system. The aganglionic region cannot transduce inhibitory signals for sphincter relaxation. This results in dysphagia and proximal esophageal dilation creating a "bird's beak" appearance.

questions.question: Which leukocyte is involved in allergic reactions?
questions.explanation: Basophils release histamine and heparin during allergic reactions and inflammation. They constitute only 0.5-1% of circulating leukocytes but play crucial roles in hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, asthma, and hay fever through mediator release.

Right-sided heart failure causes systemic venous congestion, with blood backing up into peripheral circulation. This increases capillary hydrostatic pressure, causing peripheral edema (especially legs), hepatomegaly, ascites, and jugular venous distension.
questions.question: What characterizes right-sided heart failure?
Which diuretic paradoxically reduces urinary calcium excretion?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics paradoxically REDUCE urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria) by blocking NCC in the DCT, creating intracellular Na+ depletion that secondarily upregulates basolateral Na-Ca exchange, increasing Ca2+ reabsorption. This property makes thiazides useful for treating hypercalciuria and preventing recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones. Loop diuretics increase Ca2+ excretion (calciuretic).

DIC is a life-threatening syndrome of widespread microvascular coagulation that consumes clotting factors, platelets, and fibrinogen, causing simultaneous microvascular thrombosis and uncontrolled haemorrhage. It is triggered by sepsis, obstetric emergencies, malignancy, or trauma. Laboratory findings include prolonged PT/APTT, thrombocytopenia, reduced fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimers.
questions.question: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is characterised by:
options: Systemic coagulation activation consuming clotting factors
Selective deficiency of vitamin K-dependent factors
Localised platelet plug formation at a single vessel injury site

questions.question: Compared to growth hormone, prolactin concentration is approximately:
questions.explanation: Prolactin circulates at about 1/100 the concentration of GH in non-pregnant, non-lactating individuals. Levels increase dramatically during pregnancy and lactation. Despite lower concentration, prolactin has potent effects on target tissues.

Myoepithelial cells surrounding mammary alveoli contract in response to oxytocin, not prolactin. This contraction generates 10-20 mm Hg pressure, expelling milk into the ductal system. Without oxytocin-induced contraction, milk remains in alveoli despite being produced.
questions.question: Myoepithelial cells contract in response to:

options: Anaemia due to haemolysis of abnormal cells
Anaemia due to megaloblastic changes in marrow
Anaemia resulting from failure of bone marrow
Anaemia caused by chronic blood loss
questions.explanation: Aplastic anaemia results from destruction or suppression of haematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, leading to pancytopenia (anaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia). Causes include autoimmune attack, radiation, chemotherapy, or drugs. It is distinct from haemolytic anaemia (excess destruction), iron deficiency, and megaloblastic anaemia (maturation failure).
questions.question: Aplastic anaemia is BEST defined as:

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates provide 4 kcal/g, same as proteins. Fats provide 9 kcal/g (most energy-dense), while alcohol provides 7 kcal/g. These are the Atwater factors used to calculate dietary energy content. Carbohydrates are the preferred energy source.
questions.question: How many kilocalories per gram does carbohydrate provide?

questions.explanation: Exercise produces lactic acid, CO2, heat, and 2,3-DPG, all shifting the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT (Bohr effect). A right shift means haemoglobin has LOWER oxygen affinity, facilitating oxygen unloading to metabolically active tissues. This is physiologically appropriate: the harder tissues work, the more acid they produce and the more O2 is delivered to them by haemoglobin.
questions.question: During exercise, lactic acid production SHIFTS the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction with what physiological benefit?
options: Left shift; increases oxygen loading in the lungs
No shift; exercise does not affect haemoglobin-oxygen affinity
Right shift (Bohr effect); facilitates oxygen unloading to exercising muscles
Left shift; haemoglobin retains more oxygen to reduce lactic acid toxicity
Right shift; haemoglobin carries more CO2 to buffer lactic acid

questions.question: In males, stage two puberty includes:
questions.explanation: Stage two (ages 9-15) involves testicular and scrotal growth without penile enlargement yet. Body shape changes, muscle and fat develop, aureole darkens and enlarges. Early pubic hair appears at penis base. These changes precede the more obvious penile growth of later stages.

questions.question: What is the first step in hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Vascular spasm (vasoconstriction) is the immediate response to vessel injury, reducing blood flow and loss. This reflex contraction results from direct smooth muscle injury, chemicals released by endothelial cells and platelets, and local pain receptor activation.

Transcellular fluid comprises minor specialized compartments such as CSF, synovial, pleural, pericardial, and ocular fluids. Interstitial fluid is a major division of extracellular fluid, not transcellular. Synovial fluid, however, IS a transcellular fluid, making D the correct exception here—interstitial fluid does not belong to the transcellular category.
questions.question: Transcellular fluid includes all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Ionotropic (ligand-gated) receptors are ion channels that open directly when neurotransmitter binds, causing rapid (millisecond) responses. Metabotropic receptors work through second messengers (G-proteins), causing slower but longer-lasting effects. Both types exist for many neurotransmitters.
questions.question: What type of receptor opens ion channels directly?

questions.explanation: Mass movements (strong peristaltic waves) are triggered by gastrocolic and duodenocolic reflexes after meals, moving contents toward the rectum. These reflexes are mediated by gastrin, CCK, and parasympathetic activity. Mass movements occur 1-3 times daily.
questions.question: What triggers mass movements in the colon?

questions.explanation: Estradiol stimulates breast development, female fat distribution pattern (hips, thighs), reproductive organ development, and growth acceleration. It also affects bone maturation and closure of epiphyseal plates. These estrogenic effects produce female secondary sexual characteristics.
options: Breast development and fat distribution changes
Facial hair growth and voice deepening
Muscle mass increase and linear growth
questions.question: Estradiol-17ß during female puberty stimulates:
MAO inhibitors affect neurotransmitter levels by:
questions.explanation: Monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors prevent catecholamine breakdown, increasing norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin levels. They're used as antidepressants. Dietary restrictions are necessary to avoid hypertensive crisis.

questions.question: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, extensive proteinuria leads to oedema PRIMARILY because:
questions.explanation: Loss of plasma proteins (especially albumin) in urine reduces plasma oncotic pressure. This lowers the force reabsorbing fluid at the venous end of capillaries, resulting in net movement of fluid into the interstitial space and oedema. This is classic oncotic oedema distinct from inflammatory or hydrostatic oedema.
options: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure causing oedema
Increased ADH leading to water retention

questions.question: What is the role of bile salts in digestion?
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify large fat droplets into smaller particles, increasing surface area for lipase action and forming micelles for absorption. They do not directly digest fats enzymatically. Emulsification is a physical process increasing enzyme efficiency.

The lungs partially remove serotonin (5-HT), bradykinin, adenine nucleotides, norepinephrine, and acetylcholine from blood ? one of the lungs' secondary metabolic functions. In contrast, prostaglandins, histamine, and kallikrein are synthesised and released by the lungs. This pulmonary metabolic activity forms the basis of exhaled breath condensate analysis for biomarker detection.
questions.question: Serotonin is partially removed from circulation during transit through the:

questions.explanation: Parasympathetic stimulation via vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which hyperpolarizes SA node cells, slowing their firing rate (negative chronotropic effect). This dominates at rest, maintaining resting heart rate below the SA node's intrinsic rate (~100 bpm).
questions.question: What nervous system decreases heart rate?
Tyrosine combined with two iodine atoms forms:
questions.explanation: Di-iodotyrosine (DIT) contains two iodines on the tyrosine molecule. DIT serves as the primary precursor for thyroxine (T4). Like MIT, DIT has no inherent biological activity.

options: Thickening cervical mucus to block sperm entry
Acting as spermicidal agents killing sperm
questions.question: Chemical barrier contraceptives work by:
questions.explanation: Chemical barriers contain spermicidal agents like nonoxynol-9 or octoxynol-3 that kill sperm on contact. Available as foams, tablets, creams, jellies and vaginal sponges, they are well-tolerated and inexpensive. However, they can be messy and may cause local irritation in some users.

questions.question: Normal plasma sodium concentration is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal plasma sodium concentration is 135–145 mEq/L (mmol/L). Sodium is the dominant ECF cation and primary determinant of ECF osmolality and volume. Hyponatraemia (< 135) causes cellular swelling (cerebral oedema, seizures); hypernatraemia (> 145) causes cellular shrinkage. Plasma [Na+] is regulated by ADH (water retention) and thirst, not by aldosterone which regulates Na+ balance (volume), not concentration.

questions.question: Where do pulmonary emboli typically originate?
questions.explanation: Most pulmonary emboli originate as deep vein thromboses in leg veins. When these clots dislodge, they travel through increasingly larger veins to the right heart, then lodge in pulmonary arteries, potentially causing severe respiratory compromise or death.

questions.question: What is bradycardia?
questions.explanation: Bradycardia describes heart rates below 60 bpm. While normal in trained athletes (high vagal tone), pathological bradycardia results from SA node dysfunction, AV blocks, hypothyroidism, or medications. Severe bradycardia (<40 bpm) may require pacemaker intervention.

Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in the synaptic cleft rapidly hydrolyzes ACh into acetate and choline (inactive products). This terminates the signal and allows repolarization. Choline is taken back into the terminal and reused for ACh synthesis.
questions.question: What enzyme degrades acetylcholine?
What is the mechanism of cholera toxin?
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin irreversibly activates adenylate cyclase in crypt cells, increasing cAMP and causing massive chloride (and water) secretion. Water follows chloride osmotically. Absorption remains intact but is overwhelmed. Severe dehydration can be fatal.

questions.question: Albumin is synthesized PRIMARILY in the:
questions.explanation: Albumin is synthesized exclusively in the liver (hepatocytes). It is the most abundant plasma protein and is responsible for oncotic pressure, transport of hormones, fatty acids, bilirubin, and drugs, and buffering of blood pH. Liver disease reduces albumin synthesis, lowering oncotic pressure and causing hypoalbuminaemic oedema.

questions.question: The first stage of labor ends when:
questions.explanation: Stage one ends when cervical dilation reaches 10 cm (complete dilation). This marks the transition from cervical dilation to active fetal descent and delivery. The cervix must dilate fully to permit passage of the fetal head.

questions.question: In alpha-thalassaemia, the molecular abnormality involves:
options: Decreased, absent, or abnormal alpha chains
Substitution of valine in the beta chain
questions.explanation: Alpha-thalassaemia involves decreased, absent, or structurally abnormal alpha (a) globin chains. Depending on how many alpha-globin genes are deleted or mutated (out of 4 total), clinical severity ranges from silent carrier to HbH disease to hydrops fetalis (all 4 genes affected). Beta-thalassaemia affects beta-chain synthesis.

Cardiac reserve is the difference between resting and maximal cardiac output, representing the heart's capacity to increase pumping when needed. Healthy young adults can increase output 4-5 fold, while trained athletes achieve 6-7 fold increases.
questions.question: What is cardiac reserve?

questions.explanation: Paracellular transport (between cells via leaky tight junctions) in the PCT is driven by passive electrochemical and osmotic gradients. The PCT has relatively leaky tight junctions, allowing significant paracellular Na+, Cl-, water, and solute transport. Tighter junctions in the collecting duct greatly restrict paracellular flow, allowing hormonal fine-tuning of transport rates.
questions.question: Paracellular transport in the PCT is driven primarily by:
What stimulates enterochromaffin-like cells to release histamine?
questions.explanation: Gastrin stimulates ECL cells to release histamine, which then acts on parietal cells via H2 receptors to stimulate acid secretion. This represents an important indirect pathway for gastrin's acid-stimulating effects. Vagus nerve also stimulates ECL cells.

questions.question: What is the medical term for clot dissolution?
questions.explanation: Fibrinolysis is the physiological process of clot dissolution by plasmin. This natural "clot buster" system ensures temporary clots formed in minor vessel injuries are removed after healing, preventing progressive vessel occlusion from accumulated unnecessary clots.

questions.question: What is the typical diameter of a red blood cell?
questions.explanation: Normal erythrocytes measure approximately 6-9 µm in diameter and 1-2 µm in thickness. This size allows them to pass through the smallest capillaries while maintaining adequate surface area for efficient gas exchange with surrounding tissues.

questions.question: Glucosuria in diabetes occurs when blood glucose exceeds:
questions.explanation: The renal threshold for glucose reabsorption is approximately 180 mg/dL; above this, glucose appears in urine. Glucosuria causes osmotic diuresis. The threshold may vary with age and kidney function.

Injectable contraceptives like depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) contain long-acting progestins given every 3 months. They suppress ovulation, thicken cervical mucus, and alter endometrium. Advantages include convenience and privacy; disadvantages include delayed return to fertility.
questions.question: Injectable contraceptives typically contain:
What happens to salivary sodium concentration during maximal flow rates?
questions.explanation: At high flow rates, there is less time for sodium reabsorption in the ducts, so salivary sodium concentration increases toward plasma levels. At low flow rates, more time allows greater sodium reabsorption, producing more hypotonic saliva. Flow rate inversely affects modification time.

questions.question: Which cells naturally prevent clotting in intact vessels?
questions.explanation: Intact endothelial cells release prostacyclin and nitric oxide, inhibiting platelet activation, and express thrombomodulin and heparan sulfate, which activate protein C and enhance antithrombin III respectively. These mechanisms maintain blood fluidity by preventing inappropriate coagulation.

The coronary sinus, a large vein on the heart's posterior surface, collects blood from great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein, and small cardiac vein. It empties directly into the right atrium, providing the heart's primary venous drainage route.
questions.question: What is the major venous drainage of the heart?
The absence of EEG activity indicates:
questions.explanation: Flat EEG (isoelectric recording) indicates brain death when other criteria are met. This represents cessation of cortical electrical activity. Confirmatory testing and clinical criteria are required for brain death determination.

questions.question: During which phase does potassium exit the cell to cause repolarization?
questions.explanation: During the repolarization phase, voltage-gated potassium channels open allowing potassium efflux. This outward movement of positive charges restores the negative membrane potential. Repolarization returns the membrane toward its resting state after depolarization.

Resting coronary blood flow averages approximately 225 mL/min, which represents about 4–5% of cardiac output (~5 L/min). Despite the heart comprising only about 300 g (0.5% of body weight), it extracts 70–80% of oxygen from coronary blood at rest (compared to 25% for most tissues), making it highly vulnerable to ischaemia.
questions.question: Resting coronary blood flow averages approximately:

questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones increase cardiac beta-adrenergic receptor expression and enhance catecholamine responsiveness (permissive effect). They also increase a-myosin heavy chain expression with higher ATPase activity. These effects increase heart rate and contractility.
questions.question: Thyroid hormones affect cardiac function through which mechanism?
Hyperventilation causes respiratory ALKALOSIS because:
options: Reduces PaCO2 below 40 mmHg, raising pH
It increases CO2 production by activated cells
It causes excessive retention of bicarbonate by the kidneys
It promotes lactic acid production by respiratory muscles
It increases carbonic anhydrase activity in red cells
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation blows off CO2 faster than it is produced, reducing arterial PCO2 (hypocapnia). By the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, lower CO2 increases the HCO3–/CO2 ratio, raising pH above 7.45 (respiratory alkalosis). Psychoneurosis, anxiety, altitude exposure, and CNS stimulation can cause hyperventilation. Renal compensation involves bicarbonate excretion.

Acetazolamide (CA inhibitor) causes bicarbonaturia and mild metabolic acidosis by blocking renal bicarbonate reabsorption. This mild metabolic acidosis stimulates central chemoreceptors (via reduced CSF pH), increasing ventilation and alveolar PO2 at altitude. By preventing the respiratory alkalosis that normally suppresses ventilatory drive, it allows sustained hyperventilation and reduces altitude sickness (AMS) symptoms.
options: Increasing ventilation by causing metabolic alkalosis
Stimulating ventilation via mild metabolic acidosis
Reducing cerebral blood flow and ICP
questions.question: Acetazolamide's clinical use in altitude sickness is based on which mechanism?
Which mechanism allows pepsinogen activation to pepsin?
questions.explanation: Pepsinogen is converted to active pepsin by the low pH (1-3) environment in the gastric lumen through autocatalytic cleavage. Once activated, pepsin can also activate more pepsinogen. This pH-dependent activation protects chief cells from autodigestion.

questions.question: Eosinophils are primarily involved in:
questions.explanation: Eosinophils (2% of WBCs) are specialized for allergic responses and killing parasites, particularly helminths. They degranulate, releasing toxic proteins damaging parasite surfaces. While involved in allergic inflammation, their primary evolutionary role is antiparasitic defense.

questions.question: What characterizes hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A, the most common severe hereditary clotting disorder (77% of cases), results from factor VIII deficiency. This X-linked recessive condition primarily affects males, causing prolonged bleeding after minor trauma due to impaired intrinsic pathway activation.

questions.question: The PHOSPHATE buffer system is MOST IMPORTANT in which body compartment?
questions.explanation: The phosphate buffer system (HPO42-/H2PO4-, pKa approximately 6.8) is an important buffer in two specific settings: the INTRACELLULAR fluid, where phosphate concentrations are high, and the RENAL TUBULAR FLUID, where it buffers secreted H+ as a titratable acid. It is relatively unimportant in plasma due to low phosphate concentrations there, where the bicarbonate buffer predominates.

questions.question: In erythroblastosis foetalis (haemolytic disease of the newborn), the PATHOLOGICAL sequence involves:
questions.explanation: In erythroblastosis foetalis, an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus becomes sensitised to Rh antigens at delivery of the first pregnancy. In subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies, maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses the placenta and destroys foetal RBCs. Prevention is by administering anti-D immunoglobulin (Rh-immunoglobulin) after the first delivery.
options: First pregnancy resulting in foetal hydrops immediately
Rh-positive mother and Rh-negative foetus in all pregnancies
ABO incompatibility only without Rh involvement
Destruction of maternal red cells by foetal antibodies

questions.question: Which plasma protein is primarily responsible for transport of hormones, fatty acids, and bilirubin?
questions.explanation: Albumin is the principal transport protein in plasma, binding and carrying hormones, fatty acids, bilirubin, drugs, and metal ions. Its large surface area and numerous binding sites make it extraordinarily versatile. Loss of albumin in liver disease reduces transport capacity for many metabolites and drugs.

questions.question: Gonadotropin secretion during childhood is:
questions.explanation: During childhood, gonadotropin secretion remains very low. Even slight sex steroid secretion strongly inhibits hypothalamic GnRH release. This prepubertal quiescence maintains sexual immaturity until puberty onset when these inhibitory mechanisms are overcome.

questions.question: Platelet adhesion to the damaged vessel wall occurs PRIMARILY because platelets are attracted to:
options: Collagen fibres exposed following vascular damage
Elastin fibres exposed beneath the endothelium
Fibrin strands already present in the vessel wall
Von Willebrand factor independent of collagen
