Release phase that follows budding at the membrane
Eclipse phase that follows uncoating of the genome
Adsorption phase that precedes penetration of the cell
questions.question: Infectious virus cannot be recovered from lysed cells soon after infection, although the cells are infected. Which stage explains this?

questions.explanation: Remdesivir is a prodrug analogue of adenosine nucleotide that inhibits viral RdRp. Favipiravir is a guanosine analogue prodrug with a similar target. Lopinavir inhibits protease.
questions.question: Which drug acts as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor and is an adenosine nucleotide prodrug?

options: They are the main cause of hepatocellular carcinoma in adults
They are the main cause of Kaposi sarcoma in AIDS patients
Some types transform cells in the laboratory but not in humans
They are the main cause of cervical cancer worldwide in women
They cause Burkitt lymphoma in children across tropical Africa
questions.question: Which statement about adenoviruses and malignancy is correct?
questions.explanation: Certain adenoviruses of groups A and B can transform cells by integrating DNA, but oncogenicity has not been observed in humans. Other DNA viruses such as HPV and EBV are clearly oncogenic. Laboratory transformation therefore does not predict human cancer risk.

options: Birds and pigs are reservoirs for pandemic influenza A
Influenza viruses are never found in animals
Mosquitoes carry and transmit influenza A viruses
Influenza B is the main avian reservoir host species
Influenza spreads only through ticks and fleas
questions.question: Which statement about influenza as a zoonosis is correct?
questions.explanation: Influenza A has reservoirs in birds and pigs, and mixing of strains allows antigenic shift. This explains pandemics. Influenza B is mainly human.

The combination of negative HBsAg with positive IgM anti-HBc and anti-HBs indicates recent infection from which the patient has recovered. IgM persists for around six months. This pattern separates a recovered recent infection from one that is still active.
questions.question: Which HBV marker pattern shows recent infection with recovery and immunity achieved?
options: HBsAg positive with all other markers negative in serum
HBsAg negative, total anti-HBc positive, IgM positive, anti-HBs positive
HBsAg negative with anti-HBs negative only in serum
HBsAg positive with anti-HBs positive only in serum
HBsAg positive with IgM anti-HBc negative in serum

questions.question: What is the main reason a single positive PCR result may be hard to interpret?
options: Its sensitivity can detect trace virus that does not signify disease
PCR needs four weeks of incubation to give a final result
PCR cannot be quantified in any commercial closed automated system
PCR is too insensitive to detect viral DNA in most clinical specimens
PCR detects only live virus particles and never dead virus fragments
questions.explanation: PCR can detect as little as one DNA molecule, so a positive may reflect latent or trace virus. Clinical context is therefore essential. Quantitative assays help interpretation.

options: Virions mature in the nucleus and accumulate over a long period
Host chromatin coats each newly formed capsid in the nucleus
Envelope proteins condense on the inner nuclear membrane surface
Cells transform without producing any complete virions at all
Virions bud rapidly from the cell and leave no trace inside
questions.question: A smear of cells infected with a naked icosahedral DNA virus shows dense intranuclear aggregates. What explains these structures?
questions.explanation: Naked DNA viruses that mature in the nucleus reach the surface slowly and are released on autolysis. They tend to accumulate and form highly visible inclusion bodies. RNA naked viruses are released rapidly with little accumulation.

Acute infection may end in recovery without sequelae, recovery with residual effects, death or progression to chronicity. Neurological sequelae after acute viral encephalitis illustrate recovery with residual effects. The other patterns involve persistence of virus.
questions.question: A patient recovers from an acute viral encephalitis but later has persistent neurological deficits. How is this outcome best classified?
options: Recovery with residual effects after an acute infection
Malignant transformation of the infected cells
Chronic disease with relapses and exacerbations
Silent subclinical infection lasting for life
Reactivation of a latent virus as acute disease
A fall to undetectable titre in the second specimen
A rise in antibody titre between the two specimens
Appearance of free complement in the second specimen taken
Identical antibody titres in both of the two specimens
Loss of IgM only without any change in IgG
questions.explanation: Paired sera collected in the acute and convalescent stages show a rising titre in recent infection. Specific IgM supports primary infection. Stable titres suggest past exposure.
questions.question: An early specimen is taken during acute illness and a second after recovery for antibody testing. What change confirms recent infection?

options: The vaccine contains core antigen only without surface antigen
The vaccine is a live attenuated whole virus
The vaccine contains complete infectious virions
The vaccine induces only an IgM response
The vaccine contains surface antigen but no core antigen
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant subunit vaccine made from surface antigen. It therefore induces anti-HBs but not antibody to core. Natural infection induces both.
questions.question: Why is anti-HBc absent in a person who is immune only through vaccination?

options: Rhinovirus is a family that contains the genus Picornaviridae
Picornaviridae is a genus that contains the family Rhinovirus
Rhinoviridae is a species placed under the genus Picornavirus
Picornavirus is a family that contains the genus Rhinoviridae
Picornaviridae is a family that contains the genus Rhinovirus
questions.explanation: Families carry the suffix viridae while genera carry the suffix virus. Rhinovirus is therefore a genus placed within the family Picornaviridae. The reversed or mixed pairings break this convention.
questions.question: Which pairing correctly follows the ICTV naming convention for viruses?

questions.explanation: Early transcription yields about twenty early proteins. They push the cell into S phase and create conditions suitable for viral replication. Structural proteins appear later.
options: Cleave the fibre from the penton base during virion assembly
Provide the lipid envelope used for budding from the nucleus
Reverse transcribe the viral genome into RNA inside the nucleus
Push the host cell into S phase and favour viral replication
Assemble the capsid around the viral genome inside the nucleus of cells
questions.question: What is the role of the early proteins made by adenovirus after its DNA reaches the nucleus?

options: Hepatitis E and hepatitis B only in children
questions.explanation: HBV and HCV often cause chronic disease and are oncogenic. HAV and HEV do not cause chronic infection in immunocompetent persons. Chronic infection leads to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.question: Which pair of hepatitis viruses commonly causes chronic infection?

questions.explanation: CMV persists in salivary gland cells, renal tubules and leukocytes. HSV and VZV remain in ganglia and EBV in lymphoid cells. This reflects subfamily patterns.
options: CMV and secretory glands, kidneys and leukocytes
HSV and the kidneys, bone and muscle
VZV and the salivary glands and kidneys
EBV and sensory ganglia of the face
HHV-8 and the trigeminal and sacral ganglia
questions.question: Which pair is a correctly matched herpesvirus and its major site of latency?

questions.explanation: Orf, a parapoxvirus, is acquired from sheep and goats by contact. Herpes B is from monkeys, Lassa from rodents and vesicular stomatitis from cattle. Such links guide control through animal vaccination and rodent management.
options: Rabies virus and mosquitoes as vector
Orf virus and sheep or goats
questions.question: Which pairing of zoonotic virus and reservoir is correct?

questions.explanation: VZV causes chickenpox on first infection and remains latent in ganglia. When immunity falls, it reactivates as zoster in a dermatomal distribution. Respiratory spread is the usual portal.
questions.question: Which statement about varicella-zoster virus is correct?
options: Zoster occurs only in neonates born to infected mothers
Zoster results from reactivation of latent virus when immunity weakens
Varicella is caused by herpes simplex virus in most children
Varicella results from reactivation of latent virus in the ganglia
Zoster results from a fresh infection acquired by faecal-oral spread

questions.explanation: Most bunyaviruses are arthropod-borne, such as Rift Valley fever by mosquitoes and Congo-Crimean fever by ticks. Hantaviruses are transmitted by contact with rodent excreta and cause renal and pulmonary syndromes. This explains why rodent control matters for hantavirus disease.
questions.question: Which virus family spreads by arthropods except for one genus that spreads from rodents?
options: Filoviridae with Ebola as the exception
Togaviridae with rubella as the exception
Arenaviridae with Lassa as the exception
Bunyaviridae with hantaviruses as the exception
Flaviviridae with yellow fever as the exception

questions.explanation: Person-to-person spread of Lassa, Ebola and Congo-Crimean viruses occurs through body fluids. Strict isolation and barrier nursing limit nosocomial spread. Ribavirin is used for most haemorrhagic fevers.
questions.question: A hospital outbreak spreads among staff caring for a patient with haemorrhagic fever. Which control measure is most important?
Which antiviral is considered for prophylaxis or treatment of poxvirus infections?
questions.explanation: Cidofovir is used against poxviruses and also CMV and adenovirus. Vaccination against smallpox is protective. Supportive care is also essential.

questions.question: Which mechanism is mainly responsible for liver injury in hepatitis B?
options: Autoimmune destruction of bile duct epithelium by antibody
Direct release of a toxin by the circulating virions
Mechanical obstruction of the bile ducts by the virus
Immune killing of infected hepatocytes by cytotoxic T cells
Complement-mediated lysis of erythrocytes in the sinusoids
questions.explanation: HBV is not directly cytopathic. Liver damage results when cytotoxic T cells destroy infected cells. The strength of this response shapes the outcome.

questions.question: Which diagnostic test best confirms acute measles?
questions.explanation: Measles IgM ELISA confirms acute infection, and RT-PCR or culture may also be used. Isolation precautions begin from the seventh day after exposure. It is a notifiable infection.

options: Absence of the specific surface receptor needed for attachment
Absence of a nucleus to allow viral transcription
Absence of ribosomes needed for viral protein synthesis
A defect in capsid assembly occurring inside the nucleus
Failure of the cell to support viral genome replication
questions.explanation: Infection begins when the viral attachment protein binds a specific receptor, and cells lacking it are not susceptible. Since the transfected genome replicates, later steps are intact. The defect therefore lies at attachment.
questions.question: A virus fails to infect a cell line although its genome replicates normally after transfection. What is the most probable block?
Class I major histocompatibility complex molecules are important for antiviral defence because they do what?
options: Neutralize free virions in the extracellular fluid before they enter cells
Present viral lipids to natural killer cells for subsequent cell killing
Bind complement proteins to the viral envelope outside the infected cell
Display viral protein fragments from inside the cell on its surface
Form pores in the membrane of infected cells to cause lysis
questions.explanation: MHC class I molecules display peptides from inside the cell, including viral protein fragments, so that T cells can see infection. Cytotoxic CD8 cells recognise these peptides through their T cell receptors. Antibodies and complement act outside cells.

questions.question: Overall, which arm of immunity predominantly clears an established viral infection, and which protects against reinfection?
options: Phagocytes clear infection and mucus protects against reinfection
Humoral immunity clears infection and cellular immunity protects against reinfection
Innate immunity only clears infection and nothing protects later
Complement clears infection and interferon protects against reinfection
Cellular immunity clears infection and humoral immunity protects against reinfection
questions.explanation: Because viruses replicate inside cells and spread cell to cell, resolution relies mainly on T cell function. Antibody is an important barrier against reinfection, especially at mucosal surfaces. Both arms work together.
Acyclovir is first-line therapy for HSV and VZV infections. No effective antiviral treatment exists for EBV. For CMV, ganciclovir, foscarnet and cidofovir are used.
questions.question: Which antiviral is recommended for HSV infections, orally or parenterally?

questions.explanation: Some enveloped viruses cannot fuse with the plasma membrane and require acid pH in endosomes for fusion. Neutralizing endosomal pH therefore blocks release of the nucleocapsid. Viruses that fuse at the surface would be unaffected.
questions.question: Raising endosomal pH with a weak base blocks infection by an enveloped virus. Which entry route is suggested?
options: Passive diffusion of the particle across the lipid bilayer
Injection of nucleic acid through a rigid capsid tail
Endosomal uptake with acid pH needed for membrane fusion
Docking of intact virions at the nuclear pore complex
Direct fusion with the plasma membrane at neutral pH
Absence of any viral DNA in the cell
Integration of viral DNA into the cellular genome
Production of a toxin that damages the cells
Destruction of the infected cell by lysis only
Replication of the viral genome in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: HPV DNA integrates into the cellular genome in cervical epithelium and persistent infection can lead to malignancy. Most infections clear on their own. Persistence is the key risk.
questions.question: Which feature of high-risk HPV contributes to carcinogenesis?
Which statement about the classification of influenza viruses is correct?
options: Influenza A, B and C are orthomyxoviruses and A causes most epidemics
Influenza A is a retrovirus while B and C are orthomyxoviruses
Influenza A, B and C are paramyxoviruses and C causes most epidemics
Influenza A and B are rhabdoviruses and B causes most pandemics
Influenza C undergoes antigenic shift and causes most epidemics
questions.explanation: Influenza A, B and C are enveloped negative-sense segmented RNA viruses of the family Orthomyxoviridae. Type A causes most epidemics and all pandemics. Type C is antigenically stable and mild.

questions.question: Which feature of adenovirus capsid components explains the cytopathic effect seen even before extensive replication?
options: Toxin-like activity of the penton base
Lytic enzyme activity in the envelope
Reverse transcriptase activity in the core
Phospholipase activity in the hexon proteins
Neuraminidase activity on the fibre knob
questions.explanation: The penton base carries toxin-like activity that produces cytopathic effect in host cells. The fibre has the attachment function and also acts as haemagglutinin. Hexons form most of the capsid faces.

options: Rotavirus gastroenteritis and norovirus gastroenteritis in infants
Rabies virus infection and influenza virus infection
Rhinovirus infection and respiratory syncytial virus infection
Measles virus infection and mumps virus infection
Hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus
questions.question: A virus is linked to chronic disease with relapses and exacerbations over many years. Which pair fits this pattern?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B and C viruses cause chronic infection marked by relapses and exacerbations. They can eventually lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer. The remaining pairs cause self-limited acute disease.

options: Cowdry type B bodies in neurons
Negri bodies in Ammon's horn neurons
Owl's eye inclusions in cortical cells
questions.question: Which finding on brain histology supports rabies diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions seen in neurons, particularly in the hippocampus. Their absence does not exclude rabies. Immunofluorescence is more sensitive.
Idoxuridine was approved in June 1963 as the first antiviral drug. Newer nucleoside analogues followed later. It marked the start of antiviral drug development.
questions.question: Which was the first antiviral drug approved, opening a new era in therapy?

questions.explanation: Oral ganciclovir can help prevent CMV, but its low bioavailability limits its value. Intravenous administration achieves high peak concentrations. It is potent for treating CMV.
options: Complete destruction by gastric acid in the stomach
Complete lack of in vitro activity against cytomegalovirus
Low bioavailability of about eight to nine percent
Rapid metabolism to inactive acyclovir in the liver
Inability to cross the membranes of infected cells
questions.question: What limits the use of oral ganciclovir?
Which hierarchy correctly places HIV-1 in the taxonomic system?
questions.explanation: HIV belongs to the family Retroviridae and the genus Lentivirus. Its types are HIV-1 and HIV-2, and each type is divided into subtypes such as A, B and C. Only the first arrangement respects the descending order of ranks and the suffix rules.
options: Family Hepadnaviridae, genus Lentivirus, type HIV-1, subtype B
Family Lentivirus, genus Retroviridae, type HIV-1, subtype B
Family Retroviridae, genus Lentivirus, type HIV-1, subtype B
Family Lentiviridae, genus HIV-1, type Retrovirus, subtype B
Family Retroviridae, genus HIV, type Lentivirus, subtype one

questions.question: In a haemagglutination inhibition test, what result indicates that the patient serum contains specific antibody?
questions.explanation: If the serum has antibody complementary to the virus, it blocks the haemagglutinin and agglutination is inhibited. The test uses a standard dose of four haemagglutinating units of virus. It is used for influenza and rubella.
options: Complete haemagglutination of all the red cells
Absence of haemagglutination of the red cells
Cytopathic effect in the cell culture
Colour change in the plate wells
Lysis of the sheep red cells added

questions.explanation: Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue and is first phosphorylated by thymidine kinase encoded by HSV or VZV. Cellular kinases then form the diphosphate and triphosphate. This gives selectivity for infected cells.
questions.question: Which statement about the activation of acyclovir is correct?
options: It is active as given without any phosphorylation step at all
Host DNA polymerase first converts it to the monophosphate form
It is activated by viral neuraminidase at the cell surface
It is activated by viral protease after viral protein translation
Viral thymidine kinase first converts it to the monophosphate form
Diploid RNA viruses such as retroviruses
Double-stranded DNA viruses such as poxviruses
Negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses such as rhabdoviruses
Positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses such as picornaviruses
Segmented negative-sense RNA viruses such as orthomyxoviruses
questions.explanation: When the genome is itself mRNA, naked RNA is infectious because no virion polymerase is required. Picornaviruses translate it into a polyprotein that is cleaved into mature proteins. Negative-strand and retroviral RNAs need virion enzymes first.
questions.question: Transfecting purified genomic RNA from a virus into cells yields infectious progeny without any virion enzyme. Which group does the virus most likely belong to?

options: The virus replicates only in the presence of neutralizing host antibody
The virus is shed constantly in the urine of the infected host
The virus is cleared completely from the body after the first illness
The virus stays dormant after infection, as an episome or integrated genome
The virus replicates continuously at a very low level in the host
questions.explanation: In true latency the virus remains completely dormant after primary infection, with the genome integrated or existing as an episome. In persistence, replication continues at a low level. HSV and VZV illustrate latency while HIV, HBV, CMV and EBV persist.
questions.question: HSV and VZV are said to show true latency, whereas HIV and HBV show persistence. What distinguishes true latency?
Which marker confers protection against hepatitis B and is the only marker positive after vaccination?
questions.explanation: Anti-HBs is a neutralizing antibody and a titre above ten mIU/mL is considered protective. Vaccines contain only surface antigen so core antibody does not develop. This distinguishes vaccination from natural infection.

questions.question: A virus entering the host provokes interferon production after sensing its nucleic acid. Which receptor recognises viral DNA?
questions.explanation: TLR9 is the pattern recognition receptor for viral double-stranded DNA, while others sense RNA. Activation promotes type I interferons and inflammatory cytokines. CD4 is a T cell molecule.

options: Phylum level and the ranks below it
Realm level and the ranks below it
Kingdom level and the ranks below it
Family level and the ranks below it
Order level only, with no lower ranks
questions.question: A virologist notes that classification of viruses is practically significant only from one taxonomic level downward. Which level is it?
questions.explanation: Although ICTV recognises realms, kingdoms, phyla, classes and orders, classification is really only important from the level of families downwards. Families end in viridae and genera in virus. Higher ranks are used far less in routine work.
Antemortem diagnosis in humans uses immunofluorescence on nuchal skin biopsy, corneal impressions and saliva. Virus may also be isolated from saliva. Brain biopsy is rarely done.
questions.question: Which specimen can be used for antemortem rabies diagnosis by immunofluorescence?
options: Skin biopsy, corneal impression or saliva
Throat swab, nasal swab or sputum
Stool sample, urine sample or sputum
Serum sample, plasma sample or urine
Blood culture, stool culture or urine

questions.question: Famciclovir acts as which type of agent?
questions.explanation: Famciclovir is the diacetyl 6-deoxy derivative of penciclovir. It is deacetylated and oxidised in the gut, blood and liver to give penciclovir. Penciclovir triphosphate has a long intracellular half-life.
options: An integrase inhibitor used in HIV combination therapy regimens
A prodrug converted to penciclovir after oral administration
An uncoating inhibitor used only for influenza A virus
A neuraminidase inhibitor used for influenza A and B
A topical pyrophosphate analogue used for cold sores only

questions.explanation: The p24 capsid protein forms the conical core and is detected as antigen in early infection. Gp120 and gp41 are envelope proteins, and p17 is the matrix protein. Early detection of p24 helps close the window before antibodies appear.
questions.question: Which protein forms the core of the HIV capsid and is used in diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus produces large cells with an owl's eye intranuclear inclusion. These are cytomegalic inclusion bodies. They support but do not prove the diagnosis.
questions.question: Owl's eye intranuclear inclusion bodies in cells from a transplant recipient indicate which virus?

questions.explanation: In the immune active phase the host mounts an immune response and the liver is damaged. ALT rises and HBV DNA is lower than in the tolerant phase. Sustained high viral levels increase risk of cirrhosis and carcinoma.
questions.question: During which phase of chronic hepatitis B does the host mount an immune response causing raised enzymes and inflammation?
A child is bitten by a stray dog. What is the first step in post-exposure management?
options: Waiting for symptoms before any action is taken
Immediate thorough washing of the wound with soap and water
Giving oral antibiotics only to prevent any infection
Suturing the wound tightly closed immediately after the bite occurs
Applying a bandage without cleaning the bite wound
questions.explanation: Prompt wound cleansing with soap and water, followed by antiseptic, is the first step. Human rabies immunoglobulin around the wound and vaccine follow. Suturing is avoided.

questions.question: A traveller from West Africa has fever, ulcerative pharyngitis and bleeding. Which virus is the likeliest cause?
questions.explanation: Lassa fever is caused by an arenavirus and manifests with fever and ulcerative pharyngitis followed by haemorrhage. It is endemic in West Africa. Ribavirin is used for treatment.

questions.question: Even in the inactive HBV phase, what risk remains?
questions.explanation: Though the immune response controls the virus and ALT falls, the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma persists. Complete clearance happens only in spontaneous cure when HBsAg disappears. Long-term surveillance for liver cancer therefore remains necessary in such patients.
The Dane particle of 42 nm is the complete infectious virion. The 20 nm spherical and 22 nm filamentous particles are surface antigen aggregates without genome. They are defective and excess.
questions.question: Which structure is the infective, complete hepatitis B virion?

questions.explanation: HSV and CMV produce a characteristic CPE, whereas enteroviruses do not. The CPE may be specific or non-specific. Confirmation uses immunological or molecular tests.
questions.question: Which virus produces a specific cytopathic effect in cell culture that allows presumptive identification?

options: Single-stranded DNA genome, naked, no vaccine
Single-stranded RNA genome, naked, vaccine available
Partially double-stranded DNA genome, enveloped, vaccine available
Double-stranded RNA genome, naked, no vaccine
Single-stranded RNA genome, enveloped, no vaccine
questions.question: Which characteristics fit hepatitis C virus relative to hepatitis B virus?
questions.explanation: HCV is an enveloped single-stranded RNA virus without a vaccine. HBV is a DNA virus with a recombinant vaccine. This difference determines prevention strategy.

options: Integrated proviral DNA sequences within the host cell chromosomes
Intracellular virus particles during active genome replication in cells
Viral RNA being transcribed within the nucleus of the cell
Free viral particles, thereby blocking infection of the host cells
Latent viral genomes sitting inside neurons of sensory ganglia
questions.explanation: Antibodies usually bind free virions and block infection of cells. T cells destroy infected cells. Intracellular and latent virus is out of antibody reach.
questions.question: Antibody works mainly against which stage of viral infection?
Who first discovered a retrovirus in 1910?
questions.explanation: Peyton Rous discovered avian sarcoma virus in 1910 and later received the Nobel Prize. Temin and Baltimore discovered reverse transcriptase. Montagnier isolated HIV-1 in 1983.
Single-stranded DNA viruses first form double-stranded DNA using a host DNA-dependent DNA polymerase. Afterwards they follow a typical replication cycle. They do not carry reverse transcriptase.
options: Viral thymidine kinase enzyme of the virion
Reverse transcriptase enzyme carried in the capsid
questions.question: Which enzyme converts the single-stranded genome of a parvovirus into a replicative double-stranded form?

options: Viruses possess a peptidoglycan wall that blocks entry of the drug
Viruses divide only outside cells where the drugs cannot easily reach
Viruses use host cell machinery, so few targets spare host cells
Viruses have ribosomes that are identical to those of bacteria
Viruses lack nucleic acid and therefore cannot be targeted by drugs
questions.explanation: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that rely on host cellular machinery, which makes targets that interfere with the virus but spare the host scarce. Viral variation adds to the problem. Antivirals mostly inhibit replication rather than destroy virions.
questions.question: Why is it harder to develop selectively toxic antiviral drugs than antibacterial drugs?

questions.explanation: In a sandwich ELISA the capture antibody is adsorbed to the plate, patient specimen is added and then enzyme-labelled antibody detects bound antigen. It therefore measures antigen. Indirect ELISA measures antibody.
questions.question: Which ELISA format is designed to detect antigen in a patient specimen using antibody coated on the plate?
Why is ganciclovir preferred over acyclovir for cytomegalovirus infection?
options: Ganciclovir requires no activation by any viral or cellular kinase
Ganciclovir blocks the neuraminidase enzyme found in cytomegalovirus particles
CMV lacks a DNA polymerase so that acyclovir becomes toxic
Acyclovir is not absorbed from the gut in CMV infection
CMV phosphotransferase phosphorylates it well and the triphosphate persists longer
questions.explanation: CMV-encoded phosphotransferase is a better catalyst for ganciclovir. The intracellular triphosphate half-life is about 12 hours, compared with 1 to 2 hours for acyclovir. This explains greater anti-CMV activity.
Tenofovir is a nucleotide analogue that inhibits reverse transcriptase and viral DNA polymerase. It is used in HIV and hepatitis B. Raltegravir and darunavir act on integrase and protease.
questions.question: Which agent is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor used for HIV and HBV?

options: Complex DNA viruses replicating in the host cytoplasm
Naked RNA viruses that make a single polyprotein
Helical viruses with a segmented negative-sense RNA genome
Enveloped RNA viruses with segmented genomes in cells
Naked icosahedral viruses with circular double-stranded DNA genomes
questions.explanation: Papovaviruses are naked icosahedral viruses with circular double-stranded DNA. Papillomaviruses cannot be grown in cell culture, so diagnosis relies on cytology and molecular methods. Poxviruses replicate in cytoplasm.
questions.question: Which description fits papillomaviruses?
Which class of influenza drugs acts at the release stage of replication?
questions.explanation: Zanamivir and oseltamivir inhibit neuraminidase and block release of new virions. They are active against influenza A and B. Amantadine only covers influenza A.

questions.question: Why does an infected person's blood show excess surface antigen particles in hepatitis B?
options: Infected cells overproduce HBsAg, forming non-infectious spheres and filaments
Surface antigen is made only by cells of the immune system
Infected cells release only complete virions and no extra antigen
Surface antigen is made only by cells inside the bone marrow
Surface antigen is produced by bacteria colonising the liver
questions.explanation: HBV infected hepatocytes overproduce surface protein, which assembles into 20 nm spheres and 22 nm filaments. These decoy particles may absorb neutralizing antibody. They also give a ground-glass appearance in cells.
Congo-Crimean haemorrhagic fever virus is transmitted by ticks and also spreads between people via blood and body fluids. Hospital outbreaks have occurred. Yellow fever spreads by mosquitoes only.
questions.question: Which tick-borne virus causes a haemorrhagic fever with person-to-person transmission through body fluids?

questions.explanation: Toll-like receptors detect viral products and induce type I interferons. TLR7, 8 and 9 are expressed at high levels from the start for rapid interferon release. Most other TLRs are largely inducible.
questions.question: Which innate receptors, expressed constitutively at high levels in plasmacytoid cells, give rapid interferon production?
options: Killer inhibitory receptors on NK cells

questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe anaemia with absent reticulocytes after a febrile illness. Which virus should be suspected?
questions.explanation: B19 infects erythroid precursors and can produce aplastic crisis in people with chronic haemolytic anaemia. Transfusion may be lifesaving. IgM ELISA and PCR support diagnosis.

questions.question: Why must viruses that spread by the gastrointestinal tract have specific adaptations?
options: They must avoid ciliated epithelium and mucus in the passages
They must tolerate high oxygen tension in the gut lumen
They must evade the skin keratin layer before they enter
They must resist the low temperature of the gut mucosa
They must withstand gastric acid, bile salts and digestive enzymes
questions.explanation: The gastrointestinal tract is a hostile environment with acid, bile salts and enzymes. Enteric viruses such as rotavirus and hepatitis A virus survive these. Mucus and cilia are defences of the respiratory tract.

questions.question: For which agents is electron microscopy currently most useful in the diagnostic laboratory?
options: Gastroenteritis viruses such as Norwalk-like viruses
HIV in plasma of infected patients
Hepatitis C virus in serum samples
Latent CMV in leucocytes of donors
Antibody to rubella in patient serum
questions.explanation: EM is now mainly used for Norwalk-like viruses and occasionally for herpesviruses and papillomaviruses in skin lesions. Reliable antigen and molecular methods have replaced it elsewhere. Cost and poor sensitivity limit its use.

Classical serology includes complement fixation, haemagglutination inhibition, immunofluorescence and neutralization tests. Newer techniques include RIA, EIA, particle agglutination and Western blot. Serology therefore combines older complement-based tests with newer enzyme-based assays.
questions.question: Which pair lists classical serological techniques?

options: Increasing interferon signalling leads to a failed antiviral state in neighbours
Producing more MHC class I leads to failed detection by natural killer cells
Blocking MHC class I transport leads to failed detection by cytotoxic T cells
Increasing perforin release leads to survival of infected cells in tissue
Neutralizing granzymes leads to increased apoptosis of infected target cells
questions.explanation: If MHC class I does not reach the surface, T cells cannot see viral peptides, so infection is missed. NK cells may compensate. The other pairings describe consequences that are reversed.
questions.question: Which viral evasion strategy is paired correctly with its consequence?
A fluid passes through a bacteriological filter, fails to grow on cell-free agar, yet infects cultured cells. Which property of viruses does this reflect?
options: Virions are fungal spores that are adapted to cell-free media
Virions multiply by binary fission outside the host cells
Virions are tiny filterable obligate intracellular parasites
Virions are bacteria that have lost their cell walls entirely
Virions are large enough to be retained on bacterial filters
questions.explanation: Viruses are sub-microscopic obligate intracellular parasites small enough to pass through bacteriological filters. They cannot multiply on cell-free media. Growth requires living cells.

questions.question: In post-exposure prophylaxis against rabies, where is human rabies immunoglobulin administered?
questions.explanation: Rabies immunoglobulin, at around twenty international units per kilogram, is infiltrated around and into the wound. It provides passive immunity until vaccine induced antibody appears. Vaccine is given in the other limb.

questions.question: Which statement describes the incubation period and early symptoms of rabies?
questions.explanation: Rabies incubation is usually two weeks to three months or longer, and early symptoms include fever, headache and paraesthesia at the wound. Hydrophobia, seizures and respiratory paralysis follow. The long and variable delay allows time for post-exposure treatment.
options: Usually six months with jaundice and dark urine
Usually two weeks to three months with itching at the bite
Usually two to three weeks with parotid swelling
Usually five hours with vomiting and severe diarrhoea
Usually one to two days with high fever and chills only
Segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA in helical form
Single-stranded linear DNA packaged within a naked capsid
Fully double-stranded linear DNA with inverted terminal repeats
Diploid positive-sense RNA flanked by long terminal repeats
Partially double-stranded circular DNA containing a gap
questions.question: Which genome description is characteristic of hepadnaviruses?
questions.explanation: Hepadnaviruses have a small circular DNA genome that is partially double stranded. The gap is repaired after infection. Linear DNA with terminal repeats describes adenoviruses instead.

questions.question: Which is the largest of the poxviruses that cause disease in humans?
questions.explanation: Variola virus, the orthopoxvirus causing smallpox, is large, about 230 by 300 nm. Poxviruses are large complex viruses that replicate in cytoplasm. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

questions.question: A girl develops bright red cheeks followed by a lacy rash on trunk and limbs. Which virus is responsible?
questions.explanation: Erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease, produces a slapped-cheek appearance followed by a maculopapular rash. It is caused by parvovirus B19. Adults, especially women, may have arthropathy.

questions.question: Which virus is the only one among the following that replicates in the cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: All DNA viruses except poxviruses replicate in the nucleus. Variola therefore replicates in the cytoplasm using its own enzymes. This distinguishes poxviruses from other DNA viruses.

questions.question: Which HPV types are mostly responsible for genital warts?
questions.explanation: HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types that cause most genital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk and linked to cancer. Cutaneous warts involve other types.

Parvoviruses are the smallest human viruses, 18 to 26 nm, naked and icosahedral with a linear single-stranded DNA genome. They replicate in the nucleus of actively dividing cells. Its small size and simple structure make it resistant to many disinfectants.
questions.question: Which statement about parvovirus B19 is correct?
options: It is a complex virus replicating only in the cytoplasm
It is an enveloped virus with partially double-stranded circular DNA
It is a naked icosahedral virus with linear single-stranded DNA
It is a segmented virus with eight RNA genome fragments
It is a helical virus with a negative-sense RNA genome

questions.explanation: Real-time PCR performs quantitative amplification and is available in closed systems. Closed systems also limit contamination. It is increasingly used as cost falls.
questions.question: Which technique allows viral load quantification and is used with closed automated systems?

options: It cannot enter human cells at all because of charge
Little triphosphate forms where viral thymidine kinase is absent
It is excreted by the kidney before it reaches cells
It is converted into an inert compound by human polymerase
It binds only to free virions circulating in the plasma
questions.question: Why does acyclovir cause little toxicity in uninfected cells?
questions.explanation: The first phosphorylation step depends on a viral enzyme. Uninfected cells therefore form little acyclovir triphosphate. Its affinity for viral DNA polymerase is also much greater than for human polymerase.

questions.question: Which finding is used to identify growth of influenza or parainfluenza viruses in cell culture even without a clear cytopathic effect?
questions.explanation: Infected cells acquire the ability to adsorb red blood cells, mainly with influenza and parainfluenza viruses. The identity is then confirmed by neutralization, haemadsorption inhibition, immunofluorescence or molecular tests. This property helps when cytopathic effect is absent or non-specific.
options: Neutralization of the virus by specific patient antibody
Formation of Negri bodies in infected cell cytoplasm
Agglutination of latex particles in a slide test
Haemadsorption of red blood cells to infected cells
Fixation of complement by antigen-antibody complexes in wells

questions.explanation: HBeAg is produced during active replication and is secreted into plasma. Its presence indicates high viral load and infectivity. Anti-HBe usually signals reduced replication.
questions.question: Which HBV marker indicates high viral load and high infectivity?
Which statement about monkeypox compared with smallpox is correct?
questions.explanation: Monkeypox is an orthopoxvirus zoonosis that resembles smallpox but is generally milder. Incubation is 7 to 14 days. Death has occurred in as many as one in ten in some outbreaks.
options: It is caused by a parapoxvirus found in sheep and goats
It lacks any skin lesions and is only a respiratory illness
It is spread only by the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes
It is a zoonosis with fatality up to one in ten
It is caused by a herpesvirus that is found in monkeys only

questions.explanation: These agents increase endosomal pH, which is needed for fusion, and interfere with receptor glycosylation. This is an entry-level mechanism and not a polymerase effect. They are therefore classed as entry-stage rather than replication-stage inhibitors.
options: Raise endosomal pH needed for virus-cell fusion
Block the viral integrase enzyme in cells
Terminate the growing viral DNA chains directly
Inhibit the neuraminidase enzyme of the virion
Cleave the viral polyprotein into mature proteins
questions.question: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine were studied against SARS-CoV-2 mainly because they do what?

questions.explanation: CD4 cells act as helper cells for antiviral antibody and CD8 responses. Th1 effectors produce IFN gamma, TNF alpha and IL-2 and orchestrate inflammation. They can also act as memory cells.
questions.question: Which T cell subset helps both antibody and CD8 responses and, when Th1, mainly secretes IFN gamma, TNF alpha and IL-2?
Which virus is best matched with a silent subclinical infection that persists for life?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus commonly cause silent subclinical infection that remains for life. Influenza, measles and rotavirus are cleared after acute disease. Rabies is rapidly fatal once symptoms begin.

HSV-1 is neurotropic, travels by retrograde axonal transport and becomes latent in sensory ganglia, mainly the trigeminal ganglia. HSV-2 usually reactivates from sacral ganglia. Reactivation therefore produces recurrent lesions along the territory supplied by that nerve.
questions.question: After oral herpes infection, where does HSV-1 establish latency and later reactivate?
Which animal is the most important reservoir of rabies worldwide?
questions.explanation: Dogs account for most human rabies, especially in Asia and Africa. Bats, foxes and other mammals also act as reservoirs. Transmission is mainly by bite or scratch.

questions.question: The rash of measles and rubella is attributed mainly to which immunopathologic process?
options: Immune complex deposition in the skin
Type I hypersensitivity to viral glycoproteins
Direct cytolysis of keratinocytes by virions
questions.explanation: Immune complexes can deposit in organs such as skin, brain or kidney and cause tissue injury. The rash in rubella and measles is an example. It reflects the immune response rather than virus alone.
Influenza B undergoes only minor changes. Influenza A undergoes both drift and shift. Influenza C is antigenically stable and rarely epidemic.
questions.question: Which influenza virus type does not undergo antigenic shift but only minor drift?
options: Both influenza A and B equally

questions.explanation: Rotavirus, enteric adenoviruses and hepatitis A virus enter through the gastrointestinal tract. Influenza and rhinovirus enter through the respiratory tract, while arboviruses enter through insect bites. HIV and HSV use mucosal or parenteral routes.
questions.question: Which pair of viruses commonly enter through the gastrointestinal tract?
options: West Nile and Semliki Forest viruses

questions.explanation: Measles virus is a morbillivirus and lacks neuraminidase. RSV is a pneumovirus lacking both haemagglutinin and neuraminidase. Paramyxoviruses are enveloped with helical nucleocapsids.
questions.question: Measles virus belongs to which genus and has which unusual feature among paramyxoviruses?

questions.explanation: A virus contains either DNA or RNA as genetic material, never both. Viruses such as retroviruses and hepadnaviruses use an intermediate of the other type during replication but package only one. Sensitivity to both enzymes therefore points to contamination of the preparation.
questions.question: Nuclease digestion of a purified virion genome shows sensitivity to both DNase and RNase. Which interpretation is most consistent with viral biology?
options: The genome is a retroviral hybrid made of equal parts DNA and RNA strands
The sample is a hepadnavirus that packages separate DNA and RNA chromosomes together
The preparation is contaminated because a virion carries only one nucleic acid type
The result confirms a bacteriophage that possesses a mixed nucleic acid genome type
The virus is an enveloped species that naturally carries both nucleic acid genomes

questions.question: For a virus that assembles in the nucleus, how does the envelope form?
options: Capsids pass through lysosomal membranes during their transport
Capsids fuse with Golgi vesicles that contain viral lipids
Ribosome complexes enclose the capsid on the way out
The virus synthesizes its own lipid bilayer within the cytoplasm
Nucleocapsids bud through the nuclear membrane that carries viral glycoproteins
questions.explanation: Virus-coded envelope proteins migrate to the nuclear membrane when assembly is nuclear and become embedded there. Nucleocapsids then bud through this modified cellular membrane. Lipids are always supplied by the host.

questions.question: A virus blocks transport of MHC class I molecules to the cell surface. Which cell is best placed to eliminate the infected cell?
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells cannot detect viral peptides if MHC class I is absent. Natural killer cells specialise in killing cells with reduced MHC class I. Viruses such as CMV and HIV exploit this evasion tactic.
Perforin forms pores in the membrane of the infected cell. Granzymes enter through these holes and initiate apoptosis. Granulysin attacks the membrane directly.
questions.question: Which cytotoxic granule protein creates pores in the target cell membrane so that granzymes can enter?

questions.explanation: There is no specific vaccine or antiviral for B19, so immunoglobulins are used to clear persistent infection in selected patients. Supportive transfusion treats crises. Pooled donor antibody supplies neutralizing activity that the patient cannot make.
questions.question: What is the main purpose of intravenous immunoglobulin in parvovirus B19 infection?
Which virus uses the CD4 molecule as its primary receptor?
questions.explanation: HIV binds CD4 on helper T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells through gp120. A co-receptor such as CXCR4 or CCR5 is also needed. Gp41 mediates fusion.

questions.question: Which statement about replication of double-stranded DNA viruses that use the nucleus is correct?
options: Transcription occurs only once and depends solely on a virion polymerase enzyme
Replication begins with reverse transcription of the genome in the capsid
Transcription occurs in successive rounds and depends on virus-encoded trans-acting factors
Genomes are copied directly in the cytoplasm by host cell enzymes
Replication depends on one polyprotein that is cleaved by a viral protease
questions.explanation: For nuclear double-stranded DNA viruses transcription proceeds in successive rounds and relies on virus-encoded trans-acting factors. Cellular machinery supplies the polymerase. Cytoplasmic independence is a poxvirus feature.

questions.question: A brain biopsy from a patient who died of encephalitis shows eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in hippocampal neurons. Which virus is suggested?
questions.explanation: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions seen in nerve cells, notably in the hippocampus, in rabies. They are an adjunct to diagnosis. CMV forms nuclear owl's eye inclusions.

questions.question: A person with chickenpox in childhood develops painful vesicles along one dermatome decades later. Which mechanism applies?
questions.explanation: VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia after chickenpox. When immunity falls, it reactivates and produces zoster in the skin supplied by the affected ganglion. It is an example of reactivation after latency.
options: Insect-borne transmission of a new virus from a mosquito bite
Immune complex deposition in dorsal root ganglia of the spine
Autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves after the earlier illness
Reinfection with a different strain acquired from a close contact
Reactivation of latent virus when immunity falls below effective levels

questions.question: In the complement fixation test, absence of haemolysis after sensitized sheep cells are added means what?
options: The antigen has been destroyed during incubation of the tube
Antibody is absent and complement remains free to lyse cells
The sheep red cells were agglutinated by the virus particles
The indicator system has failed completely and must be repeated
Antibody is present and complement was fixed by the reaction
questions.explanation: If complement is consumed in the antigen-antibody reaction, none is left for the indicator system and there is no lysis. This is a positive test. Free complement causes lysis in negative tests.
Serology can detect rising titres between acute and convalescent stages or specific IgM in primary infection. Unchanged IgG may reflect past exposure. Complement is not an antibody marker.
options: An unchanged antibody titre in both of the paired sera
A rising antibody titre between paired acute and convalescent sera
A negative IgM result in an early acute specimen
Detection of complement activity in the patient serum
A single low IgG titre measured in only one serum
questions.question: A serological diagnosis of acute infection can be made by which finding?

questions.explanation: Infected cells may show no apparent change, die or become transformed. Transformation is linked to oncogenic viruses. The other options are not recognised cell responses.
options: Mitosis, meiosis or fusion with neighbouring cells only
Atrophy, hypertrophy or metaplasia without any virus effect
Phagocytosis, pinocytosis or exocytosis of neighbouring cells
No apparent change, cell death or cell transformation
Differentiation, migration or complement activation of cells
questions.question: In which three ways can a cell respond to viral infection?

questions.explanation: Replicating virus produces histological changes that may be characteristic or non-specific. Histology is not sensitive or specific enough to stand alone. It serves as an adjunct.
options: They are produced solely by bacteria
They are neither highly sensitive nor specific
They appear only in uninfected cells
They form only after antibody appears
They are visible only by electron microscopy
questions.question: Why are viral inclusion bodies useful as an adjunct but unreliable as sole evidence for a diagnosis?

questions.explanation: HBsAg is the first marker detectable after infection and indicates the presence of virus. In acute infection it clears within six months. Persistence beyond six months defines chronicity.
questions.question: Which serological marker is the hallmark of hepatitis B infection and the first to appear?

questions.explanation: The immune tolerant phase features large amounts of virus with no host response, normal enzymes and little liver damage. In the immune active phase ALT rises and viral load falls. The inactive phase has low DNA.
questions.question: A patient with chronic HBV has very high HBV DNA, normal ALT and no liver inflammation. Which phase is this?

questions.explanation: HAV incubation is about 15 to 40 days, HEV about six weeks and HBV 50 to 180 days. HBV therefore has the longest incubation. This guides exposure history.
options: Hepatitis B, then hepatitis A, then hepatitis E
Hepatitis B, then hepatitis E, then hepatitis A
Hepatitis A, then hepatitis E, then hepatitis B
Hepatitis A, then hepatitis B, then hepatitis E
Hepatitis E, then hepatitis A, then hepatitis B
questions.question: Which is the order of increasing incubation period among hepatitis A, E and B?

options: An infectious disease that humans transmit to animals
A disease acquired only in hospital settings
An infectious disease of animals naturally transmissible to humans
A disease confined to arthropod vectors only
A disease of plants that is transmitted to animals
questions.explanation: A zoonosis is an animal infection naturally transmissible to humans, such as rabies and Lassa fever. Reverse zoonosis or anthroponosis is the opposite direction of transmission. Examples are rabies, Lassa fever and avian influenza.
questions.question: Which statement defines a zoonosis?

questions.explanation: Most acyclovir is excreted unchanged in urine, which is why renal function affects dosing. Its plasma half-life is short, so frequent dosing is needed for varicella-zoster. Dose adjustment is therefore needed in patients with impaired kidney function.
questions.question: More than 80 percent of acyclovir is found unchanged in which place after administration?

questions.explanation: Attachment occurs when the fibre binds the coxsackie and adenovirus receptor. The penton base then interacts with integrin to promote internalization. Uncoating follows in endosomes.
options: Envelope fusion with the membrane at neutral pH
Capsid injection of DNA through a contractile tail
Envelope glycoprotein binding to the CD4 receptor molecule
Penton base binding to sialic acid on mucin
Fibre binding to the coxsackie and adenovirus receptor
questions.question: Adenovirus enters a respiratory epithelial cell. Which receptor-mediated step comes first?

options: In the spleen, while draining lymph nodes handle local infection
In the kidney after filtration of virions from blood
In the skin where the virions first gain entry
In bone marrow where the virions replicate extensively before spread
In the thymus after migration of virions from blood
questions.explanation: Induction events occur in lymph nodes draining the site of infection or in the spleen if the virus enters blood. Antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes are retained there for effective interaction. This arrangement allows B cells and helper T cells to meet and start the response.
questions.question: Where do B cell activation and induction of adaptive immunity primarily occur when a virus enters the bloodstream?

options: It detects only free antibody that is present in the patient serum sample
It is slow but highly sensitive for detection of all clinically important viruses
It is rapid but poorly sensitive and specific and depends on specimen quality
It requires four weeks of cell culture before any result can be read
It cannot be used on nasopharyngeal specimens collected from any kind of patient
questions.question: Which statement about antigen detection by immunofluorescence is accurate?
questions.explanation: Immunofluorescence gives results in a few hours, yet the technique can be tedious and hard to interpret, and sensitivity and specificity are poor. A good specimen is essential. It is used for RSV, influenza A and adenoviruses.

questions.question: What is the principal way in which type I interferons protect uninfected cells nearby?
options: They carry viral peptides from the infected cell to T cells
They neutralize extracellular virions directly by binding the envelope
They form pores in infected membranes to cause cell lysis
They induce an antiviral state by activating many interferon-stimulated genes
They convert infected cells into antibody-secreting plasma cells
questions.explanation: Alpha and beta interferons bind the type I receptor and cause transcription of over one hundred interferon-stimulated genes. This inhibits protein synthesis and viral replication. They also raise MHC class I on neighbours.

questions.question: Which statement about viral multiplication is correct?
questions.explanation: Virus particles are produced from assembly of preformed components. They do not grow or divide themselves. This distinguishes them from cells, which increase their parts and then divide.
options: New particles arise by assembly of preformed components rather than division
Virions bud off as miniature cells that carry their own ribosomes
Virions multiply extracellularly whenever nutrients are supplied to them
Virions enlarge gradually and then divide by binary fission outside cells
Virions fuse in pairs to produce new progeny particles together

questions.question: Which sequence outlines early HIV replication after fusion?
options: Budding of virions, integration of DNA, then reverse transcription
Reverse transcription, nuclear import of the complex, then integration
Integration of DNA, reverse transcription, then fusion with membrane
Uncoating in nucleus, transcription of RNA, then membrane fusion
Translation of genome, integration of DNA, then reverse transcription
questions.explanation: After fusion, reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA. The pre-integration complex enters the nucleus and integrase inserts proviral DNA. Transcription and assembly follow, ending in budding.
Tat transactivates viral transcription by acting on the TAR region of the LTR. Rev helps export viral RNAs from the nucleus. Nef is a negative factor that also downregulates MHC class I.
questions.question: Which HIV regulatory gene product increases viral transcription by binding the TAR region?

questions.explanation: Guarnieri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions typical of smallpox. Poxviruses replicate in the cytoplasm. Negri bodies characterize rabies.
questions.question: Guarnieri bodies are characteristic of which infection?

options: Severe disease and frequent fulminant hepatitis
Protection against cirrhosis in later life
Lifelong immunity to the hepatitis B virus
Complete clearance of the hepatitis B virus
Reduced liver inflammation and milder disease
questions.question: Compared with hepatitis B alone, what does superinfection with HDV in a chronic HBV carrier often cause?
questions.explanation: HDV superinfection of a carrier often causes severe hepatitis and may be fulminant. HDV depends on HBV for envelope. Prevention of HBV prevents HDV.

Serology forms the mainstay of viral diagnosis and constitutes the bulk of the work of any virology laboratory. Most common viral infections can be diagnosed from antibody patterns. Direct detection and isolation depend heavily on specimen quality.
questions.question: A laboratory classifies its virology workload into direct detection, indirect examination and serology. Which category accounts for by far the bulk of routine work?

questions.explanation: Isolated anti-HBs without core antibody signals vaccine-induced immunity. Natural infection produces anti-HBc. Persistence of HBsAg is absent.
questions.question: In a patient with all markers negative except anti-HBs positive, what is the interpretation?
Which clinical problem is associated with persistent B19 infection?
questions.explanation: Persistent B19 infection in immunocompromised patients leads to chronic anaemia due to continued red cell precursor infection. Immunoglobulin can be used to treat or prevent persistence. Red cell precursor destruction in the marrow explains the fall in haemoglobin.

Alpha herpesviruses replicate fast and are latent in sensory ganglia, beta herpesviruses are slow and enlarge cells, and gamma herpesviruses are lymphotropic. This matches HSV and VZV, CMV and HHV-6 and 7, and EBV and HHV-8. Recognising these groups helps predict the latency site and tissue behaviour.
questions.question: Which grouping correctly places the herpesviruses by subfamily?
options: Alpha: HSV and VZV; beta: CMV and HHV-6; gamma: EBV and HHV-8
Alpha: HHV-6 and HHV-7; beta: HSV and VZV; gamma: CMV and EBV
Alpha: CMV and HHV-6; beta: HSV and VZV; gamma: EBV and HHV-8
Alpha: HSV and HHV-8; beta: EBV and HHV-6; gamma: CMV and VZV
Alpha: EBV and HHV-8; beta: CMV and HHV-6; gamma: HSV and VZV

questions.explanation: Reye syndrome is a recognised complication of influenza, associated with aspirin use in children. Pneumonia and myositis are other complications. Paracetamol is preferred for fever.
questions.question: A child recovering from influenza and treated with aspirin develops vomiting and encephalopathy with liver involvement. Which complication is described?

questions.explanation: Viral genes direct synthesis of the envelope proteins, but the lipid bilayer is acquired from host cellular membranes during budding. This explains why envelopes carry a mosaic of host and viral antigens. The membrane may be plasma or nuclear depending on the site of assembly.
questions.question: In an enveloped virion, the proteins are encoded by the virus, yet the lipids come from which source?
options: Fragments of bacterial plasma membrane present in the medium
Viral genes that encode enzymes for lipid biosynthesis
Ribosomes packaged inside the nucleocapsid core of the virion
The host cell membrane from which the particle buds
Capsid protomers that are chemically modified after assembly ends

questions.explanation: Parvoviruses lack the ability to push cells into S phase and wait in the nucleus until the cell enters it naturally. Rapidly dividing cells therefore support replication well. This explains fetal and erythroid involvement.
questions.question: Why does parvovirus B19 preferentially affect rapidly dividing cells such as red cell precursors and fetal tissues?
options: It integrates only into the quiescent chromatin of resting cells
It cannot induce S phase and must wait for the cell
It requires a lipid envelope that comes only from dividing cells
It binds only to receptors that are expressed in resting cells
It needs a reverse transcriptase that is made only in dividing cells

questions.explanation: The 17D live attenuated vaccine is used for yellow fever. It is a flavivirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. There is no vaccine for West Nile virus.
questions.question: Which vaccine strain is used to prevent yellow fever?
Regardless of where viral nucleic acid is made, which step always occurs in the cytoplasm?
options: Packaging of nucleic acid into capsids
Integration of viral DNA into chromosomes
questions.explanation: Nucleic acid may be made in the nucleus or cytoplasm depending on the virus. Protein synthesis always happens in the cytoplasm on ribosomes. Therefore nuclear viruses must export their mRNAs.

questions.question: BK polyomavirus is most commonly encountered in which setting?
questions.explanation: BK virus infects children subclinically and persists in the kidney. It reactivates in immunosuppression after organ transplant and late pregnancy. It was first isolated from the urine of a renal transplant recipient.

questions.question: A HBsAg-positive pregnant woman delivers. Which route poses a major risk to the infant?
options: Perinatal transmission from mother to infant
Faecal-oral transmission through breast milk only
Transmission through contaminated food to infant
Transmission by insect bite to the infant
Transmission by respiratory droplets to infant
questions.explanation: Vertical transmission is a major route of HBV spread and chronic infection often follows in infants. Transmission also occurs by blood, sex and shared needles. Casual contact does not transmit.

options: Mechanical blockage of bile canaliculi by virions
Shutoff of host protein synthesis by viral polymerase
Cytotoxic T cell killing of infected liver cells
Complement lysis of free circulating virions
Direct lysis caused by toxin-like viral protein
questions.explanation: HBV itself is not directly cytopathic. Damage arises when cytotoxic T lymphocytes try to clear the infection by killing infected cells. The strength of this response shapes the course of disease.
questions.question: Hepatocyte injury in hepatitis B is largely attributed to which mechanism?

questions.explanation: EM detects virions by morphology and needs at least 10 to the fifth to 10 to the sixth particles per millilitre. This limits its sensitivity. It is expensive and needs a skilled observer.
questions.question: Electron microscopy for virus detection requires roughly how many particles per millilitre of sample?
Which drug group includes ritonavir, atazanavir and darunavir?
questions.explanation: Ritonavir, atazanavir and darunavir inhibit the viral protease that cleaves polyproteins into mature proteins. They are important in HIV therapy. Integrase inhibitors include raltegravir.
Acyclovir and related analogues rely on viral kinases. Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase without activation. It is a rational choice for such resistance.
questions.question: A herpes virus isolate lacks thymidine kinase and resists acyclovir. Which drug could still work because it needs no viral kinase?
Disseminated CMV in an AIDS patient most typically produces which manifestation?
questions.explanation: In immunocompromised patients CMV disseminates to produce interstitial pneumonia, chorioretinitis, hepatitis, gastrointestinal disease and encephalitis. Ganciclovir is used for treatment. Retinitis in these patients can threaten sight if it is untreated.

questions.question: What is the first event after a hepadnavirus genome enters a new cell?
options: Reverse transcription of the genome by a virion enzyme
Integration into the host chromosome by an integrase
Cleavage of a polyprotein by a viral protease
Repair of the gapped DNA genome before viral transcription
Transcription by a virion RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
questions.explanation: Hepadnaviruses perform reverse transcription inside the maturing virion rather than after entry. On infection of a new cell the gapped genome is first repaired. Only afterwards is viral DNA transcribed and translated.

Hepatitis B and C are not spread by casual contact, coughing, sneezing, hugging or sharing utensils. Blood exposure is the principal risk. Health care and laboratory workers are exposed through needle sticks.
options: Sharing eating utensils or drinking glasses
Reusing unsterilised needles and syringes again
questions.question: Which activity is NOT a recognised way of transmitting hepatitis B or C?

questions.explanation: Retroviruses have a unique diploid positive-sense genome that is not used as mRNA. It is copied by reverse transcriptase into DNA. This places them in group VI.
options: Group VI, using the genome as a template for reverse transcription
Group IV, translating the genome directly into a single large polyprotein
Group V, transcribing the genome with a virion-associated RNA polymerase
Group III, transcribing each genome segment into separate mRNA molecules
Group II, converting the single-stranded genome into a double strand first
questions.question: Virions carry two copies of positive-sense RNA that do not act as mRNA but as templates for DNA synthesis. Which Baltimore group is this?

questions.explanation: Aerosolized ribavirin is used in severe RSV disease. Care is otherwise supportive. Diagnosis uses HeLa or Hep-2 culture, ELISA and RT-PCR.
questions.question: Which treatment is used for a severely ill hospitalised infant with RSV bronchiolitis?

options: Infection that lasts more than six days
Infection that lasts more than six months
Infection that lasts more than six years only
Infection with HBeAg present at any time
questions.question: Which statement about the definition of chronic hepatitis B is correct?
questions.explanation: Acute infection lasts under six months. Chronic infection is defined by persistent HBsAg beyond six months. It may progress to cirrhosis over two to three decades.
Parainfluenza viruses are paramyxoviruses causing minor colds, bronchitis, bronchopneumonia and croup in children. No specific treatment exists. They are detected by haemadsorption.
questions.question: Which virus family causes croup in young children and is a common cause of mild colds?

options: PCR requires four weeks of culture before it can be started
A positive result may reflect latent genomes and not active disease
PCR cannot detect any DNA viruses present in clinical specimens
PCR detects only protein antigens and never any nucleic acid
PCR always gives false negatives for every latent virus genome
questions.explanation: PCR is so sensitive that it can amplify latent genomes, for example latent CMV. A positive result then does not prove disease. Contamination can also cause false positives.
questions.question: A technologist plans PCR for a latent virus in blood from a healthy transplant donor. What is the main interpretive problem?

options: About two weeks before the spots appear
Never in the same illness episode
About twelve to twenty-four hours after them
Three weeks after the spots appear
Simultaneously with the end of incubation
questions.explanation: The maculopapular rash appears twelve to twenty-four hours after Koplik spots and lasts two to five days. Koplik spots last only one to two days. Incubation is seven to thirteen days.
questions.question: When does the measles rash appear relative to Koplik spots?
Which pairing of technique and principle is correct?
options: PCR uses sheep red blood cells, while branched DNA uses complement
PCR amplifies target nucleic acid, while branched DNA amplifies the signal
PCR amplifies the signal, while branched DNA amplifies the target nucleic acid
PCR measures patient antibody, while branched DNA measures viral antigen levels
PCR requires prior cell culture, while branched DNA requires embryonated eggs
questions.explanation: Newer molecular techniques use amplification of target nucleic acid, as in PCR, LCR and NASBA, or of the signal, as in branched DNA. Conventional hybridization is less sensitive. This distinction matters when choosing between assays for clinical use.

questions.question: Which is NOT a recognised antibody mechanism against viruses?
questions.explanation: Antibodies neutralize virions, cause agglutination, trigger phagocytosis through Fc receptors and activate complement that can damage envelopes. They do not degrade viral nucleic acid. The answer describes an invented mechanism.
options: Agglutination of virus particles into large clumps in fluid
Neutralization of the infectivity of free virions in fluid
Activation of the complement cascade on the virion surface
Activation of phagocytes through their surface Fc receptors
Cleavage of viral genomes through enzymatic activity of antibody

questions.question: Which virus group agglutinates red blood cells and can therefore be detected by the haemagglutination test?
questions.explanation: Viruses with surface haemagglutinin such as paramyxo, orthomyxo, toga, adeno and reoviruses can agglutinate red cells in suspension. The type of red cell and conditions must be controlled. It is a simple test for detecting such viruses.
options: Rhabdoviruses, filoviruses, arenaviruses, hepadnaviruses and herpesviruses
Hepadnaviruses, parvoviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses and retroviruses
Retroviruses, hepadnaviruses, herpesviruses, rhabdoviruses and filoviruses
Orthomyxoviruses, paramyxoviruses, togaviruses, adenoviruses and reoviruses
Picornaviruses, caliciviruses, astroviruses, hepadnaviruses and herpesviruses

questions.question: A clinician needs a result within hours for suspected RSV infection in a neonate. Which approach best meets this need?
questions.explanation: Direct antigen detection is rapid and can give results within hours, which is valuable for neonatal RSV infection. Serology and culture are slow. The quality of the aspirate remains critical.
options: Virus isolation in primary cell culture over weeks
Histology of lung tissue taken at autopsy
Passage of the specimen in embryonated hen eggs
Paired serology after three weeks of illness

questions.explanation: Some activated B cells become short-lived plasma cells, while others interact with helper CD4 cells to differentiate into long-lived plasma cells and memory cells. This produces high-affinity antibody. These cells sustain antibody levels and give rapid recall on re-exposure.
questions.question: Which cells generate high-affinity antibody and memory B cells after interacting with helper T cells?
options: Natural killer cells located in the liver sinusoids
Long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells in follicles
Mast cells located in the submucosa of the gut
Short-lived plasma cells located at the follicle centre
Dendritic cells located in the thymus of the host
Absence of any DNA genome in the virion particle
Replication by a virion RNA polymerase only
Replication through an RNA intermediate by reverse transcriptase
Replication carried out entirely in the cytoplasm of cells
Use of a segmented genome with eight pieces
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the replication of hepatitis B virus from other DNA viruses?
questions.explanation: HBV replicates through an RNA intermediate. A pregenomic RNA is reverse transcribed to make new DNA genomes. Part of the DNA may integrate into the host genome.

options: The virus is cleared by the immune response without persisting
The virus replicates mainly in bone marrow of the host
The virus infects only neurons and spares the liver
The virus is produced by hepatocytes lifelong after infection
The virus integrates into DNA and remains silent for life
questions.question: What is the chief reason hepatitis A does not become chronic?
questions.explanation: HAV replicates slowly in the liver without major cytopathic effect and is cleared by antibody and cellular responses. It does not persist. Hence no chronic carriers exist.

options: Rift Valley fever virus and sandfly fever virus
questions.explanation: Ebola and Marburg viruses belong to Filoviridae and cause haemorrhagic fever with high mortality. They spread by contact with body fluids. Their reservoirs remain uncertain.
questions.question: Which pair lists filoviruses?

options: Giving high-dose acyclovir as sole therapy
Starting oral oseltamivir as sole therapy
Giving hyperimmune globulin as sole therapy
Reducing immunosuppression along with supportive care
Giving aerosolized ribavirin as sole therapy
questions.question: What is the main approach to managing polyomavirus disease in transplant patients?
questions.explanation: No specific effective antiviral exists for polyomaviruses. Management involves supportive care and reduction of immunosuppression. Cidofovir and others have been tried.
Adenovirus types 3 and 7 are associated with pneumonia. Other types cause pharyngitis, keratoconjunctivitis and enteric disease. Types 40 and 41 are enteric.
questions.question: Which adenovirus types are associated with pneumonia?

questions.explanation: Binding of un-neutralized virus-antibody complexes to Fc receptors increases the number of infected cells, as seen in dengue haemorrhagic fever. This is antibody-dependent enhancement. Neutralizing antibody and NK cells would instead limit infection.
questions.question: A child with a second dengue infection from a different serotype develops haemorrhagic fever. Which mechanism most likely enhances the disease?
options: Cross-protective cytotoxic T cell response that terminates the infection
Non-neutralizing virus-antibody complexes binding Fc receptors and infecting more cells
Interferon-induced antiviral state in neighbouring uninfected tissue cells
Rapid clearance of infected cells by natural killer cell activity
Complete neutralization of virions by high-affinity antibody production

questions.explanation: The Baltimore scheme recognises that all viruses must produce positive-strand mRNA to make proteins. The route to that mRNA differs with genome type, giving seven groups. Integration, reverse transcription and virion polymerases apply only to some groups.
options: Every virus must integrate its genome into host chromosomes
Every virus must complete replication inside the host nucleus
Every virus must generate positive-sense mRNA from its genome
Every virus must carry its own RNA polymerase in the virion
Every virus must reverse transcribe its genome into DNA first
questions.question: What is the central principle underlying the Baltimore classification of viruses?

options: Chronic carrier state in most children
questions.question: Hepatitis E virus carries which characteristic clinical risk?
questions.explanation: HEV spreads by the faecal-oral route and has a high risk of fulminant hepatitis in pregnant women. It does not usually cause chronic disease. It requires no helper virus.
Antiviral drugs generally inhibit development of the virus instead of destroying it. They are therefore virustatic. Most antibiotics are bactericidal or bacteriostatic against free organisms.
questions.question: Antiviral drugs differ from most antibiotics in which important way?
options: They induce lifelong protective immunity in the host after therapy
They act only on cells that are infected by bacteria
They act only after the virus has been released from cells
They kill extracellular virions by directly lysing the viral envelope
They inhibit viral development rather than destroying the pathogen

questions.question: Which red cells does Newcastle disease virus agglutinate in the haemagglutination test?
questions.explanation: The haemagglutination test requires specific conditions such as temperature, pH and red cell type. Newcastle disease virus requires chicken red cells, whereas influenza virus works with human erythrocytes. Sheep red cells are used in the complement fixation indicator system.

questions.question: Which route lets viruses such as HIV, CMV and HBV pass from mother to child?
questions.explanation: Vertical infection occurs from mother to child, as in CMV, HIV and HBV. Insect bites, faecal-oral spread and fomites are other routes. Vertical routes include transplacental, perinatal and breast milk.

Virus first replicates at its portal of entry, which determines whether infection stays local or becomes systemic. It then spreads by blood or cerebrospinal fluid. Secondary replication occurs in susceptible target organs.
questions.question: A virus replicates at the site of entry and then spreads to distant organs through blood. In correct order, what are the stages?
options: Secondary replication, systemic spread and primary replication
Systemic spread, primary replication and shedding only
Primary replication, systemic spread and secondary replication
Primary replication, shedding and latency without spread
Systemic spread, secondary replication and primary replication
Flow of urine through the urethra
