Ciliated epithelium, mucus secretion and lower temperature
Gastric acid, bile salts and intestinal enzymes
Keratinized stratified squamous barrier of the skin
questions.question: Which respiratory defence must an inhaled virus overcome to establish infection?
questions.explanation: The respiratory tract has sophisticated immune defences and non-specific inhibitors such as ciliated epithelium, mucus and lower temperature. Viruses must evade these to replicate. Acid and bile are gut features.
Persistence of HBsAg with negative IgM anti-HBc and no anti-HBs indicates chronic infection. IgM anti-HBc helps separate acute from chronic cases. Chronic carriers do not develop anti-HBs.
questions.question: A patient has HBsAg positive, total anti-HBc positive, IgM anti-HBc negative and anti-HBs negative. What is the best interpretation?
Which laboratory test best supports recent parvovirus B19 infection?
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 does not grow readily in routine cell culture. IgM ELISA, PCR, EM and dot-blot hybridization are used. IgM indicates recent infection.
The capsid accounts for most of the virion mass and protects the nucleic acid. In naked viruses it also carries the attachment function and may contain enzymes. It has no metabolic capacity.
options: Protecting the genome and mediating attachment to host cells
Supplying lipids for the assembling virion at the membrane
Generating ATP to drive genome replication in the cytoplasm
Encoding the synthesis of envelope glycoproteins on ribosomes
Providing ribosomes for viral translation within the virion
questions.question: Which function is attributable to the capsid of a naked virus?

questions.explanation: After the acute illness there is a vigorous immune response and viral load falls to the set point. This level correlates with disease progression. Clinical latency follows.
questions.question: What feature of an HIV infection defines the steady-state viral load after primary infection?

questions.explanation: The capacity to infect a cell depends on specific surface receptors. The interaction between a capsid or envelope region and the receptor leads to infection. Without it the cell is resistant.
options: Binding of complement proteins to the viral envelope allows viral entry
Binding of viral nucleic acid to host ribosomes allows entry into cells
Binding of interferon molecules to the viral capsid allows viral entry
Binding of capsid or envelope region to a cell receptor allows infection
Binding of host antibody to the surface receptor allows viral entry
questions.question: Which sequence reflects how interaction of a viral surface region with its receptor leads to infection?
A food handler's illness is traced to an outbreak after raw shellfish consumption. Which virus best fits?
questions.explanation: Shellfish from polluted water have caused major HAV outbreaks, such as the one in Shanghai in 1988. The virus is shed in faeces and spread by food handlers and household contacts. Careful hand hygiene and safe food preparation reduce such outbreaks.

Mortality may follow when the virus undergoes a major antigenic change. Existing immunity then fails to recognise the new surface proteins. Cross-species jumps and weakened host immunity also increase mortality.
questions.question: Why does influenza virus repeatedly cause deaths even in people with prior infection?
options: Influenza integrates into host DNA and avoids all detection
Influenza suppresses all interferon production permanently in cells
Influenza has no surface antigens that antibody can recognise
Major antigenic change allows escape from existing immunity
Influenza infects only immune cells that cannot make antibody

questions.explanation: Viral haemorrhagic fevers are caused by enveloped RNA viruses from four families: Filoviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae and Flaviviridae. Ebola, Lassa, Congo-Crimean fever and yellow fever are examples. Their lipid envelope makes all four groups susceptible to common disinfectants.
questions.question: Which four virus families are the main causes of viral haemorrhagic fevers?

questions.explanation: Antigenic shift is a sudden major change when gene segments are exchanged between viruses from different hosts. Antigenic drift is gradual change through point mutation. Shift can cause pandemics.
questions.question: A new influenza A virus emerges after a segment from an animal strain replaces one in a human strain. What is this process?
Which virus group is the commonest cause of intrauterine infection and congenital abnormalities?
questions.explanation: CMV is the commonest agent of intrauterine infection with prenatal damage and congenital abnormalities. It may be acquired at birth or later through breast milk, kissing, sex and transfusion. Infection in pregnancy can therefore cause lasting damage to the fetus.

questions.question: Why is HBV considered to have a more oncogenic profile than HAV?
options: HBV cannot persist in hepatocytes after the acute phase
HAV causes chronic cirrhosis and later liver carcinoma
HBV causes only acute disease and is always cleared
HAV integrates into hepatocyte DNA and persists for many years
HBV can integrate into host DNA and cause chronic infection
questions.explanation: HBV may integrate and persist, causing chronic infection and hepatocellular carcinoma. HAV is cleared and never chronic. This explains oncogenic status.

In immune EM, specific antibody clumps virus particles together or captures them onto the grid, making them easier to recognise. This increases sensitivity and specificity. It does not need fluorescent or enzyme labels.
options: Radioisotopes mark the viral genome for detection by film
Virus-specific antibody agglutinates or captures particles on the grid
Enzyme conjugates generate colour in the wells of plates
Fluorescent labels light up the intracellular antigen in cells
Complement lyses the virions to make counting much easier
questions.question: How does immune electron microscopy improve detection of a virus?

questions.explanation: Each strand of adenovirus DNA is attached to a virus-coded protein at the 5' end, and this protein acts as a primer for DNA synthesis. This differs from retroviruses, which use tRNA. Replication occurs in the nucleus.
questions.question: Adenoviral DNA replication is initiated using which primer?
options: A tRNA molecule that is packaged within the mature virion core particle
A virus-encoded protein covalently attached to the 5' end of each strand
A cellular histone protein that is bound tightly to the viral genome
A host-derived RNA primer made by cellular primase enzyme in the nucleus
A host polymerase subunit that is bound at the 3' end of DNA

questions.question: Which pair of hepatitis viruses is transmitted by the faecal-oral route?
questions.explanation: HAV and HEV cause infectious hepatitis spread through faeces, contaminated water and food. HBV, HCV and HDV are transmitted parenterally and cause serum hepatitis. Water sanitation therefore protects against the first group but not the second.

questions.question: Which drug inhibits uncoating in influenza A only?
questions.explanation: Amantadine and rimantadine block uncoating of influenza A and have limited use because of resistance. Oseltamivir and zanamivir inhibit neuraminidase in both A and B. Amantadine therefore has a narrower spectrum than the neuraminidase inhibitors.

RNA-containing naked viruses are generally released soon after maturation, so little virus builds up. DNA viruses maturing in the nucleus accumulate and form inclusion bodies. Neither naked group takes an envelope.
options: They are released only after the cell transforms
They accumulate for long periods and form large inclusions
They leave rapidly after maturation with little intracellular accumulation
They always acquire an envelope during exit
They are released only by budding through the nucleus
questions.question: How does release of naked RNA viruses differ from that of naked DNA viruses maturing in the nucleus?

options: It requires no phosphorylation by any viral or cellular enzyme
It binds to the pyrophosphate binding site of the polymerase
It is an inorganic pyrophosphate analogue with no sugar ring
It carries an extra hydroxymethyl group on the sugar chain
It lacks a 3' hydroxyl group needed for chain extension
questions.question: Which feature of acyclovir explains why it acts as an obligate chain terminator?
questions.explanation: Acyclovir has an acyclic side chain with no 3' hydroxyl, so no further nucleotide can be added after incorporation. Ganciclovir differs by retaining a hydroxyl allowing limited extension. This difference explains why some analogues stop synthesis completely while others allow limited extension.

questions.question: Smallpox virus enters the body by which route and first replicates where?
options: Respiratory tract with local replication then lymph node spread
Gastrointestinal tract with local replication then spread to liver
Urinary tract with local replication then spread to kidney
Conjunctiva with local replication then direct invasion of brain
Skin abrasion with local replication then spread along nerves
questions.explanation: Variola is inhaled in oropharyngeal secretions, replicates locally and spreads to lymph nodes through macrophages. Primary viraemia is followed by secondary viraemia, when symptoms begin. Spread through macrophages explains why first symptoms appear only after viraemia.

Rhabdoviruses carry a negative-sense genome, which cannot be translated directly. A virion RNA-dependent RNA polymerase transcribes it into monocistronic mRNAs. Without this enzyme naked genomic RNA does nothing.
questions.question: Purified genomic RNA of rabies virus is not infectious by itself. What is the most likely reason?
options: The RNA lacks a nucleocapsid and cannot be packaged
Negative-sense RNA must first be transcribed by a virion-associated polymerase
The RNA must first be reverse transcribed by host enzymes
Its genome is DNA that requires host integration before translation
The genome is segmented into eight pieces that need reassembly

questions.explanation: Oseltamivir and zanamivir inhibit both influenza A and B, whereas amantadine covers only A and resistance is frequent. They act at release. This improves clinical usefulness.
options: They are active against rhinoviruses as well as influenza viruses
They act against influenza A and B, unlike limited amantadine
They act only against influenza A and not against influenza B
They prevent virus attachment by binding the viral haemagglutinin protein
They have no resistance problems and never fail in clinical practice
questions.question: Why are neuraminidase inhibitors preferred over amantadine for seasonal influenza?

questions.explanation: Raltegravir is an integrase inhibitor. It blocks insertion of the DNA copy into the host chromosome. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors act earlier.
options: Reverse transcription of the viral RNA genome
Integration of proviral DNA into host DNA
Cleavage of the viral polyprotein by protease
Release of new virions by viral neuraminidase
Attachment of gp120 to the CD4 receptor
questions.question: Raltegravir prevents which step in the HIV life cycle?

questions.explanation: HHV-8, also called KSHV, is linked to Kaposi sarcoma, especially in AIDS. In immunocompetent persons it generally causes only latent infection. It is a gamma herpesvirus.
questions.question: Which virus is also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus?
A patient is HBsAg negative and total anti-HBc positive with anti-HBs negative and IgM anti-HBc negative. What does this likely represent?
questions.explanation: Isolated total anti-HBc without HBsAg and IgM indicates past exposure in which anti-HBs has waned. Total anti-HBc is the most constant marker of exposure. It stays positive for life.
options: Immunity from vaccination alone without exposure
Chronic active infection with ongoing viral replication
Acute infection in the early symptomatic phase
Never exposed to the virus at any time
Past infection, cleared, with anti-HBs waned over time
The complement is consumed by the reaction in the tube
The cytopathic effect is clearly visible in the culture
The red cells agglutinate in the plate well
The cytopathic effect in the culture is blocked
The enzyme produces a coloured product in the well
questions.question: In a virus neutralization test, what indicates that the patient serum contains specific antibody?
questions.explanation: Serum is incubated with a standard virus and then inoculated into culture. If antibodies are present, infectivity is blocked and no CPE appears. Absence of antibody allows growth.

questions.question: Which biosafety level is required for laboratory work with arenaviruses such as Lassa virus?
questions.explanation: Handling of arenaviruses for diagnosis needs maximum containment, biosafety level 4. Strict isolation and barrier nursing are also required in hospitals. Ordinary laboratories must therefore refer suspected samples to reference centres.

questions.question: Which intervention given to an HIV-positive mother during pregnancy reduces transmission to the child?
questions.explanation: Giving zidovudine to the mother in pregnancy reduces vertical transmission. Without therapy about thirteen to forty percent of babies are infected. Transmission also occurs at delivery and by breast milk.

options: It is partially double-stranded circular DNA with a gap
It is diploid single-stranded RNA with two copies
It is segmented double-stranded RNA with ten segments
It is linear double-stranded DNA encoding many replication enzymes
It is circular single-stranded DNA needing host enzymes
questions.question: Which statement about herpesvirus DNA is correct?
questions.explanation: Herpesviruses have linear double-stranded DNA that encodes many enzymes needed for replication, which is why thymidine kinase-based drugs work. They are among the largest human viruses. This genetic capacity explains why viral enzymes are available as drug targets.
Dengue and Zika viruses are spread mainly by Aedes mosquitoes. Zika infection in pregnancy can cause microcephaly in the fetus. Dengue is common in tropical areas.
questions.question: Which mosquito genus transmits dengue and Zika viruses?
A liver biopsy shows apoptotic hepatocytes with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a dark pyknotic nucleus. Which inclusion-type structure is described?
questions.explanation: Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pyknotic nucleus. They are described in yellow fever and viral hepatitis. Guarnieri bodies occur in smallpox.

questions.question: Which rodent is the natural reservoir of Lassa virus?
questions.explanation: Lassa virus is carried by the multimammate rat Mastomys natalensis, which sheds virus in urine and faeces. Humans are infected by contact with excreta or contaminated food. Person-to-person spread also occurs.

questions.question: School children develop fever, sore throat and red eyes after swimming-pool exposure. Which adenoviral syndrome is likely?
questions.explanation: Pharyngoconjunctival fever presents with fever, sore throat and red eyes, mainly in school children. Keratoconjunctivitis and haemorrhagic cystitis are other adenoviral syndromes. Treatment is supportive.
HAV is heat and acid stable, which supports passage through the stomach and survival in food. It is spread by contaminated food and water, raw shellfish and close contact. Blood-borne spread is rare.
options: Transmission by respiratory droplets and aerosols only
Faecal-oral transmission through contaminated food and water
Parenteral transmission through needles and blood products
Vertical transmission from mother to child at delivery
Vector transmission by the bite of mosquitoes
questions.question: Hepatitis A virus survives gastric acid and mild heating. Which route does this property favour?

questions.explanation: PCR can detect down to one DNA molecule, so even tiny contamination can cause false positives. Interpretation of positives is also difficult. Closed automated systems reduce the risk.
questions.question: What is the chief practical problem encountered with PCR in the diagnostic laboratory?
JC polyomavirus is associated with which fatal neurological disease?
questions.explanation: JC virus persists in the kidney and in immunosuppression it reaches the brain, causing progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. It is a rare subacute and fatal disease. It was named from a patient's initials.

Ivermectin inhibits the importin heterodimer, hindering nuclear import of viral and host proteins. Remdesivir targets polymerase and ritonavir targets protease. Several agents were tested against COVID-19.
questions.question: Which drug inhibits importin alpha and beta heterodimer to block nuclear import of host and viral proteins?

questions.explanation: Tropism depends on cell receptors for the virus and on whether the cell can support viral replication. Physical barriers, local temperature and body secretions also contribute in the host. Laboratory variables do not define tropism.
questions.question: Two cell lines are exposed to the same virus, but only one becomes infected. Which pair of factors most directly determines this tissue tropism?
options: Colour of the culture medium and size of the cell nucleus used
Concentration of antibiotics and incubation time of the plate used
Age of the culture flask and number of cells initially seeded
Number of passages and pH of the washing buffer applied
Presence of specific receptors and ability of the cell to support replication
It blocks release of new virions by inhibiting viral neuraminidase
It cleaves the viral polyprotein at the wrong sites in the cell
It competes with dGTP and terminates the growing chain after incorporation
It prevents integration of viral DNA into the host chromosomes
It binds the viral envelope and prevents fusion with the cell membrane
questions.explanation: Acyclovir triphosphate competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate for viral DNA polymerase. Once incorporated, it terminates the chain and the polymerase is trapped. The exonuclease cannot remove it.
questions.question: How does acyclovir triphosphate stop viral DNA synthesis?

questions.explanation: Amantadine and rimantadine prevent uncoating of influenza A. Resistance has become widespread. Neuraminidase inhibitors act later.
questions.question: Which drug acts as an inhibitor of uncoating in influenza A infection?

options: Restrictive infection with persistence of the viral genome
Productive infection with release of progeny virions
Eclipse infection with immediate genome clearance
Abortive infection with no virion production at all
Lytic infection ending in rapid cell destruction
questions.question: Cells are only transiently permissive; a few virions form, production stops, but the genome persists and cells may transform. Which infection outcome is this?
questions.explanation: In restrictive infection cells are transiently permissive, produce a few viruses and then stop, while the genome remains. Such cells may be transformed. Productive infections release virions, whereas abortive infections yield none.

Adsorption is mediated by ionic interactions between the viral attachment protein and cell receptors and does not depend on temperature. Later steps such as penetration need energy and warmth. This is why cold incubation allows binding without entry.
options: Attachment depends on active membrane invagination by the host cell
Attachment relies on ionic interactions that are temperature independent
Attachment needs ATP generated by virion enzymes at body temperature
Attachment requires endosomal acidification at physiological temperature
Attachment is driven by viral polymerase activity inside the cell
questions.question: Virions bind to a cell line even when incubated at 4 degrees Celsius. What explains this observation?

questions.explanation: IgM anti-HAV appears early and indicates recent infection. Total antibody persists and indicates immunity. The other markers belong to other hepatitis viruses.
questions.question: Which serological marker confirms acute hepatitis A infection?
Which statement about HTLV-1 is correct?
options: It is an orthomyxovirus that causes seasonal influenza illness in adults
It is a herpesvirus that causes infectious mononucleosis
It is a papillomavirus that causes genital warts
It is a retrovirus causing adult T-cell leukaemia and myelopathy
It is a flavivirus that causes haemorrhagic fever syndrome
questions.explanation: HTLV-1 is a deltaretrovirus transmitted by breast milk, sex and blood. It causes adult T-cell leukaemia and tropical spastic paraparesis. It differs from HIV in being oncogenic.

questions.question: A gastroenteritis outbreak in children is investigated. Adenovirus ranks second to which virus as a cause of childhood gastroenteritis?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus is second to rotavirus as a cause of childhood gastroenteritis. It also causes about two to five percent of respiratory infections. Infection is common during childhood.

questions.question: The indicator system of the complement fixation test consists of which components?
questions.explanation: The indicator system contains sheep red cells, complement and specific haemolysin or amboceptor. The test system contains the suspected antigen and patient serum. The two systems compete for complement.
options: Sheep red cells, complement and haemolysin
Patient serum, sheep cells and antigen

questions.question: Why is the neutralization test preferred over haemagglutination inhibition for flavivirus immunity screening?
options: It requires no virus at all in the test
It is faster than the haemagglutination inhibition test for screening
It can be performed at the patient bedside
It uses red blood cells in plate wells
It detects antibodies missed by inhibition and is more specific
questions.explanation: Parallel tests in Nigeria showed some sera negative by HI but positive by neutralization for dengue. Neutralization is therefore more sensitive and specific for screening immunity. The method is slower but is more reliable for confirming immunity.
Group VII contains double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate through an RNA intermediate, with reverse transcription inside the particle. Hepatitis B virus is the example. HIV belongs to group VI.
questions.question: Which virus is placed in Baltimore group VII, the double-stranded DNA reverse-transcribing viruses?

questions.explanation: Penciclovir resembles ganciclovir in structure and acyclovir in activation. It is used topically for cold sores and intravenously for mucocutaneous herpes in immunocompromised patients. It acts as a DNA chain terminator.
options: It is a protease inhibitor used for treating HIV infection and AIDS
It is a neuraminidase inhibitor used for influenza A and B
It is used topically for cold sores and terminates viral DNA chains
It is an RNA polymerase inhibitor developed for treating COVID-19 only
It is an uncoating inhibitor used for influenza A infection only
questions.question: Which statement about penciclovir is accurate?
Which feature identifies respiratory syncytial virus within the Paramyxoviridae?
options: It is a segmented virus with eight genome segments
Fusion protein causes syncytia and it lacks both surface enzymes
It carries a haemagglutinin that agglutinates chick red cells in culture
It is a bullet-shaped virus carrying glycoprotein G spikes
It carries a neuraminidase that cleaves sialic acid residues
questions.explanation: RSV, a pneumovirus, causes syncytia through its fusion protein and has no haemagglutinin or neuraminidase. It causes bronchiolitis in infants. There is no viraemia.

questions.question: Which description correctly contrasts targets of direct-acting antivirals and host-directed strategies?
options: Direct agents target viral enzymes, whereas host-directed agents target cell factors
Direct agents target only host ribosomes, whereas host-directed agents target viral genomes
Direct agents target only interferons, whereas host-directed agents target viral enzymes
Direct agents target host mitochondria, whereas host-directed agents target viral capsids
Direct agents target the extracellular matrix, whereas host-directed agents target viral RNA
questions.explanation: Antiviral strategies follow two approaches: targeting the virus itself or host factors needed by it. Direct agents include inhibitors of polymerases, proteases, integrases and neuraminidases. Host-directed agents act on cell functions.

Influenza has an incubation of one to four days with abrupt fever, aches, chills and dry cough, and recovery in seven to ten days. It is seasonal and spreads easily among school children. Confirmation can be made by rapid antigen tests or molecular assays.
questions.question: An adult presents with sudden fever, myalgia, headache and dry cough in winter. Which diagnosis fits best?

questions.explanation: Ribavirin is the drug generally used in treatment of most haemorrhagic fevers. Supportive care and isolation are also needed. Vaccines exist only for some such as yellow fever.
questions.question: Which antiviral is used for most viral haemorrhagic fevers including Lassa fever?

questions.explanation: Poxviruses have evolved the factors needed for transcription and replication and so are largely independent of cellular machinery. This allows complete replication outside the nucleus. Most other DNA viruses depend on host nuclear enzymes.
questions.question: Poxviruses replicate in the cytoplasm even though they are DNA viruses. Which property makes this possible?
options: They reverse transcribe the DNA genome into RNA first
They depend on helper viruses to supply their polymerases
They carry their own enzymes for replication and transcription
They integrate into mitochondrial DNA in order to reproduce
They borrow nuclear polymerases exported into the cytoplasm

questions.question: Which open reading frame of HBV encodes the polymerase and reverse transcriptase activity?
questions.explanation: The P gene encodes the polymerase with reverse transcriptase activity. S codes for surface antigens, C for the core protein and X for a transactivator. This enzyme is the target of nucleos(t)ide analogues.

questions.question: Which structure of an enveloped virion is chiefly responsible for attachment, haemagglutination and strong antigenicity?
options: Host-derived lipid bilayer surrounding the nucleocapsid
Glycoprotein spikes projecting from the envelope surface
Protomers forming the helical nucleocapsid tube
Matrix protein lining the inner envelope face
Genomic nucleic acid inside the nucleocapsid core
questions.explanation: Spikes are glycoprotein projections rising from the envelope with enzymatic, adsorptive and haemagglutinating activity. They are highly antigenic and therefore targets for neutralizing antibody. The matrix protein mainly supports assembly rather than attachment.

options: It becomes incorporated into DNA as a chain terminator
It blocks neuraminidase action at the cell surface membrane
It needs viral thymidine kinase to become active in cells
It prevents uncoating of nucleocapsids inside the cell endosome
It mimics pyrophosphate and blocks its release from nucleoside triphosphate
questions.explanation: Foscarnet is an inorganic pyrophosphate analogue that binds the pyrophosphate site of the polymerase. It blocks pyrophosphate cleavage from nucleoside triphosphate and so halts chain extension. It needs no kinase activation.
questions.question: Foscarnet inhibits viral DNA polymerase by which mechanism?
Which effect of interferon makes nearby cells easier for T cells to recognise as infected?
options: Shutdown of antigen presentation pathways in cells
Increased expression of MHC class I molecules
Increased production of viral receptors on cells
Inhibition of perforin synthesis by cytotoxic cells
Decreased expression of the T cell receptor complex
questions.explanation: Interferon signalling makes neighbouring cells increase the number of MHC class I molecules, so surveying T cells identify infection. It therefore bridges innate and adaptive immunity. It does not neutralize virions.

questions.question: Nelfinavir is an example of which approach to antiviral drug discovery?
questions.explanation: Nelfinavir, developed in the 1990s for HIV, is cited as an example of computer-based drug discovery. Structure-guided design is used to find protease inhibitors. Such design relies on knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the viral enzyme.

options: Twenty identical equilateral triangular faces and twelve apices around the whole particle
Five-fold axes of symmetry passing through every apex of the capsid
One axis of symmetry running down the centre of a tube
Twelve vertices each occupied by a penton made of five subunits
Hexons arranged on the flat triangular faces of the shell
questions.explanation: Helical capsids are capped tubes with one axis of symmetry down the centre. Icosahedral capsids have twenty triangular faces, twelve vertices and multiple axes. Pentons and hexons belong to the icosahedral arrangement.
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes helical symmetry from icosahedral symmetry?

questions.explanation: HIV carries reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease, all encoded by the pol gene. Each can be targeted by drugs. Neuraminidase belongs to influenza.
questions.question: Which enzymes are carried in the HIV virion and are targets of antiretroviral drugs?
Which marker is the most direct and accurate indicator of HBV replication used for deciding treatment?
questions.explanation: HBV DNA directly measures replication and correlates with progression risk. It is used to decide the need for antivirals and to monitor response. Serological markers are less direct.

options: Individuals who sit beside a patient
Individuals who share a handshake only
Individuals who use the same toilet
questions.explanation: Haemodialysis, transplantation, tattooing, injecting drug use and exposure to blood increase risk. Casual contact does not. Health workers are at risk from needle sticks.
questions.question: Which group of people is at increased risk of HBV and HCV infection?
Which list contains only genera of the family Picornaviridae?
options: Orthopoxvirus, cardiovirus, rhinovirus, aphthovirus and hepatovirus
Enterovirus, cardiovirus, rhinovirus, aphthovirus and hepatovirus
Enterovirus, cardiovirus, lyssavirus, aphthovirus and hepatovirus
Enterovirus, cardiovirus, rhinovirus, aphthovirus and hepacivirus
Enterovirus, flavivirus, rhinovirus, aphthovirus and hepatovirus
questions.explanation: Picornaviridae has five genera: enterovirus, cardiovirus, rhinovirus, aphthovirus and hepatovirus. Flavivirus and hepacivirus belong to Flaviviridae, lyssavirus to Rhabdoviridae and orthopoxvirus to Poxviridae. Each decoy substitutes one foreign genus.

options: Both subsets recognise viral peptide presented only on class III molecules in tissues
CD4 cells recognise lipid antigen while CD8 cells recognise peptide on class II molecules
CD4 cells see peptide on class I and CD8 cells see peptide on class II
CD4 cells see peptide on class II and CD8 cells see peptide on class I
Both subsets recognise free virions directly in the blood without using any MHC molecule
questions.explanation: Both subsets recognise viral peptides bound to MHC. CD4 cells use class II and CD8 cells use class I. This division reflects exogenous and endogenous antigen presentation.
questions.question: Which statement about CD4 and CD8 T cell antigen recognition is correct?

questions.explanation: Gardasil is a quadrivalent vaccine protecting against HPV 6 and 11 as well as 16 and 18. Other vaccines target additional types. No specific treatment exists for established HPV infection.
questions.question: Which vaccine protects against HPV types 6 and 11, which cause most genital warts?

options: Measles, mumps, rubella and RSV viruses
Influenza A, influenza B, rabies and Lassa viruses
EBV, HTLV-1, HPV, HBV, HCV and HHV-8
Dengue, Zika, yellow fever and West Nile viruses
questions.explanation: Several chronic viral infections lead to malignancy, including EBV, HTLV-1, HPV, HBV, HCV and HHV-8. The other groups cause acute illness without a recognised oncogenic role. Persistence and integration are common mechanisms.
questions.question: Which group lists viruses all associated with human cancers?
Which two glycoproteins on the influenza envelope determine attachment and release?
questions.explanation: Haemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory cells, and neuraminidase helps cleave mucus and release progeny virions. Both undergo antigenic variation. They are the targets of vaccines and neuraminidase inhibitors.

Street virus is the wild virus from naturally infected animals with variable incubation. Fixed virus has been serially passaged, which stabilises virulence and incubation period. It is used for vaccines.
options: Fixed virus has stabilised virulence and incubation after serial passage
Fixed virus is isolated directly from naturally infected dogs
Fixed virus has a longer incubation than street virus
Fixed virus is non-neurotropic and non-virulent in rabbits
Fixed virus is the wild type found in saliva samples
questions.question: What distinguishes a fixed rabies virus from a street virus?

questions.explanation: HCV can cause arthralgia, myalgia, pruritus, paraesthesia and sicca syndrome with dry eyes, skin and mouth. These extrahepatic features reflect immune-mediated mechanisms. These features can appear before or without obvious liver symptoms.
questions.question: Which pair lists extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis C?

options: S codes core, C polymerase, P transactivator and X surface antigen
S codes capsid, C envelope, P integrase and X protease enzyme
S codes polymerase, C surface antigen, P core and X transactivator protein
S codes transactivator, C surface, P polymerase and X core protein
S codes surface antigens, C core, P polymerase and X a transactivator
questions.question: Which statement about the HBV genome open reading frames is correct?
questions.explanation: The four overlapping reading frames are S for surface proteins, C for core, P for polymerase and X for a transactivator. These derive from the same strand. Overlap of the frames allows a small genome to encode many proteins.

questions.question: A child with high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis develops small white spots on the buccal mucosa. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: The three Cs of measles are cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, followed by Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa. A maculopapular rash follows twelve to twenty-four hours later. The patient is highly infectious.
Cell culture is slow, taking up to four weeks, and sensitivity is often poor. It is also prone to bacterial contamination and toxic specimens. Rapid methods suit urgent cases.
questions.question: What is the most important disadvantage of virus isolation by cell culture for acute clinical management?
options: Results can take up to four weeks
It cannot be performed from throat swabs
It requires live patients' blood only

questions.question: What triggers a cytotoxic T cell to kill a virus-infected cell?
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells carry T cell receptors that recognise a specific peptide in MHC class I. Recognition triggers release of cytotoxic factors. Detection of reduced MHC class I is the cue for natural killer cells.
options: Binding of free virions to its surface receptor molecules
Detection of low MHC class I on the target cell surface
Its receptor recognising a viral peptide bound to MHC class I
Presence of interferon alone in the absence of any antigen
Binding of neutralizing antibody to the surface of the target cell

questions.question: Which complication is commonly the first sign of AIDS?
questions.explanation: AIDS is often heralded by thrush, herpes zoster or Pneumocystis pneumonia as CD4 cells fall. Kaposi sarcoma and lymphomas are also seen. In Africa tuberculosis is the leading killer.

options: Complex symmetry lacking a defined capsid arrangement
Helical symmetry built around a single central axis
Spiral symmetry formed by a capped protein tube
Binal symmetry made of a separate head and tail
Icosahedral symmetry built from pentons and hexons
questions.explanation: Protomers that aggregate into five- or six-membered capsomeres and condense into twenty equal triangular faces with twelve apices give cubic or icosahedral morphology. Pentons occupy the twelve vertices while hexons form the faces and edges. Helical forms instead arise when protomers form a capped tube.
questions.question: Protein protomers aggregate into pentameric and hexameric units that assemble into a shell with twenty triangular faces and twelve apices. Which symmetry is described?

options: Positive-sense mRNA made after double-strand conversion
A single capped mRNA transcribed by host polymerase two
Spliced mRNA made from a proviral DNA copy
One polycistronic mRNA cleaved after translation into proteins
Monocistronic mRNA from each genome segment
questions.explanation: Double-stranded RNA viruses such as reoviruses have segmented genomes. Every segment is transcribed individually and gives a monocistronic mRNA. This differs from picornaviruses, which make one polyprotein.
questions.question: A virus has a segmented double-stranded RNA genome, and each segment is transcribed separately. What type of mRNA results?

questions.explanation: Antibody screening by ELISA is followed by confirmatory tests such as Western blot, with PCR for infants. Antigen p24 testing can shorten the window period. Positive results from a screening test must always be confirmed.
options: Gram stain followed by culture on agar
Screening ELISA followed by confirmatory Western blot
questions.question: Which combination is standard for laboratory diagnosis of HIV infection by antibody detection?
Which hepatitis B genotype and phenotype statement is correct?
options: There are four genotypes A to D and eight different phenotypes
There are twelve genotypes and only two phenotypes
There are eight genotypes A to H and four HBsAg phenotypes
There is one genotype and one single phenotype only
There are seven genotypes and six different phenotypes
questions.explanation: HBV is classified into eight genotypes, A to H, and four HBsAg phenotypes: adw, adr, ayw and ayr. HCV has seven genotypes. Knowing the genotype can guide prognosis and choice of therapy.

questions.question: A vinegar solution applied to genital skin turns infected areas white. Which test is described?
questions.explanation: The acetic acid test uses dilute vinegar, which makes HPV-infected tissue turn white. It is a clinical aid since HPV cannot be cultured. Cytology and PCR confirm.

questions.question: An adenovirus virion appears under electron microscopy like a space vehicle. Which structure accounts for this appearance?
questions.explanation: The adenovirus capsid has 240 hexons and 12 pentons. Each penton carries a projecting fibre with a knob, giving a space-vehicle look. The fibre mediates binding to the host cell.
options: A segmented core wrapped by a thick matrix protein layer
A lipid envelope carrying club-shaped glycoprotein spikes over the whole surface
A fibre with a terminal knob projecting from each penton base
A contractile tail sheath attached to a small icosahedral head
A helical nucleocapsid coiled tightly inside a bullet-shaped outer coat

questions.question: Which aerosolized antiviral is used for severely ill hospitalised infants with RSV?
questions.explanation: Aerosolized ribavirin is used in severe RSV disease in infants. It is also used for several haemorrhagic fevers. It is a nucleoside analogue.

If HBsAg is positive, IgM anti-HBc helps separate acute from chronic infection. In limited resource settings clinical symptoms are used when IgM is unavailable. Clinical history therefore helps when the laboratory test is not available.
questions.question: Which test is recommended to differentiate acute from chronic infection when HBsAg is positive?
Type I interferons also activate which cells and induce which cytokine to promote their responses?
questions.explanation: Type I interferons activate NK cells and induce IL-12, which promotes NK responses. NK cells then release proinflammatory cytokines and kill infected cells. They also interact with dendritic cells.
Interferons raise cell resistance to viruses by inducing an antiviral state. They do not directly destroy virions. Other agents target specific viral enzymes.
questions.question: Interferons contribute to antiviral therapy by what general mechanism?
options: Cleaving viral polyproteins into mature structural proteins
Blocking neuraminidase and so preventing release of virions
Terminating viral DNA chains after phosphorylation in cells
Directly destroying virions in the plasma outside cells
Increasing the resistance of cells to viral infection

questions.question: Which hepatitis virus is classified in the family Picornaviridae, genus Hepatovirus?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A virus is a naked icosahedral single-stranded RNA virus of about 27 nm. It is heat and acid stable and spreads by the faecal-oral route. Hepatitis B belongs to Hepadnaviridae and C to Flaviviridae.

The hierarchical system groups viruses by shared virion properties and not by the cells they infect. Four main characteristics are used: nature of the nucleic acid, capsid symmetry, presence of an envelope and size of virion and capsid. Disease features and epidemiology are not core criteria.
options: Nucleic acid type, capsid symmetry, envelope presence and virion dimensions
Disease severity, vaccine availability, incubation period and overall mortality rates
Staining reaction, optimal temperature, growth rate and colony shape in culture
Host cell type, tissue pathology, seasonality and geographic spread of disease
Insect vector, reservoir species, transmission route and clinical stage of illness
questions.question: Which set of properties is used in the hierarchical classification of viruses?

questions.explanation: HDV has a small circular RNA genome of about 1.7 kb and uses HBsAg as its envelope. It therefore needs HBV coinfection or superinfection. It is unclassified or placed in Deltavirus.
questions.question: Which hepatitis virus is a defective virus that needs HBsAg to be infectious?

questions.question: Which organism produces characteristic fried rice or yellow vomit toxin?
questions.explanation: Bacillus cereus produces heat-stable emetic toxin (cereulide) causing the emetic syndrome of food poisoning, classically associated with reheated fried rice. The preformed toxin causes rapid onset (1-6 hours) nausea and vomiting. A separate diarrheal syndrome results from heat-labile enterotoxins with longer incubation (8-16 hours). The organism is a spore-forming, motile, beta-hemolytic Gram-positive rod. Spores survive cooking; subsequent storage allows germination and toxin production.

questions.question: Which test distinguishes pathogenic from non-pathogenic Neisseria?
questions.explanation: Glucose fermentation distinguishes pathogenic Neisseria: N. gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only, N. meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose. Non-pathogenic species show different fermentation patterns.

Molecular methods including PCR and antigen detection tests are required to definitively distinguish E. histolytica from the morphologically identical but non-pathogenic E. dispar. Microscopic examination cannot reliably differentiate these species as they share similar morphological features. Accurate species identification is clinically important because only E. histolytica requires treatment.
questions.question: The most reliable method for differentiating Entamoeba histolytica from Entamoeba dispar is:

questions.explanation: Sheep blood agar demonstrates beta-hemolysis characteristic of S. pyogenes, showing complete clearing around colonies. Throat swabs should be transported in Pike medium (Stuart transport medium) to maintain organism viability. Selective media containing crystal violet or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole suppress normal flora.
questions.question: Which media is used for throat swab culture to detect Streptococcus pyogenes?
Campylobacter jejuni characteristically causes:
questions.explanation: C. jejuni causes inflammatory diarrhea with fever, abdominal pain, and blood in ~10% of cases through mucosal invasion. Infection mimics appendicitis or inflammatory bowel disease. Poultry is the primary source; infection usually self-limited but complications include reactive arthritis and Guillain-Barr� syndrome.

Aedes mosquitoes transmit Rift Valley fever virus, causing large epizootics in livestock. Transovarial transmission (from adult mosquito to offspring) maintains the virus in mosquito populations. Humans acquire infection through mosquito bites or contact with infected animal tissues.
questions.question: What is the primary vector for Rift Valley fever virus transmission?
Which organism demonstrates beta-hemolysis with CAMP test positivity?
questions.explanation: Both Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) and Listeria monocytogenes demonstrate CAMP test positivity - enhanced hemolysis (arrowhead shape) at junction where test organism is streaked perpendicular to Staphylococcus aureus streak. The CAMP factor (protein) produced by GBS and Listeria enhances beta-lysin from S. aureus, creating characteristic arrowhead hemolysis. CAMP test aids GBS identification in neonatal sepsis workup and differentiates Listeria from morphologically similar organisms. Both are important perinatal pathogens requiring rapid identification.

Pathogenicity is defined as the ability of a microorganism to produce disease in a host organism. Virulence represents the degree of pathogenicity, while virulence factors are specific genetic, biochemical, or structural features enabling disease production. The outcome depends on both pathogen characteristics and host defense effectiveness.
questions.question: What defines pathogenicity in microorganisms?

questions.explanation: Transposons are mobile DNA segments capable of moving from one location to another within or between DNA molecules using transposase enzymes, frequently carrying antibiotic resistance genes. Unlike plasmids, transposons cannot replicate independently and must integrate into a replicating DNA molecule such as a chromosome or plasmid to be propagated.
questions.question: A bacterium acquires a segment of DNA that can move between plasmids and chromosomes using its own recombinase, often carrying antibiotic resistance genes, without needing a separate plasmid for replication. What is this element called?
Which bacterial structure mediates specific tissue attachment?
questions.explanation: Adhesive pili (fimbriae) are surface appendages mediating specific attachment to host cell receptors. Different pilus types recognize specific tissue receptors, explaining tissue tropism. Escherichia coli expresses various pilus types for different tissue colonization.

questions.question: A student compares Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial cell wall structures. The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The component of LPS responsible for the endotoxic activity is:
questions.explanation: Lipid A is the conserved hydrophobic anchor of LPS embedded in the outer membrane and is the primary mediator of LPS endotoxic activity. Lipid A is recognized by host TLR4-MD2 complexes, triggering NF-kB activation and massive cytokine release (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-12) causing the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), fever, hypotension, and DIC in Gram-negative sepsis. The O-specific polysaccharide chain (O antigen) is highly variable and determines Gram-negative bacterial serotyping.
options: The lipid A anchor in the outer membrane
The porin proteins spanning the outer membrane
The lipoprotein connecting LPS to peptidoglycan

questions.explanation: Many respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus and influenza, require contact and droplet precautions for most routine patient care encounters, reflecting their primary transmission through respiratory droplets and contaminated surfaces rather than longer-range airborne spread. Airborne precautions, which require a higher level of respiratory protection and negative pressure rooms, are reserved for select pathogens or specific aerosol-generating procedures with higher risk of fine particle transmission. Correctly classifying the appropriate precaution level for each pathogen is essential for both protecting healthcare workers and conserving specialized isolation resources appropriately.
questions.question: A hospital epidemiologist reviews infection control protocols and notes that a particular respiratory virus requires droplet rather than airborne precautions for most patient encounters, except during certain aerosol-generating procedures. Which infection control category applies to most routine encounters with this type of virus?
Janeway lesions in endocarditis represent:
questions.explanation: Janeway lesions are painless hemorrhagic plaques on palms and soles caused by septic microemboli from infected vegetations. These lesions contain microorganisms demonstrable by culture or histology, distinguishing them from immune-mediated Osler's nodes. Janeway lesions are more common in acute endocarditis, particularly with S. aureus.

questions.question: A laboratory scientist identifies tinea versicolor in a young man with hypopigmented patches on the trunk. The causative organism and its relationship to normal skin flora is:
questions.explanation: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is caused by Malassezia species (especially M. globosa, M. restricta, M. furfur) � lipophilic yeasts that are normal skin flora in most adults but cause superficial infection under predisposing conditions (heat, humidity, immunosuppression, oily skin). They convert from yeast to mycelial form (producing the characteristic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH preparation) and produce azelaic acid, which inhibits melanin synthesis causing the characteristic hypopigmentation. Treatment is with topical azole antifungals or selenium sulfide.
options: Microsporum canis � transmitted from cats or dogs
Epidermophyton floccosum � from direct skin contact
Malassezia species � normal skin flora becoming pathogenic

questions.question: Rocky Mountain spotted fever characteristically presents with rash spreading:
questions.explanation: RMSF caused by Rickettsia rickettsii produces a centripetal rash spreading from extremities (including palms and soles) toward the trunk. This centripetal pattern contrasts with typhus fever's centrifugal spread from trunk to extremities. Early recognition and treatment with doxycycline are crucial as untreated RMSF has high mortality.

Hantaan virus and related Old World hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in eastern Europe and Asia. New World hantaviruses like Sin Nombre and Andes viruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas. Geographic distribution follows rodent reservoir ranges.
questions.question: Which Old World hantavirus causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome?
What laboratory finding is characteristic of viral hemorrhagic fevers?
questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) characteristically develops during the hemorrhagic stage of viral hemorrhagic fevers. Leukopenia, bleeding abnormalities, and disseminated intravascular coagulation may also occur. Despite widespread bleeding manifestations, actual blood loss rarely causes death.

options: Calabar swelling, caused by Loa loa
Kala-azar sign, caused by Leishmania donovani
Winterbottom sign, caused by Trypanosoma brucei
Romana sign, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi
Chagoma alone without periorbital involvement, caused by Leishmania
questions.question: A patient from a Chagas disease-endemic region develops cardiomyopathy with conduction abnormalities decades after an initial febrile illness with unilateral periorbital swelling. Which named sign described this acute presentation, and which organism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Romana sign refers to unilateral periorbital and conjunctival swelling occurring at the site of triatomine bug faecal contamination entering through the conjunctiva, a classic acute presentation of Trypanosoma cruzi infection (Chagas disease). Following the acute phase, many patients enter a clinically silent indeterminate phase before potentially developing chronic complications decades later, including cardiomyopathy with characteristic conduction abnormalities and megacolon or megaoesophagus from autonomic nerve destruction. Recognising this biphasic natural history is important for understanding the long delay between exposure and chronic complications.

questions.question: What is the optimal pH indicator concentration in sugar fermentation media?
questions.explanation: Sugar fermentation media typically contain phenol red indicator at 0.01-0.02% concentration, optimal for detecting pH changes from carbohydrate fermentation. At this concentration, the indicator changes from red (neutral/alkaline, pH >6.8) to yellow (acidic, pH <6.8) with sufficient intensity for easy visualization while not inhibiting bacterial growth. Higher concentrations may be toxic; lower concentrations provide insufficient color development. The differential sugar concentration (0.5-1%) combined with appropriate indicator concentration creates reliable fermentation detection system essential for Enterobacteriaceae differentiation in clinical microbiology.

options: Periodic antibiotic resistance development in vivo
Host circadian rhythm affecting immune response
Cyclical reactivation from a dormant tissue reservoir
Seasonal variation in vector tick feeding behavior
Antigenic variation evading host antibody response
questions.question: A patient presents with recurring episodes of high fever separated by afebrile intervals, with a tick exposure history. Blood smear during a febrile episode shows spirochetes. Which mechanism explains the relapsing pattern of fever?
questions.explanation: Borrelia species causing relapsing fever undergo antigenic variation of their surface proteins, allowing the organism to evade the host antibody response generated against the previous antigenic variant. Each relapse corresponds to a new antigenic variant emerging and proliferating until the immune system again responds, in a cycle. This mechanism distinguishes relapsing fever from other febrile tick-borne illnesses with a more continuous clinical course.

questions.question: Ivermectin is used for treating:
questions.explanation: Ivermectin treats onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis (with limited activity against adult worms but suppressing microfilariae), strongyloidiasis, and scabies/lice. The drug enhances GABA neurotransmission, paralyzing parasites. Ivermectin cannot be used in areas co-endemic with loiasis due to encephalopathy risk in high microfilarial density infections.

Botulism is an intoxication from ingesting preformed botulinum neurotoxin in improperly preserved foods, not bacterial infection. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions causing descending flaccid paralysis. Infant botulism results from intestinal colonization and in vivo toxin production after spore ingestion.
questions.question: Botulism results from:

A child presents with fever and neck stiffness. CSF analysis is requested before antibiotics are started, given the urgency of bacterial meningitis diagnosis. Which CSF finding most strongly suggests a bacterial rather than viral cause?
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis classically produces a neutrophilic pleocytosis in the CSF along with elevated protein and depressed glucose, reflecting the intense inflammatory response to bacterial pathogens. This contrasts with the lymphocytic predominance and typically normal glucose seen in viral meningitis, which guides initial empiric management decisions. Gram stain and culture remain essential for definitive organism identification, but the CSF cell count differential provides rapid initial diagnostic guidance.
options: Mildly elevated protein with normal glucose
Clear, colorless appearance with normal cells

questions.explanation: Thayer-Martin agar selectively isolates Neisseria gonorrhoeae and N. meningitidis using antibiotics (vancomycin, colistin, nystatin, trimethoprim) inhibiting normal flora. Chocolate agar base provides required growth factors. Modified Thayer-Martin includes trimethoprim for improved selectivity.
questions.question: Which medium selectively isolates Neisseria gonorrhoeae?

questions.explanation: Source control involves drainage of abscesses, debridement of infected tissue, and removal of infected devices within 12 hours when feasible. Antibiotics alone cannot sterilize undrained abscesses or necrotic tissue. Effective source control dramatically improves sepsis outcomes and reduces mortality.
questions.question: Appropriate source control in sepsis includes:

questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates a G-protein subunit, locking adenylate cyclase in an active state and raising intracellular cyclic AMP. This drives massive chloride and water secretion into the intestinal lumen, producing the characteristic rice-water stool. Unlike Shigella, Vibrio cholerae does not invade the mucosa, explaining the absence of blood or significant inflammation.
options: Direct invasion and destruction of enterocytes
Inhibition of protein synthesis at the ribosome
Activation of adenylate cyclase increasing cyclic AMP
Formation of pores in the cell membrane
questions.question: A returning traveller from a cholera-endemic region develops profuse 'rice-water' stools. Stool culture on TCBS agar shows yellow colonies. Which toxin mechanism explains the massive fluid loss?

questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii crosses the placenta during acute maternal infection, causing congenital toxoplasmosis with varying severity depending on gestational timing. Other parasites with transplacental transmission include Plasmodium (congenital malaria) and rarely Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease). Most intestinal parasites do not cross the placenta.
questions.question: Congenital transmission occurs with:
Swimmer's itch after freshwater exposure suggests:
questions.explanation: Cercarial dermatitis ("swimmer's itch") develops within hours of exposure to schistosome cercariae penetrating skin, causing pruritic papular rash at penetration sites. The reaction results from host immune response to cercariae and their secretions. Symptoms resolve spontaneously within days. Both human and avian schistosomes cause this reaction.

Both Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria gonorrhoeae benefit from IsoVitaleX (or similar) enrichment added to chocolate agar. IsoVitaleX contains vitamins, amino acids, coenzymes, dextrose, and ferric ions providing essential growth factors. For H. influenzae, it supplies X (hemin) and V (NAD) factors. For N. gonorrhoeae, it enhances growth of fastidious strains. While standard chocolate agar (heated blood) provides sufficient factors for most isolates, enrichment improves recovery of nutritionally demanding strains from clinical specimens, particularly after antibiotic exposure or from partially treated patients.
questions.question: Which organism requires chocolate agar with IsoVitaleX enrichment?

questions.explanation: Bacterial chromosomes are typically circular, double-stranded DNA molecules located in the nucleoid region. Unlike eukaryotic linear chromosomes, they lack telomeres and histones. The chromosome is supercoiled and associated with nucleoid-associated proteins.
questions.question: What characterizes bacterial chromosomes structurally?

questions.explanation: Proteus mirabilis, a urease-producing organism, hydrolyzes urea to ammonia, alkalinizing urine and promoting precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) crystals. Struvite stones grow rapidly forming "staghorn calculi" that fill the renal pelvis. Treatment requires antibiotics, stone removal, and urease inhibitors.
questions.question: Which organism is associated with struvite kidney stone formation?
Enterovirus 71 can cause:
questions.explanation: Enterovirus 71 causes hand-foot-mouth disease and can progress to severe neurological complications including brainstem encephalitis, aseptic meningitis, and acute flaccid paralysis. Large outbreaks with neurological involvement occur in Asia-Pacific region. Case fatality reaches 10-25% with CNS involvement.

questions.question: How many blood culture sets are recommended?
questions.explanation: Three blood culture sets (each with aerobic and anaerobic bottles) collected from different sites within 24 hours detect >95% of bacteremias. Single cultures have low sensitivity. More cultures increase detection.
Legionella colonizes artificial water systems including cooling towers, hot water systems, fountains, and humidifiers. It survives within amoebae. Temperature range of 25-42�C supports growth.
questions.question: What environmental source harbors Legionella?
What enzyme synthesizes mRNA using DNA as template?
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase synthesizes mRNA using DNA as template during transcription. The enzyme reads DNA in 3' to 5' direction and synthesizes complementary RNA in 5' to 3' direction. Prokaryotes use single RNA polymerase while eukaryotes employ three types.

questions.question: Which medium grows Francisella tularensis?
questions.explanation: Francisella requires cysteine-supplemented media (cysteine-glucose-blood agar or Thayer-Martin agar). Growth is slow (2-4 days). Laboratory handling requires biosafety level 2/3 precautions.

The Filoviridae family includes three genera: Cuevavirus, Marburgvirus, and Ebolavirus. Six Ebolavirus species are recognized: Zaire, Bundibugyo, Sudan, Ta� Forest, Reston, and Bombali. These viruses cause severe hemorrhagic fever with high mortality rates.
questions.question: Which virus family includes the Ebola and Marburg viruses?

questions.explanation: TasP demonstrates that sustained viral suppression (<200 copies/mL) with ART prevents sexual HIV transmission (U=U: undetectable=untransmittable). HPTN 052, PARTNER, and Opposites Attract studies showed zero transmissions from virologically suppressed partners. Adherence maintaining suppression is critical.
questions.question: HIV treatment-as-prevention (TasP) relies on:

questions.explanation: Commercial multiplex PCR panels (e.g., FilmArray, BioFire) simultaneously detect 20+ enteric pathogens including bacteria, viruses, and parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba) in one test. These syndromic panels identify co-infections and reduce time to diagnosis compared to conventional methods but cannot assess clinical significance.
questions.question: Multiplex PCR panels for diarrheal diseases can detect:

questions.explanation: Pertussis toxin causes a characteristic absolute lymphocytosis by interfering with lymphocyte recirculation and promoting their release into peripheral blood rather than through direct bacterial proliferation effects on lymphocytes. This distinctive hematological pattern can support a clinical diagnosis of pertussis alongside the characteristic cough illness. Other Bordetella toxins primarily damage respiratory epithelium and contribute to the cough and tissue injury rather than systemic blood count changes.
questions.question: A pertussis patient's blood count shows a striking absolute lymphocytosis rather than the neutrophilia typical of most bacterial infections. Which bacterial toxin most directly explains this hematological finding?

questions.explanation: Inactivated hepatitis A vaccine provides long-lasting immunity (>20 years) and is recommended for children and high-risk adults. Two doses 6-12 months apart achieve >95% seroconversion. Post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks includes vaccine and/or immunoglobulin.
questions.question: Hepatitis A virus prevention is best achieved through:
Which antibiotic combination treats actinomycetoma effectively?
questions.explanation:
Streptomycin-TMP-SMX
Actinomycetoma responds to combinations of streptomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and dapsone if started early. Treatment duration is months to years. Surgery may be needed for advanced disease.

questions.question: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for Chlamydia trachomatis can use which specimen?
questions.explanation: NAATs detect C. trachomatis DNA/RNA from various specimens including first-void urine, endocervical/urethral swabs, and self-collected vaginal swabs. First-void urine is non-invasive and highly sensitive (95-98%) for genital infections. NAATs are the gold standard, replacing culture for chlamydial diagnosis.

questions.question: What is the characteristic colony color of Pseudomonas aeruginosa on agar?
questions.explanation: P. aeruginosa produces yellow-green pyocyanin pigment that fluoresces under UV light. This blue-green pigmentation is characteristic and aids identification. The pigment is more intense at room temperature.

questions.question: Which condition is NOT a non-suppurative sequela of Streptococcus pyogenes infection?
questions.explanation: Scarlet fever is a suppurative manifestation caused by erythrogenic toxin during active S. pyogenes infection, not a non-suppurative sequela. Non-suppurative sequelae like rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis occur weeks after infection due to immune-mediated mechanisms involving molecular mimicry. These complications are not related to direct bacterial invasion.

Nitazoxanide is the only FDA-approved drug for cryptosporidiosis, though efficacy is limited in immunocompromised patients where immune restoration is critical. The drug also has activity against Giardia and some helminths. Nitazoxanide interferes with pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase enzyme essential for anaerobic metabolism.
questions.question: Nitazoxanide is used for treating:

questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of prostatitis in sexually active men under 35 years, often presenting as chronic pelvic pain syndrome. Older men typically have bacterial prostatitis caused by E. coli and other uropathogens. Urethral swab or urine NAAT detects chlamydial infection.
questions.question: Prostatitis in young men is most commonly caused by:
A diagnostic laboratory uses a serological test that detects antigen-antibody complexes through a colour change reaction linked to an enzyme. What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) detects antigen-antibody binding using an enzyme-linked secondary antibody that produces a measurable colour change upon substrate addition, allowing both qualitative and quantitative assessment of antigen or antibody presence in a sample. It is widely used as an initial screening test for infections such as HIV, due to its high sensitivity.

Ledipasvir inhibits HCV NS5A protein essential for viral replication and assembly. Combined with sofosbuvir as single tablet regimen (Harvoni), it treats genotypes 1, 4, 5, and 6. Treatment duration is typically 12 weeks.
questions.question: Ledipasvir inhibits which HCV protein?

questions.explanation: Plasmid-mediated dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) genes confer trimethoprim resistance, often linked with sulfonamide resistance genes (sul1, sul2). Resistance has increased significantly, limiting trimethoprim use for empirical UTI therapy. Alternative mechanisms include chromosomal DHFR mutations and decreased drug permeability.
questions.question: Trimethoprim resistance in uropathogens most commonly results from:
Which genetic transfer mechanism requires cell-to-cell contact?
questions.explanation: Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact through sex pili for DNA transfer from donor to recipient bacteria. The process is unidirectional with genetic material flowing from F+ or Hfr donors to F- recipients. Plasmids and chromosomal DNA can transfer via conjugation.

Pneumococcal meningitis often complicates skull base fractures with CSF leak, allowing direct bacterial access to subarachnoid space. Other predisposing factors include cochlear implants, splenectomy, and immunodeficiency. Recurrent pneumococcal meningitis warrants investigation for anatomical defects or immune defects.
questions.question: Pneumococcal meningitis commonly complicates which condition?

questions.explanation: C-reactive protein is an acute-phase reactant synthesised by hepatocytes in response to circulating interleukin-6, released during inflammation or infection, and rises rapidly within hours of an inflammatory stimulus, making it a useful, though non-specific, marker for monitoring infection severity and response to treatment, alongside clinical assessment and other laboratory parameters.
questions.question: A laboratory measures the inflammatory marker C-reactive protein to monitor a patient's response to antibiotic therapy for a bacterial infection. What is the biological source of this acute-phase protein?
What is the primary advantage of membrane filtration in sterilization?
options: Separation of microbes without heat damage
questions.explanation: Membrane filtration physically separates microorganisms from solutions without using heat, making it ideal for heat-labile substances like serum and antibiotic solutions. Filters with pore sizes of 0.2-0.45 �m effectively remove bacteria while preserving the chemical integrity of thermolabile compounds. This method does not kill microbes but removes them from the solution.

questions.question: A patient with a penicillin allergy requires treatment for a streptococcal infection. What alternative antibiotic class is commonly used, given its similar spectrum but different mechanism of cross-reactivity risk?
questions.explanation: Macrolides such as erythromycin or azithromycin provide an effective alternative for treating streptococcal infections in patients with true penicillin allergy, as they act via a distinct mechanism (inhibiting the 50S ribosomal subunit) without the beta-lactam ring structure responsible for penicillin hypersensitivity. Cephalosporins carry a variable degree of cross-reactivity risk depending on the specific generation and side chain similarity.

Modified acid-fast staining (using cold Kinyoun or hot Ziehl-Neelsen methods) demonstrates Cryptosporidium oocysts as bright red spheres (4-6 �m) against a blue-green background. The acid-fast property distinguishes Cryptosporidium from other organisms in stool. Immunofluorescence and antigen detection methods are more sensitive alternatives.
questions.question: Cryptosporidium oocysts in stool are best demonstrated using:

questions.explanation: Respiratory multiplex PCR panels simultaneously detect 15-25 pathogens including influenza A/B, RSV, rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, pertussis, mycoplasma, and chlamydia. Rapid (1-2 hours) results guide isolation precautions and therapy. High sensitivity but clinical correlation necessary to distinguish colonization from disease.
questions.question: Respiratory multiplex PCR panels typically detect:

questions.explanation: Severe malaria is defined by the presence of one or more markers of organ dysfunction, such as jaundice, acute kidney injury, or impaired consciousness, often in combination with high parasitaemia, and requires urgent parenteral antimalarial treatment along with intensive supportive care to manage the associated complications. This contrasts with uncomplicated malaria, which lacks these severity markers and can typically be managed with oral antimalarial therapy on an outpatient or short inpatient basis. Recognising these severity criteria promptly is essential for appropriate triage and management to reduce the high mortality risk associated with untreated severe disease.
questions.question: A patient develops fever and is found to have a malaria parasite density of 12% on blood film, along with jaundice and acute kidney injury. Which feature of this presentation classifies it as severe malaria requiring intensive parenteral treatment and monitoring?
options: Asymptomatic parasitaemia detected on routine screening
Presence of multiple organ dysfunction with high parasitaemia
Fever alone without any other associated findings
Isolated headache without any other systemic findings
Mild parasitaemia below 1% with no organ involvement

questions.question: Which antibiotic should be added to cover Listeria monocytogenes in children under 3 months?
questions.explanation: Ampicillin is added to third-generation cephalosporins for neonatal meningitis coverage of Listeria monocytogenes. Cephalosporins alone do not adequately cover Listeria. This combination provides comprehensive empirical coverage.

questions.question: What process describes bacteria taking up environmental DNA?
questions.explanation: Transformation involves uptake and incorporation of naked DNA fragments from the environment by naturally competent bacteria. Griffith discovered this in pneumococci in 1928. Artificial competence can be induced in laboratory for genetic manipulation.

questions.question: What is the optimal pH for growth of most fungi?
questions.explanation: Most pathogenic fungi grow optimally at pH 5.0-6.0, which is more acidic than optimal bacterial pH (7.2-7.4). Sabouraud dextrose agar is adjusted to pH 5.6 to favor fungal growth while inhibiting many bacteria. This acidic pH combined with high glucose concentration creates selective conditions. Some bacteria-inhibiting media are adjusted even lower (pH 5.0) for maximum selectivity.

questions.question: Osler's nodes in infective endocarditis are characterized as:
questions.explanation: Osler's nodes are small, tender subcutaneous nodules on fingers or toes representing immune complex deposition or septic microemboli. These painful lesions are found in approximately 10-25% of endocarditis cases and represent a classic but uncommon sign. Janeway lesions, in contrast, are painless hemorrhagic plaques on palms or soles.

questions.question: Giardia lamblia characteristically causes:
questions.explanation: Giardiasis causes malabsorptive diarrhea with greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea), bloating, flatulence, and weight loss. Trophozoites attach to small intestinal villi causing villous atrophy and malabsorption. Diagnosis requires identifying cysts/trophozoites in stool or duodenal fluid; antigen detection tests are available.

Conjugation involves direct transfer of plasmid DNA between bacteria through pili, enabling horizontal gene transfer between unrelated species. F (fertility) plasmids carry genes encoding pilus formation and DNA transfer machinery. This mechanism is the major route for spreading antibiotic resistance genes among diverse bacterial populations.
questions.question: Which mechanism allows horizontal gene transfer between unrelated bacterial species?
A child is prescribed an antibiotic for a severe infection, but the prescriber avoids chloramphenicol due to a rare but serious dose-independent adverse effect. What is this effect?
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol carries a rare but serious risk of idiosyncratic, dose-independent aplastic anaemia, a potentially fatal bone marrow failure that can occur even after a single dose in susceptible individuals, distinguishing it from the more common dose-dependent reversible bone marrow suppression also associated with this drug. This rare risk significantly limits its modern clinical use despite broad-spectrum activity.

questions.question: Entamoeba histolytica causes tissue invasion primarily through:
questions.explanation: E. histolytica produces powerful histolytic enzymes including cysteine proteases that destroy host tissue, enabling invasion of the colonic mucosa. These enzymes break down the extracellular matrix and kill epithelial cells, facilitating parasite penetration and spread. The enzymatic activity is responsible for the characteristic flask-shaped ulcers observed in invasive amoebiasis.

Ebola virus transmission requires direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected, symptomatic individual, distinguishing it from airborne respiratory viruses and explaining why strict contact and droplet precautions, rather than airborne isolation, are central to outbreak control. This transmission pattern also explains why funeral practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals have historically contributed significantly to outbreak propagation in affected communities. Personal protective equipment and safe burial practices are key public health interventions for interrupting this transmission route during outbreaks.
options: Contaminated food or drinking water sources
Insect bites from local mosquito vectors
Casual social contact without fluid exposure
Airborne respiratory droplets while coughing nearby
questions.question: A patient returning from West Africa develops fever, severe myalgia, and bleeding from multiple sites. The patient reports contact with a sick family member who recently died of a similar illness. Direct contact with which body substance poses the highest transmission risk for this hemorrhagic fever?

questions.explanation: Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test is a non-treponemal test detecting antibodies to cardiolipin. It is sensitive but non-specific with false positives. It monitors treatment response.
questions.question: Which test is non-specific for syphilis?
What is the recommended incubation temperature for dermatophyte cultures?
questions.explanation: Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) grow optimally at 25-30�C on Sabouraud dextrose agar or dermatophyte test medium. Room temperature incubation enhances sporulation essential for identification. Higher temperatures (35-37�C) may inhibit sporulation or growth. Cultures require 1-4 weeks; examination every 3-5 days detects growth. Lactophenol cotton blue staining of microscopic mounts reveals characteristic macroconidia and microconidia morphology for species identification. Some laboratories incubate duplicate cultures at both 25-30�C and 35-37�C.

Screening immigrants from endemic areas and individuals with eosinophilia before chemotherapy, organ transplantation, or corticosteroid therapy prevents potentially fatal hyperinfection syndrome. Presumptive ivermectin treatment is often given if screening is unavailable or insensitive, given the consequences of missing occult infection.
questions.question: Screening for strongyloidiasis before immunosuppressive therapy is important because:

options: Fungal pathogens such as Aspergillus species
Encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae
Intracellular organisms such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Protozoal pathogens such as Toxoplasma gondii
questions.question: A patient with recurrent pneumonia is found to have markedly reduced serum immunoglobulin levels. Which group of organisms would this patient be most susceptible to?
questions.explanation: Humoral immunodeficiency, reflected by low immunoglobulin levels, predominantly impairs opsonisation and clearance of encapsulated extracellular bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis.
