A(i) Describe the parenteral routes of hepatitis B transmission.
A(ii) Describe the vertical (mother-to-child) routes of transmission.
A(iii) State the distribution/scale of hepatitis B infection as an occupational and global problem.
B. State the safe practice regarding timing of hepatitis B vaccination.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the chronic hepatic deformity that may follow infection.
questions.answerText:
A. Transmission routes and distribution:
(i) Parenteral: blood transfusions, serum products, sharing of needles and razors, tattooing, acupuncture, renal dialysis, organ donation.
(ii) Vertical transmission: perinatal transmission from a carrier mother to her baby, transplacental (rare), during delivery, and postnatal;
Sexual transmission and close (horizontal) contact are also routes.
(iii) Distribution: an estimated 240 million people are chronically infected with HBV,
More than 780,000 people die every year from complications of hepatitis B, including cirrhosis and liver cancer;
Hepatitis B is an important occupational hazard for health workers.
B. Safe practice: the first dose of vaccine should be given within 24 hours after birth, followed by 2 or 3 doses to complete the primary series;
Protection lasts at least 20 years and is probably lifelong.
C. Anatomical basis of the chronic hepatic deformity:
- Hepatocellular damage in HBV has an autoimmune basis.
- Persistent infection may progress through chronic persistent hepatitis or chronic active hepatitis to hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis and liver failure, with extrahepatic manifestations such as glomerulonephritis also occurring.

(i) Bacteraemia: the presence of viable bacteria in the circulating blood. Three types:
- Transient bacteraemia: transient presence of bacteria or fungi in the bloodstream for periods of several minutes; may follow manipulation of, or surgical procedures involving, infected tissue or instrumentation of colonised mucosal surfaces.
- Intermittent bacteraemia: recurrent transient infection; characteristically associated with undrained intra-abdominal abscesses.
- Continuous bacteraemia: suggests a severe infection that has overwhelmed the host defence.
(ii) The most frequent reason for negative blood cultures is previous antibiotic therapy. Culture-negative endocarditis is reported in 5–10% of cases of infective endocarditis. The HACEK group is the most common cause of Gram-negative endocarditis among people who do not abuse intravenous drugs; HACEK organisms: Haemophilus spp. (H. parainfluenzae, H. aphrophilus, H. paraphrophilus), Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella spp.
(iii) Manual blood culture preparation:
- Patient is advised to stop medication (especially antibiotics) about one week prior to sample collection if possible; take blood sample at the peak of fever if any.
- Use sterilised equipment including needle and syringe and special blood culture specimen bottles.
- Collect blood from two different sites, 15–30 minutes apart; aerobic bottle should be filled first.
- For the manual method: blood is subcultured (transferred from sample bottle to culture media in a Petri dish); most commonly used media are blood agar and MacConkey's agar.
- Incubate in the Petri dish for about 7 days, checked daily for growth; Gram stain can then be conducted.
(iv) Specific blood culture media:
- Glucose broth: useful in the diagnosis of endocarditis.
- Bile broth: useful in the diagnosis of enteric fever.
(v) Common blood culture contaminants: Staphylococcus epidermidis, Micrococcus, Diphtheroides (Corynebacterium), Propionibacterium acnes, Pseudomonas and Enterobacter. These organisms can be pathogenic under certain conditions and hence must not be overlooked — for example, enterococci were pathogens 70% of the time and Clostridium perfringens was a contaminant 77% of the time; it is sometimes difficult to differentiate pathogens from contaminants.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Sunlight: microbicidal activity is mainly due to the presence of ultraviolet rays; it is responsible for spontaneous sterilization in natural conditions. In tropical countries, sunlight is more effective in killing germs due to the combination of ultraviolet rays and heat; it provides a natural method of disinfection of water bodies such as tanks and lakes. Key limitation: sunlight is not sporicidal, hence it does not sterilize.
A(ii) Dry heat — hot air oven: introduced by Louis Pasteur; articles are exposed to high temperature (160°C) for a duration of one hour in an electrically heated oven. The oven must be fitted with a thermostat control, temperature indicator, meshed shelves, and must have adequate insulation. Mechanism: heat acts by oxidative effects as well as denaturation and coagulation of proteins.
A(iii) Moist heat — autoclave: moist heat acts by coagulation and denaturation of proteins. In an autoclave, water is boiled in a closed chamber; as pressure rises, the boiling point of water also rises. Sterilization is effectively achieved at temperature above 100°C; exposure at this temperature for 15 minutes sterilizes articles. Advantages of steam over dry air: more penetrative power than dry air; it moistens spores (moisture is essential for coagulation of proteins); condensation of steam on cooler surfaces releases latent heat; condensation of steam draws in fresh steam.
B) Filtration: membrane filters with pore sizes between 0.2–0.45 µm are used; applied to heat-labile liquids such as serum, antibiotic solutions, sugar solutions, and urea solution. Different types: earthenware filters, asbestos filters, sintered glass filters, membrane filters, and air filters. Filtration does NOT kill microbes — it separates them out; therefore it is NOT sterilization in the strict sense.
C) Medical asepsis: the state of being free from disease-causing microorganisms; concerned with eliminating the spread of microorganisms through facility practices. Three essential components: handwashing; utilizing gloves, gown and mask as indicated; cleaning equipment (also: handling linens to prevent spread). Surgical asepsis: also called "aseptic/sterile technique"; eliminates microorganisms before they enter an open surgical wound or contaminate a sterile field; all instruments, drapes, and objects that could contact the surgical wound are sterilized; all healthcare providers perform a surgical hand scrub with antimicrobial agent before donning surgical gown and gloves. Surgical asepsis is always practised in: operating rooms, special procedure or diagnostic areas, burn units, labour and delivery areas, and during invasive bedside procedures (chest tubes, central lines, catheters).
questions.question:
A) Describe the sterilization methods classified as physical methods under the following headings:
A(i) Sunlight: state the mechanism of its microbicidal activity, why it is more effective in tropical countries, and its key limitation.
A(ii) Dry heat: describe the hot air oven method — temperature, duration, and requirements of the oven — and the mechanism of action of dry heat.
A(iii) Moist heat: describe the autoclave — the principle of pressurised steam, the temperature required and the duration of exposure. State the advantages of steam over dry air.

C) Distinguish between medical asepsis and surgical asepsis, stating where surgical asepsis is always practised and giving three essential components of medical asepsis.

questions.answerText:
1. In any infection of bone, there is an attempt at repair that, if incomplete, results in chronic persistence of infection.
2. This repair is accomplished by hyperaemia of the surrounding tissue, which effects decalcification of the bone; granulation tissue forms and carries in osteoclasts and osteoblasts.
3. Necrotic cancellous bone is readily absorbed and replaced by new bone, while dead cortex is gradually absorbed about its surface and detached from living bone to form a sequestrum, a process that requires several months.
4. The sequestrum is a piece of dead bone, surrounded by infected granulation tissue trying to "eat" the sequestrum away; it appears pale, with a smooth inner surface and a rough outer surface.
5. When the sequestrum is complete, it lies in a free cavity and is less attacked by granulation tissue, so it is absorbed more slowly.
6. Meanwhile, the surrounding living bone attempts to wall off the infection by forming a thick, dense wall, the involucrum, which is dense sclerotic bone overlying the sequestrum.
7. An involucrum usually has multiple openings, the cloacae, through which exudate, bone debris, and sequestra find exit and pass through sinus tracts to the surface.
8. Constant destruction of neighbouring soft tissue leads to thin skin, which is easily traumatised, and skin epithelium grows inwards to line the sinus tract.
9. In chronic osteomyelitis of long standing, multiple cavities and sequestra exist throughout the bone.
10. The shaft becomes thickened, irregular and deformed as a functional deficit resulting from this chronic process.
11. Acute osteomyelitis left untreated or unresolved after 10 days is considered chronic, with necrotic bone as the distinguishing feature of the chronic form.
12. Complications of this spread include bone abscess, paravertebral/epidural abscess, bacteraemia, fracture, overlying soft-tissue cellulitis, and draining soft-tissue sinus tracts, with reduced limb or joint function possible, and amputation sometimes needed, especially in those with diabetes or poor blood circulation.

questions.answerText:
A(i) EPI launched: 1974 by WHO. At the start of the programme, fewer than 5% of the world's infants were immunized against the six target diseases. Six original target diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, measles, and tuberculosis.
A(ii) Diseases added to EPI during the 1990s: yellow fever and hepatitis B.
A(iii) Two types of vaccines:
- Preventive vaccine: provides protection from primary infection or disease; example — BCG.
- Therapeutic vaccine: given to infected people to prevent disease; example — tetanus serum.
B) DNA vaccines: developments in molecular biology have revolutionised vaccine science; recent developments focus on the use of DNA as a vaccine antigen. The potential of naked DNA as a vaccine antigen was discovered by chance in 1989 during a gene therapy experiment — it was shown that a gene inserted directly into a mammalian cell could induce the cell to manufacture the protein encoded by that gene. Edible vaccines: attracting increasing attention as they provide both a means of antigen production and delivery; studies in animals and phase I studies in humans have demonstrated their potential. Experimental evidence: mice fed with potatoes expressing a nontoxic fragment of the cholera toxin developed mucosal antibodies to the toxin, which reduced diarrhoea on challenge with whole cholera toxin.
C) Local antifungal agent: nystatin; poorly absorbed in the GIT; used mainly for local or superficial infections — e.g., oral or vaginal candidiasis. Systemic antifungal agent: Amphotericin B; used to treat systemic mycosis; administered parenterally; long-term therapy usually 6–10 weeks. Complications of long-term use: nephrotoxicity; electrolyte abnormalities (low K+, Mg++, Ca++); anaemia; gingival bleeding; febrile reactions; fever and chills. Because of these complications, patients must be well-hydrated.

questions.answerText:
(i) Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) with Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: a Gram-negative bean-shaped diplococcus, oxidase and catalase positive, growing on chocolate agar in 3-10% CO2.
(ii) Meninges, blood vessels and adrenal glands: the endotoxin causes blood vessel destruction, haemorrhage and sepsis; the polysaccharide capsule (serogroups A, B, C, W135) is antiphagocytic; IgA1 protease cleaves IgA.
(ii) Spread by respiratory secretions from the nasopharynx; bacteria rarely invade the bloodstream and meninges; epidemics are due to serogroups A (Africa), B (Europe), C (America); incubation 3-4 days.
(iii) N. gonorrhoeae (anogenital tract, gonorrhoea, one serotype, some penicillin-resistant, ferments glucose only) versus N. meningitidis (nasopharynx, several serotypes, all penicillin-sensitive, ferments glucose and maltose).
(iv) Treatment: cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, macrolides, penicillin (third-generation cephalosporin in children); close contacts receive oral chemoprophylaxis to eliminate carriage; polysaccharide vaccines (A and C; A, C, Y; A, C, W135, Y) are available; mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended.

A(i) Describe the general features and habitat of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
A(ii) Describe its epidemiology.
A(iii) Describe its virulence factors in acute and chronic infection.
B(i) Relate the forms of infection and other Pseudomonas species to the common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how infection may become systemic and the laboratory and treatment principles.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Gram-negative, non-fermentative, non-sporing, non-capsulated bacillus (0.5-0.8 by 1.5-3.0 um) motile by a single polar flagellum, strictly aerobic (grows 4-43 C, optimum 37 C); four pigments: pyocyanin, fluorescin, pyorubrin, pyomelanin; intrinsic resistance to antibiotics and disinfectants.
A(i) A saprophyte of warm moist environments (water, soil, sewage, gut) and hospital reservoirs (disinfectants, respiratory equipment, sinks, taps, mops); isolated from skin, throat, stool, urine, wounds and sputum of healthy people.
A(ii) One of the top three causes of opportunistic infection; about 90,000 deaths a year in about two million hospital-acquired infections; overall mortality about 50%; second commonest cause of nosocomial pneumonia (17%), sixth of bloodstream infections (8%), third of UTI (7%), fourth of surgical-site infection (8%); spread by fomites, contaminated reservoirs, food and water.
A(iii) Acute: pili and exoenzyme S for adherence (disrupts cytoskeleton, destroys IgG and IgA); exotoxin A (like diphtheria toxin, inflammation and necrosis); phospholipase C; at least four proteases (haemorrhage, necrosis); endotoxin (bacteraemia, septic shock).
A(iii) Chronic: siderophores (pyoverdin, pyochelin); alginate pseudocapsule in cystic fibrosis protects from phagocytosis and antibiotics; biofilm matrix; regulated by two-component and quorum-sensing systems.
B(i) Diseases: invasive external otitis, osteomyelitis, green nail syndrome, folliculitis, dialysis peritonitis, some diarrhoea; eye and ear infections often remain localised; wound and burn infection; pneumonia and UTI in hospital.
B(i) Other species: P. maltophilia (pneumonia, endocarditis, UTI, wound, septicaemia, meningitis); P. cepacia (nosocomial infection, chronic lung infection in cystic fibrosis, highly resistant); P. mallei (glanders); P. pseudomallei (melioidosis).
C(i) In leukaemia and lymphoma altered host defences result in sepsis; P. cepacia becomes systemic in some cystic fibrosis patients whereas P. aeruginosa remains confined to the lungs.
C(i) Melioidosis: acute septicaemia with respiratory involvement and multiple abscesses (high fatality); chronic form with caseous or suppurative foci in tissues; glanders: nasal abscesses and nodules, occupational hazard.
C(i) Diagnosis: pus, urine, blood, sputum, exudates (and environmental swabs); grows on MacConkey, nutrient, blood and EMB agar, cetrimide selective; large flat opaque colonies with grape-like smell, pyocyanin fluorescing green under UV.
C(i) Sensitivity testing: dilution (MIC, MBC) and disc diffusion (zone of inhibition).
C(i) Treatment: frequently resistant; many strains susceptible to gentamicin, tobramycin, colistin, amikacin; severe infections tigecycline, polymyxins and carbapenems; no vaccine for general use.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the upper respiratory tract.
A(ii) Describe the gross anatomy of the lower respiratory tract.
B. State how these zones of the respiratory tract relate to specific viral pathologies.
C. Explain how infection may spread from the upper to the lower respiratory tract, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A. Gross anatomy:
(i) The upper respiratory tract (URT) is the airway above the glottis or vocal cords; it includes the nose, sinuses, pharynx and larynx.
(ii) The lower respiratory tract (LRT) consists of the trachea, bronchial tubes, bronchioles and the lungs.
B. Relation of zones to pathologies:
- URT infections (URTIs) include tonsillitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis, sinusitis, otitis media, certain influenza and the common cold, and are generally of low severity.
- LRT infections (LRTIs) include tracheitis, acute bronchitis, laryngotracheobronchitis (croup), acute bronchiolitis, pneumonia and bronchopneumonia,
Are generally more serious, with the two most common being bronchitis and pneumonia.
C. Spread and functional deficit:
- RSV infects ciliated columnar epithelial cells of the upper and lower airway;
After several days, infected cells become rounded and slough into the smaller bronchioles of the lower airway.
- This sloughing mechanism is thought to be responsible for the spread of virus from the upper to the lower respiratory tract.
- Sloughed epithelial cells, mucous plugs and accumulated immune cells cause obstruction of the lower airway, producing bronchiolitis with wheezing and respiratory distress as the functional deficit.

A(i) An acute febrile systemic illness caused by Salmonella enterica serotype typhi, a Gram-negative bacillus of the Enterobacteriaceae; unlike Shigella it is motile and produces hydrogen sulphide (black colonies).
A(i) Transmission is faeco-oral: food or drink handled by an often asymptomatic carrier who sheds bacteria in stool (less commonly urine), hand-to-mouth after contaminated toilets, and sewage-contaminated water or shellfish.
A(ii) Most organisms are destroyed by gastric acid; survivors reach the terminal (distal) ileum and adhere by fimbriae to the epithelium over Peyer's patches, where macrophages are induced to attract more macrophages.
A(ii) Inside macrophages they pass through the mesenteric lymph nodes and thoracic duct to the reticuloendothelial tissues of liver, spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes, multiply to a critical density, then cause macrophage apoptosis and break into the bloodstream.
A(ii) They infect the gallbladder (bacteraemia or infected bile) and re-enter the gut in bile to re-infect Peyer's patches; bacteria not re-infecting are shed in stool.
A(iii) Incubation 3-30 days; daily remittent fever of 40-41 C with chills, headache and malaise; constipation or diarrhoea (diarrhoea commoner in children) with abdominal tenderness; fever is prolonged if untreated; also nausea, vomiting, cramps, cough.
A(iii) A disease of the poor, linked to poor sanitation, water supply, hygiene and waste disposal; commoner in rural areas and urban slums, in Africa and Asia, and in children and young adults.
B(i) Blood culture (gold standard, positive in the first week; automated systems), stool culture (second week), urine culture (third week), bone marrow aspirate culture; Widal test (patient serum with flagellar H and somatic O antigens); white cells usually reduced (leukocytosis in children or perforation), PCV and platelets reduced.
C(i) Chronic carriers shed bacteria in stool for decades, sequestered as a biofilm on gallstones or gallbladder epithelium, or intracellularly within the epithelium; a carrier's bacteria may have multiple genotypes, making outbreaks hard to trace.
C(i) Treatment: rehydration and correction of electrolytes (hypokalaemia); definitive antimicrobials - third or fourth generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone) or fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin).
C(i) Prevention: WASH (water, sanitation, hygiene), treatment of all cases, screening and treatment of carriers among food handlers.

Describe the eggs of Schistosoma haematobium, S. mansoni and S. japonicum under the following headings:
A(i) S. haematobium egg
A(ii) S. mansoni and S. japonicum eggs
B) Explain the clinical basis for why the eggs, rather than the adult worms, are responsible for the pathology of schistosomiasis.
C) Distinguish S. haematobium eggs and site of deposition from those of S. mansoni.
questions.answerText:
A(i) S. haematobium eggs possess a terminal spine and are deposited in the urinary bladder.
A(ii) S. mansoni eggs have a sharp lateral spine and are deposited around the bowel and can reach the portal veins; S. japonicum eggs are spherical with an inconspicuous spine and are deposited around the small intestine, involving the gastrointestinal tract, liver and brain.
B) The most significant pathology is associated with the schistosome eggs, not the adult worms; female schistosomes can lay hundreds or thousands of eggs per day within the venous system.
B) Production of large numbers of eggs results in chronic granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis of the urinary tract or portal venous system, whereas cercarial skin penetration and acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) are the other, earlier stages of pathology described.
C) S. haematobium eggs, with a terminal spine, are deposited in the urinary bladder, causing urethral pain, increased urinary frequency, dysuria, haematuria and bladder obstruction, and are associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
C) S. mansoni eggs, with a sharp lateral spine, are deposited around the bowel, giving rise to gastrointestinal symptoms, and can also reach the portal veins, giving rise to liver symptoms.
C) S. haematobium adult worms reside in the veins of the urinary bladder, while S. mansoni resides in the inferior mesenteric veins of the large intestine.
C) S. haematobium is most prevalent in Africa and the Middle East, whereas S. mansoni is found in Africa and Latin America, with reservoir hosts including primates, marsupials and rodents.
C) The adult worms of both species can live in copula for 10-20 years within the venous system, so the differing sites of egg deposition described (bladder versus bowel/portal veins) reflect a sustained, long-term difference in the vascular residence of each species.
C) Both species are obligate intravascular organisms, transmitted through a snail intermediate host, with the adult female beginning to release eggs approximately 5-8 weeks after infection in each case.

questions.question:
A(i) Define the parvobacteria and describe the features and habitat of Haemophilus influenzae.
A(ii) Describe its culture and identification.
A(iii) Describe its virulence factors and the diseases it causes.
A(iv) Describe the laboratory diagnosis and epidemiology.
B(i) Explain why capsulated type b strains are the more invasive and how prevention and treatment are based on this.
C(i) Distinguish between capsulated and non-capsulated H. influenzae and between H. influenzae and H. ducreyi.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Parvobacteria are small Gram-negative coccoid bacilli needing blood or blood products (Haemophilus, Bordetella, Brucella, Pasteurella, Francisella, Actinobacillus, Gardnerella); H. influenzae is pleomorphic, catalase and oxidase positive, an obligate human parasite normally in the upper respiratory tract (may colonise conjunctiva and genital tract).
A(ii) Grows on chocolate agar (blood agar only with haemolytic bacteria such as S. aureus); needs X factor (from blood) and V factor (from S. aureus colonies), giving the satellite phenomenon (large colonies near S. aureus).
A(iii) Capsule of polyribitol ribose phosphate (types a-f; type b commonest in invasive disease); IgA protease degrades secretory IgA aiding colonisation; pili for attachment.
A(iii) Encapsulated: meningitis, arthritis, osteomyelitis, cellulitis, epiglottitis, bacteraemia; transmission by respiratory droplets, incubation 2-4 days.
A(iv) Specimens: CSF, blood, sputum, synovial fluid; direct smear shows pus cells and pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli; CSF culture on chocolate agar, CSF antigen detection by agglutination.
A(iv) Invasive disease is commoner in winter after viral infections, in crowded poor families, spreading between family members; mortality in meningitis about 5% and neurological lesions in 10-15%.
B(i) From the upper respiratory tract the organism enters the bloodstream and disseminates; the type b capsule is the type mainly associated with invasive disease.
B(i) Prevention: Hib conjugate vaccine reduces morbidity and mortality; contacts of type b cases receive rifampicin for 4 days.
B(i) Treatment: ampicillin (amoxicillin) if not a beta-lactamase producer, chloramphenicol, ceftriaxone or cefuroxime.
C(i) Non-capsulated strains cause exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, sinusitis and otitis media; H. aegyptius causes conjunctivitis.
C(i) H. ducreyi causes chancroid, a sexually transmitted infection.
C(i) H. parainfluenzae and other haemolytic species are upper respiratory commensals that can cause disease in the immunocompromised.

A. Gross pathway of entry and spread:
(i) Enteroviruses enter through the gastrointestinal tract.
The pathway of spread is: virus, mouth, gut/lymphatics, lymph node, bloodstream, producing a major viraemia.
A minor viraemia follows and disseminates the virus to the CNS, heart, skin, lung and eye.
B. Relation of zones to pathology:
- Herpangina is a vesicular rash involving the pharynx and soft palate, associated with summer outbreaks of group A coxsackieviruses.
Its prodrome includes fever, vomiting, myalgia and headache.
- Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is a distinctive vesicular eruption usually caused by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71, most common in children under age 10, with fever and vesicles in the mouth and on the hands and feet.
C. Spread to a distant structure and functional deficit:
- Myopericarditis (inflammation of the myocardium and pericardium) is caused by enteroviruses, especially group B coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, accounting for 50% of all cases of acute myopericarditis.
- The virus replicates in the myofibers, leading to myofiber necrosis and focal inflammation.
This represents spread from the primary enteric site to the heart, with a cardiac functional deficit.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross pathway of enterovirus entry and spread through the alimentary tract.
B. State how zones along this pathway relate to specific clinical pathologies.
C. Explain how the virus may spread to a distant structure (the heart) and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
A) In amoebiasis, direct transport of trophozoites from the large intestine to the liver via the hepatic portal vein results in amoebic liver abscess.
A) In schistosomiasis, eggs of Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum that are swept back into the circulation lodge in the liver.
A) A granulomatous reaction surrounds these eggs and leads to fibrosis of the liver.
B) In chronic schistosomiasis, blood flow to the liver is impeded, which leads to portal hypertension, accumulation of ascites in the abdominal cavity, hepatosplenomegaly, and oesophageal varices.
B) Amoebic liver abscesses are the most common form of extra-intestinal amoebiasis.
B) Rupture of a liver abscess is an indication for dehydroemetine or emetine treatment and urgent management.
C) Pulmonary amoebiasis generally results from direct extension of the liver abscess through the diaphragm, with clinical symptoms of cough, chest pain, dyspnoea and fever, illustrating spread of hepatic pathology to a distant structure, the lung.
C) Haematogenous spread of trophozoites from the liver to other sites, such as the lungs, can also result in pulmonary infection.
C) The oesophageal varices that develop from portal hypertension in chronic hepatic schistosomiasis represent a further distant, vascular functional deficit arising from the hepatic pathology.
C) Hepatosplenomegaly, another consequence of this impeded hepatic blood flow, illustrates spread of the functional deficit to the spleen as well.
C) The clinical presentation of acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever), with fever, cough, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly and eosinophilia, further reflects this systemic spread of hepatic-associated pathology.

A(i) Gram-positive cocci in clusters (also singles, pairs, tetrads), about 1 um, non-motile, non-spore forming, mostly non-capsulated, catalase positive, oxidase negative, facultative anaerobes fermenting glucose; over 40 species; coagulase-positive (S. aureus) and coagulase-negative (CoNS: S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus and others).
A(ii) S. aureus is part of the normal microbiota (skin, nasopharynx, perineum), relatively heat resistant, salt resistant and able to survive long on dry objects; transmission is endogenous (breach in mucosal barriers) or exogenous (carrier, fomite, environment); predisposing factors: breach in skin, immune deficiency, diabetes mellitus, foreign bodies.
A(iii) Specimen depends on presentation (swab, pus, blood, aspirates); Gram stain shows clusters with many polymorphs; grows on blood and chocolate agar (golden yellow, beta-haemolytic colonies), mannitol salt agar is selective; catalase positive (streptococci negative); slide coagulase detects bound coagulase, tube coagulase detects free coagulase; novobiocin resistance identifies S. saprophyticus.
A(iv) Protein A (binds Fc of IgG, blocks opsonisation), coagulase (fibrin around bacteria), haemolysins (alpha, beta, gamma, delta), leukocidin (including Panton-Valentine), penicillinase and altered penicillin-binding proteins; spreading factors hyaluronidase, staphylokinase, lipase, protease; exotoxins exfoliatin, heat-stable enterotoxins and TSST-1 (superantigens).
A(v) Exotoxin diseases: food poisoning (preformed enterotoxin, short incubation, severe vomiting, resolves in about 24 hours), toxic shock syndrome, scalded skin syndrome. Direct invasion: folliculitis, furuncle, carbuncle, eye infections, wound infection, breast abscess, brain abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, endocarditis (in injecting drug users), pneumonia with empyema or abscess, sepsis, UTI.
B(i) S. epidermidis is normal skin flora with a predilection for plastic: skin flora enters with catheters, heart valves and CSF shunts, attaches to the device and forms biofilms that aid adherence and avoid phagocytosis; it is a hospital-acquired opportunist in the immunocompromised (sepsis, endocarditis, wounds, UTI, IV lines, prosthetic devices).
B(i) MRSA is due to the mecA gene coding for the low-affinity penicillin binding protein PBP2a, reducing affinity for penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems; strains are usually also resistant to tetracyclines, erythromycins and aminoglycosides; hospital and community forms occur; drug of choice is vancomycin.
B(i) Treatment otherwise: many strains make beta-lactamase and resist penicillin G; alternatives include cloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, cephalosporins, macrolides, clindamycin; drain abscesses; give supportive therapy; prevention by hand washing, wound cleansing, aseptic procedures and control of nasal carriage.
C(i) S. aureus: coagulase positive, ferments mannitol (golden yellow on mannitol salt agar), major pathogen with the full range of virulence factors above.
C(i) S. epidermidis: coagulase negative, skin commensal, presence in samples may indicate contamination, causes infection of lines, prostheses, heart valves and shunts.
C(i) S. saprophyticus: coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant (other CoNS susceptible), commensal of skin and mucous membranes.
C(i) S. saprophyticus causes UTI in sexually active young women (honeymoon cystitis) by massaging organisms into the bladder and adherence to urogenital epithelium, and is usually susceptible to a wide range of antibiotics.

A(i) Describe the origin of poliovirus entry and initial replication in the body.
A(ii) Describe the course of viral spread from the gut to the central nervous system.
A(iii) State the distribution of the virus within the central nervous system.
B. State the safe practice concerning physical activity/injections during poliovirus infection.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the flaccid paralysis seen in paralytic poliomyelitis.
questions.answerText:
A. Origin, course and distribution:
(i) Origin: the virus enters through the gastrointestinal tract, with replication in the gut and gut lymphatics.
(ii) Course: from the lymph node, the virus enters the bloodstream, producing a major viraemia.
A minor viraemia follows and carries the virus to the CNS, heart, skin, lung and eye.
(iii) Distribution: the virus shows predilection for the central nervous system, with extensive necrosis of neurons in the gray matter.
This affects primarily motor and autonomic neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord and the motor nuclei of the pons and medulla.
B. Safe practice:
- Physical exercise may impact the manifestations of infection,
Can provoke paralytic disease ("provocation polio"), so vigorous physical exertion should be avoided during infection.
C. Anatomical basis of the flaccid paralysis:
- Spinal paralytic poliomyelitis follows extensive necrosis of neurons in the anterior horn gray matter of the spinal cord.
- This produces weakness and flaccid paralysis of variable severity, while sensory loss is rare, since the virus predominantly affects motor rather than sensory neurons.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross role of the liver as the target organ for hepatotropic viruses.
B. State how hepatocellular damage relates to the clinical pathologies of viral hepatitis.
C. Explain how the disease may spread to a distant structure and cause a functional deficit outside the liver.
questions.answerText:
A. The liver as target organ:
(i) Viral hepatitis is a systemic disease primarily affecting the liver;
Hepatotropic viruses (HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV, HEV) have the liver as their primary tissue tropism,
Hepatocellular damage results in fever, gastrointestinal disorders and symptoms of liver damage such as jaundice.
B. Relation of hepatocellular damage to pathology:
- In HAV and HEV, cell-mediated immunity provokes immune-mediated hepatocyte injury, aggravating hepatic inflammation, usually followed by complete recovery without chronicity.
- In HBV and HCV, hepatocellular damage has an autoimmune basis.
This can progress to fulminant hepatitis, chronic persistent or chronic active hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
C. Spread to a distant structure and functional deficit:
- Extrahepatic manifestations occur;
HBV infection is associated with glomerulonephritis, representing spread of immune-complex-mediated injury to the kidney and a resulting renal functional deficit.
- HCV infection is associated with extrahepatic manifestations including diabetes mellitus and B-cell lymphoma, illustrating disease effects at sites distant from the liver.

questions.question:
(i) A farmer presents with chronic swelling of the foot with multiple draining sinuses discharging serosanguinous fluid containing granules, and an X-ray shows multiple large cavities within the foot. Identify the condition and the structures affected.
(ii) State which tissues become involved as the disease progresses.
(iii) List the differential causal categories of this condition.
(iv) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking the granules seen on microscopy to the sinus tracts and cavities seen on imaging.
questions.answerText:
(i) The condition is mycetoma (Madura foot/maduromycosis), affecting the cutaneous and subcutaneous tissue of the foot.
(ii) As the disease progresses it involves the cutaneous and subcutaneous tissue, fascia and bone, and may affect surrounding muscle, producing gross deformity and loss of function.
(iii) The two broad causal categories are actinomycotic mycetoma (actinomycetoma), caused by an actinomycete such as Nocardia or Actinomadura, and eumycetoma (eumycotic mycetoma), caused by a fungus, of which Madurella mycetomatis is by far the commonest, with others including Madurella grisea, Exophiala jeanselmei, Cladophialophora bantiana and Scedosporium apiospermum.
(iv)
- Infection results from traumatic implantation of the infectious agent into the skin, usually of the foot.
- Over time this produces subcutaneous nodules that form sinuses draining purulent material containing granules (grains), which are colonies of the infectious agent and inflammatory cells surrounded by tissue material.
- Chronic extension of this process into fascia and bone accounts for the multiple cavities seen radiographically, and secondary bacterial infection often occurs at the site of the lesion.

A(i) Agglutination tests are frequently used because they are simpler to perform, require no special equipment, and are less expensive. Direct slide agglutination test: used to identify bacteria following culture on a medium; a bacterial colony of pure growth is emulsified in physiological saline on a slide; antiserum containing specific antibody is added; the antibody binds to the bacterial antigen resulting in agglutination of the bacterial cells (antiserum + bacterial suspension = bacterial agglutination); the test must be controlled with positive and negative controls. Slide agglutination is practicable only when clumping of the organism occurs within a minute; it is unsuitable where the mixture must be incubated; it therefore cannot be used, as in a quantitative tube dilution test, to estimate the agglutinating power of the serum.
A(ii) Prozone phenomenon: the occasional inhibition of agglutination in the first tubes of an antiserum dilution series; agglutination occurs only in later tubes containing more dilute antiserum. Mechanism: partly due to the inhibiting effect of antibody concentrations in excess of the optimal ratio of antibody to antigen.
A(iii) Precipitin tests — two types:
- Tube precipitation test: examples — testing of CSF for extracellular antigens, especially H. influenzae antigen; original Lancefield method of grouping beta-haemolytic streptococci.
- Gel diffusion tests: examples — Elek gel technique (toxigenic C. diphtheriae); Biken test (detect toxin-producing faecal E. coli).
B) Indirect immunofluorescence test: unlabelled antibody combines with antigen; the antigen-antibody complex is detected by attaching a fluorescent-labelled anti-species globulin to the antibody — the antibody is therefore labelled indirectly. Fluorescent-labelled antihuman globulin is used if the antibody is of human origin. Two main uses: (1) to detect and identify unknown antigen in specimens; (2) to detect antibodies in a patient's serum using a known antigen (microorganism).
C) Applications of serological tests:
1. Diagnosis when pathogen is not present in routine specimens or is not easily isolated — e.g., syphilis, rickettsial diseases, leptospirosis, enteric fever, brucellosis, viral hepatitis, rotavirus infection and other viral diseases.
2. Identify and serotype a pathogen isolated by culture — e.g., V. cholerae O1, Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., group A Streptococcus, faecal E. coli.
3. Provide early or presumptive diagnosis of meningitis, cholera or typhoid.
4. Screen for rises in antistreptolysin O (ASO titre) in diagnosis of rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis, and other group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal complications.
5. Measure antibody levels to determine prevalence, spread, and control of infectious diseases in the community and immune status of individuals.
6. Identify pathogens using direct immunofluorescence — e.g., respiratory viruses, rabies virus, CMV, Pneumocystis jiroveci, chlamydia.
7. Screen pregnant women for syphilis and HIV infections.
8. Screen donor blood for antibody to HIV-1 and HIV-2.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Eight requirements for successful laboratory investigations:
1. Advance planning
2. Collection of adequate and appropriate specimens
3. Sufficient documentation
4. Biosafety and decontamination
5. Correct packaging
6. Rapid transport
7. Choice of a laboratory that can accurately perform the tests
8. Timely communication of results
A(ii) Transport medium: allows organisms (pathogens and contaminants) to survive; it is non-nutritive — it does not allow organisms to proliferate. Named example for bacteria: Cary Blair. Named example for viruses: virus transport medium (VTM).
A(iii) Blood for culture in adults: venous blood; adults require 5–10 mL; collect within 10 minutes of fever. If bacterial endocarditis is suspected: collect 3 sets of blood culture. Handling: collect into bottles with infusion broth, changing needle to inoculate the broth; transport upright with cushion to prevent haemolysis; wrap tubes with absorbent cotton; travel at ambient temperature; store at 4°C if unable to reach laboratory within 24 hours.
B) CSF collection: obtained by lumbar puncture, in sterile tubes, under aseptic conditions, by a trained person. Transport for bacteria: preferably in trans-isolate medium, pre-warmed to 25–37°C before inoculation, OR transport at ambient temperature (relevant pathogens do not survive at low temperatures). Transport for viruses: transport at 4–8°C (if up to 48 hours) or −70°C for longer duration.
C) Criteria for rejecting a specimen:
- Mismatch of information on the label and the request
- Inappropriate transport temperature
- Excessive delay in transportation
- Inappropriate transport medium
- Specimen received in a fixative
- Dry specimen
- Sample with questionable relevance
- Insufficient quantity
- Leakage

questions.answerText:
A. Structure under listed headings:
(i) Nucleic acid: a virus contains only one type of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, never both;
It may be single or double stranded, and single or segmented.
(ii) Capsid: the protein coat surrounding the nucleic acid, made up of structural units called capsomeres, which protects the nucleic acid from inactivation by outside conditions.
(iii) Envelope: an amorphous, lipoprotein membrane, composed of virally coded protein and host lipid, that lies outside the capsid in some viruses and is absent in naked viruses.
(iv) Symmetry: viruses show icosahedral (cubic), helical, or complex symmetry, based on the arrangement of capsomeres around the nucleic acid.
B. Clinical basis:
- Enveloped viruses (e.g. RSV, influenza, herpesviruses) are particularly labile and may lose infectivity if not adequately protected outside the host.
- This is why enveloped viruses must be transported in viral transport medium and kept cool, whereas non-enveloped viruses (adenovirus, enteroviruses) are more stable.
C. Distinguishing enveloped from non-enveloped viruses:
- A naked virus has only a protein capsid; an enveloped virus has an additional lipoprotein membrane with glycoprotein spikes arising from it.
- Examples of enveloped viruses include herpesviruses, rabies virus and influenza virus; examples of non-enveloped viruses include adenoviruses.

(i) Sporotrichosis, caused by Sporothrix schenckii, affecting the skin and subcutaneous tissue at the extremity together with the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes draining the area.

A(i) Bacteria that do not require oxygen; obligate anaerobes cannot grow if oxygen exceeds 0.5% (B. fragilis, C. perfringens, C. novyi, Porphyromonas, Fusobacterium); aerotolerant (2-8% O2); microaerophilic (e.g. C. jejuni, 5% O2); facultative anaerobes grow with or without air.
A(i) Gram-positive bacilli: spore-forming Clostridium; non-spore-forming Actinomyces, Bifidobacterium, Eubacterium, Lactobacillus, Mobiluncus, Propionibacterium; cocci Peptococcus, Peptostreptococcus, Finegoldia; Gram-negative bacilli Bacteroides, Prevotella, Porphyromonas, Fusobacterium, Leptotrichia; cocci Veillonella.

A(iii) Infections result from breakdown of a mucosal barrier with leakage of indigenous polymicrobial flora into sterile closed spaces or tissue; three factors: virulence factors, bacterial synergy and abscess formation.
A(iii) Features: putrid odour, foul exudates, gas in tissues, necrotic tissue (gangrene), abscesses, dark discoloured exudate, polymicrobial, near body surfaces inhabited, bite wounds, sulfur granules (actinomycosis), no growth of pus aerobically, failure to respond to aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones.
B(i) Mouth, head and neck: sinusitis, otitis media, periodontitis, root canal infection, abscess, ocular infection; thoracic: empyema, lung abscess, aspiration pneumonitis, necrotising pneumonia.
B(i) Abdomen: peritonitis, intra-abdominal abscess, appendicitis, liver abscess, biliary infection; pelvis: PID, pelvic abscess, bacterial vaginosis.
B(i) Skin and soft tissue: diabetic foot ulcers, abscess, gas gangrene, bite wounds; CNS: brain abscess, subdural empyema, epidural abscess.
C(i) Culture and identification are slow and expensive and most infections are mixed; endogenous infections are increasingly common in immunosuppressed hosts; empiric antibiotics are used because of inadequate culture techniques.
C(i) Most are resistant to penicillin and analogues, many cephalosporins (including third generation), tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and resistance to newer quinolones and clindamycin is emerging; about three quarters of isolates are the B. fragilis group and Gram-positive non-spore-forming rods.
C(i) Isolation and identification matter because anaerobic infections carry high morbidity and mortality and treatment varies with the species involved.
C(i) Diagnosis: direct examination and stains (odour, gas, sulfur granules, acridine orange), colony appearance, gas-liquid chromatography, PCR, rapid systems; bacteria seen in smears but not grown aerobically suggest anaerobes.

A) Describe the gross involvement of the urinary bladder in Schistosoma haematobium infection.
B) Explain how the affected zones/parts of the bladder and pelvic structures relate to the pathology described.
C) Explain why disease originating in the bladder may spread to cause a distant or systemic functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A) Infection with Schistosoma haematobium occurs mainly in Africa, Asia, Portugal, India and Egypt, with reservoirs including monkeys, baboons and chimpanzees.
A) Schistosomules develop in the liver and later migrate to the vesicle, prostatic and uterine plexus.
A) Eggs are deposited in the urinary bladder; S. haematobium eggs possess a terminal spine.
B) With S. haematobium infection, there is urinary tract involvement: urethral pain, increased urinary frequency, dysuria, and haematuria.
B) Eggs deposited in the bladder are associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
B) Production of large numbers of eggs results in chronic granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis of the urinary tract.
C) Bladder obstruction from this egg deposition and fibrosis leads to secondary bacterial infections, representing spread of the local bladder pathology to a broader urinary tract functional deficit.
C) Clinically, most infections are asymptomatic, but acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) may occur weeks after initial infection, with manifestations including fever, cough, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly and eosinophilia, reflecting systemic spread beyond the bladder itself.
C) An itchy rash (swimmer's itch) occurring within an hour after cercariae penetrate the skin is followed by headache, chills, fever, diarrhoea and eosinophilia 2-12 weeks after exposure, illustrating that the disease process is not confined to the bladder alone.
C) The eggs, not the adult worms, are responsible for the most significant pathology, and the disease syndromes coincide with the three stages of parasite development: skin penetration, egg deposition (acute schistosomiasis), and chronic granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis.
C) Treatment is with praziquantel or oxamniquine, aimed at the adult worms responsible for ongoing egg production and hence ongoing spread of this pathology.

A(i) The third-stage infective larvae, known as filariform larvae, live in the soil and penetrate the skin of a host on contact.
A(ii) The free-living form is seen in the soil, and the parasitic male is rarely seen.
A(iii) The parthenogenetic female lives embedded in the mucosa of the small intestine, producing eggs that hatch almost immediately into first-stage rhabditiform larvae, which are passed out in faeces and feed on bacteria in the soil, moulting twice into infective filariform larvae that can live up to 12 days in the soil.
A(iv) Self-infection (autoinfection) can occur if the rhabditiform larvae develop into filariform larvae by the time they reach the anus, and then penetrate the perianal skin.
A(v) In immunocompromised patients, the first-stage larvae can cause hyperinfection, referred to as disseminated strongyloidiasis, which can cause a mortality rate close to 90%; the rate of autoinfection can be increased in patients on immunosuppressive drugs, causing overwhelming numbers of larvae migrating in the lungs, which can be fatal.
C) A unique effect of autoinfection is larva currens, due to rapid migration of the larvae through the skin; this appears as a red line that moves rapidly and disappears, presenting as a chronic and recurrent serpentine urticarial rash that can persist for years.
C) An itchy rash also appears a few days after the initial infection, followed by mild respiratory symptoms within a few weeks, reflecting the anatomical route of larval penetration and subsequent migration.
C) In heavy infections, symptoms include dysentery, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain and weight loss, and very heavy infection in malnourished individuals can produce anaemia from blood loss, reflecting the intestinal site of the adult parthenogenetic female.
C) Any anthelminthic treatment, including albendazole, thiabendazole or levamisole, should be repeated after a few weeks, reflecting the ongoing risk of autoinfection responsible for these recurrent skin and systemic findings.
C) Wearing of protective shoes prevents the initial skin penetration that begins this migratory and autoinfective process.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male is admitted to hospital with a 6-week history of low-grade fever, weight loss and right hypochondrial pain. Blood cultures taken on two occasions using the manual method are negative. A BACTEC-automated culture bottle later flags positive, and Gram stain of the broth reveals Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
(i) Name the two most common organisms causing culture-positive endocarditis that also commonly cause the positive Gram stain described, and describe how the BACTEC automated blood culture system works.
(ii) Identify the blood culture bottle colour-coding for adult aerobic versus anaerobic bottles, and state the volume of blood required for each.
(iii) Explain the contents of blood culture specimen bottles, naming the specific component added to prevent clotting and why it is needed.
(iv) State the disadvantages/setbacks of blood culture, listing all limitations.
(v) State the diagnostic criteria for culture-negative endocarditis and name the most common organism group responsible, listing the specific genera.
questions.answerText:
(i) The two most common Gram-positive cocci in clusters causing endocarditis are Staphylococci and Streptococci, both Gram-positive cocci, non-motile, non-sporing, facultative anaerobes. The BACTEC automated method: specialised sample bottles that already contain culture media are placed in the BACTEC machine for 24 hours to allow the organism to multiply; if microbial growth is detected, a Gram stain is conducted from the culture bottle to confirm organisms are present and provide preliminary information about identity.
(ii) BACTEC specimen bottle colour-coding:
- Green top: adult aerobic — 5–10 mL blood.
- Orange top: anaerobic — 5–10 mL blood.
(Also: Yellow top — paediatric aerobic, 0.5–4 mL; Black top — mycobacteria, 5–10 mL; Silver top — mycoplasma, 3–5 mL.)
(iii) Contents of blood culture specimen bottles: (1) a growth medium (nutrient broth) to encourage microorganisms to multiply — the ratio of blood to broth is usually 10 mL to 200 mL; (2) an anticoagulant to prevent blood from clotting and to neutralise the natural bactericidal action of blood; (3) cooked meat or a reducing agent added to anaerobic bottles to aid growth of anaerobic bacteria.
(iv) Setbacks/limitations:
- Contamination: false positives from organisms not actually present in the blood sample; leads to unnecessary antibiotic treatment and longer hospital stays.
- Difficult organisms to culture: some organisms (e.g., mycobacteria) do not grow in culture, requiring serology or PCR.
- Time-consuming: fastidious organisms (e.g., Brucella, Mycobacterium) may require prolonged incubation times or special media.
- More false positives; lower yield of anaerobes; decreased sensitivity for fastidious pathogens; labour-intensive (requires constant inspection for growth).
(v) Culture-negative endocarditis is reported in 5–10% of cases of infective endocarditis; previous antibiotic therapy is the most frequent reason for negative blood cultures. The HACEK group is responsible for 5–10% of cases of infective endocarditis and is the most common cause of Gram-negative endocarditis among people who do not abuse intravenous drugs. HACEK genera: Haemophilus spp. (H. parainfluenzae, H. aphrophilus, H. paraphrophilus), Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella spp.; they are part of normal oropharyngeal flora, are slow growers, and prefer a carbon-dioxide-enriched atmosphere.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the source, reservoir and modes of transmission of Treponema pallidum.
A(ii) Describe its features and the course of infection through the stages.
A(iii) Describe the tertiary and other manifestations and the distribution of disease.
B(i) State the specimens and tests used for diagnosis.
C(i) Explain the basis of the deformities and deficits of congenital and late syphilis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Strict human pathogen, not naturally in any animal; infected humans secreting T. pallidum in serous transudate (chancre, condyloma latum, mucous patches) are the source.
A(i) Transmission: sexual contact through intact mucous membrane or minor abrasions, vertical transmission, transfusion of contaminated blood; occupational infection of health workers handling secondary syphilis.
A(ii) Thin coiled spirochaete (0.2 um by 5-15 um, 6-10 angular coils) with endoflagella; too thin for Gram or Giemsa stains, seen by silver impregnation (Fontana, Levaditi) or dark-field/phase contrast; cannot be cultured on artificial media; virulence factors: outer membrane protein, hyaluronidase, fibronectin.
A(ii) Primary syphilis within 3 weeks: single chancre with areola at the site (penis or scrotum in 75% of men; vulva, cervix, perineum in over 50% of women), highly infectious.
A(ii) Secondary syphilis 2-10 weeks later: spread by blood with mucocutaneous macular to papular lesions including palms and soles, condylomata lata, fever, headache, bone pain, painless generalised lymphadenopathy in 85%.
A(iii) Tertiary syphilis 3-10 years later: gumma (skin, mouth, upper respiratory tract), cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, ascending aortic aneurysm), granulomatous and meningovascular disease, neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis, general paralysis of the insane); few spirochaetes, delayed hypersensitivity.
A(iii) Non-venereal forms: endemic syphilis (bejel), pinta (T. carateum, central and south America); syphilis is worldwide, mostly large cities, hot dry climate, poor economic status and hygiene.
B(i) Serous transudate from moist lesions (dark-field microscopy, direct fluorescent antibody), serum for serology, CSF for neurosyphilis; non-treponemal tests (cardiolipin, reagin, VDRL) are non-specific; treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS, TP-PA) specific.
B(i) Treatment: penicillin drug of choice (benzathine penicillin G), doxycycline or tetracycline alternatives; prevention: early diagnosis and treatment, condoms, follow-up of contacts.
C(i) Congenital syphilis (vertical transmission) is the most severe outcome: late abortion, stillbirth, death, poor feeding, rhinitis.
C(i) Deformities: Hutchinson's teeth, saddle nose, frontal bossing, interstitial keratitis.
C(i) Late onset: neurosyphilis and involvement of the 8th cranial nerve with hearing loss.

(i) Hookworm infection (Necator americanus or Ancylostoma duodenale), presenting with iron deficiency anaemia.
(ii) Predisposing factors include walking barefoot on soil contaminated with hookworm larvae, poor sanitation, and farming or other occupations with soil contact; about 740 million people are infected worldwide, and hookworm is the second most common human helminthic infection.
(iii) A local dermatitis (ground itch) develops after larval skin penetration; larvae are carried through the veins into the heart, then the lungs, penetrate the pulmonary alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree into the pharynx, and are swallowed, developing into adult worms in the small intestine (jejunum); hookworms are voracious blood feeders that bite off pieces of mucosa and change their attachment site often, so that in heavy infection up to 100ml of blood may be lost per day, the most serious consequence of advanced infection being iron deficiency anaemia.
(iv) Ivermectin is the first drug of choice, though it must be repeated because it kills only the adult worm; thiabendazole has side effects of dizziness, vomiting and nausea; albendazole is second line and least effective; mebendazole has a higher failure rate in clinical practice.

A 45-year-old immunocompromised patient on long-term corticosteroids develops fever (38.6°C) 72 hours after abdominal surgery in hospital. He has a urinary catheter in situ and is being ventilated in the ICU. There is no prior history of infection at the time of admission.
(i) Define healthcare-associated infection (HAI), and state how this patient's infection qualifies.
(ii) State the distribution of HAIs by anatomical site, giving the percentage for each major category.
(iii) List all patient susceptibility factors and environmental factors that influence the development of HAIs.
(iv) Describe the six elements of the chain of infection, and state the control principle that must be targeted to break the chain.
(v) State the five common HAIs listed by name.
questions.answerText:
(i) A healthcare-associated infection (HAI) is defined as: "An infection occurring in a patient during the process of care in a hospital or other health-care facility which was not present or incubating at the time of admission. This includes infections acquired in the hospital but appearing after discharge, and also occupational infections among staff of the facility." This patient qualifies because fever developed 72 hours post-admission (not present at the time of admission) in the setting of healthcare delivery.
(ii) Distribution of HAIs by anatomical site: urinary tract — 35%; surgical site — 25%; lungs — 10%; bloodstream — 10%; other sites — 10% (remaining 10%).
(iii) Patient susceptibility factors: age (extremes of life — infancy and old age associated with decreased resistance to infection); immune status (patients with malignant tumours, leukaemia, diabetes mellitus, renal failure, or AIDS have increased susceptibility); underlying disease; immunosuppressive drugs or irradiation; injuries to skin or mucous membranes (bypass natural defences); malnutrition; diagnostic and therapeutic procedures (biopsies, endoscopic examinations, catheterisation, intubation/ventilation, suction, surgical procedures). Environmental factors: health care settings where both infected persons and persons at increased risk congregate; crowded conditions within hospitals; frequent transfers of patients from one unit to another; concentration of highly susceptible patients in one area (newborn infants, burn patients, ICU patients).
(iv) Six elements of the chain of infection: (1) the pathogen; (2) the portal of exit; (3) the mode of transmission; (4) the portal of entry; (5) the reservoir; (6) the host. All six must be present before transmission of infection can take place; interrupting any one of these elements breaks the chain.
(v) Five common HAIs: catheter-associated urinary tract infection; central line-associated bloodstream infection; Clostridium difficile infection; surgical site infection; ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.question:
A) Describe the gross involvement of the eye in onchocerciasis and in toxocariasis.
B) Explain how the affected zones/parts of the eye relate to the pathology described in these conditions.
C) Explain why disease originating in or near the eye may spread to a distant structure and cause a further functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A) In onchocerciasis, the worms commonly migrate to the eyes, where inflammatory changes occur.
A) In toxocariasis, caused by Toxocara canis, larvae migrate to various organs including the liver, brain and eyes, where they normally die and become calcified.
A) Humans are normally dead-end hosts in toxocariasis, ingesting eggs from soil contaminated with dog faeces.
B) In onchocerciasis, inflammatory changes in the eye lead to destruction of the retina, causing blindness, hence the name river blindness, related to the breeding habits of the Simulium fly near river banks.
B) In toxocariasis, the presence of dead larvae in the tissues provokes a delayed hypersensitivity reaction due to larval proteins, resulting in granulomatous lesions in the organs affected; in the eyes, this causes retinal damage and blindness.
B) In toxocariasis, other clinical findings include fever, hepatomegaly and eosinophilia, reflecting involvement of organs beyond the eye alongside the ocular pathology.
C) In onchocerciasis, inflammatory changes in the subcutaneous tissues beyond the eye cause destruction of elastic fibres of the skin, leading to wrinkling or sagging of the skin at the groin (hanging groin) and thickened, scaly, dry skin resembling that of a lizard (lizard skin), illustrating spread of the disease process to distant skin structures.
C) In toxocariasis, migration of larvae to the central nervous system may lead to symptoms of a space-occupying lesion, illustrating spread of the parasitic pathology from a peripheral or ocular site to a distant structure, the brain.
C) Young children are predominantly affected by toxocariasis because they are more likely to ingest contaminated soil, and this systemic route of infection explains why multiple organs, not the eye alone, are typically affected.
C) IgG is raised in the blood with significant eosinophilia in toxocariasis, a systemic immunological reflection of this spread beyond the eye.
C) Ivermectin is used to kill the microfilariae in onchocerciasis, while the adult worms, which may be responsible for ongoing microfilarial production and hence ongoing spread of disease to the eye and skin, can be killed with Suramin.

questions.question:
A patient from a river-blindness endemic area of tropical Africa presents with severely pruritic papules and nodules on the skin, wrinkling and sagging of the skin at the groin, and progressive visual impairment.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What procedure is available to remove the causative organism from the skin?
(iii) What developmental/life-cycle feature (timing of microfilarial release) is characteristic of this organism?
questions.answerText:
(i) Onchocerciasis (river blindness), caused by Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by the female black fly, Simulium.
(ii) Skin nodules can be surgically excised.
(iii) The female worms living in the skin nodules produce large numbers of microfilariae that are released into the blood circulation usually in the day, giving this infection a diurnal periodicity, in contrast to organisms with nocturnal periodicity; ivermectin is used to kill the microfilariae, and the adult worms can be killed with Suramin, especially in those with eye complications.

questions.question:
A patient from an area without access to safe drinking water develops a painful, blistering skin lesion on the lower limb that later ulcerates; on placing the limb in water, a worm is seen emerging from the ulcer.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What procedure is used to remove the causative organism?
(iii) What developmental/life-cycle event explains why this ulcer must be exposed to fresh water?
questions.answerText:
(i) Dracunculiasis (guinea worm infection), caused by Dracunculus medinensis.
(ii) Extraction of the adult worm gradually using a match stick; thiabendazole and metronidazole are given to weaken the worm and make extraction easier.
(iii) The gravid female worm releases a substance causing inflammation and blistering of the skin, which later ulcerates; when the ulcer is exposed to fresh water, the worm discharges motile larvae into the water, and these larvae are then eaten by copepods to initiate another cycle of the parasite's development.

A(i) Trophozoites of Plasmodium are generally ring-shaped, 1-2 microns in size; Plasmodium falciparum is the largest and is banana-shaped, while others are smaller and round.
A(ii) The gametocytes, the sexual forms of the parasite, are much larger, 7-14 microns in size.
B) Plasmodium falciparum disease is usually more serious because the parasites readily infect red cells of all ages, unlike P. vivax/ovale which attack younger red cells (reticulocytes) or P. malariae which prefers older erythrocytes; there is extensive thrombosis of capillaries leading to ischaemia and tissue anoxia in P. falciparum infection.
B) Sequestration, the retention of later developmental stages such as schizonts within capillaries of various organs, is characteristic of P. falciparum infection, and this is responsible for local metabolic defects, including hypoglycaemia and hypoxia, that may lead to coma and cerebral malaria.
C) P. falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria, with fever paroxysms every 48 hours, and is the most deadly of the species; P. malariae causes quartan malaria with paroxysms every 72 hours.
C) P. vivax and P. ovale cause benign tertian malaria, also with 48-hour paroxysms; P. ovale is almost exclusively found in Africa.
C) Only P. vivax and P. ovale have hypnozoites, a persistent form in the liver responsible for relapse (recrudescence infection); in P. falciparum and P. malariae infections, recurrence is due to recrudescence, an increase in parasites that have persisted at low levels in the blood, rather than relapse from a liver hypnozoite stage.
C) Merozoites are the matured form inside a schizont; the schizont ruptures in the liver (exo-erythrocytic) or blood (erythrocytic) to release merozoites, each able to re-infect other red blood cells, or liver cells in the case of vivax, ovale and malariae, but this is not so for falciparum.
C) Malaria pigment, a by-product of the growth or metabolism of the parasite, appears as the parasite grows and contributes to pathogenicity in all species, but the extent of erythrocytic destruction and degree of phagocytosis of the hyperplastic reticulo-endothelial system are notably greater in P. falciparum infection.
C) The periodicity of fever paroxysms becomes more regular as the malaria infection progresses, at 48-hour intervals for tertian species (falciparum, vivax, ovale) and 72-hour intervals for the quartan species, P. malariae.

A(i) the trophozoite
