With reference to the migration of hookworm (Necator americanus/Ancylostoma duodenale) larvae through the host:
A(i) Describe the origin of the infection.
A(ii) Describe the course taken by the larvae through the body.
A(iii) Describe the relations of the adult worm once it reaches its final site.
A(iv) Describe the distribution of clinical effects that result from this migration and attachment.
C) Explain the anatomical basis of the injury and its consequence at the site of adult worm attachment.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The larvae hatch from eggs passed in faeces into moist soil within 24 hours, moult twice into the infective third stage within five days, and penetrate the skin of a new host on contact.
A(ii) The larvae are carried through the veins into the heart, then into the lungs, penetrate the pulmonary alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree into the pharynx, and are swallowed.
A(iii) In the small intestine, the larvae develop into adult worms that live in the jejunum with the anterior end attached to the mucosa.
A(iv) A local dermatitis known as ground itch develops a few days after larval penetration; two to four weeks after infection, pneumonitis develops from the migrating larvae in the lungs, with coughing, wheezing, chest pain and fever where large numbers of larvae are involved; in heavy infection there are epigastric pains, indigestion, vomiting and constipation.
C) Hookworms are voracious blood feeders; they bite off pieces of mucosa and pass the blood through their body for nutrition and respiration, and they change their attachment site often, so that in heavy infection up to 100ml of blood may be lost per day (0.15ml for each adult worm).
C) This repeated site-changing injury to the jejunal mucosa is the anatomical basis of the most serious consequence of advanced severe infection, iron deficiency anaemia.
C) In endemic areas, this chronic blood loss is associated with retardation of intellectual, cognitive and growth development in children.
C) In infected pregnant mothers, intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity and low birth weight of newborns have been reported as further consequences of this chronic mucosal injury.
C) Both Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, the two nematode species causing hookworm infection, share this attachment-and-feeding pattern responsible for the anaemia.
C) Adult worms can live up to 1-2 years, although several years of survival have been recorded, meaning this mucosal injury and blood loss can be sustained over a prolonged period if untreated.

questions.question:
A child presents with high-grade fever, headache with photophobia, nuchal rigidity and positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs.
(i) State the likely diagnosis, the routes by which bacteria reach the meninges and the risk factors for neurological complications.
(ii) State the short-term and long-term complications and their basis.
(iii) State the management options (empiric, corticosteroid and preventive) and justify one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Bacterial meningitis: bacteria reach the meninges via the bloodstream, ear or sinus infection, a defect in the dura mater or neurosurgical procedures; leading causes are S. pneumoniae, group B streptococcus, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes and E. coli (M. tuberculosis less commonly).
(i) Pathogenesis: colonised nasopharynx or gut, bacteraemia, haematogenous spread across the blood-brain barrier into the CSF where absence of antibodies allows growth; neutrophil and cytokine response raises permeability, giving oedema and raised intracranial pressure.
(i) Risk factors for neurological complications: young age (infants in 71% of cases), delayed presentation and S. pneumoniae as the cause.
(ii) Complications arise from bacterial toxin release and the host immune response, causing neuronal damage; short term: seizures, focal neurological deficit, subdural effusion (commonest in infants under 1 year, 20-39%).
(ii) Long term: hearing loss, seizures, cognitive impairment, learning disability, epilepsy, hydrocephalus; 1 in 5 survivors have long-lasting effects and without treatment fatality can reach 70%.
(iii) Empiric antibiotic chosen by likely organism and age: third-generation cephalosporins in children to cover N. meningitidis; ampicillin added for L. monocytogenes in those under 3 months; S. pneumoniae: vancomycin with ceftriaxone and dexamethasone; H. influenzae and Pseudomonas: ceftazidime, gentamicin.
(iii) Dexamethasone is used to control inflammation (steroids are the only drug that controls the inflammatory response but only in specific situations); prevention: vaccines (Hib conjugate, meningococcal A, B, C, W, Y, pneumococcal) and chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (oral rifampin for Hib).
(iii) Justification of the option chosen: a third-generation cephalosporin started without delay reduces the risk of neurological complications.

questions.question:
A patient has fatigue, night sweats, flu-like symptoms, aching joints, petechiae, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and haematuria, with a new regurgitant murmur and positive blood cultures.
(i) Identify the structure and the condition.
(ii) State the structures and organs affected.
(iii) Give the differential (related) pathology and its distinguishing features.
(iv) Explain the clinico-pathological reasoning and the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Infective (bacterial) endocarditis: infection of the endocardial surfaces of the heart, usually one or more cardiac valves (less often mural endocardium or a septal defect).
(ii) Severe valvular insufficiency, intractable congestive heart failure and myocardial abscesses; infected and sterile emboli and immunological phenomena (haematuria, glomerulonephritis, renal infarcts, peripheral abscesses); fatal if diagnosis is delayed or treatment inadequate.
(ii) Agents: viridans streptococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci, enterococci, S. bovis.
(iii) Rheumatic heart disease: autoimmune valve damage after streptococcal infection (usually mitral), main risk factor previous streptococcal infection, diagnosed by ASO titre; infective endocarditis has no autoimmune background and risks are injecting drug use, poor dental hygiene, intravascular cannulae, soft tissue infections, cardiac surgery and pacemakers.
(iv) Pathogenesis: (1) trauma prepares the valve (platelet-fibrin deposit), (2) circulating bacteria adhere (e.g. dextran) and (3) survive and propagate the vegetation, with tissue factor and clotting activation.
(iv) Diagnosis: blood cultures (standard 5-day incubation), echocardiogram, ECG, chest X-ray, CT/MRI, blood count; treatment: broad-spectrum then targeted IV antibiotics for 4-6 weeks; surgery for large vegetations or invasion of nearby tissue; prevention by oral hygiene and skin care.

A(i) When the female black fly (Simulium) bites the victim, it deposits the parasites (larvae) on the skin.
A(ii) These larvae penetrate the body through the bite injury and migrate to the subcutaneous tissue.
A(iii) The larvae develop into male and female adult worms living in skin nodules; humans are the only definitive host.
A(iv) The female worms produce large numbers of microfilariae, which are released into the blood circulation, usually in the day (diurnal periodicity); when a fly bites another victim, it sucks up these microfilariae, which undergo further development in the fly to initiate another cycle.
A(v) The presence of microfilariae in the subcutaneous tissue provokes severe inflammatory reactions resulting in pruritic papules and nodules on the skin; the worms commonly migrate to the eyes, where inflammatory changes can lead to destruction of the retina and blindness.
C) Inflammatory changes in the subcutaneous tissues may cause destruction of elastic fibres of the skin, leading to wrinkling or sagging of the skin, especially at the groin, a condition known as hanging groin.
C) As the disease progresses, the skin becomes thickened, scaly and dry, with severe itching and scratching, resembling the skin of a lizard, hence the name lizard skin.
C) The worms commonly migrate to the eyes, where inflammatory changes can lead to destruction of the retina and blindness, hence the name river blindness, related to the breeding habits of the black fly near river banks.
C) Skin nodules containing the adult worms can be surgically excised as part of management, reflecting the subcutaneous location of the disease process responsible for these deformities.
C) Ivermectin is used to kill the microfilariae responsible for these skin and eye changes, while the adult worms can be killed with Suramin, especially in those with eye complications.
questions.question:
With reference to the migration of infective larvae in onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis:
A(i) Describe the origin of infection in onchocerciasis.
A(ii) Describe the course of the parasite once deposited on the skin in onchocerciasis.
A(iii) Describe the relations of the adult worms once established.
A(iv) Describe the further stage/branch of the parasite's life cycle involving microfilariae.
A(v) Describe the distribution of clinical effects that result.
C) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity that follows chronic infection in this condition.

questions.answerText:
A. Steps in viral replication:
(i) Attachment/adsorption: viruses must recognise and bind to specific cellular receptors on the host cell surface via particular ligands/glycoproteins.
(ii) Penetration and uncoating: enveloped viruses enter by fusion of the viral envelope with the cell membrane or by endocytosis;
Naked viruses enter by pore formation or endocytosis; uncoating releases the viral genome from its capsid so replication can occur.
(iii) Replication, assembly and release: the viral genome is replicated and transcribed into mRNA, translated into viral proteins, and new particles are assembled;
Enveloped viruses are released by budding from the plasma membrane, while naked viruses are released by rupture (lysis) of the infected cell.
B. Clinical basis for targeting replication stages:
- Since RNA viruses use viral-encoded enzymes for replication and transcription, these enzymes can potentially be targeted by antivirals.
- Amantadine and rimantadine, for example, block the penetration and uncoating of influenza virus particles, illustrating stage-specific antiviral action.
C. Distinguishing release mechanisms:
- Naked viruses are released predominantly by lysis of the host cell, either directly (cytolytic) or through immune destruction of the infected cell.
- Enveloped viruses obtain their envelope from host cell membranes by budding and may be released without necessarily lysing the host cell, sometimes permitting persistent, non-cytolytic infection, as with retroviruses.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe attachment/adsorption in the viral replication cycle.
A(ii) Describe penetration and uncoating.
A(iii) Describe replication, assembly/maturation and release.
B. Explain the clinical basis for targeting specific stages of replication with antiviral drugs.
C. Distinguish the mode of release of naked viruses from that of enveloped viruses.

(i) A child is bitten by a stray dog and, weeks later, develops apprehension, hallucinations, excessive salivation, hydrophobia and photophobia. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What predisposing factors and pathophysiologic mechanisms underlie this disease?
(iii) Outline the management of this patient.
questions.answerText:
1. Diagnosis: Rabies, encephalitic (furious) clinical form (about 80% of cases present this way).
2. Predisposing factors and pathophysiology:
- Predisposing factor: bite from a rabid, unvaccinated animal, most often a domestic dog.
- Current evidence shows the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR), neuronal cell adhesion molecule (NCAM) and p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) bind rabies virus and facilitate its entry; after receptor binding, the virus enters through the endosomal transport pathway.
- Low pH in the endosome induces membrane fusion, catalysed by glycoprotein G, enabling the viral genome to reach the cytosol; viral multiplication occurs in muscle cells and at neuromuscular junctions, then the virus migrates along peripheral neurons by retrograde axonal transport to the CNS.
3. Management:
- If seen before symptoms: thorough wound cleansing with soap and water, tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics, human rabies immune globulin infiltrated into the wound with the remainder given IM at a distant site, and rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 28.
- Once clinical disease is established, treatment is largely supportive; one reported survivor was managed with induced coma, high-dose ketamine, mechanical ventilation, heparin and ribavirin, though this approach has not been reliably successful.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin (natural reservoir), course of transmission to humans, and distribution of Lassa fever virus.
A(ii) State the family to which the causative virus belongs.
B(i) State a safe/preventive practice for reducing the spread of this disease.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical/pathological basis of a long-term complication seen in survivors of this disease.
questions.answerText:
1. Lassa virus is a member of the Arenaviridae, a family of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses.
2. Humans usually become infected with Lassa virus through exposure to food or household items contaminated with urine or faeces of infected Mastomys rats (the multimammate rat), the principal reservoir.
3. The disease is endemic in the rodent population in parts of West Africa.
4. Person-to-person infection and laboratory transmission can also occur, particularly in health care settings in the absence of adequate infection prevention and control measures.
5. Lassa fever is known to be endemic in Benin, Ghana, Guinea, Liberia, Mali, Sierra Leone, Togo and Nigeria, but probably exists in other West African countries as well.
6. It was first identified in Nigeria in 1969, and named after Lassa, a town in present-day Borno State, where it was discovered.
7. There is no vaccine or specific treatment to prevent Lassa fever; prevention requires isolating those who are infected and decreasing contact with the vector.
8. Other efforts to control the spread of the disease may include having a cat to hunt rodents, and storage of food in sealed containers.
9. Treatment is directed at addressing dehydration and reducing symptoms, and ribavirin has been recommended, though evidence to support its use is weak.
10. Some survivors experience lasting effects of the disease, which can include partial or complete deafness.
11. The virus has an affinity for highly vascular tissues, including the placenta, which is why inducing delivery is necessary for the mother's survival when infection occurs late in the third trimester.
12. Following delivery, the fetus has only a one-in-ten chance of survival regardless of the course of action taken, so the focus is always on saving the life of the mother.

questions.question:
(i) A preschool-age child presents with a history of mild trauma to the lower limb followed one to three days later by rapid onset of fever, bone pain over the lower end of the femur, general malaise, refusal to use the limb, and a rapid pulse with toxaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) Outline the pathologic basis of this condition, from the organisms reaching the affected site to the local tissue changes that follow.
(iii) Outline the initial management of this condition.
(iv) State the definitive treatment required if this condition fails to resolve.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis (of the lower end of the femur).
(ii)
- Bacteria pass through nutrient vessels to the metaphysis, where they lodge and proliferate.
- This is followed by exudation and a rise in intraosseous pressure.
- Vascular stasis follows, leading to bone necrosis and bone resorption.
- The physeal (epiphyseal) plate acts as a barrier to extension of infection into the epiphysis because it is avascular, although infection can sometimes extend into the adjacent joint.
- Once localised, bacteria induce an inflammatory reaction and cause cell death; bacteria and inflammation spread within the shaft and may percolate through the Haversian systems to reach the periosteum, forming a subperiosteal abscess.
(iii) Management requires prompt suspicion of the diagnosis within the first 3-4 days of onset, simple clinical investigations to confirm it, and initiation of a properly planned therapeutic programme; the primary treatment is parenteral (intravenous) antibiotics that penetrate bone and joint cavities, continued for at least 4-6 weeks, started on an inpatient basis.
(iv) Acute osteomyelitis unresolved after 10 days is considered chronic; surgery is then required to remove dead (necrotic) bone tissue and affected soft tissue, with the goal of controlling infection and eliminating the dead space left after removal of the necrotic bone, and treatment must be continued until the disease is eliminated.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the genome shared by the haemorrhagic fever virus (HFV) families.
A(ii) Describe the envelope shared by these families.
A(iii) List the four taxonomic families that contain the most important HFVs.
B. Explain the clinical basis of why the enveloped, zoonotic nature of these viruses restricts their geographic distribution.
C. Distinguish between the Filoviridae and Arenaviridae in structure and reservoir.
questions.answerText:
A. Shared structural features and families:
(i) Genome: all HFVs are small, single-stranded RNA viruses with small genomes (10 to 19 kilobases); genomes may be of negative, positive, or ambisense polarity depending on the specific virus.
(ii) Envelope: all HFVs are covered, or enveloped, in a fatty (lipid) coating.
(iii) The most important HFVs come from four taxonomic families: Filoviridae (Ebola and Marburg), Arenaviridae (Lassa, Junin, Machupo), Bunyaviridae (Crimean-Congo HF, Rift Valley fever, Hantaviruses),
Flaviviridae (Yellow fever, Dengue, Omsk HF, Kyasanur Forest disease).
B. Clinical basis of geographic restriction:
- The survival of these viruses is dependent on an animal or insect host, called the natural reservoir.
- The viruses are therefore geographically restricted to the areas where their host species live; with the exception of dengue virus, for which humans can now be considered the reservoir, HFVs are zoonotic and maintained in nature in mammalian hosts.
C. Distinguishing Filoviridae from Arenaviridae:
- Filoviruses (Ebola/Marburg) are non-segmented, negative-sense ssRNA, filamentous particles composed of 7 structural proteins, and attack the mononuclear phagocytic system via the spleen, lymph node and liver.
- Arenaviruses (Lassa) are enveloped, round or pleomorphic virions 50–300 nm in diameter, with a single-stranded genome divided into two RNA segments arranged in an ambisense orientation,
Are maintained in a rodent reservoir (Mastomys natalensis).

(i) Serological testing for syphilis and HIV: serological testing has proved valuable in screening detection of syphilis, HIV/AIDS, and coronavirus. Donor blood must be screened for antibody to HIV-1 and HIV-2 (to prevent transmission through blood transfusion); blood must also be screened for hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-HBc to reduce transmission of HBV in blood or blood products. Previous antibiotic therapy is the most frequent reason for negative blood cultures, but for syphilis and HIV serological tests are appropriate.
(ii) Hemagglutination inhibition test: many viruses bind to hemagglutinin molecules found at the surface of red blood cells of various animal species, causing aggregation of red cells — hemagglutination. Prevention of this aggregation (hemagglutination inhibition) by specific antiviral antibodies in the patient's serum is used for diagnostic purposes. Procedure: a virus preparation with a predetermined hemagglutinating capacity is mixed with the serum sample; after proper incubation, the residual hemagglutination capacity is measured. Both IgM and IgG antibodies are able to inhibit hemagglutination.
(iii) PCR principle: viral nucleic acid is extracted from the sample material and amplified in three successive steps. Steps of the PCR amplification cycle: (1) denaturation — double-stranded DNA is heat-denatured and separated into single strands; (2) annealing — specific target fragment is amplified by pairs of target-specific oligonucleotide primers, each hybridising to one strand; (3) extension — the hybridised primers act as an origin for heat-stable polymerase enzyme, and a complementary strand is synthesised by sequential addition of deoxyribonucleotides. These cycles are repeated 35–40 times, each resulting in exponentially increasing numbers of copies. Sensitivity: 1–10 copies of viral nucleic acid can be detected in a few hours.
(iv) Two situations requiring cautious interpretation of PCR:
1. PCR cannot distinguish between viable and replication-incompetent (dead) virus — warranting caution in interpretation of results in certain cases.
2. Sensitivity to cross-over contamination in the laboratory has caused some problems in clinical laboratory settings.
(v) Viral antigen detection in clinical specimens: specimens include nasopharyngeal aspirates, faecal specimens, vesicle fluids, tissue specimens, and serum samples. For cell-associated antigens: cells from a clinical specimen are fixed on a glass slide and viral antigens present in the cells are detected by fluorescein-labelled virus-specific antibodies (immunofluorescence). More reliable results are obtained using enzyme immunoassay or time-resolved fluoroimmunoassay (TR-FIA) using europium-labelled monoclonal antibodies. Examples: widely used for respiratory tract infections (influenza, RSV), and a simple test is available for rotavirus and adenovirus antigens in children with gastroenteritis.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Spectrum classification:
- Narrow spectrum: limited range of antibacterial activity; examples: penicillins, erythromycin, polymyxin.
- Broad spectrum: active against a wide range; examples: ampicillin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol.
A(ii) Effect classification:
- Bacteriostatic (inhibit growth without killing): examples: sulphonamides, tetracycline, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, spectinomycin.
- Bactericidal (kill bacteria): examples: cephalosporins, penicillin, aminoglycosides (gentamycin, amikacin, kanamycin, neomycin, streptomycin, tobramycin), bacitracin.
A(iii) Mechanisms of action:
1. Inhibition of cell wall synthesis: inhibition of peptidoglycan formation (vancomycin, bacitracin); interference with cross-linkages of peptidoglycan (cephalosporins, penicillin).
2. Impairment of cell membrane permeability: polymyxins, amphotericin B, nystatin.
3. Inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis by alteration of ribosomes: chloramphenicol, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, erythromycin, lincomycin.
4. Inhibition of bacterial nucleic acid synthesis: novobiocin, pyrimethamine, rifampicin; inhibition of DNA gyrase enzyme — quinolones, nalidixic acid.
5. Competitive inhibition (folate synthesis): sulphonamide competes with PABA; trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking formation of tetrahydrofolic acid necessary for nucleic acid synthesis.
B) Pharmacokinetic factors determine whether a drug is likely to reach the site of infection in adequate concentration. Knowledge of potential side effects and toxicity gives an indication of the extent to which therapeutic concentration can be safely achieved — the therapeutic index should be assessed (the ratio of toxic dose to therapeutic dose; a higher therapeutic index means greater safety margin).
C) Natural (inherent) resistance: bacteria may be inherently resistant to an antibiotic — for example, a streptomycete may have some natural gene responsible for resistance to its own antibiotic; Gram-negative bacteria are inherently resistant to penicillin because their vulnerable cell wall is protected by an outer membrane that prevents permeation of the penicillin molecule. Acquired resistance: bacteria previously sensitive to antibiotics become resistant due to changes in the bacterial genome. Driven by two genetic processes: (1) mutation and selection (vertical evolution) — spontaneous mutation imparts resistance; non-mutants killed by the antibiotic while resistant mutants survive and flourish; (2) exchange of genes between strains and species (horizontal evolution/horizontal gene transmission) — acquisition of resistance genes from another organism via transformation, transduction, or conjugation.

(i) A 28-year-old unvaccinated man returns from forestry work in a yellow-fever-endemic zone. After a mosquito-bite illness with abrupt fever, chills, headache and backache, he improves briefly, then on day 5 develops jaundice, black vomitus, albuminuria and a rising pulse with falling blood pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What is the pathologic basis of the disease as it evolves in this patient?
(iii) Outline the resuscitation and management appropriate at this stage of illness.
(iv) What is the definitive treatment of this condition?
questions.answerText:
1. Diagnosis: Yellow fever, now in the hepatorenal (intoxication) phase.
2. Pathologic basis:
- The mosquito-introduced virus multiplies locally in the skin, then spreads to local lymph nodes, liver, spleen, kidney, bone marrow and myocardium, where it may persist.
- Lesions result from localization and propagation of the virus in these organs, producing necrotic lesions in the liver and kidney and degenerative changes in the spleen, lymph nodes and heart.
- Serious disease is characterised by haemorrhage and circulatory collapse; viral injury to the myocardium may contribute to shock.
3. Resuscitation/management:
- There is no specific antiviral treatment.
- In the late intoxication stage, control bleeding and manage the renal damage.
- Also give care for malaria and bacterial infection, which may complicate the picture.
4. Definitive treatment:
- No specific antiviral drug therapy exists for yellow fever.
- Management remains supportive; prevention is by the 17D live attenuated vaccine, which is not a treatment for established disease.

questions.question:
A patient has a grayish-white exudate strongly adherent to the tonsils and pharynx after a 2-5 day incubation; the illness is later followed by damage to distant organs.
(i) State the diagnosis and the causative organism.
(ii) Explain the pathological basis of the local and systemic disease.
(iii) State the urgent management.
(iv) State the supplementary/definitive treatment, laboratory diagnosis and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae: a Gram-positive, pleomorphic, often club-shaped non-spore-forming rod, occurring only in humans, transmitted by droplets.
(ii) Local infection of tonsils, pharynx, nose and conjunctiva: the organisms multiply and produce a powerful extracellular toxin causing local cell damage; the diphtherial pseudomembrane (fibrin, dead granulocytes, necrotic epithelial cells) adheres strongly to the mucosa.
(ii) Systemic intoxication affects mainly the liver, kidneys, adrenal glands, cardiac muscle and cranial nerves, causing parenchymal degeneration.
(iii) Antitoxic serum therapy is the primary treatment and must begin as soon as diphtheria is suspected.
(iv) Penicillin or erythromycin is given as supplementary treatment.
(iv) Laboratory diagnosis: detection and identification of the organism in cultures from local foci on enriched selective media containing tellurite; toxin detection is necessary because toxin-negative strains occur.
(iv) Prevention: protective immunisation with diphtheria toxoid is the most important measure (extensive vaccination has made it rare).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the fungal cell wall under the headings: composition, the layer providing rigidity and support, and the additional polysaccharides making up the wall matrix.
A(ii) Describe the fungal cell membrane, stating the sterol it contains.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for the selective toxicity of certain antifungal agents against fungi.
B(ii) Distinguish between the basic morphologies of yeasts and moulds.
questions.answerText:
1. The fungal cell wall contains chitin, which provides rigidity and support.
2. The cell wall also contains other polysaccharides, the major ones being glucans, mannans, chitosan, and galactans.
3. The cell wall is similar in structure to that of plants but varies in chemical composition.
4. The fungal cell membrane is similar to the mammalian plasma membrane.
5. The cytoplasmic membrane contains sterols, differing from animal cells by having ergosterol rather than cholesterol.
6. The membrane regulates the passage of materials into and out of the cell by being selectively permeable.
7. The cell membrane's sterol content is what prevents many antibacterial antibiotics from being effective against fungi.
8. Antifungal selectivity is based on this difference in membrane sterol composition between the fungal cell (ergosterol) and the human host cell (cholesterol).
9. Yeasts are unicellular organisms that reproduce by budding (blastoconidia formation) or by binary fission.
10. Continuation of the budding process in yeasts can produce a chain of elongated cells called pseudohyphae.
11. Moulds are multicellular, filamentous fungi that produce hyphae which form a mycelium, with vegetative and aerial hyphae.
12. Moulds reproduce by formation of different types of spores, typically wind-dispersed, whereas yeasts typically grow rapidly within 24-48 hours as moist, mucoid colonies.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male student presents with three days of sore throat, fever, and cervical lymphadenopathy. On examination, tonsillar exudate is present. The clinical team suspects group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection and wishes to confirm this serologically.
(i) Describe what antigen tests and antibody tests are, distinguishing their purpose and the serological evidence each provides.
(ii) Describe how serum is collected for antibody tests, including volume of blood required, handling steps to separate serum, and labelling requirements for the two samples.
(iii) For this patient with suspected streptococcal infection, state the specific serological test used to screen for rises in a named antibody, and the conditions whose diagnosis it supports.
(iv) State the criteria for interpreting a positive antibody test result, and when a single serum specimen is sufficient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Antigen tests: use specific antisera or labelled antibodies to identify microorganisms by detecting their antigens in specimens or isolates; they enable early or presumptive diagnosis; they are rapid, simple to perform, and have good stability. Antibody tests: use known antigen suspensions to detect and measure antibody present in the patient's serum in response to infection; they provide indirect evidence; a significant rise in antibody titre is required to establish a serological diagnosis of most microbial diseases.
(ii) Serum collection for antibody tests: sufficient serum can be obtained for most antibody tests from 4–5 mL of venous blood. Blood is collected in a sterile universal bottle with cap and left to clot; when clotted, serum is separated from the cells using a Pasteur pipette and transferred to a sterile leakproof container. For microtechniques, a smaller volume of blood is adequate and capillary blood collected onto filter paper can be used. Labelling: the first blood sample should be labelled number 1 and the second number 2, and each sample should be dated.
(iii) For suspected streptococcal infection: the specific serological test is the ASO titre (antistreptolysin O). This is used to screen for rises in antistreptolysin O in the diagnosis of rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis, and other complications of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infections.
(iv) Criteria for positive result: at least a 4-fold rise in titre, or a single very high titre of antibody, possibly with specific IgM antibody present, may indicate recent infection. Two serum samples are taken at the acute phase and the convalescent phase (about 10–14 days apart). Single serum specimen is sufficient when testing for IgM antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), HIV infection, or when investigating newborn infants with congenital defects.

questions.question:
A child at a day-care centre develops sudden onset of explosive, watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea, preceded by nausea, loss of appetite and upper gastrointestinal uneasiness; the stools are loose, bulky and greasy, with no blood or mucus.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology?
(iv) How is this condition managed?
questions.answerText:
(i) Giardiasis due to Giardia lamblia (G. duodenalis).
(ii) Predisposing factors include poor personal hygiene, being a child, particularly in institutions or day-care centres, poor sanitation, lack of indoor plumbing, water-borne epidemics from water treatment failures, and travel to developing countries (travellers' diarrhoea).
(iii) The organism colonises the upper portions of the small intestine; the trophozoite absorbs nutrients from the intestinal lumen via pinocytosis and has no specialised feeding organelles; the acute stage usually resolves spontaneously in 3-4 days, but acute infections can also develop into long-standing subacute or chronic infections which in rare cases last for years.
(iv) Metronidazole is the drug of choice; improving personal hygiene, emphasising hand washing, sanitation and food handling are effective controls to reduce person-to-person transmission; treatment of asymptomatic household members prevents reinfection in non-endemic areas; public health measures to protect water supplies from contamination are required, and boiling or iodine treatment kills Giardia cysts, though standard chlorination does not.

1. Structure identified: the thalamus, specifically the dorsomedial thalamus ("hockey stick" sign) and pulvinar (pulvinar sign), features described in variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD).
2. Other structures affected: the cerebral cortex and cerebellum are affected, producing dementia and cerebellar symptoms such as ataxia; involuntary movements such as myoclonic jerks and choreoathetosis also occur.
3. Differential pathologies (prion diseases): Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sporadic and variant forms), kuru, fatal familial insomnia (FFI), and bovine spongiform encephalopathy-related disease.
4. Clinico-anatomical reasoning:
- Fatal familial insomnia affects the thalamus, the part of the brain that controls the sleep-wake cycle, explaining its cardinal features of insomnia, dysautonomia and neurological motor disturbance.
- Cortical and cerebellar involvement in CJD/kuru explains rapidly progressive dementia and ataxia, while spongiform change, neuronal loss and amyloid plaques with prion protein accumulation are the underlying neuropathological findings.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Small obligate intracellular parasites containing DNA, RNA and ribosomes but unable to make their own ATP; replicate by binary fission; rigid Gram-negative-like wall but hard to stain; respond to wide-spectrum antibiotics but not penicillin (lack peptidoglycan).
A(i) Species: Chlamydia trachomatis (humans only), Chlamydophila pneumoniae, C. psittaci; C. trachomatis biovars: trachoma (14 serotypes), LGV (4 serotypes), mouse.
A(ii) Enter through minute abrasions and infect non-ciliated columnar, cuboidal or transitional epithelium (urethra, endocervix, endometrium, fallopian tube, anorectum, respiratory tract, conjunctiva); LGV replicates in mononuclear phagocytes of lymphatics (granuloma, abscess, sinus tracts).
A(ii) Severe inflammatory response; re-infection causes vigorous inflammation with tissue damage; lymphoid follicles and fibrosis; no long-lasting immunity.
A(iii) A-C: trachoma; D-K: urethritis, cervicitis, inclusion conjunctivitis, neonatal conjunctivitis, infant pneumonia; L1-L3: lymphogranuloma venereum.
B(i) Trachoma: chronic suppurative eye disease (follicular conjunctivitis, scar, corneal ulceration, pannus, blindness) spread by hands, clothing, flies or birth canal; leading global cause of blindness.
B(i) Genital infection (D-K): 25% of men asymptomatic (non-gonococcal urethritis); 80% of women asymptomatic with Bartholinitis, cervicitis and PID; adult inclusion conjunctivitis by auto-inoculation; neonatal conjunctivitis from day 4 and infant interstitial pneumonia (afebrile, staccato cough, 10-20%).
B(i) LGV: painless genital lesion, fever, headache, myalgia, painful inguinal buboes that may rupture, proctitis, ulceration or genital elephantiasis; more common in men.
C(i) Damage from re-infection causes blindness and sterility; PID can lead to sterility and ectopic pregnancy.
C(i) C. pneumoniae: atypical pneumonia in 3-10% of adults, bronchitis, sinusitis; detected in atherosclerotic lesions but its role is unclear.
C(i) Diagnosis: cytology of stained scrapings for inclusion bodies, culture, IgM serology; NAATs for C. pneumoniae.
C(i) Treatment: azithromycin 1 g single dose, or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, erythromycin, ofloxacin or levofloxacin, with improved sanitation.

questions.answerText:
A. Gross anatomical divisions:
(i) Infection of the CNS may be diffuse or focal;
Meningitis implies primary infection of the meninges (the sheaths covering the brain and spinal cord), encephalitis indicates brain parenchymal involvement,
Brain abscess is the best example of a focal infection.
B. Relation of zones to pathology:
- Many patients have both meningeal and parenchymal involvement, termed meningoencephalitis.
- Viral (aseptic) meningitis is far commoner than bacterial (septic) meningitis and usually resolves without treatment.
Encephalitis presents with symptoms ranging from slight confusion to coma, with CSF showing fewer inflammatory (PMN) cells than meningitis.
C. Spread to a distant structure and functional deficit:
- Viruses gain access to the CNS by the haematogenous route (common for arthropod-borne viruses such as EEV, WEV and West Nile virus) or the neuronal route (as with HSV and rabies).
- Rabies virus travelling along peripheral nerves ultimately reaches the brainstem and other CNS structures.
This illustrates spread from a peripheral site to a distant CNS structure, with resulting brain damage and death as a severe functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. The discovery of hantaviruses dates back to 1951-1953, when United Nations troops were deployed during the border conflict between North and South Korea.
2. Hantaviruses cycle in rodent hosts, and humans become infected by coming into contact with rodent urine.
3. Rodents are persistently infected with hantaviruses but show no clinical signs; the virus is transmitted from rodent to rodent through biting, scratching, and possible aerosolisation of rodent urine.
4. Hantaviruses are divided into two groups based on location: Old World viruses are found in eastern Europe and eastern Asia, while New World viruses are found in North and South America.
5. Hantaviruses generally cause one of two clinical presentations: haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), generally caused by Old World hantaviruses, or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), generally caused by New World hantaviruses.
6. The incubation period is 7 to 21 days, followed by a clinical phase of 3-5 days; severity of illness depends on the virus, with case-fatality varying between 1 and 50%.
7. Steps for prevention in rodent-borne disease include control of rodent populations, discouraging their entry into homes, and safe clean-up of nesting areas and droppings.
8. In haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, the liver and vascular endothelium are targeted, with symptoms including haemorrhage, acute renal failure, and fever, and a mortality rate of over 15%.
9. In hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, the lungs are targeted, with symptoms including fever and acute respiratory distress, and a mortality rate of over 50%.
10. Shock and cardiac complications often contribute to death in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.
11. Rodent populations are affected by climatic conditions; warmer winters and increased rainfall make it more likely for rodent populations to survive, increasing the number of rodent reservoirs for disease, while increased rainfall accompanied by flooding can also increase human-to-rodent contact.
12. Inadequate hygiene and sanitation, as seen in some African countries, also contribute to increased rodent populations and higher risks of rodent-borne disease transmission, underscoring why rodent control and sanitation are the key preventive measures.
questions.question:

A(i) Describe the structure of endotoxin, under the headings: location, chemical composition, and the component responsible for toxicity.
A(ii) Describe the structure of exotoxins, stating their chemical nature and site of release.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why endotoxin produces non-specific effects such as fever in the host.
B(ii) Distinguish between exotoxins and endotoxins.
questions.answerText:
1. Endotoxins are an intracellular and cell-associated integral part of the Gram-negative cell wall, and are lipopolysaccharides.
2. Endotoxin is made up of toxic lipid A, an immunogenic polysaccharide core, and an antigenic O-linked series of oligosaccharides; the active part is lipid A, buried in the cell wall and released only with cell lysis.
3. Endotoxin is released from growing bacterial cells and from cells lysed as a result of effective host defence, such as lysozyme activity, or the activity of certain antibiotics such as penicillins and cephalosporins.
4. Exotoxins are bacterial products that are protein in nature, released from bacterial cells during exponential growth, and may act at tissue sites removed from the site of bacterial growth.
5. Exotoxins are produced by both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, are polypeptides with a molecular weight of 10,000-900,000, and are relatively unstable, with toxicity often destroyed rapidly by heating above 60 degrees Celsius.
6. Exotoxins are highly antigenic, stimulate formation of high-titre antitoxin which neutralises the toxin, and can be converted to antigenic, non-toxic toxoids by formalin, acid or heat, as with tetanus toxoid used for immunisation.
7. Endotoxin's toxic effects are pyrogenicity, complement activation, leukopenia/leukocytosis, and mitogenicity, and its complications are sepsis and shock.
8. Endotoxin usually produces fever in the host by the release of interleukin-1 and other mediators, and does not act through specific receptors on cells, unlike exotoxins which usually bind to specific receptors.
9. This non-specific, receptor-independent action, combined with the fact that endotoxin is a structural component shared by all Gram-negative bacteria rather than a specific secreted product, explains why its clinical effects (fever, shock, diarrhoea) are similar regardless of the infecting species.
10. Endotoxin is relatively stable, withstanding heating above 60 degrees Celsius for hours without loss of toxicity, and is not converted to toxoids.
11. Endotoxin is weakly immunogenic and its antibodies are antitoxic and protective, but the relationship between antibody titres and protection from disease is less clear than with exotoxin; endotoxin synthesis is directed by chromosomal genes, whereas exotoxin production is frequently controlled by extrachromosomal genes such as plasmids.
12. Exotoxins are moderately to highly toxic (fatal in microgram quantities) and specific in action, whereas endotoxin is moderately toxic (fatal in tens to hundreds of micrograms) and non-specific in action, causing fever, hypotension, shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

questions.question:
A) Describe the chemical methods of disinfection under the following headings:
A(i) Define disinfectants, antiseptics, chemisterilants, and microbicidal agents.
A(ii) Classify disinfectants based on three criteria, giving an example for each subgroup.
B) Describe the factors that influence the sterilization and disinfection process, listing all six factors.
C) Explain the six elements that define the epidemiology of HAIs and justify, using figures, why sterilization and disinfection are critical components of hospital infection control.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definitions:
- Disinfectants: agents applied to inanimate objects to destroy pathogenic bacteria; do not necessarily sterilize.
- Antiseptics: substances applied to skin (safe for living tissues).
- Chemisterilants: chemicals that can sterilize (achieve destruction of all forms of life).
- Microbicidal: any substance or process that kills germs (bacteria, viruses, and other microorganisms).
A(ii) Classification of disinfectants:
1. Based on consistency:
- Liquid — e.g., alcohols, phenols.
- Gaseous — e.g., formaldehyde vapour, ethylene oxide.
2. Based on spectrum of activity:
- High level, intermediate level, low level.
3. Based on mechanism of action:
- Action on membrane — e.g., alcohol, detergent.
- Denaturation of cellular proteins — e.g., alcohol, phenol.
B) Six factors influencing sterilization and disinfection:
1. The resistance of the microorganisms present.
2. Amount of bioburden present.
3. The nature of the items to be processed.
4. Access of the sterilizing agent to the items to be processed.
5. The function and use of the sterilizer or the disinfectant.
6. Resistance of the microbes (listed separately).
C) HAI epidemiology: at any one time, up to 7% of patients in developed countries and 10% of patients in developing countries will be affected by at least one HAI; HAIs are among the major causes of death and increased morbidity among hospitalised patients; organisms causing nosocomial infections can be transmitted to the community through discharged patients, staff and visitors; the economic costs are considerable — increased length of stay for infected patients is the greatest contributor to cost. Sterilization and disinfection are basic components of hospital infection control activities; failure to properly disinfect or sterilize equipment carries risk of infection and transmission of pathogens (e.g., hepatitis B virus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa); they have drastically reduced deaths due to infections and reduced the occurrence of nosocomial infections.

questions.question:
(i) A child bitten by an unvaccinated dog three weeks earlier presents with hydrophobia, apprehension and hypersalivation. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Name a procedure that can be performed on this patient to support the diagnosis.
(iii) State the anatomical landmarks relevant to this procedure.
(iv) What nerve/structure is primarily at risk in the pathogenesis of this disease?
questions.answerText:
1. Diagnosis: Rabies, encephalitic (furious) form.
2. Procedure: skin biopsy, examined for rabies antigen by immunofluorescence.
3. Anatomical landmarks: the biopsy targets the cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles, where viral antigen is detected.
4. Nerve/structure at risk:
- Peripheral motor and sensory nerve fibres, along which the virus travels by retrograde axonal transport to the CNS.
- Within the CNS, replication occurs mainly in the basal ganglia, pons and medulla, with Negri bodies found especially in pyramidal cells of Ammon's horn of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex.

(i) Leprosy (Hansen's disease), caused by Mycobacterium leprae (and M. lepromatosis): a chronic disease mainly of the skin and peripheral nerves, not highly contagious, not grown on artificial media; acquired by inhalation after prolonged contact or possibly through the skin.
(ii) M. leprae grows best in cooler tissues (skin, peripheral nerves, anterior chamber of the eye, upper respiratory tract, testes) and binds Schwann cells, causing demyelination and loss of axonal conduction; small sensory and autonomic fibres are damaged, giving anaesthesia, muscle paralysis and destruction of repeatedly injured areas.
(ii) Tuberculoid leprosy: few localised lesions, epithelioid granulomas, few or no bacilli, most benign, good cell-mediated immunity; lepromatous leprosy: numerous confluent lesions, many bacilli in foamy macrophages (globi), diffuse skin, mucosal, eye, nerve, node and organ involvement, loss of eyebrows, flat nose from cartilage destruction.
(ii) WHO groups: paucibacillary (5 or fewer lesions, negative smear) and multibacillary (more than 5 lesions, positive smear).
(iii) Diagnosis: examine skin, count patches, test sensation, look for nerve damage; leprosy is diagnosed with a lesion and definite sensory loss or positive skin smears; slit-skin smear or biopsy for globi; modified Fite stain (acid-fast, best at below 37 C); early diagnosis prevents permanent deformity.
(iv) Definitive treatment: multidrug therapy with rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine for 6 months (paucibacillary) or 12 months (multibacillary); patients are non-infectious after the first monthly dose; rifampicin-resistant leprosy: fluoroquinolones, minocycline or clarithromycin for 24 months.
(iv) Prevention: a single dose of rifampicin for close contacts over 2 years old without leprosy or tuberculosis.

questions.answerText:
A. Structure of HIV:
(i) Envelope: the virion is enveloped and spherical, 80–100 nm in diameter, with surface projections/spikes made of glycoprotein (gp120 receptor-binding and gp41 transmembrane, together gp160) dispersed evenly over the surface.
(ii) Capsid/matrix: the matrix protein (MA, p17) and capsid protein (CA, p24) form the internal structural proteins, along with the nucleoprotein (NC).
(iii) Genome and enzymes: the genome is +ssRNA, single-stranded, dimeric, 7000–11,000 nucleotides per monomer;
The genome carries the reverse transcriptase (RT), protease (PR) and integrase (IN) enzymes, encoded by the pol gene, alongside gag and env genes and six minor genes (vif, vpu, vpr, tat, rev, nef).
B. Clinical basis for antiretroviral drug classes:
- Different classes of antiretroviral drugs act at different stages of the HIV replication cycle: reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors and entry inhibitors, each targeting a specific viral structural component.
- A combination of several (typically three or four) antiretroviral drugs, known as highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), is used.
C. Distinguishing HIV-1 from HIV-2:
- HIV-1 and HIV-2 differ by 60% in genetic make-up, with the major difference in the env glycoproteins; co-infection of an individual by both viruses is possible.
- HIV-2 has lower perinatal (0.4–1.2% vs 25–35%) and sexual transmission rates, slower progression to AIDS (<0.5%/year vs 3–5%/year),
A distribution limited to West Africa, compared with the worldwide distribution of HIV-1.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the envelope of HIV.
A(ii) Describe the capsid/matrix proteins of HIV.
A(iii) Describe the genome and enzymes of HIV.
B. Explain the clinical basis for the different classes of antiretroviral drugs in relation to viral structure.
C. Distinguish between HIV-1 and HIV-2.

A) Describe the roles of specific healthcare personnel in preventing HAIs under the following headings:
A(i) The role of the physician — list all 10 responsibilities.
A(ii) The role of the microbiologist — list all 8 responsibilities.
A(iii) The role of nursing staff — list all 8 responsibilities.
B) Explain the concept of clinical risk management in the context of HAIs, defining risk, describing the IPC Risk Assessment process, and stating when risk assessment should be triggered.
C) Describe the role of the hospital pharmacist in HAI prevention, and explain the challenge created by the "illusion" that HAIs are inevitable complications of care rather than preventable adverse events.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Role of the physician (10 responsibilities):
1. Providing direct patient care using practices which minimise infection.
2. Following appropriate practice of hygiene (e.g. handwashing, isolation).
3. Serving on the IPC Committee and supporting the infection control team.
4. Protecting their own patients from other infected patients and from hospital staff who may be infected.
5. Complying with the practices approved by the IPC Committee.
6. Obtaining appropriate microbiological specimens when an infection is present or suspected.
7. Notifying cases of hospital-acquired infection to the team, and the admission of infected patients.
8. Complying with the recommendations of the Antimicrobial Use Committee regarding use of antibiotics.
9. Advising patients, visitors and staff on techniques to prevent the transmission of infection.
10. Instituting appropriate treatment for any infections they themselves have and taking steps to prevent such infections being transmitted to others, especially patients.
A(ii) Role of the microbiologist (8 responsibilities):
1. Handling patient and staff specimens to maximise the likelihood of a microbiological diagnosis.
2. Developing guidelines for appropriate collection, transport, and handling of specimens.
3. Ensuring laboratory practices meet appropriate standards.
4. Ensuring safe laboratory practice to prevent infections in staff.
5. Performing antimicrobial susceptibility testing following internationally recognised methods, and providing summary reports of prevalence of resistance.
6. Monitoring sterilization, disinfection, and the environment where necessary.
7. Timely communication of results to the IPC Committee or the hygiene officer.
8. Epidemiological typing of hospital microorganisms where necessary.
A(iii) Role of nursing staff (8 responsibilities):
1. Participating fully in the IPC Committee.
2. Promoting the development and improvement of nursing techniques and ongoing review of aseptic nursing policies, in association with the IPC Committee.
3. Developing training programmes for members of the nursing staff.
4. Supervising implementation of techniques for prevention of infections in specialised areas (operating suite, ICU, maternity unit, newborns unit).
5. Maintaining hygiene consistent with hospital policies and good nursing practice on the ward.
6. Monitoring aseptic techniques, including handwashing and use of isolation.
7. Reporting promptly to the attending physician any evidence of infection in patients under the nurse's care.
8. Initiating patient isolation and ordering culture specimens from any patient showing signs of a communicable disease when the physician is not immediately available.
B) Clinical risk management: defined as reducing the probability of negative patient outcomes by systematically assessing, reviewing, and seeking ways to prevent occurrence of HAIs. Risk: defined as the combination of the probability of occurrence of a hazard generating harm in a given scenario and the severity of that harm. IPC Risk Assessment: describes the infection risk unique to a particular institution; helps assess complexity and define actions to reduce effects; infection risks can originate from lack of hand hygiene, unsafe injection practices, poor cleaning/disinfection/sterilization, and inadequate environmental cleaning. A risk scoring system categorises risk as high, medium, or low; risk assessment is an ongoing process as infection risk changes over time. Triggers for risk assessment: when a new IPC service is established; when a new piece of clinical equipment or instrument is procured; when a new procedure or diagnostic test is implemented; when a problem in IPC practice or policy is identified; at least annually to re-evaluate IPC programme priorities.
C) Role of the hospital pharmacist: obtaining, storing and distributing pharmaceutical preparations limiting potential transmission of infectious agents; dispensing anti-infectious drugs and maintaining relevant records (potency, incompatibility, conditions of storage and deterioration); obtaining and storing vaccines/sera; providing the Antimicrobial Use Committee and IPC Committee with summary reports and trends of antimicrobial use; having available information on disinfectants, antiseptics and other anti-infectious agents; participating in development of guidelines for antiseptics, disinfectants, and handwashing products. The illusion: it has been proposed that the difference in approach toward HAIs (treating them as complications rather than preventable events) originates from factors such as the widespread belief that antimicrobials can solve all infection-related problems, the weakness of evidence supporting HAI-preventing interventions, the sense of responsibility felt by healthcare staff, and the perceived intractability of the problem. With this mindset, HAIs pose a significant challenge to the way clinical risk management is deployed in healthcare systems; HAIs are injuries related to management of care processes rather than complications of disease.

questions.question:
With reference to the migration of Trichinella spiralis larvae in the host:
A(i) Describe the origin of the infection.
A(ii) Describe the course of the larvae once ingested pork is digested.
A(iii) Describe the relations of the resulting adult worms and their larvae to host tissues.
A(iv) Describe the further stage/branch of this course involving fetal infection.
A(v) Describe the distribution of clinical effects that result from this tissue migration.
B) State the relevant procedure used in the laboratory diagnosis of this condition.
C) Explain the anatomical basis of the finding that is diagnostic of this condition on examination of the eyes.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pigs are the most important carriers and get infected by eating raw infected meat of other animals; humans get infected when they consume raw or undercooked pork.
A(ii) When the pork is digested, the cysts are released and the larvae migrate to the small intestine, where they develop into male and female worms, which mate to produce more larvae.
A(iii) The later larvae gain access into the bloodstream via the lymphatics and are spread over the tissues of the body, especially the muscles; encysted larvae can live up to 20 years in the body.
A(iv) The larvae rarely pass through the placenta to cause fetal infection.
A(v) Two to twelve days after eating undercooked pork, signs and symptoms depend on the tissues grossly affected; if the gastrointestinal tract is involved, diarrhoea or constipation may occur, followed by fever, muscle pain, periorbital oedema and eosinophilia; migration of larvae to the heart and brain may lead to congestive heart failure and central nervous system symptoms.
B) The relevant procedure for laboratory diagnosis is muscle biopsy, which may reveal the worms within muscle fibres.
C) Subconjunctival haemorrhages are diagnostic, reflecting the anatomical route by which migrating larvae spread through the vascular tissues of the body, including the delicate vasculature beneath the conjunctiva.
C) If the gastrointestinal tract is involved during the initial intestinal phase, diarrhoea or constipation may occur, reflecting the origin of this migratory process in the small intestine.
C) Fever, muscle pain and periorbital oedema follow, reflecting the spread of larvae into the muscle tissues and periorbital region of the body.
C) Migration of larvae to the heart and brain may lead to congestive heart failure and central nervous system symptoms, and death usually results from congestive cardiac failure and respiratory failure, illustrating the most severe anatomical consequence of this tissue migration.
C) Steroids plus mebendazole are used in treatment, with thiabendazole used in early infection to kill the intestinal worms before this tissue migration is complete.
C) The disease is worldwide in distribution but occurs especially in West Africa and Eastern Europe, wherever raw or undercooked pork is a source of infection.

(i) Candidaemia (Candida septicaemia)/invasive candidiasis.
(ii) Predisposing factors for invasive candidiasis include neutropenia (especially for more than 7 days), haematological or solid tumour malignancy, postsurgical intensive care admission, prolonged intravenous catheterisation, broad-spectrum or multiple antibiotic therapy, diabetes mellitus, parenteral nutrition, severe burns, being a neonate, corticosteroid therapy, and intravenous drug abuse.
(iii) Haematogenous dissemination may occur to one or more organ systems with formation of numerous microabscesses (disseminated candidiasis); Candida species have been reported to cause up to 15% of cases of sepsis in hospital patients; associated disseminated disease includes arthritis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, endocarditis and retinitis.
(iv)
- The underlying condition should be corrected first, for example removal of an implicated intravenous catheter.
- Treatment options include oral fluconazole, echinocandins, and amphotericin B with 5-flucytosine.
- Correcting the underlying condition is justified first because predisposing factors such as catheterisation and neutropenia are what allow the yeast to gain access to and persist in the bloodstream.

(i) A neutropenic patient on chemotherapy develops fever, cough and pleuritic pain with imaging suggestive of invasive pulmonary disease, while a separate patient with a history of tuberculosis is found incidentally to have a fungus ball in a pre-formed lung cavity on routine chest X-ray. Identify the organ affected in both cases and the two clinical forms described.
(ii) State the structures that may become affected if the disease disseminates.
(iii) List the differential clinical forms of pulmonary disease caused by this organism.
(iv) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning for why the fungus ball forms in a pre-formed cavity while invasive disease occurs in the neutropenic patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) The lungs are affected in both cases; this is aspergillosis, caused by species of Aspergillus, with the two forms being acute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis and non-invasive aspergillosis (aspergilloma, or fungus ball).
(ii) If the disease disseminates, abscesses may occur in the brain (cerebral aspergillosis), kidney (renal aspergillosis), heart (endocarditis, myocarditis), bone (osteomyelitis) and gastrointestinal tract, and ocular lesions (mycotic keratitis, endophthalmitis, orbital aspergilloma) may also occur.
(iii) The clinical forms of pulmonary aspergillosis include allergic aspergillosis (ranging from extrinsic asthma to allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis), non-invasive aspergillosis (aspergilloma), and acute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
(iv)
- Non-invasive aspergillosis (aspergilloma) is caused by saprophytic colonisation of pre-formed cavities usually secondary to tuberculosis or sarcoidosis; many cases are asymptomatic and found by routine chest X-ray, though haemoptysis may occur.
- Acute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is predisposed to by prolonged neutropenia, especially in leukaemia patients or bone marrow transplant recipients, and by corticosteroid therapy and cytotoxic chemotherapy; it is the most common form of aspergillosis in the immunosuppressed patient, and symptoms may mimic acute bacterial pneumonia.

questions.question:
(i) An immunocompromised patient presents with fever, a productive cough, weight loss and night sweats, and is found to have hepatosplenomegaly, with a history of exposure to soil contaminated with bird and bat droppings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the predisposing factors for this condition.
(iii) Outline the pathophysiology of this condition, from the route of entry to dissemination.
(iv) Outline the management of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Histoplasmosis (disseminated histoplasmosis), caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.
(ii) Predisposing/risk factors include a large inoculum, extremes of age, immunocompromise, and underlying emphysema; the incidence of H. capsulatum is high in soils enriched with bird and bat droppings.
(iii)
- Transmission is by inhalation of conidia of the fungus.
- Conidia develop into yeasts, are engulfed by and replicate within macrophages, and spread via the reticuloendothelial system (RES).
- This produces a granulomatous inflammatory reaction; nodules may heal with calcification, or reactivation may be precipitated by pulmonary damage.
- Clinically ill patients generally have acute pulmonary, chronic pulmonary, or disseminated disease; if untreated, the disseminated form is usually fatal.
(iv) Treatment is with itraconazole or amphotericin B; diagnosis is supported by history, microscopy of stained specimens, culture on selective media with conversion of the mould form to the yeast phase, or serologic testing (immunodiffusion and/or complement fixation).

questions.question:
A medical student is tested positive for Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) during a routine medical school screen. He is asymptomatic but further tests reveal persistent HBsAg positivity for over 8 months.
(i) State the diagnosis and distinguish between acute and chronic hepatitis B infection based on duration.
(ii) Describe the structure of the hepatitis B virus, naming the antigens/serological markers and the unusual enzymatic property of this virus.
(iii) List the routes of transmission of HBV.
(iv) List all the complications of chronic HBV infection and describe the treatment options.
questions.answerText:
(i) Chronic hepatitis B infection. Acute hepatitis B infection lasts less than six months; most adults with acute infection have acute disease but it can lead to chronic infection. Chronic hepatitis B infection lasts six months or longer; it may last a lifetime, possibly leading to serious illnesses such as cirrhosis and liver cancer. The younger the patient when infected (particularly newborns or children younger than 5), the higher the risk of chronicity.
(ii) HBV structure: HBV (Dane particle) is 42 nm in diameter; the virions are unusually stable for an enveloped virus. Genome is small, circular, partly double-stranded DNA of only 3200 bases; although a DNA virus, it encodes a reverse transcriptase and replicates through an RNA intermediate. It includes a protein kinase and a polymerase as well as a P protein attached to the genome, all surrounded by an icosahedral capsid formed by Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg). Important antigens/serological markers: HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen), HBeAg, HBcAg.
(iii) Routes of transmission: sexual contact (blood, saliva, semen, or vaginal secretions); sharing of needles (syringes contaminated with infected blood); mother to child during childbirth; blood transfusion (also via semen, saliva, milk, vaginal and menstrual secretions, amniotic fluid). It does not spread by sneezing or coughing.
(iv) Complications: scarring of the liver (cirrhosis — impairs liver's ability to function); liver cancer (increased risk); liver failure (acute liver failure requiring liver transplant); other conditions including kidney disease or inflammation of blood vessels. Treatment: Hepatitis B immune globulin may be administered within a week of exposure and to newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers to prevent and ameliorate disease. Chronic HBV: drugs targeted at the polymerase — lamivudine, entecavir, telbivudine or tenofovir (HIV reverse transcriptase inhibitors), or nucleoside analogues adefovir dipivoxil and famciclovir; pegylated interferon-α.

A) The lymphatic system is a network of vessels that collect fluid that leaks out of the blood into tissues (lymph); the thoracic duct redirects lymph back into the bloodstream.
A) Adult worms live in the lymphatics and lymph nodes, growing over approximately 9 months to mature worms that can live 5-7 years, occasionally up to 15 years.
A) Females release up to 10,000 microfilariae per day into the bloodstream.
B) The most common areas affected by acute adenolymphangitis are the inguinal nodes and the lower extremities, though the upper extremities and breast can also be affected.
B) Chronic lymphoedema is mostly seen in the lower extremities and inguinal region, initially as pitting oedema with gradual hardening of tissues, hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis.
B) The genitalia can be affected, producing hydroceles.
C) Renal involvement can occur, with chyluria (lymph discharge into urine) and loss of fat and protein causing hypoproteinaemia, and haematuria and proteinuria from possible immune complex nephritis, illustrating spread of lymphatic pathology to a distant structure, the kidney.
C) Secondary bacterial/fungal infections can also occur in the oedematous (elephantiasic) areas.
C) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, a hyperresponsiveness to microfilariae trapped in the lungs causing nocturnal wheezing, is a further distant (pulmonary) functional deficit arising from this lymphatic parasitic disease.
C) Filarial fever, fever without lymphangitis, can also occur as a systemic manifestation of this disease process.
C) Peripheral blood eosinophilia is common in this condition and may exceed 3000 per microlitre, a further systemic (haematologic) reflection of the underlying lymphatic pathology.

questions.answerText:
(i) Septic arthritis; the hip is often the site of infection in infants.
(ii) Septic arthritis develops when bacteria or other microorganisms spread through the bloodstream to a joint; it may also occur when the joint is directly infected with a microorganism from an injury or during surgery.
(iii) Management focuses on adequate and timely drainage of the infected synovial fluid, administration of appropriate antimicrobial therapy, and immobilisation of the joint to control pain; a needle aspirate is generally used initially, repeated frequently enough to prevent significant re-accumulation of fluid.
(iv) If frequent drainage is necessary, surgical drainage becomes more attractive; antibiotics are used to treat the infection, and once the patient's condition responds adequately (after about 5 days of treatment), gentle mobilisation and aggressive physical therapy are used to allow maximum post-infection joint function.

A malnourished patient (or one with a viral infection) develops an ulcerative gingivostomatitis with ulcers of the mouth and tonsillar areas.
(i) State the diagnosis and the organisms.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iv) State the diagnosis and management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Vincent's angina (ulcerative gingivostomatitis or oropharyngitis) caused by Borrelia vincentii with fusiform bacteria (Fusobacterium fusiforme).
(ii) Predisposing conditions: malnutrition and viral infections.
(iii) B. vincentii is a Gram-negative obligate anaerobe found as a normal commensal in the mouth; under these conditions it produces the ulcerative condition.
(iv) Diagnosis: demonstration of B. vincentii and fusiform bacteria in stained smears of exudate from the lesion (Giemsa, Leishman); it grows with difficulty anaerobically on enriched media.
(iv) Treatment: penicillin and metronidazole are effective.

A. Origin, course and distribution:
(i) Origin: the virus is introduced by a mosquito through the skin, where it multiplies locally.
(ii) Course: it spreads to the local lymph nodes, liver, spleen, kidney, bone marrow and myocardium, where it may persist for days.
(iii) Distribution: the virus is present in the blood early during infection, and the patient is viraemic and a source of infection for mosquitoes during this initial period.
B. Safe practice:
- Most countries insist on vaccination at least 10 days before arrival in or from an endemic zone, and on mosquito control on airplanes.
- Vaccination is contraindicated in infants younger than 9 months of age, during pregnancy, in persons with egg allergies,
In persons with altered immune systems (e.g. HIV infection with low CD4 counts, malignancy, organ transplantation).
C. Anatomical basis of the hepatorenal deformity:
- The lesions of yellow fever are caused by localisation and propagation of the virus in a particular organ, resulting in necrotic lesions in the liver and kidney.
- Degenerative changes also occur in the spleen, lymph nodes and heart,
The hepatorenal phase is characterised by rising temperature, jaundice, albuminuria and haemorrhagic symptoms, with virus injury to the myocardium contributing to shock.

A 35-year-old male with known HIV infection presents with high-grade fever, productive cough, progressive dyspnoea, and hypoxia. He is on no antiretroviral medication. On examination, breath sounds are reduced bilaterally. A chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify the causative organism.
(ii) Describe the pathological basis of this patient's increased susceptibility to this infection, linking it to his underlying condition.
(iii) List the baseline investigations that should be carried out in this patient.
(iv) State the most frequent reason for negative blood cultures in patients on treatment, and describe the definitive treatment approach.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), caused by Pneumocystis jiroveci. In HIV-positive patients, more than 75% of PUOs are due to infective causes; a patient with a low CD4 count who presents with progressive dyspnoea, a nonproductive cough and hypoxia should have evaluation for pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP).
(ii) Immunocompromised patients — those with chronic disease such as malignant tumours, leukaemia, diabetes mellitus, renal failure, or AIDS — have increased susceptibility to infections with opportunistic pathogens. Opportunistic pathogens are organisms that are normally innocuous or part of the normal bacterial flora but may become pathogenic when the body's immunological defences are compromised. Immunosuppressive drugs or irradiation may lower resistance to infection.
(iii) Baseline investigations: full blood count with differential cell count; renal electrolytes; liver function tests; C-reactive protein (CRP); erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR); clotting time; creatinine kinase; blood cultures (while not receiving antibiotics); HIV test; chest X-ray.
(iv) Previous antibiotic therapy is the most frequent reason for negative blood cultures. For definitive treatment: treatment is directed to the cause; appropriate antimicrobial agents should be chosen based on antimicrobial susceptibility testing; in life-threatening infections in hospital, antimicrobial treatment is indicated as soon as the specimen has been collected.

1. Diagnosis: Bulbar paralytic poliomyelitis.
2. Procedure: viral isolation from the throat (useful in the first week of illness) or from stool (useful for several weeks); paired serology may also be used.
3. Anatomical landmarks: the anterior horn of the spinal cord and the motor nuclei of the pons and medulla are the sites of extensive neuronal necrosis in poliomyelitis.
4. Nerves/structures at risk:
- Paralysis of muscles innervated by cranial nerves IX, X and XII, with cranial nerves IX and X most commonly affected, producing dysphagia, nasal speech and dyspnea.
- The vasomotor and respiratory centres can also be involved, leading to rapid pulse, hypoxia and circulatory collapse.

questions.answerText:
(i) Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection — a papovaviridae, subfamily Papillomavirinae. Over 100 types recognized. Risk classification:
- High risk for malignancy: small number of virus types producing lesions at high risk of progression to malignancy (e.g., cervical carcinoma).
- Intermediate risk: mucosal lesions that progress to malignancy with lower frequency, causing anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata) and laryngeal papillomas.
- Benign only: virus types associated only with benign lesions (common, flat, and plantar warts).
(ii) Transmission requires direct contact with infected individuals (sexual contact) or contaminated surfaces such as communal bathroom floors; also transmitted from mother to infant during passage down the birth canal via epithelial surface lesions such as abrasions. HPV specifically infects only surface epithelia of skin and mucous membranes; the maintenance of infection occurs in cells of the basal layer of the skin; the virus replication cycle proceeds in parallel with the steps of keratinocyte differentiation.
(iii) Pathogenesis of malignant transformation: progression to malignancy is associated with a limited number of papillomavirus types on mucosal surfaces. Two early viral proteins interact with and inactivate two cellular anti-oncoproteins: p53 (cellular growth suppressor protein) and pRb (retinoblastoma gene product). The affinity of binding between viral early proteins and p53 and pRb correlates with high risk for malignant progression. However, this interaction is only the first step; a multistep process involving alterations in expression of other cell oncoproteins and anti-oncoproteins follows, and at some point non–site-specific integration of part of the viral genome into a host cell chromosome occurs.
(iv) Laboratory identification: diagnosis of cutaneous warts involves visual inspection. For genital tract lesions: (1) determine whether HPV is present in abnormal tissue from biopsy or cervical swab; (2) determine whether the HPV type is high risk for progression to malignancy. There is no tissue culture system for recovery of the virus; HPV types are defined by molecular criteria, so typing is done by DNA hybridization reactions using defined, type-specific nucleic acid probes.
(v) Treatment and prevention: surgical removal or destruction of wart tissue with liquid nitrogen, laser vaporization, or cytotoxic chemicals (podophyllin or trichloroacetic acid); cidofovir (inhibitor of DNA synthesis — effective topically); interferon given orally causes regression of laryngeal papillomas; common warts often regress spontaneously. Prevention: all procedures for prevention of sexually transmitted diseases (safe sex practices); vaccination (HPV vaccine).

questions.answerText:
1. Diagnosis: Dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF)/dengue shock syndrome (DSS).
2. Pathologic basis:
- The second dengue infection causes an anamnestic response of dengue subgroup-specific antibodies; virus-antibody complexes form and non-neutralising enhancing antibodies promote infection of higher numbers of mononuclear cells.
- This is followed by release of cytokines, vasoactive mediators and pro-coagulants, leading to increased vascular permeability with plasma leakage into interstitial spaces, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
- Complement activation from immune complexes liberates toxic substances that cause vasodilation and hypovolaemic shock.
3. Resuscitation/management: dengue haemorrhagic fever can be treated by fluid replacement therapy for the hypovolaemic shock.
4. Definitive treatment: there is no antiviral drug therapy for dengue and no widely available licensed vaccine, so fluid replacement remains the mainstay of management.
questions.question:
