questions.answerText:
(i) Cryptococcal meningitis, caused by Cryptococcus neoformans (an encapsulated yeast).
(ii) Predisposing factors include AIDS, haematological malignancies, and immunosuppressive therapy.
(iii) The normal habitat of Cryptococcus is soil rich in organic substances, and it is very frequently found in bird (pigeon) droppings; transmission is by inhalation of yeasts, needlestick injury, or organ transplant; the portal of entry is the respiratory tract, and the organism is inhaled into the lungs before spreading haematogenously, showing a pronounced affinity for the central nervous system.
(iv) Treatment is with amphotericin B plus 5-flucytosine, followed by fluconazole, together with pressure management; diagnosis is supported by India ink preparation of cerebrospinal fluid (which demonstrates the capsule), culture, and the cryptococcal antigen (CRAG) test on serum and CSF.

A(i) Describe the source, reservoir and species of Brucella.
A(ii) Describe the routes of infection and the course of the disease.
A(iii) Describe the clinical features and treatment.
B(i) State the control measures.
C(i) Explain the basis of the chronic and multi-organ nature of the disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Brucellae are obligate parasites of animals and humans and characteristically intracellular pathogens (small Gram-negative coccoid bacilli needing blood products).
A(i) Reservoirs by species: B. melitensis - goats; B. suis - swine; B. abortus - cattle; B. canis - dogs.
A(ii) Common routes: intestinal tract (ingestion of infected milk), mucous membranes (droplets) and skin (contact with infected animal tissues).
A(ii) Disease brucellosis (undulant or Malta fever): an acute bacteraemic phase followed by a chronic stage that may extend over many years.
A(iii) Incubation 1-4 weeks; insidious onset with malaise, fever, weakness, aches and sweats.
A(iii) Susceptible to tetracyclines, rifampin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, aminoglycosides and some quinolones.
B(i) Control rests on limiting spread and possible eradication of animal infection, and pasteurisation of milk and milk products.
C(i) The chronic, multi-organ course of brucellosis reflects the intracellular habit of Brucella, which allows it to persist in tissues and organs over many years.
C(i) Related zoonoses in the same group: Pasteurella multocida (animal bite wounds; penicillin G drug of choice) and Francisella tularensis (tularaemia from rodents by contact or blood-sucking insects; streptomycin or gentamicin).
C(i) Bordetella pertussis, also a parvobacterium, causes whooping cough in humans, the only natural hosts.
C(i) All parvobacteria need blood or blood products for growth.

1. Organ/structure identified: the central nervous system (CNS), the target of West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease.
2. Structures affected: meningitis, encephalitis, and, more rarely, acute flaccid paralysis described as "West Nile polio-like paralysis," with poliomyelitis literally meaning inflammation of the spinal cord.
3. Differential arboviral pathologies:
- St Louis encephalitis (also mosquito-borne, birds as reservoir, man usually a dead-end host).
- Eastern equine encephalitis and Western equine encephalitis (mosquito-borne, birds as reservoir, horses as sentinels).
4. Clinico-anatomical reasoning:
- For every ~150 people infected with West Nile virus, about 30 have mild symptoms and about 1 has severe illness such as encephalitis or meningitis, with high fever, stiff neck, stupor, disorientation, coma, tremors, convulsions and muscle weakness.
- The majority of cases of neuroinvasive disease and fatalities are seen over 50 years of age, and the rare occurrence of flaccid paralysis reflects spinal cord (anterior horn) involvement analogous to poliomyelitis, though at much lower frequency than encephalitis.
questions.question:
(i) An elderly patient with recent mosquito exposure develops fever, stiff neck, disorientation and tremors, with some patients in similar outbreaks developing acute flaccid paralysis. Identify the organ/structure primarily affected.
(ii) What structures may be affected within this organ?
(iii) List the differential arboviral pathologies to consider.
(iv) Provide the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking the findings to the presentation.

questions.answerText:
(i) The liver and portal venous system are affected; a granulomatous reaction surrounds schistosome eggs deposited in the liver and leads to fibrosis, impeding blood flow to the liver.
(ii) This impeded blood flow leads to portal hypertension, accumulation of ascites in the abdominal cavity, hepatosplenomegaly, and oesophageal varices.
(iii) Of the schistosome species, Schistosoma mansoni (inferior mesenteric veins of the large intestine) and Schistosoma japonicum (inferior and superior mesenteric veins of the small intestine) are associated with this hepatic/intestinal presentation, whereas Schistosoma haematobium (veins of the urinary bladder) causes a urinary tract presentation instead.
(iv) The most significant pathology is associated with the schistosome eggs, not the adult worms; female schistosomes can lay hundreds or thousands of eggs per day within the venous system, and production of large numbers of eggs results in chronic granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis of the portal venous system, accounting for the hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and oesophageal varices seen.

A) Describe the history of asepsis and antimicrobial chemotherapy under the following headings:
A(i) The contributions of Paul Ehrlich to chemotherapy, including the specific concept he formulated and the first antimicrobial agent he synthesized.
A(ii) The discovery of penicillin by Fleming — year of observation, the organism he observed, what inhibited its growth, and when it came into clinical use.
A(iii) The contributions of Domagk, Chain and Florey.
B) Explain the ancient and historical evidence of chemotherapy, naming three cultures and the substances they used.
C) Describe three important observations about antimicrobial resistance in the historical context: (i) the first multiresistant organism, the year and the outbreak it occurred in; (ii) the resistance pattern of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep) to penicillin to date; (iii) the two most important pathogens to emerge in multiple drug resistant forms.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Paul Ehrlich (1854–1915): proposed the term "chemotherapy" to describe the use of chemicals that would selectively kill pathogens while having little or no effect on a patient — the concept of selective toxicity. He recognised specific chemical relationships between parasites and drugs, the development of drug resistance, and the role of combination therapy in combating resistance development. He synthesised the first antimicrobial agent in the world: salvarsan, a remedy for syphilis, in 1910.
A(ii) Fleming's discovery of penicillin: in 1928, Fleming found that the growth of Staphylococcus aureus was inhibited in a zone surrounding a contaminated blue mould (a fungus from the Penicillium genus, first observed by Fleming in 1929) in culture dishes — leading to the finding that a microorganism would produce substances that could inhibit the growth of other microorganisms. Penicillin came into clinical use in the 1940s.
A(iii) Domagk: in 1935, discovered sulphonamide — rapid development of antimicrobial chemotherapy began with this discovery; these drugs were synthetic compounds with limitations in terms of safety and efficacy. Chain and Florey: in 1940, demonstrated that penicillin (observed by Fleming) could be made into an effective chemotherapeutic substance; isolation, concentration, purification and mass production of penicillin followed; penicillin saved the lives of many wounded soldiers during World War II.
B) Ancient evidence of chemotherapy:
- Ancient Peru: Indians used bark from the cinchona tree to treat malaria (earliest evidence of successful chemotherapy).
- Egypt: Egyptians used honey for wound dressing.
- China and Greece: used bread moulds to treat skin infections (producing some raw form of antibiotics).
- India: turmeric was used to treat wounds.
C) Historical resistance observations:
(i) First multiresistant organism: in 1953, during a Shigella outbreak in Japan, a strain of the dysentery bacillus was isolated with multiple drug resistance, exhibiting resistance to chloramphenicol, tetracycline, streptomycin, and sulphanilamides.
(ii) Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep): has not fully developed resistance to penicillin — it remains a reasonable drug of choice for many types of streptococcal infections.
(iii) Two most important pathogens to emerge in multiple drug resistant forms: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Staphylococcus aureus.

A(i) AST is an in vitro test used to detect the susceptibility or resistance of microorganisms to antimicrobials such as antibiotics and antifungals. Only bacteria likely to be the causative agent(s) of an infection should be tested — not contaminants or normal flora at the site of infection. It determines which antimicrobial agents might be effective in treating infections caused by the isolated organisms.
A(ii) In clinical laboratories, susceptibility testing is usually performed by:
- Disk diffusion (Kirby-Bauer method)
- Dilution method (minimum inhibitory concentration [MIC] method)
Standards are published and frequently updated by the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), formerly the National Committee for Clinical Laboratory Standards (NCCLS).
A(iii) Procedure for inoculum preparation:
1. From the primary culture plate, touch with a loop the tops of each of 3–5 colonies of similar appearance and transfer growth to a tube of saline.
2. Compare the tube with the 0.5 McFarland turbidity standard (approximately 1.5 × 10^8 CFU/ml) and adjust the density of the test suspension to match by adding more bacteria or more sterile saline.
3. Inoculate the plate by dipping a sterile swab into the inoculum, removing excess by pressing and rotating against the side of the tube; streak all over the surface three times rotating the plate through 60° after each application; pass the swab around the edge.
4. Leave inoculum to dry for at least 3–5 minutes (but no more than 15 minutes) at room temperature.
B) Interpretation: after overnight incubation, measure the diameter of each zone (including the disk diameter) to the nearest mm. Using CLSI guidelines, report each drug as susceptible (S), intermediate (I), or resistant (R). Zone sizes are NOT reported to physicians. Three exceptions to zone-reading:
1. With sulphonamides and co-trimoxazole, slight growth within the inhibition zone should be ignored.
2. Beta-lactamase-producing staphylococci tested against penicillin with a heaped-up, clearly defined zone edge — report as resistant regardless of zone size.
3. Certain Proteus species may swarm into the area of inhibition; the zone is usually clearly outlined and the thin swarming layer should be ignored.
C) Two limitations: (1) does not provide accurate information about the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC); (2) does not provide reliable results with some antibiotic/organism combinations, such as penicillin G in N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae. If performed precisely according to standard protocol, disk diffusion yields data that can reliably predict the in vivo effectiveness of the drug in question.
questions.question:

A(ii) The two principal laboratory methods used in clinical laboratories, naming the standard-setting body that publishes guidelines for these methods.
A(iii) The disk diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) method — describe step by step the procedure for preparing the inoculum, including the turbidity standard used and the cell density it represents.
B) Explain how to interpret the results of the disk diffusion test, including the three possible categories of reporting and the specific exceptions to zone-reading stated.

A(i) Describe the modes of transmission of dermatophyte infections, and their ecological classification.
A(ii) State the factors that enhance susceptibility to these infections and the climatic conditions favouring higher incidence.
B(i) State a preventive measure against dermatophyte infection.
B(ii) Explain the pathological basis of the nail deformity seen in chronic dermatophyte infection of the nail.
questions.answerText:
1. Dermatophytoses are acquired by contact with contaminated soil, infected animals or humans, and are transmissible from person to person.
2. They are classified ecologically as geophilic (from soil), zoophilic (from animals), or anthropophilic (from humans), according to their source.
3. Susceptibility may be enhanced by moisture, warmth, and specific skin chemistry.
4. The incidence of dermatophyte infection is higher in hot, humid climates and under crowded living conditions.
5. Tinea pedis is transmitted by desquamated skin scales, usually via the feet, and may remain infectious in the environment for months or years.
6. Prevention includes avoiding direct contact with the pathogen, for example by regular disinfection of showers and wardrobes, keeping the area dry, and avoiding sharing sources of infection.
7. Treatment consists of thorough removal of infected and dead epithelial structures and application of a topical or oral antifungal such as griseofulvin or terbinafine.
8. Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) is dominantly caused by Trichophyton rubrum and T. interdigitale, and results in dystrophic nails.
9. Dermatophytes have the ability to utilise keratin as a nutrient source, and no living tissue is invaded; the keratinised stratum corneum is simply colonised.
10. However, the presence of the fungus and its metabolic products usually induces an allergic and inflammatory eczematous response in the host.
11. Chronic Candida onychomycosis, a related keratin-invading process affecting the nail, often causes detachment of the cuticle from the nail plate with complete destruction of nail tissue, illustrating how such chronic infection produces progressive nail deformity.
12. The type and severity of the host response to dermatophyte infection is often related to the species and strain of dermatophyte causing the infection, which underlies the variable degree of nail dystrophy seen clinically.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old child is brought to clinic by her mother who reports that two of the child's siblings have recently been vaccinated. The mother asks about the difference between being vaccinated and becoming immune, and whether the child's previous chickenpox illness means she is protected.
(i) Define vaccination, immunization, and immunity, and distinguish between innate and acquired immunity.
(ii) Distinguish active from passive immunity, stating an advantage and a disadvantage of each.
(iii) Explain how artificial active immunization works, including what happens during a second exposure to the same microbe.
(iv) Describe how passive immunization occurs physiologically and how it is used artificially, including the clinical situations in which artificial passive immunization is indicated.
(v) State when antiviral agents must be administered to be effective, and name the largest group of antiviral agents with its prototype drug and mechanism of action.
questions.answerText:
(i) Vaccination: the use of vaccines to stimulate the immune system to protect against infection or disease. Immunization: the process of making an individual immune or resistant to an infectious disease, typically via vaccination. Immunity: the ability of the body to defend itself. Innate immunity: the immunity you are born with (genetic). Acquired immunity: can be actively acquired (you develop the immunity in your body) or passively acquired (ready-made immunity given to you).
(ii) Active immunity advantages: imparts long-term immunity; enables herd immunity. Active immunity disadvantages: not immediate; can be suppressed or deficient; exposes host to risk of infection if not developed. Passive immunity advantages: offers immediate protection from infection; offers a window for the body to develop active immunity. Passive immunity disadvantages: does not offer long-term protection; not all infection antibodies offer protection.
(iii) Artificial active immunization: the microbe or parts of it are injected into the person before natural exposure. If whole microbes are used, they are pre-treated (attenuated vaccine). The body generates immunity (T cells and B cells with their antibodies). On second exposure, the immune response against the microbe is very efficient — this is the basis for childhood infections that a person only contracts once and then becomes immune to.
(iv) Physiological passive immunization: antibodies are transferred from mother to fetus during pregnancy, protecting the fetus before and shortly after birth. Artificial passive immunization: pre-synthesised antibodies are transferred to a person so the body does not need to produce them; normally administered by injection; antibodies are naturally broken down so protection is short-lasting. Indicated: when there has been a recent outbreak of a particular disease, or as emergency treatment for toxicity (e.g., for tetanus).
(v) Viral replication is at its peak before the appearance of signs and symptoms; for an antiviral agent to be effective, it must be administered before the appearance of symptoms. Largest group: nucleoside analogues, with acyclovir (Zovirax) as a prototype. Mechanism of action: inhibition of viral enzymes to terminate DNA synthesis. Indicated for: Herpes simplex, Herpes zoster (shingles), varicella, Epstein-Barr and CMV infections.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the classification of fungal infections according to the anatomical site or depth of tissue involved.
A(ii) State the type of fungi responsible for infections at the deepest (systemic) anatomical level.
B(i) Relate each of these anatomical categories to a representative disease.
B(ii) Explain how a systemic mycosis may spread from its primary site to distant organs and produce a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Fungal infections (mycoses) are classified according to the area of the body affected: superficial mycosis, cutaneous mycosis, subcutaneous mycosis, systemic mycosis, and opportunistic mycosis.
2. Superficial mycosis is limited to the outermost layer of the skin and hair, elicits no immune response, and is caused mostly by yeasts, as in dandruff.
3. Cutaneous mycosis is caused by dermatophytes, affects deeper levels of the epidermis, and invades the hair and nails, evoking an immune response, as in tinea (ringworm, athlete's foot, jock itch).
4. Subcutaneous mycosis is a chronic infection of subdermal tissues involving the dermis, subcutaneous tissue, muscles and fascia, resulting from puncture wounds by objects contaminated with fungal species from the soil, and may require surgical intervention.
5. Systemic mycosis primarily infects the lungs and then spreads to other organs; it is caused by virulent dimorphic fungi, and the disease can spread from organ to organ or tissue to tissue.
6. Opportunistic mycosis is caused by organisms of low pathogenicity that produce disease only under conditions of lowered immunity.
7. Histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis and paracoccidioidomycosis are examples of systemic (endemic) mycoses, all caused by dimorphic fungi with similar pathogenesis.
8. Candidiasis, aspergillosis, cryptococcosis, mucormycosis and pneumocystis pneumonia are examples of opportunistic mycoses, occurring in patients with compromised host defences.
9. In systemic mycosis, infection results from inhalation of the spores of dimorphic fungi that have their saprophytic mould forms in the soil.
10. Within the lungs the spores differentiate into yeasts, establishing a primary pulmonary infection.
11. The organisms can also result in haematogenous spread throughout the body, allowing them to reach distant organs such as the bone marrow, liver and spleen, as occurs in histoplasmosis.
12. This dissemination is often fatal, and accounts for why systemic mycoses can produce functional deficits far removed from the lungs, the original portal of entry.

questions.question:
(i) A healthcare worker sustains a needle-stick injury from a patient known to be a chronic hepatitis B carrier. What are the risk factors relevant to hepatitis B transmission in general?
(ii) What complications can follow hepatitis B infection?
(iii) What management options exist for this exposed worker, and justify the preferred approach.
questions.answerText:
1. Risk factors for HBV transmission:
- Parenteral: blood transfusions, serum products, sharing of needles/razors, tattooing, acupuncture, renal dialysis, organ donation.
- Sexual transmission and close (horizontal) contact.
- Vertical transmission: perinatal (carrier mother to baby), transplacental (rare), during delivery, and postnatal.
- Hepatitis B is an important occupational hazard for health workers.
2. Complications: - Fulminant hepatitis (about 1% of acute cases).
- Persistent infection: chronic persistent hepatitis or chronic active hepatitis, progressing to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cirrhosis and liver failure.
- Extrahepatic manifestations such as glomerulonephritis, and co-infection with HIV, HCV or HDV.
3. Management options and justification:
- Passive immunisation: hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) should be administered to non-immune individuals following exposure to HBV-infected blood.
- Active immunisation: the vaccine should also be given, since both HBIG and vaccine together are recommended following exposure.
- This combined approach is preferred because passive immunisation (HBIG) provides immediate short-term protection while active immunisation (vaccine) provides protection lasting at least 20 years and probably lifelong.

questions.question:
Describe Entamoeba histolytica under the following headings:
A(i) the trophozoite
A(ii) the cyst
B) Explain the clinical basis for why the cyst, rather than the trophozoite, is responsible for transmission of this organism.
C) Distinguish Entamoeba histolytica from Entamoeba dispar.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Trophozoites live and replicate within the large intestine, have an amorphous shape, are generally 15-30 micrometres in diameter, and move by extending a finger-like pseudopodium.
A(ii) Cysts are generally 12-15 micrometres in diameter, with cyst maturation involving two rounds of nuclear replication without cell division, giving cysts 1-4 nuclei.
B) Cysts are immediately infective upon excretion with the faeces and remain viable for weeks to months depending on environmental conditions, whereas trophozoites do not have this environmental resistance.
B) E. histolytica exhibits a typical faecal-oral life cycle, and cysts tend to predominate in formed stools, while trophozoites predominate in diarrhoeic stools; fresh stools can be examined for motile trophozoites, which exhibit progressive motility, but it is the cyst that is responsible for onward transmission.
C) E. dispar is morphologically identical to E. histolytica, and the two were previously considered to be the same species.
C) Among these Entamoeba species, only E. histolytica is pathogenic, causing amoebiasis or amoebic dysentery.
C) It is estimated that up to 10% of the world's population may be infected with either E. histolytica or E. dispar, with prevalence as high as 50% in many tropical countries.
C) There are an estimated 50 million cases of amoebiasis per year and up to 100,000 deaths, attributable to the pathogenic E. histolytica rather than E. dispar.
C) Cysts of E. histolytica have 1-4 nuclei formed by two rounds of nuclear replication without cell division, a maturation process that does not differ between E. histolytica and E. dispar.
C) Sigmoidoscopy may reveal the characteristic ulcers of invasive E. histolytica disease, especially in more severe cases, a finding attributable to the pathogenic species rather than E. dispar.

A(i) Infection is acquired by ingestion of embryonated ova either in food or drinks, or in young children from soil.
A(ii) The second stage larvae hatch in the duodenum and penetrate the wall to reach the bloodstream, are carried into the lungs, grow and moult twice in the lungs, then penetrate the alveoli and return to the intestine via the trachea and oesophagus.
A(iii) The migration of larvae in the lung causes pneumonitis with cough, chest pain and difficulty in breathing; heavy worm load in the intestine results in abdominal discomfort, anorexia, nausea and diarrhoea, and impaired absorption of protein, lactose and vitamin A resulting in protein-energy malnutrition in children.
C) Intestinal obstruction occurs when a mass of worms partially or totally blocks the bowel lumen, with symptoms such as colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and constipation.
C) There may also be occasional migration of the adult worm out of the mouth, nose, lacrimal ducts, or umbilicus, an aberrant structural consequence of this organism's course through the body.
C) The severity of symptoms tends to correlate with the worm burden.
C) Impaired absorption of protein, lactose and vitamin A, resulting in protein-energy malnutrition in children with heavy worm load, is a further structural/functional consequence of this organism's presence in the intestine.
C) The migration of larvae through the lungs itself, with growth and two moults occurring there before the larvae penetrate the alveoli to return to the gut, is part of the same course responsible for the pneumonitis described.
questions.question:
With reference to the migration of Ascaris lumbricoides larvae through the host:
A(i) Describe the origin of the infection.
A(ii) Describe the course taken by the larvae through the body.
A(iii) Describe the distribution of clinical effects that result from this migration.
C) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity or structural consequence that follows heavy or aberrant worm migration in this condition.

questions.answerText:
1. Risk factors:
- Rodent-to-human transmission from the multimammate rat, Mastomys natalensis, through inhalation of aerosolised virus or ingestion of food/materials contaminated by rodent excreta.
- Human-to-human transmission through direct contact with blood, tissues, secretions or excretions of infected persons, needle-stick or cut injuries, or inhalation of aerosolised virus, all relevant to a nurse in a hospital setting.
- Secondary human-to-human spread carries potential for nosocomial outbreaks with high case-fatality.
2. Complications:
- Abnormal bleeding, oedema of the neck/face, jaundice, persistent hypotension and shock.
- Sensorineural hearing deficit (deafness), occurring in about one-third of cases.
- In pregnancy: increased maternal mortality (>30% in the third trimester) and increased fetal/neonatal mortality (>85%).
3. Management options and justification:
- Supportive measures: monitoring fluid, electrolyte and oxygen levels.
- Ribavirin (60 mg/kg/day IV for 4 days, then 30 mg/kg/day orally) is justified because it is most effective when started within the first 6 days of illness, reducing mortality from 55–76% to 5–9% when intravenous ribavirin is given within this window.
questions.question:
(i) A nurse caring for a febrile patient in a rural West African hospital develops fever, sore throat, retrosternal pain and proteinuria that fail to respond to antimalarials and antibiotics. What are the risk factors for her infection?
(ii) What complications may follow in this illness?
(iii) What are the management options available, and justify the use of one of them.

questions.answerText:
1. The bacterial cell wall is a macromolecule composed of polysaccharide, repeating sugars (NAG and NAM), cross-linked with short chains of amino acids, known as peptidoglycan (also called murein).
2. This tough outer coat prevents rupture, protects the cell, and gives the bacterium its distinct shape.
3. Certain antibiotics, such as penicillins, work by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.
4. Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane found outside the cell wall, which is not present in Gram-positive bacteria.
5. Gram-negative bacteria have lipopolysaccharide (LPS), lipoprotein, and phospholipids in this outer membrane, which can cause some of the symptoms of Gram-negative bacterial infections, such as fever, shock and diarrhoea.
6. The Gram-negative cell envelope is more complicated than that of Gram-positive bacteria, containing lipid, phospholipid, lipid A, a periplasmic space (a fluid-filled area between the cell wall and outer membrane), and various protein porins.
7. Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria have differences in their cell wall and outer envelope, and the theory of why the Gram stain works is based on this difference.
8. Gram-negative bacteria are less sensitive to penicillin as a result of a thinner cell wall and the presence of the additional outer membrane.
9. The Gram stain is a differential stain procedure, giving different results for Gram-positive (violet-retaining) and Gram-negative organisms.
10. Gram-positive cocci in clusters is identified as Staphylococcus, while Gram-negative motile bacilli with a green sheen on EMB agar is identified as E. coli, illustrating how cell envelope characteristics assist bacterial identification.
11. Endotoxin is an integral part of the cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria specifically, being a lipopolysaccharide complex whose lipid A portion is probably responsible for toxicity.
12. Endotoxin is relatively stable, withstanding heating above 60 degrees Celsius for hours without loss of toxicity, is weakly immunogenic, and is not converted to toxoids, unlike bacterial exotoxins.

A(ii) Describe the outer membrane found in Gram-negative bacteria and its components.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for the difference in penicillin sensitivity between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
B(ii) Distinguish between the Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial cell envelope.

A patient from a filariasis-endemic area in Asia or Africa presents with chronic swelling of the lower limb, with pitting oedema progressing to hardened, hyperpigmented and hyperkeratotic skin, together with a hydrocele.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(iii) What complications are associated with this condition?
(iv) What management options exist, and justify the combination approach used in mass treatment programmes.
questions.answerText:
(i) Lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) due to Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi.
(ii) Risk factors include living in an area endemic for these filarial nematodes (endemic in 83 countries, with 1.2 billion people at risk), hyperendemic areas including Asia, India and China, and exposure to the night-feeding mosquito vectors (Culex, Aedes and Anopheles species for W. bancrofti; Anopheles and Mansonia species for B. malayi).
(iii) Complications include acute adenolymphangitis with painful lymphadenopathy, chronic/irreversible lymphedema, hydroceles, chyluria with loss of fat and protein causing hypoproteinaemia, haematuria and proteinuria from possible immune complex nephritis, secondary bacterial/fungal infections, and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia with nocturnal wheezing.
(iv) Management options include diethylcarbamazine (DEC), which reduces microfilariae concentrations and kills adult worms; albendazole, which kills adult worms; and ivermectin, which kills the microfilariae; the combination of DEC or ivermectin with albendazole, given once annually, is justified as the basis of the Global Programme for the Elimination of Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF), since together they target both the adult worms and the circulating microfilariae.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old child is brought to the paediatric clinic with a 7-day history of fever, malaise, and painless cervical lymphadenopathy. The mother reports that the child was born to an HTLV-1-positive mother and was breastfed for 2 years.
(i) State the likely diagnosis and name the virus responsible, distinguishing it from HTLV-2 in terms of associated disease.
(ii) Describe the three routes by which HTLV is transmitted, stating which is the most common mode.
(iii) Describe the pathogenesis of adult T-cell leukaemia (ATL) caused by HTLV-1, including the estimated lifetime risk of developing ATL and the typical latency period.
(iv) Describe the laboratory diagnosis of HTLV infection and the treatment and prevention options.
questions.answerText:
(i) HTLV-1 (Human T-cell Lymphotrophic Virus type 1) infection. HTLV-1 has been associated with a human malignant disease — adult T-cell leukaemia (ATL) — and a less common neurological condition, HTLV-associated myelopathy (HAM). HTLV-2 infection causes a rare form of cancer: hairy cell leukaemia (a rare, lymphocytic leukaemia usually of B-cell origin, characterised by malignant cells that look ciliated, replacing bone marrow and infiltrating the spleen causing splenomegaly).
(ii) Three routes of transmission, with most common route first:
1. Mother to fetus or newborn (most common): via infected lymphocytes either trans-placentally or in breast milk.
2. Sexual intercourse: infection transmitted by infected lymphocytes contained in semen.
3. Blood products containing intact cells: a potential source of infection. There is little evidence for transmission by cell-free fluids.
(iii) Pathogenesis of ATL: HTLV-1 infection both stimulates mitosis and immortalises T lymphocytes, which acquire an antigen-activated phenotype. The virus becomes integrated in the host cell as a provirus and transforms a polyclonal population of T cells; there is no common integration site in different tumours and no HTLV mRNA is transcribed. Over many years, infected T cells accumulate chromosomal aberrations, leading to selection of monoclonal populations with increasingly malignant phenotype. The majority of infected individuals are asymptomatic carriers with an estimated 1% lifetime chance of developing ATL. ATL typically appears 20–30 years after initial infection. Median survival after appearance of acute ATL is 6 months.
(iv) Laboratory diagnosis: screening of blood donors is done by ELISA or agglutination tests; false-positives necessitate confirmatory testing by Western blotting; test sensitivity is a problem due to low and variable antibody titres. Treatment and prevention: usual cancer chemotherapy agents have proven ineffective in treating ATL; attempts to treat HAM have been largely unsuccessful. An estimated 10–20 million people worldwide are infected with HTLV-1 or -2; 5% will eventually develop either ATL or HAM. Screening of blood donors prevents transmission by transfusion; other modes of transmission best controlled by a vaccine, but none is currently available for human use; trials of experimental vaccines are in progress.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient returns from a rural area with a 3-day history of high-grade fever and rigors. Malaria rapid diagnostic test is negative but peripheral blood film examination is requested. Blood is collected by finger prick.
(i) Describe the correct collection method for blood smears, including fixation and handling, and state the storage rule for slides.
(ii) Describe the procedure for collecting stool samples for bacterial culture, stating the transport medium used and the storage condition if testing is delayed beyond 48 hours.
(iii) Describe how nasopharyngeal swabs should be collected, including the correct technique.
(iv) List all information that must be included on the case investigation form sent with the specimen.
(v) Describe all biosafety measures for protecting self, the patient, and the environment when handling clinical specimens.
questions.answerText:
(i) Blood for smears: collect capillary blood from finger prick; make smear; fix with methanol or other fixative. Handling and transport: transport slides within 24 hours; do NOT refrigerate (refrigeration can alter cell morphology).
(ii) Stool for bacterial culture: collect freshly passed stool samples; avoid specimens from a bedpan; use sterile or clean container — do not clean with disinfectant; during an outbreak collect from 10–20 patients. Transport medium: Cary-Blair medium. For antigen detection/PCR — no transport medium. Storage: refrigerate at 4°C if testing within 48 hours; store at −70°C if longer.
(iii) Nasopharyngeal swab technique: tilt the patient's head backwards; insert a flexible fine-shafted polyester swab into the nostril and back to the nasopharynx; leave in place a few seconds; withdraw slowly using a rotating motion.
(iv) Case investigation form must include: Patient information — age (or date of birth), sex, complete address. Clinical information — date of onset of symptoms, clinical and immunization history, risk factors or contact history where relevant, antimicrobial drugs taken prior to specimen collection. Laboratory information — whether acute or convalescent specimen; other specimens from the same patient. Line listing — if a large number of patients. Receiving laboratory records: date and time when specimen was received; name and initials of person receiving specimen; record of specimen quality.
(v) Biosafety measures:
- Protect the patient: use single-use equipment; disinfect; work in a clean, dedicated area.
- Protect yourself: use personal protective equipment — disposable gloves, laboratory coats/gown, mask, protective eyewear/face shields if procedure likely to generate aerosols; have first aid kit readily accessible; do not reuse contaminated equipment; if no sharps container, collect sharps immediately to prevent needle-stick injury.
- Protect others and the environment: package samples appropriately for transport; decontaminate spills with 10% bleach after wiping the surface clean; disinfect working areas with 1% household bleach daily; soak contaminated non-disposable equipment/material in 1% household bleach for 5 minutes, wash in soapy water before re-use, sterilize if necessary; place waste in leak-proof biohazard bags; protect cleaning/decontamination personnel with protective coat and thick rubber gloves.

A. Origin, course, relations and distribution:
(i) Origin: after a bite, viral multiplication takes place in muscle cells and at neuromuscular junctions at the site of inoculation.
(ii) Course: the virus then migrates along peripheral neurons (axonal transport) to the CNS via retrograde axonal transport mechanisms.
(iii) Relations: both motor and sensory fibres may be involved, depending on the animal infected;
Replication in the CNS occurs mainly in the basal ganglia, pons and medulla.
(iv) Distribution: from the CNS, the virus migrates centrifugally along peripheral nerves (anterograde axoplasmic flow) to skeletal and cardiac muscle and salivary glands, with shedding of virus in saliva.
B. Safe site for the procedure:
- As much rabies immune globulin (RIG) as possible should be infiltrated into the wound(s).
- The remainder should be given intramuscularly at a site distant from the vaccine.
C. Anatomical basis of the deformity:
- In paralytic (dumb) rabies, early flaccid muscle weakness often begins in the bitten extremity.
- This progresses to produce quadriparesis and bilateral facial weakness, while sensory examination is usually normal, reflecting the pattern of viral spread along the affected nerve pathways.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Gram-negative curved (comma) rods of family Vibrionaceae, facultative anaerobes, oxidase positive, non-spore forming, motile with sheathed polar flagella, usually two chromosomes; tolerate alkaline media but sensitive to acid; found in surface water, marshes, river deltas, warm coastal water, shellfish and sewage.
A(i) Several species cause foodborne infection, usually from undercooked seafood found in salt water; pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains co-exist in aquatic environments, giving many genetic varieties.
A(ii) Non-halophilic: V. cholerae O1 (classical and El Tor biovar); halophilic (marine): V. parahaemolyticus, V. fluvialis, V. mimicus, V. vulnificus, V. alginolyticus; non-O1 strains share the H but not the O antigen.
A(ii) Classical versus El Tor: haemolysis negative/positive, chick cell agglutination negative/positive, polymyxin sensitive/resistant, Voges-Proskauer negative/positive; TCBS: V. cholerae yellow sucrose fermenters, V. mimicus, V. parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificus green-blue non-fermenters.
A(iii) V. cholerae has over 84 serovars; O1 agglutinated by polyvalent antiserum, serovars 2-84 are non-O1; O1 subtypes Ogawa, Inaba and Hikojima.
B(i) V. cholerae O1: cholera (epidemic disease with cholera toxin); several species cause foodborne infection from undercooked seafood; V. alginolyticus and V. vulnificus cause wound infection (pus and wound swabs).
B(i) Cholera clinical range: 75% asymptomatic, 20% mild to moderate, 2-5% severe (cholera gravis); dangerous in late pregnancy (16% fetal death in a Haiti study of 900 women).
C(i) Non-cholera Vibrio wound infection or sepsis makes patients much more ill, often with other medical conditions; may cause necrotising fasciitis or compartment syndrome.
C(i) Treatment of severe cases: doxycycline or a quinolone if ill with high fever or underlying disease; aggressive fluids and vasopressors for hypotension and septic shock.
C(i) Early fasciotomy within 24 hours can be life-saving in necrotising fasciitis; early debridement avoids amputation; serial surgical evaluation; skin grafts in recovery.
C(i) Gastroenteritis is self-limited in most patients and needs no specific therapy; antibiotics do not shorten cholera.
C(i) Gene recombination among V. cholerae can produce new virulent strains.

questions.answerText:
1. Diagnosis: Ebola virus disease (viral haemorrhagic fever).
2. Pathologic basis:
- Filoviruses (Ebola, Marburg) attack the mononuclear phagocytic system (MPS) via the spleen, lymph node and liver.
- MPS infection leads to release of inflammatory agents such as cytokines, peroxides and proteases; release of these pro-inflammatory agents causes activation of the endothelium, in turn causing procoagulant activity, loss of blood pressure regulation, and increased vascular permeability via dissociation of intercellular junctions of the endothelium.
3. Resuscitation/management:
- Basic interventions that can significantly improve chances of survival when used early include providing intravenous fluids and balancing electrolytes.
- Maintaining oxygen status and blood pressure, and treating other infections if they occur.
4. Definitive treatment: no FDA-approved vaccine or medicine (antiviral drug) is available for Ebola; experimental vaccines and treatments are under development but have not yet been fully tested for safety or effectiveness.

A) Describe the classification of oncogenic viruses under the following headings:
A(i) The two main classes (RNA vs DNA oncogenic viruses) and the general mechanism by which each class causes oncogenesis.
A(ii) Name all human cancer viruses in the table, specifying the virus family, virus name, and the human cancer each is associated with.
A(iii) Describe the structure and genome of a retrovirus, naming the key structural proteins and enzymes contained within the capsid.
B) Explain the mechanism by which HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukaemia, stating specifically why no recognised oncogene is activated and how malignancy eventually develops.
C) Explain how hepatitis B infection is prevented and controlled, including the vaccine schedule and which populations are recommended for vaccination.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Two classes of oncogenic viruses:
- RNA oncogenic viruses (retroviruses): have shown involvement in formation of cellular oncogenes.
- DNA oncogenic viruses: act by encoding viral proteins which deregulate the integrated framework of host cellular processes and prevent cell death (i.e., act on tumour suppressor genes).
A(ii) Human cancer viruses:
- RNA viruses: Retroviridae — Human T-lymphocytic virus (HTLV) → adult T-cell leukaemias; HIV → AIDS-related malignancies; Flaviviridae — Hepatitis C virus → primary liver cell cancer.
- DNA viruses: Papoviridae — Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) → cervical, vulva, penile, squamous cell carcinoma; BKV and JCV; Herpesviridae — Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) → nasopharyngeal carcinoma, African Burkitt lymphoma, B-cell lymphomas; HSV type 2 → cervical carcinomas; Hepadnaviridae — Hepatitis B → hepatocellular carcinoma; Flaviridae — Hepatitis C → hepatocellular carcinoma; Polyomaviridae — Merkel cell virus → Merkel cell carcinoma.
A(iii) Retrovirus structure: enveloped particles; viral envelope (from host cell membrane) contains spiked knobs consisting of TM (gp41, fusion/transmembrane protein) linked to SU (gp120, attachment protein); outer matrix protein MA (p17) directs entry of double-stranded DNA provirus into the nucleus; two identical copies of positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome in the capsid (diploid); major capsid protein CA (p24); nucleocapsid protein NC (p7); enzymes in the capsid: reverse transcriptase, integrase (required for DNA synthesis and integration), and protease (essential for virus assembly); a host cellular tRNA is hydrogen-bonded at the 5' end of each viral RNA as a primer for reverse transcription.
B) HTLV-1 stimulates mitosis and immortalises T lymphocytes; the virus integrates into the host cell as a provirus and transforms a polyclonal T-cell population; there is no common integration site in different tumours, no HTLV mRNA is transcribed, and no recognised oncogene is activated. Over many years of continued multiplication, infected T cells accumulate many chromosomal aberrations, leading to selection of monoclonal populations with increasingly malignant phenotype — malignancy results from chromosomal instability rather than direct oncogene activation.
C) Prevention and control of hepatitis B:
- Blood screening: screening for HBsAg and anti-HBc has helped reduce transmission via blood or blood products.
- Safe sex and avoiding lifestyles that facilitate spread of the virus.
- Vaccination: the hepatitis B vaccine is given as three or four injections over six months; you cannot get hepatitis B from the vaccine. Recommended for: newborns; children and adolescents not vaccinated at birth; those who work or live in a centre for people who are developmentally disabled; people who live with someone who has hepatitis B; health care workers, emergency workers and others who come into contact with blood.

A. Gross structure of lymphoid organs:
(i) Lymphocytes in the peripheral blood represent only about 2% of the total lymphocyte pool, the remainder being located chiefly in lymphoid organs;
The network of follicular dendritic cells in the germinal centres of lymph nodes traps antigens and stimulates an immune response.
B. Relation of lymphoid zones to pathology:
- Lymphoid organs play a central role in HIV infection;
Virus is widely disseminated to the lymphoid organs during primary infection,
The lymphoid organs become seeded.
- During the period of clinical latency, there is a high level of ongoing viral replication in these organs, with an estimated 10 billion HIV particles produced and destroyed each day.
C. Spread to a distant structure and functional deficit:
- Monocytes and macrophages play a major role in the dissemination and pathogenesis of HIV infection;
In the brain, the major cell types infected with HIV are monocytes and macrophages.
- This dissemination to the brain may have important consequences for the development of neuropsychiatric manifestations associated with HIV infection, representing a functional deficit distant from the original site of infection.

A(i) Describe bacterial virulence factors under the headings: definition, the two broad categories, and one example of each category.
A(ii) State the definition of virulence itself.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why encapsulated organisms are more virulent than unencapsulated strains of the same species.
B(ii) Distinguish between virulence factors that promote colonisation and those that damage the host.
questions.answerText:
1. Virulence is the ability of bacteria to overcome body defences and cause an infection, or the likelihood of bacteria to cause disease.
2. Virulence is a quantitative measure of pathogenicity; virulence factors are gene products (properties) that enable a microorganism to establish itself on or within a host and enhance its potential to cause disease.
3. Virulence factors influence the ability of bacteria to cause infectious disease and are divided into two categories: those that promote bacterial colonisation of the host, and those that damage the host.
4. Those that promote colonisation have properties including the ability to use motility to contact host cells, the ability to adhere to host cells and resist physical removal, the ability to invade host cells, the ability to compete for iron and other nutrients, and the ability to resist innate and adaptive immune defences.
5. Those that damage the host have properties including the ability to produce cell wall components that bind host cells and cause secretion of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, the ability to produce harmful exotoxins, and the ability to induce autoimmune responses.
6. Examples of virulence factors include fimbriae or pili, flagella, toxins, and invasins.
7. Encapsulated pneumococci and Escherichia coli strains that express Shiga-like toxins are more virulent than those that do not.
8. Virulence depends on the number of infecting microorganisms, their route of entry into the body, and the response of the host immune system.
9. Cells of virulent strains of S. pneumoniae are surrounded by a polysaccharide capsule which protects them from being digested by phagocytic white blood cells, whereas unencapsulated strains are normal microbiota of the lungs, sinuses and middle ear that do not cause disease.
10. This capsule-mediated resistance to phagocytosis is the basis for the greater virulence of encapsulated strains, which can cause pneumococcal pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis media, bacteraemia and endocarditis.
11. Capsules generally help organisms evade phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages, while pili/fimbriae serve as adherence factors that help colonise a body surface.
12. Toxins, whether intrinsic (released only after cell lysis, endotoxin) or extrinsic (secreted into the environment, exotoxins), fall under the category of virulence factors that damage the host, distinguishing them from adhesion and colonisation factors.

questions.question:
(i) A patient with a history of travel to south-western regions of the Americas presents with an acute febrile flu-like illness with fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough, malaise, headache, myalgia, night sweats and loss of appetite, together with a mild erythematous rash on the trunk and limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the population group in which this disease carries a much greater mortality rate, and the finding on examination that suggests dissemination.
(iii) Outline the pathophysiology of this condition, describing its two life cycles.
(iv) Outline the management of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Coccidioidomycosis, caused by Coccidioides immitis.
(ii) There is a much greater mortality rate in dark-skinned people (Mexicans, Filipinos, and Blacks), who are 25 times more likely to develop progressive disease and death, for reasons that are obscure; dissemination to the meninges, bones, joints and subcutaneous and cutaneous tissues may be suggested by a mild, diffuse erythematous or maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs.
(iii)
- C. immitis is a dimorphic fungus with two life cycles: it follows the saprophytic cycle in the soil and the parasitic cycle in man or animals.
- The saprophytic cycle starts in the soil with spores (arthroconidia) that develop into mycelium; the mycelium matures and forms alternating spores within itself, which are released and germinate back into mycelia.
- The parasitic cycle involves inhalation of the arthroconidia, which then form spherules that become filled with endospores.
(iv) Treatment is with itraconazole, amphotericin B, or fluconazole; diagnosis is supported by microscopy showing characteristic endosporulating spherules, culture on Sabouraud's dextrose agar and brain heart infusion agar with 5% sheep blood (a severe biohazard), and serology (latex agglutination and/or complement fixation tests for antibodies to coccidioidin and spherulin).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin (reservoir) of Lassa virus.
A(ii) Describe the routes of rodent-to-human transmission.
A(iii) Describe the routes of human-to-human transmission.
A(iv) State the geographic distribution of Lassa fever.
B. State the safe practices recommended to prevent transmission.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity (hearing deficit) that may follow the illness.
questions.answerText:
A. Origin, transmission routes and distribution:
(i) Origin: Lassa fever is a zoonosis with reservoir in the multimammate rat, Mastomys natalensis (Mastomys species complex).
(ii) Rodent-to-human transmission: inhalation of aerosolised virus, ingestion of food or materials contaminated by infected rodent excreta,
Catching and preparing Mastomys as a food source.
(iii) Human-to-human transmission: direct contact with blood, tissues, secretions or excretions of infected humans, needle-stick or cut injuries,
Inhalation of aerosolised virus.
(iv) Distribution: endemic in areas of West Africa, including Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea (the Mano River basin).
B. Safe practices: village-based programmes for rodent control and avoidance, safe food storage, wetting down surfaces before sweeping,
Hospital training programmes with a barrier nursing manual to avoid nosocomial spread.
C. Anatomical basis of the hearing deficit:
- A sensorineural hearing deficit typically appears during early convalescence, occurring in one-third of cases, and is not related to the severity of the acute illness.
- It may be bilateral or unilateral and may persist for life in up to one-third of those affected.

questions.question:
A patient who drank water from an unsafe source develops profuse watery 'rice-water' diarrhoea with occasional vomiting and abdominal cramps, thirst, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, sunken eyes and a weak radial pulse.
(i) State the diagnosis, the causative organism and its features.
(ii) Explain the pathogenic basis of the illness.
(iii) State the initial (resuscitative) management.
(iv) State the definitive treatment, the laboratory diagnosis and the preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae: a Gram-negative, highly motile, comma-shaped rod with a polar flagellum, oxidase positive, facultative anaerobe, tolerant of alkaline media but sensitive to acid; reservoirs are aquatic sources (rivers, brackish water, estuaries, shellfish, zooplankton); spread where water treatment, sanitation and hygiene are inadequate.
(ii) Infection is acquired from water containing the organism or contaminated with faeces of an infected person; the organism attaches to the intestinal mucosa by the toxin coregulated pilus without invading it, then secretes cholera toxin (5 B subunits attach to the epithelial cells, 1 A subunit is the active part).
(ii) The toxin increases cyclic AMP by activating adenylyl cyclase through the Gs pathway, causing efflux of water and sodium into the lumen, giving watery 'rice-water' stools and dehydration (thirst, hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria, kidney failure, coma, death).
(iii) The basic treatment is rehydration to replace lost fluids: oral rehydration solution (ORS) for mild dehydration; intravenous fluids when the patient is severely dehydrated and cannot take enough ORS (with rehydration, under 1% of cases die; in untreated cholera gravis up to 60% can die).
(iv) Antibiotics (usually fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines, e.g. doxycycline) are used in some cases but do not shorten the illness or the duration of pathogen excretion; the disease typically lasts 4-6 days.
(iv) Laboratory diagnosis: stool (preserved at 4 C or in Cary-Blair medium); wet preparation showing darting motility, inhibited by polyvalent antiserum; enrichment in alkaline peptone water (pH 8.6); TCBS agar gives yellow sucrose-fermenting colonies; string test in 0.5% sodium deoxycholate.
(iv) Prevention: safe water, hand washing with soap, sanitation, thorough cooking of food; oral cholera vaccine (Dukoral, Shanchol, Euvichol-Plus), each requiring two doses.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the general features, classification and staining of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
A(ii) Describe transmission and pathogenesis.
A(iii) Describe the clinical forms and laboratory diagnosis.
B(i) Relate the sites and stages of the lesions to the common pathologies of tuberculosis and its treatment.
C(i) Explain how tuberculosis spreads to distant organs and the complications produced.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Slender, non-motile, aerobic, non-capsulated, non-sporing rods (2-4 um by 0.2-0.5 um) with a waxy mycolic acid coat and high GC DNA, so not stained by Gram stain; acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen, Kinyoun) bright red on a blue background; M. tuberculosis complex includes M. bovis, M. africanum, M. canetti, M. microti.
A(ii) Spread by aerosol droplets (0.5-5 um) from active pulmonary disease; fewer than 10 bacilli may infect; latent TB is not infectious; 5-10% of non-HIV infected develop disease against 30% of those with HIV; other risks: diabetes, silicosis, smoking, malnutrition, corticosteroids, overcrowding.
A(ii) Bacilli lodge in the alveoli (upper lobe) and are ingested by macrophages, forming the primary tubercle (Ghon focus) and, with regional nodes, the Ghon complex; T-cell hypersensitivity in 4-8 weeks walls off organisms in caseating granulomas (positive Mantoux); reactivation may follow in the immunosuppressed.
A(iii) Pulmonary TB: cough over 2 weeks, haemoptysis, chest pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss and anorexia; chest X-ray shows apical and posterior upper lobe lesions and cavities; sputum AFB smear (3 specimens), egg-based Lowenstein-Jensen culture, tuberculin (PPD) test, GeneXpert, interferon-gamma release assays.
B(i) The caseous centre enlarges by liquefaction and forms an air-filled cavity in which aerobic bacilli multiply outside macrophages; when the tubercle ruptures into a bronchiole bacilli spread through the lungs.
B(i) Treatment: combination chemotherapy - 2-month intensive phase with 3-4 drugs and 4-month continuation phase with 2-3 drugs; first-line drugs isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, streptomycin, ethambutol; DOTS (directly observed treatment).
B(i) Goals: cure, prevent relapse, minimise transmission and prevent MDR-TB (resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin); XDR-TB is MDR-TB also resistant to a fluoroquinolone and a second-line injectable.
C(i) After rupture bacilli reach the vascular and lymphatic systems; in 15-20% of active cases infection spreads outside the lungs (pleura, central nervous system, lymphatics, genitourinary tract, bones and joints), more often in HIV (over 50%) and young children.
C(i) Disseminated (miliary) TB makes up about 10% of extrapulmonary cases.
C(i) Complications: meningitis, pleurisy, kidney involvement, spine (Pott's disease) and bone and joint involvement.
C(i) Prevention: screening of high-risk people, early detection and treatment, BCG vaccination.
C(i) Latent infection (most infections) shows no symptoms; about 10% of latent infections progress to active disease, which if untreated kills about half of those affected.

1. Diagnosis: Lassa fever in pregnancy, with placental infection, which carries increased maternal mortality (>30% in the third trimester) and increased fetal/neonatal mortality (>85%).
2. Procedure/intervention: evacuation of the uterus, which improves the mother's chance of survival.
3. Anatomical landmark: the uterus and placenta are the sites of infection relevant to this intervention.
4. Nerve/structure at risk: the auditory (cochlear) nerve/inner ear apparatus, since a sensorineural hearing deficit is a recognised sequela of Lassa fever, occurring in about one-third of cases during early convalescence.
questions.question:
(i) A pregnant woman in her third trimester develops Lassa fever with high viraemia and evidence of placental infection. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Name a procedure/intervention that improves the mother's chance of survival.
(iii) State the anatomical landmark(s) relevant to this intervention.

A(i) Describe a biofilm under the headings: composition, sites of formation on the body, and sites of formation on medical devices.
A(ii) State the property of biofilms that is of particular clinical importance.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for the increased antibiotic resistance seen in biofilm-associated infections.
B(ii) Distinguish between the two phases of biofilm formation.
questions.answerText:
1. Biofilms are matrix-enclosed bacterial populations that adhere to a surface and interface with each other.
2. They are responsible for things such as dental plaque and clogging of water pipes.
3. Biofilms are also formed on synthetic medical implants, including intravenous catheters, orthopaedic devices and contact lenses.
4. One property of biofilms of particular clinical importance is an increased resistance to antibiotics.
5. It has been suggested that the exopolysaccharide matrix creates an exclusion barrier to antimicrobials, or more directly complexes with them to inactivate them, accounting for this increased resistance.
6. Biofilms are formed in two phases: initial reversible adherence to a surface, followed by intercellular adhesion resulting in microcolony formation and a complex biofilm architecture.
7. Biofilm formers of medical importance include Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the lungs of patients with cystic fibrosis, and Staphylococcus epidermidis on synthetic medical implants.
8. An important aspect of biofilm formation is reduced cell-cell interaction.
9. Bacteria resist physical removal from host tissue in a related way, by biofilm-producing glycocalyx, by producing fimbriae (pili), and by non-fimbrial adhesins.
10. Glycocalyx (the sugar coat) protects and prevents drying, also protects from phagocytes, is slimy, and is often a significant component of biofilms.
11. Specific bacteria usually colonise specific tissues by mechanisms including tissue tropism, specific adherence, and biofilm formation, for example plaque forming on teeth for nutrients and protection.
12. This resistance to physical and antimicrobial clearance is what allows biofilm-associated infections on implants to persist and often require removal of the implicated device for successful treatment.

A(i) B. pertussis (whooping cough) and B. parapertussis (milder) are short Gram-negative coccobacilli living mainly in the human respiratory tract; humans are the only natural hosts.
A(i) Pathogenicity: production of endotoxin affecting the respiratory mucosa.
A(ii) Presents as acute tracheobronchitis in three stages: catarrhal (2 weeks) with fever, rhinorrhoea, sneezing, anorexia, malaise.
A(ii) Paroxysmal stage (2 weeks): violent cough followed by inspiratory whoop, vomiting, convulsions.
A(ii) Convalescent stage (4 weeks).
A(iii) Affects pre-school children and is severe in those under 1 year.
B(i) Clinical diagnosis, per-nasal swab, cough plate, swab by immunofluorescence (rapid method); enriched blood agar - Bordet-Gengou medium (potato-blood-glycerol agar) with added antibiotics.
C(i) Convalescent stage shows lymphocytosis that can mimic lymphocytic leukaemia.
C(i) Treatment: erythromycin, effective in the early stages.
C(i) Prevention: whole killed bacterial vaccine given intramuscularly in the triple DPT vaccine (safe, though CNS involvement has been reported), and an acellular vaccine formed from pertussis toxin.
C(i) Related organisms: H. influenzae, Brucella and Pasteurella belong to the same group needing blood for growth.

A(ii) Describe the stages of the disease.
A(iii) Describe the age distribution and pathogenesis.
B(i) State the appropriate specimens and media.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Gram-positive spherical cocci in pairs or chains, catalase negative, non-sporing, non-motile, facultative anaerobes, capnophilic, fastidious (blood or serum-enriched media), strong carbohydrate fermenters giving lactic acid.
A(ii) Alpha-haemolytic (incomplete lysis, green pigment), beta-haemolytic (complete lysis, clearing) and non-haemolytic (gamma); Lancefield groups (A-H, K-U) based on group-specific cell wall carbohydrate: A rhamnose-N-acetyl glucosamine, B rhamnose-glucosamine, C rhamnose-N-acetyl galactosamine, D glycerol teichoic acid.
A(ii) Sherman's divisions: pyogenic, viridans, lactic, enterococci; identification also by biochemical reactions, gene sequencing and MALDI-TOF.
A(iii) S. pyogenes (A): pharyngitis, impetigo, glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever; S. agalactiae (B): neonatal sepsis and meningitis, adult bacteraemia; groups C/G: pharyngitis and pyogenic infections; enterococcus (D): endocarditis, abdominal abscess, UTI; S. gallolyticus (bovis): endocarditis, biliary disease.
A(iii) Viridans group and others: bacteraemia, meningitis, abdominal infection, tooth abscesses, and subacute endocarditis in those with pre-existing heart disease; S. pneumoniae causes otitis media, pneumonia and meningitis.
A(iv) Hyaluronic acid capsule, M protein (hair-like, anti-phagocytic, main virulence factor, up to 150 types), F protein and fibronectin adhesion, streptolysins, NADase, hyaluronidase, streptokinases, streptodornases, pyrogenic exotoxins.
A(iv) Non-invasive disease: pharyngitis, scarlet fever (rash begins on chest and spreads), impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis; invasive: necrotising fasciitis, myositis, toxic shock, bacteraemia, puerperal fever.
B(i) Non-suppurative sequelae (rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis) are not due to direct effect of the organism but to hypersensitivity reactions; nephritogenic M types 2, 42, 49, 56, 57, 60.
B(i) Maxwell's grouping: nasty (pyogenic, mostly beta-haemolytic, exotoxins), boring (viridans, enterococci, opportunists); group C streptococci share M protein and cause similar disease and are treated with penicillin and gentamicin.
C(i) S. pyogenes: Lancefield group A, bacitracin susceptible (zone around disc), throat/skin/soft tissue and sequelae.
C(i) S. agalactiae: group B, bacitracin resistant, CAMP test positive (arrowhead haemolysis near S. aureus streak), colonises colon and vagina in 10-40% of women.
C(i) S. agalactiae virulence: haemolysins, capsule (types 1a, 1b, II-IX; type III neonatal), hyaluronidase, surface proteins; causes early and late neonatal meningitis and sepsis, chorioamnionitis, abortion, postpartum sepsis.

A(ii) Describe the classification by haemolysis and by Lancefield groups.
A(iii) Describe the pathogenic groups and diseases.
A(iv) Describe the virulence factors of Streptococcus pyogenes.

A patient presents with severe bloody diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, tenesmus, fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness, with stools containing blood, mucus and pieces of necrotic tissue.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology?
(iv) How is this condition managed?
questions.answerText:
(i) Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery) due to Entamoeba histolytica.
(ii) Predisposing factors include poor personal hygiene, oral-anal contact, and travel to or residence in tropical countries where prevalence may be as high as 50%; up to 10% of the world's population may be infected with E. histolytica or the morphologically identical but non-pathogenic E. dispar.
(iii) E. histolytica is a facultative pathogen that can live as a commensal in the large intestine or, in invasive disease, trophozoites penetrate the intestinal mucosa and kill epithelial cells; lateral and downward spread of the amoeba into the submucosa produces the classic flask-shaped ulcer with a small opening and a wide base; the amoebas can also metastasise, with direct transport of trophozoites from the large intestine to the liver via the hepatic portal vein resulting in amoebic liver abscess, and haematogenous spread to the lungs resulting in pulmonary infection.
(iv) Asymptomatic cyst passers are treated with iodoquinol, paromomycin or diloxanide furoate; metronidazole or tinidazole is recommended for all symptomatic infections; dehydroemetine or emetine is used in severe disease such as necrotic colitis, perforation of the intestinal wall, or rupture of a liver abscess; necrotic colitis requires urgent hospitalisation to restore fluid and electrolyte balance, and surgery may be needed to close perforations or for a partial colostomy.

questions.question:
A patient from central Africa presents with a slowly progressive illness marked by a painful, itchy chancre at a tsetse fly bite site weeks earlier, followed by fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and visible enlargement of the glands of the posterior cervical region; later there is personality change, daytime sleepiness and slow, shuffling gait.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the pathologic basis of this condition, according to its clinical staging?
(iii) How should this patient be managed once central nervous system involvement is present?
(iv) What is the definitive treatment for blood-stage disease without central nervous system involvement?
questions.answerText:
(i) African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), specifically the slowly developing Gambian form caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense; the enlargement of the glands of the posterior cervical region described is the characteristic Winterbottom's sign.
(ii) The disease progresses through three stages: the bite reaction (a non-pustular, painful, itchy chancre forming 1-3 weeks after the bite and lasting 1-2 weeks, leaving no scar), parasitaemia with lymph node invasion (fever, malaise, insomnia, headache, lymphadenopathy and oedema), and the central nervous system stage, marked by changes in character and personality, mental retardation, lethargy, low tremulous speech, slow shuffling gait, altered reflexes, and progressing to drowsiness, an uncontrollable urge to sleep, wasting and emaciation.
(iii) Cases with central nervous system involvement should be treated with Melarsoprol.
(iv) Blood stages of African trypanosomiasis can be treated with reasonable success with Pentamidine or Suramin.

1. Rift Valley Fever was first reported in livestock by veterinary officers in Kenya's Rift Valley in the early 1910s.
2. It is generally found in the regions of eastern and southern Africa where sheep and cattle are raised, but exists in most of sub-Saharan Africa, including West Africa.
3. Rift Valley Fever virus is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, resulting in large epizootics in livestock.
4. The virus is believed to be maintained by transovarial transmission between the mosquito and its offspring.
5. Humans are incidentally infected when bitten by infected mosquitoes or when coming into contact with infected animal tissues.
6. Most human infections occur one to two weeks following the appearance of abortion or disease in livestock, and infected humans experience flu-like symptoms with recovery after an incubation period of 2-6 days.
7. In 0.5% of cases, haemorrhagic fever develops following the initial febrile stage, and another 0.5% of cases develop retinitis or encephalitis one to four weeks after infection.
8. For viral haemorrhagic fevers spread by arthropod vectors, prevention efforts should focus on community-wide insect and arthropod control.
9. People are also encouraged to use insect repellent, proper clothing, bed nets, window screens, and other insect barriers to avoid being bitten.
10. Retinopathy occurs in 1-10% of cases, one to three weeks after the onset of symptoms, and presents with conjunctivitis and photophobia.
11. Retinopathy can lead to permanent vision loss, though death from this complication is uncommon.
12. The haemorrhagic fever form of the disease occurs 2-4 days after the onset of fever and presents with melena, haematemesis, petechiae, jaundice, shock and coma, with a case-fatality of around 50%.
