(ii) Functionally, because arteries cannot relax as quickly, blood pressure cannot adjust quickly when people stand, putting older people at risk of dizziness or fainting on standing; exchange of oxygen and nutrients to tissues occurs more slowly.
Physiotherapy assessment/treatment approach: monitor vital signs and blood pressure, calculate maximum heart rate, and perform necessary warm-ups before exercise; allow more rest periods during exercise since patients fatigue more easily, watch for signs of DVT, and ensure adequate fluid intake.
Changes to the heart and vessels are only evident when the heart must work hard (exercise or illness), so structured, monitored exercise progression is important; about 65% of clients older than 70 are medicated for hypertension, which must be considered in programme design.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises from fundamental connective-tissue changes - increased collagen crosslinking, altered matrix composition and loss of elastin - making the entire vascular system, including the heart and peripheral vessels, stiffer and less compliant.
This produces the characteristic rise in blood pressure with age and the reduction in cardiac output from compromised left ventricular contractility, both of which reduce tolerance for physical activity and exercise.
Thickening of the capillary basement membrane slows the exchange of oxygen and nutrients between blood and working tissue, further limiting exercise capacity.
Because arteries and arterioles cannot relax quickly during the cardiac cycle, orthostatic blood pressure regulation is impaired, producing risk of dizziness/fainting on standing, which has direct implications for fall risk.
Age-related changes in the heart and blood vessels are among those most responsive to lifestyle habits (exercise, sleep, diet) and medications, so they are not fixed and can be favourably influenced by rehabilitation.
Overall, these cardiovascular changes reduce exercise tolerance and increase cardiovascular risk, underlying much of the reduced physical capacity and fatigue seen in geriatric rehabilitation.

(i) Impairments: pain, reduced joint mobility. Activity limitations: difficulty with light housework, shopping, self-care activities (bathing, dressing, lacing shoes), walking and lifting. Participation restrictions: anxiety and depression associated with the struggle of chronic pain, and reduced social/occupational engagement.
(ii) Goals should address reducing pain-related disability and improving function in mobility and self-care, since those with widespread pain (upper and lower extremities and trunk) have a greater likelihood of severe difficulties in ADLs, walking and lifting.
(iii) Flexibility exercises, aerobic exercise/walking programme, strengthening exercise (isometrics, sit-to-stand, squats, open-chain exercises with cuff weights), joint mobilisation or manipulation, and treatment modalities (TENS, heat, cryotherapy).
(iv) Medication side effects such as fatigue, sedation, dizziness and confusion can limit a person's ability to participate in therapy and should be monitored; comorbid cognitive impairment can make accurate pain assessment particularly challenging, so pain assessment and treatment response must be interpreted with this in mind.
(v) Encourage positive, active coping strategies (positive self-talk, exercise) rather than passive coping strategies (hoping, praying, catastrophizing), which are less effective and associated with greater disability.
questions.question:
An elderly patient has widespread chronic pain affecting her upper and lower extremities and trunk, with difficulty in light housework, shopping and self-care.
(i) State the problem list.
(ii) State the short-term and long-term goals.
(iii) Outline the specific physiotherapy interventions with parameters.
(iv) State the precautions/contraindications.
(v) Give home/community advice and prevention measures.

(i) Describe the age-related changes in the gastrointestinal system.
(ii) State the functional consequences and the physiotherapy assessment or treatment approach.
(iii) Explain the basis of the resulting deficit or disability.
questions.answerText:
(i) The digestive system has considerable reserve, so aging affects it less than other systems; oesophageal contraction strength and upper sphincter tension decrease, though food movement is usually not impaired.
The bone structure of the jaws may change with loss of dentures, salivary gland function and saliva volume/quality diminish, and the gag reflex reduces, increasing choking risk; the stomach lining's capacity to resist damage decreases, increasing peptic ulcer risk especially with NSAID/aspirin use.
Intestinal motility decreases with age, the colon becomes hypotonic, leading to increased storage capacity, longer stool transit time and greater stool dehydration; the liver's ability to metabolise substances and withstand toxic stress decreases.
(ii) Functionally, these changes contribute to dysphagia and choking risk, atrophic gastritis, chronic constipation, faecal incontinence from loss of anal sphincter tone, lactose intolerance, and slower drug metabolism by the liver.
Physiotherapy assessment/treatment approach: take a nutritional history (number of meals/day, diet content), be alert to swallowing/choking risk during exercise sessions, and recognise that reduced physical activity and reduced exercise further worsen constipation, so encouraging mobility and exercise is part of management.
Bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine can reduce absorption of vitamin B12, iron and calcium, which is relevant to bone health and should be considered alongside musculoskeletal assessment.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises because reduced saliva, weakened gag reflex and altered oesophageal motility (presbyesophagus) together increase the risk of dysphagia and aspiration.
Reduced intestinal motility and pelvic floor weakness in older women contribute to chronic constipation and faecal incontinence, both of which can restrict participation in physiotherapy sessions and community activities.
Because the liver metabolises drugs more slowly with age, a drug dose safe in a younger person may produce dose-related side effects in an older person, so drug dosages often need to be reduced, which is relevant when medication side effects (e.g., sedation, dizziness) are suspected of affecting therapy performance.
Loss of control of the internal and external anal sphincters can cause faecal incontinence, which is usually emotionally traumatic for cognitively intact older adults and can affect participation and dignity in rehabilitation.
Most GI changes typically do not cause noticeable symptoms on their own, so significant symptoms should prompt consideration of disease rather than being attributed to normal aging alone.
Overall, gastrointestinal changes affect nutrition, continence and drug handling, all of which have downstream effects on strength, endurance and rehabilitation potential.

(i) Immobility is the inability to move or be moved independently; it is one of the "Giants of Geriatrics", a term coined by the late Prof Bernard Isaacs to highlight major illnesses associated with ageing.
This term reflects the gigantic numbers of elderly affected and the giant onslaught on victims' independence.
Difficulty or inability to perform mobility tasks is an important outcome of disease and a public health problem in older people; it is often multifactorial in origin.
(ii) Common pathologies contributing to immobility include musculoskeletal osteoarthritis (pain, muscle weakness, deconditioning), heart disease/COPD progressing to congestive cardiac failure (shortness of breath, loss of work ability), stroke (muscle weakness, abnormal gait, poor proprioception), and cataracts/macular degeneration (poor vision and falls).
Impaired mobility is therefore a common pathway for many different diseases and is associated with significant functional decline; proper evaluation allows the causes to be identified and appropriate intervention to be applied for better outcome.
(iii) Immobility negatively affects the quality of life of older people, threatens their independence, and increases both informal and formal carer needs (a burden to society).
Inactivity from immobility increases the risks of incontinence, pressure ulcers, deep vein thrombosis, osteoporosis and pulmonary embolism, and increases the risk of muscular weakness and lowered aerobic capacity, leading finally to poor physical capacity or deconditioning - a vicious spiral.
Physiotherapy prevents/manages immobility by avoiding this vicious spiral through early intervention and treatment focused on factors that will improve quality of life; early consultation is important for better outcome.
Functional assessment of the elderly is very important in a comprehensive geriatric assessment and patient management in a holistic manner, allowing problems to be identified and addressed with a coordinated plan.
Management approaches include strengthening exercise, ADL training, transfer training, gait training (e.g. with a walker), alternate stepping exercises, and safety/fall-prevention education and programmes.
An example plan of care delivers physiotherapy over six weeks (5 times weekly for 2 weeks, 3 times weekly for 3 weeks, 2 times weekly for 1 week), aiming to return the patient to safe function at home under distal caregiver supervision.
Because impaired mobility can lead to a cascade of complications, early, comprehensive, and holistic physiotherapy intervention is the core principle for preventing the secondary problems of immobility.
questions.question:
(i) Describe immobility as a geriatric syndrome in full.
(ii) State how it relates to common pathologies.
(iii) Explain how it may lead to secondary problems and how physiotherapy prevents or manages them.

questions.answerText:
(i) Maximum respiratory function gradually declines with age, with a decrease in peak airflow and gas exchange.
There is a decrease in measures of lung function such as vital capacity (the maximum amount of air breathed out after maximum inhalation), and a weakening of the respiratory muscles.
There is a decline in the effectiveness of lung defence mechanisms, and a reduction in the elasticity of lung tissue and the chest wall, along with a decline in maximal voluntary ventilation and the rate of gas diffusion.
(ii) Functionally, older people are at higher risk of developing pneumonia after bacterial or viral infections because of reduced lung defence mechanisms, and have a reduced ability to perform vigorous or intense aerobic exercise.
Physiotherapy assessment/treatment approach: plan activities with shorter durations to accommodate reduced capacity, and train airway clearance techniques and effective coughing to compensate for weakened respiratory muscles and defence mechanisms.
In healthy people these age-related changes seldom cause symptoms on their own, but are compounded by the destructive effects of heart and lung disease, especially those caused by smoking, so assessment should distinguish normal decline from disease.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises from a combination of weaker respiratory muscles, reduced chest wall and lung elasticity, and reduced vital capacity, which together lower the reserve available for increased ventilatory demand.
Reduced peak airflow and gas exchange limit the oxygen available to working tissues during exertion, contributing to reduced exercise tolerance alongside cardiovascular changes.
Decline in lung defence mechanisms increases vulnerability to respiratory infection, which can precipitate acute functional decline, falls, or immobility in an older adult.
Because the digestive-like reserve capacity of the lungs is reduced, illness (such as a chest infection) that would be tolerated in a younger person can produce disproportionate functional decline in an older adult.
These changes contribute somewhat to an older person's reduced ability to do vigorous exercise such as running, biking or mountain climbing, even in the absence of overt lung disease.
Overall, respiratory system changes reduce exercise capacity and increase infection risk, both of which are relevant to pacing and airway-clearance components of geriatric physiotherapy.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the age-related changes in the respiratory system.
(ii) State the functional consequences and the physiotherapy assessment or treatment approach.
(iii) Explain the basis of the resulting deficit or disability.

questions.answerText:
(i) A Timed Up and Go score above 13.5 seconds indicates increased fall risk, and slowed gait speed (below the usual 1.2-1.3 m/s, with 0.5 m/s only sufficient for limited community mobility) indicates reduced functional mobility; slow gait speed has been shown to be the single best predictor of functional decline and disability.
(ii) The findings reflect involvement of the musculoskeletal system (strength, endurance), the sensory systems (vision, vestibular function, proprioception) and central nervous system integration of balance and gait.
(iii) Differential considerations include postural/orthostatic hypotension, medication-related instability, cognitive impairment affecting judgement and safety, and vestibular disease.
(iv) Clinical reasoning should prioritise addressing modifiable intrinsic factors (strength, balance, medications, vision) and extrinsic environmental hazards together, since falls-prevention is most effective when several risk factors are targeted simultaneously; strengthening, endurance and balance retraining should therefore take priority alongside medication review and home modification.
questions.question:
An elderly patient is assessed with the Timed Up and Go test, scoring above 13.5 seconds, and her gait speed is measured as slower than the usual adult walking speed of 1.2-1.3 m/s.
(i) Interpret these findings.
(ii) State the systems or structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to be considered.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for treatment priorities.

questions.answerText:
A(i) A disability is any continuing condition that restricts everyday activities, attributable to an intellectual, psychiatric, cognitive, neurological, sensory or physical impairment or a combination of these.
It is usually defined in terms of restrictions in the ability to perform activities of daily living (ADL) or instrumental ADL.
A(ii) The three main underlying causes of disability are diseases, injuries, and the processes of ageing.
The borderlines between the processes of ageing, diseases of old age, and consequent functional decline are in many cases poorly understood.
A(iii) Impairments are problems in body function or alterations in body structure, e.g. paralysis or blindness.
Activity limitations are difficulties in executing activities such as walking or eating; participation restrictions are problems with involvement in life areas such as employment or transportation.
B. Disability arises from the interaction of health conditions with contextual factors - environmental and personal factors.
An individual's functional performance results from the interaction between competence and environmental demand (person-environment fit); inaccessible environments create disability by creating barriers to participation.
When competence is inadequate to respond to environmental demands, excess disability may result, so contextual factors can worsen or lessen the functional impact of the same underlying impairment in an older adult.
C. Impairment is a problem in body function or structure (organ level), while disability refers to difficulties in activity/participation resulting from impairment interacting with context.
Handicap, by contrast, is felt at the person or societal level rather than the organ level - it reflects the social disadvantage that results from impairment or disability.
Disability, impairment and handicap are therefore not synonymous, and each represents a different level at which the effect of a health condition is experienced.
questions.question:
A. Describe disability under the following headings: (i) definition (ii) causes (iii) clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the interaction between health conditions and contextual (environmental and personal) factors matters in older adults.
C. Distinguish between disability and handicap.

questions.answerText:
(i) The presentation is consistent with a femoral neck fracture (a displaced intracapsular hip fracture), given the fall, hip pain, decreased range of motion and a shortened, externally rotated limb.
(ii) Femoral neck fractures in the elderly are associated with low-energy falls; risk factors include female gender, decreased mobility and low bone density. The femoral neck's junctional location connecting the shaft to the head makes it prone to fracture, and because its blood supply runs along the neck (chiefly via the medial femoral circumflex artery), a displaced fracture can compromise healing, predisposing to non-union or avascular necrosis.
(iii) Subjective: circumstances of the fall, pain and its rating, past medical/surgical history and pre-fall functional status. Objective: observe for limb shortening/external rotation and deformity, assess pain, hip range of motion, and general observation, palpation and movement. Outcome measures: functional mobility tools such as the Timed Up and Go test and gait speed once movement is permitted, alongside standard geriatric assessment tools.
(iv) Goals are to promote healing, prevent complications and return function, aiming to return the patient to premorbid functional level. Physical therapy should begin immediately after surgery, with weight-bearing as tolerated and hip movement precautions observed depending on the surgical approach used; the patient should be educated on the limitations on hip movements, and safety/fall-prevention education should be given.
questions.question:
An elderly woman sustains a low-energy fall at home and is brought in complaining of hip pain with reduced range of hip motion; on inspection the affected lower limb appears shortened and externally rotated.
(i) State the probable diagnosis/condition.
(ii) Explain the age-related physiological or pathological basis for this presentation.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy assessment for this patient, covering subjective, objective and outcome-measure components.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management plan for this patient.

(i) Describe the effects of disuse/immobilisation on the elderly in full.
(ii) State how it relates to common pathologies.
(iii) Explain how it may lead to secondary problems and how physiotherapy prevents or manages them.
questions.answerText:
(i) Disuse/immobilisation refers to the reduced activity that follows illness, disability or hospitalisation in the elderly, and is closely linked to the geriatric giant of immobility (inability to move or be moved independently).
Common problems associated with disabling disease/disability in the elderly include pain (the most common problem, almost everywhere), generalised weakness, and contractures arising from reduced activity.
Many elderly persons suffer the effects of a specific disabling disease or disability such as arthritis and stroke; the combined effects of aging and disease place the individual at high risk for loss of functional independence and mobility.
(ii) Disuse/immobilisation relates to common pathologies including musculoskeletal disease (arthritis, contractures from inactivity) and neurological impairment (upper or lower motor neuron).
It also relates to generalised deconditioning, often leaving the elderly person homebound.
Inactivity increases the risks of incontinence, pressure ulcers, deep vein thrombosis, osteoporosis and pulmonary embolism, and increases the risk of muscular weakness and lowered aerobic capacity, leading to poor physical capacity or deconditioning.
(iii) These secondary problems (pressure ulcers, DVT, osteoporosis, pulmonary embolism, incontinence, deconditioning) can each independently worsen prognosis and further restrict mobility, creating a vicious spiral of worsening immobility.
Immobility negatively affects quality of life, threatens independence and personal autonomy, and increases both informal and formal carer needs, becoming a burden to society if not addressed.
Physiotherapy prevents/manages disuse effects through early intervention and treatment focused on factors that will improve quality of life, avoiding the vicious spiral of immobility.
Functional assessment of the elderly is very important in a comprehensive geriatric assessment and patient management in a holistic manner, so that the specific causes of disuse in an individual can be identified and addressed.
Management strategies include strengthening exercise, active and resisted exercises, transfer training, gait training with assistive devices, and safety/fall-prevention education, delivered over a defined structured period (e.g. a six-week plan of care).
Overall, because disuse/immobilisation triggers a cascade of preventable secondary complications, early, proactive, and comprehensive physiotherapy intervention is the central principle for management, aiming to interrupt the spiral of decline as soon as it is identified.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the age-related changes in the sensory (visual and auditory) system.
(ii) State the functional consequences and the physiotherapy assessment or treatment approach.
(iii) Explain the basis of the resulting deficit or disability.
questions.answerText:
(i) Ageing includes a decline in accommodation (presbyopia), glare tolerance, adaptation, low-contrast sensitivity, attentional visual fields and colour discrimination; the pupil becomes smaller and reacts more sluggishly to light, and the lens stiffens, yellows and becomes denser.
Changes occur in depth perception, making it harder to judge the height of curbs or steps, and in the ability to focus on small print; the retina becomes less sensitive, and fewer nerve cells transmit visual signals from the eyes to the brain.
Presbycusis (progressive hearing loss, especially for higher-pitched sounds) is common, along with increased wax build-up, difficulty hearing in loud places, and vestibular imbalance/tinnitus (though these are not considered normal).
(ii) Functionally, vision changes affect reading, balancing and driving, and may make an older person appear confused or disoriented in an unfamiliar environment even though they are independent and efficient in their own environment; hearing loss can alter the ability to understand speech and can cause depression and social isolation.
Physiotherapy assessment/treatment approach: approach the person directly, not from the side, and ensure proper lighting for vision changes; for hearing, reduce background noise, position yourself where the person can see you and is fairly close, and ensure you have the person's attention before speaking.
Environmental modification during assessment should use diffuse, adequate lighting while avoiding glossy or highly polished surfaces and directional/localised light, since changes in depth perception and glare tolerance increase fall risk on such surfaces.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises because reduced pupil size, lens stiffening/yellowing/denseness and retinal changes together reduce the amount and quality of light reaching the retina, impairing vision especially in low light or with glare.
Impaired depth perception directly increases the risk of misjudging curbs or steps, and impaired colour discrimination can cause misidentification of similarly shaded objects, both relevant to fall risk during mobility training.
There are three major types of hearing loss - high-frequency loss, conductive loss (muffled, poorly conducted sound) and central hearing loss (speech heard but not understood) - each requiring a different communication strategy during therapy.
Hearing loss that goes unrecognised by the individual can lead to social withdrawal, paranoia, or the perception of being deliberately excluded from conversation, which can affect engagement in group-based rehabilitation.
Because visual and auditory changes can make an older person appear cognitively confused when the underlying problem is sensory, accurate assessment must distinguish sensory impairment from cognitive impairment before concluding on cognitive status.
Overall, sensory system changes are directly relevant to fall risk, communication and participation, and require specific environmental and communication adaptations in physiotherapy practice.

questions.question:
(i) Describe polypharmacy/iatrogenic problems as a geriatric syndrome in full.
(ii) State how it relates to common presentations/pathologies.
(iii) Explain how it may lead to secondary problems and how physiotherapy-relevant management addresses them.
questions.answerText:
(i) Polypharmacy literally means "many drugs"; it reflects the problems that occur when older persons take too many, or too many of the wrong, drugs (iatrogenesis), and is one of the "Giants of Geriatrics".
An estimated 5% to 23% of hospital admissions are due to drug-related illness; unnecessary prescribing, misuse of medication and inappropriate prescriptions can contribute to the risk of drug-related illness.
Elderly people are at particular risk because of changes in drug distribution and metabolism, multiple symptoms leading to multiple drugs, expectations of "a pill for every ill", over-reliance on treating symptoms rather than comprehensive geriatric assessment, and multiple factors affecting medication adherence.
(ii) Drug-related illness often presents atypically and non-specifically as a geriatric giant itself - confusion (delirium, dementia), depression, falls, incontinence, and decreased activities of daily living.
Frequent drug side effects in the elderly include falls, arrhythmias, and confusion (from sedation or anticholinergic effects).
Other effects include dehydration from diuretics, hypotension from cardiac medications, NSAID gastropathy, digoxin toxicity (even at therapeutic levels), and insulin-induced hypoglycaemia.
Elderly patients are particularly vulnerable to side effects of major tranquilisers (delirium, extrapyramidal symptoms, arrhythmias, postural hypotension) and benzodiazepines (ataxia leading to falls/fractures, confusion, disinhibition, withdrawal symptoms), with long-acting benzodiazepines such as diazepam and flurazepam best avoided.
(iii) These drug effects can precipitate or worsen falls, incontinence, confusion/delirium, and decline in activities of daily living, compounding the other Giants of Geriatrics and reducing functional independence.
Recommendations for drug therapy in the elderly include making a diagnosis before starting multiple drug therapy (avoiding treatment of symptoms alone), beginning with a low dose and simplifying the regimen to maximise compliance, advising patients of serious drug effects, and periodically reviewing the medication list and doses.
Advanced patient age should never in itself be considered a contraindication to beneficial drug therapy in older persons, so medication review should be individualised rather than reflexively restrictive.
In falls management specifically, patients who have fallen should have their medications reviewed, altered or stopped in light of their fall risk, especially those on four or more medications.
Overall, physiotherapy-relevant management involves recognising medication side effects (e.g. sedation, dizziness, postural hypotension) as possible contributors to falls, confusion or reduced participation in therapy, and communicating these findings to the prescribing team for periodic medication review.

questions.question:
An elderly patient is screened using the Mini-Mental Status Examination and scores 20 out of 30.
(i) Interpret these findings.
(ii) State the systems or structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to be considered.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for treatment priorities.
questions.answerText:
(i) A score of 23 or lower on the Mini-Mental Status Examination is indicative of cognitive impairment, whereas a score of 24 and higher purports to identify individuals who are cognitively intact; a score of 20 therefore indicates cognitive impairment.
(ii) Cortical dementia tends to cause problems with memory, language, thinking and social behaviour, primarily affecting the cortex, while subcortical dementia affects parts of the brain below the cortex, causing changes in emotions and movement in addition to memory problems.
(iii) Differential considerations include dementia (acquired, persistent decline from previous function), delirium (sudden, sometimes rapid change in mental function with a fluctuating course, a common complication of medical illness or postoperative recovery), and depression, since these conditions share overlapping features that can make them difficult to tell apart.
(iv) An individual should not be assumed to have dementia until a thorough medical assessment has been made, given the stigma attached to dementia and the presence of ageism; clinical reasoning should therefore prioritise ruling out reversible dementia-like conditions and delirium before committing to a diagnosis of dementia and planning long-term management.

questions.question:
An elderly patient's family reports progressive memory loss and increasing difficulty performing everyday tasks over many months; the family, rather than the patient, first noticed the changes.
(i) State the probable diagnosis/condition.
(ii) Explain the age-related basis for this presentation.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy assessment.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management plan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Dementia (most likely of the Alzheimer's type, since it is the most common cause), given newly acquired cognitive impairments sufficient to interfere with social or occupational functioning, more often first noticed by family members than by the affected person.
(ii) Dementia increases with age, affecting only about 5% of people aged 71-79 years, but 24.2% of those aged 80-89 years and 37.4% of those aged 90 years and older, although dementia is not itself a normal part of the aging process.
(iii) Because cognitive impairments need to be acquired and represent a decline from a previous level, assessment should include cognitive screening (such as the Mini-Cog or Mini-Mental Status Examination, where a score of 24 or higher purports to identify individuals who are cognitively intact and 23 or lower is indicative of cognitive impairment) alongside functional status (ADLs/IADLs), often supplemented by caregiver report since the affected person may not notice the first symptoms.
(iv) The physiotherapist acts as a member of the geriatric rehabilitation team and as a resource for other caregivers of patients with cognitive impairment; management includes environmental modification to support orientation and caregiver education, alongside physical activity, which has been shown to have a comparable reduction in depressive symptoms to antidepressant medication.

A(i) Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, associated with advancing age and developing over a period of years; not all its causes are known, though a small percentage are related to gene mutations passed from parent to child.
Early-onset/familial AD is rare and develops between ages 30-60; late-onset AD is the more common form.
A(ii) Risk factors include advancing age, positive family history, being a woman, and race (African-American, Hispanic).
A(iii) In the early stages: memory impairment, lapses of judgement, subtle personality changes, depression, difficulty in ADL performance, visual-spatial problems and delusions.
In the late stages: loss of bowel and bladder control, repetitive physical behaviours (pacing, repetitive folding), loss of interest and decreased activities.
Summary features include progressive deficit of memory, progressive loss of functional skills, and behavioural disturbance, mood disorders and psychotic problems that arise and disappear.
B. Alzheimer's disease patients have plaques and tangles in their brains - plaques are clumps of the protein beta-amyloid, and tangles are fibrous tangles made of tau protein.
It is thought that these clumps damage healthy neurons and the fibres connecting them, producing the progressive cognitive decline characteristic of the disease.
Because this pathology accumulates gradually and is strongly age-associated, and because one important risk gene (APOE) increases susceptibility, Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia in older adults.
C. Alzheimer's disease typically progresses gradually from mild memory problems to problems recognising friends, family and self, driven by beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles.
Vascular dementia is caused by damage to the vessels supplying blood to the brain and shows abrupt onset, step-by-step deterioration and a fluctuating course, with problem-solving, slowed thinking and loss of focus/organisation more noticeable than memory loss.
Risk factors for vascular dementia (hypertension, smoking, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, cardiovascular/cerebrovascular disease) differ from the risk profile of Alzheimer's disease (age, family history, female gender, race).
questions.question:
A. Describe Alzheimer's disease under the following headings: (i) definition/causes (ii) risk factors (iii) clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia.
C. Distinguish between Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia.

questions.answerText:
(i) Chronic/persistent pain in the elderly, commonly related to osteoarthritis, which has a prevalence of 49.5% in those aged 65 and above.
(ii) Pain increases in incidence and prevalence after age 60 because of the cumulative burden of aging-associated illnesses such as osteoarthritis and compression fractures; six factors are proposed to alter pain perception in older adults - decreased nociceptor density, changes in the conductivity of nociceptive afferents, changes in central coding of pain, changes in segmental nociceptive reflexes, alterations in descending inhibition of pain, and psychosocial influences that alter the meaning and impact of pain - with older adults taking longer to report pain and longer for pain tenderness to resolve.
(iii) Subjective: a brief pain history covering the quality of pain, pain intensity (patient self-report preferred), location (including referred pain), and aggravating and easing factors. Objective: a full history and physical examination detailing impairments in cardiopulmonary endurance, motor function, joint mobility, motor control and posture. Outcome measures: pain intensity instruments such as the Numerical Rating Scale, Verbal Descriptor Scale, Visual Analog Scale or Faces Pain Scale, and standardised instruments such as the Multidimensional Pain Inventory or the Geriatric Pain Measure.
(iv) Therapeutic exercise (flexibility exercises, aerobic exercise/walking programme, strengthening exercise such as isometrics, sit-to-stand, squats and open-chain exercises with cuff weights), joint mobilisation or manipulation, orthotic or supportive devices (therapeutic taping, custom-fitted orthosis, braces), and treatment modalities such as TENS, heat and cryotherapy.
questions.question:
An elderly patient reports chronic joint pain that has progressively limited her mobility and activities of daily living.
(i) State the probable diagnosis/condition.
(ii) Explain the age-related basis for this presentation.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy assessment.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management plan.

questions.answerText:
(i) Immobility is often multifactorial: musculoskeletal osteoarthritis (pain, muscle weakness, deconditioning), heart disease/COPD progressing to congestive cardiac failure (loss of work ability), stroke (muscle weakness, abnormal gait, poor proprioception), and cataracts/macular degeneration (poor vision and falls).
(ii) Immobility adversely affects quality of life, threatens independence and personal autonomy, and increases formal and informal carer needs and societal burden; inactivity increases the risks of incontinence, pressure ulcers, deep vein thrombosis, osteoporosis and pulmonary embolism, and increases the risk of muscular weakness and lowered aerobic capacity, leading to poor physical capacity or deconditioning.
(iii) Management should avoid the vicious spiral of immobility through early intervention and treatment focused on factors that will improve quality of life. Early comprehensive functional assessment is justified because functional assessment of the elderly is very important in a comprehensive geriatric assessment and patient management in a holistic manner, allowing the vicious spiral of worsening immobility to be interrupted before complications such as pressure ulcers or DVT develop.
questions.question:
An elderly patient has become progressively immobile.
(i) State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications/consequences that may follow.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options, justifying one.

questions.answerText:
(i) A gradual decrease in the volume and weight of the kidneys occurs with aging, so that by the ninth decade renal size is about 70 percent of that in the third decade, with a decline in the total number of glomeruli per kidney.
The glomerular filtration rate reduces, impairing drug metabolism and excretion, so medications remain in the bloodstream longer; both concentrating and diluting ability of the kidneys deteriorate, increasing risk of dehydration and hyponatraemia.
Bladder capacity decreases and bladder muscles weaken so the impulse to urinate cannot be delayed as long; in older adults the sensation of needing to void occurs later or not at all, leading to overflow incontinence, and in men the prostate commonly enlarges.
(ii) Functionally, these changes cause urinary frequency, nocturia, urgency, incomplete bladder emptying, increased risk of urinary tract infection, and urinary incontinence, which can also increase fall risk when rushing to the toilet.
Physiotherapy assessment/treatment approach: assess fluid intake pattern, mobility and dexterity to reach the toilet, and post-voidal residual urine; treatment includes pelvic floor/Kegel exercises, bladder retraining and behavioural methods.
Because medications remain in the bloodstream longer due to reduced renal clearance, drug dosages often need to be decreased in older people, and this should be considered when interpreting fatigue, dizziness or confusion during physiotherapy sessions.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises because declining glomerular filtration and reduced concentrating/diluting capacity reduce renal reserve, so illness, dehydration or medication changes can more readily precipitate acute kidney or fluid/electrolyte problems.
Weakened bladder muscles and a later-occurring or absent sensation of bladder fullness underlie both overflow incontinence and incomplete emptying, which in turn increases susceptibility to urinary tract infection.
In women, declining oestrogen thins the urethral lining and reduces sphincter closure, increasing risk of stress incontinence; in men, prostatic enlargement gradually obstructs urine flow, which if untreated can cause urinary retention and kidney damage.
These changes, taken together, are central to the pathophysiology of the incontinence commonly seen as one of the "Giants of Geriatrics".
Because changes that occur with age do not in themselves cause disease but reduce reserve kidney function, discerning what is normal aging versus disease in the urinary tract is clinically important.
Overall, genitourinary changes reduce renal and bladder reserve, predisposing older adults to incontinence, infection, and drug-related complications relevant to physiotherapy management.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the age-related changes in the genitourinary/urinary system.
(ii) State the functional consequences and the physiotherapy assessment or treatment approach.
(iii) Explain the basis of the resulting deficit or disability.

questions.answerText:
(i) This level of endurance falls well below norms for community mobility (a gait speed of 0.5 m/s is described as sufficient only for limited community mobility), indicating severe deconditioning that limits safe independent function.
(ii) The musculoskeletal system (muscle performance and endurance) is primarily affected, in the context of generalised deconditioning.
(iii) Differential contributors, given that immobility is often multifactorial, include musculoskeletal osteoarthritis (pain, weakness), heart disease/COPD (loss of work ability), stroke (weakness, abnormal gait, poor proprioception), and cataracts/macular degeneration (poor vision and falls).
(iv) Clinical reasoning should prioritise a comprehensive functional assessment to identify which of these multifactorial contributors are present, then address them through strengthening exercise, ADL training, transfer and gait training, and safety/fall-prevention education, since functional assessment is very important in a comprehensive geriatric assessment and holistic patient management.
questions.question:
An elderly patient's functional assessment shows poor endurance, limited to walking only 4 metres before getting tired.
(i) Interpret these findings.
(ii) State the systems or structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to be considered.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for treatment priorities.

questions.answerText:
(i) Impairments: impaired balance and gait, reduced lower-limb strength. Activity limitations: unable to ambulate safely without risk of falling. Participation restrictions: reduced community and social engagement because of fear of falling.
(ii) Goals should address reducing fall risk and improving confidence in mobility, working toward safe movement in the home and community; older people who have had recurrent falls should be offered long-term exercise and gait/balance training.
(iii) Screening for risk using the Timed Up and Go test and Tinetti balance and gait scale; strengthening and endurance exercises; a balance retraining programme, shown to reduce the risk of falls over a period as short as four months.
(iv) Correct prescription of assistive devices (type, size, accommodation design) must be ensured before use; medications should be reviewed for their contribution to fall risk, especially in patients on four or more medications.
(v) Education and home modification, including grab bars in the bathroom and for outside steps, firm stair railings, automatic outside lights, higher toilets and flashlight key holders; watching for imminent signs such as grabbing objects or holding onto walls, and cautious stepping.
questions.question:
An elderly patient with recurrent falls and a fear of falling is referred for physiotherapy; she has impaired balance and gait and has reduced her outdoor activities.
(i) State the problem list, covering impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions.
(ii) State the short-term and long-term goals.
(iii) Outline the specific physiotherapy interventions with parameters.
(iv) State the precautions/contraindications.
(v) Give home/community advice and prevention measures.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Osteoporosis is a skeletal disorder characterised by a decrease in bone mass, which may result in mechanical failure of the skeleton.
The decrease in bone mass is an age-related phenomenon, beginning in the fourth decade of life.
A(ii) The decrease in bone mass is due to a relative increase of bone resorption over formation, the basis of which is unknown, though hormonal factors play a role since women are more susceptible than men.
Nutritional factors (inadequate calcium, protein and vitamin D) and sedentary lifestyle/physical inactivity also lead to bone loss.
A(iii) There is a linear decline in bone mass at about 10 percent per decade for women and 5 percent per decade for men; by the eighth and ninth decades, 30 to 50 percent of skeletal mass may be lost.
Bones become more fragile and more likely to break, especially in old age, predisposing to fracture, e.g. of the femoral neck.
B. The rate of development of osteoporosis in women accelerates after menopause, and oestrogen is critical for maintenance of bone mass in both men and women.
Because women have a faster rate of bone mass loss during and after menopause (linear decline of about 10%/decade versus 5%/decade in men), osteoporosis becomes more common and more severe in older women.
Older women who are inactive (e.g. spending many hours lying or sitting) become increasingly osteoporotic, frail, and more predisposed to falling and bone breakage.
C. Osteoporosis is a skeletal disorder involving a decrease in bone mass/mineral density, predisposing to fracture with minimal trauma.
Osteoarthritis, in contrast, is a joint disorder in which the cartilage inside a joint becomes thinner and its proteoglycans become altered, making the joint less resilient and more susceptible to damage.
Both are age-related musculoskeletal conditions, but osteoporosis affects bone mass/strength while osteoarthritis affects joint cartilage and mobility.
questions.question:
A. Describe osteoporosis under the following headings: (i) definition (ii) causes (iii) clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why osteoporosis is more common and more severe in older women.
C. Distinguish between osteoporosis and osteoarthritis.

questions.answerText:
(i) From about age 30, bone density begins to diminish in both men and women, accelerating in women after menopause due to reduced oestrogen; cartilage inside joints becomes thinner and its proteoglycans altered, making joints less resilient.
Joints become stiffer because connective tissue in ligaments and tendons becomes more rigid and brittle, limiting range of motion; loss of muscle (sarcopenia) begins around age 30, reducing muscle tissue, fibre number and size.
Fast-twitch fibres are lost faster than slow-twitch fibres, slowing contraction; by age 75 body fat typically doubles compared with young adulthood; collagen crosslinking increases, water is lost from the intervertebral discs (causing height loss) and articular cartilage.
(ii) Functionally, bones become more fragile and likely to break (predisposing to fracture), reduced range of motion and loss of shock-absorbing "bounce" occur, and increased stress is placed on joints such as the knee, predisposing to arthritis or falls.
Physiotherapy assessment should include range of motion, muscle strength/power, posture, gait and anthropometric measures (e.g. BMI, waist circumference); treatment approaches include strengthening and weight-bearing exercise, since the natural pull of contracting muscles maintains bone mineral density.
Exercise programmes should target strength, balance and endurance, since most muscle loss beyond the expected 10-15% is preventable with regular exercise, and inactivity (e.g. prolonged bed rest/sitting) accelerates osteoporosis and fall risk.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises because a decreased loss/gain ratio in bone remodelling (more breakdown than formation, believed to have a hormonal basis) causes progressive bone loss, while cartilage water loss and increased collagen crosslinking reduce joint resilience and range of motion.
Sarcopenia compounds this by reducing muscle mass, strength and contraction speed, so that the combination of weaker bones, stiffer joints and weaker muscles increases the risk of falls, fracture and functional disability.
Sedentary lifestyle and physical inactivity accelerate all these changes, creating a cycle in which reduced activity leads to further bone and muscle loss and greater fall/fracture risk.
Because oestrogen is critical for bone mass maintenance in both sexes, its decline (especially at menopause) is a key hormonal driver of the disability seen in osteoporosis-related fracture.
The loss of elasticity of tendons and muscles also means internal organs are less well supported, contributing to conditions such as uterine prolapse, bladder issues, constipation and hernia with advancing years.
Overall, these musculoskeletal changes are central to the pathophysiology of common geriatric problems such as osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, falls and immobility.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the age-related changes in the musculoskeletal system.
(ii) State the functional consequences and the physiotherapy assessment or treatment approach.
(iii) Explain the basis of the resulting deficit or disability.

questions.answerText:
(i) Femoral neck fractures are associated with low-energy falls in the elderly; risk factors include female gender, decreased mobility, and low bone density.
(ii) The junctional location of the femoral neck and the course of its blood supply (medial femoral circumflex artery running under the quadratus femoris) mean healing may be compromised, causing non-union or osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis), which is the most common complication in patients treated by open reduction internal fixation.
(iii) Management options include deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis started in the perioperative period and continued for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively, and physical therapy begun immediately after surgery with weight-bearing as tolerated and hip precautions observed per the surgical approach used. Early postoperative physical therapy is justified because the goals of treatment are to promote healing, prevent complications and return function, with the primary aim being to return the patient to her premorbid level of function.
questions.question:
An elderly woman is admitted after a low-energy fall at home with a confirmed femoral neck fracture.
(i) State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications/consequences that may follow.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options available, justifying one.

(i) Describe the principle of exercise prescription for older adults in full.
(ii) State how it relates to common age-related pathologies.
(iii) Explain how inadequate exercise leads to secondary problems and how physiotherapy addresses this through exercise prescription.
questions.answerText:
(i) The aging process can be modified by activity and exercise, although improvement occurs at a slower rate in the elderly than in younger people; benefits reported include improvement in muscle strength, muscle morphology, coordination and reaction time, and an increase in total body calcium.
Endurance training has been reported to significantly improve VO2 max, ventilatory function and maximum work output in the elderly; even low-level programmes such as walking or biking produce a training effect, though intensity and duration should be individualised to each person's physical ability.
Recommended healthy habits include exercising regularly while maintaining a triad of weight-bearing, aerobic, and balance activities, along with maintaining a comfortable weight and having regular medical checkups.
(ii) Maximum exercise capacity progressively declines with advancing age, such that daily activities like getting out of bed and walking may require a greater percentage of maximum exercise capacity in older adults, meaning some elderly function dangerously close to the point where further decline in strength or aerobic power could make them incapable of self-care or independent mobility.
This links exercise prescription directly to pathologies such as sarcopenia/frailty (loss of strength and muscle mass), osteoporosis (bone density maintained by muscle pull), cardiovascular deconditioning (reduced cardiac output and VO2max), and falls (reduced strength, balance and endurance).
(iii) Because even a small gain in strength and endurance from exercise may render a person capable of regaining a higher level of function, inadequate exercise (or prolonged inactivity/bed rest) accelerates the vicious spiral of deconditioning, immobility, falls and dependency described among the Giants of Geriatrics.
Before subjecting an older adult to an exercise programme, it is important to monitor vital signs, calculate maximum heart rate, and perform necessary warm-ups to accommodate age-related cardiovascular and musculoskeletal changes.
Physiotherapy addresses this through individualised prescription of weight-bearing, aerobic and balance exercise, adjusting intensity/duration to the person's ability, and allowing more rest periods since older adults fatigue more easily.
Exercise/physical activity has also been shown to have a comparable reduction in depressive symptoms to antidepressant medication, illustrating exercise prescription's relevance beyond musculoskeletal and cardiovascular benefit.
Because improvement occurs more slowly in the elderly, physiotherapy programmes should be progressive and sustained rather than short-term, recognising that benefits (strength, coordination, VO2max) accrue gradually.
Watching for warning signs during testing/exercise (e.g. excessive systolic/diastolic blood pressure, heart rate or respiratory rate abnormalities) is an important safety principle in prescribing exercise to this population.
Overall, structured, individualised, progressive exercise prescription is a core physiotherapy principle for both preventing and reversing the functional decline associated with aging.

(i) Impairments: pain, decreased hip range of motion, general muscle weakness, poor endurance. Activity limitations: unable to transfer without assistance, unable to walk with assistive devices without assistance, dependent for all activities of daily living. Participation restrictions: unable to return to premorbid home and community activities while dependent.
(ii) Goals should be specific, measurable and time-framed short-term goals (STGs) and long-term goals (LTGs); an example plan of care gives physiotherapy for a total of six weeks (5 times a week for 2 weeks, 3 times a week for 3 weeks, and 2 times a week for one week), aiming for the patient to benefit from strengthening exercise, ADL training and safety/fall-prevention education to function safely at home under distal caregiver supervision.
(iii) Active exercises, e.g. shoulder elevation through flexion without weight, 3 sets of 10 repetitions; resisted exercise to bilateral lower extremities, 2 sets of 10 repetitions for quadriceps, hamstrings, hip flexion, hip extension and hip abduction, with 1 kg ankle weight where tolerated; transfer training (sit-to-stand and bed-to-wheelchair), 5 times per session; gait training with a walker for 5 metres, 3 times per session; alternate stepping exercises with assistance, 2 sets of 10 repetitions.
(iv) Weight-bearing as tolerated and hip precautions must be observed according to the surgical approach used; deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis should continue for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively; the patient should be educated on the limitations on hip movements.
(v) Safety and fall-prevention education; home exercise instruction such as sit-to-stand transfer with caregiver assistance, 3 sets of 10 repetitions, 3 times daily; care coordination and communication with the caregiver.
questions.question:
An elderly woman with a femoral neck fracture has undergone surgical fixation and is now being seen for postoperative rehabilitation; she has pain, decreased hip range of motion and muscle weakness, and is unable to transfer or walk independently.
(i) State the problem list, covering impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions.
(ii) State the short-term and long-term goals.
(iii) Outline the specific physiotherapy interventions with parameters.
(iv) State the precautions/contraindications.
(v) Give home/community advice and prevention measures.

questions.answerText:
(i) Impaired muscle performance and impaired endurance with limitations in activities of daily living associated with generalised deconditioning.
(ii) Immobility of this kind is often multifactorial, related to musculoskeletal osteoarthritis (pain, weakness, deconditioning), heart disease/COPD (loss of work ability), stroke (weakness, abnormal gait, poor proprioception) or cataracts/macular degeneration (poor vision and falls); at a tissue level, age-related cartilage thinning, connective tissue stiffening and progressive sarcopenia (loss of muscle mass and strength from around age 30) underlie the weakness and reduced range of motion.
(iii) An example plan of care gives physiotherapy 5 times a week for 2 weeks, 3 times a week for 3 weeks and 2 times a week for one week (a total of six weeks), with strengthening exercise, ADL training, and safety education and fall-prevention programme/strategies so the patient can function safely at home under distal caregiver supervision.
questions.question:
A classic presentation: an elderly patient shows general muscle weakness, is unable to transfer without assistance, is unable to walk with assistive devices without assistance, is dependent for all activities of daily living, and has poor endurance limited to walking only 4 metres before getting tired.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Discuss the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy and rehabilitation management.

An elderly deconditioned patient has impaired muscle performance and endurance limiting her activities of daily living.
(i) State the problem list.
(ii) State the short-term and long-term goals.
(iii) Outline the specific physiotherapy interventions with parameters.
(iv) State the precautions/contraindications.
(v) Give home/community advice and prevention measures.
questions.answerText:
(i) Impaired muscle performance and impaired endurance, with limitations in activities of daily living associated with generalised deconditioning.
(ii) Specific, measurable, time-framed short-term and long-term goals, such as the patient benefiting from six weeks of physiotherapy with strengthening exercise, ADL training and safety education/fall-prevention programme to function safely at home under distal caregiver supervision.
(iii) Active exercises, e.g. shoulder elevation through flexion without weight, 3 sets of 10 repetitions; resisted exercise to bilateral lower extremities, 2 sets of 10 repetitions for quadriceps, hamstrings, hip flexion, hip extension and hip abduction, with 1 kg ankle weight; transfer training, sit-to-stand and bed-to-wheelchair, 5 times per session; gait training with a walker for 5 metres, 3 times per session; alternate stepping exercises with assistance, 2 sets of 10 repetitions.
(iv) Safety must be supervised throughout given the patient's dependence for transfers and ambulation and her limited endurance (walking only about 4 metres before tiring).
(v) Safety and fall-prevention education; home exercise instruction such as sit-to-stand transfer with caregiver assistance, 3 sets of 10 repetitions, 3 times daily; care coordination and communication with the caregiver.

(i) Intrinsic factors: increasing age, female gender, living alone, impaired vision, impaired cognition, impaired mobility/gait/balance, co-morbidity (circulatory disease, arthritis, neuropathy) and nutritional deficiency. Extrinsic factors: environmental hazards (poor lighting, slippery floors, loose floor coverings, uneven surfaces), improper footwear/clothing, inappropriate walking aids, and being on four or more medications.
(ii) Falls are a major reason for hospital admission, a cause of morbidity (about 10% of falls cause serious injury, 5% cause fracture), and the sixth leading cause of mortality; falls affect quality of life and independence, cause fear of falling that restricts activities, and impose high financial and public-health costs.
(iii) Options include advice on vision, multidisciplinary medication review/withdrawal, nutritional supplementation, screening (Timed Up and Go, Tinetti scale), strengthening and endurance exercise, balance retraining, education and home modification, and correct prescription of assistive devices. A multifactorial intervention targeting several risk factors at once is justified because falls-prevention effectiveness is achieved through interventions that target multiple risk factors together rather than a single factor in isolation.
questions.question:
An elderly community-dwelling person has fallen several times in the past year.
(i) State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications/consequences that may follow.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options, justifying one.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Sarcopenia is the age-related wasting of muscle; some of the decline in functional ability in older adults is secondary to sarcopenia.
Loss of muscle (sarcopenia) is a process that starts around age 30 and progresses throughout life, in which the amount of muscle tissue and the number and size of muscle fibres gradually decrease.
A(ii) The accumulated declines in strength, balance and endurance - often a consequence of inactivity - have resulted in frailty, of which sarcopenia is frequently the hallmark.
Muscles cannot contract as quickly because more fast-twitch fibres are lost than slow-twitch fibres; in the absence of disease, most loss beyond 10-15% is preventable with regular exercise, while more severe loss results from disease or extreme inactivity.
B. The major distinction between sarcopenia and cachexia is that sarcopenia is amenable to change - a sarcopenic muscle will respond to strength training exercise.
A cachexic muscle, by contrast, will not respond to strength training, because cachexia is a rapid and relentless wasting that frequently occurs as a response to one or more pathologies overwhelming the body.
This distinction has direct clinical implications: physiotherapy strengthening exercise is expected to improve sarcopenic muscle but not cachexic muscle.
Cachexia typically precedes death and is the final stage of conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic heart failure, and other terminal pathologies, explaining why it does not respond to exercise-based rehabilitation.
C. Sarcopenia is the age-related wasting of muscle that starts around age 30 and progresses gradually throughout life, and is distinct from cachexia.
Cachexia is rapid and relentless muscle wasting that frequently occurs before death, occurring with terminal disease such as cancer, and is also associated with diseases like AIDS, tuberculosis and certain infectious diseases.
While some young adults with more physiological reserve may recover from a cachectic state, most people do not, and older adults rarely recover from cachexia.
Sarcopenic muscle responds to strength training exercise, while cachexic muscle does not, making this the key clinical distinction between the two muscle-wasting conditions.
questions.question:
A. Describe sarcopenia under the following headings: (i) definition (ii) causes.
B. Explain the clinical basis for distinguishing sarcopenia from cachexia in terms of responsiveness to treatment.
C. Distinguish between sarcopenia and cachexia.

questions.answerText:
(i) Vascular dementia, the second most common type of dementia, caused by damage to the vessels that supply blood to the brain.
(ii) Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease; three forms are most common - large vessel disease, strokes, and multiple microcerebral infarcts, with abrupt onset, step-by-step deterioration, fluctuating course and emotional lability specific to this type.
(iii) Comprehensive geriatric assessment to identify treatable health problems; management of cardiovascular risk factors (treating hypertension, cholesterol, diabetes); maintaining a healthy diet and physical/social activity, which might delay onset and reduce symptoms; and environmental modification to support orientation and function.
questions.question:
A classic presentation: following a stroke, a patient shows an abrupt onset of cognitive decline with step-by-step deterioration, a fluctuating course, and emotional lability, with problem-solving, slowed thinking and loss of focus/organisation more noticeable than memory loss.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Discuss the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy and rehabilitation management.

An elderly incontinent patient is found to have a post-voidal residual urine volume greater than 100 mL on assessment.
(i) Interpret these findings.
(ii) State the systems or structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to be considered.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for treatment priorities.
questions.answerText:
(i) A post-voidal residual urine of more than 100 mL needs further investigation and referral for urodynamic studies, which can check for detrusor instability and compliance of the urethra.
(ii) The lower urinary tract is affected, including the detrusor muscle, urethral sphincter, and in men the prostate; weakened bladder muscles mean the bladder may not empty completely.
(iii) Differential types of incontinence include stress incontinence (leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure), urge incontinence (inability to delay voiding after sensing bladder fullness), overflow/neurogenic incontinence (frequent dribbling, often after stroke or with BPH, from an overdistended bladder), and functional incontinence (due to cognitive/physical impairment, psychological unwillingness or environmental barriers).
(iv) Clinical reasoning should first identify and treat contributing factors (medications, infection, atrophic vaginitis), then apply behavioural methods such as pelvic floor/Kegel exercises and bladder retraining, reserving catheters or devices for cases where other therapies have been exhausted, given the raised residual urine suggesting possible overflow/retention needing urological work-up before conservative bladder retraining alone is relied upon.

questions.question:
(i) Describe incontinence as a geriatric syndrome in full.
(ii) State how its types relate to common pathologies.
(iii) Explain how it may lead to secondary problems and how physiotherapy prevents or manages them.
questions.answerText:
(i) Incontinence is a condition of involuntary loss of urine that is a social or hygiene problem and is objectively demonstrable; it is one of the "Giants of Geriatrics".
Continence requires adequate mental function, sufficient mobility and dexterity to get to the toilet and manage clothing, motivation to be continent, adequate function of the lower urinary tract, and absence of environmental/iatrogenic barriers; failure of any of these can produce incontinence.
Ageing causes smaller bladder capacity and greater night-time glomerular filtration rate, producing more nocturia; in males the urethra is obstructed by the prostate gland, and in females it may be traumatised by frequent pregnancies.
(ii) Acute incontinence relates to delirium, restricted mobility, infection, inflammation, polyuria and pharmaceuticals.
Persistent incontinence is classified into stress (leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure, e.g. cough/laugh/exercise), urge (inability to delay voiding after sensing fullness), overflow/neurogenic (dribbling, usually after stroke or BPH), and functional (due to physical/cognitive impairment, e.g. dementia, depression, inaccessible toilets).
Each type therefore relates to different underlying pathology - stress to pelvic floor/sphincter weakness, urge to bladder overactivity, overflow to obstruction or neurogenic bladder, and functional to cognitive/physical/environmental barriers rather than the lower urinary tract itself.
(iii) Incontinence carries a huge social stigma, reduces life space and mobility, and is a huge financial and social burden to carers; because of weakened bladder muscles the bladder may not empty completely, increasing susceptibility to urinary infection.
Physiotherapy and the wider team prevent/manage incontinence by identifying and treating contributing factors (medications, infection, atrophic vaginitis), and by removing environmental/iatrogenic barriers to continence.
Physiotherapy-relevant interventions include pelvic floor or Kegel exercises, bladder retraining, and behavioural methods; devices such as catheters and incontinence pads (best for stress incontinence) are used when needed, with indwelling catheters reserved for after other therapies have been exhausted.
External sheaths/condom catheters and intermittent catheterisation are alternatives for selected patients; post-voidal residual urine greater than 100 mL warrants further investigation and urodynamic studies to check for detrusor instability and urethral compliance.
In the management of incontinence few can be cured, many can be improved, and all can be better understood, reflecting the realistic aim of physiotherapy and multidisciplinary management in this syndrome.
Overall, because incontinence has a huge social and financial impact, early identification of its type and contributing factors, followed by conservative behavioural management, is the core physiotherapy principle before progressing to devices.

(i) Slowing of the nervous system is an inherent aspect of aging; slowing of movement speed is a major clinical manifestation, and decline in muscle mass is partly a consequence of neuronal (axonal) loss.
Peripheral sensation gradually diminishes, reducing the ability to perceive excessive heat or cold; innervation declines in all tissues, affecting sympathetic, parasympathetic, sensory and motor systems, with effects on gastric motility, bladder control and blood pressure/flow regulation.
As people age, vertebrae become hard and brittle and may overgrow, reducing disc cushioning capacity and putting more pressure on the spinal cord and nerve roots; peripheral nerves conduct impulses more slowly and neurotransmitter release is impaired.
(ii) Functionally, this produces decreased sensation, slower reflexes, some clumsiness, and slower reaction time and task performance because the brain processes nerve impulses more slowly.
Physiotherapy assessment/treatment approach: assess sensation, reflexes, coordination, gait and balance; incorporate cognitive control (executive function, attention) into gait/balance assessment, since depression is associated with slower gait and anxiety with a cautious gait.
Exercise and physical therapy can help improve gait and balance disorders in older adults; the brain compensates for nerve-cell loss through redundancy (more cells than needed), formation of new connections, and production of new nerve cells in some areas after injury.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises because pressure on spinal nerve roots from vertebral overgrowth and disc changes can injure nerve fibres, resulting in decreased sensation and sometimes decreased strength and balance.
Nerve conduction slows because myelin sheaths degenerate, blood flow decreases, and nearby bone overgrowth compresses nerves; nerves also repair themselves more slowly and incompletely with age.
Decreased melatonin levels result in loss of normal sleep-wake cycles (circadian rhythms) with aging, which can further affect function and participation in rehabilitation.
Because different aspects of brain function decline at different times (short-term memory/learning early, verbal ability later, intellectual processing usually maintained absent underlying disease), the pattern of deficit varies between individuals.
Reaction time and processing slow because the brain processes nerve impulses more slowly overall, contributing to increased fall risk and slower task performance.
Overall, these nervous system changes contribute to sensory loss, slowed reflexes and gait/balance disturbance, making the nervous system a key contributor to instability and falls in older adults.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the age-related changes in the nervous system.
(ii) State the functional consequences and the physiotherapy assessment or treatment approach.
(iii) Explain the basis of the resulting deficit or disability.

(i) Describe the age-related changes in the immune system.
(ii) State the functional consequences and the physiotherapy assessment or treatment approach.
(iii) Explain the basis of the resulting deficit or disability.
questions.answerText:
(i) The cells of the immune system act more slowly with age; vaccines tend to be less protective in older adults, and cancer is more common among older adults.
Declining physiologic function and increased disease prevalence, particularly in the old-old (85 years and older), are partly a result of reduced ability of the body's homeostatic mechanisms, most importantly the immune system, to respond to stress.
This is referred to as declined immunocompetence; as the immune system slows down, autoimmune disorders become less common, and allergy symptoms may become less severe.
(ii) Functionally, older adults are more susceptible to illness and death from infections that could be prevented by vaccination, making vaccination increasingly important; some infections, such as pneumonia and influenza, are more common and more often fatal in older adults.
Physiotherapy assessment/treatment approach: be alert to atypical or subtle presentation of infection (e.g. confusion, falls, decreased function) as a possible sign of underlying illness in a frail older adult, and adjust exercise intensity/rest during acute illness given reduced homeostatic reserve.
Recognise that older adults have less ability than younger people to cope with assaults such as infection, blood loss, a high-tech environment, or loss of a significant person, so pacing and monitoring for deterioration are important during rehabilitation.
(iii) The resulting deficit arises because reduced adaptive reserve and weakened homeostatic mechanisms, especially the immune system, decrease the body's ability to respond to physical and emotional stress.
This declined immunocompetence explains the increased susceptibility to, and severity of, infections such as pneumonia and influenza in older adults, and the reduced protective benefit of vaccines compared with younger people.
Self-report of vague signs and symptoms such as lethargy, incontinence, decreased appetite and weight loss can be an indicator of underlying functional impairment or infection in this context, and should not be dismissed as normal aging.
Because chronic disease increases vulnerability to functional decline even though most older people remain functionally independent, discerning what is normal aging versus an indicator of disease or disability is important so that treatable conditions are not overlooked.
The reduction in the body's ability to respond to stress through homeostatic mechanisms is part of a broader pattern in which declining organ and system function and diminishing physiologic reserve make the body more susceptible to disease or disability.
Overall, immune system decline underlies increased infection risk and reduced resilience to physical/emotional stressors, both of which are important considerations in monitoring older adults during physiotherapy.

questions.question:
A. Describe pain in the elderly under the following headings: (i) definition (ii) categories (iii) common causes.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why pain is often under-reported and under-treated in older adults.
C. Distinguish between acute pain and chronic/persistent pain.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage; pain is "whatever the person says it is, and existing whenever the person says it does".
A(ii) Four categories of pain are recognised based on presumed source: nociceptive (from stimulation of pain receptors), neuropathic (from pathology in the peripheral or central nervous system), mixed or unspecified (from multiple or unknown sources), and psychiatric.
A(iii) Common causes include osteoarthritis (prevalence 49.5% in those 65+), other joint disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, gout/pseudogout, SLE), osteoporosis (e.g. vertebral compression fractures), cancer, cardiac ischaemia and diabetic neuropathy.
Pain increases in incidence and prevalence after age 60 because of the cumulative burden of aging-associated illnesses such as osteoarthritis and compression fractures.
B. Pain is under-reported by seniors for fear of being labelled bothersome, and is under-treated in the oldest-old (over 85) and in patients with dementia who may not adequately describe their pain.
Six factors are proposed to alter pain perception in older adults: decreased nociceptor density, changes in the conductivity of nociceptive afferents, changes in central coding of pain, changes in segmental nociceptive reflexes, alterations in descending inhibition of pain, and psychosocial influences.
Older adults have been found to take longer to report pain than younger adults, and it also takes longer for pain tenderness to resolve in them, compounding under-recognition.
These age-related changes in central and peripheral pain processing combine with other age-related losses (narrowed social networks, depression, cognitive decline) to further decrease capacity to adapt to stressors, worsening under-treatment.
C. Acute pain is the unpleasant sensation typically associated with direct tissue injury; it usually resolves readily through the healing process and lasts less than 3 months, e.g. postsurgical or musculoskeletal-injury pain.
Chronic pain (persistent pain) is an unresolved pain problem persisting after the normal period of tissue healing, continuing because of some factor other than the original injury or illness, lasting more than 3 months.
Older adults have longer pain duration and more pain sites than working-age adults; although acute pain is reported more by middle-aged adults, older adults have a higher prevalence of chronic health conditions associated with persistent pain.
Diagnoses of back and neck pain decrease after a peak in middle age, but severe back pain increases with advanced age, reflecting the shift toward chronic/persistent pain patterns in older adults.

(i) Under-reported and undertreated chronic pain in the elderly.
(ii) Pain is under-reported by seniors for fear of being labelled bothersome, and is under-treated in the oldest-old (over 85) and in patients with dementia who may not adequately describe their pain; age-related changes such as decreased nociceptor density, altered conductivity of nociceptive afferents and altered central processing mean older adults take longer to report pain and longer for tenderness to resolve.
(iii) A full history and physical examination, use of appropriate pain assessment instruments (Numerical Rating Scale, Visual Analog Scale, Faces Pain Scale, Multidimensional Pain Inventory, Geriatric Pain Measure), and therapeutic exercise, joint mobilisation, orthotic/supportive devices and modalities such as TENS, heat and cryotherapy.
questions.question:
A classic presentation: an elderly patient with joint pain under-reports her symptoms for fear of being labelled bothersome, and her pain remains undertreated.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Discuss the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy and rehabilitation management.

An elderly patient presents with joint pain, generalised muscle weakness and deconditioning, having become increasingly inactive.
(i) State the probable diagnosis/condition.
(ii) Explain the age-related physiological or pathological basis.
