Both have similar bioavailability (~80% vs 60%), half-life, and protein binding. Dose equivalence: bumetanide 1mg = furosemide 40mg = torsemide 20mg. Potency doesn't indicate efficacy; all loop diuretics achieve similar maximal effect.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of bumetanide's greater potency compared to furosemide?

questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) preventing regeneration of reduced vitamin K from vitamin K epoxide. Reduced vitamin K is essential cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, making them functional. The result is synthesis of non-functional factors.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of vitamin K antagonism by warfarin?

questions.explanation: Male condoms have a typical-use failure rate of approximately 14% within the first year, compared to perfect-use failure of 3%. This discrepancy reflects inconsistent or incorrect usage, including failure to use with every intercourse, improper application, and oil-based lubricant damage. Long-acting reversible contraceptives like implants (<1% failure) are most effective as they eliminate user error.
questions.question: Which contraceptive method has the highest typical-use failure rate?

questions.explanation: Chronic caffeine causes adaptive vasoconstriction; abrupt cessation causes rebound cerebral vasodilation and headache. Adenosine receptor upregulation also contributes. Caffeine withdrawal syndrome includes headache, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and mood disturbances, peaking 1-2 days after cessation. Gradual taper prevents severe withdrawal. Chronic caffeine use can contribute to medication overuse headache when combined with analgesics. The mechanism explains why caffeine is included in some analgesic combinations while potentially perpetuating headache cycles.
questions.question: Which mechanism explains the development of rebound headaches when caffeine intake is discontinued?
options: Downregulation of adenosine receptors causing hypersensitivity
Depletion of endogenous pain modulation systems
Cerebral vasodilation from loss of vasoconstrictor effects
Direct neurotoxicity from chronic receptor stimulation

questions.explanation: Valproate-induced hyperammonemia can occur without hepatotoxicity from carbamyl phosphate synthetase-1 inhibition. Symptoms include lethargy, vomiting, confusion, and asterixis. Ammonia levels may be markedly elevated. L-carnitine deficiency may contribute; supplementation can help. Treatment involves dose reduction or discontinuation. This idiosyncratic reaction differs from hepatotoxicity (elevated transaminases). Risk factors include genetic urea cycle defects. Ammonia should be checked in patients developing unexplained encephalopathy on valproate.
questions.question: A patient develops confusion and asterixis after valproate dose increase. Which metabolic abnormality most likely explains these symptoms?
options: Severe hypoglycemia from enhanced insulin secretion
Hyperammonemia from urea cycle enzyme inhibition
Hypocalcemia from altered vitamin D metabolism

questions.question: What is the primary mediator of the bradykinin effect on blood vessels?
questions.explanation: Bradykinin binds B2 receptors on endothelial cells, stimulating nitric oxide synthase and cyclooxygenase, producing NO and PGI2 (prostacyclin), which mediate vasodilation. This is 10 times more potent than histamine. Bradykinin also increases vascular permeability through endothelial cell contraction, contributing to edema. These mechanisms explain bradykinin's role in inflammatory responses and ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema.

Dihydropyridines preferentially dilate precapillary arterioles without affecting postcapillary venules, increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure and fluid extravasation. This mechanism differs from cardiac or renal edema. Diuretics are ineffective; ACE inhibitors or ARBs may help.
questions.question: Dihydropyridine calcium blockers cause peripheral edema through:
A patient with type 1 diabetes becomes unwell with a febrile illness and stops eating normally. What is the most important instruction regarding their basal insulin during this period?
options: Stop all insulin until eating resumes
Stop only the basal insulin component
Switch entirely to sliding scale dosing
Continue basal insulin despite reduced eating
questions.explanation: Basal insulin should never be stopped during illness, even if oral intake is reduced, because illness-related stress hormones often increase insulin requirements and abrupt cessation risks rapid development of diabetic ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes.

Tamoxifen acts as an oestrogen agonist in the liver, activating hepatic oestrogen receptors and stimulating synthesis of procoagulant proteins — particularly fibrinogen and clotting factors — while reducing natural anticoagulants (antithrombin III, protein C, protein S). This hepatic oestrogenic effect increases VTE risk approximately 2–3-fold, similar to combined oral contraceptives. The risk is highest in the first year and with increasing age. Patients with additional VTE risk factors warrant careful thromboprophylaxis assessment before starting tamoxifen.
options: Tamoxifen antagonises antithrombin III in hepatic tissue
Tamoxifen's anti-androgenic metabolites increase factor X levels
Tamoxifen directly activates platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors
Tamoxifen inhibits prostacyclin synthesis in vascular endothelial cells
Tamoxifen activates hepatic ER, increasing procoagulant protein synthesis
questions.question: A 47-year-old woman on tamoxifen for breast cancer 2 months ago is found to have a pulmonary embolism. Which pharmacological property makes tamoxifen thrombogenic?

questions.explanation: Oxazepam (along with lorazepam and temazepam — the 'LOT' group) undergoes direct Phase 2 glucuronidation without requiring Phase 1 oxidative metabolism. In elderly patients, Phase 1 hepatic oxidation (CYP450-mediated) is reduced, causing accumulation of benzodiazepines requiring this pathway. Oxazepam bypasses Phase 1, has no active metabolites, and has a shorter half-life, making it the preferred benzodiazepine in the elderly.
options: Nitrazepam primarily metabolized by reduction reactions
questions.question: An elderly patient requires long-term benzodiazepine therapy. Which benzodiazepine is MOST appropriate considering reduced hepatic Phase 1 metabolism in the elderly?

questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins essential for acetylcholine vesicle fusion and release, causing prolonged paralysis until new presynaptic terminals sprout (weeks to months). Therapeutic applications exploit this duration for treating dystonia, spasticity, hyperhidrosis, and cosmetic uses. Respiratory support may be needed in botulism.
questions.question: The duration of botulinum toxin-induced paralysis is:

questions.explanation: Prolonged nitrous oxide exposure inactivates methionine synthase (requiring vitamin B12), disrupting folate metabolism and DNA/myelin synthesis. While acute use doesn't cause problems, chronic exposure can cause megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy. The analgesic mechanism may involve endogenous opioid systems and NMDA antagonism; tachyphylaxis to analgesia can occur with continued use. Recreational abuse causing neurological complications from B12 inactivation has been reported. Occupational exposure requires scavenging systems.
options: Rapid downregulation of opioid receptor expression
Depletion of cofactors required for drug action
Inactivation of methionine synthase affecting pathways
questions.question: Which mechanism explains the development of tachyphylaxis to nitrous oxide's analgesic effects?

questions.explanation: Omeprazole acts as an enzyme inhibitor, selectively and irreversibly binding to the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells after acid-catalyzed activation. This blocks the final common pathway of acid secretion regardless of the stimulus (histamine, gastrin, or acetylcholine). Since inhibition is irreversible, acid suppression lasts until new proton pumps are synthesized (24-48 hours), explaining once-daily dosing efficacy.
options: A reversible competitive antagonist at H2 receptors
A physiological antagonist opposing acid production
A chemical antagonist neutralizing gastric acid directly
An enzyme inhibitor blocking the final acid secretion step
A non-competitive antagonist reducing Emax of histamine
questions.question: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells. This classifies omeprazole as:
In zero-order kinetics, the rate of drug elimination:
options: Is proportional to the drug concentration
Is constant and independent of drug concentration
Doubles with each doubling of drug concentration
questions.explanation: In zero-order (saturation) kinetics, the rate of drug elimination is constant and independent of drug concentration — a fixed amount of drug is eliminated per unit time. This occurs when elimination pathways are saturated. Classic examples are alcohol (ethanol) and aspirin at toxic doses. Unlike first-order kinetics, half-life is not constant with zero-order kinetics.

questions.question: What is the mechanism by which digoxin toxicity is enhanced by hypokalemia?
questions.explanation: Hypokalemia enhances digoxin binding to and inhibition of Na-K-ATPase increasing toxicity risk. Potassium and digoxin compete for the same binding site on the enzyme. Low potassium allows more digoxin binding. Loop and thiazide diuretics causing hypokalemia increase digoxin toxicity risk.

questions.question: A pregnant woman at term requires analgesia during labor. Which property makes pethidine preferable to morphine in this situation?
options: Absence of respiratory depression in the neonate
Lack of placental transfer due to ionization
Superior analgesic potency at lower doses
Preservation of uterine contractility during delivery
Reduced risk of neonatal physical dependence
questions.explanation: Pethidine, unlike morphine, does not significantly reduce uterine contractions, allowing labor to progress normally while providing analgesia. Morphine can depress uterine muscle tone, potentially prolonging labor. Both drugs cross the placenta and can cause neonatal respiratory depression, but pethidine's effect on labor progression makes it preferred.

Thiazides act primarily at the cortical diluting segment or distal tubule by inhibiting Na+-Cl- symport. They do not affect the cortico-medullary osmotic gradient, indicating lack of action at the medullary thick ascending loop. This explains their lesser efficacy compared to loop diuretics.
questions.question: What is the primary site of action for thiazide diuretics in the nephron?

questions.explanation: All loop diuretics cause metabolic alkalosis through volume contraction and enhanced distal hydrogen ion secretion driven by increased sodium delivery and secondary hyperaldosteronism. Chloride depletion perpetuates alkalosis. The contraction alkalosis is a class effect requiring chloride replacement for correction.
questions.question: Which loop diuretic is most likely to cause metabolic alkalosis?

questions.explanation: All statins are contraindicated during breastfeeding (pregnancy category X) due to cholesterol's essentiality for infant development and potential toxicity. Small amounts enter breast milk. Alternative lipid management: diet, bile acid sequestrants (not absorbed systemically), or delay treatment until breastfeeding complete. LDL-apheresis for familial hypercholesterolemia if absolutely necessary.
questions.question: Which statin is safest during breastfeeding?

questions.explanation: Ethacrynic acid is a phenoxyacetic acid derivative without sulfonamide moiety, making it suitable for patients with sulfa allergies. Most other loop and thiazide diuretics are sulphonamyl derivatives. However, ethacrynic acid has higher ototoxicity risk than other loop diuretics.
questions.question: Which diuretic is most appropriate for a patient with sulfa allergy?

questions.explanation: Ketoconazole is a weak base that requires an acidic gastric environment for dissolution and ionization before absorption. Proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole, by raising gastric pH, impair ketoconazole dissolution and reduce its oral bioavailability significantly. This clinically important interaction means ketoconazole should be given with an acidic beverage (e.g., cola) when PPIs are co-prescribed, or the PPI should be withheld if possible.
options: Increase absorption by reducing ketoconazole ionization
Reduce absorption as ketoconazole requires acidic pH for dissolution
Have no effect as ketoconazole is absorbed in the intestine
Increase absorption by improving ketoconazole gastric stability
Reduce absorption by accelerating gastric emptying time
questions.question: A patient taking omeprazole is prescribed ketoconazole. How would elevated gastric pH from omeprazole affect ketoconazole oral absorption?

questions.explanation: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu receptors, producing submaximal receptor activation even when occupying all receptors. This creates a ceiling for analgesia beyond which higher doses don't increase effect. The high receptor affinity and slow dissociation also make it difficult to reverse with naloxone.
options: Rapid development of tolerance limiting dose escalation
Preferential metabolism to antagonist metabolites at high doses
Competitive displacement by endogenous opioid peptides
Enhanced NMDA receptor activation producing anti-analgesia
Partial agonist activity at receptors with maximal response
questions.question: Which mechanism explains the analgesic ceiling effect observed with partial mu-opioid agonists like buprenorphine?
What is the mechanism of icosapent ethyl in triglyceride reduction?
questions.explanation: Icosapent ethyl (purified EPA ethyl ester) reduces triglycerides primarily by reducing hepatic VLDL synthesis and secretion. Also increases lipoprotein lipase activity and beta-oxidation. Reduces TG 20-30% at 2g twice daily, more at 4g daily. REDUCE-IT trial showed cardiovascular benefit beyond TG lowering. Better tolerated than mixed omega-3 preparations.

options: Pure antacid effect without antimicrobial action
Pure antimicrobial effect without acid suppression
Acid suppression plus antimicrobial bismuth action
Selective antiviral effect on gastric mucosa
questions.question: A patient is prescribed ranitidine bismuth citrate as part of dual therapy for H. pylori eradication. What is the combined mechanism of action that makes this agent effective?
questions.explanation: Ranitidine bismuth citrate combines H2-receptor mediated acid suppression with bismuth's direct antimicrobial activity against H. pylori and mucosal protective coating effect, providing a dual mechanism that supports its use in combination eradication regimens.

questions.question: Which property of niacin explains why pretreatment with aspirin 325 mg reduces its most troublesome adverse effect?
options: Aspirin inhibits hepatic niacin uptake reducing peak plasma drug concentration
Aspirin blocks H1 histamine receptors mediating niacin-induced vasodilation
Aspirin chelates niacin in the GI tract slowing absorption and peak drug effect
Aspirin inhibits prostaglandin D2 synthesis mediating the cutaneous flushing reaction
Aspirin neutralizes the acidic metabolites of niacin that cause skin pruritus
questions.explanation: Niacin activates GPR109A receptors on Langerhans cells in the skin, stimulating release of prostaglandin D2 and E2, which cause cutaneous vasodilation manifesting as intense flushing, warmth, and pruritus typically within 15-30 minutes of dosing. Aspirin, by irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase and reducing prostaglandin synthesis, substantially attenuates this flushing reaction when taken 30 minutes before niacin. Laropiprant, a prostaglandin D2 receptor antagonist, was also developed to reduce flushing but was withdrawn due to adverse cardiovascular effects.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of warfarin's anticoagulant effect?
questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) preventing regeneration of reduced vitamin K, essential cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. This reduces functional clotting factor synthesis. Effect delayed 2-3 days until preformed factors are depleted.

options: Formation of active metabolites with prolonged action
Enhanced lipid sequestration with delayed release
Fentanyl's longer duration than naloxone's effect
Naloxone's partial agonist activity providing minimal reversal
questions.explanation: Naloxone's duration (30-120 minutes) is shorter than most opioids including fentanyl (several hours, longer with repeated doses or infusions). As naloxone redistributes and is metabolized, opioid receptor occupation resumes, causing renarcotization with respiratory depression. This necessitates naloxone repeat boluses or continuous infusion, close monitoring, and delayed discharge. Ultra-short-acting opioids (remifentanil) less commonly cause this problem. The phenomenon emphasizes appropriate observation duration after reversal.
questions.question: A patient develops respiratory depression from fentanyl overdose. Which factor explains the potential for renarcotization after naloxone administration?
A patient develops gynecomastia while taking an H2-receptor blocker. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Cimetidine binds to dihydrotestosterone and androgen receptors causing antiandrogenic effects including gynecomastia in men and galactorrhea in women. Other H2 blockers lack this property. The antiandrogenic activity is unique to cimetidine's molecular structure.

questions.question: Which anti-anginal drug increases exercise tolerance most?
questions.explanation: Beta blockers, by reducing heart rate and contractility throughout exercise, most effectively increase exercise capacity and time to angina. They also reduce cardiovascular mortality post-myocardial infarction. Nitrates provide symptomatic relief but don't improve mortality.

Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that allosterically activates calcium-sensing receptors (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells, increasing receptor sensitivity to extracellular calcium, suppressing PTH secretion, reducing serum calcium. Used in: primary hyperparathyroidism (non-surgical candidates), secondary hyperparathyroidism (chronic kidney disease on dialysis), parathyroid carcinoma. Dose: 30-180 mg daily, titrated to PTH/calcium targets. Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, hypocalcemia. Monitor calcium, phosphate, PTH. Doesn't cure underlying disease; surgical parathyroidectomy definitive treatment primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of cinacalcet in hyperparathyroidism?

questions.explanation: Vitamin E (tocopherols) is lipid-soluble antioxidant protecting cell membranes from lipid peroxidation by scavenging free radicals, particularly in polyunsaturated fatty acids. Donates hydrogen to lipid peroxyl radicals, forming stable products, interrupting chain reactions. Regenerated by vitamin C, glutathione. Deficiency (rare, occurs in fat malabsorption, abetalipoproteinemia) causes: hemolytic anemia (red cell membrane damage), peripheral neuropathy, retinopathy, immune dysfunction. Treatment: vitamin E supplementation (depends on severity). High-dose supplementation healthy individuals not beneficial, possibly harmful (increased mortality some studies).
questions.question: What is the mechanism of vitamin E as antioxidant?

questions.explanation: Type B (Bizarre) adverse drug reactions are not based on the known pharmacological properties of the drug. They are less common, often non-dose related, pharmacologically unexpected, and generally more serious than Type A. They typically require complete drug withdrawal. They include allergic (immunological) and idiosyncratic reactions based on patient peculiarities.
questions.question: Type B adverse drug reactions differ from Type A in that Type B reactions are:
options: Based on known pharmacological properties of the drug
Less common, non-dose related, and pharmacologically unexpected
More amenable to treatment without drug withdrawal

questions.explanation: Loop diuretics inhibit Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in stria vascularis of inner ear disrupting endolymph composition essential for hearing. Usually reversible but can be permanent with high doses or rapid administration. Risk increased with aminoglycosides (additive ototoxicity). Ethacrynic acid has highest risk.
questions.question: What is the mechanism by which loop diuretics cause ototoxicity?

questions.explanation: Alpha-2 receptors located presynaptically provide autoregulatory negative feedback by inhibiting further norepinephrine release when activated. This mechanism prevents excessive sympathetic stimulation at synapses. Drugs like clonidine exploit this property to reduce sympathetic outflow centrally.
questions.question: Which adrenergic receptor subtype mediates negative feedback at nerve terminals?
Which diuretic class is specifically contraindicated in acute tubular necrosis?
questions.explanation: Osmotic diuretics like mannitol are contraindicated in acute tubular necrosis, anuria, pulmonary edema, acute LVF, CHF, and cerebral hemorrhage. They can worsen these conditions by increasing intravascular volume before diuresis occurs. Loop diuretics are preferred in renal dysfunction.

Methimazole crosses the placenta and is associated with scalp defects (aplasia cutis) and cloacal abnormalities when used in the first trimester. Propylthiouracil is preferred despite higher risk of hepatotoxicity. After the first trimester, switching to methimazole may be considered due to PTU's hepatotoxic potential.
questions.question: Which drug is contraindicated in the first trimester of pregnancy for hyperthyroidism treatment?
Compounds with molecular weight greater than 400-500 pass from liver into bile through:
options: Passing through pores by molecular size exclusion
Pinocytosis from hepatocytes to bile canaliculi
questions.explanation: Compounds of molecular weight more than 400-500 pass through the pores of bile canalicular membranes into bile. Smaller lipid-soluble and non-ionized compounds can also penetrate from liver to bile by simple diffusion. Large molecules (MW > 400-500 Da) tend to have significant biliary excretion, which is why many conjugated drug metabolites (glucuronides with high MW) are excreted in bile.

questions.question: Which statin requires dose adjustment in renal impairment?
questions.explanation: Rosuvastatin requires dose adjustment in severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min) starting at 5mg daily with maximum 10mg as it has some renal elimination (10%). Other statins are primarily hepatically eliminated requiring no renal dose adjustment. Atorvastatin and fluvastatin are safest in renal disease. Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are hydrophilic with less muscle penetration.

questions.question: Which antihypertensive drug is safe in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Methyldopa has the longest safety record in pregnancy and is considered first-line therapy for chronic hypertension during gestation. ACE inhibitors and ARBs cause fetal renal dysgenesis and are absolutely contraindicated. Labetalol and nifedipine are also acceptable alternatives.

questions.question: Which second-line antituberculosis drug requires thyroid function monitoring?
questions.explanation: Ethionamide and prothionamide (structural analogs) inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis, potentially causing hypothyroidism, especially prolonged use or baseline thyroid disease. Monitor TSH every 2-3 months. Other adverse effects: GI intolerance (severe nausea, metallic taste), hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine), psychiatric disturbances. Difficult to tolerate; poor adherence common. Dose 500-750 mg daily divided doses with meals. Reserve for MDR-TB when safer alternatives unavailable. Absorption improved with fatty foods despite GI upset.

The sublingual route bypasses the liver's first-pass metabolism, allowing glyceryl trinitrate (nitroglycerin) to enter the systemic circulation directly from the sublingual venous drainage. Since nitroglycerin undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism when swallowed, the sublingual route preserves bioavailability and ensures a rapid onset of action for angina relief.
questions.question: The sublingual route of drug administration is preferred for glyceryl trinitrate because it:
options: Has the slowest onset among oral routes
Allows for accurate and controllable dosing
Has better patient compliance than oral tablets
Produces lower peak plasma levels of the drug

questions.question: What is the mechanism of thiazide-induced hyperglycemia?
questions.explanation: Thiazides cause hyperglycemia primarily through hypokalemia impairing insulin secretion (potassium required for insulin release) and secondarily increasing insulin resistance. Chronic use increases diabetes risk 10-20%. Effect dose-dependent; lower doses (=25mg HCTZ) minimal impact. Potassium supplementation or K-sparing diuretic combination may mitigate. Benefits of blood pressure control outweigh modest diabetes risk in most patients.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of colchicine in acute gout?
questions.explanation: Colchicine binds tubulin preventing microtubule polymerization disrupting neutrophil migration, phagocytosis, and inflammatory mediator release. Inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation reducing IL-1β production. Used for acute gout attacks and prophylaxis. Narrow therapeutic index with GI toxicity (diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) limiting dosing.

questions.question: A patient taking primaquine for radical cure of P. vivax malaria develops dark urine and jaundice. Which screening test should have been performed before starting this medication?
questions.explanation: Primaquine causes haemolytic anaemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficient patients due to its oxidative metabolites, so G6PD screening before treatment is recommended, particularly in populations with higher prevalence of this enzyme deficiency.

questions.question: A drug is found to have a clearance calculated from its volume of distribution and elimination rate constant. If the half-life of this drug is shortened by disease while its volume of distribution remains constant, what happens to its clearance?
questions.explanation: Since clearance equals the elimination rate constant multiplied by volume of distribution, and the elimination rate constant is inversely related to half-life, a shortened half-life with unchanged volume of distribution results in a proportionally increased clearance.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of clomiphene in infertility treatment?
questions.explanation: Clomiphene citrate is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that antagonizes estrogen negative feedback at hypothalamus, increasing GnRH pulsatility and subsequent FSH/LH secretion, stimulating follicular development. Given days 3-7 or 5-9 of menstrual cycle. Ovulation induction rate ~80%; pregnancy rate ~40% over 6 cycles. Multiple gestation risk (8-10%, mostly twins). Adverse effects: hot flashes, visual disturbances, ovarian hyperstimulation.

Intravenous calcium gluconate is the immediate first-line treatment for severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes because it stabilizes the cardiac membrane resting potential by raising the threshold for depolarization, protecting against fatal arrhythmias within minutes. It does not lower serum potassium but provides a critical cardiac membrane protective window of 30-60 minutes during which definitive potassium-lowering treatments such as insulin-dextrose, bicarbonate, and dialysis can be arranged. Calcium gluconate must always be given first when ECG changes are present, before any other hyperkalemia treatment.
options: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to shift potassium intracellularly from extracellular space
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate to bind and eliminate potassium from the intestine
Intravenous regular insulin with dextrose to drive potassium into cells temporarily
Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize cardiac membrane against hyperkalemic effects
Intravenous furosemide to enhance renal potassium excretion in this patient
questions.question: A patient develops severe hyperkalemia of 6.8 mEq/L with peaked T-waves on ECG from ACE inhibitor and spironolactone combination. What is the most immediate treatment to protect the heart?

questions.explanation: Febuxostat is a non-purine, selective xanthine oxidase inhibitor that selectively inhibits xanthine oxidase without inhibiting other purine-metabolising enzymes, making it more selective than allopurinol. Crucially, febuxostat is almost entirely hepatically metabolised, making it safe in patients with mild-to-moderate CKD who cannot tolerate allopurinol. It is approximately 3–4-fold more potent than allopurinol 300 mg at standard doses. Febuxostat is approved for gout unresponsive to or intolerant of allopurinol, though cardiovascular safety warnings have been added post-marketing.
options: Febuxostat inhibits hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase instead of xanthine oxidase
Febuxostat is a non-purine, selective xanthine oxidase inhibitor hepatically cleared
Febuxostat is a uricosuric agent blocking URAT1 renal uric acid reabsorption
Febuxostat irreversibly inhibits xanthine oxidase via covalent bond formation
Febuxostat inhibits both xanthine oxidase and purine nucleoside phosphorylase simultaneously
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with gout intolerant to allopurinol is started on febuxostat. What distinguishes febuxostat from allopurinol mechanistically?
What thyroid medication is used for fetal/neonatal hyperthyroidism?
questions.explanation: Propylthiouracil crosses placenta less than methimazole, preferred in pregnancy first trimester despite hepatotoxicity risk (methimazole causes aplasia cutis, esophageal atresia). Treats maternal Graves' disease and prevents fetal hyperthyroidism from transplacental passage of TSH receptor antibodies. Lowest effective dose used. Consider switching to methimazole after first trimester as PTU hepatotoxicity risk ongoing. Monitor maternal TSH, free T4; fetal growth, heart rate. Beta-blockers adjunctive for symptoms.

questions.question: A patient on chronic methadone develops hypogonadism. Which mechanism explains this endocrine adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Chronic opioid use suppresses hypothalamic GnRH release through mu-opioid receptor activation, reducing LH and FSH secretion, causing hypogonadism. Men develop low testosterone (fatigue, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, osteoporosis). Women experience menstrual irregularities. This effect occurs with all chronic opioids but is particularly problematic with methadone's long half-life maintaining constant suppression. Testosterone replacement may be needed in symptomatic men. Recognition of this complication guides evaluation of symptoms in chronic opioid users.
options: Direct gonadal toxicity reducing hormone production
Enhanced aromatization of testosterone to estrogen
Pituitary adenoma formation from chronic use

questions.explanation: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy by competing with pyridoxal phosphate (active vitamin B6), impairing neurotransmitter synthesis. Pyridoxine 25-50 mg daily prevents neuropathy, particularly important in patients at high risk: diabetes, alcoholism, malnutrition, pregnancy, HIV, or uremia. Prophylactic supplementation is standard practice. Seizures from INH overdose are also treated with high-dose IV pyridoxine.
questions.question: Which antituberculosis drug requires pyridoxine supplementation?

questions.explanation: Tolvaptan hepatotoxicity mechanism is unclear; likely idiosyncratic. TEMPO trials (ADPKD) showed 3x increased ALT elevation risk; FDA restricted to =30 days use for hyponatremia. Monthly LFTs required. Contraindicated in liver disease. SAMSCA REMS program mandates monitoring. Benefits (correction of severe hyponatremia) must outweigh risks. Alternative: fluid restriction, treat underlying cause, demeclocycline, or loop diuretics cautiously.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of tolvaptan-induced hepatotoxicity?

questions.explanation: An aqueous drug solution provides the fastest oral absorption because the drug is already dissolved and does not require time for tablet disintegration or drug dissolution. Tablets and capsules must first disintegrate and dissolve before absorption can begin. Enteric-coated tablets and sustained-release preparations intentionally delay or slow drug release.
questions.question: Drug formulation affects absorption. Which formulation generally provides the fastest oral absorption?

options: Results only from deliberate drug overdose
Is restricted to Type B idiosyncratic reactions
Requires treatment, dose reduction, or caution in future use
Occurs exclusively with parenteral drug administration
Is specific to elderly and pediatric patients
questions.question: An adverse drug reaction is best defined as any noxious change at normal doses that:
questions.explanation: An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is defined as any noxious change suspected to be due to a drug that occurs at normal doses used in humans, and that requires treatment or decrease in dose, or indicates caution in future use. This definition specifically excludes trivial side effects and drug poisoning or overdose, which have their own classification categories.

Platelets store about 8% of total body serotonin, taken up from plasma rather than synthesised locally, playing a role in the clotting process, while the majority of body serotonin resides within enterochromaffin cells of the gut.
questions.question: A patient with carcinoid syndrome is noted to have markedly elevated platelet serotonin storage contributing to symptoms. What proportion of total body serotonin is normally found within platelets?
Drug distribution is defined as the process by which a drug:
questions.explanation: Drug distribution is the process by which a drug leaves the blood stream and enters the interstitial or intracellular fluid of body tissues. Following absorption or systemic administration, distribution depends on the drug's physicochemical properties. The rate and extent of distribution determine how much drug reaches target tissues and at what concentration.
options: Leaves the bloodstream and enters interstitial or intracellular fluid
Is transformed into active or inactive metabolites
Crosses the intestinal mucosa into portal circulation
Is filtered by the renal glomerulus into primary urine
Binds to plasma albumin reducing free drug levels

questions.explanation: Primidone (and its metabolite phenobarbital) enhances GABAergic inhibition, providing a mechanism distinct from beta-blockade for essential tremor. When beta-blockers fail, primidone offers approximately 60% response rate. The GABA enhancement reduces Purkinje cell firing thought to contribute to tremor. This mechanistic diversity explains why non-responders to one class may benefit from another.
options: Metoprolol through selective beta-1 receptor antagonism
Nadolol via non-selective beta receptor antagonism
Labetalol through combined alpha-beta receptor blockade
questions.question: A patient with essential tremor shows poor response to propranolol. Which alternative medication's mechanism targets different pathways?
What is the metabolic fate of histamine in the body?
questions.explanation: Histamine is primarily metabolized by diamine oxidase to imidazole acetic acid, which is further converted to imidazole acetic acid riboside. An alternative pathway involves N-methylation by histamine N-methyltransferase to form N-methylhistamine, followed by oxidation by MAO-B. These pathways ensure rapid histamine clearance from tissues.

questions.question: Cinacalcet treats secondary hyperparathyroidism by:
questions.explanation: Cinacalcet allosterically activates calcium-sensing receptors on parathyroid chief cells, increasing their sensitivity to extracellular calcium and suppressing PTH secretion. This mechanism effectively treats secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease and primary hyperparathyroidism. Hypocalcemia can occur.

questions.question: What is the biochemical basis of megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis (folate or B12 deficiency) while RNA/protein synthesis continues, causing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony. Large immature red cells (megaloblasts) with delayed nuclear maturation accumulate in bone marrow; hypersegmented neutrophils appear in peripheral blood. Both folate and B12 required for thymidylate synthesis (DNA building block). Ineffective erythropoiesis (intramedullary hemolysis) causes anemia, elevated LDH, indirect bilirubin. Treated with appropriate vitamin replacement. Distinguish from other macrocytic anemias (reticulocytosis, liver disease, hypothyroidism, alcohol).

questions.question: What is the recommended basal insulin starting dose for type 2 diabetes patients on 2000mg metformin failing to reach target?
questions.explanation: Standard basal insulin initiation in type 2 diabetes: 10 units daily (or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, use lower value) of long-acting analog (glargine, detemir, degludec) or NPH. Continue metformin (and other oral agents initially). Titrate 10-15% or 2-4 units every 3-7 days based on fasting glucose targeting 80-130 mg/dL. If fasting controlled but HbA1c elevated, add mealtime insulin. Conservative start minimizes hypoglycemia.

questions.question: The additive interaction between H1-antihistamine mepyramine and alcohol results in:
questions.explanation: Mepyramine (a first-generation H1-antihistamine) and alcohol both produce CNS depression. Their combined use causes additive worsening of drowsiness and CNS sedation. This additive interaction is clinically important — patients taking sedating antihistamines should be warned against driving or operating machinery, especially when drinking alcohol, as the combined sedation can be dangerous.
options: Reduced sedation due to mutual receptor antagonism
Enhanced analgesic effect from the combination
Reversed antihistamine effect due to alcohol competition
Worsening of drowsiness due to additive CNS depression
Increased antiallergic response from dual blockade

questions.question: Morphine requires a much higher oral dose than its intravenous dose to achieve equivalent analgesia. This discrepancy is best explained by:
questions.explanation: Morphine undergoes substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism following oral absorption via the portal vein. The liver metabolizes a large fraction of absorbed morphine before it reaches systemic circulation, reducing bioavailability to approximately 20-40%. This necessitates oral doses 3-5 times higher than IV doses to achieve equivalent plasma concentrations and analgesic effect.
options: Rapid renal clearance via glomerular filtration
Active tubular secretion reducing plasma levels
Poor lipid solubility reducing intestinal absorption
Extensive plasma protein binding in the bloodstream
Hepatic first-pass metabolism reducing systemic availability

questions.question: Tachyphylaxis differs from tolerance primarily in that tachyphylaxis:
questions.explanation: Tachyphylaxis is a rapid, acute decrease in response to an agonist drug following repeated administration within a brief period (an acute form of desensitization). Unlike tolerance which develops over a long period requiring progressively higher doses, tachyphylaxis occurs acutely, and increasing the dose will not improve the response. Classic example: repeated use of ephedrine causing tachyphylaxis.
options: Develops gradually over weeks of drug therapy
Is irreversible and requires drug discontinuation
Acute rapid decrease in response over a brief period
Is only seen with receptor antagonist drugs

questions.explanation: Hypermagnesemia (from antacids, laxatives, or preeclampsia treatment) potentiates both depolarizing and non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade by reducing acetylcholine release and decreasing muscle membrane excitability. Other acquired conditions affecting succinylcholine duration include pregnancy (reduced pseudocholinesterase), severe liver disease (reduced enzyme synthesis), malnutrition, and certain medications (metoclopramide, esmolol, cyclophosphamide). Hypothermia and electrolyte abnormalities also affect neuromuscular function. Recognition prevents inappropriate management of prolonged blockade.
questions.question: A patient experiences prolonged apnea after succinylcholine despite normal pseudocholinesterase levels. Which acquired condition might explain this?
Which antihypertensive drug can cause severe first-dose hypotension in volume-depleted patients?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors can cause precipitous blood pressure drops in patients with activated renin-angiotensin systems, particularly when volume depleted or sodium restricted. The first dose should be low and administered at bedtime. This effect is rare in uncomplicated essential hypertension.

Approximately 25% of patients receiving chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine for several years develop bluish-grey pigmentation on face and neck. Long-term use may lead to blue-black patches in sun-exposed areas. Nail beds and corneal/retinal changes may also develop.
questions.question: Which antimalarial drug causes bluish-grey pigmentation in 25% of patients receiving it for several years?
The most common cause of ACE inhibitor discontinuation is:
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitor-related cough affects approximately 15% of patients and results from bradykinin accumulation irritating bronchial afferents. This benign but bothersome side effect often necessitates switching to angiotensin receptor blockers. Cough resolves within days to weeks after discontinuation.

questions.question: Which factor explains the paradoxical improvement in motor function when dopamine agonists are added to levodopa despite causing dyskinesias?
questions.explanation: Dopamine agonists provide continuous receptor stimulation versus pulsatile levodopa effect, potentially reducing motor fluctuations and dyskinesias long-term. However, they can initially worsen dyskinesias requiring levodopa reduction. The longer half-lives smooth dopaminergic stimulation. This continuous dopaminergic theory suggests early agonist use may prevent later complications, though this remains controversial.
options: Pulsatile dopamine receptor stimulation restoring normal firing
Enhanced levodopa absorption increasing therapeutic window
Blockade of toxic dopamine metabolite formation
Selective D1 receptor stimulation sparing D2 pathways
Continuous receptor stimulation reducing wearing-off fluctuations

questions.question: Children aged 2-12 years often require higher mg/kg doses of many drugs compared to adults. This is best explained by:
questions.explanation: Children aged 2-12 have disproportionately larger livers relative to body weight and higher hepatic enzyme activity per kilogram compared to adults. Specifically, CYP3A4, CYP1A2, and other metabolizing enzymes have higher intrinsic activity per unit liver mass in children. This results in faster drug elimination and shorter half-lives for hepatically metabolized drugs, necessitating higher weight-adjusted doses and more frequent dosing in children.
options: Higher body water content in children diluting drugs more
Greater hepatic metabolic enzyme activity per body weight
Faster renal glomerular filtration rate per body weight
Better oral drug absorption through the paediatric gut
Lower plasma albumin levels increasing free drug fraction

questions.question: What is the onset time for maximal bronchodilation after inhaling salmeterol?
questions.explanation: Salmeterol reaches maximum bronchodilation at approximately 3 hours after inhalation with duration lasting about 12 hours. Despite being long-acting, it has slower onset than short-acting beta-2 agonists. It should be used twice daily for maintenance therapy, not for acute symptoms.

An inverse agonist has affinity for the receptor but a negative intrinsic activity (AI between 0 and -1), producing an effect opposite to that of the agonist. Example: beta-carbolines binding to benzodiazepine receptors produce anxiety, hypertonia, and convulsions — opposite to the anxiolytic and anticonvulsant effects of benzodiazepines. A competitive antagonist has zero intrinsic activity with no effect alone.
options: Has zero affinity for the receptor
Cannot be displaced by agonists at the receptor
Acts at allosteric sites different from the agonist site
Requires higher doses than a competitive antagonist
Has affinity and a negative intrinsic activity producing opposite effect
questions.question: An inverse agonist differs from a competitive antagonist in that an inverse agonist:

questions.explanation: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine cause photosensitivity requiring sun protection during treatment. Long-term use causes bluish-grey pigmentation in sun-exposed areas (face, hands). The pigmentation may take up to one year to resolve after discontinuation.
questions.question: Which antimalarial drug requires sun protection due to photosensitivity?

questions.explanation: Rebound insomnia following discontinuation of hypnotics (sleep medications, particularly benzodiazepines) is a Type E (End-of-treatment) adverse drug event. After prolonged use of hypnotics, brain receptors adapt; abrupt withdrawal unmasks an exaggerated return of the symptom. This is why hypnotics should be gradually tapered rather than stopped abruptly to prevent rebound insomnia and anxiety.
questions.question: The rebound phenomenon with hypnotics upon discontinuation is classified as which adverse event type?

questions.explanation: Mealtime insulin dose = carbohydrate grams ÷ insulin-to-carb ratio = 60g ÷ 15 = 4 units. Add correction dose if glucose elevated. Example: if glucose 220 mg/dL, target 120 mg/dL, correction factor 1:50: correction = (220-120)÷50 = 2 units. Total = 4 + 2 = 6 units.
questions.question: What is the appropriate insulin dose for 60g carbohydrate meal with insulin-to-carb ratio 1:15?

questions.explanation: Oxandrolone is an oral anabolic androgenic steroid that binds androgen receptors in skeletal muscle and bone, promoting anabolic effects on growth plate chondrocytes and increasing GH-IGF-1 axis responsiveness. At low doses used in constitutional growth delay, it accelerates growth velocity without significantly advancing bone age, providing a net benefit to final adult height. In Turner syndrome, when used adjunctively with GH, it amplifies growth beyond GH alone. Close monitoring of bone age is required throughout treatment.
options: Oxandrolone stimulates FSH secretion advancing puberty and oestrogenic growth
Oxandrolone directly activates IGF-1 gene expression in epiphyseal bone
Oxandrolone increases insulin secretion improving nutrient delivery to growth plates
Oxandrolone suppresses sex steroids preventing premature epiphyseal closure
Oxandrolone binds androgen receptors in growth plates and increases GH sensitivity
questions.question: A 16-year-old girl with constitutional growth delay is given low-dose oxandrolone. What is its mechanism in promoting linear growth?
Ethanol elimination at blood alcohol concentrations above 0.1% follows zero-order kinetics. This means that:
questions.explanation: Zero-order kinetics describes a process where the rate of elimination is constant — a fixed amount of drug is eliminated per unit time regardless of plasma concentration. Alcohol dehydrogenase becomes saturated at standard drinking concentrations, metabolizing approximately 10 mL of pure ethanol per hour regardless of blood alcohol level. This means drinking faster than this rate always causes blood alcohol to rise, and time to sobriety is directly proportional to the amount consumed.
options: Elimination rate is directly proportional to concentration
Elimination rate decreases as blood alcohol falls
Half-life shortens as blood alcohol concentration falls
A constant amount of ethanol is eliminated per unit time
Elimination rate doubles when the concentration doubles

questions.question: Which medication delays progression of diabetic nephropathy?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) delay diabetic nephropathy progression by reducing intraglomerular pressure (efferent arteriole dilation), decreasing proteinuria, beyond blood pressure effects. Start when microalbuminuria detected (30-300 mg/g creatinine), even if normotensive. Titrate to maximum tolerated dose. Monitor potassium, creatinine (may increase 10-20% initially; acceptable if stable). Discontinue if hyperkalemia (>5.5 mEq/L) or creatinine increases >30%. Combination ACE inhibitor + ARB not recommended (increased adverse events without added benefit).

Cabergoline is discontinued as soon as pregnancy is confirmed in women with microprolactinomas (the vast majority of cases) because pregnancy itself suppresses prolactin secretion, and the normal physiological oestrogen rise promotes pituitary lactotroph hypertrophy without causing significant microprolactinoma expansion. Data on accidental first-trimester cabergoline exposure show no increased teratogenic risk, but the drug is not needed and is stopped as a precautionary measure. Visual field assessment is performed during pregnancy; bromocriptine is used if intervention is required for macroprolactinoma expansion.
questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with hyperprolactinaemia on cabergoline conceives accidentally while still on treatment. What is the recommended management regarding cabergoline?
options: Continue cabergoline throughout pregnancy to control tumour size
Discontinue cabergoline immediately on pregnancy confirmation
Switch to bromocriptine which has superior established pregnancy safety data
Halve the cabergoline dose to minimise fetal exposure in the first trimester
Continue for first trimester only then switch to close observation

questions.question: A partial agonist when administered alone will produce:
questions.explanation: A partial agonist has affinity but sub-maximal intrinsic activity (0 < AI < 1), meaning it produces less than the maximum possible tissue response even when all receptors are occupied. When co-administered with a full agonist, a partial agonist acts as a competitive antagonist by displacing the full agonist and reducing the overall response to the partial agonist's maximum.
options: No effect at any dose level
Sub-maximal response even at full receptor occupancy
An effect equal to competitive antagonist
Inverse effect opposite to full agonist

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman with PCOS starts metformin and her physician says it will help restore ovulation. Through which mechanism does metformin restore menstrual cyclicity in PCOS?
questions.explanation: In PCOS, hyperinsulinaemia drives LH-stimulated ovarian androgen excess, disrupting follicular development and causing anovulation. Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity, lowering circulating insulin levels. Reduced insulin decreases ovarian theca cell androgen production (insulin amplifies LH-stimulated androgen synthesis) and reduces pituitary LH secretion, restoring a more physiological FSH:LH ratio enabling follicular development and ovulation. Metformin improves ovulation rates, menstrual regularity, and metabolic parameters in PCOS when combined with lifestyle modification.
options: Metformin directly suppresses androgen synthesis in ovarian theca cells
Metformin inhibits LH secretion from pituitary reducing thecal stimulation
Metformin reduces hyperinsulinaemia, decreasing androgen production and improving HPG signalling
Metformin blocks aromatase reducing oestrogen negative feedback and increasing FSH
Metformin directly stimulates ovarian follicular maturation via AMPK in granulosa cells
Check CK at baseline, then at 4-6 weeks and if new muscle symptoms develop
Monitor CK levels only if the patient develops symptomatic muscle pain or weakness
Measure CK and liver enzymes at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks only
Repeat DEXA scan to assess bone density impact of any statin rechallenge
Perform muscle biopsy before rechallenge to exclude mitochondrial myopathy
questions.question: A 60-year-old man with statin-associated myopathy is rechallenged with a different statin at lower dose. Which monitoring approach is most appropriate during this rechallenge period?
questions.explanation: When rechallenging a patient with prior statin myopathy, baseline CK must be established before starting, then rechecked at 4-6 weeks after initiation and whenever new muscle symptoms develop, to detect early subclinical myopathy before it progresses to rhabdomyolysis. The structured rechallenge protocol with systematic CK monitoring allows identification of statin-tolerant patients who can continue therapy for cardiovascular protection versus the minority with true statin intolerance requiring alternative drug classes. Asymptomatic mild CK elevations below 4 times the upper limit of normal typically do not require drug discontinuation.

questions.question: Which medication treats primary ovarian insufficiency-related symptoms?
questions.explanation: Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI, premature ovarian failure) causes hypoestrogenism requiring hormone replacement therapy (estradiol with progesterone if intact uterus) for symptom relief (hot flashes, vaginal dryness), bone health, cardiovascular protection until natural menopause age (~51). Fertility restoration rarely achievable; donor oocytes may enable pregnancy. HRT differs from menopausal HRT (higher doses, physiologic replacement). Screen for associated autoimmune conditions (thyroid, adrenal). Psychological support important. Contraception still needed (rare spontaneous ovulation possible).

options: Vitamin B12 deficiency from phenytoin-induced intrinsic factor suppression
Vitamin K deficiency from phenytoin-induced hepatic enzyme induction
Folate deficiency from phenytoin-impaired intestinal absorption and metabolism
Vitamin B6 deficiency from phenytoin inhibition of pyridoxal kinase activity
Vitamin C deficiency from phenytoin-induced renal tubular vitamin wasting
questions.question: A 35-year-old man on phenytoin for epilepsy is found to have megaloblastic anemia. Which vitamin deficiency explains this hematologic complication?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin impairs folate absorption from the intestine and interferes with folate metabolism, leading to deficiency causing megaloblastic anemia with macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, and reduced red blood cell production. Phenytoin also induces hepatic enzymes that accelerate vitamin D metabolism, causing osteomalacia with chronic use. Folate supplementation is particularly important in women with epilepsy taking phenytoin who may become pregnant, as folate deficiency during early pregnancy dramatically increases neural tube defect risk in the fetus.

Zoledronic acid can be administered as a single annual intravenous infusion due to its high potency and prolonged skeletal binding, offering a significant compliance advantage over daily or weekly oral bisphosphonate regimens for patients struggling with adherence.
questions.question: A patient with osteoporosis and poor adherence to weekly oral bisphosphonate therapy is switched to an annual intravenous formulation. Which agent is most appropriate for this purpose?

options: Potentiated warfarin effect via protein displacement
No change in warfarin levels or efficacy
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of CYP2C9 (the enzyme that metabolizes warfarin) and other CYP enzymes. Enzyme induction increases warfarin metabolism, decreasing plasma warfarin concentrations and reducing its anticoagulant effect. This drug interaction requires careful INR monitoring and warfarin dose adjustment when starting or stopping rifampicin.
questions.question: A patient taking warfarin is started on rifampicin for tuberculosis. The expected effect on warfarin therapy would be:

questions.explanation: Anticholinergics effectively treat acute extrapyramidal symptoms but may mask early signs of developing tardive dyskinesia, delaying recognition. They don't prevent tardive dyskinesia and may allow continued high-dose antipsychotic use. Once tardive dyskinesia develops, anticholinergics may worsen it. Minimizing anticholinergic use and using atypical antipsychotics reduces tardive dyskinesia risk long-term.
questions.question: A patient on haloperidol requires anticholinergic therapy for extrapyramidal symptoms. Which mechanism explains why this combination increases risk of tardive dyskinesia?
options: Enhanced haloperidol absorption with anticholinergic motility effects
Muscarinic blockade masks early dystonia warning signs

questions.explanation: Both sublingual and buccal routes bypass first-pass metabolism and provide rapid absorption. The buccal route (drug placed between cheek and gum) offers the advantage of longer contact time with the mucosa and better patient tolerance for drugs that may cause discomfort under the tongue, though absorption characteristics are otherwise similar.
options: Faster absorption than the sublingual route
Higher bioavailability than the sublingual route
No first-pass effect unlike the sublingual route
Better patient tolerance and longer drug contact time
Suitable for a wider range of drug types
questions.question: A drug is given as a buccal tablet for its advantage over sublingual administration. The main extra advantage of the buccal route is:
A patient plans to exercise vigorously two hours after their usual mealtime insulin bolus. What is the most appropriate adjustment to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia during exercise?
options: Reduce the bolus insulin dose beforehand
Increase the bolus insulin dose beforehand
Double the basal insulin that morning
questions.explanation: Exercising with active bolus insulin on board significantly increases hypoglycaemia risk, so reducing the preceding bolus dose by approximately 25 to 50%, alongside considering additional carbohydrate intake, helps prevent exercise-induced hypoglycaemia.

Vancomycin rapid infusion causes histamine release from mast cells, producing red man syndrome: flushing, pruritus, erythematous rash on face/upper torso, sometimes hypotension, tachycardia. Not true allergy; IgE-independent. Prevention: slow infusion (=60 minutes for 1 gram), pretreatment with antihistamines (diphenhydramine 25-50 mg) in susceptible patients. Distinguish from true hypersensitivity (rash, eosinophilia, organ dysfunction) requiring permanent discontinuation.
questions.question: What causes red man syndrome with vancomycin?

options: Type B bizarre reaction unrelated to aspirin action
Type D delayed carcinogenic effect of aspirin
Type A exaggeration of aspirin's pharmacological effect
Type C chronic effect requiring years of exposure
questions.question: A patient on long-term aspirin for cardiovascular prophylaxis develops gastrointestinal bleeding. This adverse effect is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: Gastrointestinal bleeding from aspirin is a Type A (Augmented pharmacological) adverse effect — a predictable, dose-related extension of aspirin's known pharmacological mechanisms. Aspirin inhibits COX-1 in gastric mucosa, reducing cytoprotective prostaglandin E2 synthesis. It also inhibits thromboxane A2-mediated platelet aggregation. Both mechanisms increase GI bleeding risk. Type A reactions are predictable, common, and dose-dependent.

questions.question: What percentage of the body's total serotonin is found in blood platelets?
questions.explanation: Eight percent of total body serotonin is found in blood platelets where it plays a role in the clotting process. The enterochromaffin cells contain 90% while the brain contains 1-2%. Platelets take up and store serotonin from plasma for release during aggregation.

Niacin (nicotinic acid, used for dyslipidemia) causes flushing via prostaglandin D2 and E2-mediated cutaneous vasodilation from skin Langerhans cells. Dose-dependent, self-limiting (1-2 hours). Prevented/minimized by: aspirin 325 mg 30 minutes pre-dose (blocks prostaglandin synthesis), gradual dose titration, taking with meals, extended-release formulations, tolerance development over weeks. Laropiprant (prostaglandin D2 receptor antagonist) combined with niacin (no longer marketed many countries). Flushing main reason for niacin discontinuation despite lipid benefits. Statins largely replaced niacin as first-line therapy.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of niacin-induced flushing?

questions.explanation: Apomorphine is a potent non-selective dopamine agonist requiring subcutaneous administration (extensive first-pass metabolism prevents oral use). It provides rapid onset (10 minutes) for acute management of unpredictable "off" periods in advanced Parkinson's disease. Duration is short (60-90 minutes). Requires antiemetic pretreatment (trimethobenzamide, not ondansetron which causes severe hypotension). Continuous subcutaneous infusion is also used for severe motor fluctuations.
options: Selective D1 receptor agonism improving motor function
Enhanced oral bioavailability enabling convenient dosing
Rapid subcutaneous administration for acute off episodes
Longer duration providing sustained motor improvement
Dual dopamine and serotonin receptor agonist activity
questions.question: Which mechanism distinguishes apomorphine's therapeutic use in Parkinson's disease from other dopamine agonists?

questions.explanation: Busulfan and other cytotoxic drugs like cyclophosphamide, bleomycin, and adriamycin produce hyperpigmentation to varying degrees, with diffuse nail pigmentation being common. The pigmentation may resolve slowly after discontinuation. Some patients develop skin darkening in sun-exposed areas.
questions.question: Which cytotoxic drug is most commonly associated with diffuse hyperpigmentation of nails?

questions.explanation: Buspirone is a partial agonist at presynaptic and postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors, providing anxiolysis through serotonergic modulation without GABA-A effects. This mechanism avoids sedation, motor impairment, and dependence associated with benzodiazepines. However, onset is delayed (2-4 weeks), limiting acute anxiety use. Lack of cross-tolerance with benzodiazepines means it can't substitute in withdrawal. Adverse effects include dizziness, headache, and nausea. It's useful for generalized anxiety disorder when dependence is a concern.
questions.question: Which mechanism explains the anxiolytic effect of buspirone without sedation or dependence liability?

questions.explanation: Loop diuretics remain effective even in renal failure with reduced GFR, unlike thiazides which lose efficacy. They act on the thick ascending loop of Henle to inhibit Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter. Their maximal natriuretic effect is much greater than other diuretic classes.
questions.question: Which diuretic class is most effective in maintaining diuresis in patients with reduced glomerular filtration rate?

questions.explanation: Dawn phenomenon is early morning (4-8 AM) hyperglycemia from nocturnal growth hormone, cortisol, and glucagon surges increasing hepatic glucose production and insulin resistance. Distinguished from Somogyi effect (rebound hyperglycemia after nocturnal hypoglycemia). Managed by increasing basal insulin dose, switching to long-acting analog, or insulin pump therapy.
questions.question: What is the dawn phenomenon in diabetes management?
A patient on vancomycin for a serious infection requires monitoring to ensure efficacy while minimising toxicity. Which parameter is most appropriate to guide ongoing dosing?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin trough levels are monitored before the next dose, typically targeting 10 to 20 mg/L depending on infection severity, to ensure adequate therapeutic exposure while reducing the risk of nephrotoxicity associated with excessive drug accumulation.

Furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide are sulfonamide derivatives that theoretically cross-react with sulfonamide antibiotic allergy. However, cross-reactivity is rare (<5%) as mechanisms differ (non-arylamine vs. arylamine sulfonamides). If concern exists, use ethacrynic acid (phenoxyacetic acid), potassium-sparing diuretics, or cautiously trial sulfonamide diuretic with antihistamine pretreatment.
questions.question: Which diuretic specifically worsens sulfa allergy symptoms?
Receptors in pharmacology are best defined as:
questions.explanation: Receptors are chemical structures, composed of protein, that receive and transduce signals that are translated into a biological response (e.g., muscle contraction, hormone secretion). A molecule binding to a receptor is called a ligand. Receptor binding initiates conformational changes leading to signal transduction, often involving generation of secondary messengers.
options: Any protein in the plasma membrane of cells
Chemical structures composed of protein that receive and transduce signals
Ion channels that allow ionic drug transport
Lipid molecules in cell membranes that bind drugs
Nuclear proteins that regulate gene expression

questions.question: Which diuretic potentiates ACE inhibitor-induced hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptors, reducing potassium excretion, while ACE inhibitors decrease aldosterone secretion, creating additive hyperkalemia risk. This combination requires careful monitoring, especially in renal impairment. Loop and thiazide diuretics cause potassium loss, opposing this effect.

questions.question: A patient develops respiratory depression from morphine overdose. Which characteristic makes naloxone's action advantageous despite its short duration?
options: Selective antagonism of respiratory effects sparing analgesia
Enhancement of endogenous opioid peptide production
Preferential distribution to respiratory center in medulla
Rapid displacement of morphine from all receptor subtypes
questions.explanation: Naloxone rapidly displaces morphine from mu, kappa, and delta receptors with higher affinity, reversing all opioid effects including life-threatening respiratory depression within 1-2 minutes. The competitive antagonism is non-selective and reversible. However, naloxone's short half-life (30-60 minutes) versus morphine's (3-4 hours) necessitates repeated dosing or infusion to prevent re-narcotization.

questions.question: Phenylephrine is contraindicated in which ocular condition?
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine causes mydriasis through alpha-1 receptor stimulation of radial pupillary muscles, which can precipitate acute angle closure in susceptible individuals. The dilated iris blocks aqueous humor drainage, increasing intraocular pressure dangerously. Open-angle glaucoma patients can typically tolerate mydriatics safely.

Chronic barbiturate use causes compensatory GABA-A receptor downregulation. Abrupt cessation unmasks reduced inhibitory capacity, causing hyperexcitability manifesting as tremor, anxiety, seizures, and potentially fatal status epilepticus. Withdrawal severity correlates with dose and duration. Gradual taper (10-20% reduction every 5-7 days) prevents severe withdrawal. Phenobarbital's long half-life provides self-tapering effect. Cross-tolerance with alcohol and benzodiazepines exists; substitution therapy may be used for withdrawal management.
options: Upregulation of excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors
Enhanced glutamate release from presynaptic terminals
Reduced inhibitory interneuron activity in cortex
Direct neuronal hyperexcitability from ion channel changes
GABA-A receptor downregulation from chronic stimulation
questions.question: Which factor explains the reduced seizure threshold in patients withdrawing from barbiturates?

questions.explanation: Tolterodine causes less dry mouth and cognitive impairment than oxybutynin while providing similar efficacy. Better tolerability improves compliance. Extended-release formulations further reduce side effects. Mechanism is non-selective muscarinic antagonism for both drugs. True bladder selectivity doesn't exist.
questions.question: Tolterodine for overactive bladder differs from oxybutynin by:
What is the mechanism of vitamin K in coagulation?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which post-translationally modifies clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, adding carboxyl groups to glutamate residues, creating calcium-binding sites essential for coagulation cascade function. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, blocking regeneration of active vitamin K, causing functional deficiency. Newborns receive prophylactic vitamin K (phytonadione 1 mg IM) to prevent hemorrhagic disease.

questions.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes is found to have persistently elevated fasting glucose. A 3 AM glucose check reveals a low reading. What adjustment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A low 3 AM glucose with subsequent fasting hyperglycaemia suggests the Somogyi effect, a rebound phenomenon following nocturnal hypoglycaemia, which is managed by reducing rather than increasing the basal insulin dose responsible for the overnight low.

Erythromycin, chloramphenicol, rifampicin, tetracycline, penicillin, contrast media, and hydantoin are secreted by active transport into bile regardless of their concentration in bile. This active biliary secretion is important for drugs excreted predominantly via the biliary route, and can be exploited for treating biliary tract infections with appropriate antibiotics.
questions.question: Which drugs are excreted by active transport into bile, irrespective of their concentration in bile?

options: Time is unrelated to the half-life
questions.question: A patient newly started on phenytoin requires several days to reach steady-state plasma concentration. What general pharmacokinetic principle determines the time required to reach steady state for most drugs?
questions.explanation: Steady-state plasma concentration is generally reached after approximately five elimination half-lives of continuous dosing, a principle that applies broadly across most drugs with first-order kinetics, although phenytoin's dose-dependent kinetics can complicate this prediction at higher doses.

Ketamine produces sympathetic nervous system stimulation, releasing catecholamines that cause bronchodilation via beta-2 receptor activation. This indirect sympathomimetic effect, combined with preserved airway reflexes and minimal respiratory depression, makes it ideal for asthmatics. Direct bronchodilator effects on smooth muscle also contribute. Ketamine is preferred for emergency intubation in severe bronchospasm.
options: Direct beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonism causing bronchodilation
Sympathetic stimulation with preserved airway reflexes
Mast cell stabilization preventing histamine release
Inhibition of inflammatory mediator synthesis in airways
questions.question: Which property makes ketamine useful for anesthesia in patients with severe bronchospasm?

options: Reduce the dose or increase dosing interval significantly
Maintain the same dose as CKD does not affect aminoglycosides
Switch to oral route only to reduce systemic exposure
Double the dose as drug is less absorbed in CKD
Increase dose frequency to compensate for reduced effect
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease (GFR 20 mL/min) requires gentamicin for severe sepsis. The dose adjustment strategy should be:
questions.explanation: Gentamicin is primarily eliminated unchanged by glomerular filtration. When renal clearance falls to 20 mL/min (1/6 of normal 120 mL/min), gentamicin half-life increases proportionally. To avoid drug accumulation and aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, the dose must be reduced or the dosing interval extended. Therapeutic drug monitoring of serum levels is essential in renally impaired patients.

questions.question: Which mechanism explains rifampicin's effectiveness against M. leprae?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase by binding its beta subunit, preventing RNA transcription. It's the most bactericidal agent against M. leprae, rapidly killing >99% of viable bacilli with first dose. Monthly supervised 600 mg doses in multidrug therapy leverage its potent bactericidal effect while minimizing resistance risk and medication costs.

PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) are monoclonal antibodies preventing PCSK9 from binding hepatic LDL receptors, thereby preventing receptor degradation and increasing LDL clearance. They lower LDL 50-70% and reduce cardiovascular events. Subcutaneous administration every 2-4 weeks is required.
questions.question: PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL by:
A patient on alendronate calls the day after starting therapy complaining of severe heartburn and dysphagia. What prescribing error most likely occurred?
questions.explanation: Oral bisphosphonates like alendronate must be taken with a full glass of plain water while remaining upright for at least 30 minutes after ingestion, as reclining allows the drug to reflux into the esophagus where its caustic properties cause esophageal erosions, ulcers, and strictures. Bioavailability is reduced by any food, beverage, or medication other than plain water, so alendronate must be taken 30-60 minutes before any food or drink. Patients with esophageal motility disorders or inability to sit upright for 30 minutes should use alternative formulations.
options: Alendronate was taken with calcium-rich milk instead of plain water only
The patient took alendronate simultaneously with other morning medications
The dose was taken after a light breakfast rather than in the fasting state
The tablet was chewed rather than swallowed whole with adequate water
The patient reclined for sleep immediately after taking alendronate orally

questions.explanation: Postprandial hyperglycemia with controlled fasting glucose requires mealtime intervention: add/increase rapid-acting insulin bolus (most effective, immediate control), add GLP-1 agonist (injectable, slows gastric emptying, modest glucose lowering, weight loss), or add SGLT-2 inhibitor (oral, modest postprandial effect, cardiovascular benefits). Choice depends on patient factors: insulin resistance degree, weight, cardiovascular risk, cost, preferences. Multiple agents often needed for optimal control.
questions.question: What is the appropriate management of persistent hyperglycemia (>180 mg/dL) two hours after meals despite optimal basal insulin?

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors block kininase II, the same enzyme responsible for degrading bradykinin in the lungs, causing accumulation that stimulates pulmonary C-fiber afferents producing a persistent dry cough in approximately 15% of patients. Switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker avoids this effect because ARBs do not inhibit bradykinin degradation. This provides equivalent blood pressure control without the cough side effect that limits ACE inhibitor adherence.
questions.question: A patient develops a persistent dry cough six weeks after starting enalapril for heart failure. Which mechanism explains this side effect?
options: ACE inhibition reducing bradykinin metabolism and causing airway dryness
Angiotensin II accumulation stimulating pulmonary J-receptor afferents
Reduced prostaglandins causing hypersensitivity bronchitis in susceptible patients
Bradykinin accumulation irritating pulmonary C-fiber afferent nerves
Direct cardiopulmonary congestion from drug-induced fluid redistribution

questions.question: The mechanism of action of digoxin involves:
questions.explanation: Digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, increasing intracellular sodium, which reduces calcium extrusion via sodium-calcium exchange, thereby increasing intracellular calcium and contractility. The drug also enhances vagal tone. Therapeutic index is narrow.

Fibrates activate PPAR-alpha, increasing lipoprotein lipase expression and reducing apoC-III, thereby enhancing triglyceride-rich lipoprotein clearance. They also reduce hepatic VLDL synthesis. These mechanisms lower triglycerides 30-50%. HDL increases 10-20% through apoA-I induction.
questions.question: Fibrates primarily lower triglycerides by:

options: The ability of the drug to bind to its receptor
The selectivity of drug for a particular receptor type
The rate of drug-receptor complex formation
Ability of drug to activate receptor after binding
The duration of drug-receptor complex occupancy
questions.explanation: Intrinsic activity (efficacy) is the ability of the drug to activate the receptor after receptor occupation. A full agonist has maximal intrinsic activity (AI = 1), a partial agonist has sub-maximal intrinsic activity (0 < AI < 1), a competitive antagonist has no intrinsic activity (AI = 0), and an inverse agonist has negative intrinsic activity (AI between 0 and -1).
questions.question: Intrinsic activity (efficacy) of a drug is defined as:
Which insulin formulation is absorbed most slowly from subcutaneous tissue?
questions.explanation: Insulin ultralente has the slowest absorption due to large zinc-insulin crystals that dissolve very slowly. It has 1-1.5 hour onset and 11-24 hour duration. Insulin glargine has replaced ultralente in many markets due to more consistent absorption profile.

questions.question: A patient on chronic acetazolamide for glaucoba develops a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. What is the underlying mechanism for this acid-base disturbance?
questions.explanation: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, reducing bicarbonate reabsorption and causing a self-limiting hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, which paradoxically reduces the drug's own diuretic efficacy over time.

All bisphosphonates carry similar risk of atypical femoral fractures with prolonged use (>5 years), though absolute risk remains low. These fractures occur in subtrochanteric or diaphyseal regions with minimal trauma. Drug holidays after 3-5 years may reduce risk in low-risk patients.
questions.question: Which bisphosphonate has the highest risk of atypical femoral fractures with long-term use?

options: Progressive muscle weakness requiring ventilatory support
Positive response to edrophonium test administration
Gradual onset over hours to days
Muscle fasciculations and miosis with excessive secretions
questions.explanation: Cholinergic crisis from excessive acetylcholinesterase inhibition causes SLUDGE symptoms (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis) plus muscle fasciculations, miosis, and paradoxical weakness from depolarization blockade. Myasthenic crisis involves weakness without cholinergic signs. Edrophonium test worsens cholinergic but improves myasthenic crisis (though risky). Treatment of cholinergic crisis requires drug cessation, atropine (for muscarinic effects), and supportive care. Distinguishing between crises is crucial for appropriate management.
questions.question: A patient develops cholinergic crisis after neostigmine overdose for myasthenia gravis. Which feature distinguishes this from myasthenic crisis?
