• Allergic rhinitis (hay fever), allergic asthma (acute and chronic; leukotrienes and prostaglandins sustain bronchospasm), food allergy, urticaria and atopic dermatitis.
• Anaphylactoid reactions are not IgE-mediated: agents directly induce mast cells and basophils to release mediators.

1. Graft rejection
• Types of graft: autograft (own tissue, always accepted); isograft (genetically identical individuals, usually takes permanently); allograft (genetically different members of the same species, usually rejected without immunosuppression); xenograft (different species, always rejected by an immunocompetent recipient).
• Recognition: rejection shows specificity, memory and self/non-self recognition; the immune response to MHC antigens is the strongest force in rejection; rejection has a sensitisation stage (T cells stimulated) and an effector stage (attack on the graft); HLA antigens on the graft presented to recipient CD4+ T cells activate them and they secrete IL-2; donor dendritic cells (passenger leukocytes) migrate to draining lymph nodes and stimulate a primary alloimmune response.
• Effector mechanisms: IL-2 activates B cells (antibody) and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells against graft HLA; CTLs destroy graft cells by perforin and granzymes; activated monocytes act by delayed-type hypersensitivity promoted by IFN-gamma; antibodies destroy the graft through classical complement and ADCC; IL-2, TNF-alpha and IFN are important mediators.
• Types: hyperacute (minutes to hours; pre-formed anti-ABO and/or anti-HLA antibodies activating complement, occluding the vascularised graft; kidney particularly susceptible); acute (days to weeks; alloreactive CD8+ and CD4+ T cells; fever and raised creatinine; mononuclear infiltration; increased MHC class I and II); chronic (months to years; slow low-grade T cell response, antibodies and non-immunological processes; progressive decline in graft function, glomerular basement membrane thickening and interstitial fibrosis).
• Sites that do not reject: cornea, brain, testes and uterus, despite genetic mismatch; specific tolerance to alloantigens is induced by exposure in utero or by injection of neonates.
2. Applications
• Prevention: ABO matching; cross-matching (donor leukocytes with recipient serum and complement, done immediately before surgery; cell death means anti-donor antibody and a contraindication); tissue typing (complement-dependent cytotoxicity with monospecific sera for class I, mixed lymphocyte reaction for class II HLA-D, PCR for gene sequences, microcytotoxicity); HLA matching is very important in bone marrow transplantation and significant in kidney transplantation.
• Immunosuppression: steroids such as prednisolone, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporin A, rapamycin and FK-506, total lymphoid irradiation, and monoclonal antibodies (methylprednisolone with or without anti-CD3 for acute rejection).
• Life-long immunosuppression does not prevent chronic rejection and gives a higher incidence of infections and malignancy.
3. Pathology
• Graft-versus-host reaction: competent donor T cells transferred to a recipient unable to reject them recognise host antigens and react against them; it needs immunocompetent T cells in the graft, an immunocompromised host and recipient antigens foreign to the donor.
• After bone marrow transplantation it develops in about two-thirds of recipients; grafted T cells proliferate in the host and reject cells with class II proteins, causing severe organ dysfunction (maculopapular rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, diarrhoea), usually 7-14 days after transplant, and many end in overwhelming infection and death.
• Reduction: antithymocyte globulin or monoclonal antibodies to remove mature T cells from donor tissue; immunotoxins such as ricin linked to anti-T cell monoclonal antibody.
questions.question:
1. Describe the immune response causing graft rejection under the following headings: types of graft, recognition of graft antigens (sensitisation stage), effector mechanisms (cellular and humoral), the types of rejection (hyperacute, acute and chronic), and situations in which rejection does not occur.
2. State the laboratory, diagnostic, vaccine or therapeutic applications used to prevent or treat rejection.
3. Explain the immunological basis of the pathology that results when the response is exaggerated or misdirected (graft-versus-host reaction).

questions.answerText:
1. Type II hypersensitivity
• Trigger and target antigens: IgG or IgM antibodies directed against cell-surface or extracellular matrix antigens (blood group antigens, drug antigens, self antigens modified by physical factors or infection, and exogenous haptens attached to cell membranes); reaction time is minutes to hours; the reaction has a sensitisation phase and an effector phase.
• Recognition: the Fc region of antigen-bound antibody initiates the reaction.
• Complement: classical pathway activation gives lysis of target cells by the C5b-C9 membrane attack complex, C3b deposition (opsonin bridging targets to macrophages and neutrophils through C3b receptors) and C5a (chemoattracts phagocytes).
• Effector cells and Fc receptors: neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages and NK cells bind through Fc receptors, giving opsonic phagocytosis and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC); when the target is too large to engulf, granule and lysosomal contents are released onto it.
• Fourth mechanism: antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction (antibodies to receptors).
• Lesion: contains antibody, complement and neutrophils.
• Regulation and resolution: for example, maternal acetylcholine receptor antibodies in a newborn are removed from the infant's circulation within 10-15 days and the symptoms disappear (symptoms last 1-2 weeks).
2. Applications
• Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test: washed patient RBCs are mixed with antiglobulin, which agglutinates cells coated with non-agglutinating antibody (IgG and C3b); positive in haemolytic disease of the newborn and immune haemolysis, and negative in non-immune haemolysis (DIC, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, PNH, sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia).
• Indirect antiglobulin test: detects unbound antibody in serum, such as anti-Rh antibodies in a mother's serum, and is used in cross-matching donor RBCs with recipient serum before transfusion (a positive result means the donor blood should not be transfused).
• Prevention: ABO and Rh blood grouping, tissue typing and cross-matching; Rho(D) immune globulin given during and after each pregnancy with an Rh+ fetus prevents haemolytic disease of the newborn; HLA typing by microcytotoxicity uses antibody and complement.
• Principle of treatment of type II hypersensitivity: not covered in the document.
3. Pathology
• Incompatible transfusion: for example anti-A antibodies of a type B recipient agglutinate type A cells and, through the classical pathway and membrane attack complex, cause massive haemolysis, with fever, chills, hypotension, shock and multi-organ failure.
• Haemolytic disease of the newborn: an Rh- mother exposed to Rh+ fetal RBCs makes anti-Rh IgG; in later pregnancies the IgG crosses the placenta and haemolyses fetal RBCs.
• Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, drug-induced reactions (penicillin with RBCs, quinine with platelets, pyramidone with granulocytes), Goodpasture's syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody), myasthenia gravis (anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody), Graves' disease (anti-TSH receptor antibody mimicking TSH) and hyperacute graft rejection.
questions.question:
1. Describe the type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic) hypersensitivity response under the following headings: trigger and target antigens, recognition, activation of complement and effector cells, mediators and effector mechanisms, and regulation and resolution.
2. State the laboratory, diagnostic, vaccine or therapeutic applications related to this response.
3. Explain the immunological basis of the pathology that results from this response.

1. Describe the cell-mediated immune response under the following headings: antigen presentation and recognition, activation of T helper cells, TH1 and TH2 effector functions, activation and killing by cytotoxic T cells, and regulation.
2. State the laboratory, diagnostic, vaccine or therapeutic applications of this response.
3. Explain the immunological basis of the pathology that results when the cell-mediated response fails, is exaggerated or is misdirected.
questions.answerText:
1. Cell-mediated immune response
• Cells: mediated by macrophages and T cells; the two main T cell populations are CD4+ helper T (TH) cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Tc or CTLs).
• Presentation and recognition: virtually any cell can act as an APC, but macrophages, dendritic cells, Langerhans cells and B cells are the professional APCs; the antigen peptide of a bacterium or virus is complexed to MHC molecules, carried to the APC surface and recognised by the TCR, which activates the T cell.
• TH cell activation: signal one is TCR binding to MHC class II-antigen; signal two (co-stimulatory) is CD28 on the TH cell binding B7 on the APC; the TH cell then secretes IL-2 and expresses the IL-2 receptor, and autocrine IL-2 drives proliferation into effector and memory TH cells.
• TH effector functions: activate and expand Tc cells, help B cells, and regulate monocyte-macrophages; TH1 cells (IL-2, IFN-gamma, TNF-beta) activate macrophages for intracellular killing; TH2 cells (IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, IL-13) act against helminths and promote class switching to IgE.
• Tc cell activation: virus-infected cells present viral antigen with MHC class I; signals are TCR binding to MHC class I-viral antigen, IL-2 from nearby activated TH cells, and CD28-B7.
• Tc cell killing: TCR binding forms a CTL-target conjugate; CTLs release perforin (forms a hole through which proteins and ions leak) and granzymes (enter through the pores and activate caspase, leading to nuclear damage and apoptosis); CTLs also express Fas ligand, which binds Fas on the target and triggers apoptosis; Tc cells destroy virus, cancer cells and cells of a transplanted organ from an HLA-unrelated donor.
• Regulation: IFN-gamma (TH1) inhibits TH2 differentiation; IL-4 (TH2) inhibits TH1 differentiation; IL-10 inhibits cytokine production by TH1 cells, macrophages and other APCs.
2. Applications
• Diagnostic skin tests for delayed-type hypersensitivity: a positive skin test reaction indicates sensitised antigen-specific TH1 cells (Mantoux tuberculin test read at 48-72 hours; patch test for contact dermatitis); the Lepromin test uses M. leprae extract.
• Class II HLA typing uses the mixed lymphocyte reaction.
• Cancer immunotherapy: high-dose IL-2 enhances the cytolytic function of CTLs and NK cells; LAK cells and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs); adjuvants such as BCG activate macrophages and raise generalised humoral and cell-mediated responses.
• BCG vaccination is listed alongside the Mantoux tuberculin test.
3. Pathology
• Failure: type IV hypersensitivity is lost with the decline in CD4+ T cells in HIV and AIDS; patients with advanced cancer show depressed T cell responses and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections.
• Exaggerated: excess delayed-type hypersensitivity damages host tissues; persisting antigen gives chronic T cell and macrophage activation and granuloma formation with tissue damage.
• Misdirected: organ-specific self-antigen-reactive T cells cause localised cellular inflammation and autoimmune disease such as type 1 diabetes mellitus; CTLs attack transplanted organs from HLA-unrelated donors and mediate acute rejection.

questions.question:
1. Describe the structure and functional organisation of the ABO and Rh blood group antigen and antibody systems under the following headings: antigens and antibodies involved, compatibility, typing and cross-matching, and prevention of incompatibility.
2. State how its parts relate to common immunological disorders.
3. Explain why the disorder may spread to distant tissues or systems and cause functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Blood group systems
• Antigens and antibodies: blood group antigens (A, B, O and Rh) on red blood cells; natural antibodies are IgM in nature (blood groups A and B isohemagglutinins); the Rh antibody made after sensitisation is anti-Rh IgG.
• Compatibility: the document tabulates recipient against donor group (a plus sign marks incompatibility): O recipients are compatible only with O donors, A recipients with O and A, B recipients with O and B, and AB recipients with all four donor groups.
• Typing and cross-matching: RBCs are mixed on a slide with antisera to A or B antigens and agglutinate if the antigen is present; the indirect antiglobulin test cross-matches donor RBCs with recipient serum (37 C for 30 minutes, then antiglobulin reagent; agglutination means antibody against donor cells and the blood should not be transfused); the direct antiglobulin test detects antibody or C3b bound to RBCs.
• Prevention: ABO matching and cross-matching immediately before surgery; Rho(D) immune globulin during and after each pregnancy with an Rh+ fetus binds fetal Rh+ RBCs in the mother and prevents her primary immune response.
2. Relation to disorders
• Incompatible blood transfusion (type II hypersensitivity): for example a type B recipient's anti-A antibodies agglutinate type A cells, and classical complement activation with the membrane attack complex causes massive haemolysis.
• Haemolytic disease of the newborn from Rh incompatibility (DAT positive, cells coated with anti-Rh antibody).
• Hyperacute graft rejection from pre-formed anti-ABO antibodies; autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and drug-induced haemolysis (DAT positive).
3. Spread and functional deficit
• In incompatible transfusion, the debris from destroyed RBCs can occlude blood vessels in the alveoli of the lungs and the glomeruli of the kidneys; within 1 to 24 hours the patient has fever, chills, itching, hives, dyspnoea, haemoglobinuria and hypotension, and in the most serious reactions shock, multi-organ failure and death.
• In haemolytic disease of the newborn, the mother's anti-Rh IgG crosses the placenta into the fetal circulation and haemolyses fetal RBCs, leaving too few cells to oxygenate the fetus; the first child is usually unaffected, and second and subsequent Rh+ fetuses are affected because memory B cells make large amounts of IgG.
• Hyperacute rejection of a kidney damages glomerular capillaries and destroys the graft, within minutes to 48 hours of surgery.

questions.question:
1. Describe the humoral (antibody-mediated) immune response under the following headings: trigger (T-dependent and T-independent antigens), recognition and B cell activation, role of T helper cells and cytokines, differentiation into plasma and memory cells, kinetics of the primary and secondary responses, effector functions of antibody, and regulation and resolution.
2. State the laboratory, diagnostic, vaccine or therapeutic applications of this response.
3. Explain the immunological basis of the pathology that results when the humoral response fails, is exaggerated or is misdirected.
questions.answerText:
1. Humoral immune response
• Trigger: the humoral response is uniquely adapted to eliminate extracellular pathogens and is characterised by production of large numbers of antibody molecules; T-dependent (TD) antigens need T and B cells to recognise the antigen in a linked fashion; T-independent (TI) antigens activate B cells without MHC class II-restricted T cell help (TI-1, mainly bacterial cell wall components such as LPS; TI-2, large polysaccharides with repeating determinants such as Ficoll, dextran, polymeric bacterial flagellin and poliomyelitis virus).
• Recognition and activation: activation of B cells by TD antigens needs two signals plus IL-2, IL-4 and IL-5 from TH cells; signal one is antigen binding to sIg and signal two is cell-to-cell contact between B cell and TH cell; the sIg-antigen complex is internalised by receptor-mediated endocytosis, cleaved into peptides by lysosomal enzymes, complexed to MHC class II and presented to the TH cell; the TCR binds the MHC class II-antigen complex forming a T-B conjugate, CD40 interacts with CD40L, and B7 interacts with CD28.
• Role of other cells: macrophages act as APCs for activation of T helper cells (with IL-1); B cells also serve as APCs.
• Differentiation: the activated B cell expresses cytokine receptors, divides many times and gives plasma cells and memory B cells.
• Primary response: the first contact with antigen; phases are lag (clonal selection and differentiation into plasma and memory cells), exponential (rapid rise in antibody), steady-state or plateau (secretion and degradation equal) and decline; IgM is secreted first, often followed by IgG; the primary response follows a lag period of 2-5 days.
• Secondary response: memory B and T cells give a response that is more rapid, of greater magnitude and longer duration, with higher-affinity antibody, a variety of isotypes in addition to IgM, and antibody levels 100-1000 times higher than the primary response; the secondary response to TI antigens resembles the primary response (no class switching or increased affinity) and memory to TI antigens is poor.
• Effector functions of antibody: activate complement (lysis of microorganisms), act as opsonin (enhancing phagocytosis), neutralise bacterial toxins, block virus infection of host cells, prevent colonisation at mucous membranes, and mediate ADCC through Fc receptors on NK cells or macrophages.
• Regulation and resolution: after removal of antigen no new plasma cells are produced, existing plasma cells die within a few days and degradation of secreted antibody causes the decline phase.
2. Applications
• Serological diagnosis: in most primary infections IgM peaks 7-10 days after onset of illness and then declines; IgG starts a few days after IgM and often persists for life; diagnosis rests on specific IgM or a significant rise in specific IgG between two samples taken 7-10 days apart.
• Laboratory estimation of immunoglobulins: single radial immunodiffusion (Mancini), immunoturbidimetry, ELISA/RIA.
• Vaccination (artificial active immunity) and passive immunity from immune serum globulins, immune globulins and gamma globulins; adjuvants (for example aluminium hydroxide) are added to vaccines to stimulate the response and can act as a depot for antigen.
3. Pathology
• Failure: humoral immunodeficiencies cause recurrent bacterial infections (severe bacteraemia, meningitis, cellulitis) and recurrent or chronic gastrointestinal infection with malabsorption and malnutrition.
• Misdirected or exaggerated: antibody-mediated hypersensitivity, IgE in type I, IgG and IgM in types II and III, and autoantibodies, for example to acetylcholine receptors (myasthenia gravis) and to the TSH receptor (Graves' disease).
• Malignant transformation of plasma cells: excess light chain synthesis produces Bence Jones protein.

questions.question:
1. Describe the induction of immunological tolerance under the following headings: definition and trigger (tolerogens), central tolerance in T and B cells, peripheral tolerance, factors determining tolerance versus response, and maintenance and termination.
2. State the laboratory, diagnostic, vaccine or therapeutic applications of tolerance.
3. Explain the immunological basis of the pathology that results when tolerance fails.
questions.answerText:
1. Immunological tolerance
• Definition and trigger: unresponsiveness to an antigen induced by previous exposure to that antigen; it is specific and the immune system otherwise functions normally; antigens that induce tolerance are tolerogens as opposed to immunogens, and one antigen can be either depending on the conditions of display (for example presence of inflammation).
• Central tolerance in T cells: in the thymus, immature T cells that recognise self antigen with high affinity are deleted by negative selection (apoptosis); low-affinity recognisers survive (positive selection) and mature into CD4 or CD8 T cells.
• Central tolerance in B cells: in the bone marrow, B cells recognising self antigen are killed, inactivated or receptor-edited.
• Peripheral tolerance: clonal deletion, clonal ignorance (self-reactive cells remain viable but do not react), clonal anergy (functional inactivation without cell death due to absent co-stimulation; antigen recognition without CD28-B7 gives anergy), and active suppression by regulatory T cells; lymphocytes that do not recognise presented self antigen in regional lymph nodes undergo anergy or apoptosis.
• Determining factors: favouring tolerance are soluble, aggregate-free, simple small antigens, oral or sometimes intravenous route, very large or very small dose, a newborn or immunologically immature host, and undifferentiated B cells with only IgM; T cells become tolerant more readily and stay tolerant longer than B cells.
• Maintenance and termination: tolerance needs persistence of antigen; it can be broken naturally (autoimmune disease) or artificially (X-irradiation, certain drugs, cross-reacting antigens); Owen observed tolerance in dizygotic bovine twins and Medawar induced tolerance in mice.
2. Applications
• Inducing tolerance to prevent rejection of organ allografts and xenografts, to treat autoimmune diseases and to treat allergic diseases.
• Terminating tolerance to treat tumours (enhance the first or second signal) and infectious diseases.
• Monoclonal antibodies that inhibit co-stimulatory signals lead to anergy in specifically reactive cells; new methods aim to induce specific tolerance to grafts without general immunosuppression; desensitisation teaches the immune system to tolerate allergic triggers.
3. Pathology
• Failure of self-tolerance results in immune reactions against self, that is autoimmunity and autoimmune diseases (illustrated in the document by the butterfly rash of systemic lupus erythematosus).
• Abnormalities in the CD4+CD25+FOXP3+ Treg population may play a role in the development of allergic disease, since Tregs suppress dysregulated responses.
• Tolerance is different from immunodeficiency and immunosuppression, which are non-specific to antigen.

questions.question:
1. Describe the structure and functional organisation of the complement system under the following headings: composition and synthesis, nomenclature, the three activation pathways and common terminal sequence, functional categories of components, and regulation.
2. State how its parts relate to common immunological disorders.
3. Explain why complement-related disorders may spread to distant tissues or systems and cause functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Complement system
• Composition and synthesis: a set of about 30 activation and regulatory glycoproteins, bound to membranes or in circulation, existing largely as inactive zymogens that must be cleaved or change conformation to activate and that interact in catalytic cascades; involved in innate and adaptive immunity; synthesised largely by hepatocytes and also by monocytes, tissue macrophages, fibroblasts and epithelial cells.
• Nomenclature: proteins designated C1 to C9 (numbers do not follow order of action); cleavage products get a lower-case letter (C3a, C5a).
• Pathways: classical (initiated by IgM or IgG antigen-antibody complexes through C1q, C1r, C1s, then C4 and C2 giving C4b2a, the C3 convertase), lectin (mannose-binding lectin and MASPs cleaving C4 and C2, antibody-independent) and alternative (spontaneous C3 hydrolysis, factor B and factor D, stabilised by properdin, with its own C3 and C5 convertases); each occurs in initiation, amplification and termination phases.
• Common terminal sequence: C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b (a single convertase can generate more than 200 C3b), C5 convertase cleaves C5, and C5b binds C6, C7, C8 and polymerised C9 to form the membrane attack complex (pore widening from 10 A to 70-100 A), which causes loss of membrane integrity and cell death.
• Functional categories: initiator components (C1q, MBL), enzymatic mediators (C1r, C1s, MASP, factor B), opsonins (C3b, C4b), inflammatory mediators (anaphylatoxins C3a, C4a, C5a), membrane attack proteins, complement receptors (CR1, CR2, C5aR) and regulatory components.
• Regulation: factor I (cleaves C3b and C4b), factor H, decay accelerating factor (DAF), C4 binding protein and anaphylatoxin inhibitor protect host cells from unintended lysis.
2. Relation to disorders
• Type II hypersensitivity: classical pathway activation gives lysis by the membrane attack complex, C3b opsonisation and C5a chemotaxis.
• Type III hypersensitivity: complexes activate the classical pathway, attract neutrophils through C5a, and complement is used up so serum complement falls in active immune complex disease (SLE).
• Complement deficiency is assessed by the total haemolytic complement test (heterozygous defects may not reduce haemolysis; homozygous defects give no haemolysis) and by the elimination method; the complement fixation test detects antibodies to pathogens.
• Activation of complement by immune complexes helps to remove them and prevents formation of large tissue-depositing lattices.
3. Spread and functional deficit
• Anaphylatoxins (C3a, C4a, C5a) enhance blood supply and attract cells, and their effects are harmful in excess (anaphylaxis); C5a acts on C5aR of neutrophils to stimulate degranulation and inflammation; in serum sickness they stimulate mast cells to release histamine and lower blood pressure.
• Circulating immune complexes that activate complement deposit in joints (arthritis), glomeruli (glomerulonephritis) and blood vessels of skin and other organs (vasculitis).
• In an incompatible transfusion, complement-mediated haemolysis leaves debris that can occlude vessels in the alveoli of the lungs and glomeruli of the kidneys, with hypotension, shock and multi-organ failure.

questions.question:
1. Describe the mast cell under the following headings: distribution and morphology, receptors and bound antibody, mediators released (primary mediators, secondary mediators and cytokines), and functions in immediate hypersensitivity.
2. Explain the clinical basis of why dysfunction (inappropriate activation) of mast cells makes a patient vulnerable to particular diseases.
3. Distinguish between the mast cell and the basophil.
questions.answerText:
1. Mast cell
• Distribution and morphology: mast cell precursors are distributed to all vascularised peripheral tissues, where they differentiate into mature mast cells; round, oval or spindle-shaped cells with numerous membrane-bound granules containing inflammatory mediators; skin, mucous membranes, respiratory tract and gastrointestinal tract have higher concentrations; they occupy a sentinel position where allergens may enter the host.
• Receptors and bound antibody: express the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcεRI: one alpha chain that binds IgE, one beta chain and two gamma chains that transduce signals); serum IgE half-life is 2-3 days whereas mast cell-bound IgE is stable for many weeks.
• Mediators: primary mediators stored in granules before activation (histamine, proteases, eosinophil chemotactic factor, neutrophil chemotactic factor, heparin); secondary mediators synthesised after activation (leukotrienes through the lipoxygenase pathway, prostaglandins and thromboxanes through the cyclooxygenase pathway, platelet-activating factor); cytokines (IL-1, IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, GM-CSF, TGF-beta, TNF-alpha).
• Functions: cross-linking of IgE by allergen aggregates the receptors and the mast cell degranulates; mediators cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction and increased mucosal secretion; histamine acts through H1, H2 and H3 receptors; leukotrienes are 100 times more potent than histamine as bronchoconstrictors.
2. Clinical basis
• Activation of IgE-bound mast cells by allergen underlies hay fever, allergic asthma, insect venom reactions, food allergy, atopic eczema, urticaria and systemic anaphylaxis (circulatory collapse, oedema, increased vascular permeability, tracheal occlusion, death).
• Mast-cell TNF-alpha in high concentration may contribute to the shock in systemic anaphylaxis, and mast-cell IL-4 increases IgE production by B cells.
• Cromolyn sodium stabilises the membrane by inhibiting mast cell degranulation.
• Vulnerability from a deficiency of mast cells: not covered in the document.
3. Mast cell versus basophil
• Mast cell: resides in tissues where allergens may enter (sentinel position); precursors mature within vascularised peripheral tissues.
• Basophil: normally resides in the circulation and enters tissues at the site of inflammation, during the late phase of the type I reaction.
• Shared feature: both express high-affinity IgE receptors and release mediators when bound IgE is cross-linked.

questions.question:
1. Describe the structure and functional organisation of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC/HLA) under the following headings: class I and class II molecules and their loci, cellular distribution, role in antigen presentation to T cells, and typing.
2. State how the MHC relates to common immunological disorders.
3. Explain why the disorder may spread to distant tissues or systems and cause functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. MHC (HLA)
• Classes and loci: MHC class I and class II molecules; HLA has three class I loci and a class II locus (HLA-D); there is a high level of polymorphism at each locus, so matching all class I and II gene loci between unrelated donors is difficult.
• Cellular distribution: all normal nucleated cells express plenty of MHC class I; MHC class II is on professional antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, Langerhans cells and B cells); antigen binding induces B cells to express large numbers of class II; IFN-gamma increases MHC class I and II on malignant cells and macrophages.
• Function: antigen peptide fragments complexed to MHC molecules are carried to the cell surface and recognised by the TCR; MHC class II-antigen presented to CD4+ TH cells; MHC class I-antigen (for example viral antigen) presented to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
• Typing: class I alleles identified by complement-dependent cytotoxic reactions with monospecific sera; class II by the mixed lymphocyte reaction; alleles now defined by PCR gene sequences; microcytotoxicity with monoclonal antibodies and complement on white blood cells.
• The detailed molecular structure of MHC molecules: not covered in the document.
2. Relation to disorders
• Graft rejection: the immune response to MHC antigens is the strongest force in rejection, and the recipient-donor match is assessed by typing MHC class I and II.
• Graft-versus-host disease: donor T cells recognise foreign recipient MHC and 'reject' cells with class II proteins.
• Tumours and viruses: tumour and virus-infected cells with low MHC class I evade CTLs but are attacked by NK cells; poor T helper activation arises when tumours lack B7 co-stimulation with class II presentation.
• HLA matching is very important in bone marrow transplantation, has significant influence on kidney transplantation, and gives no benefit in corneal transplantation.
3. Spread and functional deficit
• In graft-versus-host disease, grafted T cells proliferate in the irradiated, immunocompromised host, causing severe organ dysfunction: maculopapular rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and diarrhoea (also fever and breathlessness, usually 7-14 days after transplant); many end in overwhelming infection and death.
• Well-matched bone marrow grafts establish initially in 85% of recipients but graft-versus-host reaction develops in about two-thirds of them; the stronger the difference in transplantation antigens the more severe the reaction, and HLA differences can be fatal.
• Hyperacute rejection of a kidney (pre-formed antibodies to graft antigens) damages glomerular capillaries and destroys the graft.

questions.question:
1. Describe the spleen under the following headings: classification, structure and supply, immune functions, and non-immune functions.
2. Explain the clinical basis of why dysfunction of the spleen and its immune role would leave a patient more vulnerable to particular infections or immune complex disease.
3. Distinguish between the spleen and the lymph node.
questions.answerText:
1. Spleen
• Classification: secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organ; secondary lymphoid organs are where immune cells encounter antigen and initiate immune responses, serve as filters monitoring the contents of the extracellular fluids, and are sites for lymphocyte differentiation (T cells into killer and helper effector cells, B cells into antibody-producing plasma cells, both into long-lived memory cells).
• Structure and supply: large, ovoid organ not supplied by lymphatic vessels.
• Immune functions: filters the blood and traps blood-borne antigens; site for the initiation of adaptive immune responses; macrophages in the spleen engulf and degrade circulating immune complexes through their C3b and Fc receptors.
• Non-immune functions: iron metabolism, thrombocyte storage and haematopoiesis.
2. Clinical basis
• Because the spleen filters blood and traps blood-borne antigens, it is important in the response to systemic infections.
• Immune complexes must be removed from the circulation because they are harmful; splenic macrophages engulf and degrade them, and when complexes are not cleared they deposit in tissues and cause damage.
• Graft-versus-host disease features hepatosplenomegaly among its main symptoms.
• A named clinical condition caused by loss of the spleen: not covered in the document.
3. Spleen versus lymph node
• Spleen: large, ovoid organ not supplied by lymphatic vessels; filters blood and traps blood-borne antigens; important in systemic infections; also performs iron metabolism, thrombocyte storage and haematopoiesis.
• Lymph node: bean-shaped, encapsulated structure packed with lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells; connected to both blood and lymphatic vessels; the first to encounter antigens that enter the tissue spaces; the most specialised secondary lymphoid organ committed to regulating immune responses; ideal microenvironment for antigen-lymphocyte interaction and for organised cellular or humoral responses; site for generation and residence of memory T and B cells.

questions.question:
1. Describe the structure and functional organisation of the cytokine system of the helper T cell subsets (TH1 and TH2) and related cytokines under the following headings: TH1 cytokines, TH2 cytokines, cytokines of delayed-type hypersensitivity and mast cells, and their effects on target cells.
2. State how its parts relate to common immunological disorders.
3. Explain why the disorder may spread to distant tissues or systems and cause functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Cytokine organisation
• TH1 cytokines: IL-2 (promotes activation of antigen-specific TH and Tc cells), IFN-gamma (activates macrophages, promotes B cell proliferation and class switching to IgG1, inhibits TH2 differentiation) and TNF-beta (activates macrophages and neutrophils, promotes B cell growth and Ig production).
• TH2 cytokines: IL-4 (inhibits TH1 differentiation, chemoattracts lymphocytes, mast cells and basophils, promotes class switching to IgE), IL-5 (growth of mast cells and eosinophils, B cell proliferation and switching to IgE and IgG4), IL-6 (B cell growth and Ig production), IL-10 (inhibits cytokine production, including IFN-gamma, by TH1 cells, macrophages and other APCs; promotes B cell growth) and IL-13 (same as IL-4).
• Delayed-type hypersensitivity cytokines: macrophage migration inhibition factor keeps macrophages at the site; IFN-gamma, GM-CSF and TNF-alpha enhance microbicidal and cytolytic activity of macrophages; IL-3 and GM-CSF stimulate bone marrow monocyte output; TNF-beta and TNF-alpha up-regulate adhesion molecules on local blood vessels.
• Mast cell cytokines: IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, TNF-alpha and chemotactic factors raise adhesion molecule expression and draw cells to the site; IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils; IL-4 increases IgE production.
2. Relation to disorders
• Allergy: TH2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-13 for IgE switching; IL-5 for eosinophils) drive type I hypersensitivity, and Treg cytokines IL-10 and TGF-beta inhibit TH2 cytokine production.
• Delayed-type hypersensitivity and granuloma: TH1 cytokines (IFN-gamma, TNF) sustain macrophage activation and granuloma formation.
• Leprosy: TH1 response gives the tuberculoid form and TH2 response (IL-4, IL-5, IL-10) the lepromatous form.
• Tumours: tumour cells secrete TGF-beta or IL-10 to suppress immunity; IFN and TNF are used in therapy, and high-dose IL-2 is the approved anti-tumour interleukin.
3. Spread and functional deficit
• Mast cell TNF-alpha in high concentration may contribute to shock in systemic anaphylaxis.
• Cytokines of effector TH cells act over many cell types; IFN-gamma raising MHC class II lets TDTH cells and macrophages amplify the local inflammatory response, and cytokine-driven adhesion molecules draw leukocytes into tissues.
• TNF exhibits hemorrhagic necrosis of tumours and damages tumour vascular endothelium, reducing blood supply.
• In lepromatous leprosy the TH2-skewed response leaves M. leprae free to disseminate with systemic effects.

questions.question:
1. Describe the type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity response under the following headings: trigger and antigens, formation and clearance of immune complexes, factors favouring tissue deposition, complement and neutrophil effector mechanisms, and regulation and resolution.
2. State the laboratory, diagnostic, vaccine or therapeutic applications related to this response.
3. Explain the immunological basis of the pathology that results from this response.
questions.answerText:
1. Type III hypersensitivity
• Trigger and antigens: soluble antigen (persistent infection microbial antigen, self antigen in autoimmunity, extrinsic environmental antigen, serum protein) with IgG or IgM forms immune complexes; time of appearance is 2 to 8 hours after antigen contact.
• Formation and clearance: soluble antigens are cross-linked by antibody into a lattice; complexes are removed from circulation through C3b formation, macrophage C3b and Fc receptors (spleen), binding to RBC CR1 with stripping by liver reticuloendothelial cells (Kupffer cells); classical pathway activation inhibits formation of precipitating complexes and the alternative pathway solubilises formed complexes.
• Factors favouring deposition: complex size, charge, valency of antigen, avidity of antibody, affinity of antigen for tissue components, lattice structure, duration of antigen exposure, host response, local tissue factors and a compromised phagocytic system.
• Effector mechanisms: deposited complexes activate the classical complement pathway through C1; C5a attracts neutrophils, which cannot engulf the deposited complexes and release prostaglandins, lysosomal enzymes and free oxygen radicals that damage tissue; platelets accumulate, cause clotting and release vasoactive amines and growth factor; vascular permeability rises; serum complement is used up and levels fall during the active phase.
• Localised and systemic forms: the Arthus reaction is localised (oedema, erythema and fibrin deposition, peaking 4 to 10 hours) and serum sickness is systemic.
• Regulation and resolution: serum sickness resolves following withdrawal of the passive antibody.
2. Applications
• Laboratory diagnosis: skin test antigen (rash at 5-6 hours); direct immunofluorescence of tissue biopsy (lumpy deposits); detection of immune complexes by polyethylene glycol precipitation and ELISA/RIA; rheumatoid factor by passive latex agglutination; antinuclear antibodies by indirect immunofluorescence in SLE; heterophile antibody in serum sickness.
• Treatment: removal of the antigen source (avoidance, antibiotics for infection); anti-inflammatory drugs (aspirin, indomethacin) and corticosteroids; immunosuppressants (corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, azathioprine); plasmapheresis, which relieves symptoms only for a shorter duration and does not address the autoimmune process itself.
3. Pathology
• Serum sickness: 8 to 13 days after horse antidiphtheria serum, children developed fever, malaise, skin eruptions, arthralgia, leukopenia, lymphadenopathy and albuminuria; today most often caused by drugs (penicillin, sulfonamides and others).
• Systemic lupus erythematosus: increased circulating complexes and decreased complement; complexes deposit in the glomeruli (75% of patients have nephritis) with a granular, lumpy-bumpy appearance.
• Rheumatoid arthritis (joints), post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (Streptococcus pyogenes), chronic malaria, other infections (M. leprae, T. pallidum, hepatitis B virus, Epstein-Barr virus), and vasculitis in skin and other organs.

questions.question:
1. Describe the type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity response under the following headings: trigger and antigens, sensitisation and recognition, effector phase and mediators, the three variants, and regulation and resolution.
2. State the laboratory, diagnostic, vaccine or therapeutic applications related to this response.
3. Explain the immunological basis of the pathology that results from this response.
questions.answerText:
1. Type IV hypersensitivity
• Trigger and antigens: a T cell-mediated inflammatory response to exogenous agents (microbial antigens, sensitising chemicals) or self antigens; it is a normal part of adaptive immunity and essential for control of intracellular pathogens, but if excessive it damages host tissue; it takes more than 12 hours to develop, is transferred by T cells (CD4+) rather than serum and needs no antibody.
• Sensitisation and recognition: naive TH cells first meet antigen in secondary lymphoid organs; APCs engulf the microbe and present peptides to TDTH cells; activated TH cells become TH1 cells and effector and memory cells form.
• Effector phase: on later exposure effector T cells secrete cytokines and chemokines (IFN-gamma, TNF-beta, TNF-alpha, IL-17A, IL-1beta, macrophage migration inhibition factor, GM-CSF); macrophages are the principal effector cells; IFN-gamma raises MHC class II on macrophages so that TDTH cells and macrophages amplify each other; adhesion molecules rise; the response appears at 12 to 24 hours and peaks at 48 to 72 hours.
• Variants: contact hypersensitivity (haptens, Langerhans cells, sensitisation phase 10-14 days then elicitation) and tuberculin-type hypersensitivity, both within 72 hours; granulomatous hypersensitivity develops over 21-28 days.
• Regulation and resolution: the tuberculin response is usually self-limiting as antigen is progressively removed; if antigen is easily cleared, tissues are remodelled; TGF-beta and IL-10 from keratinocytes dampen the response and may induce anergy in TH1 cells.
2. Applications
• Mantoux tuberculin test: PPD injected intradermally and read at 48-72 hours, positive as a red, swollen area if previously exposed to M. tuberculosis (a positive result shows sensitised antigen-specific TH1 cells); Lepromin test for leprosy; BCG vaccination.
• Patch test for contact dermatitis: open method (acetone extract dried on the skin, read after 48 hours) and closed method (allergen on a taped pad, removed at 48 hours, re-read at 72 and 96 hours if negative); about 20 substances at one sitting; positive is erythema, papules or vesicles.
• Inhibition of TNF leads to breakdown of granulomas.
3. Pathology
• Granulomatous hypersensitivity, the clinically most important form: persistent antigen (usually within macrophages) drives chronic T cell activation, epithelioid cells and giant cells, with lytic enzymes destroying surrounding tissue; seen in tuberculosis, leprosy, schistosomiasis, leishmaniasis, sarcoidosis and Crohn's disease.
• Contact dermatitis (for example nickel eczematous rash) and type 1 diabetes mellitus (autoreactive T cells against organ-specific self antigen); transplant rejection.

questions.question:
1. Describe the structure and functional organisation of the thymus under the following headings: location and size, lobular organisation (cortex and medulla), T cell maturation and selection, and role in central tolerance.
2. State how its parts relate to common immunological disorders.
3. Explain why the disorder may spread to distant tissues or systems and cause functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Thymus
• Location and size: an organ found just above the heart in which T cells grow and multiply; largest before puberty (30 - 40 grams at puberty), thereafter undergoing progressive involution.
• Organisation: a bi-lobed organ; each lobe is subdivided into lobules; each lobule has a cortex (lymphocyte-rich region and site of T cell maturation) and a medulla (less cellular region and site of final screening and elimination of autoreactive cells).
• Maturation and selection: immature T cells (thymocytes) from the bone marrow mature into functional T cells; maturation involves generation of unique antigen receptors and clonal selection (negative selection about 95%, and positive selection); immature T cells (CD3+, CD4+CD8+) that recognise self antigen with low affinity mature into CD4 or CD8 T cells.
• Central tolerance: the thymus presents self antigen to newly formed T lymphocytes, and T cells recognising ubiquitous self antigen with high affinity are deleted by apoptosis (clonal deletion).
2. Relation to disorders
• Failure of self-tolerance results in immune reactions against self, that is autoimmunity; the document illustrates tolerance and autoimmunity with the butterfly rash of systemic lupus erythematosus.
• Organ-specific autoreactive T cells cause localised cellular inflammation and autoimmune disease such as type 1 diabetes mellitus.
• Malnutrition causes atrophy of the thymus and other lymphoid organs with lymphopaenia and opportunistic infections; the thymus is largest before puberty and then involutes.
• A named thymic disorder (for example absent thymus): not covered in the document.
3. Spread and functional deficit
• Systemic lupus erythematosus is a multisystem autoimmune disorder with a broad spectrum of presentations encompassing almost all organs and tissues; its immune complexes deposit in joints, kidneys, skin, heart, lungs and brain by complement activation and oxygen free radicals, and 75% of patients have nephritis.
• Autoreactive T cells against an organ-specific self antigen can produce autoimmune disease of that organ, such as type 1 diabetes mellitus.
• Why a failure of thymic selection would spread to distant organs: not covered in the document.

1. Immunoglobulin A
• Structure and forms: contains 3 CH domains and a hinge region; exists as a monomer or a dimer, in which IgA monomers are connected by a J chain and protected against proteolytic enzymes by the secretory piece.
• Subclasses: IgA1 and IgA2.
• Location: predominantly in the gastrointestinal tract, tears, sweat, saliva, breast milk (including colostrum) and external surfaces (except skin); also found in the circulation.
• Functions: prevents microbial binding to epithelia; activates complement in its aggregated form; transferred to the infant during breast feeding.
• Serum concentration, half-life and size: about 100 mg/dl; 14% of total serum Ig; half-life about 1 week (5 days); molecular weight about 160 kD (monomer).
2. Clinical basis
• Humoral immunodeficiencies: recurrent bacterial infections, and recurrent or chronic gastrointestinal infection that can result in malabsorption and malnutrition.
• In gastrointestinal allergic diseases, the lack of SIgA protein hydrolase leaves undigested protein allergen, giving food allergies.
• Breast-milk passage of antibody from mother to infant gives immediate short-term (natural passive) protection.
• A named IgA deficiency syndrome: not covered in the document.
3. IgA versus IgG
• IgA: monomer or J-chain dimer with secretory piece; 2 subclasses; found in secretions and mucosal surfaces and breast milk; 14% of serum Ig; half-life about 5 days; about 160 kD (monomer); prevents microbial binding to epithelia.
• IgG: monomer; 4 subclasses; about 75% of circulating Ig; circulates between blood and interstitial fluid; crosses the placenta; half-life about 3 weeks; about 150 kD; facilitates opsonisation, ADCC, complement activation and neutralisation of viruses and toxins.
questions.question:
1. Describe immunoglobulin A (IgA) under the following headings: structure and forms, subclasses, location, functions, and serum concentration and half-life.
2. Explain the clinical basis of why loss of mucosal antibody protection or of humoral immunity makes a patient more vulnerable to infections or disease.
3. Distinguish between IgA and IgG.

1. Describe the B lymphocyte and its plasma cell progeny under the following headings: release and tolerance in the bone marrow, receptors and antigen presentation, activation (T-dependent and T-independent), and functions.
2. Explain the clinical basis of why B cell or antibody deficiency makes a patient more vulnerable to particular infections or diseases.
3. Distinguish between the plasma cell and the memory B cell.
questions.answerText:
1. B lymphocyte
• Release and tolerance: mature B cells are released from the bone marrow in a resting state and do not secrete antibodies; resting B cells that do not contact antigen die within a few days; in the bone marrow, B cells that recognise self antigen are eliminated, inactivated or receptor-edited.
• Receptors and presentation: antigen is bound by surface immunoglobulin (sIg; IgM and IgD on naive B cells); the sIg-antigen complex is internalised by receptor-mediated endocytosis, processed into peptides and presented with MHC class II to TH cells; antigen binding induces B cells to express large numbers of class II molecules.
• T-dependent activation: needs two signals plus cytokines (IL-2, IL-4, IL-5) from TH cells; the first signal is antigen binding to sIg and the second is cell-to-cell contact with the TH cell (TCR with MHC class II-antigen, CD40 with CD40L, B7 with CD28).
• T-independent activation: TI-1 antigens (such as LPS) activate B cells without a second signal and polyclonally at high concentration; TI-2 antigens (large polysaccharides with repeating determinants) cross-link Ig and need residual non-cognate T cell help such as cytokines.
• Functions: the activated B cell divides many times into plasma cells (antibody secretion) and memory B cells; B cells also serve as antigen-presenting cells for T helper cells.
2. Clinical basis
• Humoral immunodeficiencies produce recurrent bacterial infections (severe bacteraemia, meningitis, cellulitis) and recurrent or chronic gastrointestinal infection leading to malabsorption and malnutrition.
• Memory induction to T-independent antigens is poor, with no class switching or affinity increase in the secondary response.
• On malignant transformation of plasma cells, excess light chain synthesis produces Bence Jones protein.
3. Plasma cell versus memory B cell
• Plasma cell: differentiated, antibody-secreting B cell with abundant cytoplasm rich in endoplasmic reticulum; after removal of antigen no new plasma cells are produced and the existing ones die rapidly within a few days, so antibody levels decline.
• Memory B cell: formed during the primary response; stops dividing; variable lifespan, some persisting for the life of the individual; underlies the secondary response, which is more rapid, of greater magnitude and longer duration, with higher-affinity antibody and isotypes other than IgM (antibody levels 100-1000 times higher); also explains 'original antigenic sin'.

1. Lymph node
• Classification: a secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organ; the lymphoid organs are united into a functional whole by the blood vessels and the lymphatic systems.
• Structure and connections: bean-shaped, encapsulated structure, connected to both blood and lymphatic vessels.
• Cellular content: packed with lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells.
• Functions: the most specialised secondary lymphoid organ committed to regulating immune responses; the first to encounter antigens entering tissue spaces; an ideal microenvironment for interaction between antigens and lymphocytes and for organised, productive cellular or humoral responses; site for generation and residence of memory T and B cells.
• Other roles: regional lymph nodes present self antigen to lymphocytes in peripheral tolerance (lymphocytes that do not recognise it undergo anergy or apoptosis).
2. Relation to disorders
• Contact hypersensitivity: haptens are taken up by Langerhans cells that migrate to the lymph nodes and present them to CD4+ T cells, producing effector, memory and regulatory cells.
• Acute graft rejection: donor dendritic cells migrate to the lymph nodes draining the transplanted organ and stimulate a primary alloimmune response.
• Tuberculosis: dendritic cells infected with M. tuberculosis migrate to the draining mediastinal lymph nodes and activate CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
• Serum sickness includes lymphadenopathy.
3. Spread and functional deficit
• Because nodes connect to blood and lymphatic vessels, cells primed there (effector and memory T cells) return to the tissues: after sensitisation in contact hypersensitivity, later skin exposure recruits effector T cells and monocytes to the skin, giving eczematous inflammation.
• Tuberculin reaction: T cells are recruited and activated to secrete IFN-gamma, activating macrophages to make TNF-alpha and IL-1, which act on dermal endothelium to recruit leukocytes to the skin site.
• In serum sickness the systemic immune complex disease involves fever, malaise, skin eruptions, arthralgia, leukopenia, lymphadenopathy and albuminuria.
• A general mechanism by which lymph node disease spreads: not covered in the document.
questions.question:
1. Describe the structure and functional organisation of the lymph node under the following headings: classification, structure and connections, cellular content, functions in antigen encounter and immune response, and memory.
2. State how its parts relate to common immunological disorders.
3. Explain why the disorder may spread to distant tissues or systems and cause functional deficit.

1. Describe mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) under the following headings: classification, components and sites, cellular content, and functions.
2. Explain the clinical basis of why dysfunction of mucosal and humoral defence makes a patient more vulnerable to particular infections or diseases.
3. Distinguish between MALT and the lymph node.
questions.answerText:
1. MALT
• Classification: secondary (peripheral) lymphoid tissue, a group of organised lymphoid tissues protecting the mucosal membranes lining the digestive, respiratory and urogenital systems.
• Components: Peyer's patches, appendix, tonsils and adenoids, and isolated lymphoid follicles (ILFs) in the intestine; also bronchus-associated (BALT), nasal-associated (NALT) and gut-associated (GALT) lymphoid tissues.
• Cellular content: large numbers of B cells, plasma cells (exceeding those of the spleen, lymph nodes and bone marrow combined), activated T cells and macrophages.
• Functions: important defence system against infection at epithelial layers.
2. Clinical basis
• Humoral immunodeficiencies produce recurrent or chronic gastrointestinal infection, which can cause malabsorption and malnutrition.
• IgA, found in the gastrointestinal tract and other secretions, prevents microbial binding to epithelia; in gastrointestinal allergic diseases the lack of SIgA protein hydrolase leaves undigested protein allergen, giving food allergies.
• A named MALT disorder: not covered in the document.
3. MALT versus lymph node
• MALT: diffuse and organised tissue beneath the digestive, respiratory and urogenital mucosae; contains more plasma cells than spleen, lymph nodes and bone marrow combined; defends epithelial surfaces.
• Lymph node: bean-shaped, encapsulated structure of lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells connected to blood and lymphatic vessels; the first to meet antigens entering tissue spaces; the most specialised secondary lymphoid organ for regulating immune responses; site for generation and residence of memory T and B cells.

questions.question:
1. Describe the structure and functional organisation of the immune complex and the system that clears it from the circulation under the following headings: formation of the antigen-antibody lattice, complement, macrophages and Fc/C3b receptors, red blood cells and the reticuloendothelial system.
2. State how its parts relate to common immunological disorders.
3. Explain why immune complex disease may spread to distant tissues or systems and cause functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Immune complexes and their clearance
• Formation: antigen-antibody (immune) complexes form when antibody binds antigen; each Ig molecule can combine with 2 identical antigens through its Fab region, and soluble antigen molecules are cross-linked by antibody into a lattice; type III reactions involve intermediate-sized complexes of primed antibody and free antigen.
• Complement: the Fc region of antigen-bound antibody activates complement and forms C3b, which aids efficient removal of complexes; classical pathway activation inhibits formation of precipitating complexes and the alternative pathway solubilises complexes already formed, so large lattices and their deposition in tissues are avoided.
• Macrophages: have surface receptors for C3b and the Fc region of antibody; through them, macrophages in the spleen engulf and degrade circulating complexes.
• Red blood cells and liver: complexes bind to RBC CR1 complement receptors, and reticuloendothelial cells in the liver (Kupffer cells) strip the complexes from the RBCs.
2. Relation to disorders
• Complexes are not harmful while in circulation; damage occurs when they deposit in tissues and activate complement, drawing in neutrophils and monocytes that release proteases and enzymes.
• Factors favouring deposition: size (larger complexes are more easily removed), charge, valency of antigen, avidity of antibody, affinity of antigen for tissue components, lattice structure, inefficient clearance and a compromised phagocytic system.
• Diseases: Arthus reaction, serum sickness, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, malaria, dengue haemorrhagic fever, and farmers' lung and pigeon breeder's disease; serum complement falls in the active phase.
3. Spread and functional deficit
• Circulating complexes may deposit in different tissues: synovial membrane of joints (arthritis), the glomerular basement membrane of the kidney (glomerulonephritis), and blood vessels of the skin and other organs (vasculitis).
• The site differs by disease: in SLE mainly the renal glomeruli (75% of patients have nephritis, granular deposits) and other organs including joints, skin, heart, lungs and brain; in rheumatoid arthritis the joints, sparing the kidneys.
• Infections with continued antibody production form circulating complexes that deposit in tissues, for example malarial parasite-antibody complexes in the kidney in chronic P. falciparum infection.
• Deposited complexes attract neutrophils that cannot engulf them and release enzymes and oxygen radicals; platelets clot and plug small vessels, may cause haemorrhage on bursting, and release growth factor that may cause the cellular proliferation seen in rheumatoid arthritis and lupus nephritis.
• Serum sickness features fever, malaise, skin eruptions, arthralgia, leukopenia, lymphadenopathy and albuminuria.

questions.question:
1. Describe the natural killer (NK) cell under the following headings: place in immunity, recognition of target cells, mechanisms of killing, and regulation by cytokines and antibody.
2. Explain the clinical basis of why impaired NK cell function makes a patient more vulnerable to particular diseases.
3. Distinguish between the NK cell and the cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL).
questions.answerText:
1. Natural killer cell
• Place in immunity: a specialised cell of innate (natural, non-specific) immunity.
• Recognition of target cells: tumoricidal activity is believed to relate to decreased expression of MHC class I on tumour cells; all normal nucleated cells express plenty of MHC class I, so NK cells do not lyse normal cells; virus-infected cells and many transformed cells down-regulate or lose MHC class I and are therefore destroyed by NK cells.
• Killing: NK cells release cytotoxic factors and perforins that puncture holes in tumour cells, leading to their death; through Fc receptors they mediate antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), conferring antigen specificity on these otherwise non-specific cells.
• Regulation: IL-2 and IFN-gamma produced by helper T cells in response to tumour augment NK activity; lymphokine-activated killer (LAK) cells generated by IL-2 are more than 90% NK cells.
2. Clinical basis
• In Chediak-Higashi syndrome there is marked impairment of NK cells and an associated increase in the incidence of certain types of cancer.
• Rejection of tumours by animals seems to be mediated primarily by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.
3. NK cell versus CTL
• NK cell: innate; killing is related to reduced MHC class I on the target; kills with cytotoxic factors and perforins; augmented by IL-2 and IFN-gamma; ADCC through Fc receptors.
• CTL (Tc cell): CD8+ T cell of adaptive immunity; its TCR recognises MHC class I-antigen peptide complexes on the target; activation needs three signals (TCR binding to MHC class I-viral antigen, IL-2 from nearby activated TH cells, and CD28-B7); kills by perforin and granzymes (granzymes enter through perforin pores and activate caspase, leading to apoptosis) and by Fas ligand binding Fas on the target; destroys virus-infected cells, cancer cells and cells of a transplanted organ from an HLA-unrelated donor.
