questions.question: Which condition is characterized by paresthesia in median nerve distribution?
questions.explanation: is characterized by paresthesia in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of ring finger). Symptoms are often worse at night and may be relieved by shaking the hand. The condition results from median nerve compression within the carpal tunnel.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the hepatoduodenal ligament's free edge?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa, the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum) contains the portal triad: portal vein (posteriorly), common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), and hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left). The relationship is remembered as "DAV" from right to left anteriorly (Duct, Artery, Vein). This ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen and is the structure compressed during the Pringle maneuver to control bleeding during hepatic surgery. Lymph nodes and autonomic nerve plexuses also course through this ligament.

The mental foramen is typically located on the lateral surface of the mandible below the second premolar tooth or between the first and second premolars. It transmits the mental nerve and vessels (terminal branches of the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle). The foramen position varies with age and tooth loss. It is a landmark for inferior alveolar nerve block.
questions.question: The mental foramen typically lies below which tooth?

questions.explanation: Superficial and deep parotid lymph nodes lie within or on the parotid gland substance. They drain the scalp, auricle, external acoustic meatus, and parotid gland itself. Efferents pass to the superficial and deep cervical nodes. The presence of lymph nodes within the gland complicates parotid tumor surgery and influences surgical planning.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the parotid gland?
The os coxae (pelvic bone) is formed by the fusion of three bones. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The os coxae is formed by the fusion of three bones: the ilium, ischium, and pubis. They meet at the Y-shaped cartilage in the acetabulum, which fuses at approximately age 15-17 years. The acetabulum receives contributions from all three bones, though it is formed mainly by the ischium.

questions.question: What allows drainage from infected segments?
questions.explanation: Natural drainage from infected bronchopulmonary segments can be achieved by adopting different postures (postural drainage or chest physiotherapy). For example, to drain the apical segment of the lower lobe, the patient should lie prone with the head turned to one side, allowing gravity to assist drainage.

options: Lateral plantar nerve; adducts and flexes 1st digit
Deep fibular nerve; extends and abducts 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; abducts and flexes 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; flexes and inverts foot
questions.question: Abductor hallucis, the most medially placed first layer foot muscle, is innervated by which nerve and performs which action?
questions.explanation: Abductor hallucis is innervated by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3) and performs abduction and flexion of the first digit (hallux). It originates from the medial tubercle of the calcaneal tuberosity, the flexor retinaculum, and plantar aponeurosis. It inserts into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit.

The ureter has three normal anatomical constrictions where renal calculi commonly lodge: at the pelviureteric junction (ureteropelvic junction, where renal pelvis transitions to ureter), where it crosses the pelvic brim (over the bifurcation of the common iliac artery), and at the ureterovesical junction (as it passes obliquely through the bladder wall). These constrictions appear on imaging studies and during ureteroscopy. Additional functional constrictions may occur where the ureter crosses vessels (testicular/ovarian in abdomen, uterine artery in females). Understanding these sites helps predict where stones will impact and cause obstruction.
questions.question: The ureter is constricted at which locations?
What is the functional significance of the olecranon-coronoid architecture?
questions.explanation: The olecranon fits into the olecranon fossa during extension while the coronoid fits into the coronoid fossa during flexion. This reciprocal architecture allows full range elbow motion (0-150�) while providing bony stability. The radial fossa accommodates the radial head during flexion.

The cisterna chyli is located to the right of the abdominal aorta at the L1-L2 vertebral level, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. This dilated lymphatic sac receives the right and left lumbar lymphatic trunks, intestinal trunk, and sometimes lower intercostal trunks before giving rise to the thoracic duct. The cisterna lies anterior to the vertebral bodies and posterior to the aorta, in the retroperitoneal space. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus (crossing from right to left in the thorax) to drain into the venous system.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli lies to which side of the aorta?

questions.explanation: Thoracic outlet syndrome results from compression of nerves (brachial plexus) or vessels (subclavian artery/vein) at the superior aperture of the thorax. Causes include cervical rib, abnormal first rib, scalene muscle abnormalities, or trauma. Symptoms include arm pain, paresthesias, and vascular changes.
questions.question: Which condition compresses structures at thoracic inlet?

questions.explanation: The deep circumflex iliac artery arises from the external iliac artery (just above the inguinal ligament, near the origin of the inferior epigastric artery), not from the abdominal aorta. It runs laterally along the inguinal ligament and iliac crest, supplying the lower abdominal wall muscles. The abdominal aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (inferior phrenic, suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac, SMA, IMA), paired parietal branches (four lumbar arteries), and the unpaired median sacral artery posteriorly, before bifurcating into right and left common iliac arteries at L4 level.
questions.question: Which artery typically does NOT arise from the abdominal aorta?

questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends laterally and slightly superiorly, reaching to within 1 cm of the splenic hilum in approximately 75% of individuals, lying within the splenorenal ligament along with the splenic artery and vein. This relationship is surgically significant during splenectomy, as the pancreatic tail must be identified and preserved to prevent iatrogenic pancreatitis or pancreatic fistula. The body of the pancreas lies anterior to the splenic vein (which runs along its posterior surface) and behind the posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa), separated from it by the gastrosplenic ligament.
questions.question: The tail of the pancreas extends into which ligament?

questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is the most critical structure at risk from a popliteal abscess. Compression of the popliteal artery can cause limb-threatening ischaemia of the leg and foot. A popliteal aneurysm similarly presents as a pulsatile mass and carries risk of thrombosis or rupture. The close proximity of the popliteal artery to the joint capsule and fossa floor makes it vulnerable.
questions.question: Popliteal abscesses present as swellings in the popliteal fossa. Which structure, if compressed by the abscess, produces the most serious vascular complication?
At which constriction does aortic arch cross?
questions.explanation: The second constriction is where the aortic arch lies anterior to the esophagus (22 cm from incisors, T4 level). The third is where the left main bronchus crosses anteriorly (27 cm from incisors). The fourth is at the diaphragmatic hiatus (38-40 cm from incisors, T10 level).

A hip pointer is a contusion of the iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), resulting from a direct blow in contact sports such as American football. It is extremely painful due to the multiple muscle attachments in this area. Tensor fasciae latae and sartorius originate from the ASIS and iliac crest respectively. Treatment is ice, NSAIDs, and activity modification.
options: Anterior superior iliac spine and iliac crest
questions.question: The 'hip pointer' is a contusion of which anatomical structure, common in contact sports?
What is the smallest independently resectable lung unit?
questions.explanation: The bronchopulmonary segment is the smallest part of the lung that can be surgically removed without affecting adjacent regions. Each segment has its own tertiary bronchus, arterial supply, and venous drainage. Segmentectomy preserves more lung tissue than lobectomy while treating localized disease.

options: They become lax to allow free extension
questions.question: During extension of the hip joint, the three extracapsular ligaments behave in which manner due to their spiral orientation?
questions.explanation: The fibers of all three extracapsular hip ligaments are oriented in a spiral fashion around the hip joint, causing them to become taut when the joint is extended. This stabilizes the joint in standing and reduces the amount of muscle energy required to maintain upright posture, demonstrating an important energy-conserving mechanism in bipedal locomotion.

questions.question: The sphenoid sinus drains into which location?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinuses drain into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. These sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid bone and vary greatly in size. Close relationship to the optic nerve and carotid artery makes sphenoid surgery particularly challenging.

Gracilis is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest member of the adductor group. It is the only member to cross both the hip and knee joints. Its tendon joins sartorius and semitendinosus at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia. It is used as a donor muscle in gracilis free flap reconstructive surgery due to its consistent anatomy.
questions.question: Which is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest muscle of the adductor group, uniquely crossing both hip and knee joints?
Which artery supplies the anterior nasal septum superiorly?
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) descends through the anterior ethmoidal foramen to supply the anterior superior nasal septum and lateral nasal wall. It anastomoses with branches of the sphenopalatine artery posteriorly. The artery also supplies the anterior ethmoidal cells and contributes to the blood supply of the frontal sinus.

questions.question: Which structure is derived from the ventral mesentery?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament (and lesser omentum) develops from the ventral mesentery, while the greater omentum, splenorenal ligament, gastrosplenic ligament, and transverse mesocolon all derive from the dorsal mesentery. The ventral mesentery, present only in the region of the foregut, gives rise to the falciform ligament (connecting liver to anterior abdominal wall), the lesser omentum (connecting liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum), and the coronary and triangular ligaments (connecting liver to diaphragm). The liver and gallbladder develop within the ventral mesentery, explaining their peritoneal relationships.

questions.question: The non-articular portion of the acetabulum (acetabular fossa) is formed mainly by which bone and contains what?
options: Ischium; loose connective tissue and fat
questions.explanation: The acetabular fossa is the non-articular part of the acetabulum, formed mainly by the ischium. It contains loose connective tissue and a pad of fat. The articular surface is the horseshoe-shaped lunate surface covered by hyaline cartilage. The fossa is deficient inferiorly at the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.

The tensor tympani muscle tenses the tympanic membrane by pulling the malleus medially. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3). The muscle arises from the Eustachian tube and bony canal above it. Contraction dampens excessive vibrations and reduces sensitivity to low-frequency sounds. It works synergistically with stapedius.
questions.question: Which muscle tenses the tympanic membrane?
The tensor tympani muscle arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle arises from the cartilaginous part of the Eustachian tube and the bony canal above it. The muscle runs in a bony canal parallel to the Eustachian tube. Its tendon turns laterally around the processus cochleariformis to insert on the malleus. Contraction tenses the tympanic membrane.

questions.question: Which neurovascular structure is the DEEPEST within the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint. This proximity makes the popliteal artery particularly vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures. The arrangement from deep to superficial is: artery, vein, then tibial nerve.

questions.question: Which structure lies in both superior and middle mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves pass through both the superior and middle mediastinum as they descend from the neck to the diaphragm. Similarly, the superior vena cava lies in both regions. The thymus extends from superior to anterior mediastinum. Structures can span multiple mediastinal compartments.

questions.question: Which lymph node is found in the femoral canal?
questions.explanation: Cloquet's node (node of Rosenmuller) is the most superior of the deep inguinal lymph nodes, located in the femoral canal (femoral ring) and receives lymph from the superficial and deep inguinal nodes. It drains to the external iliac nodes. The femoral canal is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath (lateral to the lacunar ligament, medial to the femoral vein) and represents a potential weakness where femoral hernias occur. Virchow's node is in the left supraclavicular fossa, Sister Mary Joseph node at the umbilicus, and Calot's node in Calot's triangle.

questions.question: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to changes in which substance?
questions.explanation: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to decreased arterial oxygen (hypoxemia), increased carbon dioxide (hypercapnia), and decreased pH (acidosis). It is located at the carotid bifurcation and is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) monitors blood pressure changes.

The right lung contains ten bronchopulmonary segments: three in the upper lobe (apical, posterior, anterior), two in the middle lobe (lateral, medial), and five in the lower lobe (superior/apical, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal). Each segment is functionally independent.
questions.question: How many bronchopulmonary segments exist in right lung?
What is the effect of diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction causes the muscle to descend (central tendon is relatively fixed by the pericardium and IVC), increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrathoracic pressure (creating negative pressure that draws air in). Simultaneously, abdominal volume decreases and intra-abdominal pressure increases, displacing abdominal viscera downward and forward. The diaphragm is responsible for about 75% of the work of quiet breathing.

The anteroposterior dimension is increased by the "pump handle" movement of the true ribs (2-7), which pushes the sternum upward and forward. This occurs during inspiration. The bucket handle movement of ribs 7-10 increases the lateral dimension, while diaphragm descent increases the vertical dimension.
questions.question: What increases the anteroposterior thoracic dimension?

questions.explanation: The external intercostal muscle is the most superficial intercostal muscle with fibers directed downward and forward. It extends from the rib tubercle posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly. The muscle is deficient anteriorly where it is replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane.
questions.question: Which muscle fibers are directed downward and forward?

questions.explanation: The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of C4, corresponding to the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) and carotid body (chemoreceptor) are located at this bifurcation. Carotid endarterectomy is performed at this crucial anatomical location.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the common carotid artery typically bifurcate?
How does the ulnar nerve's path make it vulnerable to injury?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is vulnerable at two main sites: posterior to the medial epicondyle where it's subcutaneous and easily traumatized (cubital tunnel), and at the wrist in Guyon's canal. At both locations, the nerve lies in confined spaces with minimal soft tissue protection.
options: Superficial at medial epicondyle and Guyon canal
Runs in a deep and well-protected anatomical position

questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli), a dilated lymphatic sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, is located anterior to the bodies of L1 and L2 vertebrae, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm and the abdominal aorta, and to the right of the aorta. It receives the right and left lumbar lymphatic trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvic, and abdominal walls), the intestinal trunk (from pre-aortic nodes draining abdominal viscera), and sometimes the lower intercostal trunks. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to enter the posterior mediastinum, ultimately draining into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli is located at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The regional lymph node is defined as the lymph node where lymph from an organ or body part drains to firstly. This is distinct from the sentinel lymph node, which is the first node to receive drainage from a tumor. Understanding this distinction is important for staging cancer and planning surgical interventions.
questions.question: Which lymph node receives drainage first from an organ?
The pes anserinus is located on the medial surface of the tibia. Pes anserinus bursitis presents with pain at which specific location?
questions.explanation: Pes anserinus bursitis presents with pain, swelling, and tenderness at the medial aspect of the tibia, approximately 5-7 cm below the knee joint line, at the common insertion of sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus. It is common in obese patients with knee osteoarthritis and is associated with valgus knee deformity. Treatment includes local steroid injection and physiotherapy.
options: Lateral tibial plateau of the knee
Tibial tuberosity on the anterior tibia
Posterior aspect of the medial knee
Lateral joint line of the knee
Medial tibia, 5�7 cm below the knee joint line

questions.explanation: The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus at its termination. It drains the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum, corresponding to the territory of the posterior interventricular artery. It is the second largest cardiac vein.
questions.question: Where does the middle cardiac vein run?
The aditus ad antrum connects which two structures?
questions.explanation: The aditus ad antrum is an opening in the posterior wall of the epitympanic recess that connects the middle ear cavity with the mastoid antrum. Middle ear infections can spread to the mastoid air cells through this passage causing mastoiditis. The roof of the aditus is the tegmen tympani.

The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid arteries. At the base of the neck, it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. The vein receives the facial, lingual, pharyngeal, and thyroid veins.
questions.question: Which vein forms the continuation of the sigmoid sinus?
The dorsum of the foot receives cutaneous innervation from several nerves. Which nerve supplies the skin between the 1st and 2nd toes on the dorsum?
questions.explanation: The deep fibular nerve supplies the skin of the first web space (between the 1st and 2nd toes) on the dorsum of the foot. The superficial fibular nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot. The saphenous nerve supplies the medial side (first metatarsal area), while the sural nerve supplies the lateral side (digiti minimi area). This pattern is important in assessing nerve injuries.

The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. It has a side of danger (medial side, closer to the ischial tuberosity) and a side of safety (lateral side). The quadratus femoris forms a protective muscular layer over the nerve as it passes posterior to the hip joint.
questions.question: The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) curves downward at which position between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter?
Which nerve provides motor innervation to the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5 - "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provides the entire motor innervation to the diaphragm, including both muscular portions and central tendon. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Although the lower six intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12) provide sensory innervation to the peripheral parts of the diaphragm, they contribute no motor supply. Damage to one phrenic nerve causes paralysis of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, which appears elevated on chest radiograph. Bilateral phrenic nerve injury severely compromises respiratory function, particularly in supine position.

The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas, cul-de-sac) is the peritoneal reflection between the uterus anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly, representing the most inferior extent of the peritoneal cavity in females (approximately 5.5 cm from the anus and 7.5 cm from the vaginal orifice). It is bounded laterally by the uterosacral ligaments and can be accessed through the posterior vaginal fornix for drainage of pelvic abscesses (culdocentesis) or laparoscopic procedures. Fluid, blood, or pus in the peritoneal cavity gravitates to this pouch in supine or standing positions, making it clinically significant.
questions.question: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) lies between which structures?

questions.explanation: assesses ulnar artery patency before radial artery cannulation or harvesting. Both arteries are occluded, the hand is opened (blanched), then ulnar pressure is released. Color should return within 5-15 seconds indicating adequate ulnar collateral circulation. Failure indicates insufficient ulnar supply making radial artery intervention unsafe.
questions.question: Which test assesses ulnar artery patency before radial artery cannulation?

options: They allow free rotation between tibia and fibula
They maintain tibiofibular mortise integrity for stable talus articulation
They create the lateral wall of the ankle
They only protect the interosseous vessels
They provide primary stability against valgus stress
questions.explanation: The tibiofibular ligament (syndesmosis) and interosseous membrane maintain the integrity of the tibiofibular mortise, ensuring that the distal tibia and fibula remain properly spaced for stable articulation with the trochlea tali. Disruption of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain or Maisonneuve fracture) significantly destabilizes the ankle joint and requires surgical fixation.
questions.question: The tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane form part of the ankle joint supports. These structures maintain which relationship between the tibia and fibula at the ankle?
Which muscle is paralyzed causing winged scapula?
questions.explanation: Paralysis of serratus anterior causes scapular winging due to weakness of the most powerful scapular protractor. The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies this muscle. Winging becomes more apparent when pushing against resistance, as the medial border lifts away from the chest wall.

The risorius muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally, producing a grin or grimace. It arises from the parotid fascia and inserts into the angle of the mouth. The muscle is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It works with zygomaticus major in smiling. Some individuals lack this muscle.
questions.question: Which muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally?

questions.explanation: The median nerve is the only nerve passing through the carpal tunnel. It enters the hand between the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and lies anterior to the flexor digitorum profundus tendons. Compression of this nerve within the tunnel causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: The thenar space can readily spread infection into the connective tissue canals surrounding the lumbricals. Proximally, the thenar space communicates with the space of Parona. Distally, it is continuous with lumbrical canals, which then connect to web spaces, providing routes for infection spread.
questions.question: Which space infection can spread to lumbrical canals?

questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is most vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures because it runs closest to the posterior joint capsule. Posterior dislocation puts direct traction on the artery and can cause intimal tear or complete transection. Assessment of distal pulses (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial) is mandatory after knee dislocation before any reduction attempt.
questions.question: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa and is most vulnerable in which clinical scenario?
options: Knee joint effusion without ligament injury
Posterior knee dislocation and tibial plateau fractures

questions.explanation: "Student's elbow" is olecranon bursitis resulting from repetitive pressure and trauma to the posterior elbow while leaning on desks. The subcutaneous olecranon bursa becomes inflamed and swollen. The same condition in coal miners is called "miner's elbow" due to similar repetitive trauma.
questions.question: What causes student's elbow?

options: Medial condyle of the tibia proximally
Inferior lateral supracondylar line and oblique popliteal ligament
questions.explanation: Plantaris originates from the inferior end of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur and the oblique popliteal ligament. It inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon together with gastrocnemius and soleus. Its long slender tendon can be mistaken for a nerve during surgery and is used in tendon repair surgery due to its length.
questions.question: Plantaris, a vestigial muscle, inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon. From which specific femoral site does it originate?

questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the stomach lies anterior to the body of the pancreas, separated by the lesser sac (omental bursa). The anterior surface of the pancreatic body is covered by the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the lesser sac. This relationship is clinically important as pancreatic disease can cause epigastric pain.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the body of the pancreas?
Which flexure of the colon is located at a higher position?
questions.explanation: The splenic (left colic) flexure is positioned higher than the hepatic (right colic) flexure and also forms a more acute angle. The splenic flexure is attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament. This higher position of the left flexure is clinically significant in colonoscopy and surgical procedures.

questions.question: Which hormone is produced by the pancreatic alpha cells?
questions.explanation: Glucagon is produced by alpha cells in the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) and increases blood glucose by promoting hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. It opposes insulin action. Glucagon secretion is stimulated by low blood glucose, amino acids, and sympathetic stimulation. Alpha cells constitute about 20% of islet cells and are located peripherally in the islets.

questions.question: In bones with epiphyses at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from which structure?
questions.explanation: When a bone has an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes captured this in the mnemonic 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee,' indicating the direction of nutrient arteries in the humerus and lower limb bones respectively.

The superior laryngeal artery (from superior thyroid artery) accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane. Together they supply the supraglottic larynx. The artery anastomoses with the contralateral vessel and with the cricothyroid artery. Damage during surgery can cause hematoma or bleeding.
questions.question: The superior laryngeal artery accompanies which nerve?

questions.explanation: The root (origin) of the mesentery is approximately 15 cm long, extending obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction. Despite this short root attachment, the mesentery fans out to accommodate the 5-6 meters of small bowel. The root crosses the third part of the duodenum, aorta, IVC, right psoas muscle, and right gonadal vessels.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of the mesentery root attachment?
Which muscle is NOT supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve?
questions.explanation: is supplied by the median nerve, not the musculocutaneous nerve. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies only three muscles: biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis (BBC). After supplying these muscles, it continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.question: Which carpal bones form the medial side of the carpal arch base?
questions.explanation: The medial side of the carpal arch base is formed by the pisiform bone and the hook of the hamate. The lateral side is formed by the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium bones. The flexor retinaculum bridges across this arch, converting it into the carpal tunnel.

questions.question: The sphenoid sinus relates posteriorly to which structure?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinus lies within the body of the sphenoid with the clivus and pons posterior to it. The pituitary fossa is superior, and the cavernous sinuses with internal carotid arteries are lateral. The optic chiasm lies superiorly. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses the fossa through the sphenoid sinus.

questions.question: Which part of the stomach is most anterior?
questions.explanation: The body of the stomach is the most anterior part, lying against the anterior abdominal wall in the epigastric region when the stomach is empty. The fundus extends superiorly and posteriorly beneath the left dome of the diaphragm, while the pyloric antrum angles to the right and posteriorly. The stomach's position varies with body position, respiratory phase, and degree of filling. When distended, the stomach extends inferiorly and the greater curvature becomes more anterior. The anterior surface is related to the diaphragm, anterior abdominal wall, left lobe of liver, and anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question: The quadriceps tendon continues as which structure, with the patella embedded within it, attaching to the tibial tuberosity?
questions.explanation: The tendons of the four quadriceps components unite to form the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament (also called patellar tendon) with the patella embedded within as a sesamoid bone. This inserts into the tibial tuberosity. The patellar retinacula are aponeurotic expansions that provide additional lateral stability.

The lingual artery is a branch of the external carotid artery arising at the level of the hyoid bone. It supplies the tongue through dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The artery passes deep to the hyoglossus muscle, which serves as a key surgical landmark.
questions.question: The lingual artery typically arises from which parent vessel?

options: Stabilize the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint
Prevent rotation of sacrum by vertebral column weight
Form the greater sciatic foramen with bones
Transmit the obturator nerve to the medial thigh
Form the lesser sciatic foramen with bones
questions.explanation: The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments stabilize the sacrum, prevent its rotation under body weight, and form both sciatic foramina together with bones. They do not transmit the obturator nerve, which exits through the obturator foramen to supply the medial compartment of the thigh via its anterior and posterior divisions.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments?

questions.explanation: The epitympanic recess (attic) is the upper part of the tympanic cavity above the level of the tympanic membrane. It contains the head of the malleus and body of the incus. The recess communicates posteriorly with the mastoid antrum via the aditus ad antrum. Cholesteatomas commonly develop in this region.
questions.question: The epitympanic recess contains which structure?
The aortic bifurcation occurs at which surface landmark?
questions.explanation: The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta into right and left common iliac arteries at the L4 vertebral level corresponds to a point on the anterior abdominal wall slightly below and to the left of the umbilicus (which lies at L3/L4 disc level). This surface marking is clinically useful for palpating the aorta and detecting abdominal aortic aneurysms. The bifurcation point can be located by drawing imaginary lines from the umbilicus toward the midinguinal points (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis) on each side. The median sacral artery arises from the posterior aspect of the aorta just before its bifurcation.

The cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper oesophageal sphincter and creates the first physiological constriction at 15 cm from the upper incisors. This sphincter prevents air from entering the oesophagus during respiration and regulates food entry. It is a clinically significant site for foreign body impaction and stricture formation.
questions.question: Which structure causes the first constriction of the oesophagus at 15 cm from the upper incisor teeth?

questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle. Compression at this site causes posterior interosseous syndrome with weakness of finger and thumb extensors but preserved wrist extension. The superficial branch of the radial nerve does not pass through supinator.
questions.question: What nerve passes through the supinator muscle?

questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) enters the transverse mesocolon and divides into right and left branches that supply the transverse colon. The right branch anastomoses with the right colic artery (from SMA), while the left branch anastomoses with the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric artery), forming the marginal artery of Drummond at the splenic flexure. This anastomotic connection between SMA and IMA territories provides important collateral circulation. Variation in the middle colic artery is common; occasionally it may be absent or arise as two separate vessels.
questions.question: The middle colic artery divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch that extends from the tip of the transverse process of L1 to the 12th rib, arching over the quadratus lumborum muscle. It provides attachment for some of the muscular fibers of the diaphragm. The subcostal nerve (T12) and vessels pass deep to this ligament.
questions.question: Over which muscle does the lateral arcuate ligament arch?
Which layer of the appendix contains abundant lymphoid tissue?
questions.explanation: The appendix has abundant lymphoid follicles in both the lamina propria and submucosa, unlike other parts of the intestine where lymphoid tissue is confined to the lamina propria. These follicles often extend into the submucosa, sometimes obliterating the clear boundary between layers. The appendix functions as a component of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT).

The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) is the obliterated umbilical vein that runs in the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. It joins the left branch of the portal vein at the inferior end of the fissure for the ligamentum teres. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, forming caput medusae.
questions.question: Which structure forms the falciform ligament's free edge?
The incisive foramen transmits which nerve?
questions.explanation: The incisive foramen (canal) in the anterior hard palate transmits the nasopalatine nerves, which provide sensation to the anterior palate. The foramen also transmits terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. The nasopalatine nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve via the pterygopalatine ganglion.

The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and provides primary passive support. The stylomandibular ligament is merely a thickening of the parotid capsule and contributes minimally to joint support. Other ligaments provide secondary stabilization or perform different mechanical functions in the temporomandibular complex.
questions.question: Which structure forms the primary passive support of the mandible?

questions.explanation: The anterior arch of the atlas (C1) has a facet on its posterior surface that articulates with the dens (odontoid process) of the axis (C2). The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against this facet. This atlantoaxial joint allows rotation of the head. Fracture or ligamentous injury can cause atlantoaxial instability.
questions.question: The anterior arch of C1 articulates with which structure?

questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is the most important dynamic supporter of the medial longitudinal arch, actively preventing excessive pronation during stance phase. It eccentrically controls subtalar eversion during heel strike, then concentrically re-inverts and supinates the foot at push-off. Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction leads to progressive flatfoot with excessive pronation, and is the most common cause of adult acquired flatfoot.
questions.question: Which muscle, by supporting the medial longitudinal arch, prevents excessive pronation of the foot during the stance phase of gait?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct terminates by draining into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Before termination, it receives the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal lymph trunks. The duct has no valve at its termination.
questions.question: Where does the thoracic duct terminate?
What nerve supplies the dorsal interossei muscles?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all interossei muscles (both dorsal and palmar). The deep branch of the ulnar nerve enters the palm and curves around the hook of the hamate to supply these intrinsic hand muscles. Ulnar nerve palsy causes weakness of finger abduction and adduction.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explanation: The posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle. The anterior border of trapezius forms the posterior boundary, and the middle third of the clavicle forms the base. The apex is where the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius meet at the superior nuchal line.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the right crus of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus is located in the muscular part of the right crus at T10. The oesophagus passes through it along with the anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal vessels, and lymphatics. Some fibers of the right crus form a sphincter around the oesophagus, contributing to prevention of gastro-oesophageal reflux. The left crus is smaller and does not have a hiatus.

questions.question: The scala tympani contains which fluid?
questions.explanation: The scala tympani (and scala vestibuli) contains perilymph, which has an ionic composition similar to extracellular fluid. The scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph with high potassium. Perilymph communicates with CSF via the cochlear aqueduct. The round window membrane separates the scala tympani from the middle ear.

The tonsillar branch of the facial artery provides the main blood supply, entering at the lower pole. Additional supply comes from ascending palatine (facial), ascending pharyngeal, dorsal lingual, and lesser palatine arteries. The paratonsillar vein descends from the soft palate across the capsule and is regularly divided during tonsillectomy.
questions.question: The palatine tonsil receives its blood supply primarily from which artery?

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) requires intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, for absorption in the terminal ileum. Intrinsic factor binds to B12, protecting it from degradation and facilitating its receptor-mediated uptake by ileal enterocytes. Lack of intrinsic factor (from parietal cell destruction in pernicious anemia or gastrectomy) causes B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.
questions.question: Which vitamin requires intrinsic factor for absorption?
Which olecranon bursa lies in subcutaneous connective tissue?
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous olecranon bursa is located in the subcutaneous connective tissue directly over the olecranon process. This bursa can become inflamed from repeated trauma, causing olecranon bursitis known as "student's elbow" or "miner's elbow." The other two bursae are the intratendinous and subtendinous types.

questions.question: Which bone of the foot articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, the navicular anteriorly, the tibia superiorly, and both malleoli laterally?
questions.explanation: The talus articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, navicular anteriorly, tibia superiorly, lateral malleolus laterally, and medial malleolus medially. This unique articulation pattern makes the talus the keystone of the hindfoot. The talus receives no direct muscle attachments and is entirely dependent on its articular surfaces and ligamentous connections.

options: Brachial artery damage and Volkmann's ischemia
questions.question: What is the primary concern in supracondylar fracture of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The primary concern in supracondylar fractures is brachial artery damage potentially leading to Volkmann's ischemic contracture. The artery lies in close proximity to the distal humerus and can be compressed or torn. This causes forearm muscle ischemia and subsequent flexion contracture if not promptly recognized and treated.

There are typically 11-12 thoracic sympathetic ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion commonly fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion to form the stellate ganglion. Each ganglion connects to its corresponding spinal nerve via gray and white rami communicantes. The ganglia are interconnected by interganglionic segments.
questions.question: How many thoracic sympathetic ganglia exist typically?
At what age does female breast development begin?
questions.explanation: Female breasts start developing at puberty under hormonal influence (estrogen and progesterone). They remain rudimentary in males throughout life. Most breast development in females occurs during the later months of pregnancy and lactation when the glandular tissue proliferates and becomes functional.

The lesser omentum extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver and consists of the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments. The hepatogastric portion specifically connects the lesser curvature to the liver. This double layer of peritoneum carries the left and right gastric vessels along the lesser curvature.
questions.question: Which ligament extends from the lesser curvature to the liver?

questions.explanation: Approximately 95% of duodenal ulcers occur in the first part of the duodenum (duodenal cap or bulb), particularly on the anterior or posterior wall. The duodenal cap is more mobile (intraperitoneal) and exposed to gastric acid without adequate protection. Posterior ulcers can erode into the gastroduodenal artery causing hemorrhage; anterior ulcers can perforate into the peritoneal cavity.
questions.question: Where do most duodenal ulcers occur?
The foramen ovale transmits which nerve?
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale in the greater wing of the sphenoid transmits the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve. It also transmits the accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein. The nerve supplies muscles of mastication and provides sensation to the mandibular region.

options: In the popliteal fossa immediately after bifurcation
In the middle third of the leg or lower popliteal region
At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa
At the ankle level near the malleolus only
Just posterior to the lateral malleolus at the ankle
questions.explanation: The sural nerve is typically formed in the middle third of the leg (or sometimes in the lower popliteal fossa) when the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve) unites with the sural communicating branch (from the common fibular nerve). It then descends to pass posterior to the lateral malleolus and supply the lateral side of the leg, ankle, and lateral heel. Its predictable course makes it valuable for nerve grafting.
questions.question: The medial sural cutaneous nerve and the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve unite to form the sural nerve. At what level does this union typically occur?
What muscle action is lost in Saturday night palsy?
questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy results from radial nerve compression in the axilla, causing paralysis of wrist and finger extensors. This produces the characteristic "wrist drop" deformity. The condition is named for arm compression against a chair back during intoxicated sleep.

options: At the level of the fibular head proximally
In the lower third of the leg by piercing the deep fascia
At the level of the ankle joint and mortise
In the popliteal fossa at the posterior aspect of the knee
At the level of the medial malleolus medially
questions.question: The superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies the lateral compartment of the leg. Where does it emerge as a cutaneous nerve?
questions.explanation: The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment, then pierces the deep fascia in the lower third of the leg to become cutaneous. It supplies most of the dorsum of the foot and toes (except the first web space, supplied by the deep fibular nerve, and the lateral border, supplied by the sural nerve).

questions.question: Which space lies between the vocal and vestibular folds?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal ventricle (sinus of Morgagni) is a space between the true vocal fold below and the false vocal fold (vestibular fold) above. It extends laterally into the saccule, which contains mucous glands that lubricate the vocal cords. The lateral wall is formed by the thyroid cartilage.

The median nerve is at risk in supracondylar fractures of the humerus, along with the brachial artery. These injuries are common in children from falls on outstretched hands. Nerve damage can cause loss of thumb opposition and sensation in the lateral three and one-half fingers.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in supracondylar fractures of the humerus?

questions.explanation: The obturator internus tendon exits through the lesser sciatic foramen, turns nearly 90 degrees around the smooth lesser sciatic notch (using the ischium as a pulley), and then inserts into the upper border of the greater trochanter of the femur. The gemelli muscles (superior and inferior) arise from the edges of the lesser sciatic notch and merge with the obturator internus tendon, acting as its 'cheeks.'
questions.question: The obturator internus exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen. Where does its tendon turn to insert?
options: Directly into the lesser trochanter of the proximal femur
Into the ischial tuberosity rather than into the trochanter
Into the rim of the acetabulum directly without turning
Turns 90� around the ischium then inserts into the greater trochanter's upper border
Into the trochanteric fossa on the medial femur

questions.explanation: The anterior surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, which is broad and rough and serves as attachment for the iliofemoral ligament. The posterior aspect carries the prominent intertrochanteric crest. These landmarks delineate the intracapsular portion of the femoral neck.
questions.question: Which surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, a broad rough area that is the attachment for the iliofemoral ligament?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle in the ulnar groove, making it vulnerable to injury in medial epicondyle fractures. Damage causes numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and weakness of intrinsic hand muscles. This can result in claw hand deformity.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in medial epicondyle fractures?

questions.explanation: Houston's third transverse rectal fold is the most constant and prominent, located at the level of S5 vertebra, approximately 5 cm above the anus. If this fold completely encircles the rectum, it is called Nelaton's sphincter. This fold divides the rectum into an upper chamber (containing the pre-allantoic part of the hindgut that can hold feces without triggering the defecation reflex) and a lower chamber (derived from the post-allantoic cloaca that is sensitive to distension). The fold helps support the weight of feces and prevents passage during instrumentation.
questions.question: Houston's third valve in the rectum is located at which vertebral level?
In compartment syndrome of the anterior leg compartment, which muscle is affected first, causing which specific neurological deficit?
questions.explanation: Anterior compartment syndrome initially affects the tibialis anterior and the deep fibular nerve running within the compartment. Early symptoms include foot dorsiflexion weakness and pain on passive toe flexion (stretching the anterior compartment muscles). Paraesthesia in the first web space (deep fibular nerve territory) is an early sign. Fasciotomy within 6 hours prevents permanent muscle necrosis and nerve damage.
options: Fibularis longus; loss of foot eversion first
Soleus; first presenting as loss of plantarflexion
Extensor hallucis longus; toe extension loss first
Tibialis anterior; initial loss of dorsiflexion with deep fibular nerve symptoms
Gastrocnemius; presenting first as loss of ankle plantarflexion power

questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery as it crosses the ankle to enter the foot?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot at the ankle. It passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and contributes to the toes via the deep plantar arch.

questions.question: Which is the most superficial named structure of the major neurovascular bundle in the popliteal fossa?
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve is the most superficial structure of the major neurovascular bundle in the popliteal fossa, bisecting the fossa from superior to inferior angle. The popliteal vein lies superficial to and close to the artery in the same fibrous sheath, while the popliteal artery is the deepest. The common fibular nerve exits at the superolateral angle.

options: Foot drop and high-arched cavus foot deformity
Claw toes due to loss of intrinsic muscle balance
Equinus deformity of the ankle and hindfoot
Calcaneus deformity from chronic Achilles tendon insufficiency
questions.explanation: Posterior tibial nerve palsy causes claw foot (intrinsic minus foot) due to loss of the intrinsic muscles of the sole. Without the intrinsic muscles, the extrinsic toe flexors and extensors become unopposed, causing hyperextension at the metatarsophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints. This is analogous to the intrinsic minus hand in ulnar nerve palsy.
questions.question: Posterior tibial nerve palsy causes a specific foot deformity due to loss of intrinsic muscle function. Which deformity results?

questions.explanation: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels, tail of the pancreas, and associated lymph nodes. The tail of the pancreas extends into this ligament to reach the splenic hilum. This ligament represents a portion of the dorsal mesogastrium.
questions.question: What structures pass through the splenorenal ligament?
Where is Griffiths' point located?
questions.explanation: Griffiths' point is the watershed area at the splenic flexure where the superior mesenteric artery territory (via the middle colic artery) meets the inferior mesenteric artery territory (via the left colic artery). This area has the poorest collateral circulation and is most vulnerable to ischemia in low-flow states. It is a common site for ischemic colitis.

The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle layer forming the bladder wall and consists of three poorly defined layers: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. During bladder filling, the detrusor relaxes; during micturition, it contracts to expel urine. The detrusor is innervated by parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnic nerves S2-4) for contraction.
questions.question: What muscle forms the bladder wall?
Which cells produce insulin in the pancreas?
questions.explanation: Beta cells comprise about 70% of pancreatic islet cells and are located centrally within the islets. They produce and secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose, amino acids, and incretin hormones (GLP-1, GIP). Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, making it the primary hormone for lowering blood glucose. Beta cell destruction or dysfunction causes diabetes mellitus.

questions.question: A fracture of the neck of femur characteristically produces which angular deformity of the hip?
questions.explanation: A fracture of the neck of femur characteristically results in coxa vara, reducing the neck-shaft angle below the normal 125-135 degrees. Coxa valga with an increased neck-shaft angle follows congenital dislocation of the femoral head. These deformities have different biomechanical implications for gait and joint loading.

The lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) separates the frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe. The middle cerebral artery runs in this fissure. The insula lies deep within the lateral sulcus. Strokes affecting the middle cerebral artery often involve structures around this fissure causing characteristic neurological deficits.
questions.question: Which structure separates the frontal and temporal lobes?

questions.explanation: Bronchoscopy is the procedure that allows direct visualization and examination of the trachea and bronchial tree using a flexible or rigid bronchoscope. It can be used diagnostically (to visualize lesions, take biopsies, obtain specimens) or therapeutically (to remove foreign bodies, control bleeding, place stents).
questions.question: Which procedure examines the bronchial tree?
The pampiniform plexus functions primarily to:
questions.explanation: The pampiniform plexus of veins surrounding the testicular artery in the spermatic cord functions as a countercurrent heat exchanger, cooling arterial blood before it reaches the testes and maintaining testicular temperature 2-3?C below core body temperature, essential for normal spermatogenesis. This venous network of 8-12 veins allows extensive surface area for heat exchange. Varicocele (varicosity of pampiniform plexus) can impair this cooling mechanism and potentially affect fertility. The plexus drains into a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring, with asymmetric drainage (right to IVC, left to left renal vein).

questions.question: What is the length of the female urethra?
questions.explanation: The female urethra is approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches) long and extends from the internal urethral orifice of the bladder to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule. It is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall and passes through the urogenital diaphragm. The shorter length makes females more susceptible to urinary tract infections.

The depressor labii inferioris depresses and everts the lower lip. It arises from the mandible and inserts into the skin of the lower lip. The muscle is innervated by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve. Depressor anguli oris acts primarily on the angle of the mouth, though it assists in lowering the lip.
questions.question: Which muscle depresses the lower lip?
What imaging study visualizes the bronchial tree?
questions.explanation: A bronchogram is a radiographic study where contrast medium is introduced into the bronchial tree to visualize its anatomy. This procedure has largely been replaced by CT bronchography and virtual bronchoscopy. Knowledge of bronchopulmonary segments helps in correctly interpreting bronchograms and planning interventions.

questions.question: Tibialis anterior strain causes pain along the anterolateral shin during walking or running. Which specific action does the injured muscle perform that is impaired?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot. Strain of this muscle impairs these actions, causing pain during the heel-strike phase of gait (when the muscle eccentrically controls foot plantarflexion) and during active dorsiflexion. Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) can involve the tibialis anterior among other muscles. Anterior compartment syndrome also affects it acutely.

Sliding hiatal hernia (type I) accounts for about 95% of hiatal hernias. The gastroesophageal junction and a portion of the stomach slide up through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax. It is associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Paraesophageal hernias (types II-IV) account for 5% and involve herniation of stomach alongside a normally positioned gastroesophageal junction.
questions.question: What is the most common type of hiatal hernia?
Which lymph nodes drain the sigmoid colon?
questions.explanation: The sigmoid colon drains to sigmoid nodes along the sigmoid arteries, then to inferior mesenteric nodes around the inferior mesenteric artery origin. These eventually drain to para-aortic (lateral aortic) nodes. In colorectal cancer, lymph node involvement follows this drainage pattern and is crucial for staging. The lymphatic spread of left-sided colon cancers differs from right-sided cancers. The gastrosplenic ligament, connecting the greater curvature of the stomach (fundus region) to the hilum of the spleen, contains the short gastric vessels (4-6 small arteries and veins from the splenic artery and vein). The left gastroepiploic vessels also pass through this ligament after arising from the splenic vessels near the hilum. The splenic artery and vein themselves run in the splenorenal ligament (along with the tail of the pancreas), not the gastrosplenic ligament. During splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament must be divided, ligating the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.
questions.question: Which vessel lies in the gastrosplenic ligament?
The otic ganglion provides parasympathetic innervation to which gland?
questions.explanation: The otic ganglion provides postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. Preganglionic fibers arrive via the lesser petrosal nerve from the glossopharyngeal nerve. The ganglion lies in the infratemporal fossa medial to the mandibular nerve below the foramen ovale.

questions.question: The 'screw-home mechanism' of the knee refers to which specific movement that occurs at full extension?
options: Medial rotation of the femur on the tibia in the last few degrees of extension
Both A and B describe the same event
Lateral rotation of the tibia on the femur in the last few degrees of extension
Locking of the patellofemoral joint only
Posterior translation of the tibia at full extension
questions.explanation: The 'screw-home mechanism' is the conjunct rotation that occurs in the final degrees of knee extension, when the tibia rotates laterally on the femur (in an open-chain position) or the femur rotates medially on the tibia (in a closed-chain position). Both descriptions describe the same biomechanical event. Popliteus 'unlocks' this mechanism to initiate knee flexion.

The pharynx extends from the base of the skull to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6, where it becomes continuous with the esophagus. This landmark corresponds to the level where the cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter. The transition zone is clinically significant for foreign body impaction and surgical access considerations.
questions.question: At what vertebral level does the pharynx transition to the esophagus?

options: Median nerve palsy or carpal tunnel
questions.explanation: Thenar muscle wasting occurs with median nerve palsy or chronic carpal tunnel syndrome. The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis). Chronic compression leads to visible flattening of the thenar eminence.
questions.question: Which condition causes thenar muscle wasting?

questions.explanation: Osgood-Schlatter disease is traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity, where the patellar ligament inserts during the growth phase. It affects adolescents (boys aged 12-15, girls aged 8-13) who are active in jumping and running sports. Repeated quadriceps contractions pull on the incompletely ossified tibial tuberosity. Treatment is activity modification and physiotherapy.
questions.question: Osgood-Schlatter disease involves traction apophysitis at which site in adolescents?

questions.explanation: The medial orbital wall is formed primarily by the orbital plate (lamina papyracea) of the ethmoid bone. This thin bone separates the orbit from ethmoidal air cells. Fractures can cause orbital emphysema when air enters from the sinuses. The lacrimal bone contributes anteriorly.
questions.question: The medial wall of the orbit is formed primarily by which bone?

questions.explanation: The tibial nerve gives off the medial sural cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa. This joins the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve to form the sural nerve, supplying the lateral side of the leg and ankle. The tibial nerve is the most superficial of the major neurovascular bundle in the fossa.
questions.question: The tibial nerve gives off which named cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa that contributes to forming the sural nerve?
What causes the dinner fork deformity to be visible?
questions.explanation: The "dinner fork deformity" in Colles' fracture is caused by posterior displacement of the distal radial fragment. When viewed from the side, the wrist resembles the shape of an upside-down dinner fork. The ulnar styloid process is commonly avulsed in conjunction with the radial fracture.

The caval opening (vena caval foramen) in the diaphragm is located at the T8 vertebral level in the central tendon. It transmits the inferior vena cava and terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve. The IVC is adherent to the margins of the opening, so when the diaphragm contracts during inspiration, it widens the opening and dilates the IVC, facilitating venous return.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the caval opening lie?
Which of the following is NOT among the structures passing through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits five structures: the pudendal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, internal pudendal artery and vein, and the tendon of obturator internus. The sciatic nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen. The lesser sciatic foramen enables re-entry into the perineum from the gluteal region.

questions.question: Which renal artery typically passes posterior to the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation: The right renal artery is longer than the left and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava to reach the right kidney. The left renal artery has a shorter, more direct course from the aorta to the left kidney. Both arteries arise at approximately L1-L2 level, just inferior to the superior mesenteric artery origin.

questions.question: What nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve (C5, C6) supplies both supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. The nerve passes through the suprascapular notch (under the superior transverse scapular ligament) to reach the supraspinous fossa, then through the spinoglenoid notch to the infraspinous fossa.

questions.question: Which portion of the anal canal is derived from endoderm?
questions.explanation: The anal canal above the pectinate line is derived from endoderm (hindgut), while the portion below originates from ectoderm (proctodeum). This embryological distinction explains the different characteristics of the two regions: superior to the pectinate line, the mucosa is columnar, venous drainage is to the portal system via superior rectal veins, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes, and innervation is autonomic (insensitive to pain). Below the line, the epithelium is stratified squamous, venous drainage is systemic (middle and inferior rectal veins), lymph drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and sensory innervation is via the inferior rectal nerve (painful).

The renal medulla is composed of approximately 10-12 renal pyramids in each kidney. Each pyramid has its base directed toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting medially into a minor calyx. The renal columns (columns of Bertin) extend between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus.
questions.question: How many renal pyramids typically comprise each kidney?

questions.explanation: The connective tissue septa between adjacent bronchopulmonary segments act as natural barriers preventing the spread of infection between segments. However, aggressive infections like tuberculosis and carcinoma can break through these barriers. This anatomical feature is clinically important in limiting disease spread.
questions.question: What prevents infection spread between segments?
How many fascicles does the left bundle branch divide into?
questions.explanation: The left bundle branch divides into two main fascicles: anterior and posterior (some describe a third, septal fascicle). The anterior fascicle supplies the anterior and lateral left ventricular wall; the posterior fascicle supplies the posterior and inferior wall. Left bundle branch block or fascicular blocks (hemiblocks) cause characteristic ECG patterns and may indicate underlying cardiac disease.

questions.question: Which muscle produces pronation of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Pronation of the forearm is produced by pronator teres and pronator quadratus muscles. Pronator teres is more powerful and acts during rapid or forceful pronation. Pronator quadratus maintains pronation during slow movements and is the primary pronator during unresisted pronation.

questions.question: Which structures form the boundaries of the cervicoaxillary canal (apex of axilla)?
questions.explanation: The apex of the axilla forms the cervicoaxillary canal, providing passage between the neck and axilla. It is bounded by the first rib medially, the clavicle anteriorly, and the superior border of the scapula posteriorly. Arteries, veins, lymphatics, and nerves traverse this opening to reach or leave the upper limb.
options: First rib, clavicle, and superior scapular border

questions.explanation: The posterior mediastinum is bounded anteriorly by the pericardium (which forms the heart in the middle mediastinum). Posteriorly, it is bounded by the thoracic vertebrae from T5 to T12. The posterior mediastinum contains the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, and sympathetic trunks.
questions.question: What forms the anterior boundary of posterior mediastinum?

questions.explanation: The gastroduodenal artery arises from the common hepatic artery (distal to the origin of the gastric and splenic arteries but proximal to the bifurcation into hepatic artery proper and gastroduodenal artery). It descends posterior to the first part of the duodenum, where it divides into two terminal branches: the right gastroepiploic artery (running along the greater curvature) and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (supplying the pancreatic head and duodenum). The gastroduodenal artery is intimately related to the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb and can erode into this vessel, causing life-threatening hemorrhage.
questions.question: The gastroduodenal artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The anterior belly of the digastric is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects the embryologic origin from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively.
questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric muscle is innervated by which nerve?
Which structure crosses esophagus at 27 cm?
questions.explanation: The left main bronchus crosses anterior to the esophagus creating the third anatomical constriction at 27 cm from the incisors (T5-6 level). This is where the trachea bifurcates. Foreign bodies and malignancies may cause compression at this site. Endoscopic measurements from the incisors help locate pathology.

questions.question: Which cells in pancreatic islets produce somatostatin?
questions.explanation: Delta cells (D cells) comprise about 5-10% of islet cells and produce somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion, acting as a paracrine regulator. They are located peripherally in the islets. Somatostatin also inhibits growth hormone release from the pituitary (hence the name) and has widespread inhibitory effects on the GI tract.

questions.question: Which muscle is the primary supinator of the forearm?
questions.explanation: The supinator muscle is the primary supinator of the forearm, wrapping around the proximal radius. The biceps brachii is a powerful accessory supinator, especially when the elbow is flexed. The deep branch of the radial nerve passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle.

Needle decompression for tension pneumothorax is performed in the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line on the affected side. A large-bore needle or cannula is inserted just above the 3rd rib (to avoid neurovascular bundle of 2nd intercostal space). This provides immediate temporary relief until a chest tube can be inserted.
questions.question: Where is needle decompression performed?

questions.explanation: The left kidney extends higher than the right, with its upper pole reaching the 11th rib, while the right kidney's upper pole typically reaches the 12th rib. Both kidneys lie on the diaphragm superiorly, which separates them from the pleura and lungs. The left kidney's higher position reflects the asymmetry caused by the liver on the right.
questions.question: Which rib typically crosses the upper pole of the left kidney?

questions.explanation: The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones. It drains medially into the great saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the great toe) and laterally into the small saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the little toe). This arch is the origin point of both major superficial veins of the lower limb.
questions.question: The dorsal venous arch of the foot drains medially into the great saphenous vein and laterally into which vein?
Where does the portal vein form anatomically?
questions.explanation: The portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It is approximately 8 cm long and ascends behind the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It receives the left and right gastric veins, cystic vein, and paraumbilical veins during its course.

The left gastric artery, the smallest branch of the celiac trunk, gives off esophageal branches that ascend to supply the abdominal portion of the esophagus (below the diaphragm). These esophageal branches anastomose superiorly with esophageal branches from the thoracic aorta through the esophageal hiatus, creating a potential portosystemic anastomosis (left gastric vein to portal system; esophageal veins from thoracic aorta territory to azygos system to IVC). In portal hypertension, this anastomosis may become varicose, producing esophageal varices that can rupture and cause life-threatening hemorrhage.
questions.question: The left gastric artery supplies which part of the esophagus?
How many segments are in left lower lobe?
questions.explanation: The left lower lobe typically contains four (sometimes five) bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The medial basal segment is often absent or fused with the anterior basal segment on the left side, unlike the right lower lobe which consistently has five segments.

questions.question: Which muscle originates from the styloid process and inserts on the tongue?
questions.explanation: The styloglossus muscle arises from the styloid process and inserts into the side of the tongue. It retracts and elevates the tongue during swallowing. Like all tongue muscles except palatoglossus, it is innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (XII). The muscle interdigitates with the hyoglossus.

questions.question: The chorda tympani nerve carries which type of fibers?
options: Special sensory (taste) from anterior two-thirds tongue
questions.explanation: The chorda tympani carries special sensory (taste) fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to submandibular and sublingual glands. It branches from the facial nerve in the mastoid, crosses the middle ear, and joins the lingual nerve. Damage causes loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior tongue.

questions.question: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve longer?
questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer than the right because of the embryological descent of the heart and great vessels. As the heart descends from the neck into the thorax, it carries the aortic arch (and the nerve looping under it) downward. The right subclavian artery descends less, so the right nerve is shorter.

The quadratus plantae assists flexor digitorum longus in flexing the lateral four digits. This assistance is needed because the tendons of flexor digitorum longus approach the digits from a medially oblique direction; quadratus plantae corrects this pull to a more longitudinal direction. It originates from the medial and lateral plantar surfaces of the calcaneus and is innervated by the lateral plantar nerve.
questions.question: The second layer of foot muscles contains the quadratus plantae and lumbricals. The quadratus plantae assists which extrinsic muscle in flexing the lateral four digits?
Which artery anastomoses at Sudeck's point?
questions.explanation: Sudeck's point is the watershed area at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anal verge) where the last sigmoid artery (from inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of IMA). This represents a relatively weak point in the colonic blood supply, vulnerable to ischemia during periods of low blood flow, hypotension, or ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery during surgery. Another watershed area is Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure. Both areas may develop ischemic colitis, manifesting as abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and colonoscopic evidence of mucosal ischemia.

The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the S2, S3, and S4 spinal segments, representing the sacral outflow of the parasympathetic nervous system. These nerves arise from the ventral rami of S2-S4, contribute to the inferior hypogastric plexus, and supply parasympathetic innervation to pelvic viscera (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs) and distal hindgut (from splenic flexure to upper anal canal). They stimulate bladder contraction, rectal peristalsis, and penile erection ("point"), in contrast to sympathetic innervation which promotes ejaculation ("shoot").
questions.question: The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from which spinal segments?

questions.explanation: The maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve exits the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum in the greater wing of the sphenoid. It enters the pterygopalatine fossa where it gives off branches before continuing as the infraorbital nerve. The foramen rotundum is round in shape, hence its name.
questions.question: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve exits the skull through which opening?

questions.explanation: The submental lymph nodes lie between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and drain the chin, central lower lip, floor of mouth, and tip of tongue. Efferents pass to submandibular and jugulo-omohyoid nodes. These nodes are examined when staging oral cavity cancers.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the chin?
Which structure protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture?
questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the roof of the cubital fossa, protecting the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture. Historically, this structure was called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected vital deeper structures during bloodletting. The median cubital vein lies superficial to this protective layer.
