Biceps long head tendon rupture typically occurs in elderly individuals with degenerative tendon changes. The muscle belly retracts distally creating the characteristic "Popeye" sign. Despite dramatic appearance, functional deficit is surprisingly minimal as the short head remains intact and compensates adequately.
questions.question: Which condition is associated with rupture of the biceps long head?
The transpyloric plane intersects which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane is an important anatomical landmark that passes through the first lumbar vertebra (L1), situated midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis. This plane transects numerous vital structures including the pylorus, neck of pancreas, origins of superior mesenteric artery and portal vein, duodenojejunal junction, and the hila of both kidneys. It serves as a crucial reference point for clinical examination and surgical procedures in the upper abdomen.

questions.question: What produces medial rotation of the humerus at the shoulder?
options: Subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major
questions.explanation: Medial (internal) rotation of the humerus is produced by subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, and anterior fibers of deltoid. This movement rotates the arm toward the midline so the thumb points medially. These muscles are predominantly anterior or on the subscapular surface.

questions.question: The vas deferens is derived from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The vas deferens (ductus deferens) develops from the mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct) in males under the influence of testosterone. In females, the mesonephric duct regresses due to absence of testosterone, while the paramesonephric duct (M?llerian duct) develops into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina. The epididymis also develops from the mesonephric duct, while the seminal vesicles arise as outgrowths from the distal mesonephric duct. The prostate and bulbourethral glands develop from the urogenital sinus. Understanding embryology helps explain congenital anomalies of the reproductive tract.

questions.question: The left gastric artery arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left gastric artery is the smallest of the three branches of the celiac trunk (along with splenic and common hepatic arteries), arising at the T12/L1 level. It ascends to the cardioesophageal junction, giving off esophageal branches to the abdominal esophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature of the stomach in the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the right gastric artery. It supplies both surfaces of the stomach along the lesser curvature. An aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery, running in the gastrohepatic ligament.

questions.question: Which branch of the left coronary artery supplies the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: The anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending - LAD) descends in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, anterior left ventricular wall, and anterior right ventricle. It is the most commonly affected vessel in myocardial infarction. Septal branches perforate the septum; diagonal branches supply the lateral left ventricle.

The cervical pleura drains into the internal thoracic chain anteriorly and into the intercostal chain posteriorly. The parietal pleura's lymphatic drainage follows its vascular supply pattern. Coastal and mediastinal pleura also drain to the internal thoracic chain anteriorly.
questions.question: Where does the cervical pleura lymph drain anteriorly?

questions.explanation: The cochlear aqueduct (perilymphatic duct) connects the scala tympani with the subarachnoid space, allowing communication between perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid. The aqueduct opens at the base of the petrous temporal bone. The vestibular aqueduct separately connects the endolymphatic system with the posterior cranial fossa. Patency varies among individuals.
questions.question: The cochlear aqueduct connects the scala tympani with which space?
Proximal fibular fractures (Maisonneuve fracture) associated with ankle injuries disrupt which ligament, creating ankle instability?
questions.explanation: Maisonneuve fracture involves a high (proximal) fibular fracture combined with disruption of the tibiofibular syndesmosis (inferior tibiofibular ligament complex) and interosseous membrane. This creates a unstable ankle mortise (syndesmotic diastasis) despite the intact lateral ankle. It is caused by an external rotation force. The high fibular fracture may be missed if only the ankle is radiographed.

Ischial bursitis is inflammation of the bursa separating the gluteus maximus from the ischial tuberosity, caused by prolonged sitting on hard surfaces pressing against the bones. It is sometimes called 'weaver's bottom.' Trochanteric bursitis at the greater trochanter is more common in women and associated with overuse or direct trauma.
questions.question: Inflammation of the bursa separating gluteus maximus from the ischial tuberosity, caused by prolonged sitting on hard surfaces, is termed what?
What is the total approximate length of the small intestine?
questions.explanation: The small intestine measures approximately 5 to 6 meters in length in adults, with the jejunum constituting about 40% and the ileum about 60%. Post-mortem measurements may show greater length due to loss of muscle tone. The actual functional length in vivo is considerably shorter due to tonic muscular contraction.

The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when present, drains the upper part of the head of the pancreas and opens into the duodenum at the minor duodenal papilla. This papilla is located approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. The accessory duct frequently communicates with the main pancreatic duct.
questions.question: Where does the accessory pancreatic duct open into the duodenum?
Rupture of the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon typically occurs in which demographic and in what mechanism?
options: Children; direct blow to the heel
Middle-aged men; sudden powerful plantarflexion or push-off
Young female athletes; chronic overuse with no acute event
Infants; congenital deficiency of the tendon
questions.explanation: Rupture of the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon typically occurs in middle-aged men during sudden powerful plantarflexion or push-off movements (such as jumping or sprinting). The patient feels a sharp pain, as if struck from behind. Simmond's (Thompson's) test confirms rupture: squeezing the calf with the patient prone fails to produce plantarflexion of the foot.

questions.question: Which part of the male urethra is widest?
questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra, measuring approximately 3-4 cm in length. It descends through the prostate gland from the bladder neck and contains the urethral crest on its posterior wall, with the prostatic utricle and openings of the ejaculatory ducts. The membranous urethra is the narrowest part.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the testis?
questions.explanation: The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, corresponding to their embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall and their arterial supply from the abdominal aorta. Lymphatics accompany the testicular vessels through the spermatic cord, inguinal canal, and over the pelvic brim to reach these nodes. In contrast, the scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This lymphatic drainage pattern is clinically crucial in testicular cancer staging and explains why metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes rather than inguinal nodes (unless the scrotal skin is also involved).

questions.question: Into which fibers do the bundle branches terminate?
questions.explanation: The right and left bundle branches divide into Purkinje fibers, which form a subendocardial network that rapidly conducts the impulse throughout the ventricular myocardium. Purkinje fibers are larger than regular cardiac myocytes with fewer myofibrils, specialized for rapid conduction rather than contraction. They ensure coordinated ventricular contraction from apex to base.

questions.question: The common fibular nerve winds around which specific part of the fibula to divide into its terminal branches?
questions.explanation: The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula and then divides into the deep and superficial fibular nerves. At this point it is subcutaneous and highly vulnerable to injury from fractures, tight plasters, or prolonged cross-legged sitting. Injury causes foot drop due to paralysis of the anterior and lateral leg compartment muscles.

questions.question: Which muscle produces both shoulder adduction and medial rotation?
questions.explanation: produces shoulder adduction, extension, and medial rotation. It is a powerful muscle forming part of the posterior axillary fold. The muscle is commonly used in reconstructive surgery and is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.

questions.question: What deformity results from paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles?
questions.explanation: deformity results from paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles, particularly in ulnar nerve injury. There is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints. This occurs due to unopposed action of long flexors and extensors without intrinsic muscle balance.

questions.question: Which veins drain the breast?
questions.explanation: Veins of the breast drain into both the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The pattern follows the arterial supply. During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become engorged and may be visible through the skin. Venous drainage is important in the spread of breast cancer.

The anterior tibial artery gives off the anterior tibial recurrent artery, which ascends to the front of the knee to contribute inferolaterally to the genicular anastomosis. This vessel pierces the anterior tibialis muscle and anastomoses with the inferior lateral genicular artery. Knowledge of this anastomosis is important for understanding collateral circulation when the popliteal artery is occluded.
questions.question: The anterior tibial artery runs through the anterior compartment and enters the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery. It gives off which branch that contributes to the genicular anastomosis?

questions.explanation: The median nerve is compressed between the two heads of pronator teres in pronator teres syndrome. This entrapment neuropathy causes forearm pain and median nerve sensory symptoms. Unlike carpal tunnel syndrome, palm sensation is affected as compression occurs proximal to the palmar cutaneous branch.
questions.question: Which nerve is compressed in pronator teres syndrome?

options: Flattens the medial longitudinal arch of the foot
Has no significant effect on any foot arch
Progressively flattens the transverse arch of the midfoot
Raises the medial longitudinal arch, converting foot to a rigid push-off lever
Only affects the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot
questions.question: The 'windlass mechanism' of the foot refers to tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis during toe dorsiflexion. What effect does this have on the foot arches?
questions.explanation: The windlass mechanism (described by Hicks, 1954) involves tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis as the toes dorsiflexed during push-off. This raises the medial longitudinal arch, shortens the foot, and converts it into a rigid lever for efficient propulsion. This mechanism is impaired in flatfoot (pes planus) and hallux rigidus, reducing push-off efficiency.

Klumpke's paralysis involves the C8-T1 nerve roots of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. This typically results from undue abduction of the arm, such as clutching a tree branch during a fall. The resulting claw hand deformity occurs due to paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar flexors.
questions.question: Which nerve root values are primarily involved in Klumpke's paralysis?

questions.explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle. This is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The nerve descends with the superior thyroid artery. Damage affects vocal cord tension and causes voice fatigue and difficulty with pitch variation.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?

questions.explanation: Lateral (external) rotation of the humerus is produced by infraspinatus, teres minor, and posterior fibers of the deltoid. The infraspinatus and teres minor are two of the four rotator cuff muscles. This movement rotates the arm away from the midline, making the thumb point laterally.
questions.question: What muscles produce lateral rotation of the humerus?
How many arterial arcades typically supply the ileum?
questions.explanation: The ileum is supplied by 3 to 6 tiers of arterial arcades formed by branches of the superior mesenteric artery. These multiple arcades provide collateral circulation and ensure adequate blood supply to the bowel. In contrast, the jejunum typically has only 1 to 2 arterial arcades with longer vasa recta.

The zygomatic bones form the prominence of the cheeks and lie on the inferolateral sides of the orbits. They articulate with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones. The bone has a broad connection with the maxilla medially and forms part of the zygomatic arch laterally. Fractures cause flattening of the malar eminence.
questions.question: Which bone forms the prominence of the cheek?

questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural cavity through a one-way valve mechanism but cannot escape. Progressive air accumulation increases intrapleural pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum to the opposite side. This is a life-threatening emergency causing hemodynamic compromise requiring immediate needle decompression.
questions.question: What is tension pneumothorax?

questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), provides the blood supply to the vermiform appendix. It runs through the free edge of the mesoappendix, making it vulnerable during surgical mobilization of the appendix. This is typically an end artery with minimal collateral supply, so thrombosis can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery may give off a recurrent branch that ascends toward the ileocecal junction. Variations include occasional origin from a posterior cecal artery or rarely from the superior mesenteric artery directly.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the vermiform appendix?
Which part of the duodenum is most mobile?
questions.explanation: The first part (superior part) of the duodenum, specifically its first 2 cm (duodenal cap or bulb), is the only portion that is intraperitoneal and mobile, being connected to the liver by the hepatoduodenal ligament. The remainder of the first part and all of the second, third, and fourth parts are secondarily retroperitoneal and fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. This mobility makes the duodenal bulb vulnerable to anterior displacement by posterior masses (e.g., pancreatic head tumors). The mobile first part is also the most common site of peptic ulceration.

questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the dorsum of the foot. It anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form which arch?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves inferiorly toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Via this arch, it contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones.

questions.question: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by which division of the sciatic nerve?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2). The exception is the short head of biceps femoris, which is supplied by the common fibular division. The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body.

The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve supplies all muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) via its motor root. It also supplies mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor veli palatini, and tensor tympani. These muscles derive from the first pharyngeal arch mesoderm.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication?

questions.explanation: The right upper lobar bronchus (eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the right lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is unique to the right side. All other lobar bronchi arise within the hilum. The left main bronchus divides entirely within the hilum.
questions.question: Which bronchus is given off outside the hilum?

questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung begins in the tail and runs through the entire length of the gland, receiving numerous tributaries along its course. It drains the majority of pancreatic tissue and usually joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This ampulla opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.
questions.question: Which duct drains the majority of the pancreatic tissue?
Which muscle depresses the hyoid bone after swallowing?
questions.explanation: The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing. All infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) serve this function. They are innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) except thyrohyoid which receives C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.

questions.question: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle (over the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae), passing from lateral to medial as it descends toward the pelvic brim. It is crossed anteriorly by the testicular/ovarian vessels and lies posterior to the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. The ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the external iliac artery) at the pelvic brim, providing a consistent landmark. The relationship to psoas major is maintained until the ureter reaches the pelvic inlet, where it enters the pelvis.

The corrugator cutis ani muscle, formed by fusion of fibers from the longitudinal muscle layer of the rectum and the levator ani, inserts into the skin of the anal canal at the white line (intersphincteric line, or white line of Hilton). This line represents the lower border of the internal anal sphincter and the intermuscular groove between the internal and external anal sphincters. Some longitudinal muscle fibers also blend with the puborectalis anteriorly and extend to form the rectourethralis muscle (muscle of Roux) in males, extending toward the urethra.
questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the white line of Hilton?

questions.explanation: The basilar artery terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. It is formed by union of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. The artery gives off pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine branches during its course.
questions.question: The basilar artery terminates at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx), formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses, forms the medial part of the posterior wall and medial boundary of the inguinal canal. Weakness here predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The lateral part of the posterior wall is formed by the transversalis fascia.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: The middle lobe of the right lung is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. The horizontal fissure runs along the fourth rib anteriorly. The oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from both the superior and middle lobes on the right side.
questions.question: Which fissure separates the right lung's middle lobe?

questions.explanation: The brachioradialis reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the brachioradialis tendon at the distal forearm. Absence or diminution suggests C6 nerve root or radial nerve pathology proximal to the elbow.
questions.question: What nerve root is predominantly tested by the brachioradialis reflex?
What position does the heart occupy mediastinally?
questions.explanation: The heart and pericardium are the main contents of the middle mediastinum, which also contains the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, parts of the phrenic nerves, and the main bronchi. The middle mediastinum is the central compartment of the inferior mediastinum.

questions.question: Where does the spongy urethra begin?
questions.explanation: The spongy (penile) urethra begins where the membranous urethra exits the urogenital diaphragm and extends through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans penis. It is approximately 15 cm long and has two dilated portions: the intrabulbar fossa in the bulb and the navicular fossa in the glans.

Posterior mediastinal masses are most commonly neurogenic tumors arising from sympathetic ganglia (ganglioneuroma, neuroblastoma), peripheral nerves (schwannoma, neurofibroma), or paraganglia (paraganglioma). Esophageal lesions, thoracic duct cysts, and extramedullary hematopoiesis can also occur posteriorly. In children, neuroblastoma is common.
questions.question: What typically causes posterior mediastinal masses?

questions.explanation: During pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration of pericardial fluid), the needle is typically inserted in the left 5th or 6th intercostal space near the sternum or at the infrasternal (subxiphoid) angle. The internal thoracic (mammary) artery, which runs about 1 cm lateral to the sternum, is at risk if the needle is inserted too laterally. The phrenic nerves run laterally between the pericardium and mediastinal pleura.
questions.question: Which structure is most at risk during pericardiocentesis?

questions.explanation: The arytenoid cartilages sit on the upper border of the cricoid cartilage lamina at the cricoarytenoid joints. These synovial joints allow rotation and gliding movements that abduct and adduct the vocal cords. The arytenoids are pyramidal with a vocal process (anteriorly) and muscular process (laterally).
questions.question: The arytenoid cartilages articulate with which laryngeal structure?

questions.explanation: Seven nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen: the sciatic nerve, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal nerve, inferior gluteal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerve. Together with six vessels and piriformis, these seven nerves constitute the 14 total structures passing through this foramen.
questions.question: How many nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
Which sinus receives the great cerebral vein?
questions.explanation: The straight sinus receives the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the inferior sagittal sinus. It runs in the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. The sinus drains into the confluence of sinuses (typically preferentially into the left transverse sinus). Deep cerebral structures drain via this pathway.

The medial border of the brachioradialis muscle forms the lateral (radial) boundary of the cubital fossa. This muscle is a prominent flexor of the forearm that also assists with both pronation and supination from mid-position. It originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa?

The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) enters the thigh just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. Compression of this nerve causes which specific condition?
options: Meralgia paraesthetica (burning pain on lateral thigh)
Knee pain from saphenous nerve compression
questions.explanation: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2, L3) causes meralgia paraesthetica, characterized by burning, tingling, or numbness on the anterolateral aspect of the thigh. It is a purely sensory nerve with no motor component. Common causes include obesity, pregnancy, tight belts, and direct compression. Treatment is conservative with weight loss and activity modification.

questions.question: What can cause acquired diaphragmatic hernia?
questions.explanation: Acquired diaphragmatic hernias can result from: (1) penetrating or blunt trauma causing rupture, (2) weakening around the esophageal hiatus (hiatus hernias), or (3) rarely, herniation through the central tendon after surgical procedures. Traumatic hernias require urgent surgical repair.

questions.question: Which lymphatic trunk drains the right side of the thorax?
questions.explanation: The right bronchomediastinal trunk drains lymph from the right side of the thorax. It joins with right jugular and right subclavian trunks to form the right lymphatic duct. Alternatively, these three trunks may drain independently into the right venous angle. The left bronchomediastinal trunk usually drains into the thoracic duct.

questions.question: The knee joint stability depends primarily on muscles. Which muscle group is described as the MOST important in stabilizing the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is the most important muscle group for stabilizing the knee joint. The inferior fibers of vastus medialis and lateralis are particularly important stabilizers. Quadriceps weakness leads to instability especially on stairs and inclines. Rehabilitation after any knee injury or surgery focuses heavily on quadriceps strengthening exercises.

questions.question: The profunda femoris artery arises from the femoral artery at what distance below the inguinal ligament?
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery) arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. It is the largest branch of the femoral artery and the main blood supply to the thigh muscles via perforating branches, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries.

options: Waddling gait due to hip flexor weakness
Scissor gait due to adductor spasticity
High-stepping gait due to foot drop
Antalgic gait due to hip pain
Trendelenburg gait due to gluteus medius and minimus weakness
questions.explanation: Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) palsy causes weakness of gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. This results in a Trendelenburg gait (pelvis drops to the opposite side during swing phase). Bilateral superior gluteal nerve palsy causes a characteristic waddling gait. This nerve is at risk during posterior surgical approaches to the hip.
questions.question: Superior gluteal nerve palsy results in which specific gait abnormality?
Where does central diaphragmatic pain refer?
questions.explanation: Irritation of the central part of the diaphragm (supplied by phrenic nerve C3-5) causes referred pain to the shoulder-tip because the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4) supply the skin over the shoulder. This occurs in conditions like pleurisy, pericarditis, or subphrenic abscess affecting the central diaphragm.

questions.question: What replaces thymic tissue in adults?
questions.explanation: In adults, the involuting thymus is progressively replaced by adipose (fatty) tissue. This normal age-related change is called thymic involution. Despite fatty replacement, some functional thymic tissue usually persists even in elderly individuals. On CT scans, the adult thymus appears as fatty tissue in the anterior mediastinum.

The falciform ligament divides the subphrenic space into right and left components, separating the right subphrenic space from the left. The right subphrenic space communicates posteriorly with the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position, making it a common site for fluid accumulation. The left subphrenic space is bounded by the falciform ligament on the right, the diaphragm superiorly and anteriorly, the stomach and spleen posteriorly, and the anterior layer of the left triangular ligament laterally.
questions.question: Which muscle separates the subphrenic from the subhepatic space?

questions.explanation: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It ascends to the right and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch.
questions.question: Which trunk branches from the aortic arch first?

questions.explanation: The central tendon of the diaphragm is shaped like three leaves (trifoliate). It has no bony attachments but is partially fused with the inferior surface of the fibrous pericardium. All the muscular fibers of the diaphragm insert into this central tendon.
questions.question: What shape is the central tendon?

questions.explanation: The olfactory bulbs lie on the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the anterior cranial fossa. Olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium pass through the cribriform foramina to synapse in the bulbs. The olfactory tracts extend posteriorly from the bulbs. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.
questions.question: Which space contains the olfactory bulbs?
What causes esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Esophageal varices develop due to portal hypertension (commonly from liver cirrhosis). Elevated portal venous pressure causes dilation of the portosystemic anastomoses at the lower esophagus. These dilated, tortuous veins (varices) can rupture, causing massive, life-threatening hematemesis. Treatment includes endoscopic banding and beta-blockers.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the posterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The posterior abdominal wall is formed by multiple muscles: psoas major (medially, originating from lumbar vertebrae), quadratus lumborum (laterally, between 12th rib and iliac crest), and iliacus (below iliac crest, in iliac fossa). Together these muscles, along with the diaphragm superiorly and the lumbar vertebrae and their processes, create the musculoskeletal framework of the posterior abdominal wall. The transversus abdominis wraps around from the anterolateral wall to attach to these structures. These muscles are covered anteriorly by psoas fascia, quadratus lumborum fascia, and iliac fascia respectively, with retroperitoneal organs and vessels lying anterior to these fascial layers.

questions.question: Which vessel anastomoses at Griffiths' point?
questions.explanation: Griffiths' point is the watershed area at the splenic flexure where the left branch of the middle colic artery (from superior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric artery). This represents the junction between the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories and is vulnerable to ischemia due to relatively poor collateral circulation. Another watershed area exists at Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid junction) where the last sigmoid artery meets the superior rectal artery. Both areas are susceptible to ischemic colitis during low-flow states.

questions.question: What is the significance of the median nerve's dual cord origin?
questions.explanation: The median nerve's formation from lateral and medial cords ensures it receives contributions from all nerve roots (C5-T1) except sometimes C5. This broad root distribution explains why isolated cord injuries may only partially affect median nerve function. The distinctive M-shaped formation in the axilla is clinically recognizable.
options: Has no clinical or anatomical significance
Supply from both lateral and medial cords

questions.explanation: Radiographically, diaphragmatic paralysis is recognized by elevation of the affected hemidiaphragm and paradoxical movement. On fluoroscopy, the paralyzed hemidiaphragm moves upward during inspiration (instead of descending) due to passive displacement by abdominal pressure. This is called the "sniff test."
questions.question: What indicates diaphragmatic paralysis radiographically?
What structure passes through the foramen cecum in adults?
questions.explanation: In only 1% of adults, a nasal emissary vein passes through the foramen cecum connecting nasal veins with the superior sagittal sinus. In most adults, the foramen is obliterated. In the fetus, this foramen transmitted the anterior extension of the developing superior sagittal sinus.

questions.question: Which area of the liver is devoid of peritoneal covering?
questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver is located on the diaphragmatic surface where the liver is in direct contact with the diaphragm without intervening peritoneum. This area is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament. The bare area is clinically significant as infections can spread directly between the liver and thorax.

questions.question: Which muscle closes the eyelid?
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. It has orbital, palpebral, and lacrimal parts. The muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII). The palpebral portion produces gentle closure (blinking), while the orbital portion produces tight closure (squinting). Facial nerve palsy causes inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos).

questions.question: Which muscle forms the posterior pillar of the fauces?
questions.explanation: The palatopharyngeus muscle forms the posterior pillar (palatopharyngeal arch) of the fauces. The palatoglossus forms the anterior pillar. The tonsillar fossa lies between these two pillars. Both muscles descend from the soft palate but have different innervation patterns.

questions.question: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from which vertebral bodies?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the anterolateral surfaces of the bodies and intervertebral discs of L1, L2, and L3 vertebrae (sometimes extending to L4), while the left crus arises from only L1 and L2 (sometimes L3). Both crura contribute to forming the esophageal hiatus, with muscle fibers from the right crus (and sometimes left) looping around the esophagus to create a muscular sphincter mechanism. The crura also form boundaries of the aortic hiatus, with the median arcuate ligament connecting them anterior to the aorta at T12 level.

The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, extending from the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis. It contains the portal triad (portal vein posteriorly, common bile duct anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery proper anteriorly and to the left) and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The hepatoduodenal ligament can be compressed manually (Pringle maneuver) to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding inflow to the liver. The gastrohepatic ligament forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum.
questions.question: Which ligament forms the free edge of the lesser omentum?

questions.explanation: The abducens nerve (VI) passes through Dorello's canal beneath the petrosphenoid (Gruber's) ligament at the petrous apex. The nerve then enters the cavernous sinus. Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to increased intracranial pressure causing false localizing sign. The nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle.
questions.question: Which structure passes through Dorello's canal?

questions.explanation: The Harris Hip Score (modified) and Oxford Hip Score are validated patient-reported outcome measures used to assess pain, function, and quality of life following hip conditions and hip replacement surgery. The Oxford Hip Score uses 12 questions covering pain and function, with a range of 0-48 (48 being best). These are standard outcome measures used in arthroplasty registries globally, including the Nigerian context of the MDCN setting.
questions.question: The modified Harris Hip Score and Oxford Hip Score are patient-reported outcome measures used to assess which joint?
The cribriform plate is part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is the horizontal portion of the ethmoid bone forming the roof of the nasal cavity and floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It contains numerous foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers. The crista galli projects superiorly from the midline. Fractures cause CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia from shearing of olfactory nerve fibers.

questions.question: Which zone of the hepatic acinus is most susceptible to ischemia?
questions.explanation: Zone 3 (centrilobular zone) of the hepatic acinus is furthest from the blood supply (portal triads) and is therefore most susceptible to ischemic injury, toxic injury, and hypoxia. This zone receives blood last with the lowest oxygen content. Centrilobular necrosis is characteristic of ischemic hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, and chronic passive congestion from heart failure.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the lumbar triangle of Marcille?
questions.explanation: The lumbosacral triangle (Marcille's triangle) has the medial border of psoas major forming its lateral boundary, with the body of L5 vertebra medially and the ala of sacrum as its base. The floor consists of the transverse process of L5 and the iliolumbar ligament. This triangle is clinically significant as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at its lateral angle, making it an important landmark during pelvic surgery.

The long thoracic nerve arises from nerve roots C5, C6, and C7. It supplies the serratus anterior muscle with branches to each digitation. Injury to this nerve causes scapular winging, which becomes apparent when pushing against resistance.
questions.question: What are the nerve roots of the long thoracic nerve?
The caudate lobe of the liver drains bile into which duct?
options: Both right and left hepatic ducts
questions.explanation: The caudate lobe of the liver, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe, is functionally independent, receiving blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and draining bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. It also has separate venous drainage directly into the IVC via small hepatic veins, independent of the main right, middle, and left hepatic veins. This unique drainage explains why the caudate lobe may hypertrophy in cirrhosis (where it maintains direct IVC access) and why it can function in Budd-Chiari syndrome when the main hepatic veins are occluded. The caudate process extends from the caudate lobe toward the porta hepatis.

questions.question: The pubofemoral ligament of the hip joint limits which two movements?
questions.explanation: The pubofemoral ligament supports the hip joint inferomedially and limits extension and abduction. It is triangular, attaching superiorly to the iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merging with the capsule and lower band of the iliofemoral ligament. Strain of this ligament produces groin pain worsened by extension and abduction.

The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) is the most critical ligament maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It bridges the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the navicular, directly supporting the head of the talus. Rupture of the spring ligament leads to progressive collapse of the medial longitudinal arch and adult acquired flatfoot deformity.
questions.question: Which ligament is the most important structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch, bridging the sustentaculum tali to the navicular?

questions.explanation: The geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve contains cell bodies of sensory neurons carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via chorda tympani. The ganglion is located at the genu (bend) of the facial canal in the temporal bone. Herpes zoster infection (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) causes facial paralysis and painful vesicles.
questions.question: Which ganglion contains cell bodies for taste from the anterior tongue?

questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy affects the radial nerve due to compression against the humerus, typically from sleeping with the arm over a chair back. This causes wrist drop and loss of finger extension. Sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand may also occur.
questions.question: What nerve is affected in Saturday night palsy?
The anterior cerebral arteries are connected by which vessel?
questions.explanation: The two anterior cerebral arteries are joined by the anterior communicating artery, completing the anterior portion of the Circle of Willis. This connection allows collateral flow between right and left anterior circulations. Aneurysms commonly occur at this junction.

The conjoint tendon (formed by fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) inserts onto the pubic crest and pectineal line (pecten pubis), reinforcing the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medially. The pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line and is used in some hernia repairs (Cooper's ligament repair). The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and symphysis, not the pectineal line. The lacunar ligament (medial extension of the inguinal ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line.
questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the pectineal line?

questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine draining from the collecting ducts. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces per kidney. Two to three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.
questions.question: What structure indents the apex of each renal pyramid?
What percentage of pancreatic tissue is endocrine?
questions.explanation: Only about 1-2% of the pancreatic tissue consists of endocrine islets of Langerhans, with the remaining 98-99% being exocrine acinar tissue that produces digestive enzymes. Despite representing such a small proportion, the islets are crucial for glucose homeostasis. There are approximately 1 million islets in the human pancreas, most concentrated in the tail.

Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial cavity rapidly or in large amounts, increasing intrapericardial pressure. This compresses the heart chambers, particularly the right atrium and ventricle, impairing venous return and cardiac filling. Clinical signs include Beck's triad: hypotension, elevated JVP, and muffled heart sounds. Emergency pericardiocentesis may be life-saving.
questions.question: What is cardiac tamponade?
Gastrocnemius can only plantarflex the ankle effectively under which condition?
options: When the knee is fully extended
questions.explanation: Gastrocnemius is unique in that it plantarflexes the ankle only effectively when the knee is extended, because it crosses the knee joint. When the knee is flexed, gastrocnemius becomes relatively ineffective, and soleus becomes the primary plantarflexor. Gastrocnemius also flexes the leg at the knee and is innervated by the tibial nerve (S1, S2).

questions.question: The spleen is related medially to which structure?
questions.explanation: The spleen's medial (visceral) surface has multiple impressions from adjacent organs: gastric impression anteriorly (related to stomach via gastrosplenic ligament), renal impression posteroinferiorly (related to left kidney via splenorenal ligament), colic impression inferiorly (near left colic flexure), and pancreatic impression at the hilum (tail of pancreas in splenorenal ligament). The spleen sits in the left hypochondriac region, protected by ribs 9-11. Its lateral surface is smooth and convex, molded against the diaphragm and posterolateral abdominal wall. The characteristic splenic notch marks its superior border.

Horner's syndrome results from interruption of sympathetic innervation to the eye and face, characterized by: (1) ptosis (drooping eyelid from paralysis of M?ller's muscle), (2) miosis (constricted pupil from unopposed parasympathetic action), and (3) anhidrosis (absent sweating on ipsilateral face). Pancoast tumors invading the sympathetic chain commonly cause this.
questions.question: What is Horner's syndrome triad?
Which structure forms the medial umbilical fold?
questions.explanation: The medial umbilical fold is created by the peritoneum covering the medial umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated umbilical artery. There are paired medial umbilical folds (one on each side), in contrast to the single median umbilical fold in the midline formed by the urachus remnant (median umbilical ligament). Between the median and medial folds lies the supravesical fossa, while the medial inguinal fossa (site of direct inguinal hernias) lies between the medial and lateral umbilical folds, the latter being raised by the inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.question: At which junction along the clavicle does fracture most commonly occur?
questions.explanation: The junction of the middle and outer third of the clavicle represents its weakest point. Transmission of forces during falls on the shoulder or hand frequently exceeds bone strength at this location. This indirect force mechanism is the usual cause of clavicular fracture.

The veins from the lower third of the oesophagus drain into the left gastric vein, which is part of the portal circulation. This drainage pattern creates a clinically significant portosystemic anastomosis at the gastro-oesophageal junction. In portal hypertension, these veins become dilated forming oesophageal varices that can cause life-threatening haematemesis.
questions.question: Into which vein does the lower third of the oesophagus drain venously?
What closes the pleuroperitoneal canal?
questions.explanation: The pleuroperitoneal membranes close the fetal communication between the pleural and peritoneal cavities. Failure of these membranes to close completely results in congenital diaphragmatic hernias, most commonly through the foramen of Bochdalek (posterolaterally). This is more common on the left side.

questions.question: The cutaneous innervation of the upper medial quadrant of the buttock is derived from which spinal segments?
options: L1 and T12 vertebral levels only
questions.explanation: The upper medial quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3. The upper lateral quadrant receives L1 and T12. The lower medial quadrant receives S1, 2, 3, and the lower lateral quadrant receives L2, L3. This dermatomal pattern helps localize spinal pathology.

options: Right costal margin at 9th costal cartilage
questions.question: The gallbladder fundus typically lies at which anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder typically reaches the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis muscle crosses the right costal margin (approximately at the transpyloric plane). This surface marking corresponds to the point where the gallbladder may contact the anterior abdominal wall, making it palpable when distended or inflamed. Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest with deep palpation at this point due to pain) indicates acute cholecystitis. The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum.

questions.question: What characterizes quiet expiration?
questions.explanation: Quiet expiration is a passive process resulting from elastic recoil of the lungs and relaxation of intercostal muscles and diaphragm. The ribs are depressed and the diaphragm elevated to its normal position. Lung recoil reduces size, increasing pressure inside the lungs to allow air flow outward.

questions.question: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by three bony components. Which correctly describes the roof, walls, and floor?
options: Roof: inferior fibula; walls: tibia bilaterally; floor: calcaneus
Roof: inferior tibia; walls: medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) malleoli; floor: trochlea tali
Roof: superior surface of talus; walls: tibia; floor: calcaneus
Roof: superior tibia; walls: talus on both sides; floor: navicular
Roof: fibula; walls: medial and lateral malleoli; floor: navicular
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (mortise) is formed by: the roof (inferior surface of the tibia), the lateral wall (lateral malleolus from the fibula), the medial wall (medial malleolus from the tibia), and the floor (superior surface of the talus, the trochlea tali). This mortise-and-tenon configuration provides inherent bony stability, especially during dorsiflexion.

The superior surface of the diaphragm is supplied by pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic arteries (branches of the internal thoracic artery) and the superior phrenic arteries (from the thoracic aorta). The pericardiacophrenic artery accompanies the phrenic nerve. The musculophrenic artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery.
questions.question: Which vessels supply the superior diaphragmatic surface?

questions.explanation: Depression of the scapula is produced by lower fibers of trapezius and pectoralis minor muscles. This movement lowers the shoulder and is opposite to elevation. It occurs when lowering the arm from an elevated position or during downward reaching.
questions.question: What produces scapular depression?
The ovary is suspended by which ligament from the pelvic wall?
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, suspends the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian artery (from aorta) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament must be clamped and divided during oophorectomy. The ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus medially, while the broad ligament provides only indirect support via the mesovarium. The round ligament extends from uterus to labium majus via the inguinal canal.

The phrenic nerves (C3-C5) provide somatic sensory innervation to the fibrous pericardium and parietal layer of serous pericardium. Pain from pericardial irritation is therefore sharp and well-localized, often referred to the shoulder (C4 dermatome). The visceral pericardium receives autonomic innervation and is insensitive to pain.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium?
What are the splanchnic nerves?
questions.explanation: The splanchnic nerves are branches of the thoracic sympathetic trunk that carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the abdominal viscera. The greater splanchnic nerve arises from T5-9 ganglia, the lesser from T10-11, and the least (when present) from T12. They pierce the diaphragm to reach abdominal ganglia.

questions.question: The pterygoid hamulus is part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The pterygoid hamulus is a hook-like process at the inferior end of the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone. The tensor veli palatini tendon hooks around it before inserting into the soft palate. The hamulus can be palpated intraorally posterior to the maxillary tuberosity. Fractures cause palatal dysfunction.

questions.question: What structure lies in all mediastinal regions?
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes are present in all regions of the mediastinum: paratracheal and brachiocephalic nodes in the superior mediastinum; parasternal nodes anteriorly; tracheobronchial and hilar nodes in the middle mediastinum; and paraesophageal and paravertebral nodes posteriorly. Lymphadenopathy is a common cause of mediastinal widening.

The transverse mesocolon, a broad fold of peritoneum connecting the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall, divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The supracolic compartment contains the stomach, liver, spleen, and lesser sac, while the infracolic compartment is further divided into right and left infracolic spaces by the mesentery of the small intestine. These spaces communicate laterally via the paracolic gutters. The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses the descending (second) part of the duodenum and head of pancreas, serving as an important surgical landmark.
questions.question: Which structure separates the supracolic from the infracolic compartment?

questions.explanation: The common bile duct descends posterior to the first (superior) part of the duodenum (retroduodenal portion), then continues behind or embedded in the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (infraduodenal portion). It finally passes through the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum (intraduodenal portion), joining the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla. This posterior relationship means that duodenal ulcers in the first part can erode into the bile duct or gastroduodenal artery. The duct's pancreatic portion may be compressed by pancreatic head tumors.
questions.question: The common bile duct passes posterior to which part of the duodenum?

questions.explanation: The Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube opens into the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, connecting it with the middle ear cavity. The tubal elevation and tubal tonsil surround the opening. Tensor veli palatini and salpingopharyngeus muscles open the tube during swallowing to equalize middle ear pressure.
questions.question: Which opening connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear?
What are the lingular segments?
questions.explanation: The superior and inferior lingular segments of the left upper lobe are anatomically equivalent to the middle lobe of the right lung. The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe that occupies the space below the cardiac notch. Both are supplied similarly by their respective bronchi.

The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) passes through the superficial inguinal ring after traversing the inguinal canal, unlike the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve which travels within the spermatic cord through both deep and superficial rings. The ilioinguinal nerve runs between internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, enters the inguinal canal, and emerges through the superficial ring to provide sensory innervation to the skin of the upper medial thigh, root of penis and anterior scrotum (males), or mons pubis and labium majus (females). Entrapment following hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the superficial inguinal ring in males?

questions.explanation: The superolateral border of the popliteal fossa is formed by the biceps femoris muscle. The superomedial border is formed by semimembranosus and semitendinosus. The inferolateral border is the lateral head of gastrocnemius, and the inferomedial border is the medial head of gastrocnemius. The roof is formed by skin and fascia.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the superolateral border of the diamond-shaped popliteal fossa?
Which organism are asplenic patients most susceptible to?
questions.explanation: Asplenic patients (post-splenectomy or functional asplenia) are particularly susceptible to infections with encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis. The spleen is crucial for opsonization and clearance of these organisms. Asplenic patients require vaccination against these organisms and may need prophylactic antibiotics (penicillin or amoxicillin).

questions.question: Which nerve is compressed causing handlebar palsy?
questions.explanation: "Handlebar palsy" results from ulnar nerve compression at the wrist (Guyon's canal) due to prolonged pressure from bicycle handlebars. This causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and numbness in ulnar nerve distribution. The condition is common in long-distance cyclists.

The median (central) cricothyroid ligament connects the anterior aspects of the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. It is subcutaneous in the midline between the cricothyroid muscles. This ligament is crossed by the cricothyroid arterial anastomosis and is the site for emergency cricothyroidotomy.
questions.question: The median cricothyroid ligament connects which two cartilages?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve's course around the medial epicondyle means elbow flexion stretches the nerve. Prolonged flexion (sleeping with bent elbow) can cause compression symptoms. This positional sensitivity explains why cubital tunnel syndrome symptoms may worsen at night and why sleeping with extended elbows helps.
options: Elbow flexion stretches nerve around medial epicondyle
questions.question: How does the ulnar nerve's course make hand position affect its function?

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland drains to prelaryngeal, pretracheal, and paratracheal lymph nodes, which then drain to deep cervical nodes. Lymphatic drainage follows the arterial supply. Understanding lymphatic pathways is crucial for thyroid cancer staging and surgical planning. Superior gland drainage differs from inferior drainage patterns.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the thyroid gland?

questions.explanation: Boutonniere deformity results from rupture of the central slip of the extensor mechanism over the proximal interphalangeal joint. This causes PIP joint flexion with DIP joint hyperextension. The lateral bands slip volarward, creating the characteristic deformity. Common after PIP joint injuries.
questions.question: Which condition causes boutonniere deformity?
Which cartilage forms the only complete ring in the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: The cricoid cartilage is signet-ring shaped and forms the only complete cartilaginous ring throughout the entire respiratory tract. This structural feature provides crucial stability and serves as an important landmark for emergency airway access. The cricoid is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway.

options: A single extensor tendon controls finger extension
Extrinsic extensors and intrinsics interact via extensor expansion
questions.question: How does the extensor mechanism coordinate finger extension?
questions.explanation: The extensor mechanism involves complex interaction between extensor digitorum (extrinsic) and intrinsic muscles through the extensor expansion. Intrinsic muscles (lumbricals, interossei) insert into lateral bands of the expansion, enabling MCP flexion with IP extension. This coordination is essential for normal finger function.

The ureter receives its blood supply from multiple sources along its length: the upper portion from branches of the renal artery, the middle portion from the gonadal (testicular or ovarian) arteries, and the pelvic portion from branches of the internal iliac artery (mainly superior vesical). This segmental supply means the ureter has a relatively tenuous blood supply requiring careful surgical handling.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the middle portion of the ureter?

questions.explanation: Iliopsoas is the most powerful hip flexor in the fully extended hip position. Its large cross-sectional area and optimal moment arm at the hip make it the most forceful. Rectus femoris is a significant hip flexor at lower hip flexion angles. Sartorius contributes but is much weaker due to its smaller size. Iliopsoas weakness is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated or supine position.
questions.question: The rectus femoris, sartorius, and iliopsoas all flex the hip. Of these, which is the most powerful hip flexor in the fully extended hip position?
The gracilis muscle is frequently used as a free flap in reconstructive surgery. It is most suitable because of which anatomical feature?
questions.explanation: The gracilis muscle is frequently used in reconstructive surgery because of its consistent neurovascular pedicle (medial femoral circumflex artery perforators and the obturator nerve), manageable length and bulk, and relatively small donor site morbidity. It is used for facial reanimation, limb reconstruction, and dynamic graciloplasty for sphincter reconstruction in fecal incontinence.
options: Its large bulk and dual blood supply
Its ability to plantarflex the ankle
Its broad origin from the ischial tuberosity
Its dual nerve supply from femoral and obturator nerves
Its consistent neurovascular pedicle and manageable dimensions

questions.question: Where is the ideal location for pericardiocentesis?
questions.explanation: Pericardiocentesis is typically performed by inserting a needle just to the left of the xiphoid process, angled upward and posteriorly toward the left shoulder at about 30-45 degrees. This avoids the internal thoracic vessels and enters the pericardial cavity inferior to the heart. The procedure is performed under ECG and/or ultrasound guidance.

questions.question: Five bones uniquely possess epiphyseal plates at BOTH ends. Which set correctly identifies all five?
questions.explanation: Most long bones have only one epiphyseal plate at one end; however, five bones are unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius. This feature is important in understanding growth patterns and fracture management in these bones.

The sphenopalatine foramen in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa connects it with the nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the sphenoid bone and orbital process of the palatine bone. The sphenopalatine artery and nasopalatine nerve pass through it to supply the nasal cavity and septum.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the nasal cavity through which opening?

questions.explanation: The vocalis muscle, lying parallel and inferior to the vocal cord, controls fine adjustments of cord tension. The cricothyroid provides gross tension changes by tilting the thyroid cartilage. The vocalis can selectively tense different portions of the vocal cord for pitch modulation.
questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for fine adjustments of vocal cord tension?

questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as a continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the internal and common carotid arteries. The vein joins with the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
questions.question: The internal jugular vein begins at which anatomical location?
A primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at which gestational period?
questions.explanation: The primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at the 2nd month of intrauterine life. The ischium's primary centre appears during the 4th month, and the pubis during the 5th month. At birth, the hip bone is ossified except for the iliac crest, the Y-shaped cartilage, and a strip along the inferior margin.

The superior hypogastric plexus (at the L5-S1 level, anterior to the sacral promontory) divides into right and left hypogastric nerves, which descend into the pelvis alongside the rectum to contribute to the right and left inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses. The hypogastric nerves carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers. The inferior hypogastric plexuses also receive the pelvic splanchnic nerves (preganglionic parasympathetic, S2-S4) and branches from the sacral sympathetic ganglia. The combined plexuses supply pelvic viscera with both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation.
questions.question: The superior hypogastric plexus continues inferiorly as which structure?

options: Both lateral and medial pectoral nerves
questions.question: What nerve supplies pectoralis major?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major receives dual innervation from both lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) and medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1). The lateral pectoral nerve is the primary supply. The medial pectoral nerve must pierce pectoralis minor to reach pectoralis major.

The L3 sclerotome includes the hip joint, which receives innervation partly from the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Pain from L3 root pathology can be referred to the hip joint, and hip joint disease can refer pain along L3 dermatomal distribution to the anterior thigh and knee. This bidirectional referral is explained by Hilton's law and the concept of sclerotome overlap between spinal levels.
questions.question: In the lower limb, the term 'sclerotome' refers to the area of bone and deep structures supplied by a single spinal nerve root. Hip pain from L3 sclerotome involvement can mimic pain from which structure?
options: Hip joint itself (L3 innervates the hip)

questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is a fascial extension of the prevertebral fascia that encloses the axillary artery and brachial plexus cords. This tubular sheath provides a pathway for these structures through the axilla. Local anesthetic can be injected into this sheath for brachial plexus blocks.
options: Encloses axillary artery and brachial plexus
questions.question: What is the significance of the axillary sheath?
How many secondary ossification centres does the hip bone have in total?
questions.explanation: The hip bone has five secondary ossification centres: two for the iliac crest, two for the Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and one for the ischial tuberosity. All five fuse by 20-25 years of age. The three primary centres (ilium, ischium, pubis) appear in the 2nd, 4th, and 5th months of intrauterine life, respectively.

questions.question: Which muscle lies deep to the breast medially?
questions.explanation: Two-thirds of the breast's base lies on the pectoralis major muscle. The inferolateral one-third lies on the serratus anterior and external oblique muscles. The deep fascia of these muscles forms the posterior boundary of the retromammary space behind the breast.

questions.question: What causes peau d'orange appearance?
questions.explanation: Infiltration of Cooper's ligaments by breast cancer leads to their shortening, producing tethering of the skin with a characteristic dimpled appearance resembling orange peel (peau d'orange). This is an important clinical sign of locally advanced breast cancer. The dimpling becomes more apparent when the patient raises her arms.

questions.question: Which muscle extends and adducts the wrist?
questions.explanation: produces both extension and adduction (ulnar deviation) at the wrist joint. It works with flexor carpi ulnaris to produce pure adduction by balancing extension and flexion forces. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm compartment.

questions.question: Which muscle assists triceps in elbow extension?
questions.explanation: is a small triangular muscle that assists the triceps brachii in elbow extension. It lies on the lateral aspect of the elbow, blending with the triceps. Both muscles are supplied by the radial nerve and work together to extend the elbow.

The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis when the inner thigh is stroked) is mediated by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2). The sensory stimulus from the femoral branch travels to L1-L2, and the motor response via the genital branch causes contraction of the cremaster muscle. Absence of this reflex may indicate testicular torsion.
questions.question: What is the cremasteric reflex mediated by?

questions.explanation: The cardiac impression on the left lung is larger than that on the right lung because the heart is positioned more to the left side. The left ventricle forms most of the heart's left border and creates a large concave impression on the left lung's mediastinal surface.
questions.question: Which impression is largest on the left lung?
Which carpal bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuffbox floor is formed by the scaphoid proximally and the trapezium distally. The radial artery crosses the floor of this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture.

questions.question: What nerve is at risk in Bennett's fracture?
questions.explanation: The superficial branch of the radial nerve courses over the base of the first metacarpal and is at risk in Bennett's fracture (intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the thumb metacarpal base). Injury can cause numbness over the dorsum of the thumb and radial side of the hand.

Carpal tunnel syndrome commonly results from tenosynovitis (inflammatory reactions in synovial sheaths) of tendons traversing the tunnel. Excess fluid from inflammation compresses the median nerve within the confined space. This is one of the most common causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which condition involves synovial sheath inflammation in the carpal tunnel?
Which vessel is superior in the lung root?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery is the most superior structure in the root of both lungs. The main bronchus lies posterior to the vessels. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins are the most inferior structures in the root. This anatomical arrangement is constant and important during surgery.

questions.question: How do upper left intercostal veins drain?
questions.explanation: The upper three left posterior intercostal veins typically join to form the left superior intercostal vein, which crosses the aortic arch and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein. This provides a direct connection to the superior vena cava system without crossing to the right side.

questions.question: The pharyngeal recess (of Rosenm�ller) is located in which region?
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenm�ller) is a depression in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx behind the torus tubarius (Eustachian tube opening). Nasopharyngeal carcinomas commonly arise in this recess. The recess is bounded anteriorly by the tubal elevation and posteriorly by the adenoid pad. Deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from this region.

questions.question: The superior orbital fissure transmits which cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The superior orbital fissure transmits oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), and abducens (VI) nerves. It also transmits the superior ophthalmic vein. The fissure is bounded by the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid. The optic nerve passes through the separate optic canal.

questions.question: What causes superior vena cava syndrome?
questions.explanation: Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome results from obstruction or compression of the SVC, impairing venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Most cases are caused by malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma, metastases) compressing the SVC in the mediastinum. Clinical features include facial swelling, neck vein distension, and upper body edema.

questions.question: Which artery forms the main contribution to the superficial palmar arch?
questions.explanation: The superficial palmar arch is formed primarily by the ulnar artery with contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. The arch curves across the palm at the level of the distal border of the fully extended thumb. It gives rise to three common palmar digital arteries.

CT (computed tomography) scan with contrast is the best imaging modality for visualizing mediastinal structures. It provides excellent detail of masses, lymphadenopathy, vascular structures, and anatomical relationships. MRI is also excellent, particularly for vascular and cardiac structures. Chest X-ray provides basic information but limited detail.
questions.question: Which imaging best visualizes the mediastinum?

questions.explanation: To drain the apical (superior) segment of the lower lobe, the patient should lie prone with the head turned to one side. This position allows gravity to assist drainage of secretions from this segment. Different positions are used for postural drainage of different bronchopulmonary segments.
questions.question: What position drains apical lower lobe segment?

questions.explanation: During expiration, the right dome of the diaphragm reaches as high as the fifth rib due to the upward bulge of the right lobe of the liver. The left dome ascends to the fifth intercostal space. With maximal inspiration, the domes flatten out considerably, descending several centimeters.
questions.question: At which rib does right dome reach during expiration?
Which structure indents each renal papilla?
questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces in each kidney. Two or three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.

questions.question: Which condition causes anterior dislocation of the lunate?
questions.explanation: Anterior dislocation of the lunate occurs from falling on a dorsiflexed wrist. The lunate is forced anteriorly and compresses the carpal tunnel contents including the median nerve. This causes carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms with paresthesia and thenar muscle weakness. The lunate also risks avascular necrosis.

The hypoglossal canal is located in the occipital bone above the anterolateral margin of the foramen magnum. It transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII) from the posterior cranial fossa to the neck. The canal is about 1 cm long. Skull base fractures involving this canal can cause tongue paralysis.
questions.question: Which bone contains the hypoglossal canal?

questions.explanation: McBurney's point, located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, marks the base of the appendix where it attaches to the cecum. While the position of the appendix tip is highly variable, the base is consistently located at the confluence of the three taeniae coli on the posteromedialaaspect of the cecum.
questions.question: Which structure marks McBurney's point on the abdominal surface?

questions.explanation: The levator anguli oris is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It elevates the angle of the mouth during smiling. The muscle arises from the canine fossa of the maxilla and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It lies deep to levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor muscles.
questions.question: The levator anguli oris muscle is innervated by which nerve branch?

questions.explanation: The diaphragm is highest in the supine position and after a large meal due to upward pressure from abdominal viscera. When lying on one side, the dependent (lower) diaphragm is considerably higher than the uppermost one. Position affects diaphragm function and is clinically relevant.
questions.question: Which position elevates the diaphragm highest?

questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensory innervation to the anal canal below the pectinate line, making this region sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature. The inferior rectal nerve also provides motor innervation to the external anal sphincter. Above the pectinate line, the anal canal receives autonomic innervation (from inferior hypogastric plexus), making it insensitive to pain but responsive to stretch. This difference explains why internal hemorrhoids (above pectinate line) are painless while external hemorrhoids (below the line) are painful.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation below the pectinate line?
Which movement at the wrist joint is produced by extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris?
questions.explanation: at the wrist joint (ulnar deviation) is produced by the combined action of extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris. These muscles work synergistically despite being in different compartments. The wrist joint permits movement along two axes as an ellipsoid synovial joint.

Reducing the moment arm of the hip abductors (by medializing the hip center or using a low-offset prosthesis) means the abductor muscles must generate greater force to produce the same abductor moment needed to stabilize the pelvis. This increased muscle force also increases the hip joint reaction force, potentially accelerating bearing surface wear in hip replacements. Restoring femoral offset is therefore biomechanically important.
options: Improved hip abductor muscle strength reducing the limp overall
Improved Trendelenburg gait pattern after total hip arthroplasty
Reduced abductor moment arm requiring greater muscle force and increased joint reaction force
No clinical consequence for gait or joint loading
Reduced knee and ankle pain from altered load distribution only
questions.question: The hip abductor moment is critical in preventing pelvic drop during single-leg stance. If the moment arm of the hip abductors (gluteus medius) is surgically reduced (e.g., by a high femoral offset prosthesis), what is the clinical consequence?

questions.explanation: Sympathetic efferents from the thoracic sympathetic trunk cause bronchodilation and inhibit secretion from bronchial glands. This is clinically important in conditions like asthma where bronchodilators (sympathomimetics) are used therapeutically. Parasympathetic stimulation from the vagus causes bronchoconstriction.
questions.question: What causes bronchodilation in the lungs?
Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded laterally by the sartorius muscle, medially by the adductor longus muscle, and superiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor is formed by iliopsoas (laterally) and pectineus (medially), covered by fascia. The roof is formed by fascia lata. The triangle contains (from lateral to medial): femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space/lymphatics (NAVEL mnemonic). The femoral artery, vein, and canal lie within the femoral sheath (prolongation of transversalis and iliacus fascia), while the femoral nerve lies lateral to the sheath. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for femoral vessel access.

questions.question: What causes cubital tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Cubital tunnel syndrome results from ulnar nerve compression as it passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle. This is the most common site of ulnar nerve entrapment. Symptoms include numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and intrinsic hand muscle weakness.
