The ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver), representing the obliterated left umbilical vein, runs from the umbilicus to the liver within the free inferior border of the falciform ligament. Upon reaching the liver, it continues in a fissure on the visceral surface between the left and quadrate lobes before joining the left branch of the portal vein. The ligamentum teres may remain patent in portal hypertension, allowing portosystemic anastomosis through paraumbilical veins, potentially leading to caput medusae. At the umbilicus, it connects to the median umbilical ligament (obliterated urachus).
questions.question: The ligamentum teres hepatis is found in which structure?

options: Femoral rollback during knee flexion, improving flexion range
Anterior knee stability against tibial translation only
Patellar tracking and extensor alignment correction
questions.explanation: The primary biomechanical argument for retaining the PCL in total knee replacement is that it provides femoral rollback during knee flexion: as the knee flexes, the PCL pulls the femoral condyles posteriorly, increasing flexion range and reducing quadriceps force needed for stair climbing. PCL-substituting (posterior-stabilized) designs use a cam and post mechanism to replicate this rollback when the PCL is sacrificed.
questions.question: In a total knee replacement (TKR), the posterior cruciate ligament is either retained or resected. The primary biomechanical argument for retaining the PCL is that it provides which function?

questions.explanation: The fundus and upper body of the stomach contain the highest concentration of parietal cells in the gastric glands. The cardiac region contains mainly mucous-secreting cells. The pyloric region contains mainly mucous cells and G cells (which secrete gastrin). This distribution reflects the functional specialization of different gastric regions.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach has the highest concentration of parietal cells?

questions.explanation: The areola is a dark pink-brownish circular area of skin (22-60 mm in diameter) that surrounds the nipple. Its color varies with parity and race, darkening during the second month of pregnancy. The areola contains Montgomery's glands (areola glands) which enlarge during pregnancy and lactation.
questions.question: What structure surrounds the nipple?
Tibialis posterior, inverting the foot and plantarflexing the ankle, primarily supports which arch of the foot?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is the primary dynamic supporter of the medial longitudinal arch. It inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, all three cuneiform bones, cuboid, sustentaculum tali, and bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals. Rupture of the tibialis posterior tendon leads to progressive adult flatfoot deformity (acquired pes planus).

Vagotomy involves division of the vagal trunks or branches to reduce gastric acid secretion and was historically performed for peptic ulcer disease. Truncal vagotomy (dividing the main trunks) requires a drainage procedure (pyloroplasty) as it impairs gastric emptying. Highly selective vagotomy (dividing only the branches to the acid-secreting fundus/body) preserves antral innervation and pyloric function.
questions.question: Which procedure divides the vagal trunks to reduce acid secretion?
The parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall is supplied by which vessels?
questions.explanation: The parietal peritoneum lining the anterior abdominal wall receives blood supply from the same vessels that supply the overlying abdominal wall: superior and inferior epigastric arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery, and lumbar arteries. The peritoneum overlying the diaphragm is supplied by the musculophrenic and phrenic arteries, while that in the pelvis is supplied by branches of the internal iliac artery. The visceral peritoneum covering the organs receives its blood supply from the arteries supplying those organs (celiac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries). Venous and lymphatic drainage follows arterial supply patterns.

questions.question: What sensation is lost in ulnar nerve palsy at the wrist?
questions.explanation: Ulnar nerve palsy at the wrist causes sensory loss over the medial one and one-half fingers (little finger and ulnar half of ring finger) on both palmar and dorsal aspects. The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist, so its distribution may be spared depending on injury level.

questions.question: Which condition requires nerve conduction studies for diagnosis?
questions.explanation: diagnosis is confirmed by nerve conduction studies showing delayed median nerve conduction across the wrist. These studies measure sensory and motor nerve conduction velocities. Electromyography may also show denervation changes in thenar muscles in severe cases.

questions.question: Tibial nerve injury in the tarsal tunnel (tarsal tunnel syndrome) presents with pain and paraesthesia on the sole of the foot. Which action is specifically lost?
options: Plantarflexion of toes and plantar sensation
questions.explanation: Tarsal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. It presents with pain, burning, and paraesthesia on the sole of the foot and intrinsic muscle weakness. Plantarflexion of the toes and intrinsic muscle function are impaired. Tinel's sign may be positive over the tarsal tunnel at the medial ankle.

The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen after traversing the facial canal. It then enters the parotid gland and divides into five terminal branches. Damage at this location causes complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including loss of taste to anterior two-thirds of tongue.
questions.question: The stylomastoid foramen transmits which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the hepatoduodenal ligament (free right edge of lesser omentum) containing the portal triad as its anterior boundary. The superior boundary is formed by the caudate lobe of liver covered with peritoneum, the inferior boundary by the first part of the duodenum (superior or horizontal part), and the posterior boundary by the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum and the right crus of the diaphragm. This opening, typically admitting two fingers, provides the only communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs.
questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?

questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from skin of the anterior abdominal wall follows the watershed principle: above the umbilicus drains to axillary nodes, below the umbilicus drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and the umbilicus itself drains primarily to superficial inguinal nodes though some drainage may occur to both axillary and inguinal nodes. The deep abdominal wall lymphatics drain along the deep vessels (superior epigastric, inferior epigastric, lumbar) to internal thoracic, external iliac, and para-aortic nodes. Metastatic tumor deposits at the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph node) typically indicate advanced intra-abdominal malignancy spreading via lymphatics or direct extension.
questions.question: Which lymph node group drains the skin of the umbilicus?
The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as which artery?
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as the femoral artery, lying lateral to the femoral vein. The femoral artery enters the femoral triangle at this level and gives off the profunda femoris approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to the thigh muscles.

questions.question: Which vein drains the first posterior intercostal space?
questions.explanation: The first posterior intercostal space on the right side drains into the right brachiocephalic vein. The remaining intercostal spaces on the right drain into the azygos vein. On the left, the upper three spaces typically drain into the left brachiocephalic vein through the left superior intercostal vein.

questions.question: What maintains negative intrapleural pressure?
questions.explanation: The elastic recoil of the lungs pulling inward, opposed by the chest wall's tendency to spring outward, creates and maintains the negative (sub-atmospheric) pressure in the pleural cavity. This negative pressure is essential for keeping the lungs expanded and prevents their collapse.

questions.question: How does understanding upper limb anatomy improve clinical practice?
options: Only surgeons find this clinically useful
Enables accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and complication prediction
questions.explanation: Comprehensive upper limb anatomy knowledge enables accurate clinical diagnosis (recognizing nerve injury patterns, fracture complications), appropriate treatment planning (surgical approaches, nerve blocks, rehabilitation), and complication prediction (vascular injury risk, nerve vulnerability). Integration of anatomical knowledge with clinical presentation is essential for optimal patient care.

options: It originates from the rim of the acetabulum
It is supplied exclusively by the obturator nerve
Does not cross the hip joint; supplied by the common fibular nerve
It inserts into the medial tibial condyle distally
It is classified as a medial compartment muscle
questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris does not cross the hip joint (originating from the linea aspera, not the ischial tuberosity) and therefore cannot extend the hip. It is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve, unlike all other hamstrings which are supplied by the tibial division. It only flexes the knee and laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed.
questions.question: The short head of biceps femoris differs from the other hamstrings in which critical way?

questions.explanation: Crutch palsy results from radial nerve compression in the axilla due to improperly fitted crutches pressing against the nerve. This causes wrist drop and loss of finger extension. The condition is preventable by ensuring crutches are properly adjusted to avoid axillary pressure.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in crutch palsy?
Which structure forms the floor of the maxillary sinus?
questions.explanation: The alveolar process of the maxilla forms the floor of the maxillary sinus. Roots of the upper premolar and molar teeth may project into the sinus, separated only by thin bone or mucosa. Dental infections can spread to the sinus, and tooth extraction can create an oroantral fistula. The floor is typically 1-2 cm below the nasal floor.

questions.question: What is unique about segmental blood supply?
questions.explanation: There is little anastomosis between the arteries (branches of pulmonary artery) supplying adjacent bronchopulmonary segments. This anatomical feature allows individual segments to be surgically resected without significantly affecting neighboring segments. Each segment functions as an independent unit.

questions.question: The greater omentum is attached to which part of the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The greater omentum (specifically its posterior two layers after folding back from the inferior descent) attaches to the anterior surface (and superior border) of the transverse colon and its mesocolon. The omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach, descends anterior to the small intestine, then folds back on itself and fuses with the transverse colon and mesocolon before continuing to the posterior abdominal wall. This four-layered structure contains fat and can wall off inflamed organs (giving it the name "abdominal policeman"), provides insulation, and allows mobility of abdominal contents.

questions.question: Which nerve provides sensation to the upper eyelid?
questions.explanation: The supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (branches of the frontal nerve from V1) provide sensation to the upper eyelid and forehead. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper lid. Infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial canthus and side of nose. These are all branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, superior pole of the left kidney, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum fused to the transverse mesocolon. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum (anterior two layers); superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; inferiorly by the transverse colon and mesocolon; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac appear on imaging as fluid between stomach and pancreas.

questions.question: Which nerve provides motor supply to diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. Each phrenic nerve supplies its corresponding half of the diaphragm up to the margin of the esophageal opening. Injury to the phrenic nerve results in paralysis of that hemidiaphragm with consequent elevation.

questions.question: The vermiform appendix typically arises from which part of the cecum?
questions.explanation: The vermiform appendix arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. The three taeniae coli of the cecum converge at the base of the appendix, serving as a reliable landmark for locating it during surgery. While the base of the appendix has a relatively constant position, its tip can be found in various locations: retrocecal (65%), pelvic (31%), subcecal (2.3%), preileal (1%), or postileal (0.4%). The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, runs through the mesoappendix to supply the appendix.

The major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater) in the second part of the duodenum marks the embryological and vascular transition between foregut (supplied by celiac trunk) and midgut (supplied by superior mesenteric artery). The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal, ultimately from celiac trunk) supplies the duodenum and pancreatic head above this point, while the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA) supplies structures below it. This dual blood supply creates an anastomotic arcade providing collateral circulation between the two major arterial territories and reflects the embryological division of the primitive gut.
questions.question: Which structure marks the junction of the foregut and midgut blood supply?
The main blood supply to the medial compartment of the thigh comes from which two arteries?
questions.explanation: The medial fascial compartment of the thigh receives its blood supply from the profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery via its perforating branches and from the obturator artery. The nerve supply is from the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4). The profunda femoris is the major blood supply to all three thigh compartments via its perforating branches.

The free right edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the portal triad: portal vein (posteriorly), common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), and hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left). This arrangement is remembered by the mnemonic "DAV" from anterior to posterior (Duct, Artery, Vein). The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen and can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding hepatic arterial and portal venous inflow.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum?

questions.explanation: Erb's paralysis produces the "policeman's tip hand" or "porter's tip hand" deformity. The arm hangs by the side adducted and medially rotated, the forearm is extended and pronated. This results from paralysis of muscles supplied by C5-C6 nerve roots (deltoid, biceps, brachialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus).
questions.question: What is the characteristic deformity in Erb's paralysis?

questions.explanation: has no bony attachment distally; it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. This muscle is absent in approximately 15% of people without functional deficit. It can be used as a tendon graft source in reconstructive surgery.
questions.question: Which forearm muscle has no bony attachment distally?

questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery is typically the first branch of the external carotid artery, arising just below the carotid bifurcation. It descends to supply the thyroid gland and gives off the superior laryngeal artery. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve accompanies this artery and innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
questions.question: The superior thyroid artery is typically the first branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: Six vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen: superior gluteal artery and vein, inferior gluteal artery and vein, and internal pudendal artery and vein. Together with seven nerves and the piriformis muscle, they constitute the 14 structures passing through this critical anatomical gateway from the pelvis to the gluteal region.
questions.question: How many vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen?

questions.explanation: The umbilicus typically corresponds to the level of the intervertebral disc between L3 and L4 vertebrae, though its position varies with body habitus, age, pregnancy, and previous surgery. The transumbilical plane passing through the umbilicus divides the abdomen into upper and lower halves and is used clinically to define abdominal quadrants. The skin at the umbilicus receives sensory innervation from the T10 dermatome ("belly button at T10"), making this a useful landmark for assessing spinal cord levels. In neonates, the umbilicus lies relatively higher (near L2).
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the umbilicus?

questions.explanation: The inferior meatus receives the opening of the nasolacrimal duct beneath the inferior turbinate. No paranasal sinuses drain into the inferior meatus. The maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle meatus. The posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus. The sphenoid drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.
questions.question: Which sinus opens into the inferior meatus?

questions.explanation: Chordae tendineae attach the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles, preventing the cusps from prolapsing into the atria during ventricular systole when intraventricular pressure is high. Papillary muscles contract just before ventricular contraction, tensing the chordae. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes severe valve regurgitation requiring urgent surgical repair.
questions.question: What prevents the AV valves from prolapsing into the atria?
Which muscle forms the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of this triangle consists of transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon), representing a potential weak area in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery, in contrast to indirect hernias which emerge lateral to the artery through the deep inguinal ring.

questions.question: What produces index finger independent extension?
questions.explanation: allows independent extension of the index finger, supplementing extensor digitorum action. This is particularly useful for pointing while making a fist. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm and supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the appendix. It runs in the mesoappendix (the peritoneal fold connecting the appendix to the mesentery). This is an end artery without significant anastomoses, making the appendix vulnerable to ischemia if the vessel thromboses (as in appendicitis). The artery typically runs behind the terminal ileum.
questions.question: What is the blood supply to the appendix?
What creates the aortic knuckle on X-ray?
questions.explanation: The aortic knuckle (or aortic knob) is the prominent shadow on a chest X-ray created by the aortic arch as it curves backward and to the left at the level of T4/5. This is a normal finding and an important landmark. Widening may indicate aortic aneurysm or dissection.

questions.question: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated at which surface anatomical location?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery curves to enter the tarsal tunnel and then the sole of the foot. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. The four main pulse points of the lower limb are femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.
options: Anterior surface of the ankle between malleoli
Dorsum of foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus
Midway between lateral malleolus and calcaneus

questions.explanation: The fovea centralis is a depression in the center of the macula lutea, representing the area of most acute vision. It contains only cones (no rods) and has minimal overlying retinal layers to reduce light scatter. The fovea is located temporal to the optic disc. Macular degeneration causes central vision loss.
questions.question: The fovea centralis is located in which structure?
Which nerve supplies somatic sensation below the pectinate line?
questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensation below the pectinate line, making this area sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature. Above the pectinate line, the anal canal is supplied by autonomic (visceral) nerves and is insensitive to these stimuli but sensitive to stretch. This explains why internal hemorrhoids are painless while external hemorrhoids are painful.

The azygos system provides important collateral circulation between the superior and inferior vena cava systems. If either major vein is obstructed, the azygos system can enlarge significantly to provide an alternative route for blood return to the heart. This is visible on imaging as dilated azygos and intercostal veins.
questions.question: What is the clinical significance of azygos system?
Which lymph nodes lie along the sternum?
questions.explanation: The parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum. They receive lymph from the anterior chest wall, medial breast, diaphragm, and upper abdominal wall. Efferents drain to the bronchomediastinal trunks and brachiocephalic veins.

The brachial artery lies in the anterior compartment of the arm, medial to the biceps brachii. It is accompanied by the median nerve and basilic vein. The artery is separated from the posterior compartment by the medial intermuscular septum.
questions.question: Which compartment contains the brachial artery in the arm?

options: Proximal injuries affect more muscles than distal injuries
questions.question: How does nerve injury level affect clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: Nerve injury level critically affects presentation: proximal median nerve injury affects all forearm flexors and hand muscles; carpal tunnel syndrome spares forearm muscles. Similarly, ulnar nerve injury at elbow affects forearm flexors; wrist injury doesn't. Injury level determines which muscles and sensory territories are affected.

Lymphatic drainage from the stomach first passes to regional lymph node groups along the lesser curvature (left and right gastric nodes), greater curvature (left and right gastroepiploic nodes), and around the cardia (paracardial nodes). From these first-tier nodes, lymph flows to second-tier nodes along the celiac trunk and its branches (celiac, hepatic, and splenic nodes), then to pre-aortic nodes, and finally to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This extensive lymphatic drainage explains the potential for widespread metastases in gastric cancer and the need for extended lymphadenectomy in curative surgery.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive direct drainage from the stomach?
Which part of the humerus is most commonly associated with radial nerve injury?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve winds around the spiral groove of the humerus accompanied by profunda brachii vessels. Midshaft humeral fractures frequently damage the radial nerve at this location. This results in wrist drop due to paralysis of extensor muscles and sensory loss over the dorsal hand.

questions.question: Which component comprises the majority of splenic tissue?
questions.explanation: The red pulp comprises approximately 76-79% of normal splenic tissue and consists of blood-filled sinusoids and splenic cords (cords of Billroth). The red pulp is responsible for filtering blood, removing old or damaged erythrocytes, and recycling iron. It appears red due to the large number of red blood cells in the sinusoids.

questions.question: Which vessels run with the phrenic nerve?
questions.explanation: The pericardiacophrenic vessels (branches of internal thoracic artery and vein) accompany the phrenic nerve on each side as it descends through the thorax to the diaphragm. These vessels supply the pericardium, pleura, and diaphragm. The phrenic nerve lies between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura.

The portal tract (portal triad) is located at the corners of hepatic lobules and contains branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, surrounded by connective tissue. Some also include lymphatic vessels. The portal triad delivers blood and removes bile from the hepatic lobule. The hepatic artery provides oxygen; the portal vein provides nutrients and metabolites from the GI tract.
questions.question: Which hepatic structure contains the portal triad?
How many lactiferous duct openings are on nipple?
questions.explanation: There are 15-20 lactiferous ducts that open by the same number of openings on the summit of the nipple. Each duct drains one lobe of the mammary gland. Deep to the areola, each duct has a dilated portion called the lactiferous sinus where milk can be stored.

Goblet cells that secrete mucus are abundant in the large intestinal mucosa and increase in number toward the rectum. The mucus lubricates the passage of increasingly solid feces and protects the mucosa. Large intestinal crypts (of Lieberk?hn) lack villi and contain mainly goblet cells and absorptive colonocytes. Paneth cells are found only in the small intestine.
questions.question: Which cells are characteristic of the large intestinal mucosa?
Which structure separates the oral cavity from the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the boundary between the oral cavity and oropharynx. The arch contains the palatoglossus muscle and extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the oral cavity and oropharynx, bounded by these arches.

questions.question: How many leaves does the central tendon of the diaphragm have?
questions.explanation: The central tendon is trifoliate (three-leafed), resembling a clover leaf with right, left, and middle (anterior) leaflets. The right leaflet is the largest. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right and middle leaflets. The heart in its pericardium rests on the superior surface of the central tendon.

questions.question: What is the only electrical connection between atria and ventricles?
questions.explanation: The bundle of His (AV bundle) is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and ventricles, as the fibrous skeleton of the heart electrically insulates these chambers. It arises from the AV node, penetrates the fibrous skeleton, and divides into right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum. Accessory pathways (e.g., WPW syndrome) can create additional abnormal connections.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the deep palmar arch?
options: Deep hand structures and palmar metacarpal arteries
questions.explanation: The deep palmar arch (formed primarily by radial artery) supplies blood to deep hand structures and gives off palmar metacarpal arteries. These metacarpal arteries provide important contributions to digital blood supply. The arch lies approximately 1cm proximal to the superficial arch.

questions.question: What are signs of tension pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: Signs of tension pneumothorax include: respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from affected side, hyperresonance to percussion, and absent breath sounds on the affected side. The diagnosis is clinical and treatment (needle decompression followed by chest tube) should NOT be delayed for chest X-ray confirmation.

questions.question: The porta hepatis contains which structures?
questions.explanation: The porta hepatis (gateway to the liver) on the inferior surface of the liver contains the right and left branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery proper, and hepatic ducts, along with lymphatic vessels and hepatic nerve plexuses. The structures are arranged with bile ducts anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery anteriorly and to the left, and portal vein posteriorly. The hepatic veins and IVC are not at the porta but rather on the posterior surface of the liver. The porta hepatis forms the floor of the fissure for the ligamentum venosum and is continuous with the hepatoduodenal ligament.

questions.question: What clinical sign suggests pneumomediastinum?
questions.explanation: Hamman's sign (also called Hamman's crunch) is a crunching or clicking sound synchronous with the heartbeat, heard on auscultation over the precordium in pneumomediastinum. It's caused by the heart beating against air-filled tissue. The sign is named after Dr. Louis Hamman who described it in 1939.

questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately medial to the kidney?
questions.explanation: The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially to each kidney, forming part of its posterior relation. A psoas abscess can cause confusion with renal pathology due to this proximity. The quadratus lumborum lies directly posterior to the mid-portion of the kidney, while the transversus abdominis and its aponeurosis lie posterolaterally.

questions.question: What are gray rami communicantes?
questions.explanation: Gray rami communicantes carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers from sympathetic ganglia back to all spinal nerves for distribution to blood vessels, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles throughout the body. They are "gray" because postganglionic fibers are unmyelinated. Gray rami exist at all spinal levels unlike white rami.

The scaphoid and trapezium bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. The boundaries are formed by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally, and extensor pollicis longus medially. The radial artery crosses the floor.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the anatomical snuffbox floor?
Which structure lies immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery in the carotid sheath?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the internal carotid artery within the carotid sheath. The vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the artery and vein. The sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the sheath. This anatomical arrangement is important for central venous catheterization and carotid endarterectomy.

The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4), the largest branch of the lumbar plexus, emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle near the inguinal ligament and descends in the groove between psoas and iliacus. It enters the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle. Other branches emerging from psoas major's lateral border include the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves. The obturator nerve, in contrast, emerges from the medial border of psoas, while the genitofemoral nerve pierces through its anterior surface.
questions.question: The femoral nerve emerges from which muscle's lateral border?
Which muscle retracts the mandible?
questions.explanation: The posterior (horizontal) fibers of the temporalis muscle retract (pull back) the protruded mandible. The masseter and medial pterygoid elevate, while the lateral pterygoid protrudes. Bilateral contraction of temporalis elevates the mandible; unilateral posterior fibers retract ipsilaterally.

questions.question: What is the most common primary mediastinal tumor?
questions.explanation: In adults, thymoma is the most common primary tumor of the anterior mediastinum. Overall, the most common mediastinal masses vary by location: anterior (thymoma, lymphoma, germ cell tumors - "4 T's": Thymus, Thyroid, Teratoma, Terrible lymphoma); middle (lymphadenopathy, cysts); posterior (neurogenic tumors, esophageal lesions). In children, neurogenic tumors and lymphomas are most common.

The left colic artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the distal one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, and left colic (splenic) flexure through its ascending branch. The ascending branch anastomoses with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery of Drummond. This anastomosis at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) represents the watershed between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories and is vulnerable to ischemia. The splenic flexure may be relatively poorly supplied by collaterals, making it susceptible to ischemic colitis in low-flow states.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the distal third of the transverse colon?

questions.explanation: The quadratus femoris forms a 'red carpet' muscular protective layer for the sciatic nerve as it descends in the gluteal region. This coverage is surgically important during posterior hip approaches, where quadratus femoris must be carefully reflected to avoid sciatic nerve injury. It also acts as a lateral rotator of the hip joint.
options: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.question: During a posterior approach to the hip joint, which muscle forms a 'red carpet' protecting the sciatic nerve?

questions.explanation: The radial nerve (C5-T1) is the largest branch of the brachial plexus and the most frequently injured. It arises from the posterior cord and supplies all extensor muscles of the upper limb. The nerve is particularly vulnerable in the spiral groove of the humerus.
questions.question: Which nerve is the largest branch of the brachial plexus?

questions.explanation: The duodenum is approximately 25 cm (10 inches) in length and represents the first and shortest part of the small intestine. Despite being the shortest segment, it is the widest portion of the small intestine. The duodenum is predominantly retroperitoneal except for the first 2 cm (the duodenal cap or ampulla).
questions.question: What is the standard length of the duodenum in adults?

questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery typically divides into frontal (anterior) and parietal (posterior) branches after entering the skull through the foramen spinosum. The frontal branch crosses the pterion area. The parietal branch supplies the posterior parietal region. Epidural hematomas most commonly involve the frontal branch in the pterion region.
questions.question: The middle meningeal artery commonly divides into which branches?
Which structure receives blood from both celiac and superior mesenteric arteries?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon has a dual blood supply: the right two-thirds from the middle colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery (midgut supply) and the left third from the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut supply). The junction between these territories forms the marginal artery (of Drummond) and represents the watershed area most vulnerable to ischemia.

questions.question: Which artery accompanies the hypoglossal nerve?
questions.explanation: The lingual artery arises from the external carotid at the level of the hyoid bone and is closely related to the hypoglossal nerve. The nerve crosses superficial to the artery as it loops forward. The artery divides into dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The hyoglossus muscle separates superficial from deep structures.

questions.question: Which vein forms a portosystemic anastomosis at the esophagus?
questions.explanation: At the lower esophagus, esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal system, draining to portal vein) anastomose with esophageal veins draining the middle third of the esophagus into the azygos system (systemic circulation to SVC). In portal hypertension, these anastomoses dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing massive hematemesis. This is one of four main portosystemic anastomoses (others: rectum, umbilicus, retroperitoneal). The left gastric vein ascends along the lesser curvature to drain directly into the portal vein, receiving esophageal tributaries that create the anastomosis.

questions.question: The head of the femur is directed medially, upward, and forward, forming what fraction of a sphere?
questions.explanation: The head of the femur forms two-thirds of a sphere and is directed medially, upward, and forward. It articulates with the acetabulum to form the hip joint. The fovea capitis on the head transmits blood from the obturator artery through the ligament of the head of femur.

questions.question: Where does the membranous urethra pass through?
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch), specifically through the sphincter urethrae (external urethral sphincter). This is the shortest (1-2 cm) and narrowest part of the male urethra and the least distensible. It is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter, which is under voluntary control.

questions.question: How do digital arteries ensure blood supply to fingertips?
options: Single artery to each digit only
Dual proper digital arteries with extensive anastomoses
questions.explanation: Each finger receives two proper palmar digital arteries (one on each side from common digital arteries). These anastomose extensively, providing redundant blood supply. Additional dorsal digital arteries contribute. This rich vascular network protects fingertip perfusion critical for hand function.

questions.question: What does the medial arcuate ligament overlie?
questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of the fascia covering the anterior surface of psoas major muscle. It extends from the side of the body of L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process of L1. The lateral arcuate ligament overlies quadratus lumborum muscle.

The third (horizontal or inferior) part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the right psoas major muscle, the right ureter, and the right testicular/ovarian vessels at approximately the L3 vertebral level. This portion of the duodenum runs transversely from right to left and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein, with the root of the mesentery of the small intestine crossing it obliquely. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can occur when the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly.
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta?

questions.explanation: The marginal zone, located between the white pulp and red pulp, contains specialized marginal zone B lymphocytes and macrophages that capture blood-borne antigens and particulate matter. It is the first site of contact between blood-borne antigens and the immune system. Marginal zone B cells can rapidly differentiate into antibody-producing cells without requiring T cell help.
questions.question: What is the function of the marginal zone in the spleen?

questions.explanation: The sternal part of the diaphragm consists of two small muscular slips (or sometimes just fibrous tissue) that attach to the posterior surface of the xiphoid process. These are the smallest attachments of the diaphragm and may be absent, leaving a gap (the sternocostal triangle or foramen of Morgagni) through which superior epigastric vessels and lymphatics pass.
questions.question: What attaches the diaphragm to the xiphoid process?
What is the differential for anterior mediastinal mass?
questions.explanation: The differential diagnosis for anterior mediastinal masses is remembered by the "4 T's": Thymus (thymoma, thymic hyperplasia), Thyroid (retrosternal goiter, thyroid cancer), Teratoma (and other germ cell tumors), and Terrible lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma). Age and imaging characteristics help narrow the differential.

The lateral pterygoid assists in opening the jaw against resistance (along with gravity, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric). The suprahyoid muscles provide the main force when opening against resistance. Lateral pterygoid protrudes and depresses the mandible. All other muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close the jaw.
questions.question: Which muscle opens the jaw against resistance?

questions.explanation: The suprapatellar bursa extends approximately 3-5 cm above the superior pole of the patella, beneath the quadriceps tendon, and communicates freely with the knee joint cavity. In knee effusions, fluid accumulates in this bursa as well as the joint space, creating the characteristic fluctuant fullness above the patella. Aspiration is performed by needle insertion into the suprapatellar pouch.
questions.question: The knee joint has a synovial membrane that is extensive. The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the knee joint cavity and is clinically important because it extends how far above the patella?
options: 3�5 cm above the superior patellar pole beneath the quadriceps tendon
1 cm above the superior pole of the patella
To the level of the anterior superior iliac spine
Only to the level of the patella
10 cm above the patella into the anterior thigh

questions.question: Which vein arches over the right bronchus?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus at the level of T4 before draining into the superior vena cava. This creates a characteristic arch visible on chest radiographs. The azygos arch relationship to the bronchus is an important anatomical landmark.

questions.question: Which vessel crosses anterior to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) and the root of the mesentery cross anteriorly to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant as compression by these vessels can cause superior mesenteric artery syndrome. The third part of the duodenum crosses the vertebral column from right to left at the L3 level.

questions.question: What is the most common site for peritoneal metastases in females?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in females and is therefore the most common site for peritoneal metastases, free fluid (ascites), and pelvic abscesses to collect. It can be assessed by pelvic examination (palpable through the posterior vaginal fornix) and accessed by culdocentesis for diagnostic aspiration.

questions.question: At which intercostal space does nipple usually lie?
questions.explanation: In males and most young nulliparous women, the nipple lies opposite the 4th intercostal space, approximately 10 cm from the anterior midline. This position is variable in females and changes with age, pregnancy, and parity. The position is more constant in males.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the bladder?
questions.explanation: The superior vesical arteries (usually multiple branches) arise from the patent part of the umbilical artery and supply the superior surface and upper lateral surfaces of the bladder. The umbilical artery is obliterated distally (becoming the medial umbilical ligament) but remains patent proximally. The inferior vesical artery (in males) or vaginal artery (in females) supplies the bladder base.

questions.question: Which surface landmark on the femur, below the greater trochanter, represents the insertion of the gluteus maximus?
questions.explanation: The gluteal tuberosity is located below the greater trochanter and serves as the insertion point for gluteus maximus. The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. Knowing these distinctions is critical in hip replacement surgery.

questions.question: Which structure is palpable in the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox and is palpable in this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture. The radial artery pulse can also be felt crossing the snuffbox floor.

questions.question: The hepatic portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence, though variations exist. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and lacks valves.

questions.question: Which muscle tenses the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is the only muscle that tenses (lengthens) the vocal cords by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid. It is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.question: The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is best described as the main artery of which part of a long bone?
questions.explanation: The nutrient artery, also called the medullary artery, is the main blood supply to the diaphysis of a long bone. It enters through the nutrient canal and nutrient foramen, branching within the medullary cavity. The epiphysis, metaphysis, and periosteum all have their own distinct arterial supplies from separate named vessels.

questions.question: Which layer of the gut wall contains Meissner's plexus?
questions.explanation: Meissner's (submucosal) plexus is located in the submucosa between the inner circular and the mucosa layers. It primarily regulates secretion and blood flow in the gut wall. The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers and primarily controls motility. Together these form the enteric nervous system.

questions.question: What produces circumduction at the shoulder joint?
questions.explanation: Circumduction at the shoulder joint is a sequential combination of flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction movements. This creates a conical movement pattern of the limb. Multiple muscles act in coordinated sequence to produce this composite movement.

questions.question: What is the narrowest point of esophagus?
questions.explanation: The narrowest point of the esophagus is at its origin at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. This is the most common site for foreign body impaction and the site requiring most care during esophagoscopy to avoid perforation.

The interosseous membrane between radius and ulna serves multiple functions: separates anterior and posterior compartments, provides muscle attachment surface, transmits forces from radius to ulna, and contains apertures for interosseous vessels. It maintains the spatial relationship between the two forearm bones.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the interosseous membrane?

questions.explanation: The "critical zone" in the supraspinatus tendon has relatively poor vascularity, located approximately 1cm from its humeral insertion. This hypovascular area is more susceptible to degenerative changes and tears. The zone's poor blood supply impairs healing after injury.
questions.question: What is the significance of the critical zone in the supraspinatus tendon?
The spleen develops in relation to which mesentery?
questions.explanation: The spleen develops within the dorsal mesogastrium (greater omentum) during embryonic development, explaining its position in the left upper quadrant and its peritoneal attachments. The gastrosplenic ligament (part of the dorsal mesogastrium) connects it to the greater curvature of the stomach, while the splenorenal ligament attaches it to the left kidney. Although the spleen is not a gastrointestinal organ, it receives its blood supply from the celiac trunk (via splenic artery) due to this developmental relationship. The tail of the pancreas also develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, extending into the splenorenal ligament.

The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk (a branch of the subclavian artery) and ascends to supply the lower poles of the thyroid gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerve has an intimate relationship with this artery, passing either anterior or posterior to it. The superior thyroid artery supplies the upper poles.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the thyroid gland inferiorly?

options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. It exits the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis. Injury to this nerve (during posterior hip surgery or gluteal injections) causes Trendelenburg sign due to loss of hip abduction and medial rotation. It carries no cutaneous branches.
questions.question: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies which muscles?
What nerve supplies serratus anterior?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies serratus anterior, giving branches to each muscle digitation. The nerve descends on the superficial surface of the muscle and is vulnerable to injury during axillary surgery. Damage causes scapular winging.

The phrenic nerves (C3-C5, with C4 being most important - "C3,4,5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provide all motor innervation to the diaphragm and most of its sensory innervation. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral half of the diaphragm. Peripheral parts receive additional sensory innervation from intercostal and subcostal nerves, but these provide no motor supply.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the entire diaphragm?

questions.explanation: The medial basal segment is often absent or rudimentary on the left side, or it may be fused with the anterior basal segment. This anatomical variation contributes to the left lung having fewer total segments (8-10) compared to the right lung (10 segments). This variation is clinically significant.
questions.question: Which basal segment is often absent on left?

questions.explanation: The lateral compartment contains fibularis longus and fibularis brevis, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2). Their primary actions are eversion of the foot and weak plantarflexion of the ankle. Fibularis longus also supports the transverse arch by crossing the sole. Lateral compartment injury impairs the ability to evert the foot.
questions.question: The two lateral compartment muscles, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve, primarily perform which actions?
options: Inversion and adduction of the foot

questions.explanation: In healthy adults, the apex beat (point of maximal impulse) is located in the 5th left intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line. This represents the most inferior and lateral point where the cardiac impulse can be felt. In children, the apex beat is one interspace higher (4th space). Displacement suggests cardiac enlargement or chest deformity.
questions.question: Which intercostal space corresponds to the apex beat?
Which nerves supply peripheral diaphragm sensory fibers?
questions.explanation: The peripheral part of the diaphragm (including the crura) receives sensory fibers from the lower six or seven intercostal and subcostal nerves. The central part receives sensory fibers from the phrenic nerves (C3-5). This dual innervation explains the referral patterns of pain from diaphragmatic irritation.

questions.question: Which ligament arches over the psoas major muscle?
questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch in the diaphragm that arches over the psoas major muscle, extending from the body of L1 or L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process. The sympathetic trunk passes deep to (posterior to) this ligament as it enters the abdomen. The ligament forms part of the lumbar attachment of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Which ligament limits posterior dislocation of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The lateral (temporomandibular) ligament strengthens the joint capsule laterally and prevents posterior dislocation of the mandibular condyle. It extends from the zygomatic arch to the mandibular neck. Anterior dislocation is more common, occurring when the mouth opens too wide. The sphenomandibular ligament provides passive support.

questions.question: At which location is the external intercostal muscle deficient?
questions.explanation: The external intercostal muscle is deficient anteriorly at the costochondral junction and is replaced by the external (anterior) intercostal membrane. This fibrous membrane continues the plane of the muscle to the sternum. The internal intercostal muscle conversely is deficient posteriorly at the angle of the rib.

options: Exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region
Exit from perineum to gluteal region
Passage between gluteal and adductor compartments
Entrance from gluteal to femoral triangle
questions.question: The greater sciatic foramen's primary function is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: The greater sciatic foramen (GSF) provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. In contrast, the lesser sciatic foramen (LSF) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region, enabling structures that exited the pelvis via the GSF to re-enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.

The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII), specifically by a branch from the nerve after it exits the stylomastoid foramen. The muscle elevates and retracts the hyoid bone during swallowing. It shares innervation and embryologic origin (second pharyngeal arch) with the posterior belly of digastric.
questions.question: The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The lacrimal gland receives parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Preganglionic fibers travel via the greater petrosal nerve and nerve of the pterygoid canal. Postganglionic fibers reach the gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves. The pathway originates from the superior salivatory nucleus.
questions.question: The lacrimal gland is innervated by which parasympathetic pathway?

questions.explanation: independently extends the little finger, working alongside extensor digitorum. It is located in the posterior forearm compartment and supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve. The muscle has its own compartment under the extensor retinaculum.
questions.question: Which muscle extends the little finger independently?
The lamina papyracea forms the medial wall of which structure?
questions.explanation: The lamina papyracea (orbital plate) of the ethmoid bone forms the thin medial wall of the orbit. It separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells. The name papyracea (paper-like) reflects its extreme thinness. Ethmoidal infections can erode through this wall causing orbital cellulitis or abscess.

questions.question: Why are esophageal constrictions clinically important?
questions.explanation: The four esophageal constrictions are clinically important because they are: (1) sites where swallowed foreign bodies or large food boluses lodge, (2) sites where strictures tend to form, (3) sites where esophageal cancer commonly develops, and (4) areas of resistance during esophagoscopy. The narrowest point is at the cricopharyngeus.

options: Supination optimal with flexed elbow, flexion optimal mid-pronation
questions.question: How does forearm position affect biceps function?
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is most effective as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90� (maximum mechanical advantage). As a flexor, it's most effective when the forearm is in mid-prone position. When fully supinated, the tendon is wrapped around the radius, reducing flexion efficiency.

questions.question: What is the most common position of the appendix?
questions.explanation: The retrocaecal position is the most common location of the appendix, occurring in approximately 65-75% of individuals. In this position, the appendix lies behind the caecum, which may explain atypical presentations of appendicitis. Other positions include pelvic (most common after retrocaecal), subcaecal, preileal, and postileal positions.

The caval opening for the inferior vena cava is located at the level of T8 in the central tendon. It also transmits terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve and a few lymphatic vessels. This is the highest and most anterior of the three main diaphragmatic openings.
questions.question: At which vertebral level is the caval opening?

options: Lateral joint capsule and adductor hallucis
questions.explanation: In established hallux valgus, the lateral joint capsule and the tendon of adductor hallucis contract and pull the hallux into further valgus deviation. The medial capsule becomes stretched and the medial eminence (bunion) forms. Abductor hallucis, which should abduct the hallux, migrates plantarly and becomes ineffective. Surgical correction involves release of lateral structures and medial capsule repair.
questions.question: Hallux valgus (bunion) is a deformity involving lateral deviation of the hallux. Which structure becomes contracted in established hallux valgus, pulling the hallux into further valgus?
What is the characteristic deformity produced by a Colles' fracture?
questions.explanation: Colles' fracture results from falling onto an outstretched hand, causing the distal radius fragment to displace posteriorly. The ulnar styloid process is frequently avulsed in the majority of these cases. This produces the characteristic "dinner fork deformity" when viewing the affected wrist from the side.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial and lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The canal runs obliquely (downward, forward, and medially) from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring, approximately 4 cm in length. The anterior wall is formed by external oblique aponeurosis (entire length) and internal oblique laterally; posterior wall by transversalis fascia (entire length) and conjoint tendon medially; roof by arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus; floor by inguinal ligament. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for hernia repair.

questions.question: Which test demonstrates ulnar nerve palsy?
questions.explanation: demonstrates ulnar nerve palsy by revealing adductor pollicis weakness. When gripping paper between thumb and index finger, the patient compensates for weak thumb adduction by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint (using median nerve-supplied flexor pollicis longus). This abnormal flexion indicates ulnar nerve dysfunction.

questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the orbit through which opening?
questions.explanation: The inferior orbital fissure connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the orbit. The fissure is bounded by the greater wing of sphenoid, maxilla, and palatine bone. The maxillary nerve continues through this fissure as the infraorbital nerve. The infraorbital and zygomatic nerves and vessels pass through this communication.

Serratus anterior is the most powerful protractor of the scapula, pulling it forward around the chest wall. Paralysis of this muscle causes scapular winging, where the medial border of the scapula protrudes from the back. The muscle is supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).
questions.question: What is the primary action of serratus anterior?

questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost fascial covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep inguinal ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis). These three concentric layers are acquired as the processus vaginalis descends through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent. The tunica vaginalis is the closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis, derived from the processus vaginalis.
questions.question: The transversalis fascia forms which covering of the spermatic cord?

questions.explanation: Psoas major originates from the sides of T12-L5 vertebrae and their intervening discs, as well as from the transverse processes of all lumbar vertebrae. It inserts into the lesser trochanter together with iliacus (forming iliopsoas). A psoas abscess from vertebral tuberculosis can track along this muscle to present as a groin swelling.
options: T12�L5 vertebrae, intervening discs, and all lumbar transverse processes
L1-L5 vertebral bodies only, no disc or process
T12-L4 vertebral bodies only without processes
L2-S1 vertebral levels and intervening discs
questions.question: The psoas major originates from which vertebral levels, including transverse processes?

questions.explanation: The right lung is divided into three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior) by two fissures: the oblique and horizontal fissures. The left lung has only two lobes (superior and inferior) separated by the oblique fissure. The presence of a middle lobe makes the right lung larger than the left.
questions.question: How many lobes does the right lung contain?
Which part of the pancreas is most commonly affected by tumors?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic head tumors are most common (60-70% of pancreatic cancers), followed by body (15-20%) and tail (10-15%). Head tumors often present earlier due to biliary obstruction causing jaundice. Body and tail tumors may grow larger before detection as they don't obstruct the bile duct. The head's proximity to the duodenum and bile duct makes surgical resection (Whipple procedure) more complex.

The spleen is situated in the left hypochondriac region, lying obliquely along the long axis of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left upper quadrant. It is protected by the rib cage and cannot normally be palpated unless enlarged. The spleen is related anteriorly to the stomach (via the gastrosplenic ligament), posteriorly to the left kidney (via the splenorenal ligament), superiorly to the diaphragm, and inferiorly to the left colic flexure (supported by the phrenicocolic ligament). The splenic notch on its superior border is a characteristic feature visible on imaging.
questions.question: The spleen is located in which abdominal region?

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament separates the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver on the anterior and superior surfaces, extending from the diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall to the liver surface. However, the functional division between right and left lobes (Couinaud's segmentation) is defined by the main portal fissure (Cantlie's line), an imaginary plane running from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the IVC groove posteriorly, containing the middle hepatic vein. This functional division corresponds to the distribution of the right and left branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts. The quadrate and caudate lobes, though anatomically part of the right lobe, are functionally part of the left lobe.
questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left lobes of the liver anatomically?

questions.explanation: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on the medial surface of the mandibular angle and ramus, forming a sling with the masseter on the lateral surface. It arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and pterygoid fossa. The muscle elevates and protrudes the mandible. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3).
questions.question: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on which structure?
The lesser omentum has two parts, which are:
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum consists of two continuous portions: the gastrohepatic ligament (pars flaccida, the membranous portion extending from lesser curvature of stomach to liver) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa, the thickened free right edge containing the portal triad extending from first part of duodenum to porta hepatis). These two parts form a continuous peritoneal fold connecting the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver, and together they form the anterior boundary of the lesser sac and epiploic foramen. The lesser omentum develops from the ventral mesentery and contains the portal triad in its free edge.

options: Biceps, coracobrachialis, and forearm median muscles
questions.explanation: Lateral cord injury paralyzes muscles supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve (biceps, coracobrachialis, brachialis) and muscles supplied by the median nerve except those in the hand. This results from damage to both the musculocutaneous nerve and lateral root of median nerve. Wrist and finger flexion is lost along with forearm flexion.
questions.question: Which muscles are paralyzed in injury to the lateral cord of the brachial plexus?

questions.explanation: The suprapleural membrane is attached at its apex to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra (C7). Laterally, it attaches to the internal border of the first rib and its costal cartilage. Medially, it blends with the fascia covering structures passing through the superior thoracic aperture.
questions.question: To which structure is the suprapleural membrane attached apically?

questions.explanation: The posterior sag sign (gravity drawer test) is a clinical test for posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury. The patient lies supine with the hip at 45 degrees and knee at 90 degrees. The posterior sag of the proximal tibia (relative to the femur) under gravity indicates PCL rupture. This distinguishes it from ACL injury, where the tibia sags anteriorly on the drawer test.
questions.question: The 'posterior sag sign' of the knee is a clinical test for which ligament injury?
Which bone accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm in length?
questions.explanation: The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, averaging 45 cm in length. It accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height. The femur articulates with the acetabulum superiorly and the patella and tibia inferiorly.

Barrett's esophagus is a premalignant condition where the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium (intestinal metaplasia). This occurs due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). It increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma and requires surveillance.
questions.question: What is Barrett's esophagus?

questions.explanation: The pleural cavity normally contains a small amount of serous (pleural) fluid that acts as a lubricant between the visceral and parietal pleural surfaces. This fluid is continuously produced and absorbed, maintaining a thin film that facilitates smooth lung movement during respiration.
questions.question: What contains the pleural fluid normally?
The kidney is located at which vertebral levels?
questions.explanation: The kidneys extend from approximately T12 to L3 vertebral levels, with the hilum positioned at the L1 level (transpyloric plane). The right kidney typically sits slightly lower than the left (by about half a vertebra) due to the presence of the liver superiorly. The upper poles are closer to the midline and are related to the diaphragm and ribs (left kidney: ribs 11-12; right kidney: rib 12), while the lower poles are further from the midline. The kidneys lie obliquely, with the upper poles more posterior and closer together than the lower poles.

questions.question: At what distance from the upper incisors does the aortic arch constrict the oesophagus?
questions.explanation: The aortic arch crosses anteriorly to the oesophagus creating a constriction at approximately 22.5 cm from the upper incisors. This is the second of four normal oesophageal constrictions and represents an important anatomical relationship. The arch of the aorta indents the anterior and left lateral aspects of the oesophagus at this level.

questions.question: Hilton's law states the nerve supplying a joint also supplies which other two structures?
questions.explanation: Hilton's law states: 'The nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' This explains why patients with hip joint disease may refer pain to the knee, as the posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both joints. It is fundamental in understanding referred pain patterns.
options: Ligaments of the joint and adjacent bone
Muscles moving the joint and skin covering their insertion
Tendons crossing the joint and adjacent bursae
Articular cartilage and synovial membrane only

questions.explanation: The superior oblique is the primary intortor of the eye, also producing depression and abduction. The muscle passes through the trochlea before inserting on the posterolateral superior eyeball. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV). Superior oblique palsy causes vertical diplopia, worse on downward gaze and head tilt to the affected side.
questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for intorsion of the eye?
Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the stylopharyngeus muscle?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) is the only cranial nerve that provides motor innervation to a pharyngeal muscle - the stylopharyngeus. All other pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). Stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing.

questions.question: The basilar artery is formed by the union of which vessels?
questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. It ascends in the pontine groove and terminates by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Branches include pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine arteries.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive diaphragmatic lymph from the superior surface?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the superior (thoracic) surface of the diaphragm drains into parasternal, posterior mediastinal, and phrenic lymph nodes. Lymph from the inferior (abdominal) surface drains into anterior and posterior diaphragmatic lymph nodes, phrenic nodes, and superior lumbar nodes. Lymphatic vessels from the bare area of the liver communicate through the diaphragm with posterior mediastinal nodes.

questions.question: Which structure is at risk during splenectomy?
questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends into the splenorenal ligament to reach the splenic hilum and is at risk of injury during splenectomy. The splenic vessels in the splenorenal ligament must be carefully ligated. Pancreatic fistula is a recognized complication of splenectomy. The tail represents about 30% of pancreatic tissue but is rarely the site of surgical disease.

questions.question: Which vein receives the inferior mesenteric vein?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though anatomical variations exist (occasionally draining into superior mesenteric vein or the portal vein directly). The IMV ascends from the pelvis on the left side of the inferior mesenteric artery, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries. After joining the splenic vein, blood flows to the confluence with the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas, forming the portal vein. This pathway ensures blood from the hindgut reaches the liver for processing.

questions.question: Which bone forms the hard palate posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The posterior portion of the hard palate is formed by the horizontal plates of the palatine bones. The anterior portion is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities and provides a rigid surface for the tongue during mastication.

The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac trunk and has a characteristic tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas. It runs from right to left within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-7 branches at the splenic hilum. The artery gives off numerous pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, and the left gastroepiploic artery.
questions.question: Which is the largest branch of the celiac trunk?

questions.explanation: Empyema is the accumulation of pus in the pleural cavity, usually resulting from bacterial infection (often complicating pneumonia). It requires drainage, either by chest tube insertion or surgical decortication. Empyema is distinguished from simple pleural effusion by the presence of purulent material.
questions.question: What is empyema?

questions.explanation: Scaphoid fracture requires urgent treatment to prevent avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment. Due to the unique retrograde blood supply, fractures disrupt perfusion to the proximal portion. Failure to achieve timely revascularization leads to avascular necrosis and future arthritis.
options: Scaphoid fracture with avascular necrosis risk
questions.question: Which condition requires urgent revascularization to prevent complications?

options: Tibialis anterior tendon, deep fibular nerve, dorsalis pedis artery
Tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve, FHL
Fibularis longus, fibularis brevis, sural nerve, small saphenous vein
Extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, anterior tibial artery
questions.explanation: The tarsal tunnel contains the following structures passing from anterior to posterior (using the mnemonic Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry): Tibialis posterior tendon, flexor Digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial Artery and Veins, tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus tendon. Compression within this tunnel causes tarsal tunnel syndrome with plantar foot pain and paraesthesia.
questions.question: The tarsal tunnel is formed by the flexor retinaculum and bones of the medial ankle. Which structures pass through it from anterior to posterior?

questions.explanation: The AV nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 80-90% of people (right dominant circulation) and from the left circumflex artery in the remainder (left dominant circulation). It typically arises near the origin of the posterior interventricular artery. AV node ischemia from right coronary occlusion can cause heart block.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the AV node in most people?

questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is three times stronger than its antagonist, the hamstrings. It forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh and is the great extensor of the leg. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur and is considered the largest and one of the most powerful muscle groups in the body.
questions.question: The quadriceps femoris is how many times stronger than its antagonist muscle group, the hamstrings?

questions.explanation: The neck of the bladder is the most fixed part, anchored by the puboprostatic ligaments (in males) or pubovesical ligaments (in females) and the lateral ligaments of the bladder. The remainder of the bladder is relatively mobile, allowing it to expand superiorly into the abdomen when full. The neck surrounds the internal urethral orifice.
questions.question: Which part of the bladder is most fixed in position?
The testicular vein on the left typically drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle. This anatomical difference explains the higher incidence (90%) of left-sided varicoceles, as the perpendicular drainage into the renal vein, along with the longer venous column and potential compression by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon), creates higher venous pressure on the left. The left testicular vein lacks valves or has incompetent valves, facilitating retrograde flow and varicosity formation.

questions.question: Which embryological origin corresponds to the descending colon?
questions.explanation: The descending colon is derived from the embryological hindgut, along with the distal third of the transverse colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Hindgut structures are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery and receive parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves. The midgut-hindgut junction occurs at approximately the left third of the transverse colon.

options: Allows arm to clear hip, prevents body collision
Serves to limit range of elbow motion
questions.explanation: The carrying angle (approximately 170� in males, more in females) allows the forearm to clear the hip during walking and permits objects to be carried clear of the body. Excessive carrying angle (cubitus valgus) can predispose to ulnar nerve problems at the elbow.
questions.question: What is the clinical significance of the carrying angle?
