questions.explanation: The middle cranial fossa accommodates the temporal lobes of the brain laterally and the pituitary gland centrally. The floor is formed by the greater wings and body of the sphenoid and the petrous and squamous parts of the temporal bones. The fossa is wider than the anterior fossa. Multiple foramina pierce its floor.
questions.question: Which cranial fossa contains the temporal lobes?

questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus in the diaphragm is located at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra (T10). The oesophagus passes through the muscular part of the right crus of the diaphragm at this level. This hiatus also transmits the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the oesophageal opening in the diaphragm?
The maxillary sinus ostium opens into which structure?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris. This high opening impairs natural drainage when standing upright. The sinus is the largest paranasal sinus and is present in rudimentary form at birth.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the axilla's superficial layer?
questions.explanation: The anterior wall of the axilla is formed by the pectoralis major muscle and the pectoral fascia associated with it. The pectoralis minor and clavipectoral fascia form a deeper layer. The anterior axillary fold, formed by pectoralis major bridging from thoracic wall to humerus, represents the inferiormost graspable part.

The supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries (from the ophthalmic artery of internal carotid system) supply the anterior scalp. The superficial temporal artery supplies the lateral scalp. Posterior scalp receives blood from occipital and posterior auricular arteries from the external carotid system.
questions.question: What is the primary arterial supply to the scalp anteriorly?

questions.explanation: Blood from the breast drains into both the axillary veins (via lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial tributaries) and the internal thoracic veins (via perforating veins). During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become prominent and engorged. Venous drainage pathways are important routes for cancer metastasis.
questions.question: What drains blood from the breast?

questions.explanation: "Ape hand" deformity indicates median nerve injury at the wrist affecting the recurrent branch to thenar muscles. The thumb falls back into the plane of the palm due to thenar muscle paralysis. Opposition and abduction are lost, making the hand resemble an ape's hand.
questions.question: Which position indicates median nerve injury at the wrist?
Which structure marks the junction between the nasopharynx and oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The lower border of the soft palate marks the boundary between the nasopharynx above and the oropharynx below. The soft palate can elevate to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing. The pharyngeal isthmus connects these two regions and can be voluntarily controlled.

options: Deep facial vein to pterygoid plexus
questions.question: Which vein drains the deep face?
questions.explanation: The deep facial vein connects the facial vein with the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa, draining deep facial structures. The pterygoid plexus drains via the maxillary vein to the retromandibular vein. This valveless connection provides a route for infection spread between face and cavernous sinus.

questions.question: Which vein receives the left renal vein?
questions.explanation: Both right and left renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is approximately three times longer than the right and crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC. The left renal vein receives the left suprarenal vein, left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein, and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein.

In males, the spermatic cord passes through the deep inguinal ring (an opening in the transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels). In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through. The ilioinguinal nerve passes through the superficial inguinal ring but not the deep ring - it enters the canal by piercing the internal oblique muscle.
questions.question: What passes through the deep inguinal ring?
Which part of the male urethra is least distensible?
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm), narrowest, and least distensible part of the male urethra. It passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch) surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae muscle). This segment is most vulnerable to traumatic injury, particularly in pelvic fractures, and is the most difficult to dilate or catheterize.

The superior hypogastric plexus lies anterior to the lower part of the abdominal aorta and its bifurcation, extending from approximately L4 to the upper part of the sacrum, anterior to the L5 vertebra and sacral promontory. It represents the continuation of the aortic (intermesenteric) plexus and receives lumbar splanchnic nerves carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers. The plexus divides inferiorly into right and left hypogastric nerves, which descend into the pelvis to join the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses. The superior hypogastric plexus can be blocked or surgically divided to treat intractable pelvic pain.
questions.question: The superior hypogastric plexus is located at which vertebral level?
Which muscle forms the floor of the mouth?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular floor (diaphragm) of the oral cavity, creating the mylohyoid raphe in the midline. The muscle elevates the floor during swallowing and depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed. Above the mylohyoid lie the tongue and genioglossus; below lie the geniohyoid and digastric. Mylohyoid nerve (V3) provides innervation.

The patellar reflex (knee jerk) tests the L3 and L4 nerve roots. The reflex arc involves the femoral nerve (both afferent and efferent), the L3-L4 spinal cord segments, and the quadriceps femoris muscle. An absent or diminished knee jerk suggests L3 or L4 root pathology, commonly from disc herniation at the L2/3 or L3/4 levels. The Achilles tendon reflex tests S1 and S2.
questions.question: The patellar reflex (knee jerk) tests which nerve roots?

questions.explanation: The cricoarytenoid joint permits rotation and sliding movements of the arytenoid cartilages, which directly control vocal cord abduction and adduction. Tension changes occur primarily through cricothyroid joint movement, not cricoarytenoid articulation. The L-shaped base of the arytenoid pivots at the cricoarytenoid joint to open or close the rima glottidis.
questions.question: The cricoarytenoid joint allows which specific movement of the vocal cords?

questions.explanation: The left gastric vein typically drains directly into the portal vein near its origin behind the neck of the pancreas, though it may occasionally drain into the splenic vein. The left gastric vein receives esophageal tributaries from the abdominal esophagus, creating an important portosystemic anastomosis with esophageal veins draining to the azygos system. In portal hypertension, these anastomotic channels dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing life-threatening hemorrhage. The coronary vein is an alternative name for the left gastric vein, following the course of the left gastric artery along the lesser curvature.
questions.question: The left gastric vein drains into which vessel?

questions.explanation: Each renal artery typically divides into five segmental arteries: apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior, and posterior. These are functional end arteries with no significant anastomoses, meaning occlusion of one causes infarction of that segment. This segmental anatomy allows partial nephrectomy without affecting remaining segments. Four segmental arteries arise from the anterior division; one (posterior) from the posterior division.
questions.question: How many segmental arteries typically supply each kidney?

questions.explanation: Only the upper third of the rectum is covered by peritoneum on its anterior surface, the middle third has peritoneum on its front only, and the lower third is completely devoid of peritoneal covering. Posteriorly, the rectum is retroperitoneal throughout its length. This peritoneal relationship creates the rectovesical pouch in males and rectouterine pouch in females.
questions.question: What percentage of the rectum is covered by peritoneum anteriorly?
Which lymph nodes are located along the external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein in the superficial cervical fascia. They receive drainage from the scalp and superficial neck structures. Efferent vessels drain to the deep cervical nodes. These nodes are distinct from the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein.

questions.question: Which structure lies deepest in the costal groove?
questions.explanation: The posterior intercostal veins lie deepest in the costal grooves and contain valves that direct blood flow posteriorly. The neurovascular bundle arrangement from superior to inferior is vein-artery-nerve (VAN). The veins are the largest and most superior structures in this arrangement.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between finger flexor sublimis and profundus?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes PIP joints independently of DIP joints. Flexor digitorum profundus flexes DIP joints and contributes to PIP and MCP flexion, providing power grip force. This two-layer arrangement enables independent or combined finger joint flexion for varied hand positions.
options: Both tendons have identical flexor function
FDS flexes PIP joints, FDP flexes DIP joints

questions.explanation: Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum as ferrous iron (Fe2+). Gastric acid helps convert ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous iron for absorption. Vitamin C enhances absorption while phytates and tannins inhibit it. Heme iron from meat is absorbed more efficiently than non-heme iron from plant sources.
questions.question: Where in the small intestine is iron primarily absorbed?
Which muscle is the primary flexor of the hip joint, described as the great flexor, with its traction epiphysis being the lesser trochanter?
questions.explanation: The iliopsoas is the primary flexor of the hip joint, formed by the fusion of iliacus and psoas major. Their combined tendon inserts into the lesser trochanter, which is its traction epiphysis. The iliopsoas is active in walking, running, and sitting up. Weakness of iliopsoas is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated position.

questions.question: What is the function of anconeus muscle?
questions.explanation: Anconeus is a small muscle that assists triceps brachii in elbow extension. It is located on the posterior aspect of the elbow, blending with the lateral head of triceps. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve.

questions.question: The pectineus muscle receives primary innervation from the femoral nerve and a variable additional supply from which nerve?
questions.explanation: Pectineus is primarily supplied by the femoral nerve (L2, L3), but may also receive innervation from the obturator nerve. It originates from the superior ramus of the pubis and inserts into the pectineal line of the femur just inferior to the lesser trochanter. It acts to adduct and flex the thigh and assists with medial rotation.

Adjacent bronchopulmonary segments are separated by connective tissue septa. Intersegmental veins run in these septa and serve as guides for surgically separating segments. The septa act as natural barriers preventing spread of infection between segments (though cancer and tuberculosis can break through).
questions.question: What separates adjacent bronchopulmonary segments?
At what age does the appendix typically reach its adult position?
questions.explanation: The appendix reaches its definitive adult position by puberty. In infants and young children, the appendix has a relatively higher position, which explains why appendicitis in children may present with higher abdominal pain. The growth of the cecum pulls the appendix to a lower position. The base of the appendix remains constant at the confluence of the three taeniae coli.

questions.question: What are internal hemorrhoids dilations of?
questions.explanation: Internal hemorrhoids are dilations of the internal rectal venous plexus (superior rectal veins) above the pectinate line. They are covered by insensate rectal mucosa and are therefore painless. External hemorrhoids are dilations of the external rectal venous plexus (inferior rectal veins) below the pectinate line, covered by sensitive anoderm, making them painful. Portal hypertension can cause internal hemorrhoids.

questions.question: What movements occur at the shoulder girdle during arm abduction?
questions.explanation: During shoulder joint abduction, the shoulder girdle undergoes upward rotation of the scapula. This scapular movement is essential for achieving full arm abduction beyond 90 degrees. The trapezius and serratus anterior muscles produce this upward rotation of the scapula.

The right upper lobe contains three bronchopulmonary segments: apical, posterior, and anterior. Each segment is supplied by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus and a branch of the pulmonary artery. The segments are separated by connective tissue septa allowing individual segment resection.
questions.question: How many segments are in right upper lobe?

questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, medial to the deep inguinal ring. It ascends obliquely along the medial margin of the deep ring, passing medial to it (an important landmark distinguishing direct from indirect inguinal hernias), and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Within the sheath, it ascends posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery, providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian (via internal thoracic) and external iliac arterial systems.
questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery arises from which vessel?
What is myasthenia gravis?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular disease characterized by antibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This causes muscle weakness and fatigue that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Common symptoms include ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and weakness. Treatment includes anticholinesterases, immunosuppression, and sometimes thymectomy.

questions.question: How do the three deltoid portions contribute differently to shoulder function?
options: Anterior flexes, middle abducts, posterior extends
questions.explanation: The deltoid's three portions have distinct actions: anterior fibers flex and medially rotate, middle fibers abduct (15-90�), posterior fibers extend and laterally rotate. This multipennate architecture allows the same muscle to produce different movements depending on which fibers are active.

questions.question: The oblique popliteal ligament strengthens the fibrous capsule posteriorly. It is an expansion of the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The oblique popliteal ligament is an expansion of the tendon of semimembranosus. It arises posterior to the medial tibial condyle and attaches to the central part of the posterior fibrous capsule. It is an important posterior stabilizer of the knee. The arcuate popliteal ligament is a separate structure arising from the posterior fibular head.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes are commonly called the tonsillar nodes?
questions.explanation: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are located below the angle of the mandible where the posterior belly of digastric crosses the internal jugular vein. They are commonly enlarged in tonsillitis and are therefore called tonsillar nodes. These are part of the superior deep cervical lymph node chain.

The median cubital vein connects the basilic and cephalic veins superficially in the cubital fossa. This vein is commonly used for venipuncture, blood sampling, and intravenous infusions due to its prominence and accessibility. It lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, which historically protected deeper structures during bloodletting.
questions.question: Which vein is commonly used for venipuncture in the cubital fossa?

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx, including the tonsillar region and posterior third of tongue. The vagus nerve also contributes sensation to the valleculae via the internal laryngeal branch. Referred otalgia from pharyngeal lesions occurs via glossopharyngeal pathways.
questions.question: Which cranial nerve supplies sensory innervation to the oropharynx?

questions.explanation: Nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta, supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces. The upper two spaces receive their posterior intercostal arteries from the superior intercostal artery. Each posterior intercostal artery gives branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura, and the breast.
questions.question: How many posterior intercostal arteries arise from thoracic aorta?

questions.explanation: The femoral ring (the medial compartment of the femoral sheath) is bounded medially by the lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament), laterally by the femoral vein, anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, and posteriorly by the pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) and pectineus muscle covered by fascia. The femoral ring normally contains a lymph node (Cloquet's node) and loose connective tissue. It represents a potential site of weakness where femoral hernias can occur (more common in women), protruding through the ring into the femoral canal. The rigid boundaries make strangulation a risk in femoral hernias.
questions.question: The femoral ring is bounded medially by which structure?
Why does left lung have fewer segments?
questions.explanation: The left lung has 8-10 bronchopulmonary segments (compared to 10 on the right) because the apical and posterior segments typically fuse to form an apicoposterior segment. Additionally, the medial basal segment is often absent or fused with the anterior basal segment on the left side.

The azygos vein lies posterior and to the right of the esophagus in the posterior mediastinum. The descending aorta lies posterior and to the left of the esophagus. The thoracic duct lies posterior to the esophagus. The vagus nerves form plexuses around the esophagus.
questions.question: Which vein lies posterior to the esophagus?
The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to which muscle group?
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) provides motor innervation to the infrahyoid strap muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. The thyrohyoid receives C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve. These muscles depress the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing.

questions.question: What nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres?
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres muscle. Compression at this site causes pronator teres syndrome, an entrapment neuropathy. This produces pain in the proximal forearm and sensory symptoms in the median nerve distribution.

The transtubercular plane is a horizontal plane passing through the iliac tubercles (projections on the outer lips of the iliac crests about 5 cm posterior to the anterior superior iliac spines) at the level of the L5 vertebral body. Along with the subcostal plane (through the lowest points of the costal margin at L3), it defines the superior boundaries of the right and left inguinal (iliac) regions. This plane also approximates the level of the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta and the confluence of common iliac veins to form the inferior vena cava.
questions.question: Which plane passes through the iliac tubercles?

questions.explanation: The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) arises from the lateral cord and primarily supplies pectoralis major muscle. The lateral cord also gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve. It lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery.
questions.question: Which nerve branch arises from the lateral cord?

questions.explanation: Only one small artery enters the scaphoid bone at the end closest to the thumb (distal end). This unique blood supply pattern makes the scaphoid vulnerable to avascular necrosis following fracture. The proximal fragment may lose blood supply if fracture tears the artery.
questions.question: What is the primary blood supply to the scaphoid bone?
options: Dual arterial supply proximally and distally
Direct branches from radial artery proximally

questions.explanation: Talipes equinus is a form of club foot in which the toes are directed toward the ground and the foot is fixed in plantarflexion, similar to the position of a horse's hoof. Talipes calcaneus, by contrast, leaves the heel on the ground with the toes upturned. Talipes varus fixes the foot in inversion and adduction. CTEV (congenital talipes equinovarus) is the most common club foot deformity.
questions.question: Talipes equinus is a type of club foot in which the foot is fixed in which position, resembling the hoof of a horse?
options: Toes upturned and heel on the ground
Foot fixed in inversion and adduction
Foot fixed in eversion and abduction
Toes directed downward and fixed in plantarflexion
Heel on the ground with toes inverted

questions.question: Which artery does NOT arise from the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The superior epigastric artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery (which arises from the subclavian artery), not the abdominal aorta. It descends through the thorax, enters the rectus sheath by passing between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm, and anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac artery), providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian and external iliac systems. The abdominal aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac, SMA, IMA), paired parietal branches (inferior phrenic, four lumbar), and the unpaired median sacral artery.

questions.question: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV), the only extraocular muscle not supplied by the oculomotor nerve except lateral rectus (abducens). The superior oblique passes through the trochlea (pulley) on the medial orbital roof. It intorts, depresses, and abducts the eye.

questions.question: What condition results from median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. This causes sensory disturbances in the lateral three and one-half fingers (palmer aspect) and weakness of thenar muscles. The condition commonly occurs from inflammatory reactions in flexor tendon synovial sheaths or space-occupying lesions.

questions.question: Which structure separates the frontal lobe from the orbit?
questions.explanation: The thin orbital plate (roof) of the frontal bone separates the frontal lobe of the brain from the orbital contents. Fractures can cause CSF leakage into the orbit. The anterior cranial fossa lies above this plate. The frontal sinus may pneumatize into this region of the frontal bone.

questions.question: The tibial nerve enters the tarsal tunnel and supplies intrinsic muscles of the sole via its terminal branches. Which of the following is supplied by the medial plantar nerve?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum brevis is supplied by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3). The medial plantar nerve (analogous to the median nerve) also supplies abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis, and the first lumbrical. The lateral plantar nerve (analogous to the ulnar nerve) supplies all other intrinsic muscles: abductor digiti minimi, quadratus plantae, flexor digiti minimi brevis, all interossei, lateral three lumbricals, and adductor hallucis.

questions.question: Where does the azygos vein terminate?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus at T4 to drain into the posterior aspect of the superior vena cava. This creates a communication between the SVC and IVC systems, providing collateral circulation if either is obstructed. The azygos arch is visible on chest X-rays.

options: Transverse arch first then longitudinal arches
questions.explanation: Pes planus (flat foot) is characterized by collapse of the medial longitudinal arch. The foot print of a flat foot shows increased contact with the ground medially. It can be flexible (reversible on tip-toeing) or rigid. Common causes include tibialis posterior tendon rupture, spring ligament laxity, and obesity. It can lead to secondary knee and hip pain.
questions.question: Pes planus (flat foot) is a deformity characterized by collapse of which arch?

options: Sustentaculum tali of calcaneus and talus
All five metatarsal bases and the navicular
Base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform
Plantar surface of cuboid and bases of 3rd�5th metatarsals
questions.question: The long plantar ligament, an important supporter of the lateral longitudinal arch, passes from the calcaneus to which structures?
questions.explanation: The long plantar ligament (longest ligament in the foot) passes from the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the ridges on the plantar surface of the cuboid and the bases of the 3rd-5th metatarsals. It is a primary support for the lateral longitudinal arch. In combination with the short plantar (plantar calcaneocuboid) ligament, it forms the floor of the fibularis longus tendon groove on the cuboid.

questions.question: Which axillary node group lies on pectoralis minor?
questions.explanation: The pectoral (anterior) group of axillary lymph nodes lies on the pectoralis minor muscle along the lateral thoracic vessels. This group receives most of the lymphatic drainage from the breast. From here, lymph passes to the central and then apical nodes before reaching the subclavian lymph trunk.

questions.question: The superior laryngeal nerve's internal branch provides sensation to which region?
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation above the vocal cords, including the epiglottis and vestibule. Below the cords, sensation is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. This division is clinically important for regional anesthesia during laryngoscopy.

questions.question: What type of synovial joint is the elbow classified as?
questions.explanation: The elbow joint is classified as a synovial hinge (ginglymus) joint, allowing uniaxial movement. Articulation occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus with the trochlear notch of the ulna and radial head respectively. This configuration permits flexion and extension movements.

The azygos vein passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (at T12 level) along with the aorta and thoracic duct, posterior to the diaphragmatic crura. The aortic hiatus is actually a midline gap between the crura rather than a true opening in the diaphragmatic muscle. The azygos vein drains the posterior thoracic and abdominal walls and provides important collateral circulation between the superior and inferior vena cavae. It arches over the right main bronchus to drain into the superior vena cava. The hemiazygos vein may also pass through the aortic hiatus.
questions.question: The azygos vein passes through which diaphragmatic opening?
How many subdivisions does inferior mediastinum have?
questions.explanation: The inferior mediastinum has three subdivisions: anterior (in front of the heart), middle (contains the heart), and posterior (behind the heart). The superior mediastinum lies above the horizontal plane through T4. This classification helps in understanding the location of mediastinal structures and pathology.

questions.question: What causes achalasia?
questions.explanation: Achalasia is a motility disorder characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing and loss of normal esophageal peristalsis. This causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, and progressive esophageal dilation. Treatment includes pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM).

questions.question: The hepatic artery proper typically divides into which branches?
questions.explanation: The hepatic artery proper, ascending in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) as part of the portal triad, divides near the porta hepatis into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver. The right hepatic artery gives off the cystic artery to the gallbladder. Significant anatomical variation exists in hepatic arterial anatomy (occurring in up to 45% of individuals), including replaced or accessory right hepatic arteries from the superior mesenteric artery and replaced or accessory left hepatic arteries from the left gastric artery.

questions.question: What supplies the first two intercostal spaces?
questions.explanation: The superior intercostal artery (from costocervical trunk of subclavian artery) gives off the first and second posterior intercostal arteries. These are the only posterior intercostal arteries not arising from the thoracic aorta. This arrangement provides collateral circulation if the thoracic aorta is obstructed.

questions.question: Which cartilage lies in the aryepiglottic fold?
questions.explanation: The cuneiform cartilages (cartilages of Wrisberg) are small rod-shaped elastic cartilages lying in the aryepiglottic folds anterior to the corniculate cartilages. They produce small elevations on the mucosal surface visible during laryngoscopy. The cartilages strengthen the aryepiglottic folds. Some individuals may lack these cartilages.

questions.question: Stress fractures of the metatarsals (March fractures) most commonly affect which metatarsal in soldiers and long-distance runners?
questions.explanation: Metatarsal stress fractures (March fractures) most commonly affect the second metatarsal in soldiers, runners, and military recruits after unaccustomed prolonged walking or running. The second metatarsal is the most stable midfoot ray (most protected by its surrounded cuneiforms) but is subjected to repetitive bending forces. They typically present with pain in the forefoot that worsens with activity and is relieved by rest.

questions.question: How high above the clavicle does cervical pleura extend?
questions.explanation: The cervical pleura extends approximately one inch (2.5 to 4 cm) above the medial third of the clavicle. This superior extension of the parietal pleura is reinforced by the suprapleural membrane. Understanding this anatomy is important because the pleura can be injured during procedures in the lower neck.

The internal urethral sphincter is composed of smooth muscle (a thickening of the detrusor muscle at the bladder neck) and is under involuntary autonomic control. It is controlled by sympathetic innervation (hypogastric nerves), which causes contraction to maintain continence and prevent retrograde ejaculation in males. It relaxes during micturition under parasympathetic control.
questions.question: What is the internal urethral sphincter composed of?

options: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.question: The posterior approach to the hip (Moore's approach) identifies which nerve as the critical structure to protect, found running midway between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter?
questions.explanation: The posterior (Moore's) approach to the hip must carefully protect the sciatic nerve, which runs midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. The approach involves splitting gluteus maximus and detaching the short external rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli) from the greater trochanter. These rotators must be reattached to reduce the risk of posterior hip dislocation postoperatively.

questions.question: Which region does the majority of the ileum occupy?
questions.explanation: The ileum predominantly occupies the right lower quadrant of the infracolic compartment, with the terminal ileum usually located in the pelvis. The ileum constitutes approximately 60% of the jejunoileal length. It characteristically ends at the ileocaecal junction on the medial aspect of the caecum.

questions.question: Which structure lies between the pretracheal and prevertebral fascia?
questions.explanation: The pharynx, esophagus, larynx, trachea, and thyroid gland lie between the pretracheal and prevertebral fascia. The pretracheal fascia encloses these visceral structures while the prevertebral fascia covers the vertebral column and associated muscles. The retropharyngeal space lies between these fascial layers posteriorly.

options: Deep fibular nerve; first web space sensation and dorsiflexion
Superficial fibular nerve; dorsal foot sensation and eversion strength
questions.explanation: Lateral compartment (fibular compartment) syndrome is confirmed by testing the superficial fibular nerve: eversion strength of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis) and sensation on the dorsum of the foot (superficial fibular nerve cutaneous distribution). In the anterior compartment, the deep fibular nerve is tested (first web space sensation and dorsiflexion). These clinical tests guide emergency fasciotomy decision-making.
questions.question: The peroneal (fibular) compartment syndrome is a less common variant of leg compartment syndrome. Which specific nerve function is tested to confirm lateral compartment integrity?
Which position of the appendix may cause retrocecal abscess?
questions.explanation: When the appendix is in a retrocecal position (most common position, 65-75% of cases), appendicitis can cause a retrocecal abscess. This position may also cause atypical symptoms with less peritoneal irritation and more lateral/posterior pain. The appendix may lie behind the cecum but still be intraperitoneal (covered by peritoneum) or rarely be retroperitoneal.

The femoral canal, the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally contains lymphatics and loose connective tissue. It is the site of femoral hernias, which are more common in women (due to their wider pelvis and femoral ring). Femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (unlike inguinal hernias above and medial to it). They are at high risk of strangulation due to the rigid femoral ring.
questions.question: The femoral canal, the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, contains which structures and is the site of which type of hernia?
options: Lymphatics and loose connective tissue; femoral hernia
Femoral artery and nerve; femoral hernia

questions.explanation: The posterior surface of each kidney lies on the diaphragm superiorly, then from medial to lateral on the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis muscles, separated from them by the perinephric fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat. The subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves descend obliquely posterior to the kidney on these muscles. The left kidney is related to ribs 11 and 12 posteriorly (protected by the rib cage), while the right kidney is related only to rib 12. These posterior relations are important when considering retrograde surgical approaches to the kidney or complications of renal trauma.
questions.question: The kidney is related posteriorly to which muscle?
Which lymphatic structure drains lymph from the right upper quadrant of the body?
questions.explanation: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limb. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. The duct enters the right venous angle (junction of right internal jugular and subclavian veins).

Approximately 75% of lymph from the breast drains into the axillary nodes, primarily the pectoral (anterior) group. About 20% drains to the internal mammary (parasternal) chain. The lower quadrants may drain to inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes. This drainage pattern is crucial in cancer staging.
questions.question: What percentage of lymph drains to axillary nodes?

questions.explanation: The hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and left subcostal vein. It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum, crosses at T8-9, and drains into the azygos vein. It receives lower left posterior intercostal veins.
questions.question: What forms the hemiazygos vein?

questions.explanation: The right lower lobe contains five bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The superior segment is also called the apical segment of the lower lobe and is the most dependent segment when lying supine.
questions.question: How many segments are in right lower lobe?
The cystic duct typically joins the common hepatic duct to form which structure?
questions.explanation: The cystic duct (3-4 cm long, containing spiral valves of Heister) joins the common hepatic duct (formed by union of right and left hepatic ducts at porta hepatis) to form the common bile duct. The CBD (approximately 8 cm long) descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, passes behind the first part of duodenum, through the head of pancreas, and joins the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) in the wall of the second part of duodenum. Variations in this anatomy are common and surgically important.

questions.question: What structure forms the lateral boundary of mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The mediastinum is bounded laterally by the right and left pleural cavities and their contained lungs. Anteriorly, it is bounded by the sternum; posteriorly by the thoracic vertebrae. Superiorly, it extends to the root of the neck, and inferiorly to the diaphragm.

questions.question: Which pleura has somatic sensory innervation?
questions.explanation: Only the parietal pleura has somatic sensory innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerves, making it sensitive to pain. The visceral pleura has no somatic sensory nerve supply and receives only autonomic vasomotor innervation. This explains why pleural pain is sharp and well-localized to the chest wall.

Carpal tunnel syndrome causes weakness of thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis) due to median nerve compression. This results from compression of the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Thumb opposition and abduction are particularly affected.
questions.question: What muscle weakness occurs in carpal tunnel syndrome?
The left triangular ligament of the liver attaches to which lobe?
questions.explanation: The left triangular ligament is formed by the approximation of the anterior and posterior layers of the left coronary ligament near the left end of the bare area, attaching the left lobe of the liver to the diaphragm. It is typically longer and narrower than the right triangular ligament. Division of this ligament is necessary to mobilize the left lateral segment of the liver during surgery. The ligament represents the reflection of peritoneum from the diaphragm onto the superior surface of the liver and demarcates the left lateral limit of the bare area of the liver.

questions.question: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) most commonly develops in the deep veins of the leg. Which two veins are most commonly involved initially?
questions.explanation: DVT most commonly begins in the posterior tibial and fibular veins of the calf, often in valve sinuses where flow is stagnant. From here, thrombus can propagate proximally into the popliteal and femoral veins. The deep veins are the primary concern because thrombus there can embolize to the pulmonary circulation, causing potentially fatal pulmonary embolism. Superficial thrombophlebitis occurs in the saphenous veins.

questions.question: Which vessel crosses anterior to the left renal vein?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery crosses anteriorly to the left renal vein as the vein passes from left to right to drain into the IVC. This can occasionally cause compression of the left renal vein (nutcracker syndrome), leading to left gonadal vein reflux, hematuria, or left flank pain. The left renal vein also passes anterior to the aorta.

A positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness of the gluteus medius on the stance (weight-bearing) side. Normally, gluteus medius contracts to prevent the pelvis from dropping on the swinging side. When it is weak (as in superior gluteal nerve palsy, hip abductor tendon tears, or hip joint disease), the pelvis drops toward the unsupported side. This produces the Trendelenburg lurch in gait.
questions.question: A positive Trendelenburg sign (pelvis drops on the unsupported side during single-leg stance) indicates weakness of which muscle?
Which compartment contains structures passing through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The flexor compartment of the hand receives structures passing through the carpal tunnel, including flexor tendons and the median nerve. The tunnel's confined space makes it susceptible to compression syndromes. Any lesion diminishing compartment size can result in median nerve compression.

The sigmoid colon receives its blood supply from 2-4 sigmoid arteries (sigmoidal arteries), branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. These arteries descend in the sigmoid mesocolon, anastomosing with each other and with branches from the left colic artery superiorly and the superior rectal artery inferiorly, contributing to the marginal artery along the mesenteric border. Sudeck's point, at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from anal verge), represents a watershed area where the last sigmoid artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery and is vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the sigmoid colon?
Which structure joins the posterior part of the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle?
questions.explanation: The posterior meniscofemoral ligament is a strong tendinous slip joining the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle. The coronary ligaments attach both menisci to the tibial condyles. The transverse ligament joins the anterior edges of both menisci, allowing them to move together during knee movements.

The classical hepatic lobule is a hexagonal structural unit with a central vein at its center and portal triads at the periphery (corners). Hepatocytes are arranged in plates radiating from the central vein with sinusoids between them. Blood flows from portal triads through sinusoids to the central vein. This is the histological/structural concept, though the hepatic acinus is a better functional unit.
questions.question: What is the functional unit of liver according to the lobular concept?

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery crosses the roof of the ethmoid sinuses and is at risk during frontal and ethmoidal sinus surgery. It is a branch of the ophthalmic artery and supplies the anterior ethmoidal cells, frontal sinus, and anterior nasal cavity. Damage can cause orbital hematoma or CSF leak.
questions.question: Which artery is most at risk during frontal sinus surgery?

questions.explanation: The median nerve provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. This sensory distribution is preserved in anterior interosseous syndrome (pure motor branch) but affected in carpal tunnel syndrome and more proximal median nerve injuries.
questions.question: What provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb?
Which nerve innervates the cremaster muscle?
questions.explanation: The cremaster muscle receives motor innervation from the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2), which enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring and travels within the spermatic cord. The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis in response to stroking the inner thigh) tests this nerve and the L1-L2 cord segments. The ilioinguinal nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the scrotum and adjacent thigh but does not innervate the cremaster muscle. The cremasteric artery (from inferior epigastric) provides vascular supply to the cremaster muscle and travels alongside the nerve.

questions.question: What forms the right heart border radiographically?
questions.explanation: The right border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed by the right atrium. The left border is formed primarily by the left ventricle with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. The superior border is formed by the great vessels (aorta and pulmonary artery).

The superior mesenteric artery and vein cross anteriorly over the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship can cause superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, where the duodenum is compressed between the SMA and the aorta, leading to intestinal obstruction. The third part of the duodenum passes from right to left across the vertebral column at L3.
questions.question: Which vessels cross anterior to the third part of the duodenum?
The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through which structure, then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel (formed by the flexor retinaculum and medial ankle bones), accompanying the tibial nerve. It then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries, supplying the plantar foot and contributing to the toes via the deep plantar arch. Its pulse is palpated inferoposterior to the medial malleolus.

questions.question: How many bones are present in both lower limbs combined, considering femurs, patellae, tibiae, fibulae, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges?
questions.explanation: The bones of both lower limbs total 60: 2 femurs, 2 patellae, 2 tibiae, 2 fibulae, 14 tarsals, 10 metatarsals, and 28 phalanges. This understanding is fundamental in trauma assessment and radiological interpretation. Each single lower limb contains 30 bones.

The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior third (dorsal surface) of the tongue behind the sulcus terminalis. It forms part of Waldeyer's ring with the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils. The lingual tonsil is covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. Hypertrophy can cause airway obstruction or dysphagia.
questions.question: The lingual tonsil is located on which surface of the tongue?
What defines polymastia?
questions.explanation: Polymastia is the presence of extra (supernumerary) breast tissue, which can occur anywhere along the embryonic mammary ridge (milk line) from axilla to groin. This is distinct from polythelia (extra nipples only). Supernumerary breast tissue can undergo the same pathological changes as normal breasts.

options: Only the transverse arch of the foot
The transverse arch and potentially both longitudinal arches
questions.explanation: Lisfranc joint injuries disrupt the tarsometatarsal joint complex, which is the keystone of both the transverse arch and the longitudinal arches. These injuries range from subtle ligamentous sprains to complete fracture-dislocations. Missed Lisfranc injuries lead to progressive collapse of all foot arches, chronic pain, and disability. Early anatomical reduction and fixation are essential.
questions.question: The Lisfranc joint (tarsometatarsal joint complex) connects the midfoot to the forefoot. Injury at this joint is clinically significant because it disrupts which arch?
The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with which important venous structure?
questions.explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins and deep facial veins. This valveless connection allows spread of infection from the infratemporal fossa to the cranial cavity. The plexus receives maxillary, middle meningeal, and deep temporal veins.

questions.question: Where does the left testicular vein drain?
questions.explanation: The left testicular (gonadal) vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava obliquely. This difference in drainage, along with the longer left testicular vein, explains why varicoceles are much more common on the left side (85-90% of cases).

questions.question: The hindfoot consists of which two bones?
questions.explanation: The hindfoot consists of the talus and the calcaneus. The calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest and strongest bone, absorbing shock and leveraging movement. The talus (ankle bone) articulates with the tibia and fibula superiorly and with the calcaneus inferiorly and navicular anteriorly, allowing ankle movement and weight transfer to the foot.

questions.question: How does the brachial plexus organization reflect compartment innervation?
options: Anterior divisions supply flexors, posterior divisions supply extensors
questions.explanation: Brachial plexus organization reflects compartmental function: anterior divisions supply flexor (anterior) compartment muscles while posterior divisions supply extensor (posterior) compartment muscles. This organizational pattern continues from the plexus through the peripheral nerves, reflecting embryological development.

questions.question: Which glands open into the bulbar urethra?
questions.explanation: The bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands) are paired pea-sized glands located in the urogenital diaphragm that drain via long ducts into the bulbar portion of the spongy urethra. They secrete a clear, mucoid pre-ejaculatory fluid that lubricates the urethra and neutralizes acidic urine residue. These glands are homologous to Bartholin's glands in females.

The vas deferens crosses superior to the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, then curves medially, crossing over (anterior to) the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder. At the inguinal region, the vas deferens "hooks" around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery, crossing it from lateral to medial as it exits the deep inguinal ring. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. The vas is easily palpable in the spermatic cord and feels like a firm cord or thick string.
questions.question: The vas deferens crosses which vessel during its pelvic course?
The vocal ligament is the thickened upper edge of which membrane?
questions.explanation: The vocal ligament is the thickened free upper edge of the cricothyroid membrane (conus elasticus). It extends from the vocal process of the arytenoid to the posterior surface of the thyroid cartilage. The ligament is covered by mucosa to form the true vocal cord.

questions.question: Despite its complexity with two articulations, the knee joint is primarily classified as which type of synovial joint?
questions.explanation: The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint in the body, primarily classified as a hinge-type synovial joint. It has two articulations: the tibiofemoral joint (femur with tibia, bearing most body weight) and the patellofemoral joint (femur with patella). Despite being hinge-like, the knee also allows rotation during the screw-home mechanism.

The head of the pancreas lies in the concavity formed by the C-shaped duodenum and indents the medial aspect of the second (descending) part. The pancreatic head is intimately related to the duodenum, particularly the second part where the bile and pancreatic ducts enter. This close relationship means that pancreatic head disease often affects the duodenum and vice versa.
questions.question: Which structure indents the second part of the duodenum medially?
Which structure passes through the triangular interval?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery pass through the triangular interval. This space is bounded by teres major superiorly, long head of triceps medially, and lateral head of triceps laterally. The structures then enter the spiral groove of the humerus.

involves median nerve compression between the two heads of pronator teres in the proximal forearm. Unlike carpal tunnel syndrome, this causes proximal symptoms and affects the palmar cutaneous branch. Forearm pain and median nerve sensory symptoms are characteristic.
questions.question: Which condition involves median nerve compression in the forearm?
Which bone forms the lateral wall of the nasal cavity?
questions.explanation: The lateral nasal wall is formed by the maxilla (medial surface), ethmoid bone (superior and middle conchae, and perpendicular plate), palatine bone (perpendicular plate), inferior nasal concha, and lacrimal bone. The complex three-dimensional structure creates the superior, middle, and inferior meatuses. Understanding this anatomy is essential for sinus surgery.

options: Wrist extensors stabilize wrist enabling grip strength
questions.explanation: During grip, wrist extensors isometrically contract to stabilize the wrist in slight extension. This prevents wrist flexion as finger flexors contract, optimizing finger flexor length-tension relationship for maximum grip force. This synergistic stabilization demonstrates functional muscle interaction.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist flexors and extensors in grip?

questions.explanation: Afferent (sensory) nerve fibers from the kidneys travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at T10-T12 and L1 segments. This explains the referred pain pattern of renal colic, which radiates from the loin to the groin along the distribution of these dermatomes. Ureteric pain follows a similar pattern as the ureter shares this innervation.
questions.question: Which spinal segments provide afferent innervation from the kidney?

options: Scaphoid palpation and radial artery assessment
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuffbox allows clinical palpation of the scaphoid bone (floor) and assessment of radial artery pulse (crossing the floor). Tenderness in the snuffbox after wrist trauma suggests scaphoid fracture. The borders (thumb extensor and abductor tendons) are easily identified.
questions.question: What is the clinical significance of the anatomical snuffbox?

questions.explanation: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) is a muscular bridge extending from the interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle. It carries the right bundle branch of the conducting system, ensuring coordinated activation of the papillary muscles. It prevents overdistention of the ventricle and was historically important for determining ventricular orientation.
questions.question: Which structure carries the right bundle branch in the right ventricle?

questions.explanation: The iliacus muscle is innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3). It originates from the iliac crest, iliac fossa, ala of sacrum, and anterior sacroiliac ligaments, and inserts into the tendon of psoas major and the lesser trochanter. Acting conjointly with psoas major and minor, it flexes the thigh at the hip and stabilizes the joint.
questions.question: The iliacus muscle, originating from the iliac fossa, is innervated by which nerve?
What is the normal percentage of reticulocytes in peripheral blood?
questions.explanation: Reticulocytes (immature red blood cells still containing RNA) normally comprise 0.5-1.5% of circulating red blood cells, representing the daily replacement of senescent erythrocytes. The reticulocyte count increases in hemolysis or bleeding (compensatory bone marrow response) and decreases in bone marrow failure or nutritional deficiencies. The spleen removes excessive RNA from reticulocytes (pitting function).

questions.question: The taeniae coli are thickenings of which muscle layer?
questions.explanation: The taeniae coli represent three longitudinal bands where the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the colon is thickened and concentrated, running from cecum to rectosigmoid junction. The three bands are: taenia libera (free, anteriorly on ascending and descending colon), taenia mesocolica (at mesenteric attachment), and taenia omentalis (at omental attachment). Between the taeniae, the longitudinal muscle is thin, allowing the circular muscle to create sacculations (haustra). The taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, providing a surgical landmark. At the rectosigmoid junction (about 15 cm from anus), the taeniae spread to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer in the rectum.

The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is the sensory continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve after it supplies the anterior arm muscles. It provides sensation to the lateral aspect of the forearm from elbow to wrist. This nerve emerges lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.
questions.question: What provides sensory innervation to the lateral forearm?

questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae but do not contain taste buds; they provide the rough texture of the tongue. Fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae all contain taste buds. The circumvallate papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis.
questions.question: Which papillae on the tongue do NOT contain taste buds?

questions.explanation: The left colic artery (first branch of the inferior mesenteric artery) divides into ascending and descending branches near the descending colon. The ascending branch runs superiorly to supply the left (distal) third of the transverse colon and splenic flexure, anastomosing with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery. The descending branch runs inferiorly along the descending colon, anastomosing with branches of the sigmoid arteries. This anastomotic pattern creates collateral circulation between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories, though the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) remains a watershed area vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: The left colic artery typically divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal canal is formed by the lacrimal bone and maxilla, housing the nasolacrimal duct. The duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior meatus. The valve of Hasner at the inferior opening prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction requires dacryocystorhinostomy surgery.
questions.question: The nasolacrimal duct is formed by which two bones?
What is the action of opponens digiti minimi?
questions.explanation: Opponens digiti minimi draws the fifth metacarpal forward and rotates it laterally, deepening the palm and opposing the little finger toward the thumb. It is one of the three hypothenar muscles and is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Lymphatic drainage from the appendix passes through lymph nodes in the mesoappendix to the ileocolic lymph nodes along the ileocolic artery, which subsequently drain to superior mesenteric lymph nodes along the superior mesenteric artery. From there, lymph flows to the pre-aortic nodes and eventually to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This drainage pattern follows the arterial supply (appendicular artery from ileocolic artery from SMA). Enlarged ileocolic nodes may be palpable in appendicitis and can contribute to diagnostic imaging findings in acute abdominal conditions.
questions.question: The appendicular lymph nodes drain into which nodal group?
Which nerve supplies the anterior belly of the digastric?
questions.explanation: The anterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects embryologic derivation from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively. The digastric helps open the mouth and elevate the hyoid.

The scapulothoracic "joint" is not a true anatomical joint but a functional articulation between the scapula and thoracic wall. It allows scapular movements (elevation, depression, protraction, retraction, rotation) essential for positioning the glenoid cavity. Muscle action rather than ligaments controls this "joint."
questions.question: What is the significance of the scapulothoracic joint?
options: Functional articulation allowing scapular mobility on thorax

questions.explanation: The trochanteric anastomosis is formed by four arteries: superior gluteal (SGA), inferior gluteal (IGA), medial femoral circumflex (MFCA), and lateral femoral circumflex (LFCA) arteries. Disruption of this anastomosis in femoral neck fractures leads to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
questions.question: The trochanteric anastomosis, providing the main blood supply to the head of femur, is formed by which four arteries?

options: Anterior compartment flexor with radial nerve supply
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is unique as an anterior compartment muscle (flexor) supplied by the radial nerve, which typically supplies extensors. This reflects its developmental origin from extensor muscle mass despite its eventual anterior position. It flexes the forearm most effectively from mid-prone position.
questions.question: How does the brachioradialis differ from other radial nerve-supplied muscles?
The first metatarsophalangeal joint is particularly affected by gout, forming a tophus. The big toe joint is important functionally as the propulsion point during which phase of gait?
questions.explanation: The first metatarsophalangeal joint is the primary propulsion point during the push-off (terminal stance) phase of gait. Dorsiflexion of this joint during push-off tensions the plantar aponeurosis via the windlass mechanism, raising the medial longitudinal arch and providing a rigid lever for propulsion. Hallux rigidus (stiff 1st MTP joint) severely impairs push-off and causes antalgic gait.

options: Upper and middle trapezius, levator scapulae
questions.explanation: Elevation of the scapula is caused by contraction of upper and middle fibers of trapezius and levator scapulae muscles. This movement is associated with elevation of the lateral end and depression of the medial end of the clavicle. Shoulder shrugging demonstrates this action.
questions.question: Which muscles elevate the scapula?
What predisposes the scaphoid to avascular necrosis following fracture?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid has a unique retrograde blood supply with only one small artery entering distally. Fracture through the middle disrupts blood supply to the proximal fragment, which has no alternative source. This makes the proximal fragment vulnerable to avascular necrosis if not promptly treated.

questions.question: At which level is the aortic hiatus located?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus is located at the T12 vertebral level, posterior to the diaphragm (technically behind rather than through it). It is formed by the median arcuate ligament connecting the right and left crura. It transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos vein. As it's posterior to the diaphragm, aortic flow is not impeded during diaphragmatic contraction.

The anterior mediastinum (between the sternum and pericardium) contains primarily the thymus gland (or its remnant in adults), fatty tissue, and lymph nodes. In children, the thymus is prominent; in adults, it is largely replaced by fat. This space can be involved in thymomas or lymphomas.
questions.question: What lies in the anterior mediastinum primarily?

questions.explanation: Beck's triad comprises three clinical signs of cardiac tamponade: (1) hypotension (due to reduced cardiac output), (2) elevated jugular venous pressure/JVP (due to impaired venous return), and (3) muffled/distant heart sounds (due to fluid surrounding the heart). Pulsus paradoxus (excessive decrease in systolic BP during inspiration) is another important sign.
questions.question: What are Beck's triad signs?

options: Anterior for deep flexors, posterior for extensors
Anterior for extensors, posterior for flexors
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies deep flexor muscles (flexor pollicis longus, radial half of flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus) while the posterior interosseous nerve supplies all posterior forearm extensors. This complementary distribution ensures complete innervation of forearm muscles from the radial and median nerves.
questions.question: How do the anterior and posterior interosseous nerves complement each other?
What is the marginal artery of the heart?
questions.explanation: The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery that descends along the acute margin (right border) of the heart to supply the right ventricle. The left marginal artery (branch of the circumflex or left coronary artery) supplies the left border of the heart. These marginal branches are important anatomical landmarks in cardiac catheterization and surgery.

questions.question: Which muscle protracts the eyeball?
questions.explanation: The inferior oblique muscle is the only extraocular muscle that protracts (brings forward) the eyeball along with extorsion, elevation, and abduction. It arises from the maxilla at the anteromedial orbital floor and inserts on the posterolateral inferior eyeball. The muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). It has no relationship with the common tendinous ring.

questions.question: What causes olecranon bursitis in students?
questions.explanation: Olecranon bursitis in students results from repeated trauma and pressure to the posterior elbow from leaning on desks. The subcutaneous olecranon bursa becomes inflamed and swollen. The condition is called student's elbow or miner's elbow depending on the occupation causing the repetitive trauma.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior mesenteric artery arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the anterior surface of the abdominal aorta at approximately the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), about 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. It supplies the hindgut derivatives: distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum. Its first branch is the left colic artery.

Three muscles arise from the styloid process: styloglossus, stylohyoid, and stylopharyngeus. These muscles form part of the "styloid apparatus" along with two ligaments (stylomandibular and stylohyoid). The styloid process projects downward and forward from the temporal bone. Elongation (Eagle syndrome) causes pharyngeal pain and dysphagia.
questions.question: The styloid process gives attachment to which muscles?
Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of the talus is a known complication of which type of ankle/foot injury due to the talus having no direct muscle attachments and a tenuous blood supply?
questions.explanation: Avascular necrosis is a well-recognized complication of talar neck fractures, classified by the Hawkins system. The talus receives its blood supply from branches of the posterior tibial, anterior tibial, and fibular arteries entering through its non-articular portions. Displaced talar neck fractures disrupt these vessels. Hawkins sign (subchondral osteopenia on radiograph at 6-8 weeks) is a favorable sign indicating intact blood supply.

The foramen of Morgagni is located anteriorly between the xiphoid and costal origins of the diaphragm. Hernias through this opening (Morgagni hernias) are less common than Bochdalek hernias but can allow omental fat or intestine to herniate into the anterior mediastinum. They are usually asymptomatic.
questions.question: Where is Morgagni's foramen located?

questions.explanation: The 7-12 vallate (circumvallate) papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue. Each papilla is surrounded by a circular trench containing taste buds. Von Ebner's glands open into the trenches, washing the taste buds.
questions.question: The vallate papillae are arranged in which pattern?

questions.explanation: The first (medial) lumbrical is innervated by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3), while the lateral three lumbricals are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3). The lumbricals originate from the tendons of flexor digitorum longus and insert into the medial aspect of the extensor expansion over the lateral four digits. Their dual action balances flexion and extension.
questions.question: The lumbricals of the foot flex the proximal phalanges and extend the middle and distal phalanges of the lateral four digits. The first lumbrical is innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: When the thigh and knee are flexed, the hamstrings extend the trunk. This action is important in activities such as rising from a forward-flexed position and in postural control. The hamstrings also flex the leg at the knee and extend the thigh at the hip. Semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate the leg, while biceps femoris laterally rotates it when the knee is flexed.
questions.question: When the thigh and knee are already flexed, the hamstring muscles perform which action on the trunk?
The transverse acetabular ligament converts the acetabular notch into a foramen. It also serves as the base of attachment for which intracapsular ligament?
questions.explanation: The transverse acetabular ligament bridges across the acetabular notch, converting it into a foramen for vessels and nerves, and serves as the base of attachment for the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the margin of the acetabulum that deepens it.

questions.question: Intragluteal injections are safely administered in the upper lateral quadrant. Which nerve, if inadvertently injected, causes permanent foot drop?
options: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.explanation: Inadvertent injection into the sciatic nerve causes severe pain, paralysis, and sensory loss in the leg and foot, resulting in permanent foot drop if the common fibular division is damaged. This is avoided by always using the upper lateral quadrant, away from the midway line between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter where the sciatic nerve courses.

Rupture of the long head of biceps tendon causes the characteristic "Popeye" sign, where the muscle belly retracts distally creating a prominent bulge. This typically occurs in older individuals during forceful elbow flexion. Surprisingly, functional deficit is minimal as the short head remains intact.
questions.question: What muscle action creates the Popeye sign?

options: Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
Abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis
Plantar interossei, dorsal interossei, flexor hallucis brevis
Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi
questions.explanation: The first layer of foot muscles contains three muscles: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, and abductor digiti minimi. All three originate from the medial tubercle of the tuberosity of the calcaneus and the plantar aponeurosis. Abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis are innervated by the medial plantar nerve, while abductor digiti minimi is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.
questions.question: The sole of the foot muscles are arranged in four layers. The first layer contains three muscles. Which combination is correct?
The inferior vena cava is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), to the right of the midline and anterior to the right common iliac artery. From this point, it ascends on the right side of the aorta, anterior to the vertebral column, receiving tributaries in an asymmetric pattern. The IVC passes through the diaphragm (caval opening in central tendon) at T8 level to enter the thorax and immediately empties into the right atrium. The formation level (L5) is slightly lower than the aortic bifurcation (L4).

Forearm compartment syndrome develops when increased pressure within closed fascial compartments (from edema, hemorrhage, or external compression) impairs venous drainage then arterial inflow. This causes muscle ischemia and potential Volkmann's contracture. The deep fascia and interosseous membrane create compartments limiting expansion.
questions.question: How does compartment syndrome develop in the forearm?
options: Caused through soft tissue infection alone
Elevated compartment pressure impairs tissue perfusion

questions.question: Which condition results from portal vein thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Portal vein thrombosis causes portal hypertension by obstructing blood flow to the liver, leading to increased pressure in the portal system. This can cause splenomegaly, ascites, and development of portosystemic collaterals including esophageal varices, hemorrhoids, and caput medusae. Causes include hypercoagulable states, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, and abdominal sepsis. Chronic thrombosis may lead to cavernous transformation of the portal vein.

Jersey finger results from avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus from the distal phalanx. This commonly occurs in the ring finger when a player's finger catches in another player's jersey during tackle attempts. Inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint is diagnostic.
questions.question: What causes Jersey finger?

questions.explanation: Post-splenectomy blood films show: Howell-Jolly bodies (DNA remnants) in red cells, target cells, acanthocytes, thrombocytosis, and occasionally nucleated red cells. Leukocytosis may also occur. These findings reflect loss of the spleen's filtering function that normally removes inclusions and abnormal cells. Howell-Jolly bodies are the most specific marker of asplenia or hyposplenism.
questions.question: Which blood cells may show abnormalities post-splenectomy?
Which muscle elevates the hyoid bone and pharynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle elevates the pharynx and hyoid bone during swallowing, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) depress the hyoid. Longitudinal pharyngeal muscles collectively raise the pharynx to engulf the food bolus.

The base of the axilla is formed by skin, subcutaneous tissue, and axillary fascia spanning from the fourth rib. This base is concave and forms the floor of the axillary space. The axillary fascia is continuous with the pectoral fascia anteriorly and latissimus dorsi fascia posteriorly.
questions.question: At which rib level is the axilla base formed?

questions.explanation: The adult urinary bladder has a capacity of approximately 400-600 ml, with the desire to void typically occurring at about 150-250 ml and strong urgency at 400-500 ml. The bladder is highly distensible due to its muscular wall (detrusor muscle) and transitional epithelium lining. Capacity can be reduced in pathological conditions or increased with chronic retention.
questions.question: What is the typical capacity of an adult urinary bladder?

questions.explanation: The occipital sinus lies in the attached border of the falx cerebelli and drains into the confluence of sinuses. It is the smallest of the cranial venous sinuses. The sinus communicates with the vertebral venous plexuses through the foramen magnum. It runs in the midline on the internal occipital crest.
questions.question: The occipital sinus drains into which structure?

questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, located immediately superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. Its margins, called the medial and lateral crura, are connected superiorly by intercrural fibers and give attachment to the external spermatic fascia. The superficial ring represents the external opening of the inguinal canal and transmits the spermatic cord in males or round ligament in females, along with the ilioinguinal nerve. The ring is larger in males than females, contributing to the higher incidence of inguinal hernias in males.
questions.question: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in which structure?
Which valve cusp is attached to the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: The septal cusp of the tricuspid valve is attached to the interventricular septum, while the anterior and posterior cusps are attached to the anterior and posterior ventricular walls respectively. The septal cusp receives chordae tendineae from the septal and posterior papillary muscles. Ventricular septal defects near the membranous septum can affect this cusp's support.

questions.question: What prevents the kidney from descending more than normal?
questions.explanation: The renal vessels (particularly the renal veins attached to the IVC) are the main structures preventing excessive descent of the kidneys. The renal fascia provides minimal support. Loss of perirenal fat (in cachexia) can lead to nephroptosis (floating kidney), where the kidney descends excessively with positional changes, potentially causing ureteric kinking and obstruction.

questions.question: The vaginal artery typically arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The vaginal artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (though it may arise from the uterine artery) and descends to supply the vagina. It gives off numerous branches to the anterior and posterior vaginal walls, anastomosing with branches from the uterine artery superiorly and internal pudendal artery inferiorly. This rich anastomotic network provides extensive collateral circulation to the vagina. The vagina also receives blood supply from the middle rectal and internal pudendal arteries. The upper vagina drains via uterine veins, while the lower vagina drains via internal pudendal veins.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pierce the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening (foramen venae cavae) in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level, the highest of the three major diaphragmatic openings. This opening also transmits branches of the right phrenic nerve. The esophageal hiatus (T10 level) transmits the esophagus and vagal trunks, while the aortic hiatus (T12 level) transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. The IVC opening dilates during inspiration as the diaphragm contracts and descends, facilitating venous return to the heart.
