questions.question: What is clinical significance of esophageal venous drainage?
questions.explanation: The esophageal veins form an important portosystemic anastomosis where portal venous blood (from lower esophagus draining to left gastric vein) connects with systemic venous blood (middle and upper esophagus draining to azygos system and brachiocephalic veins). In portal hypertension, these veins dilate to form esophageal varices which can rupture.

questions.question: Which muscle elevates the first rib?
questions.explanation: The scalene muscles fix and elevate the first rib during inspiration. With the first rib fixed, the external and internal intercostal muscles elevate the other ribs upward toward it. The scalene muscles are accessory muscles of respiration and are particularly active during forced inspiration.

Smith's fracture (reverse Colles' fracture) results from falling on the back of a flexed wrist. This causes volar (forward) displacement of the distal radius fragment, opposite to Colles' fracture. The mechanism is less common than the fall on an outstretched hand that causes Colles' fracture.
options: Fall on back of flexed wrist
questions.question: What causes Smith's fracture of the distal radius?
Which thigh muscle has TWO different nerve supplies from two different divisions of two different named nerves?
questions.explanation: Adductor magnus uniquely has two parts with different nerve supplies: the adductor part (obturator nerve, L2, L3, L4) and the hamstring part (tibial division of sciatic nerve). This dual origin and nerve supply reflects its dual embryological origin. Biceps femoris similarly has two heads with different nerve divisions of the sciatic nerve.

questions.question: Which muscles form the posterior wall of the axilla?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the axilla is formed by subscapularis on the anterior surface of the scapula superiorly, and teres major and latissimus dorsi inferiorly. The posterior axillary fold extends farther inferiorly than the anterior wall and can be grasped between fingers.

The anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves supply the breast. These nerves convey sensory fibers to the skin, sympathetic fibers to blood vessels, and fibers to smooth muscle in the overlying skin and nipple. Pain from breast pathology follows these dermatomes.
questions.question: Which intercostal nerves supply the breast?
The parotid duct pierces which muscle before opening into the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct pierces the buccinator muscle to open into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar tooth. The duct is approximately 5 cm long and crosses the masseter muscle superficially. Trauma to the cheek can damage the duct causing salivary fistula.

The gastrocolic ligament, part of the greater omentum, connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon. It contains the right and left gastroepiploic vessels along the greater curvature and represents the anterior two layers of the greater omentum before they descend and fold back. Division of the gastrocolic ligament provides surgical access to the lesser sac (omental bursa) and is a key step in gastric surgery, transverse colectomy, and pancreatic surgery. The avascular plane (relatively avascular window) between the gastroepiploic vessels and transverse colon can be developed to enter the lesser sac with minimal bleeding.
questions.question: The gastrocolic ligament connects the stomach to which structure?
The glossopharyngeal nerve exits the skull through which foramen?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) exits the skull through the jugular foramen along with the vagus (X) and accessory (XI) nerves. The internal jugular vein also passes through this foramen. The nerve descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein to reach the pharynx.

questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to supply the posterior and medial thigh?
questions.explanation: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery consist of three or four arteries that perforate the adductor magnus muscle, contributing to the supply of the medial and posterior thigh muscles. The lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies the lateral thigh, while the medial femoral circumflex artery supplies the femoral head and neck.

Phrenic nerve injury causes paralysis of the corresponding hemidiaphragm, which becomes elevated and moves paradoxically upward during inspiration. Causes include surgical trauma (especially cardiac surgery), tumors, neurological disease, and cervical spine injury. Bilateral phrenic nerve injury causes severe respiratory compromise. The phrenic nerve can be stimulated to pace the diaphragm in some patients.
questions.question: Which nerve injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis?

options: One centimeter distal to wrist joint
One centimeter proximal to superficial arch
questions.question: At what level does the deep palmar arch lie in the hand?
questions.explanation: The deep palmar arch is formed by the radial artery and deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery. It lies approximately one centimeter proximal to the superficial palmar arch at the level of the proximal border of the extended thumb. It gives off palmar metacarpal arteries and perforating branches.

The greater splanchnic nerve, after synapsing in the celiac ganglion, provides sympathetic innervation to foregut-derived organs including the stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, small intestine, and proximal colon (to the splenic flexure). It also carries visceral afferent fibers for pain sensation from these organs.
questions.question: Which organs receive greater splanchnic innervation?

questions.explanation: The foot contains seven tarsal bones: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiform bones (medial, intermediate, and lateral). The 26 bones of the foot include 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges. Understanding tarsal anatomy is fundamental to interpreting foot radiographs and managing tarsal fractures.
questions.question: The foot contains how many tarsal bones, and what are they?
options: Five: calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid, one cuneiform
Seven: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiforms
Six: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and two cuneiforms
Eight: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and four cuneiforms
Seven: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals

questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and vein pass between the two peritoneal layers of the mesentery along with lymph nodes, lymphatic vessels, nerves, and fat. These vessels provide the primary blood supply and drainage for the jejunum and ileum. The superior mesenteric artery gives off 15-18 branches that form the arterial arcades.
questions.question: Which structures pass between the two layers of the mesentery?

questions.explanation: Since there are 12 ribs on each side, there are 11 intercostal spaces between them. Each intercostal space contains intercostal muscles, neurovascular bundles, and lymphatics. Understanding the anatomy of these spaces is crucial for procedures like thoracentesis and chest tube insertion.
questions.question: How many intercostal spaces are present on each side?
The ankle joint allows primarily which movements?
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (talocrural joint) primarily allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, with a small degree of rotation. Inversion and eversion occur primarily at the subtalar joint (talocalcaneal articulation) and midtarsal joints. The talocrural joint has a range of approximately 20 degrees dorsiflexion and 50 degrees plantarflexion in a healthy adult.

questions.question: The lesser trochanter, the traction epiphysis of which muscle, projects from the posterior surface of the femur and points in which direction?
questions.explanation: The lesser trochanter is the traction epiphysis of the iliopsoas muscle, the great flexor of the hip joint. It projects from the posterior surface of the femur and is conical, pointing medially. It marks the lowermost fibers of the gluteus maximus insertion.

The anterior cranial fossa accommodates the frontal lobes of the brain. The floor is formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, cribriform plate of ethmoid, and lesser wings of sphenoid. The crista galli provides attachment for the falx cerebri. Fractures can cause CSF rhinorrhea through the cribriform plate.
questions.question: The anterior cranial fossa contains which lobe of the brain?

questions.explanation: Nine flexor tendons accompany the median nerve through the carpal tunnel: four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, plus the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These tendons are enclosed in synovial sheaths within the tunnel.
questions.question: What structure accompanies the median nerve through the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: The quadratus lumborum muscle forms the central posterior relation of each kidney. The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially, and the transversus abdominis muscle (its aponeurosis) lies posterolaterally. The diaphragm is posterior to the upper pole, and the subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run posterior to the kidneys.
questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately posterior to both kidneys?

questions.explanation: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, descending in the parametrium (base of the broad ligament) to reach the uterus at the level of the internal cervical os. It crosses superior to (over) the ureter approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"), an important surgical relationship. The artery ascends along the lateral margin of the uterus in a tortuous course, giving off branches to the uterus and anastomosing superiorly with the ovarian artery. During pregnancy, it enlarges significantly to supply the gravid uterus and placenta.
questions.question: The uterine artery is a branch of which vessel?
At which vertebral level does the renal artery arise from the aorta?
questions.explanation: The renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta at approximately the level of the L2 vertebral body, just inferior to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery. The right renal artery is longer than the left and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava to reach the right kidney. Each renal artery divides into five segmental arteries that are functionally end arteries.

The prostatic urethra (the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra) receives the openings of the two ejaculatory ducts on the seminal colliculus (verumontanum) and numerous prostatic ducts (15-30 openings) on either side of the urethral crest. The bulbourethral (Cowper's) gland ducts open into the bulbar portion of the spongy urethra, not the prostatic urethra. The prostatic utricle, a small blind pouch representing the remnant of the paramesonephric duct, also opens on the seminal colliculus. The internal urethral sphincter surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra.
questions.question: The prostatic urethra receives openings from which ducts?

questions.explanation: The tensor veli palatini muscle opens the auditory (Eustachian) tube during swallowing by pulling on the membranous lateral wall. The levator veli palatini also contributes. Salpingopharyngeus assists in opening the tube. This mechanism equalizes middle ear pressure with atmospheric pressure.
questions.question: Which muscle opens the auditory tube during swallowing?
Which lymph nodes drain the ovary?
questions.explanation: The ovaries drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, following the ovarian vessels along which the lymphatics ascend. This drainage pattern reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys. In contrast, the uterine fundus drains to para-aortic nodes via lymphatics following the ovarian vessels, while the uterine body drains to external iliac nodes, and the cervix drains to external iliac, internal iliac, and sacral nodes. The upper vagina drains to internal iliac nodes, while the lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

questions.question: Which muscle produces wrist flexion and abduction?
questions.explanation: produces both wrist flexion and wrist abduction (radial deviation). It is a prominent muscle in the anterior forearm, easily palpable lateral to palmaris longus. The muscle is supplied by the median nerve.

questions.question: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles. Which of the following does NOT belong to this compartment?
questions.explanation: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius. Fibularis longus belongs to the lateral compartment, along with fibularis brevis. All anterior compartment muscles are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Paralysis of these muscles causes foot drop.

questions.question: The anal columns (of Morgagni) are found in which part of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The anal columns of Morgagni are 6-10 permanent longitudinal mucosal folds in the upper 15 mm of the anal canal, above the pectinate line, containing terminal radicles of the superior rectal veins (portal system). The lower ends of adjacent columns are connected by anal valves (semilunar mucosal folds), forming the pectinate (dentate) line. Superior to each valve is a small recess called an anal sinus, into which anal glands open. The columns have a plum-red color in living subjects due to the underlying internal rectal venous plexus, and internal hemorrhoids develop from these vascular columns.

options: Pubic tubercle and anterior superior iliac spine
Medial malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine
Inguinal ligament and the femoral condyle
Anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
Pubic crest and posterior superior iliac spine
questions.question: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, defined as the midpoint between which two bony landmarks?
questions.explanation: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. At this point the femoral artery lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve. This is distinct from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, which overlies the femoral canal.

questions.question: Erector spinae and gluteus maximus work together during which functional activity?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus and erector spinae work together in rising from a forward-flexed position, simultaneously extending the hip and the trunk respectively. Gluteus maximus is the great extensor of the hip, particularly powerful in these loaded extension tasks. Weakness of either muscle group causes difficulty in rising from bending and is assessed in clinical examination of low back and hip pathology.
options: Hip abduction while in single-leg stance
Dorsiflexing the ankle during the swing phase of walking
Rising from a forward-flexed position (simultaneous hip and trunk extension)
Rotating the trunk in a sitting position

questions.question: Where is Bochdalek's foramen located?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Bochdalek (pleuroperitoneal canal) is located posterolaterally in the diaphragm. Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close this opening results in a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. These hernias are more common on the left side and can allow abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax.

questions.question: The portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The portal vein forms at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level posterior to the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein then ascends obliquely to the right in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and receives the left and right gastric veins.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor supply to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus.
questions.question: The posterior third of the tongue receives general and special sensory from which nerve?
What is the functional importance of the flexor retinaculum?
options: Prevents flexor tendon bowstringing, maintains carpal arch
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum prevents bowstringing of flexor tendons during wrist flexion, maintaining mechanical efficiency. It maintains the carpal arch and serves as origin for thenar and hypothenar muscles. However, it creates the confined carpal tunnel space predisposing to median nerve compression.

The external spermatic fascia, the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the external oblique muscle's aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. Moving inward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the innermost fascial layer is the internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring). The dartos muscle is in the scrotal wall, not directly covering the cord. These concentric layers are acquired sequentially as structures descend through abdominal wall layers.
questions.question: The spermatic cord receives its external covering from which muscle?

questions.explanation: The Thomas test assesses tightness of the hip flexors (primarily iliopsoas). The patient lies supine and holds one knee to the chest (flattening the lumbar lordosis). If the opposite hip cannot remain flat on the table (flexes up), this indicates hip flexor contracture. This is commonly found in patients with lumbar disc disease, hip osteoarthritis, and those who sit for prolonged periods.
questions.question: The Thomas test assesses tightness of which muscle group, with the patient supine and one hip fully flexed against the chest?

questions.explanation: The lower third of the oesophagus receives its arterial supply from branches of the left gastric artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk. This creates an important portosystemic anastomosis with veins draining to both portal and systemic circulations. The upper third is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery and the middle third by oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta.
questions.question: Which artery primarily supplies the lower third of the oesophagus?
What imaging localizes a chyle leak?
questions.explanation: Lymphangiography involves injecting contrast into pedal lymphatics to visualize the lymphatic system and thoracic duct, potentially identifying the site of leakage. This procedure is technically challenging and rarely performed. Modern alternatives include lymphoscintigraphy or high-resolution MRI. Diagnosis is usually made by pleural fluid analysis showing characteristic chyle properties.

questions.question: The marginal artery of Drummond connects which two arterial systems?
questions.explanation: The marginal artery of Drummond (marginal artery of the colon) is a continuous arterial arcade running along the mesenteric border of the colon, connecting the superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arterial territories. It is formed by anastomoses between the ileocolic, right colic, middle colic, left colic, and sigmoid arteries. This vessel provides crucial collateral circulation to the colon and is particularly important at the splenic flexure, where the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial distributions meet. The weakest point in this anastomotic chain occurs at Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid junction).

questions.question: Which artery typically does NOT arise directly from the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The common hepatic artery arises from the celiac trunk (along with left gastric and splenic arteries), not directly from the abdominal aorta. The aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (inferior phrenic, suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, inferior mesenteric artery), paired parietal branches (subcostal, four lumbar arteries), and the unpaired median sacral artery before bifurcating into common iliac arteries. Anatomical variations exist, with occasionally the common hepatic or left gastric arising separately from the aorta (replaced vessels).

The "safe position" (MCP joints flexed 70-90�, IP joints extended, wrist slightly extended) maintains collateral ligaments at maximum length and prevents contracture. This position is also called the "intrinsic plus" position. Prolonged immobilization in other positions can result in permanent stiffness.
options: Position maintaining ligament length and preventing contracture
questions.question: What determines the safe position for hand immobilization?
What is the most common congenital renal anomaly?
questions.explanation: Duplicated (duplex) collecting system is the most common congenital renal anomaly, occurring in 0.5-1% of the population. It can be complete (two separate ureters) or incomplete (ureters join before entering bladder). The upper pole moiety ureter inserts more medially and inferiorly in the bladder (Weigert-Meyer rule) and is prone to obstruction, while the lower pole ureter is prone to reflux.

The inferior phrenic arteries are usually the first branches of the abdominal aorta, arising immediately after it passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, though they may arise from the celiac trunk. They supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm and give off superior suprarenal arteries. Each artery has a medial and lateral branch.
questions.question: From which vessel do the inferior phrenic arteries usually arise?

questions.explanation: The iliohypogastric nerve (L1, sometimes with T12 contribution) emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle, running obliquely across the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum. It pierces the transversus abdominis muscle to run between it and internal oblique, providing motor innervation to these muscles. The nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch (skin over hip) and anterior cutaneous branch (skin above pubis). Other nerves emerging from the lateral border of psoas include ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves. The genitofemoral nerve pierces the anterior surface.
questions.question: The iliohypogastric nerve emerges from which border of psoas?

options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, and first metatarsal
Calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and all metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, and all five metatarsals
questions.question: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by which bones and is described as more rigid and making more contact with the ground?
questions.explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals. Its summit is the subtalar articulation. It is smaller, more rigid, more stable than the medial arch, and makes more contact with the ground. It bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play and has limited mobility, built to transmit weight.

questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
questions.explanation: is not part of the rotator cuff; it acts as a medial rotator and adductor of the humerus. The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. These muscles fuse with the joint capsule and stabilize the glenohumeral joint.

questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the parietal peritoneum?
questions.explanation: The parietal peritoneum receives sensory innervation from the same nerves that supply the overlying body wall region: phrenic nerve (C3-C5) for the central diaphragmatic peritoneum, lower six intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12) for the peripheral diaphragmatic and abdominal wall peritoneum, and lumbar nerves for the pelvic peritoneum. This explains why peritoneal irritation produces well-localized, sharp, somatic pain referred to specific dermatomes. In contrast, the visceral peritoneum is insensitive to touch, temperature, and laceration, being innervated only by autonomic nerves that mediate poorly localized visceral pain in response to stretch, ischemia, or chemical irritation.

options: Anterior deltoid and pectoralis clavicular head
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary shoulder flexor?
questions.explanation: Shoulder flexion is produced primarily by anterior fibers of deltoid and the clavicular head of pectoralis major. Biceps brachii and coracobrachialis provide assistance. This movement raises the arm forward in the sagittal plane.

questions.question: At what location does the brachial artery typically bifurcate into radial and ulnar arteries?
questions.explanation: The brachial artery bifurcates in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. This division occurs under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis into the radial artery (superficial) and ulnar artery (deeper). The cubital fossa provides a triangular space for this important vascular division.

questions.question: How many pulmonary veins emerge from each lung?
questions.explanation: Two pulmonary veins (superior and inferior) emerge from each lung, for a total of four pulmonary veins entering the left atrium. These veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. The openings of the pulmonary veins into the left atrium have no valves.

The duodenum is primarily retroperitoneal except for the first 2 cm of the superior (first) part, which is intraperitoneal and mobile, connecting to the liver via the hepatoduodenal ligament. The descending (second), horizontal (third), and ascending (fourth) parts are all secondarily retroperitoneal, having been covered by peritoneum during development but subsequently becoming fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. The duodenojejunal flexure marks the transition from retroperitoneal duodenum to intraperitoneal jejunum and is supported by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz).
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal?
The hyoglossus muscle separates which two important arteries?
questions.explanation: The hyoglossus muscle is a key surgical landmark separating the lingual artery into three parts: above, on, and below the muscle. The hypoglossal nerve and lingual vein lie superficially on the muscle. Deep lingual and sublingual arteries arise from the lingual artery in relation to this muscle.

The pancreatic acinus is the functional exocrine secretory unit, consisting of pyramid-shaped serous (enzyme-secreting) acinar cells arranged around a small lumen. The acinus is drained by an intercalated duct lined by centroacinar cells. Multiple acini drain into larger ducts, which eventually form the main pancreatic duct. The pancreas structurally resembles the parotid gland.
questions.question: What is the exocrine secretory unit of the pancreas called?

questions.explanation: Within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum), the structures of the portal triad are arranged from anterior to posterior and right to left as: bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and portal vein (posteriorly). This arrangement is sometimes remembered as "DAV" reading from right to left anteriorly (Duct, Artery, Vein). The hepatic artery typically lies anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the bile duct, though anatomical variations are common. Lymph nodes and autonomic nerve plexuses also travel through the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.question: The proper hepatic artery lies in which position within the portal triad?

questions.explanation: The vagus nerves (CN X, both right and left) provide all parasympathetic innervation to the heart via the cardiac plexus. The right vagus preferentially supplies the SA node (negative chronotropy - decreases heart rate), while the left vagus preferentially supplies the AV node (negative dromotropy - slows AV conduction). Vagal stimulation also decreases atrial contractility.
questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart?
Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The lateral border of the pronator teres muscle forms the medial (ulnar) boundary of the cubital fossa. The lateral boundary is formed by the medial border of brachioradialis muscle. The floor consists of brachialis and supinator muscles while the roof is formed by fascia and bicipital aponeurosis.

questions.question: Where is coarctation typically located?
questions.explanation: Aortic coarctation is typically located just distal to the left subclavian artery origin, near the site of the ligamentum arteriosum (remnant of ductus arteriosus). This is called juxtaductal coarctation. Less commonly, it may be preductal or postductal. The stenosis reduces blood flow to the lower body.

questions.question: Which nerve injury causes loss of the regimental badge sensation?
questions.explanation: injury causes loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area (lateral shoulder over deltoid). This sensory territory is supplied by the superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve, the cutaneous continuation of the axillary nerve. The injury also causes deltoid paralysis affecting shoulder abduction.

The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the 5th-9th (or sometimes 5th-10th) thoracic sympathetic ganglia. It descends on the vertebral bodies, pierces the crus of the diaphragm, and synapses in the celiac ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation to foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, pancreas, spleen, etc.).
questions.question: Where does the greater splanchnic nerve arise?

questions.explanation: The renal hilum is positioned at the level of the transpyloric plane, which corresponds to the first lumbar vertebra (L1), though the kidneys themselves extend from approximately T12 to L3. At the hilum, structures are arranged from anterior to posterior as vein, artery, and pelvis (VAP), though the renal vein is most anterior and superior. The left kidney typically sits slightly higher than the right due to the presence of the liver on the right side.
questions.question: The kidney hilum is located at which vertebral level?

options: Common fibular nerve; great saphenous vein
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve (L3, L4). It runs with the great saphenous vein along the medial leg, from the knee to the medial malleolus and then to the medial side of the foot. It provides cutaneous sensation to the medial leg, ankle, and foot. It is at risk during stripping of the great saphenous vein for varicose vein surgery or coronary bypass grafting.
questions.question: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of which nerve and runs with which vein throughout most of the leg?
Which rib does the costal pleural reflection cross midaxillarily?
questions.explanation: The costal line of pleural reflection passes obliquely, crossing the tenth rib in the midaxillary line (MAL). It crosses the eighth rib in the midclavicular line and becomes continuous posteriorly with the vertebral lines at the neck of the twelfth rib. This surface marking is crucial for safe thoracentesis.

The saphenous nerve, which runs with the great saphenous vein from the knee downward, must be identified and protected during saphenofemoral junction ligation and vein stripping. Inadvertent injury causes persistent medial leg and ankle paraesthesia. The saphenous nerve is also at risk during knee replacement surgery and medial ankle procedures. It is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve (L3, L4).
questions.question: Surgical ligation of the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction during varicose vein surgery must identify and protect which named nerve that lies immediately adjacent to the vein?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve exits the pelvis by passing through the obturator foramen, along with the obturator vessels. It then divides into anterior and posterior divisions in the obturator canal. The anterior division runs anterior to obturator externus and adductor brevis, while the posterior division runs posterior to adductor brevis. It supplies the medial compartment of the thigh.
questions.question: The obturator nerve supplies the medial compartment of the thigh. It exits the pelvis through which specific structure?
Which portion of the axillary artery lies behind pectoralis minor?
questions.explanation: The second part of the axillary artery lies directly behind (posterior to) the pectoralis minor muscle. This anatomical relationship is used to divide the artery into three parts. The second part gives off two branches: the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries.

questions.question: The pelvic splanchnic nerves synapse in which location?
questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that synapse in terminal ganglia within or very near the walls of the pelvic organs they supply (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs). This is characteristic of parasympathetic innervation, where the preganglionic fibers are long and synapse close to or within the target organ, while postganglionic fibers are very short. The fibers travel via the inferior hypogastric plexus to reach their destinations but do not synapse there. The pelvic splanchnics also provide parasympathetic innervation to the distal hindgut from the splenic flexure to the upper anal canal.

questions.question: What artery typically accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the supraspinous fossa?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular artery accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the suprascapular notch into the supraspinous fossa. Unlike the nerve which passes under the superior transverse scapular ligament, the artery passes over it. Both structures then pass through the spinoglenoid notch to reach the infraspinous fossa.

questions.question: What are the approximate dimensions of an adult kidney?
questions.explanation: Each adult kidney is approximately 10 cm long, 5 cm wide, and 2.5 cm thick, resembling a large bean in shape. The left kidney is typically slightly longer and narrower than the right. Kidney size is clinically important, as small kidneys may indicate chronic disease while enlarged kidneys suggest acute processes or masses.

The third (horizontal) part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein as they descend toward the root of the mesentery. This relationship can lead to superior mesenteric artery syndrome, where the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta (with the spine) posteriorly, causing partial or complete duodenal obstruction. Risk factors include rapid weight loss, scoliosis, surgical correction of scoliosis, and conditions causing loss of the mesenteric fat pad that normally cushions the angle between the SMA and aorta.
questions.question: The third part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by which vessels?
Which structure contains the portal triad?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament, forming the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, contains the portal triad: the portal vein (posteriorly), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right). This ligament extends from the porta hepatis to the superior border of the first part of the duodenum. The portal triad arrangement is crucial for the Pringle maneuver, where the hepatoduodenal ligament is compressed to control bleeding during hepatic surgery.

The subcostal plane is a horizontal transverse plane passing through the inferior margins of the 10th costal cartilages (lowest point of the costal margin) on each side, corresponding to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Together with the transtubercular plane (L5 level) and the two vertical midclavicular planes, it defines the nine regions of the abdomen. The subcostal plane marks important anatomical landmarks including the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery, the level of the pylorus in some individuals, and the approximate position of the inferior border of the liver.
questions.question: The subcostal plane passes through which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: is the only rotator cuff muscle that performs medial (internal) rotation of the humerus. It lies on the anterior surface of the scapula, filling the subscapular fossa. The other rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) are located posteriorly.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle performs medial rotation of the humerus?
What muscle action is tested by the OK sign?
questions.explanation: The OK sign tests anterior interosseous nerve function by assessing flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger. Inability to form the OK sign indicates anterior interosseous nerve palsy. The patient cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger.

The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and accessory (XI) nerves along with the internal jugular vein. The foramen is divided by a fibrous or bony septum into anteromedial (pars nervosa) and posterolateral (pars vascularis) compartments. Glomus jugulare tumors arise in this region.
questions.question: The jugular foramen transmits which three cranial nerves?

questions.explanation: Zenker's diverticulum is a pharyngeal pouch (false diverticulum) that herniates through Killian's dehiscence (area of weakness between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles). It occurs in the hypopharynx just above the upper esophageal sphincter. Patients present with dysphagia, regurgitation, halitosis, and risk of aspiration.
questions.question: What is a Zenker's diverticulum?

questions.explanation: The crista terminalis is a prominent vertical muscular ridge on the internal right atrial wall that marks the junction between the smooth-walled posterior sinus venarum (derived from the sinus venosus) and the rough-walled anterior part with pectinate muscles (derived from the primitive atrium). Externally, this corresponds to the sulcus terminalis groove.
questions.question: Which structure marks the junction between the smooth and rough parts of the right atrium?
Which nerve supplies the costal pleura?
questions.explanation: The costal pleura receives sensory innervation from the intercostal nerves, which correspond to the dermatomes of the overlying thoracic wall. The blood supply to costal pleura is also from intercostal vessels. This arrangement means that irritation of costal pleura causes sharp, well-localized pain.

questions.question: The popliteus muscle originates from the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and also from the lateral meniscus. It is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within which structure?
questions.explanation: The popliteus is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within the joint capsule of the knee. It passes through a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule (the popliteal hiatus) between the fibular collateral ligament and the lateral meniscus. Popliteal tendinopathy causes posterolateral knee pain during downhill walking when the PCL and popliteus are most active.

questions.question: The parotid gland duct opens opposite which tooth?
questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth. The duct crosses the masseter superficially before piercing the buccinator. A small accessory parotid gland may be present along the duct on the masseter (socia parotidis).

options: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and one cuneiform
All three cuneiforms and the first two metatarsals
Three cuneiforms, cuboid, and the talus
questions.question: The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones. Which bones constitute the midfoot?
questions.explanation: The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones: navicular, cuboid, and three cuneiform bones. The midfoot meets the forefoot at the five tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints. The three cuneiforms articulate proximally with the navicular. The midfoot provides a stable platform and distributes forces between the hindfoot and forefoot during gait.

questions.question: Soleus, unlike gastrocnemius, can plantarflex the ankle regardless of knee position because it does NOT cross the knee joint. It originates from which structures?
options: Both femoral condyles bilaterally (as in gastrocnemius origin)
Navicular tuberosity and the medial cuneiform bone distally
Head of fibula and lateral tibia condyle only
Posterior fibula head and superior quarter; soleal line, medial tibia; tendinous arch
Ischial tuberosity and posterior surface of the femur
questions.explanation: Soleus originates from the posterior aspect of the head and superior quarter of the posterior fibula, the soleal line and middle third of the medial border of the tibia, and a tendinous arch between these bony attachments. It does not cross the knee joint, so it can plantarflex the ankle regardless of knee position. Together with gastrocnemius, it inserts via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the porta hepatis?
questions.explanation: The porta hepatis transmits the portal vein, proper hepatic artery (and its right and left branches), right and left hepatic ducts, nerves (sympathetic and parasympathetic), and lymphatic vessels. These structures, except the hepatic ducts, enter the liver while the ducts exit. The portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct) is enclosed by the hepatoduodenal ligament at the free edge of the lesser omentum.

The first thoracic nerve is atypical because it has no anterior cutaneous branch. Instead, it has a large branch that joins the brachial plexus, corresponding to its lateral cutaneous branch. The second thoracic nerve is also atypical, giving rise to the intercostobrachial nerve.
questions.question: Which thoracic nerve lacks an anterior cutaneous branch?

options: Flex metacarpophalangeal joints, extend interphalangeal joints
questions.question: What is the function of the lumbricals in the hand?
questions.explanation: Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints of the fingers. This unique action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve while the medial two receive ulnar innervation.

The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from T10-11 ganglia, pierces the diaphragm, and synapses in the aorticorenal ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation primarily to the kidneys and suprarenal glands. Some fibers may also reach midgut derivatives. The nerve carries both efferent sympathetic and visceral afferent fibers.
questions.question: What does the lesser splanchnic nerve supply?
Which nerve provides bronchoconstrictors to the lung?
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic fibers that are bronchoconstrictor and secretomotor to bronchial glands. These fibers are also important for the cough reflex. The sympathetic trunk provides fibers that are bronchodilators and inhibit secretion from bronchial glands.

Fractures of the fibular neck are particularly associated with injury to the common fibular nerve, which winds around this subcutaneous location. Injury causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion), loss of eversion (superficial fibular nerve), and sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg. The nerve is also vulnerable to pressure from tight plasters or prolonged crossing of the legs.
questions.question: Fractures of the fibular neck are particularly associated with injury to which nerve, causing foot drop?

options: Fracture of the neck of femur
Congenital dislocation of the femoral head
questions.explanation: Coxa valga, with a neck-shaft angle increased above normal, is associated with congenital dislocation of the femoral head. It results in a relatively longer limb and altered gait mechanics. In contrast, coxa vara, with a reduced neck-shaft angle, follows fracture of the neck of femur.
questions.question: Coxa valga, with an increased neck-shaft angle of the femur, is characteristically associated with which clinical condition?
What does the pericardial cavity normally contain?
questions.explanation: The pericardial cavity normally contains 15-50 ml of serous pericardial fluid that lubricates the surfaces of the visceral and parietal pericardium, reducing friction during cardiac contraction. Excessive fluid accumulation (pericardial effusion) or rapid accumulation of even small volumes can cause cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise.

The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins), while the right suprarenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors that of the testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands have a rich arterial supply from three sources (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery, abdominal aorta, and renal artery respectively) but typically have only a single venous drainage pathway, creating a high arterial-to-venous ratio favoring hormone secretion.
questions.question: Which vein drains the left suprarenal gland?

options: Bases of metatarsals 2-4; medial longitudinal arch
Plantar ligaments of MTP joints; transverse arch
questions.question: The adductor hallucis has two heads. The transverse head originates from which structure and contributes to maintaining which arch?
questions.explanation: The transverse head of adductor hallucis originates from the plantar ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints. Together with the oblique head (from bases of metatarsals 2-4), it inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit. The transverse head contributes to maintaining the transverse arch by drawing the metatarsal heads together.

The median arcuate ligament is formed by the union of the medial borders of the two crura and crosses over the anterior surface of the aorta. This ligament forms the posterior boundary of the aortic opening. Occasionally, it can compress the celiac artery, causing the median arcuate ligament syndrome.
questions.question: Which ligament crosses anterior to the aorta?
What characterizes centroacinar cells?
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are pale-staining cells unique to the pancreas that represent the intra-acinar portion of the intercalated duct. They secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid in response to secretin, which neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum. This bicarbonate secretion, combined with enzymes from acinar cells, produces complete pancreatic juice. Centroacinar cells distinguish pancreatic from salivary acini.

The transverse colon is completely invested by peritoneum and suspended by the transverse mesocolon, making it freely mobile. This complete peritoneal covering classifies it as intraperitoneal. The ascending and descending colons are retroperitoneal, while the sigmoid colon and appendix also have mesenteries.
questions.question: Which part of the large intestine is completely intraperitoneal?

questions.explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering splenius capitis, levator scapulae, and scalene muscles (anterior, middle, posterior). The subclavian artery and brachial plexus emerge between the scalene muscles. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle superficially on this floor. Cervical lymph nodes lie within the triangle.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the posterior triangle?

questions.explanation: The appendicular artery arises from the ileocolic artery (the terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery) and runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to supply the vermiform appendix. The ileocolic artery divides into superior and inferior branches near the ileocecal junction, with the inferior branch giving rise to anterior cecal, posterior cecal, appendicular, and ileal branches. The appendicular artery's position in the mesoappendix makes it vulnerable during appendectomy, and its thrombosis can lead to appendicitis.
questions.question: The appendicular artery is typically a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The splenic vein joins with the superior mesenteric vein posterior to the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. The splenic vein runs from left to right along the posterior surface of the pancreas. It receives the short gastric veins, left gastroepiploic vein, pancreatic veins, and inferior mesenteric vein.
questions.question: Into which vein does the splenic vein primarily drain?
Which nerve passes through the quadrangular space?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space accompanied by the posterior circumflex humeral vessels. The space is bounded by teres minor superiorly, teres major inferiorly, long head of triceps medially, and surgical neck of humerus laterally. Injury can occur with shoulder trauma or humeral neck fractures.

The extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis, the only intrinsic muscles on the dorsum of the foot, are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L5, or S1, or both). They aid the extensor digitorum longus in extending the four medial toes and the extensor hallucis longus in extending the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint.
questions.question: The muscles of the dorsum of the foot include the extensor digitorum brevis (EDB) and extensor hallucis brevis (EHB). They are innervated by which nerve?
At what sound pressure level does the stapedius reflex typically activate?
questions.explanation: The stapedius muscle reflex activates bilaterally at sound levels above 80 dB SPL to protect the cochlea. This acoustic reflex increases ossicular chain stiffness and attenuates low-frequency sounds. Testing this reflex provides valuable information about facial nerve and auditory pathway integrity.

The right main bronchus is shorter (2.5 cm), wider, and more vertically oriented than the left main bronchus (5 cm). This anatomical difference makes the right main bronchus more susceptible to aspiration of foreign bodies. The right bronchus gives off the upper lobar bronchus outside the hilum.
questions.question: Which bronchus is shorter and more vertical?

questions.explanation: The anterior cardiac veins (3-4 small veins) drain the anterior right ventricular wall and empty directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus. They cross the atrioventricular groove and are the only cardiac veins that don't drain via the coronary sinus. During cardiac surgery, these veins must be identified to avoid injury.
questions.question: Where do the anterior cardiac veins drain?
Which plane divides the mediastinum horizontally?
questions.explanation: A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts. The inferior mediastinum is further subdivided into anterior, middle, and posterior mediastina. This anatomical division is useful for localizing pathology on imaging.

questions.question: What provides collateral drainage in SVC obstruction?
questions.explanation: In SVC obstruction, the azygos venous system (along with intercostal veins and other collaterals) provides alternative drainage pathways for blood from the upper body to reach the right atrium. These collateral vessels dilate significantly. Prominent dilated veins may be visible on the chest wall and abdomen, directing flow from above downward.

questions.question: What is the primary extensor of the thumb interphalangeal joint?
questions.explanation: extends the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and assists with extension at the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints. Its tendon forms the medial border of the anatomical snuffbox. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

questions.question: What is spontaneous pneumothorax most common in?
questions.explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is most common in young (20-40 years), tall, thin males. It typically results from rupture of apical pleural blebs (small air-filled sacs). Risk factors include smoking, Marfan syndrome, and family history. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying lung disease (COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis).

options: Injury causes motor deficit without sensory loss
questions.question: What is the significance of the anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor?
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor (no cutaneous branches) means injury produces pure motor deficit (weak thumb IP flexion, index finger DIP flexion, pronation) without sensory symptoms. This can lead to delayed diagnosis as patients lack the paresthesia typical of other nerve compression syndromes.

options: Wrist position does not affect grip strength
Strongest grip in full wrist flexion
Grip strongest with wrist in slight extension
Strongest grip in full wrist extension
Strongest grip in neutral wrist position
questions.explanation: Maximum grip strength occurs with the wrist in 20-30� extension. This position optimally lengthens finger flexors for maximum tension development while stabilizing the wrist. Full flexion or extension reduces grip strength due to passive insufficiency or active insufficiency of finger flexors.
questions.question: How does wrist position affect grip strength?

questions.explanation: White rami communicantes carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers from spinal nerves T1-L2 to the sympathetic trunk. They are white because the preganglionic fibers are myelinated. These fibers originate from intermediolateral cell columns in the thoracolumbar spinal cord. White rami exist only at T1-L2 levels.
questions.question: What are white rami communicantes?

questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunk does not innervate voluntary (skeletal) muscles, which are innervated by somatic motor neurons. The sympathetic system innervates cardiac muscle, smooth muscle in blood vessels and organs, sweat glands, and various viscera. Sympathetic fibers reach the body wall via gray rami communicantes.
questions.question: Which structure does the sympathetic trunk NOT innervate?
Where can cervical rib compress the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: A cervical rib (arising from C7) can compress the lowest trunk of the brachial plexus as it arches over the rib at the thoracic inlet. This causes T1 symptoms: pain and paresthesias along the ulnar border of the forearm and wasting of the small muscles of the hand.

questions.question: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests nucleic acids?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic juice contains DNAase and RNAase (nucleases) that digest deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid respectively into nucleotides. These nucleotides are further broken down by intestinal enzymes into nucleosides and bases for absorption. The pancreas secretes all major classes of digestive enzymes: proteases, lipases, amylase, and nucleases, making it essential for complete digestion.

questions.question: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of popliteus by dividing into which two initial divisions?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus muscle by dividing into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk. The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. The popliteal artery gives five genicular branches contributing to the genicular anastomosis.
options: Anterior tibial artery and tibioperoneal trunk
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries
Peroneal artery and posterior tibial artery directly

questions.explanation: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). M�ller's muscle (superior tarsal muscle), a smooth muscle also elevating the lid, is innervated by sympathetics. Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis (drooping eyelid) along with eye movement deficits. Horner's syndrome causes mild ptosis from sympathetic loss.
questions.question: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by which nerve?
The root of the mesentery extends from which two points?
options: Second part of duodenum to sigmoid colon
Duodenojejunal flexure to right sacroiliac joint
questions.explanation: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure (at approximately L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (at approximately S1, right of midline), a distance of about 15 cm. Along this short root, approximately 6-7 meters of small intestine (jejunum and ileum) is attached. The root crosses the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum, abdominal aorta, IVC, right ureter, right psoas major muscle, and right testicular/ovarian vessels. This oblique orientation allows the small intestine maximum mobility while maintaining vascular supply and creating the characteristic radiating pattern of jejunal and ileal vessels.

The anterior two-thirds (oral part) of the tongue develops from the first pharyngeal arch (two lateral lingual swellings and median tuberculum impar). The posterior third (pharyngeal part) develops from the third arch (copula). The second arch contribution is overgrown. This embryologic division explains the different nerve supplies.
questions.question: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: Adductor longus is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. It originates from the anterior surface of the body of the pubis, inferior to the pubic crest and lateral to the pubic symphysis, and inserts into the middle third of the medial lip of the linea aspera. Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle.
questions.question: Which muscle of the medial compartment is the most anteriorly placed, large, and fan-shaped, forming the medial boundary of the femoral triangle?
What is the normal carrying angle of the fully extended forearm?
questions.explanation: The long axis of the fully extended ulna makes an angle of approximately 170 degrees with the long axis of the humerus. This carrying angle represents the way the forearm angles away from the body when carrying objects. The obliquity is more pronounced in females than males.

The right middle lobe contains two bronchopulmonary segments: lateral and medial. This is the smallest lobe of the right lung. The middle lobe is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. Middle lobe syndrome can occur from lymph node compression.
questions.question: How many segments are in right middle lobe?
The vertebral arteries enter the skull through which opening?
questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries enter the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum after ascending through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. They unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. The vertebral arteries give off the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries before joining.

The mesoappendix is a triangular fold of peritoneum extending from the terminal ileum and its mesentery to the entire length of the appendix (base to tip), connecting it to the posterior abdominal wall. The appendicular artery (from ileocolic artery) runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix to supply the appendix. During appendectomy, the mesoappendix must be divided and the appendicular artery ligated. The mesoappendix contains fat, lymph nodes, and vessels. Occasionally, the mesoappendix may be short, leaving the distal appendix without mesenteric coverage.
questions.question: The mesoappendix is attached to which part of the appendix?

questions.explanation: Thenar muscles receive dual innervation: the recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The ulnar nerve supplies the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis and sometimes contributes to other thenar muscles.
questions.question: What nerve provides motor innervation to all thenar muscles?
Which muscle forms the deepest layer of the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The transversus abdominis is the deepest of the three flat muscles of the anterior abdominal wall (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus), with horizontally oriented fibers. Its aponeurosis joins the linea alba and contributes to the rectus sheath (anterior leaf above arcuate line, anterior to rectus below arcuate line). Deep to the transversus lies the transversalis fascia. The transversus is particularly important for increasing intra-abdominal pressure and core stability. The rectus abdominis and pyramidalis are vertical muscles lying anterior to the posterior rectus sheath (when present).

Wharton's duct (submandibular duct) is approximately 5 cm long and opens at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum. The duct runs forward on the hyoglossus muscle between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves. Stone formation is more common in this duct than in Stensen's duct due to its upward course and mucoid secretions.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of Wharton's duct?

questions.explanation: The prostate gland is related posteriorly to the anterior wall of the rectum (ampulla), separated from it by the rectovesical fascia (fascia of Denonvilliers). This relationship allows the prostate to be palpated during digital rectal examination (DRE), where the posterior surface of the gland can be assessed for size, consistency, symmetry, and nodules. The prostate is related anteriorly to the pubic symphysis (retropubic space of Retzius), superiorly to the bladder base, and inferiorly to the urogenital diaphragm. The prostatic urethra passes through the gland from base to apex.
questions.question: The prostate gland is related posteriorly to which structure?
Which structure marks the beginning of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The anal canal begins at the anorectal junction (where the rectum pierces the pelvic diaphragm formed by the levator ani muscle), located approximately one inch (2.5 cm) below and anterior to the tip of the coccyx. At this level, the puborectalis sling creates the anorectal angle. The anal canal extends approximately 3.8-4 cm to the anus (anal verge). The pectinate line divides the anal canal into upper (endodermal) and lower (ectodermal) parts. The white line of Hilton marks the lower border of the internal sphincter.

questions.question: Which part of the colon lacks taeniae coli?
questions.explanation: The rectum lacks taeniae coli, haustra, and appendices epiploicae, unlike the cecum and colon. At the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anus, at S3 level), the three taeniae spread out to form a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer encircling the rectum. The rectum can be distinguished from sigmoid colon by this absence of taeniae, its fixed retroperitoneal position, and presence of transverse folds (Houston's valves). The taeniae coli converge at the base of the appendix on the cecum, providing a surgical landmark.

questions.question: Which muscle is pierced by the superior gluteal nerve?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle (the only structure exiting above piriformis), passes between gluteus medius and minimus, and supplies these muscles plus tensor fasciae latae. All other structures exit below piriformis. The nerve does not actually pierce piriformis but rather exits superior to it. Piriformis serves as an important anatomical landmark in the gluteal region, dividing structures exiting the greater sciatic foramen into suprapiriform (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) and infrapiriform groups (all others including sciatic nerve).

questions.question: The internal spermatic fascia is derived from which structure?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost of the three fascial coverings of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia as the cord structures pass through the deep inguinal ring. This fascia is continuous with the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial ring). These three layers enclose the contents of the spermatic cord and represent contributions from each layer of the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question: What is the average weight of a normal adult spleen?
questions.explanation: The average weight of a healthy adult spleen is approximately 150 grams (about 7 ounces), though this can vary considerably. A useful mnemonic for splenic dimensions is the "odd numbers rule": 1 inch thick, 3 inches wide, 5 inches long, 7 ounces in weight, and related to ribs 9-11. The spleen can enlarge significantly in disease states (splenomegaly).

options: It is a single band with one attachment to the calcaneus
It has tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts
It consists only of the tibionavicular and posterior tibiotalar parts
It is a triangular ligament with apex on the fibula
It attaches from the fibula to the navicular, calcaneus, and talus
questions.question: The medial ligament of the ankle joint is called the deltoid ligament. Which statement correctly describes its four components?
questions.explanation: The deltoid ligament is the medial ligament of the ankle, a strong triangular ligament with its apex on the medial malleolus. It has four parts: tibionavicular (to navicular), tibiocalcaneal (to sustentaculum tali of calcaneus), and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts (to the talus). It is significantly stronger than the lateral ligaments and rarely ruptures in isolation.

options: Crossing one leg over the other (adduction)
questions.explanation: Obturator nerve injury (as can occur with obturator hernia, difficult childbirth, or pelvic fractures) causes weakness of the adductor muscles, making it difficult to cross one leg over the other (adduction). Sensory loss occurs on the medial side of the thigh. The obturator nerve does not supply the knee directly (though the posterior division gives a branch to the knee joint capsule).
questions.question: The obturator nerve exits the pelvis through the obturator foramen. Obturator nerve injury may cause difficulty with which activity due to adductor weakness?
Which structure separates thoracic from abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (at T12) marks the transition from thoracic to abdominal aorta. The descending thoracic aorta passes through this opening (actually behind the diaphragm, between the crura) to become the abdominal aorta. The thoracic duct and sometimes azygos vein also pass through this hiatus.

questions.question: Which structure forms the medial wall of the tympanic cavity?
questions.explanation: The promontory on the medial wall of the tympanic cavity is formed by the basal turn of the cochlea. The facial nerve canal runs above it. The oval and round windows are also located on the medial wall. The tympanic plexus lies on the promontory providing sensation to the middle ear mucosa.

questions.question: What structure occupies the free edge of the falciform ligament?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) occupies the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament. It is the obliterated remnant of the umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. The ligamentum teres extends from the umbilicus to the left branch of the portal vein at the porta hepatis.

questions.question: What fluid occupies the pericardial cavity?
questions.explanation: The pericardial cavity contains 15-50 ml of serous pericardial fluid, an ultrafiltrate of plasma produced by the serous pericardium. This thin film of fluid acts as a lubricant, allowing the heart to beat with minimal friction between the visceral and parietal layers of serous pericardium. Excess fluid accumulation causes pericardial effusion and potential cardiac tamponade.

questions.question: Into which vein does the right inferior phrenic vein drain?
questions.explanation: The right inferior phrenic vein usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left inferior phrenic vein is usually double, with one branch draining into the IVC and the other frequently joining the left suprarenal vein, which then drains into the left renal vein. These veins drain blood from the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the tonsillar fossa?
questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle forms the floor (bed) of the tonsillar fossa, separated from the tonsil by the tonsillar capsule. The palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus form the anterior and posterior pillars respectively. Loose areolar tissue separates the capsule from the superior constrictor, facilitating surgical dissection.

Trypsinogen is the inactive precursor (zymogen) of trypsin, a protease that digests proteins. It is activated by enterokinase in the duodenum to form trypsin, which then activates other pancreatic proteases (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) in a cascade. Pancreatic juice contains multiple proteases, each cleaving peptide bonds at specific amino acid sequences. Premature activation within the pancreas causes acute pancreatitis.
questions.question: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests proteins?

questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits the esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, esophageal branches of left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The hiatus is formed by muscle fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm. Some right crus fibers form a sling around the esophagus.
questions.question: Which structure passes through esophageal hiatus?
Why does diaphragmatic pain refer to shoulder?
questions.explanation: Pain from irritation of the central diaphragm (supplied by phrenic nerve C3-5) refers to the shoulder because the supraclavicular nerves (C3-4) supply the skin over the shoulder. This is an example of referred pain where stimuli from different areas share the same spinal cord segments.

The wrist joint is innervated by branches from three nerves following Hilton's law: median nerve (anterior interosseous branch), radial nerve (posterior interosseous branch), and ulnar nerve (deep and dorsal branches). This follows the principle that nerves supplying muscles moving a joint also supply the joint.
questions.question: What nerve innervates the wrist joint?
options: Anterior and posterior interosseous nerves only

questions.explanation: Mammary glands are modifications of sweat glands and are therefore ectodermal in origin. They develop from the mammary ridge (milk line) which extends from axilla to groin in the embryo. In humans, most of this ridge disappears except in the pectoral region where breasts develop.
questions.question: What embryonic structure forms mammary glands?

questions.explanation: The internal acoustic meatus transmits the facial nerve (VII), vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII), and labyrinthine artery. The facial nerve continues through the facial canal to exit at the stylomastoid foramen. Acoustic neuromas typically arise in this region from Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the internal acoustic meatus?

questions.explanation: Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along the femoral vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes. Afferent vessels reach the popliteal nodes from the knee joint and lymphatics accompanying leg arteries. Superficial popliteal nodes receive lymph from the region accompanying the small saphenous vein.
questions.question: Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along which vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes?
Which vessel crosses anterior to the ureter in the female pelvis?
questions.explanation: In the female pelvis, the uterine artery crosses superior (above) to the ureter near the lateral fornix of the vagina - remembered by the phrase "water under the bridge." This relationship is clinically crucial during hysterectomy to avoid inadvertent ureteric injury during ligation of the uterine artery. The ureter runs along the lateral wall of the pelvis to reach the bladder.

questions.question: What connects the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The scapular anastomoses provide collateral circulation connecting the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery. This involves suprascapular artery, dorsal scapular artery, and circumflex scapular artery. The anastomoses allow blood flow to the limb even with proximal vessel obstruction.

questions.question: What provides the blood supply to the radial nerve in the arm?
questions.explanation: The profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery accompanies the radial nerve through the spiral groove, providing its blood supply in the arm. Both structures wind around the posterior humerus together. Injury to the artery often accompanies radial nerve damage in humeral fractures.

questions.question: What predisposes elderly individuals to Colles' fracture?
questions.explanation: predisposes elderly individuals to Colles' fracture from relatively minor falls. Decreased bone density makes the distal radius unable to withstand forces that younger bone would tolerate. This is the most common wrist pathology in persons over 50 years old.

questions.question: What happens to diaphragm during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, causing its domes and central tendon to descend and flatten. This increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. As the diaphragm descends, abdominal viscera are pushed downward and the intrathoracic volume increases, reducing intrathoracic pressure.

The right upper lobar bronchus (also called eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is in contrast to the left lung where the main bronchus divides within the hilum into two lobar (secondary) bronchi. This anatomical arrangement is clinically significant.
questions.question: Where does the right upper lobar bronchus branch?

questions.explanation: The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in rudimentary form at birth. The frontal and sphenoid sinuses become evident around age seven. This developmental pattern explains why frontal sinusitis is rare in young children. All sinuses reach full development by late adolescence.
questions.question: Which paranasal sinus is present in rudimentary form at birth?

questions.explanation: The appendix drains to ileocolic lymph nodes located along the ileocolic artery, which then drain to superior mesenteric nodes. Appendiceal lymphoid tissue is abundant, earning it the nickname "intestinal tonsil." In appendicitis, lymph nodes may become enlarged and palpable. Metastatic disease from appendiceal tumors follows this lymphatic drainage pattern.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the appendix?

questions.explanation: Indirect inguinal hernias pass through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, following the path of the spermatic cord. They are the most common type of inguinal hernia and can be congenital (due to persistent processus vaginalis) or acquired. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
questions.question: Which type of inguinal hernia passes through the deep ring?

questions.explanation: The taeniae coli are three longitudinal muscle bands that are characteristic external features of the large intestine (colon) but absent from the rectum and anal canal. These bands are shorter than the colon itself, causing sacculations (haustra) to form. The small intestine has a complete, continuous longitudinal muscle layer without taeniae.
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the large intestine from the small intestine externally?
Which forearm muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve?
questions.explanation: is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Anterior interosseous syndrome results in inability to flex the thumb interphalangeal joint and index finger distal interphalangeal joint.

questions.question: Patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain) is characterized by pain around the patella, aggravated by stairs and squatting. Which muscle weakness most contributes to this condition?
questions.explanation: Patellofemoral syndrome is closely associated with weakness of the vastus medialis oblique (VMO), the distal oblique fibers of vastus medialis. VMO weakness allows the patella to track laterally in the trochlear groove, causing increased patellofemoral contact pressure and pain. VMO strengthening exercises (terminal knee extension, shallow squats) are the cornerstone of rehabilitation.

The biceps reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root, though C5 also contributes. The reflex is elicited by tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa. Absence or diminution of this reflex suggests C6 nerve root or musculocutaneous nerve pathology.
questions.question: Which nerve root is predominantly tested by the biceps reflex?
Where is the costodiaphragmatic recess most clinically important?
questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is located inferiorly between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura and is by far the more clinically important of the two pleural recesses. It is shallow during inspiration and becomes deeper during expiration. This recess can accumulate fluid in pleural effusions and is the site for thoracentesis.

The optic canal in the lesser wing of the sphenoid transmits the optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery. The central retinal vein drains alongside within the optic nerve sheath. The canal opens into the posterior orbit and connects the middle cranial fossa with the orbital cavity.
