questions.question: The optic canal transmits which two structures?
Where is the pulmonary ligament located?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary ligament is a loose fold of pleura that hangs down below the root of the lung. It is formed by the continuity of visceral and parietal pleura inferior to the hilum. It forms a sleeve allowing for expansion of the pulmonary veins during increased venous return.

questions.question: The ovarian artery crosses which structure anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The ovarian artery (arising from the aorta at L2) descends obliquely across the psoas major muscle, crosses anterior to the ureter and the common iliac vessels (or external iliac vessels), then enters the suspensory ligament of the ovary to reach the ovary in the pelvis. This long course reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall. The artery anastomoses with the uterine artery in the broad ligament. In males, the testicular artery follows a similar course but continues through the inguinal canal. The ovarian artery's relationship to the ureter is surgically important.

questions.question: The tensor tympani muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid, a branch of the mandibular division (V3). The stapedius muscle is innervated by the facial nerve. Both muscles modulate ossicular chain movement, protecting the inner ear from loud sounds and reducing physiologic noise.

questions.question: The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from the S2, S3, and S4 spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers synapse in ganglia within the bladder wall and stimulate contraction of the detrusor muscle (for micturition) while relaxing the internal urethral sphincter. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via lumbar splanchnic nerves and superior hypogastric plexus) has the opposite effect, promoting urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter. Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter comes from the pudendal nerve (S2-S4), allowing voluntary control.

questions.question: What happens to old platelets in the spleen?
questions.explanation: Old platelets, like old erythrocytes, are recognized and destroyed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The spleen also serves as a reservoir for approximately one-third of the body's platelet pool. After splenectomy, platelet counts typically rise (thrombocytosis) due to loss of platelet sequestration and destruction. Splenic platelets can be rapidly mobilized in stress or hemorrhage.

questions.question: How many cusps compose the tricuspid valve?
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve has three cusps: anterior (largest), posterior (smallest), and septal. These cusps are attached to a fibrous ring (annulus) and prevented from prolapsing into the atrium by chordae tendineae connecting to papillary muscles. The valve prevents backflow from the right ventricle to the right atrium during ventricular systole.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The pancreas is approximately 15-20 cm in length, making it one of the larger accessory digestive organs. It weighs about 90 grams and lies transversely across the posterior abdominal wall. The gland extends from the duodenal C-loop on the right to the splenic hilum on the left.

questions.question: All muscles of the medial (adductor) compartment are supplied by the obturator nerve EXCEPT which part of which muscle?
questions.explanation: All muscles of the medial compartment are supplied by the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) except the hamstring part of adductor magnus, which is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. Part of pectineus may also receive obturator supply. The dual nerve supply of adductor magnus reflects its dual embryological origin.

questions.question: The superior laryngeal nerve divides into which two branches?
questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal nerve (from the vagus) divides into internal and external branches. The internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to provide sensation above the vocal cords. The external branch descends to innervate the cricothyroid muscle. Damage to the external branch affects voice pitch control.

The iliohypogastric nerve arises from the L1 nerve root (sometimes with minor contribution from T12), emerging from the lateral border of psoas major. It runs obliquely across the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum, then pierces the transversus abdominis muscle to run between it and internal oblique, providing motor innervation to these muscles. The nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch (supplying skin over the hip) and an anterior cutaneous branch (supplying skin above the pubis), crossing above and parallel to the inguinal canal. Injury during appendectomy or hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain and sensory loss.
questions.question: Which nerve root contributes to the iliohypogastric nerve?
Where is referred pain from renal pathology typically felt?
questions.explanation: Renal and ureteric pain is typically felt in the loin (flank) and radiates to the groin and genitalia, following the T10-L1 dermatomes. Upper ureteric/renal pelvis obstruction causes loin pain, mid-ureteric obstruction causes iliac fossa pain, and lower ureteric obstruction causes suprapubic pain with urinary frequency. This radiation pattern is characteristic of renal colic from ureteric stones.

questions.question: The infraorbital foramen transmits which nerve?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital foramen on the anterior surface of the maxilla transmits the infraorbital nerve (continuation of maxillary nerve V2) and vessels. The nerve emerges about 1 cm below the infraorbital margin. It provides sensation to the lower eyelid, lateral nose, and upper lip. The foramen is a landmark for regional anesthesia.

questions.question: Which muscles aid forced expiration?
questions.explanation: In forced expiration, the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, internal/external obliques, transversus abdominis) contract forcibly. This pushes the abdominal viscera upward against the relaxed diaphragm, forcing it higher into the thorax. Quadratus lumborum also contracts to pull down the 12th rib.

questions.question: The thoracic duct begins at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins as the cisterna chyli anterior to L1 vertebra, formed by lumbar and intestinal trunks. It ascends through the aortic hiatus into the thorax. At the root of the neck, it arches forward to enter the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).

The palatoglossus muscle forms the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of the fauces). It descends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. Unlike other tongue muscles, it is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory), not the hypoglossal nerve. The muscle elevates the posterior tongue during swallowing.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the anterior pillar of the fauces?
Which structure controls voluntary defecation?
questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter, composed of skeletal muscle and innervated by the inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve), is under voluntary control and can be consciously contracted to prevent or defer defecation. The internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, autonomic control) maintains resting anal tone. The puborectalis muscle contributes to the anorectal angle and fecal continence.

The tympanic cavity is a single air-filled space without compartmentalization, though the articular disc divides the temporomandibular joint into compartments. The cavity extends into mastoid air cells posteriorly via the aditus ad antrum. The Eustachian tube provides communication with the nasopharynx.
questions.question: Which structure separates the tympanic cavity into superior and inferior compartments?

questions.explanation: Three fascial septa pass from the inner aspect of the fascia lata to the linea aspera of the femur, dividing the thigh into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments. Each compartment has distinct nerves, muscles, and vessels. Understanding compartment anatomy is critical in managing thigh compartment syndrome following trauma.
questions.question: The three fascial compartments of the thigh are separated by septa passing from the fascia lata to which bony structure?
Which structure lies immediately medial to the medial pterygoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle of the pharynx lies medial to the medial pterygoid muscle, separated by a thin fascial layer. The medial pterygoid forms part of the lateral wall of the infratemporal fossa. This relationship is important when accessing the pharyngeal space surgically.

questions.question: Which structures pierce the costocoracoid membrane of the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.explanation: The costocoracoid membrane portion of clavipectoral fascia between pectoralis minor and subclavius is pierced by three structures. These are the lateral pectoral nerve, the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery, and the cephalic vein joining the axillary vein. This membrane is continuous with the suspensory ligament of the axilla inferiorly.
options: Cephalic vein, lateral pectoral nerve, thoracoacromial artery

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes through Guyon's canal (ulnar tunnel) at the wrist alongside the ulnar artery. The canal is bounded by the pisiform and hook of hamate. Compression here causes ulnar tunnel syndrome affecting hand muscles but sparing forearm muscles.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through Guyon's canal?
Which structure is located in the pudendal canal?
questions.explanation: The pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) is a fascial tunnel in the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa, formed by the splitting of the obturator fascia covering the obturator internus muscle. It contains the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels as they pass from the lesser sciatic foramen toward the perineum. The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) provides motor innervation to perineal muscles and sensory innervation to the external genitalia and perineum. Pudendal nerve block can be performed by injecting anesthetic near the ischial spine where the nerve re-enters the pelvis.

The male urethra is approximately 20 cm (8 inches) long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) portions. It serves both urinary and reproductive functions, carrying urine and semen. The female urethra is much shorter at approximately 4 cm, serving only urinary function.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of the male urethra?
Which spinal nerve roots contribute to the lumbar plexus?
questions.explanation: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots within the substance of the psoas major muscle. The lower part of L4 joins with L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk, which contributes to the sacral plexus. The lumbar plexus gives rise to several important nerves including the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, and obturator nerves, as well as branches to the psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles.

questions.question: The internal anal sphincter is formed from which layer?
questions.explanation: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer of the rectum, extending from the anorectal junction to approximately the level of the white line of Hilton, covering the upper three-quarters of the anal canal. It is under autonomic (involuntary) control, receiving sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric plexuses) that promotes contraction and parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) that causes relaxation. This sphincter maintains resting anal tone and unconscious fecal continence, while the external anal sphincter (striated voluntary muscle supplied by inferior rectal nerve) provides voluntary control.

Downward rotation of the scapula is performed by levator scapulae, pectoralis minor, and the rhomboids. This movement is opposite to the upward rotation needed for full arm abduction. Downward rotation returns the scapula to its resting position from the upward rotated position.
questions.question: Which muscles perform downward rotation of the scapula?

questions.explanation: The interventricular septum has a small upper membranous part (approximately 1 cm) and a large lower muscular part. The membranous septum lies just beneath the aortic valve (specifically between the right and non-coronary cusps). Ventricular septal defects most commonly occur in the membranous portion near the tricuspid valve.
questions.question: Which part of the interventricular septum is membranous?

questions.explanation: Plantar interossei adduct (PAD - Plantar ADduct) and dorsal interossei abduct (DAB - Dorsal ABduct) in reference to the second digit (2nd ray), which is the anatomical axis of the foot. This is the same concept as the hand interossei, but referenced to different rays (middle finger for hand, second toe for foot). All interossei also flex the metatarsophalangeal joints.
questions.question: The fourth layer of foot muscles contains plantar interossei (3 muscles) and dorsal interossei (4 muscles). Plantar interossei adduct and dorsal interossei abduct in reference to which axis?

questions.explanation: The midtarsal joint (Chopart's joint) consists of two articulations working in concert: the talonavicular joint medially and the calcaneocuboid joint laterally. Movements at this joint complement subtalar movements to produce overall foot inversion and eversion. Chopart's amputation is performed through this joint for distal foot pathology, preserving the hindfoot for a functional stump.
questions.question: The midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint is formed by which two articulations working together?

questions.explanation: Depression of the diaphragm significantly alters the vertical (superoinferior) dimensions of the thorax. When the muscle fibers of the diaphragm contract, the domes and central tendon descend. Elevation occurs when the diaphragm relaxes. The diaphragm is the most important muscle of respiration.
questions.question: What increases vertical thoracic dimension?

questions.explanation: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins cross from left to right behind the esophagus and aorta at the levels of T8-9 and T7 respectively to drain into the azygos vein. These cross-communications provide collateral venous drainage pathways between the left and right sides of the thorax.
questions.question: What connects the azygos and hemiazygos systems?

questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is primarily a flexor of the forearm, most effective when the forearm is in mid-pronation position. It also assists with both pronation from supinated position and supination from pronated position, returning the forearm to neutral. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve despite being an anterior compartment muscle.
questions.question: What is the primary action of brachioradialis?
How many functional segments does the liver have?
questions.explanation: The liver is divided into eight functionally independent segments (Couinaud segments I-VIII) based on the distribution of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts. Each segment has its own vascular inflow, outflow, and biliary drainage, allowing surgical resection of individual segments without damaging others. This segmental anatomy is crucial for hepatic surgery and understanding disease distribution.

questions.question: Which muscle is paralyzed in ape hand deformity?
questions.explanation: "Ape hand" deformity results from thenar muscle paralysis due to median nerve injury. The thenar eminence flattens and the thumb falls back in the plane of the palm. Opposition and abduction of the thumb are lost, creating a hand resembling that of an ape.

questions.question: The seminal vesicles are located posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles are located posterior to the fundus (base) of the urinary bladder, lateral to the ampulla of the vas deferens, anterior to the rectum (separated by rectovesical fascia), and superior to the prostate gland. They are elongated, lobulated structures that produce approximately 70% of seminal fluid volume, which is alkaline and contains fructose (energy for sperm), prostaglandins, and clotting factors. The duct of each seminal vesicle joins the ampulla of the corresponding vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra.

questions.question: Which structure separates the orbit from the ethmoid sinus?
questions.explanation: The lamina papyracea (orbital plate of ethmoid) is a thin bony plate separating the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells. Its paper-like thinness makes it vulnerable to fracture and erosion. Ethmoidal infections can spread through this wall causing orbital complications. The anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina pierce this plate.

The superior boundary of the cubital fossa is formed by an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus. This line is located approximately 2-3 cm inferior to the actual position of the epicondyles. The base of this triangular depression is directed superiorly.
questions.question: Which two epicondyles are connected by the superior boundary of the cubital fossa?
The mylohyoid line of the mandible provides attachment for which muscle?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle arises from the mylohyoid line on the internal surface of the mandible. The muscle forms the floor of the mouth, separating oral cavity from neck. Below the mylohyoid line, the submandibular gland rests in the submandibular fossa. The mylohyoid nerve (V3) innervates the muscle.

questions.question: What is the ligamentum arteriosum?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, which connected the pulmonary artery to the aorta in fetal circulation, bypassing the non-functional fetal lungs. It closes functionally at birth and becomes a fibrous cord extending from the left pulmonary artery to the aortic arch.

questions.question: The foramen of Bochdalek is located in which part of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Bochdalek is a congenital posterolateral defect in the diaphragm (more common on the left side) that results from incomplete fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membrane during embryological development. This allows herniation of abdominal contents (stomach, spleen, intestines) into the thorax, potentially causing respiratory distress in neonates due to pulmonary hypoplasia. The foramen of Morgagni is an anteromedial defect between sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm. Both differ from the normal anatomical openings (caval opening in central tendon at T8, esophageal hiatus in muscular portion at T10, and aortic hiatus between crura at T12).

questions.question: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandible through which opening?
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (a branch of V3) enters the mandibular foramen on the medial surface of the mandibular ramus. It travels in the mandibular canal supplying the lower teeth and emerges at the mental foramen as the mental nerve. The mylohyoid nerve branches before entering the foramen to supply mylohyoid and anterior digastric.

questions.question: Which artery provides 60% of breast blood flow?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic artery (a branch of subclavian artery) provides approximately 60% of total breast blood flow, mainly to the medial portion through anterior and posterior perforating branches. The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th perforating branches are particularly large and significant in breast blood supply.

questions.question: What forms the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle (part of levator ani) forms a sling around the anorectal junction, creating an approximately 90-degree anorectal angle that contributes to fecal continence. During defecation, the puborectalis relaxes, straightening the anorectal angle to allow passage of feces. Paradoxical contraction of this muscle during defecation causes obstructed defecation syndrome.

questions.question: The cisterna chyli receives lymph from which trunks?
questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli) receives the intestinal trunk (draining abdominal viscera via pre-aortic nodes), right and left lumbar trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvis, and posterior abdominal wall), and sometimes the lower intercostal lymphatic trunks. It represents a dilated sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, located at L1-L2 level, anterior to the vertebral column, posterior and to the right of the aorta, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to traverse the posterior mediastinum and drain into the junction of left subclavian and internal jugular veins.

The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve by two branches in the submandibular region. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arrive via the chorda tympani, synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through without synapsing.
questions.question: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from which nerve?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at L1 and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, initially posterior to the esophagus. At T5, it moves to the left side of the esophagus and continues upward into the superior mediastinum where it arches forward to drain into the left venous angle.
questions.question: Where is the thoracic duct located initially?
The aortic hiatus transmits which structures besides the aorta?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus, located at the T12 vertebral level between the two crura of the diaphragm (posterior to the median arcuate ligament), transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein (and sometimes hemiazygos vein). The esophagus and vagal trunks pass through the esophageal hiatus at T10, while the inferior vena cava traverses the caval opening in the central tendon at T8. The aortic hiatus is actually a midline gap between the crura rather than a true opening in the diaphragm, which means structures passing through it are not constricted during diaphragmatic contraction.

questions.question: The ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres) transmits arteries from which named vessels to the femoral head?
options: Superior gluteal artery from the internal iliac
Inferior gluteal artery from the internal iliac alone
Acetabular branches of medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres transmits arteries from acetabular branches of the medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries to the head of femur. It is triangular and flat, with its apex at the fovea capitis and base at the acetabular notch. In adults, this provides only a minor blood supply compared to the retinacular vessels.

questions.question: The ACL is slack during knee flexion and taut during full extension. It prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia and which other movement?
questions.explanation: The ACL prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia (or anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur) and hyperextension of the knee joint. When the knee is flexed at a right angle, the tibia cannot be pulled anteriorly because it is held by the intact ACL. ACL rupture is detected by a positive anterior drawer test.

questions.question: Which nerve may be injured during inguinal hernia repair?
questions.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1), running through the inguinal canal between the internal oblique and external oblique, and emerging through the superficial inguinal ring, is at risk during inguinal hernia repair. Injury can cause chronic postoperative groin pain and sensory loss over the medial thigh and anterior scrotum/labium majus. The nerve should be identified and preserved during herniorrhaphy. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (running within the spermatic cord) is also vulnerable. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs lateral to the inguinal canal and may be injured during lateral approaches.

questions.question: The adductor tubercle is an important bony landmark on the medial aspect of the distal femur. Which tendon inserts here?
questions.explanation: The adductor tubercle on the medial aspect of the distal femur receives the insertion of the hamstring part of adductor magnus. This is the part of adductor magnus supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The adductor tubercle is palpable on physical examination and serves as an important landmark in knee surgery (origin of the tibial collateral ligament is just above it).

The lacrimal sac occupies the lacrimal fossa, a depression formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of the maxilla. The sac receives tears from the canaliculi superiorly and drains into the nasolacrimal duct inferiorly. Dacryocystitis (infection of the lacrimal sac) causes swelling medial to the inner canthus.
questions.question: The lacrimal sac lies in which structure?

questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur, and empties into the femoral vein after traversing the saphenous opening. It has 10-12 valves.
options: Medial marginal vein and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and posterior tibial vein
Small saphenous vein and dorsal venous arch
Anterior tibial vein and dorsal venous arch
questions.question: The great saphenous vein, the longest vein in the body, is formed at the foot by the union of which structures?
Which structure provides the main sensory innervation to the larynx above the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal vessels. Below the cords, sensation is provided by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. This sensory innervation triggers the cough reflex.

The popliteal fascia is often pierced by the small saphenous vein as it ascends from the lateral ankle to the popliteal fossa, where it enters the popliteal vein. The popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg, forming a protective covering for neurovascular structures.
questions.question: The popliteal fascia is often pierced by which superficial vein as it drains into the popliteal vein?

questions.explanation: The brachial artery is the main arterial supply to the arm and represents the continuation of the axillary artery. It begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into radial and ulnar arteries.
questions.question: Which artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm?
Which Y-shaped hip ligament, described as one of the strongest in the body, has its apex attached to the anterior inferior iliac spine?
questions.explanation: The iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) is one of the strongest ligaments in the body, triangular and Y-shaped. Its apex attaches to the anterior inferior iliac spine and its base to the intertrochanteric line. It reinforces the joint anteriorly, prevents overextension while standing, and reduces the muscle energy needed to maintain upright posture.

questions.question: What is the normal capacity of an adult stomach?
questions.explanation: The adult stomach has a mean capacity of approximately 1.5 to 2 litres when distended, though it can accommodate more. The stomach is a highly distensible organ with significant variation in capacity between individuals. At birth, the capacity is only about 30 ml, increasing to 1000 ml at puberty.

The junction of the middle and outer third of the clavicle is the weakest point. Most clavicular fractures occur at this location from indirect forces transmitted through the limb during falls. The medial fragment is typically displaced superiorly by sternocleidomastoid while the lateral fragment is displaced inferiorly by arm weight.
questions.question: What is the weakest part of the clavicle?
Which component of the quadriceps femoris is the largest and lies on the lateral side of the thigh?
questions.explanation: Vastus lateralis is the largest component of the quadriceps femoris, lying on the lateral side of the thigh. It originates from the greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera. All four quadriceps components converge into the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament inserting into the tibial tuberosity.

The rectovesical pouch (between bladder and rectum in males) is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when standing or sitting and is a common site for fluid collection, abscesses, or metastatic deposits. In females, the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is even deeper and is the most dependent peritoneal space, which can be accessed via the posterior vaginal fornix.
questions.question: Which pouch in males is the most dependent peritoneal space?

questions.explanation: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the pyloric antrum and stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid and stimulates chief cells to secrete pepsinogen. Its release is stimulated by stomach distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin secretion is inhibited by low pH (negative feedback) and by somatostatin from D cells.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates gastric acid secretion?
Which ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a double-layered peritoneal fold that connects the anterior and superior surfaces of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, extending from the umbilicus to the diaphragm. Its free inferior border contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (obliterated umbilical vein) and separates the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver. This ligament develops from the ventral mesentery and serves as an important surgical landmark during laparoscopic procedures.

questions.question: Which vein accompanies the internal thoracic artery?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic vein accompanies the artery of the same name, draining blood from the anterior chest wall, upper abdomen, and breast. It ascends to drain into the brachiocephalic vein on each side. The vein receives tributaries corresponding to the arterial branches.

options: Medial knee pain from tibial collateral ligament strain
Lateral patellar tracking with patellofemoral syndrome
questions.explanation: An increased Q angle (measured from the anterior superior iliac spine to the midpoint of the patella, then to the tibial tuberosity) predisposes to lateral patellar tracking, increasing lateral patellofemoral contact pressure and causing patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain). Women generally have larger Q angles due to their wider pelvis. VMO weakness and foot overpronation exacerbate this problem.
questions.question: The Q angle (quadriceps angle) is the angle between the line of pull of the quadriceps and the patellar ligament. An increased Q angle predisposes to which condition?

questions.explanation: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins. It traverses the popliteal fossa in the same fibrous sheath as the popliteal artery and terminates at the adductor hiatus to become the femoral vein. The small saphenous vein also drains into the popliteal vein.
options: Medial genicular and small saphenous veins
questions.question: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of which two deep leg veins?

questions.explanation: Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie in the posterior mediastinum alongside the esophagus and descending thoracic aorta. They receive lymph from the esophagus, posterior diaphragm, pericardium, and posterior intercostal spaces. Efferents drain primarily to the thoracic duct.
questions.question: Where do posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie?

questions.explanation: In flail chest (from multiple rib fractures creating a free-floating segment), the affected segment moves paradoxically: sucking inward during inspiration (when intrathoracic pressure decreases) and bulging outward during expiration (when pressure increases). This ineffective breathing causes hypoventilation, hypoxia, and impaired secretion clearance. Treatment includes positive pressure ventilation.
questions.question: What causes paradoxical breathing in flail chest?

questions.explanation: The human foot achieves its two basic functions through a segmented skeleton arranged in arches (longitudinal and transverse), supported by muscles and ligaments. This arrangement enables efficient locomotion, sparing of foot structures, and shock absorption. The arches allow the foot to adapt to uneven surfaces and serve as resilient springs to absorb shocks as in jumping.
options: Segmented bony arches supported by muscles and ligaments
Rigid flat bone platform without arching
Phalanges arranged in a single arch only
questions.question: The two basic functions of the human foot are supporting body weight and providing leverage for locomotion. These are achieved through which structural arrangement?

questions.explanation: The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion because the trochlea tali (superior articular surface of the talus) is wider anteriorly. During dorsiflexion, this wider part engages the mortise more tightly, increasing bony congruence and stability. In plantarflexion, the narrower posterior talus is in the mortise, creating relative instability and increased susceptibility to inversion sprains.
questions.question: The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion than plantarflexion. Why is this so?
options: The wider anterior trochlea tali fits more snugly in the mortise during dorsiflexion
The deltoid ligament is placed under increased tension in dorsiflexion
The calcaneus supports the talus more during dorsiflexion
The Achilles tendon tightens and mechanically limits further dorsiflexion
The lateral ligaments are tighter in dorsiflexion only

questions.explanation: The incisive canal opens inferiorly into the oral cavity at the incisive fossa in the anterior hard palate. Superiorly, it communicates with the nasal cavity. The canal transmits the nasopalatine nerve and terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. Embryologically, it marks the fusion of the primary and secondary palates.
questions.question: The incisive canal opens into which structure?
Which structure passes through the oesophageal hiatus?
questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus is located at the T10 level in the muscular part of the right crus of the diaphragm. It transmits the oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The muscular sling of the right crus acts as a physiological sphincter, helping prevent gastroesophageal reflux.

questions.question: From which aortic sinus does the right coronary artery arise?
questions.explanation: The right coronary artery arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus of the ascending aorta. It runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving off branches to the right atrium, SA node (in 60% of people), right ventricle, and posterior interventricular septum. In right-dominant circulation (70% of people), it gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.

questions.question: What nerve supplies the extensor digitorum muscle?
questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve, the deep terminal branch of the radial nerve, supplies extensor digitorum and all other extensor muscles in the posterior forearm compartment. The nerve passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle to reach the posterior compartment.

The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus. The accessory meningeal artery supplies the trigeminal ganglion and dura. Foramen ovale is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone.
questions.question: The foramen ovale transmits which additional structure besides V3?
What is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region?
questions.explanation: The greater tubercle of the humerus is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region. It projects laterally below and in front of the acromial angle. This prominence can be palpated and felt to move during rotation of the humerus.

questions.question: Which two muscles in the anterior thigh compartment cross BOTH the hip and knee joints?
questions.explanation: Both rectus femoris and sartorius cross both the hip and knee joints. Rectus femoris originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and inserts via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. Sartorius originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and inserts into the superior medial surface of the tibia. The three vasti only cross the knee joint.

questions.question: The lacteal vessels in intestinal villi drain into which nodes first?
questions.explanation: Lacteal vessels (lymphatic capillaries) in intestinal villi coalesce to form larger lymphatic vessels that drain to lymph nodes along the mesenteric border of the intestine (juxta-intestinal nodes), then to nodes along the vascular arcades in the mesentery (intermediate nodes), followed by nodes at the root of the mesentery along the superior mesenteric artery (superior mesenteric nodes), and finally to pre-aortic nodes (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric groups) before reaching the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This stepwise progression through multiple nodal stations allows for filtering and immune surveillance of intestinal lymph.

questions.question: What muscles are affected in posterior cord injury of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: Posterior cord injury affects all extensor muscles and shoulder abduction through damage to the radial and axillary nerves. The cord is formed by posterior divisions from all three trunks (C5-T1). Weakness occurs in elbow extension, wrist extension, finger extension, and shoulder abduction.

questions.question: Which nerve is tested by the prayer position?
questions.explanation: The "prayer" position (pressing palms together with fingers extended) tests median nerve function, particularly flexor digitorum superficialis. Inability to maintain all fingers in full extension with palms pressed together suggests median nerve pathology. This is a reverse of Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome.

The rectum begins as a continuation of the sigmoid colon at the level of the third sacral vertebra (S3). It extends approximately 13 cm (5 inches) before terminating as the anal canal one inch below the tip of the coccyx. The rectum follows the curvature of the sacrum and coccyx, forming the sacral and perineal flexures.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the rectum commence?
The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though variations exist (occasionally draining into the superior mesenteric vein or the confluence of splenic and superior mesenteric veins). The IMV ascends from the pelvis, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries, and runs to the left of the inferior mesenteric artery. It passes anterior to the left psoas, left ureter, and left gonadal vessels before reaching the splenic vein. From there, blood flows via the splenic vein to join the superior mesenteric vein, forming the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck.

s are intra-articular fractures of the distal phalanx resulting from avulsion of the extensor tendon. These can be associated with small dorsal fragments or larger articular fragments with volar subluxation. Jersey fractures involve avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus instead.
questions.question: What type of fracture results from avulsion of the extensor tendon from the distal phalanx?

questions.explanation: The pleural cavities are lined by mesothelium, a specialized layer of simple squamous epithelial cells. This smooth lining produces pleural fluid that lubricates the surfaces. The visceral pleura covers the lung surface while the parietal pleura lines the thoracic cavity walls.
questions.question: Which type of tissue lines the pleural cavities?

questions.explanation: The duodenojejunal flexure is located at the level of the second lumbar vertebra (L2), approximately 2.5 cm to the left of the midline. This junction is supported by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), a fibromuscular band. The flexure marks the transition from the retroperitoneal duodenum to the intraperitoneal jejunum.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the duodenojejunal flexure lie?
What is the fossa ovalis a remnant of?
questions.explanation: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale, which allowed blood to bypass the fetal lungs by shunting from the right to left atrium in utero. Functional closure occurs at birth with the first breath, though anatomical fusion may take months to years. A patent foramen ovale persists in about 25% of adults without usually causing problems.

questions.question: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot. It is found just lateral to the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. The dorsalis pedis artery (continuation of the anterior tibial artery) runs between the extensor hallucis longus tendon medially and the extensor digitorum longus tendon laterally. Absence of this pulse, along with the posterior tibial pulse, indicates peripheral arterial disease.

The levator costarum muscles are twelve small muscles connecting the transverse processes of C7 and T1-T11 vertebrae to the ribs below. They elevate the ribs and are innervated by lateral branches of the dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves. They assist in respiration and lateral flexion.
questions.question: Which muscle connects ribs to vertebrae posteriorly?

questions.explanation: The facial artery crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of the masseter muscle, where its pulse can be palpated. After crossing, it ascends toward the medial canthus as the angular artery. The artery winds around the mandible from the neck to reach the face. Facial vein crosses more anteriorly.
questions.question: The facial artery crosses which border of the mandible?

questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle. This anatomical asymmetry explains the higher incidence (90%) of left-sided varicoceles, as the longer venous column, perpendicular drainage, and potential compression of the left renal vein by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon) create higher venous pressure. The pampiniform plexus of veins in the spermatic cord converges to form a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring.
questions.question: Which vessel drains the left testis?
What nerve is at risk in anterior shoulder dislocation?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve is at risk in anterior shoulder dislocation due to its course around the surgical neck of the humerus. The nerve can be stretched or damaged when the humeral head displaces anteriorly. This results in deltoid paralysis and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.

The lateral arcuate ligament (lateral lumbocostal arch) is a thickened band of fascia covering the quadratus lumborum muscle, extending from the tip of the L1 transverse process to the 12th rib. The diaphragm's lateral muscular fibers arise from this ligament. The medial arcuate ligament crosses over psoas major (from L1 body to L1 transverse process), while the median arcuate ligament connects the right and left crura across the aortic hiatus. These ligaments can compress neurovascular structures and serve as important surgical landmarks in retroperitoneal approaches.
questions.question: The lateral arcuate ligament extends from L1 transverse process to which structure?

questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater) is located on the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum, approximately 8-10 cm distal to the pylorus. At this site, the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi. The minor duodenal papilla, located 2 cm proximal to the major papilla, receives the accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini) when present. This anatomical arrangement is crucial for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum contains the major duodenal papilla?

questions.explanation: The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura of the diaphragm through two lesser apertures in each crus. The hemiazygos vein also pierces the left crus. The sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament without piercing the diaphragm itself.
questions.question: Through which opening do splanchnic nerves pass?

questions.explanation: The splenic artery, the largest branch of the celiac trunk, takes a characteristically tortuous course to the left along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas, giving off numerous small pancreatic branches en route. It runs posterior to the stomach within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-6 terminal branches that enter the splenic hilum. Before reaching the spleen, the artery gives off the left gastroepiploic artery and short gastric arteries, which pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the greater curvature and fundus of the stomach respectively.
questions.question: The splenic artery typically runs along which organ's superior border?
The transverse cervical nerve provides sensation to which area?
questions.explanation: The transverse cervical nerve (C2-C3) emerges from the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and provides sensation to the anterior and lateral neck. It is a branch of the cervical plexus. The nerve crosses the sternocleidomastoid horizontally. Cervical plexus block affects this nerve causing anterior neck anesthesia.

The "painful arc" sign is characteristic of rotator cuff pathology, particularly supraspinatus tendonitis or tears. Pain occurs specifically during the middle range of abduction (60-120 degrees) when the greater tubercle and supraspinatus tendon pass under the acromion. Pain is absent at the start and end of abduction.
questions.question: Which condition is characterized by the painful arc sign?
The transverse sinus lies in the attached border of which dural fold?
questions.explanation: The transverse sinuses lie in the attached posterior border of the tentorium cerebelli, extending from the internal occipital protuberance to the petrous temporal bone. They receive blood from the superior sagittal sinus (or confluence) and drain into the sigmoid sinuses. The tentorium separates the cerebellum from the occipital lobes.

The foramen rotundum provides direct communication between the pterygopalatine fossa and the middle cranial fossa, transmitting the maxillary nerve. The pterygoid canal connects with the foramen lacerum region, not the middle cranial fossa proper. This anatomical relationship is crucial for understanding trigeminal nerve pathways and regional anesthesia.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the middle cranial fossa through which opening?

questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery gives off the superior laryngeal artery, which accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane. The artery supplies the laryngeal structures above the vocal cords. The cricothyroid branch runs with the external laryngeal nerve to supply the cricothyroid muscle and anastomoses across the midline.
questions.question: The superior thyroid artery gives off which laryngeal branch?

questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery originates from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), approximately 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. This vessel supplies hindgut derivatives, including the left one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Its main branches include the left colic artery, sigmoid arteries (2-4 branches), and the superior rectal artery, which represents its terminal continuation descending into the pelvis.
questions.question: The inferior mesenteric artery typically arises at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The quadrangular space is bounded superiorly by teres minor, inferiorly by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps, and laterally by the surgical neck of humerus. Through this space pass the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels. Injury to these structures can occur with shoulder trauma.
questions.question: Which muscles form the boundaries of the quadrangular space in the axilla?
options: Teres major, teres minor, long head of triceps, surgical neck of humerus
Subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi, humerus
Teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, lateral head of triceps
Deltoid, teres minor, long head of triceps, humerus

questions.question: What position drains apical pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: For draining a pneumothorax (air), which accumulates in the non-dependent (uppermost) part of the pleural cavity, the patient should be sitting upright. Air rises, so chest drain insertion for pneumothorax is typically in the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line (anteriorly and superiorly) to access the apex where air collects.

questions.question: The hepatic portal vein is formed posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. The portal vein measures approximately 8 cm in length and has no valves.

The superior mesenteric artery is the principal vessel supplying midgut derivatives, extending from just distal to the major duodenal papilla to the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon. It originates from the abdominal aorta at the L1 level, immediately below the celiac trunk. Its branches include the inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic arteries, providing blood to the duodenum (distal to ampulla), jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and right two-thirds of transverse colon.
questions.question: The superior mesenteric artery supplies which embryological division of the gut?

questions.explanation: The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node to receive drainage from a tumor. It is identified during sentinel node biopsy using radioactive tracer or blue dye. If the sentinel node is negative for cancer, downstream nodes are unlikely to be involved, potentially avoiding extensive lymph node dissection.
questions.question: What is a sentinel lymph node?

questions.explanation: are the most common complications of scaphoid fracture due to the unique blood supply. The proximal fragment often fails to heal due to inadequate blood supply. Early diagnosis and appropriate immobilization are essential to prevent these complications.
questions.question: What is the most common complication of scaphoid fracture?

questions.explanation: After splenectomy, patients have increased susceptibility to infections, particularly from encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis). This is due to loss of the spleen's role in antibody production and filtration of blood-borne pathogens. Other organs (liver, bone marrow) can partially compensate for splenic function, but immunization and antibiotic prophylaxis are necessary in asplenic patients.
questions.question: What happens to the spleen after splenectomy?

questions.explanation: The right suprarenal vein is short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava on its posterior aspect, while the left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins). This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors the pattern of testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands receive blood from three arteries (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery respectively) but drain via only one or two veins, creating a rich arterial supply with limited venous drainage.
questions.question: The right suprarenal vein drains directly into which vessel?
Where does the subclavian lymph trunk drain?
questions.explanation: The subclavian lymph trunk is formed by the union of efferent lymph vessels from the apical group of axillary nodes. It usually opens into the subclavian vein. On the left side, it may open into the thoracic duct. This represents the final pathway for breast lymph drainage.

The gastric impression is the largest and most concave of the impressions on the splenic visceral surface, reflecting contact with the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach. It lies between the superior and intermediate borders. Other impressions include renal (from left kidney), colic (from splenic flexure), and pancreatic (from pancreatic tail).
questions.question: Which structure forms the most concave impression on the splenic visceral surface?
Which movement at the hip joint has the greatest range, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees?
questions.explanation: Flexion-extension at the hip joint has the greatest range of movement, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees. Abduction-adduction has a range of 60-80 degrees, while internal-external rotation is 60-90 degrees. These ranges vary with the position of other joints and the state of surrounding soft tissues.

The arches of the foot are maintained by three factors: the shape of the bones, the strength of the ligaments, and the tone of the muscles. All three work together to maintain normal arch height. In pes planus (flat foot), ligamentous laxity and muscle weakness combine with bony changes to flatten the medial longitudinal arch.
options: Bone shape alone maintains the arches
Muscle tone alone determines arch height
Bone shape, muscle tone, and ligament strength
Tendon length, joint capsule, and synovial fluid
questions.question: The arches of the foot are described as being maintained by three factors. Which combination is correct?

questions.explanation: The posterior fontanelle (lambda) is located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures where the occipital and parietal bones meet. It is triangular and smaller than the anterior fontanelle. The posterior fontanelle typically closes by 2-3 months of age. Delayed closure may indicate hydrocephalus or skeletal dysplasia.
questions.question: The posterior fontanelle is located at which suture junction?
What are the cusps of the mitral valve?
questions.explanation: The mitral (bicuspid) valve has two cusps: anterior (aortic) and posterior (mural). The anterior cusp is larger and more mobile, positioned between the mitral orifice and aortic orifice, while the posterior cusp is shorter and attached to more of the annular circumference. Mitral valve prolapse and stenosis are common pathological conditions affecting this valve.

The central artery of the retina is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It is an end artery running in the center of the optic nerve to supply the inner layers of the retina. Occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision. The artery enters the optic nerve about 12 mm behind the eyeball.
questions.question: The central artery of the retina is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: Piriformis is innervated by branches directly from the ventral rami of S1 and S2 (sacral plexus), not the lumbar plexus. The lumbar plexus (L1-L4) innervates psoas major (L1-L4), quadratus lumborum (T12, L1-L4 via subcostal and lumbar nerves), iliacus (femoral nerve, L2-L4), and obturator externus (obturator nerve, L2-L4). Piriformis is a muscle of the gluteal region and posterior pelvic wall, exiting the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. It serves as a landmark dividing structures exiting above it (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) from those below it (all others).
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT innervated by the lumbar plexus?
Through which opening does the sympathetic trunk enter the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunks enter the abdomen from the thorax by passing deep to (posterior to) the medial arcuate ligaments. They descend on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, giving off lumbar splanchnic nerves. The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura to enter the abdomen.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the foramen transversarium?
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery and accompanying veins pass through the foramina transversaria (transverse foramina) of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. The artery typically enters at C6 and ascends to C1. The stellate ganglion lies anterior to C7 transverse process, which usually lacks a foramen transversarium. Spinal nerves exit via intervertebral foramina posteriorly.

questions.question: Which muscle flexes the elbow when the forearm is pronated?
questions.explanation: is the primary elbow flexor regardless of forearm position because it inserts on the ulna. Biceps brachii is less effective when the forearm is pronated because its supinating action is opposed. Brachialis is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.

questions.question: The left renal vein passes between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The left renal vein passes anteriorly to the aorta and posteriorly to the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) before draining into the inferior vena cava. This anatomical relationship can lead to compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA, a condition called nutcracker syndrome (or left renal vein entrapment syndrome), which may cause hematuria, left flank pain, and varicocele. The left renal vein is longer than the right (7-10 cm vs 2-4 cm) and receives the left testicular/ovarian vein, left suprarenal vein, and inferior phrenic vein before entering the IVC.

questions.question: Which two ligaments, combined with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
questions.explanation: The sacrotuberous ligament and sacrospinous ligament, in conjunction with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. They primarily stabilize the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint under the weight of the vertebral column. These ligaments are critical surgical landmarks in posterior pelvic surgery.

The lateral pterygoid muscle protrudes the mandible when both sides contract simultaneously, assisted by the medial pterygoid. Unilateral contraction causes lateral deviation to the opposite side. The muscle has superior and inferior heads inserting on the articular disc and pterygoid fovea respectively.
questions.question: Which muscle protrudes the mandible when contracted bilaterally?
The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus to continue as which artery?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus, to become the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa. The femoral vein similarly traverses the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal vein. The adductor canal lies superior to the adductor hiatus.

The aortic arch begins at the level of T4 as a continuation of the ascending aorta. It arches backwards and to the left, passing over the left main bronchus. The arch ends at the level of T4/5 by continuing as the descending thoracic aorta. The aortic arch lies entirely within the superior mediastinum.
questions.question: At which level does the aortic arch begin?
The great saphenous vein passes posterior to which bony knee landmark, approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella). This is a key landmark for identifying the vein during varicose vein surgery and for cannulation. At the ankle, it ascends anterior to the medial malleolus.

questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery enters the rectus sheath by piercing which structure?
questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac artery) ascends medial to the deep inguinal ring and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Once within the sheath, it ascends on the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery (from the internal thoracic artery). The inferior epigastric artery gives off the cremasteric artery and sometimes a pubic branch. Its position medial to the deep inguinal ring makes it an important landmark distinguishing direct (medial to vessel) from indirect (lateral to vessel) inguinal hernias.

The superior mesenteric vein lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery as they ascend from the root of the mesentery toward the pancreas. Both vessels cross anterior to the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum and the uncinate process of the pancreas. Posterior to the neck of the pancreas, the SMV joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. This relationship is important surgically, as the SMV must be identified and preserved during pancreatic and duodenal procedures. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can compress both the duodenum and potentially the SMV.
questions.question: The superior mesenteric vein lies to which side of the superior mesenteric artery?

questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery arises from the tibioperoneal trunk, which is one of the two terminal divisions of the popliteal artery (the other being the anterior tibial artery). The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and the fibular artery. The fibular artery descends alongside the fibula in the posterior compartment.
questions.question: The fibular (peroneal) artery is a branch of which vessel, making it an indirect branch of the popliteal artery?
Which structure serves as the anatomical landmark within the greater sciatic foramen, defining the relationship of all other structures to it?
questions.explanation: The piriformis muscle is the landmark structure in the greater sciatic foramen. All other structures are described relative to it: the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above it, while all seven other nerves and five vessels pass below it. This anatomical knowledge is essential for safe gluteal intramuscular injections.

Rectus femoris is the only quadriceps component that crosses the hip joint, originating from the anterior inferior iliac spine. Therefore, it can both extend the leg at the knee and flex the thigh at the hip. The three vasti originate from the femur itself and only cross the knee joint.
questions.question: Which muscle is the ONLY component of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint and can therefore flex the thigh?

questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the middle rectal artery (from anterior division of internal iliac) in the wall of the rectum, creating a portosystemic anastomosis between portal (superior rectal vein to inferior mesenteric vein to portal vein) and systemic (middle rectal vein to internal iliac vein to IVC) venous systems. The inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal) also anastomoses with these vessels at the level of the anal canal. In portal hypertension, these anastomoses may become varicose, contributing to rectal varices (internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line).
questions.question: Which artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery?
The iliolumbar ligament connects which two structures?
options: L5 transverse process to iliac crest
questions.explanation: The iliolumbar ligament extends from the transverse processes of L5 vertebra (and sometimes L4) to the iliac crest and iliac fossa. This strong ligament helps stabilize the lumbosacral junction and limits rotation at L5-S1. It forms an important surgical landmark in posterior approaches to the lumbar spine and pelvis. The ligament has superior and inferior bands; the superior band attaches to the transverse process and iliac crest, while the inferior band extends from the transverse process to the upper part of the sacral ala.

Anterior dislocation of the lunate can occur when falling on a dorsiflexed wrist. The displaced lunate compresses structures within the carpal tunnel, causing carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms. This manifests as paresthesia in median nerve distribution and weakness of thenar muscles.
questions.question: Which carpal bone can undergo anterior dislocation following a fall on a dorsiflexed wrist?
Inversion sprains of the ankle most commonly damage which ligament first?
questions.explanation: Inversion sprains of the ankle most commonly damage the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) first, as it is the weakest of the three lateral ankle ligaments. The ATFL runs from the anterior aspect of the lateral malleolus to the lateral surface of the talus and is taut in plantarflexion, the position in which inversion sprains typically occur. With more severe inversion, the CFL is next to be torn.

The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the peritoneal space between the posterior wall of the uterus/upper vagina and the anterior wall of the rectum. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in females and commonly contains loops of small intestine (ileum). It can be accessed via the posterior vaginal fornix for drainage of pelvic abscesses or fluid aspiration (culdocentesis).
questions.question: What lies in the rectouterine pouch in females?
The piriform fossa is bounded medially by which structure?
questions.explanation: The piriform fossa (recess) is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels lie in the mucosa of the piriform fossa. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in this recess. The fossa is part of the laryngopharynx.

dislocation is the most common direction for shoulder dislocation, accounting for about 95% of cases. The humeral head is forced anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest part of the joint capsule during excessive extension and lateral rotation. Superior dislocation is prevented by the coraco-acromial arch.
questions.question: What is the most common direction of shoulder dislocation?
Which branches arise from the first part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The first part of the axillary artery (from lateral border of first rib to upper border of pectoralis minor) gives off only one branch. This is the superior (highest) thoracic artery. The second part gives two branches while the third part gives three branches.

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by I cells in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to fats and proteins. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion from acinar cells and contraction of the gallbladder. Secretin, released in response to acid in the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion from duct cells. Both hormones work synergistically to produce adequate pancreatic juice.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?
What is chylothorax?
questions.explanation: Chylothorax is the accumulation of chyle (lymphatic fluid rich in triglycerides from intestinal absorption) in the pleural cavity due to thoracic duct injury. This can result from trauma, surgery, or malignancy eroding the duct. The fluid appears milky white. Treatment includes dietary modification (medium-chain triglycerides), drainage, and sometimes surgical duct ligation.

The tendon of biceps femoris at its insertion on the lateral side of the head of fibula is split into two parts by the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee joint. The common fibular nerve closely follows the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula. Injury to biceps femoris or the fibular head can therefore damage the common fibular nerve.
questions.question: The tendon of biceps femoris at its fibular head insertion is split into two parts by which ligament?

questions.explanation: is the primary adductor of the thumb, bringing it toward the palm. It is supplied by the ulnar nerve, unlike the other thenar muscles. The muscle has two heads (oblique and transverse) that converge on the base of the proximal phalanx.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary adductor of the thumb?

questions.explanation: A Baker's cyst most commonly arises from the semimembranosus bursa, located between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of gastrocnemius. It communicates with the knee joint in adults via a one-way valve mechanism, enlarging when intra-articular pressure increases (as in knee osteoarthritis or meniscal tears). It presents as a soft swelling in the medial popliteal fossa.
questions.question: A Baker's cyst (popliteal cyst) is a fluid-filled swelling in the popliteal fossa, most commonly arising from which bursae?
options: Semimembranosus bursa between semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius head
Ischial bursa over the ischial tuberosity
Trochanteric bursa over the greater trochanter

questions.explanation: Chief (peptic or zymogenic) cells in the gastric glands of the fundus and body secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin. Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin by gastric acid (HCl) and autocatalytically by pepsin itself. Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach, working optimally at pH 1.5-2. Chief cells are basophilic due to abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum for protein synthesis.
questions.question: Which cells in the gastric mucosa produce pepsinogen?
Which nerve supplies pronator quadratus?
questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus. The pronator quadratus is the deepest muscle in the anterior forearm.

The left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, a branch of the splenic artery, is the dominant vessel supplying the greater curvature of the stomach, anastomosing with the smaller right gastroepiploic artery from the gastroduodenal trunk. These vessels run along the greater curvature within the gastrocolic ligament, giving branches to both anterior and posterior surfaces of the stomach. The short gastric arteries contribute to the fundus but represent a minor component of the greater curvature blood supply.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the majority of blood to the greater curvature of the stomach?
What is Pancoast tumor?
questions.explanation: Pancoast tumor (superior sulcus tumor) is a lung cancer arising in the apex of the lung. Due to its location, it can invade the brachial plexus (causing arm pain and weakness), sympathetic chain (causing Horner's syndrome), and ribs (causing pain). Patients present with shoulder/arm pain rather than typical lung symptoms.

The palatine tonsil drains to the superior deep cervical nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric node at the angle of the jaw. The soft palate and posterior tongue also drain to these nodes. The jugulodigastric node is also called the tonsillar node due to enlargement during tonsillitis.
questions.question: The superior deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from which structure?

questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. The nerve emerges from the jugular foramen and descends across the posterior triangle. Injury during lymph node biopsy causes weakness in shoulder shrugging and difficulty turning the head against resistance.
questions.question: The spinal accessory nerve supplies which two muscles?

questions.explanation: The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the second (descending) part of the duodenum as it extends from right to left across the posterior abdominal wall. This attachment divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic (containing stomach, liver, spleen) and infracolic (containing small intestine and colon) compartments. The root also crosses anterior to the head of the pancreas and the superior mesenteric vessels. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical mobilization of the transverse colon and in understanding the spread of peritoneal infections.
questions.question: The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses which part of the duodenum?

questions.explanation: The celiac trunk emerges from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta immediately below the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, anterior to the upper part of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). It quickly trifurcates into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries, providing the principal arterial supply to foregut derivatives. The celiac ganglion and plexus surround the origin of this vessel, receiving preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the greater splanchnic nerve.
questions.question: The celiac trunk typically arises at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: Displaced clavicle fractures risk injury to the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks that pass immediately posterior to the bone. The subclavius muscle provides some protection, but severe displacement can damage these vital structures. Posteriorly, the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein are also at risk.
questions.question: Which structure is at risk in displaced clavicle fractures?
What is the clinical significance of understanding brachial plexus variations?
options: Variant plexus patterns affect nerve root contributions
Variations do not affect nerve function
questions.explanation: Prefixed brachial plexus (greater C4 contribution, less T1) and postfixed plexus (greater T2 contribution, less C5) affect nerve root distribution to terminal branches. This influences clinical presentation of nerve root injuries and may affect thoracic outlet syndrome presentation. Understanding variations aids diagnosis.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between the two palmar arches?
questions.explanation: The superficial and deep palmar arches provide redundant blood supply to the hand through extensive anastomoses. This collateral circulation protects hand perfusion even with single artery occlusion. The arches interconnect via perforating branches and palmar metacarpal communications.
options: Provide redundant blood supply with extensive anastomoses

questions.explanation: The internal iliac artery, formed by the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the L5/S1 level (pelvic brim), descends into the pelvis and typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at the level of the first sacral vertebra (S1), near the greater sciatic foramen. The posterior division gives off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries (all parietal branches), while the anterior division supplies both parietal structures (obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal) and viscera (umbilical, inferior vesical, middle rectal, uterine/vaginal in females, prostatic in males).
questions.question: The internal iliac artery typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at which vertebral level?
Where are Peyer's patches most concentrated?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are most numerous and largest in the terminal ileum, with 20-30 patches typically present in the last 60 cm of ileum. They are permanent aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the lamina propria and submucosa, located on the antimesenteric border. M cells in the epithelium overlying Peyer's patches sample antigens for immune surveillance. They can become inflamed in conditions like typhoid fever.

The deep inguinal ring, an oval opening in the transversalis fascia located lateral to the inferior epigastric artery, transmits the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament of the uterus in females. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the cremasteric artery also pass through this ring. The ilioinguinal nerve, in contrast, passes through the superficial inguinal ring after traversing the inguinal canal, while the iliohypogastric nerve runs above and parallel to the canal.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the deep inguinal ring?

questions.explanation: The right phrenic nerve passes through the superior and middle mediastinum descending on the right side of the superior vena cava (SVC) and heart. The left phrenic nerve similarly descends on the left side of the heart. Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm, providing motor and sensory innervation.
questions.question: Which nerve descends on the right side of SVC?

questions.explanation: The fibrous pericardium is the tough, inelastic outer layer of the pericardial sac composed of dense fibrous connective tissue. It prevents overdistention of the heart, protects against infection from surrounding structures, and anchors the heart in the mediastinum. It is continuous superiorly with the adventitia of the great vessels and inferiorly with the central tendon of the diaphragm.
questions.question: Which structure forms the fibrous outer layer of the pericardium?
