questions.explanation: The median umbilical fold (single, midline structure) is raised by the median umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated urachus (embryonic connection between bladder apex and umbilicus). The paired medial umbilical folds contain the medial umbilical ligaments (obliterated umbilical arteries), while the paired lateral umbilical folds contain the inferior epigastric vessels (patent). The obliterated umbilical vein forms the ligamentum teres hepatis and runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament, not in an umbilical fold. These folds create fossae on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall that are clinically significant as potential sites of herniation.
questions.question: The median umbilical fold contains which structure?

questions.explanation: For draining pleural effusion (fluid), the patient should be sitting upright leaning forward (or in lateral decubitus position with affected side down). Gravity causes fluid to accumulate in the dependent costodiaphragmatic recess. Thoracentesis is typically performed in the 7th-9th intercostal space in the posterior or midaxillary line.
questions.question: What position is best for draining pleural fluid?

questions.explanation: Below the arcuate line (linea semicircularis), located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis, the posterior rectus sheath is absent. At this level, all three aponeurotic layers (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) pass anteriorly to the rectus abdominis muscle, leaving only the transversalis fascia and peritoneum posteriorly. This anatomical arrangement creates a relative weakness that may be involved in direct inguinal hernias. The inferior epigastric vessels pierce the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line to enter the rectus sheath.
questions.question: The rectus sheath is absent posteriorly below which line?

questions.explanation: The gastric impression is a concave area on the visceral surface of the liver where it contacts the right side and lesser curvature of the stomach. Other impressions on the visceral surface include the duodenal, colic (from hepatic flexure), and renal impressions. These impressions reflect the relationships of the liver with adjacent viscera.
questions.question: Which impression is found on the visceral surface of the liver?

questions.explanation: The inferior boundary is where the medial pterygoid muscle attaches to the mandible near its angle. The fossa has no distinct floor but is limited inferiorly by this muscular attachment. Superiorly, it is bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid.
questions.question: Which structure forms the inferior boundary of the infratemporal fossa?

questions.explanation: The external acoustic meatus measures approximately 2.9 cm in length from the concha to the tympanic membrane. The lateral one-third is cartilaginous containing cerumen glands, while the medial two-thirds is bony. Understanding this anatomy is essential for safe otoscopic examination and foreign body removal.
questions.question: The external acoustic meatus is what total length?

questions.explanation: Trochanteric bursitis is a common cause of hip pain that is more likely to involve women. It is most often caused by overuse or direct trauma to the joint. It presents as lateral hip pain that may radiate down the thigh and is aggravated by lying on the affected side or climbing stairs.
questions.question: Trochanteric bursitis at the tip of the greater trochanter is more likely to occur in which gender and due to what mechanism?

questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae, voluntary striated muscle) surrounds the membranous urethra as it passes through the deep perineal space (urogenital diaphragm). This sphincter provides voluntary control of micturition and is innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). The prostatic urethra is surrounded by the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle under autonomic control) at the bladder neck. The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm) and least distensible part, making it vulnerable to injury during instrumentation and the most common site of urethral rupture in pelvic fractures.
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external sphincter?

questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises in the forearm proximal to the carpal tunnel, so palm sensation is preserved. Only sensation in the lateral three and one-half fingers (palmar aspect) is affected by carpal tunnel syndrome. This distinguishes it from more proximal median nerve injuries.
questions.question: What sensation is preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?

questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin over the parotid gland, lower ear, and angle of the mandible. It emerges at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and ascends on that muscle. The nerve is at risk during parotid surgery and facelift procedures.
questions.question: The great auricular nerve is derived from which spinal segments?

questions.explanation: The descending genicular artery is a branch of the femoral artery, contributing superomedially to the genicular anastomosis. The five genicular branches of the popliteal artery are: lateral superior, medial superior, middle, lateral inferior, and medial inferior genicular arteries. The anterior tibial recurrent artery contributes inferolaterally.
questions.question: The descending genicular artery, contributing to the genicular anastomosis superomedially, is a branch of which artery?

questions.explanation: The upper lateral quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1 and T12. This is distinct from the upper medial quadrant (L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3), lower medial quadrant (S1, 2, 3), and lower lateral quadrant (L2, 3). Clinical dermatomal mapping in this region can help identify the level of spinal pathology.
questions.question: Which cutaneous nerves supply the upper lateral quadrant of the buttock?
What causes posterior interosseous syndrome?
questions.explanation: Posterior interosseous syndrome results from compression of the posterior interosseous nerve as it passes through the supinator muscle. This causes weakness of finger and thumb extensors. Unlike complete radial nerve palsy, wrist extension is preserved as extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis are supplied proximal to the compression.

questions.question: Which muscle's fibers contribute to the conjoint tendon?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx or conjoined tendon) is formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles as they insert onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. This structure reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in its medial third, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Weakness or absence of the conjoint tendon in Hesselbach's triangle (bounded by lateral border of rectus, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric artery) predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The external oblique does not contribute to the conjoint tendon; instead, its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the canal and the superficial ring.

The calcaneal tendon (Achilles) reflex tests the S1 and S2 nerve roots. The reflex arc involves the tibial nerve (both afferent and efferent), the S1-S2 spinal cord segments, and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles. An absent ankle jerk is a hallmark of S1 root compression (commonly from L5/S1 disc herniation). The knee jerk tests L3 and L4.
questions.question: The calcaneal tendon reflex (ankle jerk) tests which nerve roots when elicited by tapping the Achilles tendon?

options: Hyperextension of the knee with foot planted
Hyperflexion of the knee in a flexed position
Direct blow to the medial knee causing varus stress
Lateral knee blow with foot planted, causing valgus force and external rotation
Twisting injury with foot in the air (open-chain)
questions.explanation: O'Donoghue's unhappy triad results from a direct blow to the lateral side of the knee with the foot planted on the ground. This creates a valgus force with external rotation of the tibia, simultaneously stressing the ACL (rotatory force), medial meniscus (compression), and tibial collateral ligament (valgus distraction). This injury pattern is classic in American football 'clipping' injuries.
questions.question: The 'unhappy triad' of the knee is also called O'Donoghue's triad. What is the mechanism of injury most commonly responsible?
The ciliary ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion receiving preganglionic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus via the oculomotor nerve. Postganglionic fibers travel in short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. Sensory fibers from V1 and sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing. The ganglion lies posterolaterally in the orbit.

Blood-borne bacteria and particulate matter are primarily filtered and phagocytosed by macrophages in the red pulp cords and sinusoids. Blood flowing through the spleen is exposed to numerous macrophages that can recognize and remove opsonized bacteria and foreign particles. This filtering function is lost after splenectomy, increasing infection susceptibility.
questions.question: Where in the spleen are blood-borne bacteria primarily filtered?
Which lymph nodes drain the lower anal canal (below pectinate line)?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from the anal canal below the pectinate line follows the drainage of the external body wall, passing to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. This reflects the embryological origin of this region from ectoderm (proctodeum) and its somatic innervation. In contrast, the anal canal above the pectinate line (derived from endoderm) drains to internal iliac nodes along the superior rectal vessels, with some drainage via middle rectal vessels also to internal iliac nodes. This dual drainage pattern is clinically important in carcinoma of the anal canal, affecting surgical planning and lymph node dissection.

Posteriorly, the obturator internus, the gemelli, and the quadratus femoris separate the hip joint from the sciatic nerve. Superiorly, piriformis and gluteus minimus are related. Anteriorly, iliopsoas, pectineus, and rectus femoris are anterior relations. Inferiorly, the tendon of obturator externus is found. These relations are vital during posterior hip surgery.
questions.question: Which muscles, posteriorly related to the hip joint, separate it from the sciatic nerve?
options: Obturator internus, gemelli, and quadratus femoris

questions.question: Which artery can be used for coronary bypass?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery is commonly used for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). It is dissected from the chest wall while maintaining its origin from the subclavian artery, then anastomosed to a coronary artery (usually left anterior descending). It provides excellent long-term patency.

questions.question: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of psoas major?
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4), formed within the psoas major from the lumbar plexus, emerges from the medial border of the muscle at the pelvic brim. It descends along the lateral wall of the pelvis, passing above the obturator vessels to reach the obturator foramen, through which it exits the pelvis to enter the medial compartment of the thigh. This medial emergence distinguishes it from other lumbar plexus branches (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves) which emerge from the lateral border, except for the genitofemoral nerve which pierces the anterior surface of psoas.

questions.question: Which segment of colon has the largest diameter?
questions.explanation: The cecum is the widest part of the large intestine (approximately 7.5 cm in diameter), and the diameter gradually decreases toward the sigmoid colon. This variation in diameter is clinically significant in colonic obstruction: according to Laplace's law, the cecum is most likely to perforate in cases of distal large bowel obstruction due to its larger diameter and thinner wall.

questions.question: Where does the right vagus form plexus?
questions.explanation: The right vagus nerve descends to the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior esophageal plexus, and continues into the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve. The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior esophageal plexus, and continues as the anterior gastric nerve.

The levator veli palatini elevates the soft palate during swallowing to close the nasopharynx. The muscle arises from the petrous temporal bone and Eustachian tube cartilage. It is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). Bilateral paralysis causes nasal regurgitation and hypernasal speech.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the soft palate?

questions.explanation: The short gastric veins drain the fundus of the stomach and flow into the splenic vein. There are typically 4-5 short gastric veins that pass through the gastrosplenic ligament. In portal hypertension, these veins can become dilated and form part of the portosystemic collateral circulation, potentially leading to gastric varices and bleeding.
questions.question: Which vein drains the fundus of the stomach?
The carotid sinus is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) at the carotid bifurcation is innervated by the carotid sinus nerve (nerve of Hering), a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid body (chemoreceptor) is also innervated primarily by IX. These receptors monitor blood pressure and blood gas levels respectively. Carotid massage can slow heart rate via this pathway.

Thoracentesis is the procedure to drain fluid from the pleural cavity by inserting a needle or catheter. It is performed just above the upper border of a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. The costodiaphragmatic recess is the usual site for this procedure.
questions.question: Which procedure drains pleural fluid?

questions.explanation: The palmaris longus tendon (when present) passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum and inserts into it along with the palmar aponeurosis. The ulnar nerve and artery also pass superficial to the retinaculum through Guyon's canal. All flexor tendons and the median nerve pass deep to the retinaculum through the carpal tunnel.
questions.question: What structure passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum?

questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct crosses the masseter muscle superficially before turning medially to pierce the buccinator. The duct runs parallel to and one finger's breadth below the zygomatic arch. Accessory parotid tissue (socia parotidis) may be present on the masseter along the duct. Facial nerve branches lie deep to the duct.
questions.question: The parotid duct crosses which muscle superficially?
The superior rectal artery is the terminal continuation of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery represents the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery after it gives off the left colic and sigmoid branches, descending into the pelvis within the sigmoid mesocolon. It crosses the left common iliac vessels at the level of S3 and divides into right and left branches that descend on either side of the rectum, penetrating its wall and anastomosing with branches of the middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal) arteries at the level of the internal anal sphincter.

questions.question: Where does referred cardiac pain typically radiate?
questions.explanation: Cardiac ischemic pain typically radiates to the left shoulder, left arm (especially the medial aspect and little finger), neck, and jaw, following the distribution of T1-T4 dermatomes that share spinal segments with cardiac afferents. This occurs because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal cord neurons. Some patients also experience epigastric discomfort or right-sided radiation.

The glenohumeral joint capsule is weakest inferiorly, making this the most common site for dislocation. The capsule is thin and lax to allow wide range of movement, particularly abduction. Superior movement of the humeral head is prevented by the coraco-acromial arch rather than capsular strength.
questions.question: What is the anatomical position of the glenohumeral joint capsule's weakest area?

questions.explanation: The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) emerges through the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle at approximately the L3/L4 level, unlike other branches of the lumbar plexus which emerge from its lateral border. After piercing psoas, it descends on the muscle's anterior surface, dividing into genital and femoral branches. The genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring to supply the cremaster muscle and scrotal/labial skin, while the femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery to supply skin over the femoral triangle.
questions.question: The genitofemoral nerve pierces which muscle?

questions.explanation: The pyloric orifice lies on the transpyloric plane at the level of the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is an important surface anatomy landmark located approximately 1.25 cm to the right of the median plane. The pyloric sphincter can be identified by a slight surface constriction and the prepyloric vein of Mayo.
questions.question: Which structure forms the upper border of the pyloric sphincter on the transpyloric plane?

questions.explanation: The medial wall of the orbit is formed by bone (primarily the orbital plate of ethmoid), not muscle. The medial rectus muscle lies within the orbit adjacent to this bony wall. The thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the orbit?
Which foramen transmits the emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus?
questions.explanation: An emissary vein passes through the foramen ovale connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus. Other emissary veins include those passing through the foramen spinosum (middle meningeal vein), mastoid foramen (sigmoid sinus), and parietal foramina (superior sagittal sinus). These valveless connections allow bidirectional flow and infection spread.

The two sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis (medial and lateral heads). They protect the tendons from compression during weight-bearing and increase the mechanical advantage of flexor hallucis brevis. Sesamoiditis (inflammation of sesamoid bones) causes plantar pain under the first metatarsal head and is common in dancers and runners.
questions.question: Sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded in the tendons of which muscle?

questions.explanation: Thenar muscles provide thumb mobility essential for opposition and precision grip. Hypothenar muscles provide little finger mobility and contribute to power grip by cupping the hand. The specialized thumb movements made possible by thenar muscles are uniquely human characteristics.
questions.question: How do the thenar and hypothenar muscles differ functionally?
options: Thenar for thumb mobility/opposition, hypothenar for little finger mobility
Thenar for power, hypothenar for precision
Thenar for extension, hypothenar for flexion

questions.explanation: The tendon of popliteus passes deep to the fibular collateral ligament, separating it from the lateral meniscus. This is why the lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus. The popliteus tendon also creates a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule allowing its passage. The biceps femoris tendon is split by the fibular collateral ligament at the fibular head.
questions.question: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament is separated from the lateral meniscus by the tendon of which muscle?
Which artery supplies the head of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas receives dual blood supply from pancreaticoduodenal arcades formed by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, representing the junction between celiac (foregut) and superior mesenteric (midgut) arterial territories. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal) divides into anterior and posterior branches that descend on their respective surfaces of the pancreatic head, anastomosing with corresponding anterior and posterior branches of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA). This rich anastomotic network provides collateral circulation between celiac and SMA systems.

Scapular protraction (abduction) is produced by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor muscles. During protraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves forward along with the scapula. This movement is used in punching, pushing, and reaching forward actions.
questions.question: Which muscles are responsible for scapular protraction?

questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra contains the openings of the two ejaculatory ducts on either side of the prostatic utricle (a small blind pouch) on the seminal colliculus (urethral crest). About 20-30 prostatic ducts also open into the prostatic urethra. The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra, measuring about 3-4 cm in length.
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra contains the ejaculatory duct openings?

questions.explanation: The optic canal is located at the apex of the orbit in the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone. It transmits the optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery from the middle cranial fossa into the orbit. The canal is approximately 10 mm long. Optic nerve compression can occur from tumors, trauma, or inflammatory processes.
questions.question: Which opening is located at the apex of the orbit?

questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) lies lateral to the femoral artery as it exits beneath the inguinal ligament, outside the femoral sheath (which contains only the femoral artery, vein, and canal). The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty/Lymphatics) describes the lateral to medial arrangement. The femoral nerve rapidly divides into branches in the femoral triangle.
questions.question: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) exits the pelvis beneath the inguinal ligament. It lies in which position relative to the femoral artery?

questions.explanation: in nerve injuries causes vasomotor changes including arteriolar dilation (making skin warmer) and loss of sweating (making skin drier). Long-standing cases develop trophic changes with dry, scaly skin and cracked nails. These changes are seen in Klumpke's paralysis and other severe nerve injuries.
questions.question: What causes vasomotor changes in nerve injuries?

questions.explanation: "Handlebar palsy" results from ulnar nerve compression at the wrist (Guyon's canal) due to prolonged pressure from bicycle handlebars. This causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and sensory changes in ulnar nerve distribution. Long-distance cyclists are particularly susceptible.
questions.question: What causes handlebar palsy in cyclists?
Where does the posterior vagal trunk primarily distribute after entering the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The posterior vagal trunk, formed mainly from the right vagus nerve, sends a large branch to the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses. This distribution extends vagal innervation to the intestines as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas. The remaining branches supply the posterior surface of the stomach.

questions.question: Which structure marks the transition from foregut to midgut?
questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla represents the embryological junction between foregut and midgut derivatives, marking the transition from celiac to superior mesenteric arterial supply. The duodenum proximal to this point receives blood from the celiac trunk (via gastroduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries), while the portion distal to it is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (via inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries). This vascular watershed reflects the embryological division of the primitive gut tube and has important implications for the blood supply and venous/lymphatic drainage patterns.

The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal throughout its length. The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular opening in the external oblique aponeurosis. The anterior wall is reinforced laterally by fibers of the internal oblique muscle as they arch over the spermatic cord.
questions.question: What forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: In adults, the Eustachian tube lies at 45� to the horizontal plane, whereas in infants it is only 10�. This more vertical orientation in children predisposes them to middle ear infections. The tube is approximately 31-38 mm long with the posterior third being osseous.
questions.question: The Eustachian tube in adults lies at what angle to the horizontal plane?
Which nerve supplies the parotid gland with sensory fibers?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) provides sensory innervation to the skin over the parotid gland and lower auricle. The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (not sensory to the gland). The facial nerve traverses the gland but doesn't innervate it. Parotid surgery risks great auricular nerve injury causing numbness.

The cardiac plexus is formed by sympathetic fibers from the cervical and upper thoracic sympathetic ganglia and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerves. The superficial cardiac plexus lies beneath the aortic arch, while the deep plexus lies between the arch and tracheal bifurcation. These plexuses distribute fibers to the conducting system, coronary vessels, and myocardium.
questions.question: What forms the superficial cardiac plexus?

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the surgical neck of the humerus, making it vulnerable to injury in fractures of this region. Damage results in paralysis of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. These fractures are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk during surgical neck fractures of the humerus?
The lateral femoral circumflex artery has three named branches. Which of these descends distally to contribute to the genicular anastomosis?
questions.explanation: The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) has three branches: ascending (to the hip joint and gluteal region), transverse (encircling the femur laterally), and descending (contributing superolaterally to the genicular anastomosis around the knee). The descending branch travels between vastus intermedius and vastus lateralis muscles and provides one of the anastomotic connections at the knee.

The parotid gland extends superiorly to the external acoustic meatus and zygomatic arch. The gland lies below and anterior to the ear, extending from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the mandible. The facial nerve divides within the gland substance into its terminal branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical).
questions.question: Which structure limits the superior extent of the parotid gland?

questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is shallow during inspiration when the lung expands into it, and becomes deeper during expiration when the lung retracts. This recess is clinically important as it is the site where pleural fluid accumulates in effusions and is the target for thoracentesis.
questions.question: Which recess is deeper during expiration?
Which effect does vagal stimulation have on the heart?
questions.explanation: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation decreases heart rate (negative chronotropy), decreases conduction velocity through the AV node, and slightly decreases contractility. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors (M2) in the SA node, AV node, and atrial muscle. The right vagus preferentially affects the SA node; the left vagus affects the AV node.

questions.question: The inferior alveolar artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It descends with the inferior alveolar nerve to enter the mandibular foramen, supplying the mandibular teeth and bone. The mylohyoid branch supplies the mylohyoid muscle. The mental artery emerges through the mental foramen.

questions.question: How many separate joints are formed collectively by the 19 bones of the hand?
questions.explanation: The 19 bones of the hand (metacarpals and phalanges) collectively form 14 separate joints. These include the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints connecting fingers to palm and interphalangeal (IP) joints between finger segments. All are synovial joints with articular cartilage covering the bone surfaces.

questions.question: What is the function of splenic red pulp?
questions.explanation: The splenic red pulp filters blood and removes old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes through selective retention and phagocytosis by macrophages in the splenic cords. It also stores platelets (about one-third of the body's platelet pool) and serves as a reservoir for iron recycled from hemoglobin. The red pulp comprises about 75% of splenic tissue.

questions.question: Which ribs produce bucket-handle movement?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, ribs 7-10 move laterally in a "bucket handle" movement, increasing the lateral (transverse) dimensions of the thoracic cavity. The upper ribs (2-7) move in a "pump handle" fashion, increasing anteroposterior diameter by pushing the sternum forward. These movements are coordinated during breathing.

Hiatus hernias (both sliding and rolling types) are far more common than congenital diaphragmatic hernias. They occur in middle-aged and older adults due to weakening of the tissues around the esophageal hiatus. Sliding hernias are much more common than rolling (para-esophageal) hernias.
questions.question: What type of hernia is most common?

questions.explanation: The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve via cranial accessory), not the hypoglossal nerve like other tongue muscles. This exception makes it technically a palatal muscle rather than a tongue muscle. The pharyngeal plexus supplies all soft palate muscles except tensor veli palatini.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the palatoglossus muscle?
The sartorius muscle, the longest muscle in the body, performs which complete combination of actions?
options: Extends hip and flexes the knee only
Adducts the hip and extends the knee
Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates hip; flexes and medially rotates knee
Flexes hip and laterally rotates the knee joint only
Abducts the hip and extends the knee only
questions.explanation: Sartorius (the tailor's muscle) acts on two joints. At the hip: it flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh. At the knee: it flexes the leg and medially rotates when the knee is flexed. The combined action of both sartorii brings the lower limb into the cross-legged sitting position typical of traditional tailors.

The transverse colon receives its arterial supply from branches of the superior mesenteric artery, specifically the middle colic artery and right colic artery branches. The junction between the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries occurs near the left third of the transverse colon. This represents the embryological boundary between midgut and hindgut derivatives.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the transverse colon?

questions.explanation: The foramen spinosum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, posterolateral to the foramen ovale. It transmits the middle meningeal artery and meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve. The foramen is located at the spine of the sphenoid. Accessory meningeal arteries may also pass through this foramen.
questions.question: Which bone contains the foramen spinosum?

questions.explanation: The proper hepatic artery arises from the common hepatic artery, which is a branch of the celiac trunk. The common hepatic artery divides into the proper hepatic artery and the gastroduodenal artery. The proper hepatic artery then divides into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver.
questions.question: From which artery does the proper hepatic artery arise?
Which structure forms the posterior wall of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver and diaphragm; and inferiorly by the transverse mesocolon. It communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow).

The wider and more vertical course of the right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter into it more easily than the left. The left bronchus is longer, narrower, and more horizontally oriented. This anatomical difference is clinically significant in aspiration and foreign body lodgment.
questions.question: Why do foreign bodies enter the right bronchus?
What nerve supplies subscapularis muscle?
questions.explanation: Subscapularis is supplied by the upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6) and lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6). Both nerves arise from the posterior cord. The lower subscapular nerve also supplies teres major muscle.

The posterior auricular artery arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery above the level of the digastric and stylohyoid muscles. It supplies the auricle, scalp behind the ear, and gives off the stylomastoid artery (which supplies the facial nerve and middle ear structures). The artery ascends between the parotid gland and mastoid process.
questions.question: The posterior auricular artery is a branch of which vessel?
Which structure is most anterior in right lung root?
questions.explanation: In both lung roots, the arrangement from superior to inferior is: pulmonary artery (uppermost), bronchus (middle), pulmonary veins (lowermost). From anterior to posterior: pulmonary veins (most anterior), pulmonary artery, bronchus (most posterior). Hilar lymph nodes are scattered throughout.

questions.question: Which muscle depresses the angle of the mouth?
questions.explanation: The depressor anguli oris (triangularis) depresses the angle of the mouth, contributing to expressions of sadness or frowning. It is a muscle of facial expression innervated by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve. The muscle arises from the mandible and inserts into the angle of the mouth.

questions.question: What is the thymus gland's primary function?
questions.explanation: The thymus gland's primary function is the maturation and education of T-lymphocytes. Na?ve T cells from bone marrow migrate to the thymus where they undergo positive and negative selection by epithelial-reticular cells. This eliminates self-reactive T cells and produces immunocompetent T cells. The thymus is crucial for cellular immunity.

The levator labii superioris elevates the upper lip. It arises from the maxilla above the infraorbital foramen and inserts into the upper lip. The muscle is innervated by the zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve. Zygomaticus major and minor also contribute to upper lip elevation but primarily act on the angle of mouth.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the upper lip?
What structure arches over right lung root?
questions.explanation: The arch of the azygos vein arches over the right lung root from behind. The right lung root lies within the groove created by the azygos arch. On the left side, the aortic arch passes over the left lung root, and the left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the upper ureter?
questions.explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the upper ureter is to the lateral aortic (para-aortic) lymph nodes, while the pelvic portion drains to the internal and external iliac nodes. This lymphatic drainage pattern follows the blood supply. The lateral aortic nodes are located around the origin of the renal arteries at the L1-L2 level.

The pulmonary valve has three semilunar (half-moon shaped) cusps: anterior, right, and left. Behind each cusp is a pulmonary sinus. The valve opens during right ventricular systole to allow blood into the pulmonary trunk and closes during diastole to prevent backflow. Unlike AV valves, semilunar valves have no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.
questions.question: How many cusps form the pulmonary valve?

questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament is a fibrous arch that unites the right and left crura anteriorly across the aortic hiatus at the T12 level. It forms the superior boundary of the aortic hiatus through which the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes azygos vein pass. Occasionally, this ligament can compress the celiac trunk causing median arcuate ligament syndrome.
questions.question: What connects the two crura anteriorly?

options: Stable scapula essential for efficient glenohumeral motion
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between scapular stability and glenohumeral mobility?
questions.explanation: A stable scapular base is essential for efficient glenohumeral motion. Scapular stabilizers (serratus anterior, rhomboids, trapezius) provide a fixed base from which glenohumeral muscles can act. Scapular winging demonstrates how loss of stability compromises shoulder function despite intact glenohumeral muscles.

Gastrocnemius strain (tennis leg) typically occurs at the musculotendinous junction of the medial head of gastrocnemius, where the thick muscle belly transitions to the thin Achilles tendon. It occurs during sudden push-off activities and presents with acute posterior calf pain. The medial head is more commonly strained than the lateral because it is larger and generates greater force.
questions.question: Gastrocnemius strain ('tennis leg') typically occurs at which specific location within the muscle?
options: At the Achilles tendon insertion on the calcaneus
At the origin from the lateral femoral condyle
At the musculotendinous junction of the medial gastrocnemius head

questions.question: Where do anterior intercostal lymphatics drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the anterior part of intercostal spaces drain into anterior intercostal nodes that lie along the internal thoracic artery. From these nodes, lymph passes to the parasternal nodes. Posterior intercostal lymphatics drain into posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.

questions.question: Which bursa is the largest in the body and lies between supraspinatus and the coraco-acromial arch?
questions.explanation: The subacromial bursa is the largest bursa in the body, positioned between the supraspinatus tendon and the coraco-acromial arch. It protects the supraspinatus tendon against friction with the acromion during arm abduction. Inflammation of this bursa is responsible for several shoulder pathologies including rotator cuff tendonitis.

Gynecomastia is enlargement of the male breast due to proliferation of glandular tissue. It can be physiological (neonatal, pubertal, elderly) or pathological (hormonal imbalance, drugs, liver disease, tumors). The condition is usually bilateral but may be asymmetric. True gynecomastia must be distinguished from fat accumulation.
questions.question: What is gynecomastia?
The ureter is crossed anteriorly at the pelvic brim by which vessel?
questions.explanation: The ureter is crossed anteriorly by the testicular vessels (in males) or ovarian vessels (in females) near the pelvic brim, as these vessels descend from their aortic origins at L2 level toward the deep inguinal ring (males) or ovary (females). The ureter then crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or proximal external iliac artery) before entering the pelvis. In females, the ureter is subsequently crossed by the uterine artery approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"), an important surgical relationship during hysterectomy. The superior vesical artery travels with the ureter in the pelvis but does not cross it.

questions.question: Which cells produce hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in the gastric glands of the stomach fundus and body secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. The acid creates an optimal pH for pepsin activation and kills ingested bacteria. Intrinsic factor is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Parietal cell loss or dysfunction can cause achlorhydria and pernicious anemia.

Multiple factors maintain gastroesophageal junction competence preventing reflux: intrinsic LES tone, extrinsic compression by right crus sling fibers, acute angle of gastric entry (angle of His), positive intraabdominal pressure on the abdominal esophageal segment, and mucosal rosette at the cardia. Disruption causes GERD.
questions.question: What maintains gastroesophageal junction competence?
The cruciate anastomosis is at the level of the lesser trochanter. Which four arteries specifically constitute this anastomosis?
options: IGA, obturator artery, MFCA, and LFCA branches
SGA, IGA, MFCA, and LFCA arterial branches
IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris
SGA, IGA, obturator, and 1st perforating branch
MFCA, LFCA, popliteal, and descending genicular
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis at the level of the lesser trochanter is constituted by four arteries: inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA), and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral circulation between the internal iliac and femoral artery systems.

questions.question: The optic nerve is surrounded by which meningeal layers?
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is covered by all three meningeal layers (dura, arachnoid, and pia) from the sclera to the optic canal. At the canal, the dura becomes continuous with the periosteum of the orbit. Increased intracranial pressure can cause papilledema due to continuity of the subarachnoid space around the optic nerve.

The true vocal cords are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium, which is firmly adherent to the underlying vocal ligament without submucosa. This accounts for the pearly white avascular appearance on laryngoscopy. The rest of the larynx is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
questions.question: What epithelium lines the true vocal cords?

questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3). It carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. The nerve provides sensation to the temporal region, auricle, and temporomandibular joint. Misdirected regeneration causes Frey's syndrome.
questions.question: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of which division?

questions.explanation: The adult heart weighs approximately 250-350 grams, representing about 0.5% of total body weight (roughly 1/200th of body weight). The heart size is often compared to a closed fist. The male heart is typically slightly larger and heavier than the female heart, correlating with body size differences.
questions.question: What percentage of body weight does the adult heart represent?
Which injury commonly causes avulsion of the medial epicondyle?
questions.explanation: Avulsion of the medial epicondyle commonly results from valgus stress to the elbow, seen in throwing athletes (tennis elbow). The common flexor origin and ulnar collateral ligament attachment create a strong pull. Repetitive throwing or acute valgus force can avulse this growth center in children or the epicondyle in adults.

The sphenoid bone articulates with all other cranial bones (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, ethmoid, zygomatic, palatine, vomer) and is called the keystone of the cranial base. It has a central body, greater and lesser wings, and pterygoid processes. The sella turcica houses the pituitary gland.
questions.question: Which bone articulates with all other cranial bones?

options: Bases of all five proximal phalanges
Bases of all five metatarsal bones
Heads of all metatarsals and bases of proximal phalanges
Only the first metatarsophalangeal joint exclusively
All tarsal bones as a group
questions.question: The plantar aponeurosis is the most important passive structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity to which structures?
questions.explanation: The plantar aponeurosis (plantar fascia) stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity (medial tubercle) to the heads of all metatarsals and the bases of the proximal phalanges. During toe extension (dorsiflexion) in push-off phase of gait, this aponeurosis is tensioned, raising the arch in a windlass mechanism. Plantar fasciitis involves inflammation at the calcaneal attachment.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial or lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The internal oblique muscle contributes to the anterior wall in the lateral third of the canal (where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament) and forms part of the roof with the transversus abdominis muscle through their arching fibers. The external oblique aponeurosis forms the entire length of the anterior wall, the transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by conjoint tendon) forms the posterior wall, and the inguinal ligament forms the floor.

questions.question: Which nerve may cause referred pain to the shoulder?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm (both pleural and peritoneal surfaces). Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (from subphrenic abscess, ruptured spleen, perforated peptic ulcer, ectopic pregnancy, liver inflammation, or cholecystitis) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip (C3-C5 dermatomes) via the phrenic nerve. This is called Kehr's sign when associated with splenic rupture. The peripheral diaphragm receives sensory innervation from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, referring pain to the chest wall and upper abdomen.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (which itself arises from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the vermiform appendix. It runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to reach the tip of the appendix. This end-artery arrangement (with minimal collateral supply) means that thrombosis or inflammation affecting the appendicular artery can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery's location in the mesoappendix requires careful ligation during appendectomy. Variations in the arterial supply are uncommon, but occasionally the appendicular artery may arise directly from a posterior cecal artery.

The left lung typically contains 8-10 bronchopulmonary segments depending on anatomical variation. The upper lobe has 4-5 segments (apicoposterior/or separate apical and posterior, anterior, superior lingular, inferior lingular) and the lower lobe has 4-5 segments (superior, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal, ? medial basal).
questions.question: What provides the total left lung segment count?
The processus vaginalis normally obliterates when?
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis through the inguinal canal, normally obliterates during the first year of life, leaving only the distal portion as the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Failure of complete obliteration leads to various clinical conditions: patent processus vaginalis allows peritoneal fluid to flow into the scrotum (communicating hydrocele) or permits herniation of abdominal contents (congenital indirect inguinal hernia). Partial obliteration with persistence of intermediate portions creates encysted hydroceles of the cord. Complete patency occurs in about 20% of adults.

In Erb's paralysis, the affected arm hangs by the side in an adducted and medially rotated position. The forearm assumes an extended and pronated posture, creating the "policeman's tip" or "porter's tip" hand deformity. This results from paralysis of muscles supplied by C5-C6 nerve roots.
questions.question: What is the characteristic position of the forearm in Erb's paralysis?

questions.explanation: The superior (apical) segment of the lower lobe is the most dependent position in the supine position. This explains why abscess formation is more common in this segment and in the posterior segment of the upper lobe, as secretions pool in dependent areas during recumbency.
questions.question: Which segment is most dependent when supine?

questions.explanation: Splenic cords (cords of Billroth) in the red pulp consist of a meshwork of reticular fibers and reticular cells, with macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and various blood cells in the interstices. Blood from open-ended capillaries percolates through these cords before re-entering the circulation via sinusoids. Macrophages in the cords phagocytose old red cells and foreign particles.
questions.question: What are splenic cords composed of?
Which nerves provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder?
questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from S2-S4 spinal segments provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder. These nerves stimulate detrusor muscle contraction and inhibit the internal urethral sphincter, promoting micturition. Sympathetic innervation from T11-L2 via the hypogastric plexus promotes urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter.

Wrist drop results from radial nerve injury, which has nerve root values C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1. However, C7 is the most critical root for wrist extension. Complete radial nerve palsy affects all extensor muscles and causes the characteristic wrist drop deformity.
questions.question: Which nerve root value is predominantly involved in wrist drop?

questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian vessels (artery and vein) and nerves passing from the lateral pelvic wall to the ovary. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus and contains no significant vessels. The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, with the ovarian vessels running in its superior lateral extension.
questions.question: Which peritoneal ligament contains the ovarian vessels?
Which structure opens into the descending duodenum at the major duodenal papilla?
questions.explanation: The hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) opens at the major duodenal papilla in the descending (second) part of the duodenum. This ampulla is formed by the union of the main pancreatic duct and common bile duct in most individuals. The sphincter of Oddi surrounds the ampulla controlling the flow of bile and pancreatic secretions.

In the mnemonic 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?' each letter corresponds to a branch of the femoral artery: Deep external pudendal, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular, Profunda femoris, Superficial circumflex iliac. The profunda femoris is the largest and most important branch, giving rise to the perforating branches and circumflex arteries.
questions.question: The femoral artery branches are recalled using the mnemonic 'Does she scream during poking sessions?' Which branch corresponds to 'D'?

questions.explanation: The inferior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the twelfth thoracic vertebra. Laterally, it is bounded by the curving costal margin formed by ribs 11 and 12. Anteriorly, the xiphisternal joint completes the boundaries, and the entire opening is closed by the diaphragm.
questions.question: Which vertebra bounds the inferior thoracic aperture posteriorly?
Which duct drains the right side of the thorax?
questions.explanation: The right lymphatic duct receives lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, right upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart, and right surface of the liver. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. This duct drains into the right venous angle.

questions.question: The popliteus muscle 'unlocks' the knee from full extension by rotating the femur by how many degrees on the fixed tibia?
questions.explanation: The popliteus muscle weakly flexes the knee and unlocks it from full extension by rotating the femur 5 degrees on a fixed tibia (or medially rotating the tibia on an unplanted limb). It originates from the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus, inserting on the posterior tibia. It is innervated by the tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1).

questions.question: Which nerve is at risk during submandibular gland surgery?
questions.explanation: All three nerves are at risk during submandibular gland surgery. The marginal mandibular nerve crosses the lower border of the mandible superficially. The hypoglossal nerve lies deep to the gland on hyoglossus. The lingual nerve lies above the gland in contact with the submandibular duct. Careful surgical technique preserves these structures.

Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are extensions of cortical tissue that project between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus. They contain interlobar arteries and veins. The cortical tissue in the columns and over the bases of pyramids contains the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules. Enlarged renal columns can mimic renal masses on imaging.
questions.question: Which structure extends between adjacent renal pyramids?

questions.explanation: The pharyngeal plexus on the middle constrictor muscle is formed primarily by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve with contributions from glossopharyngeal (sensory only) and sympathetic fibers. Motor fibers originate from the nucleus ambiguus and travel via the cranial accessory to the vagus. The plexus supplies all pharyngeal and most palatal muscles.
questions.question: The pharyngeal plexus is formed primarily by which cranial nerve?
Which structure lies posterior to the head of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava lies posterior to the head of the pancreas (separated by the right renal vein and sometimes the third part of the duodenum), along with the right renal artery and vein, aorta, and origin of the superior mesenteric artery. The superior mesenteric vein ascends posterior to the neck of the pancreas (not the head), where it joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. The common bile duct runs in a groove on (or through) the posterior surface of the pancreatic head before joining the main pancreatic duct.

options: Extensor carpi radialis longus, brevis, and ulnaris
questions.explanation: Extension at the wrist joint is produced mainly by extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris. The extensor digitorum provides assistance to this movement. All these extensors are located in the posterior compartment of the forearm.
questions.question: Which muscles produce wrist extension with assistance from extensor digitorum?

questions.explanation: The mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals (articulating with hamate) allow palmar cupping for power grip. This adaptation enables the hand to conform to cylindrical objects. The 2nd and 3rd metacarpals are relatively fixed, providing a stable platform for precision grip.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals?
options: Allow cupping of hand for power grip

questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery descends in the deep posterior compartment of the leg, alongside the fibula. It supplies the lateral and posterior compartment muscles and gives off perforating branches that pierce the interosseous membrane to supply the lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis). It terminates by anastomosing with the lateral malleolar and calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery.
options: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
questions.question: The fibular (peroneal) artery, arising from the tibioperoneal trunk, descends laterally alongside the fibula in which compartment?

questions.explanation: In life, the foramen lacerum is closed by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal arterial branches and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above the foramen within the carotid canal, not through it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large irregular opening.
questions.question: The foramen lacerum transmits which structure in life?
Which vessel typically runs in the splenorenal ligament?
questions.explanation: The splenorenal ligament connects the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney and contains the splenic artery and vein, along with the tail of the pancreas (extending to within 1 cm of the splenic hilum in about 75% of individuals). The splenic vessels run a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreatic body and tail before entering this ligament. The ligament represents the left portion of the dorsal mesogastrium. During splenectomy, the tail of the pancreas within this ligament must be identified and preserved to prevent pancreatic injury and subsequent pancreatitis or pseudocyst formation.

The obturator nerve divides into anterior and posterior divisions. The anterior division supplies adductor longus, brevis, gracilis, and pectineus (sometimes), and provides a cutaneous branch to the medial thigh. The posterior division supplies obturator externus and the adductor part of adductor magnus, and gives an articular branch to the knee joint.
questions.question: The obturator nerve divides into which two divisions upon exiting the obturator foramen?
Which nerve loops around the ligamentum arteriosum?
questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of left vagus) loops around the aortic arch and ligamentum arteriosum before ascending in the groove between trachea and esophagus to reach the larynx. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the right subclavian artery. This asymmetry reflects embryological development.

questions.question: Which structure prevents superior displacement of the humeral head?
questions.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch (formed by coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament) prevents superior displacement of the humeral head. The joint capsule is weak superiorly, making this bony-ligamentous arch essential for stability. Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability but the arch provides the structural barrier.

questions.question: Which nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome as it passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle. This is the most common site of ulnar nerve entrapment. Symptoms include numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and hand muscle weakness.

questions.question: Which nerve is tested by thumb interphalangeal flexion?
questions.explanation: Thumb interphalangeal joint flexion tests the anterior interosseous nerve through flexor pollicis longus function. Inability to flex this joint while the metacarp ophalangeal joint is stabilized indicates anterior interosseous syndrome. This is demonstrated by inability to make the OK sign properly.

questions.question: How many pulmonary veins open into left atrium?
questions.explanation: Four pulmonary veins (two from each lung) drain oxygenated blood from the lungs and open into the left atrium. These veins have no valves at their orifices. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins from each side carry blood from the respective lobes of the lungs.

The detrusor muscle is composed of smooth muscle arranged in three poorly defined layers (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal). It is under involuntary control via autonomic innervation. Parasympathetic stimulation (via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction for micturition; sympathetic stimulation (via hypogastric nerves) causes relaxation for urine storage.
questions.question: What type of muscle forms the detrusor muscle?
Which rib is most commonly fractured?
questions.explanation: The middle ribs (4-9) are most commonly fractured because they are longest and least protected. The upper two ribs are protected by the clavicle, and the lower two floating ribs are mobile and therefore swing free, avoiding fracture. Rib fractures are uncommon in children due to chest wall elasticity.

questions.question: The quadrate lobe of the liver receives blood from which branch?
questions.explanation: The quadrate lobe, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe (located between the gallbladder fossa and falciform ligament), functionally belongs to the left lobe as it receives its blood supply from the left hepatic artery and drains bile via the left hepatic duct. The functional division of the liver (Couinaud's classification) is based on vascular supply and biliary drainage rather than external anatomical features. The main portal fissure (containing the middle hepatic vein) separates functional right and left lobes, running from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC, placing the quadrate and caudate lobes functionally on the left.

questions.question: Which structure is most posterior in superior mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The esophagus is the most posterior structure in the superior mediastinum. From superficial to deep, the contents include: thymus gland, great veins (brachiocephalic veins and SVC), great arteries (aortic arch and branches), nerves (vagus and phrenic), trachea, esophagus, and thoracic duct.

The porta hepatis (transverse fissure) separates the caudate lobe (posterosuperiorly) from the quadrate lobe (anteroinferiorly) on the visceral surface of the liver. The porta hepatis contains the portal vein, hepatic artery, hepatic ducts, lymphatics, and nerves entering or leaving the liver. The caudate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis anteriorly, the IVC groove posteriorly, and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum on the left. The quadrate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis posteriorly, the gallbladder fossa on the right, and the fissure for the ligamentum teres on the left.
questions.question: Which structure separates the caudate lobe from the quadrate lobe?

questions.explanation: The upper lateral quadrant is the safe zone for intramuscular injections in the gluteal region. This avoids the sciatic nerve, which courses midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. Injections in other quadrants risk sciatic nerve injury, causing foot drop and sensory loss.
questions.question: The safe quadrant for intramuscular injection in the gluteal region is which of the following?
The middle rectal artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The middle rectal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (or occasionally from the internal pudendal artery) and passes medially in the lateral rectal ligament (lateral ligament of the rectum) to supply the lower part of the rectum. It anastomoses with branches of the superior rectal artery (from inferior mesenteric) above and inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal) below, creating collateral circulation. This vessel represents the junction between portal (superior rectal) and systemic (middle and inferior rectal) venous systems, a site of potential portosystemic anastomosis in portal hypertension.

Fourteen structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen: one muscle (piriformis), seven nerves (sciatic, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerves), and six vessels (superior and inferior gluteal arteries and veins, and internal pudendal artery and vein).
questions.question: How many total structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen?

questions.explanation: The deep perineal space (deep perineal pouch) is bounded superiorly by the inferior fascia of the pelvic diaphragm and inferiorly by the perineal membrane. In males, it contains the membranous urethra, external urethral sphincter, bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands), deep transverse perineal muscle, internal pudendal vessels, and dorsal nerve of penis. In females, it contains the urethra, external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscle, internal pudendal vessels, and dorsal nerve of clitoris (no bulbourethral glands). The space is traversed by the urethra (and vagina in females).
questions.question: Which structure passes through the deep perineal space?

questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) provide parasympathetic innervation to hindgut derivatives (distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal). The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic supply to foregut and midgut derivatives (up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon). Sympathetic supply is via lumbar splanchnic nerves and the inferior mesenteric plexus.
questions.question: Which parasympathetic nerve supplies the hindgut derivatives?

questions.explanation: The sphincter of Oddi (sphincter ampullae) surrounds the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), controlling the release of bile and pancreatic juice into the second part of the duodenum. The sphincter choledochus surrounds the terminal bile duct just before its junction with the pancreatic duct, while the sphincter pancreaticus surrounds the terminal pancreatic duct. The sphincter of Oddi coordinates the flow from both ducts, relaxing in response to cholecystokinin during digestion and contracting between meals to allow bile storage in the gallbladder.
questions.question: The hepatopancreatic ampulla is surrounded by which sphincter?
Which nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve is formed from cervical nerve roots C3, C4, and C5 ("C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"). It provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. The long course from neck to diaphragm reflects the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region.

questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to reach the posterior compartment of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The perforating branches (three or four) of the profunda femoris artery perforate the adductor magnus to supply the muscles of the medial and posterior thigh. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical approaches to the posterior thigh, where inadvertent cutting of perforating vessels can cause significant hemorrhage. They are the main blood supply to the hamstring muscles.

questions.question: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery at which landmark?
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery as it passes beneath the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis, different from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament). The femoral artery enters the femoral triangle, lying lateral to the femoral vein in the femoral sheath. Just before passing beneath the inguinal ligament, the external iliac artery gives off the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries. The femoral artery later becomes the popliteal artery after passing through the adductor hiatus.

The left inferior phrenic vein is usually doubled: one part drains into the inferior vena cava, while the other drains into the left suprarenal vein. The right inferior phrenic vein drains directly into the IVC. The superior phrenic vein (right side) also drains into the IVC.
questions.question: Where does the left inferior phrenic vein drain?
The femoral neck is intracapsular, but the greater and lesser trochanters are extracapsular. The fibrous capsule attaches anteriorly to which line on the femur?
questions.explanation: The fibrous capsule attaches anteriorly to the intertrochanteric line (making the entire femoral neck intracapsular anteriorly) and posteriorly just proximal to the intertrochanteric crest. The greater and lesser trochanters are therefore extracapsular. This distinction explains why femoral neck fractures carry different complication profiles than intertrochanteric fractures.

questions.question: The pancreas lies at which vertebral levels?
questions.explanation: The pancreas extends obliquely across the posterior abdominal wall from the C-shaped curve of the duodenum (head) to the splenic hilum (tail) at approximately L1-L2 vertebral levels, though the tail may extend slightly higher. The head lies at L1-L2, the neck crosses L1, and the body and tail run along L1-L2 as they extend to the left. The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal (except the tail, which extends into the splenorenal ligament), lying anterior to the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vessels, aorta, IVC, left kidney, and left suprarenal gland.

questions.question: Which nerve injury causes inability to form OK sign?
questions.explanation: injury causes inability to properly form the OK sign. This tests flexor pollicis longus (thumb IP flexion) and flexor digitorum profundus to index finger (DIP flexion). Patients cannot touch the thumb tip to index fingertip in a rounded configuration.

The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian artery (from abdominal aorta at L2) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully clamped and ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (connecting ovary to uterus) contains no significant vessels. The uterine artery reaches the uterus via the parametrium (base of broad ligament).
questions.question: The suspensory ligament of the ovary contains which vessels?

questions.explanation: The middle third of the esophagus (thoracic portion) drains into the azygos venous system. The upper third drains into brachiocephalic veins, and the lower third into the portal system (via left gastric vein). These represent important sites of portosystemic anastomosis where esophageal varices can develop in portal hypertension.
questions.question: How does esophageal venous drainage occur in thorax?
How many lobes does the mammary gland contain?
questions.explanation: The mammary gland is formed of 15-20 lobes, each consisting of numerous lobules. The lobes and lobules are separated by interlobar and interlobular fibrous and fatty tissue called the ligaments of Cooper. Each lobe drains through its own lactiferous duct, which opens onto the nipple summit.

questions.question: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured due to falls on an outstretched hand?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid bone crosses two rows of carpal bones forming a hinge, making it vulnerable to heavy stress during falls on outstretched hands. The fracture commonly occurs through the middle of the bone or causes complete separation into two pieces. Risk of avascular necrosis exists due to single arterial blood supply entering at the distal end.

questions.question: The gallbladder fundus projects beyond which liver border?
questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where it may contact the anterior abdominal wall. This location corresponds approximately to the point where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis crosses the right costal margin (at the transpyloric plane). The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum on all surfaces. When the gallbladder is distended or inflamed (acute cholecystitis), the fundus becomes palpable at this location, and deep palpation causes inspiratory arrest (Murphy's sign).

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the submandibular triangle?
questions.explanation: The submandibular triangle is bounded superiorly by the body of the mandible, anteroinferiorly by the anterior belly of digastric, and posteroinferiorly by the posterior belly of digastric. The floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles. The triangle contains the submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, and submandibular lymph nodes.

questions.question: Which vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, representing the final pathway for blood that has passed through the hepatic sinusoids. Unlike other veins, hepatic veins have no valves. The portal vein and its tributaries (splenic, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric veins) carry nutrient-rich but deoxygenated blood to the liver, where it mixes with oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery in the sinusoids before draining via hepatic veins. The hepatic veins and their relationship to IVC are crucial landmarks in liver surgery and transplantation.

Biceps femoris has two heads: the long head from the ischial tuberosity (in common with semitendinosus) and the short head from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur. The short head does not cross the hip joint and is supplied by the common fibular division (not tibial division) of the sciatic nerve.
questions.question: Which hamstring muscle has a short head originating from the linea aspera and NOT from the ischial tuberosity?

questions.explanation: The thymus reaches its maximum size at puberty, after which it undergoes involution (gradual shrinkage). In adults, much of the thymic tissue is replaced by adipose tissue, though some functional tissue persists. Despite involution, the adult thymus continues to produce T cells, though at a reduced rate.
questions.question: When does the thymus reach maximum size?

questions.explanation: The lesser omentum forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac, separating it from the greater sac anteriorly along with the posterior wall of the stomach. This double-layered peritoneal fold extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of duodenum to the liver. The lesser omentum consists of the hepatogastric ligament (its membranous portion) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad), with the latter forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
questions.question: Which structure separates the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs?
Why does the phrenic nerve have a long course?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve has a long course from the neck (C3-5) to the diaphragm because of embryological migration of the diaphragm. The septum transversum initially forms in the cervical region and migrates caudally during development, carrying its nerve supply (from cervical segments) with it to its final thoracic position.

The internal urethral sphincter, a thickening of smooth muscle at the bladder neck, is under involuntary autonomic control (both sympathetic and parasympathetic), in contrast to the external urethral sphincter which is skeletal muscle under voluntary somatic control via the pudendal nerve. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric nerves) causes contraction of the internal sphincter and relaxation of the detrusor, promoting urine storage. Parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation, promoting micturition. The internal sphincter prevents semen from entering the bladder during ejaculation and contributes to urinary continence.
questions.question: The internal urethral sphincter receives which type of innervation?
Which segment absorbs bile salts for enterohepatic recirculation?
questions.explanation: Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal circulation (enterohepatic recirculation). About 95% of bile salts are recycled this way, conserving the bile salt pool. Ileal disease or resection disrupts this circulation, leading to bile salt malabsorption, steatorrhea, and potential bile salt diarrhea.

The white pulp of the spleen consists of lymphoid tissue surrounding central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS) and lymphoid nodules. It is the site of immune surveillance and antibody production in response to blood-borne antigens. The white pulp contains predominantly T lymphocytes in the PALS and B lymphocytes in the lymphoid follicles.
questions.question: What is the primary immunological function of splenic white pulp?

questions.explanation: The aryepiglotticus muscle closes the laryngeal vestibule during swallowing by pulling the arytenoid cartilages toward the epiglottis. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function. The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral margins of the laryngeal inlet.
questions.question: Which muscle closes the vestibule of the larynx during swallowing?

questions.explanation: Semimembranosus originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. Its reflected attachment forms the oblique popliteal ligament. Semimembranosus is named for its membranous (flat, broad) proximal tendon, in contrast to semitendinosus which has a long round distal tendon.
questions.question: Which hamstring muscle originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia?

questions.explanation: The puboprostatic ligaments extend from the posterior aspect of the pubic bones to the prostate and bladder neck in males, anchoring these structures. In females, the equivalent structures are the pubovesical ligaments. The lateral ligaments of the bladder (containing superior vesical vessels) also contribute to bladder support and fixation.
