The arch extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue and contains the palatoglossus muscle. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the two palatoglossal arches connecting the oral cavity with the oropharynx.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper?

questions.explanation: Proximal hamstring avulsion (ischial tuberosity avulsion) occurs during sudden forceful hip flexion with the knee extended, as in the full stride of sprinting. This violent stretch exceeds the tensile strength of the proximal hamstring attachment. Athletes present with acute posterior thigh pain and inability to sprint. MRI confirms the degree of retraction of the avulsed hamstring.
options: Sudden forceful hip flexion with knee extended (sprint stride)
Slow walking on flat ground at low speed
Passive knee extension while lying down
questions.question: Hamstring injuries are common in sprinting athletes. Which specific action most commonly causes a proximal hamstring avulsion?
The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows which movements of the foot?
options: Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion at the ankle
Circumduction only, without inversion or eversion
Inversion and eversion (with associated adduction and abduction)
Pronation and supination of the ankle
questions.explanation: The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows inversion and eversion of the foot, with associated adduction and abduction. These movements occur at the subtalar joint and midtarsal joints together. True dorsiflexion and plantarflexion occur at the ankle (talocrural) joint. The summit of the lateral longitudinal arch is at the subtalar articulation.

The external urethral sphincter is composed of skeletal muscle and is under voluntary somatic control via the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). This sphincter can be consciously contracted to prevent or interrupt micturition. In males, it surrounds the membranous urethra; in females, it surrounds the middle third of the urethra at the urogenital diaphragm.
questions.question: What controls the external urethral sphincter?
From how many lumbar vertebrae does right crus arise?
questions.explanation: The right crus arises from the front of the bodies of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs. The left crus is smaller and arises only from L1 and L2. Some muscle fibers from the right crus form a sling around the esophageal opening.

questions.question: Which lymphoid structures are characteristic of the terminal ileum?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules characteristic of the ileum, especially prominent in the terminal ileum. These are permanent features of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) that play a crucial role in intestinal immunity. Peyer's patches are absent in the jejunum and located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.

questions.question: The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplying both the hip and knee joints explains which clinical observation?
options: Quadriceps weakness in obturator nerve injury
Referred pain to the knee in hip joint disease
Loss of adduction in knee joint pathology
Hip pain referred to the lumbar spine
Groin pain referred to the ankle
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, explaining the well-known clinical phenomenon of referred pain to the knee in hip joint disease. Children with Perthes disease or slipped femoral epiphysis classically present with knee pain. This is a critical clinical pearl applying Hilton's law practically.

questions.question: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Additional proprioceptive fibers from C2-C3 may contribute. Unilateral contraction of sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head ipsilaterally. Bilateral contraction flexes the neck.

The thoracentesis needle should be inserted immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein-artery-nerve) that runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib. Insertion below the rib risks injuring the intercostal vessels and nerve.
questions.question: Where should thoracentesis needle be inserted?

options: Located in a deep protected position
Superficial over lateral wrist makes it vulnerable to trauma
questions.explanation: The superficial branch of radial nerve becomes subcutaneous on the lateral wrist as it passes over the anatomical snuffbox. This superficial position makes it vulnerable to trauma (handcuff neuropathy, tight watches, wrist lacerations). Injury causes numbness over dorsal thumb and radial hand without motor deficit.
questions.question: How does the superficial branch of radial nerve course affect its vulnerability?

questions.explanation: The azygos vein is formed by the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and right subcostal vein at the level of L1-L2. It enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12. It represents the embryonic right posterior cardinal vein.
questions.question: Where does the azygos vein originate?

questions.explanation: The flexor pollicis brevis is one of the thenar muscles supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. This branch arises in the hand after the nerve passes through the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome can affect these muscles, causing thenar wasting and weakness of thumb opposition.
questions.question: Which muscle is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve?

questions.explanation: The flexor carpi radialis tendon lies in a groove between the attachments of the flexor retinaculum to bone, not within the carpal tunnel itself. The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve, four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, and the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These structures are enclosed within synovial sheaths.
questions.question: Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: A thymoma is a neoplasm (tumor) arising from the epithelial cells of the thymus gland. It is the most common primary tumor of the anterior mediastinum in adults. Thymomas are often associated with myasthenia gravis (about 30-50% of thymoma patients develop MG). Treatment typically involves surgical resection.
questions.question: What is a thymoma?
What muscle action is tested by resisted elbow extension?
questions.explanation: Resisted elbow extension primarily tests triceps brachii strength, particularly the medial head which is most active in this action. Anconeus provides minor assistance. Weakness suggests radial nerve injury or C7 nerve root pathology.

The thoracic sympathetic trunk lies anterolateral to the vertebral bodies, just lateral to the anterior longitudinal ligament. It descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum and posterior mediastinum. Each trunk has 11-12 segmental ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion often fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion.
questions.question: Where does the thoracic sympathetic trunk lie?
The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in which anatomical groove?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove between the trachea and esophagus. This location makes it vulnerable during thyroid surgery. The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch while the right loops under the subclavian artery.

questions.question: The testicular lymphatics drain to which nodes?
questions.explanation: The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, bypassing the inguinal and iliac nodes. This drainage pattern follows the testicular vessels and reflects the embryological origin of the testes high on the posterior abdominal wall. In testicular cancer, metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes, not inguinal nodes (unless scrotal skin is involved). The scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This explains why orchiectomy for testicular cancer requires high ligation of the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring to include regional lymphatics.

The ulnar artery is the larger terminal branch of the brachial artery, beginning below the elbow joint. It provides the main arterial supply to the medial forearm and forms the superficial palmar arch predominantly. The radial artery is smaller but more clinically accessible.
questions.question: Which artery is the largest terminal branch of the brachial artery?

questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain lymph from the lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, and lower anterior abdominal wall (below the umbilicus). Their efferents drain to the deep inguinal lymph nodes, which then drain to the external iliac nodes, common iliac nodes, and ultimately the para-aortic nodes. This drainage pattern explains why infections of the foot can present with inguinal lymphadenopathy.
options: Lower limb only; draining to external iliac nodes
Lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, lower anterior abdominal wall; deep inguinal nodes
Only the genitalia; draining to internal obturator nodes
Only the lower limb below the knee; popliteal nodes
Only the gluteal region; internal iliac nodes
questions.question: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain which areas of the body, and their efferents drain to which deep node group?
Which structure forms the floor of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The floor of the cubital fossa is formed by two muscles: the brachialis muscle superiorly and the supinator muscle inferiorly. The roof is formed by skin, superficial and deep fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis. The fossa contains important neurovascular structures from medial to lateral.

questions.question: Which nerve is at risk during clavicle fracture?
options: Subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks
questions.explanation: The subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks pass behind the medial third of the clavicle, separated only by the subclavius muscle. Fracture of the clavicle, especially displaced fractures, can injure these neurovascular structures. The subclavius muscle provides some protection.

Swan neck deformity involves PIP joint hyperextension with DIP joint flexion. This can result from volar plate insufficiency, FDS tendon injury, or chronic inflammatory arthritis. The deformity resembles a swan's neck in profile. It's the opposite of boutonniere deformity.
options: Central slip rupture with DIP extension deformity
Volar plate or FDS rupture with hyperextension
questions.question: What causes swan neck deformity?

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. It extends from the umbilicus to the liver, dividing the liver into anatomical right and left lobes on the diaphragmatic surface. The free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres (round ligament).
questions.question: Which ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?

questions.explanation: Flexor hallucis longus is innervated by the tibial nerve at S2 and S3. It originates from the inferior two-thirds of the posterior surface of the fibula and inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe. It flexes the great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes the ankle, and supports the medial longitudinal arch during the push-off phase of gait.
questions.question: Flexor hallucis longus is innervated by the tibial nerve at which spinal levels?
Which structure does the round ligament of the liver represent?
questions.explanation: The round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres hepatis) represents the obliterated left umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. It runs from the umbilicus to the liver within the free inferior margin of the falciform ligament, then continues in a fissure on the visceral surface between the left and quadrate lobes before joining the left branch of the portal vein. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, creating a portosystemic anastomosis that can produce caput medusae (dilated superficial veins radiating from the umbilicus). The obliterated ductus venosus forms the ligamentum venosum.

The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus contains (from superior to inferior): oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), ophthalmic division (V1), and maxillary division (V2). The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (VI) pass through the sinus cavity itself. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can affect all these structures causing ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the cavernous sinus lateral wall?
Which cruciate ligament becomes taut during knee flexion and is the stronger of the two cruciate ligaments?
questions.explanation: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) arises from the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and attaches to the medial condyle of the femur. It becomes taut during flexion of the knee and is the stronger of the two cruciate ligaments. In a weight-bearing flexed knee (walking downhill), the PCL is the main stabilizing factor preventing anterior displacement of the femur.

questions.question: Which hypothenar muscle abducts the little finger?
questions.explanation: abducts the little finger away from the ring finger. It is one of three hypothenar muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve. The muscle forms the medial border of the palm in the hypothenar eminence.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive anterior diaphragmatic drainage?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the thoracic surface of the diaphragm drains anteriorly to parasternal lymph nodes (via anterior diaphragmatic nodes) and posteriorly to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes. From the abdominal surface, drainage goes to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic, and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.

Musculocutaneous nerve injury greatly weakens forearm flexion (biceps and brachialis loss) and supination (biceps loss). Sensation is lost over the lateral forearm through the lateral cutaneous nerve. Some weak flexion remains through brachioradialis (radial nerve) and pronator teres (median nerve).
options: Forearm flexion and supination weakened, lateral forearm numbness
questions.question: How does the musculocutaneous nerve injury affect function?
Which nerve is involved in Froment's sign?
questions.explanation: Froment's sign indicates ulnar nerve palsy, demonstrating weakness of adductor pollicis. When attempting to grip paper between thumb and index finger, the patient compensates by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint (using flexor pollicis longus supplied by median nerve). This flexion indicates inability to adduct the thumb normally.

The scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph, which has high potassium and low sodium concentration (similar to intracellular fluid). The scala vestibuli and scala tympani contain perilymph. The organ of Corti lies on the basilar membrane separating scala media from scala tympani. M�ni�re's disease involves endolymphatic hydrops.
questions.question: The scala media contains which fluid?

questions.explanation: The nasal mucosa receives blood from both internal carotid (via ophthalmic artery branches: anterior and posterior ethmoidal) and external carotid (via maxillary artery branches: sphenopalatine, greater palatine) systems. The superior labial artery also contributes anteriorly. This rich dual blood supply accounts for profuse epistaxis. Kiesselbach's plexus represents arterial convergence.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies the nasal mucosa?
How is chylothorax initially managed?
questions.explanation: Initial management of chylothorax is conservative: chest tube drainage, nutritional support with medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) diet or total parenteral nutrition (TPN) to reduce chyle production, and treatment of underlying cause. Many cases resolve with conservative management. Persistent cases (>2 weeks, >1L/day drainage) may require surgical intervention.

questions.question: Where does the suspensory muscle of the duodenum attach?
questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) extends from the right crus of the diaphragm behind the pancreas to attach to the duodenojejunal flexure. It contains both smooth muscle and fibrous tissue. Contraction of this muscle widens the angle of the duodenojejunal flexure and may assist in opening the duodenum for passage of contents into the jejunum.

questions.question: Which vessel specifically supplies the bed of the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Branches of the facial and lingual arteries supply the submandibular gland, with the facial artery providing the primary vascular supply. The facial artery passes deep to the gland before crossing the mandible. Venous drainage follows corresponding veins to the internal jugular system.

questions.question: Which muscle causes nipple erection?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle cells disposed in a predominantly circular direction and radiating from the nipple base cause nipple erection. Their contraction, induced by cold, tactile, or emotional stimuli, causes erection of the nipple and wrinkling of the surrounding areola. This is an involuntary response.

questions.question: The portal vein is formed by the union of which two vessels?
questions.explanation: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein, measuring approximately 8 cm in length. The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein ascends to the porta hepatis within the free edge of the lesser omentum, positioned posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery, where it divides into right and left branches.

questions.question: Which coronary artery typically gives rise to the SA nodal artery?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people, and from the left circumflex artery in about 40%. It courses posteriorly around the superior vena cava-atrial junction to supply the SA node. Occlusion can cause sinus node dysfunction, though collateral circulation often provides some protection.

questions.question: The maxillary artery is divided into how many parts by the lateral pterygoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle divides the maxillary artery into three parts: mandibular (first), pterygoid (second), and pterygopalatine (third). Each part gives off specific branches to supply deep facial structures. The third part enters the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure.

is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle due to its vulnerable position under the acromion. The tendon passes through a narrow space (subacromial space) where it's subject to impingement. Age-related degeneration combined with repetitive overhead activities increases tear risk.
questions.question: What is the primary muscle affected in rotator cuff tears?
Which artery supplies the lateral breast?
questions.explanation: The lateral thoracic artery, a branch of the axillary artery, provides lateral mammary branches that supply the lateral portion of the breast. Additional supply comes from pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery and branches from posterior intercostal arteries in the 3rd and 4th intercostal spaces.

The quadratus lumborum receives innervation from the subcostal nerve (T12) and the upper lumbar nerves (L1-L3 or L4), reflecting its position as the most lateral muscle of the posterior abdominal wall. This muscle originates from the iliolumbar ligament and adjacent iliac crest, inserting onto the medial half of the inferior border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae. It functions to fix the 12th rib during inspiration, extend the lumbar vertebral column bilaterally, and produce lateral flexion when acting unilaterally.
questions.question: The quadratus lumborum muscle is innervated by which nerves?

questions.explanation: Pronator teres and biceps brachii are antagonistic for forearm rotation: pronator teres produces pronation while biceps produces supination. However, both can contribute to elbow flexion when pronation/supination resistance is present. This demonstrates how muscles can be synergistic for one motion while antagonistic for another.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and biceps?
options: They're antagonists: pronator teres pronates, biceps supinates

questions.explanation: From lateral to medial, the femoral triangle contains: Nerve (femoral nerve), Artery (femoral artery), Vein (femoral vein), and Empty space/Lymphatics. The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics) helps recall this order. The femoral sheath surrounds the femoral artery and vein (and the femoral canal), but not the femoral nerve.
questions.question: The contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial are arranged as which of the following?
Which structure forms the medial boundary of the carotid triangle?
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded by the sternocleidomastoid (posterolaterally), superior belly of omohyoid (inferiorly), and posterior belly of digastric (superiorly). The triangle contains the carotid bifurcation, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve, and several other structures. It is a subdivision of the anterior triangle of the neck.

questions.question: What is the thoracic duct's capacity?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct carries approximately 1-2 liters of lymph per day (though this can increase significantly after meals due to chyle from intestinal lacteals). It is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body. Injury to the thoracic duct (from trauma or surgery) can result in significant chyle leakage into the pleural cavity (chylothorax).

questions.question: Adductor brevis lies deep to which two muscles of the medial compartment?
questions.explanation: Adductor brevis lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. It originates from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis and inserts into the pectineal line and proximal part of the linea aspera. It is innervated by the anterior division of the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) and adducts the thigh and to some extent flexes it.

The internal oblique muscle originates from the lateral two-thirds of the inguinal ligament (along with the iliac crest and thoracolumbar fascia), with its fibers running superomedially. The lowermost fibers arch over the spermatic cord, contributing to the anterior wall of the inguinal canal laterally and the roof of the canal throughout its length. The external oblique muscle does not originate from the inguinal ligament; rather, its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament itself. The transversus abdominis also takes origin from the inguinal ligament laterally, contributing to the roof of the canal.
questions.question: Which muscle originates from the inguinal ligament?

questions.explanation: The testicular arteries arise directly from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta, just inferior to the renal arteries at approximately the L2 vertebral level, reflecting the embryological origin of the testes in the posterior abdominal wall. These long, slender arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major muscle, ureter, and external iliac vessels before entering the deep inguinal ring as part of the spermatic cord. The right testicular artery crosses anterior to the inferior vena cava, while the left crosses anterior to the left renal vein, then both pass through the inguinal canal to supply the testes.
questions.question: The testicular artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The breast is separated from the deep fascia covering the underlying muscles by a layer of loose areolar tissue called the retromammary space. This space allows the breast some mobility over the pectoralis major muscle. The space is important surgically as it provides a plane for mastectomy.
questions.question: What separates the breast from deep fascia?

options: Allows full flexion-extension with ligament support
questions.question: How does the elbow joint capsule weakness affect function?
questions.explanation: The elbow joint capsule is weak anteriorly and posteriorly, allowing extensive flexion-extension movement. The medial and lateral collateral ligaments provide essential stability. This capsular laxity in the movement plane while maintaining stability perpendicular to it exemplifies structure-function relationships.

questions.question: Which kidney is more commonly affected by renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma affects both kidneys with approximately equal frequency, though some studies show a slight left-sided predominance. It typically presents in the 60-70 age group and is more common in males. The classic triad of flank pain, hematuria, and palpable mass is present in only 10-15% of cases. Most are now detected incidentally on imaging.

questions.question: What drains the area above the pectinate line in the anal canal?
questions.explanation: Above the pectinate line, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes (following the superior rectal vessels). Below the pectinate line, drainage is primarily to superficial inguinal nodes. This difference is clinically important in anal cancer spread: tumors above the line metastasize to pelvic nodes, while those below spread to inguinal nodes.

The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the left vagus nerve as it descends on the anterior surface of the oesophagus. This trunk enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and supplies the anterior gastric surface. It also gives off a large hepatic branch and a pyloric branch.
questions.question: Which nerve forms the anterior vagal trunk supplying the stomach?

options: Fall on outstretched hand with wrist extended
questions.explanation: Colles' fracture typically occurs from falling onto an outstretched hand with the wrist extended. This is the most common wrist pathology in persons older than 50 years. The distal radius fractures with posterior displacement of the distal fragment, creating the characteristic "dinner fork deformity."
questions.question: What is the typical mechanism of Colles' fracture?

questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the cubital fossa roof and protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture. It distributes biceps force to the ulna and forearm fascia. Historically recognized as the grace of God tendon for protecting vital structures during bloodletting.
options: Provides muscle attachment to bicipital fascia
Reinforces cubital fossa, protects neurovascular structures
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the bicipital aponeurosis?
Which veins drain into the azygos vein?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein receives: right superior intercostal vein, lower eight right posterior intercostal veins, right bronchial vein, middle esophageal veins, and the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins from the left side. It drains much of the thoracic wall and mediastinal structures.

questions.question: What nerve provides sensation to the regimental badge area?
questions.explanation: The superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve, the sensory continuation of the axillary nerve, provides sensation to the skin over the deltoid muscle ("regimental badge" area). Loss of sensation in this area indicates axillary nerve injury. Testing sensation here helps diagnose nerve damage in shoulder trauma.

options: Does not supply any flexor muscles
Supplies brachioradialis flexor despite being an extensor nerve
questions.question: How does the radial nerve supply both flexors and extensors?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve primarily supplies extensor muscles but also innervates brachioradialis (elbow flexor) and extensor carpi radialis longus (proximal to lateral epicondyle). This reflects developmental muscle group origins. Brachioradialis, despite being anatomically anterior (flexor compartment), is functionally and embryologically an extensor group muscle.

Scarpa's fascia is the deep membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall, found inferior to the umbilicus. Superficial to it lies Camper's fascia, the fatty superficial layer. Scarpa's fascia continues inferiorly as the superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia) in the perineum and the dartos muscle and fascia in the scrotum. This fascial layer is clinically important as it can limit the spread of extravasated urine or blood in the superficial perineal space, directing fluids superiorly toward the anterior abdominal wall.
questions.question: Which layer of the anterior abdominal wall contains Scarpa's fascia?
What is pneumomediastinum?
questions.explanation: Pneumomediastinum is the presence of air in the mediastinum. It can result from alveolar rupture (from trauma, positive pressure ventilation, asthma), esophageal perforation, tracheal injury, or tracking from neck injuries. Air may dissect along tissue planes into the neck (subcutaneous emphysema) or into the pleural cavity (pneumothorax).

The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by union of internal cerebral veins and basal veins, draining into the straight sinus. The straight sinus then joins the superior sagittal sinus at the confluence of sinuses. Deep cerebral structures drain via this venous pathway.
questions.question: The great cerebral vein of Galen drains into which sinus?

questions.explanation: The hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII). The nerve provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus. Unilateral paralysis causes the tongue to deviate toward the paralyzed side when protruded.
questions.question: The hypoglossal canal transmits which cranial nerve?
What is the costocervical trunk?
questions.explanation: The costocervical trunk is a branch of the second part of the subclavian artery (posterior to scalenus anterior). It divides into the superior intercostal artery (supplying the first two intercostal spaces) and the deep cervical artery (supplying deep neck muscles). This trunk is important in collateral circulation.

The fabella is an accessory sesamoid bone occasionally found in the tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius, at the posterolateral aspect of the knee. It is present in approximately 10-30% of individuals. It can cause posterolateral knee pain (fabella syndrome) when it compresses the common fibular nerve or irritates the popliteus tendon. It is typically visible on lateral knee radiographs.
questions.question: The fabella is a sesamoid bone occasionally found in which muscle's tendon near the knee?

questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of the triangle is formed by the transversalis fascia, which may be reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. This triangle represents an area of potential weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, and direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Understanding this triangle is crucial for distinguishing direct (through the triangle) from indirect (lateral to inferior epigastric) inguinal hernias.
questions.question: Which vessel marks the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
How do the rotator cuff muscles stabilize the glenohumeral joint?
options: Through passive ligament and capsule action
Rotator cuff compresses humeral head into glenoid cavity
questions.explanation: Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability through their resting tone, actively compressing the humeral head into the glenoid cavity. The muscles form a tendinous cuff blending with the joint capsule, providing circumferential reinforcement. This active stabilization is essential given the joint's inherent bony instability.

The calcaneal apophysis (posterior calcaneal epiphysis) is a classic example of an atavistic epiphysis. Traction epiphyses arise at tendinous insertions, while pressure epiphyses form articular surfaces. Traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis in adolescents is known as Sever's disease.
questions.question: An atavistic epiphysis represents a vestigial bone once separate in ancestral species. Which of the following is a classic example in the lower limb?

questions.explanation: Full shoulder abduction beyond 90 degrees requires synchronized glenohumeral abduction and scapular upward rotation (scapulohumeral rhythm). For every 3 degrees of abduction, approximately 2 degrees occur at the glenohumeral joint and 1 degree from scapular rotation. This demonstrates upper limb integrated function.
options: Glenohumeral abduction and scapular upward rotation
questions.question: Which movements must occur together for full shoulder abduction beyond 90 degrees?
Which structure forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum is a thick connective tissue structure forming the roof of the carpal tunnel. It bridges between the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally. This converts the carpal arch into a tunnel through which flexor tendons and median nerve pass.

The deep group of the posterior compartment contains four muscles: popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and tibialis posterior. The superficial group contains three muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris. All muscles of the posterior compartment are supplied by the tibial nerve. It is the largest of the three leg compartments.
questions.question: The deep group of the posterior leg compartment contains how many muscles?
What level are nodes behind pectoralis minor?
questions.explanation: Level II nodes (middle nodes) lie behind the pectoralis minor muscle. Level I (low nodes) are lateral to pectoralis minor. Level III (upper/apical nodes) are medial to pectoralis minor. This classification is used in staging breast cancer and planning surgical lymph node dissection.

The anterior fontanelle (bregma) is located at the junction of the coronal, sagittal, and frontal (metopic) sutures where the frontal and parietal bones meet. It is diamond-shaped and typically closes by 18-24 months. The fontanelle allows skull molding during birth and accommodates brain growth. Bulging indicates increased intracranial pressure.
questions.question: The anterior fontanelle is located at the junction of which sutures?
The popliteal artery begins where the femoral artery passes through which structure in the lower thigh?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus. It then descends through the popliteal fossa and terminates at the inferior border of popliteus. The femoral artery travels through the adductor canal in the anterior thigh before reaching the hiatus.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the suprarenal medulla directly?
questions.explanation: The middle suprarenal artery (from the abdominal aorta) is unique in that it supplies the medulla directly without first passing through the cortex, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly to chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic neurons). The superior suprarenal artery (from inferior phrenic) and inferior suprarenal artery (from renal) supply primarily the cortex. This direct arterial supply to the medulla allows rapid hormone release (epinephrine and norepinephrine) in response to stress. The suprarenal glands have rich arterial supply from three sources but limited venous drainage (one vein each side).

questions.question: What drains to tracheobronchial lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: The tracheobronchial lymph nodes (superior and inferior) lie at and around the tracheal bifurcation. They receive lymph from the lungs, bronchi, trachea, and heart. These nodes are important in lung cancer staging. Efferents form the bronchomediastinal trunks which drain to the venous system or lymphatic ducts.

The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at approximately 7-8 years of age. The secondary ossification centres of the hip bone (for the iliac crest, Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and ischial tuberosity) all fuse completely by 20-25 years of age.
questions.question: The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at which approximate age?
Which rib level marks the base of breast vertically?
questions.explanation: The base of the breast extends vertically from the 2nd to 6th rib. Transversely, it extends from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line. The axillary tail of Spence extends from the upper outer quadrant into the axilla. These landmarks are important for clinical breast examination.

questions.question: Which space lies proximal to the carpal tunnel in the forearm?
questions.explanation: The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm. Its roof is formed distally by flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis. The floor consists of pronator quadratus distally and interosseous membrane proximally.

questions.question: Where does a femoral hernia emerge?
questions.explanation: Femoral hernias pass through the femoral ring (the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally occupied by a lymph node) and emerge below the inguinal ligament through the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis) in the deep fascia of the thigh. They are more common in women but overall less common than inguinal hernias. They have a high risk of strangulation due to the rigid boundaries of the femoral ring.

The fovea capitis transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur). This vascular route is clinically important, as fractures of the femoral neck can disrupt primary blood supply and lead to avascular necrosis.
questions.question: The fovea capitis of the femoral head transmits blood from which artery to the femoral head?

questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion is located in the pterygopalatine fossa and is one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head. It receives preganglionic fibers via the greater petrosal nerve and provides secretomotor innervation to lacrimal and nasal glands. The ganglion also transmits sympathetic and sensory fibers without synapsing.
questions.question: Which parasympathetic ganglion is associated with the pterygopalatine fossa?

questions.explanation: The long head of triceps crosses both the shoulder and elbow joints, performing extension at the shoulder. At the elbow, all three heads of triceps work together to produce extension. The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.
questions.question: What is the action of the long head of triceps at the shoulder?
What is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI)?
questions.explanation: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) is a rare but life-threatening condition characterized by fulminant sepsis that can progress to death within hours. It occurs in 0.1-0.4% of splenectomized patients per year, with mortality rates of 50-70%. It is most commonly caused by encapsulated bacteria, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae. Prevention includes vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis.

Anteriorly, the fibrous layer of the knee joint capsule is replaced by the quadriceps tendon (above the patella), the patella itself, and the patellar ligament (below the patella). These three structures provide strong anterior protection. The patellar retinacula blend with the capsule laterally providing additional support.
options: Patellar ligament, ACL, and synovial membrane
Fibular collateral ligament, patella, and patellar ligament
Patellar retinacula, PCL, and iliotibial tract
Tibial collateral ligament, patella, and patellar tendon
Quadriceps tendon, patella, and patellar ligament
questions.question: The fibrous capsule anteriorly is replaced by which three structures from proximal to distal?

questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle is supplied solely by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), not the pharyngeal plexus. All other pharyngeal muscles receive innervation from the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing. It is the only structure supplied by the motor component of IX.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT supplied by the pharyngeal plexus?
Which ligament connects the epiglottis to the hyoid bone?
questions.explanation: The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the anterior surface of the epiglottis to the upper border of the hyoid bone. The thyroepiglottic ligament attaches the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage. The epiglottis is also connected to the tongue by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds. These ligaments maintain epiglottic position during swallowing.

The pyramidalis muscle, a small triangular muscle anterior to the lower rectus abdominis (base on pubis, apex on linea alba), is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12). This muscle is variably present (absent in about 20% of individuals) and functions to tense the linea alba. The subcostal nerve also contributes to innervation of the abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin. The pyramidalis lies within the rectus sheath and represents a derivative of the rectus abdominis. Its clinical significance is minimal.
questions.question: Which nerve innervates the pyramidalis muscle?
Medial rotation at the hip joint is primarily performed by which three muscles?
questions.explanation: Medial rotation at the hip joint is performed primarily by gluteus medius (anterior fibers), gluteus minimus (anterior fibers), and tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation is performed by obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, and posterior fibers of gluteus medius and maximus.
options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae

questions.question: The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric fossa, located on the medial surface of the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. This differs from other short rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli) which insert into the upper border of the greater trochanter. Knowledge of this distinction is important in hip replacement approaches.

The esophagus has four anatomical constrictions where it is narrowed. The first is at its origin (C6 level, 15 cm from incisors) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. These constrictions are clinically important as sites where foreign bodies lodge and where esophageal pathology commonly occurs.
questions.question: Which constriction is at the esophageal origin?

questions.explanation: The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein within the superficial cervical fascia containing platysma. They receive drainage from the scalp and auricle. Efferents pass to the deep cervical chain.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the superficial cervical fascia?
Where are circular venous plexuses located?
questions.explanation: Circular venous plexuses are found at the base of the nipple. Veins corresponding to the arteries drain the breast, ultimately into the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The superficial veins often become prominent and dilated during pregnancy and lactation.

questions.question: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by which structure?
questions.explanation: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal vessels and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above it in the foramen's upper part but does not traverse it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large opening.

questions.question: Which arteries supply the bronchial tree?
questions.explanation: The bronchial arteries supply the bronchial tree from the main bronchi to the respiratory bronchioles. Two left bronchial arteries arise from the descending thoracic aorta, and one right bronchial artery arises from the third right posterior intercostal artery. These vessels provide oxygenated blood to airway structures.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist position and finger function?
questions.explanation: Wrist position affects finger flexor and extensor muscle lengths through tenodesis effect. Wrist extension tightens finger flexors enhancing grip while passively flexing fingers. Wrist flexion tightens extensors causing passive finger extension. This relationship is exploited in tenodesis grip for spinal cord injury patients.
options: Wrist position affects finger flexor/extensor length affecting grip

questions.question: The testicular artery arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The testicular arteries (and ovarian arteries in females) arise from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level, just inferior to the renal arteries. This high origin reflects the embryological development of the gonads on the posterior abdominal wall before testicular descent or ovarian migration. The long testicular arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major, ureter, and external iliac vessels, enter the deep inguinal ring, and travel through the inguinal canal as part of the spermatic cord to reach the testes in the scrotum.

questions.question: The lesser sac communicates with the greater sac through which opening?
questions.explanation: The lesser sac (omental bursa) communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow, foramen of Winslow), bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament, posteriorly by the IVC and right crus of diaphragm, superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum. This communication allows peritoneal fluid to flow between the two sacs and permits spread of infection or hemorrhage. The foramen typically admits two fingers and can be used surgically to access the lesser sac. Foramina of Morgagni and Bochdalek are diaphragmatic defects, not communications between peritoneal sacs.

questions.question: The nasolacrimal duct opens into which nasal meatus?
questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath the inferior turbinate. The valve of Hasner at the duct's termination prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction causes epiphora (excessive tearing) and may require dacryocystorhinostomy.

The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum and veers to the left at the level of the T5 vertebra. At the root of the neck, it arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle. This anatomical course is crucial for understanding lymphatic drainage patterns in the thorax.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct turn laterally?
Which cells are found in Brunner's glands?
questions.explanation: Brunner's glands (duodenal glands) are located in the submucosa of the duodenum and contain mucous cells that secrete alkaline mucus rich in bicarbonate. This secretion neutralizes gastric acid entering the duodenum, protecting the duodenal mucosa and providing optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme function. Brunner's glands are unique to the duodenum and are most concentrated in the first part.

questions.question: Which vessel supplies the scalp in the occipital region?
questions.explanation: The occipital artery, a branch of the external carotid, supplies the posterior scalp. It ascends on the back of the neck, pierces the trapezius attachment, and runs in the dense connective tissue layer of the scalp. The artery accompanies the greater occipital nerve. Scalp lacerations in this region can cause significant bleeding.

questions.question: The adductor magnus has two distinct parts. The hamstring part, originating from the ischial tuberosity, is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The hamstring part of adductor magnus originates from the ischial tuberosity and is supplied by the tibial nerve, unlike the adductor part which is supplied by the obturator nerve. The hamstring part inserts into the adductor tubercle of the femur and acts to extend the hip. This dual origin and nerve supply make adductor magnus a 'hybrid' muscle.

questions.question: The scala vestibuli communicates with the scala tympani through which structure?
questions.explanation: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex of the cochlea through the helicotrema. Both scalae contain perilymph. Sound vibrations travel up the scala vestibuli, through the helicotrema, and back down the scala tympani. The basilar membrane separates the scala tympani from the scala media (cochlear duct).

Approximately 99% of the pancreatic tissue is exocrine, consisting of acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes. Only about 1% consists of endocrine tissue in the form of pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans). The exocrine pancreas produces 1.5-2 liters of pancreatic juice daily containing enzymes for protein, carbohydrate, and fat digestion.
questions.question: What percentage of the pancreas is exocrine tissue?
Which muscle is NOT part of the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The iliacus muscle is part of the posterior abdominal wall, not the anterior wall, originating from the iliac fossa and inserting with psoas major onto the lesser trochanter of the femur as the iliopsoas tendon. The anterior abdominal wall muscles include three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) and two vertical muscles (rectus abdominis and pyramidalis). The iliacus is innervated by the femoral nerve and functions primarily as a hip flexor, while the anterior abdominal wall muscles are involved in trunk movement and increasing intra-abdominal pressure.

questions.question: Which part of the kidney contains the renal pyramids?
questions.explanation: The renal medulla is the inner part of the kidney containing 10-12 renal pyramids (medullary pyramids). Each pyramid has its base directed toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting medially into a minor calyx. The pyramids contain the loops of Henle and collecting ducts, giving them a striated appearance due to parallel tubules.

questions.question: At what level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate into common iliac arteries?
questions.explanation: The abdominal aorta terminates at the lower border of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4) by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries, slightly to the left of midline. This bifurcation point corresponds roughly to the level of the umbilicus and represents the transition from the abdominal aorta to the pelvic arterial system. The median sacral artery also arises from the posterior aspect of the aorta just before its bifurcation.

questions.question: The inguinal ligament extends between which two points?
questions.explanation: The inguinal ligament represents the rolled-under, thickened inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis, extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) laterally to the pubic tubercle medially. It serves as a retinaculum bridging the subinguinal space through which pass the iliopsoas muscle, femoral vessels and nerve, and lymphatics entering/leaving the thigh. The inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary (floor) of the inguinal canal and the base of Hesselbach's triangle. The lacunar ligament represents its medial extension, reflecting posteriorly to attach to the pectineal line.

questions.question: The middle cerebral artery supplies which cortical area?
questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including motor and sensory cortices for face and upper limb. It also supplies Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant hemisphere. MCA occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia more marked in upper extremity and face.

produces both flexion and supination of the forearm. It is most powerful as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90 degrees. The muscle has two heads proximally but a common tendon distally inserting on the radial tuberosity.
questions.question: Which muscle produces both flexion and supination of the forearm?

questions.explanation: The menisci are crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the tibial articular surface and act as shock absorbers. They are thicker at external margins and taper toward the center. Meniscal tears are among the most common knee injuries in athletes. The lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus.
options: Shock absorbers and joint space deepeners
Attachment points for cruciate ligaments only
Blood vessel channels for synovial membrane
Lubricating pads reducing synovial fluid production
questions.question: The menisci deepen the articular surface and act as which functional structures in the knee joint?

questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, enophthalmos) in Klumpke's paralysis results from injury to sympathetic fibers traveling with the T1 nerve root. These sympathetic fibers supply the head and neck. The association indicates severe lower trunk injury affecting both motor and sympathetic components.
questions.question: What causes Horner's syndrome in Klumpke's paralysis?

questions.explanation: The ethmoidal bulla is a rounded prominence in the lateral wall of the middle meatus formed by the underlying middle ethmoidal air cells. The hiatus semilunaris lies below it. The bulla is a key landmark during endoscopic sinus surgery. Above the bulla lies the suprabullar recess. The uncinate process lies anterior and inferior.
questions.question: The ethmoidal bulla is located in which meatus?

questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck as they pass behind it. The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body. Anteriorly, the neck is related to the pylorus of the stomach.
questions.question: Which vessels form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck?

options: Medial sural cutaneous nerve and sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve; lateral side of leg and ankle
Medial sural cutaneous nerve (from tibial nerve) and lateral sural cutaneous nerve (from common fibular nerve); lateral side of leg, ankle, and foot
Saphenous nerve and medial sural cutaneous nerve; medial leg and foot
Both sural nerves from tibial nerve; posterior leg entirely
Posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh and medial sural cutaneous nerve; posterior thigh and leg
questions.explanation: The sural nerve is formed by the union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa) and the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve. It supplies the skin of the lateral side of the leg, ankle, and lateral heel. The sural nerve is commonly harvested as a nerve graft in peripheral nerve reconstruction surgery.
questions.question: The sural nerve is formed by the union of which two nerves and supplies which area of the lower limb?

questions.explanation: At the renal hilum, the renal vein lies most anteriorly, the renal artery lies in the middle, and the renal pelvis (with the ureter) lies most posteriorly. This arrangement can be remembered as "VAP" (Vein, Artery, Pelvis) from anterior to posterior. The hilum is located on the medial border of each kidney.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the hilum of the kidney most anteriorly?
Which part of the pancreas lies within the concavity of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas lies within the C-shaped curve formed by the duodenum, specifically nestled in the concavity of the second, third, and fourth parts of the duodenum. The head is the broadest part of the pancreas. A portion of the head, the uncinate process, extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels.

questions.question: A patient presents with weakness of knee extension and reduced patellar reflex but intact hip and ankle function. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
questions.explanation: L3 root compression presents with quadriceps weakness (knee extension), reduced patellar reflex (L3 component), and sensory changes on the anteromedial thigh and medial leg. The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) supplies the quadriceps, and the knee jerk is primarily L3 and L4. Pure L3 compression spares the dorsiflexors (L4, L5) and plantarflexors (S1, S2).

The lumbar sympathetic chain enters the abdomen from the thorax by passing beneath the medial arcuate ligament (lumbocostal arch), which extends from the body of L1 vertebra to the tip of the L1 transverse process over the psoas major muscle. The chain then descends along the medial border of psoas major on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, with the right chain posterior to the inferior vena cava and the left along the left margin of the aorta. It typically contains four lumbar ganglia that give off gray rami communicantes to all lumbar nerves and lumbar splanchnic nerves to autonomic plexuses.
questions.question: The lumbar sympathetic chain enters the abdomen through which opening?

questions.explanation: There are three taeniae coli on the large intestine: the free taenia, mesocolic taenia, and omental taenia. These bands converge at the root of the appendix and disappear at the rectosigmoid junction. The taeniae are approximately 1 cm wide and their contraction creates the characteristic sacculated appearance of the colon.
questions.question: How many taeniae coli are present on the colon?
What impression is on the left lung medially?
questions.explanation: The left lung has several impressions on its mediastinal surface including: cardiac impression (the largest), aortic arch groove, descending aorta groove, subclavian artery groove, esophageal and tracheal grooves, and brachiocephalic vein groove. The aortic impressions are particularly prominent.

questions.question: What percentage of the vocal cord structure consists of the arytenoid cartilage?
questions.explanation: The arytenoid cartilage comprises 40% of the vocal cord, while the remaining 60% is membranous (cricovocal ligament covered by mucosa). This anatomical proportion is important for understanding vocal cord pathology and surgical planning. The cartilaginous portion provides the posterior attachment point for the vocal ligament.

questions.question: The lesser splanchnic nerve typically synapses in which ganglion?
questions.explanation: The lesser splanchnic nerve, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers from T10-T11 spinal segments, typically synapses in the superior mesenteric ganglion (or aorticorenal ganglion), though it may also send fibers to the celiac ganglion. Postganglionic fibers distribute along superior mesenteric artery branches to supply midgut derivatives. This nerve pierces the diaphragm (separately or with the sympathetic trunk) to reach the abdomen. The sympathetic supply causes decreased intestinal motility and secretions, vasoconstriction, and contraction of sphincters, opposing the effects of parasympathetic innervation (vagus nerve for midgut).

The oval window (fenestra vestibuli) in the medial wall of the middle ear is closed by the footplate of the stapes, held in place by the annular ligament. The stapes transmits vibrations from the ossicular chain to the perilymph of the inner ear. Otosclerosis causes abnormal bone growth fixing the stapes, resulting in conductive hearing loss.
questions.question: The oval window is closed by which structure?

questions.explanation: The Achilles (calcaneal) tendon inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus via the calcaneal tuberosity. The gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles all contribute to the calcaneal tendon. The calcaneal tendon is the strongest tendon in the body but is frequently ruptured in sudden powerful plantarflexion, such as in a jump landing. Bursae lie posterior and anterior to the tendon.
questions.question: The calcaneus is the largest and strongest bone of the foot and its primary function is to absorb shock and leverage movement. Where is the Achilles tendon inserted on the calcaneus?
Which structure passes posterior to the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava, covered by parietal peritoneum, forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), along with the right crus of the diaphragm. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant because the IVC can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver when the hepatoduodenal ligament (anterior boundary containing the portal triad) is manually compressed or clamped to control hepatic bleeding. The proximity of the IVC also means that the foramen provides a potential route for hemorrhage into the lesser sac following IVC injury.

questions.question: The infraorbital nerve is a continuation of which cranial nerve division?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve is the terminal branch of the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve. It traverses the infraorbital canal and emerges through the infraorbital foramen. The nerve provides sensation to the lower eyelid, side of nose, and upper lip.

Pleurisy (or pleuritis) is inflammation of the pleura lining the lungs. It usually occurs in conjunction with pneumonia and other lung infections. Characteristic symptoms include sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing. The inflamed pleural surfaces may produce a friction rub audible on auscultation.
questions.question: Which condition causes pleural inflammation?

questions.explanation: The psoas major muscle is innervated by the ventral rami of lumbar nerves L1 through L4, which emerge from the lumbar plexus formed within the substance of the muscle itself. This segmental innervation pattern corresponds to the muscle's extensive vertebral origins from the bodies, transverse processes, and intervertebral discs of T12 through L5. The muscle serves as the chief flexor of the thigh at the hip joint and also assists in lateral flexion of the lumbar vertebral column when acting unilaterally.
questions.question: The psoas major muscle receives innervation from which nerve roots?
Which sinus drains into the superior meatus?
questions.explanation: The posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into the superior meatus. The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses. The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct. The sphenoethmoidal recess receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the thoracic cage?
questions.explanation: The thoracic cage primarily functions to protect the lungs, heart, and great vessels from external trauma. Additionally, it provides attachment points for muscles of the thorax, upper limb, abdomen, and back. The cage also plays a vital role in the mechanics of respiration through its elastic properties.

questions.question: The jugulo-omohyoid node drains which structure primarily?
questions.explanation: The jugulo-omohyoid lymph node (principal node of the tongue) is located where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. It receives drainage from the tip and anterior tongue (along with submental nodes). The node is part of the inferior deep cervical chain. Enlargement suggests anterior oral cavity or tongue pathology.

The visceral pleura receives its arterial supply from branches of both the bronchial and pulmonary arterial systems. Venous drainage is to the pulmonary veins. Unlike the parietal pleura, the visceral pleura has no somatic sensory innervation and receives only autonomic vasomotor nerve supply.
questions.question: Which vessels supply blood to the visceral pleura?

questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle, part of the levator ani complex, forms a U-shaped sling that loops around the anorectal junction, creating the anorectal angle of approximately 90 degrees by pulling the rectum anteriorly toward the pubic symphysis. This angle is a critical component of the fecal continence mechanism, as relaxation of puborectalis during defecation straightens the anorectal angle to facilitate evacuation. Damage to the puborectalis (such as during childbirth or surgery) or its nerve supply (pudendal nerve and direct branches from S3-S4) can lead to fecal incontinence. The muscle is in tonic contraction at rest.
questions.question: Which muscle's contraction causes the anorectal angle?

questions.explanation: The cardinal ligament (Mackenrodt's ligament, transverse cervical ligament), extending from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the lateral pelvic wall, contains the uterine artery and vein along with autonomic nerve fibers and lymphatics. This ligament provides the most important support for the uterus, preventing uterine prolapse. The uterine artery crosses over the ureter ("water under the bridge") in the base of the broad ligament before reaching the uterus. During hysterectomy, the cardinal ligaments must be clamped and divided, requiring careful identification of the ureters to prevent injury.
questions.question: The cardinal ligament of the uterus contains which vessels?

questions.explanation: McBurney's point marks the base of the appendix and is located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. This is the point of maximum tenderness in acute appendicitis and guides the surgical incision. The tip of the appendix, however, can vary considerably in position.
questions.question: Which structure marks the base of the appendix on the surface?

questions.explanation: The thin orbital plate of the maxilla forms the roof of the maxillary sinus and the floor of the orbit. The infraorbital nerve and vessels run in a groove on this surface. Fractures can cause orbital contents to herniate into the sinus (blow-out fracture). Dental roots may project into the sinus floor.
questions.question: Which structure separates the maxillary sinus from the orbit?
What is the function of palmar interossei?
questions.explanation: Palmar interossei (PAD - Palmar ADduct) produce finger adduction, moving fingers toward the middle finger axis. There are three palmar interossei muscles compared to four dorsal interossei. All interossei also flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.

Complete section of a phrenic nerve results in complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the corresponding half of the diaphragm. The paralyzed hemidiaphragm shows paradoxical movement: moving upward during inspiration and downward during expiration. Unilateral paralysis is often asymptomatic; bilateral causes severe respiratory compromise.
questions.question: What happens with complete phrenic nerve section?
In the popliteal fossa, the popliteal artery lies deepest and the tibial nerve most superficially. In what order, from lateral to medial, are the structures arranged superiorly within the fossa?
options: Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
Tibial nerve, common fibular nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Common fibular nerve, popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal vein, popliteal artery, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
questions.explanation: At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve divides into the common fibular nerve (laterally, following the medial border of biceps femoris) and the tibial nerve (medially). From lateral to medial: common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, then popliteal artery (deepest). This arrangement changes inferiorly as the popliteal vein crosses to lie posterior to the artery.

The rotator cuff receives blood supply from three main sources: anterior circumflex humeral artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery, and suprascapular artery. A critical zone exists in the supraspinatus tendon with relatively poor vascularity, predisposing this area to degeneration and tears.
questions.question: What provides the primary blood supply to the rotator cuff?
options: Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral plus suprascapular

questions.question: Which muscle is the most powerful flexor of the elbow?
questions.explanation: is the most powerful and primary flexor of the elbow joint in all forearm positions. It has a larger cross-sectional area than biceps and inserts directly on the ulna. The muscle lies deep to biceps brachii in the anterior arm compartment.

questions.question: Which vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove?
questions.explanation: The great cardiac vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove alongside the anterior interventricular artery, then curves left in the coronary groove to become the coronary sinus. It drains the areas supplied by the left coronary artery (anterior left ventricle, anterior interventricular septum, and parts of right ventricle). It is the largest tributary of the coronary sinus.

options: Flexors of the knee and extensors of the hip
Extensors of the hip and adductors
Abductors of the hip and flexors of the knee
Flexors of the hip and extensors of the knee
Lateral rotators of the hip and extensors of the knee
questions.question: The anterior compartment of the thigh contains muscles functioning primarily as which two groups?
questions.explanation: The anterior compartment of the thigh contains muscles functioning as flexors of the hip and extensors of the knee. These muscles tend to atrophy rapidly with disease and often require physical therapy to restore strength, tone, and symmetry after immobilization. The anterior compartment is the largest of the three thigh compartments.

The vertebral arteries give off anterior spinal arteries before joining to form the basilar artery. The two anterior spinal arteries unite to form a single vessel descending in the anterior median fissure. The vertebral arteries also give off posterior spinal arteries. These vessels supply the cervical spinal cord before receiving reinforcement from segmental arteries.
questions.question: The vertebral artery gives off which spinal branch?

questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) passes superiorly into the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon, dividing into right and left branches. The middle colic veins (draining to the superior mesenteric vein) also pass through the mesocolon. The root of the transverse mesocolon is attached to the inferior border of the pancreas and anterior surface of the second part of the duodenum, crossing from right to left. The superior mesenteric vessels themselves lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, not within it.
questions.question: Which vessel passes through the transverse mesocolon?

questions.explanation: The middle colic artery arises from the right side of the superior mesenteric artery as it emerges from beneath the pancreas, ascending into the transverse mesocolon. It divides into right and left branches that supply the transverse colon; the right branch anastomoses with the right colic artery (from SMA), while the left branch anastomoses with the left colic artery (from IMA) forming the marginal artery of Drummond. This anastomotic connection between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories creates an important collateral pathway in cases of vascular compromise.
questions.question: The middle colic artery is a branch of which vessel?
Which structure lies in the stomach bed posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The body of the pancreas is one of the major structures forming the posterior relations or stomach bed. The stomach bed is separated from the stomach by the lesser sac (omental bursa). Other structures in the stomach bed include the left kidney, left suprarenal gland, splenic artery, transverse mesocolon, and diaphragm.

questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the transpyloric plane?
questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane, passing midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis (or midway between xiphoid and umbilicus), corresponds to the level of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and the lower border of vertebra T12. This important surgical landmark crosses numerous structures: pylorus of stomach (when supine), neck of pancreas, origin of the SMA and portal vein, duodenojejunal flexure, hila of both kidneys, fundus of gallbladder, root of transverse mesocolon, origin of IMA (at L3), and tips of ninth costal cartilages. The plane is used to define upper and lower abdominal regions in the nine-region scheme.

Olfactory nerve axons from the nasal epithelium pass through multiple foramina in the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. These first-order sensory neurons synapse in the olfactory bulb above the cribriform plate. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.
questions.question: The olfactory nerves pass through which structure?

questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic (gastrolienal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach. It is part of the greater omentum and contains the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels. This ligament provides vascular connections between the spleen and stomach.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the spleen to the greater curvature?

options: Collateral circulation bypassing proximal subclavian obstruction
questions.explanation: Scapular anastomoses provide crucial collateral circulation connecting first part of subclavian artery with third part of axillary artery. This enables continued limb perfusion even with proximal arterial obstruction. The anastomoses involve suprascapular, dorsal scapular, and circumflex scapular arteries.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the scapular anastomoses?
Which cartilage forms the Adam's apple (laryngeal prominence)?
questions.explanation: The thyroid cartilage is shield-shaped with two laminae meeting in the midline to form the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). This prominence is more acute and prominent in males. The thyroid cartilage protects the vocal cords and provides anterior attachment for the vocal ligaments.

questions.question: Which nerve passes through the mandibular notch?
questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve (from anterior division of V3) passes through the mandibular notch with the masseteric artery to supply the masseter muscle. It also provides articular branches to the temporomandibular joint. The nerve crosses lateral to the temporomandibular joint and deep to the tendon of temporalis muscle.

Cockett's perforators are the clinically most important perforating veins in the lower leg, connecting the posterior arch vein (a tributary of the great saphenous vein) to the posterior tibial veins. Their incompetence leads to venous hypertension in the gaiter area of the leg (lower medial aspect), causing lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulcers. Perforator incompetence is addressed surgically or with thermal ablation.
questions.question: Varicose veins of the great saphenous system result from incompetence of the saphenofemoral junction and perforating veins. The longest perforating vein, connecting the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins, is named what?

questions.explanation: is absent in approximately 15% of people without any functional deficit. When present, it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. The tendon is commonly harvested for use in tendon grafts and reconstructive procedures.
questions.question: Which muscle can be absent without functional deficit?

questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament (zonules of Zinn) connects the lens equator to the ciliary processes. These zonular fibers transmit tension from the ciliary muscle to the lens capsule, controlling lens shape for accommodation. When ciliary muscle contracts, zonular tension decreases, allowing the elastic lens to become more spherical for near vision.
questions.question: Which ligament suspends the lens of the eye?

questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (typically two or three major veins: right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. These veins are intersegmental in distribution, draining adjacent hepatic segments. The attachment of these large veins to the IVC helps anchor the liver in position within the abdominal cavity.
questions.question: Into which vessel do the hepatic veins drain?

questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch is the peritoneal reflection between the bladder and rectum in males. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males when upright and can contain loops of small intestine (ileum). Fluid collections or abscesses may accumulate here. In females, the analogous space is the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), which is deeper.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the rectovesical pouch in males?

questions.explanation: The right suprarenal gland is related anteriorly to the bare area of the liver and the inferior vena cava, posteriorly to the diaphragm, medially to the right celiac ganglion and IVC, and inferiorly to the upper pole of the right kidney. The left suprarenal gland has different anterior relations (stomach, pancreas, splenic artery, and lesser sac). Both glands are retroperitoneal and highly vascular, receiving arterial supply from three sources (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery) but having asymmetric venous drainage (right to IVC, left to left renal vein).
questions.question: The right suprarenal gland is related anteriorly to which structure?

questions.explanation: The suprasternal space (of Burns) lies between the investing and pretracheal layers of deep cervical fascia above the manubrium. It contains the jugular venous arch, lymph nodes, and fat. The space extends laterally behind the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Infections can collect here forming a suprasternal abscess.
questions.question: Which space lies between the pretracheal and investing layers of deep cervical fascia?
Which artery supplies the ileum?
questions.explanation: The ileum receives its blood supply from multiple ileal arteries (12-15 branches) arising from the left side of the superior mesenteric artery. These arteries run between the layers of the mesentery, forming 4-5 arcades (more numerous than in the jejunum) before giving rise to short, widely spaced vasa recta that supply the intestinal wall. The terminal ileum also receives branches from the ileocolic artery (ileal branch).
