The extensive arterial arcades create broad, low windows in the mesentery (versus the narrow, tall windows in the jejunal mesentery).

questions.question: How long is the ureter in adults?
questions.explanation: Each ureter is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. The ureter descends on the psoas major muscle, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enters the bladder at the lateral angles of the trigone. It is a muscular tube that propels urine by peristaltic contractions.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the upper third of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the upper two-thirds of the anal canal above the pectinate line. The middle rectal arteries (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal arteries (from internal pudendal) supply the lower third. This mixed blood supply creates a watershed area prone to ischemia.

questions.question: What causes scapular winging?
questions.explanation: Scapular winging results from serratus anterior paralysis due to long thoracic nerve injury. The medial border of the scapula protrudes from the back, particularly evident during pushing movements. The serratus anterior is the most powerful protractor of the scapula and its loss dramatically affects scapular stability.

questions.question: The broad ligament contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, containing multiple structures: the uterine tube in its superior free edge (mesosalpinx), the round ligament of uterus in its anteroinferior portion, the ovarian ligament posteriorly, and the ovarian vessels in its lateral extension (suspensory ligament of ovary/infundibulopelvic ligament). The broad ligament is divided into mesosalpinx (above ovary), mesovarium (posterior, supporting ovary), and mesometrium (below ovary, containing uterine vessels). It does not provide significant uterine support despite its name.

questions.question: The pampiniform plexus drains into which vein?
questions.explanation: The pampiniform plexus, a network of 8-12 veins in the spermatic cord surrounding the testicular artery, drains into a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring. The right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle, while the left testicular vein typically drains into the left renal vein at a right angle. This venous plexus serves as a countercurrent heat exchanger, cooling arterial blood before it reaches the testes. The higher incidence of left-sided varicoceles reflects the longer course and perpendicular drainage of the left testicular vein.

questions.question: The iliotibial band syndrome (runner's knee) involves friction of the iliotibial tract over which bony landmark during running?
questions.explanation: Iliotibial band syndrome involves repetitive friction of the iliotibial tract over the lateral femoral epicondyle during the flexion-extension cycle of running. This creates pain and inflammation at the lateral aspect of the knee. It is particularly common in long-distance runners. Treatment includes stretching, foam rolling, and correcting biomechanical factors such as hip abductor weakness.

The tail of the pancreas extends to the left and lies at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra (T12). The tail reaches the splenic hilum and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas, lying within the splenorenal ligament. Anteriorly, the tail is related to the splenic flexure of the colon.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the tail of the pancreas lie?
Which artery supplies the body of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The body and tail of the pancreas receive arterial supply from the splenic artery through numerous small pancreatic branches (dorsal pancreatic, greater pancreatic, caudal pancreatic arteries) as the splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreas. The head of the pancreas is supplied by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries forming anterior and posterior arcades. The pancreas has a rich blood supply with extensive anastomoses, though the pancreatic neck region may be relatively less vascular. The intimate relationship between the splenic artery and pancreas means that pancreatic pathology can affect the artery.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the large intestine?
questions.explanation: The primary function of the large intestine is absorption of water and electrolytes from the remaining indigestible food matter, converting liquid chyme into semi-solid feces. Approximately 1-2 liters of water are absorbed daily. The colon also absorbs short-chain fatty acids produced by bacterial fermentation and synthesizes vitamin K through bacterial action.

questions.question: Morton's neuroma is a painful condition of the foot involving perineural fibrosis of a digital plantar nerve. In which intermetatarsal space does it most commonly occur?
questions.explanation: Morton's neuroma most commonly occurs in the third intermetatarsal space (between the 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads), where the medial and lateral plantar nerves communicate, creating a larger nerve prone to compression. It presents with burning pain and paraesthesia in the 3rd and 4th toes, aggravated by tight footwear and weight-bearing. Mulder's click is a clinical sign on examination.

The superior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the first thoracic vertebra (T1). Anteriorly, it is bounded by the superior border of the manubrium sterni. Laterally, the medial borders of the first ribs and their costal cartilages complete the boundaries of this important opening.
questions.question: Which structure bounds the superior thoracic aperture posteriorly?

questions.explanation: The Straight Leg Raise (SLR) test assesses lumbar nerve root compression (L4-S2) and sciatic nerve irritation. A positive test reproduces sciatica (not just hamstring tightness) when the hip is passively flexed between 30-70 degrees with the knee extended. The nerve root is maximally tensioned in this range. It is used to diagnose lumbar disc herniation causing nerve root compression.
questions.question: The Straight Leg Raise (SLR) test is used to assess which structure, with a positive result occurring when sciatica is reproduced at 30-70 degrees of hip flexion?
options: Hip flexor tightness from psoas overuse
Femoral nerve root tension sign at the hip
Hamstring muscle tightness causing posterior thigh pain alone
Lumbar nerve root compression (L4�S2) with sciatic nerve irritation

questions.question: The first metatarsal is described as the shortest and thickest metatarsal and bears the most weight. Which two bones are found at its head?
questions.explanation: The head of the first metatarsal contains two sesamoid bones, which increase the mechanical advantage of the flexor hallucis brevis and protect its tendons from compression. The first metatarsal is the most important in propulsion during walking and is also the most important attachment site for several tendons, making it clinically significant in hallux valgus and gout.

The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus, extending from the uterine pole of the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus just below the uterine tube attachment. It represents the proximal remnant of the gubernaculum (the distal remnant becoming the round ligament of the uterus). The ligament lies within the broad ligament (between its layers) and contains no significant vessels. The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) connects the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian vessels; it is not directly attached to the uterus.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the ovary to the uterus?
Which vessel supplies the cecum?
questions.explanation: The cecum receives its blood supply from the ileocolic artery (terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery), which divides into superior and inferior branches. The inferior branch gives rise to anterior and posterior cecal arteries that supply the corresponding surfaces of the cecum. The ileocolic artery also gives off the appendicular artery (to appendix) and ileal branches. The superior branch of the ileocolic artery anastomoses with the right colic artery along the ascending colon. The cecum's venous drainage follows the arterial pattern, with ileocolic vein draining to the superior mesenteric vein.

Lumbricals originate from flexor digitorum profundus tendons (unique among hand muscles). This means lumbrical contraction (causing MCP flexion and IP extension) also reduces profundus tension. This coupling enables the delicate coordination needed for precision movements like writing.
options: This attachment has no special anatomical significance
FDP origin couples DIP flexion with IP extension
questions.question: What is the functional significance of lumbrical muscle origin?

questions.explanation: The right renal artery passes posterior to both the right renal vein and the inferior vena cava as it courses from the aorta (at L1-L2 level, just below the superior mesenteric artery) to the right kidney hilum. The right renal artery is longer than the left due to the aorta's left-sided position. Both renal arteries also pass posterior to the corresponding psoas major muscle and ureter. The arteries typically divide into anterior and posterior divisions before entering the hilum, supplying corresponding segments of the kidney. The right artery may give off the inferior suprarenal artery.
questions.question: The right renal artery passes posterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: The "safe triangle" for chest drain insertion is bounded by: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, a line superior to the horizontal level of the nipple (in males), and an apex below the axilla. This typically corresponds to the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line. This location minimizes risk to neurovascular structures and breast tissue.
questions.question: What is the safest chest drain insertion site?

questions.explanation: The tip of the tongue drains to submental lymph nodes. The lateral anterior two-thirds drains to submandibular nodes, while the medial anterior two-thirds drains to inferior deep cervical nodes. The posterior third drains to superior deep cervical nodes. Understanding lymphatic drainage is crucial for cancer staging.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the tip of the tongue?
The buccopharyngeal fascia covers which structure?
questions.explanation: The buccopharyngeal fascia is a thin layer covering the buccinator muscle and pharyngeal constrictor muscles externally. It is continuous anteriorly over the buccinator and posteriorly over the constrictors. The retropharyngeal space lies between this fascia and the prevertebral fascia. The fascia blends with the pterygomandibular raphe.

The cupola (or apex) is the rounded superior portion of the lung that extends into the root of the neck, reaching 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle. It is covered by cervical pleura and the suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia). The subclavian artery arches over the lung apex.
questions.question: What is the lung at the apex called?
The ophthalmic artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the internal carotid artery after it exits the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the optic canal with the optic nerve. Branches include the central retinal artery, which is an end artery supplying the retina.

Anterior interosseous syndrome involves compression of the anterior interosseous nerve, a pure motor branch of the median nerve. This causes weakness of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus to index finger, and pronator quadratus. There is no sensory loss as this is a pure motor nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve is compressed in anterior interosseous syndrome?
Which structure represents the continuation of cisterna chyli?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at the level of L1 as a continuation of the cisterna chyli, which is formed by the union of left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. The duct eventually terminates by draining into the left venous angle after receiving additional lymphatic tributaries.

options: Posterior leg compartment; loss of plantarflexion strength
Medial compartment of thigh; loss of adduction
Anterior compartment only; loss of dorsiflexion only
Posterior compartment of leg; calcaneal gait
Anterior and lateral compartments; foot drop and loss of eversion
questions.explanation: Compression of the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula paralyzes the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg, causing foot drop (inability to dorsiflex) and loss of eversion of the foot. Sensory loss occurs on the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg. The patient walks with a high-stepping gait to compensate for the foot drop.
questions.question: Compression of the common fibular nerve around the neck of the fibula results in paralysis of which compartments and what clinical presentation?

questions.explanation: The biceps reflex tests C5 nerve root integrity (with C6 contribution). The reflex is elicited by tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa while the elbow is partially flexed. Absence or diminution suggests C5 nerve root pathology or musculocutaneous nerve injury.
questions.question: Which reflex tests C5 nerve root integrity?

questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies only the gluteus maximus. It exits the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. Injury results in loss of powerful hip extension, making it impossible to rise from sitting, climb stairs, or run effectively. Since gluteus maximus has little role in gentle walking, the patient may ambulate with minimal apparent deficit on flat ground.
questions.question: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies which single muscle?
Which branch of the external carotid artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the skull through the foramen spinosum. It supplies the dura mater and inner table of the skull. Rupture of this artery causes epidural hematoma, typically from temporal bone fractures.

Piriformis syndrome occurs when the sciatic nerve is compressed by a hypertrophied or spasmodic piriformis muscle. The sciatic nerve normally passes below piriformis; in approximately 10-15% of individuals, part or all of the nerve passes through the muscle, increasing vulnerability. It presents with buttock pain radiating down the posterior thigh (mimicking lumbar disc herniation) and is exacerbated by sitting.
questions.question: Piriformis syndrome causes buttock and posterior thigh pain by compressing which nerve as it passes through or near the piriformis muscle?
The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied primarily by perforating branches of which artery?
questions.explanation: The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied by perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery, consisting of three or four arteries perforating adductor magnus. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to all three thigh compartments. The inferior gluteal artery provides additional supply to the proximal hamstrings via descending branches.

On the left side, the pleural reflection passes inferomedially to the level of the fourth costal cartilage, where it deviates to the left margin of the sternum. This creates a shallow notch corresponding to the cardiac notch of the left lung. This differs from the right side where the pleura descends vertically in the median plane.
questions.question: At which costal cartilage does left pleural reflection deviate?
How many muscles constitute the gluteal region, including the six lateral rotators?
questions.explanation: The gluteal region contains nine muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae, piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, and quadratus femoris. These perform extension, abduction, lateral rotation, and stabilization of the hip joint.

questions.question: Extensor hallucis longus, innervated by the deep fibular nerve, originates from which structure?
options: Superior half of lateral surface of tibia
Middle anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
Inferior third of anterior fibula only
questions.explanation: Extensor hallucis longus originates from the middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula and the adjacent interosseous membrane. It inserts into the dorsal aspect of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe and is innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). It extends the great toe, dorsiflexes the ankle, and can assist with foot inversion.

options: Children aged 4�10; hip pain or referred knee pain
Elderly adults; hip pain and leg shortening
Neonates; total absence of hip movement
Adolescents; lower back pain radiating to thigh
questions.question: Perthes disease (Legg-Calve-Perthes disease) is avascular necrosis of the femoral head in which age group, and the child typically presents with pain at which site?
questions.explanation: Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in young children typically aged 4-10 years. Due to the obturator nerve supplying both the hip and knee (Hilton's law), children classically present with knee pain rather than hip pain, leading to delayed diagnosis. Boys are affected four times more than girls. Treatment aims to maintain femoral head congruency within the acetabulum.

questions.question: What nerve supplies the first and second lumbricals?
questions.explanation: The lateral two lumbricals (to index and middle fingers) are supplied by the median nerve. The medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers) are supplied by the ulnar nerve. This dual innervation pattern is unique among hand muscles.

questions.question: The posterior cruciate ligament prevents anterior displacement of the femur on the tibia. Clinically, PCL injury causes a positive posterior drawer test. In what clinical position is this test performed?
options: Hip 90�, knee 90�, posterior force applied to the proximal tibia
Hip at 45 degrees flexion, knee in extension
Hip flexed, knee extended, valgus stress applied
Patient prone on table with knee extended passively
Patient standing while performing a single-leg squat
questions.explanation: The posterior drawer test for PCL integrity is performed with the patient supine, the hip at 90 degrees and the knee at 90 degrees. A posterior force is applied to the proximal tibia. Excessive posterior translation indicates PCL rupture. The starting position is important: if the tibia is already posteriorly sagged (posterior sag sign), an apparent positive anterior drawer sign may mimic ACL injury.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus commence?
questions.explanation: The oesophagus begins at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the level of the sixth cervical vertebra (C6). This anatomical landmark marks the transition point from the pharynx to the oesophagus. The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the respiratory tract.

Chordae tendineae (heart strings) are thin, strong tendinous cords that connect the papillary muscles to the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps. They prevent the valve cusps from prolapsing into the atrium during ventricular contraction. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes acute valvular regurgitation, often requiring surgical repair.
questions.question: What connects the papillary muscles to the valve cusps?
Which muscle elevates the mandible during mastication?
questions.explanation: The masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid muscles elevate the mandible during mastication. The masseter originates from the zygomatic arch and inserts on the lateral surface of the mandibular angle and ramus. It is innervated by the masseteric nerve from V3. Bilateral contraction closes the mouth and clenches the teeth.

The sella turcica (Turkish saddle) is a depression in the body of the sphenoid bone housing the pituitary gland. It is bounded anteriorly by the tuberculum sellae and posteriorly by the dorsum sellae. The cavernous sinuses lie laterally. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses this region through the sphenoid sinus.
questions.question: Which bone contains the sella turcica?

questions.explanation: During inspiration, expansion of the thoracic cavity (through rib elevation and diaphragm descent) increases intrathoracic volume and creates negative pressure within the chest. This negative pressure draws air into the lungs. The pleural cavity pressure becomes more negative, preventing lung collapse.
questions.question: What creates negative intrathoracic pressure?

questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus muscle, the lower part of the inferior constrictor, acts as the upper esophageal sphincter. It remains tonically contracted except during swallowing. Between cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus lies the dehiscence of Killian where pharyngeal diverticula (Zenker's) occur.
questions.question: The cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter for which structure?
Which structure is at risk in hook of hamate fracture?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is at risk in hook of hamate fracture as it passes through Guyon's canal adjacent to this structure. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve curves around the hook of the hamate. Fracture can cause motor weakness of intrinsic hand muscles with or without sensory symptoms.

questions.question: Which sinus receives blood from the superior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus drains posteriorly into the confluence of sinuses (torcular herophili) at the internal occipital protuberance. From here, blood typically flows into the right transverse sinus more than the left. The confluence also receives the straight sinus and occipital sinus.

questions.question: The reflected attachment of the semimembranosus tendon forms which structure posteriorly in the knee?
questions.explanation: The reflected attachment of semimembranosus forms the oblique popliteal ligament, which strengthens the fibrous capsule of the knee posteriorly. Semimembranosus inserts primarily into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. The arcuate popliteal ligament is a separate structure arising from the posterior fibular head.

questions.question: Which muscles work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction?
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction (ulnar deviation). By contracting simultaneously, they balance flexion and extension forces while producing adduction. This demonstrates how muscles from different compartments can cooperate for specific movements.

questions.question: The pectinate line in the anal canal marks the junction between which embryological structures?
questions.explanation: The pectinate line represents the mucocutaneous junction where endoderm-derived hindgut epithelium meets ectoderm-derived proctodeal epithelium at the level of the anal valves. Above this line, the anal canal has columnar epithelium, venous drainage to portal circulation, lymphatic drainage to internal iliac nodes, and autonomic innervation. Below the line, it has stratified squamous epithelium, systemic venous drainage, lymphatic drainage to superficial inguinal nodes, and somatic (pudendal) innervation.

The sinoatrial (SA) nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people and from the left circumflex artery in 40%. The SA node is located in the superior part of the crista terminalis near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It is the primary pacemaker of the heart, initiating approximately 60-100 beats per minute.
questions.question: Which artery typically supplies the SA node?

questions.explanation: The platysma is a muscle of facial expression innervated by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. It lies in the superficial cervical fascia and extends from the chest to the mandible. The muscle tenses the skin of the neck and can depress the mandible and lower lip. Facial nerve paralysis causes platysmal weakness.
questions.question: The platysma muscle is innervated by which nerve?
Where does the axillary tail extend?
questions.explanation: The axillary tail (of Spence) is a process that extends from the upper lateral part of the breast into the axilla. It passes through an opening in the deep fascia and may reach as far as the third rib. Cancer in the axillary tail presents as an axillary mass.

questions.question: What structure forms the lingula?
questions.explanation: The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe located below the cardiac notch. It is analogous to the middle lobe of the right lung. The lingula consists of superior and inferior lingular segments, which are distinct bronchopulmonary segments.

The portal vein, positioned posteriorly within the hepatoduodenal ligament (posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery), forms part of the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The entire hepatoduodenal ligament (containing the portal triad) constitutes the anterior boundary. The portal vein is the most posterior structure within this ligament, closest to the foramen. Injury to the portal vein during surgical manipulation near the epiploic foramen can cause massive hemorrhage into the lesser sac. The foramen can be occluded by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament between thumb and fingers (Pringle maneuver).
questions.question: Which vein forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) is important as a source vessel for which reconstructive flap frequently used in plastic surgery?
questions.explanation: The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) and its descending branch provide the vascular pedicle for the anterolateral thigh (ALT) free flap, one of the most commonly used free flaps in reconstructive surgery. The ALT flap is based on septocutaneous or musculocutaneous perforators from the descending branch of the LFCA, running in the intermuscular septum between vastus lateralis and rectus femoris.

The loose connective tissue layer contains emissary veins that connect the superficial scalp veins with intracranial venous sinuses. This layer is often called the danger area because infections can spread intracranially. The loose texture allows fluid and blood to spread widely in scalp injuries.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the loose connective tissue layer of the scalp?

questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is part of the ethmoid bone and forms the roof of the nasal cavity. It contains multiple foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium to the olfactory bulb. The crista galli projects upward from the cribriform plate for attachment of the falx cerebri.
questions.question: Which bone contains the cribriform plate?
What epithelium lines the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium that can stretch and accommodate changes in bladder volume without tearing. When the bladder is empty, the epithelium appears thick with 5-6 cell layers; when distended, it thins to 2-3 layers. This epithelium is impermeable to salts and water.

The sphenopalatine artery (from maxillary artery) provides the dominant blood supply to the nasal septum via posterior septal branches. The anterior ethmoidal artery and superior labial artery contribute anteriorly. Kiesselbach's plexus in the anteroinferior septum is the most common site of epistaxis.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the majority of the nasal septum?

questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus has little action during ordinary gentle walking on level ground. It acts mainly in rising from sitting, straightening up, walking upstairs, and running. This is a critical clinical distinction in assessing gluteal function and designing rehabilitation after injury.
questions.question: Despite being the great extensor of the hip joint, gluteus maximus has little action during which of the following?
Compartment syndrome of the thigh is less common than leg compartment syndrome. Which compartment of the thigh is most commonly affected following a femoral fracture?
questions.explanation: Thigh compartment syndrome most commonly affects the anterior compartment, usually following femoral shaft fractures with significant hematoma formation, crush injuries, or arterial injuries. The anterior compartment contains the quadriceps muscles and femoral neurovascular bundle. Rising compartment pressure impairs perfusion, causing ischemia. Fasciotomy must include all three thigh compartments to ensure complete decompression.
options: Only the fascial sheath around the femoral vessels

questions.question: Which bone contains the foramen rotundum?
questions.explanation: The foramen rotundum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, transmitting the maxillary nerve (V2). It connects the middle cranial fossa with the pterygopalatine fossa. The foramen is round in shape, distinguishing it from the oval foramen ovale.

questions.question: The inferior vena cava receives which vein at the L1 level?
questions.explanation: The right renal vein (shorter than the left, approximately 2-4 cm) drains into the inferior vena cava at approximately the L1-L2 level, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta. The left renal vein (longer, 7-10 cm) crosses anterior to the aorta at the same level to reach the IVC. The right renal vein receives only the right gonadal and right suprarenal veins (sometimes), while the left renal vein receives the left gonadal, left suprarenal, and left inferior phrenic veins before reaching the IVC.

Above the pectinate (dentate) line, the anal canal is lined by simple columnar epithelium (rectal-type mucosa) forming the columns of Morgagni. Below the pectinate line, it transitions to stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium (in the intermediate zone) and then stratified squamous keratinized epithelium (in the cutaneous zone). The pectinate line marks the junction of endoderm and ectoderm.
questions.question: Which epithelium lines the anal canal above the pectinate line?
The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies which teeth?
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of maxillary nerve) supplies the upper molar teeth except the mesiobuccal root of the first molar (supplied by middle superior alveolar). The nerve descends on the maxillary tuberosity and enters the posterior superior alveolar foramina. It also supplies the maxillary sinus mucosa and buccal gingiva.

The ileocecal valve prevents reflux of colonic contents (which contain bacteria) back into the sterile small intestine. It also slows the passage of ileal contents into the cecum, allowing more time for nutrient and water absorption. The valve consists of superior and inferior lips formed by mucosal folds supported by circular muscle thickening.
questions.question: What is the function of the ileocecal valve?

questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus (at T10 level, formed by muscle fibers from the right crus of the diaphragm that loop around the esophagus) transmits the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks (formed from the vagus nerves). The vagal trunks provide parasympathetic innervation to the abdominal viscera up to the splenic flexure. The left gastric artery and vein may also pass through or near this opening. The aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein pass through the aortic hiatus at T12, while the IVC passes through the caval opening at T8.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the esophageal hiatus?

questions.explanation: Fibularis tertius inserts into the dorsum of the base of the 5th metatarsal. It originates from the inferior third of the anterior surface of the fibula. Although in the anterior compartment, its eversion action makes it functionally similar to the lateral compartment muscles. It is sometimes absent as a normal variant. It is innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
questions.question: Fibularis tertius dorsiflexes the ankle and aids eversion. It inserts into which specific structure?

questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus at T12 transmits the descending thoracic aorta (which continues as the abdominal aorta), the thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. This is the lowest and most posterior of the three main openings. It lies between the crura rather than through them.
questions.question: What passes through the aortic hiatus?

questions.explanation: The sternal angle (of Louis) at the level of T4/5 marks the tracheal bifurcation, the beginning and end of the aortic arch, the upper margin of the heart, and the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum. This is one of the most important surface landmarks in thoracic anatomy.
questions.question: What landmark indicates tracheal bifurcation level?

questions.explanation: The geniculate ganglion is the sensory ganglion of the facial nerve located at the genu (bend) of the facial canal. It contains cell bodies of neurons carrying taste from the anterior tongue via chorda tympani. Herpes zoster infection here causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy and vesicles.
questions.question: The geniculate ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament (lateral lumbocostal arch) is a thickening of the fascia covering quadratus lumborum, extending from the tip of the L1 transverse process to the 12th rib. The diaphragm's lateral part arises from this ligament. The medial arcuate ligament crosses over psoas major (from L1 body to L1 transverse process tip), allowing passage of the sympathetic trunk, while the median arcuate ligament connects the diaphragmatic crura across the midline anterior to the aorta at T12. These arcuate ligaments can be sites of neurovascular compression or serve as anatomical landmarks in retroperitoneal surgery.
questions.question: Which muscle attachment defines the lateral arcuate ligament?

options: Unique opposition enabling precision pinch grip
questions.question: What is the functional significance of opposition movement?
questions.explanation: Opposition (bringing thumb pad to finger pads) is a uniquely human capability essential for precision grip. It involves flexion, abduction, and medial rotation at the thumb carpometacarpal joint. This complex movement, enabled by opponens pollicis and other thenar muscles, distinguishes human hand function.

The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of S2. This is a clinically important landmark for epidural and spinal anesthesia, as well as for assessing pelvic symmetry in musculoskeletal examination. The highest point of the iliac crest corresponds to the level of L4, used for lumbar puncture guidance.
questions.question: The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of which sacral segment?

questions.explanation: Fracture of the neck of femur disrupts the retinacular blood vessels (mainly the medial femoral circumflex artery), leading to avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head. This is the most specific complication, occurring in approximately 15-35% of displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures. It results in segmental collapse of the femoral head and severe hip arthritis if untreated.
questions.question: A fracture of the neck of femur causing coxa vara also disrupts the blood supply to the femoral head. Which named clinical complication most specifically results from this vascular disruption?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

questions.explanation: The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2), emerging through the anterior surface of psoas major, may be at risk during appendectomy if the appendix has a retrocecal position or if dissection extends medially. The nerve's genital branch enters the inguinal canal at the deep ring, while the femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament. Injury can cause sensory loss over the upper anterior thigh (femoral branch) and anterior scrotum/labium majus (genital branch), along with loss of the cremasteric reflex. The ilioinguinal nerve may also be at risk during gridiron or Lanz incisions for appendectomy.
questions.question: Which nerve may be injured during appendectomy?

questions.explanation: The ligamentum venosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus venosus, which shunted oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava during intrauterine life. It lies in a fissure on the visceral surface of the liver between the caudate and left lobes. After birth, when the ductus venosus closes, it becomes the ligamentum venosum.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the fissure for the ligamentum venosum?

questions.explanation: The adult liver weighs approximately 1500 grams, constituting about 2.5% of total body weight in healthy adults. The liver is the largest internal organ and the largest gland in the human body. In newborns, the liver is proportionally larger, contributing to the characteristic protuberant abdomen of infants.
questions.question: What is the approximate weight of an adult liver?

questions.explanation: The diaphragmatic pleura is the portion of parietal pleura that covers the superior surface of the diaphragm. It reflects onto the thoracic wall to become continuous with the costal pleura. The diaphragmatic pleura receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally.
questions.question: Which pleura covers the diaphragm's superior surface?

questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering the pharynx) and the prevertebral fascia. This potential space extends from the skull base to the mediastinum. Infections here can spread to the posterior mediastinum causing mediastinitis.
questions.question: The retropharyngeal space lies between which two fascial layers?

questions.explanation: Myositis ossificans traumatica can complicate contusions or tears of the quadriceps muscle in the anterior thigh, particularly direct blows (common in contact sports). Heterotopic bone forms within the healing hematoma over 4-8 weeks. Premature massage or passive stretching accelerates its formation. It can cause restriction of knee flexion. Most cases resolve with time and physiotherapy.
options: Quadriceps (rectus femoris) muscle tear or contusion
Adductor muscle strain of the thigh
Piriformis syndrome from external hip rotation
questions.question: Myositis ossificans is pathological bone formation within muscle that may complicate which injury about the anterior thigh?
How many posterior intercostal arteries does aorta give?
questions.explanation: The descending thoracic aorta gives off nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces (3rd-11th). The upper two spaces are supplied by the superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk. The subcostal arteries (below the 12th rib) are also given off by the thoracic aorta.

questions.question: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at which landmark?
questions.explanation: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib. The artery is divided into three parts by the anterior scalene muscle. The vertebral, internal thoracic, and thyrocervical trunk typically arise from the subclavian. The costocervical trunk arises from the second part posteriorly.

questions.question: What procedure accesses the heart anteriorly?
questions.explanation: Median sternotomy (vertical splitting of the sternum) is the standard approach for cardiac surgery, providing excellent access to the heart, great vessels, and anterior mediastinum. The sternum is later rewired together. This approach causes less pain and respiratory compromise than lateral thoracotomy.

questions.question: What causes anterior shoulder dislocation?
questions.explanation: Anterior shoulder dislocation typically results from excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus. This forces the humeral head anteriorly and inferiorly through the weakest part of the joint capsule. The anterior capsule lacks reinforcement from rotator cuff muscles, making this the most common dislocation direction.

questions.question: Which structure forms the skeleton of the nasal septum posteroinferiorly?
questions.explanation: The vomer forms the posteroinferior part of the bony nasal septum. The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the posterosuperior portion. The septal cartilage forms the anterior part. The maxillary and palatine crests provide inferior support. Septal deviation commonly occurs at the junction of vomer and cartilage.

The posterior cerebral arteries are the terminal branches of the basilar artery, which bifurcates at the upper border of the pons. They supply the occipital lobes, inferior temporal lobes, and parts of the thalamus. The posterior communicating arteries connect them to the internal carotid system.
questions.question: The posterior cerebral artery is a terminal branch of which vessel?
The facial vein commonly anastomoses with which intracranial structure?
questions.explanation: The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus. These connections lack valves, allowing bidirectional flow. Infections in the danger triangle of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis.

lumbrical canals are present in the hand as potential spaces surrounding the tendon of each lumbrical muscle. These canals lie between the index, middle, ring, and little fingers. Proximally they are continuous with one of the palmar spaces and can serve as routes for infection spread.
questions.question: How many lumbrical canals are present in the hand?

questions.explanation: The first 2 cm of the first (superior) part of the duodenum (the duodenal cap or bulb) is the most mobile as it is intraperitoneal with a mesentery. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal and relatively fixed. This mobility, combined with exposure to acid, makes the duodenal cap the most common site for duodenal ulcers (95% of duodenal ulcers occur here).
questions.question: Which segment of the duodenum is most mobile?

questions.explanation: The splenic red pulp is the primary site for destruction of old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes (red blood cells). After their normal lifespan of approximately 120 days, erythrocytes become less flexible and are selectively engulfed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The iron from hemoglobin is recycled, while other components are degraded.
questions.question: Which cells are predominantly destroyed in the splenic red pulp?
The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous inferiorly with which named structure of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous with the fascia lata of the thigh. The superficial fascia, thick in women and impregnated with large quantities of fat, accounts for the prominence of the buttock. This fascial continuity has clinical implications for spread of infections between gluteal and thigh compartments.

The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. The sheath also contains deep cervical lymph nodes along the vein. It is formed by condensation of deep cervical fascia and extends from the skull base to the thoracic inlet.
options: Carotid artery, jugular vein, vagus nerve
questions.question: The carotid sheath contains which three main structures?
The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended from which nerve?
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion hangs from the maxillary nerve (V2) by two pterygopalatine (sensory) branches in the pterygopalatine fossa. Parasympathetic fibers arrive via the nerve of the pterygoid canal (greater petrosal + deep petrosal). Postganglionic fibers supply the lacrimal gland and nasal/palatine mucosa. Sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing.

questions.question: Which position tests for carpal tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Phalen's test (passive wrist flexion for 60 seconds) provokes carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms by increasing pressure within the tunnel. Reproduction of paresthesia in the median nerve distribution within one minute is considered positive. The reverse Phalen's test uses wrist extension.

Approximately 70% of people have right-dominant circulation, where the right coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery supplying the posterior third of the interventricular septum and diaphragmatic surface. About 10% have left-dominant (circumflex gives posterior interventricular), and 20% have co-dominant (contributions from both) circulation patterns.
questions.question: What percentage of people have right-dominant coronary circulation?
The internal carotid artery enters the skull through which opening?
questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through the carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone. It ascends through the carotid canal, passes above the foramen lacerum, traverses the cavernous sinus, and emerges to give off the ophthalmic artery. The sympathetic carotid plexus surrounds the artery in the canal.

questions.question: At which level do bronchial arteries anastomose?
questions.explanation: Bronchial and pulmonary arteries anastomose at the precapillary level, creating connections between the systemic and pulmonary circulations. This anastomosis allows some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The bronchial circulation comprises only about 1-2% of cardiac output.

All the abdominal wall muscles work together to increase intra-abdominal pressure: the diaphragm contracts and descends, while the rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis contract simultaneously to compress the abdominal contents. This coordinated action is essential for defecation, micturition, parturition (childbirth), coughing, sneezing, and vomiting. The transversus abdominis is particularly important for this function. Weakness of abdominal wall muscles (from aging, pregnancy, or surgery) can impair these functions and predispose to hernias.
questions.question: Which muscle assists in raising intra-abdominal pressure?

questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve, the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, descends within the adductor canal and then exits with the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery to supply the medial side of the leg and foot. The adductor canal also transmits the femoral artery and vein. The saphenous nerve also supplies the knee joint via its branch to the articular capsule.
questions.question: The adductor canal (subsartorial or Hunter's canal) transmits structures from the femoral triangle to the popliteal fossa. Which nerve within it supplies the knee joint and descends within it?

questions.explanation: The upper pole of the left kidney is related to the spleen laterally. Other anterior relations of the left kidney include the stomach superiorly, the pancreatic body and tail centrally, the left colic flexure laterally and inferiorly, and coils of jejunum medially and inferiorly. The left suprarenal gland sits on the upper pole medially.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the upper pole of the left kidney?
Which vein accompanies the posterior interventricular artery?
questions.explanation: The middle cardiac vein ascends in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus near its termination in the right atrium. It drains blood from the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum. It is the second largest cardiac vein after the great cardiac vein.

questions.question: The superior mesenteric artery syndrome involves compression of which structure?
questions.explanation: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome results from compression of the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly and the aorta (and spine) posteriorly. This typically occurs when the aortomesenteric angle decreases (normally 25-60 degrees) due to loss of the mesenteric fat pad, which can result from rapid weight loss, cachexia, scoliosis surgery, or growth spurts in adolescents. Symptoms include postprandial epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. Left renal vein compression between the SMA and aorta is called nutcracker syndrome, a different condition.

The Circle of Willis is situated around the pituitary infundibulum and optic chiasma at the base of the brain. It provides collateral circulation when major arteries become occluded. The circle includes anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries.
options: Internal acoustic meatus and jugular foramen
Superior orbital fissure and optic canal
questions.question: The Circle of Willis is located around which anatomical structures?
Which nerve supplies rhomboid muscles?
questions.explanation: The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) supplies the rhomboid major and minor muscles, and often the levator scapulae. The nerve pierces and may supply scalenus medius before descending along the vertebral border of the scapula. Injury affects scapular retraction.

is the primary muscle producing opposition of the thumb, bringing the thumb across the palm to touch the little finger. This movement involves flexion, abduction, and medial rotation at the carpometacarpal joint. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
questions.question: What produces opposition of the thumb?
The bare area of the liver is related to which organ?
questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver is the triangular region on the posterior surface that is in direct contact with the diaphragm, devoid of peritoneal covering. This area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary ligament (superior and inferior layers) and is continuous with the groove for the inferior vena cava. The bare area represents the part of the liver that remained adherent to the diaphragm during embryological development. Small diaphragmatic veins in this region drain directly from the liver into the IVC without forming hepatic veins, and the right phrenic artery contributes to the vascular supply of this area.

Erb's paralysis results in loss of abduction and lateral rotation at the shoulder joint. This occurs due to paralysis of the deltoid, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus muscles supplied by C5-C6 nerve roots. The affected arm hangs by the side in an adducted and medially rotated position.
questions.question: What muscle action is lost in Erb's paralysis affecting shoulder movement?

questions.explanation: The musculophrenic artery is one of the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery (the other being superior epigastric). It runs along the costal margin supplying the lower intercostal spaces (7th-9th via anterior intercostal arteries), the diaphragm, and the abdominal muscles.
questions.question: What is the musculophrenic artery?

questions.explanation: The patellar ligament passes from the apex and adjoining margins of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It is a strong thick fibrous band representing the distal continuation of the quadriceps tendon. It blends with the medial and lateral patellar retinacula (aponeurotic expansions of vastus medialis and lateralis) providing additional stability.
questions.question: The patellar ligament, described as the distal part of the quadriceps tendon, ultimately attaches to which bony prominence?
Which structure passes through the transverse mesocolon?
questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) and middle colic veins (to superior mesenteric vein) pass through the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon. The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the descending duodenum, serving as an important surgical landmark dividing the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The superior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, while the inferior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the peritoneum, not within the mesocolon itself.

questions.question: What causes flail chest?
questions.explanation: Flail chest results from multiple rib fractures (usually three or more) in two or more places, creating a free-floating segment of chest wall. This segment moves paradoxically: sucking in during inspiration and blowing out during expiration. It causes respiratory distress and requires positive pressure ventilation.

Piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior share innervation from L5, S1. They also share the same insertion into the upper border of the greater trochanter and the same action as lateral rotators of the hip joint. This common heritage is useful clinically in understanding hip pathology.
questions.question: Piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior share a common innervation. What is their shared nerve root?
The ductus deferens passes medial to which vessel?
questions.explanation: The ductus deferens (vas deferens) hooks around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery at the deep inguinal ring, crossing from lateral to medial as it leaves the spermatic cord to descend into the pelvis. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. After crossing the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, the vas continues posteromedially across the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder where it dilates to form the ampulla and joins the seminal vesicle duct.

The thyroid gland is bound to the larynx and trachea by the pretracheal fascia. This attachment causes the thyroid to move with the larynx during swallowing. The isthmus overlies the second to fourth tracheal rings while the lobes extend from the thyroid cartilage downward.
questions.question: The thyroid gland is attached to which laryngeal structure?
The cremasteric artery is typically a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The cremasteric artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery (a branch of the external iliac artery) near the deep inguinal ring and accompanies the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal. It supplies the cremaster muscle and anastomoses with the testicular artery and artery of the vas deferens, contributing to the arterial supply of the spermatic cord coverings. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve also enters the cord at the deep ring to innervate the cremaster muscle, which elevates the testis in response to cold or cremasteric reflex stimulation.

The anterior drawer test of the ankle assesses the integrity of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). The test is performed with the ankle in slight plantarflexion, applying an anterior force to the heel while stabilizing the tibia. Excessive anterior translation of the talus relative to the tibia indicates ATFL rupture. This is the most commonly injured ankle ligament in inversion sprains.
questions.question: The anterior drawer test of the ankle assesses the integrity of which specific ligament?
At which vertebral levels do the kidneys typically lie?
questions.explanation: The kidneys typically extend from the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12) to the third lumbar vertebra (L3) on the posterior abdominal wall. The right kidney is slightly lower than the left due to the presence of the liver. Both kidneys move inferiorly with respiration, descending as much as 2.5 cm during diaphragmatic contraction.

The 'unhappy triad' of the knee (O'Donoghue's triad) consists of simultaneous injury to the anterior cruciate ligament, medial meniscus, and tibial (medial) collateral ligament. This injury occurs classically in American football when a valgus force is applied to a planted, slightly flexed knee. The tight adherence of the medial meniscus to the tibial collateral ligament explains their combined injury.
options: PCL, lateral meniscus, and fibular collateral ligament
ACL, lateral meniscus, and fibular collateral ligament
PCL, lateral meniscus, and tibial collateral ligament
ACL, medial meniscus, and tibial collateral ligament
ACL, medial meniscus, and ACL and fibular collateral ligament
questions.question: The 'unhappy triad' of the knee involves simultaneous injury to which three structures following a valgus force with the foot planted?

options: Base and styloid process of the 5th metatarsal only
Medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
Navicular tuberosity and the adjacent medial cuneiform bone
Bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsal bones
Calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon posteriorly
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior inserts into the medial and inferior surfaces of the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal. It originates from the lateral condyle and superior half of the lateral surface of the tibia and interosseous membrane. It is the most powerful dorsiflexor and inverts the foot, active throughout the swing phase of gait.
questions.question: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot. It inserts into which specific structures?

questions.explanation: The female external urethral orifice opens into the vestibule, the space between the labia minora, approximately 2.5 cm posterior to the clitoris and immediately anterior to the vaginal opening. The orifice is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter and may be difficult to visualize in some women. Paraurethral (Skene's) glands open on either side of the orifice.
questions.question: Where does the female urethra open externally?
What is the primary function of the tensor veli palatini muscle?
questions.explanation: The tensor veli palatini opens the Eustachian tube during swallowing and yawning, equalizing middle ear pressure. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3), unlike other palatal muscles supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. The muscle also tenses the soft palate.

The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the bile duct within the hepatoduodenal ligament as its anterior boundary, not medial. The superior boundary is the caudate lobe of the liver, the inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct), and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered by parietal peritoneum. This opening typically admits two fingers and provides communication between the greater and lesser sacs.
questions.question: Which vessel marks the medial boundary of the epiploic foramen?
What structure lies between the subscapularis tendon and the scapula?
questions.explanation: The subscapular bursa is located between the subscapularis tendon and the scapula, reducing wear and tear during shoulder movement. Unlike the subacromial bursa, the subscapular bursa communicates with the shoulder joint cavity through a gap between the superior and middle glenohumeral ligaments. This communication allows potential spread of infection or inflammatory processes.

questions.question: Which intrinsic hand muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve?
options: All interossei and medial two lumbricals
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all the interossei (palmar and dorsal) and the medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers). It also supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, and the medial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the hypoglossal triangle?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) lies in the hypoglossal triangle (muscular triangle), a subdivision of the anterior triangle bounded by the midline, superior belly of omohyoid, and sternocleidomastoid. The triangle also contains the infrahyoid muscles and thyroid gland. The nerve passes from the carotid triangle into the muscular triangle.

questions.question: Which ligament supports the uterus?
questions.explanation: The uterus is supported by multiple structures: the cardinal ligaments (most important, prevent prolapse), uterosacral ligaments (from cervix/upper vagina to sacrum, maintain position), pubocervical ligaments (from cervix to pubis), round ligaments (maintain anteverted position), broad ligaments (minimal support, mainly peritoneal folds), and the muscular pelvic floor (levator ani, particularly pubococcygeus). The perineal body also provides indirect support. Damage to these supports (especially during childbirth) can lead to uterine prolapse, cystocele, rectocele, or enterocele. The broad ligament, despite its name, provides minimal structural support.

questions.question: What arches over the left lung root?
questions.explanation: The aortic arch passes over and in front of the left lung root. The left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch. This anatomical relationship is visible on chest X-rays and CT scans and is important for understanding mediastinal anatomy.

questions.question: Which muscle adducts the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle adducts (closes) the vocal cords by internally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. Other adductors include the interarytenoid and thyroarytenoid muscles. All adductors are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Bilateral adductor paralysis causes airway obstruction.

The superficial branch of the radial nerve passes over the scaphoid bone in the anatomical snuffbox. Scaphoid fracture or associated swelling can compress this nerve branch. This causes numbness over the dorsal thumb and radial side of the hand without motor deficit.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in scaphoid fracture?

questions.explanation: The middle ear receives blood from multiple tympanic arteries: superior tympanic (middle meningeal), inferior tympanic (ascending pharyngeal), anterior tympanic (maxillary), and posterior tympanic (stylomastoid branch of posterior auricular). This rich vascular supply reflects the metabolic needs of the middle ear mucosa and ossicles.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies blood to the middle ear?

questions.explanation: The transversus thoracis (sternocostalis) is the anterior portion of the innermost intercostal layer. It is fan-shaped, spreading upward from the posterior aspect of the lower sternum to insert onto the inner surfaces of the 2nd-6th costal cartilages. It depresses the ribs during expiration.
questions.question: What is the transversus thoracis muscle?

options: Young children under 5; from excessive dorsiflexion
Adolescents aged 8�14; Achilles traction on the calcaneal apophysis
Young adults; from overuse of tibialis posterior
questions.question: Sever's disease (calcaneal apophysitis) is a traction apophysitis of the calcaneus, predominantly affecting which age group and caused by traction from which structure?
questions.explanation: Sever's disease is calcaneal apophysitis affecting adolescents aged 8-14 years (peak growth phase), caused by traction from the Achilles tendon on the calcaneal apophysis (secondary ossification centre). It presents with posterior heel pain aggravated by activity. Treatment is conservative with activity modification, heel cups, and Achilles tendon stretching. It is self-limiting once the apophysis fuses.

The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) typically joins the common bile duct within the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens at the major duodenal papilla. The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when patent, opens separately at the minor duodenal papilla approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. Anatomical variations exist, including separate openings of the pancreatic and bile ducts (pancreas divisum). The junction is surgically significant during ERCP and pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure).
questions.question: The main pancreatic duct typically joins the bile duct at which location?

questions.explanation: The right kidney's anterior surface is related superiorly to the right lobe of the liver (hepatorenal recess), the second part of the duodenum medially, and the right colic flexure and ascending colon inferiorly. Small intestine loops may also contact its anterior surface. The liver creates the largest impression on the right kidney's anterior surface.
questions.question: Which organ lies anterior to the right kidney?

questions.explanation: Trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges that project from the inner surface of the ventricles. They prevent the walls from adhering to each other during contraction, increase ventricular surface area, and may contribute to ventricular contraction. Some are attached at both ends (ridges), some at one end (bridges like the moderator band), and some are free (papillary muscles).
questions.question: What is the function of trabeculae carneae?
How many structures contribute to diaphragm development?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm develops from four embryological structures: (1) septum transversum (forming central tendon), (2) dorsal esophageal mesentery, (3) peripheral rim from body wall, and (4) pleuroperitoneal membranes (closing the pleuroperitoneal canals). Incomplete fusion of these components leads to congenital diaphragmatic hernias.

The Achilles tendon does not have a true synovial tendon sheath like finger flexor tendons. Instead, it is surrounded by a paratenon (peritenon), a loose connective tissue sheath that allows tendon gliding and contains blood vessels. Two bursae are adjacent: the retrocalcaneal bursa (between tendon and calcaneus) and the superficial calcaneal bursa (between tendon and skin). Inflammation of the paratenon causes peritendinitis (Achilles peritendinitis).
questions.question: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. It does NOT have a true tendon sheath but instead has which covering?
options: A fascial tunnel from the posterior compartment

questions.explanation: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ridge surrounding the glenoid cavity that deepens the cavity, reducing dislocation risk. It increases the articular surface area and provides attachment for some glenohumeral ligaments. This structure contributes significantly to glenohumeral joint stability despite the joint's high mobility.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the glenoid labrum?

questions.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch, formed by the coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament, prevents superior displacement of the humeral head. This structure overlies the shoulder joint superiorly. The joint capsule is weak superiorly, making the arch essential for preventing upward dislocation.
questions.question: What prevents superior displacement of the humeral head at the shoulder?

questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein arises from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch and ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus. It then passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, ascends between the heads of gastrocnemius, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
questions.question: The small saphenous vein arises on the lateral side of the foot and ascends posterior to which malleolus before entering the popliteal vein?

questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis is situated at the level of the lesser trochanter and is formed by the inferior gluteal artery, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
questions.question: The cruciate anastomosis, at the level of the lesser trochanter, provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and which major vessel?
What structure is torn in gamekeeper's thumb?
options: Ulnar collateral ligament of thumb MCP
questions.explanation: "Gamekeeper's thumb" (skier's thumb when acute) involves a tear of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint. This causes thumb instability affecting pinch grip strength. The injury historically occurred in gamekeepers from repetitive stress while killing rabbits.

Frozen shoulder results from adhesive capsulitis, causing progressive restriction of glenohumeral joint motion. The joint capsule becomes thickened and contracted. The condition typically progresses through freezing, frozen, and thawing phases over 1-3 years.
questions.question: What causes frozen shoulder?

questions.explanation: The three teniae coli (longitudinal muscle bands: taenia libera, taenia mesocolica, and taenia omentalis) of the cecum converge at the base of the vermiform appendix, providing a reliable surgical landmark for locating the appendix during appendectomy. The teniae continue along the ascending, transverse, and descending colon but disappear at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anal verge), where the longitudinal muscle coat becomes complete around the circumference of the rectum. The teniae correspond to areas where the longitudinal muscle is thickened, while the areas between are thinner, allowing formation of sacculations (haustra).
questions.question: The teniae coli converge at which structure?

questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is the presence of air in the potential space between the pleural layers, causing lung collapse. This can occur spontaneously, traumatically, or iatrogenically. Hemothorax involves blood, empyema involves pus, and pleural effusion involves abnormal fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity.
questions.question: What condition results from air in pleural cavity?

options: Middle cranial fossa and pterygopalatine fossa
questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure is a vertical opening between the lateral pterygoid plate (posteriorly) and the maxilla (anteriorly), connecting the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae. The maxillary artery and mandibular nerve branches pass through this fissure. It forms the lateral boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa.
questions.question: The pterygomaxillary fissure connects which two regions?
Which vessels supply the esophagus in thorax?
questions.explanation: In the thorax, the esophagus is supplied by esophageal branches arising directly from the anterior aspect of the descending thoracic aorta. Additional supply comes from the inferior thyroid artery superiorly and left gastric artery inferiorly. Bronchial arteries also contribute small branches. Venous drainage follows a similar pattern.

Retraction (adduction) of the scapula is produced by combined action of middle fibers of trapezius and the rhomboid muscles. During retraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves backward along with the scapula. This movement is important for pulling actions.
questions.question: What is the primary muscle for scapular retraction?

questions.explanation: Chyle has a characteristic milky white appearance due to its high lipid (triglyceride) content from intestinal fat absorption. After fasting, the fluid may appear clearer. Laboratory analysis shows elevated triglycerides (typically >110 mg/dL) and presence of chylomicrons. The fluid is odorless and has a pH of 7.4-7.8.
questions.question: What characterizes chyle fluid?

questions.explanation: Dupuytren's contracture results from progressive fibrosis of the palmar aponeurosis. Longitudinal bands thicken forming cords that cause progressive flexion contracture of fingers, typically ring and little fingers. The condition has genetic predisposition and is more common in males of Northern European descent.
questions.question: What causes Dupuytren's contracture?

questions.explanation: McBurney's (gridiron) incision for appendectomy divides (cuts) the external oblique aponeurosis in the direction of its fibers, then splits (separates) the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles in the direction of their fibers. This muscle-splitting approach preserves the neurovascular supply and provides good healing with reduced hernia risk. The incision is centered on McBurney's point.
questions.question: Which muscle does McBurney's incision divide?
What nerve root is predominantly tested by the triceps reflex?
questions.explanation: The triceps reflex predominantly tests the C7 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon. Absence or diminution suggests C7 nerve root or radial nerve pathology.

The round ligament of the uterus passes through the deep inguinal ring (homologous to the spermatic cord in males), traverses the inguinal canal, exits through the superficial inguinal ring, and terminates in the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus. It represents the distal gubernaculum (the proximal part becoming the ovarian ligament). The round ligament contains smooth muscle, vessels, and nerves, and helps maintain the anteverted position of the uterus. Rarely, indirect inguinal hernias can occur in females alongside the round ligament (canal of Nuck).
questions.question: The round ligament of the uterus passes through which opening?
Which side internal thoracic is preferred for bypass?
questions.explanation: The left internal thoracic artery is preferred for coronary bypass because of its proximity to the left anterior descending coronary artery. The right internal thoracic may also be used for right coronary or circumflex vessels. Using arterial grafts (vs. saphenous vein) provides superior long-term patency rates.

questions.question: Which part of the stomach is most common site for gastric ulcers?
questions.explanation: Gastric ulcers most commonly occur along the lesser curvature, particularly at the incisura angularis and junction of body and antrum. This distribution reflects the exposure to gastric acid and the vulnerability of this area to ischemia. Duodenal ulcers are more common overall than gastric ulcers, but gastric ulcers have higher malignancy potential.

questions.question: Full knee flexion may kink which artery, explaining the functional importance of the genicular anastomosis as collateral circulation?
questions.explanation: Full knee flexion may kink the popliteal artery, explaining why the genicular anastomosis is functionally important: it provides collateral circulation to maintain blood supply to the leg even when the popliteal artery is kinked. This anastomosis is formed by branches of the popliteal, femoral, lateral femoral circumflex, and anterior tibial arteries.

questions.question: Where is Auerbach's plexus located in the gut wall?
questions.explanation: Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa throughout the gastrointestinal tract. It controls gut motility, including peristalsis and segmentation. Damage to this plexus (as in Chagas disease or Hirschsprung disease) causes severe motility disorders. It contains both excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons.

questions.question: Which test assesses scaphoid fracture?
questions.explanation: is the classic test for scaphoid fracture. Pain with palpation in the snuffbox and/or with axial compression of the thumb suggests fracture. Even if initial radiographs are negative, clinical suspicion warrants immobilization and follow-up imaging.

The interatrial septum is the thin wall separating the right and left atria. It contains the fossa ovalis, a thumbprint-sized oval depression representing the site of the foramen ovale in the fetus. The limbus fossae ovalis is the prominent margin of the fossa. In approximately 25% of people, the foramen ovale remains probe-patent without functional significance.
questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left atria internally?
What is the functional significance of extensor expansion?
questions.explanation: The extensor expansion (extensor hood) distributes extensor digitorum force and coordinates intrinsic hand muscle action with extrinsic extensors. Intrinsic muscles insert into the expansion, enabling their unique MCP flexion with IP extension action. This complex structure allows coordinated finger movements essential for precision grip.
options: Distributes extensor force, coordinates intrinsic-extrinsic action
Fascia lata of the thigh only
Camper's fascia of the anterior abdominal wall
Transversalis fascia anteriorly and iliac fascia posteriorly
questions.question: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of which fascia, enclosing the femoral vessels and the femoral canal?
questions.explanation: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of the transversalis fascia anteriorly and the iliac fascia posteriorly, enclosing the femoral artery, femoral vein, and the femoral canal (containing lymphatics). The femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal into the femoral sheath inferior to the inguinal ligament.

questions.question: The processus vaginalis gives rise to which structure?
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis, normally obliterates during the first year of life except for its distal portion, which remains as the tunica vaginalis (a closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis). The parietal layer of tunica vaginalis lines the inner surface of the scrotum (internal spermatic fascia), while the visceral layer covers the testis and epididymis. Failure of processus vaginalis obliteration leads to patent processus (communicating hydrocele) or congenital indirect inguinal hernia. The gubernaculum guides testicular descent.

Lymph vessels from the lung drain into hilar (bronchopulmonary) nodes, and efferent lymphatics ultimately drain into the brachiocephalic vein. The lymph passes through pulmonary nodes, bronchopulmonary nodes, and tracheobronchial nodes before reaching the venous system. This pathway is important in cancer metastasis.
questions.question: Where do hilar lymphatics ultimately drain?

questions.explanation: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus (opening in the adductor magnus muscle), transitioning from the anterior compartment of the thigh to the popliteal fossa.
