options: Reduced GI motility and gastric acid secretion, slowing drug dissolution and absorption rate
Increased first-pass metabolism in older adults
Increased splanchnic blood flow significantly enhancing overall drug uptake efficiency throughout the intestine
Increased gastric acid secretion speeding dissolution
Improved intestinal villous height significantly increasing overall surface area available for absorption

questions.explanation: Locomotive handicap refers to restrictions to movement, which may be partial or total, with an example given being a person whose lower limbs are amputated. Communication handicap instead affects hearing, speech, or writing ability, while visceral handicap involves disorders of ingestion and excretion. Intellectual handicap includes impaired learning ability or memory loss, and invisible handicap includes conditions not visible from outside, such as asthma or diabetes mellitus, none of which describe amputation-related movement restriction.
questions.question: A person who has had their lower limbs amputated and experiences restrictions to movement would be classified under which type of handicap?

A falls prevention nurse recommends a specific exercise modality to an older client to improve balance and reduce fall risk. Which type of exercise is most strongly supported by the evidence for fall prevention?
questions.explanation: Tai Chi and progressive resistance training are the exercise modalities most strongly supported by evidence for fall prevention in older adults, improving balance, gait, leg strength, and coordination. Swimming provides cardiovascular benefit but is not cited as the strongest evidence-based fall prevention modality. High-intensity aerobic exercise, passive range of motion, and supine stretching alone do not provide the balance and strength training components most critical for reducing fall risk.
options: Supine stretching routines used only occasionally
Tai Chi and progressive resistance training

questions.explanation: Consistently denying an older person with dementia their meals represents neglect, defined as the failure to provide essential care such as nutrition to a person who cannot adequately advocate for themselves. Financial exploitation involves misuse of money or property, emotional abuse involves verbal or psychological harm, physical abuse involves infliction of pain or injury, and sexual abuse involves non-consensual sexual acts, none of which describe withholding food and nutrition.
questions.question: A nurse documents that an older client with dementia is consistently denied meals by the caregiver who states the client is 'not hungry.' This repeated act most accurately constitutes which form of elder abuse?

questions.explanation: For older adults with type 2 diabetes, the recommended HbA1c target is typically individualized in the range of 7.0% to 8.0%, balancing the benefits of glycaemic control against the risks of hypoglycemia, which are amplified in frail older adults with multiple comorbidities. Targets below 5.0% or below 6.0% are overly stringent and increase hypoglycemia risk in older adults, while targets above 10% represent poor control associated with increased complication risk. Exact uniform targets without individualization are not appropriate for this heterogeneous population.
questions.question: An older adult newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes is educated on the HbA1c target. Which value represents the generally recommended HbA1c target for older adults to balance glycaemic control with hypoglycemia risk?
options: A level below 5.0% strictly regardless of frailty status
Exactly 6.5%, applied without any individualization whatsoever
7.0% to 8.0%, individualized based on frailty and comorbidities

questions.explanation: The correct technique for using a standard cane with unilateral leg weakness is to hold the cane on the stronger, unaffected side and advance it simultaneously with the weaker leg, which shifts weight away from the weaker limb and improves gait stability. Holding the cane on the weaker side defeats this mechanical advantage. Prescribing a walker may sometimes be appropriate but is not the automatic correction for incorrect cane technique, and holding the cane behind the body would provide no meaningful support.
questions.question: A nurse documents that an older client is using a standard cane incorrectly by holding it on the same side as the weaker leg. What is the correct instruction?
options: Continue using the cane consistently on the same side as the weaker leg
Hold the cane behind the body for stability
Use a walker instead since all canes are considered entirely inappropriate for unilateral weakness cases
Hold the cane on the weaker side and advance it before the stronger leg
Hold the cane on the stronger side and advance it with the weaker leg simultaneously

questions.question: A client asks why she needs to urinate so urgently once she finally feels the urge, unlike when she was younger. The nurse explains this is due to a delay in which physiological process?
options: The micturition reflex, normally triggered at half-full bladder capacity, delayed in older adults
Renal filtration, which actually increases steadily and progressively with advancing age in most people overall
questions.explanation: In older adults, the micturition reflex, which normally activates when the bladder is about half full, is delayed until the bladder is nearly at capacity, producing a sudden sense of urgency. Renal filtration decreases rather than increases with age. Thirst hormone regulation, gastric emptying, and the pupillary light reflex are unrelated processes that do not explain urinary urgency.

Sildenafil belongs to the class of phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitors, which block the activity of an enzyme in blood vessel walls, allowing blood vessels in the penis to relax and fill with blood, producing an erection. Beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, and diuretics are cardiovascular medications with different mechanisms unrelated to the PDE5 pathway, and men taking nitrates for blood pressure should avoid PDE5 inhibitors.
questions.question: A male client is prescribed sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. Which mechanism of action correctly describes how this drug works?
options: It is an ACE inhibitor that specifically lowers systemic arterial blood pressure
It is a PDE5 inhibitor that relaxes blood vessels in the penis to allow filling with blood
It is a diuretic that reduces overall fluid retention
It is a calcium channel blocker that widens all peripheral arteries equally and uniformly throughout the body
It is a beta-blocker that slows heart rate

questions.question: A nurse reviewing connective tissue physiology explains that the meninges enveloping the brain and spinal cord are composed of which tissue type?
questions.explanation: The three outer membranes of the central nervous system, the meninges, are composed of connective tissue, which develops from the mesoderm and is found throughout the body including the nervous system. Epithelial and muscle tissues are separate basic tissue types unrelated to the meninges. Nervous tissue makes up the brain and spinal cord itself, not its protective coverings, and lymphoid tissue is unrelated to meningeal structure.

options: Significant excess intake of vitamins and proteins from various dietary sources
Improved digestion due to a softer diet exclusively
Potential deficiencies in vitamins and proteins from these critical food sources
Significantly decreased need for dietary fiber overall
questions.explanation: Older adults with poor dentition may avoid fibrous fruits, vegetables, and meats, which are critical sources of vitamins and proteins, leading to potential nutritional deficiencies rather than excess. A softer diet alone does not necessarily improve digestion if it lacks essential nutrients, and intrinsic factor production actually decreases with age rather than increasing. The need for dietary fiber does not decrease simply because intake of fibrous foods is reduced; rather, this avoidance itself becomes a risk factor for inadequate fiber intake.
questions.question: Oral health changes in aging, including tooth loss, gum disease, and reduced salivary production, can lead an older adult to avoid certain foods. What is the most likely nutritional consequence of avoiding fibrous fruits, vegetables, and meats?

questions.explanation: Additional CGA domains for hospitalized patients include prevention and treatment of delirium, falls prevention, improving physical function, discharge planning and support post-discharge, and nutritional support. Career counseling, cosmetic dermatology referrals, recreational travel planning, and academic tutoring are not part of the additional domains identified for hospitalized older patients undergoing CGA.
questions.question: For hospitalized older patients undergoing CGA, additional domains include prevention and treatment of delirium, falls prevention, improving physical function, discharge planning, and which other domain?

questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease causes the brain to shrink and brain cells to eventually die, producing a gradual decline in memory, thinking, behavior, and social skills that affects a person's ability to function. It is not a sudden-onset or curable condition, and while cholinesterase inhibitors may improve or slow symptom progression, they do not reverse the underlying disease. The condition extends well beyond short-term memory, eventually affecting judgment, personality, and the ability to perform everyday tasks.
options: It causes the brain to shrink and brain cells to eventually die, leading to progressive decline
It is fully and completely reversible if cholinesterase inhibitors are started very early in the disease course
It has no impact on a person's ability to perform daily tasks
It is a sudden-onset condition that can be fully cured with medication
It primarily affects only short-term memory while sparing all other cognitive functions entirely
questions.question: A nurse caring for a client with Alzheimer's disease notes that the client repeats the same questions and misplaces items in unusual locations. According to the described disease progression, which statement about Alzheimer's disease is accurate?

questions.explanation: Progressive weight loss in dementia requires assessment for contributing factors such as swallowing difficulties, environmental distractions during meals, or depression, rather than assuming it is an inevitable, unaddressable consequence of the disease. Jumping to invasive interventions like tube feeding without this assessment bypasses potentially reversible causes. A thorough, individualised assessment guides the most appropriate, least invasive intervention first.
options: Assess for underlying causes such as swallowing difficulty or distraction
Discontinue oral intake until a specialist review occurs
Immediately request insertion of a feeding tube without assessment
Assume weight loss is an expected, unavoidable part of dementia
Increase meal portion sizes without addressing other factors
questions.question: A nurse caring for an older client with dementia notes progressive weight loss despite apparently adequate food availability at meals. The most appropriate initial nursing action is to:
A nurse caring for an older client with moderate dementia notes the client repeatedly asks the same question despite being answered each time. The most appropriate nursing response is to:
options: Ignore the client until they stop asking the question
Explain in detail why repeated questions are problematic
Answer calmly and consistently each time without showing frustration
Correct the client firmly to reduce repetitive behaviour
Point out that the question has already been answered
questions.explanation: Responding calmly and consistently to repeated questions, without pointing out the repetition or showing frustration, respects the client's cognitive limitations and reduces distress, which is a recommended approach in dementia care. Correcting or ignoring the client can increase agitation and damage trust. This patient-centred communication approach supports dignity and reduces behavioural escalation.

questions.question: A nursing lecturer explains that her course examines the social, psychological, and biological aspects of aging as a whole, distinguishing it from the medical treatment of diseases in older persons. Which term best describes this field of study?
questions.explanation: Gerontology is the broad study of the social, psychological, and biological aspects of aging, distinct from geriatrics which focuses on disease management. Geriatrics, by contrast, is a medical specialty dealing with diagnosis and treatment of illnesses in older adults. Biogerontology and geroscience are narrower subfields concerned mainly with biological mechanisms of aging.

Socioemotional Selectivity Theory suggests that as people perceive time as more limited, they prioritise emotionally meaningful relationships over broader social networks, which explains this client's selective, close-relationship focus rather than complete withdrawal. This differs from disengagement theory, which describes a more general withdrawal from society. Understanding this theory helps the nurse recognise selective socialising as a purposeful, adaptive choice rather than isolation.
questions.question: A nurse observes that an older client has become more selective about social relationships, preferring a few close family members over large social gatherings, and explains this reflects a conscious prioritisation of emotionally meaningful time. This is best explained by:
options: Continuity theory describing unchanged social patterns overall
Activity theory requiring maintenance of all prior activities
Disengagement theory describing complete social withdrawal
Terror Management Theory describing avoidance of mortality
Socioemotional Selectivity Theory prioritising meaningful connections

questions.question: A 70-year-old client reports that he now feels cold much more easily than he did at age 40, even in mild weather. Which physiological change most directly explains this complaint?
questions.explanation: Loss of subcutaneous fat with aging reduces the body's natural insulation, and diminished blood flow to the skin and extremities further reduces heat retention, making older adults more sensitive to cold. The opposite changes, increased fat thickness or improved circulation, do not occur with normal aging. Sweat gland atrophy and thermoregulatory reflexes generally decline rather than improve with age.
options: Increased overall thickness of subcutaneous fat layers throughout the body
Decreased subcutaneous fat with reduced insulation and blood flow
Increased total number of active sweat glands

questions.explanation: The 'start low, go slow' principle in geriatric prescribing accounts for altered drug metabolism, increased sensitivity, and higher risk of adverse effects in older adults, aiming to achieve therapeutic benefit while minimising harm. It is a safety-focused strategy, not primarily about cost or length of stay. This principle reflects careful, individualised dose titration in this vulnerable population.
options: Longer hospital stays unrelated to medication safety
Increased cost of medication therapy for the client
Reduced medication effectiveness overall in older adults
Adverse effects from altered drug metabolism and sensitivity
Delayed therapeutic response requiring higher initial doses
questions.question: A nurse reviewing a medication administration record for an older client applies the principle of 'start low, go slow' primarily to reduce the risk of:

A nurse explains that an older adult's bladder capacity is markedly reduced compared to a younger adult's. Approximately what bladder capacity is cited for an elderly person compared to about 600 mL in a young adult?
questions.explanation: The bladder of an elderly person is described as having a capacity of less than half that of a young adult, approximately 250 mL compared to 600 mL, often containing significant residual urine. Less than 100 mL is too small to match the described value, while 400, 500, and 600 mL all exceed the cited reduced capacity for older adults.

options: Waiting for the client to request fluids independently always
Restricting fluids in the evening for all older clients
Relying solely on the client's reported thirst level alone consistently
Providing fluids only during scheduled meal times
Offering fluids proactively on a scheduled basis throughout the day
questions.explanation: Because older adults often have a blunted thirst response, proactively offering fluids on a scheduled basis throughout the day, rather than waiting for the client to feel or express thirst, helps ensure adequate hydration and reduce dehydration risk. Relying solely on reported thirst can miss early signs of inadequate intake. This proactive approach reflects individualised, needs-based nursing care.
questions.question: A nurse teaching about hydration in older adults explains that dehydration risk is increased partly because of a blunted thirst response, and recommends which strategy to support adequate intake?

questions.explanation: Care of the handicapped includes prompt assessment, corrective measures, educational treatment, vocational training, provision of employment, the design and production of special gadgets, and centers for guidance and counselling. Withholding employment opportunities permanently, avoiding guidance and counselling centers, discontinuing corrective measures after the initial assessment, and restricting access to educational treatment would all contradict the comprehensive, ongoing approach described for caring for the handicapped.
questions.question: Care of the handicapped, as outlined in community health nursing literature, includes prompt assessment, corrective measures, educational treatment, vocational training, and which additional component related to functional support?
options: Discontinuing all corrective measures after initial assessment
Designing and production of special gadgets
Avoiding centers for guidance and counselling
Urinary frequency, urgency, and urinary tract infection
Decreased risk of urinary tract infection overall
Improved bladder control compared to younger adults
Complete resolution of any urinary symptoms
Reduced need for any toileting assistance
questions.question: A nurse caring for an older client notes reduced bladder capacity and increased residual urine on assessment. This combination of changes primarily increases the client's risk for:
questions.explanation: Reduced bladder capacity and increased post-void residual urine with ageing contribute to urinary frequency, urgency, and a higher risk of urinary tract infection due to urinary stasis. This is the opposite of improved control or reduced infection risk. Recognising these changes supports proactive toileting schedules and infection prevention strategies.

options: Only intrinsic factors such as advancing age and biological gender differences are considered here
Intrinsic factors such as age-related physiological changes and extrinsic factors such as environmental hazards
Only extrinsic factors such as environmental hazards
Only psychological factors such as persistent fear of falling
Only pharmacological factors related to medication use
questions.explanation: Falls in older adults result from a combination of intrinsic factors such as age-related physiological changes, chronic conditions, and cognitive impairment, and extrinsic factors such as environmental hazards and medications. Attributing falls to only one category misses the multifactorial nature described. Pharmacological factors are part of the extrinsic category, and fear of falling is a psychological consequence and risk factor that sits within the intrinsic domain, but neither alone constitutes the full framework.
questions.question: Falls in older adults are described as having a multifactorial aetiology. Which framework correctly categorizes fall risk factors?

questions.explanation: Attributing new or changing symptoms solely to age without proper evaluation is a harmful form of ageism that can lead to missed or delayed diagnosis of serious conditions. New symptoms in older adults warrant the same thorough evaluation as in younger patients. Nurses play an important advocacy role in ensuring older clients receive appropriate diagnostic attention.
options: Appropriate clinical judgement based on solid evidence
Standard geriatric assessment protocol being followed
Correct application of comprehensive geriatric assessment
Ageism leading to under-investigation of new symptoms
Evidence-based reassurance requiring no further action
questions.question: A physician dismisses an older client's report of new chest pain as 'just part of getting old' without further evaluation. This response illustrates a harmful consequence of:
According to Terror Management Theory, which type of psychological defense against mortality anxiety is considered more adaptive and beneficial in the long run?
questions.explanation: While both proximal and distal defenses help manage mortality anxiety, distal defenses such as symbolic immortality, cultural worldview, self-esteem, and identification with something larger are considered more adaptive and beneficial over the long run. Proximal defenses including denial, distraction, repression, and rationalization are short-term strategies that merely suppress death-related thoughts temporarily rather than providing lasting meaning.
options: Short-term rationalization strategies that occur without deeper philosophical reflection
Distal defenses such as symbolic immortality and cultural worldview
Proximal defenses such as denial and distraction
Repression of death-related thoughts without any lasting cultural engagement

questions.explanation: Age-related changes in body composition, including decreased total body water and increased fat percentage, alter drug distribution, causing water-soluble drugs to reach higher concentrations and fat-soluble drugs to have prolonged effects due to accumulation in fat tissue. This is a distribution effect, not primarily related to excretion or absorption directly. Understanding this helps explain altered drug responses and prolonged effects in older adults.
options: Drug absorption exclusively within the oral cavity
Drug distribution, altering how medications spread through the body
Drug metabolism exclusively within the pancreas only specifically overall
Drug excretion exclusively through the respiratory system only
No aspect of pharmacokinetics in older adults
questions.question: A nurse caring for an older client understands that age-related decreases in total body water and increases in body fat percentage primarily affect:

questions.explanation: While basal metabolic rate declines with age and reduces overall energy requirements, the need for proteins, fiber, calcium, and vitamin D increases to maintain muscle mass, bone health, and immune function. Simple sugars, saturated fats, and trans fats are not nutrients whose increased intake is recommended for older adults. Carbohydrates alone, or sodium and potassium alone, do not capture the specific nutrients identified as having increased requirements in this context.
questions.question: The basal metabolic rate declines with age, leading to reduced energy requirements. However, the need for which nutrients actually increases to maintain muscle mass, bone health, and immune function?
options: Proteins, fiber, calcium, and vitamin D
Only sodium and potassium minerals overall

questions.explanation: Aging connective tissue undergoes decreased cellular activity, reduced matrix synthesis, and increased collagen cross-linking, which together produce reduced elasticity, increased stiffness, and brittleness in tissues such as skin, bone, and cartilage. The opposite outcomes, increased elasticity or improved healing, are not consistent with these changes. Arterial stiffness actually increases rather than decreases as part of this same process.
options: Significantly improved overall wound healing capacity
Reduced elasticity, increased stiffness, and brittleness
questions.question: An older client's skin biopsy shows decreased cellular activity, reduced extracellular matrix synthesis, and increased collagen cross-linking. What is the most likely overall consequence of these changes on tissue mechanical properties?

Oncological Emergencies: Q24–28

courses.title: Palliative Care Nursing II

questions.question:
Describe the theories of grief under the following headings:
(a) Kubler-Ross's five stages
(b) Worden's four tasks of mourning
(c) Bowlby's attachment theory
(d) continuing bonds theory
(e) Explain the rationale for using these theories in nursing care of the bereaved.
(f) Distinguish between Kubler-Ross's stages and Worden's tasks, and between grief and mourning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Kubler-Ross: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance; developed for terminally ill patients and applied to significant loss; people may not follow the stages in order, or at all. Nursing: compassionate support without pushing in denial, safe space for anger, empathic listening in bargaining, rest and monitoring for clinical depression, new routines and goals in acceptance.

(b)
Worden: accept the reality of the loss; experience the pain of grief; adjust to an environment without the deceased; relocate the deceased emotionally and move on. Nursing: honest gentle communication, safe emotional expression, practical guidance and resources, rituals and memorials.

(c)
Bowlby: people are biologically predisposed to form strong attachments; grief is the reaction to disruption of the bond; phases are protest, despair and detachment.

(d)
Continuing bonds: challenges the notion that grief requires 'letting go'; ongoing connection through memories, rituals or writing supports healing, and nurses encourage photographs and rituals.

(e)
• Grief is not linear and manifests uniquely in each person, so frameworks guide nurses without fixing a single path.
• Worden stresses that grief is an active process; suppressing grief can delay healing and result in complicated grief.
• Bowlby explains why intensity of grief is tied to the depth of attachment.
• Grief has physical effects (exhaustion, appetite change, sleep disturbance) requiring monitoring, supportive care and watchfulness for complicated grief.

(f)
• Kubler-Ross describes emotional stages experienced by the mourner; Worden describes tasks the mourner must actively accomplish to heal and adjust.
• Bowlby's final phase is gradual letting go of the attachment, whereas continuing bonds holds that an ongoing connection supports healing.
• Grief is the internal emotional experience of loss; mourning is the outward, socially and culturally prescribed expression of grief, such as rituals and behaviours.
• Bereavement is the period following the death of a loved one, with emotional, psychological and social adjustments.

(a)
Severe pain (chronic pain related to cancer progression), breathlessness (impaired gas exchange), plus the son's disagreement with the patient's wishes and a language barrier with his wife.

(b)
• Opioid therapy: opioids bind to opiate receptors (mu, kappa, delta); binding to the mu receptor stabilises the membrane so the neuron does not fire. Low-dose morphine is the gold standard for dyspnoea and reduces the perception of breathlessness by acting on CNS receptors.
• Initial choice is based on route, need for continuous versus intermittent dosing and severity of pain; generally start with non-opioids and increase stepwise; guidance is also given on nausea, constipation and anxiety.

(c)
Pain: WHAT'S UP or PQRST format with numeric/visual analogue/face scales. Breathlessness: Modified Borg Scale, RDOS if non-verbal, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, vital signs.

(d)
• Nausea, CNS depression/sedation, pruritus, constipation, delirium, and endocrine dysfunction with long-term use.
• Morphine's active metabolite (morphine-6-glucuronide) accumulates in renal failure causing neuroexcitation and prolonged CNS effects; elderly are more sensitive to fentanyl; used appropriately, opioids do not significantly compromise oxygenation.

(e)
• Goals of care: open-ended questions, respect for his wish for comfort at home and consent; team explains natural progression and limited benefit of further interventions to the son.
• Islam: spiritual care is important; consult an imam about permissibility of certain medications and end-of-life rituals.
• Language: use a professional interpreter for his wife; respect the family's request for modesty and privacy during home visits.
questions.question:
A 68-year-old man with advanced non-small cell lung cancer, for whom curative options are no longer viable, is cared for at home. He has severe pain and breathlessness and wishes to remain comfortable at home. His son requests more aggressive treatment. The family practises Islam and his wife speaks limited English. The team prescribes opioids for pain and low-dose morphine for breathlessness.
(a) State the main nursing problems.
(b) Name the main pharmacological intervention and state how it acts and how it is chosen.
(c) Describe the assessment tools and parameters used.
(d) State the safety risks and adverse effects to monitor.
(e) Discuss the ethical, cultural, spiritual and family-related considerations.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Malignant epidural spinal cord compression, a structural oncological emergency.

(b)
• Musculoskeletal and neurological (back pain, motor weakness, sensory loss below the level of compression) and bladder and bowel function (dysfunction); risk of paralysis and irreversible neurological damage.
• Pain and neurological symptoms can also disturb sleep.

(c)
• Cause: metastatic tumour invasion into the vertebral column compressing the spinal cord, which can lead to ischaemia and irreversible neurological damage.
• Severe pain may signal an underlying oncological emergency, and untreated pain can escalate rapidly.

(d)
• Treat as an emergency because delay risks irreversible damage; stabilise with airway, breathing and circulation and control symptoms with analgesics.
• Give high-dose corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone) to reduce oedema.
• Arrange urgent MRI for diagnosis, then radiation therapy or surgical decompression.
• Reasoning: timely recognition prevents severe complications and improves outcomes; do not dismiss the pain, sleep or neurological symptoms as routine.
questions.question:
A patient with metastatic cancer reports back pain that is worse at night, then develops weakness and loss of sensation below a level of the trunk, together with bowel and bladder dysfunction.
(a) Identify the syndrome.
(b) State the body systems and domains affected.
(c) Explain the contributing causes and possible alternatives.
(d) Describe your clinical reasoning and the prioritisation of care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sleep has two states, NREM and REM, which alternate cyclically through the night. NREM stage 1: light transitional sleep (5-10%) with slow eye movements and reduced muscle activity.
• Stage 2: sleep spindles and K-complexes, 40-50% of total sleep; inhibits external disturbances and consolidates learning. Stage 3: deep slow-wave sleep (15-20%), essential for physical restoration, growth and immune support.

(b)
• REM: intense brain activity, vivid dreaming and rapid eye movements; brain activity mirrors wakefulness (heightened limbic activity, decreased prefrontal activity) while the body is nearly paralysed.
• REM cycles occur about every 90 minutes and lengthen as the night progresses (about 10 minutes early, up to an hour later); infants spend up to 50% in REM, adults about 20-25%.

(c)
• The circadian rhythm is the internal clock regulating the sleep-wake cycle over about 24 hours, influenced by light and darkness; the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus is the master regulator, responding to light from the eyes.
• Melatonin promotes sleepiness and rises in darkness; cortisol peaks in the morning to promote alertness and energy.

(d)
• Sleep is essential for physical and mental health; REM supports memory consolidation, emotional processing and creative thinking.
• Reduced deep sleep impairs cellular repair and metabolic regulation; chronic disturbance is linked to cardiovascular disease, obesity and immune suppression; REM disruption leads to mood disorders, anxiety and cognitive decline.
• Circadian disruption (shift work, time-zone travel) causes poor sleep quality, sleep disorders, mood disorders and metabolic imbalances; hospitalisation and irregular treatment schedules disrupt it in cancer patients.

(e)
• NREM focuses on physical restoration, with stage 3 deep sleep supporting growth and immunity; REM is crucial for cognitive function and emotional regulation.
• NREM stage 1 is light transition and stage 2 about 40-50% of sleep; REM involves vivid dreaming, near paralysis and brain activity like wakefulness.
• Disruption to REM causes cognitive impairment and emotional instability, whereas reduced deep NREM sleep impairs cellular repair.
questions.question:
Describe the physiology of sleep under the following headings:
(a) the sleep cycle and NREM stages
(b) REM sleep
(c) the role of the circadian rhythm
(d) Explain why sleep is essential and why its disruption affects health.
(e) Distinguish between NREM sleep and REM sleep.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Terminal respiratory congestion, commonly called the 'death rattle': rattling or gurgling sounds during respiration, usually in the final hours or days of life.

(b)
• It occurs because of the inability to swallow or cough, leading to pooled secretions in the upper airway.
• Conditions that impair the cough reflex or mucociliary clearance contribute to pooling of mucus, resulting in excessive secretions and terminal congestion.
• The sound is not usually distressing to the patient but causes significant anxiety to family members, who may interpret it as suffering.

(c)
• Assess respiratory symptoms (RDOS can be used in non-verbal patients) and use anticholinergic medications such as glycopyrrolate or scopolamine to reduce secretions.
• Use positioning techniques to facilitate drainage; gentle suctioning is part of secretion management.
• Family: open communication about the nature and implications of the 'death rattle'; reassure them about the normalcy of certain respiratory symptoms at end of life and educate them; involve caregivers in care planning.
• Interdisciplinary collaboration with palliative care specialists, respiratory therapists and social workers, and spiritual advisors or counsellors for existential distress.
questions.question:
The family of a patient in the final hours or days of life is alarmed by rattling or gurgling sounds with each breath. The patient can no longer swallow or cough.
(a) Recognise the problem.
(b) State the contributing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Outline the nursing management, including support for the family.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: intentionally ending a person's life to relieve suffering, typically in terminal illness; it remains controversial and highly debated in medical and legal fields.

(b)
Legality: in many jurisdictions euthanasia is illegal, while some countries and US states (e.g. the Netherlands, Belgium, California) have legalised physician-assisted suicide under strict criteria; nurses must know local laws to avoid legal consequences.

(c)
Autonomy: proponents argue it extends autonomy by allowing individuals to choose when and how to end suffering, but ethical concerns arise about pressure on vulnerable patients.

(d)
Euthanasia raises a conflict between non-maleficence (do no harm) and beneficence (doing what is best for the patient); providers are committed to relieving suffering through palliative care and many argue euthanasia conflicts with the duty to preserve life.

(e)
Slippery slope: legalisation could lead to unintended consequences such as vulnerable individuals being coerced or pressured; safeguards are critical to prevent abuses.

(f)
• Best practices: encourage comprehensive palliative care options to relieve suffering without resorting to euthanasia.
• Respect and support decisions that match the patient's values while avoiding coercion; stay informed about local legal and ethical frameworks.

(g)
• Vulnerable patients, particularly those who feel like a burden to their families, may feel pressured to choose euthanasia; palliative patients are among the most vulnerable (physical, emotional, spiritual distress), so nurses have an ethical duty to advocate for them.
• Consent must be given without coercion; some palliative patients feel pressured by family to pursue aggressive treatment against their own wishes.

(h)
• Euthanasia is intentionally ending a person's life to relieve suffering; physician-assisted suicide is where a person may end their own life with medical assistance.
• Legally, euthanasia is illegal in many jurisdictions, whereas some countries and states have legalised physician-assisted suicide under strict criteria.
• Core ethical principles guiding nursing practice are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice.
questions.question:
Describe euthanasia under the following headings:
(a) definition
(b) legality
(c) patient autonomy
(d) non-maleficence and beneficence
(e) slippery slope
(f) best practices for the nurse
(g) Explain why vulnerable patients are at risk in relation to euthanasia.
(h) Distinguish between euthanasia and physician-assisted suicide.

Describe the management of oncological emergencies under the following headings:
(a) meaning and classification
(b) immediate interventions and stabilisation
(c) condition-specific interventions
(d) the importance of timely recognition
(e) State the monitoring and safe-practice precautions.
(f) Explain the basis of the complications and of delayed recognition.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Oncological emergencies are acute, life-threatening conditions arising from cancer or its treatment: metabolic (tumour lysis syndrome, hypercalcaemia), structural (SVCS, spinal cord compression), haematologic (febrile neutropenia, hyperviscosity) and treatment-related (chemotherapy extravasation, radiation pneumonitis).

(b)
Immediate: maintain airway, breathing and circulation; oxygen or mechanical ventilation; IV access and fluid resuscitation for hypotension or shock; analgesics, antiemetics, antipyretics; anticonvulsants (lorazepam, levetiracetam) for seizures; vasopressors for refractory hypotension.

(c)
• TLS: aggressive IV hydration, rasburicase or allopurinol, correct electrolytes, dialysis in severe renal failure. Febrile neutropenia: broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately after blood cultures, monitor for sepsis, G-CSF in some cases.
• Spinal cord compression: high-dose corticosteroids, urgent MRI, radiation or surgical decompression. SVCS: elevate head, oxygen, corticosteroids or diuretics, radiotherapy or stenting.
• Hypercalcaemia: IV saline, loop diuretics, bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) or denosumab, treat malignancy. Tamponade: urgent pericardiocentesis. SIADH: fluid restriction, hypertonic saline in severe cases.

(d)
Timely recognition prevents severe complications, improves outcomes and survival, reduces morbidity and mortality, and allows appropriate resource allocation; multidisciplinary teams and patient education support prevention.

(e)
• Monitor electrolytes and haemodynamics and correct abnormalities (hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, acidosis) promptly.
• In neutropenia, fever above 38.3 C may be the only sign as signs of infection may be subtle or absent; watch for sepsis.
• In hypercalcaemia give aggressive rehydration; in TLS prevent renal failure with prompt hydration.

(f)
• TLS: rapid destruction of tumour cells releases potassium, phosphate and uric acid, causing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and hyperuricaemia, leading to renal failure and arrhythmias; febrile neutropenia: chemotherapy suppresses bone marrow (neutrophils below 500 cells/mm3).
• Hypercalcaemia: tumours produce PTHrP or induce bone resorption, raising serum calcium; SIADH: excess ADH causes water retention and hyponatraemia.
• Delay: analgesics or sedatives and deep sleep may mask confusion or seizures, and symptoms of tamponade may be attributed to fatigue or confusion, delaying diagnosis.

(a)
• Disease progression: tumours of the brain (increased intracranial pressure) or GI tract; advanced liver or kidney disease (toxin build-up stimulates the vomiting centre).
• Medications: opioids stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone; chemotherapy and antibiotics irritate the GI mucosa. Treatment effects: abdominal radiotherapy damages the GI lining; postoperative ileus or delayed gastric emptying.

(b)
Nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing symptoms in palliative care: they cause discomfort, disrupt nutritional intake, hinder the effectiveness of treatments and contribute to anorexia, weight loss and psychological distress.

(c)
• Antiemetics by class: dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, for gastric stasis), serotonin antagonists (ondansetron, for chemotherapy-induced nausea), corticosteroids (dexamethasone, for intractable nausea and intracranial pressure), antihistamines (cyclizine, for vestibular-related nausea).
• Non-pharmacological: small frequent meals reduce nausea and bloating; sipping clear fluids or ice chips; guided imagery and mindfulness to reduce anxiety and nausea; acupressure and acupuncture; sitting upright during meals.
• Procedures if refractory: nasogastric tube or PEG decompression, venting gastrostomy in inoperable obstruction.
• Justification: corticosteroid (dexamethasone) is prioritised because it is used for intractable nausea and intracranial pressure, matching the cause in this patient; the antiemetic class is matched to the cause.
questions.question:
A patient with a brain tumour causing raised intracranial pressure, who is on opioids, has persistent nausea and vomiting.
(a) Identify the risk factors and causes contributing to the problem.
(b) State the complications and effects of the problem.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the one you would prioritise.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Assessment: severity of dyspnoea, cough and secretions using tools such as the Modified Borg Scale, and the Respiratory Distress Observation Scale (RDOS) for non-verbal patients; identify underlying causes (lung metastases, heart failure, pneumonia, pleural effusion).

(b)
Non-pharmacological: elevate the head of bed or sit upright; fan on the face (stimulates trigeminal receptors); pursed-lip breathing; guided imagery, mindfulness and relaxation; oxygen therapy for hypoxia or severe breathlessness.

(c)
Pharmacological: low-dose morphine (gold standard, reduces perception of breathlessness via CNS receptors); lorazepam for anxiety; glycopyrrolate or scopolamine for terminal secretions; dexamethasone for airway inflammation or oedema; nebulised saline or bronchodilators.

(d)
Secretions: hydration to thin secretions; gentle suctioning; anticholinergics; antitussives and chest physiotherapy for cough.

(e)
Reassure and educate patients and families about the normalcy of certain respiratory symptoms; involve caregivers (positioning, medication administration); work with palliative specialists, respiratory therapists, social workers and spiritual advisors.

(f)
• Avoid unnecessary oxygen if it does not improve comfort; perform suctioning gently.
• Use opioids appropriately, since they reduce respiratory drive while making breathing more comfortable without significantly compromising oxygenation.
• Communicate openly with families about the 'death rattle', which is not usually distressing to the patient but alarms relatives.

(g)
• Breathlessness triggers panic, which worsens dyspnoea, creating a vicious cycle; hence relaxation, counselling and anxiolytics are needed.
• Reduced lung compliance (pulmonary fibrosis, pleural effusion), airway obstruction (tumours, mucus plugs, inflammation) and accumulated secretions keep symptoms recurring.
• Persistent coughing causes fatigue, insomnia and even rib fractures in frail patients.
• Terminal congestion arises from inability to swallow or cough, so pooled secretions recur in the final hours or days.
questions.question:
Describe the management of respiratory problems (dyspnoea, cough, excessive secretions and terminal respiratory congestion) under the following headings:
(a) assessment
(b) non-pharmacological interventions
(c) pharmacological interventions
(d) secretion management
(e) emotional support and collaboration
(f) State the safe-practice precautions.
(g) Explain the basis of the recurrence, complications or failure of symptom control.

Describe the ethical decision-making framework in nursing under the following headings:
(a) meaning and purpose
(b) key steps
(c) models
(d) support structures
(e) ethical theories
(f) Explain why the framework is needed in palliative care and its impact.
(g) Distinguish between utilitarianism and deontology.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The ethical decision-making framework ensures patient care aligns with moral principles and professional standards; ethical dilemmas arise from conflicting values, principles or interests.

(b)
Key steps: identifying the issue, evaluating options and making informed choices.

(c)
• MORAL model: Massage dilemma, Outline options, Review criteria, Affirm commitment, Look back.
• Four-Quadrant approach: medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life, contextual features.
• 6-step process (Lo and Snyder): Identify, Gather, Clarify, Explore, Implement, Reflect.

(d)
Ethics committees: multidisciplinary groups offering guidance and reducing decision-making burdens; professional guidelines: ANA and ICN ethical codes give consistent decision-making standards.

(e)
Theories: principle-based (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice), virtue ethics (integrity and compassion), utilitarianism and deontology; applied to end-of-life care, resource allocation and informed consent.

(f)
• Palliative care often involves dilemmas such as balancing patient autonomy with family wishes or managing end-of-life decisions.
• Impact: ethical decision-making fosters trust, societal harmony and quality patient care; core principles guide nursing practice.
• Call to action: continuously educate on ethical challenges, uphold integrity and protect patient dignity.

(g)
• Utilitarianism: maximise well-being.
• Deontology: duty over outcomes.

(a)
Dyspnoea: a subjective sensation of breathlessness accompanied by anxiety, fatigue and fear; the unmet need is relief of anxiety and fear of being alone at night.

(b)
Respiratory system, plus psychological (anxiety, fear, panic), social (fear of being alone, dependency on others) and spiritual/existential (fear of death, uncertainty); loss of independence and reduced quality of life.

(c)
• Underlying COPD: airway narrowing and chronic inflammation cause dyspnoea and increased secretions; reduced lung compliance and airway obstruction; hypoxia; the illness, its comorbidities or their therapy.
• Anxiety and fear trigger panic, which worsens dyspnoea, creating a vicious cycle of breathlessness and emotional distress.

(d)
• The nurse must consider causes across all dimensions: the initial problem ('ineffective air exchange') is incomplete, and fear of being alone at night is a cause found through inter-dimensional assessment.
• Assess severity (Modified Borg Scale), then use non-pharmacological measures (upright position, fan, pursed-lip breathing, relaxation) and oxygen if hypoxic; low-dose morphine and lorazepam for anxiety; counselling to break the cycle.
• Involve caregivers in care planning, provide reassurance and education, and use interdisciplinary support including spiritual advisors.
questions.question:
A patient with end-stage chronic obstructive pulmonary disease complains of shortness of breath. The first impression is that it is due to ineffective air exchange in the lung, but on fuller assessment the episodes occur because of fear of being alone at night, and the patient is anxious.
(a) Identify the symptom and the unmet need.
(b) State the body systems and domains affected.
(c) Explain the contributing causes.
(d) Describe your clinical reasoning and the prioritisation of care.

Describe pain in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) definition
(b) physiology
(c) classification of types
(d) State how the types and mechanisms of pain relate to common pain problems in patients.
(e) Explain how pain spreads to affect the psychological, emotional and spiritual domains (total pain) and quality of life.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage; it is subjective, varies from person to person and from time to time, is whatever the person says it is, and is a complex bio-psychosocial event.

(b)
Physiology: transduction (stimulus converted to electrical energy in nociceptors); transmission (A-delta myelinated fibres carry sharp localised pain, C fibres carry poorly localised, burning, persistent pain via spinothalamic tracts); perception (somatosensory cortex identifies location and intensity); modulation (endogenous opioids inhibit transmission).

(c)
Types: by duration (acute or chronic), mechanism (nociceptive or neuropathic), origin (somatic or visceral) and situation (incidental, breakthrough, procedural); by source: superficial, deep somatic, visceral, psychogenic.

(d)
• Fast pain (A-delta): sharp, pricking, electric; slow pain (C fibres): dull, aching, burning, throbbing, diffuse, follows fast pain.
• Visceral pain from internal organs is diffuse at first and hard to localise; referred pain is felt in another body part; phantom limb pain develops after amputation.
• Conditions with chronic pain include cancer, fibromyalgia, spinal injury, headaches, back injury, arthritis and nerve damage; about 80% of people with advanced cancer and 50% with advanced HIV have moderate or severe pain.
• Nociceptive pain (mechanical, thermal or chemical stimulation) should be differentiated from neuropathic pain to choose the best treatment.

(e)
• Total pain: patients experience pain on physical, psychological, emotional and spiritual levels, so effective treatment requires holistic assessment.
• Pain history explores effects on quality of life, emotional and spiritual distress and coping abilities; physical symptoms such as pain coexist with anxiety or depression.
• Pain assessment in palliative care addresses emotional, psychological, spiritual and social dimensions, considering past pain experiences and cultural attitudes.
• Cancer pain is a common cause of sleep disturbance; unrelieved symptoms can cause anxiety, depression and frustration.
• Effective symptom control improves comfort, functionality and quality of life, and reduces the caregiving burden on families.

(a)
Symptom management enhances comfort, preserves dignity (prevents visible decline), improves functionality, supports emotional well-being, enhances family relationships, facilitates holistic care, promotes satisfaction and supports caregiver well-being.

(b)
• Anxiety and depression (concerns about weight loss, pain, discomfort and an uncertain illness trajectory), also in caregivers witnessing decline and anticipating loss.
• Grief and loss (anticipatory grief for health, independence and life); fear and uncertainty about progression, treatment options and symptom management.
• Spiritual and existential concerns (questions about life, death and one's place in the world); social isolation from fatigue, weakness and frequent appointments, worsening loneliness and depression.

(c)
• ACS causes severe weight loss, muscle wasting and reduced functional capacity; GI symptoms cause discomfort, disrupt nutritional intake and hinder treatment; mental health issues such as anxiety and depression compound physical distress.
• Unrelieved symptoms cause anxiety, depression and frustration, while relief fosters emotional stability, peace and acceptance.

(d)
• Uncontrolled symptoms strain relationships and cause caregiver burnout; relief lets patients engage meaningfully with family and reduces the caregiving burden.
• Symptom control maintains independence, meaningful activities, identity and purpose.
• Team: physicians, nurses, social workers (counselling, community resources, financial and logistic help), chaplains, dietitians, physical and occupational therapists, psychologists (individual and family therapy).
• Interventions: active listening and empathic communication; counselling and psychotherapy; relaxation techniques (deep breathing, mindfulness, meditation); support groups.
• Advance care planning discussions (goals of care, preferred place of care, pain and symptom management); effective management of pain, nausea and fatigue.
• At end of life, symptom control ensures a peaceful transition with dignity and minimal suffering.
questions.question:
Describe the psychosocial and emotional impact of anorexia-cachexia syndrome and gastrointestinal problems under the following headings:
(a) why symptom management matters
(b) the concerns of patients and caregivers
(c) State how the physical symptoms relate to these psychosocial concerns.
(d) Explain how the problem spreads to affect the family and functional domains and describe the team and interventions that address it.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cough and excessive secretions are common in advanced disease, often from infections, tumour obstruction or pulmonary oedema, or from the primary pulmonary pathology (unrelated causes should not be excluded).
• COPD: airway narrowing and chronic inflammation increase secretions; heart failure causes pulmonary congestion; impaired cough reflex or mucociliary clearance causes pooling of mucus; airway obstruction by tumours, mucus plugs or inflammation; reduced lung compliance.

(b)
Complications: ineffective cough causes distress; noisy breathing and discomfort; disrupted sleep (insomnia), impaired communication and fatigue; rib fractures in frail patients; reduced quality of life and anxiety about breathing.

(c)
• Pharmacological: antitussives and anticholinergics; dexamethasone for airway inflammation or oedema from tumours; nebulised saline or bronchodilators to relieve obstruction and improve mucus clearance.
• Non-pharmacological: chest physiotherapy, hydration adjustments, gentle suctioning, positioning (elevate head of bed).
• Justification: hydration is a simple first measure because it thins secretions and makes them easier to expel; if tumour-related airway inflammation or oedema is the cause, dexamethasone is preferred.
questions.question:
A frail patient with advanced lung disease has a persistent, ineffective cough with excessive secretions and noisy breathing.
(a) Identify the risk factors and causes contributing to the problem.
(b) State the complications and effects of the problem.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the one you would prioritise.

Describe pain assessment in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) approach and pain history
(b) assessment formats
(c) pain scales and tools
(d) nursing responsibilities
(e) State the safe-practice precautions in pain assessment.
(f) Explain the basis of inaccurate or failed pain assessment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Approach: establish a relationship, encourage the patient to do most of the talking, begin with a wide-angle open question, watch for clues and avoid jumping to conclusions; pain history covers effects on quality of life, emotional and spiritual distress, coping, and previous pain experience and measures that did or did not help.

(b)
• WHAT'S UP: Where, How it feels (shooting, burning, dull, sharp), Aggravating/alleviating factors, Timing, Severity (0-10, 0-5 or faces), Useful other data (itching, nausea, sedation, constipation), Perception of cause.
• PQRST: Palliative/Provocative factors, Quality, Radiation, Severity (and effect on life), Temporal factors; OLDCART may also be used.

(c)
Scales: descriptive, numeric, visual analogue, percentage, coin and face; Wong-Baker for children; FLACC for non-verbal patients; CPOT for critically ill patients unable to communicate (facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, ventilator compliance).

(d)
• Responsibilities: document location, intensity, type and factors that worsen or relieve pain; regular re-evaluation; documentation of effectiveness and follow-up; family and staff education.
• Assess subjective (patient-reported) and objective (observable) indicators holistically across physical, emotional, psychological, spiritual and social dimensions, including past pain experiences and cultural attitudes.

(e)
• Tools must be valid, reliable and relevant; choose the tool suited to the patient (FLACC or behavioural observation for non-verbal patients, Wong-Baker for children, CPOT for critically ill).
• Use gentle techniques and obtain consent; accept that pain is whatever the person says it is.
• Recognise that severe pain may signal an oncological emergency such as spinal cord compression or tumour lysis syndrome, where untreated pain can rapidly escalate.

(f)
• Pain is subjective, varies from person to person and from time to time, and is a complex bio-psychosocial event.
• Communication barriers (altered mental status, mechanical ventilation, severe pain) reduce self-report; symptoms are often underreported in ICU patients.
• Jumping to conclusions or ignoring emotional and spiritual distress (total pain) leaves the assessment incomplete.

questions.question:
Describe sleep disturbances in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) definition
(b) major types
(c) prevalence
(d) common causes
(e) State how the causes and types relate to the problems commonly seen in patients with cancer.
(f) Explain how sleep disturbance can spread to affect physical, mental, behavioural and quality-of-life domains and the recognition of oncological emergencies.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: conditions that disrupt the normal sleep cycle, leading to inadequate or poor-quality sleep (difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, waking too early, non-refreshing sleep).

(b)
Types: insomnia; sleep apnoea (obstructive or central); hypersomnia; parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors, bruxism).

(c)
Prevalence: particularly common in chronic or terminal illness; over 50% of individuals in palliative care experience sleep problems.

(d)
Medical causes: pain (cancer, arthritis), medication side effects (steroids, opioids), breathlessness, frequent urination. Psychological: anxiety, depression, emotional distress related to illness or impending death. Lifestyle: poor sleep hygiene, lack of activity, caffeine and alcohol.

(e)
• Cancer pain from tumours affecting bones, organs or nerves makes it hard to fall or stay asleep; chemotherapy, radiation, corticosteroids and opioids cause insomnia, wakefulness and circadian disruption; hospitalisation and irregular treatment schedules disrupt the sleep-wake cycle.
• Stress of diagnosis causes insomnia, anxiety and depression; brain or spinal metastases cause cognitive dysfunction and disturbed sleep; electrolyte imbalances (hypercalcaemia, tumour lysis) disrupt sleep.

(f)
• Physical: cardiovascular disease, obesity, weakened immunity, worsened pain; reduced deep sleep impairs cellular repair and metabolic regulation; sleep deprivation suppresses immunity and raises infection risk.
• Mental: anxiety, depression and cognitive impairment; REM disruption leads to mood disorders and emotional instability.
• Behavioural and quality of life: impaired concentration, decision-making and reaction times (accident risk); reduced energy, impaired daily functioning, diminished emotional well-being.
• Sedation or deep sleep from pain medication may delay recognition of emergencies such as tumour lysis syndrome or hypercalcaemia (confusion, seizures unnoticed).
• Disrupted sleep may cause cardiac tamponade symptoms (breathlessness, dizziness, chest pain) to be attributed to fatigue or confusion, delaying diagnosis.
• A vicious cycle results: sleep disturbance can contribute to or mask emergencies, and emergencies further disrupt sleep; holistic care addresses physical, emotional, psychological, social and spiritual needs.

questions.question:
Describe palliative care nursing under the following headings:
(a) definition
(b) goals
(c) distinguishing features
(d) the attitudes and principles required for successful care
(e) Explain why the patient and family are treated as one unit of care and why continuity of care, crisis prevention and caregiver support are emphasised.
(f) Distinguish between palliative care and hospice care, stating one similarity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: a scientific and humanistic approach that improves quality of life by addressing physical needs (pain and other symptoms), emotional support, psychological and spiritual care and building support systems; WHO: improves quality of life of patients with life-limiting illnesses and their families through prevention and relief of physical, psychosocial and spiritual suffering.

(b)
• Goals: promote quality of life across the illness trajectory through relief of suffering, including care of the dying and bereavement follow-up; whole-person care of physical, psychological, social, spiritual and existential aspects of patient and family.
• Also: effective pain and symptom management, psychosocial and spiritual needs, cultural values in the care plan, support in loss, grief and bereavement, ethical and legal decision-making, advocacy for wishes, therapeutic communication, collaborative practice.

(c)
Features: a 'whole-person' philosophy across the lifespan and diverse settings; the individual is central to the healing relationship; the nurse's relationship with patient and family is crucial; inter-dimensional assessment (end-stage COPD breathlessness may stem from fear of being alone at night).

(d)
• Attitudes: caring attitude (sensitivity, empathy, compassion, non-judgemental), consideration of individuality, cultural considerations, consent before treatment is given or withdrawn, choice of site of care (home whenever possible).
• Principles: good communication among professionals and with families; treatment appropriate to stage and prognosis (futile treatment given because 'you have to do something' is unethical); inter-professional, excellent, consistent, coordinated and continuous care; crisis prevention; caregiver support; continued reassessment.

(e)
• The patient and family are the unit of care; relatives of patients with advanced disease suffer considerable emotional and physical distress, especially at home, and palliative care often succeeds or fails on the support given to caring relatives.
• Continuity: continuous symptomatic and supportive care from referral until death is basic; problems most often arise when patients move between places of care.
• Crisis prevention: careful planning, forewarning patients and families of likely problems and making contingency plans to minimise physical and emotional distress.

(f)
• Palliative care is ideally implemented alongside curative care; hospice care is for those nearing end of life, with life expectancy of less than 6 months certified by a physician, for whom curative treatment is no longer an option or desired.
• Hospice is a defined integrated model focusing on comfort, dignity, quality of life and relationship closure, directed by patient/family goals; it aims to maximise quality of life in the last phases of an incurable disease.
• Similarity: both use an interdisciplinary team, aim to improve comfort and reduce complications, and are family-oriented.

(a)
Holistic assessment: physical, psychological, social and spiritual dimensions are evaluated (pain or fatigue may coexist with anxiety or depression), enabling personalised care plans. Patient and family-centred care: the patient and family are a unit of care, involved in decisions with respect for preferences, cultural values and beliefs.

(b)
Interdisciplinary collaboration (doctors, nurses, social workers, chaplains, therapists pool expertise) and communication skills (open, honest, empathetic; transparent discussion of prognosis supports shared decisions and reduces anxiety).

(c)
Cultural sensitivity (beliefs shape perception of illness, death and care; fosters trust) and ethical considerations (autonomy versus family wishes, informed consent, confidentiality, right to choose, e.g. declining life-prolonging treatment for comfort care).

(d)
Continuous reassessment, dignity and respect, and equity in care (access regardless of socioeconomic status, culture or location; fair resource allocation).

(e)
• Patients' conditions and family dynamics change over time, so ongoing assessment keeps care aligned with evolving needs; as illness progresses, priorities may shift from symptom management to emotional and spiritual support.
• Families are often primary caregivers and decision-makers, so their capacity, resources, emotional readiness, communication styles, coping and beliefs must be assessed; family involvement improves quality of care and outcomes and reduces family anxiety, depression and PTSD.

(f)
• Physical assessment: aims to alleviate suffering by identifying distressing symptoms (pain, dyspnoea, fatigue, nausea); scope is vital signs, organ systems, functional status and comfort.
• Physical tools and methods: observation, palpation, auscultation, percussion, ESAS, pain scales (NRS, VAS, FLACC, CPOT), CMSAS, e-POS.
• Psychosocial assessment: structured evaluation of mental, emotional, social and behavioural well-being to understand how these factors influence health and quality of life.
• Components: psychological (emotional state, cognitive function, coping), social (family/caregiver support, network and isolation, cultural and religious influences), economic (financial stress, access to care, employment/insurance), spiritual/existential (beliefs, meaning, end-of-life concerns).
• Psychosocial tools: patient-centred interviews, HADS, Distress Thermometer, POS, genograms/ecomaps, Caregiver Strain Index, FICA, behavioural observation.
• Both feed into a multidisciplinary approach that delivers holistic, patient-centred care.
questions.question:
Describe the principles of patient and family assessment in palliative care nursing under the following headings:
(a) holistic assessment and patient and family-centred care
(b) interdisciplinary collaboration and communication skills
(c) cultural sensitivity and ethical considerations
(d) continuous reassessment, dignity and respect, and equity in care
(e) Explain why assessment must be continuous and why the patient and family are assessed together.
(f) Distinguish between physical assessment and psychosocial assessment in terms of purpose, scope and tools.

Describe communication in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) importance
(b) key principles
(c) barriers
(d) State how each barrier leads to the common problems seen in patients and families.
(e) Explain how poor communication can spread to affect the psychosocial, family and care domains and what solutions and benefits apply.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Importance: builds trust; reduces anxiety; improves care outcomes by personalising care to values and goals; facilitates decision-making including end-of-life decisions; supports emotional well-being.

(b)
Principles: empathy (NURSE: Name, Understand, Respect, Support, Explore); active listening (paraphrasing, open-ended questions, verbal and non-verbal cues); clarity and honesty (jargon-free); cultural sensitivity; a patient- and family-centred approach.

(c)
Barriers: emotional distress; cultural and language barriers; time constraints; physical barriers (patient's condition, healthcare environment, logistics).

(d)
• Emotional distress (fear of death, uncertainty, loss) makes patients struggle to articulate needs and withdraw, leading to misunderstandings and inadequate care.
• Cultural and language barriers: different beliefs about illness, treatment and dying (death may be taboo) and language mismatch make it hard to convey information, discuss symptoms or address emotions, causing confusion, mistrust and poor adherence to care plans.
• Time constraints cause rushed interactions and families feel unheard; prognosis and end-of-life talks need careful explanation and time for questions.
• Physical barriers: fatigue, pain, breathlessness or cognitive decline make communication difficult for patients.

(e)
• Patients and families feel unheard or unsupported and fear and uncertainty about prognosis go unaddressed; families understand less about the condition and care plan, increasing stress and conflict with teams.
• Symptoms are expressed less accurately, weakening symptom management; end-of-life care may not match the patient's wishes.
• Burnout affects communication skills and training gaps hinder interactions.
• Solutions: self-care (physical activity, sleep, relaxation), peer support, workshops and role-playing exercises.
• Benefits of effective communication: better understanding and decisions, emotional support, stronger relationships, better symptom management, family satisfaction, fewer conflicts and better end-of-life planning.

questions.question:
A patient with a terminal condition is being asked about cardiopulmonary resuscitation. The family struggles with the idea of withholding CPR, while the patient's values and goals of care favour comfort and dignity.
(a) State the nursing and ethical problem.
(b) Name the intervention and the steps involved.
(c) Describe the assessment parameters to be used.
(d) State the safety, legal and ethical risks to monitor.
(e) Discuss the family, cultural and ethical considerations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Decision-making about CPR and a 'Do Not Resuscitate' (DNR) order, balancing autonomy and wishes, best interests and beneficence, and family involvement; CPR may be medically futile and prolong suffering without improving quality of life.

(b)
Hold early and ongoing conversations with the patient and family about CPR and DNR; explain possible outcomes (e.g. survival with severe disability, prolonged suffering); review goals of care to see whether CPR fits the care plan; document the DNR order and make it accessible in the medical record, informing all team members.

(c)
Assess the patient's decision-making capacity regularly (cognitive impairment or delirium from illness or medications), values and goals of care, nature of illness, prognosis and likelihood of CPR success; review advance directives (living will, durable power of attorney) and update them as the condition progresses.

(d)
• Failure to properly document a DNR can lead to legal liability if resuscitation is attempted against the patient's wishes.
• Consent must be voluntary: patients may feel pressured by family toward aggressive treatment; continuing futile CPR does not align with beneficence.

(e)
• Family members may need to take part when the patient cannot decide, including a healthcare proxy or legal representative; open honest conversations about prognosis and the patient's wishes.
• Respect cultural and religious values; family conferences and ethics committees can help resolve conflicts while advocating for the patient's wishes.

questions.question:
A patient receiving palliative care has a history of heart failure and poor protein intake and is taking steroids. The legs, ankles and feet are swollen and leave an indentation when pressed, and the abdomen is distended with discomfort and a feeling of fullness.
(a) Identify the risk factors that predispose to this problem.
(b) State the complications and effects on the patient's quality of life.
(c) Outline the management options (non-pharmacological, pharmacological and procedural) and justify the one you would prioritise.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Oedema (peripheral pitting oedema with ascites). Risk factors: heart failure (heart struggles to pump, fluid accumulates in extremities and lungs); kidney dysfunction; liver disease such as cirrhosis (ascites or leg swelling); medications, especially steroids and some antihypertensives; malnutrition (lack of protein lowers oncotic pressure so fluid leaks into tissue); lymphatic blockage after cancer treatment, surgery or radiation.

(b)
• Complications: swelling and discomfort limiting mobility (difficulty walking or wearing shoes); pain and sensitivity; breathing difficulty in pulmonary oedema; skin breakdown or infection in severe cases.
• Ascites causes abdominal discomfort and fullness affecting appetite and intake, leading to weight loss and muscle wasting; visible swelling affects body image and self-esteem (withdrawal, isolation, depression, anxiety).
• Restricted activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, moving), loss of independence, increased care needs straining family caregivers, and sleep disruption causing fatigue.

(c)
• Non-pharmacological: elevation of limbs above heart level, gentle limb massage, graduated compression stockings/bandaging.
• Pharmacological: diuretics (furosemide, spironolactone) with monitoring of electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalaemia or dehydration.
• Procedural: paracentesis drains abdominal fluid (ascites) to relieve pressure; thoracentesis removes pleural fluid; patient and family education on signs of worsening oedema and realistic expectations.
• Justification: non-pharmacological measures are the first line of defence, especially to minimise medication burden, and are prioritised for peripheral oedema; for severe ascites, paracentesis gives significant symptom relief and comfort.

(a)
Oedema (swelling) occurs when excess fluid builds up in the body tissues, leading to visible swelling, often in the legs, ankles and feet and sometimes in the abdomen or other areas.

(b)
Types: peripheral (extremities; pitting or non-pitting), pulmonary (fluid in the lungs), ascites (abdominal cavity), lymphoedema (lymphatic blockage in arms or legs), cerebral (brain tissue) and macular (macula of the eye).

(c)
Causes: heart failure; kidney dysfunction; liver disease such as cirrhosis; medications (steroids, some antihypertensives); malnutrition (lack of protein lowers oncotic pressure).

(d)
• Peripheral oedema is linked to heart failure, kidney dysfunction or venous insufficiency; pulmonary oedema to advanced heart disease or severe respiratory conditions (shortness of breath, cough, wheezing).
• Ascites is linked to liver disease or malignancy (abdominal distension, discomfort, appetite changes); lymphoedema to cancer treatment, surgery or radiation affecting lymph nodes.
• Cerebral oedema occurs with brain tumours, infections or injury (headaches, altered consciousness, neurological deficits); macular oedema with diabetes or certain cancer treatments (vision problems).

(e)
• Physical: swelling limits mobility and daily activity; swollen areas become painful or sensitive, needing medication with its own side effects; pulmonary oedema causes distressing breathlessness.
• Psychological: visible swelling affects self-esteem and body image, leading to self-consciousness, withdrawal, isolation, depression or anxiety.
• Nutritional: ascites causes fullness and discomfort, affecting appetite and intake, leading to weight loss and muscle wasting.
• Functional: restricts bathing, dressing and moving, causing loss of independence and reliance on caregivers that affects relationship dynamics.
• Family and care: increased care needs mean more frequent medical attention, straining the health system and family caregivers (stress and anxiety).
• Sleep: discomfort interferes with sleep, causing fatigue and reduced ability to cope with other symptoms; in severe cases skin breakdown or infection may occur.
questions.question:
Describe oedema in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) definition
(b) main types
(c) causes
(d) State how each type and cause relates to the common problems seen in patients.
(e) Explain how oedema can spread to affect the physical, psychological, nutritional, functional, sleep and family domains and cause deficit.

A patient with advanced ovarian or colorectal cancer, who has had previous abdominal surgery and is taking opioids, has nausea, vomiting and abdominal distension.
(a) Recognise the problem.
(b) State the contributing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Bowel obstruction, a critical and potentially life-threatening problem in palliative care; intestinal obstruction is common in advanced malignancies, particularly ovarian and colorectal cancers.

(b)
• Disease progression: tumours in the abdomen or pelvis compress or block the intestines; adhesions from prior surgery cause mechanical obstruction; hernias.
• Medications: opioids may contribute to pseudo-obstruction by reducing peristalsis. Treatment: radiotherapy causes fibrosis or scarring of the intestinal wall, leading to partial or complete obstruction.

(c)
• Palliative procedures for symptoms refractory to medical and non-medical measures: decompression by nasogastric tube or PEG to relieve nausea, vomiting and abdominal distension; stenting for colorectal or esophageal obstruction; venting gastrostomy for continuous drainage in inoperable obstruction.
• Also: antiemetics, low-fibre diet in partial obstruction, hydration, a multidisciplinary approach balancing symptom control and quality of life while respecting patient preferences, and psychosocial support for patient and caregivers.

questions.question:
A patient with lung cancer develops facial swelling, distended neck veins and swelling of the upper limbs, with shortness of breath and cough. Headache and dizziness are also present.
(a) Recognise the condition.
(b) State the contributing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS), a structural oncological emergency.

(b)
• Contributing factors: compression or obstruction of the superior vena cava by a tumour (e.g. lung cancer, lymphoma) or thrombosis.
• Pathophysiology: obstruction leads to venous congestion in the upper body, producing facial swelling, neck vein distension, upper limb oedema, dyspnoea and cough; headache, dizziness or altered mental status occur if cerebral oedema develops.

(c)
• Stabilise: maintain airway, breathing and circulation, give oxygen, secure IV access, and control symptoms.
• Elevate the head of the bed; give corticosteroids to reduce inflammation or diuretics for symptom relief.
• Radiation therapy or chemotherapy to reduce tumour size; stenting or bypass surgery in severe cases; emergency radiotherapy or stenting if indicated.
• Early recognition and management alleviate symptoms and prevent further complications.

questions.question:
Describe the physical assessment of a critically ill patient in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) purpose and scope
(b) assessment methods
(c) practical steps from preparation to documentation
(d) key considerations for the palliative care nurse
(e) State the safe-practice precautions to be observed during the assessment.
