(f) Explain the basis of the challenges that can make the assessment difficult or unreliable in critically ill patients.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Purpose and scope: to alleviate suffering by identifying distressing symptoms (pain, dyspnoea, fatigue, nausea); covers vital signs, organ systems, functional status and comfort; it informs decisions and goals and is therapeutic as well as diagnostic.

(b)
• Methods: inspection (skin colour, swelling, wounds, nutritional status, distress), palpation (tenderness, organ enlargement, fluid, masses or ascites), auscultation (breath, heart and bowel sounds), percussion (fluid, air or solid masses in chest and abdomen).
• Patient self-reporting (e.g. ESAS for symptom severity), vital signs monitoring (changes may indicate deterioration) and functional assessment (mobility, strength, activity levels).

(c)
• Steps: preparation (privacy, quiet, lighting, stethoscope, BP cuff, thermometer, pulse oximeter, hand hygiene, explain and gain consent); initial observation (appearance, posture, consciousness, orientation, non-verbal cues); vital signs including oxygen saturation compared with baseline.
• Head-to-toe examination (head and neck, skin, cardiovascular, respiratory, GI, musculoskeletal, neurological); pain assessment with standardised tools (NRS, Wong-Baker, FLACC, CPOT); psychosocial and emotional well-being; accurate documentation, prompt communication of critical findings and interdisciplinary follow-up.

(d)
Considerations: sensitivity and respect for dignity, comfort-focused rather than aggressive interventions, involving family or caregivers, building rapport, informed consent, cultural sensitivity and active listening.

(e)
• Obtain consent and explain the procedure; use gentle techniques because of fragility and pain; ensure privacy (drapes, screens, only necessary personnel); prioritise comfort over exhaustive investigations in severe pain; respect the patient's right to refuse parts of the assessment.
• Respect cultural norms on modesty, gender and handling of the body (e.g. chaperone); use professional interpreters; share findings with family only with the patient's consent; avoid coercion.

(f)
• Communication barriers: altered mental status, mechanical ventilation or severe pain limit communication, so non-verbal cues such as facial expression and body language become essential.
• Fragility and pain: touch or movement may worsen discomfort. Multisystem involvement: symptoms such as fatigue may stem from anaemia, respiratory distress or cardiac dysfunction, requiring interdisciplinary collaboration.
• Rapid changes: the condition can deteriorate quickly, so frequent reassessment and prompt intervention are needed.
• Psychological and emotional dimensions: physical symptoms such as pain or dyspnoea are intertwined with psychological distress, requiring a dual focus.

(a)
Chronic pain related to cancer progression (facial grimacing, guarding, reported pain); impaired gas exchange related to advanced lung cancer (dyspnoea, accessory muscle use); risk for infection related to impaired skin integrity from oedema and immobility; terminal respiratory congestion, fear and anxiety, and family distress.

(b)
• Respiratory (tachypnoea, hypoxia, gurgling), cardiovascular (weak pulses), integumentary (oedema, skin), abdomen (ascites and distension).
• Psychological (fear of dying, anxiety, restlessness), social (feels a burden, family distress) and spiritual/existential (fear of death).

(c)
• Cancer: tumour growth or treatment effects can obstruct airways or cause inflammation; heart failure: fluid accumulation in lungs and extremities causes pulmonary congestion and oedema; ascites relates to malignancy or liver disease.
• Gurgling reflects pooled secretions from inability to swallow or cough; anxiety and fear trigger panic that worsens dyspnoea (vicious cycle); pain is aggravated by movement and deep breathing.

(d)
• Care is sequenced as: pain, then impaired gas exchange, then infection risk.
• Gas exchange: upright/Fowler's position (lung expansion, less diaphragm pressure), prescribed oxygen (goal saturation above 90%), breathing and relaxation techniques taught to family, prescribed morphine to reduce breathlessness.
• Pain: regular assessment with a validated scale, massage and guided imagery, analgesics such as morphine for scheduled and breakthrough pain.
• Infection risk: skin hygiene, regular skin inspection, monitoring for fever and redness. Reassure and educate the family, involve them in care planning and provide emotional support.
questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman with stage IV lung cancer and chronic heart failure is receiving home-based palliative care. Findings: respiratory rate 30/min, use of accessory muscles, audible gurgling sounds, oxygen saturation 86% on room air; BP 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 98 bpm, weak but palpable peripheral pulses; grade 3 pitting oedema of both lower limbs with cool, pale, shiny skin and no breakdown; distended abdomen with ascites; dull constant pain 7/10 worse on movement and deep breathing. She fears dying, worries about being a burden, is restless and anxious, and her family is distressed and wants guidance.
(a) Identify the priority problems and needs.
(b) State the body systems and domains affected.
(c) Explain the contributing causes of the findings.
(d) Describe your clinical reasoning and the order in which care would be prioritised.

A patient with advanced illness who is receiving chemotherapy and antibiotics and has had pelvic radiotherapy has frequent watery stools.
(a) Identify the risk factors and causes contributing to the problem.
(b) State the complications and effects of the problem.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the one you would prioritise.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Diarrhoea. Disease: tumours in the colon or rectum (malabsorption or secretory diarrhoea) and endocrine tumours such as carcinoid tumours secreting hormones.
• Medications: antibiotics disrupt gut microbiota (diarrhoea or infection such as Clostridioides difficile); chemotherapy damages the intestinal lining.
• Treatment effects: pelvic or abdominal radiotherapy can cause radiation enteritis; bowel resections can cause short bowel syndrome and impaired nutrient absorption.

(b)
Diarrhoea can severely affect quality of life, causing dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, infection (e.g. Clostridioides difficile) and impaired nutrient absorption.

(c)
• Pharmacological: loperamide slows gut motility and reduces frequency; octreotide is effective for refractory diarrhoea, particularly high-output secretory diarrhoea in cancer.
• Non-pharmacological: low-fibre diet for diarrhoea; maintaining hydration prevents electrolyte imbalances and other complications.
• Justification: loperamide slows gut motility and reduces stool frequency, which suits diarrhoea caused by chemotherapy, antibiotics or radiation; octreotide is for refractory high-output secretory diarrhoea; hydration is maintained throughout to prevent dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

(a)
Chronic, slow pain carried by unmyelinated C fibres (dull, aching, more diffuse); cancer is a condition associated with chronic pain; in palliative care it is 'total pain' with physical, psychological, emotional and spiritual components.

(b)
• Transduction: the painful stimulus is converted to electrical energy at the nociceptor; transmission: C fibres relay poorly localised, burning, persistent impulses via the spinothalamic tracts.
• Perception: the somatosensory cortex identifies location and intensity with physiological and behavioural responses; modulation: endogenous opioids inhibit transmission.

(c)
• Build a relationship, let the patient do most of the talking, start with a wide-angle open question, watch for clues and avoid jumping to conclusions; obtain a pain history (effects on quality of life, emotional and spiritual distress, coping, previous pain experience and what helped).
• Use WHAT'S UP (Where, How it feels, Aggravating/alleviating factors, Timing, Severity 0-10, Useful other data, Perception) or PQRST or OLDCART; scales (numeric, visual analogue, descriptive, percentage, coin, face) must be valid, reliable and relevant.

(d)
• Treatment based on assessment: severity, nociceptive versus neuropathic, stepwise approach; start with non-opioids (acetaminophen, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors), then opioids, with adjuncts (anticonvulsants, steroids, TCAs).
• Non-pharmacological: relaxation techniques, massage therapy, music therapy, aromatherapy; ensure availability of PRN and emergency medications, staff education and pharmacy consultant use.

(e)
• Evaluation: regular re-evaluation of pain levels, documentation of pain-relief effectiveness and follow-up, and monthly drug regime reviews.
• Family: education of the patient and family about pain, and attention to their emotional and spiritual distress.
questions.question:
A patient with advanced cancer complains of a continuous dull, aching, poorly localised pain and is also anxious and worried about the illness.
(a) Identify the type and nature of the pain.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis of the pain.
(c) Describe the nursing assessment of the pain.
(d) Describe the nursing management and interventions.
(e) State how the outcome would be evaluated and how the family would be supported.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade; jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds and hypotension are Beck's triad.

(b)
• Contributing factors: cancer (e.g. lung or breast cancer) or its treatment.
• Pathophysiology: accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac compresses the heart; features include dyspnoea, chest pain, tachycardia and hypotension.

(c)
• Urgent pericardiocentesis; treat the underlying malignancy; pericardial window in recurrent cases.
• Stabilise with airway, breathing and circulation, oxygen, IV access and fluid resuscitation for hypotension, vasopressors for refractory hypotension, and analgesics for pain.
• Monitor haemodynamics; recognise early because symptoms (breathlessness, dizziness, chest pain) may be wrongly attributed to fatigue or confusion in patients with disrupted sleep, delaying diagnosis.
questions.question:
A patient with lung or breast cancer develops shortness of breath and chest pain, with a fast heart rate, low blood pressure, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.
(a) Recognise the condition.
(b) State the contributing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Outline the nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Informed consent is a cornerstone of ethical practice: patients are fully aware of the risks, benefits and alternatives of treatment and may refuse or choose interventions that match their values, including whether to continue aggressive treatment or move to comfort care.
• Consent of the patient (or those delegated) is necessary before any treatment is given or withdrawn; most patients want shared decision-making.

(b)
Capacity: nurses assess mental capacity regularly, since cognitive impairment or delirium may result from illness or medications, especially for high-risk decisions such as life-sustaining treatment or clinical trials.

(c)
Voluntariness: consent must be given without coercion; some patients feel pressured by family to pursue aggressive treatment, so nurses ensure a safe and supportive environment.

(d)
Advance directives: living wills or durable power of attorney for healthcare state wishes about resuscitation, ventilator support and feeding tubes.

(e)
Best practices: clear jargon-free explanations of options, risks and benefits; encourage questions and check understanding; review and update directives as the condition progresses; involve family, legal representatives or a healthcare proxy when necessary.

(f)
• Patients face complex decisions about treatment options, including stopping aggressive treatments; respecting autonomy upholds dignity.
• Capacity may be impaired by delirium or medications, and family pressure can override the patient's wishes.
• Hospice nurses ensure the autonomy rights of patients to choose between options and refuse any indicated treatment; in physical assessment, consent is obtained and refusal respected.

(g)
• Informed consent ensures understanding of risks, benefits and alternatives when a treatment decision is made.
• Advance directives are prepared ahead of time, expressing wishes about end-of-life care and interventions such as resuscitation, ventilation and feeding tubes.
• When a patient cannot decide, family members, legal representatives or a healthcare proxy are involved, and directives are reviewed as the condition progresses.
questions.question:
Describe informed consent in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) meaning and purpose
(b) capacity and decision-making
(c) voluntariness
(d) advance directives
(e) best practices
(f) Explain why informed consent is especially important in palliative care.
(g) Distinguish between informed consent and advance directives.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Fear of mortality; anxiety from the disrupted role as family breadwinner; isolation and helplessness from restricted ICU visits.

(b)
• Psychological support: calm empathetic emotional reassurance, frequent updates, explaining procedures; referral to a hospital counsellor for cognitive behavioural therapy.
• Family involvement: daily video calls, voice notes or written messages from family; social worker assessment of financial needs, temporary charity aid and education on community support systems.

(c)
• Patient-centred interview (open-ended questions on emotional state, coping, social support); HADS, Distress Thermometer, Palliative Outcome Scale; behavioural observation (appetite and sleep changes, withdrawal, hopelessness).
• Family: genograms/ecomaps and Caregiver Strain Index; spiritual: FICA tool. HADS was used to show reduced anxiety by the end of the stay.

(d)
• Communication barriers (intubation, sedation) and altered mental status (delirium, sedation) can mask or mimic distress and lead to underestimation of symptoms or misdiagnosis.
• Trauma-related responses such as PTSD may overlap with depression or anxiety; early attention reduces the risk of long-term psychological complications.

(e)
• Strong cultural emphasis on family made family involvement integral; regular chaplain visits offered prayers and spiritual counselling in line with his cultural background, strengthening faith and resilience.
• Respect cultural and religious practices and differing expressions of distress; use interpreters where language barriers exist; involve a multidisciplinary team of social workers, psychologists, chaplains, nurses and physicians.
questions.question:
A 56-year-old man was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit after a severe myocardial infarction. He has been stabilised medically but shows heightened anxiety, withdrawal and emotional distress. He fears dying, is worried about his role as family breadwinner and feels isolated because of restricted visiting.
(a) State the nursing problems identified.
(b) Name the interventions you would use.
(c) Describe the assessment tools and parameters used.
(d) State the safety risks and problems to monitor.
(e) Discuss the cultural, spiritual, ethical and family-related considerations.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy, a metabolic oncological emergency (elevated calcium due to cancer).

(b)
• Gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, constipation), renal/urinary (polyuria, polydipsia), neurological (confusion, lethargy, coma in severe cases); fluid and electrolyte balance.
• Weakness and fatigue may also disturb sleep.

(c)
• Tumours produce parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) or induce bone resorption, raising serum calcium.
• Alternatives: nausea and vomiting can also arise from opioids, brain tumours or advanced liver or kidney disease; constipation from opioids, dehydration or anticholinergics; confusion from metabolic imbalance or medication side effects.

(d)
• Treat as an emergency: maintain airway, breathing and circulation, secure IV access, and monitor electrolytes and haemodynamics.
• Aggressive IV hydration with saline; loop diuretics for volume repletion and calcium excretion; bisphosphonates (e.g. zoledronic acid) or denosumab; treat the underlying malignancy; antiemetics for symptom control.
• Reasoning: confusion and fatigue can delay identification of the emergency, so early recognition prevents severe complications.
questions.question:
A patient with cancer (such as breast cancer, lung cancer or multiple myeloma) has nausea, vomiting and constipation, passes large volumes of urine, is very thirsty, and is becoming confused and lethargic.
(a) Identify the syndrome.
(b) State the body systems and domains affected.
(c) Explain the contributing causes and alternative explanations.
(d) Describe your clinical reasoning and the prioritisation of care.

Several months after the death of a spouse, a person still cannot accept the loss, feels persistently hopeless, is unable to work, sleep or eat, and seems 'stuck' in mourning.
(a) Identify the problem and distinguish it from normal grief.
(b) Explain the underlying basis of the problem.
(c) Describe the nursing assessment.
(d) Describe the nursing management and interventions.
(e) State how the outcome would be evaluated and how the family would be supported.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Complicated (prolonged or pathological) grief: prolonged, intense and disrupting daily functioning, with persistent symptoms for months or years. Normal grief is temporary and evolves, and the person adjusts and begins to rebuild life.

(b)
• Grief is a natural response to loss of an attachment figure, and its intensity is tied to the depth of attachment (Bowlby).
• Suppressing or avoiding grief can delay healing and result in complicated grief or emotional complications, and may lead to depression or post-traumatic stress disorder.

(c)
• Assess emotional, physical, cognitive and behavioural manifestations: hopelessness, difficulty accepting the loss, lack of emotional healing, avoidance of reminders, fatigue, insomnia, appetite change, poor concentration.
• Assess how far grief interferes with daily functioning (work, sleep, eating) and monitor for depression and PTSD.

(d)
• Intervene early: refer to mental health professionals, grief counsellors or support groups; therapy with a licensed professional for complicated grief, trauma or depression.
• Active listening in a non-judgemental space; encourage expression of feelings; help with practical matters; promote self-care (eating, sleeping, light exercise); educate about the non-linear grieving process; promote rituals and memorials.

(e)
Family: grief affects the whole family, so facilitate open communication and family meetings, share pamphlets and community support group information, and connect them with hospice or grief support resources.

questions.question:
The team must tell a patient and family that treatment has not been as effective as hoped. The patient's culture may prefer a gradual, indirect approach to discussing prognosis, and relatives ask the nurse for details of the patient's condition.
(a) State the nursing problem.
(b) Name the communication intervention and its steps.
(c) Describe the assessment parameters used.
(d) State the risks to monitor.
(e) Discuss the ethical, cultural and family-related considerations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Delivering difficult news about diagnosis or prognosis in an emotionally challenging and ethically complex situation; the patient and family risk being overwhelmed.

(b)
The SPIKES protocol: Setting up a private, comfortable space; Perception (what the patient already knows); Invitation (how much they want to know); Knowledge (clear, compassionate information); Emotions (acknowledge and validate); Strategy and Summary (next steps with hope and reassurance).

(c)
Assess the patient's emotional and psychological readiness and adjust the approach; ask what the patient knows and how much information they want; use jargon-free language.

(d)
Emotional harm if news is delivered hastily; breach of confidentiality if information is given to unauthorised persons, even family or friends who ask; false reassurance or withholding of critical information undermines trust.

(e)
• Autonomy: the patient has the right to decide how much information to receive; legally, written consent may be needed before discussing the condition with others.
• Cultural: some cultures prefer an indirect or gradual approach; be aware of norms so news is broken respectfully.
• Beneficence: provide emotional support, time to process, referrals to counselling, chaplains or social workers, and follow-up conversations; balance patient autonomy with family input.

(a)
Mechanism: opioids bind to opiate receptors (mu, kappa, delta); the mu receptor is a 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor and binding stabilises the membrane so the neuron does not fire; mu receptors are in the periphery, dorsal root ganglia, periaqueductal grey, midbrain and gut.

(b)
Classification: 'weak' opioids (codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone); 'strong' (hydromorphone, fentanyl, morphine); hydrophilic (morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone); lipophilic (fentanyl, methadone).

(c)
Routes: IV (morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl); oral (long- and short-acting morphine and oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone, fentanyl, hydrocodone); transdermal fentanyl. Initial decisions rest on route, continuous versus intermittent dosing and severity of pain.

(d)
Water-soluble opioids: Cmax 60-90 min after oral dose, 30 min after SQ/IM, 6-10 min after IV; conjugated in liver and 90% excreted by the kidney; half-life 3-4 h with normal renal function; steady state in 4-5 half-lives.

(e)
• Morphine: low protein binding, dialyses off, active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide (10%). Fentanyl: little or no active metabolites, not dialysable. Hydromorphone: inactive metabolites. Methadone: binds mu and blocks NMDA receptors, highly protein bound, variable prolonged half-life.
• Context: start with non-opioids (acetaminophen, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors) and step up; adjuncts include anticonvulsants, steroids and TCAs.

(f)
• Morphine accumulates in renal failure; hydromorphone is the drug of choice in renal failure.
• Fentanyl: elderly are more sensitive; the effect of low subcutaneous fat on the transdermal route is unclear.
• Methadone: caution when changing from another opioid; it may prolong the QT interval (phase I metabolism).

(g)
• Potential side effects: nausea, CNS depression/sedation, pruritus, constipation, delirium, endocrine dysfunction with long-term use.
• Basis: opioids stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone (nausea); reduce peristalsis and increase water absorption from stool (constipation, pseudo-obstruction); reduce muscle coordination for swallowing; morphine-6-glucuronide accumulation causes neuroexcitation and prolonged CNS effects.
• Opioids relieve breathlessness by decreasing respiratory drive and do not significantly compromise oxygenation when used appropriately.
questions.question:
Describe opioid analgesics in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) mechanism of action
(b) classification
(c) routes and initial decisions
(d) pharmacology
(e) special notes on individual drugs
(f) State the safe-practice precautions.
(g) Explain the basis of the adverse effects and complications of opioids.

A patient with advanced lung cancer has had unintended weight loss of more than 5% of body weight over 6 months, reduced food intake with early satiety, muscle wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat. Weight loss continues despite efforts to increase intake.
(a) Identify the syndrome and state how it differs from simple loss of appetite.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis of the syndrome.
(c) Describe the nursing assessment, including history, assessment tools and laboratory markers.
(d) Describe the nursing management and interventions (nutritional, pharmacological, non-pharmacological and palliative procedures).
(e) State how the outcome of care would be evaluated and how the family would be supported.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Anorexia and cachexia syndrome (ACS). Anorexia is decreased appetite or aversion to food (a symptom, reversible with caloric intake); cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome of severe involuntary weight loss, muscle wasting and fat depletion with metabolic alteration, so muscle is lost despite adequate nutrition and it is not reversible by nutrition alone.

(b)
• Anorexia: pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) impair NPY/AgRP signalling and enhance POMC/CART signals, shifting the hypothalamus toward appetite suppression; ghrelin effects are blunted and chronic inflammation raises leptin (leptin resistance); fatigue, depression and nausea worsen it.
• Cachexia: chronic systemic inflammation (TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1, IFN-gamma) drives increased protein degradation (ubiquitin-proteasome, autophagy-lysosome) and decreased synthesis (mTOR suppressed); lipolysis; hypermetabolism; raised cortisol, insulin resistance, reduced GH/IGF-1; mitochondrial dysfunction reduces ATP.

(c)
• History: weight loss >5% in 6 months, reduced intake, early satiety, aversion to foods; physical signs: muscle wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat, signs of malnutrition.
• Tools: PG-SGA, BMI, Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis, ESAS. Laboratory: serum albumin (low in malnutrition), C-reactive protein (raised in systemic inflammation), cytokine profiles (IL-6, TNF-alpha).

(d)
• Nutritional: dietitian-led personalised plans, small frequent nutrient-dense meals, high-calorie high-protein oral supplements; tube (enteral) feeding if unable to eat but GI tract functional; parenteral nutrition only when the GI tract is non-functional.
• Pharmacological: corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone 4-8 mg/day, short-term because of side effects), progestogens (medroxyprogesterone, megestrol), anabolic agents (oxandrolone), omega-3 fatty acids and thalidomide for inflammation.
• Non-pharmacological: counselling for anxiety/depression, pleasant dining environment, eating at own pace with favourite foods, social dining, moderate exercise. Procedures: paracentesis for ascites, PEG tube, stent placement for GI obstruction.

(e)
Family support: family education on realistic expectations and supportive care; psychosocial and emotional support for patient and caregivers within a multidisciplinary team.

questions.question:
The primary caregiver of a patient with advanced disease being managed at home appears exhausted and emotionally distressed, disagrees with other relatives about the patient's care, and has limited time available.
(a) Identify the problem.
(b) Explain the underlying basis of the problem.
(c) Describe the nursing assessment of the family, including tools.
(d) Describe the nursing management and interventions.
(e) State how the outcome would be evaluated and how ongoing family support would be provided.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Caregiver burnout/strain with conflicting family opinions and limited availability, a challenge in integrating the family into assessment and care planning.

(b)
• Relatives of patients with advanced disease are subject to considerable emotional and physical distress, especially when the patient is managed at home; families are often the primary caregivers and decision-makers, and palliative care often succeeds or fails on the care and support given to them.
• Witnessing decline and anticipating loss add emotional strain.

(c)
• Assess family dynamics, relationships, roles and coping mechanisms; communication styles; coping strategies for stress, grief and decision-making; cultural and spiritual beliefs; capacity, resources and emotional readiness.
• Tools: Caregiver Strain Index (burden on primary caregivers), genograms and ecomaps; regular check-ins to gauge coping.

(d)
• Facilitate open communication in a safe space; clarify each member's role (physical care, emotional support, logistics); educate and train (medication administration, symptom management, recognising distress) to improve confidence and reduce anxiety.
• Collaborate on shared decisions; mediate conflicts with sensitivity and professionalism; offer respite care to reduce burnout; engage extended family or community resources; refer to counselling, support groups or spiritual care; hold family conferences.

(e)
• Evaluation: regular check-ins and continuous reassessment as family dynamics change.
• Family support: family involvement improves outcomes, satisfaction and reduces stress; ongoing support services and respite care.

questions.question:
Describe the management of sleep disturbance in palliative care under the following headings:
(a) sleep hygiene
(b) behavioural therapy approaches
(c) CBT-I
(d) relaxation techniques
(e) pharmacological options
(f) State the safe-practice precautions, particularly for sleep aids.
(g) Explain the basis of the complications and limitations of these interventions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sleep hygiene (non-pharmacological, first line): regular sleep schedule; dark, quiet, cool room; avoid electronics (blue light) an hour before bed; avoid caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and large meals near bedtime; regular exercise, particularly earlier in the day.

(b)
Behavioural therapy: stimulus control (bed only for sleep and intimacy); sleep restriction therapy (reduce time in bed awake to increase sleep drive); relaxation training (breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation).

(c)
CBT-I is the gold standard non-pharmacological treatment for chronic insomnia, improving sleep latency, wake time after sleep onset and sleep efficiency, with long-term benefits. Components: cognitive restructuring, sleep scheduling (consistent wake time), stimulus control (leave bed if not asleep within 10 minutes), relaxation training.

(d)
Relaxation: slow deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, autogenic training, biofeedback, hypnosis, meditation (including yoga and tai chi), chosen to fit the person's routine.

(e)
• Pharmacological, for short-term relief or when other methods are insufficient: OTC melatonin (jet lag, circadian disorders) and antihistamines such as diphenhydramine (drowsiness, next-day grogginess).
• Prescription: benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam) for short-term use in severe insomnia; non-benzodiazepine hypnotics (zolpidem, eszopiclone) with lower dependence risk but still needing caution; antidepressants (trazodone, mirtazapine) when associated with depression or anxiety.

(f)
• Individualise: consider age, medical history and concurrent conditions; older adults are more sensitive to sedatives and at higher risk of falls.
• Sleep aids can interact with other medications or exacerbate conditions such as sleep apnoea; use as a bridge to non-pharmacological interventions, ideally combined.
• Monitor for daytime drowsiness and cognitive impairment affecting alertness and memory the next day, increasing accident risk.

(g)
• Prolonged use causes dependence and tolerance, leading to addiction or reduced effectiveness; sedative-hypnotics carry risks of dependence, cognitive impairment and morning 'hangover' effects.
• Drugs provide immediate relief but do not address root causes, so they are a bridge to non-pharmacological interventions.
• Heavy sedation from pain medication may mask or delay recognition of emergencies such as tumour lysis syndrome or hypercalcaemia.

(a)
• Nutritional: dietary counselling with a dietitian and personalised meal plans; small, frequent nutrient-dense meals; high-calorie, high-protein oral supplements (e.g. Ensure, Boost).
• Enteral (tube) feeding for patients unable to eat orally but with a functional GI tract; parenteral nutrition reserved for a non-functional GI tract.

(b)
• Appetite stimulants: corticosteroids (dexamethasone 4-8 mg/day) improve appetite and energy; progestogens (medroxyprogesterone, megestrol acetate) increase appetite and body weight.
• Anabolic agents (oxandrolone, testosterone derivatives) may preserve lean body mass; anti-inflammatory agents: omega-3 fatty acids and thalidomide.

(c)
Counselling and psychosocial support for anxiety and depression; family education on realistic expectations; pleasant dining environment, eating at own pace, favourite foods, social dining; moderate exercise to stimulate appetite and maintain muscle mass.

(d)
Procedures: paracentesis to relieve ascites and improve appetite; PEG tube for long-term enteral feeding in dysphagia or obstruction; stent placement for GI obstruction to improve nutrient intake.

(e)
Assessment: weight loss above 5% in 6 months, PG-SGA, BMI, BIA, ESAS, serum albumin, CRP and cytokine profiles; care by a multidisciplinary team including dietitians.

(f)
• Use corticosteroids short-term because of side effects.
• Choose enteral feeding only with a functional GI tract and reserve parenteral nutrition for a non-functional tract.
• Allow patients to eat at their own pace and set realistic expectations with families.

(g)
• Cachexia is not reversible by nutrition alone because of severe systemic inflammation and metabolic dysregulation, and muscle loss occurs despite adequate nutrition; anorexia alone is reversible with caloric intake.
• Cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1, IFN-gamma) drive protein degradation, suppress synthesis (mTOR), cause lipolysis, hypermetabolism, cortisol excess, insulin resistance and mitochondrial dysfunction.
questions.question:
Describe the management of anorexia and cachexia syndrome under the following headings:
(a) nutritional support
(b) pharmacological interventions
(c) non-pharmacological measures
(d) palliative procedures
(e) assessment basis and team
(f) State the safe-practice precautions.
(g) Explain the basis of the limits and failure of nutritional and appetite-stimulating interventions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Bereavement: the period following the death of a loved one, with emotional, psychological and social adjustments. Loss: separation from someone or something valuable (e.g. a job, a breakup, a terminal diagnosis). Grief: a complex, non-linear emotional response to loss (sorrow, sadness, anger, guilt, even relief). Mourning: outward, socially and culturally prescribed expressions of grief.

(b)
Types: normal (temporary, evolves), complicated (prolonged, intense, disrupts functioning), anticipatory (before the death), disenfranchised (not openly acknowledged, e.g. a pet, an ex-spouse or a stigmatised death such as suicide or overdose), cumulative (multiple losses within a short time).

(c)
Emotional: sadness, guilt, anger, anxiety, disbelief, isolation; physical: fatigue, insomnia, appetite change, muscle tension, somatic complaints; behavioural: withdrawal, changed routine, avoidance of reminders; cognitive: poor concentration, memory problems, confusion, numbness.

(d)
• Persistent grief becomes complicated grief with hopelessness and difficulty accepting the loss, and may lead to depression or PTSD; cumulative grief feels never-ending; disenfranchised grief is dismissed by society.
• Anticipatory grief causes emotional stress long before death but offers a chance to address unresolved issues, prepare emotionally and discuss end-of-life care decisions; physical symptoms of grief affect overall health and need monitoring.

(e)
• Grief affects the entire family and communication can break down; facilitate family meetings and open communication. Daily tasks become hard, so help with practical matters (calls, notifying relatives, funeral arrangements); support changes in roles and routines.
• Support rituals and memorialisation; mourning practices vary across cultures and religions and must be respected; prayer, meditation or a chaplain can give solace.
• Nursing interventions: active listening, encouraging expression, assessing for complicated grief, promoting self-care, educating about the grieving process.
• Coping strategies: social support networks, physical activity, journaling and creative expression, spiritual practices, mindfulness and relaxation.
• Therapy and professional support: refer to a licensed therapist or grief counsellor when grief impairs mental health or functioning.
• Support groups provide a setting to connect with others who understand the experience.
• Self-care: remind the grieving person to eat nourishing meals, drink water, rest and do light activity; monitor insomnia, weight loss and fatigue.
questions.question:
Describe bereavement, loss, grief and mourning under the following headings:
(a) definitions
(b) types of grief
(c) manifestations of grief
(d) State how these types and manifestations relate to the common problems seen in bereaved persons.
(e) Explain how grief spreads to affect the family, social, functional and spiritual domains and describe the nursing interventions and coping strategies.
