courses.title: Orthopedics II

questions.explanation: Tendon sheath conditions such as trigger finger, de Quervain's disease, and related tendo-synovitis share a rehabilitation principle of progressing from assisted passive exercises to free active exercises. Heat therapy and wax bath therapy commonly accompany this progression. This graded approach protects the healing tendon sheath while restoring function.
questions.question: A patient recovering from acute suppurative tendo-synovitis is guided through rehabilitation similar to related tendon sheath conditions. Which shared exercise principle applies from the trigger finger and de Quervain protocols?
options: Complete avoidance of any hand movement
Passive stretching alone with no active phase
Cold immersion as the sole treatment
Progression from assisted passive to free active exercises

questions.explanation: The Cobb method for measuring scoliosis requires locating the top and bottom vertebrae of the curve, then drawing intersecting perpendiculars from the superior surface of the top vertebra and the inferior surface of the bottom vertebra, with the angle of deviation from a straight line representing the curve angle. The Ferguson method instead uses lines drawn to the center of the apex vertebra. Both methods quantify curve severity for treatment planning.
questions.question: In measuring scoliosis curves, the Cobb method specifically requires locating which two vertebrae as reference points?
options: Only the single apex vertebra of the curve
Only vertebrae showing visible rotation on X-ray
The sacral base and the first cervical vertebra
The top and bottom vertebrae of the curve
The vertebra directly above and below the sacrum

questions.explanation: In the osteoplastic method, weight is transmitted through a bone, typically the patella, that is surgically arthrodesed to the distal femur. This contrasts with the tendoplastic (supracondylar) method, where weight passes through a layer of tendinous tissue to the distal femur. Both aim to create a durable, end-bearing thigh stump.
questions.question: In amputation through the thigh, what distinguishes the osteoplastic technique from the tendoplastic technique?
options: Weight is transmitted through a metal prosthetic socket rim
Weight is transmitted through sutured muscle bellies alone
Weight is transmitted through bone arthrodesed to the femur
Weight is transmitted directly through the sciatic nerve stump
Weight is transmitted entirely through the overlying skin flap
Destruction of the femoral head and neck
questions.explanation: Osteotomy is specifically indicated in Charcot's joint of the hip when the femoral head and neck are destroyed. Reconstruction and arthrodesis remain alternative regional options depending on the extent of damage. Selecting the appropriate procedure depends on the degree of structural joint destruction present.
questions.question: A patient with Charcot's joint of the hip is scheduled for osteotomy. Which finding on assessment specifically supports this choice over reconstruction or arthrodesis?

options: Before any surgical repair takes place
Only once the cast has been worn a year
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for a repaired distal biceps tendon rupture introduces active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening as pain subsides after surgery. Heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy or heating pad therapy supports this recovery. This graded approach protects the healing tendon repair from excess strain.
questions.question: A patient recovering from surgical repair of a ruptured biceps tendon (distal end) begins physiotherapy exercises for joint movement guided by which timing principle?

questions.explanation: PNF stretching most commonly involves an isometric hold of the target muscle group followed by a static stretch of the same muscles. The patient relaxes while the physiotherapist gently stretches further for about thirty seconds. This approach both increases flexibility and improves muscular strength.
questions.question: Proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation, or PNF stretching, typically involves which sequence of muscle actions?

questions.explanation: Splinting or traction in acute septic arthritis primarily provides joint rest during the inflammatory stage. This protects the inflamed joint from further mechanical stress. Range of motion and strengthening exercises are introduced in later stages.
options: Restoration of full range of motion
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning splinting for a child with acute septic arthritis of the hip during the acute inflammatory stage. What is the primary aim of this splinting?

questions.explanation: Assisted exercise is indicated when muscle strength or coordination is inadequate to perform a movement, or when free movement causes pain, so an external force compensates for the deficiency. The physiotherapist provides this assistance, often through techniques such as sling suspension. This differs from purely passive exercise, where the patient provides no effort or intent at all.
questions.question: A physiotherapist choosing exercise type for a patient whose muscle strength is inadequate to complete a movement, but who is not in pain, should select which type of active exercise?

questions.explanation:
Volkmann's ischemic contracture results from arterial spasm following reduction of a supracondylar fracture of the humerus.
Interrupted blood flow causes necrosis and fibrosis of the forearm flexor muscles.
Early signs include a white, pulseless hand with inability to passively extend the fingers.
questions.question: Volkmann's ischemic contracture most classically follows which fracture, affecting the flexor muscles of the forearm?

options: A cervical collar for a further two to three months
Skull traction extended for a further year
Surgical arthrodesis in every case regardless of stability
questions.question: A patient with a fracture of the atlas (C1) has completed six weeks of skull traction. What follows in the described management sequence?
questions.explanation:
Fracture of the atlas is typically managed with skull traction maintained for six weeks.
After this period, a cervical collar is applied for a further two to three months to support ongoing healing.
Surgical arthrodesis is reserved for cases where conservative traction and collar management prove insufficient.

questions.question: In muscle physiology, a contraction in which the muscle changes length while tension stays relatively constant is termed?
questions.explanation: Isotonic contraction is one in which the muscle changes its length without a marked increase in tension, occurring as either concentric or eccentric movement. Isometric contraction, by contrast, involves no change in muscle length or joint angle at all. A person carrying a static object exemplifies isometric contraction of the biceps.

questions.question: Which lifestyle risk factor is specifically listed as increasing osteoporosis risk?
questions.explanation: A sedentary lifestyle with lack of physical activity is a recognized risk factor for osteoporosis. Regular weight-bearing exercise is protective rather than causative. Addressing modifiable risk factors forms part of prevention.

Metaphyseal defects appear on X-ray as small bowl-shaped defects located eccentrically, with sclerosed and scalloped bony margins. The cortex is often absent peripherally at the lesion site. Nonosteogenic fibromas show similarly sclerotic, scalloped margins with trabeculated lesions.
questions.question: On X-ray, metaphyseal defects typically appear as bowl-shaped lesions with margins that are?

questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis is characterized partly by hypertrophic bone formation, known as osteophytes, at the articular margins. This accompanies degeneration of the articular cartilage itself. Subchondral sclerosis and cyst formation are separate pathological features of the disease.
questions.question: Which pathological change in osteoarthritis refers to bone formation at the articular margins?
Early radiographic change in rheumatoid arthritis of the hand and wrist chiefly shows which finding?
options: Dense sclerosis of the joint margins
questions.explanation: Early X-ray changes in rheumatoid arthritis of the wrists and hands show osteoporosis around the affected joint. Erosion of cartilage at the periphery of the joint surface is also seen. These changes accompany the clinical criteria used for diagnosis.

questions.question: The three main aims of treatment in fractures of the femoral shaft are restoration of alignment, restoration of length, and:
options: Prevention of avascular necrosis of the femoral head
questions.explanation:
Femoral shaft fracture management targets three principal goals for a good functional outcome.
Alignment must be restored to avoid undue strain on the knee and later osteoarthritis.
Length must be maintained, and knee stiffness actively prevented through appropriate rehabilitation.

The calcaneus is usually fractured by a fall from a height, classically in window cleaners or construction workers.
Impact from below, such as in mine explosions, is another recognised mechanism.
The bone is often shattered like an eggshell with variable involvement of the subtalar joint.
questions.question: Fracture of the calcaneus is most commonly caused by which mechanism?
A physiotherapist is treating an infant with congenital torticollis and is teaching the mother a home exercise programme. What specific technique is emphasized as part of this physiotherapy plan?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for congenital torticollis includes manipulation (stretching) of the neck three times daily for a couple of months, followed by free active exercises, aiming to lengthen the shortened sternocleidomastoid muscle. Many transient cases, roughly 20%, resolve without any treatment at all, while persistent cases may eventually require surgical release. The physiotherapist's early stretching programme is therefore a key conservative intervention attempted before considering surgery.
options: Avoidance of any passive movement of the cervical spine
Manipulation (stretching) of the neck three times daily
Strengthening only of the unaffected contralateral muscle
Complete immobilization of the neck in a rigid collar
Surgical release performed immediately regardless of severity

questions.explanation: Postural affections beginning in childhood often go unnoticed until adolescence, when the body becomes heavier and the person adopts occupations requiring prolonged sitting or standing, causing the affection to increase and become symptomatic. Early diagnosis during the less symptomatic childhood period allows for more effective correction and prevention of later disability. This principle underlies the emphasis on early screening for postural deformities in children.
options: Complete resolution of growth plate activity before puberty
Increasing body weight and occupations requiring prolonged posture
Loss of all proprioceptive sensory receptor function suddenly
Development of compensatory hypertrophy of unaffected limbs
Sudden cessation of all physical activity at puberty onset
questions.question: Which factor is specifically cited as making postural affections that begin in childhood likely to increase and become symptomatic during adolescence?

questions.explanation:
Fractures involving a joint surface, or very close to it, are especially prone to stiffness.
Fibrous adhesions, cartilage injury, and prolonged immobilization all contribute mechanically to this stiffness.
Prevention relies on accurate reduction, adequate but not excessive fixation, and early active exercise.
questions.question: Which statement about intra-articular fractures and joint stiffness is most accurate?
options: Intra-articular fractures rarely cause any long-term stiffness
Intra-articular fractures are more prone to joint stiffness than fractures of the shaft away from the joint
Extra-articular fractures always cause more stiffness than intra-articular ones
Joint stiffness only follows fractures treated conservatively
Stiffness after intra-articular fracture is unrelated to immobilization duration

questions.question: Conservative management of Charcot's joint is generally described as?
questions.explanation: Conservative management of Charcot's joint, including rest, analgesics, NSAIDs and antibiotics, is symptomatic rather than curative. Surgical arthrodesis is used regionally for definitive joint stabilization. This reflects the largely irreversible nature of trophic joint destruction.

The window cut into the postoperative POP cast in chronic osteomyelitis allows access for wound dressing changes. Physiotherapy exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening are introduced as pain subsides. Heat therapy further supports the recovery process.
options: To reduce the total weight of the cast
To allow the limb to bear full weight
To enable direct heat lamp treatment
questions.question: A patient recovering from chronic osteomyelitis surgery has a POP cast with a window cut over the wound. What is the primary functional purpose of this window?

questions.explanation: Following surgical fusion for scoliosis, the physiotherapist aims to teach the child to adjust to the new corrected posture and to strengthen muscles to hold this position and perform normal function, with hydrotherapy noted as a helpful modality once the child mobilizes freely. Since a structural curve cannot be reversed by physiotherapy alone, the postoperative role instead centers on adaptation and functional strengthening around the surgically achieved correction. This differs from the non-surgical group, where the aim is instead to prevent progression of a still-flexible curve.
options: Discouraging any use of hydrotherapy throughout recovery
Teaching the child to adjust to and strengthen the new posture
Removing the surgical instrumentation within the first month
Avoiding all exercise until the fusion mass matures fully
Restoring full spinal flexibility to the pre-surgical range
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a postoperative patient following spinal arthrodesis for severe idiopathic scoliosis. What is the primary rehabilitation goal described for this surgical group?

A physiotherapist is treating a patient following surgical exploration for neurotmesis and notes the surgical note describes débridement and delayed closure rather than primary suturing. What clinical circumstance most likely justified this approach?
questions.explanation: Débridement with delayed closure is specifically indicated for open, contaminated wounds where primary suturing would risk infection, whereas primary suturing is reserved for sharply incised, clean wounds. This staged surgical decision-making directly affects the physiotherapist's postoperative timeline, since immobilization and mobilization schedules differ between primary and delayed repair approaches. Recognizing which wound type justifies each surgical strategy helps the physiotherapist anticipate the likely rehabilitation pathway.
options: A clean, sharply incised wound ideal for immediate suturing
A closed fracture with no associated soft tissue wound
An open, contaminated wound unsuitable for immediate suturing
A situation requiring no surgical intervention at all
Complete absence of any wound contamination whatsoever

questions.explanation: Rickets is a deficiency disease resulting from lack of vitamin D, a component of natural fats and oils. Osteomalacia represents the adult equivalent of this deficiency. Both conditions disturb the mineral-matrix ratio of bone.
questions.question: Rickets is fundamentally a deficiency of which vitamin?

questions.explanation: Isometric exercises by muscles surrounding the affected joint are introduced during the inflammation-resolving phase. They maintain muscle strength without stressing the healing joint. Weight-bearing and ballistic activity are deferred until later stages.
questions.question: A child with acute suppurative arthritis of the knee is in the inflammation-resolving phase. Which exercise type should the physiotherapist introduce first?
A patient with mycotic (coccidioidomycosis) infection of bone and joint is receiving immobilization with splints or plaster cast. What activity should specifically be avoided during this phase?
questions.explanation: Conservative management of coccidioidomycosis of bone and joint includes immobilization by splint or plaster cast, with weight bearing specifically avoided. Antifungal antibiotics such as amphotericin B support systemic treatment. Physiotherapy exercises progress once the infection is controlled.

Reticulum cell sarcoma of bone is a solitary lesion, distinct from the generalized or disseminated type, though it remains highly malignant and often fatal within two years. It usually affects the shaft of a long tubular bone or the pelvis. X-ray shows a large area of destruction without periosteal reaction.
questions.question: Reticulum cell sarcoma of bone differs from the disseminated lymphoma type mainly by being characterized as?
A physiotherapist is treating a patient recovering from varicose vein stripping surgery. What is the specific rehabilitation focus emphasized during recovery?
options: Application of a warm compress continuously to the legs
Exercises with legs raised while remaining ambulant
Avoidance of any walking until full wound healing
Complete bed rest with legs kept flat for six weeks
Immediate return to prolonged standing occupations
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy after varicose vein surgery encourages exercises performed with the legs raised while the patient remains ambulant, supporting venous circulation without prolonged immobility. This combination of elevation and mobilization is a recurring physiotherapy principle across most venous conditions described in the chapter. Avoiding prolonged standing or sitting further supports venous return during recovery.

Pathological fractures in Paget's disease most commonly occur in weight-bearing bones such as the femur and tibia. This relates to the thickened but weakened, deformed nature of pagetic bone. Osteoarthritis may also develop as a complication from altered mechanics.
questions.question: Pathological fractures in Paget's disease most commonly occur in?

questions.explanation: Trigger finger develops from thickening of the flexor tendon or a constriction within the tendon sheath. A nodule can be palpated opposite the metacarpophalangeal joint. The finger suddenly releases with a click after being held by a small applied force.
questions.question: Trigger finger is primarily caused by which pathological change?

options: Discouraging any use of a wheelchair under all circumstances
Improving gait in partial lesions with the aid of caliper support
Avoiding balance training for sitting or standing
Preventing the patient from returning to any occupation
Eliminating the need for any dressing adaptation training
questions.question: A patient with an incomplete cord lesion begins rehabilitation focused on returning to work. Which of the following is a stated rehabilitation goal in the text?
questions.explanation:
Rehabilitation after incomplete spinal cord injury focuses on functional independence and eventual return to work.
One specific goal described is improving gait for patients with partial lesions using caliper support.
Other goals include restoring sitting and standing balance, overcoming dressing difficulties, and permitting wheelchair use where needed.

options: Free active exercises with heat therapy
questions.question: A physiotherapist managing a fibrous dysplasia patient post-curettage and bone grafting should apply which combination of modalities?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management for fibrous dysplasia includes free active exercises, heat therapy using short-wave or infrared radiation, and wax bath therapy. Conservative treatment for the active lesion in young children delays surgery, using analgesics and diathermy. Osteotomy may later correct any existing deformity if surgery becomes necessary.

questions.question: Mallet finger conservative treatment involves splinting the DIP joint in which position for five weeks?
questions.explanation: Mallet finger is conservatively treated by applying a splint in hyperextension at the DIP joint for five weeks. Arthrodesis is reserved for cases where conservative treatment fails. This approach allows the torn extensor tendon insertion to heal.

Galeazzi fracture dislocation combines a fractured radial shaft with dislocation of the inferior radioulnar joint.
Accurate plating of the radius is the treatment of choice, since the ulna usually reduces spontaneously once the radius is fixed.
All radial shaft fracture-dislocations of this type are best treated by open reduction and internal fixation.
questions.question: A fracture of the radius combined with dislocation of the inferior radioulnar joint is called:

questions.explanation: Regional bursitis workups routinely include a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and blood uric acid level. Blood sugar is also checked, since rheumatic diseases such as gout can mimic or coexist with bursitis. X-rays may further reveal calcific deposits.
options: CBC, ESR, and blood uric acid
questions.question: Which laboratory investigations are commonly ordered for suspected regional bursitis to screen for gout and infection?

A physiotherapist is treating a patient recovering from surgical repair of a severed nerve and notes the surgical note lists 'non-cooperating patient' among factors affecting outcome. What role does this factor play in postoperative nerve recovery?
options: Non-cooperation only affects wound cosmetic appearance
This factor solely affects preoperative planning, not recovery
This factor is relevant only to intraoperative haemostasis
Patient cooperation has no documented effect on nerve recovery
Poor compliance is listed as a postoperative factor limiting results
questions.explanation: Among postoperative factors affecting nerve suture outcomes, a non-cooperating patient is specifically listed alongside infection and vicarious movements (where adjoining muscles fail to share the paralysed function) as contributors to poorer results. This highlights the physiotherapist's role in patient education and engagement as a genuine contributor to functional outcome, not merely a background consideration. Actively fostering patient cooperation with the rehabilitation programme is therefore a meaningful clinical intervention in itself.

A broad, smooth bony base with a scar placed away from the pressure area is specifically required to support the two key functions of the stump and prosthesis: walking and static weight bearing. Poor stump quality in these respects compromises comfort and gait efficiency even with a well-made prosthesis. This is why physiotherapy stump assessment routinely checks bone contour, skin coverage, and scar placement.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing an amputee stump and finds the bony end is broad, smooth, and well covered, with the scar positioned away from pressure. What functional purpose does this specific stump quality serve?
options: Enabling effective walking and static weight bearing
Guaranteeing complete absence of phantom limb sensation
Preventing any need for subsequent prosthetic adjustment
Eliminating the requirement for any further physiotherapy
Allowing the stump to regenerate lost sensory function

questions.question: Homans sign is specifically used as a clinical indicator suggesting which peripheral vascular condition?
questions.explanation: Homans sign, calf pain elicited on passive dorsiflexion of the foot, is a classical clinical indicator of deep vein thrombosis, alongside swollen calf, distended peripheral veins, and a tender cord-like vein. Superficial thrombophlebitis instead presents with an indurated, red, tender, hard cord-like vein without the same systemic risk profile. Recognizing which sign points to DVT specifically guides urgent anticoagulation decisions.

questions.question: A physiotherapist teaching a caregiver to perform passive exercise on a paralyzed limb explains why the unaffected leg must be fixed during hip abduction testing. What is the reason given?
questions.explanation: When performing passive abduction of one leg, the patient lies with the other leg fixed in abduction to prevent side flexion of the trunk during the movement. This ensures the observed range reflects true hip joint mobility rather than compensatory trunk movement. Proper patient support throughout is essential to allow the physiotherapist to move the joint through its available free range.
options: To increase resistance on the leg
To eliminate the need for support
To prevent side flexion of the trunk

questions.question: The onion-peel appearance of subperiosteal bone deposition on X-ray is a hallmark of which malignant bone tumor?
questions.explanation: Ewing's sarcoma X-ray shows marked diffuse rarefaction of the shaft with subperiosteal deposition of bone in layers, described as an onion-peel effect, along with occasional sunburst periosteal reaction. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy given overlap with chronic osteomyelitis and other round-cell tumors. Management remains highly unsatisfactory despite radiotherapy combined with chemotherapy.

questions.question: In anterior dislocation of the shoulder, the Dugas test is positive when the patient is unable to:
options: Raise the affected arm above the head
Extend the elbow of the affected side fully
Touch the opposite shoulder with the hand of the affected side
Make a fist with the affected hand
Touch the ipsilateral hip with the affected hand
questions.explanation:
The Dugas test assesses the ability to reach across and touch the opposite shoulder.
In anterior shoulder dislocation, the humeral head is displaced, preventing full adduction needed for this manoeuvre.
Inability to complete this test is therefore considered a positive finding supporting the diagnosis.

Juxtacortical osteosarcoma results from progressive proliferation and ossification of the periosteum or parosteal connective tissue, developing in juxtaposition to or continuity with bone. It most often affects the distal femur but may involve flat bones too. Unlike ordinary osteosarcoma, large parts of the lesion may remain histologically benign.
questions.question: A rare tumor from progressive ossification of periosteum or parosteal tissue, developing in continuity with bone, is best described as?

questions.explanation: Early Dupuytren's contracture is managed conservatively with night splintage and active exercises involving gentle finger stretching by the patient. Radiotherapy has a limited role in this early phase. Surgical fasciotomy is reserved for more advanced or disabling contracture.
options: Night splintage with active finger stretching
Aggressive forced finger extension under anesthesia
Full hand immobilization for one year
questions.question: A patient with Dupuytren's contracture in the early stage is being managed conservatively. Which physiotherapy-related measure is appropriate at this stage?

questions.explanation: Forequarter amputation is indicated for malignant tumors in the proximal part of the humerus, involving the neck, glenoid, or body of the scapula, or the clavicle. It is also used when breast carcinoma metastasizes into axillary lymph glands, vessels, or the brachial plexus. Hindquarter amputation instead addresses proximal femoral and pelvic malignancies.
questions.question: Forequarter amputation is specifically indicated for malignant tumors located in which anatomical region?

questions.explanation: Colles' fracture of the distal radius is a classic osteoporotic fracture occurring at the wrist. Fracture neck of femur and vertebral crush fractures are other common sites. All reflect the fragility of osteoporotic bone.
questions.question: Which fracture site is a classical presentation of osteoporosis at the wrist?

questions.explanation: The therapist must distinguish tenderness, which can be due to deep friction and can persist long after pain disappears, from pain itself, which is elicited through clinical assessment and reassessment. Deep friction massage may be given every other day once excess tenderness has worn off. This distinction guides appropriate progression of treatment frequency and intensity.
options: They are always identical in origin
Tenderness can persist after pain resolves
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to distinguish tenderness from pain during a course of deep friction massage. Why is this distinction clinically important according to the description?

questions.explanation:
After closed reduction of a dislocated hip, fixed traction in a Thomas splint is maintained for four weeks.
Once traction is discontinued, physiotherapy is carried out for a further two weeks.
Weight-bearing is then permitted, though it may be delayed to eight weeks if an acetabular rim fracture is present.
questions.question: A patient has undergone closed reduction for dislocation of the hip and is placed in fixed traction using a Thomas splint for four weeks. What is the described sequence after traction is discontinued?
options: Immediate unsupported full weight-bearing on the same day
A further eight weeks of traction before any exercise
Physiotherapy for two weeks, followed by weight-bearing
Passive hip manipulation under general anaesthesia weekly

questions.explanation: In hip disarticulation, the socket of the artificial limb is fitted with the stump fixed at a right angle so that weight is transferred onto the ischial tuberosity, since there is no femur remaining to bear load directly. This positioning principle is specific to disarticulation at this level, unlike below-knee prostheses that use tibial or patellar-tendon bearing. Correct socket alignment is essential for comfortable, efficient prosthetic gait.
options: It prevents any further growth of the remaining pelvis
It eliminates the need for any further socket adjustment
It reduces total prosthesis weight for easier mobility
Weight is thereby transferred onto the ischial tuberosity
It allows the prosthesis to be removed without unlocking
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient following hip disarticulation and notices the prosthetic socket is fitted with the stump fixed at a right angle. What is the specific rationale for this positioning?

questions.explanation: Hyperparathyroidism is characterized by a rise in serum calcium with a reciprocal fall in serum phosphate. Calcium is withdrawn from bone while urinary calcium excretion increases. Urinary phosphate excretion decreases in this condition.
questions.question: Hyperparathyroidism causes serum calcium and phosphate levels to change in which pattern?

questions.explanation: Axonotmesis involves rupture of the axons while the surrounding neural sheath remains intact, leading to Wallerian degeneration of the distal segment though the Schwann tubules are preserved. This differs from neurapraxia, a momentary conduction block without organic damage, and neurotmesis, where the sheath itself is divided. Recovery in axonotmesis is incomplete but generally better than in neurotmesis.
questions.question: Which type of peripheral nerve injury is characterized by axon rupture within an intact nerve sheath?
A patient has fracture of scaphoid managed conservatively with a cock-up plaster cast for eight to ten weeks. Physiotherapy input during this period is best described as:
options: Mandatory intensive daily resisted wrist exercises throughout immobilization
Immediate hydrotherapy started on day one of casting
Mostly unnecessary, but the physiotherapist should remain alert for complications requiring assisted exercises
Forced passive wrist extension performed weekly
Continuous electrical stimulation of thenar muscles throughout casting
questions.explanation:
Scaphoid fractures managed conservatively in a cast usually do not require active physiotherapy during immobilization.
The physiotherapist should nonetheless remain alert to complications such as non-union or Sudeck's atrophy.
Should these arise, assisted exercises become necessary as part of the complication-specific management.

Surgical treatment in achondroplasia is primarily indicated for shortened legs, with leg lengthening as the surgical option. Management overall remains largely symptomatic since the cause is unknown. This differs from surgical indications in conditions like Charcot's joint or hyperparathyroidism.
options: Shortened legs affecting stature and function
questions.question: A patient with achondroplasia is scheduled for leg lengthening surgery. What is the primary indication for this surgical procedure?

questions.explanation:
Lumbar spine dislocation or fracture-dislocation following severe trauma such as hanging requires urgent management if the patient survives.
Closed reduction under general anaesthesia is the described conservative approach where feasible.
Surgical treatment with ORIF is reserved for cases where this conservative reduction fails.
options: Immediate open surgery without any conservative attempt
Manipulation performed while the patient is fully conscious without anaesthesia
Reduction achieved solely through physiotherapy exercises
questions.question: A patient with a lumbar spine fracture-dislocation surviving a hanging injury requires closed reduction. What is the described method of achieving this reduction?

questions.explanation: A sitz bath uses two adjacent tubs of warm and cool water, sitting in one with the feet in the other and alternating. It is recommended specifically for hemorrhoids, premenstrual syndrome, and menstruation problems. This differs from warming socks, which are used to improve circulation and ease upper body congestion.
questions.question: A sitz bath, a form of hydrotherapy, is specifically recommended for which group of conditions?
Which finding on X-ray supports a diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism?
questions.explanation: Subperiosteal bone resorption is a characteristic radiographic finding of hyperparathyroidism. Additional findings include loss of the lamina dura of teeth and renal calcification. These changes reflect ongoing calcium withdrawal from bone.

Physiotherapy management of anterior poliomyelitis includes support through orthoses such as braces, splints, and plaster casts along with regular evaluation of muscle power. Passive movements are provided by the physiotherapist, complemented by massage therapy to tone muscle strength and ultrasound therapy. This ongoing evaluation guides decisions about bracing and future surgical timing.
questions.question: Following anterior poliomyelitis, a physiotherapist notices reduced muscle strength that requires ongoing monitoring. What should be regularly performed alongside orthotic support?
Fracture of the shaft of the humerus is most commonly complicated by injury to which nerve?
questions.explanation:
The radial nerve winds around the humeral shaft in the spiral groove, placing it at risk during shaft fractures.
Injury produces a wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors.
Most cases recover spontaneously, so exploration is reserved for those without recovery by eight weeks.

Muscle rupture mostly occurs at the musculotendinous junction rather than the belly. The quadriceps extensor, for example, typically ruptures just above the patella. Exceptions such as rectus femoris rupturing at mid-thigh are less common.
questions.question: Rupture of a muscle most commonly occurs at which anatomical site?
In thoracic outlet syndrome, physiotherapy exercise selection specifically targets maintenance of which two qualities in the neck muscles?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management of thoracic outlet syndrome centers on isometric and other exercises to maintain muscle power and flexibility of the neck muscles. Conservative measures also include rest and posture improvement. Surgical decompression is reserved for cases where conservative measures fail.

questions.question: A patient with a wound of the knee joint has had acute symptoms subside after surgical debridement. What guides the timing of restoring full function through exercise?
questions.explanation: Exercises for a joint wound are started once acute symptoms have subsided, with restoration of function induced slowly. Rushing this process may cause a reaction leading to residual synovitis or reactivated infection. Special attention is given to restoring quadriceps power early.
options: Delay of exercise for six months
Full range stretching on day one
Gradual, slowly induced restoration to avoid reactivating infection

questions.question: Laser electrotherapy is specifically contraindicated in cardiac patients who additionally have which device implanted?
questions.explanation: Laser electrotherapy contraindications include skin irritation, direct eye exposure, and chest application in cardiac patients especially those with a pacemaker. Low intensity laser light is otherwise used to relieve pain following soft tissue damage and facilitate tissue repair. The treatment head or probe is applied directly to the tissue being treated under controlled energy exposure.

questions.question: Reiter's syndrome arthritis typically affects joints in which distribution pattern?
questions.explanation: Arthritis in Reiter's syndrome is typically asymmetrical, affecting large weight-bearing joints such as the knee and ankle. Sacroiliitis and ankylosing spondylitis-like features may also occur. Valgus or varus deformity of the knee is a common accompanying finding.

questions.question: Which two chemotherapeutic agents are specifically listed together for treating osteogenic sarcoma?
questions.explanation: Osteogenic sarcoma chemotherapy uses methotrexate at 12 to 15 g per square meter orally or intramuscularly, combined with doxorubicin 60 to 75 mg per square meter intravenously repeated every three weeks. This combination is used alongside amputation as high as possible. Radiotherapy to the lungs remains controversial in affecting survival.

questions.question: A physiotherapist choosing between axillary and forearm support crutches for weight-bearing status should recall that axillary crutches offer which specific advantage?
questions.explanation: Axillary crutches are described as more stable than elbow crutches and are also used for partial weight-bearing instead of a stick. They require the patient to maintain good balance with the normal leg and arms strong enough to bear body weight. Forearm support crutches are reserved specifically for rheumatoid arthritis patients with hand, wrist, and elbow involvement.

questions.question: A 65-year-old patient presents with insidious knee pain, morning stiffness and crepitus but no systemic symptoms. Which physiotherapy modality is appropriate as first-line conservative management?
questions.explanation: Conservative treatment of osteoarthritis includes muscle strengthening exercises alongside heat therapy such as SWD or IR. This presentation, with insidious onset and absent systemic features, is typical of osteoarthritis. Surgery is reserved for cases where conservative measures fail.
options: Heat therapy with muscle strengthening exercises

questions.explanation: In polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, bone and cartilage fail to form normally and are replaced by fibrous tissue, resulting in weaker, more fracture-prone bone. Cautious, supervised loading protects against further pathological fracture. Complete avoidance of exercise, however, is not indicated.
options: Because the condition is fully curable with rest
Because bone and cartilage are replaced by weaker fibrous tissue
Because the patient has normal bone strength
Because loading exercises are contraindicated entirely
Because the disease is infective in origin
questions.question: A patient with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia has a pathological fracture and is undergoing rehabilitation. Why should the physiotherapist proceed cautiously with loading exercises?

questions.explanation: Gonococcal arthritis is listed among the differential diagnoses of infective arthritis, along with tuberculous, rheumatic and rheumatoid arthritis. Osteoarthritis, Charcot's joint and bone cysts have distinct, non-infective pathologies. Differentiating these conditions guides appropriate management.
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized differential diagnosis of infective arthritis?
Which portion of the palmar fascia is described as thick and strong, related to the palmar aponeurosis?
questions.explanation: The deep palmar fascia is divided into medial and lateral portions that are thin and weak, and an intermediate portion that is thick and strong. The intermediate portion forms the palmar aponeurosis. It is related to the inner four digits of the hand.

questions.question: Multiple myeloma most frequently involves which group of bones in over 90 percent of patients?
questions.explanation: Bones are involved in ninety percent of multiple myeloma patients, principally the skull, pelvis, spine, ribs, and femurs. Severe bone pain aggravated by motion and pathological fractures are typical presentations. Bone marrow aspiration biopsy confirms the diagnosis by showing sheets of plasma cells with large nuclei and nucleoli.

Following triple arthrodesis for flat foot, the postoperative POP cast positions the foot in equinus with the heel held in varus, extended with the ankle in dorsiflexion, before progressing to a walking plaster boot and then modified shoes with arch support. This specific positioning protects the surgical correction during the early fusion period. The physiotherapist should understand this cast positioning when planning the sequence of later mobilization and gait re-education.
options: Foot immobilized only above the ankle, excluding the foot
Foot in equinus with the heel held in varus position
Foot in neutral position with no ankle involvement
Foot in plantarflexion with the toes left completely free
Foot in full dorsiflexion with the heel in valgus
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with rocker bottom flat foot who underwent triple arthrodesis. What specific postoperative cast position is described for this surgery?

questions.explanation: During the fixation period after tendocalcaneus repair, physiotherapy uses non-weight bearing walking that progresses toward weight-bearing walking. Functional activities with crutches are taught by the physiotherapist during this stage. Exercises also maintain mobility of the toes, knee, and hip joints.
questions.question: A patient in a long leg cast following tendocalcaneus repair is being taught crutch walking by the physiotherapist. What weight-bearing status should be maintained during this fixation period?
options: Non-weight bearing progressing to weight bearing
Full weight bearing from day one
Partial weight bearing on the unaffected leg only
Weight bearing only on crutches without walking

questions.question: A child recovering from acute suppurative arthritis of the knee is being mobilized by the physiotherapist. Which exercise approach is prioritized to prevent muscle atrophy and stiffness?
options: Early mobilization with non-weight bearing free active exercises
Prolonged strict bedrest for several months
Complete avoidance of all joint movement
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for acute suppurative arthritis emphasizes early mobilization to prevent muscle atrophy and joint stiffness. Non-weight bearing free active exercises are performed to move the affected joint through its full range. Gait re-education with crutches, progressing to sticks, follows once pain subsides.

questions.question: Which criterion makes epiphyseal-preserving amputation particularly favoured for amputations performed in children?
options: It removes the need for nerve ligation during surgery
It shortens the overall operating time significantly
It eliminates the requirement for skin flap coverage
It avoids the need for any postoperative immobilization
It preserves the distal femoral growth epiphysis
questions.explanation: Tendoplastic (supracondylar) thigh amputation is the method of choice in children specifically because it preserves the distal femoral epiphysis, allowing continued longitudinal bone growth. This is important since children have significant remaining growth potential compared with adults. Preserving growth plates reduces the risk of disproportionate stump shortening over time.

questions.question: Physiotherapy for gonorrheal arthritis, following joint aspiration, progresses from assisted passive exercises to which stage?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management of gonorrheal arthritis progresses from assisted passive exercises to free active exercises for joint movement. This aims to strengthen weak muscles while restoring full range of motion. Splints or braces may still be used to provide comfort during the transition.
options: Passive exercises indefinitely with no progression

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient after excision of a cervical rib and is asked about the expected symptom course prior to surgery. Which description best matches the typical clinical course of cervical rib syndrome?
options: Sudden onset of complete permanent paralysis at outset
Immediate resolution without any need for intervention
Rapid, universally progressive deterioration within days
Fixed, unchanging symptoms from the moment of onset
Variable course with frequent remissions or slow progression
questions.explanation: Cervical rib syndrome is described as having a variable clinical course, with remissions or slow progression occurring frequently, which is why conservative treatment such as rest, arm support, cervical traction, and diathermy is trialled before considering surgical excision. Understanding this variable natural history helps the physiotherapist set appropriate expectations for symptom fluctuation during a course of conservative treatment. This also explains why surgery is not always the immediate first-line management choice.

questions.question: A physiotherapist wants gravity to assist ankle dorsiflexion during a mobility exercise. Which patient position achieves this according to the described technique?
options: Prone lying, foot over plinth edge
questions.explanation: For ankle dorsiflexion, the patient lies prone on a plinth with the foot over the end of the plinth, so that gravity assists the dorsiflexion movement. Alternatively, sitting with one leg crossed over the other allows the foot to move freely through dorsiflexion and plantar flexion. This gravity-assisted approach is useful when muscle strength around the ankle is reduced.

questions.question: An elderly patient with osteoarthritis is prescribed NSAIDs for pain relief. What specific caution should the physiotherapist reinforce regarding this medication in this age group?
questions.explanation: Elderly patients are especially vulnerable to NSAID toxicity, an important caution in osteoarthritis management. Analgesics and NSAIDs remain part of medical treatment despite this risk. Physiotherapists should reinforce medical advice on safe medication use alongside exercise therapy.
options: NSAIDs replace the need for exercise
NSAIDs are entirely safe at any dose
NSAIDs prevent all further joint damage
NSAIDs cure the underlying cartilage loss

questions.explanation:
Rehabilitation after meniscectomy follows a graded progression from non-weight-bearing to full weight-bearing.
The physiotherapist first teaches the patient to use elbow or axillary crutches for non-weight-bearing exercises.
This is progressed to hip hitching with partial weight-bearing and knee flexion exercises as recovery advances.
options: Elbow or axillary crutches for non-weight-bearing exercises
No walking aid is used at any stage
A single walking stick on the affected side only
Parallel bars used permanently without progression
questions.question: A patient with a torn medial meniscus proceeds to meniscectomy. Postoperative physiotherapy specifically teaches the patient to use which type of walking aid before progressing to partial weight-bearing?

questions.explanation: Exploration of the wound and soft tissue is indicated when a remnant foreign body is suspected, since it can perpetuate infection. Débridement accompanies this exploration of the joint. Removing the source of ongoing contamination reduces risk of persistent or reactivated infection.
options: Reactivated infection from a retained foreign body
questions.question: A patient with an infected joint wound requires exploration due to a suspected foreign body. What complication is this surgical exploration primarily intended to prevent?
For a patient with a ganglion cyst managed conservatively, which two specific physiotherapy modalities are indicated in the described protocol?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management of a ganglion includes free active exercises, heat therapy with short-wave or infrared radiation, and wax bath therapy. Conservative medical treatment separately includes strapping and hydrocortisone injection with lignocaine. Surgical excision remains the definitive treatment of choice despite fairly common recurrence.

questions.question: Which benign bone tumor characteristically produces a nidus of osteoid surrounded by a sclerotic zone with vague boring pain that gradually worsens?
questions.explanation: Osteoid osteoma consists of a nidus or core of osteoid and bone surrounded by a zone of sclerosis, more striking when the lesion is cortical. Pain is vague initially and gradually increases in severity, described as boring in character. Osteoblastoma instead is a granular, vascular lesion typically found in the spine or small bones.

questions.question: A spastic child shows involuntary quadriceps contraction on active knee flexion with hyperactive stretch reflexes. Which cerebral lesion site is responsible?
questions.explanation: Combined lesions of the premotor area and the motor area of the anterior central gyrus produce muscle spasticity. This explains the involuntary quadriceps contraction and hyperactive deep tendon reflexes seen on active flexion. Lesions of the main motor area alone instead cause flaccidity rather than spasticity.

questions.question: A patient with causalgia (reflex sympathetic dystrophy) is managed physiotherapeutically. Which two elements are specifically combined for this condition?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for causalgia combines isometric and other exercises to maintain muscle power and flexibility with heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy or infrared. Active and passive exercises along with warm fomentation are used conservatively. Sympathetic blocks are reserved for cases failing conservative measures.

questions.question: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome is characteristically associated with a positive result on which clinical test?
questions.explanation: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome typically shows a positive Tinel's sign, along with paresthesia in the median nerve distribution as the chief symptom. It commonly affects middle-aged women, with morning stiffness of the fingers. Severe or progressive symptoms warrant surgical decompression of the tunnel.

questions.question: A patient recovering from ORIF of a fracture involving the subtalar joint (calcaneus, Type II tongue fracture) begins weight-bearing after radiological confirmation of union. At approximately what point post-fixation is this weight-bearing typically permitted?
options: Weight-bearing is never permitted after this fracture type
questions.explanation:
Type II calcaneal fractures involving the subtalar joint are managed with reduction and axial pin or screw fixation.
Immobilization in a plaster cast is maintained for eight weeks following this fixation.
Weight-bearing is then permitted after this period, once radiological confirmation of union has been obtained.

questions.question: In ankylosing spondylitis physiotherapy, isometric exercise is specifically defined by which muscle action?
options: Muscle elongated under external traction only
questions.explanation: Isometric exercise in ankylosing spondylitis physiotherapy is defined as muscle contraction without shortening of the muscle. Isotonic exercise, by contrast, involves the muscle being contracted and shortened. Both active and passive exercise types are used alongside heat therapy in management.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with Klumpke's palsy who also shows drooping of the upper eyelid and a smaller pupil on the affected side. What additional syndrome should the physiotherapist recognize as coexisting?
questions.explanation: Ptosis, enophthalmos, and miosis alongside anhydrosis together constitute Horner's syndrome, which frequently accompanies Klumpke's (lower brachial plexus) palsy due to involvement of the cervical sympathetic fibres travelling with the first dorsal nerve root. Recognizing this cluster of eye and facial findings alerts the physiotherapist to the specific root-level involvement and helps differentiate Klumpke's from Erb-Duchenne palsy. This recognition also informs the broader multidisciplinary assessment needed for this injury.
options: Carpal tunnel syndrome from median nerve compression
Horner's syndrome from paralyzed cervical sympathetic fibres
Compartment syndrome from raised intracompartmental pressure
Thoracic outlet syndrome from subclavian artery compression

questions.question: Charcot's joint is best defined as a?
questions.explanation: Charcot's joint is defined as a trophic affection of joints that develops frequently in weight-bearing joints. It results from underlying neurological disturbance rather than infection or autoimmunity. Recognizing its trophic nature guides appropriate management.

Sling suspension lifts the limb clear of the plinth, thereby removing the friction offered by the surface of the plinth and blanket, while also supporting the weight of a heavy limb. This allows the patient to concentrate on the desired movement despite weakness. The suspension point is placed vertically over the joint being moved to allow free swinging.
questions.question: A physiotherapist wants a technique that removes friction from the plinth surface while supporting a heavy paralyzed limb during exercise. Which technique specifically achieves this according to the description?

options: Sclerosis and rounding of the fractured bone ends
Faint fracture line with early callus
questions.explanation:
Radiological union is confirmed by callus formation bridging the fracture gap.
Sclerosis with rounding-off of the bone ends instead indicates that healing has failed.
This appearance reflects bone ends that have become insulated from each other by fibrous tissue.
questions.question: On X-ray, which finding is considered a definite sign of non-union rather than normal healing?
A patient with a vertebral aneurysmal bone cyst has undergone excision of the lesion with adjoining tissue. What should guide the physiotherapist's early postoperative mobilization plan?
questions.explanation: Excision of expanded vertebral aneurysmal bone cyst lesions, along with adjoining involved tissue, is a more extensive surgery than curettage used for long bone lesions. Postoperative mobilization should therefore be gradual and protected to respect spinal healing. Physiotherapy exercises follow as part of aftercare once appropriate.
options: Return to competitive sport within days
Gradual, protected mobilization respecting spinal surgical healing
Complete avoidance of any movement indefinitely

questions.question: Abnormal forward movement of the tibia over the femur, with the knee capable of hyperextension, is most consistent with injury to which ligament?
questions.explanation:
The anterior cruciate ligament normally restrains forward translation of the tibia on the femur.
When it is torn, the tibia can be drawn abnormally forward and the knee may hyperextend.
Isolated tears are uncommon and often occur alongside injury to the medial collateral ligament or meniscus.

options: Freiberg's disease, occurring at ten to fifteen years of age
Sever's disease, occurring at ten to fifteen years of age
Osgood-Schlatter disease, occurring at ten to fifteen years of age
Kohler's disease, occurring at five to ten years of age
Perthes disease, occurring at five to fifteen years of age
questions.explanation:
Kohler's disease is osteochondritis of the navicular tarsal bone, typically affecting boys aged five to ten years.
X-ray shows fragmentation and irregularity of the epiphysis with a characteristic disc-like appearance of the navicular.
Conservative management includes rest, diathermy, strapping support, and appropriate footwear modification.
questions.question: A seven-year-old boy has foot pain and a prominent dorsal foot swelling, with X-ray showing a flattened, disc-like navicular bone. What condition and typical age range does this describe?

A physiotherapist notices a patient with suspected chronic arterial insufficiency has intermittent claudication that worsens with walking and improves with rest. Which vasospastic or occlusive condition is this pain pattern most typically associated with?
questions.explanation: Buerger's disease characteristically presents with both persistent, aching rest pain and intermittent claudication due to inflammatory occlusion of distal arteries, distinguishing it from Raynaud's disease, which is primarily cold- or stress-triggered digital colour change without claudication. Chronic venous insufficiency instead produces a dull ache worsened by prolonged standing rather than exertional claudication. Correctly distinguishing these pain patterns helps the physiotherapist appropriately direct further vascular assessment.
options: Sudeck's atrophy with burning pain worsened by movement
Chronic venous insufficiency with dull aching worse standing
Buerger's disease with rest pain and claudication
Superficial thrombophlebitis with a tender venous cord
Raynaud's disease with cold-triggered digital pallor

questions.explanation: One stick is held by the arm opposite the affected leg, giving the patient the advantage of sparing one hand free while maintaining balance. Two sticks may be used for partial weight-bearing as a progression from crutches. Sticks or frames serve as an alternative aid for maintaining balance during gait re-education.
questions.question: A patient progressing from crutches to a single stick for partial weight-bearing should hold the stick in which hand according to the described principle?
options: The arm on the same side
The arm opposite the affected leg

questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for popliteal cyst addresses muscle weakness alongside pain relief through active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening. Heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy supports this approach. This combination restores functional knee strength after the cyst is treated.
questions.question: A patient with popliteal (Baker's) cyst has muscular weakness noted alongside knee swelling. Physiotherapy exercises specifically aim to address which functional deficit alongside pain relief?

options: Immediate return to unrestricted sporting activity
Physiotherapy including active exercises of fingers, wrist, and elbow
A further six weeks of rigid immobilization without exercise
Surgical re-exploration regardless of clinical progress
questions.explanation:
Following the fixed immobilization period for an anterior Monteggia fracture dislocation, plaster is removed.
Physiotherapy is then initiated, focusing on active exercises of the fingers, wrist, and elbow.
An arm sling may continue to be used to support the limb while active movement is progressed.
questions.question: A patient recovering from Monteggia fracture dislocation has had the forearm and elbow immobilised in supination and flexion by plaster for six weeks. What comes next in management?
Which complication of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia results from orbital bone involvement?
questions.explanation: Orbital involvement in polyostotic fibrous dysplasia can lead to blindness from expanding cystic lesions. Other complications include limb shortening and deformity. Thyrotoxicosis may also occur in association with this condition.

Chronic venous insufficiency usually occurs from changes secondary to deep thrombophlebitis, where damaged valves of the deep venous channels by the thrombotic process lead to progressive leg edema and secondary skin and subcutaneous fibrosis. It may also occur from neoplastic obstruction of the pelvic veins. This differs from primary varicose veins, which stem from congenital valve paucity in the superficial system.
options: Isolated arterial embolism lodging in the popliteal artery
Changes secondary to deep thrombophlebitis damaging valves
Direct traumatic laceration of the femoral artery
Acute superficial thrombophlebitis without deep involvement
Congenital absence of the superficial saphenous system
questions.question: Chronic venous insufficiency most commonly develops secondary to which underlying process?

questions.explanation: Hammer toe combines hyperextension of the metatarsophalangeal joint with a flexed proximal interphalangeal joint, and the distal interphalangeal joint may be flexed or extended, together with a depressed, prominent metatarsal head and callosities over bony prominences. This contrasts with claw toe patterns seen in some neurological deformities. The Sir Robert Jones procedure, resecting the proximal interphalangeal joint, is the surgical treatment described.
questions.question: Hammer toe deformity is characterized by hyperextension of the metatarsophalangeal joint together with which interphalangeal joint change?
options: Ankylosis of the distal interphalangeal joint only
Complete absence of the proximal phalanx
Fixed abduction of the proximal phalanx

questions.explanation:
In children, both-bone forearm fractures are mostly undisplaced greenstick injuries in the middle third.
These can usually be managed conservatively with closed reduction and plaster immobilization.
In adults, by contrast, open reduction and internal fixation is generally the treatment of choice.
questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates management of both-bone forearm fractures in children from those in adults?
options: Children's fractures always require open reduction and internal fixation
Children's fractures are mostly undisplaced greenstick fractures managed conservatively
Adult fractures are always treated with closed reduction alone
Children's fractures typically require plating of both bones
Adults heal both-bone fractures faster than children

questions.question: Recurrent dislocation of the elbow, though rare, is usually of which type?
questions.explanation:
Recurrent dislocation of the elbow is an uncommon condition overall.
When it does occur, it is usually posterior in direction, similar to the pattern of acute elbow dislocation.
Predisposing factors include laxity of the collateral ligaments or a shallow trochlear notch of the ulna.

Cervical spondylosis shows an early loss of the normal anterior cervical convexity with reduced disc space. Osteophyte formation is described as a late radiographic finding. MRI is used to demonstrate any nerve root or spinal cord compression.
questions.question: Cervical spondylosis is characterized radiographically in its late stage by which finding?
A patient with loose bodies in the knee, confirmed on arthroscopy, undergoes surgical removal. What is the described physiotherapy management following this procedure?
options: Free active exercises combined with short-wave diathermy or infrared
Complete joint immobilization for six months
Passive-only treatment with no active exercise ever introduced
Cryotherapy as the sole postoperative treatment
questions.explanation:
Loose bodies within the knee joint typically present with a history of locking at variable angles.
Once surgically removed, either arthroscopically or by open surgery, rehabilitation begins promptly.
Physiotherapy management combines free active exercises with short-wave diathermy or infrared heat therapy.

options: Amputation above the knee in all cases
Exploration of the knee joint, shaving of cartilage, arthroplasty, or patellectomy
Total hip replacement regardless of symptoms
Spinal fusion of the lumbar spine
Excision of the entire quadriceps tendon
questions.question: A patient with chondromalacia patellae has predisposing factors including obesity and a disturbed quadriceps mechanism causing knee locking. Alongside physiotherapy, what surgical options are listed for cases involving internal derangement or arthritic changes?
questions.explanation:
Chondromalacia patellae is degeneration of the patellar articular cartilage, often linked to obesity and quadriceps imbalance.
When internal derangement or arthritic lesions are present, surgical options become relevant.
These include exploration of the joint, shaving of the involved cartilage, arthroplasty, or patellectomy depending on severity.

questions.question: Gonorrheal arthritis in males classically presents around how long after intercourse with an infected partner?
questions.explanation: Male patients with gonorrheal arthritis typically present around two weeks after intercourse with an infected partner. Symptoms include urethral discharge, dysuria, and arthralgia with swelling of joints. Movements of the affected joints become painful and restricted.

questions.question: An old unreduced dislocation of a joint is generally defined as one that has remained unreduced for approximately how long?
questions.explanation:
An old unreduced dislocation is defined by the duration it has remained unreduced.
This period is generally taken as three to four weeks following the original injury.
Beyond this point, degeneration of unbathed articular cartilage and soft tissue changes complicate reduction.

questions.question: When teaching a patient to descend stairs using crutches, the physiotherapist should instruct which sequence of actions?
questions.explanation: Going downstairs with crutches, the patient places the crutches on the step below and takes weight through them while lowering the normal leg onto that step. The physiotherapist moves down in front of the patient to ensure safety throughout. This contrasts with going upstairs, where the normal leg is lifted onto the step first while weight is borne through the crutches.
options: Crutches on lower step, then normal leg

questions.question: A patient with a nonosteogenic fibroma of the tibia has failed conservative treatment with analgesics and heat therapy. What is the next step in management before physiotherapy-focused rehabilitation?
questions.explanation: Surgical curettage of the lesion is indicated for a nonosteogenic fibroma when conservative treatment with analgesics, NSAIDs and heat therapy fails. Physiotherapy rehabilitation follows as aftercare once surgery has been performed. This staged approach reserves surgery for refractory cases.

Displacement of the biceps brachii tendon from the intertubercular groove occurs commonly amongst mountain climbers, skiers, and marchers. On contraction, the tendon dislocates out of the groove due to a weak or split fascial sheath. A reducible swelling appears over the muscle belly that decreases on contraction.
questions.question: Displacement of the biceps brachii tendon from the intertubercular groove is seen commonly among which group?

options: Stump volume has decreased, altering socket fit over time
The contralateral limb has become proportionally longer
The prosthetic socket material has permanently expanded
The prosthetic suspension system has spontaneously failed
The residual limb has regenerated additional bone length
questions.explanation: Since the stump must maintain consistent volume for a snug socket fit, significant weight change alters stump volume and produces a loose-fitting prosthesis, requiring socket adjustment or additional stump socks. This is a recognized, expected consequence of weight fluctuation in amputees rather than a prosthetic material defect. The physiotherapist should refer the patient for prosthetic review rather than assume a structural prosthesis failure.
questions.question: A patient with a below-knee stump complains the prosthesis feels loose after significant recent weight loss. What is the most likely underlying stump-related explanation?

options: Directly posterior to the tibia without lateral shift
Superiorly, wedged between tibia and fibula
In front of the ankle, overlying the lateral side of the foot
Into the subtalar joint without displacement
questions.explanation:
Forced inversion stresses all the ligaments attached to the talus, eventually dislocating it.
The talus shifts to lie in front of the ankle, overlying the lateral aspect of the foot.
Its head points medially while its calcaneal articular surface faces backwards, a characteristic deformity pattern.
questions.question: In fracture dislocation of the ankle, forced inversion causes the talus to shift into which position relative to the ankle?

questions.explanation:
Comminuted fractures of the radial head, particularly with capitellar damage, are managed by excision.
After this surgery, physiotherapy focuses on free active exercises to restore range of movement.
Heat pad therapy is used alongside exercise to help relieve pain and stiffness during recovery.
questions.question: A patient with fracture head of radius has been managed by excision due to comminution. Physiotherapy after this procedure is best described as:
options: Immediate resisted forearm rotation against weights
Strict immobilization for twelve weeks without exercise
Passive manipulation under general anaesthesia weekly
Free active exercises combined with heat pad therapy
Ice immersion as the sole modality

questions.explanation: Deep friction massage must be applied transversely across the specific tissue fibers involved, unlike superficial massage which follows the longitudinal direction parallel to blood vessels to enhance circulation. questions.question: A patient with hyperparathyroidism is noted to have hypercalcemia with nausea, restlessness and tachycardia. How should this acute presentation influence physiotherapy scheduling?

Begin aggressive gait training at once

questions.question: Volkmann's ischemic contracture of the lower limb is characterized by which deformity of the foot?
questions.explanation: Volkmann's ischemic contracture of the lower limb produces an equinovarus deformity of the foot and ankle that cannot be corrected. questions.question: A physiotherapist evaluating an irritable joint with pain at rest should select which general grade of oscillation technique to remain safe?
questions.explanation: For an irritable joint, characterized by pain at rest, muscle spasm, and insomnia, the physiotherapist should select gentler, lower-grade oscillation techniques rather than vigorous ones. Grade V, a high-velocity thrust, is reserved for stable, nonirritable joints.

questions.question: Congenital club foot (talipes equinovarus) most typically presents with which combination of deformity components?

questions.question: Mallet finger deformity results from avulsion of which tendon from the terminal phalanx?
questions.explanation: Mallet finger occurs when forced flexion tears the extensor tendon from its attachment to the phalanx. The deformity presents as persistent flexion of the terminal phalanx. Extension of the terminal phalanx is characteristically lost.

questions.question: Which type of true aneurysm is described as the commonest, with the lumen more or less equally expanded?
questions.explanation: Fusiform aneurysm is the commonest type of true aneurysm, characterized by more or less equal expansion of the arterial lumen, usually from an artery weakened by hypertension and atheroma. Saccular aneurysm instead results from localized stretching of the arterial wall due to trauma. Dissecting aneurysm involves separation of an atheromatous plaque allowing blood to insinuate between the layers of the media.

questions.question: Following knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis, a patient is placed in Buck's traction for one week postoperatively. What is the primary purpose of subsequent exercise once this period ends?
options: To replace the need for the traction
To restore quadriceps power as soon as possible
To prevent recurrence of septic arthritis
questions.explanation: After the postoperative period of Buck's traction for osteoarthritis knee surgery, exercises are started as soon as possible to restore quadriceps power. questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient recovering from ligation and division of a superficial vein for thrombophlebitis. What specific indication led to surgical rather than conservative management in this case?
questions.explanation: Surgical management of superficial thrombophlebitis, through ligation and division of the vein, is specifically indicated when the thrombus has become detached and produced emboli, a relatively rare event, since most cases are managed conservatively with rest, elevation, and anti-inflammatory measures. questions.question: A discoid meniscus producing snapping knee is described as being thicker at which region compared to the periphery?
questions.explanation: A discoid meniscus is a solid disc that is thicker in the center than at the periphery. This shape causes it to slip and produce an audible snap during knee movement. Excision of the disc is the surgical treatment of choice for severe cases.

A physiotherapist reviewing amputation aftercare notes that after a Boyd amputation, weight bearing on the stump is not permitted until how many weeks postoperatively?
questions.explanation: Following Boyd amputation, weight bearing upon the stump is only allowed after 8 weeks, while sutures are removed at 2 weeks and any internal fixator is removed at 4 weeks, with a walking cast maintained until arthrodesis is complete. This staged timeline reflects the need for solid calcaneo-tibial fusion before loading the stump. The physiotherapist must sequence rehabilitation exercises around these specific fixation and fusion milestones.

Fat embolism is a clinical entity that occurs following severe polytrauma with multiple fractures, where fat droplets from injured bone marrow or adipose tissue enter the circulation and become lodged in vessels, causing obstruction. A convex sole due to talus and calcaneus positioned in equinus

questions.question: Which visual field defect is classically associated with a pituitary adenoma causing acromegaly?
questions.explanation: Eye examination in acromegaly may reveal bitemporal hemianopsia due to compression of the optic chiasm. This occurs as the pituitary tumor enlarges superiorly. Visual field loss is an important indicator for surgical rather than radiotherapy treatment.

questions.question: Causalgia (reflex sympathetic dystrophy) is characterized by pain of which quality?
questions.explanation: Causalgia produces severe, burning pain that is often paroxysmally precipitated by friction and worse at night. Vasomotor changes include warm, dry, swollen skin that may appear red or cyanotic. Affected limbs are often held in a deformed position by spasmodic muscles.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a newborn diagnosed with Erb-Duchenne palsy following a difficult delivery. Which position is used to immobilize the arm in the relaxation position during early conservative management?

questions.question: Therapeutic ultrasound used in physiotherapy operates within which approximate frequency range?

questions.explanation: Diabetic gangrene results from three combined factors: peripheral neuritis causing trophic changes, atheroma of arteries causing ischemia, and hyperglycemia lowering tissue resistance to infection. questions.question: A patient with lumbar spine osteoarthritis and neurological symptoms is referred for imaging. Which modality is specifically indicated in this context?

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient one week after amputation performed for diabetic gangrene. Which additional monitoring consideration is specifically relevant compared with a patient amputated for trauma alone?

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to assess a patient with suspected cervical rib compression. Which specific clinical test would most appropriately be included in the assessment?
