Presence of thenar eminence wasting on examination
Presence of pain radiating into the little and ring fingers
Presence of hand sweating on the affected side only
Absence of a visible cervical rib on X-ray or CT imaging
questions.explanation: Since scalene syndrome reproduces the identical clinical picture of cervical rib compression, the key distinguishing feature is imaging: the absence of an actual cervical rib on X-ray or CT scan in scalene syndrome, since the compression instead comes from a pulled scalenus anticus muscle. The other listed findings, thenar wasting, sweating, radiating pain, and Adson's test, occur similarly in both conditions and cannot reliably differentiate them. This makes imaging essential before deciding between muscle division and rib excision as definitive surgery.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to help differentiate scalene syndrome from cervical rib syndrome in a patient with supraclavicular pain. Which investigation finding would most reliably distinguish the two conditions?
A physiotherapist is asked to justify why chronic tennis elbow uses deep transverse friction rather than only rest. What is the described purpose of this technique?
questions.explanation: Deep transverse frictions in chronic tennis elbow are applied specifically to regain mobility and stretch adhesions that have formed. This is done for five to ten minutes daily over one week. Ultrasound therapy given beforehand further prepares the tissue for this manual technique.
options: To regain mobility and stretch adhesions
To replace the need for any rest
To eliminate all future flare-ups instantly

questions.question: Which pathological finding is characteristically described in recurrent anterior dislocation of the shoulder, involving flattening of the posterolateral humeral head?
questions.explanation:
Recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation is associated with several characteristic pathological lesions.
The Hill-Sachs lesion refers specifically to flattening of the posterolateral aspect of the humeral head.
This differs from a Bankart lesion, which involves separation of the anterior glenoid labrum.

questions.question: Which type of hip dislocation is described as the commonest, with the femoral head displaced onto the dorsum ilii?
questions.explanation:
Posterior dislocation of the hip is by far the commonest type described.
In this pattern, the femoral head is displaced backward onto the dorsum ilii.
A classic mechanism is force transmitted up the femoral shaft, as in a dashboard injury during a road accident.

questions.question: For chronic rheumatoid arthritis outdoor physiotherapy, muscle power is built using slow reversals and repeated contractions combined with which activity in parallel bars?
options: Static balance on one foot only
questions.explanation: Outdoor physiotherapy for chronic rheumatoid arthritis builds muscle power through slow reversals and repeated contractions, along with resisted walking using pelvic resistance in parallel bars. Joint range is maintained with active assisted movements progressing to free active exercises. Hydrotherapy further assists through buoyancy-reduced movement.

When calcaneal spur pain is disabling and persists despite conservative measures such as heat therapy, analgesics, and heel padding, surgical excision of the spur is indicated, with weight bearing permitted after about 2 weeks postoperatively. This staged escalation from conservative to surgical care mirrors the pattern used for other painful, non-resolving orthopedic foot conditions in the chapter. The physiotherapist should recognize when persistent symptoms warrant escalation beyond continued conservative management.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with a painful calcaneal spur who has not improved with heat therapy and shoe modification. What is the next appropriate management step described?
options: Referral for unrelated cervical spine investigation
Permanent cessation of all weight-bearing activity
Surgical excision of the spur if pain remains disabling
Immediate above-knee amputation of the affected limb
Repeating the same conservative measures indefinitely

questions.explanation: Surgical amputation for malignancy aims to save life or preserve health by severing a harmful limb, improve function by removing a deformed or useless part, and substitute an artificial prosthesis from a functional standpoint. Forequarter amputation for tumor extension is additionally combined with excision of regional lymph nodes. This differs from PVD amputation, whose primary aim is limb and life salvage from ischemia.
questions.question: What is the specific surgical aim of amputation performed for a malignant tumor rather than for trauma or vascular disease?
options: To remove a harmful part and restore function via prosthesis
To delay definitive surgery until tumor markers normalize
To salvage as much bony length as technically possible only
To preserve the joint immediately proximal at all costs
To avoid any resection of surrounding lymph node tissue

questions.explanation: Pirogoff's amputation is distinguished by rotating the calcaneus forward so that it fuses directly to the tibia, preserving a weight-bearing surface. Chopart's and tarsometatarsal disarticulations were largely discarded because they tend to develop equinovarus or equinus deformity. This anatomical detail differentiates the various mid-foot amputation levels.
questions.question: During amputation through the middle of the foot, which historic procedure involves forward rotation of the calcaneus to fuse with the tibia?

questions.explanation: Quantitative CT scan and quantitative MRI provide detailed assessment of bone mineral density in osteoporosis. Plain radiographs mainly show demineralization once bone loss is advanced. These quantitative modalities aid earlier diagnosis.
questions.question: Which imaging modality provides quantitative assessment of bone mineral density beyond plain X-ray?

questions.explanation: Periarthritis shoulder, also called frozen shoulder, is common in women past the fifth decade of life. Pain is acute or insidious, worst at night, and aggravated by joint motion. Local tenderness is often found over the greater trochanter or bicipital groove.
questions.question: Periarthritis of the shoulder (frozen shoulder) is most commonly encountered in which demographic group?

options: It is the only effective treatment available
It is one of several modalities used to relieve joint symptoms
It is used exclusively for hand osteoarthritis
It cures the degenerative cartilage changes
It replaces the need for all medication
questions.question: A patient asks why traction is included among physiotherapy modalities for osteoarthritis. What is the most appropriate explanation?
questions.explanation: Traction is listed among the physiotherapy modalities used for osteoarthritis, alongside exercises, heat therapy, massage and orthoses. It contributes to symptom relief as part of a broader conservative program. It is not curative and is not restricted to one specific joint.

questions.question: A postmenopausal woman presents after sustaining a Colles' fracture with minimal trauma. What underlying condition should the physiotherapist suspect and address in the rehabilitation plan?
questions.explanation: A Colles' fracture from minor trauma in a postmenopausal woman is a classic presentation of osteoporosis, linked to postmenopausal estrogen loss. Rehabilitation should therefore incorporate osteoporosis-specific measures such as weight-bearing exercise and fall prevention. Addressing the underlying bone fragility reduces future fracture risk.

options: Immediate death from haemorrhage in nearly all cases
Permanent loss of the femoral pulse regardless of reduction
Spontaneous conversion to an anterior dislocation
Automatic development of a pathological fracture
questions.question: Dislocation or fracture-dislocation of the hip is regarded as an acute emergency mainly because delay in reduction increases the risk of:
questions.explanation:
Hip dislocation is treated as an emergency requiring priority reduction.
The longer the joint remains dislocated, the greater the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Osteoarthritis is a further long-term consequence of delayed or inadequate reduction.

In tennis elbow, passive pronation of the forearm to its full extent characteristically exaggerates pain over the lateral epicondyle. The mechanism of injury involves abrupt pronation straining the extensor aponeurotic fibers. Local tenderness is found specifically over the lateral epicondyle.
questions.question: Which finding differentiates tennis elbow pain provocation on clinical examination?
options: Exaggeration of pain with wrist flexion only
Exaggeration of pain with elbow extension only
Exaggeration of pain with finger abduction
Exaggeration of pain with shoulder external rotation
Exaggeration of pain with full passive pronation
Erosion of the adjacent vertebral body
questions.question: The earliest definite radiographic sign of tuberculous spondylitis is which finding?
questions.explanation: Erosion of the adjacent vertebral body is described as the earliest definite radiographic sign of tuberculous spondylitis. Narrowing of the intervertebral space and a perispinal abscess follow as the disease progresses. Wedging and collapse of the vertebrae represent later findings.

Following anterior transposition surgery for tardy ulnar nerve palsy, immobilization with a plaster of Paris cast is maintained for 4 to 6 weeks, with stitches removed after 2 days through a window in the cast. Physiotherapy exercises and occupational therapy follow once the cast is discontinued. This timeline guides the physiotherapist in sequencing early protective care versus later active rehabilitation.
options: 16 to 20 weeks in a POP cast
10 to 12 weeks in a POP cast
4 to 6 weeks in a POP cast
1 to 2 weeks in a POP cast
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with tardy ulnar nerve palsy following anterior transposition surgery. What is the expected duration of postoperative plaster cast immobilization?

questions.explanation: Viral causes of infective arthritis include smallpox, measles and mumps. Bacteria remain the commonest cause overall, including staphylococci and streptococci. Fungal and parasitic causes are comparatively rare.
questions.question: Which causative organism group for infective arthritis includes measles and mumps?

Application of ice packs directly over the coccyx continuously
Warm fomentation combined with short-wave or infrared therapy and analgesics
questions.explanation:
Coccygodynia describes pain in the coccyx that may follow trauma such as a fall from height.
Conservative management includes rest, warm fomentation, short-wave or infrared therapy, and analgesics.
Surgery, such as coccygectomy, is reserved for organic cases where conservative measures fail to relieve symptoms.
questions.question: A patient with coccygodynia following a fall is managed conservatively with local infiltration of lignocaine and steroid alongside physiotherapy. What additional conservative measure specifically addresses aggravation of pain by sitting?

options: To assist venous and lymphatic drainage
To bypass the need for exercise
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing swelling after knee trauma elevates the leg on pillows. What is the physiological rationale for this positioning according to the described technique?
questions.explanation: Elevating the limb assists drainage as part of the physiotherapeutic measures for post-traumatic swelling, combined with static muscle contractions controlling joint movement and free exercises for unaffected joints. This is applied both for leg swelling after knee trauma and arm swelling after upper limb trauma. The patient is advised to continue keeping the limb elevated along with regular exercise.

For patients with flat feet related to occupational strain, such as waitresses, policemen, and watchmen, well-fitting comfortable footwear is emphasized, specifically requiring the inner side of the shoe to be straight and the upper edge to fit snugly, alongside general posture correction and gait re-education. This structural footwear guidance is a practical, low-cost physiotherapy intervention appropriate for occupation-related flat foot strain. The physiotherapist should tailor this advice around the patient's specific occupational demands.
options: A pointed narrow toe box with an elevated heel
A curved outer border designed for high-impact sport
Complete absence of any arch support structure
A loosely fitting upper edge to maximize comfort
A straight inner side with a snugly fitting upper edge
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to advise a teacher-patient with strain-related flat feet (common in occupations requiring prolonged standing) about footwear modification. What specific structural feature of the shoe is emphasized?

Avoidance of any splint or exercise until surgery is planned
Night splintage combined with active finger-stretching exercises
Complete immobilization of the hand for several months
Radiotherapy as the definitive treatment at every stage
questions.explanation: Early-stage Dupuytren's contracture is managed conservatively with night splintage and active exercises involving gentle stretching of the fingers by the patient, with radiotherapy noted as having only a limited role in this early phase. Surgical fasciotomy is reserved for more advanced disease where conservative measures are unlikely to be effective. The physiotherapist's early involvement in splinting and exercise instruction can help delay or reduce the eventual need for surgical intervention.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with Dupuytren's contracture in the early stage before surgery is indicated. What specific conservative measure is recommended at this stage?
Which triad of factors, known by the name of its describer, explains the pathogenesis of deep vein thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Deep vein thrombosis pathogenesis is explained by Virchow's triad: vessel wall trauma, venous stasis, and hypercoagulability, which together promote thrombus formation typically starting in a venous tributary around a valve. Portions of the thrombus may break off to form pulmonary emboli. This mechanistic understanding underlies the preventive and anticoagulant strategies used in DVT management.
options: Charcot's triad of fever, jaundice, and abdominal pain
Beck's triad of hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distension
Waddell's triad involving nonorganic physical signs
Cushing's triad of hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing
Virchow's triad of vessel trauma, stasis, hypercoagulation

questions.question: In the classification of walking patterns, akinesia during standing is considered which type of state?
questions.explanation: Akinesia during standing is classified as a pathological state, contrasted with normal intentional standing. Similarly, small shuffling steps during walking are pathological compared with normal regular steps. Festination is likewise listed as a pathological standing pattern in the walking classification table.

Testing for lateral popliteal (common peroneal) nerve injury involves assessing dorsiflexion of the ankle with the foot resting on its lateral border, the leg hanging down from the end of the bed, and movement tested against resistance; inability to dorsiflex confirms the deficit. This mirrors the muscle testing approach used for sciatic nerve injury, since both affect similar distal musculature. The physiotherapist uses this specific positioning to isolate the movement being assessed.
options: Inversion tested with the ankle in maximum plantarflexion
Toe flexion tested with the ankle in neutral position
Dorsiflexion tested with the leg hanging and against resistance
Plantarflexion tested with the knee fully extended
Eversion tested with the great toe held in flexion
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with lateral popliteal nerve injury and foot drop. Which specific ankle movement is the priority focus of the muscle testing protocol described?
A patient with fracture of the calcaneus managed conservatively is allowed early weight-bearing. What supportive device accompanies this early mobilisation?
questions.explanation:
Isolated calcaneal fractures without significant displacement are managed with plaster and early weight-bearing.
An ankle brace is provided to support the foot as weight-bearing begins.
The physiotherapist subsequently focuses on reducing oedema, regaining ankle and foot movement, and re-educating gait.
options: Wheelchair use exclusively for six months
Solo home exercise with no supervision
questions.question: A patient with chronic rheumatoid arthritis being reviewed as an outdoor patient reports mutual encouragement from peer interactions. Which physiotherapy-associated service specifically provides this benefit?
questions.explanation: Group therapy is specifically described as providing mutual support through group meetings for chronic rheumatoid arthritis patients. Community care further supports monitoring of the patient's progress. These psychosocial elements complement muscle power and joint range training in outdoor physiotherapy.

questions.question: A patient with a compression fracture of a thoracic vertebra is managed conservatively with traction and a shield-spine brace. What physiotherapy approach is indicated?
options: Assisted exercises by the physiotherapist followed by free active exercises by the patient
Complete avoidance of any exercise for one year
Passive spinal manipulation under anaesthesia weekly
Hydrotherapy as the sole treatment from day one
questions.explanation:
Compression fractures of the vertebral body are frequently managed conservatively with bed rest, traction, and bracing.
Physiotherapy begins with assisted exercises delivered by the physiotherapist during the early recovery phase.
As strength and confidence return, the patient progresses to performing free active exercises independently.

Kocher's method reduces the shoulder through a specific sequence of manoeuvres.
Traction is applied first, followed by gradual external rotation of the arm.
Once reduced, the arm is brought across the chest and finally rotated internally to complete the manoeuvre.
questions.question: The Kocher's method of shoulder reduction proceeds through which correct sequence of manoeuvres?
options: Internal rotation, then abduction, then traction
Adduction, then external rotation, then traction
Traction, external rotation, adduction across the chest, then internal rotation

questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management of palmar and plantar fibromatosis includes free active exercises, heat therapy with SWD or IRR, and wax bath therapy. Conservative treatment separately includes analgesics, antiallergics, and local hydrocortisone injection with hyalase. Surgical reconstruction is the definitive treatment of choice once conservative measures are exhausted.
questions.question: In managing a patient with palmar fibromatosis before reconstructive surgery, which physiotherapy techniques are indicated?
options: Free active exercises, heat, wax bath

questions.question: Which sign is considered the most important clinical symptom of a fracture, while local bony tenderness is the most important clinical sign in impacted fractures?
questions.explanation:
In impacted fractures, unnatural mobility and crepitus are often absent because fragments are locked together.
Loss of function is therefore regarded as the most important presenting symptom.
Local bony tenderness becomes the key clinical sign that alerts the examiner to the fracture.

questions.question: A fracture fails to unite within the expected time, but X-ray shows no sclerosis and bone ends remain well defined. This describes which condition?
Which weight-bearing pattern is the recognized exception among lower-limb amputation stumps that bears weight through the end of the stump?
questions.explanation: Syme amputation is the classical exception to lateral bearing, functioning instead as an end-bearing stump because the heel pad skin is preserved and adapted to bear weight directly. Most other lower-limb levels rely on lateral (tibial or ischial) bearing at bony points above the amputation. This distinction guides prosthetic socket design for each level.

Support slings are used in peripheral nerve injury rehabilitation to assist movement and bear the weight of the paralysed limb, working alongside static and dynamic splints that rest paralysed muscles in an optimum position to avoid overstretching or contractures. Aerobic activity, aiming for around 30 minutes four times weekly, is also encouraged for general health benefit. This combination of support and controlled activity parallels circulatory-focused strategies used in vascular rehabilitation, though the underlying mechanism differs.
options: Support slings to bear the weight of the paralysed limb
Complete rest with no splinting of the affected limb
Isolated cryotherapy applied continuously to the limb
Avoidance of all aerobic activity throughout recovery
Passive range of motion applied only to unaffected joints
questions.question: A physiotherapist working with an amputee-equivalent nerve-injured patient uses Buerger's exercises as part of the treatment plan. In peripheral nerve injury rehabilitation, which modality serves an analogous circulatory support role for paralysed limbs?

questions.explanation: Buerger's disease is strongly associated with tobacco or cigarette smoking, alongside a possible collagen disorder and abnormal sympathetic nervous system activity, producing episodic inflammatory and thrombotic occlusion of distal arteries and veins predominantly in the legs. It typically affects men aged 20 to 40 and often terminates in gangrene. Smoking cessation is therefore a preventive cornerstone of management.
questions.question: Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is most strongly associated with which specific etiological factor?

questions.explanation: Arteriosclerosis obliterans occurs at a comparatively older age with associated hyperlipidemia and blood vessel calcification, without phlebitis, distinguishing it from Buerger's disease, which affects younger men aged 20 to 40 with a strong smoking association and superficial vein involvement. Scleroderma is a further differential showing skin changes preceding vascular changes. Correctly distinguishing these entities affects both prognosis and treatment approach.
options: Occurrence at an older age with associated hyperlipidemia
Involvement limited strictly to the upper limb vessels
Complete absence of any pain on exertion or rest
Occurrence exclusively in young women under twenty
Presence of a positive family vasospastic history only
questions.question: Arteriosclerosis obliterans is differentiated from Buerger's disease in differential diagnosis primarily by which feature?

questions.explanation: Hydrotherapy contraindications include cardiovascular disease or high blood pressure, since increased blood flow from warm water may place additional stress on the heart. Other contraindications include fever, acute inflammation, kidney disease, cancer, and pregnancy. It should never be used as a substitute for standard medical care.
options: High blood pressure or cardiovascular disease
questions.question: Contraindications to hydrotherapy specifically include which cardiovascular concern?

questions.explanation: Palmar fibromatosis, or Dupuytren's contracture, typically starts near the base of the ring or little finger. It gradually draws the affected finger into the palm through fixed flexion. The terminal phalanx characteristically remains unaffected while proximal and middle phalanges flex.
questions.question: Dupuytren's contracture most commonly begins near the base of which finger?

questions.explanation: In snapping shoulder, muscle fibers from the outer border of the short head of biceps pass distally and laterally toward the long head, sliding over the lesser trochanter as the shoulder is abducted and rotated. The click produced is usually less audible than in other snapping joints. Movements of the shoulder become painful and restricted.
questions.question: Snapping shoulder due to the short head of biceps sliding over a bony prominence occurs at which site?

questions.explanation: The T score compares a patient's bone mineral density to that of a healthy young adult, informing fracture risk. The Z score instead compares to a person of the same age and sex. Understanding which score is used helps interpret fracture risk correctly during exercise planning.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning a fall-prevention and exercise program for a patient with a T score indicating osteoporosis. What does the T score specifically compare?
options: The patient's BMD to a same-age peer
The patient's BMD to a healthy young adult's BMD
The patient's calcium level to normal range
The patient's BMD to their own baseline only
The patient's BMD to the general population mean

questions.question: For Raynaud's disease, the physiotherapist instructs contrast baths using a hot bath for three minutes followed by a cool bath for how long?
questions.explanation: Contrast bath therapy for Raynaud's disease involves immersing the hands or feet in a hot bath for three minutes, then a cool bath for one minute. This alternating temperature exposure accelerates blood flow in peripheral vessels. Active exercises to increase circulation are used alongside this modality.

Loss of bladder control before any motor or sensory change
Motor supply of upper limbs first, then lower limbs, then pain and temperature, and lastly touch
Pain and temperature loss precedes any motor involvement
Lower limb motor loss always precedes upper limb involvement

Pain and temperature sensation are affected next, with touch sensation being the last modality to be lost.

Permanent discontinuation of any cast or support
Bed rest without any cast for a further six months
Passive forced abduction stress testing of the knee

Surgical repair of the medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus, and ACL follows a staged postoperative protocol.
After the initial long leg cast and stitches are removed at two weeks, a walking cylindrical cast is applied.

questions.question: A patient recovering from injury to the medial collateral ligament of the knee, repaired surgically alongside the medial meniscus and ACL, has had the cast and stitches removed at two weeks. What is the next stage of management described?

Immediate aggressive resisted strengthening of all limbs
Foot exercises with leg elevated, modified per patient condition

Complete avoidance of any respiratory or foot exercises
questions.explanation: In fat embolism management, the physiotherapist encourages foot exercises with the leg elevated and encourages the patient to remain ambulant to maintain venous circulation, though in severe cases the patient may be confined to bed for a short period, with treatment modified according to the patient's condition. This reflects the same cautious, condition-adapted approach seen across other acute vascular emergencies. Recognizing the acuity of fat embolism helps the physiotherapist appropriately scale activity level to the patient's clinical stability.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with fat embolism syndrome following multiple long-bone fractures. What is the primary role of the physiotherapist during the acute severe phase?

High pulse pressure with left ventricular enlargement
Low pulse pressure with right ventricular hypertrophy

questions.explanation: An acquired arteriovenous fistula produces a physiological effect from arterial blood shunting into veins, resulting in high pulse pressure, left ventricular enlargement, and potentially cardiac failure. A congenital fistula instead produces a structural effect, causing veins to become dilated, tortuous, and thick-walled (arterialized). This distinction between acquired physiological and congenital structural effects is clinically important.
questions.question: An acquired arteriovenous fistula produces which physiological consequence from shunting of arterial blood into veins?

questions.explanation: The role of physiotherapy in cancer recovery is to restore strength, endurance, and vitality, making rehabilitation part of overall cancer treatment. This is achieved through aerobics, strengthening, balancing, and stretching exercises. It complements, rather than replaces, surgical, chemotherapeutic, and radiotherapeutic management.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is developing an exercise plan for a post-amputation cancer patient. According to the described role, physiotherapy exercise for such patients primarily aims to achieve what?

A patient following amputation through the middle of the foot develops recurrent equinus deformity of the residual foot. Which of the described mid-foot procedures is most associated with this specific complication?
questions.explanation: Chopart's amputation (and tarsometatarsal disarticulation) were largely discarded because of the tendency to develop equinovarus or equinus deformity postoperatively, unlike Pirogoff's or Burgess's amputations, which were developed partly to address this recurring problem. Recognizing which procedure is prone to this complication helps the physiotherapist anticipate the need for closer postoperative positioning and splinting. Persistent deformity typically requires more proximal amputation or reconstructive surgery.

questions.explanation: Kneeling is described as an unstable position because the center of gravity moves toward the front of the base, with the patient upright from the knees and lower legs supported on the floor. Modified kneeling positions include kneel sitting, half kneeling, and prone kneeling. Standing, by contrast, is an upright stable position with feet apart and arms by the sides.

questions.question: A patient with a contaminated wound near the knee joint is being managed conservatively. Which physiotherapy-relevant measure supports wound management alongside antibiotics?
Which pair of muscles ruptures most frequently according to incidence?
questions.explanation: Among muscles, the rectus femoris and biceps brachii are cited as rupturing most often. Tendons most prone to rupture include the quadriceps, supraspinatus, patellar, and tendocalcaneus tendons. Degenerative wear in elderly patients predisposes these structures to tearing.

questions.question: Which region of the spine is most often involved in Paget's disease?
questions.explanation: Paget's disease usually involves the lumbar region of the spine among its typical sites. Other frequently affected bones include the skull, sternum, ribs and femur. Small bones tend to be spared in this condition.

Physiotherapy management for a repaired ruptured biceps tendon combines heat therapy, such as shortwave or infrared, with active exercises. questions.question: For a patient with a healing ruptured biceps tendon repair, which two treatment elements form the described physiotherapy management?
options: Heat therapy and graded active exercises

questions.question: A patient with recurrent dislocation of the elbow has undergone tenodesis with the biceps tendon transferred to the coronoid process. Postoperatively, the elbow is immobilised for six weeks in which position?

As healing progresses, the physiotherapist re-educates a correct gait pattern for full weight-bearing.

questions.question: Which hormone level is characteristically low in acromegaly investigations?
questions.explanation: FSH levels are typically low in acromegaly, while growth hormone drives the disease process. Serum inorganic phosphorus and BMR are elevated. T4 and PBI usually remain normal.

Hematogenous infective arthritis generally carries a more favorable prognosis than suppurative arthritis resulting from wounds of joints. Wound-related infection can spread through fascial planes causing cellulitis or abscess. Understanding this helps set realistic recovery expectations for the patient.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a patient about a healing joint wound's more favorable course. Compared with wounds, which route of joint infection generally carries a better prognosis?

A physiotherapist notices a below-knee amputee's stump has an unusually long residual tibia and observes recurring skin breakdown. What is the most likely underlying explanation based on stump-length principles?
options: Longer stumps require no scar or pressure area monitoring
Longer stumps are poorly adapted to prosthetic fitting and circulation
Longer stumps always heal faster than standard-length stumps
Longer stumps automatically prevent phantom limb sensation
Longer stumps eliminate the need for any stump shrinker sock
questions.explanation: Longer below-knee stumps are poorly adapted to a standard prosthesis and are more prone to breakdown due to compromised circulation at the distal segment, contrasting with the ideal 15 cm level below the medial tibial condyle. In such cases weight may need to be transferred to the ischial tuberosity via an extended thigh corset. Recognizing this helps the physiotherapist anticipate recurring pressure problems in atypically long stumps.

Prepatellar bursitis occurs more often than other regional bursitis, resulting from tendinitis of the quadriceps rather than being a primary condition. Chronic friction during activities like scrubbing floors gives rise to the name housemaid's knee. The bursa separates the lower patella and upper patellar ligament from the overlying skin.
questions.question: Prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee) is chiefly the result of tendinitis of which structure?

questions.explanation: Calcitonin is used conservatively to lower serum calcium levels in hyperparathyroidism. Furosemide is a diuretic used alongside IV fluids to reduce renal calcium stone formation. Definitive cure, however, requires surgical parathyroidectomy.
questions.question: Which drug therapy is used to lower serum calcium in the conservative management of hyperparathyroidism?
A physiotherapist is treating a child with hammer toe deformity following resection of the proximal interphalangeal joint. When is weight bearing typically permitted after this procedure?
options: After 6 months of strict non-weight-bearing rest
Not until the child reaches skeletal maturity
Immediately on the day of surgery
questions.explanation: Following resection of the proximal interphalangeal joint (the Sir Robert Jones procedure) for hammer toe, weight bearing is permitted after 1 week postoperatively, with a corrective or protective orthosis such as a hallux valgus splint used during recovery. This relatively short non-weight-bearing period is consistent with other minor forefoot procedures described for toe deformities. The physiotherapist should coordinate the timing of gait progression with this specific postoperative milestone.

questions.question: Which surgical procedure is indicated for severe attacks of Raynaud's disease?
questions.explanation: Sympathectomy, involving preganglionic section of the thoracic sympathetic chain, is indicated for severe attacks of Raynaud's disease. Conservative measures include protection from cold and avoidance of smoking. Vasodilator drugs such as reserpine may also be used.

options: Risk of heart failure as a known complication
questions.question: Why might a physiotherapist be cautious about high-intensity cardiovascular exercise in a patient with longstanding acromegaly?
questions.explanation: Heart failure is a recognized complication of acromegaly, making cautious exercise prescription important. Surgical treatment is also often limited because these patients are poor risks due to heart and chest problems. This systemic risk should guide the intensity of any physiotherapy-directed activity.

The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus close to the glenohumeral joint.
Anterior dislocation places greater traction on this nerve than posterior dislocation.
Axillary nerve injury after shoulder dislocation may present as deltoid weakness and sensory loss over the 'regimental badge' area.
questions.question: Which nerve is more commonly injured in anterior dislocation of the shoulder than in posterior dislocation?
Snapping hip is chiefly caused by a tense band sliding over which bony prominence?
questions.explanation: Snapping hip results from a tense fascial band, usually the iliotibial band or gluteus maximus border, sliding over the greater trochanter. The snap occurs during flexion, adduction, or internal rotation of the hip. The condition is often painless and habitual, sometimes described as obsessive-neurotic in origin.

This crutch-foot pattern, where the right crutch moves forward followed by the left foot, then the left crutch followed by the right foot, describes a four-point gait. Progression occurs when the patient moves the right crutch and left foot together followed by the left crutch and right foot, forming a two-point gait. These patterns are used for partial weight-bearing progression.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a patient's crutch-assisted gait observes the right crutch and left foot moving together, followed by the left crutch and right foot. What gait pattern is this?
Why is reassurance about cognitive development an appropriate part of counseling for families of a child with achondroplasia?
options: Cognitive function is untestable in this condition
Mental development is generally normal despite the skeletal deformity
Cognitive delay is a certain outcome
Mental development mirrors limb shortening severity
The condition always causes intellectual disability
questions.explanation: Mental development remains normal in achondroplasia despite pronounced skeletal deformities affecting stature and limbs. This is an important reassurance point during family counseling. It also supports full participation in age-appropriate physiotherapy and developmental activities.

The lesional tissue of a nonosteogenic fibroma is grossly friable, vividly rusty colored, and contains bright yellow foci. Histologically it contains giant cells and lipid or iron-laden macrophages. It is considered a developmental defect rather than a true neoplasm.
questions.question: Grossly, the lesional tissue of a nonosteogenic fibroma is characteristically described as?

questions.explanation:
This fracture is an avulsion injury at the base of the fifth metatarsal.
It results from sudden contraction of peroneus brevis as the ankle undergoes an inversion strain.
Although a minor injury, unnecessary disability can follow if it is treated in a prolonged walking plaster.
questions.question: An avulsion fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal is caused by sudden contraction of which muscle during an inversion strain?

questions.explanation: Tendon transferring in poliomyelitis, whether to eliminate a dynamic deforming force or supplement power of a paralyzed muscle, is deferred until skeletal maturity. The same deferral applies to arthrodesis and leg-length discrepancy correction. This avoids interfering with ongoing bone growth.
questions.question: In the residual period of anterior poliomyelitis, orthopedic surgery for tendon transfer is deferred until which milestone?

options: Only once weight bearing is fully achieved
Only after knee brace removal permanently
questions.explanation: Post-fixation physiotherapy for a repaired quadriceps tendon begins non-weight bearing exercises immediately. Massage helps mobilize the tendon and reduce swelling during this stage. Weight-bearing exercises are introduced once pain subsides, with a knee brace worn until full control is regained.
questions.question: A patient recovering from surgical repair of a ruptured quadriceps tendon is in the post-fixation phase. Physiotherapy encourages non-weight bearing exercises to begin at what point?

questions.explanation: Clutton's joints refer to bilateral, painless hydrops of the knee occurring in a child with congenital syphilis. The joints show free and painless mobility, which is considered pathognomonic. This contrasts with the painful, restricted joints seen in infective arthritis.
options: Unilateral painful swelling of the wrist
Bilateral painless hydrops of the knee
questions.question: Clutton's joints, a manifestation of congenital syphilis, are characterized by what clinical feature?
Serum alkaline phosphatase in rickets and osteomalacia is typically?
questions.explanation: Alkaline phosphatase is elevated in rickets and osteomalacia, reflecting increased osteoblastic activity. Serum calcium and phosphate, by contrast, are low. This biochemical pattern helps differentiate rickets from osteoporosis.

options: Spinal cord stimulation as the primary modality
Trigger point therapy and dry needling, alongside joint mobilization and neurodynamic exercises
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the sole treatment
questions.question: A patient with recurrent shoulder dislocation is being assessed for physiotherapy input beyond exercise alone. Which additional modalities are specifically mentioned as part of physiotherapy for recurrent dislocation?
questions.explanation:
Physiotherapy for recurrent dislocation extends beyond simple strengthening exercises alone.
The described approach includes joint mobilization and alignment techniques, massage, and muscle stretches.
Neurodynamic exercises are combined with adjuncts such as trigger point therapy and dry needling as part of comprehensive care.

Curettage of the lesion is the surgical approach used for aneurysmal bone cysts located in long bones. Excision, together with adjoining involved tissue, is used instead for expanded vertebral lesions. Surgery is reserved for cases where conservative treatment fails.
questions.question: Surgical treatment for an aneurysmal bone cyst in a long bone typically involves?
A patient with a stable wedge fracture of a cervical vertebra has completed six to eight weeks in a cervical collar. What is the next physiotherapy step described?
questions.explanation:
Stable wedge fractures of the cervical spine are managed with a cervical collar for six to eight weeks.
After this period, physiotherapy introduces active and passive exercises to restore neck movement.
Heat therapy such as short-wave diathermy or infrared may be combined with these exercises for pain relief.
options: Active and passive exercises with heat therapy following collar removal
Permanent avoidance of any neck movement
Mandatory static contractions for leg and trunk muscles
Full active weight-bearing walking within the spica
Passive stretching of the hip into full extension
Hydrotherapy commenced during the acute inpatient phase
Resisted straight leg raises against maximal resistance
questions.explanation:
Patients with displaced pelvic fractures managed in a plaster spica cannot mobilise the joints directly.
Static contractions of the leg and trunk muscles are therefore mandatory to maintain muscle tone.
This maintains strength and circulation while the pelvic ring heals within the immobilising spica.
questions.question: A patient in a plaster spica following a displaced pelvic fracture requires which specific physiotherapy intervention during bed rest?
A physiotherapist is treating chronic low back pain with mechanical or manual decompression of the spine. What is this treatment technique specifically called?
questions.explanation: Spinal traction is a form of decompression therapy that relieves pressure on the spine, performed either manually or mechanically. It is indicated for herniated discs, sciatica, degenerative disc disease, pinched nerves, and low-backache. Its goal is to determine whether traction is more effective than other treatments or no treatment for low-back pain.

questions.question: In pelvic fractures, which structures are particularly vulnerable to associated visceral injury?
questions.explanation:
Displaced fractures of the anterior pelvic ring frequently damage pelvic viscera.
The male urethra and urinary bladder are particularly vulnerable to this type of injury.
The rectum may also rarely be involved, but genitourinary injury is the more characteristic association.

questions.question: Lipoma most frequently arises subcutaneously in women during which decade of life?
questions.explanation: Lipoma is the most frequent benign tumor of connective tissue, occurring mostly in women during the fifth decade of life. It usually arises subcutaneously, typically in the neck, axilla, shoulder, or back. Superficial lipomas are managed by enucleation while deep-seated ones require wide excision.

options: Risk of pathological fracture through weakened bone
Aneurysmal bone cysts heal faster than soft tissue
Aneurysmal bone cysts are always malignant
Weight-bearing has no relevance to bone lesions
questions.question: Why might a physiotherapist expect a slower, more cautious return to weight-bearing activity in a patient with an aneurysmal bone cyst compared to simple muscle strain?
questions.explanation: Aneurysmal bone cysts weaken the bone structurally, with pathological fracture listed among possible findings. This justifies a more cautious, graded approach to weight-bearing activity compared to typical soft tissue injuries. Protecting the healing bone reduces the risk of fracture during rehabilitation.

Surgery such as cryohypophysectomy is chosen when radiotherapy is hazardous, typically because visual fields are markedly reduced. When vision is preserved and the tumor is radiosensitive, radiotherapy is instead preferred. This decision reflects balancing tumor control against risk to vision.
questions.question: A patient recovering from cryohypophysectomy for acromegaly asks the physiotherapist why surgery was chosen instead of radiotherapy. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Visual field loss made radiotherapy hazardous
The patient preferred a faster recovery

questions.question: A patient with acute gout is advised on general measures alongside drug therapy. Which specific physical measure is recommended for the affected limb?
questions.explanation: General measures for acute gout mandate rest with the affected limb raised, alongside control of body weight and alcohol intake. A purine-restricted diet and adequate oral fluids support this approach. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy help prevent problems with daily activities during recovery.
options: Ice-water immersion of the entire limb

questions.question: During a Raynaud's attack, the skin of the fingers characteristically shows pallor and cyanosis while sparing which digit?
questions.explanation: Raynaud's disease produces paroxysmal bilateral symmetrical pallor and cyanosis of the fingers, typically sparing the thumbs. Bright redness of the skin follows as the attack resolves. Attacks are accompanied by numbness, tingling, and blanching that terminate spontaneously or with warmth.

questions.question: A physiotherapist selects sling suspension for a patient with weak hip abductors performing side-lying hip abduction exercise. How should the uninvolved leg be positioned?
questions.explanation: During sling suspension for hip abduction and adduction, the patient lies with the other leg fixed in abduction to prevent unwanted spine movement, while the exercising leg is supported by slings at the foot and knee. The axial suspension point is placed over the hip joint. This setup allows the weak hip abductors to move against minimal resistance.
options: Flexed fully at hip and knee
Fixed in abduction to prevent spine movement

questions.question: Which factor listed in the text most reliably delays fracture healing, regardless of the specific bone involved?
questions.explanation:
Fasciae, ligaments, or muscle caught between fracture fragments act as a barrier to callus formation.
This interposition impairs apposition of the fractured surfaces, causing delayed or non-union.
Classic examples include fractures of the patella, olecranon, and medial malleolus.
options: Cancellous rather than cortical bone type
Interposition of soft tissue between the bone ends
Adequate immobilization of the fracture site

questions.explanation: Segmental resection or total excision of bone is indicated for benign tumors and tumors of unknown malignant potential such as giant cell tumors and central cartilaginous tumors, along with juxtacortical osteosarcomas. Postoperative care involves immobilization in a long leg cast with the knee flexed twenty degrees for two months. Fibrous lesions such as bone cysts instead are managed by curettage and bone grafting.
questions.question: Segmental resection or total excision of bone is indicated for tumors of unknown malignant potential, which specifically includes?

options: Appropriate thermal, electrical, or manipulative technique
questions.question: A physiotherapist observes that a patient's active exercise causes pain, but medical treatment has already failed to control it. What is the next described approach available to the physiotherapist?
questions.explanation: When medical or surgical treatment fails to relieve pain that limits active exercise, the physiotherapist may address it through appropriate thermal, electrical, manipulative, or exercise techniques. This reflects pain being treated as a protective mechanism requiring resolution before progressing active exercise. Suitable methods for pain relief are discussed according to the specific condition being treated.

Conservative management of bursitis includes intra-articular injection of hydrocortisone acetate combined with lignocaine. Triamcinolone acetonide with lignocaine serves as an alternative. These are given alongside rest, immobilization, diathermy, and NSAIDs.
questions.question: Which intra-articular corticosteroid combination is cited for treating bursitis conservatively?

questions.explanation: Active dynamic stretches are most commonly used as a warm-up and are ideal to promote blood flow to the exercised muscle groups prior to activity. Passive static stretches, by comparison, are described as better suited for a cool-down after activity. This distinction helps the physiotherapist time each stretching type appropriately around exercise sessions.
questions.question: A physiotherapist counsels a patient about active versus passive stretching before a competitive event. Which type is recommended as most appropriate for a pre-event warm-up?
Erb-Duchenne upper arm brachial plexus lesion classically results from injury to which nerve roots?
questions.explanation: Erb-Duchenne (upper arm) brachial plexus lesion results from involvement of the C5 and C6 nerve roots, typically from traction during obstructed labour or a fall of a heavy weight onto the shoulder. This produces the classic 'waiter's tip' posture with the arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, and wrist and fingers flexed. Klumpke's lower arm lesion instead involves the C8 and T1 roots.

Plain X-ray in osteoarthritis characteristically shows asymmetric narrowing of the joint space along with osteophytes at the joint margins. MRI can reveal earlier changes missed on X-ray. CT scan is particularly useful in cervical or lumbar spondylosis with neurological involvement.
questions.question: Which imaging finding is characteristic of osteoarthritis on plain X-ray?
What is the etiology of Paget's disease according to the source material?
questions.explanation: The cause of Paget's disease is described as unknown. Despite this, characteristic pathological changes of thickened, softened and deformed bone are well documented. Management therefore remains largely symptomatic rather than curative.

Spondylolisthesis is defined as the forward slipping of a lower lumbar vertebra, usually the fifth, through the plane of the intervertebral disc below it, carrying with it the entire upper part of the spine. The essential lesion is a defective pedicle separating the vertebral body from its posterior articulation. Diagnosis is confirmed by AP and lateral X-rays showing this pedicle defect.
questions.question: Spondylolisthesis is defined as the forward slipping of which specific lumbar vertebra most commonly?
A patient with longstanding diabetic neuropathy presents with a markedly destroyed, painless, unstable ankle joint. Which condition should the physiotherapist suspect?
questions.explanation: Charcot's joint is a trophic affection of weight-bearing joints associated with diabetic neuropathy among other neurological causes. The marked joint destruction with relative painlessness reflects the underlying sensory loss. Recognizing this presentation is important given the different management approach compared to other arthropathies.

questions.question: Surgical treatment of acromegaly, when required, typically involves which procedure?
questions.explanation: Cryohypophysectomy is the surgical procedure used for acromegaly when radiotherapy is hazardous or vision is markedly reduced. Surgery is rarely required because patients are often poor surgical risks from cardiac and chest problems. The approach itself is also technically difficult.

questions.question: A patient is several weeks post-surgical treatment for an infected joint wound and is now allowed active and passive exercises. What specific muscle group requires special early attention around the knee?
questions.explanation: Special exercises are required to restore quadriceps power at the earliest possible time following joint wound management. This supports knee stability and function during rehabilitation. Neglecting quadriceps strengthening can delay functional recovery of the joint.

Dislocation of the shoulder is common because of its wide range of motion and shallow glenoid cavity.
Inadequate support from the rotator cuff ligaments and muscles further predisposes to instability.
A deep, well-fitted glenoid cavity would actually reduce rather than increase this predisposition.
questions.question: Dislocation of the shoulder is common largely because of the joint's anatomy. Which factor is NOT among the reasons given for this predisposition?
options: Inadequate support from the rotator cuff
Acute trauma with the arm in abduction

questions.question: A physiotherapist is advising a patient recovering from embolectomy for acute arterial thrombosis about resuming activity. What is the recommended activity progression during early recovery?
options: Avoid strenuous exercise but remain ambulant to maintain circulation
Resume full unrestricted strenuous exercise immediately
Begin high-resistance strength training within the first week
Remain confined to complete bed rest for several months
Avoid all walking until arterial pulses fully normalize
questions.explanation: Following embolectomy or thrombectomy for acute arterial thrombosis, the physiotherapist encourages foot exercises and remaining ambulant to maintain venous circulation, while avoiding strenuous exercise that could strain the surgical repair. In severe cases the patient may need a short period of bed confinement, with treatment modified according to the patient's condition. This balanced approach protects the repair while still promoting circulation and preventing complications like DVT.

questions.question: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) classically produces tenderness over which structure?
questions.explanation: Tennis elbow presents with pain over the outer aspect of the elbow and local tenderness over the lateral epicondyle. Passive pronation to the full extent characteristically exaggerates the pain. The condition relates to strain on the common extensor tendon attachment.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to test serratus anterior function in a patient with suspected long thoracic nerve injury. Which specific instruction should be given to the patient during this assessment?
options: Push forward against resistance while watching for scapular winging
Flex the terminal phalanx of the thumb against resistance
Grip a card firmly between the thumb and palm surface
Extend the wrist against resistance in mid-prone position
Abduct the shoulder fully while palpating the deltoid muscle
questions.explanation: Testing serratus anterior involves asking the patient to push forward, or to raise the arm, while observing for winging of the scapula with prominence of the vertebral border and inferior angle, confirming long thoracic nerve (nerve of Bell) paralysis. This test is distinct from deltoid testing, which involves raising a flexed elbow against resistance for axillary nerve assessment. Correctly selecting the test movement ensures the physiotherapist isolates the muscle and nerve genuinely in question.

questions.question: Which bone is described as the commonest long bone to fracture, being subcutaneous and prone to indirect violence from a fall on the outstretched hand?
questions.explanation:
The clavicle is subcutaneous throughout its length, making it vulnerable to both direct and indirect trauma.
A fall on the outstretched hand transmits force along the arm to fracture the bone, commonly at the junction of its outer and middle thirds.
Because of its exposed position it is regarded as the commonest long bone fracture.

Chronic venous insufficiency is distinguished from lymphedema by the presence of varicosities from incompetent perforating veins, which are typically absent in lymphedema, which instead shows brawny, thickened subcutaneous tissue and often a history of cellulitis. Both conditions must also be differentiated from congestive heart failure and renal failure, which cause bilateral edema with sacral involvement. This differential diagnosis guides appropriate targeted management.
options: Presence of pitting edema exclusively seen in lymphedema
Presence of varicosities, which are absent in lymphedema
Involvement restricted only to the upper limb in both
Presence of bilateral sacral edema seen only in lymphedema
Complete absence of any skin pigmentation changes
questions.question: Chronic venous insufficiency is differentiated from lymphedema on examination primarily by which feature?

options: Hip and knee of the same side
Ankle and foot of the same side
questions.explanation:
After internal fixation of a humeral shaft fracture, assisted active shoulder movement is started as soon as possible.
This is followed by active exercises of the fingers, wrist, and elbow to maintain distal joint mobility.
Once the fixation is removed, physiotherapy progresses to restoring full shoulder and elbow range and muscle power.
questions.question: Following internal fixation of a fracture shaft of humerus, physiotherapy during immobilization should begin with assisted active movement of the shoulder followed by active exercises of which additional joints?

questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma is diagnosed in part through Bence Jones protein in the urine, which precipitates on adding nitric acid and disappears again on warming. Other findings include marked rouleaux formation, greatly elevated ESR, and multiple punched-out lesions on X-ray. Melphalan is described as the most effective chemotherapeutic agent available.
questions.question: Bence Jones protein in urine, precipitating on adding nitric acid and disappearing on warming, is a classic finding in which malignancy?
A cerebral palsy child requires drug therapy that is both anxiolytic and muscle-relaxant. Which class of drug fits this dual action?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are anxiolytic, muscle relaxant, and anticonvulsant in action. Phenothiazines are mainly antipsychotic and anxiolytic without a muscle relaxant effect. Barbiturates are anticonvulsant and muscle relaxant but are sedating rather than primarily anxiolytic.

options: Range, power and endurance, coordination, timing
questions.question: In assessing components of movement for restoring function, which four components should a physiotherapist specifically evaluate?
questions.explanation: To restore function, the physiotherapist must assess the components of movement not functioning adequately, namely range of joint movement, muscle power and endurance, coordination of movement, and timing. This assessment applies specifically when the defect pertains to the musculoskeletal system. Good coordination and timing are vital for achieving an efficient overall movement.

questions.question: A physiotherapist selecting oscillation grade for a joint presenting with pain at rest, muscle spasm, and insomnia should treat it as which type of joint?
questions.explanation: A joint with pain at rest, muscle spasm, and insomnia is classified as irritable, guiding the physiotherapist toward gentler, lower-grade oscillation techniques. A nonirritable joint, by contrast, is painless at rest with absent spasm and insomnia, allowing more vigorous grades. Joint irritability is used specifically as a guiding factor for grading manipulative oscillation techniques.

questions.question: A patient with primary osteoarthritis affecting multiple DIP joints asks whether this pattern is common at her age of 35. What should the physiotherapist explain?
questions.explanation: Primary or idiopathic osteoarthritis rarely occurs in younger patients under 40 years, even though it commonly affects the DIP joints when it does occur. This makes early-onset presentation somewhat atypical and worth further clinical consideration. Secondary osteoarthritis, by contrast, can occur at any age due to a pre-existing disorder.
options: DIP joint involvement never occurs in osteoarthritis
This pattern is expected and common under 40
Primary osteoarthritis rarely occurs below 40 years of age
Age has no bearing on osteoarthritis presentation
This pattern only occurs in secondary osteoarthritis

questions.question: Chiropractic therapy is mainly concerned with the diagnosis and manipulative treatment of which structural region?
questions.explanation: Chiropractic therapy is a form of alternative medicine concerned with the diagnosis and manipulative treatment of mechanical disorders of the musculoskeletal system, especially misalignments of the spinal column. Chiropractors mainly focus on adjustments to the vertebrae of the spine. Osteopaths, in comparison, tend to treat a broader range of disorders beyond the spine alone.

Gait re-education mandates crutches initially to allow partial weight bearing while the joint heals. Progression to walking sticks follows once pain has diminished. This staged approach protects the joint from excessive early load.
questions.question: During gait re-education after septic arthritis, which walking aid is used initially before progressing to walking sticks?
A patient with cervical spondylosis is being treated by the physiotherapist. Which type of exercise is specifically emphasized to maintain neck muscle function?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for cervical spondylosis emphasizes isometric and other exercises to maintain muscle power and flexibility of the neck muscles. A cervical collar may be used short-term to avoid muscle atrophy from disuse. Ice packs, warm fomentation, or diathermy may also be used for symptomatic relief.

options: Weight-bearing is strictly avoided for six months
Full unsupported weight-bearing is mandatory from the first hour
Weight-bearing is never permitted after this procedure
Weight-bearing with crutches is encouraged as soon as possible
Weight-bearing is delayed until one year postoperatively
questions.explanation:
Chondromalacia patellae involves degeneration of the patellar articular cartilage, sometimes requiring arthroscopic surgery.
After shaving of the involved cartilage, an elastic crepe bandage supports the knee for one week.
Weight-bearing with the aid of crutches is encouraged as soon as possible, alongside quadriceps and hamstring exercises.
questions.question: A patient with chondromalacia patellae undergoes arthroscopic shaving of the involved cartilage. Postoperatively, an elastic crepe bandage is applied for one week. What is emphasised regarding weight-bearing in the immediate postoperative period?

questions.explanation: Surgical treatment of achondroplasia is mainly indicated for shortened legs through leg lengthening procedures. Management overall is largely symptomatic since the underlying cause is unknown. Other skeletal features are not primary surgical targets.
questions.question: Surgical treatment in achondroplasia is primarily indicated for?

questions.explanation: Embolic blockage of the central artery supplying the retina produces a flash of light followed by total and permanent blindness, a distinct regional effect from embolism elsewhere in the body. Blockage of the middle cerebral artery instead produces temporary or permanent hemiplegia, while renal artery blockage causes loin pain and hematuria. Recognizing organ-specific embolic presentations aids rapid clinical localization.
options: Engorgement and gangrene of an intestinal loop
Pain and splenomegaly from splenic involvement
Flash of light followed by total, permanent blindness
Hemiplegia that is either temporary or permanent
Pain in the loin accompanied by hematuria
questions.question: Which regional effect of arterial embolism is specifically linked to blockage of the central artery supplying the retina?

questions.explanation: Hallux valgus is characterized by valgus angulation of the great toe phalanges at the metatarsophalangeal joint together with varus deformity of the first metatarsal, producing the medially prominent 'bunion' at the first metatarsal head. Surgical options include the Keller, McBride, Lapidus, and Duncan McKeever operations depending on severity and patient age. This combination of opposite-direction deformities at adjacent joints is characteristic of the condition.
options: Rotation of the fifth metatarsal medially
Shortening of the first metatarsal only
Varus deformity of the first metatarsal
Valgus deformity of the first metatarsal
Fusion of the first and second metatarsals
questions.question: Hallux valgus is defined by valgus of the great toe phalanges combined with which additional metatarsal deformity?

questions.explanation: Volkmann's ischemic contracture results from interrupted arterial blood supply distal to an obstruction, usually from fracture or fracture-dislocation, causing ischemia of muscles and nerves that progresses to muscle replacement by fibrous tissue and ischemic contractures. This may be accompanied by paralysis if nerve involvement is severe. The roughened bony edge from the causative fracture may itself lacerate the artery.
options: Nerve replaced by regenerated Schwann cell tissue
Skin replaced by keratinized scar tissue permanently
Bone replaced by fibrous dysplastic tissue locally
Muscle replaced entirely by adipose fatty tissue
Muscle replaced by fibrous tissue causing contractures
questions.question: In Volkmann's ischemic contracture, what is the final tissue consequence of prolonged arterial obstruction distal to a fracture?

questions.explanation: Paraffin wax treatment acts as thermotherapy that helps conditions like arthritis by increasing blood flow, relaxing muscles, and reducing stiffness in joints. It is commonly used in skin-softening treatments on the hands, cuticles, and feet due to being colorless, tasteless, and odorless. This heat-based mechanism underlies its benefit for arthritic hand stiffness.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is fitting a patient with paraffin wax treatment for hand osteoarthritis. What is the primary physiological benefit expected according to the description?
options: Increased blood flow and reduced stiffness

questions.question: Obstetric paralysis is defined as an upper brachial plexus lesion involving which nerve roots?
questions.explanation: Obstetric paralysis is defined as the upper lesion of the brachial plexus due to involvement of the C5 and C6 nerve roots. The mechanism is an obstructed labor traction force on the neck. Untreated, unopposed muscle contraction fixes the limb into an internally rotated, pronated posture.

options: Complete rest with no active movement for a further two weeks
Immediate resisted wrist extension against heavy weights
Free active exercises combined with moist heat pack therapy
Passive forced manipulation of the wrist under sedation
questions.question: A patient recovering from a Colles fracture has just had the cast removed after eight weeks. What physiotherapy approach is indicated?
questions.explanation:
Following removal of the cast at six to eight weeks, active rehabilitation of the wrist is initiated.
Free active exercises are combined with moist heat pack therapy to ease stiffness and improve mobility.
The physiotherapist also remains alert for complications such as Sudeck's dystrophy, which may develop at this stage.

options: Immediate resisted overhead lifting before splint removal
Passive-only mobilisation throughout, never active exercise
No physiotherapy input is required at any stage
Forced manipulation under anaesthesia weekly during splinting
Free active exercises once the splint period is complete
questions.question: A patient with old unreduced dislocation of the shoulder has undergone open reduction and is on an abduction humeral splint. Physiotherapy is described at this stage as:
questions.explanation:
Old unreduced shoulder dislocations treated by open reduction require a structured splinting period.
The abduction humeral splint protects the joint in abduction, flexion, and external rotation for several weeks.
Once this period concludes, physiotherapy consists of free active exercises to restore shoulder function.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is preparing a treatment plan for a patient with reduced hip range from a total hip disorder screened for manipulative therapy safety first. What should precede any oscillation grading?
questions.explanation: Before grading oscillation techniques, the physiotherapist must screen for the listed contraindications, spanning traumatic, inflammatory, infective, endocrinal, malignant, mobility-related, psychological, and miscellaneous categories. Joint irritability is then used as a guiding factor for selecting the appropriate oscillation grade. This systematic screening protects the patient from harm before any manual technique is applied.

questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a patient with fracture of the metacarpals emphasizes an integrated plan involving which other professional?
questions.explanation:
Recovery from metacarpal fractures benefits from a coordinated rehabilitation approach.
Free active exercises are monitored by both the physiotherapist and the occupational therapist together.
This integrated plan addresses both physical range of motion and functional hand use in daily activities.

options: Isolated upper limb strengthening only, avoiding the back
Immediate return to unrestricted heavy lifting activities
Active exercises to strengthen the back extensor muscles
Permanent avoidance of all future physical activity
Aggressive spinal manipulation of the affected segment
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a young patient with spondylolisthesis whose acute pain has recently subsided. What is the next appropriate physiotherapy focus?
questions.explanation: Once acute pain has subsided in spondylolisthesis, active exercises to strengthen the back extensor muscles become the physiotherapy priority, alongside advice on posture, back care, and correct lifting technique, and weight loss where appropriate. Mobilization may also be used to restore movement to lumbar levels above the level of the lesion. This staged approach moves from acute symptomatic relief toward active functional strengthening as pain allows.

questions.question: A physiotherapist reassessing a patient after several deep friction massage sessions must decide when to progress from daily to alternate-day treatment. What guides this decision according to the description?
questions.explanation: Deep friction massage may be given every other day, or when the excess tenderness has worn off, guiding the transition from daily gentle massage used in a recent injury. The therapist distinguishes tenderness caused by the friction itself from the underlying pain through ongoing clinical assessment. Treatment duration also lengthens as the tissue tolerates deeper, more sustained friction.

Primary or idiopathic osteoarthritis is also known as polyarticular degenerative disease, often active in several joints simultaneously. Secondary osteoarthritis, by contrast, is termed monoarticular degenerative disease. This distinction relates to underlying cause.
questions.question: Primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis typically shows which distribution pattern?

options: Traction injury at the elbow from cubitus valgus deformity
Compression at the wrist from carpal tunnel syndrome
Stretching injury during obstructed labour delivery
Direct laceration during shoulder disarticulation surgery
Compression from a cervical rib pressing the lower trunk
questions.explanation: Median nerve injury at the wrist is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome, where compression within the tunnel produces a tardy or delayed median neuropathy requiring carpal tunnel decompression when symptoms are unrelieved. This is distinct from tardy ulnar palsy, which results from traction at the elbow due to cubitus valgus. Recognizing the compression site guides the specific surgical decompression required.
questions.question: What specific mechanism of injury is most closely associated with tardy median nerve palsy according to the described pathogenesis?

questions.explanation: Biopsy, whether needle or aspiration, is described as the confirmatory diagnostic procedure recommended before surgery when a somatic tissue tumor is suspected. Frozen section interpretation by an expert pathologist greatly helps confirm the clinical diagnosis. Nonetheless, truly accurate diagnosis ultimately depends upon full histologic study.
questions.question: Aspiration or needle biopsy in suspected bone tumors is described in the text as serving which primary role?

A baseball pitcher develops shoulder pain referred to the deltoid region with restricted movement, attributed to repeated strain. Initial conservative management includes warm fomentation, analgesics, and local infiltration with which agent?
questions.explanation:
Baseball pitcher's shoulder results from repeated severe occupational or sporting strain on the joint.
Conservative treatment includes warm fomentation, analgesics, and local infiltration.
The infiltration specifically combines lignocaine with hydrocortisone to reduce local inflammation and pain.

Preoperative assessment includes physical, social, and psychological domains, with the psychological assessment specifically covering the patient's approach to amputation and motivation to walk again. Social assessment covers financial status and living accommodation, while physical assessment covers muscle strength and joint mobility. Addressing psychological readiness early helps anticipate the mental hazard drawback associated with amputation surgery.
options: Preferred colour scheme for the eventual prosthesis
Detailed dietary history over the preceding twelve months
Family history of unrelated childhood illnesses
Occupational income bracket prior to hospital admission
Psychological approach to amputation and walking motivation
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning preoperative assessment for a patient scheduled for a lower-limb amputation. Which assessment domain should be prioritized alongside physical assessment?

questions.explanation: Acute suppurative arthritis develops abruptly rather than gradually. Rapid onset helps distinguish it from chronic inflammatory joint diseases like rheumatoid or tuberculous arthritis. Recognizing sudden onset guides urgent investigation and treatment.
questions.question: What is the usual onset of acute suppurative (infective) arthritis?

questions.explanation: Physiotherapy assessment in spina bifida mandates noting areas of anesthesia (sensory impairment) specifically to overcome the development of pressure sores, given the child's inability to sense harmful pressure in affected areas. The physiotherapist also teaches parents how to handle the child correctly and encourages progressive developmental sequences such as rolling, sitting, crawling, and standing. This sensory vigilance is a distinguishing safety priority not seen to the same degree in purely orthopedic congenital deformities.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning early intervention for an infant recently diagnosed with meningomyelocele. What is emphasized as a mandatory area of physiotherapy vigilance given the sensory impairment present?
options: Delaying all developmental handling until walking age
Focusing exclusively on upper limb strength training
Avoiding any parental involvement in handling the infant
Monitoring for pressure sores over areas of anesthesia

questions.question: On X-ray, the epiphyseal line in rickets characteristically appears?
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal line in rickets shows cupping, with a blurred and concave appearance toward the epiphysis. Demineralization and bowing accompany this finding. These features distinguish rickets from normal epiphyseal architecture.

options: Teaching free active exercises with parental presence
questions.explanation: Children recovering from Volkmann's ischemic contracture generally mobilize quickly after cast removal and require little formal treatment. The physiotherapist may still teach free active exercises as encouragement, performed in the presence of parents. This supportive role helps the child regain confidence in movement.
questions.question: A patient recovering from Volkmann's ischemic contracture in childhood mobilizes quickly after cast removal. What physiotherapy role is described for such children?
Ruptured supraspinatus tendon differs from simple supraspinatus tendonitis chiefly by which finding?
options: Pain confined strictly to night hours
A palpable gap at rupture site
questions.explanation: Ruptured supraspinatus tendon presents with a visible and palpable gap at the site of rupture, unlike simple tendonitis. Tenderness persists over the greater tuberosity and abduction is painful at ninety degrees. Most complete ruptures in this condition do not require surgical repair.

questions.question: Volkmann's ischemic contracture most commonly follows which fracture in the upper limb?
questions.explanation: Volkmann's ischemic contracture of the upper limb most often follows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus. It occasionally follows fractures of both bones of the forearm. The flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus are the muscles most severely affected.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why shortening of up to 2.5 cm after a lower limb fracture is often simply accepted rather than surgically corrected?
options: It can be compensated by pelvic tilt or a shoe raise
It always resolves spontaneously without any intervention
It cannot be measured accurately on clinical examination
It has no effect on gait regardless of magnitude
It is only relevant in fractures of the upper limb
questions.explanation:
Shortening after a lower limb fracture becomes functionally significant once it exceeds about 2.5 cm.
