Below this threshold, the pelvis can tilt to compensate, and minor differences can be managed with a shoe raise.
Greater shortening usually requires corrective osteotomy because compensation alone becomes inadequate.

Rocker bottom (vertical talus) flat foot is classified separately because the talus is positioned obliquely downward, distinguishing it from the flexible and rigid types with normal or spastic peronei. This congenital variant produces the convex sole appearance on weight bearing. Its rigid, recurrent nature typically requires surgical correction rather than conservative moulding.
options: Isolated forefoot varus without hindfoot change
Vertical (oblique downward) positioning of the talus
Absence of any tarsal joint mobility restriction
Complete absence of the calcaneus bone entirely
Fusion of the talus directly to the navicular
questions.question: Which specific deformity component is used to distinguish 'rocker bottom' flat foot from other flat foot types in classification?

questions.explanation:
Unnatural mobility is a definite sign of fracture but must be tested gently to avoid causing complications.
In an impacted fracture the fragments are driven together, so mobility is absent.
A greenstick fracture also lacks mobility because one cortex remains intact and holds the bone together.
questions.question: Eliciting unnatural mobility at a suspected fracture site is contraindicated or absent in which two conditions?
A patient recovering from septic arthritis of the hip is cleared to begin free active exercises. What loading status should these exercises follow?
questions.explanation: Non-weight bearing free active exercises are used to move the affected joint through its full range once appropriate. This protects the joint while restoring mobility. Weight bearing is introduced later during gait re-education.

Bone biopsy provides confirmatory diagnosis of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. X-ray findings of rarefaction and expansion are suggestive but not definitive alone. Biochemical tests support but do not confirm the diagnosis.
questions.question: Definitive diagnostic confirmation of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is obtained through?

questions.explanation: Electrical stimulation testing for axillary nerve injury involves inserting needles along the posterior border of the deltoid muscle to assess the motor response to stimulation. This complements the clinical test of asking the patient to raise a flexed elbow against resistance. Confirmatory imaging includes an X-ray of the shoulder to exclude fracture-dislocation.
questions.question: In investigating suspected axillary nerve injury, where are stimulating needles specifically placed for electrical testing?
options: Along the anterior border of the pectoralis major
Directly over the acromioclavicular joint line
Along the medial border of the scapula
Over the belly of the biceps brachii muscle
Along the posterior border of the deltoid muscle

questions.explanation: In superficial vein thrombosis (thrombophlebitis), anticoagulants are usually not indicated, with management instead focusing on rest, leg elevation, analgesics, elastic crepe bandaging, and antibiotics if infection is present. This differs markedly from deep vein thrombosis, where anticoagulation is a central part of management given the higher embolic risk. The physiotherapist should understand this distinction when counselling patients about expected medical treatment for each condition.
options: Anticoagulants must be continued indefinitely once started
Anticoagulants are usually not indicated in this condition
Anticoagulants are used only if surgery is being avoided
Anticoagulants completely replace the need for any rest
Anticoagulants are always mandatory in this condition
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with superficial vein thrombosis (thrombophlebitis) and is asked whether anticoagulant therapy is typically indicated. What is the correct response based on standard management?

questions.explanation: In midshaft arm amputation, the flexor muscles are sectioned 1 cm distal to the saw line so they retract properly, while the triceps tendon is divided 3 cm below the saw line for anterior transposition over the bone end. These precise measurements ensure adequate soft tissue coverage of the humeral stump. Correct muscle handling supports a functional, well-padded stump.
options: 2 cm distal to the saw line
3 cm distal to the saw line
5 cm distal to the saw line
1 cm distal to the saw line
0.5 cm distal to the saw line
questions.question: During upper-arm midshaft amputation, at what distance below the saw line are the flexor muscles of the arm sectioned to allow retraction?

questions.explanation: In rickets, weight bearing on softened, poorly mineralized long bones produces deformities such as increased anterior femoral curvature and coxa vara. This reflects the disturbed mineral-matrix ratio characteristic of the disease. Correcting these deformities involves splinting and addressing the underlying deficiency.
options: Vascular occlusion of the femoral neck
Infective destruction of the femoral head
Fibrous tissue replacement of the femur
questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a rachitic child notes increased anterior curvature of the femur and coxa vara. What is the underlying cause of these deformities?

questions.explanation: For knee flexion and extension using pendular movement, the patient sits high on a plinth with the alternate leg swinging up and down rhythmically. This technique aims to stretch adhesions restricting joint movement while improving local blood supply. Movements should remain smooth with emphasis placed at the limit of available range.
questions.question: During knee flexion-extension pendular exercise, which patient position is specified in the described technique?
Which risk factor for osteoarthritis relates to repeated mechanical stress on joints?
questions.explanation: Strenuous exercises including regular use of stairs is listed as a risk factor for osteoarthritis. Overweight and wrong posture are additional mechanical risk factors. These contrast with sedentary life, which is a separate, non-mechanical risk factor.

questions.question: What is the recommended ideal level for a below-knee amputation, measured from the medial tibial condyle?
options: 8 cm below the medial tibial condyle
15 cm below the medial tibial condyle
25 cm below the medial tibial condyle
10 cm below the medial tibial condyle
20 cm below the medial tibial condyle
questions.explanation: The ideal below-knee amputation level is 15 cm below the medial tibial condyle, with bone length varying between 12 and 18 cm depending on patient height. This level provides good leverage, healthy skin coverage, and adequate circulation for prosthetic fitting. Longer stumps tend to have poorer circulation and fit less well in a prosthesis.

questions.question: Which nerve injury classification represents rupture of axons within an intact neural sheath, with recovery expected over a few months?
questions.explanation:
Axonotmesis is a lesion in continuity where axons are disrupted but the surrounding sheath stays intact.
Because the sheath is preserved, axons can regenerate along it, so recovery occurs within months.
This differs from neurapraxia, which recovers within weeks, and neurotmesis, which is complete division.

questions.question: Which type of spina bifida is described as the rarest, characterized by a dilated central canal of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelocele is the rarest type of spina bifida, characterized by a dilated central canal of the spinal cord, with the sac containing spinal cord tissue along with nerves arising from it. Spina bifida occulta is instead the commonest type, involving failure of neural arch fusion without protrusion of the cord or membranes. Distinguishing these subtypes affects both prognosis and surgical planning.

options: The fistula produces reflex bradycardia and hypotension
The fistula causes a sudden drop in systemic blood volume
The fistula directly obstructs the coronary circulation
The fistula eliminates venous return to the right atrium
Arterial blood shunting into veins raises pulse pressure
questions.explanation: An acquired arteriovenous fistula produces a physiological effect from arterial blood shunting directly into the venous system, raising pulse pressure and potentially causing left ventricular enlargement and cardiac failure over time. Recognizing this mechanism helps the physiotherapist understand why cardiac assessment findings might accompany what initially appears to be a purely vascular limb condition. This differs from a congenital fistula, which instead produces primarily structural venous changes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify why a patient with an arteriovenous fistula shows signs of cardiac strain on assessment. What is the underlying physiological mechanism?

options: The subclavian vein rather than artery is compressed
Symptoms occur only in the lower limb rather than upper
There is no actual cervical rib present on imaging
Onset always occurs before puberty rather than after forty
Muscle wasting affects the deltoid rather than thenar group
questions.explanation: Scalene syndrome reproduces the clinical picture of cervical rib compression, including supraclavicular pain and thenar or hypothenar wasting, but there is no actual cervical rib present; instead a pulled scalenus anticus muscle stretches the lower trunk or subclavian artery against the first rib. This distinction is important because management differs, focusing on division of the muscle rather than rib excision. Both conditions share similar sensory and vasomotor findings.
questions.question: What key clinical feature differentiates scalene syndrome from true cervical rib compression?

questions.explanation: In achondroplasia, the cartilaginous base of the skull is smaller than the vertex, producing a prominent forehead and depressed nose. This cranial disproportion is a recognizable diagnostic feature. It results from the same cartilage maldevelopment affecting the limbs.
questions.question: The skull appearance in achondroplasia is typically described as having a base that is?
A march or fatigue fracture most typically affects which bones?
questions.explanation:
March fracture, also called fatigue or stress fracture, classically affects the second or third metatarsal neck.
It follows repeated stress such as prolonged marching or standing, common in soldiers and police.
Loss of muscular tone and short metatarsals predispose to this overuse injury.

options: Corticosteroids are a recognized secondary cause of osteoporosis
questions.explanation: Excessive or prolonged use of corticosteroids, along with heparin, is a recognized secondary cause contributing to osteoporosis. Recognizing this drug history alerts the physiotherapist to increased fracture risk. Exercise and handling should be adapted accordingly to protect fragile bone.
questions.question: An osteoporosis patient on prolonged corticosteroid therapy for an unrelated condition is referred for physiotherapy. How does this medication history relate to her bone health?
In managing a patient with synovitis following a penetrating joint wound with a suspected foreign body, what is the physiotherapist's expected role relative to the surgical team?
options: Support post-surgical rehabilitation after debridement and exploration
questions.explanation: Surgical exploration and débridement address synovitis and a retained foreign body, which are indications for surgery in joint wounds. The physiotherapist's role is centered on rehabilitation once acute symptoms subside. This includes active and passive exercises and later gait training with a brace.

questions.question: A physiotherapist explains the mechanism of pain relief for cervical traction to a patient with cervical radiculopathy. Which structural change is achieved by the modality?
options: Separation of disc and joint surfaces
questions.explanation: Cervical traction gently stretches the neck to separate the disc and joint surfaces in the cervical spine, applied either manually or mechanically. It is indicated for neck pain, cervical radiculopathy, herniated discs, degenerative disc disease, and pinched nerves. Its goal is to establish whether traction outperforms other treatments or no treatment for cervical neuralgia.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is counseling an osteoporosis patient on modifiable risk factors. Which two lifestyle factors should be specifically addressed?
questions.explanation: Smoking and excess alcohol intake are specific modifiable risk factors for osteoporosis identified in the source material. Addressing these alongside diet, exercise and calcium/vitamin D intake forms the general management approach. Counseling on lifestyle change supports fracture prevention.

questions.question: Excessive traction force applied during fracture immobilization predisposes to non-union chiefly because it:
questions.explanation:
Excessive traction distracts the fractured bone ends beyond their normal apposition.
This gap favours ingrowth of fibrous tissue rather than bridging bony callus.
The fibrous tissue effectively insulates the fragments from each other, promoting non-union.
options: Prevents any movement at the fracture site
Pulls the bone ends apart, favouring fibrous tissue growth that insulates them

questions.explanation: Sciatic nerve injury paralyzes all the hamstring muscles, which are the primary knee flexors, so complete inability to flex the knee together with a foot drop below the knee strongly suggests sciatic nerve involvement, especially after fractures or dislocations of the pelvis and hip. This localizes the lesion proximal to the nerve's division into its tibial and common peroneal branches. The physiotherapist should correlate the mechanism of injury (hip trauma) with this specific muscle group finding.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a patient with suspected femoral or sciatic nerve involvement after a hip fracture-dislocation notes complete inability to flex the knee. Which nerve injury is most consistent with this specific finding?

options: As one of the recognized conservative treatment modalities
As a cure for the underlying cartilage loss
As an investigation to confirm diagnosis
As a surgical alternative to arthroplasty
As a replacement for all exercise therapy
questions.question: An osteoarthritis patient asks why acupuncture is offered alongside standard physiotherapy modalities. How should the physiotherapist categorize this intervention?
questions.explanation: Acupuncture and acupressure are listed among the conservative treatment modalities for osteoarthritis, alongside exercises, traction, heat and massage. They are adjuncts rather than replacements for core physiotherapy interventions. This reflects the range of modalities available within conservative management.

questions.question: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with brown pigmented skin spots and true precocious puberty is known as?
questions.explanation: The combination of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, brown ragged-margined skin spots, and true precocious puberty defines Albright's syndrome. It may also associate with hyperthyroidism and acromegaly. This distinguishes it from simple polyostotic fibrous dysplasia without endocrine features.

Two main sources produce joint clicking sounds: intra-articular menisci and sliding tendons over bony prominences. Intra-articular menisci occur in the jaw and knee. Snapping tendons, by contrast, occur at the hip, shoulder, and peroneal tendons.
questions.question: Snapping tendons, as distinguished from intra-articular meniscal clicks, typically occur at which joints?
A patient with acute carpal tunnel syndrome managed conservatively with a wrist strap is also given physiotherapy. Which two supportive modalities are specifically listed alongside exercise?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for acute carpal tunnel syndrome combines heat therapy, such as shortwave diathermy, with wax bath therapy alongside progressive exercises. Assisted passive exercises progress toward free active exercises as symptoms improve. A wrist strap provides additional support during this conservative phase.
options: Ultrasound of the lumbar spine and fasting
Heat therapy and wax bath therapy

questions.question: A fracture of the capitellum in a child with gross displacement may show the fragment rotated through how many degrees, with its articular surface facing the fractured surface of the humerus?
questions.explanation:
In severe capitellar fracture displacement, the fragment can rotate through a full 180 degrees.
This rotation reverses the fragment so its articular cartilage faces the raw fractured humeral surface.
Such gross displacement usually requires surgical reduction rather than conservative management.

questions.question: Which type of open amputation is described as the method of choice because it affords generous drainage while eliminating dead space?
questions.explanation: Circular open amputation is regarded as the method of choice because it affords generous open drainage, eliminates dead space, precludes osteomyelitis, and preserves bone length while being quick to perform. It contrasts with open amputation using skin flaps, which risks sacrificing skin needed for later repair. The bone is divided at the most distal site to reduce sepsis risk.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked why compression massage is specifically favored in sports massage therapy. What broader category of benefit does this technique serve according to the description?
questions.explanation: Compression massage is one of several therapeutic massage techniques used in sports massage therapy, medical massage therapy, and other prescriptions of massage for optimal performance, improved mobility, and treatment of pain or discomfort. This places it alongside longitudinal gliding, kneading, and myofascial release as core massage therapy techniques. Selection of technique depends on the specific therapeutic goal.

options: Complete cord transection with no possibility of recovery
questions.question: A patient presenting after a road traffic accident with signs of spinal concussion shows loss of voluntary movement, muscle tone, and reflexes below the level of lesion. What is this clinical picture called?
questions.explanation:
Spinal concussion, also called spinal shock, is characterised by loss of all function below the level of injury.
This includes voluntary movement, muscle tone, and pain, temperature, and reflex responses.
If no recovery from spinal shock occurs within about forty-eight hours, the prognosis is considered grave.

Arthrodesis is the surgical procedure of choice for Charcot's joint of the knee. Postoperatively, the joint is immobilized in a POP spica for two to three months. Walking with knee support is then continued for about a year afterward.
questions.question: The surgical procedure of choice for Charcot's joint of the knee is?

questions.explanation: Chondromyxoid fibroma most often occurs in bones of the lower limbs, namely the femur, tibia, fibula, tarsals, and metatarsals, usually eccentrically in the metaphysis of long bones. It may occasionally involve other long or flat bones. X-rays show radiolucent lesions with thinned, bulged cortices and marginal sclerosis.
questions.question: Chondromyxoid fibroma most often occurs eccentrically in the metaphysis of which group of bones?
In classifying types of stretching described in physiotherapy technique, which of the following is listed as one of the seven primary types?
questions.explanation: The seven primary types of stretching described are static, passive, dynamic, ballistic, active isolated, isometric, and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation stretching. Each helps people of varying flexibility and needs. Active dynamic stretches are typically used as a warm-up, while passive static stretches serve better as a cool-down.

Backache and local tenderness are typical diagnostic features of Paget's disease, which commonly involves the lumbar spine. Fever and sudden swelling would suggest an infective process instead. Recognizing this pattern helps distinguish Paget's disease from other differentials during assessment.
options: Sudden severe joint swelling with fever
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient with Paget's disease affecting the lumbar spine. Which associated finding would be consistent with this diagnosis?

questions.explanation:
The deep fibres of the medial collateral ligament attach directly to the medial meniscus.
Because of this attachment, injury to the ligament frequently damages the meniscus as well.
With continued strain, the anterior cruciate ligament may also rupture as force progresses through the joint.
questions.question: Injury to the medial collateral ligament of the knee is frequently associated with damage to which other structure, due to attachment of deep fibres?

questions.explanation: Radiotherapy is used for relief of severe bony pain in Paget's disease, alongside analgesics and NSAIDs. Osteotomy is reserved for correcting faulty mechanics rather than pain relief. There is no specific treatment to halt disease progression itself.
questions.question: Which treatment modality is used specifically for relief of severe bony pain in Paget's disease?
A patient after hindquarter disarticulation is being assessed preoperatively for informed consent discussion. Which preoperative preparation step is specifically emphasized for this major procedure?
questions.explanation: Hindquarter disarticulation, being a major mutilating procedure, requires thorough preoperative preparation including bowel enema or purgative the previous night, an indwelling catheter to keep the bladder empty, skin preparation from the costal margins to both knees, and antibiotic coverage. Medical fitness to withstand this major procedure is also mandatory before proceeding. This intensive preparation reflects the scale and risk of the surgery.
options: Avoidance of any skin preparation from costal margin to knee
Bowel and bladder preparation with an indwelling catheter
Discontinuation of all antibiotic coverage prior to incision
Deferral of medical fitness assessment until after surgery
Immediate fitting of a temporary prosthesis before surgery

questions.question: Calcaneal spur develops at the attachment of which structure to the calcaneal tuberosity?
questions.explanation: Calcaneal spur develops at the attachment of the plantar fascia to the anterior plantar edge of the calcaneal tuberosity, extending into the fascia itself, typically arising from plantar fasciitis progressing into bony spur formation. It may be large and painless, large and painful, or rudimentary in size. Surgical excision of the spur is reserved for pain that persists despite conservative measures such as heel padding and physiotherapy.

options: Training a disabled person to work
questions.question: Vocational rehabilitation, as a form of occupational therapy, is specifically concerned with which patient goal?
questions.explanation: Vocational rehabilitation is described as a form of occupational therapy concerned with training a disabled person to earn a living. Its program includes aptitude testing, job training, and job placement conducted by a team including physiotherapists and speech therapists. This distinguishes it from general occupational therapy activities like basketry or gardening.

The mental hazard of amputation, where some patients cannot psychologically surmount the loss and find readjustment more difficult than after other orthopedic procedures, is listed as a drawback rather than an indication. Indications instead include uncontrolled infection, malignant tumor, deformity, and life-threatening impaired blood supply. Distinguishing drawbacks from indications helps in preoperative counselling.
questions.question: Which amputation indication is specifically classified under 'drawbacks' rather than 'specific indications' in surgical amputation planning?
options: Mental hazard of psychological readjustment after surgery
Congenital deformity rendering the limb useless
Malignant tumor that is necrosed and fungating
Impaired blood supply threatening life from toxins

questions.explanation:
Flexion forces acting on the cervical spine can produce a stable anterior wedge fracture of the vertebral body.
In this pattern, the posterior ligament complex and neural arch remain intact.
Because of this preserved stability, usually no neurological deficit occurs in association with this fracture type.
options: Bilateral upper limb paralysis is expected in all cases
Cauda equina syndrome is the typical presentation
questions.question: A patient with a stable anterior wedge fracture of a cervical vertebra from a flexion injury is assessed. What is the expected neurological status in this pattern of injury, according to the text?

A patient with a dorsal spine compression fracture and no neurological deficit is treated conservatively with a shield-spine brace. Which finding on follow-up would most strongly suggest a need to reconsider surgical treatment?
questions.explanation:
Conservative treatment is the mainstay for compression fractures without neurological compromise.
However, persistent residual pain despite adequate bracing and rest is a recognised indication for surgical treatment.
Albee's bone grafting is the described surgical option when conservative measures fail to control symptoms.
options: Residual pain despite adequate conservative management
Full painless range of spinal movement
Radiological evidence of good vertebral alignment
Relief of pain due to faulty mechanics
questions.question: A patient with Paget's disease and bowing of the leg is referred for osteotomy. What is the primary goal of this surgical procedure?
questions.explanation: Osteotomy in Paget's disease is performed for relief of pain resulting from faulty mechanical alignment of deformed bone. It does not address or cure the underlying disease process, which has no specific treatment. Physiotherapy rehabilitation follows to restore mobility after surgery.

Physiotherapy management for chondromyxoid fibroma, like other benign fibrous and cartilaginous lesions, includes free active exercises, heat therapy with SWD or IRR, and wax bath therapy. Conservative management prior to surgery includes rest, warm fomentation, massage, and analgesics or NSAIDs. Surgical curettage or excision remains the definitive treatment of choice.
options: Free active exercises, heat, wax bath
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviewing a patient with chondromyxoid fibroma post-curettage should include which physiotherapy modalities in the rehabilitation plan?
Solitary unicameral bone cyst characteristically presents in the first two decades of life and most often results in which complication?
questions.explanation: Solitary or unicameral bone cyst is frequent in the first or second decade of life and most often results in a pathological fracture, usually involving the femur, tibia, humerus, or iliac bone. X-rays show an expansile lesion with cortical thinning and a distinct sclerotic margin. Surgery is often delayed in young children with an active cyst.

questions.question: Manipulative therapy is contraindicated in a patient presenting with active ankylosing spondylitis for which listed reason category?
questions.explanation: Manipulative therapy contraindications are categorized, and active rheumatoid arthritis together with ankylosing spondylitis fall under the inflammatory category. Traumatic contraindications instead include recent fractures or acute sprains, while endocrinal contraindications include osteoporosis. Recognizing the correct contraindication category helps the physiotherapist select safer alternative techniques.

A ganglion is a cystic or partially cystic lesion originating from the synovial membrane, found near a tendon sheath or joint capsule, most frequently on the dorsal or volar wrist. It arises traumatically through herniation of synovial membranes. Recurrence is fairly common, especially with poorly performed excision.
questions.question: A ganglion cyst near the wrist is best described pathologically as originating from which structure?

options: The overall stump length is considerably shorter for storage
The radioulnar joint is deliberately sacrificed for stability
Pronation and supination movements of the forearm are retained
No skin flap coverage of the bone end is ever required
Nerve retraction above the amputation level becomes unnecessary
questions.explanation: Wrist-level amputation and disarticulation preserve the intact radioulnar joint, allowing the arm to retain supination and pronation, and avoid the need for an above-elbow cuff that would otherwise restrict elbow flexion. This functional retention is the key advantage over more proximal forearm amputation. Adequate palmar skin coverage without bony prominence is also required for a good stump.
questions.question: What is the principal advantage of wrist amputation or disarticulation over a standard forearm-level amputation?
A ten-year-old boy presents with pain, a prominent tibial tubercle, and pain aggravated by running. A cylinder walking cast is applied for eight to ten weeks. Which condition does this describe?
questions.explanation:
Osgood-Schlatter disease is an epiphysitis of the tibial tuberosity typically seen in boys aged ten to fifteen years.
It presents with pain, limping, and an unduly prominent tibial tubercle aggravated by sports activity.
Conservative management includes rest, avoidance of strenuous exercise, and a cylinder walking cast for eight to ten weeks.

questions.question: In achondroplasia, the fingertips typically reach only to which anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: In achondroplasia, the shortened arms resemble flippers, with fingertips reaching only to the greater trochanters. The fingers also diverge to resemble the spokes of a wheel. These features reflect the disproportionate limb shortening of the condition.

questions.question: A physiotherapist working with a patient with achondroplasia notes weakened muscles on examination. How should this finding influence the exercise prescription?
options: Assume weakness is unrelated to the condition
Prescribe complete rest until strength normalizes
Include supervised strengthening as part of the regular exercise program
questions.explanation: Weakened muscles are a recognized diagnostic feature of achondroplasia, supporting inclusion of supervised strengthening within the regular exercise program. This is combined with heat therapy such as SWD or IRR where appropriate. A tailored, supervised approach addresses this specific finding safely.

Moist hot packs are kept in water at a temperature of 140 to 160 degrees Fahrenheit and are wrapped in six to eight layers of towels to prevent burns. They are applied for 15 to 20 minutes and conduct heat more uniformly than dry heat. Careful layering is mandatory to separate the pack from the patient's skin.
questions.question: Moist hot packs used in physiotherapy are typically kept in water at which approximate temperature range?

questions.explanation: Following surgical fixation of a displaced biceps brachii tendon, postoperative immobilization uses an arm pouch or sling for two weeks. Physiotherapy with heat therapy and active exercises follows to restore shoulder and elbow function. This graded approach supports return of full joint movement.
questions.question: A patient status-post fixation of a ruptured biceps brachii tendon in the intertubercular groove is immobilized in an arm pouch or sling for how long postoperatively?

options: Arms adducted and internally rotated with forearm extended
Arms abducted and externally rotated, with the forearm flexed and supinated
Arms hanging fully extended at the sides
Complete paralysis of the diaphragm requiring ventilation
Normal arm posture with isolated leg involvement
questions.question: A patient with a cord lesion at the C6 level shows a characteristic arm posture. Which position is described for this level of injury?
questions.explanation:
Spinal cord injury at the C6 level produces a recognisable resting posture of the upper limbs.
Due to irritation of the C5 segment, the arms lie abducted and externally rotated.
The forearm characteristically remains flexed and supinated in this typical C6-level presentation.

Gamekeeper's thumb describes rupture of the ulnar collateral ligament, typically from forced abduction violence. The deformity shows persistent flexion of the terminal phalanx. Grasping movements of the thumb become painful and restricted.
questions.question: Gamekeeper's thumb refers to rupture of which structure?
Extension of infection from osteomyelitis of the femoral neck into the hip joint is an example of which route of infective arthritis?
questions.explanation: Local spread occurs when infection extends from a nearby focus such as osteomyelitis into an adjoining joint. This differs from direct inoculation, which involves penetrating trauma or surgery. It also differs from hematogenous spread via the bloodstream.

questions.question: A patient scheduled for parathyroidectomy is receiving preoperative calcium lactate and calciferol with milk. What is the primary purpose of this regimen?
questions.explanation: Preoperative calcium lactate and calciferol with milk prepares the patient for the metabolic shifts expected after parathyroidectomy. This same supplementation continues postoperatively for an extended period. It supports bone and calcium homeostasis around the time of surgery.
options: To replace the need for surgery entirely
To cure the parathyroid adenoma non-surgically
To prepare the patient for postoperative metabolic changes

questions.question: Why should a physiotherapist introduce restoration of function slowly after an infected joint wound has had acute symptoms subside?
options: Rapid restoration may reactivate infection or cause residual synovitis
Slow restoration avoids need for bracing
Slow restoration is required only for cosmetic reasons
Rapid restoration guarantees full range loss
questions.explanation: If function is restored too quickly after a joint wound, a reaction may develop that causes residual synovitis or reactivates the infection. Gradual, carefully paced rehabilitation avoids this risk. This principle guides pacing of both active and passive exercise.

options: A site of new bone formation
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes a patient describes a trigger point in the low back causing referred pain in the neck. According to the described phenomenon, what may the neck subsequently become?
questions.explanation: A trigger point in the back may produce referral pain in the neck, and the neck may then act as a satellite trigger point that in turn causes pain in the head. Trigger point massage therapy addresses this through cycles of isolated pressure and release. This cascading referral pattern illustrates why treating only the site of pain may be insufficient.

Surgical treatment in achondroplasia is primarily indicated for shortened legs rather than craniofacial features like the prominent forehead or depressed nose. Overall management remains largely symptomatic. This helps set realistic expectations for the patient regarding treatment goals.
options: No physiotherapy or medical input is ever needed
All craniofacial features require surgery first
Surgery mainly targets shortened legs; other features are largely symptomatic
The condition always requires spinal fusion
questions.question: A patient with achondroplasia and a prominent forehead and depressed nose asks whether these features require surgical correction. What should the physiotherapist explain about management priorities?

questions.explanation: Streptomycin may cause injury to the eighth cranial nerve, producing vertigo and deafness. Because of this toxicity, it is now used mainly for resistant organisms rather than as first-line therapy. Isoniazid remains the preferred primary agent.
questions.question: Streptomycin therapy for bone tuberculosis carries a particular risk of toxicity to which structure?

questions.explanation: Distal to the wrist, a long anterior (palmar) flap and a short posterior (dorsal) flap are used to provide thick, tough palmar skin coverage over the stump end. Above the wrist level, equal anterior and posterior flaps are instead used to distribute pressure evenly. This ratio protects the stump from the thinner, less durable dorsal skin.
options: A short anterior flap and a long lateral flap
A long posterior flap and a short anterior flap
A long anterior flap and a short posterior flap
questions.question: According to flap-length rules for the upper limb, what flap arrangement is used distal to the wrist?

questions.explanation:
The hanging cast relies on the weight of the plaster and limb to maintain reduction through gentle traction.
If this traction becomes excessive, it distracts the bone ends rather than approximating them.
Such distraction favours fibrous tissue formation between fragments, predisposing to non-union.
options: Excessive compression at the fracture site
Direct injury to the brachial artery
Distraction of the fracture ends by the weight of the cast and limb
questions.question: In fractures of the humeral shaft treated by a hanging cast method, non-union may result chiefly because this method causes:

questions.explanation: In hyperparathyroidism, calcium is withdrawn from bone, causing rarefaction (osteoporosis) and bone cyst formation, which predisposes to pathological fractures. This differs from the fibrous tissue replacement seen in fibrous dysplasia. Recognizing the calcium-driven mechanism explains the skeletal manifestations.
questions.question: A patient with hyperparathyroidism presents with backache and a pathological fracture of a rib. What underlying mechanism links these skeletal findings?
options: Rarefaction of bone from calcium withdrawal

questions.explanation: Propulsive gait is described as a stooped, stiff posture with the head and neck bent forward. Scissors gait, by contrast, involves legs flexed slightly at hips and knees with the knees and thighs crossing in a scissoring movement. Both are classified among pathological walking abnormalities requiring re-education.
questions.question: Which walking abnormality is described as a stooped, stiff posture with the head and neck bent forward?
A patient with subacromial bursitis undergoing aspiration and steroid injection is subsequently guided through physiotherapy. Which principle governs the timing of active exercise introduction?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy for subacromial bursitis introduces active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening as pain subsides after aspiration and injection. Heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy supports this recovery phase. This graded approach avoids re-irritating the treated bursa.
options: Exercises start only after six months
Exercises are never introduced in bursitis

questions.question: Subdeltoid bursitis is most often described in the text as resulting primarily from which underlying process?
questions.explanation: Subacromial bursitis occurs more often than other regional bursitis, with inflammation rarely being primary. It instead results from tendinitis of the rotator cuff, with or without calcification. Pain, swelling, and painful restricted movement are the presenting features.

questions.question: A below-knee amputation stump is ideally fashioned with the anterior flap how much longer than the posterior flap?
questions.explanation: Below-knee amputation flap design places the scar 1.0 cm above the bone end by making the anterior flap 1.0 cm longer than the posterior one. This differs from thigh amputation, where the anterior flap is 2.5 cm longer, so that the resulting scar sits away from the weight-bearing surface of the stump. Correct flap ratios reduce pressure-related scar breakdown.
options: 1.0 cm longer than the posterior flap
3.0 cm longer than the posterior flap
0.5 cm longer than the posterior flap
1.5 cm longer than the posterior flap
2.5 cm longer than the posterior flap
Early childhood, from untreated rickets exclusively
Middle adulthood, from occupational heavy lifting
Old age exclusively, from severe osteoporosis alone
Adolescence, from abnormal spine and muscle development
questions.explanation: Postural kyphosis is the commonest form of kyphosis, occurring predominantly in adolescents when the spine and surrounding muscles develop abnormally, often related to poor posture. This differs from Scheuermann's kyphosis, which also develops in adolescence but can progress to greater severity, and congenital kyphosis, which is present from birth due to abnormal spinal development in utero. Each type carries a different natural history and treatment approach.
questions.question: Postural kyphosis is described as the commonest form of kyphosis occurring predominantly during which life stage?

options: It always involves complete rupture of the rotator cuff
It cannot occur following inflammatory joint disease
It is functionally identical to a complete dislocation
It never requires any period of arm support
It involves partial tearing of the coracoclavicular ligaments and may progress to complete dislocation
questions.question: Which statement about subluxation of the shoulder is correct, as distinguished from complete dislocation?
questions.explanation:
Subluxation of the shoulder involves partial rather than complete tearing of the coracoclavicular ligaments.
If the tear progresses, complete dislocation can subsequently occur.
Subluxation may also arise secondary to inflammatory conditions such as suppurative arthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.

Following surgical repair of the supraspinatus tendon, physiotherapy encourages active exercises only once pain begins to subside. Heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy or heating pad therapy is used alongside this graded approach. This protects the healing repair while restoring joint movement and muscle strength.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient two days post repair of a ruptured supraspinatus tendon. What is the most appropriate immediate exercise approach?
options: Active exercises deferred until pain subsides
Full unrestricted range exercises at once

questions.explanation: Synovial chondromatosis is a rare lesion characterized by multiple small cartilaginous or partially ossified nodules developing within the synovial membrane of a joint, bursa, or tendon sheath. X-rays show unusual extensive ossification with multiple small irregular opacities. Synovectomy is the surgical treatment of choice.
questions.question: Multiple small cartilaginous nodules developing within the synovial membrane of a joint characterize which condition?

questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management following synovectomy for synovial chondromatosis includes free active exercises, heat therapy with SWD or IRR, and wax bath therapy. Surgical synovectomy itself is the treatment of choice for this condition. These modalities aim to restore joint mobility and function after the surgical procedure.
options: Free active exercises, heat therapy, wax bath
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning rehabilitation for a patient post synovectomy for synovial chondromatosis. What physiotherapy modalities match the described protocol?

questions.explanation:
Sudeck's dystrophy typically appears after removal of plaster following a Colles fracture of the wrist.
It presents with painful, restricted finger movement, warm shiny skin, and tenderness over the wrist.
X-ray characteristically shows osteoporosis and mottling of the carpus despite the fracture having united.
questions.question: Sudeck's dystrophy is most frequently seen as a late complication following which fracture?
A physiotherapist is treating an adolescent with idiopathic scoliosis being managed with a Milwaukee brace. What is the specific role of the physiotherapist regarding this brace-based treatment?
questions.explanation: In non-surgical scoliosis cases managed with bracing, the physiotherapist teaches the child to hold a correct position and perform active exercises to strengthen trunk muscles, while monitoring for progress and any posture deterioration alongside the brace treatment. This role is distinct from the actual manufacture and fitting of the orthosis, which remains the domain of the orthotist. Physiotherapy exercise reinforcement therefore complements, rather than replaces, the mechanical correction the brace provides.
options: Teaching the child to hold a corrected position and exercise
Discontinuing the brace immediately once pain resolves
Avoiding all communication with the treating orthopedic team
Manufacturing and fitting the brace independently
Replacing the need for any medical or orthotic review

questions.explanation: Elderly patients are especially vulnerable to NSAID toxicity when used for osteoarthritis pain relief. This caution guides careful drug selection and monitoring in this age group. Analgesics and NSAIDs nonetheless remain a mainstay of medical treatment.
questions.question: Which population requires special caution regarding NSAID use in osteoarthritis management?

questions.explanation: Wounds of the knee that are surgically closed with intact synovium, capsule and skin may later develop an extra-articular infection rather than a true intra-articular one. This distinction affects the expected clinical course and management approach. The knee's extensive synovium is relatively protective against direct intra-articular spread.
questions.question: A patient's knee wound was surgically closed, and an infection later developed outside the joint capsule rather than within it. What term best fits this presentation?

options: Direct blow to the front of a fully extended knee
Axial loading through a straight leg
Fall on the bent knee with a violent twist of tibia over femur
questions.question: Fracture of the tibial spine in children typically follows which mechanism of injury?
questions.explanation:
Fracture of the tibial spine is a rare injury seen mostly in children.
It results from a fall onto the bent knee combined with a violent twisting force of the tibia against the femur.
Undisplaced fractures may be managed by aspiration and immobilization, while displaced fragments require fixation or excision.

questions.question: The 'ape thumb' deformity of median nerve injury results specifically from paralysis affecting which movement?
questions.explanation: Median nerve injury paralyzes the thenar muscles, including abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis, resulting in the 'ape thumb' deformity where the thumb lies in the same plane as the other metacarpals rather than being opposable. The pen test and opponens test are used to assess this loss. This deformity is distinct from ulnar claw hand, which affects the ring and little fingers instead.
options: The thumb becoming permanently flexed into the palm
The thumb lying in line with the other metacarpals
The thumb rotating externally away from the palm
The thumb becoming hyperextended at the interphalangeal joint
The thumb losing all sensation without any motor loss

questions.question: A physiotherapist reviewing imaging of a suspected aneurysmal bone cyst notes heavy trabeculations and cortical erosion. How should this finding influence exercise loading in early rehabilitation?
options: Recommend permanent avoidance of all activity
Use cautious, graded loading given the structural bone changes
Assume the bone is structurally normal
questions.explanation: Radiographic findings of heavy trabeculations, loculation and cortical erosion reflect the structural weakening caused by an aneurysmal bone cyst. Cautious, graded loading protects against pathological fracture during rehabilitation. This mirrors the general principle of protecting weakened bone in other conditions in this chapter set.

questions.question: The physiotherapist's role in acromegaly management is best described as?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy plays a limited role in acromegaly, mainly through advice on moderate regular exercise. The physiotherapist may help plan and teach an activity program for the patient. Intensive interventions are not emphasized in this condition.

options: Assess and manage conservatively alongside medical treatment
questions.explanation: Local tenderness and restricted, painful movement of the adjoining joint are recognized features of fibrous metaphyseal defects and nonosteogenic fibromas. Conservative management with analgesics, NSAIDs and heat therapy is typically tried first. Physiotherapy assessment supports this conservative approach before considering surgery.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes local tenderness and restricted movement of the joint adjoining a nonosteogenic fibroma. What is the most appropriate initial physiotherapy action?
Following a supracondylar fracture of the humerus complicated by radial nerve palsy, physiotherapy management typically includes provision of which splint?
questions.explanation:
Radial nerve palsy produces wrist drop due to paralysis of wrist and finger extensors.
A wrist drop splint supports the hand in a functional position while awaiting nerve recovery.
Regular physiotherapy alongside the splint helps maintain joint range until active recovery begins.

options: Referred pain from the opposite limb
Proximity of the lesion to the joint causing secondary restriction
questions.question: A patient with an aneurysmal bone cyst reports restricted, painful movement of the adjoining joint along with local tenderness. What is the most likely explanation for these joint-related symptoms?
questions.explanation: Movements of the adjoining joint may be painful and restricted in an aneurysmal bone cyst due to the lesion's proximity and associated swelling and tenderness. This is a direct effect of the bone lesion rather than a separate joint pathology. Recognizing this helps focus assessment on the bone lesion itself.

options: It favors surgical treatment over radiotherapy
It confirms radiotherapy as first choice
It has no bearing on treatment choice
It rules out any pituitary tumor
questions.question: A patient with acromegaly is found to have visual field loss on assessment. How does this finding influence the treatment plan?
questions.explanation: Marked reduction of visual fields makes radiotherapy hazardous, shifting the treatment plan toward surgery such as cryohypophysectomy. Radiotherapy is preferred instead when the tumor is radiosensitive and vision is preserved. This finding is therefore central to treatment selection.

Connective tissue massage in Raynaud's disease begins with the sacral and lumbar area before progressing to the limbs. This sequence is described as reducing tension in the back. Active exercises to increase circulation and contrast baths further support symptomatic improvement.
questions.question: In Raynaud's disease connective tissue massage, which body region is massaged first before progressing to the limbs?

questions.explanation: Ewing's sarcoma, occurring most often in childhood between five and fifteen years, arises at the diaphysis of long bones and may affect the pelvis or skull as well. The lesion is osteolytic with mottled destruction and reactive endosteal and periosteal new bone. Radiotherapy is highly sensitive but has little effect on distant metastasis.
questions.question: Ewing's sarcoma classically arises at which site within the long bone shaft?

questions.explanation: Pendular movements are rhythmical swinging movements taken to the limit of range, used for the shoulder, hip, and knee to stretch adhesions and improve local blood supply. An example is standing in a lunge position while swinging the arm forward and back for shoulder flexion and extension. Movements should be smooth with emphasis at the range limit.
questions.question: Pendular movements used to stretch joint adhesions are best described by which quality of motion?
A patient with fracture of the clavicle in a figure-of-8 bandage asks the physiotherapist what exercises are appropriate during this period. What is the correct guidance?
questions.explanation:
Clavicle fractures usually heal well with simple conservative support such as a figure-of-8 bandage.
Because of this, they seldom require formal physiotherapy treatment in straightforward cases.
However, if complications develop leading to restricted shoulder movement or muscle weakness, physiotherapy input is then indicated.
options: Intensive daily resisted shoulder abduction is mandatory
These fractures seldom require physiotherapy unless complications restrict shoulder movement
The arm must be kept completely immobile for twelve weeks
Passive manipulation of the shoulder should begin immediately
Physiotherapy should focus solely on the contralateral limb
The tibia has an unusually rich soft tissue covering
The tibia is entirely intramedullary in structure
The tibia rarely bears any body weight
One third of the tibia lies subcutaneously
The tibia has the thickest surrounding musculature of any long bone
questions.question: Fractures of the tibia are especially prone to becoming compound (open) injuries mainly because:
questions.explanation:
The tibia is unique among long bones in having roughly one third of its surface lying just beneath the skin.
This subcutaneous position means relatively minor direct trauma can drive a fragment through the skin.
As a result, tibial fractures are particularly prone to becoming compound injuries and subsequent infection.

options: The Syme stump always requires a hip-level prosthesis instead
The Syme stump end-bears directly, unlike lateral-bearing stumps
The Syme prosthesis requires no socket fitting whatsoever
The Syme amputation eliminates the need for any prosthesis
The Syme stump cannot tolerate any weight bearing at all
questions.explanation: The Syme amputation is the classic example of an end-bearing stump, where the preserved heel pad skin bears weight directly at the stump tip, unlike below-knee amputations that rely on lateral bearing at accessible bony points. This functional difference explains why the socket design and gait feel different between the two prosthesis types. Understanding this distinction helps the physiotherapist set realistic expectations for gait training.
questions.question: A patient with a well-healed Syme amputation stump asks why their prosthesis feels different from that of a friend with a below-knee amputation. What is the most accurate physiotherapy explanation?
In a child's forearm injury, one cortex bends and breaks while the opposite cortex remains intact. What is this fracture called?
questions.explanation:
A greenstick fracture occurs in children because the periosteum is strong and pliable.
One cortex (convex side) breaks while the concave cortex bends but stays intact.
Displacement is minimal and healing is rapid, allowing early mobilization.

options: Full extension for six months without change
Ulnar deviation maintained for one year
Radial deviation only, without any flexion phase
Flexion, for two weeks, followed by a cast with the wrist in a more neutral position
No immobilisation is required after excision
questions.explanation:
Kienbock's disease involves vascular changes of the lunate bone, sometimes requiring surgical excision.
After excision, a plaster cast is initially applied with the wrist held in flexion for two weeks.
This is followed by a further period of casting with the wrist positioned more neutrally as healing progresses.
questions.question: A patient with Kienbock's disease of the lunate is managed with excision due to vascular changes. Postoperative immobilisation involves a plaster cast with the wrist in which position initially?

options: A hypoplastic and misshapen scapula lying abnormally high
A scapula fused directly to the underlying ribcage
An enlarged scapula with normal position but restricted rotation
A normally shaped scapula fixed in a depressed position
A bifid scapula with a duplicated inferior angle
questions.question: Sprengel's deformity (congenital elevation of the scapula) is characterized by which structural abnormality of the scapula?
questions.explanation: Sprengel's deformity involves a hypoplastic and misshapen scapula that lies more superiorly than normal in relation to the thoracic cage, with restricted abduction movement and, in severe forms, internal rotation of the inferior angle. Surgical treatment through muscle release or scapular excision is reserved for severe deformity and disability. Mild cases with minimal disability require no treatment.

questions.question: A patient with Charcot's joint is being managed conservatively with rest, analgesics, NSAIDs and antibiotics. What should the physiotherapist understand about the intent of this conservative approach?
options: It fully reverses the joint destruction
It targets the underlying neurological cause directly
It is symptomatic management, not a cure for the trophic joint changes
It is used only after surgery fails
It replaces the need for any surgery
questions.explanation: Conservative management of Charcot's joint, including rest, analgesics, NSAIDs and antibiotics, is described as symptomatic. It does not reverse the underlying trophic joint destruction. Surgical arthrodesis is used regionally when definitive joint stabilization is required.

Metabolic arthropathies are characterized by crystals present in the synovial fluid or articular cartilage. Gout involves sodium urate crystals, while pseudogout involves calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Identification of the crystal type distinguishes between the two conditions.
questions.question: Metabolic arthropathies are characterized by the presence of crystals in which location?
Snapping knee in adolescents is chiefly explained by which congenital abnormality?
questions.explanation: Snapping knee is attributed to a discoid cartilage that is thicker centrally than at the periphery, causing it to slip and produce an audible click. It is common among adolescents and lacks any neurotic element. Excision of the discoid disc is the surgical treatment of choice.

questions.question: Palmar fibromatosis, also known as Dupuytren's contracture, initially appears as a nodule in line with which finger?
questions.explanation: Palmar fibromatosis appears as a painless subcutaneous nodule in the palm, mostly in line with the ring finger at the distal palmar crease. More nodules and bands appear later, eventually flexing the metacarpophalangeal joints. The plantar form similarly affects the medial half of the plantar fascia, forming a hammer toe.

questions.question: Scleroderma (progressive systemic sclerosis) is characterized by tightening and hardening of which tissues?
questions.explanation: Scleroderma refers to disorders in which the skin and connective tissues progressively tighten and harden. It is a long-term, progressive disease affecting mainly middle-aged women. Raynaud's phenomenon is frequently positive in affected patients.

questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a patient's gait notices difficulty maintaining single-leg stance while swinging the other leg for heel strike. Which walking component is impaired?
questions.explanation: Points checked by the physiotherapist during walking re-education include transference of weight smoothly with control of pelvic position, and the ability to maintain weight on one leg while swinging the other for heel strike. Other checks include propulsion of the back leg and even stride length. These observations guide the walking re-education plan and choice of walking aid.

questions.question: A child with rickets is scheduled for splinting to correct bowed legs. What complements splinting in correcting deformity when needed?
questions.explanation: Deformities in rickets are corrected by splinting, with osteoclasis by manipulation used as an additional measure when required. Surgical osteotomy is reserved for older children and adults. This staged, largely conservative approach reflects the pliability of young bone.

Dysuria and pyuria are noted genitourinary diagnostic features associated with Charcot's joint, reflecting the broader neurological or systemic context of the condition. This combination should prompt broader clinical assessment rather than being dismissed. Recognizing associated systemic features supports comprehensive patient management.
options: As entirely unrelated and to be ignored
As evidence of a vitamin D deficiency
As a noted diagnostic association requiring broader clinical assessment
As proof the joint symptoms are psychosomatic
questions.question: A patient with Charcot's joint reports dysuria and pyuria alongside joint symptoms. How should the physiotherapist interpret this combination of findings?

questions.explanation:
Olecranon fractures fixed with tension band wiring benefit from relatively early mobilization.
The described physiotherapy approach is free active exercises combined with heat or short-wave therapy.
Early movement helps offset the tendency toward stiffness after this periarticular fracture.
questions.question: A patient with fracture of the olecranon has undergone tension band wiring. What is the described physiotherapy approach post-fixation?
options: Free active exercises combined with heat therapy
Complete immobilization for sixteen weeks without exercise
Passive elbow manipulation under anaesthesia at two weeks
Immediate resisted triceps strengthening against maximal load
Hydrotherapy as the only treatment offered

questions.question: Individuals with achondroplasia are noted in the source to often be occupationally employed in?
questions.explanation: The source notes that individuals with achondroplasia are usually employed in circuses due to their distinctive stature. This reflects an occupational pattern described in the text rather than a clinical feature. It is unrelated to the pathology of the condition itself.

options: Deltoid, trapezius, rhomboids, and levator scapulae
Pectoralis major, minor, serratus, and latissimus
Supinator, pronator, flexor carpi, extensor carpi
Supraspinatus, teres minor, infraspinatus, and subscapularis
questions.question: Which structures are involved in a typical shoulder cuff, according to the described anatomy?
questions.explanation: The shoulder cuff comprises the tendons of supraspinatus, teres minor, infraspinatus, and subscapularis. Little trauma may cause tears in a cuff already degenerated with age. Lesions include tendonitis, rupture, and calcification of these tendons.

Reconstruction of an old ruptured tibial collateral ligament follows a structured postoperative protocol.
A long leg cast with the knee flexed to fifteen degrees is applied, with exercises beginning at one week.
The cast is removed after four weeks, after which the patient walks in a supportive brace for three months.
options: Cast removed on the first postoperative day
Cast maintained for one year without removal
Cast removed after twenty-four hours with immediate unsupported walking
No brace is used at any stage of rehabilitation
Cast removed after four weeks, followed by walking in a brace for three months
questions.question: A patient with old rupture of the tibial (medial) collateral ligament of the knee undergoes reconstruction. Postoperatively, a long leg cast is applied with the knee flexed to fifteen degrees, and exercises begin from one week. When is the cast removed and walking in a brace begun?
A patient with cysts of the lateral meniscus undergoes surgical excision of the cyst. What is the described postoperative physiotherapy approach?
options: Complete avoidance of exercise for one year
Assisted passive exercises progressing to free active exercises
Immediate unsupported return to competitive football
Cold immersion therapy as the sole intervention
questions.explanation:
Cysts of the lateral meniscus present as a round, hard swelling with pain on the lateral side of the knee.
Surgical excision of the cyst is the definitive treatment when conservative measures are insufficient.
Postoperative physiotherapy follows the standard pattern of assisted passive exercises progressing to free active exercises.

questions.question: A patient with cervical spondylosis undergoes surgical division of dentate ligaments for intraforaminal osteophyte compression. Postoperative after-care specifically includes wearing a collar for how long?
questions.explanation: Postoperative after-care for cervical spondylosis surgery includes wearing a collar for one month. Neck exercises are started as soon as possible after surgery. This combination protects the healing surgical site while restoring cervical mobility.

questions.question: A young patient with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is prescribed weight-bearing exercise under supervision. What is the primary rationale for supervision in this condition?
options: The patient has no bone involvement
Supervision is required only for cosmetic reasons
Exercise has no relevance to this condition
Bones are weakened and prone to pathological fracture
questions.explanation: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia involves softening, bending and pathological fracture of bone due to fibrous tissue replacement. Supervised weight-bearing exercise is therefore recommended to balance activity benefits against fracture risk. This mirrors the cautious exercise approach used in other fragile-bone conditions.

questions.question: Avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment is a well-recognized complication after fracture of which carpal bone?
questions.explanation:
The scaphoid receives a retrograde blood supply entering distally, making the proximal fragment vulnerable after fracture through its waist.
Interruption of this supply leads to avascular necrosis of the proximal segment.
This complication contributes to non-union and later osteoarthritis of the wrist.

Serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase remain normal in osteoporosis, unlike in other metabolic bone diseases. Diagnosis instead relies on radiographic demineralization and bone densitometry. This biochemical normalcy helps distinguish osteoporosis from conditions like hyperparathyroidism.
questions.question: In osteoporosis, serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase are typically?
A concentric isotonic contraction is best defined by which change in the working muscle?
questions.explanation: A concentric contraction is an isotonic movement in the direction of muscle contraction, during which the working muscle shortens. Eccentric contraction is the opposite type, where the working muscle lengthens under tension. Isometric contraction differs from both by keeping muscle length constant throughout.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with excessive villous synovial thickening and boggy knee swelling. Alongside heat therapy and wax bath, what active component is indicated?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management for pigmented villonodular synovitis includes free active exercises along with heat therapy using SWD or IRR and wax bath therapy. This addresses the disability and partial loss of function caused by the swollen, boggy joint. Conservative medical treatment separately may include intra-articular hydrocortisone injection with lignocaine.

Extension injuries of the cervical spine are generally classified as stable when the posterior ligament complex is intact.
Conservative management for stable extension injuries includes heat therapy, analgesics, and a cervical collar.
Physiotherapy proceeds with assisted exercises progressing to free active exercises as the patient recovers.
questions.question: A patient with a cervical spine extension injury shows wedging of the vertebra without narrowing of the disc space on X-ray, and the injury is classified as stable. What is the appropriate conservative management?
options: Emergency laminectomy regardless of neurological status
Immediate skull traction for twelve weeks
Complete bed rest without any collar support
Heat, analgesics, and a cervical collar

questions.question: A fracture of the lateral tibial condyle from an abduction strain forcing the leg into valgus is known as:
questions.explanation:
The bumper fracture is the commonest of the tibial condylar fractures.
It is caused by an abduction strain forcing the lower leg into valgus, often from a vehicle bumper injury.
A downward thrust of body weight is usually associated with the abduction force at the time of injury.

questions.question: During an active exacerbation of arthritis in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus, the affected joints are physiotherapeutically treated similarly to which other condition?
questions.explanation: During an active exacerbation of arthritis in SLE, affected joints are treated in the same manner as rheumatoid arthritis. Between exacerbations, a program of active exercise is devised for the patient to follow daily. This maintains function while limiting further joint compromise.

options: Sudden onset with severe unremitting pain
Instant onset with total joint paralysis
Abrupt onset limited to children only
Slow onset with mild to moderate continuous pain
questions.question: Chronic suppurative arthritis differs from the acute form chiefly in which feature of onset?
questions.explanation: Chronic suppurative arthritis has a slow onset with pain that is mild to moderate and continuous, unlike the sudden severe onset of the acute form. It is more common in adults, with the knee and hip most frequently affected. Increasing deformity and sinus formation mark advanced disease.

questions.question: Keloid is differentiated from a simple hypertrophic scar by which distinctive gross appearance?
questions.explanation: Keloid is differentiated from a simple hypertrophic scar by cauliflower-like or claw-like projections caused by massive collagenized overgrowth of fibrous tissue infiltrating adjoining normal tissue. It commonly occurs on the chest wall, arm, buttock, or thigh after trauma. Local injection of hydrocortisone with hyalase and lignocaine is a conservative option.

questions.question: Medial popliteal (tibial) nerve injury produces which characteristic foot deformity from paralysis of the calf and plantar muscles?
options: Talipes equinovarus with the foot plantarflexed and inverted
Hallux valgus with lateral deviation of the great toe
Genu varum with bowing of the tibia and fibula
Pes cavus with an abnormally elevated longitudinal arch
Talipes calcaneovalgus with the foot dorsiflexed and everted
questions.explanation: Medial popliteal (tibial) nerve injury paralyzes the calf muscles and sole of the foot, resulting in talipes calcaneovalgus in which the foot is held dorsiflexed at the ankle and everted. This is the opposite deformity pattern to lateral popliteal nerve injury, which produces talipes equinovarus. Recognizing which muscle groups are paralyzed helps distinguish the two injury patterns clinically.

For leg swelling after knee trauma, the patient lies on a plinth with the leg raised on pillows, performing quadriceps exercises plus ankle and toe movements. This elevates the limb to assist drainage while static muscle contractions control joint movement. The patient is advised to keep the limb elevated between exercise sessions.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a patient's active free exercise program for restricted joint movement due to swelling of the leg after knee trauma should position the patient and apply which exercises?
A physiotherapist is treating a child with bowing of the legs and a pot belly appearance. Which underlying deficiency should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Bowing of the legs with a flabby, pot-bellied appearance is characteristic of rickets, caused by vitamin D deficiency. Recognizing this presentation guides appropriate referral for medical and nutritional management. Physiotherapy input focuses on supporting deformity correction and mobility.

questions.question: A proposed etiological factor for aneurysmal bone cyst includes which vascular disturbance?
questions.explanation: Vascular disorders such as hemorrhage and venous dilatation are proposed etiological factors for aneurysmal bone cyst, though the cause remains uncertain. Trauma, such as parosteal myositis ossificans, is another suggested factor. No single definitive cause has been established.

The described exercise program for cancer patients comprises four types: aerobics such as walking, bicycling, and running; strengthening muscles; balancing; and stretching. This combination aims to restore strength, endurance, and vitality as part of rehabilitation. It applies broadly across the various benign and malignant bone and soft tissue tumors described.
questions.question: A physiotherapist designing a cancer rehabilitation program wants to include balance training. Alongside balancing, which three other exercise categories complete the standard four-part program described?

questions.explanation: Grade IV is a small-amplitude oscillation performed at the limit of the available range, distinguishing it from Grade I, which is a small-amplitude oscillation performed at the start of that range. Grade III instead is a large-amplitude oscillation carried to the limit of range. Grade V involves a high-velocity thrust beyond voluntary patient control.
questions.question: In oscillatory joint mobilization grading, a small-amplitude oscillation performed at the very limit of available range is classified as?
Radiotherapy is considered the treatment of choice for acromegaly when?
questions.explanation: Radiotherapy is preferred when the tumor is sensitive to radiation and visual fields are preserved. When visual fields are markedly reduced, radiotherapy becomes hazardous and surgery is favored. This distinction guides treatment selection in acromegaly.
options: Tumor is radiosensitive without visual loss

questions.question: Which drug is specifically mentioned for lowering blood prothrombin levels in acute arterial injury conservative management?
questions.explanation: Dicoumarol (Warfarin), alongside phenindione, is specifically cited as an anticoagulant used to lower the blood level of prothrombin in the conservative management of acute arterial injury. Heparin is separately used as an intravenous anticoagulant in the same setting. Vasodilators such as Papaverine serve a different purpose, addressing arterial spasm rather than coagulation.

questions.question: Prolapsed intervertebral disc (PIVD) most commonly affects adults within which age range?
questions.explanation: PIVD is the main cause of low backache with pain radiating down the thigh, leg, or arm. It commonly affects adults aged thirty to fifty, most often males. Nuclear retropulsion occurs when the damaged posterior longitudinal ligament allows backward protrusion of the nucleus pulposus.

options: Sole reliance on radiotherapy for healing
Supporting mobility while protecting the healing weight-bearing bone
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy is required for relief of pain and tenderness in Paget's disease, and to assist the patient in becoming mobile as soon as possible, including after fractures. Weight-bearing bones such as the femur and tibia are most commonly affected by pathological fracture. Careful, graded rehabilitation protects the healing bone while restoring function.
questions.question: A patient with Paget's disease of the femur sustains a pathological fracture. Which physiotherapy consideration is most relevant during early rehabilitation?

questions.explanation: Paraffin wax treatment acts as a type of thermotherapy, or heat therapy, helping conditions like arthritis and fibromyalgia by increasing blood flow, relaxing muscles, and reducing joint stiffness. It is a white, colorless, odorless wax made from saturated hydrocarbons. This distinguishes it functionally from cold-based or purely mechanical modalities.
questions.question: Paraffin wax treatment functions therapeutically as which category of physical modality?

questions.explanation:
Whiplash injuries commonly affect the facet joints around the C3 to C5 levels of the cervical spine.
Gentle posteroanterior mobilizations at grade I or II help keep these facet surfaces moving without provoking pain.
Treatment can progress by upgrading the mobilization grade or changing to unilateral posteroanterior techniques as tolerated.
questions.question: A patient with whiplash injury from a rear-end collision reports paraesthesia along the ulnar border of the hand and dizziness. What physiotherapy technique targeting the facet joints is described for this condition?
options: High-velocity thrust manipulation from day one
Complete cervical immobilisation for twelve weeks
Aggressive resisted neck extension against maximal load
Posteroanterior mobilizations of the spinous processes at grade I or II
Deep transverse friction massage over the cervical facets

questions.explanation:
A sprain is specifically defined as an incomplete tear of one or more ligaments.
Critically, it is described as unrelated to overall stability of the joint, unlike subluxation.
The lateral ligaments of the ankle, including the anterior talofibular ligament, are frequently involved in ankle sprains.
questions.question: Sprain of the ankle, as distinguished from subluxation and dislocation in the text, is defined as:
options: An incomplete tear of ligament(s) unrelated to joint stability
A complete tear of the lateral ligament with instability
An incomplete loss of contact between articular surfaces
A complete loss of contact between articular surfaces
A fracture through the lateral malleolus

questions.explanation: Trendelenburg's test assesses the competency of valves in the superficial venous system and the communicating (perforating) veins between the superficial and deep systems, particularly at the saphenofemoral junction. This helps localize the site of valvular incompetence responsible for varicose vein formation. The test guides whether high ligation and stripping will be curative.
questions.question: Trendelenburg's test in varicose veins is specifically performed to assess the competency of which structures?
options: Valves within the deep femoral and popliteal arteries
Sensory nerve conduction along the saphenous nerve
Ligamentous stability at the saphenopopliteal junction only
Arterial pulsation at the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial
Valves in the superficial and communicating venous systems

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating an infant with Sprengel's deformity (congenital elevation of the scapula) using passive stretching. Which additional caregiver education component is specifically emphasized?
options: Advising complete avoidance of any physiotherapist follow-up
Advising the family to delay all care until school age
Discouraging any form of passive stretching at this stage
Recommending immediate surgical excision regardless of severity
Teaching the mother correct positioning and handling techniques
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management of Sprengel's deformity specifically includes teaching the mother how to perform passive stretching, hold the baby, and position the baby correctly in the cot, with the physiotherapist monitoring progress at regular intervals.
