Surgical treatment (muscle release or scapular excision) is reserved specifically for severe deformity and disability, while mild cases require no treatment. Caregiver education is therefore central to conservative management of this condition.

Closed manipulation for an old unreduced hip dislocation is generally attempted within the first week.
Beyond this early window, skeletal traction over three to four weeks is used instead.
If conservative measures fail altogether, open reduction, followed later by osteotomy if needed, becomes necessary.
questions.question: Old unreduced dislocation of the hip is initially managed conservatively by closed reduction within approximately what timeframe, before skeletal traction is considered?

A patient recovering from thoracic and lumbar spine fracture managed with a plaster jacket in extension develops backache and local tenderness on follow-up. What physiotherapy approach is indicated once fixation is stable?
options: Immediate discontinuation of the jacket without medical review
Permanent avoidance of exercise for the remainder of treatment
Assisted exercises progressing to free active exercises by the patient
questions.explanation:
Fractures of the thoracic and lumbar spine are frequently managed conservatively with bed rest and a plaster jacket.
Physiotherapy input follows the standard pattern of assisted exercises delivered by the physiotherapist initially.
These are then progressed to free active exercises performed by the patient as symptoms and stability allow.

The physiotherapist teaches the patient with mallet finger to hold the middle phalanx in extension while practicing controlled flexion of the affected joint. Finger kneading massage and passive stretching support this process. Progress is measured by gradually increasing flexion of the proximal interphalangeal joint.
questions.question: A patient with a ruptured extensor tendon (mallet finger) has completed splintage. The physiotherapist teaches the patient to hold the middle phalanx in which position while practicing flexion?
Pott's paraplegia most often complicates tuberculosis of the spine at which anatomical level?
questions.explanation: Pott's paraplegia is most often associated with tuberculosis of the dorsal spine because the spinal canal is narrowest there and the anterior ligament loosely confines a cold abscess. Tuberculosis is also more prevalent in the dorsal spine generally. This anatomical narrowness increases the risk of cord compression.

questions.question: Tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease) produces which spinal deformity as vertebral bodies collapse?
questions.explanation: Vertebral body collapse in tuberculous spondylitis produces a kyphotic deformity of the spine. A perispinal abscess travels along muscle planes to form a subcutaneous cold abscess at a distance. Paraplegia may follow from spinal cord compression by the abscess or displaced bone fragments.

questions.question: Codman's triangle and sunray appearance on X-ray are classic radiological features of which malignant bone tumor?
questions.explanation: Osteogenic sarcoma shows subperiosteal new bone formation causing stripping of the periosteum, radiologically described as Codman's triangle with a sunray appearance. This tumor most often affects the distal femur, then proximal tibia, then proximal humerus. Amputation as high as possible remains the surgical treatment of choice.

Snapping shoulder conservative management includes rest, heat therapy, and immobilization using a sling or arm pouch. Aspiration and needling of any calcified mass may also be performed. Surgery is reserved for very severe, persistent snapping or clicking.
questions.question: A patient with snapping shoulder due to biceps tendon displacement undergoes conservative management. Immobilization is provided using which device?

options: This length is chosen purely for improved cosmetic appearance
This length guarantees full preservation of wrist movement
This length provides adequate leverage to power the prosthesis
This length eliminates any requirement for terminal scar care
This length avoids the need for any pronation-supination use
questions.question: A physiotherapist is advising a patient with a new forearm amputation about prosthesis activation. Why is the amputation site specifically chosen at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Forearm amputation at the junction of the middle and distal thirds provides an adequately long stump for powerful activation of the artificial limb, since shorter forearm stumps are less effective in activating the prosthesis and are more difficult to fit. This length also allows pronation and supination to be preserved. The physiotherapist should relate stump length directly to expected functional prosthetic control during training.

options: Extending the plaster cast to cover additional joints indefinitely
Tightening the cast further to control spasticity
Avoiding any skin inspection to prevent disturbing the patient
Removal of the plaster cast to avoid formation of bedsores
Applying a second layer of plaster over the first
questions.question: A patient develops paraplegia in flexion following a complete spinal cord lesion. What is the priority regarding plaster cast management to prevent a specific complication?
questions.explanation:
Complete cord lesions carry a heightened risk of pressure injury because of absent sensation and prolonged immobility.
Care after cast application therefore prioritises removal of the plaster to prevent bedsore formation.
Regular skin inspection and good nursing care become essential parts of ongoing management in this patient group.

Dislocation of the lunate is a wrist injury that typically follows a fall on the outstretched hand.
After closed reduction, the wrist is initially immobilised in flexion before being brought to neutral.
Kienbock's disease, involving vascular changes in the lunate, is a recognised late complication.
options: Direct blow to the dorsum of the wrist
questions.question: Dislocation of the lunate bone typically follows which mechanism of injury?

options: Damaged articular surfaces of the joint
A single ligament injury rather than multiple
questions.question: A patient with recurrent knee instability due to an old rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament is being considered for reconstruction. According to the text, which factor would make reconstruction of little practical value?
questions.explanation:
Several criteria are considered before reconstructing an old ligament rupture of the knee.
When the articular surfaces of the joint are already damaged, reconstruction of the ligaments becomes of little practical value.
Other important factors include patient age, general health, and the strength of the surrounding stabilizing muscles.

Myositis ossificans of the elbow classically affects the brachialis muscle anterior to the joint.
A hematoma within the muscle undergoes calcification and ossification, restricting movement mechanically.
Repeated forceful manipulation during reduction is a recognized precipitating factor.
questions.question: Myositis ossificans following elbow trauma most commonly arises in which muscle?

options: Isolated root avulsion is anatomically nearly impossible
Major trauma severe enough to damage all roots is often fatal
The condition typically resolves without any intervention needed
The plexus is anatomically protected by dense fascia layers
Partial recovery almost always occurs before full paralysis sets in
questions.question: Complete brachial plexus injury is considered a rare presentation primarily because of what factor?
questions.explanation: Complete brachial plexus injury is rare because the degree of major trauma required to damage all the nerve roots frequently inflicts fatal injuries on adjoining vital structures. When it does occur, it produces complete paralysis of the upper limb with anaesthesia of the hand, forearm, and distal arm. This severity distinguishes it from the more common incomplete (upper or lower) plexus lesions.

questions.question: A patient presents with painful, restricted finger movement, warm shiny skin, and wrist tenderness four to six weeks after plaster removal for a Colles fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis guiding physiotherapy planning?
questions.explanation:
Sudeck's dystrophy characteristically appears after removal of plaster following a Colles fracture.
It presents with painful restricted movement, swollen warm shiny skin, and tenderness over the wrist and metacarpals.
Management includes anti-inflammatory analgesics alongside physiotherapy exercises to restore function.

Walking is allowed with the aid of a long leg brace after surgery for a joint wound. The brace should not be discarded until a satisfactory range of motion, especially extension, is restored. Premature removal risks compromising joint recovery.
questions.question: Following surgery for a wound of the knee joint, a patient is allowed to walk with which aid, which should not be discarded prematurely?

questions.explanation: Postoperative physiotherapy management for anterior tibial compartment syndrome includes rest with splints, heat therapy, and exercises performed under the physiotherapist's supervision. This supervised approach ensures safe progression after fasciotomy and arteriectomy. Heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy also supports recovery.
questions.question: Following anterior tibial compartment syndrome surgery, physiotherapy exercises are performed under what condition according to management guidance?

questions.explanation: Osteomalacia, the adult counterpart of rickets, is noted to be more common in females. Advanced cases of osteomalacia may progress to tetany. This gender predisposition is relevant to clinical suspicion.
questions.question: Osteomalacia is best described as the adult form of rickets and is more common in?

questions.explanation: The McBride operation is indicated in middle-aged and younger patients with moderate hallux valgus deformity, dealing primarily with soft tissue correction by freeing the adductor hallucis tendon and reattaching it to the first metatarsal. The Keller operation instead excises the base of the proximal phalanx and is more commonly used for marked discomfort with gross deformity. Choice of procedure depends on patient age and severity of the deformity.
questions.question: Which surgical procedure for hallux valgus is specifically indicated in middle-aged and younger patients with moderate deformity, focusing on soft tissue correction?

questions.explanation:
Internal derangement of the temporomandibular joint is initially managed conservatively with rest and splinting.
Surgical treatment is usually contraindicated unless pain remains severe despite adequate conservative management.
When surgery is required, options include excision of the disc, ligament repair, or reduction of dislocation depending on the finding.
options: Surgery is the first-line treatment in every case
Surgery is never indicated regardless of severity
Surgery is limited exclusively to children under ten years
Surgery always involves total joint replacement as the only option
Surgery is usually contraindicated unless pain is severe and unrelieved by conservative measures
questions.question: A patient with internal derangement of the temporomandibular joint has failed conservative treatment with rest, analgesics, warm fomentation, and mandibular splinting. Which statement about surgical treatment for this condition is correct?

questions.explanation: Acute gout results from disturbed purine metabolism or abnormal uric acid excretion, producing hyperuricemia. Any abrupt change in serum uric acid concentration may provoke an acute attack. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is characteristically painful and swollen.
questions.question: Acute gout is precipitated most typically by an abrupt change in which serum parameter?

options: Elimination of the need for antibiotics
questions.question: A patient with syphilitic bone disease has weak osteoporotic bone. Physiotherapy immobilization using splints and braces primarily aims to achieve what?
questions.explanation: Immobilization with splints or braces in syphilitic bone disease aims to provide comfort or protect weak osteoporotic bone from fracture. Assisted passive exercises are then progressed to free active exercises. This strengthens weak muscles while restoring free joint movement.

questions.question: Which fracture is described as the reverse deformity of a Colles fracture, with the distal fragment displaced anteriorly?
questions.explanation:
Smith's fracture, also called reversed Colles fracture, follows a fall onto the back of the hand.
The distal radial fragment displaces anteriorly, opposite to the direction seen in a Colles fracture.
The articular surface tilts forward, producing anterior rather than dorsal angulation.

questions.question: Morning stiffness and pain relieved by rest are diagnostic features most typical of?
questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis presents with an insidious onset, morning stiffness, and dull aching pain aggravated by joint use and relieved by rest. Systemic manifestations are notably absent. This pattern contrasts with the sudden onset and systemic features of septic arthritis.

questions.question: Which laboratory investigation directly examines the joint fluid in suspected infective arthritis?
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid analysis shows leukocytosis and allows smear and culture of the causative organism directly from the joint. Blood culture and ESR support diagnosis but do not sample the joint itself. Identifying the organism from synovial fluid guides antibiotic choice.

options: Immediately on the day of surgery
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient recovering from surgery for Kohler's (Freiberg's) disease. When is weight bearing typically permitted following excision of the affected metatarsal head?
questions.explanation: Following excision or remodeling of the metatarsal head in Kohler's (Freiberg's) disease, weight bearing is permitted after 1 week postoperatively, with a corrective or protective orthosis such as a hallux valgus splint supporting the foot during recovery. This short recovery timeline is consistent with other minor forefoot procedures for conditions like Morton's toe and hammer toe. The physiotherapist should sequence gait progression around this specific one-week milestone.

questions.question: A patient with internal derangement of the radioulnar joint has a torn articular disc confirmed on MRI. What is the described surgical management for this specific finding?
questions.explanation:
Internal derangement of the radioulnar joints may involve injury to the articular disc, ligaments, or alignment.
When the articular disc itself is torn, the described surgical management is excision of the disc.
Ruptured ligaments are managed by repair, while angulated bones are corrected by osteotomy.

Shortwave diathermy uses an inductive coil applicator capable of affecting both superficial and deep tissues, making it suitable for larger areas needing deep heating. Microwave diathermy instead mainly affects superficial tissue over small areas using a compactive plate or magnetron. This distinction guides modality selection based on target tissue depth and area size.
questions.question: A physiotherapist choosing between shortwave and microwave diathermy for a patient needing deep tissue heating in a large area should select which modality?
Which gram-positive sporing bacilli are implicated in infected joint wounds?
questions.explanation: Clostridia welchii and Clostridia tetani are gram-positive sporing bacilli associated with contaminated joint wounds. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are gram-positive but non-sporing cocci. Klebsiella and Pseudomonas are gram-negative bacilli implicated separately.

questions.question: A vertebral lesion showing vertical striations with radiating trabeculae on X-ray, arising from vascular tissue, suggests which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hemangioma of bone characteristically occurs in the vertebrae or skull, showing focal areas of low density with vertical striations within the vertebral body on X-ray. Histologically it consists of closely packed thin-walled vascular channels encased in radiating trabeculae. Small vertebral lesions may be managed by radiotherapy rather than surgery.

Congenital coxa vara is defined by a progressive decrease in the angle between the femoral neck and shaft, leading to limb shortening, a limp, and a defect in the medial part of the neck. It is confirmed radiographically by slipping of the femoral epiphysis on pelvic X-ray, and Trendelenburg's sign becomes positive as the deformity progresses. Osteotomy of the femur is used to correct the abnormal neck-shaft angle.
questions.question: Congenital coxa vara is characterized by a progressive decrease in which specific anatomical angle?
options: The angle between the acetabulum and pelvis
The angle between the femoral shaft and tibia
The angle between the tibia and fibula distally
The angle between the femoral neck and shaft
The angle between the patella and femoral condyles
Triceps and the wrist and finger extensor muscles
Flexor carpi ulnaris and the short muscles of the hand
Pronator teres and the flexor digitorum sublimis
Flexor carpi radialis and the thenar eminence muscles
Deltoid and the spinati rotator cuff muscles
questions.explanation: Ulnar nerve injury paralyzes flexor carpi ulnaris, the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, and the short intrinsic muscles of the hand, producing claw hand with clawing specifically of the little and ring fingers. Sensory loss is confined to the ulnar border of the hand and the whole little finger. The interossei and adductor pollicis tests, such as the card test, help confirm the diagnosis.
questions.question: The classic deformity of ulnar nerve injury, clawing of the ring and little fingers, results primarily from paralysis of which muscle groups?

questions.explanation: De Quervain's disease physiotherapy management includes free active exercises together with wax bath therapy. Heat therapy such as shortwave or infrared also supports conservative treatment. Surgical incision of the thickened tendon sheath is reserved for cases unresponsive to conservative measures.
questions.question: A patient with de Quervain's disease undergoes conservative treatment. Which specific physiotherapy modality, in addition to exercises, is described for this condition?

questions.explanation: Occupational therapy is defined as the use of assessment and intervention to develop, recover, or maintain meaningful activities, or occupations, of individuals, groups, or communities. It assists recovery by encouraging patients to exercise unused or disabled muscles and gain independence. It is performed by occupational therapists and occupational therapy assistants.
questions.question: Occupational therapy is defined in the text as using assessment and intervention primarily to achieve which patient outcome?

options: Ability to be given once for life
Effectiveness when combined with other antitubercular drugs
questions.explanation: Isoniazid is considered the most effective antitubercular agent, particularly when used in combination with other antitubercular drugs. Streptomycin is less effective and reserved mainly for resistant organisms. Ethambutol serves as a relatively safer substitute for PAS.
questions.question: Isoniazid is regarded as the most effective antitubercular drug chiefly because of what property?

questions.explanation: Melphalan, marketed as Alkeran, is described as the most effective alkylating agent available for multiple myeloma, typically dosed at 6 mg once daily orally for two to three weeks. It is given along with prednisone and cyclophosphamide, plus weekly vincristine. Stem cell transplantation is reserved for selective patients.
questions.question: Which chemotherapeutic agent is described as the most effective alkylating agent available for multiple myeloma?

questions.explanation: Peroneal tendon displacement commonly results from a congenitally shallow groove of the lateral malleolus, or total absence of the groove. On contraction, the tendon slips from the posterior malleolus to lie over the lateral aspect of the fibula. Swelling appears over the lateral aspect of the ankle.
questions.question: Displacement of the peroneal tendons is most often attributable to which congenital feature?
options: A shallow or absent fibular groove

questions.question: A patient with internal derangement of the ankle joint (chronic sprain) due to a ruptured lateral ligament undergoes surgical repair. What physiotherapy approach follows this repair?
options: Immediate unsupported running on uneven terrain
Passive-only treatment indefinitely with no active component
Assisted passive exercises progressing to free active exercises
Cryotherapy as the sole postoperative treatment
questions.explanation:
Internal derangement of the ankle from ligament rupture may require surgical repair when conservative measures fail.
Following repair, physiotherapy follows the standard pattern of assisted passive exercises initially.
These progress to free active exercises performed by the patient as healing and confidence improve.

options: Short-wave diathermy or infrared combined with exercises in the lying position
Immediate coccygectomy without a trial of conservative care
Deep tissue friction massage directly over the fracture site
High-intensity resisted core exercises in sitting
questions.explanation:
Fracture of the coccyx typically produces pain that worsens with sitting, walking, and coughing or defecation.
Conservative physiotherapy management includes short-wave diathermy or infrared heat therapy.
Exercises are performed with the patient in lying to avoid aggravating the pain associated with sitting.
questions.question: A patient six weeks after fracture of the coccyx continues to have pain aggravated by sitting and coughing. What physiotherapy modality is indicated according to the text?

options: A role centered on joint manipulation
A limited role, focused on moderate regular activity
questions.question: A physiotherapist is developing an exercise program for a patient with acromegaly. Which characteristic of the physiotherapy role in this condition should guide program design?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy does not play a prominent part in acromegaly management, but advice on moderate regular exercise is vital. The physiotherapist may help plan and teach an activity program tailored to the individual. This distinguishes the supportive nature of the role from disease-modifying treatment.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a patient with Charcot's joint about protecting the affected weight-bearing joint from further trauma. Why is this protection especially important in this condition?
options: Impaired sensation increases risk of unnoticed further joint damage
The joint heals faster than normal joints
There is no risk of further destruction
The joint is not weight-bearing at all
questions.explanation: Charcot's joint develops due to trophic changes from neurological disturbance, often with impaired sensation in the weight-bearing joint. This impaired sensation increases the risk of unnoticed trauma leading to further destruction. Patient education on joint protection is therefore especially important in this condition.

questions.question: Fractures of the pelvic ring at two different levels are clinically significant chiefly because they lead to:
options: Isolated stable injury with minimal displacement
Marked separation and instability of the ring
questions.explanation:
Isolated single fractures of the pelvis are usually stable because of muscular support on both sides.
However, fractures occurring at two different levels of the ring permit significant displacement.
Such double-level fractures cause marked instability with greater risk of internal haemorrhage and visceral injury.

options: Eliminating all physical activity to prevent further injury
Avoiding all forms of protective footwear entirely
Exposing the feet regularly to very cold water
Refraining from smoking, alcohol, and cold exposure
Increasing daily alcohol intake to promote vasodilation
questions.explanation: Preventive treatment for infective gangrene specifically emphasizes refraining from smoking, alcohol consumption, and cold exposure, alongside protecting pressure areas of the foot from further trauma. These lifestyle measures address the underlying vascular risk factors that predispose to tissue ischemia and gangrene. The physiotherapist plays a role in reinforcing this preventive education throughout the rehabilitation process, particularly for patients at risk of contralateral limb involvement.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a patient about preventing recurrence of infective gangrene affecting the toes. Which preventive lifestyle measure is specifically emphasized?

questions.explanation: Excision of osteophytes is a specific surgical procedure for osteoarthritis, targeting the hypertrophic bone formed at articular margins. Other surgical options include excision of loose bodies and arthroscopic débridement. Arthroplasty, by contrast, involves complete joint replacement.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked which surgical procedure removes bone overgrowth at joint margins in osteoarthritis. What is the correct term for this procedure?
Osteoporosis is defined by reduced bone mass leading to fracture risk once bone loss exceeds?
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis increases fragility such that fracture may occur with minor injury once bone loss exceeds 30%. This threshold reflects the degree of structural weakening of bone matrix. Recognizing this helps in assessing fracture risk.

options: Silver fork deformity in the opposite direction
questions.question: A Colles fracture classically produces which deformity of the wrist?
questions.explanation:
In a Colles fracture, the distal radial fragment is displaced backwards and radially with dorsal rotation.
This combination of deformities produces the characteristic 'dinner fork' silhouette of the wrist in profile.
The radial and ulnar styloid processes come to lie at the same level rather than their normal offset.

options: To replace the need for any exercise
To eliminate the need for bedrest
questions.question: A patient recovering from acute low backache with associated infection receives antibiotics alongside physiotherapy. What is the described purpose of adding antibiotics in this specific scenario?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics are added to control infection if present in cases of acute low backache with an infective cause such as discitis. Physiotherapy continues with heat therapy, traction, and a lumbar belt regardless. Exercises are performed regularly to support recovery.

Passive range of motion is where the physiotherapist or equipment moves the joint through its range with no effort at all from the patient. Active range of motion, in contrast, requires the patient to move the joint without external assistance. Relaxed passive movements are performed accurately, rhythmically, and smoothly within the free range.
questions.question: Passive range of motion exercise is defined by which key characteristic regarding patient effort?
The distal femoral metaphysis is the most frequent site for which lesion?
questions.explanation: Metaphyseal defects most often occur in the distal femoral metaphysis. Nonosteogenic fibromas tend to occur in long bones of the lower limbs, particularly tibia and fibula. Recognizing typical sites aids accurate radiographic interpretation.

Recovery of radial nerve palsy after humeral shaft fracture usually begins around eight weeks post injury.
At six weeks, therefore, continued splinting and physiotherapy is appropriate rather than premature exploration.
Exploration of the nerve is reserved for cases showing no evidence of recovery once the eight-week point is reached.
questions.question: A patient is six weeks post fracture shaft of humerus with a radial nerve palsy that has not yet shown clinical recovery. What is the appropriate physiotherapy approach at this stage?
options: Immediately refer for nerve exploration regardless of timeline
Discontinue all splinting since recovery cannot occur
Encourage full unsupported use of the hand for grip strengthening
Provide a wrist drop splint and continue regular physiotherapy while awaiting further recovery time
Apply a below-elbow cast without splint support

questions.question: A physiotherapist manages a patient with tuberculosis of bones and joints. What is the described physiotherapy role at this stage?
options: Complete withdrawal of all physical therapy
Assisted exercises provided by the physiotherapist
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management for tuberculosis of bones and joints is described simply as assisted exercises provided by the physiotherapist. This reflects the priority of systemic antitubercular treatment alongside gentle rehabilitation. General measures such as bedrest and immobilization by splint or plaster support the chemotherapy regimen.

Glomus tumor presents with excruciating, burning or lancinating pain and is exquisitely tender on local examination, located typically in the nailbed of hands or feet. It originates from a glomus body, an arteriovenous shunt structure. Excision of the small bluish-red lesion is curative.
questions.question: Glomus tumor of the nailbed is distinguished clinically from other vascular lesions by which striking feature?

questions.explanation: PNF movement patterns are named according to movements at the shoulder or hip, with the movement beginning distally and ending proximally. This nomenclature underlies patterns such as flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation combined with extension, adduction, and medial rotation. Understanding this sequence helps the physiotherapist cue the patient correctly through each phase.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes that a patient's shoulder movement pattern in PNF ends proximally rather than distally. According to the described nomenclature, where does the movement pattern begin?

questions.explanation: Beading at the costochondral junctions in rickets produces the appearance known as rickety rosary. This is one of several skeletal deformities described in the condition. Others include bowing of the legs and spinal deformities.
questions.question: The characteristic beading of the costochondral junctions in rickets is termed?

questions.explanation: Boyd amputation is the preferred method when a prosthesis will not be used, being performed on the principle of talectomy with forward shifting of the calcaneus and calcaneo-tibial arthrodesis. It affords greater length and a wider weight-bearing surface than Syme amputation, though it requires a bulkier prosthesis when one is fitted. This makes it distinct in indication from Syme amputation, which favours prosthetic use.
questions.question: Which amputation technique is specifically indicated when a prosthesis is not intended to be used, based on the principle of talectomy?

questions.explanation:
This intra-articular fracture requires perfect reduction, achieved here by Kirschner wiring or screw fixation.
Physiotherapy management following fixation combines active exercises with heat pad therapy.
Early, guided movement helps to reduce the risk of late ulnar nerve palsy and cubitus valgus deformity.
options: Immediate passive range of motion under general anaesthesia
Prolonged bed rest without any exercise for twelve weeks
Hydrotherapy commenced on day one post-surgery
Active exercises combined with heat pad therapy
questions.question: A patient with a fracture of the lateral condyle of the humerus has undergone Kirschner wire fixation. What physiotherapy approach is described for this injury?

questions.explanation: Fever is listed among the contraindications to hydrotherapy, alongside cardiovascular disease, acute inflammation, kidney disease, cancer, and pregnancy. The physiotherapist should check with the healthcare provider before proceeding in such circumstances. Hydrotherapy should never be used as a substitute for standard medical care regardless of the presenting condition.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked whether hydrotherapy pool exercise is appropriate for a patient with active fever. What should the physiotherapist advise based on the described contraindications?
options: Fever has no bearing on suitability

questions.question: A physiotherapist begins preoperative strengthening for a patient awaiting below-knee amputation. Which muscle groups should specifically be targeted in the upper limbs to prepare for crutch or wheelchair mobility?
questions.explanation: Preoperative strengthening for lower-limb amputation specifically targets shoulder extensors and adductors, elbow extensors, and hand grip strength to prepare the patient for crutch walking and wheelchair propulsion. Hip extensors, adductors, and abductors are also strengthened for later prosthetic gait. This targeted preparation reduces the functional gap during the early postoperative period before prosthetic fitting.
options: Shoulder extensors and adductors, and elbow extensors
Intrinsic muscles of the unaffected foot
Neck flexors and cervical rotator muscles
Wrist flexors and finger flexors exclusively

questions.explanation:
Reconstruction of an old ruptured fibular collateral ligament follows the Edwards-modified technique.
A long leg cast with the knee slightly flexed is applied for three weeks, alongside active quadriceps and hamstring exercises.
Weight-bearing is then allowed after four weeks as the reconstructed ligament gains adequate strength.
questions.question: A patient with an old rupture of the fibular collateral ligament undergoes reconstruction using the Edwards-modified technique. According to the described protocol, when is weight-bearing allowed?
options: Immediately on the first postoperative day
Weight-bearing is never permitted following this procedure

questions.explanation: The ischiogluteal bursa lies between the gluteus maximus muscle and the ischial tuberosity. It is caused by constant irritation or friction, typically in persons with sedentary occupations. Symptoms include pain, swelling, local tenderness, and a limp.
questions.question: Ischiogluteal bursitis (weaver's bottom) separates the gluteus maximus from which bony structure?
A physiotherapist is treating a patient with axonotmesis of the radial nerve. Which specific exercise precaution is emphasized during muscle strengthening in this condition?
questions.explanation: In nerve injury management, muscle strengthening exercises are performed with care not to damage the healing nervous tissue, watching for pin-prickling sensations, numbness, or increased pain that can impair healing. Exercises are graded appropriately, such as isometric progression and open-to-closed chain work. This cautious, graded approach differs from standard strengthening protocols used for uninjured muscle.
options: Avoiding any form of splinting throughout the recovery period
Immobilizing the limb completely for the entire recovery period
Avoiding overexertion that could impair the healing nerve tissue
Delaying all exercise until full sensory recovery has occurred
Applying maximal resistance from the very first treatment session

questions.question: Which drug class forms the mainstay of pharmacological therapy for rheumatoid arthritis according to the described management?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs, with or without analgesics, form the mainstay of pharmacological therapy for rheumatoid arthritis. Corticosteroids and disease-modifying agents are added depending on disease severity. Careful monitoring is required since underuse or overuse of these agents can be harmful.

Acute low back pain is defined as low back pain present for up to six weeks. It is most often caused by sudden injury to the muscles and ligaments supporting the back. The pain may be described as aching, burning, stabbing, sharp, or dull.
questions.question: Acute low back pain is defined by the described criteria as pain present for up to how long?

questions.explanation:
The Hippocratic method is a traditional technique for reducing shoulder dislocation.
The surgeon places the heel of the foot into the patient's axilla, taking care to avoid injuring the chest wall.
Careful leverage then brings the head of the humerus back into its normal position.
questions.question: The Hippocratic method of reducing shoulder dislocation involves the surgeon placing which body part into the patient's axilla?
options: The heel of the surgeon's foot

questions.explanation:
Barton's fracture is considered a form of Smith's fracture limited to the anterior part of the radius.
It results from a fall on the outstretched hand and produces wrist deformity with painful restricted movement.
Management mirrors Smith's fracture, with surgery reserved for cases where closed reduction fails.
questions.question: A fracture involving only the anterior part of the distal radius, essentially a variant of Smith's fracture, is known as:

questions.explanation: The T score compares the patient's bone mineral density to that of a healthy young adult. The Z score instead compares BMD to a person of the same sex and age. Fracture risk is estimated based on the T score.
questions.question: The T score in bone densitometry compares a patient's BMD to that of?

questions.explanation: The transillumination test allows the cord and nerves to be seen as dark shadows, helping distinguish meningocele from meningomyelocele. This distinction matters because meningomyelocele carries neural tissue within the sac while meningocele contains CSF alone. X-ray of the lumbosacral spine complements this by revealing bony deficiency.
questions.question: The transillumination test in a suspected spina bifida case is primarily used to distinguish which two conditions?

questions.explanation: When adhesions are associated with muscular weakness, the aim of exercise is to strengthen the muscles so they are effective specifically at the limit of joint range. This differs from managing adhesions alone with pendular stretching movements. Both approaches work together to restore functional range and strength in the affected joint.
questions.question: A physiotherapist wants to increase joint range using active free exercise for adhesions but the patient also has associated muscular weakness. What is the stated aim of exercise in this situation?
options: To bypass range of motion work
To strengthen muscles effective at range limit
To rely solely on passive movement

questions.explanation: Physiotherapy after prepatellar bursitis surgery introduces active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening as pain subsides. Heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy or heating pad therapy supports this graded approach. This protects the knee while restoring full function.
questions.question: A patient recovering from prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee) surgery undergoes physiotherapy as postoperative care. Which principle guides when active knee exercises begin?
options: Only after six months of rest
Only once the patient can jog

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating an ambulatory child with corrected club foot after cast removal. What footwear-related intervention is specifically recommended to maintain correction?
options: High-heeled shoes to maintain plantar flexion posture
Permanent avoidance of any footwear until adulthood
Footwear with no arch or ankle support whatsoever
Completely unrestricted footwear of the family's choice
A surgical shoe or an ankle and foot splint walker
questions.explanation: Once a child is already walking and has completed cast correction of club foot, a surgical shoe or an ankle and foot splint walker is required to help maintain the corrected position during ambulation. This follows the physiotherapist's earlier work using passive movements and active exercises in dorsiflexion and eversion after fixation is removed. Ongoing footwear support is therefore an essential component of relapse prevention in this condition.

questions.question: Which investigation is used to rule out malignancy in a suspected aneurysmal bone cyst?
questions.explanation: Needle aspiration biopsy is used to exclude malignancy when an aneurysmal bone cyst is suspected. X-ray shows a bulging mass with heavy trabeculations or loculation. This combination supports accurate diagnosis before treatment.

questions.question: Ruptured quadriceps femoris tendon is described as occurring most typically in which population?
questions.explanation: Rupture of the quadriceps tendon mostly occurs just above the patella, typically in elderly individuals through a zone of degeneration. Supplementing the sutures with fascial strips is described as beneficial during repair. Physiotherapy after fixation includes non-weight bearing exercises progressing to weight bearing once pain subsides.

questions.question: Which endocrine cause of osteoporosis relates specifically to loss of estrogen?
questions.explanation: Postmenopausal osteoporosis results from lack of estrogen following menopause. Senile osteoporosis, by contrast, is linked to lack of androgens. Both are secondary endocrinal causes of osteoporosis.

questions.question: In neuropraxia, what is the underlying pathological state of the nerve fibres and sheath?
questions.explanation: Neurapraxia is a concussion-type injury in which there is only a momentary loss of conduction without any organic damage, so both the nerve fibres and the nerve sheath remain intact. Recovery is almost complete because no structural regeneration is required. This contrasts sharply with axonotmesis and neurotmesis, which involve actual anatomical disruption.
options: Both nerve fibres and sheath are completely divided
The sheath is intact but all axons are severed
The fibres are intact but the sheath is disrupted
Both nerve fibres and sheath remain structurally intact

questions.question: In acute osteomyelitis, physiotherapy exercises for joint movement are introduced under which specific condition?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management of acute osteomyelitis introduces active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening as pain subsides. Heat therapy such as shortwave diathermy or heating pad therapy accompanies this approach. This graded introduction avoids aggravating the acutely infected bone.
options: Only after complete bone healing on X-ray
Only once the patient is discharged home

questions.question: A fracture heals in an abnormal anatomical position due to defective reduction and fixation. What is this termed?
questions.explanation:
Malunion describes a fracture that has united but in an abnormal anatomical position.
It results from inadequate initial reduction or loss of fixation during treatment.
Clinically it produces deformity, possible shortening, and predisposes to secondary osteoarthritis.

options: Immediate arthroscopic meniscectomy without any trial of rest
Unrestricted running training to maintain fitness
Complete avoidance of any bandage or support
Rest, analgesics, elastic crepe bandage or knee cap, and short-wave diathermy or infrared
questions.question: A footballer presents with a history of knee locking followed by sudden unlocking and effusion, with a positive McMurray's test. Conservative physiotherapy management is planned. Which combination is described?
questions.explanation:
Injury to the medial meniscus, common in footballers, presents with locking, unlocking, and effusion.
Conservative management includes rest, analgesics, and support with an elastic crepe bandage or knee cap.
Short-wave diathermy or infrared and local massage are also used alongside a period of bed rest.

options: Free active exercises and wax bath
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to assist a patient recovering from myositis ossificans excision. Which modality combination matches the described physiotherapy protocol?
questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management for myositis ossificans includes free active exercises, heat therapy with SWD or IRR, and wax bath therapy. Surgical excision is reserved only for mature lesions, usually six to twelve months post-trauma, since excising a premature lesion risks extensive recurrence. Conservative treatment beforehand includes NSAIDs and local hydrocortisone injection.

questions.question: A physiotherapist observes a patient in half-lying position experiencing discomfort during passive spinal movement caused by a cushion behind the back. What action reflects correct passive movement principle?
options: Force the position for full range
Adjust to a more comfortable position
questions.explanation: Passive movement produced during normal activity, such as a cushion inducing spinal extension or flexion, should prompt the person to adjust to a more comfortable position if discomforted. This exemplifies the harmless, everyday nature of passive movement described in the text. It contrasts with a violent external force inducing passive movement that instead results in injury, such as whiplash.

questions.question: Which vasospastic disorder is described as affecting predominantly women aged 15 to 40 with symmetrical, bilateral digital colour changes?
questions.explanation: Raynaud's disease predominantly affects women aged 15 to 40, producing intermittent, symmetrical, bilateral attacks of pallor or cyanosis in the fingers precipitated by cold or emotional stress, with arterial pulsations remaining unaffected. This helps differentiate it from Buerger's disease, which typically affects men aged 20 to 40 with impaired or absent pulses. Recognizing the demographic and pulse findings distinguishes the two vasospastic conditions.

questions.question: The patella is the commonest fracture site around the knee. Which pattern most often preserves the power and mobility of the knee because the prepatellar fibres remain intact?
questions.explanation:
Most patellar fractures are undisplaced, with the prepatellar fibrous expansion remaining intact.
Because this fibrous layer bridges the fracture, the extensor mechanism continues to function.
Knee power and mobility are therefore largely preserved compared with displaced or comminuted patterns.

questions.question: Recurrent dislocation of the patella typically occurs towards which direction?
questions.explanation:
Recurrent dislocation of the patella characteristically displaces the patella laterally.
Predisposing factors include a relaxed medial capsule, genu valgum, or flattened articular surfaces.
A patellar tendon insertion positioned too far laterally may also contribute to this recurrent instability.

Calcification of the supraspinatus tendon is confirmed radiographically by a calcified deposit above the head of the humerus. Clinically, the patient presents with shoulder pain and stiffness. Intra-articular corticosteroid injection with heat therapy forms part of conservative management.
questions.question: Calcification of the supraspinatus tendon is best confirmed by which investigation finding?

options: Young men aged twenty to forty
questions.question: Ankylosing spondylitis predominantly affects which demographic group?
questions.explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is a crippling disease that mostly affects young men between twenty and forty years of age. It chronically involves the spine, sacroiliac joints, peripheral joints, and extra-articular structures. Chest expansion becomes restricted as the disease progresses.

questions.question: Radiologically, bone ends that are flared out and sclerotic, giving an 'elephant's foot' appearance, indicate which type of non-union?
questions.explanation:
Hypertrophic non-union shows sclerotic, flared bone ends because the body is still attempting to bridge the gap.
The fracture line remains clearly visible without any bridging callus.
This contrasts with atrophic non-union, where the bone ends are narrow, rounded, and avascular.

options: Excision of the lateral end of the clavicle
questions.question: Old unreduced dislocation of the acromioclavicular joint, causing mainly cosmetic disability, is typically managed by:
questions.explanation:
An old unreduced acromioclavicular dislocation usually causes little functional disability beyond cosmetic prominence.
The treatment of choice is excision of the lateral end of the clavicle, lateral to the ligaments.
Where ligaments are completely torn, repair may be combined with the excision procedure.

Physiotherapy management for neurofibroma includes free active exercises, heat therapy using short-wave diathermy or infrared radiation, and wax bath therapy. Conservative medical treatment also includes analgesics, NSAIDs, and SWD or IR therapy for pain and numbness from nerve compression. Surgical excision is reserved for relief of persistent pain or numbness.
questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a neurofibroma patient with nerve compression numbness should apply which heat modality alongside exercise?
Which physiotherapy modality is specifically noted as beneficial for neuropathic pain relief and quality of life via aromatherapy-based technique?
questions.explanation: Massage, including aromatherapy-based approaches, is specifically cited as beneficial in managing neuropathic pain and improving quality of life in peripheral nerve injury patients. TENS and low-level laser therapy are also used as adjuvant modalities for pain reduction. These are combined with relaxation techniques and, where indicated, acupuncture.

questions.question: Sciatic nerve injury produces complete paralysis below the knee together with which specific deformity?
options: Foot drop from loss of hamstring and distal leg muscle function
Genu recurvatum from loss of quadriceps muscle power
Claw toes from isolated loss of intrinsic foot muscles only
Talipes calcaneovalgus from isolated posterior tibial paralysis
Hallux rigidus from degeneration of the first metatarsal joint
questions.explanation: Sciatic nerve injury paralyzes all the hamstrings and produces complete paralysis below the knee, resulting in foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion. Sensory loss extends below the knee with loss of joint sense at the ankle, foot, and toes. This differs from isolated lateral or medial popliteal nerve injury, which affects only the distal branches after the sciatic nerve's bifurcation.

options: Etiological factors such as arteriosclerosis are not the determining factor
Presence of uncontrolled infection is not the determining factor
Failure of medical and surgical salvage is not the determining factor
Presence of unrelieved ischemic pain is not the determining factor
Presence of established gangrene is not the determining factor
questions.explanation: In PVD amputation, the underlying etiological factors, whether arteriosclerosis, diabetes, or thromboangiitis obliterans, are deliberately set aside once salvage has failed; the decision instead rests on pain, infection, and gangrene. Amputation is performed as a salvage measure to save life and preserve remaining function. This distinguishes indication-based decision making from etiological classification.
questions.question: In amputations for peripheral vascular disease, which factor is specifically excluded from consideration as an indication for amputation?

questions.explanation: Snapping hip rarely requires surgery because it is usually painless and habitual in nature, often related to a mild obsessive-neurotic element. Patients typically prefer no treatment once the benign cause is explained. Surgery is reserved only for very severe, persistent snapping or clicking.
questions.question: A patient with snapping hip is explained that treatment is rarely needed. What is the primary reason given for avoiding surgery in most cases?
options: The condition always leads to joint destruction
Surgery is universally contraindicated in all patients
No conservative treatment options exist at all
The condition is usually painless and habitual
The hip joint cannot tolerate any anesthesia

questions.question: Anterior tibial compartment syndrome (march gangrene) primarily follows which activity?
questions.explanation: March gangrene arises in army personnel, police, or athletes after long marches or races, producing ischemic myositis of the anterior compartment muscles. Strenuous exercise causes edema and micro-hemorrhage that raises compartment pressure. The dorsalis pedis pulse becomes diminished or absent as ischemia develops.

questions.question: A patient with osteoporosis has normal serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase. How should the physiotherapist interpret this in the context of diagnosis?
options: It suggests rickets is more likely
It is consistent with osteoporosis, which typically has normal biochemistry
questions.explanation: Normal serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase is typical of osteoporosis, distinguishing it biochemically from conditions like hyperparathyroidism or rickets. Diagnosis instead relies on radiographic and densitometry findings. This reassures that biochemical normalcy does not exclude an osteoporosis diagnosis.

The Milwaukee brace is specifically used to control and correct rapidly increasing scoliosis in growing children as part of conservative management, alongside turnbuckle and localizer casts. Surgical arthrodesis of the spine is reserved for growing children with increasing curves, adolescents with severe trunk asymmetry, or older patients with uncontrollable pain. Preoperative Risser turnbuckle casting may also be used before definitive spinal fusion surgery.
questions.question: Which brace is specifically used to control and correct rapidly increasing scoliosis in growing children?

questions.explanation: Osteopathy, or osteopathic manipulative therapy, is a type of alternative medicine emphasizing manual readjustments, myofascial release, and physical manipulation of muscle tissue and bones more broadly. It differs from chiropractic, which mainly focuses on adjustments to the vertebrae of the spine. Practitioners of osteopathy are referred to as osteopaths.
questions.question: Which manipulative therapy is described as emphasizing manual readjustments, myofascial release, and physical manipulation more broadly than the spine alone?

A physiotherapist is asked why a young child undergoing thigh amputation was scheduled for a supracondylar (tendoplastic) technique instead of an osteoplastic approach. What is the most likely surgical reasoning?
options: It removes any risk of future stump revision surgery
It guarantees a shorter total hospital admission always
It avoids the need for any postoperative physiotherapy
It preserves the distal femoral epiphysis for continued growth
It is technically simpler and requires no anaesthesia
questions.explanation: The tendoplastic (supracondylar) method is specifically preferred in children because it preserves the distal femoral epiphysis, allowing the femur to continue growing, unlike the osteoplastic method which arthrodeses the patella to the femur. This growth-preserving rationale is a key surgical consideration unique to pediatric amputation. Physiotherapists should anticipate periodic prosthetic adjustment as the child's limb continues to grow.

Type II Pott's fracture, involving two malleoli, is managed with a below-knee plaster cast for four to six weeks.
Once the cast is removed, physiotherapy provides an ankle brace to support walking.
Short-wave diathermy or infrared therapy is combined with this support to aid pain relief and mobility.
options: Unsupported barefoot walking on uneven ground
Ankle brace in walking combined with short-wave diathermy or infrared
Continued strict bed rest for a further eight weeks
questions.question: A patient with a Pott's fracture Type II (bimalleolar) has completed six weeks in a below-knee plaster cast. What physiotherapy support is indicated for walking at this stage?

questions.explanation:
After meniscectomy, weight-bearing status depends partly on the presence of joint effusion.
When effusion is present, weight-bearing is withheld for one to two weeks postoperatively.
During this period, assisted quadriceps exercises are progressed gradually to free active exercises.
questions.question: Following meniscectomy for a torn medial meniscus, physiotherapy in the presence of effusion typically restricts weight-bearing for how long postoperatively?
options: Immediately full weight-bearing from day one

questions.question: A physiotherapist recognizes a patient has an obsessive psychological fixation on receiving repeated spinal manipulation without clear benefit. This is specifically classified as which type of contraindication?
questions.explanation: Obsessive neurosis for manipulative therapy is specifically classified as a psychological contraindication to continuing manual manipulation. This differs from miscellaneous contraindications such as nerve root compression, which are structural rather than psychological in origin. Recognizing this contraindication protects the patient from unnecessary or potentially harmful repeated manipulation.

questions.question: Rheumatoid arthritis is classified diagnostically by requiring how many of the seven listed criteria?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis, per the described criteria, requires at least four of the seven listed features. These include morning stiffness, symmetric joint swelling, and a positive rheumatoid factor. Failure to meet all criteria early in the disease does not exclude the diagnosis.

questions.question: A physiotherapist wants to stretch shoulder adhesions using pendular movement technique. What starting position should the patient adopt for the right shoulder?
questions.explanation: To restore flexion and extension of the right shoulder using pendular movement, the patient stands with the left leg forward in a lunge position while swinging the right arm forward and back. A similar movement pattern is used for abduction and adduction. This rhythmical swinging emphasizes stretching adhesions at the range limit.

Emergency closed amputation provides loose skin closure with adequate drainage for traumatized tissue and can be easily converted to an open amputation if infection develops. It is not intended as a final, prosthesis-ready amputation. This staged approach protects tissue viability while infection risk is still being assessed.
questions.question: What is the specific aim of the emergency (temporarily closed) amputation technique?
options: To permanently eliminate any risk of future infection
To provide loose skin closure and adequate drainage after trauma
To immediately restore full functional use of the limb
To avoid any further surgical intervention altogether
To achieve a definitive stump ready for prosthetic fitting

questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient using axillary crutches has developed nerve compression symptoms in the axilla. What is the most likely underlying cause of this presentation?
options: Excessive pressure through the axillary pad
questions.explanation: Axillary crutches transfer weight from the legs through pads positioned in the axilla to the upper body, so excessive or prolonged pressure at this point risks compressing the underlying neurovascular structures. Correct fitting and technique are essential to avoid this complication. Elbow or forearm crutches avoid direct axillary pressure by design.

questions.question: Vitamin D resistant rickets is associated with which underlying disturbance?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D resistant rickets occurs in association with renal losses of calcium or phosphorus. This differs from simple dietary or absorptive vitamin D deficiency. Recognizing this distinction affects the choice of vitamin D dosage in treatment.

questions.question: A patient one week after wrist amputation reports being pleased that they can still turn their palm up and down. What accounts for this preserved movement?
options: The elbow joint has compensated for lost forearm rotation
Amputation at this level automatically restores lost movement
The prosthesis itself actively generates all forearm rotation
The intact radioulnar joint is preserved at this amputation level
Nerve regeneration has already restored full motor control
questions.explanation: Wrist amputation and disarticulation preserve the intact radioulnar joint, allowing the arm to retain natural pronation and supination, which is a specific advantage over more proximal forearm-level amputation. This preserved movement also avoids the need for an above-elbow prosthetic cuff that would otherwise restrict elbow flexion. The physiotherapist can reassure the patient that this functional retention is an expected anatomical benefit of this amputation level, not a temporary phenomenon.

options: They never require any period of immobilization
They occur only in young, active adults
They carry a higher risk of avascular necrosis
Non-union is extremely rare because the fracture occurs in well-vascularised cancellous bone
questions.explanation:
Trochanteric fractures occur through cancellous bone with a comparatively rich blood supply.
Because the vessels supplying this region remain intact, avascular necrosis is essentially avoided.
As a result, non-union is extremely rare compared with intracapsular femoral neck fractures.
questions.question: Extracapsular (trochanteric) fractures of the femur, compared with intracapsular fractures, have which characteristic advantage regarding union?

questions.explanation:
Fractures of the phalanges commonly follow either a direct blow or a crush injury such as a door or sash.
They are more difficult to manage than metacarpal fractures because the flexor tendon sheath may be involved.
Splintage or Kirschner wire fixation is chosen depending on displacement and involvement of the sheath.
questions.question: A crush injury sustained by pressing a finger in a door or window sash most typically produces which type of fracture?

questions.explanation: Slit-lamp examination in hyperparathyroidism may reveal band keratoplasty, a calcium deposit in the cornea. This reflects the hypercalcemic state of the disease. Bitemporal hemianopsia is instead associated with pituitary tumors.
questions.question: Which eye finding may be detected on slit-lamp examination in hyperparathyroidism?

questions.explanation: Rupture of the long head of biceps tendon produces a visible bulge in the lower upper arm that becomes prominent when the elbow is flexed against resistance. Pain and local tenderness accompany the deformity. Shoulder and elbow movements become restricted.
questions.question: A bulge appearing in the lower upper arm on resisted elbow flexion is characteristic of rupture of which structure?

questions.explanation: A high protein diet adequate in calcium, such as milk and milk products, supports bone matrix and mineral content in osteoporosis management. This nutritional measure works alongside exercise, smoking cessation and reduced alcohol intake. Together these general measures aim to reduce further bone loss.
questions.question: Why is a high protein, calcium-adequate diet recommended as part of osteoporosis management alongside physiotherapy?
options: It supports bone matrix and mineral content
It replaces the need for exercise

questions.question: The supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children is notorious mainly because of its association with which type of complication?
questions.explanation:
Displaced supracondylar fractures place the brachial artery and adjacent nerves at direct risk of injury.
This neurovascular vulnerability is why the fracture demands careful, prompt reduction and close observation.
Undetected vascular compromise can progress to Volkmann's ischemic contracture of the forearm.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

questions.question: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis typically presents in which patient group, sometimes associated with hormonal imbalance?
questions.explanation:
Slipped upper femoral epiphysis is a condition of adolescence, resembling a fracture through the femoral neck.
Affected patients are often described as fatty and sexually immature, sometimes linked to hormonal imbalance such as Frohlich syndrome.
The leg becomes externally rotated with pain referred to the groin or knee and a limp.
options: Adolescents, often fatty and sexually immature

questions.explanation: After suturing a ruptured patellar tendon, a long leg cast is applied with the knee flexed and the foot held in an equinus position. Wire sutures protrude through the cast for monitoring. The cast and wires are removed after four weeks, followed by a walking cast.
questions.question: Following surgical repair of a ruptured patellar tendon, the postoperative cast is applied with the foot in which position?

questions.explanation: Myelocele is the spina bifida cystica type in which CSF discharges directly from the spinal central canal. Meningocele contains CSF only without neural tissue, while meningomyelocele has the cord or cauda equina adherent to the sac. Syringomyelocele instead shows a dilated central canal.
questions.question: Which spina bifida type is characterized by CSF discharge from the spinal central canal?

questions.explanation: When a metaphyseal defect fails to resolve along its usual course, it forms a nonosteogenic fibroma. Metaphyseal defects are usually small, innocuous and asymptomatic in children. Unlike metaphyseal defects, nonosteogenic fibromas rarely occur as multiple lesions.
questions.question: A metaphyseal defect that fails to follow its usual evolutionary course develops into a?
A patient presents with a painful, swollen long bone lesion, and needle aspiration biopsy is planned before physiotherapy referral. What is the primary purpose of this biopsy?
options: To measure serum alkaline phosphatase directly
To rule out malignancy before proceeding with management
To replace the need for X-ray
To confirm the diagnosis of osteoporosis
questions.explanation: Needle aspiration biopsy is used to rule out malignancy when an aneurysmal bone cyst is suspected. Definitive management, including physiotherapy referral, follows once malignancy has been excluded. This diagnostic step is essential before planning rehabilitation.

In middle-aged and older persons, rupture of the long head of biceps tendon usually occurs spontaneously due to a degenerative aging process. Trivial trauma may precipitate the actual tear. Most such patients do not require surgical repair.
questions.question: Rupture of the long head of biceps tendon in an elderly patient most typically results from what process?

questions.explanation: In long bones, Paget's disease characteristically begins at one end and advances toward the other. This progressive pattern is a useful radiographic clue. It contrasts with diffuse or midshaft onset seen in other bone disorders.
questions.question: In advancing long bone involvement, Paget's disease characteristically begins at which point?

questions.explanation: Trochanteric bursitis conservative management includes rest and immobilization by traction, along with diathermy and analgesics. Physiotherapy with heat therapy and active exercises follows once symptoms improve. This approach addresses the underlying tendinitis of the glutei tendons.
questions.question: In trochanteric bursitis, immobilization during conservative treatment is achieved specifically by which method?
The overactivity of the anterior pituitary lobe in gigantism and acromegaly is most commonly caused by?
questions.explanation: A benign adenoma of the anterior pituitary lobe is the usual cause of the excess growth hormone. Carcinomas are a much rarer cause. The hyperactivity specifically involves the eosinophilic portion of the gland.

Progression of weight-bearing after femoral shaft fracture with internal fixation is not based on a fixed timetable alone.
Instead, the surgeon and physiotherapist jointly assess progressive radiological union together with muscle power.
Only once adequate range of movement and strength are demonstrated is full weight-bearing then permitted.
questions.question: A patient with fracture of the femoral shaft treated with a cast brace is progressing through rehabilitation. What determines the transition from partial to full weight-bearing?
options: A fixed calendar date regardless of clinical findings
Achieving full weight-bearing on the first postoperative day
X-ray evidence of union is disregarded in this decision
Adequate union progress along with sufficient muscle power and range of movement, as assessed jointly by surgeon and physiotherapist

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to help differentiate arteriosclerosis obliterans from Buerger's disease in an older patient with lower limb claudication. Which finding would favour arteriosclerosis obliterans as the diagnosis?

questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a two-week-old infant with congenital club foot before starting treatment. What is the most important timing consideration guiding when to begin manipulation?

Timing has no effect on the eventual outcome achieved
Beginning only after the child reaches five years of age
Delaying all treatment until the child begins walking
Waiting until six months for adequate bone ossification
questions.explanation: Conservative correction of club foot should begin within the first two weeks after birth, since increasing age makes the deformity progressively more difficult to correct through manipulation alone.
