(iii) Identify the anatomical structure prolapsed in the wound and explain the clinical and therapeutic significance of its presence in the wound.
(iv) Outline the surgical management of this eye, addressing each component of the injury.
(v) State what ophthalmological emergency requires emergent lateral canthotomy and describe the clinical signs that indicate its presence.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Classification: This is a penetrating injury (one entry wound, no exit wound). Note: If both an entry and exit wound are present, it is classified as a perforating injury. An intraocular foreign body (IOFB) must always be excluded in any penetrating injury. ("N/B There may or may not be a retained intra-ocular foreign body.")

(ii)
Factors determining extent of penetrating ocular injuries:
• The size of the object.
• Its speed at the time of impact.
• Its composition.
• There is usually introduction of infection with any penetrating injury.

(iii)
Anatomical structure prolapsed: The iris (uveal tissue) is incarcerated in the corneal wound (corneal laceration with iris/uveal prolapse).
Clinical significance: This indicates full-thickness corneal injury with breakdown of the anterior chamber, posing risk of infection (endophthalmitis), ongoing iritis, and vision loss.
Therapeutic significance of iris incarceration: Management depends on the duration and extent of incarceration. The incarcerated iris may need to be reposited or excised depending on viability and duration.

(iv)
Surgical management:
• Treatment depends on the severity of the wound and associated complications (iris incarceration, flat anterior chamber, damage to intraocular contents).
• Small shelving corneal lacerations with formed AC may not require suturing (may heal spontaneously or with soft bandage contact lens).
• Medium-sized corneal lacerations usually require suturing, especially if the AC is shallow.
• Corneal lacerations with iris involvement: management depends on duration and extent of incarceration.
• Corneal laceration with lenticular (lens) damage: suture the laceration and remove the lens.
• Pad the eye and refer for surgery as soon as possible.
• Do NOT remove any penetrating object; pad and refer for surgery ASAP.

(v)
Emergency requiring lateral canthotomy:
Retrobulbar haemorrhage — indicated by: acute pain, proptosis, resistance to retropulsion, and a relative afferent pupillary defect. These signs suggest compression of the optic nerve by the haematoma. Emergent lateral canthotomy is required to decompress the orbit; refer for high-dose IV steroids.

(i)
Classification of ocular foreign bodies by anatomical location:
• Extraocular (surface) foreign bodies — on the conjunctival surface or palpebral conjunctiva.
• Corneal foreign bodies — impacted in the corneal epithelium or stroma.
• Intraocular foreign bodies (IOFB) — lodge in any structure from the anterior chamber to the retina and choroid.
• Intra-orbital foreign bodies — lodged in the orbital tissues outside the globe.

(ii)
Trajectory of conjunctival surface foreign body:
• Small foreign bodies (particles of steel, sand) impact on the conjunctival surface.
• They may be washed along the tear film into the lacrimal drainage system.
• They may adhere to the superior palpebral conjunctiva.
• They may ascend and lodge in the superior conjunctival fornix, where they produce chronic conjunctivitis (by repeated abrasion of the conjunctival and corneal surface with each blink).
• Alternatively, they may impact in the bulbar conjunctiva, or penetrate the corneal epithelium or stroma to a depth proportional to their velocity.

(iii)
Management of corneal foreign body:
• Corneal foreign bodies are extremely common and cause considerable irritation.
• If a FB is allowed to remain, there is a risk of secondary infection; organic and stone FBs carry a higher risk of infection.
• Apply topical anaesthetic to the eye.
• Careful slit-lamp examination (SLE) is essential to locate the FB precisely.
• Remove the FB under slit-lamp visualisation using a sterile 26-gauge needle.
• Magnetic removal may be useful for a deeply embedded metallic FB.
• Aftercare: antibiotic ointment is instilled together with a cycloplegic (to promote comfort and prevent ciliary spasm/pain).
• Refer if FB cannot be removed.

(iv)
Toxic effects of specific metals:
• Iron (ferrous IOFB): causes siderosis — dissociation of iron ions in the eye produces toxic effects on the retina, lens, iris, and other intraocular structures.
• Copper (cuprous IOFB): causes chalcosis — dissociation of copper ions produces toxic effects, especially on the lens (sunflower cataract) and retinal structures.

(v)
Inert intraocular materials (no toxic dissociation):
• Glass
• Plastics
• Gold
• Silver
(These materials are generally inert and may be left in the eye if removal risks further damage.)
General risks of a retained IOFB:
• Mechanical trauma to the eye.
• Introduction and perpetuation of infection.
• Toxic effects on intraocular structures (as above for iron and copper).
• The FB may lodge anywhere from the anterior chamber to the retina and choroid.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old metalworker presents with right eye pain, redness, photophobia, and the feeling of something in the eye after grinding metal without goggles. On slit-lamp examination, a metallic foreign body is seen embedded in the right corneal stroma with surrounding rust ring and corneal infiltrate. An X-ray is also ordered to exclude an intraocular foreign body.

(i) Classify the ocular foreign bodies into their anatomical locations.
(ii) Describe the trajectory of a foreign body that may ascend from the conjunctival surface and lodge in the superior conjunctival fornix, and what condition it may produce.
(iii) Describe the management of a corneal foreign body, naming the instrument used, the aftercare, and when magnetic removal is appropriate.
(iv) Describe the specific toxic effects of iron and copper intraocular foreign bodies, naming the conditions they cause.
(v) Name all the materials that are inert when retained intraocularly, and describe the general risks of an intraocular foreign body remaining in the eye.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Primary congenital glaucoma (infantile glaucoma / buphthalmos).

(ii)
Predisposing and aetiological factors:
• Incidence approximately 1 in 10,000 live births.
• Usually sporadic; autosomal inheritance has also been reported; association between autosomal recessive inheritance and mutations in the CYP1B1 gene (GLC3A).
• Bilateral in 64%–88% of cases; 60%–70% are males; diagnosed within the first year of life in 86% of cases.
• Ocular associations: sclerocornea, microcornea, megalocornea, aniridia, coloboma, lenticonus, congenital aphakia, Axenfeld's anomaly, Rieger syndrome, Peters syndrome.
• Systemic associations: chromosomal defects (Trisomy 13), inborn errors of metabolism (homocystinuria, Hurler syndrome), infections (rubella), phakomatoses (neurofibromatosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, Nevus of Ota), pluriformative syndromes (Down's syndrome, Marfan syndrome).

(iii)
Pathophysiology:
• It is believed that in primary congenital glaucoma there is an abnormal membrane overlying the trabecular meshwork called Barkan's membrane.
• This membrane obstructs aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork, causing IOP to rise.
• The elevated IOP in infancy causes the immature sclera to stretch, enlarging the globe (buphthalmos), stretching and thinning the cornea, and causing breaks in Descemet's membrane (Haab's striae).

(iv)
Management:
• Angle surgery is the preferred initial surgical intervention.
• Goniotomy: performed by making an incision across the trabecular meshwork (targeting Barkan's membrane) under direct gonioscopic visualisation; the goniotomy knife is placed through peripheral clear cornea 1 mm from the limbus; a circumferential incision is made for about 4–5 clock hours; corneal clarity must be sufficient for this procedure.
• Trabeculotomy ab externo: performed by cannulating Schlemm's canal from the external approach and tearing the trabecular meshwork into the anterior chamber; used when corneas are too cloudy for goniotomy.
• Trabeculectomy with antimetabolites.
• Implants (e.g., Molteno, Ahmed valves) — especially in refractory paediatric glaucoma.
• Assessment under anaesthesia: history of lacrimation, photophobia, blepharospasm; assess visual acuity; examine cornea; measure IOP with hand-held Perkins applanation tonometer; measure corneal diameter with calipers; fundus examination.
questions.question:
An 8-month-old male infant is brought by his mother with a 6-week history of excessive tearing, photophobia, and constant eye-blinking. On examination, both eyes appear enlarged (buphthalmos), with corneal diameters measured at 13 mm, cloudy corneas, curvilinear scars (Haab's striae) on the cornea, and elevated IOP measured with a hand-held Perkins applanation tonometer.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis?
(ii) State all the predisposing and aetiological factors, including the genetic and systemic associations.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology of why IOP is elevated in this condition.
(iv) Outline the full management, including the preferred surgical intervention and alternative surgical options.

questions.answerText:
A.
Components of the lacrimal excretory system in order:
• Superior and inferior puncta (starting points).
• Ampulla: 2 mm, perpendicular to the lid margin.
• Canaliculi: 8–12 mm, parallel to the lid margin.
• Common canaliculus: present in approximately 90% of individuals.
• Valve of Rosenmuller: located at the lateral wall of the tear sac.
• Lacrimal sac: 10 mm in length.
• Nasolacrimal duct (NLD): 12 mm, opens to the inferior nasal meatus.
• Valve of Hasner: at the distal end of the NLD.

B.
Physiology of drainage is by blinking, gravity and capillarity. Approximately 70% of drainage occurs through the inferior canaliculus; 10–20% is through evaporation. The valve of Hasner prevents nasal secretions from refluxing into the lacrimal sac.

C.
Congenital NLD obstruction: The NLD is the last structure to canalise, usually completing at birth; obstruction at its distal end is present in approximately 50% of infants at birth. Epiphora is not apparent until about 6 weeks of life (when lacrimation begins). 90% resolve spontaneously in the first year of life. Management begins with conservative measures — antibiotics and massage — progressing to irrigation and probing, then silicone intubation or dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) in older children.
Acquired epiphora: May occur at any age due to stricture or trauma. Investigated with dye disappearance test, Jones tests 1 and 2, diagnostic probing, nasal endoscopy, dacryocystography, or radionuclide scintigraphy. Treatment is mainly surgical — dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR); canalicular obstruction (from trauma, toxic drugs such as 5-FU, viral infection, or autoimmune disease) requires conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy.
questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the lacrimal excretory system, stating each component in order from the punctum to the nasal meatus.

B. Explain the physiology of tear drainage and state the valve that normally prevents nasal secretions from refluxing into the lacrimal sac.

C. Distinguish between congenital and acquired obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct — stating their typical age of presentation, underlying mechanism, and management approach for each.

Describe the anatomy and physiology of the eye in relation to ophthalmic drug formulation, including the formulation requirements for eye drops and the role of preservatives.

A(i) Describe the anatomical structures of the eye relevant to drug delivery and the categories of ophthalmic preparations.
A(ii) Describe the components of an eye drop formulation and explain the most important requirement.
B(i) Explain the role of antimicrobial preservatives in eye drops and describe benzalkonium chloride including its concentration, spectrum, and interactions.
B(ii) State the tonicity requirements for eye drops and the clinical relevance of viscosity enhancers.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Anatomical structures relevant to drug delivery: corneal epithelium; scleral epithelium; conjunctival epithelium; ciliary body and trabecular network for fluid drainage; glands (lacrimal, Meibomian, of Zeis, of Moll, of Krause, Wolfring's, Manz); conjunctival sac. Categories of ophthalmic preparations: eye drops (solutions and suspensions); eye ointments, creams and gels; contact lens solutions; parenteral products (intracorneal, intravitreous, retrobulbar injection); solid dosage forms placed in the conjunctival sac designed to release active ingredient over a prolonged period.

A(ii)
Components of eye drop formulation: active ingredient(s); vehicle (usually aqueous, occasionally oil); antimicrobial preservative; adjuvants to adjust tonicity, viscosity or pH; suitable container. The single most important requirement of eye drops is that they are sterile. Contamination with Pseudomonas aeruginosa is particularly damaging and can cause loss of the eye.

B(i)
Benzalkonium chloride (BZK) is the preservative of choice; present in over 70% of commercially produced eye drops. Used at 0.01% w/v (well tolerated up to 0.02% w/v); stable to autoclaving; rapid bactericidal action against wide range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms. Activity reduced by multivalent cations (Mg2+, Ca2+); activity reduced if heated with methylcellulose; incompatible with fluorescein and nitrates; sorbed from solutions by rubber. Enhancement: disodium edetate enhances activity against Gram-negative organisms by chelating divalent cations. Contraindicated with local anaesthetics (combination causes drying and irritation of cornea).

B(ii)
Eye drops should be made isotonic with lachrymal fluid (approximately equivalent to 0.9% w/v sodium chloride). The eye will tolerate tonicities equivalent to 0.7–1.5% w/v sodium chloride. Viscosity enhancers (methylcellulose derivatives, polyvinyl alcohol) increase residence time of the drop; most preparations adjusted to 15–25 mPas. Under normal conditions a large proportion of a 50 µl drop drains from the conjunctival sac (capacity 25 µl) within 30 seconds.

questions.question:
A patient presents with sudden severe eye pain, headache, nausea and vomiting. Examination shows a red eye with a hazy cornea, a mid-dilated non-reactive pupil, and markedly elevated intraocular pressure.

(i) State the diagnosis and the pupillary finding that is pathognomonic for it.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the condition and the bedside sign used to identify eyes at highest risk of developing it.
(iii) Outline the resuscitative/emergency principle of management, including drug classes that may be used to lower pressure acutely.
(iv) State the definitive treatment, how it works, and the recommendation for the fellow eye.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Acute angle-closure glaucoma. The mid-dilated, non-reactive pupil is pathognomonic, distinguishing it from anterior uveitis, where the pupil is typically miotic and irregular.

(ii)
The definitive treatment (see iv) works by relieving pupillary block, indicating that pupillary block is the underlying mechanism. Eyes at highest risk are identified using the Eclipse Sign: a pen torch is shone from the temporal side of the cornea, and a shadow cast on the nasal iris indicates a shallow anterior chamber; a shallow anterior chamber (narrow angle) carries the highest risk of this condition.

(iii)
Urgent reduction of intraocular pressure is required to prevent permanent vision loss. Drug classes that reduce intraocular pressure and can be used include beta-adrenergic receptor blockers (reduce aqueous humor production by the ciliary body) and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (inhibit carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body to reduce aqueous production). Miotics (parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine) also constrict the pupil and contract the ciliary muscle to increase aqueous drainage.

(iv)
The definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy. It creates a small hole in the peripheral iris, allowing aqueous to flow directly from the posterior to the anterior chamber, bypassing the pupillary block that causes angle closure. Prophylactic iridotomy in the fellow eye is also recommended because of the high risk of a contralateral attack.

questions.question:
A child aged 3 years is brought by his mother because she noticed a whitish glow in the child's left eye in photographs. There is no family history of eye problems. On examination, there is leucocoria of the left eye.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what other presentations may occur?
(ii) Describe the genetic basis of this condition, distinguishing between hereditary and non-hereditary forms.
(iii) What imaging is appropriate for diagnosis and what is absolutely contraindicated in germline cases?
(iv) Outline the treatment options from local to surgical.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Most likely diagnosis: Retinoblastoma (RB). It is the most common ocular malignancy in children; occurs in 1:15,000 live births. Presentations include: leucocoria (most common); squint; inflammatory presentation e.g. orbital cellulitis; secondary glaucoma; fungating mass (common in middle- to low-income countries due to late presentation).

(ii)
Genetic basis — Two-hit theory (1971, Knudson): deletion or inactivation of RB gene (13q14, tumour suppressor gene) by two mutations. Non-hereditary RB: both mutations occur in somatic cells; accounts for 60% of cases; all unilateral; late onset; accounts for 85% of unilateral RB; not predisposed to second non-ocular tumour; tumour is non-transmissible. Hereditary RB: first mutation is inherited via germinal cells, second occurs in somatic cells; accounts for 40% of cases; accounts for all bilateral cases and 15% of unilateral RB; early onset; prone to second non-ocular tumour e.g. pinealoblastoma.

(iii)
Imaging appropriate: B-scan; EUA; MRI is GOOD. CT scan is BAD (for germline tumours — must not be used because of radiation risk to susceptible germline mutation carriers).

(iv)
Treatment options: Local — laser (810 nm Diode, TTT), cryotherapy; Radiation — brachytherapy (rare), EBRT (never used); Chemotherapy — intravenous (risks: hearing loss, hair loss, pancytopenia, secondary leukaemia), intra-arterial, intra-vitreal; Surgery — enucleation; exenteration. Red reflex test is an important screening tool.

(i)
Specific lens pathology: True diabetic cataract (also called snowflake cataract).
Distinguishing features from other diabetic lens changes:
• True diabetic cataract: bilateral; appears as white punctate or snowflake posterior or anterior subcapsular opacities; caused by osmotic overhydration of the lens; may mature within a few days; seen in young patients with poorly controlled diabetes.
• Senile cataract: appears earlier in diabetics than in non-diabetics and may progress more rapidly; may be subcapsular, nuclear, or cortical — these are not unique in type, just earlier in onset.

(ii)
Pathophysiological mechanism of true diabetic cataract:
• The lens is avascular and depends on the aqueous humour for glucose.
• Elevated blood glucose → increased glucose entry into the lens.
• Glucose is converted to sorbitol (by aldose reductase) within the lens fibres, which cannot exit the lens easily.
• Accumulation of sorbitol → increased osmotic pressure within the lens fibres → water is drawn into the lens fibres → osmotic overhydration of the lens.
• This overhydration disrupts the lens fibre architecture → rapid opacification (bilateral white snowflake/punctate opacities).

(iii)
Refractive change and advice on glasses:
• Refractive change: Increased myopia results from hydration of the lens caused by elevated blood glucose over time (the swollen lens has increased curvature and refractive power).
• Previously poorly controlled patients with rapid improvement in diabetic control may also have transient refractive changes and transient paralysis of accommodation.
• Practical advice: It is advisable NOT to prescribe glasses until the diabetes has been controlled for 3 months (3/12) and the diabetes is stable — because refractive changes will fluctuate with blood glucose and glasses prescribed during hyperglycaemia will be inappropriate once glucose is controlled.

(iv)
Anterior segment manifestations other than the lens:
• Lids: Recurrent styes (acute staphylococcal infection of a lash follicle; treatment — hot fomentation); blepharitis (chronic staphylococcal infection of lid margin); xanthelasma (yellowish subcutaneous plaques of cholesterol and lipid at medial canthus in elderly).
• Cornea: Increased susceptibility to injury and reduced rate of healing; recurrent corneal erosion (thickening of epithelial basement membrane causing defective adhesion to stroma → recurrent breakdown of epithelium); treatment: pressure patching, cycloplegic, prophylactic AB, debridement of loose epithelium, artificial tears, bandage contact lens, anterior stromal puncture.
• Orbit: Fungal orbital cellulitis; mucormycosis (rare but common in diabetic ketoacidosis).
• Iris: Neuropathy → poor dilatation; pigment loss; neovascularisation (rubeosis iridis) → secondary glaucoma (neovascular glaucoma).

(v)
Relationship between diabetes and POAG:
• Diabetics have a higher prevalence of primary open angle glaucoma than non-diabetics.
• Conversely, approximately 10% of patients with POAG have either frank diabetes or an abnormal glucose tolerance test (GTT).
• Treatment caution: Use of non-selective beta-blockers may mask the symptoms and delay recovery from hypoglycaemia; use of acetazolamide should be with caution as it may result in metabolic acidosis.
questions.question:
A 38-year-old man with a 10-year history of poorly controlled Type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with rapidly progressive bilateral visual blurring over 2 weeks. Slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral posterior subcapsular opacities with a white snowflake appearance, and anterior chamber depth appears normal. His blood glucose on presentation is 28 mmol/L.

(i) What is the specific type of lens pathology, and distinguish it from the other lens changes seen in diabetic patients?
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological mechanism behind this lens change, linking it to the blood glucose level.
(iii) What refractive change may be associated with elevated blood glucose in diabetes, and what practical advice should be given regarding glasses prescription in such patients?
(iv) Describe the anterior segment manifestations of diabetes mellitus affecting structures other than the lens.
(v) What is the standard statement regarding the relationship between diabetes and primary open angle glaucoma?

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The normal optic disc has a pink rim (the neuroretinal rim).

A(ii)
The disc has a pale central cup; the normal cup-to-disc ratio in a normal adult eye is approximately 0.3 or less.

A(iii)
Disc margins are normally distinct.

B.
A cup-to-disc ratio of 0.6 or above is suspicious for glaucomatous optic nerve damage, particularly with notching of the neuroretinal rim, flame haemorrhages at the disc margin, or asymmetry between the two eyes; the hallmark of glaucomatous damage is progressive cupping of the disc with loss of retinal ganglion cells. In contrast, papilledema produces blurred, congested, indistinct disc margins with obliteration of the cup, beginning superiorly and inferiorly, with dilated veins, loss of the spontaneous venous pulse, and eventually flame-shaped haemorrhages around the disc.

C.
Raised intracranial pressure from an intracranial disease process produces papilledema at the optic disc, which is typically bilateral and does not cause early loss of vision (unlike anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, which causes sudden visual loss). If raised intracranial pressure persists, chronic papilledema can develop optociliary shunt vessels (collateral vessels between the central retinal and choroidal circulations at the disc) and secondary (consecutive) optic atrophy, where the disc appears pale despite ongoing swelling ("atrophic papilledema"); this reflects progressive axonal death and represents established, longer-standing optic nerve damage with eventual visual function loss.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the optic disc under the headings: (i) neuroretinal rim, (ii) central cup, (iii) disc margins.
B. State how change at each part of the optic disc relates to specific pathologies.
C. Explain why disease at a distant structure (the brain) can produce a change at the optic disc, and the functional deficit this may eventually cause.

A(i) Describe the anatomy of the optic nerve head (optic disc), stating its components, the arrangement of nerve fibres entering it, and the meaning of the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR).
A(ii) Describe the ISNT rule for the neuroretinal rim and explain what deviation from this rule signifies clinically.
B(i) Explain why peripheral retinal nerve fibres are more vulnerable to glaucomatous damage than central fibres, using the known anatomical arrangement of axons in the optic nerve.
B(ii) Describe the anatomical basis of the sequence of visual field defects that occur as glaucoma progresses from early to end stage.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Optic nerve head anatomy:
• The optic disc is where retinal ganglion cell axons leave the eye; it has no photoreceptors (blind spot).
• It consists of the neuroretinal rim (functional rim of nerve fibres) surrounding the central cup (empty excavation).
• Arrangement: Peripheral fibres run closer to the choroid and exit in the periphery of the optic nerve; fibres originating closer to the nerve head are situated closer to the vitreous and occupy a more central portion of the nerve.
• Cup-to-disc ratio (CDR): The ratio of the vertical diameter of the cup to the vertical diameter of the disc. Normal CDR ≈ 0.2; CDR ≥ 0.6 suggests glaucomatous cupping. Large optic discs have large cups even in healthy eyes; small discs have small cups.

A(ii)
ISNT rule:
• In a normal disc, the neuroretinal rim is thickest Inferiorly, then Superiorly, then Nasally, then Temporally (I > S > N > T).
• The width of the rim is measured as the distance between the border of the disc and the point where the blood vessel bends at the disc margin.
• Deviation from the ISNT rule (focal thinning or notching, especially inferiorly or superiorly) indicates glaucomatous rim loss and is an early sign of optic neuropathy.

B(i)
Peripheral fibres run closer to the choroid and exit at the periphery of the optic nerve. Because the disc rim at the superior and inferior poles is relatively thin and the peripheral fibres are more densely packed there, they are more susceptible to pressure-related ischaemia and mechanical compression; therefore, peripheral fibres are more vulnerable to glaucoma damage.

B(ii)
Sequence of visual field defects:
• Early: paracentral scotoma, Seidel scotoma — defects adjacent to the blind spot.
• Intermediate: arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma, double arcuate scotoma (ring scotoma), nasal step.
• Advanced: constriction of the peripheral field — a small central island and a small temporal island remain.
• End stage: the temporal island is slowly, quietly wiped out, leaving total blindness.

A(i)
The Eclipse Sign is the bedside sign used to estimate anterior chamber depth.

A(ii)
It is elicited by shining a light (pen torch) from the temporal side of the cornea; a shadow cast on the nasal iris indicates a shallow anterior chamber, whereas a deep anterior chamber allows light to illuminate the full iris without shadow.

A(iii)
A shallow anterior chamber detected by the Eclipse Sign indicates the highest risk for acute angle-closure glaucoma.

B.
A shallow anterior chamber indicates a narrow drainage angle, which is the anatomical prerequisite for acute angle-closure glaucoma; impaired access of aqueous humour to the trabecular meshwork leads to a dangerous rise in intraocular pressure, which is a sight-threatening emergency.

C.
In acute angle-closure glaucoma the pupil is mid-dilated and non-reactive; this is pathognomonic and is accompanied by a hazy cornea and markedly elevated intraocular pressure. In anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis), the pupil is typically miotic and irregular, and the condition is managed with a cycloplegic mydriatic and topical corticosteroid rather than emergency pressure-lowering treatment.
questions.question:
A. Describe the anterior chamber and its assessment under the headings: (i) bedside sign used to estimate depth, (ii) how the sign is elicited, (iii) significance of a positive finding.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why a shallow anterior chamber is dangerous.
C. Distinguish the pupil of acute angle-closure glaucoma from the pupil of anterior uveitis.

questions.answerText:
A.
CNV1 (ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve):
• Origin: arises from the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion.
• Course and branches: The ophthalmic division divides into three main branches — nasociliary, frontal and lacrimal nerves — which enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
• Distribution: Provides sensation to the conjunctiva, cornea, eyelids, upper face and sides of the nose. It also supplies the lacrimal gland and its passages.

C.
Facial nerve (CNVII) palsy affects the orbicularis oculi muscle (responsible for palpebral and orbital forced closure of the eyelids, winking and blepharospasm, and assisting the lacrimal pump). The effects include:
• Lagophthalmos: inability to close the eyelids fully due to orbicularis oculi paresis.
• Exposure keratopathy: due to improper wetting of the corneal surface from failure of lid closure.
• Ectropion: the lower eyelid may evert (paralytic ectropion), worsening corneal exposure.
• Impaired lacrimal pump: the orbicularis assists the lacrimal pump mechanism; its palsy leads to epiphora despite a patent drainage system.
• Upper and lower lids remain open, leaving the cornea exposed, which may lead to corneal ulceration and scarring if untreated.
questions.question:
A. Describe the origin, anatomical course, relations, branches and distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CNV1) as it relates to ocular and periocular structures.

C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformities observed in the eye and eyelid following facial nerve (CNVII) palsy, distinguishing the effects on the upper and lower eyelids, the cornea and lacrimal drainage.

A(i) Describe the course of the enlarged extraocular muscles in thyroid eye disease in relation to the optic nerve.
A(ii) State the muscle most commonly and severely involved and the movement it restricts.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the visual deficit produced when the optic nerve is compressed in this condition.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
In thyroid eye disease, the extraocular muscles become enlarged and fibrotic; at the orbital apex, this enlargement compresses the optic nerve, producing vision-threatening compressive optic neuropathy - a specific indication for orbital decompression surgery.

A(ii)
The inferior rectus muscle is most commonly and most severely affected first, causing restriction of upgaze and vertical diplopia; the medial rectus is the second most commonly involved muscle.

C.
Compression of the optic nerve by the enlarged fibrotic muscles at the orbital apex reduces visual acuity and produces a relative afferent pupillary defect - dysthyroid optic neuropathy. Colour vision loss (desaturation) often precedes acuity loss and is an early warning sign. This is a vision-threatening complication of severe thyroid eye disease requiring urgent systemic steroids and/or orbital decompression; eyelid retraction, present in up to 90% of patients, results separately from sympathetic overstimulation of Muller's muscle and from fibrosis of the levator and inferior retractor muscles.

A(i)
Genetics and molecular basis:
• The haemoglobin molecule is composed of 2 pairs of polypeptide chains: α and β. Two α genes and one β gene code for these chains, located on chromosomes 16 and 11 respectively.
• Molecular defect in HbS: results from substitution of glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain (the classical sickle mutation described by Pauling in 1949).
• Types: HbSS (homozygous): most severe systemic manifestations, early morbidity; HbSC: milder systemic manifestations, more serious ocular disease; HbS-thalassemia: severity depends on the amount of β chains present.
• Balanced polymorphism: The sickle gene has remained stable in the population despite severe clinical morbidity/mortality because HbS confers some immunity to malaria (especially P. falciparum); HbC also confers some immunity to malaria.

A(ii)
Pathophysiology of sickling:
Sequence: Intracellular polymerisation → gel formation → deformed RBC → damaged RBC membrane → potassium loss → intracellular dehydration → increased HbS polymerisation → loss of biconcave shape permanently → irreversible sickled cells (ISC).
Triggers of sickling:
• Decreased O2 concentration
• Decreased pH
• Temperature changes
• Haemoconcentration
• Stress

B(i)
Why peripheral retina and macula are most susceptible:
• Tissues with low blood flow and high O2 requirements are more prone to sickling and secondary vascular occlusion.
• The peripheral retina and macula are most susceptible to vascular occlusion because of their relatively low blood flow and high metabolic demand.
• Vascular occlusions in sickle cell retinopathy occur in the arterioles rather than the capillaries because the sphincters of the precapillary arterioles are narrower than the true capillaries.
• Additionally, RBCs containing HbS demonstrate greater vascular endothelium adherence.

B(ii)
HbSS vs HbSC ocular severity:
• HbSS: more systemic complications (vaso-occlusive events and secondary organ damage); fewer ocular complications (fewer retinal neovascularisation events) because patients develop early systemic morbidity and mortality.
• HbSC: fewer systemic complications but greater frequency and earlier onset of retinal neovascularisation; resulting in more serious proliferative sickle cell retinopathy.
• Explanation: Patients with HbSC have a higher haematocrit and higher blood viscosity than HbSS, which may promote occlusion in the peripheral retinal vasculature without the severe systemic sickling that kills HbSS patients early.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the genetics and molecular basis of sickle cell haemoglobinopathy under the headings: gene location, molecular defect, types of sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbSC, HbS-thal), and balanced polymorphism.
A(ii) Describe the pathophysiology of sickling, stating the factors that trigger it and the sequence from polymerisation to irreversible sickled cells (ISC).
B(i) Explain why the peripheral retina and macula are the structures most susceptible to vascular occlusion in sickle cell disease, using the anatomical and rheological factors involved.
B(ii) Distinguish between the ocular severity of HbSS and HbSC disease, and explain why patients with HbSC have more serious ocular disease despite milder systemic disease.

A. Describe the anatomy of the aqueous humour pathway — where it is produced, its composition, its route of circulation and its drainage mechanism.

B. State the normal range of intraocular pressure (IOP) and explain the physiological balance that maintains it.

C. Explain how disruption to aqueous drainage leads to glaucoma, and state why raised IOP is a major risk factor. Also describe what happens to the retina and optic nerve when IOP is chronically elevated.
questions.answerText:
A.
Aqueous humour:
• Production: produced by the ciliary body.
• Composition: a clear watery fluid (ultrafiltrate of plasma).
• Circulation: flows from the posterior chamber (behind the iris) through the pupil into the anterior chamber.
• Drainage: drained conventionally by the trabecular meshwork located at the anterior chamber angles (conventional outflow pathway).

B.
Normal IOP: 10–21 mmHg. This is maintained by the balance between the rate of aqueous humour production (by the ciliary body) and the rate of its drainage (through the trabecular meshwork at the anterior chamber angle). When production exceeds drainage, or drainage is impaired, IOP rises.

C.
Disruption to aqueous drainage — such as blockage of the trabecular meshwork (open-angle) or occlusion of the drainage angle (closed-angle) — raises IOP above 21 mmHg. Raised IOP is a major risk factor for glaucoma. The metabolic role of aqueous humour is to provide substrates and remove metabolites from the avascular cornea and crystalline lens. Chronically elevated IOP causes progressive mechanical damage to the optic nerve fibres at the lamina cribrosa. This results in cupping of the optic disc, optic atrophy (pale disc with cupping — glaucoma is the commonest cause of optic atrophy), and progressive visual field defects leading to blindness if untreated. Glaucomatous optic atrophy is characterised by pallor and cupping of the optic disc.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of a gradually enlarging painless lump on her upper eyelid. On examination there is a non-tender nodular swelling prominent on the conjunctival surface, and she reports occasional blurred vision in that eye.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and name the gland primarily involved.
(ii) Identify the risk factors and predisposing conditions associated with this lesion, including conditions that must be excluded.
(iii) List the complications of this condition, including its potential effect on vision.
(iv) Compare conservative and surgical management options for this patient, justifying the indication for surgical intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The most likely diagnosis is a chalazion. The gland primarily involved is the meibomian gland (deep chalazion), though it may also arise from the glands of Zeis (superficial chalazion).

(ii)
Risk factors and predisposing conditions: The chalazion forms when the meibomian gland becomes blocked, leading to chronic granulomatous inflammation of secretion extruded into adjacent tissue. It may be associated with meibomian gland dysfunction, seborrhoea, rosacea, and chronic blepharitis. Recurrent chalazia must be biopsied to exclude sebaceous cell carcinoma.

(iii)
Complications: An internal hordeolum may progress to chronic granulation forming a chalazion if untreated. Occasionally patients may experience blurred vision secondary to the astigmatic effect of the chalazion pressing on the globe.

(iv)
Management:
• Conservative: Apply warm compress and massage; more than 50% of chalazia resolve with conservative treatment. Intralesional steroid injection (0.1–0.2 ml of 10 mg/ml) or 5-fluorouracil may be used for moderately sized lesions. Antibiotic treatment is of no value as chalazia are sterile.
• Surgical: Curettage (I&C) is performed for larger lesions that do not resolve. Dissection of the granuloma for complete removal is done for the largest lesions. Biopsies on recurrent chalazia are mandatory to exclude sebaceous cell carcinoma.

(i)
Primary open angle glaucoma (POAG).
Risk factors:
• Elevated intraocular pressure level
• Older age
• Positive family history of glaucoma
• African ancestry or Latino/Hispanic ethnicity
• Thinner central corneal thickness
• Low ocular perfusion pressures
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus
• Myopia
• Genetic mutations
• Steroid responders

(ii)
Visual field defect patterns:
• Paracentral scotoma
• Seidel scotoma
• Arcuate scotoma
• Double arcuate scotoma
• Nasal step
• Visual field loss starts from the periphery; in end stage, only a central field with a small temporal island remains, which is slowly wiped out over time.

(iii)
Complications if untreated:
• Progressive optic neuropathy and permanent visual field loss
• Blindness (risk of blindness is higher in blacks)
• Vascular occlusions (branch retinal artery occlusion, central retinal vein occlusion) may occur with untreated chronic glaucoma and elevated IOP

(iv)
Classes of anti-glaucoma medications:
• Prostaglandin analogues (e.g., latanoprost): increase uveoscleral outflow — first-line choice because they are once-daily, have few systemic side effects, and provide effective diurnal IOP control.
• Beta-adrenergic antagonists (e.g., timolol): reduce aqueous production.
• Adrenergic agonists (e.g., apraclonidine): reduce aqueous production and episcleral venous pressure.
• Parasympathomimetics/miotics (e.g., pilocarpine): increase trabecular outflow.
• Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide/dorzolamide): reduce aqueous production.
• Hyperosmotic agents (e.g., mannitol): osmotically dehydrate the vitreous (used acutely).
Justification: Prostaglandin analogues are first-line as they reduce IOP most effectively with once-daily dosing and minimal systemic side effects, contrasted with beta-blockers which cause bronchospasm and bradycardia.
questions.question:
A 62-year-old man of African descent is referred for gradual, painless loss of peripheral vision bilaterally over several years. He has a family history of glaucoma. On examination, IOP is 28 mmHg in both eyes. Gonioscopy shows open angles. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral increased cup-to-disc ratio with thinning of the neuroretinal rim. Automated perimetry shows arcuate scotomas.

(i) Identify this condition and state all the risk factors for it.
(ii) State the visual field defect patterns that may be seen on perimetry.
(iii) Enumerate the complications if this condition is left untreated.
(iv) List the classes of anti-glaucoma medications available, giving one example from each class, and justify the first-line choice in this patient.

questions.answerText:
(i)
The oculomotor nerve (CN III). The combination of an ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia localises the lesion to the brainstem (midbrain), as in Weber's syndrome.

(ii)
Pupil dilation (mydriasis) occurs because the parasympathetic fibres, carried on the outer surface of CN III and vulnerable to compression, are disrupted. Complete ptosis results from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris. The "down and out" position results from paralysis of the medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique, with the lateral rectus (supplied by CN VI) unopposed. Loss of accommodation (cycloplegia) results from paralysis of the ciliary muscle.

(iii)
Pupillary involvement is the first and most important clinical determination in evaluating a third nerve palsy: a dilated, unreactive pupil (as here) suggests a compressive/surgical cause requiring urgent investigation, whereas a pupil-sparing palsy is more typical of an ischaemic/medical cause, since ischaemia affects the inner core fibres while sparing the outer parasympathetic fibres.

(iv)
As CN III courses ventrally from the midbrain, it passes through the red nucleus and the ipsilateral corticospinal tract before emerging from the ventral midbrain surface. A lesion at this level (Weber's syndrome) produces an ipsilateral CN III palsy together with contralateral hemiplegia due to corticospinal tract involvement - the classic "crossed" pattern of brainstem localisation.
questions.question:
A patient presents with a painful, dilated, non-reactive right pupil, complete ptosis, and the eye deviated "down and out". There is loss of accommodation on the same side. Neurological examination reveals contralateral hemiplegia.

(i) Identify the nerve involved and the anatomical level at which the lesion is located.
(ii) State the structures affected that explain the ocular findings.
(iii) Explain why pupil involvement is clinically significant in this presentation.
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning connecting the contralateral hemiplegia to the site of the lesion.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: primary open-angle glaucoma. Glaucoma is not a single disease entity but a group of conditions characterized by damage to the optic nerve (detected by pathological cupping of the optic disc) and loss of the field of vision. The two main types are primary open-angle glaucoma and primary angle-closure glaucoma.

(ii)
Epidemiological significance: about 60.5 million people are estimated to have glaucoma by 2010 (44.7 million with open-angle glaucoma, 15.7 million with angle-closure glaucoma); may increase to almost 80 million by 2020 due to ageing of world's population. Nigeria: prevalence 4–6%; over 4 million have the disease. Worldwide estimate of blindness due to glaucoma — 6 million (67 million prevalence); USA — 200,000 blind (4 million prevalence). Population studies suggest over half of all glaucoma cases have not been diagnosed; in developing countries, over 90% are not diagnosed.

(iii)
Reasons for late presentation and under-diagnosis: society — poor access to healthcare; patient — non-adherence to therapy; physician — inadequate therapy. Interventions are limited as the condition is not preventable; patients tend to present late; there is no simple screening test. Many suffer severe visual field loss before diagnosis.

(iv)
Changes in management: earlier diagnosis; diagnosis now based on VF + optic nerve appearance + others — NOT IOP alone; earlier treatment; more aggressive treatment to lower pressures (IOP within normal range may not be low enough). Nigeria strategies: ensure training curricula for ophthalmologists and optometrists/mid-level personnel adequately address glaucoma; ensure training centres are adequately equipped to provide essential services for glaucoma patients.
questions.question:
A 42-year-old man presents to the eye clinic with a history of progressive narrowing of his field of vision over several years. He is asymptomatic but his brother was recently diagnosed with open-angle glaucoma. IOP is 24 mmHg, and optic disc examination shows pathological cupping.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and how is glaucoma defined?
(ii) What is the epidemiological significance of this condition in Nigeria and globally?
(iii) Why do patients with this condition present late, and what are the reasons for under-diagnosis?
(iv) Outline how management of glaucoma has evolved, including what the diagnosis is now based on and the treatment target.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
• Eye with drusen and flat macula: Dry AMD (atrophic type) — characterised by drusen and maculopathy.
• Eye with subretinal haemorrhage and retinal elevation: Wet AMD (neovascular type) — characterised by choroidal neovascularisation, subretinal fluid and haemorrhage.

(ii)
Risk factors for age-related macular degeneration:
• Advancing age.
• Smoking (a recognised risk factor).
Hypertension is a risk factor for retinal vascular diseases generally.

(iii)
Vision is lost preferentially in the central field because the macula (and specifically the fovea, which provides high-resolution central vision) is primarily affected. The photoreceptors — particularly cones in the foveal region — degenerate or are damaged by the subretinal neovascularisation and haemorrhage, causing central visual loss while peripheral vision is relatively preserved.

(iv)
Management:
• Dry AMD: antioxidant supplementation (antioxidants).
• Wet AMD: laser photocoagulation; anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor) therapy.
questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of gradual, painless deterioration of vision in both eyes. She reports difficulty reading and watching television. She has a 10-year history of poorly controlled hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes per day. On fundoscopy the macula appears flat in one eye and there are small yellowish deposits (drusen) with areas of retinal elevation and subretinal haemorrhage in the other.

(i) State the diagnosis in each eye and identify the two forms of this disease.
(ii) State all risk factors for this disease.
(iii) Explain why vision is lost preferentially in the central field and which retinal structure is primarily affected.
(iv) State the management options for each form of the disease.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Spot diagnosis: Graves' ophthalmopathy (also called thyroid eye disease, thyroid orbitopathy). Most common clinical sign: eyelid retraction — it is the most common sign. It is the most common cause of eyelid retraction and the most common cause of bilateral or unilateral proptosis.

(ii)
Risk factors: smoking (associated with increased risk and severity of ophthalmopathy); associated with hyperthyroidism in 90% of patients; 6% are euthyroid (euthyroid Graves' disease). The course of ophthalmopathy does not necessarily parallel the activity of the thyroid gland or the treatment of thyroid abnormalities. More common in women. Eye findings may occur even in the absence of objective evidence of thyroid dysfunction.

(iii)
Clinical signs: eyelid retraction (most common sign); lid lag; proptosis; restrictive extraocular myopathy; optic neuropathy. Signs of injection around the insertion of the recti muscles are characteristic. The condition is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder.

(iv)
Treatment options: correction of thyroid function abnormality — anti-thyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, thyroidectomy; orbital decompression — to treat optic neuropathy, orbital congestion, advanced proptosis; topical ocular lubricants; corticosteroid treatment; orbital radiotherapy (targets lymphocytes). Prognosis: self-limiting but may run an active course of exacerbation and remissions; often improves with establishment of euthyroid state but eye disease may continue to progress; elective orbital decompression, strabismus surgery and eyelid retraction repair are usually not considered until ophthalmic signs have been stable for 6–9 months.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman of West African descent presents to the clinic with bilateral proptosis, lid retraction, and injection around the insertion of the recti muscles. She has a history of hyperthyroidism treated with radioactive iodine 2 years ago.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis and what is the most common clinical sign of this condition?
(ii) Describe the risk factors for this condition and the relationship between thyroid status and eye disease.
(iii) What are the clinical signs of this condition on ocular examination?
(iv) Outline the treatment options for this condition.

questions.answerText:
A.
The crystalline lens is a transparent, avascular, biconvex structure. It is held in position by the zonule of Zinn (suspensory ligament), which connects it to the ciliary body. It is enclosed in a semi-permeable lens capsule. The lens consists of a central nucleus surrounded by cortex and is covered by a subcapsular epithelium anteriorly.

B.
Transparency is maintained by:
• Avascularity.
• Regular arrangement of lens fibres.
• Tightly packed nature of lens cells.
• Semi-permeable nature of the lens capsule.
• The Na-K+ pump, which maintains a relatively dehydrated state.
• Continuous supply of ATP generated from glucose metabolism.
Cataract (opacification of the lens) results when these mechanisms are disrupted:
• Nuclear sclerosis: from aging (multifactorial — genetic and environmental).
• Drug-induced: corticosteroids cause posterior subcapsular cataract; phenothiazines deposit drug pigment in lens fibres.
• Traumatic: contusion or penetrating injury causes mechanical fibre damage at the site of rupture, progressing to involve the rest of the lens.
• Metabolic: diabetes causes cataract via sorbitol production; galactosaemia via galactitol production; hypocalcaemia via deranged membrane transport.
• Congenital: maternal infections (rubella, toxoplasmosis, CMV) injure lens fibres; maternal drug ingestion (thalidomide, corticosteroids) causes deranged membrane transport.

C.
Classification of cataract:
• Aetiological: age-related, drug-induced, traumatic, metabolic, complicated (post-uveitic, high myopia, retinitis pigmentosa), congenital, hereditary.
• Morphological: nuclear, cortical, anterior/posterior polar, anterior/posterior subcapsular.
• Stage of maturity: immature, mature, intumescent (swollen with imbibed water), hypermature (shrunken with wrinkled capsule), Morgagnian (hypermature with nucleus sunken in liquefied cortex).
• Chronological: congenital (since birth), infantile (first year of life), juvenile (1–13 years), developmental (1–35 years), presenile (36–49 years), senile (>50 years).
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the crystalline lens — including its structure, zones, capsule and relationship to surrounding structures.

B. Explain how the transparency of the crystalline lens is maintained and state which factors, when disrupted, lead to cataract formation — relating each mechanism to a specific cause.

C. Classify cataract by aetiology, morphology, stage of maturity and chronological age of onset, giving examples for each category.

A 45-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic with a red eye. She reports bilateral involvement, watery discharge, and no visual impairment. She has a history of rhinitis and uses contact lenses.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what are the possible aetiological categories of red eye as classified by anatomical location?
(ii) List the specific risk factors and predisposing features in the history relevant to this patient.
(iii) What are the potential sight-threatening complications of red eye that would mandate urgent referral to an ophthalmologist?
(iv) Outline the treatment options — medical, supportive, and surgical — applicable to different causes of red eye.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Most likely diagnosis: Allergic conjunctivitis. Aetiological classification by anatomical location includes: Adnexa (blepharitis, trichiasis, stye, chalazion, dacryocystitis); Conjunctiva (bacterial, viral and allergic conjunctivitis, dry eye); Sclera (scleritis, episcleritis); AC (acute angle closure glaucoma, hyphema); Uvea (iritis, iridocyclitis); Orbit/Retrobulbar (orbital cellulitis, pseudotumor, cavernous thrombosis).

(ii)
Risk factors/predisposing features: use of contact lenses; presence of allergies; systemic disease (RA, PAN, syphilis, TB); social history including alcohol ingestion; recent illness. ROS should include URTI, urethritis, arthritis, nausea and vomiting.

(iii)
Sight-threatening red flags requiring referral: Pain; Visual impairment; Abnormal lashes; Corneal involvement (hazy, abrasion, ulcer, laceration); Hyphema; Distorted pupil/Abnormal pupillary reaction; Raised IOP.

(iv)
Treatment: Medical — antimicrobials, antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, antiglaucoma agents, NSAIDs (refrain from prescribing steroids without ophthalmic consultation); Supportive — cold compress for itchy eyes/avoidance of allergens; hand washing; lid care; avoid sharing of towels, cosmetics or eye drops; saline lavage for ophthalmia neonatorum; Surgical — depends on cause: paracentesis (hyphema); iridotomy (acute angle closure glaucoma); pterygium excision; orbital decompression for vision-threatening thyroid eye disease.

questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the orbit under the following headings:
A(i) Shape, volume and bony composition.
A(ii) Contents of the orbit.
A(iii) Vascular supply and venous drainage.

B. Explain why the floor of the orbit is the most commonly fractured wall in blunt ocular trauma, and why infection from the adjacent sinuses spreads so readily into the orbit.

C. Distinguish between preseptal cellulitis and orbital cellulitis — in terms of anatomical basis, clinical features and complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Shape, volume and bony composition: The orbit is a pear-shaped (pyramidal) bony cavity. Volume is approximately 30 cc in adults. The entrance is 35 mm in height and 40 mm in width. It is composed of 7 bones: frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, ethmoid, lacrimal, maxillary and palatine.

A(ii)
Contents: The eye ball and orbital optic nerve; extraocular muscles (EOMs); ophthalmic vessels; lacrimal gland (orbital lobe); ocular motor nerves (sensory, motor, sympathetic, parasympathetic); and orbital fat and periorbita.

A(iii)
Vascular supply: The ophthalmic artery (a branch of the internal carotid artery). Venous drainage is via the superior ophthalmic vein, which drains to the cavernous sinus through the superior orbital fissure.

B.
The floor of the orbit is the weakest wall and is most likely to be fractured in blunt ocular trauma. The medial wall is separated from the ethmoidal sinus by a paper-thin wall known as the lamina papyracea, which easily allows transmission of pathogens from the sinuses into the orbit.

C.
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis: Confined to structures anterior to the orbital septum. Features include lid oedema, erythema, normal globe position, normal pupil, normal visual acuity, and normal ocular motility; chemosis and pain on eye movement are absent.
Orbital cellulitis: Involves structures behind the orbital septum. Features include fever, proptosis, chemosis, restricted ocular motility and pain. Reduced visual acuity and pupillary abnormality suggest involvement of the orbital apex. Complications include orbital apex syndrome, cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST), cranial nerve palsy, brain abscess, blindness and death.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old farmer presents with a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision three days after being struck in the eye by a piece of vegetable matter while working on his farm. Slit-lamp examination reveals a greyish-white corneal ulcer with indistinct margins and finger-like infiltrations in the adjacent stroma, together with a hypopyon in the anterior chamber. Culture and corneal biopsy are obtained.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify the causative organisms most commonly responsible for this type of infection.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological basis of how this organism gains access to the cornea and what features of its infection make it distinct from bacterial keratitis.
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitation and supportive steps that should be taken for this patient while awaiting laboratory results.
(iv) State the definitive antifungal treatment — topical and systemic — for this patient, including agents, routes and duration.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The most likely diagnosis is filamentous fungal keratitis. The causative organisms are filamentous fungi such as Aspergillus and Fusarium species.

(ii)
Filamentous fungal keratitis is more common in farmers following trauma from vegetable material. The organism gains entry through disrupted corneal epithelium. Unlike bacterial keratitis, filamentous fungal infections typically present with a greyish-white ulcer with indistinct margins and delicate finger-like infiltrations in the adjacent stroma; use of topical steroid also enhances fungal growth.

(iii)
Immediate steps include hospitalisation, corneal scraping for culture and corneal biopsy to confirm diagnosis, and cycloplegics to relieve ciliary spasm. De-epithelisation may help drug penetration.

(iv)
Definitive treatment:
• Topical: Econazole 1%, Natamycin, and Imidazole (or Furiconazole, a more recent agent) applied topically.
• Systemic: Itraconazole or Ketoconazole for 6 weeks.
• Treatment may be prolonged.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and poor glycaemic control presents with sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. The fundus view is obscured by vitreous haemorrhage.

(i) State the risk factors for the underlying retinal disease that are relevant to this patient.
(ii) State the complications of advanced disease that could explain this presentation and threaten vision further.
(iii) State the surgical/management options available, and justify the option most appropriate for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Long duration of diabetes combined with poor glycaemic control (elevated HbA1c) is the strongest risk factor for developing and progressing diabetic retinopathy; after 20 years of type 1 diabetes, up to 99% of patients develop some degree of retinopathy. Type 2 diabetes carries a particular predilection for diabetic macular oedema.

(ii)
Sudden, painless visual loss in proliferative diabetic retinopathy is most commonly caused by vitreous haemorrhage from rupture of fragile new vessels (neovascularisation at the disc or elsewhere). Rubeosis iridis (iris neovascularisation) may also develop, indicating neovascular glaucoma from anterior segment ischaemia. When media opacity (as here) prevents direct visualisation of the posterior segment, tractional retinal detachment may be present behind the haemorrhage.

(iii)
Options: panretinal photocoagulation (destroys ischaemic peripheral retina to reduce VEGF production, standard for proliferative disease), anti-VEGF therapy (targets VEGF-driven vascular permeability and neovascularisation), and vitrectomy (indicated for severe persistent vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment threatening the macula).
Justification: because the vitreous haemorrhage is obscuring the fundus, laser cannot be applied directly. B-scan ultrasonography should first be used to assess the retina behind the haemorrhage for tractional detachment; given severe persistent vitreous haemorrhage, vitrectomy is the most appropriate option to clear the media and address any tractional detachment threatening the macula.

(i)
Anterior and posterior segment ocular manifestations of diabetes:
Anterior segment:
• Lids: Recurrent styes (acute staphylococcal infection of lash follicle); blepharitis (chronic staphylococcal infection of lid margin); xanthelasma (yellowish subcutaneous plaques of cholesterol and lipid at medial canthus).
• Cornea: Increased susceptibility to injury and reduced rate of healing; recurrent corneal erosion (thickening of epithelial basement membrane leads to defective adhesion to stroma).
• Iris: Neuropathy causing poor dilatation; pigment loss; neovascularisation leading to secondary glaucoma.
• Lens: Senile cataract appearing earlier; true diabetic cataract (bilateral white punctate/snowflake opacities, osmotic overhydration); refractive changes (increased myopia from lens hydration due to elevated blood glucose).
• Orbit: Fungal orbital cellulitis, mucormycosis (rare but common in diabetic ketoacidosis).
Posterior segment:
• Diabetic retinopathy (NPDR and PDR).
• Vitreous haemorrhage.
• Optic neuropathy (diabetic papillopathy).
• Extraocular muscle palsies (diabetic cranial neuropathy).

(ii)
Risk factors for diabetic retinopathy:
• Duration of diabetes (most important).
• Poor glycaemic control (elevated HbA1c).
• Hypertension.
• Nephropathy (diabetic nephropathy / uraemia).
• Myopia.
• Vascular disease such as HTN or vasospasm.
• Race (higher in blacks).
• Family history.
• General vascular risk factors.

(iii)
Neovascular glaucoma in diabetes:
• Diabetes is the second commonest cause of neovascular glaucoma (NVG) after central retinal vein occlusion.
• The underlying cause is always severe retinal ischaemia, which stimulates the production and liberation of angiogenic factors.
• These angiogenic factors diffuse into the anterior chamber and cause the growth of new vessels on the iris (rubeosis iridis) and in the angle.
• The fibrovascular tissue in the angle leads to blockage of aqueous outflow and a consequent rise in IOP (secondary angle closure).
• NVG is an extremely painful condition and does not respond to standard glaucoma therapy.

(iv)
General principles of treatment of diabetes mellitus:
• NIDDM: diet, weight reduction, reduced alcohol consumption, exercise, oral hypoglycaemic drugs (sulphonyl ureas e.g., chlorpropamide; biguanides e.g., metformin).
• IDDM: modified diet, exogenous insulin; also treat hypertension, weight reduction, reduce fat intake, stop smoking.
Special precautions for anti-glaucoma medications in diabetics:
• Non-selective beta-blockers may mask the symptoms and delay recovery from hypoglycaemia.
• Acetazolamide (CAI) should be used with caution as it may result in metabolic acidosis in diabetics.
questions.question:
A 52-year-old man with a 15-year history of poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes mellitus is referred for a routine eye review. He has no visual symptoms. On examination, visual acuity is 6/9 bilaterally. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral dot haemorrhages, microaneurysms, hard exudates, and new vessels on the disc (NVD) in the right eye.

(i) What are the anterior and posterior segment ocular manifestations of diabetes mellitus?
(ii) State all the risk factors for development and progression of diabetic retinopathy.
(iii) Describe how neovascular glaucoma develops as a complication of diabetic retinopathy, explaining the mechanism fully.
(iv) Outline the general principles of treatment of diabetes mellitus and state what special precaution applies when prescribing anti-glaucoma medications in diabetic patients.

Describe the gross anatomy of the conjunctiva and the blood supply to it, the pathophysiology of red eye arising from it, and the distinctions between its common inflammatory pathologies.

A(i) Describe the subdivisions and anatomical relations of the conjunctiva.
A(ii) Describe the blood supply to the conjunctiva and its three sources.
B(i) Outline the pathophysiology of red eye, including the role of chemical mediators.
B(ii) Distinguish bacterial, viral and allergic conjunctivitis by their cardinal features.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The conjunctiva is a loose mucous membrane that lines the posterior surface of the eyelids and the anterior aspect of the globe. Sub-divided into: 1. Bulbar (lines the eyeball); 2. Palpebral (lines the eyelids); 3. Forniceal (lines the junction between eyeball and eyelids).

A(ii)
Arteries supplying the conjunctiva are from 3 sources: peripheral arterial arcade of the eyelid; marginal arterial arcade of the eyelid; anterior ciliary arteries.

B(i)
Red eye refers to the red appearance of the opened eye. It is a common ophthalmic symptom and sign. It may arise from causes within or outside the globe (eyeball). Chemical mediators of inflammation are any messenger that acts on blood vessels, inflammatory cells or any other cell to contribute to an inflammatory process. Causes include infectious (bacterial, viral or fungal conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, orbital cellulitis); non-infectious: allergic, immunologic, toxic, trauma, elevated IOP.

B(ii)
Bacterial conjunctivitis: purulent discharge; Viral conjunctivitis: typically watery discharge, associated with URTI; Allergic conjunctivitis: associated itching, bilateral, avoidance of allergens recommended; Vernal keratoconjunctivitis: tarsal FB-like papillae. Investigation: microbiologic — exudates/corneal scrapings for m/c/s; immunologic — VDRL, RF. Treatment differs: antimicrobials for bacterial; antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers for allergic.

A(i)
Trabecular meshwork:
• Location: Situated at the anterior chamber angle, between the base of the iris/ciliary body and the corneal endothelium, forming the inner wall of Schlemm's canal.
• Structure: Consists of a series of trabecular lamellae perforated by openings (pores); divided into uveal meshwork, corneoscleral meshwork, and the juxtacanalicular (cribriform) layer, which offers the greatest resistance to outflow.
• Function: Filters aqueous humour from the anterior chamber into Schlemm's canal and then into the episcleral venous system; maintains normal IOP of 10–21 mmHg.

A(ii)
Schlemm's canal:
• Location: A circumferential channel at the limbus, lying just external to the trabecular meshwork.
• Structure: An endothelium-lined canal; the inner wall adjoins the juxtacanalicular trabecular meshwork.
• Relationship: Aqueous passes through the trabecular meshwork → into Schlemm's canal → via collector channels → into the episcleral venous system; trabeculotomy ab externo cannulates Schlemm's canal to tear the trabecular meshwork from outside.

B(i)
In primary open angle glaucoma, there is increased resistance to aqueous outflow specifically at the juxtacanalicular (cribriform) portion of the trabecular meshwork. Despite an open angle visible on gonioscopy, outflow is impaired, causing aqueous to accumulate, IOP to rise, and progressive pressure-related damage to retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic nerve head.

B(ii)
Conventional (trabecular) outflow: aqueous flows through the trabecular meshwork → Schlemm's canal → collector channels → episcleral veins. Enhanced by miotics (parasympathomimetics, e.g., pilocarpine) and laser trabeculoplasty.
Uveoscleral (unconventional) outflow: aqueous crosses the ciliary muscle into the supraciliary and suprachoroidal space and exits through the sclera. Selectively enhanced by prostaglandin analogues (e.g., latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the trabecular meshwork under the headings: location, structure/layers, and function in aqueous outflow.
A(ii) Describe Schlemm's canal under the headings: location, structure, and its relationship to the trabecular meshwork.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis of why increased resistance in the trabecular meshwork is the primary pathologic event in primary open angle glaucoma.
B(ii) Distinguish between the trabecular (conventional) outflow pathway and the uveoscleral (unconventional) outflow pathway, stating which drug class selectively enhances each.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum. Ophthalmia neonatorum is defined as bilateral inflammation of the conjunctiva occurring in the first 28 days of life. Laboratory confirmation via eye swab: Gram stain, culture and sensitivity.

(ii)
Risk factors and modes of transmission: most common mode — during birth through contact with infected birth canal; prolonged delivery; position of baby in the birth canal (face presentation); birth trauma (e.g. forceps delivery); infected liquor amnii in mothers with ruptured membrane; cleaning of newborn with soiled clothes/fingers. Gonococcal ON is caused by Neisseria gonorrhea. The most common infective cause of ON overall is Chlamydia trachomatis; gonococcal ON is less common but causes the most severe disease.

(iii)
Complications: corneal ulceration (gonococcal ON can penetrate intact cornea); corneal opacity; globe perforation; systemic spread — sepsis/meningitis (gonococcal); otitis media/pneumonia (chlamydial); death (rare).

(iv)
Management: Admit; hourly saline lavage (till discharge is eliminated); systemic therapy — IV/IM ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg stat (max 125 mg); alternative: IM Kanamycin 75 mg/kg stat. Primary prevention: ocular prophylaxis within 1 hour of life — occ 0.5% erythromycin, occ 1% tetracycline, 2% povidone iodine solution, or gutt 1% silver nitrate (Credé method — no longer popular).
questions.question:
A neonate is brought to the clinic at day 5 of life with bilateral eye swelling and profuse purulent discharge from both eyes. The mother had untreated gonococcal infection during pregnancy, and delivery was vaginal.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and on what basis is it made?
(ii) List the risk factors and modes of transmission relevant to this presentation.
(iii) What are the complications if this condition is left untreated?
(iv) Outline the immediate management, including both systemic and topical treatment, and state the primary preventive measure.

A(i) Describe optic neuritis as an ophthalmic emergency under the headings: definition/nature, typical patient profile, clinical features (including the pupillary sign), systemic association, and treatment.
A(ii) Describe the afferent pupillary defect (APD): what it is, how it is elicited, what it indicates, and in which ophthalmic emergencies it is a key sign.
B(i) Describe the clinical features of sudden painful loss of vision and list all the differential diagnoses for this presentation.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical and physiological basis of why the pupil is mid-dilated, paralytic, and unreactive in acute angle closure glaucoma, linking this to the IOP level.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Optic neuritis as an ophthalmic emergency:
• Definition/nature: Inflammation of the optic nerve causing sudden visual loss.
• Typical patient profile: Middle-aged females.
• Clinical features: Sudden visual loss; afferent pupillary defect (APD) present; pain on eye movement; papilloedema may occur (rare) or the disc may look normal in retrobulbar neuritis.
• Systemic association: Multiple sclerosis.
• Treatment: Steroids.

A(ii)
Afferent pupillary defect (APD):
• The APD (also called the relative APD or Marcus Gunn pupil) is elicited by swinging a bright light from one eye to the other.
• In a normal response, both pupils constrict when light falls on either eye. In an APD, the affected eye fails to constrict (or dilates) when light is directed into it, compared with the normal response when light is directed into the fellow eye.
• It indicates: Asymmetric optic nerve damage (used to detect afferent pathway — retina or optic nerve — disease).
• Key sign in: Optic neuritis; traumatic optic neuropathy; retrobulbar haemorrhage; orbital apex fracture; any condition causing asymmetric optic nerve damage — used in fundus evaluation by looking for an afferent pupillary defect.

B(i)
Differential diagnoses of sudden painful loss of vision:
• Optic neuritis
• Acute angle closure glaucoma
• Trauma (ocular trauma)
• Orbital cellulitis
• Uveitis

B(ii)
Anatomical and physiological basis of mid-dilated, paralytic, unreactive pupil in acute ACG:
• The very high IOP in acute angle closure glaucoma exceeds the perfusion pressure of the iris sphincter muscle.
• Ischaemia of the iris sphincter (the muscle responsible for pupil constriction) causes it to cease functioning.
• The pupil is therefore fixed (paralytic) and unreactive — it can neither constrict to light nor to accommodation.
• It remains mid-dilated (not fully dilated nor fully constricted) because the dilator muscle is also partially impaired but less severely than the sphincter; additionally the mechanical stretching of the iris in the ischaemic state holds it mid-dilated.
• This is also why stronger miotics (pilocarpine) are to be avoided in severe attacks — the iris will be ischaemic and unresponsive to them.

A(i)
Glaucoma is not a single disease entity but a group of conditions characterized by damage to the optic nerve (detected by pathological cupping of the optic disc) and loss of the field of vision. The two main types are primary open-angle glaucoma and primary angle-closure glaucoma. About 60.5 million people are estimated to have glaucoma by 2010 (44.7 million with open-angle glaucoma and 15.7 million with angle-closure glaucoma).

A(ii)
The anterior chamber is a 3-dimensional space between the cornea and the iris. The depth of the anterior chamber is important in determining the access of aqueous to the drainage channels in the angle of the anterior chamber. When the angle is narrow, access to the angle is impaired and there is a risk of elevated intraocular pressure. The depth of the anterior chamber is influenced by the structures behind the iris.

B(i)
Classification: primary open-angle glaucoma and primary angle-closure glaucoma. Diagnosis is based on visual field, optic nerve appearance, and others — not IOP alone. Earlier and more aggressive treatment is required to lower pressures; IOP within normal range may not be low enough.

B(ii)
Glaucoma causes progressive injury to retinal ganglion cells and their axons. The specific pattern of optic atrophy (cupping) and associated visual function deficit (visual field loss) results. In developing countries, over 90% of cases are not diagnosed; many suffer severe visual field loss before diagnosis. Interventions for prevention of blindness due to glaucoma are limited as the condition is not preventable and patients tend to present late.
questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy and classification of glaucoma, explaining how its zones relate to common pathologies, and why the disease may progress to cause a specific functional deficit.

A(i) Define glaucoma and describe the two main types.
A(ii) Describe the anatomy of the anterior chamber relevant to aqueous drainage.
B(i) State the classification of glaucoma and explain how intraocular pressure relates to the pathology.
B(ii) Explain why glaucoma causes a characteristic pattern of vision loss and what functional deficit results.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Episcleritis involves only the superficial episcleral vessels. Scleritis involves the deep episcleral and scleral vessels.

A(ii)
Episcleritis is typically benign and only mildly painful. Scleritis produces severe, deep, boring eye pain, often waking the patient at night, with photophobia.

A(iii)
Episcleral vessels in episcleritis blanch with topical phenylephrine. In scleritis, the sectoral redness does not blanch with phenylephrine.

A(iv)
Episcleritis may be associated with systemic disease in only a minority of cases. Scleritis is strongly associated with systemic autoimmune disease, particularly rheumatoid arthritis.

B.
Scleritis involves the deeper scleral vessels and is strongly linked to systemic autoimmune disease (such as rheumatoid arthritis), and the pain is severe and boring in character; this deep, non-blanching involvement and systemic association make scleritis a more severe condition than the superficial, benign, self-limiting episcleritis.

C.
Episcleritis is superficial, typically benign and self-limiting, and blanches with topical phenylephrine. Scleritis is deep, does not blanch with phenylephrine, produces severe boring pain, and has a stronger systemic disease association; the blanching test with phenylephrine is the key bedside method to distinguish the two.
questions.question:
A. Describe episcleritis and scleritis under the following headings: (i) vessel layer involved, (ii) pain character, (iii) response to topical phenylephrine, (iv) systemic association.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why scleritis is regarded as the more serious of the two conditions.
C. Distinguish episcleritis from scleritis.

A. Describe the normal optic disc under the headings: (i) rim colour, (ii) central cup, (iii) margins.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.6 or above is regarded as suspicious.
C. Distinguish the optic disc changes of glaucoma from those of papilledema.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The normal optic disc has a pink rim (neuroretinal rim).

A(ii)
It has a pale central cup; the normal cup-to-disc ratio in a normal adult eye is approximately 0.3 or less.

A(iii)
The disc margins are normally distinct.

B.
A cup-to-disc ratio of 0.6 or above is suspicious for glaucomatous optic nerve damage, particularly when accompanied by notching of the neuroretinal rim, flame haemorrhages at the disc margin, or an asymmetry of more than 0.2 between the two eyes; the hallmark of glaucomatous damage is progressive cupping of the optic disc with loss of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, accompanied by characteristic visual field defects.

C.
Glaucoma produces progressive cupping of the optic disc, with an increasing cup-to-disc ratio and loss of the neuroretinal rim. Papilledema instead produces blurred, congested, and indistinct disc margins, beginning superiorly and inferiorly, with obliteration of the physiological cup, dilated veins, loss of the spontaneous venous pulse, and eventually flame-shaped haemorrhages around the disc; papilledema is bilateral and does not typically cause early vision loss, in contrast to glaucoma.

questions.question:
