A 45-year-old woman with known hyperthyroidism presents with progressive proptosis and diplopia on upgaze. Over recent weeks her visual acuity has dropped from 6/6 to 6/24 in the affected eye, and examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect.

(i) Identify the structure being compressed and the structures responsible for the compression.
(ii) State the extraocular muscle most characteristically and severely involved, and the finding this produces.
(iii) State the differential clinical sign that localises the redness of this condition to a specific site, distinguishing it from simple conjunctivitis.
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning connecting the exam findings to the diagnosis and the urgency of management, and state the first-line treatment for the active phase.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Enlarged, fibrotic extraocular muscles at the orbital apex compress the optic nerve, producing vision-threatening compressive optic neuropathy; this is a specific indication for orbital decompression surgery.

(ii)
The inferior rectus muscle is most commonly and most severely affected first, causing restriction of upgaze and vertical diplopia; the medial rectus is the second most commonly involved muscle.

(iii)
Injection and redness are characteristically located around the insertion of the recti muscles, distinguishing this from the diffuse conjunctival injection typical of conjunctivitis.

(iv)
The drop in visual acuity from 6/6 to 6/24 with a relative afferent pupillary defect indicates dysthyroid (compressive) optic neuropathy from the enlarged muscles compressing the optic nerve at the orbital apex - a vision-threatening complication requiring urgent treatment. This condition (thyroid eye disease/Graves' ophthalmopathy) is associated with hyperthyroidism in about 90% of cases. First-line treatment for the active inflammatory phase is high-dose systemic corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone); orbital decompression is reserved for vision-threatening compressive optic neuropathy or severe orbital congestion.

(i)
Retinoblastoma. Leucocoria (white pupillary reflex, "cat's eye reflex") is its most common presenting feature and is detected on the red reflex test; the incidence is approximately 1 in 15,000 live births.

(ii)
The family history and pattern described suggest the hereditary (germline) form; all bilateral cases and 15% of unilateral cases are hereditary. The responsible gene is the RB1 tumour suppressor gene, located at chromosome 13q14.

(iii)
Knudson's two-hit hypothesis: in the hereditary form, the first mutation is inherited through the germinal cells and is present in every cell of the body; the second mutation then occurs in somatic retinal cells to produce the tumour. The RB1 protein normally regulates the cell cycle by binding and inhibiting the E2F transcription factor; loss of both copies removes this inhibition, allowing uncontrolled retinal cell proliferation. Histology characteristically shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, representing true photoreceptor differentiation and specific to retinoblastoma.

(iv)
Management options include intra-arterial chemotherapy (via selective catheterisation of the ophthalmic artery through the internal carotid artery, for globe salvage) and enucleation (indicated for advanced unilateral tumours filling the vitreous with no visual potential). External beam radiotherapy is now rarely used because it increases the risk of second non-ocular tumours, particularly in germline RB1 mutation carriers. CT scanning of the orbits should be avoided in patients with germline RB1 mutations, because the ionising radiation increases the risk of second radiation-induced malignancies in these patients; MRI is preferred. Long-term follow-up is necessary in the hereditary form because of an increased lifetime risk of second non-ocular malignancies.
questions.question:
An 8-month-old infant is brought in after the parents noticed a white pupillary reflex in photographs. There is a family history of a similar eye tumour in a relative. The red reflex test confirms an absent red reflex in the affected eye.

(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing/genetic factor suggested by the family history and where the responsible gene is located.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology of this condition according to the two-hit hypothesis.
(iv) State the management options available, and the imaging modality that should be avoided and why.

A(i) Describe normal ocular flora under the headings: definition, origin/acquisition, composition, and its role in host defence.
A(ii) Describe host defence mechanisms of the eye under the headings: anatomical mechanisms and biochemical/immunological mechanisms.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis of microbacterial pathogenicity: define invasiveness, toxigenicity, and state the factors that enhance invasiveness.
B(ii) Distinguish between Gram-positive cocci and Gram-negative bacilli as causes of ocular infection: give two examples of each group, naming the specific ocular diseases they cause.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Normal ocular flora:
• Definition: Bacteria that colonise the eyelid margin and conjunctiva normally and beneficially; they reduce opportunities for pathogenic bacteria to cause infection.
• Origin/acquisition: The eye is sterile in utero but acquires normal flora during birth; flora is recurrently introduced from adjacent skin of the face, nose, and mouth.
• Composition: Mainly Staphylococcus epidermidis, S. aureus, Corynebacterium spp. and Propionibacterium acnes; with increasing age, Gram-negative bacteria also become part of the flora. The spectrum varies with age and geographic location.
• Role in defence: Interactions between the ocular surface mucosa and resident non-pathogenic bacteria reduce the opportunities for pathogenic bacteria to cause infection.

A(ii)
Host defence mechanisms:
Anatomical:
• Intact epithelium
• Eyelashes
• The blink reflex
• Tear production
• Desquamation of conjunctival and eyelid skin epithelial cells
Biochemical:
• Lipids (unsaturated and long-chained fatty acids)
• Lysozyme
• Lactoferrin
• Beta-lysin
Immunological:
• Complement system
• Immunoglobulins: IgA, IgE
• PMNs, macrophages, cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells

B(i)
Microbacterial pathogenicity:
• Virulence depends on invasiveness and toxigenicity.
• Invasiveness: the ability to enter the host, multiply, and spread; enhanced by: ability to adhere to target cells; amount of local tissue damage; production of hyaluronidase, coagulases, and haemolysins by the microorganism.
• Pathogenesis: Infection results when there is an imbalance between proliferation/invasive potential of microbes and defences of the host flora. Infection can occur via transplacental transmission, direct contact during delivery, fomites, fingers, airborne particles, sexual contact, or spread from adnexal or upper respiratory disease.

B(ii)
Gram-positive cocci vs Gram-negative bacilli:
Gram-positive cocci:
• Staphylococcus aureus: causes blepharitis, keratitis, endophthalmitis, panophthalmitis, orbital cellulitis.
• Streptococcus pneumoniae: causes dacryocystitis, conjunctivitis, hypopyon keratitis.
Gram-negative bacilli:
• Pseudomonas aeruginosa: causes hypopyon keratitis, endophthalmitis.
• Haemophilus influenzae: causes conjunctivitis, orbital cellulitis (especially in children).

questions.question:
A footballer sustains blunt trauma to the right eye during a match. He develops restricted upward eye movement, periorbital swelling, and the eye appears sunken.

(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the management indication and the imaging used to confirm it.
(iii) State the anatomical feature of the orbit that predisposes to this injury.
(iv) State the structure primarily at risk/entrapped.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Orbital floor fracture (blow-out fracture) with inferior rectus entrapment - producing restricted upgaze, vertical diplopia, enophthalmos, and periorbital emphysema/oedema.

(ii)
Immediate imaging (CT of the orbits) confirms the diagnosis; surgical repair is required if diplopia or enophthalmos is significant.

(iii)
Blunt orbital trauma can cause a blow-out fracture because the orbital floor is thin, allowing herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus below.

(iv)
The inferior rectus muscle is the structure primarily at risk, becoming herniated/entrapped in the fracture, which produces the restricted upward eye movement.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the conjunctiva — its parts, epithelial type and cell content — and state its functions.

B. State the signs and symptoms of conjunctival inflammation, and classify conjunctival infections by causative agent — listing specific organisms for each category.

C. Describe the pathology and management of vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), and explain why this condition is more common in certain climates and populations.
questions.answerText:
A.
The conjunctiva is a transparent (translucent) membrane covering the sclera and the inner surface of the eyelids. It has three parts:
• Bulbar conjunctiva: covers the sclera.
• Palpebral conjunctiva: lines the inner surface of the eyelids.
• Fornix: the cul-de-sac recess connecting bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva.
Epithelial type: non-keratinised squamous epithelium. Cell content includes goblet cells (which secrete the inner mucous layer of the tear film) and accessory lacrimal glands.
Functions: allows for ocular movement; contributes to moistening of the eye; protects the eye from pathogens via the tear film, lymphoid follicles and conjunctival lymphatics.

B.
Symptoms of conjunctival inflammation: redness, itching, discharge (mucoid in allergic disease, watery in viral disease, purulent in bacterial disease), foreign body sensation, gritty sensation.
Signs: redness, oedema, lid swelling, papillae, follicles, discharge, pre-auricular lymphadenopathy.
Classification by causative agent:
• Bacterial: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae; Gonococcal (Neisseria gonorrhoeae — hyperacute).
• Viral: adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis (serotypes 8, 11, 19 most common), molluscum contagiosum, herpes simplex.
• Chlamydial: trachoma, neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis, adult chlamydial keratoconjunctivitis.
• Allergic: simple allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, vernal keratoconjunctivitis, atopic keratoconjunctivitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis.

C.
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC): Recurrent bilateral condition affecting children and young adults; more common in males and in warm climates. Features: itching, mucoid discharge and lacrimation; frequently associated with atopy (asthma, hay fever and dermatitis). It is more common in warm climates because allergen exposure and the underlying atopic tendency are both heightened in such environments. Management: allergic conjunctivitis is treated with avoidance of allergens, antihistamines, mast cell stabilisers, and short courses of topical steroids. Artificial tears protect the epithelium. If the epithelium is ulcerated, topical steroid must be stopped, and systemic steroids used to treat associated iritis; keratoplasty may be considered for severe corneal scarring.

A(i)
Shape and walls: The orbit is pyramidal (pear-shaped). It is situated between the anterior cranial fossa above and the maxillary sinus below. Each orbit has a medial wall, lateral wall, roof (floor of anterior cranial fossa), floor (roof of maxillary sinus), base and apex. The floor is the weakest wall (most likely to be fractured in blunt ocular trauma). The medial wall is separated from the ethmoidal sinus by a paper-thin wall known as the lamina papyracea.

A(ii)
Foramina and fissures (non-exhaustive):
Key structure: the optic foramen is 18 mm posterior to the globe.
The superior ophthalmic vein drains to the cavernous sinus through the superior orbital fissure.

A(iii)
Contents: The eyeball/optic nerve occupies approximately one-fifth of the orbit. Other contents include extraocular muscles (EOM), ophthalmic vessels, lacrimal gland and nasolacrimal apparatus, ocular motor nerves (sensory, motor, sympathetic, parasympathetic), and orbital fascia and fat.

B.
The medial wall is separated from the ethmoidal sinus by the lamina papyracea — a paper-thin bony plate that easily allows direct transmission of pathogens from the ethmoidal sinus into the orbit. This is the most common route for orbital cellulitis.

C.
Thyroid eye disease (TED):
• Pathogenesis: autoimmune inflammatory disease; TSH-R stimulating IgG antibodies with cross-reactive TSH-R antigens expressed on orbital fibroblasts stimulate glycosaminoglycan deposition from fibroblasts (water retention) and adipogenesis, increasing orbital volume within a fixed bony space.
• Sex/age: F:M = 8:1; peak in females 40–44 and 60–64 years; in males 45–49 and 65–69 years.
• Clinical features: eyelid retraction (most common sign, >90%), exophthalmos (~60%), restrictive ophthalmopathy (~40%), optic nerve dysfunction (~6%); only about 5% have all classic signs with hyperthyroidism.
• Management: self-limiting with exacerbations and remissions; supportive care with topical lubricants; steroids and radiotherapy to decrease inflammation; surgical orbital decompression to expand orbital bony volume. Smoking worsens prognosis.
Orbital pseudotumour:
• Pathogenesis: idiopathic orbital inflammation.
• Sex/age: affects middle-aged individuals.
• Clinical features: pain, proptosis, restrictive myopathy.
• Management: steroids, radiotherapy, cytotoxic drugs.
questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the bony orbit under the following headings:
A(i) Shape, walls and their relationship to adjacent sinuses.
A(ii) Foramina and fissures, and the structures that pass through each.
A(iii) Contents of the orbit.

B. Explain the clinical basis of why the medial wall of the orbit is particularly susceptible to transmitting infection from the adjacent sinus.

C. Distinguish between thyroid eye disease (TED) and orbital pseudotumour — in terms of pathogenesis, clinical features, sex and age predilection, and management.

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the anterior chamber angle, naming all the normal angle structures visible on gonioscopy from anterior to posterior.
A(ii) Explain how the configuration of the anterior chamber angle forms the basis for classifying glaucoma, and state what gonioscopy reveals in each major type.
B(i) Explain how the pathology of angle closure differs from that of open angle glaucoma, linking the difference to aqueous dynamics.
B(ii) Describe how secondary glaucoma differs from primary glaucoma, and give four causes of secondary glaucoma.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Normal angle structures visible on gonioscopy, from anterior to posterior:
• Schwalbe's line — the termination of Descemet's membrane and the beginning of the trabecular meshwork.
• Trabecular meshwork — the major outflow structure, divided into a pigmented and non-pigmented portion.
• Scleral spur — a white ridge projecting inward, marking the posterior limit of the trabecular meshwork.
• Ciliary body band — the most posterior visible structure, brownish-grey in colour.
(Gonioscopy is the clinical method of examination of anterior chamber angle structures.)

A(ii)
Classification based on angle configuration:
• Open angle glaucoma: on gonioscopy the angle is fully open; reduced drainage occurs through the trabecular meshwork despite the open angle (e.g., POAG). Commoner after age 40 years; usually asymptomatic.
• Angle closure glaucoma: the angle is narrowed or closed; the peripheral iris apposes or fuses with the trabecular meshwork, preventing aqueous drainage. In acute angle closure, the angle is completely closed.
• Gonioscopy grading: Grades 0–IV (0 = closed, IV = wide open).

B(i)
In open angle glaucoma, aqueous can reach the trabecular meshwork (angle is open), but resistance within the meshwork is increased; IOP rises gradually. In angle closure, the peripheral iris physically blocks the trabecular meshwork, preventing aqueous from even reaching the outflow pathway; IOP rises rapidly and severely.

B(ii)
Primary glaucomas usually affect both eyes and are not associated with known ocular or systemic disorders that cause increased resistance to aqueous outflow or angle closure.
Secondary glaucomas are associated with ocular or systemic disorders responsible for decreased aqueous outflow; they are often asymmetric or unilateral.
Four causes of secondary glaucoma:
• Exfoliative glaucoma
• Pigmentary glaucoma
• Steroid-induced glaucoma
• Neovascular glaucoma (e.g., from diabetes or CRVO)

questions.question:
A(i) State the origin of the parasympathetic pathway for the pupillary light reflex.
A(ii) Describe its course to the ciliary ganglion.
A(iii) State its distribution via the short ciliary nerves.
C. Explain the anatomical basis for why some third nerve palsies spare the pupil while others involve it.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The parasympathetic supply to the pupil for the light reflex originates in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain.

A(ii)
Fibres from this nucleus travel with the oculomotor nerve (CN III) to synapse in the ciliary ganglion.

A(iii)
Postganglionic fibres travel via the short ciliary nerves to supply the iris sphincter muscle (causing miosis) and the ciliary muscle (causing accommodation).

C.
The parasympathetic fibres run on the outer surface of CN III and are particularly vulnerable to compression. In a "medical" (ischaemic) third nerve palsy, ischaemia affects the inner core fibres while the outer parasympathetic fibres remain intact, so the pupil is spared. In a "surgical" (compressive) palsy, such as from an aneurysm, the outer pupillary fibres are compressed first, so the pupil is involved. Because of this, whether the pupil is involved is the first clinical determination made when evaluating a third nerve palsy, and a painful, pupil-involving palsy warrants urgent neuroimaging for a compressive aneurysm.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the viral organisms causing eye disease under the headings: organism name, serotype (where applicable), and the specific ocular disease caused by each.
A(ii) Describe the fungal organisms causing eye disease: name the organisms, the diseases they cause, and the laboratory diagnostic methods used for each.
B(i) Explain the Gram stain technique step by step, identifying what each step achieves and what the final result means for classifying bacteria.
B(ii) Describe how infection of the ocular surface occurs, specifying all routes of transmission, and explain why an imbalance between the host and microbial factors leads to clinical infection.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Viral organisms causing eye disease:
• Herpes simplex type 1: facial vesicles, keratitis, retinitis.
• Herpes simplex type 2: keratitis.
• Varicella zoster: eyelid vesicles, keratitis, episcleritis, retinitis.
• Cytomegalovirus (CMV): retinitis.
• Adenovirus serotypes 3, 7, 11: pharyngoconjunctival fever.
• Adenovirus serotypes 8, 11, 19: epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC).
• Measles virus: keratitis, uveitis, associated vitamin deficiency.
• Rubella: microphthalmia, cataract, retinopathy.
• HIV: microangiopathy, opportunistic infections, Kaposi Sarcoma, Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

A(ii)
Fungal organisms causing eye disease:
• Aspergillus spp: orbital Aspergilloma, endophthalmitis, optic neuropathy.
• Mucor spp / Rhizopus spp: rhino-orbital phycomycosis.
• Candida spp: endophthalmitis, hypopyon, chorioretinitis.
• Cryptococcus neoformans: endophthalmitis, retrobulbar neuritis.
• Histoplasma capsulatum: chorioretinitis.
• Other fungal organisms: Fusarium solani, Aspergillus flavus, Candida albicans, Mucor mucorales.
Laboratory diagnosis of fungi: Clinical characteristics; morphology (hyphae, asexual spores, spore-bearing structures); Gram staining to accentuate morphology; culture on Sabouraud's agar or Brain-heart infusion broth.

B(i)
Gram stain technique (step by step):
• Flood slide with crystal violet for 30 seconds (stains purple).
• Rinse with water gently.
• Flood with Lugol's iodine for 30 seconds (turns brown).
• Rinse with water.
• Tilt slightly and decolourise with ethanol-acetone until stain ceases to wash off.
• Rinse with water.
• Counter-stain with Carbol fuchsin/neutral red for 30 seconds.
• Rinse with water.
• Blot dry — take care not to smudge.
• Examine under low and high powers.
Result: Gram-positive bacteria retain the purple crystal violet stain; Gram-negative bacteria are decolourised and take up the red counter-stain.

B(ii)
Routes of transmission of ocular surface infection:
• Transplacental transmission.
• Direct contact during delivery.
• Exposure from fomites.
• Fingers.
• Airborne particles.
• Sexual contact.
• Spread from adnexal or upper respiratory disease.
Mechanism of infection: Infection results when there is an imbalance between
• proliferation of the microbes and the invasive potential of the microbes
• the defences by other microbes that make up the flora and the host. When pathogen virulence exceeds host defence capacity, clinical infection ensues.

(i)
Two co-existing pathologies:
• Hyphema (haemorrhage into the anterior chamber) — from blunt trauma.
• Blow-out fracture of the orbital floor — with entrapment of the inferior rectus/orbital contents.

(ii)
Mechanisms and structures injured:
• Hyphema: Severe blunt trauma causes antero-posterior compression with simultaneous equatorial expansion and a transient but severe increase in IOP. Bleeding is from the vessels of the peripheral iris or anterior ciliary body. The anterior chamber fills with blood ranging from a microscopic haze to complete filling.
• Blow-out fracture: Blunt trauma to the orbit increases intraorbital pressure, fracturing the thinnest orbital wall (floor). The most common sites of rupture are in a circumferential arc parallel to the corneal limbus at the insertion of the rectus muscles, or in the orbital bones especially the medial wall and floor. Entrapment of the medial rectus leads to defective adduction and abduction.

(iii)
Grading of hyphema:
• Grade 0: RBCs (microhyphema, detectable only with slit-lamp)
• Grade I: Blood fills less than 1/3 of the anterior chamber
• Grade II: Blood fills 1/3 to 1/2 of the anterior chamber
• Grade III: Blood fills more than 1/2 of the anterior chamber
• Grade IV: Eight-ball hyphema (total filling)
Approximately 20% of all hyphemas rebleed, typically at 3–4 days after the initial bleed; rebleeding carries a worse prognosis than the primary bleed.

(iv)
Emergency management priorities:
• Restrict activity/play; shield the eye.
• Refer immediately for specialist care.
• If no signs of orbital fracture or optic neuropathy: rest, analgesics, cold compresses to control oedema and discomfort.
• Patient must NOT blow the nose — because if the sinuses are injured, blowing forces infected sinus contents into the orbit, leading to orbital cellulitis.
• For retrobulbar haemorrhage (acute pain, proptosis, resistance to retropulsion, afferent pupillary defect): emergent lateral canthotomy is required; refer for high-dose IV steroids.
• Immediately refer patients with orbital fractures.

(v)
Anatomical basis:
• Blow-out fracture of the orbital floor causes entrapment of orbital contents (including the inferior rectus muscle and/or perimuscular fat) within the fracture site.
• The trapped inferior rectus cannot function normally; restricted upward gaze (limitation of elevation) results from mechanical restriction of the entrapped inferior rectus.
• Enophthalmos (posterior displacement of the globe) occurs because the bony orbital volume is increased by the fracture, and herniation of orbital fat reduces the retrobulbar support of the globe.
questions.question:
A 22-year-old male is brought to casualty after being struck in the right eye with a squash ball. He reports pain, reduced vision, and double vision. On examination: ecchymosis of right eyelid, subconjunctival haemorrhage, blood visible in the anterior chamber, restricted upward gaze, and enophthalmos. Plain X-ray of orbit shows a floor fracture. IOP is elevated on the right.

(i) Identify the two co-existing pathologies, naming each precisely.
(ii) For each pathology, state the mechanism and the specific ocular structures injured, using the standard classification of blunt trauma complications.
(iii) State the grading system used for the anterior chamber blood collection, and what percentage of such cases rebleed and when.
(iv) Enumerate the emergency management priorities for this patient, including what the patient must be instructed NOT to do and why.
(v) Explain the anatomical basis of the restricted upward gaze and enophthalmos.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Chemical burn from an alkali agent - domestic alkali burns from detergents and disinfectants are the most common type of domestic chemical eye injury. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis, allowing continued deep tissue penetration even after initial exposure has ended, giving alkali burns a worse prognosis than acid burns (which cause coagulative necrosis, forming a protective barrier that limits further penetration).

(ii)
Immediate and copious irrigation with water or normal saline at the scene, before any other intervention, is the single most important first-aid step; irrigation should be maintained until the patient reaches an ophthalmologist.

(iii)
Debridement of necrotic tissue is performed because necrotic tissue perpetuates inflammation and impairs epithelial healing. Intense topical steroid therapy is recommended in the first week (it inhibits the acute leukocyte inflammatory reaction in the corneal stroma), but is avoided in the 2nd-3rd week (as it may impair collagen synthesis needed for healing), and may be resumed after the 3rd week. A bandage contact lens protects the migrating ocular surface epithelium and reduces pain from exposed corneal nerves. The overall objective of therapy is to prevent secondary corneal inflammation, ulceration, and infection.
questions.question:
A patient presents with a red, painful eye and blurred vision shortly after a household alkali (detergent) splash to the eye.

(i) State the diagnosis and the pathological basis of the tissue damage caused.
(ii) State the first and most critical resuscitative management step.
