questions.answerText:
A(i)
The sympathetic nerve fibres serving the face, eye, and eyelids originate in the hypothalamus and travel to the C8–T2 level of the spinal cord. Second order neurons (pre-ganglionic) leave the cord and travel over the lung apex to the subclavian and carotid arteries; these fibres terminate in the superior cervical ganglion. Third order neurons (post-ganglionic) leave the ganglion and travel with the internal carotid artery to enter the skull, course through the cavernous sinus, and enter the orbit with the ophthalmic artery and ciliary nerves.

A(ii)
Horner's Syndrome features: 1. Ptosis; 2. Miosis; 3. Hypochromia; 4. Anhydrosis. Pre-ganglionic causes: lung apex tumour (Pancoast's tumour); mediastinal mass; neck lesions (thyroidectomy, thyroid neoplasm, trauma, lymphadenopathy). Post-ganglionic causes: migraine variants (cluster headache, Raeder's syndrome); cavernous sinus or orbital lesion; internal artery dissection; carotid-cavernous fistula; nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

B(i)
These sympathetic fibres allow pupil dilation and cause eyelid opening of about 2–3 mm; disruption at any level causes the opposite — miosis and ptosis. Hypochromia of the iris reflects loss of sympathetic control of melanin distribution.

B(ii)
Pre-ganglionic causes originate from C8–T2 and affect the lung apex/neck region; post-ganglionic causes follow the internal carotid artery. Pupillary involvement is key: a pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in an older patient with diabetes/hypertension indicates ischaemic demyelination, whereas pupil involvement suggests compressive lesion requiring urgent neuroimaging.
questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, and clinical significance of the oculosympathetic pathway, including the anatomical basis of the deformity after injury and the safe interpretation of clinical signs.

A(i) Describe the origin and three-neuron course of the sympathetic nerve fibres serving the eye and eyelids.
A(ii) List the features of the clinical syndrome that results from disruption of this pathway and its causes by level.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the features of this syndrome.
B(ii) Distinguish pre-ganglionic from post-ganglionic causes and explain the importance of pupillary involvement in localizing a lesion.

A(i) Describe the aim, anatomical basis, and mechanism of action of trabeculectomy (guarded fistula) for lowering IOP, including the role of the scleral flap and the bleb.
A(ii) Outline the pre-operative management of a glaucoma patient before trabeculectomy, covering all the steps.
B(i) Describe the post-operative management of a patient following trabeculectomy, including what features to assess, how to monitor the bleb, and how to manage post-operative IOP spikes.
B(ii) Enumerate the early and late complications of filtration surgery, naming the most disastrous late complication and explaining why it is so serious.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Aim, anatomy, and mechanism:
• Aim: To create an alternate route of drainage to the episcleral veins through a subconjunctival reservoir (bleb).
• Mechanism: A guarded fistula (opening) is created through the limbal sclera (under a partial-thickness scleral flap/trapdoor). Aqueous drains from the anterior chamber → through the fistula in the trabecular meshwork → under the scleral flap → into the subconjunctival bleb → absorbed into the episcleral venous system, bypassing the blocked TM.
• The bleb overlies the trapdoor-like scleral flap opening; a peripheral iridectomy is created to prevent iris from blocking the internal ostium.
• Antimetabolites (5-FU, Mitomycin C) are added to prevent scarring/fibrosis of the bleb.

A(ii)
Pre-operative management:
• Confirm diagnosis and severity (IOP, gonioscopy, visual fields).
• Ensure pre-operative documentation of all clinical details.
• Obtain informed consent (risks, benefits, expected outcomes of surgery).
• Cross-check IOP; confirm need for surgery.
• Control excessively high IOPs (ideally IOP should be <35 mmHg before surgery).
• Stop miotics a few days before surgery (to reduce bleeding and post-operative inflammation).
• Usually do NOT dilate trabeculectomy patients (unlike cataract patients).

B(i)
Post-operative management:
• Monitor IOP at every visit.
• Assess integrity of the bleb (should be relatively avascular, raised, and diffuse).
• Assess anterior chamber depth.
• Perform Seidel's test to exclude leakage at the conjunctival edge.
• Control inflammation with steroids initially 4–6× daily for at least 2 months.
• Manage peri-operative IOP spikes with: massaging of bleb, suture lysis, adjustable sutures, bleb revision, needling of bleb, and/or additional medication.
• Patient needs lifetime follow-up (lifetime risk of endophthalmitis through bleb/fistula).

B(ii)
Complications of filtration surgery:
Early complications:
• Conjunctival button-hole (predisposing to leaking bleb)
• Shallow anterior chamber (from overfiltration, aqueous misdirection or leaking bleb)
• Hyphaema
Late complications:
• Polycystic bleb (prone to rupture from mild trauma)
• Blebitis (bleb infection)
• Endophthalmitis — the most disastrous complication; the entire eye may be lost because endophthalmitis can progress to panophthalmitis, destroying all intraocular structures. The bleb/fistula provides a permanent route for bacteria to enter the eye throughout the patient's lifetime.

questions.question:
A young man presents 6 hours after a stick injury to the eye. Examination reveals a corneo-scleral laceration with uveal tissue prolapsed at the wound, and no exit wound is found. Visual acuity in both eyes is recorded at presentation.

(i) State the diagnosis, its classification/grade, and whether it is a penetrating or perforating injury.
(ii) State the surgical procedure indicated and the specific technique used at this stage of presentation.
(iv) State the structure/complication at risk if repair is delayed or the wound is mishandled.
questions.answerText:
(i)
This is a Grade 1 corneo-scleral laceration (Eagling classification), involving uveal prolapse in the anterior segment. Because there is only an entry wound with no exit wound, it is classified as a penetrating injury (a perforating injury has both an entry and an exit wound).

(ii)
As presentation is within 24 hours, the uveal prolapse should be repositioned and the laceration repaired, suturing the cornea with 10-0 nylon. (If presentation were beyond 24 hours, the prolapsed uvea would instead be excised before wound closure to prevent infection.) Visual acuity of both eyes must be recorded at first examination for medicolegal documentation.

(iv)
Delayed or mishandled repair risks infection, hypotony, and sympathetic ophthalmia - a rare, feared, bilateral granulomatous uveitis that can occur in the uninjured eye following penetrating trauma with uveal tissue disruption, particularly with delayed repair.

A(i)
The macula/posterior pole is the central retinal zone where diabetic macular oedema and the macular star of hypertensive retinopathy occur.

A(ii)
The peripheral retina is the zone where ischaemia-driven neovascularisation characteristically develops.

B.
At the macula/posterior pole: diabetic macular oedema (from capillary permeability changes) is the most common cause of visual impairment in diabetic patients, particularly type 2 diabetics; the macular star of Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy forms from hard exudates accumulating in the outer plexiform layer, radiating from the fovea. At the periphery: retinal ischaemia stimulates neovascularisation - "new vessels at the disc" (NVD) or "new vessels elsewhere" (NVE) in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and "sea-fan" neovascularisation arising from peripheral arteriovenous anastomoses in sickle cell retinopathy. Cotton wool spots (ischaemic infarction of nerve fibre layer axons) and microaneurysms (localised outpouchings of capillary walls where pericytes are absent) may be seen in either zone and are pre-proliferative/early signs.

C.
Severe retinal ischaemia triggers excessive VEGF production, which diffuses anteriorly from the retina to stimulate neovascularisation on the iris (rubeosis iridis) and the trabecular meshwork. This leads to neovascular glaucoma, a devastating complication with markedly elevated intraocular pressure due to angle occlusion by fibrovascular tissue, which is extremely difficult to treat and often results in blindness.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the retina under the zones: (i) macula/posterior pole, (ii) peripheral retina.
B. State how pathology at each zone characteristically presents in retinal vascular disease.
C. Explain how disease in the retina can spread to a distant structure (the iris) and the serious complication this produces.

questions.answerText:
A.
Visual acuity (VA) is a measure of the visual perceptive ability of the eye. It depends on:
• the focusing (dioptric) mechanism of the eye
• retinal status
• the optic nerve
• central nervous system mechanisms.
VA is measured by the smallest object which can be clearly seen at a certain distance (usually 6 metres or 20 feet by convention).
Optical principle: For two separate points to be distinguished by the retina, two individual cones must be stimulated while the area between them remains unstimulated. The average diameter of a cone in the macular region is 0.004 mm; a normal eye appreciates a retinal image of 0.004 mm. An object must subtend a visual angle of 1 minute of arc to produce such an image. Snellen letters are designed so that their edges subtend a visual angle of 1 minute of arc at a specified distance.
Chart design: the largest line is read at 60 m, subsequent lines at 36, 24, 18, 12, 9, 6 and 5 m respectively.
Results expressed as a fraction: numerator = patient's distance from chart; denominator = the smallest line seen. Normal vision at 6 m = 6/6. If unable to read from 6 m, distance is reduced to 3 m, 1 m, then recorded as counting fingers (CF), hand movements (HM), or light perception (LP).

B.
Requirements for accurate VA measurement:
• Even illumination of the chart.
• VA of each eye tested separately.
• Corrective spectacles for each eye should be worn.
• Pin-hole test of each eye.
• Careful instruction of the patient.
Test types: Snellen, E-chart, Landolt's C (adults); pictorial charts, Sheridan-Gardiner, Worth's ivory ball test, preferential looking with optokinetic disc (for children).
Pinhole test: The pinhole theoretically allows only one ray of light from each point of an object to pass through the principal axis to the retina, forming a clear image regardless of the refractive state. If VA improves with pinhole, the reduction is due to refractive error; no improvement suggests ocular pathology or neurological disease.

C.
Visual handicap: defined as a reduction of VA or field of vision such that a person is unable to adequately carry out their normal daily activities. Normal range of vision is 6/5–6/18.
WHO categories:
• Category 0: VA ≥ 6/18 — normal vision.
• Category 1: VA <6/18 to ≥6/60 — visual impairment.
• Category 2: VA <6/60 to ≥3/60 (CF at 3 m) — severe visual impairment.
• Category 3: VA <3/60 to ≥1/60 (CF at 1 m) — blind.
• Category 4: VA <1/60 to light perception — blind.
• Category 5: No light perception — blind.
• Visual field: If the central visual field (CVF) is <10 degrees but >5 degrees around fixation, the patient is in category 3. If CVF <5 degrees around fixation, the patient is in category 4.
questions.question:
A. Describe visual acuity (VA) measurement using the Snellen chart — including the definition of VA, the optical principle underlying the chart, how results are expressed, and the test distance used.

B. State all the requirements for accurate VA measurement and explain the role of the pinhole test in distinguishing refractive error from ocular pathology.

C. Define visual handicap, state the WHO categories of visual impairment with their corresponding VA ranges, and explain the role of visual field in categorising a patient's level of disability.

A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency unit after his eye was struck by a sharp broom stick while sweeping. On examination, visual acuity is reduced in the affected eye, there is a visible corneo-scleral laceration, and the lens appears damaged.

(i) What is the diagnosis and how is this injury classified under the Eaglings classification system?
(ii) What is the mechanism and what activities commonly lead to this type of injury?
(iii) Describe the specific surgical management appropriate to this grade.
(iv) State the visual prognosis for each grade of injury.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Penetrating eye injury (Grade 2 — corneo-scleral laceration with lens damage). Eaglings classification: Grade 1 — corneo-scleral laceration + uveal (UV) prolapse, usually in the anterior part; Grade 2 — corneo-scleral laceration with lens damage; Grade 3 — injury confined to the posterior segment, around limbus + vitreous loss; Grade 4 — combination of anterior and posterior segment (with corneo-scleral laceration, lens damage, and vitreous loss) — collapsed globe, most severe form.

(ii)
Mechanism: a penetrating eye injury has entry into the globe. In adults, common causes include RTA windshield and broken spectacles; in children, mostly sharp toys and broom sticks. 75% of injuries occur in people <30 years of age; 1/3 are children <10 years of age; males more affected than females because males are more active and adventurous.

(iii)
Surgical management Grade 2: if minimal or no capsule rupture, leave lens alone during primary repair; if capsule is damaged, attempt to aspirate/mop up remaining lens matter (SLM) and repair laceration. Suture laceration with 10 nylon for cornea.

(iv)
Visual prognosis: Grade 1 — excellent; Grade 2 — fair; Grade 3 — poor; Grade 4 — poor.

(i)
Diagnosis: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation burn to the eyes (photokeratitis / arc eye / welder's flash).

(ii)
Source of injury: Welding arc — ultraviolet radiation is the most common cause of light-induced ocular injury.
All sources of this type of radiation:
• Welding arcs.
• Carbon arcs.
Prevention note: Ultraviolet burns may be prevented by use of ordinary crown glass or regular glass lenses (or UV-protective lenses) as they absorb the UV rays.

(iii)
Full clinical presentation and structures affected:
Symptoms (range from mild to severe):
• Mild irritation and foreign body sensation.
• Severe photophobia, pain, and spasm of the lids (blepharospasm).
Signs on examination:
• Varying lid oedema.
• Conjunctival hyperaemia.
• Punctate roughening of the corneal epithelium, which stains with fluorescein.
Structures affected:
• Corneal epithelium: punctate damage (the primary structure affected in UV burns).
• Conjunctiva: hyperaemia.
• Lids: oedema and blepharospasm.
• Lens: UV radiation damages the lens and leads to cataract formation.
• Note: UV radiation does NOT damage the retina (unlike visible and infrared radiation).

(iv)
Emergency management:
• Topical anaesthetic drops to allow examination and reduce pain.
• Antibiotic ointment to prevent secondary infection.
• Cycloplegic drops to reduce ciliary spasm and pain.
• Patching of the eye (24-hour follow-up is mandatory for corneal abrasion/UV injury).
• Analgesics for pain relief.
• Reassurance — the condition is usually self-limiting and recovers within 24–48 hours with epithelial regeneration.

(v)
Chronic infrared exposure:
• Chronic exposure to infrared (IR) light is seen in glass blowers and metal furnace stokers.
• These workers develop cataract after many years of exposure (infrared cataract/glassblower's cataract).
• Acute infrared burns are usually of little consequence and produce only temporary lid oedema and erythema, with little or no damage to the globe.
• Other signs: conjunctival hyperaemia, circum-corneal injection, watering, and mucopurulent discharge.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old welding apprentice presents with bilateral eye pain, intense photophobia, foreign body sensation, and inability to open his eyes, approximately 4 hours after welding without protective goggles. On slit-lamp examination, punctate staining of the corneal epithelium with fluorescein is seen bilaterally, and conjunctival hyperaemia is noted.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What is the source of injury in this case, and list all the sources of this type of radiation?
(iii) Describe the full clinical presentation, and what anatomical structures are affected?
(iv) Outline the emergency management of this patient.
(v) Describe the ocular effects of chronic infrared exposure and who is at risk.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Refractive errors (myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism, presbyopia) result in an unfocussed image falling on the retina. Refractive errors affect persons of all ages and ethnic groups; they are the main cause of vision impairment.

A(ii)
Epidemiological burden: there are estimated to be 153 million people with visual impairment due to uncorrected refractive errors (presenting visual acuity <6/18 in the better eye, excluding presbyopia). Globally, uncorrected refractive errors are the main cause of vision impairment in children aged 5–15 years. The prevalence of myopia (short-sightedness) is increasing dramatically among children, particularly in urban areas of South-East Asia. Refractive error is the 4th most important cause of blindness (definition <3/60) and an important cause of blindness after ARMD (46%) and glaucoma (17%).

B(i)
Options for correcting refractive errors: spectacles — the simplest, cheapest, and most widely used method; contact lenses — not suitable for all patients or environments; corneal refractive surgery — entails reshaping the cornea by laser. Uncorrected refractive errors are increasingly being addressed in national plans for the prevention of blindness; low-cost, good-quality spectacles are becoming available.

B(ii)
Vision 2020 strategy: aim — to eliminate avoidable visual impairment due to uncorrected refractive errors and reduce the magnitude of uncorrected presbyopia. Strategy — establish comprehensive eye-care services so that refraction services with provision of suitable correction tools are available at all levels, including during outreach activities. Consequences of uncorrected refractive errors: lost education and employment opportunities; lower productivity; impaired quality of life. The VISION 2020 global initiative intensively promotes awareness of the extent of uncorrected refractive errors and the means for correcting them.
questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the eye relevant to refractive errors, how refractive errors relate to common pathologies in different age groups, and explain why uncorrected refractive errors spread their functional impact to education and employment.

A(i) Define refractive errors and name the four types with a brief description of each.
A(ii) Describe the epidemiological burden of refractive errors globally and in children.
B(i) Describe the options available for correcting refractive errors.
B(ii) Explain the Vision 2020 strategy for addressing refractive errors and state the functional consequences of leaving them uncorrected.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Presbyopia — defined as loss of accommodation with age. Refractive mechanism: Accommodation is the ability of the eye to increase its dioptric (converging) power so that near objects are seen clearly. In the accommodated state, the ciliary muscles contract, releasing tension on the zonules, and the elastic lens returns to a more rounded shape suitable for near vision. In the resting state, when the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the zonules pull tight, keeping the lens flattened for distant vision. With ageing, the elasticity of the lens decreases, reducing the ability to change shape.

(ii)
Predisposing factors and progressive anatomical changes: There is gradual loss of power of accommodation with age. The infant is capable of 14 dioptres of accommodation, but this drops gradually to about 4 dioptres at age 45 years, resulting in increasing difficulty seeing near objects after age 40–45 years. The lens nucleus scleroses with ageing (increased weight, thickness and hardening), reducing its flexibility; the ciliary muscle weakens over time.

(iii)
Correcting lens: A convergent (convex/converging) lens is used for reading. Optical principle: the convergent lens of power equal to the weakness in accommodation is used to bring near objects to a focus on the retina instead of behind it.

(iv)
Management: The purpose of the correcting lens is to deviate rays from near objects so that they focus on the retina. Reading addition (near add) is calculated as: the dioptric power required = the dioptric loss in accommodation. Patients are prescribed ready-made or custom reading spectacles. The near add increases as presbyopia progresses with age. The pin-hole test helps confirm that any additional reduced distance acuity is due to refractive error and not ocular pathology.
questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents complaining that he cannot read fine print and has to hold books further away than he used to. He is otherwise emmetropic (no distance refractive error). He is told he needs reading glasses for the first time.

(i) State the diagnosis, defining the refractive mechanism and physiological process that explains this change with age.
(ii) List the predisposing factors and the progressive anatomical changes in the lens and ciliary apparatus that lead to this condition.
(iii) State the appropriate correcting lens and the optical principle of correction.
(iv) State the management including the lens power calculation principle used to select the correct reading addition.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Pathogenesis of hypertensive eye disease:
Two main vascular mechanisms:
• Microvascular occlusion:
• Basement membrane thickening.
• Compromise of luminal area.
• Reduction of blood flow, therefore reduction in perfusion.
• Resulting in ischaemia.
• Microvascular leakage:
• Decrease in number and integrity of endothelial cells.
• Reduction in the number of pericytes (which are wrapped around capillaries and are responsible for structural integrity of the vessel wall).
• Distension of capillary walls and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, leading to leakage of plasma constituents into the retina.
• Consequence: haemorrhages, diffuse or localised retinal oedema, and deposition of hard exudates.

A(ii)
Modified Scheie's Classification of Hypertensive Retinopathy:
• Grade 0: No changes.
• Grade 1: Barely detectable arterial narrowing.
• Grade 2: Obvious arterial narrowing with focal irregularities (copper wire appearance, unusual AV crossing, microaneurysms).
• Grade 3: Grade 2 + hard exudates, haemorrhages, soft exudates (silver wire appearance).
• Grade 4: Grade 3 + optic disc swelling (papilloedema).

B(i)
Mechanisms of arteriolar changes:
• Hypertension is basically an arteriolar disease affecting fine arteriolar vessels on the retina.
• The arteriolar wall thickens and becomes brittle.
• Cracks occur in the walls — leading to leakage of blood and plasma.
• The lumen becomes progressively narrower.
• Eventually occlusion occurs.
• Deposition of high cholesterol compounds (as in atherosclerosis) further complicates the picture.
• Narrowing + occlusion = ischaemia.

B(ii)
Most common retinal findings and their basis:
• Generalised/focal arterial constriction: from arteriolar wall thickening and smooth muscle hypertrophy.
• Haemorrhages: leakage of blood through cracked vessel walls (flame-shaped from superficial layers, dot/blot from deeper layers).
• Hard exudates: leakage of serum lipoproteins that accumulate in the outer plexiform layer.
• Soft exudates (cotton wool spots): ischaemia leading to degeneration/swelling of axons (coagulative necrosis of the nerve fibre layer).
• Retinal oedema: increased vascular permeability.
• Papilloedema: ischaemia and leakage at the optic disc.
• Other vascular accidents: CRAO, CRVO, BRVO from occlusion.
• Traction bands and retinal detachment (in severe/chronic hypertension).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the pathogenesis of hypertensive eye disease, explaining the two main vascular mechanisms that produce retinal changes.
A(ii) Describe the Modified Scheie's Classification of hypertensive retinopathy, stating the features at each grade.
B(i) Explain why the retinal vessels in hypertension undergo the specific changes described, linking arteriolar wall thickening, lumen changes, and the blood-retinal barrier.
B(ii) State the most common retinal findings in hypertension and describe how ischaemia and leakage produce each retinal lesion type.

A(i) Describe prostaglandin analogues under the headings: mechanism of action, examples, ocular side effects, systemic side effects, and dosing frequency.
A(ii) Describe beta-adrenergic antagonists used in glaucoma under the headings: mechanism of action, types (selective vs non-selective), examples of each, ocular side effects, and systemic side effects.
B(i) Describe carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs) in glaucoma management: mechanism of action, formulations (oral and topical), examples, and special precautions relevant to patients with diabetes and those sensitive to sulphonamides.
B(ii) Distinguish between hyperosmotic agents and parasympathomimetics (miotics) in terms of mechanism, examples, ocular side effects, and their specific roles in acute glaucoma management.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Prostaglandin analogues:
• Mechanism: Increase uveoscleral outflow by acting at the FP receptor; also increase trabecular outflow (some agents).
• Examples: Latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost, unoprostone.
• Ocular side effects: Iris and hair pigmentation; cystoid macular oedema; conjunctival hyperaemia; burning/stinging; itching; tearing; periocular skin pigmentation; eyelash growth; uveitis; keratitis.
• Systemic side effects: Flu-like symptoms; muscle pain; headaches; joint pain; hypertension.
• Dosing frequency: Once daily; effective diurnal control of IOP.

A(ii)
Beta-adrenergic antagonists (beta-blockers):
• Mechanism: Reduce aqueous production by blocking beta-adrenergic receptors in the ciliary epithelium.
• Types: Non-selective (affect B1 and B2 receptors): Carteolol, levobunolol, metipranolol, Timolol; B1-selective (cardioselective): Betaxolol.
• Ocular side effects: Burning, redness, dry eye.
• Systemic side effects: Reduced heart rate/heart block; bronchospasm (non-selective agents); may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms (important in diabetics — do NOT use non-selective beta-blockers in diabetics on insulin/oral agents without caution).
• Note: Loss of IOP-lowering efficacy with prolonged use (due to upregulation of beta-adrenergic receptors) often requiring adjunctive therapy.

B(i)
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs):
• Mechanism: Reduce aqueous production by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body, producing acidosis that decreases aqueous secretion.
• Formulations: Oral — acetazolamide (Diamox), methazolamide; Topical — dorzolamide 2% (Trusopt), brinzolamide 1%.
• Systemic side effects: Diuresis, muscle cramps, paraesthesia, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, anaemia with thrombocytopenia.
• Special precautions: Acetazolamide should be used with caution in patients sensitive to sulphonamides (cross-reactivity). In diabetic patients, acetazolamide may result in metabolic acidosis — use with caution. Avoid in significant renal failure.

B(ii)
Hyperosmotic agents vs Miotics (Parasympathomimetics):
Hyperosmotic agents:
• Mechanism: Osmotically dehydrate the vitreous by increasing plasma osmolality, drawing water out of the eye, thereby reducing IOP acutely.
• Examples: Mannitol (IV), glycerol (oral).
• Side effects: Rebound rise in IOP; expansion of blood volume; headache.
• Role: Acute emergency reduction of IOP (e.g., in acute angle closure glaucoma, pre-operatively).
Miotics (Parasympathomimetics):
• Mechanism: Increase trabecular aqueous outflow by contracting the ciliary muscle which opens the trabecular lamellae and widens the Schlemm's canal drainage pathway.
• Examples: Pilocarpine 2%, 4%; carbachol.
• Ocular side effects: Brow ache, miosis, iris cysts, risk of retinal detachment.
• Systemic side effects: Increased secretions, abdominal cramps.
• Role in acute angle closure: Gutt pilocarpine every 15 minutes until the pupil is responsive (mild to moderate attacks only); stronger miotics avoided in severe attacks as the iris will be ischaemic and unresponsive.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the sympathetic pathway supplying the eye under the following headings: order of neuron, origin, and the course/structures traversed by each order.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the associated features (ptosis, anhidrosis) differ depending on which order of neuron is affected.
C. Distinguish a preganglionic cause of the resulting syndrome from a postganglionic cause, giving an example of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
First-order (central) neuron: originates in the hypothalamus and descends to synapse at the C8-T2 level of the spinal cord.
A(ii) Second-order (preganglionic) neuron: leaves the spinal cord and travels, passing near the lung apex and through the mediastinum, to synapse at the superior cervical ganglion.
A(iii) Third-order (postganglionic) neuron: travels from the superior cervical ganglion along the internal carotid artery to reach the eye; sympathetic innervation controls pupillary dilation and elevation of the upper lid via Muller's muscle.

B.
Ptosis in the resulting syndrome is partial (about 1-2 mm) rather than complete, because only Muller's muscle (a sympathetically innervated accessory lid elevator contributing 1-2 mm of lid elevation) is denervated; the main elevator, the levator palpebrae superioris, is supplied by the oculomotor nerve and remains intact.
Facial sweating fibres travel with the sympathetic pathway up to the superior cervical ganglion; anhidrosis therefore accompanies lesions at the first- or second-order (preganglionic) level.
Hypochromia iridis (a lighter iris colour on the affected side) may also occur, most pronounced in congenital or longstanding cases, because sympathetic denervation prevents normal melanin development in the iris.

C.
A preganglionic (second-order) cause is a mass compressing the sympathetic chain between the superior cervical ganglion and T1 - for example, a neck mass (lymphadenopathy, tumour, or surgical trauma, as in radical neck dissection) or a Pancoast's tumour at the lung apex, or a mediastinal mass compressing the fibres as they pass over the lung apex.
A postganglionic (third-order) cause is internal carotid artery dissection, affecting the fibres after they leave the superior cervical ganglion and travel along the carotid artery.

(i)
Diagnosis: Optic neuritis. Identifying features: sudden visual loss, pain on eye movement, afferent pupillary defect (APD — also described as RAPD), reduced visual acuity, disc oedema with hyperaemia, middle age predominantly in females, and dischromatopsia (impaired colour vision). The systemic condition most associated with optic neuritis is multiple sclerosis.

(ii)
Predisposing factors: The condition predominantly affects middle-aged females. Multiple sclerosis is the most important associated systemic condition. Inflammation is the underlying mechanism.

(iii)
Pathophysiology: Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve. Inflammation demyelinates the nerve fibres, impairing axonal conduction and leading to sudden visual loss. Signs of optic nerve dysfunction include reduced visual acuity, diminished light brightness sensitivity, dyschromatopsia, afferent pupillary conduction defect, and visual field defects. Disc changes on fundoscopy include oedema, hyperaemia, paleness and atrophy.

(iv)
Treatment: Steroids (systemic corticosteroids) are used to reduce inflammation and shorten the episode. Further neurological evaluation for multiple sclerosis is also required.
questions.question:
A 38-year-old man presents with sudden painful loss of vision in the right eye, pain on eye movement, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). He is a middle-aged female. Visual acuity is reduced. Fundoscopy shows disc oedema with hyperaemia.

(i) State the diagnosis, giving the identifying clinical features, and name the systemic condition most associated with it.
(ii) State the predisposing factors for this condition.
(iii) Outline the pathophysiology and explain why visual loss occurs suddenly.
(iv) State the treatment.

questions.answerText:
(i)
The patient most likely has Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR). Classification into non-proliferative (NPDR) and proliferative (PDR): NPDR includes mild (annual follow-up), moderate (6–8 months), severe (3–4 months); PDR requires treatment. Proliferative stage is characterised by neovascularization.

(ii)
Risk factors: type of diabetes and its duration; control of DM (in type 1 IDDM, good control reduces risk of progression; also in type 2 NIDDM); hypertension — high diastolic BP in young individuals, high systolic BP in older individuals can worsen retinopathy; pregnancy in women; hyperlipidaemia; onset of puberty; ethnicity; DR is increasingly becoming a major cause of blindness in the 20–60 age group.

(iii)
Mechanisms of vision loss in DR: macular ischaemia; macular oedema; vitreous haemorrhage; preretinal haemorrhage; epiretinal membrane formation; retinal detachment; neovascular glaucoma. DR is a chronic progressive, potentially sight-threatening disease of the retinal microvasculature associated with prolonged hyperglycaemia.

(iv)
Treatment for PDR: anti-VEGF drugs (bevacizumab/Avastin 1.25 mg, ranibizumab/Lucentis 0.5 mg, aflibercept/Eyelea 2 mg) — used as adjunct to laser treatment or primary treatment for diabetic macular oedema; laser photocoagulation (panretinal); corticosteroids for refractory macular oedema — inhibit expression of VEGF; vitrectomy — indicated for severe persistent vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment involving or threatening the macular, premacular haemorrhage. Recommended follow-up for PDR: recommend treatment immediately.
questions.question:
A 50-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with gradual blurring of vision. Fundoscopy reveals multiple dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, and new vessel formation.

(i) What stage of diabetic retinopathy does this patient most likely have, and what is the classification used?
(ii) Identify the risk factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the mechanisms by which vision may be lost in diabetic retinopathy.
(iv) Outline the treatment options for this stage of diabetic retinopathy.

A(i) Describe the course of the retinal arterioles and veins in relation to each other, in particular at arteriovenous crossing points.
A(ii) State the normal arterial-to-venous (A:V) ratio on fundoscopy.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the venous changes seen at arteriovenous crossings in chronic hypertension, and distinguish Salus' sign from Gunn's sign.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
At arteriovenous crossing points, the artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath.

A(ii)
The normal arterial-to-venous ratio on fundoscopy is approximately 2:3, meaning arteries appear narrower than veins; arteries appear bright red while veins appear purplish. A reduction in this ratio below 1:2 suggests significant arteriolar narrowing, as seen in hypertensive retinopathy.

C.
Chronic hypertension causes arteriosclerotic thickening and increased rigidity of the arteriolar wall. Because the artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath at crossing points, this thickened, rigid arteriolar wall compresses the underlying vein.
Gunn's sign (arteriovenous nipping) is the deflection, constriction, or banking of blood in the vein distal to the crossing, caused by this compression.
Salus' sign is the deflection or bending of the vein at the crossing itself, away from its usual course, caused by the same arteriolar rigidity.
Further arteriolar wall thickening produces copper wiring (moderate arteriosclerosis, giving a copper-coloured light reflex) progressing to silver wiring (severe arteriosclerosis, where the wall is so opaque the blood column is no longer visible).
These arteriosclerotic changes (AV nicking, copper/silver wiring) are structural and do NOT regress after blood pressure is controlled, unlike the acute hypertensive changes (haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates, papilledema), which typically improve over months once blood pressure is controlled.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old with known sickle cell disease (HbSC genotype) presents for routine eye screening. Fundoscopy shows peripheral fan-shaped new vessels resembling a marine organism.

(i) State the risk factors/genotype relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications that can occur if this finding is untreated.
(iii) State the management options, with justification for the option most appropriate here.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Sickle cell retinopathy is driven by vaso-occlusion of peripheral retinal vessels by rigid, sickled red blood cells, causing ischaemia and neovascularisation; haemoglobin S polymerises under hypoxia, acidosis, and dehydration, deforming red blood cells. Paradoxically, SC disease (compound heterozygous, as in this patient) is more commonly associated with severe proliferative sickle cell retinopathy than SS disease, likely due to higher red cell viscosity, even though SS disease causes the worst systemic disease.

(ii)
The "sea-fan" appearance described is Goldberg Stage III neovascularisation, arising from peripheral arteriovenous anastomoses at areas of retinal ischaemia. Although sea-fan lesions may auto-infarct in 20-60% of cases without treatment, they carry a risk of vitreous haemorrhage (Stage IV) if they bleed, and can progress to Stage V (fibrovascular proliferation with tractional retinal detachment), requiring vitrectomy and surgical retinal detachment repair.

(iii)
Wide-field fundus fluorescein angiography is the most useful investigation for detecting peripheral non-perfusion, arteriovenous anastomoses, and neovascularisation, as standard fundoscopy may miss peripheral lesions. Peripheral laser scatter photocoagulation, applied to non-perfused peripheral retina identified on angiography, is the appropriate management here: it destroys ischaemic peripheral retina (the source of VEGF), reducing the angiogenic stimulus and promoting regression of the sea-fan lesion, reducing the risk of vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment. Non-proliferative lesions (salmon patches, black sunbursts) do not routinely require treatment, as they often auto-infarct spontaneously - unlike this proliferative (sea-fan) stage, which carries vision-threatening risk.

questions.question:
A woman brings her 6-month-old daughter with a 4-week history of constant watering of the left eye with intermittent mucopurulent discharge. The mother reports that the child was not brought for the 6-week postnatal check. On examination, the infant has a normal eye examination apart from epiphora and discharge on the left side. Pressure over the lacrimal sac produces mucoid regurgitation.

(i) State the diagnosis and its embryological basis.
(ii) Name the procedure used to confirm that the drainage system is patent.
(iii) State the anatomical landmark and specific passage that is found obstructed in this condition.
(iv) State the embryological variant that may complicate access during dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).
(v) State the sequence of management steps from conservative to surgical, with timing for each.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction. Embryological basis: The nasolacrimal duct starts as a cord of ectodermal cells; it is the last part of the excretory system to canalise, usually completing at or shortly after birth. Obstruction at the distal end is present in approximately 50% of infants at birth. Epiphora is not apparent until approximately 6 weeks of life, when lacrimation begins.

(ii)
The procedure used to confirm patency is probing and syringing (diagnostic probing and irrigation of the lacrimal system).

(iii)
The obstruction is typically at the distal end of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD), at or proximal to the valve of Hasner, which is the valve at the inferior nasal meatus.

(iv)
Embryological variant relevant to this area: The common canaliculus is present in approximately 90% of individuals; its absence or variant anatomy may complicate surgical access.

(v)
Sequence of management:
• Conservative (from birth): topical antibiotics and lacrimal sac massage. 90% of cases resolve in the first year of life.
• Probing and irrigation: for children in whom obstruction persists beyond the first year of life.
• Silicone intubation (bicanalicular stenting): for cases failing simple probing.
• Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR): for older children or those with persistent obstruction after intubation.

questions.question:
A 3-day-old neonate is brought with bilateral purulent eye discharge. On examination there is marked lid oedema, severe mucopurulent discharge from both eyes and chemosis. The mother reports an unprotected sexual contact prior to pregnancy.

(i) State the most likely causative organism and the diagnosis.
(ii) State the embryological and pathophysiological basis by which this organism can infect the intact corneal epithelium — distinguishing it from other bacterial pathogens.
(iii) Outline the immediate management steps for this neonate.
(iv) State the definitive topical and systemic antibiotic treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Most likely causative organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Diagnosis: Gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis (hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis of the newborn / ophthalmia neonatorum).

(ii)
Pathophysiological basis: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is one of the only bacterial agents capable of invading intact corneal epithelium (others being Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Listeria species and Haemophilus species). Most other bacteria require prior loss of corneal epithelial integrity (e.g. due to contact lens wear, ocular surface disease, trauma or bullous keratopathy) before they can cause keratitis. This virulence property accounts for the severity and rapidity of corneal destruction in gonococcal infection.

(iii)
Immediate management:
• Hospitalise the neonate.
• Perform regular copious irrigation of the conjunctival sac to mechanically clear the exudate and reduce bacterial load.
• Obtain corneal scrapings and cultures.
• Notify and treat the mother and her sexual partner.

(iv)
Definitive treatment:
• Topical: quinolones and bacitracin eye drops.
• Systemic: intravenous cefoxitin or cefotaxime.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the course of the retinal vein in relation to the artery at an arteriovenous crossing point.
A(ii) State the primary mechanism of visual loss when the vein becomes occluded at such a crossing.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the visual deficit that develops.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
At arteriovenous crossing points, the artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath; in branch retinal vein occlusion, compression of the vein at such a crossing causes venous obstruction.

A(ii)
The primary mechanism of visual loss in branch retinal vein occlusion is macular oedema and macular ischaemia secondary to the venous occlusion, which leads to retinal haemorrhages, macular oedema, and macular ischaemia in the affected sector.

C.
Because the artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath at the crossing point, compression of the vein by the artery leads to venous obstruction in the sector of retina it drains. This causes retinal haemorrhages and, most importantly for vision, macular oedema and macular ischaemia, which are the primary drivers of visual loss in this condition. Anti-VEGF therapy and laser photocoagulation are used for the resulting macular oedema; neovascularisation may develop as a secondary complication.

questions.question:
Describe the epidemiology of childhood blindness, including the definition, magnitude, regional variation, and the spectrum of causes with particular reference to avoidable blindness.

A(i) Define childhood blindness using WHO/UNICEF parameters and state the prevalence ranges by income level.
A(ii) Describe the epidemiological burden of childhood blindness globally, including child blind-years and annual incidence.
B(i) Describe the causes of childhood blindness and how they vary by region and income level.
B(ii) Describe the control framework for childhood blindness from primary to tertiary levels of intervention.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Childhood blindness (CB) definition: age range 0–15 years (UNICEF); blindness — VA <3/60 in better eye or central field <10°; severe visual impairment — VA <6/60–3/60 in better eye; moderate VI — VA <6/18–6/60 in better eye; mild VI — VA <6/12–6/18 in better eye. Prevalence ranges: high income — 0.3/1,000; middle income — 0.5/1,000; low income — 0.7/1,000; very low income — 0.9/1,000; overall range 0.2–1.5 (average 0.7)/1,000.

A(ii)
Epidemiological burden: it has been estimated that there are 1.4 million blind children in the world (1 million in Asia, 300,000 in Africa). 500,000 children become blind each year (nearly one per minute). Although the number of blind children is relatively low, they have a lifetime of blindness ahead, with an estimated 75 million blind-years — second only to cataract. 50% of blind children die within 1–2 years. Many die in childhood from underlying causes: measles, meningitis, rubella, prematurity, genetic diseases, and head injuries. Most blind children are either born blind or become blind before their fifth birthday.

B(i)
Causes by region: avoidable causes — treatable (cataract, ROP, refractive errors, low vision); preventable (corneal scarring from vitamin A deficiency, measles, traditional eye remedies, ROP). Low-income countries: corneal scarring in Africa and poorer countries in Asia; cataract; glaucoma. High- and middle-income countries: retinopathy of prematurity; refractive errors everywhere, particularly South-East Asia. Only 30–40% of all causes of CB are avoidable. U5MR is a good indicator of magnitude of CB.

B(ii)
Control framework: promotion and prevention; early detection ± treatment; early detection and referral; secondary level care — strengthen diagnosis and management of less complex cases; tertiary level care — specialist training and services for surgical correction of cataract, congenital glaucoma, and corneal scarring, including long-term follow-up. Children's vision loss requires paediatric and ophthalmic care, especially in severe cases.

(i)
Most likely diagnosis: age-related macular degeneration (AMD/ARMD). Age-related macular degeneration is the commonest cause of blindness in industrialised countries. It affects the macula, leading to central visual loss. Visual loss from this condition is uncommon among persons under the age of 50.

(ii)
Risk factors: non-modifiable — age (prevalence increases, uncommon under 50); ageing population globally. Modifiable — smoking (a potentially modifiable risk factor); obesity. Regular eye examinations are recommended particularly for persons with symptoms. AMD is responsible for 8.7% of all blindness (3 million persons) due to eye diseases. Its prevalence is likely to increase in absolute numbers globally as a consequence of population ageing.

(iii)
Global epidemiological burden: age-related macular degeneration is responsible for 8.7% of all blindness (3 million persons) due to eye diseases. Its prevalence is likely to increase in absolute numbers as a consequence of population ageing. It is the commonest cause of blindness in industrialised countries.

(iv)
Management strategies (Vision 2020): aim — to prevent and reduce vision loss from AMD and improve functioning vision and quality of life of persons with functional low vision. Strategies: health education programmes to increase awareness about potentially modifiable risk factors, particularly smoking and obesity; regular eye examinations particularly for persons with symptoms, with prompt referral to centres with appropriate facilities for diagnosis and treatment of wet AMD; low-vision care. There is no treatment for dry AMD beyond risk factor modification; low-vision aids are used for those with residual functional vision.
questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with a painless gradual decline in central vision. She lives in a high-income country. Fundoscopy reveals drusen deposits and macular changes. She is a heavy smoker and is obese.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what does it commonly affect?
(ii) Describe the risk factors for this condition including modifiable and non-modifiable factors.
(iii) What is the global epidemiological burden of this condition?
(iv) Outline the management strategies including the Vision 2020 approach.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Spot diagnosis: Ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis).
Most likely organism given presentation at day 3: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum — typically presents within the first 2–5 days of life; gonococcal infection causes hyperacute conjunctivitis and ophthalmia neonatorum; associated with maternal gonococcal cervicitis).

(ii)
Other organisms causing ophthalmia neonatorum:
• Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D–K): the most common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis; typically presents at 5–14 days.
• Staphylococcal and Streptococcal species (bacterial conjunctivitis).
• Chemical (silver nitrate prophylaxis — chemical ophthalmia).
Diagnostic approach:
• Swab for microscopy, culture and sensitivity (M/C/S).
• Copious saline irrigation before swabbing.
• Gram stain (to differentiate staining properties) and Giemsa stain (to identify inflammatory cells and intracellular inclusions for Chlamydia).
• Culture on appropriate media (chocolate agar for Neisseria and Haemophilus influenzae).

(iii)
Pathogenesis and mode of acquisition:
• Infection is acquired during passage through the infected birth canal (direct contact during delivery).
• The eye is sterile in utero; it acquires organisms from the maternal genital tract during birth.
• The conjunctival mucosa is susceptible to infection when the normal flora has not yet been established and host defences are immature.
• Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes hyperacute conjunctivitis with profuse purulent discharge and can penetrate intact corneal epithelium, risking corneal perforation and blindness.

(iv)
Management:
• Swab for M/C/S (taken before starting treatment).
• Copious saline irrigation of both eyes.
• Broad-spectrum antibiotics: quinolones (topical), and IM Ceftriaxone (for gonococcal infection — systemic treatment essential).
• Treat parents: both parents must be treated for the sexually transmitted infection, and sexual contacts traced.
• Refer if in doubt — ophthalmology referral for specialist assessment and monitoring of corneal involvement.
• Educate on contacts and prevention.
questions.question:
A 3-day-old neonate is brought to the hospital with bilateral eye discharge and marked eyelid swelling. The mother had a history of untreated genital discharge during pregnancy. The discharge is profuse, mucopurulent, and the eyelids are difficult to open due to oedema.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis, and which organism is most likely given the timing of presentation?
(ii) State the other organisms that can cause this condition, and describe the diagnostic approach.
(iii) Describe the pathogenesis and mode of acquisition of this infection.
(iv) Outline the complete management of this neonate and who else must be treated.

A 35-year-old woman with a 2-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus is referred by her rheumatologist after being on prolonged high-dose chloroquine therapy. She is asymptomatic but reports some difficulty with colour discrimination. Fundoscopy is performed and the macula is examined carefully.

(i) Identify the fundoscopic sign to be looked for in this patient and state its name.
(ii) Name the other drugs known to cause abnormal corneal or retinal deposits.
(iii) Identify the macular structure affected and explain why central vision is preferentially impaired.
(iv) State the differential pathologies that must be excluded in a patient with maculopathy presenting with impaired central colour vision.
(v) State the management and screening principle for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The fundoscopic sign to look for is the 'bull's eye maculopathy' pattern of toxic maculopathy from chloroquine. The condition is toxic maculopathy due to chloroquine, in which the additive dose exceeding 300 g causes poor central vision and characteristic macular changes.

(ii)
Other drugs known to cause abnormal corneal or retinal deposits:
• Chloroquine, amiodarone, amodiaquine, meperidine, indomethacin, chlorpromazine and tamoxifen — cause abnormal corneal depositions.
• Chrysiasis: deposit of gold in the cornea due to chronic administration in rheumatoid arthritis.
• Phenothiazines: deposit drug pigment in lens fibres (cataract).

(iii)
The macular photoreceptors — specifically the cone cells of the fovea centralis — are the primary structure affected. Central vision is preferentially impaired because the macula and fovea are responsible for fine detail and colour discrimination; the cone cells are concentrated here and are selectively toxic to chloroquine accumulation.

(iv)
Differential pathologies with maculopathy and impaired central colour vision:
• Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) — dry and wet types.
• Diabetic macular oedema.
• Macular hole (from trauma, myopia, senility, idiopathic or solar retinopathy).
• Retinitis pigmentosa (also causes maculopathy).
• Optic neuritis (causes dyschromatopsia and central field loss).
• Retinal vein occlusion with macular oedema.

(v)
Management and screening: Education of the patient and prescribing physician about the risk of toxic maculopathy. Regular ophthalmological screening (including fundoscopy and visual field testing) for all patients on cumulative doses approaching or exceeding 300 g of chloroquine. If toxic maculopathy is detected, chloroquine should be discontinued. Low vision aids may be required for patients with established central visual loss.

A.
Microscopic layers of the retina from the vitreous inward:
• Internal limiting membrane.
• Nerve fibre layer.
• Ganglion cell layer.
• Inner plexiform layer.
• Inner nuclear layer.
• Outer plexiform layer.
• Outer nuclear layer.
• External limiting membrane.
• Layer of rods and cones.
• Retinal pigment layer (adjacent to choroid).
Structures visible on fundoscopy (the fundus): the retina, the optic nerve head, the macula, and the retinal vessels.

B.
Types of retinal detachment:
• Rhegmatogenous RD: caused by a full-thickness break (tear or hole) in the retina, allowing fluid from the vitreous to pass through and separate the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium. Associated with posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) and vitreous traction. Clinical features: sudden visual loss, flashes of light, floaters, and metamorphopsia (distorted vision).
• Tractional RD: caused by fibrovascular membranes on the retinal surface that pull the neurosensory retina away from the RPE without a retinal break; classically associated with proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
• Exudative (secondary) RD: no retinal break; fluid accumulates beneath the retina from a sub-retinal source (e.g. inflammation, tumour, or vascular disease).

C.
If the macula is involved in a rhegmatogenous RD, the photoreceptors of the macula (the fovea and its surrounding cones) become deprived of nutrients from the choroid, leading to irreversible damage and permanent loss of central vision. The longer the macula remains detached, the less likely full central vision recovery.
Surgical options: management is an emergency. Options include:
• Scleral buckle surgery (indentation of the eye wall to relieve vitreous traction).
• Intravitreal gas injection (pneumatic retinopexy — to tamponade the break).
• Vitrectomy (surgical removal of vitreous and internal repair).
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the retina — its layers from innermost to outermost, and the anatomical structures visible on fundoscopy.

B. Describe the three types of retinal detachment (rhegmatogenous, tractional and exudative) — stating the mechanism, distinguishing pathological features and clinical presentation of each.

C. Explain why rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, if involving the macula, leads to permanent visual loss, and state the surgical options for retinal detachment.

A. Describe the progression of Vitamin A deficiency in the eye under the headings: (i) earliest functional symptom, (ii) conjunctival sign, (iii) corneal signs leading to scarring.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why children are particularly at risk of rapid progression to blindness.
C. Distinguish a sign associated with chronic, longstanding deficiency from signs associated with rapid, acute deficiency.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Night blindness (nyctalopia) is the earliest symptom of Vitamin A deficiency, because retinol is an essential component of rhodopsin (visual purple) in rod photoreceptors, which mediate scotopic (dim light) vision; rhodopsin regeneration requires a constant supply of Vitamin A.

A(ii)
A Bitot's spot (WHO grade X1B) is a raised, silvery-white, foamy, triangular patch of keratinised epithelium on the bulbar conjunctiva, most commonly temporal, representing metaplasia of the conjunctival epithelium.

A(iii)
Corneal xerosis (X2) begins in the lower nasal quadrant of the cornea as punctate keratopathy, progressing to haziness and dryness; without treatment this progresses to keratomalacia (X3A/X3B - corneal softening, melting and ulceration), which directly precedes and causes irreversible corneal scarring (XS).

B.
Bitot's spots in children under 5 years are highly specific for active Vitamin A deficiency, and this age group is at particular risk because deficiency can progress rapidly through night blindness, corneal xerosis, and keratomalacia to irreversible scarring; urgent high-dose Vitamin A therapy at the keratomalacia stage can prevent progression to scarring if given promptly.

C.
Bitot's spots in older children (above age 5) are often inactive, representing a chronic remnant of past deficiency rather than current active deficiency, and may persist despite adequate current Vitamin A status. In contrast, night blindness, corneal xerosis, and keratomalacia are signs associated with rapid, acute deficiency, requiring urgent treatment.

(i)
Diagnosis: Acid chemical burn to both eyes (occupational ocular chemical injury).
Type: Acid burn — battery acid (sulphuric acid is among the most commonly implicated acids).

(ii)
Comparison of alkali vs acid burns:
• Prevalence: Alkali burns are twice as common as acid burns, since alkalis are more widely used at home and in industry.
• Common alkalis: ammonia, sodium hydroxide (lye), lime.
• Common acids: sulphuric, sulphorous, hydrofluoric, acetic, chromic, and hydrochloric acids.
• Depth of penetration: Alkalis penetrate deeper than acids.
• Pathological reason: Acids coagulate surface proteins (coagulative necrosis), forming a protective barrier that limits further penetration. Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis, which allows them to penetrate deeper into ocular tissues.

(iii)
Immediate emergency treatment:
• Copious irrigation is crucial to minimise duration of contact with the chemical and normalise the pH in the conjunctival sac.
• Normal saline should be used to irrigate the eye for about 30 minutes or until pH is normalised.
• Double eversion of the eyelids should be performed so that any retained particulate matter trapped in the fornices may be removed.
• Debridement of necrotic areas of corneal epithelium should be performed to allow proper re-epithelialisation.

(iv)
Medical treatment:
• Steroids: to reduce inflammation (to be monitored and time-limited).
• Ascorbic acid: to promote wound healing.
• Cycloplegic: to reduce pain (ciliary spasm).
• Ointments: to reduce ulceration and allow re-epithelialisation.

(v)
Severe complications:
• Symblepharon: adhesion between the fornix (palpebral) conjunctiva and the bulbar conjunctiva.
• Necrosis of corneal and conjunctival tissues.
• Stromal corneal opacification.
• Anterior chamber penetration resulting in iris and lens damage.
• Ciliary body damage.
• Hypotony and phthisis bulbi.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old factory worker is rushed to the eye casualty after battery acid splashed into both eyes at work. He is in severe pain, with swollen lids and reduced vision. On examination both eyes show conjunctival hyperaemia, chemosis, and areas of limbal ischaemia with corneal opacity.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and classify the type of chemical agent involved?
(ii) Compare alkali and acid burns with respect to prevalence, common agents implicated, and depth of tissue penetration — giving the pathological reason for the difference.
(iii) State the immediate emergency treatment, specifying agent, duration, and any preparatory steps.
(iv) State the medical treatment, listing all agents and their specific roles.
(v) Describe the severe complications that may occur if treatment is inadequate.

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the conjunctiva relevant to trachoma under the zones: (i) tarsal conjunctiva, (ii) lid margin, (iii) cornea.
B. State how the WHO grading of trachoma (TF, TI, TS, TT, CO) reflects anatomical progression through these zones.
C. Explain how disease confined to the conjunctiva can spread to a distant structure (the cornea) and cause blindness.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The tarsal conjunctiva is the site of the chronic follicular conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, and C.

A(ii)
The lid margin is the site where trichiasis (in-turned eyelashes) develops after chronic conjunctival scarring.

A(iii)
The cornea is the site of the disease's most advanced, blinding stage.

B.
Chronic infection produces follicular and intense inflammatory changes on the tarsal conjunctiva, then conjunctival scarring (TS); scarring distorts the lid margin, producing trichiasis (TT), the in-turned lashes that mechanically abrade the cornea; repeated abrasion finally produces corneal opacity (CO), the most advanced WHO grading stage, which directly causes blindness by obstructing the visual axis and is irreversible.

C.
Because trachoma begins as a conjunctival infection but progressively scars the tarsal conjunctiva and distorts the lid margin, the resulting trichiasis brings the eyelashes into repeated mechanical contact with the cornea - a structure distant from the original site of infection. This chronic corneal abrasion leads to corneal opacity, which is irreversible; making this progression the rationale for the SAFE strategy, in which Surgery (correction of trichiasis) is the only direct treatment for established trichiasis and late-stage disease, alongside Antibiotics, Face washing, and Environmental improvement to control the earlier conjunctival infection before it progresses.

A(i)
Structural layers of the eyelid from anterior to posterior:
• Skin and subcutaneous tissue: thinnest in the body; no subcutaneous fat.
• Muscles of protraction: mainly orbicularis oculi; narrows the palpebral fissure and assists the lacrimal pump.
• Orbital septum: sheet of fibrous tissue from periosteum of upper and lower orbital rims; fuses with levator aponeurosis above the superior tarsal border and with the capsulopalpebral fascia in the lower lid.
• Orbital fat: posterior to the orbital septum, anterior to the levator aponeurosis.
• Muscles of retraction: levator muscle and aponeurosis (superior tarsal muscle/ Müller's in the upper lid); capsulopalpebral fascia and inferior tarsal muscle in the lower lid.
• Tarsus: dense plate of connective tissue; skeleton for the lids; 10–12 mm upper lid, 4 mm lower lid vertically; 1 mm thick.
• Conjunctiva: non-keratinised squamous epithelium containing goblet cells and accessory lacrimal glands.

A(ii)
Glands: Meibomian glands originate in the tarsus (25 in the upper lid, 20 in the lower lid) and secrete the oily outer layer of the tear film. Glands of Zeis are sebaceous glands associated with eyelash follicles. Accessory lacrimal glands (Krause and Wolfring) contribute to the aqueous tear layer.
Eyelashes: 100 in the upper lid, 50 in the lower lid, in 2–3 irregular rows.

A(iii)
Arterial supply: from the internal carotid via the ophthalmic artery, and from the external carotid via facial branches; good anastomosis aids wound healing. Venous drainage: pretarsal through angular and superficial temporal veins; post-tarsal through orbital veins. Lymphatics: submandibular nodes medially; preauricular nodes laterally, then anterior cervical nodes.

B.
Hordeolum and lid infections are found more frequently in persons with diabetes, other debilitating illness, chronic blepharitis, and seborrhoea — all of which impair immune defence and normal lid margin flora, creating an environment conducive to staphylococcal overgrowth.

C.
Hordeolum (stye): acute suppurative nodular inflammation. An external hordeolum (stye) occurs in the anterior eyelid, involving the glands of Zeis or lash follicles, usually caused by staphylococcal infection. An internal hordeolum involves the meibomian gland. Features: pain, redness, localised purulent abscess; may suppurate on the conjunctival surface or skin.
Chalazion: chronic granuloma that forms when the meibomian gland (deep chalazion) or glands of Zeis (superficial chalazion) become blocked; generally painless, slowly enlarging nodule without acute inflammation. Both involve glandular blockage but chalazion is sterile and chronic, while hordeolum is acute and infective. In recurrent chalazia, biopsy must be performed to exclude sebaceous cell carcinoma.
questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the eyelid under the following headings:
A(i) Structural layers from anterior to posterior.
A(ii) Glandular content of the eyelid and their secretory products.
A(iii) Arterial supply, venous drainage and lymphatic drainage.

B. Explain the clinical basis of why lid infections are more common in persons with diabetes, seborrhoea or chronic blepharitis.

C. Distinguish between a hordeolum (stye) and a chalazion — in terms of the gland involved, pathophysiology, clinical features, and the serious condition that must be excluded in a recurrent case.

Describe the gross anatomy of the lens, how its changes relate to cataract pathology, and explain why blindness from cataract is avoidable and how it may spread to cause systemic burden.

A(i) Define cataract and describe its aetiological classification.
A(ii) Describe the risk factors for cataract development, distinguishing definite from possible risk factors.
B(i) Explain why cataract is described as avoidable blindness and describe the barriers to surgery in poor communities.
B(ii) Explain the global epidemiological burden of cataract and the cost-effectiveness of surgical intervention.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cataract is clouding of the lens of the eye which impedes the passage of light (WHO definition). Cataract is severe opacification and clouding of the lens. Aetiological classification: congenital; trauma-related; secondary; age-related (senile). Although most cases are related to the ageing process, occasionally children can be born with the condition, or a cataract may develop after eye injuries, inflammation, and some other eye diseases.

A(ii)
Definite risk factors: age (strongest — prevalence increases with age); diabetes mellitus; smoking; steroids (used for RA, asthma, organ transplant); sunlight; sex (female at greater risk). Possible risk factors: alcohol; hypertension; severe diarrhoea. Protection: aspirin; antioxidants. Cataract in children is due mainly to genetic disorders. Women are at greater risk than men and are less likely to have access to services.

B(i)
Avoidable blindness is defined as blindness which could be either treated or prevented by known, cost-effective means. Up to 80% of the world's blindness is avoidable. Barriers to uptake of cataract surgery in poor communities: lack of awareness; poor quality of service; high cost of treatment; limited access. Main limitations are lack of resources and political will to address cataract blindness as a global public health issue.

B(ii)
Globally, cataract is the single most important cause of blindness; responsible for 50% of global blindness. There are estimated to be almost 18 million people who are bilaterally blind from cataract (represents almost half of all causes of blindness due to eye diseases globally). Cataract surgery has been shown to be one of the most cost-effective healthcare interventions. In well-managed eye units, one ophthalmologist is able to undertake 1,000–2,000 or more operations a year with adequate support staff and infrastructure.

A(i)
Classification of common eye medications: 1. Antimicrobial (anti-infective) — antibacterial (chloramphenicol, genticin, rifamycin, povidone-iodine), antiviral (zovirax/acyclovir), antifungal, antihelminthic, antiprotozoal; 2. Anti-allergic — mast cell stabiliser (opticrom), antihistamines/receptor antagonist (alomide); 3. Mydriatics/cycloplegics — atropine 1%, mydriacyl, phenylephrine 2.5%, 5%, 10%; 4. Antiglaucoma — carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, beta-adrenergic receptor blockers, miotics/parasympathomimetics; 5. Corticosteroids — prednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone; 6. Local anaesthetics; 7. Others.

A(ii)
Corticosteroids: indication — uveitis (anterior/posterior). Forms: topical; injectable; tablets. Examples: prednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone. Side effects: raised IOP (10P), cataract, infections. Note: refrain from prescribing steroids without ophthalmic consultation.

B(i)
Antiglaucoma medications: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; beta-adrenergic receptor blockers; miotics or parasympathomimetics; others. Mydriatics/cycloplegics: atropine 1%; mydriacyl (tropicamide); phenylephrine 2.5%, 5%, 10%. Miotics such as pilocarpine constrict the pupil and contract the ciliary muscle, increasing drainage from the anterior chamber. Mydriatics and cycloplegics such as atropine dilate the pupil and paralyse the ciliary muscle, facilitating examination of the interior of the eye.

B(ii)
Local anaesthetics: injectable — xylocaine ± adrenaline; topical — tetracaine HCl drops, xylocaine jelly, xylocaine spray. Critical interaction: it is important not to use benzalkonium chloride with local anaesthetics — the combination of the anaesthetic abolishing the blink reflex and the preservative solubilising the oily layer results in drying of the eye and irritation of the cornea.
questions.question:
