questions.explanation: Vaso-occlusive crisis is precipitated by dehydration, hypoxia, and infection, causing sickled cells to obstruct microvasculature. Hydration reduces blood viscosity and promotes microcirculatory flow, while prompt analgesia prevents escalating tissue ischaemia. Cold application is avoided because it causes vasoconstriction, worsening sickling.

questions.question: A patient with chronic sinusitis develops a complication where infection spreads to the orbit, causing eyelid swelling, redness, and pain with eye movement. This complication is termed:
questions.explanation: Orbital cellulitis is a serious complication in which infection, often originating from sinusitis, spreads into the tissues surrounding the eye (the orbit), causing eyelid swelling, redness, pain with eye movement, and potentially threatening vision if untreated. Conjunctivitis is limited to the conjunctiva without orbital involvement, a hordeolum is a localized eyelid gland infection, and presbycusis and tinnitus are unrelated auditory conditions.

options: Total Erb-Klumpke injury affecting C5 to T1 is present
MRI confirms complete nerve root avulsion on imaging
Complete paralysis with circulatory problems is confirmed
Surgical nerve repair is performed in the first week of life
Recovery of biceps function occurs within the first 3 weeks
questions.question: The prognosis for brachial plexus injury is most favourable when:
questions.explanation: The prognosis for brachial plexus injury is generally good, with most babies recovering completely within 3 weeks. The prognosis is most favourable when biceps function recovers within the first 3 weeks. Babies with no recovery of biceps function by 3 months, and those with total brachial plexus injury (C5-T1) showing no recovery by 1 month, are referred for surgical exploration and possible microsurgical nerve repair.

questions.question: An intraoperative complication involving electrocautery devices causing vascular injury occurs through:
options: Unintended thermal injury to blood vessel walls from energy spread
Electromagnetic interference with vascular monitoring equipment
Pressure necrosis from prolonged application to vessel walls
Chemical burn from conductive gel used with the device
Direct mechanical laceration of vessels by the cautery electrode
questions.explanation: Electrocautery and other energy-based devices can cause unintended thermal injury to blood vessels through lateral energy spread beyond the intended target site. This thermal damage to vessel walls weakens their integrity, potentially causing immediate or delayed hemorrhage, and can occur even when the vessel is not directly in contact with the device.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient on a fentanyl transdermal patch for chronic pain notes the patient is febrile with a temperature of 39°C. This is clinically significant because fever can
options: increase fentanyl absorption from the patch
completely inactivate the fentanyl within the patch
have no effect on drug absorption at all
cause the patch to lose adhesion only
questions.explanation: Elevated skin temperature from fever increases blood flow to the skin and can accelerate the release and absorption of fentanyl from a transdermal patch, increasing the risk of opioid toxicity and respiratory depression. This is why external heat sources near patches are also avoided. The fever does not inactivate or reverse the drug's action.

questions.question: Sweet taste is primarily transduced through which cellular mechanism?
questions.explanation: Sweet taste activates G-protein-coupled receptors (T1R2-T1R3) linked to gustducin, initiating a second messenger cascade involving phospholipase C and IP3. This cascade releases calcium from internal stores, depolarizing the receptor cell and triggering neurotransmitter release. Similar G-protein mechanisms mediate bitter and umami taste transduction.

questions.question: Into which vessel do the hepatic veins drain?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (typically two or three major veins: right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. These veins are intersegmental in distribution, draining adjacent hepatic segments. The attachment of these large veins to the IVC helps anchor the liver in position within the abdominal cavity.

questions.question: A midwife is asked to explain the standard WHO regimen for active management of the third stage of labour as a complete package. Which three components make up this regimen?
questions.explanation: Active management of the third stage of labour, as recommended by WHO, comprises three key components: administration of a uterotonic drug, usually oxytocin, shortly after birth, controlled cord traction to assist placental delivery once separation is confirmed, and uterine massage after placental delivery to maintain good uterine tone. This package has been shown to significantly reduce the incidence and severity of postpartum haemorrhage compared with expectant management. Consistent application of all three components maximises the protective benefit.
options: Uterotonic administration, manual placental removal, and antibiotics
Uterotonic administration, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage
Delayed cord clamping, uterine massage, and immediate breastfeeding
Controlled cord traction, episiotomy, and uterine massage
Uterotonic administration, cervical examination, and fundal massage

questions.question: A client who had a vitrectomy with gas bubble insertion is being discharged. Which specific instruction is MOST important for the nurse to include?
questions.explanation: Gas bubbles inserted during vitrectomy expand at altitude, so clients must avoid air travel until the bubble has fully resorbed to prevent a dangerous rise in intraocular pressure. Reading, sleep position restrictions, caffeine intake and permanent avoidance of corrective lenses are not the critical safety concerns here. This instruction directly prevents a serious ocular complication during air travel.
options: Avoid lying flat while sleeping only
Avoid air travel until the gas bubble fully resolves
Avoid caffeine intake for six weeks
Hand, foot, and mouth disease exclusively
questions.question: A midwife caring for a child with a vesicular rash appearing in crops at different stages of healing, along with mild fever, diagnoses:
questions.explanation: Chickenpox is characterised by a vesicular rash appearing in successive crops, so lesions at different stages of development, from macules to vesicles to crusted lesions, are present simultaneously, distinguishing it from other rash illnesses. It is usually accompanied by mild fever and generalised itching. This pattern of lesions at varying stages is a key diagnostic feature that differentiates chickenpox from conditions with more uniform rash presentations.

questions.question: Which body of law in Nigeria governs the relationship and disputes between private individuals, such as a nurse and a patient in a civil claim, rather than between individuals and the state?
questions.explanation: Private, or civil, law governs relationships and disputes between individuals or private entities, such as tort claims for negligence between a nurse and patient or contract disputes, whereas public law governs relationships between individuals and government authorities, including constitutional, criminal, and administrative law.

questions.question: A woman develops sudden-onset chest pain, dyspnoea, and cardiovascular collapse immediately after delivery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency occurring during or immediately after delivery. Amniotic fluid (containing fetal squamous cells, lanugo, meconium) enters the maternal circulation, causing an anaphylactoid-like reaction with sudden cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and DIC. Management is supportive with resuscitation and ICU care. Mortality remains high (up to 40%).
options: Eclamptic seizure with acute cardiovascular compromise
Pulmonary embolism from postpartum deep vein thrombosis
Uterine rupture with haemorrhage into the peritoneal cavity
Amniotic fluid embolism causing cardiorespiratory collapse
Massive postpartum haemorrhage with hypovolaemic shock

questions.question: The MOST appropriate nursing response to discovering that a colleague has been charting care that was not actually provided is:
questions.explanation: Falsification of nursing records—charting care not provided—is a serious professional and legal violation that endangers patient safety. It constitutes fraud, a quasi-intentional tort, and a criminal offence in some jurisdictions. The appropriate response is to report through the correct professional channel (charge nurse, nursing management, or NMCN). Failing to report protects the colleague at the expense of patient safety and professional integrity.
options: Correct the documentation without informing the colleague
Discuss with the colleague and provide informal counselling only
Report the falsification through the appropriate professional channel
Ignore the issue to protect the professional relationship
Document the observation in the patient's medical record

questions.question: A patient with severe metabolic acidosis is showing deep, rapid breathing on assessment. The nurse should recognise this breathing pattern as:
questions.explanation: Kussmaul breathing is a deep, rapid respiratory pattern that represents the body's compensatory attempt to blow off carbon dioxide and correct severe metabolic acidosis. It is a recognisable clinical sign, often seen in diabetic ketoacidosis. Identifying this pattern helps confirm the acid-base disturbance suspected on blood gas analysis.
options: Normal breathing requiring no further clinical concern
Kussmaul breathing, a compensatory respiratory response
Agonal breathing indicating imminent cardiac arrest
Biot's breathing indicating increased intracranial pressure

questions.question: The descending genicular artery, contributing to the genicular anastomosis superomedially, is a branch of which artery?
questions.explanation: The descending genicular artery is a branch of the femoral artery, contributing superomedially to the genicular anastomosis. The five genicular branches of the popliteal artery are: lateral superior, medial superior, middle, lateral inferior, and medial inferior genicular arteries. The anterior tibial recurrent artery contributes inferolaterally.

questions.question: A ventilated patient's low-pressure alarm sounds continuously. The nurse should first check for:
options: Kinking of the ventilator tubing itself
Circuit disconnection or a significant air leak
Biting down on the endotracheal tube
Airway obstruction from thick secretions present
questions.explanation: A low-pressure alarm typically indicates a disconnection or leak in the ventilator circuit, cuff, or connections, allowing delivered volume to escape. This differs from a high-pressure alarm, which suggests obstruction or resistance. Prompt identification of the leak source restores effective ventilation.

questions.question: A woman with vulval carcinoma is assessed for lymph node spread. Besides the inguinal nodes, which other nodal group commonly receives lymphatic drainage from the vagina?
questions.explanation: The vagina drains lymph to the inguinal nodes inferiorly and to the internal iliac nodes from its middle and upper portions. Awareness of this dual drainage pattern guides staging and surgical clearance in vulvovaginal malignancy. The upper vagina shares drainage pathways with the cervix through the internal iliac chain.

The classic presentation of placenta praevia is painless, bright red vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester without uterine tenderness, contractions, or fetal distress (in early episodes). The uterus is soft and non-tender. Malpresentation is common because the low-lying placenta prevents cephalic engagement. Diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasound - vaginal examination is contraindicated until praevia is excluded.
options: Cervical ectropion — contact bleeding from cervical tissue
Vasa praevia — fetal vessel rupture over the os
Uterine rupture — with maternal shock and fetal distress
Placenta praevia — painless lower segment bleeding
questions.question: A woman at 32 weeks presents with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding with no uterine tenderness. The most likely diagnosis is:

options: Immediate administration of oxytocin and fluid resuscitation only
Manual removal of the placenta and uterine packing
Emergency caesarean section after maternal stabilisation
Insertion of a Bakri balloon for tamponade
Application of a B-Lynch suture to compress the uterus
questions.explanation: Massive haemorrhage from placenta praevia with maternal shock requires emergency caesarean section as the definitive treatment. Simultaneous resuscitation (IV fluids, blood transfusion, oxygen) is initiated immediately. The surgical team, anaesthetist, neonatal team, and blood bank must be alerted. Caesarean section stops the haemorrhage by delivering the placenta. Balloon tamponade and compression sutures may be used intraoperatively if postpartum atony occurs.
questions.question: A woman at 34 weeks with known placenta praevia experiences a sudden massive haemorrhage with maternal shock. What is the definitive treatment?
A woman on long-term antihypertensive therapy conceives while taking an ACE inhibitor. This drug class is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because it causes:
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors cross the placenta and impair fetal renal blood flow, leading to oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, and skull ossification defects when used in the second and third trimesters. Women taking these drugs should be switched to pregnancy-safe alternatives as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Early first-trimester exposure carries lower but still notable risk of cardiac and renal malformation.

The 4 T's of PPH are: Tone (uterine atony - most common, ~70%); Trauma (lacerations of cervix, vagina, perineum, uterine rupture); Tissue (retained placenta or placental fragments); and Thrombin (coagulopathy - DIC, pre-existing clotting disorders). This mnemonic guides systematic assessment and management. Uterine atony must always be excluded and treated first.
questions.question: The "four T's" mnemonic for causes of postpartum haemorrhage lists which four categories?

options: Expected finding in a multiparous woman only
questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman in labour identifies that the fetal head has receded between contractions on repeated examination despite adequate contractions. This finding is called the 'bouncing head sign' and suggests:
questions.explanation: A 'bouncing' fetal head that recedes between contractions rather than descending progressively suggests the head is failing to engage, often due to cephalopelvic disproportion, and warrants further assessment of pelvic adequacy and fetal size. This is an abnormal finding, not a sign of normal progress or an adequate pelvis. Persistent findings of this nature require prompt obstetric review to plan safe delivery.

Cardiotocography provides continuous, non-invasive assessment of fetal heart rate patterns and can reveal early signs of fetal compromise such as reduced variability or decelerations in a woman with antepartum haemorrhage. It complements maternal clinical assessment and ultrasound in guiding the urgency of delivery. Continuous monitoring is particularly important given the risk of placental insufficiency accompanying bleeding.
questions.question: A woman with antepartum haemorrhage of unclear origin has her fetal wellbeing assessed as part of ongoing evaluation. Which non-invasive test is routinely used to help detect fetal compromise in this situation?
options: Chorionic villus sampling, assessing fetal chromosomes
Cardiotocography, assessing fetal heart rate patterns
Biophysical liver function tests on the mother

questions.explanation: Improved activity tolerance in a previously hypothyroid patient would be evidenced by the patient's own report of increased energy and the ability to perform daily activities without the excessive fatigue that characterised their hypothyroid state, reflecting improved metabolic function with treatment. This outcome evaluation relies on functional, patient-reported improvement rather than an isolated, unmeasured laboratory value. Recognising this type of evidence supports accurate evaluation of nursing care outcomes.
options: The patient's TSH level remains unmeasured
The patient reports increased energy and can complete daily activities without excessive fatigue
The patient reports no change in energy levels at all
The patient has stopped taking levothyroxine altogether
The patient's weight has increased significantly further
questions.question: A nurse evaluates that a patient with hypothyroidism has achieved the outcome 'Adequate Activity Tolerance' after a period of treatment. Which finding would best support this evaluation?
A woman with confirmed PID reports fever of 39°C, severe abdominal pain, and a palpable adnexal mass. This presentation most strongly suggests which complication requiring hospital admission?
questions.explanation: A palpable adnexal mass accompanied by high fever and severe pain in a woman with PID strongly suggests tubo-ovarian abscess, a serious complication requiring inpatient intravenous antibiotics and close monitoring for possible surgical drainage. Uncomplicated cervicitis, candidiasis, and bacterial vaginosis do not typically produce a palpable mass or this degree of systemic illness. Prompt recognition prevents progression to abscess rupture and peritonitis.

questions.question: A nurse advocates for a patient requesting access to their own health records. This reflects which NMCN ethical obligation?
options: Nurses must ensure only physicians can access patient records
Nurses must advocate for clients requesting access to health records subject to legal requirements
Nurses are responsible for releasing records to all who request them
Nurses may restrict patient access to records for clinical safety
Nurses must always obtain physician approval before sharing records with patients
questions.explanation: The NMCN Code requires nurses to advocate for clients requesting access to their own health records, subject to legal requirements. This reflects the patient's right to information as part of informed consent and autonomy. While legal constraints may apply in specific circumstances, nurses are obligated to support rather than obstruct patients' efforts to access their own health information.

questions.question: The evaluation for infertility referral requires documentation of ovulation, which is best assessed by which investigation?
questions.explanation: Ovulation is most practically assessed by mid-luteal serum progesterone measurement (typically on day 21 of a 28-day cycle), which should be elevated above 30 nmol/L if ovulation has occurred. Alternatively, LH detection kits measure the LH surge that precedes ovulation by approximately 24 to 36 hours, allowing prediction of the fertile window. Both methods provide objective evidence of ovulatory function as part of the infertility evaluation prior to referral.
options: Serum FSH and LH measurement on day 1 of the menstrual cycle
Basal body temperature charting over one menstrual cycle only
Endometrial biopsy to confirm secretory phase transformation
Mid-luteal serum progesterone or LH detection on ovulation kits
Pelvic ultrasound to visualise follicle development on day 2

questions.question: Carboprost (prostaglandin F2a analogue) used in PPH is specifically contraindicated in which maternal condition?
questions.explanation: Carboprost is contraindicated in women with asthma because prostaglandin F2a is a potent bronchospastic agent that can trigger severe bronchoconstriction and potentially fatal bronchospasm in asthmatic patients. This is a critical contraindication to remember in emergency PPH management. In asthmatic women with PPH unresponsive to oxytocin and ergometrine, misoprostol (prostaglandin E1, which is a bronchodilator) is a safer alternative uterotonic agent.

A goal focused on the client's ability to identify non-pharmacological strategies reflects the educational domain of nursing care, empowering the client with knowledge and skills for ongoing self-management of pain after discharge. Education is a core, independent nursing function distinct from dependent functions such as medication administration. Effective client education supports long-term self-efficacy in managing chronic pain beyond the immediate hospital stay.
questions.question: A nurse develops a care plan for a client with chronic pain that includes the goal: 'Client will identify at least two non-pharmacological strategies for pain management by discharge.' This goal primarily reflects which domain of nursing intervention?
The cornerstone of management for puerperal psychosis secondary to severe puerperal sepsis is:
options: Immediate electroconvulsive therapy without any antibiotics
Prompt treatment of the underlying infection with antibiotics
Discharge planning with no further medical treatment
Permanent separation of mother and infant
questions.explanation: When puerperal psychosis arises secondary to severe infection, treating the underlying sepsis with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care is the essential first step, since resolving the infective and metabolic disturbance often leads to significant improvement in the psychiatric symptoms. Psychiatric treatments may still be needed but should accompany, not replace, treatment of the causative infection. Multidisciplinary care involving obstetric, medical, and psychiatric teams gives the best outcome.

questions.question: When preparing a patient for adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma, the nurse's primary priority preoperatively is:
options: Ensuring NPO status for at least 12 hours before surgery
Obtaining informed consent for bilateral adrenal removal
Blood pressure control and volume expansion with medications
Arranging postoperative ICU admission for monitoring
Restricting all physical activity to prevent catecholamine release
questions.explanation: The primary preoperative priority for a patient with pheochromocytoma is achieving adequate blood pressure control and volume expansion with alpha-adrenergic blocking agents (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10-14 days before surgery. Pheochromocytoma patients are chronically vasoconstricted due to excess catecholamines, causing volume depletion. Alpha blockade allows vessels to dilate, requiring volume expansion to fill the dilated vascular space. Adequate preparation prevents life-threatening intraoperative hypertensive crises.

Progressive dysphagia beginning with solid foods and advancing to liquids is the hallmark symptom of a mechanical obstructive lesion in the oesophagus — most commonly oesophageal carcinoma or tight peptic stricture. As the lumen narrows progressively, the patient compensates by swallowing softer foods, then liquids only. This symptom pattern demands urgent endoscopic evaluation. In contrast, dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset, or intermittent dysphagia, suggests motility disorders such as achalasia or oesophageal spasm.
options: Mechanical obstruction progressively narrowing the oesophageal lumen
Motility disorder with intermittent oesophageal spasm
Normal ageing changes in the oesophageal muscles
questions.question: A patient with oesophageal cancer presents with progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids. The nurse understands this pattern indicates:

questions.explanation: Implantation occurs between days 6 and 10 after fertilization (approximately days 20-24 of a 28-day cycle, during the window of implantation). The endometrium must be in the secretory (luteal) phase, prepared by progesterone. Implantation involves apposition, adhesion, and invasion of the syncytiotrophoblast into the decidua. Early implantation bleeding may be mistaken for a light period.
questions.question: Implantation of the blastocyst normally occurs on approximately which day after fertilization?
options: Day 14–16 — after the corpus luteum has fully formed
Day 6–10 — at the blastocyst stage in the endometrium
Day 12–14 — coinciding with the LH surge
Day 3–4 — at the morula stage entering the uterus
Day 1–2 — immediately after fertilization in the tube
perform immediate artificial rupture of further membranes
questions.explanation: In cord prolapse, relieving pressure on the compressed cord is an immediate priority, achieved by manually elevating the presenting part off the cord or positioning the woman in a knee-chest or exaggerated Sims' position while urgent delivery, usually by caesarean section, is arranged. These measures aim to preserve fetal oxygenation until delivery can be achieved. Continuous fetal heart monitoring during this time helps assess ongoing fetal condition.
questions.question: A woman has a spontaneous rupture of membranes at term and cord prolapse is identified on examination. While awaiting emergency delivery, the immediate nursing action to relieve cord compression is to:

questions.explanation: The median nerve provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. This sensory distribution is preserved in anterior interosseous syndrome (pure motor branch) but affected in carpal tunnel syndrome and more proximal median nerve injuries.
questions.question: What provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb?
A client presents with a fracture where the bone has broken through the overlying skin, exposing bone fragments. Which classification applies?
questions.explanation: An open, or compound, fracture is specifically distinguished from a closed fracture by a break in the skin that exposes the fracture site to the external environment, increasing infection risk. Greenstick fractures involve incomplete breaks typically in children, while stress fractures result from repetitive load and pathological fractures occur through abnormal bone. This classification determines the urgency of infection prevention measures.

Chest X-ray is NOT part of routine IMCI nutritional assessment. IMCI nutritional assessment includes: weighing the child and comparing with WHO growth charts for weight-for-age, measuring MUAC (middle upper arm circumference) for children 6 months to 5 years, checking for bilateral pitting oedema of the feet, and looking for visible severe wasting. These clinical tools are practical, low-cost, and effective in identifying children requiring nutritional intervention without the need for X-ray.
options: Weight-for-age using growth chart to identify underweight
MUAC measurement to detect acute malnutrition directly
Presence of bilateral pitting oedema of the feet
Chest X-ray to identify pulmonary nutritional complications
Visible severe wasting assessed by looking at the child
questions.question: IMCI states that all sick children under 5 should be assessed for nutritional status. The assessment includes all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Postpartum blues are transient, mild mood changes that typically resolve within 2 weeks without treatment, often related to hormonal fluctuations after delivery. Postpartum depression is a persistent clinical condition with significant depressive symptoms requiring assessment and management, including counselling and potentially antidepressant therapy. Depression does not exclusively affect primiparae, and both conditions can affect any postpartum woman.
options: Postpartum blues involves suicidal ideation while depression causes transient mood changes only
Depression is self-limiting and resolves within 2 weeks without treatment
Depression occurs only in primiparae while blues affect multiparae exclusively
Blues are transient mild mood swings, while depression is a persistent clinical condition
Blues require antidepressant therapy while depression responds to hormonal treatment only
questions.question: Postpartum depression is a recognized complication after childbirth. It differs from postpartum blues primarily because:

questions.explanation: Tetracyclines bind to calcium in developing bones and teeth, causing permanent discolouration of the fetal teeth and inhibition of bone growth when used during pregnancy. This risk applies particularly from the second trimester onward, when fetal tooth mineralisation begins. Safer alternative antibiotic classes are therefore used for infections in pregnant women.
questions.question: A pregnant woman requires antibiotic treatment but tetracyclines are avoided. The main reason tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy is that they:
options: cause discolouration of fetal teeth and bones

questions.question: The terminal sac period of lung development extends from:
questions.explanation: The terminal sac period extends from 26 weeks to birth, during which terminal sacs (primitive alveoli) form and capillaries establish close contact with the epithelium. The epithelium thins from cuboidal to squamous, creating the blood-air barrier. Surfactant production by type II pneumocytes begins during this period.

questions.question: A healthcare provider who performs life-sustaining care on a competent patient who clearly refused treatment may be charged with:
options: Negligence and malpractice for substandard care delivery
Assault and battery for providing care without valid consent
Libel and slander for misrepresenting patient consent
False imprisonment for restricting the patient's free movement
Abandonment for inappropriate continuation of care
questions.explanation: A healthcare provider can be charged with assault and battery for providing life-sustaining care without consent. All persons have the right to accept or reject treatment, and performing care on a competent patient who has clearly refused violates this fundamental right. This is particularly relevant in end-of-life care, where a patient's explicit refusal of life-prolonging measures must be respected.

questions.question: An older client undergoing cancer chemotherapy is at increased risk for which complication due to age-related reductions in bone marrow reserve?
options: A paradoxical and unexpected improvement in immune function overall entirely
Significantly accelerated tumour growth resulting from treatment
Myelosuppression leading to increased infection risk, anaemia, and bleeding tendency
questions.explanation: Age-related reductions in bone marrow reserve make older adults receiving chemotherapy more susceptible to myelosuppression, leading to increased infection risk from neutropenia, anaemia from reduced erythropoiesis, and bleeding tendency from thrombocytopenia. Hypercalcaemia and hypercoagulability are separate oncological complications not specifically related to bone marrow reserve reduction. Chemotherapy does not accelerate tumour growth, and immune function does not paradoxically improve from treatment in older adults with reduced reserve.

questions.question: A 'susceptible host' in the chain of infection within the perioperative context refers to a patient who:
options: Has reduced ability to resist infection due to illness or immunosuppression
Has fully intact immune defences with no risk factors
Has received complete vaccination against all pathogens
Has no surgical incision or invasive access present
Is scheduled only for minor outpatient procedures
questions.explanation: A susceptible host is someone whose natural defences are compromised by factors such as illness, immunosuppression, malnutrition, or extremes of age, increasing vulnerability to infection following pathogen exposure. Fully intact immune defences or absence of any invasive access would reduce, not increase, susceptibility. Identifying susceptible hosts allows targeted, enhanced infection prevention measures.

options: Continue indefinitely until delivery is achieved
Be applied without maternal effort involved
Only be applied during a contraction and coordinated with maternal pushing
Exceed three pulls if no descent occurs
questions.question: A midwife assists with a vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery. An important safety limit taught for this procedure is that traction should:
questions.explanation: Vacuum-assisted delivery requires traction to be applied only during contractions and coordinated with maternal pushing efforts, mimicking normal expulsive forces and reducing risk of trauma. If there is no descent after a limited number of pulls, usually three, the procedure should be abandoned in favour of alternative delivery methods. Continuous or excessive traction increases the risk of scalp trauma and fetal injury.

questions.question: A midwife teaches a pregnant woman to recognise danger signs requiring immediate care-seeking. Which of the following would be classified as a TRUE danger sign in pregnancy?
options: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Mild fatigue in the first trimester
questions.explanation: Severe headache with visual disturbance is a recognised danger sign in pregnancy, potentially indicating severe pre-eclampsia, and requires immediate assessment and care-seeking. Mild ankle swelling, occasional round ligament discomfort, first-trimester fatigue, and occasional Braxton Hicks contractions are all common, generally benign findings in pregnancy that do not typically require urgent evaluation, though ongoing monitoring remains important. Distinguishing true danger signs from normal pregnancy discomforts is an essential part of patient education.

options: Fixed tissues take up stain more selectively
Cells rapidly deteriorate through drying out and autolysis after removal
Fixation prevents tissue shrinkage during microtomy
Unfixed tissues react with embedding media
Blood supply continues to alter tissue composition after removal
questions.explanation: After removal from the body, tissues lose their blood supply, causing cellular enzymes (lysosomes) to begin digesting cellular components (autolysis) and the tissue to dry out. Immediate fixation halts these processes by cross-linking proteins and denaturating enzymes. Delay in fixation results in artefacts that compromise histological and diagnostic interpretation.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly explains why tissue fixation must be performed immediately after tissue removal from the body?
A nurse caring for a patient with acute gastritis should advise avoiding which substance that irritates the gastric mucosa?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit protective prostaglandin synthesis in the gastric mucosa, increasing susceptibility to irritation, erosion, and bleeding. Patients with gastritis are advised to avoid these medications and instead use bland, small, frequent meals to reduce mucosal irritation. Antacids and other prescribed gastroprotective agents support mucosal healing.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient receiving rapid intravenous fluids should recognise that the electrolyte with the highest concentration in extracellular fluid, and therefore most important to monitor during fluid therapy, is:
questions.explanation: Sodium is the predominant cation in extracellular fluid and plays a central role in determining plasma osmolality and fluid distribution between compartments. Monitoring sodium levels during intravenous therapy helps detect and prevent complications such as hyponatraemia or hypernatraemia from inappropriate fluid administration. This makes sodium a key focus of fluid balance assessment.

options: X-linked deletion causing hypogonadism and failure of secondary sex development
Missing Y chromosome causing primary male infertility with normal testosterone levels
Duplication of Y chromosome causing hyperandrogenism and aggressive infertility
Autosomal trisomy causing bilateral cryptorchidism and azoospermia
An extra X chromosome leading to low testosterone, reduced muscle mass and infertility
questions.question: Klinefelter Syndrome affects males by causing which reproductive health complication?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter Syndrome occurs in males who have an extra X chromosome (47,XXY). This chromosomal abnormality may cause low testosterone levels, reduced muscle mass, and infertility. It represents one of the most common chromosomal causes of male infertility. Understanding Klinefelter Syndrome is important for reproductive health nurses providing fertility counselling and hormonal health management for affected male clients.

Patients with scleritis should be advised to wear sunglasses to protect their eyes from UV radiation and bright light that can exacerbate photosensitivity. They should also avoid contact sports or activities that may cause eye trauma, which can worsen scleral inflammation or lead to perforation in a weakened sclera. This protective advice is part of a comprehensive nursing education plan that complements pharmacological management.
options: Apply topical lubricants every hour to prevent corneal ulceration
Use cold compresses continuously to reduce scleral vascularity
Remove contact lenses permanently to prevent scleral trauma
Wear sunglasses and avoid activities that may cause eye injury
Perform gentle periorbital massage to improve scleral blood flow
questions.question: A nurse educating a patient with scleritis about eye protection should include which SPECIFIC advice?
Lactoferrin found in colostrum and breast milk functions primarily to:
options: Stimulate alveolar cell proliferation for milk production
Provide iron to the neonate to prevent anaemia early
Provide immunological humoral defence to the newborn
Facilitate fat digestion and absorption in neonatal gut
Promote bowel motility to pass meconium effectively
questions.explanation: Lactoferrin is a humoral factor found in colostrum and breast milk that provides immunological defence to the newborn. It functions primarily as an antimicrobial agent by binding iron and making it unavailable to iron-dependent bacteria, thereby inhibiting bacterial growth. Lactoferrin also has anti-inflammatory properties and contributes to immune system modulation in the developing neonatal gut.

options: It causes the brain to shrink and brain cells to eventually die, leading to progressive decline
It is fully and completely reversible if cholinesterase inhibitors are started very early in the disease course
It has no impact on a person's ability to perform daily tasks
It is a sudden-onset condition that can be fully cured with medication
It primarily affects only short-term memory while sparing all other cognitive functions entirely
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease causes the brain to shrink and brain cells to eventually die, producing a gradual decline in memory, thinking, behavior, and social skills that affects a person's ability to function. It is not a sudden-onset or curable condition, and while cholinesterase inhibitors may improve or slow symptom progression, they do not reverse the underlying disease. The condition extends well beyond short-term memory, eventually affecting judgment, personality, and the ability to perform everyday tasks.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a client with Alzheimer's disease notes that the client repeats the same questions and misplaces items in unusual locations. According to the described disease progression, which statement about Alzheimer's disease is accurate?
A nurse is caring for a patient with aplastic anaemia and a platelet count of 15,000/mm³. The most appropriate nursing precaution is to:
questions.explanation: Severe thrombocytopenia markedly increases bleeding risk from minor trauma, including gum trauma and injection sites. A soft toothbrush and avoidance of intramuscular injections minimise mucosal and tissue bleeding. Any invasive procedure should be deferred or covered with platelet support where possible.
options: Allow contact sports as tolerated by the patient
Encourage vigorous flossing to prevent gum disease
Use a soft toothbrush and avoid intramuscular injections
Administer aspirin for any reported discomfort
Apply firm rubbing when giving a bed bath

questions.explanation: Poor venous return and increased venous pressure in the legs contribute to increased distensibility of leg veins during and after pregnancy. This, combined with postpartum immobility, hypercoagulability (increased clotting factors during pregnancy), and endothelial changes, predisposes to DVT. The Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial damage) is the mechanism, with venous stasis being a significant component in the early puerperium.
questions.question: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a recognized complication of the puerperium. Which physiological change from pregnancy MOST predisposes the mother to this risk?
options: Reduction in clotting factor concentrations after placental delivery
Activity in almost all body systems including blood volume changing during the postnatal adjustment
Haemoconcentration causing increased blood viscosity after fluid redistribution
Low protein diet in the immediate postpartum period reducing albumin levels
Decreased venous return and increased venous pressure in the legs from prolonged immobility and physiology

questions.explanation: The fundamental principle of cord stump care is to keep it clean and dry, avoiding the application of unnecessary substances such as powders, oils, or traditional remedies that can introduce infection or delay natural drying and separation. Exposure to air supports the drying process that leads to normal separation. This simple, evidence-based approach reduces the risk of omphalitis while allowing the stump to heal naturally.
options: apply antiseptic powder liberally every hour
cover the stump tightly with an occlusive dressing
apply alcohol repeatedly throughout each day
submerge the stump in water frequently
keep the stump clean and dry, avoiding unnecessary substances
questions.question: A midwife teaches a cardinal rule of cord stump care to prevent complications and premature or delayed separation. This rule is to:

questions.explanation: Osteoporosis as a predisposing factor for pathological fractures is defined as a condition of reduced bone density and microarchitectural deterioration that weakens bone strength and increases fracture risk from minimal trauma. Osteomyelitis is a bone infection, osteosarcoma is a bone malignancy, and osteoarthritis is a joint disease rather than a systemic bone density disorder. Osteomalacia involves defective bone mineralisation rather than purely reduced density, distinguishing it from osteoporosis.
questions.question: A client is diagnosed with reduced bone density and microarchitectural deterioration, predisposing them to fractures from minimal trauma. Which condition does this describe?
A client's imaging reveals a tumour arising from cells lining the small bile passages within the liver. Which type of liver cancer does this describe?
questions.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma begins specifically in the cells lining the bile ducts, distinguishing it from hepatocellular carcinoma which arises from hepatocytes. Angiosarcoma originates from vascular endothelial cells and hepatoblastoma is a paediatric tumour, while hepatic adenoma is a benign lesion. This origin determines the specific treatment approach for cholangiocarcinoma.

A child with measles and signs of severe disease (clouding of cornea, deep mouth ulcers, severe complications) in IMCI is classified as 'Severe Complicated Measles' requiring urgent referral with pre-referral treatment including Vitamin A (which significantly reduces measles case fatality by correcting measles-induced Vitamin A deficiency). Children with uncomplicated measles are managed at home with Vitamin A, paracetamol for fever, and return visit in 2 days.
options: Treating at home with vitamin A and follow-up in 5 days
Giving oral antibiotics and vitamin A then discharge home
Urgent referral after vitamin A and pre-referral treatment
Vaccination with live attenuated measles vaccine to boost immunity
Management with paracetamol and tepid sponging at home only
questions.question: IMCI management of a child with measles and signs of severe complications includes:
Misoprostol is used in PPH management. By which route is it most commonly administered as a first-line measure immediately after delivery?
questions.explanation: Misoprostol (a prostaglandin E1 analogue) is inserted rectally immediately after the baby is delivered as part of PPH management. Rectal administration allows for rapid absorption and uterotonic effect even in haemorrhaging patients who may have poor peripheral perfusion. Sublingual administration is also used in some protocols. Misoprostol is particularly valuable in resource-limited settings where parenteral uterotonics may be unavailable.

questions.question: A patient's PaO2 is 55 mmHg on room air, well below the ICU target range. This finding indicates the patient requires:
questions.explanation: A PaO2 of 55 mmHg is significantly below the expected normal range and reflects hypoxaemia requiring supplemental oxygen and further evaluation for the underlying cause. Delaying oxygen therapy risks worsening tissue hypoxia. Ongoing respiratory assessment guides the level of support needed.
options: Only reassurance without objective clinical reassessment
Immediate discontinuation of all oxygen therapy
Fluid restriction as the primary corrective measure
No intervention since the value is within limits
Supplemental oxygen and further respiratory assessment

questions.explanation: A pulmonary capacity is defined as the sum of two or more volumes, while a volume represents a single component of the breathing cycle. The four basic volumes (TV, IRV, ERV, RV) cannot be subdivided further, but capacities (IC, VC, FRC, TLC) combine these volumes to provide more comprehensive information about lung function. This distinction is clinically important as capacities often better indicate overall respiratory reserve and functional ability.
questions.question: A capacity differs from a volume because it:
A woman with a history of migraine with aura is requesting contraception. Which method should be AVOIDED because of increased stroke risk?
questions.explanation: Migraine with aura is associated with an increased baseline risk of ischaemic stroke, and oestrogen-containing contraceptives further amplify this risk through effects on coagulation and vascular tone. Progestin-only and non-hormonal methods do not carry this same risk elevation. Current guidelines therefore classify combined oestrogen methods as unsuitable for this client group.

Febrile states are recognised as a potential trigger for multiple sclerosis relapses, likely because heat further impairs conduction in already demyelinated fibres. Fever does not cure symptoms or reverse demyelination, and it is not unrelated to MS activity. This effect involves central, not merely peripheral, nerve conduction.
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis develops a fever from an unrelated infection and experiences worsening neurological symptoms. What should the nurse recognise about this pattern?
options: Fever is unrelated to MS activity
Fever only affects the peripheral nerves
Febrile states can trigger MS relapse

questions.explanation: Wharton's jelly is rich in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), a type of cord tissue stem cell under extensive study as a potential treatment for a wide range of serious health conditions. Like cord blood, cord tissue can be banked and stored for future use. MSCs from Wharton's jelly have advantages over other sources as they are easily harvested, ethically uncontroversial, and exhibit immunomodulatory properties.
questions.question: Wharton's jelly is rich in which type of stem cells that are currently under extensive study for therapeutic use?
options: Haematopoietic stem cells similar to those in cord blood
Embryonic stem cells with pluripotent differentiation ability
Mesenchymal stem cells - a type of cord tissue stem cell
Neural crest stem cells for nervous system regeneration
Endothelial progenitor cells for vascular regeneration therapy

questions.explanation: A defining morphological feature of chronic inflammation is concurrent tissue destruction with attempts at healing through fibrosis and angiogenesis, reflecting the prolonged, simultaneous processes of injury and repair. Acute inflammation, by contrast, is typically limited to vascular changes and neutrophilic infiltration without significant fibrosis. The presence of fibrosis alongside mononuclear cells therefore points strongly toward a chronic inflammatory process.
questions.question: A liver biopsy from a patient with long-standing hepatitis shows fibrosis alongside a mononuclear infiltrate, a pattern seen only in chronic and not acute inflammation. This finding is:

questions.explanation: Linear skull fractures in newborns usually require no specific treatment because they are not displaced and heal spontaneously with good outcomes in the absence of associated complications. Depressed skull fractures, on the other hand, may require surgical intervention. Antibiotic therapy is indicated only if there is cerebrospinal fluid leakage through the ear or nose, suggesting meningeal breach and risk of meningitis.
options: CT-guided aspiration of any associated subdural haematoma
Prophylactic antibiotics and lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
No specific treatment as linear fractures usually heal spontaneously
Emergency neurosurgical craniectomy to release intracranial pressure
Skull traction device to realign the fractured bone segments
questions.question: Linear skull fracture in a newborn detected after a prolonged or difficult instrumental birth most commonly requires:

questions.explanation: The vesical (upper) part of the urogenital sinus is continuous with the allantois, which constricts to form the urachus connecting the bladder apex to the umbilicus. The vesical portion forms most of the urinary bladder. The allantois eventually obliterates to become the median umbilical ligament in the adult.
questions.question: The vesical part of the urogenital sinus is continuous with:
Which of the following is a fetal indication for emergency referral of a pregnant woman during antenatal care?
options: Blood pressure of 125/80 mmHg on routine antenatal measurement
Absent or markedly reduced fetal movements detected by the mother
Fundal height measuring 1 cm less than the gestational age in weeks
Mild ankle oedema appearing in the third trimester of pregnancy
Haemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL responding to oral iron supplementation
questions.explanation: Absent or markedly reduced fetal movements are an important fetal warning sign that may indicate fetal distress, placental insufficiency, or fetal compromise requiring urgent assessment with cardiotocography (CTG) and obstetric ultrasound. This is an acute fetal indication for emergency referral. Maternal indications for referral include severe preeclampsia, haemorrhage, obstructed labour, uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes, and severe anaemia unresponsive to initial treatment.

options: Discard the pack and restart after her next period
Stop the pack immediately and await withdrawal bleeding
Take the missed pills now and use backup contraception
Continue as scheduled without any additional precaution
Double the next scheduled dose only once
questions.question: A woman using combined oral contraceptives reports missing two consecutive pills in the second week of her pack. The most appropriate advice is to:
questions.explanation: Missing two pills reduces contraceptive efficacy and requires the woman to take the most recently missed pill immediately, continue the remaining pack as scheduled, and use a backup method such as condoms for seven days. Discarding the pack unnecessarily increases the risk of an unintended pregnancy. Emergency contraception should also be considered if unprotected intercourse occurred in the preceding days.

options: Airway obstruction or respiratory failure needing oxygenation
Management of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease at home
questions.question: The primary indication for endotracheal intubation in a patient is:
questions.explanation: Endotracheal intubation is indicated when patients cannot breathe effectively or maintain adequate oxygenation due to airway obstruction or respiratory failure. It is also used during general anesthesia and cardiopulmonary arrest. Short-term intubation is preferred, as prolonged use risks vocal cord damage and surrounding tissue injury.

questions.question: A patient reports increasing alcohol consumption and social withdrawal as ways of coping with ongoing financial stress. The nurse recognises these behaviours as:
questions.explanation: Maladaptive coping strategies, such as substance use and social withdrawal, may provide temporary relief but ultimately worsen physical and psychological health and can create additional problems. Recognising these patterns allows the nurse to intervene early with healthier coping alternatives and appropriate referrals. Left unaddressed, these behaviours often perpetuate a harmful cycle of stress.

questions.question: A patient recovering from smoking cessation reports increased sputum production in the weeks following quitting. The nurse explains this occurs because:
options: New mucus production has permanently increased
Nicotine withdrawal directly stimulates the lungs
Lung tissue is being damaged by withdrawal
Ciliary function is recovering and clearing retained mucus
Airway inflammation is worsening after cessation
questions.explanation: After smoking cessation, previously paralyzed cilia begin to regain function and start clearing mucus and debris that had accumulated in the airways over time. This temporary increase in sputum production is a positive sign of airway healing, not worsening disease. Patients should be reassured this typically resolves within several weeks.

The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen after traversing the facial canal. It then enters the parotid gland and divides into five terminal branches. Damage at this location causes complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including loss of taste to anterior two-thirds of tongue.
questions.question: The stylomastoid foramen transmits which cranial nerve?
A nurse discovers that hand hygiene supplies are inaccessible at the point of care. Based on recognized reasons for non-compliance, the MOST appropriate immediate action is to:
questions.explanation: Inaccessible hand hygiene supplies are a recognized barrier to compliance. The most appropriate action is to report and rectify the situation to ensure supplies are available at the point of care. Proceeding without hand hygiene violates infection control principles and cannot be justified by inconvenience.
options: Report the inaccessibility and ensure supplies are restocked
Don sterile gloves without performing hand hygiene first
Proceed with the procedure and document the limitation
Request the patient's family member to assist with access
Use the nearest sink, even if further from the patient

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected acute cholecystitis should anticipate that pain will most typically be aggravated by:
questions.explanation: Fatty meals stimulate cholecystokinin release, causing gallbladder contraction against an obstructed or inflamed cystic duct, which intensifies right upper quadrant pain in cholecystitis. Recognising this trigger helps differentiate biliary pain from other abdominal causes. Dietary fat restriction is often advised while awaiting definitive treatment.

questions.question: The primary nursing priority in initial assessment of a crush injury patient is:
options: Immediate measurement of serum myoglobin and creatine kinase levels
Assessment of airway, breathing, circulation (ABCs), and neurological status
Surgical referral for immediate fasciotomy before any assessment is completed
Psychological assessment for post-traumatic stress disorder risk stratification
Collection of blood and urine samples for laboratory analysis and culture
questions.explanation: The primary nursing priority in the initial assessment of a crush injury patient is the primary assessment: ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) and neurological status. This follows the standard ABCDE approach to trauma assessment. Only after the primary survey are secondary assessment (focused on the affected area) and laboratory investigations undertaken.

questions.question: A nurse admits an older client whose family reports sudden confusion, fluctuating attention, and disturbed sleep-wake pattern over the past two days, following a urinary tract infection. This presentation is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Sudden onset of confusion with fluctuating attention, often triggered by an acute illness such as infection, is characteristic of delirium, which is typically reversible with treatment of the underlying cause. Dementia, in contrast, develops gradually over months to years without the acute fluctuation pattern. Recognising delirium promptly is critical because it signals an underlying medical problem requiring urgent evaluation.
options: Chronic schizophrenia with a new acute exacerbation
Dementia, a chronic and gradually progressive decline
Delirium, an acute and potentially reversible confusion
Normal ageing with no clinical significance at all
Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

questions.question: Which nursing assessment tool is MOST appropriate for measuring pain severity in an ophthalmic patient post-operatively?
questions.explanation: The numerical pain rating scale from 0 to 10 is the most appropriate and commonly used validated tool for measuring subjective pain severity in post-operative ophthalmic patients. It provides a simple, reproducible baseline for evaluating effectiveness of pain interventions and for monitoring progress. Snellen charts measure visual acuity, tonometry measures eye pressure, and the Glasgow Coma Scale assesses consciousness rather than pain.
options: Numerical pain rating scale from zero to ten

questions.explanation: Thick, copious purulent discharge that rapidly reaccumulates after cleaning, together with lid crusting on waking, is characteristic of bacterial conjunctivitis, commonly caused by organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae. Viral conjunctivitis more typically produces a watery discharge, while allergic conjunctivitis produces stringy mucoid discharge with prominent itching. Distinguishing these presentations guides whether topical antibiotics are indicated.
questions.question: A patient presents with a thick, purulent, yellow-green discharge that reaccumulates rapidly after wiping, along with lid crusting. This is most consistent with:
options: Giant papillary conjunctivitis from contact lenses

questions.explanation: In cord prolapse, the immediate priority is to relieve pressure on the cord by manually elevating the presenting part off the cord, which preserves fetal circulation and oxygenation while urgent transfer for delivery, usually caesarean section, is arranged. Attempting to replace the cord into the uterus is not recommended as it does not prevent compression and may cause further complications. Positioning the woman in knee-chest or exaggerated Sims' position also helps reduce cord compression.
questions.question: A midwife is called to a woman with a prolapsed umbilical cord visible at the vulva while the fetal head remains high. The FIRST priority action is to:
options: Attempt to replace the cord into the uterus
Apply firm fundal pressure to expedite delivery
Relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part manually
Clamp and cut the cord immediately
Administer oral fluids and reassess in 30 minutes

questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock occurs due to disruption of sympathetic outflow following spinal cord injury or severe central nervous system trauma, resulting in loss of vasomotor tone, widespread vasodilation, and often bradycardia rather than the compensatory tachycardia seen in other shock states. The skin typically remains warm because of the vasodilation, distinguishing it clinically from the cold, clammy skin of hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock. Management focuses on restoring vascular tone and supporting blood pressure.
questions.question: A patient with a spinal cord injury above the mid-thoracic level develops sudden hypotension with a paradoxically slow heart rate and warm skin. This presentation is MOST consistent with:

options: Adrenocortical suppression after a single dose
questions.explanation: Etomidate is known to cause transient adrenocortical suppression by inhibiting 11-beta-hydroxylase, even after a single induction dose, which is a key reason it is used cautiously, particularly in critically ill patients. It is valued for its cardiovascular stability rather than causing hypertension or bronchospasm. It is not a neuromuscular blocking agent and does not itself cause prolonged paralysis.
questions.question: A patient receiving etomidate for rapid sequence induction should be monitored for which recognised adverse effect?

questions.explanation: Fruity-smelling breath from ketone production, deep rapid Kussmaul breathing as a compensatory response to metabolic acidosis, and altered consciousness together are classic features of diabetic ketoacidosis, a complication most commonly seen in type 1 diabetes due to absolute insulin deficiency. This differs from hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, which is more typical in type 2 diabetes and usually lacks significant ketosis. Rapid recognition is critical given the life-threatening nature of this complication.
options: Simple dehydration from reduced fluid intake
questions.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes presents with fruity-smelling breath, deep rapid breathing, and confusion. What life-threatening complication should the nurse suspect?

questions.explanation: Mastoiditis occurs when middle ear infection spreads to the adjacent mastoid bone, producing swelling, tenderness and characteristic outward displacement of the pinna. Otosclerosis involves gradual bony changes without acute infection, while serous otitis media presents with effusion rather than mastoid swelling. Presbycusis and Meniere's disease are unrelated degenerative and inner ear conditions respectively.
questions.question: A client with long-standing untreated otitis media develops swelling, redness, and tenderness behind the ear with outward displacement of the pinna. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

questions.explanation: Extensive myocardial damage reduces the heart's pumping ability, lowering cardiac output, while compensatory vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance in an attempt to maintain blood pressure. This combination produces the hallmark hypotension and poor perfusion of cardiogenic shock. Recognising this pattern guides the choice of inotropic support.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient in cardiogenic shock after extensive myocardial infarction should anticipate which haemodynamic finding?
options: Low blood volume with normal cardiac contractility
Normal cardiac output with normal blood pressure
Low cardiac output with elevated systemic vascular resistance
High cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance
High cardiac output with high blood pressure

questions.explanation: Breast development (thelarche) is usually the first visible sign of puberty in girls, beginning around ages 9-13. This precedes menarche by approximately 2-3 years and is driven by rising estrogen levels. Pubic and axillary hair growth typically follow breast development as secondary manifestations.
questions.question: Which is typically the first sign of puberty in girls?

questions.explanation: Preoperative smoking cessation and blood glucose optimization represent patient health optimization—a component of perioperative preparation that addresses modifiable risk factors. Smoking impairs wound healing, and hyperglycemia promotes bacterial growth; optimizing both significantly reduces postoperative complication rates.
questions.question: Encouraging preoperative smoking cessation and optimizing blood glucose in diabetic patients before surgery are examples of which perioperative preparation component?
options: Patient education to improve postoperative self-care ability
Medication management for perioperative drug interactions
Coordination of care between surgical and medical teams
Psychological support to reduce preoperative anxiety levels
Patient health optimization to reduce surgical risk factors

questions.question: A patient placed in the lithotomy position for a prolonged gynaecological procedure is at increased risk of which nerve injury?
questions.explanation: In the lithotomy position, the common peroneal nerve is vulnerable to compression against the fibular head from leg supports, particularly during prolonged procedures, and can result in foot drop if unrecognised. Ulnar and radial nerve injuries are more typically associated with improper arm positioning in the supine position, while brachial plexus injury is linked to excessive arm abduction rather than leg positioning.
options: Ulnar nerve injury at the elbow
Common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular head
Brachial plexus injury from arm abduction
Radial nerve injury at the humeral groove
Facial nerve injury from mask pressure

questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman with a persistent occipito-posterior position anticipates that if the head fails to rotate anteriorly, the MOST likely outcome is:
questions.explanation: When the occiput fails to rotate fully anteriorly, the head may become arrested in the transverse diameter, known as deep transverse arrest, or may rotate posteriorly and deliver face-to-pubis. Both scenarios often require instrumental assistance or caesarean section if progress stalls. Close monitoring of descent and rotation is therefore essential in persistent occipito-posterior positions.
options: Deep transverse arrest or face-to-pubis delivery
Complete resolution without further monitoring needed

questions.question: A woman going through menopause and her husband going through andropause both report irritability and reduced concentration. From a nursing management perspective, what is the most appropriate approach to their shared symptoms?
options: Ignoring symptoms since they resolve without intervention
Prescribing identical hormone therapy to both without assessment
Individualised counselling and symptom-focused support for each partner
Referring both exclusively to a psychiatrist without assessment
Advising complete cessation of all physical activity
questions.explanation: Because symptoms and underlying hormonal changes differ between menopause and andropause, individualised assessment and counselling tailored to each partner's specific needs is the appropriate nursing approach. Blanket, non-individualised interventions risk inappropriate or ineffective management. Supportive counselling addresses the emotional as well as physical dimensions of these transitions.

While approximately 9-10 liters of fluid enter the GI tract daily (2L ingested, 7-8L secreted), about 8-8.5 liters are absorbed in the small intestine through osmosis following solute absorption, leaving only 1-1.5L to enter the colon. The colon further absorbs 0.9-1.4L, leaving 100-200ml in feces. Despite the colon's efficiency (absorbing 90% of water it receives), the small intestine handles the larger absolute volume. Diseases affecting the small intestine cause more severe diarrhea than colonic diseases.
questions.question: The primary site of water absorption in the GI tract is the:

questions.explanation: Correct walking frame technique involves moving the frame forward first and then stepping into it, allowing the frame to provide stable weight-bearing support before the client shifts weight, reducing fall risk. Moving the frame after stepping, or leaning backward, undermines its stabilising purpose. Proper technique education is an important nursing responsibility to maximise the safety benefit of assistive devices.
options: Forward first, then step into it with weight-bearing support
While leaning quite heavily backward onto the frame
Only when finally reaching a designated resting point eventually
Simultaneously with rapid, quick stepping movements
After both feet have already stepped forward fully
questions.question: A nurse is educating an older client on the correct use of a walking frame to reduce fall risk. The nurse should emphasise that the client should move the frame:
A mother asks what the 'Amount' criterion within FADUA complementary feeding guidance refers to. The correct explanation is that it refers to:
questions.explanation: The 'Amount' criterion within FADUA refers to offering a quantity of complementary food appropriate to the infant's age, growing energy needs, and limited stomach capacity, gradually increasing portion size as the infant grows. Offering too little fails to meet nutritional requirements, while portions that are excessively large may overwhelm a young infant. This criterion works alongside frequency and density to ensure overall adequate nutrient intake.
options: the total number of different food types offered
the food quantity relative to stomach capacity
the exact weight of the infant
the cost of the food ingredients
the colour variety of foods offered

questions.explanation: The perineal body separates the vagina from the anal canal posteriorly. It is a pyramidal fibromuscular mass at the centre of the perineum into which multiple pelvic floor muscles insert. Its integrity is essential for pelvic floor support and continence. Damage to the perineal body during childbirth (as in third- or fourth-degree perineal tears) can result in faecal incontinence if not properly repaired.
questions.question: The perineal body separates the vagina from which structure posteriorly?

options: Hypovolaemic shock from significant fluid loss
Obstructive shock from a mechanical circulatory cause
Cardiogenic shock from impaired pump function
Compensated shock with no haemodynamic compromise
questions.question: A nurse caring for a septic patient notes warm, flushed skin despite hypotension and tachycardia. This presentation reflects which type of shock?
questions.explanation: Distributive shock, such as septic shock, causes widespread vasodilation leading to warm, flushed skin despite hypotension, in contrast to the cool periphery seen in hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock. This distinction helps guide diagnosis and targeted treatment such as vasopressor therapy alongside fluids. Recognising the warm shock pattern is key to identifying a distributive cause.

options: 100-200ml after each loose stool as a Plan A guide
50-100ml after each loose stool as appropriate amount
250ml after each loose stool to ensure adequate rehydration
200-400ml after each loose stool for children under 2
10-20ml per kg after each loose stool based on weight
questions.explanation: IMCI Plan A (home treatment for no dehydration) specifies: after each loose stool, give 50-100 ml of ORS for children under 2 years, and 100-200 ml for children aged 2-10 years. Additionally, continue feeding normally, increase fluids, and return immediately if danger signs develop. Mothers should be shown how to prepare ORS correctly (dissolve one sachet in one litre of clean water) and given enough sachets for 2 days of home treatment.
questions.question: When counselling mothers on giving ORS at home (Plan A in IMCI), the nurse should advise giving ORS after each loose stool in the following amount for children under 2 years:
Guaifenesin is classified as an:
questions.explanation: Guaifenesin is an expectorant that increases respiratory tract fluid secretions, reducing mucus viscosity and making it easier to cough up and expectorate. The mechanism involves stimulating vagal gastric reflexes and directly stimulating respiratory tract secretory cells. Expectorants are used for productive coughs in conditions like acute bronchitis or upper respiratory infections where facilitating mucus clearance is beneficial. Unlike mucolytics that chemically break down mucus, expectorants work by increasing hydration of secretions. Clinical evidence for expectorant efficacy is limited, and adequate hydration is equally important.

questions.question: The Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV) given in Nigeria's schedule protects against Streptococcus pneumoniae, which causes:
options: Meningococcal meningitis and septicaemia in school-age children
Pneumonia, meningitis, septicaemia, and otitis media in children
Haemophilus influenzae type b diseases in unimmunised children
Respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis in the first year of life
Pertussis whooping cough and laryngotracheobronchitis syndrome
questions.explanation: The Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV) protects against Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus), which causes pneumonia, meningitis, bacteraemia, and otitis media (middle ear infection) in children. Pneumococcal disease is a leading cause of vaccine-preventable childhood mortality globally. PCV is given at 6, 10, and 14 weeks in Nigeria's schedule. The conjugate vaccine formulation ensures immunogenicity in infants under 2 years, who do not respond well to plain polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccines.

options: Advocate for honest, sensitive disclosure to the patient
Tell the patient a falsely optimistic prognosis instead
Avoid the patient entirely to sidestep the conflict
Agree to withhold the information as requested
Discuss the prognosis only with the family present
questions.question: A nurse is asked by a physician to withhold a poor prognosis from a competent patient at the family's request. The nurse's most appropriate response, guided by the principle of veracity, is to:
questions.explanation: The principle of veracity supports a competent patient's right to honest information about their own condition, even when family members request otherwise, and the nurse should advocate for sensitive, truthful disclosure. Withholding information from a competent patient undermines their autonomy and ability to make informed decisions. Skilled communication can balance honesty with compassion in delivering difficult news.

options: Encourage very hot spicy meals for taste
Provide frequent gentle saline mouth rinses
Restrict all oral fluids until healed
Apply firm scrubbing with a hard toothbrush
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-induced mucositis causes painful oral ulceration that impairs nutrition if untreated. Frequent gentle saline rinses cleanse the mouth without further irritating fragile mucosa, promoting comfort and healing. Hot, spicy, or acidic foods and harsh brushing would worsen mucosal trauma.
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with leukaemia who reports painful mouth ulcers preventing adequate oral intake. The most appropriate nursing intervention is to:
Congenital syphilis in a neonate born to an untreated infected mother most characteristically presents with which clinical feature?
options: Absent red reflex in both eyes
Sunset sign of both eyes bilaterally
Cataracts present at the time of birth
questions.explanation: Congenital syphilis classically presents with persistent nasal discharge known as snuffles, along with skin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities such as periostitis, resulting from transplacental spirochaete transmission. The sunset sign is instead associated with hydrocephalus, while cataracts and cardiac murmurs are more typical of congenital rubella syndrome. Early recognition allows prompt penicillin treatment of both mother and infant.

options: Withhold all anaesthesia until allergy resolves
Proceed without mentioning the allergy history
Alert the anaesthetist to verify true allergy
Substitute atropine for the induction agent
questions.question: A patient with a known egg allergy is scheduled for induction with propofol. What is the MOST appropriate nursing action?
questions.explanation: Historically propofol was thought to be contraindicated in egg allergy, but current evidence suggests the lecithin component is not the allergenic egg protein, so the nurse should alert the anaesthetist to verify the nature and severity of the allergy rather than assume automatic contraindication. Cancelling surgery outright is not necessary for most egg allergies. Atropine is not an induction agent.

Once the catecholamine-secreting tumour is removed, the sudden loss of previously high circulating catecholamine levels can cause a significant and sometimes profound drop in blood pressure, so close haemodynamic monitoring is essential in the immediate postoperative period. This risk is specific to the abrupt hormonal change following tumour removal. Anticipating this complication allows for timely fluid or vasopressor support if needed.
options: Sudden hypotension from abrupt withdrawal of excess catecholamines
questions.question: A patient recovering from adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma has their blood pressure monitored very closely in the immediate postoperative period. What complication is this monitoring specifically aimed at detecting?

questions.explanation: In the early hyperdynamic phase of septic shock, profound peripheral vasodilation reduces systemic vascular resistance, and the heart initially compensates by increasing output to maintain blood pressure, producing warm extremities despite hypotension. This contrasts with the cold, clammy presentation typical of hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock. As sepsis progresses, however, myocardial depression and worsening capillary leak can eventually overwhelm this compensatory hyperdynamic state.
options: The myocardium becomes hyperfunctional independent of preload
Intravascular volume is markedly increased above normal
Widespread vasodilation reduces peripheral resistance while the heart compensates
Sympathetic outflow is completely abolished early in sepsis
Bacterial toxins directly increase myocardial contractility permanently
questions.question: A patient in early septic shock is noted to have a hyperdynamic circulation with warm extremities despite hypotension. Cardiac output may be preserved or even increased early in septic shock because:

questions.explanation: For patients with low health literacy, simple demonstration combined with plain-language verbal explanation is more effective than dense written material or rapid, unsupported verbal instruction. Visual and hands-on components reinforce understanding beyond text alone. Tailoring teaching method to literacy level improves retention and correct skill performance.
options: An online self-directed course requiring independent reading
A lengthy written pamphlet with technical medical terminology
Simple demonstration paired with plain-language verbal explanation
A single verbal explanation delivered at a rapid pace
A recorded lecture delivered without any visual demonstration
questions.question: Which preoperative teaching method is MOST appropriate for a patient with low health literacy who needs to learn wound care?

questions.explanation: The "dinner fork deformity" in Colles' fracture results from posterior displacement of the distal radial fragment.
