options: High-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma with 60-70% recurrence
Carcinoma in situ requiring intravesical BCG therapy
Papilloma with benign behaviour and under 5% recurrence
PUNLMP with very low malignant transformation rate
Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma with 50-70% recurrence
questions.question: A 70-year-old man has haematuria. Biopsy shows papillary urothelial architecture with mild nuclear atypia, preserved polarity, and rare mitoses. How is this classified and what is the expected recurrence risk?

questions.explanation:
Biomphalaria snails serve as intermediate hosts for S. mansoni in Africa
and South America. Different schistosome species require specific snail
species: Bulinus for S. haematobium, Oncomelania for S. japonicum.
Control measures targeting snails reduce transmission.
questions.question: Which intermediate host transmits Schistosoma mansoni?

questions.explanation: Rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults) result from vitamin D deficiency causing inadequate bone mineralization. Widened epiphyseal plates, delayed closure, bowing deformities, and fractures occur in children. Causes include dietary deficiency, malabsorption, and renal disease. Elevated alkaline phosphatase, decreased calcium/phosphate, and elevated PTH are characteristic. Vitamin D supplementation is curative.
questions.question: Rickets results from deficiency of:
Which enzyme deficiency causes phenylketonuria?
questions.explanation:
Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU with phenylalanine
accumulation. Untreated cases develop mental retardation, seizures, and
hypopigmentation. Dietary phenylalanine restriction prevents neurologic
damage when started early.

questions.question: A child presents with chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Sweat chloride testing is markedly elevated. Which underlying defect explains this combination of findings?
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis results from mutations in the CFTR gene encoding a chloride channel, leading to thick secretions affecting the lungs, pancreas, and sweat glands, with elevated sweat chloride being a key diagnostic test. Pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption and failure to thrive, while thickened airway secretions predispose to recurrent infections. Newborn screening has improved early detection and outcomes in affected infants.

questions.question: Papillary renal cell carcinoma type 1 is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Type 1 papillary RCC shows papillae/tubules lined by small cells with scant basophilic cytoplasm and low-grade nuclei. Favorable prognosis. Multifocality common. Trisomies 7 and 17, loss of Y chromosome occur. Hereditary papillary RCC syndrome (MET mutations) predisposes. Type 2 has larger cells, eosinophilic cytoplasm, high-grade nuclei, worse prognosis.

questions.question: What is the screening test for hereditary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Screening for hereditary hemochromatosis involves measuring the percentage transferrin saturation (serum iron divided by total iron binding capacity). Values persistently above 45-50% warrant further investigation. Genetic testing for HFE mutations (particularly C282Y and H63D) confirms the diagnosis. Liver biopsy with iron quantification may be performed.

questions.question: Which mutation is most important in familial gastric cancer?
questions.explanation: CDH1 mutations are found in familial gastric cancers and in 50% of sporadic diffuse tumors. The loss of E-cadherin function, encoded by CDH1, seems to be a key step in the development of diffuse gastric cancer. Other genetic alterations include FAP, MSI, and hypermethylation of several genes.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis typically affects males around age 30, with 70% male predominance. It is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel diseases (particularly ulcerative colitis), pancreatitis, and idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis. The disease is characterized by beading on radiographs.
questions.question: What is the characteristic age and gender distribution of primary sclerosing cholangitis?

questions.explanation: In endemic areas, infestation by liver flukes, particularly Opisthorchis sinensis and Clonorchis species, is a major risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma. Other risk factors include primary sclerosing cholangitis, hepatolithiasis, fibropolycystic liver disease, and viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV). Chronic inflammation and cholestasis promote carcinogenesis.
questions.question: What is the major risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma in endemic areas?

A 7-year-old girl presents with a vulvar mass. Biopsy shows benign-appearing cells forming tubules and trabeculae with Call-Exner body-like structures, associated with gonadoblastoma. Which karyotype is most commonly associated?
questions.explanation: Gonadoblastoma occurs almost exclusively in patients with gonadal dysgenesis and a Y chromosome (46,XY phenotypic females, or mosaic 45,X/46,XY individuals). It is composed of germ cells and sex cord stromal cells forming nests, and may coexist with or give rise to dysgerminoma. The presence of a Y chromosome in a phenotypic female with streak gonads mandates prophylactic gonadectomy to prevent malignant transformation. TSPY (testis-specific protein on Y chromosome) is considered the key gene driving gonadoblastoma risk in this setting.

questions.question: Angelman syndrome is confirmed by maternal UBE3A point mutation. If the mother carries the mutation, recurrence risk in future pregnancies is:
questions.explanation: UBE3A mutations cause Angelman syndrome only when maternally inherited because paternal UBE3A is imprinted and silenced in neurons. If the mother carries a UBE3A mutation, 50% of children inherit the maternal mutant copy and express Angelman syndrome. The other 50% inherit the normal maternal allele and are unaffected. Maternal carrier testing is therefore essential before accurate recurrence risk counseling can be provided to the family planning further pregnancies.
options: Less than 1% as UBE3A mutations are usually sporadic events
Zero percent since maternal imprinting silences the gene always
100% as mothers transmit all mutations to every child
50% of children receiving the maternal mutant allele affected
25% applying standard autosomal recessive inheritance ratios

questions.explanation:
Type III hyperlipoproteinemia involves apolipoprotein E mutation causing
remnant lipoprotein accumulation. Both cholesterol and triglycerides are
elevated. Palmar xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis occur.
questions.question: What distinguishes Type III hyperlipoproteinemia from other types?

options: Loss of dopaminergic neurons with Lewy bodies
Plaques of beta-amyloid and neurofibrillary tangles
Huntingtin protein aggregates in striatal neurons
Spongiform vacuolation from prion protein accumulation
Demyelination of nigrostriatal white matter tracts
questions.question: A 70-year-old man presents with resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity responding well to levodopa. Which pathological finding is expected in the substantia nigra?
questions.explanation: Parkinson disease is characterised by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with Lewy bodies — eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions composed of misfolded alpha-synuclein filaments. Loss of neuromelanin-containing neurons produces gross pallor of the substantia nigra. The dopaminergic deficit in the nigrostriatal pathway explains the motor symptoms and their response to levodopa replacement. SNCA gene mutations (alpha-synuclein) and LRRK2 mutations cause familial Parkinson disease. Lewy bodies are also found in the locus coeruleus and dorsal vagal nucleus.

Giant condyloma acuminatum (Buschke-Lwenstein tumor) shows massive exophytic growth with local destruction but lacks metastatic potential. HPV 6 and 11 association. Histologically benign-appearing with papillomatosis and koilocytosis but deeply infiltrative. Differential includes verrucous carcinoma. Wide surgical excision required; recurrence common. May undergo malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.question: Buschke-Lwenstein tumor (giant condyloma) is characterized by:
Hassall's corpuscles are characteristic structures found in which thymic compartment?
questions.explanation:
Hassall's corpuscles are concentric whorls of keratinized
epithelial cells found in the thymic medulla, increasing in number with
age. Their exact function remains unclear but may involve regulatory T
cell development. These structures are pathognomically thymic and aid in
histological identification of thymic tissue.

Homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency causes homogentisic acid
accumulation producing dark urine. Ochronosis develops with pigment
deposition in connective tissues. Arthritis affects large joints in
later life.
questions.question: Which defect causes alkaptonuria?

options: Atresia of the duodenum at the level of the ampulla
Failure of midgut rotation causing volvulus
Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction
Absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel
questions.explanation: Pyloric stenosis results from hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer of the pylorus, causing progressive gastric outlet obstruction that produces the classic projectile, non-bilious vomiting and a palpable 'olive' mass on examination. This is distinct from intestinal malrotation with volvulus, which classically causes bilious vomiting due to obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater. Ultrasound demonstrating thickened, elongated pyloric muscle confirms the diagnosis.
questions.question: A 6-week-old male infant presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds and is found to have a palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium. Which underlying pathological process explains this presentation?

questions.explanation: VHL disease (VHL gene mutation on 3p25) predisposes to multiple bilateral clear cell renal cell carcinomas, cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, pancreatic cysts/neuroendocrine tumors. Renal cysts precede carcinomas. Surveillance includes annual abdominal imaging. Nephron-sparing surgery preferred for tumors >3cm. Germline VHL mutations also occur in 50% of sporadic clear cell RCCs.
questions.question: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with:
What dietary management treats urea cycle disorders?
questions.explanation:
Protein restriction limits ammonia production while essential amino acid
supplementation prevents deficiency. Sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate
provide alternative nitrogen disposal. Liver transplantation is
curative.

questions.question: What complication is indicated by green-black necrotic gallbladder?
questions.explanation: Gangrenous cholecystitis is characterized by a green-black necrotic organ with transmural necrosis. This severe complication of acute cholecystitis results from vascular compromise and tissue death. It carries high risk of perforation, peritonitis, and sepsis, and requires emergency surgical intervention.

FMR1 premutation alleles (55-200 CGG repeats) in males over 50 cause Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia, intention tremor, and cognitive decline. The premutation produces excess FMR1 mRNA that sequesters RNA-binding proteins, causing toxic gain of function distinct from the full mutation mechanism of Fragile X syndrome. The grandfather transmitted his premutation to the mother, who underwent further repeat expansion to a full mutation in her son, causing Fragile X syndrome through complete absence of FMR protein.
options: Full mutation FMR1 expansion expressing late in adult males
FMR1 deletion causing neurodegeneration in older adult males
FMR1 premutation causing FXTAS from toxic RNA gain of function
Normal FMR1 repeat range with coincidental cerebellar disease
Somatic FMR1 mutation accumulating in cerebellar neurons only
questions.question: Fragile X syndrome is diagnosed in a boy with intellectual disability. His maternal grandfather has late-onset ataxia and tremor. The grandfather's neurological disorder results from:
What is linitis plastica?
questions.explanation: Linitis plastica ("leather bottle stomach") describes diffuse gastric cancer with extensive desmoplastic reaction stiffening the gastric wall, causing rigid, non-distensible stomach. The mucosa may appear grossly normal while tumor infiltrates diffusely through the wall. This pattern is characteristic of signet ring cell carcinoma (diffuse type) but can occur with breast or lung metastases. Prognosis is very poor.

questions.question: Which extraintestinal manifestation is characteristic of familial adenomatous polyposis?
questions.explanation: Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium is a characteristic extraintestinal manifestation of familial adenomatous polyposis. Variant syndromes include Gardner syndrome (osteomas, epidermal cysts, desmoid tumors, dental abnormalities) and Turcot syndrome (CNS tumors including medulloblastomas and glioblastomas).

Approximately 70% of prostatic adenocarcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, accessible to digital rectal examination. This differs from BPH originating in transition zone. Peripheral zone cancers may not cause obstructive symptoms until advanced. Transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy samples peripheral zone preferentially.
questions.question: Which prostatic zone is most commonly affected by adenocarcinoma?
What are the clinical consequences of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Clinical consequences of chronic pancreatitis include chronic abdominal pain (most common symptom), malabsorption from exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea, weight loss), and diabetes mellitus from endocrine insufficiency. Patients may develop obstructive jaundice from fibrosis around the bile duct, and have 40% lifetime risk of pancreatic cancer. Complications also include pseudocysts and splenic vein thrombosis.

questions.question: Which vitamin supplementation helps some organic acidemias?
questions.explanation:
Some methylmalonic acidemia cases respond to vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
supplementation. Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA
mutase. Mut- variants retain partial enzyme responsiveness.

questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with recurrent urinary tract infections and is found on imaging to have dilated ureters with reflux of contrast into the renal pelvis during voiding cystourethrogram. Which underlying mechanism best explains this finding?
questions.explanation: Vesicoureteric reflux results from an incompetent valve mechanism at the ureterovesical junction, normally formed by the oblique, submucosal course of the distal ureter through the bladder wall, allowing retrograde flow of urine into the ureter and renal pelvis during voiding. This predisposes to recurrent urinary tract infections and, if severe or longstanding, renal scarring. Grading reflux severity on voiding cystourethrogram guides decisions regarding prophylactic antibiotics or surgical correction.

questions.question: Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) confers how much increased breast cancer risk?
questions.explanation: ADH confers 4-5 times increased breast cancer risk. This proliferative lesion with atypia shows some but not all features of DCIS (extent <2mm or <2 duct spaces). Excision ensures no adjacent DCIS exists. Annual surveillance mammography recommended. Chemoprevention with tamoxifen or raloxifene reduces risk in high-risk patients.

questions.question: Craniopharyngioma arises from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation:
Craniopharyngiomas derive from Rathke's pouch remnants
(embryonic precursor of anterior pituitary), occurring in suprasellar
region. Two types exist: adamantinomatous (children, calcifications,
"wet keratin") and papillary (adults, BRAF V600E mutations). Despite
being benign (WHO grade I), location causes visual and endocrine
dysfunction.

questions.question: Inflammatory breast cancer is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer shows extensive dermal lymphatic invasion causing breast erythema, edema, and peau d'orange (resembling orange peel) without discrete mass. Rapidly progressive and aggressive with poor prognosis. Skin punch biopsy demonstrates tumor in lymphatics. Staging is T4d regardless of tumor size. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery and radiation provides best outcomes.

Primary ovarian insufficiency affects most galactosemia females despite
lactose-free diet. Mechanism involves toxic galactose metabolite
accumulation. Fertility preservation options are limited.
questions.question: Which galactosemia complication occurs despite treatment?

questions.explanation: Symptoms of hemochromatosis typically occur after accumulation of 20 grams of iron, usually after age 40. Clinical manifestations include micronodular cirrhosis (100%), diabetes mellitus from pancreatic deposition (75%), and skin pigmentation (65%). There is also a 200-fold increased risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (20% risk).
questions.question: At what total body iron level do symptoms of hemochromatosis typically appear?
Which Turner syndrome variant has best prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Mosaicism with 46,XX cell line improves prognosis with milder phenotype
and possible fertility. Degree of mosaicism affects phenotypic severity.
Some mosaic individuals are nearly normal.

questions.question: Seminal vesicle epithelium is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicle epithelium shows tall columnar cells with abundant cytoplasm containing golden-brown lipofuscin pigment, nuclear pleomorphism (degenerative atypia), and complex architecture. May contaminate prostate biopsies and mimic adenocarcinoma. Distinguished by typical cytology, lack of AMACR, and absence of basal cells (normal for seminal vesicle). Awareness prevents over-diagnosis.

questions.question: What age group typically develops Leber hereditary optic neuropathy?
questions.explanation:
LHON typically manifests between ages 15-35, predominantly in males.
Environmental factors like smoking and alcohol may trigger disease.
Point mutations in complex I genes are causative.

questions.question: Salpingitis isthmica nodosa is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Salpingitis isthmica nodosa shows epithelial diverticula extending into hypertrophied muscularis of isthmic portion, creating nodular thickening. May follow chronic inflammation or represent developmental anomaly. Associated with infertility and ectopic pregnancy. Demonstrates intact epithelial lining distinguishing from adenomyosis. Usually bilateral. Conservative surgical treatment for symptomatic cases.

questions.question: Docetaxel chemotherapy in prostate cancer works by:
questions.explanation: Docetaxel is a taxane stabilizing microtubules and preventing depolymerization, causing mitotic arrest and apoptosis. First chemotherapy showing survival benefit in metastatic CRPC. Given with prednisone every three weeks. Side effects include myelosuppression, neuropathy, fatigue, and nail changes. Cabazitaxel (second-line taxane) treats docetaxel-resistant disease.

questions.question: What maternal PKU effect threatens pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
High maternal phenylalanine during pregnancy causes fetal PKU syndrome
with microcephaly, intellectual disability, and cardiac defects. Occurs
even if fetus doesn't have PKU. Strict diet before conception prevents
damage.

questions.question: Which reproductive technology helps Klinefelter syndrome fertility?
questions.explanation:
Testicular sperm extraction (TESE) with intracytoplasmic sperm injection
enables biological paternity in some KS men. Focal spermatogenesis may
persist despite azoospermia. Success rates vary.

options: Annual CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis for all organ screening
Whole-body MRI to minimize ionizing radiation exposure risk
Annual PET-CT to detect metabolically active early malignancies
Regular mammography starting at age 25 as sole modality
Annual ultrasound of abdomen and pelvis only for soft tissue
questions.question: A 35-year-old with Li-Fraumeni syndrome (germline TP53 mutation) undergoes cancer surveillance. The imaging modality of choice for surveillance is:
questions.explanation: Li-Fraumeni syndrome patients have germline TP53 mutations, making them hypersensitive to ionizing radiation-induced DNA damage and secondary malignancies. CT and PET-CT, which involve significant ionizing radiation exposure, are relatively contraindicated for surveillance. Whole-body MRI (using the LIFSCREEN protocol) can survey the entire body without radiation, detecting adrenocortical carcinomas, sarcomas, brain tumors, and breast cancers in a single annual examination. Annual breast MRI from age 20 complements whole-body MRI for breast cancer surveillance in female carriers.

Tay-Sachs disease shows cherry-red macular spot from ganglioside
accumulation in retinal ganglion cells. Central retina appears red while
surrounding ganglion cells appear white. Hexosaminidase A deficiency
causes GM2 ganglioside accumulation.
questions.question: Which lysosomal storage disease causes cherry-red spot on macula?

questions.explanation:
Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile
anesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane) and succinylcholine in genetically
susceptible individuals (RYR1 or CACNA1S mutations). Uncontrolled
calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum causes sustained muscle
contraction, hyperthermia, hypermetabolism, and rhabdomyolysis.
Dantrolene (blocks calcium release) is life-saving treatment.
questions.question: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by which agents?
Cribriform pattern in prostatic adenocarcinoma corresponds to Gleason pattern:
questions.explanation: Cribriform architecture (irregular glands with sieve-like pattern) represents Gleason pattern 4, indicating higher-grade disease. Clean, well-formed cribriform glands may be pattern 3, but most cribriform patterns are 4. Gleason pattern 5 shows solid sheets, cords, or single cells. Recognition of pattern 4 is critical for risk stratification and treatment decisions.

questions.question: What is the most frequent malignant tumor of the biliary tract?
questions.explanation: Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the most frequent malignant tumor of the biliary tract. It is more common in women and strongly associated with gallstone disease. The tumor may be exophytic or infiltrating, with most being adenocarcinomas (papillary or poorly differentiated). Survival rate is dismal.

Panacinar emphysema predominantly affects lung bases in a1-AT
deficiency. Neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls without
sufficient a1-AT inhibition. Disease accelerates with smoking.
questions.question: What lung pathology characterizes a1-antitrypsin deficiency?
What is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism of cholesterol gallstone formation?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol gallstone formation occurs when cholesterol concentration exceeds the solubilizing capacity of bile salts (supersaturation), leading to cholesterol nucleation into monohydrate crystals. This is facilitated by four conditions: supersaturation, gallbladder hypomotility, accelerated cholesterol crystal nucleation, and hypersecretion of mucus in the gallbladder.

questions.question: Sjogren syndrome is characterized by which pathological features?
questions.explanation:
Sjogren syndrome shows lymphocytic infiltration (mainly
CD4+ T cells) destroying salivary and lacrimal glands, causing dry mouth
(xerostomia) and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). Anti-SSA (Ro)
and anti-SSB (La) antibodies are characteristic. The disease can be
primary or secondary to other autoimmune diseases (RA, SLE). Increased
risk of B-cell lymphoma exists.

questions.question: What is the function of normal a1-antitrypsin?
questions.explanation:
a1-antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase preventing proteolytic lung
damage. The protease-antiprotease balance maintains lung integrity.
Deficiency shifts balance toward proteolysis causing emphysema.

Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma contains
"popcorn" or L&H (lymphocytic and histiocytic) cells with multilobated
nuclei resembling popped corn, distinct from classic Reed-Sternberg
cells. These cells are CD20+ and CD15/CD30 negative, representing a
different disease entity from classical Hodgkin. The prognosis is
generally excellent but late relapses occur.
questions.question: Which morphological cell variant is specifically found in lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma?

questions.explanation: Patients with cirrhosis usually die due to progressive liver failure, complications of portal hypertension (particularly variceal bleeding), or development of hepatocellular carcinoma. The specific cause depends on the etiology and stage of cirrhosis. Hepatorenal syndrome, sepsis, and hepatic encephalopathy are also important causes of mortality.
questions.question: What is the most common cause of death in cirrhosis?
What are sanded nuclei in hepatitis B infection?
questions.explanation: Sanded nuclei are hepatocellular nuclei with a finely granular, pale eosinophilic appearance of the larger central part of the nucleus, due to massive accumulation of HBcAg. Special stains including Victoria blue, immunoperoxidase, and Shikata Orcein stain can be used to demonstrate viral antigens.

questions.question: What is the hallmark of familial adenomatous polyposis?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is diagnosed by the presence of ≥100 adenomatous polyps in the colorectum, germline APC mutation, or family history with any number of adenomas at young age. Untreated patients develop colorectal cancer by age 40 with nearly 100% penetrance. Prophylactic colectomy is recommended. Attenuated FAP has <100 polyps with later onset.

questions.question: What is the size distinction between micronodular and macronodular cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: Micronodular cirrhosis has nodules less than 3 mm in diameter, while macronodular cirrhosis has nodules greater than 3 mm. Mixed micro-macronodular cirrhosis comprises approximately equal numbers of nodules greater than and less than 3 mm. The nodular pattern may evolve over time as the disease progresses.

questions.question: What histologic type comprises most gallbladder carcinomas?
questions.explanation: Most gallbladder carcinomas are adenocarcinomas, either papillary (better prognosis) or poorly differentiated infiltrating type. Less common variants include squamous cell carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and neuroendocrine tumors. The tumors may grow exophytically into the lumen or infiltrate diffusely through the wall into adjacent liver, causing diagnostic challenges on imaging.

Most club foot cases represent deformations from uterine
constraint (oligohydramnios, breech position, multiple gestations)
affecting normally formed feet. The deformation is correctible with
early intervention. Some cases may represent malformations (particularly
bilateral cases or those with other anomalies) requiring different
management approaches.
questions.question: Club foot (talipes equinovarus) is typically an example of which process?

questions.explanation: Parathyroid carcinoma diagnosis requires demonstration of invasion into adjacent structures, vascular invasion, or metastases. Cytologic features are unreliable. These rare tumors cause severe hypercalcemia (often >14mg/dL) and markedly elevated PTH. Complete surgical excision with negative margins provides best outcomes. Local recurrence is common.
questions.question: Parathyroid carcinoma can be distinguished from adenoma by:
Potter sequence results from which primary defect?
questions.explanation:
Potter sequence results from bilateral renal agenesis (or
severe dysplasia) causing severe oligohydramnios, which leads to
pulmonary hypoplasia (from inadequate thoracic space), limb positioning
defects, and characteristic facies. The oligohydramnios is the critical
factor allowing mechanical compression effects. Pulmonary hypoplasia
causes neonatal death.

questions.question: A 20-year-old woman has an ovarian mass with Schiller-Duval bodies and markedly elevated serum AFP. Which tumour is this finding most characteristic of?
questions.explanation: Yolk sac tumour (endodermal sinus tumour) is characterised by Schiller-Duval bodies — glomeruloid structures with a central blood vessel surrounded by tumour cells — representing yolk sac differentiation. AFP is markedly elevated, serving as a diagnostic and monitoring marker. It most commonly affects young women and girls. BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin) chemotherapy is highly effective. Serum AFP should normalise after complete resection; failure to do so or subsequent rise signals residual or recurrent disease requiring restaging and salvage chemotherapy.
options: Embryonal carcinoma producing both AFP and hCG
Hepatoid carcinoma of primary ovarian origin
Immature teratoma with hepatic tissue differentiation

questions.explanation:
Amniocentesis with hexosaminidase A assay or DNA testing detects
Tay-Sachs prenatally. Chorionic villus sampling enables earlier
diagnosis. Carrier screening allows prevention through reproductive
choices.
questions.question: What prenatal test detects Tay-Sachs disease?
Renal cell carcinoma in end-stage renal disease occurs in:
questions.explanation: Acquired cystic kidney disease develops in end-stage kidneys after prolonged dialysis (>3 years), increasing RCC risk 100-fold. Multiple bilateral cysts contain atypical epithelium. RCCs are often multiple, bilateral, and papillary. Screening with imaging recommended. Native nephrectomy considered for high-risk patients (men, longer dialysis duration, larger cysts).

questions.question: Parkinson disease pathology involves:
questions.explanation: Parkinson disease shows loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra with Lewy bodies (a-synuclein aggregates). Motor symptoms include resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability. Most cases are sporadic; familial forms involve SNCA, parkin, and LRRK2 mutations. Levodopa/carbidopa provides symptomatic relief but doesn't prevent progression. Dementia may develop late.

Pott disease is tuberculous spondylitis causing vertebral destruction with kyphotic deformity (gibbus formation) and potential spinal cord compression. Results from hematogenous spread from pulmonary or extrapulmonary focus. Infection may extend into paravertebral tissues forming cold abscesses. Chronic course with back pain and neurologic deficits. Requires prolonged anti-tuberculous therapy; surgery for instability/neurologic compromise.
questions.question: Pott disease refers to:
Guillain-Barré syndrome involves which pathological process?
questions.explanation:
Guillain-Barré syndrome involves immune-mediated
peripheral nerve demyelination (sometimes axonal damage) causing
ascending paralysis following infections (Campylobacter jejuni common
trigger). Molecular mimicry between microbial and peripheral nerve
antigens drives autoimmunity. CSF shows elevated protein without
pleocytosis (albuminocytologic dissociation). Most patients recover with
supportive care and immunotherapy.

Alzheimer disease shows extracellular amyloid- plaques (neuritic plaques) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau). Neuronal loss and cortical atrophy occur, particularly affecting hippocampus and temporal lobes. APP, presenilin-1, and presenilin-2 mutations cause familial cases. ApoE4 allele increases sporadic disease risk. Progressive memory impairment and dementia characterize clinical course.
questions.question: Alzheimer disease is characterized by:

questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans appears as encapsulated budding yeasts highlighted by India ink preparation or mucicarmine stain showing thick polysaccharide capsule. The organism causes meningitis in immunocompromised hosts, particularly AIDS patients. Latex agglutination detects capsular antigen in CSF and serum. Treatment involves amphotericin B and flucytosine.
questions.question: Cryptococcal meningitis is diagnosed by demonstrating:

A 7-year-old presents with recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, and conductive hearing loss. Skeletal survey shows multiple healed fractures of varying ages. Which differential diagnosis must be carefully excluded given overlapping features?
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta can present with multiple fractures of varying ages, which may superficially resemble non-accidental injury, making careful clinical correlation with additional features such as blue sclerae, family history, and hearing loss essential to avoid misdiagnosis in either direction. This distinction carries significant social and legal implications, requiring a thorough and balanced clinical evaluation. Genetic testing and skin biopsy for collagen analysis can support the diagnosis when clinical features are ambiguous.

options: Elevated plasma VLCFAs and phytanic acid from peroxisomal failure
Elevated urine sulfatides and galactocerebrosides from myelin
Absent hexosaminidase A and B with GM2 ganglioside elevation
Elevated urine organic acids with elevated propionic acid levels
Elevated plasma sphingomyelin with Niemann-Pick liver infiltration
questions.question: An infant with Zellweger syndrome has cerebral gyral abnormalities and absent peroxisomes on liver biopsy. The biochemical hallmarks confirming peroxisomal biogenesis failure include:
questions.explanation: Zellweger syndrome is the most severe peroxisome biogenesis disorder caused by PEX gene mutations preventing peroxisome assembly. All peroxisomal functions fail simultaneously: VLCFA beta-oxidation (elevating plasma C26:0), phytanic acid alpha-oxidation (elevating phytanic acid), and plasmalogen synthesis. Absent peroxisomes on liver electron microscopy with elevated VLCFAs and pipecolic acid confirm the diagnosis. Infants present with hypotonia, seizures, cerebral migration defects, hepatic dysfunction, and typically die within the first year without definitive treatment options.

Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) is diagnosed by germline mutations in mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM), characteristic family history (Amsterdam criteria), or tumor features (MSI-high, loss of MMR protein expression). Unlike FAP, polyposis is absent. CRC develops at younger age (mean 45 years) with right-sided predominance. Multiple cancer risks exist.
questions.question: What characterizes Lynch syndrome diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Pyridoxine-unresponsive homocystinuria from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is treated with a methionine-restricted diet supplemented with cysteine (which becomes essential when CBS is deficient). Betaine is added as adjunct therapy in pyridoxine-nonresponders by providing an alternative pathway to remethylate homocysteine to methionine, thereby reducing homocysteine levels. Folic acid and B12 address remethylation pathway defects (MTHFR deficiency or cobalamin disorders) rather than CBS deficiency. Anticoagulation addresses the complication but not the underlying metabolic cause.
questions.question: A 28-year-old man with homocystinuria has homocysteine of 85 umol/L and cardiac thrombus. Pyridoxine trial shows no response. The treatment of choice is:
options: High-dose pyridoxine to maximize residual CBS enzyme activity
Betaine to remethylate homocysteine via alternative pathway
Folic acid and B12 to remethylate elevated homocysteine levels
Anticoagulation alone to prevent thromboembolic complications

questions.question: Sheehan syndrome results from:
questions.explanation: Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis) results from obstetric hemorrhage with hypotension causing ischemic infarction of enlarged pregnancy-related pituitary. The low-pressure portal circulation supplying the gland cannot increase despite physiologic gland enlargement, creating vulnerability. Manifestations include failure to lactate, amenorrhea, and hypopituitarism.

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant has jaundice and pale stools. Liver biopsy shows marked bile duct proliferation with bile plugs and portal fibrosis. Intraoperative cholangiogram shows complete obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Biliary atresia results from progressive fibro-obliterative destruction of the extrahepatic (and sometimes intrahepatic) bile ducts in infancy, producing marked ductular proliferation, bile plugging, and portal fibrosis on biopsy. Early diagnosis is critical since timely Kasai portoenterostomy can restore bile flow and delay or avoid the need for liver transplantation.

Fetal alcohol syndrome features include smooth philtrum,
thin vermillion border of upper lip, short palpebral fissures, and
midface hypoplasia. Prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency and CNS
dysfunction (intellectual disability, attention deficits) complete the
syndrome. No safe alcohol threshold in pregnancy exists.
options: Smooth philtrum and thin upper lip
questions.question: Fetal alcohol syndrome demonstrates which characteristic facial features?
Which myotonic dystrophy feature distinguishes it from other muscular dystrophies?
questions.explanation:
Myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation) is pathognomonic of myotonic
dystrophy. Grip myotonia and percussion myotonia are demonstrable. CTG
repeat expansion in DMPK gene causes disease.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man has odynophagia. Endoscopic biopsy of an oesophageal ulcer shows multinucleated giant cells with ground-glass nuclei and intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus oesophagitis classically produces multinucleated epithelial giant cells with ground-glass intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a halo (Cowdry type A bodies), typically at the ulcer edge. Cytomegalovirus oesophagitis instead causes large cells with both intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions, typically located in the ulcer base within endothelial or stromal cells.

Oligodendrogliomas demonstrate sheets of cells with round nuclei surrounded by clear cytoplasmic halos (fried egg appearance - fixation artifact). Delicate branching capillaries (chicken-wire vasculature) and calcifications are typical. 1p/19q codeletion predicts chemosensitivity and favorable prognosis. Seizures are common presenting symptom. WHO grade 2 and 3 (anaplastic) exist.
questions.question: Oligodendrogliomas characteristically show:

questions.explanation:
Neurons show marked ballooning from GM2 ganglioside accumulation.
Membranous cytoplasmic bodies appear on electron microscopy. Progressive
neuronal loss causes brain atrophy.
questions.question: What pathologic finding characterizes Tay-Sachs brain?

questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus oesophagitis occurs predominantly in immunocompromised patients and produces enlarged cells, typically endothelial or stromal, with characteristic 'owl's eye' intranuclear inclusions and granular intracytoplasmic inclusions, usually located within the ulcer base rather than at the squamous edge as seen in herpes infection.
questions.question: A 60-year-old immunocompromised man has odynophagia. Biopsy of an oesophageal ulcer base shows enlarged cells with both intranuclear 'owl's eye' inclusions and granular intracytoplasmic inclusions. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is highly specific for primary biliary cholangitis, present in >90% of cases. It targets the E2 component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. While ANA and ANCA may also be present, AMA is the diagnostic hallmark. The florid duct lesion with granulomatous destruction of bile ducts is the characteristic histologic finding.
questions.question: What is the most specific antibody for primary biliary cholangitis?

questions.explanation: Borderline tumors (tumors of low malignant potential) show epithelial proliferation, stratification, and atypia without stromal invasion. These tumors affect younger women with excellent prognosis (95% five-year survival for stage I). Non-invasive implants may occur on peritoneal surfaces. Conservative surgery preserving fertility is appropriate. Recurrence and late malignant transformation occasionally occur.
questions.question: Ovarian serous borderline tumor is characterized by:

questions.explanation: Mucinous carcinomas show clusters of tumor cells floating in abundant extracellular mucin pools. Occur in older women with favorable prognosis. Usually low-grade, ER-positive, HER2-negative. Gelatinous gross appearance. Pure mucinous carcinomas have better outcomes than mixed forms. Rare axillary metastases. Hormone therapy is effective.
questions.question: Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma is characterized by:
What is the mechanism of zidovudine?
questions.explanation:
Zidovudine (AZT) is nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor that
terminates viral DNA chain synthesis. The drug competes with natural
nucleotides during reverse transcription. Zidovudine was first approved
antiretroviral medication.

BRCA1 mutations confer 40-50% lifetime ovarian cancer risk; BRCA2 mutations confer 15-25% risk. These germline mutations also increase breast cancer risk. Prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing reduces ovarian cancer risk by 80-90% and breast cancer risk by 50%. High-grade serous carcinomas are the predominant histologic type in BRCA mutation carriers.
questions.question: BRCA1 mutation carriers have lifetime risk of ovarian cancer of approximately:

questions.explanation: Linear, branching calcifications outline ductal architecture, highly suspicious for high-grade DCIS particularly comedo type with central necrosis. Pleomorphic, fine linear, or fine linear branching calcifications warrant biopsy. Benign calcifications are typically coarse, popcorn-like (fibroadenoma), or rim calcifications (fat necrosis). Mammographic screening effectively detects early DCIS.
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman has mammographic calcifications described as linear and branching. This suggests:

questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic (necrotizing) pancreatitis is a severe form characterized by extensive tissue destruction, interstitial hemorrhage, fat necrosis, and vascular damage with bleeding into the pancreatic parenchyma and retroperitoneum. It appears as a red-black hemorrhagic mass. Edematous (interstitial) pancreatitis is milder with edema and minimal necrosis. Hemorrhagic pancreatitis carries higher mortality (20-50% versus <5%).
questions.question: What distinguishes hemorrhagic pancreatitis from edematous pancreatitis?

A 6-month-old presents with hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, and is found to have markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein. Imaging reveals a solitary liver mass. Which tumour is most likely in this age group?
questions.explanation: Hepatoblastoma is the most common paediatric liver malignancy, typically presenting before three years of age with an abdominal mass and markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein, which also serves as a useful tumour marker for monitoring treatment response. This contrasts with hepatocellular carcinoma, which more commonly occurs in older children with underlying chronic liver disease. Surgical resection combined with chemotherapy has improved outcomes for this tumour.

Osteopetrosis ("marble bone disease") results from
defective osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, causing dense, brittle
bones that fracture easily. The medullary cavity fills with bone,
causing marrow failure (anemia, thrombocytopenia). Infantile form
(autosomal recessive) is severe; adult form (autosomal dominant) is
milder. Bone marrow transplant can cure severe disease.
questions.question: Osteopetrosis results from which cellular defect?

questions.explanation:
Zellweger syndrome results from defective peroxisome assembly affecting
multiple enzymes. Severe hypotonia, seizures, and liver dysfunction
cause neonatal death. Absence of peroxisomes on liver biopsy is
diagnostic.
questions.question: Which peroxisomal disorder causes Zellweger syndrome?
The most common cause of death in cervical cancer patients is:
questions.explanation: Bilateral ureteral obstruction from parametrial extension causes hydronephrosis, renal failure, and uremia - the leading cause of death in cervical cancer. Tumor encases ureters preventing drainage. Urinary diversion or stenting may provide palliation. Prevention through early detection and treatment is essential, highlighting importance of screening programs.

Infantile hypercalcemia occurs in 15% of Williams cases, may cause
nephrocalcinosis. Calcium restriction and close monitoring are
necessary. Mechanism remains incompletely understood.
questions.question: Which Williams syndrome metabolic abnormality requires monitoring?

questions.explanation: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia results from mutations in the Bruton tyrosine kinase gene, which is essential for B-cell maturation, leading to absent or markedly reduced B cells and immunoglobulins of all classes while T-cell numbers and function remain normal. This selective humoral defect predisposes to recurrent bacterial infections, typically becoming apparent after maternal antibody protection wanes around six months of age. Regular intravenous immunoglobulin replacement is the mainstay of management.
questions.question: A 1-year-old presents with recurrent infections and is found to have absent B cells and markedly reduced immunoglobulin levels of all classes, with normal T-cell numbers. Which underlying genetic defect best explains this presentation?
What is Trousseau sign in pancreatic carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Trousseau sign refers to migratory thrombophlebitis (superficial thrombophlebitis affecting different veins) associated with visceral malignancies, particularly pancreatic adenocarcinoma. This paraneoplastic phenomenon results from a hypercoagulable state induced by tumor-secreted procoagulant factors. It may be the presenting feature of occult malignancy.

questions.question: What percentage of Angelman syndrome results from UBE3A mutations?
questions.explanation:
UBE3A mutations account for 10% of Angelman syndrome cases. Maternal
deletions cause 70%, imprinting defects 5%, and paternal UPD 2-5%. Some
cases remain genetically unexplained.

questions.question: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumor of kidney occurs in:
questions.explanation: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumors (MEST) occur predominantly in perimenopausal women, often with history of estrogen therapy or oral contraceptives. Cystic and solid components with epithelium and spindle cell stroma. Estrogen/progesterone receptors positive. Benign behavior; surgical excision curative. May represent spectrum with cystic nephroma. Rare malignant variants reported.

Mallory-Denk bodies are intracytoplasmic hyaline inclusions composed of intermediate filaments (particularly cytokeratins 8 and 18) that are characteristic of alcoholic hepatitis, though they can be seen in other liver diseases. They appear as eosinophilic, rope-like cytoplasmic inclusions, often in ballooned hepatocytes.
questions.question: What are Mallory-Denk bodies?

questions.explanation: Lissencephaly (smooth brain) results from defective neuronal migration producing absent or decreased gyri (agyria/pachygyria) and abnormal cortical lamination. LIS1 and DCX gene mutations cause different forms. Severe intellectual disability, seizures, and motor impairment occur. Most patients die in early childhood. Imaging shows characteristic smooth cortical surface with thickened cortex.
questions.question: Lissencephaly is characterized by:
What prevents Tay-Sachs disease in screened populations?
questions.explanation:
Comprehensive carrier screening in Ashkenazi population reduced
Tay-Sachs incidence by 90%. Carrier couples use prenatal diagnosis or
IVF with genetic testing. Prevention through screening is highly
effective.

questions.question: Medullary carcinoma of kidney occurs in:
questions.explanation: Renal medullary carcinoma affects young African Americans (median age 20) with sickle cell trait/disease. Extremely aggressive tumor presenting with advanced metastatic disease. Arises from collecting ducts in renal medulla. Histology shows reticular/microcystic pattern with neutrophils. Loss of SMARCB1/INI1 expression. Median survival <1 year despite chemotherapy. Often misdiagnosed as collecting duct carcinoma.
options: Young patients with sickle cell trait

questions.explanation: Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN, germ cell neoplasia in situ) is the precursor to invasive germ cell tumors (except spermatocytic seminoma). Large atypical cells with clear cytoplasm along basement membrane characterize ITGCN. OCT4, PLAP, and CD117 positive. Present in adjacent testis in >90% of germ cell tumors. Progresses to invasion in 50% within 5 years.
questions.question: Post-pubertal germ cell tumors arise from:
Luminal A breast cancers are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Luminal A tumors express estrogen receptors at high levels, are HER2 negative, and show low proliferation rates with Ki67 <14%. These cancers have the best prognosis among invasive carcinomas and respond well to endocrine therapy. They typically arise in postmenopausal women and exhibit favorable histologic features.

Elastin haploinsufficiency causes supravalvular aortic stenosis and
other vascular abnormalities. The 7q11.23 deletion involves elastin and
25-27 adjacent genes. Cardiovascular complications require monitoring.
questions.question: Which Williams syndrome feature results from elastin gene deletion?
Which organism is specifically associated with gastric MALT lymphoma pathogenesis?
questions.explanation:
Helicobacter pylori chronic gastritis drives proliferation
of gastric MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) through continuous
antigenic stimulation, eventually leading to lymphoma in susceptible
individuals. Early-stage MALT lymphomas often regress with H. pylori
eradication alone. This represents one of the clearest examples of
infection-driven lymphomagenesis.

questions.question: A newborn presents with recurrent pulmonary infections and failure to thrive. Sweat chloride testing is markedly elevated. Pancreatic histology shows ductal obstruction by thick mucus and acinar atrophy with fibrosis. What is the underlying genetic defect?
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis results from CFTR mutations causing defective chloride and bicarbonate transport, leading to thick, viscous secretions that obstruct pancreatic ducts, causing acinar atrophy and fibrosis, along with thick pulmonary secretions predisposing to recurrent infections. The elevated sweat chloride test is diagnostic and reflects the same channel defect in sweat glands.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man has a colonic adenocarcinoma. Molecular testing shows wild-type KRAS. What is the most direct clinical relevance of this finding?
questions.explanation: Wild-type KRAS status is required for colorectal cancer patients to potentially benefit from anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody therapies such as cetuximab or panitumumab, since activating KRAS mutations downstream of EGFR render these therapies ineffective. KRAS testing is therefore a standard predictive biomarker test in metastatic colorectal cancer management.

Tuberous sclerosis complex results from mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes, affecting the mTOR signalling pathway, and characteristically presents with hypopigmented 'ash-leaf' macules, seizures from cortical tubers, and cardiac rhabdomyomas, which may be identified even prenatally on fetal echocardiography. This combination of dermatological, neurological, and cardiac findings reflects the multisystem nature of this condition. Regular surveillance for renal angiomyolipomas and other systemic manifestations is important in long-term management.
questions.question: A 3-year-old presents with hypopigmented skin macules, seizures, and cardiac rhabdomyomas identified on echocardiography. Which underlying genetic condition best explains this combination of findings?
A 2-year-old with Gaucher disease type 1 has massive splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. The most appropriate established first-line treatment is:
options: Splenectomy to immediately relieve hematological cytopenias
Bone marrow transplantation for definitive disease cure
Enzyme replacement therapy with intravenous imiglucerase
Substrate reduction therapy with miglustat as primary option
Dietary glucocerebroside restriction to reduce substrate load
questions.explanation: Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with imiglucerase or velaglucerase alfa is the established first-line treatment for symptomatic Gaucher disease type 1. Intravenous recombinant glucocerebrosidase reduces glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages, improving organomegaly, hematological parameters, and bone disease. Substrate reduction therapy is a second-line option. Splenectomy worsens bone disease by redirecting storage to marrow. BMT carries significant mortality risk and is not standard care for non-neuronopathic type 1 disease.

questions.question: What is the classic triad of hereditary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation:
Classic triad includes cirrhosis from hepatic iron overload, diabetes
from pancreatic damage, and bronze skin from iron and melanin
deposition. Arthropathy, hypogonadism, and cardiomyopathy also occur.

questions.question: In immune complex-mediated (type III) hypersensitivity, which factor most influences where complexes deposit in tissues?
questions.explanation:
Small, soluble immune complexes circulate longer and
deposit in vessel walls, glomeruli, and joints based on hemodynamic
factors and complex size. Large complexes are rapidly cleared by the
reticuloendothelial system preventing tissue deposition. The
size-solubility characteristics determine whether complexes cause
systemic or localized disease manifestations.

questions.question: What is the strongest risk factor for gallbladder carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Gallstones are the strongest risk factor for gallbladder carcinoma, present in 80-90% of cases. Chronic cholecystitis and recurrent trauma from stones promote malignant transformation. Other risk factors include porcelain gallbladder (calcified wall), choledochal cysts, chronic Salmonella typhi infection, and anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction. The risk is proportional to stone size (stones >3cm have higher risk).

questions.question: What imaging modality best assesses liver fibrosis non-invasively?
questions.explanation: MRI with elastography (MR elastography) is the most accurate non-invasive imaging modality for assessing liver fibrosis, measuring tissue stiffness. Transient elastography (FibroScan) is more widely available and also highly effective. Ultrasound detects cirrhosis morphology (nodularity, surface irregularity) but doesn't quantify fibrosis well. These techniques reduce need for biopsy. Serum biomarker panels (APRI, FIB-4) provide additional non-invasive assessment.

A significantly raised level of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) greater than 500 ng/ml strongly suggests hepatocellular carcinoma. Continuously rising values, even if less than 100 ng/ml, are also highly suspicious. However, not all HCCs produce elevated AFP, and levels can be elevated in other conditions including hepatitis and cirrhosis.
questions.question: What serum marker level strongly suggests hepatocellular carcinoma?

options: Tuberous sclerosis with cortical tubers and subependymal nodules
NF2 with bilateral acoustic schwannomas and meningiomas
questions.question: A 60-year-old woman presents with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance disturbance. MRI reveals a cerebellopontine angle mass. Histology shows Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies and Antoni B myxoid areas. Which syndrome predisposes to bilateral lesions?
questions.explanation: Schwannomas (acoustic neuromas/vestibular schwannomas) most commonly arise from the superior vestibular nerve at the cerebellopontine angle. Histologically, Antoni A (hypercellular, palisading Verocay bodies) and Antoni B (hypocellular, myxoid) areas are characteristic. S100 protein is strongly positive. Bilateral acoustic schwannomas are pathognomonic of Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2), caused by germline NF2 (merlin) mutations on chromosome 22q. NF2 also predisposes to multiple meningiomas and ependymomas. NF1 is characterised by cafe-au-lait spots, cutaneous neurofibromas, and optic gliomas.

Inclusion body myositis shows characteristic rimmed
vacuoles (basophilic-rimmed spaces) on trichrome stain and congophilic
amyloid deposits containing beta-amyloid and phosphorylated tau.
Endomysial inflammation (like polymyositis) is present. The disease
affects older men, involves distal and proximal muscles, and is
refractory to immunosuppression.
questions.question: The pathognomonic pathological finding in inclusion body myositis is:
A 50-year-old woman has watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, and achlorhydria. A pancreatic tumour is identified and resected, with symptom resolution. What hormone is most likely overproduced?
questions.explanation: VIPoma (Verner-Morrison syndrome) is caused by a vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, producing the classic triad of watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, and achlorhydria due to VIP's effects on intestinal secretion and gastric acid suppression. Surgical resection of the tumour typically resolves the syndrome.

Crohn's disease characteristically produces transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas and discontinuous skip lesions, most often affecting the terminal ileum. Ulcerative colitis, in contrast, is limited to mucosa and submucosa, is continuous, and always involves the rectum, lacking the granulomas seen here.
questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents with right lower quadrant pain, fever, and a palpable mass. Resection of the terminal ileum shows transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, and skip lesions. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation:
Giant cell (temporal) arteritis affects medium and large
arteries, particularly cranial vessels (temporal, ophthalmic, posterior
ciliary). Histology shows granulomatous inflammation with giant cells,
intimal thickening, and fragmented internal elastic lamina. The disease
causes headache, jaw claudication, and vision loss (medical emergency).
Diagnosis requires temporal artery biopsy; treatment is high-dose
corticosteroids.
questions.question: Giant cell arteritis characteristically affects which vessels?

questions.explanation: PID causes tubal scarring and adhesions predisposing to ectopic pregnancy by impeding normal ovum transport. Other complications include chronic pelvic pain, tubo-ovarian abscess, infertility, and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis). Early antibiotic treatment reduces long-term sequelae. IUD use slightly increases PID risk.
questions.question: Pelvic inflammatory disease complications include:

questions.explanation: Ovarian carcinomas preferentially spread by exfoliation of cells into peritoneal cavity with implantation throughout abdomen (omentum, peritoneal surfaces, diaphragm). Ascites develops. Lymphatic spread to pelvic and para-aortic nodes occurs. Hematogenous spread to liver, lung is late. Surface location and lack of capsule facilitate transcoelomic spread.
questions.question: Ovarian carcinoma most commonly spreads by:
A child with Prader-Willi syndrome has maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15. The mechanism making this equivalent to paternal deletion is:
options: Both maternal copies are silenced by an X-inactivation analogy
Maternal UPD15 means no paternal allele to express imprinted PWS genes
Maternal disomy causes excess UBE3A imprinting on both alleles
Both copies carry fully methylated maternal imprint silencing PWS genes
Uniparental disomy expands CAG trinucleotide repeats at PWS locus
questions.explanation: In Prader-Willi syndrome, the critically paternally expressed genes (SNRPN and snoRNAs at 15q11-q13) are normally silenced on the maternal allele by imprinting. When a child has maternal UPD15, no paternal allele is present to express these genes. Both copies carry maternal imprinting marks silencing the PWS critical region, producing identical outcome to paternal deletion: complete absence of paternal gene expression. Methylation PCR detects only the methylated maternal pattern without the paternal unmethylated band in both mechanisms.

options: Test both parents to determine de novo versus inherited status
Repeat the microarray analysis at 6 months interval
Diagnose a syndrome from phenotypic features alone
Discard result and perform standard G-banded karyotype
questions.explanation: Parental microarray testing is the most productive next step for a VUS, as inheritance pattern significantly influences interpretation. A de novo variant carries much higher pathogenic probability than the same variant inherited from a phenotypically normal parent. Whole genome sequencing would not clarify copy number variant significance at this stage. Standard karyotype misses submicroscopic variants that chromosomal microarray is specifically designed to detect at genome-wide resolution.
questions.question: Chromosomal microarray returns a variant of uncertain significance in a child with developmental delay. The most productive next step is:
An AIDS patient with CD4 count of 30 cells/uL develops fever, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy. Blood cultures at 14 days grow acid-fast bacilli. The missed prophylaxis was:
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) disseminated infection occurs predominantly at CD4 counts below 50 cells/uL. Weekly azithromycin (1200 mg) or daily clarithromycin is the recommended prophylaxis at this threshold. Blood cultures growing acid-fast bacilli after 14 days indicates slow-growing MAC rather than M. tuberculosis. TMP-SMX prevents PCP and toxoplasmosis but not MAC. Isoniazid prevents TB reactivation in LTBI-positive patients but does not cover MAC infection at any stage of HIV disease.
options: Isoniazid preventive therapy to prevent latent TB reactivation
TMP-SMX double-strength to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia
Fluconazole prophylaxis to prevent cryptococcal meningitis
Weekly azithromycin or daily clarithromycin for MAC prevention

questions.explanation:
Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I) is the most common
pediatric brain tumor, typically cerebellar, showing biphasic pattern
with piloid (hair-like) cells, Rosenthal fibers, and eosinophilic
granular bodies. It's well-circumscribed (not diffusely infiltrative)
with excellent prognosis after complete resection. BRAF fusion
(KIAA1549-BRAF) is characteristic.
questions.question: Pilocytic astrocytoma is characterized by which features?
options: Benign piloid tumor with Rosenthal fibers
Salmonella typhi causing typhoid vertebral osteitis
questions.explanation: Pott disease (tuberculous spondylitis) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis haematogenously seeding the vertebral bodies, typically affecting the thoracolumbar junction. Caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells are characteristic. Intervertebral disc destruction leads to vertebral collapse and the characteristic angular kyphosis (gibbus deformity). Cold (psoas) abscess formation is common. Treatment requires prolonged anti-tuberculous chemotherapy; surgical decompression is indicated for neurological compromise or instability.
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with chronic back pain and gibbus deformity. MRI shows vertebral body destruction. Bone biopsy reveals caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells. Which organism is responsible?

questions.explanation: Chromosomal microarray (CMA) is the recommended first-line test for clinically suspected 22q11.2 deletion because it detects the deletion at higher resolution than FISH, identifies atypical deletions not covered by a single FISH probe, and simultaneously surveys for other copy number variants modifying the phenotype. Standard G-banded karyotype usually misses the 3 Mb deletion at its resolution limit even at 850 bands. FISH confirms known deletion positions but lacks CMA's genome-wide coverage. CMA has replaced FISH as the primary diagnostic tool at most genetics centers internationally.
questions.question: A 22q11.2 deletion is strongly suspected clinically. The best first-line diagnostic method when G-banded karyotype is non-diagnostic is:
options: G-banded karyotype repeated at 850-band higher resolution
PCR of short tandem repeat markers in the deleted region
FISH with 22q11.2-specific probe for rapid bedside screening
Chromosomal microarray detecting copy number variants genome-wide
Next-generation sequencing of the TBX1 coding exons only

questions.question: Ankylosing spondylitis is strongly associated with which HLA type?
questions.explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis shows strong association with
HLA-B27 (90% of patients vs. 6-8% of general population). This
seronegative spondyloarthropathy causes inflammatory back pain,
sacroiliitis, and progressive spinal fusion ("bamboo spine").
Extra-articular manifestations include anterior uveitis, aortic
regurgitation, and apical pulmonary fibrosis. Young males are
predominantly affected.

Holoprosencephaly results from failure of prosencephalon to divide into cerebral hemispheres, lateral ventricles, and olfactory/optic bulbs. Alobar (most severe), semilobar, and lobar forms exist. Midline facial anomalies (cyclopia, cleft lip/palate) occur. Associated with trisomy 13, maternal diabetes, and sonic hedgehog pathway mutations. Severe forms are incompatible with life.
questions.question: Holoprosencephaly results from:

questions.explanation: Guillain-Barr syndrome is acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy often following respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (Campylobacter jejuni common trigger). Molecular mimicry causes autoantibodies against myelin. Ascending paralysis with areflexia develops. CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein, normal cells). Respiratory failure may require ventilation. Plasmapheresis or IVIG hastens recovery; most patients recover fully.
questions.question: Guillain-Barr syndrome typically follows:

questions.explanation: Fibroadenomas are the most common benign breast tumors in women under 30 years, presenting as mobile, well-circumscribed masses. These biphasic tumors contain proliferating stromal and epithelial elements responsive to hormonal stimulation. Most measure 2-3cm and may increase during pregnancy or regress after menopause. Multiple or bilateral fibroadenomas occur in 15-20% of patients.
questions.question: Fibroadenoma of the breast typically occurs in:

questions.explanation: Collecting duct carcinomas (Bellini duct carcinomas) are rare aggressive tumors arising from medullary collecting ducts. Occur in younger patients. Present at advanced stage. Histology shows tubulopapillary architecture with desmoplastic stroma in medulla. High-grade cytology. Poor prognosis despite aggressive treatment. Must distinguish from upper tract urothelial carcinoma and metastatic adenocarcinoma.
questions.question: Collecting duct carcinoma arises from:

questions.explanation: Acute epiglottitis was historically most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b before the introduction of effective conjugate vaccines, presenting with rapid onset of fever, drooling, and a characteristic tripod positioning to maximise airway patency. The classic 'thumbprint sign' on lateral neck X-ray reflects epiglottic swelling. This is a paediatric emergency requiring careful airway management, as examination manoeuvres can precipitate complete airway obstruction.
questions.question: A 6-year-old presents with fever, drooling, and a preference for sitting upright with the neck extended ('tripod position'). Lateral neck X-ray shows a swollen epiglottis. Which organism has historically been most associated with this presentation prior to widespread vaccination?

options: Decreased trabecular mass with normal osteoid width
Widened osteoid seams with defective mineralisation
Mosaic cement lines with large irregular osteoclasts
Fibrous tissue replacing haematopoietic marrow spaces
Dense woven bone with prominent osteoblastic rimming
questions.question: A 70-year-old woman fractures her hip after a minor fall. DEXA scan shows a T-score of -2.8. Which histological finding distinguishes her condition from osteomalacia?
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is defined by decreased bone mass (T-score of -2.5 or below) with normal bone mineralisation and architecture but reduced trabecular bone volume and connectivity. Histologically, there is thinning and loss of trabecular plates with normal osteoid width, distinguishing it from osteomalacia where osteoid seams are widened due to defective mineralisation. Post-menopausal osteoporosis results from oestrogen deficiency increasing osteoclast activity. DEXA scanning guides treatment with bisphosphonates or denosumab for fracture prevention.

Ghon complex consists of a 1-1.5 cm area of parenchymal consolidation
(Ghon focus) combined with involvement of regional hilar lymph nodes.
This develops within 3 weeks of primary infection when granuloma
formation occurs. The combination of the lung lesion and lymph node
involvement distinguishes it from isolated Ghon focus.
options: Area of consolidation with hilar lymph node
questions.question: What is the characteristic microscopic finding in Ghon complex of primary tuberculosis?
What percentage of Down syndrome results from maternal nondisjunction?
questions.explanation:
Approximately 95% of Down syndrome cases result from meiotic
nondisjunction producing trisomy 21. Maternal age strongly influences
nondisjunction risk. Translocation and mosaicism account for remaining
cases.

Prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL or T-PLL) shows larger
cells with prominent nucleoli, higher white blood cell counts, and more
aggressive behavior than CLL. Massive splenomegaly is characteristic.
Prognosis is worse than CLL with poor response to conventional therapy.
T-PLL is even more aggressive than B-PLL.
questions.question: Prolymphocytic leukemia differs from CLL by which feature?
Churg-Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is characterized by:
questions.explanation:
EGPA features asthma, eosinophilia, and necrotizing
vasculitis with eosinophil-rich granulomas. p-ANCA (anti-MPO) is
positive in 40-60%. Classic presentation includes: asthma, peripheral
eosinophilia >10%, and vasculitis affecting =2 extrapulmonary organs.
Cardiac involvement (myocarditis, coronary vasculitis) is major cause of
mortality. Corticosteroids are mainstay treatment.

questions.question: Dermatomyositis in adults is associated with which complication?
questions.explanation:
Adult dermatomyositis associates with underlying
malignancy (ovary, lung, pancreas, stomach, colorectal) in 15-30% of
cases, particularly in patients >40 years. The myositis may precede,
coincide with, or follow cancer diagnosis. Cancer screening is
essential. Juvenile dermatomyositis rarely associates with malignancy
but often follows viral infections.

Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of the bile duct associated with abnormal pancreaticobiliary ductal union, allowing reflux of pancreatic enzymes into the biliary tree and causing chronic inflammation. This chronic irritation significantly increases the lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, making surgical excision of the cyst the recommended definitive treatment.
questions.question: A 3-year-old child has a cystic dilatation of the common bile duct on imaging, with recurrent jaundice and abdominal pain. What complication is this child at increased long-term risk of developing?

questions.explanation:
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome involves gastrin-secreting
tumors (gastrinomas), usually pancreatic or duodenal, causing massive
gastric acid hypersecretion and severe peptic ulcer disease (including
jejunal ulcers). About 25% occur with MEN-1 syndrome. Diagnosis requires
elevated fasting gastrin (>1000 pg/mL) and positive secretin
stimulation test. Treatment includes proton pump inhibitors and tumor
resection.
questions.question: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from:

questions.explanation: Dysplastic nodules are distinguished from regenerative cirrhotic nodules by the presence of cellular atypia/dysplasia. They are larger than cirrhotic nodules and show low-grade or high-grade dysplasia. High-grade dysplastic nodules have significant risk of progressing to hepatocellular carcinoma. They represent an important preneoplastic lesion in the cirrhotic liver.
questions.question: What distinguishes dysplastic nodules from regenerative nodules?

questions.explanation: PSA, a serine protease liquefying seminal coagulum, is produced by prostatic secretory epithelial cells. Both benign and malignant prostatic tissue produces PSA, limiting specificity. Factors elevating PSA include BPH, prostatitis, instrumentation, and carcinoma. PSA velocity and density improve diagnostic accuracy. Free-to-total PSA ratio helps distinguish cancer from benign disease.
questions.question: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is produced by:
Which metachromatic leukodystrophy enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation:
Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes sulfatide accumulation in
metachromatic leukodystrophy. Demyelination affects central and
peripheral nervous systems. Metachromatic granules appear on toluidine
blue staining.

questions.question: The transformation zone of the cervix is important because:
questions.explanation: The transformation zone, where squamous metaplasia replaces columnar epithelium, is most vulnerable to HPV infection and carcinogenic transformation. This dynamic area moves with hormonal changes and age. Adequate sampling of the transformation zone is essential for effective Pap smear screening. CIN lesions preferentially develop in this region.
options: Site of origin for most cervical cancers
It is resistant to HPV infection

questions.explanation: Acute appendicitis typically begins with luminal obstruction, often by a faecolith, leading to increased intraluminal pressure, bacterial overgrowth, and transmural neutrophilic infiltration of the appendiceal wall. Mesenteric adenitis instead causes abdominal pain from inflamed lymph nodes without primary appendiceal wall involvement, and the appendix itself remains histologically normal.
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with right iliac fossa pain. Appendicectomy specimen shows transmural neutrophilic infiltration with luminal obstruction by a faecolith. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasms predominantly affect young women, showing characteristic pseudopapillary architecture with degenerative cystic change and nuclear beta-catenin accumulation due to CTNNB1 mutations activating Wnt signalling. They generally have low malignant potential and a favourable prognosis after complete surgical resection.
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman has a solid pancreatic mass. Histology shows monomorphic cells with pseudopapillary architecture, degenerative cystic change, and positivity for beta-catenin nuclear staining. What is the diagnosis?
What is the histologic appearance of most cholangiocarcinomas?
questions.explanation: Most cholangiocarcinomas are adenocarcinomas that resemble bile duct epithelium and produce mucin. They typically show marked desmoplasia (dense fibrous stroma), which makes them firm and fibrous. The tumors may form glands or tubular structures but do not secrete bile, distinguishing them from hepatocellular carcinoma. Rarely, mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma variants occur.

questions.question: Auer rods in myeloblasts are pathognomonic for which condition?
questions.explanation:
Auer rods (crystallized azurophilic granules appearing as
pink needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions) are specific for acute myeloid
leukemia and exclude lymphoblastic leukemia. They're most abundant in
APL (M3) where they may appear as bundles ("faggot cells"). Their
presence confirms myeloid lineage.

questions.question: What neonatal feature suggests Prader-Willi syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Severe neonatal hypotonia with poor feeding characterizes early PWS.
Later childhood shows transition to hyperphagia and obesity. Small hands
and feet with hypogonadism are typical.

questions.question: What are the three mechanisms causing acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis results from inappropriate activation of pancreatic enzymes by three mechanisms: (1) pancreatic duct obstruction (gallstones, tumors), (2) primary acinar cell injury (alcohol, drugs, ischemia, viruses), and (3) defective intracellular transport of pro-enzymes within acinar cells. All lead to premature trypsinogen activation, triggering autodigestion.

Creatine kinase elevation 50-100 times normal indicates muscle damage.
CK levels are elevated from birth before weakness appears. Serial CK
measurements track disease progression.
questions.question: What laboratory finding is markedly elevated in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

questions.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolemia most commonly results from LDL receptor (LDLR) mutations reducing hepatic clearance of LDL particles from the circulation. Without adequate LDL receptor recycling, LDL-cholesterol accumulates in plasma and deposits in arterial walls (causing premature atherosclerosis) and tendons (causing xanthomata). Heterozygotes have approximately twice normal LDL levels; homozygotes have severely elevated levels with childhood atherosclerotic events. Apolipoprotein B mutations (familial defective apoB) and PCSK9 gain-of-function mutations cause phenotypically similar disease through different mechanisms.
options: LDL receptor deficiency reducing hepatic LDL particle clearance
Apolipoprotein B mutation preventing LDL receptor binding
PCSK9 gain-of-function degrading LDL receptors excessively
Cholesterol ester transfer protein overactivity raising LDL levels
Hepatic lipase deficiency allowing IDL to accumulate as LDL
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with familial hypercholesterolemia has LDL of 8.2 mmol/L and tendon xanthomata. The molecular mechanism of LDL accumulation is:

questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori gastritis is characterized by intraepithelial neutrophils that may form pit abscesses, along with subepithelial plasma cells, lymphocytes, and lymphoid aggregates. The antrum is mostly affected. Endoscopy shows erythematous, coarse or nodular appearance of the mucosa.
questions.question: Which histologic feature is characteristic of Helicobacter pylori gastritis?

questions.explanation:
Heterosexual transmission accounts for majority of global HIV infections
particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Vertical transmission and injection
drug use also contribute significantly. Pattern varies by region and
population.
questions.question: What is the primary mode of HIV transmission globally?

A 45-year-old woman taking long-term anabolic steroids develops a liver mass. Biopsy shows a well-demarcated lesion of benign-appearing hepatocytes without portal tracts or bile ducts. What is the diagnosis?
