questions.explanation: Hepatocellular adenoma is a benign hepatocyte tumour strongly associated with oral contraceptive and anabolic steroid use, characteristically lacking portal tracts and bile ducts since it derives purely from hepatocytes without the normal lobular architecture. Focal nodular hyperplasia, by contrast, contains a central fibrous scar with portal tract elements.

questions.question: Alzheimer disease is pathologically characterized by which lesions?
questions.explanation:
Alzheimer disease shows: (1) neurofibrillary tangles
(hyperphosphorylated tau protein) intracellularly, (2) senile (neuritic)
plaques (extracellular amyloid-beta deposits with dystrophic neurites),
and (3) amyloid angiopathy. The disease causes progressive cortical
atrophy, particularly temporal and parietal lobes. ApoE4 allele is major
genetic risk factor.

Osteosarcomas spread hematogenously, predominantly to lungs (most common), then bones and brain. Presence of pulmonary metastases significantly worsens prognosis. Skip metastases (tumor deposits in same bone) also occur. Approximately 20% have detectable metastases at diagnosis; micrometastases likely exist in most. Chemotherapy targets micrometastatic disease improving survival from 20% to 60-70%.
questions.question: Osteosarcoma most commonly metastasizes to:

questions.explanation: Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) is the most common renal tumour in children. Favourable histology shows the classic triphasic pattern without anaplasia. Anaplasia (unfavourable histology) is defined by tripolar or multipolar mitotic figures, nuclear enlargement three times or more compared to adjacent cells, and hyperchromasia. Diffuse anaplasia is associated with TP53 mutations and confers significantly worse prognosis with chemotherapy resistance. Standard treatment is nephrectomy with actinomycin D and vincristine; diffuse anaplasia requires additional doxorubicin.
questions.question: A 4-year-old child presents with a painless abdominal mass. CT reveals a large renal mass. Histology shows triphasic pattern: blastemal, epithelial, and stromal components. Which feature indicates unfavourable histology with poorer prognosis?
options: Presence of all three histological components equally
Diffuse anaplasia with nuclear enlargement and abnormal mitoses
Predominance of blastemal over epithelial component
Cystic spaces within the epithelial component of tumour

questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma, endemic in Africa and associated with EBV, shows t(8;14)(q24;q32) in 80% of cases, placing MYC under the constitutive influence of the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer. MYC overexpression drives explosive proliferation with nearly 100% Ki-67 index. The starry-sky pattern reflects numerous tingible body macrophages engulfing apoptotic tumor cells. MYC is also translocated to light chain loci in the remaining 20% of cases. Holoendemic malaria acts as a cofactor by suppressing EBV immunity in endemic African populations.
options: t(14;18) placing BCL2 under immunoglobulin heavy chain control
t(11;14) placing CCND1 under immunoglobulin heavy chain control
t(8;14) placing MYC under immunoglobulin heavy chain control
t(2;5) producing NPM-ALK fusion in anaplastic large cell lymphoma
questions.question: An 8-year-old African child has a rapidly enlarging jaw mass over 4 weeks. Biopsy reveals a starry-sky pattern. The cytogenetic finding is:

questions.explanation: The Ishak modification of the hepatic activity index (HAI) is a histological scoring system for grading necroinflammatory activity (0-18) and staging fibrosis (0-6) in chronic hepatitis. It provides standardized assessment of disease severity. Other systems include Knodell HAI, METAVIR, and Scheuer. Clinical scoring includes Child-Pugh, MELD, and ALBI for cirrhosis severity.
questions.question: What is the Ishak scoring system used for?
Burkitt lymphoma shows which characteristic cytogenetic abnormality?
questions.explanation:
All Burkitt lymphoma variants show MYC rearrangement, most
commonly t(8;14) juxtaposing MYC with immunoglobulin heavy chain locus.
Variants include t(2;8) and t(8;22) with light chain loci. The
translocation causes constitutive MYC expression driving rapid
proliferation (nearly 100% proliferation fraction).

questions.question: Dermatomyositis is characterized by which muscle pathology?
questions.explanation:
Dermatomyositis shows characteristic perifascicular
atrophy, perivascular and perimysial inflammation (predominantly B cells
and CD4+ T cells), and capillary damage. Perifascicular fibers show
MHC-I upregulation. Adult dermatomyositis associates with malignancy in
15-30% of cases. The diagnosis requires both muscle and skin
manifestations.

Pancreatic pseudocysts develop after acute or chronic pancreatitis when leaked pancreatic enzymes and fluid become walled off by fibrous and granulation tissue, lacking a true epithelial lining. This distinguishes them from true cysts and neoplastic cystic lesions, all of which possess an epithelial lining of varying type.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man has chronic pancreatitis with a fluid collection lacking an epithelial lining, surrounded by fibrous and granulation tissue. What is the diagnosis?
What is the characteristic shape of ulcers in amebiasis?
questions.explanation: In amebiasis, amebae attach to the colonic epithelium, induce apoptosis, invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria, creating characteristic flask-shaped ulcers. This recruits neutrophils and causes tissue damage. Parasites may penetrate splanchnic vessels and embolize to the liver to produce abscesses.

questions.question: The pathognomonic histological feature of rheumatoid nodules is:
questions.explanation:
Rheumatoid nodules show central zone of fibrinoid necrosis
surrounded by palisading epithelioid macrophages and peripheral chronic
inflammation. These subcutaneous nodules occur over pressure points
(elbows, fingers) in seropositive patients. Similar lesions can occur in
lungs and other organs. Their presence indicates more severe, erosive
disease.

questions.question: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is defined by which criteria?
questions.explanation:
MGUS diagnostic criteria: serum M-protein <3 g/dL, bone
marrow plasma cells <10%, no end-organ damage (hypercalcemia, renal
failure, anemia, bone lesions). MGUS progresses to myeloma at ~1%/year.
Risk stratification based on M-protein level, isotype, and free light
chain ratio guides monitoring frequency.

Esophageal adenocarcinoma pathogenesis involves progression over time with accumulation of genetic and epigenetic changes, most notably abnormalities of p53. Other molecular alterations include amplification of c-ERB-B2, cyclin D1 and cyclin E, mutation of RB gene, allelic loss of p16/INK4a, and increased epithelial expression of TNF and NFκB.
questions.question: Which genetic abnormality is most commonly associated with esophageal adenocarcinoma?

questions.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) shows marked female predominance with 90% of patients being women, typically presenting around age 50. It is associated with other autoimmune conditions including Sjögren syndrome, scleroderma, and thyroid disease. Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is present in >90% of cases and is highly specific.
questions.question: What percentage of patients with primary biliary cholangitis are female?

questions.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy type 1 follows autosomal recessive inheritance from homozygous SMN1 deletion. When both parents are confirmed carriers (each with one SMN1 deletion on one chromosome), Mendelian ratios give 25% recurrence risk for each pregnancy (25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% unaffected). Prenatal diagnosis by SMN1 copy number analysis in chorionic villus samples or amniocytes is available. Newborn screening and early treatment with nusinersen, risdiplam, or onasemnogene abeparvovec before symptom onset dramatically improves motor outcomes in presymptomatic infants.
options: 25% for each pregnancy with autosomal recessive inheritance
50% for each pregnancy as one parent is always an obligate carrier
Zero as SMN1 deletion is almost always a de novo mutation
10% empirical risk adjusted for parental carrier testing results
75% as both parents carry the deletion on both chromosomes
questions.question: A couple has a child with spinal muscular atrophy type 1 from homozygous SMN1 deletion. Both parents are confirmed carriers. The recurrence risk in future pregnancies is:
Prion diseases are characterized by which pathological change?
questions.explanation:
Prion diseases (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, kuru, fatal
familial insomnia) show spongiform change (vacuolation of neuropil),
neuronal loss, and gliosis without inflammation. Misfolded prion protein
(PrPSc) converts normal PrPC to pathological form, propagating disease.
No effective treatment exists; diseases are invariably fatal.

Single cholesterol stones are typically ovoid, while multiple stones become faceted (multifaceted with flat surfaces) due to compression against each other in the gallbladder. This geometric adaptation allows maximum packing. The number of facets corresponds to the number of adjacent stones. Faceting is a characteristic gross feature distinguishing solitary from multiple stones.
questions.question: What causes faceting of multiple gallstones?
Berry aneurysms are associated with:
questions.explanation: Berry aneurysms occur at arterial bifurcations in Circle of Willis due to congenital weakness in vessel wall media. Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, and genetic conditions (adult polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome). Most remain asymptomatic until rupture. Large aneurysms may cause mass effect. Screening recommended in high-risk families.

questions.question: Multiple myeloma is characterized by which laboratory findings?
questions.explanation:
Myeloma produces monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein)
creating a sharp spike on serum protein electrophoresis, most commonly
IgG (50%) or IgA (20%). Some cases secrete only light chains (15%)
detected in urine (Bence-Jones protein). The M-protein level correlates
with tumor burden.

questions.question: A newborn presents with congenital absence of thymus and parathyroids with cardiac anomalies. Which pharyngeal pouches failed to develop properly?
questions.explanation:
DiGeorge syndrome results from failed development of third
and fourth pharyngeal pouches, which normally give rise to thymus,
parathyroids, and portions of great vessels. This causes T cell
immunodeficiency (thymic hypoplasia), hypocalcemia (parathyroid
absence), and cardiac defects. The syndrome often associates with
22q11.2 deletion.

questions.question: Which a1-antitrypsin variant causes most severe disease?
questions.explanation:
ZZ phenotype causes severe a1-AT deficiency with serum levels 10-15% of
normal. Homozygotes develop emphysema and liver disease. The Z mutation
causes protein misfolding and retention.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman has a partial hydatidiform mole. Which feature distinguishes a partial mole from a complete mole?
questions.explanation: Partial hydatidiform mole characteristically shows triploid karyotype (most commonly 69,XXY from dispermy), presence of foetal or embryonic tissue including foetal red blood cells within villi, and only focal trophoblastic hyperplasia with two populations of villi (hydropic and normal). Complete moles show purely androgenetic 46,XX or 46,XY karyotype, diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia, and complete absence of foetal tissue. Partial moles carry lower malignant potential (approximately 2-4% risk of GTN) compared to complete moles (approximately 15-20%).
options: Uniform trophoblastic hyperplasia affecting all villi
Higher risk of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
Purely androgenetic diploid karyotype in all cases
Complete absence of embryonic or foetal tissue
Presence of foetal red blood cells within villous stroma

questions.question: What is the most common colonic polyp?
questions.explanation: Hyperplastic polyps are the most common polyps in the colon, typically occurring in the 6th to 7th decade of life. They are small, sessile mucosal protrusions with exaggerated crypt architecture and have no malignant potential. It is important to distinguish them from sessile serrated adenomas.

questions.question: Serous ovarian tumors are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Serous tumors contain epithelium resembling fallopian tube with ciliated columnar cells. High-grade serous carcinomas are the most common and lethal ovarian malignancies, often presenting with advanced-stage disease. Psammoma bodies (laminated calcifications) are characteristic. Low-grade serous carcinomas follow stepwise progression from borderline tumors.

questions.question: Renal involvement in multiple myeloma classically shows which histological lesion?
questions.explanation:
Myeloma kidney shows intratubular casts of Tamm-Horsfall
protein complexed with light chains, causing tubular obstruction, giant
cell reaction, and renal failure. The casts appear fractured with
surrounding inflammation. Light chain deposition disease and AL
amyloidosis are other myeloma-associated renal lesions.

FAP results from germline APC mutations causing hundreds
to thousands of colorectal adenomatous polyps developing in adolescence,
with 100% progression to colorectal cancer by age 40 without colectomy.
Extra-colonic manifestations include duodenal adenomas, desmoid tumors,
osteomas, epidermoid cysts, and CHRPE (congenital hypertrophy of retinal
pigment epithelium). Prophylactic colectomy is required.
questions.question: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by mutations in which gene?

A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes develops proteinuria and CKD. Renal biopsy shows diffuse glomerulosclerosis with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and thickened glomerular basement membranes. What mechanism primarily drives these histological changes?
options: Immune complex deposition in glomerular basement membrane
Direct toxic effect of exogenous insulin on mesangial cells
Non-enzymatic glycation and advanced glycation end-product accumulation
Hypertensive arteriolar sclerosis alone causing glomerulosclerosis
Amyloid deposition of islet amyloid polypeptide in glomeruli
questions.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is driven by chronic hyperglycaemia causing non-enzymatic glycation of proteins and accumulation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) that cross-link collagen, thicken basement membranes, and expand mesangium. Hyperfiltration from glomerular hypertension, PKC activation, VEGF upregulation, and TGF-beta-mediated fibrosis further contribute. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis) are pathognomonic of diabetic nephropathy. Microalbuminuria is the earliest clinical marker. ACE inhibitors and SGLT-2 inhibitors slow progression independently of blood pressure.

questions.question: What clinical triad characterizes Kearns-Sayre syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Progressive external ophthalmoplegia, retinitis pigmentosa, and cardiac
conduction defects characterize Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Large mtDNA
deletions cause disease. Onset before age 20 distinguishes from CPEO.

questions.question: The most common location for endometriosis is:
questions.explanation: Ovaries are the most common site for endometriosis, followed by pelvic peritoneum, uterosacral ligaments, and rectovaginal septum. Ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) result from cyclic hemorrhage. Rare sites include umbilicus, surgical scars, lung (catamenial pneumothorax), and brain. Deep infiltrating endometriosis involves rectovaginal septum and bowel.

questions.question: Which cardiac defect most commonly associates with Down syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Endocardial cushion defects (atrioventricular canal defects) occur in
40% of Down syndrome patients with heart disease. Complete
atrioventricular canal shows both atrial and ventricular septal defects.
Congenital heart disease affects 40-50% of Down syndrome individuals.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with bone pain and elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. Skull X-ray shows a cotton-wool appearance. Which histological finding is most characteristic of this condition?
questions.explanation: Paget disease of bone is characterised histologically by a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone with prominent irregular cement lines, giving a jigsaw-puzzle appearance reflecting repeated cycles of bone resorption and formation. Osteoclasts are abnormally large and numerous in the lytic phase; the mixed and sclerotic phases show chaotic bone deposition. Elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased osteoblastic activity. Sarcomatous transformation occurs in less than 1% but carries very poor prognosis.
options: Reactive woven bone around central necrotic core
Sheets of plasma cells replacing haematopoietic marrow
Mosaic lamellar bone pattern with prominent cement lines
Osteoid production by pleomorphic spindle-shaped cells
Fibrous replacement of medullary cavity with woven bone

questions.question: Which laboratory test confirms HIV infection?
questions.explanation:
HIV diagnosis requires positive ELISA screening test confirmed by
Western blot showing antibodies to viral proteins. Fourth-generation
assays detect both antibodies and p24 antigen. HIV RNA PCR confirms
viremia.

questions.question: MELAS syndrome presents with stroke-like episodes at age 12 and lactic acidosis. The most common mitochondrial mutation in MELAS is at:
options: Large 4977 bp deletion of the mitochondrial genome region
Nuclear POLG gene causing progressive mtDNA replication errors
MT-TL1 tRNA-leucine gene at position m.3243A>G mutation
MT-ND4 gene at position m.11778 causing complex I defect
MT-ATP6 gene causing ATP synthase subunit 6 deficiency
questions.explanation: MELAS is most commonly caused by the m.3243A>G point mutation in MT-TL1 encoding mitochondrial tRNA-Leucine(UUR). This impairs translation of mitochondrially encoded respiratory chain subunits, reducing oxidative phosphorylation. The 4977 bp deletion characterizes Kearns-Sayre syndrome. MT-ND4 mutation at m.11778 causes Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. POLG mutations cause progressive external ophthalmoplegia and mitochondrial depletion syndromes. The m.3243A>G mutation also causes maternally inherited diabetes and deafness at lower heteroplasmy levels.

questions.question: Which Angelman syndrome feature distinguishes it from Prader-Willi?
questions.explanation:
Inappropriate laughter and happy demeanor characterize Angelman syndrome
("happy puppet"). Severe mental retardation, ataxia, and seizures
occur. UBE3A gene mutations on maternal chromosome cause disease.

options: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairing platelet maturation
Direct viral infection of megakaryocytes only
Peripheral platelet destruction with compensatory marrow response
Bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells
questions.question: A child presents with recurrent epistaxis and is found to have a platelet count of 15,000/microlitre with megakaryocytes prominent on bone marrow biopsy. Which mechanism best explains this combination of findings?
questions.explanation: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causes peripheral destruction of antibody-coated platelets by splenic macrophages, while the bone marrow compensates by increasing megakaryocyte numbers, distinguishing it from marrow failure states. This pattern of low peripheral platelets with normal or increased marrow megakaryocytes is a key diagnostic clue. Most childhood cases follow a viral illness and resolve spontaneously.

questions.question: Which urea cycle defect causes hyperammonemia?
questions.explanation:
OTC deficiency is most common urea cycle disorder causing severe
hyperammonemia. X-linked inheritance affects males severely while
females show variable manifestations. Ammonia toxicity causes
encephalopathy.

questions.question: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by:
questions.explanation: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) results from abnormal prion protein (PrPSc) causing spongiform encephalopathy. Sporadic (85%), familial (10-15%), and acquired (iatrogenic, variant) forms exist. Rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and EEG changes occur. Spongiform change, neuronal loss, and gliosis without inflammation characterize pathology. No treatment exists; universally fatal. 14-3-3 protein in CSF aids diagnosis.

The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score predicts 3-month mortality in cirrhotic patients using serum creatinine, bilirubin, and INR. Scores range from 6-40, with higher scores indicating greater mortality risk. MELD is used for liver transplant allocation based on mortality risk. MELD-Na includes sodium for better prediction. Unlike Child-Pugh, MELD uses only objective variables.
questions.question: What does the MELD score predict?

questions.explanation: Precursor lesions for hepatocellular carcinoma include large cell change, small cell change (cellular dysplasia), dysplastic nodules, and macro-regenerative nodules. These represent progressive steps in hepatocarcinogenesis, with accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations leading from dysplastic changes to frank malignancy.
questions.question: What are the precursor lesions for hepatocellular carcinoma?
options: Large cell change and small cell change

questions.question: What is the most common primary malignancy metastasizing to lymph nodes in adults?
questions.explanation:
Lung carcinoma is the most common malignancy overall and
frequently metastasizes to regional and distant lymph nodes early in the
disease course. Mediastinal and supraclavicular node involvement is
common. The presence and extent of nodal metastases significantly
impacts staging and treatment decisions in lung cancer.

Luminal A tumors (ER-high, HER2-negative, low Ki67 <14%, low-grade) have most favorable prognosis with excellent response to endocrine therapy alone. Luminal B (ER-positive, HER2-negative or positive, higher Ki67, higher grade) has intermediate prognosis requiring chemotherapy plus endocrine therapy. HER2-enriched and triple negative have worst outcomes.
questions.question: Which breast cancer molecular subtype has best prognosis?

questions.explanation:
Carcinoid tumors (well-differentiated neuroendocrine
tumors) most commonly arise in small intestine (particularly ileum),
followed by appendix. Appendiceal carcinoids are usually benign; small
bowel carcinoids frequently metastasize. Carcinoid syndrome (flushing,
diarrhea, bronchospasm, right-sided valvular disease) occurs with liver
metastases from midgut carcinoids releasing serotonin into systemic
circulation.
questions.question: Carcinoid tumors most commonly arise in which location?

questions.explanation: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but serious third-trimester complication associated with defective mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, producing diffuse microvesicular steatosis on biopsy. This pattern differs from HELLP syndrome, which is characterised more by hepatic haemorrhage, periportal necrosis, and fibrin deposition related to microangiopathic injury.
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops nausea, right upper quadrant pain, and abnormal liver enzymes. Biopsy shows diffuse microvesicular steatosis without significant inflammation. What is the diagnosis?
Lytic bone metastases are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Breast carcinoma produces mixed lytic and blastic metastases while multiple myeloma, renal cell carcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, and lung carcinoma typically cause lytic lesions. Prostate carcinoma characteristically produces blastic (sclerotic) metastases. Bone metastases commonly involve axial skeleton (vertebrae, pelvis, ribs). Bisphosphonates reduce skeletal complications.

questions.question: What gross appearance is characteristic of diffuse gastric carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Diffuse gastric carcinomas are usually composed of signet ring cells and may be difficult to appreciate as a mass. Desmoplasia stiffens the wall, giving a leather bottle appearance called linitis plastica. These tumors show loss of E-cadherin function and have a poorer prognosis than intestinal type tumors.

Trisomy 18 shows characteristically low levels of pregnancy-associated
plasma protein A and beta-hCG. Unconjugated estriol is also low. This
biochemical pattern differs from trisomy 21.
questions.question: Which prenatal screening marker suggests trisomy 18?

options: Direct endothelial cell injury and necrosis
questions.explanation:
Histamine released from mast cells binds to H1 receptors
on endothelial cells, causing rapid contraction that widens
intercellular gaps in venules. This immediate transient response peaks
within 15-30 minutes and is reversible, representing the earliest phase
of increased vascular permeability. Antihistamines can effectively block
this specific mechanism of leakage.
questions.question: In acute inflammation, which mechanism primarily causes endothelial cell contraction leading to immediate transient vascular permeability?

options: It has better prognosis than conventional urothelial carcinoma
It is frequently misdiagnosed and presents at advanced stage
It is uniquely radiosensitive and managed without surgery
It specifically requires intravesical BCG therapy only
It harbours mutations exclusive to this bladder variant
questions.question: A 65-year-old woman has a bladder biopsy showing urothelial carcinoma with cells having abundant pink cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei mimicking plasmacytes. GATA3 is positive. What is the significance of identifying this morphological variant?
questions.explanation: Plasmacytoid variant urothelial carcinoma is an aggressive morphological variant mimicking plasma cells or lobular breast carcinoma, characterised by CDH1 (E-cadherin) loss. Its bland appearance and diffuse non-cohesive growth frequently lead to underdiagnosis and understaging, with extensive peritoneal and retroperitoneal spread at diagnosis. GATA3 and p63 positivity confirm urothelial origin. Peritoneal carcinomatosis is common and requires inclusion of peritoneum in surgical specimens. It carries a worse prognosis than conventional urothelial carcinoma and typically requires radical cystectomy, though often presents at unresectable stage.

Galactose is converted by aldose reductase to galactitol,
which accumulates in lens causing osmotic swelling and cataract
formation. Galactose-1-phosphate accumulation in liver and kidney causes
organ damage. Early lactose/galactose dietary restriction prevents
complications but must be maintained lifelong.
questions.question: Galactosemia causes cataracts through accumulation of which metabolite?
Ewing sarcoma is characterized by which molecular abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Ewing sarcoma shows t(11;22) translocation (85% of cases)
creating EWS-FLI1 fusion protein (or less commonly other EWS-ETS
fusions). The tumor comprises small round blue cells (primitive
neuroectodermal tumor family) affecting long bone diaphyses and pelvis
in children/adolescents. CD99 (MIC2) is characteristically positive.
Onion-skin periosteal reaction is radiographic feature.

questions.question: Which HCC growth pattern is most common?
questions.explanation: The trabecular (plate-like) pattern is the most common histologic pattern in well and moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinomas. Tumor cells grow in cords or plates of variable thickness (often more than 3 cells thick, unlike normal liver) separated by sinusoid-like blood spaces. This recapitulates the normal liver architecture.

questions.question: What is the characteristic vascular change in cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: In cirrhosis, capillarization of sinusoids occurs with loss of endothelial cell fenestrations and deposition of basement membrane material in the space of Disse. This impairs exchange between blood and hepatocytes. Additionally, vascular shunting develops (portal vein-hepatic vein and hepatic artery-portal vein shunts), disrupting normal hepatic blood flow and contributing to portal hypertension.

HTLV-1 (human T-lymphotropic virus 1) is endemic in Japan,
Caribbean, and parts of Africa/South America, causing ATLL in 2-5% of
infected individuals after decades of latency. The viral Tax protein
activates NF-?B and other growth pathways. The disease presents with
characteristic "flower cells" and hypercalcemia.
questions.question: Adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is specifically associated with which retroviral infection?
Ductal adenocarcinoma of prostate characteristically shows:
questions.explanation: Prostatic ductal adenocarcinoma arises from periurethral ducts, showing papillary and cribriform architecture with tall columnar epithelium resembling endometrial carcinoma. May present with hematuria. Often high-grade (Gleason pattern 4) with poor prognosis. PSA and PSAP positive confirm prostatic origin. May occur pure or mixed with acinar adenocarcinoma.

options: Neuroblastoma from adrenal medulla catecholamine-secreting cells
Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) from kidney metanephric blastema
Hepatocellular carcinoma from hepatomegaly and liver overgrowth
Pancreatoblastoma from pancreatic overgrowth in BWS syndrome
Rhabdomyosarcoma from somatic overgrowth of skeletal muscle
questions.question: A 3-year-old with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome presents with a rapidly growing abdominal mass. The tumor most likely arising from BWS-associated organomegaly is:
questions.explanation: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) from 11p15.5 imprinting abnormalities is associated with markedly elevated risk of embryonal tumors, most commonly Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) occurring in approximately 5-7% of BWS patients. Other associated tumors include hepatoblastoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma. Tumor surveillance with abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until age 8 years (for Wilms tumor) and alpha-fetoprotein every 3 months until age 4 years (for hepatoblastoma) is the standard of care for all confirmed BWS patients.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man has chronic constipation and intermittent left iliac fossa pain. Colonoscopy shows multiple sac-like outpouchings in the sigmoid colon without inflammation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diverticulosis refers to the presence of asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic colonic diverticula without active inflammation, common with ageing and low dietary fibre intake. Diverticulitis describes the same anatomical lesions complicated by inflammation or infection, distinguished clinically by fever, leucocytosis, and localised peritoneal signs.

questions.question: Male breast carcinoma most commonly presents as:
questions.explanation: Male breast cancer typically presents as subareolar mass or nipple changes due to limited breast tissue. Most are invasive ductal carcinomas expressing hormone receptors. Risk factors include BRCA2 mutations, Klinefelter syndrome, and prior radiation exposure. Prognosis is similar to female breast cancer when stage-matched.

Amsterdam II criteria are clinical diagnostic criteria for Lynch syndrome: ≥3 relatives with Lynch-associated cancers (CRC, endometrial, etc.), ≥2 successive generations affected, ≥1 diagnosis before age 50, ≥1 first-degree relative of the other two, and exclusion of FAP. These criteria identify high-risk families warranting genetic testing. Revised Bethesda guidelines broaden testing recommendations.
questions.question: What is the Amsterdam II criteria?

questions.explanation: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells, presenting as dura-based masses compressing but not invading brain. Whorled pattern with psammoma bodies is characteristic of meningothelial type. Multiple variants exist (fibrous, transitional, psammomatous). Most are WHO grade 1; atypical (grade 2) and anaplastic (grade 3) show increased proliferation. NF2 gene loss on chromosome 22q occurs.
questions.question: Meningiomas most commonly arise from:

A 5-year-old presents with progressive neurological decline, a cherry-red spot on fundoscopic examination, and exaggerated startle response to sound. Which underlying enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Tay-Sachs disease results from hexosaminidase A deficiency, causing GM2 ganglioside accumulation within neurons, leading to progressive neurodegeneration, a cherry-red macular spot from ganglion cell swelling around the relatively preserved fovea, and an exaggerated startle response. This combination of neurological and ophthalmological findings is highly suggestive of this specific lysosomal storage disease. The condition is more prevalent in certain populations, including those of Ashkenazi Jewish descent, supporting targeted carrier screening.

questions.question: Which Huntington disease feature results from CAG repeat expansion?
questions.explanation:
CAG repeat expansion in huntingtin gene causes chorea (involuntary
movements). Repeat length inversely correlates with age of onset.
Striatal neurodegeneration produces movement disorder.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of death from portal hypertension complications?
questions.explanation: Rupture and bleeding from esophagogastric varices is a very important cause of death in persons with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. These thin-walled, dilated veins in the lower esophagus and gastric fundus are prone to rupture, causing massive, potentially fatal upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. This represents a medical emergency requiring urgent intervention.

options: CD4 count below 200 or AIDS-defining illness
questions.question: What defines AIDS according to CDC criteria?
questions.explanation:
AIDS diagnosis requires CD4 count below 200 cells/? or presence of
AIDS-defining opportunistic infection regardless of CD4 count.
Twenty-six conditions including PCP, toxoplasmosis, and certain cancers
define AIDS.

questions.question: What genetic mechanism causes most Angelman syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Maternal deletion of 15q11-13 accounts for 70% of Angelman syndrome.
UBE3A mutations (10%) and imprinting defects (5%) also occur. Paternal
uniparental disomy causes 2-5% of cases.

questions.question: Polycystic kidney disease (autosomal dominant) is caused by mutations in:
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) results from PKD1 (chromosome 16, 85% of cases) or PKD2 (chromosome 4, 15%) mutations affecting polycystin proteins in cilia. Progressive cyst formation causes renal enlargement and insufficiency. Presents in adulthood. Associated with hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, cardiac valvular disease. Leading genetic cause of end-stage renal disease.

questions.question: What is the characteristic microscopic pattern of alcoholic hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Alcoholic hepatitis is characterized by macrovesicular steatosis with inflammation, ballooning degeneration, satellitosis (ballooned hepatocyte surrounded by neutrophils), Mallory-Denk bodies, and chicken wire fibrosis (perivenular and pericellular/perisinusoidal fibrosis). These features are characteristic for fatty liver disease.

Caudate and putamen show severe neuronal loss and atrophy. GABAergic
medium spiny neurons preferentially degenerate. Cortical atrophy
develops in later stages.
questions.question: What brain region shows predominant pathology in Huntington disease?

questions.explanation:
The t(14;18) translocation places BCL-2 gene under control
of immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer, causing overexpression of the
anti-apoptotic BCL-2 protein. This prevents normal programmed cell death
of germinal center B cells, allowing accumulation of long-lived cells
susceptible to additional mutations. The translocation is present in
about 85% of follicular lymphomas.
questions.question: In follicular lymphoma, which translocation is most characteristically associated with the disease pathogenesis?

questions.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome results from a somatic activating mutation in the GNAS gene, causing the triad of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (predisposing to fractures), irregular 'coast of Maine' café-au-lait macules, and endocrine hyperfunction such as precocious puberty. This irregular border pattern distinguishes the café-au-lait macules from the smoother 'coast of California' borders typical of neurofibromatosis type 1. The mosaic nature of this condition reflects its origin from a post-zygotic somatic mutation rather than germline inheritance.
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with recurrent fractures and is found to have multiple café-au-lait macules with irregular ('coast of Maine') borders, along with precocious puberty. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
What physical finding suggests familial hypercholesterolemia?
questions.explanation:
Tendon xanthomas particularly in Achilles tendon suggest familial
hypercholesterolemia. Corneal arcus before age 45 and xanthelasmas also
occur. These signs indicate chronic severe hypercholesterolemia.

Fat-poor/fat-invisible angiomyolipomas lack detectable fat on imaging, mimicking renal cell carcinoma. Diagnosis challenging; may require biopsy showing HMB-45 and Melan-A positivity (melanocytic markers) confirming smooth muscle origin. Most occur sporadically in middle-aged women. Treatment reserved for symptomatic/large (>4cm) lesions due to hemorrhage risk.
questions.question: Angiomyolipoma without fat is important to recognize because:
What immune response dominates early schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation:
Early immune response to schistosome eggs is dominated by Th1 cells
producing IFN-?. This represents type IV hypersensitivity causing
granuloma formation around eggs. Chronic infection shifts toward Th2
response with increased fibrosis from IL-13.

questions.question: Bowenoid papulosis differs from Bowen disease by:
questions.explanation: Bowenoid papulosis shows similar histology to Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) but occurs in younger sexually active individuals as multiple pigmented papules, typically regressing spontaneously. HPV 16 association. Despite histologic atypia, malignant behavior is uncommon. Conservative management appropriate; excision if persistent. Represents viral-induced dysplasia rather than true malignancy.

questions.question: A 4-year-old with recurrent hypoglycemia and seizures has liver glycogen accumulation. Fasting glucose falls to 1.8 mmol/L with lactic acidosis and hyperlipidemia. The enzyme deficient is:
options: Liver phosphorylase causing hepatomegaly without significant hypoglycemia
Debranching enzyme causing moderate hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly
Branching enzyme causing progressive cardiomyopathy and cirrhosis
Phosphofructokinase causing exercise intolerance rather than hypoglycemia
Glucose-6-phosphatase causing hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and lactic acidosis
questions.explanation: Glycogen storage disease type Ia (Von Gierke disease) results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency in the liver, kidney, and intestine. Inability to release free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate causes severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis (from diverted glucose-6-phosphate through glycolysis), hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia. Hepatomegaly is massive from glycogen and lipid accumulation. Management involves continuous glucose feeding to prevent hypoglycemia. Liver phosphorylase deficiency (GSD VI) and debranching enzyme deficiency (GSD III) cause milder hypoglycemia without significant lactic acidosis.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive headache, personality change, and focal seizures. MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis. Biopsy shows pseudopalisading necrosis with microvascular proliferation. What is the WHO grade of this tumour?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma (WHO Grade 4) is characterised by pseudopalisading necrosis (tumour cells lining necrotic areas), microvascular (endothelial) proliferation, high mitotic activity, and marked nuclear pleomorphism. Ring enhancement on MRI reflects blood-brain barrier breakdown around necrosis. EGFR amplification, PTEN loss, and CDKN2A deletion are common. IDH-wildtype glioblastoma has median survival of approximately 15 months with maximal safe resection, temozolomide, and radiotherapy (Stupp protocol). IDH-mutant glioblastoma has marginally better prognosis.
options: WHO Grade 1 pilocytic astrocytoma with biphasic pattern
WHO Grade 3 anaplastic oligodendroglioma with 1p/19q codeletion

questions.question: In granulomatous inflammation, what triggers the transformation of macrophages into epithelioid cells?
questions.explanation:
Persistent antigen stimulation and chronic IFN-? secretion
from T cells cause macrophage transformation into epithelioid cells with
enhanced secretory capacity. These modified macrophages have abundant
cytoplasm and reduced phagocytic ability but excel at antigen
presentation. This specialized differentiation is hallmark of
granulomatous inflammation.

questions.question: Immune hydrops fetalis due to Rh incompatibility requires which previous maternal exposure?
questions.explanation:
Rh disease requires prior maternal sensitization to D
antigen (usually from previous Rh+ pregnancy, transfusion, or
fetomaternal hemorrhage) to generate IgG antibodies. The first Rh+
pregnancy typically produces only IgM that doesn't cross placenta.
RhoGAM (anti-D immunoglobulin) given prophylactically prevents
sensitization.

Positive predictive value for trisomy 21 is 90-95% but lower for
trisomies 13 and 18. False positives occur from confined placental
mosaicism. Diagnostic testing confirms positive results.
questions.question: What is the positive predictive value of cfDNA for trisomy 21?

questions.explanation:
Unbalanced segregation produces offspring with partial monosomy for one
chromosome and partial trisomy for another. Severity depends on
imbalanced segments. Balanced carrier parents have recurrence risk.
questions.question: Which chromosomal imbalance results from unbalanced translocation?
Which Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome feature increases embryonal tumor risk?
questions.explanation:
Hemihypertrophy associates with increased Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma
risk in BWS. Tumor surveillance with abdominal ultrasound and
alpha-fetoprotein monitoring is recommended. Imprinting defects at 11p15
cause BWS.

questions.question: Which TORCH infection is most commonly associated with congenital cataracts and cardiac defects?
questions.explanation:
Congenital rubella syndrome causes classic triad of
cataracts, cardiac defects (patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary
stenosis), and sensorineural deafness. First trimester infection carries
highest risk of severe anomalies. Widespread vaccination has nearly
eliminated congenital rubella in developed countries.

Type 1 diabetes results from T-cell mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells, often triggered by environmental factors in genetically susceptible individuals. Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltration) precedes clinical disease. HLA-DR3 and DR4 associations exist. Autoantibodies against GAD, insulin, and IA-2 are detectable. Absolute insulin deficiency causes ketoacidosis risk.
questions.question: Diabetes mellitus Type 1 results from:

questions.explanation:
Chronic immune activation from HIV and opportunistic
infections drives progressive T cell exhaustion and activation-induced
cell death, contributing more to CD4 depletion than direct viral
killing. This persistent activation depletes naive T cells and
accelerates immunosenescence. The inflammatory state also recruits new
targets for infection.
questions.question: Which mechanism is most important for HIV-mediated CD4+ T cell depletion in established infection?
Invasive lobular carcinoma characteristically shows:
options: Signet ring cells in single file pattern
questions.explanation: Invasive lobular carcinoma demonstrates discohesive growth due to loss of E-cadherin expression, forming single-file strands and targetoid periductal/perivascular patterns. Cells may contain intracytoplasmic mucin (signet ring cells). These tumors show predilection for bilateral disease and unusual metastatic sites including gastrointestinal tract, peritoneum, and leptomeninges.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome is characterized by elevated LH levels with normal or low FSH, resulting in an increased LH:FSH ratio. This hormonal imbalance leads to excess androgen production, chronic anovulation, and formation of multiple subcapsular follicular cysts. Insulin resistance often coexists and contributes to the pathophysiology.
questions.question: A 28-year-old nulliparous woman has bilateral ovarian enlargement with multiple subcapsular cysts. Serum studies would most likely show elevated:

questions.explanation:
AA amyloid derives from serum amyloid A (acute phase
protein) in chronic inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis,
inflammatory bowel disease, and chronic infections. This represents
reactive (secondary) systemic amyloidosis affecting kidneys, liver, and
spleen. Treating underlying inflammation can halt progression.
questions.question: Which type of amyloid is associated with chronic inflammatory diseases?

questions.explanation: Schiller-Duval bodies are glomeruloid structures with central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within cystic space, pathognomonic for yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor). AFP production aids diagnosis and monitoring. Highly malignant but chemosensitive. Occur in children and young women. Combination chemotherapy (BEP regimen) achieves excellent cure rates.
questions.question: Schiller-Duval bodies are characteristic of:

A 45-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice. Biopsy of the gallbladder shows transmural neutrophilic infiltration with mucosal ulceration following cystic duct obstruction by a stone. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute calculous cholecystitis results from cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone, causing bile stasis, gallbladder wall distension, and secondary bacterial infection with transmural neutrophilic inflammation and mucosal ulceration. Acalculous cholecystitis follows the same pathway but without an obstructing stone, typically in critically ill patients.

questions.question: Which oxygen-dependent bactericidal mechanism is most potent in neutrophils for killing ingested microorganisms?
questions.explanation:
The myeloperoxidase-halide system converts H2O2 to
hypochlorous acid (HOCl), the most efficient bactericidal agent in
neutrophils. This system is more potent than other oxygen-dependent
mechanisms and requires myeloperoxidase enzyme stored in azurophilic
granules. Deficiency causes increased susceptibility to certain fungal
and bacterial infections.

questions.question: A child with recurrent infections is found to have absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray, hypocalcaemia, and cardiac outflow tract abnormalities. Which embryological structures are most likely affected?
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome results from abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to thymic hypoplasia (causing T-cell immunodeficiency), parathyroid hypoplasia (causing hypocalcaemia), and associated cardiac outflow tract defects. This combination of findings reflects the shared embryological origin of these structures. A 22q11.2 microdeletion is the most common underlying genetic cause.

options: TDP-43 inclusions in frontotemporal lobar degeneration
Alpha-synuclein aggregates forming neuronal Lewy bodies
Huntingtin aggregates forming neuronal intranuclear inclusions
questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive cognitive decline, memory loss, and positive amyloid PET scan. Histology shows neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. Which protein forms the neurofibrillary tangles?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer disease shows two hallmark lesions: neuritic plaques (extracellular deposits of beta-amyloid Abeta42 surrounded by dystrophic neurites) and neurofibrillary tangles (intraneuronal aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau protein forming paired helical filaments that disrupt microtubule function). Amyloid accumulation is thought to be the initiating event (amyloid cascade hypothesis). APOE epsilon4 allele is the major genetic risk factor. APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2 mutations cause familial early-onset Alzheimer. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine provide symptomatic benefit.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Alcohol and gallstones together account for approximately 80% of acute pancreatitis cases. Gallstones cause 40-50% (more common in females), alcoholism causes 30-40% (more common in males with M:F ratio 6:1). Other causes include hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, drugs, trauma, ERCP, infections, and autoimmune disease. About 10-20% are idiopathic.

questions.question: Which cytokine produced by TH2 cells is most directly responsible for stimulating B cells to undergo class switching to IgE?
questions.explanation:
IL-4 is the primary cytokine driving B cell class
switching to IgE production, central to type I hypersensitivity
reactions. TH2 cells secreting IL-4 create a microenvironment favoring
allergic responses over cell-mediated immunity. IL-13 can also promote
IgE production but IL-4 is the dominant and most direct stimulus.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents with gynecomastia and small firm testes. The laboratory finding distinguishing primary from secondary hypogonadism is:
options: Low luteinizing hormone (LH) indicating pituitary failure
Elevated FSH and LH with low testosterone indicating primary failure
Low FSH with elevated testosterone indicating androgen resistance
Normal FSH with elevated estradiol indicating adrenal estrogen excess
Elevated prolactin suppressing gonadotropin axis secondarily
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome causes primary testicular failure with seminiferous tubule hyalinization and reduced Leydig cell function. The hypergonadotropic hypogonadism pattern shows elevated FSH and LH (reflecting lost negative feedback from testis) combined with low testosterone. This distinguishes primary testicular failure from secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism where LH and FSH are low or inappropriately normal. Gynecomastia results from elevated estradiol-to-testosterone ratio. Testosterone replacement therapy corrects hypogonadism but does not restore fertility without assisted reproductive techniques.

questions.question: During the late phase of type I hypersensitivity, which cell type is primarily responsible for sustaining the inflammatory response?
questions.explanation:
Eosinophils recruited by IL-5 and eotaxin sustain
late-phase reactions through release of major basic protein and other
mediators causing tissue damage. This occurs 2-24 hours after initial
exposure and can persist for days without additional antigen exposure.
Eosinophil-derived products contribute significantly to chronic allergic
inflammation.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with an epiphyseal lesion at the distal femur after skeletal maturity. Biopsy shows multinucleated giant cells evenly distributed among mononuclear stromal cells. What is the most appropriate primary treatment?
options: Systemic chemotherapy followed by restaging biopsy
En bloc wide resection with prosthetic reconstruction
Radiation therapy alone as the primary modality
Intralesional curettage with local adjuvant therapy
Transcatheter arterial embolisation as sole treatment
questions.explanation: Giant cell tumour (GCT) of bone, characterised by multinucleated giant cells among mononuclear stromal cells, occurs in epiphyses of skeletally mature individuals. The standard treatment is intralesional curettage followed by local adjuvants (phenol, liquid nitrogen, or argon beam) with bone grafting or cementation. Wide resection is reserved for recurrent or expendable bone lesions. Denosumab (anti-RANKL) is used for unresectable or recurrent GCT, which has a local recurrence risk of approximately 20%.

questions.question: Which sleeping position is most strongly associated with increased SIDS risk?
questions.explanation:
Prone sleeping increases SIDS risk 2-13 fold, possibly
impairing arousal from sleep and reducing heat dissipation. The "Back
to Sleep" campaign reducing prone sleeping has decreased SIDS incidence
by over 50%. Side sleeping also carries increased risk compared to
supine positioning.

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis demonstrates a strong male predominance with a male to female ratio of 3-4:1. It is a disorder of multifactorial inheritance associated with Turner syndrome and trisomy 18. The condition is caused by hyperplasia of the muscularis propria causing persistent gastric outlet obstruction.
questions.question: What is the male to female ratio in congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

questions.explanation: HSV-1 encephalitis shows predilection for temporal lobes and orbital frontal cortex, causing hemorrhagic necrosis. Patients present with fever, altered mental status, and seizures. CSF shows lymphocytosis, elevated protein, and positive HSV PCR. MRI demonstrates temporal lobe abnormalities. Early acyclovir treatment improves outcomes; untreated disease has >70% mortality with severe neurologic sequelae.
questions.question: Herpes simplex encephalitis characteristically involves:

options: Observation with repeat biopsy in 5 years
questions.explanation: High-grade dysplasia confined to the epithelium without invasion is treated by endoscopic mucosal resection or ablation, which removes the at-risk mucosa while avoiding the morbidity of major surgery. Oesophagectomy is reserved for invasive carcinoma. PPIs alone do not address the dysplastic tissue.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with chronic GERD has biopsy of the distal oesophagus showing high-grade dysplasia confined to the epithelium without invasion. What is the most appropriate management?

questions.explanation: Renal angiomyolipomas (AMLs) in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) grow through mTORC1 pathway activation from TSC1/TSC2 mutations. Everolimus (an mTOR inhibitor) reduces AML volume by approximately 50% and is the preferred first-line treatment for AMLs exceeding 3 cm in TSC patients, avoiding nephron loss from surgery. The risk of spontaneous hemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome) increases with lesions above 3-4 cm, particularly those containing large aneurysms greater than 5 mm. Embolization is reserved for acute bleeding. Malignant transformation of AML in TSC is extremely rare.
questions.question: A 10-year-old with tuberous sclerosis complex has a 4.5 cm renal angiomyolipoma found on surveillance imaging. The most appropriate management is:
options: Radical nephrectomy to prevent malignant transformation
Annual surveillance alone as lesions rarely cause symptoms
Surgical wedge resection to preserve maximum renal parenchyma
Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor) to reduce tumor size non-surgically
Arterial embolization reserved only for acute hemorrhage events
CIN 1 best managed by watchful waiting and repeat smear
CIN 3 (carcinoma in situ) requiring excisional treatment
Invasive squamous cell carcinoma stage IA1
High-grade VAIN managed with topical fluorouracil
questions.question: A 25-year-old woman has abnormal Pap smear showing HSIL. Biopsy of the transformation zone shows dysplastic cells extending through the full epithelial thickness without invasion. How should this finding be classified?
questions.explanation: CIN 3 (carcinoma in situ) is characterised by full-thickness dysplasia of the cervical squamous epithelium without invasion through the basement membrane. It corresponds to HSIL on cytology. Untreated CIN 3 carries approximately 30-70% risk of progression to invasive carcinoma over 10-30 years. Treatment options include LLETZ (large loop excision of transformation zone) or cold knife conisation to achieve clear margins. Unlike CIN 1 (which often regresses spontaneously), CIN 3 requires excisional treatment. Adequate post-treatment surveillance is mandatory.

questions.question: A newborn fails to pass meconium within 48 hours and has abdominal distension. Rectal biopsy is taken to confirm a diagnosis before surgery. What histochemical stain helps confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase staining shows increased activity in hypertrophic nerve fibres within the lamina propria and muscularis mucosae in Hirschsprung's disease, supporting the diagnosis when combined with the absence of ganglion cells on routine and immunohistochemical staining (e.g., calretinin). This is a key ancillary technique in confirming aganglionosis.

questions.question: Abruptio placentae is associated with:
questions.explanation: Placental abruption (premature separation) complicates 1% of pregnancies, associated with hypertension, trauma, cocaine use, smoking, and thrombophilias. Causes fetal hypoxia and maternal hemorrhage. Retroplacental hematoma with compression of placental tissue occurs. DIC may develop. Immediate delivery necessary. Recurrence risk is 10-25% in subsequent pregnancies.

questions.question: Which HIV gene encodes reverse transcriptase?
questions.explanation:
The pol gene encodes viral enzymes including reverse transcriptase,
integrase, and protease. Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA to DNA
for integration. Antiretroviral drugs targeting these enzymes form
treatment backbone.

questions.question: Which hepatotropic virus is most associated with development of chronic hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C virus is most strongly associated with development of chronic hepatitis, with approximately 85% of acutely infected individuals becoming chronically infected. This makes HCV a major cause of chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. HBV also causes chronic hepatitis but at lower rates (about 10%).

questions.question: Smudge cells (basket cells) on peripheral blood smear are characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation:
Smudge cells (disrupted lymphocytes) occur in CLL due to
increased cellular fragility during slide preparation. While not
specific, numerous smudge cells suggest CLL. Other findings include
lymphocytosis (often >50,000/μL), autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and
hypogammaglobulinemia from immune dysfunction.

Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, resulting from deficient or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor, which impairs platelet adhesion to the vascular subendothelium, producing mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet count and morphology. This contrasts with haemophilia, which typically causes deep tissue and joint bleeding rather than mucocutaneous symptoms. Specific assays measuring von Willebrand factor antigen and activity are required for diagnosis.
questions.question: A child presents with recurrent epistaxis, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. Platelet count and morphology are normal, but bleeding time is prolonged. Which underlying disorder is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation:
Aspergillus demonstrates narrow (3-6μm) septate hyphae
with characteristic acute-angle (45°) dichotomous branching. This
differs from Mucor (broad nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching)
and Candida (yeast and pseudohyphae). Angioinvasion is typical in
invasive aspergillosis.
options: Narrow septate hyphae with acute branching
questions.question: Aspergillus species in tissue typically shows which morphological feature?

questions.explanation:
Massive muscle breakdown releases myoglobin, which is
nephrotoxic and precipitates in renal tubules (especially with
hypovolemia and aciduria), causing acute tubular necrosis and
obstruction. Myoglobin also depletes nitric oxide causing
vasoconstriction. Compartment syndrome, toxins, medications, and
metabolic myopathies cause rhabdomyolysis. Aggressive fluid
resuscitation prevents kidney injury.
questions.question: Rhabdomyolysis can lead to acute kidney injury through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Low-grade dysplasia detected in flat mucosa during ulcerative colitis surveillance warrants confirmation by an expert pathologist and increased surveillance frequency, as it carries a risk of progression to high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma. Colectomy is generally reserved for high-grade dysplasia, multifocal dysplasia, or a dysplasia-associated lesion or mass.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis for 10 years undergoes surveillance colonoscopy. Biopsy shows architectural distortion with low-grade dysplasia in flat mucosa. What is the most appropriate next step?

questions.explanation:
LEMS involves antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated
calcium channels, impairing acetylcholine release. Unlike myasthenia
gravis, strength improves with repeated muscle contraction. Associated
with small cell lung cancer in 50-60% of cases (paraneoplastic) or
occurs as autoimmune disorder. EMG shows incremental response to
repetitive stimulation.
questions.question: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome involves antibodies against:
What is the most common histologic subtype of HCC?
questions.explanation: The trabecular (plate-like) pattern is the most common in well and moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinomas. Tumor cells grow in cords of variable thickness separated by sinusoid-like blood spaces. Other patterns include pseudoglandular, acinar, compact, scirrhous, and fibrolamellar variants.

Achondroplasia results from autosomal dominant mutations in fibroblast
growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3). These mutations cause constitutive
activation of the receptor inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation.
Affected individuals have normal trunk size but shortened limbs and are
usually normal in biological functions.
questions.question: Which genetic mutation is associated with achondroplasia?
A 17-year-old is diagnosed with neurofibromatosis type 1 after finding cafe-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules. The most important surveillance finding to monitor for in adolescence is:
questions.explanation: Plexiform neurofibromas in NF1 carry approximately 8-13% lifetime risk of transformation to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST), which is the leading cause of NF1-related mortality. MPNSTs are aggressive sarcomas with poor prognosis when not detected early. Surveillance includes clinical examination for rapid growth, pain, or firmness changes in known plexiform neurofibromas, and whole-body MRI every 1-2 years in high-risk patients. Optic pathway gliomas are important in young children (under age 7) but rarely appear after age 10; MPNST risk persists lifelong.
options: Renal artery stenosis causing secondary hypertension in NF1
Plexiform neurofibroma transformation to malignant MPNST
Optic pathway glioma causing visual loss in NF1 children
Cardiac rhabdomyoma from NF1 germline mutation penetrance

questions.question: What is the characteristic ulcer pattern in shigellosis?
questions.explanation: Shigellosis principally affects the colon, with the terminal ileum occasionally involved. A granular and hemorrhagic mucosa exhibits numerous shallow serpiginous ulcers. Severe superficial inflammation is seen in the sigmoid colon and rectum, with accumulation of neutrophils in damaged crypts forming crypt abscesses.

Portal hypertension causes blood to be diverted from the high-pressure portal system into lower-pressure systemic venous channels through portosystemic collaterals, including those at the gastro-oesophageal junction, rectum, and umbilicus. These collateral veins, normally thin-walled, become dilated and tortuous, forming varices that are prone to rupture and haemorrhage.
options: Direct neoplastic invasion of submucosal veins
Diversion of portal blood through portosystemic collaterals
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with portal hypertension has variceal bleeding. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism leading to varix formation?
What age characterizes typical Huntington disease onset?
questions.explanation:
Mean onset occurs at 35-40 years with gradual progression over 15-20
years. Larger CAG repeats cause earlier onset. Juvenile cases (under age
20) show rigid-akinetic syndrome.

questions.question: A 7-year-old with phenylketonuria maintained on a phenylalanine-restricted diet has excellent metabolic control. The most important micronutrient to supplement in PKU dietary management is:
questions.explanation: When phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) is deficient or absent, tyrosine cannot be synthesized from phenylalanine, making tyrosine conditionally essential in PKU. Without adequate tyrosine supplementation, patients develop tyrosine deficiency causing poor growth, impaired neurotransmitter synthesis (dopamine, norepinephrine), and pigmentation abnormalities. The amino acid formula used in PKU management is specifically formulated to provide tyrosine, essential amino acids, and micronutrients while excluding or limiting phenylalanine. Sapropterin (BH4 analogue) can increase PAH enzyme responsiveness in BH4-responsive PKU variants.
options: Vitamin B12 because meat restriction reduces dietary intake
Tyrosine as it becomes essential when PAH activity is absent
Zinc because phenylalanine competes for zinc absorption directly
Folate because phenylalanine hydroxylase requires folate cofactor
Iron because the PKU diet is poor in iron-containing foods

questions.question: Hydatidiform mole is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Hydatidiform moles show hydropic swelling of chorionic villi with varying degrees of trophoblastic proliferation. Complete moles (46,XX or 46,XY, all paternal) lack fetal tissue; partial moles (triploidy) contain fetal parts. Markedly elevated -hCG occurs. "Snowstorm" ultrasound appearance is characteristic. Risk of persistent gestational trophoblastic disease requires -hCG monitoring.

questions.question: A child with Marfan syndrome undergoes echocardiography. The aortic root diameter threshold typically prompting prophylactic surgical intervention is:
questions.explanation: Current guidelines recommend prophylactic aortic root replacement at 4.5-5.0 cm, or earlier with rapid progression exceeding 5 mm per year, family history of early dissection, significant aortic regurgitation, or planned pregnancy. Fibrillin-1 deficiency impairs elastic fiber integrity predisposing to dissection. Beta-blockers and ARBs (losartan) reduce wall stress to slow progression. Surveillance imaging every 6-12 months is mandatory once aortic root dilation is identified on initial echocardiographic screening of Marfan patients.
options: 3.0 cm in any patient regardless of progression rate
4.5 to 5.0 cm or rapid progressive dilatation rate
Any measurement above the population age-adjusted norm
6.0 cm to avoid premature and unnecessary surgery
3.5 cm given high familial dissection risk factor

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman taking long-term methotrexate for psoriasis develops abnormal liver enzymes. Biopsy shows pericellular and periportal fibrosis without significant steatosis or inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is a recognised cause of drug-induced hepatic fibrosis, characteristically producing periportal and pericellular fibrosis with relatively mild inflammation or steatosis, distinct from the more inflammatory pattern of autoimmune hepatitis or the bile duct-centred injury of primary biliary cholangitis. Cumulative dose and duration of therapy are key risk factors.

options: Liver ultrasound for hepatoblastoma risk every 3 months
Annual chest X-ray for increased mediastinal lymphoma risk
Renal ultrasound for Wilms tumor risk every 3 months to age 8
Annual whole-body MRI for sarcoma risk assessment
Surveillance for leukemia and solid tumors including neuroblastoma
questions.explanation: Sotos syndrome from NSD1 haploinsufficiency is an overgrowth syndrome associated with a modestly elevated cancer risk (approximately 2-4%), including cases of leukemia (ALL, AML), Wilms tumor, hepatocellular carcinoma, and neuroblastoma. Unlike BWS where tumor surveillance is protocol-driven, Sotos tumor surveillance does not have a standardized guideline but clinicians remain vigilant for hematological malignancies given the NSD1 role in chromatin regulation. Parents should be educated about symptoms of malignancy. The cancer risk is much lower than in BWS (5-7%) or hemihyperplasia (5%), and routine surveillance imaging is debated in current literature.
questions.question: A 4-year-old boy with Sotos syndrome (NSD1 deletion) has advanced bone age, macrocephaly, and learning disability. The tumor surveillance required in Sotos syndrome is:

questions.explanation: Anencephaly results from failure of anterior neuropore closure, causing absence of forebrain and calvarium. Area cerebrovasculosa (vascular connective tissue) replaces brain tissue. Brainstem remnants may be present allowing live birth, but survival beyond days is rare. Polyhydramnios occurs (impaired fetal swallowing). Most pregnancies are detected prenatally and terminated.
questions.question: Anencephaly results from failure of:

questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis, caused by APC mutations, leads to hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomas with near-certain progression to colorectal cancer if untreated, usually by the third or fourth decade. Prophylactic colectomy is therefore recommended once polyps are detected, as surveillance alone cannot adequately reduce cancer risk in this condition.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man has multiple colonic polyps with a family history of colorectal cancer. Genetic testing reveals an APC gene mutation. What is the most appropriate management?

questions.explanation:
CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 gene causes fragile X syndrome. Premutation
has 55-200 repeats while full mutation exceeds 200 repeats. Expansion
occurs during maternal transmission.
questions.question: What molecular mechanism causes fragile X syndrome?

questions.explanation:
Nodular sclerosis subtype shows fibrous bands dividing the
lymph node into nodules containing lacunar variant RS cells. This is the
most common Hodgkin subtype (65-70%), typically affecting young adults
with mediastinal mass. Collagen deposition distinguishes it from other
subtypes.
questions.question: Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically shows which feature?
Granulosa cell tumors produce which hormone?
questions.explanation: Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord-stromal neoplasms secreting estrogen, causing precocious puberty in children and endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma in adults. Call-Exner bodies (eosinophilic fluid in follicle-like spaces) are characteristic. Adult type occurs perimenopausal while juvenile type affects younger patients. Late recurrences may occur decades after initial diagnosis.

Cervical adenocarcinomas arise from endocervical glandular epithelium, representing 15-20% of cervical cancers. HPV 16 and 18 are etiologic agents. Endocervical adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) is the precursor lesion. These tumors are more difficult to detect on Pap smear and have worse prognosis than squamous cell carcinomas at similar stages.
questions.question: Cervical adenocarcinoma most commonly arises in:

questions.explanation: Enzalutamide is a second-generation androgen receptor antagonist blocking AR nuclear translocation, DNA binding, and coactivator recruitment. More potent than bicalutamide. Effective in castration-resistant prostate cancer pre- and post-chemotherapy. Side effects include fatigue, hypertension, and rarely seizures. Resistance develops through AR splice variants, mutations, or bypass mechanisms.
questions.question: Enzalutamide works by:
Benign prostatic hyperplasia primarily affects which zone?
questions.explanation: BPH arises predominantly in the transition zone surrounding the proximal urethra, causing urethral compression and obstructive symptoms. Prostatic adenocarcinoma typically originates in the peripheral zone. Nodular hyperplasia involves both stromal and epithelial proliferation under androgenic stimulation, particularly by dihydrotestosterone.

questions.question: Legionella pneumophila is best detected using which culture medium?
questions.explanation:
Legionella requires specialized BCYE agar supplemented
with L-cysteine and iron for culture, as it won't grow on standard
media. Urinary antigen testing provides rapid diagnosis for L.
pneumophila serogroup 1 (most common). The organism is a fastidious
gram-negative rod transmitted via contaminated water aerosols.

Granulomas are not seen in ulcerative colitis but are a hallmark feature of Crohn disease, occurring in approximately 35% of cases. Ulcerative colitis is characterized by crypt architecture distortion, cryptitis, crypt abscesses, increased mucosal chronic inflammation, eosinophils, lymphoid aggregates, and mucin depletion in regenerating epithelium.
questions.question: What histologic feature is NOT seen in ulcerative colitis?

questions.explanation: Fibrocystic change with usual-type (non-atypical) ductal hyperplasia (UDH) confers a slightly increased relative risk (1.5-2 times) of subsequent breast carcinoma compared to non-proliferative disease, which has no increased risk. UDH, cysts, adenosis, and apocrine metaplasia without atypia fall into the proliferative disease without atypia category. Atypical ductal hyperplasia or atypical lobular hyperplasia increases risk 4-5 times. LCIS carries 8-10 times relative risk. No specific intervention beyond routine mammographic surveillance is required for UDH alone.
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with cyclic breast pain and bilateral nodularity. Biopsy shows cysts, apocrine metaplasia, adenosis, and usual-type ductal hyperplasia without atypia. What is the correct breast cancer risk classification?
options: High risk requiring chemoprevention and enhanced surveillance
Slightly increased risk without specific intervention needed
No increased risk equivalent to non-proliferative disease
Moderate risk requiring annual MRI breast screening
Very high risk equivalent to BRCA1 mutation carriers

questions.question: Arteriovenous malformations most commonly present with:
questions.explanation: AVMs are congenital vascular malformations with direct arteriovenous connections without intervening capillary bed, creating high-flow shunts. Hemorrhage (50%), seizures (25%), and headaches (25%) are presentations. Annual bleeding risk is 2-4%. Tangled vessels ("bag of worms") appear on imaging. Treatment options include surgical resection, endovascular embolization, and stereotactic radiosurgery.

In severe hemochromatosis, the liver shows the most severe hemosiderin deposition, followed (in decreasing order) by pancreas, myocardium, pituitary gland, adrenal gland, thyroid and parathyroid glands, joints, and skin. Hemosiderin is deposited in hepatocytes initially, then in Kupffer cells and bile duct epithelium.
questions.question: Which organ shows the most severe hemosiderin deposition in hemochromatosis?

questions.explanation: Juvenile polyps are characterized histologically by dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris. They are common in the rectum and may be sporadic or syndromic. Surface epithelial erosion with underlying granulation tissue and reactive epithelial proliferation may occur.
questions.question: What is the characteristic histologic feature of juvenile polyps?

questions.explanation:
Osteosarcoma predominantly affects metaphyseal regions
around the knee (distal femur 40%, proximal tibia 20%) in adolescents
during growth spurts. The tumor produces osteoid/bone matrix (diagnostic
feature). Radiographs show mixed lytic-sclerotic lesion with periosteal
reaction (Codman triangle, sunburst pattern). Lung is the most common
metastatic site.
questions.question: Osteosarcoma most commonly arises in which location?

questions.explanation:
Gonadal mosaicism affects only germ cells while somatic tissues remain
normal. Parents are phenotypically normal but transmit mutations through
gametes. Multiple affected offspring may occur.
questions.question: What distinguishes gonadal mosaicism from somatic mosaicism?

questions.explanation:
Vascular EDS (Type IV) causes spontaneous arterial rupture particularly
of medium-sized vessels. Bowel perforation and uterine rupture during
pregnancy also occur. Median survival is 50 years.
questions.question: Which Ehlers-Danlos syndrome complication causes mortality?

questions.explanation: Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) shows disease progression (rising PSA, new metastases, or symptom progression) despite castrate testosterone levels (<50 ng/dL or 1.7 nmol/L) from surgical or medical castration. Mechanisms include androgen receptor amplification/mutations, intratumoral androgen synthesis, and bypass pathways. Novel hormonal agents (abiraterone, enzalutamide), chemotherapy, and immunotherapy treat CRPC.
questions.question: Castration-resistant prostate cancer is defined as:

questions.explanation: Intussusception, where a proximal segment of bowel telescopes into a distal segment, classically presents with intermittent colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and 'red currant jelly' stool reflecting mucosal ischaemia, with ultrasound demonstrating a characteristic 'target' or 'doughnut' sign on cross-section. This is the most common cause of bowel obstruction in infants beyond the neonatal period. Air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and often therapeutic in reducing the intussusception.
questions.question: A 9-month-old presents with intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and passage of red, jelly-like stool. Abdominal ultrasound shows a 'target sign'. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
What size adenoma has highest malignancy risk?
questions.explanation: Adenomas >2cm have significantly higher malignancy risk (35-50%) compared to <1cm adenomas (<1%). Risk also increases with villous architecture (villous>tubulovillous>tubular) and high-grade dysplasia. The combination of large size, villous features, and high-grade dysplasia confers highest risk. Adenomas ≥1cm warrant surveillance colonoscopy at shorter intervals due to increased malignant potential.

questions.question: Gastric adenocarcinoma of intestinal type is associated with:
questions.explanation:
Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma develops through
multistep process: chronic H. pylori gastritis ? chronic atrophic
gastritis ? intestinal metaplasia ? dysplasia ? carcinoma. This type is
decreasing in incidence with H. pylori eradication. Diffuse-type gastric
cancer (signet ring cells) is less associated with H. pylori and has
worse prognosis.

The Baveno VI consensus provides criteria for stratifying variceal bleeding risk in cirrhotic patients, helping determine who needs endoscopic screening. Patients with liver stiffness <20kPa and platelet count >150,000/μL have very low risk of large varices and can avoid screening endoscopy. This reduces unnecessary procedures while identifying high-risk patients. It represents evidence-based portal hypertension management.
questions.question: What is the Baveno VI consensus used for?

questions.explanation: Caput medusae refers to dilated periumbilical and abdominal wall veins radiating from the umbilicus, resembling Medusa's snake hair.
