It represents portosystemic shunting through recanalized umbilical and paraumbilical veins (ligamentum teres) in portal hypertension. Blood flow may be toward (portal hypertension) or away from (IVC obstruction) the umbilicus. The pattern is distinctive but occurs in only 15% of cirrhotic patients.
questions.question: What is caput medusae?
What is the recommended Lynch syndrome screening test for CRC?
questions.explanation: Universal tumor screening for Lynch syndrome uses microsatellite instability (MSI) testing or immunohistochemistry (IHC) for mismatch repair (MMR) proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) on all colorectal cancers. Loss of MMR protein expression or MSI-high prompts germline testing. MLH1-deficient tumors need BRAF/promoter methylation testing to distinguish Lynch (germline) from sporadic (somatic). This identifies ~3% Lynch syndrome patients.

questions.question: Which genomic imprinting disorder shows paternal deletion?
questions.explanation:
Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of paternally expressed genes at
15q11-13. Maternal uniparental disomy also causes PWS. Paternal deletion
accounts for 70% of cases.

questions.question: A patient with chronic granulomatous disease has recurrent catalase-positive bacterial infections. Which biochemical defect underlies this condition?
questions.explanation:
Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH
oxidase, preventing superoxide and subsequent H2O2 generation essential
for killing. Catalase-positive organisms (like Staphylococcus aureus)
destroy any H2O2 they produce, leaving no substrate for residual
bactericidal activity. This explains the specific susceptibility pattern
and granuloma formation.

Chicken wire fibrosis refers to perivenular and pericellular (perisinusoidal) fibrosis that is characteristic of fatty liver disease, both alcoholic and non-alcoholic. This pattern of collagen deposition around individual hepatocytes and along sinusoids creates a network resembling chicken wire on microscopy, distinguishing it from other patterns of hepatic fibrosis.
questions.question: What is chicken wire fibrosis?

questions.explanation: Craniopharyngiomas derive from squamous epithelial remnants of Rathke pouch, presenting as suprasellar masses causing hypopituitarism and visual defects. Adamantinomatous type (children) shows calcification and "machine oil" cyst fluid; papillary type (adults) lacks calcification. Histology resembles ameloblastoma. Complete resection is difficult due to adherence to critical structures.
questions.question: Craniopharyngiomas arise from remnants of:

questions.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1 or TSC2 mutations) causes subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, cortical tubers, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas, and facial angiofibromas. SEGAs arise near foramen of Monro, potentially causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Large cells with glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm characterize these WHO grade 1 tumors. mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) shrink tumors.
questions.question: Subependymal giant cell astrocytomas occur in:

questions.explanation: Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign) is a characteristic paraneoplastic phenomenon in pancreatic adenocarcinoma, occurring in 10-20% of patients. Superficial thrombophlebitis affects different veins sequentially, resulting from tumor-produced procoagulant factors creating a hypercoagulable state. It may be the presenting feature of occult pancreatic cancer and often precedes diagnosis by months. Other manifestations include portal/splenic vein thrombosis.
questions.question: What paraneoplastic phenomenon is associated with pancreatic cancer?

questions.explanation: Bacterial tracheitis often develops as a secondary bacterial infection following initial viral croup, with sudden clinical deterioration, high fever, and thick purulent tracheal secretions that can cause life-threatening airway obstruction, frequently requiring intubation for airway management and secretion clearance. Staphylococcus aureus is a common causative organism in this condition. Distinguishing this from simple viral croup is critical given the more aggressive management required.
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with high fever, severe sore throat, and a barking cough that suddenly worsens with high fever and toxic appearance, requiring intubation for thick purulent tracheal secretions. Which condition, often a complication of viral croup, is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure occurring in advanced liver disease without primary kidney abnormality. Severe splanchnic vasodilation and reduced effective arterial blood volume trigger intense renal vasoconstriction (preserving perfusion to vital organs), causing decreased GFR and sodium retention. Kidneys are structurally normal and can function if transplanted. It represents a severe complication with poor prognosis.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of hepatorenal syndrome?

questions.explanation:
Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes GM2 ganglioside accumulation in
neurons. Progressive neurodegeneration causes death by age 4. Cherry-red
macular spot and seizures are characteristic.
questions.question: What enzyme deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease?
What characterizes small cell change in the liver?
questions.explanation: Small cell change (small cell dysplasia) consists of smaller-than-normal hepatocytes with normal-sized, often hyperchromatic, oval or angulated nuclei. These cells have increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and may form small clusters or nodules. Like large cell change, it represents a preneoplastic condition with molecular alterations predisposing to HCC development.

questions.question: What causes immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome?
questions.explanation:
IRIS occurs when recovering immune system mounts vigorous inflammatory
response to subclinical infections. Symptoms paradoxically worsen
despite virologic control. Common triggers include tuberculosis,
cryptococcosis, and CMV.

questions.question: A child presents with recurrent bacterial infections and delayed umbilical cord separation. Neutrophil studies show absence of CD18 expression. Which process is primarily impaired?
questions.explanation:
CD18 is the common β chain of β2 integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1)
essential for firm leukocyte adhesion to ICAM-1 on endothelium. Without
functional integrins, neutrophils cannot arrest rolling or transmigrate
to infection sites despite normal chemotaxis and phagocytic capacity.
This defines leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-1) with
characteristic clinical presentation.

questions.question: What is the third leading cause of cancer death in the United States?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma represents the third leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States, recently surpassing breast and prostate cancers. Despite accounting for only about 3% of new cancer diagnoses, it causes approximately 7% of cancer deaths due to extremely poor prognosis. The 5-year survival rate is less than 10%, reflecting late diagnosis and aggressive biology.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy has recurrent intussusception and hyperpigmented macules around the lips. Polypectomy shows polyps with an arborising smooth muscle core covered by normal epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by STK11 mutations, producing hamartomatous polyps with a characteristic arborising smooth muscle core and mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation, particularly around the lips and oral mucosa. These polyps can cause intussusception due to their size, and patients have an increased risk of various cancers.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman develops painful vesicles on her vulva. Tzanck smear would most likely show:
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus infection produces multinucleated giant squamous cells with intranuclear viral inclusions (Cowdry type A) visible on Tzanck smear. The characteristic "3 Ms" - multinucleation, margination of chromatin, and nuclear molding - help diagnose herpetic infections. HSV-2 typically causes genital lesions while HSV-1 causes orofacial disease.

Burkitt lymphoma shows diffuse sheets of monotonous
intermediate-sized cells with high mitotic rate and apoptosis, creating
a "starry-sky" pattern from scattered tingible body macrophages. These
benign macrophages phagocytose apoptotic debris, appearing as pale stars
against the dark tumor cell background. This pattern reflects the
extremely high proliferation rate.
questions.question: Which morphological pattern is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma on histological examination?

questions.explanation: Classical seminomas are exquisitely radiosensitive; low-dose radiation to para-aortic and pelvic nodes effectively treats early-stage disease. However, chemotherapy (BEP regimen) increasingly preferred to avoid long-term radiation toxicity (secondary malignancies, cardiovascular disease). Non-seminomatous germ cell tumors are radioresistant requiring chemotherapy and surgery.
questions.question: Which testicular tumor is most radiosensitive?

questions.explanation:
Production of osteoid or bone matrix by malignant cells is
the diagnostic hallmark of osteosarcoma. Various subtypes exist based on
predominant matrix (osteoblastic, chondroblastic, fibroblastic). The
tumor shows marked pleomorphism, mitotic activity, and infiltrative
growth. Treatment requires neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by
limb-salvage surgery or amputation.
questions.question: The diagnostic histological feature of osteosarcoma is:

questions.explanation: Once in the intestine, Shigella organisms are taken up by M cells (microfold cells). Shigella then proliferates intracellularly, escapes into the lamina propria, and is phagocytosed by macrophages, in which they induce apoptosis. All Shigella species carry virulence plasmids encoding a type III secretion system.
questions.question: How does Shigella typically invade the intestinal mucosa?
A 3-year-old girl presents with grape-like polypoid vaginal masses. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides) presents as polypoid grape-like masses protruding from the vagina in infants and young children. Histology shows small round blue cells with eosinophilic rhabdomyoblasts beneath an intact epithelium (cambium layer). Treatment involves conservative surgery and chemotherapy with generally favorable prognosis.

questions.question: What distinguishes fibrolamellar HCC from conventional HCC?
questions.explanation: Fibrolamellar HCC is an uncommon variant that usually arises in non-cirrhotic livers of adolescents or young adults. Tumor cells grow in sheets or small trabeculae separated by hyalinized collagen bundles with a characteristic lamellar pattern. It generally has a better prognosis than conventional HCC.
options: Arises in non-cirrhotic livers of young adults
Arises in cirrhotic livers of elderly

questions.explanation: Portopulmonary hypertension is pulmonary arterial hypertension (mean PAP >25mmHg) associated with portal hypertension, involving pulmonary vasoconstriction and remodeling. Hepatopulmonary syndrome involves pulmonary vasodilation with hypoxemia. Both are serious complications of cirrhosis but have opposite pathophysiology. Portopulmonary hypertension may contraindicate liver transplantation if severe, while hepatopulmonary syndrome may improve post-transplant.
questions.question: What distinguishes portopulmonary hypertension from hepatopulmonary syndrome?
What distinguishes primary HIV infection from AIDS?
questions.explanation:
Primary HIV infection shows high viral load but CD4 count remains above
500 cells/?. Acute retroviral syndrome occurs 2-4 weeks post-infection.
AIDS develops when CD4 falls below 200 or opportunistic infections
occur.

questions.question: Necrotizing enterocolitis in premature infants most commonly affects which intestinal region?
questions.explanation:
NEC predominantly affects the terminal ileum, cecum, and
right colon, possibly related to their watershed blood supply and
bacterial colonization patterns. Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in bowel
wall) is characteristic. Severe cases progress to perforation,
peritonitis, and sepsis requiring surgical resection.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by which karyotype?
questions.explanation:
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) affects 1:500-1:1000 males,
often diagnosed during evaluation for infertility. Additional X
chromosome(s) inactivate like in normal females, but inactivation is
incomplete affecting genes escaping X-inactivation. Variants include
48,XXXY and 48,XXYY with more severe phenotypes.

questions.question: Which maple syrup urine disease variant shows intermittent symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Intermittent MSUD shows symptoms only during illness or increased
protein intake. Higher residual enzyme activity permits normal periods.
Classic form causes continuous severe symptoms.

questions.question: Hairy cell leukemia is characterized by cells expressing which combination of markers?
questions.explanation:
Hairy cell leukemia cells characteristically express
CD11c, CD25, and CD103, a relatively unique immunophenotype among B cell
disorders. The "hairy" cells have distinctive thread-like cytoplasmic
projections visible on peripheral blood smears. The disease responds
dramatically to purine analogs like cladribine.

Lymphocyte-predominant HL shows CD20+ popcorn (L&H) cells
unlike classical HL (CD15+/CD30+ RS cells). This represents a distinct
entity with B-cell origin, excellent prognosis, but higher relapse rate.
It may transform to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
questions.question: Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma differs from classical types by which feature?

options: Ductal prostatic adenocarcinoma with papillary growth
questions.explanation: Foamy gland carcinoma of the prostate shows large glands with xanthomatous (foamy) cytoplasm filled with vesicular lipid vacuoles and dense eosinophilic secretions, closely resembling benign glands but lacking a basal cell layer (confirmed by absent HMCK/34betaE12 and p63). It is a morphological variant of prostatic adenocarcinoma and is often underdiagnosed. Despite its bland cytology (nucleoli may be inconspicuous), it behaves as a conventional prostatic carcinoma. Recognising absence of basal cells and AMACR positivity are key diagnostic features.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man has a prostatic biopsy showing large glands with abundant pale cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and intraluminal crystalloids, without a basal cell layer. HMCK (34betaE12) and p63 are negative. This carcinoma pattern is termed:
Endometriosis is definitively diagnosed by:
questions.explanation: Definitive diagnosis requires histologic demonstration of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus. Laparoscopic visualization with biopsy provides tissue for confirmation. Hemosiderin-laden macrophages indicate prior hemorrhage. Treatment options include hormonal suppression (OCPs, GnRH agonists), surgical ablation/excision, or hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

questions.question: During induction phlebotomy in hereditary hemochromatosis, the ferritin target indicating adequate iron depletion is:
questions.explanation: Iron depletion targets serum ferritin below 50 ng/mL and transferrin saturation below 50% during induction weekly phlebotomy. Each session removes approximately 200-250 mg of iron. Maintenance phlebotomy every 2-4 months prevents re-accumulation. Achieving ferritin near zero causes iatrogenic iron deficiency anemia; the below 50 ng/mL target balances effective iron removal against this complication. Liver biopsy to confirm iron depletion is rarely needed when ferritin targets are clinically achieved through the phlebotomy program.
options: Normal range below 300 ng/mL for ongoing monitoring
Below 1000 ng/mL to prevent phlebotomy-related anemia
Below 50 ng/mL with transferrin saturation below 50%
Zero ng/mL confirming absolute complete iron removal
Below 200 ng/mL appropriate for the maintenance phase

questions.explanation:
Increased nuchal translucency on first-trimester ultrasound suggests
Down syndrome. Combined with maternal serum screening (PAPP-A, hCG),
risk assessment guides amniocentesis decisions. Cell-free fetal DNA
testing provides non-invasive screening.
questions.question: Which Down syndrome feature helps with prenatal diagnosis?

questions.explanation: The eccentric hyperdense scolex (the larval tapeworm head) visualized within the cystic lesion on CT or MRI is pathognomonic for neurocysticercosis and most specifically distinguishes it from brain abscess. Brain abscesses show thick irregular ring enhancement with debris but lack a scolex. Pyogenic abscesses and tuberculomas cannot be reliably distinguished by enhancement pattern or edema alone. Serology (EITB assay) and history of T. solium exposure support the diagnosis. Albendazole combined with corticosteroids is the standard antiparasitic treatment for viable parenchymal cysts.
options: Ring enhancement pattern on contrast CT scanning
Perilesional edema exceeding the lesion size itself
Eccentric scolex dot within the cyst cavity identifying the larva
Single lesion rather than multiple simultaneous ring lesions
Absence of fever or systemic inflammatory response signs
questions.question: CT brain shows a ring-enhancing lesion with an eccentric hyperdense dot in a seizure patient from a T. solium endemic region. The feature most specifically excluding brain abscess is:

A 3-year-old presents with a palpable abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. Imaging shows a renal mass, and histology reveals blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements. Which tumour is most consistent with this description?
questions.explanation: Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) is the most common paediatric renal malignancy and classically shows a triphasic histological pattern of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements recapitulating normal nephrogenesis. Its tendency to remain confined to one side without crossing the midline helps distinguish it clinically from neuroblastoma, which often crosses the midline. WT1 gene mutations are implicated in a subset of cases.

questions.question: What is a Virchow node?
questions.explanation: Virchow's node represents metastasis to the supraclavicular sentinel lymph node from gastric adenocarcinoma. Sister Mary Joseph nodule refers to metastasis to the periumbilical region. Depth of invasion, nodal metastasis, and distant metastasis at diagnosis are the primary determinants of prognosis.

Appendiceal carcinoid (well-differentiated neuroendocrine) tumours are the most common appendiceal neoplasm, typically found incidentally at the tip, showing uniform cells with characteristic salt-and-pepper chromatin and positivity for neuroendocrine markers chromogranin and synaptophysin. Tumours under 2 cm without other risk features are usually adequately treated by appendicectomy alone.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man has an incidental 1.5 cm tumour at the appendiceal tip on histology, composed of uniform cells with 'salt and pepper' chromatin, positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Krukenberg tumors are metastatic signet-ring cell adenocarcinomas to ovaries, most commonly from gastric (70%) or less commonly from colorectal, appendiceal, or breast primaries. Bilateral ovarian involvement with preservation of ovarian shape occurs. Mucin-filled signet-ring cells within cellular stroma are characteristic. Presentation may precede primary tumor identification.
questions.question: Krukenberg tumor most commonly metastasizes from:
A 25-year-old man has hundreds of colonic polyps and pigmented ocular fundus lesions (CHRPE). What gene mutation underlies this condition?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by APC gene mutations and is associated with congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), a useful clinical marker that can predate colonic polyposis. STK11 mutations instead cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, characterised by hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation rather than CHRPE.

questions.question: Which cellular component is specifically responsible for wound contraction during healing by secondary intention?
questions.explanation:
Myofibroblasts are specialized cells containing
contractile actin filaments (similar to smooth muscle) that actively
pull wound edges together. These cells differentiate from fibroblasts
under influence of TGF-β and are crucial for reducing large defect
sizes. Excessive myofibroblast activity can lead to pathological
contractures in some anatomical locations.

Invasive lobular carcinoma characteristically infiltrates as single files (Indian file pattern) and targetoid rings around ducts (periductal spread), attributed to loss of E-cadherin cell adhesion molecule. It most commonly belongs to the Luminal A molecular subtype (ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative, low Ki-67), explaining its relatively favourable prognosis. Lobular carcinoma tends to be bilateral and multicentric. It lacks discrete masses on imaging and may be underestimated by mammography, making MRI particularly useful for accurate staging.
options: Luminal A with low-grade hormone receptor expression
Luminal B with high Ki-67 proliferation index
Luminal B with absent hormone receptor expression
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman undergoes mastectomy for invasive breast carcinoma. Histology shows cells infiltrating singly in an Indian file pattern with targetoid periductal spread. What molecular subtype is most commonly associated with this pattern?

options: Pulmonary hypertension from congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula
Complete heart block from 45,X associated cardiac conduction disease
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from sex chromosome dosage effects
Atrial fibrillation from abnormal cardiac development at 45,X
Bicuspid aortic valve with risk of progressive aortic root dilation
questions.question: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea, short stature, and webbing of the neck. Karyotype reveals 45,X. The most likely cardiovascular complication requiring surveillance is:
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with bicuspid aortic valve in approximately 16% and coarctation of the aorta in 11% of patients. Progressive aortic root dilation occurs in Turner syndrome regardless of valve morphology due to intrinsic aortopathy from haploinsufficiency of X-linked vascular genes. Annual cardiovascular surveillance with echocardiography or cardiac MRI and management of hypertension is essential. Aortic dissection risk is approximately 25 times the general population risk, particularly during pregnancy, emphasizing the importance of lifelong aortic monitoring.

Untreated PKU causes severe mental retardation from phenylalanine
neurotoxicity. Dietary restriction started in first weeks of life
prevents damage. Compliance throughout childhood is essential.
questions.question: Which PKU complication occurs without dietary treatment?

questions.explanation:
Comprehensive newborn screening includes PKU, galactosemia, MSUD,
homocystinuria, and many others. Specific disorders vary by
jurisdiction. Early treatment prevents irreversible damage.
questions.question: What metabolic disorder is universally screened in newborns?
What is the most common cause of death in HCC patients?
questions.explanation: Common causes of death in HCC include liver failure with hepatic coma, cachexia, gastrointestinal or esophageal variceal bleeding, and rupture of the tumor with fatal hemorrhage. The specific cause depends on tumor burden, underlying liver function, and presence of cirrhosis. Many patients have multifactorial terminal events involving both tumor and liver failure.

Exon skipping using antisense oligonucleotides converts out-of-frame to
in-frame mutations. This produces partially functional dystrophin
similar to Becker phenotype. Eteplirsen targets exon 51 deletions.
questions.question: What therapy shows promise for Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
What percentage of the normal iron pool is stored in the liver?
questions.explanation: The normal iron pool is 2-6 grams, with approximately 0.5 g (about 8-25%) stored in the liver, and 98% of that hepatic iron is in hepatocytes. In hemochromatosis, total body iron may exceed 50 grams. Excessive iron cannot be eliminated and is directly toxic through lipid peroxidation and DNA interactions.

Stromal invasion with basement membrane breach distinguishes invasive from in situ carcinoma. Irregular nests, cords, or single cells infiltrating stroma with desmoplastic response are seen. Lymphovascular invasion may be present. p16 immunostain is diffusely positive in high-grade lesions. Invasion determines staging and treatment approach.
questions.question: Which finding suggests invasive rather than in situ cervical carcinoma?
Bartholin gland cysts result from:
questions.explanation: Bartholin gland cysts develop from obstruction of the gland's excretory duct, causing accumulation of mucoid secretions. These may become infected, forming abscesses requiring incision and drainage. The glands are located at posterolateral aspects of the vaginal introitus and normally produce mucus for lubrication. Rarely, adenocarcinoma may arise.

questions.question: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Papillary carcinomas show characteristic nuclear features including clearing (Orphan Annie eyes), grooves, pseudoinclusions, and psammoma bodies. True papillae with fibrovascular cores may be present. These tumors spread via lymphatics to regional nodes but have excellent prognosis. RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations are common. Most common thyroid malignancy (75-85%).

questions.question: A 35-year-old man has chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption after extensive ileal resection for Crohn's disease. What specific deficiency is most directly attributable to the loss of terminal ileum?
questions.explanation: The terminal ileum is the exclusive site of vitamin B12 absorption, mediated by intrinsic factor-B12 complex binding to specific ileal receptors. Resection or disease of the terminal ileum, as occurs in Crohn's disease, therefore causes vitamin B12 deficiency, while other nutrients are absorbed more proximally and are less specifically affected by terminal ileal loss.

Leiomyomas show various cytogenetic abnormalities including deletions of 7q, trisomy 12, rearrangements of 6p21 (HMGA2 gene), and deletions of 1p. MED12 mutations occur in 70% of fibroids. These benign smooth muscle tumors are hormone-responsive (estrogen and progesterone), explaining growth during reproductive years and regression after menopause.
questions.question: Leiomyomas are associated with which chromosomal abnormality?

questions.explanation: Renal oncocytomas are benign tumors composed of oncocytes (cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm packed with mitochondria). Mahogany brown color and central stellate scar are characteristic. Occur in older adults. Cannot reliably distinguish from chromophobe RCC preoperatively. Surgical excision is curative. Familial oncocytosis (Birt-Hogg-Dub syndrome) causes multiple bilateral oncocytomas.
questions.question: Oncocytoma is characterized by:

A 60-year-old woman with longstanding gallstones develops a gallbladder mass. Biopsy shows malignant glands invading the muscularis with dystrophic calcification nearby. What predisposing factor is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Porcelain gallbladder, characterised by dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall from chronic cholelithiasis and inflammation, is a well-recognised risk factor for gallbladder adenocarcinoma. The chronic irritation from longstanding stones promotes a metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence in the gallbladder epithelium over time.

Streptococcus pneumoniae causes most adult bacterial meningitis, followed by Neisseria meningitidis. Haemophilus influenzae incidence decreased dramatically with vaccination. Classic triad includes fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, decreased glucose, and elevated protein. Empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone plus vancomycin) should begin immediately; dexamethasone reduces complications.
questions.question: Bacterial meningitis in adults is most commonly caused by:
What causes swimmer's itch in schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation:
Swimmer's itch results from cercarial penetration of skin with death of

larvae. This early reaction causes pruritic rash with edema and erythema
occurring within 24 hours. The reaction resolves spontaneously within 10
days.

Tumor cells arrive via afferent lymphatics and first lodge
in the subcapsular (marginal) sinus beneath the lymph node capsule.
Progressive growth replaces the sinus then invades cortex and medulla,
eventually effacing normal architecture. This predictable pattern allows
sentinel node biopsy to stage early metastasis.
questions.question: Metastatic carcinoma initially enters lymph nodes through which anatomical structure?

questions.explanation: Hepatoblastoma is the most common liver tumor of early childhood and rarely occurs over the age of 3 years. It is associated with WNT signaling pathway activation, APC gene mutations, familial adenomatous polyposis, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. The tumor may be epithelial type or mixed epithelial and mesenchymal type.
questions.question: What is the most common primary liver tumor in early childhood?
What is the gender predilection for esophageal adenocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: Esophageal adenocarcinoma demonstrates a strong male predominance, being seven times more common in men than women. The tumor arises from Barrett esophagus and longstanding GERD, is more common in Caucasians, and typically involves the distal third of the esophagus.

Macrophage-tropic HIV strains use CCR5 coreceptor for cell entry. T-cell
tropic strains use CXCR4. CCR5-?32 deletion confers resistance to HIV
infection. Maraviroc blocks CCR5 preventing viral entry.
questions.question: Which HIV coreceptor is used by macrophage-tropic strains?
Which adult-onset variant of Tay-Sachs presents differently?
questions.explanation:
Adult Tay-Sachs variant causes psychiatric symptoms, ataxia, and motor
neuron disease. Residual hexosaminidase activity permits survival to
adulthood. Progressive but slower course than infantile form.

ART aims to suppress viral replication to undetectable levels preserving
immune function. Sustained suppression prevents disease progression and
transmission. Current therapy cannot eradicate latent viral reservoirs.
questions.question: What is the goal of antiretroviral therapy?

questions.explanation: Sentinel lymph node biopsy identifies first draining axillary node(s) using radiotracer and/or blue dye, providing accurate staging while avoiding complete axillary dissection morbidity. Negative sentinel node(s) predicts negative axillary basin in 95-97%. Macrometastases or multiple positive sentinel nodes may warrant completion dissection. Z0011 and AMAROS trials reduced axillary surgery indications.
questions.question: Sentinel lymph node biopsy in breast cancer:

questions.explanation:
Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) has poorest prognosis with 90% mortality
in first year. Severe malformations affect multiple organ systems.
Median survival is 3-15 days.
questions.question: Which aneuploidysexually affects newborn viability most?

options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I producing no orotic acid
N-acetylglutamate synthase proximal causing no orotic acid
Ornithine transcarbamylase whose block diverts to orotic acid
Arginase causing elevated arginine with no orotic acid rise
questions.question: A neonate with severe hyperammonemia of 800 umol/L, respiratory alkalosis, and elevated urine orotic acid has a urea cycle defect. The specific enzyme most likely deficient is:
questions.explanation: Elevated orotic acid distinguishes OTC deficiency from proximal urea cycle defects. When OTC is deficient, carbamoyl phosphate accumulates and enters the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, producing orotic acid as a diagnostic byproduct. CPS1 and NAGS deficiencies are proximal and show no orotic acid elevation. OTC deficiency is X-linked; affected males suffer severe neonatal crises while female heterozygotes show variable severity depending on X-inactivation patterns favoring the mutant allele in hepatocytes.

questions.question: Which genetic pathway is most commonly activated in hepatoblastoma?
questions.explanation: Hepatoblastoma is strongly associated with WNT signaling pathway activation. Genetic associations include APC gene mutations, familial adenomatous polyposis, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and chromosomal abnormalities. FOXG1, a regulator of the TGF-β pathway, is also highly expressed in these tumors.

Pathologic stage (TNM) is the most important prognostic factor, incorporating tumor size, local invasion (renal vein, perirenal fat, adrenal, Gerota fascia), lymph nodes, and distant metastases. Five-year survival: stage I 95%, stage II 88%, stage III 59%, stage IV 20%. Grade, subtype, sarcomatoid features, tumor necrosis, and vascular invasion provide additional prognostic information.
questions.question: The most important prognostic factor in renal cell carcinoma is:
Mycosis fungoides is characterized by which clinical presentation?
options: Progressive cutaneous patches, plaques, and tumors
questions.explanation:
Mycosis fungoides progresses through patch, plaque, and
tumor stages over years to decades. Early lesions show epidermotropism
of atypical T cells forming Pautrier microabscesses. Despite the name,
it's a T-cell lymphoma, not a fungal infection. Sézary syndrome
represents leukemic phase with erythroderma.

questions.question: Hyperviscosity syndrome in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia results from which property of IgM?
questions.explanation:
IgM exists as pentamers with very high molecular weight
(900 kDa) compared to IgG (150 kDa), causing blood hyperviscosity at
lower concentrations. Symptoms include visual disturbances (retinal vein
engorgement), bleeding, headaches, and altered consciousness. Emergency
plasmapheresis rapidly removes IgM and relieves symptoms.

questions.question: Which cells characteristically infiltrate the mucosa in reflux esophagitis?
questions.explanation: In reflux esophagitis, histology shows eosinophils and neutrophils infiltrating the mucosa along with basal zone hyperplasia. Endoscopy reveals hyperemia of the mucosa. Complications include ulceration, hematemesis, melena, stricture formation, and Barrett esophagus.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis develops fever and abdominal pain. Ascitic fluid analysis shows a neutrophil count above 250 cells/microlitre with a single bacterial organism on culture. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in cirrhotic patients with ascites due to bacterial translocation across the gut wall, typically producing monomicrobial infection with an ascitic neutrophil count exceeding 250 cells/microlitre. Secondary peritonitis, by contrast, usually involves multiple organisms from a perforated viscus and requires surgical source control.

Salmonella species cause osteomyelitis in sickle cell patients more frequently than general population, though Staphylococcus aureus remains most common overall. Bone infarctions from vaso-occlusive crises predispose to infection. Multiple bones may be involved. Distinguishing infarction from infection is challenging. Prolonged antibiotic therapy is required.
questions.question: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease is most commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: Spina bifida results from failure of caudal neural tube closure, producing defects in posterior vertebral arches and neural tissue. Spina bifida occulta (vertebral defect only), meningocele (meninges protrude), and myelomeningocele (neural tissue protrudes) represent severity spectrum. Folic acid supplementation during pregnancy reduces incidence. Associated with Arnold-Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus.
questions.question: Spina bifida results from:

questions.explanation:
Lobar pneumonia shows homogeneous consolidation of an
entire lobe or large portion thereof, typically caused by Streptococcus
pneumoniae. The inflammatory exudate spreads through alveolar pores of
Kohn producing confluent involvement. This contrasts with
bronchopneumonia's patchy pattern.
questions.question: Lobar pneumonia is characterized by which pattern of lung involvement?
Which intestinal segment is always involved in ulcerative colitis?
questions.explanation: Ulcerative colitis always involves the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous pattern. Disease may be limited (proctitis, proctosigmoiditis) or extensive (pancolitis). The small intestine is normal except for possible backwash ileitis in severe pancolitis. Rectal involvement distinguishes it from Crohn disease.

Invasive ductal carcinoma NST (no special type, previously NOS) accounts for 70-80% of invasive breast cancers. These show variable glandular/tubular formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic activity. Nottingham grading system (SBR score) evaluates tubule formation, nuclear grade, and mitotic count. Stromal desmoplasia is characteristic. Axillary node metastases are common.
questions.question: The most common histologic type of invasive breast cancer is:

questions.explanation: Neuroblastomas arise from neural crest-derived sympathetic ganglia or adrenal medulla, predominantly in children <5 years. Abdominal masses crossing midline, bone pain, and periorbital ecchymosis occur. N-myc amplification predicts aggressive behavior. Elevated urinary catecholamines (VMA, HVA) aid diagnosis. Prognosis varies dramatically with age and stage; infants with 4S disease may regress spontaneously.
questions.question: Neuroblastoma most commonly arises in:
Which skin layer contains Merkel cells?
questions.explanation: Merkel cells are specialized mechanoreceptors located in the basal layer of the epidermis, particularly concentrated in touch-sensitive areas. These neuroendocrine cells form synaptic connections with sensory nerve fibers and contain dense-core neurosecretory granules. Merkel cell carcinoma is an aggressive neuroendocrine malignancy arising from these cells.

questions.question: Spermatocytic seminoma differs from classic seminoma by:
questions.explanation: Spermatocytic seminomas occur in older men (mean age 55), show indolent behavior, rarely metastasize, and don't arise from IGCN. Histology shows cells of varying sizes including filamentous chromatin. These tumors lack lymphocytic infiltrate and express CD117 weakly. Local excision is curative; adjuvant therapy is unnecessary.

Endometriosis requires histological confirmation showing both endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity. Haemosiderin-laden macrophages support the diagnosis in the absence of glands and stroma (burnt-out lesions). Ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) contain old haemorrhagic fluid and are lined by endometrioid epithelium. The pathogenesis involves retrograde menstruation, coelomic metaplasia, and lymphovascular dissemination. Endometriosis is associated with infertility, dyspareunia, and increased risk of ovarian endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas.
options: Adhesion tissue between pelvic organs alone
Decidualised stromal cells with spiral arterioles
Endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus
Endometrial-type columnar cells without associated stroma
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with dysmenorrhoea and infertility undergoes laparoscopy showing powder-burn lesions on the ovaries and pouch of Douglas. What is required for definitive histological diagnosis?

questions.explanation:
Thick bile obstructs intrahepatic bile ducts causing focal biliary
cirrhosis. Approximately 5% of CF patients develop clinically
significant liver disease. Portal hypertension may complicate cirrhosis.
questions.question: What liver complication develops in cystic fibrosis?

questions.explanation:
Acute ATLL characteristically presents with hypercalcemia
(from osteoclast-activating factors), lytic bone lesions,
lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and skin lesions. Peripheral blood
shows "flower cells" with polylobulated nuclei. Prognosis is poor
despite aggressive chemotherapy; allogeneic transplant offers best
survival chance.
questions.question: Which finding is characteristic of acute ATLL presentation?

questions.explanation: Verrucous carcinoma is well-differentiated exophytic squamous cell carcinoma variant showing pushing borders, minimal cytologic atypia, and rare metastases. Locally destructive requiring wide excision. HPV 6/11 association (low-risk types). Differential includes condyloma acuminatum and giant condyloma. Radiation contraindicated due to anaplastic transformation risk. Excellent prognosis with complete excision.
questions.question: Verrucous carcinoma of penis is characterized by:

A 4-year-old presents with high spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, and generalised lymphadenopathy, along with markedly elevated ferritin levels. Which subtype of juvenile idiopathic arthritis is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis is characterised by quotidian (daily spiking) fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, lymphadenopathy, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers including ferritin, reflecting a prominent systemic inflammatory component distinct from the other subtypes which are predominantly articular. This systemic inflammation also carries risk of macrophage activation syndrome, a life-threatening complication requiring prompt recognition. Treatment often targets specific inflammatory cytokine pathways given the systemic nature of this subtype.

Yolk sac tumors (endodermal sinus tumors) are highly malignant germ cell neoplasms producing AFP. Characteristic Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures) are pathognomonic. These tumors occur in children and young adults, presenting with rapidly enlarging pelvic mass. Combination chemotherapy with BEP regimen achieves excellent cure rates.
questions.question: Yolk sac tumors produce which tumor marker?
What percentage of pancreatic cancers arise from the head of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: Most pancreatic carcinomas arise from the head of the pancreas. This location often leads to early obstruction of the common bile duct, producing jaundice. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is an infiltrating ductal carcinoma that represents the third leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States.

options: Weakness at sites of vasa recta penetration
questions.explanation: Colonic diverticula are pseudodiverticula that herniate through natural weak points in the muscularis where the vasa recta penetrate the bowel wall to supply the mucosa. Increased intraluminal pressure, often from a low-fibre diet, promotes herniation at these points, particularly in the sigmoid colon.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man has sigmoid diverticulitis. Resection specimen shows outpouchings of mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis at sites where blood vessels penetrate the bowel wall. What predisposes to this pattern?
Ghon complex in tuberculosis consists of which components?
questions.explanation:
Ghon complex comprises the primary lung parenchymal focus
(Ghon focus, usually subpleural) plus involved draining lymph nodes,
representing primary tuberculosis. This typically heals with
calcification creating a Ranke complex. Reactivation usually occurs in
lung apices, not at the primary site.

Chronic pancreatitis carries a 40% lifetime risk of developing pancreatic cancer. The chronic inflammation, fibrosis, oxidative stress, and repeated cellular injury promote malignant transformation. This risk is significantly elevated compared to the general population. Hereditary pancreatitis has even higher cancer risk (40% by age 70). Surveillance is challenging due to background parenchymal changes.
questions.question: What percentage of chronic pancreatitis patients develop pancreatic cancer?
Coccidioides immitis in tissue forms which characteristic structure?
questions.explanation:
Coccidioides forms large spherules (20-80μm) containing
numerous endospores in tissue, representing the parasitic phase.
Spherule rupture releases endospores that develop into new spherules.
The mycelial (hyphal) phase occurs in soil/culture. Endemic areas
include southwestern US and parts of Mexico/South America.

options: Any gastric cancer with elevated AFP
questions.question: What defines AFP-producing gastric cancer?
questions.explanation: AFP-producing gastric carcinoma is a rare variant (1-15% of gastric cancers) with serum AFP >100ng/mL and often hepatoid morphology (resembling hepatocytes or HCC). These tumors show worse prognosis with frequent liver metastases. AFP may be useful for monitoring. Differential diagnosis includes metastatic HCC, germ cell tumors, and primary gastric cancer with hepatoid differentiation.

questions.question: Chondrosarcoma most commonly arises in:
questions.explanation: Chondrosarcomas are malignant cartilage-producing tumors occurring in middle-aged to older adults (40-60 years), affecting pelvis, proximal femur, and shoulder girdle. Histologic grading (1-3) predicts behavior. Grade 1 lesions are well-differentiated with low metastatic potential; grade 3 tumors are aggressive. Surgical resection is treatment; chemotherapy and radiation have limited efficacy.

questions.question: What histologic feature is characteristic of autoimmune hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Portal plasma cell infiltration is highly characteristic of autoimmune hepatitis. Other features include interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis), emperipolesis, hepatocyte rosette formation, variable fibrosis, and lobular necroinflammatory activity. The presence of numerous plasma cells in the portal inflammatory infiltrate helps distinguish it from viral hepatitis.

questions.question: What dietary modification treats maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation:
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes leucine,
isoleucine, and valine accumulation. Dietary restriction of these amino
acids prevents neurologic damage. The name derives from sweet-smelling
urine.

CLL/SLL shows a characteristic immunophenotype:
CD5+/CD20+/CD23+ with dim surface immunoglobulin. The aberrant
coexpression of T-cell marker CD5 on B cells is diagnostically useful.
CD23 helps distinguish CLL from mantle cell lymphoma (which is
CD5+/CD23-).
questions.question: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma cells characteristically express which markers?
What is the primary neurotoxin in hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Ammonia and its metabolites are the primary neurotoxins in hepatic encephalopathy, though pathogenesis is multifactorial. Ammonia derives from gut bacterial protein breakdown and inadequate hepatic urea cycle detoxification. Other contributing factors include false neurotransmitters (octopamine), neuroinhibitors (GABA, endogenous benzodiazepines), manganese deposition, and aromatic amino acid imbalances. Blood ammonia levels correlate imperfectly with encephalopathy severity.

Only IgG antibodies can cross the placenta via FcRn
receptors, allowing maternal anti-Rh antibodies to reach and destroy
fetal red cells. IgM antibodies (like anti-ABO) cannot traverse the
placenta despite causing transfusion reactions. This selective placental
transfer explains why Rh incompatibility requires previous sensitization
for clinically significant disease.
questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is most commonly involved in type II hypersensitivity reactions causing hemolytic disease of the newborn?

questions.explanation:
Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic
lymphoma secreting monoclonal IgM, causing hyperviscosity syndrome
(visual disturbances, bleeding, neurological symptoms). The high
molecular weight of IgM pentamers increases serum viscosity at lower
concentrations than other immunoglobulins. Plasmapheresis provides rapid
symptomatic relief.
questions.question: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is characterized by which immunoglobulin type?
Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from:
questions.explanation: Medullary carcinomas arise from calcitonin-producing C cells, appearing as solid tumors with amyloid stroma. Familial cases occur in MEN 2A and 2B syndromes with RET proto-oncogene mutations requiring prophylactic thyroidectomy. Serum calcitonin serves as tumor marker. CEA is also elevated. Prognosis worse than differentiated thyroid cancers.

questions.question: What causes the distinctive cry in Cri-du-chat syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Laryngeal and neurologic abnormalities cause the characteristic cry.
Small larynx with reduced muscle tone affects vocalization. Severity
correlates with deletion size.

questions.question: The antiretroviral mechanism that prevents HIV from integrating proviral DNA into the host chromosome is:
options: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors blocking viral DNA synthesis
Protease inhibitors preventing Gag-Pol polyprotein cleavage
CCR5 antagonists blocking coreceptor binding to viral gp120
Fusion inhibitors preventing HIV envelope-host membrane merging
Integrase strand transfer inhibitors blocking chromosomal insertion
questions.explanation: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs: raltegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir) block the strand transfer step of HIV integration, preventing proviral DNA insertion into the host chromosome. This is mechanistically distinct from reverse transcription inhibition (NRTIs/NNRTIs) and polyprotein processing inhibition (PIs). INSTIs have become preferred first-line components due to high potency, favorable tolerability, and high genetic barrier to resistance, particularly for dolutegravir and bictegravir in current WHO and national treatment guidelines.

questions.question: Which variant requires parental testing for interpretation?
questions.explanation:
VUS requires parental testing to determine if de novo or inherited. De
novo VUS more likely pathogenic. Inherited from normal parent suggests
benign. Classification may change with additional data.

questions.question: Which cystic fibrosis complication results from pancreatic insufficiency?
questions.explanation:
Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency causes malabsorption of fats and
fat-soluble vitamins. Thick secretions obstruct pancreatic ducts leading
to fibrosis. Steatorrhea and failure to thrive result.

questions.question: Testicular microlithiasis is associated with:
questions.explanation: Testicular microlithiasis (calcifications in seminiferous tubules) detected on ultrasound associates with increased testicular cancer risk, particularly with other risk factors (cryptorchidism, prior cancer, testicular atrophy, infertility). Isolated microlithiasis without risk factors may not require intensive surveillance. Annual self-examination recommended. Pathogenesis involves degenerating cells forming calcifications.

The incubation period for hepatitis B virus ranges from 2 to 26 weeks. HBV is a DNA virus with 8 genotypes distributed around the world. The mature virus is called the Dane particle, a 42nm spherical double-layered particle containing HBcAg, HBeAg, HBsAg, HBx, and Pol (polymerase).
questions.question: What is the incubation period for hepatitis B virus?
Active surveillance for prostate cancer is appropriate for:
questions.explanation: Active surveillance monitors low-risk localized prostate cancer with serial PSA, DRE, and repeat biopsies, deferring treatment until progression. Appropriate for very low-risk and low-risk disease (Gleason =6, PSA <10, <3 positive cores, <50% involvement per core, clinical stage T1c-T2a). Avoids treatment morbidity (incontinence, erectile dysfunction) while maintaining curability.

questions.question: A 6-year-old presents with multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and small cutaneous nodules along peripheral nerves. Which gene mutation is most associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 results from mutations in the NF1 gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor protein, causing the combination of café-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, and neurofibromas along peripheral nerves. This contrasts with neurofibromatosis type 2, which is characterised predominantly by bilateral vestibular schwannomas with fewer cutaneous findings. Regular monitoring for associated complications, including optic gliomas and skeletal abnormalities, is important in affected children.

Oncocytoma is characterised by large cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm from mitochondrial accumulation. It is distinguished from chromophobe RCC (eosinophilic variant) by: negative Hale colloidal iron stain (diffusely positive in chromophobe RCC), a characteristic spoke-wheel vascular pattern on gross examination, no perinuclear halos, and absence of multiple chromosomal monosomies. CK7 is diffusely positive in chromophobe RCC but negative or focally positive in oncocytoma. Oncocytoma is benign with excellent prognosis after excision.
options: Negative Hale colloidal iron stain and spoke-wheel vasculature
Presence of perinuclear halos and plant-cell-like borders
Multiple chromosomal monosomies on cytogenetic analysis
CK7 strong diffuse positivity on immunohistochemistry
Raisinoid irregular nuclear contours on high power
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman undergoes nephrectomy. Histology shows a renal tumour composed of large cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm due to mitochondrial accumulation. Hale colloidal iron stain is negative. What distinguishes this from chromophobe renal cell carcinoma?

questions.explanation:
Mesangioproliferative or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis occurs
in hepatosplenic schistosomiasis. Immune complex deposition contributes
to glomerular injury. Proteinuria and hematuria may develop with
progressive renal dysfunction.
questions.question: Which glomerular lesion is associated with hepatosplenic schistosomiasis?
Adenomatoid tumor arises from:
questions.explanation: Adenomatoid tumors are benign mesothelial neoplasms of epididymis or tunica vaginalis, presenting as small firm nodules in young adults. Histology shows tubular/glandular structures lined by flattened mesothelial cells. May mimic adenocarcinoma. Immunostains (calretinin, WT1 positive) confirm mesothelial origin. Simple excision is curative; no recurrence or malignant potential.

questions.question: Fibrous dysplasia is characterized by which pathological feature?
questions.explanation:
Fibrous dysplasia shows replacement of normal bone with
fibro-osseous tissue containing irregular woven bone trabeculae
("Chinese characters" pattern) without normal maturation. Caused by
GNAS mutations (activating Gsa). Monostotic form affects single bone;
polyostotic form (including McCune-Albright syndrome with endocrine
abnormalities and café-au-lait spots) affects multiple bones.

questions.question: Phyllodes tumor differs from fibroadenoma by exhibiting:
questions.explanation: Phyllodes tumors show greater stromal cellularity, increased mitotic activity, stromal overgrowth, and infiltrative borders compared to fibroadenomas. The leaf-like architecture results from stromal expansion into cystic spaces. Benign phyllodes tumors have low recurrence risk while malignant variants may metastasize hematogenously, typically to lungs.

questions.question: What is the characteristic chromosomal region involved in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome involves the 11p15.5 region where multiple
imprinted genes reside. Abnormal imprinting patterns affect gene
expression from maternal versus paternal chromosomes. The syndrome
features organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, and predisposition
to embryonal tumors.

Struma ovarii contains functional thyroid tissue that rarely (5%) causes clinical hyperthyroidism. Radioiodine uptake demonstrates functional thyroid tissue. Malignant transformation (papillary thyroid carcinoma) occurs in 5% of cases. Treatment involves surgical excision; radioablation for functional tumors or malignancy. Thyroid function monitoring is essential postoperatively.
questions.question: Struma ovarii may cause:
What seizure type is most common in Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Tonic-clonic seizures occur in majority of Wolf-Hirschhorn patients,
often medication-resistant. Status epilepticus is common. Seizures
typically begin in infancy or early childhood.

Continue

8:35 PM

questions.question: Which organic acidemia causes characteristic odor?
questions.explanation:
Isovaleric acidemia produces "sweaty feet" odor from accumulated
isovaleric acid. Metabolic acidosis and hyperammonemia occur during
crises. Glycine supplementation conjugates isovalerate for excretion.

Sézary cells show characteristically convoluted,
cerebriform nuclei resembling the brain's surface. These circulating
malignant T cells define Sézary syndrome (erythroderma, lymphadenopathy,
leukemia). Flow cytometry showing CD4+/CD7- immunophenotype aids
diagnosis. The syndrome represents advanced-stage cutaneous T-cell
lymphoma.
questions.question: Sézary cells in peripheral blood have which characteristic morphology?

questions.explanation: Testicular plasmacytomas represent extramedullary involvement by multiple myeloma, rarely presenting as isolated mass. Clonal plasma cell proliferation produces monoclonal immunoglobulin. Systemic workup essential to exclude multiple myeloma. Treatment involves radiation and/or chemotherapy. Solitary plasmacytoma has better prognosis than myeloma with testicular involvement.
questions.question: Plasmacytoma of testis is associated with:
A 65-year-old man has cirrhosis. His serum bilirubin, INR, and creatinine are used to calculate a score predicting 3-month mortality for transplant allocation. What is this score called?
questions.explanation: The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score uses serum bilirubin, creatinine, and INR to objectively predict 3-month mortality in patients with cirrhosis and guides organ allocation priority for liver transplantation. The Child-Pugh score also assesses liver disease severity but incorporates additional clinical variables such as ascites and encephalopathy.

questions.question: Which factor increases HIV transmission risk during sexual contact?
questions.explanation:
Genital ulcers from STIs increase HIV transmission by disrupting mucosal
barriers and recruiting target cells. High viral load in genital
secretions increases infectivity. Male circumcision reduces transmission
risk.

questions.question: Which achondroplasia feature results from FGFR3 mutation?
questions.explanation:
FGFR3 mutations cause constitutive receptor activation inhibiting
chondrocyte proliferation. Shortened limbs with normal trunk create
disproportionate dwarfism. Intelligence and organ function remain
normal.

questions.question: Which complication develops in adults with osteogenesis imperfecta?
questions.explanation:
Progressive conductive hearing loss from otosclerosis affects many OI
adults. Blue sclera result from thin sclera revealing choroid.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta causes abnormal tooth structure.

Integrase inhibitors prevent viral DNA integration into host chromosome.
Raltegravir and dolutegravir block integrase enzyme. Integration is
essential for viral replication making this effective therapeutic
target.
questions.question: Which antiretroviral drug class prevents viral integration?

questions.explanation: Cerebral malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum shows parasitized erythrocytes sequestered in cerebral capillaries causing ring hemorrhages and Drck granulomas. Coma develops despite antimalarial treatment in severe cases. Microvascular obstruction, cytokine release, and endothelial damage contribute to pathology. High mortality in children; survivors may have neurologic sequelae.
questions.question: Cerebral malaria is characterized by:
Homer-Wright rosettes are characteristic histological structures in which pediatric tumor?
questions.explanation:
Homer-Wright pseudorosettes show tumor cells arranged
concentrically around central neuropil (tangle of neuritic processes)
without a true lumen. These are characteristic but not pathognomonic of
neuroblastoma. The cells express neuron-specific enolase and
synaptophysin, confirming neural differentiation.

questions.question: Hereditary hemochromatosis patients with established cirrhosis remain at elevated HCC risk despite successful iron depletion. The persistent risk factor after phlebotomy is:
questions.explanation: Once cirrhosis is established in hereditary hemochromatosis, hepatocellular carcinoma risk remains markedly elevated (170-200 times population risk) even after complete iron depletion. Cirrhosis itself, regardless of etiology, creates an environment of chronic hepatocyte injury, regenerative pressure, and accumulated genomic instability predisposing to HCC. Surveillance with 6-monthly ultrasound and AFP measurement must continue indefinitely in cirrhotic HH patients. Iron depletion before cirrhosis develops can reduce HCC risk to near-normal levels, emphasizing early screening and treatment.
options: Residual iron in hepatic regenerative nodules causing oxidative damage
Established cirrhosis independently predisposing to HCC development
HFE C282Y mutation directly activating oncogene transcription
Elevated serum ferritin continuing to stimulate hepatocyte proliferation
Concurrent alcohol use unmasked after iron depletion therapy

questions.question: What cardiac complication occurs in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
questions.explanation:
Dilated cardiomyopathy develops in virtually all DMD patients by late
teens. Cardiac fibrosis affects left ventricular wall. ACE inhibitors
and beta-blockers slow progression.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has ascites, mild encephalopathy, and a bilirubin of 3 mg/dL. Using bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and encephalopathy, his disease severity is classified into three categories. What is this classification called?
questions.explanation: The Child-Pugh classification stratifies cirrhosis severity into classes A, B, and C using bilirubin, albumin, INR/prothrombin time, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy, helping predict prognosis and surgical risk. Unlike the MELD score, which is purely numerical and objective, Child-Pugh includes subjective clinical assessments of ascites and encephalopathy severity.

Villous adenomas carry a substantially higher risk of malignant transformation compared with tubular adenomas, with risk increasing proportionally with the percentage of villous component and the degree of dysplasia. This is why histological subtyping of colonic adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous) is clinically important in dictating surveillance intervals.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man has a colonic biopsy showing a polyp with villous architecture covering more than 75% of its surface and high-grade dysplasia. Compared with tubular adenomas, what is the most important clinical implication of villous architecture?
Seminal vesicle invasion by prostate cancer indicates:
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicle invasion defines pathologic stage pT3b, indicating locally advanced disease with worse prognosis. May occur by direct extension through ejaculatory duct or extraprostatic spread. Imaging (MRI) detects preoperatively. Patients require multimodal therapy with surgery, radiation, and/or hormonal therapy. Five-year biochemical recurrence-free survival approximately 50%.

questions.question: What is the cell of origin for mantle cell lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Mantle cell lymphoma derives from naive B cells in the
mantle zone surrounding germinal centers, characterized by lack of
somatic hypermutation in immunoglobulin genes. These cells express CD5
(like CLL) but also express cyclin D1 due to t(11;14) translocation. The
naive cell origin explains aggressive behavior despite small cell
morphology.

Cell-free DNA screening is appropriate for increased aneuploidy risk
including advanced maternal age. Also offered for positive serum
screening or fetal anomalies. Not diagnostic, requires confirmation.
questions.question: Which indication makes cell-free fetal DNA screening appropriate?
Can cirrhosis regress after successful treatment?
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is potentially reversible after successful treatment of chronic liver disease (e.g., viral hepatitis eradication, alcohol cessation). Cessation of chronic damage allows hepatocyte recovery and modulates the microenvironment. The inflammatory-to-resolution balance shifts, immune cells adjust phenotypes, myofibroblasts undergo senescence/apoptosis, and matrix degradation occurs. However, reversal is partial and depends on disease duration/severity.

Brain parenchyma (usually at gray-white junction) is the
most common metastatic site, appearing as multiple well-circumscribed
masses with surrounding vasogenic edema. Lung, breast, melanoma, kidney,
and colon are common primaries. Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis involves
meninges, presenting with cranial neuropathies and positive CSF
cytology.
questions.question: The most common site of CNS metastases is:
What is the mode of inheritance of hereditary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder of excessive iron storage. It is the most common single gene disorder in whites, affecting 1/220 of Northern European ancestry as homozygotes and 1/11 as heterozygotes. Males are affected more than females (80%) because menstruation and pregnancy delay iron accumulation in women.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents with testicular mass and hemoptysis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Choriocarcinoma presents with hemorrhagic pulmonary metastases causing hemoptysis before testicular mass is apparent. Markedly elevated -hCG and rapid hematogenous spread characterize these aggressive tumors. Gynec omastia may occur from -hCG. Despite poor prognosis historically, modern chemotherapy (BEP, EP) achieves 70-80% cure rates even with metastatic disease.

Persistent villous atrophy despite strict adherence to dietary modification should prompt reconsideration of the original diagnosis, as conditions such as autoimmune enteropathy, common variable immunodeficiency, or other causes of villous atrophy can mimic coeliac disease histologically. This distinction is important, as management and prognosis differ significantly between these conditions. Reassessment of serology, genetic testing, and consideration of alternative diagnoses is warranted in cases of apparent treatment failure.
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with chronic diarrhoea and is found to have villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytosis on duodenal biopsy. Despite strict dietary modification, symptoms persist and biopsy findings do not improve. Which alternative diagnosis should be reconsidered?
options: Autoimmune enteropathy or an alternative cause of villous atrophy
Irritable bowel syndrome without organic pathology
Functional abdominal pain without further investigation
Definite confirmation of coeliac disease regardless of response
Simple lactose intolerance requiring no further workup

questions.explanation:
Progressive obstructive pulmonary disease with chronic
infections (Pseudomonas, Burkholderia) causes respiratory failure and
cor pulmonale, accounting for >90% of CF mortality. Thick mucus impairs
mucociliary clearance, creating ideal conditions for bacterial
colonization. Median survival has improved to approximately 40 years
with modern therapy.
questions.question: Which organ system manifestation is the leading cause of death in cystic fibrosis patients?
What ocular manifestation characterizes Marfan syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Upward lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) occurs from weakened suspensory
ligaments. This distinguishes Marfan from homocystinuria showing
downward dislocation. Myopia and retinal detachment also occur.

questions.question: The most common paratesticular tumor in children is:
questions.explanation: Paratesticular rhabdomyosarcoma arises from spermatic cord in boys (median age 5 years), showing embryonal or alveolar histology. Presents as painless inguinal/scrotal mass. Radical inguinal orchiectomy with retroperitoneal lymph node dissection plus chemotherapy provides treatment. Prognosis excellent (>90% five-year survival) with modern multimodal therapy.

Next-generation sequencing with high depth detects low-level mosaicism
in gonadal tissue. Standard methods may miss mosaicism below 10-20%.
Testicular or ovarian biopsy is rarely performed.
questions.question: Which technique detects low-level gonadal mosaicism?

options: Toxoplasma gondii causing focal retinochoroiditis with vitritis
Herpes simplex virus causing acute peripheral retinal necrosis
Cytomegalovirus causing necrotizing retinitis at CD4 below 50
Cryptococcus neoformans causing choroidal granuloma formation
questions.question: An AIDS patient with CD4 count of 50 cells/uL develops progressive visual loss with perivascular yellow-white retinal infiltrates and hemorrhage. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: CMV retinitis is the leading cause of visual impairment in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 50 cells/uL. Funduscopy shows yellow-white granular retinal infiltrates with hemorrhage along vascular arcades, producing a characteristic pizza-pie or brushfire pattern. Toxoplasma causes focal retinochoroiditis with vitritis rather than the vascular perivascular infiltrates of CMV. Treatment requires systemic ganciclovir or valganciclovir. ART improving CD4 above 100 cells/uL allows discontinuation of maintenance therapy once immune reconstitution is confirmed.

questions.question: What GI manifestation occurs in newborns with cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Meconium ileus results from thick inspissated meconium obstructing
distal ileum. This occurs in 10-15% of CF newborns. Bowel perforation
may complicate the obstruction.

Tubular carcinomas are well-differentiated tumors composed of angulated tubules in desmoplastic stroma, with excellent prognosis. Usually small (<1cm), grade 1, node-negative, and ER-positive. Axillary metastases rare. Ten-year survival approaches 100%. May be associated with radial scars and often multifocal. Requires complete excision with negative margins.
questions.question: Tubular carcinoma has which prognosis?
Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma has which recurrence risk?
questions.explanation: Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinomas show organized papillae with minimal cytologic atypia. Recur in 50-70% but rarely progress to muscle-invasive disease (<5%). Surveillance cystoscopy monitors for recurrence. Transurethral resection treats recurrences. Intravesical chemotherapy (mitomycin) reduces recurrence rates. Excellent prognosis with appropriate management.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man with a history of atopy has dysphagia and food impaction. Biopsy of the mid-oesophagus shows more than 15 eosinophils per high-power field confined to the mucosa. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is an antigen-driven, often allergy-associated condition producing dense eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal mucosa (typically over 15 eosinophils per high-power field), commonly causing dysphagia and food impaction in young adults with atopic history. While GERD can also cause mucosal eosinophilia, it is usually less pronounced and concentrated distally.

options: Furosemide infusion with intravenous fluid hydration
Bisphosphonate infusion to acutely lower serum calcium
Dietary calcium restriction and vitamin D avoidance
Calcitonin injection for acute hypercalcemia control
questions.question: A 2-year-old with Williams syndrome has serum calcium of 3.1 mmol/L and overly sociable behavior. The most appropriate initial management is:
questions.explanation: Williams syndrome hypercalcemia results from dysregulated vitamin D metabolism with increased intestinal calcium absorption. Management centers on dietary calcium restriction and avoiding vitamin D supplementation, which would exacerbate calcium elevation. Parathyroid hormone is typically normal or suppressed, making parathyroidectomy inappropriate. Furosemide and hydration are reserved for acute severe hypercalcemia but do not address the underlying metabolic mechanism of Williams syndrome.

Meckel diverticulum represents a remnant of the omphalomesenteric duct and frequently contains ectopic gastric or pancreatic mucosa, with the gastric tissue producing acid that can ulcerate adjacent ileal mucosa, causing painless rectal bleeding. The technetium-99m pertechnetate scan ('Meckel scan') detects this ectopic gastric mucosa, aiding diagnosis. This is the most common congenital gastrointestinal anomaly, often remembered by the 'rule of twos' regarding its epidemiological features.
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with painless rectal bleeding, and a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows uptake in the right lower quadrant corresponding to ectopic gastric mucosa. Which congenital anomaly is most consistent with this finding?

questions.explanation: Pigment stones may be black (sterile) or brown (associated with infection). Black pigment stones form in sterile bile from unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, while brown stones are associated with biliary infection by bacteria (E. coli) or parasites (Ascaris lumbricoides, Opisthorchis sinensis) that promote bilirubin deconjugation.
questions.question: What distinguishes black from brown pigment stones?
Which organ is most commonly affected in systemic amyloidosis?
questions.explanation:
Kidneys are most commonly and severely affected in
systemic amyloidosis, presenting with proteinuria and nephrotic
syndrome. Amyloid deposits in glomeruli, blood vessels, and
interstitium. Renal involvement is major cause of morbidity and
mortality. Renal biopsy with Congo red staining establishes diagnosis.

COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase) maps within the 22q11.2 deleted region and metabolizes dopamine in the prefrontal cortex. Haploinsufficiency elevates synaptic dopamine predisposing to psychosis; approximately 30% of 22q11.2 deletion patients develop schizophrenia. TBX1 drives cardiac and thymic defects rather than psychiatric manifestations. The COMT Val158Met polymorphism on the remaining allele further modulates psychosis risk in affected individuals.
options: VEGF altering cerebral vessel formation patterns
questions.question: A child with 22q11.2 deletion develops schizophrenia at age 16. The gene most responsible for this psychiatric complication within the deleted region is:
Which chromosomal translocation is characteristic of anaplastic large cell lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
The t(2;5) translocation creates NPM-ALK fusion protein
with constitutive ALK tyrosine kinase activity in approximately 60% of
systemic ALCL cases. ALK-positive cases occur in younger patients with
better prognosis than ALK-negative variants. ALK immunohistochemistry is
diagnostically and prognostically important.

Oligodendroglioma is defined by IDH mutation AND 1p/19q codeletion (per the 2021 WHO Classification of CNS Tumours). Histologically, cells have round nuclei with perinuclear haloes (fried-egg artefact) and delicate branching capillaries (chicken-wire pattern). The 1p/19q codeletion results from an unbalanced whole-arm translocation. Oligodendrogliomas are chemosensitive (PCV or temozolomide regimen) and have better prognosis than IDH-mutant astrocytomas without codeletion. The combined molecular and histological definition is now mandatory for diagnosis.
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with seizures. MRI shows a well-defined frontal lobe lesion. Histology shows cells with perinuclear haloes (fried-egg appearance) and chicken-wire capillary pattern. Molecular testing shows 1p/19q codeletion and IDH mutation. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: Pilocytic astrocytoma with biphasic histological pattern
Central neurocytoma with neuronal differentiation markers

questions.explanation: HPV type 2 is the most common cause of verruca vulgaris (common warts), followed by types 1 and 4. These low-risk HPV types cause benign epithelial proliferation with characteristic koilocytic atypia, hyperkeratosis, and papillomatosis. Warts typically regress spontaneously within months to years as cell-mediated immunity develops.
questions.question: Verruca vulgaris is most commonly associated with HPV type:
Which third of the esophagus is most commonly affected by adenocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: Adenocarcinomas typically occur in the distal third of the esophagus and may invade the adjacent gastric cardia. They arise in a background of Barrett esophagus and longstanding GERD, are commoner in Caucasians, and are seven times more common in men than women.

questions.question: A newborn presents with ambiguous genitalia, hyponatraemia, and hyperkalaemia. Hormonal assays reveal elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Which enzyme deficiency best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common cause of ambiguous genitalia in genetic females, resulting from impaired cortisol and aldosterone synthesis with shunting of precursors toward androgen production, explaining both virilisation and salt-wasting crisis. Elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone is a key diagnostic marker reflecting the enzymatic block. Prompt recognition of the salt-wasting form is critical given the life-threatening risk of adrenal crisis in untreated infants.

questions.question: The most important prognostic factor in bladder cancer is:
questions.explanation: Depth of invasion (stage) is the most critical prognostic factor. Non-muscle-invasive (Ta, T1, Tis) has 90% five-year survival. Muscle-invasive (T2-T4) has 50% five-year survival even with cystectomy. Lymph node involvement (N+) and distant metastases (M1) confer worse prognosis (<10% five-year survival). Grade, variant histology, and lymphovascular invasion provide additional information.

questions.question: What is the infectious form of schistosomes transmitted to humans?
questions.explanation:
Cercariae are the infectious larval form that penetrate human skin. They
develop in snails from miracidia hatched from eggs. Proteolytic enzymes
help cercariae penetrate keratinized skin layers to reach blood vessels.

Hepatocellular carcinoma typically shows a trabecular growth pattern recapitulating normal liver architecture, with malignant hepatocytes producing bile and staining positive for HepPar-1, a marker of hepatocellular differentiation. Cholangiocarcinoma instead arises from bile duct epithelium, forming glandular structures with mucin rather than bile production.
