questions.question: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has a new liver mass. Biopsy shows trabecular arrangement of malignant hepatocytes with increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and bile production. Immunostain is positive for HepPar-1. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Amiodarone-induced liver injury can produce phospholipidosis, in which the drug accumulates within hepatocyte lysosomes and forms characteristic lamellated inclusions due to inhibition of phospholipid degradation. This pattern, alongside steatohepatitis-like changes, distinguishes amiodarone toxicity from other causes of drug-induced liver injury.
questions.question: A 70-year-old man taking long-term amiodarone develops liver dysfunction. Biopsy shows hepatocytes with lamellated, lysosomal inclusions resembling those seen in phospholipid storage disorders. What is the underlying mechanism?

options: Fertilisation of a normal oocyte by two spermatozoa simultaneously
Chromosomal non-disjunction during maternal meiosis II
Fertilisation of an anucleate oocyte by haploid sperm with duplication
Partial chromosomal endoreduplication of maternal genome
Fusion of two haploid oocytes followed by fertilisation
questions.question: A 22-year-old woman presents with a complete hydatidiform mole with karyotype 46,XX. FISH reveals both X chromosomes are paternal in origin. What is the primary mechanism?
questions.explanation: Complete hydatidiform mole most commonly arises from fertilisation of an enucleated (anucleate) egg by a haploid sperm that then undergoes duplication, producing 46,XX (androgenetic diploid). Alternatively, two spermatozoa may fertilise the anucleate egg producing 46,XY or 46,XX. In both mechanisms, all genetic material is paternal (androgenetic). Complete moles show diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia, hydropic villi, and absent foetal parts. They carry approximately 15-20% risk of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia and require serial hCG monitoring post-evacuation.

Autoimmune adrenalitis causing primary adrenal insufficiency accounts for 70-90% of Addison disease in developed countries. Adrenal antibodies target 21-hydroxylase. Clinical manifestations develop after >90% destruction: weakness, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Tuberculosis remains common cause globally. May occur as isolated disease or with polyglandular autoimmune syndromes.
questions.question: Addison disease most commonly results from:

questions.explanation: Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma forms gland-like structures and arises through a stepwise sequence from chronic gastritis to atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma, often linked to H. pylori. Diffuse-type carcinoma instead shows discohesive single cells infiltrating the wall, often with signet-ring morphology, and is associated with E-cadherin loss.
questions.question: A 58-year-old man with chronic atrophic gastritis develops a gastric mass. Biopsy shows malignant glands infiltrating as cohesive structures with desmoplastic stroma. What gastric carcinoma subtype is this?

questions.explanation:
Fibrillin-1 mutations cause defective elastic fibers in aortic media
predisposing to dissection. Aortic root dilation and mitral valve
prolapse also occur. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of
mortality.
questions.question: Which Marfan syndrome feature results from fibrillin-1 deficiency?

questions.explanation:
Neurogenic atrophy (from denervation) shows angular
atrophic fibers in groups and fiber type grouping (from reinnervation by
sprouting axons converting fiber types). This contrasts with myopathic
atrophy showing random distribution. ATPase staining demonstrates fiber
type grouping. Causes include motor neuron disease, nerve injury, and
spinal muscular atrophy.
questions.question: Neurogenic atrophy shows which characteristic pattern?
Varicocele is more common on which side?
questions.explanation: Left-sided varicoceles are more common (90%) due to longer left testicular vein, perpendicular drainage into left renal vein, and absent/incompetent valves. Right-sided or acute onset varicocele warrants evaluation for retroperitoneal mass obstructing venous drainage. "Bag of worms" appearance on physical examination. May cause infertility through increased scrotal temperature; surgical ligation improves sperm parameters.

options: CFTR gene transcription in bronchial airway epithelium
CFTR mRNA splicing causing critical exon 10 skipping
CFTR channel gating function after successful membrane insertion
CFTR protein degradation by extracellular matrix proteases
CFTR protein folding and endoplasmic reticulum trafficking
questions.explanation: The F508del mutation deletes phenylalanine at position 508, causing severe protein misfolding. The misfolded CFTR protein is recognized by ER quality control and targeted for proteasomal degradation before reaching the apical membrane. Modulators like elexacaftor correct folding (class II mutation). Channel gating mutations (class III, e.g., G551D) are corrected by ivacaftor alone. F508del is present in approximately 70% of CF alleles globally and its identification guides eligibility for targeted CFTR modulator combination therapies.
questions.question: Sweat chloride testing confirms CF in a neonate with meconium ileus. The F508del CFTR mutation affects which specific processing step:

questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1 gene mutation on chromosome 17) presents with caf-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas, optic pathway gliomas, and skeletal dysplasias. Increased malignancy risk (malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors) exists. Learning disabilities are common. Diagnosis requires meeting two of seven clinical criteria.
questions.question: A 5-year-old child presents with caf-au-lait macules and axillary freckling. This suggests:

questions.explanation:
Osteomalacia (adults) and rickets (children) result from
defective bone mineralization due to vitamin D deficiency, phosphate
deficiency, or renal tubular disorders. Unmineralized osteoid
accumulates. Adults develop bone pain and fractures; children show
growth retardation, bowing deformities, and rachitic rosary
(costochondral prominence). Serum calcium and phosphate are low;
alkaline phosphatase is elevated.
questions.question: Osteomalacia results from which metabolic defect?
Paget disease of the nipple is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Paget disease represents extension of underlying ductal carcinoma into nipple epidermis, appearing as large pale cells with abundant cytoplasm (Paget cells). These malignant cells migrate through the epidermis singly or in small groups, often accompanied by underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma. Clinically presents as eczematous nipple lesion.

questions.question: What is the 5-year survival rate for large hepatocellular carcinomas?
questions.explanation: The 5-year survival of large hepatocellular carcinomas is dismal, with the majority of patients dying within the first 2 years. Common causes of death include cachexia, gastrointestinal or esophageal variceal bleeding, liver failure with hepatic coma, and rupture of the tumor with fatal hemorrhage.

Progressive pulmonary disease causes most CF morbidity and mortality.
Thick mucus obstructs airways promoting chronic bacterial infections.
Bronchiectasis, respiratory failure, and cor pulmonale develop.
questions.question: Which organ system manifestation causes most CF mortality?

questions.explanation:
Prenatal and postnatal overgrowth with macrosomia characterizes BWS.
Macroglossia may cause feeding and airway difficulties. Neonatal
hypoglycemia from islet cell hyperplasia requires monitoring.
questions.question: What growth pattern characterizes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?

questions.explanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma is graded according to histologic differentiation into well differentiated, moderately differentiated, poorly differentiated, and undifferentiated types. Well-differentiated tumors closely resemble normal hepatocytes with trabecular pattern. Poorly differentiated tumors show solid growth, marked pleomorphism, and loss of hepatocellular features. Grade correlates with prognosis.
questions.question: How is HCC graded histologically?

questions.explanation:
HIV preferentially infects memory and activated CD4+ T
cells which express higher levels of CCR5/CXCR4 coreceptors and are
metabolically active, supporting viral replication. This selective
tropism explains rapid depletion of memory responses. Resting naive T
cells are relatively resistant to productive infection.
questions.question: HIV preferentially infects which subset of T lymphocytes through CD4 receptor binding?
options: Naive T cells in lymph nodes

questions.explanation:
Serum a1-AT levels identify deficiency with values below 50 mg/dL
suggesting homozygous deficiency. Phenotyping or genotyping confirms
specific mutation. Screening is recommended for early-onset emphysema.
questions.question: What screening test identifies a1-antitrypsin deficiency?

questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae cause most epididymitis in sexually active men <35 years. Older men develop epididymitis from uropathogens (E. coli, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas) related to urinary tract abnormalities or instrumentation. Presentation includes scrotal pain, swelling, dysuria. Doppler ultrasound shows increased testicular blood flow (versus decreased in torsion).
questions.question: Epididymitis in sexually active young men is most commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: Dysgerminomas are histologically identical to testicular seminomas, composed of sheets of large cells with clear cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and lymphocytic infiltrate. These malignant germ cell tumors occur in young women, often associated with gonadal dysgenesis. Most are confined to ovary at diagnosis. Treatment with surgery and chemotherapy yields excellent prognosis.
questions.question: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of:
Follicular thyroid carcinoma is diagnosed by demonstrating:
questions.explanation: Follicular carcinoma requires histologic evidence of capsular and/or vascular invasion to distinguish from follicular adenoma. These tumors spread hematogenously to bones and lungs. Minimally invasive variants have excellent prognosis while widely invasive forms behave aggressively. Hrthle cell (oncocytic) variant shows similar behavior. RAS mutations are common.

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers are ductal adenocarcinomas arising from pancreatic duct epithelium. Other less common types include acinar cell carcinoma, pancreatoblastoma, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, and neuroendocrine tumors. The predominance of adenocarcinoma reflects the anatomy, with extensive ductal epithelium at risk. Most are poorly differentiated at diagnosis with extensive desmoplasia.
questions.question: What percentage of pancreatic cancers are adenocarcinomas?
What is the first-line diagnostic investigation for suspected portal hypertension?
questions.explanation: While the gold standard for diagnosing portal hypertension is measurement of hepatic venous pressure gradient via portal vein catheterization, ultrasound is the non-invasive first-line investigation that can detect signs of portal hypertension. It is widely available, cost-effective, and provides valuable anatomical and hemodynamic information.

options: Borderline phyllodes tumour requiring wide excision
Benign phyllodes tumour with minimal stromal atypia
Malignant phyllodes tumour with high-grade stroma
Juvenile fibroadenoma with abundant myxoid stroma
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has a well-circumscribed 3 cm breast mass. Core needle biopsy shows a biphasic tumour with increased stromal cellularity, leaf-like projections into cystic spaces, and more than 4 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phyllodes tumours are classified as benign, borderline, or malignant based on stromal cellularity, atypia, mitotic activity, stromal overgrowth, and margin characteristics. Borderline phyllodes shows moderate stromal cellularity, mild atypia, 4-9 mitoses per 10 HPF, and microscopically infiltrative margins. Malignant phyllodes has marked stromal atypia, 10 or more mitoses per 10 HPF, and permeative margins. Unlike fibroadenoma, phyllodes has purely stromal malignant potential. Wide local excision with clear margins is required; local recurrence correlates with grade and margin status.

Anticipation in myotonic dystrophy occurs through intergenerational CTG repeat expansion in DMPK. Congenital DM1 almost exclusively results from maternal transmission during which the largest expansions occur, often exceeding 1000 repeats. Children with congenital DM1 have profound hypotonia, respiratory failure, and feeding difficulties reflecting greater toxic RNA accumulation. The mechanism of maternal bias relates to greater repeat instability during female meiosis compared with male gametogenesis, producing catastrophically large expansions in offspring.
options: Maternal antibodies crossing placenta causing neonatal myositis
De novo mitochondrial mutations occurring during oogenesis
Paternal modifying genes worsening maternal transmission severity
X-linked expression amplified only in female-to-male transmission
Child inheriting a massively expanded maternal CTG repeat
questions.question: A mother with myotonic dystrophy type 1 has a child with congenital myotonic dystrophy requiring ventilation at birth. This intergenerational worsening is explained by:

questions.explanation: Multicystic dysplastic kidney represents developmental anomaly with non-functional kidney replaced by cysts of varying sizes separated by dysplastic tissue. Usually unilateral; bilateral is lethal. Associated with ureteral atresia/obstruction. Detected prenatally on ultrasound. Contralateral kidney normal. Nephrectomy or observation (involution occurs). No malignant potential.
questions.question: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is characterized by:

questions.explanation: Peyronie disease causes fibrous plaques in tunica albuginea of penis, resulting in curvature, pain, and erectile dysfunction. Etiology unclear; may involve repetitive trauma with abnormal healing. Association with Dupuytren contracture exists. Conservative management includes oral medications, injections; surgical correction for severe deformity. Plaques contain dense collagen with variable inflammation.
questions.question: Peyronie disease involves:

options: Fourth to sixth week of life
Second to third month of life
Second to third week of life
questions.question: At what age do infants with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically present?
questions.explanation: Infants with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis characteristically present with persistent projectile non-bilious vomiting by the second to third week of life. Physical examination reveals an ovoid abdominal mass measuring 1-2 cm with left to right hyperperistalsis during and after feeding. The condition requires surgical intervention for definitive management.

questions.question: Call-Exner bodies are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Call-Exner bodies are small follicle-like spaces containing eosinophilic fluid surrounded by granulosa cells, characteristic of granulosa cell tumors. These sex cord-stromal tumors secrete estrogen. Nuclear grooves (coffee-bean nuclei) are also typical. Adult type occurs perimenopausal; juvenile type in children/young adults. Late recurrences (10-20 years) require prolonged surveillance.

Fc receptors on phagocytes binding to IgG-coated bacteria
provide the most potent engulfment signal, initiating phagocytosis
immediately upon contact. While C3b aids recognition, it requires
additional activation signals for effective engulfment unlike Fc
receptor engagement. This explains why antibody deficiencies cause
severe susceptibility to encapsulated bacterial infections.
questions.question: During phagocytosis, which opsonin provides the strongest signal for neutrophil engulfment of bacteria?

questions.explanation:
Ashkenazi Jewish population has 1 in 30 carrier frequency for Tay-Sachs
disease. Carrier screening is recommended before pregnancy. The disease
causes progressive neurodegeneration with death by age 4-5 years.
questions.question: What ethnic group has highest Tay-Sachs carrier frequency?
Which finding is most characteristic of phenylketonuria if untreated?
questions.explanation:
Untreated PKU causes severe intellectual disability,
seizures, behavioral problems, and neurological impairment from toxic
phenylalanine metabolite accumulation. Early dietary restriction of
phenylalanine prevents brain damage, making newborn screening critical.
Patients also show decreased pigmentation (hypophenylalaninemia reduces
melanin synthesis).

questions.question: Langhans giant cells are characteristically seen in which pathological process?
questions.explanation:
Langhans giant cells (multinucleated with nuclei arranged
in a peripheral horseshoe pattern) are typical of tuberculous and other
immune granulomas. They differ from foreign body giant cells (randomly
scattered nuclei). The cells form from macrophage fusion and are
involved in antigen presentation and containment.

questions.question: SIADH is most commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: Small cell lung carcinoma frequently produces ectopic ADH causing SIADH with hyponatremia, concentrated urine despite low serum osmolality, and euvolemia. Other causes include CNS disorders, pulmonary infections, and various medications. Treatment involves fluid restriction, hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic hyponatremia, and vasopressin receptor antagonists (vaptans).

Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer caused by germline CDH1 mutations carries a very high lifetime risk of diffuse-type gastric cancer, which is often multifocal and difficult to detect endoscopically due to submucosal spread. Prophylactic total gastrectomy is therefore recommended in mutation carriers, as surveillance endoscopy alone has limited sensitivity for this infiltrative cancer subtype.
questions.question: A 35-year-old man with a family history of diffuse gastric cancer undergoes genetic testing revealing a germline CDH1 mutation. What is the most appropriate management to prevent gastric cancer?
What clinical finding helps distinguish homocystinuria from Marfan syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Homocystinuria causes downward lens dislocation while Marfan syndrome
shows upward dislocation. Both conditions present with tall stature and
arachnodactyly. Thromboembolism occurs in homocystinuria but not Marfan.

Polyarteritis nodosa involves medium-sized muscular
arteries with transmural necrotizing inflammation, fibrinoid necrosis,
and aneurysm formation. Glomeruli and pulmonary vessels are typically
spared (unlike microscopic polyangiitis). Affects kidneys, heart, liver,
GI tract causing infarctions. Associated with HBV infection in some
cases. Treatment requires corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.
questions.question: Polyarteritis nodosa characteristically involves which vessel size?

questions.explanation: Osteosarcoma classically arises in the metaphysis of long bones during the adolescent growth spurt, producing malignant osteoid matrix and a characteristic 'sunburst' periosteal reaction from rapid, disorganised new bone formation breaking through the cortex. This is distinct from the 'onion-skin' pattern of Ewing sarcoma, which reflects a different growth pattern within bone. Pulmonary metastasis is the most common site of spread, influencing prognosis and follow-up imaging.
questions.question: A 16-year-old presents with knee pain and a destructive metaphyseal lesion with a 'sunburst' periosteal reaction on X-ray. Biopsy shows malignant cells producing osteoid matrix. Which tumour is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation:
Gonadal mosaicism complicates recurrence risk counseling since seemingly
unaffected parents may have multiple affected children. Standard
Mendelian predictions don't apply. Empiric recurrence risks are used.
questions.question: What counseling challenge does gonadal mosaicism present?

questions.explanation: Prostatic adenocarcinoma characteristically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases, contrasting with osteolytic lesions from most other cancers. Axial skeleton (lumbar spine, pelvis) is preferentially involved. Elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects osteoblastic activity. Bone scan detects metastases before radiographically apparent. Spinal cord compression may occur.
questions.question: A 70-year-old man presents with bone pain and elevated serum PSA. Bone scan would most likely show:

A 50-year-old woman undergoes thyroidectomy for a 2 cm thyroid nodule. Histology shows papillary projections, Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and intranuclear inclusions. Which molecular alteration is most commonly identified in this tumour?
questions.explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common thyroid malignancy and is characterised by BRAF V600E mutation in approximately 40-60% of sporadic cases. BRAF V600E constitutively activates the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, promoting tumour growth and dedifferentiation. The diagnostic nuclear features — Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, intranuclear pseudoinclusions, and psammoma bodies — are critical for diagnosis even in metastatic lymph nodes. BRAF mutation is associated with higher risk of recurrence and radioiodine resistance compared to BRAF wild-type PTC.
options: RAS point mutation driving follicular carcinoma pathway
PAX8-PPARG fusion gene in follicular carcinoma
BRAF V600E mutation activating the MAPK pathway
RET point mutation in MEN2 syndrome tumours

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with longstanding heartburn undergoes endoscopy showing salmon-coloured mucosa above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: This patient has Barrett's oesophagus, a precursor lesion for adenocarcinoma. Without evidence of dysplasia or malignancy, periodic surveillance endoscopy with biopsy is recommended to detect progression early. Aggressive treatments like surgery or radiotherapy are reserved for confirmed dysplasia or cancer.

Balanced translocation carriers receive genetic counseling regarding
recurrence risks and reproductive options. Preimplantation genetic
diagnosis or prenatal testing available. Extended family screening
identifies additional carriers.
questions.question: What follow-up is recommended after identifying balanced translocation carrier?

A 52-year-old woman has a painless axillary lymph node metastasis. No primary breast lesion is found on mammography or ultrasound. Breast MRI detects a 6 mm enhancing lesion. Which is the most appropriate next management step?
questions.explanation: When axillary lymph node metastasis is detected without an identifiable primary breast lesion on standard imaging, breast MRI is the most sensitive modality and can detect occult primaries in 50-75% of cases. MRI-guided core biopsy of any detected lesion should be performed to confirm the primary origin and guide treatment planning. Immunohistochemistry (ER, PR, HER2, GATA3, mammaglobin) on the nodal metastasis helps establish breast origin. Treatment includes systemic therapy and breast-directed treatment (radiotherapy or mastectomy) regardless of whether the primary is excised.
options: Mastectomy must be performed without further tissue confirmation
MRI-guided biopsy of the detected enhancing lesion
Isolated axillary nodal disease is never of breast origin
Axillary lymph node dissection without breast treatment
Invasive lobular carcinoma with atypical features
Tubular carcinoma with well-formed angulated glands
Mucinous carcinoma with extracellular mucin pools
questions.explanation: Medullary carcinoma (invasive carcinoma with medullary features) has specific histological criteria: syncytial growth pattern occupying over 75% of the tumour, pushing borders, prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, high nuclear grade, and no glandular differentiation. Despite being triple-negative and high-grade, it carries a paradoxically favourable prognosis compared to other triple-negative carcinomas. It is associated with BRCA1 mutations and occurs predominantly in younger women. The lymphocytic infiltrate likely reflects an immune response contributing to better outcomes.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging 8 cm breast mass. Biopsy shows invasive carcinoma with lymphocytic infiltrate, pushing margins, and syncytial growth pattern. ER, PR, and HER2 are all negative. What subtype best describes this tumour?

options: Arylsulfatase A deficiency with sulfatide accumulation in myelin
Hexosaminidase A deficiency with GM2 ganglioside accumulation
Sphingomyelinase deficiency with sphingomyelin storage in tissues
questions.question: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is confirmed by metachromatic material in urine sediment. The enzyme deficient and substrate accumulating are:
questions.explanation: Arylsulfatase A (ARSA) deficiency causes MLD, with sulfatide (cerebroside-3-sulfate) accumulation in lysosomes of oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, and renal tubular cells. Sulfatides stain metachromatically (orange-brown with acidic cresyl violet) due to their sulfate groups. MLD affects both central and peripheral myelin, causing progressive motor and cognitive deterioration. Urine sulfatide excretion is elevated. Pseudo-ARSA deficiency (low enzyme activity without sulfatide accumulation) must be excluded by measuring urinary sulfatide excretion directly before initiating treatment.

Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) shows excessive collagen
deposition causing skin thickening, vascular damage with intimal
proliferation, and organ fibrosis (lungs, kidneys, GI tract, heart).
Limited cutaneous form (CREST syndrome) has better prognosis than
diffuse cutaneous form. Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) and
anti-centromere antibodies have diagnostic value.
questions.question: Systemic sclerosis is characterized by which pathological process?
Which inflammatory bowel disease is most associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis?
questions.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis. Approximately 70-80% of PSC patients have IBD, and conversely, about 5% of ulcerative colitis patients develop PSC. The association with Crohn disease is less common. PSC can precede, coincide with, or follow IBD diagnosis.

questions.question: A child presents with recurrent fractures from minimal trauma, blue sclerae, and a family history of similar findings. Skin biopsy shows abnormal collagen fibril structure. Which protein defect underlies this condition?
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta most commonly results from mutations affecting type I collagen synthesis or structure, the predominant collagen type in bone, skin, and sclera, explaining the combination of fragile bones and blue sclerae from scleral thinning revealing underlying choroidal vasculature. Disease severity varies widely depending on the specific mutation and its effect on collagen assembly. This contrasts with Marfan syndrome, which results from fibrillin gene mutations affecting connective tissue elasticity.

Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant transformation in mature cystic teratomas (1-2% incidence), usually occurring in postmenopausal women. Rapidly growing mass, elevated CA-125, and imaging changes suggest transformation. Prognosis is poor. Other transformations include adenocarcinoma, melanoma, sarcoma, and carcinoid. Complete surgical excision with staging required.
questions.question: Teratoma with malignant transformation most commonly develops:

questions.explanation: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is a rare but serious complication of longstanding, poorly controlled coeliac disease, arising from an aberrant intraepithelial T-cell population that loses normal surface markers such as CD8 and acquires clonal proliferative capacity. This should be suspected when symptoms worsen despite strict dietary gluten avoidance.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with longstanding coeliac disease develops worsening symptoms despite strict gluten avoidance. Biopsy shows an atypical lymphocyte population with loss of normal CD8 expression infiltrating the small bowel epithelium. What complication is suspected?

questions.explanation:
Intrapartum transmission occurs through exposure to maternal blood and
genital secretions during delivery. Maternal antiretroviral therapy
dramatically reduces transmission risk. Cesarean section before membrane
rupture further decreases risk.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of mother-to-child HIV transmission during delivery?
A patient develops keloid formation following a minor surgical procedure. Which pathological process best explains this abnormality of tissue repair?
questions.explanation:
Keloids result from excessive and uncontrolled collagen
deposition extending beyond original wound boundaries, representing
pathological ECM accumulation. Unlike hypertrophic scars which remain
within wound margins, keloids demonstrate continued growth driven by
dysregulated fibroblast activity. This occurs more frequently in
genetically predisposed individuals, particularly those of African
descent.

Brain abscesses frequently arise from contiguous infections (otitis, mastoiditis, sinusitis) or hematogenous spread from distant foci (endocarditis, lung abscess). Streptococcus species are most common; polymicrobial infections occur. Ring-enhancing lesions with central necrosis appear on imaging. Treatment combines prolonged antibiotics with surgical drainage for large abscesses. Mortality remains significant despite therapy.
questions.question: Brain abscess most commonly results from:

questions.explanation: Radium-223 is a calcium mimetic alpha-emitting radiopharmaceutical preferentially targeting osteoblastic bone metastases. Delivers high-energy radiation to metastatic sites with minimal damage to surrounding tissue. Improves survival and reduces skeletal events in metastatic CRPC with bone metastases. Side effects include myelosuppression. First alpha-emitter approved for cancer therapy.
questions.question: Radium-223 dichloride treats metastatic prostate cancer by:

questions.explanation: Tuberculous salpingitis results from hematogenous spread from pulmonary focus, causing chronic granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis. Patients present with chronic pelvic pain, infertility, and constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis requires high index of suspicion; culture and PCR aid identification. Treatment involves prolonged multi-drug anti-tuberculous therapy.
questions.question: Tuberculous salpingitis characteristically presents with:

options: Valine causing branch-chain amino acid pathway blockade
Isoleucine accumulating in CSF to produce seizures directly
Alloisoleucine present only in MSUD but not directly neurotoxic
Leucine causing cerebral edema via competitive transport inhibition
questions.explanation: Leucine is the most neurotoxic of the three elevated branched-chain amino acids in MSUD. Elevated leucine causes cerebral edema, impairs myelination, competitively inhibits large neutral amino acid transport across the blood-brain barrier, and reduces serotonin and dopamine synthesis. Treatment during acute crisis uses BCAA-free intravenous amino acid solutions to reduce leucine urgently. Monitoring leucine levels specifically guides treatment intensity, as leucine normalization correlates most closely with neurological recovery in affected neonates.
questions.question: In maple syrup urine disease with elevated leucine, isoleucine, and valine, the most neurotoxic amino acid driving encephalopathy in acute crisis is:

A 50-year-old woman has a large multiloculated pancreatic cyst on imaging. Cyst fluid analysis shows high CEA and mucin. Biopsy shows mucinous epithelium with ovarian-type stroma. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mucinous cystic neoplasms occur almost exclusively in women, typically in the pancreatic body or tail, and are characterised by mucinous epithelium overlying distinctive ovarian-type stroma. High cyst fluid CEA reflects the mucinous nature. Serous cystadenomas instead show glycogen-rich cuboidal epithelium with low CEA and lack ovarian-type stroma.

questions.question: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by:
options: Insulin resistance and beta cell dysfunction
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance (decreased tissue sensitivity) combined with progressive beta cell failure unable to compensate. Obesity, particularly visceral adiposity, contributes through inflammatory adipokines. Amyloid deposition (amylin) in islets occurs. Most patients eventually require insulin. Complications include macrovascular and microvascular disease.

The adenoma-carcinoma sequence typically requires 5-10+ years for progression from adenoma to carcinoma, providing a window for screening and prevention. Molecular alterations accumulate stepwise: APC mutation → KRAS mutation → loss of tumor suppressors → p53 mutation. This long timeline explains screening efficacy. However, some serrated polyps may progress faster, and interval cancers do occur.
questions.question: What is the polyp-cancer sequence timeline?

A 48-year-old woman has pruritus and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Liver biopsy shows granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts with anti-mitochondrial antibodies positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune disease targeting small interlobular bile ducts, producing granulomatous duct destruction (florid duct lesions) and is highly associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies. Primary sclerosing cholangitis instead affects larger ducts with concentric 'onion-skin' periductal fibrosis and lacks anti-mitochondrial antibody positivity.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with bloody nipple discharge. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Intraductal papillomas are the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge, arising within lactiferous sinuses near the nipple. These benign lesions consist of fibrovascular cores covered by epithelial and myoepithelial cells. Large duct papillomas are usually solitary while small duct papillomas may be multiple and associated with slightly increased cancer risk.

Courvoisier sign is a palpable, enlarged, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient, classically indicating pancreatic head carcinoma causing distal bile duct obstruction. The gallbladder distends because obstruction is gradual, allowing dilation without inflammation. This distinguishes it from choledocholithiasis, which typically causes a non-distended, tender gallbladder. The sign has limited sensitivity but good specificity.
questions.question: What sign indicates enlarged non-tender gallbladder with jaundice in pancreatic cancer?
Lytic bone lesions in multiple myeloma result from which mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Myeloma cells secrete factors (RANKL, MIP-1a) activating
osteoclasts while suppressing osteoblasts, causing lytic lesions without
new bone formation. This leads to hypercalcemia, pathologic fractures,
and bone pain. Lesions appear as punched-out radiolucencies on
radiographs; bisphosphonates reduce skeletal complications.

High concentrations of monoclonal immunoglobulin coat red
cell surfaces, reducing their mutual repulsion and causing stacking
(rouleaux). This produces markedly elevated ESR and increased blood
viscosity. The finding is suggestive but not specific for myeloma, as
any cause of hypergammaglobulinemia can produce rouleaux.
questions.question: Rouleaux formation on blood smear in multiple myeloma results from:

questions.explanation:
Acrodermatitis enteropathica results from severe zinc deficiency causing
periorificial and acral dermatitis. Zinc is essential for numerous
enzymes and transcription factors. The condition can be inherited as
autosomal recessive or acquired from malabsorption or inadequate intake.
questions.question: Which trace element deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica?

questions.explanation: Alcoholic steatosis first appears in the perivenular region (zone 3) and spreads to other regions if drinking persists. This pattern relates to the hepatic acinus model where zone 3 has the lowest oxygen tension and highest concentration of alcohol-metabolizing enzymes. Steatosis may disappear within 1 month after alcohol cessation.
questions.question: Which zone of the liver acinus is first affected by alcoholic steatosis?
What age group is affected by fibrolamellar HCC?
questions.explanation: Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma typically arises in non-cirrhotic livers of adolescents or young adults (15-40 years). Tumor cells grow in sheets or trabeculae separated by hyalinized collagen bundles with characteristic lamellar pattern. It has better prognosis than conventional HCC and lacks association with viral hepatitis or cirrhosis.

Abiraterone acetate inhibits CYP17A1, blocking androgen synthesis in testes, adrenal glands, and prostate tumor. Reduces testosterone to undetectable levels. Requires concurrent prednisone to prevent mineralocorticoid excess from upstream steroid accumulation. Effective in metastatic CRPC. Side effects include hypertension, hypokalemia, fluid retention, and hepatotoxicity. Resistance mechanisms include bypass pathways.
questions.question: Abiraterone acetate inhibits:

questions.explanation:
Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine-rhodamine stains demonstrate
acid-fast bacilli due to mycobacterial cell wall mycolic acid content.
The organisms appear as thin red rods (Ziehl-Neelsen) or fluorescent
rods (fluorochrome stains). Culture remains gold standard but requires
weeks; molecular tests provide rapid diagnosis.
questions.question: Which stain is most appropriate for identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis in tissue?

questions.explanation:
Miliary TB results from hematogenous dissemination
producing innumerable small (millet seed-sized) granulomas throughout
lungs and other organs. This represents failure of immune containment
with bacillemia, most common in immunocompromised patients. Chest
radiograph shows diffuse micronodular pattern.
questions.question: Miliary tuberculosis results from which dissemination pattern?
What is the characteristic morphologic hallmark of hyperplastic polyps?
questions.explanation: The morphologic hallmark of hyperplastic polyps is the serrated surface architecture created by delayed shedding of mature goblet and absorptive cells, leading to crowding. These polyps result from decreased epithelial cell turnover and defective proliferation and maturation of normal epithelium.

questions.question: A patient with precursor B-ALL shows t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome. This confers which prognostic implication?
questions.explanation:
The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creating BCR-ABL
fusion in ALL indicates high-risk disease with poor response to
conventional chemotherapy. This same translocation defines chronic
myeloid leukemia but has worse implications in ALL. Tyrosine kinase
inhibitors combined with intensive chemotherapy improve outcomes but
prognosis remains guarded.

questions.question: What is the recommended colorectal cancer screening age?
questions.explanation: Current guidelines recommend starting colorectal cancer screening at age 45 for average-risk individuals (reduced from 50 due to rising young-onset CRC). High-risk individuals (family history, IBD, hereditary syndromes) start earlier. Screening options include colonoscopy every 10 years, annual FIT, or other modalities. Early detection significantly reduces CRC mortality through polyp removal and early-stage diagnosis.

options: Meganeurites with storage vacuoles in swollen cortical neurons
Gaucher cells with wrinkled tissue-paper cytoplasm in marrow
Metachromatic granules in oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells
Foamy macrophages with sphingomyelin in reticuloendothelial system
Globoid multinucleated macrophages in perivenular white matter
questions.question: Krabbe disease presents in an infant with peripheral neuropathy and severe white matter disease. The pathognomonic cell type on brain biopsy is:
questions.explanation: Krabbe disease is caused by galactocerebrosidase (GALC) deficiency accumulating psychosine (galactosylsphingosine), a highly cytotoxic metabolite destroying oligodendrocytes. The pathognomonic finding is globoid cells - large multinucleated perivascular macrophages containing PAS-positive undegraded galactocerebroside - in the white matter. Rapid demyelination follows oligodendrocyte death. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in asymptomatic neonates identified through expanded newborn screening can modify the disease course before severe neurological damage accumulates irreversibly.

The most important synergism for hepatocellular carcinoma development in sub-Saharan Africa is between chronic hepatitis B virus infection and consumption of aflatoxin-contaminated foodstuffs. This combination exponentially increases HCC risk compared to either factor alone, making it a critical public health concern in endemic regions.
questions.question: What is the most important synergism for HCC development in sub-Saharan Africa?
Congenital mesoblastic nephroma occurs in:
questions.explanation: Congenital mesoblastic nephroma is the most common renal tumor in neonates and infants <6 months. Benign spindle cell tumor resembling infantile fibromatosis. Classic (fibrous) and cellular variants exist; cellular type has ETV6-NTRK3 fusion. Presents as abdominal mass. Complete surgical excision is curative. Excellent prognosis; recurrence rare. Must distinguish from Wilms tumor and rhabdoid tumor.

Onion skin fibrosis refers to concentric layers of periductal fibrosis around bile ducts in primary sclerosing cholangitis, resembling the layers of an onion on microscopy. This represents the healing response to chronic bile duct inflammation and destruction. As disease progresses, affected ducts may become obliterated, leaving only a fibrous scar (tombstone scar).
questions.question: What is onion skin fibrosis?
What is the characteristic endoscopic appearance of Barrett esophagus?
options: Red velvety mucosa from gastroesophageal junction
questions.explanation: Barrett esophagus appears endoscopically as red velvety mucosa extending upward from the gastroesophageal junction. Both endoscopic and histologic evidence of intestinal metaplasia are required for diagnosis. The characteristic histologic finding is the presence of goblet cells in the columnar epithelium.

questions.question: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is most strongly linked to which condition?
questions.explanation:
EATL develops in patients with longstanding celiac disease
(gluten-sensitive enteropathy), presenting with abdominal pain,
perforation, or obstruction. Type I EATL associates with celiac disease;
Type II EATL occurs independently. Strict gluten-free diet compliance
may reduce but not eliminate risk. Prognosis is poor.

questions.question: What is Y-90 radioembolization?
questions.explanation: Yttrium-90 (Y-90) radioembolization delivers radioactive microspheres via hepatic artery catheterization, lodging in tumor microvasculature and delivering localized beta radiation. It treats unresectable HCC, particularly with portal vein thrombosis (TACE contraindication). Radiation dose to tumor exceeds external beam by 10-20x with minimal liver toxicity. It may downstage tumors or serve as bridge to transplantation.

questions.question: The most common cause of death in untreated chronic lymphocytic leukemia is:
questions.explanation:
Hypogammaglobulinemia from suppressed normal B-cell
function causes recurrent bacterial infections, the leading cause of
death in CLL. The defect worsens with disease progression and treatment.
Intravenous immunoglobulin replacement reduces infection frequency in
severely affected patients. Autoimmune cytopenias also cause significant
morbidity.

In decreasing order of severity, hemosiderin deposition occurs in liver (most severe), pancreas, myocardium, pituitary gland, adrenal gland, thyroid and parathyroid glands, joints, and skin. Pancreatic iron deposition leads to diabetes mellitus ("bronze diabetes"), while cardiac deposition causes arrhythmias and cardiomyopathy.
questions.question: Which organ shows the second most severe iron deposition after the liver?
Cowper glands (bulbourethral glands) may be mistaken for:
questions.explanation: Cowper gland acini in prostate specimens (particularly apex) may mimic adenocarcinoma due to location in skeletal muscle and perineural location. Distinguished by mucinous columnar epithelium, basal cells present, lobular architecture, and negative AMACR. Awareness of this pitfall prevents false-positive cancer diagnosis on biopsy or TURP specimens.

questions.question: Which chromosome is most commonly involved in translocations associated with Burkitt lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
The t(8;14) translocation juxtaposes c-MYC oncogene
(chromosome 8) with immunoglobulin heavy chain locus (chromosome 14),
causing constitutive MYC expression and uncontrolled proliferation.
Alternative translocations t(2;8) and t(8;22) involve light chain loci
but are less common. All variants result in MYC dysregulation.

questions.question: Granulomatous prostatitis may result from:
questions.explanation: Nonspecific granulomatous prostatitis follows BCG intravesical therapy for bladder cancer, representing iatrogenic implantation. Other causes include infectious (TB, fungi in immunocompromised), post-surgical, and idiopathic (likely ruptured ducts/acini). Histology shows epithelioid granulomas, sometimes with necrosis. Must exclude infectious etiologies. Usually requires no treatment.

Nearly 100% of endemic (African) Burkitt lymphoma cases
are EBV-positive, compared to 15-20% of sporadic cases. The virus
contributes to pathogenesis through immunosuppression and chronic B-cell
stimulation. Endemic cases typically present with jaw/facial masses in
young children.
questions.question: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma is most strongly associated with which pathogen?

A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive renal failure and proteinuria. Kidney biopsy shows extracellular deposits that are Congo red positive. Which precursor protein is most likely involved if she has rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation:
AA amyloid derives from serum amyloid A protein, an acute
phase reactant produced by the liver during chronic inflammatory
conditions like rheumatoid arthritis. This represents secondary
(reactive) systemic amyloidosis, contrasting with AL amyloid from plasma
cell disorders. The chronic inflammatory stimulus drives sustained SAA
production, providing substrate for amyloid fibril formation.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is found to have ovarian involvement in a mucinous appendiceal neoplasm. Gelatinous mucin fills the peritoneal cavity. What is this condition?
questions.explanation: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is characterised by gelatinous mucinous ascites dissecting peritoneal surfaces and omentum. The vast majority originate from low-grade mucinous appendiceal neoplasms (LAMN) rather than primary ovarian mucinous tumours, which were historically misdiagnosed as the source. CK20-positive/CK7-negative immunophenotype and CDX2 positivity support appendiceal origin. Ovarian involvement is secondary. Treatment involves cytoreductive surgery combined with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC). Prognosis depends on tumour grade and completeness of cytoreduction.
options: Pseudomyxoma peritonei from appendiceal mucinous neoplasm
Pseudomyxoma peritonei from primary ovarian mucinous tumour
Diffuse peritoneal endometriosis with mucinous change
Ovarian mucinous cystadenoma with peritoneal rupture
Green-brown nipple discharge and periareolar inflammation
questions.question: Mammary duct ectasia presents with:
questions.explanation: Duct ectasia involves dilatation of subareolar ducts with thick secretions and periductal chronic inflammation, presenting with nipple discharge (green-brown, sticky), nipple retraction, and periareolar mass. Occurs in perimenopausal women. Ruptured ducts cause granulomatous inflammation. Excision of involved ducts provides treatment if symptomatic.

Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is distinguished from simple steatosis by the presence of inflammation (lobular and portal) and hepatocyte ballooning degeneration in addition to steatosis. NASH may also show Mallory-Denk bodies and perisinusoidal (chicken wire) fibrosis. Simple steatosis has fat without significant inflammation or ballooning. NASH carries risk of progression to cirrhosis, while simple steatosis generally does not.
questions.question: What distinguishes NASH from simple steatosis histologically?
Which is the most common viable autosomal trisomy?
questions.explanation:
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most common viable
autosomal trisomy (1:700 live births) with survival to adulthood
possible. Trisomy 18 and 13 are less common and usually lethal in
infancy. Trisomy 16 is the most common trisomy overall but causes first
trimester miscarriage, not live birth.

questions.question: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colorectal cancer involves which sequence of mutations?
questions.explanation:
The classic adenoma-carcinoma sequence involves: (1) APC
mutation (initiation), (2) KRAS mutation (polyp growth), (3) TP53
mutation/LOH (progression to carcinoma). Additional mutations (DCC,
SMAD4) contribute. This multistep process takes years, explaining why
screening colonoscopy with polypectomy prevents cancer. Serrated pathway
represents alternative route.

questions.question: What distinguishes thanatophoric dysplasia from achondroplasia?
questions.explanation:
Thanatophoric dysplasia is lethal form of skeletal dysplasia from severe
FGFR3 mutations. Respiratory insufficiency from thoracic hypoplasia
causes neonatal death. More severe phenotype than achondroplasia.

Niemann-Pick disease types A and B result from acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (SMPD1 mutations), causing sphingomyelin accumulation in lysosomes of neurons, macrophages, and visceral organs. Type A has severe neurological involvement from profound enzyme deficiency below 5%. The cherry-red spot in type A reflects sphingomyelin storage in retinal ganglion cells contrasting with the pale surrounding macula. Glucocerebroside accumulation characterizes Gaucher disease; galactocerebroside accumulation characterizes Krabbe disease specifically.
options: GM2 ganglioside in swollen cortical neuronal cytoplasm
Galactocerebroside in globoid perivascular white matter macrophages
Sphingomyelin in neuronal and visceral organ lysosomes
Sulfatide within oligodendrocyte and Schwann cell myelin
questions.question: A child with Niemann-Pick type A has progressive psychomotor deterioration with sphingomyelinase activity at 5% of normal. The primary substrate accumulating in neuronal lysosomes is:
Which pathological feature becomes universal in Down syndrome patients by age 40?
questions.explanation:
All Down syndrome individuals develop Alzheimer-type
neuropathological changes (amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles) by
age 40, though not all develop clinical dementia. This relates to APP
gene location on chromosome 21 with gene dosage effect. Average age of
dementia onset is 50-60 years, earlier than sporadic Alzheimer's.

options: Downregulation of MHC class I expression
questions.explanation:
Viruses like influenza undergo frequent mutations in
surface glycoproteins (antigenic drift/shift), creating variants
unrecognized by existing antibodies. This genetic instability allows
escape from immune surveillance despite previous exposure or
vaccination. The high error rate of viral polymerases facilitates this
continuous antigenic evolution.
questions.question: Which mechanism best explains how some viruses achieve immune evasion through antigenic variation?
Priapism is defined as:
questions.explanation: Priapism involves persistent erection unrelated to sexual stimulation lasting >4 hours, causing ischemic damage if untreated. Causes include sickle cell disease, medications (phosphodiesterase inhibitors, antipsychotics), malignancy, and trauma. Ischemic (low-flow) type requires emergency aspiration and intracavernosal injection; non-ischemic (high-flow) from arterial-lacunar fistula has better prognosis.

options: Echocardiography to screen for bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation
Pelvic ultrasound to confirm the presence of streak gonads
Bone density scan to quantify degree of osteoporosis at diagnosis
Thyroid function tests to detect autoimmune hypothyroidism
Renal ultrasound to identify horseshoe kidney malformation
questions.question: A 16-year-old girl with Turner syndrome (45,X) presents for evaluation. The single most important investigation at diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Congenital cardiovascular malformations occur in approximately 30% of Turner syndrome patients, most commonly bicuspid aortic valve (16%), coarctation of the aorta (11%), and aortic root dilation. These carry life-threatening risks including aortic dissection (25 times population risk). Echocardiography at diagnosis identifies structural defects requiring surgical or surveillance planning. While renal anomalies, hypothyroidism, streak gonads, and low bone density are all important to assess, cardiac screening takes highest priority given acute mortality risk.

Severe cholera presents with stools resembling rice water following an abrupt onset of watery diarrhea and vomiting after an incubation period of 1 to 5 days. The rate of diarrhea may reach 1 liter per hour. Mortality for severe cholera is about 50% without treatment, with most deaths occurring within the first 24 hours.
questions.question: What is the characteristic appearance of cholera stools?

questions.explanation:
Previous child with de novo chromosomal abnormality, advanced maternal
age, abnormal screening, or ultrasound anomalies justify diagnostic
testing. Balanced translocation carriers have higher recurrence risk.
questions.question: Which indication justifies prenatal diagnostic testing?

options: Testicular germ cell tumour including seminoma
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) increases the risk of testicular germ cell tumour by approximately 3-5 fold compared to normally descended testes. The elevated scrotal temperature impairs spermatogenesis and DNA repair mechanisms, predisposing to malignant transformation. Even after orchidopexy, the risk remains elevated, though early orchidopexy (before age 2) may reduce but does not eliminate this risk. The contralateral descended testis also carries increased risk. Annual self-examination and ultrasound surveillance are recommended in men with a history of cryptorchidism.
questions.question: A 35-year-old man with cryptorchidism is found to have testicular microlithiasis on ultrasound. Which condition does cryptorchidism most significantly increase the risk of developing?
Which organism characteristically causes cold abscesses without acute inflammatory features?
questions.explanation:
Tuberculous abscesses ("cold abscesses") lack the
warmth, erythema, and acute purulence of pyogenic abscesses due to
granulomatous rather than neutrophilic response. They contain caseous
material and may track along tissue planes. Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's
disease) classically produces psoas abscesses.

questions.question: Which cytogenetic abnormality in AML indicates favorable prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Core binding factor AMLs with t(8;21), inv(16), or
t(16;16) and APL with t(15;17) have favorable prognosis with high cure
rates using standard chemotherapy. Complex karyotype, monosomy 5/7, and
TP53 mutations indicate adverse risk. FLT3-ITD (internal tandem
duplication) confers poor prognosis; FLT3 inhibitors improve outcomes.

The antrum is the most common site for gastric adenocarcinoma. The lesser curvature is more commonly involved than the greater curvature. Tumors may be classified as intestinal or diffuse type according to the Lauren classification, with intestinal forms creating bulky tumors with glands.
questions.question: What is the most common site for gastric adenocarcinoma?
Placental infarction is associated with:
questions.explanation: Placental infarcts result from uteroplacental vascular insufficiency, commonly associated with maternal hypertension, pre-eclampsia, and thrombophilias. Small peripheral infarcts (<5% placental volume) are normal. Extensive infarction (>10%) causes fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, and fetal demise. Gross examination shows firm, pale, wedge-shaped lesions. Microscopic examination reveals villous ischemic necrosis.

Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) from MLH1 or MSH2 mutations confers a 50-80% lifetime risk of colorectal cancer, compared to 4-5% in the general population. Lynch syndrome causes defective DNA mismatch repair, leading to microsatellite instability. Cancers develop at younger ages (mean approximately 45 years), predominantly in the right colon. Surveillance colonoscopy every 1-2 years beginning at age 20-25 significantly reduces mortality. Lynch syndrome also confers elevated risk for endometrial, ovarian, gastric, and urinary tract cancers.
options: Slightly elevated at 10% lifetime risk compared to 5% general risk
Two to three times elevated with a 15% overall lifetime risk
Approximately 50 to 80% lifetime risk compared to 4 to 5% general
Similar to general population since MLH1 penetrance is low
Universal 100% requiring prophylactic total colectomy at age 20
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with Lynch syndrome has a germline MLH1 mutation. Her lifetime risk of colorectal cancer compared to the general population is:

A 55-year-old man with chronic alcohol use presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Serum lipase is markedly elevated. CT shows peripancreatic fat necrosis. What is the underlying mechanism of pancreatic injury?
options: Premature activation of pancreatic enzymes within acinar cells
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis, commonly caused by alcohol or gallstones, results from premature intra-acinar activation of digestive enzymes such as trypsinogen, leading to autodigestion of pancreatic tissue, fat necrosis, and inflammation. This enzymatic autodigestion, rather than infection or autoimmune attack, is the central mechanism of acinar cell injury.

options: LDL receptor deficiency causing severe hypercholesterolemia
VLDL overproduction from hepatic insulin resistance pattern
ApoC-II deficiency preventing LPL enzyme activation in capillaries
Hepatic lipase deficiency causing IDL and HDL accumulation
Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causing chylomicron accumulation
questions.explanation: Familial lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency causes massive chylomicronemia with triglycerides exceeding 20-50 mmol/L. Without LPL, dietary triglycerides in chylomicrons cannot be hydrolyzed in peripheral capillaries. The creamy plasma (lactescence) results from chylomicron accumulation. Acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomata, and lipemia retinalis are the cardinal manifestations. ApoC-II deficiency presents identically but is distinguished by LPL activity normalized on addition of normal serum. Treatment involves strict fat restriction to less than 20% of calories from fat to prevent recurrent pancreatitis.
questions.question: A 19-year-old presents with acute abdomen and creamy plasma after centrifugation. Triglycerides are 58 mmol/L. The most likely enzymatic defect is:
What enzyme elevation is characteristic of cholangiocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: Cholangiocarcinomas typically cause elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl-transpeptidase (GGT) due to cholestasis. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) may be mildly elevated. Bilirubin is elevated in extrahepatic or perihilar tumors causing biliary obstruction. The cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme elevation helps distinguish cholangiocarcinoma from hepatocellular injury patterns.

Primary biliary cholangitis (formerly primary biliary cirrhosis) typically affects women around age 50, with 90% female predominance. It is associated with other autoimmune conditions including Sjögren syndrome, scleroderma, and thyroid disease. Anti-mitochondrial antibody is the characteristic serologic marker.
questions.question: What is the characteristic age and gender distribution of primary biliary cholangitis?
What percentage of the pancreas is exocrine tissue?
questions.explanation: The exocrine pancreas constitutes approximately 80% of the pancreatic mass, comprising acini that produce digestive enzymes and ducts that transport secretions to the duodenum. The remaining 20% consists of endocrine tissue (islets of Langerhans) producing hormones including insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin. The exocrine pancreas is subject to inflammatory and neoplastic diseases.

questions.question: Neurocysticercosis is caused by:
questions.explanation: Neurocysticercosis results from Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) larvae forming cysts in brain parenchyma. Most common parasitic CNS infection worldwide. Seizures are primary manifestation. Imaging shows cystic lesions with scolex. Cyst degeneration triggers inflammation and calcification. Treatment combines antiparasitics (albendazole/praziquantel) with corticosteroids to reduce inflammation.

Tubal serous carcinomas are rare but increasing in recognition. Many ovarian high-grade serous carcinomas likely originate in fallopian tube fimbria as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinomas (STIC). p53 mutations are early events. Bilateral salpingectomy may prevent significant proportion of ovarian cancers. Presentation and treatment mirror ovarian carcinoma.
questions.question: Fallopian tube carcinoma is most commonly:

A 50-year-old man has a colonic polyp removed. Histology shows a serrated 'saw-tooth' luminal architecture with proliferation confined to the base of crypts and no nuclear atypia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyperplastic polyps show a serrated, saw-tooth luminal architecture with proliferation restricted to the crypt base and no cytological atypia, generally carrying minimal malignant potential. Sessile serrated lesions, in contrast, show serration extending to the crypt base with architectural distortion and basal dilation, carrying greater malignant potential via the serrated neoplasia pathway.

questions.question: Which three malignancies show highest tendency for splenic metastases?
options: Melanoma, lymphoma, and germ cell tumors
Brain, bone, and soft tissue sarcomas
questions.explanation:
Melanoma, lymphomas, and testicular germ cell tumors have
particular tropism for splenic metastases, likely related to rich blood
supply and immunologic microenvironment. Despite this, splenic
metastases from solid tumors remain uncommon overall. Isolated splenic
metastases are rare and may be amenable to splenectomy.

options: Trientine chelation with urgent liver transplant evaluation
Penicillamine as primary copper chelation for liver failure
Zinc acetate alone to block intestinal copper absorption
Dietary copper restriction as sole intervention approach
Plasmapheresis to remove circulating free copper rapidly
questions.explanation: Wilson disease with acute hepatic failure requires urgent evaluation for liver transplantation, as the condition can be rapidly fatal. Trientine is preferred over penicillamine in acute liver failure due to fewer adverse effects. Liver transplantation corrects the underlying hepatic copper metabolism defect permanently. Zinc therapy is used for maintenance or presymptomatic cases but is entirely inadequate in acute failure. Penicillamine can paradoxically worsen neurological symptoms acutely and is avoided in neurological or acute hepatic presentations of Wilson disease.
questions.question: A child with Wilson disease presents with Kayser-Fleischer rings, liver failure, and hemolytic anemia. The treatment of choice for acute liver failure is:
A 60-year-old man has haematuria and a 4 cm renal mass on CT showing clear cells and prominent sinusoidal vasculature. Biopsy shows VHL gene loss. Which chromosomal alteration is characteristic?
questions.explanation: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), the most common RCC subtype, is characterised by biallelic inactivation of the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p25, through deletion of 3p (loss of heterozygosity) combined with mutation or methylation of the remaining allele. VHL protein loss prevents HIF ubiquitination, leading to VEGF overexpression and angiogenesis — the rationale for VEGFR-targeted therapy (sunitinib, pazopanib). Sporadic ccRCC shows chromosome 3p deletion in approximately 90% of cases; VHL germline mutations cause hereditary ccRCC in Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.
options: Deletion of chromosome 3p with VHL mutation or methylation
Gain of chromosome 7 and loss of chromosome Y
t(X;1) translocation with TFE3 gene rearrangement
1p and 19q codeletion in sporadic renal lesions
Trisomy 7 and trisomy 17 on renal cytogenetics

questions.explanation:
Severe OI (Type II) shows multiple fractures and bone deformities on
prenatal ultrasound. Lethal perinatal form has shortened, deformed
limbs. Molecular testing confirms collagen mutations.
questions.question: Which osteogenesis imperfecta finding aids prenatal diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Triple negative breast cancers lack ER, PR, and HER2 expression, precluding targeted therapies. These aggressive tumors occur in younger women, show basal-like gene expression patterns, and have high recurrence rates. BRCA1-associated cancers are frequently triple negative. Chemotherapy remains the primary systemic treatment option with limited effectiveness.
questions.question: Which breast cancer subtype has the worst prognosis?

questions.explanation: Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1) is characterised by dense IgG4-positive lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, storiform ('swirling') fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis, often mimicking pancreatic cancer clinically and radiologically. Unlike adenocarcinoma, it characteristically responds dramatically to corticosteroid therapy, an important diagnostic and therapeutic clue.
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman has obstructive jaundice and elevated serum IgG4. Pancreatic biopsy shows dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is more vertically oriented and slightly wider than the left, making it the more common site for foreign body lodgement following aspiration, a pattern that persists into adulthood. This anatomical predisposition is important to recognise when localising suspected foreign body aspiration on imaging or during bronchoscopic retrieval. Delayed diagnosis can lead to recurrent pneumonia or bronchiectasis in the affected lung segment.
options: Longer left main bronchus compared to right
Narrower right main bronchus compared to left
More vertical and wider right main bronchus
Absence of a carina in young children
Smaller right lung volume compared to left
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with chronic cough and recurrent pneumonia, and bronchoscopy reveals a foreign body in the right main bronchus. Which anatomical feature explains the predisposition to right-sided foreign body aspiration in this age group?

questions.explanation: A polymorphonuclear leukocyte (PMN) count greater than 250 cells/mm³ in ascitic fluid in the absence of an intra-abdominal, surgically treatable source of infection indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. The ascitic fluid in portal hypertension is typically serous with less than 3 g/dL of protein.
questions.question: What polymorphonuclear leukocyte count in ascitic fluid suggests spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
Which opportunistic infection most commonly affects AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 200?
questions.explanation:
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia occurs when CD4 counts fall below 200
cells/?. Bilateral interstitial infiltrates and hypoxemia are
characteristic. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis prevents PCP.

questions.question: A 6-year-old with cystic fibrosis consistently grows mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa in sputum. The clinical significance of mucoid colony morphology is:
options: Beta-lactamase production conferring broad antibiotic resistance
Hypervirulence phenotype increasing systemic bacteremia risk
Indicator of chronic Aspergillus fungal co-infection presence
Alginate biofilm formation making eradication extremely difficult
Marker of the acute virulent Pseudomonas infection phase
questions.explanation: Mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa in CF lungs produces excess alginate, forming thick biofilms within bronchial secretions. Biofilm-embedded bacteria are phenotypically resistant to antibiotics and shielded from host immune defenses, making eradication virtually impossible once chronic infection is established. Management shifts from eradication to chronic suppression with inhaled antibiotics. The mucoid phenotype emerges from mutations under selective pressure of host immunity and antibiotic exposure within the viscid CF lung microenvironment over time.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis has a liver biopsy showing dense plasma cell-rich lymphocytic infiltrate, interface hepatitis, and emperipolesis. Serology shows positive anti-smooth muscle antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune hepatitis classically shows plasma cell-rich interface hepatitis with emperipolesis, where lymphocytes penetrate hepatocytes, alongside autoantibodies such as anti-smooth muscle antibody (type 1) or anti-LKM-1 (type 2). Primary biliary cholangitis instead targets bile ducts with granulomatous duct destruction and anti-mitochondrial antibodies.

Serous carcinomas are aggressive type II tumors showing papillary architecture with marked nuclear atypia, resembling ovarian serous carcinomas. p53 mutations are nearly universal. Arise in atrophic endometrium of elderly women. High propensity for myometrial invasion, lymphovascular invasion, and extrauterine spread. Poor prognosis requires aggressive treatment.
questions.question: Endometrial serous carcinoma characteristically shows:

questions.explanation:
Cri-du-chat syndrome from 5p15 deletion causes characteristic
high-pitched cat-like cry in infancy. Microcephaly, intellectual
disability, and typical facies occur. The cry becomes less distinctive
with age.
questions.question: Which chromosomal deletion syndrome shows cat-like cry?
What causes hypogonadism in male cirrhotic patients?
questions.explanation: Hypogonadism in male cirrhotic patients results from hyperestrogenism (impaired hepatic estrogen metabolism) and decreased testosterone production. Elevated estrogen suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary axis, reducing LH and FSH. This causes testicular atrophy, decreased libido, impotence, gynecomastia, and feminization. Alcohol has additional direct toxic effects on Leydig cells. Spider angiomas and palmar erythema also reflect hyperestrogenism.

TdT is a nuclear enzyme expressed in precursor
(lymphoblastic) T and B cells but lost during normal maturation, making
it a marker of lymphoblastic leukemias/lymphomas. Mature lymphoid
neoplasms are TdT negative, aiding in distinguishing precursor from
peripheral lymphomas. The enzyme adds random nucleotides during V(D)J
recombination.
questions.question: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) positivity is most characteristic of which lymphoid neoplasms?

questions.explanation: Ulcerative colitis is closely related to Crohn disease but is limited to the colon and rectum. The small intestine is normal except for mild mucosal inflammation of the distal ileum (backwash ileitis) in severe cases of pancolitis. The disease always involves the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous fashion.
questions.question: Which chronic inflammatory bowel disease is limited to the colon and rectum?
What characterizes the florid duct lesion in primary biliary cholangitis?
questions.explanation: The florid duct lesion in primary biliary cholangitis is characterized by active destruction of interlobular bile ducts by lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, often with granulomatous features. This immune-mediated bile duct destruction leads to progressive loss of small ducts (ductopenia), cholestasis, and eventually biliary cirrhosis. The process is insidious and progressive.

questions.question: What is gallstone ileus?
questions.explanation: Gallstone ileus occurs when a large gallstone erodes through the gallbladder wall into adjacent bowel (usually duodenum), creating a cholecystoenteric fistula. The stone then travels distally and may impact at the ileocecal valve, causing small bowel obstruction. This rare complication is more common in elderly patients with chronic cholecystitis. The classic radiographic triad is pneumobilia, intestinal obstruction, and ectopic gallstone.

options: Sessile polyp with serration throughout crypt
questions.question: What defines sessile serrated lesion?
questions.explanation: Sessile serrated lesions (SSL, formerly sessile serrated adenomas/polyps) are characterized by serration extending to the crypt base, often with horizontal growth along the crypt base ("boot-shaped" crypts). Unlike hyperplastic polyps (serration only in upper crypt), SSLs have malignant potential via the serrated pathway with BRAF mutations and CpG island methylation. They're more common in the right colon.

questions.question: What fold increase in hepatocellular carcinoma risk exists in hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Patients with hereditary hemochromatosis have a 200-fold increased risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma, with a lifetime risk of approximately 20%. This dramatically elevated risk results from chronic iron-induced oxidative stress, DNA damage, and cirrhosis. HCC may develop even in non-cirrhotic hemochromatosis patients, though cirrhosis significantly increases risk.

questions.question: In X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's), which stage of B cell development is primarily arrested?
questions.explanation:
BTK (Bruton tyrosine kinase) deficiency arrests
development at the pre-B cell stage, preventing maturation to
immunoglobulin-expressing B cells. The bone marrow shows absent mature B
cells despite normal pre-B cells. This explains the profound
hypogammaglobulinemia and absence of B cells in peripheral blood.

questions.question: Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy shows diffuse and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) with basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and hyaline arteriosclerosis. Microalbuminuria precedes overt proteinuria and renal failure. ACE inhibitors or ARBs slow progression. Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease.

questions.question: Juxtaglomerular cell tumor causes:
questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cell tumors (reninomas) secrete renin causing secondary hypertension, hypokalemia, and hyperaldosteronism in young patients. Small cortical masses. Elevated plasma renin and aldosterone with lateralization on renal vein sampling confirm diagnosis. Histology shows polygonal cells with renin granules. Surgical excision is curative with immediate blood pressure normalization.

Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies are highly specific
for SLE (though anti-Sm antibodies share similar specificity) and
correlate with disease activity and renal involvement. These antibodies
form circulating immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli causing
nephritis. While other autoantibodies occur in SLE, anti-dsDNA has both
diagnostic and prognostic significance.
questions.question: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus develops immune complex glomerulonephritis. Which antibody specificity is most diagnostic?
Corpora amylacea are:
questions.explanation: Corpora amylacea are rounded basophilic polyglucosan bodies accumulating in astrocytic processes with aging, found in subependymal, subpial, and perivascular regions. These represent degenerative change and increase with age. Not associated with pathologic significance, though abundant corpora amylacea may indicate chronic stress. Composed of glucose polymers with ubiquitin.

Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD, endocardial cushion defect) is the most common congenital heart disease in Down syndrome, occurring in approximately 40% of affected children. Complete AVSD involves both ASD and VSD components with a common AV valve. Early echocardiographic screening at birth is essential because untreated AVSD leads to irreversible pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger syndrome). Surgical repair before 6 months prevents this complication. While tetralogy, VSD, and PDA also occur in Down syndrome, AVSD is the most frequent and surgically urgent.
questions.question: Down syndrome from standard trisomy 21 nondisjunction requires cardiac investigation at birth. The most important echocardiographic finding to exclude urgently is:
options: Tetralogy of Fallot requiring early palliative Blalock-Taussig shunt
Patent ductus arteriosus causing left-to-right shunt and plethora
Atrioventricular septal defect with common AV valve involvement
Transposition of great arteries requiring balloon atrial septostomy
Coarctation of aorta causing differential blood pressure in limbs

questions.explanation: PML results from JC polyomavirus reactivation in immunosuppressed patients causing demyelination. Oligodendrocytes show enlarged nuclei with viral inclusions. Multifocal white matter lesions develop without mass effect or enhancement. Progressive neurologic deficits occur. No specific treatment exists; reconstituting immunity (antiretroviral therapy in AIDS) may stabilize disease. Prognosis is poor.
questions.question: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by:

questions.explanation: Acute mastitis during lactation is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), which gains entry through cracked or fissured nipples. The bacteria colonise the infant's nasopharynx and are transmitted to the breast during feeding. Inadequate breast emptying and milk stasis predispose to abscess formation. Treatment includes antibiotics (cloxacillin or vancomycin for MRSA), continued breastfeeding or expression, and incision and drainage if a fluctuant abscess forms. Ultrasound guides aspiration of deep abscesses.
options: Streptococcus agalactiae from neonatal oropharyngeal flora
Staphylococcus aureus entering via cracked nipple skin
Klebsiella pneumoniae from descending lymphatic infection
questions.question: A lactating woman develops a tender, erythematous, fluctuant breast mass after nipple fissuring. Which organism is most likely responsible for this complication?

questions.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations) causes multiple bilateral renal angiomyolipomas (80%), cysts, and occasionally renal cell carcinomas.
