Angiomyolipomas contain blood vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue. Fat-containing masses on CT are characteristic. Large tumors (>4cm) risk spontaneous hemorrhage requiring intervention. mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) shrink angiomyolipomas.
questions.question: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with which renal tumor?

questions.explanation: DES exposure in utero causes vaginal adenosis (persistence of columnar epithelium) predisposing to clear cell adenocarcinoma in adolescents and young adults. The medication was used to prevent miscarriage from 1940s-1970s before this association was discovered. Characteristic histology shows hobnail cells with clear cytoplasm and tubulocystic architecture.
questions.question: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina is associated with in utero exposure to:

questions.explanation: Duct ectasia involves dilation of subareolar ducts containing thick, lipid-laden secretions and foamy macrophages. Periductal chronic inflammation and fibrosis develop, potentially causing nipple retraction and discharge. The condition occurs in perimenopausal women and may mimic carcinoma clinically. Plasma cell mastitis describes prominent plasma cell infiltration.
options: Lactiferous duct dilation with inspissated secretions
questions.question: Duct ectasia of the breast characteristically shows:

questions.explanation:
Chondrosarcoma occurs in adults (40-60 years), affecting
axial skeleton (pelvis, shoulder, ribs) more than appendicular skeleton.
The tumor produces cartilage matrix. Most are primary (de novo); some
arise from pre-existing enchondromas or osteochondromas. Histological
grading (I-III) predicts behavior. Treatment is surgical; chemotherapy
and radiation are ineffective.
questions.question: Chondrosarcoma most commonly arises in which patient population and location?

questions.explanation: The Ghon complex consists of the Ghon focus (primary parenchymal subpleural lesion, usually in the lower or mid-lung zone) combined with enlarged ipsilateral hilar or tracheobronchial lymph nodes representing lymphatic spread. Together these two calcified components form the Ranke complex on imaging. Most primary TB complexes heal and calcify, representing contained infection. Progressive primary TB occurs when the immune response fails to contain the infection, particularly in immunocompromised or malnourished individuals with inadequate cellular immunity.
questions.question: In primary tuberculosis, the two components forming the Ghon complex on imaging are:
options: Pleural effusion and parenchymal lower lobe consolidation
Ghon focus and ipsilateral hilar lymph node calcification
Cavitary lesion with upper lobe satellite fibrotic nodules
Miliary nodules with bilateral symmetrical hilar adenopathy
Ghon focus with surrounding perihilar inflammatory pneumonitis

questions.question: What inheritance pattern characterizes achondroplasia?
questions.explanation:
Achondroplasia shows autosomal dominant inheritance though 80% represent
new mutations. Advanced paternal age increases mutation risk.
Homozygosity is lethal.

questions.question: What clinical course characterizes infantile Tay-Sachs disease?
questions.explanation:
Infantile Tay-Sachs shows rapid progressive neurodegeneration leading to
death by 4 years. An exaggerated startle response to sound is
characteristic. No effective treatment exists.

questions.question: A 2-year-old presents with recurrent infections, eczema, and is found to have an elevated IgM level with low IgG and IgA. Which underlying mechanism best explains this immunoglobulin pattern?
questions.explanation: Hyper-IgM syndrome results from defective CD40 ligand signalling required for immunoglobulin class switching from IgM to IgG and IgA, leading to elevated or normal IgM with deficient IgG and IgA, predisposing to recurrent bacterial and opportunistic infections. This contrasts with X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, where all immunoglobulin classes are reduced due to a block earlier in B-cell development. Recognising this specific pattern guides appropriate immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis strategies.

questions.question: Which Leber hereditary optic neuropathy feature is characteristic?
questions.explanation:
LHON causes acute or subacute bilateral central vision loss from optic
nerve degeneration. Males are predominantly affected despite maternal
inheritance. Visual loss is usually permanent.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man has bronze skin pigmentation, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy. Liver biopsy with Perls' stain shows blue-staining pigment within hepatocytes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hereditary haemochromatosis results from excessive intestinal iron absorption, typically due to HFE gene mutations, leading to iron deposition in the liver, pancreas, heart, and skin. Perls' Prussian blue stain demonstrates iron as blue-staining granules within hepatocytes. The triad of bronze skin, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy reflects multi-organ iron deposition.

Salmonella flagellin activates TLR5 on host cells, increasing the local inflammatory response. Bacterial lipopolysaccharide activates TLR4. Salmonella also secretes molecules that induce epithelial release of the eicosanoid hepoxilin A3, and mucosal TH17 immune responses limit infection to the colon.
questions.question: Which toll-like receptor is activated by Salmonella flagellin?

questions.explanation:
High-energy demanding tissues like brain and muscle are most vulnerable
to mitochondrial dysfunction. Oxidative phosphorylation defects impair
ATP production. Neurons and myocytes show greatest sensitivity.
questions.question: Which organ systems are most vulnerable to mitochondrial dysfunction?

questions.explanation:
Reed-Sternberg cells and Hodgkin cells in classical Hodgkin lymphoma are
derived from germinal center B cells. These cells have undergone somatic
hypermutation with crippled immunoglobulin genes preventing normal B
cell function. The malignant cells comprise only small percentage of
tumor mass with reactive inflammatory cells forming bulk.
questions.question: Which cell type is the malignant cell in Hodgkin lymphoma?

questions.explanation: Osteoid osteomas cause severe nocturnal pain dramatically relieved by aspirin/NSAIDs due to prostaglandin production by tumor. Small (<2cm) cortical lesions with central nidus surrounded by reactive sclerosis appear on imaging. Most occur in proximal femur and tibia in adolescents and young adults. Surgical excision or radiofrequency ablation is curative.
questions.question: Osteoid osteoma characteristically presents with:

questions.explanation:
Delayed-type hypersensitivity (type IV) is characterized
by CD4+ T cell and macrophage accumulation around venules, creating
perivascular cuffing. These T cells recognize presented antigen and
secrete IFN-?, activating macrophages that mediate tissue damage. This
classic pattern distinguishes cell-mediated from antibody-mediated
immune reactions.
questions.question: A tuberculin skin test demonstrates delayed-type hypersensitivity. Which cells predominate in the perivascular infiltrate at 48 hours?

questions.explanation: Microscopic examination in cholestasis reveals green-brown plugs of bile in canaliculi, brown pigment in Kupffer cells, and droplets of bile in hepatocytes (feathery degeneration). Prolonged cholestasis leads to bile duct proliferation, portal inflammation, and eventually biliary fibrosis and cirrhosis.
questions.question: What is the characteristic microscopic finding in cholestasis?

options: XYY males have increased risk of violent criminal behavior
The boy will be infertile and require testosterone replacement
Testosterone therapy is needed to normalize height velocity
XYY is associated with tall stature but normal intelligence and fertility
Psychiatric medications are required to prevent antisocial behavior
questions.question: A 14-year-old boy is found to have 47,XYY karyotype after referral for severe acne and tall stature. The most important information for the family is:
questions.explanation: 47,XYY syndrome is associated with tall stature and may include mild learning difficulties, but intelligence and fertility are typically normal or near-normal. The historical association with criminality was a significant overestimate derived from ascertainment bias in prison populations. Population studies show no meaningful increase in violent behavior. Most XYY males are identified incidentally during prenatal diagnosis or investigation for another condition. Counseling should emphasize the generally favorable prognosis and avoid the harmful stigmatization associated with historical case reports.

IGCN represents carcinoma in situ of testis, showing large atypical germ cells with clear cytoplasm, enlarged nuclei, and prominent nucleoli along basement membrane of seminiferous tubules. Placental-like alkaline phosphatase and OCT4 expression aid diagnosis. Approximately 50% progress to invasive germ cell tumors within five years if untreated.
questions.question: Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (IGCN) is characterized by:

questions.explanation: The rectum is invariably affected in Hirschsprung disease, with variable proximal extension. The aganglionic segment undergoes functional obstruction while the proximal unaffected colon shows progressive dilation and hypertrophy, forming a megacolon. Diagnosis requires histological documentation of absent ganglion cells in the affected segment.
questions.question: Which intestinal segment is always affected in Hirschsprung disease?

questions.explanation: Xp11 translocation RCCs involve TFE3 or TFEB gene fusions, occurring predominantly in children and young adults (25% of pediatric RCC). Also occurs after chemotherapy. Histology shows clear cells and papillae. Immunostains for TFE3 aid diagnosis. Aggressive behavior in adults; better prognosis in children. Resistance to conventional therapies but may respond to MET inhibitors.
questions.question: Xp11 translocation renal cell carcinoma characteristically occurs in:

questions.explanation:
Holoprosencephaly from failed forebrain division is characteristic of
trisomy 13. Midline facial defects, cleft lip/palate, and polydactyly
are also seen. Multiple malformations suggest chromosomal abnormality.
questions.question: What ultrasound finding suggests trisomy 13?

A 50-year-old man undergoes radical nephroureterectomy for a renal pelvis tumour. Histology shows urothelial carcinoma invading the muscularis propria (T2). Which feature most strongly predicts disease-specific survival?
questions.explanation: The most important prognostic factor in upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) is pathological stage (depth of invasion) and histological grade. T2 (muscularis propria invasion) carries substantially worse prognosis than non-muscle-invasive disease. Stage for stage and grade for grade, UTUC has similar prognosis to bladder urothelial carcinoma. Radical nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision is the standard treatment for high-grade non-metastatic UTUC. Adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy improves survival in pT2-T4 or node-positive disease following surgery.
options: Pathological stage and grade of the tumour
Tumour size exceeding 3 cm in greatest dimension
Lymphovascular invasion in the urothelial carcinoma
Concomitant carcinoma in situ in the ureter
Multifocality of urothelial carcinoma in the upper tract

questions.explanation: Central diabetes insipidus results from ADH deficiency due to hypothalamic or posterior pituitary damage. Patients present with polyuria (>3L/day) and polydipsia with dilute urine (specific gravity <
questions.question: Diabetes insipidus results from deficiency of:
Paget disease of bone is characterized by which histological feature?
questions.explanation:
Paget disease shows abnormal bone remodeling with
increased osteoclast and osteoblast activity, producing disorganized
woven bone in a mosaic "jigsaw puzzle" pattern. Affected bones are
enlarged, deformed, and prone to fracture. Complications include
high-output heart failure (increased vascularity), nerve compression,
and rarely osteosarcoma. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly
elevated.

questions.question: Which genetic alteration is most frequently found in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?
questions.explanation:
KRAS mutations occur in over 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas
and are considered initiating events. These mutations lead to
constitutive activation of downstream signaling pathways including
RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade. KRAS mutations typically occur early in
pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia progression before other genetic
alterations accumulate.

Approximately 50% of Shigella patients progress from watery diarrhea to a dysenteric phase. The disease is typically self-limited, characterized by about 6 days of diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain. The subacute presentation may involve several weeks of waxing and waning diarrhea.
questions.question: What percentage of Shigella infections progress to the dysenteric phase?

questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is histologically defined by diffuse bridging fibrosis connecting portal and central regions, with formation of regenerative nodules that disrupt the normal hepatic lobular architecture, representing the end stage of many chronic liver diseases. This irreversible architectural distortion impairs normal hepatic blood flow and function, contributing to portal hypertension and liver failure. Recognising this pattern on biopsy is important for staging and prognosis in chronic liver disease.
questions.question: A patient with chronic liver disease undergoes biopsy showing bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules disrupting normal architecture. Which term best describes this histological pattern?
What mutation causes most cystic fibrosis cases?
questions.explanation:
?F508 deletion accounts for approximately 70% of CF alleles. This
mutation causes misfolding and degradation of CFTR protein. Over 2000
different CFTR mutations have been identified.

questions.question: Perineural invasion in prostate adenocarcinoma indicates:
questions.explanation: Perineural invasion by malignant glands is highly specific for prostate adenocarcinoma. Tumor cells track along nerve sheaths, serving as low-resistance pathway for spread. Intraneural invasion portends worse prognosis with increased extraprostatic extension risk. Finding perineural invasion on biopsy confirms malignancy even when other features are ambiguous.

questions.question: Which plexuses are absent in Hirschsprung disease?
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease is characterized by the absence of both Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus and Meissner's (submucosal) plexus in the affected segment. This results from arrested migration of neural crest cells from proximal to distal, leading to functional obstruction. The rectum is always affected with variable proximal involvement.

questions.question: Targeted therapy for clear cell RCC includes:
questions.explanation: Clear cell RCC responds to VEGF pathway inhibitors (sunitinib, pazopanib, bevacizumab, cabozantinib, axitinib) and mTOR inhibitors (temsirolimus, everolimus). VHL loss causes HIF accumulation, upregulating VEGF. Recent addition of checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, ipilimumab) improves outcomes. Combination immunotherapy or immunotherapy plus VEGF inhibitor now first-line.

Blastomyces shows broad-based budding (in contrast to
Cryptococcus with narrow-based budding) with thick, refractile cell wall
and large size (8-15μm). The organism causes granulomatous inflammation
in lungs and disseminates to skin and bone. Endemic areas include
Mississippi and Ohio River valleys.
questions.question: Blastomyces dermatitidis is characterized by which morphological feature?
Adenomyosis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Adenomyosis requires endometrial glands and stroma at least 2mm (one low-power field) below the endometrial-myometrial junction. Diffuse or focal patterns cause uterine enlargement, dysmenorrhea, and menorrhagia. Hysterectomy specimen shows thickened myometrium with hemorrhagic foci. Medical management includes NSAIDs and hormonal therapy; hysterectomy provides definitive cure.

Ataxia-telangiectasia results from mutations in the ATM gene, which is critical for DNA double-strand break repair, leading to progressive cerebellar degeneration, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, and increased cancer susceptibility. The combined neurological and immunological features distinguish it from isolated immunodeficiency syndromes. Increased sensitivity to ionising radiation is also a notable feature requiring caution with diagnostic imaging in affected patients.
questions.question: A 10-year-old presents with progressive ataxia, telangiectasia of the conjunctivae, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Which underlying defect explains this combination of neurological and immune findings?

questions.explanation: Williams syndrome hemizygous deletion of 7q11.23 includes the elastin gene. Elastin deficiency causes supravalvular aortic stenosis through abnormal smooth muscle proliferation narrowing the aorta above the valve. Peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis is also common. Ventricular and atrial septal defects characterize Down syndrome, while tetralogy of Fallot is associated with 22q11.2 deletion rather than Williams syndrome.
questions.question: Williams syndrome requires cardiac surgery. The defect most likely needing intervention results from hemizygous elastin deletion at 7q11.23:
options: Ventricular septal defect in perimembranous position
Tetralogy of Fallot with right ventricular hypertrophy
Supravalvular aortic stenosis above the aortic valve
Atrial septal defect in ostium secundum position
Patent ductus arteriosus in premature neonatal period
Discohesive cells resembling lobular breast carcinoma
questions.question: Plasmacytoid variant of urothelial carcinoma is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma shows discohesive cells with eccentric nuclei infiltrating diffusely, resembling signet-ring cells or lobular breast carcinoma. Loss of E-cadherin occurs. Highly aggressive with peritoneal spread. Difficult to diagnose due to subtle infiltration. Requires immunostains (GATA3, CK7, CK20, uroplakin) to confirm urothelial origin. Poor prognosis despite aggressive treatment.

questions.question: What metabolite accumulates in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy?
questions.explanation:
ABCD1 gene mutations impair peroxisomal beta-oxidation of very long
chain fatty acids. VLCFA accumulation damages myelin and adrenal cortex.
Elevated plasma VLCFA levels confirm diagnosis.

questions.question: A complete hydatidiform mole most commonly has which karyotype?
questions.explanation: Most complete moles result from monospermic fertilization of an empty ovum followed by duplication of the paternal haploid genome, producing 46,XX karyotype. Dispermic fertilization accounts for remaining cases producing 46,XX or 46,XY. Complete moles lack fetal tissue and show diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia with high malignant potential.

questions.question: Which glycogen storage disease causes massive hepatomegaly?
questions.explanation:
Von Gierke disease (Type I) from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes
massive hepatomegaly from glycogen accumulation. Severe hypoglycemia,
lactic acidosis, and hyperuricemia occur. Growth retardation and hepatic
adenomas develop.

questions.question: A 2-year-old child has painless rectal bleeding. Technetium-99m scan shows uptake in the right lower quadrant. Resection shows ileal mucosa containing ectopic gastric mucosa. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum resulting from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct, often containing ectopic gastric or pancreatic mucosa. Ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid that can ulcerate adjacent ileal mucosa, causing painless rectal bleeding. The technetium-99m scan detects uptake by the gastric mucosa, aiding diagnosis.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of polyps required for diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is diagnosed when a minimum of 100 adenomatous polyps are present in the colorectum. It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations of the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene. Untreated patients have a 100% risk of developing colorectal carcinoma.

Nephrogenic adenoma (nephrogenic metaplasia) is benign reactive proliferation of urothelium forming tubules resembling renal tubules, occurring after injury (instrumentation, stones, infection, BCG). May mimic adenocarcinoma. PAX8 positive confirms renal-type differentiation. No malignant potential. Usually asymptomatic; observation appropriate. May recur but remains benign.
questions.question: Nephrogenic adenoma of bladder is:

questions.explanation: Ductal carcinoma in situ represents neoplastic proliferation of epithelial cells confined within ducts without basement membrane invasion. High-grade DCIS carries substantial risk of progression to invasive carcinoma if untreated. Comedo-type DCIS with central necrosis has particularly aggressive behavior and requires complete excision with adequate margins.
questions.question: Which breast lesion shows the highest risk for subsequent development of invasive carcinoma?

A 60-year-old woman has chronic watery diarrhoea with a normal-appearing colon on colonoscopy. Biopsy shows more than 20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 surface epithelial cells without a thickened collagen band. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytic colitis is a microscopic colitis subtype defined by increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (typically over 20 per 100 surface epithelial cells) without the thickened subepithelial collagen band seen in collagenous colitis. Both conditions present with chronic watery diarrhoea and a macroscopically normal colon, making biopsy essential for diagnosis.

questions.question: Brodie abscess represents:
questions.explanation: Brodie abscess is localized chronic osteomyelitis forming well-circumscribed intraosseous abscess with surrounding sclerosis, typically in metaphysis of long bones. Results from contained infection without systemic symptoms. Staphylococcus aureus is usual organism. Radiographically appears as lucent lesion with sclerotic rim. Treatment involves curettage and antibiotics.

Anticipation describes increasing severity and earlier onset in
successive generations. Progressive CGG expansion during maternal
transmission causes anticipation. Premutation carriers have affected
grandchildren through full mutation development.
questions.question: What phenomenon explains worsening severity in fragile X across generations?
Which trisomy shows longest survival?
questions.explanation:
Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is compatible with survival to adulthood.
Modern medical care extends lifespan to 60+ years. Trisomies 13 and 18
are typically lethal in infancy.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman has multiple cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, cutaneous nodules, and optic pathway gliomas on MRI. Which mutation is responsible?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1/Recklinghausen disease) is caused by NF1 gene mutations on chromosome 17q11, encoding neurofibromin (a RAS-GTPase activating protein/tumour suppressor). Diagnostic criteria include six or more cafe-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, optic pathway glioma, two or more Lisch nodules, distinctive bony lesions, or a first-degree relative with NF1. NF1 is autosomal dominant with 100% penetrance but variable expressivity. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST) is the most serious complication.
options: TSC1 mutation causing hamartin loss of function
PTCH1 mutation in the Hedgehog signalling pathway

questions.explanation:
Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes glucocerebroside accumulation in
Gaucher disease. Type 1 (non-neuronopathic) is most common showing
hepatosplenomegaly and bone involvement. Gaucher cells are lipid-laden
macrophages.
questions.question: Which enzyme is deficient in Gaucher disease?

questions.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional renal failure occurring in advanced cirrhosis, caused by splanchnic vasodilation and reduced effective renal perfusion without intrinsic kidney pathology, hence the bland urinalysis. It is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out other causes of renal failure such as acute tubular necrosis, hypovolaemia, or obstruction.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis develops worsening ascites despite diuretics, along with progressive renal failure and a bland urinalysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which substance is primarily responsible for the apple-green birefringence seen in amyloid deposits under polarized light microscopy?
questions.explanation:
Congo red stain binds specifically to the beta-pleated
sheet configuration characteristic of all amyloid proteins, producing
the pathognomonic apple-green birefringence under polarized light
microscopy. This property distinguishes amyloid from other hyaline
materials and is essential for definitive diagnosis. The staining
pattern remains consistent regardless of the precursor protein type.
options: Congo red staining of beta-pleated sheets

questions.question: What causes the dark urine in alkaptonuria?
questions.explanation:
Homogentisic acid oxidizes to dark polymer on exposure to air turning
urine black. This benign finding may alarm patients. Connective tissue
pigmentation (ochronosis) causes later complications.

Courvoisier sign is an enlarged non-tender gallbladder associated with jaundice, classically seen in pancreatic head carcinoma. It occurs when the tumor obstructs the common bile duct, leading to gallbladder distension. This distinguishes pancreatic cancer from choledocholithiasis, which typically causes a tender, non-distended gallbladder.
questions.question: What is Courvoisier sign?
Endometrial clear cell carcinoma is associated with:
questions.explanation: Clear cell carcinomas are rare type II tumors with clear or hobnail cells, similar aggressive behavior to serous carcinomas. p53 mutations and HNF-1 expression occur. Tubulocystic, papillary, and solid patterns exist. High stage at presentation with poor prognosis. No association with estrogen stimulation or endometrial hyperplasia.

questions.question: What is the characteristic CSF finding in cryptococcal meningitis?
questions.explanation:
Cryptococcal meningitis shows elevated protein, low glucose, lymphocytic
pleocytosis, and elevated opening pressure. India ink preparation
reveals encapsulated yeast in 50-80% of cases. Cryptococcal antigen
testing is highly sensitive.

questions.question: What laboratory finding suggests mitochondrial disease?
questions.explanation:
Elevated blood and CSF lactate from impaired oxidative metabolism
suggests mitochondrial disease. Lactate-to-pyruvate ratio helps
distinguish from other causes. Exercise testing shows exaggerated
lactate response.

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl presents with grape-like polypoid vaginal masses protruding from the introitus. Biopsy shows primitive round cells beneath intact vaginal epithelium with a condensed subepithelial cambium layer. What is this tumour?
questions.explanation: Sarcoma botryoides (botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma) is the most common vaginal malignancy in girls under 5 years, presenting as grape-like polypoid masses. The cambium layer — a condensed subepithelial zone of primitive rhabdomyoblasts — is pathognomonic. Cells may show cross-striations and express desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1 on immunohistochemistry. Treatment involves multiagent chemotherapy (VAC regimen) followed by conservative surgery. Modern multimodal treatment has significantly improved survival while preserving bladder and sexual function.
options: Clear cell adenocarcinoma from in utero DES exposure
Endodermal sinus tumour of vaginal origin
Papillary squamous cell carcinoma of the vagina
Benign fibroepithelial stromal polyp of vagina

questions.explanation: Leiomyosarcomas show high mitotic activity (>10 mitoses/10 HPF), significant nuclear atypia, and coagulative tumor cell necrosis. These aggressive malignancies arise de novo rather than from leiomyomas. Hematogenous spread to lungs is common. Poor prognosis with 50% five-year survival. Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is treatment.
questions.question: Leiomyosarcoma differs from leiomyoma by showing:
What is the most characteristic gross appearance pattern of HCC?
questions.explanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma can present with three main gross patterns: unifocal (usually large) mass, multifocal widely distributed nodules of variable size, or a diffusely infiltrative mass. The pattern depends on tumor biology, underlying liver disease, and stage at diagnosis. All patterns can occur with or without background cirrhosis.

questions.question: What distinguishes Type I from Type II osteogenesis imperfecta?
questions.explanation:
Type I OI is mildest form compatible with normal lifespan while Type II
is perinatally lethal. Type III shows progressive deformity and Type IV
has variable severity. All result from COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations.

questions.question: A male infant with classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency) is treated with galactose-free formula from day 3 of life. Despite excellent dietary compliance, the most common long-term complication is:
questions.explanation: Despite early dietary galactose elimination, classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency) is associated with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) in approximately 80% of female patients, causing early menopause, infertility, and need for hormone replacement therapy. The mechanism involves endogenous galactose production (from cellular metabolism) accumulating as toxic galactose-1-phosphate in ovarian tissue during critical fetal development, irreversibly damaging the primordial follicle pool before dietary intervention can begin. This complication occurs regardless of early treatment initiation, distinguishing it from other manifestations that respond to dietary therapy.
options: Hepatocellular carcinoma from residual galactose-1-phosphate toxicity
Renal tubular dysfunction from ongoing galactitol nephrotoxicity
Premature ovarian insufficiency in female patients despite treatment
Progressive visual impairment from bilateral cataracts reforming
Severe intellectual disability from neurological galactitol toxicity

questions.explanation: Children with Down syndrome have a significantly increased risk of acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia, often preceded by a transient myeloproliferative disorder in the neonatal period. GATA1 gene mutations are frequently implicated in the pathogenesis of this leukaemia subtype in this population. Recognising this association is important for monitoring children with Down syndrome for haematological abnormalities.
questions.question: A child with Down syndrome develops easy bruising and is found to have a markedly elevated white cell count with blasts showing megakaryocytic markers on immunophenotyping. Which leukaemia subtype is most associated with this combination?

questions.explanation:
Approximately 95% of males with CF are infertile due to
congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD), though
spermatogenesis is normal. CBAVD can occur as isolated finding with mild
CFTR mutations. Fertility is possible through surgical sperm retrieval
and assisted reproduction.
questions.question: Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens in males is associated with which condition?
What is the most common cause of acute liver failure requiring transplantation in the United States?
questions.explanation: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is the most common cause of acute liver failure needing transplantation in the United States. Toxicity occurs from direct hepatocellular injury when toxic metabolites overwhelm hepatic glutathione stores. This is a preventable cause of acute liver failure, highlighting the importance of safe medication use.

ATP7B gene mutations impair hepatic copper excretion into bile. Copper
accumulates in liver, brain, cornea, and kidneys. Hepatic cirrhosis and
neuropsychiatric symptoms develop.
questions.question: What causes copper accumulation in Wilson disease?
What percentage of chromosomal microarray results show VUS?
questions.explanation:
Variants of uncertain significance occur in 5-10% of clinical
microarrays. These create counseling challenges and require follow-up.
Databases improve VUS interpretation over time.

questions.question: Which 22q11.2 deletion syndrome feature is most common?
questions.explanation:
Conotruncal cardiac defects occur in 75% of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
cases. Tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch, and truncus
arteriosus are typical. DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome phenotype
varies widely.

questions.question: Oncotype DX recurrence score predicts benefit from:
questions.explanation: Oncotype DX analyzes 21 genes in ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative breast cancer, providing recurrence score predicting chemotherapy benefit. Low scores (<11) indicate excellent prognosis with endocrine therapy alone; high scores (>25) benefit from chemotherapy. Intermediate scores (11-25) may be managed based on clinical-pathologic features. TAILORx trial guides treatment decisions.

Mitochondrial DNA shows maternal inheritance since oocytes provide all
mitochondria. Heteroplasmy affects phenotype severity. Males cannot
transmit mtDNA mutations to offspring.
questions.question: Which mitochondrial disorder inheritance pattern differs from nuclear genes?

questions.explanation:
Modified Gomori trichrome stain reveals ragged red fibers from
subsarcolemmal mitochondrial accumulation. These abnormal mitochondria
contain paracrystalline inclusions on electron microscopy. Muscle biopsy
aids diagnosis.
questions.question: Which tissue shows ragged red fibers in mitochondrial diseases?

questions.explanation: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involves clonal proliferation of dendritic cells with characteristic kidney-shaped (reniform) nuclei, positive for CD1a and S100, often with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy. Clinical presentation ranges from isolated bone lesions to multisystem disease involving skin, lymph nodes, and viscera. This distinguishes it from Ewing sarcoma, which shows small round blue cells without histiocytic markers.
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with bone pain, lytic skull lesions, and a skin rash. Biopsy of a lesion shows cells with kidney-shaped nuclei and positive CD1a and S100 staining. Which condition is most likely?
options: Eosinophilic granuloma alone without systemic involvement

questions.question: What finding suggests chronic rather than acute cholecystitis?
questions.explanation: Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses (outpouchings of mucosal epithelium through the muscular wall) are characteristic of chronic cholecystitis. Other chronic features include wall thickening, fibrosis, chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages), and possible calcification. Acute cholecystitis shows edema, hemorrhage, neutrophilic infiltration, and possible necrosis. The two may coexist (acute on chronic).

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids. Barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus with a 'bird's beak' narrowing at the lower end. Manometry shows failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, causing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis. The bird's beak sign on barium swallow and impaired sphincter relaxation on manometry are classic. Diffuse spasm shows a corkscrew pattern instead, and scleroderma shows reduced sphincter tone, not failure to relax.

questions.question: A 9-year-old presents with progressive kyphoscoliosis, gait ataxia, and absent deep tendon reflexes alongside cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing reveals a trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin gene. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Friedreich ataxia results from a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin gene, causing progressive degeneration of the spinocerebellar tracts and dorsal columns, producing ataxia, absent reflexes, and skeletal abnormalities such as kyphoscoliosis, along with characteristic cardiomyopathy contributing significantly to mortality. This combination of neurological and cardiac findings distinguishes it from other inherited ataxias. Genetic confirmation of the repeat expansion establishes the diagnosis.

questions.question: Which condition is associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome?
questions.explanation: Plummer-Vinson syndrome, also known as Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome, is associated with esophageal webs. These are vascularized fibrous tissue covered by mucosa protruding into the lumen, typically in the upper esophagus. The syndrome also includes iron-deficiency anemia, glossitis, and increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.question: A 1-year-old presents with hypotonia, tongue fasciculations, and absent deep tendon reflexes, with normal cognitive development. Genetic testing reveals a deletion in the SMN1 gene. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy results from SMN1 gene mutations, causing degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, producing progressive symmetric muscle weakness and hypotonia while sparing cognitive function, distinguishing it from many other severe infantile neuromuscular conditions. Tongue fasciculations reflect denervation of bulbar musculature. Newer disease-modifying therapies targeting SMN protein production have significantly improved outcomes when administered early in the disease course.

options: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with papillary architecture
questions.explanation: Papillary renal cell carcinoma (pRCC) type 1 is characterised by papillae lined by small cells with scanty pale cytoplasm and low-grade nuclei, and is associated with trisomy 7, trisomy 17, and loss of chromosome Y. MET gene mutations (chromosome 7q31) drive hereditary papillary RCC type 1. Psammoma bodies may be present. Type 2 pRCC shows pseudostratified eosinophilic cells with high-grade nuclei and is associated with CIITA mutations and CDKN2A loss, carrying worse prognosis. pRCC overall has better prognosis than clear cell RCC stage-for-stage.
questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents with haematuria and a 2 cm papillary renal mass. Histology shows papillae lined by cells with foamy (clear) cytoplasm, psammoma bodies, and papillary architecture. Chromosome analysis shows trisomy 7 and trisomy 17. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation:
The red pulp, comprising about 75% of splenic tissue,
contains macrophage-rich cords of Billroth and vascular sinusoids that
filter blood and remove aged/damaged red cells. This "open
circulation" allows prolonged cell-macrophage interaction.
Hypersplenism results from excessive red pulp function causing
cytopenias.
questions.question: Which splenic compartment is primarily responsible for filtering blood and removing senescent erythrocytes?

questions.explanation:
Approximately 40% of neuroblastomas arise in the adrenal
medulla, 25% in abdominal paravertebral sympathetic ganglia, and 15% in
posterior mediastinum. These neural crest-derived tumors can occur
anywhere along the sympathetic chain. Adrenal location often presents as
abdominal mass in young children.
questions.question: Neuroblastoma most commonly arises from which anatomical location?

questions.explanation: CIN3 (high-grade dysplasia/carcinoma in situ) shows diffuse atypia involving full epithelial thickness with loss of maturation and orientation. CIN1 (low-grade dysplasia) demonstrates koilocytic atypia mainly in upper layers with preserved maturation. CIN2 shows intermediate features with atypia extending through lower two-thirds of epithelium.
questions.question: CIN3 differs from CIN1 by showing:

questions.explanation: Emperipolesis refers to the phenomenon where one cell penetrates into another intact cell, commonly seen in autoimmune hepatitis where lymphocytes are found within hepatocytes. This is distinct from phagocytosis. Along with hepatocyte rosette formation and prominent plasma cells, it is a helpful diagnostic feature of autoimmune hepatitis.
questions.question: What is emperipolesis in autoimmune hepatitis?
What is the prognosis for cholangiocarcinoma at diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The outlook for cholangiocarcinoma is very dismal because it is rarely resectable at the time of diagnosis. These tumors are typically advanced at presentation due to insidious onset and lack of early symptoms. The 5-year survival rate is less than 10% overall, though early-stage resectable tumors have better outcomes. Most patients present with unresectable or metastatic disease.

Nontyphoid Salmonella infection is usually due to Salmonella enteritidis. Transmission is most commonly through contaminated food, particularly raw or undercooked meat, poultry, eggs, and milk. Infection is most common in young children and the elderly.
questions.question: What is the most common cause of nontyphoid Salmonella infection?

A 45-year-old man has recurrent hypoglycaemia with episodes of confusion relieved by eating. Imaging localises a pancreatic tail mass. Biopsy shows uniform cells in a trabecular pattern, positive for insulin and chromogranin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Insulinoma is the most common functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, characteristically causing fasting hypoglycaemia with neuroglycopenic symptoms relieved by glucose ingestion (Whipple's triad). Histologically these tumours show the typical organoid/trabecular pattern of neuroendocrine tumours with chromogranin positivity, and immunostaining confirms insulin production.

options: Disseminated tuberculosis destroying the adrenal cortex
Autoimmune adrenalitis causing primary Addison disease
Bilateral adrenal metastases from lung carcinoma
Amyloidosis infiltrating and replacing the adrenal cortex
questions.explanation: Autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison disease) is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developed countries, accounting for approximately 80% of cases. Anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies are present in over 80% and confirm autoimmune aetiology. It may occur in isolation or as part of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome Type 1 or 2. In developing countries, tuberculosis remains the leading cause. Presentation includes hyperpigmentation (from elevated ACTH and MSH), fatigue, weight loss, and salt craving. Treatment requires lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement.
questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents with primary adrenal insufficiency. Investigations show elevated ACTH, low cortisol, and autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2). What is the most common cause in developed countries?

questions.explanation:
Histoplasma appears as small (2-4μm) oval yeast
predominantly within macrophages and other phagocytes. Despite the name,
it's unencapsulated; the clear area around organisms in H&E sections is
artifact. GMS and PAS stains highlight the organisms better than H&E.
questions.question: Histoplasma capsulatum characteristically appears as:

questions.explanation: Immunotherapy historically included high-dose IL-2 and interferon-alpha with modest responses. Checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab targeting PD-1; ipilimumab targeting CTLA-4) revolutionized treatment. Combination nivolumab/ipilimumab or pembrolizumab/axitinib are first-line for advanced disease. Durable responses occur in 40-50%. Immune-related adverse events require management.
questions.question: Immunotherapy for renal cell carcinoma includes:

questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma shows a characteristic 'starry sky' histological pattern, with scattered pale macrophages (the 'stars') consuming apoptotic tumour cells against a dark background of densely packed malignant lymphocytes, reflecting the tumour's extremely high proliferation rate. MYC gene translocation, most commonly t(8;14), is the defining genetic abnormality driving this aggressive lymphoma. The endemic (African) form classically presents with jaw involvement and is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection.
questions.question: A 6-year-old presents with a rapidly enlarging jaw mass. Biopsy shows a 'starry sky' pattern of small blue cells with high mitotic activity. Cytogenetics reveals a MYC gene translocation. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Gliosis represents reactive astrocytic proliferation with hypertrophy and increased GFAP expression in response to CNS injury. Astrocytes fill areas of neuronal loss, forming glial scars. While initially protective, chronic gliosis may impede regeneration. Gemistocytic astrocytes (abundant pink cytoplasm) and Rosenthal fibers may be seen. Gliosis is a nonspecific response to diverse injuries.
questions.question: Gliosis represents:
What percentage of gallstones afflict adult populations in developed countries?
questions.explanation: Gallstones (cholelithiasis) afflict 10% to 20% of adult populations in developed countries. The vast majority (>80%) are "silent," and most individuals remain free of biliary pain or other complications for decades. There are two general classes: cholesterol stones (>80%) and pigment stones.

questions.question: Mature cystic teratomas (dermoid cysts) most commonly contain:
questions.explanation: Mature cystic teratomas contain well-differentiated tissues from all three germ layers, most prominently skin with hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and keratin debris (producing characteristic greasy contents). Teeth and bone may be present. Complications include torsion, rupture, and rarely malignant transformation (usually squamous cell carcinoma). Struma ovarii contains predominantly thyroid tissue.

Approximately 30-40% of thymoma patients develop
myasthenia gravis, though 85% of myasthenia patients do not have
thymoma. The association suggests disrupted immune tolerance from
abnormal thymic environment. Other autoimmune phenomena (pure red cell
aplasia, hypogammaglobulinemia) also associate with thymomas.
questions.question: What percentage of thymoma patients develop myasthenia gravis?

questions.explanation:
Organic acid accumulation from enzyme deficiencies causes metabolic
acidosis. Ketosis, hyperammonemia, and hypoglycemia frequently coexist.
Emergency treatment includes hydration and alkalization.
questions.question: What causes the acidosis in organic acidemias?

questions.explanation: Pseudomembranous colitis results from Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B following disruption of normal flora by antibiotics, producing the characteristic volcano-like eruption of inflammatory debris from damaged crypts that coalesces into a pseudomembrane. Shiga toxin instead causes haemorrhagic colitis with thrombotic microangiopathy, a different histological pattern.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man develops bloody diarrhoea after starting broad-spectrum antibiotics. Colonic biopsy shows a 'volcano' eruption of neutrophils and mucin bursting from crypts, forming an adherent pseudomembrane. What is the causative toxin?
Lynch syndrome increases risk of which urologic malignancy?
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) caused by mismatch repair gene mutations increases upper tract urothelial carcinoma risk 14-75 fold. These cancers show microsatellite instability and loss of MMR protein expression. Screening urinalysis in Lynch syndrome recommended. Also increases risk of colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, stomach, and other cancers.

questions.question: The presence of which cytokine is essential for differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into Th1 cells during tuberculosis infection?
questions.explanation:
Antigen-presenting cells produce IL-12 when stimulated by mycobacterial
antigens through TLR2 receptors. IL-12 is crucial for inducing naive
CD4+ T cells to differentiate into the Th1 subset that produces IFN-?.
This Th1 differentiation is essential for activating macrophages to
control mycobacterial infection effectively.

Echinococcus granulosus metacestode forms hydatid cysts in liver and
lungs. Cysts contain laminated membrane, germinal layer, and
protoscolices in brood capsules. Dogs are definitive hosts with sheep as
intermediate hosts; humans are accidental hosts.
questions.question: Which tapeworm causes hydatid cyst disease?

options: Decreased bone mass with abnormal mineralization
Decreased bone mass with normal mineralization
Normal bone mass with decreased mineralization
questions.question: Osteoporosis is defined as:
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis involves decreased bone mass and density with normal mineralization, increasing fracture risk. Postmenopausal estrogen deficiency and aging are primary causes. T-score =-2.5 on DEXA scan defines osteoporosis. Vertebral compression fractures, hip and wrist fractures are common. Prevention includes calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise. Treatment involves bisphosphonates, denosumab, or teriparatide.

Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) confers approximately 4-5 times increased relative risk of developing invasive breast carcinoma compared to women without proliferative changes. This risk doubles to 8-10 times if a first-degree family history of breast cancer coexists. ADH has some features of low-grade DCIS but is too small or architecturally incomplete to qualify. Management includes excision to exclude adjacent DCIS, enhanced surveillance, and consideration of chemoprevention with tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors in high-risk individuals.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has atypical ductal hyperplasia on core needle biopsy. She enquires about her increased breast cancer risk. Which figure most accurately represents her relative risk increase?
options: 1.5 times increased relative to women without proliferative disease
15-20 times increased relative to the general population
8-10 times increased relative to non-proliferative disease
2-3 times increased relative to the general population
4-5 times increased relative to the general population

questions.question: What skin finding characterizes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Skin hyperextensibility with cigarette-paper scarring characterizes most
EDS types. Collagen defects impair wound healing producing atrophic
scars. Joint hypermobility and easy bruising also occur.

Epidural hematomas typically result from middle meningeal artery laceration by temporal bone fracture. Blood accumulates between skull and dura, producing biconvex (lentiform) hematoma on CT. Classic "lucid interval" precedes neurologic deterioration as hematoma expands. Rapid surgical evacuation is lifesaving. Arterial bleeding allows rapid accumulation distinguishing from slower-developing subdural hematomas.
questions.question: Epidural hematoma most commonly results from:

questions.explanation:
HIV primarily infects CD4+ T helper cells through binding of viral gp120
to CD4 receptor. Coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4 are also required for viral
entry. Progressive CD4+ T cell depletion causes immunodeficiency.
questions.question: What is the primary cell infected by HIV?

questions.explanation:
Oligodendrogliomas with IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion
have much better prognosis and chemosensitivity than those lacking this
molecular signature. The codeletion results from unbalanced
translocation t(1;19). These tumors typically occur in frontal lobes of
younger adults and show "fried egg" appearance with perinuclear halos
and calcification.
questions.question: Which mutation is characteristic of oligodendrogliomas with favorable prognosis?

questions.explanation:
Chromosomal microarray detects aneuploidies plus submicroscopic
deletions/duplications missed by karyotype. It's first-tier test for
developmental disabilities. Cannot detect balanced rearrangements.
questions.question: Which chromosomal abnormality detection method is most comprehensive?

questions.explanation:
Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes galactocerebroside accumulation.
This globoid cell leukodystrophy causes severe demyelination. Infantile
form causes death by age 2.
questions.question: Which substrate accumulates in Krabbe disease?

questions.explanation:
Self-injurious behaviors particularly head-banging and hand-biting
characterize Smith-Magenis syndrome. Sleep disturbances from inverted
melatonin rhythm are problematic. 17p11.2 deletion or RAI1 mutations
cause SMS.
questions.question: Which Smith-Magenis syndrome feature distinguishes it from other intellectual disability syndromes?

questions.explanation: Among chronic HBV-infected patients, 15-40% may develop advanced alcoholic liver diseases including alcoholic hepatitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma. The progression is influenced by factors including alcohol consumption, viral load, concurrent infections, and host immune response.
questions.question: What percentage of heavy drinkers develop hepatitis B cirrhosis following chronic infection?

questions.explanation: Aflatoxin B1, produced by Aspergillus flavus and parasiticus fungi that contaminate stored grains and nuts, is a major dietary risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma in Africa and Asia. It causes specific TP53 mutations (codon 249 ser→arg). The synergism between aflatoxin exposure and chronic HBV infection exponentially increases HCC risk.
questions.question: Which dietary toxin is most associated with HCC in Africa?

questions.explanation: Oesophageal varices arise from portal hypertension, usually due to cirrhosis, which forces blood through portosystemic collateral channels including submucosal oesophageal veins. These thin-walled veins become dilated and tortuous and are prone to rupture. This differs from Mallory-Weiss tears, which result from mechanical mucosal injury during vomiting.
questions.question: A 60-year-old alcoholic presents with haematemesis. Endoscopy reveals dilated, tortuous submucosal veins at the lower oesophagus. What is the underlying mechanism?

A 65-year-old woman has rectal bleeding and tenesmus. Biopsy of a rectal mass shows malignant glands extending into but not beyond the muscularis propria, with no lymph node involvement on resection. What TNM stage best describes this tumour?
questions.explanation: Colorectal cancer staging using the TNM system classifies tumours invading into but not through the muscularis propria, without nodal or distant metastases, as Stage I (T1-T2, N0, M0). Stage II tumours extend through the muscularis propria into surrounding tissue, while Stage III indicates nodal involvement and Stage IV indicates distant metastasis.

questions.question: What prenatal diagnostic test has lowest miscarriage risk?
questions.explanation:
Amniocentesis carries approximately 1 in 300-500 miscarriage risk when
performed after 15 weeks. CVS has slightly higher risk. Modern
techniques have improved safety.

Helicobacter pylori shows tropism for gastric epithelia and is concentrated within the superficial mucus overlying epithelial cells. The organism causes a predominantly antral gastritis initially. Pangastritis, mucosal atrophy, reduced acid secretion, and intestinal metaplasia are key factors underlying H. pylori-associated disease progression.
questions.question: What is the tropism of Helicobacter pylori?

questions.explanation: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis produces periportal (Symmers clay-pipe) fibrosis from granulomatous inflammation around portal vein radicals stimulated by egg antigens. This fibrosis obstructs portal flow, causing presinusoidal portal hypertension with massive splenomegaly and esophageal varices. Hepatocyte architecture is remarkably preserved, explaining why hepatic synthetic function remains intact until late stages. Variceal bleeding thus occurs with preserved liver function tests, distinguishing this pattern from alcohol-related cirrhosis where hepatocytes are directly destroyed.
options: Micronodular cirrhosis from progressive hepatocyte necrosis
Centrilobular fibrosis from hepatic vein outflow obstruction
Sinusoidal fibrosis from stellate cell activation and collagen
Periportal pipestem fibrosis from portal egg granuloma formation
Biliary fibrosis from granulomatous bile duct cholangitis
questions.question: A patient with hepatosplenic schistosomiasis develops hematemesis from esophageal varices. The type of hepatic fibrosis responsible is:

questions.explanation:
Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma shows the highest EBV
association (>70%), particularly in HIV-positive patients and
developing countries. EBV-encoded proteins like LMP-1 may drive
Reed-Sternberg cell proliferation through NF-?B pathway activation. This
subtype has the worst prognosis and most advanced presentation.
questions.question: Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma has the strongest association with Epstein-Barr virus infection?
Which congenital malformation results from failure of neural tube closure?
questions.explanation:
Spina bifida results from failure of posterior neural tube
closure, ranging from occult lesions to severe myelomeningocele with
exposed neural tissue. The defect occurs by day 28 of gestation. Folate
supplementation periconceptually reduces risk by approximately 70%,
though mechanism remains incompletely understood.

While AFP >500 ng/ml strongly suggests hepatocellular carcinoma, no single cutoff is absolutely diagnostic. Continuously rising values, even <100 ng/ml, are highly suspicious. However, some HCCs are AFP-negative, and elevated AFP can occur in hepatitis and cirrhosis without HCC. AFP should be interpreted with clinical context and imaging findings.
questions.question: What AFP level is diagnostic of HCC?

questions.explanation: Non-ketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH) results from deficiency of the glycine cleavage enzyme (GCS) complex in the mitochondrial matrix, normally comprising P-, H-, T-, and L-proteins. Glycine accumulates in plasma and disproportionately in CSF because glycine acts as a co-agonist at NMDA receptors, causing severe neonatal seizures, hypotonia, and encephalopathy. The elevated CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio exceeding 0.08 is diagnostic. Sodium benzoate reduces plasma glycine; NMDA antagonists may reduce seizure burden but prognosis remains poor in neonatal-onset forms.
questions.question: A newborn is diagnosed with non-ketotic hyperglycinemia. Plasma glycine is 500 umol/L and CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio is markedly elevated at 0.12 (normal less than 0.04). The enzyme deficient is:
options: Glycine cleavage enzyme complex in mitochondrial matrix
Glycine reductase in the anaerobic glycine cleavage pathway
D-amino acid oxidase in peroxisomal glycine catabolism
Serine hydroxymethyltransferase in folate one-carbon metabolism
Unabsorbed bile acids stimulate colonic secretion
Direct mucosal toxicity of bile acids
Osmotic effect of unabsorbed fat alone
questions.explanation: Bile acids are normally reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via active transport; when this segment is resected or diseased, unabsorbed bile acids pass into the colon where they stimulate colonic water and electrolyte secretion, causing secretory diarrhoea. This differs from the osmotic diarrhoea of fat malabsorption, which results from unabsorbed fatty acids rather than bile acids.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man has chronic diarrhoea and bile acid malabsorption following ileal resection. What is the mechanism underlying his diarrhoea?
Prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) is characterized by:
questions.explanation: High-grade PIN shows cytologically atypical cells (enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli) within architecturally preserved prostatic ducts with intact basal cell layer. This is the presumed precursor to prostatic adenocarcinoma. Low-grade PIN is no longer reported. Isolated PIN on biopsy warrants close follow-up; 30-50% develop carcinoma within years.

Benign fibroepithelial polyps arise in prostatic urethra of boys, presenting with hematuria, obstruction, or urinary tract infection. Polypoid masses with fibrovascular cores and benign epithelium occur. Simple transurethral resection is curative. No malignant potential. Must distinguish from botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma which occurs in similar age group but shows malignant features.
questions.question: Prostatic urethral polyps occur in:
What percentage of colorectal cancers show microsatellite instability?
questions.explanation: Approximately 10-15% of colorectal cancers exhibit microsatellite instability (MSI), resulting from defective DNA mismatch repair. About 3% have Lynch syndrome (hereditary), while 12% have sporadic MSI (MLH1 promoter hypermethylation). MSI tumors are often right-sided, mucinous, poorly differentiated, with lymphocytic infiltrate. They have better prognosis than microsatellite-stable tumors and respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

questions.question: What clinical syndrome results from schistosome egg embolization to brain?
questions.explanation:
Schistosome eggs can embolize to brain causing focal neurologic deficits
including seizures. Granulomatous inflammation around eggs creates
space-occupying lesions. Spinal cord involvement causes transverse
myelitis with paraplegia.

questions.question: What is the characteristic appearance of cholesterol stones?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol stones occur exclusively in the gallbladder and are classically hard and pale yellow. They may be radiolucent when composed entirely of cholesterol or radio-opaque when calcium is present (10-20% of cases). Single stones are ovoid, while multiple stones become faceted due to compression against each other.

High-grade papillary urothelial carcinomas show architectural disorder, marked cytologic atypia, and high mitotic rate. Recur in 70-80% with progression to muscle invasion in 30-50%. Require aggressive surveillance and intravesical BCG therapy if non-invasive. Presence of high-grade disease warrants complete staging including upper tracts. Patients with muscle invasion require radical cystectomy.
questions.question: High-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma is characterized by:

questions.explanation: 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome) causes thymic hypoplasia producing T-cell lymphopenia, hypoparathyroidism producing hypocalcemia, and conotruncal cardiac defects from TBX1 haploinsufficiency. B-cells remain normal because they develop in bone marrow independent of the thymus. This is the most common microdeletion syndrome, occurring in approximately 1 in 4000 live births with highly variable phenotypic expression.
questions.question: A 3-year-old presents with conotruncal cardiac defect, hypocalcemia, and recurrent infections. Immunophenotyping reveals severe T-cell lymphopenia with normal B-cell counts. The most likely genetic mechanism is:
options: Point mutation in GATA2 transcription factor

questions.question: What is the most common site for intestinal tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Intestinal tuberculosis usually establishes infection in the ileocecal region where lymphoid tissue is abundant. The tubercle bacillus, protected from digestion by its waxy capsule, passes into the small bowel. Infection may also involve the colon, jejunum, appendix, rectum, and duodenum.

questions.question: Which amino acid accumulates in homocystinuria?
questions.explanation:
Cystathionine synthase deficiency causes methionine and homocysteine
accumulation. Clinical features include lens dislocation, marfanoid
habitus, mental retardation, and thromboembolism. Homocysteine damages
vascular endothelium.

options: Endometrial atrophy from chronic progesterone excess
Excess prolactin causing follicular development arrest
Autoimmune destruction of ovarian follicular granulosa cells
Premature follicular atresia from FSH receptor mutations
questions.explanation: PCOS is characterised by anovulatory cycles resulting from insulin resistance, elevated LH, and androgen excess that impair follicular maturation. Chronic anovulation means no corpus luteum forms, so progesterone is not produced. Unopposed oestrogen stimulation leads to endometrial hyperplasia and risk of endometrial carcinoma if untreated. Menstrual irregularity ranges from oligomenorrhoea to amenorrhoea. The multiple subcapsular follicles on ultrasound represent arrested follicular development. Treatment includes lifestyle modification, metformin, and hormonal contraceptives to restore regular cycles and protect the endometrium.
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with PCOS has irregular menses and bilateral polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Which pathological mechanism best explains her menstrual irregularity?

questions.explanation: Alagille syndrome is a JAG1/NOTCH2-related disorder causing intrahepatic bile duct paucity, characteristic facial features, cardiac defects (commonly pulmonary stenosis), butterfly vertebrae, and posterior embryotoxon of the eye. This multisystem pattern, particularly the skeletal and facial findings, distinguishes it from isolated biliary atresia, which lacks these extrahepatic features.
questions.question: A 25-year-old man has cholestatic jaundice and a triangular facies. Liver biopsy shows paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts in portal tracts. He also has a cardiac murmur and butterfly vertebrae. What is the diagnosis?

A 4-year-old presents with recurrent epistaxis and is found to have markedly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time that corrects with mixing studies. Factor VIII level is markedly reduced. Which inheritance pattern is most consistent with this condition?
questions.explanation: Haemophilia A, resulting from factor VIII deficiency, follows X-linked recessive inheritance, predominantly affecting males while female carriers usually have intermediate factor levels and are typically asymptomatic. The prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time correcting with mixing studies indicates a factor deficiency rather than a circulating inhibitor. Severity of bleeding correlates with the degree of factor VIII deficiency, guiding prophylactic treatment decisions.

options: Demyelination with macrophage infiltration and axonal injury
Loss of oligodendrocytes and myelin with complete axonal sparing
Wallerian degeneration of axons without inflammatory infiltrate
Neuronal loss with reactive astrocytosis only
Amyloid deposition in periventricular white matter
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has relapsing episodes of limb weakness and optic neuritis. MRI shows periventricular white matter lesions. CSF shows oligoclonal bands. What pathological change characterises the active multiple sclerosis lesion?
questions.explanation: Active multiple sclerosis plaques show T-lymphocyte and macrophage infiltration, myelin breakdown (macrophages laden with myelin debris), oligodendrocyte loss, and early axonal injury evidenced by amyloid precursor protein (APP) accumulation. Chronic plaques show dense astrogliosis (sclerosis) with loss of axons, myelin, and oligodendrocytes. The periventricular and juxtacortical distribution reflects venular inflammation. Remyelination occurs in shadow plaques. Natalizumab, fingolimod, and dimethyl fumarate are disease-modifying therapies targeting lymphocyte trafficking and activation.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man undergoes liver biopsy for abnormal liver enzymes. Histology shows steatosis affecting less than 5% of hepatocytes, with no inflammation or fibrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Simple hepatic steatosis, often termed non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in the absence of alcohol use, refers to fat accumulation in hepatocytes without significant inflammation or fibrosis. It is generally considered a benign and reversible stage, in contrast to steatohepatitis, which involves additional inflammatory and fibrotic changes with progression risk.

questions.question: What characterizes alcoholic cirrhosis initially?
questions.explanation: Alcoholic cirrhosis classically presents as micronodular cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis) with nodules <3mm diameter. The uniform small nodules reflect diffuse injury pattern. Over time, it may evolve to mixed pattern as some nodules enlarge through continued regeneration. The liver is initially enlarged and fatty (4-6kg), becoming smaller, fibrotic, and bile-stained as cirrhosis advances. Steatosis may "burn out."

Rotavirus is a major cause of acute viral gastroenteritis, particularly in children. Other viral causes include norovirus and adenovirus. For hepatotropic viruses specifically, hepatitis A virus is more common in children, but rotavirus causes the majority of viral gastroenteritis episodes requiring medical attention in pediatric populations.
questions.question: Which virus causes the majority of acute viral hepatitis in children?

questions.explanation: Juvenile polyps are the most common colonic polyps in children, characterised by cystically dilated glands within an oedematous, inflamed lamina propria without epithelial dysplasia. They differ from adenomatous polyps, which show dysplastic epithelium, and from Peutz-Jeghers polyps, which have a distinctive arborising smooth muscle core.
questions.question: A 6-year-old child presents with rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy reveals a single pedunculated polyp in the rectum. Histology shows dilated, cystic glands with abundant lamina propria and inflammatory cells, but no dysplasia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Elevated urine sulfatides on thin-layer chromatography analysis
Elevated plasma very long-chain fatty acids particularly C26:0
Elevated plasma galactocerebroside on high-performance HPLC
Absent hexosaminidase A in leukocyte enzyme activity assay
Elevated plasma phytanic acid on gas chromatography analysis
questions.explanation: X-ALD results from ABCD1 mutations impairing peroxisomal VLCFA transport, causing accumulation of C26:0, C25:0, and C24:0 in plasma and tissues. Plasma VLCFA analysis (C26:0/C22:0 ratio) is the primary diagnostic marker. Saturated VLCFAs disrupt myelin and adrenocortical cells. Elevated phytanic acid characterizes Refsum disease; elevated sulfatides indicate MLD. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in early cerebral ALD when MRI lesion score is low can halt demyelination progression before severe neurological impairment develops irreversibly.
questions.question: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy presents in a 7-year-old boy with behavioral change, seizures, and adrenal insufficiency. The biochemical marker confirming peroxisomal VLCFA oxidation failure is:

A 35-year-old woman presents with weight loss, heat intolerance, and palpitations. She has exophthalmos and pretibial myxoedema. TSH is suppressed with elevated free T4. Which antibody mediates the hyperthyroidism?
questions.explanation: Graves disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI/TRAb) — IgG antibodies directed against TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells — that mimic TSH and constitutively activate the receptor, causing diffuse thyroid hyperplasia and excess hormone production. Exophthalmos and pretibial myxoedema result from cross-reactive immune responses to orbital fibroblasts and dermis. Radioiodine ablation, antithyroid drugs (carbimazole/propylthiouracil), or thyroidectomy are treatment options depending on clinical circumstances.
options: TSH receptor stimulating (TRAb) antibodies mimicking TSH
Anti-thyroglobulin IgG antibodies against storage protein
Anti-TPO antibodies blocking follicular cell function
Anti-nuclear antibodies cross-reacting with TSH receptor
Anti-TSH antibodies neutralising circulating TSH activity

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant has projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds. Examination reveals a palpable 'olive-shaped' mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the underlying pathology?
questions.explanation: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis results from hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the pyloric circular muscle layer, narrowing the gastric outlet and causing projectile non-bilious vomiting, typically in firstborn males around 2-8 weeks of age. The palpable 'olive' represents the thickened pylorus. Bilious vomiting would instead suggest an obstruction distal to the ampulla, such as malrotation.

questions.question: A newborn presents with bilious vomiting on the first day of life, and abdominal X-ray shows a 'double bubble' sign. Which underlying anomaly is most consistent with this finding?
questions.explanation: Duodenal atresia produces the classic 'double bubble' sign on abdominal X-ray, representing distended, gas-filled stomach and proximal duodenum proximal to the atretic segment, and is strongly associated with Down syndrome. This contrasts with malrotation with volvulus, which typically shows a more non-specific or 'corkscrew' appearance on contrast studies rather than the discrete double bubble. Early surgical correction is required given the complete obstruction this anomaly causes.

Ground glass hepatocytes are characteristic of chronic HBV infection. These are parenchymal liver cells with a finely granular and pale appearance of their cytoplasm due to massive amounts of HBsAg in smooth endoplasmic reticulum. The "ground glass" area is often separated from the cell membrane by a clear halo.
questions.question: What is the characteristic histologic feature of hepatocytes in chronic HBV infection?
Which skeletal feature is characteristic of Marfan syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Arachnodactyly describes abnormally long, slender fingers and toes. Tall
stature with arm span exceeding height is typical. Pectus deformities
and scoliosis commonly occur.

X-linked agammaglobulinaemia follows X-linked recessive inheritance, explaining the family history pattern affecting maternal uncles (related through carrier mothers) while sparing direct paternal relatives, a pattern useful for distinguishing X-linked from autosomal immunodeficiency syndromes. Absent lymphoid tissue reflects the failure of B-cell maturation and subsequent lack of germinal centre formation in lymph nodes and tonsils. Genetic counselling for at-risk family members is an important component of comprehensive care.
questions.question: A 2-year-old with recurrent infections is found to have absent tonsils and lymph nodes on examination, alongside a family history of similar findings in maternal uncles. Which inheritance pattern is most consistent with this presentation?
How do metastatic liver tumors typically appear grossly?
questions.explanation: Metastatic liver tumors may appear as a single nodule or multiple nodules of varying sizes throughout the liver. Multiple nodules are more common. They are typically well-demarcated from surrounding liver parenchyma, often with central necrosis creating umbilication. Massive hepatomegaly may occur with extensive metastatic disease, potentially leading to liver failure.

Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind and activate TSH receptors causing hyperthyroidism, diffuse goiter, and orbital complications (exophthalmos, pretibial myxedema). Histology shows follicular hyperplasia with tall columnar epithelium forming papillary projections and scalloped colloid. Smoking increases ophthalmopathy risk. Treatment options include antithyroid drugs, radioiodine, or surgery.
questions.question: Graves disease is caused by antibodies against:

questions.explanation:
Calf pseudohypertrophy from fat and connective tissue replacement is
characteristic. Dystrophin absence causes sarcolemmal fragility and
muscle fiber necrosis. Progressive proximal weakness begins in early
childhood.
questions.question: Which Duchenne muscular dystrophy feature results from dystrophin absence?

questions.explanation:
Takayasu arteritis ("pulseless disease") affects young
women (typically <40 years), more common in Asian populations. This
granulomatous vasculitis involves aortic arch and its branches, causing
absent pulses, claudication, and renovascular hypertension. Histology
resembles giant cell arteritis. Angiography shows arterial stenosis and
aneurysms. Corticosteroids and immunosuppression are treatments.
questions.question: Takayasu arteritis primarily affects which patient population?
Prostate adenocarcinoma arising in the transition zone accounts for:
questions.explanation: Transition zone cancers account for only 5-10% of prostate adenocarcinomas while 70% arise peripherally. Anterior zone cancers (5-10%) are difficult to detect by DRE and transrectal biopsy. Transition zone cancers may present earlier due to obstructive symptoms. Some evidence suggests different biology and better prognosis for transition zone tumors.

BPH shows proliferation of both epithelial and stromal elements with preservation of basal cell layer (p63, HMWCK positive). Prostate adenocarcinoma demonstrates infiltrative small glands lacking basal cells, often with prominent nucleoli and AMACR expression. Papillary hyperplasia, clear cell cribriform hyperplasia, and atypical adenomatous hyperplasia are benign mimics requiring careful distinction.
questions.question: Which finding distinguishes benign prostatic hyperplasia from prostate cancer on microscopy?

questions.explanation: Long-standing ulcerative colitis is associated with increased risk of dysplasia and adenocarcinoma. Colectomy is recommended for patients with any degree of dysplasia in a raised sessile lesion (DALM - dysplasia-associated lesion or mass). Other long-term problems include chronic anemia, hypoalbuminemia, sclerosing cholangitis, and arthritis.
questions.question: What long-term complication is associated with ulcerative colitis?
What defines chronic hepatitis duration?
questions.explanation: Chronic hepatitis is defined as liver disease with persistent necroinflammatory activity lasting longer than 6 months. It is associated with progressive fibrosis that ultimately leads to liver cirrhosis and is morphologically characterized by portal inflammation, interface hepatitis, parenchymal inflammation, necrosis, and fibrosis.

questions.question: Which female DMD carrier manifestation results from unfavorable lyonization?
questions.explanation:
Female carriers may develop cardiomyopathy from skewed X-inactivation.
Most carriers are asymptomatic but 8% show muscle weakness. Cardiac
screening is recommended.

questions.question: What organisms are associated with brown pigment stone formation?
questions.explanation: Brown pigment stones are associated with biliary infection by Escherichia coli, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Opisthorchis sinensis. These organisms produce β-glucuronidase that deconjugates bilirubin glucuronide, promoting precipitation of calcium bilirubin salts. Brown stones are soft, earthy, and more common in intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. They indicate biliary stasis and infection.

options: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with eosinophilic change
Papillary renal cell carcinoma type 2 eosinophilic variant
Collecting duct carcinoma with tubular architecture
