questions.question: A 55-year-old man has a renal mass showing cells with perinuclear haloes, plant-cell-like borders, and multiple monosomies (chromosomes 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17, 21). What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma shows characteristic cells with pale (chromophobic) cytoplasm with perinuclear halos, plant-cell-like borders, and a combination of large pale and smaller eosinophilic cells. Hale colloidal iron stain shows diffuse cytoplasmic positivity. The hallmark cytogenetic finding is multiple monosomies (chromosomes 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17, 21). It arises from type B intercalated cells of collecting ducts. Chromophobe RCC has better prognosis than clear cell RCC. It can be difficult to distinguish from oncocytoma, particularly in the eosinophilic variant.

Triple X syndrome (47,XXX) often goes undetected as phenotype is mild.
Tall stature and minor learning difficulties may occur. Most women are
fertile with normal intelligence.
questions.question: Which sex chromosome aneuploidy shows mildest phenotype?

questions.explanation:
Congenital myotonic dystrophy occurs through maternal transmission of
large CTG expansions. Severe hypotonia, respiratory distress, and
feeding difficulties occur at birth. Mental retardation is common.
questions.question: Which parent transmits severe congenital myotonic dystrophy?

questions.explanation:
Breast milk contains both free virions and infected maternal cells
capable of transmitting HIV. Transmission risk increases with higher
maternal viral load and breast lesions. Formula feeding eliminates this
transmission route where safe alternatives exist.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of HIV transmission through breast milk?

questions.explanation: Nested urothelial carcinoma shows deceptively bland-appearing nests infiltrating muscularis propria, easily mistaken for benign von Brunn nests. Irregular distribution, confluent growth, and deeper infiltration distinguish from benign nests. High stage at diagnosis common due to subtle appearance. Requires careful evaluation and liberal use of immunostains. Poor prognosis.
questions.question: Nested variant of urothelial carcinoma may be mistaken for:
Rhabdoid tumor of kidney is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Rhabdoid tumors are highly aggressive malignancies showing SMARCB1 (INI1, SNF5) inactivation on chromosome 22q11. Occur in infants <2 years. Rhabdoid cells (eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions) are characteristic. Often metastatic at presentation. Brain involvement occurs. Poor prognosis despite intensive therapy; median survival <12 months.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has invasive breast carcinoma: ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative, low Ki-67, and low Oncotype DX recurrence score. Which molecular subtype does this represent?
options: Luminal B subtype with intermediate-risk prognosis
Luminal A subtype with the best overall prognosis
Claudin-low subtype with stem cell-like features
questions.explanation: Luminal A breast carcinoma is characterised by ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative expression with low Ki-67 (proliferative index below 14%) and low Oncotype DX scores. It has the best overall prognosis among breast cancer molecular subtypes and typically responds well to endocrine therapy alone without the need for chemotherapy. Luminal B shares hormone receptor positivity but shows higher Ki-67, possible HER2 amplification, and higher recurrence scores, indicating intermediate prognosis and greater chemotherapy benefit.

Choriocarcinoma shows propensity for hematogenous spread, most commonly to lungs producing hemorrhagic metastases. Brain, liver, and vagina are other common sites. Despite aggressive behavior, these tumors are exquisitely chemosensitive with cure rates exceeding 90% even with metastatic disease. Serial -hCG monitoring guides treatment.
questions.question: Choriocarcinoma metastasizes primarily to:
Celiac disease shows which characteristic small bowel histology?
questions.explanation:
Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) shows
villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial
lymphocytes (>25-30 per 100 enterocytes) in small bowel, most severe in
duodenum/proximal jejunum. Anti-tissue transglutaminase and
anti-endomysial antibodies are diagnostic. The disease associates with
HLA-DQ2/DQ8. Strict gluten-free diet reverses changes and prevents
complications (T-cell lymphoma, adenocarcinoma).

Endometriosis manifests as ectopic endometrial tissue causing cyclic hemorrhage, inflammation, and scarring. Powder-burn lesions represent hemosiderin-laden deposits on peritoneal surfaces. Ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) and dense adhesions may develop. Retrograde menstruation, coelomic metaplasia, and lymphatic/hematogenous spread explain ectopic endometrium.
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has cyclic pelvic pain and infertility. Laparoscopy reveals powder-burn lesions on peritoneal surfaces. This describes:

questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy results from the cirrhotic liver's failure to clear nitrogenous waste, particularly ammonia, which is normally converted to urea via the urea cycle. Elevated ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier and disturbs neurotransmission, contributing to confusion and asterixis, especially when precipitated by gastrointestinal bleeding, which increases nitrogenous substrate load.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis develops confusion and asterixis after a gastrointestinal bleed. What metabolic abnormality is most directly implicated in this presentation?
Central core disease is characterized by which muscle fiber abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Central core disease shows well-demarcated cores in muscle
fiber centers lacking oxidative enzymes (pale on NADH stain) due to RYR1
mutations. This congenital myopathy causes proximal weakness and
predisposes to malignant hyperthermia. The histological appearance is
distinctive but clinical severity varies.

In high hepatitis B prevalence regions like South East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, hepatocellular carcinoma typically presents in the 20-40 year age group. This is approximately 20-40 years earlier than in Western countries where HCC peaks at 60+ years. The younger age reflects perinatal HBV transmission and earlier onset of chronic liver disease.
questions.question: At what age does HCC typically present in high-risk areas?
HER2-positive breast cancers benefit from:
questions.explanation: HER2-positive cancers (HER2 amplification/overexpression) respond to HER2-targeted therapies: trastuzumab (Herceptin), pertuzumab, and T-DM1. These agents transformed HER2-positive disease from worst to intermediate prognosis. Dual HER2 blockade (trastuzumab + pertuzumab) with chemotherapy is standard for metastatic disease. Cardiotoxicity requires monitoring.

Pompe disease (GSD type II) results from acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency in lysosomes, causing lysosomal glycogen accumulation. The infantile form presents with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, severe hypotonia, and respiratory failure within the first months. Enzyme replacement therapy with alglucosidase alfa has transformed survival outcomes. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes GSD type I (Von Gierke disease) with hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia rather than the cardiomyopathy and hypotonia that dominate Pompe disease presentation.
options: Lysosomal compartments via acid alpha-glucosidase activity
Hepatocyte cytoplasm on glycogen granules for glucose release
Sarcoplasmic reticulum on calcium-handling troponin proteins
Cytosolic glycogen particles via debranching enzyme activity
Mitochondria via the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
questions.question: A 4-month-old with Pompe disease has cardiomegaly, profound hypotonia, and lysosomal glycogen on muscle biopsy. The enzyme deficient acts within:
Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma characteristically presents with which features?
questions.explanation:
AITL presents with fever, weight loss, rash,
lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia,
and autoimmune cytopenias. Histology shows proliferation of follicular
dendritic cells and high endothelial venules. EBV-positive B cells are
often present. Prognosis is generally poor.

Phyllodes tumor recurrence correlates with histologic grade (benign, borderline, malignant based on stromal cellularity, mitoses, atypia, margins) and surgical margins. Benign phyllodes with negative margins rarely recur. Malignant variants may metastasize hematogenously (lungs). Wide local excision with 1cm margins is standard. Mastectomy for large lesions or recurrent disease.
questions.question: Phyllodes tumor recurrence risk correlates with:

questions.explanation: HFE gene mutation testing (particularly for C282Y and H63D mutations) is the most specific test for hereditary hemochromatosis. While transferrin saturation >45-50% is used for screening and is highly sensitive, genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. Liver biopsy with quantitative iron measurement can assess iron burden and fibrosis stage.
questions.question: Which laboratory test is most specific for hereditary hemochromatosis?

questions.explanation: Ulcerative colitis characteristically causes continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and extending proximally without skip lesions, with histology showing crypt abscesses and architectural distortion but typically lacking the granulomas and transmural inflammation seen in Crohn disease. This continuous, mucosa-limited pattern, confined to the colon, helps distinguish it from Crohn disease, which can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract in a discontinuous, transmural pattern. Long-term risk of colorectal cancer necessitates surveillance colonoscopy in longstanding disease.
questions.question: A patient presents with chronic abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. Colonoscopy shows continuous mucosal inflammation limited to the colon, beginning in the rectum. Biopsy shows crypt abscesses and architectural distortion without granulomas. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?

options: Prostate carcinoma with characteristic blastic response
Hodgkin lymphoma with predominantly blastic involvement
Bronchial carcinoid with mixed lytic and blastic changes
Renal cell carcinoma with vascular lytic destruction
Medullary thyroid carcinoma with variable bone response
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with known breast carcinoma has vertebral collapse on X-ray. Bone biopsy reveals lytic destruction without new bone formation. Which primary tumour most characteristically produces purely lytic bone metastases?
questions.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma characteristically produces purely lytic (destructive) bone metastases with extensive vascularity, leading to pathologic fractures and severe haemorrhage during surgical intervention. Breast and lung carcinoma can produce mixed lytic/blastic metastases. Prostate carcinoma classically produces blastic (sclerotic) metastases. The mnemonic BLT with a Kosher Pickle (Breast, Lung, Thyroid, Kidney, Prostate) covers common primaries metastasising to bone, with prostate being predominantly blastic and kidney being typically lytic.

options: Polymerisation of abnormal haemoglobin under low oxygen conditions
Mechanical fragmentation of red cells in small vessels
Osmotic fragility leading to red cell lysis
Autoimmune destruction of red cell membranes
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with recurrent bone pain, dactylitis, and is found to have sickle-shaped red cells on peripheral blood smear during a painful crisis. Which underlying mechanism explains the vaso-occlusive episodes?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease results from a point mutation causing haemoglobin S, which polymerises under conditions of low oxygen tension, dehydration, or acidosis, distorting red cells into a rigid sickle shape that occludes small vessels and causes painful vaso-occlusive crises. Dactylitis in young children reflects vaso-occlusion in the small bones of the hands and feet, often an early presenting feature. Hydroxyurea therapy reduces crisis frequency by increasing fetal haemoglobin production, which interferes with polymerisation.

questions.question: Male breast cancer is associated with:
questions.explanation: BRCA2 mutations confer higher male breast cancer risk than BRCA1. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) increases risk through estrogen excess. Other risk factors include radiation exposure, liver disease, and obesity. Most are ER-positive invasive ductal carcinomas presenting as subareolar mass. Treatment mirrors female breast cancer. Prognosis similar when stage-matched.

options: Eosinophilic oesophagitis, with risk of stricture only
Barrett oesophagus, with risk of adenocarcinoma
Plummer-Vinson syndrome, with risk of web formation
Oesophageal varices, with risk of haemorrhage
Achalasia, with risk of aspiration pneumonia
questions.explanation: Barrett oesophagus results from chronic acid reflux causing metaplastic transformation of the normal squamous oesophageal epithelium into intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, and this metaplastic change carries an increased long-term risk of progression through dysplasia to oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Regular endoscopic surveillance with biopsy is recommended to detect dysplastic changes early. This metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence is an important model in understanding cancer development from chronic inflammatory injury.
questions.question: A patient with longstanding gastro-oesophageal reflux disease undergoes endoscopic biopsy showing replacement of normal squamous epithelium with columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Which condition is most consistent with this finding, and which complication is of greatest long-term concern?

questions.explanation: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors (androblastomas) secrete androgens causing virilization with hirsutism, temporal balding, clitoromegaly, and voice deepening. Occur in young women (mean age 25). Testosterone and androstenedione levels are elevated. Most are low-grade and unilateral; surgical excision is curative. Rare poorly differentiated forms have malignant potential.
questions.question: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors produce:
Which T cell maturation stage occurs specifically within the thymic cortex?
questions.explanation:
T cell precursors become double-positive (CD4+CD8+) in the
thymic cortex where they undergo positive selection based on MHC
restriction. Cells that fail positive selection die by neglect through
apoptosis. The cortex appears darker microscopically due to dense
lymphocyte packing.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent acute pancreatitis. Imaging shows two separate pancreatic ducts draining the dorsal and ventral pancreas separately into the duodenum. What is the embryological basis of this finding?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic divisum results from failure of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds' ducts to fuse during embryogenesis, leaving the dorsal duct draining through the smaller minor papilla as the dominant outflow route. This relative outflow restriction can predispose to recurrent pancreatitis due to impaired drainage.

questions.question: Schwannomas most commonly affect which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation:
Vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) arise from CN
VIII, presenting with unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance
problems. Histology shows Antoni A (compact) and Antoni B (loose) areas
with Verocay bodies. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic
for neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2 gene mutation on chromosome 22).

Endometrial clear cell carcinoma is classified as a Type II (p53-associated, oestrogen-independent) endometrial carcinoma along with serous carcinoma. Histologically, hobnail cells with prominent nuclei line glandular spaces and papillae, and hyalinised stroma may be prominent. Despite lower stage at diagnosis compared to serous carcinoma, clear cell carcinoma has a poor prognosis. It is not driven by oestrogen excess (unlike Type I endometrioid carcinoma) and does not respond reliably to progestogen therapy. TP53 mutations and loss of mismatch repair proteins may both be present.
options: It is strongly associated with oestrogen excess and obesity
It is a Type II tumour with p53 mutations and poor prognosis
It has the best prognosis of all endometrial carcinoma types
It is universally associated with Lynch syndrome mutations
It responds well to progestogen therapy in all stages
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows clear cell carcinoma with hobnail cells lining tubules and papillae, with hyalinised stroma. Which statement about this tumour is most accurate?

questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cell (JG cell) tumour is a rare benign cortical renal tumour causing secondary hypertension and hypokalaemia through autonomous renin secretion. It predominantly affects young adults. Histologically, cells resemble JG cells with distinctive rhomboid membrane-bound PAS-positive renin granules on electron microscopy. Surgical excision is curative with resolution of hypertension. Renin immunostaining confirms the diagnosis. It must be distinguished from other renin-secreting tumours; unlike most renal tumours, it causes hypertension through hormonal mechanism rather than mass effect or renal compression.
questions.question: A 3-year-old boy has hypertension and elevated renin levels. CT shows a small cortical renal tumour. Histology shows cells resembling juxtaglomerular cells with rhomboid renin granules on electron microscopy. What is the diagnosis?
options: Wilms tumour with renin-secreting blastemal component
Clear cell RCC with paraneoplastic renin secretion
Metanephric adenoma with tubular epithelial features
Juxtaglomerular cell tumour causing secondary hypertension
Congenital mesoblastic nephroma in an older child

questions.explanation:
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma preferentially affects
head/neck (especially orbit) and genitourinary tract in young children
(median age 6 years). The embryonal subtype has better prognosis than
alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. Orbital location has best prognosis due to
early detection and favorable biology.
questions.question: Rhabdomyosarcoma embryonal subtype most commonly arises in which location?

questions.explanation: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease results from accumulation of an abnormally folded, protease-resistant form of prion protein, which causes characteristic spongiform vacuolar changes in neuronal tissue without eliciting a significant inflammatory response, distinguishing it from infectious encephalitis. This rapidly progressive course with myoclonus and ataxia is a key clinical clue prompting consideration of prion disease. The absence of inflammation reflects the unique pathogenesis of prion-mediated neurodegeneration through protein misfolding rather than classic infectious or immune mechanisms.
questions.question: A patient with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and ataxia is found to have spongiform changes on brain biopsy without significant inflammatory infiltrate. Which underlying pathological process best explains this presentation?

questions.explanation: Pituitary adenomas represent approximately 10% of primary intracranial neoplasms, classified as microadenomas (<1cm) or macroadenomas (=1cm). Most are sporadic; 5% occur with MEN1 syndrome. Functioning adenomas cause hyperpituitarism while non-functioning adenomas present with mass effect. Immunohistochemistry identifies hormonal product.
questions.question: Pituitary adenomas account for what percentage of intracranial tumors?
A 40-year-old man with Crohn's disease develops a fistula between the terminal ileum and sigmoid colon. What underlying histological feature best explains this complication?
questions.explanation: Crohn's disease is characterised by transmural inflammation extending through the full thickness of the bowel wall, which predisposes to complications such as fistula formation, abscesses, and strictures as inflammation breaches serosal surfaces and adheres to adjacent structures. Ulcerative colitis, being limited to mucosa and submucosa, does not characteristically cause fistulae.

questions.question: Radial scar of breast is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Radial scars (complex sclerosing lesions) show central fibroelastic core with radiating ducts, mimicking invasive carcinoma architecturally and mammographically. Benign lesions but may harbor atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma. Complete excision ensures accurate diagnosis and rules out associated malignancy. Slightly increased breast cancer risk exists.

Chronic pancreatitis results from recurrent acinar injury and progressive fibrosis, leading to glandular atrophy, ductal dilatation, and calcification, with eventual exocrine insufficiency causing steatorrhoea. Alcohol is the most common cause in adults. This contrasts with acute pancreatitis, which lacks the chronic fibrotic and calcific changes.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man with recurrent alcoholic pancreatitis has chronic abdominal pain and steatorrhoea. Imaging shows pancreatic calcifications and a dilated, irregular main duct. What is the diagnosis?
Testicular torsion requires surgical intervention within:
questions.explanation: Testicular viability decreases rapidly after six hours of torsion; salvage rates drop dramatically beyond this window. Bell clapper deformity (abnormal high attachment of tunica vaginalis) predisposes to torsion. Acute onset testicular pain without trauma in adolescent suggests torsion requiring emergency exploration. Contralateral orchiopexy prevents bilateral loss.

The t(2;5) translocation creates NPM-ALK fusion protein in
systemic ALCL, leading to constitutive ALK tyrosine kinase activation.
ALK-positive cases occur more in younger patients and have better
prognosis than ALK-negative variants. Immunohistochemistry for ALK
protein is diagnostically useful and prognostically significant.
questions.question: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) characteristically shows which chromosomal rearrangement?

questions.explanation:
Type II pneumocytes synthesize, store, and secrete
pulmonary surfactant (phospholipids and proteins) that reduces alveolar
surface tension. Surfactant production accelerates after 35 weeks
gestation and during labor. Deficiency causes respiratory distress
syndrome in premature infants requiring exogenous surfactant
administration.
questions.question: Which cells produce surfactant in the developing lung?

questions.explanation: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy results from amyloid- deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessel walls, weakening them and causing lobar hemorrhages in elderly patients. Multiple hemorrhages at different stages may occur. Associated with Alzheimer disease. APOE e4 and e2 alleles increase risk. No specific treatment exists; recurrent hemorrhages are common.
questions.question: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes:

questions.explanation:
Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens causes obstructive
azoospermia in 98% of CF males. CFTR mutations affect development of
reproductive structures. Sperm production is normal but cannot be
transported.
questions.question: What causes male infertility in cystic fibrosis?
What skeletal feature distinguishes achondroplasia?
questions.explanation:
Rhizomelic shortening affects proximal limb segments (humerus, femur)
more than distal segments. Macrocephaly with frontal bossing is
characteristic. Spinal stenosis may cause neurologic complications.

The spleen is crucial for clearing encapsulated bacteria
(Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria
meningitidis) through antibody production and phagocytosis. Asplenic
patients require prophylactic antibiotics and vaccines against these
organisms. Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) can be rapidly
fatal.
questions.question: Patients with asplenia have markedly increased susceptibility to which category of infections?
Composite lymphoma refers to which situation?
questions.explanation:
Composite lymphoma describes two or more distinct lymphoma
types occurring simultaneously in the same patient (often same lymph
node). Classic example is follicular lymphoma with DLBCL. This differs
from transformation (one lymphoma evolving into another). Recognition
requires careful morphologic and immunophenotypic evaluation.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) typically affects
thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, causing vertebral destruction, kyphosis
(gibbus deformity), and paravertebral abscesses that may track to psoas
muscle. The infection spreads hematogenously from primary pulmonary
focus. Cord compression can cause paraplegia. Granulomatous inflammation
with caseation is seen histologically.
questions.question: Tuberculous osteomyelitis characteristically affects which anatomical site?

A 13-year-old presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and is found on biopsy to have Reed-Sternberg cells within a background of reactive lymphocytes and eosinophils. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Hodgkin lymphoma is characterised by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells, large binucleate cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli giving an 'owl's eye' appearance, within a reactive background of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells. The nodular sclerosis subtype is most common in adolescents and young adults and carries a generally favourable prognosis with modern combination therapy. This contrasts with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which shows malignant lymphocyte proliferation without Reed-Sternberg cells.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man with jaundice has a liver biopsy showing ground-glass hepatocytes with cytoplasmic accumulation of viral surface antigen. What is the most likely infection?
questions.explanation: Ground-glass hepatocytes reflect accumulation of hepatitis B surface antigen within the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of chronically infected hepatocytes, a hallmark finding in chronic hepatitis B infection. This feature is not seen in hepatitis A, C, or E, which lack a comparable integrated viral protein accumulation pattern.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with bloody diarrhoea undergoes colonoscopy showing continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum extending proximally, with crypt abscesses on biopsy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ulcerative colitis produces continuous mucosal and submucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and extending proximally without skip areas, with crypt abscesses and architectural distortion on biopsy. Crohn's colitis instead shows discontinuous, transmural disease that may spare the rectum, a key distinguishing feature.

questions.question: Wilms tumor most commonly presents with which clinical finding?
questions.explanation:
Wilms tumor typically presents as large, smooth, firm
abdominal mass detected by parents or during routine examination.
Hematuria occurs in only 15-20% of cases. The mass crosses midline
distinguishing it from neuroblastoma which usually doesn't.
Hypertension can occur from renin production.

questions.question: Type II endometrial carcinoma is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Type II carcinomas are high-grade serous or clear cell tumors arising in atrophic endometrium of older women, harboring p53 mutations. These aggressive cancers lack hormone receptor expression and have poor prognosis. Type I cancers are endometrioid adenocarcinomas with PTEN mutations arising from hyperplasia in estrogen-stimulated endometrium.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents with painless testicular enlargement and elevated -hCG. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Choriocarcinoma produces markedly elevated -hCG from syncytiotrophoblasts and shows rapid hematogenous spread, particularly to lungs. These highly aggressive tumors cause hemorrhagic metastases and may present with metastatic symptoms. Pure choriocarcinoma is rare; most occur in mixed germ cell tumors. Extremely chemosensitive despite aggressive behavior.

questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency in the autosomal recessive form?
questions.explanation:
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes toxic
accumulation of deoxyadenosine metabolites particularly harmful to
lymphocytes, resulting in SCID. This represents about 15% of SCID cases
and is one of the few forms amenable to enzyme replacement therapy. The
toxic metabolites interfere with DNA synthesis affecting both T and B
cell development.

questions.question: A 6-month-old male presents with hyperammonemia after a normal newborn screen. Plasma amino acids show markedly elevated citrulline but urine shows no orotic acid. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Citrullinemia type 1 results from argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1) deficiency, causing citrulline accumulation (often markedly elevated to greater than 1000 umol/L) with hyperammonemia. Unlike OTC deficiency, there is no orotic acid elevation because the block is downstream of carbamoyl phosphate utilization. Unlike CPS1 deficiency, citrulline is elevated rather than low. Argininosuccinic aciduria would show elevated argininosuccinate alongside elevated citrulline. Treatment includes arginine supplementation, sodium benzoate as nitrogen scavengers, and dietary protein restriction to minimize ammonia production.
options: OTC deficiency with elevated orotic acid in urine always
CPS1 deficiency with low citrulline and no orotic acid
Citrullinemia type 1 from argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency
Argininosuccinic aciduria from lyase deficiency after citrulline step
Arginase deficiency with elevated arginine and spastic diplegia

questions.question: A 2-year-old presents with failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and foam cells with a 'crinkled tissue paper' appearance on bone marrow biopsy. Enzyme assay reveals deficient glucocerebrosidase activity. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Gaucher disease results from deficient glucocerebrosidase activity, causing accumulation of glucocerebroside within macrophages, producing the characteristic 'crinkled tissue paper' appearance of Gaucher cells on bone marrow examination. Hepatosplenomegaly and bone involvement are prominent clinical features, distinguishing it from Tay-Sachs disease, which predominantly affects the central nervous system without significant organomegaly. Enzyme replacement therapy has substantially improved outcomes for this condition.

questions.question: Where do most pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas arise?
questions.explanation: Most pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (60-70%) arise in the head of the pancreas. This location often leads to earlier presentation due to common bile duct obstruction causing jaundice. Tumors of the body (15%) and tail (5-10%) present later with pain or metastases. Despite earlier detection of head tumors, overall prognosis remains poor for all locations.

The activated B-cell (ABC) subtype shows
CD10-/BCL-6-/MUM1+ (post-germinal center origin) with worse prognosis
than germinal center B-cell (GCB) subtype (CD10+ and/or BCL-6+). Gene
expression profiling defines these subtypes most accurately, predicting
response to standard chemotherapy and guiding targeted therapy
selection.
questions.question: Which immunophenotype indicates post-germinal center B-cell origin in DLBCL?

questions.explanation:
Myeloma kidney (cast nephropathy) results from massive
light chain filtration overwhelming tubular reabsorptive capacity,
causing intratubular cast formation with giant cell reaction and tubular
damage. The casts are composed of Tamm-Horsfall protein complexed with
light chains. This acute kidney injury is often precipitated by
dehydration or contrast exposure.
questions.question: Which renal lesion is specifically caused by light chain deposition in multiple myeloma?
Why is hemochromatosis more common in males than females?
questions.explanation: Hemochromatosis affects 80% males because menstruation and pregnancy delay iron accumulation in women, postponing clinical manifestations. Women typically present later, often postmenopausally. The disease has autosomal recessive inheritance, so both sexes inherit mutations equally, but physiologic iron loss in premenopausal women provides protection.
options: Menstruation and pregnancy delay iron accumulation

questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with chronic anaemia and is found to have target cells and microcytosis on peripheral blood smear, with haemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased haemoglobin A2 and F. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia trait results from reduced beta-globin chain production, causing a compensatory relative increase in haemoglobin A2 and sometimes haemoglobin F, alongside microcytic anaemia with target cells on peripheral smear. This electrophoresis pattern helps distinguish it from iron deficiency anaemia, which would not show this characteristic increase in haemoglobin A2. Genetic counselling is important given the risk of more severe disease (beta-thalassaemia major) in offspring of two carrier parents.

questions.question: The thymus is located in which anatomical region?
questions.explanation:
The thymus occupies the anterior superior mediastinum
behind the sternum, overlying the great vessels and pericardium. This
location is clinically relevant for radiographic interpretation and
surgical access. Thymic masses can compress adjacent structures causing
superior vena cava syndrome.

questions.question: Bowen disease of penis involves:
questions.explanation: Bowen disease represents squamous cell carcinoma in situ appearing as well-demarcated erythematous plaque on penile shaft or scrotum. HPV 16 association exists. Histology shows full-thickness atypia with numerous mitoses. Erythroplasia of Queyrat refers to CIS on glans or inner prepuce. Both progress to invasive carcinoma in 10% if untreated. Complete excision or topical therapy treats disease.

Splenic marginal zone lymphoma presents with splenomegaly,
cytopenias, and circulating villous lymphocytes (short polar cytoplasmic
projections). Bone marrow shows intrasinusoidal infiltration.
Splenectomy often produces durable remissions. The disease is generally
indolent with good prognosis.
questions.question: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma characteristically presents with:

questions.explanation:
Autosomal dominant mutations in the PRSS1 gene encoding cationic
trypsinogen cause hereditary pancreatitis from childhood. These
mutations render activated trypsin resistant to normal inactivation
mechanisms leading to persistent enzyme activity. The continued trypsin
activity results in recurrent bouts of pancreatitis through
autodigestion of pancreatic tissue.
questions.question: Which protein mutation renders activated trypsin resistant to inactivation in hereditary pancreatitis?

A 40-year-old man has epigastric pain unresponsive to standard PPI dosing. Biopsy from the gastric antrum shows no H. pylori, but a markedly elevated fasting serum gastrin is noted, along with a positive secretin stimulation test. Where is the most likely site of the underlying tumour?
questions.explanation: Gastrin-secreting tumours (gastrinomas) causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome arise most commonly in the duodenum, followed by the pancreas, often within the 'gastrinoma triangle'. A paradoxical rise in gastrin after secretin administration is diagnostic and distinguishes gastrinoma from other causes of hypergastrinaemia such as atrophic gastritis.

questions.question: The most common primary brain tumor in adults is:
questions.explanation:
Glioblastoma (WHO grade IV astrocytoma) is the most common
and aggressive primary brain malignancy in adults, median survival 12-15
months despite maximal therapy. It shows necrosis, microvascular
proliferation, marked cellular atypia, and high mitotic activity.
IDH-wildtype glioblastomas (primary, older patients) have worse
prognosis than IDH-mutant (secondary, younger patients).

Multiple myeloma is plasma cell malignancy causing "punched-out" lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and anemia. Monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) appears in serum/urine. Bone marrow shows >10% clonal plasma cells. Complications include pathologic fractures, hyperviscosity, and amyloidosis. Treatment involves chemotherapy, proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, and stem cell transplantation.
questions.question: A 60-year-old woman presents with back pain and pathologic fracture. Bone biopsy shows plasma cells. The most likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone malignancy in children and adolescents, typically affecting metaphyses of long bones around the knee. Peak incidence is during growth spurt. Radiating sunburst pattern or Codman triangle (elevated periosteum) appears on X-ray. Histology shows malignant cells producing osteoid. Treatment combines neoadjuvant chemotherapy and limb-salvage surgery.
questions.question: The most common primary bone tumor in children is:

questions.explanation: The primary aim of treatment in peptic ulcer disease is eradication of Helicobacter pylori, which is associated with 85-100% of duodenal ulcers and 65% of gastric ulcers. Treatment involves combination antibiotic therapy along with acid suppression. Successful eradication significantly reduces ulcer recurrence rates.
questions.question: What is the primary aim of treatment in peptic ulcer disease?

questions.explanation: Aflatoxin B1 exposure causes a characteristic TP53 mutation at codon 249 (serine to arginine substitution, 249ser→arg). This specific mutation serves as a molecular signature of aflatoxin-induced hepatocarcinogenesis. The mutation impairs p53 tumor suppressor function, contributing to malignant transformation when combined with chronic HBV infection.
questions.question: What TP53 mutation is characteristic of aflatoxin-induced HCC?
Which stain demonstrates iron deposits in tissues?
questions.explanation:
Prussian blue (Perls) stain demonstrates ferric iron as blue deposits in
hepatocytes. Hepatic iron index quantifies iron loading. Liver biopsy
shows cirrhosis with extensive iron deposits.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man has PSA of 18 ng/mL and prostate biopsy showing adenocarcinoma with cribriform glands and perineural invasion. Gleason score is 4+4=8. What does this grade most accurately indicate?
options: Low-grade tumour with excellent prognosis on surveillance
Grade applicable only to transition zone tumours
Intermediate-grade tumour amenable to active surveillance
Grade that cannot predict biochemical recurrence risk
High-grade tumour with significant metastatic potential
questions.explanation: Gleason grade 4+4=8 corresponds to Grade Group 4 in the ISUP grading system, indicating high-grade prostatic adenocarcinoma with poorly formed, fused, or cribriform glands. Gleason pattern 4 shows glands that are poorly formed, fused, or have cribriform architecture; pattern 5 adds solid sheets and single infiltrating cells. GS 8-10 carries high risk of biochemical recurrence, metastasis, and cancer-specific mortality. Treatment typically involves radical prostatectomy with lymph node dissection or radiotherapy with long-term androgen deprivation therapy.

questions.question: Gout results from deposition of which crystal type?
questions.explanation:
Gout results from monosodium urate crystal deposition in
joints and soft tissues due to hyperuricemia. Crystals are needle-shaped
and negatively birefringent under polarized light. Acute attacks cause
intense inflammation (neutrophils phagocytosing crystals). Chronic
tophaceous gout shows aggregated crystals with giant cell reaction.
First MTP joint (podagra) is classically affected.

questions.question: A 2-year-old presents with a white pupillary reflex noted by the parents. Examination reveals a retinal mass, and genetic testing identifies a mutation in a tumour suppressor gene. Which gene is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Retinoblastoma results from biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene, which normally regulates the cell cycle by controlling progression through the G1-S checkpoint. Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is a classic presenting sign requiring urgent ophthalmological evaluation. Hereditary cases involve a germline mutation and carry increased risk of bilateral disease and second malignancies.

questions.question: Urothelial carcinoma in situ is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) shows flat urothelium replaced by cells with high-grade nuclear atypia without invasion. Represents aggressive intra-epithelial malignancy with high progression risk to muscle-invasive disease (50% at 5 years if untreated). May appear as velvety red patches cystoscopically or be invisible. Requires aggressive treatment with BCG or cystectomy.

ATLL is endemic where HTLV-1 infection is prevalent:
southwestern Japan, Caribbean islands, and parts of West/Central Africa.
Transmission occurs through breastfeeding, sexual contact, and blood
products. Only 2-5% of infected individuals develop ATLL after decades
of latency. The acute form presents with hypercalcemia and lytic bone
lesions.
questions.question: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is endemic in which geographic regions?

options: Lipohyalinosis of small penetrating perforating arteries
Berry aneurysm of the middle cerebral artery
Amyloid deposition in cortical vessel walls
Venous sinus thrombosis causing venous infarction
questions.explanation: Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage most commonly occurs in the basal ganglia (putamen and thalamus), pons, and cerebellum, supplied by small penetrating arteries that develop lipohyalinosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis) from chronic hypertension. These weakened small vessels rupture spontaneously. Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms (small aneurysms of perforating arteries) are a predisposing lesion. Lobar haemorrhages in elderly normotensive patients more typically result from cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Management involves blood pressure control and monitoring for cerebral herniation.
questions.question: A 75-year-old hypertensive man collapses with spontaneous intraparenchymal haemorrhage in the putamen and internal capsule. Which pathological lesion most predisposes to this location of haemorrhage?
Neuronophagia refers to:
questions.explanation: Neuronophagia describes microglial cells (rod cells) clustering around and phagocytosing injured or dying neurons, indicating acute neuronal injury. Seen in viral encephalitis, ischemia, and other acute insults. Represents innate immune response to clear cellular debris. Microglial nodules (aggregates without neuron remnants) also indicate inflammation.

questions.question: Hydatidiform mole is diagnosed by ultrasound showing:
questions.explanation: Characteristic "snowstorm" or "bunch of grapes" ultrasound appearance results from multiple hydropic villi. Markedly elevated -hCG for gestational age, enlarged uterus, and theca lutein ovarian cysts occur. No fetal heart tones in complete mole. Partial mole may show abnormal fetal parts. Suction curettage evacuates molar tissue; serial -hCG monitoring detects persistent disease.

Crohn disease classically produces discontinuous 'skip lesions' with intervening normal mucosa, transmural inflammation extending through the full bowel wall thickness, and non-caseating granulomas on biopsy, distinguishing it from the continuous, mucosa-limited inflammation of ulcerative colitis. This transmural inflammatory pattern explains the characteristic complications of fistula and abscess formation seen in Crohn disease, which are uncommon in ulcerative colitis. Disease can affect any segment of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus.
questions.question: A patient develops chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, and perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy shows skip lesions with cobblestone mucosa, and biopsy reveals transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Parkinson disease is characterised by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with surviving neurons containing Lewy bodies composed predominantly of aggregated alpha-synuclein protein, producing the classic clinical triad of resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia. This contrasts with Alzheimer disease, where tau and amyloid-beta are the principal pathological proteins involved. The same alpha-synuclein pathology, when more widespread, underlies the related condition of dementia with Lewy bodies.
questions.question: A patient develops progressive resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia. Brain biopsy at autopsy shows loss of pigmented neurons in the substantia nigra with eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions. Which protein composes these characteristic inclusions?

questions.explanation: Small cell neuroendocrine carcinomas show chromatin pattern nuclear atypia, scant cytoplasm, and neuroendocrine marker expression (synaptophysin, chromogranin, CD56). PSA usually negative or focal. Aggressive behavior with early metastasis. Platinum-based chemotherapy (as for lung small cell) provides treatment. Often admixed with acinar adenocarcinoma. Poor prognosis.
questions.question: Small cell carcinoma of prostate is characterized by:

questions.explanation:
Mucicarmine stains the thick polysaccharide capsule of
Cryptococcus red/pink; India ink shows capsule as clear halo around
yeast. The capsule is crucial for virulence and diagnosis. GMS and PAS
also stain the organisms. Cryptococcosis occurs primarily in
immunocompromised patients with predilection for CNS.
questions.question: Cryptococcus neoformans in tissue is best highlighted by which stain?

questions.explanation: Hydroceles result from serous fluid accumulation between visceral and parietal layers of tunica vaginalis. Communicating hydroceles in infants result from patent processus vaginalis connecting peritoneal cavity. Acquired hydroceles follow infection, trauma, or tumor. Transillumination demonstrates fluid. Large symptomatic hydroceles require surgical repair; small asymptomatic ones observed.
questions.question: Hydrocele is characterized by:
Where do Entamoeba histolytica cysts colonize after passing through the stomach?
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica cysts are resistant to gastric acid and pass through the stomach without harm. They then colonize the epithelial surface of the colon and release trophozoites. Dysentery develops when amebae attach to colonic epithelium, induce apoptosis, invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria.

IRIS occurs when ART rapidly suppresses HIV replication, allowing restoration of immune function including rising CD4 counts and improved pathogen-specific immunity. The reconstituted immune system mounts an exuberant inflammatory response against pre-existing opportunistic infections or residual antigens. MAC-associated IRIS typically presents within 1-3 months of ART initiation with fever, lymphadenitis, and systemic inflammation despite falling HIV viral load. Management involves continuing ART while treating the underlying OI; corticosteroids are reserved for severe or life-threatening IRIS presentations.
options: Rapid immune recovery causing exuberant response to MAC antigens
ART drugs directly activating macrophage inflammatory cascades
MAC developing drug resistance causing uncontrolled infection
Cross-reactive antibodies from coincidental immunization exposure
ART-induced cytokine suppression unmasking subclinical MAC
questions.question: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome develops 3 weeks after ART initiation in a patient with disseminated MAC. The underlying pathophysiologic mechanism is:

questions.explanation:
Tandem mass spectrometry screens for 30+ metabolic disorders including
amino acid, organic acid, and fatty acid oxidation defects. Single blood
spot analyzes multiple analytes. Early detection enables treatment.
questions.question: Which newborn screening detects most disorders?
POEMS syndrome in plasma cell dyscrasia includes which features?
questions.explanation:
POEMS syndrome (rare variant of plasma cell dyscrasia)
comprises: Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal
protein, and Skin changes. Sclerotic (not lytic) bone lesions and
elevated VEGF are characteristic. Treatment differs from typical
myeloma, often including radiation for localized disease.
options: Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein, skin changes

questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori is present in almost all patients with duodenal ulcers, with association rates of 85-100%. The bacterium is also found in 65% of patients with gastric ulcers. H. pylori is associated with poverty, colonization in childhood in high prevalence areas, and humans are the only host.
questions.question: What percentage of patients with Helicobacter pylori have duodenal ulcers?
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma characteristically shows:
questions.explanation: Clear cell RCC (70-80% of RCCs) shows cells with clear cytoplasm (glycogen and lipid-rich) arranged in nests/alveoli separated by delicate branching vasculature. VHL gene alterations (3p loss) are characteristic. Arises from proximal tubule. Grades 1-4 based on nuclear features. Higher grades show sarcomatoid dedifferentiation. Responds to VEGF/mTOR inhibitors.

questions.question: What percentage of patients with gallstones are asymptomatic?
questions.explanation: Approximately 70-80% of individuals with gallstones are asymptomatic. The vast majority (>80%) of gallstones are "silent," and most people remain free of biliary pain or other complications for decades. Symptomatic patients may present with spasmodic colicky abdominal pain, cholecystitis, or complications.

questions.question: AL amyloidosis is most commonly associated with which condition?
questions.explanation:
AL amyloid consists of immunoglobulin light chains (lambda
more than kappa) produced by clonal plasma cells in myeloma, MGUS, or
other plasma cell dyscrasias. This primary systemic amyloidosis affects
heart, kidneys, liver, tongue, and peripheral nerves. Cardiac
involvement causes restrictive cardiomyopathy.

questions.question: The most important predictor of biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy is:
questions.explanation: Positive surgical margins significantly predict biochemical recurrence (rising PSA), though not all patients with positive margins recur. Margin location, extent, and Gleason grade influence recurrence risk. Other predictors include pathologic stage (extraprostatic extension, seminal vesicle invasion), Gleason score, and preoperative PSA. Adjuvant radiation therapy may benefit high-risk patients.

questions.question: What cell type is the major source of collagen in cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: Perisinusoidal stellate cells (hepatic stellate cells, Ito cells) are the major source of collagen in cirrhosis. When activated by reactive oxygen species, cytokines, and growth factors, they transform into myofibroblasts that produce types I and III collagen and other extracellular matrix components in the space of Disse.

Turcot syndrome associates colorectal polyposis with CNS tumors. Type 1 (mismatch repair deficiency) develops glioblastomas, while Type 2 (APC mutation, FAP variant) develops medulloblastomas. This distinction helps genetic counseling. CNS tumors may present before colon cancer, so neurologic symptoms in FAP families warrant evaluation. The syndrome is rare but has significant implications for surveillance and management.
questions.question: What brain tumor is associated with Turcot syndrome?

questions.explanation:
Chromosomal microarray identifies pathogenic CNVs in 15-20% of
unexplained developmental delay cases. Yield is higher than karyotype
(3%) but lower than exome sequencing (25-30%).
questions.question: What is the diagnostic yield of chromosomal microarray for unexplained developmental delay?

options: 50% based on theoretical unbalanced gamete production
Less than 1% due to universal trisomic embryo lethality
10 to 15% from empirical liveborn outcome studies
questions.explanation: Despite theoretical 33% segregation risks, empirical data show liveborn trisomy 13 risk from a balanced 13;14 Robertsonian translocation is approximately 1-2%, owing to prenatal lethality filtering most trisomic conceptuses. Overall empirical recurrence risk for unbalanced offspring cited in counseling is 10-15%. Theoretical risks markedly overestimate actual liveborn outcomes and should never be quoted directly to families without empirical data adjustment.
questions.question: A balanced Robertsonian 13;14 translocation carrier asks about liveborn trisomy 13 risk. The correct empirical figure for genetic counseling is:
The most significant risk factor for trisomy 21 is which maternal characteristic?
questions.explanation:
Advanced maternal age shows strong correlation with
trisomy 21 risk: 1:1500 at age 20, 1:350 at age 35, 1:100 at age 40, and
1:25 at age 45. This reflects increased meiotic nondisjunction with
oocyte aging. However, most babies are born to younger mothers due to
higher birth rates in younger age groups.

questions.question: A partial mole characteristically contains:
questions.explanation: Partial moles result from dispermic fertilization producing triploid conceptuses (69,XXY most common). Fetal tissue is present but nonviable. Chorionic villi show focal edema with scalloped borders and trophoblastic hyperplasia is focal. Risk of persistent gestational trophoblastic disease exists but choriocarcinoma development is extremely rare.

questions.question: How much can hepatic lymph flow increase in cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: Normal thoracic duct lymph flow is 800 to 1000 mL/day. With cirrhosis, hepatic lymphatic flow may approach 20 L/day, exceeding thoracic duct capacity. Hepatic lymph is rich in proteins and low in triglycerides, reflected in protein-rich ascitic fluid. This percolates from the liver surface into the peritoneal cavity.

questions.question: What distinguishes Prader-Willi from Angelman syndrome genetically?
questions.explanation:
Both syndromes involve chromosome 15q11-13 but differ in parental
origin. PWS has paternal deletion while Angelman has maternal deletion.
This demonstrates genomic imprinting effects.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of ascites formation in cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: Ascites formation in cirrhosis involves multiple mechanisms: sinusoidal hypertension drives fluid from sinusoids into space of Disse, hypoalbuminemia decreases oncotic pressure, hepatic lymph percolates into peritoneum (thoracic duct capacity exceeded), and splanchnic vasodilation triggers renal sodium/water retention via RAAS activation. The combination creates portal hypertension-related ascites with high SAAG.

questions.question: Which testicular tumor has the best prognosis?
questions.explanation: Spermatocytic seminomas occur in older men (mean age 55), show indolent behavior with rare metastases (<1%), and don't arise from intratubular germ cell neoplasia. Local excision is curative. Classic seminomas also have excellent prognosis (95% five-year survival stage I) but can metastasize. Choriocarcinoma has worst prognosis though chemosensitive.

options: Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma with collagen band formation
Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma in immunosuppressed patient
Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma with LP cells
Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma associated with older adults
Lymphocyte-rich classical Hodgkin lymphoma with sparse RS cells
questions.explanation: Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common subtype in young adults and characteristically involves the mediastinum. Collagen bands divide lymphoid tissue into nodules, and the lacunar variant of Reed-Sternberg cells (retracted within fixation artifact lacunae) is the hallmark finding. Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical fever) is a classical association. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma features CD20-positive popcorn cells and lacks classic RS cells with the CD15 and CD30 positivity seen in classical HL subtypes.
questions.question: A 22-year-old with mediastinal mass, pruritus, and cyclical fever has biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells with lacunar morphology. The specific Hodgkin lymphoma subtype is:

A 7-year-old boy has cerebellar ataxia and hydrocephalus. MRI shows a cystic posterior fossa mass with an enhancing mural nodule. Biopsy shows biphasic pattern with Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies. What is the expected molecular finding?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO Grade 1) predominantly arises in children in the cerebellum, optic pathway, and hypothalamus. The KIAA1549-BRAF tandem duplication/fusion is present in over 70% of cases, especially cerebellar ones. This distinguishes it from the BRAF V600E point mutation seen in glioblastoma and some diffuse gliomas. Rosenthal fibres (hyaline, eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped deposits in astrocyte processes) and eosinophilic granular bodies are characteristic. Pilocytic astrocytoma has excellent prognosis; complete surgical resection is often curative.
options: BRAF V600E point mutation driving MAPK pathway activation
BRAF deletion resulting in loss of kinase domain activity
BRAF amplification causing constitutive ERK signalling
KIAA1549-BRAF gene fusion from chromosome 7q tandem duplication
BRAF rearrangement with ROS1 as the partner gene

questions.explanation: Metanephric adenomas are rare benign epithelial tumors resembling embryonic kidney, occurring in adults (mean age 40). Small uniform cells forming tubules/papillae. May be mistaken for Wilms tumor or papillary RCC. WT1 positive. Excellent prognosis; simple excision curative. Incidental finding in most cases. Metanephric stromal tumor and metanephric adenofibroma are related entities.
questions.question: Metanephric adenoma is characterized by:

questions.explanation:
Klinefelter men have 20-50 fold increased breast cancer risk compared to
normal males. Absolute risk remains low. Gynecomastia doesn't increase
cancer risk but may delay diagnosis.
questions.question: What breast cancer risk exists in Klinefelter syndrome?

questions.explanation: Invasive aspergillosis demonstrates septate hyphae with acute-angle (45-degree) branching and tendency for vascular invasion causing hemorrhagic infarction. Aspergillus fumigatus is most common species. Galactomannan assay aids diagnosis. Neutropenic patients are particularly susceptible. Voriconazole or amphotericin B provides treatment.
questions.question: Aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients characteristically shows:

questions.explanation:
Deletion or duplication analysis detects mutations in 65-70% of DMD
cases. Sequencing identifies remaining mutations. Muscle biopsy shows
dystrophin absence on immunohistochemistry.
questions.question: Which genetic test confirms Duchenne muscular dystrophy diagnosis?

A child presents with palpable purpura on the buttocks and lower limbs, abdominal pain, and haematuria. Renal biopsy shows IgA deposition in the mesangium. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis affecting skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys, with renal biopsy findings indistinguishable from IgA nephropathy on light microscopy. The palpable purpura distribution over dependent areas such as buttocks and legs is a classic clinical clue. Most cases in children are self-limited, though renal involvement can occasionally progress to chronic kidney disease.

Chronic peptic ulcers characteristically show four histological zones: superficial fibrinoid necrosis, an underlying neutrophilic infiltrate, granulation tissue, and a base of fibrosis. This layered appearance reflects long-standing mucosal injury and healing. Acute stress ulcers, in contrast, are shallow and lack the organised fibrotic base.
questions.question: A 40-year-old man with epigastric pain undergoes endoscopy showing a clean-based ulcer at the duodenal bulb. Biopsy of the ulcer edge shows fibrinoid necrosis, granulation tissue, and fibrosis in layers. What does this layering represent?
Gynecomastia results from:
questions.explanation: Gynecomastia develops when estrogen effects exceed androgen effects, stimulating ductal epithelial proliferation and stromal development. Causes include physiologic (puberty, aging), pathologic (liver disease, testicular tumors), and drug-induced (spironolactone, cimetidine). Histology shows ductal proliferation without lobule formation, increased periductal stroma, and variable inflammation.

Squamous cell carcinoma remains the most common esophageal
cancer globally, particularly in Asia, Africa, and developing countries.
Risk factors include smoking, alcohol, hot beverages, and nutritional
deficiencies. In Western countries, adenocarcinoma (associated with
Barrett esophagus and GERD) is now more common. Both types have poor
prognosis.
questions.question: The most common type of esophageal carcinoma worldwide is:

A 2-year-old presents with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, worse at night. Neck X-ray shows subglottic narrowing described as a 'steeple sign'. Which viral pathogen is most commonly responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus and produces the characteristic barking cough and stridor from subglottic airway narrowing, visualised as the 'steeple sign' on neck radiography due to loss of the normal shouldering of the subglottic airway. This viral aetiology and clinical pattern contrasts with the bacterial cause and more severe presentation of epiglottitis. Most cases are managed supportively, with corticosteroids reducing symptom severity and hospitalisation need.

Katayama fever is acute toxemic schistosomiasis occurring 1-3 months
post-infection. This immune complex-mediated syndrome causes fever,
hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and dysentery. Most
cases involve S. japonicum and resolve after several weeks.
questions.question: What characterizes Katayama fever?
What is the characteristic gross appearance of cavernous hemangioma?
questions.explanation: Cavernous hemangiomas, the most common benign liver tumors, appear as blood-filled spongy masses with a soft, compressible consistency. They are composed of large, dilated vascular channels lined by endothelium and filled with blood. These lesions are usually incidental findings and rarely cause symptoms unless very large or complicated by hemorrhage or thrombosis.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with breast pain and lumpy texture that varies with menstrual cycle. This describes:
questions.explanation: Fibrocystic change represents exaggerated physiologic response to hormonal stimulation, causing cyclic mastalgia and nodularity. Features include cyst formation, stromal fibrosis, and adenosis. Most women show some fibrocystic changes; clinical significance depends on presence of proliferative epithelial changes with or without atypia determining cancer risk.

questions.question: What characterizes the epithelial type of hepatoblastoma?
questions.explanation: The epithelial type of hepatoblastoma is composed of small polygonal fetal cells or smaller embryonal cells forming acini, tubules, or papillary structures that vaguely recapitulate liver development. The mixed epithelial and mesenchymal type contains foci of mesenchymal differentiation including primitive mesenchyme, osteoid, cartilage, or striated muscle.

questions.question: What is a pancreatic pseudocyst?
questions.explanation: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic fluid (rich in amylase and other enzymes) enclosed by a wall of fibrous or granulation tissue, lacking an epithelial lining (hence "pseudo"). It develops weeks after acute pancreatitis as enzyme-rich fluid dissects through tissue planes. Pseudocysts may resolve spontaneously, persist, become infected, rupture, or hemorrhage.

In typhoid fever, mucosal shedding creates oval ulcers oriented along the axis of the ileum, overlying Peyer's patches. Histologically, ulcers show minimal inflammatory cells, chiefly mononuclear cells (plasma cells, histiocytes, and lymphocytes), often with histiocytes showing erythrophagocytosis.
questions.question: What is the characteristic appearance of typhoid ulcers in the ileum?

questions.explanation: Cholangiocarcinomas have greater propensity for extrahepatic spread than hepatocellular carcinoma, including metastases to regional lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and adrenal glands. They also show invasion along peribiliary nerves to the abdomen (perineural invasion). This aggressive spread pattern contributes to the poor prognosis despite being adenocarcinomas.
questions.question: How do cholangiocarcinomas differ from HCC in metastatic pattern?

questions.explanation:
Gag polyprotein forms viral core structure essential for budding from
infected cells. Protease cleaves Gag into matrix, capsid, and
nucleocapsid proteins. Immature virions bud with uncleaved Gag proteins.
questions.question: Which HIV protein is required for viral budding?

questions.explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis) is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is characterised by dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centre formation and Hurthle cell (oxyphilic) metaplasia of follicular cells. Anti-TPO (thyroid peroxidase) antibodies are elevated in over 95% of cases. Progressive autoimmune destruction reduces thyroid function. It carries increased risk of B-cell lymphoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma. Treatment is thyroid hormone replacement. Unlike Graves disease, TSH receptor stimulating antibodies are absent.
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight gain, and constipation. Thyroid biopsy shows dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centre formation and Hurthle cell change. Anti-TPO antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Riedel fibrosing thyroiditis with dense sclerosis
Papillary thyroid carcinoma with sclerosing stroma

questions.question: The starry sky pattern in Burkitt lymphoma results from:
questions.explanation:
Tingible body macrophages containing phagocytosed
apoptotic tumor cell debris appear as pale "stars" scattered among
densely packed dark tumor cells creating the starry sky pattern. This
reflects the extremely high proliferation and apoptosis rate
characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.question: What causes MELAS syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like
episodes result from mtDNA mutations. Point mutations in tRNA genes are
most common. Ragged red fibers appear on muscle biopsy.

questions.question: Which medication is most strongly associated with hepatocellular adenomas?
questions.explanation: Both oral contraceptives and anabolic steroids are strongly associated with development of hepatocellular adenomas. These benign neoplasms develop from hepatocytes and show three subtypes: HNF1-α inactivated (minimal malignant potential), β-catenin activated (high malignant risk), and inflammatory (significant malignant potential). Risk increases with duration and dose of hormone use.

questions.question: Wegener granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is characterized by which antibody?
questions.explanation:
GPA shows c-ANCA (cytoplasmic pattern, anti-proteinase 3)
positivity in 90% of cases. The disease causes necrotizing granulomatous
inflammation of upper/lower respiratory tract and necrotizing
glomerulonephritis. Classic triad: sinusitis/nasal lesions, lung
nodules/cavities, and glomerulonephritis. Treatment requires
cyclophosphamide or rituximab with corticosteroids.

Inflammatory bowel disease commonly presents in young adults, though it can occur at any age. Ulcerative colitis is rare in the first decade with a major peak at 15-25 years and a minor peak in the 7th decade. Both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis show familial association.
questions.question: At what age range does inflammatory bowel disease typically present?
What distinguishes diagnostic from screening prenatal tests?
questions.explanation:
Diagnostic tests (amniocentesis, CVS) provide definitive karyotype while
screening tests (cfDNA, serum markers) assess risk probability. Positive
screening requires diagnostic confirmation. Invasive procedures carry
miscarriage risk.

questions.question: What is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism in acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis results from inappropriate release and activation of pancreatic enzymes, which may be due to three mechanisms: pancreatic duct obstruction, primary acinar cell injury, or defective intracellular transport of pro-enzymes within acinar cells. This leads to autodigestion of pancreatic tissue.

questions.question: A 70-year-old presents with recurrent lobar intracerebral haemorrhages without significant hypertension history. Brain biopsy shows amyloid deposition within the walls of cortical and leptomeningeal vessels. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy results from amyloid-beta deposition within the walls of small and medium cortical and leptomeningeal vessels, weakening them and predisposing to recurrent lobar haemorrhages, typically in elderly patients without the deep haemorrhage pattern seen in hypertensive disease. This condition is also associated with an increased risk of cognitive decline. Recognising this distinct haemorrhage pattern and location is important for guiding further management, including caution with anticoagulation.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man has a colonic polyp showing tubulovillous architecture with high-grade dysplasia but no invasion through the muscularis mucosae. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Adenomas with high-grade dysplasia confined above the muscularis mucosae (carcinoma in situ) carry no risk of lymph node metastasis since lymphatics are absent above this layer, so complete endoscopic polypectomy with histological confirmation of clear margins is curative, followed by surveillance colonoscopy to detect recurrence or new lesions.

Intravenous augmentation therapy provides purified a1-AT from pooled
plasma. This slows emphysema progression in severely deficient patients.
Liver transplantation cures both liver and lung disease.
questions.question: Which treatment option exists for a1-antitrypsin deficiency?

A 40-year-old woman has a 5 cm ovarian mass. Histology shows granulosa cells arranged around small spaces containing eosinophilic material (Call-Exner bodies) and elevated serum inhibin. Which hormone does this tumour most likely produce?
questions.explanation: Granulosa cell tumours (sex cord-stromal tumours) produce oestrogen, which stimulates the endometrium causing hyperplasia (manifesting as postmenopausal bleeding or precocious puberty in girls). Call-Exner bodies (small follicle-like structures with eosinophilic material) are pathognomonic. Inhibin A and B are useful serum markers for monitoring recurrence. Granulosa cell tumours carry low malignant potential but can recur late (10-30 years after resection). FOXL2 C402G mutation is present in over 95% of adult-type granulosa cell tumours and aids molecular diagnosis.
options: Inhibin suppressing FSH without steroid production

questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease shows a significant male predominance with a male to female ratio of 4:1. The condition is associated with Down syndrome and involves heterozygous loss of function mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase RET gene. Complications include risk of perforation, sepsis, enterocolitis, and fluid derangement.
questions.question: What is the male to female ratio in Hirschsprung disease?

questions.explanation:
Ashkenazi Jewish population has 1 in 30 carrier frequency justifying
screening. French-Canadian and Cajun populations also show increased
frequency. Carrier testing enables informed reproductive decisions.
questions.question: Which population should undergo Tay-Sachs carrier screening?
What bacteria commonly colonizes CF lungs?
questions.explanation:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa chronically colonizes CF lungs forming biofilms.
Mucoid strains predominate producing alginate polysaccharide.
Burkholderia cepacia complex also causes problematic infections.

Macrocephaly with frontotemporal atrophy distinguishes glutaric acidemia
Type I. Striatal injury during metabolic crises causes dystonia. Lysine
and tryptophan restriction prevents crises.
questions.question: What distinguishes glutaric acidemia Type I?

questions.explanation:
Insatiable appetite and food-seeking behavior lead to severe obesity
causing major morbidity. Hypothalamic dysfunction impairs satiety
signaling. Strict dietary control and environmental restriction are
necessary.
questions.question: Which Prader-Willi syndrome feature causes major morbidity?

questions.explanation: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma most commonly arises from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), a stepwise sequence of increasing epithelial dysplasia within small ducts driven by accumulating KRAS and other mutations. Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms are a less common but clinically important precursor, typically arising in larger ducts and producing visible mucin-filled cysts.
questions.question: A 65-year-old man has a pancreatic head mass causing obstructive jaundice. Biopsy shows malignant glands with marked desmoplastic stroma infiltrating perineural spaces. What is the most common precursor lesion?

A 60-year-old man has haematuria. Cystoscopy shows a flat erythematous patch. Biopsy shows full-thickness nuclear atypia of the urothelium with dyscohesion, without papillary architecture or stromal invasion. What is the management of choice?
questions.explanation: Urothelial carcinoma in situ (CIS) is a high-grade flat non-invasive urothelial carcinoma characterised by full-thickness cellular atypia, loss of cell polarity, and dyscohesion without invasion. It is treated with intravesical BCG (bacillus Calmette-Guerin) immunotherapy, achieving complete response in approximately 70% of cases. BCG works by inducing local Th1 immune response killing tumour cells. Failure to respond to BCG is an indication for radical cystectomy. CIS carries significant progression risk to muscle-invasive disease if inadequately treated; close surveillance is essential.
options: Transurethral resection and intravesical mitomycin C
Immediate radical cystectomy without further delay
Observation with repeat cystoscopy in 6 months only
External beam pelvic radiotherapy as sole treatment

questions.question: What treatment removes excess iron in hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation:
Regular phlebotomy removes excess iron preventing organ damage if
started before cirrhosis develops. Each unit of blood removes
approximately 250 mg iron. Treatment continues lifelong with monitoring.

questions.question: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from deletion of which chromosome region?
questions.explanation:
Cri-du-chat (cat cry) syndrome results from deletion of
chromosome 5p, causing characteristic high-pitched, mewing cry in
infancy, intellectual disability, microcephaly, and distinctive facial
features. The cry results from laryngeal and CNS abnormalities and
becomes less pronounced with age. Most cases are de novo deletions.

questions.question: A patient with progressive chorea, behavioural changes, and a family history of similar findings is found to have a trinucleotide repeat expansion. Brain imaging shows marked atrophy of the caudate nucleus. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Huntington disease results from a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene, causing progressive neuronal loss particularly affecting the caudate nucleus and putamen, producing the characteristic combination of chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbance. This autosomal dominant condition shows genetic anticipation, with repeat expansion often increasing in subsequent generations, particularly with paternal transmission. Caudate atrophy on imaging, alongside the characteristic clinical triad and family history, supports the diagnosis.

Ewing sarcoma, characterised by small round blue cells expressing CD99 (MIC2), harbours the t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation in approximately 85% of cases, creating the EWS-FLI1 fusion oncogene. This translocation is pathognomonic and distinguishes Ewing from other small round blue cell tumours. Molecular confirmation of this translocation is essential for definitive diagnosis and prognostication.
questions.question: A 10-year-old boy presents with fever, bone pain, and a diaphyseal lytic lesion in the femur. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells positive for CD99. Which chromosomal translocation is characteristic of this tumour?
What is the primary route of transmission for cholera?
questions.explanation: Cholera is transmitted by drinking contaminated water, though it can also be present in food. The causative organism is Vibrio cholerae, which shows marked seasonal variation in most climates due to rapid bacterial growth at warm temperatures. Animal reservoirs include shellfish and plankton.

Additional X chromosomes worsen phenotype with greater intellectual
impairment and skeletal abnormalities. Classic 47,XXY shows mild
phenotype. Each extra X chromosome increases severity.
questions.question: Which Klinefelter syndrome variant shows severe phenotype?

questions.explanation:
DLBCL cells are typically 4-5 times larger than small
lymphocytes with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant
cytoplasm. This aggressive lymphoma represents the most common NHL
(30-40% of cases). Immunophenotyping shows CD20 positivity; BCL-6
rearrangement is common.
questions.question: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is characterized by cells of which size relative to normal lymphocytes?
Spermatic cord lipoma presents as:
questions.explanation: Spermatic cord lipomas are benign adipose tissue masses presenting as soft, reducible inguinal swellings mimicking inguinal hernia ("cord lipoma hernia"). Occur in adults. Ultrasound demonstrates homogeneous echogenic mass. Simple excision during hernia repair is appropriate. No malignant potential. Must distinguish from well-differentiated liposarcoma which shows cellular atypia.

questions.question: In community-acquired pneumonia, which organism is most common overall?
questions.explanation:
Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) remains the most
common cause of community-acquired pneumonia across all age groups,
though incidence has decreased with vaccination. The organism is
identified in sputum/blood cultures and by urinary antigen testing.
Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci are characteristic.

questions.question: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia has what progression risk to carcinoma?
