questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia has <1% progression risk to carcinoma and often regresses with progestin therapy or after anovulatory cycles resolve. Atypical hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia) carries 25-30% progression risk over 10-20 years, requiring treatment. Hysterectomy is definitive; progestin therapy may be attempted in young women desiring fertility.

questions.question: A patient with longstanding hypertension develops a sudden focal neurological deficit. CT shows a haemorrhage centred in the basal ganglia. Which vessel pathology most commonly underlies this type of intracerebral haemorrhage?
options: Venous sinus thrombosis with venous infarction
Embolic occlusion of a cortical artery
Rupture of a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis
questions.explanation: Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage classically occurs in deep brain structures such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, and pons, resulting from rupture of small penetrating arterioles weakened by chronic hypertension, forming microscopic Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms. This contrasts with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which typically causes lobar haemorrhages in the cortical and subcortical regions of elderly patients. Strict blood pressure control is a key modifiable risk factor for preventing this type of haemorrhage.

questions.question: What are the neurologic signs of hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Neurologic signs of hepatic encephalopathy include asterixis (flapping tremor), rigidity, hyperreflexia, non-specific EEG changes, and possible seizures. Asterixis is the characteristic sign—inability to maintain posture with brief lapses in muscle tone. The spectrum ranges from subtle cognitive impairment (West Haven grade 1) to coma (grade 4). Cerebral edema occurs in acute liver failure but not typically in chronic disease.

questions.question: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis shows multifocal demyelinating plaques in white matter with relative axonal preservation initially. Perivenular inflammation with T lymphocytes and macrophages occurs. Oligodendrocyte loss with astrogliosis develops. Clinical relapses and remissions correlate with inflammation and repair. CSF shows oligoclonal bands. MRI demonstrates periventricular white matter lesions. Disease-modifying therapies reduce relapse rates.

Atrioventricular septal defects (endocardial cushion
defects) occur in 40% of Down syndrome cardiac anomalies, much higher
than in general population. Overall, ~40-50% of Down syndrome patients
have congenital heart disease. Ventricular septal defects are also
common. Cardiac evaluation is essential in all Down syndrome patients.
questions.question: Which cardiac defect is most common in Down syndrome?

A 55-year-old man with a 20-year history of heavy alcohol use has a liver biopsy showing micronodular regeneration surrounded by bands of fibrosis. What complication is this patient at highest risk of developing?
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis, regardless of cause, is the strongest risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma due to chronic hepatocyte injury, regeneration, and accumulated genetic alterations. Alcoholic cirrhosis with micronodular regeneration and fibrous septa places this patient at substantially elevated risk, warranting regular surveillance with imaging and alpha-fetoprotein measurement.

Among the three hepatocellular adenoma subtypes, β-catenin activated tumors have high risk of malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma. Inflammatory subtype also carries significant malignant potential. In contrast, HNF1-α inactivated tumors have minimal risk of malignant transformation.
questions.question: Which hepatocellular adenoma subtype has the highest risk of malignant transformation?
Which gene is mutated in juvenile polyposis syndrome?
questions.explanation: Juvenile polyposis syndrome is associated with mutations in SMAD4, which encodes a cytoplasmic intermediate in the TGF-β signaling pathway. BMPR1A, a kinase in the TGF-β superfamily, is mutated in some cases. The syndrome carries an increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Acute intermittent porphyria results from a partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase, causing accumulation of porphyrin precursors that are excreted in urine and darken on exposure to light and air. Attacks are often triggered by fasting, infection, or certain medications that increase haem precursor demand. The characteristic abdominal pain without peritoneal signs, alongside neuropsychiatric symptoms, helps distinguish this from surgical causes of abdominal pain.
questions.question: A child presents with recurrent abdominal pain, dark urine after fasting or illness, and a family history of similar episodes. Urine turns dark on standing due to excess porphyrin precursors. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
Condyloma acuminatum is caused by HPV types:
questions.explanation: HPV types 6 and 11 are low-risk viruses causing benign genital warts (condyloma acuminatum) without significant malignant potential. These papillary lesions show koilocytic atypia histologically. High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 cause cervical dysplasia and carcinoma by inactivating p53 and RB tumor suppressors through E6 and E7 viral proteins.

Excessive salt loss in sweat predisposes to hyponatremic dehydration
particularly in hot weather. Infants may present with failure to thrive
and electrolyte abnormalities. Increased salt intake prevents
dehydration.
questions.question: Which CF complication results from salt loss in sweat?

questions.explanation:
Wound tensile strength typically reaches 70-80% of normal
skin by 3 months post-injury and rarely improves substantially beyond
this point. This limitation results from differences in collagen
organization between scar tissue and normal dermis. The healed wound
never fully replicates the complex architecture of uninjured tissue
despite adequate collagen deposition.
questions.question: During wound healing by primary intention, what is the approximate maximum percentage of tensile strength recovered compared to unwounded skin?

questions.explanation:
HIV-associated dementia involves subcortical structures causing
psychomotor slowing and motor dysfunction. Cortical functions remain
relatively preserved initially. Brain shows multinucleated giant cells
and white matter pallor.
questions.question: Which HIV-associated dementia characteristic distinguishes it from other dementias?

questions.explanation: SCO syndrome shows seminiferous tubules containing only Sertoli cells without germ cells. Causes include Klinefelter syndrome, Y chromosome deletions, cryptorchidism, radiation/chemotherapy, and idiopathic. Azoospermia with normal to slightly small testes, normal testosterone, elevated FSH occur. Testicular biopsy confirms diagnosis. Sperm extraction occasionally successful in focal SCO.
questions.question: Sertoli cell-only syndrome (SCO) is characterized by:
What distinguishes osteogenesis imperfecta from other skeletal dysplasias?
questions.explanation:
Blue sclera results from defective type I collagen allowing visibility
of underlying choroidal veins. This sign along with hearing loss and
dental abnormalities characterizes osteogenesis imperfecta. The
condition exists as clinical spectrum from type 1 to type 4 with varying
severity.

Krukenberg tumor is metastatic adenocarcinoma to the ovaries, classically from gastric cancer (also colon, breast, appendix). Bilateral ovarian masses with signet ring cells are characteristic. The metastatic route is likely lymphatic or hematogenous. Krukenberg tumors account for 1-2% of ovarian tumors. They indicate advanced disease (stage IV) with poor prognosis. Primary gastric tumor may be occult.
questions.question: What is Krukenberg tumor?
What is the most important prognostic factor in colorectal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: The two most important prognostic factors in colorectal carcinoma are depth of invasion and the presence or absence of lymph node metastases. Invasion into the muscularis propria confers significantly reduced survival, which is decreased further by the presence of lymph node metastases. These factors form the basis of TNM staging.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6 cm ovarian cyst lined by tall columnar mucin-secreting epithelium without atypia or invasion, with stromal ovarian invasion absent. The cyst shows complex papillary architecture with stratification up to 3 cell layers. How should this be classified?
questions.explanation: Mucinous borderline tumour (atypical proliferative mucinous tumour) is characterised by complex papillary or glandular architecture with mucin-secreting columnar epithelium showing mild to moderate nuclear atypia and stratification (up to 3 cell layers), but without destructive stromal invasion. It differs from benign cystadenoma (no atypia or complexity) and invasive mucinous carcinoma (stromal invasion present). Mucinous borderline tumours are almost always unilateral. They have an excellent prognosis with surgery alone. Bilateral mucinous tumours should raise suspicion for a metastatic appendiceal or GI primary rather than a primary ovarian tumour.
options: Benign mucinous cystadenoma without borderline features
Mucinous cystadenoma with focal simple hyperplasia
Mucinous borderline tumour (atypical proliferative mucinous tumour)

questions.explanation:
Newborn screening measures blood phenylalanine levels at 24-48 hours of
life. Elevated levels prompt confirmatory testing and dietary
intervention. Early detection and treatment prevent mental retardation.
questions.question: What screening test detects PKU in newborns?
Pregnancy-associated breast cancer (PABC) is defined as cancer diagnosed:
options: During pregnancy or within 5 years postpartum
During pregnancy or within 1 year postpartum
questions.explanation: PABC is breast cancer diagnosed during pregnancy or within one year postpartum. Often presents at advanced stage due to dense breast tissue delaying detection and attribution of symptoms to physiologic changes. Usually high-grade, ER-negative. Treatment requires multidisciplinary approach. Chemotherapy can be administered after first trimester. Termination doesn't improve outcomes.

questions.question: Embryonal carcinoma produces which tumor markers?
questions.explanation: Embryonal carcinomas produce both AFP and -hCG, showing primitive epithelial cells forming papillary structures, sheets, and glands. Highly aggressive with rapid growth and early metastasis. Usually occurs in mixed germ cell tumors. Pure embryonal carcinoma is rare in ovary (more common in testis). Combination chemotherapy required.

questions.question: Which mutation class prevents CFTR protein synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Class I mutations introduce premature stop codons preventing CFTR
protein production. These nonsense mutations cause severe disease.
Different mutation classes require different therapeutic approaches.

questions.question: What is transarterial chemoembolization (TACE)?
questions.explanation: Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) delivers concentrated chemotherapy directly into hepatic arteries feeding HCC, followed by arterial occlusion with embolic agents. This creates high local drug concentration with tumor ischemia while sparing normal liver (dual blood supply). TACE is first-line for intermediate-stage HCC (BCLC-B). Complications include post-embolization syndrome and rarely hepatic failure. Repeated sessions may be needed.

Chromophobe RCC shows large pale cells with prominent cell membranes ("plant-like"), perinuclear halos, and irregular wrinkled nuclei (raisinoid). Hale colloidal iron stains cytoplasm. Multiple chromosome losses occur. Arises from intercalated cells of collecting ducts. Better prognosis than clear cell RCC. Difficult to distinguish from oncocytoma; Birt-Hogg-Dub syndrome predisposes to both.
questions.question: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma cells contain:

questions.explanation: Prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and INR are the most common coagulation abnormalities in cirrhosis, reflecting decreased hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Factor VII has the shortest half-life, causing early PT prolongation. Thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism, decreased thrombopoietin production, and DIC-like consumption also occur. The MELD score uses INR for severity assessment.
questions.question: What coagulation defect is most common in cirrhosis?

options: Ependymoma arising from the fourth ventricle ependyma
Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumour with SMARCB1 loss
Primitive neuroectodermal tumour of cerebral hemisphere
Choroid plexus carcinoma from posterior fossa plexus
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumour in children, arising in the cerebellar vermis and frequently invading the fourth ventricle. Homer Wright rosettes (ring arrangements of tumour cells around neuropil fibrils, without a central lumen) indicate neuroblastic differentiation. Molecular subgroups include WNT-activated (best prognosis), SHH-activated, and non-WNT/non-SHH Groups 3 and 4. Treatment involves surgical resection, craniospinal irradiation (in children over 3 years), and chemotherapy. SMARCB1 (INI1) loss characterises atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumours, which must be excluded in infants.
questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with headache, vomiting, and an MRI showing a posterior fossa midline mass. Histology shows sheets of small primitive cells with Homer Wright rosettes and synaptophysin positivity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Deficiency of the terminal complement components (C5 through C9), which form the membrane attack complex, is specifically associated with increased susceptibility to recurrent Neisseria infections, as this pathway is particularly important for direct lysis of these organisms. This contrasts with C3 deficiency, which causes more generalised susceptibility to pyogenic bacterial infections due to impaired opsonisation. Recognising this specific deficiency pattern guides targeted vaccination and prophylaxis strategies.
options: C3 deficiency causing recurrent pyogenic infections
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with recurrent meningococcal infections despite vaccination. Laboratory testing reveals absence of the terminal complement complex. Which complement component deficiency is most associated with this specific susceptibility?

options: LDH reflecting total tumour bulk and metabolism
CA-125 from epithelial component of the tumour
questions.question: A 25-year-old man has a painless testicular mass with serum AFP of 5,000 ng/mL. Histology reveals a reticular/microcystic pattern with Schiller-Duval bodies. Which tumour marker confirms this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Yolk sac tumour (endodermal sinus tumour) of the testis produces alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) — the oncofoetal protein normally produced by the yolk sac, liver, and GI tract in foetal life. Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures) are pathognomonic. AFP is the definitive tumour marker for monitoring; failure of AFP to normalise after orchidectomy indicates residual or metastatic disease. Pure seminoma does NOT elevate AFP — any AFP elevation in apparent seminoma indicates non-seminomatous elements, fundamentally changing treatment management. BEP chemotherapy is standard for metastatic disease.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency classically causes panlobular (panacinar) emphysema predominantly in the lower lobes, in contrast to centrilobular emphysema of smoking which preferentially affects upper lobe respiratory bronchioles. Without A1AT, neutrophil elastase degrades alveolar walls throughout the entire acinus including alveolar ducts and sacs. Smoking dramatically accelerates progression. The lower lobe predominance reflects greater blood flow and neutrophil trafficking to dependent lung zones where greater cumulative elastase burden accumulates over time.
questions.question: An alpha-1 antitrypsin ZZ homozygote presents with emphysema at age 40 without significant smoking history. The characteristic lung pathology pattern is:
options: Panlobular emphysema predominantly affecting lower lung zones
Centrilobular emphysema predominantly affecting upper lung zones
Bullous emphysema with giant apical blebs causing pneumothorax
Paraseptal emphysema immediately adjacent to pleural surfaces
Scar emphysema following previous pneumonia or tuberculosis

questions.explanation:
Myeloma requires =10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells (or
biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus evidence of end-organ damage (CRAB
criteria: hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions).
Smoldering myeloma has =10% plasma cells or M-protein =3 g/dL without
end-organ damage. Higher plasma cell percentages correlate with worse
prognosis.
questions.question: Plasma cell myeloma is definitively diagnosed when bone marrow plasma cells exceed:
Gaucher disease causes massive splenomegaly through accumulation of which substance?
questions.explanation:
Gaucher disease results from glucocerebrosidase deficiency
causing glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages (Gaucher cells),
leading to massive hepatosplenomegaly. These storage macrophages have
characteristic "crinkled paper" cytoplasm. The spleen can reach
enormous sizes (>3000g) requiring splenectomy or enzyme replacement
therapy.

options: Alloantibody formation against minor blood group antigens
Transfusion-transmitted hepatitis B despite vaccination protocol
Progressive hemolytic anemia from splenomegaly and hypersplenism
Graft-versus-host disease from transfused allogeneic lymphocytes
Iron overload causing cardiac failure, endocrinopathy, and cirrhosis
questions.explanation: Each unit of packed red blood cells contains approximately 200-250 mg of iron, which the body cannot excrete. Without chelation therapy (deferoxamine, deferasirox, or deferiprone), transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia major patients accumulate sufficient iron within 5-10 years to cause cardiomyopathy (the leading cause of death), endocrine failure (hypogonadism, diabetes, hypothyroidism), and hepatic cirrhosis. Regular monitoring of serum ferritin and liver iron concentration by MRI guides chelation intensity. Adherence to chelation therapy dramatically improves survival and quality of life in thalassemia major.
questions.question: A 3-year-old child with beta-thalassemia major requires regular transfusions. The most serious long-term complication of chronic transfusion without chelation is:

options: Immediate biochemical screening with ceruloplasmin and urine copper
Liver biopsy to confirm copper accumulation in hepatocytes
Empirical penicillamine treatment without biochemical confirmation
Annual surveillance starting at school age without testing now
Genetic testing for ATP7B mutation as the definitive initial screen
questions.explanation: Siblings of Wilson disease probands have a 25% risk of being affected (autosomal recessive inheritance). Biochemical screening with serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper is recommended for all first-degree relatives including asymptomatic siblings at the time of proband diagnosis. Presymptomatic treatment prevents irreversible organ damage. While ATP7B mutation analysis is valuable (particularly when the proband's mutations are known), biochemical screening is faster, less expensive, and clinically validated. Liver biopsy is reserved for equivocal biochemistry. Empirical treatment without diagnosis is inappropriate.
questions.question: A 6-year-old boy has Wilson disease. His 3-year-old asymptomatic sibling requires evaluation. The most appropriate management for the sibling is:
What is the hallmark histologic feature of chronic viral hepatitis?
questions.explanation: The defining histologic feature of chronic viral hepatitis is mononuclear portal infiltration. Interface hepatitis refers to inflammatory cells at the portal region involving the bordering hepatocytes (formerly called piecemeal necrosis). Additional features include parenchymal inflammation, necrosis, and variable degrees of fibrosis.

questions.question: What treatment improves final height in Turner syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Growth hormone therapy started in childhood improves final adult height
by 5-10 cm. Earlier initiation provides better results. Estrogen
replacement at puberty develops secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.question: What is Sister Mary Joseph nodule?
questions.explanation: Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a periumbilical metastatic nodule, typically from gastric, ovarian, colorectal, or pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Named after Sister Mary Joseph who noted this sign assisting Dr. William Mayo. It represents peritoneal spread with umbilical implantation, indicating advanced disease (stage IV). Physical examination of the umbilicus is important in patients with abdominal malignancies.

questions.question: A patient with progressive cognitive decline undergoes brain biopsy showing extracellular amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer disease is characterised histologically by extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, predominantly affecting the hippocampus and cortical association areas responsible for the characteristic memory and cognitive decline. This combination of pathological hallmarks distinguishes it from other dementias, such as Lewy body dementia, which is characterised by alpha-synuclein-containing Lewy bodies instead. Definitive diagnosis traditionally requires postmortem histological confirmation, though clinical criteria and biomarkers increasingly support diagnosis in life.

questions.question: Amyloidosis as a complication of multiple myeloma most commonly affects which organ first?
questions.explanation:
AL amyloidosis from myeloma most commonly affects heart
(restrictive cardiomyopathy) and kidneys (nephrotic syndrome), though
any organ except brain can be involved. Macroglossia, periorbital
purpura, and peripheral neuropathy are characteristic. Cardiac
involvement determines prognosis; advanced cardiac amyloidosis has
median survival <6 months without treatment.

questions.question: The most useful immunohistochemical markers for prostate adenocarcinoma are:
options: p63 and high molecular weight cytokeratin
AMACR (p504S) and absence of basal cells
questions.explanation: Prostate adenocarcinomas lack basal cells (p63 and high molecular weight cytokeratin negative) and express AMACR (racemase), an enzyme involved in fatty acid metabolism. Triple stain cocktail (p63, HMWCK, AMACR) aids diagnosis. PSA and PSAP demonstrate prostatic origin but don't distinguish benign from malignant. Complete absence of basal cell layer confirms carcinoma.

Testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) develop in males with congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to chronic ACTH stimulation of aberrant adrenal cells in testes. Bilateral masses near rete testis occur. Histology shows cells resembling adrenal cortex. Intensive glucocorticoid suppression may shrink tumors. Important to recognize to avoid unnecessary orchiectomy.
questions.question: Testicular adrenal rest tumors occur in:

options: Obesity causing excess adipose tissue oestrogen conversion
Chronic alcohol consumption causing hepatic dysfunction
Anabolic steroid use for athletic performance
questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with a subareolar breast mass confirmed as invasive ductal carcinoma on biopsy. Which risk factor is most strongly associated with male breast carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY karyotype) is the strongest risk factor for male breast cancer, increasing lifetime risk approximately 50-fold compared to 46,XY males. The persistently elevated oestrogen-to-androgen ratio in Klinefelter syndrome drives ductal proliferation. BRCA2 mutation is the most important hereditary factor in male breast cancer generally. Male breast carcinoma is usually invasive ductal carcinoma and presents at an older age. Prognosis is similar stage-for-stage to female breast carcinoma when matched for molecular subtype.

Progressive cardiac conduction defects cause sudden death in myotonic
dystrophy. Pacemaker placement may be required. Dilated cardiomyopathy
also occurs.
questions.question: What cardiac complication requires monitoring in myotonic dystrophy?

questions.explanation: Adenomyosis represents extension of endometrial glands and stroma into the myometrium at least 2mm below the basalis layer. The condition causes diffuse uterine enlargement, dysmenorrhea, and menorrhagia. Hormonal therapy or hysterectomy provides definitive treatment. Imaging shows thickened junctional zone and myometrial cysts.
questions.question: Adenomyosis is defined as:
Sclerosing adenosis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Sclerosing adenosis shows proliferation of small acini distorted and compressed by dense stromal fibrosis, mimicking invasive carcinoma. Myoepithelial cells remain intact around acini, distinguishing it from carcinoma. This proliferative lesion without atypia confers 1.5-2 times increased breast cancer risk. Calcifications may be visible mammographically.

questions.question: Which schistosome species causes urinary bladder carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Schistosoma haematobium inhabits pelvic venous plexus depositing eggs in
bladder wall. Chronic inflammation and granuloma formation predispose to
squamous cell carcinoma. IARC classifies S. haematobium as definite
human carcinogen for bladder cancer.

options: Hypotension, edema, lactic acidosis, pulmonary edema
Hematuria, elevated creatinine, lung disease, pericarditis
Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets
questions.question: HELLP syndrome consists of:
questions.explanation: HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is severe complication of pre-eclampsia/eclampsia. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatocellular injury occur. Patients present with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, malaise. Hepatic subcapsular hematoma or rupture may develop. Immediate delivery and supportive care essential. Maternal and fetal mortality significant.

Large metastatic implants in the liver often have defective blood supply leading to central necrosis, which creates a depressed appearance on the surface called umbilication. This characteristic finding can be seen on imaging and at gross examination. The tumor outgrows its blood supply, causing ischemic necrosis in the center while the periphery remains viable.
questions.question: What characterizes umbilication in liver metastases?

questions.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is characterized by "beading" on cholangiography (ERCP or MRCP), showing alternating strictures and dilations of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts. This distinctive pattern results from fibrosing inflammatory obliteration of bile ducts. Histologically, onion skin fibrosis (concentric periductal fibrosis) around medium and small intrahepatic ducts is characteristic.
questions.question: What is the characteristic radiographic finding in primary sclerosing cholangitis?

questions.explanation: Isolated or combined pituitary hormone deficiencies with hypoplastic anterior pituitary on MRI frequently result from mutations in transcription factors essential for pituitary organogenesis, including PROP1, POU1F1 (Pit-1), HESX1, LHX3, and LHX4. These transcription factors regulate pituitary progenitor cell differentiation into hormone-secreting cell types during embryonic development. PROP1 mutations cause combined deficiency of GH, TSH, prolactin, LH, and FSH in variable combinations. Genetic testing of pituitary development transcription factors is indicated in all children with hypoplastic anterior pituitary and idiopathic growth hormone deficiency.
options: Rathke cleft cyst compressing the pituitary gland from above
SOD1 gain-of-function mutation causing oxidative pituitary damage
Autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis from maternal antibodies
Transcription factor mutation during pituitary organogenesis
Previous neonatal hypoxic ischemic injury to hypothalamus
questions.question: A 6-year-old child has isolated growth hormone deficiency and MRI shows hypoplastic anterior pituitary. Pituitary hypoplasia in this context most likely results from:

questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) causes bilateral vestibular schwannomas, other schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas. NF2 gene on chromosome 22q encodes merlin tumor suppressor. Patients present with hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance problems. Histology shows Antoni A (dense) and Antoni B (loose) patterns with Verocay bodies. Treatment includes observation, surgery, or stereotactic radiosurgery.
questions.question: Acoustic schwannomas are associated with:
A newborn male has urethral opening on the ventral penile surface. This anomaly is termed:
questions.explanation: Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of urethral folds during embryonic development, leaving abnormal ventral urethral opening. Severity varies from glanular to perineal locations. Associated findings may include chordee (penile curvature), cryptorchidism, and inguinal hernias. Surgical correction is typically performed before two years of age.

questions.question: The pathognomonic cell of Hodgkin lymphoma is:
questions.explanation:
Reed-Sternberg cells (large binucleated or multinucleated
cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli) are required for Hodgkin
lymphoma diagnosis. Classic RS cells show "owl's eye" appearance.
Variants include lacunar cells (nodular sclerosis) and popcorn cells
(lymphocyte predominant). RS-like cells can occur in other conditions
requiring appropriate context.

questions.question: What is the characteristic ulcer pattern in intestinal tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Intestinal tuberculosis presents with circular ulcers of varying size in the transverse plane of the bowel. As the ulcers heal, reactive fibrosis may cause a circumferential stricture of the bowel lumen. Mesenteric lymph nodes are typically enlarged and display caseous necrosis.

questions.question: What percentage of acute pancreatitis cases are attributable to alcoholism in males?
questions.explanation: In alcoholism-related acute pancreatitis, males are affected more commonly than females with a male to female ratio of 6:1. In contrast, acute pancreatitis associated with biliary disease is more common in females. Alcohol and gallstones are the two most prominent causes of acute pancreatitis.

Down syndrome children have 10-20 fold increased risk of
acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia (particularly
megakaryoblastic type). However, they often respond well to chemotherapy
with outcomes comparable to or better than non-Down syndrome cases.
Transient myeloproliferative disorder unique to Down syndrome can
resolve spontaneously.
questions.question: Individuals with Down syndrome have markedly increased risk for which malignancy?

questions.explanation: LCIS represents discohesive proliferation of monotonous cells expanding lobules, serving as marker of increased bilateral breast cancer risk (both ductal and lobular types) rather than obligate precursor. Management options include surveillance, chemoprevention (tamoxifen/raloxifene), or bilateral prophylactic mastectomy for high-risk patients. Excision not required if diagnosed on core biopsy matching imaging.
options: Precursor to invasive lobular carcinoma only
Risk indicator for future bilateral cancer
questions.question: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) is considered:
What defines the lacunar variant of Reed-Sternberg cells in nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Lacunar cells have multilobated nuclei and abundant pale cytoplasm that
retracts in formalin fixation. This retraction creates an empty space or
lacunae around the nucleus giving characteristic appearance. These cells
are pathognomonic of nodular sclerosis subtype of classical Hodgkin
lymphoma.

Medullary carcinoma of the colon is a histologic subtype associated with microsatellite instability (MSI-H), characterized by poor differentiation, solid growth pattern, and prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. Despite poor differentiation, it has better prognosis than conventional adenocarcinoma. MLH1 hypermethylation (sporadic MSI) or Lynch syndrome may be present. The term "medullary" refers to the solid, soft appearance.
questions.question: What characterizes medullary carcinoma of the colon?

options: Juvenile polyposis syndrome without malignancy risk
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with increased malignancy risk
Familial adenomatous polyposis with universal colorectal cancer
questions.explanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is characterised by hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps and characteristic perioral and mucocutaneous pigmented macules, and although the polyps themselves are hamartomatous rather than classically pre-malignant, affected individuals have a significantly increased lifetime risk of various malignancies, including gastrointestinal and gynaecological cancers. This distinguishes it from familial adenomatous polyposis, which carries a near-universal risk of colorectal cancer specifically from adenomatous polyps. Regular surveillance for malignancy is recommended throughout life in affected individuals.
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with recurrent abdominal pain and is found to have multiple gastrointestinal polyps on endoscopy, along with perioral pigmented macules. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation, and which complication carries increased long-term risk?

questions.explanation: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and characteristically shows normal-appearing glomeruli on light microscopy, with diffuse podocyte foot process effacement only visible on electron microscopy. This contrasts with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which shows visible scarring on light microscopy. Most children respond well to corticosteroid therapy, supporting the generally favourable prognosis of this condition.
questions.question: A 6-year-old presents with periorbital and facial oedema, frothy urine, and hypoalbuminaemia. Renal biopsy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy with normal light microscopy. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Ischaemic colitis typically affects watershed areas such as the splenic flexure, which receive marginal blood supply from two vascular territories. Histology shows mucosal necrosis, hyalinised lamina propria, and atrophic 'withered' crypts. The clinical context of vascular risk factors and acute onset supports ischaemia over inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.question: A 70-year-old hypertensive man on dialysis presents with sudden abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. Colonic biopsy shows mucosal necrosis with hyalinised lamina propria and withered crypts, most prominent at the splenic flexure. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation:
Deletion of 17p eliminates the TP53 tumor suppressor gene,
conferring very poor prognosis in multiple myeloma with resistance to
conventional therapies. This is considered a high-risk cytogenetic
abnormality along with t(4;14) and t(14;16). Detection influences
treatment decisions favoring more aggressive initial approaches.
questions.question: In plasma cell myeloma, which cytogenetic abnormality is associated with poorest prognosis?
Clear cell sarcoma of kidney differs from Wilms tumor by:
questions.explanation: Clear cell sarcoma of kidney (bone-metastasizing renal tumor of childhood) shows propensity for bone and brain metastases unlike Wilms tumor. Worse prognosis requires aggressive chemotherapy. Occurs in slightly older children (mean age 3 years). Histology shows clear cells in nested/cystic patterns. BCOR gene alterations are characteristic. Not related to Wilms tumor despite renal location.

questions.question: In homocystinuria from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, the feature best distinguishing it from Marfan syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Homocystinuria and Marfan syndrome share ectopia lentis, arachnodactyly, and tall stature, making clinical distinction difficult. Homocystinuria is uniquely characterized by intellectual disability (absent in Marfan) and thromboembolic events due to homocysteine-induced endothelial damage and platelet activation. In homocystinuria, lens displacement is typically inferior, while in Marfan syndrome it is superior. Elevated plasma homocysteine and urine amino acid analysis confirm the biochemical diagnosis of homocystinuria conclusively.
options: Ectopia lentis with lens displacement in affected patients
Arachnodactyly and tall stature with dolichostenomelia
Aortic root dilation requiring echocardiographic surveillance
Pectus excavatum deformity from chest wall connective tissue

questions.question: At what age does the thymus typically reach its maximum absolute weight?
questions.explanation:
The thymus reaches maximum absolute weight (20-50g) at
puberty, though relative size peaks in infancy. Progressive involution
then occurs with fatty replacement throughout adulthood, leaving minimal
lymphoid tissue in elderly. Despite involution, residual thymic tissue
maintains limited T cell production throughout life.

questions.question: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) causes:
questions.explanation: Primary hyperaldosteronism from adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia causes hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Excessive aldosterone promotes sodium retention and potassium wasting. Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio aids screening. Muscle weakness, polyuria, and polydipsia result from hypokalemia. Surgical adrenalectomy cures adenomas; spironolactone treats bilateral hyperplasia.

Meningiomas derive from arachnoid cap cells of the
meninges, representing most common benign intracranial tumor. They're
more frequent in women (progesterone receptors present) and may grow
during pregnancy. Most are WHO grade I (benign) with excellent prognosis
after resection. Loss of chromosome 22 (NF2 gene) is common.
questions.question: Meningiomas arise from which cell type?

questions.explanation: Hereditary hemochromatosis is the most common single gene disorder in whites, with 1/220 of Northern European ancestry being homozygous for the mutation and 1/11 being heterozygous. The C282Y mutation in the HFE gene accounts for the majority of cases. Despite high carrier frequency, disease penetrance is incomplete.
questions.question: What is the most common single gene disorder in whites?

questions.explanation:
The t(15;17) translocation creating PML-RARA fusion
defines acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, AML-M3). This unique fusion
protein responds to all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) inducing
differentiation. APL presents with DIC from promyelocyte granule
release. ATRA plus arsenic trioxide achieves >90% cure rates.
questions.question: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is characterized by which translocation?

questions.explanation:
Goodpasture syndrome involves anti-glomerular basement
membrane antibodies (specifically against a3 chain of type IV collagen)
causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.
Linear IgG deposition along GBM is pathognomonic on immunofluorescence.
The disease affects young men predominantly. Plasmapheresis removes
antibodies; immunosuppression prevents new antibody formation.
questions.question: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies against which target?

questions.explanation:
Increased protein catabolism during illness or high protein intake
exceeds limited enzyme capacity. Branched-chain amino acids and
ketoacids accumulate causing metabolic crisis. Prompt treatment prevents
neurologic damage.
questions.question: What triggers metabolic crisis in maple syrup urine disease?
What facial feature characterizes Williams syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Elfin-like facies with full cheeks, wide mouth, and stellate iris
pattern are characteristic. Periorbital fullness and short upturned nose
contribute to appearance. Recognition enables clinical diagnosis.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Serology is positive for anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Coeliac disease is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy producing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis, with anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies being highly specific serological markers. Tropical sprue produces similar histology but follows travel to endemic areas and lacks the specific serology.

questions.question: The most common site of distant metastasis from prostate cancer is:
questions.explanation: Bone metastases occur in 80-90% of men dying from prostate cancer, predominantly affecting axial skeleton (lumbar spine, pelvis, ribs, femur). Osteoblastic lesions are characteristic. Skeletal complications include pain, fractures, spinal cord compression, and bone marrow suppression. Bisphosphonates and denosumab reduce skeletal-related events. Radium-223 targets bone metastases.

questions.question: What is hepatopulmonary syndrome?
questions.explanation: Hepatopulmonary syndrome occurs in 15-30% of cirrhotic patients, characterized by intrapulmonary vascular dilations causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxemia (PaO2 <70mmHg). Patients develop platypnea (dyspnea when upright) and orthodeoxia (oxygen desaturation when upright). Contrast echocardiography with late appearance of bubbles in left heart confirms diagnosis. It may improve with liver transplantation.

options: Immunofluorescence showing dominant mesangial IgA deposits
Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence
Electron microscopy showing uniform GBM thinning
Silver stain showing spike pattern on glomerular basement membrane
PAS staining showing Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular lesions
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has proteinuria, haematuria, and hypertension. Renal biopsy shows mesangial hypercellularity. Which staining confirms the diagnosis of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, defined by dominant or codominant mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, often with IgG and C3. Light microscopy shows mesangial hypercellularity and matrix expansion. Electron microscopy confirms mesangial electron-dense deposits. It frequently presents after upper respiratory or GI infection (synpharyngitic haematuria). Prognosis varies; 20-30% reach ESRD within 20 years. RAS blockade (ACE inhibitors/ARBs) slows progression. Corticosteroids are added for persistent proteinuria over 1 g per day despite RAS blockade.

questions.question: Which stain is most specific for demonstrating amyloid deposits?
questions.explanation:
Congo red produces pathognomonic apple-green birefringence
under polarized light due to binding to amyloid's beta-pleated sheet
structure. This is the gold standard for amyloid diagnosis. Other stains
(thioflavin T, crystal violet) can suggest amyloid but lack Congo red's
specificity.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man undergoes colonic resection for a mass. Histology shows malignant glands with marked mucin production filling more than 50% of the tumour volume. What is the histological subtype?
questions.explanation: Mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon is defined by extracellular mucin comprising more than 50% of the tumour, often associated with microsatellite instability and a distinct prognosis compared with conventional adenocarcinoma. Signet-ring cell carcinoma instead shows intracellular mucin displacing the nucleus, a different and generally more aggressive pattern.

questions.question: What characterizes NAFLD spectrum?
questions.explanation: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) comprises a full spectrum of conditions from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis (NASH), fibrosis, and cirrhosis. The progression from benign steatosis to advanced disease is influenced by metabolic syndrome components, genetic factors, and environmental factors. Not all patients with steatosis progress to advanced disease.

questions.question: Microscopic polyangiitis differs from GPA by which feature?
questions.explanation:
Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) causes necrotizing
vasculitis of small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles) WITHOUT
granulomas, distinguishing it from GPA. It typically shows p-ANCA
(anti-MPO) positivity. Common manifestations include rapidly progressive
glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis (hemoptysis). Treatment is
similar to GPA.

questions.question: A 7-month-old with Tay-Sachs disease develops macrocephaly. The direct mechanism causing progressive head enlargement is:
questions.explanation: GM2 ganglioside accumulates within neuronal lysosomes, causing progressive ballooning and enlargement of neurons throughout the brain. This lysosomal engorgement physically enlarges neurons contributing to macrocephaly despite eventual neuronal loss. The process is not hydrocephalus and CSF pathways remain patent in early disease. The characteristic neuropathological finding is lipid-laden swollen neurons with membranous cytoplasmic bodies on electron microscopy, distinguishable from the demyelinating lesions seen in leukodystrophies.
options: Neuronal ballooning from lysosomal GM2 ganglioside engorgement
Obstructive hydrocephalus from brainstem granuloma formation
Megalencephaly from excess abnormal myelination deposition
Cerebral edema from blood-brain barrier disruption and leak
Increased CSF from choroid plexus infiltration by lipid

questions.explanation:
Follicular lymphoma is characterized by t(14;18) translocation in
approximately 90% of cases. This translocation juxtaposes the bcl-2 gene
with the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus leading to bcl-2
overexpression. Bcl-2 overexpression inhibits apoptosis allowing
prolonged survival of malignant B cells.
questions.question: Which chromosomal translocation is characteristic of follicular lymphoma?
What is porcelain gallbladder?
questions.explanation: Porcelain gallbladder refers to calcification of the gallbladder wall in chronic cholecystitis. The calcification may be extensive, creating a hard, brittle organ visible on imaging. Porcelain gallbladder is associated with increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma and is often an indication for prophylactic cholecystectomy.

questions.question: Which cell type is primarily infected by Mycobacterium tuberculosis during initial pulmonary exposure?
questions.explanation:
M. tuberculosis enters macrophages through phagocytosis mediated by
mannose receptors and complement receptors. The bacteria replicate
within phagosomes by preventing phagolysosome formation through blocking
calcium signaling and protein assembly. This initial infection in
macrophages occurs during the first 3 weeks before cell-mediated
immunity develops.

questions.question: Which Turner syndrome complication requires lifelong monitoring?
questions.explanation:
Bicuspid aortic valve and aortic coarctation predispose to aortic
dissection. Regular echocardiography monitors aortic root dilation.
Dissection risk persists lifelong requiring surveillance.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11/LKB1 mutation) shows
hamartomatous polyps throughout GI tract (especially small bowel) and
characteristic perioral/buccal melanotic macules. Polyps can cause
intussusception and bleeding. Increased cancer risk exists (GI,
pancreas, breast, ovary, testis) requiring surveillance. The hamartomas
show branching smooth muscle core.
questions.question: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is characterized by:
Myelodysplastic syndrome is characterized by which feature?
options: Normal blood counts with marrow fibrosis
questions.explanation:
MDS shows peripheral cytopenias despite hypercellular
marrow due to ineffective hematopoiesis with dysplastic changes
(nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony, abnormal granulation, binucleation).
The disorder represents pre-leukemic clonal stem cell expansion. Risk of
AML transformation varies by MDS subtype; high-risk disease progresses
to AML in 30-40% of cases.

Sturge-Weber syndrome shows facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in trigeminal distribution with ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis causing seizures, intellectual disability, and focal neurologic deficits. GNAQ somatic mutation occurs. Characteristic "tramtrack" cortical calcifications appear on imaging. Glaucoma may develop. Treatment targets seizure control and complications.
questions.question: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterized by:

options: No, not required but common background
questions.question: Is cirrhosis a prerequisite for hepatocellular carcinoma development?
questions.explanation: While HCC is usually identified in a background of cirrhosis, cirrhosis per se is not a premalignant lesion and is not required for hepatocarcinogenesis. The most important underlying factors are viral infections (HBV, HCV) and toxic injuries (aflatoxin, alcohol), which can cause HCC even without cirrhosis.

questions.question: A 3-year-old presents with delayed separation of the umbilical cord, recurrent bacterial infections, and a markedly elevated peripheral white cell count with absent pus formation at infection sites. Which underlying defect explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency results from defects in integrin molecules required for neutrophil adhesion to vascular endothelium and subsequent migration to sites of infection, causing markedly elevated peripheral neutrophil counts (as cells cannot leave the bloodstream) alongside paradoxically absent pus formation at infection sites due to impaired neutrophil recruitment. Delayed umbilical cord separation is a classic early clinical clue. This contrasts with chronic granulomatous disease, where neutrophils reach infection sites but cannot effectively kill ingested organisms.
options: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairing neutrophil migration
Absent neutrophil production from the bone marrow

questions.question: Periventricular calcifications on neuroimaging suggest which congenital infection?
questions.explanation:
CMV causes characteristic periventricular calcifications,
microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and sensorineural hearing loss. It's the
most common congenital infection in developed countries (0.5-2% of live
births). Most infected infants are asymptomatic at birth but may develop
hearing loss or neurodevelopmental delays later.

Paget disease represents intraepidermal spread of adenocarcinoma cells from underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma, presenting as eczematous nipple changes. Large pale malignant cells (Paget cells) with abundant cytoplasm infiltrate epidermis. Biopsy confirms diagnosis. Underlying carcinoma requires identification and treatment. Mastectomy or breast-conserving surgery with radiation treats disease.
questions.question: Paget disease of the nipple is associated with underlying:
Which syndrome is characterized by gonadal dysgenesis and nephropathy with germline WT1 mutations?
questions.explanation:
Denys-Drash syndrome features gonadal dysgenesis, early-onset
nephropathy, and Wilms tumor from dominant-negative WT1 mutations. The
nephropathy presents as diffuse mesangial sclerosis leading to renal
failure. Male pseudohermaphroditism results from gonadal dysgenesis.

Sequestrum is devitalized bone fragment separated from viable bone by granulation tissue, serving as nidus for persistent infection. Involucrum (reactive new bone formation) surrounds dead bone. Sinus tracts may develop draining purulent material. Surgical debridement removing sequestrum combined with prolonged antibiotics is necessary for cure. Biofilm formation on dead bone protects bacteria from antibiotics.
questions.question: Sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis refers to:

questions.explanation: Alcoholic cirrhosis classically presents as micronodular cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis), though it may evolve to a mixed pattern over time. Steatosis and ballooned hepatocytes may "burn out" in advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis. The liver initially becomes enlarged, yellow, and greasy, then becomes red with bile-stained areas and visible nodules.
questions.question: What is the classic cirrhosis pattern in alcoholic liver disease?

questions.explanation: Endometriomas result from ectopic endometrial tissue in the ovary that undergoes cyclic bleeding, producing cysts filled with dark brown altered blood resembling chocolate. The hemorrhage triggers inflammation and fibrosis causing pelvic adhesions and infertility. These lesions respond to hormonal fluctuations and may cause severe dysmenorrhea.
questions.question: Chocolate cysts of the ovary are characteristic of:
A 65-year-old woman with primary sclerosing cholangitis develops a hilar bile duct mass. Biopsy shows malignant glands with desmoplastic stroma and mucin production. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile duct epithelium and is strongly associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis, presenting as a desmoplastic, mucin-producing glandular tumour at the hilum (Klatskin tumour) or more peripherally. Unlike hepatocellular carcinoma, it does not produce bile and typically stains for biliary/glandular markers rather than HepPar-1.

Serous tumors are bilateral in 20-30% of benign cases and 65% of malignant cases. Mucinous tumors are bilateral in only 5%. Endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas show bilaterality in 10-15%. Metastatic tumors (Krukenberg) characteristically involve both ovaries. Dermoid cysts are bilateral in 10-15% but usually asynchronous.
questions.question: Which ovarian tumor is most commonly bilateral?
Polymyositis differs from dermatomyositis by which feature?
questions.explanation:
Polymyositis shows endomysial inflammation with CD8+ T
cells invading non-necrotic muscle fibers (unlike dermatomyositis's
perifascicular pattern). No skin manifestations occur. MHC-I expression
is upregulated on muscle fibers. The disorder is less common than
dermatomyositis and diagnosis requires excluding inclusion body myositis
and muscular dystrophies.

questions.question: Normal spleen weight in adults typically ranges within which parameters?
questions.explanation:
Normal adult spleen weighs approximately 150-200 grams
(similar to kidney) with dimensions around 12cm length, 7cm width, and
3cm thickness. Weights exceeding 400-500 grams indicate pathological
splenomegaly requiring investigation. The spleen can massively enlarge
(>1000g) in myeloproliferative disorders and chronic hemolytic anemias.

Deletion 17p (TP53 loss) and TP53 mutations confer very
poor prognosis with resistance to conventional chemotherapy, median
survival <3 years without novel agents. Deletion 11q (ATM loss) also
indicates high-risk disease. Isolated deletion 13q has favorable
prognosis. FISH testing should be performed in all CLL patients.
questions.question: Which factor indicates high-risk disease in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?

questions.explanation: Rosenthal fibers are eosinophilic corkscrew-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions composed of aggregated intermediate filaments and heat shock proteins, characteristically found in pilocytic astrocytomas. Also seen in Alexander disease (genetic disorder affecting astrocytes) and chronic gliosis. These inclusions represent astrocytic stress response and are not specific for neoplasia.
questions.question: Rosenthal fibers are seen in:

questions.explanation:
Beta-2-microglobulin accumulates in long-term dialysis
patients because it's not efficiently cleared by dialysis membranes.
Amyloid deposits in joints, bones, and carpal tunnel causing destructive
arthropathy. Modern high-flux dialysis membranes have reduced incidence.
Renal transplantation resolves the condition.
questions.question: Dialysis-related amyloidosis is composed of which protein?

questions.explanation: Sarcomatoid (spindle cell) dedifferentiation occurs in any RCC subtype, representing high-grade transformation with extremely poor prognosis. Median survival <12 months. Presents at advanced stage with metastases. Spindle cells may show heterologous differentiation (bone, cartilage, skeletal muscle). Requires aggressive chemotherapy; checkpoint inhibitors show promise. Diagnosis requires identification of epithelial component.
questions.question: Sarcomatoid differentiation in renal cell carcinoma indicates:

questions.explanation: Spider angiomas (spider nevi) and palmar erythema in chronic liver disease result from impaired hepatic metabolism of estrogen, leading to hyperestrogenemia. This causes arteriolar dilatation and vascular proliferation in characteristic distributions. Other effects of hyperestrogenemia include gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, and loss of male escutcheon. These stigmata help identify chronic liver disease clinically.
questions.question: What causes spider angiomas in chronic liver disease?
Reed-Sternberg cells in classical Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically express which immunophenotypic markers?
questions.explanation:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma Reed-Sternberg cells typically
express CD15 and CD30 but lack B cell (CD20) and T cell (CD3) markers,
representing an unusual immunophenotype. This contrasts with
lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin where cells are CD20+ and CD15/CD30
negative. The CD15/CD30 positivity aids in distinguishing Hodgkin from
non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

Adrenal insufficiency from adrenocortical destruction distinguishes
X-ALD from other leukodystrophies. Very long chain fatty acids
accumulate in brain white matter and adrenal cortex. Lorenzo's oil may
slow progression.
questions.question: Which X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy feature distinguishes it from other leukodystrophies?
Seminoma is characterized histologically by:
options: Uniform clear cells with lymphocytic infiltrate
questions.explanation: Classic seminomas contain sheets of large uniform cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and central nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Fibrous septae contain lymphocytic infiltrate with occasional granulomas. Tumor cells express OCT4 and CD117 (c-kit). Excellent radiosensitivity and generally favorable prognosis characterize seminomas.

Oral hairy leukoplakia results from EBV replication in oral epithelium
causing white patches on tongue lateral borders. The lesions cannot be
scraped off unlike candidiasis. This marker indicates significant
immunosuppression.
questions.question: What causes oral hairy leukoplakia in AIDS?

options: Degree of nuclear atypia and mitotic activity
Capsular or vascular invasion through the capsule
Presence of papillary architecture within follicles
RAS mutation demonstrated by molecular pathology testing
Tumour size exceeding 4 cm in greatest dimension
questions.explanation: Follicular thyroid carcinoma cannot be distinguished from follicular adenoma on cytology (FNA cannot diagnose it) or nuclear features — the diagnosis requires histological demonstration of capsular invasion (penetration through the entire capsule) or vascular invasion (tumour within endothelium-lined vascular channels). Minimally invasive follicular carcinoma shows only capsular breach; widely invasive carcinoma shows extensive vascular invasion with worse prognosis. Nuclear features of PTC are absent. Adequate sampling of the entire capsule is critical and requires permanent histological sections, not frozen sections.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man has a thyroid tumour with follicular growth pattern and thick fibrous capsule. The definitive diagnosis of follicular carcinoma versus adenoma depends on demonstrating:

questions.explanation:
Gaucher cells are enlarged macrophages with crinkled tissue paper
cytoplasm from glucocerebroside accumulation. They infiltrate bone
marrow, liver, and spleen. PAS-positive material fills cytoplasm
creating characteristic appearance.
questions.question: What is the characteristic cell in Gaucher disease?

questions.explanation:
SIDS peaks between 2-4 months of age when physiologic
systems regulating arousal, cardiorespiratory control, and sleep-wake
cycles are maturing. The triple-risk model suggests vulnerable infant,
critical developmental period, and environmental stressor must coincide.
Incidence drops sharply after 6 months.
questions.question: What is the peak age incidence for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)?
How does rapid weight reduction affect gallstone risk?
questions.explanation: Rapid weight reduction increases gallstone risk by causing bile supersaturation with cholesterol from mobilization of adipose tissue cholesterol. This occurs with very low-calorie diets, bariatric surgery, or rapid weight loss from any cause. Gallbladder stasis during reduced caloric intake also contributes. Prophylactic ursodeoxycholic acid may be given during rapid weight loss programs.

Maturation arrest involves failure of germ cells to progress beyond spermatocyte or early spermatid stage. May be partial or complete. Causes include genetic abnormalities, radiation, chemotherapy, hormonal disorders, and varicocele. Testicular biopsy shows orderly maturation up to arrest point. Distinguishing from hypospermatogenesis important. Some patients achieve fertility with assisted reproductive techniques.
questions.question: Maturation arrest of spermatogenesis shows:
options: Arrest at spermatocyte or spermatid stage

questions.question: A 50-year-old man undergoes resection of a gastric wall mass. Histology shows spindle cells with positive CD117 (c-KIT) immunostaining. What is the cell of origin?
questions.explanation: Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of gut motility, and characteristically express CD117 (KIT) due to activating KIT mutations. This distinguishes GIST from true smooth muscle tumours (leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma), which are desmin and smooth muscle actin positive but KIT negative.

Mammary duct ectasia (plasma cell mastitis) characteristically shows dilated subareolar ducts filled with inspissated secretions and a prominent periductal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Multicoloured bilateral nipple discharge, nipple retraction, and subareolar masses are typical clinical features. Periductal fibrosis from repeated episodes may simulate carcinoma clinically. It predominantly affects perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. The condition is benign and managed conservatively; duct excision may be needed for persistent or recurrent symptoms.
options: Intraductal papilloma causing obstruction and discharge
Ductal carcinoma in situ with comedonecrosis
Mammary duct ectasia with periductal mastitis
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with thick grey-green bilateral nipple discharge. Biopsy shows dilated subareolar ducts filled with amorphous secretions and periductal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which developmental milestone regresses in Tay-Sachs disease?
questions.explanation:
Progressive neurodegeneration causes loss of all previously acquired
milestones. Initial development appears normal until 6 months.
Developmental regression with seizures follows ganglioside accumulation.

questions.question: Hutchinson teeth and saddle nose deformity are late manifestations of which congenital infection?
questions.explanation:
Late congenital syphilis (after age 2) manifests with
Hutchinson teeth (notched incisors), saddle nose, saber shins, and
eighth nerve deafness. Early manifestations include hepatosplenomegaly,
rash, and osteochondritis. Maternal screening and treatment prevent
congenital transmission.

options: External beam radiation followed by wide resection
Immediate amputation of the affected limb
Intralesional curettage and bone grafting alone
questions.question: A 14-year-old boy presents with knee pain and swelling for 3 months. X-ray shows a lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis with a sunburst periosteal reaction. Biopsy reveals malignant cells producing osteoid. What is the most appropriate next step after diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone malignancy in adolescents, is treated with neoadjuvant (pre-operative) chemotherapy to shrink the tumour and target micrometastases, followed by limb-salvage surgery with wide margins. This approach has improved 5-year survival from under 20% to over 60%. Amputation is reserved for cases where adequate margins cannot be achieved with limb-salvage techniques.

questions.question: Which cytokine recruits eosinophils to Hodgkin lymphoma tissue?
questions.explanation:
Reed-Sternberg cells secrete IL-5 which specifically recruits
eosinophils to the tumor microenvironment. The cytokine production by
malignant cells explains the characteristic mixed inflammatory
infiltrate. IL-6 recruits plasma cells while TGF-?stimulates fibroblast
proliferation.

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is characterised by 11p15.5 dysregulation (loss of imprinting of IGF2 and silencing of CDKN1C/p57), causing overgrowth features including macroglossia, hemi-hypertrophy, omphalocele, and Wilms tumour risk. Perilobar nephrogenic rests (PLNR) are the precursor lesions in BWS-associated Wilms tumour and are bilateral and multifocal. WT1 mutations (chromosome 11p13) characterise WAGR syndrome and Denys-Drash syndrome. BWS patients require regular renal ultrasound surveillance every 3 months until age 7 to detect Wilms tumour at an early, resectable stage.
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with bilateral renal tumours on CT. Histology reveals triphasic Wilms tumour bilaterally with adjacent perilobar nephrogenic rests. Which genetic syndrome should be suspected?
options: WAGR syndrome with WT1 deletion and aniridia
Denys-Drash syndrome with WT1 missense point mutation
Perlman syndrome with DICER1 germline mutation

questions.question: The most important prognostic factor in non-Hodgkin lymphoma is:
questions.explanation:
Histologic grade (indolent vs. aggressive) and stage
combine as the most important prognostic determinants. The International
Prognostic Index (IPI) incorporates age, stage, LDH, performance status,
and extranodal sites. Molecular features (MYC/BCL2 rearrangements, cell
of origin) increasingly guide prognosis and treatment.

Protease inhibitors prevent cleavage of viral polyproteins producing
immature non-infectious virions. These drugs revolutionized HIV
treatment when combined with reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
Resistance develops through protease gene mutations.
questions.question: Which HIV regimen component prevents viral maturation?
Which laboratory marker predicts HIV disease progression?
questions.explanation:
HIV RNA viral load predicts disease progression and treatment response.
Higher viral loads indicate faster CD4 decline. Undetectable viral load
on treatment prevents disease progression and transmission.

questions.question: What is a mucocele of the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: Mucocele (hydrops) of the gallbladder occurs with cystic duct obstruction, typically by a stone. The gallbladder becomes markedly distended with clear, sterile mucus secreted by the mucosal lining. Bile is reabsorbed, leaving behind mucoid secretions. This represents a chronic process distinct from acute cholecystitis. The distended gallbladder may be palpable.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman has unilateral nipple eczema that has failed topical treatment. Biopsy shows large pale cells with prominent nucleoli within the nipple epidermis. What is the underlying breast finding most likely present?
options: Invasive lobular carcinoma with pagetoid epidermal spread
Squamous cell carcinoma of the nipple skin
Underlying ductal carcinoma involving subareolar ducts
Lobular carcinoma in situ extending along nipple ducts
questions.explanation: Paget disease of the nipple presents as eczematoid changes and is characterised histologically by large malignant Paget cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli within the nipple epidermis. It invariably indicates an underlying ductal carcinoma, which may be DCIS or invasive, involving the subareolar ducts with intraepidermal spread. It should not be confused with Paget disease of bone. Mammography and MRI are essential to identify the underlying carcinoma. Treatment depends on the extent of the underlying breast lesion.

Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) causes globotriaosylceramide accumulation. Angiokeratomas appear in the bathing trunk distribution (periumbilical, scrotum, buttocks) in childhood, often decades before renal or cardiac manifestations develop. They result from lipid deposition in vascular endothelium. Xanthomata suggest hyperlipidemia; shagreen patches and ash-leaf spots characterize tuberous sclerosis; cafe-au-lait spots are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 rather than with Fabry disease.
questions.question: A 35-year-old man with Fabry disease develops end-stage renal disease. The earliest recognizable skin lesion preceding renal failure by years was:
options: Xanthomata on extensor tendons from lipid accumulation
Shagreen patches on the lower back from collagen dysplasia
Ash-leaf hypopigmented macules from melanocyte absence
Cafe-au-lait spots on trunk suggesting neurofibromatosis overlap
Angiokeratomas in bathing trunk distribution from vasculopathy

questions.question: Which genetic polymorphism is most associated with NAFLD progression?
questions.explanation: Polymorphisms of genes involving lipid metabolism, particularly PNPLA3, APOC3, and adiponectin, are associated with NAFLD. PNPLA3 polymorphism is one of the strongest genetic determinants of NAFLD progression. Polymorphisms in genes for lipid transport such as PPARA and PPARG also contribute.

Hepatoblastoma can produce erythropoietin causing
secondary polycythemia, distinguishing it from hepatocellular carcinoma
(which typically causes no paraneoplastic effects in children). Other
associations include precocious puberty from gonadotropin production and
osteopenia. Alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated and useful for
monitoring.
questions.question: Hepatoblastoma is associated with which paraneoplastic syndrome?

questions.explanation:
p24 is the most abundant HIV core protein and appears
early during acute infection before antibodies develop, making it
valuable for early diagnosis. The p24 antigen test combined with
antibody detection improves diagnostic sensitivity during the window
period. Declining p24 levels correlate with antibody appearance and
clinical latency.
questions.question: Which viral glycoprotein is most abundant and widely used for diagnosing HIV infection through antigen detection?

questions.explanation: HPV 16 is the most common high-risk type causing 50-60% of cervical carcinomas, followed by HPV 18 (10-15%). Types 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 account for remaining cases. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause condylomas without significant malignant potential. HPV vaccines targeting types 16 and 18 prevent majority of cervical cancers.
questions.question: Which cervical HPV type is most commonly associated with cervical carcinoma?

questions.explanation: Necrotising enterocolitis results from a combination of intestinal ischaemia and bacterial invasion of the bowel wall in premature infants, with gas-forming organisms producing the characteristic pneumatosis intestinalis seen radiographically. This is distinct from Hirschsprung disease, which causes obstruction from aganglionic bowel rather than ischaemic necrosis. Early recognition and bowel rest are critical to prevent perforation.
questions.question: A premature infant develops bloody stools, abdominal distension, and pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal X-ray. Which underlying process best explains this presentation?
options: Ischaemic bowel injury with bacterial gas production
Congenital absence of intestinal ganglion cells

questions.question: What is pancreatic divisum?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic divisum is the most common congenital pancreatic anomaly, occurring in 5-10% of the population. It results from failure of fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts during embryologic development. Most cases are asymptomatic, but some may predispose to pancreatitis due to inadequate drainage of the dorsal pancreas through the minor papilla.

questions.question: A 25-year-old has dark urine on voiding, lower back pain, and ochronosis of ear cartilage. Urine turns black on alkalinization. The deficient enzyme causing this disorder is:
questions.explanation: Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency in the tyrosine catabolism pathway, causing homogentisic acid accumulation. Homogentisic acid oxidizes to a dark polymer (alkapton) deposited in connective tissues (ochronosis) and excreted in urine, which blackens on standing or alkalinization. The condition leads to premature arthritis from cartilage and joint damage. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes tyrosinemia type I with acute liver failure rather than the ochronosis and darkening urine of alkaptonuria.
options: Tyrosine aminotransferase causing tyrosine derivative deposits

questions.question: Follicular lymphoma cells carry the t(14;18) translocation. The direct oncogenic consequence preventing cell death is:
questions.explanation: The t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation juxtaposes BCL2 on chromosome 18 with the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer on chromosome 14, causing BCL2 overexpression. BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein; its constitutive expression prevents normal germinal center B-cell apoptosis, allowing accumulation of neoplastic cells. This explains the indolent clinical behavior with slow accumulation rather than rapid proliferation. The t(8;14) drives MYC overexpression in Burkitt lymphoma; cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14) characterizes mantle cell lymphoma.
options: MYC overexpression driving explosive cellular proliferation
BCL2 overexpression preventing follicular center B-cell apoptosis
BCL6 translocation disrupting germinal center apoptosis signals
Cyclin D1 overexpression accelerating G1-S cell cycle transition
IGH-PAX5 fusion causing pre-B cell differentiation arrest

questions.question: In the most common form of esophageal atresia with fistula, which anatomical configuration is present?
questions.explanation: The most common form of esophageal atresia features the proximal esophagus ending as a blind sac while the distal portion forms a tracheoesophageal fistula. This configuration accounts for approximately 87% of cases (Type C in Gross's classification). Patients present with paroxysmal suffocation from food aspiration, pneumonia, and severe fluid and electrolyte imbalances.
options: Proximal blind sac with upper tracheoesophageal fistula
Distal blind sac with lower tracheoesophageal fistula
Complete esophageal continuity with H-type fistula
Bilateral blind pouches without any fistula connection
Proximal blind sac with distal tracheoesophageal fistula

questions.explanation:
AIDS wasting results from cytokine-mediated hypermetabolism similar to
cancer cachexia. TNF-a and IL-1 increase metabolic rate and muscle
protein breakdown. Wasting exceeds that explained by reduced caloric
intake.
questions.question: What causes wasting syndrome in AIDS?

questions.explanation:
Klebsiella pneumoniae produces thick, bloody, mucoid
sputum resembling currant jelly due to extensive tissue destruction and
hemorrhage. This organism causes necrotizing pneumonia typically in
alcoholics and diabetics, with propensity for upper lobe involvement and
abscess formation. The mucoid capsule aids virulence.
questions.question: Which pneumonia characteristically produces currant jelly sputum?

questions.explanation:
Ulcerative colitis invariably involves rectum and extends
proximally in continuous, uninterrupted fashion (proctitis, left-sided
colitis, or pancolitis). The inflammation is limited to mucosa and
submucosa (unlike Crohn's transmural pattern). "Backwash ileitis"
(terminal ileum involvement) occurs only with pancolitis. Pseudopolyps
(islands of preserved/regenerating mucosa) are characteristic.
questions.question: Ulcerative colitis characteristically involves which intestinal segment?
What are Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses?
questions.explanation: Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses are outpouchings of the mucosal epithelium through the gallbladder wall, characteristic of chronic cholecystitis. They represent herniation of mucosa into or through the muscular layer. Other features of chronic cholecystitis include wall thickening, chronic inflammation, and possible calcification (porcelain gallbladder).

Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) persist in red
cells when the spleen cannot perform its "pitting" function of
removing inclusions. Their presence indicates functional or anatomical
asplenia, increasing infection risk particularly from encapsulated
bacteria. Other findings include target cells and acanthocytes.
questions.question: Howell-Jolly bodies in erythrocytes indicate which functional deficiency?

questions.explanation: Vertebral osteomyelitis is most common in adults, usually from hematogenous spread or direct extension from soft tissue infection. Staphylococcus aureus predominates. Back pain, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers occur. MRI shows vertebral and disc space involvement with paravertebral soft tissue changes. Blood cultures may identify organism. Prolonged intravenous antibiotics required; surgery for abscess drainage or instability.
questions.question: Pyogenic osteomyelitis in adults most commonly affects:
Huntington disease is caused by:
questions.explanation: Huntington disease results from CAG repeat expansion in huntingtin gene on chromosome 4, causing mutant protein aggregation and neuronal death. Striatal atrophy (caudate and putamen) produces chorea and psychiatric symptoms. Autosomal dominant inheritance with anticipation (earlier onset, more severe in successive generations). No disease-modifying therapy exists; symptomatic management only.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has multiple gastric ulcers refractory to PPI therapy. Biopsy shows hyperplasia of the gastric mucosa with no H. pylori. Serum gastrin is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour, usually in the pancreas or duodenum, causing markedly elevated gastrin, gastric acid hypersecretion, and multiple refractory peptic ulcers. Menetrier's disease causes giant rugal hypertrophy with protein loss but normal or low gastrin, distinguishing it from this presentation.

Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi, with transmission occurring from person to person or via food or contaminated water. Humans are the sole reservoir for these organisms. In endemic areas, children and adolescents are most often affected.
questions.question: What is the most common mode of transmission for typhoid fever?
Which immunodeficiency is characterized by thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections in males?
