questions.explanation:
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder affecting
WAS protein involved in actin cytoskeleton regulation, causing the
classic triad of thrombocytopenia, eczema, and immunodeficiency.
Progressive T cell depletion and inability to respond to polysaccharide
antigens cause recurrent infections. The syndrome carries increased risk
of autoimmunity and lymphoma.

Reactive plasmacytosis (infections, autoimmune diseases)
shows polyclonal plasma cell expansion with diverse immunoglobulin
expression, while myeloma is monoclonal (single light chain type by
immunohistochemistry/flow cytometry). Flow cytometry showing aberrant
CD56+/CD19- immunophenotype also supports myeloma diagnosis.
questions.question: Which finding distinguishes reactive plasmacytosis from plasma cell myeloma?

A 6-month-old presents with severe anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal changes described as 'hair-on-end' appearance on skull X-ray. Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows absent haemoglobin A. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia major results from near-complete absence of beta-globin chain production, causing severe anaemia requiring regular transfusion, with marked extramedullary haematopoiesis producing hepatosplenomegaly and characteristic skull changes from marrow expansion ('hair-on-end' appearance). This severe presentation contrasts with the generally asymptomatic beta-thalassaemia trait. Regular transfusion therapy, while life-sustaining, necessitates iron chelation therapy to prevent transfusion-related iron overload.

Krukenberg tumours are bilateral ovarian metastases characterised by signet ring cells (mucin-filled malignant cells) embedded in cellular ovarian stroma. The most common primary is gastric carcinoma (diffuse-type with signet ring features), accounting for approximately 75% of cases. Colorectal, breast (lobular), and appendiceal tumours may also metastasise to ovaries. Krukenberg tumours typically preserve ovarian shape, are bilateral, and involve the stroma prominently. Discovery of bilateral ovarian masses with signet ring cells should prompt systematic search for a gastric primary.
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman has bilateral ovarian masses. Histology shows signet ring cells filled with intracytoplasmic mucin embedded in cellular ovarian stroma. What is the most common primary site for this secondary tumour?
options: Gastric carcinoma with signet ring differentiation
Colon carcinoma with haematogenous ovarian spread
Breast lobular carcinoma with ovarian metastasis

questions.question: Which Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome feature is pathognomonic?
questions.explanation:
Broad nasal bridge continuing to forehead creates "Greek warrior
helmet" appearance. 4p16.3 deletion causes severe intellectual
disability and growth retardation. Seizures affect 90% of patients.

Barrett esophagus shows replacement of normal stratified
squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing
goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), resulting from chronic
gastroesophageal reflux. This metaplasia predisposes to esophageal
adenocarcinoma through dysplasia-carcinoma sequence. Surveillance
endoscopy with biopsies is recommended for monitoring dysplasia.
questions.question: Barrett esophagus is characterized by which metaplastic change?

questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is caused by mutations in the APC gene on chromosome 5q21. The tumors are morphologically similar to sporadic adenomas but occur in much greater numbers, with 100% risk of colorectal carcinoma in untreated patients.
questions.question: What is the mode of inheritance of familial adenomatous polyposis?
Which cells form the center of schistosomal granulomas?
questions.explanation:
Schistosome eggs occupy the center of granulomas surrounded by
inflammatory cells. Eosinophils are prominent in the cellular infiltrate
along with macrophages and lymphocytes. Granulomas obstruct
microvascular flow causing ischemic tissue damage.

Adrenal Cushing syndrome from a unilateral cortisol-secreting adenoma is best treated by surgical adrenalectomy (laparoscopic if feasible) of the affected gland. The contralateral adrenal is suppressed by chronic elevated cortisol, necessitating steroid replacement post-operatively until the HPA axis recovers, which may take months to years. Medical treatment with steroidogenesis inhibitors (metyrapone, ketoconazole) is reserved for patients awaiting surgery or those unfit for operation. Bilateral adrenalectomy is reserved for bilateral disease or failed previous unilateral surgery.
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents with hypertension, weight gain, purple striae, and proximal muscle weakness. 24-hour urinary free cortisol is elevated and dexamethasone suppression is incomplete. CT shows a 3 cm unilateral adrenal adenoma. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Chronic medical management with metyrapone alone
High-dose dexamethasone suppression as definitive therapy
Bilateral adrenalectomy to prevent any recurrence risk
Pituitary irradiation for presumed corticotroph adenoma
Unilateral adrenalectomy of the adenoma-bearing gland

questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency impairs the red cell's ability to generate reduced glutathione, leaving it vulnerable to oxidative stress from triggers such as fava beans, certain drugs, and infections, resulting in haemoglobin denaturation visible as Heinz bodies. This X-linked condition shows variable severity depending on the specific enzyme variant. Avoidance of known oxidative triggers is a key management strategy in affected individuals.
questions.question: A child with recurrent haemolytic episodes after eating fava beans is found to have red cells with Heinz bodies on peripheral smear during an acute episode. Which enzyme deficiency explains this presentation?
Osteoporosis is defined by which measurement?
questions.explanation:
Osteoporosis is defined by bone mineral density T-score =
-2.5 (2.5 standard deviations below young adult mean). Osteopenia (low
bone mass) is T-score between -1.0 and -2.5. Risk factors include age,
female sex, estrogen deficiency, corticosteroid use, smoking, and
calcium/vitamin D deficiency. Fragility fractures (hip, vertebral,
wrist) are major complications.

5-alpha-reductase inhibitors block conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), reducing prostate volume by 20-30% and improving urinary symptoms in BPH. Finasteride inhibits type 2 enzyme; dutasteride inhibits types 1 and 2. Lower PSA by approximately 50% (must double result for screening). May reduce prostate cancer incidence but increase high-grade tumor detection.
questions.question: Dutasteride and finasteride work by inhibiting:

questions.explanation: Reflux esophagitis is the most common type of esophagitis, resulting from gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The squamous epithelium of the esophagus is normally protected by submucosal glands and the lower esophageal sphincter. Conditions that decrease lower esophageal sphincter tone, such as alcohol, tobacco, pregnancy, and hiatal hernia, predispose to reflux.
questions.question: What is the most common type of esophagitis?

questions.explanation: Compensated cirrhosis involves hepatic fibrosis without clinical complications—patients are asymptomatic or have minor symptoms. Decompensated cirrhosis features complications including ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice, or hepatorenal syndrome. Decompensation marks a critical transition with dramatically reduced survival (50% 5-year versus 80-90% compensated). Child-Pugh and MELD scores assess severity and predict outcomes.
questions.question: What defines compensated versus decompensated cirrhosis?

questions.explanation: Mesotheliomas arise from mesothelial lining of tunica vaginalis, presenting as hydrocele or scrotal mass in elderly men. Asbestos exposure history in 40%. Papillary and tubulopapillary patterns occur. Diagnosis requires immunohistochemistry (calretinin, WT1, D2-40 positive; CEA, MOC31 negative). Radical orchiectomy with hemiscrotectomy treats disease. High local recurrence; metastases uncommon but possible.
questions.question: Malignant mesothelioma of tunica vaginalis presents with:

A 65-year-old woman has vulvar pruritus of 5 years duration. Biopsy shows hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy with loss of rete ridges, homogeneous collagenous dermis, and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate. Which statement about this condition is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Lichen sclerosus of the vulva shows thinned epidermis with loss of rete ridges, hyperkeratosis, and a homogenised pale dermis with underlying lymphocytic infiltrate. It occurs across all ages including prepubertal girls and carries approximately 4-5% lifetime risk of squamous cell carcinoma via the non-HPV differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia pathway. Regular long-term follow-up is therefore essential. High-potency topical corticosteroids (clobetasol) are first-line treatment. TP53 mutations are frequently found in associated carcinomas.
options: It is associated with approximately 4-5% risk of SCC
It has no malignant potential and requires no follow-up
It invariably progresses to vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia
It is caused by HPV infection requiring specific vaccination
It occurs exclusively in postmenopausal women only

questions.question: Turner syndrome results from which chromosomal abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Turner syndrome (45,X) affects 1:2500 female births,
though 99% of 45,X conceptuses abort spontaneously. Mosaicism
(45,X/46,XX) occurs in ~50% of cases with milder phenotype. Complete
absence of one sex chromosome is the only viable monosomy in humans.
Loss of SHOX gene on X causes short stature.

Approximately 90-95% of heavy drinkers develop hepatic steatosis (fatty liver), the earliest and most common form of alcoholic liver disease. However, only up to 35% progress to develop advanced alcoholic liver diseases including alcoholic hepatitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma. The progression depends on multiple host and environmental factors.
questions.question: What percentage of heavy drinkers develop hepatic steatosis?

questions.explanation: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) most commonly results from rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm (80% of non-traumatic cases). Berry aneurysms form at arterial branch points of the circle of Willis, particularly the anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating artery, and middle cerebral artery bifurcation. They are associated with ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and coarctation of the aorta. Vasospasm (3-14 days post-bleed) is the major cause of delayed neurological deficit. Treatment involves surgical clipping or endovascular coiling. Nimodipine reduces vasospasm incidence.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man has sudden-onset severe thunderclap headache and neck stiffness. CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. Most cases are caused by rupture of which lesion?
options: Arteriovenous malformation at the Sylvian fissure
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy of superficial cortical vessels
Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage into subarachnoid space
Septic embolic mycotic aneurysm after endocarditis
Berry (saccular) aneurysm at the circle of Willis

questions.question: CA-125 is elevated in:
questions.explanation: CA-125 (MUC16) is elevated in 80% of epithelial ovarian cancers, particularly serous type, but lacks specificity. Benign conditions causing elevation include endometriosis, PID, menstruation, pregnancy, liver disease, and congestive heart failure. Most useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence. Screening asymptomatic women is not recommended due to low positive predictive value.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man from a hepatitis B endemic region has elevated alpha-fetoprotein and a liver mass with arterial enhancement and venous washout on imaging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma typically arises in a background of chronic hepatitis B or cirrhosis and shows the classic imaging pattern of arterial phase hyperenhancement with portal venous phase washout, alongside elevated alpha-fetoprotein. This imaging and biochemical pattern is sufficiently specific that biopsy can sometimes be avoided for diagnosis in cirrhotic patients.

NOD2 (nucleotide oligomerization binding domain 2) has been identified as a susceptibility gene in Crohn disease. Loss of function mutations in NOD2 make it less effective at recognizing and combating luminal microbes and may impair regulation of immune responses to prevent excessive activation by luminal microbes.
questions.question: Which NOD2 gene alteration is associated with Crohn disease susceptibility?

questions.explanation: Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL gene mutation on 3p) causes cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas, retinal angiomas, renal cell carcinomas, pheochromocytomas, and pancreatic cysts/tumors. Hemangioblastomas show abundant capillaries with intervening stromal cells (produce erythropoietin causing polycythemia). Cyst with enhancing mural nodule is characteristic. Multiple lesions require surveillance.
questions.question: Hemangioblastomas are associated with:

questions.explanation: Fuhrman grading (1-4) evaluates nuclear size, irregularity, and nucleolar prominence. Grade 1: small uniform nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli; Grade 2: slight irregularity, visible nucleoli; Grade 3: marked irregularity, prominent nucleoli; Grade 4: bizarre pleomorphic nuclei, chromatin clumping. Higher grades predict worse outcomes. Now replaced by WHO/ISUP grading in clear cell RCC.
questions.question: Fuhrman grading of renal cell carcinoma is based on:

questions.explanation:
Clonorchis sinensis inhabits biliary tree causing chronic cholangitis
and periductal fibrosis. Chronic infection predisposes to
cholangiocarcinoma with highest rates in Southeast Asia. The parasite is
transmitted through raw or undercooked freshwater fish.
questions.question: Which trematode causes liver fluke infection associated with cholangiocarcinoma?

options: Fibrillin-1 in elastic fibres of vascular walls
Perlecan in basement membranes of vessels
Type I collagen in bone and connective tissue matrix
Fibulin-5 in extracellular matrix of aortic wall
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) results from mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 genes encoding type I collagen, the predominant structural protein of bone, skin, and sclerae. Defective collagen leads to abnormally brittle bones prone to fracture with minimal trauma. Blue sclerae occur because the underlying choroid shows through thin collagen-deficient sclerae. Hearing loss results from otosclerosis. Severity ranges from mild (Type I) to perinatally lethal (Type II). Bisphosphonates reduce fracture frequency in moderate-to-severe forms.
questions.question: A newborn presents with multiple fractures sustained during delivery, blue sclerae, and progressive hearing loss. The underlying molecular defect involves which protein?

options: Staphylococcus aureus entering via haematogenous seeding
Escherichia coli from ascending urinary tract infection
questions.question: A 25-year-old woman with sickle cell disease presents with fever and localised bone pain. Which organism is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in this population?
questions.explanation: Salmonella species are the most common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease patients, though Staphylococcus aureus remains most common in the general population. Functional asplenia from repeated splenic infarcts and impaired phagocytic function predispose sickle cell patients to encapsulated organisms. The diaphysis is preferentially affected due to microvascular occlusion from sickling. Multifocal involvement is common, and prompt antibiotic treatment covering Salmonella is essential.

options: Progesterone therapy followed by repeat biopsy
questions.question: A 50-year-old postmenopausal woman has an endometrial biopsy showing glands with nuclear atypia, complex branching, and back-to-back arrangement with scanty stroma and no myometrial invasion. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (atypical endometrial hyperplasia/endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia) carries approximately 30% risk of concurrent endometrial carcinoma and 30% risk of subsequent progression if untreated. Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive treatment in women who have completed childbearing. Progestogen therapy (oral medroxyprogesterone or LNG-IUS) is reserved for women who strongly desire fertility preservation, with close surveillance. Coexisting carcinoma must be excluded before any conservative management is attempted.

Empyema of the gallbladder is characterized by frank pus in the lumen, resulting from bacterial superinfection in acute cholecystitis. Common organisms include E. coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus. The gallbladder is tense and distended with purulent material. This represents severe acute cholecystitis requiring urgent cholecystectomy and antibiotics. Sepsis and perforation are significant risks.
questions.question: What complication involves pus in the gallbladder lumen?

A 65-year-old smoker with chronic alcohol use presents with dysphagia. Endoscopic biopsy of a mid-oesophageal mass shows keratinising squamous cell carcinoma. Which risk factor combination most strongly predisposes to this tumour type?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus is strongly associated with tobacco and alcohol use, which act synergistically to damage the squamous epithelium. In contrast, adenocarcinoma is linked to GERD, obesity, and Barrett's oesophagus. H. pylori is associated with gastric, not oesophageal, malignancy.

Cholesterol stones are radiolucent when composed entirely of cholesterol monohydrate. However, 10-20% contain sufficient calcium to be radio-opaque. In contrast, 50-75% of pigment stones are radio-opaque due to calcium content. Only about 10-15% of all gallstones are visible on plain radiographs. Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality for gallstone detection.
questions.question: What percentage of cholesterol stones are radiolucent?

options: Vermis hypoplasia with enlarged fourth ventricle
questions.explanation: Dandy-Walker malformation includes cerebellar vermis hypoplasia/agenesis, cystic dilatation of fourth ventricle, and enlarged posterior fossa. Hydrocephalus commonly develops. Associated anomalies include agenesis of corpus callosum and other CNS malformations. Clinical features include developmental delay, ataxia, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. Shunt placement treats hydrocephalus.
questions.question: Dandy-Walker malformation consists of:

questions.explanation: Approximately 40% of individuals with cirrhosis are asymptomatic, with the condition discovered incidentally through imaging, abnormal laboratory tests, or during evaluation for other conditions. Symptomatic patients may experience anorexia, weight loss, weakness, and manifestations of portal hypertension including ascites and variceal bleeding.
questions.question: What percentage of individuals with cirrhosis are asymptomatic?
A 40-year-old man with chronic osteomyelitis undergoes X-ray showing a sequestrum within an involucrum. Which best describes the sequestrum in this context?
options: Dead cortical bone separated from viable surrounding bone
New periosteal reactive bone encasing the infected area
Granulation tissue lining the chronic bone sinus tract
Sclerotic reactive bone formed around the abscess wall
Fibrous scar tissue replacing necrotic haematopoietic marrow
questions.explanation: A sequestrum is a fragment of dead cortical bone that has been separated from viable surrounding bone due to interruption of blood supply in chronic osteomyelitis. The surrounding reactive new bone (involucrum) encases the sequestrum, which cannot be revascularised and harbours bacteria protected from antibiotics and immune cells. Surgical removal (sequestrectomy) of the sequestrum is necessary for cure. Brodie abscess represents a localised form of subacute osteomyelitis contained by reactive bone without a true sequestrum.

Extrahepatic metastasis from hepatocellular carcinoma is mostly hematogenous, with the lungs being the most common target organ. Regional lymphatic metastasis to portal and periportal lymph nodes is frequent, though distant lymph nodes are rarely involved. Bone, adrenal glands, and brain are less common sites.
questions.question: What is the most common site of extrahepatic HCC metastasis?
What distinguishes Taenia solium from Taenia saginata infection?
questions.explanation:
Taenia solium causes cysticercosis when humans ingest eggs from
contaminated food. Oncospheres develop into cysticerci in tissues
particularly brain, muscle, and eyes. T. saginata does not cause
cysticercosis as humans are definitive hosts only.

Invasion into blood vessels, particularly the portal vein, is a characteristic feature of hepatocellular carcinoma. This vascular invasion is important for staging and prognosis. Tumor thrombus in the portal vein can extend to involve major branches and may even reach the main portal vein.
questions.question: What is the most characteristic vascular invasion pattern in HCC?

options: They frequently undergo malignant transformation to sarcoma
They arise from endometrial stromal cells during menopause
Red degeneration occurs characteristically during pregnancy
Chromosomal changes are rare and diagnostically unhelpful
They are associated with BRCA2 germline mutations
questions.explanation: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumours associated with HMGA2 and MED12 mutations. Red (carneous) degeneration occurs during pregnancy when rapid growth outpaces blood supply, causing haemorrhagic infarction with gross red-brown discolouration. This presents with acute severe abdominal pain and tenderness during pregnancy. Malignant transformation to leiomyosarcoma is extremely rare (less than 0.1%) and does not represent progression from existing leiomyomas. Submucosal fibroids most commonly cause heavy menstrual bleeding.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding. Hysterectomy reveals multiple well-defined rubbery whorled masses within the myometrium with interlacing smooth muscle bundles and no necrosis. Which statement about these lesions is correct?
Which urea cycle disorder shows hyperammonemia without elevated orotic acid?
questions.explanation:
CPS deficiency causes hyperammonemia without orotic aciduria. OTC
deficiency shows both findings. CPS catalyzes the first step before
orotic acid production.

Orchiopexy should be performed before age two years to prevent irreversible testicular damage and preserve fertility potential. Cryptorchidism increases testicular cancer risk 3-10 fold even after surgical correction, requiring lifelong surveillance. The contralateral descended testis also shows slightly elevated cancer risk, suggesting inherent developmental abnormality.
questions.question: A 2-year-old boy presents with failure of testicular descent. The most appropriate management involves:

questions.explanation:
Becker muscular dystrophy shows milder phenotype with ambulation
preserved past age 16. In-frame dystrophin mutations produce partially
functional protein. Cardiac involvement may be prominent.
questions.question: What distinguishes Becker from Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

questions.explanation: Osteochondromas (exostoses) are bony projections capped by cartilage, continuous with underlying bone marrow. Most common benign bone tumor, arising from metaphyseal surface near growth plates. Hereditary multiple exostoses (autosomal dominant) carries higher malignant transformation risk. Malignant change suggested by cartilage cap thickness >2cm or growth after skeletal maturity.
questions.question: Osteochondroma is characterized by:

questions.explanation:
Standard karyotyping detects balanced translocations by visualizing
chromosome structure. Microarray cannot detect balanced rearrangements
as no net gain/loss occurs. Family studies identify carriers.
questions.question: Which technique detects balanced translocations?

questions.explanation: CFRD results from progressive islet cell loss due to pancreatic fibrosis causing insulin deficiency, while concurrent lung infection, inflammation, and glucocorticoid therapy increase insulin resistance. Unlike type 1 diabetes, ketoacidosis is rare because residual insulin and intact glucagon secretion limit lipolysis. Unlike type 2, the primary defect includes genuine insulin insufficiency not resistance alone. Insulin therapy is standard for CFRD; oral hypoglycemics have limited demonstrated efficacy. CFRD significantly worsens pulmonary outcomes and nutritional status in CF patients.
options: Treatment requires oral hypoglycemics rather than insulin injections
Ketoacidosis is a common complication as seen in type 1 diabetes
It resolves completely after successful bilateral lung transplantation
Fasting hyperglycemia alone defines CFRD without postprandial changes
Insulin deficiency and resistance coexist with intact glucagon secretion
questions.question: Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes differs fundamentally from type 1 and type 2 diabetes because:
What is the characteristic growth pattern of right-sided colon cancers?
questions.explanation: Proximal or right-sided colon tumors tend to be polypoid and exophytic with predominantly intraluminal growth. They do not usually cause obstruction due to the large caliber of the cecum and ascending colon. In contrast, distal or left-sided tumors tend to produce napkin ring constrictions and luminal narrowing.

HIV retinopathy causes cotton-wool spots from retinal ischemia. These
microinfarctions appear as white fluffy patches distinct from CMV
retinitis. CMV causes hemorrhagic necrotizing retinitis with potential
blindness.
questions.question: Which opportunistic infection causes cotton-wool spots on retinal examination?

A 48-year-old woman undergoes breast biopsy for mammographic calcifications described as linear and branching. Histology shows high-grade nuclei with central necrosis confined within ducts. What is the correct classification?
options: Lobular carcinoma in situ grade 3 with pleomorphism
Invasive micropapillary carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion
Invasive carcinoma NST with ductal origin
Atypical ductal hyperplasia with focal calcification
questions.explanation: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with comedonecrosis (comedo-type) shows high-grade nuclear morphology with central luminal necrosis and calcification within distended ducts, without invasion through the basement membrane. Extensive calcification makes it detectable on mammography as linear and branching microcalcifications. High-grade comedo DCIS has greater risk of progression to invasive carcinoma and local recurrence after excision. Treatment involves excision with clear margins; adjuvant radiotherapy reduces recurrence. Tamoxifen reduces contralateral cancer risk in ER-positive DCIS.

Most Klinefelter cases are diagnosed during evaluation for infertility
or hypogonadism. Mild phenotype often escapes detection. Prenatal
diagnosis through amniocentesis is increasing.
questions.question: At what age is Klinefelter syndrome typically diagnosed?

questions.explanation:
Pneumocystis pneumonia typically occurs when CD4 counts
fall below 200 cells/mm³, serving as an AIDS-defining threshold and
indication for prophylaxis. This opportunistic infection rarely occurs
at higher counts unless other immunosuppressive factors exist. The CD4
count stratifies risk for specific opportunistic infections.
questions.question: At what CD4+ T cell count does the risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia significantly increase in HIV infection?
Which CNS infection shows Negri bodies?
questions.explanation: Rabies virus causes fatal encephalitis with pathognomonic Negri bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions) in hippocampal and Purkinje neurons. Transmission occurs through infected animal bites. Hydrophobia and aerophobia develop. Post-exposure prophylaxis with vaccine and immunoglobulin prevents disease if given promptly. No treatment exists once symptoms appear; outcome is nearly always fatal.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman has pernicious anaemia and gastric biopsy showing atrophy and intestinal metaplasia confined to the fundus and body, with antral sparing. Which antibody is most specific to this condition?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis is characterised by autoantibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor, leading to achlorhydria, loss of intrinsic factor, and vitamin B12 deficiency causing pernicious anaemia. It selectively involves the fundus and body, sparing the antrum, unlike H. pylori gastritis which favours the antrum.

questions.question: What distinguishes Edwards from Patau syndrome phenotypically?
questions.explanation:
Edwards (trisomy 18) shows clenched hands with overlapping fingers,
rocker-bottom feet, and micrognathia. Patau (trisomy 13) has
holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, and polydactyly. Both are lethal.

VSD is most common cardiac defect in trisomy 18, occurring in 90% of
cases. Other defects include patent ductus arteriosus and tetralogy of
Fallot. Cardiac malformations contribute to poor prognosis.
questions.question: What cardiac defect occurs most frequently in trisomy 18?
Which 47,XYY syndrome feature is most consistent?
questions.explanation:
Tall stature above 97th percentile is most consistent XYY feature.
Intelligence is usually normal with mild learning difficulties.
Behavioral problems occur no more than general population contrary to
historical beliefs.

Lung carcinoma causes most brain metastases, followed by breast, melanoma, renal cell, and colorectal carcinomas. Metastases typically occur at gray-white junction where tumor emboli lodge in narrowing vessels. Multiple lesions are common. Circumscribed masses with surrounding vasogenic edema appear on imaging. Treatment includes surgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, whole-brain radiation, and systemic therapy.
questions.question: Cerebral metastases most commonly originate from:
What is the gender predilection for gallbladder carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Gallbladder carcinoma is more common in women, consistent with the female predominance of cholelithiasis. Risk factors include gallstones, chronic cholecystitis, porcelain gallbladder, and possibly parasitic infestations. Recurrent trauma and chronic inflammation from gallstones are thought to contribute to carcinogenesis.

The most common cause of Prader-Willi syndrome is paternal deletion of 15q11-q13, removing paternally expressed imprinted genes including SNRPN. Methylation analysis detects absence of the paternal methylation pattern, confirming this mechanism. Angelman syndrome arises from loss of maternal contribution through maternal deletion or paternal UPD. Maternal UPD15, the second most common PWS mechanism, also shows absence of paternal imprint but requires microsatellite testing for definitive differentiation.
options: Prader-Willi syndrome from maternal UPD chromosome 15
Angelman syndrome from paternal UPD of chromosome 15
questions.question: A neonate with hypotonia and poor feeding has methylation analysis showing absence of paternal methylation imprint at 15q11-q13. The most likely diagnosis is:
What molecular pathway characterizes sessile serrated lesions?
questions.explanation: Sessile serrated lesions are characterized by BRAF mutations, hypermethylation of the MLH1 promoter, and microsatellite instability. This "serrated pathway" to CRC differs from the traditional adenoma-carcinoma sequence. SSLs can progress to colorectal cancer, particularly right-sided, mucinous, poorly differentiated tumors. CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP-high) is characteristic. Detection and complete removal are crucial for cancer prevention.

questions.question: Senile cardiac amyloidosis is most commonly composed of which protein?
questions.explanation:
Wild-type transthyretin (formerly senile cardiac amyloid)
deposits in hearts of elderly men causing restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Unlike mutant transthyretin (familial amyloidosis), this represents
age-related amyloid accumulation without hereditary predisposition.
Newer treatments targeting transthyretin show promise.

questions.question: What is the most common site of extranodal involvement in Burkitt lymphoma endemic variant?
questions.explanation:
Endemic Burkitt lymphoma predominantly affects children in Africa and
commonly involves the jaw and facial bones. The tumor shows strong
association with Epstein-Barr virus infection occurring in
malaria-endemic regions. Jaw involvement creates characteristic facial
swelling distinguishing endemic from sporadic variants.

Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-producing tumors of chromaffin cells causing paroxysmal hypertension, headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. The "rule of 10s": 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% malignant, 10% familial (MEN 2, VHL, NF1). Urinary metanephrines/catecholamines confirm diagnosis. Preoperative alpha-blockade prevents hypertensive crisis during resection.
questions.question: Pheochromocytoma produces which hormones?

options: Direct recognition of donor MHC molecules
questions.explanation:
Direct allorecognition occurs when recipient T cells
recognize intact donor MHC molecules on graft dendritic cells,
triggering a uniquely strong response because many T cells cross-react
with allogeneic MHC. This explains why acute rejection is so common
despite immunosuppression. Indirect recognition becomes more important
in chronic rejection.
questions.question: In acute transplant rejection, which pathway of T cell recognition is primarily responsible for the strong initial response?

questions.explanation:
Parathyroid hypoplasia causes hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism.
Neonatal seizures may result from low calcium. Calcium and vitamin D
supplementation treats hypocalcemia.
questions.question: What causes hypocalcemia in DiGeorge syndrome?

questions.explanation:
Azoospermia from seminiferous tubule dysgenesis occurs in
nearly 100% of Klinefelter cases, causing infertility (though testicular
sperm extraction sometimes succeeds). Testosterone levels are often
low-normal with elevated gonadotropins. Small firm testes are
characteristic. Gynecomastia develops in ~50% due to
testosterone/estrogen imbalance.
questions.question: Which clinical feature is most consistent in Klinefelter syndrome?

questions.explanation:
Myasthenia gravis involves antibodies against nicotinic
acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing receptor
internalization and complement-mediated destruction. This produces
fatigable weakness improving with rest or anticholinesterase inhibitors.
Thymoma or thymic hyperplasia is present in most patients. Thymectomy
often improves symptoms.
questions.question: Myasthenia gravis results from antibodies against which target?

questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome is characterised by a facial port-wine stain in the trigeminal nerve distribution, particularly the ophthalmic division, associated with an underlying leptomeningeal vascular malformation that can cause seizures, glaucoma, and intellectual disability due to associated cortical involvement. This contrasts with neurofibromatosis type 1, which presents with café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas rather than a vascular birthmark. Early recognition allows for monitoring of associated neurological and ophthalmological complications.
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with a port-wine stain in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, along with seizures and intellectual disability. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Wilms tumor is the most common renal malignancy in children, peak age 2-5 years. Presents as asymptomatic abdominal mass. Syndromic associations include WAGR (Wilms, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, mental retardation), Denys-Drash, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes. WT1 and WT2 gene alterations occur. Triphasic histology (blastemal, epithelial, stromal). Excellent prognosis (90% cure) with surgery and chemotherapy.
questions.question: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) most commonly occurs in:

questions.explanation: While all components of metabolic syndrome contribute to NAFLD, central obesity is most strongly associated with disease development and severity. The prevalence and severity of fatty liver increase with the number of metabolic syndrome components present: central obesity, hyperglycemia (≥5.6 mmol/L), hypertriglyceridemia, reduced HDL cholesterol, and hypertension.
questions.question: Which metabolic syndrome component is most strongly associated with NAFLD?

questions.explanation: Craniopharyngioma arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch and classically presents as a suprasellar, often calcified, cystic mass causing visual field defects from optic chiasm compression and endocrine dysfunction from pituitary and hypothalamic involvement. The bitemporal visual field loss reflects compression of the crossing nasal retinal fibres at the optic chiasm. Surgical resection carries risk of significant endocrine and hypothalamic complications given the tumour's critical location.
questions.question: A 7-year-old presents with recurrent severe headaches, vomiting, and bitemporal visual field loss. MRI reveals a suprasellar calcified cystic mass. Which tumour is most consistent with this presentation?
Which prophylaxis prevents Mycobacterium avium complex in AIDS?
questions.explanation:
Azithromycin or clarithromycin prophylaxis prevents MAC when CD4 counts
fall below 50 cells/?. MAC causes disseminated infection with fever,
diarrhea, and wasting. Blood cultures yield acid-fast bacilli.

questions.question: Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes both involve deletion of which chromosome?
questions.explanation:
Both involve chromosome 15q11-q13, but paternal deletion
causes Prader-Willi (hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity) while maternal
deletion causes Angelman (ataxia, seizures, inappropriate laughter).
This demonstrates genomic imprinting where gene expression depends on
parent of origin. Uniparental disomy can also cause these syndromes.

questions.question: Radical cystectomy in men includes removal of:
questions.explanation: Radical cystectomy in men removes bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles, and pelvic lymph nodes (standard template). In women, includes bladder, urethra, anterior vaginal wall, uterus, and ovaries. Urinary diversion via ileal conduit, continent cutaneous reservoir, or orthotopic neobladder reconstructs urinary tract. Perioperative chemotherapy improves outcomes in muscle-invasive disease.

questions.question: Krukenberg tumors represent:
questions.explanation: Krukenberg tumors are metastatic signet ring cell carcinomas, most commonly from gastric origin, involving both ovaries. The tumor cells produce abundant mucin displacing nuclei peripherally creating signet ring appearance. Other sources include colorectal, breast, and appendiceal primaries. Ovarian enlargement may precede identification of primary tumor.

Fibrostenotic Crohn's disease represents one of the major disease phenotypes, where chronic transmural inflammation with fissuring ulcers leads to progressive fibrosis and luminal narrowing, producing strictures that can cause obstructive symptoms. This contrasts with the penetrating/fistulising phenotype, where transmural inflammation instead leads to fistula or abscess formation.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has chronic abdominal pain and is found to have a strictured segment of terminal ileum on imaging. Biopsy from resection shows transmural lymphoid aggregates and fissuring ulcers extending into the muscularis. What complication of the underlying disease does this strictured segment represent?

questions.explanation:
WAGR syndrome results from contiguous gene deletion at
11p13 including WT1 (Wilms tumor) and PAX6 (aniridia) genes. Affected
individuals have ~50% risk of Wilms tumor. Genitourinary anomalies and
intellectual disability complete the syndrome. Regular screening for
tumor development is essential.
options: Wilms, ambiguous genitalia, growth retardation, renal dysplasia
Wilms, adrenal hyperplasia, gonadal dysgenesis, rhabdomyosarcoma
Wilms, agenesis of kidney, genital duplication, radial defects
questions.question: WAGR syndrome includes which constellation of abnormalities?

questions.explanation: Renal medullary carcinoma is a highly aggressive tumour virtually exclusively occurring in patients with sickle cell trait (not disease) or other haemoglobinopathies. It arises from the calyceal epithelium of the renal medulla. SMARCB1 (INI1) deletion is the molecular hallmark, demonstrated by loss of nuclear INI1 immunostaining. It presents in young patients (median age approximately 22) with advanced stage at diagnosis and extremely poor prognosis. It is often confused with collecting duct carcinoma but SMARCB1 loss is the distinguishing molecular feature.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with sickle cell trait presents with a renal medullary mass. Histology shows high-grade carcinoma with sheet-like, tubular, and micropapillary patterns with desmoplastic stroma and intravascular sickling. What is this tumour?
options: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma in sickle cell trait
Collecting duct carcinoma of Bellini arising centrally
Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
Renal medullary carcinoma exclusively in sickle cell trait
Papillary renal cell carcinoma type 2 with necrosis

questions.question: Marginal zone lymphoma of MALT type most commonly arises in which organ?
questions.explanation:
Gastric MALT lymphoma is most common, associated with
chronic H. pylori gastritis creating acquired MALT. The t(11;18)
translocation is specific for MALT lymphoma. Early-stage disease often
regresses completely with H. pylori eradication, representing a unique
example of antibiotic treatment curing lymphoma.

questions.question: Which B symptoms must be present to append B designation to Hodgkin lymphoma stage?
questions.explanation:
B symptoms include unexplained fever >38°C, drenching
night sweats, and unintentional weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight
over 6 months. Their presence (stage designation "B" vs "A" without
symptoms) has prognostic significance and influences treatment
intensity. Pruritus, though common, is not a B symptom.

options: Approximately 20% arising in the transition zone
Approximately 70-80% arising in the peripheral zone
Approximately 40% in the anterior fibromuscular stroma
questions.explanation: Approximately 70-80% of prostatic adenocarcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, making it the primary target for systematic biopsy. The transition zone accounts for approximately 15-20% and the central zone for approximately 5-10%. Transition zone cancers are typically well-differentiated and often detected incidentally in TURP chips. Peripheral zone cancers are palpable on digital rectal examination when large enough. Benign prostatic hyperplasia predominantly affects the transition zone. The peripheral zone's proximity to the rectal wall makes it accessible for TRUS-guided biopsy.
questions.question: A 70-year-old man with bladder outlet obstruction and elevated PSA undergoes TRUS biopsy targeting the peripheral zone. What percentage of prostate adenocarcinomas arise in the peripheral zone?

questions.explanation:
Umbilical cord blood transplant before symptom onset improves outcomes
in Krabbe disease. Donor-derived cells provide enzyme crossing
blood-brain barrier. Newborn screening enables presymptomatic treatment.

options: HPV types 16 and 18 causing high-grade dysplasia
HPV types 6 and 11 causing condyloma acuminatum
HPV types 31 and 33 causing intermediate-risk lesions
HPV types 45 and 56 causing flat condylomata
HPV types 51 and 52 causing subclinical infection
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy presents with a painful penile lesion. Biopsy shows squamous epithelium with koilocytes (perinuclear haloes with nuclear wrinkles) and hyperkeratosis, without invasion. Which HPV types are most responsible?
questions.explanation: Condyloma acuminatum (genital warts) is caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, which cause benign squamoproliferative lesions with koilocytic change (perinuclear cytoplasmic clearing with nuclear wrinkling/raisinoid nuclei). These types are not oncogenic. High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 cause penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) and penile squamous cell carcinoma. HPV vaccines targeting types 6, 11, 16, and 18 (quadrivalent) or additionally types 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 (nine-valent) prevent both warts and high-grade dysplasia. Koilocytosis is the histological hallmark of productive HPV infection.

questions.question: What is pipestem fibrosis in schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation:
Pipestem fibrosis describes periportal liver fibrosis from chronic S.
mansoni or S. japonicum infection. Portal vein obstruction causes portal
hypertension without cirrhotic nodules. The liver surface appears bumpy
with granulomas and fibrotic bands.

Ruptured berry aneurysms cause 80% of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. Anterior communicating artery is the most common location. Sudden severe "thunderclap" headache occurs. CT shows blood in basal cisterns. Complications include rebleeding, vasospasm causing delayed ischemia, and hydrocephalus. Aneurysm securing by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping prevents rebleeding.
questions.question: Subarachnoid hemorrhage most commonly results from:

options: Diaphragmatic hernia allowing abdominal organ herniation
questions.question: A neonate develops respiratory distress shortly after birth, and chest X-ray shows bowel loops within the thoracic cavity with mediastinal shift. Which embryological defect explains this finding?
questions.explanation: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia results from incomplete closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal during development, allowing abdominal contents to herniate into the thoracic cavity and compress the developing lung, often causing pulmonary hypoplasia. The resulting mediastinal shift and bowel loops on chest imaging are diagnostic. Antenatal diagnosis allows for delivery planning at a centre equipped for immediate neonatal surgical care.

questions.question: A female obligate carrier of X-ALD has normal plasma VLCFA levels. The most reliable confirmatory carrier detection test is:
options: ABCD1 gene mutation analysis once the familial variant is known
Adrenal stimulation test for subclinical adrenocortical insufficiency
Enzyme activity assay for ABCD1 protein in peripheral leukocytes
Skin fibroblast VLCFA analysis for elevated C26:0 fatty acids
Brain MRI for early white matter changes in female carriers
questions.explanation: Because VLCFA elevation can be normal in 15-20% of obligate female X-ALD carriers due to skewed X-inactivation favoring the normal allele in leukocytes, ABCD1 gene mutation analysis is definitive for female carrier detection when the familial mutation is known. Targeted mutation analysis offers near-100% sensitivity once the pathogenic ABCD1 variant is characterized in the index case. Female carriers may develop adrenomyeloneuropathy in mid-adulthood but are generally much less severely affected than hemizygous males with full cerebral or spinal cord ALD presentation.

Homozygous FH causes cholesterol levels 600-1000 mg/dL with severe
premature atherosclerosis. Myocardial infarction occurs in childhood or
adolescence. LDL apheresis and liver transplantation are treatment
options.
questions.question: At what cholesterol level do homozygous FH patients present?
What are the typical presenting symptoms of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas present as liver masses with nonspecific signs and symptoms including weight loss, pain, anorexia, and ascites, without early jaundice. In contrast, extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas present with biliary obstruction causing jaundice, acholic stools, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Location determines clinical presentation pattern.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with chronic H. pylori infection has a gastric biopsy showing a dense lymphoid infiltrate with lymphoepithelial lesions invading glands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Gastric MALT lymphoma arises from chronic antigenic stimulation by H. pylori, producing a low-grade B-cell lymphoma with lymphoepithelial lesions where lymphocytes infiltrate and destroy glands. Many early-stage cases regress after H. pylori eradication, a feature unique to this lymphoma subtype among gastrointestinal malignancies.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: The most common cause of chronic pancreatitis is alcohol abuse, particularly in middle-aged males. Other causes include obstruction of the duct with stones or tumor, autoimmune diseases, and hereditary pancreatitis. The disease typically follows repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis with progressive pancreatic damage.

questions.question: A patient presents with relapsing episodes of visual disturbance, limb weakness, and sensory symptoms over several years. MRI shows multiple periventricular white matter lesions. CSF shows oligoclonal bands. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system characterised by relapsing-remitting episodes of neurological dysfunction, with MRI showing characteristic periventricular white matter lesions disseminated in space and time, and CSF analysis often revealing oligoclonal bands reflecting intrathecal antibody production. This chronic relapsing pattern distinguishes it from acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, which typically follows a single monophasic course after an infectious trigger. Disease-modifying therapies aim to reduce relapse frequency and slow disability accumulation.

questions.question:
An athlete in a racquet sport develops pain on the outer aspect of the elbow after repetitive wrist/forearm use, diagnosed as tennis elbow.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Name the assessment/intervention approach used for this injury.
(c) Outline a prevention strategy for this injury.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tennis elbow - a recognised example of overuse syndrome.
(b)
Recognition as an overuse syndrome (caused by load too great, poor technique/posture, faulty equipment, or inappropriate posture/anatomy) and management with PRICES and qualified modalities (cold/heat, ultrasound, electrical stimulation), followed by an individual therapeutic exercise programme.

Correcting technique/posture, ensuring adequate/appropriate equipment, adequate training and conditioning, and adequate rest, since these are the stated causes of overuse injury when they are inadequate.

Biceps femoris tendinopathy - a sprint-associated injury.

Classified as a chronic/sub-acute (overuse) injury and managed with PRICES (Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support) and qualified modalities (cold/heat, ultrasound, electrical stimulation).

The musculotendinous unit of biceps femoris (part of the hamstring), subjected to repetitive microtrauma.

Adequate warm-up, adequate/appropriate training and conditioning, good/right sporting technique, and adequate rest/recovery period.

questions.answerText:

• Extrinsic: poor/bad facilities, faulty/bad equipment, psychological factor, climatic conditions, poor kits/wears; also level of competition, playing surface, and weather
(b)
• PRICES (Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support)

questions.question:
(a) Describe a sample weekly training/exercise programme as a staged process.
(b) Relate the components of this programme to common sports pathologies.
(c) Explain why inadequate adherence to such a programme may lead to re-injury or functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Monday to Friday: 5 minutes warm-up, 45 minutes aerobic activity, 10 minutes cool-down and stretching.
• Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday: 5 minutes warm-up, 30 minutes resistance training, 10 minutes cool-down and stretching.
• Saturday and/or Sunday: sports, walking, hiking, biking or swimming.
• Health-professional recommendations add: about 30 minutes of moderate aerobic activity daily (or three 10-minute sessions); resistance exercise for 8–10 exercises stressing major muscle groups at least twice a week; and flexibility/balance activities for 10 minutes, 2 days a week.
(b)
• Adequate cardiovascular, strength, and flexibility training addresses the health-related fitness components (cardiovascular fitness, strength, flexibility, muscular endurance, body composition) linked to avoiding injury and maintaining function.
• Poor/inadequate training and conditioning is an intrinsic risk factor for sports injury.
• Weakness in muscles, tendons and ligaments is a cause of sports injuries, which resistance training in the weekly programme is designed to address.
• Exercise programmes for older adults should be based on physical fitness level and health status, reflecting individual injury-risk profiles.
(c)
• Skipping the warm-up or cool-down components of the weekly programme removes the protective effect against muscular injury and post-exercise soreness/spasm.
• Not meeting the resistance/flexibility recommendations may leave muscular strength and flexibility deficits, both linked to injury risk and daily function.
• Increasing intensity too quickly, rather than following a structured weekly plan, is a cause of sports injury.

questions.question:

questions.answerText:

• Components: Protect (e.g., crutches, immobilisation), Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support.
• Adjunct technique: qualified use of modalities - cold or heat, ultrasound, electrical stimulation.
• Progression technique: development and supervision of an individual therapeutic exercise programme.
(b)
• Modalities must be used by qualified personnel.
• The therapeutic exercise programme is evaluated and modified as progress deems necessary.
• Return to competition is confirmed through functional testing rather than a fixed timeline.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Warm-up activities are necessary to prepare the body for vigorous physical activity, increasing performance and decreasing risk of muscular injury.
• A comprehensive warm-up takes about 30 minutes: 5 minutes of light aerobic activity (jogging, non-cutting linear drills), then at least 15 minutes stretching all primary muscles used for the sport.
• This is followed by 5 minutes of sport-specific drills (full running, multi-directional skills) and 5 minutes of high-intensity, multi-directional sprinting/jumping activity that is sport specific.
• After activity, the athlete should spend 5 to 10 minutes stretching all primary muscles, at least 30 to 60 seconds each.
(b)
• Poor/inadequate warm-up is an intrinsic risk factor for sports injury.
• Not warming up properly is among the reasons most sports injuries are avoidable.
• The purpose of the warm-up (raising heart rate, warming muscles, improving blood flow) is to reduce muscular/soft-tissue injuries (sprains, strains).
• Cool-down stretching is aimed at preventing muscle soreness and spasms, related to muscle strain risk.
(c)
• Skipping or shortening the warm-up increases the risk of muscular injury, since the warm-up's purpose is explicitly to decrease this risk.
• Not stretching adequately after activity may increase muscle soreness and spasms.
• General prevention advice reiterates the importance of warm-up and cool-down for the athlete.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications: needed because an athlete participating in sports sweats, and this fluid loss must be replaced with equal amounts of fluids.
• Technique/parameters: drink fluids before, during, and after each practice/game; to avoid stomach cramps from drinking large amounts at once, drink about one cup of water (or a sports drink) every 15 to 20 minutes.
• Precautions: avoid drinks with carbonation and caffeine.
• Additional precaution: in hot, humid weather, the athlete can become dehydrated faster, so consider decreasing or stopping the activity when it is too hot.
(b)
• Fluids should be taken in small, regular amounts (about one cup every 15–20 minutes) rather than large volumes at once, to avoid stomach cramps.
• Carbonated and caffeinated drinks should be avoided.
• Activity should be decreased or stopped in excessively hot, humid conditions due to faster dehydration.
• Recognise dehydration symptoms early: thirstiness, weakness, headache, dark-coloured urine, and slight weight loss.
(c)
• Sweating during sports activity causes fluid loss that must be replaced with equal amounts of fluids.
• Hot, humid weather increases the rate at which an athlete becomes dehydrated.

(a) Describe the principles of bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), including its indications and technique.
(b) State how BIA should be safely and accurately applied.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications: used as a method of measuring body fat percentage.
• Technique: a low-level, safe electrical current is sent through the body; the current passes easily through muscle tissue (which contains a large amount of fluid) but travels slowly through fat tissue.
• Parameters: the resistance encountered as the current passes through fat tissue is called bioelectrical impedance; with the addition of the person's height, gender and weight, the device computes body fat percentage.
• A variety of BIA devices exist, e.g., Omron and Tanita.
(b)
Accurate results require inputting the person's correct height, gender and weight alongside the impedance measurement.
(c)
The method relies on the physiological fact that electrical current passes more easily through fluid-rich muscle tissue than through fat tissue, creating measurable impedance.

(a)

questions.answerText:
(a)
• BMI is a method of estimating a person's body fat level from weight and height; Metric BMI = weight (kg) / [height (m)]²; English BMI = weight (lb) / [height (in)]² × 703.
• BMI classification: below 18.5 underweight; 18.5–24.9 normal; 25.0–29.9 overweight; 30.0 and above obese (Class I 30–34.9, Class II 35–39.9, Class III 40 and greater).
• Waist-to-hip ratio measures the ratio of waist to hip circumference; the higher the ratio, the higher the risk of heart disease and other obesity-related disorders.
• Risk of heart disease rises sharply for women with ratios above 0.8 and for men with ratios above 1.0.
(b)
• Individuals with BMI in the overweight/obese categories (25.0 and above) carry excess body fat, which places strain on joints, muscles and bones and increases injury risk.
• Body fat around the abdomen and hips (the apple shape), reflected in waist-hip ratio, may be a more consistent predictor of heart problems/health risk than BMI.
• Individuals with waist-hip ratios above the thresholds (0.8 for women, 1.0 for men) are more vulnerable to heart disease and obesity-related disorders.
• Excess body fat is also linked to a number of health problems such as heart disease and diabetes.
(c)
• BMI is calculated purely from weight and height, giving an indirect estimate of body fat; waist-hip ratio is calculated from waist and hip circumference measurements.
• BMI classifies individuals into underweight, normal, overweight, and three obesity classes; waist-hip ratio is interpreted against sex-specific risk thresholds (0.8 for women, 1.0 for men).
• BMI has been found to correlate strongly with other, more complicated direct measures of body fat, including underwater weighing.
• Waist-hip ratio (reflecting abdominal/hip fat distribution) may be a more consistent predictor of heart problems and health risk than BMI.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications: used as a common method of determining a person's body composition and body fat percentage.
• Technique: the tester pinches the skin at the site and pulls the fold away from underlying muscle so only skin and fat tissue is held, then measures thickness in millimetres using special skinfold calipers; two measurements are taken and averaged.
• Sites: measurements are generally taken on the right side of the body, at locations including triceps, pectoral, subscapula, midaxilla, abdomen, suprailiac, and quadriceps (the exact sites vary with the protocol used).
• Parameters: results rely on formulas that convert the measurements into an estimate of body fat percentage according to the person's age and gender.
(b)
• Measurements should be taken at the correct anatomical sites, generally on the right side of the body.
• Two measurements should be taken at each site and averaged to improve accuracy.
(c)
The method is based on the principle that a pinched skinfold isolates skin and subcutaneous fat tissue from underlying muscle, allowing its thickness to be measured.

questions.answerText:

Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) sprain/tear - a soccer-associated knee injury.
(b)
• Mechanism: falling, twisting, or getting hit (the recognised causes of a sprain).
• Tissue pathology: the ligament, which connects bones at the joint, is stretched or torn, ranging from Type I (minimal stretch/tear, mild), Type II (some fibres torn completely, moderate), to Type III (entire ligament torn, marked instability, severe).
(c)

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principles of the Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire (PAR-Q), including its indications, purpose and technique.
(b) State how PAR-Q findings should be safely applied and any precautions to observe.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications: used as a self-screening tool by anyone planning to start an exercise programme, often administered by fitness trainers or coaches.
• Purpose: to identify the small number of adults for whom physical activity may be inappropriate, or who should seek medical advice on the type of activity most suitable for them.
• Technique: answer yes/no to questions covering a doctor-diagnosed heart condition, chest pain during or in the past month without physical activity, dizziness/loss of consciousness, a bone or joint problem, blood-pressure/heart medication, and any other reason not to exercise.
• Trigger for referral: one or more 'yes' answers, being over age 40, being inactive, or having health concerns.
(b)
• If one or more 'yes' answers are given, being over 40, inactive, or concerned about health, the person should consult a physician before a fitness test or before substantially increasing activity, and ask for medical clearance and information about exercise limitations.
• If all answers are 'no', the person can be reasonably sure they can exercise safely with low risk of medical complications.
• Even with all 'no' answers, it is still important to start slowly and increase activity gradually.
• A fitness assessment may also be helpful to determine where to begin.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principles of hydrostatic underwater weighing, including its indications and technique.
(b) State how hydrostatic underwater weighing should be safely applied.
(c) Explain the physical basis of hydrostatic underwater weighing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications: used as a method to determine body composition (body fat to lean mass), considered the gold standard for body composition assessment.
• Technique: the person is first weighed on dry land, then gets into a large tank of water.
• Technique: sitting on a special scale, the person is lowered underwater and asked to expel all air from the lungs and remain motionless while underwater weight is measured.
• Parameters: the procedure is repeated three times and averaged; a special calculation then determines lean weight, fat weight, and percentage body fat.
(b)
• The person must remain motionless underwater while weight is measured, and must fully expel air from the lungs for accuracy.
• Measurements are repeated three times and averaged to improve accuracy.
(c)
The method uses Archimedes' Principle of displacement to determine a person's total body density and hence body composition.

(a)
• Definition: acute (traumatic) injuries typically result from single events.
• Features: immediate onset of pain, associated with obvious deformity, and impaired function.
• Duration: classified as occurring in less than 72 hours.
• Examples/causes: sudden injuries such as cuts and sprains, usually caused by accidents such as a sudden impact or an awkward movement.
(b)
• The sport itself is the greatest predictor of injury risk, with contact sports such as football topping the list.
• Poor technique and structural abnormalities can contribute to the development of injuries.
• Sudden injury can be difficult to avoid, though damage can be minimised by wearing appropriate safety equipment.
• Intrinsic factors (e.g., fatigue, unstable joint integrity, poor fitness) and extrinsic factors (e.g., poor facilities, bad equipment) also raise vulnerability.
(c)
• Acute injuries result from a single event, with immediate pain, obvious deformity and impaired function, occurring in less than 72 hours.
• Chronic/sub-acute injuries result from repetitive microtrauma to bone, ligament and musculotendinous units, developing over more than 72 hours.
• Acute injury examples include cuts and sprains from sudden impact or awkward movement; chronic injury examples fall under overuse syndrome (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome, tendonitis, bursitis, tennis elbow, shin splints).
• Chronic/overuse causes include load too great for conditions, poor technique or posture, faulty equipment, and inappropriate posture or anatomy, whereas acute injury is linked to accidents/trauma rather than repetitive load.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fitness tests must be specific: they must assess an individual's fitness for the activity or sport in question (e.g., a running endurance test is of little use for assessing improvement in cycling endurance).
• Fitness tests must be valid: they must measure the component of fitness they are supposed to (e.g., checking whether a sit-and-reach test measures hamstring flexibility alone or other factors too).
• Fitness tests must be reliable/objective: a test is objective when it produces the same results for the same individual regardless of the tester or technician (also called intertester reliability).
• Many factors need to be considered when choosing a test for fitness testing to be accurate and worthwhile: specificity, validity, objectivity and reliability.
(b)
• When performing a repeat test, it is important to limit as many variables as possible by keeping conditions/circumstances the same as the previous test.
• Factors affecting results include time of day, weather conditions, environment (surface/noise/other people), and use of a different assessor.
• Further factors: accuracy of measurements, whether the test protocol was followed exactly as before, and time since the athlete's last meal.
• Further factors: the athlete's emotions, state of hydration, health (recent colds/illness), and any medication being taken.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Muscular strength is defined as the ability of a muscle to exert a force to overcome a resistance; it is usually assessed by measuring the maximum amount of weight a person can lift one time (Repetition Maximum Testing, 1RM).
• Muscular strength is vitally important not only in sports but in day-to-day life, enabling tasks such as lifting heavy bags, avoiding injuries, maintaining good posture, and remaining independent in older age.
• Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle to make repeated contractions over a period of time, or to contract without becoming exhausted; it is assessed by counting the maximum number of repetitions of a contraction a person can perform to fatigue.
• Muscular endurance is important in sports such as football (repeated running and kicking), tennis (repeated arm swinging) and swimming (repeating the stroke).
(b)
• Athletes with poor muscular strength may struggle to perform sport tasks, are more prone to injuries, and may have difficulty maintaining good posture.
• Athletes with poor muscular endurance may struggle to sustain repeated actions required in their sport, such as repeated running/kicking (football), swinging (tennis), or strokes (swimming).
• Strength testing measures the maximal force a muscle group can exert at one time, while muscle endurance testing measures how long a muscle group can contract and release before fatiguing, so deficits in either domain create different vulnerabilities.
• Sports with high demands for sustained repetitive effort place athletes with low muscular endurance at particular disadvantage.
(c)
• Muscular strength is the ability to exert force against resistance, assessed via 1RM (maximum weight lifted once); muscular endurance is the ability to sustain repeated contractions, assessed by counting repetitions to fatigue.
• Strength testing measures maximal force at one time; endurance testing measures duration/repetitions before fatigue.
• Strength is important for tasks such as lifting and avoiding injury; endurance is important for sustained repetitive sporting actions (e.g., running, swinging, swimming strokes).
• Both are components of health-related physical fitness, alongside cardiovascular fitness, flexibility, and body composition.
