The gradual onset over repeated training, with no single traumatic event, and duration beyond 72 hours, supports classification as a chronic/overuse rather than acute/traumatic injury.

questions.question:
A soccer player receives a direct knock to the front of the thigh during a match and develops pain, swelling, bruising, and reduced knee movement.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Outline the predisposing factors for this injury.
(c) Describe the pathophysiology of the injury.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management of the injury.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Quadriceps contusion - a soccer-associated injury.
(b)
• Contact sports such as football/soccer carry the greatest predictor of injury risk among sports.
• Extrinsic factors such as poor/inappropriate kits/wears or lack of appropriate protective equipment, and psychological factors, are also risk factors.
(c)
Sports injuries are commonly caused by overuse, direct impact, or the application of force greater than the body part can structurally withstand; here the mechanism is direct impact.
(d)
• PRICES (Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support) and qualified modalities (cold/heat, ultrasound, electrical stimulation).
• An individual therapeutic exercise programme evaluated and modified as progress requires.
• Return to competition guided by functional testing.

(a)
Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain - a soccer-associated knee injury.
(b)
• Predisposing (intrinsic) factors: fatigue, inadequate warm-up, unstable joint integrity, inadequate training/conditioning, poor fitness, poor motor control, inadequate rest, poorly healed prior injury.
• Predisposing (extrinsic) factors: poor/bad facilities, faulty/bad equipment, climatic conditions, poor kits/wears; contact sports carry the greatest injury risk of all sports.
(c)
• Caused by falling, twisting, or getting hit (the recognised causes of a sprain).
• The ligament, which connects bones at the joint, becomes stretched or torn, ranging from Type I (minimal stretch/tear) through Type II (some fibres torn completely) to Type III (entire ligament torn, marked instability).
(d)
• PRICES (Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support) and qualified modalities (cold/heat, ultrasound, electrical stimulation).
• An individual therapeutic exercise programme that is evaluated and modified as progress requires.
• Return to competition guided by functional testing.
questions.question:
A soccer player receives a blow to the outer side of the knee during a tackle and develops pain and swelling on the inner side of the knee.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Outline the predisposing factors for this injury.
(c) Describe the pathophysiology of the injury.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management of the injury.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Risk factors for sports injuries are characteristics and behaviours of athletes (intrinsic) and characteristics of the sport and environment (extrinsic) associated with injury risk.
• Intrinsic (subject) factors include age, sex, skill, level of fitness, use of protective equipment, playing position, and game strategies; also fatigue, inadequate warm-up, body typing, substance abuse, unstable joint integrity, inadequate training/conditioning, inappropriate nutrition, poor fitness, disregard for rules, psychological factors, poor motor control, poor kits, inadequate rest, poorly healed injury, and poor hydration.
• Extrinsic (sport/game) factors include level of competition, playing surface, and weather; also poor/bad facilities, bad equipment, psychological factor, climatic condition, and poor kits/wears.
• Some extrinsic risk factors can be modified, e.g., rule changes, protective equipment, ankle supports, and safer athletic equipment.
(b)
• The sport itself is the greatest predictor of injury risk, with contact sports such as football topping the list.
• Overuse also increases injury risk, particularly in athletes with intense training demands.
• Athletes with poor fitness, inadequate training/conditioning, inadequate warm-up, or poorly healed prior injuries are more vulnerable.
• Sports played on poor surfaces, in adverse weather, or with poor facilities/equipment increase vulnerability for all participants.
(c)
• Intrinsic risk factors relate to the athlete's own characteristics and behaviours (e.g., age, fitness, fatigue, motor control, hydration).
• Extrinsic risk factors relate to the sport and environment (e.g., playing surface, weather, facilities, equipment).
• Intrinsic factors are generally athlete-modifiable through training, conditioning, and behaviour change.
• Extrinsic factors are typically addressed through rule changes, protective/safer equipment, and improved facilities.
questions.question:
(a) Describe risk factors for sports injury under the headings of definition, categories, and examples.
(b) Explain why certain athletes or sports are more vulnerable based on these risk factors.
(c) Distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic risk factors.

(a) Describe periodization as a process, including how training load/volume is structured over time.
(b) Relate inadequate periodization to common sports pathologies.
(c) Explain why inadequate periodization/management may lead to re-injury or functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Periodization is the process of consistently and slowly increasing training load and volume, with periodic recovery days or weeks.
• It is the best way to produce long-term, sustainable fitness gains while avoiding injury and burnout.
• Systematic planning for injury prevention (which includes periodization) involves analysing the problem and risk factors, studying behaviour determinants, designing an intervention, and implementing it.
• The evaluation phase of injury-prevention planning examines effects at the levels of implementation, intervention, determinants, behaviour, and incidence of injury.
(b)
• Poor training methods are the most common cause of sports injury.
• Increasing exercise intensity too quickly, without periodised progression, is linked to overuse/chronic injuries (repetitive microtrauma to bone, ligament and musculotendinous units).
• Participating at too high a level, too quickly, results in injury.
• Overuse injury arises when load is too great for the athlete's conditioning, which periodization is designed to manage.
(c)
• Muscles need 48 hours to recover after a workout; not allowing this recovery (poor periodization) risks injury.
• Not stopping activity when pain develops during exercise is also a cause of injury.
• Complete healing and adequate rest/recovery are among the prevention measures for sports injuries, underscoring the risk of re-injury without them.

(a)
• Warm-up activities are necessary to prepare the body for vigorous physical activity; they increase performance and decrease the risk of muscular injury.
• A comprehensive warm-up includes light aerobic activity to raise heart rate and warm muscles (improving blood flow for stretching), followed by stretching, sport-specific drills, and high-intensity multi-directional sprinting/jumping.
• Cool-down (post-activity stretching) involves at least 5 to 10 minutes stretching all primary muscles used, holding each stretch 30 to 60 seconds.
• The purpose of cool-down stretching is to prevent muscle soreness and spasms.
(b)
• Athletes in sports requiring sudden, high-intensity, or multi-directional movement (e.g., sprinting) are especially reliant on an adequate warm-up to reduce injury risk.
• Inadequate warm-up is an intrinsic risk factor for sports injury.
• Skipping proper warm-up is among the common, avoidable causes of sports injuries.
• Athletes who omit the cool-down stretch may be more vulnerable to muscle soreness and spasms following vigorous activity.
(c)
• Warm-up occurs before activity and is structured around light aerobic work, stretching, and sport-specific/high-intensity drills, over approximately 30 minutes.
• Cool-down occurs after activity and consists of 5 to 10 minutes of stretching all primary muscles, each held 30 to 60 seconds.
• Warm-up aims to increase performance and decrease the risk of muscular injury during activity.
• Cool-down aims to prevent muscle soreness and spasms following activity.
questions.question:
(a) Describe warm-up and cool-down under the headings of definition, purpose, and technique.
(b) Explain why certain athletes or sports are more vulnerable without adequate warm-up/cool-down.
(c) Distinguish warm-up from cool-down.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Overtraining occurs when the skills required by an athlete are continually repeated and become physically and/or mentally too demanding.
• Signs include: lack of motivation to participate; getting tired quickly.
• Further signs: irritability and unwillingness to cooperate with coaches and teammates; decreased ability to achieve training goals.
• Further signs: deterioration in execution of sport plays; slower times in distance sports.
(b)
• Competitive athletes have a high risk of overuse injuries due to the intense nature of their training and overuse of specific muscle groups.
• Overuse syndrome is a large group of conditions resulting from using the body in a repetitive way.
• Causes of overuse injury include load too great for conditions, poor technique/posture, faulty equipment, and inappropriate posture/anatomy.
• Overtraining and overuse injury both stem from training demands exceeding the athlete's capacity to recover.
(c)
• Taking frequent rest breaks during practices/games reduces injury risk, with break length being age and sport specific.
• The greater the intensity of the sport on muscles/joints, the more rest is needed during practice/games; hydration during rest breaks is also advised.
• Immediate reporting of injuries is encouraged as a preventive measure.
questions.question:
(a) Describe overtraining as a process, including its definition and the signs that mark its progression.
(b) Relate overtraining to common sports pathologies.
(c) Explain why inadequate management of overtraining may lead to functional deficit.

A long-distance runner develops gradual pain along the inner shin after a rapid increase in training mileage.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Describe the mechanism of injury and the tissue pathology involved.
(c) Describe the acute/initial management of the injury.
(d) Describe the rehabilitation and return-to-play criteria for the injury.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Medial tibial stress syndrome - a long-distance-running-associated injury.
(b)
A chronic/overuse injury caused by repetitive microtrauma to bone, developing over more than 72 hours; overuse causes include load too great for conditions, poor technique/posture, faulty equipment, and inappropriate posture or anatomy.
(c)
Management follows PRICES - Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support; qualified use of modalities (cold or heat, ultrasound, electrical stimulation).
(d)
Rehabilitation uses an individual therapeutic exercise programme, evaluated and modified as progress requires; return to competition is guided by functional testing.

(a)
• Stage 1 (acute/protective): PRICES - Protect (e.g., crutches, immobilisation), Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support.
• Stage 2 (modality-assisted): qualified use of modalities such as cold or heat, ultrasound, or electrical stimulation.
• Stage 3 (therapeutic exercise): development and supervision of an individual therapeutic exercise programme.
• Stage 4 (progression and return): evaluation and modification of the programme as progress deems necessary, followed by return to competition guided by functional testing.
(b)
• This staged process applies to sports injuries including sprains, strains, and overuse (chronic) conditions such as tendinopathies, stress fractures, and shin splints.
• Acute-stage protection/rest/ice/compression/elevation/support addresses the immediate pain, swelling and impaired function seen in acute (traumatic) injuries.
• Therapeutic exercise and progressive evaluation address the repetitive microtrauma underlying chronic/overuse injuries.
• Functional testing before return to competition is relevant across both injury categories to confirm readiness.
(c)
• Skipping or shortening protection/rest stages may aggravate the initial injury given the need for adequate rest and complete healing.
• Muscles need 48 hours to recover after a workout; returning to activity without allowing this recovery is linked to injury.
• Returning to competition without functional testing removes the check that confirms readiness, risking re-injury.
• Adequate rest/recovery period and complete healing are among the general measures to prevent (re-)injury.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the treatment, rehabilitation and reconditioning process as a staged sequence.
(b) Relate this staged process to common sports pathologies.
(c) Explain why inadequate management at any stage may lead to re-injury or functional deficit.

A sprinter suddenly grabs the back of the thigh and pulls up while accelerating during a race, diagnosed as a hamstring strain.
(a) List the intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors that could have predisposed this athlete to injury.
(b) Outline the physiotherapy management options available.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Intrinsic: fatigue, inadequate warm-up, age, body type, substance abuse, unstable joint integrity, inadequate training/conditioning, inappropriate nutrition, poor fitness, disregard for rules, psychological factors, poor/defective motor control (e.g., tight hamstring muscles in a gymnast), poor kits, inadequate rest, poorly healed prior injury, poor hydration; also sex, skill, fitness level, playing position, and game strategies
• Extrinsic: poor/bad facilities, faulty/bad equipment, psychological factor, climatic conditions, poor kits/wears; also level of competition, playing surface, and weather
(b)
• PRICES (Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Support)
• Qualified use of modalities (cold/heat, ultrasound, electrical stimulation)
• An individual therapeutic exercise programme, evaluated and modified as needed
• Return to competition guided by functional testing

questions.question:
(a) Describe a conditioning programme as a staged process, including timing and the skills it should address.
(b) Relate inadequate conditioning to common sports pathologies.
(c) Explain why inadequate conditioning may lead to re-injury or functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A conditioning programme should be preseason and progressive during the season.
• It is beneficial to start the programme at least two to four weeks prior to the season.
• The programme should address flexibility, strength, balance/coordination, endurance, agility, and sport-specific skills.
• It should progressively prepare and maintain the body for the demands of the sport.
(b)
• Sports injuries frequently occur in athletes who have been sedentary and are then expected to perform at sport level without preseason training.
• Poor training methods, including increasing intensity too quickly, are the most common cause of sports injury.
• Weakness in muscles, tendons, and ligaments (addressed by a strength/flexibility conditioning programme) is a cause of sports injuries.
• Inadequate training and conditioning is an intrinsic risk factor for injury.
(c)
• Without adequate conditioning, an athlete is more likely to be injured when returning to or beginning sport-level activity.
• Muscles need 48 hours to recover after a workout, so inadequate recovery within a conditioning programme raises injury risk.
• Complete healing and adequate rest/recovery are among the general measures to prevent (re-)injury.

questions.question:
A runner rapidly increases training intensity and volume without adequate recovery and subsequently develops an overuse injury.
(a) Identify the tissue/structure most likely affected and the mechanism.
(b) Discuss the contributing factors to the condition.
(c) State differential diagnoses to consider.
(d) Explain the clinical reasoning that supports the diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Overuse syndrome broadly affects bone, ligament, and musculotendinous units through repetitive microtrauma.
(b)
Overuse is attributed to load too great for the athlete's conditioning, poor technique or posture, faulty/poor equipment, and inappropriate posture or anatomy; poor training methods (the most common cause of injury) include increasing exercise intensity too quickly and not stopping when pain develops, noting that muscles need 48 hours to recover after a workout.
(c)
Any of the chronic/overuse injuries, e.g., plantar fasciitis, stress fracture of the second metatarsal, medial tibial stress syndrome, tendinopathies (Achilles, biceps femoris, jumper's knee), shin splints, or carpal tunnel syndrome.
(d)
The gradual symptom development linked to a rapid increase in training load and insufficient recovery time is consistent with poor training methods, the most common cause of sports injury.

(a)
• Physical fitness's multidimensional characteristics can be divided into health-related and skill-related fitness.
• Health-related fitness includes cardiovascular (aerobic) fitness, strength, flexibility, muscular endurance, and body composition.
• Skill-related fitness includes speed, reaction time, agility, balance, coordination, and power, important for the more technical aspects of many sports.
• Physical fitness overall is the capacity to carry out daily activities without undue fatigue, and to meet ordinary and unusual demands of daily life safely and effectively.
(b)
• Athletes lacking cardiovascular fitness may struggle to sustain submaximal exercise, since circulatory and respiratory systems must work together to supply oxygen to the muscles.
• Poor muscular strength reduces the ability to perform tasks, avoid injuries, and maintain good posture.
• Poor flexibility can increase injury risk and reduce efficient performance of skills such as gymnastics, dancing, or diving.
• Deficits in skill-related components (e.g., poor balance or agility) are linked to greater risk in sports requiring quick changes of direction or contact, such as football and rugby.
(c)
• Health-related fitness (cardiovascular fitness, strength, flexibility, muscular endurance, body composition) forms the overall health status.
• Skill-related fitness (speed, reaction time, agility, balance, coordination, power) is important for performing the more technical aspects of sport.
• Health-related fitness underpins general health and daily function, while skill-related fitness underpins sport-specific performance.
• Both are components of the same multidimensional concept of physical fitness.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the components of physical fitness under the headings of health-related and skill-related fitness.
(b) Explain why certain athletes or sports are more vulnerable to deficits in these components.
(c) Distinguish health-related fitness from skill-related fitness.

(a) Describe a ligament sprain under the headings of definition, causes, clinical features, and classification/grading.
(b) Explain why certain athletes or sports are more vulnerable to sprains.
(c) Distinguish between a sprain and a strain.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; ligaments connect bones at a joint.
• Causes: falling, twisting, or getting hit.
• Clinical features: pain, swelling, bruising, inability to move the joint, and sometimes a felt pop or tear.
• Classification: Type I mild (minimal stretch/tear), Type II moderate (some fibres torn completely), Type III severe (entire ligament torn, marked joint instability).
(b)
• Ankle and wrist sprains are common, so sports involving running, jumping, cutting or falling raise exposure.
• Intrinsic factors (fatigue, inadequate warm-up, unstable joint integrity, poor fitness, poor motor control) increase susceptibility.
• Extrinsic factors (poor facilities, bad equipment, adverse climatic conditions) add further risk.
• The sport itself is the greatest predictor of injury risk, with contact sports topping the list; overuse also increases risk.
(c)
• A sprain involves a ligament (bone-to-bone); a strain involves a muscle or tendon (tendon connects muscle to bone).
• Sprain causes: falling, twisting, or getting hit; strain causes: twisting or pulling, occurring suddenly or developing over time.
• Sprain symptoms: pain, swelling, bruising, inability to move the joint; strain symptoms: pain, muscle spasms, swelling, trouble moving the muscle.
• Common sprain sites: ankle and wrist; common strain sites: back and hamstring.

questions.question:
A transplant recipient on cyclosporine develops rising creatinine, tremor, hypertension and gum overgrowth.
(a) Identify the drug and the adverse effects.
(b) Explain the mechanism and basis of toxicity.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic basis.
(d) State the management and alternative.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cyclosporine: nephrotoxicity (in the majority of patients; major indication to modify or stop therapy), tremor, hirsutism, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, gum hyperplasia, hyperkalaemia, hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia and anaphylaxis with IV use.
(b)
It inhibits calcineurin through cyclophilin binding, blocking IL-2 synthesis.
(c)
• Lipophilic and highly hydrophobic cyclic undecapeptide, given IV or orally (soft gelatin capsule 20-50% bioavailability); biphasic elimination with terminal half-life 5-18 h; extensively metabolised by CYP3A in the liver (also gut and kidney), excreted via bile into faeces.
• Drug monitoring is essential; tremor can be an early sign of rising plasma concentration.
(d)
• Nephrotoxicity may be minimised by concomitant calcium channel blockers; tacrolimus is an alternative with similar toxicities but 10-100 times more potency and is used as rescue therapy.
• Dose reduction or modification is indicated for nephrotoxicity.

(a)
Natural: streptomycin, neomycin, kanamycin, tobramycin, gentamicin; semi-synthetic: amikacin (from kanamycin) and netilmicin (from sisomicin).
(b)
• Two amino sugars joined to a non-sugar aminocyclitol by an O-glycosidic bond; the aminocyclitol is 2-deoxystreptamine in most, streptidine (not central) in streptomycin.
• All are sulphate salts, highly water-soluble, whose solutions are stable for months; more active in alkaline pH; gentamicin and neomycin are stable over a wide pH range and to autoclaving; physically incompatible with penicillins.
(c)
Bind irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit (and chelate Mg2+): block initiation, cause mRNA mis-reading and break polysomes into monosomes; bactericidal with a post-antibiotic effect.
(d)
• They are highly polar basic drugs, ionised in solution, so poorly absorbed orally, distributed only extracellularly, not penetrating brain or CSF, and almost entirely excreted unchanged in urine.
• A low margin of safety gives nephrotoxicity (proximal tubular), ototoxicity (8th nerve) and neuromuscular paralysis; levels must be monitored and doses adjusted in renal insufficiency (Cockcroft-Gault).
• Resistance: aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (phosphorylation, acetylation, adenylation, plasmid-mediated, the most important), efflux, and 16S rRNA methylation; pus binds and inactivates them.
(e)
• Gentamicin (from Micromonospora purpurea) is the most used, potent against Pseudomonas, Proteus, Klebsiella, relatively more nephrotoxic, ineffective against M. tuberculosis.
• Amikacin is a less toxic semisynthetic kanamycin derivative with the broadest activity, resistant to inactivating enzymes, used for hospital Gram-negative infections and MDR-TB.
• Neomycin is too toxic for parenteral use and is topical or oral (bowel preparation, hepatic coma), often with bacitracin or polymyxin B.
• Tobramycin is superior against Pseudomonas and Proteus, with probably lower toxicity; netilmicin resists many modifying enzymes but is less active on P. aeruginosa.
• Streptomycin develops ribosomal resistance fast, so it is used only in combination (TB, plague, tularemia, brucellosis).
questions.question:
(a) Classify the aminoglycosides.
(b) Describe the general structure and pharmacophore.
(c) State the mechanism of action.
(d) Explain the chemical basis of their pharmacokinetic limitation, toxicity and resistance.
(e) Distinguish gentamicin from amikacin and neomycin.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Primaquine, the least toxic and most effective 8-aminoquinoline; it causes haemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals, shown by dark brown urine.
(b)
It is converted to electrophiles that generate reactive oxygen species and interfere with the electron transport chain.
(c)
• It is essentially the only drug against liver (exoerythrocytic) forms, giving radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale (hypnozoites); it kills gametocytes of all four species but is relatively ineffective against asexual erythrocytic forms; given as the diphosphate (15 mg daily for 14 days for vivax).
• Higher dosages or prolonged use cause GI distress, nausea, headache, pruritus and leukopenia.
(d)
• It is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency and pregnancy.
• Used alongside blood schizonticides for P. vivax and P. ovale infections.
questions.question:
A patient given an 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial to eradicate liver hypnozoites of P. vivax develops dark brown urine and haemolysis.
(a) Identify the drug and the adverse effect.
(b) Explain the mechanism of action and the likely mechanism of toxicity.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic and clinical basis.
(d) State the management and contraindications.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Multibacillary leprosy (6 or more lesions, smear positive): dapsone 100 mg daily, clofazimine 50 mg daily plus 300 mg monthly, and rifampicin 600 mg monthly under supervision, for 12 months.
(b)
Rifampicin is the most bactericidal against M. leprae; dapsone is leprostatic (PABA analogue); clofazimine binds mycobacterial DNA with anti-inflammatory activity; multidrug therapy was introduced to reduce prevalence and the resistance seen with monotherapy.
(c)
• The paucibacillary regimen should never be given to a multibacillary patient; if uncertain, treat as multibacillary.
• If dapsone cannot be taken, replace with clofazimine; if clofazimine cannot be taken, ofloxacin 400 mg or minocycline 100 mg for 12 months; if rifampicin cannot be taken, a 6-month three-drug (clofazimine, ofloxacin, minocycline) then 18 months of two drugs.
(d)
• Monthly clinic visits with direct observation of rifampicin; urinalysis, CBC, creatinine and liver function tests; yearly skin scrapings; monitor for 5-10 years after treatment (relapse about 1%).
• Warn about lepra reactions; clofazimine discolours skin (reddish brown) and is contraindicated in pregnancy; dapsone causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; rifampicin enzyme induction interacts with drugs.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old adult (60 kg) has skin lesions with loss of sensation, a positive skin smear and 8 patches; WHO multidrug therapy is planned.
(a) Identify the type of leprosy and the drugs.
(b) Justify the combination.
(c) Identify the interactions or antagonism and the replacement options.
(d) State the monitoring and precautions.

(a) Give the chemical class, name and structure of artemisinin.
(b) State its properties, derivatives and synthesis.
(c) State its assay methods.
(d) State the SAR and the structural basis of its metabolism and activation.
(e) Explain the basis of resistance and the loss of activity after structural change.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A sesquiterpene lactone with an internal peroxide (endoperoxide) linkage, from Qinghaosu, used in China for over 1000 years; systematic name is a 3,6,9-trimethyl-3,12-epoxy-12H-pyrano[4,3-j]-1,2-benzodioxepin-10(3H)-one.
(b)
• Soluble in organic solvents and almost insoluble in water, so soluble derivatives are used clinically; artesunate and dihydroartemisinin are water-soluble, artemether is lipid-soluble (oil-soluble methyl ether), arteether is more lipophilic than artemether and crosses the BBB for cerebral malaria.
• Synthesis (Roth and Acton, 1989): conversion from artemisinic acid by reduction of the exocyclic methylene group and photo-oxidation of dihydroartemisinic acid in CH2Cl2 at -78°C.
• Artemether is stable in neutral aprotic solvents up to at least 150°C.
(c)
It lacks chromophores, so direct UV assay is poor; assay by derivatisation or acid/base methods, best by HPLC-MS-MS or HPLC with electrochemical detection.
(d)
• SAR: H at C-1 and C-7 essential; substitution at C-2 and C-3 loses activity; CH3 at C-4 increases activity; the peroxide linkage is indispensable; the C-12 ketone may not be essential.
• Activation: metabolised to the active dihydroartemisinin by O-demethylation (artemether), O-deethylation (arteether) and ester hydrolysis (artesunate); inactive desoxyartemisinin and 9,10-dihydroxy products also form.
• Mechanism: the endoperoxide is cleaved (haem iron implicated) to free radicals that damage parasite membranes and proteins; artesunate autoinduces its own metabolism (CYP2B6, CYP3A4).
(e)
• Little cross-resistance with quinoline antimalarials; active against chloroquine-resistant strains; artemisinin resistance is mediated by kelch13 mutations.
• Loss of the peroxide linkage abolishes activity.
• Monotherapy is discouraged because of resistance; short monotherapy courses (under 7 days) are followed by recrudescence.

(a)
• Nitrogen mustards (chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, estramustine, ifosfamide, mechlorethamine, melphalan), aziridine (thiotepa), nitrosoureas (carmustine, lomustine, streptozocin), platinum complexes (carboplatin, cisplatin, oxaliplatin), alkyl sulphonate (busulphan).
• Non-classic alkylators: altretamine, dacarbazine, procarbazine, temozolomide.
(b)
• They form covalent bonds with amino, carboxyl, sulphydryl and phosphate groups in DNA, RNA and proteins.
• They depend on cell proliferation for activity but are cell-cycle nonspecific; the historical origin is the 1940 use of mustine in lymphoma by Gilman and Goodman.
(c)
• Nitrosoureas are highly lipid soluble and cross the BBB, useful for CNS tumours, and are chemically unstable.
• Platinum complexes show structural differences between carboplatin and cisplatin that lead to different toxicities.
(d)
• Alkylators are powerful local vesicants causing local tissue necrosis, cytopenias with marrow suppression, pulmonary fibrosis and haemorrhagic cystitis.
• Cyclophosphamide metabolites cause haemorrhagic cystitis (prevented by mesna) and the drug causes alopecia, sterility and SIADH.
(e)
• Cisplatin and carboplatin are both platinum complexes classed as cell-cycle nonspecific agents (increasing dose increases kill).
• Oxaliplatin is a third platinum complex in the list.
• Busulphan is an alkyl sulphonate used in the haemato-oncology regimens listed.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the alkylating agents with examples.
(b) Describe their general structure/mode of reaction and mechanism of action.
(c) State the pharmacological properties of nitrosoureas and platinum complexes.
(d) Explain the chemical basis of their toxicities.
(e) Distinguish cisplatin from carboplatin.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• First-line: isoniazid, rifamycins (rifampin, rifabutin, rifapentine), pyrazinamide, ethambutol and streptomycin.
• Second-line (intolerance, resistance or contraindication): bedaquiline, clofazimine, cycloserine, delamanid, ethionamide, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, linezolid, para-aminosalicylic acid, pretomanid, thioacetazone, amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin and carbapenems plus clavulanate.
(b)
• Mycobacteria are hard to treat because of the cell wall, efflux pumps and host location; combinations prevent resistance. Active TB: two months of four drugs then four months of isoniazid and rifampicin; latent TB: isoniazid alone for six to nine months or alternatives.
• Chemoprophylaxis with isoniazid for six months is given to newborns of mothers with TB, children under 6 years with a positive tuberculin test and contacts with co-morbidities.
(c)
• Isoniazid blocks mycolic acid synthesis (prodrug activated by KatG): hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuritis. Rifampicin inhibits RNA synthesis via rpoB: hepatotoxicity, orange discolouration.
• Pyrazinamide is converted by pncA pyrazinamidase to pyrazinoic acid, inhibiting FAS1, and is activated in acid: hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia.
• Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferase III (arabinogalactan synthesis), bacteriostatic: optic neuritis, hyperuricaemia. Streptomycin binds the 30S subunit: ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, vertigo.
(d)
• MDR-TB is resistant to isoniazid and rifampin and is treated with second-line drugs including bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid and pretomanid; moxifloxacin-type fluoroquinolones are central for pulmonary MDR-TB.
• XDR-TB is resistant to rifampicin, isoniazid, at least one injectable (amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin) and any fluoroquinolone; it is treated with effective second-line drugs.
• Bedaquiline targets ATP synthase subunit c, is metabolised by CYP3A4 and causes cardiovascular toxicity; linezolid causes bone marrow suppression and irreversible peripheral and optic neuropathy.
• Capreomycin should not be given with other drugs damaging cranial nerve VIII; protease inhibitors with rifampicin risk liver toxicity and sub-therapeutic levels.
• Ethionamide neurological symptoms are relieved by pyridoxine; cycloserine causes CNS effects such as tremor, psychosis and convulsions.
questions.question:
(a) List the first-line and second-line antituberculous drugs.
(b) State the rationale for combination therapy and the treatment durations.
(c) State the mechanism of action and main adverse effects of each first-line drug.
(d) Describe the treatment of MDR-TB and XDR-TB with the key precautions.

(a) State the factors in the selection of an antimicrobial agent.
(b) Describe host factors and site of infection.
(c) Relate to examples of drugs affected by each factor.
(d) State the trade-offs, limitations and complications of antimicrobial therapy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Selection depends on the identity of the organism and its susceptibility, the site of infection, the safety of the agent, and patient factors (immune status, renal and hepatic function, perfusion, pregnancy, lactation, age) and cost.
• Identification uses Gram stain, immunologic methods and PCR, with final identification by culture before therapy; susceptibility by Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion, MIC dilution and E-test.
(b)
• Host factors: previous adverse reactions, age, genetic or metabolic abnormalities, pregnancy, renal and hepatic function, site of infection.
• Site: concentrations must exceed the MIC at the infection site; the BBB excludes many antibiotics and inflammation increases penetration; endocarditis vegetations and bone impair penetration; pus inactivates aminoglycosides.
(c)
• Age: infants and elderly vulnerable; chloramphenicol and sulphonamides avoided in neonates; tetracycline avoided in children.
• Genetics: isoniazid acetylators (polyneuritis in slow); sulphonamides, nitrofurantoin and chloramphenicol cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
• Pregnancy: tetracycline hepatic necrosis; ampicillin levels lower; nearly all antimicrobials appear in breast milk; renal excretion matters for most; erythromycin, azithromycin, chloramphenicol and clindamycin need caution in hepatic impairment.
• Lipid-soluble chloramphenicol crosses the BBB better than aminoglycosides; ceftriaxone or chloramphenicol are used for meningitis.
(d)
• Poor perfusion (diabetic lower limbs) limits access; immunocompromised patients need higher bactericidal doses; poor kidney function (10% or less) causes accumulation.
• Complications: hypersensitivity (penicillin rash to anaphylaxis), direct toxicity (aminoglycoside ototoxicity), superinfection (Candida) after broad-spectrum therapy.
• Empiric therapy may be needed in acutely ill patients before culture results; bacteriostatic drugs rely on host defences.

questions.question:
(a) Define PEP, PrEP, PMTCT and OI prophylaxis.
(b) State the regimens used for each.
(c) Explain the rationale for the regimens.
(d) State the doses and durations.
(e) State the precautions and adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• PEP is the use of antiretrovirals in an HIV-negative person after a specific high-risk exposure within 72 hours (occupational and non-occupational); PrEP is for key populations and sero-discordant couples at risk.
• PMTCT prevents transmission from mother to child during pregnancy, labour, childbirth or breastfeeding; OI prophylaxis includes cotrimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT) and isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT).
(b)
• PEP: dolutegravir 50 mg/TDF/3TC once daily for 28 days (or, per WHO, TDF/FTC + LPV/r or ATV/r for 28 days).
• PrEP: lamivudine 300 mg/TDF 300 mg once daily.
• PMTCT: mother continues HAART; infant nevirapine (replaced by AZT if unavailable); high-risk infants nevirapine plus zidovudine for 6 weeks, plus a further 6 weeks if breastfed.
(c)
• The PEP regimen is tolerable, potent, conveniently administered and has minimal drug interactions; three drugs (dual NRTI backbone plus integrase inhibitor) are given for all exposures.
• CPT is effective against PCP, S. pneumoniae, toxoplasmosis and cryptosporidiosis and is given to all PLHIV regardless of CD4 or WHO stage.
(d)
• IPT: isoniazid 300 mg daily for 6 months in adults (10 mg/kg/day to maximum 300 mg in children) with pyridoxine; CPT: adults 960 mg daily; infant NVP 10-15 mg and 20 mg doses by age and weight.
• Exclude active TB before IPT; if active TB develops, stop IPT and begin DOT.
(e)
• PrEP drugs are only for people at risk, not for HIV management, and do not prevent other STIs or pregnancy.
• Avoid efavirenz in pregnancy (controversially teratogenic); continue maternal therapy through breastfeeding.
• Pyridoxine treats isoniazid numbness, tingling and burning.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old with sepsis and a reduced creatinine clearance is to receive gentamicin.
(a) Identify the drug and the principal adverse effects expected.
(b) Explain the mechanism of toxicity and risk factors.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic basis and the dose-adjustment method.
(d) State the prevention and management steps.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Gentamicin (aminoglycoside): nephrotoxicity (direct proximal tubular damage, reversible if caught early), ototoxicity (8th cranial nerve; irreversible vestibular and auditory damage) and neuromuscular paralysis.
(b)
Risk factors: high troughs, prolonged therapy, underlying renal dysfunction and concomitant nephrotoxins; neuromuscular paralysis after rapid IV infusion, especially in myasthenia gravis or with succinylcholine.
(c)
• Highly polar basic drugs, poor oral bioavailability, poorly distributed and poorly protein-bound, not metabolised, nearly all excreted unchanged in urine, so doses must be adjusted in renal insufficiency.
• Cockcroft-Gault: CrCl = (140 - age) x weight (kg) / (sCr x 72), multiplied by 0.85 for females; corrected dose = normal dose x patient CrCl / normal CrCl.
(d)
Monitor levels; avoid dehydration and other renal toxic drugs; give a large single dose (multiple small doses cause failure and renal toxicity); check renal clearance; avoid in renal failure, but it is safe in liver failure.

(a)
Tissue amoebicides: nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, tinidazole, ornidazole, secnidazole) and isoquinolines (emetine, dehydroemetine); luminal: hydroxyquinolines (iodoquinol, clioquinol), dichloroacetamides (diloxanide furoate), and the aminoglycoside paromomycin.
(b)
Intestinal amoebiasis (asymptomatic to bloody diarrhoea and colitis) and extraintestinal (liver abscess; lungs, brain); the cyst is infective and resistant, the trophozoite is invasive; only E. histolytica needs treatment (diagnosis: stool microscopy, ELISA, PCR).
(c)
• Metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 10 days or tinidazole 2 g daily for 6 days, followed by diloxanide furoate 500 mg three times daily for 10 days or another luminal agent.
• Metronidazole plus paromomycin is recommended for cyst carriers; chloroquine or dehydroemetine only when metronidazole is contraindicated.
(d)
• Metronidazole kills trophozoites but not cysts and is well absorbed so luminal levels may be sub-therapeutic; luminal agents eradicate trophozoites in the lumen.
• Iodoquinol acts in the bowel lumen but not on trophozoites in the wall or tissues; 90% is retained in the intestine; chloroquine is concentrated in the liver but is not effective for intestinal disease.
(e)
• Metronidazole: nausea, metallic taste, disulfiram-like reaction; potentiates coumarins; phenytoin/phenobarbital accelerate elimination; tinidazole is somewhat better tolerated.
• Iodoquinol: diarrhoea, neurotoxicity with prolonged high dosing, iodine toxicity; contraindicated in iodine intolerance; caution in optic neuropathy, renal or thyroid disease.
• Chloroquine: pruritus, hypotension with bolus IV, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
• Diloxanide furoate acts by chelating ferrous ions: side effects fever/chills, hypersensitivity, thyroid enlargement, diarrhoea.
• Paromomycin: skin rash, flatulence, abdominal cramps; nitazoxanide is also active against E. histolytica.
• Prevention: hand washing, boiling water, avoiding raw vegetables and street foods.
questions.question:
(a) Classify amoebicides into tissue and luminal agents with examples.
(b) Describe the disease forms, diagnosis and the cyst and trophozoite stages relevant to drug action.
(c) State the regimens for amoebic colitis, liver abscess and cyst carriers.
(d) State the rationale for combining a tissue agent with a luminal agent.
(e) State the adverse effects, interactions and precautions of the agents.

Quinine is a short-acting quinoline methanol with a half-life of 10-14 hours. A structurally related analogue is made by placing trifluoromethyl groups on the quinoline ring and replacing the quinuclidine with a piperidine.
(a) Identify the analogue.
(b) Predict the effect on metabolic stability, lipophilicity and duration.
(c) Justify through SAR and basicity.
(d) Name the related drugs and the risk of cross-resistance.
(e) State the rationale.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mefloquine (9RS,2'SR-alpha-(2'-piperidyl)-2,8-bis(trifluoromethyl)-4-quinoline methanol), an analogue of quinine.
(b)
The CF3 on the carbon next to the quinoline nitrogen makes the molecule more stable to metabolism and highly lipid soluble, giving an elimination half-life of 15-33 days (about 3 weeks average), much longer than quinine.
(c)
Mefloquine is monobasic despite two nitrogens: basicity comes from the piperidine nitrogen, while the quinoline nitrogen is not basic because of the electron-withdrawing CF3 and the resonance effect of the benzene ring.
(d)
Cross-resistance between mefloquine, halofantrine and quinine occurs in some regions because all three are quinoline methanols (aryl amino alcohols).
(e)
• Rationale: to obtain a stable, lipophilic, long-acting blood schizonticide for multi-resistant P. falciparum; its exact mechanism is unknown.
• Properties to expect: bioavailability above 85%, food raises absorption about 40%, protein binding about 98%, Vd about 20 L/kg; contraindicated with quinine and halofantrine (cardiac arrest) and in active depression.

questions.question:
A chemist acylates the free para-amino group of a sulphonamide with a phthalyl or succinyl group and, in another analogue, replaces it with a nitro group; a third analogue moves the amino group to the ortho position.
(a) Predict the effect of each change on activity.
(b) Justify through SAR.
(c) Name the useful derivatives and their uses.
(d) State the rationale for the modification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Moving the amino group from the para position causes loss of activity; any ring substituent also reduces or abolishes activity.
• Substituting the NH2 with R loses activity unless the substituent can easily form NH2 in vivo; phthalyl and succinyl groups are such groups, and NO2, NHCOOCH3 and NHOH also retain activity.
(b)
The free p-NH2 and sulphamido group mimic PABA; groups easily converted into free NH2 regenerate the active species in vivo.
(c)
• Succinyl and phthalyl sulphathiazole are intestinal sulphonamides, pro-drugs not absorbed from the GI tract; sulphamethizole is a urinary sulphonamide (rapid absorption, slow excretion, high urinary concentration).
• Other classes: systemic (sulphadiazine short-acting, sulphomethoxin long-acting), ophthalmic (sulphacetamide) and topical (sulphadiazine for burns).
(d)
• The rationale for gut-restricted pro-drugs is local intestinal action.
• Compounds with a heterocyclic aromatic ring on N are active.

questions.question:
A kidney transplant recipient is maintained on cyclosporine, sirolimus and azathioprine and is also given allopurinol and a calcium channel blocker.
(a) Identify the drugs and their classes.
(b) Justify the combination.
(c) Identify interactions and antagonism.
(d) State monitoring and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cyclosporine (calcineurin inhibitor), sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor), azathioprine (antiproliferative antimetabolite, prodrug of mercaptopurine); allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor).
(b)
Sirolimus is synergistic with cyclosporine; the drugs act at different sites of T-cell activation (calcineurin, mTOR, purine synthesis); glucocorticoids are commonly combined to prevent and treat rejection.
(c)
• Allopurinol inhibits inactivation of azathioprine (dose reduction needed); cyclosporine nephrotoxicity may be minimised by concomitant calcium channel blockers; cyclosporine increases P-glycoprotein activity.
• Cyclosporine is metabolised by CYP3A and excreted in bile, so CYP3A inducers/inhibitors are expected to matter.
(d)
• Cyclosporine drug monitoring is essential (20-50% bioavailability from original soft gelatin capsule); tremor may be an early sign of rising levels; monitor renal function, blood count and liver function; nephrotoxicity is the major reason for stopping.
• Sirolimus: myelosuppression (platelets); azathioprine: bone marrow suppression.

(a)
Pentavalent antimony (SbV) compounds such as sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam) are the classic drug for all forms of leishmaniasis.
(b)
Only amastigotes are susceptible; activity depends on in vivo reduction of SbV to the more toxic SbIII.
(c)
SbV acts on several targets: inhibiting parasite glycolysis, fatty acid beta-oxidation and ADP phosphorylation; nonspecific blocking of SH groups of amastigote proteins; and inhibition of DNA topoisomerase I.
(d)
• Used for visceral leishmaniasis; given IM or IV (intralesional also tried); distributes to plasma, liver and spleen; half-life about 2 hours; biotransformed in the liver to SbIII; about 50% is excreted in urine over 24-76 hours.
• Long courses allow antileishmanial levels to accumulate in liver and spleen.
• Adverse effects: nausea, abdominal pain, myalgia, pancreatic inflammation, cardiac arrhythmia, hepatitis; significant resistance has emerged.
• Alternatives for antimony-resistant disease: liposomal amphotericin B (drug of choice), pentamidine, miltefosine and paromomycin (aminosidine).
questions.question:
A patient from an endemic area presents with irregular fever, weight loss, anaemia and enlarged spleen and liver; amastigotes are found in bone marrow and visceral leishmaniasis (kala azar) is diagnosed. The classic drug is a pentavalent antimonial.
(a) Identify the drug class and examples.
(b) State the features responsible for activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action.
(d) State the therapeutic use and key adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The cell wall contains peptidoglycan in all bacteria except Mycoplasma; peptidoglycan is unique to prokaryotes with no eukaryotic counterpart.
• Layers have backbones of alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid with peptide side-chains cross-linked into a lattice; Gram-positive walls may have up to 40 layers and resist about 20 atm internal osmotic pressure (about 5 atm in Gram-negatives).
(b)
• Cycloserine, a D-alanine analogue, competitively prevents addition of the two terminal alanines (it inhibits racemase).
• Vancomycin inhibits release of the building-block unit from its carrier; bacitracin blocks dephosphorylation and so regeneration of the lipid carrier.
• Penicillins, cephalosporins and other beta-lactams inhibit the final transpeptidation by covalently binding penicillin-binding proteins, preventing cross-links.
(c)
• Beta-lactams include penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem) and the monobactam aztreonam; glycopeptides include vancomycin, teicoplanin, dalbavancin and telavancin.
• Glycopeptides bind cell-wall peptides (Ala-Ala), block cross-linking and transglycosylation; the weak wall leads to osmotic lysis and bactericidal action.
• Bacitracin is a polypeptide that also inhibits teichoic acid synthesis and is used topically for skin and eye infections.
(d)
• Resistance: beta-lactamases (penicillinases, cephalosporinases) destroy beta-lactams (clavulanic acid, sulbactam and tazobactam inhibit them); vancomycin-resistant S. aureus has developed.
• Beta-lactam adverse effects: hypersensitivity (rash to anaphylaxis) with cross-allergy, diarrhoea and nephritis; aztreonam does not necessarily cross-react with penicillin allergy.
• Vancomycin: red-man syndrome related to infusion rate (infuse over at least 60 minutes); negligible oral absorption, so IV for systemic infection.
• Cycloserine: dose-related CNS toxicity (headache, tremor, acute psychosis, convulsions); used for TB resistant to first-line drugs.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure of the bacterial cell wall and explain why peptidoglycan is a selective target.
(b) State the points of peptidoglycan synthesis blocked by cycloserine, vancomycin, bacitracin and the beta-lactams.
(c) Relate these to the examples of each group and explain the cellular basis of the effect.
(d) State the main resistance mechanisms and adverse effects of beta-lactams, vancomycin and cycloserine.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Isoniazid (INH) is isonicotinic acid hydrazide (pyridine-4-carbohydrazide), a synthetic derivative of nicotinic acid, a hydrazine derivative antitubercular.
(b)
It chelates partly (Cu+); assay by bromometric titration with KBrO3 using ethoxychrysoidine as indicator.
(c)
• A prodrug that inhibits synthesis of mycolic acid, essential for the cell wall; interferes with enzyme systems requiring pyridoxal phosphate as co-enzyme.
• Activated by the bacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG to a nicotinoyl radical, which reacts with NAD+ to form adducts inhibiting cell-wall enzymes and with NADP+ to inhibit nucleic acid synthesis; FAS2 is inhibited by isoniazid.
(d)
• Metabolised by N-acetylation (hepatic NAT2 isoforms) to N-acetylisoniazid/acetylhydrazine, a hepatotoxic metabolite; dehydrazination also occurs; excreted in urine.
• Genetic polymorphism: fast acetylators t1/2 1-2 h, slow acetylators 2-5 h; polyneuritis is more frequent in slow acetylators.
(e)
Mutation or inactivation of KatG results in resistance.
(f)
• Toxicity: hepatotoxicity (raised AST, ALT), peripheral neuritis if pyridoxine is not given, sideroblastic anaemia, haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency.
• Other toxicities: convulsions, optic neuritis, muscle twitching, ataxia, mental abnormalities and a lupus-like syndrome.
• Interaction: inhibits the metabolism of phenytoin and carbamazepine, raising their plasma concentrations.
• Uses: kills intracellular and extracellular bacilli; crosses CSF, placenta and tuberculous cavities; used in treatment and prophylaxis.
• Isoniazid alone is used for latent TB; with rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol or streptomycin for active TB.
questions.question:
(a) Give the chemical name, structure and chemical class of isoniazid.
(b) State its chemical properties, synthesis and assay where given.
(c) State its mechanism of action and how it is activated.
(d) Describe the structural basis of its metabolism and the effect of acetylator status.
(e) Explain the basis of resistance.
(f) State its toxicity, uses and drug interactions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Rifampicin (CYP inducer) with nevirapine or protease inhibitors: PIs and rifampicin lead to a high risk of liver toxicity and sub-therapeutic levels of both drugs; avoid NVP and PIs in rifampicin-based TB therapy.
(b)
Standard TB therapy is isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid + rifampicin for 4 months.
(c)
• Isoniazid preventive therapy 300 mg daily for 6 months is for latent TB after excluding active disease; with pyridoxine.
• Rifampicin induces its own metabolism and interacts with many drugs (corticosteroids, oral anticoagulants, hypoglycaemics, digitalis, contraceptives).
(d)
Monitor liver function (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide), peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine), visual acuity (ethambutol), viral load and CD4.
questions.question:
A patient with HIV and newly diagnosed active TB is to be started on rifampicin-based TB therapy together with antiretrovirals.
(a) Identify the drugs and the interaction problem.
(b) Justify the choice of regimen.
(c) Identify what to avoid and the preventive therapy options.
(d) State the monitoring and precautions.

(a) Give the chemical class and structure of rifampicin.
(b) State its properties, chemical instability and assay.
(c) State its mechanism of action.
(d) Describe its metabolism, enzyme-inducing action and interactions.
(e) Explain the basis of resistance.
(f) State its uses and toxicity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Rifampicin is a semisynthetic macrocyclic antibiotic of the ansamycin/rifamycin class (macrolide with a non-aliphatic ansa bridge); rifampin, rifapentine and rifabutin form the rifamycin group.
(b)
Supplied as capsules and oral suspension; unstable to moisture; in alkaline pH and O2 it is oxidised to a quinone, and acid hydrolysis gives 3-formylrifampicin; assayed by UV spectrophotometry.
(c)
• Inhibits RNA synthesis by binding the beta subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB) to form a stable drug-enzyme complex; bacterial but not mammalian polymerase.
• A sterilizing agent for intracellular and extracellular bacilli and caseous necrosis; bactericidal for M. tuberculosis, S. aureus, N. meningitidis and H. influenzae.
(d)
• Absorbed to variable extents (food affects it except rifabutin); metabolised by microsomal beta-esterases and cholinesterases; drug and metabolites excreted in bile.
• An enzyme inducer that induces its own metabolism; interacts with corticosteroids, oral hypoglycaemics, oral anticoagulants, dapsone, phenytoin, digitalis and steroidal contraceptives.
(e)
rpoB mutations (codons 526 and 531) account for 86% of resistance; efflux pumps contribute; monoresistance occurs with rifapentine or rifabutin in AIDS and multicavitary TB; cross-resistance may occur.
(f)
• Uses: tuberculosis, leprosy, MAC, Legionnaires' disease, prophylaxis of meningococcal disease and H. influenzae meningitis, brucellosis.
• Hepatotoxicity (especially in alcoholics and the elderly), flu-like syndrome (hypersensitivity), GI disturbances.
• Orange-tan discolouration of skin, urine, faeces, saliva, tears and contact lenses.
• Teratogenic potential is unknown and it crosses the placenta, so it is best avoided in pregnancy.
• It is part of two- and three-drug leprosy regimens and is most bactericidal against M. leprae.

questions.question:
Proflavine (3,6-diaminoacridine) precipitates in saline solution and cannot be used in injections. A methyl is placed at position 4 or a quaternary methochloride is made.
(a) Predict the effect on compatibility and use.
(b) Justify through SAR.
(c) Name the derivatives and related dyes.
(d) State the rationale for the modification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The methyl group at position 4 gives compatibility with saline solutions (injection use); proflavine methochloride is the derivative.
(b)
SAR of acridine dyes: degree of ionisation increases effectiveness; an optimal molecular size and shape are required for activity.
(c)
• Acriflavine, proflavine and 9-aminoacridine are acridine dyes; thiazine dyes (methylene blue); azo dyes (amaranth, resorcin brown); triphenylmethane dyes (gentian violet, brilliant green, malachite green).
• Triphenylmethane SAR: removal of one phenyl group decreases activity; a diethyl/dimethylamino group is required; they are incompatible with mineral acids and bases and form a colourless carbinol base with NaOH.
(d)
• Rationale: to avoid precipitation in saline so that the dye can be formulated for injection; acridine dyes otherwise are topical agents for skin infections.
• Methylene blue: antiseptic in urinary conditions and treatment of cyanosis from sulphonamides.

(a)
Targets: cell membrane (ergosterol instead of cholesterol), the cell wall (absent in mammalian cells), and DNA synthesis/mitosis.
(b)
• Polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin) bind ergosterol, form transmembrane pores and cause leakage of ions and small molecules; amphotericin B also generates toxic free radicals.
• Azoles inhibit 14-alpha-sterol demethylase; allylamines/benzylamines (terbinafine, naftifine, butenafine) inhibit squalene epoxidase, causing squalene accumulation (fungicidal).
• Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) noncompetitively inhibit beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase causing osmotic lysis.
• Flucytosine is converted by cytosine deaminase to 5-FU and then 5-fluorodeoxyuridylic acid, which inhibits thymidylate synthase (DNA synthesis); griseofulvin binds tubulin and disrupts the mitotic spindle.
(c)
• Selectivity: amphotericin B's ergosterol affinity is 500 times its cholesterol affinity; flucytosine enters via cytosine permeases that mammals lack; drugs against the wall have a high therapeutic index.
• Amphotericin B still binds cholesterol at therapeutic doses, accounting for toxicity; fungi are eukaryotes with similar metabolic pathways, so selective agents are harder to make.
(d)
• Resistance: decreased ergosterol (amphotericin B); mutated P450 and efflux pumps (azoles); Candida species resistance to fluconazole.
• Amphotericin B toxicity: cytokine storm (TNF-alpha, IL-1) causing fever, chills and hypotension; renal toxicity (tubular acidosis, hypokalaemia); anaemia; lipid formulations are less toxic.
• Azoles: hepatotoxicity, interactions through P450 inhibition; terbinafine hepatotoxicity, Stevens-Johnson syndrome; flucytosine bone marrow suppression, contraindicated in pregnancy.
• Echinocandins: generally well tolerated, headache, fever and abnormal liver function tests; griseofulvin induces hepatic enzymes and reduces coumarin and contraceptive effect.
• Griseofulvin is also fetotoxic.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the cellular targets of antifungal therapy.
(b) State the mechanism of action of each antifungal group.
(c) Relate to examples and explain selective toxicity.
(d) State the resistance mechanisms and adverse effects.

(a) Describe the cell cycle and the three general populations of body cells.
(b) Distinguish cell cycle-specific from non-specific agents.
(c) Relate to the examples of each class given.
(d) Explain why the dose-exposure relationship and phase-specificity affect efficacy.
(e) State the trade-offs and limitations in terms of toxicity and resistance.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cells are terminally differentiated (permanent G0), proliferating, or currently quiescent (temporary G0); phases: G1, S (DNA synthesis), G2 (pre-mitotic) and M (division).
(b)
• Cell cycle-specific agents (CCSA): increasing exposure increases total cell kill; antimetabolites are S-phase specific and vinca alkaloids M-phase specific.
• Cell cycle-nonspecific agents (CCnSA): increasing dose increases total cell kill; alkylating agents and platinum complexes.
(c)
• Antimetabolites: methotrexate, 5-FU, cytarabine, 6-MP, 6-TG, hydroxyurea, fludarabine; vinca: vincristine, vinblastine; alkylators: busulfan, chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, procarbazine, dacarbazine, cisplatin.
• Others listed: anthracyclines and epipodophyllotoxins (etoposide, G2/late S), asparaginase, corticosteroids, thalidomide, bortezomib, tamoxifen, ATRA and tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
(d)
• Rapidly proliferating cells are most sensitive; S-phase agents act best in tumours with a high growth fraction; antimetabolite dose-response curves plateau, except 5-FU.
• Etoposide induces G2 arrest and preferentially kills cells in G2 and late S; methotrexate kills cells in S phase and its polyglutamates are selectively retained in tumour cells.
(e)
• Bone marrow suppression limits tolerable chemotherapy; the therapeutic index is low and bone marrow and GI cells are the most sensitive normal cells.
• Alkylators are vesicants (necrosis, cytopenias, pulmonary fibrosis, haemorrhagic cystitis); nitrosoureas are lipid-soluble and chemically unstable.
• Acquired resistance arises from inadequate dosage, wrong combination, mutation, multidrug resistance genes and poorly exposed necrotic tumour.
• Treatment-free periods allow recovery of normal tissues; combination of phase-specific and non-specific agents is used.

questions.question:
A hospitalised, immunocompromised patient presents with fever and suspected Gram-negative bacillary septicaemia. An aminoglycoside obtained from Micromonospora purpurea is chosen and given together with a penicillin.
(a) Identify the drug and its chemical class.
(b) State the structural features of the class that are responsible for its activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(d) State its spectrum of activity and therapeutic uses.
(e) State the key adverse effects and the basis for them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Gentamicin, an aminoglycoside obtained from Micromonospora purpurea; it is the most commonly used aminoglycoside, more potent than streptomycin with a broader spectrum.
(b)
• Aminoglycosides contain amino sugars: two amino sugars joined to a non-sugar aminocyclitol by an O-glycosidic bond; in most the aminocyclitol is 2-deoxystreptamine.
• They are highly water-soluble sulfate salts that ionize in solution and are more active in alkaline pH.
(c)
• Binds irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit: blocks protein synthesis at the initiation complex stage, causes mis-coding of RNA (non-functional or toxic proteins) and breaks polysomes into non-functional monosomes.
• Bactericidal at higher concentrations; strong irreversible binding gives a post-antibiotic effect, allowing a prolonged dosage interval.
(d)
• Spectrum: Gram-negative aerobes (Pseudomonas, Proteus, E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Serratia); Gram-positive aerobes usually with beta-lactams; ineffective against M. tuberculosis.
• Uses: serious Gram-negative bacillary infections; septicaemia, sepsis and fever in immunocompromised patients with penicillins; pelvic infections with metronidazole; SABE; UTI; synergy with ampicillin, penicillin G, ticarcillin, ceftriaxone and vancomycin.
(e)
• Nephrotoxicity (direct proximal tubular damage, reversible if caught early), ototoxicity (8th cranial nerve, irreversible vestibular and auditory damage) and neuromuscular paralysis after rapid IV infusion.
• Risk factors: high troughs, prolonged therapy, underlying renal dysfunction, concomitant nephrotoxins; relatively low margin of safety, so levels must be monitored; gentamicin is relatively more nephrotoxic.

(a)
Nucleosides: abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine, zidovudine; nucleotide: tenofovir (TDF, TAF); adefovir is also listed for hepatitis B.
(b)
They are analogues of natural nucleosides/nucleotides that must be phosphorylated by host kinases to the 5'-triphosphate derivative to be active.
(c)
• The triphosphates compete with host cellular triphosphates and act as false substrates for viral reverse transcriptase; incorporation into the growing viral DNA chain causes chain termination.
• NRTIs bind competitively to reverse transcriptase preventing addition of another nucleotide.
(d)
• Mammalian alpha-DNA polymerase is relatively resistant to NRTIs, but gamma-DNA polymerase in host mitochondria is fairly sensitive, which may account for unwanted effects such as lactic acidosis.
• Class adverse effect: lactic acidosis; specific: zidovudine anaemia, stavudine neuropathy and lipodystrophy, abacavir allergic reaction (HLA-B*5701 negative needed for ABC/3TC + DTG).
• Uses: HIV with other ARVs; lamivudine, adefovir and tenofovir also treat hepatitis B.
(e)
• TAF has better effects on bone and kidney and is preferable in bone or kidney disease; TDF gives higher tenofovir levels, with better lipid-lowering effect.
• 3TC and FTC are equivalent drugs (3TC may replace FTC in all regimens); keeping 3TC or FTC in second line increases the activity of AZT or TDF.
• Combination cautions: ddI + d4T additive toxicity, d4T + AZT antagonism, ddI + TDF reduced efficacy and increased toxicity.
• Anaemia: avoid AZT; renal disease: avoid TDF; hepatitis B: use TDF.

(b) Describe the general structure and pharmacophore requirements.

(d) Explain the chemical or biochemical basis of their selectivity, toxicity and limitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tetracyclines (bacteriostatic, 30S ribosome binders); resistance arises when the concentrating mechanism becomes less effective and bacteria acquire the capacity to pump tetracyclines out.
• A plasmid-mediated 'protection' protein that protects the ribosomal binding site from tetracyclines is also described.
(b)
Target: tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and block aminoacyl-tRNA access to the acceptor site; protection protein shields this site; reduced uptake and efflux lower intracellular drug; an inactivating enzyme for tetracyclines is not described.
(c)
General principles given: susceptibility testing (disc diffusion, MIC, E-test) before therapy and choosing an agent by organism, site and host factors.
(d)
Doxycycline lacks the 6-OH and is more stable with increased action.
questions.question:
A patient with a rickettsial or mycoplasma infection fails tetracycline therapy.
(a) Identify the drug class and the likely mechanism of resistance.
(b) Explain the basis in terms of the target, drug uptake, efflux or inactivation.
(c) State the strategy to overcome it.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is caused by the acid-fast bacillus Mycobacterium leprae; classified by the Ridley-Jopling system (TT, BT, BB, BL, LL) and by WHO as paucibacillary (5 or fewer lesions) or multibacillary (6 or more).
(b)
Dapsone: PABA analogue, competitive inhibitor of dihydropteroate synthase; rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase and is the most bactericidal; clofazimine binds mycobacterial DNA and has anti-inflammatory activity; minocycline is an alternative.
(c)
• PB: dapsone daily plus rifampicin monthly under supervision for 6 months; MB: dapsone, clofazimine daily and rifampicin monthly plus clofazimine 300 mg monthly for 12 months.
• Adult doses: dapsone 100 mg daily, rifampicin 600 mg monthly, clofazimine 50 mg daily plus 300 mg monthly; patients with a positive skin smear or uncertain diagnosis get the MB regimen.
• If dapsone cannot be taken, replace with clofazimine; if clofazimine cannot be taken, ofloxacin 400 mg or minocycline 100 mg; single-lesion PB uses a single dose of rifampicin, ofloxacin and minocycline (not for pregnant women or children under 5).
• For rifampicin-intolerant MB: clofazimine, ofloxacin and minocycline for 6 months then two drugs for 18 months; clarithromycin may be used for rifampicin- and ofloxacin-resistant disease.
(d)
• Type 1 reaction (reversal) is delayed-type hypersensitivity in borderline leprosy, treated with NSAIDs and high-dose prednisone 40-60 mg/day tapered.
• Type 2 reaction (ENL) in lepromatous leprosy (nodules, fever, high TNF-alpha, immune complexes) is treated with prednisolone, clofazimine or thalidomide; mild ENL with aspirin.
• If prednisolone exceeds 4 months, add clofazimine 50 mg as prophylaxis against steroid-accelerated multiplication.
• Dapsone adverse effects: sulphone syndrome, haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency, peripheral neuropathy; clofazimine: reddish-brown skin discolouration, corneal pigmentation, contraindicated in pregnancy.
• Dapsone resistance has been reported after monotherapy; relapse after multidrug therapy about 1%; monitor with CBC, creatinine and liver function tests.
• Single-dose rifampicin is used as post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts (600 mg for those aged 15 or older).
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
8-aminoquinolines (primaquine, pamaquine, quinocide), 4-aminoquinolines (chloroquine, amodiaquine, sontoquine, hydroxychloroquine), and quinoline methanols (quinine, mefloquine); piperaquine is a bisquinoline.
(b)
• 4-Amino-7-chloroquinolines with a basic side chain at C-4: chloroquine is 7-chloro-4-[4-(diethylamino)-1-methylbutylamino]quinoline; amodiaquine is a 4-aminoquinoline related to chloroquine.
• SAR: methyl at C-3 reduces activity and at C-8 abolishes it; C-7 is the best site for halogen; a hydroxyl on an ethyl of the terminal nitrogen reduces toxicity and increases blood level (hydroxychloroquine).
(c)
CQ diffuses into the parasite digestive vacuole (pH 4.7), is protonated and trapped, caps haemozoin and prevents biocrystallisation of haem; the haem-chloroquine complex is toxic, disrupts membranes and causes lysis.
(d)
• The pKa of the quinoline nitrogen is 8.5; at lysosomal pH 4.6 ionisation traps the drug, which concentrates in the parasite food vacuole and potentiates its action.
• Large distribution into adipose tissue, accumulation in liver, spleen, kidney and retina, and half-life of 1-2 months (poor for prophylaxis); a loading dose is needed because of tissue binding.
• Metabolism: N-dealkylation, C-hydroxylation, N-oxidation; desethylchloroquine is bioactive with a long half-life; excretion increases with urine acidification.
• Widespread P. falciparum resistance (PfCRT mutations) limits its use; long-term use causes retinopathy; pruritus is prominent in black Africans (70%).
(e)
• Amodiaquine is effective against some chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum; it is metabolised by CYP2C8 to N-desethylamodiaquine, which is responsible for most of its antimalarial action (amodiaquine itself is three times more potent but its blood concentration is low).
• Amodiaquine is used in ACTs; CYP2C8*2, *3, *4 poor metabolisers show lower efficacy and higher toxicity; agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity limit prolonged use.
• Amodiaquine also inhibits haemoglobin digestion and glutathione-dependent destruction of ferriprotoporphyrin IX; it is an inhibitor of CYP2D6 and CYP2C9.
• Chloroquine is no longer first line, but still used for P. vivax and extraintestinal amoebiasis.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the quinoline antimalarials.
(b) Describe the general structure and pharmacophore of the 4-aminoquinolines.
(c) State the mechanism of action of chloroquine.
(d) Explain the chemical basis of the potency, selectivity and limitation of chloroquine (accumulation, resistance, toxicity).
(e) Distinguish chloroquine from amodiaquine.

An HIV-positive patient with recurrent oral and oesophageal candidiasis, treated long-term with fluconazole, stops responding.
(a) Identify the likely mechanism of resistance and the drug class affected.
(b) Explain the basis in terms of target, uptake, efflux or inactivation.
(c) State the strategies to overcome it.
(d) Justify the choice of each alternative.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Azole resistance: Candida species are the most notable pathogens to develop resistance to fluconazole, and resistance develops readily.
(b)
Mechanisms are mutation of the fungal P450 enzyme (the 14-alpha-sterol demethylase target) and overexpression of multidrug efflux transporter proteins; no drug-inactivating enzyme is described.
(c)
• Ravuconazole, a fluconazole derivative, has expanded activity including against the relatively resistant C. krusei and C. glabrata; voriconazole spectrum includes Candida species.
• Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) are primary therapy for oesophageal candidiasis and candidaemia; amphotericin B can also be used.
(d)
• Echinocandins act on a different target (beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase of the cell wall, absent in mammalian cells), so target-site azole resistance does not apply; they are given parenterally and are generally well tolerated.
• Echinocandins have also been used in combination with amphotericin B, flucytosine, itraconazole or voriconazole in refractory fungal infections.
• Risk factors listed include HIV infection and long-term antibiotic use.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman, and later a nursing mother with a small child, are prescribed a tetracycline for a rickettsial infection.
(a) Identify the drug class and the adverse effect expected.
(b) Explain the chemical basis of the toxicity.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic basis and interactions.
(d) State the management and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tetracyclines: tooth discolouration and effects on bones and teeth in pregnancy, lactation or childhood; pregnant women are vulnerable to acute fatty necrosis of the liver, pancreatitis and probably renal damage.
(b)
Tetracyclines chelate calcium and other metals and bind connective tissue in bone and teeth, which affects teeth and bones.
(c)
• Secreted in milk (affecting the infant); concentrated in liver and spleen; excreted mainly in urine by glomerular filtration; all except doxycycline accumulate in and enhance renal failure.
• Chelation with milk, iron, non-systemic antacids and sucralfate reduces absorption; incomplete GI absorption is better on an empty stomach; doxycycline and minocycline are well absorbed regardless of food.
(d)
They should not be used in pregnancy, lactation or children; avoid in patients on diuretics (raised blood urea); do not mix injectable tetracyclines with penicillin or inject intrathecally.

questions.question:
A patient with a high-grade lymphoma is to receive a multidrug regimen including cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone.
(a) Identify the drugs and their classes.
(b) Justify the combination.
(c) Identify the toxicities and interactions that must be managed.
(d) State the supportive care, monitoring and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cyclophosphamide (alkylating agent), doxorubicin (anthracycline), vincristine (vinca alkaloid, M-phase), and prednisolone (corticosteroid); a regimen means a combination given in timed cycles.
(b)
Different mechanisms with additive or synergistic effects; different dose-limiting toxicities allow full doses; different resistance patterns minimise cross-resistance; all are active as single agents in haemato-oncology.
(c)
Doxorubicin cardiotoxicity (limit cumulative dose below 550 mg/m2), cyclophosphamide haemorrhagic cystitis, vincristine peripheral neuropathy and ileus, myelosuppression and mucositis.
(d)
• Pre-therapy assessment and counselling; IV fluids and allopurinol or rasburicase to prevent tumour lysis syndrome and urate nephropathy; antiemetics (metoclopramide, dexamethasone, ondansetron); antibiotic prophylaxis for febrile neutropenia.
• G-CSF and erythropoietin; analgesics and nutrition; response assessed by complete response (disappearance of disease at 4 weeks), partial response (50% decrease) or progression (25% increase); monitor full blood count, cardiac function and LFTs.

questions.question:
A neonate treated with an antibiotic that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit develops vomiting, refusal to suck, irregular respiration, abdominal distension, cyanosis and loose green stools, then becomes flaccid and ashen-grey.
(a) Identify the drug and the syndrome.
(b) Explain the mechanism and basis of the toxicity.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic basis and other toxicities.
(d) State the management or alternative.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chloramphenicol causing gray baby syndrome (overdose in neonates); it binds the 50S subunit and prevents binding of the aminoacyl-tRNA end to the acceptor site (bacteriostatic, broad spectrum).
(b)
Hepatic function in the neonate is undeveloped by adult standards; chloramphenicol and sulphonamides should be avoided in infants. Death occurs in 40% within 20 days.
(c)
• Lipid-soluble, crosses the BBB rapidly, primarily excreted or detoxified in the liver (use with caution in hepatic impairment); the primary OH is the site of salt formation (palmitate, sodium succinate) hydrolysed in vivo.
• Other toxicities: haematological (anaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anaemia, irreversible marrow depression), haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, hypersensitivity and GIT effects.
(d)
• Only avoidance in neonates is stated.
• In adults it is used for typhoid fever, bacterial meningitis, rickettsial diseases and brucellosis.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the forms of leishmaniasis and trypanosomiasis.
(b) List the first-line and alternative drugs for each.
(c) State the mechanism of action of each drug.
(d) State the adverse effects, resistance and special precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Leishmaniasis: cutaneous, mucocutaneous, diffuse cutaneous and visceral (kala azar, fatal in over 95% untreated); trypanosomiasis: African (T. b. gambiense chronic, T. b. rhodesiense acute) and American (Chagas disease, T. cruzi).
(b)
• Leishmaniasis: pentavalent antimony (classic); amphotericin B, pentamidine, miltefosine and paromomycin (aminosidine) as alternatives.
• Trypanosomiasis: early gambiense pentamidine, early rhodesiense suramin; CNS stage melarsoprol or eflornithine (NECT recommended); Chagas disease nifurtimox and benznidazole.
(c)
• SbV: reduced to SbIII, inhibits glycolysis, beta-oxidation, ADP phosphorylation, topoisomerase I; amphotericin B binds ergosterol precursors forming pores; pentamidine binds kinetoplast DNA in mitochondria.
• Miltefosine (alkylphosphocholine) modulates cell receptors, inositol metabolism, phospholipase and protein kinase C leading to apoptosis; paromomycin binds the 30S subunit; eflornithine inhibits ornithine decarboxylase; nifurtimox generates reactive oxygen species.
• Melarsoprol is an arsenical (melarsen oxide plus dimercaprol); suramin is a sulphonated naphthylamine.
(d)
• Antimony: nausea, myalgia, pancreatitis, arrhythmia, hepatitis, resistance; amphotericin B: fever, rigor, thrombophlebitis, hypokalaemia, renal dysfunction (lipid formulations less toxic).
• Pentamidine: myalgia, pain at injection site, tachycardia, reversible hypoglycaemia (2%); resistance linked to reduced mitochondrial accumulation; paromomycin: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity.
• Miltefosine: GI disturbance and renal toxicity; teratogenic, contraindicated in pregnancy; not effective for L. braziliensis, L. guyanensis, L. mexicana.
• Melarsoprol: reactive encephalopathy in 5-10% (stop and give corticosteroids and anticonvulsants); suramin: anaphylaxis with filariasis, nephrotoxicity; eflornithine: anaemia, diarrhoea, leukopenia, convulsions.
• Pentamidine does not cross the BBB; eflornithine is only active against T. b. gambiense and is expensive and hard to give.
• Cutaneous leishmaniasis is generally self-limiting over 3-18 months but other forms need therapy.

questions.question:
A patient presents with thickened, discoloured toenails; a dermatophyte (Trichophyton rubrum) onychomycosis is diagnosed and an allylamine tablet is prescribed.
(a) Identify the drug class and drug.
(b) State the structural features of the class.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(d) State the therapeutic use and the key adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Allylamine antifungals: terbinafine (also naftifine; butenafine is a benzylamine; amorolfine).
(b)
