An allylamine is an organic compound, the simplest stable unsaturated amine; terbinafine is available orally and topically.
(c)
Inhibits squalene epoxidase, blocking conversion of squalene to squalene epoxide (lanosterol, then ergosterol); accumulation of toxic squalene makes them fungicidal; only amorolfine inhibits the pathway at a later stage.
(d)
• Oral terbinafine treats onychomycosis (tinea unguium), tinea corporis, cruris, pedis and capitis; elimination half-life about 300 hours with accumulation in skin, nails and fat; topical cream for superficial infections.
• Adverse effects: liver toxicity, myalgia, rash, GI disturbance, taste and visual disturbance, insomnia, depression, headache, blood dyscrasia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, neutropenia; not recommended in renal or hepatic failure or pregnancy.

(a)
Tetracycline, oxytetracycline and demeclocycline are shorter-acting; doxycycline and minocycline are long-acting (chlortetracycline was the first, 1948).
(b)
• Broad-spectrum, with a hydronaphthacene nucleus of four fused rings; most have five chiral carbons (4, 4a, 5a, 6, 12a), with 5-OH six (oxytetracycline, minocycline).
• SAR: C4 dimethylamino (alpha orientation), the C2 amide, C10-C12 conjugation and H at 5a are required; Cl or CH3 at C9 reduces activity; bulky groups on the C2 amide N have no significant effect.
(c)
Bacteriostatic; bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and prevent access of aminoacyl-tRNA to the acceptor site, so the peptide chain fails to grow.
(d)
• Amphoteric with three pKa values (tricarbonyl methane about 3.3, phenolic beta-diketone about 7.5, dimethylamino about 9.4); aqueous solutions are unstable and stabilised with excess acid.
• They chelate Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe and Al to form insoluble complexes, so milk, antacids and iron reduce absorption; chelation affects teeth and bones.
• At pH 2-6 C4 epimerisation gives epitetracycline with reduced activity; 6-OH tetracyclines form anhydrotetracycline in strong acid with loss of activity.
• At pH 7.5 with heat tetracycline forms isotetracycline (6-OH attacks the C11 carbonyl, lactone formation); oxytetracycline gives epimeric apoxytetracyclines.
(e)
• Doxycycline lacks the 6-OH (deoxytetracycline), preventing isotetracycline formation and giving stability and increased action.
• Doxycycline and minocycline are completely absorbed regardless of food and highly protein bound; tetracycline is moderately bound.
• All tetracyclines except doxycycline accumulate and enhance renal failure.
• Resistance (class): efflux pumping, reduced uptake and plasmid-mediated ribosomal protection protein.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the tetracyclines.
(b) Describe the general structure and SAR.
(c) State the mechanism of action.
(d) Explain the chemical basis of the instability and chelation of tetracyclines.
(e) Distinguish tetracycline from doxycycline.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mefloquine is an aryl amino alcohol, a quinoline methanol and analogue of quinine: 9RS,2'SR-alpha-(2'-piperidyl)-2,8-bis(trifluoromethyl)-4-quinoline methanol; trade name Lariam, 250 mg tablets of the hydrochloride (228.0 mg base).
(b)
• A monobasic drug although it has two nitrogens: the basicity is on the piperidine nitrogen, while the quinoline nitrogen is not basic because of the electron-withdrawing CF3 and the resonance of the benzene ring.
• Assay: non-aqueous titration of 0.350 g in 15 ml anhydrous formic acid and 40 ml acetic anhydride with 0.1 M perchloric acid, potentiometric end point; 1 ml equals 41.48 mg.
(c)
A blood schizonticide; exact mechanism unknown; used alone for prophylaxis and cure in multi-resistant P. falciparum, and as an ACT with artesunate (Artequin).
(d)
• The CF3 next to the quinoline nitrogen makes the molecule more stable to metabolism and highly lipid soluble, giving a half-life of 15-33 days (2-4 weeks).
• Bioavailability over 85%, food raises absorption about 40%, Vd about 20 L/kg, protein binding about 98%, crosses the placenta, minimal excretion in milk, hepatic clearance about 30 mL/min, mainly bile and faeces.
(e)
• Resistance is selected in multi-drug resistance areas of Southeast Asia; cross-resistance with halofantrine and quinine as all three are quinoline methanols.
• Contraindicated with hypersensitivity to quinine/quinidine, active depression (prophylaxis), G6PD deficiency, nursing mothers; not with quinine or halofantrine (cardiac arrest).
• Adverse effects: vomiting, dizziness, syncope, extra-systoles.
• Mefloquine causes haemorrhagic anaemia in G6PD deficiency.
questions.question:
(a) Give the chemical name, class and structure of mefloquine.
(b) State its physicochemical properties and assay.
(c) State its mechanism and uses.
(d) State the structural basis of its metabolism and long half-life.
(e) Explain the basis of resistance, toxicity and loss of activity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A prodrug is inactive or poorly active until converted in the body (or the target) to the active drug by enzymes.
(b)
• Prontosil (a dye active only in vivo) is split to sulfanilamide; proguanil is oxidised by CYP2C19 to cycloguanil; isoniazid is activated by KatG; pyrazinamide by pncA pyrazinamidase; ethionamide by EthA.
• Cyclophosphamide is activated to 4-hydroxy metabolites; azathioprine is a prodrug of mercaptopurine; baloxavir marboxil is a prodrug of baloxavir acid; chlorproguanil-dapsone acts as a prodrug.
(c)
• Ester prodrugs of ampicillin (bacampicillin, pivampicillin, talampicillin) are hydrolysed in vivo; the C4 COOH of cephalosporins allows esters and prodrugs.
• Succinyl and phthalyl sulphathiazole are not absorbed from the GI tract and act in the intestine; acedapsone (NH2 replaced by CH3CO) is a latent, less toxic form of dapsone.
• Chloramphenicol palmitate (tasteless oral suspension) and sodium succinate (injectable, water-soluble) are hydrolysed in vivo to the base; depot salts procaine penicillin G (once daily) and benzathine penicillin G (once monthly) give prolonged action.
• Acyclovir, penciclovir and valaciclovir require viral thymidylate kinase for the first phosphorylation, giving selectivity for infected cells.
(d)
• Dependence on enzymes means variability: CYP2C19 poor metabolisers reduce cycloguanil formation; slow/fast acetylators vary isoniazid effects; KatG mutation causes isoniazid resistance.
• Salts such as the palmitate show polymorphism, and the thermodynamically stable form has low oral bioavailability.
• Prodrugs may appear inactive in vitro (prontosil did not work in the test tube).
• Metabolites of prodrugs can be toxic (acetylhydrazine from isoniazid is hepatotoxic).
questions.question:
(a) Describe the prodrug approach in chemotherapy.
(b) Relate the principle to the examples of prodrugs given.
(c) Explain why prodrugs improve absorption, stability, selectivity or duration.
(d) State the trade-offs and limitations that result.

An infant, whose immune system is immature, is at risk of invasive infection by an encapsulated bacterium, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and a vaccine is chosen.
(a) Identify the vaccine type.
(b) State the structural features responsible for immunogenicity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action.
(d) State the use and the key adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A conjugate vaccine (the Hib vaccine is a conjugate vaccine).
(b)
Conjugate vaccines are developed against bacteria with an outer polysaccharide coating that disguises the antigen; bacterial antigens or toxins that an infant can recognise are linked to the polysaccharide coat.
(c)
The linkage helps the immature immune system react to the polysaccharide coating and defend against the bacterium; it is an active immunisation that builds memory and takes days to weeks.
(d)
• Used in infants and children, who are especially vulnerable to such bacteria.
• General vaccine adverse effects: local pain, swelling, redness, nodule; fever, malaise, headache; hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis (rare); faulty technique reactions.

(a)
A coherent set of actions promoting use of antimicrobials that ensures sustainable access to effective therapy for all who need them; coordinated interventions to select the optimal regimen, dose, duration and route.
(b)
• Core elements: AMS priority for hospital management and action plan, a multidisciplinary AMS committee and team, treatment guidelines, a hospital formulary with approved/restricted antibiotics, audit and ward rounds.
• Also training of professionals, monitoring of antibiotic use (appropriateness, quantity) and AMR of key bacteria, a hospital antibiogram and feedback to prescribers.
(c)
• Access: 20 antibiotics, first or second choice, narrow spectrum or low toxicity (amoxicillin, benzylpenicillin, gentamicin, doxycycline, cefalexin, metronidazole, SMX/TMP).
• Watch: 11 antibiotics with higher resistance potential for limited indications (ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, clarithromycin, meropenem, vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam).
• Reserve: 8 last-resort antibiotics for MDR/XDR infections (colistin, linezolid, cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, plazomicin, fosfomycin IV, polymyxin B).
(d)
Fixed-dose combinations without clear indication: 22% of consumption in 75 countries, 92% not approved by the US FDA and over 80% not compatible with the EML.
(e)
• Selection depends on the organism and its susceptibility (Gram stain, culture, disc diffusion, MIC, E-test), the site of infection and host factors (age, genetics, pregnancy, renal and hepatic function).
• Empiric therapy begins before culture results in acutely ill patients, after specimens are taken; antibiotics should exceed the MIC at the infection site (CSF penetration, abscess, endocarditis).
• Trade-offs: broad-spectrum agents can cause superinfection; prophylaxis risks resistance; combinations may be antagonistic or more toxic; resistance justifies susceptibility testing.
• Host examples: tetracycline avoided in children and pregnancy; chloramphenicol and sulphonamides avoided in neonates; sulphonamides, nitrofurantoin and chloramphenicol cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
• Isoniazid neuropathy is more frequent in slow acetylators.
questions.question:
(a) Define antimicrobial stewardship.
(b) Describe the core elements of a hospital stewardship programme.
(c) Describe the AWaRe classification with examples.
(d) Explain the rationale for the 'not recommended' group.
(e) State the general principles of selection of an antimicrobial and the trade-offs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Inactivation by aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (phosphorylation, acetylation, adenylation), plasmid-mediated, is the most important mechanism.
(b)
Aminoglycosides.
(c)
Other mechanisms: decreased drug uptake/efflux pumps and target-site modification (16S rRNA methylation decreases binding to the 30S ribosome); the enzymes modify the drug so it cannot bind its target.
(d)
• Use amikacin, which has the broadest activity and special role in hospitals where gentamicin- and tobramycin-resistant organisms are prevalent; netilmicin is also relatively resistant to the inactivating enzymes.
• Amikacin is a less toxic semisynthetic kanamycin derivative, used as a reserve drug for hospital-acquired Gram-negative bacillary infections; 15 mg/kg/day in 1-3 doses.
• Combine with beta-lactams for synergy; monitor levels and renal function because of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
questions.question:
In a hospital, many Gram-negative isolates are resistant to gentamicin and tobramycin.
(a) Identify the likely mechanism of resistance.
(b) Name the drug class.
(c) Explain the basis in terms of target, uptake and drug inactivation.
(d) State the strategy to overcome it and justify the choice.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Cyclophosphamide, a nitrogen mustard alkylating agent; others in the class include chlorambucil, ifosfamide, mechlorethamine, melphalan.
(b)
It forms active metabolites (4-hydroperoxycyclophosphamide, 4-aldophosphamide, 4-HOCy) in the liver; inactivation is by aldehyde dehydrogenase (high in early haematopoietic stem cells, megakaryocytes and intestinal epithelial stem cells).
(c)
Metabolites cross-link tumour cell DNA by forming covalent bonds with DNA, RNA and protein groups; the drug has no phase specificity (cell-cycle nonspecific) and is also potently immunosuppressive.
(d)
• Used for lymphoma and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; routes oral, IV, IM, intrapleural; bioavailability 75%, half-life 3-12 h, excreted in urine.
• Adverse effects: alopecia (40-60%), nausea and vomiting, GI toxicity, leukopenia, amenorrhoea, sterility; SIADH and fatal cardiotoxicity at high doses.
• Haemorrhagic cystitis is prevented by IV fluids, frequent urination and mesna; contraindicated in hypersensitivity; also used as an immunosuppressant, where large doses may cause pancytopenia and haemorrhagic cystitis.
questions.question:
A patient with non-Hodgkin lymphoma is treated with a nitrogen mustard that requires hepatic activation.
(a) Identify the drug class and the drug.
(b) State the structural or metabolic features responsible for activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action.
(d) State the therapeutic use and the key adverse effects with their basis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tyrosine kinase inhibitors: imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, gefitinib, erlotinib, sorafenib, sunitinib; proteasome inhibitor bortezomib; ATRA (tretinoin); arsenic trioxide.
• Monoclonal antibodies: rituximab, alemtuzumab, trastuzumab (Herceptin), cetuximab, bevacizumab.
(b)
• Imatinib (a 2-phenylaminopyrimidine) inhibits the tyrosine kinase activity of the BCR-ABL1 fusion protein from the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22), and PDGF and c-kit, inhibiting proliferation and inducing apoptosis.
• Gefitinib and erlotinib inhibit EGFR (HER1); bortezomib inhibits the 26S proteasome.
• Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells; alemtuzumab anti-CD52; trastuzumab HER2; cetuximab EGFR; bevacizumab binds VEGF.
(c)
• Indications: imatinib for CML, GIST, ALL, systemic mastocytosis; dasatinib and nilotinib for imatinib-resistant CML; gefitinib/erlotinib NSCLC; bortezomib myeloma; rituximab CD20-positive B-cell NHL; alemtuzumab chemo-refractory CLL; trastuzumab HER2 breast cancer; cetuximab and bevacizumab colorectal cancer.
• Selectivity arises from targeting abnormal fusion proteins or surface markers (BCR-ABL1, CD20, HER2) of malignant cells.
(d)
• Imatinib: nausea, vomiting, muscle cramps, fatigue, hypopigmentation, oedema, hepatotoxicity; oral bioavailability 98%, protein binding 98%, hepatic metabolism, faecal elimination.
• Interactions: imatinib reduces acetaminophen metabolism (toxicity), dexamethasone decreases imatinib effect, imatinib decreases levothyroxine effect; take with food and water; avoid grapefruit and St John's wort.
• Nanomedicines (polymer nanoparticles, liposomes) such as liposomal doxorubicin improve pharmacokinetics, biodistribution and reduce clearance.
• Resistance: acquired resistance is addressed by second-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib) for CML.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the molecularly targeted therapies and monoclonal antibodies in cancer.
(b) State the mechanism of each with examples.
(c) Relate to the indications and explain the cellular basis of selectivity.
(d) State the adverse effects, interactions and limitations.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Methotrexate (folic acid analogue antimetabolite): mucositis, GI ulceration (bleeding or perforation), myelosuppression and pulmonary fibrosis; nerve root irritation and convulsions with intrathecal use; liver cirrhosis and osteoporosis with chronic therapy.
(b)
It is S-phase specific; it depletes reduced folate (THF) needed for nucleotide synthesis, and rapidly proliferating normal cells of marrow and GI tract are most sensitive.
(c)
• Penicillins reduce tubular secretion of methotrexate, thus increasing the risk of toxicity.
• MTX polyglutamates are selectively retained in tumour cells.
(d)
Avoid co-administration of penicillins; supportive care measures listed include antiemetics, antibiotics for febrile neutropenia and G-CSF.
questions.question:
A patient with leukaemia on high-dose methotrexate develops mouth ulcers, diarrhoea and low blood counts, and has also been given a penicillin.
(a) Identify the drug and the adverse effects.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the toxicity.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic/interaction basis.
(d) State the management or alternative.

A child with P. falciparum malaria in Nigeria fails chloroquine, and a follow-up case shows delayed parasite clearance after artemisinin treatment.
(a) Identify the likely mechanisms of resistance.
(b) Name the drugs affected.
(c) State the strategies to overcome it and justify them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mutations in genes encoding essential parasite proteins are mostly implicated.
(b)
Chloroquine, quinine and mefloquine (PfCRT and pfmdr1 mutations); SP (DHFR and DHPS mutations); artemisinin (kelch13 mutations; reported in Southeast Asia in 2008 and spreading to Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda).
(c)
• ACTs (fast artemisinin plus long-acting partner) were adopted after resistance to quinine, chloroquine and SP; they aim to prevent resistance, give rapid cure and prevent recrudescence.
• Current approaches: triple ACTs, ACT plus single low-dose primaquine, artemether-lumefantrine plus amodiaquine; non-artemisinin combinations such as ganaplacide-lumefantrine, M5717-pyronaridine and cipargamin.
• Mefloquine resistance is cross-resistant with halofantrine and quinine because all three are quinoline methanols; amodiaquine may remain active against chloroquine-resistant strains.
• Quinine retained activity in cerebral malaria , but resistance to quinine was first reported in the 1980s.

questions.question:
(a) Classify antimalarial drugs by chemical group and by stage of action.
(b) List the WHO-recommended first-line, second-line and severe-malaria treatments.
(c) State the rationale for ACTs and the recommended combinations.
(d) Describe chemoprophylaxis and radical cure.
(e) State resistance mechanisms and the adverse effects of key drugs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Chemical groups: natural (artemisinin, quinine), 8-aminoquinolines (primaquine), 4-aminoquinolines (chloroquine, amodiaquine), 9-aminoacridines, DHFR inhibitors (proguanil, pyrimethamine), phenanthrene methanols (halofantrine), sulphonamides and antibiotics (doxycycline).
• By stage: blood schizonticides (quinine, chloroquine, artemisinins), tissue schizonticides/radical cure (primaquine, tafenoquine), causal prophylactics, and gametocidal/transmission-blocking drugs (primaquine, artemisinins).
(b)
First line in Nigeria: artemether-lumefantrine and artesunate-amodiaquine; quinine is second line and for severe malaria; IV artesunate is first line for severe malaria (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily) followed by a full ACT course; quinine 20 mg salt/kg loading then 10 mg/kg 8-hourly if artesunate is unavailable.
(c)
• ACTs pair a fast-acting artemisinin with a long-acting partner to give rapid cure, prevent recrudescence and prevent resistance; monotherapy is discouraged.
• Six WHO ACTs: artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, artesunate-mefloquine, artesunate-sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, artesunate-pyronaridine.
(d)
Prophylaxis: mefloquine, chloroquine, pyrimethamine, doxycycline, proguanil; SP is used for IPTp and seasonal chemoprevention with amodiaquine; primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days gives radical cure of vivax (hypnozoites).
(e)
• Mutations in PfCRT and pfmdr1 cause chloroquine, quinine and mefloquine resistance; DHFR and DHPS mutations cause SP resistance; kelch13 mutations mediate artemisinin resistance.
• Responses to resistance: triple ACT, ACT plus single low-dose primaquine, artemether-lumefantrine plus amodiaquine, and non-artemisinin combinations (ganaplacide-lumefantrine, cipargamin).
• Quinine: cinchonism, hypoglycaemia, black water fever; chloroquine: pruritus, retinopathy; primaquine: haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; amodiaquine: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity.
• Mefloquine: neuropsychiatric effects, should not be used with quinine or halofantrine (cardiac arrest); artemisinins: QT prolongation.
• Fansidar: haematological reactions; avoid with other anti-folics.
• Quality: 63.9% of antimalarial products in Nigeria failed quality tests in a WHO survey.

questions.question:
A woman in late pregnancy with a urinary tract infection is given a sulphonamide, and her G6PD-deficient relative on the same drug develops dark urine.
(a) Identify the drug class and the adverse effects.
(b) State the pharmacokinetic basis.
(c) State the management and alternatives.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sulphonamides: kernicterus in newborns of mothers given the drug near the end of pregnancy; haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; crystalluria; skin rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hypersensitivity, photosensitivity, GI upset.
(b)
Sulphonamides are well absorbed orally, penetrate CSF, cross the placenta and enter breast milk; N-acetylation in the liver reduces solubility, giving crystalluria; excreted by the kidney.
(c)
• Sulphonamides should be avoided in neonates and in G6PD deficiency (also nitrofurantoin and chloramphenicol); cephalosporins are used for UTI especially in pregnancy.
• Sulphamethoxazole (with trimethoprim) is the main systemic sulphonamide used.
• Primaquine, mefloquine and dapsone also cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

(a)
Production of beta-lactamases (penicillinase) that inactivate penicillins; the drug class is the beta-lactams.
(b)
The strained amide bond of the fused beta-lactam nucleus is very reactive and is attacked by nucleophiles, including penicillinase, which cleaves it to penicilloic acid (inactive).
(c)
• Use a penicillinase-resistant penicillin (methicillin, nafcillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin) or a combination of a penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (clavulanic acid with amoxicillin or ticarcillin; sulbactam; tazobactam).
• Other options: carbapenems (developed against beta-lactamase-producing organisms) or vancomycin for MRSA.
(d)
• Penicillinase-resistant penicillins have a bulky side chain that sterically hinders the enzyme; clavulanic acid is a weak antibiotic but a potent suicide inhibitor of beta-lactamase.
• MRSA is resistant to all antibiotics except vancomycin and possibly ciprofloxacin, rifampin and imipenem/cilastatin; vancomycin-resistant S. aureus has developed.
questions.question:
A patient with a Staphylococcus aureus infection fails treatment with benzylpenicillin because the isolate produces an enzyme that destroys the drug.
(a) Identify the likely mechanism of resistance and the drug class.
(b) Explain the basis in terms of the chemistry of the drug.
(c) State the strategies to overcome it.
(d) Justify the choices.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Isoniazid (with pyridoxal phosphate) + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol for two months, then isoniazid and rifampicin alone for a further four months.
(b)
• Combination therapy is used in tuberculosis to prevent the emergence of resistant organisms; choice depends on age, health, latent or active disease, site and resistance of the strain.
• Pyridoxine is given because isoniazid causes peripheral neuritis through pyridoxine depletion.
(c)
• Isoniazid: hepatotoxicity (raised ALT/AST); inhibits metabolism of phenytoin and carbamazepine. Rifampicin: enzyme inducer interacting with corticosteroids, oral hypoglycaemics, anticoagulants, dapsone, phenytoin, digitalis and contraceptives; orange discolouration of body fluids.
• Pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia (competes with uric acid secretion, may provoke gout, not a reason to halt therapy). Ethambutol: optic neuritis (reduced acuity, loss of red-green discrimination).
(d)
• Adverse-effect indicators named are AST/ALT, uric acid and visual acuity.
• Latent TB: six to nine months of daily isoniazid, or three months of weekly isoniazid/rifapentine (12 doses), or isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide for two months then isoniazid and rifampicin for four months; ethambutol need not be used.
questions.question:
A newly diagnosed adult with active pulmonary tuberculosis starts standard short-course therapy.
(a) Identify the drugs and the duration of the intensive and continuation phases.
(b) Justify the combination and the role of pyridoxine.
(c) Identify the key interaction and adverse-effect precautions for each drug.
(d) State the monitoring parameters and the standard treatment of latent TB.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Natural immunity is acquired during normal biological experiences; artificial immunity follows medical procedures (vaccines and immune sera); active immunity requires an immune stimulus, builds memory and takes days to develop, passive immunity transfers antibodies with immediate but short-lived protection and no memory.
(b)
Vaccine types: inactivated (killed), live attenuated, toxoid, subunit, conjugate, DNA, recombinant vector, mRNA; sera/antisera provide passive immunisation.
(c)
• Inactivated: pertussis, typhoid, Salk polio, influenza, cholera; live attenuated: measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, yellow fever, rotavirus; toxoid: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (formalin-detoxified toxins); conjugate: Hib; recombinant subunit: hepatitis B (yeast).
• Conjugate vaccines link bacterial antigens to the polysaccharide coat so immature infant immune systems respond; mRNA vaccines instruct cells to make the spike protein; DNA vaccines make host cells produce the antigen.
(d)
• Inactivated vaccines are safe (even in immunocompromised) but need multiple doses and adjuvants; live vaccines need one dose but can cause severe reactions in the immunodeficient and are destroyed by heat and light.
• Antisera are used in immunocompromised, acutely ill patients but are regulated and used in public health settings.
• Duration: cholera months; TAB two years; DPT 3-5 years; BCG 5 or more years; yellow fever 10 years; MMR solid.
• Effectiveness: yellow fever 100%; measles, mumps, rubella and DT 99%; polio, BCG, hepatitis B, pertussis 80-95%; TAB, cholera, killed influenza 40-60%.
• Hazards: local and general reactions; faulty technique; hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, serum sickness 7-12 days after antiserum); neurological reactions (post-vaccinial encephalitis); provocative reactions.
• The cold chain (cold rooms, deep freezers, ice-lined refrigerators, cold boxes, vaccine carriers, ice packs) prevents vaccine failure from poor storage.
• Routes: IM/deep SC (most), oral (Sabin), intradermal (BCG), scarification (smallpox), intranasal (live influenza).
• Boosters (DT, MMR) maintain waning immunity.
questions.question:
(a) Define natural and artificial, active and passive immunity.
(b) Describe the types of vaccines and sera with examples.
(c) Relate each type to the examples and explain why each strategy produces protection.
(d) State the advantages, limitations, hazards and the cold chain.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Chloramphenicol is an amphenicol with a chloride on the side chain, a nitro group at the para position and a free OH group; thiamphenicol replaces NO2 with methylsulphonyl.
(b)
• The primary OH group is the site of salt formation; salts are hydrolysed in vivo to release the base; the palmitate is insoluble and tasteless (oral suspension) and shows polymorphism, the thermodynamically stable form having low oral bioavailability.
• The sodium succinate is water-soluble (injection); the pure base is used in capsules; solutions hydrolyse (unstable) and undergo light-induced reactions; there is no free carbonyl so it does not react with semicarbazide, hydrazine or hydroxylamine.
(c)
• It binds the 50S subunit and prevents binding of the aminoacyl-tRNA end to the acceptor site; bacteriostatic and broad spectrum, bactericidal to H. influenzae, N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae.
• Uses: typhoid fever, bacterial meningitis, rickettsial diseases and brucellosis; it crosses the BBB rapidly because it is lipid-soluble.
(d)
• Activity is lost by removal or transfer of Cl to the ring, by replacing or moving the nitro group to ortho or meta, by esterifying the OH (unless the ester is easily cleaved in vivo), and by alkyl or alkoxy groups on the aryl ring.
• Replacing NO2 with methylsulphonyl (thiamphenicol) improves activity.
(e)
• Adverse effects: irreversible bone marrow depression, aplastic anaemia, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, gray baby syndrome.
• Neonates have undeveloped hepatic function, so chloramphenicol and sulphonamides should be avoided.
• Resistance: acetyltransferases inactivate chloramphenicol.
• Caution in hepatic impairment since it is primarily detoxified in the liver.
questions.question:
(a) Give the chemical class, structure and key structural features of chloramphenicol.
(b) State its chemical properties, salts and stability.
(c) State its mechanism and uses.
(d) State the SAR.
(e) Explain the structural basis of toxicity and the loss of activity.

(a) State the uses of prophylactic antimicrobials.
(b) Describe examples across bacterial, mycobacterial, protozoal and viral infections.
(c) Explain why prophylaxis reduces infection and relate to the drugs used.
(d) State the trade-offs and limitations of prophylaxis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Antibiotic prophylaxis is used in specific situations: prevention of streptococcal infection in rheumatic heart disease, dental extraction in patients with prosthetic valves, TB or meningitis in close contacts, and presurgical treatment (GI procedures, hysterectomy, caesarean, joint replacement, open fracture).
(b)
• Meningococcal and H. influenzae meningitis prophylaxis with rifampicin; isoniazid chemoprophylaxis for 6 months (newborns of TB mothers, children under 6 years with positive tuberculin, contacts).
• Leprosy: single-dose rifampicin for contacts (600 mg aged 15 and over, 450 mg 10-14 years, 300 mg 6-9 years, 10-15 mg/kg for younger).
• Malaria: mefloquine, chloroquine, pyrimethamine, doxycycline, proguanil, atovaquone-proguanil; SP for IPTp and seasonal chemoprevention; causal prophylaxis (primary tissue schizonticides).
• HIV: PEP within 72 hours for 28 days, PrEP, PMTCT; OIs: cotrimoxazole and isoniazid preventive therapy.
(c)
• Causal prophylactics kill parasites once they emerge from the liver, blocking the link between exoerythrocytic and erythrocytic stages; suppressive drugs suppress the erythrocytic phase.
• Rifampicin and isoniazid are active against the target bacilli; HAART components prevent integration and reverse transcription in exposed persons.
(d)
• Indiscriminate use causes resistance and superinfection, so prophylaxis is restricted to situations where benefits outweigh risks.
• Chloroquine's long half-life (1-2 months) is not good for prophylaxis; mefloquine is not for patients with depression; doxycycline cannot be used in pregnancy.
• PrEP does not prevent other STIs or pregnancy; IPT needs exclusion of active TB.
• Pyrimethamine and proguanil act slowly; proguanil must be taken daily.

(a)
Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antibiotic and antiprotozoal; the structure has 2-hydroxyethyl, nitro and methyl groups at C1, C2 and C5 respectively .
(b)
• Active against anaerobic bacteria (Bacteroides, Clostridium) and protozoa (amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis); also bacterial vaginosis and H. pylori eradication, and surgical prophylaxis.
• Penetrates CSF very well regardless of inflammation; adult dose 400 mg three times daily for 10 days for amoebiasis.
(c)
• The nitro group is chemically reduced in anaerobic bacteria and sensitive protozoa; the reactive reduction products (nitroso radicals) disrupt DNA and inhibit nucleic acid synthesis.
• It has little effect on human and aerobic bacterial cells because the reductive activation occurs in anaerobes.
(d)
• Activity is based on the nitro group; tinidazole and ornidazole are analogues; secnidazole carries a methyl on the 2-hydroxyethyl group, has a broad anaerobic spectrum, a longer half-life and is given as a single dose rather than multiple doses.
• Tinidazole 1 g (4 tablets) at once or 2 g daily for 6 days.
(e)
• Adverse effects: nausea, headache, dry mouth, metallic taste, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, dark urine, neutropenia.
• Interactions: potentiates coumarin anticoagulants; phenytoin and phenobarbital speed its elimination; cimetidine decreases clearance.
• E. histolytica can survive sub-therapeutic metronidazole in vitro, and metronidazole is less effective against cysts.
• Bicyclic nitroimidazoles (delamanid, pretomanid) are also used for MDR/XDR-TB, inhibiting mycolic acid and protein synthesis; delamanid is associated with QT prolongation.
questions.question:
(a) Give the chemical class, name and structure of metronidazole.
(b) State its properties and uses.
(c) State its mechanism of activation.
(d) Describe the structural basis of its metabolism, activity and the basis of related analogues.
(e) Explain the basis of toxicity and loss of activity.

(a) Describe the polyene antifungals: classification, source and structure.
(b) State the pharmacophore and the mechanism of action.
(c) Explain the chemical basis of their instability, toxicity and resistance.
(d) Distinguish amphotericin B from nystatin.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin, candicidin, rimocidin, filipin, natamycin, hamycin) are products of Streptomyces; amphotericin B comes from Streptomyces nodosus.
• Structure: macrocyclic lactone with a sequence of conjugated double bonds, a heavily hydroxylated region opposite and often a mycosamine (aminoglycoside) group.
(b)
They bind ergosterol in the fungal membrane, form pores with leakage of K+, Na+, H+, Cl-, enzymes and small organic molecules; amphotericin B also generates toxic free radicals on oxidation.
(c)
• Properties: acidic, basic, amphoteric or non-ionic; inactivated by acids and bases; poor solubility and stability; high toxicity.
• Human cells use cholesterol, but amphotericin B and filipin still bind cholesterol at therapeutic doses (500-fold lower affinity), accounting for side effects.
• Resistance to amphotericin B is due to decreased ergosterol content; Candida lusitaniae and C. guilliermondii, Fusarium, Trichosporon and Pseudallescheria boydii are resistant.
• Toxicity: infusion reactions (TNF-alpha and IL-1 release), renal toxicity, hypokalaemia, anaemia (reduced erythropoietin); lipid formulations (Amphotec, Abelcet, AmBisome) reduce nephrotoxicity.
(d)
• Amphotericin B is given only IV (intrathecal in chronic meningitis), negligible oral absorption, for severe systemic infections (aspergillosis, blastomycosis, cryptococcosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis); also antileishmanial.
• Nystatin is a structural relative that acts by the same pore-forming mechanism but is not absorbed from any route and is used topically for skin, vaginal and oral candidiasis.
• Natamycin is used for superficial yeast and mould infections of the eye.
• Elimination half-life of amphotericin B about 24 hours, present in blood up to 4 weeks.

questions.question:
An HIV-positive adult on antiretroviral therapy is started on cotrimoxazole preventive therapy and later develops shigellosis.
(a) Identify the drugs in cotrimoxazole.
(b) Justify the combination.
(c) Identify interactions or antagonism and special-population cautions.
(d) State the dose and monitoring/precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sulphamethoxazole and trimethoprim (co-trimoxazole).
(b)
• The two drugs block bacterial nucleotide (folate) synthesis at two points in the pathway; this sequential blockade is more successful than either alone, they potentiate one another (synergism) and the result is bactericidal.
• It is effective for P. jirovecii pneumonia, shigellosis, systemic salmonella infections, UTI and some non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections; CPT is effective prophylaxis against PCP, S. pneumoniae, toxoplasmosis and cryptosporidiosis.
(c)
• Anti-folic drugs such as sulphonamides, trimethoprim and sulphamethoxazole should not be used while the patient receives Fansidar (antagonism/additive toxicity); trimethoprim can cause folate deficiency and blood disorders; sulphonamides cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
• Sulphonamides should be avoided in the neonate; trimethoprim/sulphamethoxazole itself can induce aseptic meningitis.
(d)
• CPT is given to all PLHIV regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage: adults 960 mg daily; infants under 6 months 120 mg daily; 6 months-5 years 240 mg; 6-14 years 480 mg; started from 6 weeks in exposed infants.
• Monitoring of blood counts is implied by the toxicities listed.

(a)
Erythromycin (a mixture of A, B and C; A greater), clarithromycin, azithromycin, telithromycin, oleandomycin, spiramycin, tylosin; 14-, 15- and 16-membered ring macrolides.
(b)
A macrocyclic lactone ketone of 12-17 atoms, with one or two amino sugars glycosidically linked, and neutral (deoxy) sugars linked directly or through amino sugars; a dimethylamino group on the sugar gives basicity.
(c)
Usually bacteriostatic; bind reversibly to 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and block the translocation reaction of polypeptide elongation.
(d)
• Stable in neutral solution; acid hydrolyses the glycoside bond; base saponifies the lactone bond.
• Lipophilic, so readily concentrated in tissues and intracellular sites; excellent tissue and cellular penetration, useful in intracellular infections.
• Resistance: altered target sites and ribosomal methylation preventing binding; cross-resistance among all macrolides.
(e)
• Gram-positive activity: clarithromycin > erythromycin > azithromycin; Gram-negative (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, Neisseria): azithromycin > clarithromycin > erythromycin; none against Enterobacteriaceae.
• Erythromycin, clarithromycin and telithromycin have 14-membered rings, azithromycin a 15-membered ring.
• All are eliminated by the liver; GI side effects occur in up to 33%, especially with erythromycin; best used in atypical pneumonia.
• Uses: Mycoplasma, Legionnaires' disease, Chlamydia, diphtheria, pertussis, streptococci, Campylobacter, H. pylori, alternative to penicillin for endocarditis prophylaxis, skin and soft tissue infection.
• Adverse effects: skin eruption, eosinophilia, cholestatic hepatitis, jaundice; use with caution in hepatic impairment; poor CSF penetration so not for meningitis.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the macrolides.
(b) Describe the general structure and pharmacophore.
(c) State the mechanism of action.
(d) Explain the chemical basis of their stability, tissue penetration and resistance.
(e) Distinguish erythromycin from azithromycin and clarithromycin.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Virological failure (plasma viral load 1000 copies/ml or more on consecutive measurements 6 months after starting ART), with immunological failure suggested by falling CD4.
(b)
The NNRTI efavirenz (and nevirapine) have a low genetic barrier: a single mutation leads to class resistance.
(c)
NNRTIs bind reverse transcriptase near its catalytic site; mutation of that site abolishes binding. Adherence assessment is the baseline for success.
(d)
• Switch to second line: one boosted PI plus two NRTIs (for example TDF + 3TC + ATV/r or LPV/r), based on the history of prior ARVs; include at least two new ARVs.
• Keep 3TC or FTC, which increases the activity of AZT or TDF; do not keep the NNRTI in the second-line regimen (no benefit, additive toxicity).
• Lopinavir, indinavir and saquinavir must be boosted with ritonavir; PIs with rifampicin risk toxicity; the patient must be able to adhere to a more complicated regimen.
questions.question:
A patient on tenofovir, lamivudine and efavirenz for 8 months still has a plasma viral load above 1000 copies/ml on two consecutive measurements and a falling CD4 count.
(a) Identify the type of failure and likely resistance mechanism.
(b) Name the drug class affected.
(c) Explain the basis (target, genetic barrier).
(d) State the strategy to overcome it and justify it.

(a) Give the class, source and structure of doxorubicin.
(b) State its pharmacokinetic properties and indications.
(c) State its mechanism of action.
(d) State the structural basis of its toxicity, especially cardiotoxicity.
(e) Explain the dose limits and the related drugs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Doxorubicin (Adriamycin) is an anthracycline antibiotic obtained from Streptomyces; anthracyclines have a tetrahydrotetracene quinone structure/chromophore (daunorubicin, rhodomycin).
(b)
• 75% protein bound; volume of distribution 20-30 L/kg; metabolised predominantly in the liver to doxorubicinol; half-life 1-3 h; clearance 8-20 mL/min/kg; excreted in faeces (40-50%) and urine (5-12%).
• Indications: acute myeloblastic leukaemia and lymphoma; given IV only.
(c)
Intercalates between DNA base pairs, impairs topoisomerase II function and inhibits replication and transcription; anthracyclines inhibit topoisomerases I and II.
(d)
• Cardiotoxicity (about 30%) is related to free radical production; epirubicin and mitoxantrone are structurally related with the same cardiotoxicity and marrow suppression.
• Other adverse effects: neutropenia (52%), anaemia (52%), leukopenia (42%), thrombocytopenia (24%), vomiting (22%).
(e)
• Limit lifetime cumulative dose to below 550 mg/m2; monitor full blood count, cardiac function and liver function tests.
• No dose adjustment in renal impairment; adjust in mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment; contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment.
• Pregnancy category D; enters breast milk and is not recommended in lactation.
• Liposomal doxorubicin (PLGA/Doxil) and liposomal daunorubicin (DaunoXome) are nanomedicine formulations that improve pharmacokinetics and biodistribution and reduce clearance.
• Anthracyclines are listed as cell-cycle dependent anti-mitotic antibiotics.

questions.question:
A treatment-naive adult with HIV, normal renal function, is started on tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir.
(a) Identify the classes of the three drugs.
(b) State the structural or functional feature responsible for activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action of each at its molecular target.
(d) State the therapeutic use and the key adverse effect linked to the mechanism.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tenofovir (a nucleotide) and lamivudine (a nucleoside) are NRTIs; dolutegravir is a second-generation integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI).
(b)
NRTIs are analogues of natural nucleosides/nucleotides that require phosphorylation to their 5'-triphosphate; INSTIs target integrase.
(c)
• NRTIs are phosphorylated by host kinases and compete with natural triphosphates as false substrates for reverse transcriptase, causing chain termination in proviral DNA synthesis.
• Dolutegravir inhibits the viral integrase enzyme that inserts viral DNA into host cell DNA to form the provirus.
(d)
• Used in combination with other ARVs for HIV; lamivudine and tenofovir also treat hepatitis B; TDF/3TC/DTG is the preferred first-line regimen.
• Class adverse effect of NRTIs is lactic acidosis from mitochondrial toxicity (host gamma-DNA polymerase is fairly sensitive, alpha-DNA polymerase relatively resistant).
• TDF causes renal toxicity and reduced bone density; TAF has better bone and kidney effects while TDF has better lipid-lowering effects.
• Dolutegravir: hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity and neural tube defects early in pregnancy; lamivudine is generally well tolerated.

questions.question:
Gentamicin and tobramycin are inactivated in a hospital by aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, so semisynthetic derivatives of kanamycin and sisomicin were prepared.
(a) Identify the derivatives.
(b) Predict the effect on resistance, spectrum and toxicity.
(c) Justify through the mechanism of resistance.
(d) State their uses and the rationale.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Amikacin is a semisynthetic derivative of kanamycin; netilmicin is a semisynthetic derivative of sisomicin.
(b)
• Amikacin is less toxic than its parent with the broadest antimicrobial activity and remains active against organisms resistant through inactivating enzymes.
• Netilmicin is relatively resistant to aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes, is more active against Klebsiella, Enterobacter and staphylococci, and less active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa; it is not metabolised by most aminoglycoside-metabolising enzymes.
(c)
The most important resistance mechanism is inactivation by aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (phosphorylation, acetylation, adenylation); derivatives that are poor substrates for the enzymes escape it.
(d)
• Amikacin (15 mg/kg/day in 1-3 doses): hospital-acquired Gram-negative bacillary infections where gentamicin and tobramycin resistance prevail, and MDR-TB with other drugs.
• Netilmicin has doses and pharmacokinetics similar to gentamicin and may act on gentamicin-resistant bacteria.

(a)
• Natural: benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) and phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V); beta-lactamase-resistant: flucloxacillin, methicillin, temocillin (also cloxacillin, nafcillin).
• Broad spectrum: ampicillin, amoxicillin, pivampicillin; extended spectrum with antipseudomonal activity: carbenicillin, ticarcillin, azlocillin, piperacillin.
(b)
• Penicillins are penam (penicillanic acid) derivatives: a 4-thia-1-azabicyclo[3.2.0]heptane in which the beta-lactam ring is a cyclic amide with cis orientation.
• Requirements: a properly substituted amino side chain and a free carboxylic group; three chiral carbons, absolute configuration 3S, 5R, 6R.
(c)
Inhibit the final transpeptidation by forming covalent bonds with penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidase and carboxypeptidase), preventing cross-links; the result is osmotic lysis (bactericidal).
(d)
• The strained amide bond of the fused beta-lactam nucleus is very reactive: easily hydrolysed to penicilloic acid and attacked by nucleophiles (NaOH, NH3, alkoxides, penicillinase) and electrophiles (HCl, Zn2+, Cu2+).
• Free acids are strong acids (pKa 2.5-3.0) and not water soluble, so Na or K salts are used; they are unstable in aqueous solution and incompatible with heat, moisture, metals, acids, alkalis and oxidizing agents.
• Acid-stable (oral): a powerful electron-attracting group on the amino side chain prevents acidic rearrangement (ampicillin, amoxicillin, penicillin V, cloxacillin).
• Penicillinase-resistant: a bulky side-chain group gives steric hindrance (methicillin, nafcillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin); broad spectrum: high hydrophilic character of the amino side chain.
(e)
• Cephalosporins resemble penicillins except for a dihydrothiazine ring with a double bond (cepham, 5-thia-1-azabicyclo[4.2.0]octene); absolute configuration 6R, 7R; physicochemical properties similar to penicillins.
• Cephalosporins derive from 7-aminocephalosporanic acid (R1 on the 7-acylamide, R2 at the 3-acetoxymethyl); cephalosporin C from the mould Cephalosporium is beta-lactamase resistant but of low activity.
• Cephalosporins are described as more beta-lactamase resistant, broader spectrum, more active on Gram-negative bacteria, with low serum binding and renal excretion.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the penicillins with examples.
(b) Describe the general structure of the penicillins and the structural requirements for activity.
(c) State the mechanism of action.
(d) Explain the chemical basis of the instability of penicillins and how structural modification produces acid-stable, penicillinase-resistant and broad-spectrum penicillins.
(e) Distinguish the penicillins from the cephalosporins in structure and properties.

(a) Give the chemical class and general structure of sulphonamides.
(b) State the physicochemical properties (acidity, basicity, solubility, ionization) and assay methods.
(c) State the SAR.
(d) Describe the metabolism and the structural basis of its toxicity.
(e) Explain the basis of loss of activity or resistance.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sulphonamides are p-aminobenzenesulphonamides, structural analogues of PABA, which is the basis for their action; they are bacteriostatic antimetabolites.
• Requirements: an unsubstituted or easily split substituted amino (NH2) group, para position of the amino and sulphamido groups, and no other substituent on the ring.
(b)
• Basic property from NH2 (soluble in acids); acidic property from the sulphamido group (SO2NHR); overall weak acids that form sodium salts with increased water solubility.
• Acidity varies with the electron-withdrawing effect of the R substituent; they exist as anions at physiological pH, and maximum activity is with pKa between 6.0 and 7.5 (about 50% ionization), the negative SO2N-H being responsible for activity.
• Assay: sodium nitrite titration, non-aqueous titration, UV spectrophotometry.
(c)
• Activity lost: change of the para position; any substituent on the ring; R on NH2 unless easily converted to NH2 in vivo (phthalyl, succinyl salts).
• Activity retained or increased: NO2, NHCOOCH3 or NHOH replacing NH2 (converted in vivo to NH2); a heterocyclic aromatic ring on N gives active compounds.
(d)
• Metabolised by N-acetylation in the liver, which increases hydrophobic character and reduces aqueous solubility (insoluble metabolite, e.g. of sulfathiazole), leading to crystalluria; excreted by the kidneys.
• Other toxicities: haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hypersensitivity, photosensitivity, and kernicterus in newborns of mothers given sulphonamides near the end of pregnancy.
(e)
• They compete with PABA for dihydropteroate synthetase and the effect is overcome by excess PABA; resistant strains produce more PABA.
• Their importance has declined with increasing resistance; sulphamethoxazole (with trimethoprim) and sulfasalazine remain systemically used.
• Succinyl and phthalyl sulphathiazole are pro-drugs not absorbed from the GI tract.

(a)
Fluorination at position 6 and a piperazine substitution at position 7 of the quinolone gave the fluoroquinolones (introduced in 1986); nalidixic acid is a non-fluorinated 1,8-naphthyridine.
(b)
Higher potency, expanded broad-spectrum activity, slow development of resistance, better tissue penetration and good tolerability.
(c)
• Activity increases with lipophilicity (fluorine at C6 aids tissue penetration), piperazinyl at C7, cyclopropyl at N1 (ciprofloxacin) and ring condensation at 1,8-, 5,6- and 7,8-positions.
• Replacing COOH with an isothiazolo ring retains activity (acidic N proton mimics COOH); modifying or removing the C4 keto group or the C3 COOH reduces activity.
(d)
• Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin and others.
• A halogen at C8 increases phototoxicity (lomefloxacin) whereas NH2 at C5 or C8 reduces photoreaction (sparfloxacin).
(e)
To expand the spectrum and prevent development of resistance; the result is broad spectrum, low toxicity, good oral absorption and poor brain penetration.
questions.question:
Nalidixic acid, the first quinolone, has low potency, a narrow spectrum and rapidly developing resistance. Structural modification of the quinolone nucleus produced a new class.
(a) Identify the structural modifications and the resulting class.
(b) Predict the effect on potency, spectrum, tissue penetration and resistance.
(c) Justify through SAR, including changes that reduce activity.
(d) Name improved analogues.
(e) State the rationale for the modification.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The phenylglycine-based 7-acyl side chain with an unsubstituted amino group gives good oral absorption and stability to gastric acid; a bulky group on R2 gives beta-lactamase resistance.
(b)
• Activity depends on the reactivity of the beta-lactam ring, the nature and spatial arrangement of peripheral substituents (R1 on the 7-acylamide, R2 at 3-acetoxymethyl) and the skeleton.
• Aromatic or heteroaromatic substituted acetic acid residues with polar groups (OH, carboxyl, sulpho) on the 7-beta-acylamino enhance activity; a heterocyclic ring on the 7-acyl chain gives broad spectrum.
• C3 substituent affects activity, metabolic stability, pharmacokinetics and adverse effects; C7 substitution affects beta-lactam stability and plasma protein binding; COOH at C4 allows esters and pro-drugs.
(c)
Oral: cephalexin, cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefdinir; beta-lactamase resistant (bulky R2): cefuroxime.
(d)
• Overall activity is determined by the reactivity of the lactam ring and the nature and arrangement of R1 and R2, which potentiate beta-lactamase stability; the natural cephalosporin C is beta-lactamase resistant but of low activity, so semi-synthetic modification of 7-ACA improves it.
• Generations: 1st good Gram-positive, 2nd more Gram-negative, 3rd enhanced Gram-negative, 4th (cefepime) anti-pseudomonal, 5th (ceftaroline) active against MRSA.
questions.question:
A chemist modifies the 7-acyl side chain and the 3-substituent of a cephalosporin nucleus: a phenylglycine-based side chain with a free amino group is introduced, and in another analogue a bulky group is placed at R2.
(a) Predict the effect on oral activity and beta-lactamase stability.
(b) Justify through SAR.
(c) Name the analogues.
(d) State the rationale.

A woman with HIV, CD4 count 300 cells/mm3, has anaemia, renal disease and hepatitis B, and wishes to become pregnant.
(a) Identify the antiretroviral drugs to avoid and the adverse effects they cause.
(b) Explain the mechanism of the toxicity.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic or class basis.
(d) State the preferred drugs and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Avoid zidovudine (anaemia), tenofovir disoproxil (renal toxicity), nevirapine in women with CD4 above 250 (hepatotoxicity and severe rash) and efavirenz in women of child-bearing intent (controversially teratogenic).
(b)
Zidovudine: anaemia, neutropenia and myopathy are listed; TDF: renal toxicity and reduced bone mineral density.
(c)
NRTI toxicity relates to sensitivity of mitochondrial gamma-DNA polymerase; nevirapine and efavirenz have a low genetic barrier; TDF produces higher tenofovir levels than TAF.
(d)
• With hepatitis B use tenofovir (also lamivudine); with renal or bone disease TAF is preferable to TDF; avoid zidovudine in anaemia; abacavir/lamivudine + dolutegravir in HLA-B*5701 negative.
• Dolutegravir is associated with neural tube defects in early pregnancy; AZT is the preferred NRTI in pregnancy yet anaemia is a contraindication.

questions.question:
A patient with a urinary tract infection responds initially to a fluoroquinolone but then fails treatment.
(a) Identify the drug class and its molecular targets.
(b) Identify the likely mechanisms of resistance.
(c) Explain the basis in terms of the target, drug uptake and drug inactivation.
(d) State the strategy or structural feature that reduces the propensity for resistance.
(e) Justify the choice of a fluoroquinolone over nalidixic acid.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fluoroquinolones (bactericidal synthetic quinolones) target DNA gyrase (Gram-negative bacteria) and topoisomerase IV (Gram-positive bacteria).
• They bind the A subunit of DNA gyrase with high affinity and interfere with strand cutting and resealing.
(b)
Resistance results from alteration of the enzymatic targets, decreased outer-membrane permeability or development of efflux mechanisms.
(c)
• Chromosomal point mutations in the quinolone-binding region give DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV with reduced affinity for the drug; drugs are effluxed across bacterial membranes.
• No quinolone-modifying or inactivating enzymes have been identified in bacteria; resistance to fluoroquinolones is slow to develop.
(d)
In tuberculosis, adding C8 halogen and C8 methoxy groups markedly reduces the propensity for resistance (moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin, levofloxacin); first-generation agents are more susceptible to resistance.
(e)
Fluoroquinolones have high potency, broad spectrum, slow development of resistance, better tissue penetration and good tolerability, whereas nalidixic acid has low potency, narrow spectrum, rapid resistance and limited utility.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the biology of the parasite stages relevant to drug action.
(b) State the mechanism of action of each antimalarial group.
(c) Relate each mechanism to examples and explain the cellular basis of selectivity.
(d) State the main resistance mechanisms and adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sporozoites invade liver cells (pre-erythrocytic stage); merozoites invade red cells, digest haemoglobin to globin and toxic haem, and polymerise haem to harmless haemozoin; some form gametocytes; P. vivax/ovale hypnozoites persist in the liver.
(b)
• Chloroquine: concentrated in the acidic food vacuole, inhibits haem polymerisation to haemozoin; the haem-drug complex damages membranes and causes lysis; quinine has a similar action; amodiaquine inhibits haemoglobin digestion.
• Artemisinins: the endoperoxide is cleaved (haem iron) to free radicals that damage parasite membranes and proteins.
• Antifolates: sulphadoxine inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, pyrimethamine and cycloguanil (from proguanil) inhibit DHFR, acting synergistically; atovaquone inhibits cytochrome bc1 and collapses the mitochondrial membrane potential.
• Primaquine is converted to electrophiles generating reactive oxygen species that interfere with the electron transport chain; mefloquine's mechanism is unknown.
(c)
• Selectivity: the folate pathway is bacterial/parasitic; drugs concentrate in infected erythrocytes (quinine uptake) and in the acidic food vacuole.
• Blood schizonticides: quinine, chloroquine, mefloquine, artemisinins; tissue schizonticides: primaquine, tafenoquine; transmission-blocking: primaquine, artemisinins.
(d)
• Resistance: PfCRT and pfmdr1 mutations (chloroquine, quinine, mefloquine); DHFR/DHPS mutations (SP); kelch13 (artemisinin); cross-resistance among quinoline methanols.
• Adverse effects: quinine cinchonism, hypoglycaemia, black water fever; chloroquine retinopathy; primaquine haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; mefloquine neuropsychiatric effects.
• Artemisinins prolong QT intervals; amodiaquine agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity.
• Antifolics (SP) cause haematological reactions and Stevens-Johnson syndrome-type reactions of the sulphonamide component.

questions.question:
(a) Classify mycoses by site and describe the main fungal infections.
(b) List the first-line and alternative antifungals for superficial, subcutaneous and systemic mycoses.
(c) State the rationale for the choice of drug in each.
(d) State the combinations used.
(e) State the adverse effects, interactions and precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Superficial (skin, hair, nails: tinea, onychomycosis, thrush), subcutaneous (tropical), systemic (primary or opportunistic: aspergillosis, cryptococcosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystosis, sporotrichosis) and allergic mycoses (ABPA).
• Risk factors: broad-spectrum antibiotics, steroids, HIV, cancer chemotherapy, diabetes, extremes of age, catheters, transplantation.
(b)
• Superficial: topical azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole), terbinafine, griseofulvin, nystatin for mucosal candidiasis, terconazole vaginal, natamycin eye.
• Systemic: fluconazole (candidiasis, cryptococcal and coccidioidal meningitis), voriconazole (aspergillosis), itraconazole (blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, sporotrichosis), amphotericin B (severe systemic), echinocandins (candidaemia, salvage aspergillosis).
(c)
• Terbinafine accumulates in skin, nails and fat (half-life about 300 hours) and treats onychomycosis and tinea; griseofulvin treats dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton).
• Fluconazole penetrates CSF excellently with a low adverse-effect profile; amphotericin B penetrates CSF poorly and is used IV (intrathecal in chronic meningitis).
(d)
Flucytosine with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis (synergy through enhanced uptake); echinocandins combined with amphotericin B, flucytosine, itraconazole or voriconazole in refractory infections.
(e)
• Amphotericin B: infusion reactions, renal toxicity, anaemia; flucytosine: marrow suppression; azoles: hepatotoxicity and P450 interactions; terbinafine: hepatotoxicity.
• Griseofulvin induces hepatic enzymes (reduces coumarin and oral contraceptive effect), is fetotoxic and teratogenic; ketoconazole is hepatotoxic and not for aspergillosis.
• Terbinafine is not recommended in renal or hepatic failure or pregnancy; flucytosine contraindicated in pregnancy.
• Fungicides are agricultural chemicals, distinguished from antifungal drugs used for treating infections in animals and humans.

(a)
Four classes: calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), antiproliferative agents (mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine), mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus), and glucocorticoids (prednisone); also cytotoxic agents (cyclophosphamide, methotrexate) and immunosuppressive antibodies.
(b)
• Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin; the complex inhibits calcineurin, a phosphatase needed to activate NF-AT, blocking IL-2 and other cytokine synthesis by activated T cells.
• Tacrolimus (macrolide from Streptomyces tsukubaensis) binds FKBP-12 and likewise inhibits calcineurin; it is 10-100 times more potent than cyclosporine.
• Sirolimus (from Streptomyces hygroscopicus) binds FKBP and blocks mTOR, inhibiting interleukin-driven T-cell proliferation.
• Azathioprine (prodrug of mercaptopurine) interferes with purine metabolism required for lymphoid proliferation; cyclophosphamide destroys proliferating lymphoid cells; glucocorticoids have broad anti-inflammatory effects on cellular immunity.
(c)
• Cyclosporine is a cyclic undecapeptide from Beauveria nivea; it is specific for T-helper (Th1) cells and acts mainly on the primary immune response, preferentially inhibiting antigen-triggered signalling in T lymphocytes; it increases TGF-beta.
• Sirolimus is synergistic with cyclosporine; hydroxychloroquine decreases T-cell activation; methotrexate is used in rheumatoid arthritis.
(d)
• Cyclosporine: nephrotoxicity (major reason to modify therapy), tremor, hirsutism, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, gum hyperplasia, hyperkalaemia, hepatotoxicity; metabolised by CYP3A.
• Sirolimus: myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia), hepatotoxicity, diarrhoea, hypertriglyceridaemia; tacrolimus has similar toxicity to cyclosporine.
• Azathioprine: bone marrow suppression; dose reduction with allopurinol; hepatic dysfunction.
• Cyclophosphamide: pancytopenia, haemorrhagic cystitis.
• Glucocorticoids: used for transplant rejection and GVHD.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the immunosuppressive drugs.
(b) State the mechanism of action of each class with examples.
(c) Relate each to the examples and explain the cellular basis of selectivity for T cells.
(d) State the main adverse effects and interactions.

(a) Define selective toxicity and explain why it is relative rather than absolute.
(b) Describe the biochemical differences between microorganisms and humans that chemotherapy exploits.
(c) Relate these to examples of antibacterial, antifungal and antiprotozoal drugs.
(d) Explain why selective toxicity improves safety and state the limitations and trade-offs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Selective toxicity is the ability of a drug to kill an invading microorganism without harming host cells; it underlies the effectiveness of antimicrobials.
• It is relative rather than absolute, so drug concentration must be carefully controlled to attack the organism while being tolerated by the host.
(b)
• Drugs exploit processes important to the pathogen but not the host; bacteria are prokaryotes while protozoa, fungi and helminths are eukaryotes, and viruses use host-cell machinery.
• Peptidoglycan is unique to prokaryotes; the folate biosynthetic pathway occurs in bacteria but not humans (humans use preformed folate, bacteria lack the transport).
(c)
• Sulfonamides compete with PABA at bacterial dihydropteroate synthetase (absent from human cells); trimethoprim inhibits bacterial DHFR, which is about 50,000 times more sensitive than the human enzyme.
• Fungi use ergosterol rather than cholesterol; amphotericin B's affinity for ergosterol is 500 times its affinity for cholesterol.
• Flucytosine enters fungi through cytosine-specific permeases that mammals lack; echinocandins target the cell wall (beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase), which mammalian cells lack.
• Eflornithine inhibits ornithine decarboxylase in parasite and host equally; selectivity arises from rapid turnover of the mammalian enzyme versus the stable parasite enzyme.
(d)
• The ideal drug combines selective toxicity, favourable pharmacokinetics, few side effects, a high therapeutic index and little resistance; there is no perfect drug.
• Fungi are eukaryotes with metabolic pathways similar to humans, so selective antifungals are harder to develop; amphotericin B still binds cholesterol at therapeutic doses, explaining its side effects.
• Selectivity does not prevent hypersensitivity, direct toxicity (aminoglycoside ototoxicity) or superinfection from altered flora.
• Sulfonamides are bacteriostatic and not ideal for patients with weakened immune systems.

questions.question:
A patient presents early in an influenza A illness (first 48 hours) and an antiviral that blocks release of new virions is chosen.
(a) Identify the drug class and examples.
(b) State the feature or target responsible for activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(d) State the spectrum, use and key adverse effects, and the alternative classes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Neuraminidase inhibitors: oseltamivir, zanamivir, laninamivir and peramivir.
(b)
The target is the viral neuraminidase, a protein enzyme on the surface of the virion.
(c)
Neuraminidase severs the bond between the viral coat and host sialic acid (neuraminic acid); inhibition prevents escape of newly replicated virus.
(d)
• Used for influenza A and B and only effective in the early stage of infection; side effects are GI (nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhoea).
• Alternatives: amantadine and rimantadine (M2 ion channel blockers, block H+ influx needed for coat disassembly; influenza A only; side effects dizziness, slurred speech, insomnia); baloxavir marboxil (prodrug; inhibits cap-dependent endonuclease; influenza A and B).

questions.question:
A child in Nigeria presents with fever, headache, vomiting and chills; uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria is confirmed and a fixed-dose artemisinin combination is prescribed.
(a) Identify the combination and its chemical classes.
(b) State the structural features responsible for activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action.
(d) State the therapeutic use and administration requirement.
(e) State key adverse effects and interactions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem), first-line therapy in Nigeria; artemether is an oil-soluble methyl ether of artemisinin (a sesquiterpene lactone endoperoxide), lumefantrine an arylamino alcohol like halofantrine.
(b)
The endoperoxide bridge is indispensable for antimalarial activity; artemether lacks chromophores and a nitrogen-containing ring.
(c)
• The endoperoxide is cleaved (heme iron implicated) to free radicals that damage parasite membranes and bind covalently to membrane proteins.
• It acts on schizonts/trophozoites and gametocytes.
(d)
• First-line for acute uncomplicated malaria: 20/120 mg tablets, adults four tablets in six doses over 3 days (0, 8, 24, 36, 48, 60 h); artemether gives rapid parasite reduction, lumefantrine long-lasting action preventing recrudescence.
• It must be given with fatty food or milk; fat increases absorption about 2-fold for artemether and up to 16-fold for lumefantrine.
(e)
• Most common: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dizziness; rare neutropenia, anaemia, haemolysis, raised liver enzymes, allergy.
• Artemisinins prolong the QT interval: avoid with tricyclic antidepressants and phenothiazines; both drugs are metabolised by CYP3A4.

questions.question:
A patient on long-term chloroquine complains of blurred vision and itching, and another patient on amodiaquine develops agranulocytosis.
(a) Identify the drug and the adverse effects.
(b) Explain the mechanism or basis of the toxicity.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic and pharmacogenetic basis.
(d) State the management and alternative.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chloroquine: retinopathy (long-term or large doses), pruritus, GI upset, headache, urticaria; amodiaquine: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity, aplastic anaemia, lassitude.
(b)
Chloroquine accumulates in the retina (selectively); the itching occurs on genetic bases and interaction with opioid receptors, increased in malaria fever and more prominent in black Africans (70%).
(c)
• Chloroquine has large tissue distribution (liver 500 times blood concentration), half-life 3-10 days (some sources give 1-2 months), metabolised to desethylchloroquine; amodiaquine is metabolised by polymorphic CYP2C8 to N-desethylamodiaquine, and *2, *3, *4 poor metabolisers show lower efficacy and higher toxicity.
• About 3.6% of the East African population studied is at high risk for poor response to amodiaquine.
(d)
Alternatives: artemisinin combinations; amodiaquine only with artesunate; contraindicated in severe liver impairment and hypersensitivity, with caution in G6PD deficiency, kidney disease and pregnancy.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of pharmacogenetic and pharmacokinetic variability in chemotherapy.
(b) Relate it to the examples given for antimicrobial and anticancer drugs.
(c) Explain why individualised dosing improves efficacy or safety.
(d) State the trade-offs and limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Individual differences in absorption, distribution and clearance cause variation in AUC and may produce variation in toxicity or idiosyncratic reactions; in high-dose chemotherapy this can cause significant variation in morbidity and mortality.
• Overcoming variation in clearance is a fundamental goal; individualised treatment aims for a uniform target AUC and clinical result; BSA-based dosing (mg/m2) is the common attempt.
(b)
• Isoniazid: NAT2 acetylation polymorphism (fast acetylators t1/2 1-2 h, slow 2-5 h; polyneuritis more frequent in slow acetylators).
• Proguanil: CYP2C19 polymorphism affects formation of cycloguanil (poor metabolisers 4.8% in Nigerians); amodiaquine: CYP2C8*2, *3, *4 poor metabolisers with lower efficacy and higher toxicity (3.6% of an East African population).
• Dapsone: slow and fast acetylators; G6PD deficiency causes haemolysis with primaquine, sulphonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin and chloramphenicol.
• Cyclophosphamide: aldehyde dehydrogenase levels determine inactivation in stem cells; lumefantrine levels are lower in children and day-7 levels of 280 ng/ml or below predict failure; fatty food raises absorption up to 16-fold.
(c)
• Aminoglycoside doses are adjusted to creatinine clearance by the Cockcroft-Gault formula; azathioprine is reduced with allopurinol; cyclosporine requires drug monitoring.
• Knowing genotype or phenotype helps predict poor response or toxicity (pharmacovigilance in regions with high CYP2C8 variant frequency).
(d)
• BSA dosing does not fully remove variability; high interindividual variability (CV 58-80% for artemether, 148-154% for lumefantrine) persists and is reduced in malaria and fed state.
• Genotyping requires knowledge of allele prevalence in populations; only limited data are available (for example, East African and Nigerian studies).
• Children and pregnant women need newer dosing guides because exposures differ.

(a)
Rifampicin: mutations in rpoB (86% of cases, codons 526 and 531), efflux pumps; isoniazid: mutation or inactivation of KatG, the catalase-peroxidase that activates the prodrug.
(b)
Rifamycins (RNA synthesis inhibitors) and the hydrazide isoniazid (mycolic acid synthesis inhibitor); resistance to both of these two most potent first-line drugs defines multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB).
(c)
Rifampicin binds the beta subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB); mutated target loses binding. Isoniazid without KatG is not converted to the nicotinoyl radical that forms NAD/NADP adducts.
(d)
• Treat with second-line drugs: bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, pretomanid; moxifloxacin-type fluoroquinolones are central; capreomycin or amikacin injectables; carbapenems with clavulanate; ethionamide.
• If also resistant to an injectable and a fluoroquinolone, it is XDR-TB, treated with effective second-line drugs.
• Justification: new classes act at different targets (ATP synthase subunit c for bedaquiline; mycolic acid/protein synthesis for delamanid/pretomanid; ribosome A site for linezolid), avoiding the resistance mechanisms above; adverse effects (bedaquiline cardiotoxicity, linezolid neuropathy) limit use.
questions.question:
A patient with pulmonary TB on standard therapy remains sputum-positive; laboratory testing shows resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin.
(a) Identify the likely mechanisms of resistance for each drug.
(b) Name the drug classes and the type of TB.
(c) Explain the basis in terms of the target and activation.
(d) State the strategy to overcome it and justify it.

A patient with invasive aspergillosis is not responding to fluconazole and amphotericin B-resistant moulds are suspected.
(a) Identify the likely cause of failure and the drugs affected.
(b) Explain the basis in terms of target and drug properties.
(c) State the strategy to overcome it.
(d) Justify the choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Fluconazole is not effective against aspergillosis; amphotericin B is active against most fungi except Aspergillus terreus and Scedosporium spp (resistance is attributed to decreased ergosterol content).
(b)
Fluconazole lacks aspergillus activity; amphotericin B resistance is due to decreased ergosterol in the fungal membrane, its binding target.
(c)
• Voriconazole is the drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis and other moulds (Fusarium, Scedosporium), and is fungicidal against all Aspergillus species; posaconazole is potent against Aspergillus and active against Zygomycetes.
• Itraconazole treats aspergillosis; echinocandins (caspofungin) can be salvage therapy for Aspergillus, and combinations have been used in refractory disease.
(d)
• Voriconazole gives better outcomes in allogeneic bone marrow transplant recipients, CNS infection and disseminated disease; available orally and parenterally.
• Precautions: hepatic P450 inhibition (reduce cyclosporine/tacrolimus), contraindicated with ritonavir, rifampin and rifabutin; hepatotoxicity (dose reduction); visual disturbance; avoid IV cyclodextrin vehicle in renal failure.

(a)
Eflornithine, originally developed as an anticancer agent, is the only alternative to melarsoprol for late-stage disease and is effective in both early and late stages of T. b. gambiense infection.
(b)
Melarsoprol is melarsen oxide (trivalent organic arsenical) combined with the chelator dimercaprol.
(c)
• Eflornithine is a specific irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, a key enzyme of polyamine metabolism, slowing cell proliferation.
• Parasite and human enzymes are equally susceptible; selectivity arises because the mammalian enzyme turns over rapidly while the parasite enzyme is stable.
(d)
• Active only against T. b. gambiense; usually curative even for late CNS stages resistant to arsenicals; synergistic with melarsoprol; NECT (nifurtimox-eflornithine) is recommended by WHO after melarsoprol resistance; less successful in AIDS patients.
• Early-stage therapy is pentamidine (gambiense) or suramin (rhodesiense); melarsoprol is the standard CNS drug but causes fatal reactive encephalopathy in 2-10%.
(e)
Eflornithine: anaemia (48%), diarrhoea (39%), leukopenia (27%), convulsions (7%), reversible hearing loss; large doses need IV fluid (fluid overload risk); dose pharmacokinetics: t1/2 about 200 minutes, over 80% renal excretion.
questions.question:
A patient from West Africa has fever, lymphadenopathy and headache, and later confusion, disturbed sleep and poor coordination; Trypanosoma brucei gambiense with CNS involvement is diagnosed.
(a) Identify the most appropriate drug and its class.
(b) State the chemical feature responsible for activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(d) State the spectrum and therapeutic use.
(e) State the key adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) plus vancomycin (alternative: vancomycin + rifampin + aztreonam), covering S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis, the likely pathogens in this age group.
(b)
Ceftriaxone has sustained reliable CSF bactericidal activity despite high protein binding; vancomycin gives cover for resistant pneumococci and reaches up to 22% of serum levels with inflamed meninges; meningitis demands a bactericidal regimen with adequate CSF penetration.
(c)
• Dexamethasone should be given before or with the first antibiotic dose in children (reduces cerebral oedema, TNF-alpha and IL-1; fewer hearing losses); concomitant dexamethasone may reduce vancomycin CSF penetration (29% in rabbits) but higher doses (60 mg/kg/day) overcome this.
• A rash with amoxicillin is a hypersensitivity concern; beta-lactam cross-sensitivity is stated for penicillins and cephalosporins (about 10%), and aztreonam does not cross-react with penicillin.
(d)
• Monitor temperature and mental status, daily CBC, electrolytes, glucose and renal function (SIADH), improvement within 24-48 h, CSF sterile after 18-24 h; duration for N. meningitidis 7 days, S. pneumoniae 10-14 days.
• Ceftriaxone 80-100 mg/kg/day in children (12-24 h interval); vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day.
questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy (20 kg) has fever 40°C, stiff neck, positive Brudzinski and Kernig signs, petechial rash, lethargy and photophobia; his CSF Gram stain is negative and he has a history of a skin rash with amoxicillin.
(a) Identify the likely drugs for empiric therapy.
(b) Justify the combination.
(c) Identify the interactions, adjuncts and precautions.
(d) State the monitoring and duration.

Quinine, a cinchona alkaloid, undergoes chemical modifications in the laboratory: the vinyl group is oxidised to carboxyl, the 6-methoxy group is demethylated, and the C9 hydroxyl and quinuclidine ring are altered.
(a) Identify the parent and the modified compounds.
(b) Predict the effect on antimalarial activity.
(c) Justify through SAR including stereochemistry.
(d) Name the analogue that restores activity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Parent: quinine (6-methoxy-alpha-(5'-vinyl-2'-quinuclidinyl)-4'-quinoline methanol); modified compounds: quitenine, cupreine, dihydrocupreine and optochin.
(b)
• Oxidation of the vinyl group to COOH (quitenine) causes complete loss of activity; esterifying the carboxyl partly restores it.
• Demethylation (HBr/AcOH or BCl3) gives cupreine with remarkably reduced activity; reduction of cupreine gives dihydrocupreine, which lacks activity.
(c)
• Alkylating the 6-hydroxyl of dihydrocupreine gives alkyl hydrocupreine (optochin), which restores activity.
• Configuration at C2 and C9 matters: activity is high in erythro forms (quinine, quinidine, cinchonine, cinchonidine) and low or absent in threo forms (9-epi compounds).
• Loss of the C9 OH (quinidinone) abolishes activity; breaking the quinuclidine ring at C2 (quinicine) abolishes activity.
(d)
Optochin (alkyl hydrocupreine) restores activity.

(a)
Binding (CD4 then CCR5 or CXCR4), fusion (gp41), reverse transcription, integration, replication/transcription, assembly, budding and maturation by protease.
(b)
• NRTIs are phosphorylated to 5'-triphosphates, compete with host triphosphates as false substrates for reverse transcriptase and cause chain termination (zidovudine, lamivudine, tenofovir, abacavir, emtricitabine).
• NNRTIs bind a hydrophobic pocket near the catalytic site, locking reverse transcriptase inactive (efavirenz, nevirapine, etravirine, rilpivirine).
