• PIs bind the cleavage site of the inactive polyproteins, giving defective non-infectious virions (atazanavir, darunavir, lopinavir, ritonavir).
• INSTIs inhibit integrase (dolutegravir, raltegravir); fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide binds gp41 (ibalizumab binds CD4); maraviroc blocks CCR5-gp120; maturation inhibitors block polyprotein conversion; lenacapavir blocks the capsid.
(c)
• Mammalian alpha-DNA polymerase is relatively resistant to NRTIs, but mitochondrial gamma-DNA polymerase is fairly sensitive, accounting for toxicity (lactic acidosis).
• Maraviroc needs a tropism test because some HIV enters through CXCR4; ritonavir is used as a booster for other PIs and is not effective alone; PIs are 80-95% metabolised by CYP450.
(d)
• NNRTIs (efavirenz, nevirapine) have a low genetic barrier: a single mutation causes class resistance; HIV-2 is inactive to NNRTIs (does not respond to nevirapine).
• NRTIs: lactic acidosis, anaemia (AZT), neuropathy and lipodystrophy (d4T), hypersensitivity (ABC); NNRTIs: rash, CNS effects (EFV), hepatotoxicity (NVP).
• PIs: paraesthesia, rhabdomyolysis, lipodystrophy, hyperglycaemia; atazanavir raises bilirubin; INSTIs: headache, nausea, diarrhoea, rare hepatitis.
• Enfuvirtide: injection-site and hypersensitivity reactions, flu-like symptoms; maraviroc: fever, insomnia, cough.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the HIV life cycle steps.
(b) State the mechanism of action of each class of antiretroviral with examples.
(c) Relate to examples and explain the cellular basis of selectivity and toxicity.
(d) State the resistance and adverse effects of each class.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Artesunate and dihydroartemisinin are water-soluble (artesunate as sodium salt: oral, IM, IV); artemether is lipid-soluble (oral and IM); arteether is more lipophilic than artemether and crosses the BBB.
(b)
SAR: H at C-1 and C-7 essential; substitution at C-2 and C-3 loses activity; CH3 at C-4 increases activity; the peroxide linkage is indispensable, so its removal abolishes activity; the C-12 ketone may not be essential.
(c)
• Artemether (with lumefantrine) and artesunate (with amodiaquine) in ACTs; IV artesunate first line for severe malaria; arteether for cerebral malaria; dihydroartemisinin with piperaquine; all are converted to the active metabolite dihydroartemisinin.
• Artemisinin soluble derivatives find great clinical use because the parent is almost insoluble in water.
(d)
• To obtain soluble, administrable derivatives (oral, parenteral, rectal) active against chloroquine-resistant strains with little cross-resistance to quinolines.
• Artemisinin has no UV chromophore, so analytical assay is by HPLC-MS-MS.
questions.question:
Artemisinin is poorly soluble in water and short-acting. Chemists prepare the water-soluble artesunate, the oil-soluble artemether and the more lipophilic arteether, and test removal of the endoperoxide and substitutions at C-2 and C-3.
(a) Predict the effect on solubility, administration and activity.
(b) Justify through SAR.
(c) Name the derivatives and their uses.
(d) State the rationale for the modification.

(a) Explain how antivirals differ from viricides and describe viral replication.
(b) Classify antiviral drugs by mechanism with examples.
(c) State the mechanism of each class and relate to examples.
(d) State the uses, adverse effects and limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antivirals inhibit development or reproduction of viruses rather than destroying them; viricides (Lysol, sodium hypochlorite, benzalkonium chloride) destroy virus particles and are not medication.
• Replication: entry, transcription, translation, assembly, budding/release; retroviruses use reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease.
(b)
Classes: viral DNA polymerase inhibitors, neuraminidase inhibitors, coat disassembly (M2) inhibitors, endonuclease inhibitors, NS protease inhibitors.
(c)
• Aciclovir, valaciclovir and penciclovir are guanosine analogues phosphorylated first by viral thymidylate kinase then host kinases; the triphosphates compete with GTP and cause chain termination.
• Ribavirin is a nucleoside analogue (alters nucleotide pool or interferes with mRNA synthesis); foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analogue binding the pyrophosphate site of viral DNA polymerase.
• Oseltamivir, zanamivir, laninamivir and peramivir inhibit viral neuraminidase, preventing release of new virions (cleavage of the bond to host sialic acid).
• Amantadine and rimantadine block the M2 ion channel, preventing H+ influx and acidification needed for disassembly; baloxavir marboxil (prodrug) inhibits cap-dependent endonuclease.
• HCV agents: NS3/4A protease inhibitors, NS5A inhibitors, NS5B inhibitor sofosbuvir; combinations such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir treat all six genotypes.
(d)
• Uses: aciclovir for herpes; ganciclovir, valganciclovir, cidofovir for CMV; ribavirin for RSV, Lassa fever and hepatitis C; neuraminidase inhibitors for influenza A and B early; M2 blockers only influenza A.
• Neuraminidase inhibitors cause GI symptoms; amantadine dizziness, slurred speech and insomnia; neuraminidase inhibitors work only in early infection.
• HPV has no effective drugs (treatment is cryotherapy, laser); several viral diseases lack cure; dormant viruses (herpes) recur when the immune system is compromised.

questions.question:
A traveller to a malaria-endemic area is given a fixed combination of an analogue of ubiquinone and a biguanide prodrug for prophylaxis.
(a) Identify the drugs and their doses.
(b) Justify the combination.
(c) Identify the pharmacogenetic or interaction issue and the toxicity.
(d) State the metabolic basis and monitoring/precautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Atovaquone (an analogue of ubiquinone) and proguanil (Malarone): 1000/400 mg ATQ/PG as prophylaxis, or taken for 3 days for treatment; atovaquone is not used alone except with proguanil.
(b)
• Atovaquone inhibits the malarial cytochrome bc1 complex, collapsing the mitochondrial membrane potential; death follows indirect inhibition of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (pyrimidine biosynthesis).
• Proguanil, acting through a mechanism distinct from cycloguanil, lowers the concentration at which atovaquone inhibits pyrimidine synthesis and collapses the membrane potential; the synergy is due to the prodrug itself, not to cycloguanil.
(c)
• Proguanil has little activity itself but is oxidised to cycloguanil (DHFR inhibitor) by CYP2C19, which is polymorphic; poor metabolisers (*2, *3 alleles) occur in 4.8% of Nigerians studied.
• Proguanil is highly effective against pre-erythrocytic forms of P. falciparum and has a slow action on erythrocytic forms; it must be taken daily; it is more concentrated in the kidney than the liver.
(d)
PG Cmax 150-220 ng/ml, Tmax 3 h, half-life 14-17 h, bioavailability 70-90%, protein binding about 75%; assay by non-aqueous titration with perchloric acid and mercuric acetate.

(a)
Amphotericin B and flucytosine; in combination they are the treatment of choice for cryptococcal meningitis.
(b)
• Synergy: amphotericin-induced damage to the fungal plasma membrane enhances flucytosine uptake; flucytosine, selectively taken up through cytosine permeases, is converted to 5-FU and inhibits thymidylate synthase (DNA synthesis).
• Flucytosine has wide distribution and excellent CNS penetration, whereas amphotericin B penetrates the CSF poorly (intrathecal therapy may be needed for meningeal disease).
(c)
• Amphotericin B: infusion reactions (cytokine storm), renal toxicity (cumulative, dose-related; avoid aminoglycosides and cyclosporine), hypokalaemia, anaemia; lipid formulations reduce toxicity.
• Flucytosine: dose-dependent bone marrow suppression (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia), nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, hepatic dysfunction; contraindicated in pregnancy.
(d)
Pre-treatment with antipyretics or hydrocortisone and slower infusion minimise infusion reactions; maintain euvolaemia, replace electrolytes; monitor blood count, renal and liver function.
questions.question:
An HIV-positive patient with cryptococcal meningitis is given a polyene together with a fluorinated pyrimidine antimetabolite.
(a) Identify the drugs.
(b) Justify the combination.
(c) Identify the interactions and toxicity limits.
(d) State the monitoring parameters and precautions.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Proguanil (chloroguanide, Paludrine) is 1-(4-chlorophenyl)-5-isopropylbiguanide hydrochloride, reported as the first antimalarial antifolate in 1945 (ICI); a synthetic biguanide derivative.
(b)
• A white crystalline solid sparingly soluble in water; molecular weight 290.22, formula C11H16ClN5.HCl.
• SAR: halogen substitution (Cl, Br) increases activity; a second Cl on the phenyl ring (chloroproguanil) enhances activity but is more toxic.
• Assay: non-aqueous titration with 0.1 M perchloric acid with mercuric acetate to remove chloride, potentiometric end point.
(c)
• Through cycloguanil it inhibits parasitic DHFR, disrupting folate synthesis and blocking purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis for DNA, so nuclear division fails at schizont formation in erythrocytes and liver; effective against pre-erythrocytic forms of P. falciparum.
• With atovaquone (Malarone) the synergy is due to proguanil itself, not cycloguanil; chlorproguanil with dapsone (LapDap) acts as a prodrug like SP.
(d)
• Proguanil has little antimalarial activity but is oxidised in the liver to cycloguanil (CYP2C19), which inhibits DHFR.
• Disposition: Cmax 150-220 ng/ml, Tmax 3 h, t1/2 14-17 h, bioavailability 70-90%, protein binding about 75%, more concentrated in kidney than liver; cycloguanil Cmax 12-69 ng/ml, Tmax 5-7 h.
(e)
• CYP2C19 is polymorphic: *1 wild type (extensive metabolisers); *2 and *3 variant alleles (poor metabolisers); Nigerians had 4.8% PMs and 4.7% with mutated alleles in healthy subjects (*2), and 1% PM alleles in sickle cell patients using it daily.
• It is the sequential-blocking partner of sulphonamides and dapsone in the folate pathway (with pyrimethamine).
• Slow action against erythrocytic forms; no action on P. vivax hypnozoites; must be taken daily.
questions.question:
(a) Give the chemical name, class and structure of proguanil.
(b) State its properties, SAR and assay.
(c) State its mechanism of action and uses.
(d) Describe the structural basis of its metabolism and activation.
(e) Explain the basis of pharmacogenetic variability and loss of activity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
There is no cure; clinical goals are halting progression and preventing OIs; virological goal is viral load below 50 copies/ml; immunological goal is CD4 above 500 cells/mm3; epidemiological goal is reduced transmission.
(b)
• NRTIs (abacavir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, tenofovir, zidovudine), NNRTIs (efavirenz, etravirine, nevirapine, rilpivirine), PIs (atazanavir, darunavir, lopinavir, ritonavir), INSTIs (dolutegravir, raltegravir, elvitegravir, cabotegravir).
• Fusion inhibitor (enfuvirtide), CCR5 antagonist (maraviroc), maturation inhibitors, and capsid inhibitor (lenacapavir).
(c)
• HAART combines at least three ARVs from at least two classes, attacking the virus from different directions, stopping replication and reducing resistance; two NRTIs form the backbone plus a PI or INSTI as base.
• First line (naive): preferred TDF + 3TC + DTG; alternative ABC + 3TC + DTG; second line: TDF + 3TC + ATV/r or AZT + 3TC + ATV/r (or DRV/r); third line DRV/r + DTG with or without NRTIs.
(d)
• Substitution replaces one or two drugs of the same class for toxicity, co-morbidity, pregnancy or interaction; switching replaces two or more drugs from another class for failure.
• Failure (after at least 6 months): clinical (new OI or malignancy), immunological (CD4 fall more than 30% from peak, return to baseline, or persistently below 100), virological (plasma viral load 1000 copies/ml or more on consecutive measurements).
(e)
• NRTI class effect lactic acidosis; abacavir hypersensitivity (do not rechallenge); TDF renal toxicity and reduced bone density; zidovudine anaemia and neutropenia.
• Efavirenz CNS effects and teratogenicity concern; nevirapine hepatotoxicity and severe rash; atazanavir hyperbilirubinaemia; lopinavir pancreatitis; dolutegravir hepatotoxicity and neural tube defects early in pregnancy.
• Rifampicin with PIs gives high risk of liver toxicity and sub-therapeutic levels; avoid AZT in anaemia, TDF in renal disease, NVP in women with CD4 above 250.
• Combinations to avoid: ddI + d4T, d4T + AZT (antagonistic), ddI + TDF; 3TC and FTC are equivalent.
• Monitoring is clinical, laboratory (viral load, CD4) and adherence; virological suppression is the key outcome.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the goals of antiretroviral therapy.
(b) List the classes of antiretrovirals with examples.
(c) State the first-line, second-line and third-line regimens and the rationale for combination.
(d) State how treatment failure is defined and how substitution differs from switching.
(e) State the adverse effects, interactions and precautions of key drugs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Artemether plus lumefantrine; other WHO-recommended ACTs: artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, artesunate-mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine and artesunate-pyronaridine.
(b)
• Artemether is absorbed fast (Tmax up to 1 h) and cleared rapidly (t1/2 2-3 h) giving rapid parasite reduction; lumefantrine absorbs slowly (Tmax 4-8 h) with t1/2 3-10 days, preventing recrudescence.
• Monotherapy for under 7 days is frequently followed by recrudescence; the dual effect may reduce selective pressure for resistance; a 3-day course encourages compliance. 28-day cure rate 100% for AL versus 54.5% for artemether alone.
(c)
Fatty food increases absorption (artemether 2-fold, lumefantrine up to 16-fold); both are metabolised by CYP3A4; lumefantrine is up to 99.9% protein bound and adsorbed by antacids.
(d)
• Day 7 lumefantrine level of 280 ng/mL or below predicts treatment failure, and AUC of lumefantrine and time above MIC determine cure.
• Lumefantrine levels are lower in children; newer guides are needed for children and pregnant women. Artemisinins prolong QT, so avoid with drugs of similar potential.
questions.question:
A malaria programme in Nigeria adopts artemether-lumefantrine rather than artemisinin monotherapy.
(a) Identify the drugs involved and other recommended ACTs.
(b) Justify the combination (pharmacokinetic complementarity, resistance, recrudescence).
(c) Identify interaction or special administration issues.
(d) State the monitoring parameter predictive of failure and the precautions.

(a) Describe the folate pathway and its importance in bacteria and humans.
(b) State the mechanism of sulphonamides, trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole.
(c) Relate each part to the examples given (PAS, dapsone, pyrimethamine, proguanil, sulphadoxine).
(d) Explain the selective toxicity and state the resistance mechanisms and adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Folate is required for DNA synthesis in bacteria and humans; humans cannot synthesise it and obtain it from the diet via uptake mechanisms, whereas most bacteria lack these and synthesise it de novo.
• Pathway: PABA plus pteridine form dihydropteroate (dihydropteroate synthetase), then dihydrofolate, reduced by dihydrofolate reductase (NADPH) to tetrahydrofolate, needed for purines, pyrimidines and thymidylate.
(b)
• Sulphonamides competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthetase (mimicking PABA, reversible, bacteriostatic).
• Trimethoprim, a trimethoxybenzylpyrimidine resembling the pteridine moiety, selectively inhibits bacterial DHFR; it is bacteriostatic.
• Co-trimoxazole blocks the pathway at two points (sequential blockade); the drugs potentiate each other (synergism) and the effect is bactericidal.
(c)
• Para-aminosalicylic acid is a PABA/sulphonamide-like substrate of dihydropteroate synthase (folP1/P2); dapsone is a PABA analogue and competitive inhibitor of dihydropteroate synthase.
• Pyrimethamine and proguanil (via cycloguanil) inhibit DHFR; sulphadoxine inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; sulphadoxine plus pyrimethamine act synergistically.
(d)
• Bacterial DHFR is about 50,000 times more sensitive to trimethoprim than the human enzyme, giving selective toxicity.
• Resistance: DHFR altered so it becomes insensitive to trimethoprim; resistant strains produce more PABA; mutations in DHFR and DHPS genes cause resistance to sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine.
• Trimethoprim: folate deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia on long-term use, nausea, vomiting, blood disorders and rashes.
• Sulphonamides: crystalluria, rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, kernicterus.
• Co-trimoxazole is effective for P. jirovecii pneumonia, shigellosis, systemic salmonella infections and UTI.

(a)
• Antimetabolites: folate analogs (methotrexate, pemetrexed), purine analogs (fludarabine, 6-MP, 6-TG), adenosine analogs (cladribine, pentostatin), pyrimidine analogs (cytarabine, 5-FU, gemcitabine, capecitabine, floxuridine) and hydroxyurea.
• Natural products: antitumour antibiotics (bleomycin, dactinomycin, anthracyclines, mitomycin), epipodophyllotoxins (etoposide, teniposide), microtubule agents (vinca alkaloids, taxanes), camptothecin analogs (irinotecan, topotecan), asparaginase.
(b)
• Antimetabolites are structural analogues of nucleic acid precursors that compete with metabolites for an enzyme's catalytic or regulatory site, or substitute for a metabolite; they act in S-phase.
• Methotrexate is a folic acid analogue; folate must be reduced by DHFR to THF to give one-carbon units for nucleotides; MTX polyglutamates are retained in tumour cells.
• Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (inhibiting DNA synthesis without interfering with RNA or protein synthesis), though the precise mechanism is not known.
(c)
• Bleomycin intercalates DNA at G-C and G-T sequences; anthracyclines intercalate and inhibit topoisomerases I and II; etoposide inhibits topoisomerase II (G2 arrest); camptothecins inhibit topoisomerase I and interrupt DNA elongation.
• Vinca alkaloids (from Vinca rosea) enhance microtubular disassembly (M-phase); taxanes (semisynthetic from yew) promote microtubular assembly and stability.
(d)
• Rapidly proliferating cells are most sensitive; this explains selectivity for tumours with high growth fraction and toxicity to marrow and GI mucosa.
• Methotrexate: mucositis, GI ulceration, myelosuppression, pulmonary fibrosis, nerve root irritation and convulsions (intrathecal), cirrhosis and osteoporosis (chronic).
• Vincristine: peripheral neuropathy, ileus, SIADH, myelosuppression; etoposide: nausea, thrombocytopenia, alopecia, leucopenia.
• Resistance: intrinsic or acquired (dose, combination, mutation, multidrug-resistance gene).
questions.question:
(a) Classify the antimetabolites and natural-product anticancer drugs.
(b) State the mechanism of action of each group.
(c) Relate these to the examples given.
(d) Explain the cellular basis of selectivity and the main adverse effects and resistance.

A transplant patient is given a drug that is a prodrug of mercaptopurine, and the patient is also taking allopurinol.
(a) Identify the drug and its relation to the parent.
(b) Predict the effect of allopurinol on the drug's inactivation and the consequence.
(c) Justify through the metabolic pathway.
(d) Name related drugs and state the rationale for the modification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Azathioprine, a prodrug of mercaptopurine that functions as an antimetabolite; azathioprine and mercaptopurine interfere with purine metabolism at steps required for lymphoid cell proliferation.
(b)
Drug inactivation depends on xanthine oxidase, so the dose must be reduced in patients receiving allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) to avoid toxicity.
(c)
Inhibiting the enzyme that inactivates the drug raises its level; the main toxicity is bone marrow suppression, and hepatic dysfunction (very high ALP, mild jaundice) can occur, particularly with pre-existing hepatic dysfunction.
(d)
Related drug: mercaptopurine (6-MP), also used in haemato-oncology; azathioprine blocks cellular immunity and serum antibody responses and benefits maintenance of renal allografts.

questions.question:
A patient with chronic myeloid leukaemia (Philadelphia chromosome) responds to imatinib and later relapses.
(a) Identify the likely mechanism of resistance and the drug.
(b) Name the drug class affected.
(c) Explain the basis in terms of the target.
(d) State the strategy to overcome it and justify it.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Imatinib, a 2-phenylaminopyrimidine tyrosine kinase inhibitor that inhibits the BCR-ABL1 fusion protein from t(9;22), with inhibition of PDGF and c-kit; relapse is imatinib resistance.
(b)
Molecularly targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).
(c)
The target is the tyrosine kinase activity of BCR-ABL1.
(d)
• Dasatinib and nilotinib are used for imatinib-resistant CML.
• Imatinib adverse effects (nausea, muscle cramps, oedema, hepatotoxicity) and interactions (dexamethasone reduces its effectiveness) are given.

(a)
Efavirenz (an NNRTI), whose controversial teratogenicity makes it a drug to avoid in pregnancy; efavirenz also causes CNS toxicity (headache, fatigue, sleep disturbance, dizziness, depression) and rash.
(b)
NNRTIs bind reverse transcriptase near the catalytic site and denature it.
(c)
Efavirenz and nevirapine have a low genetic barrier (a single mutation leads to class resistance) and are inactive against HIV-2; nevirapine causes hepatotoxicity especially in women with CD4 above 250.
(d)
• Avoid efavirenz in women of child-bearing potential and in the first trimester; AZT is the preferred NRTI in pregnancy; dolutegravir is associated with neural tube defects early in pregnancy.
• Mother continues the pre-conception HAART through pregnancy, breastfeeding and thereafter; infant gets nevirapine started 6-72 hours after birth until one week after stopping breastfeeding (6 weeks if not breastfed).
• High-risk infants (mother not virally suppressed) also get zidovudine for 6 weeks, and breastfed high-risk infants a further 6 weeks of dual prophylaxis; scheduled caesarean can reduce transmission; cotrimoxazole from 6 weeks of age.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman living with HIV, planning to breastfeed, is on a regimen containing efavirenz.
(a) Identify the drug and the adverse effect or concern.
(b) Explain the mechanism and risk.
(c) State the pharmacokinetic or class basis.
(d) State the management, preferred alternatives and infant prophylaxis.

(a) Define bacterial resistance and describe how it spreads.
(b) Describe the biochemical mechanisms of resistance with examples.
(c) Relate these mechanisms to named antibiotic classes.
(d) Explain the strategies that limit resistance and their trade-offs or limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bacteria are resistant if growth is not halted by the maximum level of antibiotic tolerated by the host.
• Resistance spreads by transfer of bacteria between people, by transfer of resistance genes between bacteria (plasmids, R-factors, via transduction or conjugation) and between genetic elements within bacteria (transposons).
(b)
• Production of enzymes that inactivate the drug (beta-lactamases, acetyltransferases for chloramphenicol, kinases for aminoglycosides).
• Alteration of binding sites (ribosomes: aminoglycosides, erythromycin, penicillin); reduced drug uptake (tetracyclines); altered enzymes (DHFR insensitive to trimethoprim).
(c)
• Aminoglycosides: modifying enzymes, efflux, 16S rRNA methylation; quinolones: gyrase/topoisomerase mutations, efflux, no modifying enzymes; macrolides: methylation of ribosomes with cross-resistance.
• Rifampicin: rpoB mutations; isoniazid: KatG mutation; sulphonamides: resistant strains produce more PABA; amphotericin B: decreased ergosterol content; azoles: mutated P450 and efflux transporters.
• MRSA is resistant to all antibiotics except vancomycin and possibly ciprofloxacin, rifampin and imipenem/cilastatin.
(d)
• Strategies: single most specific agent to reduce superinfection and resistance; combination in TB and HIV to prevent resistant organisms; susceptibility testing (disc diffusion, MIC, E-test); stewardship.
• Beta-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam) restore beta-lactam activity; amikacin and netilmicin resist aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes.
• Limitations: combinations may cause superinfection, antagonism or increased toxicity; prophylaxis restricted to situations where benefit outweighs risk.
• Resistance to vancomycin and artemisinin has emerged, showing that resistance can follow even last-line agents.

(a)
Meninges (pia, arachnoid, dura) with subarachnoid CSF; CSF flows unidirectionally so intrathecal antibiotics barely reach the ventricles; the blood-brain barrier (tight junctions) excludes poorly lipid-soluble drugs and inflammation increases penetration.
(b)
Neonates: group B streptococci, E. coli, Listeria; 1 month-4 years: H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis; elderly: pneumococci, meningococci, enteric Gram-negatives, Listeria; post-neurosurgery: enteric Gram-negatives, staphylococci, Pseudomonas.
(c)
• Neonates: ampicillin + cefotaxime (alternative ampicillin + gentamicin); infants and children, and adults 2-50 years: cefotaxime or ceftriaxone + vancomycin (alternative vancomycin + rifampin + aztreonam).
• Elderly: ampicillin, cefotaxime or ceftriaxone + vancomycin; post-neurosurgical or penetrating head trauma: vancomycin + ceftazidime (alternative cefepime or meropenem); risk factors: vancomycin + ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + ampicillin.
(d)
• Very good penetration: chloramphenicol, metronidazole, TMP-SMX, linezolid; good when inflamed: penicillins, cephalosporins, meropenem, aztreonam, rifampin; poor: aminoglycosides, macrolides, clindamycin, vancomycin.
• Aminoglycosides have a low therapeutic index and reduced activity in acidic purulent CSF; oral cephalosporins cannot be recommended.
• Dexamethasone reduces cerebral oedema and TNF-alpha and IL-1 release; given before or with the first antibiotic dose in adults with pneumococcal meningitis and in children; adverse effects: GI bleeding, mental changes, hyperglycaemia.
(e)
• Duration: N. meningitidis and H. influenzae 7 days, S. pneumoniae 10-14, group B streptococci 14-21, Listeria 21 or more, Gram-negative bacilli 21 days.
• Monitor temperature, mental status, daily CBC, electrolytes, glucose, renal function; CSF culture is usually sterile after 18-24 hours; repeat lumbar puncture if the response is inadequate.
• Beta-lactams may transiently amplify inflammation by lysing cell walls, attenuated by corticosteroids.
• SIADH (hyponatraemia) needs fluid restriction and, if severe, 3% NaCl.
• High doses raise the likelihood of adverse effects; a CT scan is needed before lumbar puncture in patients with papilloedema, seizure or focal deficit.

(a) Describe the anatomical and physiological barriers relevant to treatment of meningitis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• DNA viruses (herpesviruses, varicella zoster, HBV, CMV, HPV, adenovirus) replicate in the nucleus; RNA viruses (HIV, HCV, influenza, measles, rabies) use RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; retroviruses use reverse transcriptase and integrase.
• Dormant viruses (herpes labialis, zoster) recur when immunity falls; host defences include intact skin, T-lymphocytes, NK cells and gene silencing.
(b)
• Herpes: aciclovir; CMV: ganciclovir, valganciclovir, valaciclovir, cidofovir, foscarnet; RSV, Lassa fever, hepatitis C: ribavirin; influenza: neuraminidase inhibitors, amantadine/rimantadine, baloxavir.
• Hepatitis C: NS3/4A inhibitors, NS5A inhibitors, sofosbuvir; combinations glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Mavyret), sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa), sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir (Vosevi); HIV: HAART.
(c)
• Aciclovir, valaciclovir, penciclovir (guanosine analogues) are phosphorylated first by viral thymidylate kinase, then by host kinases, and their triphosphates compete with GTP causing chain termination; this makes them selective for infected cells.
• Foscarnet binds the pyrophosphate site of DNA polymerase; ribavirin alters the nucleotide pool or mRNA synthesis; neuraminidase inhibitors stop release; M2 blockers stop disassembly; baloxavir inhibits viral mRNA initiation.
• HCV protease inhibitors block cleavage of the polyprotein into functional proteins; combination covers all six genotypes.
(d)
• Neuraminidase inhibitors: GI effects, only early infection; amantadine: dizziness, slurred speech, insomnia, no action on influenza B.
• Viral infections with no effective antiviral drugs include HPV (warts treated by cryotherapy, laser); HIV has no cure but viral load can be undetectable.
• Antiviral drugs inhibit viruses rather than destroying them, unlike viricides.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the types of viruses and viral replication relevant to drug action.
(b) List the antiviral drugs for herpes, CMV, influenza, hepatitis C and HIV.
(c) State the mechanism of each and the rationale for the choice.
(d) State the adverse effects, resistance and viral diseases lacking effective drugs.

(a) State the subgroups of protein synthesis inhibitors and their ribosomal targets.
(b) Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides and chloramphenicol.
(c) Relate each to its examples and explain the basis of selective toxicity or bactericidal versus bacteriostatic action.
(d) State the main resistance mechanisms and adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Subgroups: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides, clindamycin and amphenicols; aminoglycosides and tetracyclines inhibit the 30S subunit, macrolides the 50S subunit.
• Chloramphenicol binds the 50S subunit; linezolid-type oxazolidinones block aminoacyl-tRNA interaction with the A site of the peptidyl transferase centre.
(b)
• Aminoglycosides bind irreversibly to 30S, block initiation, cause mRNA mis-coding and break up polysomes; tetracyclines block aminoacyl-tRNA access to the acceptor site.
• Macrolides bind reversibly to 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and block translocation of the elongating polypeptide; chloramphenicol blocks binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the 50S acceptor site.
(c)
• Examples: streptomycin, gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, netilmicin; tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline; erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin.
• Aminoglycosides are bactericidal (unique among protein synthesis inhibitors), with a post-antibiotic effect; tetracyclines, macrolides (usually) and chloramphenicol are bacteriostatic.
(d)
• Aminoglycoside resistance: inactivating enzymes (phosphorylation, acetylation, adenylation; plasmid-mediated, the most important), efflux/decreased uptake, 16S rRNA methylation.
• Tetracycline resistance: reduced concentrating mechanism, efflux pumps, plasmid-mediated ribosomal protection protein; macrolide resistance: altered target sites by ribosomal methylation, with cross-resistance among macrolides.
• Aminoglycoside adverse effects: nephrotoxicity, irreversible ototoxicity, neuromuscular paralysis; tetracyclines: GI, photosensitivity, tooth discolouration.
• Macrolide adverse effects: GI (up to 33%), cholestatic hepatitis; chloramphenicol: marrow toxicity, gray baby syndrome.
• Monitoring and avoidance of renal toxins are essential for aminoglycosides.

(a)
Azoles are subdivided into imidazoles (ketoconazole, clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole, butoconazole, oxiconazole, sertaconazole, sulconazole, tioconazole), triazoles (itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, terconazole, ravuconazole) and thiazoles (abafungin).
(b)
An azole is a five-membered aromatic ring with two double bonds, one nitrogen and at least one other non-carbon atom (imidazole, oxazole or thiazole); a triazole contains three nitrogens in the ring.
(c)
• The azoles (except abafungin) inhibit the fungus-specific CYP450 enzyme 14-alpha-sterol demethylase, blocking the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol.
• Decreased ergosterol and accumulation of 14-alpha-methyl sterol disrupt the packing of phospholipid acyl chains, so membrane-associated enzymes (including electron transport) fail and the cell dies.
• Abafungin instead inhibits fungal sterol 24-C-methyltransferase (Erg6) and is used topically.
(d)
• Azoles are not completely selective for the fungal P450 and also inhibit hepatic P450 enzymes, so drug-drug interactions are important.
• Ketoconazole potently inhibits hepatic P450 and, at therapeutic doses, adrenal and gonadal P450 (17,20-lyase, side-chain cleavage), lowering steroid hormone synthesis; high doses cause adrenal insufficiency, gynecomastia and impotence.
• Voriconazole inhibits hepatic P450 (lower cyclosporine or tacrolimus doses) and is contraindicated with ritonavir, rifampin and rifabutin.
(e)
• Ketoconazole needs gastric acid for absorption (not for achlorhydria, antacids, H2-blockers, PPIs), penetrates CSF and urine poorly, is hepatotoxic and is not effective for aspergillosis.
• Fluconazole has nearly 100% oral bioavailability independent of gastric pH, diffuses into CSF, sputum, urine and saliva, is renally excreted, and is the drug of choice for systemic candidiasis and cryptococcal and coccidioidal meningitis.
• Fluconazole is not effective against aspergillosis; resistance develops readily (mutated P450 and efflux transporters), and it raises levels of amitriptyline, cyclosporine, phenytoin and warfarin.
• Fluconazole 150 mg single dose treats vaginal candidiasis; triazoles have replaced amphotericin B in systemic mycoses with less liver toxicity than ketoconazole.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the azole antifungals with examples.
(b) Describe the general structure and pharmacophore of an azole.
(c) State the mechanism of action.
(d) Explain the chemical or biochemical basis of selectivity limits, interactions and toxicity.
(e) Distinguish ketoconazole from fluconazole.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Select drugs active as single agents, especially those inducing complete remission; use drugs with different mechanisms and additive or synergistic cytotoxicity.
• Combine drugs with different dose-limiting toxicities so full doses can be used; use each at optimal dose and schedule; give at consistent intervals with a treatment-free period as short as possible.
• Use drugs with different patterns of resistance to minimise cross-resistance.
(b)
Examples: alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide), antimetabolites (methotrexate, 6-MP), vinca alkaloids (vincristine, M-phase), anthracyclines (doxorubicin) and corticosteroids; regimen means timed cycles and courses, with neoadjuvant or adjuvant use.
(c)
• Cell cycle-specific agents (antimetabolites S-phase, vinca M-phase) increase kill with exposure; non-specific agents (alkylators, platinum) with dose; combining them covers different phases.
• Bone marrow suppression determines the upper limit of tolerable chemotherapy and rapidly proliferating cells are most sensitive; therapeutic index is low, with marrow and GI cells most sensitive.
• Supportive care is needed: IV fluids, allopurinol or rasburicase for tumour lysis, antiemetics, antibiotic prophylaxis for febrile neutropenia, G-CSF, bisphosphonates, anticoagulation.
• Resistance may be intrinsic or acquired; causes include inadequate dosage, wrong combination, mutation, multidrug resistance gene and poor exposure of large necrotic tumours.
(d)
• Antimicrobial combinations are indicated for preventing resistance (TB, HIV), polymicrobial infections, critically ill patients and synergism (enterococcal endocarditis).
• A single specific agent is otherwise advisable to reduce superinfection and resistance; combinations may cause superinfection, antagonism or toxicity.
• HAART uses at least three ARVs; TB short-course therapy uses four drugs then two.
questions.question:

(b) Relate them to the examples of drugs and regimens given.
(c) Explain why combinations improve efficacy and state the trade-offs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Dapsone (DDS) is a sulphone: 4,4'-sulphonyldianiline (diamino diphenyl sulphone), the oldest, cheapest and most widely used antileprosy drug, with antibacterial, antiprotozoal and antifungal effects.
(b)
Assay: amperometric titration with 0.1M sodium nitrite.
(c)
• A structural analogue of PABA and competitive inhibitor of dihydropteroate synthase, inhibiting folate synthesis; leprostatic (bactericidal and bacteriostatic against mycobacteria).
• Part of a 2-drug regimen for paucibacillary and a 3-drug regimen for multibacillary leprosy.
(d)
• Absorption is complete orally; highly bound to plasma protein and concentrated in infected muscle; metabolised by acetylation (genetic polymorphism, slow and fast acetylators) and N-oxidation with glucuronic and sulphate conjugation.
• Acedapsone replaces NH2 with CH3CO, a latent form that is less toxic.
(e)
• Resistance reported in Southeast Asia, most commonly to dapsone, after prior monotherapy; of 230 strains tested 3 relapsing strains were resistant, 2 dapsone-resistant and 1 dapsone- and rifampicin-resistant.
• Toxicity: sulphone syndrome (fever, dermatitis, methaemoglobinaemia), haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency, peripheral neuropathy.
• Chlorproguanil-dapsone (LapDap) was combined for malaria, acting like SP.
• Dapsone is also used for malaria as a sulfone.
• Almost all antileprosy drugs have adverse effects that limit their use.

(b) State its chemical properties and assay.
(c) State its mechanism of action.
(d) Describe its metabolism and the structural modification that gives acedapsone.
(e) Explain the basis of resistance and toxicity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antiseptics are used on living tissues with limited spectrum; disinfectants are for inanimate objects, bactericidal, with rapid irreversible lethal effect and possible adverse effect on tissues; both have different chemical structures.
• Groups: alcohols, phenols, biphenols, acids and derivatives, hydroxyquinolines, halogens, amidines and guanidines, quaternary ammonium compounds, metals, dyes, peroxides, nitrofurans.
(b)
• Alcohols and phenols act by protein denaturation and coagulation; hydroxyquinolines (chloroxine) by metal chelation; QACs by cell membrane disruption, protein denaturation and enzyme inactivation.
• Peroxides (H2O2, KMnO4, ozone, sodium perborate) are oxidising agents releasing nascent oxygen.
(c)
• Phenol SAR: electron-withdrawing groups (halogens) increase activity (p-chlorophenol, hexachlorophene).
• QACs (benzalkonium chloride, benzethonium chloride) have cationic surface activity and broad spectrum; a long aliphatic chain (optimal C12) and cationic head are needed.
(d)
• Halogens: iodine compounds; chlorine compounds (chloramine-T forms hypochlorous acid; halazone for water purification); amidines: chlorhexidine (preservative, dental plaque), chloroazodine (urinary).
• Dyes (acridine, thiazine, azo, triphenylmethane) are coloured topical agents for skin infections.
• Metals: mercury (thiomersal) and silver (AgNO3, antibacterial at low concentration) are no longer in use because of toxicity.
• Nitrofurans are used for UTI but limited by hypersensitivity; formaldehyde is a miscellaneous agent.
• Acids: acetic and salicylic acid, with sodium benzoate, p-hydroxybenzoates and parabens as derivatives.
questions.question:
(a) Distinguish antiseptics from disinfectants and classify them.
(b) Describe the general structure and mode of action of the main groups.
(c) Explain the SAR and chemical basis of activity of phenols and quaternary ammonium compounds.
(d) Distinguish the halogen compounds, dyes and metals and state their limits.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acid stability and oral activity
• A depot preparation with prolonged action
• Pro-drugs that hydrolyse in vivo (not in vitro) to ampicillin.
(b)
A powerful electron-attracting group on the amino side chain prevents acidic rearrangement (acid-stable); a bulky side chain gives penicillinase resistance by steric hindrance; high hydrophilic character of the amino side chain gives broad Gram-negative action.
(c)
• Acid stable: ampicillin, amoxicillin, penicillin V, cloxacillin; depot: procaine penicillin G (once daily), benzathine penicillin G (once monthly); ester pro-drugs: bacampicillin, pivampicillin, talampicillin.
• Acid-stable and penicillinase-resistant: cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin (bulky electron-attracting side chains); extended spectrum antipseudomonal: carbenicillin, ticarcillin, piperacillin.
(d)
• Natural penicillins have low toxicity and high activity but are inactivated by penicillinase and acid, so synthetic modifications improve activity and bioavailability.
• Penicillin G is given IM, penicillin V orally, because route depends on gastric acid stability.
questions.question:
Benzylpenicillin is acid-labile and short-acting. A chemist (a) introduces a strong electron-attracting group on the amino side chain, (b) converts it to a procaine or benzathine salt, and (c) forms an ester at the carboxyl of ampicillin.
(a) Predict the effect of each modification.
(b) Justify through SAR.
(c) Name the improved analogues.
(d) State the rationale.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Nitroimidazole class: metronidazole is the drug of choice for extraluminal amoebiasis; tinidazole and ornidazole are analogues.
(b)
Activity is based on the nitro group; the structure has 2-hydroxyethyl, nitro and methyl groups at C1, C2 and C5 respectively.
(c)
• The nitro group is chemically reduced in anaerobic bacteria and sensitive protozoa; reactive reduction products are responsible, forming nitroso radicals that disrupt DNA and inhibit nucleic acid synthesis, with little effect on human and aerobic cells.
• The mechanism against Entamoeba histolytica itself is described as unknown, while the reduction mechanism is given for anaerobes and sensitive protozoa.
(d)
• It kills trophozoites but not cysts; it eradicates intestinal and extraintestinal tissue infection and is active against anaerobes (bacteroides, clostridium), giardiasis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis and H. pylori eradication.
• Liver abscess: metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 10 days or tinidazole 2 g daily for 6 days, then diloxanide furoate 500 mg three times daily for 10 days (or another luminal amoebicide) must always follow.
• Because it is well absorbed, colonic luminal levels may be sub-therapeutic and it is less effective against cysts, so it is contraindicated in asymptomatic cyst carriers; luminal agents are paromomycin or iodoquinol.
(e)
• Nausea, headache, dry mouth, metallic taste, and a disulfiram-like (Antabuse) reaction with alcohol; dark urine, neutropenia and paraesthesias are infrequent.
• It potentiates coumarin anticoagulants; phenytoin and phenobarbital accelerate its elimination; cimetidine may decrease its clearance; taking it with meals lessens GI irritation.
questions.question:
A patient presents with bloody, mucoid diarrhoea and abdominal pain; Entamoeba histolytica is found, and a liver abscess is later diagnosed. A nitroimidazole is started.
(a) Identify the drug class and the most likely drug.
(b) State the structural feature responsible for activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(d) State the spectrum, therapeutic uses and the luminal agent that must follow.
(e) State the key adverse effects linked to its structure and chemistry.

questions.question: A renal biopsy is stained with a combined connective tissue trichrome method to help characterise interstitial fibrosis alongside standard periodic acid-Schiff staining. Explain the clinical reasoning for adding this stain, the underlying principle, the expected colour pattern, and the precaution needed for consistent interpretation across biopsies.
questions.answerText: A trichrome stain is added because quantifying interstitial fibrosis is an important prognostic factor in many forms of chronic kidney disease, and while periodic acid-Schiff shows basement membranes and general architecture well, a trichrome method gives a clearer, more specific colour contrast between collagenous fibrosis and normal tubular and glomerular tissue for more confident grading. The principle involves the use of multiple dyes with different molecular sizes and tissue affinities applied sequentially, so that collagen, muscle and nuclei each take up a differently coloured dye based on tissue permeability, producing a multicoloured image that separates fibrous tissue clearly from cellular elements. In a kidney with significant interstitial fibrosis, trichrome staining shows collagen deposition as a distinctly coloured green or blue area clearly separated from the differently coloured tubular epithelium and muscle, allowing more reproducible fibrosis quantification than routine staining alone. The precaution is to standardise staining time and reagent concentration carefully, since trichrome methods are particularly sensitive to technical variation, which can shift colour balance and affect the reproducibility of fibrosis grading between different biopsies or laboratories.

questions.question: A blood smear examined for suspected relapsing fever is stained and viewed using dark-ground illumination rather than standard bright-field microscopy alone. Explain the clinical reasoning for this technique, the underlying principle, the expected appearance of the spirochetes, and the precaution needed for reliable detection.
questions.answerText: Dark-ground illumination is used because the causative spirochetes of relapsing fever are extremely thin, poorly refractile organisms that are difficult to visualise clearly against a standard bright background, whereas this illumination technique makes even faint, thin structures stand out brightly against a dark background, greatly improving detection sensitivity. The principle is that dark-ground illumination blocks the direct light path to the objective lens and instead relies on light scattered by structures within the specimen, so that even organisms too thin to be seen by absorption of light under bright-field conditions become visible as bright objects against a dark background. In a positive case, actively motile, corkscrew-shaped spirochetes are seen as bright, moving structures weaving between blood cells, a distinctive appearance supporting the diagnosis. The precaution is to examine fresh, unstained or minimally processed material promptly, since organism motility, an important diagnostic feature under dark-ground examination, is lost if the specimen is allowed to dry out or degrade before observation.

Assessing the integrity of the thyroid capsule and its relationship to any nodular lesion is essential for distinguishing benign follicular adenomas, which do not breach the capsule, from follicular carcinomas, which characteristically show capsular or vascular invasion, a distinction that fundamentally changes the patient's diagnosis and management. The precaution is to sample and embed the specimen so that the full circumference or at least multiple representative areas of the capsule are included and correctly oriented in the sections examined, since a biopsy or resection specimen sampled only from the central portion of a nodule, without adequate capsular representation, cannot reliably exclude capsular invasion even if none is seen in the limited material examined.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected chronic autoimmune thyroid disorder has a thyroid biopsy examined, and the technologist ensures the specimen is oriented so that both the fibrous capsule and the underlying parenchyma are visible in the same section. Why does capsular assessment matter in thyroid pathology, and what precaution ensures it is not missed?

questions.answerText: Fading is clinically significant because archived slides may need to be reviewed months or years later for comparison with new biopsies, second opinions, or research, and faded staining could prevent accurate reassessment of the original skin lesion's histological features. The principle is that certain mounting media allow slow oxidation or evaporation-related changes that gradually degrade dye-tissue complexes, particularly for stains not chemically stabilised against long-term light or air exposure, meaning mounting medium choice directly affects how well the original staining is preserved over time. A properly mounted archival slide retains close to its original colour intensity and contrast even after years of storage, allowing confident retrospective review; a poorly mounted slide may fade to the point that fine architectural or nuclear detail becomes difficult to interpret. The precaution is to use mounting media specifically validated for long-term stain stability and to store archived slides away from direct light and extremes of temperature and humidity.
questions.question: A laboratory scientist notes that a batch of stained slides from a skin excision shows unexpectedly faded colour after several months in storage and traces the cause to an unsuitable mounting medium. Explain the clinical consequence of this fading, the underlying principle, the expected appearance of a properly mounted archival slide, and the precaution needed to ensure long-term diagnostic value.

questions.answerText: Nervous tissue is delicate and prone to excessive hardening and brittleness with harsh clearing agents, so cedarwood oil or similar gentle clearing agents are preferred because they clear tissue without the aggressive dehydrating and hardening action of reagents like chloroform or xylene, preserving the fine architecture of white and grey matter needed to assess myelin loss. The disadvantage that must still be monitored is that gentler clearing agents work far more slowly and are considerably more expensive, so processing schedules must allow for a longer clearing time, and the technologist must confirm complete clearing before proceeding to wax infiltration, since incompletely cleared tissue will not infiltrate evenly with wax.
questions.question: A technologist processing central nervous system tissue from a patient with suspected demyelinating disease avoids chloroform and instead selects a clearing agent recommended for delicate neural tissue. What principle guides this choice, and what disadvantage of the alternative should still be monitored?

questions.answerText: Toluidine blue at a carefully controlled acidic pH is used because mast cell granules contain heparin and other sulphated mucopolysaccharides that produce a striking metachromatic colour change under these specific conditions, allowing even scattered or increased mast cell populations to be readily identified within the dermis. The principle is that the degree and character of metachromasia depend on the density and arrangement of sulphated groups on the tissue substrate as well as the staining pH, so a specifically buffered pH is required to reliably elicit the characteristic mast cell granule colour change. In a positive case, mast cell cytoplasmic granules stain a vivid reddish-purple against the blue background of the surrounding orthochromatic tissue, making increased mast cell numbers or abnormal infiltrates easy to identify and quantify. The precaution is to prepare and verify the buffer pH precisely before each staining run, since deviation from the validated pH can weaken or abolish the metachromatic effect, potentially causing a genuine increase in mast cells to be under-appreciated.
questions.question: A dermal biopsy from a patient with suspected mast cell disease is stained with toluidine blue at a specifically buffered acidic pH to identify mast cell granules. Explain the clinical reasoning, the underlying principle, the expected staining appearance of a positive result, and the precaution regarding buffer pH control.

questions.answerText: Buffering matters because unbuffered formalin becomes acidic over time and in the presence of tissue, and this acidity both slows fixation quality and promotes formation of dark artefactual pigment in blood-containing biopsy tissue, either of which could interfere with accurate assessment of the small, diagnostically critical prostate needle cores used for cancer grading. The principle is that formaldehyde in aqueous solution tends to oxidise to formic acid over time, and without an adequate buffering system to neutralise this drift, the working solution's pH falls progressively, altering its fixation characteristics and promoting unwanted pigment formation in blood-rich tissue. With correctly buffered formalin maintained near neutral pH, prostate biopsies fix consistently with good nuclear and cytoplasmic preservation free from pigment artifact, supporting reliable Gleason grading. The precaution is to periodically verify the pH of working formalin solutions rather than assuming the buffering system remains effective indefinitely, replacing or re-buffering solutions that have drifted outside the validated neutral pH range.
questions.question: A histology laboratory checks that its formalin working solution used for fixing a batch of prostate needle biopsies is buffered to a neutral pH using an appropriate buffering system rather than used as an unbuffered stock solution. Explain the clinical reasoning for this buffering requirement, the underlying principle, the expected fixation quality with correctly buffered formalin, and the precaution needed to maintain consistent buffering over time.

questions.answerText: Blade quality matters because a dull or improperly bevelled knife produces uneven, torn or compressed sections that can distort the fine architectural and cytological features, such as pattern of melanocytic growth and depth of invasion, that are essential for accurately diagnosing and staging a possible melanoma. The principle is that a microtome knife must maintain a precise, uniformly sharp cutting facet at the correct bevel angle to shear through tissue cleanly without dragging, tearing or compressing cellular structures. With a properly sharpened knife, sections are thin, smooth and free from chatter or compression artifact, allowing accurate measurement of tumour thickness; a dull knife produces uneven thickness, tissue folds and compression that can obscure or falsely alter the apparent depth of invasion. The precaution is to inspect and, when necessary, hone or replace the knife before cutting diagnostically critical specimens, and to test cutting quality on a trial section before committing the true diagnostic block.
questions.question: A microtome operator sharpens the knife and checks its bevel angle carefully before sectioning a skin biopsy for suspected melanoma, rather than using a knife that has been in continuous use without maintenance. Explain why blade quality matters to the clinical outcome, the principle behind proper sharpening, the expected section quality, and the precaution needed to maintain diagnostic accuracy.

A 60-year-old man undergoes excision of a suspicious skin nodule on the scalp. The surgeon places the specimen in a wide-mouthed bottle of 10% formal saline before sending it to the laboratory. Why did the surgeon fix the tissue in this fluid before dispatch, and what must the laboratory scientist verify on receipt?
questions.answerText: Fixation is requested to halt autolysis and putrefaction that begin the moment tissue loses its blood supply, and to harden the specimen enough for later cutting while preserving cellular and tissue architecture close to the living state. Formaldehyde works by cross-linking proteins through methylene bridges, rendering them insoluble and resistant to digestion by the tissue's own lysolytic enzymes. Adequately fixed tissue should be firm, pale tan-grey, and free of a soft, mushy, or foul-smelling centre; a soft or discoloured core indicates incomplete penetration and impending autolysis, which would make later diagnosis unreliable. The laboratory scientist must confirm that fixative volume is at least ten times the tissue volume, that the specimen has not dried out in transit, and that the block was thin enough (ideally 3-5 mm) for the fixative to penetrate fully before further processing.

Mitochondrial and other enzyme activities central to diagnosing metabolic myopathies decline rapidly once tissue is removed from its blood supply, and any delay allows enzyme degradation that would give falsely weak or absent staining reactions unrelated to the patient's actual disease. The tissue is therefore rapidly frozen unfixed, a process called quenching, most safely performed by plunging it into isopentane pre-cooled in liquid nitrogen, which freezes the tissue almost instantaneously and minimises ice-crystal artefact while preserving enzyme activity for subsequent cryostat sectioning and histochemical enzyme staining.
questions.question: A muscle biopsy from a child with suspected mitochondrial myopathy must reach the laboratory and be processed within one to two hours of removal. Why is this narrow time window so critical, and what technique is used once the tissue arrives?

questions.answerText: Eosin staining intensity and selectivity are strongly influenced by the concentration of the working solution, the staining time, and residual alkalinity left in the tissue from the preceding blueing step, since an alkaline environment reduces eosin's ability to bind cleanly and produces washed-out, non-differential staining. The precaution is to ensure sections are adequately rinsed and slightly acidified after blueing before eosin is applied, to use a correctly prepared and not overly diluted eosin solution, and to differentiate briefly in alcohol afterward so that the cytoplasm, collagen, and red cells regain good tinctorial contrast rather than a uniform pink haze.
questions.question: A technologist notices eosin staining appears unusually pale and diffuse in a batch of gastric biopsies, obscuring the distinction between different cytoplasmic components. What factor commonly affects eosin's staining quality, and what precaution restores good contrast?

A patient with chronic cough, weight loss, and cavitary lung disease on chest radiograph is suspected of having pulmonary tuberculosis, and a lymph node biopsy is stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen method. What is the underlying principle of this stain, and what colour confirms the presence of acid-fast bacilli?
questions.answerText: The Ziehl-Neelsen method exploits the unique waxy, high-lipid mycolic acid content of the mycobacterial cell wall, which allows these organisms to bind strongly to carbol fuchsin when heat is applied to enhance dye penetration, and then to resist decolourisation by a subsequent acid-alcohol wash that would remove the stain from all other, non-acid-fast bacteria and tissue components. A positive result shows slender, bright red bacilli against a contrasting blue methylene blue counterstained background, confirming the presence of acid-fast organisms consistent with tuberculosis; the precaution is to examine multiple fields carefully, since bacilli can be scanty even in genuinely infected tissue, and a negative stain does not fully exclude the diagnosis.

questions.question: A liver biopsy from an infant with suspected mitochondrial hepatopathy is examined by electron microscopy specifically to assess mitochondrial number, size and internal cristae structure. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle, the expected abnormal findings, and the precaution needed to avoid a misleading ultrastructural impression.
questions.answerText: This test is requested because mitochondrial hepatopathies are defined by structural abnormalities of the mitochondria themselves, including altered number, size, shape and internal cristae architecture, changes only resolvable at the ultrastructural level that can support this specific diagnosis in an infant with unexplained liver dysfunction. The principle is that the exceptional resolving power of electron microscopy allows direct visualisation of individual mitochondrial internal architecture, including the cristae folds of the inner membrane, features entirely beyond the resolution of light microscopy but central to recognising mitochondrial pathology. Abnormal findings may include markedly increased mitochondrial numbers, unusual pleomorphic shapes, or disorganised, reduced or abnormal cristae structure, patterns that support the suspected diagnosis when interpreted alongside biochemical and clinical findings. The precaution is to compare findings against normal age-matched mitochondrial appearance where possible, since mitochondrial morphology can vary somewhat with tissue handling and normal physiological state, and isolated minor variation should not be over-interpreted as definitively pathological without corroborating evidence.

questions.question: A patient with suspected amyloidosis affecting the kidney has a biopsy examined, and the laboratory scientist ensures that all glassware used for the associated silver impregnation reticulin stain has been thoroughly acid-washed beforehand. Why is this precaution necessary, and what would happen if it were omitted?
questions.answerText: Silver solutions used in reticulin staining are extremely sensitive to contamination, and residual organic material, detergent, or metal ions left on glassware from previous use can cause the silver to precipitate prematurely or deposit non-specifically throughout the tissue and background rather than being selectively reduced at the reticulin fibres, producing a heavily blackened, uninterpretable section. Acid-washing removes these contaminants and ensures the glassware is chemically clean, so the silver solution reacts only with the intended tissue components, giving a crisp, selectively stained reticulin pattern rather than a diffusely blackened artefact.

questions.question: A patient with a palpable thyroid nodule undergoes fine needle aspiration cytology to determine whether surgery is needed. Why is this technique preferred as a first-line investigation, and what precaution during needle withdrawal prevents specimen loss?
questions.answerText: Fine needle aspiration cytology is preferred as a first-line investigation because it is quick, minimally invasive, avoids the scarring and recovery time of an open biopsy, and provides sufficient cellular material in most cases to distinguish benign from suspicious or malignant thyroid nodules, guiding whether surgical excision is warranted. The precaution during the procedure is to release the syringe piston, relieving suction, before the needle is withdrawn from the nodule, since maintaining negative pressure while withdrawing risks drawing the aspirated cellular material up into the syringe barrel itself rather than leaving it within the needle hub and shaft where it can be expelled cleanly onto slides for staining.

questions.question: A patient with a suspected varicose vein excision is examined with Verhoeff's elastic stain to assess the venous wall architecture, and the technologist uses ferric chloride as the differentiating agent after silver impregnation. What role does this differentiating step play, and what precaution prevents overshooting the correct endpoint?
questions.answerText: After the tissue is impregnated with the haematoxylin-based elastic stain solution, ferric chloride acts as a differentiator, selectively removing excess non-specific staining from collagen and other background structures while leaving the more strongly bound elastic fibre staining intact, sharpening the contrast between the black elastic fibres and their surroundings. The precaution is to monitor the differentiation step under the microscope at intervals rather than fixing a rigid time, since over-differentiation can strip staining from the elastic fibres themselves, understating the true elastic content of the vessel wall and potentially masking genuine pathology.

Understanding the normal baseline cellularity of these fluids matters because any significant increase in cellularity, particularly of atypical or clearly malignant-appearing cells, immediately stands out as abnormal against this expected sparse background, making cellularity itself a useful first clue even before detailed cytological assessment of individual cells begins. The principle is that these serous cavity fluids are normally produced and reabsorbed in a dynamic balance that keeps free cellular content low, so any pathological process disrupting this balance, whether inflammatory, infective or malignant, characteristically increases both fluid volume and cellularity. In malignant ascites, the fluid typically shows increased cellularity with clusters or single atypical cells showing nuclear pleomorphism, an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and sometimes distinctive architectural clustering patterns that stand out from the sparse mesothelial cell population expected in benign fluid. The precaution is to carefully distinguish reactive, proliferating mesothelial cells, which can themselves show some atypical features in benign inflammatory conditions, from truly malignant cells, since mesothelial hyperplasia can occasionally mimic malignancy and requires careful, experienced cytological assessment, sometimes supported by immunocytochemistry, before a diagnosis of malignancy is confirmed.
questions.question: A patient with ascites of unknown cause has peritoneal fluid submitted for cytology, and the laboratory notes that pleural and peritoneal fluids normally contain very few cells under non-pathological conditions. Explain why this baseline expectation matters to the clinical interpretation, the underlying principle, the expected abnormal finding in malignant ascites, and the precaution needed before concluding malignancy.

questions.answerText: Tap water is often slightly alkaline and can gradually differentiate or extract the acid fuchsin component of the van Gieson stain if the section remains in prolonged contact with it, weakening the intended red collagen staining and shifting the overall colour balance. The precaution is to differentiate and rinse the section quickly, following the manufacturer's or laboratory's standard operating procedure precisely, and to mount the section promptly in an appropriate medium after dehydration, rather than leaving it soaking in water, since prolonged washing compromises the specific red-yellow contrast the stain is designed to demonstrate.
questions.question: A laboratory technologist notices that a van Gieson-stained section has become discoloured after being left too long in tap water during the washing step. What precaution should have been taken, and why does this matter for the final result?

questions.answerText: A minimum specimen number requirement exists because, as with any test relying on intermittent shedding of abnormal cells, examining too few specimens risks a falsely reassuring negative result simply due to inadequate sampling opportunity rather than genuine absence of malignancy, and adhering to a validated minimum improves the reliability of a truly negative overall report. The principle is the same cumulative sensitivity concept underlying multiple specimen collection, where each additional independent specimen adds incremental probability of detecting malignant cells if genuinely present, meaning overall diagnostic confidence in a negative result depends directly on how many adequately collected specimens have been examined. With the recommended minimum met and all specimens negative, the laboratory can report a result with a reasonably low likelihood of a missed malignancy, appropriately calibrated to the inherent limitations of the technique. The precaution is that if the clinically recommended minimum number of specimens cannot be obtained for any reason, this limitation should be explicitly stated in the report, and the reduced confidence in a negative result communicated clearly to the requesting clinician rather than implying the same level of reassurance as a fully complete series.
questions.question: A histopathology-linked cytology laboratory ensures at least the recommended minimum number of separate sputum specimens are collected from a patient with suspected lung malignancy before reporting a negative overall result. Explain the clinical reasoning for this minimum specimen requirement, the underlying principle, the expected effect on overall diagnostic sensitivity, and the precaution needed if the minimum cannot be met.

questions.answerText: Cytological examination of peritoneal fluid can directly identify malignant cells shed from intra-abdominal or pelvic tumours into the peritoneal cavity, offering a rapid, minimally invasive means of confirming malignant involvement without requiring surgical exploration or biopsy, which is particularly valuable in patients who may not be fit for more invasive procedures. The precaution is to submit an adequate volume of fluid, typically at least fifty millilitres where possible, for concentration by centrifugation, since a very small fluid volume may contain too few malignant cells to be reliably detected even when malignant involvement of the peritoneum is genuinely present.
questions.question: A patient with suspected malignant ascites has peritoneal fluid sent for cytology alongside biochemical analysis. Why is cytological examination considered a key diagnostic test in this setting, and what precaution regarding specimen volume improves diagnostic yield?

A cytogenetics request accompanies a bone marrow trephine biopsy from a patient with suspected leukaemia, and the technologist is asked to prepare touch imprint smears from the fresh specimen before it is placed into fixative. Why is this step performed first, and what precaution preserves cell morphology on the smear?
questions.answerText: Touch imprint or impression smears capture individual intact cells directly from a fresh cut surface onto a slide before fixation and processing distort or destroy cellular detail, giving rapid access to well-preserved nuclear and cytoplasmic morphology that is valuable for same-day cytological screening while the tissue proceeds through slower routine processing. The precaution is to touch the freshly cut, blood-free surface gently and briefly onto the slide without smearing or applying pressure, and to fix or air-dry the resulting imprint promptly, since delay or rough handling causes cell distortion and compromises the diagnostic value of the smear.

A dual screening approach is used because chronic non-healing ulcers can have a wide range of infectious causes, and applying both common bacterial and mycobacterial stains as an initial broad screen efficiently narrows the differential diagnosis before committing to more specific and resource-intensive testing for less common organisms. The principle is that each stain targets a different category of organism based on distinct cell wall properties, so a negative result on one does not exclude infection by an organism in the other category, making combined screening more comprehensive than either test alone. If both stains are negative, common bacterial and mycobacterial causes become less likely, appropriately shifting clinical suspicion toward other infectious agents such as fungi or atypical organisms, or toward a non-infectious cause of the ulcer. The precaution is to recognise that negative special stains reduce but do not eliminate the possibility of infection, since organism density below the detection threshold of histology can still be clinically significant, and further targeted testing or clinical correlation may still be warranted.
questions.question: A skin biopsy from a patient with a chronic ulcer of uncertain cause is examined with both Gram and Ziehl-Neelsen stains to broadly screen for bacterial and mycobacterial organisms before considering other causes. Explain the clinical reasoning for this dual screening approach, the underlying principle, the expected outcome if both are negative, and the precaution needed before excluding infection.

questions.answerText: Succinate dehydrogenase is a key mitochondrial enzyme that catalyses the reversible oxidation of succinic acid to fumaric acid as part of the citric acid cycle, and the histochemical method demonstrates its activity by incubating fresh, unfixed frozen sections with a substrate and a tetrazolium salt that is reduced to an insoluble, visible blue formazan precipitate specifically at sites of enzyme activity, typically concentrated within mitochondria along muscle fibres. In normal muscle, fibres show an even, fine granular blue reaction reflecting the normal distribution of mitochondria; abnormal, coarse, or excessively intense subsarcolemmal staining, sometimes described as ragged appearance, indicates mitochondrial proliferation and supports a mitochondrial myopathy, and the precaution is to ensure the tissue reaches the laboratory fresh and unfixed, since enzyme activity is rapidly lost after removal from the blood supply.
questions.question: A 10-year-old boy with progressive muscle weakness is suspected of having a mitochondrial myopathy, and a fresh frozen muscle biopsy is examined for succinate dehydrogenase activity. What is the underlying principle of this enzyme test, and what result indicates abnormal mitochondrial function?

A skin biopsy from a patient with suspected pseudoxanthoma elasticum-related vascular calcification undergoes Verhoeff's elastic fibre staining with a specific differentiating agent applied after the initial iron haematoxylin step. Explain the clinical reasoning for this differentiation step, the underlying principle, the expected final appearance of elastic fibres, and the precaution needed to avoid under- or over-differentiation.
questions.answerText: The differentiation step is necessary because the initial iron haematoxylin-based staining in this method deposits stain non-selectively throughout the tissue, and a subsequent differentiating agent is required to selectively remove excess stain from everything except the elastic fibres, revealing them with the sharp, selective contrast needed to assess their integrity in this vascular disorder. The principle is that differentiation exploits differences in how strongly various tissue components retain the initially applied stain complex, allowing controlled, timed removal of unwanted staining from collagen, muscle and other elements while genuine elastic fibre staining, more resistant to this removal process, is preserved. With correct, carefully timed differentiation, elastic fibres appear crisply stained black against a clear, appropriately counterstained background, allowing confident assessment of fibre fragmentation or calcification; incorrect timing leaves either excessive background staining obscuring the fibres or over-differentiated fibres that appear falsely weak or fragmented. The precaution is to monitor the differentiation step visually under the microscope at intervals rather than relying on a fixed time alone, since tissue and reagent variability can affect how quickly appropriate differentiation is achieved.

questions.question: A histopathology department decalcifies a vertebral biopsy and checks the endpoint by gently flexing the tissue with forceps rather than sending it for radiography. Explain why this practical method was used, the underlying principle, the expected sign of completion, and the precaution needed to avoid an inaccurate assessment.
questions.answerText: Physical flexibility testing is a quick, low-cost bedside-laboratory method to judge whether enough mineral has been removed for the tissue to be safely sectioned, useful when radiographic confirmation is unavailable or would delay turnaround. The principle is that as calcium salts are progressively dissolved and removed, the tissue loses its rigidity and becomes pliable, so gentle flexing gives an indirect but practical indication of the degree of decalcification achieved. Correctly judged, the tissue should feel uniformly soft and slightly springy without any hard or gritty areas remaining, at which point sectioning becomes possible without damaging the microtome knife or tearing tissue; if hard areas remain undetected, the knife will tear or skip through the block, distorting the section. The precaution is to test at multiple points along the specimen, not just the edges, since decalcification proceeds from the surface inward and the centre of a large fragment may remain incompletely treated even when the edges feel soft.

questions.question: A histology laboratory notices that paraffin blocks containing a series of skin biopsies keep coming out with poor infiltration in the deeper dermis. Why might vacuum infiltration help in this situation, and for which other tissue type is it specifically valuable?
questions.answerText: Vacuum infiltration reduces the pressure above the molten wax bath, drawing out trapped air and gases from within the tissue and allowing wax to penetrate deeply into small vascular spaces, follicular structures, and dense connective tissue that would otherwise resist infiltration under normal atmospheric pressure. This is particularly valuable for lung tissue, whose air-filled alveolar spaces would otherwise trap air and prevent the wax from reaching the alveolar walls, and it is equally useful for urgent biopsies where thorough infiltration must be achieved quickly. The precaution is to maintain the recommended vacuum pressure and temperature so that the tissue is not overheated or damaged during the accelerated process.

Zenker's fluid is preferred over formal saline because the mercuric chloride component gives markedly sharper nuclear and cytoplasmic detail, which aids accurate classification of lymphoid architecture and cell morphology in suspected lymphoma. The principle is that mercuric chloride acts as a protein-precipitating fixative that produces intense chromatin clumping and crisp cytoplasmic granularity, complemented by potassium dichromate which stabilises cytoplasmic elements, giving a combined nuclear-cytoplasmic fixative superior to formalin alone. When correctly used, sections show brilliant staining and well-defined follicular and interfollicular detail; failure to remove residual mercury pigment leaves fine black-brown crystalline deposits that can be mistaken for haemosiderin or melanin and obscure cellular detail. The scientist must thoroughly wash the tissue after fixation, treat sections with an iodine-thiosulphate sequence to remove mercuric pigment before staining, and avoid using this fixative before X-ray-based analytical techniques since mercury interferes with such methods.
questions.question: A lymph node excised for suspected lymphoma is sent fixed in Zenker's fluid rather than plain formal saline. What was the clinical reasoning for this choice, what is the underlying chemical principle, what result is expected, and what precautions minimise false interpretation?

A pathologist requests ultrathin sections of a renal biopsy for electron microscopy and specifies that these must be far thinner than routine paraffin sections. What section thickness range is typically used, and why is such extreme thinness necessary?
questions.answerText: Ultrathin sections for transmission electron microscopy are typically cut in the range of 60 to 90 nanometres, vastly thinner than the 3 to 5 micrometre sections used for routine light microscopy, because the electron beam used in this technique has very limited penetrating power through dense resin-embedded tissue, and only sections this thin allow sufficient electrons to pass through to form a clear image at the very high magnifications needed to resolve subcellular structures such as basement membrane layers and cell organelles.
