An infant presents with meconium ileus in the neonatal period and later develops recurrent respiratory infections and malabsorption.
(i) State the risk factors for this condition.
(ii) State its complications.
questions.answerText:
(i) This is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation of the CFTR gene on chromosome 7q31.2 (classified into mutation classes 1-5); phenotypic severity is modified by other genetic polymorphisms such as transforming growth factor beta 1 (which affects neutrophil function) and by environmental modifiers such as infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
(ii) Complications include pancreatic mucus plugging with atrophy, fibrosis and squamous metaplasia; meconium ileus of the small intestine; hepatic bile duct plugging, ductular proliferation, portal inflammation, steatosis and focal biliary cirrhosis; salivary gland duct dilation and glandular atrophy; pulmonary airway obstruction and infection with mucus gland hyperplasia/hypertrophy; and azoospermia/infertility in 95% of males, with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
Airway infection, obstructive pulmonary disease, and cor pulmonale are stated as the common causes of death.

(i) Hypertensive heart disease is a consequence of the effect of raised blood pressure on the heart, causing pressure overload and ventricular hypertrophy. Right-sided hypertensive heart disease (cor pulmonale) results from pulmonary hypertension, while left-sided hypertensive heart disease (concentric hypertrophy) results from systemic hypertension. Cor pulmonale itself may be acute or chronic, and its causes are usually disorders of the lungs.
(ii) The criteria for diagnosis of hypertensive heart disease caused by systemic hypertension are left ventricular hypertrophy (usually concentric) in the absence of other cardiovascular pathology, plus a clinical history of hypertension or pathological evidence of hypertension in other organs (e.g., the kidney). The hypertrophy usually exceeds 2.0 cm in wall thickness (normal 1.3-1.5 cm), and heart weight may exceed 500g (normal female 300-350g, male 350-400g). Microscopy shows increased transverse diameter of myocytes, evidenced by nuclear enlargement, with accompanying interstitial fibrosis. Complications of left-sided hypertensive heart disease include atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, congestive cardiac failure or sudden death. Right-sided hypertensive heart disease (cor pulmonale) similarly produces right-sided hypertrophy in response to raised pulmonary vascular resistance arising from lung disease. This represents an anatomical deformity (chamber hypertrophy and dilation) of the heart following the sustained pressure injury imposed by the diseased pulmonary or systemic circulation. Complications of hypertension generally include ischaemic heart disease, congestive heart failure and stroke, showing the wider downstream effects of sustained vascular pressure overload. Adequate therapeutic control of the underlying hypertension allows these patients to enjoy normal longevity and die of unrelated causes.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the pulmonary and systemic circulatory basis of hypertensive heart disease.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the cardiac deformity that follows sustained pressure injury.

A young adult presents with episodes of bloody diarrhoea. Endoscopy shows continuous mucosal involvement from the rectum proximally, loss of haustral folds, and no skip lesions.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List the risk factors.
(iii) List the complications.
(iv) Discuss the surgical/management options, justifying one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Ulcerative colitis.
(ii) Higher incidence in Westerners; occurs at any age, rare in the first decade, major peak 15-25 years, minor peak in the 7th decade; familial association; smoking reduces the risk of ulcerative colitis (in contrast to Crohn disease, in which smoking increases risk).
(iii) Mortality is uncommon and occurs due to fulminant disease (toxic colitis); mortality may also result from associated complications including colorectal carcinoma, primary sclerosing cholangitis, therapeutic complications and thromboembolic disease; long-standing ulcerative colitis is associated with increased risk of dysplasia (low or high grade) and adenocarcinoma.
(iv) Mild to moderate disease does not require colectomy. Colectomy is recommended for patients with any degree of dysplasia in a raised sessile lesion (dysplasia-associated lesion or mass, DALM) - justified because such dysplastic lesions carry an increased risk of progression to colorectal adenocarcinoma.

(i) Infective endocarditis.
(ii) Cardiac/vascular abnormalities predisposing to infective endocarditis include rheumatic heart disease, myxomatous mitral valve, degenerative calcific valvular stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, prosthetic cardiac valves, valvular grafts and indwelling vascular catheters. Host factors include neutropenia, immunodeficiency, diabetes mellitus, and alcohol and intravenous drug abuse; right-sided valves are commonly affected in IV drug abusers, while the aortic and mitral valves are most commonly affected overall.
(iii) Colonisation or invasion of the heart valves, mural endocardium or other cardiovascular sites by a microbiologic agent leads to bulky, friable vegetations composed of thrombotic debris and organisms, with destruction of cardiac tissue. Most cases are caused by alpha-haemolytic streptococci viridans (50-60%) and Staphylococcus aureus (10-20%, especially in IV drug abusers). Vegetations may erode into the underlying myocardium to produce ring abscesses, and systemic embolisation may cause septic infarcts in organs such as the spleen, kidneys, lungs and brain.
(iv) Prompt diagnosis and effective treatment is critical. Acute endocarditis (a destructive, tumultuous infection of a previously normal valve) is treated with antibiotics and surgery, though more than 50% of patients still die within days to weeks. Subacute endocarditis, caused by organisms of low virulence affecting previously damaged valves, usually recovers after antibiotic therapy.

questions.answerText:
(i) The average age of presentation is 32 years. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) genome is found in Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells in some subtypes, and its LMP-1 protein upregulates NF-kB, driving monoclonal B-lymphocyte proliferation into RS cells; mutation of the C-REL oncogene has also been implicated.
The lymphocyte-depleted subtype is associated with HIV infection and, especially in underdeveloped countries, with EBV.
(ii) The disease spreads predictably and by contiguity, starting first with a single lymph node, then to the spleen, liver, bone marrow and other tissues (disseminated extranodal extension).
The described fever, night sweats and weight loss are "B symptoms" indicating more advanced disease; poor prognostic parameters are age over 60 years, poor Karnofsky performance status, elevated LDH, more than one site of extranodal extension, and stage III or IV disease.
(iii) A localised extranodal extension (suffix E) group often benefits from radiotherapy, and bulky disease or a nodal mass greater than 10 cm is an indication to commence therapy irrespective of stage. Radiotherapy is justified as the option linked to benefit in localised extranodal disease.
questions.question:
A young adult presents with painless enlargement of a group of lymph nodes, unexplained fever above 38 degrees C, drenching night sweats, and weight loss of more than 10% of body weight over the preceding 6 months.
(i) State the risk factors/associations for the underlying condition.
(ii) State its complications.

Within hours of receiving a kidney transplant, a previously sensitised recipient develops sudden graft failure.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is hyperacute rejection of the renal transplant.
(ii) Preformed antidonor antibodies, already present in the recipient's circulation before transplantation, destroy the renal vasculature and cause outright necrosis of the kidney cortex, within minutes to hours of transplantation.
Such preformed antibodies may arise from a previously rejected kidney transplant, from exposure to paternal antigens in multiparous women, or from previous blood transfusion (presensitisation). This antibody-mediated injury to the graft vasculature is described as rejection vasculitis.

questions.question:
A patient presents with headache, visual abnormalities and abnormal eye movements; imaging shows a mass in the region of the sella turcica.
(i) Identify the structure involved, its location and its relations.
(ii) Name the structures compressed or invaded and the clinical effect on each.
(iii) State the differential pathologies of a sellar mass and the features that separate them.
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning that links the mass to hypopituitarism and to hormonal syndromes.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pituitary gland: a small bean-shaped organ at the base of the brain within the sella turcica, in close proximity to the optic chiasm and cavernous sinuses; it is attached to the hypothalamus by the pituitary stalk and enlarges during pregnancy; the anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) forms 80% and the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) stores oxytocin and vasopressin.
(ii) A macroadenoma produces mass effects: headache, visual abnormalities and compression of the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and abducens (VI) nerves with abnormal eye movements; invasive adenomas may erode the sella turcica and extend into the cavernous and sphenoid sinus.
- Compression and atrophy of the normal gland causes hypopituitarism, which is noted clinically when 75% or more of the gland is lost.
(iii) Pituitary adenoma: 10% of intracranial neoplasms, commonest at 30-50 years, monomorphous cells with no reticulin (unlike normal gland); null cell adenomas present as large masses (>1 cm); atypical adenomas (Ki-67 at least 3%, p53 staining or brain invasion) recur more; carcinoma is diagnosed only when there is metastasis.
- Craniopharyngioma: 1-5% of intracranial neoplasms, derived from Rathke's pouch, sellar or suprasellar, benign and slow growing, in children or adolescents (symptoms may be delayed 20 years or more); adamantinomatous or papillary, often cystic with calcification and thick brownish "machine oil" fluid; causes pituitary hypo- or hyperfunction, diabetes insipidus and visual disturbance.
- Others that present with mass effects and can mimic an adenoma: meningiomas and pilocytic astrocytoma; pituitary hyperplasia (due to excessive stimulation, nodular or diffuse, non-neoplastic) may simulate an adenoma; pituitary apoplexy (haemorrhage into an adenoma) gives rapid headache and diplopia, with hypopituitarism and diabetes insipidus.
(iv) Hormone-secreting adenomas add syndromes: prolactinoma (about 30% of adenomas; galactorrhoea, infertility and amenorrhoea in females, decreased libido and impotence in males); GH adenoma (gigantism before epiphyseal closure, acromegaly after it; elevated IGF-1); ACTH adenoma (Cushing disease; Nelson syndrome after adrenalectomy); TSH adenomas are rare.
- Hypopituitarism gives GH, TSH, ACTH and ADH deficiency features: growth retardation and fasting hypoglycaemia in infants, hypothyroidism, hypoadrenalism and diabetes insipidus.

(i) The breast is a modified sweat gland (skin appendage), functional in females during lactation and rudimentary in males; it develops along the milk line (mammary ridge) from epidermal thickenings extending from axilla to perineum: ectoderm gives skin, nipples and ductal system, mesoderm gives fat and blood vessels. Anomalies: amastia, polymastia, polythelia, congenital nipple inversion; milk line remnants (supernumerary nipples or breast, ectopic breast); accessory axillary breast tissue can be a site of origin of cancer even after prophylactic mastectomy.
(ii) Six to 10 major ducts extend from the nipple and branch into smaller ducts, ending as lobules (15-25 lobes, each with a lactiferous duct: large duct, small duct, terminal duct, ductules or acini); the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) is the functional unit of the mammary parenchyma; superficial portions of the major ducts are lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium.
(iii) The rest of the duct-lobular system has a double-layered epithelium: luminal cells (positive for EMA and lactalbumin) and myoepithelial cells (positive for SMA and S-100); stroma is loose connective and adipose tissue, interlobular and intralobular (specialized).
(iv) After puberty the duct system expands into numerous TDLUs; changes are most profound in reproductive years under estrogen, progesterone and prolactin; estrogen and rising progesterone increase cell proliferation and the number of acini per lobule, and the fall in hormones at menstruation induces lobular regression.
(v) The epithelial component is under 10% of the volume of the non-lactating breast but is pathologically more significant because most lesions originate from it (ducts collect and drain, lobules secrete); benign and malignant lesions can arise from any element. In a series of breast lesions about 40% prove fibrocystic changes, 10% cancer, 7% fibroadenoma, 13% miscellaneous benign lesions and 30% show little or no pathology; over 90% of symptomatic lesions are benign, most presenting as palpable, sometimes painful nodules.
(vi) No increased risk: adenosis, cystic change, apocrine metaplasia, mild hyperplasia; slight risk (1.5-2 times): sclerosing adenosis, moderate to florid hyperplasia, papillomas; moderate risk (4-5 times): atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia; substantial risk (8-10 times): DCIS and LCIS.
(vii) Fibroadenoma: commonest benign tumour and cause of breast lump; biphasic stromal and epithelial proliferation from unopposed estrogenic effect; adolescence to adulthood, commoner under 30, often multiple and bilateral; painless lump; well-encapsulated rubbery grey-white nodule with slit-like spaces, myxoid stroma (collagenized in older women), pericanalicular or intracanalicular ducts; two-thirds harbour MED12 driver mutations. Phyllodes tumour: biphasic proliferation with a leaf-like pattern; most present in the sixth decade as a large lump, possibly with pain and ulceration; whorled grey-white mass, sometimes massive with bulbous protrusions; majority have MED12 mutations; graded benign, borderline or malignant.
(viii) Phyllodes tumour differs from fibroadenoma by higher cellularity, higher mitotic rate, nuclear pleomorphism, stromal overgrowth and infiltrative borders; low-grade lesions resemble fibroadenomas but are more cellular and mitotically active, and high-grade lesions may be difficult to distinguish from sarcomas. Behaviour: fibroadenoma carries a mild increase in later breast cancer risk and regresses after menopause or calcifies; benign-appearing phyllodes tumours have only a slight propensity to recur, while malignant ones likely have additional mutations such as TERT.

questions.question:
(i) State the origin of human malaria infection.
(ii) Describe the course of the parasite within the human host from inoculation to red cell invasion.
(iii) State the distribution of the parasite's asexual erythrocytic stages across Plasmodium species.
(iv) How is the diagnosis confirmed?
(v) Explain the anatomical basis of the splenic changes that follow chronic malarial infection.
questions.answerText:
(i) The vector is the female Anopheles mosquito, which injects sporozoites into the bloodstream of humans when taking a blood meal; the sporozoites invade liver cells by binding to hepatocyte receptors for the serum proteins thrombospondin and properdin.
(ii) In the liver, the parasites develop to form schizonts, from which several thousand merozoites develop (about 30,000 merozoites are released when each infected hepatocyte ruptures); in P. vivax and P. ovale, a proportion of the liver-stage parasites (hypnozoites) remain dormant in hepatocytes for months or years, and this exoerythrocytic stage is asymptomatic. When liver cells rupture, merozoites are released into the bloodstream and rapidly invade red blood cells using a lectin-like molecule that binds sialic acid residues on glycophorin molecules on the red cell surface, invading by active membrane penetration.
(iii) P. falciparum infects erythrocytes of all ages, P. vivax and P. ovale infect young erythrocytes, and P. malariae infects older erythrocytes; erythrocytic schizogony varies between species, taking 36-48 hours for P. falciparum, 48 hours for P. ovale and P. vivax, and 72 hours for P. malariae.
(iv) The gold standard is microscopy, using a thick blood film to determine the density of infestation and a thin film for species determination.
(v) During the acute attack, the spleen is enlarged, weighing about 500 g, and is soft and diffusely pigmented, with congestion and reticulo-endothelial hyperplasia microscopically, and macrophages containing engulfed parasites and red cells; haemorrhages and infarcts may be present.
This acute enlargement reflects the reticulo-endothelial system's response to clearing parasitised and damaged red cells, and to accumulating malarial pigment, during ongoing parasitaemia.
In persons resident in an endemic area, there is continuous low-level parasitaemia even without symptoms, a phenomenon known as concomitant immunity or premunition, in which both cell-mediated and antibody-mediated immunity are involved against malaria.
With repeated or chronic infection, the spleen becomes very large, up to 1000 g, and becomes fibrotic, with a brittle, thick capsule and fibrous trabeculae, and may show foci of mineralisation known as Gandy-Gamna bodies.
This chronic fibrotic enlargement is anatomically distinct from the acute, soft, congested splenomegaly of an acute attack, reflecting the transition from a reactive hyperplastic response to an organised fibrotic remodelling of the splenic architecture after repeated antigenic and haemolytic insults.
This chronic massive splenomegaly of greater than 5 kg, occurring in the falciparum-malaria-endemic region and with no other known cause, constitutes the syndrome of hyperimmune malarial splenomegaly (tropical splenomegaly syndrome).
The anatomical basis of this deformity is therefore repeated cycles of reticulo-endothelial hyperplasia and pigment deposition during successive parasitaemic episodes, culminating in progressive fibrous trabecular thickening and capsular brittleness of the spleen.
This fibrotic, brittle, massively enlarged spleen is structurally and functionally distinct from the normal spleen, representing the chronic anatomical sequel of repeated malarial injury.

questions.question:
An 18-month-old child, recently weaned following the birth of a younger sibling and now fed almost exclusively on a carbohydrate-based diet, presents with generalized oedema, a distended abdomen, and patches of skin showing alternating hyperpigmentation, desquamation and hypopigmentation. The hair shows loss of colour in bands.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
(i) Kwashiorkor.
(ii) Kwashiorkor occurs when protein deprivation is relatively more severe than the deficit in total calories; it is the commonest form of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) in impoverished countries of Southeast Asia and in African children weaned too early and then fed almost exclusively a carbohydrate diet; less severe forms occur worldwide in persons with chronic diarrhoeal states in which protein is not absorbed, or with chronic protein loss from protein-losing enteropathies, nephrotic syndrome, or extensive burns.
(iii) Marked protein deprivation causes severe depletion of the visceral protein compartment (represented mainly by liver protein stores), and the resultant hypoalbuminaemia gives rise to generalised or dependent oedema, masking the weight loss; there is relative sparing of subcutaneous fat and muscle mass (unlike marasmus); the small bowel shows decreased mitotic index in the crypts with mucosal atrophy and loss of villi/microvilli, with concurrent loss of small intestinal enzymes (often disaccharidase deficiency); the liver becomes enlarged and fatty from reduced synthesis of the carrier protein component of lipoproteins; thymic and lymphoid atrophy (more marked than in marasmus) causes defects in immunity and secondary infections; nutrient and vitamin deficiencies cause apathy, listlessness and loss of appetite.

(i) The squamocolumnar junction (epidermidalization) is the transformation zone, the site where carcinomas or precancerous lesions develop; at puberty hormonally induced eversion of the cervix exposes columnar cells to the acidic environment, causing metaplasia to squamous epithelium, so this area is one of changing cells.
(ii) The normal cervix has a narrow transformation zone with an abrupt transition from columnar (sometimes via metaplastic) to squamous epithelium; HPV is probably most infectious to cells near this junction, infecting immature basal squamous cells through the vagina (for example at intercourse) or breaks in the epithelium; the cervix is more vulnerable than vulva and vagina because it has large areas of immature epithelium.
(iii) HPV causes 99.8% of cervical cancer (types 16 and/or 18 in 70.9%); high-risk types are 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45 and others, low-risk types 6, 11, 42 and 44. Risk factors: early coitarche, multiple partners, a male partner with multiple partners, genital warts, oral contraceptives, multiparity, smoking, HIV/AIDS, no circumcision in the partner, diet. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is a reversible precancerous disorder lasting months to 20 years that sheds abnormal cells detectable on Pap smear (also called dysplasia, SIL, GIN); CIN1 shows koilocytosis, CIN2-3 shows integrated viral DNA with no koilocytes, and about 20% of CIN3 become invasive cancer when the basement membrane is breached. Invasive tumours: squamous carcinoma (95%; 25-45 years in this environment; fungating, exophytic or endophytic granular eroded lesions; non-keratinising nests or keratin pearls); adenocarcinoma is second commonest, arises at the squamocolumnar junction and extends into the endocervical canal, with adenocarcinoma in situ as precursor (HPV 16 and 18) and a worse prognosis than squamous carcinoma.
(iv) HPV replicates episomally in basal cells expressing early genes E1, E2, E4, E5, E6 and E7 and late genes L1 and L2 in superficial cells; on integration E6 binds p53 and promotes its degradation, and E7 binds hypophosphorylated Rb for proteasomal degradation and inhibits p21 and p27, so infected cells continue through the cell cycle. Other lesions: acute cervicitis (red, swollen cervix with pus, neutrophils) and chronic cervicitis (hyperaemia, erosions, lymphocytes and plasma cells) from lactobacillary disturbance, chlamydia, gonococci or HSV-2; endocervical polyps (commonest cervical growths, spotting, curettage curative); cervical leiomyomas.
(v) Direct extension into the parametrium compresses the ureters, causing hydroureters, hydronephrosis and renal failure, the most common cause of death; invasion of vagina, bladder and rectum may cause fistulae, and the commonest causes of death are pelvic wall extension, obstructive uropathy, pyelonephritis and uraemia rather than metastasis.
(vi) Lymph node metastasis occurs, and distant metastasis is to liver, lungs and bone marrow. Clinical features are post-coital bleeding, bleeding after douching and foul smell; progression is slow over many years, so Pap smear is advised in all women once sexually active. Screening (Pap smear or liquid-based cytology, VIA/VILI, HPV-DNA testing) should cover at least 80% of sexually active women aged 25-65 in an organised community-based programme; average age at diagnosis is 45 years (range 19-75).

questions.question:
A patient who has been immobile after major surgery develops swelling of the calf, and some days later suffers sudden breathlessness and collapse.
(i) State the risk factors for the underlying condition.
(ii) State the complications that may follow it.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors follow Virchow's triad: hypercoagulability, endothelial cell injury, and stasis/abnormal blood flow.
Specific factors named include congestive heart failure, inactivity of the lower extremities, trauma, surgery, burns, injury to vessels, procoagulant substances released from tissues, and reduced tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) activity.
(ii) A thrombus may propagate, embolise, dissolve, become organised, or undergo recanalisation.
Over 95% of pulmonary emboli arise from deep vein thromboses proximal to the popliteal vessels; a large embolus may lodge as a pulmonary "saddle" thromboembolus.
Sudden death may occur as a result of blockage of blood flow through the lungs.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old farmer from an endemic riverine community presents with progressive abdominal distension, hepatosplenomegaly, fatigue, and blood-stained stools. There is a history of chronic exposure to slow-moving fresh water.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) State the procedure that would confirm the diagnosis.
(iii) State the anatomical site(s) primarily involved.
(iv) State the vessel/structure placed at risk by the disease process.
questions.answerText:
(i) Chronic hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (most often due to Schistosoma mansoni, the species chiefly responsible for hepatic disease in South America, Africa and the Middle East, producing this pattern of chronic egg-induced disease with fever, fatigue, abdominal pain, and blood-stained stools).
(ii) Confirmatory procedure: microscopy of stool or urine for eggs, tissue biopsy for histology, or DNA probes; liver biopsy would demonstrate the periportal (pipestem) fibrosis and pinpoint granulomas described for this condition.
(iii) Anatomical sites: adult worm pairs migrate to and reside in the portal (S. mansoni, S. japonicum, S. mekongi) blood venules; the liver is darkened by regurgitated heme-derived pigment, has a bumpy surface, and cut surfaces show pinpoint granulomas; pinhead-sized granulomas composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, neutrophils and eosinophils around the schistosome egg are scattered throughout the gut, liver and other involved organs; the colon may show inflammatory patches or pseudopolyps.
(iv) Structure at risk: widespread fibrosis with portal enlargement without intervening regenerative nodules (pipestem fibrosis) may obliterate the portal veins, leading to portal hypertension and congestive splenomegaly, accounting for this patient's hepatosplenomegaly.

(i) Osteomyelitis is usually due to pyogenic bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism; others include Mycobacteria, Salmonella, Pseudomonas, Eikenella and Pasteurella); routes of transmission of infection are haematogenous spread, direct inoculation, and contiguous spread. In a child, infection typically follows innocuous mucosal injury with spread of microbes to the nutrient arteries of bone; the nidus of infection is at the metaphysis, where pus formation begins, matching this patient's site of tenderness.
(ii) Complications include septic arthritis, bone necrosis, septicaemia, pathologic fracture, squamous cell carcinoma (from a chronically draining sinus), and amyloidosis; progression leads to chronic osteomyelitis characterised by bone destruction and new bone formation with a draining sinus tract - the focus of dead bone is the sequestrum, the area of new bone formed around it is the involucrum, and the opening through which it drains is the cloaca.
(iii) Early drainage of the abscess together with antimicrobial therapy directed at the causative organism (most often Staphylococcus aureus) is justified to arrest progression from subperiosteal abscess to sequestrum/involucrum/cloaca, and to prevent complications such as septic arthritis and pathologic fracture, before chronic osteomyelitis becomes established.
questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy presents with a two-day history of fever, irritability, and refusal to bear weight on the left leg. There is localized warmth, swelling, and tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis.
(i) List the risk factors/route of infection relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications that may arise.
(iii) Outline the management options, justifying one.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma).
(ii) Sporadic Wilms tumour accounts for 90% of cases. Recognised syndromes are WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, mental retardation), with constitutional deletion of 11p13 involving WT1 and PAX6, tumours developing after a second-hit mutation of the remaining WT1 allele; Denys-Drash syndrome (90% risk), with gonadal dysgenesis/male pseudo-hermaphroditism and early-onset nephropathy due to a dominant-negative missense mutation in the zinc-finger region of WT1; and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, with hemihypertrophy, organomegaly, macroglossia, omphalocele and large cells in the adrenal cortex, due to an imprinting defect in the 11p15.5 region.
(iii) Grossly the tumour is large, solitary and well-circumscribed (10% bilateral or multicentric), with grey foci of haemorrhage, cyst formation and necrosis on cut section.
Microscopically it is triphasic, with blastemal (sheets of small blue cells), stromal (myxoid or fibroblastic) and epithelial (abortive tubules or glomeruli) components; 5% show anaplasia associated with p53 mutations, and nephrogenic rests are regarded as precursor lesions.
questions.question:
A child presents with a large abdominal mass, haematuria, abdominal pain, features of intestinal obstruction and hypertension.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology/morphology of this tumour.

A woman presents with progressive right upper quadrant/epigastric pain, mild fever, anorexia, tachycardia, sweating, nausea and vomiting.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List the risk factors for the underlying condition.
(iii) List the complications that may arise.
(iv) Discuss the surgical/management options, justifying one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute (calculous) cholecystitis - an acute abdominal emergency; precipitated in 90% of cases by obstruction of the gallbladder neck or cystic duct by a stone.
(ii) Risk factors for the underlying gallstones: demography (northern Europeans, North/South Americans, Native Americans, Mexican Americans for cholesterol stones; Asians and rural populations for pigment stones); advancing age; female sex hormones (female gender, oral contraceptives, pregnancy); obesity and metabolic syndrome; rapid weight reduction; gallbladder stasis; inborn disorders of bile acid metabolism; hyperlipidemia syndromes; for pigment stones - chronic haemolytic syndromes, biliary infection, and gastrointestinal disorders (Crohn disease, ileal resection/bypass, cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency).
(iii) Complications: empyema (pure pus), perforation, fistulas, erosion of the gallstone into adjacent bowel (gallstone ileus), mucocele with obstruction of gallbladder outflow; the gallbladder may become gangrenous (green-black necrotic organ) or "emphysematous" from invasion by gas-producing organisms.
(iv) This is an acute abdominal emergency arising from obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone; management should address the obstructing stone given the risk of empyema, perforation, fistula formation and gangrenous change.

(i) The meninges comprise three membranes (dura, arachnoid, pia) and three spaces (epidural, subdural, subarachnoid containing CSF); epidural haemorrhage usually follows trauma with injury to a dural artery (for example the middle meningeal artery), occasionally to a venous sinus, often shows a lucid interval and grossly is a biconvex haematoma.
(ii) Subdural haemorrhage usually results from injury to the bridging veins, through acceleration-deceleration movements or spontaneously; onset is more insidious; causes include coagulation disorders, tumours and haemangiomas; it may be acute or chronic depending on organisation, and the haematoma adheres to the convexity of the brain.
(iii) Subarachnoid haemorrhage occurs between the pia and arachnoid, primary (within the space) or secondary (by extension); causes: aneurysm (berry, fusiform, infective), arteriovenous malformation, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, coagulopathies and neoplasms. Intracerebral haemorrhage: hypertension is the commonest cause (also of ganglionic haemorrhage); others are trauma, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, aneurysms and vascular malformations, neoplasms, vasculitis and bleeding diathesis; it may be lobar, ganglionic or brainstem.
(iv) Diffuse axonal injury is widespread transection of axons from shearing forces between brain layers, characterised by axon bulbs, and clinically may cause deep coma from which severe cases may not recover.
(v) The brain receives 15% of the resting cardiac output and 20% of total body oxygen consumption, with cerebral blood flow of about 50 mL per minute per 100 g of tissue, and is highly aerobic. Global ischaemia (ischaemic or hypoxic encephalopathy) follows generalised reduction of cerebral perfusion (cardiac arrest, shock, severe hypotension) and produces laminar necrosis. Focal ischaemia follows reduction or cessation of flow to a localized area from large-vessel disease (embolic or thrombotic arterial occlusion, often on atherosclerosis) or small-vessel disease (vasculitis, or occlusion from arteriosclerotic lesions in hypertension), giving brain infarction.
(vi) Types of infarct: carotid (including occlusion) 15%, lacunar 26%, cardioembolic 19%, cryptogenic 36% and miscellaneous 4%; causes include atherosclerosis, Moya Moya disease, sickle cell disease, homocystinuria, fibromuscular dysplasia and HIV-associated pathologies. By size: cystic infarcts lie in the territory of a major artery (MCA, ACA, PCA) or its branch and exceed 1 cm; lacunar infarcts are up to 1 cm, grossly visible, and most common in basal ganglia, deep white matter and basis pontis; microinfarcts are seen only histologically. Evolution: acute 0-48 hours, subacute 2-4 days, chronic from 5 days onwards, with liquefaction and cavitation in the chronic phase.

questions.question:
(i) State the origin of human schistosomal infection.
(ii) Describe the course taken by the organism from skin penetration to maturity.
(iii) State the distribution of the adult worm pairs and their eggs within the body.
(iv) How is the diagnosis confirmed?
(v) Explain the anatomical/pathological basis of the hepatic deformity that follows chronic infection.
questions.answerText:
(i) Schistosomiasis is caused by mammalian blood flukes (trematodes) known as Schistosoma, transmitted by freshwater snails living in slow-moving water of tropical rivers, lakes and irrigation ditches, with man as the definitive host and the snail as the intermediate host (Bulinus for S. haematobium/S. intercalatum, Biomphalaria for S. mansoni, Oncomelania for S. japonicum).
(ii) The infectious larvae (cercariae) penetrate human skin with the aid of proteolytic enzymes that degrade the keratinised layer, migrate into the peripheral blood vessels, and travel to the lungs and then to the hepatic vessels, where they mature and mate.
(iii) The mature male and female worm pairs migrate out and settle in the portal blood venules (S. mansoni, S. japonicum and S. mekongi) or the pelvic blood venules (S. haematobium); the females produce hundreds of eggs daily, and the eggs' proteases aid their passive transfer across the intestinal and bladder walls so that eggs are shed in stool or urine, with some eggs embolising to the brain, lungs, placenta, genitals or skin, where granulomas form around them.
(iv) Diagnosis is by microscopy of stool or urine, tissue histology, and DNA probes.
(v) Chronic disease is egg-induced chronic granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis in many organs, with pinhead-sized granulomas composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, neutrophils and eosinophils scattered throughout the gut, liver and other involved organs, centred on the schistosome egg.
In the liver, this is compounded by darkening from regurgitated heme-derived pigment and a bumpy surface, with pinpoint granulomas visible on cut surfaces.
The chronic immune response shifts from an early Th1-dominant reaction (producing interferon-gamma, which stimulates macrophages to secrete TNF, IL-1 and IL-6, causing fever) to a dominant Th2 response in chronic disease, although Th1 cells persist.
Th2 cells produce IL-13, which increases fibrosis by stimulating collagen synthesis.
This results in widespread fibrosis with portal enlargement without intervening regenerative nodules, the characteristic "pipestem fibrosis", which gives the liver its deformed, bumpy external appearance.
This pipestem fibrosis may obliterate the portal veins, leading to portal hypertension and congestive splenomegaly.
Portal hypertension and congestive splenomegaly are therefore the direct anatomical consequences of this periportal fibrotic deformity of the liver in chronic schistosomiasis.
This pattern of periportal fibrosis with portal enlargement but without intervening regenerative nodules anatomically distinguishes schistosomal "pipestem fibrosis" from other causes of chronic liver fibrosis, and directly explains the portal hypertension and splenomegaly that follow.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old presents with fever, fatigue, weight loss and headache most intense along the course of the temporal artery; examination reveals a thickened, nodular, tender vessel, and there are ocular symptoms ranging from diplopia to blindness.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List the predisposing factors.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology.
(iv) Outline the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Giant cell (temporal) arteritis - a medical emergency.
(ii) It is the most common form of vasculitis among older individuals (greater than 50 years); it affects large to small-sized arteries principally in the head, especially the temporal arteries, but also the vertebral and ophthalmic arteries (risking permanent blindness), and can affect other arteries such as the aorta (giant cell aortitis).
(iii) T-cell-mediated immune response against a vessel wall antigen induces cytokine production (especially TNF); anti-endothelial cell antibodies and anti-smooth muscle cell antibodies are found in about two-thirds of patients. Microscopy shows intimal thickening with or without thrombosis, medial granulomatous inflammation centred on the internal elastic lamina with fragmentation of the lamina, and giant cells in 75% of cases.
(iv) Responds well to steroids/anti-TNF therapies.

(i) In chronic rheumatic heart disease, the mitral valve is virtually always deformed (90% of cases); the aortic and tricuspid valves are variably affected, and the pulmonary valve is rarely affected. The cardinal valvular changes are leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and shortening, thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords, producing "fish-mouth" or "button-hole" stenosis.
(ii) With tight mitral stenosis, the left atrium progressively dilates and may harbour mural thrombi in its appendage or wall. In dilated cardiomyopathy, four-chamber dilation is also commonly accompanied by mural thrombi, while primary valvular defects are absent. The long-standing congestive changes in the lungs caused by mitral stenosis may induce pulmonary vascular and parenchymal changes leading to right ventricular hypertrophy.
(iii) Complications of rheumatic heart disease include increased vulnerability to recurrence with subsequent pharyngitis and worsening of the cardiac valves. Embolisation from the left atrial mural thrombi is a recognised complication, and infective endocarditis may develop on the deformed valves. Cardiac failure is also a recognised complication of chronic rheumatic heart disease. In infective endocarditis, vegetations are bulky and friable and may erode into the underlying myocardium to produce ring abscesses. Systemic embolisation from these vegetations may occur, causing septic infarcts in several distant organs, including the spleen, kidneys, lungs and brain. Embolisation to the brain thus represents a distant functional deficit (stroke/septic infarct) arising from a primary valvular abnormality. This illustrates how structural deformity of the heart valves can translate into remote organ dysfunction through thrombus formation and embolisation.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the heart valves affected in chronic rheumatic heart disease.
(ii) State how the parts of the heart relate to the common pathological changes seen.
(iii) Explain how disease of the heart valves may spread to cause a functional deficit in a distant structure (the brain).

questions.answerText:
(i) Benign prostatic (nodular) hyperplasia: hyperplasia of prostatic stromal and epithelial cells forming large, fairly discrete nodules in the periurethral region; it arises in the transitional and periurethral zones (beginning in the submucosa of the proximal urethra), whereas carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone. It is not a precursor lesion for prostatic carcinoma.
(ii) Risk factors: advancing age (about 20% of men over 40, 70% by 60 and 90% by 80 years); commoner in blacks than whites and least common in Asia; androgens are required, and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is the ultimate mediator of prostatic growth.
- DHT is produced by prostatic stromal and a few basal cells through type 2 5α-reductase; it binds nuclear androgen receptors and stimulates transcription of genes for growth factors and their receptors, which stimulate proliferation of stromal cells and inhibit death of epithelial cells.
(iii) The nodules compress the urethra into a slit-like orifice; the gland weighs 60-100 g; histology shows glandular proliferation with small to large, cystically dilated glands lined by an inner columnar and an outer cuboidal layer.
- Increased outflow resistance leads to bladder hypertrophy and distension with retention of urine; failure to empty completely leaves residual urine, a common source of infection of the bladder and kidney; some patients present with acute urinary retention requiring emergency catheterisation.
(iv) Options: surgical (prostatectomy); medical (α-blockers such as tamsulosin, which inhibit α1-adrenergic receptors and reduce prostatic smooth muscle tone; 5α-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride, which inhibit DHT synthesis and shrink the prostate); transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP).
- Justification: because DHT is the ultimate mediator of growth, a 5α-reductase inhibitor removes the growth stimulus, causing shrinkage with improvement of symptoms; surgery is the mainstay of treatment.
questions.question:
A man older than 50 years presents with increased urinary frequency, nocturia, difficulty starting and stopping the urinary stream and overflow dribbling.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and the prostatic zones in which it arises, contrasting these with the zone of origin of prostatic carcinoma.
(ii) State the risk factors, the incidence with age and the hormonal basis of the condition.
(iii) Describe the pathology and the complications, including how outflow obstruction leads to retention and infection.
(iv) List the treatment options and justify one of them.

A patient is found to have a medullary carcinoma of the thyroid together with parathyroid hyperplasia and a pheochromocytoma.
(i) State the diagnosis and the other conditions in its group.
(ii) State the genetic predisposition and the pathophysiology.
(iii) Describe the origin, morphology and clinical features of the thyroid and adrenal tumours.
(iv) State the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (Sipple syndrome): parathyroid hyperplasia, medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma. The MEN syndromes are inherited diseases with proliferative lesions (hyperplasia, adenomas, carcinomas) of multiple endocrine organs: MEN-1 (Wermer) has pituitary, parathyroid and pancreatic tumours; MEN-2B has pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple neuromas or ganglioneuromas and Marfanoid habitus, without parathyroid hyperplasia.
(ii) MEN-2A is due to a gain-of-function mutation in the RET proto-oncogene on chromosome 10q11.2 (MEN-2B has a point substitution in RET); MEN-1 is due to a loss-of-function mutation in the Menin tumour suppressor gene on 11q13. Features: early onset of tumours, multiple and multifocal organ involvement, usually more aggressive than sporadic tumours, and often preceded by hyperplasia.
(iii) Medullary carcinoma: arises from parafollicular C cells (calcitonin, CEA, serotonin, VIP); about 5% of thyroid malignancies; 80% sporadic, otherwise familial MEN-2; solitary in sporadic cases but bilateral in syndromic cases; polygonal or spindle cells with amyloid in the stroma and calcitonin demonstrable in tumour cells.
- Pheochromocytoma: secretes catecholamines (VMA in urine); well circumscribed; small clusters of cells (Zellballen pattern) with finely granular cytoplasm; the "10% tumour" (10% are bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% not associated with hypertension and 10% malignant); malignancy is confirmed by metastases; sustained or paroxysmal attacks of raised blood pressure, a correctable cause of hypertension.
- Parathyroid hyperplasia enlarges all glands, with chief cell or clear cell hyperplasia in a nodular or diffuse pattern.
(iv) Related syndromes for the differential: von Hippel-Lindau (chromosome 3p: phaeochromocytoma, islet cell tumour, renal cell carcinoma, CNS haemangioblastoma, retinal angiomas) and Carney complex (2p and 17q: myxomas, schwannomas, spotty pigmentation, Sertoli cell tumours, adrenocortical disease, GH-secreting pituitary tumours).

(i) Cryptorchidism (incomplete descent of the testis): complete or incomplete failure of the intra-abdominal testis to descend into the scrotal sac; found in approximately 1% of 1-year-old boys; usually an asymptomatic incidental finding; unilateral in about 85% of cases.
(ii) Descent occurs in two morphologically and hormonally distinct phases: the transabdominal phase, in which the testis comes to lie in the lower abdomen or brim of the pelvis, is controlled by Müllerian-inhibiting substance; the inguinoscrotal phase, in which the testis descends through the inguinal canal into the scrotal sac, is androgen dependent and possibly mediated by androgen-induced release of calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.
- Arrest within the inguinal canal is the commonest; arrest within the abdomen accounts for only 5-10% of cases; the precise cause is poorly understood.
- It may be isolated or accompanied by other genitourinary malformations such as hypospadias.
(iii) Most inguinal cryptorchid testes descend spontaneously into the scrotum during the first year of life. A testis kept in the inguinal canal is exposed to trauma and crushing against ligaments and bones, and an inguinal hernia accompanies it in some cases.
- From about 2 years the malpositioned testis undergoes atrophic change: arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization and thickening of the basement membrane of the tubules, and increased interstitial stroma with prominent Leydig cells.
- Testicular dysfunction results, and the undescended testis is at greater risk of developing testicular cancer than a descended testis.
(iv) Surgical correction (orchiopexy) for those that remain undescended, performed before the age of two years, before histologic deterioration sets in.
questions.question:
A one-year-old boy is found on routine examination to have an empty scrotal sac on one side. The finding is asymptomatic and incidental.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis, its frequency and its laterality.
(ii) Explain the embryologic basis, naming the two phases of testicular descent, the hormonal control of each and the commonest site of arrest.
(iii) Describe the natural history, and the pathological changes and risks if the testis remains malpositioned.
(iv) State the definitive treatment and its timing.

questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital aganglionic megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease).
(ii) Male-to-female ratio 4:1; associated with Down syndrome; heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase RET gene.
(iii) Arrest of migration (proximal to distal) of neural crest cells into the aganglionic segment, producing functional obstruction and colonic dilation proximal to the affected segment. There is absence of Auerbach's (myenteric) and Meissner's (submucosal) plexus; the rectum is always affected, with variable proximal involvement and progressive dilation and hypertrophy of the unaffected proximal colon (megacolon). Diagnosis is confirmed by absence of ganglion cells.
(iv) Complications include perforation, sepsis, enterocolitis and fluid derangement.
questions.question:
A neonate presents with delayed passage of meconium and progressive abdominal distension. A contrast study shows a transition zone with a dilated proximal colon.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List the predisposing factors.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology.
(iv) Outline the management.

questions.answerText:
(i) Invasive breast carcinoma (most are of no special type). Risk factors: female sex, advancing age, lifetime oestrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, first child after 30, not breastfeeding, postmenopausal obesity), family history and genes (BRCA1 on 17q21 and BRCA2 on 13q12 account for up to 25% of familial cases; TP53/Li-Fraumeni, PTEN/Cowden, CHEK2, ATM), proliferative breast disease (atypical hyperplasia 4-5 times, DCIS and LCIS 8-10 times), radiation, alcohol, high-fat diet and pesticides.
- Risk is reduced by early pregnancy (before 20 years), prolonged breastfeeding, oophorectomy (75%), bilateral prophylactic mastectomy (about 90%) and chemoprevention with ER antagonists.
(ii) Metastasis to axillary nodes, internal mammary nodes, skin, bones, lung, liver and adrenals; locally advanced disease invades skin or skeletal muscle (extension to pectoral muscles), and inflammatory carcinoma shows extensive invasion of dermal lymphovascular channels; Paget's disease is spread of malignant cells to the nipple skin.
- Poor prognostic indicators: distant metastasis, 4 or more involved nodes (axillary nodal status is the most important factor when there is no distant metastasis), tumour size over 2 cm, locally advanced disease, lymphovascular invasion, inflammatory carcinoma, HER2-positive or triple-negative profile, high grade, poor response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and some special types (metaplastic, micropapillary, medullary).
(iii) The goals are to control local disease and to prolong survival by treating known or potential distant metastases. Options: hormonal therapy with tamoxifen (ER antagonist), trastuzumab (anti-HER2 antibody) with chemotherapy, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
- Justification for hormonal therapy in receptor-positive tumours: 80% of tumours with both oestrogen and progesterone receptors respond to hormonal manipulation, about 40% with only one receptor, and under 10% with neither; ER-positive patients have a higher likelihood of tamoxifen response. Trastuzumab suits HER2-overexpressing tumours, although cardiac toxicity may limit its use.
questions.question:
A woman presents with a hard breast lump, nipple retraction and peau d'orange skin change.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and its risk factors, including genetic, reproductive and protective factors.
(ii) State the complications: the sites of spread and the indicators of poor prognosis.
(iii) List the management options and justify one on the basis of tumour receptor status.

A heavy smoker presents with cough, haemoptysis and chest pain; chest imaging shows a central hilar mass. Another patient's imaging shows a peripheral lung nodule.
(i) Identify the organ/structure and the likely tumour type in each location.
(ii) Describe the structures compressed/affected by each tumour type.
(iii) List the differential histological pathologies.
(iv) Discuss the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking tumour site to its clinical behaviour.
questions.answerText:
(i) The central hilar mass is typically a squamous cell (bronchogenic) carcinoma or small cell carcinoma; the peripheral nodule is typically an adenocarcinoma or large cell carcinoma.
(ii) The central squamous cell (bronchogenic) carcinoma typically involves the hilar lymph nodes and spreads to other parts from there, producing mainly localised effects of respiratory distress but may cause skeletal and brain metastasis; small cell carcinoma, also central, is notorious for widespread distant metastasis including to the CNS and skin.
(iii) Broad histological divisions are small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC - squamous, adenocarcinoma or large cell carcinoma); adenocarcinomas are further typed as solid, acinar, mucinous, papillary and micropapillary; squamous tumours tend to be central, have the highest rates of cavitation and metastasise late, whereas adenocarcinoma and large cell tumours are peripheral and tend to metastasise early.
(iv) Adenocarcinomas may present like pneumonic changes in the lung, are the type typically associated with scars, and spread within and outside the lung to involve the liver, brain, skin, kidneys and adrenals; lymphatic invasion may produce intractable pleural effusion with chest X-ray changes of lymphangitis carcinomatosa. The pain-poor lung parenchyma often permits a mass to grow undiscovered until it invades another structure such as a blood vessel, cough receptor, pleural pain receptor or distant site, explaining late presentation with symptoms and signs of the tumour.

(i) The lymphoid immune system is divided into two major functional regions: the primary immune organs (sites of initial maturation of immune-competent cells - B cells in the bone marrow, T cells in the thymus) and the secondary immune organs (sites of antigen-driven replication and differentiation into committed effector cells - lymph nodes, spleen, and the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lining the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts).
(ii) After initial maturation in the primary immune organs, "virgin" B and T lymphocytes travel via the peripheral blood and home to specific sites within the lymph node; B cells home to the primary and secondary follicles of the cortex and to the medullary cords, while T cells home to the paracortex, although the separation of B and T lymphocytes is not absolute and both cell types are present throughout the lymph node.
(iii) Lymph node histology is dynamic: in the absence of immune stimulation, follicles are primary follicles, whereas in the presence of immune stimulation they become secondary follicles or germinal centres.
(iv) Recognising lymph node pathology requires familiarity with this normal anatomy and cytology, because lymph node hyperplasia is an exaggeration of this normal histology, with expansion of all regions or selective expansion of a single region.
Follicular hyperplasia (expansion of the follicular/cortical region) occurs in collagen vascular diseases, systemic toxoplasmosis, and syphilis;
parafollicular hyperplasia (expansion of the paracortex) occurs in skin diseases, viral infections, and drug reactions;
sinus histiocytosis occurs adjacent to cancer or with infections, so the site of expansion corresponds to the anatomical zone reacting to the particular stimulus.
(v) Both are lymphomas usually affecting lymph nodes and visceral organs, characterised by malignant cells within a background inflammatory infiltrate.
Pattern: classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) shows a diffuse, interfollicular or nodular pattern, whereas nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) is nodular, at least in part.
Tumour cells: CHL shows classic Reed-Sternberg cells, mononuclear or lacunar variants (CD15-positive in 85%, CD30-positive in over 95%, CD45-negative, CD20 negative or weakly positive, EBV-positive in 50%), whereas NLPHL shows lymphocytic/histiocytic or "popcorn" cells (CD15-negative, CD30-negative, CD20-positive, CD45-positive, EBV-negative).
Background: CHL has lymphocytes, histiocytes, eosinophils and plasma cells with common fibrosis and background T-cells outnumbering B-cells, whereas NLPHL has a predominantly lymphocytic/histiocytic background, rare fibrosis, and background B-cells outnumbering T-cells.
Additional markers: nuclear BCL6 and epithelial membrane antigen are negative in the Reed-Sternberg cells of CHL but positive in NLPHL, and CD57-positive T-cells are absent in CHL but present in NLPHL.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the anatomical organization of the lymphoid immune system under the headings of primary and secondary immune organs.
(ii) Describe the sites of B lymphocyte and T lymphocyte homing within the lymph node.
(iii) Describe the histological variation seen in lymph node follicles.
(iv) Explain the clinical basis for the different patterns of lymph node hyperplasia.
(v) Distinguish between classical Hodgkin lymphoma and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.

A 6-year-old child from a malaria-endemic region presents with a rapidly enlarging jaw mass. A lymph node biopsy shows sheets of monomorphic medium-sized lymphoid cells with numerous interspersed tingible-body macrophages producing a 'starry sky' appearance.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
(i) Burkitt's lymphoma (endemic type).
(ii) Endemic Burkitt's lymphoma occurs in childhood, characteristically with jaw involvement, and is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) in 95% of cases; malaria is also associated with the endemic form (there are also sporadic and AIDS-related forms).
(iii) Burkitt's lymphoma is a mature B-cell neoplasm (CD10, CD19, CD20 positive) characterised by translocations involving chromosome 8 and the c-myc and immunoglobulin gene loci: t(8;14) in 75% of cases, t(2;8) in 15%, and t(8;22) in 10%; histology shows the starry sky pattern, and Burkitt cells have 3-5 nucleoli with lipid vacuoles in the cytoplasm.

(i) Renal cell carcinoma is classified into clear cell carcinoma, papillary carcinoma, chromophobe carcinoma, Xp11 translocation carcinoma, collecting duct (Bellini duct) carcinoma and medullary carcinoma. Contd: renal cell carcinomas represent about 3% of all newly diagnosed cancers and account for 85% of renal cancers in adults.
(ii) Risk factors for renal cell carcinoma include tobacco use, obesity (particularly in women), hypertension, unopposed oestrogen therapy, and exposure to asbestos, petroleum products and heavy metals. Most renal cancer is sporadic, but unusual autosomal dominant familial forms occur, including Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome, hereditary papillary carcinoma, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome.
(iii) Clear cell carcinoma is the most common type, accounting for 70% to 80% of renal cell cancers. Clear cell carcinoma is made up of cells with clear or granular cytoplasm and is nonpapillary in growth pattern. Papillary carcinoma accounts for 10% to 15% of renal cancers. Papillary carcinoma is characterised by a papillary growth pattern and occurs in both familial and sporadic forms. Chromophobe carcinoma, by comparison, represents about 5% of renal cell cancers and is composed of cells with prominent cell membranes and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, usually with a halo around the nucleus. The Xp11 translocation carcinoma is a genetically distinct subtype that often occurs in young patients and is defined by translocations of the TFE3 gene at Xp11.2. Collecting duct (Bellini duct) carcinoma represents about 1% or less of renal epithelial neoplasms and arises from collecting duct cells in the medulla, forming glands within a prominent fibrotic stroma. Medullary carcinoma is morphologically similar to collecting duct carcinoma and is seen in patients with sickle cell trait.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the classification of Renal Cell Carcinoma.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis (risk factors) for the development of Renal Cell Carcinoma.
(iii) Distinguish between Clear cell carcinoma and Papillary carcinoma of the kidney.

questions.answerText:
(i) Leprosy (Hansen disease) is a slowly progressive contagious disease of skin and peripheral nerves caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an acid-fast obligate intracellular organism that secretes no toxin (virulence rests on its cell wall); transmitted by aerosol from upper respiratory tract lesions, inhaled bacilli are taken up by alveolar macrophages; it disseminates through blood but grows in cold tissues of skin and extremities; low communicability, prolonged skin contact needed, incubation about 3 years.
(ii) Leprosy is a bipolar disease determined by the host cellular immune response: a T cell-mediated response gives tuberculoid leprosy, anergy gives lepromatous leprosy; borderline (dimorphous) leprosy has features of both and may upgrade or downgrade during treatment. Tuberculoid: CD4+ TH cells release IL-2 and IFN-γ, forming well-developed granulomas with few surviving bacilli (paucibacillary); nerve damage occurs early, with granulomas forming in nerve sheaths. Lepromatous: lack of T cell-mediated immunity; diffuse lesions with macrophages stuffed with bacilli (multibacillary); many CD8+ suppressor T cells secrete IL-10 (inhibits TH cells) and IL-4 (induces antibody production); the non-protective antibody forms antigen-antibody complexes causing erythema nodosum leprosum (vasculitis) and glomerulonephritis; nerve damage occurs late. A chromosomal locus called Bcg has been found to determine and regulate individual immunologic responsiveness to mycobacterial antigens.
(iii) Tuberculoid: begins with localized flat skin lesions that develop hyperpigmented elevated margins and pale centres; nerve involvement later dominates, with peripheral nerves thickened and hard, and nerves enclosed in granulomatous reaction destroyed; skin lesions show a marked inflammatory reaction around skin appendages including the subepidermal zone. Lepromatous: peripheral nerves, particularly the ulnar and peroneal nerves, are invaded by bacteria; the disease also involves skin, anterior eye, upper airways down to the larynx, testes, hands and feet, and may involve liver, spleen, bone, kidney and muscle; first sign is an ill-defined hypopigmented macule on trunk or buttocks, then macules, papules or nodules on face, earlobes and wrists.
(iv) Destruction of nerves enclosed in granuloma causes extensive skin anaesthesia, skin and muscle atrophy, proneness to trauma and development of indolent skin ulcers. Contractures, paralysis and autoamputation of toes and fingers may ensue; facial nerve damage causes eyelid paralysis, keratitis and corneal ulceration.
(v) Invasion of the ulnar and peroneal nerves gives loss of sensation with trophic changes (claw hand and foot drop); skin lesions are hypoaesthetic or anaesthetic, and coalescing nodules produce a leonine facies with lepra (Virchow) foamy cells and globi of bacilli beneath a grenz zone. Further changes: loss of nasal septum or laryngeal stricture, inguinal and axillary lymphadenopathy with foamy histiocytosis, testicular involvement with gynaecomastia and sterility, and amyloid in late stages.

(i) Pelvic inflammatory disease is infection of pelvic organs extending beyond the uterine corpus; Neisseria gonorrhoeae (a Gram-negative diplococcus, sexually transmitted) and Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K) are the most common agents, though most infections are polymicrobial, and it is commoner in sexually promiscuous women. After postpartum endometritis or endometrial curettage the agents are staphylococci, streptococci, coliforms and Clostridium perfringens; Actinomyces israelii (a Gram-positive filamentous rod found in 4% of normal individuals) is increasingly associated with intrauterine devices.
(ii) Gonococcal infection ascends through the cervix to the endometrial cavity (acute endometritis) and the fallopian tube (acute salpingitis), and may spread to the ovary causing a tubo-ovarian abscess; the result is bilateral acute suppurative salpingitis, salpingo-oophoritis, pyosalpinx, with hydrosalpinx on resolution. Actinomyces enters the uterine cavity through the tail of the intrauterine device, ascends the fallopian tube, ovary and broad ligament and may form a tubo-ovarian abscess, with drainage tracts containing sulphur granules.
(iii) Presentation is lower abdominal pain, fever, vaginal discharge, bilateral adnexal tenderness and marked discomfort on cervical manipulation (Chandelier sign). Complications: rupture of a tubo-ovarian abscess causing life-threatening peritonitis, infertility from scarring of healed tubes, increased risk of ectopic pregnancy, and intestinal obstruction from fibrous bands and adhesions.
(iv) The purulent inflammatory reaction at every site rarely resolves completely and leaves dense fibrous adhesions and distortion of the organs, especially the fallopian tube, which is a cause of infertility.
(v) Actinomycosis produces extensive fibrosis and scarring of the female genital tract. In lymphogranuloma venereum (chlamydial serotypes L1-L3) a painless vesicle is followed by enlarged inguinal nodes that may rupture into fistulae, and third-stage scarring obstructs lymphatics, producing genital elephantiasis and rectal strictures.
(vi) Gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis (primary painless indurated papule; secondary rash, lymphadenopathy and condyloma lata; tertiary aortitis and gummas), Gardnerella (bacterial vaginosis) and Trichomonas vaginalis (purulent vaginal discharge, flagellated trophozoites) affect the lower tract; tuberculosis causes salpingitis and endometritis.
(vii) HSV-2 causes papules, vesicles and ulcers with latency in lumbosacral ganglia, condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6 and 11) causes koilocytic warts, molluscum contagiosum causes pearly papules with molluscum bodies, and Candida albicans (favoured by diabetes, oral contraceptives and pregnancy) forms adherent white plaques.

(i) Oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
(ii) In its most common form, the proximal part of the oesophagus ends as a blind sac and the distal part forms a tracheo-oesophageal fistula. Up to half of patients have other congenital anomalies, and one-fifth have VACTERL syndrome (vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, renal dysplasia and limb abnormalities). Polyhydramnios develops because amniotic fluid cannot reach the stomach; prenatal diagnosis is suggested by polyhydramnios, a prominent oesophageal pouch, and a small or absent stomach bubble with fluid-filled bowel loops on ultrasound.
questions.question:
A newborn develops paroxysmal choking, cyanosis and food aspiration with attempted feeds, with recurrent pneumonia; the antenatal history reveals polyhydramnios.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Describe the embryologic variant seen in this condition.

questions.answerText:
(i) Between 1% and 3% of patients with pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis have osseous infection; the organisms are usually blood borne from a focus of active disease, though direct extension from a pulmonary focus or tracheobronchial nodes into adjacent vertebrae, or lymphatic spread, is possible.
(ii) The infection is usually solitary but may be multifocal in AIDS; the spine (especially thoracic and lumbar) is the commonest site, followed by knee and hips. It tends to be more destructive and resistant to treatment than pyogenic osteomyelitis; patients present with pain on motion, localized tenderness, low-grade fevers, chills and weight loss.
(iii) In the spine the infection breaks through the intervertebral disc to involve multiple vertebrae and extends into soft tissue, where it can form an ilio-psoas abscess.
(iv) Severe destruction of vertebrae (Pott's disease) may cause skeletal deformities and neurologic deficits.
(v) Syphilis (T. pallidum) and yaws (T. pertenue) rarely involve bone because treatment is achieved before that stage; in congenital syphilis bone lesions appear at the fifth month of gestation and are fully developed at birth, with spirochaetes localising in areas of endochondral ossification (osteochondritis) and in the periosteum (periostitis). In acquired syphilis bone disease begins early in the tertiary stage, 2-5 years after the initial infection, affecting the bones of the nose, palate, skull and extremities, especially the tibia; the saber shin is produced by massive periosteal bone deposition on the medial and anterior surfaces of the tibia.
(vi) Pyogenic haematogenous osteomyelitis is bacterial seeding from the blood, primarily in children, most commonly in the rapidly growing, highly vascular metaphysis where sluggish flow in capillary loops predisposes to thrombosis, necrosis and seeding. It presents as an acute systemic illness with malaise, fever, chills, leukocytosis and throbbing pain. Infants are prone to arthritis of the adjacent joint through metaphyseal-epiphyseal vascular connections; predisposing factors include diabetes, sickle cell disease, AIDS, intravenous drug abuse, steroids and prosthetic devices, and organisms are chiefly S. aureus (80% from age 4 years) with Salmonella in sickle cell disease. Antibiotics with surgical drainage are usually curative, but 5-25% become chronic and complications include pathologic fracture, endocarditis and sepsis, whereas tuberculous osteomyelitis is more resistant to treatment.

(i) The spleen is located in the left hypochondrial region beneath the 9th to 11th ribs, weighs 150-200g and measures about 12cm in length, 7cm in width and 3cm in thickness in a normal adult. It has a smooth and glistening capsule, and is bordered by the diaphragm, kidney, pancreas, splenic flexure and stomach.
(ii) About half of the organ is red pulp, containing red blood cells and macrophages, traversed by vascular sinusoids and capillaries separated by the cords of Billroth, a sponge-like labyrinth of macrophages that filters blood as it slowly seeps through. The other half is white pulp, made up of lymphocytes (seen grossly as grey specks/Malpighian follicles), containing about 25% of the body's total T-cells in the periarteriolar sheath and about 15% of total B-cells in the germinal centre.
(iii) In portal hypertension the red pulp exceeds 50% of the splenic volume. Long-standing splenic congestion leads to fibrosis.
(iv) Hypersplenism is characterised by splenomegaly with a fall in one or more peripheral blood cell lines (pancytopenia) and bone marrow hyperplasia of the deficient cell lines. Phagocytosis in the red pulp cords removes red cells with reduced elasticity, pits inclusion bodies such as Heinz bodies, and removes bacteria, cell debris and abnormal macromolecules (for example in Gaucher's disease).
(v) Because it is the largest mononuclear/phagocytic unit, the spleen readily becomes enlarged following systemic, inflammatory, haematological and metabolic disorders, and is also a site of secondary spread from melanoma, lymphomas and testicular germ cell tumours. The spleen can resume extramedullary haemopoiesis as a compensatory fetal role, for example during chronic haemolytic anaemia and idiopathic myelofibrosis. Hypersplenism produces a distant functional deficit by causing a decrease in one or more blood cell lines in the peripheral blood, compensated for by hyperplasia of those cell lines in the bone marrow. This pancytopenia is corrected by splenectomy, confirming the spleen as the cause of the distant marrow/peripheral-blood functional deficit.
questions.question:
(i) State the location, weight and dimensions of the spleen, and describe its capsule.
(ii) Describe the red pulp and white pulp that make up the organ.
(iii) State how the red pulp is affected in portal hypertension and long-standing congestion.
(iv) State how the organ's compartments relate to hypersplenism.
(v) Explain how splenic disease produces a functional deficit at a distant site, and how this is confirmed.

A 15-year-old boy presents with a painful, enlarging mass around the knee of two months' duration, with a recent pathological fracture. X-ray shows an osteolytic lesion with periosteal elevation described as a 'Codman triangle' and a 'sunburst' pattern.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
(i) Osteosarcoma.
(ii) Osteosarcoma is associated with Paget's disease, fibrous dysplasia, bone infarction, radiation exposure to bone, prosthetic implants, and the Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, and retinoblastoma.
(iii) Osteosarcoma is a malignant tumour of bone characterised by production of bone matrix by the tumour cells; clinically it presents with a painful mass and pathological fractures, and radiologic features include the Codman triangle, a sunburst pattern, and an osteolytic picture on x-ray, all present in this patient.

(i) The pancreas has an exocrine component made up of acinar cells (which secrete digestive enzymes, including amylase and lipase in active form, and others such as proteases, elastase and phospholipase that require cleavage by trypsin) drained by a ductal system, and an endocrine component, the islets of Langerhans.
In chronic disease the gland grossly becomes hard, sometimes with extremely dilated ducts and visible calcified concretions, and there is parenchymal fibrosis with a reduced number and size of acini and variable dilation of the pancreatic ducts.
(ii) Acinar cell injury (from alcohol, drugs, trauma, ischaemia, viruses or metabolic injury) or pancreatic duct obstruction leads to release and activation of intracellular proenzymes and lysosomal enzymes, producing acute pancreatitis, with proteolysis, fat necrosis (from lipase and phospholipase) and haemorrhage (from elastase).
Long-standing ductal obstruction, toxic-metabolic injury and oxidative stress instead produce chronic pancreatitis, in which there is relative sparing of the islets of Langerhans early on, although in late-stage disease the endocrine pancreas is also affected, with remaining islets becoming embedded in sclerotic tissue, fusing, and eventually disappearing; so the exocrine (acinar) component is affected earlier and the endocrine (islet) component only in advanced disease.
Pancreatic ducts of all sizes may contain variably calcified proteinaceous material, and there is hyperplastic or atrophic ductal epithelium with squamous metaplasia.
The ductal system is also the site of origin of mucin-producing cystic neoplasms: serous cystadenoma arises from glycogen-rich cuboidal cells around small cysts, mucinous cystic neoplasms arise in the body or tail with mucin-filled cysts lined by mucinous columnar epithelium, and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms arise within the main pancreatic duct or its branches, more often in the head of the pancreas.
(iii) In acute pancreatitis, the released and activated pancreatic enzymes are not confined to the gland: trypsin generation converts prekallikrein to its active form (activating the kinin system) and activates factor XII (activating the clotting and complement systems), so the pathological process becomes systemic rather than remaining localised to the pancreas.
This accounts for disseminated intravascular coagulation and for acute respiratory distress syndrome, which results from alveolar capillary injury at a site distant from the pancreas.
Increased microvascular permeability produces hypovolaemia and peripheral vascular collapse (shock), compounded by endotoxaemia arising from breakdown of the barrier between gastrointestinal flora and the bloodstream.
Renal failure follows from acute tubular necrosis, again a distant functional deficit driven by the systemic effects of the pancreatic insult.
Fat necrosis is not confined to the pancreatic substance but extends to peripancreatic and extrapancreatic fat, with released fatty acids combining with calcium to form insoluble salts (soap formation).
In this way a primarily glandular, exocrine-cell injury generates circulating activated proteases and inflammatory mediators that produce distant organ dysfunction (lung, kidney, coagulation system) well beyond the pancreas itself.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the components of the pancreas relevant to its exocrine and endocrine pathology.
(ii) State how these components relate to the common pathologies of the pancreas.
(iii) Explain why disease of the pancreas may spread to affect distant structures, causing functional deficit.

A newborn delivered several weeks before term develops rapid, laboured breathing within hours of birth, and on examination the lungs are noted to be airless.
(i) State the diagnosis and explain why its incidence rises the earlier a baby is born.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of this condition, including the gross and microscopic appearance of the lungs and the composition and fate of the hyaline membranes.
(iii) State what is indicated regarding definitive treatment of this condition, and list its complications.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease.
Its incidence increases with a decrease in gestational age, because the fundamental defect is pulmonary immaturity.
(ii) The defect is deficiency of surfactant produced by type II alveolar cells; surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and the work of keeping alveoli open, and its production is accelerated after 35 weeks and during labour.
Grossly, the lungs are normal size, solid, reddish purple, airless, and sink in water.
Microscopically, the alveoli are poorly developed and collapsed, with necrotic debris in the terminal bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
Eosinophilic hyaline membranes line the respiratory tree, consisting of fibrin and cellular debris from necrotic type II pneumocytes; the membranes either break off and are phagocytosed, or are reorganised by fibroblasts and incorporated into the alveolar wall. This disease is never seen in stillborn infants.
(iii) Complications include retinopathy of prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, patent ductus arteriosus, and intraventricular haemorrhage.

(i) The paired Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts develop into the fallopian tubes, uterus and vaginal wall; anomalies are agenesis (failure of the ducts to develop, usually with other urogenital anomalies and absent vagina and tubes), didelphys (failure to fuse, with double vagina), duplex bicornis (common wall fails to degenerate), septus (incomplete resorption of the fused wall) and bicornuate uterus (two horns, common cervix).
(ii) Menstrual phase: without blastocyst hCG the granulosa and theca cells degenerate and progesterone falls; the endometrium breaks down, spiral arteries collapse and stroma disintegrates, with menses on day 28. Proliferative phase: rapid growth of glands and stroma from the basal layer, glands becoming coiled and pseudostratified; secretory phase: ovulation on day 14, progesterone transforms the endometrium, glandular cells develop glycogen-rich subnuclear vacuoles by day 17 with stromal oedema, and pregnancy carries it to a hypersecretory state.
