(iii) Dysfunctional uterine bleeding is bleeding without an organic abnormality, related to the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis; commonest cause is anovulation (prolonged oestrogen without a post-ovulatory progesterone rise) at menarche and perimenopause, from endocrine disorders, granulosa cell tumours or obesity and malnutrition; inadequate luteal phase is an ovulatory cause; organic causes are leiomyoma, polyps, hyperplasia, adenocarcinoma, endometritis, pregnancy and IUCD. Acute endometritis follows delivery or miscarriage with retained products (group A streptococci, staphylococci) and is treated by curettage and antibiotics; chronic endometritis occurs with chronic PID, retained products, IUCD or tuberculosis, and plasma cells are diagnostic.
(iv) Endometriosis is endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus (ovaries, ligaments, rectovaginal septum, pelvic peritoneum, bowel, appendix, cervical, vaginal and tubal mucosa, laparotomy scars, umbilicus), causing infertility, dysmenorrhoea and chronic pelvic pain, with brown-fluid chocolate cysts (endometriomas); theories: benign metastasis, coelomic metaplasia and extrauterine stem cells. Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium, in continuity with the endometrium, with irregular nests separated from the basalis by at least 2 cm, causing menorrhagia, colicky dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and pelvic pain.
(v) Polyps are sessile or pedunculated, oestrogen-responsive with little progesterone response, may become hyperplastic and can transform to malignancy; endometrial hyperplasia (increased gland-to-stroma ratio from prolonged oestrogen: anovulation, obesity, menopause, PCOS, granulosa cell tumours, oestrogen therapy) is non-atypical or atypical (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia), with PTEN inactivation, and atypical forms progress to adenocarcinoma. Endometrial carcinoma is the commonest invasive cancer of the female genital tract, peaking at 55-65 years with postmenopausal bleeding; Type I endometrioid (over 80%) arises with hyperplasia, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, infertility and unopposed oestrogen; Type II serous (about 15%) arises a decade later in atrophic endometrium, poorly differentiated, with p53 mutation in at least 90%.
(vi) Leiomyoma (fibroid) is the commonest tumour in women (25% in reproductive life), commoner in blacks, oestrogen responsive (regresses or calcifies at menopause, enlarges in pregnancy), intramural (most), submucosal (bleeding) or subserosal; rarely leiomyosarcoma.
(vii) Endometriosis may reach distant sites such as bone, lung and brain by blood and lymphatics (benign metastasis theory), and involvement of the rectal wall causes pain on defaecation and of the bladder wall causes dysuria; large intramural fibroids interfere with bowel or bladder function.
(viii) Malignant mixed Müllerian tumours occur in menopausal women, usually with prior radiation therapy, and endometrial carcinoma tends to occur concurrently with breast carcinoma.

questions.question:
A woman presents with post-coital bleeding, bleeding after douching and a foul-smelling discharge.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and its risk factors, including the causative agent and the high-risk and low-risk types.
(ii) State the complications, local and distant.
(iii) State the management options available and justify one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Carcinoma of the cervix (squamous cell carcinoma in 95%). HPV is the most important cause (99.8% of cervical cancers; types 16 and/or 18 in 70.9%): high-risk types 16, 18, 31, 33 and others cause invasive cancer, whereas low-risk types 6 and 11 cause condylomas.
- Risk factors: early age at first intercourse, multiple sexual partners, a male partner with multiple previous partners, genital warts or infections, oral contraceptive use, multiparity, smoking, immune status (HIV/AIDS), lack of circumcision in male partners, diet and family history.
- Precursor: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, reversible and lasting from a few months to 20 years; about 20% of CIN3 progress to invasive cancer; viral E6 and E7 proteins bind p53 and Rb and drive progression.
(ii) Local extension into the parametrium compresses the ureters, causing hydroureters, hydronephrosis and renal failure, the most common cause of death; bladder and rectal involvement may lead to fistula formation; lymph node metastasis occurs; distant metastasis is to the liver, lungs and bone marrow.
(iii) Secondary prevention by screening: Pap smear (liquid-based cytology), visual inspection with acetic acid or iodine (VIA/VILI) and HPV-DNA testing, covering at least 80% of sexually active women aged 25-65 in an organised, community-based programme.
- Justification for Pap smear: the cancer progresses slowly over many years, so it should be performed in all women once sexually active; it detects precursor lesions by shed abnormal cells before invasion and has had a remarkable effect on cervical cancer mortality.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the structure of the tooth.
(ii) State the essential requirements for the development of dental caries.
(iii) Describe the stages of enamel caries.
(iv) Explain the clinical basis for why acute pulpitis and apical periodontitis commonly follow untreated caries.
(v) Distinguish between gingivitis and periodontitis.
questions.answerText:
(i) The tooth is made predominantly of dentin capped by a hard shell of enamel; the root, beneath the surface, is surrounded by a layer of cementum, and the periodontal membrane is wedged between the root and the alveolar bone, allowing the tooth to move slightly within the bone.
(ii) The essential requirements for the development of dental caries are cariogenic (acidogenic) bacteria, bacterial plaque, and a fermentable bacterial substrate (sugar); viridans streptococci such as Streptococcus mutans are implicated, being acidogenic (producing lactic acid from sucrose), able to survive at low pH, possessing an attachment mechanism to adhere to the smooth tooth surface, and producing insoluble plaque polysaccharides (glucans) that enable the bacteria to adhere to each other and to the tooth surface.
(iii) The stages of enamel caries are: an early submicroscopic lesion; a phase of non-bacterial enamel crystal destruction; cavity formation; and bacterial invasion of enamel.
(iv) Dental caries is the progressive bacterial damage to teeth exposed to saliva, and its ultimate effect is to break down the enamel and dentin and open a path for bacteria to reach the pulp.
Inflammation usually follows this bacterial invasion of the pulp, which is why acute pulpitis and apical periodontitis are very common causes of toothache; the progressive stages of caries (submicroscopic lesion, crystal destruction, cavity formation, bacterial invasion of enamel) provide a direct anatomical pathway from the tooth surface, through the dentin, to the pulp.
Dental caries is prevented by fluoridation of hydroxyapatite in enamel to form fluoro-apatite (calcium fluorophosphate), achieved through fluorine in drinking water and toothpaste, which strengthens the enamel barrier against this progression.
(v) Gingivitis is the inflammation of the oral mucosal soft tissue surrounding the teeth, often due to accumulation of dental plaque and calculus (calcified plaque), with features including erythema, oedema, bleeding, changes in contour, and loss of soft tissue adaptation to the teeth.
Types of gingivitis include plaque-related gingivitis, necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, medication-related gingivitis (e.g. phenytoin, calcium channel blockers), allergic gingivitis, and specific infection-related gingivitis; pre-existing gingivitis may become more severe in early pregnancy and poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.
Periodontitis is an inflammatory process that affects the supporting structures of the teeth - the periodontal ligaments, alveolar bone, and cementum - and may follow persisting gingivitis; the patient may complain of gingival bleeding, recession, or unpleasant taste.
Tooth loss may follow the destruction of the periodontal ligaments in periodontitis, whereas gingivitis, confined to the soft tissue surrounding the teeth, does not itself cause tooth loss.
Periodontal disease is most frequently localised but can also be a component of systemic diseases, including AIDS, leukaemia, Crohn disease, diabetes, Down syndrome, sarcoidosis, and syndromes associated with neutrophil defects (Chediak-Higashi syndrome, agranulocytosis, cyclic neutropenia).
In summary, gingivitis is inflammation limited to the gingival soft tissue around the tooth, while periodontitis extends to destroy the deeper supporting structures - the periodontal ligament, alveolar bone, and cementum.

(i) Meningocele or myelomeningocele: primary failure of neural tube closure, in which mesenchyme destined to form the posterior elements remains trapped laterally, causing a wide spina bifida; most frequently located in the thoracolumbar area.
(ii) Primary neurulation occurs at 3-4 weeks of gestation and ends with creation of the neural tube, which gives rise to the CNS above the S2 segment (epidermis externally, and neural crest at the junction of neural tube and epidermis); closure starts at the cervico-medullary junction and extends cranially and caudally; the cephalic neuropore closes around day 25 and the caudal neuropore around day 29 (corresponding to S2).
- Congenital malformations account for 1-20% of post-neonatal deaths; causes: idiopathic 40-60%, multifactorial 20-25%, chromosomal 10-15%, Mendelian 2-10%, maternal disease 6-8%, transplacental infection 2-3%.
(iii) Failures of closure: myeloschisis and craniorachischisis (neural folds fail to meet and fuse; flattened plate-like mass of nervous tissue with no overlying skin or membrane; most aborted); anencephaly (failure of the anterior neuropore to close; brain and calvarium absent and replaced by area cerebrovasculosa; remnants of brainstem and pituitary so the infant is born alive); encephalocele (midline bony defect through which brain protrudes, commonest occipital; prognosis depends on the amount of cerebral tissue herniated).
- Later disorders: diverticulation at weeks 5-6 (arrhinencephaly, holoprosencephaly); migration at 2-5 months (micrencephaly, lissencephaly, pachygyria, polymicrogyria, heterotopia); sulcation at 5-6 months (agyria, pachygyria, micropolygyria); maturation from the third trimester to postnatal life (megalencephaly, Arnold-Chiari and Dandy-Walker malformations).
questions.question:
A newborn has a defect of the thoracolumbar vertebral column with a wide spina bifida.
(i) State the diagnosis and the developmental process that has failed.
(ii) Explain the embryologic basis, including the timing of neuropore closure and the derivatives of the neural tube.
(iii) Describe the embryologic variants: failures of closure elsewhere in the neuraxis and the disorders of later stages of development.

(i) Describe the arteriosclerosis subtypes and the structure of the atheromatous plaque.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for the sites commonly affected by atherosclerosis.
(iii) Distinguish between Atherosclerosis and Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Arteriosclerosis is a broad term for hardening, thickening and loss of elasticity of arteries with accompanying narrowing of the vascular lumen; it has three subtypes - atherosclerosis, Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis, and arteriolosclerosis. Contd: the atheromatous plaque shows intimal thickening with lipid accumulation and has three main components - cells (macrophages, smooth muscle cells), connective tissue extracellular matrix, and intracellular/extracellular lipid, with a core rich in cholesterol and its esters.
(ii) Atherosclerosis commonly develops at sites predisposed to haemodynamic disturbance, such as vessel ostia and bifurcation points. The distribution of atheromatous plaques is mainly the abdominal aorta (especially at the ostia of its main branches), the coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, descending thoracic aorta, internal carotid arteries and vessels of the circle of Willis. Fatty streaks, present universally in children, are an important possible precursor of these atheromatous plaques.
(iii) Atherosclerosis is a chronic vascular disease characterised by intimal thickening with accumulation of lipids, inflammatory cells, fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells. Atherosclerosis usually affects medium to large sized arteries and produces stenosis and ultimately ischaemia. Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis is typically an incidental finding, usually seen in thick, muscular arteries. It is typically more prevalent with advancing age, though it can also occur at younger ages. Monckeberg sclerosis is characterised by dystrophic calcification of the tunica media of the vessels, unlike the intimal process of atherosclerosis. The third subtype, arteriolosclerosis, is either hyaline or hyperplastic and causes thickening of microvessel walls with luminal narrowing that may induce downstream ischaemic injury, seen in hypertension and diabetes. Complications of atherosclerotic plaques include calcification, ulceration, haemorrhage, thrombosis, aneurysmal dilation and infection.

questions.question:
An 18-month-old child presents with a large abdominal mass, fever, weight loss, bone pains, and respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology/morphology of this tumour.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is neuroblastoma.
(ii) Most cases are sporadic, but 1-2% are familial; the tumour has a prevalence of 1 in 7000 live births and a median age at diagnosis of 18 months.
It arises most often in the adrenal medulla (40%), the paravertebral region of the abdomen (25%), and the posterior mediastinum (15%).
(iii) Grossly the tumour may have a pseudocapsule and appear fleshy.
Histologically it is composed of small primitive cells with dark nuclei and scant cytoplasm, set in eosinophilic fibrillary material (neuropil), with Homer-Wright pseudorosettes in which cells are concentrically arranged around a central space filled with neuropil.
Immunohistochemistry is positive for neurone-specific enolase and PHOX2B. A variant with larger cells is called ganglioneuroblastoma.

questions.question:
A light-skinned adult presents with a pigmented lesion on sun-exposed skin that is asymmetrical, with an irregular border, varied colour and differential structure.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and the clinical rule used to suspect it.
(ii) List the predisposing factors, including the differences in dark-skinned patients.
(iii) Explain the molecular pathophysiology and the histological features.
(iv) Name the clinicopathological types, the prognostic factors and the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Malignant melanoma: a common and lethal skin cancer arising from melanocytes; the features fit the ABCD rule (asymmetry, border, colour, differential structure).
(ii) Usually due to ultraviolet light exposure; light-skinned whites are commonly affected; tumours are grouped into those in chronic sun-damaged skin and those in non-chronic sun-damaged skin; in blacks the acral sites and mucous membranes are affected.
- Melanocytic nevi may progress to melanoma and mark increased risk, so they are monitored; xeroderma pigmentosum (decreased repair of sunlight-induced DNA damage) predisposes to skin cancers including melanoma.
(iii) Acquired activating mutations in NRAS or BRAF (Ras pathway) occur in nevi and melanoma; in normal melanocytes activated RAS or BRAF gives only limited proliferation followed by permanent arrest through accumulation of p16/INK4a (inhibitor of CDK4 and CDK6); this protective response is disrupted in melanoma and its precursor lesions.
- Histology: many growth patterns are possible; cells are usually pleomorphic epithelioid cells with cherry-red nucleoli.
(iv) In situ melanoma (confined to the epidermis, may persist for months to years, simple excision often curative); superficial spreading (middle age; back in both sexes, legs in females; haphazard colours); nodular (fifth-sixth decade, males 2:1, often misdiagnosed as blood blister, haemangioma, dermal nevus or polyp); acral lentiginous (blacks and orientals; palms, soles, terminal phalanges and mucous membranes; aggressive with early metastasis); amelanotic.
- Prognostic factors: Breslow thickness, Clark's level, vascular invasion, male sex, mitotic index, ulceration, tumour regression and tumoural lymphocytic infiltration.

(i) Neurocysticercosis, caused by Taenia solium.
(ii) Stool examination for eggs/proglottids, tissue examination for cysticerci cysts, and scans (CT, MRI).
(iii) Cysticercosis is caused by ingestion of T. solium eggs in food contaminated by infested human stool; the oncosphere hatches in the small intestine, penetrates into the bloodstream, and then disseminates to muscles, the brain (causing neurocysticercosis), the heart, the eye, and the skin; in the upper small intestine, tapeworms can also cause mild abdominal pain, distension, anorexia and nausea, though infection is often asymptomatic, with central nervous system symptoms manifesting as epilepsy, matching this patient's seizures.
(iv) The cysts cause symptoms due to pressure and inflammatory response in the organ in which they lodge; cysticerci cysts are ovoid, white-to-opalescent, grape-sized, and contain an invaginated scolex and hooklets in clear fluid, with neurocysticercosis described as showing a larva containing an invaginated neck region within the brain.
(v) Eggs within the proglottid (tapeworm segment) are passed in the stool of an infected human; when a person ingests T. solium eggs from contaminated food, the oncosphere hatches in the small intestine, penetrates the intestinal wall, enters the bloodstream, and migrates to encyst as cysticerci, which can survive for years, in contrast to taeniasis proper (upper intestinal tapeworm infection), which follows ingestion of undercooked meat containing cysticerci that excyst in the small intestine.

questions.answerText:
(i) The genes that code for the most important transplantation antigens are clustered in a small segment of chromosome 6; this cluster constitutes the human MHC, also known as the HLA complex.
(ii) There are three categories, based on chemical structure, tissue distribution and function: Class I and Class II, which encode cell surface glycoproteins, and Class III, which encodes components of the complement system (e.g. C2, C4), enzymes such as 21-hydroxylase and the cytochrome P450 system, and TNF-alpha and TNF-beta (lymphotoxin).
(iii) The principal physiologic function of the cell-surface histocompatibility molecules is to bind peptide fragments of foreign proteins for presentation to antigen-specific T cells; because T cells can recognise only membrane-bound antigens, histocompatibility antigens are critical to the induction of T-cell immunity, and they also code for antigens that evoke rejection of transplanted organs and serve as determinants of disease susceptibility.
(iv) Individuals who are HLA-B27 positive have a 90-100-fold greater chance of developing ankylosing spondylitis, one of several HLA-B27-associated inflammatory disorders that also include post-infectious arthropathies such as post-gonococcal arthritis, Yersinia arthritis, Reiter's syndrome, and acute anterior uveitis.
This association may be explained by the presentation of B-27 on the cell surface with its peptide-binding groove unoccupied, thus enabling bacterial products to easily occupy it, or by the groove being abnormally available for interaction with peptides of microorganisms.
(v) Class I antigens are glycoproteins expressed on all nucleated cells and platelets, encoded by three closely linked loci (HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C), each a heterodimer of a polymorphic heavy chain non-covalently linked to a smaller, non-polymorphic peptide called beta-2-microglobulin.
Class I molecules present peptides derived from cytoplasmic (endogenous) proteins, digested by proteasomes from endogenous viral proteins, complexed with the class I chain and beta-2-microglobulin within the endoplasmic reticulum and transported to the surface for binding to the T-cell receptor on CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells, which are therefore Class I MHC-restricted.
Class II antigens are glycoproteins found on antigen-presenting cells, macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells, coded for in the HLA-D region with three sub-regions (HLA-DP, HLA-DQ and HLA-DR), each a heterodimer of a polymorphic alpha-chain and beta-chain, with expression inducible by interferon-gamma.
Class II molecules present exogenous antigens (such as extracellular microbes and soluble proteins) that are first internalised and processed within endosomes or lysosomes, associated with the class II heterodimer within the endoplasmic reticulum, and transported to the surface to interact with the T-cell receptor of CD4-positive helper T cells, which are therefore Class II MHC-restricted.
Thus Class I molecules are restricted to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and present endogenous (cytoplasmic) antigens, whereas Class II molecules are restricted to CD4+ helper T cells and present exogenous antigens.
Both Class I and Class II molecules possess an antigen-binding groove formed by their respective polymorphic domains, and many alleles exist within the population for both classes, identifiable by serological typing or DNA typing (PCR, RFLP, restriction enzyme digestion).
The type of MHC molecules T cells encounter during maturation also shapes the functional repertoire of mature peripheral T cells, linking both classes to genetic regulation of T-cell mediated immune responses.
questions.question:

(ii) Name the three categories of HLA genes and their loci.
(iii) State the general role of histocompatibility molecules.
(iv) Explain the clinical basis for the association between HLA-B27 and ankylosing spondylitis.

(i) Describe the classification (structure) of colonic polyps.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for the differing malignant potential of colonic polyps.
(iii) Distinguish between the Hyperplastic polyp and the Adenomatous (tubular) polyp.
questions.answerText:
(i) Colonic polyps may be sessile or pedunculated, and are either neoplastic or non-neoplastic. Contd: non-neoplastic polyps include inflammatory, hamartomatous and hyperplastic types; neoplastic polyps (colonic adenomas) are intraepithelial neoplasms and are the precursors of colorectal carcinoma.
(ii) Hyperplastic polyps arise from decreased epithelial cell turnover and delayed shedding of surface epithelial cells, causing a pile-up of goblet cells and defective maturation. This delayed shedding produces the serrated surface architecture that is the morphological hallmark of hyperplastic polyps, which have no malignant potential. Colonic adenomas are characterised by dysplasia (nuclear hyperchromasia, elongation and stratification), and the prevalence of adenomas correlates with that of colorectal carcinoma, though the majority of adenomas do not progress to cancer.
(iii) Hyperplastic polyps are the commonest polyp in the colon, occurring in the 6th to 7th decade. They are usually found in the left colon, typically less than 5mm in diameter, and are smooth, nodular mucosal protrusions, usually multiple. Their crypts are elongated with relatively normal crypt bases and mature goblet and absorptive cells. Colonic adenomas vary in size and may be pedunculated or sessile, with a velvety surface. Adenomas show epithelial dysplasia and an architecture that is tubular, tubulovillous or villous. An adenoma is classified as tubular if the villous component is less than 25%, villous if more than 75%, and tubulovillous if between 25% and 75%. Unlike hyperplastic polyps, adenomas are benign neoplasms with malignant potential, and their prevalence increases dramatically with age.

(i) Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina arising in vaginal adenosis: adenocarcinoma is rare (under 0.14% of those exposed) but frequent in young women whose mothers were treated with DES during pregnancy, usually at ages 15-20; the probable precursor is vaginal adenosis, seen as red granular patches different from the pale pink vaginal mucosa.
(ii) Surgery and irradiation have eradicated DES-related tumours in up to 80% of patients.
(iii) In utero the vagina and the outer part of the cervix are initially covered by columnar (endocervical-type) epithelium, normally replaced by squamous epithelium advancing up from the urogenital sinus; with DES exposure the columnar epithelium persists into adult life as vaginal adenosis; the squamocolumnar junction (transformation zone) is the site where carcinomas or precancerous lesions develop.
(iv) The tumour can also occur in the cervix.
(v) Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts form the fallopian tubes, uterus and vaginal wall; Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts regress or remain as vestigial rests that may form cysts in the cervix or vagina (Gartner duct cysts along the lateral vaginal walls).
- Septate or double vagina results from failure of total fusion of the Müllerian ducts (with uterus didelphys); vaginal atresia or total absence (very uncommon) results from failure of fusion of the Müllerian duct with the urogenital sinus.
- Uterine variants: agenesis (failure of the Müllerian ducts to develop, usually with absent vagina and tubes), didelphys (failure to fuse), duplex bicornis (common wall fails to degenerate), septus (incomplete resorption of the wall) and bicornuate (two horns with a common cervix).
- The differential in young girls is embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides): polypoid, grape-like vaginal masses in infants and girls under 5 years, treated by conservative surgery and chemotherapy.
questions.question:
A young woman in her teens, whose mother took diethylstilbestrol during pregnancy, has red granular patches on the vaginal mucosa and later develops a vaginal adenocarcinoma.
(i) State the diagnosis and the precursor lesion.
(ii) State the treatment stated to eradicate these tumours.
(iii) Explain the embryologic development of the vaginal and cervical epithelium that accounts for the precursor lesion, naming the anatomical landmarks.
(iv) State the other site of the tumour and the structures at risk.
(v) Describe the embryologic variants: the developmental anomalies of the Müllerian and Wolffian ducts.

questions.answerText:
(i) The growing cartilage/bone of the skeleton is affected - this is a skeletal dysplasia (osteochondrodysplasia), specifically achondroplasia, the most common form of dwarfism, due to mutations in FGFR3 (autosomal dominant inheritance).
(ii) Achondroplasia presents with a normal trunk size but shortened limbs; affected individuals are usually normal in other biological functions.
(iii) The differential diagnosis is thanatophoric dysplasia (thanatophoric dwarfism), which is also due to mutations in FGFR3 but is a lethal form of dwarfism, unlike achondroplasia.
(iv) The normal trunk size with markedly shortened limbs, absence of respiratory distress, and otherwise normal biological function in this infant are consistent with achondroplasia rather than the lethal thanatophoric dysplasia, since both share the same mutated gene (FGFR3) but differ in severity and outcome.

questions.answerText:
(i) The prostate is retroperitoneal and encircles the neck of the bladder and urethra; it has no distinct capsule; it is classically divided into five lobes (posterior, middle, anterior and two lateral) and histologically is a compound tubuloalveolar gland; testicular androgens play an important role in its maturation and function.
(ii) In the adult the gland is divided into peripheral, central, transitional and periurethral regions.
(iii) Only three entities of note affect the prostate: inflammation, benign hyperplasia and carcinoma; benign hyperplasia arises in the transitional and periurethral zones and its nodules compress the urethra, whereas carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone (70% of patients), so urinary obstruction is usually a late event in cancer. Inflammation: acute bacterial prostatitis (E. coli and other Gram-negative rods, enterococci, staphylococci; intraprostatic reflux of urine or lymphohaematogenous spread; after catheterisation, cystoscopy, urethral dilation or prostatic resection); chronic bacterial (recurrent UTI, poor antibiotic penetration; low back pain, dysuria); chronic abacterial (over 10 leucocytes per high power field, negative cultures); granulomatous (fungal, after BCG, non-specific).
(iv) Carcinoma is a disease of men over 50, commoner in blacks and rare in Asians; about 90% never cause trouble in a lifetime; risk factors: age, race, family history, hormone levels (androgens), high fat or red meat intake, low vitamin A and beta-carotene, germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations; low fat, soy, lycopene, selenium and vitamins D and E are protective. Most are adenocarcinomas with well-defined glands (smaller, lined by a single layer of cuboidal or low columnar cells, outer basal cell layer absent) with perineural invasion; high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia is the precursor lesion.
(v) Patients present with a prostate readily palpable on digital rectal examination; local extension involves periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicle and base of the bladder, and in advanced disease causes ureteral obstruction. Lymphatic spread is to the obturator and para-aortic lymph nodes.
(vi) Haematogenous spread is to bones (lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine and ribs in descending order of frequency), skull, lungs and liver; osteoblastic metastases on radionuclide bone scan are virtually diagnostic. Clinical features: prostatism (nocturia, frequency, urgency, urgent incontinence, hesitancy, terminal dribbling, weak stream), general features of malignancy, local infiltration and distant metastasis; complications involve musculoskeletal, renal, CNS, infective and other systems.
(vii) Grading uses the Gleason system (five patterns; primary plus secondary grade out of ten: score 2-6 well differentiated, 7 moderate, 8-10 poor) and staging uses TNM or Whitmore-Jewett; investigations are digital rectal examination, ultrasound, X-rays, PSA (density and velocity) and PAP. Treatment: chemotherapy is not useful; hormonal therapy (LHRH analogues suppress LHRH to establish androgen deprivation), surgery (radical prostatectomy; orchidectomy in metastatic disease) and radiotherapy (external beam and interstitial).

questions.question:
An antenatal ultrasound in a male fetus shows an enlarged, extremely irregular, multicystic kidney with dilatation of the collecting system.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Describe the embryologic variant/basis of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Renal dysplasia with hydronephrosis due to obstruction of the urinary tract.
(ii) Renal dysplasia is a sporadic disorder, almost always cystic, unilateral or bilateral, resulting grossly in an enlarged, extremely irregular, multicystic kidney. Hydronephrosis is dilatation of the collecting system or the ureter, or both, with or without obstruction, and is often seen on prenatal ultrasound (about 50% of dilatation occurs without obstruction). Causes of bilateral obstruction include posterior urethral valves; other causes include ureterocele and neurogenic bladder; renal dysplasia may result from such obstruction.

(i) Adult (autosomal dominant) polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
(ii) ADPKD is the most common kidney disease (1:1,000), accounts for 10% of transplant/dialysis patients, and is due to mutation of the polycystin I gene (ADPKD-1, chromosome 16p13.3) or the PKD-2 gene (chromosome 4q21); symptoms appear in adult life and renal failure follows 5-10 years thereafter; associated conditions include cerebral aneurysms (20%) and diverticulosis coli. The autosomal recessive form (ARPKD) is a rarer developmental anomaly (1:30,000) presenting in childhood, due to the PKHD1 gene (chromosome region 6p21-23) encoding the protein fibrocystin, with kidneys usually enlarged; the infantile/juvenile forms may develop congenital hepatic fibrosis (bland periportal fibrosis with proliferation of well-differentiated biliary ductules).
questions.question:
An adult presents with bilaterally enlarged, palpable kidneys (over 3,000g), hypertension and a family history of similar kidney disease; renal failure develops several years later.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Describe the embryologic/genetic variant of this condition.

questions.answerText:
(i) In acute malaria, the spleen is enlarged (weighing about 500 g), soft, and diffusely pigmented, with congestion, reticulo-endothelial hyperplasia, macrophages containing engulfed parasites and red cells, and possible haemorrhages and infarcts.
In chronic malaria, the spleen becomes very large (up to 1000 g), fibrotic, with a brittle, thick capsule and fibrous trabeculae, and may show foci of mineralisation (Gandy-Gamna bodies); massive splenomegaly of greater than 5 kg with no other known cause, in a falciparum-endemic region, constitutes hyperimmune malarial (tropical) splenomegaly syndrome.
In typhoid fever, the spleen is enlarged, soft, with pale red pulp, sinus histiocytosis, reticulo-endothelial proliferation with prominent Malpighian corpuscles, and typhoid nodules.
In schistosomiasis, splenomegaly is congestive, occurring as a consequence of periportal (pipestem) fibrosis obliterating the portal veins and causing portal hypertension, rather than from direct parasitic infiltration of the splenic parenchyma itself as seen in malaria or typhoid.
(ii) In malaria, the acute-stage splenic enlargement (soft, congested, pigmented, with reticulo-endothelial hyperplasia) reflects an active reactive response to ongoing parasitaemia, whereas the chronic-stage enlargement (large, fibrotic, brittle) reflects cumulative fibrous remodelling after repeated parasitaemic episodes.
In typhoid fever, splenic enlargement with typhoid nodules corresponds to the systemic phase of the illness, paralleling the hepatic involvement (typhoid nodules also seen in liver, bone marrow, and lymph nodes) that occurs as the mononuclear phagocyte system is seeded by circulating bacilli.
In schistosomiasis, the congestive splenomegaly is a chronic-stage phenomenon, developing as periportal fibrosis progressively obstructs portal venous outflow over the course of long-standing egg-induced granulomatous inflammation in the liver.
(iii) In malaria, splenic pathology does not spread to or produce a functional deficit at a distant structure; the acute spleen may develop internal haemorrhages and infarcts, and the chronic spleen becomes fibrotic and brittle, with both changes confined to the organ itself. In typhoid fever, the parallel involvement of the liver, bone marrow and lymph nodes reflects independent seeding of these separate reticulo-endothelial sites by circulating bacilli, rather than spread from the spleen. In schistosomiasis the direction of causation is reversed: periportal hepatic fibrosis causes portal hypertension, which in turn produces congestive splenomegaly, so here the spleen is the site of a distant effect of hepatic disease rather than a source of spread. Across all three diseases, the spleen functions as a reticulo-endothelial organ that reacts to, rather than spreads, the underlying systemic infective or fibrotic process.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross pathological appearance of the spleen in malaria, typhoid fever, and schistosomiasis.
(ii) State how these splenic changes relate to the stage (acute versus chronic) of each disease.
(iii) Explain whether splenic disease in these conditions produces functional deficit at a distant structure.

questions.answerText:
(i) The mass arises from the thymus, which is pyramidal, encapsulated, has two fused lobes with an outer cortex and inner medulla, and lies behind the sternum in the superior mediastinum; thymomas are tumours of adults over 40 years (M:F 1:1) and are commonly found in the antero-superior mediastinum.
(ii) Differential pathologies are the three classes of thymoma: benign/encapsulated thymoma, malignant thymoma type 1 (cytologically benign but biologically aggressive/locally invasive), and malignant thymoma type 2/thymic carcinoma (cytologically malignant; commonest variants are squamous cell carcinoma and lymphoepithelioma).
(iii) Thymomas are usually associated with autoimmune diseases, especially myasthenia gravis, and also Cushing syndrome, pernicious anaemia, dermatomyositis, polymyositis, pure red cell aplasia, Graves disease and acquired gamma-globulinaemia.
This association is explained by the tumour disturbing the environment normally required in the thymus for negative selection of self-reacting lymphocytes.
questions.question:
A middle-aged adult is found to have a mass in the antero-superior mediastinum, and also has muscle weakness that worsens with sustained activity.
(i) Identify the organ/structure from which this mass arises.
(ii) List the differential pathologies for this mass.

questions.answerText:
(i) Unilateral renal agenesis is compatible with normal life if no other abnormalities exist, with the opposite kidney undergoing compensatory hypertrophy; bilateral agenesis is incompatible with life. Ectopic kidneys lie either just above the pelvic brim or sometimes within the pelvis. Congenital renal disease is grouped into congenital anomalies, parenchymal defects (renal dysplasia), obstruction of the urinary tract (hydronephrosis), cystic diseases, metabolic diseases and syndromes.
(ii) Vascular causes of chronic renal failure include large vessel disease (bilateral renal artery stenosis) and small vessel disease (ischaemic nephropathy, haemolytic-uraemic syndrome, vasculitis). Glomerular causes are subclassified into primary glomerular disease (e.g., focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, IgA nephritis) and secondary glomerular disease (e.g., diabetic nephropathy, lupus nephritis). Obstructive causes include bilateral kidney stones and diseases of the prostate.
(iii) In chronic renal failure, fluid overload and vasoactive hormone production raise blood pressure, leading to hypertension and congestive heart failure. Urea accumulates causing azotaemia and uraemia, with symptoms ranging from lethargy to pericarditis and encephalopathy. Hyperkalaemia produces symptoms ranging from malaise to fatal cardiac arrhythmias, and decreased erythropoietin synthesis leads to anaemia. Reduced phosphate excretion with hypocalcaemia (vitamin D3 deficiency) causes secondary and later tertiary hyperparathyroidism, with renal osteodystrophy and vascular calcification. Fluid volume overload can progress to life-threatening pulmonary oedema, and gastrointestinal effects include nausea, vomiting, oesophagitis, gastritis, ulceration and colitis. Skin manifestations include pruritus, uraemic frost and hyperpigmentation, illustrating how renal failure produces functional deficits across the heart, brain, bone marrow, bones, lungs, gut and skin.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross/positional anatomy of congenitally abnormal kidneys.
(ii) State how the causes of chronic renal failure relate to different parts/components of the kidney.
(iii) Explain how chronic renal failure produces functional deficits in distant structures.

questions.answerText:
(i) Herniation is displacement of brain structures from one compartment to another, resulting from a mass lesion or raised intracranial pressure; the pressure rises when there is an increase in volume of solid tissue (tumours), tissue fluid (oedema) or vascular contents (haemorrhage).
(ii) Subfalcine (cingulate) herniation displaces the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri and may compress branches of the anterior cerebral artery.
(iii) Transtentorial uncal and hippocampal herniation: a hemispheric mass lesion displaces the uncus and all or part of the hippocampus through the tentorial opening, and may damage the oculomotor nerve and posterior cerebral arteries.
(iv) Central herniation: bilateral anterior hemispheric or centrally situated mass lesions displace the diencephalon and/or upper midbrain downward into the tentorial opening.
(v) Tonsillar herniation is displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum; it is life-threatening, causing brainstem compression and compromising the vital respiratory and cardiac centres in the medulla oblongata.
(vi) The rate of growth, rather than size, is often the more critical factor; the location of the mass relative to CSF and venous outflow is important, and increased pressure is also related to tissue oedema; the brain is a complex organ (2% of total body water) in a protective bony case, with no lymphatics, CSF circulation and limited immune surveillance.
(vii) Generalised brain swelling from increased tissue water shows flattened gyri, narrow sulci, prominent pacchionian granulations, increased brain weight, obstruction of the subarachnoid space and decreased ventricular size, with bony erosion in chronic cases, and may accompany congestive swelling (increased cerebral blood volume). Vasogenic oedema results from breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, occurs around tumours or trauma and diffusely in white matter, with enlarged extracellular spaces and swollen perivascular astrocyte foot processes; cytotoxic oedema results from impaired cell Na+-K+ pump, is intracellular and mainly in grey matter, and hypoxia is the commonest cause; interstitial (hydrocephalic) oedema occurs around the lateral ventricles when intraventricular CSF crosses the ependyma into periventricular white matter.
(viii) Hydrocephalus is excessive accumulation of CSF that considerably enlarges the ventricles, from obstruction to CSF circulation (obstructive, non-communicating), overproduction of CSF or failure of absorption at the arachnoid granulations (communicating).
(ix) Complications of meningitis include subdural effusion, cranial nerve palsy, vasculitis, abscess, hydrocephalus, mental retardation, seizures, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome and SIADH; tuberculous meningitis has a basal, thick gelatinous exudate with obliterative endarteritis and possible tuberculomas.
(x) Metastatic tumours make up 50% of CNS tumours, commonly from small cell lung carcinoma, breast carcinoma, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and colon carcinoma; 80% lie in the cerebral cortex, 50% are multiple and at the grey-white junction; the vertebral column is a common site for breast and prostatic metastases (thoracic 60%, cervical 20%, lumbar 20%).

(i) In malaria, the liver is enlarged with a slatey-grey appearance from hemozoin staining, with enlarged Kupffer cells containing malarial pigment, parasites and parasitised red cells; pigment is also found in parenchymal cells, the sinusoids and other vessels are usually congested, and focal areas of fatty change may be seen.
In typhoid fever, there is hepatomegaly with the striking feature of typhoid nodules (collections of macrophages and lymphocytes with central necrosis and bacilli), also seen in the bone marrow and lymph nodes, together with typhoid abscesses; cholangitis is rarer, while the gallbladder is the usual seat of the carrier state, with chronic cholecystitis and gallstones.
In schistosomiasis, the liver is darkened by regurgitated heme-derived (iron-free) pigment, the surface is bumpy, and cut surfaces show pinpoint granulomas, with widespread fibrosis and portal enlargement without intervening regenerative nodules (pipestem fibrosis).
In amoebiasis, amoebae embolise through the portal circulation to the liver in about 40% of cases, producing a usually solitary (or less often multiple) discrete abscess, typically in the right lobe, with scant inflammatory reaction, a shaggy fibrinous lining, and chocolate-coloured/anchovy sauce material.
(ii) In malaria, the involvement is diffuse throughout the hepatic parenchyma and sinusoids, reflecting the pigment-laden Kupffer cells and parasitised red cells circulating through the sinusoidal system.
In typhoid, involvement is nodular (typhoid nodules scattered through the parenchyma), reflecting seeding of the mononuclear phagocyte system by circulating bacilli, paralleling similar nodules in bone marrow and lymph nodes.
In schistosomiasis, involvement is periportal, centred on the portal tracts where the egg-induced granulomas and resultant pipestem fibrosis develop, sparing the lobular parenchyma itself.
In amoebiasis, involvement is typically a single discrete abscess, most often in the right lobe, reflecting the pattern of portal venous embolisation of amoebae from the colon rather than diffuse or periportal involvement.
(iii) In schistosomiasis, the periportal pipestem fibrosis may obliterate the portal veins, leading to portal hypertension and congestive splenomegaly, a distant structural change at the spleen resulting from the hepatic disease process.
In amoebiasis, the hepatic abscess can rupture to form a discharging sinus draining through the body wall, and rare complications include empyema thoracis, broncho-pleural fistulae, pericardial abscesses, and metastatic abscesses in the kidney and brain, all distant structures affected by spread from the primary hepatic lesion.
In typhoid fever, seeding of the mononuclear phagocyte system is not confined to the liver but occurs in parallel at the bone marrow, spleen and lymph nodes, and the biliary tract itself (gallbladder) can become the site of the chronic carrier state, so that hepatobiliary involvement has direct downstream consequences for the carrier status and infectivity of the patient.
In malaria, hepatic Kupffer cell involvement occurs alongside similar reticulo-endothelial involvement of the spleen, so that both organs reflect, rather than cause, the same underlying systemic parasitaemic process; the hepatic changes themselves are not considered the source of a distant deficit in malaria specifically.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross pathological appearance of the liver in malaria, typhoid fever, schistosomiasis, and amoebiasis.
(ii) State how the site/zone of hepatic involvement differs between these conditions.
(iii) Explain why liver disease in these conditions may produce a functional deficit at a distant structure.

questions.answerText:
(i) Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumour), associated with WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, Aniridia, Genital anomalies, and mental Retardation).
(ii) WAGR syndrome carries an approximately 33% lifetime risk of developing Wilms tumour and results from constitutional (germline) deletions of chromosome 11p13; the WT1 deletion in WAGR syndrome represents the "first hit", and development of the tumour occurs when a nonsense or frameshift mutation affects the second WT1 allele (the "second hit"). Grossly the tumour has a characteristic tan-to-gray colour with well-circumscribed margins; histologically there are tightly packed blue cells consistent with the blastemal component and interspersed primitive tubules representing the epithelial component, with focal anaplasia (hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei and abnormal mitoses) in some cases.

(i) Acute diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).
(ii) This is the prototype of diffuse post-infectious glomerulonephritis with enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli. Light microscopy shows proliferating endothelium and mesangium with infiltration by neutrophils and monocytes, and crescents in severe cases. Immunofluorescence shows a granular "lumpy-bumpy" capillary wall pattern of IgG, IgM and C3. Electron microscopy shows discrete amorphous subepithelial humps (antigen-antibody complexes) with small subendothelial/mesangial deposits. Diagnosis is supported by raised ASO titre, low complement, nephritic syndrome and hypertension.

questions.answerText:
(i) The normal liver weighs 1400-1600g and is mahogany brown, with a dual blood supply - two-thirds from the portal vein and one-third from the hepatic artery. Lobules are oriented around the terminal tributaries of the hepatic (central) vein, with portal tracts at the lobule's periphery; the functional unit is the hepatic acinus. The acinus has three zones - zone 1 (periportal), zone 2 (intermediate) and zone 3 (perivenular).
(ii) Zone 1 (periportal) hepatocytes receive the most oxygenated blood and are therefore insensitive to ischaemic injury; they perform gluconeogenesis, beta-oxidation of fatty acids and cholesterol synthesis. Zone 1 hepatocytes are susceptible to viral hepatitis and to haemochromatosis. Zone 3 (perivenular/centrilobular) hepatocytes are the site of centrilobular necrosis caused by ischaemia, drugs and toxins.
(iii) Cirrhosis is defined as a diffuse process with fibrous septa and conversion of the normal architecture into structurally abnormal (micro or macro) regenerating nodules. Increased resistance to blood flow in the sinusoids, with compression of the central vein and arteriovenous shunting, raises portal pressure (portal hypertension). Portosystemic shunting produces oesophagogastric varices, whose rupture and bleeding is a leading cause of death in cirrhosis. Shunting of blood from the portal to the systemic circulation, together with severe loss of hepatocellular function, allows ammonia and aromatic amino acid derivatives to reach the brain. This produces hepatic encephalopathy - a neuropsychiatric disturbance with rigidity, hyperreflexia, non-specific EEG changes, seizures and asterixis, that can progress to coma. Hepatic encephalopathy thus represents a distant (cerebral) functional deficit arising from liver disease, morphologically associated with oedema and an astrocytic reaction in the brain.

A newborn, the second child of the same mother, is born jaundiced, anaemic and grossly oedematous.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is immune hydrops fetalis due to Rh D blood group incompatibility between mother and fetus.
(ii) On first exposure, the mother forms IgM antibodies, which do not cross the placenta, so a first pregnancy is unaffected; a second pregnancy provokes an IgG antibody response, which crosses the placenta and destroys fetal red cells, causing haemolysis.
Haemolysis leads to anaemia, which causes tissue hypoxia of the liver and heart. Hepatic hypoxia reduces plasma protein production and oncotic pressure, while cardiac hypoxia causes cardiac failure and increased hydrostatic pressure; together these produce generalised oedema and anasarca.
Concurrent ABO incompatibility protects the mother against Rh immunisation, because fetal red cells entering the maternal circulation are quickly removed by anti-A or anti-B IgM, which does not cross the placenta, so the mother does not develop anti-RhD antibodies and future pregnancies are protected.

(i) The mass most commonly arises from the kidney (Wilms tumour) or from the adrenal medulla/paravertebral sympathetic tissue (neuroblastoma).
(ii) Wilms tumour presents with a large abdominal mass, haematuria, pain, intestinal obstruction and hypertension; it is a large, solitary, well-circumscribed mass, bilateral or multicentric in 10% of cases.
Neuroblastoma presents with a large abdominal mass, fever, weight loss, bone pains, and respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms; it arises most often in the adrenal medulla (40%), the paravertebral region of the abdomen (25%), or the posterior mediastinum (15%).
(iii) Differentials for a large paediatric abdominal mass include Wilms tumour and neuroblastoma, both classed among the malignant "small round blue cell tumours" of childhood, alongside leukaemia, retinoblastoma, immature teratoma, lymphoma/Hodgkin lymphoma, hepatoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma and CNS tumours.
(iv) On cut section, Wilms tumour shows homogenous grey foci of haemorrhage, cyst formation and necrosis, and is microscopically triphasic (blastemal, stromal and epithelial elements forming abortive tubules or glomeruli); 5% show anaplasia associated with p53 mutations, and nephrogenic rests are regarded as precursor lesions.
It may be associated with WAGR syndrome (11p13 deletion involving WT1 and PAX6), Denys-Drash syndrome (WT1 zinc-finger mutation, gonadal dysgenesis, early-onset nephropathy) or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (hemihypertrophy, organomegaly, macroglossia, omphalocele, 11p15.5 imprinting defect).
Neuroblastoma, by contrast, may show a pseudocapsule and a fleshy cut surface, and is composed histologically of small primitive cells with Homer-Wright pseudorosettes and neuropil, positive for neurone-specific enolase and PHOX2B.

(i) Testicular torsion (twisting of the spermatic cord). Predisposing factors: incomplete descent, absence of scrotal ligaments, atrophy of the testis so that it is abnormally mobile within the tunica vaginalis, and abnormal attachment of the testis to the epididymis.
(ii) The twisted cord cuts off the venous drainage of the testis; the arteries remain patent and continue to supply blood, producing intense vascular engorgement followed by haemorrhagic infarction (twisting may also cut off the arterial supply).
(iii) It is an emergency: the testis must be manually untwisted within six hours of onset to remain viable. Structures involved: spermatic cord, tunica vaginalis, the attachment of the testis to the epididymis and the scrotal ligaments.
(iv) The structure at risk is the testis itself, which loses viability if not untwisted in time. The contralateral testis is surgically fixed to the scrotum to prevent a catastrophic recurrence, since the abnormality affects both testes.
(v) Neonatal torsion occurs in utero or shortly after birth and is not associated with any anatomic defect; adult torsion, typically seen in adolescents, is associated with a bilateral anatomic defect (clapper-bell abnormality) that increases mobility of the testes.

questions.answerText:
(i) Ewing's sarcoma: a primitive malignant bone neoplasm of children, second in frequency to osteosarcoma, highly aggressive and associated with a chromosomal translocation identical to that in primitive neuroectodermal tumours; X-ray shows a destructive lytic tumour with a periosteal reaction producing layers of reactive bone (onion-skin appearance).
(ii) Metaphysis of long bones: osteosarcoma, osteochondroma (10-30 years), osteoid osteoma (femur and tibia, 10-20 years) and haematogenous osteomyelitis; epiphysis: giant cell tumour (20-40 years); shoulder, pelvis, proximal femur and ribs: chondrosarcoma (40-60 years); small bones of hands and feet: enchondroma (20s-40s); spine: osteoblastoma.
(iii) Osteosarcoma: malignant cells produce bone matrix (osteoid formation is the gold standard); 75% under 20 years, male 1.6:1; metaphysis with almost 50% around the knee; grows outward lifting the periosteum and inward into the medullary cavity; painful enlarging mass, sometimes pathologic fracture; about 20% have pulmonary metastases at diagnosis; 5-year survival 60%.
- Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis shares malaise, fever, chills, leukocytosis and throbbing pain (metaphyseal, children); antibiotics with surgical drainage are usually curative.
- Osteoid osteoma (under 2 cm, nocturnal pain relieved by aspirin) and osteoblastoma (dull pain not relieved by aspirin); both are treated by conservative surgery.
- Giant cell tumour: osteoclast-like giant cells with mononuclear cells; giant cells alone are not diagnostic; biopsy is necessary. Chondrosarcoma: cartilaginous matrix, enlarging painful mass, blood-borne spread mainly to lungs. Enchondroma: well-circumscribed radiolucency with a thin rim of dense bone (O-ring sign). Fibrous dysplasia: ground-glass appearance on x-ray; monostotic, polyostotic or with café-au-lait spots (McCune-Albright).
(iv) Treatment of Ewing's sarcoma is chemotherapy and surgery with or without radiation, which has increased 5-year survival to approximately 75%.

A patient with symptoms of hyperglycaemia is found to have a random glucose level of at least 200.
(i) State the diagnosis and the criteria used to confirm it.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diabetes mellitus: a chronic disorder of carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism resulting from relative or absolute insulin deficiency, with hyperglycaemia as a common feature. Diagnosis: random glucose of at least 200 with symptoms; fasting glucose of at least 126 on more than one occasion; abnormal OGTT (over 200 two hours after a 75 g glucose load); HbA1c of at least 6.5%.
(ii) Type 1 (about 10%): absolute insulin deficiency from β-cell destruction, immune mediated or idiopathic, with genetic, autoimmune and environmental factors; 90% of β cells are lost before metabolic changes appear. Type 2 (80-90%): combination of peripheral insulin resistance and inadequate β-cell secretory response.
- Type 2 pathogenesis: genetic and environmental factors with a proinflammatory state; obesity-related insulin resistance is induced by adipokines, free fatty acids and chronic adipose inflammation; β cells first compensate by hypersecretion, then fail and diabetes ensues.
- Other types: genetic β-cell defects (MODY 1-6 involving HNF4A, GCK, HNF1A, PDX1, HNF1B and NEUROD1; neonatal diabetes from KCNJ11 and ABCC8 mutations; MIDD from mitochondrial DNA mutation; proinsulin conversion and insulin gene defects), insulin receptor mutations, exocrine pancreatic disease (chronic pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, neoplasia, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis), endocrinopathies (acromegaly, Cushing syndrome, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, glucagonoma), infections (CMV, coxsackie B, congenital rubella), drugs (glucocorticoids, thyroid hormone, interferon-α, protease inhibitors), genetic syndromes (Down, Klinefelter, Turner, Prader-Willi) and gestational diabetes.
(iii) Type 1: T-cell leukocytic infiltration of islets (insulitis) with progressive β-cell depletion, later small indistinct or absent islets. Type 2: ill-defined reduction in islet cell mass, fibrous tissue accumulation in some islets and amyloid deposition; the newborn of a diabetic mother shows islet cell hyperplasia.
(iv) Whatever the type, the complications are the same; diabetes ranks first as a cause of end-stage renal disease, adult blindness and non-traumatic lower extremity amputation.
- Insulin physiology: glucose entering β cells through GLUT-2 triggers Ca2+-induced release of stored insulin; insulin increases glucose transport into striated muscle and, to a lesser extent, adipocytes, promotes glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis and lipogenesis, and inhibits lipolysis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Pott disease - a presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in which disease is seen in the spinal vertebrae.
(ii) Tuberculosis is diagnosed by finding Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a clinical specimen; this includes acid-fast bacilli smear (Ziehl-Neelsen stain), bacteriological culture tests (Lowenstein-Jensen media, or the BACTEC radiometric culture system, taking 9-16 days, with mycobacterial culture requiring 2-6 weeks for interpretation), and a complete medical evaluation including medical history, physical examination, chest x-ray, and microbiological examination of sputum or other appropriate samples, which may also include a tuberculin skin test, other scans/x-rays, and surgical biopsy for histology.
(iii) The spinal vertebrae; disseminated tuberculosis most commonly involves, in order, the lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, and bone marrow, reflecting the lymphohaematogenous spread by which vertebral disease is seeded.

(i) Colorectal adenocarcinoma.
(ii) Diet (low fibre, high fat and refined carbohydrates, red meat); obesity and physical inactivity; alcohol and cigarette smoking; inflammatory bowel disease; age; genetic factors; race (aspirin and other NSAIDs are protective).
(iii) Distal/left-sided tumours tend to produce napkin-ring constrictions and cause obstruction, in contrast to proximal/right-sided tumours, which tend to be polypoid/exophytic and do not usually cause obstruction.
(iv) Colectomy is used in the context of familial adenomatous polyposis, where it protects against colorectal carcinoma, and in ulcerative colitis, where it is recommended for any degree of dysplasia in a dysplasia-associated lesion or mass (DALM).

questions.answerText:
(i) The stomach comprises the cardia, fundus, body and antrum, ending at the pylorus, with a lesser curvature and a greater curvature. Gastric carcinoma may form large masses, diffusely infiltrate, or stiffen the wall (desmoplasia) to give a "leather bottle" appearance called linitis plastica.
(ii) Chronic gastritis caused by Helicobacter pylori is often limited to the antrum with occasional involvement of the cardia, but can extend to involve the body and fundus with progressive mucosal atrophy. In such pan-gastritis, damage to the antrum and cardia is typically more advanced, with the body and fundus becoming markedly thinned. Peptic ulcers are located along the lesser curvature, near the interface of the body and antrum. Gastric adenocarcinoma most commonly involves the gastric antrum, with the lesser curvature more involved than the greater curvature. The adjacent cardia may also be invaded by tumours arising near the gastro-oesophageal junction.
(iii) Gastric carcinoma is described as intestinal or diffuse in growth pattern, with the intestinal type forming bulky tumours with glands and the diffuse type infiltrating widely with a signet-ring appearance. The gross growth pattern determines local spread; the wall may become rigid (linitis plastica) once desmoplasia stiffens it. Depth of invasion, nodal metastasis and distant metastasis at diagnosis determine prognosis. Distant lymphatic spread may reach the supraclavicular sentinel lymph node, known as Virchow's node. Metastasis to Virchow's node illustrates how a gastric primary tumour can produce a clinically detectable change at a site remote from the stomach, via the lymphatic route.

questions.answerText:
(i) The brain - this presentation is cerebral malaria, one of the recognised forms of severe/complicated malaria (caused mostly by Plasmodium falciparum), together with severe anaemia, renal failure, pulmonary oedema/ARDS, circulatory collapse (algid malaria), abnormal bleeding/DIC, repeated generalised convulsions, acidaemia/acidosis, macroscopic haemoglobinuria, and hyperbilirubinaemia.
(ii) Grossly there is cerebral oedema/congestion with a pink appearance of the brain, petechiae in the white matter, and gross features of raised intracranial pressure; microscopically the capillaries and venules are congested and filled with parasitised red blood cells, there is blockage of blood vessels by parasitised red cells, ring haemorrhages are characteristic, and Durck's granulomas are seen.
(iii) The kidney (slightly enlarged, petechial haemorrhages, malarial pigment in glomeruli, cortico-medullary capillaries with parasitised red cells and haemoglobin in tubules, acute tubular necrosis and renal failure); the heart (dilated and flabby, pericardial/endocardial petechiae, congested capillaries with parasitised red cells, focal hypoxic lesions and interstitial infiltrates); the lungs (congested and oedematous with occasional parasitised erythrocytes, fibrin deposition causing shock lung/ARDS); the gastrointestinal tract (oedematous, congested, focal/diffuse haemorrhage, parasitised red cells in mucosal vessels); the liver (enlarged, slatey-grey from hemozoin, enlarged Kupffer cells containing pigment/parasites/parasitised red cells); and the spleen (enlarged, soft, diffusely pigmented, congestion and reticuloendothelial hyperplasia).
(iv) Destruction of erythrocytes releases cytokines (TNF, IFN-gamma, IL-1) that suppress red cell production, increase fever, and stimulate reactive nitrogen species causing tissue damage; sequestration of parasitised erythrocytes in small vessels (as seen in the brain) causes blockage and capillary/venular congestion, accounting for the convulsions and impaired consciousness in this child through capillary obstruction and the resulting hypoxic injury to the brain.

questions.answerText:
(i) The infratentorial compartment (cerebellum and fourth ventricle): in children 70% of CNS tumours are infratentorial whereas in adults 70% are supratentorial; primary CNS tumours account for 20% of all cancers in children. Hydrocephalus results from obstruction to CSF circulation (obstructive, non-communicating type): medulloblastoma grows rapidly and occludes CSF flow, and fourth-ventricle ependymomas may cause hydrocephalus.
(ii) Raised pressure depends on rate of growth and on the location of the mass relative to CSF and venous outflow; tonsillar herniation (cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum) is life-threatening because it compresses the brainstem and the vital respiratory and cardiac centres in the medulla oblongata.
(iii) Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1): commonly in the cerebellum of children and young adults; cystic with a tumour nodule in the cyst wall; bipolar astrocytes with long hair-like processes, Rosenthal fibres, microcysts and calcification; very slow growing with an excellent prognosis.
- Ependymoma: arises from the ependymal lining of the ventricles or central canal, in the fourth ventricle in children and young adults; highly cellular with regular nuclei, rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes; may cause hydrocephalus.
- Medulloblastoma: second commonest CNS tumour of childhood after astrocytomas; occurs exclusively in the cerebellum; derived from the fetal external granular layer; extremely cellular, anaplastic small round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, high nucleocytoplasmic ratio and Homer-Wright pseudorosettes.
(iv) All CNS tumours are biologically malignant; malignant tumours spread by direct infiltration and may disseminate within the CNS via CSF (medulloblastoma seeds through CSF); medulloblastoma is highly malignant yet radiosensitive. Some patients with pilocytic astrocytoma have survived more than 40 years after incomplete resection.

questions.answerText:
(i) Takayasu arteritis affects large to medium-sized vessels - the entire length of the aorta and its branches, especially the aortic arch and its great vessels, as well as the pulmonary artery. Giant cell (temporal) arteritis affects large to small arteries principally in the head - especially the temporal arteries, but also the vertebral and ophthalmic arteries - and can also affect the aorta (giant cell aortitis). Takayasu arteritis occurs in patients under 50 years of age, whereas giant cell arteritis occurs in patients over 50 years.
(ii) In Takayasu arteritis, there is transmural fibrous thickening of the aorta with severe luminal narrowing of the involved arteries. Symptoms principally include ocular disturbances and marked weakening of the pulses in the upper extremities, giving rise to the name "pulseless disease." The clinical features and histology of Takayasu arteritis are the same as those of giant cell arteritis, the only exception being the age of occurrence. In giant cell arteritis, involvement of the ophthalmic and vertebral arteries can cause permanent blindness. Microscopy in giant cell arteritis shows intimal thickening with or without thrombosis, medial granulomatous inflammation centred on the internal elastic lamina with fragmentation of the lamina, and giant cells in 75% of cases. The pathogenesis of giant cell arteritis is a T-cell-mediated immune response against a vessel wall antigen, inducing cytokine production (especially TNF), with anti-endothelial cell and anti-smooth muscle cell antibodies found in about two-thirds of patients. Clinically, patients present with fever, fatigue, weight loss, facial pain or headache most intense along the course of the temporal artery, and ocular symptoms ranging from diplopia to complete blindness. Both conditions illustrate how inflammatory injury to the wall of a large vessel produces luminal narrowing and downstream ischaemic deformity - pulse loss in Takayasu arteritis, visual loss in giant cell arteritis.

(i) State the origin/portal of entry of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
(ii) Describe the course of spread of the organism within the body.
(iii) State the distribution of extrapulmonary tuberculosis.
(iv) How is the diagnosis confirmed?
questions.answerText:
(i) The major source of transmission is humans with active pulmonary tuberculosis, who release mycobacteria present in their sputum into the environment; humans are the only reservoir for M. tuberculosis, and oropharyngeal or intestinal tuberculosis can also be contracted by drinking milk contaminated with Mycobacterium bovis.
(ii) Following entry, M. tuberculosis is phagocytosed by macrophages and, in the first three weeks after infection (primary tuberculosis, in nonsensitised individuals), replicates within macrophages by inhibiting phagosome maturation and phagolysosome formation, proliferating in pulmonary alveolar macrophages and air spaces and causing bacteraemia with seeding of multiple sites; there are two pathophysiological types of clinical tuberculosis - primary, in nonsensitised individuals, and secondary, in sensitised individuals, occurring shortly after primary disease or, more often, years later by reactivation of latent infection or exogenous re-infection.
From about three weeks post-infection, Toll-like receptor 2 stimulation by mycobacterial ligands promotes IL-12 production by antigen-presenting cells, driving differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into the Th1 subset, which secrete interferon-gamma that activates macrophages, stimulating granuloma formation with caseous necrosis and formation of Langhans-type giant cells.
(iii) Organisms draining through lymphatics may enter the venous blood and circulate back to the lung, producing miliary pulmonary disease, or disseminate through the systemic arterial system as systemic miliary tuberculosis, most prominent in the liver, bone marrow, spleen, adrenals, meninges, kidneys, fallopian tubes and epididymis, but able to involve any organ, including the osteo-articular system (e.g. Pott disease), skin, heart, and genito-urinary tract.
Systemic symptoms across this distribution are related to cytokines released by activated macrophages (TNF and IL-1) and include malaise, anorexia, cachexia, low-grade remittent fever (appearing each late afternoon and then subsiding), and night sweats.
(iv) Diagnosis rests on finding the organism in an appropriate clinical specimen (most often sputum) by acid-fast bacilli smear (Ziehl-Neelsen stain) and bacteriological culture, together with medical history, physical examination, chest X-ray, tuberculin skin testing where indicated, and surgical biopsy for histology.

(i) Blood supply: the renal artery gives arcuate and interlobar branches, then an interlobular artery, from which an afferent arteriole supplies each glomerulus; capillary loops within the glomerulus are supported by mesangium, which functions in both filtration and phagocytosis, and are lined by fenestrated endothelium.
(ii) Cellular components: epithelial cells (visceral/podocytes and parietal), mesangial cells and endothelial cells.
(iii) Filtration barrier: capillary loops are surrounded by podocytes whose foot processes form slits; a negative (anionic) charge on the foot processes normally keeps negatively charged proteins from filtering through. Contd: Bowman's space: filtered fluid (water, waste products and some solutes to be recovered later) collects initially in Bowman's space; the glomerular basement membrane has three layers (lamina rara externa, lamina densa, lamina rara interna) made of collagen IV, laminin, proteoglycans, fibronectin and entactin.
(iv) Clinical basis: in Minimal Change Disease, electron microscopy shows only fusion (effacement) of the podocyte foot processes, with other nonspecific changes. This effacement abolishes the normal charge barrier so that albumin leaks out selectively, producing the proteinuria of nephrotic syndrome; light microscopy is otherwise near-normal.
(v) Light microscopy: Minimal Change Disease shows few if any changes (other than those secondary to proteinuria); Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis shows segmental sclerosis (mesangial matrix material, collapse, basement-membrane-like material, hyalinosis) in some, especially juxtamedullary, glomeruli. Immunofluorescence: Minimal Change Disease is usually negative, may have mesangial IgM; Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis is usually negative except in the sclerotic segment, which may show IgM and C3. Proteinuria: Minimal Change Disease proteinuria is selective, typically in children; Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis proteinuria is non-selective and more often accompanied by haematuria and hypertension. Response to treatment: Minimal Change Disease is 85% responsive to steroids with excellent prognosis; Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis is only about 15% responsive to steroids. Outcome: over one-third of Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis cases progress to end-stage renal disease, whereas Minimal Change Disease has an excellent prognosis. Aetiology: idiopathic Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis accounts for 10-35% of nephrotic syndrome in children and adults and is also associated with sickle cell disease, obesity and HIV/heroin use, unlike Minimal Change Disease.
