(ii) Describe the cellular components of the glomerulus.
(iii) Describe the filtration barrier and Bowman's space.
(iv) Explain the clinical basis for the proteinuria seen in Minimal Change Disease.
(v) Distinguish between Minimal Change Disease and Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Ovarian tumours are epithelial (serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, seromucinous, Brenner, undifferentiated; each benign, borderline or malignant), mesenchymal, mixed epithelial-mesenchymal, sex cord-stromal (pure stromal, pure sex cord, mixed), germ cell, germ cell-sex cord stromal, miscellaneous, mesothelial, soft tissue, tumour-like lesions, and lymphomas and myeloid tumours.
(ii) About 80% are benign and occur mostly in women aged 20-45 years; malignant tumours occur between 40 and 65 years; major risk factors are nulliparity and family history, with single status, gonadal dysgenesis and low parity; genetic factors are BRCA1, BRCA2, HER2/neu and p53, and HER2/neu overexpression is associated with poor prognosis.
(iii) Most ovarian cancers have spread beyond the ovary at diagnosis, so they account for a disproportionate number of deaths from cancers of the female genital tract.
(iv) Cysts are the commonest cause of enlarged ovaries: a few arise from invaginated surface epithelium (simple serous cysts) but most from follicles; follicular cysts (unruptured or sealed follicles) are lined by granulosa and theca cells; corpus luteum cysts (delayed resolution of the central cavity) are unilocular, 3-5 cm, lined by yellow luteinised granulosa cells, with menstrual irregularity from continued progesterone. Polycystic ovarian (Stein-Leventhal) syndrome: excess androgen, menstrual irregularity, 12 or more small subcapsular cysts, chronic anovulation, decreased fertility, hirsutism, acne and male hair distribution; increased androgen from ovary and adrenal through abnormal regulation of 17α-hydroxylase, following excess LH.
(v) The commonest tube disorders are infection, inflammation, ectopic pregnancy and endometriosis; tuberculous salpingitis causes infertility; tumours are uncommon, but serous ovarian cysts are suggested to arise from tubal neoplasms; paratubal cysts and hydatids of Morgagni are Müllerian remnants of little significance.
(vi) Serous tumours are cystic neoplasms ('serous' describes the cyst fluid) including the commonest malignant ovarian tumours, with epithelium like that of the fallopian tube; Type I cancers arise from benign lesions (endometriosis or cystadenoma) through borderline to low-grade carcinoma; Type II are high grade and arise from tubal in-situ lesions or ovarian inclusion cysts. Mucinous tumours occur in mid adult life and are mostly benign or borderline; benign ones have tall columnar cells with apical mucin and no cilia, borderline show stratification and papillary growth, malignant show confluent growth; pseudomyxoma peritonei (mucinous ascites, cystic implants, adhesions, both ovaries) may cause intestinal obstruction and death.
(vii) Endometrioid tumours have tubular glands, may arise from endometriosis and sometimes coexist with endometrial cancer (favourable outcome suggests independent origin); clear cell tumours are uncommon, with large epithelial cells with abundant clear cytoplasm.
(viii) Fibromas (fibroblasts; unilateral in 90%; Meigs syndrome of fibroma, right hydrothorax and ascites) and thecomas (plump spindle cells with lipid droplets) are stromal tumours; granulosa cell tumours are sex cord-stromal. Teratomas are the commonest germ cell tumours, mostly benign, containing tissue from three germ layers (ectoderm: skin, sebaceous glands, hair follicles; mesoderm: tooth, cartilage; endoderm: gastric glands); immature teratoma is malignant; the other germ cell tumours listed are dysgerminoma (identical to testicular seminoma), yolk sac tumour, mixed germ cell tumour and embryonal carcinoma. Metastatic tumours come mostly from tumours of Müllerian origin (uterus, tube, opposite ovary) and others from breast, GIT, pancreas and gall bladder, for example Krukenberg tumour, mostly of gastric origin.

(i) The lung lobule is the smallest anatomic subunit of the lung, comprising a cluster of 3-5 terminal bronchioles with its appended acinus. The acinus comprises respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs whose walls are formed by alveoli. The conducting airway consists of respiratory transitional epithelium, bronchial mucous glands, cartilage in a C-shape and then circular pattern down to the segmental bronchioles, and submucosal muscle fibres. The gaseous exchange airway consists of the alveoli and alveolar walls together with septal and interstitial capillaries.
(ii) Obstructive diseases affect the conductive airway and may also involve external sources such as the muscles of respiration, pleural problems and central control. Restrictive diseases affect the interstitial tissue and gaseous exchange at the interalveolar septa and are mostly localised lesions. The more central squamous cell (bronchogenic) carcinoma arises near the conducting airways, while adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma are typically peripheral, arising in the gas-exchanging portion of the lung.
(iii) The central squamous cell carcinoma typically involves the hilar lymph nodes and spreads to other parts from there, producing mainly localised respiratory distress but occasionally skeletal and brain metastasis. Small cell carcinoma, though also central, is notorious for producing widespread distant metastasis, including to the CNS and skin. Peripheral adenocarcinoma spreads within and outside the lung to involve the liver, brain, skin, kidneys and adrenal glands, and lymphatic invasion may cause lymphangitis carcinomatosa with intractable pleural effusion. Lung cancer is probably the most common cause of paraneoplastic syndrome, with oat (small) cell carcinoma causing Cushing syndrome (ACTH-like substance) and hyponatraemia (inappropriate ADH secretion), and squamous cell carcinoma causing hypercalcaemia (parathormone-like substance). These remote endocrine and metastatic effects illustrate how a primary lesion within the bronchial tree can cause functional deficits in distant organs such as the brain, bones, skin and endocrine/electrolyte balance.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the lung lobule and acinus.
(ii) State how the parts of the respiratory tract relate to obstructive versus restrictive lung disease and to tumour location.
(iii) Explain how lung carcinoma may spread to cause a functional deficit in distant structures.

A 3-week-old male infant is brought in with persistent, forceful (projectile) non-bilious vomiting after feeds, present since the second to third week of life. He remains hungry and irritable after each episode.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Outline the embryologic/pathologic basis of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
(ii) A disorder of multifactorial inheritance; associated with Turner syndrome and trisomy 18. It is caused by hyperplasia of the muscularis propria, which produces persistent gastric outlet obstruction; male-to-female ratio is 3-4:1.

questions.question:
A patient with known liver cirrhosis is found on imaging to have a large hepatic mass with a tumour thrombus extending into the portal vein.
(i) Identify the organ/structure and the likely lesion.
(ii) Describe the structures compressed/affected by the lesion.
(iii) List the differential/precursor pathologies.
(iv) Discuss the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking the background disease to this lesion.
questions.answerText:
(i) Liver mass consistent with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); it may appear as a unifocal (usually large) mass, multifocal widely distributed nodules of variable size, or a diffusely infiltrative mass.
(ii) Invasion into blood vessels, particularly the portal vein, is characteristic of HCC; regional lymphatic metastasis is frequent though distant lymph nodes are rarely involved; extrahepatic metastasis is mostly haematogenous, with the lungs being the most common target.
(iii) Precursor/background lesions include large cell change, small cell change, dysplastic nodules and macro-regenerative nodules, typically arising in a background of cirrhosis with risk factors of HBV, HCV, aflatoxin B1, alcohol, hereditary haemochromatosis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson disease and metabolic syndrome.
(iv) Cirrhosis is the usual background for HCC but is not itself required for, or a premalignant lesion of, hepatocarcinogenesis; the most important underlying factors are viral infection (HBV, HCV) and toxic injury (aflatoxin, alcohol), and synergism between risk factors (notably HBV together with consumption of aflatoxin-contaminated foodstuffs) exponentially increases the risk of HCC; the characteristic invasion of the portal vein explains the tumour thrombus and the pattern of haematogenous spread.

(i) The diagnosis is Graves disease.
(ii) Graves disease is an organ-specific autoimmune disease; genetic factors are stated to play a role in its development, though no further detail is given.
(iii) Autoantibodies are directed against the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor on thyroid epithelial cells; these autoantibodies mimic the effect of TSH, activating receptor-coupled adenylate cyclase and stimulating production of the thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodothyronine.
Because production of these autoantibodies is not regulated, unlike the production of TSH itself, the thyroid is overstimulated, resulting in excessive production of thyroid hormones.
questions.question:
A patient presents with features of excess thyroid hormone production.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology of this condition.

questions.answerText:
(i) Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid and may be euthyroid, hyperthyroid or hypothyroid; endemic goitre (over 10% of the population) is due to dietary iodine deficiency; sporadic goitre shows female predominance in young adults and is due to physiological demand, excess dietary calcium, goitrogens (cruciferous vegetables such as cabbage, cauliflower, brussels sprouts and cassava, which interfere with iodine uptake and inhibit T3 and T4 formation) or hereditary enzyme defects.
(ii) Low thyroid hormone raises TSH, which stimulates the gland and causes hyperplasia and hypertrophy of follicular cells; the gland enlarges to make best use of limited iodine.
(iii) Diffuse goitre is grossly non-nodular with enlarged hyperplastic follicles filled with colloid and no fibrosis; multinodular goitre shows enlarged follicles lined by flattened inactive cells with focal unencapsulated nodules and degenerative changes (fibrosis, old haemorrhage, calcification, cystic change).
(iv) Because the enlargement compensates for limited iodine the patient is often euthyroid, though may be toxic or hypofunctioning; a large goitre may extend retrosternally (plunging goitre) and pressure symptoms are a common complaint; long-standing multinodular goitre predisposes to follicular carcinoma.
(v) Hypothyroidism lowers the metabolic rate: weight gain, cold intolerance and cool skin, thinning hair with loss of the lateral eyebrows (Queen Anne sign), raised diastolic pressure, bradycardia and heart failure; it is cretinism when it occurs in infancy or childhood and myxoedema in older children and adults, caused by Hashimoto thyroiditis and iodine deficiency.
(vi) Graves: autoimmune, with anti-TSH receptor antibody (thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin) stimulating the receptor and raising T3 and T4; commonest cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism; age 20-40, F:M about 7:1, more common in western races. Hashimoto: antibodies to thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase; commonest cause of hypothyroidism where iodine is sufficient though it may first present with hyperthyroidism; F:M 10-20:1, age 45-65, can occur in children.
(vii) Graves: diffusely enlarged, non-nodular gland; tall hyperplastic follicular cells forming papillae without fibrovascular cores, pale colloid with scalloped edges, lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centres. Hashimoto: destruction of follicles then fibrosis, widespread lymphoid infiltrate with reactive follicles, epithelium replaced by metaplastic Hurthle cells.
(viii) Acute thyroiditis follows congenital sinuses linking thyroid to pharynx and is painful, possibly with abscess; subacute thyroiditis is viral (coxsackie, mumps), may mimic pharyngitis and is self-limiting; lymphocytic thyroiditis is silent, commoner in women, with anti-peroxidase antibodies, and is a probable precursor of Hashimoto; rare hyperthyroid causes: adenoma, postpartum thyroiditis, amiodarone, iodinated contrast, struma ovarii and hydatidiform mole (TSH-like hCG).
(ix) Adenoma is a single encapsulated follicular nodule with activating TSH-receptor mutation (raised cAMP) or RAS mutation in 20%; capsule integrity separates it from follicular carcinoma. Carcinomas: papillary (75-85%, Orphan Annie nuclei, psammoma bodies, lymph node spread, good prognosis, usual type in children, RET/PTC and radiation), follicular (10-20%, capsular and vascular invasion, blood spread to lung, bone, liver), medullary (5%, C cells, amyloid, MEN-2) and anaplastic (5%, elderly, rapid, radiosensitive, no surgery, p53); Hashimoto thyroiditis predisposes to papillary carcinoma and B cell lymphoma.

(i) A teratoma. Most sacrococcygeal teratomas are mature (benign, 75%); teratomas are the most common tumours of infancy, and the sacrococcygeal region is the most common site (40% of childhood teratomas), with two peaks in incidence, about 2 years of age (congenital) and late adolescence/early adulthood - the benign forms are encountered in younger infants (younger than 4 months) while malignant forms occur in an older age group.
(ii) Approximately 10% of sacrococcygeal teratomas are associated with other congenital anomalies such as meningocele and spina bifida; other midline sites for childhood teratomas include the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and head and neck, and gonadal sites include the testis and ovaries.
(iii) The differential pathological components are mature teratoma (75%), immature teratoma, and malignant teratoma (12%), the last usually admixed with another germ cell tumour component such as an endodermal sinus tumour.
(iv) Sacrococcygeal teratomas show a female preponderance (F:M ratio of 4:1) with a frequency of 1 in 20,000 to 40,000 live births; the midline location reflects the totipotent germ cell origin typical of teratomas, and the coexistence with neural tube defects such as meningocele and spina bifida in a minority of cases supports a close relationship between the sacrococcygeal region's developmental field and the tumour.
questions.question:
A female infant is noted at birth to have a large mass arising from the sacrococcygeal region in the midline. Imaging shows a mixed cystic and solid mass without involvement of the vertebral canal.
(i) Identify the likely nature of this mass.
(ii) State the structures/organs that may be affected or associated.
(iii) State the differential pathological components that should be considered.
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning supporting the diagnosis.

questions.answerText:
(i) The lymph node is an encapsulated organ made up of cortex, paracortex and medulla. The cortex contains naive B-cells that make up the primary follicles.
(ii) The paracortex contains mainly T-cells. The medulla (the filter) often contains the secondary follicles made up of antigen-activated B-cells within the germinal centre; macrophages, dendritic cells and plasma cells are also found there.
(iii) Follicular hyperplasia is enlargement of the cortical secondary follicles and an increase in their number. In follicular hyperplasia, the medulla may be compromised.
(iv) Reticular hyperplasia/sinus histiocytosis is prominence of the medullary sinuses. In reticular hyperplasia/sinus histiocytosis, the cortex may be compromised; this can be seen in reaction to cancer even when there are no tumour cells in the node.
(v) Metastatic tumour cells reaching a lymph node first enter the subcapsular sinus, and this is perhaps the single most important staging and prognostic feature of tumours. Hodgkin lymphoma spreads predictably, starting first with a single node. It then spreads to the spleen, liver, bone marrow and other tissues (disseminated extranodal extension). This orderly, predictable pattern of spread is why staging is crucially important in Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the capsule of a lymph node and the three regions found deep to it.
(ii) State which cells predominate in each of these regions.
(iii) Describe what happens to the cortex and medulla in follicular hyperplasia.
(iv) Describe what happens to the cortex and medulla in reticular hyperplasia/sinus histiocytosis.
(v) Explain where within the node metastatic tumour cells first arrive, and the order in which Hodgkin lymphoma spreads to distant tissues.

questions.answerText:
(i) The most widely accepted mechanism of atherosclerosis is the "response to injury hypothesis," which regards it as a chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall initiated by focal chronic endothelial injury. This begins with insudation of lipoproteins (mainly LDL and cholesterol) into the vessel wall and their oxidation. Blood monocytes and other leukocytes adhere to the endothelium, migrate into the intima and transform into macrophages and foam cells. Platelets adhere to focal areas of endothelial denudation or to adherent leukocytes. Factors released from activated platelets, macrophages and vascular cells cause smooth muscle cells to migrate from the media into the intima. Smooth muscle cells then proliferate within the intima and elaborate extracellular matrix, and lipid accumulates, forming the mature plaque.
(ii) Non-modifiable risk factors for the initiating endothelial injury include increasing age, male gender, family history and genetic abnormalities. Potentially controllable risks include hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, cigarette smoking and diabetes mellitus. Lesser risks include obesity, physical inactivity, stress, homocysteine, postmenopausal oestrogen deficiency, high carbohydrate diet, alcohol, lipoproteins, unsaturated fat intake and Chlamydia pneumoniae. The resulting deformity of the vessel wall - the atheromatous plaque - can undergo calcification, ulceration, haemorrhage, thrombosis, aneurysmal dilation or infection. These complications explain the downstream consequences of atherosclerotic injury, including stenosis and ischaemia in the territory supplied by the affected artery.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the course of the pathogenic process ("the response to injury hypothesis") by which atherosclerosis develops within the arterial wall.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the complications (deformity) that follow this injury to the vessel wall.

questions.answerText:
(i) The Lauren classification of gastric carcinoma, based on the presumed pathogenetic mechanism, divides tumours into intestinal type (53%), diffuse type (33%) and mixed type. Contd: the WHO classification, based on histologic appearance alone, divides tumours into papillary, tubular, mucinous or signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma, with tubular and papillary carcinomas generally having a better prognosis than mucinous and signet-ring carcinomas.
(ii) The intestinal type predominates in high-risk areas and develops from precursor lesions related to chronic atrophic gastritis, particularly that associated with intestinal metaplasia. It is commoner in the elderly (mean age 55 years) with a male-to-female ratio of 2:1. Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with multifocal mucosal atrophy and intestinal metaplasia that underlie susceptibility to the intestinal type.
(iii) Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma exhibits an intestinal morphology, forming bulky tumours composed of glandular structures with variable differentiation. In better-differentiated intestinal-type tumours, most cells are columnar and mucin-secreting; poorly differentiated variants have a predominantly solid pattern. The adjacent gastric mucosa in intestinal-type carcinoma often shows chronic gastritis with widespread intestinal metaplasia. Diffuse carcinoma shows rare glandular formation, with most tumour cells growing individually and a typical signet-ring appearance. The diffuse type is usually poorly demarcated and infiltrates widely, and intestinal metaplasia of the adjacent mucosa is conspicuously lacking. The diffuse type is commoner in younger patients, has an approximately equal sex distribution, and has no identifiable precursor lesion, unlike the intestinal type. The intestinal-type tumours are known to have a better prognosis than the diffuse-type tumours.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the classification systems (Lauren and WHO) used for gastric carcinoma.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis for the occurrence of the intestinal type in high-risk populations.
(iii) Distinguish between the Intestinal type and Diffuse type of gastric carcinoma.

questions.answerText:
(i) The liver has a dual blood supply - two-thirds from the portal vein and one-third from the hepatic artery. Branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile ducts run together within the portal tracts at the periphery of each liver lobule. Portosystemic shunts develop where the systemic and portal circulations share capillary beds. Shunt sites include veins around and within the rectum, the cardio-oesophageal junction, the retroperitoneum, and the falciform ligament of the liver (periumbilical and abdominal wall collaterals).
(ii) Anatomical basis of the deformity after injury: cirrhosis is the major intrahepatic cause of increased resistance to portal blood flow. This results from increased resistance to flow in the sinusoids and compression of the central vein. Anastomoses between the arterial and portal systems impose arterial pressure on the normally low-pressure portal venous system, increasing portal blood flow. At the rectal shunt site, dilated veins manifest as haemorrhoids. At the cardio-oesophageal junction, shunting produces oesophagogastric varices, whose rupture and bleeding is a major cause of death. At the retroperitoneum/falciform ligament, shunting produces periumbilical and abdominal wall collaterals, seen clinically as caput medusae. Congestive splenomegaly, with associated haematologic abnormalities from hypersplenism, also results from the raised portal pressure.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the portal venous system and the sites of portosystemic shunting.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity that develops at the shunt sites after liver injury (cirrhosis).

questions.answerText:
(i) The thymus develops at about the 8th week from the 3rd and 4th branchial pouches, alongside the lower pair of parathyroid glands. It is pyramidal in shape, encapsulated, has two fused lobes with an outer cortex and inner medulla, and lies behind the sternum in the superior mediastinum, weighing 10-35g at birth, 20-50g at puberty, and 5-15g in adults thereafter.
(ii) Thymic epithelial cells and immature T-lymphocytes (thymocytes) predominate, alongside Hassall corpuscles, dendritic cells, a few B-cells and polymorphonuclear cells; prothymocytes originate in the bone marrow and migrate to the thymus to mature. In the cortex, pre-T cells become CD2, 3, 4 and 8-positive and TdT-negative as T-cell receptor gene rearrangement begins; in the medulla the cells selectively lose either CD4 or CD8 positivity, so the mature T-cell leaving in the peripheral blood is either CD4-positive (helper) or CD8-positive (cytotoxic).
(iii) Hypoplasia/aplasia of the thymus is associated with DiGeorge syndrome (also known as velocardiofacial syndrome, a 22q11.2 deletion). DiGeorge syndrome presents with defective cell-mediated immunity and hypoparathyroidism.
(iv) Thymic nodular hyperplasia is associated with chronic inflammatory and immunologic states, including myasthenia gravis, Graves disease, SLE, scleroderma and rheumatoid arthritis. It is characterised by reactive lymphoid follicles with prominent pale germinal centres.
(v) Thymomas, arising from the thymic epithelial cells, are classified as benign/encapsulated, malignant type 1/invasive, or malignant type 2/thymic carcinoma, and occur in adults over 40 years (M:F 1:1), commonly in the antero-superior mediastinum. Thymomas are usually associated with autoimmune diseases, especially myasthenia gravis, and also Cushing syndrome, pernicious anaemia, dermatomyositis, polymyositis, pure red cell aplasia, Graves disease and acquired gamma-globulinaemia. This association is explained by the tumour disturbing the thymic environment normally required for negative selection of self-reacting lymphocytes. The functional deficit at the distant neuromuscular junction in myasthenia gravis (antibodies against acetylcholine receptors blocking neuromuscular transmission, causing muscle weakness) illustrates how disturbed thymic selection produces disease at a distant structure.
questions.question:
(i) State the embryological origin, shape, weight and location of the thymus.
(ii) State the cell populations of the thymus and describe how T-cells mature within it.
(iii) State the condition associated with thymic hypoplasia/aplasia.
(iv) State the condition associated with thymic nodular hyperplasia, and describe its appearance.
(v) Explain how a thymic tumour produces a functional deficit at a distant structure.

A child presents with an acute systemic illness with malaise, fever, chills and throbbing pain over a site in a long bone; the blood count shows leukocytosis.
(i) State the diagnosis and the routes by which the organism reaches bone.
(ii) List the predisposing factors and the causative organisms by age group.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology, including why the metaphysis is the commonest site and why infants are prone to arthritis.
(iv) State the investigations, management and complications.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute (pyogenic) haematogenous osteomyelitis: an acute or chronic inflammatory process of bone and its structures, including marrow, secondary to infection; the organism reaches bone by haematogenous spread (most common route), extension from a contiguous site or direct implantation.
(ii) Predisposing factors: diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, AIDS, intravenous drug abuse, alcoholism, chronic steroid use, immunosuppression, chronic joint disease, peripheral vascular disease, a prosthetic orthopaedic device (independent risk factor), recent orthopaedic surgery or open fracture.
- Organisms: newborns (under 4 months) S. aureus, Enterobacter and group A and B streptococci; 4 months to 4 years S. aureus, group A streptococci, H. influenzae and Enterobacter; 4 years to adult S. aureus (80%), group A streptococci, H. influenzae and Enterobacter; adults S. aureus, occasionally Enterobacter or streptococci; sickle cell disease S. aureus and Salmonella; MRSA and Kingella kingae are increasingly reported.
(iii) The condition primarily occurs in children; the commonest site is the rapidly growing, highly vascular metaphysis of growing bones, where sharp angling and sluggish flow in the metaphyseal capillary loops (distal metaphysis) predispose to thrombosis, localised necrosis and bacterial seeding.
- Vascular connections between metaphysis and epiphysis make infants prone to arthritis of the adjacent joint (shoulder or hip when the intracapsular metaphyseal end of the humerus or femur is infected); untreated infection spreads to the subperiosteal space after crossing the cortex; despite its name the onset may be slow and insidious.
(iv) X-rays, biopsy and cultures help diagnosis; antibiotics combined with surgical drainage are usually curative; in 5-25% of cases the infection fails to resolve and persists as chronic infection; complications include pathologic fracture, endocarditis and sepsis.

questions.question:
A middle-aged man with hypertension, cigarette smoking and diabetes mellitus presents with severe substernal chest pain lasting more than 30 minutes.
(i) Identify the organ/structure most likely involved.
(ii) Describe the structures/tissue affected by the pathological process over time.
(iii) List the differential clinical pathologies to consider.
(iv) Discuss the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking risk factors to the event and its complications.
questions.answerText:
(i) Myocardium in the distribution of a major coronary artery; most infarcts are transmural, in which ischaemic necrosis involves the full thickness (or nearly so) of the ventricular wall, while a small percentage are subendocardial infarcts.
(ii) In ischaemic myocytes, ATP depletion begins within seconds; contractility is lost within less than 2 minutes; ATP falls to 50% by 10 minutes and 10% by 40 minutes; irreversible cell injury occurs at 20-40 minutes; microvascular injury occurs after more than 1 hour.
(iii) Differential clinical manifestations of ischaemic heart disease: angina pectoris (stable/typical angina, Prinzmetal variant angina, unstable/crescendo angina), chronic ischaemic heart disease with heart failure, and sudden cardiac death; all result from imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, which in 90% of cases is due to reduced coronary blood flow from atherosclerosis.
(iv) Pathogenesis involves atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary vessels, intraluminal thrombosis over plaques, platelet aggregation and vasospasm; predisposing risk factors include hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, genetic hypercholesterolemia, hyperlipoproteinemia and obesity. Complications include contractile failure/heart failure, arrhythmias, myocardial rupture, pericarditis, right ventricular infarction, infarct extension/expansion, mural thrombosis, ventricular aneurysm, papillary muscle dysfunction and progressive late heart failure.

(i) Hydatidiform mole (complete or partial): cystic swelling of the chorionic villi with variable trophoblastic proliferation; occurs in women in active reproductive life, in teenagers and at 40-50 years; usually diagnosed in early pregnancy (average 9 weeks); highest incidence in south-east Asia.
(ii) Complete mole: genetic material entirely paternal, from fertilisation of an empty ovum lacking functional maternal DNA; about 90% are monospermic with duplication of the haploid set (46XX), about 10% dispermic (46XX or 46XY); grossly swollen villi resembling a bunch of grapes; all villi enlarged and scalloped with central cisterns and circumferential trophoblastic proliferation; no fetal tissue or vessels.
- Partial mole: fertilisation of an egg by two sperms (triploid 69XXY or 69XXX, rarely 69XYY; tetraploid 92XXXY) or by a single sperm that failed meiotic reduction; two populations of villi with only some enlarged; focal, less marked trophoblastic hyperplasia; fetal parts or fetal blood vessels may be seen; the fetus usually dies after about 10 weeks and the mole is aborted.
(iii) Predisposing factors: reproductive age extremes (under 20 and over 40), nulliparity, blood group A (stronger if the husband is group O), history of abnormal pregnancy or prior mole (20-fold greater risk of another mole), folic acid and carotene deficiency, Asian, African or Latin American ethnicity; contraception has no definite link to mole risk, though contraception is useful during β-hCG monitoring because a supervening pregnancy would distort the values.
(iv) Complete mole carries a 2.5% risk of choriocarcinoma and a 10% risk of invasive mole; partial mole has an increased risk of persistent disease but almost never evolves into choriocarcinoma; an invasive mole penetrates or perforates the uterine wall, may embolise to lungs or brain without growing there, and may regress even without chemotherapy.
- Choriocarcinoma is rapidly invasive and metastasises to lungs, vagina, brain, liver and bone but responds well to treatment: evacuation of the uterus followed by chemotherapy, which is usually curative.
questions.question:
A woman in her teens presents in early pregnancy with vaginal bleeding, a uterus larger than dates, passage of small grape-like masses and rapidly rising hCG levels.
(i) State the diagnosis, its types and the ages at which it occurs.
(ii) Explain the cytogenetic and pathologic basis, contrasting the complete and partial forms.
(iii) State the predisposing factors and the resuscitation or immediate management.
(iv) State the risks of progression and the definitive treatment of progressive disease.

(i) Describe the functional respiratory unit of the lung and its grouping into lobules and lobes.
(ii) Describe the distribution within the lobule of the three named types of emphysema.
(iii) State how smoking-related disease and pulmonary oedema typically distribute within the lung.
(iv) State the lung disease that underlies many cases of spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults, and why.
(v) Explain how chronic lung disease and pulmonary embolism each produce a functional deficit at the distant structure of the heart.
questions.answerText:
(i) The functional respiratory unit of the lung is the acinus, running from the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli, grouped into lobules and lobes, and covered by the pleura.
(ii) Emphysema is classified by its distribution within the lobule into four major types. Centriacinar (centrilobular) emphysema is the most common form (over 95% of clinically significant cases), occurring mainly in heavy smokers with COPD; the central/proximal parts of the acini are affected while distal alveoli are spared. Panacinar emphysema uniformly enlarges the acinus from the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli, occurring more in the lower zones and anterior margins of the lung, usually most severe at the bases.
(iii) In smoking-related disease generally, the upper two-thirds of the lungs are more severely affected, with large alveoli seen on the cut surface and apical blebs or bullae in advanced disease. Pulmonary oedema accumulates initially in the basal regions of the lower lobes, because hydrostatic pressure is greatest at these dependent sites.
(iv) Distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema spares the proximal acinus, is more striking adjacent to the pleura and lobular septa, and is usually more severe in the upper half of the lungs. It underlies many cases of spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.
(v) Advanced interstitial fibrotic lung disease produces diffuse scarring (end-stage/honeycomb lung), which may eventually cause secondary pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale). A large pulmonary thromboembolus (such as a "saddle" embolus) can similarly cause sudden death from blockage of blood flow through the lungs, or acute right-sided heart failure (acute cor pulmonale). Recurrent pulmonary thromboemboli can also cause pulmonary hypertension by reducing the functional cross-sectional area of the pulmonary vascular bed, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure of at least 25 mmHg at rest, classified into groups including that due to left heart failure and that due to lung disease and/or hypoxia.

(i) Carbon monoxide (CO) is one of the common air pollutants (alongside sulfur dioxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, lead and particulate matter) contributing to outdoor smog, and is also an important indoor air pollutant, along with tobacco smoke, nitrogen dioxide and asbestos.
(ii) Chronic poisoning by CO forms carboxyhaemoglobin, which may give rise to hypoxia; acute poisoning is generally a consequence of accidental exposure or a suicide attempt, and in light-skinned individuals is marked by a characteristic generalised cherry-red colour of the skin and mucous membranes, resulting from high levels of carboxyhaemoglobin.
(iii) Chronic carboxyhaemoglobin-related hypoxia can insidiously evoke widespread ischaemic changes in the central nervous system, particularly marked in the basal ganglia and lenticular nuclei; there may be permanent neurologic sequelae such as impairment of memory, vision, hearing, and speech.
If death from acute poisoning occurs rapidly, morphologic changes may not be present; with longer survival, the brain may be slightly oedematous, with punctate haemorrhages and hypoxia-induced neuronal changes.
(iv) The permanent neurologic sequelae of CO poisoning, impairment of memory, vision, hearing, and speech, follow from chronic carboxyhaemoglobin-induced hypoxia causing widespread ischaemic changes in the central nervous system.
These ischaemic changes are particularly marked in the basal ganglia and lenticular nuclei.
The basal ganglia and lenticular nuclei are therefore the anatomical structures whose ischaemic injury underlies the permanent neurologic deficits described.
In cases of longer survival after acute poisoning, the brain may show slight oedema with punctate haemorrhages, reflecting ongoing hypoxic-ischaemic injury at the tissue level.
These hypoxia-induced neuronal changes in the brain are the structural correlate of the functional deficits (memory, vision, hearing, and speech impairment) that persist after the acute exposure has resolved.
This localisation to the basal ganglia and lenticular nuclei explains why the resulting neurologic deficit is often selective rather than a global encephalopathy.
The anatomical basis of the deficit is thus the particular vulnerability of the basal ganglia and lenticular nuclei to hypoxic-ischaemic injury from carboxyhaemoglobin-mediated tissue hypoxia.
questions.question:
(i) State the origin/source of carbon monoxide exposure.
(ii) Describe the course by which carbon monoxide produces tissue hypoxia.
(iii) State the distribution of tissues/organs typically affected.
(iv) Explain the anatomical basis of the permanent neurologic deficit that may follow carbon monoxide poisoning.

A(i)
A reactor produces neutrons from controlled chain fission of U-235; targets capture neutrons (neutron activation) and become radioactive.
A(ii)

Traditional, digital, laboratory (Abbe) and inline process (Rayleigh, typically for gases). The Abbe refractometer, the most common bench-top device, was developed by Ernst Abbe with a built-in thermometer.

A(i)
A polarimeter is an instrument used to measure the angle of rotation caused by passing polarised light through an optically active substance; it shows whether the substance rotates plane-polarised light to the left, to the right, or not at all.
A(ii)
Light source, polarizer, sample tube, analyzer and detector; the plane-polarised light is rotated through an angle α read from the detector, (+) dextro and (-) laevo. Digital polarimeters also exist.
A(iii)
Observed rotation depends on concentration and tube length, temperature and wavelength; the sodium D line (about 589 nm) is usually used and temperature mostly 298 K; the solvent must be optically inactive.
A(iv)
α = [α] × l × c. Example: 0.5245 g diluted to 10.0 mL = 5.245 g/100 mL; [α] = -30.0°, l = 1.00 dm, so α = -157°.
B(i)
The tendency of molecules to rotate plane-polarised light (d or l, clockwise or anticlockwise) and the extent of rotation (α); specific rotation is a property of chirality.
B(ii)
Optical purity = specific rotation of the mixture / specific rotation of the pure enantiomer. The enantiomeric excess (ee) tells how much excess of one enantiomer is in the mixture; an enantiomerically pure sample has only one enantiomer.
B(iii)
Naturally occurring nicotine is levorotatory, [α]D = -166.4°; (+)-nicotine is physiologically less active and (-)-nicotine is more toxic.

C(iii)

C(iv)

A(i)
Pure water has small amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻ and very low conductivity; dissolved electrolytes furnish ions and raise it; ionic conductance is conduction by the ions present.
A(ii)
Nature of electrolyte, concentration, size of ions and their solvation, and nature and viscosity of solvent.
A(iii)
Conductivity decreases on dilution (fewer ions per unit volume) for weak and strong electrolytes; molar conductivity increases on dilution (larger volume per mole); at zero concentration it is the limiting molar conductivity (λ∞).
A(iv)
Transference number: fraction of total current carried by cations or anions; t₊ + t₋ = 1. Cell constant example: 1.29 cm⁻¹ (129 m⁻¹) from 0.1 M KCl.
B(i)
Ions of all electrolytes migrate independently as the solution is diluted; in dilute solution ions are so far apart there is no interaction.
B(ii)
The difference in equivalent conductance of a pair of electrolytes with the same counter ion is the same at the same temperature and solvent (e.g. K and Li salts).
B(iii)
Λ₀ = nc λ c + na λ a; for Ca₃(PO₄)₂: Λ₀ = 3 λ(Ca²⁺) + 2 λ(PO₄³⁻).
B(iv)
Λ₀ (PhCOOH) = Λ₀ (PhCOONa) + Λ₀ (HCl) - Λ₀ (NaCl), since a weak electrolyte's value at infinite dilution cannot be found experimentally.
C(i)
At infinite dilution no attraction exists between ions, so the ionic conductance of chloride is the same in NaCl or KCl and the difference between NaCl and KCl is the difference between Na⁺ and K⁺.
C(ii)
Weak-electrolyte Λ₀ cannot be measured directly.
C(iii)
Molar conductivity rises as concentration falls and reaches the limiting value (λ∞) as concentration approaches zero.
C(iv)
A strong acid dissociates completely, giving many ions and high conductance; a weak acid dissociates partially, giving few ions and low conductance.

E = E½ - (0.0591/n) log [i/(id - i)]; at i = id/2 the log term is zero; id = limiting - residual current.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Polarimetry measures the optical rotation of compounds that rotate plane-polarised light. Ordinary light has waves vibrating in all planes at right angles to the direction of propagation; plane-polarised light vibrates in a single plane (obtained with polarizers such as a Nicol prism).
A(ii)
A compound that rotates plane-polarised light to the left or right is optically active; one that does not rotate it is optically inactive. Dextrorotatory (+ or d) = clockwise rotation viewed through the polarimeter; laevorotatory (- or l) = counter-clockwise rotation.
A(iii)
The d and l designations are different from the D and L configurations and from the R and S forms in stereochemistry; the assignment of R or S has no relationship with the optical rotation (+) or (-).
A(iv)
Light source, polarizer, sample compartment/polarimeter tube (10 cm = 1 dm), analyzer, and detector/eyepiece.
B(i)
Specific rotation [α]T(λ) = α/(l c). α = observed rotation in degrees; l = cell path length in dm (1 dm = 10 cm; standard tube 1.00 dm); c = concentration in g/mL for a pure liquid (its density) or g per 100 mL for a solution. A further note gives [α] = 100 α/(l c).
B(ii)
The coniine solution in ethanol is dextrorotatory with specific rotation 16°, measured at 298 K using plane-polarised light of the sodium D line (589.6 nm in that example). T and D are conditions of measurement, not mathematical terms.
B(iii)
α depends on the solvent, temperature, wavelength, concentration of the isomer and path length; it depends on the number of optically active molecules the light meets. If the compound is optically active the solvent must be inactive.
B(iv)
Pure (S)-2-butanol, 10.0 cm tube, sodium D line, 20 °C, α = +104°, density 0.805 g/mL: [α] = +104/(1.00 × 0.805) = +129°. Molecular rotation = [α] × M/100.
C(i)
Asymmetric (chiral) carbon centres carry four different substituents; chiral compounds are non-superimposable mirror images and can rotate plane-polarised light. Specific rotation is a property of chirality.
C(ii)
The solvent must be optically inactive; α varies with solvent, temperature, wavelength, concentration and path length; a 50/50 racemic mixture has no effect on plane-polarised light.
C(iii)
Enantiomers are chiral molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of one another. Diastereomers are stereoisomers whose molecules are non-superimposable but not mirror images.
C(iv)
Optically active substances made in the laboratory often occur as a 50/50 mixture of two enantiomers (racemic mixture/racemate), which has no effect on plane-polarised light; a single enantiomer rotates it (e.g. nicotine natural form is levorotatory, [α]D = -166.4°).

A(i)
UV/visible spectroscopy is the interaction of molecules with UV/visible radiation: electrons are promoted from the ground state to excited levels (HOMO to LUMO), usually outer valence electrons (σ, π, n). Ultraviolet 190-400 nm; visible 400-780 nm.
A(ii)
Each electronic transition has vibrational and rotational transitions: E electronic > E vibrational > E rotational, so electrons reach sublevels.
A(iii)
E = hc/λ; ΔE (kJ/mol) = h ν = 1.19 × 10⁵ / λ (nm).
A(iv)
σ to σ*: methane 125 nm, ethane 135 nm (not in 200-700 nm). n to σ*: 150-250 nm. π to π* (unconjugated): below 200 nm. n to π*: about 300 nm. Also charge-transfer, d-d and f-f.
B(i)
Longer conjugation lowers the π to π* energy gap, so λ max increases and ε roughly doubles per added double bond (acetone n-π* 270 nm; methyl vinyl ketone 324 nm; β-carotene 455 nm; lycopene 474 nm).
B(ii)
π to π* is 10 to 100 times more intense than n to σ* or n to π*; allowed transitions have ε above 10,000, forbidden n to π* about 10-100.
B(iii)
Spin rule: same multiplicity (S-S, T-T allowed; S-T forbidden); LaPorte rule: opposite parity; ε = 0.87 × 10²⁰ P a with P above 0.01 allowed.
B(iv)
Charge-transfer (donor to acceptor, e.g. SCN- with Fe(III)); d-d (splitting increases with ligand field strength); f-f (4f/5f, sharper).
C(i)
A chromophore is the group responsible for absorption (e.g. C=C-C=C, NO₂); an auxochrome is a saturated group with little intrinsic absorption that modifies absorption when attached to a chromophore.
C(ii)
Bathochromic (red) shifts the maximum to longer wavelength; hypsochromic (blue) to shorter.
C(iii)
Hyperchromic increases absorption intensity; hypochromic decreases it.
C(iv)
Singlet: all spins paired, multiplicity 1; triplet: parallel spins, total spin 1, multiplicity 3.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Refractometry measures how light is refracted when it passes through a substance. Refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (or air) to its speed in the medium (nD = V air / V liquid); it is dimensionless.
A(ii)
Light travels more slowly in media other than vacuum (vacuum > air > water > glass) because of absorption and re-emission by atoms; when speed changes at a boundary, direction changes. Into a denser medium light bends towards the normal; into a less dense medium, away from it.
A(iii)
n = sin(φa)/sin(φb), i.e. n₁ sin(θ₁) = n₂ sin(θ₂), where φa/φb are the angles of incidence and refraction and n the refractive indices of the two media. It applies to any waves; the refracted angle depends on light speed, which depends on wavelength.
A(iv)
The critical angle is the incident angle at which refracted light becomes parallel to the boundary (refraction angle 90°, sin = 1): n₁ sin(θc) = n₂ sin 90°. Smaller angles pass through, larger ones are reflected; refractometers detect the light/dark boundary.
B(i)
r = (1/d) (n² - 1)/(n² + 2), where d is density; specific refraction is refractivity divided by density (Lorentz and Lorenz equation).
B(ii)
A (or R) = r × M = [(n² - 1)/(n² + 2)] × (M/d), where M is molecular weight and d density.
B(iii)
Temperature (for many organic liquids n falls about 0.0005 per °C; water about 0.0001 per °C), wavelength (n decreases as wavelength increases, so indices at different wavelengths cannot be compared) and pressure (n increases with pressure through density; less marked for liquids than gases).
B(iv)
nD²⁰ = sodium D line (589.3 nm) at 20 °C; other lines: hydrogen C 656.3 nm, F 486.1 nm, mercury G 435.8 nm. Most organic liquids 1.3 to 1.5/1.7. nD²⁰: water 1.3330, acetone 1.3588, isopropanol 1.3772, ethyl acetate 1.3742.
C(i)
It is a physical property characteristic of a pure compound; like melting point it confirms identity or assesses purity by comparison with literature values; the closer to the literature value, the purer the sample.
C(ii)
The density and crystalline structure dictate the RI; materials whose physical properties are approximately equal have similar RI, so different substances may not be distinguished.
C(iii)
Specific refraction (r) is the refractivity divided by density; molar refraction (A) is the product of specific refraction and molecular weight.
C(iv)
At smaller incident angles rays pass the boundary (bending towards the normal in a denser medium); at angles larger than the critical angle they are reflected back.

A(ii)
Identical labels on both the container and the shield.
A(iii)
Stated activity at a given time and date and an expiry time reflect the fall in activity with physical half-life.
A(iv)
Intravenous injections, gases, aerosols, oral solutions and capsules; kits and nuclide generators are included.
B(i)
Never touch radioactive material with the hand; use forceps or suitable instruments; no eating or drinking where it is present; wear protective clothing.
B(ii)
Special storage conditions must appear on the label.
B(iii)
α: Perspex and thin rubber gloves; β: 1 cm Perspex; γ: about 15 cm lead for high-energy rays.
B(iv)
5 mSv/year (0.5 rem/year) for the personnel concerned.
C(i)
Short half-lives mean rapid loss of activity, so short-lived products are prepared at or near the point of use.
C(ii)
About 2 weeks after delivery (5 half-lives, yield about one thirtieth), so supplied weekly.
C(iii)
Decay period for waste disposal is calculated from half-life; spent fuel and radioactive waste require careful management.
C(iv)
Shielding and strict protocols protect staff but α emitters are not used in preparations because internal exposure is severe; safety versus availability and cost are noted.

questions.question:

C(iv) Distinguish allowed from forbidden transitions.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Peaks and valleys; absorptivity (ε or A(1%,1cm)) = intensity; wavelength of maximum absorption (λ max) = position; these depend on the extent of conjugation.
A(ii)
Absorbance: strength of absorption of radiation, dimensionless; A(1%,1cm): absorbance of a 1% solution in a 1 cm cuvette.
A(iii)
Its lone pair joins the π system of the chromophore, lowering π and π* energies and narrowing the gap, giving a red shift.
A(iv)
Benzene 255 nm; phenol 270 nm; phenolate 287 nm; aniline 280 nm; anilinium ion 254 nm (no auxochrome, like benzene).
B(i)
Ethene vs butadiene: smaller π to π* gap in butadiene; longer conjugation gives longer wavelength.
B(ii)
Polarity alters solute-solvent interaction: fine structure when interaction is small (benzene in hexane, vapour phase); conjugated dienes and aromatics shift little; in α,β-unsaturated carbonyls π to π* red shifts and n to π* blue shifts.
B(iii)
Ionisable auxochromes (-OH, -NH₂) change species: phenol to phenolate 270 to 287 nm; use buffer or work at the isosbestic point.
B(iv)
Non-planarity lowers λ max (biphenyl 250 vs 237 nm; ε 19,000 vs 10,250); trans isomers absorb at longer λ max than cis (stilbenes).
C(i)
Vibrational and rotational sublevels of the excited state broaden bands.
C(ii)
Solvents must be transparent at the analytical wavelength; the cut-off is where absorbance approaches 1 against water.
C(iii)
π to π* is far more intense (ε above 10,000 allowed); n to π* is weak (10-100) and forbidden.
C(iv)
Allowed: transition probability P above 0.01; forbidden: P below 0.01.

questions.question:

C(ii) Distinguish E electronic, vibrational and rotational.
C(iii) Distinguish absorption from emission spectroscopy.
C(iv) Distinguish UV from IR spectroscopy.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The study of interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter, giving absorption, emission or transmitted radiation.
A(ii)
E = h ν; c = λ ν; E = hc/λ; wavenumber = 10^4/λ (micrometres); ΔE (kJ/mol) = 1.19 × 10^5/λ (nm).
A(iii)
X-ray: bond breaking; UV/visible: electronic; infrared: vibrational; microwave: rotational; radio frequency (NMR): nuclear and electron spin.
A(iv)
E total = E trans + E elec + E vib + E rot + E nucl.
B(i)
Absorption: transition to a higher level with energy transferred to the absorber; emission: transition to a lower level; nonradiative decay if no radiation is emitted.
B(ii)
Strongly interact when energies are equal (E₁ = E₂, λ₁ = λ₂).
B(iii)
Violet 400-420, indigo 420-440, blue 440-490, green 490-570, yellow 570-585, orange 585-620, red 620-780 nm.
B(iv)
IR gives bond type, NMR types of protons, MS molecular weight, X-ray atom distribution.
C(i)
Collision: particle-to-particle, energy lost as heat; coupling: wave matches the particle's wave property and promotes to a higher level.
C(ii)
E electronic > E vibrational > E rotational.
C(iii)
AAS measures absorbed light; AES measures emitted light.
C(iv)
UV: electronic transitions (200-700 nm); IR: vibrations (4000-400 cm⁻¹).

Compounds with ionisable protons exist as interconvertible species in equilibrium; the amount of each depends on pH, and the chromophore type and absorptivity depend on the species present.
A(ii)
Phenol to phenolate: λ max 270 to 287 nm, ε 72 to 271. Aniline 280 nm vs anilinium ion 254 nm.
A(iii)

pH change from CO₂ dissolution and variable absorptivity cause deviation; remedy: isosbestic point and buffers.
B(i)
Absorbance difference at a defined wavelength between two samples in one of which a physical or chemical property of the drug is changed; uses reactions selective to the analyte (e.g. pH changes for acidic and basic drugs).
B(ii)
A13 = AD + AM; A10 = AB + AM; ΔA = A13 - A10 = AD - AB; ΔA = KC (AM = interfering substance).

A calibration curve of ΔA against concentration.

C(ii)

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Rules allow λ max to be calculated for conjugated systems; values are reliable to ± 5 nm; they do not apply to crossed conjugated or aromatic systems.
A(ii)
Parent butadiene 217 nm; each extending double bond +30; each alkyl substituent or ring residue +5; homoannular diene +36; exocyclic double bond +5.
A(iii)
OAcyl 0; alkoxy (RO) 6; S-alkyl 30; Cl or Br 5; N-alkyl2 60 nm.
A(iv)
More conjugated double bonds mean less energy for the transition and longer wavelength; λ max can predict the number of conjugated double bonds.
B(i)
217 (parent) + 36 (homoannular) + 30 (extension) + 5 (one exocyclic) + 15 (three alkyl) + 0 (acyl) = 303 nm calculated vs 304 nm actual in hexane.
B(ii)
A: 217 + 36 + 30 + 0 + 20 (4 alkyl) = 303 nm; B: 217 + 30 + 10 (2 exocyclic) + 25 (5 alkyl) = 282 nm; C: 217 + 36 + 60 + 15 + 25 = 353 nm.
B(iii)
Six-ring α,β-unsaturated ketone 215; five-ring 202; aldehyde 207; +39 homoannular diene; +30 extension; +5 exocyclic; alkyl α 10, β 12, γ and higher 18 nm.
B(iv)
OH α 35, β 30, δ 50; OAc 6; OMe α 35, β 30, γ 17, δ 31; S-alkyl β 85; Cl α 15 nm.
C(i)
They lower the energy of the π to π* transition (auxochrome lone pairs extend the π system).
C(ii)
Accuracy ± 5 nm; not for crossed conjugated or aromatic systems.
C(iii)
Homoannular: both double bonds in one ring (+36 diene; +39 enone). Exocyclic: double bond attached to a ring (+5).
C(iv)
Dienes use base 217 nm; α,β-unsaturated ketones use 215 nm (six-ring), 202 (five-ring), 207 (aldehyde), values in ethanol for π to π*.

questions.question:
A. IR regions and features
A(i) State the IR regions and wavenumber relation.
A(ii) Describe the two main parts of the spectrum.
A(iii) State the four primary regions.
A(iv) State what controls intensity.
B. Characteristic frequencies
B(i) Give the hydrocarbon values.
B(ii) Give the O and N values.

C(i) State Hooke's law relation.
C(ii) State the effect of hydrogen bonding.
C(iii) State ring size, field effect and conjugation.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Near 12500-4000 cm⁻¹ (0.8-2.5 micrometres), mid 4000-400 (2.5-25), far 400-20 (25-500); wavenumber = 10^4/λ (micrometres); E = hc ν, so wavenumber is proportional to energy.
A(ii)
Fundamental frequency region 4000-1500 cm⁻¹ (functional groups); fingerprint region 1500-500 cm⁻¹ (bending vibrations, unique to each molecule).
A(iii)
Bonds to H (O-H, N-H, C-H), triple bonds, double bonds, single bonds plus fingerprint; boundaries about 2700, 2000, 1600, 400 cm⁻¹.
A(iv)
The change in dipole moment (stretching more than bending); band area is not directly proportional to concentration; carbonyls are strong; bands described s, m, w, br.
B(i)
sp³ C-H below 3000 (2800-3000); sp² C-H 3000-3100; sp C-H about 3300; C=C 1620-1680; C(triple bond)C 2100-2260; aromatic bands about 1500 and 1600; CH₂ bend about 1460, CH₃ about 1380.
B(ii)
O-H 3200-3400 strong broad (monomeric 3590-3650 sharp); C-O alcohols 1050-1260, ethers 1050-1150; primary amine N-H doublet 3200-3500; secondary single; tertiary none.
B(iii)
Aldehyde 1720-1740 (C-H doublet 2720, 2820); ketone 1705-1725; ester 1735-1750; acid 1700-1725 with O-H 2400-3500; anhydride 1740-1770 and 1810-1840; acid halide 1770-1820; amide 1640-1680.
B(iv)
Nitro 1300-1380 and 1500-1570; nitrile 2100-2280; C-Cl 600-800; C-Br and C-I outside the useful range.
C(i)
Frequency = (1/2 π c) √(K/μ); K = force constant (bond strength), μ = reduced mass; lighter atoms and stronger bonds give higher frequency (C-H > C-C > C-N > C-O; C(triple bond)C > C=C > C-C).
C(ii)
Lowers and broadens absorption of interacting bonds (OH, NH); IR distinguishes intermolecular from intramolecular hydrogen bonding.
C(iii)
Ring strain raises frequency; electronegative atoms raise carbonyl frequency (ketone < ester < acid halide); conjugation lowers it by about 20-40 cm⁻¹.
C(iv)
Main use is detecting functional groups and bond types; fingerprint region identifies a compound; IR preferred to UV for identification; peak area is not proportional to concentration.

A(i)
The burner-nebulizer is an inefficient sampling device: only a small fraction of the sample reaches the flame and the atomised sample passes quickly through the light path.
A(ii)
The sample is placed directly in a graphite tube heated in programmed steps to remove solvent and matrix and atomize the rest; all analyte is atomised and retained in the light path for longer.
A(iii)
Drying; ashing (burning off interfering organic species; molecules have broad absorption bands); vaporization of analyte atoms.
A(iv)
Drying 125 °C for 20 s; ashing 1200 °C for 60 s; vaporization 2700 °C for 10 s.
B(i)
Hollow cathode lamp or electrodeless discharge tube (e.g. Zn lamp for Zn), graphite furnace atomizer, monochromator, detector, readout.
B(ii)
1-100 µL injected by syringe; furnace reaches about 2500 °C in stages.
B(iii)
A = ε c l (Beer's law applies to AAS but not to AES, where I = kc).
B(iv)
FAAS measures light absorbed by unexcited atoms and needs a light source; FAES measures light emitted by excited atoms and needs none.
C(i)
Greater sensitivity because more atoms are in the light path, and less sample is needed.
C(ii)
To remove organic matter that would interfere with the elemental analysis.
C(iii)
A different lamp for each element, though some multi-element lamps exist.

A(i) Define the method and its principle.
A(ii) State the factors affecting conductivity of ionic solutions.
A(iii) List the types of conductometric titration.
A(iv) State the practical rules for accurate results.

B(i) Describe the strong acid-strong base curve.
B(ii) Describe the weak acid-strong base curve.
B(iii) Describe the other acid-base curves.
B(iv) Describe displacement and precipitation titrations.
C. Applications and limitations
C(i) State the advantages.
C(ii) State the disadvantages.
C(iii) List the applications.
C(iv) State why conductance measurement alone is of limited value.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A titrant of known concentration is added in measured volumes to the analyte while conductance is measured; one ion is replaced by another of different ionic conductance, so conductivity varies; conductance is plotted against titrant volume and no indicator is needed.
A(ii)
Nature of the electrolyte, concentration, size of the ions and their solvation, and nature and viscosity of the solvent.
A(iii)
Acid-base, replacement/displacement, redox, precipitation, complexometric and non-aqueous titrations.
A(iv)
Smaller conductivity of the replacing ion is better (cations with lithium salts, anions with acetates); small angle between curve branches; correct for dilution by multiplying conductance by (V + V')/V; reagent 10-20 times more concentrated, with a micro burette; salt and reagent should be strong electrolytes.
B(i)
HCl with NaOH: high initial conductance (mobile H⁺), falling to equivalence as H⁺ is replaced by Na⁺ and water forms, then rising sharply because of OH⁻.
B(ii)
Acetic acid with NaOH: low initial conductance, slight fall (replacement and suppression by common acetate ion), then rise as CH₃COONa forms; curved near equivalence (hydrolysis); steeper rise after equivalence (OH⁻).
B(iii)
Strong acid-weak base (H2SO4 with NH4OH): falls then almost horizontal. Weak acid-weak base: like the weak acid curve, then constant. Strong + weak acid mixture: two break points (strong acid neutralised first).
B(iv)
Sodium acetate with HCl (acetate replaced by chloride; limits Ka/original concentration not above 5 × 10⁻³); NH₄Cl with NaOH falls. Precipitation/complex titrations need solubility or dissociation below 5%; KCl with AgNO₃ shows little change (Cl⁻ replaced by NO₃⁻) then a rise; end point at the intersection of two lines.
C(i)
No indicator; suitable for coloured, turbid, very dilute solutions, weak acids/bases and mixtures; graphical end point; suits relatively incomplete reactions (phenol, Ka = 10⁻¹⁰); precision better than 1%.
C(ii)
High salt levels mask conductance changes; limited for redox because high H₃O⁺ masks changes; conductance is non-specific; slightly ionised salts give poor results.
C(iii)
Water pollution in rivers and lakes; alkalinity of fresh water; salinity of sea water; deuterium in water-deuterium mixtures; purity of distilled and deionised water; tracing antibiotics; solubility of sparingly soluble salts (AgCl, BaSO₄).
C(iv)
Conductance measures current-carrying capacity and total ionic strength, so direct measurement helps only if the electrolyte is alone or other ions are known; titrations converting ions to non-ionic form are of more value.

A(i)
Based on the voltage-current relationship when an external potential is applied to a cell; species are oxidised or reduced at the electrode surface at characteristic potentials, which identify the species; the current-voltage curve is a voltammogram.
A(ii)
It must be completely polarised so current is proportional to concentration, have a small surface area (microelectrode), not be readily contaminated and keep reproducible surface behaviour; the continuously dropping mercury electrode gives polarography.
A(iii)
Working electrode: renewable mercury drop, polarised, used as cathode. Counter electrode: normally the anode, a pool of large area, low current density, non-polarised (ideal depolarised electrode). A reference electrode is also shown in the circuit.
A(iv)
Capillary glass tubing 10-15 cm long, diameter 0.05 mm, connected to a mercury reservoir of adjustable height; drop time 1-5 s; drop diameter 0.5 mm.
B(i)
Residual current, limiting current, diffusion current (limiting minus residual) and half-wave potential E½.
B(ii)
E½ is the potential at half the limiting current and is independent of concentration; E = E½ - (0.0591/n) log [i/(id - i)]; a plot of E against log [i/(id - i)] is a straight line of slope -0.0591/n.
B(iii)
id = KC (K = Ilkovic constant); calibration curve method (wave heights of several standards plotted) and standard addition method (record the unknown, add a known amount of the same ion, record again, calculate from the two wave heights).
B(iv)
K = 607 n D^(1/2) m^(2/3) t^(1/6); with temperature, matrix and capillary constant, id is proportional to C.
C(i)
Reproducible data from a fresh, smooth, self-renewing surface; no cleaning; not contaminated by deposited metal; high overpotential for H⁺ reduction; reduction into amalgam is favourable; drop area can be calculated from drop weight.
C(ii)
More positive than about +0.4 V vs SCE mercury dissolves (anodic wave; oxidised near +0.25 V in non-complexing medium), so poor for oxidations; capillary blocks; mercury is toxic; drop size changes with time.
C(iii)
Dissolved oxygen gives two waves (O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O₂; H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H2O), removed by sparging with N₂ or Ar for 5-20 min; polarographic maxima are suppressed with gelatin, detergents, Triton X-100.
C(iv)
Charging (residual) current limits the lowest determinable concentration to about 10⁻⁵ M; migration current is reduced by supporting electrolyte (KNO₃, NaCl, Na3PO4); convection avoided by an unstirred solution.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The definite time required for half of the original atoms of a radioisotope to decay; each radionuclide has a distinct value; most medical radioisotopes lie between minutes and months.
A(ii)
The time required for the body to eliminate one-half of an administered dose by the regular process of elimination; the chemical characteristics of all isotopes of an element are identical, so stable and radioactive isotopes are eliminated alike.
A(iii)
The time required for radioactivity to fall to 50% of the original activity through the combined action of radioactive decay and biological elimination.
A(iv)
t½ = 0.693/λ.
B(i)
Natural secretion and excretion rates of the atoms from the organism also affect how long radioactivity persists, so physical half-life is not the only determinant of clearance.
B(ii)
ln (N/N₀) = -λ t; rate of decay = λ N; N₀ = initial atoms, N = atoms at time t.
B(iii)
In calculation of in vivo dosimetry and in blood volume and tissue isotope concentration studies.
B(iv)
Radioactive and normal atoms of the same element behave chemically alike; the fate of a drug is followed by giving a small amount in radioactive form and observing its radiations.
C(i)
Short half-life radioisotopes must be prepared at or near the point of use by pharmacy staff.
C(ii)
The activity decayed between purchase and use, and the decay period for waste disposal.
C(iii)
Tc-99m half-life about 6 hours (imaging); Mo-99 parent 66.2 hours; I-131 about 8 days (thyroid treatment).
C(iv)
Short-lived isotopes suit imaging but cannot be transported far; radiation dose in the body depends on both decay and elimination.

A(i)
Transmitted intensity falls exponentially with concentration and path length: A = log (I₀/I) = kcl = log (1/T) = 2 - log (%T).
A(ii)
A = kcl = ε C l; k is A(1%,1cm) with c in %w/v, ε is molar absorptivity with C in mol/dm³, l usually 1 cm; k and ε are linked through molecular weight M. Measurement is at λ max for sensitivity.
A(iii)
Determine λ max, prepare the sample for its matrix, generate a calibration curve (minimum 5 concentrations) from pure reference compound, measure sample absorbance and read the concentration from the curve.
A(iv)

B(i)

B(iii)
At λ 1: A total = AA = KA(λ₁) CA; at λ 2: A total = KA(λ₂) CA + KB(λ₂) CB; solve.
B(iv)
A(λ₁) = kx(λ₁) Cx + ky(λ₁) Cy and A(λ₂) = kx(λ₂) Cx + ky(λ₂) Cy solved simultaneously (e.g. pethidine hydrochloride injection stabilised with chlorocresol).
C(i)
UV is more useful quantitatively because most drugs are aromatic (UV active); IR is more popular for identification; radically different molecules with similar chromophores give similar broad spectra.
C(ii)
Dilute, non-particulate, chemically stable (not in equilibrium), monochromatic. Deviations: instrumental (exit slit, stray light), chemical (pH change from CO₂, variable absorptivity), real (above 10⁻² M).
C(iii)
Broad zero-order spectra (e.g. benzocaine adulterated with cocaine), weak absorption of UV-inactive compounds, non-specific absorption/matrix interference; remedies: difference spectrophotometry, derivative spectroscopy (2nd order), chemical derivatisation.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Radioactivity is the spontaneous transformation of one nucleus into another nuclide, accompanied by emission of charged particles or electromagnetic radiation. A radionuclide is not in a stable energy state but gains stability by emitting radiation.
A(ii)
The decay constant (λ) is the probability of decay in unit time (fraction disintegrating per unit time). The moment a single atom decays is unpredictable, but the whole population obeys the exponential law; decay is independent of temperature, pressure, concentration or catalyst.
A(iii)
dN/dt = rate of decay (activity) in dps or dpm; rate of decay = λ N. N₀ = atoms originally present at t = 0; N (Nt) = atoms remaining at time t.
A(iv)
Time for half the radioactive nuclei to decay or for activity to fall to half; distinct for each radionuclide. Examples stated: I-131 about 8 days, P-32 14.3 days, Sr-90 28.8 years, Mo-99 66.2 hours.
B(i)
t½ = ln 2 / λ = 0.693/λ.
B(ii)
ln (N/N₀) = -λ t; log N = log N₀ - 0.693 t / (2.303 t½), so a graph of log N against time is used.
B(iii)
Knowing t½ is needed to determine the activity decayed between purchase and use and the decay period for waste disposal. Practice problems (1000 Bq falling to 600 Bq in 2 h.
B(iv)
Becquerel (Bq) = 1 dps (SI); curie (Ci) = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ dps (2.2 × 10¹² dpm) = 37 GBq.
C(i)
Most medical radioisotopes have half-lives of minutes to months; those with short half-lives must be prepared at or near the point of use because rapid decay prevents transport over long distances.
C(ii)
The activity in the container, the time and date at which it will have the stated activity, and the expiry date and time.
C(iii)
Shelf-life is typically 2 weeks after delivery; the Mo-99 parent has then undergone 5 half-lives and its yield is about one thirtieth of the initial activity; generators are supplied weekly.
C(iv)
Short half-life limits transport and storage and activity falls with time, so activity must be calculated for the time of use; the half-life must suit the application.

A(i)
Test refractometry for detecting tampering with opioid solutions; a hand-held refractometer (about $300, about 15 s per assay) compares with distilled water, reading in degrees.
A(ii)
Alfentanil 500 µg/mL, fentanyl 50, sufentanil 50, morphine 10 mg/mL in saline, Ringer's lactate, dextrose in saline or water; dilutions 1:2, 1:4, 1:8; six samples each.
A(iii)
Undiluted fentanyl, sufentanil and distilled water read zero; morphine and alfentanil read similarly, but differ (P < 0.05); dilutions of 1:2 or 1:4 in saline or Ringer's lactate could go undetected.
A(iv)

B(i)
Quality control of rodent anaesthetic mixtures (ketamine, xylazine, acepromazine, buprenorphine) in water.
B(ii)
Temperature-compensated refractometer, zero with water, 100% with stock, dilutions 75, 50, 25%, plot refraction against percentage stock.
B(iii)
Linear graphs; refraction of mixtures is additive; final concentration = drug weight/final volume (e.g. 225 mg in 6.0 mL).
B(iv)
Assesses single drug dilutions and verifies mixtures when components are known and in range.
C(i)
Refraction varies directly with solute concentration; speed of light varies with density; temperature and wavelength are controlled.
C(ii)
Urine specific gravity, serum protein, detection of diversion of midazolam, morphine sulfate, meperidine.
C(iii)
Refraction is the difference between the index of water and the solution.
C(iv)
Fails when diluents have similar values; works only with known components.

questions.question:
Describe the criteria for admission to and discharge from intensive care under the following headings:
(a) definition of critical care and guiding principles for admission
(b) the prioritisation (priority) model
(c) the diagnosis and objective parameter models and other factors considered
(d) discharge criteria.
(e) Explain why admission criteria are needed.
(f) Distinguish between admission criteria and discharge criteria.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Critical care is a service for patients with potentially recoverable conditions who can benefit from more detailed observation and invasive treatment than wards can safely provide; admission is appropriate if the condition is potentially reversible, the patient can reasonably be expected to survive, and the outcome is in reasonable doubt.
• Guiding steps: review co-morbidities and response to treatment, formulate a prognosis, discuss risks and burdens with patient and carers, and agree treatment ceilings in advance. Admission may be precluded by the patient's condition, co-morbidities, or a capacitated patient's refusal.

(b)
• Priority 1: unstable, needing intensive treatment and monitoring (ventilator support, vasoactive infusions), no therapy limits. Priority 2: intensive monitoring, may need immediate intervention. Priority 3: unstable with reduced likelihood of recovery, limits may be set.
• Priority 4: generally not appropriate - category A too well to benefit (e.g. stable diabetic ketoacidosis), category B too sick to benefit (e.g. irreversible brain damage, brain-dead non-donors); admission only individually at the ICU Director's discretion.

(c)
• Diagnosis model lists conditions by system (cardiac, pulmonary, neurologic, drug overdose, gastrointestinal, endocrine, renal, haematology, obstetric, multi-system, surgical); objective parameters include pulse under 40 or over 150, MAP under 60, respiratory rate over 35, PaO2 under 50, pH under 7.1 or over 7.7.
• Other factors: diagnosis and prognosis, severity of illness and coexisting disease, age, availability of treatment, response to treatment, recent cardiopulmonary arrest, anticipated quality of life and the patient's wishes.

(d)
Discharge when haemodynamics are stable, respiratory status is stable (extubated, stable ABGs, patent airway), oxygen requirement is not more than 60%, inotropes/vasopressors/vasodilators are no longer needed, dysrhythmias are controlled, and neurologic status is stable with seizures controlled.

(e)
• Critical care is a limited, scarce and costly resource that must target those most likely to benefit; shortages can reduce access, force transfers and terminate urgent and elective procedures.
• Decisions should be objective, ethical and transparent, and early referral improves recovery, reduces organ dysfunction and may reduce length of stay and costs.

(f)
• Admission criteria identify who should enter ICU (reversible condition, benefit from intensive treatment).
• Discharge criteria apply once physiology has stabilised and ICU care is no longer necessary, and are based on admission criteria, the admitting criteria of the next lower level of care and the availability of resources.
• Where deterioration is irreversible and active interventions no longer beneficial, therapy is withdrawn in the ICU; if a bed is needed the patient goes to the ward.

(a)
Defibrillation is indicated when a shockable rhythm is present - ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (in children 2-4 J/kg is recommended); signs of both are identical and they are differentiated only by ECG.

(b)
• An AED is a 'smart' defibrillator: it interprets the ECG rhythm, decides whether a shock is required, delivers the shock and guides the operator with voice and message prompts.
• Steps: switch on (it switches on automatically when the lid is opened); attach pads to the casualty's bare chest; analyse rhythm - do not touch the victim; if shock indicated, stand clear; deliver the shock; immediately resume CPR 30:2.
• If no AED is available, give CPR every moment, always if an AED is not available within 5 minutes; if the victim starts breathing normally, place in the recovery position.

(c)
The rescuer giving the shock is responsible for their own safety and for the safety of other people around the victim.

(d)
Safety measures: do not touch the victim during analysis and stand clear during the shock.

(e)
• Survival falls with delay to defibrillation: 90% at 1 minute, 50% at 5 minutes, 30% at 7 minutes and 2-5% at 10-12 minutes.
• Early resuscitation and prompt defibrillation within 1-2 minutes can result in over 60% survival; ventricular fibrillation has a better outlook than asystole if CPR is immediate.
• CPR is resumed at once after the shock because compressions at best provide only 30% of normal perfusion to brain and heart and cerebral damage is irreversible after 3-5 minutes.
• AEDs are easier than CPR and extend defibrillation beyond healthcare professionals to trained citizens.
• An implantable cardioverter defibrillator similarly detects arrhythmia or asystole and delivers a shock as secondary prevention after ventricular fibrillation/tachycardia arrest.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Institutional constraints or policies that stop nurses acting on their ethical beliefs, such as being compelled to provide treatments they believe are futile or not in the patient's best interest (e.g. continuing aggressive treatment at the family's request).
• Contributing factors: resource limitations, increased patient mortality, rapid ethically charged decisions and staffing shortages.

(b)
The nurse knows the ethically appropriate action but is constrained from taking it, leading to psychological disequilibrium and emotional suffering.

(c)
Frustration, guilt and professional dissatisfaction; anxiety, burnout, uncertainty and self-doubt.

(d)
• Job dissatisfaction, decreased quality of patient care, increased turnover intentions, strained team relationships and communication breakdown that compromise patient safety.
• Also legal and ethical uncertainty with risk of liability, personal distress affecting mental health, delays in treatment and damage to professional reputation.

(e)
The ethics committee monitors unit practices and identifies recurring ethical challenges (preventive ethics).

(f)
• Create a supportive work environment where nurses discuss ethical concerns and seek guidance; policies for ethical consultations and resources for coping.
• Ethics committees provide case consultation, conflict resolution and support, reduce moral distress and clarify complex situations.
• Institutions should offer regular ethics training, peer support, clear protocols and open dialogue; train emotional resilience.
• Promote interdisciplinary collaboration (ethics rounds, team-building workshops, ethics consultation services) and simulation-based learning and mentorship.
• Nurses should advocate for patient-centred care, improve communication skills and reflect on their practice.
