questions.answerText:
(a)
Emergency nursing care is the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of perceived, actual or potential, sudden or urgent, physical or psychosocial problems that are primarily episodic or acute.

(b)
• A separate specialty whose common goal is to restore physiological or psychological stability to the severely ill patient; it uses the nursing process and needs knowledge and skill beyond the nurse generalist.
• Its core knowledge applies to medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and psychiatry; emergencies occur in the community, on a nursing unit or in the ED, so nurses in any area must assess, prioritise and intervene quickly.

(c)
Emergency nursing encompasses independent, dependent and interdependent interventions.

(d)
• Disaster: a serious disruption of the functioning of a community or society causing widespread human, material, economic or environmental losses that exceed its ability to cope with its own resources.
• Disaster epidemiology is the use of epidemiology (study of distribution and determinants of health events in populations) to assess short- and long-term adverse health effects of disasters and predict consequences of future ones.
• Roles/uses: identify priority health problems, causes and risk factors; rapid needs assessment; demographic studies; surveillance; outbreak investigation; programme monitoring and evaluation; surveys.

(e)
• Emergency nurses are often responsible for life-and-death decisions, placing them at high legal risk, so priorities must be set quickly on sound knowledge and judgment.
• They must make triage decisions to expedite care and are at high risk of injury or illness from exposure to infections such as hepatitis, AIDS or other communicable diseases.

(f)
• Independent interventions are unique to nursing: management of the environment, teaching, counselling and initiating referrals.
• Dependent interventions are prescribed by appropriate health care personnel.
• Interdependent interventions (for comparison) are determined by multidisciplinary collaboration.

A 68-year-old widowed woman with advanced COPD and intermittent respiratory failure has been admitted after an exacerbation with acute respiratory distress and hypoxaemia. Despite non-invasive ventilation and medications she is getting worse. Her family is considering invasive mechanical ventilation if she deteriorates further, while she has verbally expressed a wish to avoid such measures and prefers comfort care.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) Identify the ethical problem and the principles involved.
(c) Describe the immediate nursing interventions.
(d) Give the rationale and state how the care is evaluated.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clinical status: worsening respiratory function, acute respiratory distress and hypoxaemia despite non-invasive ventilation and medications; 10-year history of COPD with smoking, hypertension and heart disease and frequent hospitalisations.
• Patient's expressed wishes (verbal preference for comfort care), the family's differing wishes, and her values (Christian faith, retired teacher, widow).

(b)
• Ethical dilemmas: autonomy versus beneficence, informed consent, conflicting family wishes, and palliative care versus aggressive treatment.
• Principles involved: respect for autonomy, beneficence and non-maleficence, and justice.

(c)
• Advocacy for her wishes, education and emotional support for patient and family, and ethics consultation.
• Provide adequate information for informed consent and use a four-quadrant analysis: medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life and contextual features (legal, social, cultural).
• Hold a family meeting with the interdisciplinary team (physician, nurse, social worker, chaplain), explain the prognosis and treatment limitations and address the family's emotional concerns.

(d)
• Rationale: the decision should be patient-centred, focused on her values and her right to make informed choices about her care, with the family's complex emotions handled with empathy and professionalism.
• Evaluation: her wishes are respected and the family reach consensus; where consensus leads to comfort care, palliative care with pain management and emotional support follows.

questions.question:
Describe monitoring of vital signs in the intensive care unit:
(a) what vital signs are and the aims of monitoring
(b) modes of monitoring
(c) parameters monitored with their normal values.
(d) Explain how the findings guide nursing decisions.
(e) Explain why monitoring findings may be misinterpreted or fail, and how this is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Vital signs indicate life: pulse/heart rate, respiration, blood pressure, temperature, pupillary constriction to light and level of consciousness; end-tidal CO2, blood gases, electrolytes and pain are also monitored.
• Aim: there are limits compatible with life, so regular monitoring identifies deviations so corrective measures are instituted promptly.

(b)
Non-invasive: pulse/heart rate, blood pressure, pupillary reaction, temperature, respiration. Invasive: arterial blood pressure, central venous pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, cardiac output, left atrial pressure.

(c)
• Pulse 60-90/min (13 years and above); blood pressure 94-140/62-88 mmHg (over 13 years); temperature 36.2-37.2 degrees C; end-tidal CO2 35-45; oxygen saturation 90-100%; hourly urine output 0.5-1 ml/kg/hr.
• ABG: pH 7.33-7.45, PCO2 35-45 mmHg, PO2 75-100 mmHg, HCO3 22-28, BE +/-2; Glasgow Coma Scale 3-15; sodium 135-145 and potassium 3.5-4.5 meq/l, checked 4-hourly or more often.

(d)
• Invasive blood pressure monitoring is continuous and the most reliable; a high core with low peripheral temperature may indicate low cardiac output or infection.
• Equal reactive pupils mean the upper brainstem and third cranial nerve are intact, while unilateral dilatation and non-reactivity with depressed consciousness suggests impaired brainstem function.
• Intubated patients need more vigilance for CO2 retention, secretions in the tube and tube dislodgement; abnormal electrolyte readings are promptly corrected.
• Baseline ABG 5-10 minutes after ICU admission; repeat 30 minutes after ventilator changes, 45 minutes to 1 hour after extubation and 30 minutes after suctioning.

(e)
• Related cautions: pupil dilatation is not a reliable sign of arrest, and the 5Ps of compartment syndrome are not reliable in patients with decreased consciousness.
• Prevention: combine several parameters and invasive/continuous monitoring rather than relying on a single sign.

(a)
• Patients unable to maintain volitional intake: comatose patients, major surgery, trauma, burns, sepsis, gastrointestinal failure, severe anorexia nervosa, kidney or liver failure; also little or no intake for 5 days with none expected for 5 more.
• TPN is used when the GI tract is not functional, cannot be accessed, or feeding is inadequate.

(b)
Parenteral nutrition is to be adopted only when absolutely necessary.

(c)
• Screen with MUST (BMI, weight loss, acute disease score); feed by the safest, simplest, most effective route; start about 25 kcal/kg/day (rising to 30), protein 1.25 g/kg/day, fluid 30 ml/kg/24 hours plus 100-200 ml per degree of temperature.
• TPN: doctor decides, dietitian decides the regime, pharmacy makes the bag aseptically; start low and build up; usually via central line, with strict asepsis when handling lines.

(d)
Nurses identify history and weight, optimise and monitor intake; NG feeding with head of bed at 30 degrees, not started at night; monitor U&Es, phosphate, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs, fluid balance, haematology, weight.

(e)
• Risk of aspiration and tube displacement; high aspirates; constipation; diarrhoea; ileus; intolerance (?sepsis); line sepsis.
• Manage with prokinetics, nasojejunal feeding or drugs; for ileus avoid opioids, optimise fluid balance and electrolytes, give a trickle of feed; avoid overfeeding.
• Overfeeding causes lactic acidosis, hyperglycaemia, increased infections, liver impairment and persistent pyrexia.

(f)
• Enteral feeding preserves intestinal mucosal structure and function, is more physiological and reduces infectious complications; use the gut if you can, as bowel function may recover within 12 hours.
• Jejunal feeding may reduce aspiration and often increases the dose of enteral nutrition delivered; TPN is started on day 3-7 only if optimised enteral feeding fails.
• Specialised sterile-packed feeds replaced mixed feeds given via NG tube because of infection risk.

Describe adult basic life support (CPR) under the following headings:
(a) indications
(b) contraindications (when CPR is not indicated)
(c) preparation and rescuer safety
(d) steps, including compression and rescue breath technique
(e) rescuer responsibilities and when to stop.
(f) State the complications of CPR and how each is prevented.
(g) Explain the rationale for key steps (compression technique, 30:2 ratio, airway opening, barrier devices).
questions.answerText:
(a)
Unexpected cardiac arrest, especially in otherwise healthy people: malignant arrhythmia, acute myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, intoxication, electrocution, drowning, acute suffocation, severe trauma, stroke; age is not a restriction.

(b)
Not indicated: definitive biological death; arrest witnessed 15 or more minutes earlier; terminal incurable disease; trauma without chance of survival; a living will (where accepted) or written DNR.

(c)
Rescuer safety is the first priority (traffic, falling masonry, electrocution, toxic fumes, infection); wear gloves and use barrier devices (face shield, pocket mask with one-way valve); place victim supine on a firm flat surface.

(d)
• Shake shoulders and ask 'Are you all right?'; if unresponsive shout for help, open the airway (head tilt-chin lift; jaw thrust if cervical spine injury suspected), look/listen/feel for normal breathing (gasps are agonal), call 112.
• 30 compressions: heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, other hand on top, fingers interlocked, rate 100/min, depth 4-5 cm, equal compression and relaxation; change operator every 2 minutes when possible.
• 2 rescue breaths: pinch nose, seal lips, blow about 1 second until the chest rises (6-7 ml/kg, about 500 ml), allow chest to fall; continue 30:2.

(e)
Stop if the victim breathes normally (recovery position), medical help takes over, the rescuer is exhausted, or after 20 minutes without circulation (earlier if biological death signs appear); use compression-only CPR if unable or unwilling to give breaths.

(f)
• Gastric distension (often in children): avoid overinflating the lungs and use a volume that makes the chest rise.
• Rib fractures: correct hand position, keep hands on the chest wall, avoid 'dancing on the chest'; aspiration of gastric contents: prevent gastric distension and use the recovery position in unconscious victims.

(g)
• Thoracic pump theory: compressions propel blood out of the thorax by raising intrathoracic pressure, so compression and relaxation are equal, pressure is fully released and hands stay in contact; compressions give at best 30% of normal brain and heart perfusion.
• Expired air contains 16-18% oxygen, enough to keep haemoglobin over 80% saturated; 30:2 is one uniform ratio in adults; head tilt-chin lift opens the airway in the unconscious patient.
• Barrier devices prevent blood-borne and airborne pathogen transmission (no documented case of transmission, but use whenever possible); all human blood and body fluids are regarded as infectious.

questions.question:
Describe sudden cardiac arrest under the following headings:
(a) causes
(b) pathophysiology
(c) clinical features
(d) complications and outcome.
(e) State the diagnostic and monitoring measures.
(f) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cardiac: coronary artery disease (leading cause), myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, hypertensive heart disease/left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and arrhythmic syndromes (long QT, Wolff-Parkinson-White, Brugada).
• Non-cardiac (15-25%): trauma, bleeding (GI bleeding, aortic rupture, intracranial haemorrhage), overdose, drowning, pulmonary embolism, poisoning; also electrolyte imbalance, respiratory failure, cocaine/amphetamine use.

(b)
The heart abruptly beats abnormally or irregularly; without organised electrical activity the ventricles do not contract consistently, so the heart cannot generate adequate cardiac output.

(c)
About 50% have no warning; otherwise non-specific chest pain, fatigue, blackouts, dizziness, shortness of breath, weakness, vomiting. At arrest: no palpable pulse, rapid loss of consciousness and breathing (loss of cerebral perfusion), blue-tinged skin, dilated pupils, convulsions.

(d)
Survival with treatment is about 8% and many survivors have significant disability; brain cells are irreversibly damaged after 3-5 minutes without perfusion.

(e)
• Recognition: unresponsive, absent/abnormal breathing, no carotid pulse (check no more than 10 seconds); ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia have identical signs and are differentiated only by ECG.
• After return of circulation: intensive monitoring of vital signs, neurological status and response to treatment, ECG and chest x-ray, BUN, creatinine and electrolytes, and identification of the underlying cause.

(f)
• Immediate: call for help, CPR at once, defibrillate shockable rhythms, advanced life support (airway, medications such as epinephrine every five minutes); targeted temperature management (24 hours, 32-36 degrees C) if circulation returns without consciousness.
• Nursing diagnoses: Decreased cardiac output/risk for decreased cardiac output, Ineffective breathing pattern, Activity intolerance/risk for activity intolerance.
• Administer prescribed medications, oxygen and IV solutions; monitor closely; encourage rest, semirecumbent position; assist with physical care.
• Give emotional support to patient and family; communicate clearly and work as a team with physicians and other specialists.
• Educate patient and family on cause, risk factors and prevention (healthy diet, exercise, smoking cessation, blood pressure and cholesterol control; ICD for survivors of VF/VT arrest) and plan discharge.

(a)
• Earthquakes and other disasters, terrorist attacks and war, building collapse, industrial incidents such as mining, motor vehicle crashes, falls, objects dropped on the foot, hands shut in doors, machinery and trench collapse.
• Non-trauma: immobility against a firm surface for more than one hour (e.g. surgery, stroke, intoxication, drug overdose, elderly with hip fracture), own body compressing tissue, MAST pants, carbon monoxide poisoning.

(b)
• Compression reduces blood flow and oxygen, cells turn to anaerobic metabolism and leak lactic acid, potassium, myoglobin and purines; once the force is released, toxic substances enter the systemic circulation.
• Compartment syndrome: raised pressure in a confined muscle space causing ischaemia and necrosis. Rhabdomyolysis: muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin, which can cause kidney failure. Crush syndrome: compartment syndrome plus rhabdomyolysis plus SIRS.

(c)
Local: pain, swelling, discoloration, decreased sensation. Systemic: tachycardia, hypotension, fever, oliguria, altered mental status; myoglobinuria (red or brown urine); the 5Ps of compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis, pulselessness).

(d)
Acute kidney failure, compartment syndrome, infection, amputation, long-term disability and PTSD.

(e)
• Primary assessment of airway, breathing, circulation and neurological status; secondary assessment focused on the affected area (pain, swelling, sensation, compartment signs).
• Laboratory tests: creatine kinase, myoglobin, electrolytes and renal function tests; the 5Ps are not reliable in unconscious patients.

(f)
• Early fluid resuscitation to maintain blood pressure and prevent kidney failure; pain management for comfort and cooperation.
• Monitor closely for compartment syndrome and prepare for fasciotomy if necessary.
• Rhabdomyolysis management: alkalinisation of urine, diuresis and electrolyte monitoring; nutritional support to prevent muscle wasting and promote healing.
• Psychological support for anxiety, fear and PTSD; patient education, discharge planning and rehabilitation.
questions.question:
Describe severe crush injury under the following headings:
(a) causes
(b) pathophysiology (including compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis and crush syndrome)
(c) clinical features
(d) complications.
(e) State the diagnostic and monitoring measures.
(f) Outline the nursing management.

Describe infection control measures in the ICU under the following headings:
(a) indications
(b) contraindications (personnel restrictions)
(c) preparation (policies, environment, equipment)
(d) steps/routine measures and nursing responsibilities.
(e) State the complications of failure and how they are prevented or managed.
(f) Explain the rationale for key steps.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Needed because about one in four ICU patients acquires nosocomial organisms if the stay exceeds 3 days; measures cover three areas - personnel, environment and equipment.

(b)
Any staff member with a respiratory infection must be exempted from patient care for the period; no one is exempted from infection control rules.

(c)
Hand washing policies, a dress code and an orientation/education programme; a unit with distinct common and clean/sterile areas, clean entry, changing rooms before patient areas, about 210 cm between beds, good ventilation without open windows, an isolation room with hand washing facilities.

(d)
• Wash hands before each patient contact with alcohol-based rub; remove rings and cracked or chipped nail polish; scrub attire not worn outside and changed daily; visitors in gown and cap with minimal visitation.
• Equipment: sterilise properly, keep sterile items covered until use, wash, disinfect and sterilise reusables; change Cheatle forceps and jars daily.
• IV lines and sets every three days; urethral catheters and Ryle's tubes every 5-7 days; suction and oxygen tubing on alternate days; ventilator tubing and transducer dome every fifth day; suction bowls daily; oral toileting three times daily; laminar flow for injections where available.
• Keep aseptic technique in procedures, daily cleaning and dusting, periodic general washing down and prompt removal of waste; use personal protective equipment, disposable items and surveillance.

(e)
• Nosocomial infections such as MRSA blood stream/catheter-related infection and C. difficile diarrhoea; microorganism invasion can destroy well performed surgery or truncate recovery.
• Prevention: surveillance with accurate documentation and reporting, standard infection control principles (environmental hygiene, hand washing, PPE, safe sharps disposal), aseptic dressing and venepuncture; management of established infection: stop antibiotics for C. difficile.

(f)
• Hands and clothes of staff, tracheal tubes, urinary bags and catheters, linens and visitors' apparel are reservoirs, so hand hygiene, barrier measures and minimal visitation reduce spread.
• Reusable equipment and invasive lines are changed on schedule to prevent microbial build-up.
• Everyone participates in controlling infection in the ICU.

questions.question:
An adult cardiac arrest survivor has regained spontaneous circulation but has not regained consciousness.
(a) Identify the condition and the therapy that is indicated.
(b) Name the therapy, its parameters and methods.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after the therapy.
(d) State the documentation and communication/escalation required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) without return of consciousness after cardiac arrest; cooling adults in this situation improves outcomes.

(b)
• Targeted temperature management (previously therapeutic hypothermia): typically a 24-hour period with a target temperature of 32-36 degrees C (90-97 degrees F).
• Methods: ice packs or cold-water circulating pads applied directly to the body, or infusion of cold saline; followed by gradual rewarming over the next 12 to 24 hours.
• It is associated with improved survival and better neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

(c)
• Before: once circulation is restored the patient needs intensive monitoring and support in hospital; identification and treatment of the underlying cause.
• During: continuously assess vital signs, neurological status and response to treatment; give medications as prescribed; provide emotional support to patient and family.
• After: monitor through gradual rewarming; care may involve medications, cardiac procedures and ongoing rehabilitation; educate patient and family on cause of arrest, risk factors and prevention.

(d)
Clear, concise communication is essential for teamwork; nurses communicate with other providers, the patient and the family, and collaborate with physicians, therapists and other specialists.

questions.question:
Describe nosocomial infection in the ICU under the following headings:
(a) definition and key terms (prevalence, virulence, susceptibility)
(b) causative organisms and reservoirs
(c) classification.
(d) Explain why ICU patients are vulnerable to nosocomial infection.
(e) Distinguish between MRSA and Clostridium difficile infection.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection has existed for a long time with little effort to curtail it. Prevalence: number of people with a defined disease per defined population at a point in time.
• Virulence: ability of a microorganism to produce toxins or disease. Susceptibility: ability of an individual to be infected on contact with an affected person, which reflects individual defences.

(b)
• Organisms: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Aerobacter. Reservoirs: patient wounds, hands and clothes of staff, tracheal tubes, urinary bags and catheters.
• More reservoirs: bladder irrigation solutions, sinks and sink-traps, patient linens, and visitors' and relatives' apparel.

(c)
Exogenous sources and endogenous sources; Jones and Fix classify MRSA and Clostridium difficile.

(d)
• Approximately one in four ICU patients acquires nosocomial organisms if the stay is more than 3 days, with increasing risk as the stay is prolonged.
• Infection is a major problem in ICUs; in Nigeria there is no proper documentation, but this does not mean it is absent. Not all patients are affected, which reflects individual susceptibility.

(e)
• MRSA: a health care-associated blood stream and catheter-related infection; spread by close contact with an infected person.
• MRSA is resistant to methicillin, amoxicillin, penicillin and other antibiotics.
• Clostridium difficile: a common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.
• It is spread through faeces or any surface, device or material contaminated with faeces.
• The best way of treating C. difficile is to stop the antibiotics.

questions.question:
A child is being resuscitated by a rescuer who is overinflating the lungs with rescue breaths and lifting the hands off the chest wall between compressions.
(a) Identify the risk factors for CPR complications.
(b) State the potential complications.
(c) State the monitoring parameters and the preventive nursing measures, and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Overinflation of the lungs (gastric distension is often seen in children), incorrect hand position, removing the hands from the chest wall ('dancing on the chest') and an unconscious victim (risk of aspiration).

(b)
Gastric distension, rib fractures, and aspiration of gastric content or other fluids.

(c)
• Monitor chest rise with each breath and give an appropriate volume (6-7 ml/kg) over 1-1.5 seconds, making the chest visibly rise.
• Monitor hand position and compression technique: in children the lower third of the sternum (one finger above the xiphoid process), depth one third of the chest, 100 compressions per minute.
• Prevention: avoid overinflating the lungs; correct hand position; keep hands on the chest wall; place unconscious breathing victims in the recovery position.
• Priority intervention: prevent gastric distension by giving only a volume that makes the chest rise.
• Justification: preventing gastric distension is the measure to prevent aspiration of gastric contents, which also requires the recovery position in unconscious victims.

(a)
• Each value falls in the objective admission parameters for intensive care: pulse over 150 or under 40, MAP under 60, respiratory rate over 35, PaO2 under 50, pH under 7.1 or over 7.7, potassium under 2.0 or over 7.0; anuria and cyanosis are acute-onset physical findings.
• Together they indicate a critically ill, unstable patient.

(b)
Cardiovascular (rate and perfusion pressure), respiratory (oxygenation, breathing rate, cyanosis), acid-base/metabolic (pH), electrolyte (potassium) and renal (anuria) function.

(c)
• Cardiac: acute myocardial infarction with complications, cardiogenic shock, complex arrhythmias; pulmonary: acute respiratory failure, massive pulmonary embolism with instability, upper airway obstruction.
• Renal/electrolyte: hyperkalaemia with dysrhythmias or muscle weakness, acute rhabdomyolysis with renal insufficiency, renal replacement therapy in an unstable patient; multi-system: severe sepsis/septic shock, multi-organ dysfunction syndrome, poly-trauma.

(d)
• Priority: recognise that the patient meets criteria and refer early - early referral improves chances of recovery, reduces organ dysfunction and may reduce length of stay; any patient needing 50% or more inspired oxygen should at least be managed in a high dependency unit.
• Start continuous monitoring: heart rate, blood pressure, end-tidal CO2, oxygen saturation, arterial blood gases, electrolytes (4-hourly or more often) and hourly urine output.
• Promptly correct abnormal electrolyte readings and support airway, breathing and circulation.
• Decisions rest on the patient's condition being potentially reversible; admission should follow objective, ethical and transparent processes.
questions.question:
A patient referred for ICU admission has newly discovered findings: pulse above 150 beats/min, mean arterial pressure below 60 mmHg, respiratory rate above 35 breaths/min, PaO2 below 50 mmHg, pH below 7.1, serum potassium above 7.0 mEq/L, anuria and cyanosis.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the body systems or functions affected.
(c) State the possible causes/differentials.
(d) State the nursing priorities and the reasoning for the actions taken.

Describe ethics in critical care nursing under the following headings:
(a) definition of ethics
(b) the core principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, fidelity)
(c) veracity, accountability, privacy and confidentiality.
(d) Explain why ethical consideration is essential in critical care.
(e) Distinguish between autonomy and paternalism.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ethics is the branch of philosophy dealing with the principles of right and wrong behaviour; the rules or code of conduct used to decide whether an action is acceptable; in nursing, the moral principles and values guiding practice.

(b)
• Autonomy: the right to make informed, uncoerced decisions, supported by informed consent (disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, competence). Beneficence: actively promoting well-being and preventing or removing harm.
• Non-maleficence: do no harm, balancing risks and benefits and minimising harm (e.g. double checking doses, speaking up against unsafe practice). Justice: fairness and equity in care and resource allocation, regardless of background.
• Fidelity: loyalty, trustworthiness, keeping promises, confidentiality and patient advocacy.

(c)
• Veracity: the obligation of truth-telling, giving honest information on diagnosis, prognosis and options, balanced with compassion. Accountability: taking responsibility for actions and outcomes and acknowledging errors.
• Privacy: the right to control access to personal information; confidentiality: the duty to protect information from unauthorised disclosure without consent or legal justification.

(d)
• The high-stakes nature of life-saving interventions demands respect for patient autonomy and dignity.
• Respecting informed decisions fosters trust and upholds dignity even in life-threatening conditions; this includes advocating the choice to decline interventions.
• Common issues: end-of-life care, informed consent, futile treatments, confidentiality, resource allocation and moral distress.

(e)
• Autonomy honours a person's right to decide for themselves, even when choices differ from professional recommendations.
• Paternalism limits a person's autonomy for their perceived best interest; it is common when providers override patient preferences and is justified as acting in the patient's best interest.
• Balancing autonomy and beneficence is a recognised challenge in implementation.

questions.question:
An ICU patient's gastrointestinal tract is not functioning adequately, enteral feeding has been optimised without success, and total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central line is prescribed.
(a) Identify the condition and the indication for the therapy.
(b) Name the therapy and the access routes.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after the therapy.
(d) State the safety checks and complications to watch for.
(e) State the documentation and communication/escalation required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications for TPN: the GI tract is not functional, cannot be accessed, or GI feeding is inadequate; it is adopted only when absolutely necessary, optimising enteral feeding first.
• If the patient is not absorbing, start TPN on day 3-7 depending on nutritional state.

(b)
Total parenteral nutrition; usually a central line in ICU (keep a clean port, 5-lumen); short term - PIC or PICC (needs a different formula); long term - tunnelled subclavian (Hickman) catheter or subcutaneous port.

(c)
• Before: the doctor decides the patient needs it; the dietitian sees the patient and decides the regime; the bag is ordered from pharmacy and made up aseptically to requirements; screen nutrition status and weigh the patient.
• During: start low and build up; observe strict asepsis when handling the lines.
• After: monitor bloods - U&Es, phosphate, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs, fluid balance, haematology, weight, and trace elements if long term.

(d)
• Complications: line sepsis; overfeeding with lactic acidosis, hyperglycaemia, increased infections, liver impairment (alkaline phosphatase, ALT, GGT, acalculous cholecystitis) and persistent pyrexia.
• Avoid overfeeding.

(e)
Communication: doctors and nurses identify history; nurses weigh; doctors, dietitians and nurses optimise intake and monitor - nursing collaboration with the nutrition team.

(a)
• Moral distress: nurses are unable to act according to their ethical beliefs because of institutional constraints or policies.
• Features: frustration, guilt and professional dissatisfaction; also anxiety, burnout, uncertainty and self-doubt.

(b)
• Predisposing factors: being compelled to give treatments believed futile or not in the patient's best interest (e.g. at the family's request), institutional constraints, resource limitations, increased patient mortality and rapid ethically charged decisions.
• Mechanism: the nurse knows the ethically appropriate action but is constrained from taking it, leading to psychological disequilibrium and emotional suffering.

(c)
• Create a supportive work environment where nurses can discuss ethical concerns and seek guidance; provide policies for ethical consultation and resources for coping.
• Ethics committees offer case consultation, conflict resolution and support for providers, reducing moral distress and giving clarity; preventive ethics includes support systems for staff moral distress.
• Institutions should provide regular ethics training, peer support, clear protocols and open dialogue; nurses should stay informed on guidelines, advocate for patient-centred care and collaborate with teams.
• Interdisciplinary collaboration through ethics rounds and ethics consultation services supports shared responsibility for ethical decisions.
questions.question:
A critical care nurse is required to continue aggressive treatment for a terminally ill patient at the family's request, although she believes palliative care would be more appropriate; she feels frustrated and guilty.
(a) Identify the problem indicated.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the underlying mechanism.
(c) Outline the management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Compartment syndrome: the classic 5Ps are pain out of proportion, pallor, paraesthesias, paralysis and pulselessness.

(b)
• Predisposing factors: crush injuries and non-trauma compression such as immobility against a firm surface for more than one hour, stroke, intoxication, drug overdose, an elderly person with a hip fracture.
• Pathophysiology: internal swelling raises pressure within a confined muscle compartment, causing tissue damage and inhibiting perfusion, leading to ischaemia and necrosis.
• Compression also causes anaerobic metabolism and cell leakage of lactic acid, potassium and myoglobin; rhabdomyolysis can lead to kidney failure.

(c)
• Observe closely for signs and symptoms of compartment syndrome and prepare for fasciotomy if necessary; the 5Ps are not very reliable in patients with decreased consciousness.
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation and neurological status, then focus on pain, swelling, sensation and compartment signs; check creatine kinase, myoglobin, electrolytes and renal function.
• Give early fluid resuscitation, pain management, alkalinisation of urine, diuresis and electrolyte monitoring; give psychological support.
questions.question:
An elderly patient with a hip fracture who lay immobile against a firm surface for more than one hour now has a limb with pain out of proportion, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis and pulselessness.
(a) Identify the condition indicated.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiology.
(c) Outline the nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Comatose patients and other critically ill patients unable to maintain volitional intake need nutrition support by the safest, simplest, most effective route.

(b)
Enteral nutrition via nasogastric tube (PEG/gastrostomy for long-term feeding; jejunal feeding is an alternative); enteral feeding preserves intestinal mucosal structure and function, is more physiological and reduces infectious complications.

(c)
• Before: screen for malnutrition (MUST), take the history and weight; the dietitian calculates the prescription - about 25 kcal/kg/day initially, protein 1.25 g/kg/day, fluid 30 ml/kg/24 hours.
• During: keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees because of aspiration risk in ICU; do not start the feed at night; watch for tube displacement and high aspirates.
• After: monitor U&Es, phosphate, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs, fluid balance, haematology and weight.

(d)
Complications: aspiration, displacement, high aspirates and inadequate calories, constipation, diarrhoea, ileus, intolerance (?sepsis); manage with prokinetics, nasojejunal feeding or drugs, avoid opioids in ileus, and avoid overfeeding.

(e)
Nurses, doctors and dietitians share the roles of history, weight, optimising intake and monitoring.
questions.question:
A comatose ICU patient who cannot maintain volitional intake and has a functioning gut is to be fed through a nasogastric tube.
(a) Identify the condition and the indication for the therapy.
(b) Name the therapy/equipment and its advantages.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after the therapy.
(d) State the safety checks and complications to watch for.
(e) State the documentation and communication/escalation required.

A patient who has been in the ICU for more than three days has a tracheal tube, a urinary catheter, intravenous lines and a wound.
(a) Identify the risk factors for nosocomial infection.
(b) State the potential complications.
(c) State the monitoring parameters and the preventive nursing measures, and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• About one in four ICU patients acquires nosocomial organisms if the stay is more than 3 days, and the risk rises as the stay is prolonged.
• Reservoirs: the patient's wound, tracheal tubes, urinary bags and catheters, hands and clothes of staff, bladder irrigation solutions, sinks and sink-traps, linens, and visitors' apparel.
• Usual organisms: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Aerobacter species.

(b)
• Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) blood stream and catheter-related infection; Clostridium difficile antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.
• Invasion by microorganisms can destroy even well performed surgery or truncate recovery.

(c)
• Monitoring: surveillance with accurate documentation and reporting of cases and temperature recording for all suspicious cases.
• Prevention: wash hands before each patient contact (alcohol-based hand rub); remove rings; wear PPE; aseptic technique for procedures; isolation room for infected patients; minimal visitation with visitors in gowns and caps.
• Change IV lines and sets every three days, catheters and Ryle's tubes every five to seven days, suction and oxygen tubing on alternate days, ventilator tubing every fifth day; suction bowls daily; oral toileting three times daily.
• Priority: hand hygiene before every patient contact, because the hands and clothes of staff are a reservoir for microbes.
• IV infusion sets, catheters and cannulae are also changed every 24 hours using aseptic technique.

questions.question:
A critically ill ICU patient has dehydration and shock, sepsis and is receiving medications with potential nephrotoxic effects.
(a) Identify the risk factors for acute renal failure.
(b) State the potential complications.
(c) State the monitoring parameters and the preventive nursing measures, and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Prerenal: reduced blood flow to the kidneys (dehydration, shock). Intrarenal: damage to kidney tissue (sepsis, medications). Postrenal: urinary tract obstruction (kidney stones, blood clots).
• Acute renal failure can occur in critically ill ICU patients or be the cause of ICU admission.

(b)
Electrolyte imbalance, fluid overload, infection, acid-base imbalance and increased risk of death; progression through the oliguric phase (under 400 ml in 24 hours) and the polyuric phase (3-6 L/day).

(c)
• Monitor vital signs, urine output (hourly 0.5-1 ml/kg/hr), fluid intake and output, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and electrolytes, and watch for fluid overload and electrolyte imbalance.
• Imaging such as ultrasound or CT helps identify the cause; nurses document and interpret findings and communicate them to the team.
• Prevention: early identification and management of risk factors, maintain adequate hydration, monitor medications with potential nephrotoxic effects, treat infections and underlying conditions promptly, and educate patients on risk factors.
• Priority: maintain adequate hydration/fluid management, because prerenal failure often requires addressing the underlying cause of decreased blood flow.
• Ensure adequate protein and calorie intake and give diuretics and antibiotics as prescribed; dialysis if necessary to remove waste products and excess fluid.

questions.question:
An unconscious ICU patient with a depressed level of consciousness is found to have one pupil dilated and not reacting to light, while the other pupil is normal and reactive.
(a) Identify the condition or problem indicated.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Unilateral pupil dilatation and non-reactivity with a depressed level of consciousness suggests impaired brainstem function.
• Unequal pupils in an unconscious patient is also an acute-onset physical finding that supports ICU admission.

(b)
• Pathophysiology: equal, normal and reactive pupils imply that the upper brainstem and the third cranial nerve are intact; loss of this pattern indicates that this pathway is impaired.
• Neurologic conditions that warrant ICU admission include acute stroke with altered mental status, coma (metabolic, toxic or anoxic), intracranial haemorrhage with potential for herniation, status epilepticus and progressive neuromuscular dysfunction requiring respiratory support.

(c)
• Observe pupillary reaction closely, as it is essential in patients with neurological problems; monitor level of consciousness with the Glasgow Coma Scale (total 3-15: eye opening 1-4, best verbal response 1-5, best motor response 1-6).
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation and neurological disability (Glasgow Coma Scale) as in the primary survey; ICU patients are mostly intubated, so monitor the respiratory pattern for CO2 retention, secretions in the tube and tube dislodgement.
• Continue monitoring vital signs, end-tidal CO2 (35-45), oxygen saturation (90-100%), arterial blood gases and hourly urine output (0.5-1 ml/kg/hr).

questions.question:
Describe the assessment and recognition of cardiac arrest:
(a) the signs of cardiac arrest
(b) the initial assessment sequence.
(c) Explain how the findings guide nursing decisions and actions.
(d) Explain why the assessment may fail or be misinterpreted, and how this is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Unconsciousness within seconds and no response to tapping the shoulders or asking if the person is all right; absence of normal breathing - apnoea or last gasps 1-3 minutes after arrest.
• No pulse on a large artery (carotid or femoral; check for no more than 10 seconds); changed appearance (colour change, blue-tinged skin); dilated pupils and convulsions may occur.

(b)
• Kneel beside the victim, shake the shoulders and ask 'Are you all right?'; if unresponsive shout for help, open the airway, then look, listen and feel for normal breathing (apnoea or gasps).
• Check for signs of functional circulation: breathing, coughing, movement, skin condition, responsiveness and pulse.

(c)
• If the person responds: leave as found, find out what is wrong and reassess regularly.
• If unresponsive and not breathing normally: call 112, give 30 chest compressions, then 2 rescue breaths, and continue 30:2 until help arrives.
• Loss of consciousness is the most immediate and crucial sign; early action limits brain damage, since cortex cells are irreversibly damaged after 3-5 minutes without perfusion.

(d)
• Pupil dilatation (mydriasis) is not reliable.
• Agonal breathing (barely, heavy, noisy or gasping breathing) occurs in up to 40% of arrests and must be recognised as a sign of arrest, not confused with normal breathing.
• Checking for a pulse is for experienced rescuers only and limited to 10 seconds; time estimates under stress are not precise (arrest witnessed 15 or more minutes earlier).
• Stressing conditions can lead to an inadequate situation assessment; the signs of ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are identical and differentiated only by ECG.

questions.question:
Describe foreign body airway obstruction (choking) under the following headings:
(a) causes
(b) pathophysiology and types
(c) clinical features
(d) complications.
(e) State the diagnostic and monitoring measures.
(f) Outline the management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mostly occurs during eating and is commonly witnessed, giving an opportunity for early intervention; in children, foreign bodies such as small toys or toys that can be dismantled into small parts.

(b)
Airway obstruction may be mild (partial) or severe (complete); in an unconscious patient the tongue obstructs the airway; all relief manoeuvres work by raising intrathoracic pressure to expel the foreign body.

(c)
• Mild: suffocation, difficult intense inspiration, neck and thorax soft tissue retraction, hoarse (croupy) noisy inspiration and barking cough.
• Severe: difficult intense inspiratory effort, powerful breathing movements, retraction, no audible breathing, non-cooperation, restlessness, convulsions, coma and blue skin colour.

(d)
Progression to convulsions, coma and cyanosis; in children the chain is choking, hypoxia, hypercapnia, apnoea, bradycardia and cardiac arrest.

(e)
• Recognise mild versus severe obstruction from the signs; a potentially treatable condition.
• In 50% of cases more than one manoeuvre is necessary, so the response must be monitored.

(f)
• Conscious patient with partial blockage: encourage the victim to cough (much more effective than any other manoeuvre) and add several hits to the back.
• Heimlich manoeuvre (several thrusts, 5); in children back blows, chest thrusts and abdominal compression.
• Unconscious patient: tilt the head backward and lift the chin; begin CPR - in choking start with 5 initial breaths in children and adults.
• Compression-only CPR is contraindicated in sudden cardiac arrest due to choking.
• After childhood airway obstruction transfer to a hospital with an anaesthesiologist or intensivist as soon as possible.

questions.question:
A ward patient who earlier complained of new chest pain, dizziness and shortness of breath is found suddenly unresponsive, not breathing normally (only gasping) and with no palpable carotid pulse; the skin looks blue-tinged.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings that confirm the emergency.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnoses/problems.
(c) Describe the immediate nursing interventions and resuscitation/stabilisation measures.
(d) Give the rationale for these actions and state how the care is evaluated.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Responsiveness: shake the shoulders and ask loudly 'Are you all right?' - no response.
• Breathing: look, listen and feel for normal breathing - absent, or only gasps (agonal breathing), which is a sign of cardiac arrest and must not be mistaken for normal breathing.
• Circulation: no palpable carotid pulse (check for no more than 10 seconds); blue-tinged skin, dilated pupils (not reliable) and convulsions may also be present.

(b)
Sudden loss of blood flow because the heart fails to pump effectively (cardiac arrest), with loss of cerebral perfusion; nursing diagnoses: Decreased cardiac output and Ineffective breathing pattern.

(c)
• Call for help/activate the emergency response system at once; protect yourself (gloves, barrier device) and place the patient supine on a firm flat surface.
• Start chest compressions: heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, other hand on top, rate 100-120/min, depth 4-5 cm, equal compression and relaxation; change compressor every 2 minutes when possible.
• Give 30 compressions : 2 rescue breaths (if trained) with visible chest rise; interrupt CPR as little as possible.
• Attach AED/defibrillator pads to the bare chest, do not touch the patient during rhythm analysis, stand clear for a shock (ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shockable), then resume CPR immediately.
• Advanced life support includes defibrillation, airway management and medications as prescribed (epinephrine is generally given every five minutes).

(d)
• Rationale: early CPR improves blood and oxygen flow to vital organs and, by keeping the brain supplied, decreases neurological damage; chest compressions make the greatest difference; brain cortex cells are irreversibly damaged after 3-5 minutes without perfusion.
• Evaluation: continue CPR until help arrives or the patient breathes normally/regains consciousness (then recovery position); once circulation returns, continuously assess vital signs, neurological status and response to treatment, and treat the underlying cause.
• Give emotional support to patient and family and communicate clearly within the team.

questions.question:
A patient rescued after prolonged compression of a limb has tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria and red-brown urine; laboratory tests show raised creatine kinase and myoglobin with abnormal electrolytes and renal function.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the body systems or functions affected.
(c) State the possible causes/differentials.
(d) State the nursing priorities and the reasoning for the actions taken.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Red or brown urine indicates myoglobinuria; raised creatine kinase and myoglobin indicate muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis), which releases myoglobin with the potential to cause kidney failure.
• Tachycardia, hypotension and oliguria are systemic manifestations of a severe crush injury.

(b)
Musculoskeletal (muscle damage), renal (acute kidney failure risk), cardiovascular (tachycardia, hypotension) and metabolic/electrolyte balance (release of lactic acid, potassium, myoglobin and purines).

(c)
• Crush syndrome - a combination of compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis and systemic inflammatory response syndrome; compartment syndrome.
• Cause of compression: disasters, collapsed buildings, industrial or motor vehicle accidents, or non-trauma immobility over one hour.

(d)
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation and neurological status first; focus assessment on pain, swelling, sensation and compartment signs.
• Early fluid resuscitation to maintain blood pressure and prevent kidney failure; manage rhabdomyolysis with urine alkalinisation, diuresis and electrolyte monitoring.
• Monitor for compartment syndrome and prepare for fasciotomy; provide pain management, nutritional support and psychological support.
• Reasoning: prognosis depends on severity, time to treatment and complications; early diagnosis and aggressive management improve it.

(a)
• End-tidal CO2 (measured by capnostat) and PCO2 above 35-45, pH below 7.33-7.45 and saturation (pulse oximeter) below 90-100% show CO2 retention with inadequate oxygenation.
• Arterial blood gas analysis is the single most important test for evaluating respiratory and metabolic disorders.

(b)
Respiratory function (ventilation and gas exchange) and acid-base balance.

(c)
Problems that occur in intubated patients: retention of CO2, secretions in the endotracheal tube and tube dislodgement.

(d)
• Monitor the respiratory pattern closely since intubated patients need more vigilance, to identify these problems promptly.
• Repeat ABG 30 minutes after a change in ventilator parameters and 30 minutes after suctioning (baseline ABG is taken 5-10 minutes after ICU admission).
• Check electrolytes 4-hourly between ABGs or more often and correct abnormal readings promptly.
• Protect against infection: aseptic technique, suction bowls changed daily, oral toileting three times daily, suction tubing changed on alternate days and ventilator tubing every fifth day.
questions.question:
An intubated ICU patient has end-tidal CO2 and arterial PCO2 above the normal range (35-45), arterial pH below the normal range (7.33-7.45) and oxygen saturation below 90%.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the body system or function affected.
(c) State the possible causes.
(d) State the nursing priorities and the reasoning for the actions taken.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Triage comes from the French trier, to sort: sorting of casualties by severity and the immediacy of treatment needed to determine priority of care and the proper site for treatment; all systems share a hierarchy based on the potential for loss of life.

(b)
Emergent: life threatening, highest priority, seen immediately. Urgent: serious but not immediately life threatening, seen within 1 hour. Non-urgent: episodic illness addressed within 24 hours without increased morbidity.

(c)
• Red (immediate): life-threatening but survivable with minimal intervention, e.g. sucking chest wound, airway obstruction, shock, tension pneumothorax. Yellow (delayed): can wait hours, e.g. stable abdominal wounds, soft tissue injuries, most eye and CNS injuries.
• Green (minimal): minor injuries delayed hours to days and moved away from the main triage area, e.g. upper extremity fractures, sprains, small lacerations. Black (expectant): survival unlikely even with definitive care, separated but not abandoned, given comfort measures.

(d)
Triage nurses collect vital signs, history, neurologic findings and diagnostic data: circumstances and time of injury or illness, loss of consciousness, prior health, medications (insulin, digitalis, anticoagulants), allergies, bleeding tendencies, last meal and last tetanus immunisation.

(e)
• Emergency care must be rendered without delay, so triage decisions expedite care; every nurse should know the colour-coded tagging system used by the facility and community.
• In a disaster the fundamental principle is to do the greatest good for the greatest number, with decisions based on likelihood of survival and consumption of available resources.
• Patients with conditions associated with high mortality are assigned low priority in a disaster, even if conscious.

(f)
• Routine hospital triage directs all available resources to the most critically ill patients, regardless of potential outcome.
• Field triage (or hospital triage during a disaster) uses scarce resources to benefit the most people possible.
• This distinction affects triage decisions.
• A nurse may serve as the triage officer during a disaster.
questions.question:
Describe triage under the following headings:
(a) definition and origin
(b) the three-category system
(c) the NATO four-colour categories
(d) data collected at triage.
(e) Explain the clinical and ethical basis of triage decisions in emergencies and disasters.
(f) Distinguish between routine emergency department triage and disaster (field) triage.

Describe acute renal failure under the following headings:
(a) causes
(b) pathophysiology and stages
(c) clinical features
(d) complications.
(e) State the diagnostic and monitoring measures.
(f) Outline the nursing management, including prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Prerenal: reduced blood flow to the kidneys (e.g. dehydration, shock). Intrarenal: damage to kidney tissue (e.g. sepsis, medications). Postrenal: obstruction of the urinary tract (e.g. kidney stones, blood clots).
• The cause determines treatment: prerenal - address decreased blood flow; intrarenal - manage the source of damage or support kidney function; postrenal - remove the obstruction to restore urine flow.

(b)
• An abrupt deterioration of renal function (now also called acute renal injury) with inability to filter waste, leading to accumulation of metabolic wastes, fluids and electrolytes, usually followed by reduced urinary output.
• Four stages: initiation (onset of injury); oliguric (less than 400 ml in 24 hours); diuresis/polyuric (3-6 L of urine per day); recovery (slow, up to one year).

(c)
Decreased urine output, oedema, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, confusion, shortness of breath and high blood pressure.

(d)
Electrolyte imbalance, fluid overload, infection, acid-base imbalance and increased risk of death.

(e)
• Comprehensive history and physical examination, vital signs, urine output assessment, laboratory tests (blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, electrolytes) and imaging (ultrasound, CT scan).
• These identify the cause, assess severity of injury and guide treatment; nurses document and interpret findings and communicate them to the team.

(f)
• Fluid management: maintain fluid balance and avoid overload; electrolyte management: correct imbalances (usually high potassium and sodium).
• Give medications as prescribed (diuretics, antibiotics); provide nutritional support with adequate protein and calories; dialysis therapy if necessary to remove waste products and excess fluid.
• Monitor fluid intake and output closely and watch for fluid overload or electrolyte imbalance.
• Prevention: early identification of risk factors, adequate hydration, monitoring nephrotoxic medications, prompt treatment of infections and patient education.

(a)
For a patient with an emergent or urgent health problem: stabilisation, provision of critical treatments and prompt transfer to the appropriate setting (ICU, operating room, general care unit) are the priorities.

(b)
Triage nurses collect vital signs, history, neurologic findings and diagnostic data: circumstances and time of injury or illness, onset of symptoms, unconsciousness, prior health, medications, allergies, bleeding tendencies, last meal and tetanus immunisation.

(c)
• Primary survey (ABCD): patent airway; adequate ventilation with resuscitation when necessary; evaluate and restore cardiac output by controlling haemorrhage and treating shock; neurologic disability by Glasgow Coma Scale.
• Secondary survey: complete health history and head-to-toe assessment; diagnostic and laboratory tests; ECG electrodes, arterial lines or urinary catheters; splinting of suspected fractures; cleaning and dressing of wounds.
• Then medical and nursing diagnoses are formulated, initial treatment started and disposition planned.

(d)
ED staff work collaboratively; nurses must be able to assess, prioritise and intervene quickly and must know which procedures each nurse may perform.

(e)
Risks to the nurse: high risk of injury or illness from exposure to infections such as hepatitis and AIDS; high legal risk from life-and-death decisions.

(f)
• The primary survey focuses on stabilising life-threatening conditions, so it is done first.
• In trauma patients the cervical spine is protected and chest injuries are assessed first.
• The secondary survey completes assessment and testing after stabilisation, allowing correct diagnoses and disposition.
questions.question:
Describe the primary and secondary survey in emergency nursing under the following headings:
(a) indications
(b) preparation (triage data)
(c) steps of the primary and secondary survey
(d) nursing responsibilities.
(e) State the complications and how they are prevented or managed.
(f) Explain the rationale for key steps.

A patient with acute respiratory failure is admitted to the ICU and requires ventilatory support through a tracheal tube.
(a) Identify the condition and the priority of admission.
(b) Name the therapy/equipment involved.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after the therapy.
(d) State the safety checks and complications to watch for.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support is a Priority 1 ICU admission: critically ill, unstable, needing intensive treatment and monitoring that cannot be provided outside the ICU, with no limits on therapy.

(b)
Ventilatory support through an endotracheal (tracheal) tube; most ICU patients are intubated, which calls for more vigilance.

(c)
• Before/on admission: take baseline arterial blood gases 5-10 minutes after admission with the initial FiO2.
• During: monitor the respiratory pattern, end-tidal CO2 (normal 35-45) and oxygen saturation (90-100%); repeat ABG 30 minutes after changing ventilator parameters and 30 minutes after suctioning; check electrolytes 4-hourly.
• After extubation: ABG 45 minutes to 1 hour afterwards.

(d)
• Watch for retention of CO2, secretions in the tube and tube dislodgement; maintain asepsis because tracheal tubes are reservoirs for microbes.
• Infection safeguards: change suction tubing and oxygen tubing on alternate days, ventilator tubing every fifth day, suction bowls daily; oral toileting three times daily for intubated patients.

questions.question:
An ICU patient who has been receiving antibiotics develops diarrhoea.
(a) Identify the condition or problem most likely present.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Clostridium difficile (C. diff) infection, a common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

(b)
• Predisposing factor: antibiotic therapy (it is a cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea); ICU stay of more than 3 days increases the risk of acquiring nosocomial organisms.
• Transmission: through the faeces or any surface, device or material contaminated with faeces.

(c)
• The best way of treating it is to stop the antibiotics.
• Apply standard infection control principles: hospital environmental hygiene, hand washing, use of fluid-repellent PPE and safe disposal of sharps; use disposable items where possible and prompt removal of waste.
• Provide an isolation room with hand washing facilities for an infected patient.
• Surveillance: accurate documentation and reporting of cases, with temperature recording for suspicious cases.

questions.question:
A child (over 1 year and before puberty) who was choking on a small toy collapses, is unresponsive and is not breathing normally.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings.
(b) Identify the problem and its pathway.
(c) Describe the immediate nursing interventions and resuscitation measures.
(d) Give the rationale and state how the care is evaluated.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Airway: look for obstruction - foreign bodies (small toys) are a common cause. Breathing: look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds. Circulation: signs of circulation (movements, coughing, skin colour, breathing); check the pulse (if an experienced health provider) for no more than 10 seconds.

(b)
• Choking (foreign body airway obstruction) is the most common cause of vital function failure in children; the chain is choking, hypoxia, hypercapnia, apnoea, bradycardia, cardiac arrest.
• Primary cardiac arrest and ventricular fibrillation are uncommon in children, and hypoxia develops faster because of the high metabolic rate.

(c)
• Open the airway as in adults; start with 5 initial breaths (also for choking), each blown steadily over 1-1.5 seconds at 6-7 ml/kg so that the chest visibly rises; use a paediatric-size self-inflating bag.
• Compress the lower third of the sternum (one finger above the xiphoid process) to one third of the chest depth at 100 compressions per minute.
• Use 30:2 for 1 minute when alone or without paediatric training, then call 155 (112); the generally preferred ratio is 15:2 for in-hospital CPR with two rescuers. The precordial thump is contraindicated in children.
• For foreign body airway obstruction use back blows, chest thrusts and abdominal compression; all raise intrathoracic pressure and expel the foreign body, and in 50% of cases more than one manoeuvre is needed.

(d)
• Rationale: hypoxia is the cause of arrest, so ventilation is started first with initial breaths; avoid overinflation to prevent gastric distension and use the recovery position in an unconscious victim to prevent aspiration.
• Evaluation: signs of circulation and normal breathing return; continue until help arrives.

questions.question:
Describe informed consent in critical care nursing:
(a) definition and elements
(b) how it applies when patients lack capacity.
(c) Explain how it guides nursing decisions.
(d) Explain why it may fail or cause harm in critical care, and how this is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Informed consent ensures the patient has sufficient information to decide - risks, benefits and alternatives of treatment - and respects autonomy and self-determination; it is a cornerstone of autonomy.
• Elements: disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness and competence; the patient must be able to ask questions and consent willingly.

(b)
• Critical care patients may be unconscious, heavily sedated or lack capacity; decisions then rely on advance directives (a legal document outlining care preferences if the person cannot communicate) and surrogate decision-makers (next of kin or legally appointed proxies).
• With no advance directive, emergency treatment principles permit life-saving interventions without consent, guided by beneficence.

(c)
• For unconscious patients autonomy is upheld by respecting advance directives or consulting surrogate decision-makers.
• Nurses advocate by facilitating communication, clarifying treatment goals and resolving conflicts through ethics consultation, balancing ethics and advocacy.

(d)
• Surrogates may not fully understand the implications of treatment, may delay or refuse decisions through emotional distress, or decide against medical recommendations or the patient's perceived preferences.
• Emergency interventions such as intubation often proceed without explicit consent, raising questions of overriding autonomy; cultural or religious beliefs (for example rejecting blood transfusion) may conflict with care.
• A patient's religious belief on blood must be respected: giving blood without their knowledge is an assault; if unconscious or a child, blood may be given against relatives' decision because of the fundamental right to life.
• Prevention: educate surrogates, follow institutional policies for emergency interventions, use ethics consultation and encourage documentation of advance directives.
• Cultural competence and open communication help nurses respect beliefs while advocating patient well-being.
• Family meetings with the interdisciplinary team support shared decision-making.

(a)
• Core and peripheral temperatures are monitored because they indicate peripheral perfusion and cardiac output; a high core and low peripheral temperature may indicate low cardiac output and is also an indicator of infection.
• Urine output should be monitored hourly at 0.5-1 ml/kg/hr; output below this, with a rate above the normal range (13 years and above 60-90 beats/min), supports poor perfusion.

(b)
Cardiovascular function (cardiac output and peripheral perfusion) and renal perfusion/urinary function; also the infection/inflammatory response.

(c)
• Low cardiac output or infection; conditions in the ICU diagnosis model include cardiogenic shock, severe sepsis or septic shock and multi-organ dysfunction syndrome.
• Reduced renal blood flow from dehydration or shock (prerenal) may reduce urine output.

(d)
• Monitor core and peripheral temperature, pulse, blood pressure (invasive monitoring is continuous and the most reliable), hourly urine output, arterial blood gases and electrolytes.
• Temperature recording and accurate documentation of suspicious cases support infection surveillance; correct abnormal readings promptly and report deviations so corrective measures are instituted promptly.
• Regular monitoring is needed because there are limits compatible with life.
questions.question:
An ICU patient's chart shows a high core temperature with a low peripheral temperature, a heart rate above the normal range for age, and hourly urine output persistently below the recommended range.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the body system or function affected.
(c) State the possible causes/differentials.
(d) State the nursing priorities and the reasoning for the actions taken.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Veracity is the ethical obligation of truth-telling in the patient-caregiver relationship, grounded in respect for patient autonomy so individuals can make informed decisions.
• In critical care it means honest, transparent information on diagnoses, prognoses and treatment options, even when the news is difficult; it builds trust.

(b)
Breaking bad news (life-altering or terminal diagnoses such as organ failure or advanced cancer); disclosing medical errors (medication mistakes, procedural complications) to the patient or family; end-of-life decisions; futility conversations.

(c)
• Deliver the truth compassionately, considering the patient's emotional readiness and cultural values; balance veracity with compassion to maintain trust and address emotions.
• Give accurate information about the benefits, risks and likelihood of success of CPR or artificial ventilation so decisions to continue or withdraw treatment are informed.
• When treatment cannot help (e.g. irreversible multi-organ failure) communicate this clearly; nurses acknowledge errors and take corrective action transparently, which supports accountability and patient safety.

(d)
• Veracity can conflict with beneficence or non-maleficence; white lies told to protect feelings or prevent harm erode trust, and overuse leads to a slippery slope of dishonesty.
• Some cultures prefer an indirect approach to sharing grim prognoses, which can conflict with veracity.
• Fear of litigation or damaged trust may cause hesitancy in full disclosure; families with unrealistic expectations or in denial make futility discussions difficult.
• Prevention: transparency and open communication that strengthen trust and accountability; cultural competence training, active listening and open-mindedness; incident reporting systems for learning-focused error management.
• Regular training and professional development, clear policies and protocols, and adherence to legal and ethical nursing codes.
• Family meetings with the interdisciplinary team to explain prognosis compassionately.
questions.question:
Describe veracity (truth-telling) in critical care nursing:
(a) definition and basis
(b) situations in which it applies.
(c) Explain how it guides nursing decisions and communication.
(d) Explain why it may fail or cause harm, and how this is prevented.

An older male patient in the ICU is a cigarette smoker with high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity and diabetes, takes little physical exercise, has a family history of heart disease, and has survived a previous episode of sudden cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation.
(a) Identify his risk factors for sudden cardiac arrest.
(b) State the potential complications.
(c) State the monitoring parameters and the preventive nursing measures, and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Risk factors: age (arrest becomes more common with age), male sex (affected more often), cigarette smoking (current and former smokers), high blood pressure, high cholesterol, lack of physical exercise, obesity, diabetes, family history; a prior episode of sudden cardiac arrest increases the risk of future episodes.
• Heredity, gender and age cannot be changed; tobacco use, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes and overweight/obesity can be changed.

(b)
• Recurrent sudden cardiac arrest/death: the heart abruptly beats in an abnormal or irregular rhythm, with no organised electrical activity, no consistent ventricular contraction and inadequate cardiac output.
• Loss of cerebral perfusion causes rapid loss of consciousness and cessation of breathing; survival with treatment is about 8% and many survivors have significant disability.

(c)
• Monitor vital signs (pulse, blood pressure) and heart sounds; monitor ECG and chest x-ray changes closely; monitor laboratory status (BUN, creatinine), electrolytes and nutrition; assess neurological status and response to treatment.
• Preventive measures: promote healthy diet, exercise and smoking cessation; blood pressure control and cholesterol lowering; administer medications as prescribed; oxygen by nasal prongs or face mask as indicated; IV solutions as prescribed.
• Encourage rest, semirecumbent in bed or chair, and assist with physical care; give emotional support to patient and family; educate on the cause of arrest, risk factors and prevention.
• Priority intervention: an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) - a battery-powered device that monitors the heart's electrical activity and delivers a shock when an arrhythmia or asystole is detected.
• Justification: ICDs are used as secondary prevention in people who survived sudden cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia, which is this patient's history.

questions.question:
A trauma patient brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle crash is unconscious with a suspected chest injury and signs of shock.
(a) State the priority nursing assessment findings to obtain.
(b) Identify the problem and its triage priority.
(c) Describe the immediate nursing interventions and stabilisation measures.
(d) Give the rationale and state how the care is evaluated.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Triage data: vital signs and history, neurologic assessment findings and diagnostic data; circumstances, precipitating events, location and time of injury; whether the patient was unconscious after injury; how the patient reached hospital.
• Also ask the patient or companion about prior health status, medical/surgical history, medications (hormones, insulin, digitalis, anticoagulants), allergies, bleeding tendencies, time of last meal and date of last tetanus immunisation.
• Primary survey findings: airway patency, breathing/ventilation and chest injuries, circulation (haemorrhage, shock) and neurologic disability using the Glasgow Coma Scale.

(b)
• An emergent patient: life threatening, highest priority and seen immediately; conditions such as airway obstruction, shock, tension pneumothorax or a sucking chest wound fall in the immediate (red) category.
• Formal nursing diagnoses are formulated once the patient has been assessed, stabilised and tested.

(c)
• Primary survey (ABCD): establish a patent airway with the cervical spine protected; provide adequate ventilation using resuscitation measures when necessary; assess chest injuries first.
• Evaluate and restore cardiac output by controlling haemorrhage, preventing and treating shock and maintaining effective circulation; determine neurologic disability with the Glasgow Coma Scale.
• Secondary survey: complete health history and head-to-toe assessment, diagnostic and laboratory tests, ECG electrodes, arterial lines or urinary catheters, splinting of suspected fractures, cleaning and dressing of wounds.

(d)
• Rationale: the primary survey focuses on stabilising life-threatening conditions and emergency care must be rendered without delay; emergent patients need stabilisation, critical treatment and prompt transfer to the appropriate setting.
• Evaluation: the patient has been assessed, stabilised and tested; medical and nursing diagnoses are formulated, initial important treatment is started and plans for disposition (ICU, operating room or general care unit) are made.

(a)
• End-of-life care is comprehensive support in the final stages of terminal illness that focuses on comfort, dignity and quality of life rather than cure.
• Decisions involve initiating, withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatments such as mechanical ventilation, dialysis and vasopressors; withdrawal is discontinuing treatment that no longer benefits the patient, guided by autonomy, beneficence and non-maleficence.

(b)
An advance directive is a legal document stating care preferences if the person cannot communicate; a DNR order reflects a patient's wish not to be resuscitated; palliative care in critical care manages symptoms and improves quality of life for patients and families through an interdisciplinary approach addressing physical, emotional and spiritual needs.

(c)
• Nurses honour documented wishes (autonomy), advocate for the patient's best interest and facilitate discussions between patient, family and medical team.
• Priority 3 patients may have limits on therapy such as no intubation or CPR; if deterioration is irreversible, withdrawal of therapy is carried out in the ICU and keeping patients when care is futile is discouraged.
• Administering high doses of painkillers for relief in a terminally ill patient follows the principle of double effect: the intent is pain relief, not death.

(d)
• Withdrawal of life support can be perceived as euthanasia, and families may see withholding care as giving up, insisting on aggressive treatment despite the patient's directive.
• Nurses experience moral distress when made to give treatment they think futile.
• Prevention: a family meeting with the interdisciplinary team (physician, nurse, social worker, chaplain) to explain prognosis and treatment limits, address emotional concerns and build consensus.
• Transparent, empathetic communication, advance directives, ethics committees and the four-quadrant approach (medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life, contextual features) also help.
• In the case described, the family agreed to transition to palliative care and the patient was extubated and given comfort care.
• Emotional resilience training and peer support for nurses are also recommended.
questions.question:
Describe end-of-life decisions in critical care:
(a) end-of-life care, withholding and withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment
(b) advance directives, DNR orders and palliative care.
(c) Explain how these guide nursing decisions.
(d) Explain why they may cause conflict or harm, and how this is prevented.

questions.explanation: The second-class lever is called the lever of power because the effort arm is always greater than the load arm, giving a constant mechanical advantage. This means less effort force is needed to overcome the load. However, the movement produced is slow. The existence of pure second-class levers in the human body is still debated.
options: The effort arm always exceeds the load arm, creating mechanical advantage
The fulcrum is between effort and load, amplifying speed of movement
The load arm always exceeds the effort arm, requiring high force output
The effort is positioned furthest from fulcrum for maximum torque
Both arms are equal length, distributing force equally throughout
questions.question: The second-class lever is referred to as the 'lever of power' because:

questions.explanation: Torque (also called moment of force) is calculated as the product of force and the moment arm — which is the perpendicular distance from the force's line of action to the axis of rotation (T = Fd). The greater the torque acting at the axis, the greater the tendency for rotation to occur. Its unit is Newton-meters (Nm).
options: The cosine of the angle between force and the lever segment
Velocity at which the body segment undergoes angular motion
Mass of the body segment multiplied by its angular velocity
Perpendicular distance from the force's line of action to axis
The ratio of force arm to resistance arm in lever calculation
questions.question: Torque is defined as the rotary effect created by a force, calculated as the product of force and:

options: The presence of large intra-articular fibrocartilaginous discs
Extremely lax capsuloligamentous structures permitting multiaxial motion
The large muscle mass crossing these joints in multiple directions
The absence of collateral ligaments restricting rotational motion
Reciprocally convex and concave spheroidal bone surfaces present
questions.question: The factor most responsible for allowing hip and shoulder joints to move in three planes is:
questions.explanation: Ball and socket (spheroidal) joints have the surfaces of the articulating bones shaped reciprocally as convex and concave, allowing rotations in all three planes of movement. This spherical geometry permits triaxial motion with three degrees of freedom. The hip and shoulder joints are the primary examples of spheroidal joints.

Kinetic friction comes into operation once maximal static friction has been overcome and has constant values that are always lesser than maximum static friction. Static friction includes sliding and rolling subtypes. The coefficient of friction and normal reaction force are the two factors affecting friction magnitude.
options: Greater in magnitude and variable depending on applied speed
Equal in magnitude but opposite in direction of application
Greater and acts only after the body begins to accelerate
