Variable and depends on surface hardness and temperature
Constant and always lesser than maximum static friction
questions.question: Kinetic friction compared to maximum static friction is:

questions.explanation: The anatomical reference position is the erect standing position with all body parts with feet slightly separated, arms hanging relaxed at the sides, and the palms of the hands facing forward (supinated). It is a universally accepted reference position used to describe regions, spatial relationships of the body, and to refer to body positions including in goniometry.
options: Subject seated with hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees each
Subject supine lying with arms extended and palms facing down
Subject standing with feet together and arms crossed over chest
Erect standing with feet slightly separated, arms hanging, palms forward
Subject prone lying with arms at sides and head in neutral position
questions.question: The anatomical reference position is accepted universally and described as:

questions.explanation: Two-joint muscles can produce force with a significant transverse component affecting movement at two joints simultaneously, unlike one-joint muscles that produce force primarily in line with a single segment. This allows energy transfer between joints and contributes to coordinated multi-joint movement patterns. In rehabilitation, understanding two-joint muscle mechanics helps explain why exercises must address both joints a muscle crosses.
options: Force with transverse component across segments
questions.question: The key functional advantage of two-joint muscles is their ability to produce:

questions.explanation: The elastic behavior of muscle has two components: the parallel elastic component (PEC), provided by the muscle membrane (sarcolemma), and the series elastic component (SEC), found inside the tendon. PEC is named because the membrane is parallel to the muscle fiber, while the tendon is in series (in line) with it. Both have viscoelastic properties.
options: The tendon which lies in series with the contractile component
The muscle membrane (sarcolemma) parallel to muscle fibers
The endomysium surrounding individual muscle fiber cells
The titin protein connecting the Z line to the M line
The actin-myosin cross bridge linkages during active contraction
questions.question: The parallel elastic component (PEC) of muscle's elastic behavior is provided by:

questions.explanation: Mechanical work equals force applied against resistance multiplied by the displacement of that resistance in the direction of force application. During isometric contractions, no mechanical work is performed despite high muscular tension because no displacement occurs. Physiotherapists use work calculations to quantify exercise demands and compare the metabolic costs of different therapeutic activities.
questions.question: Mechanical work is defined as force multiplied by:
Kinematics is the study of motion:
questions.explanation: Kinematics describes motion patterns including displacement, velocity, and acceleration without reference to the forces causing those motions. It addresses the 'what' of movement. In contrast, kinetics examines the forces causing motion. Physiotherapists use kinematics for observational gait analysis and movement screening before selecting quantitative force-based assessments to confirm clinical hypotheses.

Articular cartilage can reduce contact stress at a joint by approximately 50 percent through load distribution over a wider area. This property is exploited in conservative management of osteoarthritis, where weight reduction and muscle strengthening further decrease joint stress. In aquatic therapy, buoyancy reduces compressive loads and supports the remaining cartilage function.
questions.question: Articular cartilage is known to reduce contact stress at a joint by approximately:
The coefficient of friction is primarily influenced by which two factors?
questions.explanation: Two factors influence the coefficient of friction: (1) the relative roughness and hardness of the surfaces in contact — rougher and harder surfaces increase the coefficient — and (2) the type of molecular interaction between the surfaces — greater molecular and mechanical interaction increases the coefficient of friction.
options: Surface roughness/hardness and molecular interaction between surfaces
Normal reaction force and the velocity of the sliding body
Body mass and contact area between the two opposing surfaces
Ambient temperature and lubricating fluid film at the interface
Applied force magnitude and duration of contact between surfaces

questions.question: During observational gait analysis (OGA), the recommended procedural approach is to:
options: Observe only the lower limbs since upper limb motion is secondary
Analyze one entire gait cycle then focus on cadence and speed
Focus solely on the sagittal plane as it contains the most information
Begin observing at the hip since hip pathology drives most gait deviations
Observe the entire process first, then examine each joint segment beginning at foot and ankle
questions.explanation: In OGA, the procedure includes examining the patient from the front, back, and side; first observing the gait pattern as an entire process, then examining each joint segment beginning with the foot and ankle. The examiner should determine visually if the patient's performance is significantly different for each observed segment and gait cycle phase.

options: Be used for community ambulation outside the clinical setting
Fold for portable use and transport to the patient's home setting
Be adjusted to accommodate users of all heights automatically
Provide feedback on weight distribution through electronic sensors
Determine which ambulatory device the patient will likely require next
questions.explanation: One key advantage of the parallel bar is that it can be used to determine which other ambulatory device the user will use, because the patient's performance within the parallel bar indicates their ability to use other types of ambulatory devices. It also provides maximum stability and requires the least amount of coordination.
questions.question: One key advantage of the parallel bar over other ambulatory devices is that it can:
The classic gait terminology term equivalent to Rancho Los Amigos 'Loading Response' is:
options: Heel strike, the first event as the heel contacts the ground
Mid-stance, the period when one limb alone supports the body
Push-off, the terminal propulsive phase of the stance period
Foot flat, when the entire foot comes into contact with ground
Heel-off, when the heel begins to rise from the walking surface
questions.explanation: In classic gait terminology, 'Foot Flat' is equivalent to the Rancho Los Amigos 'Loading Response' phase. 'Heel Strike' corresponds to 'Initial Contact,' 'Mid-stance' remains the same, 'Heel-off' corresponds to 'Terminal Stance,' and 'Toe-off' corresponds to 'Preswing.' The Rancho system is more precise and widely used clinically.

Anthropometry is the science of measuring body dimensions including height, weight, girth, segment lengths, and body density. These measurements provide essential data for equipment prescription (wheelchair dimensions, orthotic sizing), exercise parameter setting, and biomechanical modelling. Physiotherapists use anthropometric data to individualise rehabilitation equipment and exercise parameters to patient-specific body proportions.
questions.question: The science of measuring body dimensions including height, weight, girth, and segment lengths is called:
Muscle function reaches peak efficiency at which temperature:
questions.explanation: Muscle function reaches peak efficiency at 38.5 degrees Celsius, balancing enhanced enzyme kinetics, nerve conduction, and contractile speed without risking thermal damage. Below this temperature, metabolic processes are slowed; above it, protein denaturation and hyperthermia become concerns. This rationale underpins the physiotherapist's use of thermal agents and warm-up protocols before therapeutic exercise.

questions.question: Static flexibility is the ROM achieved when a body segment is moved by:
questions.explanation: Static flexibility is the range of motion achieved when a body segment is passively moved by an external source such as a physiotherapist, rather than by the patient's own muscle activity. It better represents the tissue's intrinsic extensibility and capsular-ligamentous restriction. Differentiating static from dynamic flexibility helps identify whether limitations are passive structural or active neuromuscular in origin.
options: Passive external force from the therapist

questions.question: The functional excursion of a muscle is described as the distance a muscle can shorten after being:
questions.explanation: Functional excursion is the distance that a muscle is capable of shortening after it has been elongated to its maximum. It represents the total range over which the muscle can operate. This excursion depends on fiber arrangement and whether the muscle crosses one or multiple joints.
options: Fully contracted in the inner range without external resistance
Warmed up through concentric activity to optimal temperature
Stimulated electrically to maximal twitch contraction force
Elongated to its maximum, which is its full excursion range
Held isometrically at a constant length for a set time period

questions.question: Oscillatory motion is characterized by:
options: Motion being rapidly reversed after short excursions around an equilibrium
Continuous unidirectional movement in a single straight line path
Progressive acceleration in the direction of the applied force vector
Circular motion around a fixed axis at constant angular velocity
Translation combined with rotation in a general combined motion
questions.explanation: Oscillation is characterized by motion being rapidly reversed after short excursions. It involves repeated back-and-forth movement around an equilibrium point. This is distinct from translational (linear or curvilinear) motion and rotational motion. Examples include vibration and pendular movements.

questions.question: Resistance to a physiotherapy exercise is MOST effective when applied at:
options: The proximal end of the limb to reduce joint compression
The midpoint of the lever to evenly distribute the load
Right angles (90°) to the lever for maximum perpendicular torque
An acute angle to the bone to increase the stabilizing component
A distance equal to the effort arm to ensure balanced torques
questions.explanation: Resistance must be applied at right angles (90°) to the lever system for maximum effectiveness. If applied at less than 90°, the full effect of the lever system will not be maximal. The further the point of application from the fulcrum (joint), the more effective the resistance due to the longer resistance arm increasing the resistive torque.

options: Proportional to their masses and to the square of the distance
Inversely proportional to the product of their two total masses
Proportional to mass product and inversely to distance squared
Constant regardless of separation when masses remain unchanged
Equal to the product of individual masses divided by distance
questions.question: The Law of Gravitation states that gravitational force between two bodies is:
questions.explanation: Newton's Law of Gravitation states that all bodies are attracted to one another with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Algebraically: Fg = Gm1m2/d². This represents one of the most significant contributions to the scientific revolution.

questions.question: The hip joint's triaxial classification permits movements in:
questions.explanation: Ball-and-socket joints are triaxial, permitting movements in three planes: sagittal (flexion-extension), frontal (abduction-adduction), and transverse (medial-lateral rotation). Assessment of all three movement planes is therefore essential in hip joint evaluation, as restriction in any one plane may affect function in the others through compensatory movement patterns.

questions.question: The condition for a body in dynamic equilibrium is that it is:
options: Completely at rest with all forces and torques summing to zero
Accelerating at a constant rate with no net external torque
Rotating about a fixed axis with constant angular momentum
Moving at constant velocity with balanced forces and torques
In periodic oscillation about a fixed point of equilibrium
questions.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium applies to bodies in motion. According to Newton's second law, a body in equilibrium is either motionless (static equilibrium) or moving at constant velocity (dynamic equilibrium). In both cases, there is no net force or net torque — the forces and torques are balanced.

questions.question: The behavioral property unique to muscle tissue (not shared by other tissues) is:
options: Extensibility, which is the ability to increase in length when stretched
Elasticity, the ability to return to normal resting length after stretch
Irritability (contractility), the ability to respond to a stimulus by developing tension
Viscoelasticity, the time-dependent stretching and recoiling property
Compliance, the passive property of yielding to applied deformation
questions.explanation: Irritability (the ability to respond to a stimulus by developing tension, also known as contractility) is the behavioral property unique to muscle tissue and is not shared by other biological tissues. Extensibility and elasticity are common to many biological tissues. The ability to develop tension is traditionally referred to as contraction.

questions.question: The coefficient of restitution of a therapeutic ball is a dimensionless value ranging from:
questions.explanation: The coefficient of restitution ranges from 0 to 1, representing the ratio of post-impact to pre-impact velocity difference. Values near 1 indicate elastic impact with minimal energy loss, while values near 0 indicate plastic impact. In therapeutic exercise, the coefficient of restitution of balls, surfaces, and orthotic materials affects impact forces transmitted to patients' joints and tissues.

questions.question: The most common lever class in human limbs is the third-class lever. In this lever, the effort is applied:
questions.explanation: Third-class levers have the effort applied between the fulcrum and the load, producing mechanical disadvantage but generating greater velocity and range of movement at the load end. The elbow joint exemplifies this with the biceps insertion between the elbow joint (fulcrum) and the hand (load). This sacrifices mechanical efficiency for speed and range, critical for limb function.

The forearm walker provides forearm support rather than handgrips, making it the appropriate choice for patients with wrist or hand pathology, reduced grip strength, or conditions requiring that weight be borne through the forearm rather than the wrist and hand. It is otherwise similar in design and function to the standard walking frame.
questions.question: The forearm walker's primary clinical indication over the standard walker is for patients with:
options: Reduced balance and poor coordination requiring maximum support
Obesity or extreme body weight requiring a reinforced frame design
Wrist or hand pathology requiring forearm rather than hand weight bearing
Lower limb weakness requiring bilateral upper limb support simultaneously
Community-level ambulation requiring portability and adjustable height

questions.explanation: The stretch-shortening cycle involves eccentric contraction immediately followed by concentric contraction, with the transition time between phases being critical for maximising elastic energy release and stretch reflex contribution. The SSC produces greater force and power than concentric contraction alone at lower metabolic cost. Plyometric training programmes in rehabilitation exploit the SSC to restore and enhance explosive power after lower limb injury.
questions.question: The stretch-shortening cycle that underpins plyometric training follows which correct sequence:

options: Axially through a body in a compressive squeezing manner
Axially through a body in a tensile pulling stretch manner
Perpendicular to the surface causing joint compression load
Parallel or tangent to a surface, causing parts to slide
Obliquely at approximately 45 degrees to the bone long axis
questions.question: Shear force is uniquely characterized by being directed:
questions.explanation: Shear is a force directed parallel to or tangent to a surface. It tends to cause one portion of an object to slide, displace, or shear with respect to another portion. This differs from compression (axial pressing) and tension (axial pulling). Shear forces are particularly relevant in spinal biomechanics and in joint pathomechanics.

questions.question: Tibialis anterior controls foot descent immediately after heel strike by contracting:
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior contracts eccentrically immediately after heel strike to control the rate of foot descent to the floor, preventing foot slap. In stroke rehabilitation, weakness of tibialis anterior results in foot drop during swing phase and uncontrolled foot descent after initial contact. Physiotherapy interventions include electrical stimulation, ankle-foot orthotics, and targeted neuromuscular re-education of dorsiflexors.

Middle range is the arc between the middle of the outer range and the middle of the inner range, where muscles are neither fully stretched nor contracted. Most daily activities including walking, reaching, and sit-to-stand transitions occur in this range, which is also where muscles generate the most consistent force. Middle range training is the functional training zone most relevant to ADL rehabilitation.
options: Only at joint extremes of motion
At the fully shortened position only
From full stretch to full contraction
questions.question: Most activities of daily living occur in which muscle working range:
Neutralizer muscles function to:
options: Provide isometric support to proximal joints for distal movement
Produce movement of a body segment by primary agonist action
Prevent unwanted accessory actions when agonists contract
Simultaneously contract with antagonists to stabilize the joint
Reduce velocity of movement by decelerating the body segment
questions.explanation: Neutralizer muscles prevent unwanted accessory actions that normally occur when agonists contract. For example, when only elbow flexion is desired, pronator teres acts to neutralize (counteract) the supination action of biceps brachii, which would otherwise produce both elbow flexion and forearm supination simultaneously.

options: A narrow base of support with a high center of gravity position
The line of gravity passing through the edge of the support base
A wide base of support, low COG, and central line of gravity
Equal mass distribution above and below the transverse plane
Maximum friction at the base with minimal contact surface area
questions.question: In a stable equilibrium, the most stable configuration exists when the body has:
questions.explanation: Stable equilibrium is most effectively achieved when the COG is as low as possible, the base of support (BOS) is wide, and the line of gravity falls near the center of the BOS. The classic example is supine lying. Forces acting on the body in stable equilibrium tend to restore it to its original position after displacement.

CGA does NOT replace OGA — it serves as an adjunct to aid in understanding visual impressions of a patient's gait impairment more precisely and sometimes more accurately. CGA is used as part of surgical decision-making when all conservative treatments have been exhausted and surgical intervention is being contemplated.
questions.question: Clinical Gait Analysis (CGA) is considered a substitute for OGA when:
options: All clinical conditions since CGA always provides more accurate data
OGA reliability is low due to therapist's limited experience in gait
CGA is NOT a substitute — it serves as an adjunct to OGA findings
The patient requires surgical intervention without prior conservative care
OGA is too time-consuming relative to the information provided

questions.explanation: Elasticity is the property of muscle and connective tissue enabling it to return to its original resting length following passive stretching. This property is clinically relevant in assessing tissue response to stretching interventions — elastic tissues recoil after stretch, while plastic deformation results in permanent elongation. Physiotherapists use sustained stretching techniques to promote plastic changes in shortened structures during contracture management.
questions.question: The muscle property allowing return to its original length after passive stretching is called:
Rubber-tipped crutch ferrules and wheelchair brake extensions are added to assistive devices to:
questions.explanation: Rubber-tipped ferrules on crutches and wheelchair brakes increase friction at the contact surfaces, providing safety by preventing unintended slipping and sliding. The rubber material increases the coefficient of friction compared to metal or smooth surfaces. Physiotherapists select these additions as non-pharmacological safety interventions in fall prevention programmes for patients with balance deficits.

Movements in the sagittal plane (flexion and extension) occur around a frontal (coronal) axis oriented side to side through the joint. Understanding the plane-axis relationship is fundamental for physiotherapists when selecting exercise directions and applying resistance. Errors in plane identification lead to misapplication of strengthening and mobilisation techniques.
questions.question: Movements in the sagittal plane occur around which axis:

options: Near the joint with insertion far from joint (stabilizer type)
At the midpoint of the segment with equal effort distribution
Away from the joint with insertion near to the joint (rotator)
Distal to the joint with a long tendon providing excursion
Proximal to insertion with a large moment arm for torque
questions.question: A 'spurt' muscle is defined as one whose origin is:
questions.explanation: Spurt muscles are mainly rotator muscles that have their origin away from the joint and their insertion near the joint (e.g., biceps muscle). They are primarily responsible for rotation of the bone. In contrast, shunt muscles (e.g., brachioradialis) have their origin near the joint and insertion away from the joint, functioning primarily as stabilizers.

options: Remains constant in length as myosin filament length is unchanged
Decreases in length as actin slides into the central H zone region
Increases in length as the overlap of actin and myosin increases
Disappears completely when the sarcomere reaches maximum shortening
Divides into two equal halves at peak concentric contraction force
questions.explanation: During sarcomere shortening, the A band does not change in length, indicating that the length of the myosin filaments does not change. The H zone disappears as actin filaments slide into it, the I bands shorten as actin and myosin overlap increases, and the Z lines move closer together. Actin filament length also remains constant.
questions.question: During sarcomere shortening, the A band:
Antagonist muscles primarily become active during which phase of a movement?
options: Deceleration (negative acceleration) phase of body segment motion
Acceleration phase when the agonist is generating peak force
Initial recruitment phase before the agonist reaches peak torque
The isometric holding phase at the end range of motion
Throughout the entire range of motion equally with the agonist
questions.explanation: Antagonists are primarily active during deceleration or negative acceleration of a body segment, acting eccentrically as the agonists contract concentrically. Agonists are particularly active during acceleration. Co-contraction of agonists and antagonists enhances stability at the joint that the muscles cross.

questions.question: Average velocity of walking is calculated as:
options: Step length (m) multiplied by cadence (steps per minute)
Stride length divided by the time to complete one full cycle
Cadence multiplied by stride width in the transverse plane
Distance walked divided by the number of strides completed
Step frequency multiplied by the double support percentage
questions.explanation: Average velocity (m/min) = step length (m) × cadence (steps/min). Velocity is the distance covered by the body in unit time and is usually measured in m/s or m/min. The formula demonstrates why both step length and cadence are important determinants of walking speed.

questions.question: The force-generating capacity of muscle per unit cross-sectional area equals:
questions.explanation: The force-generating capacity of muscle per physiological cross-sectional area equals 90 N/cm squared. This value is used to estimate muscle forces in biomechanical models and explains why pennate muscles with larger cross-sections produce greater absolute forces. Physiotherapists apply this concept when understanding why muscle hypertrophy from resistance training improves strength output independently of neural adaptations.

questions.question: Protraction of the scapula is synonymous with which movement term?
options: Scapular retraction (adduction) moving the shoulder girdle backward
Scapular elevation moving the shoulder girdle superiorly upward
Scapular abduction moving the shoulder girdle forward anteriorly
Scapular depression moving the shoulder girdle inferiorly downward
Scapular upward rotation during glenohumeral abduction motion
questions.explanation: Protraction is scapular abduction — the forward movement of the shoulder girdle anteriorly away from the spine. Retraction is scapular adduction — movement backward toward the spine. These movements occur in the transverse plane and are important for scapulothoracic rhythm and shoulder function.

questions.question: Increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously to generate greater muscle force is the definition of:
questions.explanation: Multiple fibre summation (spatial summation) involves recruiting additional motor units simultaneously to increase overall muscle contraction intensity. This mechanism operates according to the Henneman size principle, with slow-twitch units recruited first, followed by fast-twitch units as force demands increase. Physiotherapists apply this concept when progressively loading exercises to achieve higher force outputs in rehabilitation programmes.

questions.question: Research indicates that flexibility reduction with ageing or inactivity is primarily due to:
questions.explanation: Research demonstrates that reduction in joint flexibility results from decreased physical activity levels rather than the aging process itself. Maintaining regular stretching and movement preserves flexibility across the lifespan. This evidence supports physiotherapy programmes emphasising continued activity and regular stretching to prevent flexibility loss in sedentary patients, older adults, and those after prolonged immobilisation.

questions.question: The term 'proximal' in anatomical directional terminology means:
options: Located toward the front (anterior aspect) of the body surface
Located toward the skin surface rather than deep tissues
Located closer to the head than to the feet in the body
Located on the same side of the body as the reference point
Located closer to the trunk or to the reference point of origin
questions.explanation: Proximal means closer to the trunk or closer to the reference point (origin). Its opposite is distal, meaning away from the trunk or further from the reference point. These terms are primarily used for limb segments. For example, the shoulder is proximal to the elbow, and the elbow is proximal to the wrist.

options: Dense fibrous bands holding two bones with extremely limited motion
Articulating bones held together by a thin layer of hyaline cartilage
A fibrocartilaginous disc separating hyaline cartilage from bone
A synovial membrane lining secreting fluid for reduced friction
Periosteum-continuous fibrous tissue with eventual bony ossification
questions.question: Synchondroses differ from other amphiarthrodial joints by consisting of:
questions.explanation: Synchondroses (meaning 'held by cartilage') are amphiarthrodial joints where articulating bones are held together by a thin layer of cartilage. Examples include sternocostal joints and epiphyseal plates before ossification. They absorb shock and permit more motion than synarthrodial joints but less than diarthrodial joints.

options: Located on the same side of the body as the reference structure
Located toward the surface of the body rather than centrally
Located toward the head rather than toward the feet of the body
Located on the other (opposite) side of the body from the reference
Located below rather than above the reference point in the body
questions.question: The contralateral term in positional anatomy refers to:
questions.explanation: Contralateral means on the OTHER (opposite) side of the body from the reference point. Ipsilateral means on the SAME side. These terms are clinically important in describing symptoms, findings, and treatment targets, particularly in neurological and orthopedic rehabilitation where asymmetry between sides is a key consideration.

questions.question: A patient is told the fractured skull suture cannot be mobilised. Skull sutures are classified as:
questions.explanation: Synarthroses are fibrous, immovable joints that absorb shock but permit little or no motion, making mobilisation inappropriate. Skull sutures are the classic example, bonded by fibrous tissue that begins to ossify in early adulthood. Understanding this classification prevents inappropriate manual therapy application to inherently immovable joints.

options: SEC is already partially stretched in the active state
Active state always produces longer EMD
Muscle temperature is lower at rest
questions.question: EMD is significantly shorter when contraction is initiated from an already-active state compared to resting because the:
questions.explanation: EMD is significantly shorter when contraction is initiated from an already-active or pre-tensed state, because the Series Elastic Component is already partially stretched and force can be transmitted to bone more rapidly. This underpins physiotherapy warm-up protocols and neuromuscular training for fall prevention and sport injury prevention, where pre-activation strategies reduce the window of vulnerability before protective force generation.

Valgus describes the distal segment of a joint deviating laterally away from the midline, as in genu valgum (knock-knees) where the lower leg deviates laterally relative to the thigh. This contrasts with varus, where the distal segment deviates medially. Accurate valgus-varus documentation is critical for monitoring knee alignment, selecting bracing options, and planning surgical referrals in knee osteoarthritis management.
questions.question: Valgus deformity describes the distal joint segment:

questions.explanation: When motor neurons are destroyed, neighbouring intact nerve fibres give off collateral branches that supply the denervated muscle fibres, creating enlarged motor units called macromotor units. This compensatory reinnervation partially restores function but produces less refined motor control. Physiotherapists must account for this when setting expectations for strength and coordination recovery in post-injury rehabilitation.
questions.question: Following motor neuron injury causing partial paralysis, adjacent nerve fibres innervate paralysed fibres through:

questions.explanation: A walker (zimmer frame) is best prescribed for users with poor balance and coordination. It is also the best device to prescribe to the elderly, the obese, and for long-distance ambulation in users who lack endurance. It can be used to decrease weight bearing to both lower extremities simultaneously.
options: Has poor balance and coordination or lacks upper limb strength
Needs to bear full weight on both lower extremities immediately
Requires a device primarily to reduce weight bearing on one limb
Needs to improve lateral stability and practice stair climbing
Has strong upper limbs and good trunk stability for bipedal walking
questions.question: A walker (zimmer frame) is BEST prescribed in preference to crutches when the patient:

questions.explanation: The force-velocity relationship demonstrates that as contraction velocity increases, the maximum force a muscle can develop decreases inversely. This applies specifically to maximally activated muscle and explains why fast movements generate less force than slow ones at maximum effort. Clinically, this guides physiotherapists in prescribing high-velocity low-load versus low-velocity high-load training based on functional goals.
questions.question: As concentric contraction velocity increases, maximum force production:
Walking base (stride width) is defined as:
options: The distance between heel contact of the same foot in one cycle
The distance from initial contact to toe-off in the stance phase
The side-to-side distance between the line of step of the two feet
The anteroposterior distance traversed during one full stride cycle
The width of the foot sole contact during the loading response phase
questions.explanation: Walking base (stride width) is defined as the side-to-side distance between the line of step of the two feet. It reflects the mediolateral placement of the feet relative to each other. An excessively wide walking base may indicate balance impairment, while a narrow base may indicate a different postural strategy.

questions.question: Tropomyosin in the thin filament serves to:
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin is a tube-shaped molecule that wraps around the actin filament, fitting into a groove created by the intertwining actin helices. It prevents muscle contraction by blocking the active site on actin until the proper signal (calcium binding to troponin C) arrives to move tropomyosin aside and expose the active sites.
options: Bind calcium ions and trigger the contraction cascade in muscle
Wrap around actin and prevent muscle contraction until proper signal
Connect adjacent actin monomers to form the double helix structure
Anchor the thin filament to the Z-line through troponin-T linkage
Provide the active site for myosin cross-bridge head attachment

questions.explanation: Elevated body temperature shifts the force-velocity curve upward and to the right, producing higher maximum isometric tension and faster maximum shortening velocity. This occurs because enzymatic reactions accelerate with temperature elevation, improving cross-bridge cycling rates. Physiotherapists exploit this by using thermal modalities before exercise to temporarily enhance muscle performance in patients with limited function.
questions.question: Elevated body temperature shifts the force-velocity curve toward:
options: Higher maximum tension and velocity values

questions.explanation: Terminal stance and pre-swing (push-off) phases generate forward propulsion primarily through concentric activity of the ankle plantarflexors, particularly gastrocnemius and soleus. This propulsive force is the largest contributor to forward progression in normal gait. Weakness of ankle plantarflexors significantly reduces gait speed and efficiency, requiring specific rehabilitation targeting.
questions.question: Forward propulsion during normal gait is primarily generated during:
Tendon action of a two-joint muscle refers to:
options: Active contraction generating force transmitted via the tendon
Passive resistance to muscle stretch causing joint compression
Elastic energy storage in the tendon during eccentric loading
Active shortening of the tendon during concentric contraction
Passive tension without active contraction producing joint motion
questions.explanation: Tendon action is a passive tension without active muscle contraction that may produce movement at a joint when the muscle is elongated over two or more joints simultaneously. For example, if the wrist is allowed to flex by gravity, the digits will automatically extend without contraction of the finger extensors due to passive tension in the tendon.

questions.question: A body at rest remains at rest unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force. This is Newton's:
questions.explanation: Newton's first law (law of inertia) states that a body maintains its state of rest or constant velocity unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force. In clinical practice, this principle explains why increasing patient mass requires greater muscle forces to initiate and stop movements. Inertia also explains the challenge of restarting movement after prolonged immobilisation.

questions.question: The body achieves static equilibrium when:
questions.explanation: Static equilibrium requires that net force equals zero, resulting in either a stationary state or constant velocity. For upright standing, all gravitational, ground reaction, and muscular forces must sum to zero. Physiotherapists assess postural equilibrium through balance testing and treat equilibrium deficits by strengthening postural muscles, improving proprioception, and modifying the base of support through mobility aid prescription.

options: Are composed primarily of elastic fibers rather than collagen fibers
Can contract actively when stimulated by appropriate neural input
Do not respond to mechanical stress by hypertrophy or atrophy
Cannot contract but are slightly extensible and elastic passive tissues
Hypertrophy in response to stretch but atrophy under compressive load
questions.explanation: Tendons (connecting muscles to bones) and ligaments (connecting bones to other bones) are passive tissues composed primarily of collagen and elastic tissues. Like muscles, they are slightly extensible and elastic, but unlike muscles, they cannot contract. When stretched beyond their elastic limits during injury, they remain stretched and can only be returned to original length through surgery.
questions.question: Tendons and ligaments differ from muscles in that tendons and ligaments:

questions.explanation: Kinetic friction occurs between surfaces in relative motion and is responsible for shear forces on immobile patients' skin when repositioned or when they slide down the bed. This shear, combined with pressure, accelerates pressure injury formation. Physiotherapists advise on repositioning techniques, friction-reducing sheet materials, and pressure-redistributing mattresses to manage kinetic friction-related skin integrity issues.
questions.question: Friction causing skin damage in immobile patients during repositioning is classified as:
The swing phase of the gait cycle accounts for what percentage of the cycle?
options: 60-62% of the total gait cycle in normal walking speed
50% of the total gait cycle equally sharing with stance
30-35% of the total gait cycle in normal walking
25% of the total gait cycle alongside double support
38-40% of the total gait cycle in normal adult gait
questions.explanation: The swing phase accounts for 38-40% of the normal gait cycle. The stance phase, in contrast, accounts for 60-62%. The three components of the swing phase (using Rancho Los Amigos terminology) are Initial Swing, Mid-Swing, and Terminal Swing. The double support periods together account for 25% of the cycle.

questions.question: When quadriceps muscles lengthen under tension during stair descent, the type of contraction occurring is:
questions.explanation: Eccentric contraction occurs when external torque exceeds muscular torque, causing the muscle to lengthen under tension while still producing force. This occurs in the quadriceps during stair descent and in the hamstrings during the terminal swing phase of gait. Eccentric contractions generate greater forces than concentric contractions at lower metabolic cost, making them efficient for deceleration and energy absorption.

questions.question: During loading response in gait, the quadriceps contracts to control knee flexion in which mode:
questions.explanation: The quadriceps contracts eccentrically during the loading response phase of gait to control the knee flexion that occurs as body weight is accepted, preventing knee collapse. This eccentric demand is clinically important because patients with quadriceps weakness compensate with trunk lean or increased hip extension to avoid knee flexion during loading. Quadriceps eccentric strengthening is therefore fundamental to gait rehabilitation.

options: One axis with one degree of freedom in a single plane
Three axes with three degrees of freedom in all planes
No axes, with only limited non-axial translational gliding
Two or more axes but fewer than three planes simultaneously
Two axes with two degrees of freedom in two cardinal planes
questions.explanation: Biaxial joints allow motion around two axes of rotation and have two degrees of freedom. They include condyloid (ovoid/ellipsoidal) and saddle (sellar) joints. In contrast, uniaxial joints have one degree of freedom, triaxial joints have three degrees of freedom, and non-axial joints have limited motion in any direction.
questions.question: In joint classification by motion capability, a biaxial joint allows motion around:

questions.explanation: Muscles create forward progression of the body by creating rotations of the lower limb segments using concentric contractions. They also act to stabilize and support the body's COM and limbs, and will turn off when not needed to counteract ground reaction forces (GRFs), thereby conserving metabolic energy.
options: Eccentric loading to absorb ground reaction forces efficiently
Isometric holding at key points to maintain upright posture
Gravity-assisted pendular swing of the limb segments forward
Concentric contractions creating rotations of lower limb segments
Co-contraction of agonist-antagonist pairs for joint stiffness
questions.question: During gait, muscles create forward progression of the body primarily through:
The limitation of observational gait analysis (OGA) includes that it is:
questions.explanation: The limitation of observational gait analysis is that it is subjective, with accuracy dependent on the physiotherapist's skill level. Despite this, OGA remains the most common method of gait analysis in clinical practice because it requires little investment in equipment, time, and expense, and is appropriate to characterize most gait pathologies.
options: Expensive requiring specialized equipment and software processing
Unable to capture temporal and spatial parameters during analysis
Limited to use in research settings and not applicable clinically
Only applicable to patients with neurological gait deviations
Subjective with accuracy dependent on the physiotherapist's skill

questions.question: Isometric exercises are ideal for an acutely painful knee because isometric contraction occurs when:
questions.explanation: Isometric contraction occurs when the muscular torque equals the opposing resistive torque, producing zero net torque and therefore no joint movement or change in muscle length. This allows force generation without joint movement, making isometric exercises ideal for early post-surgical rehabilitation, acute injury management, and situations where joint movement is contraindicated.

questions.question: Tendons function as passive force transmitters and are correctly classified as:
questions.explanation: Tendons are slightly extensible and elastic but cannot contract voluntarily, functioning as passive force transmitters between contracting muscle and the bone it moves. Their elastic properties allow energy storage during loading and release during propulsion in the stretch-shortening cycle. In ACL graft rehabilitation, understanding tendon-to-bone healing timelines determines when progressive loading is safe without risking graft failure.

questions.question: The components of the stance phase in order using Rancho Los Amigos terminology are:
options: Heel strike, foot flat, mid-stance, heel-off, push-off sequentially
Initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance, preswing
Weight acceptance, single support, double support, push-off, pre-swing
Opposite toe-off, heel rise, opposite initial contact, toe-off sequentially
Initial contact, midstance, terminal stance, initial swing, preswing
questions.explanation: The stance phase components using Rancho Los Amigos terminology in order are: Initial Contact (heel strike), Loading Response (foot flat), Midstance, Terminal Stance, and Preswing (toe-off). These five phases together constitute the 60-62% of the gait cycle spent in stance phase.

Linear momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity. It represents the quantity of motion a body possesses and is the key variable in impulse-momentum relationships. In clinical biomechanics, momentum analysis is used to assess gait patterns, understand forces during falls, and design safe deceleration strategies in return-to-sport programmes following lower limb injury.
questions.question: Linear momentum is defined as the product of:

options: Flexion and extension in the sagittal plane of movement
Abduction and adduction in the frontal plane of motion
Rotation around the longitudinal axis in the transverse plane
Circumduction combining movements in multiple planes
Adduction bringing the distal segment toward the midline
questions.explanation: Condyloid joints have one articulating bone surface with an ovular convex shape and the other reciprocally shaped concave. They permit flexion, extension, adduction, abduction, and circumduction — but NOT axial rotation around the longitudinal axis. Examples include the 2nd to 5th metacarpophalangeal joints and radiocarpal joints.
questions.question: Condyloid (ovoid/ellipsoidal) joints are characterized by permitting all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Replace clinical observation with objective technology in all cases
Document joint ranges of motion at each phase of the gait cycle
Measure electromyographic activity of lower limb muscles only
Assist in treatment decisions for complex, poorly understood walking problems
Determine ambulatory device prescription for all patients post-injury
questions.question: The goal of Clinical Gait Analysis (CGA) is specifically to:
questions.explanation: The goal of CGA is to assist in treatment decision-making for individuals with complex and not easily understood walking problems. It also answers questions concerning bracing and medication efficacy, and assesses efficacy of surgical interventions. CGA does not replace OGA but serves as an adjunct.

In the human body, the bone serves as the rigid lever, the joint serves as the fulcrum/pivot, and the muscular contraction provides the force (effort). The load or resistance to be overcome is provided by the weight of the body segment or any external resistance being applied.
options: Bone = fulcrum, joint = effort force, muscle = load resistance
Joint = lever arm, muscle = fulcrum, bone = resistive load
Bone = lever, joint = fulcrum, muscle = effort force (E)
Muscle = fulcrum, joint = lever, bone = resistive load (R)
Bone = effort arm, joint = resistance arm, muscle = fulcrum
questions.question: In the human body, the bone, joint, and muscle correspond to lever components as follows:

options: Gliding (plane) joints permitting only non-axial translations
Ball and socket joints permitting triaxial motion
Pivot (trochoid) joints permitting uniaxial rotation only
questions.question: The atlantoaxial joint and the distal radioulnar joint share what common classification?
questions.explanation: Both the atlantoaxial joint and the distal radioulnar joint are classified as pivot (trochoid/screw) joints, permitting rotation around one axis only. They are uniaxial joints with one degree of freedom. The atlantoaxial joint allows head rotation while the distal radioulnar joint participates in pronation/supination of the forearm.

options: Zero degrees as the starting reference position for all measurements
180 degrees representing maximum extension of all joint positions
90 degrees representing the midpoint of any joint's total motion
A negative value indicating deviation from the neutral alignment
The endpoint of measurement for all sagittal plane joint motions
questions.question: In the 0-180 degrees notation system for ROM, the anatomical position represents:
questions.explanation: In the 0-180 degrees notation system (most widely used), the anatomical position represents 0 degrees as the universal starting reference point for all ROM measurements except transverse plane rotations. Motion proceeds from 0 toward 180 degrees. Three notation systems exist: 0-180, 180-0, and 360 degree systems.

questions.question: Kinetic friction, compared to sliding static friction, characteristically has:
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction has constant values that are always lesser than maximum static friction. It comes into operation once maximal static friction has been overcome. Friction is greater when surfaces are irregular and reduced when surfaces become more polished.
options: Higher values and increases with increasing velocity of the body
Equal values since both arise from the same surface interaction
Constant values that are always lower than maximum static friction
Variable values depending on the normal force and body shape
Lower values that decrease progressively as sliding velocity rises
Loading response, the early stance weight acceptance phase
Midstance, the period of single limb support during stance
Preswing, corresponding to the toe-off event in the cycle
Initial swing, the earliest phase of the limb's swing period
Terminal stance, the late stance phase before preswing begins
questions.question: The classic gait term 'heel-off' corresponds to which Rancho Los Amigos phase?
questions.explanation: In classic gait terminology, 'Heel-off' corresponds to the Rancho Los Amigos 'Terminal Stance' phase. Terminal stance begins when the heel rises and ends when the opposite foot makes initial contact. During this phase, the body moves forward over the planted forefoot, preparing for the push-off that transitions to preswing.

options: The load and the resistance point of force application
The muscle's origin and the joint it crosses functionally
The joint center and the distal insertion of the muscle tendon
The joint (fulcrum) and the point of muscle insertion (effort)
The center of gravity and the supporting base of the segment
questions.question: In the human body, the effort arm is defined as the distance between:
questions.explanation: In the human body, the effort arm is the distance between the joint (acting as the fulcrum) and the point of insertion of the muscle (where effort is applied). The load arm is the distance between the joint and the loaded part of the body. The ratio of effort arm to load arm determines the mechanical advantage of the system.

In first-class levers, the fulcrum lies between the load and the effort, as seen at the atlanto-occipital joint during neck extension. First-class levers can be either mechanically advantageous or disadvantageous depending on relative arm lengths. Physiotherapists use this to explain resistance positioning in exercise and assistive device prescription.
questions.question: In first-class levers the fulcrum is positioned:
Double support in the gait cycle refers to the period when:
options: Both feet are in the swing phase simultaneously during running
One foot is in initial contact while the other is in midstance
The body's weight is supported entirely on one limb alone
Both lower limbs are simultaneously in the terminal stance phase
Both feet are simultaneously in contact with the ground surface
questions.explanation: Double support is the period of time when both feet are in contact with the ground. It occurs twice in a gait cycle — at the beginning and end of stance phase (referred to as initial and terminal double-limb stance). The two periods of double-limb support represent 25% of the entire gait cycle. Double support is absent during running.

Biceps brachii flexing the elbow joint is the classic example of a third-class lever. The fulcrum is the elbow joint, the effort is the biceps muscle contraction at its insertion on the radius, and the load is the weight of the forearm and any held object. The effort lies between the fulcrum and the load — defining third class.
questions.question: The action of the biceps brachii flexing the elbow joint is classified as:
options: First-class lever since the joint lies between effort and load
Second-class lever since there is always mechanical advantage
Third-class lever since biceps insertion is between joint and load
A pulley system without a classifiable lever arrangement type
A compound lever of both first and third class combined

questions.question: General motion during cycling is correctly defined as a:
options: Pure rotation around a fixed axis
questions.explanation: General motion combines translational and rotational components simultaneously, as demonstrated in cycling where joints rotate while the body translates forward. Most real-world human movements are general motion rather than pure rotation or translation. Understanding this combination guides physiotherapists in selecting appropriate assessment tools and exercise interventions that replicate functional movement complexity.

questions.question: The physiotherapist explains to a patient with ruptured Achilles tendon that tendons differ from cartilage in that they:
options: Can heal and sometimes regenerate entirely
Cannot heal at all after rupture
questions.explanation: Unlike articular cartilage, tendons can not only heal following rupture but in some cases regenerate entirely. This regenerative capacity depends on adequate vascular supply, appropriate mechanical loading, and the phase of healing. Conservative physiotherapy management of Achilles tendon rupture exploits this healing potential through controlled progressive loading protocols.

Cadence is defined as the number of steps per unit time. In normal gait, cadence is approximately 100-115 steps per minute. Cadence varies among individuals and is subject to cultural and social influences. It is one of the parameters used in gait evaluation and can be computed using observational or technological methods.
questions.question: Normal cadence in gait is approximately:
options: 80-90 steps per minute in comfortable walking conditions
120-130 steps per minute in typical adult ambulation
60-70 steps per minute in normal comfortable walking
100-115 steps per minute in normal adult gait
145-160 steps per minute in comfortable adult walking

questions.question: A 'wheel and axle' arrangement in the human trunk is represented by:
options: Abdominal muscles as wheel, spinal column as axle for rotation
Ribcage as wheel, thoracic vertebrae serving as the axle
Diaphragm as wheel, lumbar spine serving as the rotational axle
Erector spinae as wheel, pelvis serving as the rotational axle
Latissimus dorsi as wheel, thoracic spine as the rotational axis
questions.explanation: In the trunk, the wheel and axle arrangement is represented by the abdominal muscles as the wheel and the spinal column as the axle around which the wheel rotates. Wheel and axle systems are designed to gain speed. Other wheel and axle examples involve rotational movements at joints where large movements of the 'wheel' correspond to smaller axle rotation.

questions.question: Having extremely low, extremely high, or asymmetrical flexibility significantly increases a patient's risk of:
questions.explanation: Injury risk increases when joint flexibility is extremely low (restricting movement), extremely high (reducing stability), or unbalanced between dominant and non-dominant limbs. All three states impair normal biomechanics and neuromuscular control. Physiotherapists routinely assess bilateral flexibility symmetry as part of injury prevention screening, particularly in athletes and post-surgical populations.

questions.question: Qualitative gait analysis appropriately guides the physiotherapist by:
questions.explanation: Qualitative analysis (observational gait assessment) identifies movement deviations and clinical patterns that direct the physiotherapist toward which specific parameters require quantitative measurement. This hierarchy of assessment is time-efficient and clinically practical, using systematic observation to formulate hypotheses that quantitative testing then confirms or refutes. Neither approach alone provides complete biomechanical understanding.

options: Concentric muscle contraction is required to maintain the direction
Isometric contraction is needed to prevent excessive joint motion
No concentric contraction is needed, though eccentric may be required
Maximum muscle force is generated to accelerate the body segment
Co-contraction of agonists and antagonists controls the movement
questions.explanation: If a movement of a lower limb joint is occurring in the SAME direction as the GRF, then NO concentric contraction is needed (though eccentric contraction may be required to control the force). If movement occurs in the OPPOSITE direction of GRF, muscles must contract concentrically to overpower the GRF.
questions.question: When a lower limb joint movement occurs in the SAME direction as the ground reaction force:
A pulley in the musculoskeletal system functions to achieve which of the following?
questions.explanation: In the body, a pulley consists of a grooved wheel turning on an axle with a cable in the groove. Pulleys serve three functions: to change the direction of force, to modify the effect of a force, and to obtain mechanical advantage. The peroneus tendon running over the lower end of the fibula is an example in the human body.
options: Amplify force by providing greater moment arm length
Change direction of force, modify effect, or gain mechanical advantage
Convert linear muscle force directly into angular joint motion
Reduce friction at tendon-bone interfaces during movement
Stabilize bone ends against shear during high-load activities

questions.question: Regular exercise results in which specific adaptations in tendons and ligaments?
questions.explanation: Like bones, tendons and ligaments respond to altered habitual mechanical stress by hypertrophying or atrophying. Regular exercise over time results in increased size and length as well as increased strength of their junctions with bones. Unlike articular cartilage, they can not only heal following rupture but in some cases regenerate entirely.
options: Decreased collagen density with increased elastic fiber proportion
Reduction in tendon cross-sectional area due to efficient remodeling
Increased size, length, and stronger junctions with the bones
Conversion from type I to type III collagen throughout the tissue
Decreased stiffness and increased compliance during loading cycles
Double upright posts joined distally by a single post with ferrule
A single forearm cuff and a single upright post with one ferrule
An axillary pad providing support in the axillary region for loading
Two points of proximal contact with both the axilla and hand grip
A wider base and longer overall length than axillary crutches normally
questions.explanation: The elbow crutch (Lofstrand/Canadian crutch) has a single forearm cuff (vinyl-coated, leather, plastic or rubber), a handgrip, and a single upright vertical post covered with a ferrule distally. In contrast, the axillary crutch has an axillary bar with axillary pad, a handgrip, and double upright vertical posts joined distally by a single post.
questions.question: The elbow crutch (Lofstrand/Canadian) differs from the axillary crutch by having:

options: All body parts moving in a straight line as in ice skating on rollers
All body parts moving at the same angular velocity around a joint
Curved motion where the path is not a straight line trajectory
Compound motion combining both translation and rotation together
Motion rapidly reversed after short excursions around equilibrium
questions.question: Linear motion in kinesiology is specifically characterized by:
questions.explanation: In linear motion (a form of translational motion), all body parts move in a straight line. Examples include ice skating and skating on rollers, where the body moves linearly along the ice. Curvilinear motion is also a form of translation, but the line of motion is curved (as in falling from a height).

The stance phase accounts for 60-62% of the normal gait cycle. The swing phase accounts for the remaining 38-40%. The two periods of double-limb support (occurring at the beginning and end of stance phase) represent 25% of the total gait cycle.
options: 60-62% of the gait cycle in normal ambulation
38-40% of the gait cycle in normal ambulation
50% of the gait cycle equally divided with swing
70-75% of the gait cycle in normal ambulation
45-48% of the gait cycle in normal ambulation
questions.question: The stance phase accounts for what percentage of the normal gait cycle?

questions.explanation: Average velocity (m/min) = step length (m) × cadence (steps/min). This formula demonstrates that walking speed is a product of both step length and cadence. To increase walking speed, one can increase step length, cadence, or both. Clinically, gait training may focus on either parameter depending on the patient's specific deficits.
questions.question: Gait velocity expressed as m/min can be calculated from which combination?
options: Step length (m) multiplied by cadence (steps per minute)
Stride length (m) divided by cadence (steps per minute)
Step length divided by gait cycle time in seconds
Cadence multiplied by double support duration percentage
Stride width multiplied by number of strides per minute

questions.question: The same change in momentum can be achieved by large force over short time OR small force over long time. This combined quantity is:
questions.explanation: Impulse (force times time) equals change in momentum, so the same momentum change can be produced by a large force over a short time or a small force over a longer time. This principle guides rehabilitation progressions — early post-injury patients use low force over longer contact times, progressing to higher force short-duration tasks as tissues adapt.

In a third-class lever, the effort is located between the fulcrum and the load, making the effort arm always shorter than the load arm. This creates a mechanical disadvantage — more effort force is required to move the load. However, third-class levers gain speed and range of motion. Biceps flexing the elbow is the classic example.
questions.question: A third-class lever always has a mechanical disadvantage because:
options: The fulcrum is positioned between the effort and the load
The effort arm is longer than the load arm in the system
The load is located between the fulcrum and the effort
The fulcrum and load coincide at the same spatial point
The effort is between the fulcrum and load, making effort arm shorter
Reduced myosin ATPase activity requiring strength training reversal
Selective hypertrophy due to tonic low-level activation patterns
Rapid atrophy that is NOT prevented by isometric exercise alone
Conversion to Type IIa fibers if the immobilization period is long
Increased oxidative enzyme concentration due to disuse adaptation
questions.explanation: Type I (slow twitch) fibers are likely to atrophy rapidly during immobilization, and this atrophy is NOT prevented by isometric exercises. In contrast, atrophy of Type II (fast twitch) fibers may be prevented by isometric contractions during immobilization. This has important clinical implications for rehabilitation after injury or surgery requiring immobilization.
questions.question: Type I fibers are particularly susceptible to which specific clinical finding during immobilization?

options: Adequate oxygen, glucose supply, and phosphocreatine availability
Normal body temperature, proper hydration, and neural drive
Motor unit synchrony, proper muscle length, and pennation angle
Neural stimulus, available calcium, and ATP for energy supply
Proper joint alignment, muscle resting length, and tendon integrity
questions.explanation: For skeletal muscle contraction to occur, three conditions are essential: there must be a neural stimulus, calcium must be available in the muscle cells (released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum), and ATP must be available for energy. The calcium binds to troponin C, exposing actin's active sites for myosin cross-bridge formation.
questions.question: For skeletal muscle contraction to occur, three essential conditions must be met, which include:

questions.explanation: Fatigued muscles lose their capacity to contribute to joint stability, making injuries significantly more common at the end of sporting activities when fatigue accumulates. This is particularly relevant for the knee and ankle joints, where muscular co-contraction plays a critical stabilising role. Physiotherapists incorporate fatigue-resistance training in late rehabilitation stages to prepare patients for real sports demands.
options: Has no effect on joint stability
questions.question: Fatigued muscles compromise joint stability primarily because fatigue:

options: 1 kg of mass at 1 meter per second squared (1 m/s²)
1 gram of mass at 9.8 meters per second squared (9.8 m/s²)
1 kg of mass at 9.8 meters per second squared (9.8 m/s²)
1 kg of mass to a velocity of 1 meter per second (1 m/s)
1 pound of mass at 1 foot per second squared (1 ft/s²)
questions.explanation: One Newton is defined as the force required to accelerate 1 kilogram of mass at 1 meter per second squared (1 m/s²), expressed as F = ma. Force has four characteristics: magnitude, direction, line of application, and point of application. Force causes a body to accelerate proportionally to the force causing the motion.
questions.question: The unit of measurement for force in the SI (metric) system is the Newton, where 1 Newton is defined as the force that accelerates:
Static flexibility differs from dynamic flexibility in that static flexibility represents:
questions.explanation: Static flexibility is ROM when a body segment is passively moved (e.g., by a physiotherapist) and is a better indication of the relative tightness or laxity of a joint in terms of injury potential. Dynamic flexibility is the ROM achievable by actively contracting the relevant muscles. Static and dynamic flexibility are independent of each other.
options: Passively achieved ROM indicating relative tightness or laxity of joint
ROM achieved by active muscular contraction during free movement
ROM recorded at maximum voluntary effort without any assistance
The instant maximum ROM at rest without any warm-up activity
Joint motion recorded during high-speed dynamic functional activities

questions.explanation: Reducing leverage involves applying resistance closer to the joint (fulcrum), which decreases the moment arm and therefore reduces the torque demands on the painful or swollen joint. This allows continuation of strengthening exercises without aggravating joint irritation. As symptoms resolve, the physiotherapist progressively increases leverage by moving resistance further from the joint to increase exercise demands systematically.
questions.question: Reducing leverage in the presence of pain and swelling means applying resistance:
options: At the end of the lever

questions.explanation: Cadence is defined as the number of STEPS per unit time. In normal gait, cadence is about 100-115 steps per minute. A stride consists of two steps (one right and one left), so stride frequency is approximately half of cadence. Cadence is subject to cultural, social, and individual variation.
options: The forward velocity of the body's center of gravity per second
The time taken to complete one full gait cycle in seconds
The distance traveled per unit time measured in meters per minute
The number of steps taken per unit time, measured in steps/minute
The number of strides completed in one minute of walking
questions.question: The term 'cadence' in gait analysis specifically refers to:
Static equilibrium requires that the sum of all torques acting on a body must equal:
questions.explanation: For a body to be in static equilibrium, three conditions must be satisfied: the sum of all vertical forces must equal zero (SFv = 0), the sum of all horizontal forces must equal zero (SFh = 0), and the sum of all torques must equal zero (ST = 0). These three conditions collectively define static equilibrium.
options: Zero, as one of three conditions for static equilibrium
The weight of the body times its height above support
The product of the base of support and center of gravity height
The net moment generated by all active muscle groups
The gravitational moment arm times the body segment mass

questions.question: PROM is generally slightly greater than AROM because:
questions.explanation: PROM (passive range of motion) is usually slightly greater than AROM because each joint has a small amount of available motion that is not under voluntary control. This extra range, known as the accessory range, can only be achieved when the patient's muscles are fully relaxed and an external force moves the joint.
options: The examiner applies greater force than voluntary muscle effort
Each joint has a small amount of motion not under voluntary control
Passive movement bypasses pain inhibition of muscular contraction
The articular surfaces are more congruent when passively positioned
Capsular slack is taken up by the examiner's manipulative technique
The quantity of matter composing a body measured in kilograms
The gravitational force on a body (Wt = mass × g), a force in Newtons
A scalar quantity with magnitude but no directional component
The product of specific weight and the volume of the body
Constant regardless of location due to its intrinsic nature
questions.question: Weight differs from mass in that weight is:
questions.explanation: Weight is the amount of gravitational force exerted on a body, calculated as mass multiplied by acceleration due to gravity (Wt = mag). Weight is a force and its real unit is the Newton (N). Unlike mass, weight varies with gravitational acceleration. A body's weight is assumed to act at its COG.

options: Body mass index with heavier children having more cartilage growth
Both height and weight equally as the child grows and develops
Hormonal levels of growth hormone and IGF-1 in adolescence
Increases in the child's height but NOT correlating with weight change
Muscle strength around the joint stimulating cartilage proliferation
questions.explanation: Articular cartilage increases as the child's height increases during normal growth, though weight change was not found to correlate with cartilage accrual at the knee. This finding suggests that skeletal lengthening, rather than body weight loading alone, drives cartilage development during childhood growth.
questions.question: Articular cartilage accrual during growth is correlated with:
Stride length is defined as the distance between:
questions.explanation: Stride length is defined as the distance between any two successive points of heel contact of the SAME foot. In normal gait, the stride length is double the step length. This is different from step length, which is the distance between corresponding successive heel contact points of the OPPOSITE feet.
options: Corresponding successive heel contact points of opposite feet
The side-to-side distance between lines of step of the two feet
Any two successive heel contact points of the same foot
The midpoint of the foot at initial contact and at toe-off
The center of gravity horizontal displacement over one full step
Equal left and right sections along a vertical midline axis
Anterior and posterior sections along a vertical coronal plane
Superior and inferior sections along a horizontal transverse plane
Medial and lateral sections along an oblique diagonal plane
Ipsilateral and contralateral sections relative to dominant side
questions.question: The sagittal plane divides the body into which two sections?
questions.explanation: The sagittal (median) plane passes vertically through the body dividing it into equal right and left sections. It is also called the anteroposterior plane. Movements in the sagittal plane occur around the frontal (coronal) axis and include flexion, extension, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion.

options: Producing synovial fluid and absorbing nutritional metabolites
Generating proprioceptive signals and resisting shear forces
Providing vascular supply and neural innervation to the joint
Synthesizing collagen and regenerating after mechanical injury
Distributing loads over a wide area and allowing minimal friction motion
questions.explanation: Articular cartilage serves two important functions: (1) it distributes loads at the joint over a wide area to reduce stress at any contact point (can reduce contact stress by 50%), and (2) it allows movement of the articulating bones with minimal friction and wear. It is a dense, white, soft, porous, permeable, and hydrated connective tissue.
questions.question: Articular cartilage serves two important biomechanical functions, which include:

options: Simultaneous flexion or extension occurs at both joints crossed
Flexion at one joint and extension at the other occur together
Isometric contraction occurs at both joints simultaneously
Eccentric lengthening happens at both joints at the same time
One joint extends while the other adducts in a combined motion
questions.question: A concurrent pattern of two-joint muscle action occurs when:
questions.explanation: A concurrent pattern occurs when simultaneous movement of flexion (or extension) occurs at two joints crossed by a two-joint muscle. In contrast, a countercurrent pattern occurs when one of the two joint muscles shortens rapidly at both joints while its antagonist lengthens correspondingly, gaining tension at both ends — e.g., rapid loss of tension in rectus femoris when hip flexes and knee extends simultaneously.

questions.question: The frontal (coronal) plane divides the body into:
questions.explanation: The frontal (coronal) plane passes vertically through the body dividing it into front (anterior) and back (posterior) sections. Movements in the frontal plane occur around the sagittal axis and include abduction/adduction, lateral flexion, elevation/depression of the shoulder girdle, and radial/ulnar deviation.
options: Equal right and left halves along the vertical midline axis
Upper and lower segments at the transverse horizontal level
Medial and lateral portions relative to the body's long axis
Ipsilateral and contralateral halves relative to movement direction

questions.explanation: Ambulatory devices are mobility devices that assist in transfer of users from one point to another and require ACTIVE participation of users during mobilization. Mobility devices (like wheelchairs) require passive participation. Ambulatory devices include parallel bars, walking sticks, tripod stands, elbow crutches, axillary crutches, zimmer frames, and wheelchairs.
options: Passive participation of users without active physical engagement
Prescription only by licensed physiotherapists and physicians
Four-point contact with the ground for maximum stability always
Active participation of users during the mobilization process
The patient to be non-weight-bearing on at least one lower extremity
questions.question: Ambulatory devices differ from mobility devices in that ambulatory devices require:
Type I fibres are highly fatigue-resistant because they possess:
questions.explanation: Type I (slow-twitch oxidative) fibres resist fatigue because of their high oxidative enzyme concentration, abundant mitochondria, and rich capillary supply supporting sustained aerobic ATP production. These characteristics make the soleus ideal for postural control and prolonged low-level activities. Physiotherapists prescribe endurance training for these fibre-type adaptations in patients with postural fatigue or early ambulation goals.

questions.question: The wheeled walker differs from the standard walker specifically in that:
options: It requires the user to lift the entire frame forward during ambulation
It has forearm supports replacing the standard handgrip design
It is designed specifically for pediatric users with smaller dimensions
The ferrules are replaced by wheels allowing rolling rather than lifting
It provides less stability than the standard walker due to its rolling base
questions.explanation: The wheeled walker has the same design as the standard walker except the ferrules are replaced by wheels. This eliminates the need to lift the frame entirely during ambulation, making it easier for users with reduced arm strength or coordination. The standard walker requires strength and grip power to lift the entire frame forward.

In concentric contraction, muscular tension produces a torque greater than the resistive torque at the joint, causing the muscle to shorten. The resulting joint movement is in the direction of the net torque generated by the muscle. The external force (load) is lesser than the muscle's internal force in concentric contraction.
questions.question: Concentric muscular contraction produces joint movement in the direction of:
options: The opposing resistance force applied by the external load
Gravity, since concentric contraction requires no energy output
The antagonist muscle group's line of pull across the joint
The net torque generated by the contracting muscle group
The line of gravity regardless of the muscle's line of pull

questions.explanation: The endomysium covers individual muscle fibers and helps prevent the signal for muscle activation from spreading from one muscle fiber to an adjacent fiber. This allows fine control of activation of individual fibers. The epimysium covers the whole muscle and the perimysium covers bundles of fibers (fasciculi). Together, these sheaths also make up the muscle's elastic component.
options: Transmitting force from the contractile component to the tendon
Providing the parallel elastic component of the muscle unit
Supplying nutrients and oxygen directly to each muscle fiber
Preventing muscle fiber rupture during eccentric overload exercise
Preventing activation signals from spreading between adjacent fibers
questions.question: The endomysium surrounding individual muscle fibers serves the specific function of:
Which of the following BEST represents a body in static equilibrium?
questions.explanation: A body in static equilibrium is completely at rest — it is motionless. Supine lying is the classic example of stable static equilibrium. Running and walking involve acceleration and deceleration, while a rolling ball or rotating joint may represent dynamic equilibrium but not static equilibrium.
options: A person running at constant speed on a level treadmill
A person lying supine, completely motionless on a flat surface
A ball rolling at uniform speed across a frictionless plane
A joint rotating at constant angular velocity during exercise
A person walking at comfortable speed with consistent cadence

questions.explanation: AROM (active range of motion) is the amount of joint motion attained by an individual during unassisted joint motion.
