Information obtained from AROM includes the patient's willingness to move, muscle strength, coordination, and the available ROM. PROM, in contrast, provides information about articular surface integrity and soft tissue extensibility.
options: Willingness to move, muscle strength, coordination, and ROM
Articular cartilage integrity and synovial membrane health
Capsular and ligamentous extensibility and joint laxity
Intra-articular pathology and effusion within the joint space
Passive extensibility of muscles and connective tissue length
questions.question: The AROM obtained during goniometric measurement specifically provides information about:

questions.explanation: Extensibility is the ability of muscle to be passively stretched beyond its normal resting length. Limited extensibility causes restricted passive ROM as encountered in hamstring tightness, and is assessed using straight leg raise or knee extension measurements. Physiotherapy interventions targeting extensibility include sustained static stretching, proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation techniques, and progressive passive ROM exercises.
options: Returned to original length after stretch
questions.question: Extensibility is the muscle property defined as the ability to be:
Arthrokinematics, as distinct from osteokinematics, refers to the:
questions.explanation: Arthrokinematics refers to the movement of joint surfaces — specifically slides (glides), spins, and rolls occurring at the articular surfaces. Osteokinematics, in contrast, describes the movement of the shafts of bones, usually expressed as rotatory motion in one of the three cardinal planes.
options: Movement of bone shafts described in cardinal planes and axes
Movement of joint surfaces including slides, spins, and rolls
Range of joint motion measured by standard goniometric methods
Force produced at the joint during active muscular contraction
Angular displacement of body segments around fixed joint axes

questions.question: During post-fracture ankle assessment, the physiotherapist asks the patient to bring the dorsum of the foot toward the shin. This movement is:
questions.explanation: Dorsiflexion decreases the angle between the dorsal foot and the anterior tibia, occurring in the sagittal plane around a frontal axis. It is assessed routinely after ankle fractures and Achilles tendon pathology. Limited dorsiflexion indicates tightness of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex or posterior capsule restriction.

options: Fast oxidative-glycolytic, combining speed with fatigue resistance
Slow oxidative with small diameter and high endurance capacity
Fast glycolytic with few mitochondria and rapid fatigue onset
Intermediate in speed only, but predominantly glycolytic in nature
Fast twitch with purely aerobic metabolism and white coloration
questions.explanation: Type IIa fibers are fast oxidative-glycolytic (FOG) fibers — they share characteristics intermediate between Type I and Type IIb. They have a fast contraction velocity, very high capacity for generating ATP by oxidative metabolism, and are resistant to fatigue. They are used during sustained power activities such as sprinting or repeated near-maximal lifts.
questions.question: Muscle fibers classified as Type IIa are characterized by being:

questions.explanation: Factors influencing joint flexibility include the shapes of the articulating bone surfaces, intervening muscle or fatty tissue that may terminate movement at the extreme of ROM, and laxity/extensibility of collagenous tissues and muscles crossing the joint. The number and type of motor units are neuromuscular factors affecting strength, not flexibility.
questions.question: Factors influencing joint flexibility include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: The shapes of the articulating bone surfaces at the joint
The number and type of motor units within the crossing muscles
Laxity and extensibility of collagenous tissues and muscles crossing
Intervening muscle or fatty tissue that may terminate movement
The joint-specific nature of flexibility limiting generalizations across joints

questions.question: The primary factor increasing joint stability in a patient with generalised hypermobility is:
questions.explanation: Strong ligaments and surrounding muscles are the primary factors increasing joint stability by resisting displacement of the articulating bone ends. In hypermobility syndromes, ligamentous laxity reduces passive restraint, making active neuromuscular stabilisation through targeted muscle strengthening the cornerstone of treatment. The physiotherapist emphasises proprioceptive and co-contraction training to compensate for passive insufficiency.

options: Blood flow to the muscle only
Distance from joint and angle of pull
questions.explanation: A muscle's moment arm depends on both the distance from its attachment to the joint axis of rotation and the angle between its line of pull and the bone. The moment arm determines how efficiently a muscle converts tension into joint torque. Changes in joint angle alter the moment arm, explaining why muscle strength tests show angle-dependent torque curves which physiotherapists use to identify weak points in the ROM.
questions.question: A muscle's moment arm is primarily determined by:

options: 50% of the user's weight for moderate weight bearing conditions
75% of the user's weight for near full weight bearing scenarios
10% of the user's weight for touch-down weight bearing only
25% of the user's weight when minimal stability is needed
40% of the user's weight in post-operative rehabilitation settings
questions.question: A standard cane can typically support up to what percentage of a user's body weight?
questions.explanation: A standard cane is typically used when minimal stability is needed and can support up to 25% of a user's weight. Canes are also known as walking sticks and are the most basic ambulatory assistive device. They have a horizontal bar with a crook or T-shape handgrip at one end and the tip covered by a ferrule.

options: Using force plates to quantify the ground reaction force patterns
Employing electromyography to confirm clinical gait observations
Using video-tape recording to allow repeated review of gait
Training the patient to perform a standardized walking protocol
Having multiple physiotherapists observe and vote on deviations
questions.explanation: The reliability of observational gait analysis (OGA) can be improved by using video-tape recording, which allows repeated review of gait parameters. Additionally, ROM at various joints can be examined through goniometric measurements on screen. Video recording partially compensates for the subjective nature of real-time visual observation.
questions.question: Reliability of observational gait analysis can be specifically improved by:
Type I muscle fibres are preferred for endurance activities because they have the:
questions.explanation: Type I (slow-twitch oxidative) fibres possess the highest mitochondrial density and oxidative enzyme concentration, supporting sustained aerobic metabolism with minimal fatigue. Their dark red colour reflects high myoglobin content. In rehabilitation, endurance-based low-load exercises preferentially recruit Type I fibres, making them ideal for early strengthening in deconditioned patients before progressing to higher-intensity work.

Contractility is the ability of muscle to contract and develop internal tension or force against resistance when appropriately stimulated. In upper motor neuron lesions, spasticity increases the neural drive to contractile elements, heightening resistance to passive stretch and producing increased resting tone. Physiotherapy management of spasticity targets the contractile response through positioning, stretching, functional electrical stimulation, and task-specific training.
options: Develop tension against resistance when stimulated
Respond to external chemical stimuli only
Return to original length after stretch
questions.question: Contractility is the muscle property defined as the ability to:

options: Can support 100% of body weight unlike canes during all activities
Require less coordination and upper limb strength than walking sticks
Are lighter and more portable than standard walking canes or sticks
Provide more proprioceptive feedback through the upper extremity
Improve balance, improve lateral stability, and can be used for stair climbing
questions.explanation: Advantages of crutches include: reducing weight bearing on one lower limb, improving balance, improving lateral stability, and the ability to be used for stair climbing. Disadvantages include requiring upper limb support, coordination, and trunk stability. Crutches have two contact points with the body, making them more stabilizing than canes.
questions.question: The advantage of crutches over canes for improving lateral stability is that crutches:

questions.explanation: Intrinsic muscles both originate and insert within the body part they act upon (e.g., small hand muscles), while extrinsic muscles arise outside or proximal to the part they move. In spinal cord injury rehabilitation, understanding this distinction helps identify which muscles remain innervated and accessible for functional retraining versus which require substitution strategies or orthotic support.
questions.question: Intrinsic muscles differ from extrinsic muscles because intrinsic muscles:
options: Are always larger than extrinsic muscles
Arise from outside the part they move
Are located within the body part they act upon
Have only one point of attachment
Never cross more than one joint
Study of joint force and resistance measurement methods
Bone alignment and structural deformity classification
Limb position in space relative to gravitational reference
Electromechanical analysis of joint kinematics during motion
questions.explanation: Goniometry is derived from two Greek words: gonia meaning angle and metron meaning measure. It is the technique of measuring angles, specifically those created at human joints by the bones of the body. It is an important part of comprehensive evaluation of joints and surrounding soft tissues.
questions.question: Goniometry is a technique derived from Greek words meaning:

questions.explanation: Adult axillary crutches range from 48 to 60 inches (122–153 cm). They are available in pediatric, youth, adult, and tall adult sizes. In contrast, adult walkers have a height range of 32 to 37 inches (81–92 cm). Most canes are usually between 25 and 40 inches long.
questions.question: The adult axillary crutch height ranges from approximately:
options: 48 to 60 inches (122–153 cm) in adult standard sizing range
32 to 37 inches (81–92 cm) in adult standard sizing range
60 to 72 inches (152–183 cm) in adult standard sizing range
24 to 32 inches (61–81 cm) in adult standard sizing range
36 to 48 inches (91–122 cm) in adult standard sizing range
Inversely related to contact area so smaller joints are more stable
Greater with larger contact area between articulating bone surfaces
Independent of contact area but determined only by ligament laxity
Dependent on contact area only during high-speed dynamic activities
Proportional to contact area squared for all synovial joint types
questions.question: Joint stability, as a factor of contact area, is stated as:
questions.explanation: Contact area between articulating bone surfaces is one of the factors influencing joint stability. The larger the contact area between the articulating bones, the more stable the joint. Some people have more or less stable joints due to slight anatomical variations in the shape and size of the articulating bone surfaces.

Muscular strength is specifically defined as the ability of a given muscle or muscle group to generate torque at a particular joint, derived from both the amount of tension the muscle can develop and its moment arm length. This definition is clinically applied in torque measurement using dynamometry and guides loading parameters in progressive resistance exercise programmes.
questions.question: Muscular strength is specifically defined as the ability to generate:

questions.explanation: Active insufficiency occurs when a two-joint muscle cannot shorten enough to produce full range of motion at all joints it crosses simultaneously, because it has run out of contractile range. Rectus femoris exemplifies this when trying to achieve full knee flexion with full hip flexion. Physiotherapists design rehabilitation programmes that account for two-joint muscle length limitations.
questions.question: A patient cannot fully flex the hip while simultaneously fully flexing the knee. This failure to achieve full ROM at both joints is called:
Warm-up reduces electromechanical delay because elevated muscle temperature:
questions.explanation: Warm-up reduces electromechanical delay by increasing temperature-dependent enzyme activity, enhancing nerve conduction velocity, and reducing Series Elastic Component stiffness. These changes collectively accelerate force transmission from contractile element to bone. Physiotherapists use structured warm-up protocols for EMD reduction as part of injury prevention, particularly before high-speed activities demanding rapid protective muscle activation.
options: Has no proven effect on EMD
Reduces EMD and enhances muscle function
Biochemical changes in collagen cross-linking from the aging process
Reduced physical activity levels rather than the aging process itself
Progressive fibrosis of the articular cartilage and joint capsule
Calcification of the joint capsule and surrounding soft tissues
Age-related decrease in synovial fluid production and viscosity
questions.question: Reduction in joint flexibility with aging is attributed to:
questions.explanation: Reduction in joint flexibility with aging is due to reduced levels of physical activity and not to changes caused by the aging process itself. This distinction is clinically important because it suggests that age-related inflexibility is potentially preventable and reversible through appropriate physical activity interventions.

The sagittal plane passes vertically through the body, dividing it into equal right and left halves. Flexion and extension movements at most joints occur in this plane around a frontal axis. Physiotherapists must distinguish this from the frontal (coronal) plane and transverse (horizontal) plane when prescribing planar-specific exercises or interpreting movement analysis data.
questions.question: The plane that divides the body into right and left halves is the:

options: Hamstrings unable to stretch fully during straight leg raise
Finger flexors unable to make a tight fist with the wrist flexed
Quadriceps unable to fully extend the knee in terminal range
Hip flexors unable to reach full range when knee is extended
Gastrocnemius unable to plantarflex with the knee extended
questions.question: Active insufficiency of a two-joint muscle is best exemplified by:
questions.explanation: Active insufficiency occurs when a two-joint muscle cannot shorten to the extent required to produce full range of motion at all joints it crosses simultaneously. The classic example is the finger flexors being unable to produce as tight a fist when the wrist is flexed as when the wrist is in neutral position, because the finger flexors are already shortened over the wrist.

Articular cartilage has little or no intrinsic ability to heal or regenerate once damaged because it lacks direct blood supply and contains few repair cells. Injuries therefore tend to progress toward osteoarthritis. Rehabilitation must aim to reduce joint loading, maintain surrounding muscle strength, and prevent further cartilage degradation through appropriate exercise selection.
questions.question: The primary concern in rehabilitation when articular cartilage is damaged is:
Gait is most comprehensively defined as:
options: The rhythmic alternating swing of the lower limbs during walking
A series of rhythmical alternating movements of trunk and limbs producing forward COG progression
The forward displacement of the center of pressure during ambulation
The ground reaction force pattern generated during bipedal locomotion
Sequential stance and swing phases occurring at 60% and 40% ratios
questions.explanation: Gait is defined as a series of rhythmical, alternating movements of the trunk and limbs that result in the forward progression of the center of gravity. It can also be described as the manner of walking or stepping, bearing, or carriage while moving.

options: Combination of flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation
Rotation of the forearm to bring the palm from supination to pronation
Movement of the thumb across the palm toward the little finger
Lateral flexion of the trunk combining with forward trunk flexion
Horizontal movement of the arm medially across the frontal plane
questions.explanation: Circumduction is a combination of flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, and rotation — a composite movement creating a cone of motion. It is possible at ball-and-socket joints (hip, shoulder), condyloid joints (metacarpophalangeal, radiocarpal), and saddle joints (CMC of thumb). The distal end of the limb traces a circular path.
questions.question: Circumduction is best defined as:

options: At the level of the umbilicus in the midabdominal region
Midway between the hips, a few centimeters in front of S2
At the level of the posterior superior iliac spine bilaterally
At the level of L3 between the two anterior superior iliac spines
At the level of the greater trochanters of the femora bilaterally
questions.explanation: The center of gravity (COG) during walking is located midway between the hips, a few centimeters in front of the second sacral segment (S2). Least energy consumption occurs when the COG travels in a straight line. Determinants of gait act to minimize vertical and lateral oscillation of the COG to conserve energy.
questions.question: The center of gravity during walking is located approximately:

questions.explanation: Ball-and-socket joints such as the hip and shoulder permit rotations in all three planes, making them triaxial joints with three degrees of freedom. This mobility allows flexion-extension, abduction-adduction, and internal-external rotation. Knowledge of joint classification guides the physiotherapist in choosing appropriate therapeutic movements and assessing functional restrictions.
questions.question: The hip joint is capable of movement in three planes. This joint type is classified as:

questions.explanation: Eccentric contraction acts as a braking mechanism to control movement speed by resisting and absorbing force when external torque exceeds muscular torque. This energy absorption protects tendons and joint structures from impact loading. Eccentric exercises are prescribed in tendinopathy rehabilitation because they promote tendon collagen remodelling and improve load tolerance of the musculotendinous unit.
questions.question: The primary mechanical function of eccentric contraction in patellar tendinopathy rehabilitation is:

options: It can be used for stair climbing with maximum safety guaranteed
It provides the least amount of coordination demand for users
It can be prescribed to any patient regardless of weight or diagnosis
It enables the patient to practice gait with minimal therapist input
It provides maximum stability and creates confidence while reducing fear of falling
questions.explanation: The parallel bar provides maximum stability (the patient is positioned between two bars allowing additional stability), requires the least amount of coordination, and is the best device to practice ambulation at the onset of training. It creates confidence in the patient and reduces fear of falling, making it optimal for initial ambulatory training.
questions.question: The parallel bar provides which advantage that makes it most suitable for initiating ambulatory training?

questions.explanation: Type IIB (fast glycolytic) fibres contain high glycolytic enzyme concentrations supporting rapid anaerobic ATP production, but have few mitochondria and low oxidative capacity. This makes them powerful but highly susceptible to fatigue when anaerobic substrates deplete. In hamstring rehabilitation, the physiotherapist addresses both fast-twitch power capacity and fatigue resistance through combined high-intensity and moderate-intensity training components.
options: Slow twitch rate and low speed
High glycolytic and low oxidative capacity
questions.question: Type IIB fibres fatigue most rapidly because they have:

options: Lock at pre-set intervals to ensure measurement reproducibility
Measure torque generated at the joint during passive motion
Remain parallel to the stationary arm throughout measurement
Automatically reset to zero degrees at the anatomical position
Move freely over the goniometer body during joint measurement
questions.explanation: The moving arm of the universal goniometer is attached to the fulcrum at the center of the goniometer's body by a screw-like device that allows the arm to move freely over the body. The stationary arm cannot be moved independently as it is a structural part of the goniometer body. Arms may vary from 1 to 16 inches in length.
questions.question: The movable arm of the universal goniometer is attached to the fulcrum by a device that allows it to:

questions.explanation: Passive insufficiency occurs when a two-joint or multi-joint muscle is unable to stretch to the extent required for full range of motion in the opposite direction at all the joints it crosses. An example is the limited wrist extension possible when fingers are fully extended, as the extensor digitorum longus is on full stretch over both joints.
options: Cannot shorten enough to complete full concentric movement range
Generates insufficient force due to being in the outer range
Fails to activate due to inadequate neural motor unit drive
Cannot stretch enough to allow full ROM in the opposite direction
Becomes fatigued after prolonged low-intensity eccentric activity
questions.question: Passive insufficiency occurs when a two-joint muscle:

questions.explanation: The knee menisci are examples of articular fibrocartilage that serve multiple roles: distribution of loads over joint surfaces, improvement of the fit of the articulating surfaces, limitation of translation (slip) of one bone relative to another, protection of the periphery, lubrication, and shock absorption during dynamic activities.
options: Load distribution, fit improvement, and limiting translational motion
Active stabilization through muscular attachment on meniscal tissue
Producing lubricin and hyaluronic acid for synovial fluid formation
Acting as a secondary bone end to increase bony joint congruence
Providing proprioceptive afferent signals to the spinal cord alone
questions.question: The knee menisci as examples of fibrocartilage serve the function of:

options: Fully stretched position to midpoint of the available full range
Midpoint of the full range to full relaxation position eccentrically
Midpoint of full range to full contraction (shortest position)
Resting length to the midpoint of maximum lengthening
Full contraction (inner range) to the resting length position
questions.explanation: A muscle is working in the inner range when it contracts concentrically from the midpoint of the full range to full contraction (shortest position). Alternatively, eccentric inner range work occurs from full contraction back to the midpoint. Inner range exercises are used to gain or maintain movement in the direction of muscle pull and to train extensor muscles for joint stabilization.
questions.question: Inner range of muscle work occurs when a muscle contracts concentrically from:

questions.explanation: Biomechanics is the investigation of human movements by means of concepts of classical physics and their derivatives in the practical arts of engineering. It operates on the premise that the human body functions as a machine comprising a multilever system subject to classical laws of physics.
options: Psychological and sociocultural dimensions of purposeful activity
Developmental changes in movement quality across the lifespan
Neurophysiological control mechanisms of voluntary motor action
Structural and functional interrelation of musculoskeletal tissues
Concepts of classical physics and their engineering derivatives
questions.question: Biomechanics is most precisely described as the investigation of human movement through:

questions.explanation: Inertia is the tendency for a body to maintain its current state of motion whether at rest or moving at constant velocity. Mechanically, inertia implies resistance to acceleration. It has no unit of measurement and is directly proportional to the mass of a body — heavier bodies have greater inertia.
questions.question: Inertia in mechanics is best defined as a body's resistance to:
options: Gravitational pull that acts at the center of gravity
Frictional forces at the interface between two surfaces
Acceleration, being directly proportional to body mass
Compressive load applied axially along the body segment
Rotational torque generated by eccentric muscular force

questions.explanation: The moment arm (also called force arm or lever arm) is the shortest distance between the force's line of action and the axis of rotation. It is used in calculating torque: T = F × d(perpendicular). A force directed through the axis of rotation produces no torque since the moment arm equals zero in that case.
options: Angular velocity times the radius of the rotating segment
Product of applied force and the resulting joint displacement
Cross product of the position vector and the force vector
Ratio of the resistive to the effort force in lever systems
Force arm or lever arm, being the shortest distance to axis
questions.question: The 'moment arm' in torque calculation is also known as the:

questions.explanation: Before issuing an ambulatory device, the clinician must check that the ferrules (rubber tips) and wheels are not worn to the point where no tread is showing or not aligned. Ferrules act as friction devices, and if worn out, minimal friction creates a potential risk factor for fall. Other checks include padding condition, matching pairs, structural integrity, and tight nuts/bolts.
questions.question: The most critical rule for a clinician before issuing an ambulatory device relates to checking:
options: Ferrule and wheel condition to ensure sufficient friction and tread
The patient's grip strength to ensure adequate handling ability
The patient's ability to perform the gait pattern independently
Insurance authorization and documentation of medical necessity
The patient's balance on the device before releasing independently

questions.question: The inferior tibiofibular joint is correctly classified as which type of joint?
questions.explanation: The inferior tibiofibular joint (inferior tibiofibular ligament) is a syndesmosis — a synarthrodial joint where dense fibrous tissue bands hold the bones together permitting only extremely limited movement. Other examples of syndesmoses include the coracoacromial joint, the mid-radioulnar joint, and the mid-tibiofibular joint.
options: A synchondrosis held by hyaline cartilage between the bone ends
A symphysis with a fibrocartilaginous disc between the bones
A syndesmosis held together by dense fibrous ligamentous bands
A diarthrosis (synovial joint) with a small articular cavity
A hinge joint permitting slight flexion and extension motion

questions.question: Symphyses differ from synchondroses in that symphyses have:
options: Hyaline cartilage lining the entire articular surface directly
No intervening tissue between the two opposing bony surfaces
A complete synovial membrane and articular cartilage covering
Only fibrocartilage without any hyaline cartilage component
Thin plates of hyaline cartilage separating a fibrocartilaginous disc from bone
questions.explanation: Symphyses are amphiarthrodial joints in which thin plates of hyaline cartilage separate a fibrocartilaginous disc from the bone. Examples include vertebral joints and the pubic symphysis. Synchondroses, in contrast, have articulating bones held together directly by a thin layer of hyaline cartilage without a fibrocartilaginous disc.

options: Maximum force output of the muscle at optimal fiber length
The product of the moment arm and the muscle's physiological cross-section
Zero, meaning neither agonist nor antagonist is generating force
Zero because the muscle torque equals the opposing resistive torque
Twice the gravitational torque ensuring joint stability during load bearing
questions.explanation: Isometric contraction occurs when the opposing torque at the joint equals the torque produced by the muscle, resulting in a net torque of zero. The muscle length remains unchanged and no joint movement occurs. When muscles on opposite sides of a joint simultaneously contract isometrically, the cross-sectional area of the tense muscles increases.
questions.question: Isometric contraction occurs when the net torque at the joint equals:

options: The effort (calf muscle) is located between fulcrum and load
The fulcrum (metatarsal head) is between effort and body weight
The muscle insertion is closer to the joint than the load is
The load (body weight) is between the fulcrum and the effort
The effort arm is always shorter than the resistance arm
questions.question: The gastrocnemius/soleus complex during ankle plantarflexion is classified as a second-class lever because:
questions.explanation: In plantarflexion of the ankle by the gastrocnemius/soleus, the metatarsophalangeal joints are the fulcrum, the calf muscles provide the effort (inserting at the calcaneus, away from the fulcrum), and the body weight (load) is transmitted through the ankle joint, which lies between the fulcrum and the effort. This places the load between fulcrum and effort — a second-class arrangement.

questions.question: Dorsiflexion at the ankle is defined as:
questions.explanation: Dorsiflexion is defined as bringing the toes toward the tibia (anterior shin), thereby reducing the angle between the dorsum of the foot and the anterior tibia. Its opposite is plantarflexion (pointing the toes to the floor). Both occur in the sagittal plane around the frontal (transverse) axis at the talocrural joint.
options: Pointing the toes inferiorly away from the shin in plantarflexion
Inward rotation of the sole of the foot in the frontal plane
Bringing the toes toward the tibia, reducing the ankle angle
Outward rotation of the sole of the foot away from the midline
Extension of the toes at the metatarsophalangeal joints only

questions.question: Dynamic flexibility must be sufficient specifically to ensure:
questions.explanation: Dynamic flexibility — the ROM achievable by actively contracting the relevant muscles — must be sufficient not to restrict the ROM needed for daily living, even though static flexibility is a better indicator of injury potential. Static and dynamic flexibility are independent, so both should be assessed in clinical practice.
options: ROM adequate for the requirements of daily living activities
Maximal range in all planes exceeding functional requirements
Symmetry between dominant and non-dominant joint motion
ROM comparable to static flexibility in all joints tested
Range exceeding the 90th percentile for the patient's age group

questions.explanation: A motor unit is defined as a single motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers innervated by that motor neuron. All fibers in a motor unit are of the same type. Motor units are typically confined to one muscle and localized within that muscle. A single mammalian motor unit may contain from 100 to 2000 fibers.
options: All motor neurons innervating a single skeletal muscle entirely
A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates
A group of motor neurons controlling a single movement pattern
All fast-twitch fibers within one fasciculus of a given muscle
A motor neuron, its axon, and the single muscle fiber it contacts
questions.question: A motor unit is defined as:

questions.explanation: Medial refers to a direction or movement toward the midline of the body, while lateral refers to movement away from it. Accurate use of directional terminology is essential for documenting postural deviations and movement impairments. Confusion between medial and lateral can lead to errors in treatment planning.
questions.question: The positional term describing movement toward the body midline is:

options: The acquisition of culturally specific movement patterns in sport
Growth, physical development, nutrition, and the aging process
Neurological control of motor patterns and reflex integration
Psychological aspects of self-image and cultural communication
Pathological movement resulting from neuromuscular disorders
questions.question: Developmental kinesiology studies the relationship of kinesiology to:
questions.explanation: Developmental kinesiology studies the relationship of kinesiology to growth, physical development, nutrition, and aging. It examines how movement capabilities change across the lifespan from infancy through old age. This branch complements exercise physiology and structural-functional kinesiology within the broader field.

questions.question: Crutches are considered better ambulatory devices for stabilization than walking sticks because:
questions.explanation: Crutches have two contacts with the body (hand and elbow, or hand and axilla) which makes them better ambulatory devices for stabilization compared to canes, which have only one contact with the body (hand). Crutches are the most commonly prescribed ambulatory devices and are used in pairs.
options: They provide four points of floor contact through their broad base
They transfer force through the forearm rather than the wrist
They have two contact points with the body (hand and elbow/axilla)
They can support up to 100% of body weight unlike walking sticks
Their bilateral use creates a more stable base of support in all planes

questions.explanation: The three components of the swing phase in Rancho Los Amigos terminology in correct order are: Initial Swing (from toe-off), Mid-Swing (limb advances past the stance limb), and Terminal Swing (limb decelerates before initial contact). These three phases together constitute the 38-40% of the gait cycle in swing.
options: Pre-swing, initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing phases
Toe-off, limb advancement, foot clearance, terminal swing
Initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing in correct sequence
Loading response, initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing
Pre-swing, limb unloading, mid-swing, terminal swing phases
questions.question: The components of the swing phase in Rancho Los Amigos terminology, in correct order, are:
Most joints in the human body function as which class of lever predominantly?
options: Exclusively first class levers providing maximum force output
Exclusively second class levers providing mechanical advantage
Equal distribution between all three lever classes throughout
A combination of second and third class with equal prevalence
Third class levers are most prevalent, with first class also common
questions.explanation: Most human body joints function as either first or third class levers, with third class being most prevalent. First-class levers can provide speed or force advantage; second-class levers always provide force advantage; third-class levers (most common) always require greater effort than load, providing speed and range at the cost of force.

questions.question: After lumbar disc surgery, the physiotherapist classifies intervertebral discs as:
questions.explanation: Intervertebral discs form amphiarthroses — slightly movable joints that absorb shock and permit more motion than synarthroses while lacking a full synovial cavity. In rehabilitation after disc surgery, understanding this classification helps set realistic expectations for spinal mobility restoration.

questions.question: Synarthroses are joints that permit little or no motion and are best exemplified by:
options: The pubic symphysis allowing slight movement during childbirth
Sutures of the skull, the only pure synarthrosis in humans
The inferior tibiofibular joint permitting minimal torsional play
The epiphyseal plate prior to ossification in the growing child
The sternocostal joints between the sternum and costal cartilage
questions.explanation: Synarthroses (syn = together; arthron = joint) are immovable joints that can absorb shock but permit little or no motion. Sutures of the skull are the only pure example of suture-type synarthroses in humans. The fibrous tissue between the bones begins to ossify in early adulthood eventually becoming completely replaced by bone.

Ambulatory device pairs should always be matching pairs — a clinician should not issue a mismatched pair. Uneven ambulatory devices lead to poor posture which can result in musculoskeletal disorders. This is one of the pre-issuance checks a clinician must perform, along with checking ferrule condition, padding, structural integrity, and tight nuts/bolts.
options: Inability to perform axillary weight bearing on the affected limb
Reduced friction between crutch ferrule and the floor surface
Excessive pressure on the axilla creating brachial plexus injury
Poor posture due to uneven height leading to musculoskeletal disorders
Reduced confidence in the patient reducing compliance with the device
questions.question: A mismatched pair of crutches issued by a clinician would most likely result in:
The structural feature that makes hinge joints highly stable is:
questions.explanation: In hinge joints, strong collateral ligaments restrict movement to a planar hinge-like motion around one axis. The ligamentous constraint, combined with the bony congruity between the convex and concave surfaces, contributes to stability. Examples are the ulnohumeral and interphalangeal joints, which are inherently more stable than ball-and-socket joints.
options: The ball-and-socket shape providing circumferential bony support
The intervertebral disc absorbing compressive and shear forces
Strong collateral ligaments restricting movement to planar hinge motion
Articular cartilage thickness providing maximum load distribution
Reciprocally shaped surfaces with high contact area throughout ROM
Outward lateral rotation of the sole of the foot externally
Dorsiflexion combined with abduction of the forefoot segment
Plantarflexion combined with abduction at the subtalar joint
Eversion with abduction and dorsiflexion in combined movement
Inward medial rotation of the sole of the foot toward the midline
questions.question: Inversion of the foot is defined as:
questions.explanation: Inversion is the inward (medially directed) rotation of the sole of the foot. Eversion is the outward (laterally directed) rotation of the sole. These movements occur primarily at the subtalar (talocalcaneal) joint. Inversion and eversion take place in the horizontal/frontal plane depending on the classification system used.

options: Fully stretched position to midpoint concentrically
questions.question: Outer range exercises are prescribed for post-stroke extensor weakness because outer range works the muscle from:
questions.explanation: Outer range contraction occurs from the fully stretched muscle position to the midpoint of full range during concentric work. These exercises are prescribed for muscle re-education because they challenge the neuromuscular system at elongated positions where motor control is most impaired. They train muscles at their weakest functional point.

questions.question: Gait kinetics is defined as the study of:
options: Joint angles and segment positions throughout the gait cycle
Forces and moments that cause movement during walking
Temporal and spatial parameters such as step and stride lengths
Electromyographic activity of muscles during the gait cycle
Visual observation of body posture and movement patterns
questions.explanation: Gait kinetics is the study of the forces and moments that cause movement during walking. It focuses on forces acting on the body from external sources (gravity and ground reaction forces) and internal sources (muscle contractions) that produce gait motion. This is distinct from gait kinematics, which describes movement without reference to the forces causing it.

questions.question: Circumduction is possible at condyloid and ball-and-socket joints because these joint types:
questions.explanation: Circumduction — a cone-shaped movement combining flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction in sequence — is possible at condyloid joints (biaxial) and ball-and-socket joints (triaxial) because these joints permit motion in multiple planes. Hinge and pivot joints are uniaxial and cannot produce circumduction. Shoulder and hip circumduction exercises are used in rehabilitation to restore multi-plane functional mobility.
options: Are hinge joints permitting one plane
Are pivot joints permitting rotation only
Permit motion in multiple planes simultaneously
Are suture joints bonded by fibrous tissue
Are plane joints permitting gliding only
Purely translational motion with linear displacement of all segments
Purely rotational motion around fixed joints without translation
A composite of rotations at joints and linear motion of body parts
Oscillatory motion involving rapid reversal of limb segment direction
Curvilinear translation of the entire body in a non-straight path
questions.explanation: General motion (as in cycling) is a composite of rotations at the joints (ankle, knee, and hip), linear motion of the head on a smooth road, non-linear motion of other body parts (particularly on uneven roads). General motion combines both translational and rotational components making it the most common type of motion in daily activities.
questions.question: General motion, as exemplified by cycling, is described as:
The self-lubricating mechanism of articular cartilage works because:
options: It deforms under loading, exuding synovial fluid to the joint surface
It secretes lubricin protein directly from chondrocytes continuously
The synovial membrane absorbs load and releases fluid when compressed
Microvasculature within cartilage pumps fluid to the surface during motion
Collagen fibers of the articular surface absorb fluid during relaxation phases
questions.explanation: Articular cartilage is a soft, porous, permeable, hydrated tissue that deforms under loading, thereby exuding synovial fluid. This self-pressurized fluid film provides lubrication during joint motion. Cartilage has little or no ability to heal or regenerate on its own once damaged, and injuries tend to progress toward arthritis.

Maximum torque is produced when force is applied perpendicular (90 degrees) to the lever system, because the entire force contributes to rotation with no component wasted on compression or distraction of the joint. When force is applied at acute or obtuse angles, the rotatory component decreases and a translatory component appears. Physiotherapists must position resistance at right angles to the bone for maximal therapeutic torque.
questions.question: Maximum torque at a joint is produced when resistance is applied to the bone at:

questions.explanation: Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. During standing and gait, the ground reaction force is the equal and opposite response to the patient's foot pushing against the ground. Ground reaction force analysis is fundamental in gait assessment and prosthetic fitting, as it reveals how forces are distributed through the lower limb during functional movements.
questions.question: When a patient pushes against the floor during a standing transfer, the floor pushes back with equal and opposite force. This illustrates Newton's:
Radial deviation at the wrist is defined as moving the wrist:
questions.explanation: Radial deviation is movement of the wrist toward the radius (laterally toward the thumb side). Ulnar deviation is movement of the wrist toward the ulna (medially toward the little finger side). Both movements occur in the frontal (coronal) plane around the sagittal axis, at the radiocarpal (wrist) joint.
options: In the sagittal plane reducing the angle between hand and forearm
In the sagittal plane increasing the angle between hand and forearm
Toward the ulna (medially), reducing the carrying angle at the wrist
Toward the radius (laterally), in the frontal plane of the wrist
Into pronation rotating the forearm to bring the palm facing down

questions.question: Ankle plantarflexion at push-off during gait exemplifies which lever class:
questions.explanation: Ankle plantarflexion during heel-off (push-off) represents a second-class lever system, with the metatarsophalangeal joints as the fulcrum, body weight as the load between fulcrum and effort, and the gastrocsoleus as the effort at the heel. Second-class levers always have mechanical advantage greater than one, enabling the calf muscles to lift body weight efficiently during gait.

options: The entire force contributes to rotation
questions.explanation: The rotatory component of force is maximised at 90 degrees to the bone because at this angle the entire applied force contributes to rotation with no force component creating joint compression or distraction. At all other angles, force is split between rotatory and translatory components. Physiotherapists apply resistance perpendicular to the bone to achieve maximum joint torque for accurate manual muscle testing.
questions.question: Resistance applied perpendicular to the bone maximises therapeutic torque because at 90 degrees:

options: Frontal (coronal) axis that runs horizontally side to side
Sagittal axis that runs horizontally from front to back
Longitudinal (vertical) axis running superiorly to inferiorly
Oblique axis running diagonally through the joint center
Mediolateral axis perpendicular to the plane of motion itself
questions.explanation: The transverse plane divides the body into top and bottom sections and movements within it occur around the longitudinal (vertical) axis. Examples of transverse plane motions include medial/lateral rotation, left/right trunk rotation, pronation/supination, and horizontal adduction/abduction.
questions.question: Movements occurring in the transverse plane take place around the:

questions.explanation: Valgus refers to the distal segment of a joint deviating LATERALLY (away from the midline). In contrast, varus refers to the distal segment deviating MEDIALLY (toward the midline). These positional terms are used to describe skeletal deformities at multiple joints, including the knee (genu valgum/varum) and the ankle/hindfoot.
questions.question: Valgus deformity is specifically defined as the distal segment of a joint deviating:
options: Medially toward the body's midline (e.g., genu varum alignment)
Laterally away from the body's midline (e.g., genu valgum)
Anteriorly in the sagittal plane creating a flexion contracture
Posteriorly creating a fixed extension deformity at the joint
Inferiorly due to gravity causing sag in the dependent position

questions.question: Articular cartilage has limited healing capacity primarily because it:
questions.explanation: Articular cartilage lacks direct blood supply and contains chondrocytes with limited proliferative capacity, severely restricting its intrinsic ability to heal or regenerate after damage. Injuries to articular cartilage tend to progress with further wearing of the articulating surfaces, leading to osteoarthritis. Joint replacement surgery becomes necessary when conservative rehabilitation strategies can no longer maintain acceptable pain and function.
options: Has excessive blood supply preventing healing
Lacks direct vascular and cellular regenerative capacity
Has a rapid cell turnover rate
Contains too many growth factor receptors

questions.question: Mechanical power during a patient's lifting task equals work performed:
questions.explanation: Mechanical power equals the amount of work performed in a given time (P equals work divided by time, or equivalently Force times velocity). Peak power output is a critical measure in return-to-sport assessments, distinguishing athletes who have recovered strength but not power production capacity. Physiotherapists incorporate power testing and training as a distinct phase of late-stage rehabilitation.

questions.question: An offset cane differs from the standard cane specifically by having:
questions.explanation: The offset cane is similar to the standard cane but the proximal component of the horizontal shaft is offset anteriorly, thereby creating a straight offset handle. This design places the user's weight more directly over the base of support. The vertical bar is adjustable to fit the user.
options: A four-legged broad base for maximum floor contact stability
Forearm support replacing the standard handgrip design
The proximal shaft offset anteriorly creating a straight offset handle
An adjustable wrist strap for additional security during ambulation
A contoured ergonomic grip reducing wrist extension forces

questions.explanation: Powder reduces friction between therapist's hands and the patient's skin by filling surface irregularities and decreasing the coefficient of kinetic friction, allowing smooth effleurage and petrissage strokes without skin irritation. Adequate lubrication prevents micro-trauma and allows the therapist to modulate pressure more precisely for effective massage delivery.
options: Allow the skin to warm faster
questions.question: Powder is applied during massage treatment to the patient's skin in order to:
Which goniometric instrument uses gravity on pointers and fluid levels to measure motion?
options: Universal goniometer with a stationary and a movable arm
Electrogoniometer using electronic transducers for joint angle
Tape measure used for linear distance during spinal movement
Visual estimation using a standardized observational protocol
Gravity-dependent (inclinometer) using pendulum or fluid bubble
questions.explanation: The gravity-dependent goniometer (inclinometer) uses the effect of gravity on pointers and fluid levels to measure joint position and motion. It has two types: the pendulum goniometer (360° protractor with a weighted pointer) and the fluid/bubble goniometer. It is particularly useful for spinal range of motion measurement.

questions.question: The single support phase of gait represents the period when:
options: Both feet are simultaneously in contact with the ground surface
The body's weight is supported on one limb with the other swinging
The foot transitions from heel strike to foot flat contact position
The hip and knee both move into extension during propulsion phase
The trailing limb is in pre-swing preparing for toe-off from ground
questions.explanation: Single support is the period when the body's weight is supported on one limb while the other advances in swing. It is one of the three functional tasks of gait. Single support is the most demanding phase for the supporting limb and corresponds to the period from opposite toe-off to opposite initial contact.

questions.question: At an elevated position with zero velocity, the body possesses only:
questions.explanation: A body at an elevated position with zero velocity possesses only potential energy (PE equals weight times height), with no kinetic energy because velocity is zero. As it descends, potential energy converts to kinetic energy. In suspension therapy, physiotherapists manipulate position to alter gravitational potential energy demands, reducing effective limb weight and enabling therapeutic movement in weak or pain-inhibited patients.

questions.question: The relationship among force, mass, and acceleration during patient mobilisation is described by Newton's:
questions.explanation: Newton's second law (law of acceleration) states F equals mass times acceleration, meaning a force applied to a body causes acceleration proportional to force magnitude and inversely proportional to mass. Physiotherapists use this principle when calculating forces needed to mobilise patients, prescribe exercise loads, or analyse gait deviations related to mass asymmetries.

Type IIb (fast glycolytic) fibers have a white coloration, fewer mitochondria, lower myoglobin concentration, and are associated with anaerobic metabolism. They have a large diameter, fast twitch speed, greater force of contraction, and complete a single twitch in a short time. However, they fatigue easily with high force/power/speed production but low endurance.
options: High myoglobin content and dark red coloration with many mitochondria
Intermediate properties between Type I and Type IIb in all parameters
High oxidative capacity and strong resistance to fatigue development
Large diameter, few mitochondria, and rapid fatigue during activity
Slow contraction velocity with high endurance and aerobic metabolism
questions.question: Type IIb (fast glycolytic) muscle fibers are characterized by having:

questions.explanation: Varus refers to the distal segment of a joint deviating MEDIALLY (toward the midline). Genu varum (bow-leggedness) describes medial deviation of the legs at the knee. Valgus (the opposite) refers to lateral deviation. These positional terms are important in orthopedic assessment, particularly for lower limb alignment analysis.
options: Medially toward the body's midline, as in genu varum (bow legs)
Laterally away from the body's midline, as in genu valgum
Anteriorly creating a recurvatum deformity at the joint site
Posteriorly creating a fixed flexion deformity at the joint
Superiorly above the joint line due to ligamentous laxity
questions.question: The term 'varus' in anatomical terminology refers to the distal segment deviating:

questions.explanation: Perfectly plastic impact occurs when at least one body deforms permanently and bodies do not separate after collision, with all relative kinetic energy converted to heat and deformation. Most biological tissue responses to impact lie between perfectly elastic and perfectly plastic extremes. Understanding impact characteristics helps physiotherapists design landing strategies to reduce peak impact forces and minimise tissue deformation injury risk.
questions.question: Perfectly plastic impact is characterised by:

options: An offset proximal shaft creating a straight offset handle design
A single tip with an adjustable ferrule for uneven terrain use
A four-legged base angled from shaft for maximal lateral stability
Forearm support rather than hand grip at the proximal end
A broad base with four contact points for greater floor stability
questions.explanation: The quadripod cane (quad cane) is similar to the standard cane but has a broad base of support with four points of support for floor contact. The hemi cane also has four contact points but the legs are angled from the shaft to increase stability. These designs provide greater stability than a single-tip standard cane.
questions.question: The quadripod cane differs from the standard cane by having:
The most common method of gait analysis in clinical practice is:
questions.explanation: Observational gait analysis (OGA) is the most common method of analysis and identifying gait problems in the clinic. It involves visual observation of critical gait parameters and requires little investment in equipment, time, and expense. Its reliability can be improved by using video-tape recording, and it is appropriate to characterize most gait pathologies.
options: Observational gait analysis (OGA) using visual observation of parameters
Computer-based CGA using Vicon 512 motion capture systems
Electromyographic analysis with surface and fine-wire electrodes
Force plate analysis measuring ground reaction forces during ambulation
Video-accelerometry using wearable inertial measurement unit sensors

questions.question: Fatigue's effect on joint stability is clinically important because fatigued muscles:
questions.explanation: Fatigue reduces a muscle's ability to contribute to joint stability, which is why injuries are more common in sporting activities when fatigue has set in. Tension in muscles is particularly important in joints such as the knee and shoulder where bone configurations are not particularly stable. Weak and fatigued muscles cause low stability.
options: Increase co-contraction, creating excessive compressive joint loading
Shift activity from Type II to Type I fibers reducing stability further
Produce higher joint torques that paradoxically increase instability
Release excessive calcium reducing the efficiency of cross-bridge cycling
Are less able to contribute to joint stability, increasing injury risk
Mass, centre of mass, and radius of gyration
questions.explanation: Body segment parameters include mass, centre of mass location, and radius of gyration for each segment. These are essential for calculating forces, torques, and energies during movement analysis. Physiotherapists use these parameters in biomechanical modelling of pathological movements, prosthetic design calculations, and evidence-based exercise prescription that accounts for individual anthropometric variations.
questions.question: Body segment parameters required per segment for biomechanical modelling are:

options: Slow twitch (ST) → Type IIa → Type IIb in ascending intensity
Type IIb → Type IIa → Type I in ascending exercise intensity
Type IIa → Type I → Type IIb as exercise intensity increases
All motor units activated simultaneously regardless of intensity
Type IIa → Type IIb → Type I in descending activation threshold
questions.question: The order of motor unit recruitment from lowest to highest intensity exercise is:
questions.explanation: The order of motor unit recruitment follows the Henneman size principle: slow twitch (Type I) motor units have lower thresholds and are activated first even during rapid movements. As exercise intensity and fatigue progress, Type IIa units are recruited next, followed by Type IIb. The CNS recruits only ST fibers during low-intensity exercise.

questions.question: The mechanical factor that MOST directly reduces stability in a standing person is:
options: Increasing body mass through increased muscle hypertrophy
A higher center of gravity position relative to the base of support
Increasing foot width to create a broader base of support
Greater friction between the foot and the supporting surface
Reduced horizontal distance between the COG and BOS boundary
questions.explanation: Of the mechanical factors affecting stability, the height of the COG relative to the BOS is critical — the higher the COG position, the lesser the stability. Other factors include body mass, friction, size of the BOS, and the horizontal location of the COG relative to the BOS boundary.

questions.question: The three functional tasks of the gait cycle are:
questions.explanation: The three functional tasks of the gait cycle are: (1) weight acceptance — accepting the body's weight as it transfers to the newly contacting limb; (2) single limb support — supporting the body on one limb while the other advances; and (3) limb advancement — advancing the swinging limb forward for the next step.
options: Initial contact, mid-stance, and terminal swing phases of gait
Loading response, single limb support, and pre-swing phases
Heel strike, foot flat, and toe-off in the classic terminology
Weight acceptance, single limb support, and limb advancement
Stance phase, swing phase, and double support together

questions.question: A physiotherapist places a patient in anatomical position before goniometry. The palm orientation in this position is:
questions.explanation: In the anatomical reference position the palms face anteriorly (forward), with the body erect, feet slightly apart, and arms at the sides. This standardized posture is the universal starting point for goniometric measurement and ensures consistency across assessors. Deviation from this position before measurement introduces systematic error in ROM documentation.

Syndesmoses (meaning 'held by bands') are synarthrodial joints where dense fibrous tissue bands hold the bones together, permitting only extremely limited movement. Examples include the coracoacromial joint, mid-radioulnar joint, mid-tibiofibular joint, and the inferior tibiofibular ligament.
questions.question: Syndesmoses are classified under which joint category and characterized by:
options: Freely movable (diarthrosis) with a synovial membrane lining
Slightly movable (amphiarthrosis) held by hyaline cartilage
Immovable (synarthrosis) with bony fusion between articulating surfaces
Immovable (synarthrosis) held together by dense fibrous tissue bands
Slightly movable (amphiarthrosis) with a fibrocartilaginous disc present
Restore the body to its original pre-displacement position
Maintain the center of gravity at exactly the same height
Increase the displacement away from the original position
Dissipate gradually until the body returns to neutral state
Transfer momentum to the supporting surface beneath it
questions.question: Unstable equilibrium occurs when displacement causes forces to:
questions.explanation: Unstable equilibrium is characterized by forces that, when a body is given an initial displacement, tend to increase that displacement further. It occurs when the COG is high, the base of support (BOS) is small, and the relationship between COG and BOS is difficult to maintain. Examples include a cone balanced on its apex or a person in standing.

questions.question: A first-class lever is characterized by the arrangement:
questions.explanation: In a first-class lever, the fulcrum (F) is located between the effort (E) and the load (L), giving the arrangement E-F-L. Depending on where the fulcrum lies relative to the load and effort, a first-class lever can provide either mechanical advantage (force lever) or speed advantage. Head nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint is an example.
options: Fulcrum between the effort and load in a force-amplifying arrangement
Fulcrum located between the effort and load (E-F-L arrangement)
Load between the fulcrum and effort providing mechanical advantage
Effort between the fulcrum and load requiring speed advantage
Load and effort on the same side of the fulcrum with torque balance

questions.explanation: In traction therapy, adequate friction between the patient and the treatment surface is essential to provide counter-traction, preventing the patient from sliding toward the traction force and ensuring the therapeutic force is directed to the target joint. Without sufficient friction, the patient slides and traction force is dissipated rather than creating therapeutic joint distraction. Proper positioning and non-slip materials optimise counter-traction.
questions.question: For effective cervical traction therapy, friction between the patient and the treatment surface must be:

questions.explanation: Middle range is any distance from the middle of the outer range to the middle of the inner range. In this range, the muscle is neither fully stretched nor fully contracted. It is the part of the range in which many muscles work most of the time during ADL, and exercises in this range are used to maintain muscle tone and power.
options: The portion from full stretch to the midpoint of full range
Any distance from the middle of outer range to middle of inner range
The portion from full contraction to midpoint of full range
Only the zone where the muscle generates maximum active force
The range from 25% to 75% of total joint range of motion
questions.question: Middle range of muscle work is the range in which many muscles work during ADL, defined as:

options: Moderate and balanced symmetrically between both limbs
High only on the dominant side with normal non-dominant side
Within one standard deviation of the normative range for age
Extremely low, extremely high, or unbalanced between sides
Slightly higher than normal due to recent stretching exercise
questions.explanation: Risk of injury is increased when joint flexibility is extremely low (reduced mobility increases strain), extremely high (hyperlaxity reduces stability), or unbalanced between the dominant and non-dominant sides of the body (asymmetry predisposes to injury). High strength and flexibility together are desirable for injury prevention.
questions.question: The risk of injury related to joint flexibility is increased when flexibility is:

options: Mass per unit volume measured in kilograms per cubic meter
Weight per unit cross-sectional area measured in Pascals
Volume per unit mass expressed as liters per kilogram
Mass multiplied by gravitational acceleration at body center
Weight per unit volume with the SI unit of Newton per cubic meter
questions.question: Specific weight differs from density in that specific weight is defined as:
questions.explanation: Specific weight is defined as weight per unit volume, with the SI unit of N/m³ (Newton per cubic meter). It is proportional to density given that weight is proportional to mass. Density, in contrast, is mass per unit volume (kg/m³). These two quantities are related but measure different physical properties.

options: Type IIB first, then IIA, then ST
Only Type I fibres ever activated
ST first, then Type IIA, then Type IIB
Type IIA first, then IIB, then ST
questions.question: Motor unit recruitment during increasing force production follows which order from lowest to highest threshold:
questions.explanation: Motor unit recruitment follows the size principle, activating slow-twitch (ST/Type I) units first at low forces, then Type IIA, and finally Type IIB (fast glycolytic) units at highest force demands. This orderly recruitment optimises metabolic efficiency by using fatigue-resistant units for sustained tasks. Exercise intensity must be sufficient to recruit higher-threshold units for maximum strength training benefit.

questions.question: The pennate fiber arrangement allows muscles to generate MORE force than parallel-fibered muscles because:
questions.explanation: Pennate fiber arrangement allows more fibers to be packed per unit volume than a parallel arrangement. Because pennate muscles contain more muscle fibers per unit of muscle volume, they can generate more force than parallel-fibered muscles of the same size. However, pennate muscles cannot shorten as much, limiting range of motion.
options: Fibers are longer and can shorten over a greater absolute distance
More fibers can be packed per unit volume, increasing cross-sectional area
The angle of pennation reduces internal friction between fibers
The tendon transmits force more efficiently in a pennate arrangement
Shorter pennate fibers require fewer motor units for full activation

questions.explanation: Newton's second law (Law of Acceleration) states that force applied to a body causes acceleration of that body proportional to the force magnitude, in the direction of the force, and inversely proportional to the body's mass (F = ma). This law expresses the interrelationship among force, mass, and acceleration.
questions.question: Newton's Law of Acceleration states that force applied to a body causes acceleration:
options: Proportional to force, in force's direction, inversely to mass
Proportional to mass and inversely proportional to applied force
Equal to the reaction force in the direction of impending motion
Constant regardless of mass when applied in a vacuum medium
Proportional to the square of velocity and body cross-section

questions.question: Co-contraction of agonists and antagonists primarily serves to:
questions.explanation: Co-contraction of agonists and antagonists enhances stability at the joint that the muscles cross. While agonists are primarily active during acceleration and antagonists during deceleration, simultaneous activation of both compresses the joint and improves its resistance to displacement, particularly important in joints with inherently low bony stability.
options: Produce maximum power output during explosive athletic movements
Enhance joint stability at the joint that the muscles cross
Reduce metabolic cost by sharing the work between muscle groups
Maximize range of motion through reciprocal inhibition mechanisms
Provide proprioceptive feedback to the CNS during fast movements

questions.question: The hemi cane differs from the standard quadripod cane by having:
questions.explanation: The hemi cane has four points of floor contact but the legs are angled from the shaft to increase stability of the cane. The standard quadripod has a broad base with four contact points but without the specific leg angling of the hemi cane. Both provide more stability than the single-tip standard cane.
options: A single point of contact with a straight vertical shaft design
An offset proximal shaft creating a straight handle configuration
Four legs angled from the shaft to increase stability of the cane
A forearm cuff providing support beyond the standard handgrip only
A broader base with straight legs and no angling from the shaft

questions.question: The maximum comfortable walking speed (CWS) in normal adults is approximately:
questions.explanation: While comfortable walking speed averages 80 m/min (1.4 m/s; 5.0 km/h), the maximum comfortable walking speed is 2.5 m/s (9.0 km/h; 5.6 mph). The average CWS is the speed of least energy consumption per unit time. Walking at speeds above or below CWS increases the energy cost per unit distance traveled.
options: 80 metres per minute or 5.0 km/h under comfortable conditions
1.0 m/s or approximately 3.6 km/h in normal adult ambulation
2.5 m/s or approximately 9.0 km/h at maximal walking speed
1.8 m/s or approximately 6.5 km/h at brisk walking pace
0.8 m/s or approximately 2.9 km/h in elderly adults normally
One-quarter (25%) of its normal resting length maximally
Three-quarters (75%) of its normal resting length maximally
The full 100% of its resting length in optimal conditions
One-third (33%) of its normal resting length maximally
One-half (50%) of its normal resting length maximally
questions.question: A single muscle fiber can shorten during concentric contraction by up to approximately:
questions.explanation: A single muscle fiber can shorten up to approximately half (50%) of its normal resting length during concentric contraction. This limit is determined by the sliding filament mechanism and the structural arrangement of the actin and myosin filaments within the sarcomere. Fiber architecture (parallel vs. pennate) also influences total muscle excursion.

Tendons respond to regular mechanical loading by hypertrophying — increasing in cross-sectional size, length, and strength of their bone junctions — following Wolff's law applied to connective tissue. This adaptive response underlies the physiological rationale for progressive tendon loading in tendinopathy rehabilitation. Insufficient loading leads to atrophy, while appropriately graded loading promotes collagen remodelling and improved mechanical properties.
options: Increasing in size and junction strength
questions.question: Tendons respond to regular mechanical loading during rehabilitation by:

options: In its shortest position at full contraction and maximum effort
Generating its highest force output at optimal length-tension
At the midpoint of the available range with neutral muscle tone
Transitioning between eccentric and concentric contraction types
Most fully relaxed or extended, working from full stretch to midpoint
questions.explanation: Outer range is nearest to the point at which the muscle is most fully relaxed/extended. It is achieved when a muscle contracts concentrically from the fully stretched position to the midpoint of the full range. Extreme outer range is difficult due to an adverse angle of pull, with some muscular effort used to compress joint surfaces rather than produce movement.
questions.question: Outer range of muscle work is described as nearest to the point where the muscle is:

questions.explanation: Ball and socket (spheroidal) joints have reciprocally convex and concave articulating surfaces permitting rotations in all three planes of movement. They are triaxial with three degrees of freedom. The hip and shoulder joints are the primary examples. This is in contrast to uniaxial (hinge, pivot), biaxial (condyloid, saddle), and nonaxial (gliding) joints.
options: Two planes: sagittal and frontal simultaneously and independently
One cardinal plane with accessory rotation in a single direction
The transverse plane only due to the spherical articulating surface
All three planes of movement (triaxial, three degrees of freedom)
The sagittal plane only with the greatest range of flexion-extension
questions.question: Ball and socket (spheroidal) joints are the only joints permitting rotations in:
The typical electromechanical delay (EMD) range in human skeletal muscle is:
questions.explanation: Electromechanical delay in humans ranges from 20 to 100 milliseconds, representing the interval between muscle stimulation and onset of force production during which the Series Elastic Component must be stretched. Muscles with higher fast-twitch fibre proportions have shorter EMDs. Prolonged EMD following injury indicates impaired neuromuscular readiness and increased joint vulnerability during rapid loading.

options: The muscle's line of action and the perpendicular to the joint axis
The tendon's direction and the midline of the body at rest
The joint angle and the perpendicular to the anatomical plane
Two adjacent muscle fibers within a pennate muscle arrangement
The long axis of the bone and the line of pull of the muscle
questions.question: The angle of pull of a muscle is defined as the angle between:
questions.explanation: The angle of pull is the angle between the long axis of the bone and the line of pull of the muscle. Force is most effective when applied perpendicular to the lever (90° angle of pull). If the angle of pull is small, little movement will be produced. The angle of pull changes as the joint moves through its range of motion.

Endurance training over time leads to the conversion of fast twitch (FT) fibers to slow twitch (ST) fibers. Additionally, within FT fibers, strength training, endurance training, and concentric and eccentric isokinetic training all cause conversion of Type IIb to Type IIa fibers. Thus training significantly modifies fiber type composition.
options: Conversion of Type IIa fibers to Type IIb fast glycolytic fibers
Conversion of Type I slow oxidative fibers to Type IIb fibers
Hypertrophy of Type IIb fibers without alteration in fiber type
Selective atrophy of Type I fibers with Type II fiber dominance
Conversion of fast twitch (FT) fibers to slow twitch (ST) fibers
questions.question: Endurance training leads to which specific adaptation in fiber type composition?

options: Minimizing energy expenditure by reducing ground resistance
Creating forward momentum through increased ground contact
Providing cushioning for joint surfaces during heel strike
Stabilizing the hindfoot during the mid-stance loading phase
Exerting important influence to prevent sliding of the foot
questions.explanation: Friction exerts an important influence during many daily activities including walking, where it prevents the foot from sliding on the ground. Kinetic friction is reduced when surfaces become more polished. Adhesive materials between surfaces increase frictional resistance. Friction is a force and its unit is the Newton (N).
questions.question: The role of friction during normal walking is BEST described as:

options: Twice per cycle — at the beginning and end of each stance phase
Once per cycle during the transition between swing and stance
Three times per cycle at each initial contact and mid-stance
Continuously throughout the stance phase except during mid-stance
Only once, during the loading response phase of ambulation
questions.explanation: Double support occurs twice in a gait cycle — at the beginning and end of stance phase, referred to as initial and terminal double-limb stance. The two periods of double-limb support together represent 25% of the gait cycle. As walking speed increases, the duration of double support decreases, and at running speed, double support is completely absent.
questions.question: In normal gait, the double support periods occur:
During isokinetic dynamometer testing for hamstring strain, contraction velocity remains constant throughout ROM. This contraction type is called:
questions.explanation: Isokinetic contraction involves constant velocity of movement throughout the entire range of motion, requiring specialised dynamometer equipment. This modality allows measurement of torque at multiple joint angles and specific velocities, enabling detailed strength profiling. Isokinetic testing is used to quantify hamstring-to-quadriceps strength ratios and identify residual deficits before return-to-sport clearance.

questions.question: When articular cartilage is damaged, the clinical progression typically involves:
options: Progressive wear away of bone end coating leading toward arthritis
Spontaneous regeneration through chondroblast proliferation activity
Revascularization and fibroblast invasion replacing cartilage fully
Calcification of the damaged area providing structural stability
Hypertrophy of adjacent cartilage compensating for damaged areas
questions.explanation: Articular cartilage has little or no ability to heal or regenerate on its own once damaged. Injuries tend to progress, with more and more of the protective coating of the articulating bone ends being worn away, thereby leading to arthritis. This progressive degradation is why cartilage damage is clinically significant and often requires intervention.

Saddle (sellar) joints have both articulating bone surfaces shaped like the seat of a riding saddle. The possible movements are similar to condyloid joints (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction) but greater ranges of motion are permitted due to the reciprocal curvatures. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the primary example.
questions.question: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is classified as a saddle (sellar) joint, characterized by:
options: One convex and one concave surface allowing full triaxial motion
Both surfaces shaped like a riding saddle allowing greater ROM than condyloid
A purely flat non-axial surface permitting translational gliding
A ball-and-socket configuration permitting three planes of rotation
A pivot arrangement permitting rotation around a single vertical axis

questions.explanation: Frontal plane movements occur around the sagittal axis. These include abduction and adduction of the limbs, lateral flexion of the trunk, elevation and depression of the shoulder girdle, and radial/ulnar deviation at the wrist and inversion/eversion of the foot.
questions.question: In the frontal plane, which of the following movements occurs around the sagittal axis?
options: Flexion and extension at the hip and knee joints
Internal and external rotation at the glenohumeral joint
Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion at the talocrural joint
Abduction and adduction of the limbs at respective joints
Pronation and supination of the forearm along its length
Wheels instead of ferrules to allow rolling rather than lifting
Forearm support rather than handgrips for proximal arm weight bearing
A higher frame to accommodate taller or bariatric user populations
A pediatric-sized frame with adjustable height for growing children
