A seat attachment allowing the user to sit when fatigued during use
questions.question: The forearm walker differs from the standard walker by providing:
questions.explanation: The forearm walker is basically the same as the standard walking frame but with forearm support rather than handgrips. This allows weight bearing through the forearm rather than the wrist and hand, which is useful for patients with wrist or hand pathology, reduced grip strength, or conditions requiring forearm support.

questions.question: Muscle work capacity depends on which two combined factors:
questions.explanation: Muscle work capacity depends on physiological cross-section (which determines force capacity) together with the total distance the muscle can shorten (which determines displacement). Work equals force times displacement, so both factors must be optimised in rehabilitation. Targeting only hypertrophy without restoring full functional excursion will limit overall work capacity and functional recovery.

Classification by motion capabilities — synarthroses (immovable), amphiarthroses (slightly movable), and diarthroses (freely movable) — is most clinically relevant because it directly informs joint mobilisation strategies. Systems based solely on tissue type do not provide functional movement information. Diarthroses are the primary target of mobilisation techniques.
questions.question: When classifying joints to determine which are amenable to mobilisation, the most clinically relevant system classifies joints based on:

questions.explanation: Pennate muscles pack more muscle fibres per cross-sectional area due to their oblique fibre arrangement, providing greater force generation capacity compared to parallel-fibered muscles of equal volume. While individual pennate fibres are shorter and shorten through a smaller range, the collective force from more fibres exceeds that of parallel muscles. Physiotherapists consider muscle architecture when predicting strength deficits and designing targeted strengthening interventions.
options: Greater cross-sectional area with more fibres
questions.question: Pennate muscles generate greater absolute force than parallel-fibered muscles of equal volume because they have:

options: Being double the stride length in symmetrical walking conditions
The right step length equaling the left step length in symmetry
The distance between two successive contacts of the same foot
Varying by 15-20% between the dominant and non-dominant sides
Being measured from toe-off of one foot to initial contact of the other
questions.question: Step length in normal gait is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Step length is defined as the distance between corresponding successive points of heel contact of the OPPOSITE feet. In normal, symmetrical gait, the right step length equals the left step length. The stride length is double the step length. Step length asymmetry is an indicator of gait pathology.

questions.question: Inner range exercises for terminal knee extension work the muscle from the midpoint of range to:
questions.explanation: Inner range contraction occurs from the midpoint of full range to the position of full muscle contraction during concentric effort. This range is used to maintain joint movement in the direction of muscle pull and to train extensor muscles for stabilisation at end range. Quadriceps terminal extension exercises exemplify inner range training.

Concentric contraction produces sarcomere shortening which decreases muscle length but increases its cross-sectional diameter, creating visible gaster (belly) enlargement. This mechanical property allows palpation of muscle activity and is used in manual muscle testing to confirm contraction quality. In superficial muscles, this diameter increase is clinically observable and provides real-time biofeedback during exercise sessions.
questions.question: Visible bulging of the muscle belly during concentric contraction is produced by:
Active insufficiency of a two-joint muscle occurs when the muscle cannot:
questions.explanation: Active insufficiency occurs when a two-joint or multi-joint muscle cannot shorten sufficiently to achieve full range of motion at all joints it crosses simultaneously, because it has run out of contractile range. Rectus femoris active insufficiency prevents simultaneous full hip flexion and knee extension. Physiotherapists design exercises that avoid positions of active insufficiency or progressively develop range in those challenging positions.
options: Stretch for full range when elongated
Shorten enough for full ROM at all crossed joints simultaneously

questions.explanation: At the elbow joint, flexion and extension take place in the sagittal plane around the frontal (coronal) axis. Pronation and supination, as well as medial and lateral rotation, take place in the horizontal (transverse) plane around the vertical axis. This plane-axis relationship is consistent across all joints.
options: Flexion and extension occurring in the sagittal plane
Pronation and supination in the horizontal plane
Medial and lateral rotation in the horizontal plane
Abduction and adduction in the frontal coronal plane
Circumduction combining multiple plane movements equally
questions.question: In the sagittal plane of the elbow joint, which motion pair correctly occurs around the frontal axis?

questions.explanation: The longer the lever arm (leverage) when applying resistance, the more effective the resistive program. Progression in exercise is achieved by increasing leverage — moving the point of resistance application further from the joint. If there is much pain or swelling, leverage should be lowered to reduce joint torque.
options: Decrease the lever arm length to increase resistance progressively
Increase the lever arm length to progressively increase resistance
Maintain a constant lever arm and increase repetitions only
Decrease the angle of pull to shift load toward the joint axis
Move the resistance proximally to shorten the effective load arm
questions.question: When progressing a patient's exercise program using leverage, the CORRECT approach is to:

options: Flexion and extension in the sagittal plane around the frontal axis
Abduction, adduction, and circumduction in the frontal plane
Rotation around one axis only, as in the atlantoaxial joint
Biaxial motion allowing both rotation and translation movements
Triaxial motion because the cylindrical surface allows all rotations
questions.question: A pivot (trochoid/screw) joint is classified as uniaxial and permits specifically:
questions.explanation: Pivot (screw/trochoid) joints permit rotation around one axis only, making them uniaxial with one degree of freedom. Examples are the atlantoaxial joint (allowing head rotation) and the distal radioulnar joint (allowing pronation/supination). The cylindrical bony configuration within a bony or fibrous ring restricts motion to rotation.

Titin (also called connectin) connects the Z line to the M line in the sarcomere and stabilizes myosin in the longitudinal axis. It limits the range of motion of the sarcomere and contributes to the passive stiffness of muscle. Nebulin, in contrast, stabilizes actin by binding with actin monomers and extends from the Z line within the I band.
options: Stabilize actin by binding with individual actin monomer subunits
Block the active site on actin until the calcium signal activates it
Connect Z line to M line and limit sarcomere range of motion
Provide structural lattice work in the extracellular matrix only
Anchor the T-tubule system to the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
questions.question: Titin (connectin) protein in the sarcomere functions to:
Pressure is defined as force distributed over a given area and its SI unit is:
questions.explanation: Pressure is force distributed over a given area. Its units are Newton/cm² or Pascals (Pa), where 1 Pascal equals 1 Newton/m². This distinguishes pressure from specific weight (N/m³) and torque (Nm). Understanding pressure is important in clinical contexts such as pressure ulcer prevention and orthotic fitting.
options: Newton per cubic meter (N/m³) relating force to volume
Pascal (Pa), where 1 Pascal equals 1 Newton per square meter
Newton-meter (Nm) representing torque or moment of force
Kilogram per square centimeter relating mass to contact area
Newton per kilogram (N/kg) expressing specific force per mass

questions.question: Pre-stretching an actively tensed muscle before concentric contraction results in force generation that is:
questions.explanation: Pre-stretching an actively tensed muscle before concentric contraction results in greater force generation than concentric-only contraction. This SSC enhancement comes from stored elastic energy in the Series Elastic Component and activation of the myotatic stretch reflex. Physiotherapists exploit this in plyometric training and functional movement retraining to restore and enhance explosive force generation capacity following musculoskeletal injury.

options: Develops maximum force in response to a single neural stimulus
Undergoes rapid cross-bridge cycling in the outer range zone
Fatigues completely after repeated high-frequency stimulation
Is repeatedly activated so that maximum tension is maintained
Transitions from fast to slow twitch composition after training
questions.question: Tetanus in muscle physiology refers to the state when a fiber:
questions.explanation: A fiber that is repeatedly activated so that its maximum tension is maintained for a time is said to be in tetanus. Tension present during tetanus may be 4 times the peak tension during a single twitch. In humans, motor units are generally activated in a volley of nerve impulses.

Passive insufficiency occurs when a two-joint muscle such as the hamstrings cannot stretch enough to allow full range of motion at all joints it crosses simultaneously. With both the hip flexed and the knee extended, the hamstrings are elongated maximally over two joints, reaching their extensibility limit before full range is achieved. This is clinically relevant in hamstring stretching and neural tension testing interpretation.
questions.question: Resistance encountered when stretching hamstrings with knee extended and hip fully flexed before full ROM is achieved is an example of:
Shoulder medial and lateral rotation occur in which plane:
questions.explanation: Rotational movements such as medial and lateral rotation occur in the transverse (horizontal) plane around a vertical longitudinal axis. This plane divides the body into superior and inferior halves. Rotational impairments identified in the transverse plane guide the physiotherapist toward specific rotator cuff strengthening or mobilisation strategies depending on the underlying pathology.

questions.question: A stationary body possesses what amount of linear momentum:
questions.explanation: A stationary body has zero velocity, and since momentum equals mass times velocity, its momentum is zero regardless of mass. Only bodies in motion possess momentum. This concept is relevant when teaching patients that initiating movement from rest requires overcoming inertia to build momentum, explaining why the first steps after prolonged bed rest feel particularly effortful.

options: Movements without regard to forces — displacement, time, velocity
Forces and moments that cause movement patterns during walking
Electromyographic patterns of muscle activity during ambulation
Ground reaction forces and joint reaction forces during gait
Internal joint torques generated by muscular contraction in gait
questions.explanation: Gait kinematics is the study of movements during walking without regard to the forces that produce them. It encompasses displacement, time, velocity, and joint angles. Gait kinetics, in contrast, is the study of the forces and moments that cause movement during walking, including gravity, ground reaction forces, and muscle forces.
questions.question: Gait kinematics specifically studies:

options: Looking straight ahead since this reduces awareness of floor hazards
Walking on snowy, icy, rainy, or slippery surfaces with the device
Wearing rubber-soled footwear which increases friction excessively
Using the device bilaterally as asymmetrical use improves balance
Carrying items in a bag since this does not affect walking stability
questions.question: A patient ambulating with a cane or crutch should be specifically cautioned to avoid:
questions.explanation: Users should avoid snowy, icy, or rainy conditions, and should not walk on slippery surfaces with ambulatory devices. Spilled liquids should be wiped up to avoid slipping. Items such as scatter rugs and extension cords that may cause tripping should be removed. A non-skid bath mat should be used in the shower or tub.

Motion description (kinematics) appropriately precedes force analysis (kinetics) because understanding what movement occurs guides the investigation of which forces need to be measured or calculated. Observational analysis identifies clinically relevant deviations before expensive or time-consuming kinetic measurements are applied selectively. This sequential approach ensures efficient and focused quantitative biomechanical assessment in clinical and research settings.
options: Is always less important than kinetics
Guides investigation of which forces to measure
questions.question: Motion description (kinematics) appropriately precedes force analysis (kinetics) because motion description:

questions.explanation: Maximum muscular power occurs at approximately one-third of maximum isometric force and one-third of maximum shortening velocity. This represents the optimal trade-off between the force-velocity relationship and allows maximum rate of work production. Physiotherapists designing power training programmes target this range through plyometrics and loaded movement velocities corresponding to the power peak.
questions.question: Maximum muscular power output occurs at approximately what fraction of maximum velocity and force:

questions.explanation: Gliding (plane/arthroidal) joints have nearly flat articulating bone surfaces and permit only non-axial gliding motion. Examples include intermetatarsal, intercarpal, intertarsal joints, and the facet joints of vertebrae. Because motion is non-axial, these joints do not have a specific degree of freedom in the traditional sense.
questions.question: Gliding (plane) joints permit which specific type of motion?
options: Non-axial gliding only, as the articulating surfaces are nearly flat
Uniaxial rotation about a single perpendicular axis of motion
Biaxial motion including flexion, extension, abduction, adduction
Triaxial motion in all three cardinal planes simultaneously
Hinge-like planar motion restricted by strong collateral ligaments

questions.explanation: There is a progressive age-related reduction in the number of motor units and muscle fibers, and a reduction in the size of Type II fibers specifically. This is not related to sex or training status. Infants and children have significantly smaller proportions of Type IIb fibers than adults, and obese adults also have lower proportions of Type IIb fibers than non-obese individuals.
questions.question: Age-related changes in muscle fiber composition are characterized by:
options: Selective loss of Type I fibers with preservation of Type II fibers
Conversion of Type IIb to Type I fibers in all elderly individuals
Progressive reduction in motor units, fibers, and size of Type II fibers
Increased proportion of Type IIb relative to Type I fibers with aging
No significant change in fiber type ratio but reduced fiber diameter

questions.explanation: Motor units are activated asynchronously during sustained contractions, which helps produce smooth contractions and delays the early onset of fatigue. Asynchronous activation minimizes fatigue by allowing the most fatigue-resistant muscle fibers (Type I and IIa) to be preferentially active while Type IIb units rest. This is the body's strategy for prolonged submaximal effort.
questions.question: Asynchronous activation of motor units during sustained contractions primarily serves to:
options: Minimize fatigue by allowing alternation of active motor units
Maximize peak force by synchronizing all units at peak tension
Reduce proprioceptive feedback to the muscle spindles uniformly
Ensure all motor units reach tetanus simultaneously at low loads
Prevent calcium accumulation in the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores

questions.explanation: The center of gravity (COG) is the point around which a body's weight is equally balanced regardless of position. In men, the COG is located at approximately 56% of height, while in women it is at approximately 55% of height. Generally, the COG is about 6 inches (approximately 30 cm) above the crotch.
options: 50% of standing height at the level of the umbilicus
56% of standing height slightly above the pelvic brim
60% of standing height at the level of the lower ribcage
45% of standing height below the anterior superior iliac spine
65% of standing height at the level of the xiphoid process
questions.question: The center of gravity in men is located at approximately what percentage of standing height?

questions.explanation: Procedural considerations in observational gait analysis (OGA) require an open and unobstructed area for examination. This allows the examiner to observe the gait pattern from the front, back, and side without physical barriers, and enables full observation of each joint segment through each gait cycle phase.
options: Allow unrestricted observation of the entire gait pattern without barriers
Ensure the force platforms are properly calibrated before testing
Position reflective markers without interference from furniture
Facilitate video recording from all three cardinal planes simultaneously
Allow the patient to walk at maximum speed without decelerating
questions.question: An open, unobstructed area for examination is recommended in OGA specifically to:

options: A person can walk for the greatest distance without stopping
The highest cadence is achieved during continuous ambulation
Maximum step length occurs with normal cadence patterns
The greatest forward progression of the center of gravity occurs
There is least energy consumption per unit distance traveled
questions.question: Comfortable walking speed (CWS) is specifically defined as the speed at which:
questions.explanation: Comfortable walking speed (CWS) is the characteristic speed at which there is least energy consumption per unit distance. In normal gait, CWS is approximately 80 metres per minute (5.0 km/h; 1.4 m/s; 3.1 mph). Maximum walking speed is approximately 2.5 m/s (9.0 km/h; 5.6 mph).

options: Forces restoring the body precisely to its original position
Progressive increase in displacement from the original state
Increased instability with each successive small displacement
Complete loss of contact with the supporting surface below
No change in the height or position of the center of gravity
questions.question: In neutral equilibrium, displacement of the body results in:
questions.explanation: In neutral equilibrium, despite displacement, the height and position of the COG remains the same. Examples include a cone on its side, a rolling ball on a flat plane, and rotation of the upper and lower limbs with the patient in a lying position. Neither restoring nor destabilizing forces are produced.

questions.question: The interphalangeal joints and the ulnohumeral joint are both classified as:
questions.explanation: Hinge joints (ginglymus) have one convex and one concave articulating surface. Strong collateral ligaments restrict movement to a planar hinge-like motion. The ulnohumeral joint and interphalangeal joints are uniaxial hinge joints allowing only flexion and extension. They have one degree of freedom around the frontal (transverse) axis.
options: Condyloid joints permitting flexion, extension, and circumduction
Saddle joints permitting motions similar to condyloid with more ROM
Hinge (ginglymus) joints permitting uniaxial flexion and extension
Ball and socket joints permitting rotations in all three planes
Pivot joints permitting rotation around only one longitudinal axis

questions.explanation: The sarcomere is the smallest functional contractile unit of skeletal muscle, bounded by Z lines and containing interdigitating actin and myosin filaments. It is within the sarcomere that the sliding filament mechanism of contraction occurs. Understanding sarcomere biology is clinically relevant in conditions like muscle contracture, where shortened sarcomere numbers reduce extensibility and limit functional ROM.
questions.question: The smallest contractile unit of skeletal muscle capable of shortening is the:
Impulse is the product of force and the time over which it acts and is expressed as:
questions.explanation: Impulse is defined as J = Ft (force multiplied by the time over which it acts). A large change in a body's state of motion can result from either a small force acting over a long time or a large force acting for a short time. Impulse is related to the change in momentum of a body.
options: The ratio of change in velocity to the time interval elapsed
Force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the axis
Change in momentum divided by the elapsed time period
J = Ft, where J is impulse, F is force and t is time
The integral of torque with respect to angular displacement

questions.explanation: Balance is defined as an individual's ability to control equilibrium — that is, to increase or reduce stability as needed. This distinguishes balance from stability, which is the resistance to disruption of equilibrium. Balance requires dynamic neuromuscular control to adapt to changing conditions.
options: Control equilibrium by increasing or reducing stability as needed
Maintain the center of gravity directly over the base of support
Resist all linear and angular accelerations without displacement
Prevent the line of gravity from falling outside the base of support
Sustain a constant velocity of the center of gravity during motion
questions.question: Balance is mechanically defined as an individual's ability to:
A patient using an ambulatory device should be instructed to NOT look down because:
options: Looking down reduces peripheral vision for obstacle detection
Looking straight ahead helps maintain good posture and prevents musculoskeletal disorders
Looking down increases compression on the cervical spine vertebrae
Head position affects balance via the vestibular system in the ear
Downward gaze reduces cadence and walking speed significantly
questions.explanation: Users should not look down but always look straight ahead. This helps the user maintain a good posture and prevents musculoskeletal disorders resulting from sustained cervical flexion. Users should also not use ambulatory devices when feeling dizzy or drowsy, not walk on slippery surfaces, and wear well-fitting, low-heel footwear.

questions.question: Supination of the forearm is defined as the movement that brings:
questions.explanation: Supination is the movement of the forearm that brings the palm to face anteriorly (upward in the anatomical position) or toward the ceiling when the arm is at the side. Pronation is the opposite — the movement of the forearm to make the palm face posteriorly (downward). These movements occur in the horizontal/transverse plane.
options: The palm of the hand to face posteriorly (downward in standing)
The palm of the hand to face anteriorly (upward in anatomical position)
The thumb toward the body's midline in the frontal plane movement
The forearm into extension at the elbow in the sagittal plane
The dorsum (back) of the hand to face anteriorly toward viewer

questions.explanation: The two types of friction are static friction (the force preventing initial motion between surfaces at rest) and kinetic friction (the force opposing motion between already-moving surfaces). Static friction is generally greater than kinetic friction. In traction therapy, static friction between the patient and the treatment table is essential to maintain counter-traction, while therapeutic surfaces use materials to optimise the coefficient of friction.
questions.question: The two main types of friction relevant to physiotherapy practice are:

options: Laterally away from the midline in the frontal plane of the body
Medially across the body in the horizontal transverse plane
Superiorly toward the head in an elevated arc of movement
Inferiorly returning to the anatomical position from flexion
Posteriorly extending the arm behind the plane of the trunk
questions.explanation: Horizontal adduction occurs when the arm (flexed at 90 degrees) moves medially across the body in the horizontal (transverse) plane. Horizontal abduction occurs when the flexed arm moves laterally away from the midline in the same plane. These movements are important in activities requiring cross-body reach and sport-specific arm actions.
questions.question: Horizontal adduction of the upper limb occurs when the arm, flexed at 90 degrees, moves:
Doubling running speed quadruples kinetic energy because kinetic energy relates to velocity by a:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy equals one-half times mass times velocity squared, meaning doubling velocity quadruples kinetic energy. This quadratic relationship has significant clinical implications for impact forces during falls, running, and explosive movements. Physiotherapists apply this principle when advising patients on fall risk management and when designing speed-progressive return-to-sport protocols following lower limb injuries.

Head nodding is an example of a first-class lever. The fulcrum is the atlanto-occipital joint (located between the load and the effort). The load is the weight of the skull and the effort comes from the muscular contractions in the posterior muscles of the neck.
questions.question: The atlanto-occipital joint during head nodding represents which class of lever?
options: First class lever with the fulcrum between effort and load
Second class lever with load between effort and fulcrum
Third class lever with effort between fulcrum and load
A compound pulley system not classifiable as a lever class
Second class lever with effort arm shorter than load arm

questions.question: A practical advantage of observational gait analysis over clinical gait analysis is that OGA:
options: Provides three-dimensional data on all joint kinematics simultaneously
Requires little investment in equipment, time, and expense to perform
Eliminates inter-rater variability in identifying gait deviations
Is the gold standard for pre-surgical decision-making in complex cases
Can measure electromyographic activity of deep hip muscles directly
questions.explanation: Observational gait analysis (OGA) requires little investment in equipment, time, and expense. It is appropriate to characterize most gait pathologies and is the most common method of analysis in clinical settings. CGA requires specialized technology (motion capture, force plates, EMG), making it significantly more expensive and time-consuming.

questions.question: At shortened muscle lengths following contraction, tension generation is reduced because of:
questions.explanation: At shortened muscle lengths, actin-myosin filament overlap reduces, decreasing the number of cross-bridges that can form and thus reducing tension generation. Additionally, elastic components cannot contribute pre-tension at shortened positions. This length-tension relationship explains why muscles in shortened positions are weaker and why full-range training is essential for complete rehabilitation.

questions.question: The sarcomere is defined as:
options: The entire myofibril from one motor end plate to the terminal end
A single myofilament of actin or myosin within a muscle fiber
The region of the muscle fiber enclosed by the Z-line network
The contractile protein complex including actin, myosin, and titin
The basic structural and contractile unit of skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: The sarcomere is the basic structural (and contractile) unit of skeletal muscle. It is the smallest contractile unit capable of force production and shortening. At each end of a sarcomere are Z lines, with the H zone in the middle (myosin without actin), I bands at the ends (actin only), and the A band representing the full length of the myosin filaments.

questions.question: Qualitative and quantitative gait analysis methods are best described as:
questions.explanation: Qualitative observational analysis guides quantitative analysis by identifying relevant movement deviations and directing which parameters to measure objectively. Qualitative insights allow efficient allocation of quantitative measurement resources and formulation of testable clinical hypotheses. Together, they provide comprehensive biomechanical understanding — observational efficiency combined with objective measurement precision — that neither method achieves independently.

In translation, all body parts move in the same direction, through the same distance, and at the same time. Translation can be linear (all body parts move in a straight line, as in ice skating), curvilinear (line of motion is curved), or non-linear. This contrasts with rotation, where all body parts move through the same angle.
options: At different speeds, through the same distance, in the same direction
Through the same angle, at the same time, in the same direction
At different times, through different distances, in varying directions
In circular paths around a fixed central axis of rotation
In the same direction, through the same distance, at the same time
questions.question: In translational motion, all body parts move:

questions.explanation: Eccentric contraction occurs when the opposing joint torque is greater than the torque produced by tension in the muscle, causing the muscle to lengthen while it contracts. The external load is greater than the internal force produced by the muscle. Eccentric contraction acts as a braking mechanism to control movement speed.
options: Maintaining constant length while generating maximum tension
Shortening while producing torque greater than the resistive torque
Shortening rapidly to accelerate the body segment forward
Producing zero net torque as active and passive forces balance
Lengthening while contracting as external load exceeds internal force
questions.question: Eccentric contraction is characterized by the muscle:

questions.explanation: Possible roles of articular fibrocartilage include distribution of loads, improvement of fit of articulating surfaces, limitation of translation between bones, protection of the periphery, lubrication, and shock absorption. Articular fibrocartilage is a passive structure and does NOT actively contract. Examples include intervertebral discs and knee menisci.
options: Distribution of loads over joint surfaces to reduce contact stress
Improvement of the fit between the articulating bone surfaces
Active muscular contraction to control joint motion dynamically
Protection of the periphery of the articular surface from damage
Lubrication and shock absorption during dynamic joint loading
questions.question: Articular fibrocartilage (menisci/discs) serves all of the following roles EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Pronator teres acts as a neutraliser during elbow flexion, counteracting the unwanted supination produced by biceps brachii. Neutralisers contract to eliminate undesired secondary actions of the primary mover, allowing only the intended movement to occur. Recognition of neutraliser function is important in electromyographic analysis and helps explain why isolated weakness of neutralisers leads to unwanted compensatory movements.
questions.question: Pronator teres counteracts the unwanted supination produced by biceps brachii during elbow flexion. This muscle role is classified as:
Density of a body is defined as mass per unit volume with the standard SI unit of:
questions.explanation: Density combines a body's mass with its volume and is defined as mass per unit volume. The standard SI unit is kg/m³ (kilograms per cubic meter). Density can also be expressed as kg/cm³ or kg/liter. It is related to specific weight, which is weight per unit volume (N/m³).
options: Kilograms per cubic meter (kg/m³) expressing mass-volume ratio
Newtons per square meter (N/m²) expressing force per area
Kilograms per Newton (kg/N) expressing mass-to-weight ratio
Joules per cubic meter (J/m³) relating energy to volume
Pascals (Pa) expressing force distributed over a given area

questions.question: At the molecular level, muscle contraction is triggered when calcium binds to:
questions.explanation: Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind to troponin C, causing conformational changes that move tropomyosin away from actin's active sites, allowing myosin cross-bridges to attach and generate force. This calcium-troponin interaction is the fundamental regulatory switch for skeletal muscle contraction. Calcium dysregulation can contribute to abnormal muscle tone and spasticity seen after neurological injury.

The physiological cross-section of a muscle determines its potential force of contraction. Absolute muscle strength is recognized as 3–4 kg per square centimeter of cross-section. The physiological cross-section is defined as the area of a section that cuts every muscle fiber making up the muscle at its level of hypertrophy.
questions.question: The physiological cross-section of a muscle determines its potential for:
options: Force production, with absolute strength recognized at 3-4 kg/cm²
Speed of contraction based on the number of sarcomeres in series
Endurance capacity based on mitochondrial density per fiber
Excursion length based on fiber length along the muscle axis
Recruitment threshold based on motor neuron size and diameter

questions.question: In Rancho Los Amigos terminology, the gait cycle consists of which eight phases?
questions.explanation: The Rancho Los Amigos terminology describes the gait cycle using eight phases: Initial contact, Loading response, Midstance, Terminal stance, Preswing, Initial swing, Mid-swing, and Terminal swing. This standardized system replaced the older classic terminology (heel strike, foot flat, mid-stance, heel-off, toe-off, initial swing, mid-swing, heel strike).
options: Heel strike, foot flat, mid-stance, heel-off, toe-off, initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing
Initial contact, foot flat, mid-stance, heel-off, push-off, initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing
Loading response, mid-stance, terminal stance, pre-swing, initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing, initial contact
Initial contact, opposite toe-off, heel rise, opposite initial contact, toe-off, initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing
Initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance, preswing, initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing
Ability to measure both active and passive joint motion accurately
Standardized use across all healthcare and research settings globally
Versatility in measuring joint position and motion at multiple joints
Compatibility with electrogoniometer and inclinometer data outputs
Ability to record both linear and angular displacement simultaneously
questions.explanation: The universal goniometer is described as 'universal' because of its versatility — it can be used to measure joint position and motion at virtually all peripheral joints. It is the most common instrument used in clinical settings and is produced in various sizes and shapes though the basic design with a body and two arms remains consistent.
questions.question: The universal goniometer is described as 'universal' specifically because of its:

options: Effort arm to load arm (EA:LA), enabling small force to become larger
Load arm to effort arm (LA:EA), quantifying the speed advantage
Applied force to the resulting velocity of the body segment
Torque produced to the angular displacement of the joint
Normal force to frictional force at the articular surface
questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage is the ability to turn a small force into a larger force or movement. It is the ratio of the effort arm to the load arm (EA:LA). When the effort arm is greater than the load arm (as in second-class levers), mechanical advantage exists. Third-class levers always have mechanical disadvantage because the load arm exceeds the effort arm.
questions.question: Mechanical advantage in a lever system is defined as the ratio of:
Above 38.5 degrees Celsius, body functions become:
questions.explanation: Temperatures above 38.5 degrees Celsius become dangerous for body functions because protein denaturation, heat stroke risk, and enzymatic dysfunction begin to occur as thermal limits are exceeded. This establishes the upper safe limit for therapeutic heat application and vigorous exercise warm-up. Physiotherapists monitor patient responses to thermal modalities to ensure temperatures remain within the therapeutic window.

courses.title: Gross Anatomy

questions.question: The dorsum of the foot receives cutaneous innervation from several nerves. Which nerve supplies the skin between the 1st and 2nd toes on the dorsum?
questions.explanation: The deep fibular nerve supplies the skin of the first web space (between the 1st and 2nd toes) on the dorsum of the foot. The superficial fibular nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot. The saphenous nerve supplies the medial side (first metatarsal area), while the sural nerve supplies the lateral side (digiti minimi area). This pattern is important in assessing nerve injuries.

assesses ulnar artery patency before radial artery cannulation or harvesting. Both arteries are occluded, the hand is opened (blanched), then ulnar pressure is released. Color should return within 5-15 seconds indicating adequate ulnar collateral circulation. Failure indicates insufficient ulnar supply making radial artery intervention unsafe.
questions.question: Which test assesses ulnar artery patency before radial artery cannulation?

options: Allows full flexion-extension with ligament support
questions.question: How does the elbow joint capsule weakness affect function?
questions.explanation: The elbow joint capsule is weak anteriorly and posteriorly, allowing extensive flexion-extension movement. The medial and lateral collateral ligaments provide essential stability. This capsular laxity in the movement plane while maintaining stability perpendicular to it exemplifies structure-function relationships.

questions.question: The sphenoid sinus drains into which location?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinuses drain into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. These sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid bone and vary greatly in size. Close relationship to the optic nerve and carotid artery makes sphenoid surgery particularly challenging.

The popliteal fascia is often pierced by the small saphenous vein as it ascends from the lateral ankle to the popliteal fossa, where it enters the popliteal vein. The popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg, forming a protective covering for neurovascular structures.
questions.question: The popliteal fascia is often pierced by which superficial vein as it drains into the popliteal vein?

questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus has little action during ordinary gentle walking on level ground. It acts mainly in rising from sitting, straightening up, walking upstairs, and running. This is a critical clinical distinction in assessing gluteal function and designing rehabilitation after injury.
questions.question: Despite being the great extensor of the hip joint, gluteus maximus has little action during which of the following?

questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits the esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, esophageal branches of left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The hiatus is formed by muscle fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm. Some right crus fibers form a sling around the esophagus.
questions.question: Which structure passes through esophageal hiatus?
The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). M�ller's muscle (superior tarsal muscle), a smooth muscle also elevating the lid, is innervated by sympathetics. Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis (drooping eyelid) along with eye movement deficits. Horner's syndrome causes mild ptosis from sympathetic loss.

questions.question: Which rib level marks the base of breast vertically?
questions.explanation: The base of the breast extends vertically from the 2nd to 6th rib. Transversely, it extends from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line. The axillary tail of Spence extends from the upper outer quadrant into the axilla. These landmarks are important for clinical breast examination.

The geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve contains cell bodies of sensory neurons carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via chorda tympani. The ganglion is located at the genu (bend) of the facial canal in the temporal bone. Herpes zoster infection (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) causes facial paralysis and painful vesicles.
questions.question: Which ganglion contains cell bodies for taste from the anterior tongue?

questions.explanation: The oval window (fenestra vestibuli) in the medial wall of the middle ear is closed by the footplate of the stapes, held in place by the annular ligament. The stapes transmits vibrations from the ossicular chain to the perilymph of the inner ear. Otosclerosis causes abnormal bone growth fixing the stapes, resulting in conductive hearing loss.
questions.question: The oval window is closed by which structure?
Inflammation of the bursa separating gluteus maximus from the ischial tuberosity, caused by prolonged sitting on hard surfaces, is termed what?
questions.explanation: Ischial bursitis is inflammation of the bursa separating the gluteus maximus from the ischial tuberosity, caused by prolonged sitting on hard surfaces pressing against the bones. It is sometimes called 'weaver's bottom.' Trochanteric bursitis at the greater trochanter is more common in women and associated with overuse or direct trauma.

The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels (arteries and veins, 4-6 pairs) passing from the splenic vessels near the hilum to the gastric fundus, and the left gastroepiploic vessels running to the greater curvature. The splenic artery, splenic vein, and tail of the pancreas run in the splenorenal ligament, not the gastrosplenic ligament. These two ligaments together connect the spleen to the stomach and posterior abdominal wall. Division of the gastrosplenic ligament is necessary during splenectomy, requiring ligation of the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels to devascularize the spleen.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the gastrosplenic ligament?

questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries give off anterior spinal arteries before joining to form the basilar artery. The two anterior spinal arteries unite to form a single vessel descending in the anterior median fissure. The vertebral arteries also give off posterior spinal arteries. These vessels supply the cervical spinal cord before receiving reinforcement from segmental arteries.
questions.question: The vertebral artery gives off which spinal branch?

questions.explanation: Psoas minor originates from the sides of T12 and L1 vertebrae and their intervening disc. It inserts into the pectineal line and iliopubic eminence. When present, it acts conjointly with psoas major and iliacus in flexing the thigh at the hip. Its long slender tendon is occasionally used as a landmark in pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Psoas minor, a variable muscle absent in approximately 40% of individuals, originates from which vertebral levels?
What is the significance of the critical zone in the supraspinatus tendon?
questions.explanation: The "critical zone" in the supraspinatus tendon has relatively poor vascularity, located approximately 1cm from its humeral insertion. This hypovascular area is more susceptible to degenerative changes and tears. The zone's poor blood supply impairs healing after injury.

The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, located immediately superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. Its margins, called the medial and lateral crura, are connected superiorly by intercrural fibers and give attachment to the external spermatic fascia. The superficial ring represents the external opening of the inguinal canal and transmits the spermatic cord in males or round ligament in females, along with the ilioinguinal nerve. The ring is larger in males than females, contributing to the higher incidence of inguinal hernias in males.
questions.question: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in which structure?

questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery arises from the tibioperoneal trunk, which is one of the two terminal divisions of the popliteal artery (the other being the anterior tibial artery). The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and the fibular artery. The fibular artery descends alongside the fibula in the posterior compartment.
questions.question: The fibular (peroneal) artery is a branch of which vessel, making it an indirect branch of the popliteal artery?
Which muscle can be absent without functional deficit?
questions.explanation: is absent in approximately 15% of people without any functional deficit. When present, it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. The tendon is commonly harvested for use in tendon grafts and reconstructive procedures.

questions.question: How many renal pyramids typically comprise each kidney?
questions.explanation: The renal medulla is composed of approximately 10-12 renal pyramids in each kidney. Each pyramid has its base directed toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting medially into a minor calyx. The renal columns (columns of Bertin) extend between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus.

The pampiniform plexus of veins surrounding the testicular artery in the spermatic cord functions as a countercurrent heat exchanger, cooling arterial blood before it reaches the testes and maintaining testicular temperature 2-3?C below core body temperature, essential for normal spermatogenesis. This venous network of 8-12 veins allows extensive surface area for heat exchange. Varicocele (varicosity of pampiniform plexus) can impair this cooling mechanism and potentially affect fertility. The plexus drains into a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring, with asymmetric drainage (right to IVC, left to left renal vein).
questions.question: The pampiniform plexus functions primarily to:

questions.explanation: The splenic (left colic) flexure is positioned higher than the hepatic (right colic) flexure and also forms a more acute angle. The splenic flexure is attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament. This higher position of the left flexure is clinically significant in colonoscopy and surgical procedures.
questions.question: Which flexure of the colon is located at a higher position?

questions.explanation: The anterior wall of the axilla is formed by the pectoralis major muscle and the pectoral fascia associated with it. The pectoralis minor and clavipectoral fascia form a deeper layer. The anterior axillary fold, formed by pectoralis major bridging from thoracic wall to humerus, represents the inferiormost graspable part.
questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the axilla's superficial layer?

questions.explanation: During grip, wrist extensors isometrically contract to stabilize the wrist in slight extension. This prevents wrist flexion as finger flexors contract, optimizing finger flexor length-tension relationship for maximum grip force. This synergistic stabilization demonstrates functional muscle interaction.
options: Wrist extensors stabilize wrist enabling grip strength
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist flexors and extensors in grip?
What is the functional significance of the bicipital aponeurosis?
questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the cubital fossa roof and protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture. It distributes biceps force to the ulna and forearm fascia. Historically recognized as the grace of God tendon for protecting vital structures during bloodletting.
options: Provides muscle attachment to bicipital fascia
Reinforces cubital fossa, protects neurovascular structures

questions.question: The medial ligament of the ankle joint is called the deltoid ligament. Which statement correctly describes its four components?
questions.explanation: The deltoid ligament is the medial ligament of the ankle, a strong triangular ligament with its apex on the medial malleolus. It has four parts: tibionavicular (to navicular), tibiocalcaneal (to sustentaculum tali of calcaneus), and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts (to the talus). It is significantly stronger than the lateral ligaments and rarely ruptures in isolation.
options: It is a single band with one attachment to the calcaneus
It has tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts
It consists only of the tibionavicular and posterior tibiotalar parts
It is a triangular ligament with apex on the fibula
It attaches from the fibula to the navicular, calcaneus, and talus

questions.question: What percentage of the small intestine length does the jejunum constitute?
questions.explanation: The jejunum constitutes approximately 40% of the total length of the small intestine beyond the duodenum. This represents about 2.5 meters of the 5-6 meter total small bowel length. The jejunum is characterized by being thicker-walled, more vascular, and having more prominent plicae circulares than the ileum.

questions.question: Which vessel specifically supplies the bed of the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Branches of the facial and lingual arteries supply the submandibular gland, with the facial artery providing the primary vascular supply. The facial artery passes deep to the gland before crossing the mandible. Venous drainage follows corresponding veins to the internal jugular system.

The ulnar nerve's course around the medial epicondyle means elbow flexion stretches the nerve. Prolonged flexion (sleeping with bent elbow) can cause compression symptoms. This positional sensitivity explains why cubital tunnel syndrome symptoms may worsen at night and why sleeping with extended elbows helps.
questions.question: How does the ulnar nerve's course make hand position affect its function?
options: Elbow flexion stretches nerve around medial epicondyle

questions.explanation: The deep circumflex iliac artery arises from the external iliac artery (just above the inguinal ligament, near the origin of the inferior epigastric artery), not from the abdominal aorta. It runs laterally along the inguinal ligament and iliac crest, supplying the lower abdominal wall muscles. The abdominal aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (inferior phrenic, suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac, SMA, IMA), paired parietal branches (four lumbar arteries), and the unpaired median sacral artery posteriorly, before bifurcating into right and left common iliac arteries at L4 level.
questions.question: Which artery typically does NOT arise from the abdominal aorta?
At which vertebral levels do the kidneys typically lie?
questions.explanation: The kidneys typically extend from the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12) to the third lumbar vertebra (L3) on the posterior abdominal wall. The right kidney is slightly lower than the left due to the presence of the liver. Both kidneys move inferiorly with respiration, descending as much as 2.5 cm during diaphragmatic contraction.

The posterior tibial pulse is palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery curves to enter the tarsal tunnel and then the sole of the foot. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. The four main pulse points of the lower limb are femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.
options: Anterior surface of the ankle between malleoli
Dorsum of foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus
Midway between lateral malleolus and calcaneus
questions.question: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated at which surface anatomical location?

questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin of the lateral scalp posterior to the auricle. It ascends along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The greater occipital nerve (C2) provides sensation to the posterior scalp. Both nerves can be involved in occipital neuralgia.
questions.question: The lesser occipital nerve is derived from which spinal segments?

questions.explanation: Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm accompanied by approximation of vocal folds and closure of the glottis. It commonly results from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings. It may also occur in pleurisy, peritonitis, or pericarditis affecting the diaphragm.
questions.question: What causes hiccup?
Which vessel supplies the cecum?
questions.explanation: The cecum receives its blood supply from the ileocolic artery (terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery), which divides into superior and inferior branches. The inferior branch gives rise to anterior and posterior cecal arteries that supply the corresponding surfaces of the cecum. The ileocolic artery also gives off the appendicular artery (to appendix) and ileal branches. The superior branch of the ileocolic artery anastomoses with the right colic artery along the ascending colon. The cecum's venous drainage follows the arterial pattern, with ileocolic vein draining to the superior mesenteric vein.

The median nerve is the only nerve passing through the carpal tunnel. It enters the hand between the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and lies anterior to the flexor digitorum profundus tendons. Compression of this nerve within the tunnel causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?

options: Right costal margin at 9th costal cartilage
questions.question: The gallbladder fundus typically lies at which anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder typically reaches the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis muscle crosses the right costal margin (approximately at the transpyloric plane). This surface marking corresponds to the point where the gallbladder may contact the anterior abdominal wall, making it palpable when distended or inflamed. Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest with deep palpation at this point due to pain) indicates acute cholecystitis. The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum.

The coracoacromial ligament runs between the coracoid process and acromion of the scapula. Unlike other shoulder ligaments, it does not cross a joint or permit movement. It forms part of the coraco-acromial arch that prevents superior displacement of the humeral head.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the coracoid process to the acromion of the scapula?

options: Lateral joint capsule and adductor hallucis
questions.question: Hallux valgus (bunion) is a deformity involving lateral deviation of the hallux. Which structure becomes contracted in established hallux valgus, pulling the hallux into further valgus?
questions.explanation: In established hallux valgus, the lateral joint capsule and the tendon of adductor hallucis contract and pull the hallux into further valgus deviation. The medial capsule becomes stretched and the medial eminence (bunion) forms. Abductor hallucis, which should abduct the hallux, migrates plantarly and becomes ineffective. Surgical correction involves release of lateral structures and medial capsule repair.

questions.question: Which renal artery typically passes posterior to the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation: The right renal artery is longer than the left and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava to reach the right kidney. The left renal artery has a shorter, more direct course from the aorta to the left kidney. Both arteries arise at approximately L1-L2 level, just inferior to the superior mesenteric artery origin.

questions.question: The foot contains how many tarsal bones, and what are they?
questions.explanation: The foot contains seven tarsal bones: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiform bones (medial, intermediate, and lateral). The 26 bones of the foot include 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges. Understanding tarsal anatomy is fundamental to interpreting foot radiographs and managing tarsal fractures.
options: Five: calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid, one cuneiform
Seven: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiforms
Six: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and two cuneiforms
Eight: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and four cuneiforms
Seven: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals

questions.question: What is the characteristic position of the forearm in Erb's paralysis?
questions.explanation: In Erb's paralysis, the affected arm hangs by the side in an adducted and medially rotated position. The forearm assumes an extended and pronated posture, creating the "policeman's tip" or "porter's tip" hand deformity. This results from paralysis of muscles supplied by C5-C6 nerve roots.

The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) has three branches: ascending (to the hip joint and gluteal region), transverse (encircling the femur laterally), and descending (contributing superolaterally to the genicular anastomosis around the knee). The descending branch travels between vastus intermedius and vastus lateralis muscles and provides one of the anastomotic connections at the knee.
questions.question: The lateral femoral circumflex artery has three named branches. Which of these descends distally to contribute to the genicular anastomosis?
The obturator nerve exits the pelvis through the obturator foramen. Obturator nerve injury may cause difficulty with which activity due to adductor weakness?
questions.explanation: Obturator nerve injury (as can occur with obturator hernia, difficult childbirth, or pelvic fractures) causes weakness of the adductor muscles, making it difficult to cross one leg over the other (adduction). Sensory loss occurs on the medial side of the thigh. The obturator nerve does not supply the knee directly (though the posterior division gives a branch to the knee joint capsule).
options: Crossing one leg over the other (adduction)

questions.question: What structures pass through the splenorenal ligament?
questions.explanation: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels, tail of the pancreas, and associated lymph nodes. The tail of the pancreas extends into this ligament to reach the splenic hilum. This ligament represents a portion of the dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.question: Which vessel is superior in the lung root?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery is the most superior structure in the root of both lungs. The main bronchus lies posterior to the vessels. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins are the most inferior structures in the root. This anatomical arrangement is constant and important during surgery.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes lie along the sternum?
questions.explanation: The parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum. They receive lymph from the anterior chest wall, medial breast, diaphragm, and upper abdominal wall. Efferents drain to the bronchomediastinal trunks and brachiocephalic veins.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the structures passing through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits five structures: the pudendal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, internal pudendal artery and vein, and the tendon of obturator internus. The sciatic nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen. The lesser sciatic foramen enables re-entry into the perineum from the gluteal region.

questions.question: The pes anserinus on the superior medial tibia is formed by the combined insertion of which three muscles?
questions.explanation: The pes anserinus (goose's foot) is formed by the common tendinous insertion of sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus on the superior medial surface of the tibia. These three muscles belong to three different thigh compartments yet all cross both the hip and knee joints and share this common insertion. Pes anserinus bursitis is a clinical condition here.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior mesenteric artery arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the anterior surface of the abdominal aorta at approximately the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), about 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. It supplies the hindgut derivatives: distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum. Its first branch is the left colic artery.

In a sliding hiatus hernia, the upper stomach and lower esophagus slide upward through the lax hiatus into the chest. The competence of the gastroesophageal junction is often disturbed, allowing peptic juice to regurgitate into the esophagus, causing heartburn, esophagitis, bleeding, and potentially stricture formation.
questions.question: Which hiatus hernia causes reflux?

questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli is located to the right of the abdominal aorta at the L1-L2 vertebral level, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. This dilated lymphatic sac receives the right and left lumbar lymphatic trunks, intestinal trunk, and sometimes lower intercostal trunks before giving rise to the thoracic duct. The cisterna lies anterior to the vertebral bodies and posterior to the aorta, in the retroperitoneal space. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus (crossing from right to left in the thorax) to drain into the venous system.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli lies to which side of the aorta?

questions.explanation: Femoral hernias pass through the femoral ring (the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally occupied by a lymph node) and emerge below the inguinal ligament through the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis) in the deep fascia of the thigh. They are more common in women but overall less common than inguinal hernias. They have a high risk of strangulation due to the rigid boundaries of the femoral ring.
questions.question: Where does a femoral hernia emerge?
The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for which tendon?
questions.explanation: The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for the flexor hallucis longus tendon on its inferior surface. It also receives the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon and serves as the attachment for the spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) and the deltoid ligament medially.

The second part of the axillary artery lies directly behind (posterior to) the pectoralis minor muscle. This anatomical relationship is used to divide the artery into three parts. The second part gives off two branches: the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries.
questions.question: Which portion of the axillary artery lies behind pectoralis minor?

questions.explanation: The aryepiglotticus muscle closes the laryngeal vestibule during swallowing by pulling the arytenoid cartilages toward the epiglottis. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function. The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral margins of the laryngeal inlet.
questions.question: Which muscle closes the vestibule of the larynx during swallowing?

questions.explanation: The median sacral artery arises from the posterior aspect of the abdominal aorta just before its bifurcation at the L4 level (or sometimes from the aortic bifurcation itself). This small, unpaired vessel descends in the midline anterior to the sacrum and coccyx, supplying the posterior pelvic wall and anastomosing with the lateral sacral arteries (from internal iliac). It represents a caudal continuation of the dorsal aorta and may give small lumbar arteries. The median sacral artery is occasionally injured during presacral surgery or during anterior approaches to the spine.
questions.question: The median sacral artery arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The sternal part of the diaphragm consists of two small muscular slips (or sometimes just fibrous tissue) that attach to the posterior surface of the xiphoid process. These are the smallest attachments of the diaphragm and may be absent, leaving a gap (the sternocostal triangle or foramen of Morgagni) through which superior epigastric vessels and lymphatics pass.
questions.question: What attaches the diaphragm to the xiphoid process?
Where can cervical rib compress the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: A cervical rib (arising from C7) can compress the lowest trunk of the brachial plexus as it arches over the rib at the thoracic inlet. This causes T1 symptoms: pain and paresthesias along the ulnar border of the forearm and wasting of the small muscles of the hand.

questions.question: Which trunk branches from the aortic arch first?
questions.explanation: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It ascends to the right and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch.

The lateral thoracic artery, a branch of the axillary artery, provides lateral mammary branches that supply the lateral portion of the breast. Additional supply comes from pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery and branches from posterior intercostal arteries in the 3rd and 4th intercostal spaces.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the lateral breast?

questions.explanation: The marginal artery (of Drummond) is a continuous arterial arcade running along the mesenteric border of the colon, formed by anastomoses between branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries. It provides collateral circulation and ensures blood supply if one major artery is occluded. Weak points exist, particularly at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck's point).
questions.question: What is the arterial arcade along the colon's mesenteric border called?
The tensor tympani muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid, a branch of the mandibular division (V3). The stapedius muscle is innervated by the facial nerve. Both muscles modulate ossicular chain movement, protecting the inner ear from loud sounds and reducing physiologic noise.

questions.question: The pubofemoral ligament of the hip joint limits which two movements?
questions.explanation: The pubofemoral ligament supports the hip joint inferomedially and limits extension and abduction. It is triangular, attaching superiorly to the iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merging with the capsule and lower band of the iliofemoral ligament. Strain of this ligament produces groin pain worsened by extension and abduction.

The thoracic duct terminates by draining into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Before termination, it receives the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal lymph trunks. The duct has no valve at its termination.
questions.question: Where does the thoracic duct terminate?
What nerve supplies the dorsal interossei muscles?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all interossei muscles (both dorsal and palmar). The deep branch of the ulnar nerve enters the palm and curves around the hook of the hamate to supply these intrinsic hand muscles. Ulnar nerve palsy causes weakness of finger abduction and adduction.

questions.question: Which intercostal nerves supply the breast?
questions.explanation: The anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves supply the breast. These nerves convey sensory fibers to the skin, sympathetic fibers to blood vessels, and fibers to smooth muscle in the overlying skin and nipple. Pain from breast pathology follows these dermatomes.

questions.question: Which epithelium lines the anal canal above the pectinate line?
questions.explanation: Above the pectinate (dentate) line, the anal canal is lined by simple columnar epithelium (rectal-type mucosa) forming the columns of Morgagni. Below the pectinate line, it transitions to stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium (in the intermediate zone) and then stratified squamous keratinized epithelium (in the cutaneous zone). The pectinate line marks the junction of endoderm and ectoderm.

questions.question: Where does referred cardiac pain typically radiate?
questions.explanation: Cardiac ischemic pain typically radiates to the left shoulder, left arm (especially the medial aspect and little finger), neck, and jaw, following the distribution of T1-T4 dermatomes that share spinal segments with cardiac afferents. This occurs because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal cord neurons. Some patients also experience epigastric discomfort or right-sided radiation.

questions.question: Which of the following muscles is NOT among the six small lateral rotators of the hip joint?
questions.explanation: The six small lateral rotators of the hip joint are: quadratus femoris, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, obturator externus, and piriformis. Gluteus medius is primarily an abductor and medial rotator of the hip, not a lateral rotator. Gluteus medius is sometimes referred to as the 'rotator cuff of the hip' for its stabilizing role.

questions.question: Which vessel supplies the nasal mucosa?
questions.explanation: The nasal mucosa receives blood from both internal carotid (via ophthalmic artery branches: anterior and posterior ethmoidal) and external carotid (via maxillary artery branches: sphenopalatine, greater palatine) systems. The superior labial artery also contributes anteriorly. This rich dual blood supply accounts for profuse epistaxis. Kiesselbach's plexus represents arterial convergence.

questions.question: What is the length of the female urethra?
questions.explanation: The female urethra is approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches) long and extends from the internal urethral orifice of the bladder to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule. It is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall and passes through the urogenital diaphragm. The shorter length makes females more susceptible to urinary tract infections.

The laryngeal ventricle (sinus of Morgagni) is a space between the true vocal fold below and the false vocal fold (vestibular fold) above. It extends laterally into the saccule, which contains mucous glands that lubricate the vocal cords. The lateral wall is formed by the thyroid cartilage.
questions.question: Which space lies between the vocal and vestibular folds?
Which vein receives the left renal vein?
questions.explanation: Both right and left renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is approximately three times longer than the right and crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC. The left renal vein receives the left suprarenal vein, left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein, and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein.

options: Bases of all five metatarsals only
Three cuneiforms and navicular bones only
Navicular and talus bones only proximally
Calcaneus and cuboid of the lateral column only
Three cuneiforms and cuboid proximally; five metatarsal bases distally
questions.explanation: The transverse arch is formed proximally by the three cuneiforms and the cuboid, and distally by the bases of the five metatarsals. When both feet are approximated, the medial borders form a complete transverse arch, with each foot representing a half dome. The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, contributing the bony factor to the transverse arch.
questions.question: The transverse arch is formed proximally by which bones?

questions.explanation: The "painful arc" sign is characteristic of rotator cuff pathology, particularly supraspinatus tendonitis or tears. Pain occurs specifically during the middle range of abduction (60-120 degrees) when the greater tubercle and supraspinatus tendon pass under the acromion. Pain is absent at the start and end of abduction.
questions.question: Which condition is characterized by the painful arc sign?
What prevents the kidney from descending more than normal?
questions.explanation: The renal vessels (particularly the renal veins attached to the IVC) are the main structures preventing excessive descent of the kidneys. The renal fascia provides minimal support. Loss of perirenal fat (in cachexia) can lead to nephroptosis (floating kidney), where the kidney descends excessively with positional changes, potentially causing ureteric kinking and obstruction.

The radial nerve (C5-T1) is the largest branch of the brachial plexus and the most frequently injured. It arises from the posterior cord and supplies all extensor muscles of the upper limb. The nerve is particularly vulnerable in the spiral groove of the humerus.
questions.question: Which nerve is the largest branch of the brachial plexus?
Which branch of the external carotid artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the skull through the foramen spinosum. It supplies the dura mater and inner table of the skull. Rupture of this artery causes epidural hematoma, typically from temporal bone fractures.

questions.question: The superior laryngeal nerve's internal branch provides sensation to which region?
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation above the vocal cords, including the epiglottis and vestibule. Below the cords, sensation is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. This division is clinically important for regional anesthesia during laryngoscopy.

questions.question: What procedure accesses the heart anteriorly?
questions.explanation: Median sternotomy (vertical splitting of the sternum) is the standard approach for cardiac surgery, providing excellent access to the heart, great vessels, and anterior mediastinum. The sternum is later rewired together. This approach causes less pain and respiratory compromise than lateral thoracotomy.

questions.question: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from which vertebral bodies?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the anterolateral surfaces of the bodies and intervertebral discs of L1, L2, and L3 vertebrae (sometimes extending to L4), while the left crus arises from only L1 and L2 (sometimes L3). Both crura contribute to forming the esophageal hiatus, with muscle fibers from the right crus (and sometimes left) looping around the esophagus to create a muscular sphincter mechanism. The crura also form boundaries of the aortic hiatus, with the median arcuate ligament connecting them anterior to the aorta at T12 level.

questions.question: The scala vestibuli communicates with the scala tympani through which structure?
questions.explanation: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex of the cochlea through the helicotrema. Both scalae contain perilymph. Sound vibrations travel up the scala vestibuli, through the helicotrema, and back down the scala tympani. The basilar membrane separates the scala tympani from the scala media (cochlear duct).

questions.question: Which structure marks McBurney's point on the abdominal surface?
questions.explanation: McBurney's point, located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, marks the base of the appendix where it attaches to the cecum. While the position of the appendix tip is highly variable, the base is consistently located at the confluence of the three taeniae coli on the posteromedialaaspect of the cecum.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the ovary?
questions.explanation: The ovaries drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, following the ovarian vessels along which the lymphatics ascend. This drainage pattern reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys. In contrast, the uterine fundus drains to para-aortic nodes via lymphatics following the ovarian vessels, while the uterine body drains to external iliac nodes, and the cervix drains to external iliac, internal iliac, and sacral nodes. The upper vagina drains to internal iliac nodes, while the lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

questions.question: At how many points is the ureter typically constricted?
questions.explanation: The ureter has three normal physiological constrictions: (1) at the pelviureteric junction where the renal pelvis joins the ureter, (2) where it crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and (3) at the vesicoureteric junction where it pierces the bladder wall. These are the most common sites for ureteric stone impaction.

is a small triangular muscle that assists the triceps brachii in elbow extension. It lies on the lateral aspect of the elbow, blending with the triceps. Both muscles are supplied by the radial nerve and work together to extend the elbow.
questions.question: Which muscle assists triceps in elbow extension?

options: Knee joint effusion without ligament injury
Posterior knee dislocation and tibial plateau fractures
questions.question: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa and is most vulnerable in which clinical scenario?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is most vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures because it runs closest to the posterior joint capsule. Posterior dislocation puts direct traction on the artery and can cause intimal tear or complete transection. Assessment of distal pulses (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial) is mandatory after knee dislocation before any reduction attempt.

options: It originates from the rim of the acetabulum
It is supplied exclusively by the obturator nerve
Does not cross the hip joint; supplied by the common fibular nerve
It inserts into the medial tibial condyle distally
