It is classified as a medial compartment muscle
questions.question: The short head of biceps femoris differs from the other hamstrings in which critical way?
questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris does not cross the hip joint (originating from the linea aspera, not the ischial tuberosity) and therefore cannot extend the hip. It is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve, unlike all other hamstrings which are supplied by the tibial division. It only flexes the knee and laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed.

A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts. The inferior mediastinum is further subdivided into anterior, middle, and posterior mediastina. This anatomical division is useful for localizing pathology on imaging.
questions.question: Which plane divides the mediastinum horizontally?
What causes Volkmann's ischemic contracture?
questions.explanation: Volkmann's ischemic contracture results from compartment syndrome causing forearm muscle ischemia. Increased pressure in the closed fascial compartment impairs venous outflow and subsequently arterial inflow. Untreated ischemia leads to muscle necrosis and subsequent flexion contracture of the fingers and wrist.

questions.question: Where is the AV node situated?
questions.explanation: The AV node is located in the lower part of the interatrial septum, within the triangle of Koch (bounded by the tricuspid annulus, coronary sinus orifice, and tendon of Todaro). It receives the impulse from the SA node and, after a physiological delay allowing atrial contraction, transmits it to the ventricles via the bundle of His. Its blood supply is typically from the right coronary artery.

Anterior interosseous syndrome involves compression of the anterior interosseous nerve, a pure motor branch of the median nerve. This causes weakness of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus to index finger, and pronator quadratus. There is no sensory loss as this is a pure motor nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve is compressed in anterior interosseous syndrome?

questions.explanation: The left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein drains into the left renal vein, while the right gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein also receives the left suprarenal vein and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein. This arrangement makes the left testicular vein more prone to varicocele formation.
questions.question: Which vein drains into the left renal vein?

questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament, forming the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, contains the portal triad: the portal vein (posteriorly), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right). This ligament extends from the porta hepatis to the superior border of the first part of the duodenum. The portal triad arrangement is crucial for the Pringle maneuver, where the hepatoduodenal ligament is compressed to control bleeding during hepatic surgery.
questions.question: Which structure contains the portal triad?

questions.explanation: Smith's fracture (reverse Colles' fracture) results from falling on the back of a flexed wrist. This causes volar (forward) displacement of the distal radius fragment, opposite to Colles' fracture. The mechanism is less common than the fall on an outstretched hand that causes Colles' fracture.
options: Fall on back of flexed wrist
questions.question: What causes Smith's fracture of the distal radius?

questions.explanation: The true vocal cords are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium, which is firmly adherent to the underlying vocal ligament without submucosa. This accounts for the pearly white avascular appearance on laryngoscopy. The rest of the larynx is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
questions.question: What epithelium lines the true vocal cords?

options: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi
Plantar interossei, dorsal interossei, flexor hallucis brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
questions.question: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, and flexor digiti minimi brevis. Flexor hallucis brevis and adductor hallucis are supplied by branches of the medial and lateral plantar nerves respectively. The adductor hallucis assists in maintaining the transverse arch of the foot by drawing the metatarsals medially.

questions.question: The transverse acetabular ligament converts the acetabular notch into a foramen. It also serves as the base of attachment for which intracapsular ligament?
questions.explanation: The transverse acetabular ligament bridges across the acetabular notch, converting it into a foramen for vessels and nerves, and serves as the base of attachment for the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the margin of the acetabulum that deepens it.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves inflammation of the first dorsal compartment containing abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons. Repetitive thumb and wrist motion causes the condition. Finkelstein's test (ulnar deviation of wrist with thumb flexed in palm) reproduces pain.
questions.question: What causes de Quervain's tenosynovitis?

options: Proximal injuries affect more muscles than distal injuries
questions.question: How does nerve injury level affect clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: Nerve injury level critically affects presentation: proximal median nerve injury affects all forearm flexors and hand muscles; carpal tunnel syndrome spares forearm muscles. Similarly, ulnar nerve injury at elbow affects forearm flexors; wrist injury doesn't. Injury level determines which muscles and sensory territories are affected.

questions.question: What connects the two crura anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament is a fibrous arch that unites the right and left crura anteriorly across the aortic hiatus at the T12 level. It forms the superior boundary of the aortic hiatus through which the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes azygos vein pass. Occasionally, this ligament can compress the celiac trunk causing median arcuate ligament syndrome.

The scapulothoracic "joint" is not a true anatomical joint but a functional articulation between the scapula and thoracic wall. It allows scapular movements (elevation, depression, protraction, retraction, rotation) essential for positioning the glenoid cavity. Muscle action rather than ligaments controls this "joint."
questions.question: What is the significance of the scapulothoracic joint?
options: Functional articulation allowing scapular mobility on thorax

questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the 5th-9th (or sometimes 5th-10th) thoracic sympathetic ganglia. It descends on the vertebral bodies, pierces the crus of the diaphragm, and synapses in the celiac ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation to foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, pancreas, spleen, etc.).
questions.question: Where does the greater splanchnic nerve arise?

questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) is a fibromuscular band arising from the right crus of the diaphragm near the esophageal hiatus that inserts onto the duodenojejunal flexure and sometimes the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supports the duodenojejunal junction and marks the transition from retroperitoneal (fixed) duodenum to intraperitoneal (mobile) jejunum. This landmark is important radiologically (widening suggests a mass in the pancreatic head) and surgically (identifies the site where the small bowel becomes mobile during laparotomy and marks the upper limit of superior mesenteric artery distribution).
questions.question: The ligament of Treitz suspends which structure?

questions.explanation: The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus. These connections lack valves, allowing bidirectional flow. Infections in the danger triangle of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.question: The facial vein commonly anastomoses with which intracranial structure?

questions.explanation: A sliding hiatal hernia is the most common type of diaphragmatic hernia (95% of hiatal hernias), where the gastroesophageal junction and part of the stomach slide up through the oesophageal hiatus into the thorax. This is often associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). In paraesophageal hernias, the gastroesophageal junction remains in place, but part of the stomach herniates alongside the esophagus.
questions.question: What type of hernia occurs through the oesophageal hiatus?
The spleen is located in which abdominal region?
questions.explanation: The spleen is situated in the left hypochondriac region, lying obliquely along the long axis of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left upper quadrant. It is protected by the rib cage and cannot normally be palpated unless enlarged. The spleen is related anteriorly to the stomach (via the gastrosplenic ligament), posteriorly to the left kidney (via the splenorenal ligament), superiorly to the diaphragm, and inferiorly to the left colic flexure (supported by the phrenicocolic ligament). The splenic notch on its superior border is a characteristic feature visible on imaging.

The cardinal ligament (Mackenrodt's ligament, transverse cervical ligament), extending from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the lateral pelvic wall, contains the uterine artery and vein along with autonomic nerve fibers and lymphatics. This ligament provides the most important support for the uterus, preventing uterine prolapse. The uterine artery crosses over the ureter ("water under the bridge") in the base of the broad ligament before reaching the uterus. During hysterectomy, the cardinal ligaments must be clamped and divided, requiring careful identification of the ureters to prevent injury.
questions.question: The cardinal ligament of the uterus contains which vessels?

questions.explanation: The corrugator cutis ani muscle, formed by fusion of fibers from the longitudinal muscle layer of the rectum and the levator ani, inserts into the skin of the anal canal at the white line (intersphincteric line, or white line of Hilton). This line represents the lower border of the internal anal sphincter and the intermuscular groove between the internal and external anal sphincters. Some longitudinal muscle fibers also blend with the puborectalis anteriorly and extend to form the rectourethralis muscle (muscle of Roux) in males, extending toward the urethra.
questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the white line of Hilton?

questions.explanation: The paired nasal bones articulate superiorly with the frontal bone at the frontonasal suture. Laterally, they attach to the frontal processes of the maxillae, and inferiorly to the upper lateral nasal cartilages. Fractures of the nasal bones are the most common facial fractures. The bones provide support for the nasal bridge.
questions.question: The nasal bones articulate superiorly with which bone?

questions.explanation: The middle suprarenal artery (from the abdominal aorta) is unique in that it supplies the medulla directly without first passing through the cortex, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly to chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic neurons). The superior suprarenal artery (from inferior phrenic) and inferior suprarenal artery (from renal) supply primarily the cortex. This direct arterial supply to the medulla allows rapid hormone release (epinephrine and norepinephrine) in response to stress. The suprarenal glands have rich arterial supply from three sources but limited venous drainage (one vein each side).
questions.question: Which artery supplies the suprarenal medulla directly?

questions.explanation: Avascular necrosis is a well-recognized complication of talar neck fractures, classified by the Hawkins system. The talus receives its blood supply from branches of the posterior tibial, anterior tibial, and fibular arteries entering through its non-articular portions. Displaced talar neck fractures disrupt these vessels. Hawkins sign (subchondral osteopenia on radiograph at 6-8 weeks) is a favorable sign indicating intact blood supply.
questions.question: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of the talus is a known complication of which type of ankle/foot injury due to the talus having no direct muscle attachments and a tenuous blood supply?

questions.explanation: Opponens digiti minimi draws the fifth metacarpal forward and rotates it laterally, deepening the palm and opposing the little finger toward the thumb. It is one of the three hypothenar muscles and is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
questions.question: What is the action of opponens digiti minimi?
Which muscle is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve?
questions.explanation: The flexor pollicis brevis is one of the thenar muscles supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. This branch arises in the hand after the nerve passes through the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome can affect these muscles, causing thenar wasting and weakness of thumb opposition.

questions.question: The parotid duct pierces which muscle before opening into the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct pierces the buccinator muscle to open into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar tooth. The duct is approximately 5 cm long and crosses the masseter muscle superficially. Trauma to the cheek can damage the duct causing salivary fistula.

questions.question: Which muscle lies deep to the breast medially?
questions.explanation: Two-thirds of the breast's base lies on the pectoralis major muscle. The inferolateral one-third lies on the serratus anterior and external oblique muscles. The deep fascia of these muscles forms the posterior boundary of the retromammary space behind the breast.

questions.question: The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as which artery?
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as the femoral artery, lying lateral to the femoral vein. The femoral artery enters the femoral triangle at this level and gives off the profunda femoris approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to the thigh muscles.

questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery as it crosses the ankle to enter the foot?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot at the ankle. It passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and contributes to the toes via the deep plantar arch.

questions.question: Which nerve innervates the pyramidalis muscle?
questions.explanation: The pyramidalis muscle, a small triangular muscle anterior to the lower rectus abdominis (base on pubis, apex on linea alba), is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12). This muscle is variably present (absent in about 20% of individuals) and functions to tense the linea alba. The subcostal nerve also contributes to innervation of the abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin. The pyramidalis lies within the rectus sheath and represents a derivative of the rectus abdominis. Its clinical significance is minimal.

questions.question: Which ligament is the most important structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch, bridging the sustentaculum tali to the navicular?
questions.explanation: The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) is the most critical ligament maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It bridges the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the navicular, directly supporting the head of the talus. Rupture of the spring ligament leads to progressive collapse of the medial longitudinal arch and adult acquired flatfoot deformity.

The right suprarenal vein is short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava on its posterior aspect, while the left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins). This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors the pattern of testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands receive blood from three arteries (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery respectively) but drain via only one or two veins, creating a rich arterial supply with limited venous drainage.
questions.question: The right suprarenal vein drains directly into which vessel?

questions.explanation: The iliohypogastric nerve (L1, sometimes with T12 contribution) emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle, running obliquely across the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum. It pierces the transversus abdominis muscle to run between it and internal oblique, providing motor innervation to these muscles. The nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch (skin over hip) and anterior cutaneous branch (skin above pubis). Other nerves emerging from the lateral border of psoas include ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves. The genitofemoral nerve pierces the anterior surface.
questions.question: The iliohypogastric nerve emerges from which border of psoas?

questions.explanation: The medial femoral circumflex artery wraps around the posterior side of the femur, supplying the femoral neck and head via retinacular vessels. In femoral neck fractures, this artery is easily damaged, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head. This is the most critical complication of intracapsular femoral neck fractures.
questions.question: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head following a femoral neck fracture is most likely due to disruption of which artery?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all interosseous muscles including the first dorsal interosseous. This muscle is easily visible and palpable on the dorsum of the hand between the thumb and index finger. Testing its strength (finger abduction) helps assess ulnar nerve function.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the first dorsal interosseous muscle?
The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) curves downward at which position between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. It has a side of danger (medial side, closer to the ischial tuberosity) and a side of safety (lateral side). The quadratus femoris forms a protective muscular layer over the nerve as it passes posterior to the hip joint.

questions.question: The processus vaginalis gives rise to which structure?
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis, normally obliterates during the first year of life except for its distal portion, which remains as the tunica vaginalis (a closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis). The parietal layer of tunica vaginalis lines the inner surface of the scrotum (internal spermatic fascia), while the visceral layer covers the testis and epididymis. Failure of processus vaginalis obliteration leads to patent processus (communicating hydrocele) or congenital indirect inguinal hernia. The gubernaculum guides testicular descent.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the hypoglossal triangle?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) lies in the hypoglossal triangle (muscular triangle), a subdivision of the anterior triangle bounded by the midline, superior belly of omohyoid, and sternocleidomastoid. The triangle also contains the infrahyoid muscles and thyroid gland. The nerve passes from the carotid triangle into the muscular triangle.

questions.question: The left colic flexure is supported by which ligament?
questions.explanation: The phrenicocolic ligament extends from the splenic (left colic) flexure of the colon to the diaphragm at the level of the 10th and 11th ribs, helping to support and maintain the position of the splenic flexure. This ligament forms a shelf that supports the inferior pole of the spleen, preventing its downward displacement. The ligament also serves as a barrier between the left paracolic gutter and the area around the spleen, potentially limiting the spread of infection or fluid collections between these compartments during pathological processes.

The left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, a branch of the splenic artery, is the dominant vessel supplying the greater curvature of the stomach, anastomosing with the smaller right gastroepiploic artery from the gastroduodenal trunk. These vessels run along the greater curvature within the gastrocolic ligament, giving branches to both anterior and posterior surfaces of the stomach. The short gastric arteries contribute to the fundus but represent a minor component of the greater curvature blood supply.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the majority of blood to the greater curvature of the stomach?

questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is located inferiorly between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura and is by far the more clinically important of the two pleural recesses. It is shallow during inspiration and becomes deeper during expiration. This recess can accumulate fluid in pleural effusions and is the site for thoracentesis.
questions.question: Where is the costodiaphragmatic recess most clinically important?

questions.explanation: The tendon of biceps femoris at its insertion on the lateral side of the head of fibula is split into two parts by the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee joint. The common fibular nerve closely follows the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula. Injury to biceps femoris or the fibular head can therefore damage the common fibular nerve.
questions.question: The tendon of biceps femoris at its fibular head insertion is split into two parts by which ligament?
Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the submandibular triangle?
questions.explanation: The submandibular triangle is bounded superiorly by the body of the mandible, anteroinferiorly by the anterior belly of digastric, and posteroinferiorly by the posterior belly of digastric. The floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles. The triangle contains the submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, and submandibular lymph nodes.

questions.question: The femoral ring is bounded medially by which structure?
questions.explanation: The femoral ring (the medial compartment of the femoral sheath) is bounded medially by the lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament), laterally by the femoral vein, anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, and posteriorly by the pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) and pectineus muscle covered by fascia. The femoral ring normally contains a lymph node (Cloquet's node) and loose connective tissue. It represents a potential site of weakness where femoral hernias can occur (more common in women), protruding through the ring into the femoral canal. The rigid boundaries make strangulation a risk in femoral hernias.

questions.question: The hypoglossal canal transmits which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII). The nerve provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus. Unilateral paralysis causes the tongue to deviate toward the paralyzed side when protruded.

questions.question: Which muscles work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction?
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction (ulnar deviation). By contracting simultaneously, they balance flexion and extension forces while producing adduction. This demonstrates how muscles from different compartments can cooperate for specific movements.

The external intercostal muscle is the most superficial intercostal muscle with fibers directed downward and forward. It extends from the rib tubercle posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly. The muscle is deficient anteriorly where it is replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane.
questions.question: Which muscle fibers are directed downward and forward?
Which muscle fibers form the conjoint tendon?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx) is formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, inserting onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. This tendon reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in its medial third, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Weakness or absence of the conjoint tendon in the area medial to the inferior epigastric artery predisposes to direct inguinal hernias, which protrude through Hesselbach's triangle bounded by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the body of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the stomach lies anterior to the body of the pancreas, separated by the lesser sac (omental bursa). The anterior surface of the pancreatic body is covered by the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the lesser sac. This relationship is clinically important as pancreatic disease can cause epigastric pain.

questions.question: Which condition causes thenar muscle wasting?
questions.explanation: Thenar muscle wasting occurs with median nerve palsy or chronic carpal tunnel syndrome. The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis). Chronic compression leads to visible flattening of the thenar eminence.
options: Median nerve palsy or carpal tunnel

questions.explanation: The cystic artery, most commonly arising from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle (75% of cases), provides the primary blood supply to the gallbladder. It typically divides into superficial (supplying the peritoneal surface) and deep (supplying the hepatic surface) branches. Anatomical variations are common, with the cystic artery occasionally arising from the left hepatic, common hepatic, gastroduodenal, or superior mesenteric arteries. Careful identification during cholecystectomy is essential to avoid injury to aberrant vessels or the right hepatic artery. The gallbladder may also receive small arterial branches from the liver bed.
questions.question: Which artery supplies blood to the gallbladder?
Which position elevates the diaphragm highest?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is highest in the supine position and after a large meal due to upward pressure from abdominal viscera. When lying on one side, the dependent (lower) diaphragm is considerably higher than the uppermost one. Position affects diaphragm function and is clinically relevant.

The base of the vermiform appendix has a constant anatomical location at the posteromedial wall of the cecum where the three taeniae coli converge, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. This convergence provides a reliable surgical landmark for locating the appendix during appendectomy, even when the appendix tip occupies a variable position (retrocecal, pelvic, subcecal, pre-ileal, or post-ileal). McBurney's point (one-third the distance from ASIS to umbilicus) represents the surface marking of the appendix base and is the site of maximal tenderness in appendicitis, but is not the actual anatomical landmark for finding the appendix during surgery.
questions.question: The appendix base is located at which anatomical landmark?

questions.explanation: The first 2 cm of the first (superior) part of the duodenum (the duodenal cap or bulb) is the most mobile as it is intraperitoneal with a mesentery. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal and relatively fixed. This mobility, combined with exposure to acid, makes the duodenal cap the most common site for duodenal ulcers (95% of duodenal ulcers occur here).
questions.question: Which segment of the duodenum is most mobile?

questions.explanation: The apex of the heart is formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and is the most inferior and lateral cardiac point. It lies deep to the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line in adults (4th space in children). The apex beat (point of maximal impulse) can normally be palpated at this location during systole.
questions.question: What is the most inferior part of the heart?

questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the bile duct within the hepatoduodenal ligament as its anterior boundary, not medial. The superior boundary is the caudate lobe of the liver, the inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct), and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered by parietal peritoneum. This opening typically admits two fingers and provides communication between the greater and lesser sacs.
questions.question: Which vessel marks the medial boundary of the epiploic foramen?
At what location does the brachial artery typically bifurcate into radial and ulnar arteries?
questions.explanation: The brachial artery bifurcates in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. This division occurs under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis into the radial artery (superficial) and ulnar artery (deeper). The cubital fossa provides a triangular space for this important vascular division.

questions.question: Which organ lies anterior to the right kidney?
questions.explanation: The right kidney's anterior surface is related superiorly to the right lobe of the liver (hepatorenal recess), the second part of the duodenum medially, and the right colic flexure and ascending colon inferiorly. Small intestine loops may also contact its anterior surface. The liver creates the largest impression on the right kidney's anterior surface.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the upper ureter?
questions.explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the upper ureter is to the lateral aortic (para-aortic) lymph nodes, while the pelvic portion drains to the internal and external iliac nodes. This lymphatic drainage pattern follows the blood supply. The lateral aortic nodes are located around the origin of the renal arteries at the L1-L2 level.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pierce the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening (foramen venae cavae) in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level, the highest of the three major diaphragmatic openings. This opening also transmits branches of the right phrenic nerve. The esophageal hiatus (T10 level) transmits the esophagus and vagal trunks, while the aortic hiatus (T12 level) transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. The IVC opening dilates during inspiration as the diaphragm contracts and descends, facilitating venous return to the heart.

questions.question: Which component of the quadriceps femoris is the largest and lies on the lateral side of the thigh?
questions.explanation: Vastus lateralis is the largest component of the quadriceps femoris, lying on the lateral side of the thigh. It originates from the greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera. All four quadriceps components converge into the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament inserting into the tibial tuberosity.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the vermiform appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), provides the blood supply to the vermiform appendix. It runs through the free edge of the mesoappendix, making it vulnerable during surgical mobilization of the appendix. This is typically an end artery with minimal collateral supply, so thrombosis can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery may give off a recurrent branch that ascends toward the ileocecal junction. Variations include occasional origin from a posterior cecal artery or rarely from the superior mesenteric artery directly.

questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to reach the posterior compartment of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The perforating branches (three or four) of the profunda femoris artery perforate the adductor magnus to supply the muscles of the medial and posterior thigh. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical approaches to the posterior thigh, where inadvertent cutting of perforating vessels can cause significant hemorrhage. They are the main blood supply to the hamstring muscles.

The hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) opens at the major duodenal papilla in the descending (second) part of the duodenum. This ampulla is formed by the union of the main pancreatic duct and common bile duct in most individuals. The sphincter of Oddi surrounds the ampulla controlling the flow of bile and pancreatic secretions.
questions.question: Which structure opens into the descending duodenum at the major duodenal papilla?

questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur, and empties into the femoral vein after traversing the saphenous opening. It has 10-12 valves.
options: Medial marginal vein and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and posterior tibial vein
Small saphenous vein and dorsal venous arch
Anterior tibial vein and dorsal venous arch
questions.question: The great saphenous vein, the longest vein in the body, is formed at the foot by the union of which structures?

questions.explanation: Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are extensions of cortical tissue that project between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus. They contain interlobar arteries and veins. The cortical tissue in the columns and over the bases of pyramids contains the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules. Enlarged renal columns can mimic renal masses on imaging.
questions.question: Which structure extends between adjacent renal pyramids?

questions.explanation: The peripheral part of the diaphragm (including the crura) receives sensory fibers from the lower six or seven intercostal and subcostal nerves. The central part receives sensory fibers from the phrenic nerves (C3-5). This dual innervation explains the referral patterns of pain from diaphragmatic irritation.
questions.question: Which nerves supply peripheral diaphragm sensory fibers?
Which muscle forms the floor of the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular floor of the oral cavity, separating it from the neck. It arises from the mylohyoid line of the mandible and inserts into the median raphe and hyoid bone. The muscle is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve from the mandibular division. It elevates the floor of the mouth during swallowing.

The oesophagus begins at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the level of the sixth cervical vertebra (C6). This anatomical landmark marks the transition point from the pharynx to the oesophagus. The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the respiratory tract.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus commence?

questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver, the part of the posterior surface devoid of peritoneal covering and in direct contact with the diaphragm, receives blood supply from the right phrenic artery (and sometimes left phrenic artery). This triangular area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary and right triangular ligaments. The bare area lies between the two layers of the coronary ligament and is continuous with the inferior vena cava, which is embedded in a groove on the posterior surface. Small diaphragmatic veins from the bare area drain directly into the IVC.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the bare area of the liver?
Which injury commonly causes avulsion of the medial epicondyle?
questions.explanation: Avulsion of the medial epicondyle commonly results from valgus stress to the elbow, seen in throwing athletes (tennis elbow). The common flexor origin and ulnar collateral ligament attachment create a strong pull. Repetitive throwing or acute valgus force can avulse this growth center in children or the epicondyle in adults.

Crutch palsy results from radial nerve compression in the axilla due to improperly fitted crutches pressing against the nerve. This causes wrist drop and loss of finger extension. The condition is preventable by ensuring crutches are properly adjusted to avoid axillary pressure.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in crutch palsy?

questions.explanation: The gastric impression is the largest and most concave of the impressions on the splenic visceral surface, reflecting contact with the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach. It lies between the superior and intermediate borders. Other impressions include renal (from left kidney), colic (from splenic flexure), and pancreatic (from pancreatic tail).
questions.question: Which structure forms the most concave impression on the splenic visceral surface?

questions.explanation: The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk (a branch of the subclavian artery) and ascends to supply the lower poles of the thyroid gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerve has an intimate relationship with this artery, passing either anterior or posterior to it. The superior thyroid artery supplies the upper poles.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the thyroid gland inferiorly?
Which structure passes posterior to the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava, covered by parietal peritoneum, forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), along with the right crus of the diaphragm. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant because the IVC can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver when the hepatoduodenal ligament (anterior boundary containing the portal triad) is manually compressed or clamped to control hepatic bleeding. The proximity of the IVC also means that the foramen provides a potential route for hemorrhage into the lesser sac following IVC injury.

The transverse colon receives its arterial supply from branches of the superior mesenteric artery, specifically the middle colic artery and right colic artery branches. The junction between the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries occurs near the left third of the transverse colon. This represents the embryological boundary between midgut and hindgut derivatives.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the transverse colon?

questions.explanation: The optic nerve is covered by all three meningeal layers (dura, arachnoid, and pia) from the sclera to the optic canal. At the canal, the dura becomes continuous with the periosteum of the orbit. Increased intracranial pressure can cause papilledema due to continuity of the subarachnoid space around the optic nerve.
questions.question: The optic nerve is surrounded by which meningeal layers?
What is pneumomediastinum?
questions.explanation: Pneumomediastinum is the presence of air in the mediastinum. It can result from alveolar rupture (from trauma, positive pressure ventilation, asthma), esophageal perforation, tracheal injury, or tracking from neck injuries. Air may dissect along tissue planes into the neck (subcutaneous emphysema) or into the pleural cavity (pneumothorax).

questions.question: The fibula does NOT form part of the knee joint. Its role in relation to the knee is best described as what?
questions.explanation: The fibula does not form part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella. Its role is only to provide attachment for knee joint structures: the fibular collateral ligament (from the lateral epicondyle of the femur to the fibular head) and the biceps femoris tendon. The fibula mainly serves as a muscle attachment site and forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise.
options: Articulates with the lateral femoral condyle
Provides attachment for knee joint structures only

questions.question: Which muscle opens the jaw against resistance?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid assists in opening the jaw against resistance (along with gravity, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric). The suprahyoid muscles provide the main force when opening against resistance. Lateral pterygoid protrudes and depresses the mandible. All other muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close the jaw.

Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of the triangle is formed by the transversalis fascia, which may be reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. This triangle represents an area of potential weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, and direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Understanding this triangle is crucial for distinguishing direct (through the triangle) from indirect (lateral to inferior epigastric) inguinal hernias.
questions.question: Which vessel marks the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
The superior hypogastric plexus is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The superior hypogastric plexus lies anterior to the lower part of the abdominal aorta and its bifurcation, extending from approximately L4 to the upper part of the sacrum, anterior to the L5 vertebra and sacral promontory. It represents the continuation of the aortic (intermesenteric) plexus and receives lumbar splanchnic nerves carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers. The plexus divides inferiorly into right and left hypogastric nerves, which descend into the pelvis to join the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses. The superior hypogastric plexus can be blocked or surgically divided to treat intractable pelvic pain.

questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is intraperitoneal?
questions.explanation: Only the first 2 cm of the first (superior) part of the duodenum, known as the duodenal cap or ampulla, is intraperitoneal. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, lying posterior to the peritoneum. This intraperitoneal portion is the most common site for duodenal ulceration (duodenal cap ulcers).

The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though anatomical variations exist (occasionally draining into superior mesenteric vein or the portal vein directly). The IMV ascends from the pelvis on the left side of the inferior mesenteric artery, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries. After joining the splenic vein, blood flows to the confluence with the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas, forming the portal vein. This pathway ensures blood from the hindgut reaches the liver for processing.
questions.question: Which vein receives the inferior mesenteric vein?

questions.explanation: The abducens nerve (VI) passes through Dorello's canal beneath the petrosphenoid (Gruber's) ligament at the petrous apex. The nerve then enters the cavernous sinus. Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to increased intracranial pressure causing false localizing sign. The nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle.
questions.question: Which structure passes through Dorello's canal?
The foramen of Bochdalek is located in which part of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Bochdalek is a congenital posterolateral defect in the diaphragm (more common on the left side) that results from incomplete fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membrane during embryological development. This allows herniation of abdominal contents (stomach, spleen, intestines) into the thorax, potentially causing respiratory distress in neonates due to pulmonary hypoplasia. The foramen of Morgagni is an anteromedial defect between sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm. Both differ from the normal anatomical openings (caval opening in central tendon at T8, esophageal hiatus in muscular portion at T10, and aortic hiatus between crura at T12).

questions.question: The middle meningeal artery typically arises from which artery?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and supplies the dura mater and calvarium. The artery runs in grooves on the inner skull surface. Rupture causes epidural hematoma with the classic lucid interval.

questions.question: A Baker's cyst (popliteal cyst) is a fluid-filled swelling in the popliteal fossa, most commonly arising from which bursae?
options: Semimembranosus bursa between semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius head
Ischial bursa over the ischial tuberosity
Trochanteric bursa over the greater trochanter
questions.explanation: A Baker's cyst most commonly arises from the semimembranosus bursa, located between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of gastrocnemius. It communicates with the knee joint in adults via a one-way valve mechanism, enlarging when intra-articular pressure increases (as in knee osteoarthritis or meniscal tears). It presents as a soft swelling in the medial popliteal fossa.

questions.question: Which artery primarily supplies the lower third of the oesophagus?
questions.explanation: The lower third of the oesophagus receives its arterial supply from branches of the left gastric artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk. This creates an important portosystemic anastomosis with veins draining to both portal and systemic circulations. The upper third is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery and the middle third by oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta.

questions.question: Where does the right upper lobar bronchus branch?
questions.explanation: The right upper lobar bronchus (also called eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is in contrast to the left lung where the main bronchus divides within the hilum into two lobar (secondary) bronchi. This anatomical arrangement is clinically significant.

questions.question: What are signs of tension pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: Signs of tension pneumothorax include: respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from affected side, hyperresonance to percussion, and absent breath sounds on the affected side. The diagnosis is clinical and treatment (needle decompression followed by chest tube) should NOT be delayed for chest X-ray confirmation.

The superior, middle, and inferior pharyngeal constrictors form the muscular lateral and posterior walls of the pharynx. The superior constrictor extends from the pterygoid hamulus and pterygomandibular raphe to the median raphe. Gaps between the constrictors allow passage of nerves and vessels.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the pharynx?

options: Fall on outstretched hand with wrist extended
questions.explanation: Colles' fracture typically occurs from falling onto an outstretched hand with the wrist extended. This is the most common wrist pathology in persons older than 50 years. The distal radius fractures with posterior displacement of the distal fragment, creating the characteristic "dinner fork deformity."
questions.question: What is the typical mechanism of Colles' fracture?

questions.explanation: Venae cordis minimae (smallest cardiac veins or Thebesian veins) are tiny veins that drain directly into the cardiac chambers (mainly the atria) without joining larger veins. They provide a small amount of deoxygenated blood directly to the left heart, contributing to the physiological shunt. They are difficult to visualize without specialized techniques.
questions.question: What are the smallest cardiac veins called?
Which structure is involved in trigger finger?
questions.explanation: Trigger finger involves stenosis of the flexor tendon sheath, particularly at the A1 pulley. A nodule develops on the flexor tendon that catches on the pulley during finger flexion/extension, causing triggering or locking. Release of the A1 pulley is curative.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial or lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The internal oblique muscle contributes to the anterior wall in the lateral third of the canal (where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament) and forms part of the roof with the transversus abdominis muscle through their arching fibers. The external oblique aponeurosis forms the entire length of the anterior wall, the transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by conjoint tendon) forms the posterior wall, and the inguinal ligament forms the floor.

questions.question: The ductus deferens passes medial to which vessel?
questions.explanation: The ductus deferens (vas deferens) hooks around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery at the deep inguinal ring, crossing from lateral to medial as it leaves the spermatic cord to descend into the pelvis. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. After crossing the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, the vas continues posteromedially across the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder where it dilates to form the ampulla and joins the seminal vesicle duct.

The two ureteric orifices form the superolateral angles (corners) of the triangular trigone. The internal urethral orifice forms the inferior angle. The interureteric ridge connects the two ureteric orifices forming the base of the triangle. The trigone remains smooth even when the bladder is empty, unlike the rest of the bladder mucosa which is rugose when empty.
questions.question: Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the bladder trigone?

questions.explanation: An emissary vein passes through the foramen ovale connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus. Other emissary veins include those passing through the foramen spinosum (middle meningeal vein), mastoid foramen (sigmoid sinus), and parietal foramina (superior sagittal sinus). These valveless connections allow bidirectional flow and infection spread.
questions.question: Which foramen transmits the emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus?

questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas receives dual blood supply from pancreaticoduodenal arcades formed by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, representing the junction between celiac (foregut) and superior mesenteric (midgut) arterial territories. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal) divides into anterior and posterior branches that descend on their respective surfaces of the pancreatic head, anastomosing with corresponding anterior and posterior branches of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA). This rich anastomotic network provides collateral circulation between celiac and SMA systems.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the head of the pancreas?

questions.explanation: Each renal artery typically divides into five segmental arteries: apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior, and posterior. These are functional end arteries with no significant anastomoses, meaning occlusion of one causes infarction of that segment. This segmental anatomy allows partial nephrectomy without affecting remaining segments. Four segmental arteries arise from the anterior division; one (posterior) from the posterior division.
questions.question: How many segmental arteries typically supply each kidney?
Which structure is at risk in hook of hamate fracture?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is at risk in hook of hamate fracture as it passes through Guyon's canal adjacent to this structure. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve curves around the hook of the hamate. Fracture can cause motor weakness of intrinsic hand muscles with or without sensory symptoms.

questions.question: Which vessels enter the liver at the porta hepatis?
questions.explanation: The porta hepatis (gateway of the liver) is a transverse fissure through which the portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic ducts pass. The portal vein and hepatic artery enter the liver while the hepatic ducts (right and left) exit. Lymphatic vessels and nerves also traverse the porta hepatis, which is bounded by the hepatoduodenal ligament.

questions.question: Superior gluteal nerve palsy results in which specific gait abnormality?
options: Waddling gait due to hip flexor weakness
Scissor gait due to adductor spasticity
High-stepping gait due to foot drop
Antalgic gait due to hip pain
Trendelenburg gait due to gluteus medius and minimus weakness
questions.explanation: Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) palsy causes weakness of gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. This results in a Trendelenburg gait (pelvis drops to the opposite side during swing phase). Bilateral superior gluteal nerve palsy causes a characteristic waddling gait. This nerve is at risk during posterior surgical approaches to the hip.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist position and finger function?
questions.explanation: Wrist position affects finger flexor and extensor muscle lengths through tenodesis effect. Wrist extension tightens finger flexors enhancing grip while passively flexing fingers. Wrist flexion tightens extensors causing passive finger extension. This relationship is exploited in tenodesis grip for spinal cord injury patients.
options: Wrist position affects finger flexor/extensor length affecting grip

questions.question: What characterizes centroacinar cells?
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are pale-staining cells unique to the pancreas that represent the intra-acinar portion of the intercalated duct. They secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid in response to secretin, which neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum. This bicarbonate secretion, combined with enzymes from acinar cells, produces complete pancreatic juice. Centroacinar cells distinguish pancreatic from salivary acini.

questions.question: What is the most common position of the appendix?
questions.explanation: The retrocaecal position is the most common location of the appendix, occurring in approximately 65-75% of individuals. In this position, the appendix lies behind the caecum, which may explain atypical presentations of appendicitis. Other positions include pelvic (most common after retrocaecal), subcaecal, preileal, and postileal positions.

The lesser omentum forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac, separating it from the greater sac anteriorly along with the posterior wall of the stomach. This double-layered peritoneal fold extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of duodenum to the liver. The lesser omentum consists of the hepatogastric ligament (its membranous portion) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad), with the latter forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
questions.question: Which structure separates the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs?

questions.explanation: The gluteal tuberosity is located below the greater trochanter and serves as the insertion point for gluteus maximus. The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. Knowing these distinctions is critical in hip replacement surgery.
questions.question: Which surface landmark on the femur, below the greater trochanter, represents the insertion of the gluteus maximus?
The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot. It is found just lateral to the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. The dorsalis pedis artery (continuation of the anterior tibial artery) runs between the extensor hallucis longus tendon medially and the extensor digitorum longus tendon laterally. Absence of this pulse, along with the posterior tibial pulse, indicates peripheral arterial disease.

questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the orbit through which opening?
questions.explanation: The inferior orbital fissure connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the orbit. The fissure is bounded by the greater wing of sphenoid, maxilla, and palatine bone. The maxillary nerve continues through this fissure as the infraorbital nerve. The infraorbital and zygomatic nerves and vessels pass through this communication.

The corniculate cartilages (cartilages of Santorini) are small conical nodules of elastic cartilage that sit on the apex of each arytenoid cartilage. They are located in the posterior part of the aryepiglottic folds. The cuneiform cartilages lie more anteriorly in the aryepiglottic folds. Both are visible on laryngoscopy as small elevations.
questions.question: Which cartilage caps the apex of the arytenoid?
The menisci deepen the articular surface and act as which functional structures in the knee joint?
options: Shock absorbers and joint space deepeners
Attachment points for cruciate ligaments only
Blood vessel channels for synovial membrane
Lubricating pads reducing synovial fluid production
questions.explanation: The menisci are crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the tibial articular surface and act as shock absorbers. They are thicker at external margins and taper toward the center. Meniscal tears are among the most common knee injuries in athletes. The lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus.

The cricoid cartilage is signet-ring shaped and forms the only complete cartilaginous ring throughout the entire respiratory tract. This structural feature provides crucial stability and serves as an important landmark for emergency airway access. The cricoid is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway.
questions.question: Which cartilage forms the only complete ring in the respiratory tract?

questions.explanation: Infiltration of Cooper's ligaments by breast cancer leads to their shortening, producing tethering of the skin with a characteristic dimpled appearance resembling orange peel (peau d'orange). This is an important clinical sign of locally advanced breast cancer. The dimpling becomes more apparent when the patient raises her arms.
questions.question: What causes peau d'orange appearance?

questions.explanation: In SVC obstruction, the azygos venous system (along with intercostal veins and other collaterals) provides alternative drainage pathways for blood from the upper body to reach the right atrium. These collateral vessels dilate significantly. Prominent dilated veins may be visible on the chest wall and abdomen, directing flow from above downward.
questions.question: What provides collateral drainage in SVC obstruction?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4), formed within the psoas major from the lumbar plexus, emerges from the medial border of the muscle at the pelvic brim. It descends along the lateral wall of the pelvis, passing above the obturator vessels to reach the obturator foramen, through which it exits the pelvis to enter the medial compartment of the thigh. This medial emergence distinguishes it from other lumbar plexus branches (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves) which emerge from the lateral border, except for the genitofemoral nerve which pierces the anterior surface of psoas.
questions.question: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of psoas major?

questions.explanation: The lingual artery arises from the external carotid at the level of the hyoid bone and is closely related to the hypoglossal nerve. The nerve crosses superficial to the artery as it loops forward. The artery divides into dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The hyoglossus muscle separates superficial from deep structures.
questions.question: Which artery accompanies the hypoglossal nerve?
The vaginal artery typically arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The vaginal artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (though it may arise from the uterine artery) and descends to supply the vagina. It gives off numerous branches to the anterior and posterior vaginal walls, anastomosing with branches from the uterine artery superiorly and internal pudendal artery inferiorly. This rich anastomotic network provides extensive collateral circulation to the vagina. The vagina also receives blood supply from the middle rectal and internal pudendal arteries. The upper vagina drains via uterine veins, while the lower vagina drains via internal pudendal veins.

questions.question: What is the functional unit of liver according to the lobular concept?
questions.explanation: The classical hepatic lobule is a hexagonal structural unit with a central vein at its center and portal triads at the periphery (corners). Hepatocytes are arranged in plates radiating from the central vein with sinusoids between them. Blood flows from portal triads through sinusoids to the central vein. This is the histological/structural concept, though the hepatic acinus is a better functional unit.

questions.question: What is the eparterial bronchus?
questions.explanation: The eparterial bronchus is the right upper lobar bronchus, so named because it arises above (epi-) the pulmonary artery. All other bronchi are hyparterial (below the pulmonary artery). This anatomical feature is unique to the right lung and has embryological significance.

The psoas major muscle is innervated by the ventral rami of lumbar nerves L1 through L4, which emerge from the lumbar plexus formed within the substance of the muscle itself. This segmental innervation pattern corresponds to the muscle's extensive vertebral origins from the bodies, transverse processes, and intervertebral discs of T12 through L5. The muscle serves as the chief flexor of the thigh at the hip joint and also assists in lateral flexion of the lumbar vertebral column when acting unilaterally.
questions.question: The psoas major muscle receives innervation from which nerve roots?

questions.explanation: The interventricular septum has a small upper membranous part (approximately 1 cm) and a large lower muscular part. The membranous septum lies just beneath the aortic valve (specifically between the right and non-coronary cusps). Ventricular septal defects most commonly occur in the membranous portion near the tricuspid valve.
questions.question: Which part of the interventricular septum is membranous?

questions.explanation: The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen after traversing the facial canal. It then enters the parotid gland and divides into five terminal branches. Damage at this location causes complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including loss of taste to anterior two-thirds of tongue.
questions.question: The stylomastoid foramen transmits which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius. Fibularis longus belongs to the lateral compartment, along with fibularis brevis. All anterior compartment muscles are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Paralysis of these muscles causes foot drop.
questions.question: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles. Which of the following does NOT belong to this compartment?

options: Directly into the lesser trochanter of the proximal femur
Into the ischial tuberosity rather than into the trochanter
Into the rim of the acetabulum directly without turning
Turns 90� around the ischium then inserts into the greater trochanter's upper border
Into the trochanteric fossa on the medial femur
questions.question: The obturator internus exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen. Where does its tendon turn to insert?
questions.explanation: The obturator internus tendon exits through the lesser sciatic foramen, turns nearly 90 degrees around the smooth lesser sciatic notch (using the ischium as a pulley), and then inserts into the upper border of the greater trochanter of the femur. The gemelli muscles (superior and inferior) arise from the edges of the lesser sciatic notch and merge with the obturator internus tendon, acting as its 'cheeks.'

The root of the mesentery of the small intestine extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure (at approximately L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (at approximately S1, right of midline), a distance of about 15 cm. Along this short root, approximately 6-7 meters of small intestine (jejunum and ileum) is attached. The root crosses the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum, abdominal aorta, IVC, right ureter, right psoas major muscle, and right testicular/ovarian vessels. This oblique orientation allows the small intestine maximum mobility while maintaining vascular supply and creating the characteristic radiating pattern of jejunal and ileal vessels.
options: Second part of duodenum to sigmoid colon
Duodenojejunal flexure to right sacroiliac joint
questions.question: The root of the mesentery extends from which two points?

questions.explanation: Circumduction at the shoulder joint is a sequential combination of flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction movements. This creates a conical movement pattern of the limb. Multiple muscles act in coordinated sequence to produce this composite movement.
questions.question: What produces circumduction at the shoulder joint?

questions.explanation: "Gamekeeper's thumb" (skier's thumb when acute) involves a tear of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint. This causes thumb instability affecting pinch grip strength. The injury historically occurred in gamekeepers from repetitive stress while killing rabbits.
options: Ulnar collateral ligament of thumb MCP
questions.question: What structure is torn in gamekeeper's thumb?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve has a long course from the neck (C3-5) to the diaphragm because of embryological migration of the diaphragm. The septum transversum initially forms in the cervical region and migrates caudally during development, carrying its nerve supply (from cervical segments) with it to its final thoracic position.
questions.question: Why does the phrenic nerve have a long course?

questions.explanation: The right ventricle typically has three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal) corresponding to the three cusps of the tricuspid valve. Each papillary muscle gives chordae tendineae to two adjacent cusps. The left ventricle has only two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior), which are larger and stronger, each providing chordae to two cusps of the mitral valve.
questions.question: How many papillary muscles are in the right ventricle?
Which vessel crosses anterior to the left renal vein?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery crosses anteriorly to the left renal vein as the vein passes from left to right to drain into the IVC. This can occasionally cause compression of the left renal vein (nutcracker syndrome), leading to left gonadal vein reflux, hematuria, or left flank pain. The left renal vein also passes anterior to the aorta.

The "prayer" position (pressing palms together with fingers extended) tests median nerve function, particularly flexor digitorum superficialis. Inability to maintain all fingers in full extension with palms pressed together suggests median nerve pathology. This is a reverse of Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which nerve is tested by the prayer position?
The otic ganglion provides parasympathetic innervation to which gland?
questions.explanation: The otic ganglion provides postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. Preganglionic fibers arrive via the lesser petrosal nerve from the glossopharyngeal nerve. The ganglion lies in the infratemporal fossa medial to the mandibular nerve below the foramen ovale.

questions.question: The posterior third of the tongue receives general and special sensory from which nerve?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor supply to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus.

questions.question: What are the approximate dimensions of an adult kidney?
questions.explanation: Each adult kidney is approximately 10 cm long, 5 cm wide, and 2.5 cm thick, resembling a large bean in shape. The left kidney is typically slightly longer and narrower than the right. Kidney size is clinically important, as small kidneys may indicate chronic disease while enlarged kidneys suggest acute processes or masses.

questions.question: Which structure separates the liver bare area from the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: In the bare area of the liver, there is no peritoneum between the liver and the diaphragm - they are in direct contact. This area is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament. The direct contact allows potential spread of infection between the liver and thorax, and provides a route for extraperitoneal collateral circulation.

questions.question: The central artery of the retina is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The central artery of the retina is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It is an end artery running in the center of the optic nerve to supply the inner layers of the retina. Occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision. The artery enters the optic nerve about 12 mm behind the eyeball.

questions.question: What defines the lower limit of the body of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The body of the stomach extends from the cardiac orifice to the level of the incisura angularis, a constant notch on the lesser curvature. This angular notch serves as a reliable anatomical landmark separating the body from the pyloric portion. The incisura angularis becomes more prominent when the stomach is distended.

questions.question: Which structure carries the right bundle branch in the right ventricle?
questions.explanation: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) is a muscular bridge extending from the interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle. It carries the right bundle branch of the conducting system, ensuring coordinated activation of the papillary muscles. It prevents overdistention of the ventricle and was historically important for determining ventricular orientation.

questions.question: The kidney is related posteriorly to which muscle?
questions.explanation: The posterior surface of each kidney lies on the diaphragm superiorly, then from medial to lateral on the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis muscles, separated from them by the perinephric fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat. The subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves descend obliquely posterior to the kidney on these muscles. The left kidney is related to ribs 11 and 12 posteriorly (protected by the rib cage), while the right kidney is related only to rib 12. These posterior relations are important when considering retrograde surgical approaches to the kidney or complications of renal trauma.

questions.question: Which structure causes the first constriction of the oesophagus at 15 cm from the upper incisor teeth?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper oesophageal sphincter and creates the first physiological constriction at 15 cm from the upper incisors. This sphincter prevents air from entering the oesophagus during respiration and regulates food entry. It is a clinically significant site for foreign body impaction and stricture formation.

The first posterior intercostal space on the right side drains into the right brachiocephalic vein. The remaining intercostal spaces on the right drain into the azygos vein. On the left, the upper three spaces typically drain into the left brachiocephalic vein through the left superior intercostal vein.
questions.question: Which vein drains the first posterior intercostal space?

questions.explanation: is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle due to its position under the acromion. Repetitive overhead activities and age-related degeneration increase tear risk. The painful arc (pain during mid-abduction) is characteristic of supraspinatus tendonitis or tears.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle is most commonly torn?
Which vessel supplies blood to the middle ear?
questions.explanation: The middle ear receives blood from multiple tympanic arteries: superior tympanic (middle meningeal), inferior tympanic (ascending pharyngeal), anterior tympanic (maxillary), and posterior tympanic (stylomastoid branch of posterior auricular). This rich vascular supply reflects the metabolic needs of the middle ear mucosa and ossicles.

has no bony attachment distally; it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. This muscle is absent in approximately 15% of people without functional deficit. It can be used as a tendon graft source in reconstructive surgery.
questions.question: Which forearm muscle has no bony attachment distally?

questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) extends from the right crus of the diaphragm behind the pancreas to attach to the duodenojejunal flexure. It contains both smooth muscle and fibrous tissue. Contraction of this muscle widens the angle of the duodenojejunal flexure and may assist in opening the duodenum for passage of contents into the jejunum.
questions.question: Where does the suspensory muscle of the duodenum attach?
Which surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, a broad rough area that is the attachment for the iliofemoral ligament?
questions.explanation: The anterior surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, which is broad and rough and serves as attachment for the iliofemoral ligament. The posterior aspect carries the prominent intertrochanteric crest. These landmarks delineate the intracapsular portion of the femoral neck.

questions.question: What is the lung at the apex called?
questions.explanation: The cupola (or apex) is the rounded superior portion of the lung that extends into the root of the neck, reaching 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle. It is covered by cervical pleura and the suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia). The subclavian artery arches over the lung apex.

In the female pelvis, the uterine artery crosses superior (above) to the ureter near the lateral fornix of the vagina - remembered by the phrase "water under the bridge." This relationship is clinically crucial during hysterectomy to avoid inadvertent ureteric injury during ligation of the uterine artery. The ureter runs along the lateral wall of the pelvis to reach the bladder.
questions.question: Which vessel crosses anterior to the ureter in the female pelvis?

questions.explanation: Renal and ureteric pain is typically felt in the loin (flank) and radiates to the groin and genitalia, following the T10-L1 dermatomes. Upper ureteric/renal pelvis obstruction causes loin pain, mid-ureteric obstruction causes iliac fossa pain, and lower ureteric obstruction causes suprapubic pain with urinary frequency. This radiation pattern is characteristic of renal colic from ureteric stones.
questions.question: Where is referred pain from renal pathology typically felt?
The optic canal transmits which two structures?
questions.explanation: The optic canal in the lesser wing of the sphenoid transmits the optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery. The central retinal vein drains alongside within the optic nerve sheath. The canal opens into the posterior orbit and connects the middle cranial fossa with the orbital cavity.

questions.question: The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric fossa, located on the medial surface of the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. This differs from other short rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli) which insert into the upper border of the greater trochanter. Knowledge of this distinction is important in hip replacement approaches.

The profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery) arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. It is the largest branch of the femoral artery and the main blood supply to the thigh muscles via perforating branches, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries.
questions.question: The profunda femoris artery arises from the femoral artery at what distance below the inguinal ligament?
Which sinus receives blood from the superior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus drains posteriorly into the confluence of sinuses (torcular herophili) at the internal occipital protuberance. From here, blood typically flows into the right transverse sinus more than the left. The confluence also receives the straight sinus and occipital sinus.

The phrenic nerves pass through both the superior and middle mediastinum as they descend from the neck to the diaphragm. Similarly, the superior vena cava lies in both regions. The thymus extends from superior to anterior mediastinum. Structures can span multiple mediastinal compartments.
questions.question: Which structure lies in both superior and middle mediastinum?
