The quadrangular space is bounded superiorly by teres minor, inferiorly by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps, and laterally by the surgical neck of humerus. Through this space pass the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels. Injury to these structures can occur with shoulder trauma.
questions.question: Which muscles form the boundaries of the quadrangular space in the axilla?
options: Teres major, teres minor, long head of triceps, surgical neck of humerus
Subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi, humerus
Teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, lateral head of triceps
Deltoid, teres minor, long head of triceps, humerus

questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper, separating it from the oropharynx. The arch extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue and contains the palatoglossus muscle. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the two palatoglossal arches connecting the oral cavity with the oropharynx.

The cervical pleura drains into the internal thoracic chain anteriorly and into the intercostal chain posteriorly. The parietal pleura's lymphatic drainage follows its vascular supply pattern. Coastal and mediastinal pleura also drain to the internal thoracic chain anteriorly.
questions.question: Where does the cervical pleura lymph drain anteriorly?
The 'unhappy triad' of the knee involves simultaneous injury to which three structures following a valgus force with the foot planted?
questions.explanation: The 'unhappy triad' of the knee (O'Donoghue's triad) consists of simultaneous injury to the anterior cruciate ligament, medial meniscus, and tibial (medial) collateral ligament. This injury occurs classically in American football when a valgus force is applied to a planted, slightly flexed knee. The tight adherence of the medial meniscus to the tibial collateral ligament explains their combined injury.
options: PCL, lateral meniscus, and fibular collateral ligament
ACL, lateral meniscus, and fibular collateral ligament
PCL, lateral meniscus, and tibial collateral ligament
ACL, medial meniscus, and tibial collateral ligament
ACL, medial meniscus, and ACL and fibular collateral ligament

questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises in the forearm proximal to the carpal tunnel, so palm sensation is preserved. Only sensation in the lateral three and one-half fingers (palmar aspect) is affected by carpal tunnel syndrome. This distinguishes it from more proximal median nerve injuries.
questions.question: What sensation is preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?
The rectus sheath is absent posteriorly below which line?
questions.explanation: Below the arcuate line (linea semicircularis), located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis, the posterior rectus sheath is absent. At this level, all three aponeurotic layers (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) pass anteriorly to the rectus abdominis muscle, leaving only the transversalis fascia and peritoneum posteriorly. This anatomical arrangement creates a relative weakness that may be involved in direct inguinal hernias. The inferior epigastric vessels pierce the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line to enter the rectus sheath.

The pericardial cavity normally contains 15-50 ml of serous pericardial fluid that lubricates the surfaces of the visceral and parietal pericardium, reducing friction during cardiac contraction. Excessive fluid accumulation (pericardial effusion) or rapid accumulation of even small volumes can cause cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise.
questions.question: What does the pericardial cavity normally contain?
The cisterna chyli receives lymph from which trunks?
questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli) receives the intestinal trunk (draining abdominal viscera via pre-aortic nodes), right and left lumbar trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvis, and posterior abdominal wall), and sometimes the lower intercostal lymphatic trunks. It represents a dilated sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, located at L1-L2 level, anterior to the vertebral column, posterior and to the right of the aorta, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to traverse the posterior mediastinum and drain into the junction of left subclavian and internal jugular veins.

Displaced clavicle fractures risk injury to the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks that pass immediately posterior to the bone. The subclavius muscle provides some protection, but severe displacement can damage these vital structures. Posteriorly, the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein are also at risk.
questions.question: Which structure is at risk in displaced clavicle fractures?

questions.explanation: The gluteal region contains nine muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae, piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, and quadratus femoris. These perform extension, abduction, lateral rotation, and stabilization of the hip joint.
questions.question: How many muscles constitute the gluteal region, including the six lateral rotators?
What is Horner's syndrome triad?
questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome results from interruption of sympathetic innervation to the eye and face, characterized by: (1) ptosis (drooping eyelid from paralysis of M?ller's muscle), (2) miosis (constricted pupil from unopposed parasympathetic action), and (3) anhidrosis (absent sweating on ipsilateral face). Pancoast tumors invading the sympathetic chain commonly cause this.

questions.question: How many functional segments does the liver have?
questions.explanation: The liver is divided into eight functionally independent segments (Couinaud segments I-VIII) based on the distribution of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts. Each segment has its own vascular inflow, outflow, and biliary drainage, allowing surgical resection of individual segments without damaging others. This segmental anatomy is crucial for hepatic surgery and understanding disease distribution.

questions.question: The hindfoot consists of which two bones?
questions.explanation: The hindfoot consists of the talus and the calcaneus. The calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest and strongest bone, absorbing shock and leveraging movement. The talus (ankle bone) articulates with the tibia and fibula superiorly and with the calcaneus inferiorly and navicular anteriorly, allowing ankle movement and weight transfer to the foot.

The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus contains (from superior to inferior): oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), ophthalmic division (V1), and maxillary division (V2). The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (VI) pass through the sinus cavity itself. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can affect all these structures causing ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the cavernous sinus lateral wall?

questions.explanation: The ACL prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia (or anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur) and hyperextension of the knee joint. When the knee is flexed at a right angle, the tibia cannot be pulled anteriorly because it is held by the intact ACL. ACL rupture is detected by a positive anterior drawer test.
questions.question: The ACL is slack during knee flexion and taut during full extension. It prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia and which other movement?
Which muscle is NOT innervated by the lumbar plexus?
questions.explanation: Piriformis is innervated by branches directly from the ventral rami of S1 and S2 (sacral plexus), not the lumbar plexus. The lumbar plexus (L1-L4) innervates psoas major (L1-L4), quadratus lumborum (T12, L1-L4 via subcostal and lumbar nerves), iliacus (femoral nerve, L2-L4), and obturator externus (obturator nerve, L2-L4). Piriformis is a muscle of the gluteal region and posterior pelvic wall, exiting the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. It serves as a landmark dividing structures exiting above it (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) from those below it (all others).

The medial side of the carpal arch base is formed by the pisiform bone and the hook of the hamate. The lateral side is formed by the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium bones. The flexor retinaculum bridges across this arch, converting it into the carpal tunnel.
questions.question: Which carpal bones form the medial side of the carpal arch base?
Which position tests for carpal tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Phalen's test (passive wrist flexion for 60 seconds) provokes carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms by increasing pressure within the tunnel. Reproduction of paresthesia in the median nerve distribution within one minute is considered positive. The reverse Phalen's test uses wrist extension.

questions.question: Which thigh muscle has TWO different nerve supplies from two different divisions of two different named nerves?
questions.explanation: Adductor magnus uniquely has two parts with different nerve supplies: the adductor part (obturator nerve, L2, L3, L4) and the hamstring part (tibial division of sciatic nerve). This dual origin and nerve supply reflects its dual embryological origin. Biceps femoris similarly has two heads with different nerve divisions of the sciatic nerve.

questions.question: The carotid sheath contains which three main structures?
questions.explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. The sheath also contains deep cervical lymph nodes along the vein. It is formed by condensation of deep cervical fascia and extends from the skull base to the thoracic inlet.
options: Carotid artery, jugular vein, vagus nerve

questions.explanation: Seven tendons insert into the greater trochanter: gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, piriformis, obturator internus, obturator externus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior. The concentration of these insertions makes the greater trochanter a key landmark in hip anatomy. Avulsion fractures at this site carry significant functional implications.
questions.question: How many tendons insert into the greater trochanter of the femur?

questions.explanation: The infraorbital foramen on the anterior surface of the maxilla transmits the infraorbital nerve (continuation of maxillary nerve V2) and vessels. The nerve emerges about 1 cm below the infraorbital margin. It provides sensation to the lower eyelid, lateral nose, and upper lip. The foramen is a landmark for regional anesthesia.
questions.question: The infraorbital foramen transmits which nerve?

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the surgical neck of the humerus, making it vulnerable to injury in fractures of this region. Damage results in paralysis of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. These fractures are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk during surgical neck fractures of the humerus?

questions.explanation: The sigmoid colon receives its blood supply from 2-4 sigmoid arteries (sigmoidal arteries), branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. These arteries descend in the sigmoid mesocolon, anastomosing with each other and with branches from the left colic artery superiorly and the superior rectal artery inferiorly, contributing to the marginal artery along the mesenteric border. Sudeck's point, at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from anal verge), represents a watershed area where the last sigmoid artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery and is vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the sigmoid colon?

questions.explanation: The talus articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, navicular anteriorly, tibia superiorly, lateral malleolus laterally, and medial malleolus medially. This unique articulation pattern makes the talus the keystone of the hindfoot. The talus receives no direct muscle attachments and is entirely dependent on its articular surfaces and ligamentous connections.
questions.question: Which bone of the foot articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, the navicular anteriorly, the tibia superiorly, and both malleoli laterally?

questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery represents the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery after it gives off the left colic and sigmoid branches, descending into the pelvis within the sigmoid mesocolon. It crosses the left common iliac vessels at the level of S3 and divides into right and left branches that descend on either side of the rectum, penetrating its wall and anastomosing with branches of the middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal) arteries at the level of the internal anal sphincter.
questions.question: The superior rectal artery is the terminal continuation of which vessel?
Which hypothenar muscle abducts the little finger?
questions.explanation: abducts the little finger away from the ring finger. It is one of three hypothenar muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve. The muscle forms the medial border of the palm in the hypothenar eminence.

The zygomatic bones form the prominence of the cheeks and lie on the inferolateral sides of the orbits. They articulate with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones. The bone has a broad connection with the maxilla medially and forms part of the zygomatic arch laterally. Fractures cause flattening of the malar eminence.
questions.question: Which bone forms the prominence of the cheek?

questions.explanation: produces shoulder adduction, extension, and medial rotation. It is a powerful muscle forming part of the posterior axillary fold. The muscle is commonly used in reconstructive surgery and is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.
questions.question: Which muscle produces both shoulder adduction and medial rotation?
Which part of the male urethra is least distensible?
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm), narrowest, and least distensible part of the male urethra. It passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch) surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae muscle). This segment is most vulnerable to traumatic injury, particularly in pelvic fractures, and is the most difficult to dilate or catheterize.

The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass through the gastrosplenic ligament (omentum) to supply the fundus. These vessels represent 5-7 small branches that provide blood to the superior portion of the greater curvature. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the greater curvature to the spleen.
questions.question: Which vessels pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to the fundus?
To which structure is the suprapleural membrane attached apically?
questions.explanation: The suprapleural membrane is attached at its apex to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra (C7). Laterally, it attaches to the internal border of the first rib and its costal cartilage. Medially, it blends with the fascia covering structures passing through the superior thoracic aperture.

Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal circulation (enterohepatic recirculation). About 95% of bile salts are recycled this way, conserving the bile salt pool. Ileal disease or resection disrupts this circulation, leading to bile salt malabsorption, steatorrhea, and potential bile salt diarrhea.
questions.question: Which segment absorbs bile salts for enterohepatic recirculation?

questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane, passing midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis (or midway between xiphoid and umbilicus), corresponds to the level of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and the lower border of vertebra T12. This important surgical landmark crosses numerous structures: pylorus of stomach (when supine), neck of pancreas, origin of the SMA and portal vein, duodenojejunal flexure, hila of both kidneys, fundus of gallbladder, root of transverse mesocolon, origin of IMA (at L3), and tips of ninth costal cartilages. The plane is used to define upper and lower abdominal regions in the nine-region scheme.
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the transpyloric plane?

questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is three times stronger than its antagonist, the hamstrings. It forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh and is the great extensor of the leg. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur and is considered the largest and one of the most powerful muscle groups in the body.
questions.question: The quadriceps femoris is how many times stronger than its antagonist muscle group, the hamstrings?

questions.explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals. Its summit is the subtalar articulation. It is smaller, more rigid, more stable than the medial arch, and makes more contact with the ground. It bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play and has limited mobility, built to transmit weight.
questions.question: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by which bones and is described as more rigid and making more contact with the ground?
options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, and first metatarsal
Calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and all metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, and all five metatarsals

questions.explanation: Psoas major originates from the sides of T12-L5 vertebrae and their intervening discs, as well as from the transverse processes of all lumbar vertebrae. It inserts into the lesser trochanter together with iliacus (forming iliopsoas). A psoas abscess from vertebral tuberculosis can track along this muscle to present as a groin swelling.
questions.question: The psoas major originates from which vertebral levels, including transverse processes?
options: T12�L5 vertebrae, intervening discs, and all lumbar transverse processes
L1-L5 vertebral bodies only, no disc or process
T12-L4 vertebral bodies only without processes
L2-S1 vertebral levels and intervening discs

questions.question: Which constriction is at the esophageal origin?
questions.explanation: The esophagus has four anatomical constrictions where it is narrowed. The first is at its origin (C6 level, 15 cm from incisors) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. These constrictions are clinically important as sites where foreign bodies lodge and where esophageal pathology commonly occurs.

The posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle. The anterior border of trapezius forms the posterior boundary, and the middle third of the clavicle forms the base. The apex is where the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius meet at the superior nuchal line.
questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck?

questions.explanation: Smooth muscle cells disposed in a predominantly circular direction and radiating from the nipple base cause nipple erection. Their contraction, induced by cold, tactile, or emotional stimuli, causes erection of the nipple and wrinkling of the surrounding areola. This is an involuntary response.
questions.question: Which muscle causes nipple erection?
What is clinical significance of esophageal venous drainage?
questions.explanation: The esophageal veins form an important portosystemic anastomosis where portal venous blood (from lower esophagus draining to left gastric vein) connects with systemic venous blood (middle and upper esophagus draining to azygos system and brachiocephalic veins). In portal hypertension, these veins dilate to form esophageal varices which can rupture.

The splenic artery gives off the short gastric arteries (vasa brevia, 4-6 vessels) near the splenic hilum, which pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the fundus of the stomach. The splenic artery also gives off the left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, which runs along the greater curvature in the gastrocolic ligament. The left gastric artery arises from the celiac trunk (not splenic artery), while the right gastric and gastroduodenal arteries arise from the hepatic artery proper and common hepatic artery respectively. The short gastric vessels create collateral circulation to the stomach and must be ligated during splenectomy.
questions.question: The splenic artery gives off which gastric vessels?

questions.explanation: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib. The artery is divided into three parts by the anterior scalene muscle. The vertebral, internal thoracic, and thyrocervical trunk typically arise from the subclavian. The costocervical trunk arises from the second part posteriorly.
questions.question: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at which landmark?

questions.explanation: The spleen develops within the dorsal mesogastrium (greater omentum) during embryonic development, explaining its position in the left upper quadrant and its peritoneal attachments. The gastrosplenic ligament (part of the dorsal mesogastrium) connects it to the greater curvature of the stomach, while the splenorenal ligament attaches it to the left kidney. Although the spleen is not a gastrointestinal organ, it receives its blood supply from the celiac trunk (via splenic artery) due to this developmental relationship. The tail of the pancreas also develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, extending into the splenorenal ligament.
questions.question: The spleen develops in relation to which mesentery?

questions.explanation: In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through the inguinal canal and exits via the superficial inguinal ring to terminate in the subcutaneous tissue and labium majus. The ilioinguinal nerve also passes through the superficial ring in both sexes (after traversing the canal). The round ligament is homologous to the gubernaculum testis in males (proximal gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament in females). Indirect inguinal hernias are much less common in females but can occur alongside the round ligament in the canal of Nuck (persistent processus vaginalis in females).
questions.question: The superficial inguinal ring transmits which structure in females?

questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiform bones, and the 1st-3rd metatarsals. Its summit is the superior articular facet of the talus, making the talus the keystone of this arch. It is larger, higher, more mobile, and more resilient than the lateral longitudinal arch, dynamically changing most during movement.
questions.question: The medial longitudinal arch has the greatest height and is formed by which bones?
options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, and 1st-3rd metatarsals
Talus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and two cuneiforms
Calcaneus, talus, and first metatarsal only

questions.explanation: Cubital tunnel syndrome results from ulnar nerve compression as it passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle. This is the most common site of ulnar nerve entrapment. Symptoms include numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and intrinsic hand muscle weakness.
questions.question: What causes cubital tunnel syndrome?

questions.explanation: The primary biomechanical argument for retaining the PCL in total knee replacement is that it provides femoral rollback during knee flexion: as the knee flexes, the PCL pulls the femoral condyles posteriorly, increasing flexion range and reducing quadriceps force needed for stair climbing. PCL-substituting (posterior-stabilized) designs use a cam and post mechanism to replicate this rollback when the PCL is sacrificed.
questions.question: In a total knee replacement (TKR), the posterior cruciate ligament is either retained or resected. The primary biomechanical argument for retaining the PCL is that it provides which function?
options: Femoral rollback during knee flexion, improving flexion range
Anterior knee stability against tibial translation only
Patellar tracking and extensor alignment correction

questions.explanation: The Achilles tendon does not have a true synovial tendon sheath like finger flexor tendons. Instead, it is surrounded by a paratenon (peritenon), a loose connective tissue sheath that allows tendon gliding and contains blood vessels. Two bursae are adjacent: the retrocalcaneal bursa (between tendon and calcaneus) and the superficial calcaneal bursa (between tendon and skin). Inflammation of the paratenon causes peritendinitis (Achilles peritendinitis).
questions.question: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. It does NOT have a true tendon sheath but instead has which covering?
options: A fascial tunnel from the posterior compartment

questions.explanation: The transverse humeral ligament extends between the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus. It holds the tendon of the long head of biceps brachii within the intertubercular (bicipital) groove. The synovial membrane of the shoulder joint forms a tubular sheath around this tendon.
questions.question: Which ligament holds the long head of biceps tendon in the intertubercular groove?

questions.explanation: The left renal artery passes posterior to the left renal vein as it courses from the aorta (at L1-L2 level, just below the superior mesenteric artery) to the left kidney hilum. The right renal artery, longer than the left, passes posterior to the IVC and right renal vein. Both renal arteries also pass posterior to the corresponding psoas major muscle and ureter. The left renal vein is longer than the right and receives the left gonadal vein, left suprarenal vein, and left inferior phrenic vein before draining into the IVC. This relationship is important in renal transplantation surgery.
questions.question: The left renal artery passes posterior to which structure?
Where is Auerbach's plexus located in the gut wall?
questions.explanation: Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa throughout the gastrointestinal tract. It controls gut motility, including peristalsis and segmentation. Damage to this plexus (as in Chagas disease or Hirschsprung disease) causes severe motility disorders. It contains both excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons.

The pulmonary ligament is a loose fold of pleura that hangs down below the root of the lung. It is formed by the continuity of visceral and parietal pleura inferior to the hilum. It forms a sleeve allowing for expansion of the pulmonary veins during increased venous return.
questions.question: Where is the pulmonary ligament located?

options: Lateral plantar nerve; adducts and flexes 1st digit
Deep fibular nerve; extends and abducts 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; abducts and flexes 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; flexes and inverts foot
questions.explanation: Abductor hallucis is innervated by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3) and performs abduction and flexion of the first digit (hallux). It originates from the medial tubercle of the calcaneal tuberosity, the flexor retinaculum, and plantar aponeurosis. It inserts into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit.
questions.question: Abductor hallucis, the most medially placed first layer foot muscle, is innervated by which nerve and performs which action?
Which is the most superficial named structure of the major neurovascular bundle in the popliteal fossa?
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve is the most superficial structure of the major neurovascular bundle in the popliteal fossa, bisecting the fossa from superior to inferior angle. The popliteal vein lies superficial to and close to the artery in the same fibrous sheath, while the popliteal artery is the deepest. The common fibular nerve exits at the superolateral angle.

The middle lobe of the right lung is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. The horizontal fissure runs along the fourth rib anteriorly. The oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from both the superior and middle lobes on the right side.
questions.question: Which fissure separates the right lung's middle lobe?
What is the function of the ileocecal valve?
questions.explanation: The ileocecal valve prevents reflux of colonic contents (which contain bacteria) back into the sterile small intestine. It also slows the passage of ileal contents into the cecum, allowing more time for nutrient and water absorption. The valve consists of superior and inferior lips formed by mucosal folds supported by circular muscle thickening.

After splenectomy, patients have increased susceptibility to infections, particularly from encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis). This is due to loss of the spleen's role in antibody production and filtration of blood-borne pathogens. Other organs (liver, bone marrow) can partially compensate for splenic function, but immunization and antibiotic prophylaxis are necessary in asplenic patients.
questions.question: What happens to the spleen after splenectomy?
Which muscle crosses the sole diagonally in a groove on the cuboid, and in so doing provides the most important muscular support for the transverse arch?
questions.explanation: Fibularis longus crosses the sole of the foot diagonally in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, inserting into the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This diagonal course provides critical support to the transverse arch by pulling the first metatarsal medially and maintaining the dome of the transverse arch. It is the most important muscular support for this arch.

questions.question: How high above the clavicle does cervical pleura extend?
questions.explanation: The cervical pleura extends approximately one inch (2.5 to 4 cm) above the medial third of the clavicle. This superior extension of the parietal pleura is reinforced by the suprapleural membrane. Understanding this anatomy is important because the pleura can be injured during procedures in the lower neck.

options: Bases of all five proximal phalanges
Bases of all five metatarsal bones
Heads of all metatarsals and bases of proximal phalanges
Only the first metatarsophalangeal joint exclusively
All tarsal bones as a group
questions.question: The plantar aponeurosis is the most important passive structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity to which structures?
questions.explanation: The plantar aponeurosis (plantar fascia) stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity (medial tubercle) to the heads of all metatarsals and the bases of the proximal phalanges. During toe extension (dorsiflexion) in push-off phase of gait, this aponeurosis is tensioned, raising the arch in a windlass mechanism. Plantar fasciitis involves inflammation at the calcaneal attachment.

is the classic test for scaphoid fracture. Pain with palpation in the snuffbox and/or with axial compression of the thumb suggests fracture. Even if initial radiographs are negative, clinical suspicion warrants immobilization and follow-up imaging.
questions.question: Which test assesses scaphoid fracture?
Into which vein does the right inferior phrenic vein drain?
questions.explanation: The right inferior phrenic vein usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left inferior phrenic vein is usually double, with one branch draining into the IVC and the other frequently joining the left suprarenal vein, which then drains into the left renal vein. These veins drain blood from the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

questions.question: The lesser sac communicates with the greater sac through which opening?
questions.explanation: The lesser sac (omental bursa) communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow, foramen of Winslow), bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament, posteriorly by the IVC and right crus of diaphragm, superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum. This communication allows peritoneal fluid to flow between the two sacs and permits spread of infection or hemorrhage. The foramen typically admits two fingers and can be used surgically to access the lesser sac. Foramina of Morgagni and Bochdalek are diaphragmatic defects, not communications between peritoneal sacs.

questions.question: Which structure forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The superior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe (caudate process) of the liver covered with peritoneum. The inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad, and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum along with the right crus of the diaphragm. The foramen provides communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs and typically admits two fingers, serving as a surgical landmark and potential route for accessing the lesser sac.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the hepatoduodenal ligament (free right edge of lesser omentum) containing the portal triad as its anterior boundary. The superior boundary is formed by the caudate lobe of liver covered with peritoneum, the inferior boundary by the first part of the duodenum (superior or horizontal part), and the posterior boundary by the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum and the right crus of the diaphragm. This opening, typically admitting two fingers, provides the only communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs.

questions.question: Which two epicondyles are connected by the superior boundary of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The superior boundary of the cubital fossa is formed by an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus. This line is located approximately 2-3 cm inferior to the actual position of the epicondyles. The base of this triangular depression is directed superiorly.

The cruciate anastomosis is situated at the level of the lesser trochanter and is formed by the inferior gluteal artery, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
questions.question: The cruciate anastomosis, at the level of the lesser trochanter, provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and which major vessel?

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. It extends from the umbilicus to the liver, dividing the liver into anatomical right and left lobes on the diaphragmatic surface. The free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres (round ligament).
questions.question: Which ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?

questions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism occurs when the pulmonary artery is obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumor cells, or other foreign particles. This can result in respiratory distress, chest pain, and potentially fatal cardiovascular collapse. Risk factors include prolonged immobilization, surgery, and hypercoagulable states.
questions.question: What condition involves pulmonary artery obstruction?

questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch is the peritoneal reflection between the bladder and rectum in males. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males when upright and can contain loops of small intestine (ileum). Fluid collections or abscesses may accumulate here. In females, the analogous space is the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), which is deeper.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the rectovesical pouch in males?
The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the nasal cavity through which opening?
questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine foramen in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa connects it with the nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the sphenoid bone and orbital process of the palatine bone. The sphenopalatine artery and nasopalatine nerve pass through it to supply the nasal cavity and septum.

questions.question: The lateral arcuate ligament extends from L1 transverse process to which structure?
questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament (lateral lumbocostal arch) is a thickened band of fascia covering the quadratus lumborum muscle, extending from the tip of the L1 transverse process to the 12th rib. The diaphragm's lateral muscular fibers arise from this ligament. The medial arcuate ligament crosses over psoas major (from L1 body to L1 transverse process), while the median arcuate ligament connects the right and left crura across the aortic hiatus. These ligaments can compress neurovascular structures and serve as important surgical landmarks in retroperitoneal approaches.

The anterior mediastinum (between the sternum and pericardium) contains primarily the thymus gland (or its remnant in adults), fatty tissue, and lymph nodes. In children, the thymus is prominent; in adults, it is largely replaced by fat. This space can be involved in thymomas or lymphomas.
questions.question: What lies in the anterior mediastinum primarily?

questions.explanation: The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII), specifically by a branch from the nerve after it exits the stylomastoid foramen. The muscle elevates and retracts the hyoid bone during swallowing. It shares innervation and embryologic origin (second pharyngeal arch) with the posterior belly of digastric.
questions.question: The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?
Where does the right bundle branch travel?
questions.explanation: The right bundle branch descends in the interventricular septum and crosses to the right ventricular free wall via the moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) to reach the anterior papillary muscle. From there, it divides into Purkinje fibers that spread throughout the right ventricle. This pathway ensures coordinated right ventricular contraction and explains why the moderator band is functionally important.

The superior epigastric artery is the other terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery. It descends behind the rectus abdominis muscle supplying it and the anterior abdominal wall. It anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac), providing collateral circulation between subclavian and external iliac arteries.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior body wall superiorly?

questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve contains preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the T5-T9 levels of the spinal cord, which synapse in the celiac ganglion. This nerve pierces the diaphragm separately or with the sympathetic trunk and provides sympathetic innervation to the foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and small intestine to mid-duodenum) via the celiac plexus. The lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11) supplies the midgut, while the least splanchnic nerve (T12) and lumbar splanchnic nerves supply the hindgut and pelvic organs via the superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses.
questions.question: The greater splanchnic nerve carries preganglionic fibers from which spinal levels?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at L1 and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, initially posterior to the esophagus. At T5, it moves to the left side of the esophagus and continues upward into the superior mediastinum where it arches forward to drain into the left venous angle.
questions.question: Where is the thoracic duct located initially?
How do upper left intercostal veins drain?
questions.explanation: The upper three left posterior intercostal veins typically join to form the left superior intercostal vein, which crosses the aortic arch and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein. This provides a direct connection to the superior vena cava system without crossing to the right side.

The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm, including both the pleural and peritoneal surfaces, in addition to its motor supply to the entire diaphragm. Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (such as in subphrenic abscess, perforated peptic ulcer, or ruptured spleen) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve, as both derive from the C3-C5 dermatomes. The peripheral parts of the diaphragm receive sensory innervation from the lower six intercostal nerves and subcostal nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the central part of the diaphragm?
Which vein forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The portal vein, positioned posteriorly within the hepatoduodenal ligament (posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery), forms part of the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The entire hepatoduodenal ligament (containing the portal triad) constitutes the anterior boundary. The portal vein is the most posterior structure within this ligament, closest to the foramen. Injury to the portal vein during surgical manipulation near the epiploic foramen can cause massive hemorrhage into the lesser sac. The foramen can be occluded by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament between thumb and fingers (Pringle maneuver).

questions.question: What causes pleural friction rub?
questions.explanation: A pleural friction rub is caused by inflamed visceral and parietal pleural surfaces rubbing against each other during respiration. The sound is typically described as creaking or grating and occurs in both inspiration and expiration. It is heard when pleural fluid is absent or minimal.

The inferior mediastinum has three subdivisions: anterior (in front of the heart), middle (contains the heart), and posterior (behind the heart). The superior mediastinum lies above the horizontal plane through T4. This classification helps in understanding the location of mediastinal structures and pathology.
questions.question: How many subdivisions does inferior mediastinum have?
Which left upper lobe segments are fused?
questions.explanation: In the left upper lobe, the apical and posterior segments typically fuse to form a single apicoposterior segment. The left upper lobe therefore typically contains: apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingular, and inferior lingular segments. This fusion accounts for the lower total segment count.

questions.question: What does the medial arcuate ligament overlie?
questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of the fascia covering the anterior surface of psoas major muscle. It extends from the side of the body of L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process of L1. The lateral arcuate ligament overlies quadratus lumborum muscle.

The elbow joint is classified as a synovial hinge (ginglymus) joint, allowing uniaxial movement. Articulation occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus with the trochlear notch of the ulna and radial head respectively. This configuration permits flexion and extension movements.
questions.question: What type of synovial joint is the elbow classified as?

questions.explanation: The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus, extending from the uterine pole of the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus just below the uterine tube attachment. It represents the proximal remnant of the gubernaculum (the distal remnant becoming the round ligament of the uterus). The ligament lies within the broad ligament (between its layers) and contains no significant vessels. The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) connects the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian vessels; it is not directly attached to the uterus.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the ovary to the uterus?

questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar artery arises from the basilar artery just before its terminal bifurcation. It supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum, cerebellar nuclei, and superior cerebellar peduncle. The artery courses around the pons below the oculomotor nerve. Occlusion causes ipsilateral cerebellar signs and contralateral pain/temperature loss.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum?

questions.explanation: Klumpke's paralysis involves the C8-T1 nerve roots of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. This typically results from undue abduction of the arm, such as clutching a tree branch during a fall. The resulting claw hand deformity occurs due to paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar flexors.
questions.question: Which nerve root values are primarily involved in Klumpke's paralysis?

questions.explanation: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots within the substance of the psoas major muscle. The lower part of L4 joins with L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk, which contributes to the sacral plexus. The lumbar plexus gives rise to several important nerves including the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, and obturator nerves, as well as branches to the psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles.
questions.question: Which spinal nerve roots contribute to the lumbar plexus?

questions.explanation: Iliotibial band syndrome involves repetitive friction of the iliotibial tract over the lateral femoral epicondyle during the flexion-extension cycle of running. This creates pain and inflammation at the lateral aspect of the knee. It is particularly common in long-distance runners. Treatment includes stretching, foam rolling, and correcting biomechanical factors such as hip abductor weakness.
questions.question: The iliotibial band syndrome (runner's knee) involves friction of the iliotibial tract over which bony landmark during running?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum and veers to the left at the level of the T5 vertebra. At the root of the neck, it arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle. This anatomical course is crucial for understanding lymphatic drainage patterns in the thorax.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct turn laterally?

options: Medial genicular and small saphenous veins
questions.explanation: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins. It traverses the popliteal fossa in the same fibrous sheath as the popliteal artery and terminates at the adductor hiatus to become the femoral vein. The small saphenous vein also drains into the popliteal vein.
questions.question: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of which two deep leg veins?

questions.explanation: The third (horizontal or inferior) part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the right psoas major muscle, the right ureter, and the right testicular/ovarian vessels at approximately the L3 vertebral level. This portion of the duodenum runs transversely from right to left and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein, with the root of the mesentery of the small intestine crossing it obliquely. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can occur when the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly.
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta?
The taeniae coli are thickenings of which muscle layer?
questions.explanation: The taeniae coli represent three longitudinal bands where the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the colon is thickened and concentrated, running from cecum to rectosigmoid junction. The three bands are: taenia libera (free, anteriorly on ascending and descending colon), taenia mesocolica (at mesenteric attachment), and taenia omentalis (at omental attachment). Between the taeniae, the longitudinal muscle is thin, allowing the circular muscle to create sacculations (haustra). The taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, providing a surgical landmark. At the rectosigmoid junction (about 15 cm from anus), the taeniae spread to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer in the rectum.

The appendix reaches its definitive adult position by puberty. In infants and young children, the appendix has a relatively higher position, which explains why appendicitis in children may present with higher abdominal pain. The growth of the cecum pulls the appendix to a lower position. The base of the appendix remains constant at the confluence of the three taeniae coli.
questions.question: At what age does the appendix typically reach its adult position?

questions.explanation: The parietal peritoneum lining the anterior abdominal wall receives blood supply from the same vessels that supply the overlying abdominal wall: superior and inferior epigastric arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery, and lumbar arteries. The peritoneum overlying the diaphragm is supplied by the musculophrenic and phrenic arteries, while that in the pelvis is supplied by branches of the internal iliac artery. The visceral peritoneum covering the organs receives its blood supply from the arteries supplying those organs (celiac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries). Venous and lymphatic drainage follows arterial supply patterns.
questions.question: The parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall is supplied by which vessels?

questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends to the left and lies at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra (T12). The tail reaches the splenic hilum and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas, lying within the splenorenal ligament. Anteriorly, the tail is related to the splenic flexure of the colon.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the tail of the pancreas lie?

questions.explanation: Rib notching on chest X-ray is a characteristic sign of aortic coarctation. The dilated, tortuous intercostal arteries (providing collateral circulation) erode the inferior margins of the posterior ribs (typically 3rd-8th ribs bilaterally). This creates scalloped indentations visible on radiographs. The first two ribs are usually spared.
questions.question: What sign indicates coarctation on chest X-ray?
The superior orbital fissure transmits which cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The superior orbital fissure transmits oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), and abducens (VI) nerves. It also transmits the superior ophthalmic vein. The fissure is bounded by the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid. The optic nerve passes through the separate optic canal.

The lesser omentum extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver and consists of the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments. The hepatogastric portion specifically connects the lesser curvature to the liver. This double layer of peritoneum carries the left and right gastric vessels along the lesser curvature.
questions.question: Which ligament extends from the lesser curvature to the liver?
Which artery supplies the superior surface of the bladder?
questions.explanation: The superior vesical arteries (usually multiple branches) arise from the patent part of the umbilical artery and supply the superior surface and upper lateral surfaces of the bladder. The umbilical artery is obliterated distally (becoming the medial umbilical ligament) but remains patent proximally. The inferior vesical artery (in males) or vaginal artery (in females) supplies the bladder base.

questions.question: At what vertebral level does the inferior angle of the scapula typically lie?
questions.explanation: The inferior angle of the scapula is positioned at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra (T7) and overlies the seventh rib. This serves as a convenient landmark for counting ribs along the lateral chest wall during thoracotomy procedures. The angle moves laterally and forwards around the chest wall during scapular movement.

questions.question: The celiac trunk typically arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The celiac trunk emerges from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta immediately below the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, anterior to the upper part of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). It quickly trifurcates into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries, providing the principal arterial supply to foregut derivatives. The celiac ganglion and plexus surround the origin of this vessel, receiving preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the greater splanchnic nerve.

Delta cells (D cells) comprise about 5-10% of islet cells and produce somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion, acting as a paracrine regulator. They are located peripherally in the islets. Somatostatin also inhibits growth hormone release from the pituitary (hence the name) and has widespread inhibitory effects on the GI tract.
questions.question: Which cells in pancreatic islets produce somatostatin?
What characterizes quiet expiration?
questions.explanation: Quiet expiration is a passive process resulting from elastic recoil of the lungs and relaxation of intercostal muscles and diaphragm. The ribs are depressed and the diaphragm elevated to its normal position. Lung recoil reduces size, increasing pressure inside the lungs to allow air flow outward.

questions.question: The anterior cerebral arteries are connected by which vessel?
questions.explanation: The two anterior cerebral arteries are joined by the anterior communicating artery, completing the anterior portion of the Circle of Willis. This connection allows collateral flow between right and left anterior circulations. Aneurysms commonly occur at this junction.

The thoracic duct begins at the level of L1 as a continuation of the cisterna chyli, which is formed by the union of left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. The duct eventually terminates by draining into the left venous angle after receiving additional lymphatic tributaries.
questions.question: Which structure represents the continuation of cisterna chyli?

questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve is the terminal branch of the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve. It traverses the infraorbital canal and emerges through the infraorbital foramen. The nerve provides sensation to the lower eyelid, side of nose, and upper lip.
questions.question: The infraorbital nerve is a continuation of which cranial nerve division?

questions.explanation: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) is a rare but life-threatening condition characterized by fulminant sepsis that can progress to death within hours. It occurs in 0.1-0.4% of splenectomized patients per year, with mortality rates of 50-70%. It is most commonly caused by encapsulated bacteria, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae. Prevention includes vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis.
questions.question: What is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI)?

questions.explanation: G cells are enteroendocrine cells located primarily in the pyloric antrum (also in duodenum) that secrete gastrin in response to gastric distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion by parietal cells and has trophic effects on gastric mucosa. Gastrinomas (tumors secreting gastrin) cause Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with severe peptic ulcer disease.
questions.question: Which cell type produces gastrin hormone?

questions.explanation: Natural drainage from infected bronchopulmonary segments can be achieved by adopting different postures (postural drainage or chest physiotherapy). For example, to drain the apical segment of the lower lobe, the patient should lie prone with the head turned to one side, allowing gravity to assist drainage.
questions.question: What allows drainage from infected segments?

questions.explanation: The costal pleura receives sensory innervation from the intercostal nerves, which correspond to the dermatomes of the overlying thoracic wall. The blood supply to costal pleura is also from intercostal vessels. This arrangement means that irritation of costal pleura causes sharp, well-localized pain.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the costal pleura?
The Straight Leg Raise (SLR) test is used to assess which structure, with a positive result occurring when sciatica is reproduced at 30-70 degrees of hip flexion?
questions.explanation: The Straight Leg Raise (SLR) test assesses lumbar nerve root compression (L4-S2) and sciatic nerve irritation. A positive test reproduces sciatica (not just hamstring tightness) when the hip is passively flexed between 30-70 degrees with the knee extended. The nerve root is maximally tensioned in this range. It is used to diagnose lumbar disc herniation causing nerve root compression.
options: Hip flexor tightness from psoas overuse
Femoral nerve root tension sign at the hip
Hamstring muscle tightness causing posterior thigh pain alone
Lumbar nerve root compression (L4�S2) with sciatic nerve irritation

questions.question: The median umbilical fold contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The median umbilical fold (single, midline structure) is raised by the median umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated urachus (embryonic connection between bladder apex and umbilicus). The paired medial umbilical folds contain the medial umbilical ligaments (obliterated umbilical arteries), while the paired lateral umbilical folds contain the inferior epigastric vessels (patent). The obliterated umbilical vein forms the ligamentum teres hepatis and runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament, not in an umbilical fold. These folds create fossae on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall that are clinically significant as potential sites of herniation.

"Handlebar palsy" results from ulnar nerve compression at the wrist (Guyon's canal) due to prolonged pressure from bicycle handlebars. This causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and numbness in ulnar nerve distribution. The condition is common in long-distance cyclists.
questions.question: Which nerve is compressed causing handlebar palsy?

questions.explanation: The lesser omentum consists of two continuous portions: the gastrohepatic ligament (pars flaccida, the membranous portion extending from lesser curvature of stomach to liver) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa, the thickened free right edge containing the portal triad extending from first part of duodenum to porta hepatis). These two parts form a continuous peritoneal fold connecting the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver, and together they form the anterior boundary of the lesser sac and epiploic foramen. The lesser omentum develops from the ventral mesentery and contains the portal triad in its free edge.
questions.question: The lesser omentum has two parts, which are:

questions.explanation: The posterior (Moore's) approach to the hip must carefully protect the sciatic nerve, which runs midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. The approach involves splitting gluteus maximus and detaching the short external rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli) from the greater trochanter. These rotators must be reattached to reduce the risk of posterior hip dislocation postoperatively.
options: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.question: The posterior approach to the hip (Moore's approach) identifies which nerve as the critical structure to protect, found running midway between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter?
What happens to diaphragm during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, causing its domes and central tendon to descend and flatten. This increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. As the diaphragm descends, abdominal viscera are pushed downward and the intrathoracic volume increases, reducing intrathoracic pressure.

Intersegmental veins running in the connective tissue septa between segments serve as guides for surgical separation during segmentectomy. The surgeon can identify these veins and use them to define segmental boundaries, allowing precise resection of diseased segments while preserving healthy lung tissue.
questions.question: What guides surgical segmental resection?

questions.explanation: A stable scapular base is essential for efficient glenohumeral motion. Scapular stabilizers (serratus anterior, rhomboids, trapezius) provide a fixed base from which glenohumeral muscles can act. Scapular winging demonstrates how loss of stability compromises shoulder function despite intact glenohumeral muscles.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between scapular stability and glenohumeral mobility?
options: Stable scapula essential for efficient glenohumeral motion

questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the middle rectal artery (from anterior division of internal iliac) in the wall of the rectum, creating a portosystemic anastomosis between portal (superior rectal vein to inferior mesenteric vein to portal vein) and systemic (middle rectal vein to internal iliac vein to IVC) venous systems. The inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal) also anastomoses with these vessels at the level of the anal canal. In portal hypertension, these anastomoses may become varicose, contributing to rectal varices (internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line).
questions.question: Which artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery?

questions.explanation: The tegmen tympani (thin plate of petrous temporal bone) forms the roof of the tympanic cavity, separating it from the middle cranial fossa and temporal lobe. Fractures or erosion can cause CSF otorrhea or meningitis. The tegmen also roofs the mastoid antrum. It represents the superior wall of the middle ear cavity.
questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the tympanic cavity?

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) supplies the anterior superior nasal septum. The sphenopalatine artery supplies the posterior septum while the superior labial artery supplies anteroinferiorly. These vessels anastomose in Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), the most common site of anterior epistaxis.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the nasal septum anteriorly?

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament divides the subphrenic space into right and left components, separating the right subphrenic space from the left. The right subphrenic space communicates posteriorly with the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position, making it a common site for fluid accumulation. The left subphrenic space is bounded by the falciform ligament on the right, the diaphragm superiorly and anteriorly, the stomach and spleen posteriorly, and the anterior layer of the left triangular ligament laterally.
questions.question: Which muscle separates the subphrenic from the subhepatic space?
Which structures pass between the two layers of the mesentery?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and vein pass between the two peritoneal layers of the mesentery along with lymph nodes, lymphatic vessels, nerves, and fat. These vessels provide the primary blood supply and drainage for the jejunum and ileum. The superior mesenteric artery gives off 15-18 branches that form the arterial arcades.

questions.question: What predisposes the scaphoid to avascular necrosis following fracture?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid has a unique retrograde blood supply with only one small artery entering distally. Fracture through the middle disrupts blood supply to the proximal fragment, which has no alternative source. This makes the proximal fragment vulnerable to avascular necrosis if not promptly treated.

questions.question: What percentage of pancreatic tissue is endocrine?
questions.explanation: Only about 1-2% of the pancreatic tissue consists of endocrine islets of Langerhans, with the remaining 98-99% being exocrine acinar tissue that produces digestive enzymes. Despite representing such a small proportion, the islets are crucial for glucose homeostasis. There are approximately 1 million islets in the human pancreas, most concentrated in the tail.

The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3). It carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. The nerve provides sensation to the temporal region, auricle, and temporomandibular joint. Misdirected regeneration causes Frey's syndrome.
questions.question: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of which division?
Which veins drain the breast?
questions.explanation: Veins of the breast drain into both the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The pattern follows the arterial supply. During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become engorged and may be visible through the skin. Venous drainage is important in the spread of breast cancer.

questions.question: Which structure separates the oral cavity from the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the boundary between the oral cavity and oropharynx. The arch contains the palatoglossus muscle and extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the oral cavity and oropharynx, bounded by these arches.

The upper lateral quadrant is the safe zone for intramuscular injections in the gluteal region. This avoids the sciatic nerve, which courses midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. Injections in other quadrants risk sciatic nerve injury, causing foot drop and sensory loss.
questions.question: The safe quadrant for intramuscular injection in the gluteal region is which of the following?
Which hormone stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?
questions.explanation: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by I cells in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to fats and proteins. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion from acinar cells and contraction of the gallbladder. Secretin, released in response to acid in the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion from duct cells. Both hormones work synergistically to produce adequate pancreatic juice.

DVT most commonly begins in the posterior tibial and fibular veins of the calf, often in valve sinuses where flow is stagnant. From here, thrombus can propagate proximally into the popliteal and femoral veins. The deep veins are the primary concern because thrombus there can embolize to the pulmonary circulation, causing potentially fatal pulmonary embolism. Superficial thrombophlebitis occurs in the saphenous veins.
questions.question: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) most commonly develops in the deep veins of the leg. Which two veins are most commonly involved initially?

questions.explanation: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is located at the junction between the manubrium and body of sternum, corresponding to the level of the second costal cartilage. This landmark lies at the vertebral level of T4/T5 and marks important anatomical boundaries. It is also the level of tracheal bifurcation and the beginning and end of the aortic arch.
questions.question: Which costal cartilage articulates with the sternal angle?

questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It descends with the inferior alveolar nerve to enter the mandibular foramen, supplying the mandibular teeth and bone. The mylohyoid branch supplies the mylohyoid muscle. The mental artery emerges through the mental foramen.
questions.question: The inferior alveolar artery is a branch of which vessel?
Which muscle protrudes the mandible when contracted bilaterally?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle protrudes the mandible when both sides contract simultaneously, assisted by the medial pterygoid. Unilateral contraction causes lateral deviation to the opposite side. The muscle has superior and inferior heads inserting on the articular disc and pterygoid fovea respectively.

questions.question: Which structure forms the primary passive support of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and provides primary passive support. The stylomandibular ligament is merely a thickening of the parotid capsule and contributes minimally to joint support. Other ligaments provide secondary stabilization or perform different mechanical functions in the temporomandibular complex.

The long thoracic nerve arises from nerve roots C5, C6, and C7. It supplies the serratus anterior muscle with branches to each digitation. Injury to this nerve causes scapular winging, which becomes apparent when pushing against resistance.
questions.question: What are the nerve roots of the long thoracic nerve?
Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, superior pole of the left kidney, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum fused to the transverse mesocolon. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum (anterior two layers); superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; inferiorly by the transverse colon and mesocolon; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac appear on imaging as fluid between stomach and pancreas.

The cremaster muscle receives motor innervation from the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2), which enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring and travels within the spermatic cord. The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis in response to stroking the inner thigh) tests this nerve and the L1-L2 cord segments. The ilioinguinal nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the scrotum and adjacent thigh but does not innervate the cremaster muscle. The cremasteric artery (from inferior epigastric) provides vascular supply to the cremaster muscle and travels alongside the nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve innervates the cremaster muscle?

questions.explanation: The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous with the fascia lata of the thigh. The superficial fascia, thick in women and impregnated with large quantities of fat, accounts for the prominence of the buttock. This fascial continuity has clinical implications for spread of infections between gluteal and thigh compartments.
questions.question: The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous inferiorly with which named structure of the thigh?

questions.explanation: The external spermatic fascia is the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, derived from the external oblique aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. The three concentric fascial coverings of the cord (from outside to inside) are: external spermatic fascia (from external oblique), cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia). Each layer is acquired as the processus vaginalis and accompanying structures descend through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent.
questions.question: The external spermatic fascia is derived from which layer?
From how many lumbar vertebrae does right crus arise?
questions.explanation: The right crus arises from the front of the bodies of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs. The left crus is smaller and arises only from L1 and L2. Some muscle fibers from the right crus form a sling around the esophageal opening.

questions.question: The prostate gland is related posteriorly to which structure?
questions.explanation: The prostate gland is related posteriorly to the anterior wall of the rectum (ampulla), separated from it by the rectovesical fascia (fascia of Denonvilliers). This relationship allows the prostate to be palpated during digital rectal examination (DRE), where the posterior surface of the gland can be assessed for size, consistency, symmetry, and nodules. The prostate is related anteriorly to the pubic symphysis (retropubic space of Retzius), superiorly to the bladder base, and inferiorly to the urogenital diaphragm. The prostatic urethra passes through the gland from base to apex.

questions.question: Which ligament connects the spleen to the greater curvature?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic (gastrolienal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach. It is part of the greater omentum and contains the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels. This ligament provides vascular connections between the spleen and stomach.

The anterior arch of the atlas (C1) has a facet on its posterior surface that articulates with the dens (odontoid process) of the axis (C2). The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against this facet. This atlantoaxial joint allows rotation of the head. Fracture or ligamentous injury can cause atlantoaxial instability.
questions.question: The anterior arch of C1 articulates with which structure?

questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in females and is therefore the most common site for peritoneal metastases, free fluid (ascites), and pelvic abscesses to collect. It can be assessed by pelvic examination (palpable through the posterior vaginal fornix) and accessed by culdocentesis for diagnostic aspiration.
questions.question: What is the most common site for peritoneal metastases in females?

questions.explanation: Skene's glands (paraurethral glands) are small glands that open via ducts on either side of the external urethral orifice in females. They are homologous to the male prostate and secrete mucus. They can become infected causing urethritis or form cysts. Bartholin's glands (greater vestibular glands) are homologous to Cowper's glands and open into the vestibule lateral to the vaginal orifice.
questions.question: Which glands open into the female urethra?

options: Internal acoustic meatus and jugular foramen
Superior orbital fissure and optic canal
questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis is situated around the pituitary infundibulum and optic chiasma at the base of the brain. It provides collateral circulation when major arteries become occluded. The circle includes anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.question: The Circle of Willis is located around which anatomical structures?

questions.explanation: The maxillary vein is formed from the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa. It joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein within the parotid gland. The pterygoid plexus communicates with cavernous sinus and facial veins without valves.
questions.question: Which vein drains the pterygoid venous plexus?

questions.explanation: diagnosis is confirmed by nerve conduction studies showing delayed median nerve conduction across the wrist. These studies measure sensory and motor nerve conduction velocities. Electromyography may also show denervation changes in thenar muscles in severe cases.
questions.question: Which condition requires nerve conduction studies for diagnosis?

questions.explanation: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein, measuring approximately 8 cm in length. The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein ascends to the porta hepatis within the free edge of the lesser omentum, positioned posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery, where it divides into right and left branches.
questions.question: The portal vein is formed by the union of which two vessels?

questions.explanation: The splenic vein joins with the superior mesenteric vein posterior to the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. The splenic vein runs from left to right along the posterior surface of the pancreas. It receives the short gastric veins, left gastroepiploic vein, pancreatic veins, and inferior mesenteric vein.
questions.question: Into which vein does the splenic vein primarily drain?

questions.explanation: The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery that descends along the acute margin (right border) of the heart to supply the right ventricle. The left marginal artery (branch of the circumflex or left coronary artery) supplies the left border of the heart. These marginal branches are important anatomical landmarks in cardiac catheterization and surgery.
questions.question: What is the marginal artery of the heart?
Which procedure divides the vagal trunks to reduce acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Vagotomy involves division of the vagal trunks or branches to reduce gastric acid secretion and was historically performed for peptic ulcer disease. Truncal vagotomy (dividing the main trunks) requires a drainage procedure (pyloroplasty) as it impairs gastric emptying. Highly selective vagotomy (dividing only the branches to the acid-secreting fundus/body) preserves antral innervation and pyloric function.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa is formed by the obturator internus muscle covered by obturator fascia, which contains the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) housing the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. The medial wall is formed by the levator ani and external anal sphincter. The fossa is bounded posteriorly by the gluteus maximus and sacrotuberous ligament, anteriorly by the posterior border of the urogenital diaphragm, and inferiorly by skin. The fossa contains fat and is a potential space for abscess formation.

The middle constrictor arises from the greater and lesser horns of the hyoid bone and the stylohyoid ligament.
