It is the weaker of the two cruciate ligaments with relatively poor blood supply. It becomes taut in full extension and prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia.

questions.question: The testicular artery arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The testicular arteries (and ovarian arteries in females) arise from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level, just inferior to the renal arteries. This high origin reflects the embryological development of the gonads on the posterior abdominal wall before testicular descent or ovarian migration. The long testicular arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major, ureter, and external iliac vessels, enter the deep inguinal ring, and travel through the inguinal canal as part of the spermatic cord to reach the testes in the scrotum.

questions.question: What is the subcostal muscle?
questions.explanation: The subcostalis muscle is an incomplete sheet on the inner surface of the lower ribs near their angles. Its fibers cross more than one intercostal space (unlike intercostal muscles which span single spaces). It is part of the innermost layer of thoracic wall muscles.

questions.question: Where does the spongy urethra begin?
questions.explanation: The spongy (penile) urethra begins where the membranous urethra exits the urogenital diaphragm and extends through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans penis. It is approximately 15 cm long and has two dilated portions: the intrabulbar fossa in the bulb and the navicular fossa in the glans.

questions.question: Where in the spleen are blood-borne bacteria primarily filtered?
questions.explanation: Blood-borne bacteria and particulate matter are primarily filtered and phagocytosed by macrophages in the red pulp cords and sinusoids. Blood flowing through the spleen is exposed to numerous macrophages that can recognize and remove opsonized bacteria and foreign particles. This filtering function is lost after splenectomy, increasing infection susceptibility.

The articular disk is a fibrocartilaginous structure that lies over the superior surface of the ulna. It effectively prevents direct articulation between the ulna and carpal bones at the wrist joint. The ulna therefore does not participate in the radiocarpal (wrist) joint, with articulation occurring only with the radius.
questions.question: Which ligament prevents the ulna from articulating with the carpal bones at the wrist joint?

questions.explanation: The loose connective tissue layer contains emissary veins that connect the superficial scalp veins with intracranial venous sinuses. This layer is often called the danger area because infections can spread intracranially. The loose texture allows fluid and blood to spread widely in scalp injuries.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the loose connective tissue layer of the scalp?
Which artery supplies the AV node in most people?
questions.explanation: The AV nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 80-90% of people (right dominant circulation) and from the left circumflex artery in the remainder (left dominant circulation). It typically arises near the origin of the posterior interventricular artery. AV node ischemia from right coronary occlusion can cause heart block.

questions.question: Which nerve branch arises from the lateral cord?
questions.explanation: The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) arises from the lateral cord and primarily supplies pectoralis major muscle. The lateral cord also gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve. It lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery.

options: Plantarflexion of toes and plantar sensation
questions.question: Tibial nerve injury in the tarsal tunnel (tarsal tunnel syndrome) presents with pain and paraesthesia on the sole of the foot. Which action is specifically lost?
questions.explanation: Tarsal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. It presents with pain, burning, and paraesthesia on the sole of the foot and intrinsic muscle weakness. Plantarflexion of the toes and intrinsic muscle function are impaired. Tinel's sign may be positive over the tarsal tunnel at the medial ankle.

The cochlear aqueduct (perilymphatic duct) connects the scala tympani with the subarachnoid space, allowing communication between perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid. The aqueduct opens at the base of the petrous temporal bone. The vestibular aqueduct separately connects the endolymphatic system with the posterior cranial fossa. Patency varies among individuals.
questions.question: The cochlear aqueduct connects the scala tympani with which space?

questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle is the sole abductor of the vocal cords, externally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are adductors or tensors of the vocal cords. Bilateral paralysis of this muscle causes life-threatening airway obstruction requiring immediate intervention.
questions.question: Which muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords?

questions.explanation: The tibial nerve gives off the medial sural cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa. This joins the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve to form the sural nerve, supplying the lateral side of the leg and ankle. The tibial nerve is the most superficial of the major neurovascular bundle in the fossa.
questions.question: The tibial nerve gives off which named cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa that contributes to forming the sural nerve?
Which papillae on the tongue do NOT contain taste buds?
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae but do not contain taste buds; they provide the rough texture of the tongue. Fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae all contain taste buds. The circumvallate papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis.

options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. It exits the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis. Injury to this nerve (during posterior hip surgery or gluteal injections) causes Trendelenburg sign due to loss of hip abduction and medial rotation. It carries no cutaneous branches.
questions.question: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies which muscles?

questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx), formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses, forms the medial part of the posterior wall and medial boundary of the inguinal canal. Weakness here predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The lateral part of the posterior wall is formed by the transversalis fascia.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: The "dinner fork deformity" in Colles' fracture results from posterior displacement of the distal radial fragment. When viewed laterally, the wrist resembles an upside-down dinner fork with the handle representing the forearm and the fork head representing the displaced hand segment.
questions.question: What produces the dinner fork deformity?
Which position of the appendix may cause retrocecal abscess?
questions.explanation: When the appendix is in a retrocecal position (most common position, 65-75% of cases), appendicitis can cause a retrocecal abscess. This position may also cause atypical symptoms with less peritoneal irritation and more lateral/posterior pain. The appendix may lie behind the cecum but still be intraperitoneal (covered by peritoneum) or rarely be retroperitoneal.

The lacrimal gland receives parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Preganglionic fibers travel via the greater petrosal nerve and nerve of the pterygoid canal. Postganglionic fibers reach the gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves. The pathway originates from the superior salivatory nucleus.
questions.question: The lacrimal gland is innervated by which parasympathetic pathway?
The spinal accessory nerve supplies which two muscles?
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. The nerve emerges from the jugular foramen and descends across the posterior triangle. Injury during lymph node biopsy causes weakness in shoulder shrugging and difficulty turning the head against resistance.

questions.question: Which condition causes anterior dislocation of the lunate?
questions.explanation: Anterior dislocation of the lunate occurs from falling on a dorsiflexed wrist. The lunate is forced anteriorly and compresses the carpal tunnel contents including the median nerve. This causes carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms with paresthesia and thenar muscle weakness. The lunate also risks avascular necrosis.

questions.question: The piriform fossa is bounded medially by which structure?
questions.explanation: The piriform fossa (recess) is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels lie in the mucosa of the piriform fossa. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in this recess. The fossa is part of the laryngopharynx.

questions.question: What is tension pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural cavity through a one-way valve mechanism but cannot escape. Progressive air accumulation increases intrapleural pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum to the opposite side. This is a life-threatening emergency causing hemodynamic compromise requiring immediate needle decompression.

questions.question: The genitofemoral nerve pierces which muscle?
questions.explanation: The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) emerges through the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle at approximately the L3/L4 level, unlike other branches of the lumbar plexus which emerge from its lateral border. After piercing psoas, it descends on the muscle's anterior surface, dividing into genital and femoral branches. The genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring to supply the cremaster muscle and scrotal/labial skin, while the femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery to supply skin over the femoral triangle.

questions.question: The tibial nerve enters the tarsal tunnel and supplies intrinsic muscles of the sole via its terminal branches. Which of the following is supplied by the medial plantar nerve?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum brevis is supplied by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3). The medial plantar nerve (analogous to the median nerve) also supplies abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis, and the first lumbrical. The lateral plantar nerve (analogous to the ulnar nerve) supplies all other intrinsic muscles: abductor digiti minimi, quadratus plantae, flexor digiti minimi brevis, all interossei, lateral three lumbricals, and adductor hallucis.

questions.question: Which lymph node group drains the skin of the umbilicus?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from skin of the anterior abdominal wall follows the watershed principle: above the umbilicus drains to axillary nodes, below the umbilicus drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and the umbilicus itself drains primarily to superficial inguinal nodes though some drainage may occur to both axillary and inguinal nodes. The deep abdominal wall lymphatics drain along the deep vessels (superior epigastric, inferior epigastric, lumbar) to internal thoracic, external iliac, and para-aortic nodes. Metastatic tumor deposits at the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph node) typically indicate advanced intra-abdominal malignancy spreading via lymphatics or direct extension.

questions.question: What causes Jersey finger?
questions.explanation: Jersey finger results from avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus from the distal phalanx. This commonly occurs in the ring finger when a player's finger catches in another player's jersey during tackle attempts. Inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint is diagnostic.

questions.question: The fibrous capsule anteriorly is replaced by which three structures from proximal to distal?
questions.explanation: Anteriorly, the fibrous layer of the knee joint capsule is replaced by the quadriceps tendon (above the patella), the patella itself, and the patellar ligament (below the patella). These three structures provide strong anterior protection. The patellar retinacula blend with the capsule laterally providing additional support.
options: Patellar ligament, ACL, and synovial membrane
Fibular collateral ligament, patella, and patellar ligament
Patellar retinacula, PCL, and iliotibial tract
Tibial collateral ligament, patella, and patellar tendon
Quadriceps tendon, patella, and patellar ligament

questions.explanation: Palmar interossei (PAD - Palmar ADduct) produce finger adduction, moving fingers toward the middle finger axis. There are three palmar interossei muscles compared to four dorsal interossei. All interossei also flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.
questions.question: What is the function of palmar interossei?
The ciliary ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion receiving preganglionic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus via the oculomotor nerve. Postganglionic fibers travel in short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. Sensory fibers from V1 and sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing. The ganglion lies posterolaterally in the orbit.

questions.question: How do extrinsic thumb muscles complement thenar muscles?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic thumb muscles (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus and brevis, flexor pollicis longus) provide power and basic positioning. Thenar muscles provide fine motor control and opposition. This combination enables the thumb's unique versatility in human hand function.
options: Extrinsic muscles for precision grip only
Extrinsic for power grip, thenar for precision control

questions.question: What epithelium lines the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium that can stretch and accommodate changes in bladder volume without tearing. When the bladder is empty, the epithelium appears thick with 5-6 cell layers; when distended, it thins to 2-3 layers. This epithelium is impermeable to salts and water.

questions.question: At which rib level is the axilla base formed?
questions.explanation: The base of the axilla is formed by skin, subcutaneous tissue, and axillary fascia spanning from the fourth rib. This base is concave and forms the floor of the axillary space. The axillary fascia is continuous with the pectoral fascia anteriorly and latissimus dorsi fascia posteriorly.

The thymus consists of two elongated lobes and is a large organ in the fetus, occupying the thoracic cavity behind the sternum. It secretes lymphopoietin and plays a crucial role in T-lymphocyte maturation. After puberty, the thymus undergoes involution and is gradually replaced by adipose tissue.
questions.question: How many lobes does the thymus consist of?

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament (and lesser omentum) develops from the ventral mesentery, while the greater omentum, splenorenal ligament, gastrosplenic ligament, and transverse mesocolon all derive from the dorsal mesentery. The ventral mesentery, present only in the region of the foregut, gives rise to the falciform ligament (connecting liver to anterior abdominal wall), the lesser omentum (connecting liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum), and the coronary and triangular ligaments (connecting liver to diaphragm). The liver and gallbladder develop within the ventral mesentery, explaining their peritoneal relationships.
questions.question: Which structure is derived from the ventral mesentery?
The splenic artery typically runs along which organ's superior border?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery, the largest branch of the celiac trunk, takes a characteristically tortuous course to the left along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas, giving off numerous small pancreatic branches en route. It runs posterior to the stomach within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-6 terminal branches that enter the splenic hilum. Before reaching the spleen, the artery gives off the left gastroepiploic artery and short gastric arteries, which pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the greater curvature and fundus of the stomach respectively.

Shoulder stability requires both extrinsic factors (rotator cuff muscles, long head of biceps, negative intra-articular pressure, scapular position) and intrinsic factors (glenoid labrum, glenohumeral ligaments, joint capsule). Loss of either extrinsic or intrinsic factors increases dislocation risk.
questions.question: How do extrinsic and intrinsic factors contribute to shoulder stability?
options: Both extrinsic and intrinsic stabilizers are essential

questions.question: What causes Dupuytren's contracture?
questions.explanation: Dupuytren's contracture results from progressive fibrosis of the palmar aponeurosis. Longitudinal bands thicken forming cords that cause progressive flexion contracture of fingers, typically ring and little fingers. The condition has genetic predisposition and is more common in males of Northern European descent.

The azygos vein passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (at T12 level) along with the aorta and thoracic duct, posterior to the diaphragmatic crura. The aortic hiatus is actually a midline gap between the crura rather than a true opening in the diaphragmatic muscle. The azygos vein drains the posterior thoracic and abdominal walls and provides important collateral circulation between the superior and inferior vena cavae. It arches over the right main bronchus to drain into the superior vena cava. The hemiazygos vein may also pass through the aortic hiatus.
questions.question: The azygos vein passes through which diaphragmatic opening?
The 'dancer's fracture' is an avulsion fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal. Which tendon's avulsion causes this fracture?
questions.explanation: The dancer's fracture is an avulsion fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal, caused by the fibularis brevis tendon pulling off its insertion during a sudden inversion injury or fall. The fibularis brevis inserts into the dorsal surface of the tuberosity (styloid process) at the base of the fifth metatarsal. This is the most common fracture in the foot and must be distinguished from the Jones fracture (metaphyseal stress fracture).

questions.question: Which nerve roots form the lower trunk?
questions.explanation: The lower trunk is formed by union of C8 and T1 nerve roots. Injury to the lower trunk causes Klumpke's paralysis with claw hand deformity. The lower trunk continues as the medial cord after giving off no branches in the neck.

questions.question: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) exits the pelvis beneath the inguinal ligament. It lies in which position relative to the femoral artery?
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) lies lateral to the femoral artery as it exits beneath the inguinal ligament, outside the femoral sheath (which contains only the femoral artery, vein, and canal). The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty/Lymphatics) describes the lateral to medial arrangement. The femoral nerve rapidly divides into branches in the femoral triangle.

The musculophrenic artery is one of the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery (the other being superior epigastric). It runs along the costal margin supplying the lower intercostal spaces (7th-9th via anterior intercostal arteries), the diaphragm, and the abdominal muscles.
questions.question: What is the musculophrenic artery?
Which part of the stomach lies superior to the cardiac notch?
questions.explanation: The fundus is the dilated, dome-shaped portion of the stomach that lies superior to the level of the cardiac orifice and cardiac notch. It is usually filled with gas and is in contact with the left dome of the diaphragm. The fundus can be distinguished radiographically as the gas bubble seen in upright chest X-rays.

Nine flexor tendons accompany the median nerve through the carpal tunnel: four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, plus the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These tendons are enclosed in synovial sheaths within the tunnel.
questions.question: What structure accompanies the median nerve through the carpal tunnel?
What percentage of body weight does the adult heart represent?
questions.explanation: The adult heart weighs approximately 250-350 grams, representing about 0.5% of total body weight (roughly 1/200th of body weight). The heart size is often compared to a closed fist. The male heart is typically slightly larger and heavier than the female heart, correlating with body size differences.

The third (horizontal) part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein as they descend toward the root of the mesentery. This relationship can lead to superior mesenteric artery syndrome, where the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta (with the spine) posteriorly, causing partial or complete duodenal obstruction. Risk factors include rapid weight loss, scoliosis, surgical correction of scoliosis, and conditions causing loss of the mesenteric fat pad that normally cushions the angle between the SMA and aorta.
questions.question: The third part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by which vessels?

questions.explanation: The anterior two-thirds (oral part) of the tongue develops from the first pharyngeal arch (two lateral lingual swellings and median tuberculum impar). The posterior third (pharyngeal part) develops from the third arch (copula). The second arch contribution is overgrown. This embryologic division explains the different nerve supplies.
questions.question: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch?
The appendicular lymph nodes drain into which nodal group?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from the appendix passes through lymph nodes in the mesoappendix to the ileocolic lymph nodes along the ileocolic artery, which subsequently drain to superior mesenteric lymph nodes along the superior mesenteric artery. From there, lymph flows to the pre-aortic nodes and eventually to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This drainage pattern follows the arterial supply (appendicular artery from ileocolic artery from SMA). Enlarged ileocolic nodes may be palpable in appendicitis and can contribute to diagnostic imaging findings in acute abdominal conditions.

The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular floor (diaphragm) of the oral cavity, creating the mylohyoid raphe in the midline. The muscle elevates the floor during swallowing and depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed. Above the mylohyoid lie the tongue and genioglossus; below lie the geniohyoid and digastric. Mylohyoid nerve (V3) provides innervation.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the mouth?

questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx or conjoined tendon) is formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles as they insert onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. This structure reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in its medial third, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Weakness or absence of the conjoint tendon in Hesselbach's triangle (bounded by lateral border of rectus, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric artery) predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The external oblique does not contribute to the conjoint tendon; instead, its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the canal and the superficial ring.
questions.question: Which muscle's fibers contribute to the conjoint tendon?
The cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter for which structure?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus muscle, the lower part of the inferior constrictor, acts as the upper esophageal sphincter. It remains tonically contracted except during swallowing. Between cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus lies the dehiscence of Killian where pharyngeal diverticula (Zenker's) occur.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the parotid gland with sensory fibers?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) provides sensory innervation to the skin over the parotid gland and lower auricle. The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (not sensory to the gland). The facial nerve traverses the gland but doesn't innervate it. Parotid surgery risks great auricular nerve injury causing numbness.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive anterior diaphragmatic drainage?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the thoracic surface of the diaphragm drains anteriorly to parasternal lymph nodes (via anterior diaphragmatic nodes) and posteriorly to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes. From the abdominal surface, drainage goes to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic, and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.

questions.question: Which vein forms the left border of the hepatocystic triangle (Calot's)?
questions.explanation: Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) has three boundaries: the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially (not a vein, despite the question's misdirection), and the inferior surface of the liver superiorly. Within this triangle lie the cystic artery and Calot's lymph node. The correct answer addresses that the common hepatic duct (not a vein) forms the medial boundary. Understanding this triangle's anatomy is crucial for safe cholecystectomy, as the cystic artery must be identified within it before ligation. Anatomical variations in this region are common.

Wrist drop results from radial nerve injury, which has nerve root values C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1. However, C7 is the most critical root for wrist extension. Complete radial nerve palsy affects all extensor muscles and causes the characteristic wrist drop deformity.
questions.question: Which nerve root value is predominantly involved in wrist drop?

questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal canal is formed by the lacrimal bone and maxilla, housing the nasolacrimal duct. The duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior meatus. The valve of Hasner at the inferior opening prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction requires dacryocystorhinostomy surgery.
questions.question: The nasolacrimal duct is formed by which two bones?
Which organism are asplenic patients most susceptible to?
questions.explanation: Asplenic patients (post-splenectomy or functional asplenia) are particularly susceptible to infections with encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis. The spleen is crucial for opsonization and clearance of these organisms. Asplenic patients require vaccination against these organisms and may need prophylactic antibiotics (penicillin or amoxicillin).

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the caval opening lie?
questions.explanation: The caval opening (vena caval foramen) in the diaphragm is located at the T8 vertebral level in the central tendon. It transmits the inferior vena cava and terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve. The IVC is adherent to the margins of the opening, so when the diaphragm contracts during inspiration, it widens the opening and dilates the IVC, facilitating venous return.

questions.question: Which carpal bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuffbox floor is formed by the scaphoid proximally and the trapezium distally. The radial artery crosses the floor of this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture.

The left bundle branch divides into two main fascicles: anterior and posterior (some describe a third, septal fascicle). The anterior fascicle supplies the anterior and lateral left ventricular wall; the posterior fascicle supplies the posterior and inferior wall. Left bundle branch block or fascicular blocks (hemiblocks) cause characteristic ECG patterns and may indicate underlying cardiac disease.
questions.question: How many fascicles does the left bundle branch divide into?

questions.explanation: The right middle lobe contains two bronchopulmonary segments: lateral and medial. This is the smallest lobe of the right lung. The middle lobe is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. Middle lobe syndrome can occur from lymph node compression.
questions.question: How many segments are in right middle lobe?

questions.explanation: The tibiofibular ligament (syndesmosis) and interosseous membrane maintain the integrity of the tibiofibular mortise, ensuring that the distal tibia and fibula remain properly spaced for stable articulation with the trochlea tali. Disruption of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain or Maisonneuve fracture) significantly destabilizes the ankle joint and requires surgical fixation.
questions.question: The tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane form part of the ankle joint supports. These structures maintain which relationship between the tibia and fibula at the ankle?
options: They allow free rotation between tibia and fibula
They maintain tibiofibular mortise integrity for stable talus articulation
They create the lateral wall of the ankle
They only protect the interosseous vessels
They provide primary stability against valgus stress

questions.explanation: The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) at the carotid bifurcation is innervated by the carotid sinus nerve (nerve of Hering), a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid body (chemoreceptor) is also innervated primarily by IX. These receptors monitor blood pressure and blood gas levels respectively. Carotid massage can slow heart rate via this pathway.
questions.question: The carotid sinus is innervated by which nerve?

options: Increases the weight of the quadriceps
Increases mechanical advantage in knee extension
questions.explanation: The patella is a true sesamoid bone serving as a pulley that improves the angle of pull of the quadriceps tendon, resulting in greater mechanical advantage in knee extension. Patellectomy significantly reduces knee extension strength. The patella slides within the trochlear groove during knee movements and is protected by thick hyaline cartilage on its posterior surface.
questions.question: The patella, embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon, serves as a pulley with what biomechanical benefit?
The seminal vesicles are located posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles are located posterior to the fundus (base) of the urinary bladder, lateral to the ampulla of the vas deferens, anterior to the rectum (separated by rectovesical fascia), and superior to the prostate gland. They are elongated, lobulated structures that produce approximately 70% of seminal fluid volume, which is alkaline and contains fructose (energy for sperm), prostaglandins, and clotting factors. The duct of each seminal vesicle joins the ampulla of the corresponding vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra.

The foramen rotundum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, transmitting the maxillary nerve (V2). It connects the middle cranial fossa with the pterygopalatine fossa. The foramen is round in shape, distinguishing it from the oval foramen ovale.
questions.question: Which bone contains the foramen rotundum?
What is the exocrine secretory unit of the pancreas called?
questions.explanation: The pancreatic acinus is the functional exocrine secretory unit, consisting of pyramid-shaped serous (enzyme-secreting) acinar cells arranged around a small lumen. The acinus is drained by an intercalated duct lined by centroacinar cells. Multiple acini drain into larger ducts, which eventually form the main pancreatic duct. The pancreas structurally resembles the parotid gland.

questions.question: What is the functional significance of the scapular anastomoses?
options: Collateral circulation bypassing proximal subclavian obstruction
questions.explanation: Scapular anastomoses provide crucial collateral circulation connecting first part of subclavian artery with third part of axillary artery. This enables continued limb perfusion even with proximal arterial obstruction. The anastomoses involve suprascapular, dorsal scapular, and circumflex scapular arteries.

Boutonniere deformity results from rupture of the central slip of the extensor mechanism over the proximal interphalangeal joint. This causes PIP joint flexion with DIP joint hyperextension. The lateral bands slip volarward, creating the characteristic deformity. Common after PIP joint injuries.
questions.question: Which condition causes boutonniere deformity?

questions.explanation: The ulnar artery is the larger terminal branch of the brachial artery, beginning below the elbow joint. It provides the main arterial supply to the medial forearm and forms the superficial palmar arch predominantly. The radial artery is smaller but more clinically accessible.
questions.question: Which artery is the largest terminal branch of the brachial artery?

questions.explanation: at the wrist joint (ulnar deviation) is produced by the combined action of extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris. These muscles work synergistically despite being in different compartments. The wrist joint permits movement along two axes as an ellipsoid synovial joint.
questions.question: Which movement at the wrist joint is produced by extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris?

questions.explanation: Zone 3 (centrilobular zone) of the hepatic acinus is furthest from the blood supply (portal triads) and is therefore most susceptible to ischemic injury, toxic injury, and hypoxia. This zone receives blood last with the lowest oxygen content. Centrilobular necrosis is characteristic of ischemic hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, and chronic passive congestion from heart failure.
questions.question: Which zone of the hepatic acinus is most susceptible to ischemia?

questions.explanation: The body of the pancreas is one of the major structures forming the posterior relations or stomach bed. The stomach bed is separated from the stomach by the lesser sac (omental bursa). Other structures in the stomach bed include the left kidney, left suprarenal gland, splenic artery, transverse mesocolon, and diaphragm.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the stomach bed posteriorly?

questions.explanation: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV), the only extraocular muscle not supplied by the oculomotor nerve except lateral rectus (abducens). The superior oblique passes through the trochlea (pulley) on the medial orbital roof. It intorts, depresses, and abducts the eye.
questions.question: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The tympanic plexus on the promontory of the middle ear is formed primarily by the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's nerve). Contributions also come from the caroticotympanic nerves (sympathetic). The plexus provides sensation to the middle ear mucosa. The lesser petrosal nerve arises from this plexus.
questions.question: The tympanic plexus is formed primarily by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The L3 sclerotome includes the hip joint, which receives innervation partly from the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Pain from L3 root pathology can be referred to the hip joint, and hip joint disease can refer pain along L3 dermatomal distribution to the anterior thigh and knee. This bidirectional referral is explained by Hilton's law and the concept of sclerotome overlap between spinal levels.
options: Hip joint itself (L3 innervates the hip)
questions.question: In the lower limb, the term 'sclerotome' refers to the area of bone and deep structures supplied by a single spinal nerve root. Hip pain from L3 sclerotome involvement can mimic pain from which structure?

questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, suspends the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian artery (from aorta) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament must be clamped and divided during oophorectomy. The ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus medially, while the broad ligament provides only indirect support via the mesovarium. The round ligament extends from uterus to labium majus via the inguinal canal.
questions.question: The ovary is suspended by which ligament from the pelvic wall?
Which structure lies in both superior and posterior mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The esophagus, vagus nerves, and thoracic duct all pass through both the superior and posterior mediastinum. The esophagus descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum into the posterior mediastinum before piercing the diaphragm at T10. Understanding these relationships is important for interpreting imaging.

The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve supplies all muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) via its motor root. It also supplies mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor veli palatini, and tensor tympani. These muscles derive from the first pharyngeal arch mesoderm.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication?

questions.explanation: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on the medial surface of the mandibular angle and ramus, forming a sling with the masseter on the lateral surface. It arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and pterygoid fossa. The muscle elevates and protrudes the mandible. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3).
questions.question: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on which structure?
Which muscles form the posterior wall of the axilla?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the axilla is formed by subscapularis on the anterior surface of the scapula superiorly, and teres major and latissimus dorsi inferiorly. The posterior axillary fold extends farther inferiorly than the anterior wall and can be grasped between fingers.

questions.question: What connects breast skin to deep fascia?
questions.explanation: The ligaments of Cooper are fibrous strands that connect the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major, passing through the breast tissue. They provide structural support to the breast. Infiltration of these ligaments by breast cancer causes their shortening, producing the characteristic peau d'orange appearance.

The lateral ligaments of the ankle are: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL), and the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). The ATFL is the weakest and most commonly injured in ankle sprains. The CFL is the intermediate in strength, and the PTFL is the strongest. Together they stabilize the lateral side of the ankle joint.
options: Anterior tibiotalar, posterior tibiotalar, and calcaneofibular
Anterior talofibular, tibiocalcaneal, and posterior talofibular
Anterior talofibular, posterior talofibular, and calcaneofibular
questions.question: The lateral ligaments of the ankle include which three named ligaments?

questions.explanation: Scapular protraction (abduction) is produced by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor muscles. During protraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves forward along with the scapula. This movement is used in punching, pushing, and reaching forward actions.
questions.question: Which muscles are responsible for scapular protraction?

questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy results from radial nerve compression in the axilla, causing paralysis of wrist and finger extensors. This produces the characteristic "wrist drop" deformity. The condition is named for arm compression against a chair back during intoxicated sleep.
questions.question: What muscle action is lost in Saturday night palsy?
Where does the portal vein form anatomically?
questions.explanation: The portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It is approximately 8 cm long and ascends behind the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It receives the left and right gastric veins, cystic vein, and paraumbilical veins during its course.

questions.question: The anterior cranial fossa contains which lobe of the brain?
questions.explanation: The anterior cranial fossa accommodates the frontal lobes of the brain. The floor is formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, cribriform plate of ethmoid, and lesser wings of sphenoid. The crista galli provides attachment for the falx cerebri. Fractures can cause CSF rhinorrhea through the cribriform plate.

A small area of the posterior surface of the stomach near the cardia (where the two layers of lesser omentum separate to enclose the stomach) is "bare" and in direct contact with the left crus of the diaphragm, lacking peritoneal covering. This represents the only part of the stomach not completely invested by peritoneum. The rest of the stomach is completely covered by visceral peritoneum: anteriorly and posteriorly by peritoneum continuous with the greater and lesser omenta, and along its curvatures where the gastrosplenic, gastrohepatic, and gastrocolic ligaments attach. The bare area can be a site where gastric perforation communicates directly with the retroperitoneum.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach is LEAST covered by peritoneum?

questions.explanation: Colles' fracture results from falling onto an outstretched hand, causing the distal radius fragment to displace posteriorly. The ulnar styloid process is frequently avulsed in the majority of these cases. This produces the characteristic "dinner fork deformity" when viewing the affected wrist from the side.
questions.question: What is the characteristic deformity produced by a Colles' fracture?

questions.explanation: The superior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the first thoracic vertebra (T1). Anteriorly, it is bounded by the superior border of the manubrium sterni. Laterally, the medial borders of the first ribs and their costal cartilages complete the boundaries of this important opening.
questions.question: Which structure bounds the superior thoracic aperture posteriorly?

questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve, after synapsing in the celiac ganglion, provides sympathetic innervation to foregut-derived organs including the stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, small intestine, and proximal colon (to the splenic flexure). It also carries visceral afferent fibers for pain sensation from these organs.
questions.question: Which organs receive greater splanchnic innervation?

questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) descends into the pelvis within the sigmoid mesocolon and crosses the left common iliac vessels (artery and vein) at approximately the S3 vertebral level before dividing into right and left branches that descend along the rectum. This anatomical relationship makes the superior rectal vessels vulnerable to injury during operations on the sigmoid colon or rectum. The artery eventually terminates by piercing the muscular wall of the rectum and anastomosing with the middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal) arteries.
questions.question: The superior rectal artery crosses which vessel at S3 level?
The angle of inclination (neck-shaft angle) of the femur is approximately how many degrees in adults?
questions.explanation: The angle of inclination of the femoral neck to the shaft is approximately 135 degrees in adults. A decrease below 120 degrees defines coxa vara, while an increase above 140 degrees defines coxa valga. This angle is greater in children and decreases with skeletal maturity. It is critical for hip biomechanics and prosthetic design in hip arthroplasty.

The scaphoid bone crosses two rows of carpal bones forming a hinge, making it vulnerable to heavy stress during falls on outstretched hands. The fracture commonly occurs through the middle of the bone or causes complete separation into two pieces. Risk of avascular necrosis exists due to single arterial blood supply entering at the distal end.
questions.question: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured due to falls on an outstretched hand?

questions.explanation: Pronator teres and biceps brachii are antagonistic for forearm rotation: pronator teres produces pronation while biceps produces supination. However, both can contribute to elbow flexion when pronation/supination resistance is present. This demonstrates how muscles can be synergistic for one motion while antagonistic for another.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and biceps?
options: They're antagonists: pronator teres pronates, biceps supinates

questions.question: Which nerve injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis?
questions.explanation: Phrenic nerve injury causes paralysis of the corresponding hemidiaphragm, which becomes elevated and moves paradoxically upward during inspiration. Causes include surgical trauma (especially cardiac surgery), tumors, neurological disease, and cervical spine injury. Bilateral phrenic nerve injury causes severe respiratory compromise. The phrenic nerve can be stimulated to pace the diaphragm in some patients.

The free right edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the portal triad: portal vein (posteriorly), common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), and hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left). This arrangement is remembered by the mnemonic "DAV" from anterior to posterior (Duct, Artery, Vein). The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen and can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding hepatic arterial and portal venous inflow.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum?
What nerve supplies subscapularis muscle?
questions.explanation: Subscapularis is supplied by the upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6) and lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6). Both nerves arise from the posterior cord. The lower subscapular nerve also supplies teres major muscle.

The superior intercostal artery (from costocervical trunk of subclavian artery) gives off the first and second posterior intercostal arteries. These are the only posterior intercostal arteries not arising from the thoracic aorta. This arrangement provides collateral circulation if the thoracic aorta is obstructed.
questions.question: What supplies the first two intercostal spaces?
The spermatic cord receives its external covering from which muscle?
questions.explanation: The external spermatic fascia, the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the external oblique muscle's aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. Moving inward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the innermost fascial layer is the internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring). The dartos muscle is in the scrotal wall, not directly covering the cord. These concentric layers are acquired sequentially as structures descend through abdominal wall layers.

questions.question: The inferior mesenteric artery typically arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery originates from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), approximately 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. This vessel supplies hindgut derivatives, including the left one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Its main branches include the left colic artery, sigmoid arteries (2-4 branches), and the superior rectal artery, which represents its terminal continuation descending into the pelvis.

questions.question: What causes olecranon bursitis in students?
questions.explanation: Olecranon bursitis in students results from repeated trauma and pressure to the posterior elbow from leaning on desks. The subcutaneous olecranon bursa becomes inflamed and swollen. The condition is called student's elbow or miner's elbow depending on the occupation causing the repetitive trauma.

The ankle joint (talocrural joint) primarily allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, with a small degree of rotation. Inversion and eversion occur primarily at the subtalar joint (talocalcaneal articulation) and midtarsal joints. The talocrural joint has a range of approximately 20 degrees dorsiflexion and 50 degrees plantarflexion in a healthy adult.
questions.question: The ankle joint allows primarily which movements?
The inguinal ligament extends between which two points?
questions.explanation: The inguinal ligament represents the rolled-under, thickened inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis, extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) laterally to the pubic tubercle medially. It serves as a retinaculum bridging the subinguinal space through which pass the iliopsoas muscle, femoral vessels and nerve, and lymphatics entering/leaving the thigh. The inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary (floor) of the inguinal canal and the base of Hesselbach's triangle. The lacunar ligament represents its medial extension, reflecting posteriorly to attach to the pectineal line.

questions.question: How many cusps form the pulmonary valve?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve has three semilunar (half-moon shaped) cusps: anterior, right, and left. Behind each cusp is a pulmonary sinus. The valve opens during right ventricular systole to allow blood into the pulmonary trunk and closes during diastole to prevent backflow. Unlike AV valves, semilunar valves have no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.

The portal tract (portal triad) is located at the corners of hepatic lobules and contains branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, surrounded by connective tissue. Some also include lymphatic vessels. The portal triad delivers blood and removes bile from the hepatic lobule. The hepatic artery provides oxygen; the portal vein provides nutrients and metabolites from the GI tract.
questions.question: Which hepatic structure contains the portal triad?

questions.explanation: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale, which allowed blood to bypass the fetal lungs by shunting from the right to left atrium in utero. Functional closure occurs at birth with the first breath, though anatomical fusion may take months to years. A patent foramen ovale persists in about 25% of adults without usually causing problems.
questions.question: What is the fossa ovalis a remnant of?

questions.explanation: In adults, the Eustachian tube lies at 45� to the horizontal plane, whereas in infants it is only 10�. This more vertical orientation in children predisposes them to middle ear infections. The tube is approximately 31-38 mm long with the posterior third being osseous.
questions.question: The Eustachian tube in adults lies at what angle to the horizontal plane?

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor innervation to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).
questions.question: Which nerve provides general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue?

questions.explanation: Gastric ulcers most commonly occur along the lesser curvature, particularly at the incisura angularis and junction of body and antrum. This distribution reflects the exposure to gastric acid and the vulnerability of this area to ischemia. Duodenal ulcers are more common overall than gastric ulcers, but gastric ulcers have higher malignancy potential.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach is most common site for gastric ulcers?
Which bone accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm in length?
questions.explanation: The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, averaging 45 cm in length. It accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height. The femur articulates with the acetabulum superiorly and the patella and tibia inferiorly.

questions.question: The jugular foramen transmits which three cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and accessory (XI) nerves along with the internal jugular vein. The foramen is divided by a fibrous or bony septum into anteromedial (pars nervosa) and posterolateral (pars vascularis) compartments. Glomus jugulare tumors arise in this region.

questions.question: How long is the ureter in adults?
questions.explanation: Each ureter is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. The ureter descends on the psoas major muscle, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enters the bladder at the lateral angles of the trigone. It is a muscular tube that propels urine by peristaltic contractions.

questions.question: Which ligament arches over the psoas major muscle?
questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch in the diaphragm that arches over the psoas major muscle, extending from the body of L1 or L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process. The sympathetic trunk passes deep to (posterior to) this ligament as it enters the abdomen. The ligament forms part of the lumbar attachment of the diaphragm.

Lund's node (Calot's node) is located within Calot's triangle, bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver. This lymph node frequently becomes enlarged in cases of cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed during cholecystectomy. Calot's triangle is an important surgical landmark for identifying the cystic artery, which typically lies within this triangle. Careful dissection of this area is crucial during laparoscopic cholecystectomy to avoid injury to the hepatic ducts or right hepatic artery.
questions.question: Which lymph node is characteristically found in Calot's triangle?
Which hamstring muscle originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia?
questions.explanation: Semimembranosus originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. Its reflected attachment forms the oblique popliteal ligament. Semimembranosus is named for its membranous (flat, broad) proximal tendon, in contrast to semitendinosus which has a long round distal tendon.

questions.question: What is the characteristic deformity in Erb's paralysis?
questions.explanation: Erb's paralysis produces the "policeman's tip hand" or "porter's tip hand" deformity. The arm hangs by the side adducted and medially rotated, the forearm is extended and pronated. This results from paralysis of muscles supplied by C5-C6 nerve roots (deltoid, biceps, brachialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus).

options: Deep fibular nerve; first web space sensation and dorsiflexion
Superficial fibular nerve; dorsal foot sensation and eversion strength
questions.question: The peroneal (fibular) compartment syndrome is a less common variant of leg compartment syndrome. Which specific nerve function is tested to confirm lateral compartment integrity?
questions.explanation: Lateral compartment (fibular compartment) syndrome is confirmed by testing the superficial fibular nerve: eversion strength of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis) and sensation on the dorsum of the foot (superficial fibular nerve cutaneous distribution). In the anterior compartment, the deep fibular nerve is tested (first web space sensation and dorsiflexion). These clinical tests guide emergency fasciotomy decision-making.

The superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve, the sensory continuation of the axillary nerve, provides sensation to the skin over the deltoid muscle ("regimental badge" area). Loss of sensation in this area indicates axillary nerve injury. Testing sensation here helps diagnose nerve damage in shoulder trauma.
questions.question: What nerve provides sensation to the regimental badge area?
What determines the safe position for hand immobilization?
options: Position maintaining ligament length and preventing contracture
questions.explanation: The "safe position" (MCP joints flexed 70-90�, IP joints extended, wrist slightly extended) maintains collateral ligaments at maximum length and prevents contracture. This position is also called the "intrinsic plus" position. Prolonged immobilization in other positions can result in permanent stiffness.

questions.question: Which ligament crosses anterior to the aorta?
questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament is formed by the union of the medial borders of the two crura and crosses over the anterior surface of the aorta. This ligament forms the posterior boundary of the aortic opening. Occasionally, it can compress the celiac artery, causing the median arcuate ligament syndrome.

questions.question: What nerve root value is the musculocutaneous nerve?
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve has nerve root values C5, C6, and C7. It arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. The nerve supplies three muscles (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) before continuing as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

The palmaris longus tendon (when present) passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum and inserts into it along with the palmar aponeurosis. The ulnar nerve and artery also pass superficial to the retinaculum through Guyon's canal. All flexor tendons and the median nerve pass deep to the retinaculum through the carpal tunnel.
questions.question: What structure passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum?

questions.explanation: Multiple factors maintain gastroesophageal junction competence preventing reflux: intrinsic LES tone, extrinsic compression by right crus sling fibers, acute angle of gastric entry (angle of His), positive intraabdominal pressure on the abdominal esophageal segment, and mucosal rosette at the cardia. Disruption causes GERD.
questions.question: What maintains gastroesophageal junction competence?
Which area of the liver is devoid of peritoneal covering?
questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver is located on the diaphragmatic surface where the liver is in direct contact with the diaphragm without intervening peritoneum. This area is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament. The bare area is clinically significant as infections can spread directly between the liver and thorax.

Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the chorda tympani (from facial nerve) synapse in the submandibular ganglion suspended from the lingual nerve. Postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion also reach the gland via the facial artery plexus.
questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the submandibular gland?
What structure forms the lingula?
questions.explanation: The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe located below the cardiac notch. It is analogous to the middle lobe of the right lung. The lingula consists of superior and inferior lingular segments, which are distinct bronchopulmonary segments.

The detrusor muscle is composed of smooth muscle arranged in three poorly defined layers (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal). It is under involuntary control via autonomic innervation. Parasympathetic stimulation (via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction for micturition; sympathetic stimulation (via hypogastric nerves) causes relaxation for urine storage.
questions.question: What type of muscle forms the detrusor muscle?

questions.explanation: Three fascial septa pass from the inner aspect of the fascia lata to the linea aspera of the femur, dividing the thigh into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments. Each compartment has distinct nerves, muscles, and vessels. Understanding compartment anatomy is critical in managing thigh compartment syndrome following trauma.
questions.question: The three fascial compartments of the thigh are separated by septa passing from the fascia lata to which bony structure?

questions.explanation: The posterior mediastinum is bounded anteriorly by the pericardium (which forms the heart in the middle mediastinum). Posteriorly, it is bounded by the thoracic vertebrae from T5 to T12. The posterior mediastinum contains the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, and sympathetic trunks.
questions.question: What forms the anterior boundary of posterior mediastinum?

questions.explanation: The female external urethral orifice opens into the vestibule, the space between the labia minora, approximately 2.5 cm posterior to the clitoris and immediately anterior to the vaginal opening. The orifice is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter and may be difficult to visualize in some women. Paraurethral (Skene's) glands open on either side of the orifice.
questions.question: Where does the female urethra open externally?
What nerve innervates the wrist joint?
questions.explanation: The wrist joint is innervated by branches from three nerves following Hilton's law: median nerve (anterior interosseous branch), radial nerve (posterior interosseous branch), and ulnar nerve (deep and dorsal branches). This follows the principle that nerves supplying muscles moving a joint also supply the joint.
options: Anterior and posterior interosseous nerves only

questions.question: What artery typically accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the supraspinous fossa?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular artery accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the suprascapular notch into the supraspinous fossa. Unlike the nerve which passes under the superior transverse scapular ligament, the artery passes over it. Both structures then pass through the spinoglenoid notch to reach the infraspinous fossa.

questions.question: Which vessel passes through the transverse mesocolon?
questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) passes superiorly into the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon, dividing into right and left branches. The middle colic veins (draining to the superior mesenteric vein) also pass through the mesocolon. The root of the transverse mesocolon is attached to the inferior border of the pancreas and anterior surface of the second part of the duodenum, crossing from right to left. The superior mesenteric vessels themselves lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, not within it.

On the left side, the pleural reflection passes inferomedially to the level of the fourth costal cartilage, where it deviates to the left margin of the sternum. This creates a shallow notch corresponding to the cardiac notch of the left lung. This differs from the right side where the pleura descends vertically in the median plane.
questions.question: At which costal cartilage does left pleural reflection deviate?

questions.explanation: Maximum grip strength occurs with the wrist in 20-30� extension. This position optimally lengthens finger flexors for maximum tension development while stabilizing the wrist. Full flexion or extension reduces grip strength due to passive insufficiency or active insufficiency of finger flexors.
options: Wrist position does not affect grip strength
Strongest grip in full wrist flexion
Grip strongest with wrist in slight extension
Strongest grip in full wrist extension
Strongest grip in neutral wrist position
questions.question: How does wrist position affect grip strength?
Which structure forms the floor of the tonsillar fossa?
questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle forms the floor (bed) of the tonsillar fossa, separated from the tonsil by the tonsillar capsule. The palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus form the anterior and posterior pillars respectively. Loose areolar tissue separates the capsule from the superior constrictor, facilitating surgical dissection.

questions.question: The quadriceps tendon continues as which structure, with the patella embedded within it, attaching to the tibial tuberosity?
questions.explanation: The tendons of the four quadriceps components unite to form the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament (also called patellar tendon) with the patella embedded within as a sesamoid bone. This inserts into the tibial tuberosity. The patellar retinacula are aponeurotic expansions that provide additional lateral stability.

questions.question: The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones. Which bones constitute the midfoot?
options: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and one cuneiform
All three cuneiforms and the first two metatarsals
Three cuneiforms, cuboid, and the talus
questions.explanation: The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones: navicular, cuboid, and three cuneiform bones. The midfoot meets the forefoot at the five tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints. The three cuneiforms articulate proximally with the navicular. The midfoot provides a stable platform and distributes forces between the hindfoot and forefoot during gait.

questions.question: The arytenoid cartilages articulate with which laryngeal structure?
questions.explanation: The arytenoid cartilages sit on the upper border of the cricoid cartilage lamina at the cricoarytenoid joints. These synovial joints allow rotation and gliding movements that abduct and adduct the vocal cords. The arytenoids are pyramidal with a vocal process (anteriorly) and muscular process (laterally).

questions.question: How do the medial and lateral intermuscular septa organize the arm?
questions.explanation: The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach from the deep brachial fascia to the humerus, dividing the arm into anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) compartments. Each compartment contains muscles with similar functions and common innervation. This organization is essential for understanding compartment syndromes.

questions.question: What is the narrowest point of esophagus?
questions.explanation: The narrowest point of the esophagus is at its origin at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. This is the most common site for foreign body impaction and the site requiring most care during esophagoscopy to avoid perforation.

questions.question: Which opening connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear?
questions.explanation: The Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube opens into the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, connecting it with the middle ear cavity. The tubal elevation and tubal tonsil surround the opening. Tensor veli palatini and salpingopharyngeus muscles open the tube during swallowing to equalize middle ear pressure.

The masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid muscles elevate the mandible during mastication. The masseter originates from the zygomatic arch and inserts on the lateral surface of the mandibular angle and ramus. It is innervated by the masseteric nerve from V3. Bilateral contraction closes the mouth and clenches the teeth.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the mandible during mastication?

questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch (between bladder and rectum in males) is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when standing or sitting and is a common site for fluid collection, abscesses, or metastatic deposits. In females, the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is even deeper and is the most dependent peritoneal space, which can be accessed via the posterior vaginal fornix.
questions.question: Which pouch in males is the most dependent peritoneal space?
Which artery supplies the upper third of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the upper two-thirds of the anal canal above the pectinate line. The middle rectal arteries (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal arteries (from internal pudendal) supply the lower third. This mixed blood supply creates a watershed area prone to ischemia.

The gastrosplenic ligament, a peritoneal fold connecting the greater curvature of the stomach (fundus region) to the hilum of the spleen, contains the short gastric arteries and veins (vasa brevia). These 4-6 small vessels branch from the splenic artery and vein near the splenic hilum to supply the gastric fundus. The left gastroepiploic vessels run in the greater omentum along the greater curvature, while the splenic vessels themselves course through the splenorenal ligament connecting the spleen to the left kidney, along with the tail of the pancreas.
questions.question: The gastrosplenic ligament contains which vessels?

questions.explanation: The posterior meniscofemoral ligament is a strong tendinous slip joining the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle. The coronary ligaments attach both menisci to the tibial condyles. The transverse ligament joins the anterior edges of both menisci, allowing them to move together during knee movements.
questions.question: Which structure joins the posterior part of the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle?
Where does the posterior vagal trunk primarily distribute after entering the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The posterior vagal trunk, formed mainly from the right vagus nerve, sends a large branch to the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses. This distribution extends vagal innervation to the intestines as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas. The remaining branches supply the posterior surface of the stomach.

The ileum receives its blood supply from multiple ileal arteries (12-15 branches) arising from the left side of the superior mesenteric artery. These arteries run between the layers of the mesentery, forming 4-5 arcades (more numerous than in the jejunum) before giving rise to short, widely spaced vasa recta that supply the intestinal wall. The terminal ileum also receives branches from the ileocolic artery (ileal branch). The extensive arterial arcades create broad, low windows in the mesentery (versus the narrow, tall windows in the jejunal mesentery).
questions.question: Which artery supplies the ileum?

questions.explanation: The ovarian artery (arising from the aorta at L2) descends obliquely across the psoas major muscle, crosses anterior to the ureter and the common iliac vessels (or external iliac vessels), then enters the suspensory ligament of the ovary to reach the ovary in the pelvis. This long course reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall. The artery anastomoses with the uterine artery in the broad ligament. In males, the testicular artery follows a similar course but continues through the inguinal canal. The ovarian artery's relationship to the ureter is surgically important.
questions.question: The ovarian artery crosses which structure anteriorly?
Which muscles aid forced expiration?
questions.explanation: In forced expiration, the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, internal/external obliques, transversus abdominis) contract forcibly. This pushes the abdominal viscera upward against the relaxed diaphragm, forcing it higher into the thorax. Quadratus lumborum also contracts to pull down the 12th rib.

The cricoarytenoid joint permits rotation and sliding movements of the arytenoid cartilages, which directly control vocal cord abduction and adduction. Tension changes occur primarily through cricothyroid joint movement, not cricoarytenoid articulation. The L-shaped base of the arytenoid pivots at the cricoarytenoid joint to open or close the rima glottidis.
questions.question: The cricoarytenoid joint allows which specific movement of the vocal cords?

questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is shallow during inspiration when the lung expands into it, and becomes deeper during expiration when the lung retracts. This recess is clinically important as it is the site where pleural fluid accumulates in effusions and is the target for thoracentesis.
questions.question: Which recess is deeper during expiration?

questions.explanation: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins), while the right suprarenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors that of the testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands have a rich arterial supply from three sources (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery, abdominal aorta, and renal artery respectively) but typically have only a single venous drainage pathway, creating a high arterial-to-venous ratio favoring hormone secretion.
questions.question: Which vein drains the left suprarenal gland?
Which space contains the olfactory bulbs?
questions.explanation: The olfactory bulbs lie on the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the anterior cranial fossa. Olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium pass through the cribriform foramina to synapse in the bulbs. The olfactory tracts extend posteriorly from the bulbs. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.

The aryepiglotticus muscle, running in the aryepiglottic fold, pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis, closing the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It acts like a purse-string sphincter. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function.
questions.question: Which muscle pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis?
What maintains negative intrapleural pressure?
questions.explanation: The elastic recoil of the lungs pulling inward, opposed by the chest wall's tendency to spring outward, creates and maintains the negative (sub-atmospheric) pressure in the pleural cavity. This negative pressure is essential for keeping the lungs expanded and prevents their collapse.

questions.question: The vermiform appendix typically arises from which part of the cecum?
questions.explanation: The vermiform appendix arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. The three taeniae coli of the cecum converge at the base of the appendix, serving as a reliable landmark for locating it during surgery. While the base of the appendix has a relatively constant position, its tip can be found in various locations: retrocecal (65%), pelvic (31%), subcecal (2.3%), preileal (1%), or postileal (0.4%). The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, runs through the mesoappendix to supply the appendix.

questions.question: The adductor canal (subsartorial or Hunter's canal) transmits structures from the femoral triangle to the popliteal fossa. Which nerve within it supplies the knee joint and descends within it?
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve, the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, descends within the adductor canal and then exits with the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery to supply the medial side of the leg and foot. The adductor canal also transmits the femoral artery and vein. The saphenous nerve also supplies the knee joint via its branch to the articular capsule.

The left ventricular wall is 8-12 mm thick, approximately three times thicker than the right ventricle (3-5 mm), reflecting the higher pressure it must generate to pump blood through the systemic circulation. The left ventricle forms the apex and most of the left border and diaphragmatic surface of the heart. It contains two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior).
questions.question: Which chamber has the thickest myocardial wall?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve exits the pelvis by passing through the obturator foramen, along with the obturator vessels. It then divides into anterior and posterior divisions in the obturator canal. The anterior division runs anterior to obturator externus and adductor brevis, while the posterior division runs posterior to adductor brevis. It supplies the medial compartment of the thigh.
questions.question: The obturator nerve supplies the medial compartment of the thigh. It exits the pelvis through which specific structure?

questions.explanation: Mammary glands are modifications of sweat glands and are therefore ectodermal in origin. They develop from the mammary ridge (milk line) which extends from axilla to groin in the embryo. In humans, most of this ridge disappears except in the pectoral region where breasts develop.
questions.question: What embryonic structure forms mammary glands?
The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from the S2, S3, and S4 spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers synapse in ganglia within the bladder wall and stimulate contraction of the detrusor muscle (for micturition) while relaxing the internal urethral sphincter. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via lumbar splanchnic nerves and superior hypogastric plexus) has the opposite effect, promoting urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter. Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter comes from the pudendal nerve (S2-S4), allowing voluntary control.

Pain from irritation of the central diaphragm (supplied by phrenic nerve C3-5) refers to the shoulder because the supraclavicular nerves (C3-4) supply the skin over the shoulder. This is an example of referred pain where stimuli from different areas share the same spinal cord segments.
questions.question: Why does diaphragmatic pain refer to shoulder?

questions.explanation: In life, the foramen lacerum is closed by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal arterial branches and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect.
