questions.question: The left gastric vein drains into which vessel?

questions.explanation: The internal thoracic artery (a branch of subclavian artery) provides approximately 60% of total breast blood flow, mainly to the medial portion through anterior and posterior perforating branches. The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th perforating branches are particularly large and significant in breast blood supply.
questions.question: Which artery provides 60% of breast blood flow?

questions.explanation: The valleculae (spaces between the tongue base and epiglottis) receive sensory innervation from the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus). The glossopharyngeal nerve also contributes sensation to this region. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in the valleculae. These spaces are bounded by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds.
questions.question: The vallecular receives sensory innervation from which nerve?

questions.explanation: The common iliac arteries, terminal branches of the abdominal aorta, bifurcate into external and internal iliac arteries at approximately the L5/S1 level (lumbosacral junction), anterior to the sacroiliac joint at the pelvic brim. This bifurcation point corresponds to a point just medial to the midinguinal point on the anterior abdominal wall. The ureter crosses anterior to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the external iliac artery just distal to it), a relationship that is surgically significant. The right common iliac artery is crossed anteriorly by the superior rectal vessels, while the left is related to the sigmoid mesocolon.
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery?

questions.explanation: Duplicated (duplex) collecting system is the most common congenital renal anomaly, occurring in 0.5-1% of the population. It can be complete (two separate ureters) or incomplete (ureters join before entering bladder). The upper pole moiety ureter inserts more medially and inferiorly in the bladder (Weigert-Meyer rule) and is prone to obstruction, while the lower pole ureter is prone to reflux.
questions.question: What is the most common congenital renal anomaly?

options: Quadriceps (rectus femoris) muscle tear or contusion
Adductor muscle strain of the thigh
Piriformis syndrome from external hip rotation
questions.explanation: Myositis ossificans traumatica can complicate contusions or tears of the quadriceps muscle in the anterior thigh, particularly direct blows (common in contact sports). Heterotopic bone forms within the healing hematoma over 4-8 weeks. Premature massage or passive stretching accelerates its formation. It can cause restriction of knee flexion. Most cases resolve with time and physiotherapy.
questions.question: Myositis ossificans is pathological bone formation within muscle that may complicate which injury about the anterior thigh?

options: Common fibular nerve; great saphenous vein
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve (L3, L4). It runs with the great saphenous vein along the medial leg, from the knee to the medial malleolus and then to the medial side of the foot. It provides cutaneous sensation to the medial leg, ankle, and foot. It is at risk during stripping of the great saphenous vein for varicose vein surgery or coronary bypass grafting.
questions.question: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of which nerve and runs with which vein throughout most of the leg?

questions.explanation: The levator costarum muscles are twelve small muscles connecting the transverse processes of C7 and T1-T11 vertebrae to the ribs below. They elevate the ribs and are innervated by lateral branches of the dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves. They assist in respiration and lateral flexion.
questions.question: Which muscle connects ribs to vertebrae posteriorly?
Where is the ideal location for pericardiocentesis?
questions.explanation: Pericardiocentesis is typically performed by inserting a needle just to the left of the xiphoid process, angled upward and posteriorly toward the left shoulder at about 30-45 degrees. This avoids the internal thoracic vessels and enters the pericardial cavity inferior to the heart. The procedure is performed under ECG and/or ultrasound guidance.

questions.question: Houston's third valve in the rectum is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: Houston's third transverse rectal fold is the most constant and prominent, located at the level of S5 vertebra, approximately 5 cm above the anus. If this fold completely encircles the rectum, it is called Nelaton's sphincter. This fold divides the rectum into an upper chamber (containing the pre-allantoic part of the hindgut that can hold feces without triggering the defecation reflex) and a lower chamber (derived from the post-allantoic cloaca that is sensitive to distension). The fold helps support the weight of feces and prevents passage during instrumentation.

Most long bones have only one epiphyseal plate at one end; however, five bones are unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius. This feature is important in understanding growth patterns and fracture management in these bones.
questions.question: Five bones uniquely possess epiphyseal plates at BOTH ends. Which set correctly identifies all five?

questions.explanation: The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac trunk and has a characteristic tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas. It runs from right to left within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-7 branches at the splenic hilum. The artery gives off numerous pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, and the left gastroepiploic artery.
questions.question: Which is the largest branch of the celiac trunk?
The greater omentum is attached to which part of the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The greater omentum (specifically its posterior two layers after folding back from the inferior descent) attaches to the anterior surface (and superior border) of the transverse colon and its mesocolon. The omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach, descends anterior to the small intestine, then folds back on itself and fuses with the transverse colon and mesocolon before continuing to the posterior abdominal wall. This four-layered structure contains fat and can wall off inflamed organs (giving it the name "abdominal policeman"), provides insulation, and allows mobility of abdominal contents.

questions.question: Which forearm muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve?
questions.explanation: is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Anterior interosseous syndrome results in inability to flex the thumb interphalangeal joint and index finger distal interphalangeal joint.

questions.question: Where is the SA node located anatomically?
questions.explanation: The SA node is located in the upper part of the crista terminalis in the right atrium, near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It consists of specialized pacemaker cells that spontaneously depolarize, initiating the cardiac impulse at a rate of 60-100 bpm. It is the primary pacemaker, overriding other potential pacemaker sites due to its faster rate.

The aortic arch crosses anteriorly to the oesophagus creating a constriction at approximately 22.5 cm from the upper incisors. This is the second of four normal oesophageal constrictions and represents an important anatomical relationship. The arch of the aorta indents the anterior and left lateral aspects of the oesophagus at this level.
questions.question: At what distance from the upper incisors does the aortic arch constrict the oesophagus?

questions.explanation: Maisonneuve fracture involves a high (proximal) fibular fracture combined with disruption of the tibiofibular syndesmosis (inferior tibiofibular ligament complex) and interosseous membrane. This creates a unstable ankle mortise (syndesmotic diastasis) despite the intact lateral ankle. It is caused by an external rotation force. The high fibular fracture may be missed if only the ankle is radiographed.
questions.question: Proximal fibular fractures (Maisonneuve fracture) associated with ankle injuries disrupt which ligament, creating ankle instability?
The maxillary artery is divided into how many parts by the lateral pterygoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle divides the maxillary artery into three parts: mandibular (first), pterygoid (second), and pterygopalatine (third). Each part gives off specific branches to supply deep facial structures. The third part enters the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure.

questions.question: Which nerve is compressed in radial tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Radial tunnel syndrome involves compression of the posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) in the proximal forearm. Compression typically occurs at the arcade of Frohse (fibrous arch at the proximal edge of supinator). Unlike radial nerve palsy, wrist extension is preserved as the extensor carpi radialis muscles are supplied proximal to the compression.

questions.question: What happens with complete phrenic nerve section?
questions.explanation: Complete section of a phrenic nerve results in complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the corresponding half of the diaphragm. The paralyzed hemidiaphragm shows paradoxical movement: moving upward during inspiration and downward during expiration. Unilateral paralysis is often asymptomatic; bilateral causes severe respiratory compromise.

The thoracic duct begins as the cisterna chyli anterior to L1 vertebra, formed by lumbar and intestinal trunks. It ascends through the aortic hiatus into the thorax. At the root of the neck, it arches forward to enter the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).
questions.question: The thoracic duct begins at which vertebral level?
Which bone contains the foramen spinosum?
questions.explanation: The foramen spinosum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, posterolateral to the foramen ovale. It transmits the middle meningeal artery and meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve. The foramen is located at the spine of the sphenoid. Accessory meningeal arteries may also pass through this foramen.

options: Biceps, coracobrachialis, and forearm median muscles
questions.question: Which muscles are paralyzed in injury to the lateral cord of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: Lateral cord injury paralyzes muscles supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve (biceps, coracobrachialis, brachialis) and muscles supplied by the median nerve except those in the hand. This results from damage to both the musculocutaneous nerve and lateral root of median nerve. Wrist and finger flexion is lost along with forearm flexion.

questions.question: What muscle action is tested by resisted elbow extension?
questions.explanation: Resisted elbow extension primarily tests triceps brachii strength, particularly the medial head which is most active in this action. Anconeus provides minor assistance. Weakness suggests radial nerve injury or C7 nerve root pathology.

questions.question: The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplying both the hip and knee joints explains which clinical observation?
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, explaining the well-known clinical phenomenon of referred pain to the knee in hip joint disease. Children with Perthes disease or slipped femoral epiphysis classically present with knee pain. This is a critical clinical pearl applying Hilton's law practically.
options: Quadriceps weakness in obturator nerve injury
Referred pain to the knee in hip joint disease
Loss of adduction in knee joint pathology
Hip pain referred to the lumbar spine
Groin pain referred to the ankle

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all the interossei (palmar and dorsal) and the medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers). It also supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, and the medial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve.
options: All interossei and medial two lumbricals
questions.question: Which intrinsic hand muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve?
Which breast quadrant has highest cancer frequency?
questions.explanation: About 60% of breast carcinomas occur in the upper lateral quadrant. This quadrant contains the most breast tissue including the axillary tail. The upper outer quadrant should receive particular attention during breast examination. Lymphatic drainage from this area goes primarily to the pectoral axillary nodes.

questions.question: Which bursa is the largest in the body and lies between supraspinatus and the coraco-acromial arch?
questions.explanation: The subacromial bursa is the largest bursa in the body, positioned between the supraspinatus tendon and the coraco-acromial arch. It protects the supraspinatus tendon against friction with the acromion during arm abduction. Inflammation of this bursa is responsible for several shoulder pathologies including rotator cuff tendonitis.

Each lung has three borders: anterior, posterior, and inferior. The anterior border is where the costal and mediastinal surfaces meet. The posterior border is thick and extends from C7 to T10. The inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
questions.question: How many borders does each lung possess?

questions.explanation: The scaphoid bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox and is palpable in this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture. The radial artery pulse can also be felt crossing the snuffbox floor.
questions.question: Which structure is palpable in the anatomical snuffbox?

questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia is derived from the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring. The cremasteric muscle and fascia are derived from the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. The external spermatic fascia is derived from the external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial inguinal ring. These layers represent the layers of the abdominal wall through which the testis descended.
questions.question: Which layer of the spermatic cord is derived from transversalis fascia?
Where do posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie?
questions.explanation: Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie in the posterior mediastinum alongside the esophagus and descending thoracic aorta. They receive lymph from the esophagus, posterior diaphragm, pericardium, and posterior intercostal spaces. Efferents drain primarily to the thoracic duct.

The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel (formed by the flexor retinaculum and medial ankle bones), accompanying the tibial nerve. It then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries, supplying the plantar foot and contributing to the toes via the deep plantar arch. Its pulse is palpated inferoposterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.question: The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through which structure, then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries?

questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal nerve (from the vagus) divides into internal and external branches. The internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to provide sensation above the vocal cords. The external branch descends to innervate the cricothyroid muscle. Damage to the external branch affects voice pitch control.
questions.question: The superior laryngeal nerve divides into which two branches?
What nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve (C5, C6) supplies both supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. The nerve passes through the suprascapular notch (under the superior transverse scapular ligament) to reach the supraspinous fossa, then through the spinoglenoid notch to the infraspinous fossa.

questions.question: The transverse cervical nerve provides sensation to which area?
questions.explanation: The transverse cervical nerve (C2-C3) emerges from the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and provides sensation to the anterior and lateral neck. It is a branch of the cervical plexus. The nerve crosses the sternocleidomastoid horizontally. Cervical plexus block affects this nerve causing anterior neck anesthesia.

Anconeus is a small muscle that assists triceps brachii in elbow extension. It is located on the posterior aspect of the elbow, blending with the lateral head of triceps. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve.
questions.question: What is the function of anconeus muscle?
What is Pancoast tumor?
questions.explanation: Pancoast tumor (superior sulcus tumor) is a lung cancer arising in the apex of the lung. Due to its location, it can invade the brachial plexus (causing arm pain and weakness), sympathetic chain (causing Horner's syndrome), and ribs (causing pain). Patients present with shoulder/arm pain rather than typical lung symptoms.

questions.question: The subcostal plane passes through which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The subcostal plane is a horizontal transverse plane passing through the inferior margins of the 10th costal cartilages (lowest point of the costal margin) on each side, corresponding to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Together with the transtubercular plane (L5 level) and the two vertical midclavicular planes, it defines the nine regions of the abdomen. The subcostal plane marks important anatomical landmarks including the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery, the level of the pylorus in some individuals, and the approximate position of the inferior border of the liver.

questions.question: How many vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: Six vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen: superior gluteal artery and vein, inferior gluteal artery and vein, and internal pudendal artery and vein. Together with seven nerves and the piriformis muscle, they constitute the 14 structures passing through this critical anatomical gateway from the pelvis to the gluteal region.

options: Injury causes motor deficit without sensory loss
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor (no cutaneous branches) means injury produces pure motor deficit (weak thumb IP flexion, index finger DIP flexion, pronation) without sensory symptoms. This can lead to delayed diagnosis as patients lack the paresthesia typical of other nerve compression syndromes.
questions.question: What is the significance of the anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor?

options: Variant plexus patterns affect nerve root contributions
Variations do not affect nerve function
questions.question: What is the clinical significance of understanding brachial plexus variations?
questions.explanation: Prefixed brachial plexus (greater C4 contribution, less T1) and postfixed plexus (greater T2 contribution, less C5) affect nerve root distribution to terminal branches. This influences clinical presentation of nerve root injuries and may affect thoracic outlet syndrome presentation. Understanding variations aids diagnosis.

questions.question: What fluid occupies the pericardial cavity?
questions.explanation: The pericardial cavity contains 15-50 ml of serous pericardial fluid, an ultrafiltrate of plasma produced by the serous pericardium. This thin film of fluid acts as a lubricant, allowing the heart to beat with minimal friction between the visceral and parietal layers of serous pericardium. Excess fluid accumulation causes pericardial effusion and potential cardiac tamponade.

Downward rotation of the scapula is performed by levator scapulae, pectoralis minor, and the rhomboids. This movement is opposite to the upward rotation needed for full arm abduction. Downward rotation returns the scapula to its resting position from the upward rotated position.
questions.question: Which muscles perform downward rotation of the scapula?

questions.explanation: Mallet finger deformity results from extensor tendon avulsion from the distal phalanx (terminal extensor tendon rupture). This causes inability to actively extend the distal interphalangeal joint, which droops in flexion. The injury commonly occurs from forced flexion of an extended fingertip.
options: Extensor tendon avulsion at distal phalanx
questions.question: What causes mallet finger deformity?

questions.explanation: The breast is separated from the deep fascia covering the underlying muscles by a layer of loose areolar tissue called the retromammary space. This space allows the breast some mobility over the pectoralis major muscle. The space is important surgically as it provides a plane for mastectomy.
questions.question: What separates the breast from deep fascia?
Which vessels form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck as they pass behind it. The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body. Anteriorly, the neck is related to the pylorus of the stomach.

dislocations represent the most prevalent direction of glenohumeral joint dislocation. They typically result from excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus. The humeral head is forced anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest part of the joint capsule, which lacks reinforcement from rotator cuff muscles.
questions.question: What is the most common direction of glenohumeral joint dislocation?

questions.explanation: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve to the otic ganglion. These fibers originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus. After synapsing in the otic ganglion, postganglionic fibers travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to provide secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland.
questions.question: The lesser petrosal nerve carries which type of fibers?

questions.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch, formed by the coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament, prevents superior displacement of the humeral head. This structure overlies the shoulder joint superiorly. The joint capsule is weak superiorly, making the arch essential for preventing upward dislocation.
questions.question: What prevents superior displacement of the humeral head at the shoulder?
Which structure lies within Calot's triangle?
questions.explanation: Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) is bounded by the cystic duct inferiorly, common hepatic duct medially, and inferior surface of the liver (or right lobe) superiorly. Within this triangle lies the cystic artery (typically arising from the right hepatic artery) and Lund's lymph node (Calot's node), which may be enlarged in cholecystitis or cholangitis. The triangle serves as a crucial surgical landmark during laparoscopic cholecystectomy for identifying and safely isolating the cystic duct and artery (the "critical view of safety") before ligation and division. Anatomical variations in this region are common and must be carefully identified.

The descending colon is derived from the embryological hindgut, along with the distal third of the transverse colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Hindgut structures are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery and receive parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves. The midgut-hindgut junction occurs at approximately the left third of the transverse colon.
questions.question: Which embryological origin corresponds to the descending colon?

questions.explanation: Extrinsic hand muscles (arising in forearm) provide power for grip and basic finger movements. Intrinsic hand muscles (arising in hand) provide precision movements, finger positioning, and the unique lumbrical action (MCP flexion with IP extension). This combination enables both powerful and precise hand function.
questions.question: How do intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles work together?
options: Extrinsic for power grip, intrinsic for precision

questions.explanation: In only 1% of adults, a nasal emissary vein passes through the foramen cecum connecting nasal veins with the superior sagittal sinus. In most adults, the foramen is obliterated. In the fetus, this foramen transmitted the anterior extension of the developing superior sagittal sinus.
questions.question: What structure passes through the foramen cecum in adults?
The sphenoid sinus relates posteriorly to which structure?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinus lies within the body of the sphenoid with the clivus and pons posterior to it. The pituitary fossa is superior, and the cavernous sinuses with internal carotid arteries are lateral. The optic chiasm lies superiorly. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses the fossa through the sphenoid sinus.

questions.question: Genu valgum (knock-knees) and genu varum (bow-legs) are deformities of which joint?
questions.explanation: Genu valgum (knock-knees) and genu varum (bow-legs) are angular deformities of the knee joint. In genu valgum, the knees touch while the ankles are separated; in genu varum, the ankles touch while the knees are separated. Both can be physiological in early childhood but persistent deformity after age 7 years requires investigation and possible surgical correction.

questions.question: Why are esophageal constrictions clinically important?
questions.explanation: The four esophageal constrictions are clinically important because they are: (1) sites where swallowed foreign bodies or large food boluses lodge, (2) sites where strictures tend to form, (3) sites where esophageal cancer commonly develops, and (4) areas of resistance during esophagoscopy. The narrowest point is at the cricopharyngeus.

options: When the knee is fully extended
questions.explanation: Gastrocnemius is unique in that it plantarflexes the ankle only effectively when the knee is extended, because it crosses the knee joint. When the knee is flexed, gastrocnemius becomes relatively ineffective, and soleus becomes the primary plantarflexor. Gastrocnemius also flexes the leg at the knee and is innervated by the tibial nerve (S1, S2).
questions.question: Gastrocnemius can only plantarflex the ankle effectively under which condition?

questions.explanation: The upper medial quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3. The upper lateral quadrant receives L1 and T12. The lower medial quadrant receives S1, 2, 3, and the lower lateral quadrant receives L2, L3. This dermatomal pattern helps localize spinal pathology.
questions.question: The cutaneous innervation of the upper medial quadrant of the buttock is derived from which spinal segments?
options: L1 and T12 vertebral levels only

questions.explanation: The crista terminalis is a prominent vertical muscular ridge on the internal right atrial wall that marks the junction between the smooth-walled posterior sinus venarum (derived from the sinus venosus) and the rough-walled anterior part with pectinate muscles (derived from the primitive atrium). Externally, this corresponds to the sulcus terminalis groove.
questions.question: Which structure marks the junction between the smooth and rough parts of the right atrium?
How many leaves does the central tendon of the diaphragm have?
questions.explanation: The central tendon is trifoliate (three-leafed), resembling a clover leaf with right, left, and middle (anterior) leaflets. The right leaflet is the largest. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right and middle leaflets. The heart in its pericardium rests on the superior surface of the central tendon.

questions.question: The pterygoid hamulus is part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The pterygoid hamulus is a hook-like process at the inferior end of the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone. The tensor veli palatini tendon hooks around it before inserting into the soft palate. The hamulus can be palpated intraorally posterior to the maxillary tuberosity. Fractures cause palatal dysfunction.

The puborectalis muscle (part of levator ani) forms a sling around the anorectal junction, creating an approximately 90-degree anorectal angle that contributes to fecal continence. During defecation, the puborectalis relaxes, straightening the anorectal angle to allow passage of feces. Paradoxical contraction of this muscle during defecation causes obstructed defecation syndrome.
questions.question: What forms the anorectal angle?

questions.explanation: Reducing the moment arm of the hip abductors (by medializing the hip center or using a low-offset prosthesis) means the abductor muscles must generate greater force to produce the same abductor moment needed to stabilize the pelvis. This increased muscle force also increases the hip joint reaction force, potentially accelerating bearing surface wear in hip replacements. Restoring femoral offset is therefore biomechanically important.
questions.question: The hip abductor moment is critical in preventing pelvic drop during single-leg stance. If the moment arm of the hip abductors (gluteus medius) is surgically reduced (e.g., by a high femoral offset prosthesis), what is the clinical consequence?
options: Improved hip abductor muscle strength reducing the limp overall
Improved Trendelenburg gait pattern after total hip arthroplasty
Reduced abductor moment arm requiring greater muscle force and increased joint reaction force
No clinical consequence for gait or joint loading
Reduced knee and ankle pain from altered load distribution only

questions.question: Injury to the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa would result in which functional deficit?
questions.explanation: Tibial nerve injury causes paralysis of the flexor muscles in the leg and the intrinsic muscles in the sole of the foot, resulting in inability to plantarflex the ankle or flex the toes, with loss of sensation on the sole. Foot drop with inability to dorsiflex and evert is the result of common fibular nerve injury, a distinct clinical presentation.
options: Foot drop and complete inability to evert the foot
Isolated loss of knee extension with intact plantarflexion
Leg flexor and intrinsic foot muscle paralysis with plantarflexion and toe flexion loss
Loss of hip extension strength at the gluteus maximus
Inability to abduct the hip in the coronal plane

questions.explanation: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery provides the main blood supply, entering at the lower pole. Additional supply comes from ascending palatine (facial), ascending pharyngeal, dorsal lingual, and lesser palatine arteries. The paratonsillar vein descends from the soft palate across the capsule and is regularly divided during tonsillectomy.
questions.question: The palatine tonsil receives its blood supply primarily from which artery?

questions.explanation: Gracilis is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest member of the adductor group. It is the only member to cross both the hip and knee joints. Its tendon joins sartorius and semitendinosus at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia. It is used as a donor muscle in gracilis free flap reconstructive surgery due to its consistent anatomy.
questions.question: Which is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest muscle of the adductor group, uniquely crossing both hip and knee joints?

questions.explanation: The puboprostatic ligaments extend from the posterior aspect of the pubic bones to the prostate and bladder neck in males, anchoring these structures. In females, the equivalent structures are the pubovesical ligaments. The lateral ligaments of the bladder (containing superior vesical vessels) also contribute to bladder support and fixation.
questions.question: Which ligaments anchor the bladder neck in males?
Where do hilar lymphatics ultimately drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the lung drain into hilar (bronchopulmonary) nodes, and efferent lymphatics ultimately drain into the brachiocephalic vein. The lymph passes through pulmonary nodes, bronchopulmonary nodes, and tracheobronchial nodes before reaching the venous system. This pathway is important in cancer metastasis.

Pronator quadratus is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus. The pronator quadratus is the deepest muscle in the anterior forearm.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies pronator quadratus?

questions.explanation: The common bile duct descends posterior to the first (superior) part of the duodenum (retroduodenal portion), then continues behind or embedded in the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (infraduodenal portion). It finally passes through the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum (intraduodenal portion), joining the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla. This posterior relationship means that duodenal ulcers in the first part can erode into the bile duct or gastroduodenal artery. The duct's pancreatic portion may be compressed by pancreatic head tumors.
questions.question: The common bile duct passes posterior to which part of the duodenum?

questions.explanation: The taeniae coli are three longitudinal muscle bands that are characteristic external features of the large intestine (colon) but absent from the rectum and anal canal. These bands are shorter than the colon itself, causing sacculations (haustra) to form. The small intestine has a complete, continuous longitudinal muscle layer without taeniae.
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the large intestine from the small intestine externally?

questions.explanation: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ridge surrounding the glenoid cavity that deepens the cavity, reducing dislocation risk. It increases the articular surface area and provides attachment for some glenohumeral ligaments. This structure contributes significantly to glenohumeral joint stability despite the joint's high mobility.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the glenoid labrum?
The cremasteric artery is typically a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The cremasteric artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery (a branch of the external iliac artery) near the deep inguinal ring and accompanies the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal. It supplies the cremaster muscle and anastomoses with the testicular artery and artery of the vas deferens, contributing to the arterial supply of the spermatic cord coverings. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve also enters the cord at the deep ring to innervate the cremaster muscle, which elevates the testis in response to cold or cremasteric reflex stimulation.

questions.question: Where are circular venous plexuses located?
questions.explanation: Circular venous plexuses are found at the base of the nipple. Veins corresponding to the arteries drain the breast, ultimately into the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The superficial veins often become prominent and dilated during pregnancy and lactation.

questions.question: The superior mesenteric artery syndrome involves compression of which structure?
questions.explanation: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome results from compression of the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly and the aorta (and spine) posteriorly. This typically occurs when the aortomesenteric angle decreases (normally 25-60 degrees) due to loss of the mesenteric fat pad, which can result from rapid weight loss, cachexia, scoliosis surgery, or growth spurts in adolescents. Symptoms include postprandial epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. Left renal vein compression between the SMA and aorta is called nutcracker syndrome, a different condition.

The iliacus muscle is part of the posterior abdominal wall, not the anterior wall, originating from the iliac fossa and inserting with psoas major onto the lesser trochanter of the femur as the iliopsoas tendon. The anterior abdominal wall muscles include three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) and two vertical muscles (rectus abdominis and pyramidalis). The iliacus is innervated by the femoral nerve and functions primarily as a hip flexor, while the anterior abdominal wall muscles are involved in trunk movement and increasing intra-abdominal pressure.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the anterior abdominal wall?

questions.explanation: is characterized by paresthesia in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of ring finger). Symptoms are often worse at night and may be relieved by shaking the hand. The condition results from median nerve compression within the carpal tunnel.
questions.question: Which condition is characterized by paresthesia in median nerve distribution?

questions.explanation: Although no anatomical sphincter exists, a physiological lower esophageal sphincter (LES) mechanism prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction. This involves: (1) increased smooth muscle tone in the distal esophagus, (2) acute angle of entry (angle of His), (3) compression by the right crus of the diaphragm, (4) positive intra-abdominal pressure on the abdominal esophagus. LES dysfunction causes gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
questions.question: Which structure prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction?

questions.explanation: The left gastric artery, the smallest branch of the celiac trunk, gives off esophageal branches that ascend to supply the abdominal portion of the esophagus (below the diaphragm). These esophageal branches anastomose superiorly with esophageal branches from the thoracic aorta through the esophageal hiatus, creating a potential portosystemic anastomosis (left gastric vein to portal system; esophageal veins from thoracic aorta territory to azygos system to IVC). In portal hypertension, this anastomosis may become varicose, producing esophageal varices that can rupture and cause life-threatening hemorrhage.
questions.question: The left gastric artery supplies which part of the esophagus?

questions.explanation: The mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals (articulating with hamate) allow palmar cupping for power grip. This adaptation enables the hand to conform to cylindrical objects. The 2nd and 3rd metacarpals are relatively fixed, providing a stable platform for precision grip.
options: Allow cupping of hand for power grip
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals?

questions.explanation: The pancreas extends obliquely across the posterior abdominal wall from the C-shaped curve of the duodenum (head) to the splenic hilum (tail) at approximately L1-L2 vertebral levels, though the tail may extend slightly higher. The head lies at L1-L2, the neck crosses L1, and the body and tail run along L1-L2 as they extend to the left. The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal (except the tail, which extends into the splenorenal ligament), lying anterior to the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vessels, aorta, IVC, left kidney, and left suprarenal gland.
questions.question: The pancreas lies at which vertebral levels?

questions.explanation: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2). The exception is the short head of biceps femoris, which is supplied by the common fibular division. The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body.
questions.question: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by which division of the sciatic nerve?
Which structure separates the orbit from the ethmoid sinus?
questions.explanation: The lamina papyracea (orbital plate of ethmoid) is a thin bony plate separating the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells. Its paper-like thinness makes it vulnerable to fracture and erosion. Ethmoidal infections can spread through this wall causing orbital complications. The anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina pierce this plate.

questions.question: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve exits the skull through which opening?
questions.explanation: The maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve exits the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum in the greater wing of the sphenoid. It enters the pterygopalatine fossa where it gives off branches before continuing as the infraorbital nerve. The foramen rotundum is round in shape, hence its name.

questions.question: How many nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: Seven nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen: the sciatic nerve, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal nerve, inferior gluteal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerve. Together with six vessels and piriformis, these seven nerves constitute the 14 total structures passing through this foramen.

questions.question: The lymphatics of the lower limb follow the saphenous vein and drain to which lymph node group?
questions.explanation: The superficial lymphatics of the lower limb accompany the great saphenous vein and drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. The deep lymphatics accompany the deep vessels and drain to the deep inguinal and then external iliac nodes. The popliteal nodes drain the posterior leg and lateral foot (accompanying the small saphenous vein). Lymphedema of the lower limb can follow radical inguinal lymph node dissection.

The parotid gland extends superiorly to the external acoustic meatus and zygomatic arch. The gland lies below and anterior to the ear, extending from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the mandible. The facial nerve divides within the gland substance into its terminal branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical).
questions.question: Which structure limits the superior extent of the parotid gland?
What arches over the left lung root?
questions.explanation: The aortic arch passes over and in front of the left lung root. The left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch. This anatomical relationship is visible on chest X-rays and CT scans and is important for understanding mediastinal anatomy.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the thoracic cage?
questions.explanation: The thoracic cage primarily functions to protect the lungs, heart, and great vessels from external trauma. Additionally, it provides attachment points for muscles of the thorax, upper limb, abdomen, and back. The cage also plays a vital role in the mechanics of respiration through its elastic properties.

questions.question: Which structure is NOT retroperitoneal?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon is intraperitoneal, suspended by the transverse mesocolon from the posterior abdominal wall. The ascending and descending colon are secondarily retroperitoneal (covered by peritoneum anteriorly only), as is most of the duodenum (except the first 2 cm) and the pancreas (except the tail which extends into the splenorenal ligament). Secondarily retroperitoneal structures were initially suspended by mesentery during development but became fused to the posterior body wall. Primarily retroperitoneal organs (kidneys, suprarenal glands, ureters, aorta, IVC) were never suspended by mesentery.

The superior and inferior lateral genicular arteries encircle the fibular collateral ligament at the lateral aspect of the knee, contributing to the lateral genicular anastomosis. The superior lateral genicular artery passes above the lateral condyle of the femur, while the inferior lateral genicular artery passes below the lateral tibial condyle. Together they provide important collateral circulation around the knee.
questions.question: The superior lateral genicular artery and the inferior lateral genicular artery both branch from the popliteal artery. Between them, what structure do they encircle at the lateral aspect of the knee?

questions.explanation: Sudeck's point is the watershed area at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anal verge) where the last sigmoid artery (from inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of IMA). This represents a relatively weak point in the colonic blood supply, vulnerable to ischemia during periods of low blood flow, hypotension, or ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery during surgery. Another watershed area is Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure. Both areas may develop ischemic colitis, manifesting as abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and colonoscopic evidence of mucosal ischemia.
questions.question: Which artery anastomoses at Sudeck's point?

questions.explanation: The right bronchial vein drains into the azygos vein, while the left bronchial vein drains into the accessory hemiazygos vein. These veins return deoxygenated blood from the bronchial tree. The pulmonary veins, in contrast, carry oxygenated blood from the alveoli to the left atrium.
questions.question: Where does the right bronchial vein drain?
Sever's disease (calcaneal apophysitis) is a traction apophysitis of the calcaneus, predominantly affecting which age group and caused by traction from which structure?
questions.explanation: Sever's disease is calcaneal apophysitis affecting adolescents aged 8-14 years (peak growth phase), caused by traction from the Achilles tendon on the calcaneal apophysis (secondary ossification centre). It presents with posterior heel pain aggravated by activity. Treatment is conservative with activity modification, heel cups, and Achilles tendon stretching. It is self-limiting once the apophysis fuses.
options: Young children under 5; from excessive dorsiflexion
Adolescents aged 8�14; Achilles traction on the calcaneal apophysis
Young adults; from overuse of tibialis posterior

questions.question: The nasolacrimal duct opens into which nasal meatus?
questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath the inferior turbinate. The valve of Hasner at the duct's termination prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction causes epiphora (excessive tearing) and may require dacryocystorhinostomy.

questions.question: Which cardiac chamber forms most of the anterior surface?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart. The right atrium contributes to the right portion of this surface, and a small part of the left ventricle forms the left border. This anterior position makes the right ventricle most vulnerable to anterior chest trauma. The left ventricle forms most of the diaphragmatic surface and left border.

questions.question: What causes paradoxical breathing in flail chest?
questions.explanation: In flail chest (from multiple rib fractures creating a free-floating segment), the affected segment moves paradoxically: sucking inward during inspiration (when intrathoracic pressure decreases) and bulging outward during expiration (when pressure increases). This ineffective breathing causes hypoventilation, hypoxia, and impaired secretion clearance. Treatment includes positive pressure ventilation.

The renal hilum is positioned at the level of the transpyloric plane, which corresponds to the first lumbar vertebra (L1), though the kidneys themselves extend from approximately T12 to L3. At the hilum, structures are arranged from anterior to posterior as vein, artery, and pelvis (VAP), though the renal vein is most anterior and superior. The left kidney typically sits slightly higher than the right due to the presence of the liver on the right side.
questions.question: The kidney hilum is located at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: Goblet cells that secrete mucus are abundant in the large intestinal mucosa and increase in number toward the rectum. The mucus lubricates the passage of increasingly solid feces and protects the mucosa. Large intestinal crypts (of Lieberk?hn) lack villi and contain mainly goblet cells and absorptive colonocytes. Paneth cells are found only in the small intestine.
questions.question: Which cells are characteristic of the large intestinal mucosa?
The stylomastoid artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The stylomastoid artery arises from the posterior auricular artery and enters the stylomastoid foramen to supply the facial nerve in its bony canal, the mastoid air cells, and the stapedius muscle. It anastomoses with the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery. The artery follows the facial nerve through the temporal bone.

questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the parietal peritoneum?
questions.explanation: The parietal peritoneum receives sensory innervation from the same nerves that supply the overlying body wall region: phrenic nerve (C3-C5) for the central diaphragmatic peritoneum, lower six intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12) for the peripheral diaphragmatic and abdominal wall peritoneum, and lumbar nerves for the pelvic peritoneum. This explains why peritoneal irritation produces well-localized, sharp, somatic pain referred to specific dermatomes. In contrast, the visceral peritoneum is insensitive to touch, temperature, and laceration, being innervated only by autonomic nerves that mediate poorly localized visceral pain in response to stretch, ischemia, or chemical irritation.

options: First rib, clavicle, and superior scapular border
questions.question: Which structures form the boundaries of the cervicoaxillary canal (apex of axilla)?
questions.explanation: The apex of the axilla forms the cervicoaxillary canal, providing passage between the neck and axilla. It is bounded by the first rib medially, the clavicle anteriorly, and the superior border of the scapula posteriorly. Arteries, veins, lymphatics, and nerves traverse this opening to reach or leave the upper limb.

questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, medial to the deep inguinal ring. It ascends obliquely along the medial margin of the deep ring, passing medial to it (an important landmark distinguishing direct from indirect inguinal hernias), and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Within the sheath, it ascends posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery, providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian (via internal thoracic) and external iliac arterial systems.

The alveolar process of the maxilla forms the floor of the maxillary sinus. Roots of the upper premolar and molar teeth may project into the sinus, separated only by thin bone or mucosa. Dental infections can spread to the sinus, and tooth extraction can create an oroantral fistula. The floor is typically 1-2 cm below the nasal floor.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the maxillary sinus?

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) requires intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, for absorption in the terminal ileum. Intrinsic factor binds to B12, protecting it from degradation and facilitating its receptor-mediated uptake by ileal enterocytes. Lack of intrinsic factor (from parietal cell destruction in pernicious anemia or gastrectomy) causes B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.
questions.question: Which vitamin requires intrinsic factor for absorption?

questions.explanation: Aortic coarctation is typically located just distal to the left subclavian artery origin, near the site of the ligamentum arteriosum (remnant of ductus arteriosus). This is called juxtaductal coarctation. Less commonly, it may be preductal or postductal. The stenosis reduces blood flow to the lower body.
questions.question: Where is coarctation typically located?

questions.explanation: The areola is a dark pink-brownish circular area of skin (22-60 mm in diameter) that surrounds the nipple. Its color varies with parity and race, darkening during the second month of pregnancy. The areola contains Montgomery's glands (areola glands) which enlarge during pregnancy and lactation.
questions.question: What structure surrounds the nipple?

questions.explanation: The mediastinal surface faces the mediastinum and contains the hilum where structures enter and leave the lung. This surface is in contact with the heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, and other mediastinal structures. The hilum is located on this surface opposite the bodies of T5, T6, and T7 vertebrae.
questions.question: Which surface of the lung faces the mediastinum?

questions.explanation: The costomediastinal recess is located behind the sternum where the costal pleura doubles back to become mediastinal pleura. It is more conspicuous on the left side in the region around the cardiac notch. This recess allows for cardiac expansion without lung compression.
questions.question: Where is the costomediastinal recess located?
Which paranasal sinus is present in rudimentary form at birth?
questions.explanation: The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in rudimentary form at birth. The frontal and sphenoid sinuses become evident around age seven. This developmental pattern explains why frontal sinusitis is rare in young children. All sinuses reach full development by late adolescence.

questions.question: The hepatic artery proper typically divides into which branches?
questions.explanation: The hepatic artery proper, ascending in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) as part of the portal triad, divides near the porta hepatis into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver. The right hepatic artery gives off the cystic artery to the gallbladder. Significant anatomical variation exists in hepatic arterial anatomy (occurring in up to 45% of individuals), including replaced or accessory right hepatic arteries from the superior mesenteric artery and replaced or accessory left hepatic arteries from the left gastric artery.

options: Flex metacarpophalangeal joints, extend interphalangeal joints
questions.explanation: Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints of the fingers. This unique action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve while the medial two receive ulnar innervation.
questions.question: What is the function of the lumbricals in the hand?

questions.explanation: The median nerve provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. This sensory distribution is preserved in anterior interosseous syndrome (pure motor branch) but affected in carpal tunnel syndrome and more proximal median nerve injuries.
questions.question: What provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb?
Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae, voluntary striated muscle) surrounds the membranous urethra as it passes through the deep perineal space (urogenital diaphragm). This sphincter provides voluntary control of micturition and is innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). The prostatic urethra is surrounded by the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle under autonomic control) at the bladder neck. The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm) and least distensible part, making it vulnerable to injury during instrumentation and the most common site of urethral rupture in pelvic fractures.

questions.question: Which vein drains the fundus of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The short gastric veins drain the fundus of the stomach and flow into the splenic vein. There are typically 4-5 short gastric veins that pass through the gastrosplenic ligament. In portal hypertension, these veins can become dilated and form part of the portosystemic collateral circulation, potentially leading to gastric varices and bleeding.

questions.question: What produces flexion at the wrist joint?
options: Flexor carpi ulnaris and radialis, flexor digitorum superficialis
questions.explanation: Flexion at the wrist is produced mainly by flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi radialis muscles. The flexor digitorum superficialis provides assistance to this movement. All wrist movements are performed by forearm muscles crossing the wrist joint.

The vertebral arteries enter the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum after ascending through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. They unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. The vertebral arteries give off the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries before joining.
questions.question: The vertebral arteries enter the skull through which opening?
What is the primary concern in supracondylar fracture of the humerus?
options: Brachial artery damage and Volkmann's ischemia
questions.explanation: The primary concern in supracondylar fractures is brachial artery damage potentially leading to Volkmann's ischemic contracture. The artery lies in close proximity to the distal humerus and can be compressed or torn. This causes forearm muscle ischemia and subsequent flexion contracture if not promptly recognized and treated.

questions.question: Which structure passes through both greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hook around the ischial spine (covered by sacrospinous ligament), and re-enter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. This unique course makes the pudendal nerve vulnerable to compression at the ischial spine (pudendal neuralgia). The nerve to obturator internus follows a similar course. No other major structures pass through both foramina; the sciatic nerve and other gluteal region structures exit only through the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.question: Which muscle, by supporting the medial longitudinal arch, prevents excessive pronation of the foot during the stance phase of gait?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is the most important dynamic supporter of the medial longitudinal arch, actively preventing excessive pronation during stance phase. It eccentrically controls subtalar eversion during heel strike, then concentrically re-inverts and supinates the foot at push-off. Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction leads to progressive flatfoot with excessive pronation, and is the most common cause of adult acquired flatfoot.

questions.question: Through which opening does the sympathetic trunk enter the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunks enter the abdomen from the thorax by passing deep to (posterior to) the medial arcuate ligaments. They descend on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, giving off lumbar splanchnic nerves. The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura to enter the abdomen.

The esophageal hiatus (at T10 level, formed by muscle fibers from the right crus of the diaphragm that loop around the esophagus) transmits the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks (formed from the vagus nerves). The vagal trunks provide parasympathetic innervation to the abdominal viscera up to the splenic flexure. The left gastric artery and vein may also pass through or near this opening. The aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein pass through the aortic hiatus at T12, while the IVC passes through the caval opening at T8.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the esophageal hiatus?

questions.explanation: A fracture of the neck of femur characteristically results in coxa vara, reducing the neck-shaft angle below the normal 125-135 degrees. Coxa valga with an increased neck-shaft angle follows congenital dislocation of the femoral head. These deformities have different biomechanical implications for gait and joint loading.
questions.question: A fracture of the neck of femur characteristically produces which angular deformity of the hip?

questions.explanation: is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle due to its vulnerable position under the acromion. The tendon passes through a narrow space (subacromial space) where it's subject to impingement. Age-related degeneration combined with repetitive overhead activities increases tear risk.
questions.question: What is the primary muscle affected in rotator cuff tears?
How many total structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: Fourteen structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen: one muscle (piriformis), seven nerves (sciatic, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerves), and six vessels (superior and inferior gluteal arteries and veins, and internal pudendal artery and vein).

questions.question: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the ulnar nerve?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C7, C8, T1). The medial cord also gives rise to the medial pectoral nerve, medial cutaneous nerve of arm and forearm, and the medial root of the median nerve. Injury to the medial cord affects all these structures.

At the lower esophagus, esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal system, draining to portal vein) anastomose with esophageal veins draining the middle third of the esophagus into the azygos system (systemic circulation to SVC). In portal hypertension, these anastomoses dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing massive hematemesis. This is one of four main portosystemic anastomoses (others: rectum, umbilicus, retroperitoneal). The left gastric vein ascends along the lesser curvature to drain directly into the portal vein, receiving esophageal tributaries that create the anastomosis.
questions.question: Which vein forms a portosystemic anastomosis at the esophagus?

questions.explanation: The human foot achieves its two basic functions through a segmented skeleton arranged in arches (longitudinal and transverse), supported by muscles and ligaments. This arrangement enables efficient locomotion, sparing of foot structures, and shock absorption. The arches allow the foot to adapt to uneven surfaces and serve as resilient springs to absorb shocks as in jumping.
options: Segmented bony arches supported by muscles and ligaments
Rigid flat bone platform without arching
Phalanges arranged in a single arch only
questions.question: The two basic functions of the human foot are supporting body weight and providing leverage for locomotion. These are achieved through which structural arrangement?
The anterior ethmoidal foramen transmits which structures?
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal foramen in the medial orbital wall transmits the anterior ethmoidal nerve (from nasociliary) and vessels (from ophthalmic artery). These structures supply the anterior ethmoidal air cells, frontal sinus, and upper nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the ethmoid and frontal bones at the frontoethmoidal suture.

options: Anterior compartment flexor with radial nerve supply
questions.question: How does the brachioradialis differ from other radial nerve-supplied muscles?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is unique as an anterior compartment muscle (flexor) supplied by the radial nerve, which typically supplies extensors. This reflects its developmental origin from extensor muscle mass despite its eventual anterior position. It flexes the forearm most effectively from mid-prone position.

questions.question: What causes achalasia?
questions.explanation: Achalasia is a motility disorder characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing and loss of normal esophageal peristalsis. This causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, and progressive esophageal dilation. Treatment includes pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM).

questions.question: Which pleura covers the diaphragm's superior surface?
questions.explanation: The diaphragmatic pleura is the portion of parietal pleura that covers the superior surface of the diaphragm. It reflects onto the thoracic wall to become continuous with the costal pleura. The diaphragmatic pleura receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally.

The straight sinus receives the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the inferior sagittal sinus. It runs in the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. The sinus drains into the confluence of sinuses (typically preferentially into the left transverse sinus). Deep cerebral structures drain via this pathway.
questions.question: Which sinus receives the great cerebral vein?
Which structure forms the upper border of the pyloric sphincter on the transpyloric plane?
questions.explanation: The pyloric orifice lies on the transpyloric plane at the level of the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is an important surface anatomy landmark located approximately 1.25 cm to the right of the median plane. The pyloric sphincter can be identified by a slight surface constriction and the prepyloric vein of Mayo.

The right coronary artery arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus of the ascending aorta. It runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving off branches to the right atrium, SA node (in 60% of people), right ventricle, and posterior interventricular septum. In right-dominant circulation (70% of people), it gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.
questions.question: From which aortic sinus does the right coronary artery arise?

questions.explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle. This is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The nerve descends with the superior thyroid artery. Damage affects vocal cord tension and causes voice fatigue and difficulty with pitch variation.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?

questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra contains the openings of the two ejaculatory ducts on either side of the prostatic utricle (a small blind pouch) on the seminal colliculus (urethral crest). About 20-30 prostatic ducts also open into the prostatic urethra. The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra, measuring about 3-4 cm in length.
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra contains the ejaculatory duct openings?

questions.explanation: Biceps long head tendon rupture typically occurs in elderly individuals with degenerative tendon changes. The muscle belly retracts distally creating the characteristic "Popeye" sign. Despite dramatic appearance, functional deficit is surprisingly minimal as the short head remains intact and compensates adequately.
questions.question: Which condition is associated with rupture of the biceps long head?
What is the primary action of brachioradialis?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is primarily a flexor of the forearm, most effective when the forearm is in mid-pronation position. It also assists with both pronation from supinated position and supination from pronated position, returning the forearm to neutral. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve despite being an anterior compartment muscle.

questions.question: The great auricular nerve is derived from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin over the parotid gland, lower ear, and angle of the mandible. It emerges at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and ascends on that muscle. The nerve is at risk during parotid surgery and facelift procedures.

questions.question: What can cause acquired diaphragmatic hernia?
questions.explanation: Acquired diaphragmatic hernias can result from: (1) penetrating or blunt trauma causing rupture, (2) weakening around the esophageal hiatus (hiatus hernias), or (3) rarely, herniation through the central tendon after surgical procedures. Traumatic hernias require urgent surgical repair.

questions.question: The transpyloric plane intersects which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane is an important anatomical landmark that passes through the first lumbar vertebra (L1), situated midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis. This plane transects numerous vital structures including the pylorus, neck of pancreas, origins of superior mesenteric artery and portal vein, duodenojejunal junction, and the hila of both kidneys. It serves as a crucial reference point for clinical examination and surgical procedures in the upper abdomen.

The appendix drains to ileocolic lymph nodes located along the ileocolic artery, which then drain to superior mesenteric nodes. Appendiceal lymphoid tissue is abundant, earning it the nickname "intestinal tonsil." In appendicitis, lymph nodes may become enlarged and palpable. Metastatic disease from appendiceal tumors follows this lymphatic drainage pattern.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the appendix?
Which muscle is the primary flexor of the hip joint, described as the great flexor, with its traction epiphysis being the lesser trochanter?
questions.explanation: The iliopsoas is the primary flexor of the hip joint, formed by the fusion of iliacus and psoas major. Their combined tendon inserts into the lesser trochanter, which is its traction epiphysis. The iliopsoas is active in walking, running, and sitting up. Weakness of iliopsoas is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated position.

questions.question: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from which nerve?
questions.explanation: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve by two branches in the submandibular region. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arrive via the chorda tympani, synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through without synapsing.

The aortic arch begins at the level of T4 as a continuation of the ascending aorta. It arches backwards and to the left, passing over the left main bronchus. The arch ends at the level of T4/5 by continuing as the descending thoracic aorta. The aortic arch lies entirely within the superior mediastinum.
questions.question: At which level does the aortic arch begin?

questions.explanation: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer of the rectum, extending from the anorectal junction to approximately the level of the white line of Hilton, covering the upper three-quarters of the anal canal. It is under autonomic (involuntary) control, receiving sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric plexuses) that promotes contraction and parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) that causes relaxation. This sphincter maintains resting anal tone and unconscious fecal continence, while the external anal sphincter (striated voluntary muscle supplied by inferior rectal nerve) provides voluntary control.
questions.question: The internal anal sphincter is formed from which layer?
Which nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome as it passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle. This is the most common site of ulnar nerve entrapment. Symptoms include numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and hand muscle weakness.

options: Superior gluteal artery from the internal iliac
Inferior gluteal artery from the internal iliac alone
Acetabular branches of medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries
questions.question: The ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres) transmits arteries from which named vessels to the femoral head?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres transmits arteries from acetabular branches of the medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries to the head of femur. It is triangular and flat, with its apex at the fovea capitis and base at the acetabular notch. In adults, this provides only a minor blood supply compared to the retinacular vessels.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The lateral border of the pronator teres muscle forms the medial (ulnar) boundary of the cubital fossa. The lateral boundary is formed by the medial border of brachioradialis muscle. The floor consists of brachialis and supinator muscles while the roof is formed by fascia and bicipital aponeurosis.

questions.question: What sphincter is at the gastroesophageal junction?
questions.explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a physiological sphincter at the gastroesophageal junction. Unlike the anatomical upper esophageal sphincter, the LES has no distinct anatomical structure but represents a zone of increased smooth muscle tone. The right crus fibers looping around the esophagus contribute to sphincter function.

questions.question: How many posterior intercostal arteries does aorta give?
questions.explanation: The descending thoracic aorta gives off nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces (3rd-11th). The upper two spaces are supplied by the superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk. The subcostal arteries (below the 12th rib) are also given off by the thoracic aorta.

The aditus ad antrum is an opening in the posterior wall of the epitympanic recess that connects the middle ear cavity with the mastoid antrum. Middle ear infections can spread to the mastoid air cells through this passage causing mastoiditis. The roof of the aditus is the tegmen tympani.
questions.question: The aditus ad antrum connects which two structures?

options: Extensor carpi radialis longus, brevis, and ulnaris
questions.explanation: Extension at the wrist joint is produced mainly by extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris. The extensor digitorum provides assistance to this movement. All these extensors are located in the posterior compartment of the forearm.
questions.question: Which muscles produce wrist extension with assistance from extensor digitorum?
Which ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a double-layered peritoneal fold that connects the anterior and superior surfaces of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, extending from the umbilicus to the diaphragm. Its free inferior border contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (obliterated umbilical vein) and separates the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver. This ligament develops from the ventral mesentery and serves as an important surgical landmark during laparoscopic procedures.

The primary function of the large intestine is absorption of water and electrolytes from the remaining indigestible food matter, converting liquid chyme into semi-solid feces. Approximately 1-2 liters of water are absorbed daily. The colon also absorbs short-chain fatty acids produced by bacterial fermentation and synthesizes vitamin K through bacterial action.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the large intestine?

questions.explanation: When a bone has an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes captured this in the mnemonic 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee,' indicating the direction of nutrient arteries in the humerus and lower limb bones respectively.
questions.question: In bones with epiphyses at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from which structure?
Fibularis longus crosses the sole diagonally after turning medially in a groove on which bone, ultimately inserting into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform?
questions.explanation: After descending in the lateral compartment and passing behind the lateral malleolus, fibularis longus turns medially in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, crossing the sole diagonally to insert into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This unique oblique course allows it to support the transverse arch of the foot.

questions.question: What is the stellate ganglion?
questions.explanation: The stellate ganglion is formed by fusion of the inferior cervical ganglion with the first thoracic ganglion. It lies anterior to the neck of the first rib. Stellate ganglion block (local anesthetic injection) can provide sympathetic blockade for upper limb pain or vascular conditions. Damage causes Horner's syndrome.

questions.question: Which type of tissue lines the pleural cavities?
questions.explanation: The pleural cavities are lined by mesothelium, a specialized layer of simple squamous epithelial cells. This smooth lining produces pleural fluid that lubricates the surfaces. The visceral pleura covers the lung surface while the parietal pleura lines the thoracic cavity walls.

questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the posterior triangle?
questions.explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering splenius capitis, levator scapulae, and scalene muscles (anterior, middle, posterior). The subclavian artery and brachial plexus emerge between the scalene muscles. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle superficially on this floor. Cervical lymph nodes lie within the triangle.

questions.question: What structure lies anterior to lung apex?
questions.explanation: Anterior to the lung apex lies the brachiocephalic vein (left side has left brachiocephalic vein crossing; right side has right brachiocephalic vein). The subclavian artery arches over the apex (groove on apex). Posteriorly lies the neck of the first rib and sympathetic trunk. Medially is the trachea and esophagus.

questions.question: How do the thenar and hypothenar muscles differ functionally?
options: Thenar for thumb mobility/opposition, hypothenar for little finger mobility
Thenar for power, hypothenar for precision
Thenar for extension, hypothenar for flexion
questions.explanation: Thenar muscles provide thumb mobility essential for opposition and precision grip. Hypothenar muscles provide little finger mobility and contribute to power grip by cupping the hand. The specialized thumb movements made possible by thenar muscles are uniquely human characteristics.

questions.question: What creates the aortic knuckle on X-ray?
