questions.explanation: The aortic knuckle (or aortic knob) is the prominent shadow on a chest X-ray created by the aortic arch as it curves backward and to the left at the level of T4/5. This is a normal finding and an important landmark. Widening may indicate aortic aneurysm or dissection.

The inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac artery) ascends medial to the deep inguinal ring and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Once within the sheath, it ascends on the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery (from the internal thoracic artery). The inferior epigastric artery gives off the cremasteric artery and sometimes a pubic branch. Its position medial to the deep inguinal ring makes it an important landmark distinguishing direct (medial to vessel) from indirect (lateral to vessel) inguinal hernias.
questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery enters the rectus sheath by piercing which structure?
The medial wall of the orbit is formed primarily by which bone?
questions.explanation: The medial orbital wall is formed primarily by the orbital plate (lamina papyracea) of the ethmoid bone. This thin bone separates the orbit from ethmoidal air cells. Fractures can cause orbital emphysema when air enters from the sinuses. The lacrimal bone contributes anteriorly.

questions.question: Which structure crosses esophagus at 27 cm?
questions.explanation: The left main bronchus crosses anterior to the esophagus creating the third anatomical constriction at 27 cm from the incisors (T5-6 level). This is where the trachea bifurcates. Foreign bodies and malignancies may cause compression at this site. Endoscopic measurements from the incisors help locate pathology.

questions.question: Which hormone stimulates gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the pyloric antrum and stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid and stimulates chief cells to secrete pepsinogen. Its release is stimulated by stomach distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin secretion is inhibited by low pH (negative feedback) and by somatostatin from D cells.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of the mesentery root attachment?
questions.explanation: The root (origin) of the mesentery is approximately 15 cm long, extending obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction. Despite this short root attachment, the mesentery fans out to accommodate the 5-6 meters of small bowel. The root crosses the third part of the duodenum, aorta, IVC, right psoas muscle, and right gonadal vessels.

The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from S2-S4 spinal segments provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder. These nerves stimulate detrusor muscle contraction and inhibit the internal urethral sphincter, promoting micturition. Sympathetic innervation from T11-L2 via the hypogastric plexus promotes urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter.
questions.question: Which nerves provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder?

questions.explanation: The quadratus lumborum receives innervation from the subcostal nerve (T12) and the upper lumbar nerves (L1-L3 or L4), reflecting its position as the most lateral muscle of the posterior abdominal wall. This muscle originates from the iliolumbar ligament and adjacent iliac crest, inserting onto the medial half of the inferior border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae. It functions to fix the 12th rib during inspiration, extend the lumbar vertebral column bilaterally, and produce lateral flexion when acting unilaterally.
questions.question: The quadratus lumborum muscle is innervated by which nerves?
Which muscle forms the floor of the posterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The posterior abdominal wall is formed by multiple muscles: psoas major (medially, originating from lumbar vertebrae), quadratus lumborum (laterally, between 12th rib and iliac crest), and iliacus (below iliac crest, in iliac fossa). Together these muscles, along with the diaphragm superiorly and the lumbar vertebrae and their processes, create the musculoskeletal framework of the posterior abdominal wall. The transversus abdominis wraps around from the anterolateral wall to attach to these structures. These muscles are covered anteriorly by psoas fascia, quadratus lumborum fascia, and iliac fascia respectively, with retroperitoneal organs and vessels lying anterior to these fascial layers.

questions.question: The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses which part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the second (descending) part of the duodenum as it extends from right to left across the posterior abdominal wall. This attachment divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic (containing stomach, liver, spleen) and infracolic (containing small intestine and colon) compartments. The root also crosses anterior to the head of the pancreas and the superior mesenteric vessels. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical mobilization of the transverse colon and in understanding the spread of peritoneal infections.

The anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six spaces arise from the internal thoracic artery, which is a branch of the subclavian artery. These arteries anastomose with the posterior intercostal arteries. The internal thoracic artery descends behind the costal cartilages approximately half an inch from the lateral border of the sternum.
questions.question: Where do the upper six anterior intercostal arteries arise?

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid system. It supplies the anterior and middle ethmoidal air cells and frontal sinus. The artery enters the nasal cavity through the anterior ethmoidal foramen and supplies the anterior nasal septum.
questions.question: The anterior ethmoid artery is a branch of which parent vessel?

questions.explanation: Plantar fasciitis classically presents with severe pain at the medial calcaneal tubercle with the first steps of the morning or after prolonged sitting. This is due to the plantar fascia shortening during inactivity and being suddenly stretched during initial weight-bearing. The condition is associated with obesity, excessive pronation, and prolonged standing on hard surfaces.
options: Sitting in a chair for prolonged periods
First steps after waking or after prolonged sitting
questions.question: Plantar fasciitis involves inflammation at the calcaneal attachment of the plantar aponeurosis. Which activity typically aggravates this condition due to tensioning of the fascia?

questions.explanation: The sella turcica (Turkish saddle) is a depression in the body of the sphenoid bone housing the pituitary gland. It is bounded anteriorly by the tuberculum sellae and posteriorly by the dorsum sellae. The cavernous sinuses lie laterally. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses this region through the sphenoid sinus.
questions.question: Which bone contains the sella turcica?

questions.explanation: The Harris Hip Score (modified) and Oxford Hip Score are validated patient-reported outcome measures used to assess pain, function, and quality of life following hip conditions and hip replacement surgery. The Oxford Hip Score uses 12 questions covering pain and function, with a range of 0-48 (48 being best). These are standard outcome measures used in arthroplasty registries globally, including the Nigerian context of the MDCN setting.
questions.question: The modified Harris Hip Score and Oxford Hip Score are patient-reported outcome measures used to assess which joint?

questions.explanation: The anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending - LAD) descends in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, anterior left ventricular wall, and anterior right ventricle. It is the most commonly affected vessel in myocardial infarction. Septal branches perforate the septum; diagonal branches supply the lateral left ventricle.
questions.question: Which branch of the left coronary artery supplies the interventricular septum?
How many secondary ossification centres does the hip bone have in total?
questions.explanation: The hip bone has five secondary ossification centres: two for the iliac crest, two for the Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and one for the ischial tuberosity. All five fuse by 20-25 years of age. The three primary centres (ilium, ischium, pubis) appear in the 2nd, 4th, and 5th months of intrauterine life, respectively.

The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, extending from the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis. It contains the portal triad (portal vein posteriorly, common bile duct anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery proper anteriorly and to the left) and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The hepatoduodenal ligament can be compressed manually (Pringle maneuver) to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding inflow to the liver. The gastrohepatic ligament forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum.
questions.question: Which ligament forms the free edge of the lesser omentum?

questions.explanation: The white pulp of the spleen consists of lymphoid tissue surrounding central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS) and lymphoid nodules. It is the site of immune surveillance and antibody production in response to blood-borne antigens. The white pulp contains predominantly T lymphocytes in the PALS and B lymphocytes in the lymphoid follicles.
questions.question: What is the primary immunological function of splenic white pulp?

questions.explanation: The sternocostal triangles (foramina of Morgagni) are small gaps between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm. The superior epigastric vessels (terminal branches of internal thoracic artery and vein) and lymphatic vessels pass through these triangles. They connect the thoracic and abdominal cavities and are potential sites for diaphragmatic hernias.
questions.question: Which structures pass through the sternocostal triangle?

questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensation below the pectinate line, making this area sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature. Above the pectinate line, the anal canal is supplied by autonomic (visceral) nerves and is insensitive to these stimuli but sensitive to stretch. This explains why internal hemorrhoids are painless while external hemorrhoids are painful.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies somatic sensation below the pectinate line?

questions.explanation: Three muscles arise from the styloid process: styloglossus, stylohyoid, and stylopharyngeus. These muscles form part of the "styloid apparatus" along with two ligaments (stylomandibular and stylohyoid). The styloid process projects downward and forward from the temporal bone. Elongation (Eagle syndrome) causes pharyngeal pain and dysphagia.
questions.question: The styloid process gives attachment to which muscles?

questions.explanation: Approximately 99% of the pancreatic tissue is exocrine, consisting of acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes. Only about 1% consists of endocrine tissue in the form of pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans). The exocrine pancreas produces 1.5-2 liters of pancreatic juice daily containing enzymes for protein, carbohydrate, and fat digestion.
questions.question: What percentage of the pancreas is exocrine tissue?

questions.explanation: The olecranon fits into the olecranon fossa during extension while the coronoid fits into the coronoid fossa during flexion. This reciprocal architecture allows full range elbow motion (0-150�) while providing bony stability. The radial fossa accommodates the radial head during flexion.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the olecranon-coronoid architecture?
Which structure separates the thenar and midpalmar spaces of the hand?
questions.explanation: The medial palmar septum joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone. This septum separates the thenar space (thumb side) from the midpalmar space (ulnar side). Each space contains specific flexor tendons and lumbrical muscles.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the deep inguinal ring?
questions.explanation: The deep inguinal ring, an oval opening in the transversalis fascia located lateral to the inferior epigastric artery, transmits the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament of the uterus in females. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the cremasteric artery also pass through this ring. The ilioinguinal nerve, in contrast, passes through the superficial inguinal ring after traversing the inguinal canal, while the iliohypogastric nerve runs above and parallel to the canal.

questions.question: Soleus, unlike gastrocnemius, can plantarflex the ankle regardless of knee position because it does NOT cross the knee joint. It originates from which structures?
questions.explanation: Soleus originates from the posterior aspect of the head and superior quarter of the posterior fibula, the soleal line and middle third of the medial border of the tibia, and a tendinous arch between these bony attachments. It does not cross the knee joint, so it can plantarflex the ankle regardless of knee position. Together with gastrocnemius, it inserts via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
options: Both femoral condyles bilaterally (as in gastrocnemius origin)
Navicular tuberosity and the medial cuneiform bone distally
Head of fibula and lateral tibia condyle only
Posterior fibula head and superior quarter; soleal line, medial tibia; tendinous arch
Ischial tuberosity and posterior surface of the femur

questions.question: Which structure passes through the superficial inguinal ring in males?
questions.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) passes through the superficial inguinal ring after traversing the inguinal canal, unlike the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve which travels within the spermatic cord through both deep and superficial rings. The ilioinguinal nerve runs between internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, enters the inguinal canal, and emerges through the superficial ring to provide sensory innervation to the skin of the upper medial thigh, root of penis and anterior scrotum (males), or mons pubis and labium majus (females). Entrapment following hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain.

The superior mesenteric artery and vein cross anteriorly over the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship can cause superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, where the duodenum is compressed between the SMA and the aorta, leading to intestinal obstruction. The third part of the duodenum passes from right to left across the vertebral column at L3.
questions.question: Which vessels cross anterior to the third part of the duodenum?

options: Anterior deltoid and pectoralis clavicular head
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary shoulder flexor?
questions.explanation: Shoulder flexion is produced primarily by anterior fibers of deltoid and the clavicular head of pectoralis major. Biceps brachii and coracobrachialis provide assistance. This movement raises the arm forward in the sagittal plane.

questions.question: What occurs in splenic white pulp?
questions.explanation: The white pulp, consisting of periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) and lymphoid follicles, is the site of immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens and antibody production. T cells in the PALS respond to blood-borne antigens, while B cells in follicles produce antibodies. The marginal zone between red and white pulp contains specialized macrophages and B cells for antigen capture.

questions.question: Which muscle adducts the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle adducts (closes) the vocal cords by internally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. Other adductors include the interarytenoid and thyroarytenoid muscles. All adductors are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Bilateral adductor paralysis causes airway obstruction.

The middle meningeal artery typically divides into frontal (anterior) and parietal (posterior) branches after entering the skull through the foramen spinosum. The frontal branch crosses the pterion area. The parietal branch supplies the posterior parietal region. Epidural hematomas most commonly involve the frontal branch in the pterion region.
questions.question: The middle meningeal artery commonly divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: The profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery accompanies the radial nerve through the spiral groove, providing its blood supply in the arm. Both structures wind around the posterior humerus together. Injury to the artery often accompanies radial nerve damage in humeral fractures.
questions.question: What provides the blood supply to the radial nerve in the arm?

questions.explanation: The cystic artery most commonly (in about 75% of cases) arises from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle (bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver). However, significant anatomical variations exist, with the cystic artery occasionally arising from the left hepatic, gastroduodenal, or even superior mesenteric artery. The artery typically passes posterior to the common hepatic duct before reaching the gallbladder, where it divides into superficial (supplying the peritoneal surface) and deep (supplying the hepatic surface) branches. Careful identification during cholecystectomy prevents inadvertent injury to aberrant vessels.
questions.question: The cystic artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The iliohypogastric nerve arises from the L1 nerve root (sometimes with minor contribution from T12), emerging from the lateral border of psoas major. It runs obliquely across the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum, then pierces the transversus abdominis muscle to run between it and internal oblique, providing motor innervation to these muscles. The nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch (supplying skin over the hip) and an anterior cutaneous branch (supplying skin above the pubis), crossing above and parallel to the inguinal canal. Injury during appendectomy or hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain and sensory loss.
questions.question: Which nerve root contributes to the iliohypogastric nerve?

questions.explanation: The tensor fasciae latae inserts into the iliotibial tract (iliotibial band), a thickened lateral band of fascia lata running from the iliac crest to the lateral condyle of the tibia. It assists in flexion, abduction, and medial rotation of the hip, and helps stabilize the extended knee. Tightness of this structure is associated with iliotibial band syndrome.
questions.question: The tensor fasciae latae muscle inserts into which named structure that runs to the lateral condyle of the tibia?
What connects the papillary muscles to the valve cusps?
questions.explanation: Chordae tendineae (heart strings) are thin, strong tendinous cords that connect the papillary muscles to the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps. They prevent the valve cusps from prolapsing into the atrium during ventricular contraction. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes acute valvular regurgitation, often requiring surgical repair.

The floor of the inguinal canal is formed by the inguinal ligament (the rolled-under inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis) throughout most of its length, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament. The inguinal ligament extends from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. The roof is formed by the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, while the anterior wall is formed by the external oblique aponeurosis and the posterior wall by the transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: The posterior intercostal veins lie deepest in the costal grooves and contain valves that direct blood flow posteriorly. The neurovascular bundle arrangement from superior to inferior is vein-artery-nerve (VAN). The veins are the largest and most superior structures in this arrangement.
questions.question: Which structure lies deepest in the costal groove?
The 'hip pointer' is a contusion of which anatomical structure, common in contact sports?
questions.explanation: A hip pointer is a contusion of the iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), resulting from a direct blow in contact sports such as American football. It is extremely painful due to the multiple muscle attachments in this area. Tensor fasciae latae and sartorius originate from the ASIS and iliac crest respectively. Treatment is ice, NSAIDs, and activity modification.
options: Anterior superior iliac spine and iliac crest

questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately medial to the kidney?
questions.explanation: The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially to each kidney, forming part of its posterior relation. A psoas abscess can cause confusion with renal pathology due to this proximity. The quadratus lumborum lies directly posterior to the mid-portion of the kidney, while the transversus abdominis and its aponeurosis lie posterolaterally.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of phrenic nerve paralysis?
questions.explanation: The most common cause of phrenic nerve paralysis is surgical trauma, particularly during cardiac surgery, thoracic surgery, or neck dissection. The nerve runs along the lateral aspect of the pericardium between the mediastinal pleura and pericardium, making it vulnerable. Other causes include tumors, cervical spine disease, neurological disorders, and idiopathic paralysis.

questions.question: The vocal ligament is the thickened upper edge of which membrane?
questions.explanation: The vocal ligament is the thickened free upper edge of the cricothyroid membrane (conus elasticus). It extends from the vocal process of the arytenoid to the posterior surface of the thyroid cartilage. The ligament is covered by mucosa to form the true vocal cord.

questions.question: Which two muscles in the anterior thigh compartment cross BOTH the hip and knee joints?
questions.explanation: Both rectus femoris and sartorius cross both the hip and knee joints. Rectus femoris originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and inserts via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. Sartorius originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and inserts into the superior medial surface of the tibia. The three vasti only cross the knee joint.

questions.question: What connects superior and inferior epigastric arteries?
questions.explanation: The superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath behind the rectus abdominis muscle. This provides an important collateral pathway between the subclavian artery (via internal thoracic and superior epigastric) and the external iliac artery (via inferior epigastric), bypassing the abdominal aorta.

questions.question: The popliteal artery begins where the femoral artery passes through which structure in the lower thigh?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus. It then descends through the popliteal fossa and terminates at the inferior border of popliteus. The femoral artery travels through the adductor canal in the anterior thigh before reaching the hiatus.

The submental lymph nodes lie between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and drain the chin, central lower lip, floor of mouth, and tip of tongue. Efferents pass to submandibular and jugulo-omohyoid nodes. These nodes are examined when staging oral cavity cancers.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the chin?

questions.explanation: The adductor tubercle on the medial aspect of the distal femur receives the insertion of the hamstring part of adductor magnus. This is the part of adductor magnus supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The adductor tubercle is palpable on physical examination and serves as an important landmark in knee surgery (origin of the tibial collateral ligament is just above it).
questions.question: The adductor tubercle is an important bony landmark on the medial aspect of the distal femur. Which tendon inserts here?

questions.explanation: Portal vein thrombosis causes portal hypertension by obstructing blood flow to the liver, leading to increased pressure in the portal system. This can cause splenomegaly, ascites, and development of portosystemic collaterals including esophageal varices, hemorrhoids, and caput medusae. Causes include hypercoagulable states, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, and abdominal sepsis. Chronic thrombosis may lead to cavernous transformation of the portal vein.
questions.question: Which condition results from portal vein thrombosis?

questions.explanation: The splenic vein runs along the posterior surface of the pancreas (in a groove or embedded within the pancreatic substance) from the splenic hilum to the posterior aspect of the neck of pancreas, where it joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. It receives numerous small pancreatic veins, the inferior mesenteric vein (typically), and the left gastric and left gastroepiploic veins. Its intimate relationship with the pancreas means that acute pancreatitis can cause splenic vein thrombosis, potentially leading to left-sided portal hypertension (sinistral portal hypertension) with isolated gastric varices and splenomegaly.
questions.question: The splenic vein lies posterior to which organ?

questions.explanation: The basilar artery terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. It is formed by union of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. The artery gives off pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine branches during its course.
questions.question: The basilar artery terminates at which vertebral level?
What nerve root is predominantly tested by the triceps reflex?
questions.explanation: The triceps reflex predominantly tests the C7 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon. Absence or diminution suggests C7 nerve root or radial nerve pathology.

Nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta, supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces. The upper two spaces receive their posterior intercostal arteries from the superior intercostal artery. Each posterior intercostal artery gives branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura, and the breast.
questions.question: How many posterior intercostal arteries arise from thoracic aorta?

questions.explanation: The supraspinatus muscle initiates the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction. The middle fibers of the deltoid then take over from 15-90 degrees. Beyond 90 degrees, scapular rotation by trapezius and serratus anterior is essential for achieving full overhead abduction.
questions.question: Which muscles initiate the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction?

questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules characteristic of the ileum, especially prominent in the terminal ileum. These are permanent features of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) that play a crucial role in intestinal immunity. Peyer's patches are absent in the jejunum and located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
questions.question: Which lymphoid structures are characteristic of the terminal ileum?

questions.explanation: Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum as ferrous iron (Fe2+). Gastric acid helps convert ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous iron for absorption. Vitamin C enhances absorption while phytates and tannins inhibit it. Heme iron from meat is absorbed more efficiently than non-heme iron from plant sources.
questions.question: Where in the small intestine is iron primarily absorbed?

questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded by the sternocleidomastoid (posterolaterally), superior belly of omohyoid (inferiorly), and posterior belly of digastric (superiorly). The triangle contains the carotid bifurcation, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve, and several other structures. It is a subdivision of the anterior triangle of the neck.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the carotid triangle?
Which space is safest for chest tube insertion?
questions.explanation: The fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line (the safe triangle) is commonly used for chest tube insertion. The tube should be inserted just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. This position allows effective drainage of air (which rises) and fluid (which gravitates inferiorly).

questions.question: What is the most common complication of scaphoid fracture?
questions.explanation: are the most common complications of scaphoid fracture due to the unique blood supply. The proximal fragment often fails to heal due to inadequate blood supply. Early diagnosis and appropriate immobilization are essential to prevent these complications.

questions.question: The second layer of foot muscles contains the quadratus plantae and lumbricals. The quadratus plantae assists which extrinsic muscle in flexing the lateral four digits?
questions.explanation: The quadratus plantae assists flexor digitorum longus in flexing the lateral four digits. This assistance is needed because the tendons of flexor digitorum longus approach the digits from a medially oblique direction; quadratus plantae corrects this pull to a more longitudinal direction. It originates from the medial and lateral plantar surfaces of the calcaneus and is innervated by the lateral plantar nerve.

The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies serratus anterior, giving branches to each muscle digitation. The nerve descends on the superficial surface of the muscle and is vulnerable to injury during axillary surgery. Damage causes scapular winging.
questions.question: What nerve supplies serratus anterior?

questions.explanation: Pleurisy (or pleuritis) is inflammation of the pleura lining the lungs. It usually occurs in conjunction with pneumonia and other lung infections. Characteristic symptoms include sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing. The inflamed pleural surfaces may produce a friction rub audible on auscultation.
questions.question: Which condition causes pleural inflammation?
The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows which movements of the foot?
options: Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion at the ankle
Circumduction only, without inversion or eversion
Inversion and eversion (with associated adduction and abduction)
Pronation and supination of the ankle
questions.explanation: The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows inversion and eversion of the foot, with associated adduction and abduction. These movements occur at the subtalar joint and midtarsal joints together. True dorsiflexion and plantarflexion occur at the ankle (talocrural) joint. The summit of the lateral longitudinal arch is at the subtalar articulation.

questions.question: What connects the azygos and hemiazygos systems?
questions.explanation: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins cross from left to right behind the esophagus and aorta at the levels of T8-9 and T7 respectively to drain into the azygos vein. These cross-communications provide collateral venous drainage pathways between the left and right sides of the thorax.

questions.question: Which structure gives rise to the right and left bundle branches?
questions.explanation: The bundle of His (AV bundle) penetrates the fibrous skeleton and descends along the posterior edge of the membranous interventricular septum before dividing into right and left bundle branches. The right bundle branch continues down the right side of the septum, while the left bundle branch crosses to the left side and divides into anterior and posterior fascicles.

options: Subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major
questions.question: What produces medial rotation of the humerus at the shoulder?
questions.explanation: Medial (internal) rotation of the humerus is produced by subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, and anterior fibers of deltoid. This movement rotates the arm toward the midline so the thumb points medially. These muscles are predominantly anterior or on the subscapular surface.

The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) supplies the rhomboid major and minor muscles, and often the levator scapulae. The nerve pierces and may supply scalenus medius before descending along the vertebral border of the scapula. Injury affects scapular retraction.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies rhomboid muscles?

questions.explanation: Trochanteric bursitis is a common cause of hip pain that is more likely to involve women. It is most often caused by overuse or direct trauma to the joint. It presents as lateral hip pain that may radiate down the thigh and is aggravated by lying on the affected side or climbing stairs.
questions.question: Trochanteric bursitis at the tip of the greater trochanter is more likely to occur in which gender and due to what mechanism?
The midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint is formed by which two articulations working together?
questions.explanation: The midtarsal joint (Chopart's joint) consists of two articulations working in concert: the talonavicular joint medially and the calcaneocuboid joint laterally. Movements at this joint complement subtalar movements to produce overall foot inversion and eversion. Chopart's amputation is performed through this joint for distal foot pathology, preserving the hindfoot for a functional stump.

"Handlebar palsy" results from ulnar nerve compression at the wrist (Guyon's canal) due to prolonged pressure from bicycle handlebars. This causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and sensory changes in ulnar nerve distribution. Long-distance cyclists are particularly susceptible.
questions.question: What causes handlebar palsy in cyclists?

questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the internal carotid artery within the carotid sheath. The vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the artery and vein. The sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the sheath. This anatomical arrangement is important for central venous catheterization and carotid endarterectomy.
questions.question: Which structure lies immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery in the carotid sheath?

options: Medial condyle of the tibia proximally
Inferior lateral supracondylar line and oblique popliteal ligament
questions.explanation: Plantaris originates from the inferior end of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur and the oblique popliteal ligament. It inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon together with gastrocnemius and soleus. Its long slender tendon can be mistaken for a nerve during surgery and is used in tendon repair surgery due to its length.
questions.question: Plantaris, a vestigial muscle, inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon. From which specific femoral site does it originate?
What imaging localizes a chyle leak?
questions.explanation: Lymphangiography involves injecting contrast into pedal lymphatics to visualize the lymphatic system and thoracic duct, potentially identifying the site of leakage. This procedure is technically challenging and rarely performed. Modern alternatives include lymphoscintigraphy or high-resolution MRI. Diagnosis is usually made by pleural fluid analysis showing characteristic chyle properties.

questions.question: Fractures of the fibular neck are particularly associated with injury to which nerve, causing foot drop?
questions.explanation: Fractures of the fibular neck are particularly associated with injury to the common fibular nerve, which winds around this subcutaneous location. Injury causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion), loss of eversion (superficial fibular nerve), and sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg. The nerve is also vulnerable to pressure from tight plasters or prolonged crossing of the legs.

questions.question: Which intercostal space corresponds to the apex beat?
questions.explanation: In healthy adults, the apex beat (point of maximal impulse) is located in the 5th left intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line. This represents the most inferior and lateral point where the cardiac impulse can be felt. In children, the apex beat is one interspace higher (4th space). Displacement suggests cardiac enlargement or chest deformity.

questions.question: What nerve supplies the first and second lumbricals?
questions.explanation: The lateral two lumbricals (to index and middle fingers) are supplied by the median nerve. The medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers) are supplied by the ulnar nerve. This dual innervation pattern is unique among hand muscles.

questions.question: What is empyema?
questions.explanation: Empyema is the accumulation of pus in the pleural cavity, usually resulting from bacterial infection (often complicating pneumonia). It requires drainage, either by chest tube insertion or surgical decortication. Empyema is distinguished from simple pleural effusion by the presence of purulent material.

The adult liver weighs approximately 1500 grams, constituting about 2.5% of total body weight in healthy adults. The liver is the largest internal organ and the largest gland in the human body. In newborns, the liver is proportionally larger, contributing to the characteristic protuberant abdomen of infants.
questions.question: What is the approximate weight of an adult liver?
From which vessel do the inferior phrenic arteries usually arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior phrenic arteries are usually the first branches of the abdominal aorta, arising immediately after it passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, though they may arise from the celiac trunk. They supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm and give off superior suprarenal arteries. Each artery has a medial and lateral branch.

The oesophagus is a muscular tube approximately 25 cm long extending from the cricoid cartilage to the stomach. This measurement represents the standard adult oesophageal length and is clinically important for endoscopic procedures. The length may vary slightly between individuals based on body habitus.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of the oesophagus in an adult?

questions.explanation: The iliolumbar ligament extends from the transverse processes of L5 vertebra (and sometimes L4) to the iliac crest and iliac fossa. This strong ligament helps stabilize the lumbosacral junction and limits rotation at L5-S1. It forms an important surgical landmark in posterior approaches to the lumbar spine and pelvis. The ligament has superior and inferior bands; the superior band attaches to the transverse process and iliac crest, while the inferior band extends from the transverse process to the upper part of the sacral ala.
questions.question: The iliolumbar ligament connects which two structures?
options: L5 transverse process to iliac crest

questions.explanation: The scaphoid and trapezium bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. The boundaries are formed by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally, and extensor pollicis longus medially. The radial artery crosses the floor.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the anatomical snuffbox floor?

questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris. This high opening impairs natural drainage when standing upright. The sinus is the largest paranasal sinus and is present in rudimentary form at birth.
questions.question: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into which structure?

questions.explanation: The anterior bellies of the right and left digastric muscles form the lateral boundaries of the submental triangle. The hyoid bone forms the base (inferior boundary), and the mylohyoid muscle forms the floor. The triangle contains submental lymph nodes and is located in the midline below the chin.
questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric forms part of which triangle?

questions.explanation: The transverse head of adductor hallucis originates from the plantar ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints. Together with the oblique head (from bases of metatarsals 2-4), it inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit. The transverse head contributes to maintaining the transverse arch by drawing the metatarsal heads together.
options: Bases of metatarsals 2-4; medial longitudinal arch
Plantar ligaments of MTP joints; transverse arch
questions.question: The adductor hallucis has two heads. The transverse head originates from which structure and contributes to maintaining which arch?
The gastroduodenal artery typically arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The gastroduodenal artery arises from the common hepatic artery (distal to the origin of the gastric and splenic arteries but proximal to the bifurcation into hepatic artery proper and gastroduodenal artery). It descends posterior to the first part of the duodenum, where it divides into two terminal branches: the right gastroepiploic artery (running along the greater curvature) and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (supplying the pancreatic head and duodenum). The gastroduodenal artery is intimately related to the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb and can erode into this vessel, causing life-threatening hemorrhage.

questions.question: What predisposes elderly individuals to Colles' fracture?
questions.explanation: predisposes elderly individuals to Colles' fracture from relatively minor falls. Decreased bone density makes the distal radius unable to withstand forces that younger bone would tolerate. This is the most common wrist pathology in persons over 50 years old.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the distal third of the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The left colic artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the distal one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, and left colic (splenic) flexure through its ascending branch. The ascending branch anastomoses with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery of Drummond. This anastomosis at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) represents the watershed between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories and is vulnerable to ischemia. The splenic flexure may be relatively poorly supplied by collaterals, making it susceptible to ischemic colitis in low-flow states.

During inspiration, expansion of the thoracic cavity (through rib elevation and diaphragm descent) increases intrathoracic volume and creates negative pressure within the chest. This negative pressure draws air into the lungs. The pleural cavity pressure becomes more negative, preventing lung collapse.
questions.question: What creates negative intrathoracic pressure?

questions.explanation: The junction of the middle and outer third of the clavicle represents its weakest point. Transmission of forces during falls on the shoulder or hand frequently exceeds bone strength at this location. This indirect force mechanism is the usual cause of clavicular fracture.
questions.question: At which junction along the clavicle does fracture most commonly occur?
Which muscle produces wrist flexion and abduction?
questions.explanation: produces both wrist flexion and wrist abduction (radial deviation). It is a prominent muscle in the anterior forearm, easily palpable lateral to palmaris longus. The muscle is supplied by the median nerve.

questions.question: Which ligament connects the epiglottis to the hyoid bone?
questions.explanation: The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the anterior surface of the epiglottis to the upper border of the hyoid bone. The thyroepiglottic ligament attaches the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage. The epiglottis is also connected to the tongue by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds. These ligaments maintain epiglottic position during swallowing.

The lumbosacral triangle (Marcille's triangle) has the medial border of psoas major forming its lateral boundary, with the body of L5 vertebra medially and the ala of sacrum as its base. The floor consists of the transverse process of L5 and the iliolumbar ligament. This triangle is clinically significant as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at its lateral angle, making it an important landmark during pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the lumbar triangle of Marcille?
What is the effect of diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction causes the muscle to descend (central tendon is relatively fixed by the pericardium and IVC), increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrathoracic pressure (creating negative pressure that draws air in). Simultaneously, abdominal volume decreases and intra-abdominal pressure increases, displacing abdominal viscera downward and forward. The diaphragm is responsible for about 75% of the work of quiet breathing.

Each foot has 26 bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges (the great toe has 2 phalanges; the other four toes each have 3 phalanges). Understanding foot bone anatomy is fundamental to podiatry, orthopaedics, and diagnosis of stress fractures, Lisfranc injuries, and other foot pathologies.
questions.question: Podiatry is the medical specialty dealing with the study and care of the feet. The foot has how many bones in total (tarsals + metatarsals + phalanges)?
Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
questions.explanation: is not part of the rotator cuff; it acts as a medial rotator and adductor of the humerus. The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. These muscles fuse with the joint capsule and stabilize the glenohumeral joint.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between the two palmar arches?
options: Provide redundant blood supply with extensive anastomoses
questions.explanation: The superficial and deep palmar arches provide redundant blood supply to the hand through extensive anastomoses. This collateral circulation protects hand perfusion even with single artery occlusion. The arches interconnect via perforating branches and palmar metacarpal communications.

questions.question: Which rib does the costal pleural reflection cross midaxillarily?
questions.explanation: The costal line of pleural reflection passes obliquely, crossing the tenth rib in the midaxillary line (MAL). It crosses the eighth rib in the midclavicular line and becomes continuous posteriorly with the vertebral lines at the neck of the twelfth rib. This surface marking is crucial for safe thoracentesis.

questions.question: The broad ligament contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, containing multiple structures: the uterine tube in its superior free edge (mesosalpinx), the round ligament of uterus in its anteroinferior portion, the ovarian ligament posteriorly, and the ovarian vessels in its lateral extension (suspensory ligament of ovary/infundibulopelvic ligament). The broad ligament is divided into mesosalpinx (above ovary), mesovarium (posterior, supporting ovary), and mesometrium (below ovary, containing uterine vessels). It does not provide significant uterine support despite its name.

The ulnar nerve passes through Guyon's canal (ulnar tunnel) at the wrist alongside the ulnar artery. The canal is bounded by the pisiform and hook of hamate. Compression here causes ulnar tunnel syndrome affecting hand muscles but sparing forearm muscles.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through Guyon's canal?

questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella). This is a key landmark for identifying the vein during varicose vein surgery and for cannulation. At the ankle, it ascends anterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.question: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to which bony knee landmark, approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella?

questions.explanation: The celiac ganglion, the largest of the prevertebral (preaortic) ganglia, receives preganglionic sympathetic fibers primarily via the greater splanchnic nerve (T5-T9), with contributions from the lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11). These preganglionic fibers synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers distribute along arterial branches from the celiac trunk to supply foregut derivatives. The vagus nerve also contributes parasympathetic fibers to the celiac plexus, but these pass through without synapsing. The celiac plexus surrounds the origin of the celiac trunk and is the largest autonomic plexus in the body.
questions.question: The celiac ganglion receives preganglionic fibers via which nerve?

questions.explanation: The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment, then pierces the deep fascia in the lower third of the leg to become cutaneous. It supplies most of the dorsum of the foot and toes (except the first web space, supplied by the deep fibular nerve, and the lateral border, supplied by the sural nerve).
options: At the level of the fibular head proximally
In the lower third of the leg by piercing the deep fascia
At the level of the ankle joint and mortise
In the popliteal fossa at the posterior aspect of the knee
At the level of the medial malleolus medially
questions.question: The superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies the lateral compartment of the leg. Where does it emerge as a cutaneous nerve?

questions.explanation: The left gastric artery is the smallest of the three branches of the celiac trunk (along with splenic and common hepatic arteries), arising at the T12/L1 level. It ascends to the cardioesophageal junction, giving off esophageal branches to the abdominal esophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature of the stomach in the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the right gastric artery. It supplies both surfaces of the stomach along the lesser curvature. An aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery, running in the gastrohepatic ligament.
questions.question: The left gastric artery arises from which vessel?
Semitendinosus inserts into the medial surface of the superior part of the tibia, joining which two muscles to form the pes anserinus?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus joins sartorius and gracilis at the pes anserinus on the superior medial surface of the tibia. As its name implies, semitendinosus has a long rounded distal tendon. All three pes anserinus muscles cross both the hip and knee joints from three different compartments, making this insertion a multi-compartment landmark.

The medial fascial compartment of the thigh receives its blood supply from the profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery via its perforating branches and from the obturator artery. The nerve supply is from the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4). The profunda femoris is the major blood supply to all three thigh compartments via its perforating branches.
questions.question: The main blood supply to the medial compartment of the thigh comes from which two arteries?

options: Supination optimal with flexed elbow, flexion optimal mid-pronation
questions.question: How does forearm position affect biceps function?
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is most effective as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90� (maximum mechanical advantage). As a flexor, it's most effective when the forearm is in mid-prone position. When fully supinated, the tendon is wrapped around the radius, reducing flexion efficiency.

questions.question: How many lobes does the mammary gland contain?
questions.explanation: The mammary gland is formed of 15-20 lobes, each consisting of numerous lobules. The lobes and lobules are separated by interlobar and interlobular fibrous and fatty tissue called the ligaments of Cooper. Each lobe drains through its own lactiferous duct, which opens onto the nipple summit.

questions.question: The lingual tonsil is located on which surface of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior third (dorsal surface) of the tongue behind the sulcus terminalis. It forms part of Waldeyer's ring with the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils. The lingual tonsil is covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. Hypertrophy can cause airway obstruction or dysphagia.

Radiographically, diaphragmatic paralysis is recognized by elevation of the affected hemidiaphragm and paradoxical movement. On fluoroscopy, the paralyzed hemidiaphragm moves upward during inspiration (instead of descending) due to passive displacement by abdominal pressure. This is called the "sniff test."
questions.question: What indicates diaphragmatic paralysis radiographically?
Which branches arise from the first part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The first part of the axillary artery (from lateral border of first rib to upper border of pectoralis minor) gives off only one branch. This is the superior (highest) thoracic artery. The second part gives two branches while the third part gives three branches.

questions.question: Which structure marks the base of the appendix on the surface?
questions.explanation: McBurney's point marks the base of the appendix and is located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. This is the point of maximum tenderness in acute appendicitis and guides the surgical incision. The tip of the appendix, however, can vary considerably in position.

questions.question: Which nerve injury causes loss of the regimental badge sensation?
questions.explanation: injury causes loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area (lateral shoulder over deltoid). This sensory territory is supplied by the superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve, the cutaneous continuation of the axillary nerve. The injury also causes deltoid paralysis affecting shoulder abduction.

The glenohumeral joint capsule is weakest inferiorly, making this the most common site for dislocation. The capsule is thin and lax to allow wide range of movement, particularly abduction. Superior movement of the humeral head is prevented by the coraco-acromial arch rather than capsular strength.
questions.question: What is the anatomical position of the glenohumeral joint capsule's weakest area?

options: Subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks
questions.explanation: The subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks pass behind the medial third of the clavicle, separated only by the subclavius muscle. Fracture of the clavicle, especially displaced fractures, can injure these neurovascular structures. The subclavius muscle provides some protection.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk during clavicle fracture?

questions.explanation: Adjacent bronchopulmonary segments are separated by connective tissue septa. Intersegmental veins run in these septa and serve as guides for surgically separating segments. The septa act as natural barriers preventing spread of infection between segments (though cancer and tuberculosis can break through).
questions.question: What separates adjacent bronchopulmonary segments?
What provides the primary blood supply to the rotator cuff?
questions.explanation: The rotator cuff receives blood supply from three main sources: anterior circumflex humeral artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery, and suprascapular artery. A critical zone exists in the supraspinatus tendon with relatively poor vascularity, predisposing this area to degeneration and tears.
options: Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral plus suprascapular

questions.explanation: s are intra-articular fractures of the distal phalanx resulting from avulsion of the extensor tendon. These can be associated with small dorsal fragments or larger articular fragments with volar subluxation. Jersey fractures involve avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus instead.
questions.question: What type of fracture results from avulsion of the extensor tendon from the distal phalanx?

questions.explanation: At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve divides into the common fibular nerve (laterally, following the medial border of biceps femoris) and the tibial nerve (medially). From lateral to medial: common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, then popliteal artery (deepest). This arrangement changes inferiorly as the popliteal vein crosses to lie posterior to the artery.
questions.question: In the popliteal fossa, the popliteal artery lies deepest and the tibial nerve most superficially. In what order, from lateral to medial, are the structures arranged superiorly within the fossa?
options: Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
Tibial nerve, common fibular nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Common fibular nerve, popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal vein, popliteal artery, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve

questions.explanation: The caudate lobe, although anatomically part of the right lobe, is functionally part of the left lobe based on blood supply and biliary drainage. It receives blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and drains bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. Similarly, the quadrate lobe receives blood from the left hepatic artery and drains into the left hepatic duct.
questions.question: Which lobe of the liver is functionally part of the left lobe?
Which nerve provides motor innervation to the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5 - "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provides the entire motor innervation to the diaphragm, including both muscular portions and central tendon. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Although the lower six intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12) provide sensory innervation to the peripheral parts of the diaphragm, they contribute no motor supply. Damage to one phrenic nerve causes paralysis of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, which appears elevated on chest radiograph. Bilateral phrenic nerve injury severely compromises respiratory function, particularly in supine position.

questions.question: What are Rotter's nodes?
questions.explanation: Rotter's nodes (interpectoral nodes) lie between the pectoralis major and minor muscles. They are part of the axillary lymphatic drainage pathway. During modified radical mastectomy, these nodes may be removed along with the pectoral fascia. Their involvement affects staging and prognosis.

The linea alba is a fibrous raphe extending in the midline from the xiphoid process superiorly to the pubic symphysis inferiorly, formed by the fusion of aponeuroses from both sides (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis from each side). It separates the right and left rectus abdominis muscles and is relatively avascular (appearing white, hence its name), making it an ideal site for midline surgical incisions. The linea alba is wider above the umbilicus and narrows below it. Diastasis recti (separation of recti muscles) involves widening of the linea alba, particularly common during pregnancy and in obesity.
questions.question: The linea alba extends between which two points?
Which effect does vagal stimulation have on the heart?
questions.explanation: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation decreases heart rate (negative chronotropy), decreases conduction velocity through the AV node, and slightly decreases contractility. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors (M2) in the SA node, AV node, and atrial muscle. The right vagus preferentially affects the SA node; the left vagus affects the AV node.

questions.question: Which vessel forms the left heart border?
questions.explanation: The left border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed almost entirely by the left ventricle, with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. This border extends from the 2nd left costal cartilage to the apex beat in the 5th intercostal space.

questions.question: The rectus abdominis muscle inserts onto which structures?
questions.explanation: The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and pubic symphysis and inserts superiorly onto the xiphoid process and the costal cartilages of ribs 5-7. The muscle is intersected by three or four tendinous intersections that are firmly adherent to the anterior rectus sheath, creating the characteristic "six-pack" appearance in individuals with low body fat. These intersections represent remnants of the segmental myotomes from which the muscle develops and typically occur at the level of the xiphoid process, umbilicus, and midway between these landmarks.

questions.question: Which structure separates the caudate lobe from the quadrate lobe?
questions.explanation: The porta hepatis (transverse fissure) separates the caudate lobe (posterosuperiorly) from the quadrate lobe (anteroinferiorly) on the visceral surface of the liver. The porta hepatis contains the portal vein, hepatic artery, hepatic ducts, lymphatics, and nerves entering or leaving the liver. The caudate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis anteriorly, the IVC groove posteriorly, and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum on the left. The quadrate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis posteriorly, the gallbladder fossa on the right, and the fissure for the ligamentum teres on the left.

The conjoint tendon (formed by fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) inserts onto the pubic crest and pectineal line (pecten pubis), reinforcing the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medially. The pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line and is used in some hernia repairs (Cooper's ligament repair). The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and symphysis, not the pectineal line. The lacunar ligament (medial extension of the inguinal ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line.
questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the pectineal line?
Which muscles elevate the scapula?
options: Upper and middle trapezius, levator scapulae
questions.explanation: Elevation of the scapula is caused by contraction of upper and middle fibers of trapezius and levator scapulae muscles. This movement is associated with elevation of the lateral end and depression of the medial end of the clavicle. Shoulder shrugging demonstrates this action.

questions.question: The vas deferens is derived from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The vas deferens (ductus deferens) develops from the mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct) in males under the influence of testosterone. In females, the mesonephric duct regresses due to absence of testosterone, while the paramesonephric duct (M?llerian duct) develops into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina. The epididymis also develops from the mesonephric duct, while the seminal vesicles arise as outgrowths from the distal mesonephric duct. The prostate and bulbourethral glands develop from the urogenital sinus. Understanding embryology helps explain congenital anomalies of the reproductive tract.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the superficial cervical fascia?
questions.explanation: The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein within the superficial cervical fascia containing platysma. They receive drainage from the scalp and auricle. Efferents pass to the deep cervical chain.

The anterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects embryologic derivation from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively. The digastric helps open the mouth and elevate the hyoid.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the anterior belly of the digastric?
Which muscle extends the little finger independently?
questions.explanation: independently extends the little finger, working alongside extensor digitorum. It is located in the posterior forearm compartment and supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve. The muscle has its own compartment under the extensor retinaculum.

questions.question: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by which structure?
questions.explanation: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal vessels and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above it in the foramen's upper part but does not traverse it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large opening.

options: Sustentaculum tali of calcaneus and talus
All five metatarsal bases and the navicular
Base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform
Plantar surface of cuboid and bases of 3rd�5th metatarsals
questions.explanation: The long plantar ligament (longest ligament in the foot) passes from the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the ridges on the plantar surface of the cuboid and the bases of the 3rd-5th metatarsals. It is a primary support for the lateral longitudinal arch. In combination with the short plantar (plantar calcaneocuboid) ligament, it forms the floor of the fibularis longus tendon groove on the cuboid.
questions.question: The long plantar ligament, an important supporter of the lateral longitudinal arch, passes from the calcaneus to which structures?

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament separates the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver on the anterior and superior surfaces, extending from the diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall to the liver surface. However, the functional division between right and left lobes (Couinaud's segmentation) is defined by the main portal fissure (Cantlie's line), an imaginary plane running from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the IVC groove posteriorly, containing the middle hepatic vein. This functional division corresponds to the distribution of the right and left branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts. The quadrate and caudate lobes, though anatomically part of the right lobe, are functionally part of the left lobe.
questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left lobes of the liver anatomically?
What is significant about the 3rd right posterior intercostal?
questions.explanation: The 3rd right posterior intercostal artery typically gives off the right bronchial artery (though the origin is variable). The two left bronchial arteries usually arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta. Bronchial arteries provide the nutrient blood supply to the bronchial tree and lung tissue.

The right gastric artery usually arises from the hepatic artery proper near the porta hepatis, though it may occasionally branch from the gastroduodenal or left hepatic artery. It descends to the pylorus, then ascends along the lesser curvature of the stomach within the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the left gastric artery (the smallest but most consistent branch of the celiac trunk). This anastomotic network along the lesser curvature provides collateral circulation and must be carefully ligated during gastric resections to avoid ischemia or bleeding.
questions.question: The right gastric artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: Small cricothyroid arterial branches from the superior thyroid arteries anastomose across the median cricothyroid ligament. This anastomosis crosses the ligament horizontally and must be considered during emergency cricothyroidotomy. The vessels typically run superiorly along the cricothyroid membrane.
questions.question: Which artery forms an anastomosis across the median cricothyroid ligament?
Which nerve pierces the left dome of diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome of the diaphragm to supply the abdominal surface. The right phrenic nerve passes through the caval opening in the central tendon. Both phrenic nerves provide motor supply to the entire diaphragm and sensory supply to its central portion.

The parotid (Stensen's) duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth. The duct crosses the masseter superficially before piercing the buccinator. A small accessory parotid gland may be present along the duct on the masseter (socia parotidis).
questions.question: The parotid gland duct opens opposite which tooth?

questions.explanation: The sacrotuberous ligament and sacrospinous ligament, in conjunction with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. They primarily stabilize the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint under the weight of the vertebral column. These ligaments are critical surgical landmarks in posterior pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Which two ligaments, combined with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?

questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) is a fibromuscular band arising from the right crus of the diaphragm near the esophageal hiatus (some sources describe both crura contributing), passing posterior to the pancreas to insert onto the duodenojejunal flexure and sometimes the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supports the duodenojejunal junction at the posterior abdominal wall and marks the transition from fixed (retroperitoneal) duodenum to mobile (intraperitoneal) jejunum. This landmark is important surgically and radiologically, as widening of the angle suggests a mass in the pancreatic head.
questions.question: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) arises from which structure?

questions.explanation: The lateral cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery (behind pectoralis minor). The medial cord lies medially and the posterior cord lies posteriorly to the second part. Below pectoralis minor, the cords give rise to their terminal branches.
questions.question: Which cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery?

questions.explanation: Initial management of chylothorax is conservative: chest tube drainage, nutritional support with medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) diet or total parenteral nutrition (TPN) to reduce chyle production, and treatment of underlying cause. Many cases resolve with conservative management. Persistent cases (>2 weeks, >1L/day drainage) may require surgical intervention.
questions.question: How is chylothorax initially managed?
Which peritoneal ligament contains the ovarian vessels?
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian vessels (artery and vein) and nerves passing from the lateral pelvic wall to the ovary. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus and contains no significant vessels. The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, with the ovarian vessels running in its superior lateral extension.

The ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane. It attaches medially to the ischium posteroinferior to the acetabulum and laterally to the greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament. Like all three extracapsular hip ligaments, it becomes taut during extension, stabilizing the joint in the standing position.
questions.question: Which hip joint ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane and attaches medially to the ischium just posteroinferior to the acetabulum?
What lies posterior to the male urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: In males, the seminal vesicles and ampullae of the vas deferens lie posterior to the bladder base, and the rectum lies posterior to these structures, separated by the rectovesical fascia (Denonvilliers' fascia). The rectovesical pouch of peritoneum separates the upper part of the bladder from the rectum. In females, the vagina lies directly posterior to the bladder.

questions.question: Which compartment contains structures passing through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The flexor compartment of the hand receives structures passing through the carpal tunnel, including flexor tendons and the median nerve. The tunnel's confined space makes it susceptible to compression syndromes. Any lesion diminishing compartment size can result in median nerve compression.

questions.question: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, defined as the midpoint between which two bony landmarks?
options: Pubic tubercle and anterior superior iliac spine
Medial malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine
Inguinal ligament and the femoral condyle
Anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
Pubic crest and posterior superior iliac spine
questions.explanation: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. At this point the femoral artery lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve. This is distinct from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, which overlies the femoral canal.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the adductor hiatus?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus (opening in the adductor magnus muscle), transitioning from the anterior compartment of the thigh to the popliteal fossa. The adductor hiatus is located at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the thigh. The femoral vein also passes through this opening. This question tests knowledge of lower limb anatomy in relation to pelvic structures, as the femoral vessels are continuations of the external iliac vessels that pass beneath the inguinal ligament.

The anal canal begins at the anorectal junction (where the rectum pierces the pelvic diaphragm formed by the levator ani muscle), located approximately one inch (2.5 cm) below and anterior to the tip of the coccyx. At this level, the puborectalis sling creates the anorectal angle. The anal canal extends approximately 3.8-4 cm to the anus (anal verge). The pectinate line divides the anal canal into upper (endodermal) and lower (ectodermal) parts. The white line of Hilton marks the lower border of the internal sphincter.
questions.question: Which structure marks the beginning of the anal canal?
What produces opposition of the thumb?
questions.explanation: is the primary muscle producing opposition of the thumb, bringing the thumb across the palm to touch the little finger. This movement involves flexion, abduction, and medial rotation at the carpometacarpal joint. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.

questions.question: How do the rotator cuff muscles stabilize the glenohumeral joint?
options: Through passive ligament and capsule action
Rotator cuff compresses humeral head into glenoid cavity
questions.explanation: Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability through their resting tone, actively compressing the humeral head into the glenoid cavity. The muscles form a tendinous cuff blending with the joint capsule, providing circumferential reinforcement. This active stabilization is essential given the joint's inherent bony instability.

The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint. This proximity makes the popliteal artery particularly vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures. The arrangement from deep to superficial is: artery, vein, then tibial nerve.
questions.question: Which neurovascular structure is the DEEPEST within the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint?
What is the primary extensor of the thumb interphalangeal joint?
questions.explanation: extends the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and assists with extension at the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints. Its tendon forms the medial border of the anatomical snuffbox. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

questions.question: Which vessels supply blood to the visceral pleura?
questions.explanation: The visceral pleura receives its arterial supply from branches of both the bronchial and pulmonary arterial systems. Venous drainage is to the pulmonary veins. Unlike the parietal pleura, the visceral pleura has no somatic sensory innervation and receives only autonomic vasomotor nerve supply.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer than the right because of the embryological descent of the heart and great vessels. As the heart descends from the neck into the thorax, it carries the aortic arch (and the nerve looping under it) downward. The right subclavian artery descends less, so the right nerve is shorter.
questions.question: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve longer?

options: The cuboid and calcaneus being wedge-shaped
The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being wedge-shaped
The plantar surfaces of all tarsals being flat
questions.explanation: The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, with their broader surfaces dorsally and narrower surfaces plantarly, providing the bony factor to the transverse arch. The ligaments (deep transverse metatarsal ligament and interosseous ligaments), the muscle fibularis longus, the transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior all contribute to maintaining this arch.
questions.question: Which factor provides the bony contribution to the transverse arch, with the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being specifically wedge-shaped?

questions.explanation: The hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and left subcostal vein. It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum, crosses at T8-9, and drains into the azygos vein. It receives lower left posterior intercostal veins.
questions.question: What forms the hemiazygos vein?
