questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove between the trachea and esophagus. This location makes it vulnerable during thyroid surgery. The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch while the right loops under the subclavian artery.
questions.question: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in which anatomical groove?

questions.explanation: The suprasternal space (of Burns) lies between the investing and pretracheal layers of deep cervical fascia above the manubrium. It contains the jugular venous arch, lymph nodes, and fat. The space extends laterally behind the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Infections can collect here forming a suprasternal abscess.
questions.question: Which space lies between the pretracheal and investing layers of deep cervical fascia?
The left renal vein passes between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The left renal vein passes anteriorly to the aorta and posteriorly to the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) before draining into the inferior vena cava. This anatomical relationship can lead to compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA, a condition called nutcracker syndrome (or left renal vein entrapment syndrome), which may cause hematuria, left flank pain, and varicocele. The left renal vein is longer than the right (7-10 cm vs 2-4 cm) and receives the left testicular/ovarian vein, left suprarenal vein, and inferior phrenic vein before entering the IVC.

The thoracentesis needle should be inserted immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein-artery-nerve) that runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib. Insertion below the rib risks injuring the intercostal vessels and nerve.
questions.question: Where should thoracentesis needle be inserted?

questions.explanation: Flexion-extension at the hip joint has the greatest range of movement, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees. Abduction-adduction has a range of 60-80 degrees, while internal-external rotation is 60-90 degrees. These ranges vary with the position of other joints and the state of surrounding soft tissues.
questions.question: Which movement at the hip joint has the greatest range, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees?
The cribriform plate is part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is the horizontal portion of the ethmoid bone forming the roof of the nasal cavity and floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It contains numerous foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers. The crista galli projects superiorly from the midline. Fractures cause CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia from shearing of olfactory nerve fibers.

The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limb. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. The duct enters the right venous angle (junction of right internal jugular and subclavian veins).
questions.question: Which lymphatic structure drains lymph from the right upper quadrant of the body?
Where does the axillary tail extend?
questions.explanation: The axillary tail (of Spence) is a process that extends from the upper lateral part of the breast into the axilla. It passes through an opening in the deep fascia and may reach as far as the third rib. Cancer in the axillary tail presents as an axillary mass.

The deep palmar arch (formed primarily by radial artery) supplies blood to deep hand structures and gives off palmar metacarpal arteries. These metacarpal arteries provide important contributions to digital blood supply. The arch lies approximately 1cm proximal to the superficial arch.
options: Deep hand structures and palmar metacarpal arteries
questions.question: What is the primary function of the deep palmar arch?
Which structure separates the frontal and temporal lobes?
questions.explanation: The lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) separates the frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe. The middle cerebral artery runs in this fissure. The insula lies deep within the lateral sulcus. Strokes affecting the middle cerebral artery often involve structures around this fissure causing characteristic neurological deficits.

The spleen lies deep to the left 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left hypochondrium. This relationship provides protection but also means that fractures of these ribs can lead to splenic rupture. The long axis of the spleen follows the line of the 10th rib. The spleen's position varies with respiration and body posture.
questions.question: Which ribs typically protect the spleen?

questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, enophthalmos) in Klumpke's paralysis results from injury to sympathetic fibers traveling with the T1 nerve root. These sympathetic fibers supply the head and neck. The association indicates severe lower trunk injury affecting both motor and sympathetic components.
questions.question: What causes Horner's syndrome in Klumpke's paralysis?
The teniae coli converge at which structure?
questions.explanation: The three teniae coli (longitudinal muscle bands: taenia libera, taenia mesocolica, and taenia omentalis) of the cecum converge at the base of the vermiform appendix, providing a reliable surgical landmark for locating the appendix during appendectomy. The teniae continue along the ascending, transverse, and descending colon but disappear at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anal verge), where the longitudinal muscle coat becomes complete around the circumference of the rectum. The teniae correspond to areas where the longitudinal muscle is thickened, while the areas between are thinner, allowing formation of sacculations (haustra).

questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left paracolic gutters?
questions.explanation: The mesentery of the small intestine, with its oblique root extending from the duodenojejunal flexure (L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (S1, right of midline), divides the infracolic compartment into right and left infracolic spaces. These spaces communicate laterally with the right and left paracolic gutters respectively. The paracolic gutters are depressions lateral to the ascending and descending colon where peritoneal fluid can track between the pelvis and upper abdomen. The right paracolic gutter communicates with the hepatorenal recess, providing a pathway for infection spread.

Hoarseness after cardiac surgery often results from injury to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve during manipulation of the aortic arch or ligamentum arteriosum. The nerve's close relationship to the aorta makes it vulnerable during surgery. Injury causes paralysis of the ipsilateral vocal cord, resulting in hoarseness and weak voice.
questions.question: What causes hoarseness after cardiac surgery?
What condition results from air in pleural cavity?
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is the presence of air in the potential space between the pleural layers, causing lung collapse. This can occur spontaneously, traumatically, or iatrogenically. Hemothorax involves blood, empyema involves pus, and pleural effusion involves abnormal fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity.

The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the left vagus nerve as it descends on the anterior surface of the oesophagus. This trunk enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and supplies the anterior gastric surface. It also gives off a large hepatic branch and a pyloric branch.
questions.question: Which nerve forms the anterior vagal trunk supplying the stomach?
Which structure forms the posterior wall of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver and diaphragm; and inferiorly by the transverse mesocolon. It communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow).

questions.question: Which muscle protracts the eyeball?
questions.explanation: The inferior oblique muscle is the only extraocular muscle that protracts (brings forward) the eyeball along with extorsion, elevation, and abduction. It arises from the maxilla at the anteromedial orbital floor and inserts on the posterolateral inferior eyeball. The muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). It has no relationship with the common tendinous ring.

options: Cephalic vein, lateral pectoral nerve, thoracoacromial artery
questions.explanation: The costocoracoid membrane portion of clavipectoral fascia between pectoralis minor and subclavius is pierced by three structures. These are the lateral pectoral nerve, the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery, and the cephalic vein joining the axillary vein. This membrane is continuous with the suspensory ligament of the axilla inferiorly.
questions.question: Which structures pierce the costocoracoid membrane of the clavipectoral fascia?

questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery gives off the anterior tibial recurrent artery, which ascends to the front of the knee to contribute inferolaterally to the genicular anastomosis. This vessel pierces the anterior tibialis muscle and anastomoses with the inferior lateral genicular artery. Knowledge of this anastomosis is important for understanding collateral circulation when the popliteal artery is occluded.
questions.question: The anterior tibial artery runs through the anterior compartment and enters the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery. It gives off which branch that contributes to the genicular anastomosis?
Which artery passes through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae?
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery ascends through the transverse foramina (foramina transversaria) of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. It enters the foramen of C6 and ascends to C1, then passes posteriorly around the lateral mass of atlas before entering the foramen magnum. The vertebral vein accompanies the artery through these foramina.

The phrenic nerve is formed from cervical nerve roots C3, C4, and C5 ("C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"). It provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. The long course from neck to diaphragm reflects the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region.
questions.question: Which nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?

questions.explanation: The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied by perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery, consisting of three or four arteries perforating adductor magnus. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to all three thigh compartments. The inferior gluteal artery provides additional supply to the proximal hamstrings via descending branches.
questions.question: The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied primarily by perforating branches of which artery?

questions.explanation: The interureteric ridge (interureteric fold) is a smooth muscular ridge connecting the two ureteric orifices and forms the posterior boundary (base) of the trigone. The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the internal bladder base with the two ureteric orifices forming the superolateral angles and the internal urethral orifice forming the inferior angle.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the bladder trigone?

questions.explanation: Reticulocytes (immature red blood cells still containing RNA) normally comprise 0.5-1.5% of circulating red blood cells, representing the daily replacement of senescent erythrocytes. The reticulocyte count increases in hemolysis or bleeding (compensatory bone marrow response) and decreases in bone marrow failure or nutritional deficiencies. The spleen removes excessive RNA from reticulocytes (pitting function).
questions.question: What is the normal percentage of reticulocytes in peripheral blood?
The os coxae (pelvic bone) is formed by the fusion of three bones. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The os coxae is formed by the fusion of three bones: the ilium, ischium, and pubis. They meet at the Y-shaped cartilage in the acetabulum, which fuses at approximately age 15-17 years. The acetabulum receives contributions from all three bones, though it is formed mainly by the ischium.

The brachioradialis reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the brachioradialis tendon at the distal forearm. Absence or diminution suggests C6 nerve root or radial nerve pathology proximal to the elbow.
questions.question: What nerve root is predominantly tested by the brachioradialis reflex?

questions.explanation: The lumbar plexus is formed within the substance of the psoas major muscle from the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots. The plexus gives rise to branches that emerge from different borders of the muscle: lateral border (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral nerves), anterior surface (genitofemoral nerve), and medial border (obturator nerve). The psoas major also receives direct motor innervation from L1-L4 nerve roots. The lumbar plexus supplies the anterior abdominal wall, external genitalia, and anterior and medial thigh.
questions.question: The lumbar plexus is formed within which muscle?
The superior deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from which structure?
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil drains to the superior deep cervical nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric node at the angle of the jaw. The soft palate and posterior tongue also drain to these nodes. The jugulodigastric node is also called the tonsillar node due to enlargement during tonsillitis.

The transverse colon has a dual blood supply: the right two-thirds from the middle colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery (midgut supply) and the left third from the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut supply). The junction between these territories forms the marginal artery (of Drummond) and represents the watershed area most vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: Which structure receives blood from both celiac and superior mesenteric arteries?

questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein has 10-12 valves that are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh. These valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also contain valves directing blood from superficial to deep venous systems. Incompetence of these valves leads to varicose veins most commonly in the leg.
questions.question: The great saphenous vein has 10-12 valves. These are more numerous in which segment of the vein?

questions.explanation: Morton's neuroma most commonly occurs in the third intermetatarsal space (between the 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads), where the medial and lateral plantar nerves communicate, creating a larger nerve prone to compression. It presents with burning pain and paraesthesia in the 3rd and 4th toes, aggravated by tight footwear and weight-bearing. Mulder's click is a clinical sign on examination.
questions.question: Morton's neuroma is a painful condition of the foot involving perineural fibrosis of a digital plantar nerve. In which intermetatarsal space does it most commonly occur?

questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) is the obliterated umbilical vein that runs in the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. It joins the left branch of the portal vein at the inferior end of the fissure for the ligamentum teres. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, forming caput medusae.
questions.question: Which structure forms the falciform ligament's free edge?
Where does the thoracic sympathetic trunk lie?
questions.explanation: The thoracic sympathetic trunk lies anterolateral to the vertebral bodies, just lateral to the anterior longitudinal ligament. It descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum and posterior mediastinum. Each trunk has 11-12 segmental ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion often fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion.

The chorda tympani carries special sensory (taste) fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to submandibular and sublingual glands. It branches from the facial nerve in the mastoid, crosses the middle ear, and joins the lingual nerve. Damage causes loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior tongue.
options: Special sensory (taste) from anterior two-thirds tongue
questions.question: The chorda tympani nerve carries which type of fibers?
Which condition involves median nerve compression in the forearm?
questions.explanation: involves median nerve compression between the two heads of pronator teres in the proximal forearm. Unlike carpal tunnel syndrome, this causes proximal symptoms and affects the palmar cutaneous branch. Forearm pain and median nerve sensory symptoms are characteristic.

questions.question: Which muscle is the ONLY component of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint and can therefore flex the thigh?
questions.explanation: Rectus femoris is the only quadriceps component that crosses the hip joint, originating from the anterior inferior iliac spine. Therefore, it can both extend the leg at the knee and flex the thigh at the hip. The three vasti originate from the femur itself and only cross the knee joint.

questions.question: What type of hernia is most common?
questions.explanation: Hiatus hernias (both sliding and rolling types) are far more common than congenital diaphragmatic hernias. They occur in middle-aged and older adults due to weakening of the tissues around the esophageal hiatus. Sliding hernias are much more common than rolling (para-esophageal) hernias.

The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung begins in the tail and runs through the entire length of the gland, receiving numerous tributaries along its course. It drains the majority of pancreatic tissue and usually joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This ampulla opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.
questions.question: Which duct drains the majority of the pancreatic tissue?
The scala media contains which fluid?
questions.explanation: The scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph, which has high potassium and low sodium concentration (similar to intracellular fluid). The scala vestibuli and scala tympani contain perilymph. The organ of Corti lies on the basilar membrane separating scala media from scala tympani. M�ni�re's disease involves endolymphatic hydrops.

The quadratus lumborum muscle forms the central posterior relation of each kidney. The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially, and the transversus abdominis muscle (its aponeurosis) lies posterolaterally. The diaphragm is posterior to the upper pole, and the subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run posterior to the kidneys.
questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately posterior to both kidneys?

questions.explanation: The hilum of the spleen faces anteromedially toward the stomach, receiving the splenic artery (which divides into 5-6 branches before entering) and giving exit to the splenic vein. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the hilum to the greater curvature of the stomach and contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. The splenorenal ligament connects the hilum to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and tail of the pancreas. The splenic hilum typically shows a distinct notch (splenic notch) on its superior border, a characteristic feature visible on cross-sectional imaging.
questions.question: The hilum of the spleen faces which direction?

questions.explanation: The posterior fontanelle (lambda) is located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures where the occipital and parietal bones meet. It is triangular and smaller than the anterior fontanelle. The posterior fontanelle typically closes by 2-3 months of age. Delayed closure may indicate hydrocephalus or skeletal dysplasia.
questions.question: The posterior fontanelle is located at which suture junction?

options: Sural nerve and posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh
Tibial nerve and common fibular nerve
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve divides at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa (or sometimes higher in the thigh or even within the pelvis) into the tibial nerve (medial and larger) and the common fibular nerve (lateral and smaller). The tibial nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole, while the common fibular nerve innervates the anterior and lateral leg compartments.
questions.question: The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body. At the level of the popliteal fossa, it divides into which two terminal branches?

options: Meralgia paraesthetica (burning pain on lateral thigh)
Knee pain from saphenous nerve compression
questions.question: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) enters the thigh just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. Compression of this nerve causes which specific condition?
questions.explanation: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2, L3) causes meralgia paraesthetica, characterized by burning, tingling, or numbness on the anterolateral aspect of the thigh. It is a purely sensory nerve with no motor component. Common causes include obesity, pregnancy, tight belts, and direct compression. Treatment is conservative with weight loss and activity modification.

The cricothyroid joint between the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage allows anteroposterior tilting (rotation). This movement elongates or shortens the vocal cords, changing their tension. Cricothyroid muscle contraction tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, tensing the cords. The joint is a synovial joint with a capsule and ligaments.
questions.question: The cricothyroid joint allows which movement?

questions.explanation: The first (medial) lumbrical is innervated by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3), while the lateral three lumbricals are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3). The lumbricals originate from the tendons of flexor digitorum longus and insert into the medial aspect of the extensor expansion over the lateral four digits. Their dual action balances flexion and extension.
questions.question: The lumbricals of the foot flex the proximal phalanges and extend the middle and distal phalanges of the lateral four digits. The first lumbrical is innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones. It drains medially into the great saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the great toe) and laterally into the small saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the little toe). This arch is the origin point of both major superficial veins of the lower limb.
questions.question: The dorsal venous arch of the foot drains medially into the great saphenous vein and laterally into which vein?
The prostate is divided into how many lobes?
questions.explanation: The prostate gland is classically described as having five lobes: anterior (fibromuscular, no glandular tissue), posterior (palpable on digital rectal exam, common site of carcinoma), median (between ejaculatory ducts, may enlarge to cause bladder outlet obstruction), and right and left lateral lobes (largest, common site of benign prostatic hyperplasia). Modern zonal anatomy describes peripheral zone (70%, site of most cancers), central zone (25%, around ejaculatory ducts), transitional zone (5%, surrounds urethra, site of BPH), and anterior fibromuscular stroma. The median lobe may project into the bladder when enlarged, causing urinary symptoms.

options: Deep facial vein to pterygoid plexus
questions.explanation: The deep facial vein connects the facial vein with the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa, draining deep facial structures. The pterygoid plexus drains via the maxillary vein to the retromandibular vein. This valveless connection provides a route for infection spread between face and cavernous sinus.
questions.question: Which vein drains the deep face?

questions.explanation: The middle third of the esophagus (thoracic portion) drains into the azygos venous system. The upper third drains into brachiocephalic veins, and the lower third into the portal system (via left gastric vein). These represent important sites of portosystemic anastomosis where esophageal varices can develop in portal hypertension.
questions.question: How does esophageal venous drainage occur in thorax?

options: Scaphoid palpation and radial artery assessment
questions.question: What is the clinical significance of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuffbox allows clinical palpation of the scaphoid bone (floor) and assessment of radial artery pulse (crossing the floor). Tenderness in the snuffbox after wrist trauma suggests scaphoid fracture. The borders (thumb extensor and abductor tendons) are easily identified.

questions.question: The femoral canal, the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, contains which structures and is the site of which type of hernia?
options: Lymphatics and loose connective tissue; femoral hernia
Femoral artery and nerve; femoral hernia
questions.explanation: The femoral canal, the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally contains lymphatics and loose connective tissue. It is the site of femoral hernias, which are more common in women (due to their wider pelvis and femoral ring). Femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (unlike inguinal hernias above and medial to it). They are at high risk of strangulation due to the rigid femoral ring.

questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The anterior belly of the digastric is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects the embryologic origin from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively.

questions.question: The incisive canal opens into which structure?
questions.explanation: The incisive canal opens inferiorly into the oral cavity at the incisive fossa in the anterior hard palate. Superiorly, it communicates with the nasal cavity. The canal transmits the nasopalatine nerve and terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. Embryologically, it marks the fusion of the primary and secondary palates.

questions.question: Compartment syndrome of the thigh is less common than leg compartment syndrome. Which compartment of the thigh is most commonly affected following a femoral fracture?
questions.explanation: Thigh compartment syndrome most commonly affects the anterior compartment, usually following femoral shaft fractures with significant hematoma formation, crush injuries, or arterial injuries. The anterior compartment contains the quadriceps muscles and femoral neurovascular bundle. Rising compartment pressure impairs perfusion, causing ischemia. Fasciotomy must include all three thigh compartments to ensure complete decompression.
options: Only the fascial sheath around the femoral vessels

questions.question: The Lisfranc joint (tarsometatarsal joint complex) connects the midfoot to the forefoot. Injury at this joint is clinically significant because it disrupts which arch?
options: Only the transverse arch of the foot
The transverse arch and potentially both longitudinal arches
questions.explanation: Lisfranc joint injuries disrupt the tarsometatarsal joint complex, which is the keystone of both the transverse arch and the longitudinal arches. These injuries range from subtle ligamentous sprains to complete fracture-dislocations. Missed Lisfranc injuries lead to progressive collapse of all foot arches, chronic pain, and disability. Early anatomical reduction and fixation are essential.

The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, bypassing the inguinal and iliac nodes. This drainage pattern follows the testicular vessels and reflects the embryological origin of the testes high on the posterior abdominal wall. In testicular cancer, metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes, not inguinal nodes (unless scrotal skin is involved). The scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This explains why orchiectomy for testicular cancer requires high ligation of the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring to include regional lymphatics.
questions.question: The testicular lymphatics drain to which nodes?
Which portion of the anal canal is derived from endoderm?
questions.explanation: The anal canal above the pectinate line is derived from endoderm (hindgut), while the portion below originates from ectoderm (proctodeum). This embryological distinction explains the different characteristics of the two regions: superior to the pectinate line, the mucosa is columnar, venous drainage is to the portal system via superior rectal veins, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes, and innervation is autonomic (insensitive to pain). Below the line, the epithelium is stratified squamous, venous drainage is systemic (middle and inferior rectal veins), lymph drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and sensory innervation is via the inferior rectal nerve (painful).

The floor (inferior boundary) of the lesser sac is formed by the transverse colon and its mesocolon, along with the fusion of the anterior and posterior layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac (omental bursa) is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; posteriorly by the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and posterior abdominal wall; superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac are typically detected as fluid between the stomach and pancreas on imaging.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the lesser sac?

questions.explanation: The 'screw-home mechanism' is the conjunct rotation that occurs in the final degrees of knee extension, when the tibia rotates laterally on the femur (in an open-chain position) or the femur rotates medially on the tibia (in a closed-chain position). Both descriptions describe the same biomechanical event. Popliteus 'unlocks' this mechanism to initiate knee flexion.
questions.question: The 'screw-home mechanism' of the knee refers to which specific movement that occurs at full extension?
options: Medial rotation of the femur on the tibia in the last few degrees of extension
Both A and B describe the same event
Lateral rotation of the tibia on the femur in the last few degrees of extension
Locking of the patellofemoral joint only
Posterior translation of the tibia at full extension

questions.question: The hyoglossus muscle separates which two important arteries?
questions.explanation: The hyoglossus muscle is a key surgical landmark separating the lingual artery into three parts: above, on, and below the muscle. The hypoglossal nerve and lingual vein lie superficially on the muscle. Deep lingual and sublingual arteries arise from the lingual artery in relation to this muscle.

questions.question: Which valve cusp is attached to the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: The septal cusp of the tricuspid valve is attached to the interventricular septum, while the anterior and posterior cusps are attached to the anterior and posterior ventricular walls respectively. The septal cusp receives chordae tendineae from the septal and posterior papillary muscles. Ventricular septal defects near the membranous septum can affect this cusp's support.

is the primary adductor of the thumb, bringing it toward the palm. It is supplied by the ulnar nerve, unlike the other thenar muscles. The muscle has two heads (oblique and transverse) that converge on the base of the proximal phalanx.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary adductor of the thumb?

questions.explanation: The scalene muscles fix and elevate the first rib during inspiration. With the first rib fixed, the external and internal intercostal muscles elevate the other ribs upward toward it. The scalene muscles are accessory muscles of respiration and are particularly active during forced inspiration.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the first rib?

questions.explanation: The 7-12 vallate (circumvallate) papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue. Each papilla is surrounded by a circular trench containing taste buds. Von Ebner's glands open into the trenches, washing the taste buds.
questions.question: The vallate papillae are arranged in which pattern?

questions.explanation: The hepatic (right colic) flexure is related posteriorly to the lower part of the right kidney and anteriorly to the liver and gallbladder. This relationship means that right renal pathology may manifest as right upper quadrant pain mimicking hepatobiliary disease. The hepatic flexure is more mobile than the splenic flexure, attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the hepatocolic ligament (part of the greater omentum). The flexure receives blood supply from the right colic artery (from SMA) and right branch of the middle colic artery, with anastomoses forming the marginal artery.
questions.question: The hepatic flexure is related posteriorly to which structure?

questions.explanation: "Student's elbow" is olecranon bursitis resulting from repetitive pressure and trauma to the posterior elbow while leaning on desks. The subcutaneous olecranon bursa becomes inflamed and swollen. The same condition in coal miners is called "miner's elbow" due to similar repetitive trauma.
questions.question: What causes student's elbow?
Which structure passes through the transverse mesocolon?
questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) and middle colic veins (to superior mesenteric vein) pass through the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon. The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the descending duodenum, serving as an important surgical landmark dividing the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The superior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, while the inferior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the peritoneum, not within the mesocolon itself.

questions.question: What structure forms the lateral boundary of mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The mediastinum is bounded laterally by the right and left pleural cavities and their contained lungs. Anteriorly, it is bounded by the sternum; posteriorly by the thoracic vertebrae. Superiorly, it extends to the root of the neck, and inferiorly to the diaphragm.

The external acoustic meatus measures approximately 2.9 cm in length from the concha to the tympanic membrane. The lateral one-third is cartilaginous containing cerumen glands, while the medial two-thirds is bony. Understanding this anatomy is essential for safe otoscopic examination and foreign body removal.
questions.question: The external acoustic meatus is what total length?
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all laryngeal muscles EXCEPT which one?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles receive innervation from the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The cricothyroid is also the only intrinsic muscle located externally on the larynx.

The spleen's medial (visceral) surface has multiple impressions from adjacent organs: gastric impression anteriorly (related to stomach via gastrosplenic ligament), renal impression posteroinferiorly (related to left kidney via splenorenal ligament), colic impression inferiorly (near left colic flexure), and pancreatic impression at the hilum (tail of pancreas in splenorenal ligament). The spleen sits in the left hypochondriac region, protected by ribs 9-11. Its lateral surface is smooth and convex, molded against the diaphragm and posterolateral abdominal wall. The characteristic splenic notch marks its superior border.
questions.question: The spleen is related medially to which structure?
The calcaneal tendon reflex (ankle jerk) tests which nerve roots when elicited by tapping the Achilles tendon?
questions.explanation: The calcaneal tendon (Achilles) reflex tests the S1 and S2 nerve roots. The reflex arc involves the tibial nerve (both afferent and efferent), the S1-S2 spinal cord segments, and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles. An absent ankle jerk is a hallmark of S1 root compression (commonly from L5/S1 disc herniation). The knee jerk tests L3 and L4.

questions.question: Which layer of the appendix contains abundant lymphoid tissue?
questions.explanation: The appendix has abundant lymphoid follicles in both the lamina propria and submucosa, unlike other parts of the intestine where lymphoid tissue is confined to the lamina propria. These follicles often extend into the submucosa, sometimes obliterating the clear boundary between layers. The appendix functions as a component of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT).

questions.question: Which structure indents each renal papilla?
questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces in each kidney. Two or three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.

Lymph nodes are present in all regions of the mediastinum: paratracheal and brachiocephalic nodes in the superior mediastinum; parasternal nodes anteriorly; tracheobronchial and hilar nodes in the middle mediastinum; and paraesophageal and paravertebral nodes posteriorly. Lymphadenopathy is a common cause of mediastinal widening.
questions.question: What structure lies in all mediastinal regions?

questions.explanation: The facial artery crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of the masseter muscle, where its pulse can be palpated. After crossing, it ascends toward the medial canthus as the angular artery. The artery winds around the mandible from the neck to reach the face. Facial vein crosses more anteriorly.
questions.question: The facial artery crosses which border of the mandible?

questions.explanation: The costocervical trunk is a branch of the second part of the subclavian artery (posterior to scalenus anterior). It divides into the superior intercostal artery (supplying the first two intercostal spaces) and the deep cervical artery (supplying deep neck muscles). This trunk is important in collateral circulation.
questions.question: What is the costocervical trunk?

questions.explanation: The gastrohepatic ligament (pars flaccida) forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum, extending from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of the duodenum to the liver (extending to the fissure for ligamentum venosum and porta hepatis). It contains the right and left gastric vessels along the lesser curvature, and in some individuals, an aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery arising from the left gastric artery. The lesser omentum is continuous with the hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa), which forms its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver?
Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the tip of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The tip of the tongue drains to submental lymph nodes. The lateral anterior two-thirds drains to submandibular nodes, while the medial anterior two-thirds drains to inferior deep cervical nodes. The posterior third drains to superior deep cervical nodes. Understanding lymphatic drainage is crucial for cancer staging.

The heart and pericardium are the main contents of the middle mediastinum, which also contains the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, parts of the phrenic nerves, and the main bronchi. The middle mediastinum is the central compartment of the inferior mediastinum.
questions.question: What position does the heart occupy mediastinally?

questions.explanation: The external intercostal muscle is deficient anteriorly at the costochondral junction and is replaced by the external (anterior) intercostal membrane. This fibrous membrane continues the plane of the muscle to the sternum. The internal intercostal muscle conversely is deficient posteriorly at the angle of the rib.
questions.question: At which location is the external intercostal muscle deficient?
What is the blood supply to the appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the appendix. It runs in the mesoappendix (the peritoneal fold connecting the appendix to the mesentery). This is an end artery without significant anastomoses, making the appendix vulnerable to ischemia if the vessel thromboses (as in appendicitis). The artery typically runs behind the terminal ileum.

During shoulder joint abduction, the shoulder girdle undergoes upward rotation of the scapula. This scapular movement is essential for achieving full arm abduction beyond 90 degrees. The trapezius and serratus anterior muscles produce this upward rotation of the scapula.
questions.question: What movements occur at the shoulder girdle during arm abduction?

questions.explanation: extend the interphalangeal joints while simultaneously flexing the metacarpophalangeal joints. This coordinated action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. Extensor digitorum extends the metacarpophalangeal joints but cannot independently extend interphalangeal joints without intrinsic muscle assistance.
questions.question: What muscle initiates finger extension at interphalangeal joints?

questions.explanation: The pleuroperitoneal membranes close the fetal communication between the pleural and peritoneal cavities. Failure of these membranes to close completely results in congenital diaphragmatic hernias, most commonly through the foramen of Bochdalek (posterolaterally). This is more common on the left side.
questions.question: What closes the pleuroperitoneal canal?
What forms the central tendon embryologically?
questions.explanation: The septum transversum is the mesodermal mass that forms the central tendon of the diaphragm. Initially located in front of the embryonic head, it migrates caudally during head folding. During this migration, cervical myotomes and nerves contribute muscle and nerve supply, explaining the phrenic nerve's long course from C3-5.

questions.question: The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly adheres to which extracapsular ligament, making it more vulnerable to sporting injury?
questions.explanation: The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly attached to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament at its midpoint. This attachment makes it less mobile and more vulnerable to injury than the lateral meniscus. The tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus are often torn together in contact sports as part of the classic 'unhappy triad.'

The phrenic nerves carry pain sensation from the parietal peritoneum and parietal pleura covering the central part of the diaphragm. Irritation here causes referred pain to the C3-C5 dermatomes (neck and shoulder, especially shoulder tip). Peripheral parts of the diaphragm receive sensory supply from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, with referred pain to the trunk wall.
questions.question: Which nerve carries pain sensation from the parietal peritoneum covering the diaphragm?

questions.explanation: The areola glands of Montgomery are intermediate in structure between lactiferous and sweat glands. They are greatly enlarged in pregnancy and lactation as subcutaneous tubercles. Their oily secretion acts as a protective lubricant during lactation, preventing nipple cracking.
questions.question: What are Montgomery's glands?
The inferior vena cava receives which vein at the L1 level?
questions.explanation: The right renal vein (shorter than the left, approximately 2-4 cm) drains into the inferior vena cava at approximately the L1-L2 level, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta. The left renal vein (longer, 7-10 cm) crosses anterior to the aorta at the same level to reach the IVC. The right renal vein receives only the right gonadal and right suprarenal veins (sometimes), while the left renal vein receives the left gonadal, left suprarenal, and left inferior phrenic veins before reaching the IVC.

The lesser trochanter is the traction epiphysis of the iliopsoas muscle, the great flexor of the hip joint. It projects from the posterior surface of the femur and is conical, pointing medially. It marks the lowermost fibers of the gluteus maximus insertion.
questions.question: The lesser trochanter, the traction epiphysis of which muscle, projects from the posterior surface of the femur and points in which direction?
How many structures contribute to diaphragm development?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm develops from four embryological structures: (1) septum transversum (forming central tendon), (2) dorsal esophageal mesentery, (3) peripheral rim from body wall, and (4) pleuroperitoneal membranes (closing the pleuroperitoneal canals). Incomplete fusion of these components leads to congenital diaphragmatic hernias.

The oesophageal hiatus is located at the T10 level in the muscular part of the right crus of the diaphragm. It transmits the oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The muscular sling of the right crus acts as a physiological sphincter, helping prevent gastroesophageal reflux.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the oesophageal hiatus?
Which structure lies in the hilum of the kidney most anteriorly?
questions.explanation: At the renal hilum, the renal vein lies most anteriorly, the renal artery lies in the middle, and the renal pelvis (with the ureter) lies most posteriorly. This arrangement can be remembered as "VAP" (Vein, Artery, Pelvis) from anterior to posterior. The hilum is located on the medial border of each kidney.

The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery pass through the triangular interval. This space is bounded by teres major superiorly, long head of triceps medially, and lateral head of triceps laterally. The structures then enter the spiral groove of the humerus.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the triangular interval?

questions.explanation: The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching lowest fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, along with contributions from the transversalis fascia. These arching fibers cross from lateral to medial, forming the superior boundary of the canal. The internal oblique muscle also contributes to the anterior wall laterally, where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament. The conjoint tendon (formed by the fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) reinforces the posterior wall medially but does not form the roof.
questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the inguinal canal?
Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the stylopharyngeus muscle?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) is the only cranial nerve that provides motor innervation to a pharyngeal muscle - the stylopharyngeus. All other pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). Stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing.

questions.question: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by three bony components. Which correctly describes the roof, walls, and floor?
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (mortise) is formed by: the roof (inferior surface of the tibia), the lateral wall (lateral malleolus from the fibula), the medial wall (medial malleolus from the tibia), and the floor (superior surface of the talus, the trochlea tali). This mortise-and-tenon configuration provides inherent bony stability, especially during dorsiflexion.
options: Roof: inferior fibula; walls: tibia bilaterally; floor: calcaneus
Roof: inferior tibia; walls: medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) malleoli; floor: trochlea tali
Roof: superior surface of talus; walls: tibia; floor: calcaneus
Roof: superior tibia; walls: talus on both sides; floor: navicular
Roof: fibula; walls: medial and lateral malleoli; floor: navicular

questions.question: The renal fascia (Gerota's fascia) encloses which structures?
questions.explanation: The renal fascia (Gerota's fascia), a condensation of connective tissue, encloses the kidney, perirenal fat, and suprarenal gland on each side, forming a distinct compartment. It consists of anterior and posterior layers that fuse laterally but remain open medially and inferiorly, allowing potential communication between the two sides medially and extension of infection or hemorrhage inferiorly. The fascia separates the perirenal space (containing kidney, suprarenal gland, and perirenal fat) from the posterior pararenal space posteriorly and anterior pararenal space anteriorly. This fascial envelope is important in limiting the spread of renal infections and tumors.

questions.question: Into which chamber does the coronary sinus drain?
questions.explanation: The coronary sinus, the main venous drainage vessel of the heart, opens into the right atrium between the inferior vena cava orifice and the tricuspid valve. It lies in the posterior part of the coronary (atrioventricular) groove and receives the great, middle, and small cardiac veins, along with other tributaries. A small Thebesian valve may partially cover its orifice.

questions.question: The fovea capitis of the femoral head transmits blood from which artery to the femoral head?
questions.explanation: The fovea capitis transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur). This vascular route is clinically important, as fractures of the femoral neck can disrupt primary blood supply and lead to avascular necrosis.

questions.question: The caudate lobe of the liver drains bile into which duct?
options: Both right and left hepatic ducts
questions.explanation: The caudate lobe of the liver, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe, is functionally independent, receiving blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and draining bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. It also has separate venous drainage directly into the IVC via small hepatic veins, independent of the main right, middle, and left hepatic veins. This unique drainage explains why the caudate lobe may hypertrophy in cirrhosis (where it maintains direct IVC access) and why it can function in Budd-Chiari syndrome when the main hepatic veins are occluded. The caudate process extends from the caudate lobe toward the porta hepatis.

The thenar space can readily spread infection into the connective tissue canals surrounding the lumbricals. Proximally, the thenar space communicates with the space of Parona. Distally, it is continuous with lumbrical canals, which then connect to web spaces, providing routes for infection spread.
questions.question: Which space infection can spread to lumbrical canals?

questions.explanation: Thenar muscles receive dual innervation: the recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The ulnar nerve supplies the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis and sometimes contributes to other thenar muscles.
questions.question: What nerve provides motor innervation to all thenar muscles?
Which type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia is most common?
questions.explanation: Bochdalek hernias are the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia, occurring through a posterolateral defect in the diaphragm due to failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close. They are more common on the left side (85%) and allow abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax, potentially causing respiratory distress in newborns. They represent a failure of normal diaphragm development.

questions.question: Which vein passes through the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein (formed by union of maxillary and superficial temporal veins) passes through the parotid gland substance. It divides into anterior and posterior divisions within the gland. The anterior division joins the facial vein; the posterior joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular. The facial nerve and external carotid artery also traverse the gland.

questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for fine adjustments of vocal cord tension?
questions.explanation: The vocalis muscle, lying parallel and inferior to the vocal cord, controls fine adjustments of cord tension. The cricothyroid provides gross tension changes by tilting the thyroid cartilage. The vocalis can selectively tense different portions of the vocal cord for pitch modulation.

The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing. All infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) serve this function. They are innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) except thyrohyoid which receives C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.question: Which muscle depresses the hyoid bone after swallowing?

questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends into the splenorenal ligament to reach the splenic hilum and is at risk of injury during splenectomy. The splenic vessels in the splenorenal ligament must be carefully ligated. Pancreatic fistula is a recognized complication of splenectomy. The tail represents about 30% of pancreatic tissue but is rarely the site of surgical disease.
questions.question: Which structure is at risk during splenectomy?
What typically causes posterior mediastinal masses?
questions.explanation: Posterior mediastinal masses are most commonly neurogenic tumors arising from sympathetic ganglia (ganglioneuroma, neuroblastoma), peripheral nerves (schwannoma, neurofibroma), or paraganglia (paraganglioma). Esophageal lesions, thoracic duct cysts, and extramedullary hematopoiesis can also occur posteriorly. In children, neuroblastoma is common.

The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from T10-11 ganglia, pierces the diaphragm, and synapses in the aorticorenal ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation primarily to the kidneys and suprarenal glands. Some fibers may also reach midgut derivatives. The nerve carries both efferent sympathetic and visceral afferent fibers.
questions.question: What does the lesser splanchnic nerve supply?
At what age does female breast development begin?
questions.explanation: Female breasts start developing at puberty under hormonal influence (estrogen and progesterone). They remain rudimentary in males throughout life. Most breast development in females occurs during the later months of pregnancy and lactation when the glandular tissue proliferates and becomes functional.

The base of the heart is formed primarily by the left atrium and a small portion of the right atrium. It is the posterior surface facing the vertebral column and esophagus. The four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the base. The term "base" refers to the posterior aspect, opposite to the apex, not to the inferior surface.
questions.question: Which chamber primarily forms the base of the heart?

questions.explanation: Perirenal (perinephric) fat is a layer of adipose tissue that lies outside the fibrous capsule and inside the renal fascia (Gerota's fascia). It cushions and protects the kidney. The renal fascia encloses both the kidney and suprarenal gland, while pararenal fat lies external to the renal fascia and forms part of the retroperitoneal fat.
questions.question: Which layer directly surrounds the kidney outside the fibrous capsule?
Which bone forms the hard palate anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The palatine processes of the right and left maxillae form the anterior three-quarters of the hard palate. The horizontal plates of the palatine bones form the posterior quarter. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities. The incisive foramen transmits the nasopalatine nerve anteriorly.

questions.question: Where does the membranous urethra pass through?
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch), specifically through the sphincter urethrae (external urethral sphincter). This is the shortest (1-2 cm) and narrowest part of the male urethra and the least distensible. It is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter, which is under voluntary control.

The inferior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the twelfth thoracic vertebra. Laterally, it is bounded by the curving costal margin formed by ribs 11 and 12. Anteriorly, the xiphisternal joint completes the boundaries, and the entire opening is closed by the diaphragm.
questions.question: Which vertebra bounds the inferior thoracic aperture posteriorly?
The foramen ovale transmits which nerve?
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale in the greater wing of the sphenoid transmits the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve. It also transmits the accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein. The nerve supplies muscles of mastication and provides sensation to the mandibular region.

questions.question: Which immune cells are found in splenic white pulp?
questions.explanation: The splenic white pulp consists primarily of T and B lymphocytes organized around central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS containing T cells) and in lymphoid follicles (containing B cells). The white pulp is responsible for immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens and antibody production. It represents about 15-25% of splenic tissue and increases in infections.

questions.question: Where do the anterior cardiac veins drain?
questions.explanation: The anterior cardiac veins (3-4 small veins) drain the anterior right ventricular wall and empty directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus. They cross the atrioventricular groove and are the only cardiac veins that don't drain via the coronary sinus. During cardiac surgery, these veins must be identified to avoid injury.

Gastrocnemius strain (tennis leg) typically occurs at the musculotendinous junction of the medial head of gastrocnemius, where the thick muscle belly transitions to the thin Achilles tendon. It occurs during sudden push-off activities and presents with acute posterior calf pain. The medial head is more commonly strained than the lateral because it is larger and generates greater force.
options: At the Achilles tendon insertion on the calcaneus
At the origin from the lateral femoral condyle
At the musculotendinous junction of the medial gastrocnemius head
questions.question: Gastrocnemius strain ('tennis leg') typically occurs at which specific location within the muscle?

questions.explanation: Hamman's sign (also called Hamman's crunch) is a crunching or clicking sound synchronous with the heartbeat, heard on auscultation over the precordium in pneumomediastinum. It's caused by the heart beating against air-filled tissue. The sign is named after Dr. Louis Hamman who described it in 1939.
questions.question: What clinical sign suggests pneumomediastinum?
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head can also occur after dislocation of the hip joint without fracture. How long after dislocation should the hip be reduced to minimize avascular necrosis risk?
questions.explanation: Emergency reduction of a dislocated hip should ideally be performed within 6 hours to minimize the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Prolonged dislocation stretches and compresses the retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head. The risk of avascular necrosis increases significantly after 6 hours. Posterior hip dislocations, the most common type, also risk sciatic nerve injury.

Afferent (sensory) nerve fibers from the kidneys travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at T10-T12 and L1 segments. This explains the referred pain pattern of renal colic, which radiates from the loin to the groin along the distribution of these dermatomes. Ureteric pain follows a similar pattern as the ureter shares this innervation.
questions.question: Which spinal segments provide afferent innervation from the kidney?

questions.explanation: The bones of both lower limbs total 60: 2 femurs, 2 patellae, 2 tibiae, 2 fibulae, 14 tarsals, 10 metatarsals, and 28 phalanges. This understanding is fundamental in trauma assessment and radiological interpretation. Each single lower limb contains 30 bones.
questions.question: How many bones are present in both lower limbs combined, considering femurs, patellae, tibiae, fibulae, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges?
The inferior vena cava is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), to the right of the midline and anterior to the right common iliac artery. From this point, it ascends on the right side of the aorta, anterior to the vertebral column, receiving tributaries in an asymmetric pattern. The IVC passes through the diaphragm (caval opening in central tendon) at T8 level to enter the thorax and immediately empties into the right atrium. The formation level (L5) is slightly lower than the aortic bifurcation (L4).

options: Its large bulk and dual blood supply
Its ability to plantarflex the ankle
Its broad origin from the ischial tuberosity
Its dual nerve supply from femoral and obturator nerves
Its consistent neurovascular pedicle and manageable dimensions
questions.question: The gracilis muscle is frequently used as a free flap in reconstructive surgery. It is most suitable because of which anatomical feature?
questions.explanation: The gracilis muscle is frequently used in reconstructive surgery because of its consistent neurovascular pedicle (medial femoral circumflex artery perforators and the obturator nerve), manageable length and bulk, and relatively small donor site morbidity. It is used for facial reanimation, limb reconstruction, and dynamic graciloplasty for sphincter reconstruction in fecal incontinence.

The pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenm�ller) is a depression in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx behind the torus tubarius (Eustachian tube opening). Nasopharyngeal carcinomas commonly arise in this recess. The recess is bounded anteriorly by the tubal elevation and posteriorly by the adenoid pad. Deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from this region.
questions.question: The pharyngeal recess (of Rosenm�ller) is located in which region?

questions.explanation: Thumb interphalangeal joint flexion tests the anterior interosseous nerve through flexor pollicis longus function. Inability to flex this joint while the metacarp ophalangeal joint is stabilized indicates anterior interosseous syndrome. This is demonstrated by inability to make the OK sign properly.
questions.question: Which nerve is tested by thumb interphalangeal flexion?

questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery is the principal vessel supplying midgut derivatives, extending from just distal to the major duodenal papilla to the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon. It originates from the abdominal aorta at the L1 level, immediately below the celiac trunk. Its branches include the inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic arteries, providing blood to the duodenum (distal to ampulla), jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and right two-thirds of transverse colon.
questions.question: The superior mesenteric artery supplies which embryological division of the gut?

questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) provides motor innervation to the infrahyoid strap muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. The thyrohyoid receives C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve. These muscles depress the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing.
questions.question: The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to which muscle group?
What is the normal capacity of an adult stomach?
questions.explanation: The adult stomach has a mean capacity of approximately 1.5 to 2 litres when distended, though it can accommodate more. The stomach is a highly distensible organ with significant variation in capacity between individuals. At birth, the capacity is only about 30 ml, increasing to 1000 ml at puberty.

The ileum predominantly occupies the right lower quadrant of the infracolic compartment, with the terminal ileum usually located in the pelvis. The ileum constitutes approximately 60% of the jejunoileal length. It characteristically ends at the ileocaecal junction on the medial aspect of the caecum.
questions.question: Which region does the majority of the ileum occupy?

questions.explanation: The gastric impression is a concave area on the visceral surface of the liver where it contacts the right side and lesser curvature of the stomach. Other impressions on the visceral surface include the duodenal, colic (from hepatic flexure), and renal impressions. These impressions reflect the relationships of the liver with adjacent viscera.
questions.question: Which impression is found on the visceral surface of the liver?

questions.explanation: The right phrenic nerve passes through the superior and middle mediastinum descending on the right side of the superior vena cava (SVC) and heart. The left phrenic nerve similarly descends on the left side of the heart. Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm, providing motor and sensory innervation.
questions.question: Which nerve descends on the right side of SVC?

options: 3�5 cm above the superior patellar pole beneath the quadriceps tendon
1 cm above the superior pole of the patella
To the level of the anterior superior iliac spine
Only to the level of the patella
10 cm above the patella into the anterior thigh
questions.explanation: The suprapatellar bursa extends approximately 3-5 cm above the superior pole of the patella, beneath the quadriceps tendon, and communicates freely with the knee joint cavity. In knee effusions, fluid accumulates in this bursa as well as the joint space, creating the characteristic fluctuant fullness above the patella. Aspiration is performed by needle insertion into the suprapatellar pouch.
questions.question: The knee joint has a synovial membrane that is extensive. The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the knee joint cavity and is clinically important because it extends how far above the patella?

questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including motor and sensory cortices for face and upper limb. It also supplies Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant hemisphere. MCA occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia more marked in upper extremity and face.
questions.question: The middle cerebral artery supplies which cortical area?
Which vein lies posterior to the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein lies posterior and to the right of the esophagus in the posterior mediastinum. The descending aorta lies posterior and to the left of the esophagus. The thoracic duct lies posterior to the esophagus. The vagus nerves form plexuses around the esophagus.

The nutrient artery, also called the medullary artery, is the main blood supply to the diaphysis of a long bone. It enters through the nutrient canal and nutrient foramen, branching within the medullary cavity. The epiphysis, metaphysis, and periosteum all have their own distinct arterial supplies from separate named vessels.
questions.question: The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is best described as the main artery of which part of a long bone?

questions.explanation: The duodenojejunal flexure is located at the level of the second lumbar vertebra (L2), approximately 2.5 cm to the left of the midline. This junction is supported by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), a fibromuscular band. The flexure marks the transition from the retroperitoneal duodenum to the intraperitoneal jejunum.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the duodenojejunal flexure lie?
At which vertebral level does the rectum commence?
questions.explanation: The rectum begins as a continuation of the sigmoid colon at the level of the third sacral vertebra (S3). It extends approximately 13 cm (5 inches) before terminating as the anal canal one inch below the tip of the coccyx. The rectum follows the curvature of the sacrum and coccyx, forming the sacral and perineal flexures.

The central tendon of the diaphragm is shaped like three leaves (trifoliate). It has no bony attachments but is partially fused with the inferior surface of the fibrous pericardium. All the muscular fibers of the diaphragm insert into this central tendon.
questions.question: What shape is the central tendon?

questions.explanation: The 19 bones of the hand (metacarpals and phalanges) collectively form 14 separate joints. These include the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints connecting fingers to palm and interphalangeal (IP) joints between finger segments. All are synovial joints with articular cartilage covering the bone surfaces.
questions.question: How many separate joints are formed collectively by the 19 bones of the hand?
The mental foramen typically lies below which tooth?
questions.explanation: The mental foramen is typically located on the lateral surface of the mandible below the second premolar tooth or between the first and second premolars. It transmits the mental nerve and vessels (terminal branches of the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle). The foramen position varies with age and tooth loss. It is a landmark for inferior alveolar nerve block.

questions.question: What forms the right heart border radiographically?
questions.explanation: The right border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed by the right atrium. The left border is formed primarily by the left ventricle with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. The superior border is formed by the great vessels (aorta and pulmonary artery).

The palatoglossus muscle forms the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of the fauces). It descends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. Unlike other tongue muscles, it is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory), not the hypoglossal nerve. The muscle elevates the posterior tongue during swallowing.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the anterior pillar of the fauces?

questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver is the triangular region on the posterior surface that is in direct contact with the diaphragm, devoid of peritoneal covering. This area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary ligament (superior and inferior layers) and is continuous with the groove for the inferior vena cava. The bare area represents the part of the liver that remained adherent to the diaphragm during embryological development. Small diaphragmatic veins in this region drain directly from the liver into the IVC without forming hepatic veins, and the right phrenic artery contributes to the vascular supply of this area.
questions.question: The bare area of the liver is related to which organ?

questions.explanation: The left ventricle forms most of the left (pulmonary) border of the heart, with a small contribution from the left auricle (atrial appendage) superiorly. The left border extends from the second left intercostal space to the apex in the fifth intercostal space. This border is related to the left lung and pleura, separated by the pericardium.
questions.question: Which chamber forms most of the left border of the heart?
Which muscle forms the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of this triangle consists of transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon), representing a potential weak area in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery, in contrast to indirect hernias which emerge lateral to the artery through the deep inguinal ring.

The levator anguli oris is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It elevates the angle of the mouth during smiling. The muscle arises from the canine fossa of the maxilla and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It lies deep to levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor muscles.
questions.question: The levator anguli oris muscle is innervated by which nerve branch?

questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle, part of the levator ani complex, forms a U-shaped sling that loops around the anorectal junction, creating the anorectal angle of approximately 90 degrees by pulling the rectum anteriorly toward the pubic symphysis. This angle is a critical component of the fecal continence mechanism, as relaxation of puborectalis during defecation straightens the anorectal angle to facilitate evacuation. Damage to the puborectalis (such as during childbirth or surgery) or its nerve supply (pudendal nerve and direct branches from S3-S4) can lead to fecal incontinence. The muscle is in tonic contraction at rest.
questions.question: Which muscle's contraction causes the anorectal angle?

options: Lateral tibial plateau of the knee
Tibial tuberosity on the anterior tibia
Posterior aspect of the medial knee
Lateral joint line of the knee
Medial tibia, 5�7 cm below the knee joint line
questions.question: The pes anserinus is located on the medial surface of the tibia. Pes anserinus bursitis presents with pain at which specific location?
questions.explanation: Pes anserinus bursitis presents with pain, swelling, and tenderness at the medial aspect of the tibia, approximately 5-7 cm below the knee joint line, at the common insertion of sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus. It is common in obese patients with knee osteoarthritis and is associated with valgus knee deformity. Treatment includes local steroid injection and physiotherapy.

The right lung in a healthy adult male weighs approximately 600 grams when filled with air, while the left lung weighs about 550 grams. The lungs are spongy, elastic organs that are pinkish in healthy individuals. In city dwellers, they may appear darker due to accumulation of carbon particles.
questions.question: What is the lung weight in a healthy adult male?
Which part of the bladder is most fixed in position?
questions.explanation: The neck of the bladder is the most fixed part, anchored by the puboprostatic ligaments (in males) or pubovesical ligaments (in females) and the lateral ligaments of the bladder. The remainder of the bladder is relatively mobile, allowing it to expand superiorly into the abdomen when full. The neck surrounds the internal urethral orifice.

questions.question: Which three joints does pectoralis minor movement affect?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor affects the sternoclavicular, scapulothoracic, and glenohumeral joints through its action on scapular position. It produces depression, downward rotation, and protraction of the scapula. These scapular movements influence the position and function of the clavicle and shoulder joint.

questions.question: What is the space of Disse in the liver?
questions.explanation: The space of Disse is the perisinusoidal space between the fenestrated endothelium lining the hepatic sinusoids and the hepatocytes. It contains hepatic stellate cells (fat-storing cells that can become fibrogenic), microvilli from hepatocytes, and allows exchange of materials between blood and hepatocytes. In cirrhosis, this space becomes fibrotic (capillarization), impairing hepatocyte function and exchange.

questions.question: How does the musculocutaneous nerve injury affect function?
questions.explanation: Musculocutaneous nerve injury greatly weakens forearm flexion (biceps and brachialis loss) and supination (biceps loss). Sensation is lost over the lateral forearm through the lateral cutaneous nerve. Some weak flexion remains through brachioradialis (radial nerve) and pronator teres (median nerve).
options: Forearm flexion and supination weakened, lateral forearm numbness

questions.question: The testicular vein on the left typically drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle. This anatomical difference explains the higher incidence (90%) of left-sided varicoceles, as the perpendicular drainage into the renal vein, along with the longer venous column and potential compression by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon), creates higher venous pressure on the left. The left testicular vein lacks valves or has incompetent valves, facilitating retrograde flow and varicosity formation.

The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula and then divides into the deep and superficial fibular nerves. At this point it is subcutaneous and highly vulnerable to injury from fractures, tight plasters, or prolonged cross-legged sitting. Injury causes foot drop due to paralysis of the anterior and lateral leg compartment muscles.
questions.question: The common fibular nerve winds around which specific part of the fibula to divide into its terminal branches?

questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater) is located on the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum, approximately 8-10 cm distal to the pylorus. At this site, the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi. The minor duodenal papilla, located 2 cm proximal to the major papilla, receives the accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini) when present. This anatomical arrangement is crucial for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum contains the major duodenal papilla?
A positive Trendelenburg sign (pelvis drops on the unsupported side during single-leg stance) indicates weakness of which muscle?
questions.explanation: A positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness of the gluteus medius on the stance (weight-bearing) side. Normally, gluteus medius contracts to prevent the pelvis from dropping on the swinging side.
