(c) Calculate the genotype group of a person with one slow and one fast allele.
(d) Predict the effect of the slow acetylator status.
(e) State the dosing consequence.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A phenomenon in which a drug is metabolized at a specific location before reaching systemic circulation, reducing its active concentration and bioavailability; the liver is the main site, but lungs, GI tract and vasculature also contribute.
(b)
• Absorption from the GI tract into the portal vein to the liver
• Hepatic metabolism by enzymes such as CYP450 into more water-soluble metabolites
• Reduced systemic bioavailability, since only the unmetabolized fraction reaches the circulation.
(c)
Enzyme activity (e.g. CYP2D6 polymorphisms), hepatic and GI health, route of administration, age, and drug interactions (inducers such as rifampicin increase, inhibitors such as ketoconazole decrease metabolism); plasma protein levels and GI motility are also named.
(d)
Lipophilicity (propranolol), solubility, molecular size, and drug formulation (sustained-release forms alter absorption rate and first-pass metabolism).
(e)
Bioavailability of orally given drugs is reduced; extensive first-pass: lidocaine, morphine; bypass: lithium and IV nitroglycerin.
(f)
Lipophilic drugs are absorbed easily but are extensively metabolized in the gut wall and liver; water-soluble drugs are less readily absorbed, which limits their first-pass metabolism.
(g)
Inducers (rifampicin) increase and inhibitors (ketoconazole) decrease metabolism; genetic polymorphisms in CYP2D6 alter drug metabolism and guide personalized therapy.
(h)
Reduced first-pass metabolism in liver disease necessitates dose adjustments to avoid toxicity.
(i)
First-pass often includes Phase I metabolism, but not all Phase I is first-pass: IV drugs bypass first-pass yet still undergo Phase I; Phase I converts lipophilic to hydrophilic compounds, while first-pass is a phenomenon that reduces oral bioavailability.
(j)
Nitroglycerin given orally undergoes significant liver first-pass and reduced bioavailability; sublingual or IV delivery enters the systemic circulation directly for rapid effect.
(k)
Drugs with high first-pass metabolism require higher doses or alternative routes (e.g. sublingual nitroglycerin).
(l)
Tamoxifen is a prodrug (first-pass converts it to active metabolites); aceclofenac is an active drug with an active metabolite similar to diclofenac, whose first-pass metabolism reduces bioavailability.
questions.question:
Discuss the first-pass effect.
(a) Define the first-pass effect.
(b) State the three-step mechanism.
(c) State the physiologic factors affecting it.
(d) State the physicochemical factors affecting it.
(e) State the parameter it reduces and the drugs given as examples that undergo or bypass it.
(f) Explain why lipophilic drugs undergo extensive first-pass metabolism.
(g) Explain the effect of drug interactions and genetic polymorphism on it.
(h) Explain the effect of liver disease on it.
(i) Distinguish first-pass effect from Phase I metabolism.
(j) Distinguish the route-related situations using IV and sublingual nitroglycerin.
(k) State the clinical consequence for dosing.
(l) State the examples of prodrug and active drug.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Metabolism is an enzyme-mediated process.
(b)
In neonates, phenytoin, barbiturates, analgesics and cardiac glycosides have plasma half-lives 2-3 times longer than in adults.
(c)
• Let adult half-life = t½(adult).
• Neonate t½ = 2 x t½(adult) to 3 x t½(adult).
(d)
Neonates and infants have lower enzyme activity (not fully developed), so metabolism is slower (e.g. paracetamol); in the elderly enzyme activity decreases, giving increased drug concentrations and a higher risk of adverse reactions.
(e)
Careful dosing is needed in neonates to avoid toxicity (paracetamol).
questions.question:
A neonate and an elderly patient are each given drugs normally cleared by hepatic metabolism, such as paracetamol and phenytoin.
(a) State the type of process by which these drugs are cleared.
(b) State the relationship between neonatal and adult half-lives.
(c) Calculate the half-life of a neonate relative to an adult using the reported 2 to 3 fold factor, showing the steps.
(d) Predict the effect of age on enzyme activity and exposure.
(e) State the dosing consequence.

Discuss the design of dosage regimens.
(a) Define dosage regimen and an optimal multiple dosage regimen.
(b) Describe the approaches to design (empirical, individualized, population averages with fixed and adaptive models).
(c) State the assumptions and the model used for population-average regimens.
(d) State the two adjustable parameters.
(e) Explain the effect of dose size on the plasma concentration-time profile.
(f) Explain the effect of increasing the dosing interval with unchanged dose on Cmax, Cmin, Cav and Cmax/Cmin.
(g) State the effect of a shorter dosing interval on accumulation and toxicity.
(h) Relate the design to the examples of penicillin and digoxin.
(i) State the examples of drugs needing minimum effective concentration or avoidance of toxic concentration.
(j) Explain why larger doses less frequently do not give the same result as smaller doses more frequently.
(k) State the limitation or trade-off of each approach.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A dosage regimen is the manner in which a drug is taken; an optimal multiple dosage regimen gives suitable doses by a suitable route with sufficient frequency to keep plasma concentration within the therapeutic window, without excessive fluctuations or accumulation, for the whole therapy.
(b)
Empirical (physician's clinical data and experience); individualized (based on the individual patient's pharmacokinetics); population averages (most often used): fixed model (average parameters used directly) or adaptive model (average parameters plus weight, age, sex, body surface area and pathophysiology such as renal disease).
(c)
All pharmacokinetic parameters are assumed constant during therapy; calculations use the open one-compartment model (two-compartment if β replaces KE and Vd,ss replaces Vd).
(d)
The dose size (quantity given each time) and the dosing frequency (time interval between doses); both govern the amount of drug in the body.
(e)
Therapeutic and toxic responses depend on dose size; the greater the dose size, the greater the fluctuation between Css,max and Css,min and the greater the chance of toxicity.
(f)
With the dose unchanged and the interval increased, Cmax, Cmin and Cav decrease but Cmax/Cmin increases; the opposite occurs when the interval is reduced.
(g)
A shorter dosing interval (higher frequency) results in greater drug accumulation in the body and toxicity.
(h)
Penicillin (wide therapeutic index): larger doses at longer intervals; digoxin (narrow therapeutic index): small, frequent doses.
(i)
Antibiotics need a minimum effective concentration maintained at all times; phenytoin (narrow therapeutic index) must not exceed the toxic concentration.
(j)
A proper balance of dose size and frequency is desired; larger doses less frequently cannot give minimum fluctuations, whereas smaller doses more frequently give smaller fluctuations.
(k)
Empirical is not very accurate; individualized is the most accurate but quite expensive (suited to hospitalised patients); population-average regimens become invalid if parameters change.

(a)
Stereoselectivity is a reaction property where one stereoisomer is preferred over another; metabolic stereoselectivity occurs when enzymes favor one enantiomer; chirality means non-superimposable on the mirror image, optical activity is rotation of plane-polarized light, R/S configuration uses Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules.
(b)
Substrate stereoselectivity (enantiomers metabolized at different rates, no stereoisomeric metabolites) → product stereoselectivity (one substrate gives stereoisomeric metabolites in differing proportions) → substrate-product stereoselectivity (combination, may involve chiral inversion).
(c)
Substrate: (S)- and (R)-omeprazole (CYP3A4 and CYP2C19); product: phenytoin by CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 to differing ratios of (S)/(R) p-hydroxyphenylhydantoin; substrate-product: thalidomide (hypnotic and teratogenic effects).
(d)
CYP2C9 (S-warfarin, preferentially metabolized), CYP3A4 ((R)-verapamil), and non-P450 enzymes: alcohol dehydrogenase (S-ibuprofen) and aldehyde oxidase (zonisamide).
(e)
Biological targets (enzymes, receptors) are chiral, so enantiomers differ in binding, absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and pharmacodynamics, e.g. (S)-ketamine is more effective than (R)-ketamine.
(f)
Polymorphisms in CYPs, UGTs, NATs and AKRs change active sites and enantiomer-specific metabolism, e.g. CYP2C9 and warfarin, CYP2D6 with metoprolol and codeine, NAT2 with isoniazid.
(g)
(S)-omeprazole is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 (sulfone) and (R)-omeprazole by CYP2C19 (hydroxyomeprazole and 5-O-desmethylomeprazole); (S)-omeprazole was cleared more slowly in vivo, giving a significant difference in oral bioavailability.
(h)
Esomeprazole, the (S)-enantiomer, was developed as an individual drug with significantly greater efficacy than omeprazole and comparable tolerability and safety.
(i)
In substrate stereoselectivity, enantiomers are metabolized at varying rates without stereoisomeric metabolites; in product stereoselectivity, one substrate yields different stereoisomeric metabolites in differing proportions.
(j)
Chiral inversion is the conversion of one enantiomer into its mirror image within the body; thalidomide's pure (R) or (S) enantiomer shows both hypnotic and teratogenic effects.
(k)
Chiral analysis techniques (chiral chromatography, NMR) are complex and time-consuming; matrix effects interfere with separation; achieving enantiomeric enrichment is difficult at low concentrations.
(l)
CYP2C9 preferentially metabolizes the more active (S)-warfarin, which affects warfarin's anticoagulant activity and dosing requirements.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Albumin binding in the blood stream is the primary mechanism that prolongs half-life.
(b)
• Lipidation is covalent attachment of lipids to peptides and increases metabolic stability; after subcutaneous administration, irreversible noncovalent polymers form at the injection site and act as a depot.
• Once in the blood stream, binding to albumin becomes the primary mechanism for prolonging half-life.
(c)
The depot delays absorption into the blood stream and the half-life is prolonged.
(d)
Prolonged half-life prolongs drug action.

Liraglutide, a lipidated peptide, is given subcutaneously to a patient and shows a prolonged duration of action.

A patient takes propranolol orally; the patient is elderly with liver disease.
(a) Identify the parameter affected by lipophilicity and physiological state.
(b) Explain the factors responsible.
(c) Predict the change in drug exposure and effect.
(d) State the clinical consequence.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The extent of first-pass metabolism.
(b)
• Lipophilic drugs (e.g. propranolol) are absorbed easily, undergo extensive distribution and more pronounced first-pass metabolism; plasma protein levels, GI motility and enzyme activity also influence first-pass.
• Age-related reductions in first-pass metabolism (nitrates, propranolol, phenobarbital, nifedipine) raise the risk of toxic effects; liver disease reduces first-pass metabolism.
(c)
Reduced first-pass metabolism leads to greater exposure and a higher risk of toxicity.
(d)
Reduced first-pass metabolism in liver disease necessitates dose adjustments to avoid toxicity.

(a)
A drug metabolite is a product formed in drug metabolism, usually via hepatic enzymes, either an intermediate or an end-product, usually more hydrophilic for easy excretion.
(b)
Active metabolites (same or different pharmacological activity from the parent drug), inactive metabolites and toxic metabolites.
(c)
Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G): a smaller portion of morphine is glucuronidated to M6G, which retains potency, has strong mu-opioid receptor affinity and greater pain-relieving power than morphine in animal studies.
(d)
Ipronazid (antidepressant) is metabolized by N-dealkylation to isoniazid (antitubercular).
(e)
Inactive metabolites have no medicinal effect, e.g. morphine-3-glucuronide, the product of the larger portion of morphine metabolized.
(f)
Acetaminophen's NAPQI binds macromolecules in hepatocytes (particularly mitochondrial proteins), causing direct damage, plus oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation and inflammation.
(g)
Codeine is a prodrug metabolized by CYP2D6 to morphine, the active compound responsible for analgesia.
(h)
Significance: pharmacokinetics, toxicity, personalized medicine, disease diagnosis and monitoring, and drug discovery and development.
(i)
Morphine + UDP-glucuronic acid → morphine glucuronide (Phase II glucuronidation).
(j)
Under normal conditions glutathione detoxifies NAPQI by conjugation; in overdose glutathione stores are depleted, leading to liver cell damage.
(k)
Activated charcoal within 1-2 hours of ingestion limits absorption; N-acetylcysteine (oral or IV, IV preferred in severe cases) replenishes glutathione, enhances sulfation and neutralizes NAPQI.
(l)
Active metabolites can prolong or intensify the drug's impact, sometimes causing toxicity or unique effects of their own.
questions.question:
Discuss the classification of drug metabolites.
(a) Define a drug metabolite.
(b) State the classes of metabolites.
(c) Describe active metabolites with the same pharmacological activity as the parent drug.
(d) Describe active metabolites with different pharmacological activity from the parent drug.
(e) Describe inactive metabolites with an example.
(f) Describe toxic metabolites and the mechanism of NAPQI toxicity.
(g) Relate the classes to the prodrug example of codeine.
(h) State the clinical significance of metabolite classification.
(i) Relate metabolite formation to the pathway of morphine glucuronidation.
(j) Explain how glutathione and overdose change NAPQI handling.
(k) State the clinical management of acetaminophen toxicity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
NAT1 and NAT2 are on chromosome 8, each with an open reading frame of 870 base pairs; NAT1 is involved in folate metabolism and is less polymorphic, NAT2 metabolizes aromatic amines (isoniazid, sulphonamides, hydralazine) and is highly polymorphic.
(b)
Slow: non-functional or less functional NAT2 (homozygous slow alleles); intermediate: mix of functional and less functional alleles (heterozygous); rapid: fully functional or hyperactive NAT2 (homozygous fast alleles).
(c)
Classification uses the ratio of acetylated to non-acetylated drug forms to classify slow or fast acetylators.
(d)
Phenotypic: test dose (isoniazid or caffeine) with urine or blood measurement; genotypic: PCR-RFLP, real-time PCR and next-generation sequencing of NAT2 SNPs.
(e)
Each person inherits two NAT2 copies; two slow alleles give reduced activity, while two rapid alleles or one rapid and one slow allele give higher activity.
(f)
North American and European populations: 40%-70% slow acetylators; Asian populations: 10%-20% slow acetylators.
(g)
Phenotypic: directly assesses activity and considers all factors but is invasive, time-consuming and affected by diet, liver function and co-medications; genotypic: non-invasive, definitive and unaffected by external factors but does not account for environmental or epigenetic factors.
(h)
Slow acetylators: adverse reactions, drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide), isoniazid hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy, sulfasalazine hemolytic anaemia, and increased bladder cancer risk.
(i)
Fast acetylators: reduced drug efficacy because of lower drug levels, increased cancer risk (e.g. colorectal) and increased risk of toxicity.
(j)
Dose adjustment of isoniazid, rifampicin and hydralazine by acetylator status, alternative medications, monitoring of drug levels, liver function and side effects, and genetic testing.
(k)
Drugs affected: isoniazid, procainamide, sulphonamides, dapsone, hydralazine and caffeine.
(l)
Genetic testing predicts acetylation status and guides personalized therapy to optimize efficacy and minimize toxicity.
questions.question:
Discuss acetylation polymorphism and its pharmacogenetic basis.
(a) Describe the NAT1 and NAT2 genes (location, function, polymorphism).
(b) Describe the acetylator phenotypes and the genotypes behind them.
(c) State the equation or ratio used to classify acetylators.
(d) State the phenotypic and genotypic testing methods.
(e) Explain how the two NAT2 alleles determine activity.
(f) Explain the population distribution of slow acetylators.
(g) Explain the advantages and limitations of phenotypic and genotypic testing.
(h) State the consequences in slow acetylators.
(i) State the consequences in fast acetylators.
(j) Explain the management and dose adjustment.
(k) State the drugs affected by acetylation polymorphism.
(l) State the role of genetic testing.

A drug is given by repeated intravenous bolus doses Xo with a dosing interval τ equal to its half-life.
(a) Identify the dosing regimen type.
(b) State the relationships for accumulation and steady state.
(c) Calculate the amount in the body just after each of the first four doses and just before the next dose, and the steady-state limits, showing each step.
(d) Explain the effect of changing the dose size or the interval.
(e) Reason to the therapeutic choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A multiple-dose intravenous bolus regimen with τ = t½.
(b)
At plateau Xss,min = 1Xo, Xss,max = 2Xo, (Xss,max - Xss,min) = Xo and Xss,max/Xss,min = 2.
(c)
• Dose 1: X = 1Xo; before dose 2: 1/2 Xo = 0.5Xo.
• Dose 2: X = (1 + 1/2)Xo = 1.5Xo; before dose 3: (1/2 + 1/4)Xo = 0.75Xo.
• Dose 3: X = (1 + 1/2 + 1/4)Xo = 1.75Xo; before dose 4: (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8)Xo = 0.875Xo.
• Dose 4: X = (1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8)Xo = 1.875Xo; before dose 5: (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16)Xo = 0.9375Xo.
• The values approach Xss,max = 2Xo and Xss,min = 1Xo; about 5 half-lives are needed to reach steady state.
(d)
The extent of accumulation is independent of dose size and is a function of the dosing interval and the elimination half-life; if τ < t½ accumulation is greater, and vice versa.
(e)
A proper balance of dose size and dosing frequency gives steady-state concentration with minimum fluctuations; accumulation occurs because previous doses are not completely removed.

questions.question:
Discuss the factors influencing drug metabolism.
(a) State the genetic factors (CYP2D6 metabolizer types).
(b) State the environmental factors: diet, smoking, alcohol, pollutants.
(c) State the age-related differences in neonates and in the elderly.
(d) State the gender-related differences in Phase I and Phase II.
(e) State the receptor-interaction factors that affect metabolism.
(f) Explain the effect of liver disease on enzymes.
(g) Explain the effect of kidney disease, inflammation and cancer on enzymes.
(h) Explain the physicochemical factors (lipophilicity, chemical structure, polar surface area).
(i) State the parameters (clearance) altered by low protein intake.
(j) Distinguish drug concentration effects: high versus low concentration.
(k) Explain how age affects first-pass metabolism with examples.
(l) State the consequences of induction and inhibition.
questions.answerText:
(a)
CYP2D6 polymorphism gives poor metabolizers (reduced or absent activity, increased exposure, adverse effects), extensive metabolizers (normal) and ultra-rapid metabolizers (increased activity, reduced efficacy).
(b)
Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 (simvastatin); cigarette smoke induces CYP450; prolonged ethanol induces CYP2E1 (more NAPQI, glutathione exhaustion); pesticides inhibit CYP450, reducing clearance.
(c)
Neonates and infants have underdeveloped enzymes and slower metabolism (paracetamol; phenytoin and other half-lives 2-3 times longer); in the elderly enzyme activity decreases, raising drug concentrations and adverse reaction risk.
(d)
CYP3A4 is up to 50% more active in adult Caucasian women; men have more active alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenase (higher ethanol bioavailability in women); women have lower glucuronidation activity; P-glycoprotein is more active in men; menstrual cycles do not affect enzyme activity.
(e)
Tight binding gives slower metabolism (e.g. irreversible inhibitors); high receptor occupancy prolongs action and delays metabolism (e.g. methadone).
(f)
Cirrhosis replaces functioning tissue with fibrous tissue: CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 downregulated, CYP2E1 upregulated, glucuronidation unaffected (lorazepam, diazepam); chlordiazepoxide and prednisone conversions are slower.
(g)
Kidney disease: reduced renal blood flow, altered transporter expression, uremic toxins inhibit enzymes; inflammation: IL-6 downregulates CYP3A4, 2D6, 2C9, 1A2; cancer: downregulation of CYP3A4, 2C9, 2D6 and upregulation of CYP1A2.
(h)
Lipophilic drugs (propranolol) undergo extensive distribution and more pronounced first-pass metabolism; chemical structure and functional groups determine route and extent (benzodiazepines); lower polar surface area gives more extensive metabolism.
(i)
Low protein intake reduces the clearance of drugs like phenazone and theophylline by 20-40%.
(j)
High drug concentration gives zero-order kinetics (constant rate); low concentration gives first-order kinetics; e.g. phenytoin is zero-order at therapeutic levels because of enzyme saturation.
(k)
Age-related reductions in first-pass metabolism raise toxicity risk for nitrates, propranolol, phenobarbital and nifedipine.
(l)
Induction (rifampicin on oral contraceptives, barbiturates on warfarin) lowers effect; inhibition (ketoconazole or erythromycin on terfenadine) raises concentration.

questions.question:
A patient receiving doxorubicin is at risk of cardiotoxicity, and a liposomal or PEGylated formulation is proposed.
(a) Identify the distribution parameter affected.
(b) Explain the factors responsible for cardiac damage.
(c) Predict the change in drug distribution and effect with the modified formulations.
(d) State the supportive therapies.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Exposure and uptake of the drug in cardiac tissue.
(b)
• Doxorubicin undergoes redox cycling to a semiquinone radical, producing superoxide anions and hydrogen peroxide; with iron (Fenton reaction) it gives hydroxyl radicals, causing lipid peroxidation and calcium dysregulation.
• It accumulates in mitochondria, inhibits electron transport chain enzymes, increases ROS and depletes ATP.
(c)
Liposomal formulation (e.g. Doxil) reduces exposure to cardiac tissue; PEGylation improves drug distribution and reduces cardiac uptake.
(d)
Adjuncts: dexrazoxane (iron chelator), vitamin E and coenzyme Q10, beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors.

(a)
A multiple-dose intravenous bolus regimen with τ = t½ (and τ < t½ in the separate case).
(b)
The extent of accumulation is a function of the dosing interval and elimination half-life and is independent of dose size; when τ < t½ accumulation is greater.
(c)
• At τ = t½, Xss,min = 1Xo and Xss,max = 2Xo (original dose).
• For a doubled dose (Xo becomes 2Xo), Xss,min = 2Xo and Xss,max = 4Xo; the ratio Xss,max/Xss,min remains 2.
(d)
The greater the dose size, the greater the fluctuation between Css,max and Css,min and the chance of toxicity; a shorter interval increases accumulation and toxicity.
(e)
Balance dose size and frequency: smaller doses more frequently give smaller fluctuations; larger doses less frequently do not.
questions.question:
A drug is given by repeated intravenous bolus doses Xo with the dosing interval equal to its half-life; the dose is then doubled, and in a separate case the interval is shortened below the half-life.
(a) Identify the dosing regimen type.
(b) State the relationships for accumulation and steady state.
(c) Calculate Xss,max and Xss,min for the original dose Xo and for the doubled dose when τ = t½, showing the steps.
(d) Explain the effect of changing the dose size and the interval on accumulation.
(e) Reason to the therapeutic choice.

A patient with a history of prolonged ethanol intake takes an overdose of acetaminophen (paracetamol).
(a) Identify the elimination pathways.
(b) Write the relevant pathway equations in plain text.
(c) Calculate the fraction conjugated if 5-10% goes to the toxic pathway, showing each step.
(d) Predict the effect of enzyme induction by ethanol and of glutathione depletion.
(e) State the clinical management consequence.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Major pathways: Phase II glucuronidation (UGT) and sulfation (sulfotransferases) to non-toxic water-soluble conjugates; minor pathway: Phase I oxidation by CYP2E1 and CYP3A4 to NAPQI.
(b)
Paracetamol → (UGT, sulfotransferases) → glucuronide or sulfate conjugate → urine; Paracetamol → (CYP2E1, CYP3A4) → NAPQI → (glutathione conjugation) → detoxified.
(c)
• Toxic fraction = 5-10%.
• Fraction not going through the toxic pathway, by difference = 100% - 10% = 90% up to 100% - 5% = 95% (conjugation is the main route).
(d)
• Prolonged ethanol induces CYP2E1, increasing toxic metabolites (NAPQI).
• In overdose glutathione stores are depleted, so NAPQI is not detoxified, causing liver cell damage and acute liver failure.
(e)
Activated charcoal within 1-2 hours of ingestion limits absorption; N-acetylcysteine (IV preferred in severe cases) replenishes glutathione, enhances sulfation and neutralizes NAPQI.

(a)
Codeine is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6 to morphine (the active compound responsible for analgesia); the patient has extra gene copies with normal activity (ultra-rapid metabolizer).
(b)
Ultrarapid metabolizers require higher doses and shortened dosing intervals (e.g. every 8 hours).
(c)
Ultra-rapid metabolizers metabolize drugs very quickly; respiratory depression and even death have occurred in ultrarapid-metabolizer children taking codeine after surgery.
questions.question:
A child who is an ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizer is given codeine for pain relief after surgery.
(a) Identify the process and the model of metabolism involved.
(b) State the dosing implication for an ultrarapid metabolizer.
(c) Interpret the result and the clinical outcome in the child.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Exposure to the statin (systemic exposure).
(b)
Decreased function at SLCO1B1 increases exposure to statins; atorvastatin also involves CYP3A4 inhibition.
(c)
Higher statin exposure leads to statin-induced myalgias.
(d)
The pharmacist recommended switching atorvastatin to pravastatin (to minimize statin-associated adverse events from CYP3A4 inhibition) and fluoxetine to citalopram; she reported minor pain and improved wellbeing; preemptive testing would have identified the drug-gene interactions.
questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman on atorvastatin and warfarin has leg pain and weakness; testing shows decreased SLCO1B1 function and intermediate CYP2C9 and CYP2D6 metabolizer status.
(a) Identify the parameter affected by the SLCO1B1 finding.
(b) Explain the factors responsible for the statin problem.
(c) Predict the change in drug exposure and effect.
(d) State the clinical consequence or therapy change.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A multiple-dose regimen designed on population averages (fixed or adaptive model) using the open one-compartment model.
(b)
Generally each dose is given at an interval equal to the half-life; wide therapeutic index: larger doses at longer intervals (more than t½); narrow therapeutic index: small doses at frequent intervals (less than t½).
(c)
• At τ = t½ (IV), Xss,max = 2Xo and Xss,min = 1Xo.
• Ratio = 2Xo/1Xo = 2.
(d)
Cmax, Cmin and Cav decrease but Cmax/Cmin increases; the opposite occurs when the interval is reduced.
(e)
Penicillin: larger doses at longer intervals without toxicity problems; digoxin: small frequent doses give the least fluctuations, similar to constant rate infusion or a controlled-release system.
questions.question:
Penicillin (wide therapeutic index) and digoxin (narrow therapeutic index) are both to be given on a repeated schedule.
(a) Identify the dosing regimen type.
(b) State the rule for choosing the dose size and interval relative to the half-life.
(c) Calculate Xss,max/Xss,min for an interval equal to the half-life with IV dosing, showing the steps.
(d) Explain the effect of increasing the interval with the dose unchanged on Cmax, Cmin, Cav and Cmax/Cmin.
(e) Reason to the therapeutic choice for each drug.

Discuss Phase I and Phase II drug metabolism.
(a) Define Phase I and Phase II metabolism.
(b) State the Phase I reactions and enzymes.
(c) State the Phase II reactions and enzymes.
(d) State the factors affecting drug metabolism.
(e) State the parameter or share of Phase I metabolism handled by CYP450.
(f) Explain why Phase I creates a handle for Phase II.
(g) Explain the role of the CYP450 catalytic reactions with oxygen.
(h) Explain the glucuronidation reaction mechanism.
(i) Distinguish Phase I from Phase II in terms of the effect on polarity and activity.
(j) Distinguish toxic metabolite formation from detoxification using paracetamol.
(k) Distinguish prodrug activation from detoxification.
(l) State the drug-drug interaction example for UGT.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Phase I is functionalization (introducing or exposing functional groups); Phase II is conjugation, attaching an endogenous molecule to the drug or its Phase I metabolite to increase water solubility.
(b)
Oxidation (addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen, CYP450), reduction (e.g. nitro groups to amines) and hydrolysis (esterases, amidases); enzymes include CYP450, flavin-containing monooxygenases (FMOs) and esterases.
(c)
Glucuronidation (UGTs), sulfation (sulfotransferases), acetylation (N-acetyltransferases), methylation (methyltransferases), and conjugation with amino acids or glutathione (GSTs).
(d)
Genetic polymorphisms (e.g. CYP2D6, UGT1A1, NAT1/NAT2), age, gender, disease, diet, smoking, alcohol, drug interactions and physicochemical properties (lipophilicity, chemical structure, polar surface area) affect metabolism.
(e)
CYP450 is responsible for about 75% of Phase I metabolism.
(f)
Many xenobiotics are lipophilic and almost chemically inert; Phase I provides a 'handle' of functional groups with which Phase II conjugating species react.
(g)
CYP450 catalyzes oxidation reactions (hydroxylation, dealkylation, desulfuration), often by transfer of an oxygen atom from molecular oxygen to the substrate.
(h)
UGT enzymes transfer glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid to lipophilic substrates bearing hydroxy, thiol, amino, sulfonamide or carboxy groups, giving O-, N-, S- and C-glucuronides.
(i)
Phase I makes drugs more polar and sometimes activates or deactivates them; Phase II adds hydrophilic molecules, increases hydrophilicity and decreases receptor affinity.
(j)
Paracetamol is mainly glucuronidated and sulfated (non-toxic, water-soluble conjugates); a small fraction (5-10%) is oxidized by CYP2E1/CYP3A4 to toxic NAPQI.
(k)
Prodrugs need metabolism for activation (codeine to morphine via CYP2D6); detoxification converts drugs to polar water-soluble compounds that can be excreted.
(l)
Lamotrigine with valproic acid is presumed to elevate rash risk but also increases anticonvulsive efficacy; zomepirac with probenecid increases zomepirac plasma concentration, partly due to UGT inhibition.
