questions.answerText:
(a)
• The quadrilateral socket, named for its quadrilateral shape in the transverse plane, is designed for ischial weight bearing on the posterior brim and remains an option for long-term wearers, those with a long residual limb, or those who need upper-extremity aids for trunk stability.
• The ischial containment socket (ICS) extends the socket trimlines proximally and contours the medial aspect to capture the ischial tuberosity inside the socket rather than on the brim, allowing more effective hip and pelvic stabilizing forces and improved mediolateral trunk control, especially benefiting a short residual limb.
• Both socket types can be fabricated rigid or as a flexible thermoplastic inner socket supported by a graphite-reinforced laminated frame, which improves comfort, proprioception, and accommodation of volume change.

(b)
Suspension options include a hard socket with wool or cotton socks suspended by a Silesian belt or total elastic suspension (TES) belt; a pelvic band and hip joint; suction suspension using a one-way air valve; and silicone or elastomeric gel liners with a lanyard or pin attachment providing pseudosuction suspension.

(c)
• Selection is based on residual limb length, activity level, hand function/coordination needed to manage suspension, skin/scar condition, and expected residual limb volume stability, since suction requires a stable limb volume and is not ideal for a preparatory prosthesis with rapid shrinkage.
• Belt-type suspensions are simple to don and adaptable for impaired hand function, acceptable for low activity levels, while suction and gel-liner suspension are preferred, whenever feasible, for more secure suspension across a wider range of activities.
• a pelvic band and hip joint is added when extra suspension security or rotation control is needed, especially for a short residual limb.

(d)
• Malalignment of the transfemoral prosthesis commonly produces distal femur pain.
• Difficulty pulling proximal soft tissue fully into a suction socket can cause an adductor roll - a painful compression of soft tissue in the medial groin between the socket and pelvis - that can lead to skin breakdown.
• Poor socket fit or malalignment is reflected in gait deviations such as lateral trunk bending, medial groin pain, or poor mediolateral prosthetic control during mid-stance.
• These problems may require socket modification, changes to donning technique, or external vacuum pumps to elongate residual tissue for a better fit.
• Achieving and maintaining a comfortable, well-aligned socket fit is one of the most important determinants of prosthetic acceptance and function.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the two main socket designs used for the transfemoral prosthesis and how each achieves weight-bearing and stability.
(b) Classify the main suspension options available for the transfemoral prosthesis.
(c) What criteria guide selection of a socket design and suspension system for a given individual?
(d) What are the effects of poor socket fit or malalignment in the transfemoral prosthesis?

(a) List the categories of terminal devices used with body-powered upper-limb prostheses.
(b) Describe the design and function of voluntary-opening versus voluntary-closing terminal devices, including typical prehensile forces.
(c) What features characterize a cosmetic (passive) hand?
(d) Explain the functional basis for choosing a hook over a hand terminal device.
(e) Distinguish a hook-style terminal device from an active (functional) hand terminal device.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Terminal devices for body-powered prostheses can be hooks, functional or active hands, cosmetic or passive hands, or special terminal devices for specific activities (such as a bowling-ball attachment or golf-club holder).

(b)
• Voluntary-opening terminal devices, most commonly the Dorrance 5X, 5XA, and 7 hooks, are powered through the cabling system to open, relying on springs or rubber bands to provide closing prehensile force, typically 5 to 10 lb.
• Voluntary-closing terminal devices allow the individual to apply a variable prehensile force through the control cable, capable of up to 20 to 25 lb (9 to 11 kg), and provide indirect sensory feedback through cable force, but require constant cable tension to sustain grasp, which is difficult during dynamic tasks.

(c)
Passive (cosmetic) hands are lighter than active hands and can be passively positioned but provide little or no function; a cosmetic glove tinted to the individual's skin color covers both active and passive hands.

(d)
• Hook-style terminal devices provide the equivalent of a lateral pinch grip, whereas active hand terminal devices provide a three-point chuck action,
• so the choice depends on the type of grasp and visualization needed for the task, with hooks generally favored for function and durability and hands favored for cosmesis.
• A quick-disconnect wrist option allows easy interchange between a hook and a hand, which is especially important for an individual with a bilateral upper-limb amputation.

(e)
• A hook-style terminal device provides a lateral pinch grip and, in the voluntary-opening form, relies on springs or rubber bands for a closing force of 5 to 10 lb.
• An active (functional) hand terminal device instead provides a three-point chuck grasp pattern, is heavier, and can interfere with the user's ability to see the object being grasped.
• Voluntary-opening active hands are more cosmetic but heavier and provide lower prehensile forces than hooks.
• Voluntary-closing devices of either type can generate substantially higher prehensile force than voluntary-opening devices, at the cost of requiring sustained cable tension to maintain grip.
• All conventional body-powered prostheses combine the chosen terminal device with a socket, suspension, control cable system, and any needed interposing joints according to the amputation level.

(a)
Prosthetic feet are grouped by major functional feature into rigid keel, flexible keel, single/multiaxial, and dynamic response (energy-storing) categories.

(b)
• The solid ankle cushion heel (SACH) foot is the least expensive and most commonly prescribed foot; it has no moving parts and consists of a wooden or composite keel with a compressible foam heel and toes that flex under load, simulating the heel and forefoot rocker mechanisms of the normal foot.
• It is durable and lightweight, and is a cost-effective choice for juveniles who need frequent foot changes because of growth.
• The SACH foot is appropriate for individuals with a lower activity level (K1-K2) whose ambulation is primarily limited to level surfaces.
• Flexible keel feet (e.g., the SAFE II) replace the SACH's rigid keel with a flexible one that bends with controlled stiffness from mid-stance through preswing, giving some inversion/eversion and a smoother rollover for low-to-moderate activity individuals.
• Dynamic-response (energy-storing) feet, such as the Flex-foot, Springlite, Seattle foot, and impulse feet, incorporate elastic elements that store energy during limb loading and mid-stance and return it at push-off, and are particularly suitable for running and jumping activities.

(c)
The dynamic energy characteristics were expected to make ambulation more efficient by reducing oxygen consumption through returning stored energy at push-off, but objective studies of this metabolic benefit have been mixed, with the benefit primarily seen at faster walking speeds.

(d)
• The SACH foot has no moving parts and a rigid keel providing a fixed, simple heel-cushion response suited to level-surface, lower-activity ambulation.
• The dynamic-response foot instead uses elastic, spring-like elements that actively store and return energy during loading and push-off.
• This makes the dynamic-response foot suited to higher-activity individuals engaged in running or jumping, whereas the SACH foot is the most cost-effective, durable, low-maintenance option for lower-activity or pediatric users.
• Selection of a specific foot within a functional category is otherwise largely empiric, based on matching the foot's functional characteristics to the individual's expected activity needs.
• Occasionally another characteristic such as adjustable heel height, cosmesis, or being waterproof becomes the primary determinant of foot selection.
questions.question:
(a) List and briefly describe the major functional categories of prosthetic feet.
(b) What materials and design features characterize the SACH foot, and what are its indications?
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis for why dynamic-response (energy-storing) feet are believed to make ambulation more efficient.
(d) Distinguish the SACH foot from the dynamic-response (energy-storing) foot in terms of design and function.

A patient with a transtibial amputation is observed during gait analysis to shift her trunk laterally toward the prosthetic side during mid-stance, with a medial or lateral thrust of the socket against the residual limb noted at this point in the gait cycle.
(a) Identify the gait deviation being described.
(b) What prosthetic causes could account for this deviation?
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis for why this deviation occurs.
(d) What corrective measures should be taken?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is a medial or lateral socket thrust with lateral trunk shift over the prosthesis occurring during mid-stance.

(b)
Possible causes include the prosthetic foot being set too far outset or inset, or a socket that has become loose.

(c)
Malalignment of the foot relative to the socket, or loss of a snug socket-limb fit, alters the mediolateral line of the ground reaction force relative to the residual limb, producing an uneven thrust against the socket wall; the patient compensates by shifting the trunk laterally over the prosthesis.

(d)
Management is to realign the prosthesis, replace the socket, or adjust the number of socks worn to restore a snug, well-aligned fit.

questions.question:
(a) Classify the types of knee joint mechanisms used in a knee-ankle-foot orthosis (KAFO), including locking mechanisms.
(b) Compare metal/leather and plastic materials used in orthotic fabrication.
(c) What criteria guide selection of a free, offset, or locked knee joint, and choice of material?
(d) What are the effects of poor orthotic alignment at the knee joint?
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A free-flexing knee joint is indicated when mediolateral instability or genu recurvatum may be present but knee extension strength is adequate for weight bearing.
• a posterior offset knee joint provides stance-phase stability by placing the joint axis behind the anatomical knee, while still allowing swing-phase flexion, used when knee extensors are weak.
• Locking knee joints include the drop-ring lock (dropping over the joint in full extension, sometimes with a spring-loaded pull rod), the cam lock (spring-loaded, easier to release, useful with flexor spasticity),
• and the bail (Swiss) lock, a lever bow that snaps into locked position on full extension and unlocks automatically when pressed upward.

(b)
Plastic materials are lightweight, allow total contact and adjustable flexibility, and are more cosmetic, while metal/leather orthoses offer greater durability and, in skilled hands, built-in adjustability, and are preferred for fluctuating edema, soft-tissue wounds, hyperhidrosis, or plastic intolerance.

(c)
• A free knee joint is selected when adequate knee extension strength exists despite mediolateral instability or recurvatum; an offset knee joint is selected when extensor weakness causes buckling; a locked knee is selected when instability is severe enough that mechanical stability in stance is required, accepting a stiff-knee gait.
• Material selection depends on clinical purpose and patient characteristics: plastic when lighter weight/cosmesis/total contact is valued and edema is stable, and metal/leather when durability, adjustability for growth, or accommodation of fluctuating edema or skin sensitivity is required.

(d)
• An offset knee joint is not fail-proof: knee instability can occur if the floor is uneven, the knee is not fully loaded/extended, or the ankle is allowed to dorsiflex more than about 10 degrees, so in such cases a knee lock may be a better choice.
• Even when mechanically locked, an anatomical knee with weak extensors would bend slightly on weight bearing if not further stabilized by straps above and below the patella or a patellar pad/strap.
• Close correlation between the orthotic and anatomic knee joint centers of rotation is mandatory when joint motion is required; a discrepancy in the axis of motion could produce pain, joint swelling, and skin breakdown.
• Biomechanical malalignment of the orthosis can prevent a borderline patient from becoming a functional ambulator, while patients with better recovery may be able to compensate for inadequate alignment.
• Adjustability of alignment is an advantage for early rehabilitation transfer but is also a risk, since patients or caregivers without proper knowledge may alter the alignment, or components may loosen with use over time.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the design of flexion-control orthoses (Jewett and CASH) and their mechanism of action.
(b) Describe the custom-molded plastic body jacket as a flexion-extension-lateral-rotary control orthosis.
(c) What materials are used in each?
(d) Explain the biomechanical basis for why flexion-control orthoses are contraindicated in unstable fractures or where extension must be prohibited.
(e) Distinguish the Jewett/CASH orthoses from the custom-molded body jacket in terms of control and construction.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Flexion-control orthoses (anterior hyperextension braces) function to extend the thoracolumbar region using a three-point pressure system without abdominal compression; examples are the Jewett brace and the cruciform anterior spinal hyperextension (CASH) brace.

(b)
• The custom-molded plastic body jacket, fabricated from polypropylene via a plaster cast, is the orthotic apparatus of choice for maximum immobilization, providing total contact with reliefs over bony prominences to control flexion, extension, lateral motion,
• and thoracolumbar rotation together, using abdominal compression in addition to shell-based three-point forces.

(c)
• The Jewett brace consists of a metal anterior and lateral frame with lateral pads, a sternal pad, a suprapubic pad, and a posterior thoracolumbar pad.
• the CASH orthosis consists only of an anterior metal frame shaped like a cross with pads at the ends and is easier to don and doff and better tolerated than the Jewett; both prevent only flexion, not lateral or rotary movement.

(d)
• The Jewett and CASH braces work by producing hyperextension forces on the posterior elements, which can actually induce fracture or worsen instability or displacement in an unstable spine.
• They are therefore contraindicated in unstable fractures or in conditions such as spondylolisthesis where extension must be prohibited.

(e)
• The Jewett and CASH orthoses are relatively lightweight, prefabricated metal-frame devices that control only flexion through a three-point system, without abdominal compression and without control of lateral bending or rotation.
• The custom-molded body jacket, by contrast, is a total-contact, individually molded plastic device that controls flexion, extension, lateral motion, and rotation together.
• Because the body jacket distributes forces over a much larger contact area, it provides greater comfort and support for maximum immobilization compared with the small, focused pad pressures of the Jewett brace.
• The body jacket's abdominal compression also reduces myoelectric activity of the erector spinae and reduces pressure on the vertebrae and discs, an effect not produced by the simpler flexion-control braces.
• Selection between these devices depends on whether isolated flexion control is sufficient (Jewett/CASH) or whether comprehensive multi-planar immobilization is required (custom body jacket).

questions.question:
(a) Describe how a patient is measured and fitted for axillary crutches, and the principles for correct crutch-walking technique.
(b) Describe the four-point and three-point (with swing-through) crutch gait patterns.
(c) What errors in crutch fitting or technique can occur?
(d) What effect do these errors have on function and safety?
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Axillary crutch length should approximate the distance from the anterior fold of the axilla to the bottom of the heel (plus 3-5 cm) or to a point 6 inches in front of the anterolateral border of the foot, with the handpiece set to allow 20 to 30 degrees of elbow flexion.
• Full-length crutches should be gripped firmly to the body using the shoulder adductors rather than by pressing the crutches up into the axilla, and should be held at a slight outward angle about 4 inches away from the feet.
• postural muscles, particularly the gluteus medius, must be strong to maintain pelvic balance during weight transference.

(b)
• The four-point gait is used when the patient cannot support full weight on both legs but has good coordination; it is the safest pattern but requires the most coordination, advancing one crutch, then the opposite foot, then the other crutch, then the other foot, in sequence.
• The three-point gait is used when the patient cannot support weight on one leg but has normal use of the arms, upper body, and other leg: weight is distributed between the sound leg and both crutches, both crutches are advanced together, and the affected leg is swung forward without bearing weight.
• once balance and strength improve, this can progress to a three-point swing-through pattern where the leg is swung beyond the crutches.

(c)
• Fitting the crutches too long or too short, or fitting the handpiece so the elbow is not at 20-30 degrees of flexion, is a common measurement error.
• Allowing the patient to bear weight by pressing up into the axilla rather than gripping with the shoulder adductors is a technique error.
• Progressing to three-point swing-through or four-point gait before adequate balance, coordination, or strength (especially of the gluteus medius and shoulder depressors/triceps) has been established is an error in training sequence.

(d)
• Incorrect crutch length or axillary pressure can cause neurological compression injury in the axillary area, known as crutch palsy.
• Poor postural control or inadequate gluteus medius strength compromises pelvic balance during weight transfer, increasing fall risk and producing an inefficient, uneven gait.
• Choosing a gait pattern that exceeds the patient's current coordination or strength reduces safety and the likelihood of independent, functional ambulation.

(a)
Suspension systems for the transtibial prosthesis can be grouped into straps (e.g., the supracondylar cuff strap), sleeves (rubber, neoprene, or elastic), gel liners with locking mechanisms (pin or lanyard), and suction.

(b)
• Suction suspension uses a one-way air valve ported to the bottom of the socket combined with an airtight sleeve to create a partial vacuum during swing phase; this vacuum can be generated by pistoning of the limb or by a vacuum pump (vacuum-assisted socket suspension, VASS).
• The supracondylar cuff strap uses the normal anatomic flare of the femoral condyles for suspension and is inexpensive, easy to apply, and comfortable in sitting.
• Silicone or elastomeric gel liners use either a distal metal pin that inserts into a locking mechanism, or a Velcro lanyard strap, so that friction and suction between the liner and residual limb provide suspension.

(c)
• Selection depends on activity level and hand function/coordination (belt/strap suspension for lower activity or impaired grip), presence of scarring or skin grafts (favoring gel liners,
• which reduce shear), the need for security during running/sports (favoring gel liners or suction), and stability of residual limb volume, since suction and gel liners work best with a stable volume and are less suited to a preparatory prosthesis with rapid shrinkage.

(d)
• A supracondylar strap or sleeve that is poorly fitted can allow pistoning of the prosthesis and reduced comfort or heat/dermatitis, particularly with neoprene sleeves.
• Inadequate suspension with residual limb volume loss, if not corrected by sock adjustment or a new socket, can produce a choke syndrome,
• where impaired venous return combined with lost total contact leads to distal edema, tenderness, and eventually verrucous hyperplasia and hyperpigmentation.
• According to the transtibial gait deviation pattern, inadequate suspension combined with an overly long prosthesis causes the prosthetic foot to drag during swing phase.
• Poor suspension also contributes to jerky knee motion from a loose socket noted during loading response.
• Correcting suspension problems (shortening the limb, modifying suspension, or replacing the socket) restores normal swing clearance and stance stability and helps prevent progression to skin breakdown.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the suspension systems available for the transtibial prosthesis.
(b) Describe how suction (vacuum-assisted) suspension works.
(c) What criteria determine the choice of suspension system for a given transtibial amputee?
(d) What effects result from poor suspension or an ill-fitting suspension system?

A patient with a transfemoral prosthesis is observed to bend or shift her trunk laterally toward the prosthetic side during mid-stance.
(a) Identify this gait deviation.
(b) List the possible prosthetic and patient-related causes.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis for this deviation.
(d) What corrective measures correspond to each cause?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is lateral trunk bending or shift over the prosthesis during mid-stance.

(b)
Possible causes include an abducted prosthetic limb from too much socket abduction or the foot set too far outset, a prosthesis that is too long or too short, medial groin pain, poor mediolateral prosthetic control or poor socket fit, weak hip abductors, or a short residual limb.

(c)
An abducted or malaligned socket, an incorrect prosthetic length, or weak hip abductor musculature all disturb the normal mediolateral balance of forces at the hip during single-limb stance, so the patient shifts the trunk laterally over the prosthesis to keep the center of gravity over a reduced or shifted base of support and reduce the effort otherwise required of the hip abductors.

(d)
Management is cause-specific: realign the prosthesis if the limb is abducted or the foot is outset; shorten or lengthen the prosthesis as appropriate; adjust socket fit if there is medial groin pain or poor socket fit; provide gait training and strengthening for weak hip abductors; and for a short residual limb, the deviation may need to be accepted or a hip joint added to the prosthesis.

questions.question:
A prosthetist recommends a hydraulic (fluid-control) knee unit for a K3-level individual with a transfemoral amputation who frequently changes walking speed for community and vocational activities.
(a) What device has been selected, and what are its principal features and functions?
(b) What functions must this knee unit fulfil during stance and swing?
(c) What alignment and fitting considerations should guide its use?
(d) What problems can arise from poor knee selection or alignment, and how are they corrected?
(e) What education should the patient receive regarding use and care of this component?
questions.answerText:
(a)
A single-axis hydraulic knee unit has been selected; its fluid-control mechanism responds to changing gait speeds during swing and, in some designs, provides hydraulic resistance to knee flexion during weight bearing in stance, giving reliable performance for a more active amputee, though at higher cost, greater weight, and more maintenance than simpler knees.

(b)
The prosthetic knee must provide stability during stance to prevent buckling (through alignment or mechanical means), allow knee motion during swing to permit toe clearance, allow adequate flexion for sitting, and control heel rise of the shank by assisting or resisting acceleration and deceleration of the shank during swing.

(c)
Selection and alignment are based on matching the stance-phase stability features and swing-control aspects of the knee to the individual's anticipated activity level and usage, including correct alignment of the knee to prevent buckling under load.

(d)
• Knee buckling in early stance can result from an excessive heel lever, incorrect prosthetic knee alignment, or weak hip extensors, corrected by realigning the limb, reducing heel stiffness, realigning the knee-alignment relationship, or gait training and strengthening.
• Uneven heel rise from knee friction that is too tight or too loose is corrected by adjusting knee friction or damping; circumduction of the prosthetic limb during swing from inadequate knee flexion or a knee that is too stiff is also corrected by adjusting knee friction or damping.

(e)
The patient should understand the function of the knee component so the prosthesis can be used optimally, including correct donning of the prosthesis, and should know that new gait deviations or pain may indicate a fit or alignment problem requiring review by the prosthetic team.

(a)
• K0 describes a patient who does not have the ability or potential to ambulate or transfer safely with or without assistance, and for whom a prosthesis does not enhance quality of life or mobility.
• K1 describes a potential household ambulator, including transfers, with the ability or potential to use a prosthesis for transfer or ambulation on level surfaces at a fixed cadence.
• K2 describes a potential limited community ambulator, with the ability or potential for ambulation traversing low-level environmental barriers such as curbs, stairs, or uneven surfaces.
• K3 describes a community ambulator using variable cadence, able to traverse most environmental barriers, who may have vocational, therapeutic, or exercise activity demanding prosthetic use beyond simple locomotion.
• K4 describes a high-activity user whose ambulation exceeds basic ambulation skills, exhibiting high impact, stress, or energy levels typical of a child, active adult, or athlete.

(b)
• Medicare requires that the functional level of the individual with an amputation be taken into account when prescribing a prosthesis, and the K-code limits which components can be used when fabricating the device.
• Although only formally required for Medicare, the K-code classification serves as a simple, useful hierarchical framework for classifying the mobility potential of all individuals with a lower-limb amputation.
• Hydraulic or pneumatic knee units and dynamic-response feet are matched to K3/K4 individuals who change cadence frequently or engage in higher-impact activity, while a SACH foot and simpler locking or weight-activated stance-control knees are matched to K1/K2 individuals with lower activity and level-surface ambulation.

(c)
• Prescribing a component designed for a higher K-level than the patient's actual function (for example, a complex fluid-control knee for a K1 patient with poor voluntary control) provides features the patient cannot safely or effectively use, adding cost, weight, and maintenance without functional benefit.
• Prescribing a component designed for a lower K-level than the patient's actual activity (for example, a simple constant-friction knee for a K3/K4 athlete) fails to provide the swing/stance control and durability the patient's activity demands, risking instability or component failure.
• Because collaboration between the physician, prosthetist, and therapist is essential in developing an individualized prescription, empiric experience together with correct K-level classification guides appropriate component selection to maximize comfort, match components to mobility needs,
• and achieve acceptable cosmesis for that individual's functional level.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the Medicare "K" code functional classification system for lower-limb prosthesis users, K0 through K4.
(b) How is this classification used as a criterion for prescribing lower-limb prosthetic components?
(c) What are the effects of prescribing a mismatched component relative to the patient's K-level?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The process begins with taking measurements of the residual limb and marking out pressure-sensitive and pressure-tolerant areas.
• A negative cast of the residual limb is then made.
• The cast is filled with plaster to create a positive mold of the limb.
• The positive mold is modified to optimize socket fit, a process called rectification, building up pressure-tolerant areas and relieving pressure-sensitive areas such as bony prominences, nerves, and tendons.
• A check (test/diagnostic) socket, usually transparent plastic, is then fabricated so the clinician can fully view the fit and make changes, with multiple fittings sometimes necessary.
• Once the fit is satisfactory, the socket is laminated using fiberglass, carbon fiber, and resin to create the custom definitive socket.
• Foot, knee (if needed), and other components are then attached (assembling), followed by an alignment process to ensure appropriate function and respect for the body's biomechanical structure, and finally cosmetic finishing.

(b)
• Inadequate rectification - either insufficient relief over pressure-sensitive areas (bony prominences, nerves, tendons) or insufficient build-up over pressure-tolerant areas - is a fundamental error that undermines overall socket fit.
• Failing to use the transparent check socket to verify fit before lamination, or proceeding to definitive lamination despite an unresolved check-socket problem, is also an error in the process.

(c)
• Inadequate relief over pressure-sensitive regions leads to localized high pressure, pain, blistering, or skin breakdown when the prosthesis is worn.
• Inadequate loading of pressure-tolerant regions means load is not properly distributed, again predisposing to discomfort and skin problems and reducing overall comfort and acceptance of the prosthesis.
• Because comfort depends directly on appropriate force distribution between the residual limb and socket, errors carried through rectification and check-socket fitting into the definitive socket can lead to prosthetic rejection or repeated need for socket replacement.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the steps involved in fabricating a prosthetic socket, from initial measurement to the definitive socket.
(b) What errors during rectification or check-socket fitting can occur?
(c) What effect do these errors have on comfort, fit, and function of the finished prosthesis?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Spinal orthoses protect the spinal column through three mechanisms: control of motion, trunk support, and spinal alignment.
• Control of motion depends on the flexibility of the device, ranging from minimal restriction that acts as a kinesthetic reminder (soft collars, lumbar corsets) to more restrictive braces that limit intersegmental motion in flexion-extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation.
• Trunk support is achieved by an increase in intra-abdominal (thoracoabdominal) pressure, reducing the demand on the spinal extensor musculature and the vertical loading and intradiscal pressure on the thoracolumbar spine.
• spinal alignment is achieved through a three-point force system, with the corrective component ideally located midway between opposing forces above and below it.

(b)
Spinal orthoses are classified by the joints/regions they encompass: cervical (CO), cervicothoracic (CTO), thoracolumbosacral (TLSO), lumbosacral (LSO), and sacroiliac (SO) orthoses, each with multiple designs within the category.

(c)
• The desired physiologic effect must be decided before prescribing, so that the least restrictive device capable of achieving the goal is ordered; for example, if thoracoabdominal trunk support alone is sufficient to reduce compressive spinal forces and muscular stress, joint-motion stabilization should not be required.
• Once the treatment goal has been achieved and the device is no longer needed, it should be discarded.

(d)
• Negative effects of bracing include weakness, atrophy, and contracture from restriction of motion and muscular activity, and skin irritation from poor fit, hygiene, or pin-site shear/pressure that can progress to ulceration, pain, or infection.
• Impaired ambulation and balance can result from the limitation in motion and the weight of the device (as with a halo), increasing dependence in activities of daily living.
• Eating and swallowing may be compromised by the head and neck position imposed by some cervical orthoses, and restricted chest wall motion can decrease pulmonary capacity and increase energy consumption; psychological dependence on the brace can also develop.
• Patient factors reducing tolerance include a short, stout neck with no defined chin (harder to fit a cervical collar), and pendulous breasts, a short trunk, thoracic kyphosis, or an obese abdomen (harder to fit cervicothoracic or thoracolumbosacral appliances).
• Effective bracing therefore depends on correct fit, patient compliance, body habitus, and the ability to minimize these negative effects, alongside patient education on donning/doffing, wearing schedule, skin checks, and hygiene.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the three physiologic mechanisms by which spinal orthoses achieve their protective effect.
(b) Classify spinal orthoses into their major groups by the spinal regions they encompass.
(c) What principle guides the choice of the least restrictive device for a given indication?
(d) What are the negative effects of spinal bracing, and what patient factors reduce tolerance of a brace?

A child with cerebral palsy is assessed to have less than 10 degrees of ankle dorsiflexion with the knee fully extended and is a nonambulatory child requiring ankle stability.
(a) What assessment finding is central to orthotic decision-making here?
(b) Which type of ankle-foot orthosis would be selected for this child?
(c) Justify this choice against a dynamic AFO and a posterior leaf spring AFO.
(d) What functional outcome is expected?
(e) What follow-up/rehabilitation considerations apply?
questions.answerText:
(a)
The key assessment finding is limited passive ankle dorsiflexion (less than 10 degrees with the knee fully extended), reflecting a fixed rather than easily correctable equinus.

(b)
A rigid (solid) ankle-foot orthosis is selected.

(c)
A rigid AFO provides full posterior coverage and does not allow ankle movement, enabling toe clearance during swing and complete stability of the foot and ankle, which is appropriate for a child with less than 10 degrees of dorsiflexion or for ankle stability in a nonambulatory child with cerebral palsy; a dynamic AFO is only appropriate where the foot and ankle deformity can be corrected passively with minimal force, and a posterior leaf spring AFO is intended for mild spastic equinus with flexibility at the ankle, neither of which suits a fixed limitation of this degree.

(d)
The rigid AFO is expected to provide complete stability of the foot and ankle and enable toe clearance during the swing phase.

(e)
Ongoing follow-up should reassess passive dorsiflexion range and skin tolerance, since progression of the contracture or skin changes would require reconsideration of the orthosis type.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old, right-handed female homemaker sustains a short transhumeral level of amputation following a motor vehicle accident.
(a) How is the level of her amputation classified, and how would her residual limb be assessed?
(b) What pre-prosthetic management should she receive?
(c) Give body-powered and externally powered prosthetic prescriptions for her, and explain which type of power may be preferable given her residual limb length.
(d) Describe the prosthetic training she will need to use the prosthesis for daily and homemaking activities.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Transhumeral amputation level is classified by the length of the residual humerus measured from the acromion: humeral neck (<30%), short transhumeral (30-50%), standard transhumeral (50-90%), and elbow disarticulation (90-100%); her amputation is at the short transhumeral level.

(b)
• Pre-prosthetic management parallels lower-limb care: soft dressings with stump shrinkers or compressive stockinettes are most commonly used, with removable rigid dressings advocated in some centers for residual limb protection, edema control, and pain reduction.
• Therapy should strengthen proximal shoulder girdle muscles (trapezius, serratus anterior, pectoralis major) and any residual deltoid or biceps function, alongside education and psychological support during the grieving-type response to limb loss.

(c)
• Body-powered: double-wall plastic laminate socket, constant-friction wrist unit, No. 5XA (lightest weight) terminal device, internal alternating-locking elbow with turntable, figure-8 harness, Bowden double-control cable. External-powered: double-wall plastic laminate socket, Otto Bock myoelectric hand, Utah myoelectric elbow, figure-8 harness.
• Because of her short residual limb, external power may be more comfortable and functional but will be heavier and considerably more expensive than body power.

(d)
Training includes general strengthening and range-of-motion exercises, checking prosthetic fit and control adjustment, gradually increasing wearing tolerance, and specific skills to activate, position, and lock the elbow and to control the terminal device for grasping, releasing, and positioning objects during homemaking, occupational, and recreational activities.

questions.question:
A patient with an unstable upper cervical fracture, who is not a surgical candidate, is fitted with a halo device to provide nonsurgical stabilization and allow early mobilization.
(a) What device has been prescribed, and what are its principal components?
(b) What alignment and fitting checks should be performed after application?
(c) What complications can arise with this device?
(d) How should common pin-related problems be identified and managed?
(e) What education should the patient and caregivers receive regarding safety and device care?
questions.answerText:
(a)
A halo cervicothoracic orthosis is prescribed; it consists of a rigid open or closed-back stabilizing ring fixed to the cranium by (commonly four) skeletal traction pins, supporting rods, and a superstructure connecting the ring to a fleece-lined plastic vest.

(b)
The preferred pin placement is anterolateral above the frontal orbital rim and posterolateral below the largest diameter of the skull, avoiding the temporalis muscle and cranial nerves; pins should be tightened 24-48 hours after insertion and again at one week; vest strap tension should be checked periodically since increasing strap tension decreases motion (especially lateral bending), and adequate space must be maintained between the shoulders and vest straps to avoid excessive cervical distraction.

(c)
Reported complications include loss of spinal reduction, failure to develop spinal stability, pressure sore development, pin loosening, pin-site pain, pin-tract infection, brain abscess, local osteoporosis, acute equilibrium impairment, forehead scarring, dysphagia, pin penetration of the skull, halo ring migration, cranial nerve palsy, brachial plexopathy, reduced vital capacity, periorbital edema, cervical muscle atrophy, and epileptic seizures.

(d)
Pin loosening (a visible pin tip or a pin that can be manually rotated) is managed by retightening or reinserting the pin elsewhere; pin-site infection is managed with daily cleansing using sterile cotton-tip applicators with antimicrobial soap and normal saline (avoiding hydrogen peroxide, povidone-iodine, or alcohol, which interfere with healing), with culture and sensitivity testing if drainage or erythema is present.

(e)
Patients and caregivers should be taught that the halo affects balance and gait (slower walking speed, reduced arm swing), so safe street-crossing/community ambulation training and a home safety evaluation to prevent falls are needed; they should never lift, turn, or move the patient by pulling on the vest, rods, or superstructure, should not arbitrarily adjust the vest straps without consulting the physician, and pin-site care should be performed daily, more frequently if crusting or drainage is present.

questions.question:
A patient with a transfemoral prosthesis is noted to swing the prosthetic limb outward in a wide arc (circumduction) rather than flexing the knee normally during the swing phase of gait.
(a) Identify this gait deviation.
(b) What prosthetic causes can produce this deviation?
(c) Explain the biomechanical reasoning behind each cause.
(d) What corrective measures should be applied?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is circumduction of the prosthetic limb during swing phase.

(b)
Causes include inadequate knee flexion or a knee that is too stiff, or a prosthesis that is too long combined with inadequate suspension.

(c)
If the knee will not flex adequately or is too stiff, or if the limb is effectively too long because of poor suspension allowing the limb to drop, the patient cannot achieve adequate toe clearance through normal knee and hip flexion, so the limb is swung outward in an arc to clear the ground instead.

(d)
Correction involves adjusting knee friction or damping to permit adequate swing-phase knee flexion, and adjusting the prosthesis length or modifying the suspension system if the limb is functionally too long.

questions.question:
(a) Classify the three general types of upper-limb prostheses.
(b) Describe the myoelectric control systems available for externally powered prostheses.
(c) What criteria guide the choice between body-powered, externally powered, and cosmetic prostheses?
(d) What are the effects of poor prosthetic fit, harness adjustment, or electrode positioning on function?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Upper-limb prostheses are divided into three general types: conventional (body-powered), externally powered (battery-powered, myoelectric, and/or switch-controlled), and passive or cosmetic prostheses.

(b)
• Externally powered (myoelectric) prostheses use surface electrodes in the socket to detect muscle action potentials.
• a dual-electrode system positioned over antagonist muscles allows natural, intuitive control with proportional control so the speed or strength of activation varies with contraction intensity.
• When electrode sites are limited, single-site controllers use the amplitude of one electrode's signal (weak contraction closes, strong contraction opens), and sequential/multistate controllers use one electrode pair with a brief co-contraction to switch between functions.
• hybrid prostheses combine myoelectric and body-powered components and may provide better function for some individuals than either type alone.

(c)
• Body-powered prostheses are moderate cost, moderately lightweight, most durable, and provide the highest sensory feedback through the cable, but require the most body movement and harnessing.
• Externally powered prostheses offer improved comfort from reduced harness needs, better control, and greater lifting capacity and terminal device grip force at more proximal levels, but are heavier, more expensive, and require more maintenance and a longer training period.
• Cosmetic prostheses are the lightest and provide the best appearance and least harnessing but offer the least function, and are chosen for individuals not candidates for or not desiring an active prosthetic limb.
• Because it is difficult to predict which type of power an individual will prefer, a preparatory prosthetic phase is typically used to trial different terminal devices and power types before definitive prescription.

(d)
• A stable residual limb volume is needed for a myoelectric fitting to ensure consistent socket fit and reproducible electrode position and skin contact; instability compromises reliable control.
• Poor harness fit or adjustment in body-powered systems reduces the mechanical advantage and consistency of cable-operated control, undermining function of the terminal device or elbow.
• Common reasons for prosthesis rejection include limited usefulness, excessive weight, residual limb pain, and poor durability (particularly cited for myoelectric prostheses), reflecting how poor fit or component mismatch can undermine acceptance and use.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female day care teacher sustains an open comminuted distal femur fracture while mountain climbing and ultimately undergoes a mid-thigh transfemoral amputation after developing osteomyelitis.
(a) What general principle guides selection of the level of her amputation in this trauma/infection-related case?
(b) What pre-prosthetic management is relevant to her case?
(c) Give a provisional and definitive prosthetic prescription for her, and explain the reasoning behind the choices, including the addition of a cosmetic cover to her provisional limb.
(d) Describe the prosthetic training and gait re-education she requires given her high activity level.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The underlying principle in choosing the amputation level is to preserve as much limb length as possible consistent with wound healing, an acceptable soft-tissue envelope, and functional prosthetic fitting; in trauma complicated by infection such as osteomyelitis, this must be balanced against the morbidity of further limb salvage, resulting here in a mid-thigh transfemoral level.

(b)
Pre-prosthetic management includes wound care and control of infection, prevention of hip flexion and abduction contracture (common after transfemoral amputation) through positioning and range-of-motion exercises, and strengthening of hip extensors, hip flexors, and gluteus medius to compensate biomechanically for lost limb function.

(c)
• Provisional prescription: total-contact thermoplastic ischial containment socket, TES belt suspension, hydraulic knee unit, lightweight dynamic-response foot, and a cosmetic foam cover.
• Definitive prescription: total-contact carbon-fiber-reinforced ischial containment suction-frame socket with a thermoflex liner, a thigh rotator, a swing-and-stance-phase-control hydraulic knee unit, and a split-toe flex-foot with a cosmetic foam cover.
• The provisional endoskeletal design with belt suspension and hydraulic knee was chosen to easily accommodate the major residual limb volume changes expected soon after amputation while recognizing her high physical activity level; the cosmetic cover, not usually added at the provisional stage, reflected her work with small children and her desire not to frighten them.
• The definitive changes eliminated the belt suspension for more secure suction suspension and accommodated her recreational and competitive sports activities, and the thigh rotator was added so she could sit on the floor to work with the children in her class.

(d)
Training should include the standard progression of weight-shifting and balance work, progressive ambulation, and management of uneven terrain, stairs, and ramps, with additional practice specific to her vocational needs (working on the floor with children) and her recreational and competitive sports activities, taking into account the mechanical attributes of her dynamic-response and hydraulic components, such as loading the toe during mid-to-late stance to capture energy for push-off assistance.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the categories of cervical orthoses (CO) and cervicothoracic orthoses (CTO), with examples of each.
(b) What materials are used in soft versus rigid cervical collars?
(c) What is a contraindication for rigid cervical collars?
(d) Explain the biomechanical basis for why a soft collar provides less motion restriction than a rigid collar or halo.
(e) Distinguish a soft cervical collar from a hard (rigid) cervical collar.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cervical orthoses (COs) encircle the cervical spine alone, while cervicothoracic orthoses (CTOs) extend into the thoracic spine for greater control of the lower cervical spine; examples of CTOs include the SOMI and Minerva, or any rigid collar fitted with an anterior or posterior extension piece.

(b)
• A soft cervical collar is prefabricated foam rubber with a cotton stockinette covering and Velcro closures, worn posteriorly (or reversed anteriorly if limiting flexion is the goal).
• Rigid prefabricated collars (Philadelphia, Miami J, Aspen, Newport, Malibu, and prehospital collars such as Stifneck, Ambu, and NecLoc) are used for prehospital immobilization or long-term management of mid-cervical bony or ligamentous injuries, postoperative stabilization, or post-halo removal.

(c)
Rigid collars are contraindicated if spinal instability exists, since they cannot substitute for the stabilization needed in an unstable spine.

(d)
• The soft collar, made of soft foam material, can only provide warmth, psychological reassurance, and a kinesthetic reminder to limit motion; it lacks the structural rigidity to provide true mechanical support.
• Rigid collars and CTOs achieve greater motion restriction through their rigid shell design and broader anatomical contact (mandible-to-sternum anteriorly and occiput-to-upper-thoracic-spine posteriorly for the Philadelphia collar),
• and the halo achieves the greatest restriction by fixing the cranium via skeletal pins.

(e)
• The soft cervical collar is a foam device that provides minimal restriction and mainly serves as a kinesthetic reminder not to move, appropriate for mild muscular spasm or soft-tissue injury such as some whiplash presentations.
• The hard (rigid) cervical collar is a molded plastic shell with internal padding that provides substantially greater structural motion restriction and is used for mid-cervical bony or ligamentous injury, postoperative stabilization, or stable upper cervical fractures.
• Rigid collars carry specific complications not typically seen with soft collars, such as pressure ulcer formation at the occiput, chin, clavicles, and ears, and reduced maximal mouth opening that could complicate emergency intubation.
• Soft collars have been studied particularly in whiplash management, where prolonged use compared with early mobilization/exercise has been associated with slower return to work and no clear reduction in pain.
• The choice between soft and rigid collars therefore depends on whether true structural immobilization or only symptomatic/kinesthetic support is required.

questions.question:
A young man with a transradial amputation is being considered for a myoelectric prosthesis. On assessment, electromyographic biofeedback testing shows he can reliably and independently contract and relax both his forearm flexor and extensor muscle groups, and his residual limb volume has stabilized after healing.
(a) What assessment findings support proceeding with a myoelectric fitting?
(b) What type of prosthesis and control system would be selected for him?
(c) Justify this choice against body-powered and single-site control alternatives.
(d) What functional outcome can be expected?
(e) What does his rehabilitation/training plan need to include?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Before prescribing a myoelectric prosthesis, the individual's ability to reliably contract and relax at least one muscle group in the residual limb should be ascertained using electromyographic biofeedback equipment or a myoelectric tester; a stable residual limb volume is also needed to ensure consistent socket fit and reproducible electrode position and skin contact, both of which are present in this case.

(b)
A dual-electrode myoelectric (externally powered) prosthesis with proportional control is selected, using two electrode sites positioned over antagonist muscles.

(c)
This dual-site system allows natural and intuitive control - activation of the forearm flexors closes the terminal device while activation of the extensors opens it - compared with a single-site controller (used only when an inadequate number of electrode sites are available, where a weak contraction closes and a strong contraction opens the device) and compared with a body-powered prosthesis, which is lighter, more durable, and less costly but requires more body movement and more extensive harnessing.

(d)
With proportional control, the speed or strength of terminal device activation varies with the intensity of muscle contraction, and the self-suspending socket design possible at the transradial level can eliminate the need for a harness.

(e)
Training with an externally powered prosthesis is more complex than with a body-powered one and generally takes more time, as the individual must learn to separate, modulate, and sustain voluntary muscle contractions in the selected control muscles to operate the prosthesis.

(a)
The LSU reciprocating gait orthosis consists of bilateral knee-ankle-foot orthoses with posterior offset knee joints and knee locks, posterior plastic ankle-foot and thigh pieces, a custom-molded pelvic girdle, and special thrust-bearing hip joints, coupled together with a cam mechanism and a thoracic extension with Velcro straps.

(b)
The cam mechanism provides hip stability by preventing simultaneous bilateral hip flexion, while still allowing free hip flexion on one side coupled with reciprocal extension of the contralateral hip during a weight-shifted step, enabling a four-point reciprocal gait pattern when the patient uses two crutches; this orthosis has also been used together with functional electrical stimulation to facilitate ambulation.

(c)
The pelvic band is controversial because several studies indicate it increases lumbar excursion and displacement of the center of gravity during ambulation, potentially increasing energy cost.

(d)
For most people with paraplegia who are candidates for a Scott-Craig-type orthosis, pelvic bands probably are not necessary, although they may improve standing balance, especially when flexor spasticity is severe; this trade-off between stability and energy cost should guide whether a pelvic band is retained.

(e)
The patient must be trained to use two crutches together with the device's cam-controlled reciprocal hip motion to achieve a four-point gait pattern, and to understand how the knee locks and thigh/ankle-foot pieces function together for donning, doffing, and safe ambulation.
questions.question:
A patient with paraplegia from a spinal cord injury is prescribed a Louisiana State University (LSU) reciprocating gait orthosis to enable ambulation with crutches.
(a) What are the principal components of this device and their functions?
(b) How does the device achieve a reciprocal gait pattern?
(c) What controversy applies to the pelvic band component used in orthoses of this type?
(d) How should pelvic band use be decided, and what benefit might it still offer?
(e) What patient education is required for functional use of the device?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Carpal tunnel syndrome commonly results from overuse of the wrist and hand, causing inflammation within the carpal tunnel; immobilizing the wrist for part or all of the day and night often helps resolve symptoms.

(b)
• A static wrist-hand orthosis is prescribed, positioning the wrist in neutral (0 degrees of extension) while allowing full freedom of thumb and finger movement, fabricated from thermoplastic material.
• The biomechanical rationale rests on the three-point control concept (a strong force at the joint with counterforces applied proximal and distal to it) and on immobilizing the inflamed structures to relieve overuse-related irritation.

(c)
• Fitting must respect tissue tolerance, since there are more than 30 pressure-sensitive bony prominences in the wrist, hand, and fingers; higher pressures (100-300 mm Hg) are tolerated only 2 to 4 hours continuously while lower pressures (20-50 mm Hg) are tolerated up to 12 hours, so pressure should be distributed over a larger surface area and a wearing schedule set accordingly.
• The natural transverse and longitudinal arches of the hand should also be preserved in the design of this static positioning orthosis.

(d)
• Failure to observe pressure-duration guidelines risks skin breakdown over bony prominences; the orthosis should be evaluated on and off the patient to confirm proper construction, fit, and function, with appropriate instruction of the patient and family.
• Follow-up should monitor symptom resolution and the skin under the orthosis, and adjust the wearing schedule (part-day versus full day/night wear) as tolerated.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old office worker presents with hand numbness, tingling, and nocturnal wrist pain related to repetitive wrist and hand activity, consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome.
(a) What is the functional problem underlying her symptoms?
(b) What orthosis would be prescribed, and what are its joint positioning, materials, and biomechanical rationale?
(c) What principles should guide the fitting and checkout of this orthosis to protect the skin and underlying tissues?
(d) What precautions, complications, and physiotherapy follow-up considerations apply to this orthosis?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Gait training begins with weight-shifting and balance activities while the patient remains in the parallel bars.
• Once weight shifting and balance are mastered, a program of progressive ambulation begins in the parallel bars and advances toward the most independent level of ambulation possible with or without gait aids, with specific focus on transfers, knee stability, equal step lengths,
• and avoiding lateral trunk bending.
• After mastering ambulation on flat, level surfaces, the patient progresses to managing uneven terrain, stairs, ramps, curbs, and techniques for falling and getting up from the ground.
• Higher-functioning individuals additionally receive training in driving, recreation, and vocational activities, taking into account the mechanical attributes of the prescribed components.

(b)
Wearing tolerance is built gradually: initially the prosthesis is worn only 15 to 20 minutes before removal to check the skin, with wearing time gradually increased as tolerance to weight bearing improves, until full-time wear is achieved after several weeks.

(c)
• An error in this process is progressing gait training before weight-shifting and balance skills are mastered, risking falls or reinforcement of poor gait patterns.
• Advancing wearing time too quickly, without adequate skin checks, risks missing early signs of excessive pressure or irritation.
• Failing to individualize the plan to the prescribed components (for example, not teaching the toe-loading technique needed to activate a dynamic-response foot or trigger a prosthetic knee into swing) means the patient will not obtain the intended functional benefit.

(d)
• Skipping or rushing early balance and weight-shifting training predisposes to persistent gait deviations, such as lateral trunk bending or uneven step length, and instability.
• Progressing wearing time without regular skin checks can lead to unrecognized pressure areas, blistering, or skin breakdown, interrupting prosthetic use and rehabilitation.
• An appropriately staged, individualized program is necessary to achieve safe, efficient community ambulation and to avoid the complications and setbacks associated with rushed or poorly monitored training.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the sequence of gait training for a new lower-limb amputee, from initial weight-shifting activities to advanced skills.
(b) How is wearing tolerance for the prosthesis built up over time?
(c) What errors in gait training or wearing schedule progression can occur?
(d) What effect do these errors have on gait quality and rehabilitation outcome?

(a) Describe the design and function of the axillary crutch, Lofstrand (forearm) crutch, triceps crutch, and platform (forearm-support) crutch.
(b) What component prevents slippage and increases stability at the base of a crutch?
(c) Explain the functional basis for choosing a Lofstrand crutch over an axillary crutch.
(d) Distinguish the axillary crutch from the Lofstrand crutch.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Axillary crutches, the most common type, are made of hardwood or aluminum with two upright shafts and connecting links, including a padded upper support, a middle handpiece, and a lower extension piece with regularly spaced holes for height adjustment.
• The Lofstrand crutch consists of a molded handpiece, a molded forearm piece bent posteriorly just above the handpiece, and a single length-adjustable aluminum tubular shaft.
• the forearm piece extends 4-5 cm below the elbow with a forearm cuff with a narrow anterior opening.
• The triceps crutch extends just above the elbow with a single aluminum upright attached to bilateral uprights; it is rarely prescribed but may benefit individuals with triceps weakness.
• Forearm support (platform) crutches may be prescribed when hand, wrist, or forearm conditions prevent safe or comfortable weight bearing, such as weakness of triceps or grasp, or arthritic conditions of the upper-extremity joints.

(b)
A soft rubber tip, similar to that used on canes, is attached to the bottom of the crutch to increase contact surface area and provide stability.

(c)
• Good upper-extremity strength, joint integrity, and range of motion are essential to maximize benefit with crutches, since shoulder flexors and depressors, elbow and wrist extensors, and finger flexors must have normal or good strength.
• the Lofstrand crutch's released handpiece frees the hands to perform activities, which is a significant advantage where hand use between steps is needed.
• Lofstrand crutches are typically lighter in weight than axillary crutches, reducing the assistive-device mass the user must manage during gait, though good upper-extremity strength and adequate trunk balance remain minimum requirements for safe use.

(d)
• The axillary crutch has a padded upper support that rests near the axilla and provides increased stability and load-bearing capacity but restricts hand use and, if leaned upon, can cause axillary neurological compression injury (crutch palsy).
• The Lofstrand crutch instead attaches at the forearm via a cuff and can be released without losing the crutch, freeing the hands, but demands good trunk balance and upper-extremity strength since it lacks the axillary support surface.
• Overall, the axillary crutch is chosen when maximal stability/load transfer is needed, while the Lofstrand crutch is chosen when freeing the hands for activity is a priority and the patient has adequate balance and strength.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the figure-of-eight (spica) bandaging technique used for residual limb shaping and edema control, including the required materials.
(b) Describe the role of elastic shrinkers and the PPAM aid as alternatives or adjuncts.
(c) What errors in bandaging technique can occur?
(d) What effect do these errors, and correct technique, have on the residual limb and prosthetic fitting?
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Limb shaping begins as soon as the surgical drain is removed, using elastic bandaging applied immediately, with the transtibial limb shaped conically and the transfemoral limb shaped cylindrically.
• above-knee or through-knee amputations require a 4.5 m long, 15 cm (6 in) wide bandage, while below-knee amputation uses a 10 cm (4 in) wide bandage.
• The ascending spica (figure-of-eight) technique starts with two circular turns, then wraps diagonally around the joint to form a figure eight, overlapping two-thirds of the previous layer, with firm tension distally that decreases gradually moving proximally, and the end secured with pins, tape, or fastening.
• pressure must be greater distally than proximally, with all turns diagonal, to disperse terminal edema.

(b)
• Elastic shrinkers, available in various sizes, lengths, and pressure gradients, may be used instead of bandage wrapping once the stump is mature and fully healed, and are generally easier for the patient to apply, though less adjustable for changes in limb volume.
• The Pressure Post-Amputation Mobilization Aid (PPAM) consists of an outer inflatable sleeve, an inner invaginated plastic bag, a metal frame with a rocker base, and a pump with a gauge; it reduces edema and enhances early mobility and can be used as early as 5 to 7 days postoperatively with the consultant's consent.

(c)
• A key bandaging error is using circular (rather than diagonal) turns, which produces a tourniquet effect that impairs venous return.
• Applying more pressure proximally than distally, rather than the required distal-to-proximal pressure gradient, is another error that fails to disperse terminal edema properly.
• Failing to anchor the bandage above the proximal joint allows it to slide off the stump, and continuing to wear a bandage that causes increasing pain (suggesting excessive tightness) risks impaired circulation or nerve compression.

(d)
• Correct figure-of-eight bandaging with a distal-to-proximal pressure gradient disperses edema, promotes a conical or cylindrical residual limb shape, and conditions the limb to the pressure it will experience in the prosthetic socket.
• Errors such as circular wrapping or reversed pressure gradients can cause a tourniquet effect, impaired circulation, discomfort, or an improperly shaped or persistently edematous limb, delaying readiness for prosthetic fitting.
• Rewrapping is required if the patient reports increased pain, since this indicates the wrap is likely too tight and compromising circulation or placing pressure on peripheral nerves.

(a)
He has the ability to ambulate on level surfaces at a fixed cadence, typical of the limited or unlimited household ambulator (K1) or the limited community ambulator who can traverse only low-level barriers such as curbs or stairs (K2), rather than the variable-cadence community ambulator (K3) or high-activity user (K4).

(b)
A solid ankle cushion heel (SACH) foot is selected.

(c)
The SACH foot is the least expensive and most commonly prescribed foot, is durable and lightweight with no moving parts, and is appropriate for individuals with a lower activity level (K1-K2) whose ambulation is primarily limited to level surfaces; dynamic-response feet are particularly suited to running and jumping, and multiaxial feet are appropriate for uneven terrain or cutting/pivoting at speed, neither of which matches his anticipated activity, so these alternatives would add cost and maintenance without matched benefit.

(d)
With a well-fitted SACH foot he should achieve safe, functional prosthetic ambulation for household and limited community activities on level surfaces.

(e)
The rehabilitation plan should continue gait training progressing from parallel bars to independent ambulation on level surfaces, with follow-up visits during the first 6 to 18 months to manage the expected loss of residual limb volume with sock adjustments or socket modification, and yearly review once the limb has stabilized.
questions.question:
A 68-year-old man with a transtibial amputation resulting from diabetic vascular disease is evaluated after preparatory prosthetic use. He is a household and limited community ambulator with a fixed cadence and no plans for uneven terrain or running.
(a) What assessment findings support classifying him at this functional (K) level?
(b) Which prosthetic foot would be selected for him?
(c) Justify this choice against dynamic-response and multiaxial alternatives.
(d) What functional outcome is anticipated with this foot?
(e) Outline the rehabilitation plan going forward.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Noninvasive vascular studies help predict wound healing at the transtibial level: an absolute ankle Doppler blood pressure of 70 mm Hg or greater, an ankle-brachial index of 0.5 or greater, and transcutaneous oxygen pressure greater than 20 to 30 mm Hg are all suggestive of a greater likelihood of healing, along with adequate nutritional status (albumin at or above 3.5 g/dL) and lymphocyte count above 1,500; postoperatively, muscle imbalance and positioning predispose to knee flexion contracture in the transtibial residual limb.

(b)
Pre-prosthetic management for a dysvascular transtibial amputation typically lasts 6 to 10 weeks and includes wound care (soft, semi-rigid, or rigid dressings), pain control, edema control, and a postoperative therapy program of range-of-motion exercises and early mobilization to prevent knee flexion contracture, along with strengthening of muscle groups that biomechanically substitute for lost limb function.

(c)
• Provisional prescription: total-contact PTB thermoplastic socket, foam liner (soft insert), neoprene sleeve suspension, lightweight alignable shank, and a SACH foot - a lightweight design providing a stable base to learn walking, with a soft liner that is easy to modify as residual limb volume changes.
• Definitive prescription: exoskeletal design, total-contact laminated PTB socket, silicone suction suspension, and a lightweight multiaxial foot, chosen because of his desire to return to gardening activities, requiring a more durable and stable prosthesis on uneven ground with secure suspension that would not be damaged when kneeling.

(d)
Gait training begins with weight-shifting and balance activities in the parallel bars, progresses to ambulation in the parallel bars and then to the most independent level of ambulation possible with or without gait aids, followed by training on uneven terrain, stairs, ramps, curbs, and falling and getting up from the ground; wearing tolerance is built gradually, starting at 15 to 20 minutes with skin checks, until full-day wear is achieved.
questions.question:
A 72-year-old retired man with type II diabetes and peripheral vascular disease undergoes a transtibial amputation for an infected, nonhealing ulcer and gangrenous foot.
(a) What factors would be assessed preoperatively regarding likelihood of healing at this level, and what residual limb problem is anticipated postoperatively?
(b) What pre-prosthetic management is required before he can be fitted with a prosthesis?
(c) Give a provisional and a definitive prosthetic prescription for him, and explain the reasoning behind each.
(d) Outline the gait training and rehabilitation program he will undergo.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• An articulated (hinged) AFO has an adjustable hinge at the ankle with a plantarflexion stop allowing controlled, adjustable range of motion, and must be worn with a laced or Velcro-closure shoe for stability.
• A rigid (solid) AFO provides full posterior coverage and allows no ankle movement, enabling toe clearance during swing and complete stability of the foot and ankle.
• A dynamic AFO (DAFO) is made from thin, flexible thermoplastic custom-fit to the foot, helping maintain neutral alignment and circumferential foot control, appropriate only where the deformity can be passively corrected with minimal force.
• A ground reaction (floor reaction) AFO is a custom-fabricated molded plastic support whose anterior shell redistributes extension and ground-reaction forces closer to the knee, giving more leverage than other designs.
• it is used for spina bifida, brain or spinal cord injury, post-polio paralysis, cerebral palsy, osteoarthritis, and adult acquired flatfoot.

(b)
A posterior leaf spring AFO offers flexibility at the ankle allowing passive dorsiflexion for a smoother knee-to-ankle motion, with a flexible posterior foot plate that stores and returns energy with each step; it is typically made from carbon composites, copolymer polypropylene, or Ortholen, and is best for mild spastic equinus.

(c)
An articulated AFO is often a good choice for medial/lateral instability, stroke (CVA), and stress fractures, but is not an appropriate option for patients with diabetes or fluctuating edema.

(d)
• By redistributing extension and ground-reaction forces to a point closer to the knee joint, the ground reaction AFO's anterior shell provides a knee-extension moment during stance, useful when weak knee/ankle musculature would otherwise allow knee buckling, provided hip extension strength and knee range of motion are adequate.
• This mechanism also underlies the related patellar tendon-bearing floor reaction orthosis, which immobilizes the foot and ankle in slight equinus to produce a knee extension force during stance in patients with normal hip extension strength, full knee extension range, and no significant flexor spasticity.

(e)
• The rigid AFO allows no ankle motion and is chosen for children with cerebral palsy with less than 10 degrees of dorsiflexion or for ankle stability in nonambulatory children.
• The posterior leaf spring AFO, by contrast, permits passive dorsiflexion and stores energy in its flexible posterior foot plate to assist forward propulsion, making it suitable for milder spastic equinus rather than a fixed, more severe limitation,
• and it does not provide the rigid support of the solid design where complete stability is required.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the design features of the articulated, rigid, dynamic (DAFO), posterior leaf spring, and ground reaction ankle-foot orthoses.
(b) What materials are used in the posterior leaf spring AFO?
(c) What are the indications and contraindications for the articulated AFO?
(d) Explain the biomechanical basis of the ground reaction (floor reaction) AFO.
(e) Distinguish the rigid AFO from the posterior leaf spring AFO.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Transradial amputations are classified by the length of the bony forearm measured from the medial epicondyle: very short (<35%), short (35-55%), and long (55-90%); his is a long residual limb, which enhances the forearm lever for lifting and retains 60-120 degrees of supination-pronation motion (compared with less than 60 degrees in a short residual limb).

(b)
Pre-prosthetic management includes education about the rehabilitation process and realistic expectations, and postoperative wound care with soft dressings, stump shrinkers, or elastic stockinettes, or a removable rigid dressing; a rigid dressing is especially advantageous at the transradial level because it is easy to suspend and allows immediate or early postprosthetic fitting by attaching a hook, harness, and control system to the cast.

(c)
• Body-powered prescription: double-wall plastic laminate socket, quick-change locking wrist unit, No. 7 heavy-duty ("Farmer's hook") terminal device, flexible elbow hinges, triceps pad, figure-8 harness, and a Bowden single-control cable. External-powered prescription: double-wall plastic laminate socket with a self-suspending design and an Otto Bock Greifer (myoelectric hook) terminal device.
• Body power is lightest in weight, most durable, and least expensive; however, if more than 6 to 7 lb of pinch force is necessary for his drill-press work, the Greifer can provide up to 35 lb of pinch force, favoring external power if heavier grip force is required.

(d)
• Training includes general strengthening and range-of-motion exercises for the residual limb, and checking that the prosthesis fits comfortably with a properly adjusted control system.
• The prosthesis should be removed every 15 to 30 minutes initially to check for pressure or irritation, with wearing time gradually increased as skin tolerance improves.
• He should be instructed in donning and removing the prosthesis, adjusting sock plies, and cleaning and caring for the residual limb and prosthesis.
• Specific skills practiced include controlling the terminal device, and grasping, releasing, transferring, and positioning objects for functional and occupational (drill-press) activities under therapist guidance.
questions.question:
A 24-year-old right-handed man sustains a work-related crush injury to his right hand, resulting in a long transradial level of amputation. He plans to return to work operating a drill press.
(a) What residual-limb feature determines the classification of a transradial amputation, and how would this residual limb be assessed?
(b) What pre-prosthetic management should this man receive before prosthetic fitting?
(c) Give a body-powered and an externally powered prosthetic prescription for him, and explain the reasoning for choosing between the two for his occupational needs.
(d) Describe the prosthetic training and control training he will require to use this prosthesis functionally.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is early knee flexion, or "drop off," occurring from mid-stance to terminal stance.

(b)
The underlying cause is an inadequate toe lever.

(c)
An inadequate toe lever can result from the prosthetic foot being dorsiflexed too much, the foot being positioned too far posterior, or the foot keel being too soft or flexible; any of these shortens the effective forefoot lever arm needed to support forward progression of the body over the foot in terminal stance, so the shank and knee "drop off" the end of the lever rather than rolling smoothly over it.

(d)
Correction involves realigning the prosthesis or replacing the foot to restore an adequate toe lever.
questions.question:
During gait analysis of a patient with a transtibial prosthesis, the examiner notes that the knee flexes early and the limb appears to "drop off" as the patient moves from mid-stance into terminal stance, rather than smoothly rolling over the foot.
(a) Identify this gait deviation.
(b) What is the underlying prosthetic cause?
