questions.answerText:
(a)
Prosthetic knee units range from simple single-axis constant-friction joints to polycentric (four-, five-, six-bar) joints, weight-activated stance-control knees, fluid-control (pneumatic or hydraulic) knees, and microprocessor-controlled knees.

(b)
• The primary purposes of the prosthetic knee are to provide stability during stance (through alignment or mechanical means to prevent buckling), permit knee motion during swing for toe clearance, allow adequate flexion for sitting,
• and control heel rise of the shank by assisting or resisting shank acceleration and deceleration during swing.
• Single-axis constant-friction knees are simple, durable, and low-maintenance but provide only constant single-cadence swing control and no stance control, making them excellent for pediatric users or those with good voluntary control.
• Polycentric knees give varying stability through stance and shorten the shank during swing for better toe clearance, useful for knee disarticulations and long or short transfemoral levels.
• Weight-activated stance-control knees provide a braking mechanism when weight is applied with the knee slightly flexed, useful for geriatric patients with a short residual limb but less responsive for an active walker.
• Hydraulic and pneumatic knees respond to changing gait speeds and are used for K3/K4 individuals who change cadence frequently, at higher cost and weight; microprocessor-controlled knees use onboard computer regulation of swing or stance resistance for the most active patients, at the highest cost and weight.

(c)
• Selection is based primarily on matching the stance-phase stability features and swing-control aspects of the knee to the individual's anticipated activity level and usage, as reflected in the Medicare K-level classification,
• and on residual limb length, since a long knee-disarticulation-level limb limits the choice of knee units that maintain symmetric knee centers with the sound side.

(d)
• Poor knee selection or alignment causes documented gait deviations in the transfemoral amputee, including knee buckling in early stance from incorrect prosthetic knee alignment.
• Uneven heel rise in initial swing results from knee friction being too tight or too loose, and circumduction during swing results from inadequate knee flexion or a knee that is too stiff.
• These problems are corrected by realigning the knee-alignment relationship or adjusting knee friction/damping, underscoring that correct knee selection and alignment are central to safe, efficient prosthetic gait.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
A custom-molded plastic (polypropylene) thoracolumbosacral body jacket, fabricated from a plaster cast of the patient, is prescribed; it provides total contact to soft tissues with reliefs over bony prominences, distributing forces over a large area, with the superior and inferior anterior sections restricting flexion, the posterior shell forces combined with anterior abdominal compression resisting extension, the upper and lower lateral aspects limiting lateral trunk motion, and the combination of these forces limiting thoracolumbar rotation; abdominal compression also reduces pressure on the vertebrae/discs and reduces myoelectric activity of the erector spinae.

(b)
Proper fit requires that the inferior border of the anterior shell rest one-half inch above the pubic symphysis, that the trim follow the inguinal fold when the patient is sitting, and that the superior border encompass the sternal notch; posteriorly, the shell should extend from the spine of the scapula to the sacrococcygeal junction, containing the upper gluteal mass while leaving the axillae and trochanters free.

(c)
If the anterior-inferior border is too long, the patient will have difficulty sitting forward and performing sit-to-stand transfers because the brace blocks the forward trunk motion required; if the patient complains of pain around the pubis during transfer training, the orthotist must be contacted to trim the brace.

(d)
Extra precautions must be taken when fitting a jacket to an insensate patient, although the total-contact design is generally better tolerated in this population; Plastizote lining and ventilation holes make the jacket more comfortable and breathable.

(e)
Jackets can be washed and modified as needed, and can even be modified to accommodate a drain; the patient/caregiver should be instructed in donning and doffing, the wearing schedule, whether to sleep and shower in the brace, and daily skin checks beneath the brace to detect irritation or pressure problems.
questions.question:
A patient requiring maximum immobilization of the thoracolumbar spine (for example after a spinal fracture or surgery) is fitted with a custom-molded polypropylene body jacket.
(a) What device has been prescribed, and what are its principal components and how do they achieve immobilization?
(b) What alignment and fitting checks (trim lines/landmarks) should be verified?
(c) What problems can occur if the anterior-inferior border of the jacket is fitted too long, and how is this corrected?
(d) What additional precautions apply to an insensate patient, and what features improve comfort?

A patient recovering from a stroke walks with the affected foot striking the ground on the forefoot first, bearing weight on the lateral border of the foot, with the ankle remaining plantarflexed and inverted throughout the gait cycle, and knee hyperextension noted in stance.
(a) What is the diagnosis and underlying functional problem?
(b) What orthosis would be prescribed, including its joint control, attachment, and biomechanical rationale?
(c) What should be checked or included when fitting this orthosis?
(d) What precautions and physiotherapy follow-up are relevant?
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is an equinovarus deformity, the most common pathologic lower-limb posture seen after central nervous system injury such as stroke; it creates an unstable base of support, with limited ankle dorsiflexion preventing forward progression of the tibia over the foot in stance, causing knee hyperextension and loss of the propulsive phase in terminal stance/preswing, while a sustained plantarflexed and inverted posture during swing creates a limb-clearance problem.

(b)
An ankle-foot orthosis is prescribed to control the abnormal ankle posture during stance and swing; an ankle inversion strap or pad is used to control the inversion, the orthosis is attached to an orthopedic shoe, and a plantar flexion stop is included to control excessive ankle plantar flexion; if ankle clonus is triggered in stance, a dorsiflexion stop is added, set just before the point where clonus appears.

(c)
When cognition and sensation are intact, a molded plastic ankle-foot orthosis with an inversion control wing build-up is preferred; a long plastic foot-plate with soft padding, a toe strap, and an extra-depth shoe with a high toe box can be used to accommodate an abnormal flexed toe posture.

(d)
The dorsiflexion stop should be set carefully to avoid triggering the stretch response of clonus; ongoing physiotherapy follow-up should reassess the abnormal posture, skin tolerance under the straps/pads, and the adequacy of ankle control during stance and swing as recovery progresses.

(a)
• The patella tendon-bearing (PTB) total contact socket has been the internationally accepted standard transtibial socket since the 1960s; it is fabricated from a cast modified to specific weight-bearing (SWB) regions that are pressure-tolerant, with relief over bony prominences such as the tibial crest, fibula, and distal tibia.
• The PTB-Supracondylar (PTBSC) variant has high medial and lateral sidewalls extending over the femoral condyles for enhanced mediolateral stability and self-suspension,
• and the PTB-Supracondylar/Suprapatellar (PTBSCSP) variant further extends the anterior socket to encompass the patella, adding wall stiffness and limiting genu recurvatum.
• both are used mainly for short residual limbs.

(b)
The total surface-bearing (TSB) socket, made practical by gel and elastomeric liner systems, is fabricated from a cast with minimal modification and, when used with gel liners, is believed to distribute pressure more uniformly within the socket.

(c)
PTB sockets can be fit as hard sockets without a liner or, more commonly, with a closed-cell foam liner such as Pe-Lite, which is easy to modify for volume change during the preparatory phase, while roll-on silicone or elastomeric gel liners are generally recommended for use with the TSB design.

(d)
• The SWB modifications relieve pressure over bony prominences that are pressure-intolerant (the tibial crest, fibula head, and distal tibia) while loading pressure-tolerant soft-tissue areas.
• This selective loading protects vulnerable structures from breakdown while allowing the residual limb to bear the weight-bearing forces required for standing and walking.

(e)
• The PTB socket uses selective (specific) weight bearing, with rigid contouring that relieves pressure-intolerant bony regions and concentrates load on defined pressure-tolerant areas.
• The TSB socket instead aims for more uniform pressure distribution over the whole residual limb surface, made possible by a conforming gel or elastomeric liner rather than rigid, selectively contoured socket walls.
• Gel liners used with TSB sockets are recommended for residual limbs with scarring or compromised skin integrity because they reduce shear, whereas Pe-Lite liners used with PTB sockets are valued for ease of modification during the preparatory phase.
• The relative advantages of TSB versus PTB total-contact sockets remain poorly understood, and empiric trial often guides the choice between them for an individual amputee.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the design features of the patella tendon-bearing (PTB) total contact socket and its main variants.
(b) Describe the total surface-bearing (TSB) socket design.
(c) What liners are used with these sockets?
(d) Explain the biomechanical rationale for the specific weight-bearing (SWB) modifications used in the PTB socket.
(e) Distinguish the PTB socket from the TSB socket.

(a) Outline the four-phase process of prosthetic rehabilitation following lower-limb amputation.
(b) Describe the wound dressing options available during the immediate postoperative period and their features.
(c) What complications or errors can occur during postoperative/pre-prosthetic management?
(d) What effect do these complications have on prosthetic fitting and rehabilitation outcome?
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Prosthetic rehabilitation is organized into four phases: pre-prosthetic management, postoperative care, prosthetic fitting and training, and long-term follow-up care.
• Pre-prosthetic management begins when the decision to amputate is made (or after a traumatic amputation) and ends with fitting of a prosthesis.
• it includes evaluating premorbid function, coexisting disease, and social support, and starting range-of-motion, conditioning, and positioning therapy.

(b)
• Postoperative wound care options include soft dressings (elastic bandage or compressive stockinette), semi-rigid dressings (Unna casts), rigid dressings (plaster or fiberglass casts, removable or nonremovable), and air splints.
• Soft dressings are readily available and allow frequent wound inspection but provide limited edema control and can cause a tourniquet effect if poorly applied.
• Rigid dressings reduce wound-healing time and can be combined with a pylon and foot as an immediate or early postoperative prosthesis for early weight bearing, but they prevent wound inspection and carry a risk of wound breakdown if incorrectly applied.

(c)
• A common error is poor application of elastic wraps causing a tourniquet effect and inadequate edema control.
• Failure to position the residual limb correctly, or using pillows under the limb, predisposes to knee flexion contracture in transtibial patients and hip flexion/abduction contracture in transfemoral patients.
• Use of rigid dressings without adequate experience or monitoring has led some centers to abandon early postoperative prostheses in dysvascular amputees because of residual limb trauma and wound-healing problems.

(d)
• Contractures resulting from poor positioning interfere with achieving a comfortable, correctly aligned prosthetic fit and delay or limit successful ambulation.
• Delayed wound healing, poorly fitted early postoperative devices, or uncontrolled edema prolong the pre-prosthetic phase (typically 6 to 10 weeks in dysvascular amputees) and can compromise the eventual quality of the residual limb for prosthetic fitting.
• Careful attention to wound management, edema control, and contracture prevention during this phase is essential to achieving a well-shaped, mature residual limb ready for successful prosthetic fitting and training.

(a)
Orthotic treatment is indicated because the curvature is progressing during a period of rapid growth (puberty) and the angle of curvature is significant; a 20-degree curve is generally considered an indication for bracing, curves of 25 to 30 degrees prompt bracing, and curves over 40 to 45 degrees are more likely to require surgery, so her 30-degree flexible curve with significant remaining growth falls into the bracing range rather than observation or surgery.

(b)
A low-profile thoracolumbosacral orthosis (such as the Boston brace, Providence brace, or Charleston Bending Brace) would be selected.

(c)
A high-profile brace such as the Milwaukee brace is an alternative for higher curves; low-profile TLSOs are generally preferred when the curve pattern allows, while surgery is reserved for curves that are more severe (over 40 to 45 degrees), and a curve of 50 degrees or more predisposes to cardiopulmonary complications and is difficult to brace.

(d)
The goal of bracing is to hold the spinal curvature at the degree of curvature present at the time of diagnosis, preventing further progression during the remaining growth period.

(e)
The brace is typically worn 23 hours per day, with 1 hour off for bathing and exercise, and the curve should continue to be monitored with periodic x-rays until skeletal maturity (approximately 15 years of age in girls and 18 in boys) to confirm the curve remains controlled.
questions.question:
A 13-year-old girl is found on screening to have a right thoracic curve measured at 30 degrees on Cobb angle, confirmed as a flexible, idiopathic curve using the Adam's forward bending test, with significant growth remaining.
(a) What assessment findings support the decision to brace rather than simply observe or proceed to surgery?
(b) Which type of orthosis would be selected for her?
(c) Justify this choice against a high-profile brace and against surgical management.
(d) What is the expected outcome of bracing?
(e) What follow-up/rehabilitation plan should accompany bracing?

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is a stable upper cervical fracture requiring restriction of cervical motion to allow healing without surgery.

(b)
A rigid cervical orthosis (such as the Philadelphia, Miami J, Aspen, Newport, or Malibu) or a sternal-occipital-mandibular immobilizer (SOMI) may be used as first-line treatment instead of a halo for stable upper cervical fractures; the SOMI limits flexion but, because it lacks posterior thoracic support, cannot limit extension, making it particularly suitable for atlantoaxial instability with an intact dens or for bedridden patients since it lacks posterior thoracic coverage.

(c)
When assessing fit, the chin should be centered in the anterior piece of the collar - if the chin extends beyond the collar edge it is too small, and if it falls inside the collar it is too large - and the patient should be familiar with proper donning and doffing procedures.

(d)
Studies of these devices used for stable upper cervical fractures have shown stable fracture healing without increased disability or neurologic compromise on follow-up, and they are cost-effective and easily applied; the physician should nonetheless monitor for pressure ulcer formation at common sites such as the occipital protuberance, chin, clavicles, and ears, and educate the patient about the effect of the collar on activities such as driving (reduced neck rotation increasing the blind spot).
questions.question:
A patient sustains an isolated lateral mass fracture of the atlas (a stable upper cervical fracture) and is being managed conservatively rather than surgically.
(a) What is the diagnosis and functional problem requiring orthotic management?
(b) What orthosis (or orthoses) would be prescribed, and what is the biomechanical rationale for the choice, including the SOMI as an alternative?
(c) What should be checked when fitting the device to ensure it is appropriately sized and functioning?
(d) What precautions, complications, and follow-up are relevant to this device?

(a) Describe the process of pin site selection, insertion, and tightening for a halo device.
(b) Describe the ongoing pin site care and cleaning process.
(c) What errors or complications in pin care can occur?
(d) What effect do these errors have on outcome, and what serious complications must be watched for?
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The preferred pin placement is anterolateral above the frontal orbital rim and posterolateral below the largest diameter of the skull (the parietal-occipital region), positions chosen to avoid piercing the temporalis muscle and injuring the frontal/temporal fossa and nearby cranial nerves.
• More than four pin sites may be used in pediatric patients, those with thin skulls, certain skull fractures, or other conditions compromising the usual fixation points; using six pins can give greater halo strength without increasing pin-site complications.
• Pins are typically retightened 24 to 48 hours after insertion and again at one week.

(b)
• Pin sites should be cleansed daily using sterile cotton-tip applicators with antimicrobial soap and normal saline; crusts should be gently removed with a saline-soaked applicator, since leaving crusts in place can cause fluid buildup that predisposes to infection.
• Topical ointments should be avoided because they can obstruct fluid drainage and increase infection risk, and cleansing agents such as povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide, and alcohol have been associated with pin corrosion, interference with bacterial autolysis, and disruption of healing.

(c)
• Pin loosening - evidenced by a visible pin tip, a pin that can be manually rotated, clicking/grating/creaking sounds, a sensation of looseness, pain at the pin site, or headache - is the most frequent complication.
• Pin-site infection, indicated by drainage or erythema, requires laboratory culture and sensitivity testing to identify an infectious organism; noncompliance with pin-site care can, rarely, progress to pin-site myiasis (maggots).
• External forces applied by lifting or moving the patient by the vest, rods, or superstructure can loosen pins and affect spinal alignment.

(d)
• Pin penetration of the skull has been linked in case reports to epidural abscess, brain abscess (sometimes presenting with confusion, psychosis, or other mentation changes), and even epileptic seizures arising from scar tissue at the pin site, sometimes appearing years after halo removal.
• Loose pins are managed by retightening or removing and reinserting them elsewhere, while infected pin sites require appropriate antimicrobial cleansing and, if needed, culture-directed treatment.
• Reported complications of halo vest use also include loss of spinal reduction, failure to develop spinal stability, pressure sores, local osteoporosis, acute equilibrium impairment, forehead scarring, dysphagia, halo ring migration, cranial nerve palsy, brachial plexopathy, reduced vital capacity, periorbital edema, and cervical muscle atrophy.
• Because changes in mentation, headache, eye pain, fever, or seizures can herald a brain abscess in a patient with (or with a history of) halo pins, clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion and investigate promptly if these signs appear.

(a)
He lacks the finger flexor and intrinsic hand muscle strength needed for gross grasp and fine motor pinch, but retains active wrist extension that can be harnessed for hand function.

(b)
A tenodesis prehension (flexor hinge) orthosis is prescribed; this dynamic wrist-hand-finger orthosis uses active wrist extension to regain gross grasp and fine motor pinch. The Rehabilitation Institute of Chicago design uses a non-elastic cord crossing the wrist, hand, and MCP joint to create three-jaw chuck pinch with active wrist extension, while the more traditional metal flexor hinge design uses an adjustable rigid rod, with the size of the hand opening adjusted by changing the length of the rod.

(c)
The rigid rod length (or cord tensioning in the design incorporating a non-elastic cord) should be adjusted to set the appropriate size of the hand opening for the tasks the patient needs to perform, and the coupling between wrist extension and finger/thumb closure should be checked to confirm reliable three-jaw chuck pinch is achieved.

(d)
As with other static and dynamic hand orthoses, the MCP joints should be positioned near flexion and the IP joints in extension with the thumb held in opposition to maintain collateral ligament length and prevent contracture; follow-up should monitor the strength and reliability of active wrist extension and adjust or replace worn components as needed to maintain effective prehension.
questions.question:
A patient with C6-level tetraplegia has retained some voluntary wrist extension strength but little or no long finger flexor or intrinsic hand muscle strength.
(a) What is the functional problem this orthosis must address?
(b) What orthosis would be prescribed, and how does its design achieve prehension?
(c) What should be checked when fitting and adjusting this orthosis?
(d) What precautions and physiotherapy follow-up are relevant to his ongoing use of this device?

questions.question:
A. Describe glycosides as a class of herbal drug constituents under:
A(i) classification and examples (cardiac, anthraquinone, cyanogenic)
A(ii) plant sources
A(iii) chemical tests
A(iv) uses.
B(i) Explain the basis of their toxicity, limitations and loss of activity.
C(i) Distinguish between cardiac glycosides and anthraquinone glycosides.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Classes: cardiac glycosides/cardenolides (digoxin, lanatosides, ouabain), anthraquinone glycosides and cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin).
A(ii)
Digitalis lanata (digoxin and lanatosides); Acokanthera spp. (ouabain); Asclepiadaceae (rich in cardenolides); Elaeodendron (cardiotoxic glycosides); Cassia podocarpa and C. alata (anthraquinone glycosides); cassava (cyanogenic glycosides).
A(iii)
Keller-Kiliani test for deoxy sugars in cardiac glycosides; Borntrager's test for anthraquinone-containing plants.
A(iv)
Cardiotonic action of digoxin; laxative use of anthraquinone glycosides (Cassia species).
B(i)
• Some glycosides are readily decomposed during boiling and are attacked by enzymes soon after harvest.
• Digitalis loses activity on storage through moisture-driven hydrolysis and enzyme reactivation.
• Cardiac glycosides are toxic: Elaeodendron ordeal poison and Acokanthera arrow poison (ouabain).
• Cassava cyanogenic glycosides rise up to the fifth month, so older tissues are safer.
• Ingested plant-derived cardiac glycosides are inactivated by digoxin-specific Fab antibodies (Digibind, DigiFab).
C(i)
• Cardiac glycosides act on the heart and are tested by Keller-Kiliani; anthraquinone glycosides act as laxatives and are tested by Borntrager's test.
• Biological standardisation applies to digitalis; anthraquinone-containing drugs such as cascara need prolonged storage to convert irritant anthranols to anthraquinones.

(i)
NIPRISAN, a multicomponent herbal product on the Nigerian market made from local plants including Piper guineense and Eugenia caryophyllus.
(ii)
General rule: standardise the plant material, extract and dosage form.
(iii)
Other antisickling compounds are p-hydroxybenzaldehyde, lawsone and phenylalanine.
(iv)
Risk: constituents of Piper guineense vary with season and geography; efficacy in humans needs clinical trials, of which few have been published.
(v)
• Hydroxyurea and long-term blood transfusions are the only disease-modifying therapies for sickle cell disease.
• Pain management with Cannabis sativa seed oil and leaves has been reported; clinical proof of herbal products is needed, so such products should be used only with medical supervision.
questions.question:
A patient with sickle cell disease asks about a multicomponent herbal product developed by NIPRD from local plants, instead of hydroxyurea or blood transfusion.
(i) Identify the herbal remedy and its plant components.
(ii) State the general rule for standardising it.
(iii) Name other antisickling compounds.
(iv) Identify the risk.
(v) State the safe-use or alternative recommendation.

A powdered plant extract (about 5 g in benzene, filtered) is shaken with ammonia solution and the lower ammoniacal layer turns pink-red to violet. The plant is traditionally used as a purgative; related laxative drugs include Cassia podocarpa, Cassia alata, cascara and rhubarb.
(i) Identify the class of constituent and the likely type of crude drug.
(ii) State the characteristic identification test and the constituent.
(iii) State the distinguishing features from related drugs.
(iv) State the clinical or quality consequence (include storage and seasonal effects).
questions.answerText:
(i)
The result indicates free hydroxy-anthraquinones; anthraquinone glycosides occur in laxative drugs such as Cassia podocarpa and Cassia alata.
(ii)
• Borntrager's test: extract shaken with benzene and filtered, ammonia solution added and shaken; a pink, red or violet colour in the lower ammoniacal phase indicates free hydroxy-anthraquinones.
• Borntrager's test is also used to ensure that a plant still contains the active ingredient before use as a raw material.
(iii)
• Anthranols (irritant) are converted to anthraquinones (less irritant): in cascara by storage for at least 1 year; in rhubarb by oxidation in warmer weather.
• Rhubarb anthraquinone and anthranol levels fluctuate through the year.
(iv)
• Laxatives are among drugs imported into Nigeria, so production from the many herbs used as purgatives was recommended.
• Harvest season and storage change potency and irritancy, so collection and storage must be controlled.

(i)
Variation in active constituents leading to inferior quality (not adulteration).
(ii)
• Climatic change can alter the constituents; Jamaican ginger grown in Nigeria may produce a drug of inferior quality.
• Chromolaena odorata growing in Côte d'Ivoire has leaf essential oil rich in geijerene and regeijerene and is active mainly against Gram-negative organisms; the Nigerian plant has less of these terpenes and acts mainly on Gram-positive organisms.
(iii)
• Piper guineense shows geographical and seasonal variation in amides; rhubarb anthranols change to anthraquinones in warm weather.
• Nigerian ginger, if cropped at the right time, carefully scraped and dried, can meet British Pharmacopoeia standards for official Jamaican ginger.
(iv)
• Cultivation is desirable when wild plants are scarce, sparsely distributed or inaccessible, to improve yield, under government control (cannabis) or for a desired variety.
• Plantations should be decentralised across ecological zones to minimise pest infestation and prevent change in active constituents from geographical variation; WHO weed contamination guidelines apply.
• Cultivation has risks: disease, insects, fire, hurricanes; some plants cannot be cultivated.
questions.question:
A drug company tries to grow Jamaican ginger in Nigeria and finds the drug inferior, while wild Chromolaena odorata (Eupatorium odoratum) from two countries shows different antibacterial activity.
(i) Identify the liability (deterioration, adulteration, toxicity, interaction, variation).
(ii) Explain the underlying cause or pathway.
(iii) Differentiate related plants or preparations affected by geography or season.
(iv) Reason to cultivation, collection, regulatory or therapeutic choices.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Deterioration: some drugs, e.g. digitalis, lose active constituents on storage; mould and insect attack also occur in the tropics.
(ii)
• Digitalis re-absorbs sufficient moisture (10-12 per cent), causing hydrolysis and reactivating endogenous enzymes that act on the active principles.
• Some glycosides are attacked by enzymes after harvest, and volatile oils volatilise.
(iii)
• Cascara bark is kept at least 1 year so that anthranols are converted to less irritant anthraquinones: prolonged storage improves quality.
• In rhubarb, anthranols in winter are converted by oxidation to anthraquinones in warmer weather.
(iv)
• Keep storage times to a minimum, dry quickly, keep drying and extraction apparatus close to the plantation, and avoid damp storage.
• Standardise digitalis biologically; prepared digitalis is leaf powder diluted with inert leaf powder to give 1 unit of activity per 100 mg.
• Digitalis lanata is the source of digoxin and lanatosides (cardiotonic).
• Regulatory: official galenicals follow pharmacopoeial procedures and limits.
questions.question:
A batch of digitalis leaf is stored in a humid tropical store for a long time and later shows low potency, while another drug (cascara bark) stored for a year is found to be less irritant.
(i) Identify the liability (deterioration, adulteration, toxicity, interaction) for the digitalis.
(ii) Explain the underlying cause or pathway.
(iii) Differentiate this from cascara and other drugs whose constituents change on storage or after harvest.
(iv) Reason to the storage, standardisation and formulation choices that follow.

questions.answerText:
(i)
A traditional mixture of plant materials (leaves, barks, roots) possibly with animal products; herb-sellers know local names but not necessarily botanical names, and may know only a few remedies.
(ii)
• Purchase complete recipes for a specific ailment and attempt to identify the components; ask the seller to supply materials for a disease; a follow-up with the herbalist is needed.
• Obtain botanical names from a reputable taxonomist or herbarium.
(iii)
• Only experienced collectors or botanists can identify crumbled dried leaves, roots and barks.
• Inactive ingredients may be added to confuse, so experimental testing may miss synergism or potentiation.
(iv)
• Inert material can dilute actives (reduced efficacy) and cause adverse effects, making the therapeutic index unfavourable.
• Sellers are motivated by profit; stabilisers and flavourings may also be added.
(v)
Verify the plants through a taxonomist and herbarium specimens, and test safety and activity before use.

A researcher buys a ready-made dried and crushed remedy for a disease from a market herb-seller who knows only local names. The mixture has crumbled leaves, roots and barks and the researcher wants to study its efficacy.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• Physostigma venenosum (Fabaceae), commonly called Calabar bean or ordeal bean.
• Efik-speaking people of Cross River State, Nigeria used its extracts in the trial of persons accused of witchcraft, sorcery or murder.
(ii)
• The bean contains physostigmine (eserine) at a concentration of about 0.15%.
• Related alkaloids are eseramine, physovenine, calabatine and geneserine, among others.
(iii)
• The alkaloid physostigmine is responsible for the toxic effects of the bean.
• It affects heart contractibility and induces respiratory paralysis, which can result in death.
• Two to three beans are enough to be lethal.
(iv)
• The main antidote is atropine, a slightly less toxic tropane alkaloid.
• Physostigmine is also used to reverse plant toxin-induced central anticholinergic syndromes.
(v)
Physostigmine (eserine) is a muscle relaxant (peripherally acting) and an ophthalmological preparation; Physostigma is a plant drug suitable for production in developing countries.
(vi)
The amount of toxic ingredient in a plant part varies from season to season.
questions.question: Describe Physostigma venenosum (Calabar bean) under the following: (i) botanical name, family, common names and the traditional use that gives it the name ordeal bean; (ii) constituents, with the principal alkaloid and its concentration; (iii) the pharmacological basis of its toxic effects and the amount that is lethal; (iv) the antidote and the reason it is used; (v) the other medicinal uses of the constituent; (vi) the basis of reduced quality or variation in toxin content.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Ricin and abrin are toxalbumins: protein toxins that are plant lectins with a specific affinity for animal cell receptors.
• Ricin is a protein toxin of molecular weight 60-65 kDa; abrin is a protein of about 60-65 kDa and a type II ribosome-inactivating protein.
A(ii)
• Ricin: the seeds of Ricinus communis, known as castor bean or castor oil plant.
• Abrin: the seeds of Abrus precatorius, known as crabs' eye, rosary pea or jequirity bean.
A(iii)
• Ricin affects cells at the ribosomal level, resulting in cell death.
• Abrin inhibits protein synthesis, probably by inactivating the 60S ribosomal subunit and interfering with chain elongation.
B(i)
• Abrin has a lethal dose in man as low as 0.1 to 1.0 µg/kg; death usually occurs 36-72 h after exposure, depending on route of entry and dose.
• Ricin treatment is decontamination and supportive care; ricin has the potential to be used as a biological weapon; few effective antidotes exist for most plant toxins.
B(ii)
Abrus seeds that are chewed cause clinical signs, whereas seeds swallowed whole may not cause any problems at all.
C(i)
• Ricin and abrin have similar structure, properties and mechanism of toxic action.
• Abrin is 75 times more toxic than ricin.

questions.answerText:

Cinchona officinalis (Rubiaceae); the part used is the bark; Cinchona species are listed.
(ii)
Quinine is the antimalarial constituent; the anti-arrhythmic constituent listed for Cinchona spp. is quinidine.
(iii)
Therapeutic use: antimalarial (quinine) and anti-arrhythmic (quinidine).
(iv)
• Rauwolfia serpentina and other species yield the anti-arrhythmic ajmaline.
• Rubiaceae is known for alkaloid content, which supports targeted screening of the family.

questions.answerText:
(i)
About 10% of plants have been investigated; screening validates reported activity, enables structure-activity studies, supplies information on active structure required by regulators and gives chemotaxonomic evidence.
(ii)
• Biological screening (searching for the physiological effect) and phytochemical screening (searching for the compound); random sampling needs identification confirmed at collection; targeted screening uses families such as Asclepiadaceae (cardenolides) and Rubiaceae (alkaloids).
• Traditional-use screening collects plants with the informant and verifies names at a herbarium; computer-assisted screening predicts activity but has challenges of collection, rare plants and confirmation.
(iii)
• Bench-top bioassays must be reliable, reproducible, sensitive and cheap: brine shrimp lethality (general toxicity), antimicrobial and antisickling tests.
• Use at least two animal models; penicillin is toxic to guinea pigs but not humans; mice for preliminary work, rats more reliable for cardiovascular tests; in vitro tests are preferred for speed.
(iv)
• Behavioural profile covers awareness, orientation, mood, vocalisation, restlessness, touch and pain response.
• Neurological profile includes central excitation, motor incoordination (somersault test), muscle tone and pinna reflex.
• Autonomic profile: pupil size, ear colour (red vasodilation, white vasoconstriction), heart and respiratory rate, salivation and urination; toxicity by approximate LD50 from log dose versus deaths.
• Guinea pig ileum: responses compared with histamine (blocked by promethazine) and serotonin (blocked by methysergide); analgesia by hot plate (55 °C) and tail immersion (50 °C); cardiovascular tests in anaesthetised rats with a cannulated femoral artery and kymograph.
(v)
• Alkaloids: Mayer's and Dragendorff's after 1% HCl; tannins: FeCl3 gives blue-black, green or blue-green; anthraquinones: Borntrager's test; saponins: frothing then blood haemolysis test.
• Extraction: fresh material macerated with solvent, suction-filtered, evaporated under vacuum at about 45 °C and dried to constant weight.
(vi)
Confirmatory tests avoid false positives (e.g. Dragendorff's) and screening supports safety and efficacy evidence; limitations: finding a suitable, affordable animal model is a challenge when many extracts and fractions are tested, and plant identity must be confirmed to ensure reproducibility.
questions.question: Describe screening of plants for bioactive agents as an approach: (i) reasons for screening and the proportion of plants investigated; (ii) the two procedures for isolation of bioactive agents and the sampling approaches (random, targeted, traditional use, herbarium-based, computer-assisted); (iii) bench-top bioassays and animal-model choices; (iv) behavioural, neurological and autonomic profiles, isolated guinea pig ileum, analgesia and cardiovascular tests; (v) phytochemical screening tests for alkaloids, tannins, anthraquinones and saponins; (vi) why it improves safety, quality or efficacy and what limitations result.

Describe standardisation of herbal medicines as a principle: (i) why traditional preparations are criticised and how traditional healers attempt standardisation; (ii) the stages of preparation that must be controlled; (iii) the methods used in pharmacopoeias and compendia, with examples; (iv) the role of plant nomenclature, collection, post-harvest processing and the African Pharmacopoeia and WHO guidelines; (v) why the approach improves safety, quality and efficacy and what limitations or trade-offs result.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Criticisms: potions are not standardised and doses are vague (e.g. one small tumblerful three times daily) and not related to age or weight.
• Traditional standardisation is imprecise and varies from tribe to tribe, e.g. arrow poisons are tested on a tortoise's foot or an antelope and the boiling time is not specified.
(ii)
• Control collection of the plant, extraction procedure, first galenical (liquid extract, tincture) and dosage form (tablet, capsule).
• Some galenicals, e.g. digitalis, must be standardised biologically rather than by weight or chemical assay.
(iii)
• Pharmacopoeial methods: lower limit of active constituents, physical, physicochemical, pharmacognostic, chemical, biological, final dosage form, toxicity testing and bioavailability.
• Examples: Borntrager's test for anthraquinones, Keller-Kiliani test for deoxy sugars in cardiac glycosides, saponification values, total alkaloid titration, disintegration test for tablets; prepared digitalis is diluted to one unit of activity per 100 mg.
(iv)
• Plants have several names or one name for several plants; formularies with photographs or line drawings and pharmaceutical names reduce substitution (e.g. Aristolochia in Chinese herbs).
• Geography, season, age, plant part and time of day change constituents; quick drying and minimal storage prevent loss; the African Pharmacopoeia (OAU/STRC, 1985-86) gives African names, description and habitat.
• WHO guidelines are to be used worldwide together with African Pharmacopoeia standards.
(v)
• Right-quality drug, correct collection time, minimum active content and a specified extraction ratio give constant effects and a meaningful dose.
• Toxicity tests (acute, chronic, therapeutic index) and bioavailability checks (e.g. benzoic acid adsorbing sulphadimidine) improve safety.
• Limitations: lack of data on labile active constituents and reproducible assays; simple methods (e.g. titration) may assume one alkaloid; additives and compression may hinder release.

A(i)
A poisonous plant is one that, when touched or ingested in enough quantity, can be harmful or fatal; poisoning may occur by contact, ingestion, absorption or inhalation; over 4,000 species are known.
A(ii)
Examples: Conium maculatum, Physostigma venenosum, Ricinus communis, Abrus precatorius, Mucuna pruriens, Aconitum species and Elaeodendron.
A(iii)
Toxic principles are biochemically diverse; alkaloids are the most abundant; others are toxalbumins (ricin, abrin), cardiac glycosides and serotonin with mucunain.
A(iv)
Physostigmine affects heart contractibility and causes respiratory paralysis; ricin and abrin act at the ribosome; aconitine causes arrhythmias.
B(i)
• The amount of toxic ingredient varies from season to season; plants may contain several toxic principles in different parts.
• Not all parts are poisonous: castor oil is expressed from beans that also contain highly toxic ricin.
• Antidotes: atropine for Calabar bean, physostigmine for central anticholinergic syndromes and digoxin-specific Fab antibodies for cardiac glycosides; few effective antidotes exist.
• Many poisonous plants were used for supposed therapeutic properties.
C(i)
• Ordeal plants are used in trial by ordeal (a test of guilt or innocence by severe pain or terror); Physostigma venenosum was used by the Efik people of Cross River State.
• Arrow poisons are applied to arrows (e.g. Acokanthera, Strophanthus, Mucuna hairs); many arrow poison plants were also used in ordeals by poison.
• Elaeodendron (cardiotoxic glycosides) was used as an ordeal poison in southern Africa and Conium maculatum was used to execute Socrates in 399 BC.

questions.answerText:

Zanthoxylum zanthoxyloides Waterman (syn. Fagara zanthoxyloides Lam.), family Rutaceae; the part used is the root.

Constituents: faragonine and burkinabines A, B and C.

Therapeutic uses: antisickling agent, antimicrobial and anticancer.

(i)
Fangji is one herb referring to multiple species: Aristolochia fangchi (family Aristolochiaceae) or Stephania tetrandra and Cocculus trilobus (Menispermaceae).
(ii)
Standardisation is by a pharmaceutical name defining the species, plant part and any special process or cultivating condition.

Only the Aristolochia species contain aristolochic acid (AA), shown by independent analytical data.

• Risk is substitution/adulteration exposing patients to renotoxic AA-containing Aristolochia species (also guan mutong, guang fangji, hanzhong fangji).
• Confusion in nomenclature and imprecise labelling may lead to inadvertent use of toxic herbal species.

Use the pharmaceutical name so that species are identified and substitution or adulteration avoided; additional measures are needed to ensure consumer safety.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Azadirachta indica A. Juss (Meliaceae), commonly called neem; the part used is the leaf.
(ii)
The major compound is azadirachtin.
(iii)
Uses: antiplasmodial and insecticidal activity.
(iv)
Neem leaf extract is used to treat fever and needs no incantation.
(v)
• Medicinal plants already in use, e.g. Azadirachta indica, should be standardised and formulated into an appropriate dosage form for patients.
