Juss (neem): (i) botanical name, family, common name and part used; (ii) the major constituent; (iii) the pharmacological basis of its uses; (iv) the traditional use for fever and whether incantation is required; (v) why standardisation and formulation are recommended; (vi) the need for toxicological checks and the basis of reduced quality.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• A traditional healer is recognised by the community as competent to provide health care using vegetable, animal and mineral substances; a herbalist specialises in herbs; a bone setter treats fractures with splints and medicaments.
• Ritual rites may be preventive or curative; incantations are plays on words used to conjure up efficacies into a medicine, and their effect cannot be easily proved experimentally.
(ii)
Lambo's five causes: physical, psychological, astral influences, spiritual and esoteric; only physical causes are recognised by orthodox practitioners.
(iii)
Diagnosis includes anamnesis, observation of the patient, visual and clinical examination, biological examination (taste, smell, sight, ants on urine), divination (seeds, 16 seeds and 256 Odu), mind-changing drugs, astronomical signs and dream analysis.
(iv)
• Preparations may be liquid, solid, semi-solid or gaseous; decoctions, infusions, powders, ointments, liniments, enemas and incisions rubbed with powdered drug are used; solvents include water, oils, honey, palm wine and gin.
• Treatment may be multi-component with preservatives, flavours and colours; diet and fasting are part of treatment.
(v)
• Hydrotherapy: hot baths for fever, steam inhalation for catarrh; blood-letting by cupping for rheumatism or migraine.
• Bone setting uses splints and Cissus quadrangularis (30 g per litre of water), taken three times daily and used to bathe the part.
• Psychotherapy and faith healing; TBAs use herbs such as male Carica papaya root with seven melegueta seeds and Blighia sapida bark.
(vi)
• Value: the patient is treated as a whole; many practitioners are good psychotherapists and TBAs have been trained in Ghana, Niger, Nigeria and Cuba.
• Limitations: no pathology, imprecise diagnosis, intra-uterine abortifacients risk uterine rupture, and male and female circumcision are associated with neo-natal tetanus and female circumcision with septicaemia.
• The practices vary in quality, so retraining and legal control are needed.
questions.question: Describe traditional medicine as a system, covering its methods and techniques: (i) the terms healer, herbalist, bone setter, ritual rites and incantation; (ii) the five causes of disease; (iii) methods of diagnosis; (iv) forms and routes of treatment; (v) hydrotherapy, blood-letting, bone setting, psychotherapy and obstetrics; (vi) why the approach has value and what limitation or trade-off (including harmful practices) results.

Describe traditional medicine as a system in developing countries: (i) the advantages of traditional medicine (cost, accessibility, acceptability, manpower, drug source, natural products, convenience); (ii) examples of retraining, e.g. traditional birth attendants; (iii) the disadvantages; (iv) the problems of integration or co-recognition with orthodox medicine; (v) why the approach improves access and what limitation or trade-off results, including toxic examples.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Traditional medicine is cheaper than orthodox medicine; drugs account for 10-30% of health costs in developed countries but 30-50% in many developing countries.
• It is more accessible: 60-85% of people in developing countries rely on it; 85% of Swazis use traditional healers and there were 5,000 healers in Swaziland (about 1:110).
• It has wider acceptability, being rooted in culture, and nomads have their own practitioners.
• Practitioners can add health manpower, share the culture of patients and use skilful psychotherapy and counselling.
• It is a potential source of new and cheap drugs, e.g. reserpine from Rauwolfia and vinblastine from Catharanthus roseus.
• Multi-component preparations treat all ailments in one decoction; patients avoid long queues and tests.
(ii)
Retrained TBAs in Niger (15-day course at US$21 each) lowered maternal and child mortality; Philippines hilots were retrained after 75% of births were found to be hilot-attended.
(iii)
• Disadvantages: lack of scientific proof of efficacy; imprecise diagnosis (e.g. 'stomach trouble'); lack of pathology; treating symptoms rather than disease.
• No established standards of training, no self-regulation, no follow-up of patients and no unbiased record of practitioners' ability.
(iv)
Integration needs retraining and legal control; strain arises from theoretical incompatibility (traditional systems treat the whole person within a metaphysical structure that experiment cannot prove or destroy).
(v)
• Natural products are claimed to be more readily accepted by the body, yet some are toxic in minute doses (eserine, strychnine) and comfrey contains hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids (lasiocarpine causing liver cancer in rodents).
• A national drug policy incorporating traditional medicine is needed; no documented evidence that aqueous decoctions have greater bioavailability.

questions.question:
A village preparer places a plant drug with the whole of the extraction liquid in a closed vessel for 7 days with occasional shaking, strains it, presses the marc, mixes the liquids and clarifies by settling and pouring off. Another preparer pours boiling water on the herb and leaves it for 10-15 minutes like tea.
(i) Identify the type of each preparation and the method used.
(ii) Name the solvent, process and key steps.
(iii) Predict the effect on constituent stability.
(iv) State the rationale for choosing each method.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The first is a maceration; the second is an infusion.
(ii)
• Maceration: plant material with the whole of the menstruum (extraction liquid) in a closed vessel for 7 days, shaken occasionally, strained and the marc pressed; the liquids are mixed and clarified by subsidence or filtration; traditionally subsidence then decantation is more common.
• Infusion: boiling water poured on a specific quantity of plant material and left 10-15 minutes, similar to tea in a teapot; infusions are dilute solutions and can also be made in edible oil or vinegar.
(iii)
Infusion's short contact with boiling water avoids the prolonged heating that can decompose glycosides in a decoction.
(iv)
• Maceration is the official method for tinctures; official galenicals follow pharmacopoeial maceration, percolation or decoction procedures with defined weight, solvent volume and time.
• Cold percolation and hot aqueous extraction (decoction) are also listed among extraction stages.

questions.question:
A patient presents with severe cardiac toxicity (ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation) after taking homemade medicated liquor containing aconite and a traditional medicine containing Aconitum carmichaeli.
(i) Identify the herbal remedy and the plants involved.
(ii) Name the toxic marker constituents.
(iii) Identify the risk (toxicity, adulteration, contamination, interaction).
(iv) State the safe-use or alternative recommendation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Aconitum species, including A. carmichaeli and A. kusnezoffii, used in traditional medicine and in homemade medicated liquor.
(ii)
Toxicity derives primarily from diester diterpene alkaloids: aconitine, mesaconitine and hypaconitine.
(iii)
• Risk is toxicity: poisonings were reported from homemade medicated liquor and traditional medicine containing A. carmichaeli.
• Severe cardiac toxicity: ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, eventually death; other cases showed bradycardia and hypotension.
• Combined overdose of A. kusnezoffii and A. carmichaeli also caused bradycardia and hypotension; A. kusnezoffii aconitine poisoning cases are reported.
(iv)
• Few effective antidotes exist for most plant toxins.
• General safeguard: toxic herbs must be removed from general use and toxicity checks done.

(i)
Lawsonia inermis / L. alba (Lythraceae); the leaves are used.
(ii)
The compound is lawsone (2-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone).
(iii)
• The leaves were found to inhibit sickling and to increase the oxygen affinity of HbSS blood.
• Increasing oxygen affinity reduces sickling, as also described for p-hydroxybenzaldehyde from Sorghum bicolor.
(iv)
• Sickle cell disease is hereditary; HbS replaces glutamic acid by valine in the β-chain, and red cells sickle at low oxygen tension.
• Complications are acute and chronic: chronic pain and painful episodes, musculoskeletal problems, stroke, pulmonary hypertension and septicaemia.
(v)
• Cajanus cajan seed aqueous decoction (phenylalanine); Sorghum bicolor leaves and seeds; Acacia xanthophloea stem and roots; Cannabis sativa for pain.
• NIPRISAN (NIPRD) combines local plants including Piper guineense and Eugenia caryophyllus.
(vi)
• Hydroxyurea and long-term transfusion are the only disease-modifying therapies.
• Few clinical studies of herbal therapies have been published, so efficacy in humans is unproven.
questions.question: Describe Lawsonia inermis / L. alba in sickle cell disease research: (i) botanical name, family and part used; (ii) the constituent responsible and its chemical name; (iii) the pharmacological basis of its activity; (iv) the underlying pathology of sickling; (v) the other plant remedies and multicomponent herbal product used for the disease; (vi) the limitations of herbal therapies for the disease.

Describe Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench as a medicinal plant in sickle cell disease research: (i) botanical name, family and parts used; (ii) the traditional use; (iii) the compound believed responsible and its pharmacological basis; (iv) the pathology of sickle cell disease that explains the target; (v) other plants and compounds for sickle cell anaemia and pain; (vi) why quality, adulteration or limitations of such plants matter.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench, family Poaceae; the leaves and seeds are used.
(ii)
The leaves and seeds are used as a blood builder in anaemia associated with sickle cell disease.
(iii)
The compound believed responsible is p-hydroxybenzaldehyde, which increases the oxygen affinity of HbS.
(iv)
• Sickle haemoglobin (HbS) is a structural variant of HbA caused by a missense mutation replacing glutamic acid with valine in the β-chain.
• Red blood cells sickle under conditions of low blood oxygen tension.
• Anaemia is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in sickle cell disease and may be due to malaria parasitaemia and septicaemia.
(v)
• Acacia xanthophloea stem and roots; Cajanus cajan seed aqueous decoction (phenylalanine); Lawsonia inermis leaves (lawsone).
• Cannabis sativa seed oil and leaves relieve pain; Zanthoxylum zanthoxyloides root is an antisickling agent.
• NIPRISAN was developed by NIPRD from Piper guineense and Eugenia caryophyllus.
(vi)
• Hydroxyurea and long-term blood transfusion are the only disease-modifying therapies, so herbal products need clinical trials.
• Clinical trials are the proof of efficacy in humans and few have been published.

questions.question:
A root drug is a source of reserpine, used for hypertension and listed among plant drugs suitable for production by developing countries; it is cited as an example of a natural resource that can substitute for imported bulk drugs.
(i) Identify the plant, family and part used.
(ii) Name the active constituents responsible for activity.
(iii) State the therapeutic uses of the constituents.
(iv) State related species, uses in traditional practice and its role in local drug production.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Rauwolfia serpentina (Apocynaceae); the part used is the root.
(ii)
Reserpine is the drug; ajmaline is another constituent from Rauwolfia serpentina and other species.
(iii)
Use: hypertension and control of blood pressure; ajmaline is listed as an anti-arrhythmic.
(iv)
• Rauwolfia vomitoria is also listed as an antihypertensive plant.
• Traditional practitioners give sedative decoctions, often including roots of Rauwolfia species, to mentally disturbed patients.
• Reserpine from Rauwolfia is cited as an example of using Africa's flora as a substitute for imported bulk drugs.
• Reserpine is a cheap known drug source from traditional medicine.

questions.question: Describe Chromolaena odorata (Eupatorium odoratum): (i) botanical names and the geographical sources studied; (ii) the leaf constituents and the class of compounds; (iii) the pharmacological basis of antibacterial activity and how it differs by country; (iv) the basis of variation in constituents with geography, season and age; (v) the standardisation implications; (vi) the basis of reduced quality.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Chromolaena odorata (Eupatorium odoratum), studied from Côte d'Ivoire and Nigeria.
(ii)
Plants from Côte d'Ivoire produce leaf essential oil rich in the terpenes geijerene and regeijerene.
(iii)
• The Côte d'Ivoire plant has antibacterial activity especially against Gram-negative organisms.
• The Nigerian plant has less of these two terpenes and is mainly antibacterial against Gram-positive organisms.
(iv)
• A plant growing wild in one country need not yield the same constituents as the same plant in another, and its biological activity may differ.
• Constituents also vary with season, plant age, plant part and even time of day.
(v)
• Collection of wild plants is practical when plants grow readily, but cultivation in ecological zones controls variation.
• Plant nomenclature and synonyms should be recorded for accurate research.
(vi)
Volatile oils are lost if drying is delayed, and mould and insect attack occur if the material is damp or stored too long.

(i)
Loss of viability on drying or freezing: recalcitrant seeds cannot be stored in conventional seed banks.
(ii)
Recalcitrant seeds cannot withstand desiccation to moisture contents below 20%.
(iii)
• Orthodox seeds dry to 3% (oily) or 7% (starchy) moisture and keep for long periods at low temperature; intermediate seeds dry to 10-12% but further drying or cold injures them.
• Orthodox seeds are stored at −18 °C or cooler for the long term, and at 5-10 °C for the short and medium term.
(iv)
• Field gene banks (live plants) are the traditional choice for vegetatively propagated species and those with recalcitrant seeds, but face pests, drought, flood, vandalism and high cost.
• In vitro culture (slow growth for short and medium term) and cryopreservation at −196 °C in liquid nitrogen suit germplasm that cannot be dry seed-stored.
• The choice depends on duration, storage behaviour, human and financial resources, and institutional and technological capacity.
• Botanical gardens keep living collections of one or a few individuals per species; pollen storage suits some species and DNA banking is an emerging technique.
questions.question:
A conservation team must store seeds of a medicinal plant that cannot withstand desiccation below 20% moisture, and also vegetatively propagated plants such as banana and pineapple that rarely produce seeds.
(i) Identify the liability (deterioration, loss of viability, genetic loss).
(ii) Explain the underlying cause or pathway.
(iii) Differentiate related seed types and storage methods.
(iv) Reason to the storage, formulation, regulatory or conservation choice.

A. Describe solid and semi-solid herbal dosage forms as a class under:
A(i) classification and types
A(ii) sources and method of preparation
A(iii) chemical or quality tests
A(iv) the basis for selecting a dosage form.
B(i) Explain the basis of limitation or loss of activity in these forms.
C(i) Distinguish between powders, dry extract powders and granules, and between capsules and tablets.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Solid forms: teabags, powders, dry extract powders, granules, tablets and capsules; semi-solid forms: ointments, balms, creams and pastes.
• Other forms include inhalations, medicated oils (coconut or palm kernel oil base), liniments for aches and pains, and herbal soaps.
A(ii)
• Teabag: ground herb (single or mixed) sufficient for one dose as an infusion; ointment: semi-solid greasy preparation for skin, rectum or nasal mucosa.
• Medicated oils: herbal material, extract or fresh juice mixed, macerated or boiled in fixed oil.
A(iii)
Quality tests for these forms: disintegration tests for tablets and quality control tests used for synthetic drugs are required.
A(iv)
• The dosage form depends on the physical or physicochemical properties of the drug, the route of administration, biological properties, processing conditions, biopharmaceutical aspects and dose.
• Dosage forms should be as close as possible to the traditional form, e.g. a dry powder taken with food should remain a powder.
B(i)
• Adjuvants added to make tablets can affect release of the active constituents of the extract.
• A tablet compressed too hard may not disintegrate, so the active ingredient cannot be released for absorption.
C(i)
• Powder: ground herb in coarse or fine particles (nanopowders excluded); dry extract powder: obtained by evaporating the extraction solvent, with excipients, stabilisers or preservatives; granules: dried fluid extract in agglomerated spherical particles, reconstituted as "herbal tea" or used for tablets or capsules.
• Capsule: herbal substance in a hard (two-piece) or soft (one-piece) shell; tablet: extract powder, plant powder or granule blended with excipients and compressed to a defined shape and size.
• Bioavailability of the final solid forms: attention is given to the amount of active principle in a usable form.

(i)
Mucuna pruriens L. (Fabaceae), velvet bean; it also appears in the list of plant drugs as the source of L-Dopa for antiparkinsonism.
(ii)
• The fruits are covered with persistent pale-brown or grey trichomes causing irritating blisters on skin contact.
• The compounds responsible for the itch are a protein, mucunain, and serotonin (6-hydroxytryptamine).
(iii)
Other stinging plants that need careful handling are Urtica and Tragia species.
(iv)
• Ingestion causes coughing, convulsions, twisting and death by suffocation; the hairs are a component of arrow poisons and a murder poison.
• Researchers should handle it with care to avoid irritation and distress to informants.
• Not all poisonous plants are only toxic; many have been used for their supposed therapeutic properties.
questions.question:
A fruit is covered with persistent pale-brown or grey trichomes that cause irritating blisters on contact with skin. The hairs are a component of arrow poisons and have been used as a murder poison; ingestion causes coughing, convulsions, twisting and death by suffocation. A field researcher is about to handle it.
(i) Identify the crude drug.
(ii) State the characteristic identification features and constituents.
(iii) Name other stinging plants that need careful handling.
(iv) State the clinical, safety or quality consequence.

A research team sends a patient with a doctor-diagnosed ailment to a herbalist, who is not told of the researchers' interest, and the patient returns with a ready-made powdered herbal drug that improves the condition.
(i) Identify the remedy and how its identity can be established.
(ii) Outline how the remedy can be prepared, recorded and standardised.
(iii) State what general standardisation of the remedy covers.
(iv) Identify the risk (quackery, adulteration, interaction, outside treatments).
(v) State the safe-use recommendation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A traditional herbal remedy whose components may not be easily identifiable; a follow-up visit to the herbalist may be needed to learn the actual composition, especially for a powdered drug or mixture.
(ii)
• Analyse the traditional medicine to identify its components and assess efficacy; collect the plant with the informant and deposit a voucher specimen in a herbarium.
• Only record remedies proven beneficial in a doctor-diagnosed ailment; exclude incantations or rituals performed without the patient's knowledge.
(iii)
General standardisation covers collection, extraction, galenical form, dosage form, toxicity and bioavailability.
(iv)
• Quack herbalists exist and practitioner proficiency varies; additional treatments could confound results unless the patient is under strict surveillance.
• Inert ingredients may be added and the herbalist may hide knowledge (poisonous plants).
(v)
Keep the patient under surveillance, observe before and after treatment, determine dosage and note toxic side effects before wider use.

questions.question: Describe Piper guineense (Piper guiniense) as a medicinal plant: (i) botanical name and part studied; (ii) the amides present and how their pattern changes by collection season and location; (iii) its use in sickle cell disease; (iv) the basis of variation in potency; (v) the standardisation implications; (vi) the basis of reduced quality.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Piper guineense (written Piper guiniense in one place); roots from Fume in the Volta region of Ghana were analysed.
(ii)
• Roots collected in June/July 1974 and September/October 1975 contained mainly wisanine and dihydrowisanine, with no piperine.
• Roots collected in January/February 1975 contained dihydropiperine, piperine and N-isobutyl-trans-2-trans-4-eicosadienamide as the major amides.
(iii)
Piper guineense is one of the local plants in NIPRISAN, a multicomponent product developed by NIPRD to manage sickle cell disease.
(iv)
• Active constituents vary in quantity and quality from season to season and with geography; the variation may be slight or significant.
• This matters when the plant is used in traditional medicine.
(v)
Collection season, geography, plant part and age must be controlled to give a consistent constituent profile.
(vi)
Storage should be minimal to avoid mould and insect attack and loss of constituents.

(i)
• Nigeria (about 200 million people) imports over 70% of its pharmaceutical drugs; pharmaceutical imports doubled between 2013 and 2018 (US$400 million to over US$800 million) and were $756.63 million in 2023.
• African drug importation is projected at USD 56-70 billion by 2030 (USD 28.56 billion in 2017).
(ii)
Reduce unwarranted importation (only essential drugs), produce some pharmaceuticals locally, use local medicinal plants as substitutes, cultivate on a large scale for export of excess, and direct research to local problems collaboratively.
(iii)
High cost of patent technology, contract formulation for multinationals, plants running at about 30-40% capacity because bulk drugs are imported, and low technology know-how.
(iv)
• Primary processing: powders for tabletting or capsules; aqueous extracts freeze-dried; alcoholic extracts evaporated; isolation of pure constituents; actives must be standardised.
• Category A plants are already used in health care, are commercial crude drugs or are cultivated in developing countries; category B plants are used widely and cultivated on a large scale; Azadirachta indica should be standardised and formulated.
• Dosage forms should be close to traditional forms; toxicological checks and international standards are required; plantations are decentralised across ecological zones with plants near the plantation.
• Adding value by exporting extracts gives about 10X added value; Reserpine from Rauwolfia is an example of a bulk drug substitute.
(v)
• Industrialised nations should develop simple machinery, allowing for water shortage (borehole) and irregular electricity (generating set), maintain facilities and spare parts and train staff.
• Regional collaboration (ECOWAS or AU) supports technology transfer.
(vi)
• Standardised local drugs reduce import dependence and rural migration, and extracts ease transport.
• Limitations: naira instability and high drug prices, scarce foreign exchange, cost of technology, pests and risk of constituent change.
questions.question: Describe considerations for local production of drugs from medicinal plants as an approach: (i) the import problem for Nigeria and Africa; (ii) the proposals for self-reliance; (iii) the factors responsible for low production capacity; (iv) the primary processing options and the procedures for producing drugs from plants; (v) the role of industrialised nations; (vi) why the approach improves quality and self-reliance and what limitation or trade-off results.

Two extracts from the same plant are tested: one shaken with water gives persistent frothing; the other (5 g in 10 mL distilled water, stirred and filtered) gives a blue-black precipitate with ferric chloride. The plant family is also known to yield steroidal sapogenins.
(i) Identify the constituent classes.
(ii) State the characteristic identification and confirmatory tests.
(iii) State the distinguishing features from false positives.
(iv) State the clinical or quality consequence.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Frothing indicates saponins and the blue-black precipitate indicates tannins.
(ii)
• Saponins: frothing in water is preliminary evidence; the blood haemolysis test confirms by haemolysing red blood cells.
• Tannins: ferric chloride reagent added to the filtrate; a blue-black, green or blue-green precipitate indicates tannins.
(iii)
• The haemolysis test is used to eliminate false-positive frothing results.
• Phytochemical tests must be simple, rapid and able to handle many samples; extracts should be used on the day of collection to prevent physiological changes.
(iv)
• Searching for plants that yield steroidal sapogenins is an example of targeted screening; diosgenin (Dioscorea sp., bulb) is used in partial synthesis of steroid hormones.
• Confirmatory tests are needed before reporting a class, and a voucher specimen should be kept.

questions.question:
A herbal laboratory prepares three liquid preparations: (a) an alcoholic liquid extract produced by percolation so that 1 mL contains the extractive from 1 g of herbal material; (b) an alcoholic or hydroalcoholic extract made from 1 part herbal material and 5-10 parts solvent; (c) an extract prepared like (b) but with glycerine as the solvent.
(i) Identify the type of each preparation and the method used.
(ii) Name the solvent, process and key steps.
(iii) State how fixed extraction conditions affect the concentration limits of the extracts.
(iv) State the rationale for choosing the method and the other liquid dosage forms.
questions.answerText:
(i)
(a) is a fluid extract (percolation); (b) is a tincture; (c) is a herbal glycerite.
(ii)
• Fluid extract: alcoholic liquid, 1 mL = extractive of 1 g of herbal material.
• Tincture: usually ethanol of suitable concentration or wine, 1 part herbal material to 5-10 parts solvent; the water to alcohol ratio should be recorded.
• Glycerite: glycerine is used in the extraction instead of alcohol and water.
(iii)
A fixed plant-to-solvent ratio and specified weight, volume and period of extraction give extracts of known concentration limits.
(iv)
• Alcoholic extracts can be evaporated to dryness with a rotary evaporator and the dry extract tabletted or encapsulated.
• Other liquid forms: infusions, decoctions, herbal alcoholic beverages (bitters/wines), syrups, oral emulsions and suspensions.
• Dosage form depends on the physical properties of the drug, route, biological properties, processing conditions, biopharmaceutical aspects and dose.

(i)
A herbal syrup (liquid), a dry powder kept as a powder, and capsules (solid dosage forms).
(ii)
• Syrup: viscous liquid containing honey, sugars or other sweeteners, made by dissolving, mixing, suspending or emulsifying herbal extracts or decoctions in the sweet solution.
• Capsule: herbal substance enclosed in a hard (body and cap) or soft, soluble gelatin or other shell; stages: grinding, extraction, filtration, concentration, spray or freeze drying.
(iii)
Standardisation of active constituents gives uniform actives with every preparation.
(iv)
• If a preparation is used as a decoction, the standardised form should preferably be liquid, made more palatable for children.
• A dry powder mixed with food should remain in that form; forms close to the traditional one are more acceptable and cheap to produce.
• Selection depends on drug properties, route, biological properties, processing conditions, biopharmaceutical aspects and dose.
questions.question:
A decoction used traditionally is to be standardised for children, while a dry powder normally mixed with food and a dry extract are also to be developed. The team plans to dissolve the extract in a sweet viscous base and fill the dry extract into soluble shells.
(i) Identify the type of preparations and the method used.
(ii) Name the solvent, process and key steps.
(iii) State the benefit of standardising the active constituents.
(iv) State the rationale for choosing the dosage form.

A. Describe the important plant drugs suitable for production by developing countries under:
A(i) classification by therapeutic group
A(ii) plant sources and parts
A(iii) the chemical constituents and tests
A(iv) uses.
B(i) Explain the basis of their value and the limitations or toxicity linked to some of them.
C(i) Distinguish between drugs for the cardiovascular group and drugs for ophthalmological or muscle relaxant use.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Groups: analgesics and antipyretics; antigout; antiprotozoal; antimigraine; antineoplastic; antiparkinsonism; cardiovascular (antihypertensive, antiarrhythmic, cardiotonic); laxatives; muscle relaxants; ophthalmological; oxytocics; respiratory.
A(ii)
• Papaver somniferum (morphine, codeine); Gloriosa superba (colchicine); Cephaelis ipecacuanha (emetine); Claviceps purpurea (ergotamine, ergometrine); Catharanthus roseus (vinblastine, vincristine); Mucuna pruriens (L-Dopa).
• Rauwolfia serpentina/vomitoria, Voacanga africana (antihypertensives); Cinchona spp. (quinidine); Digitalis lanata (digoxin); Cassia podocarpa and C. alata (anthraquinone glycosides).
• Physostigma venenosum (physostigmine), Chondrodendron tomentosum, Pilocarpus sp. (pilocarpine); Ephedra species (ephedrine); Theobroma cacao (theophylline as aminophylline).
A(iii)
Chemical tests: Borntrager's for anthraquinones and Keller-Kiliani for cardiac glycosides.
A(iv)
Uses include analgesia, anti-gout, antineoplastic, antiparkinsonism, hypertension, cardiotonic, laxative, glaucoma, oxytocic and respiratory.
B(i)
• Plants are a source of over 25% of prescribed drugs and substitute for imported bulk drugs; producing extracts for export adds about 10 times value.
• Drugs from plants require standardisation of active constituents to give uniform actives, plus toxicological checks and international standards.
• Some constituents are toxic (physostigmine, eserine) or lose activity (digitalis).
C(i)
• Cardiovascular: reserpine, ajmaline, quinidine, digoxin and lanatosides; ophthalmological: pilocarpine and physostigmine; muscle relaxants: physostigmine and Chondrodendron source.
• Pilocarpus jaborandi (Rutaceae) leaf treats glaucoma and dry mouth.

questions.question:
A dried plant extract (about 0.5 g) is heated with 5 mL of 1% aqueous hydrochloric acid on a water bath and filtered. One mL of the filtrate gives turbidity with Mayer's reagent and a second 1 mL gives a precipitate with Dragendorff's reagent. The plant belongs to a family known for alkaloids.
(i) Identify the class of constituent indicated.
(ii) State the identification tests and other reagents that can be used.
(iii) State how this finding is distinguished from false positives and what confirmation is needed.
(iv) State the quality or research consequence and what must be confirmed about the plant at collection.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The result indicates the possible presence of alkaloids.
(ii)
• Tests: 0.5 g extract in 5 mL of 1% aqueous HCl on a water bath, filtered; 1 mL treated with Mayer's reagent and 1 mL with Dragendorff's reagent.
• Turbidity or precipitation with either reagent indicates possible alkaloids; Wagner's reagent, picric acid solution or tannic acid solution can also be used.
(iii)
• Dragendorff's reagent may give false-positive reactions in non-alkaloidal extracts, so confirmatory tests must be done.
• Alkaloid extracts can be checked by thin-layer chromatography against reference compounds; total alkaloid can be found by acid/base titration (which assumes the major alkaloid is the only one).
(iv)
• Rubiaceae is known for alkaloid content; targeted screening of such families is more efficient.
• Plant identification must be confirmed at collection (or before the screen) and a voucher specimen deposited in a herbarium.

questions.question:
A leaf-derived herbal drug is a source of vinblastine and vincristine and is listed among the antineoplastic plant drugs suitable for production by developing countries.
(i) Identify the plant, its family and the part used.
(ii) Name the essential active constituents responsible for the activity.
(iii) State the therapeutic use of the constituents.
(iv) State how this drug is classed among drugs of natural origin and why traditional medicine is valued as a source of such drugs.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Catharanthus roseus (Apocynaceae); the part used is the leaf.
(ii)
The essential active constituents are vinblastine and vincristine (antineoplastic group).
(iii)
Therapeutic use: vinblastine is used to treat Hodgkin's disease, leukemia, testicular and neck cancer.
(iv)
• It is a drug of natural origin not used in modern medicine for the same ailment as in traditional medicine (group 2).
• Traditional medicine is a potential source of new drugs and of cheap known drugs such as vinblastine from Catharanthus roseus.
• Medicinal plants are the source of over 25% of worldwide prescribed drugs, directly or indirectly.

questions.question:
A. Describe alkaloids as a class of toxic and medicinal plant constituents under:
A(i) classification and examples
A(ii) plant sources and families
A(iii) chemical tests
A(iv) mechanism of action of examples.
B(i) Explain the basis of their toxicity and limitation as drugs.
C(i) Distinguish between alkaloids and cardiac glycosides.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Alkaloids are the most abundant class of toxic principles in poisonous plants; examples are piperidine, tropane and diester diterpene alkaloids.
• Examples: coniine, N-methyl-coniine, conhydrine (Conium); physostigmine, eseramine (Physostigma); aconitine, mesaconitine, hypaconitine (Aconitum); scopolamine and atropine.
A(ii)
Sources: Conium maculatum, Physostigma venenosum, Aconitum species and Datura metel; the Rubiaceae family is known for alkaloid content; Rauwolfia serpentina yields reserpine.
A(iii)
Extract in 1% aqueous HCl on a water bath, then Mayer's and Dragendorff's reagents (turbidity or precipitation); Wagner's reagent, picric acid or tannic acid may also be used.
A(iv)
Physostigmine affects heart contractibility and induces respiratory paralysis; reserpine is used in hypertension.
B(i)
• Toxicity: four Conium leaves are said to be a lethal dose; two to three Calabar beans are lethal; aconitine causes ventricular tachycardia, fibrillation, bradycardia and hypotension.
• Dragendorff's reagent can give false positives in non-alkaloidal extracts.
• Few effective antidotes exist; atropine is used for Calabar bean poisoning and physostigmine for central anticholinergic syndromes.
• Alkaloid extracts standardised only by total alkaloid titration assume the major alkaloid is the only one present.
• Reserpine from Rauwolfia and quinine from Cinchona show the same class also gives useful drugs (hypertension; antimalarial).
C(i)
• Cardiac glycosides (cardenolides) occur e.g. in Asclepiadaceae and Elaeodendron, are tested by Keller-Kiliani (deoxy sugars), and are antagonised by digoxin-specific Fab antibodies.
• Alkaloids are detected by Mayer's and Dragendorff's reagents, whereas cardiac glycosides are identified by the Keller-Kiliani test.

questions.question:
A traditional healer places a plant drug in cold water, brings it to the boil, simmers it for about 15 minutes (sometimes up to 1 hour), lets it stand for a further 15 minutes and decants it. The pot is often left on the heat at home and the liquid becomes darker.
(i) Identify the type of preparation and the method used.
(ii) Name the solvent, process and key steps.
(iii) Predict the effect of prolonged contact with heat and water on constituent yield, potency and stability.
(iv) State the rationale for choosing this method and the dosage form advice for standardised versions.
(v) Distinguish it from an infusion and a maceration.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A decoction; it is the usual traditional herbal preparation and is not the same as a concoction (a many-ingredient soup or drink).
(ii)
Solvent is water; plant placed in cold water, brought to boil, simmered about 15 min or longer (up to 1 h), stood a further 15 min, then decanted or filtered.
(iii)
• The extract becomes darker and probably stronger as more constituent is extracted while water stays in contact with the drug.
• Adding more water dilutes the medicament and may need a completely new preparation.
• Boiling may alter many active constituents, e.g. some glycosides are readily decomposed.
(iv)
• Decoctions are the traditional form; standardised preparations should preferably stay liquid (made more palatable for children).
• Fixed plant-to-solvent ratio and defined extraction are needed before a dose is meaningful.
(v)
• Infusion: boiling water poured on a specific quantity of drug and left 10-15 minutes, like tea in a teapot.
• Maceration: drug plus the whole menstruum in a closed vessel for 7 days with occasional shaking, then strained and the marc pressed.

questions.question:
A farmer uses cassava leaves as a vegetable and for starch for pharmaceutical use. Young and old tissues and different times of day are harvested.
(i) Identify the liability (toxicity, deterioration, adulteration, interaction).
(ii) Explain the underlying cause or pathway and time dependence.
(iii) Differentiate this variation from other plants whose constituents vary with age, season or geography.
(iv) Reason to the harvesting, formulation, regulatory or therapeutic choice.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Toxicity from cyanogenic glycosides in cassava (Manihot esculenta).
(ii)
• Cyanide content of cassava tissues increases up to the fifth month and declines from the sixth month.
• Diurnal variation: cyanogenic glucosides were highest in leaves and stems at about 2 p.m., when SCN⁻ levels were lowest.
• Glucose is needed for forming linamarin, so optimum concentrations are expected in the daytime when photosynthesis and enzymes are at optimum.
(iii)
• Ocimum gratissimum gives most volatile oil per weight when young; Mentha viridis changes oil composition with maturity; Piper guineense amides vary seasonally and geographically.
• Rhubarb anthranols oxidise to anthraquinones in warm weather; Chromolaena odorata varies with geography.
(iv)
• From toxicological considerations, older cassava tissues are safer sources of food and medicine for humans.
• This matters for populations using cassava leaves as a vegetable and for cassava starch for pharmaceutical use; the time of collection should be decided with such facts in mind.

questions.question:
A. Describe liquid herbal dosage forms as a class of herbal preparations under:
A(i) classification and types
A(ii) solvents, sources and method of preparation
B(i) Explain the basis of activity, limitation or loss of potency of these forms.
C(i) Distinguish between a decoction and an infusion, and between a tincture and a glycerite.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Liquid dosage forms are oral preparations: solutions, medicated syrups and suspensions, plus fluid extracts, decoctions, infusions, tinctures, glycerites, herbal alcoholic beverages (bitters/wines) and oral emulsions.
A(ii)
• They are made by dissolving the herbal preparation in aqueous or non-aqueous solvent, suspending it in a medium or incorporating it into one phase of an oil-and-water system.
• Syrups: viscous liquids with honey, sugars or other sweeteners, prepared by dissolving, mixing, suspending or emulsifying extracts or decoctions.
• Infusions can also be prepared in edible oil or vinegar.
B(i)
• Containers that are not airtight lead to deterioration, which is serious mainly in liquid preparations.
• Prolonged boiling alters constituents such as glycosides, and heating in the pot makes a decoction stronger.
• Palatability can be improved for children while keeping the traditional liquid form.
• Potency is tied to the stated plant-to-solvent ratio (fluid extract 1 mL = 1 g herb; tincture 1 part herb to 5-10 parts solvent).
C(i)
• Decoction: cold water brought to boil, simmered about 15 minutes to 1 hour, stood 15 minutes; infusion: boiling water poured on herbs and steeped for a short time (10-15 minutes).
• Tincture: alcohol/hydroalcohol extract, 1 part herb to 5-10 parts solvent; glycerite: made like a tincture with glycerine as the solvent.

questions.question: Describe Conium maculatum (poison hemlock) under the following: (i) botanical name, common name, geographical source and plant parts that contain toxins; (ii) constituents and their class; (iii) the basis of its toxicity and lethal dose; (iv) its historical use; (v) the basis of variability in toxic content or reduced quality.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• Conium maculatum, commonly known as poison hemlock; it grows in Europe and Asia.
• All vegetative organs, flowers and fruits contain alkaloids.
(ii)
It contains piperidine alkaloids: coniine, N-methyl-coniine, conhydrine, pseudoconhydrine and γ-coniceine.
(iii)
The toxicity is due to these alkaloids; as little as four leaves are said to constitute a lethal dose.
(iv)
• It is famous as a poison and its extract was used to execute Socrates in Athens in 399 BC.
• It is cited among plants used as ordeal or execution poisons.
(v)
• The amount of toxic ingredient in a single plant part varies from season to season.
• Poison plant toxic principles are distributed in different portions of the plant and many plants contain more than one toxic principle.

(i)
(a) powdered drug (comminution); (b) aqueous extract in powder form (freeze-dried); (c) alcoholic extract (tincture/alcoholic extract) as dry extract; (d) isolated active constituent.
(ii)
• (b) uses water; (c) uses a solvent such as alcohol with a rotary evaporator; the dried extract can be tabletted or encapsulated.
• Stages of herbal formulation: grinding, extraction (hot aqueous decoction, cold percolation, solvent extraction), filtration, concentration, spray drying and freeze drying.
• Scheme: juices by pressing and filtration; oils by pressing; volatile oils by distillation; syrup or tincture; liquid or solid extract; active principle by purification, fractional precipitation or crystallisation.
(iii)
Standardisation of active constituents in the powder or extract gives uniform actives each time the drug is prepared.
(iv)
• Primary processing machinery should be near the plantation to minimise deterioration and loss of active constituents such as volatile oils.
• Extracts also ease the logistics of transporting large quantities of plant material, and such units aid rural development.
questions.question:
A unit near a medicinal plantation processes dried plant material in four ways: (a) grinding in a mill to a powder for tabletting or encapsulation; (b) extracting in water as infusion, decoction or tisane and freeze-drying the extract; (c) extracting with alcohol and evaporating to dryness with a rotary evaporator before tabletting; (d) isolating a pure active constituent and adding excipients before tabletting or encapsulation.
(i) Identify each type of preparation and the method used.
(ii) Name the solvent, process and key steps.
(iii) State the benefit of standardising the active constituents in the powder or extract.
(iv) State the rationale for locating the plant near the plantation and for standardising active constituents.

questions.answerText:
(i)
To discover new medicines, validate traditional medicine (efficacy and safety), develop phytopharmaceuticals and standardised herbal products, and preserve traditional knowledge.
(ii)
• Enquire from villagers: survey widely, give a small token (dash or cola), visit the village head first (foreign researchers), use an interpreter and be patient with elders.
• Herbarium specimens are taken to villagers; two-dimensional dried specimens are hard to recognise and a toxic plant may be reported as medicinal; plants must be native to the locality; handle stinging plants such as Mucuna pruriens, Urtica or Tragia with care.
(iii)
• Herbalist: establish trust, negotiate fair compensation, assure confidentiality; incantations, restricted knowledge and reluctance about poisonous plants may arise.
• Herb-sellers know local names and some remedies but add inert materials; scientific publications give botanical names but have limitations (incorrect translation, chemical races, e.g. Hunteria umbellata = Picralima nitida).
• Climate affects constituents (Jamaican ginger grown in Nigeria is inferior); collect all synonyms.
• Students may invent data and informants may be sceptical; families are a reliable source (parents, mothers for women's and children's ailments) but religion may limit sharing.
• Training is by apprenticeship typically 5 years or more with fees and language proficiency; folk tales may be distorted.
• Patient surveys: a patient with a doctor-diagnosed ailment is sent to a herbalist; only record remedies that proved beneficial, exclude incantations, keep the patient under strict surveillance.
(iv)
• Confirm by information from two or more individuals from different parts of the locality and by collecting plant specimens identified by a botanist.
• Quack practitioners and varying proficiency affect reliability.
(v)
A combination of approaches is needed; limitations include cost, cultural sensitivity, misidentification and secrecy.
questions.question: Describe the methods of obtaining information on medicinal plants as a principle in ethnobotanical research: (i) why pharmacists study these methods; (ii) the methods themselves (villagers, herbarium specimens, herbalists, herb-sellers, scientific literature, students, family members, training, folk tales, patient surveys); (iii) examples and challenges of each; (iv) how reliability is confirmed; (v) why this approach improves quality and what limitations or trade-offs result.

A. Describe drugs of natural origin as a class under:
A(i) classification into the three groups with examples
A(ii) sources (plant, animal, microbial)
A(iii) chemical examples
B(i) Explain the basis of their value and limitation as drugs, including the origin of penicillin.
C(i) Distinguish between drugs derived directly from traditional remedies and synthetic derivatives of natural products.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Group 1: drugs derived directly from traditional remedies and used for the same ailments, e.g. digitalis and senna.
• Group 2: drugs of natural origin not used in modern medicine for the same ailment as in traditional medicine, e.g. Catharanthus roseus.
• Group 3: synthetic derivatives of natural products, e.g. heroin and some antimalarials.
A(ii)
Plants (digitalis, senna, Catharanthus), fungi (Penicillium notatum gave penicillin) and animals (insulin from the pancreas, thyroid extract from the thyroid gland).
A(iii)
Penicillin G is the example structure; plant drugs listed include reserpine, quinine, morphine and vinblastine.
B(i)
• Penicillin was discovered when a mould (Penicillium notatum) on an agar plate prevented growth of other micro-organisms; derivatives are now available as tablets, capsules, injection and ointment.
• Developed countries still rely on plants and animals for some orthodox drugs.
• Research on traditional plants is needed to find new therapeutic agents or richer sources of natural drugs.
C(i)
• Group 1 drugs are used (in whatever dosage form) for the same ailments as in traditional medicine, e.g. digitalis and senna.
• Group 3 drugs are synthetic derivatives of natural products, e.g. heroin and some antimalarials.
• Insulin and thyroid extract are replacement therapy from animal sources, a separate category from plant drugs.

questions.question:
A leaf drug called devil's trumpet, containing scopolamine, is used as a sedative; the hyoscine:hyoscyamine ratio of a related Datura species is known to change with plant age.
(i) Identify the plant, family and part used.
(ii) Name the active constituents responsible for activity.
(iii) State the therapeutic use of the constituents.
(iv) State the effect of harvest age, the antidote and the toxic syndrome.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Datura metel L. (Apocynaceae), devil's trumpet; the part used is the leaf.
(ii)
Scopolamine (hyoscine) is the major compound; hyoscyamine (atropine) is the related alkaloid named with it for Datura stramonium.
(iii)
Therapeutic use: sedative.
(iv)
• In Datura stramonium the hyoscine:hyoscyamine ratio is higher in young seedlings and lower in mature fruiting plants, so plant age affects composition.
• Physostigmine is used to reverse plant toxin-induced central anticholinergic syndromes.

questions.question: Describe the guidelines for research on medicinal plants for local drug production as an approach: (i) the four research guidelines of a multidisciplinary team; (ii) the two major approaches to investigating medicinal plants; (iii) the steps of the purely scientific approach and its ultimate goal; (iv) the steps of the approach that incorporates useful and harmless herbs into the health care system and its ultimate goal, with countries given as examples; (v) the general considerations (documentation, herbarium specimens, animals, facilities, medicinal plant garden); (vi) why the approach improves safety, quality or efficacy and what limitation results.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Identify health conditions treatable by traditional drugs as effectively as western drugs; identify agents (plants or other natural substances); standardise drugs and raw materials (pharmacognosy, quality, safety); develop technology for collection, selection, cultivation, extraction and processing into galenicals.
(ii)
Approach A is a purely scientific exercise that may or may not lead to isolation of bioactive agents; approach B incorporates useful, harmless medicinal plants into modern health care of a developing country.
(iii)
• Group plants by family or constituents (alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids), isolate major and minor secondary metabolites, test for activities (anticancer, anti-inflammatory) and study structure-activity relationships for synthetic analogues.
• Goal: pure compounds and dosage forms that pass Dunlop Committee, FDA and NAFDAC requirements; occult powers of herbs are ignored because they cannot be measured.
(iv)
• Test efficacy of claims in animal models, observe patients before and after treatment, determine therapeutic doses, note toxic side effects and unexpected activities, and study mode of action.
• Goal: standardised galenicals or teas, close to the form used by the populace so they pass regulatory requirements more easily; toxic herbs are removed; followed in Mali, Ghana, Madagascar and Nigeria.
(v)
• Documentation of herbs is urgent because many practitioners are old and records are lacking; ACCT (Paris) and AU/STRC (Lagos) have carried out ethnobotanical surveys.
• Plants should be collected by the person who prepares the remedy, identified, labelled and deposited in a herbarium (e.g. FRIN, Unilag) before publication.
• Mice, rats, guinea pigs (similar metabolism to man) and sub-human primates are used; cost and ethics must be considered.
• A pharmacology and a chemical laboratory in close proximity and a medicinal plant garden near the laboratory are required.
• Rigorous requirements for pure compounds may be short-circuited by toxicity tests in animals and observation of patients already using the remedy.
(vi)
Standardisation, toxicity checks and efficacy testing improve safety and quality; the limitation is that the occult/inexplicable aspect of traditional medicine cannot be tested scientifically, and approach B gives less emphasis to pure compounds.

questions.question: Describe Ocimum gratissimum L. (African basil): (i) botanical name, family, common names and part used; (ii) the major constituents; (iii) its uses; (iv) how plant age and morphological part affect oil yield and composition; (v) the basis of quality loss, adulteration or variation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Ocimum gratissimum L. (Lamiaceae); commonly called African basil; the leaf is used.
(ii)
• The major compounds are volatile oil and eugenol.
• Eugenol is also the main compound of clove (Syzygium aromaticum) whole essential oil.
(iii)
Uses: spice and treatment of digestive system disorders such as stomach-ache and diarrhoea.
(iv)
• It produces most volatile oil per unit leaf weight when young because the number of oil-secreting hairs does not increase appreciably as the leaf grows.
• The relative composition of terpenoids in its oil does not vary with age.
• Leaf is richest in oil (3.2-4.1 per cent), then inflorescence (0.5-1.4 per cent), while stem has traces only; collecting the stem only adds bulk.
• It should be harvested in the early stages of development.
(v)
• Volatile oils are lost if drying or processing is delayed, so quick drying and nearby processing minimise loss.
• Unwanted matter that only increases bulk and could cause adulteration should be excluded.
• Aerial parts should not be collected wet with dew or rain, which causes decomposition and mould during storage.

A(i)
Volatile oils are terpenoid-containing oils; examples named include eugenol, zingiberene, geijerene and regeijerene, and compounds such as carvone and cineole in essential-oil drugs.
A(ii)
Clove (Syzygium aromaticum, Myrtaceae) flower bud: whole essential oil and eugenol (spice); Ocimum gratissimum leaf (volatile oil, eugenol); Zingiber officinale rhizome (gingerols, zingiberene, shogaols).
A(iii)
Determination of carvone or cineole is used for essential-oil drugs; saponification values are used for oils.
B(i)
• Volatile oils volatilise soon after harvest, so quick drying, immediate processing and processing apparatus near the plantation are advised; aromatic drugs retain aroma with quick drying.
• Oil content varies with age and part: young Ocimum leaf is richest and stem has traces; Mentha viridis oil composition changes markedly with maturity.
• Geography changes oil composition (Chromolaena odorata: geijerene and regeijerene differ between Côte d'Ivoire and Nigeria).
• Containers that are not airtight lose volatile aroma; a perfect seal is considered important only for volatile-oil preparations.
C(i)
• Volatile oils are obtained by distillation; oils (such as expressed oil) are obtained by pressing.
• Medicated oils use fixed oils (coconut oil, palm kernel oil) as base or vehicle in which the herb is mixed, macerated or boiled.
• Volatile-oil (aromatic) drugs are dried quickly at an appropriate temperature so that they retain their aroma.
questions.question:
A. Describe volatile (essential) oils as a class of herbal constituents under:
A(i) classification and general chemistry
A(ii) plant sources, parts and uses
A(iii) chemical tests and quality assessment
B(i) Explain the basis of their loss, limitation or variation in composition.
C(i) Distinguish between volatile oils and fixed oils.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Plants are endangered by over-collecting, unsuitable agriculture and forestry, urbanisation, pollution, habitat destruction and fragmentation, invasive alien species and climate change; traditional health care depends on wild plants.
(ii)
• In situ conserves species in natural habitats through national parks, forest reserves, wild nurseries and biosphere reserves, e.g. Olokemeji, Afi, Gambari and Akure forest reserves, Oban Biosphere Reserve and eight national parks (about 3% of land).
• Limitations of in situ: natural catastrophes, genetic drift, invasive species, illegal exploitation, sectorialism and lack of knowledge.
(iii)
• Ex situ conservation outside the native habitat: seed storage, DNA, pollen, in vitro (slow growth, cryopreservation), field gene banks and botanical gardens.
• Choice depends on duration, storage behaviour (orthodox, recalcitrant or intermediate seeds), human and financial resources, and institutional capacity.
(iv)
• Seed banking: dried seeds (3-7% moisture) at −18 °C or cooler; secure and compact, but costly and risks loss of genetic diversity at regeneration.
• Field gene banks keep live plants for vegetatively propagated or recalcitrant species but face pests, drought, flood and cost.
• In vitro culture uses explants in sterile medium and cryopreservation at −196 °C in liquid nitrogen; pollen storage is cheap but conserves only paternal material; DNA banking suits research and gene discovery.
(v)
• Biodiversity has three classes: genetic, species and ecosystem diversity, linked to chemodiversity for drug discovery.
• Actions: protected areas, species recovery, gene banks, ecosystem restoration, public awareness, slowing climate change and local community benefit.
(vi)
• Reduced biodiversity means fewer natural chemicals and less potential for medical applications, so conservation sustains drug discovery.
• Trade-offs: costs, regeneration problems, technical limits and the need for combined in situ and ex situ methods.
questions.question: Describe conservation of medicinal plants as an approach: (i) why conservation is needed and the threats; (ii) in-situ conservation with Nigerian examples; (iii) ex-situ conservation methods and the factors that decide the technique; (iv) seed banking, field gene banks, in vitro, pollen and DNA storage with their advantages and disadvantages; (v) the three classes of biodiversity and the actions recommended to reduce loss; (vi) why conservation improves sustainability and what limitation or trade-off results.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Acokanthera species (A. longiflora and A. friesiorum); activity is attributed to the cardiac glycoside ouabain (G-strophanthin).
(ii)
Ouabain content was estimated by colorimetric assay; the Keller-Kiliani test detects deoxy sugars in cardiac glycosides.
(iii)
• Other poisons: Landolphia parvifolia roots plus Strophanthus eminii seeds (with snakes' tongues and heads sometimes added); Drimia or Scilla species in the Ulipa area.
• Despite varied composition, the methods of preparation are similar: boiling chopped components in water to a black sticky mass.
(iv)
• No concentration of plant material or boiling time is specified; longer boiling degrades actives; poison is often smeared with enough to kill several victims.
• Potency tests: the Dorobo prick a tortoise's foot with a poisoned arrowhead; another tribe shoots an antelope and judges the poison too weak if urine and faeces are found on its track.
• Elaeodendron (southern Africa ordeal poison) also contains cardiotoxic glycosides; digoxin-specific Fab antibodies inactivate ingested cardiac glycosides.
questions.question:
Chopped plant parts are boiled in water to give a black sticky mass smeared on arrows. The poison is prepared from species of Acokanthera such as A. longiflora and A. friesiorum; its activity is attributed to a cardiac glycoside whose content was found by colorimetric assay. Other tribes use roots of Landolphia parvifolia with seeds of Strophanthus eminii, or Drimia/Scilla species.
(i) Identify the crude drug and the toxic principle.
(ii) State the characteristic identification tests and constituent.
(iii) State the distinguishing features from related arrow poisons.
(iv) State the clinical, quality or standardisation consequence.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Toxicity and drug interaction.
(ii)
• In a traditional decoction, drug-drug interactions take place in the pot, whereas in orthodox practice mixed drugs interact in the patient's stomach if the prescriber takes inadequate care.
• Comfrey (Symphytum officinale) contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that are highly hepatotoxic; lasiocarpine causes liver cancer in rodents at 50 parts per million.
• Some plant constituents are toxic even in minute doses: eserine (Physostigma venenosum) and strychnine (Strychnos species).
(iii)
• Components in traditional preparations may act as preservatives, flavours or colours; modern paediatric products are also flavoured and coloured.
• Traditional multi-component preparations treat all ailments in one decoction; orthodox practice may need three or four tablets and an injection.
• Comfrey is the most common herbal tea sold to the American public, yet toxic.
(iv)
• Toxicity tests (acute, chronic, therapeutic index) are needed before a plant is accepted in a traditional cure.
• The claim that natural products are better tolerated is not safe to assume.
• European regulators accept long use without toxicity reports only if the mode of use is unchanged.
questions.question:
A patient is given a multi-component traditional decoction for several ailments, containing non-medicinal components, while also taking tablets and capsules prescribed by an orthodox doctor. The decoction contains plants known to hold highly toxic constituents such as eserine and strychnine, and another patient drinks comfrey tea regularly.
(i) Identify the liability (toxicity, interaction, deterioration, adulteration).
(ii) Explain the underlying cause or pathway.
(iii) Differentiate traditional and orthodox practice and related toxic plants.
(iv) Reason to formulation, regulatory or therapeutic choices.

questions.answerText:
(i) The parallel bar is a fixed apparatus with a pair of horizontal bars on vertical posts, used for standing and ambulatory training. It is a medical ambulatory device with two parallel horizontal bars on fixed four legs; the user holds the horizontal bars at wrist height and moves forward, backward, and sideways, usually in front of a standing mirror.
(ii) Four advantages: (1) Maximum stability — the user is positioned between two parallel bars, giving further stability in addition to the presence of therapists at either side. (2) Least coordination required — the presence of the two parallel bars makes coordination easier as users hold onto the bars while moving. (3) Best device to practice ambulation, particularly at the onset of ambulatory training — creates confidence in the patient and reduces the fear of falling. (4) Can be used to determine the other ambulatory device the user will use subsequently — the patient's performance in the parallel bar indicates their ability to use other types of ambulatory device.
(iii) The parallel bar is used to determine the next device because the patient's performance within it indicates their ability to use other ambulatory devices. Clinicians observe balance, strength, coordination, and endurance during parallel bar gait and use this to select the appropriate crutch, walker, or cane for the next stage of rehabilitation.
(iv) Pre-issuing checklist risk factors: check that ferrules and wheels are not worn to the point where no tread is showing or not aligned (worn ferrules reduce friction and are a fall risk); that support areas are properly padded (prevents soft tissue damage and provides comfort); that pairs are matching (unmatched pairs lead to poor posture and musculoskeletal disorder); that devices are not cracked, warped, or damaged (prevents breakage and fall); that nuts and bolts are tight (prevents collapse during use).
(v) Rules for the patient: do not look down but always look straight ahead (maintains good posture and prevents musculoskeletal disorders); do not use when feeling dizzy or drowsy (prevents fall); do not walk on slippery surfaces; avoid snowy, icy, or rainy conditions; do not put weight on the affected foot if not advised; ensure ferrules are present; wear well-fitting, low-heel footwear; carry needed items in a fanny pack, apron with pockets, or knapsack to keep hands free.
questions.question:
A post-operative patient who has been on bed rest for 4 weeks is beginning ambulatory rehabilitation. The physiotherapist decides to start gait re-education in the parallel bar.
(i) Describe the parallel bar as an ambulatory device: its structure and the way users move within it.
(ii) State all four advantages of the parallel bar, explaining the physiological and psychological basis of each.
(iii) Explain how the parallel bar is used to determine which other ambulatory device the patient will use subsequently.
(iv) Identify the risk factors the physiotherapist must address before the patient progresses to other ambulatory devices, using the pre-issuing checklist.
(v) State the rules the patient must follow when using any ambulatory device.

A physiotherapy student is testing a patient's hamstring flexibility. When the patient is in supine with the hip fully flexed, attempts to extend the knee fully are limited and the patient reports tightness and pain in the posterior thigh. In a separate test with the hip in a neutral position, full knee extension is easily achieved.
(i) Name and define the phenomenon demonstrated when the hip is fully flexed, identifying the muscle group involved and explaining why the limitation occurs in terms of the range of muscle extensibility and the number of joints the muscle crosses.
(ii) Define passive insufficiency and give a classic example.
(iii) Define active insufficiency and give a classic example of this phenomenon.
(iv) Explain the concept of tendon action of two-joint muscles, and give a classic example.
(v) State the factors on which the functional excursion (amplitude) of a muscle depends.
questions.answerText:
(i) The phenomenon demonstrated is passive insufficiency of the hamstring muscles. The hamstrings are a two-joint (bi-articular) muscle group crossing both the hip and the knee. For muscles that pass over two or more joints, the range of muscle length is lesser than the sum of the ROMs of all the joints over which the muscle passes. When the hip is fully flexed, the hamstrings are already lengthened over the hip joint; attempting to simultaneously extend the knee further lengthens the muscle beyond the limit of its extensibility, causing tightness and pain.
(ii) Passive insufficiency is defined as: the muscle cannot be stretched beyond certain limits without causing pain. The classic example: when a person tries to flex the hip fully with maximal knee extension, he usually feels pain in the hamstring muscle if he has tight hamstrings.
(iii) Active insufficiency occurs when a muscle which crosses two or more joints produces simultaneous movement at all of the joints it crosses and soon reaches a length at which it can no longer generate a useful amount of tension — i.e., the muscle cannot shorten beyond a certain limit without losing tension. The classic example: maximal hip flexion with knee extension from a supine lying position.
(iv) Tendon action is a passive tension without active muscle contraction that may produce movement of a joint if the muscle is elongated over two or more joints simultaneously. The exact example provided: if the wrist is allowed to flex by the weight of the hand, the digits will automatically extend without contraction of the finger extensors. By reversing the wrist movement, the fingers will partially flex.
(v) The functional excursion (amplitude) of a muscle depends on: the arrangement of muscle fibres (for pinnate muscles it depends on the cosine of the angle of theta of the tendon); whether the muscle is a one-joint or a multi-joint muscle. Any muscle crossing a single joint is normally capable of shortening sufficiently and is extensible enough to permit a full range of motion in the opposite direction.

questions.question:
A(i) Define an axis and a plane of motion as used in kinesiology, and state the relationship between the two.
A(ii) For each of the three cardinal planes, name it, state how it divides the body, and give the axis in which movement within that plane occurs.
B(i) Describe the plane and axis of the following movements at the shoulder joint: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction; and at the ankle joint: dorsiflexion/plantarflexion, inversion/eversion.
B(ii) Distinguish between kinematics and kinetics as divisions of kinesiology, giving the focus of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) An axis is a line about which movement takes place. A plane is the surface that lies at right angles to the axis, and in which movement takes place.
A(ii)
- Sagittal (median) plane: passes vertically through the body, dividing it into equal right and left halves; movement occurs in the coronal (frontal) axis.
- Frontal (coronal) plane: passes vertically through the body, dividing it into front and back; movement occurs in the sagittal axis.
- Transverse (horizontal) plane: divides the body into cephalic (upper) and caudal (lower) portions; movement occurs in the vertical axis.
B(i) Shoulder joint: flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane and frontal axis; abduction and adduction occur in the frontal plane and sagittal axis. Ankle joint: dorsiflexion and plantarflexion occur in the sagittal plane and in the frontal axis; inversion and eversion occur in the horizontal plane and vertical axis.
B(ii) Kinematics is the study of the description of motion — including displacement, velocity, and acceleration — without regard to the forces that produce them; it explains geometry of motion, how far, how fast, and how consistent. Kinetics focuses on the cause/course of different types of motion, specifically the effects of forces upon the motion of material bodies and the mechanism by which physical or chemical change is affected.

questions.question:
A(i) Define mechanical work, give its algebraic expression, and explain the distinction between positive and negative mechanical work in terms of muscle contraction type. State the unit of measurement.
A(ii) Define power in mechanics, give its algebraic expression including its relationship to force and velocity, and state what peak power is strongly associated with. Give the unit of measurement.
B(i) Define mechanical energy and name its two forms. For each form, give the definition and algebraic expression, and state the unit of measurement. Specify what the reference surface for potential energy is in biomechanical applications.
B(ii) Explain the relationship between kinetic and potential energy changes in human gait.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Mechanical work is defined as force applied against a resistance multiplied by the displacement of the resistance in the direction of the force. Algebraically: W = F × d. Muscles perform positive work when they contract concentrically (shorten) to produce tension that results in motion of a body segment. Muscles perform negative work when they contract eccentrically (lengthen while producing tension). When contraction is isometric (muscle length remains the same), no mechanical work is done. Positive mechanical work typically requires greater caloric expenditure than performing the same amount of negative mechanical work. Unit: Joule (J).
A(ii) In mechanics, power is the amount of mechanical work performed in a given time. Power (P) = Work/Change in time; equivalently, P = F × d/t = Force × velocity. Peak power is strongly associated with maximum isometric strength. Ability to perform mechanical power is critical for athletes competing in explosive track and field events. Unit: Watts.
B(i) Mechanical energy is defined generally as the capacity to do mechanical work. Two forms: Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy of motion — only bodies in motion have kinetic energy; KE = ½mv² (half the body's mass multiplied by the square of its velocity). Potential energy (PE) is the energy of position (stored energy) — PE = weight × height = mgh (body's weight multiplied by its height above a reference surface). The reference surface is usually the floor or ground. Changes in potential energy in biomechanical applications are usually based on changes in the body's height, since the weight of a body is typically fixed. Unit: Joule (J).
B(ii) The centre of gravity is midway between the hips, a few centimetres in front of S2, and that the least energy is consumed if the centre of gravity travels in a straight line. During gait, the centre of gravity oscillates vertically and laterally. As the centre of gravity rises (e.g., at midstance), potential energy increases and kinetic energy decreases; as it falls (e.g., at double support), potential energy decreases and kinetic energy increases. This reciprocal exchange reduces the net metabolic energy required for walking.

A(i) Organisational hierarchy: Whole muscle (covered by epimysium) → many fasciculi, each a small bundle of muscle fibres (covered by perimysium) → muscle fibres, which are long multinucleated cells that generate force when stimulated (covered by endomysium) → myofibrils, composed of → myofilaments (actin: thin filament; myosin: thick filament). The sarcomere is the smallest/most basic contractile unit capable of force production and shortening. The connective tissue sheaths ensure that force generated is transferred to the tendon and ultimately to the bone. The endomysium also helps prevent the signal for muscle activation from spreading from one muscle fibre to an adjacent fibre, allowing fine control of individual fibre activation.
A(ii) At rest the sarcomere has: Z lines at each end; I bands at both ends of the sarcomere (containing only actin filaments); A band in the middle (containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments, representing the length of myosin filaments); H zone in the middle of the sarcomere (contains myosin but not actin); M line in the middle of the H zone (proteins hold myosin filaments in place). When the sarcomere shortens: actin filaments slide over myosin; the H zone disappears (actin slides into it); the I bands become shorter; the A band does not change in length (the length of myosin filaments does not change). When the sarcomere relaxes, the H zone and I bands return to their original size; the A band remains unchanged.
B(i) Tropomyosin is a tube-shaped molecule that wraps around the actin filament, fitting into a groove created by the intertwining of the actin molecule helices; it prevents muscle contraction until the proper signal arrives. Troponin is made up of three regulatory protein subunits: Troponin I (binds to actin, holds the troponin–tropomyosin complex to actin); Troponin T (has affinity for tropomyosin, holds troponin to tropomyosin); Troponin C (has affinity for calcium ions, and this affinity is the stimulus within the muscle fibre that causes muscle activation by causing the active site on the actin molecule to be exposed).
B(ii) Titin/Connectin connects the Z line to the M line in the sarcomere and stabilizes myosin in the longitudinal axis; it also limits the range of motion of the sarcomere and contributes to the passive stiffness of muscle. Nebulin extends from the Z line and is localized to the I-band; it stabilizes actin by binding with the actin monomers.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the organisational hierarchy of skeletal muscle from whole muscle to the level of the myofilament, naming each level and the connective tissue sheath that surrounds it.
A(ii) Describe the structure of the sarcomere at rest: name all its zones and lines, state what each zone contains (actin, myosin, or both), and explain what happens to each zone when the sarcomere shortens according to the sliding filament theory.
B(i) Name and describe the two regulatory proteins wrapped around the actin filament, stating the role of each in controlling muscle contraction.
B(ii) Describe the two non-contractile proteins titin/connectin and nebulin: their location within the sarcomere and their functional roles.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Unless restrained, the arms tend to swing in opposition to the legs: the right arm swings forward as the left leg swings forward, and vice versa. This is a reflex action that tends to balance pelvic rotation. Its purpose is to counterbalance the rotation of the pelvis, keeping the upper and lower body in coordinated, energy-efficient opposition.
A(ii) Maximum flexion of the elbow and shoulder occurs at the moment of initial contact (IC) of the contralateral foot. Maximum extension of both joints (elbow and shoulder) occurs at the moment of IC of the ipsilateral foot.
B(i) Prevention of arm swinging causes the upper trunk to rotate in the same direction as the pelvis, thus causing an awkward gait. Instead of the normal counter-rotation that balances pelvic rotation, the upper body moves in phase with the pelvis, disrupting the coordinated, energy-efficient gait pattern and producing an asymmetric, awkward appearance.
B(ii) Three functional tasks of the gait cycle: (1) Weight acceptance — the body accepts full weight on the advancing limb; occurs during initial contact and loading response. (2) Single limb support — the entire body weight is supported by one limb while the other advances; occurs during midstance and terminal stance. (3) Limb advancement — the limb is unloaded and advanced forward; occurs during preswing, initial swing, midswing, and terminal swing.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the action of the upper extremities during normal walking: what the arms normally do in relation to the legs, what type of reflex drives this, and what purpose it serves.
A(ii) State what happens at maximum flexion and maximum extension of the elbow and shoulder during gait, specifying at which gait event each maximum occurs and which foot's event is referenced (ipsilateral vs contralateral).
B(i) Explain what happens to gait quality if arm swinging is prevented, including the effect on trunk rotation and the overall quality of gait.
B(ii) Summarise the three functional tasks of the gait cycle, and for each task state the gait cycle phases (in Rancho Los Amigos terminology) during which it occurs.

A patient post-stroke is observed swinging her left leg out laterally in a semicircle and forward during the swing phase, with the knee stiff and the foot in slight plantarflexion.
(i) Name this gait pattern and classify it according to the taxonomy of pathological gaits, identifying the specific neurological cause.
(ii) Describe the predisposing factors and biomechanical reason the patient uses circumduction to advance the limb, including the effect of spasticity on the knee and ankle.
(iii) Explain how the severity of gait deviations caused by muscular weakness or joint limitation varies, and apply this to the management planning for this patient.
(iv) Describe the observational gait analysis procedure the physiotherapist should follow for this patient and the parameters to document.
questions.answerText:
(i) The patient demonstrates circumductory gait. This is classified as a spastic type of gait caused by muscular paralysis from upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL). It is listed under types of pathological gait due to neurological disturbance, under spastic muscular paralysis.
(ii) Predisposing factors include upper motor neuron lesion causing spasticity (increased tone). Spasticity of the knee extensors prevents normal knee flexion during swing. Spasticity of the plantarflexors keeps the foot in plantarflexion (equinus), making foot clearance impossible with a normal swing. The patient therefore swings the limb outward and forward in a semicircle (circumduction) to achieve foot clearance without the knee bending. There can be great variation depending on severity: if a muscle is weak, how weak it is; if joint motion is limited, how limited it is.
