(iii) Severity of deviation varies: if a muscle is weak, the degree of weakness determines the deviation; if joint motion is limited, the degree of limitation determines the pattern. Management must therefore be tailored to the severity. For this patient, management targets spasticity reduction and gait re-education. CGA (using Vicon 512 and force plates) can provide quantitative data for complex gait problems to assist in treatment decision-making, including bracing and medication efficacy.
(iv) Observational gait analysis procedure: open and unobstructed area for examination; examine the patient from front, back, and side; observe the gait pattern as an entire process then examine each joint segment, beginning with foot and ankle; determine visually if the patient's performance is significantly different for each observed segment and gait cycle phase. Reliability can be improved by videotape recording. ROM at various joints can be examined through goniometric measurements. Parameters to document: gait cycle, centre of gravity, step length, pelvic tilt, stride length, pelvic rotation, walking base/stride width, lateral shifting, cadence, walking velocity, comfortable walking speed, shoulder alignment, and arm swing.

questions.question:
During a muscle testing session, a physiotherapy student notices that a patient can perform strong isolated knee extension but when the hip is extended at the same time as the knee is extended, the range of knee extension is incomplete and the patient complains the quadriceps 'give out'. The reverse is also observed: when the hip is flexed and the knee fully flexed simultaneously, the knee flexion is limited.
(i) Identify the muscle group involved and classify it by the number of joints it crosses, using the standard classification system. Identify specifically which muscle within the group is the two-joint muscle most relevant to this observation.
(ii) For the first observation (strong knee extension when the hip is not extended, loss of extension when hip is also extended), name the phenomenon and explain the kinesiological mechanism.
(iii) For the second observation (limited knee flexion when hip is also flexed), name the phenomenon and explain the kinesiological mechanism using the hamstrings as the antagonist.
(iv) Explain the concept of tendon action and describe how the clinician could use a wrist/finger example to demonstrate this principle during patient education.
(v) State the functional implications for exercise prescription: what range of muscle work is most practical during ADL and why.
questions.answerText:
(i) The muscle group is the quadriceps femoris. It is classified as a two-joint muscle because the rectus femoris crosses both the hip joint and the knee joint. One-joint muscles (e.g., vastus medialis) cross one joint only; two-joint muscles (e.g., rectus femoris) cross two joints; multi-joint muscles (e.g., finger flexors) cross multiple joints. The rectus femoris is the two-joint component most relevant to this observation.
(ii) First observation: active insufficiency of the rectus femoris. Active insufficiency occurs when a muscle crossing two or more joints produces simultaneous movement at all joints it crosses and soon reaches a length at which it can no longer generate a useful amount of tension. The classic example is maximal hip flexion with knee extension from supine lying causing active insufficiency — the same principle applies here in reverse (active extension of both joints simultaneously exhausts the shortening capacity of rectus femoris).
(iii) Second observation (limited simultaneous hip flexion and full knee flexion): passive insufficiency of the hamstrings. The hamstrings cross both the hip and knee; when the hip is flexed (which elongates the hamstrings over the hip) and full knee flexion is simultaneously attempted (which further elongates them over the knee), the hamstrings reach the limit of their extensibility. When a person tries to flex the hip fully with maximal knee extension, pain is felt in the hamstring — the same mechanism limits full knee flexion when the hip is also fully flexed.
(iv) Tendon action is passive tension without active muscle contraction that may produce movement of a joint when the muscle is elongated over two joints simultaneously. The wrist/finger example: if the wrist is allowed to flex by the weight of the hand, the digits will automatically extend without contraction of the finger extensors. By reversing the wrist movement (extending it), the fingers will partially flex. The clinician can demonstrate this by passively flexing and extending the patient's wrist while observing the passive finger movement.
(v) The middle range is the part of the range in which many muscles work most of the time during ADL. It is practical because the muscle is neither fully stretched nor fully contracted, and the angle of pull is more favourable than at the extremes. Exercises in middle range are used to maintain muscle tone and muscle power.

(i) Goniometry is the technique of human joint measurement. It is derived from two Greek words: gonia meaning angle, and metron meaning measure. It is the measurement of angles, especially angles created at human joints by bones of the body.
(ii) The universal goniometer is described as universal because of its versatility. Its body can be made of metal or plastic. The design always includes a body (which resembles a protractor and may form a full or half circle) and two long extensions called arms. One arm is fixed (stationary) and cannot be moved independently of the body — it is a structural part of the body. The other arm is movable and is attached to the fulcrum in the center of the goniometer's body by a screw-like device that allows it to move freely over the body. The arms may vary in length from 1 to 16 inches.
(iii) The starting position for all ROM measurements except rotations in the transverse plane is the anatomical position, which represents 0 degrees in the 0–180 degree system. Elbow flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane and frontal axis.
(iv) The stationary arm is aligned parallel to the longitudinal axis of the proximal segment of the joint. The movable arm is aligned parallel to the longitudinal axis of the distal segment of the joint. Bony landmarks — not soft tissue contours — are used for alignment. Alignment of the arms is more important than placement of the fulcrum over the approximate joint axis.
(v) Required information in a goniometric recording includes: type and make of goniometer used, side of the body, joint and motion measured, ROM including the beginning and terminal ROMs, and type of motion measured. Hypomobility is presented as 0–50 degrees flexion (example). Hypermobility is presented as 10–0–100 degrees.
questions.question:
A physiotherapy student is about to measure the range of motion of a patient's elbow joint using a universal goniometer.
(i) Define goniometry and state the Greek derivation of the word.
(ii) Describe the design of a universal goniometer, including all its named components, and distinguish the stationary arm from the movable arm in terms of their structural role.
(iii) State the zero starting position for ROM measurements (except rotations in the transverse plane) and the plane and axis in which elbow flexion and extension occur.
(iv) Explain how the alignment of the goniometer's arms should be performed, specifying what type of landmark is used and the correct alignment of each arm.
(v) List the information that must be included in a goniometric recording and give an example of how hypomobility and hypermobility are recorded in the 0–180 degree system.

questions.answerText:
(i) The patient demonstrates a foot drop (stepping) gait. According to the standard classification, this is a flaccid type of paralytic gait caused by lower motor neuron disease (LMNL). In spastic gait (e.g., scissoring gait or circumductory gait), paralysis results from upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL), muscle tone is increased, and the limb typically swings in an arc or crosses the midline. In foot drop, tone is reduced or absent and the limb is lifted excessively to clear the dropped foot.
(ii) The predisposing factor is lower motor neuron paralysis affecting the muscles responsible for dorsiflexion. The nerves and muscles at risk are those that produce dorsiflexion, which is illustrated as occurring in the sagittal plane and frontal axis. The weakness leads to inability to achieve the initial contact (heel strike) correctly, disrupting the loading response.
(iii) Untreated, the patient may develop joint stiffness from abnormal loading, falls risk due to the raised gait compensation, and progressive musculoskeletal disorder from asymmetric posture. Unmatched or improperly issued ambulatory devices contribute to poor posture leading to musculoskeletal disorder.
(iv) Physiotherapy management includes gait re-education, strengthening of available musculature, and prescription of an ambulatory assistive device. Elbow crutches (Lofstrand/Canadian crutch) are appropriate because they improve balance and provide lateral stability, can be used for stair climbing, and reduce weight bearing on the affected lower limb. The clinician must check that ferrules are not worn, that devices are not cracked or damaged, and that nuts and bolts are tight before issuing the device. The user should wear well-fitting, low-heel footwear and should not look downward during ambulation.
questions.question:
A 32-year-old man who sustained a lower motor neuron injury presents with inability to dorsiflex the right foot during walking. On observation, he lifts his right hip and knee excessively during the swing phase to clear the foot from the ground.
(i) Name the gait pattern demonstrated, classify it according to its neurological basis, and distinguish it from the scissoring gait seen in spastic conditions.
(ii) Identify the predisposing factors and neurological deficit that produce this gait, including the muscles that are weak or paralysed.
(iii) State the complications and secondary impairments that may develop if this gait pattern is left unmanaged.
(iv) Describe the physiotherapy management options for this patient; justify the use of an ambulatory assistive device if one would be appropriate.

questions.answerText:
(i) The patient demonstrates an antalgic (limping) gait, which is caused by pain. The stance phase is shortened on the affected (right) side because the patient tries to minimise the time spent weight-bearing on the painful limb. The stance phase normally accounts for 60–62% of the gait cycle; in antalgic gait it is reduced on the affected side. The gait falls under the category of pathological gaits due to pain.
(ii) The three functional tasks of the gait cycle are weight acceptance, single limb support, and limb advancement. Weight acceptance — which occurs at initial contact and loading response — is most compromised because it requires full tolerance of ground reaction forces on the painful limb.
(iii) Observational gait analysis parameters to examine include: step length (the right step length will be shorter), stride length (reduced), walking base/stride width, cadence (steps per minute; may be altered), comfortable walking speed (will be reduced below the normal ~80 m/min), pelvic tilt, pelvic rotation, lateral shifting, shoulder alignment, and arm swing. The right stance time will be shortened relative to the left.
(iv) Physiotherapy management is directed at the underlying cause of pain. Gait re-education should begin in the parallel bar (which provides maximum stability and requires least coordination), progressing to an appropriate ambulatory device. If an ambulatory device is needed, a cane used on the unaffected side can reduce load on the painful limb by up to 25% of body weight. Ferrules (rubber tips) must be checked before issuing any device. The clinician should also ensure the patient wears well-fitting, low-heel footwear and remove environmental hazards.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old male patient presents to the physiotherapy clinic walking with a noticeably shortened stance phase on the right lower limb, leaning his trunk over the affected side, and spending the minimum time possible weight-bearing on that leg.
(i) Identify the type of pathological gait pattern demonstrated and its kinesiological basis, including which phase of the gait cycle is primarily affected and why.
(ii) State the functional tasks of the gait cycle and explain which task is most compromised in this patient.
(iii) Describe the key observational gait analysis parameters the physiotherapist should examine, including spatial and temporal gait parameters that would be abnormal.
(iv) Outline the principles of physiotherapy management and exercise prescription appropriate to a pain-based gait deviation of this nature.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Type I (slow-twitch) fibres: they reach peak force production at a slow rate and generate small force. They have higher oxidative metabolism and excellent mitochondrial density. They are fatigue-resistant and can continue to contract over long periods of time with little decrement in force production. They are well suited for endurance performance, including maintaining posture and prolonged activities.
A(ii) Type II (fast-twitch) fibres: they develop force very rapidly and demonstrate high-force-production capability. Unlike Type I fibres, they do not display an abundance of mitochondria or a generous blood supply, resulting in a tendency to fatigue easily. They are best suited for explosive, powerful, short-duration activities.
B(i) The major fibre types — slow-twitch (Type I) and fast-twitch (Type II) — are established at birth. However, subtle changes take place within the two types of fibres over the entire life span. These changes are related to the types of activities performed, hormonal concentrations, and aging.
B(ii) The physiological cross section of a muscle is defined as the area of a section that cuts every muscle fibre making up the muscle and represents its level of hypertrophy. It determines a muscle's potential force of contraction. Absolute muscle strength is recognised to be 3–4 kg per square centimetre of cross section. The physiological cross section is an indication of the muscle's work capacity together with the distance the muscle can shorten as it functions in the human body: work = force × distance.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe Type I (slow-twitch) muscle fibres: their rate of force development, force output, metabolic properties, mitochondrial characteristics, fatigue resistance, and the functional activities for which they are best suited.
A(ii) Describe Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibres: their rate of force development, force output, blood supply, mitochondrial characteristics, fatigue tendency, and the type of activities for which they are best suited.
B(i) State when the major fibre types are established and describe the factors that can produce changes within the two types over the life span.
B(ii) Define the physiological cross section of a muscle, state the recognised absolute muscle strength per unit area, and explain its relationship to muscle hypertrophy and work capacity.

A physiotherapy student is treating a patient with weakness of the biceps brachii muscle and is designing a progressive resistance exercise programme.
(i) Using the lever system framework, identify which class of lever is formed by the elbow joint during biceps-assisted elbow flexion; define the three components of the lever system as they apply to this joint.
(ii) State the mechanical advantage (or disadvantage) of a third class lever and explain why this class is described as a 'lever of velocity'. Calculate conceptually the relative moment arms of the rectus femoris at the hip versus the knee.
(iii) Give two additional examples of third class levers and two examples of first class levers in the human body.
(iv) Apply the clinical implications of leverage to this patient's exercise programme: state the effect of lever arm length on resistance, how to progress the programme, and where and at what angle to apply resistance for maximum effect.
questions.answerText:
(i) Biceps-assisted elbow flexion forms a third class lever. The bone (radius and ulna, the forearm bones) serves as the rigid bar/lever. The elbow joint serves as the fulcrum/pivot. The biceps muscle at its point of insertion provides the effort/force. The load is the weight of the forearm (and any object held in the hand).
(ii) In a third class lever there is always a mechanical disadvantage, because the load arm is greater than the effort arm and the effort is located between the fulcrum and the load. It is called a lever of velocity because the short effort arc at the muscle insertion corresponds to a much longer arc at the hand/foot end, conferring great tangential (speed) velocity. The rectus femoris moment arm is approximately 3–4 cm at the hip joint and approximately 4.4 cm at the knee joint, making it more effective as a knee extensor than a hip flexor.
(iii) Third class lever examples: iliopsoas flexing the hip joint; hamstring flexing the knee joint. First class lever examples: the skull (as rigid bar) with the atlanto-occipital joint as fulcrum and posterior neck muscles as effort (nodding); the humerus with the glenohumeral joint as fulcrum and supraspinatus as effort in shoulder abduction.
(iv) Clinical implications: Force is most effective when applied perpendicular (at right angles) to the lever — that is, at 90 degrees to the bone. The resistance must be applied at right angles to the lever system; if applied at less than 90 degrees, the effect is not maximal for weak muscles that need strengthening. The longer the lever arm (leverage) when applying resistance, the more effective the resistive programme. If there is much pain or swelling, lower the leverage. Progression is achieved by increasing leverage (applying resistance more distally from the joint/fulcrum).

questions.question:
A teenager is referred to physiotherapy with a structural right leg length discrepancy of 3 cm. On observation, when walking he shows ipsilateral lateral trunk lean, apparent ipsilateral hip and knee flexion, and equinus posture of the shorter limb.
(i) Name the category of pathological gait to which this condition belongs, and list all the gait types within that same category.
(ii) Identify the risk factors and underlying cause of the gait deviation, and explain the kinesiological rationale for each compensatory strategy used (lateral trunk lean, knee flexion, equinus posture).
(iii) State the complications and secondary impairments that can arise from an unmanaged leg length discrepancy gait, drawing on gait analysis and muscle function principles.
(iv) Describe the physiotherapy management options, and justify the use of footwear modification based on the precautions for ambulatory device use.
questions.answerText:
(i) Leg length discrepancy is placed under pathological gaits due to leg length discrepancy, and equinus gait is also placed in this category. Other gait types in the same pathological gait section include: antalgic/limping gait, psoatic gait (due to pain); circumductory, scissoring, dragging/paralytic, robotic gait (spastic paralysis); lurching, waddling, gluteus maximus, quadriceps, foot drop/stepping gait (flaccid paralysis); ataxic gait (cerebellar), stamping gait (loss of kinesthetic sensation), festinant gait (basal ganglia); and equinus, equinovarus, calcaneal, knock/bow knee, genu recurvatum gait (abnormal deformities).
(ii) The structural short leg means the centre of gravity — which is normally midway between the hips, a few centimetres in front of S2, and optimally travels in a straight line — deviates laterally and vertically. Compensatory strategies: lateral trunk lean toward the short side shifts the body's centre of gravity over the shorter limb to reduce the pelvic drop. Hip and knee flexion on the longer side effectively shortens the longer limb to allow the foot to clear the ground and level the pelvis. Equinus posture (plantarflexion) on the shorter side effectively lengthens that limb. All these compensate for the discrepancy but distort the normal gait cycle.
(iii) Secondary impairments from unmanaged discrepancy: asymmetric muscle loading can cause weakness on one side and adaptive shortening or overstretching on the other; pelvic obliquity can produce scoliosis; uneven ambulatory devices or ill-fitting footwear leads to poor posture and musculoskeletal disorder; falls risk increases; energy expenditure increases beyond the comfortable walking speed of approximately 80 m/min.
(iv) Physiotherapy management includes orthotic/shoe lift prescription, muscle stretching and strengthening, and gait re-education. Footwear modification is justified because users of ambulatory devices must wear well-fitting, low-heel footwear, and a non-skid bath mat or rubber-soled shoe is recommended on the uninjured/shorter foot. Items that may cause tripping must be removed. Footwear that lifts the heel of the shorter limb reduces the biomechanical compensations described above.

questions.question:
A physiotherapist is prescribing a progressive exercise programme for a patient with quadriceps weakness. She plans to progress from muscle re-education exercises to exercises for joint stabilisation.
(i) Define range of muscle work, and name and define the three sub-ranges into which the full range is divided.
(ii) Describe the characteristics of the outer range: when it is used concentrically and eccentrically, why the extreme outer range is difficult, and for what purpose it is prescribed.
(iii) Describe the characteristics of the inner range: when it is used concentrically and eccentrically, why the extreme inner range is difficult, and for what purpose it is prescribed.
(iv) Describe the characteristics of the middle range and state for what purposes exercises in this range are used.
(v) Explain how range of muscle length is measured and how it differs for a muscle traversing a single joint versus a muscle traversing two or more joints.
questions.answerText:
(i) Range of muscle work is the amount of shortening or lengthening of a muscle as it acts to produce or control movements; it is the excursion a muscle makes as it contracts to produce movement at a joint. The maximum excursion during contraction equals the full range. The full range is divided into three parts: outer range, middle range, and inner range.
(ii) Outer range: it is nearest to the point at which the muscle is most fully relaxed/extended. Concentrically — a muscle works in the outer range when it contracts concentrically from the fully stretched position to the midpoint of the full range. Eccentrically — when a muscle contracts eccentrically from the midpoint of full range to full relaxation. Extreme outer range is difficult because of the adverse angle of pull of the muscle, with some of the muscle's effort used to compress joint surfaces. Outer range exercises are used for muscle re-education.
(iii) Inner range: nearest to the point at which the muscle is in its shortest position. Concentrically — a muscle works in the inner range when it contracts concentrically from the midpoint of full range to full contraction. Eccentrically — when a muscle contracts eccentrically from full contraction to the midpoint of full range. Extreme inner range is difficult to perform because it requires a greater number of motor units and the muscle's angle of pull is not favourable. Inner range exercises are used to gain or maintain movement of a joint in the direction of muscle pull, and to train some extensor muscles for stabilising joints.
(iv) Middle range is any distance from the middle of the outer range to the middle of the inner range. The muscle is neither fully stretched nor contracted. It is the part of the range in which many muscles work most of the time while producing movement during ADL. Exercises in middle range are used to maintain muscle tone and muscle power.
(v) Range of muscle length is measured in terms of degrees of joint motion and represents the length of the muscle. For muscles that traverse only one joint, the ROM of the joint equals the range of muscle length. For muscles that pass over two or more joints, the range of muscle length is lesser than the sum of the ROMs of the joints over which the muscle passes. To measure the ROM over which muscles pass, the muscle must be slackened over one joint to determine the full range over the other joint.

questions.question:
A child presents with bilateral toe-walking: both heels are off the ground throughout the entire stance phase, the ankles are held in continuous plantarflexion, and the knees and hips are slightly hyperextended.
(i) Name this gait pattern and classify it within the taxonomy of pathological gaits.
(ii) Identify the joint and movement most affected, state the plane and axis in which the affected movement occurs, and describe which muscles/structures are shortened and which are overstretched or compressed.
(iii) Explain the kinesiological effect of continuous equinus on the centre of gravity and on the functional tasks of the gait cycle, including which task is most disrupted and why.
(iv) Describe the differential gait patterns classified alongside equinus gait, and provide the kinesiological reasoning that distinguishes equinus gait from equinovarus gait.
(v) State the principles of physiotherapy management and exercise prescription appropriate for this child.
questions.answerText:
(i) The child demonstrates equinus gait, caused by abnormal deformity. Equinus gait is classified under types of pathological gait due to abnormal deformities, alongside equinovarus, calcaneal, knock and bow knee, and genu recurvatum gait. It is also mentioned under pathological gait due to leg length discrepancy.
(ii) The ankle joint is most affected; the movement deficient is dorsiflexion (which occurs in the sagittal plane and frontal axis). The plantarflexors (calf muscles, including the gastrocnemius/soleus complex) are shortened and overactive. The dorsiflexors and the posterior capsule are overstretched. Sustained equinus also compresses the anterior talotibial joint surfaces.
(iii) In equinus gait, the heel never contacts the ground; therefore the normal initial contact (heel strike) is absent, and loading response is abnormal. Weight acceptance — the functional task requiring transfer of body weight onto the forward limb at heel strike — is severely disrupted. The centre of gravity, normally located midway between the hips a few centimetres in front of S2, is elevated because the patient is constantly on tiptoe; this increases energy expenditure above the comfortable walking speed of approximately 80 m/min.
(iv) Differential gait patterns listed alongside equinus: equinovarus, calcaneal, knock and bow knee, genu recurvatum. Equinovarus gait involves both equinus (plantarflexion) and varus (the distal segment of the joint deviates medially), so the foot is plantarflexed and inverted. In pure equinus gait the foot is plantarflexed but not inverted/adducted.
(v) Physiotherapy management is directed at the cause (e.g., spasticity, contracture, or congenital anomaly). Exercise prescription includes stretching of the plantarflexors through outer range eccentric exercises and passive stretching. Inner range dorsiflexion exercises are used to gain or maintain movement in the direction of dorsiflexion. Gait re-education with an appropriate ambulatory device should include checks of ferrules and proper footwear with well-fitting, flat rubber-soled shoes.

(i) The axillary crutch (also known as the standard crutch) has the following components: axillary bar covered with an axillary pad; a hand grip; and double upright vertical posts joined distally by a single vertical post (which allows height adjustment) covered with a ferrule. The vertical posts and short horizontal bars are made of different materials including wood, hard plastic, stainless steel, aluminium steel, and iron. Adult axillary crutch range is from 48 to 60 inches (122–153 cm). It is available in paediatric, youth, adult, and tall adult sizes.
(ii) The elbow crutch (also known as Lofstrand and Canadian crutch) has the following components: a single forearm cuff (vinyl-coated, leather, plastic, or rubber); a hand grip; and a single upright vertical post (which allows height adjustment) covered with a ferrule distally. Adjustment of the handgrip and upright bar is by a push-button mechanism. The vertical bar is made of different materials including wood, hard plastic, stainless steel, aluminium steel, and iron.
(iii) Crutches have two contacts with the body — hand and elbow (for elbow crutch) or hand and axilla (for axillary crutch) — which make them better ambulatory devices for stabilisation of the user. Advantages: used to reduce weight bearing on one lower limb; used to improve balance; used to improve lateral stability; can be used for stair climbing. Disadvantages: need upper limb support and coordination; need trunk stability and support.
(iv) Clinician checks before issuing: ferrules and wheels are not worn to the point where no tread is showing or not aligned; support areas are properly padded; pair is a matching pair (uneven pair leads to poor posture and musculoskeletal disorder); device is not cracked, warped, or damaged; nuts and bolts are tight. User rules: do not look down but always look straight ahead; do not use when feeling dizzy or drowsy; do not walk on slippery surfaces; avoid snowy, icy, or rainy conditions; do not put weight on the affected foot if not advised; ensure ferrules and wheels are present; wear well-fitting, low-heel footwear.
(v) If crutch gait is performed incorrectly — particularly if the user looks down — correct posture is not maintained, which can result in musculoskeletal disorders. In gait, prevention of normal arm swinging causes the upper trunk to rotate in the same direction as the pelvis, thus producing an awkward gait. With crutches, improperly balanced crutch use similarly disrupts normal trunk and pelvic rotation, leading to compensatory lateral trunk lean and asymmetric arm swing.
questions.question:
A patient with a right lower limb fracture is being mobilised on partial weight-bearing. The physiotherapist needs to prescribe the most appropriate crutch.
(i) Name and describe the components of an axillary crutch (standard crutch), including all structural parts and the height range available.
(ii) Name and describe the components of an elbow crutch (Lofstrand/Canadian crutch), including all structural parts and how height adjustment is achieved.
(iii) State the advantages and disadvantages of crutches as a category of ambulatory device, including why two contact points with the body give crutches a particular advantage.
(iv) State the precautions and rules for use that clinicians must check before issuing crutches and that users must follow during ambulation.
(v) Identify what compensatory movement pattern may develop in the patient's trunk and upper limbs if crutch gait is performed incorrectly, using principles of gait analysis.

A(i) Describe the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction: what slides over what, what causes the sliding, and how the striation pattern changes from rest to contraction.
A(ii) Describe the sequence of events in excitation-contraction coupling from the arrival of a neural impulse at the motor end plate to the release of calcium and the exposure of the active site on actin, naming all structures involved.
B(i) State the three conditions that must be present for muscle contraction to occur.
B(ii) Define the motor unit, and explain the functional significance of the endomysium in controlling muscle activation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The sliding filament theory: actin (thin) filaments slide over myosin (thick) filaments. This causes shortening. At rest, actin and myosin filaments have a repeating pattern of light (actin or myosin filaments alone) and dark (overlapping actin and myosin) areas. In the contracted (fully shortened) state, the striation pattern changes: the H zone disappears as actin filaments slide into it; the I bands become shorter as actin and myosin slide over each other; the Z lines come closer to the ends of the myosin filaments. The A band does not change in length (myosin filament length does not change). When the sarcomere relaxes, the H zone and I bands return to original size; the A band remains unchanged.
A(ii) Excitation-contraction coupling sequence: (1) A neural stimulus arrives at the motor end plate (neuromuscular junction), the junction of the motor neuron's axon and the muscle fibre it stimulates. (2) The impulse spreads across the muscle fibre's sarcolemma, then down the transverse tubules (T-tubules) into the core of the fibre. (3) The T-tubules reach the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), a depot store for calcium that surrounds the myofibrils. (4) DHP (dihydropyridine) receptors, acting as voltage sensors, cause a sudden release of Ca²⁺ from the SR into the cytosol. (5) Calcium ions bind to Troponin C, which has an affinity for calcium, causing the troponin–tropomyosin complex to shift and expose the active sites on the actin molecules, allowing myosin cross-bridges to bind and produce contraction.
B(i) Three conditions required for contraction: there must be a neural stimulus; there must be calcium in the muscle cells; ATP must be available for energy.
B(ii) The motor unit is the individual motor neuron plus the muscle fibres it stimulates. The endomysium is the connective tissue covering individual muscle fibres; it helps prevent the signal for muscle activation from spreading from one muscle fibre to an adjacent fibre, thereby allowing fine control of the activation of individual fibres.

(i) Observational gait analysis (OGA) is the most common method of analysing and identifying gait problems in the clinic. It involves visual observation of critical gait parameters and is appropriate to characterise most gait pathologies. It requires little investment in equipment, time, and expense. Clinical gait analysis (CGA), sometimes called quantitative gait analysis, is the process whereby gait characteristics are measured, abnormalities identified, causes postulated, and treatment proposed. The process is facilitated by the use of technology — specialised, computer-interfaced video cameras, electromyography, and force platforms (e.g., Vicon 512 motion capture system and force plates).
(ii) Uses of CGA: to assist in treatment decision-making for individuals with complex and not easily understood walking problems; to answer questions concerning bracing and medication efficacy; to assess efficacy of surgical interventions. CGA is used as part of the surgical decision-making process when all conservative treatments have been exhausted and surgical intervention is being contemplated — this is when it is most important.
(iii) Procedural steps for OGA: (a) an open and unobstructed area for examination; (b) examine the patient from the front, back, and side; (c) observe the gait pattern as an entire process, then examine each joint segment beginning with the foot and ankle; (d) determine visually if the patient's performance is significantly different for each observed segment and gait cycle phase.
(iv) Reliability of OGA can be improved by using videotape recording. ROM at various joints can also be examined through goniometric measurements on screen. Limitations: it is subjective, and accuracy is dependent on the physiotherapist's skill level.
(v) CGA does not replace OGA. It serves as an adjunct to aid in understanding visual impressions of a patient's gait impairment more precisely and sometimes more accurately. OGA remains the primary clinical tool, with CGA providing additional objective data for complex cases.
questions.question:
A consultant asks the physiotherapy team to perform gait analysis on a patient with a complex movement disorder who has failed conservative management and is being considered for surgical intervention.
(i) Distinguish between observational gait analysis (OGA) and clinical gait analysis (CGA/quantitative gait analysis): define each, state the technology involved in CGA, and explain the goal of CGA in treatment decision-making.
(ii) State the specific uses of CGA, including when it is most important in the surgical pathway.
(iii) Describe the procedural steps for OGA, including the sequence of observation and the parameters examined for each joint segment.
(iv) State how reliability of OGA can be improved and what its limitations are.
(v) Explain why CGA does not replace OGA, stating the relationship between the two methods.

questions.answerText:
(i) The patient demonstrates a waddling gait (also called lurching gait). This is classified as a flaccid type of gait due to muscular paralysis caused by lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL).
(ii) The functional task compromised is single limb support. During single limb support, the entire body weight must be transferred through and supported by one limb while the other advances. The centre of gravity — located midway between the hips, a few centimetres in front of S2 — must be maintained over the base of support. Failure to stabilise the pelvis causes the characteristic lateral drop.
(iii) The structures that are weak or insufficiently active are the hip abductor muscles on the weight-bearing side, responsible for maintaining pelvic level during single support. The compensatory movement is excessive lateral trunk lean toward the affected (weight-bearing) side, which shifts the centre of gravity over the support limb to reduce the hip abductor moment required.
(iv) Other gait patterns causing altered pelvis or trunk movement include: antalgic gait (trunk lean toward painful side to offload the joint), gluteus maximus gait (another flaccid gait with backward trunk lean at heel strike), psoatic gait (caused by pain from the psoas muscle), and equinus gait (caused by abnormal deformity). These are distinguished by history, the phase in which the deviation occurs, the direction of trunk lean, and whether the deviation is related to pain, deformity, or paralysis.
(v) During observational gait analysis the physiotherapist should observe: pelvic tilt, pelvic rotation, lateral shifting, shoulder alignment, and arm swing. The arms normally swing in opposition to the legs — the right arm swings forward as the left leg swings forward and vice versa. This is a reflex action that tends to balance pelvic rotation. Prevention of arm swinging causes the upper trunk to rotate in the same direction as the pelvis, producing an awkward gait.
questions.question:
During observational gait analysis, a physiotherapist notices that a patient sways her trunk excessively from side to side with each step, dropping the pelvis on the unsupported side during the single-limb support phase.
(i) Identify the gait pattern demonstrated and classify it according to the type of neurological disturbance responsible.
(ii) State the single limb support functional task that is compromised, and explain the kinesiological basis of why this task demands stability at the support limb.
(iii) Identify the structures that are weak or insufficiently active to maintain pelvic stability during single limb support, and describe the compensatory trunk movement employed.
(iv) Outline the differential gait problems that also cause an altered pelvic or trunk pattern during ambulation, and explain the kinesiological reasoning used to distinguish them from the pattern in this patient.
(v) State what the physiotherapist should observe in relation to arm swing, shoulder alignment, and lateral shifting when conducting observational gait analysis of this patient.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Law of Inertia (Newton's first law): a body will maintain a state of rest or constant velocity unless acted on by an external force that changes that state. Application: muscles must generate force to initiate or change movement against inertia. Law of Acceleration (Newton's second law): a force applied to a body causes an acceleration of that body of a magnitude proportional to the force, in the direction of the force, and inversely proportional to the body's mass (F = ma). Application: muscle contraction force produces acceleration of the body segment proportional to the force and inversely proportional to segment mass. Law of Reaction (Newton's third law): for every applied force there is an equal and opposite reaction. Application: during walking, the ground reaction force acts equal and opposite to the body's force on the ground.
A(ii) The Law of Gravitation states that all bodies are attracted to one another with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Algebraically: Fg = Gm1m2/d2. Galileo's work demonstrating that the acceleration of a falling body is constant (not proportional to its weight) and that space, time, and velocity are the important factors provided the impetus for the emergence of kinesiology as a science — to know, prove, and explain in mathematical terms.
B(i) Momentum is defined as the quantity of motion that an object possesses; linear momentum equals the product of an object's mass and its velocity (M = mv). A static body has no velocity and hence no momentum. In humans, changes in momentum are brought about by changes in velocity. Unit: kg·m/s (kg·m·s⁻¹). Impulse = Ft (force × time). Since F = ma and a = (V2 − V1)/t, then F = m(V2 − V1)/t, hence Ft = mV2 − mV1; impulse equals change in momentum (I = Ft = ΔM).
B(ii) The coefficient of restitution describes the relative elasticity of an impact. It has no unit and ranges from 0 to 1. A value close to 1 indicates a more elastic impact; a value close to 0 indicates a more plastic impact. In a perfectly elastic impact, the relative velocities of the two bodies after impact are the same as before. In a perfectly plastic impact, at least one body deforms and does not return to its original shape, and the bodies do not separate. Most impacts are neither perfectly elastic nor perfectly plastic, but something in between.
questions.question:
A(i) State Newton's three laws of motion — including both the original Newtonian statement and the common-name used for each law — and explain how each is applicable to muscular function.
A(ii) State the Law of Gravitation, including its algebraic expression, and explain its significance to the emergence of kinesiology as a science.
B(i) Define impulse and momentum, including the unit of measurement for momentum, and state the mathematical relationship between impulse, force, time, and change in momentum.
B(ii) Define the coefficient of restitution, state its range of values and what the extreme values indicate, and distinguish between a perfectly elastic and a perfectly plastic impact.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Two principal functions of the skeleton: Protection — e.g., the skull protects the brain; the rib cage protects the heart and lungs; the spinal column protects the spinal cord. Locomotion or movement — the skeleton forms the framework enabling movement.
A(ii) Five bone types by shape: Long bones — e.g., femur. Short bones — e.g., metatarsals. Flat bones — e.g., frontal bones. Irregular bones — e.g., vertebrae. Sesamoid bones — rounded masses found in certain tendons of muscles; e.g., patella.
B(i) Bone composition: approximately 25% water, 30% organic material, and 45% mineral. The two minerals responsible for hardness are calcium phosphate and a little amount of magnesium salt. The organic matter consists of fibrous material that gives bone its toughness and resilience.
B(ii) Structure of a long bone from innermost to outermost: marrow (innermost) → surrounded by spongy bone layer → surrounded by compact bone layer → covered by a hard outside layer called periosteum. Other functions of individual bones: attachment of tendons and muscles; formation of red blood cells and some white blood cells.
questions.question:
A(i) State the two principal functions of the skeleton and give specific examples of the protective function for three anatomical regions.
A(ii) Classify bones by shape into five types, giving the Latin terminology and one anatomical example for each.
B(i) Describe the composition of bone: state the approximate proportions of water, organic material, and mineral matter. Name the two minerals responsible for hardness and the type of organic matter that gives bone toughness and resilience.
B(ii) Describe the structure of a long bone from innermost to outermost layer, naming each layer, and state the other functions of individual bones beyond forming the skeleton.

A(i) Name the three connective tissue sheaths of skeletal muscle, state what each surrounds, and explain how they function in force transmission to the tendon and bone.
A(ii) Explain the elastic component of muscle and state what structural elements contribute to it.
B(i) Name four types of classification that are applied to skeletal muscles according to their general limb appearance (contractors vs expanders). Define each type and give examples.
B(ii) Explain the function of the connective tissue in the endomysium specifically in relation to neural activation of individual muscle fibres, and describe the significance of the sarcolemma in impulse spread during muscle contraction.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Three connective tissue sheaths: Epimysium — covers the whole (intact) muscle. Perimysium — covers the bundles of muscle fibres (fasciculi). Endomysium — covers the individual muscle fibres. Connective tissue function: ensures that any force generated by the muscle will be transferred to the tendon and ultimately to the bone.
A(ii) The muscle's connective tissue sheaths make up the elastic component of muscle, which contributes to force and power production. Additionally, the non-contractile proteins within the sarcomere (including titin/connectin and nebulin) also contribute to the elastic component of the muscle fibre.
B(i) Classification by general limb appearance: Contractors — those muscles that pull the body into approximation of the fetal position, i.e., flexors, adductors, and medial rotators. Expanders — those muscles that expand or open up the body, i.e., extensors, abductors, and lateral rotators. (Note: contractors and expanders are the two categories in this classification; further sub-types are not named under this heading.)
B(ii) The endomysium helps prevent the signal for muscle activation from spreading from one muscle fibre to an adjacent fibre, thereby allowing fine control of the activation of individual fibres. The sarcolemma is the muscle fibre's membrane; the impulse detected at the motor end plate spreads across the sarcolemma, then down into the transverse tubules (T-tubules), which penetrate into the core of the fibre, reaching the sarcoplasmic reticulum — the depot store for calcium — initiating the sequence that leads to contraction.

A(i) A pulley is a wheel-type device with a rope or cable running over it. It consists of a grooved wheel which turns on an axle with a cable running in the groove in opposite directions. Its three functions: to change the direction of force; to modify the effect of a force; to obtain mechanical advantage.
A(ii) The three types of pulley and their lever equivalents: single fixed pulley corresponds to a first class lever; single movable pulley corresponds to a second class lever; combination of pulleys (block and tackle). Human body example: the peroneus tendon runs over the lower end of the fibula, and the tendon of the rectus femoris runs over the patella, acting as pulleys to redirect the line of pull of those muscles.
B(i) The angle of pull is the angle between the long axis of the bone and the line of pull of the muscle. If the angle of pull is small, then little movement will be produced. Force is most effective when it is applied perpendicular to the lever (i.e., at 90 degrees to the bone), where all the muscle's force produces rotatory movement.
B(ii) Clinical implications for resistance exercise: (1) The resistance must be applied at right angles to the lever system — if applied at less than 90 degrees the effect will not be maximal for the weak muscles being strengthened. (2) The longer the lever arm (leverage) when applying resistance, the more effective the resistive programme. (3) Application of resistance further away from the fulcrum or joint makes the resistance more effective. Conversely, if there is much pain or swelling, lower the leverage to reduce the demand on the muscle; increase leverage for progression.
questions.question:
A(i) Define a pulley as a simple machine, describe its structure, and state its three functions.
A(ii) Name the three types of pulley, state which class of lever each type corresponds to, and give one example of how a pulley is demonstrated in the human body with anatomical details.
B(i) Define the angle of pull, state how it is measured, and explain the relationship between the angle of pull and the amount of movement produced.
B(ii) Explain the clinical implications of the angle of pull for resistance exercise in physiotherapy, using the three principles of levers and application of force.

A(i) Distinguish between spatial gait parameters and temporal gait parameters. List all the temporal gait parameters and provide the definition of each.
A(ii) List all the spatial gait parameters, define each, and state the normal relationship between step length, stride length, and walking base in a normal gait.
B(i) Define velocity (as a gait parameter) and comfortable walking speed (CWS): give the algebraic expression for average velocity, state the average and maximum CWS values, and explain the significance of CWS in terms of energy consumption.
B(ii) Explain how each of the following pathological changes would alter spatial and temporal gait parameters: (a) pain causing shortened stance on one side; (b) neurological weakness causing foot drop; (c) a significantly widened walking base.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Spatial gait parameters describe the distances and angles associated with walking, providing insights into how a person moves. Temporal gait parameters are measurements related to the timing and duration of events during walking. Temporal gait parameters: Cadence — the number of steps taken per minute (steps/minute); Step time — the time it takes to complete one step (from heel strike to heel strike of the opposite foot); Stride time — the time to complete one full gait cycle (from heel strike of one foot to the next heel strike of the same foot); Stance time — the duration of time when a foot is in contact with the ground; Swing time — the duration of time when a foot is not in contact with the ground; Double support time — the duration when both feet are in contact with the ground simultaneously; Gait velocity (speed) — the speed at which a person walks, calculated by multiplying cadence by stride length; Gait symmetry — the degree of similarity in step length and stance time between the two legs.
A(ii) Spatial gait parameters: Step length — the distance between the heel strike of one foot and the heel strike of the opposite foot; in normal gait, right step length equals left step length. Stride length — the distance between successive points of initial contact of the same foot; in normal gait, stride length is double the step length. Step width (walking base/stride width) — the lateral (side-to-side) distance between the line of progression of the left and right foot. Foot angle — the angle between the foot's longitudinal axis and the direction of progression.
B(i) Velocity: distance covered by the body in unit time, usually measured in m/s. Average velocity (m/min) = step length (m) × cadence (steps/min). CWS is the speed of least energy consumption per unit distance. Average CWS = 80 m/min (5.0 km/h; 1.4 m/s; 3.1 mph). Maximum CWS = 2.5 m/s (9.0 km/h; 5.6 mph). At CWS there is least energy consumption, so deviating above or below it increases metabolic cost.
B(ii) (a) Pain causing shortened stance: step length on the painful side decreases (gait symmetry is lost); stance time is reduced on that side; double support time changes; comfortable walking speed decreases. (b) Foot drop: the patient compensates by excessive hip and knee flexion during swing (stepping gait) — swing time and step height are altered; initial contact is abnormal (toe rather than heel strike). (c) Widened walking base: step width increases markedly, as in ataxic gait; this improves balance but increases the lateral deviation of the centre of gravity from the ideal straight-line path, increasing energy expenditure.

A(i) Aristotle (384–322 BC) — a Greek philosopher — is regarded as the 'Father of Kinesiology'. He was the first to describe the action of muscles in causing movement, specifically contraction, pressing, and pushing. His explanation was a precursor to Newton's 3 Laws of Motion.
A(ii) Galen (131–201 AD), a Roman [Aelius/Claudius Galenus], was a surgeon and philosopher and the first team physician in history. He was the first to distinguish between motor nerves and sensory nerves, though he termed nervous impulses as 'animal spirits'. He was also the first to distinguish between agonists and antagonists and to define joint terminologies like diarthrosis and synarthrosis. His work was regarded as a myth and kept in a cooler (i.e., suppressed/ignored) for about a thousand years.
B(i) Alfonso Borelli (1580–1679), Galileo's student, proved that 'bones act as levers and muscles function according to mathematical principles', without prejudice to his appreciation that contraction of muscle involves a complex chemical process.
B(ii) Galileo Galilei (1564–1645), Italian, studied medicine. He proposed and was convinced that nature is written in mathematical symbols, and he changed course to mathematics in search of laws responsible for physical phenomena. He proved that the acceleration of a falling body is constant and not proportional to its weight; rather, space, time, and velocity are important factors. He also proved that the trajectory of a projectile through a resistance-free medium is a parabola. His work provided the impetus for the emergence of kinesiology as a science — to know, prove, and explain in mathematical terms. He saw movements as kinesiological events.
questions.question:
A(i) Name the scientist described as the 'Father of Kinesiology', state his dates, nationality, and the specific contributions attributed to him, including what his explanation is said to be a precursor of.
A(ii) Describe the contributions of Galen (131–201 AD) to kinesiology, including the specific distinctions he was first to make and what happened to his work afterwards.
B(i) Describe the contribution of Alfonso Borelli to kinesiology, including what he proved about bones and muscles and what he acknowledged about muscle contraction.
B(ii) Describe the contribution of Galileo Galilei (1564–1645) to kinesiology: what he proposed, what he proved, and what impetus his work provided for the field.

A researcher wishes to record dynamic joint angles during walking gait for a patient with knee dysfunction, requiring continuous measurement throughout the gait cycle.
(i) Identify the most appropriate instrument for this research purpose and explain why the universal goniometer would be inadequate for this task.
(ii) Describe the structure of the electrogoniometer: its arms, how they are applied to the patient, the mechanism by which joint position change is detected, and how the output is expressed.
(iii) State the disadvantage of the electrogoniometer that restricts its use.
(iv) Name the other methods used in research for measuring joint motion.
(v) State the starting position and the plane and axis for measuring knee flexion and extension using the 0–180 degree notation system.
questions.answerText:
(i) The most appropriate instrument is the electrogoniometer, which is used primarily in research to obtain dynamic joint measurements. The universal goniometer is designed for static measurements at a point in time; it requires manual alignment and positioning for each reading, making continuous dynamic measurement during gait impractical.
(ii) Most electrogoniometers have two arms like the universal goniometer; the arms are attached to the proximal and distal segments of the joint being measured. A potentiometer is connected to the two arms. A change in joint position causes the resistance in the potentiometer to vary. The resultant change in voltage can be used to indicate the amount of joint motion, providing a continuous electronic output throughout movement.
(iii) Disadvantage: electrogoniometers are expensive and take time to calibrate, hence they are restricted in use to research settings rather than clinical settings.
(iv) Other methods used in research for measuring joint motion: radiographs, photographs, films, videotapes.
(v) Starting position for all ROM measurements except rotations in the transverse plane is the anatomical position, which represents 0 degrees in the 0–180 degree system. Knee flexion takes place in the sagittal plane and frontal axis. Knee extension takes place in the sagittal plane and frontal axis.

A(i) The stance phase accounts for 60–62% of the gait cycle. The swing phase accounts for 38–40% of the gait cycle. Double support is the period of time when both feet are in contact with the ground simultaneously. It occurs twice in a gait cycle — at the beginning and end of the stance phase (referred to as initial and terminal double-limb stance). The two periods of double-limb support together represent 25% of the gait cycle.
A(ii) Classic stance phase components: heel strike, foot flat, mid stance, heel off, toe off. Rancho Los Amigos stance components: initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance, preswing. Swing phase components (both terminologies): initial swing, mid swing, terminal swing.
B(i) Step length is the distance between corresponding successive points of heel contact of the opposite feet; in normal gait the right step length equals the left step length. If stance time is shortened on one side (due to pain or weakness), the step length on the affected side decreases and symmetry is lost. Stride length is double the step length in normal gait; an asymmetric stance time therefore reduces stride length. Cadence is the number of steps per unit time (normally about 100–115 steps per minute); compensatory increased cadence may occur on the unaffected side.
B(ii) Gait kinetics is the study of the forces and moments that cause movement during walking, focusing on the forces that act on the body — both from external sources (gravity and ground reaction forces) and from internal sources (muscle contractions) — to produce motion. Gait kinematics refers to the study of movement patterns during walking, focusing on displacement, velocity, and acceleration of body segments and joints without considering the forces that cause these movements. It analyses how we walk rather than why we walk.
questions.question:
A(i) State the proportion of the gait cycle occupied by the stance phase and the swing phase, and define double support — including when it occurs and what proportion of the gait cycle it represents.
A(ii) List all components of the stance phase in order (both classic and Rancho Los Amigos terminology) and all components of the swing phase.
B(i) Explain how alteration of stance time on one side (as seen in painful or paralytic conditions) affects cadence, step length, and stride length.
B(ii) Describe gait kinetics and gait kinematics, and explain how forces acting on the body during gait are categorised.

questions.answerText:
(i) The patient demonstrates scissoring gait. This is classified as a spastic type of gait due to muscular paralysis from upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL). Spastic paralysis results in a circumductory gait, scissoring gait, dragging or paralytic gait, or robotic gait (quadriplegic), depending on the level of lesion.
(ii) Predisposing factors for pathological gait in general include: pain, joint ROM limitation, muscular weakness/paralysis, neurological deficits (UMNL/LMNL), and leg length discrepancy. For scissoring gait specifically, the cause is spastic muscular paralysis from UMNL, with increased tone in the hip adductors and medial rotators causing the thighs to cross during swing.
(iii) In spastic gait (e.g., scissoring), muscle tone is increased, producing stiff, resistive movements; in flaccid gait (e.g., foot drop/stepping gait, waddling gait, gluteus maximus gait), muscle tone is reduced or absent, producing weak, unsupported movements. There can be great variation depending upon the severity of the problem — specifically, how weak the muscle is or how limited joint motion is.
(iv) Assessment: The physiotherapist conducts observational gait analysis, examining gait cycle, centre of gravity, step length, stride length, walking base/stride width, cadence, walking velocity, pelvic tilt, pelvic rotation, lateral shifting, shoulder alignment, and arm swing. Computer-based gait analysis (Vicon 512 and force plates) may be used for complex presentations. Management includes spasticity management, ROM exercises to maintain or improve joint range, gait re-education, and prescription of an appropriate assistive device. Elbow crutches can be used to improve balance and lateral stability and for stair climbing. Progression involves gradual increase in resistance using leverage principles: resistance applied at right angles to the limb, with progression by increasing the lever arm distance from the fulcrum.
questions.question:
A patient with an upper motor neuron lesion is observed walking. Both thighs are adducted and cross each other with each step, producing a crossing or scissoring pattern. The limbs appear stiff.
(i) Name this gait pattern and classify it according to the neurological and biomechanical basis.
(ii) Identify the predisposing factors and causes for this category of gait disorder.
(iii) Describe how this pattern differs biomechanically from flaccid paralytic gait patterns, using the classification of the two types.
(iv) State what assessment parameters the physiotherapist should examine, and describe the physiotherapy management approach, including any ambulatory device considerations and exercise principles relevant to a spastic condition.

An elderly woman with mild right hip osteoarthritis presents to physiotherapy needing minimal gait support. She is ambulant and her balance is adequate but she experiences pain at the right hip during single limb stance.
(i) Identify the most appropriate ambulatory device for this patient and state the maximum weight it can support.
(ii) Name and describe the four types of cane, including their structural differences.
(iii) State the rule regarding which hand the cane should normally be held in and explain the kinesiological basis for this in terms of the lever system and load on the hip joint.
(iv) State the precautions and rules for use of ambulatory devices that apply to this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) The most appropriate ambulatory device is a cane (walking stick). A cane can support up to 25% of a user's weight and is typically used when minimal stability is needed.
(ii) Four types of cane: Standard cane — a single-point straight cane with a crook or T-shaped handle. Offset cane — similar to the standard cane but the proximal component of the horizontal shaft is offset anteriorly, creating a straight offset handle. Quadripod — similar to the standard cane but has a broad base with four-point support for floor contact (a tripod variant also exists). Hemi cane — also has four-point support for floor contact but the legs are angled from the shaft to increase stability.
(iii) Cane height is adjustable and the vertical bar can be made of various materials. A cane is used when minimal stability is needed and can support up to 25% of a user's weight. The rule is to hold the cane in the contralateral (unaffected) hand, using it on the side opposite the painful hip. The kinesiological basis using lever principles: the cane in the contralateral hand creates an additional moment arm on the opposite side, reducing the demand on the ipsilateral hip abductors and the compressive load on the painful hip joint during single limb stance.
(iv) Precautions and rules: clinician must check that ferrules and wheels are not worn to where no tread is showing; support areas are properly padded; device pair is matching and not cracked, warped, or damaged; nuts and bolts are tight. User rules: not to look down but always look straight ahead; not to use when feeling dizzy or drowsy; not to walk on slippery surfaces; avoid snowy, icy, or rainy conditions; ensure ferrules are present; wear well-fitting, low-heel footwear; use a non-skid bath mat in the shower or tub; carry needed items in a fanny pack, apron with pockets, or knapsack to keep hands free.

questions.question:
A(i) Define kinesiology, stating the two Greek words from which it is derived and the three fields of science on which it is based.
A(ii) Define biomechanics and state what is meant by the human body functioning as 'a machine comprising a multilever system'. Explain the two broad areas of application of biomechanics.
B(i) Define the three main themes of biomechanics — safety, effectiveness, and efficiency — and explain the distinction between efficient movement and effective movement.
B(ii) List and define all the named divisions of kinesiology (at least five divisions), giving a one-line description of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Kinesiology is the science of human movement using the principles of biological properties involving a mechanical perspective — the scientific study of human movement from the point of view of physical sciences. It is derived from the Greek words kinein (to move) and logos (to discourse). It is based on three fields of science: biomechanics, musculoskeletal anatomy, and psychological mechanisms.
A(ii) Biomechanics is the investigation of human movements by means of the concepts of classical physics and their derivatives in the practical arts of engineering. The human body functions as a machine comprising a multilever system in that the bones serve as levers, the joints as fulcrums (axes for rotational moment), and the muscles provide the forces for the effort to produce angular motion. All three types of lever are represented in the body. Two broad areas of application: (1) improvement of performance; (2) prevention/treatment of injury.
B(i) Safety — concerns related to movement that prevent harm. Effectiveness — maximisation of output; determining the most appropriate sequencing of segments to accomplish a given movement. Efficiency — economy of energy expenditure; work done with minimum energy expenditure. Distinction: effective movement is optimally efficient; however, a maximally efficient movement is not necessarily biomechanically effective.
B(ii) Divisions of kinesiology: Kinematics — explains terms such as acceleration, velocity, and position; geometry of motion; description of the motion of points, objects, or body parts without reference to forces producing the motion. Kinetics — focuses on the cause/course of different types of motion; effects of forces upon the motion of material bodies. Behavioral Kinesiology — science of structure and processes of human movements and their modification by inherent factors, environmental events, and therapeutic intervention. Structural and Functional Kinesiology — interrelation between form and function of the body. Exercise Physiology — correlation between kinesiology and basic sciences such as physiology and biochemistry. Developmental Kinesiology — relationship of kinesiology to growth, physical development, nutrition, and aging. Psychological Kinesiology — study of mutualities of movement and meaning as implied in self-image, aesthetic expression, cultural communication, personality, and motivation.

questions.question:
A(i) Define range of motion (ROM) and state the three notation systems used to define it, giving the anatomical position equivalents in each system.
A(ii) Distinguish between active range of motion (AROM) and passive range of motion (PROM): define each, state what information each type provides, and explain why PROM is usually slightly greater than AROM.
B(i) Describe the gravity-dependent goniometer (inclinometer): its two types, their mechanism of function, and their clinical advantages and disadvantages compared with the universal goniometer.
B(ii) State the causes of adaptive shortening and loss of range of motion.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Range of motion refers to the amount of motion available at a joint. Three notation systems are used: the 0–180 degree system, the 180–0 degree system, and the 360 degree system. In the 0–180 degree system, upper and lower limb joints are at 0 degrees for flexion/extension and adduction/abduction when the body is in the anatomical position. In the 180–0 degree and 360 degree systems, the anatomical position equals 180 degrees.
A(ii) AROM is the amount of joint motion attained by an individual during an unassisted joint motion. Information from AROM includes willingness to move, muscle strength, coordination, and joint ROM. PROM is the amount of motion achieved by an examiner without the patient's assistance; the patient remains relaxed and plays no role in producing the motion. Information from PROM relates to integrity of the articular surfaces and extensibility of the joint capsule, associated ligaments, and muscles. PROM is usually slightly greater than AROM because each joint has a small amount of available motion that is not under voluntary control.
B(i) The gravity-dependent goniometer, also known as an inclinometer, uses the effect of gravity on pointers and fluid levels to measure joint position and motion. Its two types are: (1) the pendulum goniometer, which has a 360-degree protractor with a weighted pointer hanging from its centre; and (2) the fluid/bubble goniometer, which is similar to a carpenter's level but has a 360-degree scale and a fluid-filled circular chamber containing a bubble. These goniometers are attached to or held on the distal segment. The proximal segment must be positioned vertically or horizontally for accurate measurement. Advantage: they may be easier to use in certain situations because they do not require alignment to bony landmarks. Disadvantage: they are difficult to use on small joints or where there is soft tissue deformity or oedema.
B(ii) Causes of adaptive shortening and loss of range of motion: prolonged immobilisation, restricted mobility, connective tissue or neuromuscular diseases, tissue pathology due to trauma, congenital and/or acquired bony deformities.

A(i) Functional excursion (amplitude) is the full range of extensibility and contractility of a muscle — the distance that a muscle is capable of shortening after it has been elongated to its maximum. For muscles in general it averages 57% of their resting length. For pinnate muscles, functional excursion depends on the cosine of the angle theta of the tendon.
A(ii) Contractility is the capacity of the muscle to produce tension between its ends. Distensibility is the ability of the muscle to be stretched or lengthened by an outside force up to a certain limit; the muscle suffers no harm so long as it is not stretched beyond its physiological limits. Factors determining absolute contractility (how much a muscle can shorten): length and arrangement of fibres (for pinnate muscles, cosine angle of theta of the tendon); structure of the joint; number of joints traversed; resistance of antagonists; presence of a load opposing the muscle.
B(i) Spurt muscles are mainly rotator muscles that have their origin away from the joint and their insertion near the joint — example: biceps muscle. Shunt muscles are mainly stabilizer muscles that have their origin near the joint and their insertion away from the joint — example: brachioradialis.
B(ii) A spurt muscle inserts close to the joint (short moment arm), so when it contracts its line of pull is directed largely perpendicular to the bone — that is, it produces primarily rotatory force (torque) to move the lever. A shunt muscle inserts far from the joint, so its line of pull is directed largely along the long axis of the bone — producing a stabilizing (compressive) force that holds the joint surfaces together. Force is most effective when applied perpendicular to the lever; the angle of pull is the angle between the long axis of the bone and the line of pull of the muscle: if the angle of pull is small, little movement will be produced.
questions.question:
A(i) Define functional excursion (amplitude) of a muscle. State the average magnitude of functional excursion relative to resting length and what it depends on for pinnate muscles.
A(ii) Define and distinguish contractility from distensibility of a muscle. List all the factors that determine how much a muscle can shorten (absolute contractility).
B(i) Explain the concept of spurt muscles versus shunt muscles: define each, state the typical location of origin and insertion relative to the joint, and give one example of each.
B(ii) Explain how a spurt muscle's design makes it primarily a rotator, and how a shunt muscle's design makes it primarily a stabilizer, with reference to the moment arm and angle of pull concepts.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Agonists are muscles that contract to perform a certain action. Prime movers are muscles that make the major contribution in any contraction — e.g., iliopsoas in hip flexion. Secondary movers cross the same joint but make less contribution; they are also called accessory or assisted movers, and act sometimes as prime movers when force required increases or paralysis occurs — e.g., sartorius in hip flexion.
A(ii) Antagonists are muscles that oppose the prime movers: they relax and lengthen progressively to allow agonists to move, so that movement is controlled but not impeded. For every action there are agonists and antagonists — e.g., gluteus maximus is the antagonist for iliopsoas.
B(i)
- Conjoint synergists: two muscles acting together to produce a movement that neither could produce alone; they are considered prime movers and are parallel to each other — e.g., tibialis anterior and peroneus tertius working together to produce dorsiflexion.
- Neutralizer synergists: muscles that neutralize or cancel the undesired action of other prime or secondary movers — e.g., wrist extensors neutralizing the unwanted wrist flexion that occurs when finger flexors contract to grasp an object; or lateral rotators neutralizing undesired medial rotation of adductors during hip adduction.
- Stabilizer synergists: muscles that surround the proximal joint, contracting isometrically to allow the distal joint to move smoothly — e.g., the rotator cuff muscles all contribute opposing tension to support the humeral head against the glenoid fossa when the arm is moved and the hand reaches for an object.
B(ii) Fixators are muscles that contract in both agonists and antagonists simultaneously, especially under stress conditions, so that tension develops inside both groups to prevent any degree of freedom. This occurs in normal physiological conditions during strenuous effort and increased demand — e.g., during standing on one leg.
questions.question:
A(i) Define agonists (prime movers and secondary movers) and explain the distinction between the two, giving an example of each from the hip joint.
A(ii) Define antagonists and describe their role during movement; give an example at the hip joint.
B(i) Define each of the three types of synergists — conjoint, neutralizer, and stabilizer — and give one example of each.
B(ii) Define fixators, describe the conditions under which they act, and give an example.

A(i) Define a joint and classify joints according to their mobility into three types, naming the Latin terminology and giving anatomical examples for each type.
A(ii) For freely movable (synovial) joints, describe their structural features: capsule, lining, fluid, and articular surface covering.
B(i) Name and give examples of the four types of movable joints, and state one movement or example available at each.
B(ii) Distinguish between the first and second class levers as found in the human body. For each class, identify the arrangement of fulcrum, load, and effort; describe one human body example (including the fulcrum, load, and effort); and state the mechanical advantage for each class.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A joint is formed where two bones meet. Joints are classified by mobility into three types: Fixed joints (synarthroses) — provide no movement; example: sutures between the skull bones. Slightly movable joints (amphiarthroses) — found in the pelvis; examples: symphysis pubis and sacroiliac joint. Freely movable joints (diarthroses) — permit free movement.
A(ii) Freely movable joints are enclosed in a fibrous capsule supported by ligaments. The capsule is lined by synovial membrane with synovial fluid inside the capsule. The bone surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage.
B(i) Four types of movable joints: Ball and socket articulations — hip and shoulder joints (allow multi-directional movement). Hinge articulation — knee joint (full hinge); elbow joint (partial hinge); permit flexion/extension. Pivot articulation — radius and ulna joint; axis of the cervical region; permit rotation. Gliding joint — tarsal joint of the ankle; carpal joint of the wrist; permit gliding/sliding.
B(ii) First class lever — fulcrum between load and effort (FLE). Example: nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint. The skull is the rigid bar; the atlanto-occipital joint is the fulcrum; the weight of the skull is the load; the posterior neck muscle contractions provide the effort. Mechanical advantage: first class levers are speed levers if the force arm (FA) is shorter than the resistance arm (RA). Second class lever — load between fulcrum and effort; there is always mechanical advantage because the effort arm is greater than the load arm; it is the lever of power — movement is powerful but slow. Example: gastrocnemius/soleus plantarflexing the ankle joint. The bones of the foot are the lever; the metatarsal joints form the fulcrum; the effort is the muscular contraction of the calf muscles; the load is the weight of the body. The existence of this class in the human body is still debated but these are cited examples.

questions.question:
A(i) Classify skeletal muscles according to (a) shape and fascicular architecture, (b) myoglobin content, and (c) type of contractile activity (tonic vs phasic), giving examples and functional implications for each classification.
A(ii) Classify skeletal muscles according to (a) the number of joints they cross (one-joint, two-joint, multi-joint) and (b) their relative stabilizing and rotatory components (spurt vs shunt muscles), giving one example for each.
B(i) List the five properties of skeletal muscles and give a brief definition of each.
B(ii) Distinguish between concurrent and countercurrent patterns of action of two-joint muscles, and give an example for each pattern.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
(a) By shape and fascicular architecture: parallel (spindle) — muscles designed for speed have parallel fibres; oblique, e.g., pinnate — muscles designed for strength; spiral, e.g., supinator.
