(b) By myoglobin content: red muscles contain more red fibres and are responsible for movements requiring slow action for a long time (e.g., antigravity muscles); white muscles contain more white fibres and are responsible for movements requiring rapid action for a short time.
(c) By type of contractile activity: tonic muscles (stabilizers) demonstrate continuous low-level contractile activity required to maintain a given posture; phasic muscles (mobilizers) demonstrate rapid (fast twitch) activity required when changing from one position to another.
A(ii)
(a) By number of joints: one-joint muscle (e.g., vastus medialis); two-joint muscle (e.g., rectus femoris); multi-joint muscle (e.g., finger flexors).
(b) By relative stabilizing/rotatory components: spurt muscles are mainly rotator muscles with origin away from the joint and insertion near the joint — e.g., biceps muscle; shunt muscles are mainly stabilizer muscles with origin near the joint and insertion away from the joint — e.g., brachioradialis.
B(i) Five properties of skeletal muscles: Irritability — ability to respond to a stimulus; Contractility — capacity to produce tension between its ends; Relaxation — giving up of tension (opposite of contraction; both progress from zero to maximal values over finite time); Distensibility — ability to be stretched or lengthened by an outside force up to a certain limit without harm; Elasticity — ability to recoil to its original length when an outside force is removed.
B(ii) Concurrent pattern: simultaneous movement of flexion or extension occurs in two joints of the two-joint muscle. Countercurrent pattern: one of the two-joint muscles shortens rapidly at both joints while its antagonist lengthens correspondingly and gains tension at both ends — e.g., the rapid loss of tension in the rectus femoris and corresponding gain of tension in the hamstrings when the hip is flexed and the knee is extended simultaneously.

A(i) A scalar quantity is described by magnitude alone — examples: mass, volume, distance, speed. A vector quantity requires description of both magnitude and direction — examples: force, momentum, impulse, displacement, velocity, acceleration. For vector quantities, direction must be specified in addition to magnitude; they follow the parallelogram law for addition.
A(ii) Friction refers to a force that acts at the interface of surfaces in contact in the opposite direction to an impending motion. Two types of friction: static friction and kinetic friction. Kinetic friction comes into operation once maximal static friction has been overcome; kinetic friction has constant values lesser than maximum static friction. Two subtypes of static friction: sliding friction and rolling friction.
B(i) Two factors affecting the magnitude of maximal static friction or kinetic friction: coefficient of friction and normal reaction force. Two factors influencing the coefficient of friction: (1) relative roughness and hardness of the surfaces in contact — the rougher and harder, the greater the coefficient of friction; (2) type of molecular interaction between the surfaces — the greater the molecular and mechanical interaction, the greater the coefficient of friction.
B(ii) Increasing friction: (1) ferrules of crutches and canes (to grip the floor safely); (2) brakes and wheels in wheelchairs, shoulder wheels, bicycle ergometers; (3) patient and bed clothing in traction application. Reducing friction: (1) use of powder or lotion in massage; (2) suspension therapy; (3) using polished or powdered table or surface for exercise.
questions.question:
A(i) Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities, list at least three examples of each, and explain what additional description is required for vector quantities.
A(ii) Define friction as a force, state the two types of friction and the two subtypes of static friction, and explain the relationship between static friction and kinetic friction in terms of their magnitudes.
B(i) State the two main factors that affect the magnitude of maximal static friction or kinetic friction, and describe the two factors that influence the coefficient of friction.
B(ii) Describe three clinical applications of friction in physiotherapy: two that require increasing friction and two that require reducing friction.

A patient is observed walking with progressively quickening, short, shuffling steps, leaning forward, and appearing as though he is chasing his own centre of gravity. He has difficulty stopping once he has started walking.
(i) Identify this gait pattern by name and state the neurological disorder responsible for it.
(ii) Describe the biomechanical and kinesiological basis of this gait deviation, including its effect on the centre of gravity and comfortable walking speed.
(iii) Identify the predisposing factors (types of neurological disturbance) that produce this class of gait.
(iv) Describe the principles of physiotherapy gait assessment and management relevant to this patient, including the observational and computer-based methods of gait evaluation.
questions.answerText:
(i) The patient demonstrates festinant gait, which is caused by basal ganglia dysfunction. This is classified as an abnormal gait due to neurological disturbance.
(ii) In festinant gait the centre of gravity (located midway between the hips, a few centimetres in front of S2) is displaced anteriorly, causing the patient to accelerate to keep up with it. Normally the least energy is consumed when the centre of gravity travels in a straight line; the forward lean disrupts this and increases energy expenditure. The comfortable walking speed, normally about 80 m/min, is disturbed in festinant gait as the patient cannot regulate cadence or step length effectively.
(iii) Neurological disturbances causing pathological gait are classified as: muscular paralysis (spastic or flaccid), cerebellar dysfunction (ataxic gait), loss of kinesthetic sensation (stamping gait), and basal ganglia dysfunction (festinant gait). Festinant gait arises specifically from basal ganglia dysfunction.
(iv) Observational gait analysis (OGA) is the most common and appropriate method for characterising this gait pathology in the clinic. The physiotherapist should examine: gait cycle, centre of gravity, step length, stride length, walking base/stride width, cadence, walking velocity, pelvic tilt, pelvic rotation, lateral shifting, shoulder alignment, and arm swing. Computer-based evaluation using the Vicon 512 motion capture system and force plates may be used for quantitative gait analysis (CGA) when treatment decision-making is complex. CGA assists in answering questions concerning bracing and medication efficacy and assessing efficacy of surgical interventions, but does not replace OGA.

(i) The patient demonstrates ataxic gait, caused by cerebellar dysfunction. It is classified under pathological gait due to neurological disturbance (specifically cerebellar dysfunction).
(ii) The neurological basis is cerebellar dysfunction, which impairs coordination of muscle activity and balance. This differs from stamping gait (caused by loss of kinesthetic sensation), in which the patient loses proprioceptive input and compensates by slapping the foot hard on the ground to generate feedback. In ataxic gait, the incoordination is due to loss of cerebellar timing/coordination, not loss of proprioception.
(iii) Observational gait analysis parameters most abnormal: walking base/stride width (markedly widened to improve stability), step length (irregular, asymmetric — the right step length does not equal the left), cadence (irregular, not the normal 100–115 steps per minute), comfortable walking speed (below the normal approximately 80 m/min), and shoulder alignment. The centre of gravity deviates unpredictably rather than travelling in a straight line, increasing energy expenditure.
(iv) Physiotherapy management includes gait re-education with an ambulatory device. A walker (zimmer frame) is the appropriate device because it is best for users with poor balance and coordination, can decrease weight bearing to both lower extremities, is best to prescribe to the elderly and obese, and can be used to train endurance. The clinician must check before issuing: that ferrules and wheels are not worn to the point where no tread is showing; that support areas are properly padded; that the pair is matching (an uneven pair leads to poor posture and musculoskeletal disorder); that the device is not cracked or damaged; and that nuts and bolts are tight. The user should not look downward during ambulation.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old patient with cerebellar dysfunction presents with wide-based, staggering, uncoordinated gait with irregular step lengths and difficulty maintaining a straight path.
(i) Name this gait pattern and classify it within the pathological gait taxonomy.
(ii) Identify the specific risk factors and neurological basis for this gait pattern and explain how it differs from the stamping gait caused by loss of kinesthetic sensation.
(iii) State the parameters of observational gait analysis that would be most abnormal in this patient, and explain the impact of this gait on cadence, walking base, and comfortable walking speed.
(iv) Describe the physiotherapy management approach for this patient, including the principles of ambulatory device prescription.

questions.answerText:
(i) The patient demonstrates stamping gait. This is classified as a gait caused by loss of kinesthetic sensation, under the category of pathological gait due to neurological disturbance.
(ii) The predisposing factor is loss of kinesthetic (proprioceptive) sensation from the lower limbs. Without proprioceptive feedback, the patient cannot feel where the foot is in space during the swing phase. The kinesiological rationale for forceful heel strike: the patient stamps the foot hard on the ground to generate maximum somatosensory and vibration feedback through the foot, compensating for the lost proprioception. Visual input (watching the ground) replaces proprioception as the feedback mechanism.
(iii) Stamping gait is caused by loss of kinesthetic sensation. Festinant gait is caused by basal ganglia dysfunction (a separate neurological disturbance), producing progressively quickening small steps as if chasing the displaced centre of gravity. Ataxic gait is caused by cerebellar dysfunction, producing wide-based, uncoordinated, staggering movement without the distinctive forceful heel-strike pattern. All three are classified under neurological causes of pathological gait but arise from distinct mechanisms.
(iv) Observational gait analysis parameters most abnormal: arm swing (altered to aid balance); shoulder alignment; lateral shifting; step length (may be increased to widen base); walking base/stride width (may be widened); cadence (reduced below normal 100–115 steps/minute); comfortable walking speed (reduced below approximately 80 m/min); gait cycle (abnormal in timing because of the forced deliberate heel strike); pelvic tilt and rotation. The patient will also look downward during walking, which affects posture.
(v) A cane or walker would be appropriate. A standard cane provides minimal stability for those who need it; a walker (zimmer frame) is best for users with poor balance and coordination and is best to prescribe to the elderly. The clinician must check all ferrules before issuing, ensure the device is not cracked or damaged, that nuts and bolts are tight, and that support areas are padded. The patient must be educated not to look downward but to look straight ahead, and not to walk on slippery surfaces.
questions.question:
A patient with posterior column spinal cord involvement is observed walking with excessively forceful heel strikes, slapping both feet hard onto the ground. He watches the ground as he walks and loses his balance if he closes his eyes.
(i) Name this gait pattern and classify it according to the neurological classification.
(ii) Describe the predisposing factor (type of neurological dysfunction) and explain the kinesiological rationale for the compensatory strategy of forceful heel strike.
(iii) Distinguish this gait pattern from festinant gait and ataxic gait using the classification of basal ganglia and cerebellar dysfunction.
(iv) State which parameters of observational gait analysis would be most abnormal in this patient, using the full list of gait evaluation parameters.
(v) Describe the physiotherapy management approach, including the ambulatory device most likely to be appropriate and the justification for its prescription.

courses.title: Histopathology

questions.explanation: Chloroform is the most ideal clearing agent for central nervous system tissues, lymph nodes, and embryos because it causes little shrinkage and does not harden tissues excessively. It is good for large blocks despite not being a classical clearing agent as it doesn't render tissues transparent.
questions.question: Which clearing agent is specifically recommended for central nervous system tissues?
options: Chloroform for minimal shrinkage and hardening

questions.question: What function does iodine serve in Gram staining?
questions.explanation: Iodine acts as mordant, forming dye-lake complex that colors both Gram positive and negative cells blue-black initially. This complex formation between crystal violet and iodine creates large molecules within bacterial cells, with subsequent differential extraction by alcohol or acetone distinguishing bacterial types.

questions.question: What component links the endoplasmic reticulum to the nucleus?
questions.explanation: The endoplasmic reticulum is continuous with the outer layer of the nuclear membrane, creating an integrated membrane system. This connection facilitates transport between nucleus and cytoplasm. The structural continuity coordinates nuclear and cytoplasmic functions.

questions.question: What oxidizing agent is used first in Gomori's reticulin method?
questions.explanation: The 0.5% aqueous potassium permanganate oxidation for two minutes prepares tissue for silver impregnation by exposing aldehyde groups. Subsequent 2% potassium metabisulfite treatment removes permanganate color while sensitizing with ferric ammonium sulfate enhances silver uptake by reticulin fibers.

After initial toluidine blue staining, uranyl nitrate extraction creates color contrast by selectively removing dye from non-metachromatic tissues. Acid mucopolysaccharides and mucoproteins retain the red or purple metachromatic color while other tissue constituents appear blue.
questions.question: In uranyl nitrate method, what color do acid mucopolysaccharides display?

questions.explanation: Elastic tissue demonstrates autofluorescence, appearing greenish-yellow when stained or blue if unstained under ultraviolet light. This intrinsic fluorescence property, combined with resistance to solvents and enzymes except pancreatic elastase, provides multiple identification approaches for elastic fiber demonstration and confirmation.
questions.question: What characteristic fluorescence do elastic fibers exhibit?

questions.explanation: Dehydration, clearing, and embedding stages are collectively called processing, which can be done manually or by automatic machine. This standardized procedure prepares tissues for sectioning. Proper processing is essential for quality sections.
questions.question: What is the collective term for dehydration, clearing, and embedding?

questions.explanation: The rotary microtome is most ideal for routine and research work, and is excellent for cutting serial sections. The tissue block moves up and down in a flat plane across the knife-edge, with handle-operated advancement after each section. Serial sections adhere forming ribbons for sequential analysis.
questions.question: Which microtome is specifically designed to produce serial ribbon sections?
Which alum haematoxylin requires no ripening period?
questions.explanation: Mayer's acid alum haematoxylin is ready for immediate use as no ripening is required. This is a general purpose stain that is stable for several months after preparation.

Thermal modules work on Peltier effect principles discovered in 1834: passing electric current through two different conductors causes absorption or generation of heat at their junction, depending on current direction. Rutherford adapted this in 1964 to both knife holders and block stages in microtomes.
options: Peltier effect with absorption or generation of heat at conductor junctions
questions.question: What principle underlies thermo-electric cooling in modern freezing microtomes?

options: Formation of two identical daughter cells
questions.question: What marks the completion of telophase?
questions.explanation: Telophase concludes with cytoplasmic membrane division creating two identical daughter cells. Chromosomes become thread-like, nucleoli appear, and nuclear membranes reform. Each daughter cell is an exact replica of the parent cell.

questions.question: What color indicates sites of cholinesterase activity in the thiocholine method?
questions.explanation: Dark brown coloration from cupric sulphide marks sites of cholinesterase activity in the thiocholine method. Cholinesterases hydrolyze acetylthiocholine to liberate thiocholine, which is then precipitated as its cupric salt. Treatment with dilute ammonium sulphide for two minutes converts the copper complex to dark brown cupric sulphide.
Haematoxylin is extracted from the core or heartwood of the tree Haematoxylin campechianum native to Campeche in Mexico. Today the tree is grown commercially mainly in Jamaica for dye production.
questions.question: Which tree provides natural haematoxylin dye?
In orcein-methylene blue method, what color do elastic fibers appear?
questions.explanation: Synthetic orcein in acidified 70% alcohol demonstrates fine and delicate elastic fibers in light to deep brown shades depending on fiber abundance and staining duration. Nuclei counterstained with methylene blue in acetic acid appear blue, providing excellent contrast for elastic fiber visualization and photography.

Biopsies and blocks not more than 3 mm thick are cleared in 20-30 minutes in xylene. Tissues should never be left in xylene for more than 2 hours as it tends to make tissues excessively hard and brittle, especially brain and blood-containing tissues.
questions.question: What is the recommended clearing time for 3-5 mm biopsies in xylene?

questions.explanation: Dehydration for electron microscopy starts with 40% alcohol as the lower grade, with subsequent concentrations and grade numbers depending on tissue type. This gradual dehydration process prevents excessive tissue shrinkage and structural damage. The progression through ascending alcohol grades ensures proper water removal before clearing.
questions.question: What is the starting alcohol concentration for EM tissue dehydration?
What advantage does FNAC have over cone biopsy?
questions.explanation: Fine needle aspiration cytology is less traumatic than the cone biopsy method it has largely superseded. FNAC provides rapid preliminary diagnosis with minimal patient discomfort. The technique is fairly inexpensive and can be performed on outpatient basis with quick results.

questions.question: What gap distance separates anti-roll plate from knife edge?
questions.explanation: The anti-roll plate is positioned so that its edge is parallel and almost even with the knife edge with about 70 μm gap between them. This prevents sections from curling during cutting.

questions.question: How should control material potency be verified for Best's carmine method?
questions.explanation: Rabbit liver from animals fed carrot for three days provides standardized positive control material with consistently high glycogen content. Alternative known positive materials may be used, but this specific preparation offers reliable verification of staining solution potency.
options: Rabbit liver fed carrots three days

questions.question: What structure ensures proper chromosome separation during mitosis?
questions.explanation: The mitotic spindle formed by achromatic fibers between centrioles is essential for chromosome separation. Without this spindle, cell division cannot occur. Spindle fibers attach to centromeres and pull chromatids to opposite poles.

options: It does not render tissues transparent (not a classical clearing agent)
questions.question: Why is chloroform's end-point difficult to assess during clearing?
questions.explanation: Chloroform is not a classical clearing agent as it does not render tissues transparent, making its end-point difficult to assess. Despite this limitation, it is excellent for CNS tissues due to minimal shrinkage. De-alcoholization time for 3-5 mm tissues is 5-20 hours.

options: To prevent reagent exhaustion and ensure complete alcohol removal
questions.question: Why should clearing reagents be used in amounts not less than 10 times tissue volume?
questions.explanation: Clearing fluids should be used in amounts not less than 10 times the volume of tissue to prevent reagent exhaustion. Adequate volume ensures complete alcohol removal and prevents contamination with extracted alcohol. Insufficient volume leads to incomplete clearing and poor wax infiltration.

questions.question: Why must plastic forceps be used during silver staining procedures?
questions.explanation: Metallic forceps cause non-specific silver precipitation on slides, creating artifacts that obscure true reticulin staining. Plastic forceps eliminate this problem while glassware must be thoroughly washed in 10% nitric acid then rinsed in distilled water to remove metallic contaminants.

questions.question: Why are mitochondria called the powerhouse of cells?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are involved in cell respiration, generating ATP through oxidative phosphorylation. They contain enzymes for aerobic metabolism. The energy produced powers cellular activities and synthetic processes.

questions.question: Why must the embedding mold be filled with fresh molten wax?
options: To ensure complete tissue encasement in uncontaminated wax
questions.explanation: After placing tissue in the mold, it is filled with more molten wax to ensure complete encasement in fresh, uncontaminated wax free of clearing agent. This provides uniform support around all tissue surfaces. Fresh wax ensures optimal block quality and sectioning characteristics.

Pleural and peritoneal fluid specimens are centrifuged at 300 rpm for 10 minutes, or cytospun at 1500 rpm for 10 minutes. Thin smears are made from sediment, at least two smears per specimen. Any clots formed are fixed and processed histologically to complement cytological examination.
questions.question: At what speed are pleural fluids centrifuged for smear preparation?
What dehydration sequence follows staining completion?
questions.explanation: After staining, sections are dehydrated through graded alcohols: 70%, 90% and two changes of absolute alcohol before passing into two changes of xylene for clearing and mounting.

questions.question: What defines a compound fixative?
options: Two or more simple fixatives combined
questions.explanation: Compound fixatives contain two or more simple fixatives mixed to obtain combined effects on tissues. This combination approach achieves properties no single fixative possesses. Most routine fixatives are compound formulations.

options: Sharper staining from sequential reagent addition
questions.explanation: Adding 10% HCl solution to tissue already containing 10% potassium ferrocyanide (in half the ferrocyanide volume) produces sharper staining than pre-mixed solutions. Potassium ferrocyanide's slower diffusion compared to HCl ensures its presence when acid releases ferric ions, maximizing Prussian blue formation at iron deposit sites.
questions.question: What improvement does Gomori's 1952 modification provide for Perl's method?
Which eosin variant is most frequently utilized?
questions.explanation: Eosin Y (yellowish) is the most frequently used and is readily soluble (4% w/v in water and 2% w/v in ethanol). It is the standard counterstain with haematoxylin in routine histopathology.

questions.question: Which embedding medium is specifically recommended for large blocks and dense bone?
questions.explanation: Paraplast and embeddol are more resilient than paraffin wax, allowing large blocks and dense bone blocks to be cut fairly easily. These synthetic wax mixtures provide superior support and cutting characteristics. Their resilience prevents block crumbling during sectioning of difficult tissues.

Complete dryness at any stage causes formation of insoluble compounds that resist decolourization by ethyl ether-acetone mixtures. Gentle blotting without complete drying between steps maintains optimal staining chemistry while preventing artifact formation that compromises bacterial demonstration quality.
questions.question: What happens if sections dry completely during Gram staining?
What temperature maintains slides during drying before staining?
questions.explanation: After picking up sections from the floating out bath, slides are placed on hot plate at 45°C to dry before staining. This temperature ensures proper section adhesion without wax degradation.

questions.question: What refractive index characterizes optimal mounting media?
questions.explanation: Mounting medium must have a refractive index close to that of glass (1.518) for optimal microscopic examination. Canada balsam and DPX both have refractive indices of 1.52, making them suitable mounting media.

The chromophoric bond, specifically the quinonoid structure of basic fuchsin, is broken when treated with sulphur dioxide. This structural disruption eliminates the color-producing mechanism, rendering the leucofuchsin completely colorless until aldehydes restore the bond.
questions.question: What structural feature makes leucofuchsin colorless?

questions.explanation: With freezing microtomes, serial sections cannot be cut because there is continuous thawing and freezing of tissue during operation. This prevents sections from adhering to form ribbons. Cryostats overcome this by maintaining constant temperature for tissue, knife, and sections.
options: Continuous thawing and freezing prevents ribbon formation
questions.question: Why can't serial sections be cut on freezing microtomes?

options: Ferricyanide reduction to ferrocyanide forming dark blue iron complex
questions.question: What is the principle of Schmorl's method for lipofuscin?
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin reduces ferricyanide to ferrocyanide, forming dark blue iron ferrocyanide complex. Fresh 1% potassium ferricyanide mixed with 1% ferric chloride and distilled water provides iron ferricyanide solution that, after 10-minute room temperature staining, demonstrates lipofuscin and other reducing substances as blue deposits.

questions.question: Which condition produces thick and thin bands (chatters)?
questions.explanation: Thick and thin lines in each section (chatters) result from the knife vibrating owing to hardness of the object, excessive tilt, or movement caused by play on slides of the microtome especially sledge type.

questions.question: Which mounting medium characteristic prevents stain fading?
questions.explanation: A good mounting medium must be non-reactive and will not change color or pH over time. It should not cause loss of staining over long periods, protecting specimens for years.

questions.question: Which tissue characteristic results from inadequate fat removal?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous tissues, breast and fatty tissues tend to give soft blocks and mushy sections mainly due to inadequate removal of fat. These tissues are better processed in vacuum baths with blocks not more than 2 mm thick.

questions.question: Which statement about PAS reaction specificity is most accurate?
questions.explanation: The PAS reaction is histochemically specific for substances containing 1,2-glycol groups but not diagnostic alone since many tissue components give positive reactions. Value increases when used with enzymatic controls, blocking techniques, or additional staining methods for definitive identification.

The optimal knife angle for routine paraffin sectioning is typically 3-5°, though this varies slightly with tissue type and consistency. Liver and fatty tissues may require different angles. Proper knife angle is critical for obtaining smooth sections without compression or chatter.
questions.question: What is the optimal knife angle for routine paraffin sectioning?

questions.explanation: Stock aqueous eosin solution is generally prepared in 5% w/v concentration using tap water or distilled water. It is considered very stable due to the alkalinity of tap water.
questions.question: What stock concentration applies to aqueous eosin solutions?

questions.explanation: Long storage, particularly at low temperature, causes paraformaldehyde precipitation in formalin. This can be prevented by room temperature storage or removed by filtration. The precipitate doesn't adversely affect fixing properties.
questions.question: What causes white precipitate formation in stored formalin?

questions.explanation: Attachment of section to slide can be facilitated by the use of special holder fitted with a section cup. This makes the mounting process easier and more reliable for frozen sections.
questions.question: What attachment facilitates frozen section mounting?
What is the basis of the 'nadi' reaction for cytochrome oxidase?
questions.explanation: The 'nadi' reaction for cytochrome oxidase is based on the enzyme catalyzing the oxidative reaction between alpha-naphthol and dimethyl-para-phenylenediamine to form indophenol blue. This oxidative coupling produces a bluish-violet color at sites of enzyme activity. Unfixed fresh cryostat sections must be used for this demonstration.

Wooden holders with deep serrations are coated with 4% celloidin or 16% LVN, and the trimmed celloidin block is pressed firmly into position. A thread is tied around them for 30-60 minutes while celloidin sets. After reintroduction to 70% alcohol for 30 minutes, the cutting surface is trimmed.
options: Coated with celloidin solution and pressed together with thread securing
questions.question: How are celloidin blocks attached to wooden holders?
What characteristic makes lead citrate effective for EM staining?
questions.explanation: Lead citrate is a cytoplasmic stain that intensifies cellular membrane and inclusion details in thin sections. It possesses electron-dense metal essential for proper contrast in cellular components during photomicrography. This contrasts with uranyl acetate which preferentially stains nuclear material.

questions.question: What thickness needle is typically used for fine needle aspiration cytology?
questions.explanation: Needles with thickness of 0.5-0.9 mm are used for fine needle aspiration cytology, with length depending on organ location. A sterile syringe with appropriate needle is the basic requirement, sometimes with special handle for single-hand grip. This allows the other hand to palpate and immobilize mobile masses during aspiration.

options: Inadequate processing, insufficient dehydration, or improper wax infiltration
questions.question: What causes tissue fragmentation and poor ribbon formation during sectioning?
questions.explanation: Tissue fragmentation and poor ribboning indicate inadequate processing, particularly insufficient dehydration or clearing, or improper wax infiltration. Fatty tissues like liver require meticulous processing with adequate time in each reagent. Incomplete processing leaves clearing agent or water preventing proper wax support.

options: To prevent air bubbles from being trapped beneath the tissue
questions.explanation: When embedding, the tissue is placed with the surface to be cut facing downward to prevent air bubbles from being trapped beneath the cutting surface. Trapped air creates gaps that cause section fragmentation. Proper orientation ensures complete wax support under the tissue.
questions.question: Why must the tissue cutting surface face downward during embedding?

questions.explanation: To obtain ribbons of sections, it is important that the upper and lower surfaces of the block are parallel. Cutting of ribbon sections is an eloquent testimony of experience of a good microtomist.
questions.question: Which structural requirement enables proper ribbon formation?

questions.explanation: Tissue blocks of 3-5 mm thickness require 12-24 hours in 10% formalin for complete fixation at room temperature. Fixative penetrates approximately 1 mm per hour from all surfaces. Adequate fixation ensures cellular preservation throughout the entire tissue block.
questions.question: What is the recommended fixation time for a 3-5 mm thick tissue block in formalin?
How do nuclear fixatives differ chemically from cytoplasmic fixatives?
questions.explanation: Nuclear fixatives have pH less than 4.6 or contain glacial acetic acid for chromatin preservation. Cytoplasmic fixatives have different pH ranges. This pH distinction reflects their selective action on cellular components.

questions.question: Which component acts as an activator in the leucine aminopeptidase incubating medium?
questions.explanation: Potassium cyanide at 0.02 M concentration serves as an activator in the leucine aminopeptidase incubating medium. This extremely poisonous substance must be handled with extreme care during preparation and use. The activator enhances enzyme activity during the 20-minute to two-hour incubation period at 37degrees C.

questions.question: What causes metachromatic color changes in dye solutions?
questions.explanation: The original color results from single molecular form in solution. These dyes polymerize, and as more polymers (dimers and trimers) are formed, the solution changes color producing metachromatic effects.

options: Cedar wood oil for improved cutting qualities
questions.explanation: Cedar wood oil imparts proper consistency to dense fibrous tissues, improving cutting qualities. Despite being slow and expensive, it provides superior results for difficult tissues. The oil allows easy cutting of sections from fibrous tumors and dense connective tissue.
questions.question: Which clearing agent imparts proper consistency to dense fibrous tissues?
What causes knife vibration producing chatter marks?
questions.explanation: The knife when not properly clamped will tend to jump, especially on striking hard tissues. Also, excessive tilt will make it vibrate and chattering is likely to occur, creating lines of unequal thickness parallel to the knife edge.

questions.question: Which method releases ribbons adhered to cardboard?
questions.explanation: Usually sections do not adhere to the cardboard and they are released by inserting the scalpel blade obliquely under the line of adhesion. The cut sections are then floated out in the water bath.
The most commonly used iron salts are ferric chloride and ferric ammonium sulphate (iron alum). These iron salts serve as both oxidising agents and mordants for haematoxylin staining.
questions.question: Which iron salt serves dual function as oxidant and mordant?

questions.explanation: Acetic acid destroys the lipid-fixing property of formaldehyde when used together, despite both being present in some fixatives. Acetic acid also destroys mitochondria and Golgi elements. However, the combination provides excellent nuclear fixation for specific applications.
questions.question: What happens when acetic acid and formaldehyde are used together in fixatives?
options: They enhance each other's fixing properties
The acetic acid destroys lipid fixation

questions.question: What combination differentiates tubercle bacilli from leprosy bacilli?
options: Decolorization resistance: tuberculosis greater than leprosy
questions.explanation: Tubercle bacilli resist 1-3% acid-alcohol decolorization more strongly than leprosy bacilli, which require gentler 0.5-1% aqueous sulphuric acid treatment. M. tuberculosis demonstrates alcohol-fastness while M. leprae shows only acid-fastness, requiring modified Fite-Faraco-Wade method with oil deparaffinization and controlled decolorization for optimal demonstration.

Brain and embryos require more gradual dehydration beginning with 50% alcohol with smaller intervals between different grades. Their delicate structure is easily damaged by rapid dehydration. Standard protocols starting at 70% alcohol are too harsh for these fragile tissues.
questions.question: Which tissue type requires the most gradual dehydration starting at lower alcohol concentrations?
options: Muscle tissue with dense connective tissue
Brain and embryos with delicate structure

questions.question: Which adhesive is considered best for section attachment?
questions.explanation: Aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APES) is the best section adhesive. Clean slides are dipped in 2% APES in acetone, drained twice, and finally dipped in distilled water before long-term storage.

questions.question: What is calculated in the karyopyknotic index?
questions.explanation: The karyopyknotic index (KPI) calculates the percentage of superficial cornified squamous cells with pyknotic nuclei among 200 total squamous cells counted. These cells show condensed, deeply stained, structureless nuclei with pink-red cytoplasm. Smears are taken at 3-4 day intervals throughout the menstrual cycle for meaningful hormonal assessment.

Aerosol fixative sprays contain alcohol and wax-the alcohol fixes the smear while wax sets to provide a water-soluble protective film. This combination is effective for smears sent by post to distant laboratories. Alternatively, completely fixed smears may be air-dried and placed in suitable carriers after wax coating.
questions.question: Which fixative component provides a water-soluble protective film for postal specimens?

questions.explanation: Iodine forms a complex with glycogen that produces a characteristic mahogany brown color, while other tissue constituents appear yellow. Though permanent preparations fade after several months, this method provides rapid glycogen visualization with distinctive color differentiation.
questions.question: What color does glycogen appear in Lugol's iodine method?
Why should sections not remain in alcohol excessively?
questions.explanation: Certain stains are soluble in alcohol, especially low grade alcohols, so sections should not be left in alcohol for more time than necessary-usually a minute or less is sufficient.

questions.question: What happens to specimens after slide examination and filing?
questions.explanation: Gross specimens are kept for at least one month before disposal, allowing time for additional sections if needed. Slides are dried at 37°C for about two weeks before filing. This retention period ensures specimen availability for review.
options: Immediately disposed of to save space
To create parallel opposite sides for serial sections and prevent cracking
questions.question: What is the purpose of trimming paraffin blocks before sectioning?
questions.explanation: Excess wax is trimmed so the block forms a four-sided prism with opposite sides parallel to produce serial sections. Trimming away excess wax also prevents blocks from cracking. At least 2 mm of wax should surround the tissue block for structural support.

Ferric iron combines with potassium ferrocyanide in acid solution forming ferric ferrocyanide (Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃), an insoluble blue precipitate called Prussian blue. This specific histochemical reaction identifies hemosiderin and ferric salts definitively, distinguishing them from other brownish tissue pigments.
questions.question: What chemical compound forms in Perl's Prussian blue reaction?
Which chemical test reagent indicates the presence of calcium in decalcifying fluid?
questions.explanation: Saturated aqueous ammonium oxalate (0.5 ml) added to alkalinized decalcifying fluid produces white cloudiness or precipitate if calcium is present. Absence of cloudiness after 20-30 minutes indicates complete decalcification. This is the standard chemical endpoint test.

questions.question: When does hemosiderin appear after hemoglobin release?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin breakdown produces iron-free hematoidin and iron-containing hemosiderin approximately 2-3 days after red cell lysis. This timing distinguishes acute from chronic hemorrhage histologically, with hemosiderin accumulation indicating blood breakdown products' temporal progression and macrophage phagocytic activity.

questions.question: What artifact may form during fixation or staining?
questions.explanation: Some pigments result from fixation or precipitation of staining solutions. These artifacts are distinguished from natural pigments and removed. Recognition prevents misinterpretation of tissue sections.

questions.question: Which remedy addresses faulty feed mechanism?
questions.explanation: Sections cut sometimes thick, sometimes thin indicate a faulty feed mechanism which may lack oil. The knife may be improperly clamped or the block holder is loose requiring correction of the respective defect.

questions.question: What disadvantage affects semi-automatic knife sharpening machines?
questions.explanation: Manual feeding of the knife across the revolving wheel causes uneven pressure and variation in the rate of honing resulting in uneven knife edge. This is the main disadvantage of semi-automatic machines.

questions.question: When are centrioles and centrosome visible in cells?
questions.explanation: The centrosome (cell center) containing centrioles is only visible during cell division. At other times, it appears as a clear cytoplasmic area near the nucleus. Their visibility correlates with their active role in mitosis.

Formal saline (10% formalin in 0.85% saline) is ideal for post-mortem specimens and prolonged storage due to its tolerance, even fixation, and ability to restore natural color. It allows tissues to remain immersed for extended periods without excessive hardening.
questions.question: Which fixative provides the best preservation for post-mortem specimens?
What technical factor most affects elastic fiber demonstration quality?
options: Fixation type minimal impact, staining duration critical
questions.explanation: Elastic fibers' chemical resistance makes most fixatives acceptable, with staining method and duration being critical factors. Aldehyde-fuchsin requires 5-10 minutes, orcein 30 minutes, resorcin-fuchsin 6-18 hours for optimal results. Prolonged oxidation steps and proper differentiation control also significantly impact final demonstration quality.

questions.question: What characteristic distinguishes collagen fibers?
questions.explanation: Collagen consists of thick (140 nm), tough white protein fibers commonly found in bones and cartilage. The enzyme collagenase can dissolve collagen. These fibers provide tensile strength to connective tissues.

questions.question: Why are sections floated in warm water after cutting?
questions.explanation: Sections are floated in warm water to flatten them and remove compression wrinkles from microtomy. This produces smooth sections for mounting on slides. The temperature must be carefully controlled to avoid tissue damage.

questions.question: What is the concentration of Orange G in the OG 6 solution?
questions.explanation: Orange G solution (OG 6) contains 0.5% Orange G (CI No. 16230) in 95% alcohol with 0.015 g phosphotungstic acid per 100 ml. This solution stains acidophilic superficial cells for 2 minutes during Papanicolaou staining. The orange stain provides contrast with the subsequent eosin-azure staining of other cell types.

questions.question: What is added to 95% alcohol to enhance cytological fixation?
questions.explanation: Three percent glacial acetic acid is added to 95% alcohol to enhance fixation properties for cytological specimens. This acidified alcohol provides improved nuclear detail preservation compared to alcohol alone. The acetic acid component aids in nuclear chromatin demonstration during subsequent staining procedures.

Celloidin is superior for very hard tissues or tissues with varying consistency, allowing thicker sections and causing minimal shrinkage. It's particularly useful for central nervous system specimens. However, processing is slower and serial sections are difficult.
options: Allows thinner sections to be cut
Better for hard tissues and varying consistency
questions.question: What advantage does celloidin have over paraffin wax?
Which decalcifying agent is specifically recommended for teeth?
questions.explanation: Ebner's fluid (sodium chloride solution 50 ml, distilled water 50 ml, hydrochloric acid 1 ml) is very ideal for teeth. It is fairly rapid-acting and hastens dehydration as decalcified tissue can be transferred directly to 90% alcohol. Nuclear staining is slightly affected.

Precautionary measures are necessary when handling chloroform as its vapor is toxic and anesthetic. It must be used in well-ventilated rooms and tightly closed containers. Despite being non-inflammable, its toxicity requires careful handling and proper ventilation to protect personnel.
questions.question: What precautions are necessary when handling chloroform as a clearing agent?
options: Use in well-ventilated rooms as vapor is toxic and anesthetic
Mix with alcohol for better results

questions.question: Which tissue component does Alcian blue at pH 1.0 help distinguish?
questions.explanation: At pH 1.0, Alcian blue selectively stains only strongly sulphated mucoproteins while carboxylated mucoproteins remain unstained. This pH-dependent selectivity, combined with varying electrolyte concentrations, enables differentiation between strongly and weakly sulphated mucosubstances.

questions.question: Why must sections be floated on water bath after cutting?
questions.explanation: Sections are floated on water bath at 40-45°C to flatten compression wrinkles that occur during cutting. The gentle heat allows compressed wax to expand, flattening the section. Temperature must be controlled - excessive heat causes tissue distortion, insufficient heat leaves wrinkles.
options: To flatten compression wrinkles before mounting

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of tissue fixation in histopathology?
options: To enhance tissue staining properties only
To facilitate rapid tissue processing procedures
To increase tissue permeability for embedding media
To prevent autolysis and putrefaction of tissues
To remove excess water from tissue specimens
questions.explanation: Fixation prevents autolysis (self-digestion by cellular enzymes) and putrefaction (bacterial decomposition) which begin within 30 minutes post-mortem. This preservation maintains cellular and tissue architecture for accurate microscopic examination. Without proper fixation, tissue specimens rapidly deteriorate making diagnosis impossible.

questions.question: What method demonstrates copper in liver tissue?
questions.explanation: Rubeanic acid combines with copper salts producing colored copper rubeanate complex, demonstrating increased hepatic copper in cirrhosis and Wilson's disease. This specific chemical reaction provides definitive copper identification when clinical history and tissue location suggest copper storage disorder diagnosis.

questions.question: Why can't the routine chemical test be used with Perenyi's decalcifying fluid?
questions.explanation: When ammonia is added to Perenyi's fluid during the standard chemical test, a precipitate forms immediately regardless of calcium presence. This false-positive result makes the routine test unusable. A modified test requiring acetic acid dissolution of the precipitate must be used.
options: Perenyi's fluid contains no acid components
Calcium oxalate is soluble in Perenyi's
A precipitate forms when ammonia is added
Chromic acid interferes with color reactions

questions.explanation: When using the planoconcave knife, the concave surface should face upwards for optimal performance. This orientation is critical for proper cutting action and section quality.
questions.question: What positioning ensures proper concave surface orientation during planoconcave use?

questions.explanation: Blood and grossly congested tissues, muscles, and fibrous connective tissues tend to become excessively hard if left more than 3 hours in wax. However, brain, skin, dense bone tissues, and breast materials with retained secretions require longer infiltration time due to density and composition.
options: Blood and grossly congested tissues with retained fluid
Brain tissue with high lipid content
questions.question: Which tissue type requires the longest wax infiltration time?
What is the recommended tissue thickness for adequate decalcification?
questions.explanation: Tissue blocks should be 2-4 mm thick, cut with a fine hacksaw or fretsaw, to allow adequate acid penetration during decalcification. Thicker blocks result in incomplete decalcification at centers. Proper thickness ensures even calcium removal throughout the tissue.

questions.question: What pH is maintained in the phosphate buffer for the 'nadi' reagent?
questions.explanation: The M/15 phosphate buffer containing 9.465 g Na2HPO4 per liter is maintained at pH 5.8 for the 'nadi' reagent preparation. This slightly acidic pH is optimal for the cytochrome oxidase catalyzed reaction between alpha-naphthol and dimethyl-para-phenylenediamine. Both reagent components are prepared as 0.1% solutions in 1% sodium chloride with this buffer.

Van Gieson counterstaining after elastic fiber demonstration provides collagen (red) and muscle (yellow) differentiation, creating comprehensive connective tissue visualization. This combination, particularly with resorcin-fuchsin, produces excellent photographic contrast between black elastic fibers and red-yellow surrounding tissues.
questions.question: Why is van Gieson often combined with elastic fiber stains?

questions.explanation: Orientation is the proper placement of tissue blocks on the microtome and this must be in such a way as to facilitate the cutting of sections of uniform thickness. All microtomes have adjusting mechanisms for block orientation.
questions.question: Which orientation ensures uniform thickness section production?

questions.explanation: Treating control slide with 10% aqueous sodium carbonate or sodium hydroxide removes calcium salts, producing negative von Kossa reaction. This control confirms that positive staining results from calcium presence rather than non-specific silver deposition, validating pathological calcification identification.
questions.question: What control verifies von Kossa method specificity?
options: Slide treated with sodium carbonate showing negative result

questions.question: Why must tissues be thoroughly washed after potassium dichromate fixation?
questions.explanation: Tissues fixed in potassium dichromate-containing solutions must be thoroughly washed in running tap water before dehydration to prevent formation of an insoluble precipitate. The dichromate reacts with alcohol if not removed. Washing ensures clean processing and prevents artifacts.
options: To prevent formation of insoluble precipitate during dehydration

questions.question: Why must complete dryness be avoided during Brown-Brenn staining?
questions.explanation: Complete dryness at any stage creates insoluble compounds that resist ethyl ether-acetone decolorization, producing false positive Gram reactions. Gentle blotting between steps maintains optimal moisture for proper staining chemistry while preventing solution pooling, ensuring accurate Gram positive/negative bacterial differentiation in tissue sections.
options: Forms insoluble compounds resistant to decolorization

questions.question: Which component in the acid phosphatase indoxyl method serves as an additional oxidizing agent?
questions.explanation: Potassium ferricyanide combined with potassium ferrocyanide acts as additional oxidizing agents to improve enzyme localization in acid phosphatase demonstration. These agents enhance the oxidation of indoxyl derivatives to insoluble indigo blue precipitates. The oxidizing action ensures precise marking of enzyme activity sites at acid pH.
The tissue block selected by the pathologist during cut up may be put in boiling buffered formalin for about 2-3 minutes and cooled before freezing and sectioning for rapid diagnosis.
questions.question: Which fixation method suits rapid cryostat diagnosis?
What combination identifies argentaffin cells in intestinal mucosa?
questions.explanation: Argentaffin cells demonstrate silver reduction (Masson-Fontana positive) without external reducing agents and Schmorl's method positivity through ferricyanide reduction. These enterochromaffin cells' granules, containing serotonin precursors, reduce silver solutions directly and reduce ferricyanide, distinguishing them from argyrophilic cells requiring reducing agents for silver demonstration.

options: Combined alcian blue-PAS with diastase control
questions.question: What staining combination characterizes mucin-secreting carcinomas?
questions.explanation: Mucin-secreting carcinomas demonstrate alcian blue positivity (acid mucins) and/or PAS positivity resistant to diastase digestion (neutral mucins). This combination, with mucicarmine confirmation of epithelial mucins, characterizes mucinous adenocarcinomas distinguishing them from glycogen-rich tumors (PAS-positive, diastase-labile) and assists tumor classification.

options: To ensure proper sectioning and ribbon formation
questions.explanation: Using clean, high-grade paraffin wax is essential for proper infiltration, block formation, and sectioning quality. Contaminated or low-grade wax causes sectioning difficulties, poor ribbon formation, and artifacts. Fresh wax ensures optimal tissue support and section quality.
questions.question: Why must embedding be performed in clean, high-grade paraffin wax?

questions.explanation:
Vacuum infiltration hastens wax penetration by removing air and clearing agent rapidly under negative pressure, making it desirable for urgent biopsies requiring rapid results. Total wax infiltration time can be reduced to 60 minutes (three 20-minute changes) in vacuum. This technique facilitates same-day diagnosis.

SECTION E: MICROTOMY AND SECTION CUTTING (Questions 111-140)
options: Vacuum accelerates wax penetration reducing total processing time
questions.question: Why is vacuum infiltration specifically recommended for urgent biopsies?
Which stain requires air-dried smears fixed with methanol?
questions.explanation: Romanowsky stains require smears to be air-dried then fixed with methanol for five minutes before staining. Alternatively, specimens may be fixed in ether-alcohol before Romanowsky staining. The most popular Romanowsky stains for fluids and effusions are Giemsa and Leishman stains.

Thin sections for transmission electron microscopy appear grey in reflected light colors, indicating proper thickness for electron penetration. These sections are cut at 50-90 nm and collected on copper grids for staining and examination. The grey reflection indicates sections thin enough for electrons to pass through during microscopy.
questions.question: What colored appearance do thin EM sections have in reflected light?
What reaction may iron ore pigments give in lung tissue?
questions.explanation: Iron ore pigments in miners' lungs contain variable iron forms that may react positively with Prussian blue (ferric iron) and Turnbull blue (ferrous iron) methods. Their variably colored appearance combined with positive iron reactions distinguishes them from pure carbon deposits in anthracosis.
options: Prussian blue and Turnbull blue positive

questions.question: What process generates ATP in cellular metabolism?
questions.explanation: Catabolic reactions generate ATP through oxidation of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins via glycolysis, fatty acid oxidation, and proteolysis. This energy currency powers anabolic reactions. The cycle coordinates energy production and utilization.

questions.question: At what angle are most knife wedges inclined in standard configuration?
questions.explanation: Most knives are wedge shaped with the edge inclined at an angle of about 15 degrees. The wedge faces are polished so that sections do not stick to them but will move on the surface.

Frozen sections are thicker (10-15 μm) than paraffin sections, providing less cellular detail. However, they enable rapid diagnosis during surgery when immediate decisions are needed. The technique sacrifices some quality for speed.
questions.question: What limits frozen section use compared to paraffin sections?
How many chromosomes are in normal human diploid cells?
questions.explanation: Normal body cells contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs (diploid set), with one chromosome of each pair from each parent. This includes 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Sex cells contain haploid sets of 23 chromosomes.

questions.question: What is the role of acetic acid in Alcian blue staining solution?
questions.explanation: Glacial acetic acid maintains the staining solution at pH 2.5, which is critical for Alcian blue's selectivity toward acid mucosubstances. The acidic environment allows the copper phthalocyanine basic dye to specifically react with acid groups in tissues through salt linkage formation.

questions.question: Why are early morning urine specimens preferred for cytology?
questions.explanation: Early morning urine specimens are preferred because they contain larger cell concentrations due to relatively long bladder residence overnight. This increases diagnostic yield for detecting abnormal cells in urinary tract disorders. The concentrated specimen provides better cellular material than random daytime collections.

Vacuum impregnation produces negative pressure that hastens extrusion of air bubbles and clearing agent from tissue, resulting in rapid wax penetration. This is especially important for lung tissues with air-filled alveoli. The vacuum eliminates air that would prevent wax infiltration.
questions.question: Why is vacuum infiltration particularly useful for lung tissues?
options: Vacuum hastens extrusion of air bubbles and clearing agent from air-filled spaces

questions.explanation: Thyroid epithelium peroxidase is labile and can be eliminated by treating sections with 10% formalin for 10-15 minutes. In contrast, leucocyte peroxidase enzyme is stable and remains unaffected by this treatment. This differential stability allows selective demonstration of leucocyte enzyme when both are present in tissue sections.
questions.question: Which peroxidase is labile and can be eliminated by formalin treatment?
What must be done before staining paraffin sections?
questions.explanation: Paraffin must be removed (dewaxed) and tissues rehydrated through graded alcohols before aqueous stains can penetrate. This reverses the processing steps. Incomplete dewaxing prevents proper staining.

questions.question: Where in cells are vacuoles primarily located?
questions.explanation: Vacuoles are compartments in the cytoplasm lined by membranes, containing water, salts, and nutrients. They store materials and maintain osmotic balance. The membrane-bound structure allows selective transport.

questions.question: What ranges describe the typical tilt angle variation during microtomy?
questions.explanation: Tilt angle varies between 10-40 degrees depending on the angle of the cutting facet. The appropriate tilt must be set to avoid compression and ensure proper section cutting.

The identifying label (written in pencil on quality paper like Whatman filter paper) is immersed in the wax during embedding to maintain permanent identification. Ball-point pen ink is soluble in alcohol and cannot be used. The label survives all processing and storage.
questions.question: Why must identification labels be placed in the embedding mold with tissue?
options: For permanent identification that survives processing

questions.explanation: One minute to two in each of two changes of xylene is usually adequate to give transparency to the section and completely remove alcohol. Insufficient clearing renders sections opaque.
questions.question: Which clearing duration ensures complete alcohol removal?
Which fixative produces hard brittle tissue blocks?
questions.explanation: The production of hard brittle blocks is due to prolonged fixation in fixatives such as Zenker's or Helly's fluid, and it may lead to the production of fragmented sections causing knife chattering.

questions.question: What initiates paraffin section preparation for staining?
questions.explanation: Before staining, the first preparatory step is removal of paraffin wax (dewaxing) because paraffin wax is not permeable to stains. It is removed with xylene in two or three minute changes.

questions.question: Which microtome type moves the knife rather than the tissue block?
options: Sliding microtome where knife moves across stationary block
questions.explanation: The sliding microtome is unique in that the block remains stationary while the microtome knife moves during cutting. All other common microtome types move the tissue block past a stationary or pivot-mounted knife. This design is particularly suited for celloidin embedding.

Secondary fixation complicates the processing schedule and requires extra precaution when handling mercuric chloride solutions. Pigment removal from sections adds another step. These considerations have reduced the technique's popularity despite improved results.
questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of secondary fixation technique?

options: To prevent false-positive endpoint reactions from calcium in tap water
questions.question: Why should distilled water be used to prepare decalcifying fluids?
questions.explanation: Distilled water prevents false-positive endpoint reactions caused by calcium ions naturally present in ordinary tap water. Using tap water would indicate calcium presence even when tissue decalcification is complete. Distilled water ensures accurate endpoint determination.

Longitudinal scratches occur when the knife edge is serrated or is coated with debris from previous sections. Similar scratches may be due to particles of dust in the wax or minute spicules of calcium or silica in the tissue.
questions.question: What causes longitudinal scratches on cut sections?
Which tissue type should be used for oxidative enzyme demonstrations?
questions.explanation: Fresh frozen unfixed tissue should be used for cryostat sections in oxidative enzyme demonstrations to preserve enzyme activity. Oxidative enzymes including dehydrogenases, diaphorases, oxidases, and peroxidases are involved in catalyzing Krebs cycle reactions. These enzymes are labile and require fresh tissue to maintain their catalytic properties.

questions.question: Which equipment depth specification applies to staining sinks?
questions.explanation: The sink should be shallow, about 13 cm deep, and should have an efficient slide washing tray, usually of stainless steel, that can be placed in the sink for proper workflow.

questions.question: Why is acid fuchsin used in van Gieson stain?
questions.explanation: Acid fuchsin combines with picric acid to form a complex having great affinity for collagen fibers in acidic solution. This picrofuchsin complex selectively stains collagen red while picric acid alone colors muscle and cytoplasm yellow, exploiting differential binding affinities of acid aniline dyes.

options: Prussian blue positive control showing expected blue color
questions.question: What confirms adequate fixation for iron pigment demonstration?
questions.explanation: Known hemosiderin-positive control tissue (spleen, liver with iron overload) processed and stained identically should demonstrate expected blue iron deposits. Positive control validation confirms adequate neutral formalin fixation preventing acid dissolution, proper reagent preparation (fresh ferrocyanide-HCl mixture), and correct technique ensuring diagnostic reliability.

Nitro blue tetrazolium (Nitro BT or NBT) at 1 mg/ml concentration is used to demonstrate succinate dehydrogenase activity. The tetrazolium salt accepts transferred hydrogen and is reduced to water-insoluble colored formazan pigment. Blue-purple deposits of formazan mark sites of enzyme activity after 30 minutes incubation at 37degrees C.
questions.question: Which tetrazolium salt is used to demonstrate succinate dehydrogenase activity?

questions.explanation: Secretion granules are small globules that coagulate into granules on fixation, involved in cellular secretion. They represent stored secretory products. The granules are released through exocytosis.
questions.question: What characterizes secretion granules in cytoplasm?

questions.explanation: The spermatozoan's sex chromosome (X or Y) determines embryo sex, as all ova contain X chromosomes. XX combination produces female offspring, XY produces male. This mechanism explains equal sex ratios at conception.
questions.question: What determines embryo sex at fertilization?

questions.explanation: Tissues must be dehydrated because water (from fixative) is not miscible with paraffin wax. Alcohol removes water through a series of graded concentrations. This dehydration is essential before infiltration with wax embedding medium.
options: Water is not miscible with paraffin
questions.question: Why must tissues be dehydrated before paraffin embedding?
Why are metachromatic preparations considered impermanent?
questions.explanation: Metachromatic color changes are inherently unstable and tend to fade during permanent mounting procedures. Though methods are quick and simple, they don't reliably produce permanent preparations, limiting their utility for archival purposes despite diagnostic value.

Absolute alcohol in Carnoy's fluid provides superior glycogen preservation through rapid dehydration and protein precipitation. Carnoy's fluid (absolute alcohol, chloroform, glacial acetic acid) fixes and dehydrates simultaneously. Glycogen is precipitated but not chemically fixed by alcohol.
questions.question: Which fixative component is specifically recommended for glycogen preservation?

questions.explanation: Lapping compounds made up of suspensions of alumina or diamond grit aid the sharpening process by being continuously recirculated by means of a built-in pump in semi-automatic machines.
questions.question: Which component aids sharpening in semi-automatic machines?

questions.explanation: Acid phosphatase demonstrates maximum enzymatic activity at pH 5.0, which is within the acidic range. This enzyme hydrolyses orthophosphate at acid pH and is inhibited by fluoride but not activated by magnesium. The optimal pH differentiates it from alkaline phosphatase which functions best at pH 9.0-10.0.
questions.question: What is the optimal pH for acid phosphatase enzyme activity?
What working solution ratio is recommended for Weigert's iron hematoxylin?
questions.explanation: Equal volumes of solution A (1g hematoxylin in 100ml 95% ethanol) and solution B (29% ferric chloride with HCl) are mixed immediately before use. This fresh working solution remains effective for two days, providing reliable nuclear staining before van Gieson counterstaining.
An experienced section cutter can produce ribbons of sections of up to 10 inches long. The ribbons can be laid out on a cardboard sheet in serial order for systematic processing.
questions.question: What maximum ribbon length can experienced cutters achieve?
Why is flaming no longer permitted in Ziehl-Neelsen staining?
questions.explanation: Current Health and Safety regulations prohibit flaming practice previously used for heating carbol fuchsin on slides. Alternative heating methods include waterbath incubation at 37°C for 1 hour, 56°C for 30 minutes, or overnight room temperature staining, maintaining effectiveness while eliminating fire hazards and chemical vapor ignition risks.

questions.question: Which microtome component requires regular calibration for accurate section thickness?
questions.explanation: The micrometer screw or thickness gauge that controls advancement distance requires regular calibration to ensure accurate section thickness. Wear or mechanical drift causes inaccurate advancement. Quality control includes periodic verification using calibration standards and maintenance records.

questions.question: What prevents ribbon formation when block is too warm?
questions.explanation: When the knife edge or wax block is too warm, the section lifts from the knife on the upstroke (rotary microtome) or backstroke (sliding microtome with fixed knife), preventing ribbon formation completely.

questions.question: Which decalcifying agent works by chelation rather than acid action?
questions.explanation: EDTA (ethylene diamine tetra-acetic acid) works by chelating calcium ions rather than acid dissolution. It is extremely slow (3+ weeks) but produces excellent staining results with minimal artifacts. It is employed for microscopic studies where urgency is not a factor.
Canada balsam is an oleoresin collected from blisters in the bark of the balsamea (Abies balsamea) fir tree native to the eastern half of Canada. It is prepared by dissolving in xylene.
questions.question: What natural tree source provides Canada balsam?

questions.explanation: Propylene oxide (epoxypropane) is a commonly used transitional fluid for electron microscopy, being miscible with both ethanol and embedding medium. Other clearing agents include xylene and toluene, which serve as media transitional between dehydration and embedding stages. These agents must be compatible with the epoxy resin embedding media.
questions.question: Which transitional fluid is commonly used as a clearing agent in EM?

questions.explanation: Fast Red TR diazonium salt couples with liberated naphthol to produce a brown precipitate at sites of alkaline phosphatase activity. The coupling azo-dye method requires incubation of 15-60 minutes for paraffin sections, though it may extend to 12 hours with Fast Red TR. This contrasts with Fast Black B which produces black coloration.
questions.question: Which diazonium salt produces a brown color when demonstrating alkaline phosphatase activity?
What fixative initiates cryostat H&E staining procedure?
questions.explanation: The air-dried section is fixed in pure acetone for 20 seconds at the beginning of the cryostat H&E staining method. This provides rapid fixation while preserving tissue architecture.

The section thickness control is usually set at 5-10 μm for frozen sections and the automatic advance mechanism is engaged. This thickness provides adequate tissue detail for rapid diagnostic purposes.
questions.question: Which thickness setting applies to frozen section cutting?
What pH is used for the phosphate buffer in acridine orange staining?
questions.explanation: Phosphate buffer at pH 6.0 is prepared by mixing 87.8 ml of 0.067 M potassium dihydrogen phosphate with 12.2 ml of 0.067 M disodium hydrogen orthophosphate. This specific pH allows acridine orange to demonstrate DNA as green and RNA as orange-red fluorescence. The buffer is used for staining solution preparation and washing steps.

options: Formation of yellow nitrous oxide discoloration
questions.question: What is the primary disadvantage of nitric acid decalcification?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid forms nitrous oxide which imparts yellow coloration to tissues that may affect staining reactions. Adding 0.1% urea temporarily inhibits yellow color formation. Despite rapid action (1-3 days), this discoloration is a significant disadvantage for diagnostic work.

Thin sections for transmission electron microscopy are cut at 50-90 nm thickness to allow electron penetration and photon transmission to the fluorescent screen. These ultra-thin sections appear grey in reflected light colors and are cut with diamond knives or fresh glass knives. This thickness contrasts with thick sections cut at 0.5-2 um for orientation.
questions.question: What section thickness range is used for thin sections in TEM?

options: Superior cytological detail and nuclear staining
questions.explanation: Zenker's fluid provides excellent cytological detail and brilliant staining of nuclei and connective tissue fibers with acid aniline dyes. It gives superior results compared to formal saline for small pieces of liver and spleen. However, it requires removal of mercuric chloride pigment.
questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using Zenker's fluid over formal saline?

questions.explanation: Dark ground illumination provides optimal spirochete detection in smears and sections, particularly valuable for syphilitic specimen examination. This technique exploits light scattering by spirochetes' helical structure against dark background, enabling visualization of living organisms without staining, though silver impregnation methods provide permanent preparations.
questions.question: What illumination method best detects spirochetes?
What mounting medium preserves metachromatic staining longest?
questions.explanation: Glycerine jelly mounting preserves metachromatic staining better than resinous media, though metachromasia remains inherently variable and impermanent. For toluidine blue and thionin methods, glycerine jelly provides acceptable temporary preservation, though complete permanence remains unachievable with current metachromatic techniques requiring repeated staining for archival purposes.

Freshly mixed equal parts of 0.3% potassium permanganate and 0.3% sulphuric acid oxidize tissues for 5 minutes before resorcin-fuchsin application. Following 5% oxalic acid bleaching and thorough washing, tissues achieve optimal elastic fiber staining with the complex resorcin-fuchsin-ferric chloride solution.
options: Equal parts potassium permanganate and sulphuric acid
questions.question: What substance oxidizes tissues before resorcin-fuchsin staining?

questions.explanation: Rinsing sections in 15% ethanol for 5 minutes after formalin-saline fixation removes excess formalin from the tissue. This step prevents interference with subsequent counterstaining and mounting procedures. The ethanol rinse also initiates partial dehydration before final mounting in glycerine jelly or synthetic resin.
questions.question: What is the purpose of using 15% ethanol after formalin-saline in succinate dehydrogenase method?

options: Dried white copper sulphate turns blue
questions.question: How can water contamination of the final absolute alcohol bath be detected?
questions.explanation: Dried white anhydrous copper sulphate placed in the alcohol will show a tinge of blue if water is present. A layer of copper sulphate covered with filter paper kept at the jar bottom serves as a continuous indicator. The salt turns blue when water contamination occurs.

questions.question: What tissue characteristic necessitates firm fast cutting strokes?
questions.explanation: Hard tissues like thyroid are best cut with firm fast strokes, while soft tissues like brain require slow smooth cutting action. The tissue hardness determines the appropriate cutting technique.
Some dyes somehow produce colors different from their own color and that produced in other parts of the tissue. This phenomenon is known as metachromasia, seen mainly with basic dyes.
questions.question: Which phenomenon describes dyes producing different colors?

questions.explanation: The sides of the cutting edge are called cutting facets and the angle formed between the cutting facets where they meet is known as the bevel angle or facet angle. This is normally about 27°33".
questions.question: What structural element is called when cutting facets meet angularly?
What appearance characterizes asbestos in tissues?
questions.explanation: Asbestos occurs as long thin crystalline needles or elongated beaded rods with large rounded ends, appearing gold-yellow when unstained. Positive Prussian blue reactions combined with distinctive morphology enable easy identification in unstained sections from lung biopsies or autopsy specimens.
options: Long thin crystalline needles or beaded rods

questions.explanation: Acetic acid causes swelling of tissues, especially collagen fibers, when used alone. Its use in compound fixatives is to counteract the shrinking effect of other reagents. Pure acetic acid disrupts tissue architecture and cannot be used as a sole fixative.
questions.question: Which fixative component causes excessive shrinkage when used alone?
Which cells are classified in the maturation index?
questions.explanation: The maturation index classifies non-cornified squamous epithelial cells as superficial, intermediate, and parabasal based on morphology and staining reactions. At least 200 squamous cells are counted with each class expressed as percentage. High oestrogenic activity shows predominant superficial-intermediate cells while low activity shows predominant parabasal cells.

questions.question: What is the minimum fixation time for cytological smears in alcohol-ether?
questions.explanation: The minimum fixation time in any of the standard cytological fixatives including alcohol-ether mixture is at least 15 minutes. Prompt and proper fixation while smears are still wet is essential for preserving cell morphology. The alcohol-ether fixative consists of equal parts of diethyl ether and 95% alcohol.

questions.question: What enzyme activity underlies the benzidine method for hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Peroxidase enzyme transfers oxygen from hydrogen peroxide to oxidize benzidine into blue dye, demonstrating hemoglobin in erythrocytes. Though applicable to frozen and paraffin sections, benzidine's carcinogenic properties necessitate substitutes like 3-amino-9 ethylcarbazole for safer hemoglobin demonstration.

Ferrous salts combine with potassium ferricyanide forming Turnbull's blue precipitate (Fe₃[Fe(CN)₆]₂), staining ferrous iron blue. This reaction distinguishes ferrous from ferric iron, though ferric iron can convert to ferrous iron with ammonium sulfide, forming black iron sulfide (Quincker's reaction) before Turnbull blue demonstration.
questions.question: What color do ferrous salts appear in Turnbull's blue reaction?
How are exogenous pigments distinguished from endogenous?
questions.explanation: Endogenous pigments like melanin and hemosiderin are produced within the body, while exogenous pigments like coal dust are foreign particles that are phagocytosed. The distinction reflects their origin and significance in pathology.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of cryostat over traditional freezing microtome?
questions.explanation: The cryostat's main advantage is maintaining tissue block, knife, and section at the same temperature (-15°C to -30°C) in the refrigerated cabinet. This eliminates difficulties like thawing of unfixed tissues with knife freezing attachment and obtaining thin sections. Constant temperature prevents freeze-thaw artifacts.
options: Maintains tissue block, knife, and section at same temperature

questions.explanation: Epithelial mucins are optimally demonstrated using both techniques in combination, as they complement each other's capabilities. PAS effectively stains neutral mucopolysaccharides while Alcian blue targets acid mucopolysaccharides, providing comprehensive mucin characterization.
questions.question: Which methods work best together for demonstrating epithelial mucins?
