questions.question: The hand piece of a crutch should be positioned to allow approximately how many degrees of elbow flexion when the elbow is extended and lined up with the wrist?
To avoid fatigue during coordination training, the course material recommends which specific practice?
options: A short rest after two or three repetitions
questions.explanation: Patients should have a short rest after two or three repetitions during coordination training to avoid fatigue, since fatigue can degrade movement quality and engram formation. High repetition of precise, correctly performed movement is still required overall, but must be paced with adequate rest. Various sensory inputs such as instruction, touch, and visual feedback are also used to enhance performance during training.

questions.question: A one-arm-drive wheelchair is specifically designed to enable propulsion under which circumstance?
options: Using a foot pedal mechanism only
Using one arm via a special push rim
Using a motor controlled by a caregiver
Using both legs without arm help
questions.explanation: A one-arm-drive wheelchair allows a patient to propel the manual chair using only one arm, employing a push handle or specially designed push rim connected by a lever to both wheels. This design is particularly useful for patients with hemiplegia or unilateral upper limb impairment. It enables greater independence in mobility compared to standard bilateral hand rim propulsion.

questions.question: Conventional manual wheelchairs typically have rear wheels of approximately what diameter compared to powered wheelchairs?
options: 30 inches, compared to 10 inches on powered chairs
16 inches, compared to 22 inches on powered chairs
24 inches, compared to 14 inches on powered chairs
14 inches, compared to 24 inches on powered chairs
questions.explanation: Conventional manual wheelchairs usually have a 24-inch diameter large rear wheel, while powered wheelchairs typically use a smaller 14-inch wheel since propulsion is motor-driven rather than manual. This size difference reflects the different mechanical demands of manual versus powered mobility. Wheel size selection can also affect ride comfort and the ability to negotiate obstacles.

questions.question: A patient post-right total knee replacement reports a loud slapping sound during walking. Which gait deviation best accounts for this?
options: Circumduction from excessive hip flexor tone
Foot drop from peroneal nerve palsy
Rocking horse gait from gluteus maximus inhibition
questions.explanation: A slapping foot contact occurs when ankle dorsiflexors fail to eccentrically control foot lowering after heel strike, causing the forefoot to slap the ground. This pattern is classic for peroneal nerve palsy — a recognised complication of knee surgery from positioning or tourniquet pressure. The nerve injury impairs dorsiflexion, producing characteristic foot drop gait with a slapping contact sound.

questions.question: Neurodevelopmental treatment, or NDT, is best described as which type of therapeutic approach?
options: An approach limited strictly to muscle re-education
A pharmacological treatment targeting spasticity symptoms
A purely strength-based resistance training program
A surgical intervention for movement disorders
A holistic approach targeting coordination beyond muscle function
questions.explanation: NDT is described as a holistic approach dealing with the quality of coordination patterns rather than isolated muscle function alone, addressing developmental, perceptual-cognitive, emotional, social, and functional aspects of the person. This comprehensive view distinguishes NDT from narrowly focused strengthening protocols. Bobath's 1990 framework emphasizes treating the whole person rather than isolated impairments.

As walking speed increases, the duration of all component phases diminishes, but the swing phase decreases the least while double support duration approaches zero. This differential change reflects the biomechanical demand of clearing the limb quickly at higher speeds. In running, double support disappears completely and swing time exceeds stance time.
questions.question: As walking speed increases, which gait cycle component decreases the least in duration?

options: Endurance through distance covered in six minutes
Walking speed on a 10-metre straight surface
Balance and fall risk in structured environments
Cadence and stride length over a fixed distance
Gait symmetry between left and right step lengths
questions.explanation: The Six-Minute Walk Test quantifies cardiovascular and cardiopulmonary endurance by measuring the maximum distance a patient can walk in six minutes at their own self-selected pace. It reflects integrated cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal function over sustained effort. For gait rehabilitation, it captures endurance limitations that short-distance speed tests cannot detect, particularly for community ambulation planning where sustained walking is required.
questions.question: A physiotherapist selects the six-minute walk test as a primary outcome measure in a cardiac rehabilitation gait programme. Which parameter does this test most directly quantify?

options: Use only during inpatient hospital stays
questions.question: Forearm crutches, also called Lofstrand or Canadian crutches, are most often selected for patients requiring which type of crutch use?
questions.explanation: Forearm crutches, known as Lofstrand, elbow, or Canadian crutches, feature a cuff around the forearm and are most often used by patients requiring long-term crutch use. Their design reduces axillary pressure compared with underarm crutches, making them more suitable for extended daily use. This makes them a common choice for patients with chronic lower limb impairments.

questions.question: The stance phase of the gait cycle typically occupies approximately what proportion of a single cycle at normal walking speed?
questions.explanation: At normal walking speed, the stance phase occupies approximately 60 percent of the gait cycle while the swing phase occupies the remaining 40 percent. This proportion shifts as speed changes, with the stance phase shortening relative to swing as walking becomes faster. In running, double support disappears entirely and the swing phase becomes proportionally longer.

options: Reducing walker frame weight with titanium components
Teaching the patient to slide the walker forward
Recommending power wheelchair for community use
questions.question: A patient cannot lift a standard walker due to bilateral forearm arthritis. Which walker modification best addresses this barrier?
questions.explanation: Platform walkers feature forearm troughs that bear the patient's weight through the forearms rather than requiring wrist extension and hand grip. This design accommodates patients with wrist flexion contractures, hand deformities, severe arthritis, or pain preventing standard handle grip. The forearm platform distributes load over a larger area, eliminating the hand and wrist demands that make standard walkers impossible in inflammatory arthritis.

questions.question: Genu valgum contributes to an increased Q-angle primarily through which mechanical effect?
questions.explanation: Genu valgum increases the obliquity of the femur, which concomitantly increases the obliquity of the quadriceps pull and consequently raises the lateral displacing force on the patella. This mechanical chain links a proximal alignment abnormality to distal patellofemoral instability. Recognizing genu valgum as a contributing factor supports targeted assessment of lower limb alignment in patients with anterior knee pain.

options: Modifying the plan or storing information for reuse
Preventing any correction of the movement
Bypassing the need for future motor planning
Permanently eliminating all proprioceptive sensory input
questions.question: Following execution of a movement, sensory feedback supplied to the central nervous system serves which of the following purposes?
questions.explanation: Sensory feedback returned to the central nervous system after a movement allows the system to modify the plan during execution, confirm that the task goal was achieved, or store the information for future performance of the same task. This feedback loop is essential for refining motor skills through practice. Without such feedback, motor learning and error correction would not be possible.

questions.question: A patient with hip osteoarthritis demonstrates a positive Trendelenburg sign. Which exercise should the physiotherapist prioritise to correct pelvic dropping during gait?
questions.explanation: The Trendelenburg sign indicates stance-side hip abductor weakness — specifically gluteus medius — causing pelvic drop on the contralateral swing side. The targeted intervention is progressive hip abductor strengthening to build sufficient muscle force to maintain pelvic level during single-limb stance. Exercises progress from non-weight-bearing hip abduction to functional weight-bearing activities on the affected limb.

questions.question: At the autonomous stage of motor learning, attention demands are best characterized by which feature?
options: Movement is largely automatic, freeing attention for tactical choices
Feedback must be given after every repetition
Cognitive activity is at its highest level
questions.explanation: The autonomous stage is characterized by accurate, consistent, and efficient movement requiring little or no cognitive activity, allowing attention to be directed toward tactical decisions rather than movement mechanics. This differs sharply from the initial stage, where movements demand a clear mental image and close conscious control. Practice at this stage focuses on results, speed, and skill application in novel situations.

options: Timing of muscle contraction and relaxation
questions.explanation: Electromyography, or EMG, records the timing of muscle contraction and relaxation throughout the gait cycle, revealing which muscle groups are active during specific phases. Surface electrodes offer a non-invasive method but may pick up activity from deeper or adjacent antagonist muscles. This limitation must be considered when interpreting EMG data from large muscle groups such as the plantarflexors.
questions.question: Electromyography is used during gait analysis primarily to determine which physiological event?

options: Base width, stride length, and arm swing
questions.explanation: A thorough gait analysis checklist includes symmetry, smoothness, cadence, base width, stride length, arm swing, and positions of the head, trunk, pelvis, knee, ankle, and foot. These observational parameters allow clinicians to systematically identify deviations from normal walking patterns. Physiological measures such as blood pressure are not part of this specific biomechanical checklist.
questions.question: Which combination of parameters is included in a comprehensive gait analysis checklist alongside symmetry and smoothness?
Forearm support crutches, sometimes called platform or gutter crutches, are specifically designed to assist patients with which condition?
options: Isolated ankle sprain needing brief support
Complete absence of lower limb function
Arthritic hand or wrist involvement needing support
questions.explanation: Forearm support crutches, also called adjustable arthritic, platform, or gutter crutches, have padded forearm troughs and adjustable handles that assist patients who need more support due to conditions such as arthritis affecting hand or wrist grip. This design distributes weight through the forearm rather than requiring a strong hand grip. Such crutches are particularly useful for patients with rheumatoid arthritis or similar joint conditions.

questions.question: Successful crutch walking with full-length crutches depends heavily on adequate strength of which muscle groups?
questions.explanation: Taking weight on full-length crutches by pressing down on extended arms and hands depends largely on the strength of the triceps and the depressor muscles of the shoulder girdle. These muscles must often be strengthened before crutch use begins in earnest. Insufficient upper limb strength can compromise safety and independence during ambulation.

options: Forearm crutches for upper limb support
Hip hiking training as primary compensation
Bilateral ankle-foot orthoses for toe clearance
Electrical stimulation of hip abductors bilaterally
questions.explanation: Bilateral ankle-foot orthoses prevent bilateral foot drop by maintaining the ankle in neutral or slight dorsiflexion during swing phase, enabling toe clearance and heel strike. AFOs address the deficit directly at the level of the impairment rather than relying on compensatory hip hiking or circumduction. In Guillain-Barré syndrome, where peripheral nerve recovery may occur, AFOs provide immediate functional ambulation while recovery progresses.
questions.question: A patient with bilateral foot drop from Guillain-Barré syndrome requires gait training. Which assistive strategy best addresses swing phase clearance deficit?

questions.explanation: An engram is a postulated physical or biochemical change in neural tissue representing a stored memory of a movement pattern. Research indicates that thousands to millions of precise repetitions are required to form and perfect an engram. This concept underlies why coordination training emphasizes high repetition of correctly performed movements.
questions.question: An engram, as a component of coordinated movement, is best described as which of the following?
options: A device used to measure coordination
A structural abnormality of the joint
A biochemical change in neural tissue representing memory
A type of muscle contraction pattern only
A sensory receptor located in muscle spindles

questions.explanation: A gait cycle spans from heel strike of one foot until the same heel contacts the ground again, defining the full cycle duration. This cyclical definition allows clinicians to compare timing of events consistently across different individuals. Stride length is similarly measured between successive heel strikes of the same foot.
questions.question: A complete gait cycle is best described as beginning and ending with which event?
options: Initial swing of the same foot
Heel strike of the same foot

questions.explanation: Cognitive learning theory considers both external factors like information and the internal thought process, viewing the learner as an information processor who absorbs, operates on, and stores knowledge. This contrasts with behaviorism, which focuses solely on observable stimulus-response patterns without regard to internal cognition. Cognitive theory emerged in the 1950s as a shift away from purely behaviorist explanations of learning.
questions.question: Cognitive learning theory differs from behaviorism primarily by emphasizing which additional factor in the learning process?
options: Passive reception of knowledge without processing
The learner's internal thought processing of information

questions.question: A patient cannot dorsiflex past neutral but compensates with circumduction and hip-hiking. Which approach best addresses the root cause?
questions.explanation: Hip hiking and circumduction are compensatory strategies for foot drop — not primary impairments. Clinical reasoning requires distinguishing the primary problem (dorsiflexion deficit) from the compensation. Effective rehabilitation addresses the underlying cause: restoring dorsiflexion through stretching or nerve recovery, and prescribing an ankle-foot orthosis to maintain dorsiflexion during swing if range cannot be restored. Training compensation strategies alone leaves the primary deficit unaddressed.
options: Practising circumduction for better limb clearance
Strengthening hip flexors to increase swing height
Restoring ankle dorsiflexion or prescribing an AFO
Fitting a platform walker for balance support

questions.question: Hemi-height wheelchairs are specifically designed to accommodate patients who require which propulsion method?
questions.explanation: Hemi-height wheelchairs have a lower seat-to-floor height of 17.5 inches or less, allowing patients to propel and control the chair using one leg placed on the ground. This design accommodates patients with hemiplegia who retain function in one lower limb. The lower seat height facilitates effective floor contact for foot-driven propulsion.
options: Propulsion using a powered joystick only
Propulsion and control using one leg
Propulsion using bilateral leg drive only

questions.question: A patient post-lumbar discectomy demonstrates excessive forward trunk lean throughout stance phase. Which primary muscular deficit most likely accounts for this?
options: Tibialis anterior weakness causing foot drop
Hip extensor or ankle plantarflexor weakness
questions.explanation: Forward trunk inclination during stance compensates for weakness in the hip extensors or ankle plantarflexors. When these muscles cannot maintain upright posture against body weight, the trunk leans forward to shift the centre of gravity anterior to the hip joint, reducing extensor demand. Clinical assessment should differentiate between these two muscle groups to direct targeted strengthening intervention.

options: Isolated quadriceps spasticity from pyramidal lesion
Hip flexor spasticity limiting terminal stance extension
Hip abductor weakness causing pelvic obliquity
questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy demonstrates excessive knee flexion throughout stance phase (crouch gait). Which primary deficit does this pattern most typically indicate?
questions.explanation: Crouch gait in cerebral palsy typically results from hamstring spasticity preventing full knee extension during stance, often combined with insufficient plantarflexor force to stabilise the knee passively. Gastrocnemius weakness or overlengthening from previous intervention can eliminate the plantarflexor contribution to knee stability. Careful gait analysis is required to differentiate primary spastic hamstrings from secondary crouch due to plantarflexor insufficiency.

questions.question: To distinguish true improvement from measurement error, which statistical concept must the gait outcome measure have established?
options: Concurrent validity with other gait measures
Face validity for patient acceptance assessment
Content validity confirmed by expert panel
questions.explanation: The Minimal Detectable Change (MDC) represents the smallest change in score that exceeds measurement error at a specified confidence level, distinguishing true change from measurement noise. Without knowing the MDC, a clinician cannot determine whether an improvement represents real recovery or random test-retest variation. Patient-specific changes must exceed the MDC threshold before being attributed to genuine functional improvement rather than measurement imprecision.

questions.question: The role of the patella as a pulley in the extensor mechanism means that its dysfunction would primarily impair which movement?
questions.explanation: Because the patella functions as a pulley redirecting quadriceps force to the patellar tendon and tibial tuberosity, any dysfunction in its position or tracking directly impairs efficient knee extension force transmission. This can manifest clinically as quadriceps lag, anterior knee pain, or instability during activities requiring knee extension. Restoring proper patellar alignment and tracking is therefore central to managing many knee pathomechanical disorders.

Motor imagery activates overlapping neural pathways — primary motor cortex, supplementary motor area, cerebellum — to those used in actual movement. This provides additional practice repetitions between physical sessions, accelerating engram formation and motor programme consolidation. Combined physical and mental practice shows superior outcomes to physical practice alone in stroke rehabilitation. Mental practice is clinically valuable when physical practice is limited by fatigue, pain, or access.
options: Mass practice produces stronger engrams than rest alone
Mental rehearsal activates similar neural pathways to physical practice
Physical repetition is the only effective training method
Mental imagery works only for upper extremity tasks
Mental practice is only useful in the cognitive learning stage
questions.question: A physiotherapist plans to use mental practice between physical gait training sessions. Which motor learning principle supports this approach?

questions.explanation: At C6 tetraplegia, patients retain wrist extension and some radial wrist flexion but lack hand grip and finger function. Knobbed or lugged hand rims provide contact surfaces that the hand can hook onto during the push stroke, enabling propulsion despite absent grip. Standard smooth hand rims cannot be effectively propelled without functional grip. This specific adaptation enables independence in manual wheelchair mobility, which is a key rehabilitation goal at the C6 level.
questions.question: A physiotherapist prescribes a wheelchair for a patient with C6 tetraplegia. Which specific feature enables independent manual propulsion at this level?
options: Standard hand rims with friction coating
Lugged or knobbed hand rims for grip

questions.explanation: Video recording uniquely enables repeated viewing of the same gait cycle, slow-motion analysis of rapid movements, frame-by-frame examination, goniometric measurement from frozen frames, and permanent records for comparison over time. These capabilities overcome fundamental limitations of real-time observation — human attention cannot process all joints simultaneously, and some deviations occur too rapidly for reliable live detection.
options: Enables repeated viewing and slow-motion examination
Replaces clinical reasoning with automatic analysis
Measures EMG muscle activation during each phase
Eliminates the need for clinical training entirely
questions.question: What advantage does video recording provide over real-time gait observation?

questions.explanation: Rigid frame wheelchairs lack the collapsing cross brace found in folding frame chairs, instead folding into a box shape by removing the back and wheels. Folding frame wheelchairs, in contrast, use a cross brace connecting the two side frames and fold vertically for storage. This structural distinction affects the chair's weight, rigidity, and ease of transport.
options: Inability to remove the back or wheels
Absence of a collapsing cross brace connecting the side frames
Requirement for a wider doorway to pass through
Folding vertically rather than into a box shape
Presence of a collapsing cross brace connecting the side frames
questions.question: A rigid frame wheelchair, compared to a folding frame wheelchair, is best distinguished by which structural feature?
Correct posture during crutch gait training requires attention to knee position primarily to avoid which complication?
questions.explanation: Care must be taken during crutch training to ensure the knees are not hyperextended, since correct posture requires the head erect, shoulders level, and hips and knees appropriately extended without locking. Hyperextension can strain posterior knee structures over repeated gait cycles. Postural muscle strength, particularly gluteus medius, is also essential for maintaining pelvic balance during weight transfer.

The handpiece of axillary crutches must be positioned to create 20–30 degrees of elbow flexion. This angle optimises force transmission through the arms, reduces fatigue, and allows effective push-down through the handpiece during weight bearing. It can be estimated as two to three finger widths below the anterior axillary fold. Excessive or insufficient elbow flexion impairs mechanical advantage and increases injury risk.
questions.question: When prescribing axillary crutches, which elbow angle should the handpiece create to ensure effective force transmission?

options: The olecranon tip, arm fully extended
The top surface of the shoulder
The wrist crease, arm extended overhead
The bottom of a 90-degree bent elbow
questions.explanation: Armrest height is measured from the sitting surface to the bottom of the elbow when flexed at 90 degrees, ensuring the armrest supports the forearm in a neutral, comfortable position. Correct armrest height promotes good postural alignment and reduces shoulder strain during prolonged sitting. This measurement complements back height and seat measurements in comprehensive wheelchair fitting.
questions.question: Armrest height for wheelchair measurement is determined from the sitting surface to which reference point?
Fine motor skills, as a type of coordination, are best exemplified by which activity?
options: Walking up a flight of stairs
questions.explanation: Fine motor skills require coordinated movement of small muscles such as those of the hands and face, exemplified by activities like writing, drawing, and buttoning a shirt. This differs from gross motor skills, which involve large muscle groups in activities such as walking or lifting. Hand-eye skills form a third category, coordinating visual input with hand movement.

questions.question: When measuring a patient for full-length axillary crutches, the measurement should be taken from the anterior axillary fold to which landmark?
questions.explanation: Full-length crutches are measured from the anterior fold of the axilla to the medial malleolus, allowing extra distance so the crutch top sits comfortably below the axilla during use. This measurement approach prevents excessive pressure on the axillary neurovascular structures. Using an incorrect measurement landmark can predispose the patient to nerve compression or poor postural alignment.

options: Cognitive demands of the home environment
questions.question: A patient's gait velocity is significantly higher on linoleum than on carpet at home. Which environmental factor best explains this discrepancy?
questions.explanation: Surface characteristics — compliance, traction, and irregularity — significantly affect gait performance. Carpet provides less stable, less predictable footing than linoleum, requiring more cautious stepping to maintain balance. Patients with balance deficits show greater speed reduction on carpet than neurologically intact individuals. This discrepancy highlights the importance of assessing gait in real-world environments and directing community training to include varied surfaces.

options: Front, back, and lateral views combined
Side view only for sagittal plane assessment
Back view only for posterior assessment
Overhead view for base of support assessment
Front view only for bilateral comparison
questions.question: During observational gait analysis, which combination of views allows assessment of all three planes of motion?
questions.explanation: Comprehensive gait assessment requires anterior, posterior, and bilateral lateral views. Frontal views reveal lateral trunk lean, pelvic obliquity, arm swing asymmetry, and base of support. Lateral views assess sagittal plane motion including trunk lean, knee flexion-extension, ankle motion, and limb clearance. No single plane captures all clinically relevant deviations; multi-plane observation is essential for thorough gait analysis.

questions.question: A patient completes 10 metres of walking in 15 seconds. Which community ambulation category does this place the patient in?
questions.explanation: 10 metres divided by 15 seconds equals 0.67 m/s. This speed falls between the household ambulation threshold (approximately 0.4 m/s) and full community ambulation threshold (approximately 1.0 m/s), indicating limited community ambulation capability. The patient can manage short community distances in controlled settings but will struggle with longer distances and challenging environments. This classification directly informs goal setting.

questions.question: A patient demonstrates a double tapping sound with foot contact during functional gait assessment. Which ataxic gait type does this most specifically indicate?
questions.explanation: The double tapping sound of sensory ataxia results from throwing the foot forward and landing heel first then toe, due to loss of proprioceptive feedback for controlled placement. Patients compensate by watching their feet constantly. This heel-toe double tap is pathognomonic for sensory ataxia from posterior column dysfunction. Cerebellar ataxia presents with irregular, wide steps but typically a single contact sound.
options: Frontal ataxia with magnetic gait pattern
Mixed ataxia with multiple combined deficits

questions.question: For restoration of optimal function, the science of physiotherapy requires knowledge of normal movement together with which other element?
questions.explanation: Restoring optimal function demands knowledge of normal movement, a qualitative and quantitative description of abnormal movement, and an understanding of its causes. Rating or grading the abnormality further completes the knowledge base of physiotherapy. Together these elements form the structured clinical reasoning process central to pathokinesiology.
options: Description and causes of abnormal movement

questions.question: Two-point crutch gait is most appropriately prescribed for a patient who demonstrates which combination of abilities?
questions.explanation: Two-point gait is prescribed when a patient cannot fully support weight on both legs but demonstrates good coordination and adequate arm strength, since it mimics a natural reciprocal walking pattern with alternating limb and crutch movement. This gait pattern requires more dynamic balance than the three or four point patterns. It is often used for patients with bilateral but partial lower limb weakness.
options: Limited leg weight-bearing but good coordination and arm strength
Bilateral upper limb paralysis with normal legs
Severe balance impairment needing maximal stability
Full weight-bearing on both legs unassisted
No usable upper limb strength at all

questions.explanation: Mobility assistive devices include wheelchairs, scooters, walkers, canes, crutches, and lower limb orthoses such as calipers, all designed to enhance movement for people with physical disabilities. This differs from hearing aids, which address auditory impairment, or classroom tools like page-turners, which support educational participation. Correct categorization helps clinicians match device type to specific functional need.
questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a mobility-type assistive device ?
A patient demonstrates hip hiking on the right during right swing phase. Which primary deficit should the physiotherapist investigate as the underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Hip hiking (elevating the pelvis on the swing side) is a compensation for inadequate ground clearance during right swing phase. The therapist must identify which mechanism impairs clearance: ankle dorsiflexor weakness (foot drop), insufficient knee flexion, inadequate hip flexion, or leg length discrepancy. Hip hiking is the compensation; the underlying cause must be identified for effective treatment.
options: Right hip abductor weakness in stance

questions.question: Anti-tippers, as a wheelchair component, are specifically designed to prevent which occurrence?
questions.explanation: Anti-tippers are extensions of the lower rail installed on the rear wheels to prevent posterior tipping of at-risk patients, such as those with impaired trunk control or high-level spinal cord injury. This safety feature is particularly important during activities that shift the center of gravity backward, such as ascending ramps. Along with wheel locks, anti-tippers form part of the safety components of a well-fitted wheelchair.
options: Loss of seat cushion pressure over time
Lateral wheel slippage on wet surfaces
The lateral epicondyle of the femur
questions.question: The Q-angle is measured using landmarks that include the anterior superior iliac spine, the center of the patella, and which third landmark?
questions.explanation: The Q-angle is measured as the angle formed by a line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the center of the patella, and a second line from the patella center to the tip of the tibial tuberosity, typically using a goniometer. This three-point measurement captures the combined influence of pelvic width, femoral alignment, and tibial position on patellar tracking forces. Standardized landmark identification is essential for reliable Q-angle measurement.

A telemetry system for measuring ground foot force allows wireless or remote capture of forces generated during gait or standing without restricting natural movement. This differs from goniometers, which measure joint angles rather than reaction forces. Telemetry exemplifies how pathokinesiology incorporates advanced instrumentation for objective movement analysis.
questions.question: Which instrument listed among pathokinesiological measurement tools is specifically used to measure ground foot force via remote sensing?

options: Decreasing prosthetic heel height to reduce knee extension
Widening the base of the prosthetic foot
Increasing dorsiflexion resistance in the prosthetic ankle
Shortening the prosthetic limb by one centimetre
Increasing prosthetic heel height to raise the socket
questions.question: A patient post-amputation walks with excessive lumbar lordosis and knee hyperextension during stance. The cause is identified as excessive prosthetic heel height. Which modification addresses this?
questions.explanation: Excessive prosthetic heel height creates a position of relative knee extension during midstance by pushing the tibia backward, producing the observed knee hyperextension and compensatory lumbar lordosis. Reducing the heel height repositions the foot-shank relationship, allowing the tibia to advance normally during stance and relieving the recurvatum tendency. Prosthetic alignment modifications are the primary approach to gait deviation correction before considering component changes.

options: Increased plantarflexion elevating pelvis for clearance
Increased knee flexion during loading response
questions.explanation: When a limb has a knee flexion contracture, the contralateral limb must elevate the pelvis through increased plantarflexion to allow the stiff contractured limb to clear the ground during its swing phase. This compensatory plantarflexion acts as vaulting on the uninvolved side and is a hallmark of arthrogenic gait that the physiotherapist must identify during systematic observational analysis.
questions.question: A patient with a 30-degree knee flexion contracture is referred for gait analysis. Which compensatory mechanism in the contralateral limb would you expect during stance?

options: Objective strength, balance, and safety are demonstrated
A fixed time period of six weeks elapses
Insurance coverage for the device expires
The therapist believes the patient appears ready
questions.question: A patient achieved independent community ambulation using a single-point cane. What criteria must be met before cane abandonment?
questions.explanation: Assistive device discontinuation requires objective demonstration of adequate strength, balance, endurance, and safety for independent ambulation in all intended environments without the device. Subjective reports, elapsed time, or insurance limitations are insufficient criteria. Objective measures such as the Timed Up and Go, 10-Metre Walk Test, and Berg Balance Scale provide appropriate benchmarks for safe and evidence-based device progression.

options: Every point shifts equally in one direction
Direction of movement reverses periodically over time
Points rotate about a fixed axis
questions.question: Translatory motion is characterized chiefly by which feature of the moving body?
questions.explanation: In translatory, or linear, motion every point of the moving object travels the same direction and distance with no change in orientation. A sliding block on an incline is a classic example since each particle experiences identical displacement. This contrasts with rotatory motion where points sweep different arc lengths about an axis.

The parapodium's defining advantage over traditional standing braces is that children can sit while wearing the device, enabling movement between standing and seated positions without removal. Conventional standing braces are fixed frames requiring removal for sitting. The sit-down capability significantly increases the parapodium's functional utility in classroom and daily life settings.
options: The child can sit while wearing the device
Allows full weight bearing through crutches only
questions.question: A child with spina bifida is fitted with a parapodium. Which feature most distinguishes this device from conventional standing braces?
When documenting gait analysis findings in a patient's clinical record, which elements are most critical?
options: Subjective patient impressions and feelings about gait
Objective measurements, deviations, analysis, and plan
Bilateral shoe wear patterns and footwear type
Insurance authorisation codes and billing information
Therapist experience level and training background
questions.explanation: Comprehensive gait documentation records objective measurements (speed, cadence, stride length), specific deviations observed by phase and segment, analysis of underlying causes versus compensatory patterns, and the resulting treatment plan. This format allows meaningful comparison over time, guides intervention decisions, facilitates team communication, and demonstrates clinical reasoning for professional documentation standards.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the five theories of motor learning identified in the course material?
questions.explanation: The five identified theories of motor learning are behaviorism, cognitive, constructivism, humanism, and connectivism learning theories. Constructivism specifically holds that the learner builds upon previous experience and understanding to construct new knowledge through active engagement. Each theory offers a different lens for designing therapeutic motor learning interventions.

options: Inability to sense limb position without visual guidance
questions.explanation: Frenkel exercises are designed to help patients compensate for the inability to sense where their arms and legs are positioned in space without looking, a deficit commonly seen in ataxic conditions. These exercises are explicitly intended for coordination training rather than strengthening. Commands are given slowly and evenly, with exercises performed to counting in a well-lit environment.
questions.question: Frenkel exercises were specifically designed to address which functional deficit?

questions.explanation: Hemi-height wheelchairs feature seat-to-floor heights of 17.5 inches or less compared to the standard 19.5 inches, enabling patients to reach the floor comfortably with one or both feet for propulsion. This is particularly beneficial for hemiplegic patients who use foot propulsion on the less affected side. The lower height facilitates a more natural foot contact pattern and reduces energy expenditure during self-propulsion.
questions.question: During wheelchair prescription for a hemiplegic patient, which wheelchair type allows foot-driven propulsion at a lower seat height?

questions.explanation: The logical gait training progression moves from maximum support in parallel bars to an appropriate assistive device based on demonstrated improvements in strength, balance, and weight-bearing tolerance. Advancing prematurely to community ambulation or stairs without intermediate device training creates safety risk. The parallel bars to assistive device transition bridges supported and more independent ambulation effectively.
questions.question: A physiotherapist begins gait training with a post-operative hip patient in parallel bars. When parallel bar goals are achieved, what is the correct next step?
options: Progress to an appropriate assistive device
Return to bed rest for consolidation
Commence stair training without a device
Preventing axillary nerve injury from crutch pressure
Advancing the crutches forward during swing phase
Supporting full body weight through the crutches
Controlling trunk sway during double limb support
Maintaining crutch tip contact on uneven ground
questions.question: During preparation for gait training, a physiotherapist strengthens shoulder depressors before axillary crutch instruction. What specific functional demand necessitates this?
questions.explanation: Shoulder depressors contract to lower the shoulder girdle, transferring body weight through the arms and crutches. When a patient uses crutches for full weight bearing, these muscles must isometrically support the entire body weight. Without adequate shoulder depressor strength, the patient cannot effectively unload the lower extremities or maintain stable crutch contact. This preparatory strengthening is a mandatory pre-crutch training requirement.

options: Bilateral forearm crutches for upper extremity use
Walker for four-point broad base support
questions.question: A physiotherapist selects a device for a patient with severe bilateral lower extremity weakness and impaired balance. Which provides maximum stability?
questions.explanation: Walkers provide maximum stability among ambulatory assistive devices through four-point contact, a wide base of support, and bilateral upper extremity loading. For patients with severe bilateral weakness and impaired balance, walkers offer the most secure platform for safe ambulation. While walkers sacrifice some manoeuvring ability, their stability advantage is critical for patients at high fall risk who require maximum support.

The course material lists physical and biosciences together with liberal arts and communication skills as qualifying prerequisites underpinning pathokinesiology. Communication skills support patient interaction and interdisciplinary collaboration, while biosciences supply the scientific grounding. Together these prerequisites prepare students for the analytical and interpersonal demands of clinical practice.
questions.question: Which qualifying prerequisite area is identified as essential preparation for the foundation of pathokinesiology alongside biosciences?

questions.explanation: Backward walking recruits hip and knee extensors eccentrically in patterns distinct from forward gait, providing therapeutic variation that may reduce anterior knee pain. Research indicates backward walking reduces patellofemoral compressive forces while still activating quadriceps, making it valuable in patellofemoral and post-surgical knee rehabilitation. The novel movement challenge also stimulates neuroplastic adaptations not achieved through forward walking alone.
questions.question: A physiotherapist includes backward walking training in a knee rehabilitation programme. What specific therapeutic benefit justifies this?
options: Eccentrically loading knee extensors in different patterns
Reducing fall risk from postural sway
Strengthening hip flexors for swing phase

questions.explanation: Disorder is defined as a medical condition involving disturbance to the usual functioning of the mind or body, distinct from movement itself which is simply a change of location or position. Combining the two terms yields movement disorder, an abnormal disturbance of motion. This distinction underlies why pathokinesiology studies disordered rather than normal motion alone.
questions.question: In the definition of movement disorder, the word disorder specifically refers to which concept?
options: A disturbance of usual body or mind function

questions.question: A tilt-in-space wheelchair frame configuration allows which specific functional adjustment?
options: The armrests fold flat against the frame
The footrests swing away completely from the frame
The rear wheels detach for transport only
The seat width increases without changing depth
The seat orients backward while maintaining body alignment
questions.explanation: A tilt-in-space configuration allows the seat frame to orient backward relative to the wheelchair frame while maintaining the patient's body alignment and joint angles, unlike a reclining back which changes the seat-to-back angle. This feature is useful for pressure redistribution and postural management in patients unable to independently shift weight. It differs functionally from a recliner wheelchair, which instead opens the hip angle by reclining the backrest.

questions.question: During Frenkel exercises, patients are instructed to perform each exercise how many times before resting to avoid fatigue?
questions.explanation: Frenkel exercises should be performed not more than four times per exercise, with rest between each to avoid fatigue, since fatigue undermines the precise sensory-motor learning these exercises target. The complete routine takes approximately half an hour and is typically performed twice daily. Exercises are kept within normal range of motion to avoid overstretching muscles during training.

questions.question: Electrogoniometry is classified among pathokinesiological tools primarily for measuring which parameter?
questions.explanation: Electrogoniometers, or Elgons, are mobility measurement instruments that record dynamic joint angles throughout a movement cycle, unlike conventional goniometers that capture single static positions. They belong to the broader group of pathokinesiological measurement tools alongside inclinometers and flexiometers. Such continuous data is valuable for analyzing gait and other repetitive movements.

options: Whether muscle tone is normal, low, or absent
questions.question: Before recommending a wheelchair, assessing the patient's neurological status specifically evaluates which characteristic?
questions.explanation: Neurological status assessment for wheelchair selection specifically evaluates whether the patient has normal, low, or no muscular tone, since tone abnormalities significantly influence seating and positioning needs. This assessment works alongside evaluation of orthopaedic status, sensation, and functional status to build a complete clinical picture. Tone abnormalities may necessitate specialized seating inserts or postural supports within the wheelchair.

options: Pelvis hiked, level, or dropped assessment
questions.explanation: Gait analysis specifically evaluates whether the pelvis is hiked, level, dropped, or fixed during walking, which directly relates to hip abductor strength, notably gluteus medius function. A dropped pelvis on the swing side is characteristic of a positive Trendelenburg sign. This observation forms part of a systematic checklist used when analyzing pathological gaits.
questions.question: A gait pattern in which the pelvis drops excessively on the swing side due to hip abductor weakness is best described using which observational term from gait analysis?

options: Complete immobilization of the knee joint
Quadriceps isometric exercise emphasizing vastus medialis
questions.question: Which conservative management strategy is specifically listed for reducing an excessive Q-angle?
questions.explanation: Management for reducing an excessive Q-angle includes custom-made functional orthoses and quadriceps isometric strengthening exercises with specific emphasis on the vastus medialis. Strengthening this muscle helps counteract the lateral pull on the patella by improving medial stabilization. Surgery is reserved as a further option when conservative measures prove insufficient.

questions.question: Three-point crutch gait is indicated for a patient presenting with which clinical pattern?
questions.explanation: Three-point gait is used when a patient cannot support weight on one leg but has normal strength in both upper limbs, the trunk, and the unaffected leg. The affected leg is kept off the floor while weight is shared between the crutches and the sound leg. This pattern is common after unilateral lower limb injury or surgery requiring non-weight-bearing precautions.
options: Inability to bear weight on both legs equally
Normal strength present in all four limbs
Complete paralysis of both lower limbs
One weak leg but normal arms and other leg

questions.question: A physiotherapist finds 15 degrees of dorsiflexion available but the patient presents with an equinus gait pattern. Which finding best distinguishes spastic from structural contracture cause?
options: Absent ankle jerk reflex on clinical examination
Better dorsiflexion when the knee is flexed
Range of motion improving with slow passive stretch
Equinus worsening with increased walking speed
Presence of ankle clonus on rapid dorsiflexion
questions.explanation: Ankle clonus — repetitive rhythmic oscillation triggered by rapid passive dorsiflexion — is a hallmark of upper motor neuron spasticity indicating CNS origin of the equinus. Its presence confirms neurologically mediated plantarflexion rather than a fixed structural contracture. This differentiation is clinically crucial: spastic equinus responds to antispastics or botulinum toxin, while structural contracture requires serial casting or surgical lengthening procedures.

options: Frenkel coordination exercises using visual feedback
Vestibular rehabilitation with head movement exercises
Speed training on varied surfaces outdoors
Strength training for proximal hip muscles
Balance board training with eyes closed exclusively
questions.explanation: The clinical picture — wide-based gait, floor watching, inability to walk without vision — describes sensory ataxia from peripheral neuropathy causing proprioceptive loss. Frenkel exercises were specifically designed to retrain coordination when proprioception is impaired by substituting visual feedback. Patients watch limb movements during structured, precise exercises to compensate for absent joint position sense, directly addressing the underlying mechanism.
questions.question: An elderly patient with diabetes presents with wide-based irregular gait, floor-watching, and inability to walk in the dark. Which intervention directly addresses the underlying mechanism?
The quadriceps angle, or Q-angle, is best defined as the angle formed between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The Q-angle is defined as the angle formed by the vector for the combined pull of the quadriceps muscle, primarily the rectus femoris, and the line of pull of the patellar tendon. It represents a key measure of patellofemoral biomechanics relevant to lateral patellar tracking forces. Alterations in this angle directly influence the lateral force exerted on the patella during knee extension.
options: The quadriceps muscle pull and the patellar tendon
The patella and the femoral condyle surface

questions.question: Cadence in gait analysis specifically refers to which measurable parameter?
questions.explanation: Cadence is defined as the number of steps completed per unit of time, typically expressed as steps per minute. It is one of several descriptive parameters used alongside speed and stride length to characterize an individual's walking pattern. Changes in cadence often accompany alterations in overall walking speed.
options: Duration of the swing phase alone
Angle of hip flexion at heel strike
Velocity of the center of gravity
Number of steps completed per unit time

questions.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease freezes at a doorway during gait training. Which cueing strategy most directly exploits motor learning principles?
questions.explanation: External visual cues such as floor markers exploit intact visual processing to bypass the impaired basal ganglia motor initiation responsible for freezing. The visual target provides an attentional focus and rhythm cue, activating alternative cortical motor pathways. This evidence-based strategy directly applies motor learning principles — task-specific practice with appropriate external feedback — to improve gait initiation.
options: Asking the patient to rest before proceeding
Providing manual resistance at the pelvis
Practising backward walking on flat surfaces
Using visual floor markers as stepping targets

questions.question: A force plate is primarily included among pathokinesiological measurement tools because it quantifies which variable?
questions.explanation: A force plate, sometimes paired with telemetry systems, records ground foot force generated during standing or gait. This objective kinetic data complements kinematic measures like goniometry to give a full picture of movement quality. Such instrumentation supports the scientific, measurable foundation that pathokinesiology requires.

options: Diurnal variation in motivation affecting performance
Uhthoff's phenomenon from heat-related neurological worsening
Spasticity increasing with daily warming temperatures
Psychological anxiety causing afternoon performance decline
Normal fatigue from daily activities after meals
questions.explanation: Uhthoff's phenomenon describes temporary worsening of neurological symptoms in multiple sclerosis with increased core body temperature, commonly occurring with physical activity or later in the day after cumulative activity-related heat. This should prompt scheduling intensive rehabilitation sessions earlier in the day when core temperature is lower and neurological function is preserved. Cooling strategies during rehabilitation may also extend effective training time.
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis whose gait is significantly worse in afternoon sessions demonstrates which phenomenon?

options: Active engagement building upon prior experience
questions.question: Constructivism learning theory holds that the learner acquires new understanding primarily through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Constructivism holds that learners build upon previous experience and understanding to construct new knowledge through active engagement, such as experiments or real-world problem solving. This contrasts with the passive view of teaching where the learner is treated as an empty vessel to be filled with knowledge. Applying constructivism in rehabilitation might involve patient-led problem solving during functional task practice.

options: A sensory receptor for joint position
A ligamentous restraint against varus stress
A pulley increasing quadriceps mechanical advantage
A shock absorber for axial loading
questions.explanation: The patella functions as a pulley that increases the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps muscle during knee extension, redirecting the line of pull over the femoral condyles. This pulley mechanism is essential for efficient force transmission from the quadriceps to the tibial tuberosity via the patellar tendon. Disruption of this mechanism, as in patella alta or baja, can significantly impair extensor efficiency.
questions.question: The patella functions biomechanically within the knee extensor mechanism primarily as which of the following?

questions.explanation: Regular wheelchair maintenance includes checking tire pressure, inspecting for worn cushions or padding, and tightening nuts, bolts, and screws weekly to prevent equipment failure. Keeping the chair clean also helps identify developing problems early. These simple self-maintenance tasks reduce the risk of unexpected breakdowns that could inconvenience or endanger the user.
questions.question: Regular self-maintenance tasks recommended for all wheelchair users include which of the following?
options: Disassembling the motor for inspection weekly
Repainting the wheelchair every six months
Removing the wheels for storage nightly
Checking tire pressure and tightening loose screws

questions.question: A patient's tandem walking is severely impaired while standard gait appears adequate. Which aspect of gait control does tandem walking specifically challenge?
options: Hip flexion strength for swing phase advancement
Mediolateral balance in a narrow base
Quadriceps endurance for prolonged stance phase
questions.explanation: Tandem walking reduces the base of support to nearly zero width, maximally challenging mediolateral balance control. This extreme narrowing reveals balance impairments not apparent during normal-width gait where a wider base accommodates moderate instability. Cerebellar dysfunction, peripheral vestibular disorders, and proprioceptive loss commonly impair tandem walking before causing obvious abnormality in standard gait, making it a sensitive screen for subtle balance disorders.

Behaviorism learning theory is concerned only with observable stimulus-response behaviors that can be studied systematically, applying drilled routines and positive reinforcement to build learning. This contrasts with cognitive learning theory, which emphasizes internal thought processes alongside external information. Behaviorist applications in therapy might include repetitive drills paired with positive feedback for correct performance.
questions.question: Behaviorism learning theory, as applied to motor learning, is primarily concerned with which type of phenomena?

questions.explanation: Pelvic rotation, together with pelvic tilt, knee flexion in stance, and foot and ankle mechanisms, is identified as a classic determinant of gait that smooths the pathway of the center of gravity. These determinants collectively minimize the energy cost of walking by reducing vertical and lateral displacement. Loss of any determinant can increase energy expenditure and produce visible gait deviations.
questions.question: Which pelvic movement is listed among the classic determinants of gait that reduce vertical excursion of the center of gravity?
Festinating gait, characterized by short shuffling accelerating steps, is most typically associated with which neurologic condition?
questions.explanation: Festinating gait is specifically linked to Parkinsonian pathology, presenting as small shuffling steps with progressive acceleration and difficulty initiating or stopping movement. This differs from ataxic or cerebellar gait, which shows a wide-based, unsteady pattern rather than festination. Recognizing this pattern helps differentiate basal ganglia dysfunction from cerebellar disease.

options: Right hip extensor weakness from gluteus maximus
Left quadriceps weakness in swing preparation
Right tibialis anterior weakness causing foot drop
Bilateral hamstring weakness during terminal swing
Right hip abductor weakness from gluteus medius
questions.explanation: Trunk shifting toward the right stance limb during right single-limb support is the classic compensation for right gluteus medius weakness — Trendelenburg compensation. Moving the trunk over the stance hip reduces the lever arm and moment demand on the weak abductors, preventing the pelvis from dropping. This identifies the right gluteus medius as the primary target for progressive strengthening interventions.
questions.question: During gait training in parallel bars, the therapist observes heavy trunk shift to the right during right single-limb stance. Which muscle weakness requires targeted intervention?

options: Mild balance impairment needing supervision only
Normal upper limb strength with no impairment
Unable to propel a manual chair due to weakness
Temporary mobility need after minor injury
Preference for outdoor recreational use only
questions.question: Power wheelchairs are primarily indicated for patients who present with which characteristic?
questions.explanation: Power wheelchairs help patients who are unable to propel a manual wheelchair due to physical weakness, lack of endurance, or a need for constant movement throughout the day. They consist of a powered base, motor, batteries, and a control device operated by the user to direct movement. Some powered wheelchairs also allow control of tilt, leg-rest position, and communication devices.

questions.question: Ambulatory assistive devices are prescribed primarily to achieve which combination of functional goals?
questions.explanation: Ambulatory assistive devices such as canes, crutches, and walkers are prescribed to improve balance and stability, reduce lower limb pain, and provide sensory feedback while assisting acceleration during locomotion. These functional goals directly address common impairments seen in orthopaedic and neurological patients. Device selection should always align with which of these specific functional goals is most relevant to the patient.
options: Improve balance and reduce lower limb pain
Increase muscle mass and bone density
Provide permanent immobilization of the limb
Replace the need for surgical intervention
Eliminate the need for gait training

questions.question: A physiotherapist has a patient practise crossing a road at a pedestrian signal. What gait parameter does this primarily train?
questions.explanation: Road crossing training specifically addresses the requirement to walk sufficient distance within a fixed time — the pedestrian signal countdown. This targets speed maintenance over a required distance, a specific community ambulation demand not arising in clinic-based training. Failure to achieve adequate speed within signal time creates significant fall risk and community participation barriers, making this task-specific training essential for community integration.
options: Speed maintenance over specific timed distances
Backward walking on uneven pavement surfaces
Energy conservation through reduced step count

questions.question: Vertical oscillation of the center of gravity during gait reaches its lowest point at which phase of the cycle?
questions.explanation: The center of gravity oscillates twice per gait cycle, reaching its highest point at mid-stance and its lowest point during double support. This oscillation typically ranges from 2 to 5 centimeters depending on stride length and walking speed. Excessive oscillation can indicate compensatory or pathological gait patterns requiring further evaluation.

The pelvis remains relatively level in the sagittal plane during gait, showing only a small mean excursion of approximately 3 degrees. This relative stability of the pelvis contrasts with the larger angular excursions seen at the hip, knee, and ankle joints. Minimal pelvic excursion helps conserve energy by limiting unnecessary trunk movement during walking.
questions.question: The pelvis in the sagittal plane during normal gait shows a mean excursion of approximately how many degrees?

options: Right quadriceps femoris during loading response
Right hamstrings failing to control extension
Right tibialis anterior during heel strike
Right hip abductors during single support phase
questions.explanation: Hamstring weakness allows the knee to snap into hyperextension during terminal swing and stance as the muscles fail to control the decelerating limb. The absent eccentric hamstring control allows knee extension to proceed beyond neutral into genu recurvatum. This must be differentiated from quadriceps spasticity and plantarflexor contracture, which can also push the knee into recurvatum through different mechanisms.
questions.question: During stance phase assessment, the patient's knee hyperextends into genu recurvatum on the right. Which muscle group weakness most commonly produces this sign?

questions.explanation: Perry's classification orders stance phase sub-phases as initial contact, loading response, mid-stance, terminal stance, and pre-swing. Loading response directly follows initial contact and represents the period of weight acceptance onto the limb. This detailed sub-classification allows precise description of both normal and pathological gait patterns.
questions.question: According to Perry's functional classification, which sub-phase immediately follows initial contact within the stance phase?

questions.explanation: The flexiometer is grouped with inclinometers and goniometers under mobility measurement equipment used to quantify joint motion. It differs from pain rating instruments such as the visual analogue scale, which assess subjective symptom intensity rather than physical movement. Correct categorization helps clinicians select the right tool for a given pathokinesiological assessment.
questions.question: A flexiometer would most appropriately be classified under which category of pathokinesiological measurement?

options: Directly touching the feet with no gap
At least 12 inches away from the feet
About 4 inches away, angled slightly outward
Positioned in front of the toes only
questions.explanation: When standing, crutches should be held at a slight outward angle from the body and positioned about 4 inches away from the feet, providing a stable base of support. This positioning balances stability with ease of movement during the gait cycle. Incorrect crutch placement can compromise balance and increase fall risk.
questions.question: When a patient is standing with crutches, they should be positioned at what approximate distance from the feet?

options: Keeping the load close to the body centre
Twisting through the trunk during the transfer
Using a wide base of support throughout
Maintaining natural spinal curves with bent knees
questions.explanation: Safe transfer technique requires maintaining natural spinal curvature and bending through the knees, not flexing the trunk forward at the waist. Forward trunk bending dramatically increases compressive and shear forces on lumbar discs and places erector spinae in a mechanically disadvantaged position. Bent-knee lifting keeps the spine in a protected neutral curve while using the stronger quadriceps and gluteals to perform the work.
questions.question: A caregiver bent forward at the waist throughout a patient transfer from wheelchair to bed. Which body mechanics principle was violated?

options: Left hand, opposite to the painful hip
Either hand based on patient comfort
Both hands using a bilateral cane
Right hand, same side as the painful hip
Alternating hands with each step taken
questions.explanation: The cane is held in the hand contralateral to the involved limb to distribute weight away from the painful side. During right stance phase, the left-held cane bears weight simultaneously, reducing load on the arthritic right hip. This mirrors the normal reciprocal pattern of arm-leg movement. Holding the cane ipsilaterally would not effectively reduce joint load and may worsen gait mechanics.
questions.question: A physiotherapist prescribes a cane for a patient with right hip osteoarthritis. In which hand should the cane be held?
During discharge planning for a patient who completed gait rehabilitation, which information is most essential for the referring physician?
questions.explanation: Professional discharge documentation must include objective gait parameters at discharge (velocity, distance, device used, observed deviations), functional goals achieved and those still outstanding, remaining impairments, ongoing rehabilitation needs, equipment or home modification recommendations, and follow-up plans. This provides the referring physician with actionable clinical information enabling appropriate ongoing medical management.
options: The physiotherapist's personal opinion of patient motivation
The number of physiotherapy sessions attended only
Financial cost of rehabilitation to the health service
Comparison to other patients with similar diagnoses
Objective gait parameters, goals achieved, and recommendations

questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the three sub-phases of the swing phase according to Perry's classification?
questions.explanation: Perry's functional classification divides the swing phase into initial swing, mid-swing, and terminal swing. This complements the five stance sub-phases, giving a total of eight functionally distinct gait events. Recognizing these sub-phases helps clinicians pinpoint where pathological deviations occur during walking.

options: Assess the cognitive, physical, and perceptual status of the patient
Select a powered wheelchair by default
Consult only the patient's family without clinical assessment
Purchase the most expensive model available
Immediately measure the patient for wheelchair dimensions
questions.question: The first step recommended in the process of selecting an appropriate wheelchair is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Principles of selecting an appropriate wheelchair begin with assessing the patient's cognitive, physical, and perceptual status, followed by discussing transportation and housing, evaluating sitting and mobility, and finally measuring the patient for the wheelchair. This sequential approach ensures the selected device matches the patient's overall functional context, not just body dimensions. Skipping early assessment steps risks prescribing a chair unsuitable for the patient's home or cognitive capacity.

options: Gross motor skills involving large muscle groups
Motor learning at the associative learning stage
Fine motor skills involving small hand muscles
Gross motor skills involving upper extremity function
Locomotor skills including walking and running
questions.explanation: Handwriting requires precise coordination of small muscles in the hand and fingers — fine motor skills. The ability to perform gross motor activities independently while struggling with fine motor tasks reflects the distinct neurological demands of these two skill categories. In cerebral palsy, fine motor impairment may persist even when gross motor function improves, requiring specifically targeted fine motor intervention programmes.
questions.question: A patient with cerebral palsy can perform gross motor skills independently but struggles with handwriting. Which motor skill category is impaired?

questions.explanation: Object-interaction skills include prehension activities such as reaching, grasping, throwing, catching, kicking, trapping, dribbling, and striking. These are distinct from locomotion skills, which involve moving the body through space, and postural skills, which involve maintaining balance. Correctly classifying a task supports targeted rehabilitation planning based on the specific skill domain impaired.
questions.question: Object-interaction skills within the motor skill classification would most appropriately include which activity?

questions.explanation: In spastic hemiplegia, hamstrings typically show abnormal prolonged activation during midswing, where they should be relatively quiet allowing free limb advancement. Excessive hamstring tone during swing phase resists knee extension and hip flexion, contributing to stiff-legged gait. EMG objectively identifies this pathological timing, differentiating it from weakness and guiding decisions about orthotics, botulinum toxin, or surgical intervention.
questions.question: In a patient with spastic hemiplegia, electromyography would most likely detect prolonged hamstring activation during which gait phase?
options: Midswing phase when the limb advances
The capacity to sense joint position
The strength generated by a muscle group
The ability to initiate, maintain, or stop an activity
The storage of movement patterns in memory
questions.explanation: Volition is defined as the ability to initiate, maintain, or stop an activity or motion, representing a fundamental component of coordinated movement. It works alongside perception and engram formation to produce smooth, purposeful motor output. Impairment of volition, as seen in some neurological conditions, can significantly disrupt coordinated movement despite intact muscle strength.
questions.question: Volition, as a component of coordinated movement, is best defined as which ability?

questions.explanation: Steppage gait results from dorsiflexor weakness causing foot drop, requiring excessive hip flexion to lift the foot clear during swing phase. Ankle dorsiflexion is primarily an L4–L5 function, with L5 specifically providing motor supply to tibialis anterior. L5 radiculopathy from disc herniation causes weakness in the common peroneal nerve distribution, including tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus, producing foot drop and steppage gait.
questions.question: A patient with L5 radiculopathy is observed using a high-stepping gait pattern. Which nerve root deficit produces this steppage gait?

questions.explanation: Wheelchair armrests help the patient with balance, posture, control, and alignment, and are typically padded for comfort with padding extending the length of the armrest. Armrests can vary in length and may be height-adjustable or removable to facilitate transfers. Their design directly influences a patient's postural stability and ease of performing functional tasks while seated.
questions.question: The armrest of a wheelchair primarily assists the patient with which combination of functions?
Kinematic analysis of locomotion is conducted objectively by recording the movement of which type of anatomical reference points?
questions.explanation: Kinematics of locomotion is studied by recording movement of surface landmarks such as the head summit, iliac crest, and joint centres along bone long axes. Projecting these landmarks onto sagittal, frontal, and horizontal planes yields a three-dimensional movement record. This approach allows objective quantification of joint motion during walking without invasive measurement.

questions.question: Which term best describes the scientific study of human movement as it relates to abnormal conditions affecting posture and movement?
questions.explanation: Pathokinesiology specifically merges the study of disease processes (patho) with movement science (kinesiology). It examines how trauma, disease, or congenital defects alter normal movement and posture. Plain kinesiology, by contrast, studies movement without reference to pathology.

Full-length crutches must be gripped firmly to the body by the adductor muscles of the shoulder rather than by pressing the crutch top up into the axilla, which risks neurovascular compression. This technique protects the brachial plexus and axillary vessels from sustained pressure injury. Proper technique instruction is therefore a critical safety component of crutch training.
questions.question: Full-length crutches should be gripped firmly against the body using which muscle action, rather than pressing upward into the axilla?

options: 0.3 m/s indicating severe community ambulation limitation
0.6 m/s indicating moderate limitation in community
questions.explanation: 10 metres divided by 25 seconds equals 0.4 m/s. This speed corresponds to the boundary of household ambulation, indicating the patient can manage basic indoor mobility but faces severe restrictions in community settings. Speeds below 0.4 m/s indicate primarily therapeutic or household ambulation. This finding warrants intensive gait rehabilitation targeting speed improvement alongside balance and endurance to progress toward limited community ambulation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing an elderly patient records a 10-metre Walk Test time of 25 seconds. Converting this to a velocity, which statement is most clinically accurate?

questions.explanation: Lateral pelvic displacement is one of the determinants of gait that works together with pelvic and knee motion to keep the center of gravity's pathway smooth and energy-efficient. Excessive or absent lateral displacement can indicate compensatory strategies or musculoskeletal weakness. This determinant is closely observed during clinical gait analysis for signs of pathology.
questions.question: Lateral displacement of the pelvis during normal gait primarily serves which biomechanical purpose?
options: Eliminating the need for ankle dorsiflexion
Preventing knee flexion at heel strike
Minimizing side-to-side displacement of the center of gravity

questions.explanation: Device progression requires objective demonstration of improved strength, balance, endurance, and weight-bearing tolerance before advancing to less supportive devices. Progression based on time elapsed, patient preference, or administrative convenience without functional criteria creates fall risk. Specific benchmarks — adequate hip abductor and knee extensor strength, balance on a single limb — must be met and documented before transitioning to the less stable forearm crutch.
questions.question: When assessing readiness for device progression from a walker to forearm crutches, which parameter is most important?
options: Time elapsed since the initial assessment
Insurance approval for the new device
Improved strength, balance, and weight-bearing tolerance
Availability of crutches in the physiotherapy department

questions.question: In a perfect translatory motion, which statement correctly describes the velocity of different points on the moving body?
options: Only the leading edge has measurable velocity
Velocity varies according to distance from the axis
Every point experiences the same velocity at all instances
Distal points move faster than proximal points
Velocity is zero throughout the motion
questions.explanation: During perfect translatory motion, each point of the body experiences identical velocity at every instant because there is no rotation or change in orientation. This uniformity distinguishes translation from rotation, where velocity varies with distance from the axis of rotation. Recognizing this distinction is fundamental to analyzing complex human movements that blend both motion types.

questions.question: According to the foundational comparison drawn in the course material, pathokinesiology serves physiotherapy in the same way which discipline serves medicine?
questions.explanation: Pathology, the study of disease processes following trauma or malfunction, is described as the knowledge base of medicine and surgery. Pathokinesiology occupies an analogous foundational role for physiotherapy, explaining abnormal movement following disease, trauma, or congenital defect. This parallel justifies treating pathokinesiology as the core science underpinning physiotherapy practice.

questions.question: The swing phase knee flexion of approximately 70 degrees is primarily required to achieve which functional outcome?
options: Control of lateral pelvic tilt motion
Stabilization of the limb during double support
Foot clearance from the floor during swing
Generation of propulsive force at push-off
questions.explanation: Approximately 70 degrees of knee flexion during swing phase is necessary to shorten the effective limb length and clear the foot from the floor as it advances forward. Without adequate swing phase flexion, patients may exhibit compensatory strategies such as hip hiking or circumduction. This flexion angle represents the second of the two knee flexion cycles occurring per gait cycle.

questions.question: A patient notes severe knee pain on hills but pain-free gait on flat ground. Which training element should be prioritised in community ambulation training?
questions.explanation: The principle of task-specific training requires practising the exact activities causing functional limitation. Since hills provoke pain, progressive inclined surface training — starting at minimal gradient and systematically increasing slope — directly prepares the patient for this specific challenge. Community ambulation training must include all anticipated environmental challenges rather than only flat surfaces to ensure the patient can manage real community terrain safely.
options: Progressive incline and decline walking training
Balance board training for proprioceptive challenge
