Increasing cadence on flat surfaces for speed
Backward walking on flat terrain for strength
Treadmill training at controlled constant speed

questions.explanation: At heel strike, the ankle sits in a neutral position between dorsiflexion and plantarflexion before rapidly moving into plantarflexion to bring the entire foot into contact with the ground, known as foot-flat. This rapid plantarflexion allows smooth loading response during early stance. The ankle subsequently moves into dorsiflexion as the tibia advances over the fixed foot.
questions.question: At the moment of heel strike, the ankle joint position is best described as which of the following?
Elbow, or forearm, crutches are measured from the ground to which anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: Elbow crutches, also called forearm or Lofstrand crutches, are measured from the point of the elbow to the ground rather than from the axilla. This differs from full-length axillary crutches, which use the axillary fold as the proximal landmark. Correct measurement ensures the forearm cuff and handgrip sit at an appropriate height for efficient weight transfer.
options: The point of the patient's elbow
The anterior fold of the axilla
The tip of the olecranon plus 10 centimeters

questions.explanation: Active paraplegic patients who play sport require ultralight rigid frame wheelchairs optimised for performance — low rolling resistance, optimal push mechanics, cambered wheels for stability during turns, and rigid frames reducing energy loss during propulsion. Hospital folding chairs are heavy and inefficient. Power chairs are inappropriate for active sport. Ultralight rigid wheelchairs enable the high-performance demands of sport wheelchair activities while also providing efficient daily community mobility.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is selecting a wheelchair for outdoor community use by an active paraplegic patient who plays sport. Which wheelchair type is most appropriate?

questions.explanation: Four-point crutch gait is indicated for patients who can bear weight on both lower extremities but require support due to coordination impairment, weakness, or poor balance. Each crutch and foot moves independently, providing constant three-point support. It requires greater coordination than two-point gait but provides superior stability for patients who cannot safely manage the two-point or swing patterns that momentarily reduce contact points.
options: One non-weight-bearing limb with good coordination
One leg weight-bearing with weak upper extremities
Normal gait requiring only minimal support
Both legs bearing weight with coordination impairment
questions.question: Which patient characteristics specifically indicate four-point crutch gait over other crutch patterns?

questions.explanation: Seat depth is measured from the back of the buttocks to a pen firmly placed in the popliteal fossa, ensuring the seat adequately supports the thigh without placing pressure behind the knee. This measurement approach avoids excessive seat length that could compress popliteal vessels and nerves. Correct seat depth contributes significantly to pressure management and seating comfort.
options: A pen placed firmly in the popliteal fossa
The tip of the medial malleolus bone
questions.question: Seat depth for wheelchair measurement is determined from the back of the buttocks to which anatomical reference point?
A physiotherapist identifies that a post-stroke patient has reached the associative stage of motor learning for gait. What training modification is most appropriate at this stage?
options: Simplify the task by removing all environmental demands
Introduce varied practice conditions and reduce feedback frequency
Provide maximum feedback after every step taken
Return to bilateral support in parallel bars only
Stop training until the cognitive stage is fully mastered
questions.explanation: In the Associative stage, the basic movement pattern is established and the patient now needs to refine and adapt the skill. Varied practice conditions (different surfaces, speeds, environments) promote transfer to real-world walking. Reducing feedback frequency forces the patient to rely on intrinsic feedback, developing self-assessment ability essential for autonomous stage performance. Continuing maximum feedback or simplifying the task would prevent progression to the autonomous stage required for community ambulation.

questions.question: Frenkel exercises specifically require good environmental lighting primarily to support which aspect of the training?
questions.explanation: Good lighting is essential during Frenkel exercises because the patient must be able to watch the movement of their legs, compensating visually for lost proprioceptive feedback. This visual substitution strategy is central to the exercise's therapeutic mechanism. Without adequate visual feedback, the exercises would fail to achieve their intended coordination-building purpose.

options: External tibial torsion with foot pronation
Internal tibial torsion with foot supination
Reduced hip range of motion only
questions.explanation: High Q-angle is associated with femoral anteroversion, external tibial torsion, foot pronation, and a laterally displaced tibial tubercle, forming a chain of lower limb malalignment. These combined factors compound the lateral force acting on the patella during knee extension. Recognizing this cluster of findings helps clinicians identify patients at heightened risk for patellofemoral pathology.
questions.question: Femoral anteroversion is associated with a high Q-angle together with which other described finding?

options: Plan selection, execution, task identification, sensory gathering
Sensory gathering, execution, plan selection, task identification
Task identification, sensory gathering, plan selection, execution
Execution, sensory gathering, task identification, plan selection
questions.explanation: Motor control begins with identifying the task, followed by gathering sensory information from the environment, perceiving that information, and selecting an appropriate movement plan. The plan is then coordinated within the central nervous system and executed through motor neurons to the muscles. Sensory feedback from the resulting movement subsequently informs modification, goal acknowledgment, or storage of the motor pattern for future use.
questions.question: Which sequence best represents the process by which motor control produces a movement, beginning with task identification?
A reciprocal walker is distinguished from other walker types by which mechanical feature?
options: An electric motor assisting forward movement
A swivel joint allowing alternating movement of each side
A single central wheel beneath the frame
Four fixed wheels with no folding capability
A rigid frame with no adjustable height
questions.explanation: A reciprocal walker has a swivel joint that allows each side of the walker to move alternately, mimicking a more natural reciprocal gait pattern, and is commonly used by patients recovering from hip replacement surgery. This differs from a standard walker, which must be lifted and repositioned as a single unit. The reciprocal design can support a more physiological gait pattern during early postoperative rehabilitation.

options: Feet strapped to a fixed board
Head turned fully to one side
Both legs elevated above heart level
Head raised on a pillow to watch every movement
questions.explanation: The starting position for lying exercises requires the head to be raised on a pillow so the patient can watch every leg movement, reinforcing the visual compensation strategy central to Frenkel training. This positioning ensures the patient receives continuous visual feedback throughout each sliding heel exercise. Progression continues from simple single-leg movements to more complex bilateral patterns as ability improves.
questions.question: The starting position for the earliest Frenkel exercises performed while lying down primarily requires which patient positioning detail?

options: Developing treatment strategies to remediate performance problems
Avoiding the need for patient assessment
Eliminating the need for practice repetition
questions.explanation: Applying motor control and learning theory helps therapists identify issues in motor performance and develop treatment strategies to remediate performance problems. It also supports evaluating the effectiveness of chosen intervention strategies over time. Selecting the appropriate motor learning strategy and control theory is essential for achieving optimal rehabilitation outcomes.
questions.question: Understanding motor control and motor learning theory primarily helps therapists achieve which clinical outcome?

questions.explanation: Back height is measured from the sitting surface to the inferior angle of the scapula for patients with adequate trunk control. This provides sufficient lumbar and lower trunk support while allowing free scapular movement and arm function for propulsion. A higher back limits shoulder mobility required for pushing. Patients with poor trunk control may require higher backs, but this compromises functional upper extremity use for self-propulsion.
questions.question: When fitting a wheelchair back height for a patient with adequate trunk control, where should the top of the backrest be positioned?
options: At the top of the patient's shoulders
At the inferior angle of the scapula
At the level of the iliac crests
At the nape of the neck for head support

questions.question: An assistive device is best defined as any instrument that primarily serves which purpose?
questions.explanation: An assistive device is defined as any instrument that helps someone do something that they might not otherwise be able to do well or at all, commonly addressing mobility, vision, dexterity, or hearing loss. This broad definition covers devices ranging from wheelchairs to adapted pencil grips. The core purpose is functional enhancement rather than cure of the underlying condition.
options: Providing entertainment during rehabilitation sessions only
Replacing the need for physical therapy entirely
Eliminating the need for patient assessment
Helping a person do an otherwise difficult task
In a darkened room to reduce visual distractions
Outdoors for a varied surface challenge
In a well-lit room for visual feedback
At high temperature to facilitate nerve conduction
questions.question: A physiotherapist conducting Frenkel exercises for multiple sclerosis must conduct sessions where?
questions.explanation: Adequate lighting is fundamental to Frenkel exercise effectiveness because vision substitutes for impaired proprioception. Patients must clearly see their limb movements to compensate for absent joint position sense through visual feedback. Well-lit environments enable precise visual monitoring of each exercise. Darkened environments would eliminate the compensatory visual pathway, making the exercises therapeutically ineffective and potentially dangerous.

options: Possessing full degrees of freedom for performance
Complete automation without any conscious input
Reducing movement complexity to a single joint
Gaining a few extra degrees of freedom
questions.question: The advanced stage of motor learning, situated between initial and expert stages, is best characterized by which feature?
questions.explanation: The advanced stage of motor learning is marked by the individual gaining a few additional degrees of freedom, permitting movement across more of the articulations involved in the task compared to the initial stage. This represents an intermediate step between the highly simplified initial stage and the fully coordinated expert stage. Progression through these stages reflects the gradual refinement of motor control during skill acquisition.

Anthropometric tape and tape rule are used to record body segment lengths and girths, providing baseline measurements relevant to device fitting and movement analysis. This differs from goniometers, which measure joint angles rather than linear body dimensions. Accurate anthropometric data supports proper prescription of assistive devices discussed later in the course.
questions.question: An anthropometric tape is primarily used in pathokinesiological assessment to measure which patient characteristic?

questions.explanation: Total hip angle excursion rises from about 40 degrees during slow walking to approximately 54 degrees during fast walking, reflecting the greater range of motion demanded at higher speeds. This increase parallels similar speed-related changes seen at other joints during gait. Such data provide reference values for identifying restricted or excessive hip motion in pathological gait.
questions.question: The total hip joint angle excursion during gait increases from approximately 40 degrees in slow walking to what value during fast walking?
The smaller front wheels of a conventional wheelchair are specifically referred to by which term?
questions.explanation: The smaller front wheels of a conventional wheelchair are called casters, distinct from the larger rear wheels that carry the hand rims used for propulsion. Casters enhance maneuverability, particularly for turning in confined spaces. Understanding this terminology is essential when discussing wheelchair components and maintenance procedures.

Rotatory, or angular, motion occurs when a body moves about a fixed axis while the radius of motion remains constant, as seen in shoulder circumduction. This differs from translatory motion where there is no axis and every point shifts identically. Human motion typically combines both rotatory and translatory components simultaneously.
questions.question: Rotatory motion occurring during shoulder circumduction is best explained by which characteristic?
options: The radius of motion continually changes
The body rotates about a fixed axis
Displacement is identical at every point

questions.explanation: Normative data show women typically have a higher Q-angle than men, attributed in part to a wider pelvis, with values such as approximately 17 degrees in women compared to 14 degrees in men in some populations. This anatomical difference contributes to a greater predisposition among women toward patellofemoral tracking disorders and certain sports injuries. Recognizing sex-based normative differences is important when interpreting an individual patient's Q-angle measurement.
questions.question: According to normative data cited in the course material, which group typically demonstrates a higher Q-angle value?
options: Elderly men, compared to young men
Children, compared to adults of either sex

questions.question: The initial knee flexion of approximately 15 degrees occurring immediately after heel strike serves primarily which functional purpose?
questions.explanation: The early stance knee flexion of about 15 degrees functions primarily as a shock absorption mechanism, cushioning the impact of body weight transfer onto the limb. This differs from the larger swing phase knee flexion of about 70 degrees, which instead serves to clear the foot from the ground. Loss of this early flexion can increase joint loading and discomfort during walking.

The cane should be held in the hand opposite the involved leg, allowing the cane and the unaffected leg to share the load during the stance phase of the affected limb. This technique widens the effective base of support on the affected side and reduces joint loading. Holding the cane on the same side as the involved leg would fail to provide this biomechanical advantage.
options: The hand matching hand dominance only
Either hand since side makes no difference
The hand on the involved side
The hand opposite the weak leg
questions.question: A patient using a single cane for lower limb weakness should hold it in which hand?

questions.explanation: The knee comprises three joints in total, two tibiofemoral compartments and one patellofemoral joint, working together to allow flexion, extension, and limited rotation. The patellofemoral joint specifically governs the interaction between the patella and femoral trochlear groove. This structural complexity contributes to the knee's susceptibility to a wide range of pathomechanical disorders.
questions.question: The knee joint complex is composed of the tibiofemoral joint together with which other articulation?

options: Sensory ataxia from proprioceptive pathway loss
En bloc turning with rigid pivot pattern
Marche a petit pas with slow shuffling steps
Festination with forward centre of gravity displacement
questions.explanation: Festination in Parkinson's disease involves involuntary acceleration of steps combined with a forward-falling tendency where the centre of gravity advances ahead of the feet. The shortening, quickening steps represent an attempt to catch up with the displaced centre of gravity. This differs from retropulsion and must be managed through external cueing, stride lengthening, and environmental modification strategies.
questions.question: A 70-year-old with Parkinson's disease shows rapidly accelerating small steps that are difficult to stop. Which gait phenomenon is being observed?

questions.explanation: Pain rating scales such as the visual analogue scale, verbal rating scale, and McGill Pain Questionnaire quantify subjective pain experience rather than physical movement parameters. They are distinct from mobility tools like goniometers, which measure joint angles objectively. Both categories together provide a comprehensive pathokinesiological assessment of a patient's condition.
questions.question: The McGill Pain Questionnaire and visual analogue scale are examples of which category of pathokinesiological measurement?
A physiotherapist observes a patient rising on the stance-side toes during contralateral swing. What does this vaulting pattern indicate?
questions.explanation: Vaulting elevates the body over the stance limb by rising on the toes, creating clearance for a functionally long swing-side limb. This compensates for conditions making the swing limb effectively too long — a stiff knee, limited hip or knee flexion, foot drop, or true leg length discrepancy. The therapist should identify which swing-limb problem drives the compensation to plan appropriate targeted intervention.
options: Antalgic avoidance of heel contact pain
Hip flexor weakness causing inadequate swing
Compensation for a functionally long swing limb

questions.explanation: An increased Q-angle increases the resultant lateral force on the patella, predisposing toward lateral displacement and potential patellar instability or dysplasia. This lateral vector arises because the combined quadriceps pull and patellar tendon line create an angulated force imbalance. Clinically, this predisposition is a key consideration when evaluating anterior knee pain and patellar tracking disorders.
questions.question: An increased Q-angle predisposes the patella toward which specific direction of displacement?

questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity requires repetitive, intensive, task-specific practice to drive cortical map reorganisation. For gait recovery, this means practising walking itself at sufficient intensity (high repetitions per session) and with appropriate challenge. Evidence consistently shows that task-specific walking practice produces cortical and spinal reorganisation exceeding that from non-specific exercise. Low-frequency, passive, or non-functional training does not adequately drive the neuroplastic change required.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies neuroplasticity principles in planning gait rehabilitation for a stroke patient. What does this specifically require?
options: Passive range of motion to maintain joint mobility
Electrical stimulation of weakened muscles only
Careful avoidance of difficult or challenging tasks
Once-weekly sessions for nervous system recovery time

questions.explanation: Parapodium suitability hinges critically on adequate upper extremity coordination and strength, since independent ambulation within the device requires using forearm crutches or a walker for forward propulsion through weight-shifting. Without sufficient arm function, the child cannot achieve independent ambulation even if well-fitted in the parapodium. Full pre-prescription assessment evaluates upper extremity function alongside bone integrity and absence of deep cognitive impairment.
questions.question: A child with L3–L4 myelomeningocele is being considered for a parapodium. Which factor is most important in determining suitability?
options: Upper extremity function for crutch ambulation
Height and body weight measurements only

questions.explanation: Motor skills are defined as tasks requiring voluntary control over the movements of joints and body segments in order to achieve a specific goal, such as walking, writing, or riding a bicycle. This voluntary, goal-directed nature distinguishes motor skills from simple reflexive movements. The study of their acquisition and performance falls under motor learning and control.
questions.question: Motor skills are best defined as tasks requiring which combination of abilities?
options: Voluntary control over movement to achieve a goal

questions.question: A patient with bilateral hip abductor weakness presents with which characteristic gait pattern?
questions.explanation: Bilateral gluteus medius paralysis creates a waddling or duck gait, where the trunk lurches side-to-side with each step because neither hip abductor group can maintain pelvic level. Unlike unilateral Trendelenburg gait, bilateral involvement produces symmetrical waddling. The wide-based, side-to-side pattern is distinctive and characteristic of bilateral hip abductor pathology such as muscular dystrophy.
options: Trendelenburg gait with ipsilateral trunk lean
Steppage gait with excessive hip flexion
Waddling gait with bilateral lateral trunk sway
Gluteus maximus gait with backward trunk shift
Scissoring gait with adductor crossing pattern

questions.explanation: Balance relies on three sensory systems: visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive. Peripheral neuropathy eliminates proprioceptive input while macular degeneration impairs visual feedback — removing two of the three balance systems simultaneously. When visual compensation for lost proprioception is also unavailable, fall risk increases dramatically. This dual-system loss is more dangerous than either deficit alone.
options: Peripheral neuropathy alone without visual loss
Visual loss alone without proprioceptive impairment
Both proprioceptive and visual sensory loss combined
Macular degeneration with intact peripheral vision
Neuropathy in feet only without ankle involvement
questions.question: A 78-year-old patient with macular degeneration and peripheral neuropathy is assessed for fall risk. Which combination creates the greatest fall vulnerability?
A hemi walker is best described as a device combining features of which two other assistive devices?
questions.explanation: The hemi walker is a combination of a walker with a quad cane, providing a wider base of support and is majorly used by hemiplegic patients not yet ready to progress to a simple quad cane. It offers more stability than a standard cane while still being operable with a single hand. This makes it a useful transitional device during recovery from hemiplegia.
options: A parapodium and a standard walker
A walker and a quad cane
A wheelchair and a standard cane
A rolling walker and axillary crutches

questions.question: A physiotherapist teaches a patient with L4 spinal cord injury to use a parapodium. How does the device achieve weight shifting for ambulation?
options: By shifting body weight back and forth between limbs
Through electrical stimulation of hip flexors
Using foot pedals driving the frame forward
By activating remaining lower extremity muscles
questions.explanation: Users achieve independent parapodium ambulation by shifting body weight laterally from one side to the other, creating a natural walking motion. With the joints locked, this weight shift unloads one limb and advances the opposite side of the frame in a controlled pattern mimicking gait. Upper extremity crutches or a walker provide forward progression and stability during the weight-shifting manoeuvre.

questions.question: A standard manual wheelchair is designed with which wheel size configuration to allow patient-driven propulsion?
options: Equal-sized wheels on all four corners
Large front wheels and small rear wheels
Rear wheels only with no casters
Small front casters and large hand-rimmed rear wheels
A single central drive wheel only
questions.explanation: Most manual wheelchairs are designed with small front wheels, called casters, and large rear wheels fitted with hand rims that allow the patient to mechanically propel the chair using body power. This configuration balances maneuverability from the small front casters with efficient propulsion from the larger rear wheels. Manual wheelchairs can be propelled using both arms, both legs, or a combination of one arm and one leg.

Caregivers are instructed to bend their knees and maintain a natural curve in their back during transfers specifically to protect their own back from injury while assisting the patient to stand. This technique distributes lifting force through the stronger leg muscles rather than the spine. Proper caregiver body mechanics are essential for sustainable, safe delivery of manual transfer assistance.
questions.question: During a car-to-wheelchair transfer, the caregiver should bend the knees and maintain a natural back curve primarily to protect which body region?

questions.explanation: The Parapodium is a high-quality aluminium standing aid especially designed for children, functioning as an excellent supplement to a child's wheelchair by enabling independent standing and simulated walking movement. It is described as difficult to use with older patients due to its design and intended population. This makes it a pediatric-specific device within the broader category of standing orthoses.
questions.question: The Parapodium is specifically designed as a standing aid primarily for which patient population?
During a Frenkel exercise session, the physiotherapist notes the patient completes movements correctly but inconsistently. Which motor learning stage does this describe?
questions.explanation: Frequent errors and high variability characterise the Cognitive (initial) stage of motor learning, where the patient is consciously trying to understand and execute the task. Movement quality is inconsistent because the motor programme is not yet established. The therapist should provide simple clear instructions, reduce task complexity, allow rest between repetitions, and ensure maximum visual feedback during Frenkel exercises until consistency improves and the patient progresses to the Associative stage.
options: Autonomous stage with automatic movement execution
Associative stage with consistent but imperfect performance
Skill decay from fatigue and inattention
Cognitive stage with frequent errors and high variability
Engram consolidation requiring only brief practice

questions.explanation: Gait velocity equals stride length multiplied by cadence. Increasing cadence while maintaining stride length directly increases walking speed in direct proportion. This relationship guides clinical interventions targeting speed — therapists may cue faster stepping rate while monitoring stride length to optimise overall velocity. Understanding this equation allows precise prescription of gait training parameters.
questions.question: During gait retraining the physiotherapist instructs a patient to increase cadence. What is the expected effect on walking speed?
options: Speed decreases as stride length shortens
Speed is unaffected without stride length change
Speed decreases as double support lengthens
Speed increases proportionally to cadence rise
Speed only changes in fast walkers

questions.question: A physiotherapist observes a patient with a right hip replacement who walks with the trunk lurching forward during initial right stance. Which primary muscle deficit causes this 'gluteus maximus gait'?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus gait (forward trunk lurch at initial contact) results from hip extensor weakness. When gluteus maximus cannot maintain the hip in extension against body weight, the trunk lurches forward to shift the ground reaction force anterior to the hip joint, passively stabilising it. This is commonly seen post-hip surgery and must be differentiated from hip flexor contracture, which requires targeted progressive hip extensor strengthening.
options: Right hip abductor weakness causing pelvic drop
Right hip extensor weakness causing forward trunk lean
Right quadriceps weakness causing knee buckling
Right plantarflexor weakness causing calcaneal gait
Right tibialis anterior weakness causing foot drop

questions.question: During the cognitive or initial stage of motor learning, the individual primarily simplifies movement by which strategy?
questions.explanation: In the initial cognitive stage, the learner simplifies a new movement by reducing the degrees of freedom, essentially limiting how many joints move independently to make the task manageable. This contrasts with the expert stage, where all degrees of freedom are used in a coordinated, effective manner. This progressive increase in freedom characterizes the pathway from novice to skilled performance.
options: Reducing the degrees of freedom used

questions.question: A physiotherapist monitors Borg RPE during treadmill training for COPD rehabilitation. The patient reports 15 at 0.7 m/s. How should intensity be modified?
options: Immediately stop the session due to exertion risk
Increase speed substantially for greater cardiovascular benefit
Reduce speed to minimise any respiratory demand
Maintain current intensity within target training range
Switch from treadmill to seated cycling for safety
questions.explanation: Borg RPE 15 (hard) falls within the recommended training intensity range of 12–17 for cardiovascular conditioning, corresponding to approximately 70–85% of maximum heart rate. This indicates appropriate aerobic training intensity that will produce cardiovascular adaptations. Stopping at this level would prevent training benefit. Maintaining the current workload optimises the cardiovascular training stimulus while remaining within safe parameters for COPD rehabilitation.

questions.question: Which principle is most critical for designing a home exercise programme for gait rehabilitation following stroke?
options: Providing only verbal instructions without written material
Prescribing maximum intensity exercises for faster gains
Specific achievable exercises with written instructions
Exercising only in supervised clinic settings
Using standardised exercises same for all stroke patients
questions.explanation: Effective home programmes require specific exercises targeting identified impairments, written and pictorial instructions enabling independent correct performance, appropriate difficulty matching current ability, and clear progression criteria. Generic standardised programmes reduce adherence. Verbal instructions alone are insufficient as patients may not recall detail after sessions. Achievable exercises maintain motivation while progressively challenging functional movement patterns.

options: Body function — physiological and psychological functions
questions.explanation: The ICF Activity domain encompasses the execution of tasks and actions by an individual, including walking. Walking speed, measured on specific gait tasks such as the 10-metre walk test or Timed Up and Go, directly quantifies activity-level performance. This contrasts with Body Function (physiological measures like muscle strength or joint range) and Participation (community involvement, social roles). Comprehensive gait rehabilitation documentation should address all ICF levels.
questions.question: Improved walking speed after stroke rehabilitation is best classified under which level of the ICF framework?

options: Hip hiking for functional leg lengthening
questions.question: A post-CVA patient walks with the right leg in extension, plantarflexion, and internal rotation, swinging the limb outward in an arc. Which strategy is this patient employing?
questions.explanation: Circumduction is the hallmark compensation for hemiplegic gait, where spastic extension at hip and knee with plantarflexion prevents normal limb shortening for swing phase clearance. The leg swings laterally in a semicircular arc to advance without dragging. This pattern compensates for inadequate hip flexion, knee flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion — all consequences of lower extremity spasticity following cerebrovascular accident.

questions.question: The Insall-Salvati ratio is used clinically to assess which specific relationship?
questions.explanation: The Insall-Salvati ratio compares the height of the patella to the length of the patellar ligament, providing an objective radiographic method to identify patella alta or baja. This ratio supplements clinical Q-angle measurement by confirming vertical patellar positioning on imaging. Accurate identification of patellar height abnormalities informs both conservative and surgical management planning.
options: Depth of the trochlear groove relative to patellar thickness
Height of the patella relative to the length of the patellar ligament
Length of the quadriceps tendon relative to hamstring length
Width of the femoral condyles relative to tibial plateau
Angle of tibial torsion relative to femoral anteversion

questions.question: A physiotherapist measures stride length improved from 1.0 m to 1.3 m over four weeks of training. At a cadence of 100 steps per minute, what is the new walking speed?
options: Speed unchanged despite improved stride length
Speed decreased due to energy cost increase
questions.explanation: Walking speed equals stride length multiplied by cadence in strides per minute. At 100 steps/min cadence equals 50 strides/min. Initial speed: 1.0 m x 50 = 50 m/min. New speed: 1.3 m x 50 = 65 m/min. This represents a 30% speed improvement from the same cadence, demonstrating how stride length gains directly translate to functional velocity improvements.

Perry's 1992 measurements found adults walking at a free pace averaged approximately 82 meters per minute with a mean stride length of 1.4 meters. This established normative data serves as a reference point for identifying abnormally slow or fast gait in clinical populations. Cadence at this pace averaged 113 steps per minute.
questions.question: Perry measured the mean free walking velocity of adults to be approximately which value?
Back height measurement for wheelchair fitting is taken from which anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: Back height is measured from the bottom of the inferior angle of the scapula, providing adequate trunk support while allowing free scapular movement for patients who propel the chair manually. This measurement ensures the backrest neither restricts arm movement nor fails to provide sufficient trunk stability. Correct back height selection varies depending on whether a patient requires more or less trunk support.
options: The top of the seventh cervical vertebra
The top of the iliac crest
The bottom of the inferior angle of the scapula
The base of the sacrum only

questions.explanation: Kinesiology integrates kinematics, the description of motion, with kinetics, the forces producing motion, into one analytical science. This dual focus allows clinicians to understand both how a movement looks and why it occurs. Pathokinesiology later applies this same dual lens to abnormal movement.
questions.question: Kinesiology is most accurately defined as the analytical study of which combined phenomena?
Compared with women, men typically demonstrate which combination of gait characteristics at free walking speed?
options: Longer stride length and slower cadence
Shorter stride length and slower cadence
Shorter stride length and faster cadence
Longer stride length and faster cadence
Equal stride length and equal cadence
questions.explanation: Men generally walk faster than women while showing a longer stride length combined with a slower cadence compared to women. This sex-based difference reflects variation in limb length and gait strategy rather than overall walking speed alone. Such normative differences are considered when interpreting individual gait analysis data.

questions.question: During stair training for a patient with bilateral peroneal neuropathy, which sequence of progression is correct?
options: Begin on high stairs then progress to lower steps
Begin without rails for maximum challenge
Begin stair training only when crutches are abandoned
Begin ascending with rails, then alternating feet, then descent
Begin with descent then progress to ascent training
questions.explanation: Standard stair progression begins with ascent rather than descent because going up requires less eccentric muscle control and is generally safer. Initial ascent is performed with bilateral rail support using step-to-gait pattern. As competence improves, the patient progresses to alternating feet with rail support, then to descent which requires greater eccentric quadriceps and balance control. Independent stair management without rails is the final progression goal.

options: Discomfort and fatigue with prolonged use
Excessive cost compared to other crutch types
Complete inability to bear any body weight
Requirement for constant supervision by a therapist
questions.explanation: Underarm crutches are the most common crutch type and are easy to use and balance, but they can lead to discomfort and fatigue with prolonged use due to pressure in the axillary region. This disadvantage contrasts with forearm crutches, which are often preferred for long-term use because they distribute pressure differently. Selecting crutch type should consider both immediate ease of use and long-term comfort.
questions.question: Underarm, or axilla, crutches are noted in the course material to carry which particular disadvantage despite being easy to balance?

options: Slightly greater than the supine measurement
Substantially lower than the supine measurement
questions.explanation: Data comparing supine and standing Q-angle measurements show standing values are generally slightly greater than supine values in both men and women. This positional difference reflects the added influence of weight-bearing alignment on patellofemoral mechanics. Clinicians should note which position was used when interpreting or comparing Q-angle measurements over time.
questions.question: The Q-angle measured in the standing position compared with the supine position is generally which of the following?
Progression in Frenkel exercise programming follows which general sequence of patient positioning?
questions.explanation: Frenkel exercises progress from exercises performed while lying down, to exercises while sitting, and finally to exercises while standing, reflecting increasing postural demand and complexity. Later stages incorporate stair climbing and upper extremity coordination tasks such as tracing diagrams on a backboard. This graded progression ensures foundational coordination is established before advancing to more challenging functional tasks.

Critical parapodium pre-prescription assessment includes evaluation of upper extremity coordination and strength needed for crutch or walker use to enable independent ambulation. Children must have adequate arm strength to use crutches alongside the parapodium for forward movement. Insufficient upper extremity function would have predicted difficulty with independent parapodium ambulation, potentially indicating the need for a different device.
options: Height and weight above device limits
Insufficient upper extremity coordination and strength
questions.question: A paediatric physiotherapist notes a child wearing a parapodium struggles to stand due to poor upper extremity strength. Which pre-prescription finding should have predicted this difficulty?
An excessively extended knee during stance phase, sometimes called locked knee hyperextension gait, is most closely associated with weakness of which muscle?
questions.explanation: Quadriceps weakness leads patients to compensate by hyperextending the knee during stance to achieve passive joint stability, producing a locked knee gait pattern. This compensatory hyperextension substitutes for the active quadriceps control normally required to stabilize the knee. Over time this pattern can predispose the posterior knee structures to strain.

questions.question: A physiotherapist treats a patient with Parkinson's disease and addresses dual-task gait requirements in community ambulation training. Which cognitive function is most critical to train?
questions.explanation: Community ambulation demands divided attention — simultaneously managing walking mechanics, environmental navigation, obstacle avoidance, and conversation. Parkinson's disease impairs the basal ganglia's ability to automatise gait, forcing it to compete for limited attentional resources. Dual-task training progressively challenges divided attention during walking, improving the ability to allocate cognitive resources between simultaneous demands and reducing fall risk in the community.
options: Divided attention for simultaneous gait tasks
Processing speed for rapid decision making
Executive function for goal setting only

questions.question: A gait deviation caused specifically by weakness of the ankle dorsiflexors is best classified under which category listed in the gait deviation classification?
questions.explanation: Drop foot or steppage gait resulting from ankle dorsiflexor weakness is categorized as an isolated motor weakness gait problem rather than a purely neurologic or structural cause. This classification distinguishes weakness-driven compensations from central nervous system pathology such as spasticity. Correct classification informs whether treatment should target strengthening or neurological rehabilitation.

options: The Parapodium allows the child to sit down from the device
Only the standing brace can be used by children
The standing brace allows sitting while the Parapodium does not
The standing brace is lighter in weight than the Parapodium
The Parapodium requires crutches for use while the brace does not
questions.question: A key functional difference between the Parapodium and a standard standing brace is which of the following?
questions.explanation: The Parapodium allows the child to transition to sitting directly from the device, whereas the standing brace is a fixed frame that does not offer this possibility. Both devices lock the hips and knees into extension for standing, but their flexibility for postural transitions differs significantly. This difference makes the Parapodium more versatile for children needing to alternate between sitting and standing throughout the day.

options: It proves humans only translate, never rotate
It demonstrates linear displacement of every particle
It illustrates constant-radius motion about a fixed axis
It eliminates the need for goniometry
questions.question: Why is rotatory motion exemplified by the earth's motion about its own axis considered relevant to human movement analysis?
questions.explanation: The earth spinning on its axis exemplifies pure rotatory motion, where every point moves about a fixed axis at a constant radius, analogous to joint motion such as hip circumduction. This conceptual example helps students distinguish rotatory from translatory motion in human joints. Both motion types typically combine during functional human activity such as walking.

options: Deterioration in balance requiring more support
Increased walking speed and improved confidence
Greater reliance on bilateral weight bearing
Increased fall risk from single limb instability
questions.question: A patient's double support time decreased compared to the initial assessment. What does this most likely indicate?
questions.explanation: Double support time decreases as walking speed increases. When patients improve in balance, strength, and confidence, they spend less time in the safe bilateral weight-bearing position. Reduced double support time is therefore a positive prognostic indicator in rehabilitation, reflecting greater walking speed and reduced need for conservative bilateral support. Conversely, increased double support time in initial assessment indicates instability requiring cautious bilateral weight bearing.

Berg Balance Scale scores of 41–56 indicate low fall risk, 21–40 indicate moderate fall risk requiring balance intervention, and 0–20 indicate high fall risk requiring wheelchair mobility. A score of 38 places this patient in the moderate risk category, indicating targeted balance training is required to reduce fall risk and improve functional independence. Rehabilitation should include progressive balance challenges, strength training, and may include assistive device modification to improve safety and confidence.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assesses a patient using the Berg Balance Scale and scores 38 out of 56. What does this score indicate regarding the patient's fall risk and rehabilitation implications?
options: Low fall risk; discharge with a home programme
High fall risk; supervision required for all mobility
Moderate fall risk; balance training intervention needed

questions.explanation: Gait is defined simply as the manner or style of walking, encompassing speed, cadence, and pattern of limb movement. It is described using parameters such as locomotion speed in meters per second and steps completed per unit time. This definition underlies all subsequent gait cycle and gait analysis concepts.
options: The manner or style of walking
The total distance covered per session
The strength of lower limb muscles
The range of motion at the ankle
questions.question: Gait is most precisely defined as which of the following?
A key disadvantage of using surface electrodes for EMG during gait analysis is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Surface EMG electrodes, while non-invasive, may inadvertently record electrical activity from deeper muscles or adjacent antagonists rather than purely the target muscle. This cross-talk can complicate interpretation of which specific muscle is generating the recorded signal. Despite this limitation, surface electrodes remain useful for large superficial muscle groups such as the plantarflexors.
options: Inability to detect any muscle activity
Interference with joint range of motion
Recording activity from deeper or adjacent muscles

questions.question: A physiotherapist determines a patient's gait velocity is 0.6 m/s. What does this speed most importantly predict regarding community ambulation?
options: Full unlimited community ambulation is achievable
Speed predicts increased risk of hospitalisation and fall
Speed is appropriate for athletic rehabilitation goals
questions.explanation: Gait velocity strongly predicts health outcomes, fall risk, and survival. Speeds below 0.8 m/s are associated with increased hospitalisation risk, and speeds below 1.0 m/s typically preclude reliable community ambulation. At 0.6 m/s, this patient falls in the range associated with significant fall risk, poor community function, and adverse health outcomes. Clinical gait velocity assessment thus provides important prognostic information.

questions.question: A recliner-type wheelchair frame primarily allows which specific movement?
questions.explanation: A recliner wheelchair has a back that reclines away from the seat, allowing the patient's head and trunk to be lowered while opening the seat-to-back hip angle. This differs from a tilt-in-space chair, which maintains the hip angle by moving the entire seat-back unit together. Recliner chairs are often selected for patients needing periodic postural change without transferring out of the chair.
options: The wheelbase widens for outdoor terrain
The seat tilts backward while preserving hip angle
The back reclines to lower the head and trunk
The seat width adjusts to fit patient size
The footrests elevate independent of the seat

questions.question: Standard wheelchair frame height is typically what distance from the seat to the floor?
questions.explanation: Standard wheelchair height is typically 19.5 inches from the seat to the floor, while hemi-height chairs measure 17.5 inches or lower to allow propulsion and control using one leg. The appropriate height depends on the patient's own height, propulsion method, arm length, trunk length, and transfer status. Selecting the correct frame height supports efficient propulsion and safe functional transfers.

In the three-point swing-through gait, once balance and strength have improved, the patient moves the unaffected leg beyond the crutches rather than stopping level with them as in the standard three-point pattern. This variant allows for faster, more efficient ambulation once the patient has mastered basic three-point technique. It represents a progression toward more advanced and functional crutch mobility.
questions.question: In the swing-through variant of the three-point gait, the patient advances the unaffected leg to which position relative to the crutches?
options: Only up to the level of the crutches
Halfway between start and the crutches
To the side of the crutches only

questions.explanation: The majority of sagittal ankle motion during gait occurs in the plantarflexion range of 0 to approximately negative 20 degrees, while dorsiflexion motion of 0 to positive 10 degrees occurs only during stance phase. This asymmetry reflects the ankle's role in absorbing shock and generating propulsion primarily through plantarflexor activity. Restriction of plantarflexion range can therefore have a pronounced effect on gait efficiency.
questions.question: Most sagittal plane motion of the ankle during the gait cycle occurs within which range?
options: Plantarflexion range of 0 to negative 20 degrees
Inversion range of the subtalar joint only
Eversion range of the subtalar joint only
A fixed neutral position maintained throughout stance
Dorsiflexion range of 0 to positive 30 degrees

questions.question: A patient with spastic diplegia uses a scissoring gait pattern with crossing thighs. Which intervention most directly targets the responsible muscle group?
questions.explanation: Scissor gait results from bilateral hip adductor spasticity in spastic diplegia, causing the thighs to cross forward at midline with each step. Management targets the hip adductors through tone-reducing interventions: botulinum toxin injection, dorsal rhizotomy, oral antispastics, orthopaedic procedures such as adductor release, and physiotherapy including stretching, orthotics, and functional gait training.

questions.question: When performing a wheelchair-to-car transfer, the gait belt should be positioned in which location on the patient?
questions.explanation: The gait belt should be placed below the ribcage and above the hips during a wheelchair-to-car transfer, allowing the caregiver to hold the belt rather than the patient's arm, which reduces injury risk to the patient. This positioning provides a secure and centrally located point of control during the transfer. Correct gait belt placement is a fundamental safety measure in all transfer techniques described in the course material.
options: Around the neck for added leverage
Below the ribcage and above the hips
At the level of the knees
Increased cadence and improved stride length
Better arm swing and reduced postural stoop
Reduced double support time and wider base
Decreased foot drag and improved heel strike
questions.question: A patient's 10-metre walk test improves from 20 to 14 seconds after six weeks of Parkinson's disease rehabilitation. Which parameter change most directly accounts for this improvement?
questions.explanation: Walking speed improvement from 0.5 to 0.71 m/s reflects increased gait velocity. Since velocity equals stride length multiplied by cadence, improvement comes from either or both parameters. In Parkinson's disease rehabilitation, cueing strategies including rhythmic auditory stimulation and visual cues, along with stride lengthening exercises, specifically target the characteristically reduced stride length and cadence. Improving both simultaneously produces observed speed gains.

Visual monitoring is the fundamental therapeutic mechanism of Frenkel exercises, substituting for impaired proprioception. Patients must watch every movement of their limbs throughout each exercise repetition. Closing the eyes eliminates the visual compensatory feedback that the exercise depends upon, removing its therapeutic benefit. The therapist must immediately correct the technique, instructing the patient to maintain continuous visual focus on the moving limb.
questions.question: A Frenkel exercise patient closes their eyes between repetitions. What correction should be made and why?
options: Allow eye closure to improve proprioceptive retraining
Eyes should be partially closed to reduce distraction
Eye closure is acceptable if movements are accurate
No correction needed — eye position is irrelevant
The patient must keep eyes open for visual feedback
Complex paediatric cerebral palsy surgical planning
Initial assessment of a simple ankle sprain
Elderly patient learning basic walking aids
questions.question: Quantitative 3D gait analysis is most appropriate for which clinical scenario?
questions.explanation: Three-dimensional motion capture gait analysis is resource-intensive and clinically indicated for complex cases requiring precise quantification to guide major decisions — particularly cerebral palsy surgical planning where data from multiple joints in all three planes informs decisions about multiple simultaneous procedures. It provides kinematic and kinetic data impossible to obtain through observational analysis alone.

Frenkel exercise guidelines specify that each exercise should not exceed four repetitions initially to prevent fatigue. Fatigue significantly impairs coordination performance and undermines the precise movement quality essential for engram formation. Rest periods between exercises are mandatory. Exceeding four repetitions risks poor-quality movement that reinforces incoordination rather than correcting it, defeating the therapeutic purpose.
questions.question: During Frenkel exercise training for sensory ataxia, fatigue is observed after three repetitions. What is the correct clinical response?
options: Push through fatigue to build coordination endurance
Double the repetitions to challenge the patient
Limit to four repetitions per exercise with rest
Stop the session and rest before continuing

questions.question: A patient presenting with an excessive Q-angle due to a wide pelvis and genu valgum would most likely also be predisposed to which condition?
questions.explanation: A wide pelvis combined with genu valgum increases the Q-angle and predisposes the patient to lateral patellar displacement, sometimes termed patellar dysplasia, due to the resultant increased lateral pull on the patella. This risk is compounded in patients who also have patella alta, since the protective effect of the lateral trochlear lip is reduced. Recognizing this combination of risk factors supports early preventive intervention such as targeted strengthening.

The vertical ground reaction force shows a double-peaked curve: the first peak during loading response and the second during terminal stance push-off. A reduced second peak on the right indicates diminished propulsive force generation, commonly from plantarflexor weakness or pain at push-off. This kinetic finding would not be detected by observational analysis alone and directs targeted plantarflexor strengthening.
questions.question: A force plate analysis reveals a reduced second peak in the vertical ground reaction force curve on the right. What does this indicate?
options: Increased loading response on the right
Adequate single limb support phase duration
Reduced push-off propulsive force on the right

questions.explanation: The Polgon is a specialized goniometric device using polarized light to measure joint angles, falling under mobility measurement equipment alongside conventional and electrogoniometers. It provides an alternative method for capturing joint position data with potentially greater precision. Such tools illustrate the breadth of instrumentation available for pathokinesiological assessment.
questions.question: The polarized light goniometer, also called the Polgon, is primarily used to assess which aspect of human motion?
Stride length is defined as the distance measured between which two events?
options: Mid-stance to mid-swing of the same limb
Heel strike to toe-off of the same foot
Heel strike of one foot to opposite heel strike
Toe-off to toe-off of opposite feet
Heel strike of a foot to its next heel strike
questions.explanation: Stride length is the distance between the heel strike of one foot and the heel strike of that same foot after a complete gait cycle. This distinguishes it from step length, which is measured between the heel strikes of opposite feet. Stride length varies with walking speed and cadence in healthy individuals.

options: Quadriceps and hamstrings for knee stability
Biceps and deltoids for arm swing pattern
Triceps and shoulder depressors for push-down
questions.question: Which muscle group must be specifically strengthened before axillary crutch walking, due to the demands of supporting body weight?
questions.explanation: Crutch walking requires strong triceps for elbow extension during push-down and shoulder depressors to support body weight through the shoulders and arms. Without adequate strength in these muscles, the patient cannot effectively transfer weight off the lower extremities. Pre-crutch strengthening exercises targeting triceps and shoulder depressors are mandatory before gait training begins to ensure safe and effective crutch use.

options: Head and neck for postural alignment
Knee joint as the primary lever arm
questions.explanation: Standard systematic observational gait analysis begins at the distal segments (foot and ankle) and progresses superiorly through knee, hip, pelvis, trunk, and upper extremities. This distal-to-proximal sequencing ensures primary deviations at ground contact are identified before examining compensatory patterns that may appear at proximal segments. Beginning proximally risks misidentifying compensations as primary pathology.
questions.question: A physiotherapy student begins a systematic observational gait analysis. Which body segment should be observed first according to standard protocol?

options: Severe visual impairment affecting depth perception
Complete lower limb paralysis with intact arms
Normal strength but impaired cognition only
Lack of strength to lift the walker with each step
Excessive upper limb strength requiring resistance
questions.explanation: Rolling walkers have wheels on the front legs to assist movement for patients who cannot lift the walker due to lack of strength, allowing them to push rather than lift the device forward with each step. This design reduces the energy cost of ambulation for weaker patients. Standard walkers, by contrast, require sufficient strength to lift and reposition the device with each step.
questions.question: Rolling walkers are equipped with wheels on the front legs primarily to assist patients who present with which limitation?
Four-point crutch gait is generally considered the safest pattern but requires which additional demand compared to other patterns?
options: Complete absence of upper limb involvement
Greater coordination due to constant weight shifting
Less coordination than any other pattern
Simultaneous movement of both crutches together
No requirement for balance at all
questions.explanation: Four-point gait is regarded as the safest crutch gait pattern because three points of contact remain on the ground at most times, but it demands greater coordination since the patient must constantly shift weight in a specific sequence. This makes it more cognitively demanding despite its inherent stability. It is typically prescribed when a patient cannot fully support weight on either leg.

In pathological gait, heel strike may not occur normally, with other parts of the foot contacting the ground first due to weakness, deformity, or pain. This alters the subsequent loading and progression through stance phase. Recognizing an absent or altered heel strike is a key observational skill in gait analysis.
questions.question: In pathological gait, which stance phase event may fail to occur as it does in normal walking?
Motor control is best defined as the process by which the central nervous system achieves which outcome?
options: Storing long-term memories unrelated to movement
questions.explanation: Motor control is defined as an area of natural science exploring how the central nervous system produces purposeful, coordinated movement through interaction with the rest of the body and the environment. It encompasses processes ranging from simple reflex loops to complex neural networks spanning the central and peripheral nervous systems. This foundational process underlies the initiation, direction, and grading of voluntary movement.

options: Expensive equipment availability in the clinic
Examiner skill and systematic observation experience
Time of day of the assessment session
Weather conditions and ambient lighting levels
questions.question: Observational gait analysis accuracy depends primarily on which factor?
questions.explanation: Observational analysis reliability correlates strongly with clinician skill level, knowledge of normal and abnormal gait patterns, and systematic observation experience. Without a structured approach — sequentially observing each joint from foot to head in each plane — the clinician's attention is split across too many variables simultaneously. A systematic protocol prevents this by focusing attention on one segment at a time, using video to enable repeated viewing.

The knee completes two cycles of flexion and extension per gait cycle, the first occurring shortly after heel strike for shock absorption and the second during swing phase to clear the foot. The initial flexion following heel strike is approximately 15 degrees, while swing phase flexion averages about 70 degrees. This dual-cycle pattern distinguishes knee kinematics from the single-cycle pattern at the hip.
questions.question: How many cycles of flexion and extension does the knee joint complete during a single gait cycle?
A physiotherapist teaches three-point crutch gait following non-weight-bearing right ankle surgery. What is the correct sequence of limb advancement?
questions.explanation: Three-point gait accommodates one non-weight-bearing limb with a normal contralateral leg. Both crutches advance simultaneously with the non-weight-bearing limb, then the sound limb swings through. The sequence is crutches-and-affected-limb together, then sound limb. This provides stability for the weight-free limb while maintaining forward progression using the normal leg and bilateral crutch support.
options: Right foot forward, then both crutches advance
Both crutches forward together, then left foot advances
Left foot forward alone, then crutches follow
Crutches and right foot advance, then left foot
Left crutch forward, then right crutch, then left foot

questions.explanation: As the tibia moves forward over the fixed foot in closed chain motion, the ankle reaches approximately 10 degrees of dorsiflexion before heel-off initiates a second wave of plantarflexion. This second plantarflexion wave peaks at about 20 degrees near toe-off. Most sagittal plane ankle motion during gait occurs within the plantarflexion range rather than dorsiflexion.
questions.question: During closed chain motion in stance phase, the tibia advancing over a fixed foot places the ankle into approximately how many degrees of dorsiflexion?
A quad cane differs from a standard cane primarily by which structural feature?
options: Four small feet giving a wider base
A retractable spike tip for ice
A curved handle for bilateral use
A single large wheel at the base
questions.explanation: A quad cane has four small feet that provide a wider base of support compared to a standard single-tipped cane, offering greater stability for patients with more significant balance impairment. This makes it an intermediate option between a standard cane and more supportive devices like a walker. The hemi walker offers even greater support by combining features of a walker with the quad cane design.

questions.question: A wheelchair user develops a sacral pressure ulcer. Which positioning change most directly reduces sacral loading?
options: Increasing seat depth to distribute femoral load
Adding armrests for upper extremity pressure relief
Raising footrests to reduce hamstring tension
Tilt-in-space to redistribute load off the sacrum
Reducing seat width for better lateral support
questions.explanation: Tilt-in-space systems orient the entire seat unit backward, transferring weight from the ischial/sacral area toward the posterior thighs and back. This pressure redistribution reduces sustained loading on bony prominences vulnerable to pressure ulcers. Unlike recliner wheelchairs which increase sacral shear forces, tilt maintains the seat-back relationship unchanged, preventing shear at the interface — the gold standard for managing sacral pressure.

When braced ambulation requires significantly elevated energy expenditure, cardiovascular conditioning becomes prerequisite to functional use. If the patient lacks the cardiopulmonary reserve to sustain the required energy output, braced walking becomes impractical for daily activities. Physiotherapy must incorporate cardiovascular endurance training alongside gait training. Energy cost assessment also guides decisions about wheelchair use for longer versus shorter functional community distances.
questions.question: A patient with bilateral KAFOs requires 300% more energy than normal gait. What does this finding suggest for rehabilitation planning?
options: The orthoses are properly fitted and functioning correctly
The patient should immediately transition to a wheelchair
Gait training should stop to prevent exhaustion
Speed must be increased to reduce energy cost per metre
Cardiovascular fitness training is essential for functional use

questions.question: To update a gait rehabilitation protocol, which level of evidence most strongly informs it?
questions.explanation: Evidence-based practice requires integrating the best available evidence with clinical expertise and patient values. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials represent the highest level of evidence, synthesising multiple studies to reduce individual study bias. This is followed by individual RCTs, then observational studies, case series, and expert opinion. Protocol development should prioritise systematic review evidence where available.
options: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials
Expert clinical opinion from senior practitioners
Individual case studies with positive clinical outcomes

questions.explanation: Leg rest length is measured from a pen firmly placed in the popliteal fossa to the bottom of the heel, ensuring the footplate sits at an appropriate height to support the lower leg without excessive pressure. questions.answerText:
(i) Primary hyperparathyroidism. It is about twice as likely to affect women as men, and most cases are diagnosed between 50 and 60 years of age; the prevalence is about 1-4 per 1000 in the general population.
(ii) It most commonly results from a sporadic PTH-secreting solitary adenoma of the parathyroid chief cells (about 85% of cases), multiglandular hyperplasia, or parathyroid carcinoma. Clinical forms include symptomatic disease (fragility fractures, kidney function impairment, gastrointestinal disturbances, and cognitive/social dysfunction) or asymptomatic hypercalcaemia presenting with fatigue, mild depression or malaise.
(iii) Biochemically, primary hyperparathyroidism shows increased calcium, decreased phosphate, and increased intact PTH; this differs from secondary hyperparathyroidism (decreased calcium, increased phosphate, increased iPTH) and tertiary hyperparathyroidism (increased calcium, increased phosphate, increased iPTH).
(iv) Parathyroidectomy is always the definitive treatment for symptomatic disease; antiresorptive drugs - oestrogen, bisphosphonates, raloxifene, and cinacalcet - are used to reduce PTH-driven bone resorption when surgery is not immediately undertaken.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Acetylcholine is synthesized in the cholinergic nerve ending from choline and acetylcoenzyme A, a reaction catalysed by choline acetyltransferase (CAT); choline uptake into the nerve terminal is the rate-limiting step. Synthesized acetylcholine is stored in vesicles at the nerve terminal, together with ATP.
A(ii) Acetylcholine is released from the nerve terminal by a calcium-dependent mechanism of exocytosis in response to a nerve action potential; there is a "readily releasable" pool near the membrane and a "reserve pool" that replenishes it.
A(iii) The action of acetylcholine is terminated by acetylcholinesterase, which hydrolyses it to inactive choline and acetate; butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) in the liver and plasma hydrolyses exogenous esters.
A(iv) Cholinergic receptors are divided into muscarinic (M1-M5) and nicotinic (NM at the neuromuscular junction, NN at autonomic ganglia) receptors.
B. Irreversible anticholinesterases (organophosphates) phosphorylate the active site of acetylcholinesterase, forming a stable bond so that the enzyme cannot be readily regenerated by hydrolysis; this produces a long duration of action with excessive accumulation of acetylcholine at all cholinergic sites, causing widespread peripheral and central effects, whereas reversible anticholinesterases are only slowly hydrolysed and their effect wears off as the enzyme is regenerated.
C. Muscarinic receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors found at postganglionic parasympathetic effector sites (heart, smooth muscle, glands) with responses that are slower and either excitatory or inhibitory; nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels found at the skeletal neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, and their activation always causes a rapid increase in Na+ and Ca2+ permeability, depolarization and excitation.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Acetylcholine (ACh) is synthesised within the cholinergic neuron from choline and acetyl coenzyme A by choline acetyltransferase; choline uptake is the rate-limiting step and can be inhibited by hemicholinium and triethylcholinium. ACh is stored in vesicles along with ATP and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), transported into vesicles by a high-affinity vesicular transporter that can be inhibited by vesamicol.
A(ii) ACh is released from the cholinergic nerve terminal by a calcium-dependent mechanism of exocytosis in response to a nerve action potential; there is a readily releasable pool and a reserve pool. Black widow spider venom (alpha-latrotoxin) causes massive release of ACh, while botulinum and tetanus toxins inhibit exocytosis of ACh.
A(iii) The action of ACh is terminated by acetylcholinesterase (AChE), which hydrolyses it to choline and acetate; butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) in the liver and plasma hydrolyses exogenous esters.
B. The Tensilon (edrophonium) test can distinguish flaccid paralysis from cholinergic crisis from that due to myasthenia gravis: edrophonium worsens the paralysis caused by cholinergic crisis but strengthens the muscle in myasthenia gravis.
C. In a cholinergic crisis there is excessive accumulation of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, which over-stimulates nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate; this leads to flaccid paralysis of skeletal muscle and respiratory failure because the intercostal muscles and diaphragm can no longer respond normally to the persistently high acetylcholine levels, and this element (respiratory arrest) cannot be reversed by atropine, which only blocks the muscarinic effects.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Statins are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that catalyses an early, rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. The reduced free cholesterol content of hepatocytes increases synthesis and reduces degradation of LDL receptors; the greater number of hepatic LDL receptors increases removal of LDL from the blood. Statins also lower LDL by enhancing removal of LDL precursors (VLDL, IDL) and decreasing hepatic VLDL production, accounting for their triglyceride-lowering effect.
A(ii) Intestinal absorption varies between 30% and 85%. Most statins are given as active beta-hydroxy acids, except simvastatin and lovastatin, which are inactive lactones requiring hepatic transformation. There is extensive first-pass hepatic uptake, so systemic bioavailability is 5-30%; more than 95% of statins and their metabolites are protein-bound (except pravastatin, 50% bound); plasma concentrations peak in 1-4 hours; half-lives are 1-4 hours except for atorvastatin and rosuvastatin (about 20 hours).
A(iii) Adverse effects: hepatotoxicity (rare, about one case per million person-years; ALT should be checked at baseline and after 3 months for high doses); myopathy, whose risk rises with plasma statin concentration and is increased by factors that inhibit statin catabolism, including concomitant fibrates (especially gemfibrozil), cyclosporine, digoxin, warfarin, macrolides, azole antifungals, niacin, HIV protease inhibitors, amiodarone and nefazodone; and statins are not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
B. Combining a statin with a fibrate, particularly gemfibrozil, increases the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis because the fibrate diminishes statin catabolism, raising plasma statin concentrations; the combination is usually used cautiously and with a low-dose statin, and is particularly useful in patients with hypertriglyceridaemia and high LDL-C.
C. Statins lower LDL-C by inhibiting hepatic cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase), which increases LDL-receptor expression and LDL clearance; bile-acid sequestrants instead bind negatively charged bile acids in the gut, preventing their reabsorption and depleting the hepatic bile-acid pool, which increases hepatic LDL-receptor production by a different route and thereby increases LDL clearance - an effect that is partially offset by compensatory upregulation of HMG-CoA reductase, which is why combining a statin with a resin is more effective than either agent alone.
