A 50-year-old woman is given a drug for treatment of hypertension. Over the next several weeks, she finds the drug becomes progressively less effective at the same dose and her blood pressure is no longer controlled.
(i) Identify the two possible pharmacodynamic mechanisms responsible for this reduced drug response.
(ii) Define tachyphylaxis and explain why increasing the dose will not restore the response once it has occurred.
(iii) A different antihypertensive (an enzyme inducer) is then added. Explain the pharmacokinetic mechanism by which this could further reduce the effect of the first drug.
(iv) Upon review, her dose is increased. Explain how the concept of the dose-response relationship can be used to determine the new required dose.
(v) Explain the concept of receptor regulation by drugs, specifically how prolonged agonist use and prolonged antagonist use each alter receptor numbers.
questions.answerText:
(i) Two pharmacodynamic mechanisms of reduced drug response: (1) Tolerance: a gradual decreased response to a drug, requiring a higher dose to achieve the same initial response; it develops over a long period of time. (2) Downregulation: a reduction in the total number of receptors due to prolonged receptor activation (e.g. by chronic use of an agonist or prolonged inhibition of metabolism of a neurotransmitter).
(ii) Tachyphylaxis is a rapid decrease in response to an agonist drug following repeated administration within a brief period; it is an acute form of desensitization. Increasing the dose of the drug will not improve the response because the available receptors are already maximally stimulated or desensitized; there are no additional receptors available to respond to a higher dose.
(iii) If the added antihypertensive is an enzyme inducer (e.g. a barbiturate), it will stimulate hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, increasing the rate of metabolism of the first antihypertensive drug. This increases clearance, shortens the half-life, and reduces steady-state plasma concentration, thereby further reducing its antihypertensive effect (pharmacokinetic antagonism).
(iv) The dose-response relationship describes the magnitude of the response as a function of exposure to a drug. Drug dose-response involves the principles of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics and can be used to determine the required dose and frequency to achieve the desired response. Increasing the dose shifts the effect along the dose-response curve toward the maximum achievable effect (efficacy), provided the drug has sufficient intrinsic activity.
(v) Receptor regulation by drugs: downregulation: prolonged use of an agonist or prolonged inhibition of metabolism of a neurotransmitter leads to a reduction in the total number of receptors, resulting in reduced response. Upregulation: prolonged deprivation of interaction with physiological ligands (e.g. chronic use of a receptor antagonist) leads to an increase in the number of receptors. Example of rebound: following abrupt withdrawal of a beta-blocker, the increased number of beta-receptors causes a rebound phenomenon such as rebound hypertension.

(i) Drugs cross the placenta primarily by simple diffusion. Lipid-soluble, unionized drugs enter foetal blood from maternal circulation. The foetus may therefore be exposed to all drugs taken virtually by the mother. Penetration is least with drugs possessing high degree of ionization and/or low lipid solubility.
(ii) Mammary glands epithelium has a lipoid membrane which separates blood with pH 7.4 from milk with pH 6.6. Weak bases diffuse rapidly and attain higher levels in breast milk than in plasma. Fat-soluble drugs diffuse easily into breast milk (e.g. tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, isoniazid). Acidic drugs are poorly diffused into breast milk.
(iii) Sulfonamides can displace bilirubin from plasma protein binding sites. The displacement of bilirubin leads to kernicterus (free bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier and damages the brain of the neonate).
(iv) Drugs emerge in the breast milk 30-90 minutes after administration and secretion persists for more than one hour.
(v) Newborn babies have less ability to metabolize drugs than adults; they have limited ability to conjugate drugs with glutamic acid, glycine, and glutathione. The microsomal enzymes are not well developed in newborns; therefore the incidence of drug toxicity is higher in newborn babies than in adults.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman is given a sulfonamide antibiotic during the last weeks of pregnancy and continues breastfeeding postpartum. Her newborn develops prolonged jaundice.
(i) Explain the pharmacokinetic mechanism by which the drug reached the neonate during pregnancy.
(ii) Explain the mechanism by which the drug passes into breast milk, and identify which class of drugs (acidic or basic) reaches higher concentrations in breast milk than in plasma.
(iii) State the consequence of this drug in the neonate in relation to bilirubin protein binding.
(iv) State the timing of drug appearance in breast milk and duration of secretion after maternal administration.
(v) Explain why newborn babies have higher drug toxicity rates than adults in general, relating to drug metabolism.

A medical student attends a pharmacology viva and is shown a drug chart where a patient developed hypoglycaemic coma while on insulin and was later found to also be taking a sulfonamide antibiotic.
(i) Identify the pharmacokinetic mechanism causing this adverse interaction.
(ii) Explain the specific molecular basis of how the sulfonamide caused this interaction.
(iii) State the clinical consequence of this interaction in this patient.
(iv) Name two other drugs that are known to cause similar displacement interactions and describe their clinical consequences.
(v) List four factors that determine the extent of plasma protein binding of a drug.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pharmacokinetic mechanism is competitive displacement from plasma protein binding sites. Drugs with less affinity can be displaced from protein binding by other compounds having higher affinity, resulting in a higher concentration of free drug.
(ii) Sulfonamides have higher affinity for plasma protein (albumin) binding sites than tolbutamide and can competitively displace it. Tolbutamide (an oral hypoglycaemic agent) is displaced from its binding site, leading to a sudden increase in free tolbutamide, which causes an exaggerated hypoglycaemic effect.
(iii) The clinical consequence is hypoglycaemic coma due to excess free tolbutamide in circulation acting at its receptor without restraint.
(iv) Two other examples: (a) Displacement of bilirubin by sulfonamides or salicylates in neonates leading to kernicterus (free bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes brain damage). (b) Displacement of warfarin by phenylbutazone leading to haemorrhage (excess free warfarin causes uncontrolled anticoagulation).
(v) Four factors that determine the extent of plasma protein binding: (1) the drug's affinity to the protein molecule; (2) number of protein binding sites; (3) protein concentration; (4) drug concentration.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old asthmatic uses a salbutamol inhaler. During an acute attack, he is unable to use his inhaler effectively and is brought to a clinic. The attending doctor needs to choose between intravenous and intramuscular routes.
(i) State the time to onset of action for the intravenous route and explain the pharmacokinetic reason for this speed.
(ii) Compare the onset of action time for the intramuscular route with the intravenous route and explain the reason for any difference.
(iii) List two advantages of the intravenous route over the intramuscular route.
(iv) List two disadvantages of the intravenous route compared with the intramuscular route.
(v) State what type of preparation can be given intramuscularly to produce slow, sustained drug release, and give one clinical example.
questions.answerText:
(i) Intravenous route: 30-60 seconds. When the drug is injected intravenously, it directly reaches the blood stream and the effect is produced immediately. The absorption phase is bypassed; bioavailability is 100%.
(ii) Intramuscular route: 10-20 minutes. The drug is injected into large skeletal muscles; absorption is fast but must still occur across tissue before reaching the blood stream, unlike IV where there is no absorption phase. Therefore onset is slower than IV.
(iii) Two advantages of IV: (a) precise, accurate, and almost immediate onset of action; (b) large quantities can be given; (c) can be used in unconscious patients; (d) one main advantage is that the dose response to drug is accurately measurable (any two accepted).
(iv) Two disadvantages of IV over IM: (a) greater risk of adverse effects including high concentration attained rapidly and risk of embolism; (b) expertise required; (c) recovery not easy; (d) expensive; (e) must be given slowly; (f) it is the most risky route (any two accepted).
(v) Repository and slow-release preparations (depot or reservoir preparations) can be given intramuscularly using insoluble salts or suspensions in non-aqueous vehicles. Clinical example: contraceptive implants (subcutaneous) which provide sustained release over months or even years.

questions.question:
A patient is admitted after taking an overdose of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, a weak acid). The clinical pharmacologist recommends alkalinizing the urine.
(i) Using the principle of ionization, explain why alkalinization of urine promotes the excretion of aspirin.
(ii) Name the two renal mechanisms by which drugs are eliminated, and explain which one handles most aspirin elimination.
(iii) Explain the concept of renal clearance and define a clearance factor >1.0 in terms of tubular secretion.
(iv) State the approximate glomerular filtration rate in adults and the volume of plasma filtered per minute.
(v) State how acidification of urine would affect aspirin excretion and explain why.
questions.answerText:
(i) Aspirin is a weak acid. Alkalinization of urine increases the degree of ionization of a weak acid, promoting its excretion in urine and reducing its reabsorption into blood. Ionized forms of drug are unable to cross the lipid tubular membrane; therefore they cannot be reabsorbed and are excreted in urine.
(ii) Two renal mechanisms: glomerular filtration and tubular secretion (with tubular reabsorption being the opposing process). Renal excretion = glomerular filtration + tubular secretion - tubular reabsorption. Drugs not bound to plasma protein, in a free state, are easily filtered by renal glomeruli.
(iii) Renal clearance of a drug is defined as the volume of plasma in millilitres which contains the quantity of drug eliminated in urine by the kidney in one minute. When the clearance of a drug is greater than that of inulin (120 ml/min), this shows that the drug is actively secreted by the renal tubuli. A clearance factor >1.0 means the filtered drug is not reabsorbed by the convoluted tubuli and a proportion is actively secreted; e.g. a drug with renal clearance of 180 ml/min has a clearance factor of 1.5, meaning the filtered drug is not reabsorbed and one-third is actively secreted.
(iv) About 1200-1300 ml of blood flows through the renal glomeruli per minute, from which about 120-130 ml of primary urine is formed per minute. Drugs in free state soluble in 120-130 ml of plasma are eliminated per minute.
(v) Acidification of urine decreases the degree of ionization of weak acid, thereby enhancing its absorption (reabsorption from the tubule) and reducing its elimination in urine. Therefore, acidifying the urine in aspirin overdose would worsen toxicity by causing more aspirin to be reabsorbed.

(i) Cerebral hypoxia/ischaemia triggers a cascade of successive events: triggering of programmed apoptosis; energy imbalance (membrane paralysis); massive neurotransmitter release (glutamate); an inflammatory reaction with production of arachidonic acid (a source of free radicals); and endogenous thrombolysis with reperfusion phenomena.
The lesion extends progressively; there are intermediary zones where intact cells are "paralysed" and thus susceptible to recovery, and there is selective vulnerability, as some anatomic structures of the brain (e.g. striatum, hippocampus) die more rapidly than others.
(ii) Indications: clinical diagnosis of stroke; onset of symptoms to time of drug administration less than or equal to 4.5 hours; CT scan showing no haemorrhage or oedema of more than 1/3 of the MCA territory; age 18 years or above; consent by patient or surrogate.
Contraindications: sustained BP >185/110 mmHg despite treatment; platelets <100,000; HCT <25%; glucose <50 or >400 mg/dL; use of heparin within 48 hours with prolonged PTT or elevated INR; rapidly improving symptoms; prior stroke or head injury within 3 months, or prior intracranial haemorrhage; major surgery in preceding 14 days; minor stroke symptoms; gastrointestinal bleeding in preceding 21 days; recent myocardial infarction; coma or stupor.
(iii) The definitive treatment is thrombolysis using recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA), e.g. alteplase, administered within 4.5 hours of the first clinical signs.
Thrombolytic (fibrinolytic) agents convert entrapped plasminogen to plasmin and initiate local fibrinolysis by binding to fibrin in a clot, disrupting the embolus and attacking the cause of the ischaemia/hypoxia.
In highly-selected patients, acute thrombolytic treatment reduces disability and improves outcome, although there is a risk of increased mortality from haemorrhage, requiring adequate patient selection.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents within hours of onset of a focal neurological deficit consistent with stroke. What is the underlying pathophysiologic cascade in ischaemic stroke?
(ii) Outline the indications and contraindications for thrombolytic therapy.
(iii) What is the definitive thrombolytic treatment, its mechanism, and its time window?

questions.answerText:
(i) Pharmacogenetics is the aspect of pharmacology that studies the genetic basis of variable responses (efficacy and safety/tolerability) of individuals to pharmacotherapeutic agents. Genetic polymorphism is the occurrence of two or more genetically determined phenotypes in a population, with each allelic variation occurring in >1% of a population. This variation may result from SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) or indels (insertions/deletions).
(ii) CYP2D6. CYP3A subfamily is responsible for the metabolism of about 50% of clinically used drugs, while CYP2D6 is involved in about 25% of clinically used drugs.
(iii) For codeine, the poor metabolizer phenotype results in failure to convert codeine to its active metabolite morphine (via O-dealkylation). Without morphine production, the patient receives no analgesia despite dose escalation.
(iv) Example: metoprolol (a CVS drug metabolized by CYP2D6). In poor metabolizers, metoprolol is not metabolized normally; the drug accumulates, and the poor metabolizer phenotype results in predisposition to adverse effects such as bradycardia or hypotension.
(v) Phenotyping involves drug administration followed by determination of metabolic ratio; individuals may exhibit normal, lower, higher, or no enzyme activity. Drawback: tedious and time-consuming; confounding influence of other CYP enzymes; impractical to carry out before drug administration. Genotyping employs molecular biology techniques to target specific polymorphic sites; specificity for any particular gene is guaranteed and easily adapted to patient management. Drawback: environmental influences including drug interactions cannot be determined; influence of rare alleles different from the selected cannot be determined.
questions.question:
A physician prescribes codeine to a patient for pain relief. The patient is later found to be a poor metabolizer of CYP2D6 and experiences no analgesia despite the dose being increased.
(i) Explain the pharmacogenetic basis of variable drug response in terms of genetic polymorphism.
(ii) Identify the CYP isoform involved and state the proportion of clinically used drugs metabolized by this isoform.
(iii) Explain why the poor metabolizer phenotype results in lack of efficacy specifically for codeine, naming the relevant active metabolite.
(iv) State one other drug metabolized by CYP2D6 where the poor metabolizer phenotype leads to adverse effects (not lack of efficacy), and explain why.
(v) Distinguish between pharmacogenetics phenotyping and genotyping methods, including one drawback of each.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The aminoglycosides include streptomycin, neomycin, paromomycin, kanamycin, gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin and spectinomycin; except for gentamicin (produced by the mold Micromonospora purpurea), the aminoglycosides are produced by members of the genus Streptomyces.
Mechanism of action: all bind to a non-enzymic site on the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, causing an abnormality in codon:anticodon recognition, resulting in misreading of the mRNA and hence production of defective bacterial protein; their effect is bactericidal and is enhanced by agents that interfere with cell wall synthesis; they have minimal action against anaerobic organisms.
A(ii) They are polycations and highly polar; not absorbed in the GIT, but rapidly absorbed after intramuscular or subcutaneous injection, and can also be given intravenously or intrathecally.
Binding to plasma protein is minimal; they do not enter cells and do not cross the blood-brain barrier, but they penetrate the eye and reach high concentration in secretions and body fluids, and they cross the placenta.
Half-life is 2-3 hours; elimination is by glomerular filtration in the kidney, with 50-60% of a dose excreted unchanged within 24 hours.
B(i) Aminoglycosides are most widely used against gram-negative enteric organisms and act at the bacterial ribosome (30S subunit) as their site of action; they may be given together with a penicillin in infections caused by streptococcus, pseudomonas or listeria; streptomycin and kanamycin are also active against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Streptomycin is virtually entirely reserved for the treatment of tuberculosis, and may be used with tetracycline for plague or brucellosis; neomycin and framycetin are too toxic for parenteral use and are used only topically or to reduce bacterial flora of the gut before surgery.
C(i) The unwanted effects of aminoglycosides include ototoxicity (vertigo, ataxia and loss of balance), nephrotoxicity, and paralysis due to neuromuscular blockade.
Because aminoglycosides are eliminated by glomerular filtration in the kidney, with a large proportion excreted unchanged, they achieve high renal concentrations, which is consistent with their nephrotoxic potential.
Resistance to aminoglycosides can occur through inactivation by microbial enzymes carried on plasmids, failure of penetration, or lack of binding of the drug to the ribosome due to a mutation altering the binding site on the 30S subunit (streptomycin alone); netilmicin and amikacin are not affected by the common inactivating enzymes.
Their narrow therapeutic index, combined with minimal plasma protein binding and predominantly renal elimination, underlies the clinical need to monitor renal function and auditory/vestibular function during therapy.
This combination of ribosomal site of action, renal route of elimination and inner-ear tissue penetration together explains why the same drug class produces both nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity as its principal dose-limiting adverse effects.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the source, classification and mechanism of action of the aminoglycosides.
A(ii) Describe the pharmacokinetics of the aminoglycosides.
B(i) State the therapeutic use and site of action of the aminoglycosides.
C(i) Explain the pharmacological basis of aminoglycoside ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

questions.answerText:
(i) ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema.
(ii) ACE inhibitors inhibit the enzyme ACE (kininase II), which also breaks down bradykinin; angioedema, like the associated dry irritant cough, is attributable to accumulation/potentiation of kinins (bradykinin) rather than to the renin-angiotensin pathway itself. It is rare but potentially fatal.
(iii) The offending ACE inhibitor should be stopped immediately, and the airway should be managed as angioedema can be life-threatening.
(iv) An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) should be substituted; a dry cough attributable to ACE inhibitors should trigger switching to an ARB, since ARBs block the angiotensin II receptor directly rather than inhibiting ACE, and so do not cause the same accumulation of bradykinin/kinins responsible for cough and angioedema.
questions.question:

(ii) Describe the pathological basis of this adverse effect, naming the pathway affected.
(iii) Describe the immediate management of this reaction.
(iv) Name the definitive/alternative class of drug that should be substituted, and explain why it is less likely to cause this reaction.

questions.answerText:
(i) The most appropriate route is intravenous (IV). The drug is either injected as a bolus or infusion into one of the superficial veins; the drug directly reaches the blood stream and the effect is produced immediately (within 30-60 seconds). The absorption phase is bypassed and bioavailability is 100%.
(ii) Subcutaneous injection should be avoided in shock patients due to vasoconstriction. Absorption by the subcutaneous route is slow because it is less vascular, and vasoconstriction associated with shock further impairs absorption, making the route unreliable in this emergency.
(iii) Intravenous: onset within 30-60 seconds; drug directly enters the blood stream without an absorption phase; bioavailability is 100%. Intramuscular: onset within 10-20 minutes; the drug is injected into large skeletal muscles (deltoid, triceps, gluteus maximus); absorption must still occur from muscle tissue before reaching systemic circulation; bioavailability is less than 100% due to binding to connective tissues.
(iv) Specific disadvantages of the IV route: (a) greater risk of adverse effects including high concentration attained rapidly and risk of embolism; (b) expertise required; (c) recovery not easy once administered; (d) expensive (syringe and needle required); (e) repeated dose dependent on patency of vein; (f) must be given slowly.
(v) Bioavailability is the relative amount (fraction) of drug from the administered dosage form that enters systemic circulation; also, the rate and extent of drug absorption into systemic circulation. For IV administration, bioavailability is 100% (f = 1). For intramuscular administration, bioavailability is less than 100% (f < 1) due to binding to connective tissues.
questions.question:

(i) State the most appropriate route of administration for this emergency, explaining the pharmacokinetic rationale.
(ii) Explain why subcutaneous injection should be avoided in this patient and state the relevant mechanism.
(iii) Compare the onset of action of the intravenous and intramuscular routes for emergency drug administration, explaining the pharmacokinetic basis for the difference.
(iv) State the specific disadvantages of the intravenous route that make it more risky than intramuscular administration.
(v) Define bioavailability and state its value for IV administration compared with intramuscular administration.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Vitamin D comprises a number of structurally related sterol compounds; it is a fat-soluble vitamin. Vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol) is produced by ultraviolet irradiation of ergosterol in plants and is not the naturally occurring form; vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is made by ultraviolet irradiation of 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin.
Vitamin D3 undergoes successive hydroxylations: first in the liver, to form 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, and second in the proximal tubules of the kidney, under the control of parathyroid hormone, to form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
A(ii) Vitamin D promotes active transport of calcium and phosphate in the gut (increasing absorption) and in the renal tubules (reducing excretion).
B(i) Indications for vitamin D use include treatment/prevention of rickets and osteomalacia, osteoporosis, hypoparathyroidism, psoriasis, and renal osteodystrophy in chronic kidney disease.
C(i) Deficiency of vitamin D causes rickets in growing children, osteomalacia, and hypocalcaemia.
Because vitamin D promotes active transport of calcium and phosphate in the gut, increasing their absorption, and in the renal tubules, reducing their excretion, its deficiency reduces the calcium and phosphate available for bone mineralization.
Sources of vitamin D are exposure to sunlight, fish oil, and egg yolks; inadequate synthesis or intake, or failure of the hydroxylation steps in the liver and kidney, therefore leads to reduced circulating 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
With reduced active vitamin D, less calcium and phosphate are absorbed from the gut and more is lost in the urine, producing the hypocalcaemia that characterizes deficiency states.
In growing children, whose bones are still being actively mineralized, this manifests as rickets, a failure of normal bone mineralization at the growth plates.
In adults, where growth plates have closed, the same defect in bone mineralization manifests as osteomalacia rather than rickets.
This illustrates why the same underlying pharmacological defect (impaired vitamin D-dependent calcium/phosphate handling) produces different named clinical syndromes depending on the skeletal maturity of the patient.
This is the basis for treating both rickets/osteomalacia and vitamin D-deficiency states with therapeutic vitamin D, to restore active transport of calcium and phosphate at the gut and renal tubule.

questions.answerText:
A. The major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand are wall stress (intraventricular pressure, ventricular radius/volume, wall thickness), heart rate, and contractility. Determinants of coronary blood flow are: increased myocardial oxygen demand normally leads to increased coronary blood flow in the normal heart; the duration of diastole (coronary blood flow drops to almost nil during systole); damage to the endothelium of coronary vessels, which alters their ability to dilate; and increased coronary vascular resistance, caused by metabolic products and autonomic activity, which reduces coronary blood flow.
B. Angina pectoris is chest pain caused by accumulation of metabolites resulting from ischaemia; the imbalance between oxygen delivery and myocardial oxygen demand is the primary pathophysiological mechanism behind angina pectoris. Drugs used to increase oxygen delivery include coronary vasodilators and anti-thrombotic drugs, while drugs used to decrease oxygen demand include vasodilators (organic nitrates, calcium channel blockers) which reduce afterload and preload, and cardioinhibitory drugs (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers) which reduce heart rate and contractility.
C. Unstable angina, in particular, is an acute coronary syndrome in which there is a change in the character, frequency and duration of previously stable chest pain; if the imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand is not corrected, the ischaemia can progress, so that anti-thrombotic (anticoagulant and antiplatelet) drugs are used specifically to prevent thrombus formation and progression to a more severe distant/further functional deficit such as myocardial infarction.

(i) Triptans are a class of analgesic used in migraine management. Under the general classification of analgesics, triptans are recognised as a specific class alongside narcotic (opioid) analgesics and NSAID analgesics. The choice of analgesic therapy depends on assessment of pain intensity using the 3-step analgesic ladder.
(ii) The WHO 3-step analgesic ladder classifies analgesics as: Non-narcotic analgesics (including NSAIDs and p-aminophenol derivatives such as paracetamol) for mild to moderate pain; narcotic (opioid) analgesics — morphine and related compounds — for moderate to severe pain; and analgesic adjuvants. The choice of analgesic therapy is dependent on assessment of pain intensity.
(iii) Codeine is another alkaloid found in opium (1 to 2%). It is used in cough-suppressant drugs and anti-diarrhoeal preparations. Routes of administration include: injected (subcutaneously or intramuscularly) and oral — medical preparations of codeine are made in combination with other chemicals and are available in the form of tablets and syrups. Codeine is very rarely abused as its analgesic effects are mild and severe side effects (e.g. convulsions) are often experienced. It can be combined with acetaminophen or aspirin. It is a short-acting opioid taken by mouth with effect lasting a few hours per dose.
(iv) Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid classified as a short-acting (immediate release) opioid. It is available in lollipop form and may be used for the management of breakthrough pain. A long-acting patch form is also available which can be effective for up to 72 hours. Fentanyl is listed as a pure opioid agonist that binds to MOR (mu opioid receptor) with high affinity (+++) and has low affinity for KOR (+) and no significant affinity for DOR or NOR.
(v) Methadone is a fully synthetic opioid. It is effective when administered orally, so it is usually taken in the form of tablets. Methadone is commonly used as a weaning drug for some opioids or heroin and is also useful in the management of chronic pain. It is effective orally and lasts for about 4–6 hours at a time. It is classified as a short-acting opioid (immediate release).

questions.answerText:
A(i) The beta-lactam antibiotics comprise the sub-classes: Penicillins, Cephalosporins, Monobactam, and Carbapenem.
A(ii) Penicillins were originally sourced from Penicillium moulds; their mechanism of action involves inhibition of cross-linkage between units of peptidoglycan.
Peptidoglycan consists of a polysaccharide (N-acetyl muramic acid and N-acetyl glucosamine) and a pentapeptide; the bacterial transpeptidase enzyme (also known as penicillin-binding protein) binds the penicillin because it resembles its original substrate, D-alanyl-D-alanine, so the overall mechanism is inhibition of cell wall synthesis, disrupting the functional stability of the bacterium.
A(iii) Resistance mechanisms include altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs); reduced influx/increased efflux; and inactivating enzymes (beta-lactamases), of which there are four classes — Class A (extended-spectrum beta-lactamases that degrade penicillins and some cephalosporins plus carbapenems, inhibited by beta-lactamase inhibitors), Class B (destroys all except aztreonam), Class C (degrades cephalosporins) and Class D (degrades cloxacillin, inhibited by beta-lactamase inhibitors).
Plasmid-mediated synthesis of beta-lactamase enzyme is the major resistance mechanism, while reduced cell penetration and altered target site (PBP) are minor mechanisms.
B(i) Because resistance to penicillins is chiefly caused by plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase enzymes that inactivate the drug, beta-lactamase inhibitors (sulbactam, clavulanic acid, tazobactam) are combined with penicillins to protect them from this inactivation and restore antibacterial activity.
This is clinically justified because Class A and Class D beta-lactamases are specifically inhibited by these agents, extending the drugs' usefulness against resistant organisms.
By contrast, Class B beta-lactamases destroy all beta-lactams except aztreonam, and Class C beta-lactamases degrade cephalosporins, so inhibitor combinations do not overcome every resistance mechanism.
C(i) Penicillins are narrow-spectrum (benzylpenicillin, phenoxymethylpenicillin), aminopenicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin), anti-staphylococcal (methicillin, nafcillin, oxacillin) and antipseudomonal (carbenicillin, ticarcillin) agents.
Cephalosporins are derived from Cephalosporium species, with a ring structure derived from 7-aminocephalosporanic acid, and are classified into generations: 1st generation (cephalothin, cefazolin, cefalexin), 2nd generation (cefuroxime, cefoxitin, cefaclor, cefproxil), 3rd generation (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, with antipseudomonal ceftazidime and cefoperazone), 4th generation (cefepime, cefquinome) and 5th generation (ceftobiprole, ceftolozane).
Newer cephalosporin generations are characterized by increased efficacy in gram-negative infections and decreased frequency of dosing.
Both classes share the same fundamental mechanism (inhibition of cell wall synthesis) and the same major resistance mechanism (plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase production), but differ in their source organism, ring structure and generational spectrum of activity.

(i) Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis) — an acute, life-threatening, hypermetabolic state induced by excessive release of thyroid hormones in an individual with thyrotoxicosis.
(ii) It is a decompensated state of thyroid hormone-induced severe hypermetabolism involving multiple systems, due to increased release (with or without increased synthesis) of thyroid hormone; hypertension may be followed by congestive heart failure associated with hypotension and shock, and the condition is almost invariably fatal if left untreated.
(iii) Supportive measures; antiadrenergic drugs such as propranolol (60-80 mg orally every 4-6 hours, or intravenously 0.5-1 mg over 10 minutes then 1-2 mg over 10 minutes every few hours) to minimize sympathomimetic symptoms, cardioselective beta blockers (atenolol, metoprolol) in reactive airway disease, calcium channel blockers when beta blockers are contraindicated, or intravenous esmolol for rapid titration; iodine preparations; glucocorticoids; bile acid sequestrants.
(iv) High-dose thionamides — propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole; PTU has a theoretical advantage because of its early onset of action and its capacity to inhibit peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 — together with treatment of the underlying precipitating condition.

questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors/predisposing factors for Type 1 (juvenile) diabetes mellitus: genetic predisposition; autoimmune disorders with antibodies developed against islet beta cells; infections, especially viral infections; modifiable factors such as obesity, hypertension and low physical activity may also predispose to diabetes generally.
Type 1 DM has early onset (below 35 years), is often of normal weight, has a lower likelihood of family history (<20%), and results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells with decreased insulin levels.
(ii) Complications: hyperglycaemia leads to reduced glucose utilisation, glucosuria, hyperosmolar diuresis, frequent urination and dehydration.
Increased lipolysis raises free fatty acids, generating ketone bodies (acetone, acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) and ketoacidosis.
Chronic hyperglycaemia forms advanced glycosylated end products (AGEs) via HbA1c and sorbitol pathways, damaging the lens, retina, blood vessels, peripheral nerves and renal tubules.
There is increased incidence of urinary tract infection, vaginal candidosis and skin infections from hyperglycaemia and glycosuria.
(iii) Management of Type 1 DM is with insulin and diet (Type 1 DM has decreased insulin levels and requires insulin plus diet, unlike Type 2 which may be managed with diet, oral hypoglycaemics, exercise or insulin).
Insulin should be administered 15-20 minutes prior to meals; rapid-acting or short-acting (regular/crystalline zinc) insulin is used for acute correction, as regular insulin is the only preparation that can be given intravenously.
Insulin is preferred/justified as the definitive agent in Type 1 DM because these patients have an absolute insulin deficiency from autoimmune beta-cell destruction, so oral agents that rely on stimulating endogenous insulin secretion or reducing insulin resistance are not appropriate.

A(i) Describe the hormones essential for lactogenesis and their control.
A(ii) Describe the milk ejection reflex.
B(i) Explain how this system relates to disorders of lactation.
C(i) Explain why hyperprolactinaemia, a pituitary hormone disorder, produces a distant effect (hypogonadism).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Oxytocin, prolactin and cortisol are essential for lactogenesis; growth hormone, insulin and thyroxine play facultative roles.
Suckling stimulates sensory receptors in the nipple, sending nerve impulses via the spinothalamic tract (T4, T5, T6) to the mesencephalon and hypothalamus, decreasing prolactin inhibiting factor (dopamine) and thereby increasing synthesis and release of prolactin.
Maintenance of lactation requires normal non-pregnant levels of prolactin; absence of prolactin means lactation does not occur, as seen with hypophysectomy, postpartum pituitary necrosis, or destructive disease of the hypothalamic-pituitary system; ingestion of dopamine agonists (e.g. bromocriptine, L-dopa) results in failure of lactation.
A(ii) The milk ejection reflex is the mechanism by which milk is transported from the alveoli to the nipple: suckling stimulates sensory fibres in the nipple, sending impulses to the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, causing synthesis and release of oxytocin, which contracts the myoepithelial cells and releases milk into the lactiferous ducts and sinuses.
Release of oxytocin becomes a conditioned response in lactating women, requiring only visual stimulation or conscious thought.
B(i) Galactopoiesis (maintenance of milk production once established) depends on regular and frequent milk removal from the mammary gland, which stimulates further milk production via regular suckling and synthesis/release of oxytocin and prolactin.
Reduced milk production can occur when catecholamines, produced during stress and anxiety, antagonize the action of oxytocin on myoepithelial cells, with norepinephrine causing vasoconstriction.
C(i) Prolactin's primary function is to stimulate and maintain lactation, but it also decreases sexual drive and reproductive function.
Hyperprolactinaemia, whether from a pituitary disorder or from drugs that block dopamine D2 receptors (removing the inhibitory effect of dopamine on prolactin release), causes hypogonadism, manifesting as infertility, oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea and galactorrhea in premenopausal women, and loss of libido and erectile dysfunction in men.
This occurs because excess prolactin, though secreted from the pituitary, exerts a systemic reproductive-suppressive effect distant from the pituitary itself, on gonadal function.
This is the basis for treating hyperprolactinaemia-associated hypogonadism with D2 receptor agonists such as bromocriptine and cabergoline, which restore the normal dopamine-mediated inhibition of prolactin release, thereby relieving the distant reproductive effect.
This mirrors the ADH pathway (also a posterior pituitary hormone) and the ACTH pathway (an anterior pituitary hormone) in illustrating a recurring principle: a pituitary hormone released in excess produces its major clinical effect not at the pituitary itself, but at a distant target organ or axis.

(i) Prostaglandins (PGE2 and PGI2), the major prostaglandins synthesised by the gastric mucosa, are involved in protecting the stomach against erosive and necrotising stimuli, including NSAIDs; endogenous PGs bind to the EP3 receptor on parietal cells, inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and decreasing intracellular cyclic AMP, which decreases acid secretion, and PGs mediate cytoprotective effects such as increasing mucosal blood flow and stimulating gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion. NSAIDs deplete these protective prostaglandins, predisposing to erosive and necrotising mucosal injury.
(ii) Misoprostol, a PGE1 analogue, was introduced for co-administration with NSAIDs to minimise gastric damage by replacing depleted PGE1 in prostaglandin-inhibiting therapies; it is the only drug shown to protect both the stomach and duodenum from NSAID-induced erosions and ulcers, though it is less effective as a healing agent, and gives less pain relief, than H2-antagonists and proton pump inhibitors.
(iii) Proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole) block the H+K+ ATPase proton pump of the parietal cell, irreversibly binding to the sulfhydryl group of cysteine on the enzyme, and are a mainstay for ulcer healing.
H2-receptor antagonists (e.g. ranitidine, nizatidine) are also used; if H. pylori infection is present, eradication therapy (e.g. a proton pump inhibitor or H2RA plus amoxicillin plus metronidazole as triple therapy) helps prevent recurrence and may be potentially curative.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification of barbiturates by duration of action:
- Long-acting: Phenobarbital (phenobarbitone) — has the least lipid-solubility, slow GI absorption, slow onset, and long duration of action (6–8 hours).
- Intermediate-acting: Amobarbital — has moderate lipid-solubility, moderate GI absorption, moderate onset, and moderate duration of action (4–6 hours).
- Short-acting: Pentobarbital — has high lipid-solubility, rapid GI absorption, rapid onset, and short duration of action (2–4 hours).
- Ultrashort-acting: Thiopental — has very high lipid-solubility, very rapid onset (within 30 seconds), and very short duration of action (20–30 minutes).
A(ii) Benzodiazepines act very selectively on GABA-A receptors by binding to a regulatory site distinct from the GABA binding site, thereby enhancing receptor affinity for GABA and facilitating the opening of GABA-activated chloride channels. Barbiturates act on the same GABA-A receptor system but differ from benzodiazepines: they can directly activate the chloride channel at higher doses and are not limited to enhancing GABA's effects. The neurobiology of anxiety disorders is underpinned by the balance between excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) neurotransmission, with GABA inhibition primarily mediated by the ionotropic GABA-A receptor.
B(i) Barbiturate pharmacokinetic properties are directly related to their lipid solubility, which governs: the rate of GI absorption; the speed of onset; the duration of action; and the rate of redistribution from CNS to peripheral tissues. Thiopental's very high lipid-solubility accounts for its rapid CNS penetration and its very short duration of action (20–30 minutes) as it redistributes rapidly to peripheral tissues. Phenobarbital's low lipid-solubility accounts for its slow onset and prolonged duration of action (6–8 hours). Unlike benzodiazepines, barbiturates affect hepatic microsomal enzymes and therefore have more drug interactions.
B(ii) Benzodiazepines in acute overdose are considerably less dangerous than other sedative-hypnotic drugs — they cause prolonged sleep without serious depression of respiration or cardiovascular centre. Barbiturates, by contrast, carry a much greater risk in overdose. Barbiturates have a narrower safety margin than benzodiazepines, which have a wide safety margin (minor effect on respiratory and vasomotor centres). Flumazenil is a specific competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine receptor that can be used in benzodiazepine overdose; no equivalent specific reversal agent exists for barbiturates.
B(iii) Specific uses of barbiturates: phenobarbital is used as an established antiepileptic drug (AED) licensed before 2000, used as a first-line or adjunctive treatment in epilepsy. In the withdrawal of barbiturates (phenobarbital and primidone), the risk of rebound seizures is particularly great; if a drug needs to be withdrawn rapidly due to life-threatening side effects, a benzodiazepine can be used to cover the withdrawal phase. The phenobarbital withdrawal regimen is 15–30 mg every 2 weeks as part of a drug change, and 15–30 mg every 4 weeks for total withdrawal. Benzodiazepines have largely replaced barbiturates because benzodiazepines have: lower liability for drug abuse; no effect on hepatic microsomal enzymes (fewer drug interactions); no change in normal sleep pattern (no depression of REM sleep); no hangover effect; and a wide safety margin.

questions.answerText:
(i) Thiazide diuretics are recommended as a good first-line choice for hypertension (along with calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, or angiotensin II receptor antagonists); current guidelines suggest starting patients over the age of 55 years, and those of African/Afro-Caribbean ethnicity, on calcium channel blockers or thiazide diuretics.
Thiazide diuretics should not be used in pregnancy, and gout may be worsened by thiazide diuretics, while kidney stones may be improved by thiazide-type diuretics.
(ii) Adverse effects include hypokalaemia (weakness, fatigue, muscle cramp, cardiac arrhythmias), acute saline depletion (dehydration, decreased BP), dilutional hyponatraemia, magnesium depletion, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia, and GIT and CNS disturbances; doses in excess of 25 mg per day of hydrochlorothiazide incur an unacceptable risk of hypokalaemia.
(iii) Thiazide and loop diuretics deplete circulating potassium unless combined with a potassium-sparing diuretic or supplemental potassium.
Directly acting potassium-sparing agents (triamterene and amiloride) are non-steroidal organic bases that decrease potassium excretion independent of aldosterone, and are used in conjunction with loop and thiazide diuretics to prevent hypokalaemia and also augment antihypertensive action; spironolactone is justified as an alternative option in that it inhibits aldosterone, increasing sodium excretion while decreasing potassium excretion, directly counteracting the potassium loss caused by thiazides.

(i) An elderly diabetic patient on a long-acting oral hypoglycaemic agent presents with an acute neurologic emergency mimicking a stroke. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology?
(iv) What is the management?
questions.answerText:
(i) Severe hypoglycaemia (sulfonylurea-induced), which may present as an acute neurologic emergency mimicking a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) in the elderly.
(ii) Renal and hepatic impairment, and being elderly and taking a long-acting sulfonylurea; the longer the half-life of the agent, the more likely it is to cause hypoglycaemia.
(iii) Sulfonylureas act as insulin secretagogues; hypoglycaemia (including coma) is a recognized adverse reaction, especially in renal and hepatic impairment and in the elderly on long-acting drugs, because metabolism and excretion of the drug and its active metabolites are impaired, prolonging the hypoglycaemic action.
(iv) Severe hypoglycaemia can be treated with glucagon, which is used for its action on hyperglycaemia (it enhances gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis); diazoxide, which has a potent hyperglycaemic action, is also used to treat hypoglycaemia.

questions.question:
Describe the factors affecting drug metabolism (biotransformation) under the following headings:
A(i) Describe how animal species and sex affect drug metabolism, giving one specific example for each.
A(ii) Describe how age (neonates and elderly) affects drug metabolism and the clinical implications for drug toxicity.
B(i) Explain how pathological conditions and body temperature affect drug metabolism.
B(ii) Describe the cytochrome P450 (CYP) system in detail: its location, the three main families involved in drug metabolism, the proportion of drugs metabolized by CYP3A4, and how CYP genes/enzymes are named.
B(iii) Explain enzyme induction and inhibition by the CYP system, with one example of a CYP3A4 inducer and one inhibitor.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Animal species: drug metabolism varies in different animals; O-demethylation of codeine takes place easily in humans but does not occur in dogs; conjugation with sulfuric acid is well developed in cats but glucuronidation does not occur in cats. Sex: most drugs metabolize faster in male than in female humans; this may be due to the male hormone (testosterone) effect; high levels of progesterone and pregnandiol in pregnancy are responsible for weak glucuronic and sulfuric acid conjugation processes.
A(ii) Age: fetus and newborn babies have less ability to metabolize drugs than adults; newborn babies have limited ability to conjugate drugs with glutamic acid, glycine, and glutathione; acetylation and conjugation with sulfuric acid are well developed in newborns; the incidence of drug toxicity is higher in newborn babies because microsomal enzymes are not well developed; children however metabolize phenobarbital and diazoxide faster than adults. In elderly people, the microsomal enzyme is reduced; drugs therefore have more potent effects and longer duration of action; the rate of occurrence of drug toxicity is more in elderly people than in young people.
B(i) Pathological conditions: liver disease reduces biotransformation of drugs and prolongs their duration of action; radioactive radiation decreases activity of microsomal enzymes (with the exception of reductase enzymes); starvation inhibits microsomal enzymes in males whereas in females, starvation can stimulate drug metabolism. Body temperature: drugs are metabolized faster in febrile conditions; as a result, drugs have a faster onset of action and shorter duration of action during febrile conditions.
B(ii) Cytochrome P450 enzymes are heme-containing enzymes involved in Phase I drug metabolism (oxidation), found in great abundance in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of the liver. A CYP gene (and enzyme) is identified with the family numeral (e.g. 1, 2, 3), subfamily letter (e.g. A, B, C), and specific enzyme numeral (e.g. 1, 2, 3); for example CYP2D6, CYP3A4. The three main families involved in drug metabolism in the liver are CYP1, CYP2, CYP3. CYP3A subfamily is responsible for the metabolism of about 50% of clinically used drugs; CYP2D6 is involved in about 25%.
B(iii) CYP3A4 inducers: rifampicin and carbamazepine. These increase enzyme activity, increasing metabolism of substrates such as midazolam, felodipine, lovastatin, buspirone, and sildenafil, reducing their plasma concentration and efficacy. CYP3A4 inhibitors: atazanavir, cimetidine, clarithromycin, ketoconazole. These reduce enzyme activity, increasing plasma concentration of CYP3A4 substrates and potentially causing toxicity.

questions.question:
Describe the routes of drug administration under the following headings:
A(i) Define local routes of drug administration and list the topical sites of application, giving one example of a dosage form for each.
A(ii) Describe deeper tissue routes of administration as local routes, giving three examples.
B(i) Describe the oral (peroral) route in full: its advantages, limitations, and the concept of first-pass effect as it applies to this route.
B(ii) Describe the parenteral routes of injection, listing the types, the speed of onset for each, and the specific advantages and disadvantages of subcutaneous injection.
B(iii) Explain the factors that guide the choice of route of drug administration in clinical practice.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Local routes of drug administration are used for localized lesions at accessible sites; systemic absorption of drug is minimal or absent; systemic side effects or toxicity are also absent or minimal. Topical sites: Skin - applied as ointment, cream, lotion, powder, paste, spray. Mucous membrane - mouth (lozenges, mouth washes). Eyes/Ear/nose - drops, ointment, irrigation, nasal spray. GIT - non-absorbable drugs given orally e.g. MgOH, sucrafate, neomycin. Bronchi and lungs - inhalations, aerosols e.g. nebulized solution or fine powder - salbutamol. Urethra - jellies e.g. lidocaine. Vagina - pessaries, vaginal tablets, inserts, cream. Anal - ointment, suppositories.
A(ii) Deeper tissue routes: certain deep tissues can be approached without the drug entering the systemic circulation or with minimal systemic circulation. Examples: intra-articular injections; intrathecal; retrobulbar injection.
B(i) The oral route is the oldest and commonest mode of drug administration. Advantages: safer, more convenient, needs no assistance, non-invasive, often painless, and cheap; solids and liquid dosage available. Limitations: action is slower and thus not suitable for emergencies; unpalatable drugs may be difficult to administer; may cause nausea and vomiting; cannot be used for uncooperative, vomiting, or unconscious patients; certain drugs are not absorbed; some are destroyed by the digestive juice or in the liver. First-pass effect: drugs absorbed perorally are initially transported to the liver via the portal vein, where they may be metabolized before reaching systemic circulation, reducing bioavailability.
B(ii) Parenteral routes include: Subcutaneous (SC) - drug deposited in loose subcutaneous tissue; absorption is slow because it is less vascular; should be avoided in shock patients due to vasoconstriction; provides sustained release (e.g. contraceptive implants); onset 5-30 minutes. Intramuscular (IM) - drug injected into large skeletal muscles including deltoid, triceps, gluteus maximus; absorption is fast, and it is less painful; onset 10-20 minutes. Intravenous (IV) - drug directly reaches the blood stream; effects produced immediately; onset 30-60 seconds; most risky route. Intradermal (ID) - drug injected into the surface of the skin; example: BCG.
B(iii) Factors guiding choice of route of drug administration: physical and chemical properties of the drug (solid/liquid/gas, solubility, stability, pH); site of desired action - local or generalized; rate and extent of absorption of that drug from the different routes; effect of digestive juice and first-pass metabolism on the drug; rapidity with which the response is desired: routine or emergency; accuracy of dose required; condition of the patient (unconscious, vomiting).

questions.question:
(i) A patient on parenteral treatment for a gram-negative infection develops vertigo, ataxia and loss of balance together with reduced urine output. Which drug class is responsible, and what is the diagnosis?
(ii) Name the mechanism of action of this drug class.
(iii) What are the adverse effects/monitoring parameters relevant to this presentation?
(iv) State a contraindication or caution relevant to this drug class.
questions.answerText:
(i) Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin, streptomycin, kanamycin, tobramycin, amikacin); the diagnosis is aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity (vertigo, ataxia, loss of balance) with accompanying nephrotoxicity.
(ii) Aminoglycosides bind to a non-enzymic site on the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, causing an abnormality in codon:anticodon recognition; this results in misreading of the mRNA and hence production of defective bacterial protein. Their effect is bactericidal and is enhanced by agents that interfere with cell wall synthesis.
(iii) Unwanted effects: ototoxicity (vertigo, ataxia, loss of balance), nephrotoxicity, and paralysis due to neuromuscular blockade. Elimination is by glomerular filtration in the kidney, with 50-60% of a dose excreted unchanged within 24 hours, so renal function should be monitored.
(iv) They do not cross the blood-brain barrier and are not absorbed in the GIT, but they do cross the placenta; caution is required given their nephrotoxic and ototoxic potential, and their bactericidal effect is minimal against anaerobic organisms.

A(i) Receptors are chemical structures, composed of protein, that receive and transduce signals that is translated into a biological response (e.g. muscle contraction, hormone secretion). A molecule that binds to a receptor is called a ligand and can be a protein, peptide, neurotransmitter, hormone, drug, toxin, etc. Receptors specifically recognize and bind to ligands. This binding initiates a conformational change in the receptor protein leading to a series of biochemical reactions (signal transduction), often involving the generation of secondary messengers.
A(ii) By location: Transmembrane receptors include ligand-gated ion channels, G protein-coupled receptors, and enzyme-linked hormone receptors. Intracellular receptors are those found inside the cell, and include cytoplasmic receptors and nuclear receptors.
B(i) Type 1: Ligand-gated ion channels (ionotropic receptors) - examples are fast neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and GABA. Type 2: G protein-coupled receptors (metabotropic receptors) - includes receptors for several hormones and slow transmitters e.g. dopamine, glutamate; composed of seven transmembrane alpha helices. Type 3: Kinase-linked receptors (receptor tyrosine kinase) - the insulin receptor is an example. Type 4: Nuclear receptors. Type 5: Voltage-sensitive ion channels.
B(ii) Loss of receptor function: Myasthenia Gravis is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies destroy nicotinic acetylcholine receptors located in skeletal muscle. Gain of receptor function: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus can be associated with a gain-of-function mutation, resulting in increased expression of the a2A-adrenergic receptor, a GPCR that prevents or suppresses the secretion of insulin.
B(iii) Affinity is the ability of the drug to combine with the receptor. Intrinsic activity (efficacy) is the ability of the drug to activate the receptor after receptor occupation. Agonist: has both affinity and maximal intrinsic activity, AI = 1. Competitive antagonist: has affinity but no intrinsic activity, AI = 0. Partial agonist: has affinity and suboptimal intrinsic activity, AI is between 0 to 1. Inverse agonist: has affinity but a negative intrinsic activity, between 0 to -1.

questions.answerText:
(i) The antidiuretic hormone (ADH/arginine vasopressin) pathway, acting via renal V2 receptors, is implicated.
(ii) The water permeability of the renal collecting duct cells, mediated by aquaporin-2 water channels inserted into the apical membrane following V2 receptor activation and cAMP-dependent protein kinase A activity, is affected; this normally allows water reabsorption in proportion to the population of aquaporin-2 channels.
(iii) Differential causes: central diabetes insipidus (a failure of ADH secretion, so collecting tubules are impermeable to water — can follow neurosurgery, head injury, or diseases such as sarcoid infiltrating the posterior pituitary) and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (ADH secretion is normal, but there is a defect in the V receptor or signalling mediators making the kidneys unresponsive to ADH). In either disease, the net effect is increased excretion of water, producing polyuria, polydipsia and possible electrolyte imbalance.
(iv) Urine volume is reduced and urine osmolarity increased by vasopressin administration if the diabetes insipidus is due to deficiency of ADH (central), but not when it is due to unresponsiveness of the kidney to ADH (nephrogenic); aqueous vasopressin or lypressin injection can therefore be used to differentiate neurogenic from nephrogenic DI, while desmopressin (2 micrograms intramuscularly) is now the preparation of choice for this purpose, with dosing individualized by measuring 24-hour urine.

A(i) Describe the neuro-endocrine system linking the hypothalamus, pituitary and target endocrine glands.
A(ii) Describe the categories of drugs that act on hypothalamic and pituitary hormones.
B(i) Explain how this system relates to thyroid disease.
C(i) Explain why a disorder of thyroid hormone release can produce distant, multi-organ effects (thyroid storm).
questions.answerText:
A(i) The hypothalamus connects intimately with the nervous system and the pituitary; the pituitary gland (the 'master gland') connects with other target endocrine glands, which include the thyroid, pancreas, adrenal, pituitary and ovaries.
The control of metabolism, growth and reproduction is mediated by a combination of neural and endocrine systems located in the hypothalamus and pituitary gland; the pituitary consists of an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis).
The hormones of the anterior pituitary are regulated by hypothalamic neuropeptides called releasing or inhibiting factors/hormones, produced in the hypothalamus and reaching the pituitary via the hypophyseal portal system; interaction with their receptors activates genes that promote synthesis of protein precursors.
A(ii) Drugs that mimic or block the effects of hypothalamic and pituitary hormones have applications in three primary areas: as replacement therapy for hormone deficiency states; as antagonists for diseases caused by excess production of pituitary hormones; and as diagnostic tools for identifying endocrine abnormalities.
Hypothalamic hormones include thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH), corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH), gonadotropin releasing hormone (GRH), and prolactin inhibiting hormone (dopamine), in addition to GHRH and somatostatin.
B(i) The thyroid is one of the target glands connected to the pituitary within this neuro-endocrine system, so disorders of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid relationship, or of the thyroid gland itself, disturb the regulated release of thyroid hormone.
Excessive release of thyroid hormone in a person with thyrotoxicosis produces the hypermetabolic state that underlies thyroid disease, and in its most extreme form, thyroid storm.
C(i) Thyroid storm is a decompensated state of thyroid hormone-induced, severe hypermetabolism involving multiple systems and is the most extreme state of thyrotoxicosis.
Because thyroid hormone acts systemically to drive metabolism, its excessive release produces distant effects across organ systems: fever, tachycardia and hypertension (cardiovascular), and neurological and gastrointestinal abnormalities.
Hypertension may be followed by congestive heart failure that is associated with hypotension and shock (cardiac decompensation).
Chest radiography may show cardiac enlargement due to congestive heart failure and pulmonary edema; head CT may be needed to exclude other neurologic conditions contributing to the presentation.
Thus a single gland's hormone excess, acting through its widespread metabolic receptors, produces a multi-system crisis that is almost invariably fatal if left untreated.

(i) The parathyroid hormone (PTH) - vitamin D - calcium axis is implicated; this presentation is hypercalcaemia.
(ii) PTH exerts minute-to-minute control of blood calcium; it acts through PTH1R on bone, stimulating IL-6 secretion which promotes osteoclast differentiation, stimulating RANKL production and inhibiting osteoprotegerin (OPG), thereby promoting calcium mobilization from bone; on the renal tubule it activates 1-alpha-hydroxylase and increases calcium reabsorption; on the GI tract it indirectly increases calcium and phosphate absorption via calcitriol.
(iii) Major causes of hypercalcaemia: hyperparathyroidism, cancer, thiazide diuretics. Minor causes: hypervitaminosis D, sarcoidosis, thyrotoxicosis, adrenal insufficiency.
(iv) Treatment includes saline diuresis (rehydration with saline and diuresis with furosemide); bisphosphonates (inhibit osteoclast action, e.g. intravenous pamidronate and zoledronate); calcitonin (blocks osteoclasts and promotes calciuria); denosumab (an antibody against RANKL, used for hypercalcaemia of malignancy resistant to bisphosphonate); corticosteroids (inhibit 1-alpha-hydroxylase, used in calcitriol-mediated hypercalcaemia such as sarcoidosis and tuberculosis); gallium nitrate (inhibits bone resorption); and plicamycin (a cytotoxic antibiotic, used only when other therapies fail) — the choice is reasoned by matching the mechanism of the causative pathway (e.g. corticosteroids for calcitriol-mediated causes, denosumab for bisphosphonate-resistant malignancy).

(ii) Toxicity is defined as a 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration above 150 ng/mL (compared with an optimal range of 30-60 ng/mL, insufficiency of 20-30 ng/mL, and deficiency below 20 ng/mL).

A(i) Acute ischaemic stroke treatment involves a therapeutic cocktail of thrombolysis, antithrombotics, antiplatelet agents, neurocytoprotectors, and other co-therapies (antihypertensives, osmotic diuretics, intravenous fluid, insulin for hyperglycaemia, anticonvulsants, antipyretics).
A(ii) Thrombolytic (fibrinolytic) agents such as recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA, alteplase) convert entrapped plasminogen to plasmin and initiate local fibrinolysis by binding to fibrin in a clot, aiming to disrupt the embolus. Aspirin, given at 75-300 mg as soon as diagnosis is confirmed, is an antiplatelet agent aiming to minimise the size of the infarction, limit extension of the thrombus, and reduce the risk of early recurrence of stroke.
B(i) In highly-selected patients, acute treatment of ischaemic stroke with thrombolytic therapy reduces disability and improves outcome; however, there is a risk of increased mortality by haemorrhage, so there is a need for adequate patient selectivity in terms of indications and contraindications for thrombolysis.
B(ii) Contraindications to thrombolysis include sustained BP >185/110 mmHg despite treatment, platelet count <100,000, prolonged PTT or elevated INR, prior stroke or head injury within 3 months, prior intracranial haemorrhage, major surgery in the preceding 14 days, and coma or stupor; these exist because thrombolysis carries a risk of bleeding, and if this occurs within the cranium, it produces intracranial haemorrhage, causing damage to brain tissue distant from the original occluded vessel and worsening rather than improving neurological outcome; higher doses of aspirin similarly have little advantage and only worsen gastrotoxicity, and dual antiplatelet/anticoagulant combinations carry a high risk of bleeding complications, so are not routinely used.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Drug abuse: drug use without medical supervision, or drug use that is not generally accepted on medical grounds. Tolerance: the decrease in pharmacological effect on repeated administration of a drug; it develops over time. Drug dependence: an adaptive state that results from repeated administration of a drug; characterised by tolerance and production of withdrawal symptoms upon cessation, which propels the person to continue drug use (relapse); hence drug taking becomes compulsive, taking precedence over other needs. Physical dependence: discontinuation of drugs results in characteristic withdrawal syndromes (e.g. myalgia, tremors, sweating, convulsions — negative reinforcement); develops as a result of tolerance produced by a resetting of homeostatic mechanisms in response to repeated drug use. Psychological dependence: drug discontinuation produces emotional distress or mental disturbance; intensity may vary from desire and craving for the drug to compulsive drug-seeking behaviour.
A(ii) Categories of dependence-producing drugs:
1. Drugs used for medicinal purposes: general anaesthetics (propofol, ketamine); sedatives and tranquillizers — benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, flunitrazepam), barbiturates; opioid analgesics (morphine, methadone); some psychostimulants (amphetamine, cocaine, caffeine); hallucinogens (LSD, mescaline, phencyclidine/PCP).
2. Non-therapeutic drugs: nicotine and ethanol.
B(i) The common feature of dependence-inducing drugs (opioids, nicotine, amphetamines, ethanol, and cocaine) is that they have a positive reinforcing action ('reward') through activation of the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway. Dopamine is released during rewarding or pleasurable stimuli (such as food, sex, drugs, etc.), creating positive feelings that reinforce the behaviour. Although for some of these drugs, their primary sites of action may be elsewhere in the brain, they all increase the extracellular level of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens.
B(ii) Addiction is marked by a change in behaviour caused by biochemical changes in the brain after continued drug/substance abuse. It involves continuous use of drugs despite negative consequences; taking high risks to obtain the drugs; and is a complex state that involves both psychological and physical dependence. The main characteristic that distinguishes addiction from dependence is the combination of mental and physical dependence with uncontrollable behaviour in obtaining and using a substance. It involves persistent use of the drug despite harm to oneself and others. Dependence is characterised by: strong desire or sense of compulsion to take a substance; difficulty in controlling drug use; presence of a physiological withdrawal state; tolerance; neglect of alternative pleasures and interests.
B(iii) Host (user) variables: in general, the effects of drugs vary among individuals. Individuals may show variation in blood levels to the same dose of a drug. Polymorphism of genes that encode enzymes involved in absorption, metabolism, and excretion, and in receptor-mediated responses, may contribute to different degrees of reinforcement or euphoria among individuals. Susceptibility to dependence can be inherited. Environmental variables: initiating and continuing illegal drug use appear to be influenced significantly by societal norms and peer pressure. The memory of previous drug-induced experiences can be very intense and long-lasting, giving rise to craving triggered by cues such as experiencing the environment associated with previously taking the drug, the sight of drug-administration paraphernalia, or direct rewarding effects of the drug.

questions.answerText:
(i) This is an acute dystonic reaction — prolonged tonic muscle contractions occurring usually within 24–96 hours of dosage initiation or dosage increase. The presentation here (torticollis — head drawn to one side, tongue protrusion) is consistent with dystonia. They may be life threatening (e.g. pharyngeal-laryngeal dystonia). Other dystonic presentations include trismus, glossospasm, blepharospasm, oculogyric crisis, and retrocollis. They occur primarily with FGAs. Risk factors include younger patients (especially male) and use of high-potency agents and high doses — haloperidol at 15 mg/day is a high-potency FGA at a high dose. First-generation antipsychotics are more likely to be associated with movement disorders, particularly drugs that bind tightly to dopaminergic neuroreceptors such as haloperidol.
(ii) Treatment includes IM or IV anticholinergics or benzodiazepines: benztropine mesylate 2 mg, or diphenhydramine 50 mg may be given IM or IV; or diazepam 5–10 mg slow IV push; or lorazepam 1–2 mg IM may be given. Relief usually occurs within 15–20 minutes of IM injection or 5 minutes of IV administration. Prophylactic anticholinergic medications are reasonable when using high-potency FGAs (e.g. haloperidol and fluphenazine), in young men, and in patients with a prior dystonia. Dystonia can be minimized by using lower initial doses of FGAs and by using SGAs instead of FGAs.
(iii) Anticholinergic effects include constipation, urinary retention, dry mouth, blurred vision. These effects are common with low-potency first-generation antipsychotics and clozapine. Anticholinergic side effects most likely to occur with low-potency FGA, clozapine, and olanzapine include impaired memory, dry mouth, constipation, tachycardia, blurred vision, inhibition of ejaculation, and urinary retention. Elderly patients are especially sensitive to these side effects. Dry mouth can be managed with increased intake of fluids, oral lubricants (Xerolube), ice chips, or sugarless chewing gum or hard candy. Constipation can be treated with increases in exercise, fluid, and dietary fibre intake.
(iv) Akathisia symptoms include subjective complaints (feelings of inner restlessness) and/or objective symptoms (pacing, shifting, shuffling, or tapping feet). Treatment with anticholinergics is disappointing; reduction in antipsychotic dose may be the best intervention. Alternatively, switch to an SGA, although akathisia occasionally occurs with SGAs. Quetiapine and clozapine appear to have the lowest risk. Benzodiazepines may be used but not in patients with a history of substance abuse. Propranolol (up to 160 mg/day), nadolol (up to 80 mg/day), and metoprolol (up to 100 mg/day) are reported to be effective.
(v) Sexual dysfunction is very common, and up to 49% of patients taking antipsychotic drugs report problems with sexual dysfunction (low libido, diminished arousal). Both FGAs and SGAs can impair arousal and orgasm in men and women.

A(i) Describe the three possible mechanisms of action of methylxanthines.
A(ii) List their pharmacological actions on the CNS, CVS and smooth muscle.
A(iii) List their adverse effects and drug interactions.
B(i) What monitoring precaution follows from their narrow margin of safety?
B(ii) Explain the pharmacologic basis of sudden death following rapid intravenous injection of methylxanthines.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Methylxanthines act by three possible mechanisms: release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; inhibition of phosphodiesterase, which degrades cAMP, leading to increased cAMP levels (causing bronchodilatation, cardiac stimulation and vasodilatation); and blockage of adenosine receptors (adenosine contracts smooth muscle, especially bronchial smooth muscle, and dilates cerebral blood vessels).
A(ii) CNS: they are CNS stimulants. CVS: they stimulate the heart, increase contractility and heart rate (tachycardia), dilate blood vessels including the coronary artery, reduce peripheral resistance, but constrict cranial vessels (used for migraine, especially caffeine). Smooth muscle: relaxation in all smooth muscle including bronchi and kidney (mild diuretic effect by inhibiting tubular reabsorption of sodium and water); they cause contraction of skeletal muscle, increased gastric acid and pepsin secretion, increased BMR, and inhibit release of histamine and other mediators from mast cells and inflammatory cells.
A(iii) Adverse effects (dose-dependent, as theophylline has a narrow margin of safety): dyspepsia, headache, nervousness, insomnia, tremors, vomiting, palpitations; rapid IV injection causes syncope and sudden death. Interactions: agents that induce theophylline metabolism (smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbitone) decrease its plasma levels; agents that inhibit its metabolism (erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives) increase its plasma levels; it enhances the effects of diuretics and hypoglycaemic agents.
B(i) Because theophylline has a narrow margin of safety (narrow therapeutic index), therapeutic drug monitoring is especially important with its use, to keep plasma levels within the safe range and avoid dose-dependent toxicity.
B(ii) Adverse effects of methylxanthines occur in a dose-dependent manner because of the narrow margin of safety; rapid IV injection produces a sudden high plasma concentration that stimulates the heart (increasing contractility and heart rate) beyond a safe threshold, and this cardiac stimulation is stated to cause syncope and sudden death.

A(i) Insulin secretagogues include sulfonylureas and meglitinides.
A(ii) First-generation sulfonylureas: chlorpropamide, tolbutamide, tolazamide and acetohexamide (tolbutamide is shortest-acting, chlorpropamide longest-acting). Second-generation: glibenclamide, glipizide, gliclazide and glimepiride, which are more potent than first-generation agents. Meglitinides (nateglinide, repaglinide) act like sulfonylureas without the sulfonylurea moiety, have short duration of action and low risk of hypoglycaemia, and are used for postprandial hyperglycaemia.
A(iii) Sulfonylureas can cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain.
B(i) Biguanides (metformin, and phenformin which was withdrawn because of lactic acidosis) are preferred agents for obese patients because they are weight neutral; metformin is first-line therapy for type 2 DM and the only oral agent demonstrated to reduce macrovascular events in type 2 DM.
B(ii) Biguanides decrease blood glucose by increasing glucose uptake and utilisation in skeletal muscle, reducing hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis) and inhibiting intestinal glucose absorption; because they do not increase serum insulin concentration, they do not cause hypoglycaemia (euglycaemic agents), unlike sulfonylureas, which act as insulin secretagogues and can cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain.
Biguanides are contraindicated in renal impairment, alcohol intake, cardiac failure and chronic lung disease because inhibition of gluconeogenesis predisposes to lactic acidosis, a risk not shared in the same way by sulfonylureas.
