A 60-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been on chlorpromazine for several years. She now presents with repetitive, involuntary lip-smacking, tongue protrusion, and facial grimacing, which worsen with stress.
(i) What is the diagnosis and its classic clinical presentation?
(ii) What are the risk factors for developing this condition?
(iii) What other adverse effects of antipsychotic drugs affect the cardiovascular system and body weight?
(iv) What is hyperprolactinaemia in the context of antipsychotic use, and which drugs most commonly cause it?
(v) What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and what are its features?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is tardive dyskinesia (TD), a chronic extrapyramidal symptom characterised by abnormal involuntary movements of the tongue, lips, face, trunk, and extremities, occurring with chronic antipsychotic therapy. The classic presentation is buccolingual-masticatory (BLM) or orofacial movements. Symptoms may become severe enough to interfere with chewing, wearing dentures, speech, respiration, or swallowing. Facial movements include frequent blinking, brow arching, grimacing, upward deviation of the eyes, and lip smacking. Restless choreiform and athetotic movements of the limbs occur in later stages. Movements may worsen with stress, decrease with sedation, and disappear with sleep.
(ii) Risk factors for tardive dyskinesia include: duration of antipsychotic therapy; higher dose; possibly cumulative dose; increasing age; occurrence of acute extrapyramidal symptoms; poor antipsychotic response; diagnosis of organic mental disorder; diabetes mellitus; mood disorders; and possibly female gender.
(iii) Cardiovascular symptoms: all antipsychotics may cause ECG changes such as prolonged QT interval and orthostatic hypotension. Orthostatic hypotension occurs with the low-potency first-generation antipsychotic drugs such as chlorpromazine and thioridazine, and with second-generation antipsychotic drugs such as clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine, and quetiapine. Weight gain: the common adverse effect of antipsychotic drugs is weight gain, which can rapidly occur and is difficult to control. It is not dose-dependent and is mostly reported in adults and children. The first-generation antipsychotic drugs such as chlorpromazine and thioridazine cause high-risk weight gain, but risk is greatest with use of second-generation antipsychotic drugs such as clozapine and olanzapine, which may cause more weight gain compared to other atypical antipsychotic drugs.
(iv) Hyperprolactinaemia occurs mostly within a few weeks of beginning treatment or increasing the dosage but can also arise after long-term stable use. It is common with the use of any first-generation antipsychotic drug as well as second-generation antipsychotic drugs such as risperidone, and is dose dependent. An increase in prolactin levels may be caused by blocking of dopamine in the hypothalamus and it results in galactorrhoea in men. Physicians routinely measure serum prolactin levels.
(v) Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening reaction caused by the use of antipsychotic drugs but is rare. NMS is characterised by labile blood pressure, tachypnoea, tachycardia, sialorrhoea, and flushing, skin pallor. The idiosyncratic reactions to antipsychotic drugs include cardiopulmonary arrest, aspiration pneumonias, and myoglobinuric renal failure — with special reference to clozapine.

A. Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate (HR) x stroke volume (SV). Heart rate is determined primarily by the cardiac innervation: sympathetic stimulation (beta1) increases heart rate while parasympathetic stimulation (M2) decreases it. Stroke volume depends on the inotropic state (a positive inotrope makes the ventricle work harder at a given filling pressure; sympathetic beta1 stimuli are positive inotropes), preload (ventricular end-diastolic volume/pressure) and afterload (the impedance against which the ventricle must eject). By the Frank-Starling law, the output of the heart is proportional to venous inflow up to a certain point.
B. In heart failure, the fundamental defect is a decrease in cardiac output relative to the needs of the body; the ventricular function curve is shifted down and to the right so that output is reduced at all fibre lengths, and the heart moves from a normal point on the curve to a "heart failure" point, with increased end-diastolic volume/pressure as the ventricle expands.
C. The fall in cardiac output reduces carotid sinus firing and renal blood flow; reduced renal blood flow triggers increased renin release and a rise in angiotensin II, causing renal vasoconstriction, sodium retention and stimulation of aldosterone secretion, so that the heart's failure to maintain output produces a functional/compensatory deficit in the kidney, manifesting as sodium and water retention and worsening oedema.
questions.question:
A. Describe the determinants of cardiac output and how they operate in the normal heart.
B. State how these determinants are altered in the common pathology of heart failure.
C. Explain how the resulting compensatory changes produce a functional deficit in a distant organ.

questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors/predisposing conditions: simple loss of functional myocardium as in myocardial infarction; chronic hypertension; valvular disease; coronary artery disease; and a variety of cardiomyopathies.
(ii) Complications (neuroendocrine/compensatory changes): reduced cardiac output triggers decreased carotid sinus firing and decreased renal blood flow; this leads to increased sympathetic discharge (causing increased force, rate and preload) and increased renin release, raising angiotensin II (causing vasoconstriction, sodium retention, continuing myocyte damage/remodelling, and stimulating aldosterone secretion). Aldosterone causes sodium retention, potassium loss and myocardial fibrosis, both of which may lead to arrhythmias. These compensatory responses eventually worsen the failing heart.
(iii) Management options: diuretics (loop diuretics, thiazides) to decrease preload and relieve oedema; neuroendocrine antagonists - ACE inhibitors, beta-receptor antagonists, angiotensin receptor blockers, aldosterone antagonists; positive inotropic drugs such as digitalis glycosides, beta agonists, and phosphodiesterase inhibitors; vasodilators such as nitroprusside, nitrates and hydralazine; and nesiritide.
(iv) ACE inhibitors are justified in chronic heart failure because they reduce afterload and salt/water retention by blocking formation of angiotensin II, thereby reducing vascular tone and aldosterone secretion; chronic failure is best treated with diuretics plus an ACE inhibitor and, if tolerated, a beta blocker.

questions.answerText:
(i) Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH); such peptides that act on the V2 receptor are produced by certain tumours (e.g. small cell carcinoma of the lung) and can cause significant water retention and dangerous hyponatraemia.
(ii) Demeclocycline and conivaptan (tolvaptan is also an antagonist of vasopressin receptors); lithium also has ADH-antagonist effects but is never used for this purpose because of its greater toxicity.
(iii) ADH antagonists oppose the actions of ADH and other naturally occurring peptides that act on the V2 receptor; conivaptan and tolvaptan are antagonists of vasopressin (V2) receptors, developed to offset the fluid retention resulting from excessive vasopressin production associated with hyponatraemia or acute heart failure, and have diuretic activity.
(iv) Conivaptan and tolvaptan may cause demyelination with serious neurologic consequences if hyponatraemia is corrected too rapidly; conivaptan may also cause infusion site reactions, and demeclocycline (like other tetracyclines) causes bone and teeth abnormalities in children younger than 8 years; lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus as a toxic effect.

- Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs): irreversible non-competitive inhibitors e.g. phenelzine, tranylcypromine; reversible MAO-A-selective inhibitors e.g. moclobemide

- Classical tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) e.g. imipramine, desipramine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, clomipramine
- Newer, mixed 5-HT and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors e.g. venlafaxine, duloxetine, milnacipran
- Noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors e.g. bupropion, reboxetine, atomoxetine
- Monoamine receptor antagonists e.g. mirtazapine, trazodone, mianserin
A(ii) SSRIs inhibit 5-HT reuptake, increasing synaptic 5-HT. However, the increase in synaptic 5-HT levels is less than expected because increased activation of 5-HT1A receptors on the soma and dendrites of 5-HT-containing raphe neurons inhibits these neurons, thus reducing 5-HT release. On prolonged drug treatment, the elevated level of 5-HT in the somatodendritic region desensitises the 5-HT1A receptors, reducing their inhibitory effect on 5-HT release from nerve terminals. The need to desensitise somatodendritic 5-HT1A receptors explains the slow onset of antidepressant action, accounting for the 2–4 week delay in therapeutic effect.
B(i) The main immediate effect of TCAs is to block the uptake of amines by nerve terminals by competition for the binding site of the amine transporter. Most TCAs inhibit noradrenaline and 5-HT uptake but have much less effect on dopamine uptake. In addition to their effects on amine uptake, most TCAs affect other receptors including muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine receptors, and 5-HT receptors. The antimuscarinic effects of TCAs do not contribute to their antidepressant effects but are responsible for various side effects including dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, and postural hypotension. TCAs may also cause ventricular dysrhythmias associated with prolongation of the QT interval.
B(ii) TCAs bind strongly to plasma albumin, most being 90–95% bound at therapeutic plasma concentrations. They also bind to extravascular tissues, which accounts for their generally very large distribution volumes (usually 10–50 l/kg). Extravascular sequestration, together with strong binding to plasma albumin, means that haemodialysis is ineffective as a means of increasing drug elimination.
B(iii) SSRIs are less likely than TCAs to cause anticholinergic side effects and are less dangerous in overdose. In contrast to MAOIs, SSRIs do not cause 'cheese reactions'. However, in combination with MAOIs, SSRIs can cause a 'serotonin syndrome' characterised by tremor, hyperthermia, and cardiovascular collapse, from which deaths have occurred. Paroxetine and fluoxetine are not used in combination with TCAs, whose hepatic metabolism they inhibit through an interaction with CYP2D6, for fear of increasing TCA toxicity.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Furosemide is a high-ceiling/loop diuretic that attaches to the Cl- binding site of the Na+-K+-2Cl co-transporter, inhibiting its transport function at the thick ascending loop of Henle; it also acts on the proximal tubule and abolishes the corticomedullary osmotic gradient, blocking free water clearance.
A(ii) It is rapidly absorbed orally, with about 60% bioavailability, low lipid solubility, and is highly bound to plasma proteins; it is partially conjugated with glucuronic acid and mainly excreted unchanged.
A(iii) Adverse effects include metabolic alkalosis, nausea, diarrhoea, hyperuricaemia (by decreasing renal excretion of uric acid) and allergic interstitial nephritis; it also causes hyperglycaemia, and increases K+ and Ca2+ excretion.
A(iv) It interacts with oral hypoglycaemic agents, decreasing their hypoglycaemic effect; aminoglycosides increase its ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; ethacrynic acid causes transient deafness.
B(i) Given the risk of hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia and hyperglycaemia, electrolyte and blood glucose status should be observed during furosemide therapy, and hearing should be monitored when it must be combined with an aminoglycoside.
B(ii) Furosemide has a weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitory effect and interacts with aminoglycosides to increase ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; ethacrynic acid similarly causes transient deafness, indicating that loop diuretics acting on the thick ascending loop of Henle affect ion transport processes shared with the inner ear, and combining them with another ototoxic agent (aminoglycosides) compounds this effect on the auditory system.

questions.answerText:
(i) Drugs are excreted by the kidney through glomerular filtration. Drugs not bound to plasma protein, in a free state, are easily filtered by renal glomeruli irrespective of their physical or chemical properties (ionized, non-ionized, lipid-soluble or water-soluble). Drugs bound to plasma proteins are not filtered. About 1200-1300 ml of blood flows through the renal glomeruli per minute, from which about 120-130 ml of primary urine is formed per minute.
(ii) Many carrier-mediated transport systems are present in the epithelium of the renal tubule; they transport organic ions from blood to urine against their concentration gradient. This is an active process divided into two types: one type is for acidic drugs and the other is for basic drugs. Elimination of drugs through tubular secretion is faster than through glomerular filtration. Drugs with higher affinity to the carrier system competitively inhibit transport of other drugs; for example, probenecid blocks the excretion of penicillins and cephalosporins.
(iii) Acidification of urine decreases the degree of ionization of weak acid, thereby enhancing its absorption (reabsorption) and reducing its elimination in urine. Alkalinization of urine increases the degree of ionization of weak acid, promoting its excretion in urine and reducing its reabsorption into blood. Therefore alkalinization of urine is used to enhance excretion of weak acid drugs (e.g. in salicylate poisoning).
(iv) The microsomal enzyme is reduced in elderly people; drugs therefore have a more potent effect and longer duration of action. In renal failure, tubular secretion and glomerular filtration are reduced, leading to drug accumulation. The clinical implication is the need for dose reduction.
(v) Renal clearance of drugs is defined as the volume of plasma in millilitres which contains the quantity of drug eliminated in urine by the kidney in one minute. Clearance factor = renal clearance of any drug / renal clearance of inulin = 60/120 = 0.5. This means that half of the drug filtered by the glomeruli is reabsorbed in the convoluted tubuli.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Beta blockers include atenolol, bisoprolol, betaxolol, carteolol, carvedilol, labetalol, metoprolol, nadolol, nebivolol, oxprenolol, penbutolol, pindolol, propranolol and timolol; mixed alpha+beta blockers include bucindolol, carvedilol and labetalol.
A(ii) Antagonists of beta-adrenergic receptors regulate blood pressure by reduction of myocardial contractility and cardiac output, reduction in secretion of renin with a resultant fall in angiotensin II levels, and reduction in aldosterone levels.
B(i) Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker, blocking beta1 and beta2 with equal potency; asthmatics have been reported to have worsening symptoms when using beta-blockers, so metoprolol (equipotent to propranolol at beta1 but less potent at beta2) has an advantage in hypertensive patients with asthmatic symptoms.
Non-selective beta-blockers in a patient on insulin therapy block the recovery from hypoglycaemia and mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia, i.e. palpitations, tremors and anxiety.
Beta-blockers should not be used in patients with heart block greater than first degree, and heart failure may be worsened by non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers used alongside them; JNC8 does not recommend beta-blockers as initial hypertension therapy.
B(ii) Sudden discontinuation of some beta-adrenergic blockers produces a withdrawal syndrome similar to sympathetic hyperactivity, exacerbating symptoms of coronary artery disease and causing rebound hypertension; propranolol should not be withdrawn abruptly as this can cause nervousness, tachycardia, angina and rebound hypertension, effects on the heart and vasculature distant from the receptor blockade site itself, reflecting the loss of the drug's chronic suppression of sympathetic/renin-angiotensin activity.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Cardiac glycosides include a steroid nucleus and a lactone ring, usually with one or more sugar residues; they are often called "digitalis" because several come from the digitalis (foxglove) plant.
A(ii) Digitalis glycosides decrease sodium transport out of the cardiac cell by inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase (sodium pump); the resulting accumulation of sodium increases intracellular calcium via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, which is responsible for the positive inotropic effect on cardiac contractility.
A(iii) Digitalis glycosides are no longer considered first-line drugs in heart failure: careful studies show that while digoxin may improve functional status (reduce symptoms) it does not prolong life, whereas other agents (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, vasodilators) may be equally effective, less toxic, and some do prolong life. The half-lives of cardiac glycosides are long, they accumulate significantly, and dosing must be carefully designed and monitored.
B. Serum potassium concentration should be maintained between 4.0 and 5.0 mmol/L, since hypokalaemia (along with hypoxaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypothyroidism and myocardial ischaemia) precipitates digitalis toxicity.
C. In toxicity, excessive inhibition of the Na+/K+-ATPase produces excessive intracellular calcium accumulation, which underlies the cardiac toxicity of ventricular and supraventricular dysrhythmias and all degrees of AV block seen in digitalis toxicity; bradyarrhythmias and AV block may respond to atropine or may require a temporary pacemaker, and antidigoxin antibodies are available for massive overdose.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Arterial vasodilators: hydralazine, minoxidil, diazoxide, fenoldopam. Arterial and venous vasodilator: sodium nitroprusside.
A(ii) Vasodilators act directly on the smooth muscle of arteries to relax their walls; hydralazine causes direct relaxation of arteriolar smooth muscle without dilating capacitance vessels; minoxidil is metabolised by hepatic enzymes to an active molecule that produces arteriolar vasodilation, resembling hydralazine and diazoxide; sodium nitroprusside is metabolised by blood vessels to nitric oxide, activating guanylyl cyclase to form cyclic GMP and cause vasodilatation of both arterioles and venules.
B(i) Hydralazine induces vasodilation and stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, causing increased heart rate and contractility, increased plasma renin activity and fluid retention, all of which counteract its antihypertensive effect; this can be resolved by combining a sympatholytic agent and a diuretic.
Minoxidil is a potent stimulator of renin secretion (mediated by renal sympathetic stimulation) and causes reflex increase in myocardial contractility, plus adverse effects of salt and fluid retention, cardiovascular effects and hypertrichosis; it is more beneficial combined with a diuretic and a beta-adrenergic receptor blocker.
B(ii) The metabolism of nitroprusside by smooth muscle produces cyanide as well as nitric oxide; cyanide is metabolised in the liver by rhodanase to thiocyanate, and toxicity from accumulation of thiocyanate results in lactic acidosis, a systemic/metabolic effect distant from the blood vessel wall where the vasodilator mechanism itself acts; sodium thiosulfate can prevent this by supplying the sulphur donor for thiocyanate formation.

(i) A patient develops redistribution of body fat, a puffy face, hirsutism, increased appetite, osteoporosis and hypertension after prolonged high-dose glucocorticoid therapy. What are the risk factors for this condition?
(ii) What complications are associated with it?
(iii) State the treatment options and justify the use of one of them.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cushing syndrome is caused by hypersecretion of glucocorticoids (hypercortisolism) resulting from excessive release of ACTH by the anterior pituitary or an adrenal tumor; it may also result from excessive, chronic, exogenous use of glucocorticoids (patients given daily doses of 100 mg or more of hydrocortisone, or the equivalent, for longer than 2 weeks develop iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome).
(ii) Complications include osteoporosis (from the catabolic and antianabolic effects of glucocorticoids on bone), hypertension, metabolic effects such as growth inhibition, diabetes, muscle wasting, salt retention, and psychosis.
(iii) Treatment options include adjuvant therapy after surgery using inhibitors of steroidogenesis or receptor antagonists: ketoconazole (non-selectively inhibits P450c17, C17,20-lyase, 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and P450c11), metyrapone (a relatively selective inhibitor of steroid 11-hydroxylation), aminoglutethimide (blocks conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, used in conjunction with ketoconazole and metyrapone), mifepristone (antagonist at the steroid receptor) and mitotane (nonselective cytotoxic action). Ketoconazole is a justified choice as it non-selectively inhibits multiple steroidogenic enzymes to reduce cortisol excess, although it carries the adverse effect of hepatotoxicity that requires monitoring.

A(i) Levodopa is the natural precursor to dopamine in the brain; it is administered because, unlike dopamine, it can cross the blood–brain barrier, and is then converted to dopamine by endogenous aromatic amino acid decarboxylase. It is administered with the peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitors carbidopa (co-careldopa: Sinemet®) or benserazide (co-beneldopa: Madopar®). The decarboxylase inhibitor blocks the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, allowing a lower dose of levodopa to be administered. Immediate-Release (IR) levodopa starts at 50 mg three times daily, titrated to maximum 600 mg/day, and should be taken 30 minutes before food as protein can critically interfere with absorption. Controlled-Release (CR) preparations include Sinemet CR (carbidopa/levodopa 50/200) and Half Sinemet CR (carbidopa/levodopa 25/100). Levodopa in CR preparations has a bioavailability of 60–70%, less than the 90–100% of IR formulations. CR preparations may help in simplifying drug regimens, relieving nocturnal akinesia, and reducing end-of-dose deterioration.
A(ii) Ergot-derived dopamine agonists — Cabergoline (administered once daily with plasma half-life of 63–68 hours); ergot derivatives run the risk of pleuropulmonary fibrosis and are not routinely used anymore. Non-ergot derived dopamine agonists (now the agents of choice): ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine. Dopamine agonists stimulate dopamine receptors, both post- and pre-synaptically, bypassing the degenerating nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons. Principal side effects: nausea and vomiting, postural hypotension, hallucinations, confusion, and, in some cases, major behavioural problems linked to impulse control disorders.
B(i) Selegiline and rasagiline are inhibitors of MAO-B. Inhibition of this enzyme slows the breakdown of dopamine, effectively having a 'levodopa-sparing' effect in the striatum, resulting in both a mild therapeutic effect and possible delay in or reduction of motor complications. A single daily dose of 5 or 10 mg of selegiline is prescribed. Both selegiline and rasagiline may be used as de novo or adjunctive treatments in PD. Amantadine has multiple modes of action including facilitation of presynaptic dopamine release, blocking dopamine reuptake, an anticholinergic (nicotinic antagonist) effect, and may act as a weak NMDA receptor antagonist. It is more commonly used as an antidyskinetic agent in advanced disease — the only drug licensed for such use. Daily doses of 100–400 mg may be used.
B(ii) Antimuscarinic drugs (trihexyphenidyl, orphenadrine) can have a moderate effect in reducing tremor but do not have any significant benefit on bradykinesia. The use of antimuscarinic agents has declined because of troublesome side effects, including constipation, urinary retention, cognitive impairment, and toxic confusional states. In selected younger patients, an antimuscarinic drug may still be helpful, but close monitoring is advised.
B(iii) The five proposed major mechanisms for neuronal death in Parkinson's disease: protein aggregation; disruption of autophagy; changes in cell metabolism or mitochondrial function; neuroinflammation; and breakdown of the blood–brain barrier resulting in vascular leakiness. Epidemiology: the prevalence of PD increases with age, affecting less than 0.5% of people in their 60s and 2.5% of those older than 80 years. The usual age at time of diagnosis ranges between 55 and 65 years. Overall, a higher preponderance of PD is reported among males. The estimated crude prevalence of PD in Nigeria is lower (10 to 249/100,000) compared to studies published in Europe (65.6 to 12,500/100,000). Environmental factors such as pesticide exposure, rural living, agricultural occupation, well water drinking, and head injury are all associated with an increased risk.

questions.answerText:
A(i) PTH is an 84-amino acid polypeptide endocrine hormone produced by the parathyroid glands; it is secreted into the circulation in response to low calcium levels, and exerts minute-to-minute control of blood calcium.
A(ii) On bone, PTH (via PTH1R) stimulates IL-6 secretion promoting osteoclast differentiation, stimulates RANKL production, inhibits osteoprotegerin (OPG), and promotes calcium mobilization.
On the renal tubule, PTH activates 1-alpha-hydroxylase, increases calcium reabsorption, and increases phosphaturia.
On the GI tract, PTH indirectly increases calcium and phosphate absorption via calcitriol.
A(iii) The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) is a G-protein coupled receptor expressed in chief cells, renal tubule, bone, brain and GI tract; it is extremely sensitive to small percentage changes in ionized calcium; its activation inhibits PTH secretion, and its activation in the renal tubule inhibits calcium reabsorption.
B(i) Major causes of hypercalcaemia include hyperparathyroidism, cancer, and thiazide diuretics; minor causes include hypervitaminosis D, sarcoidosis, thyrotoxicosis and adrenal insufficiency.
Clinical manifestations of hypercalcaemia are fatigue, mood changes, confusion, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, polyuria and weakness; these follow from excess PTH driving bone calcium mobilization, renal calcium reabsorption and gut calcium absorption beyond physiological need.
C(i) PTH raises serum calcium — it stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption (calcium mobilization from bone), increases renal calcium reabsorption, and indirectly increases intestinal calcium absorption via calcitriol.
Calcitonin, by contrast, is a minor regulator that inhibits osteoclastic bone resorption, reduces both calcium and phosphate reabsorption as well as that of Na, K and Mg, decreases gastrin secretion and reduces gastric acid output while increasing secretion of Na, K, Cl and water in the gut.
Thus PTH and calcitonin act in opposing directions on serum calcium: PTH raises it while calcitonin lowers it, which is why calcitonin is used therapeutically (by blocking osteoclasts and promoting calciuria) in the treatment of hypercalcaemia.
This opposing regulatory relationship between PTH and calcitonin, alongside vitamin D, forms the basis of the calcium homeostatic axis.
Vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) complements PTH by potentiating its action on renal calcium absorption and by mediating intestinal calcium reabsorption, while providing feedback inhibition of PTH release.

A(iii) Describe the role of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR).

questions.answerText:
A(i) The primary aim of epilepsy treatment is to control seizures using one drug, with the lowest effective dose causing the fewest side effects possible. Established AEDs (licensed before 2000) include: carbamazepine (Tegretol), clobazam, clonazepam, ethosuximide, gabapentin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, phenytoin (Epanutin), piracetam, primidone, sodium valproate (Epilim), tiagabine, topiramate, and vigabatrin. Since 2000, new AEDs have been introduced: eslicarbazepine acetate, brivaracetam, felbamate, lacosamide, levetiracetam (Keppra), oxcarbazepine, perampanel, pregabalin (Lyrica), stiripentol, rufinamide, and zonisamide. The newer AEDs are generally used as second-line drugs when treatment with established first-line drugs has failed; exceptions are levetiracetam and oxcarbazepine.
A(ii) Tonic-clonic seizures — first-line: carbamazepine (Tegretol), lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, sodium valproate (Epilim); adjunctive: levetiracetam (Keppra), clobazam, topiramate. Focal seizures — first-line: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, sodium valproate; adjunctive: brivaracetam, clobazam, eslicarbazepine, gabapentin, lacosamide, perampanel, phenytoin (Epanutin), pregabalin (Lyrica), topiramate, zonisamide. Myoclonic seizures — first-line: levetiracetam, sodium valproate, clonazepam, topiramate, piracetam; adjunctive: clobazam.
B(i) Carbamazepine is a first-line drug for generalised tonic-clonic seizures and focal seizures. It is not effective in absence seizures and myoclonic seizures, where it may even be deleterious. It acts through blockage of voltage-gated sodium channels. Adverse events may occur in up to a third of people treated but only about 5% require drug withdrawal, usually because of skin rash, GI disturbances, or hyponatraemia. Dose-related adverse reactions including ataxia, dizziness, blurred vision, and diplopia are common. Idiosyncratic reactions such as skin rash occur in up to 10%. Serious adverse events including hepatic failure and bone marrow depression are extremely uncommon. Carbamazepine exhibits auto-induction — it induces its own metabolism as well as inducing the metabolism of other drugs; it should therefore be introduced at low dosage, steadily increased over a month.
B(ii) Sodium valproate is a broad-spectrum AED, effective over the complete range of seizure types, but with particular value in idiopathic generalised epilepsies. This is mainly due to its broad mechanism of action — known to act on voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, and also in the turnover of GABA. Adverse effects include nausea, diarrhoea, weight gain, alopecia, skin rash, and thrombocytopenia. Sodium valproate is more teratogenic than other commonly used AEDs and should be avoided in women of childbearing age. TDM should only be performed in cases of suspected toxicity, deterioration in seizure control, to check adherence, or to monitor drug interactions.
B(iii) Status epilepticus is traditionally defined as ongoing seizure activity for ≥30 minutes, but a seizure that lasts longer than 5 minutes warrants pharmacological intervention. Initial management is supportive: secure airway and resuscitate; administer oxygen; assess cardiorespiratory function; establish intravenous access. In the community, buccal midazolam (10 mg) is first-line treatment; rectal diazepam is an alternative if preferred or buccal midazolam is not available. First-line AED for hospital management is intravenous lorazepam; if unavailable, intravenous diazepam or buccal midazolam. If seizures continue, intravenous phenytoin or valproate or phenobarbital should be administered as second-line treatment. In refractory status, general anaesthesia with propofol, midazolam, or thiopentone may be necessary.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Psychosis refers to a severe form of mental disorder where there is gross disorganization of personality and severe impairment in social functions. It is characterized by a disconnection from reality — the patient fails to realize what is real and what is not. Positive symptoms are usually what the public perceives when thinking about schizophrenia: hallucinations, delusions, and disorganization. Negative symptoms include apathy, avolition, blunted affect, and poverty of speech; a decreased ability to experience pleasure (anhedonia) and social withdrawal can lead to significant functional impairment, even when positive symptoms are relatively absent.
A(ii) First-generation (Typical) antipsychotics — Low potency: Chlorpromazine (100–800 mg/day), Triflupromazine (50–200 mg/day), Thioridazine (100–400 mg/day). High potency: Fluphenazine (1–10 mg/day), Haloperidol (5–20 mg/day), Pimozide (2–6 mg/day), Thiothixene (5–60 mg/day). Second-generation (Atypical) antipsychotics: Aripiprazole (10–30 mg/day), Clozapine (100–300 mg/day), Molindone (50–70 mg/day), Olanzapine (2.5–20 mg/day), Quetiapine (50–400 mg/day), Risperidone (2–8 mg/day).
B(i) First-generation antipsychotics are competitive inhibitors at a variety of receptors (noradrenergic, cholinergic, and histaminergic), but their antipsychotic effects reflect competitive blocking of dopamine D2 receptors. First-generation antipsychotics are more likely to be associated with movement disorders, particularly for drugs that bind tightly to dopaminergic neuroreceptors such as haloperidol. Second-generation antipsychotic drugs appear to owe their unique activity to blockade of both serotonin (5-HT2A) and dopamine (D2) receptors. Most SGAs differ from older medications in that serotonin (5-HT2) receptor binding exceeds their affinity for dopamine D2 receptors; this is largely the basis for the lower overall risk of extrapyramidal side effects (EPSE) with the atypical drugs.
B(ii) Evidence indicates abnormal neurotransmission systems in the dopaminergic, serotonergic, and glutaminergic systems, with interplay between the systems such that one system may affect others. There is an imbalance in the amount of neurotransmitters, most notably dopamine: overactivity accounts for the positive symptoms of schizophrenia and underactivity in another part of the brain may account for the negative symptoms. Glutamatergic dysfunction may be genetically linked as well as causative in the cognitive impairments and negative symptoms of this disorder.
B(iii) Antipsychotics are indicated for: schizophrenia; psychotic symptoms associated with brain impairment (injuries); the manic phase of bipolar affective disorder until lithium (drug of choice) becomes effective; nausea and vomiting (phenothiazines affect the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the medulla); intractable hiccups (mechanism of action unclear for phenothiazines); and as maintenance therapy for mania and psychoses.
questions.question:

A(i) Define psychosis, and distinguish between positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
A(ii) Classify antipsychotic drugs into first-generation (FGA) and second-generation (SGA) groups, giving examples and dose ranges.
B(i) Compare the mechanism of action and extrapyramidal risk of FGAs and SGAs.
B(ii) Describe the pathophysiology (aetiology) of schizophrenia.
B(iii) State the indications for antipsychotic drugs beyond schizophrenia.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Psychosis refers to a severe form of mental disorder where there is gross disorganisation of personality and severe impairment in social functions; it is characterised by a disconnection from reality. It is a group of disorders (spectrum) characterised by thought disorder, abnormal behaviour, defective cognition, delusion, and hallucination. Neurosis is a less severe form of mental disorder with minor impairment in social and personality function; sense of reality, reasoning, and insight are retained; hallucinations and delusions are absent. Examples of neurosis are generalised anxiety disorders, conversion and dissociative disorders, obsessive compulsive disorders, and phobic disorders.
A(ii) Psychotic disorders are classified as: Organic brain syndromes (Cognitive Disorders) — delirium, dementia, amnestic syndrome, organic delusional syndrome, organic hallucinations, organic affective syndrome, and organic personality syndrome. Functional disorders — no underlying cause can be defined; memory and orientation are mostly retained but emotion, thought, reasoning, and behaviour are seriously altered; examples include schizophrenia, paranoid states, and mood (affective) disorders.
B(i) Schizophrenia is characterised by delusion, hallucination, and lack of insight. The symptoms are organised into two main domains: positive and negative.
Positive symptoms: hallucinations (auditory, visual, or other senses); delusions (persecutory, paranoid, grandiose, etc.); disorganised thinking/speech; grossly disorganised or abnormal motor behaviour (including catatonia); unusual behaviour; combativeness, agitation, and hostility; ideas of reference.
Negative symptoms: diminished emotional expression (body language); avolition/psychomotor retardation; alogia (decreased speech); anhedonia (decreased ability to feel pleasure); asociality (lack of socialisation); affective flattening; social withdrawal.
B(ii) Bipolar disorder (mania and depression): Mania — elation and irritable mood, reduced sleep, hyperactivity, uncontrollable thought and speech, may be associated with reckless or violent behaviour. Depression — sadness, loss of interest and pleasure, worthlessness, guilt, physical and mental slowing, melancholia, self-destructive ideation. Types of depression include: persistent depressive disorder; bipolar disorder; seasonal affective disorder; psychotic depression; and perinatal depression.
B(iii) Organic brain syndromes are divided into 2 major subgroups: Acute — delirium or acute confusional state secondary to diseases or drug use such as uraemic encephalopathy, intoxication, drug overdose. Chronic — dementia; the patient generally retreats to simple, familiar situations and resists involvement in others. The symptoms represent organic deficits due to brain damage and psychological reactions to deficits; some causes are treatable. There is a progressive change in the total behaviour of the patient; other prominent features are confusion, disorientation, defective memory, disorganised thought and behaviour.
questions.question:
Describe the pathophysiology, classification, and treatment of psychotic disorders under the following headings:
A(i) Define psychosis and distinguish it from neurosis, giving examples of each.
A(ii) Classify psychotic disorders into organic and functional types, with examples under each.
B(i) Describe the features of schizophrenia, including its positive and negative symptoms.
B(ii) Describe bipolar disorder (mania and depression).
B(iii) Describe the classification and features of organic brain syndromes, distinguishing between the acute and chronic forms.

A(i) State the classification of high-ceiling (loop) diuretics.
A(ii) Describe their site and mechanism of action.
A(iii) State their pharmacokinetics.
A(iv) List their adverse effects and interactions.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for preferring loop diuretics over thiazides in acute pulmonary oedema and renal impairment.
B(ii) Distinguish between loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics.
questions.answerText:
A(i) High ceiling/high efficacy diuretics act on the Na+-K+-2Cl cotransporter and include sulphamoyl derivatives (furosemide, bumetanide), phenoxyacetic acid derivatives (ethacrynic acid), and mercurial diuretics.
A(ii) The major site of action is the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where furosemide attaches to the Cl- binding site of the co-transporter, inhibiting the Na+-K+-2Cl cotransporter; it also acts on the proximal tubule, abolishes the corticomedullary osmotic gradient, and blocks free water clearance.
A(iii) Furosemide is rapidly absorbed orally, has a bioavailability of about 60%, low lipid solubility, and is highly bound to plasma proteins; it is partially conjugated with glucuronic acid and mainly excreted unchanged.
A(iv) Adverse effects: metabolic alkalosis, nausea, diarrhoea, hyperuricaemia, allergic interstitial nephritis, hyperglycaemia; increased K+ and Ca2+ excretion. Interactions: decreases the hypoglycaemic effect of oral hypoglycaemic agents; increases ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity with aminoglycosides; ethacrynic acid can cause transient deafness.
B(i) Its maximal natriuretic effect is much greater than other classes, and the diuretic response increases with dose increase, making it useful for acute pulmonary oedema and treatment of hypertensive emergency/CHF; it is also used in forced diuresis in poisoning.
Loop diuretics remain effective in renal impairment, whereas thiazides are not effective in renal failure.
B(ii) Thiazides act primarily at the cortical diluting segment/distal tubule, inhibiting Na+-2Cl symport, and do not affect the corticomedullary osmotic gradient (indicating lack of action at the medullary thick ascending limb), unlike loop diuretics.
Thiazides are effective in mild to moderate oedema and are better for maintenance therapy and are first-line agents for hypertension, whereas loop diuretics are high-ceiling agents used for oedema of cardiac, hepatic or renal origin, including renal failure.

A(i) Adverse drug reaction is defined as any noxious change which is suspected to be due to a drug, which occurs at normal doses used in man, and that requires treatment or decrease in the dose or indicates caution in the future use of the same drug. This definition excludes trivial side effects and poisoning or overdose. They are more common with multiple drug therapy and in the elderly.
A(ii) Type A (Augmented): based on pharmacological properties of the drug; common, dose related, and mostly preventable; e.g. orthostatic hypotension with antihypertensives. Type B (Bizarre): based on peculiarities of the patient; less common, non-dose related, more serious; includes immunologic (e.g. allergic reaction with radiocontrast agents) and idiosyncratic reactions (e.g. hemolytic anaemia due to G6PD deficiency). Type C (Chronic): effects after chronic administration, e.g. analgesic nephropathy, or tardive dyskinesia after antipsychotics. Type D (Delayed): difficult to diagnose, e.g. teratogenic effects of thalidomide, carcinogenic effects of stilbestrol during pregnancy. Type E (End of treatment): withdrawal effects, e.g. opioids, antiepileptics, anxiolytics, rebound phenomenon with hypnotics.
B(i) Drug dependence is defined as a state in which use of drugs for personal satisfaction is accorded a higher priority than other basic needs, even with awareness of its risk to health. Psychological dependence: the individual believes that optimal well-being is only achieved through the action of the drug; may progress from liking to craving or compulsive drug use; examples: opioids, cocaine, benzodiazepines. Physical dependence: an altered physiological state produced by repeated use of drug which necessitates the continued presence of drug to maintain physiological equilibrium; discontinuation results in withdrawal syndrome; examples: alcohol, opioids, antidepressants, stimulants like cocaine.
B(ii) Teratogenicity is the capacity of a drug to cause fetal abnormalities when administered to the pregnant mother. Embryo has very dynamic biological systems, and certain drug effects are often irreversible. At fertilization and implantation (first 2 weeks): failure of pregnancy. During organogenesis (3 weeks to 3 months): deformities are produced. During growth and development (above 3 months): developmental and functional abnormalities can occur. NSAIDs can cause premature closure of ductus arteriosus. It is wise to avoid all drugs during pregnancy unless there are compelling reasons.
B(iii) Drug-induced disease (iatrogenic) is functional disturbance caused by drugs which persists even after the offending drug has been discontinued. Examples: peptic ulcer by NSAIDs; hepatitis by isoniazid; vaginal discharge by some antibiotics.
questions.question:
Describe the adverse effects of drugs under the following headings:
A(i) Define adverse drug reaction and distinguish it from trivial side effects and overdose.
A(ii) Describe the ABCDE classification of adverse drug reactions, defining each type with one example.
B(i) Define drug dependence, distinguish between psychological and physical dependence, and give two examples of drugs causing each.
B(ii) Define teratogenicity and explain how drugs can affect the embryo at different stages of pregnancy, with one specific drug example.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Affinity refers to the strength of binding between a drug and its receptor; a high-affinity agonist or antagonist is less likely than a low-affinity drug to dissociate from a receptor once bound. Potency is the amount of drug required to produce 50% of the maximal response the drug is capable of inducing. Dissociation constant is the concentration of drug required in solution to achieve 50% occupancy of its receptors.
A(ii) A strong agonist causes maximal effects even though it may occupy only a small fraction of the receptors; a weak agonist must be bound to many more receptors than a strong agonist to produce the same effect; a partial agonist fails to produce maximal effects even when all receptors are occupied, activating them in the same way but not evoking a great response however high the concentration; a full agonist can activate the receptor-effector system to the maximum extent of which the system is capable.
A(iii) The four main kinds of regulatory protein that are primary drug targets are receptors, enzymes, carrier molecules (transporters), and ion channels; for a drug to be useful it must act selectively (show high binding-site specificity), though no drug acts with complete specificity.
B(i) A partial agonist is a drug which fails to produce maximal effects even when all the receptors are occupied by it, since it binds to the same receptor and activates it in the same way as a full agonist but does not evoke as great a response no matter how high the concentration, giving it a lower ceiling of effect than a full agonist.
B(ii) A competitive antagonist competes with the agonist for the receptor; while the receptor is occupied by the antagonist, the agonist is prevented from binding, but if the antagonism can be overcome by a high dose of agonist, it is surmountable. A non-competitive antagonist binds to a site other than the agonist-binding domain, inducing a conformational change so that the agonist no longer recognises its binding domain, and high doses of agonist cannot overcome this, so it is considered insurmountable.
questions.question:
A(i) Define affinity, potency and dissociation constant as used in receptor pharmacology.
A(ii) Describe the types of agonists.
A(iii) Describe the four main kinds of regulatory protein that serve as primary drug targets.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for the ceiling effect of partial agonists.
B(ii) Distinguish between competitive and non-competitive antagonism.

(i) A patient with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus is found to have abnormal insulin secretion or action. What are the risk factors for developing this metabolic disorder?
(ii) What complications is the patient at increased risk of developing?
(iii) State the drug options for management and justify the use of one class.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycaemia and altered metabolism of lipids, carbohydrate and protein, from abnormality of insulin secretion or action, insufficient insulin secretion, or impaired response to insulin; genetic and environmental factors are risk factors, and the disease is classified as Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM, type 1, about 10%) and Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (NIDDM, type II, about 90%).
(ii) Increased risk of complications from vascular disease: retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, cardiovascular diseases, and infections.
(iii) Options are Insulin and Non-insulin agents. Non-insulin: metformin (biguanide); sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, gliclazide, glimepiride); meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide); thiazolidinediones (rosiglitazone, pioglitazone); alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, miglitol, voglibose); DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, saxagliptin, vildagliptin, linagliptin, alogliptin); SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, empagliflozin); GLP-1 receptor agonists (exenatide, liraglutide and others). Insulin is required by all IDDM patients and many NIDDM patients. Metformin is a justified first choice as it is an anti-hyperglycaemic (not hypoglycaemic) agent that does not cause insulin release and carries less risk of hypoglycaemia than sulphonylureas.

questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of opioid analgesics under the following headings:
A(i) Define the terms opium, opioid, opiate, and narcotic.
A(ii) Describe the opioid receptors — their names, locations in the CNS, and cellular mechanism of activation.
B(i) Classify opioids by their receptor activity into pure agonists, partial agonists, and antagonists, giving examples.
B(ii) State the differences between opioid and non-opioid analgesics under at least five headings.
B(iii) Describe the short-term effects and less common adverse reactions of opioid analgesics.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definitions:
- Opium: A mixture of alkaloids from the poppy plant Papaver somniferum.
- Opioid: Any naturally occurring, semi-synthetic, or synthetic compound that binds specifically to opioid receptors and shares the properties of one or more of the naturally occurring endogenous opioids.
- Opiate: Any naturally occurring opioid derived from opium (e.g. morphine).
- Narcotic: From the Greek meaning 'to numb or deaden'. Often used to denote an opioid but also widely used to describe drugs of addiction, hence includes non-opioid compounds.
A(ii) Opioid receptors are distributed throughout the CNS with high concentrations in the nuclei of tractus solitarius, peri-aqueductal grey area (PAG), cerebral cortex, thalamus, and the substantia gelatinosa (SG) of the spinal cord. They have also been found on peripheral afferent nerve terminals and many other organs. The current nomenclature approved by the International Union of Pharmacology is: MOR – μ (mu) opioid peptide receptor; KOR – κ (kappa) opioid peptide receptor; DOR – δ (delta) opioid peptide receptor; NOR (nociceptin orphanin FQ peptide receptor); ZOR (zeta receptor). Subtypes exist: MOR (μ1,2,3), KOR (k1,2&3), DOR (δ1&2). Opioid receptors are coupled with inhibitory G-proteins; activation closes voltage-sensitive calcium channels, stimulates potassium efflux leading to hyperpolarization, and reduces cyclic adenosine monophosphate production.
B(i) Pure opioid agonists (morphine, diamorphine, pethidine, and fentanyl) bind to opioid receptors avidly and demonstrate high intrinsic activity. Partial opioid agonists (buprenorphine, pentazocine) bind to opioid receptors but produce a sub-maximal effect compared to pure agonists and so have less intrinsic activity. Opioid antagonists (naloxone, naltrexone) have receptor affinity but no intrinsic activity.
B(ii) Differences between opioid and non-opioid analgesics:
- Opioids act centrally on special pain receptors; non-opioids act peripherally on injured body tissues.
- Opioids cause addiction/dependence; non-opioids do not produce tolerance or physical dependence.
- Opioids are Schedule II/III controlled drugs; non-opioids are not controlled drugs.
- Notable adverse effects of opioids: sedation, respiratory depression; non-opioids: gastric irritation, bleeding problems.
- Opioids are used for severe pain and do not have a ceiling effect; non-opioids have anti-inflammatory effect, are used for mild/moderate pain, and have a ceiling effect in analgesia (a maximum dose beyond which analgesic effect does not increase).
B(iii) Short-term effects include: short-lived state of euphoria; mental clouding; drowsiness, apathy, decreased physical activity; reduced heart rate and blood pressure; constipation; constriction of pupils (miosis); nausea, vomiting; dysphoria; increased sensitivity to pain after initial effects wear off; itchy skin. Less common side effects and adverse reactions include: confusion, hallucinations, delirium, hypothermia, bradycardia (slow heart rate), tachycardia (rapid heart rate), and raised intracranial pressure.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the zones of the adrenal cortex it regulates.
A(ii) Describe the regulation of ACTH release within this axis.
B(i) Explain how disorders of this axis relate to Addison's disease and Cushing's syndrome.
C(i) Explain why adrenal insufficiency, a disorder of the adrenal gland, produces a distant effect on the skin (hyperpigmentation).
questions.answerText:
A(i) ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex: the outer zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); the middle zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol); the inner zona reticularis secretes androgens (DHEA and DHEA-S).
ACTH is processed from the precursor protein pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), from which alpha-MSH is also derived; it acts through melanocortin receptor 2 (MC-2).
A(ii) ACTH release is regulated by a diurnal (sleep-wake) rhythm of the hypothalamus through CRH and arginine vasopressin (AVP) acting on the corticotropes, by negative feedback at multiple sites of the HPA axis, by positive regulation from interleukins and alpha-TNF, and by the stress response, which overrides the negative feedback.
B(i) In Addison's disease (primary adrenocortical insufficiency), the adrenal cortex fails to respond to ACTH administration; features include weakness, fatigue, weight loss, hypotension and hyperpigmentation, and treatment is with replacement hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone.
In Cushing's syndrome, hypersecretion of glucocorticoids results from excessive ACTH release by the anterior pituitary or from an adrenal tumor; cortisol levels and the dexamethasone suppression test are used for diagnosis, since dexamethasone fails to suppress cortisol release in these patients.
Thus the same HPA axis, when hypoactive, produces Addison's disease, and when hyperactive (or with autonomous adrenal secretion), produces Cushing's syndrome.
C(i) Because ACTH is derived from the same precursor peptide, POMC, as alpha-MSH (the first 13 amino acids of ACTH are similar to alpha-MSH), a rise in ACTH — as occurs when the adrenal cortex fails to respond and negative feedback is lost in primary adrenal insufficiency — also increases melanocortin receptor stimulation in the skin.
This shared precursor origin is the pharmacological/physiological basis for hyperpigmentation being a characteristic feature of Addison's disease alongside weakness, fatigue, weight loss and hypotension.
This demonstrates how a hormone with a primary action on the adrenal cortex (ACTH) can, through a shared biosynthetic precursor, produce a clinically important effect at a completely distant organ (the skin).
Conversely, in secondary or tertiary adrenocortical insufficiency, caused by defects in CRH production by the hypothalamus or ACTH production by the pituitary, hyperpigmentation does not occur to the same degree because ACTH levels are low or normal rather than elevated.
This distinction between primary and secondary/tertiary insufficiency in terms of ACTH level, and hence in terms of hyperpigmentation, is a key clinico-pharmacological feature of the HPA axis.
Secondary and tertiary adrenocortical insufficiency are caused by a defect in CRH production by the hypothalamus or in ACTH production by the pituitary, and are also treated with hydrocortisone.

(i) The four cardinal motor features of Parkinson's disease are: tremor when at rest (pill-rolling tremor); cogwheel rigidity (jerky resistance when limbs are moved); bradykinesia (slowness of initiation of voluntary movement, with progressive reduction in speed of repetitive actions) — which is a prerequisite feature for diagnosis; and postural instability (impairment of righting reflexes, leading to impaired gait and increased risk of falling).
(ii) At the cellular level, degeneration of dopaminergic neurons (axons and soma) projecting from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) to the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) leads to a loss of dopamine at the terminal end. There is considerable reserve in this pathway, and a loss of more than 50% of nigral neurones occurs before overt motor features appear. The normal inhibitory influence of dopamine on cholinergic neurons is significantly diminished, which results in the overproduction of acetylcholine, triggering abnormal signalling and resulting in loss of muscle movements.
(iii) Levodopa remains the most effective and first-line oral symptomatic treatment for PD. It is administered with the peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitors carbidopa or benserazide; carbidopa plus levodopa is known as co-careldopa (Sinemet®) and benserazide plus levodopa is co-beneldopa (Madopar®). The decarboxylase inhibitor blocks the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, allowing a lower dose of levodopa to be administered. Levodopa readily crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted by endogenous aromatic amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine, then stored in surviving nigrostriatal nerve terminals. Immediate-Release (IR) levodopa starts at 50 mg three times daily and can be titrated to a maximum dose of 600 mg/day. It should be taken 30 minutes before food, as protein diet can critically interfere with absorption.
(iv) The most commonly encountered side effects are nausea, vomiting, and orthostatic hypotension. Later in illness, levodopa may cause vivid dreams, nightmares, or precipitate a confusional state. A wearing-off effect may develop, in which the patient finds that the effect of the medicine does not last until their next dose. Dyskinesia (involuntary movements) may develop after years of treatment. Clinically relevant drug interactions include hypertensive crises with MAO-A inhibitors (e.g. phenelzine) — levodopa should be avoided for at least 2 weeks after stopping the inhibitor. Levodopa can also enhance the hypotensive effects of antihypertensive agents and may antagonize the action of antipsychotics. The absorption of levodopa may be reduced by concomitant administration of oral iron preparations.
(v) Other drug classes include: dopamine agonists (e.g. ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine — non-ergot; cabergoline — ergot derived); apomorphine (most potent non-selective dopamine agonist, given by subcutaneous injection); COMT inhibitors (tolcapone, entacapone) which increase the amount of levodopa entering the CNS; MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline and rasagiline) which slow the breakdown of dopamine; amantadine — used as an antidyskinetic agent in advanced disease; and antimuscarinic agents (trihexyphenidyl, orphenadrine) which reduce tremor but have no significant benefit on bradykinesia.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressive slowness of movement, a resting tremor in his right hand described as 'pill-rolling', and rigidity of his limbs. His handwriting has become very small. He is diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.
(i) What are the four cardinal motor features of Parkinson's disease ?
(ii) What is the pathophysiological basis of Parkinson's disease at the cellular level?
(iii) What first-line drug treatment is indicated, including its administration, mechanism, and the rationale for combination therapy?
(iv) What are the major side effects and clinically relevant drug interactions of levodopa?
(v) What other drug classes are available for Parkinson's disease treatment?

(i) A patient presents with chest pain on exertion. On further assessment, describe how the pattern of pain and precipitating factors would allow you to identify which of the three types of angina is present.
(ii) State the physiological determinants that are disturbed in each case.
(iii) Give the differential diagnosis among the three types based on their underlying cause.
(iv) Give the clinico-pharmacological reasoning for the choice of drug in each type.
questions.answerText:
(i) Classic (atherosclerotic) angina is usually angina of effort but may be silent (ambulatory), usually due to atheromatous obstruction of large coronary vessels. Vasospastic angina (variant or Prinzmetal's angina) is secondary to transient spasm of localised portions of blood vessels, usually with underlying atheroma. Unstable angina is an acute coronary syndrome present when there are episodes of angina at rest and a change in the character, frequency and duration of chest pain and its precipitating factors, in a previously stable pattern.
(ii) The major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand disturbed are wall stress (intraventricular pressure, ventricular radius/volume, wall thickness), heart rate, and contractility; determinants of coronary blood flow (which may instead be reduced) include the duration of diastole and increased coronary vascular resistance from damaged endothelium, metabolic products or autonomic activity.
(iii) Classic angina is due to atheromatous obstruction of large coronary vessels; vasospastic angina is due to transient coronary artery spasm; unstable angina is an acute coronary syndrome with changing pattern of previously stable angina, including angina at rest.
(iv) In angina of effort, drugs act by reducing myocardial oxygen requirements through decreased venous return, reduced intracardiac volume, decreased arterial blood pressure, and decreased intraventricular pressure and left ventricular volume - achieved with organic nitrates, calcium channel blockers, and beta-blockers. In variant angina, relief comes from relaxation of epicardial coronary artery smooth muscle to relieve coronary spasm - organic nitrates and calcium channel blockers are used, as these also increase myocardial oxygen supply by reversing arterial spasm. In unstable angina, dilation of epicardial coronary arteries, reduced oxygen demand, and decreased platelet aggregation (with anti-thrombotic drugs) are important.

questions.question:
(i) A woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill develops venous thrombosis. What component of the drug is responsible, and what is the diagnosis?
(ii) State the mechanism of action of the combined oral contraceptive pill.
(iii) What adverse effects/disadvantages are related to this component?
(iv) State a contraindication relevant to this presentation.
questions.answerText:
(i) The estrogen component (ethinyl estradiol) of the combined oral contraceptive (COC) pill; the diagnosis is COC-associated venous thrombosis.
(ii) The COC pill suppresses secretion of LH and ovulation; it thickens cervical mucus and causes atrophy of the endometrium; the estrogen component suppresses FSH and prevents maturation of the follicle, stabilizes the endometrium with improved cycle control, and potentiates the action of progesterone.
(iii) Disadvantages of the COC are related mostly to estrogen content and include excessive weight gain, glucose intolerance, venous thrombosis, cerebrovascular accident (CVA), hypertension, myocardial infarction, and gall stone formation.
(iv) Contraindications include past history of thrombosis, ischaemic heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, coagulopathy, previous CVA, severe hypertension, focal migraine, transient ischaemic attacks, hyperlipidaemia, and a combination of risk markers.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the classification and members of the benzimidazole antihelmintics.
A(ii) Describe their mechanism of action.
A(iii) Describe their pharmacokinetic profiles.
B(i) State the therapeutic use of mebendazole and albendazole.
C(i) Explain the pharmacological basis of the low systemic toxicity of mebendazole.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Examples of benzimidazoles include albendazole, mebendazole and thiabendazole; the usefulness of thiabendazole has declined because of its toxicity. They are active against both the larval and adult stages of nematodes, and are also ovicidal for Ascaris and Trichuris.
A(ii) The primary mode of action of benzimidazoles is inhibition of microtubule polymerization by binding to beta-tubulin; the selective toxicity of these agents against helminths results from their higher affinity for parasite beta-tubulin compared with host tubulin.
Other biochemical changes following exposure include inhibition of mitochondrial fumarate reductase, glucose transport, and coupling of oxidative phosphorylation.
A(iii) Thiabendazole is soluble in water and well absorbed orally, reaching peak plasma concentration rapidly.
Mebendazole and albendazole are poorly soluble in aqueous solution; the low systemic bioavailability of mebendazole results from poor absorption, plasma binding, and rapid first-pass hepatic metabolism; co-administration of cimetidine increases plasma levels of mebendazole, possibly by inhibiting first-pass CYP450-mediated metabolism.
The small proportion of absorbed mebendazole is almost entirely bound to plasma proteins and is extensively metabolized; conjugates of mebendazole and its metabolites are found in bile, with little unchanged drug in urine. Albendazole is variably and erratically absorbed orally, with absorption enhanced by fatty foods and bile salts, and is rapidly metabolized in the liver to albendazole sulfoxide, which has potent activity against nematodes.
B(i) Mebendazole is an effective drug for treatment of nematode infections.
Albendazole is the drug of choice for treating cystic hydatid disease due to Echinococcus granulosus.
C(i) Because mebendazole has low systemic bioavailability, arising from poor absorption, high plasma protein binding of the small absorbed fraction, and rapid first-pass hepatic metabolism, very little of the active drug reaches the systemic circulation.
Immobilization and death of susceptible gastrointestinal parasites occur slowly, and their clearance from the GI tract may not be complete until several days after treatment, reflecting the drug's predominantly luminal/local site of action.
This pharmacokinetic profile — poor systemic absorption combined with selective affinity for parasite beta-tubulin over host tubulin — is the basis for benzimidazoles having excellent safety profiles (with the exception of thiabendazole).
Albendazole, by contrast, is rapidly metabolized to albendazole sulfoxide, which retains potent antinematodal activity, allowing it to be effective in tissue-invasive infections such as cystic hydatid disease.

A(i) Adrenoceptors are classified into alpha (alpha1 and alpha2) and beta (beta1, beta2 and beta3) receptors; alpha1 has subtypes alpha1A, alpha1B and alpha1D, and alpha2 has subtypes alpha2A, alpha2B and alpha2C.
A(ii) Adrenergic receptors are membrane-bound G-protein-coupled receptors that function primarily by increasing or decreasing intracellular cyclic AMP and by acting on the phosphatidylinositol cycle; agonist binding at beta receptors raises intracellular cAMP via adenylyl cyclase activation, with downstream effects mediated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA).
A(iii) alpha1 receptors are found mainly in vascular smooth muscle (contraction), the pupillary dilator muscle (mydriasis) and the heart (increased force of contraction); alpha2 receptors are found on adrenergic nerve terminals (inhibition of transmitter release) and platelets (aggregation); beta1 receptors are found in the heart (increased rate and force of contraction) and the juxtaglomerular apparatus (increased renin release); beta2 receptors are found in respiratory, uterine and vascular smooth muscle (relaxation) and the liver (glycogenolysis); beta3 receptors are found in fat cells (lipolysis).
B. Selective agents are preferred because they can produce the desired therapeutic effect on one tissue while avoiding unwanted effects mediated by other adrenoceptor subtypes; for example, cardioselective beta1 blockers lower blood pressure and heart rate with less risk of bronchoconstriction than non-selective beta blockers, which can precipitate bronchospasm in asthmatic patients by also blocking beta2 receptors.
C. alpha1 receptors are mainly postsynaptic, located on effector organs such as vascular smooth muscle where their stimulation causes contraction and increased force of cardiac contraction; alpha2 receptors are mainly presynaptic, located on adrenergic nerve terminals where their stimulation inhibits further release of noradrenaline (a negative feedback/autoregulatory mechanism), and are also found on platelets, where they promote aggregation, and in the pancreas, where they decrease insulin release.

questions.answerText:
(i) The emergency diagnosis is status epilepticus. Status epilepticus is traditionally defined as ongoing seizure activity for ≥30 minutes; from a pragmatic point of view, a seizure that lasts longer than 5 minutes warrants pharmacological intervention. Initial management is supportive and may include: secure airway and resuscitate; administer oxygen; assess cardiorespiratory function; establish intravenous access. During seizures, the individual should not be moved unless in a dangerous place. No attempt should be made to open the person's mouth or force anything between the teeth. When the seizure stops, the person should be turned into the recovery position and the airway checked for any blockage.
(ii) In the community, buccal midazolam (10 mg) is first-line; rectal diazepam is an alternative. First-line AED for hospital management is intravenous lorazepam; if unavailable, intravenous diazepam or buccal midazolam should be administered. If seizures continue, intravenous phenytoin or valproate or phenobarbital should be administered as second-line treatment. In refractory status epilepticus, general anaesthesia with propofol, midazolam, or thiopentone may be necessary.
(iii) The hallmark of epilepsy is a rather rhythmic and repetitive hyper-synchronous discharge of neurons, either localised in an area of the cerebral cortex or generalised throughout the cortex, which can be observed on an EEG. Generalised seizures involve initial activation of both hemispheres of the brain simultaneously; focal seizures start in a localised area of the brain. The area from which the abnormal discharge originates is known as the epileptic focus. In focal seizures, the discharge may remain localised or may spread to adjacent areas, recruiting more neurons as it expands throughout the brain via cortical and subcortical routes.
(iv) Febrile convulsions may occur in the young without epilepsy. Brief events are managed conservatively with the primary aim of reducing the child's temperature — tepid sponging and use of paracetamol are usual. Prolonged febrile convulsions lasting ≥10–15 minutes, or in a child with risk factors, require active management to avoid brain damage. The drug of choice is diazepam by intravenous or rectal administration. Prophylactic management may be required in some children, such as those with pre-existing risk factors or a history of previous prolonged seizures.
(v) Other conditions may cause impairment or loss of consciousness which can be misdiagnosed as epilepsy; these include syncope, breath-holding attacks, transient ischaemic attacks, and psychogenic attacks. People may also present with acute symptomatic seizures or provoked seizures as a result of other problems such as drugs, metabolic dysfunction, infection, head trauma, or flashing lights (photosensitive seizures). These conditions have to be clearly ruled out before a diagnosis of epilepsy is made. Epilepsy must only be diagnosed when at least one of the three defining ILAE conditions is present.
questions.question:
A 17-year-old male is brought to hospital after a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure lasting 40 minutes. He has had previous brief seizures. He is on no medications.
(i) What is the emergency diagnosis, and what are the initial management steps?
(ii) What first-line and second-line drug treatments are used in hospital for this emergency?
(iii) What is the hallmark of epilepsy on EEG, and how does focal versus generalised epilepsy differ in terms of onset?
(iv) Describe the features and management of febrile convulsions as an important differential in young patients.
(v) What factors must be ruled out before a diagnosis of epilepsy is made?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Receptors are subject to regulation and homeostatic control. Left unregulated, receptors may be over-stimulated, which may lead to pathological changes; therefore regulation helps protect cells. Cellular mechanisms of increased response: (1) Super/hypersensitivity: refers to an enhanced response to an agonist; may occur as a result of unmasking of receptors (removal of masking protein increases activity) or accentuation of signal amplification (increase in receptor activity, e.g. increased enzymatic activity). (2) Synergism: when two receptors produce a combined effect that is greater than the sum of their individual effects. (3) Upregulation: increase in the number of receptors due to prolonged deprivation of interaction with their physiological ligands (e.g. chronic use of a receptor antagonist).
A(ii) Desensitization: reduced response to an agonist drug due to over-activation of a receptor (high doses, prolonged exposure to agonist). Downregulation: a reduction in the total number of receptors due to prolonged receptor activation (e.g. by chronic use of an agonist or prolonged inhibition of metabolism of a neurotransmitter). Tachyphylaxis: a rapid decrease in response to an agonist drug following repeated administration within a brief period; an acute form of desensitization; increasing the dose will not improve the response. Tolerance: a gradual decreased response to a drug, requiring a higher dose to achieve the same initial response. Distinction: tolerance develops over a long period of time, whereas tachyphylaxis is an acute event.
B(i) Disease states may alter the number of available receptors and affect their activity, either through loss or gain of function. Loss of receptor function: Myasthenia Gravis is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies destroy nicotinic acetylcholine receptors located in skeletal muscle. Gain of receptor function: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus can be associated with a gain-of-function mutation resulting in increased expression of the a2A-adrenergic receptor, a GPCR that prevents or suppresses the secretion of insulin.
B(ii) Downregulation: continuous exposure to an agonist leads to a reduction in the number of receptors, resulting in reduced response. Example: reduced response to beta-adrenergic agonist in asthmatics on long-term use. Upregulation: continuous exposure to an antagonist leads to an increased number of receptors. Example: rebound phenomenon following abrupt withdrawal of a beta-blocker, resulting in rebound hypertension.
B(iii) Microorganisms or malignant cells show resistance in chemotherapy, while normal host cells exhibit tolerance to pharmacodynamic drugs. Resistance refers to a genetically determined unresponsiveness of microorganisms or tumour cells to a drug; tolerance refers to a decreased response in normal host cells after repeated administration.

A(i) Major NAT2 substrates: INH (isoniazid), procainamide, sulfonamides, hydralazine. Of the 27 variants described, NAT2*5, *6, *7, *14 are slow activity alleles common among Caucasians and Africans. Phenotypes: slow and fast acetylators. Clinical consequences of slow acetylator phenotype: (a) slow acetylators on isoniazid (INH) - fast acetylators may not benefit from the antituberculous effect of INH; (b) slow acetylators on procainamide may predispose to drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); (c) fast acetylators on hydralazine may not benefit from its antihypertensive effect.
A(ii) TPMT (thiopurine S-methyltransferase) metabolizes three important drugs: 6-mercaptopurine, azathioprine, and 6-thioguanine. TPMT gene polymorphisms result in high, normal, or low/no TPMT activity. Clinical consequence: deficient TPMT activity causes severe bone marrow depression (accumulation of thioguanine nucleotides leads to myelosuppression).
B(i) Drug transporters influence absorption, distribution, and elimination; they mostly belong to the ABC (e.g. MDR1) or SLC (e.g. SerT) families. The P-glycoprotein is the product of the MDR1 gene, a member of the ATP-binding Cassette (ABC) protein. Notable substrates of P-glycoprotein include: digoxin, quinidine, verapamil, colchicine, morphine, clarithromycin, etoposide, vinblastine, efavirenz, ritonavir, tamoxifen, cyclosporin, tacrolimus, dexamethasone.
B(ii) Importance of pharmacogenetics for personalized medicine: dose optimization and personalized medicine: doses and dosing regimens would be determined by the individual's genetic make-up; avoidance of dose-dependent adverse drug reactions. Example 1: imatinib and tyrosine kinase receptor in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Example 2: trastuzumab and HER2 target in breast cancer. Also: reduction in the cost of healthcare delivery; development of novel medicines.
B(iii) Two notable HLA-associated adverse drug reactions: (1) abacavir hypersensitivity is strongly associated with HLA-B*5701 allele; screening for this allele before prescribing abacavir prevents the reaction. (2) Carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) is associated with HLA-B*1502 allele.
