questions.answerText:
A(i) Non-opioid analgesics are analgesics that do not bind to opioid receptors in the brain and hence do not have CNS effects. They are used orally to manage mild to moderate pain such as acute pain of skeletal muscle (orthopaedic) or oral (dental) origin and inflammation associated with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. They act primarily in peripheral tissues to inhibit the formation/synthesis of prostaglandins. The two main classes are: NSAIDs (including salicylates, indole derivatives, fenamates, propionic acid derivatives, oxicam derivatives, phenylacetic acid derivatives, pyrazolone derivatives, and others) and p-Aminophenol derivatives (e.g. acetaminophen/paracetamol, phenacetin, acetanilide).
A(ii) The COX enzyme catalyses the conversion of arachidonic acid into prostaglandin. The enzyme has 2 known isoforms, COX-1 and COX-2. Inhibition of COX-2 (PG, PGE2, PGI2) is responsible for the analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory activities of the salicylates. Inhibition of COX-1 (Thromboxane, TXA2) is responsible for antiplatelet activity and exposes the stomach lining, increasing the chance of stomach ulcer and/or bleeding (GIT effects). The COX-1 enzyme regulates many cellular processes, including platelet aggregation, kidney afferent arteriole vasodilation, and gastric mucosa acid protection. COX-2-specific NSAIDs work by preferentially inhibiting COX-2.
B(i) Aspirin irreversibly and non-selectively inhibits the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), which converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2 (PGH2). PGH2 is converted to prostaglandins (mediators of pain, inflammation, and fever) and thromboxane. Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation and eventual thrombus formation. For antiplatelet activity, low dose (75–100 mg) is usually given because the cyclooxygenase pathway within the platelet is more sensitive to low dose of aspirin. Adult dose is 325–975 mg. Clinical uses include prophylaxis of myocardial infarction. Contraindications: children under 8 years of age, peptic ulcer, bleeding disorder, late pregnancy. Adverse effects include: GI effects (nausea, vomiting, gastric irritation → bleeding → ulceration → perforation); increased depth of respirations; excessive bleeding; uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation; delayed onset of labour; at low doses, decreased renal urate excretion; salicylism (tinnitus, nausea, vomiting).
B(ii) p-Aminophenol derivatives (prototype: acetaminophen/paracetamol) inhibit central prostaglandin synthesis presumably through a selectivity for COX-2 with relatively little or no activity on COX-1. They have both analgesic and antipyretic activity. Acetaminophen is primarily used for its analgesic and antipyretic activity, particularly in patients unable to tolerate salicylates. There is no gastric irritation unlike the salicylates. They are less effective in blocking peripheral prostaglandin synthesis (unlike the salicylates), hence they do not have anti-inflammatory activity and do not affect platelet function. Adverse effects include skin rash, haemolytic anaemia, renal dysfunction, and tubular necrosis.
B(iii) Non-opioids have a ceiling effect in analgesia: a maximum dose beyond which analgesic effect does not increase. Non-opioids have an upper limit of pain relief that can be achieved. Once that upper limit or ceiling is reached, increasing the dosage will not provide any further pain relief. Opioids, on the other hand, tend not to have a ceiling effect — the more you take, the more pain relief you will get.

A 70-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has been on levodopa/carbidopa for 5 years. He now experiences unpredictable motor fluctuations: periods of good movement control alternating with episodes of near-complete immobility ('off' periods) and involuntary writhing movements of his limbs during the 'on' state.
(i) What are the motor complications described here, and what is the mechanism of the wearing-off phenomenon?
(ii) What COMT inhibitors are available, and how do they work to address wearing-off?
(iii) What are the non-motor features of Parkinson's disease, and why are they clinically significant?
(iv) What surgical approaches are available for Parkinson's disease management?
(v) What are the five proposed major mechanisms for neuronal death in Parkinson's disease?
questions.answerText:
(i) The wearing-off effect occurs when the patient finds that the effect of the medicine does not last until their next dose is due. The premature wearing off of the anti-Parkinsonian effects of levodopa and fluctuations in the response with the development of involuntary movements known as dyskinesia typically occur after a number of years of treatment and relate as much to the duration of disease. The involuntary writhing movements are dyskinesia, which develops after years of treatment.
(ii) COMT inhibitors — tolcapone and entacapone — represent a useful addition to the range of therapies for PD. COMT itself is a ubiquitous enzyme found in the gut, liver, kidney, and brain. Both tolcapone and entacapone act primarily as peripheral COMT inhibitors, and by so doing increase the amount of levodopa that enters the CNS by inhibiting the peripheral conversion of levodopa to the inert 3-O-methyldopa. When entacapone is prescribed, a 200 mg dose is usually given with each dose of levodopa administered, up to a frequency of 10 doses/day. Entacapone is also marketed as a compound tablet containing levodopa and carbidopa (Stalevo®). Tolcapone is hepatotoxic and requires strict liver function monitoring; entacapone studies have not shown any derangement of liver function, thus it is more commonly used.
(iii) A range of non-motor features encompassing autonomic, cognitive, and psychiatric problems are seen in nearly all cases of PD and have a pronounced effect on quality of life. They can precede disease onset and tend to become more prominent as the condition evolves. These include: postural hypotension (a leading cause of hospitalisation for patients with PD); constipation (pathology in the enteric nervous system); depression (affecting approximately 40% of patients); paranoia and hallucinations; dementia (80% of PD patients); sleep disorders (especially REM sleep behavioural disorder); and restless leg syndrome and limb pain.
(iv) Surgical approaches for management of PD include both lesioning (-otomies) and deep brain stimulation (a high-frequency signal that functionally turns off the nucleus being stimulated). The intervention is costly but significant benefits can be gained, especially for patients who have previously had a good response to levodopa but are experiencing major motor fluctuations or dyskinesia. New potential surgical approaches also include the delivery of growth factors, dopamine cells, and viral vectors (for the delivery of growth factors or enzymes required for dopamine synthesis).
(v) The five proposed major mechanisms for neuronal death in Parkinson's disease are: protein aggregation; disruption of autophagy; changes in cell metabolism or mitochondrial function; neuroinflammation; and breakdown of the blood–brain barrier resulting in vascular leakiness.

questions.question:
A. Describe vitamin D under the following headings:
A(i) sources and activation pathway
A(ii) circulating/active forms
A(iii) actions on target organs
B. State the form of vitamin D that must be used therapeutically in a patient whose activation pathway is impaired, and why.
C. Explain the basis of the skeletal deformity that results from chronic deficiency of this vitamin.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Vitamin D can be synthesised in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol under ultraviolet light, or absorbed from the diet as vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) or vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol, plant form). In the liver, cholecalciferol undergoes 25-hydroxylation to 25(OH) vitamin D (calcifediol); in the kidney, calcifediol undergoes 1-alpha-hydroxylation, catalysed by 1-alpha-hydroxylase, to produce 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D (calcitriol). 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity is increased by decreased serum calcium, increased PTH, and decreased serum phosphate.
A(ii) The main circulating/active forms are 25-hydroxyvitamin D and the active hormone 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol); insufficiency is 20-30 ng/mL, deficiency is below 20 ng/mL, and toxicity is above 150 ng/mL of 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
A(iii) Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, increases renal reabsorption of calcium and phosphate, and increases osteoclast activity; active vitamin D metabolites are required for normal mineralisation of bone.
B. In patients with conditions that impair vitamin D activation, such as chronic kidney disease, liver disease, or hypoparathyroidism, an already-activated form such as calcitriol is required, since these patients cannot adequately perform the hydroxylation steps needed to activate cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol.
C. Deficiency of active vitamin D metabolites causes abnormal mineralisation of bone; this is called rickets when it occurs in the growing skeleton of children and adolescents, producing skeletal deformity, and osteomalacia when it occurs in the adult skeleton.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old chronic alcoholic is admitted after his family reports he had a tonic-clonic seizure approximately 36 hours after his last drink. He is agitated, diaphoretic, tachycardic, and reports seeing 'insects crawling on the walls'.
(i) What is this presentation consistent with, and what is the mechanism of alcohol dependence?
(ii) What are the withdrawal symptoms of alcohol?
(iii) What pharmacological interventions are used for alcohol withdrawal and long-term management of alcohol dependence?
(iv) What are the effects of alcohol dependence on organ systems and cognition?
(v) What is the mechanism by which alcohol produces cross-tolerance to benzodiazepines, and what is the clinical risk?
questions.answerText:
(i) This presentation is consistent with alcohol withdrawal syndrome, including delirium tremens (which occurs 48–96 hours after the last drink). The mechanism of alcohol dependence: the common feature of dependence-inducing drugs including ethanol is that they have a positive reinforcing action ('reward') through activation of the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway. Dopamine is released during rewarding or pleasurable stimuli, creating positive feelings that reinforce the behaviour. All these drugs increase the extracellular level of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. Alcohol produces positive reinforcing effects such as euphoria and reduction of anxiety. Heavy consumers of alcohol acquire tolerance and develop a state of physical dependence.
(ii) Withdrawal symptoms of alcohol include: alcohol craving; tremor; irritability; nausea; sleep disturbance; tachycardia; hypertension; profuse sweating; perceptual distortion; seizures (6–48 hours after last drink); visual (and occasionally auditory or tactile) hallucinations (12–48 hours after last drink); delirium tremens (48–96 hours after last drink; rare in uncomplicated withdrawal); severe agitation; confusion; fever; diarrhoea; dilated pupils.
(iii) For detoxification: severe cases require general evaluation; attention to hydration and electrolytes; vitamins, especially high-dose thiamine; and a sedating medication with cross-tolerance to alcohol. To block or diminish withdrawal symptoms, a short-acting benzodiazepine such as oxazepam can be used at 15–30 mg every 4–6 hours according to the stage and severity of withdrawal. Complete abstinence is the objective of long-term treatment, accomplished mainly by behavioural approaches. Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase (the second step in ethanol metabolism), resulting in accumulation of acetaldehyde, which produces an unpleasant flushing reaction when alcohol is ingested, helping the patient resist taking a drink. Naltrexone (an opioid antagonist) blocks some of the reinforcing properties of alcohol and has resulted in a decreased rate of relapse.
(iv) Effects of alcohol dependence include: depression; risk of suicide among alcoholics is one of the highest of any diagnostic category; cognitive deficits that usually improve after weeks to months of abstinence; more severe recent memory impairment associated with specific brain damage caused by nutritional deficiencies (e.g. thiamine deficiency); and complications including liver disease, cardiovascular disease, endocrine and GI effects.
(v) Alcohol produces cross-tolerance to other sedatives such as benzodiazepines. These may be relatively safe in overdose when given alone but potentially are lethal in combination with alcohol. Ethanol is classed as a CNS depressant because it produces sedation and sleep; it acts on inhibitory (GABA) systems. Benzodiazepines similarly enhance GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission, explaining the mechanistic basis for cross-tolerance.

questions.question:
(i) A postmenopausal woman is found to have abnormal loss of bone predisposing her to fractures. List the risk factors that predispose to this diagnosis.
(ii) State the major complication of this condition.
(iii) Outline the pharmacological management options.
(iv) Justify the use of one class of drug as first-line therapy.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: loss of gonadal function as in menopause; adverse effect of long-term glucocorticoid administration; hyperparathyroidism; malabsorption syndrome; and alcohol abuse and cigarette smoking.
(ii) Osteoporosis is an abnormal loss of bone predisposing to fractures.
(iii) Management options: bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, zoledronate); selective estrogen receptor modulators (raloxifene, tamoxifen); teriparatide (recombinant PTH 1-34, stimulates new bone formation); calcitonin; and denosumab (a RANKL inhibitor).
(iv) Chronic bisphosphonate therapy is justified as first-line therapy because it is used commonly to prevent and treat all forms of osteoporosis and has been shown to increase bone density and reduce fractures; denosumab is at least as effective as potent bisphosphonates and avoids gastrointestinal side effects, but bisphosphonates remain the most commonly used agents.

(i) Methanol poisoning.
(ii) Methanol is metabolised to formic acid, leading to increased lactic acidosis and subsequent inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation; wilful or accidental ingestion produces severe life-threatening consequences including coma.
(iii) Ethanol competes for methanol receptors (for the alcohol dehydrogenase enzyme), and at high concentration displaces methanol, thereby promoting its elimination from the system; alteration of toxic metabolite formation is achieved because ethanol competes for the active site of the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, inhibiting formation of formaldehyde and formic acid in methanol poisoning. Pyrazole or 4-methylpyrazole can also be used to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase in this poisoning.
(iv) Intravenous administration of a high dose of ethanol, usually in combination with folate, is given as treatment.

A 45-year-old man is admitted after overdose of a basic drug. Management includes acidification of urine to promote drug excretion.
(i) Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch principle, explain why acidification of urine promotes excretion of a basic drug.
(ii) Describe tubular secretion as a mechanism of drug excretion from the kidneys, including whether it requires energy and how competitive inhibition operates in this system.
(iii) A second drug is given that blocks the active transport carrier for basic drugs. State how this would affect the excretion of the overdosed drug.
(iv) State the biliary excretion mechanisms and identify which drugs are excreted this way, including the minimum molecular weight for pore passage.
(v) Explain enterohepatic circulation, including which type of drugs undergo it and when it is terminated.
questions.answerText:
(i) Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pKa = pH + log (nonionized/ionized). Acidification of urine increases the degree of ionization of a weak base, thereby increasing its elimination in urine. Ionized molecules are charged, polar, relatively water-soluble and lipid-insoluble; they poorly penetrate membranes and therefore cannot be reabsorbed from the renal tubule, resulting in their excretion.
(ii) Many carrier-mediated transport systems are present in the epithelium of the renal tubule; they transport organic ions from blood to urine against their concentration gradient. This is an active process (requires energy). It is divided into two types: one for acidic drugs and one for basic drugs. Elimination of drugs through tubular secretion is faster than through glomerular filtration. Competitive inhibition: drugs with higher affinity to the carrier system competitively inhibit transport of other drugs with lower affinity; e.g. probenecid blocks the excretion of penicillins and cephalosporins transported by the same carrier system.
(iii) If the active transport carrier for basic drugs is blocked, the overdosed basic drug cannot be actively secreted into the tubule; only glomerular filtration would operate, significantly reducing the rate of drug excretion and prolonging the drug's half-life and potential toxicity.
(iv) Secretion of drugs into the bile by the liver occurs by simple diffusion through pores and by active transport. Only drugs soluble in lipid and non-ionized penetrate from liver to bile by diffusion. Compounds of molecular weight more than 400-500 pass through the pores into the bile. Drugs such as erythromycin, chloramphenicol, rifampicin, tetracycline, penicillin, contrast media, and hydantoin are secreted by active transport into the bile.
(v) Enterohepatic circulation: lipid-soluble drugs passing into the intestine from the bile are reabsorbed into the blood stream. This process continues until the drug undergoes biotransformation and loses its lipophilic properties. Enterohepatic circulation prolongs the duration of action of lipophilic drugs. It is terminated when the drug undergoes biotransformation and loses its lipophilic (fat-soluble) properties.

A(i) ACE inhibitors competitively inhibit the activity of ACE (also called kininase II) to prevent formation of the active octapeptide angiotensin II from the inactive decapeptide angiotensin I; this occurs in blood and tissues including the kidney, heart, blood vessels, adrenal gland and brain. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that promotes aldosterone release and facilitates sympathetic activity.
A(ii) All ACE inhibitors bind to tissue and plasma protein; free drug is eliminated relatively rapidly by the kidney, predominantly by glomerular filtration. Captopril is absorbed and eliminated rapidly; enalapril is an inactive pro-drug requiring hydrolysis to the active form, enalaprilat; lisinopril is an analogue of enalapril and is itself active.
A(iii) Adverse effects include: dry, irritant cough in about 15% of patients (attributable to accumulation of bradykinin); first-dose hypotension in essential hypertension; angioedema (rare but potentially fatal); hyperkalaemia due to reduced aldosterone; impairment of renal function (caution in bilateral renal artery stenosis); and rare taste disturbance, skin rashes and urticaria.
B. The dry cough and angioedema are both attributable to accumulation of bradykinin (kinin potentiation), since ACE (kininase II) normally also degrades bradykinin, and inhibiting the enzyme allows kinins to accumulate in the affected tissues.
C. ACE inhibitors act by inhibiting the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and, by the same action, cause bradykinin accumulation (hence cough/angioedema); ARBs act by directly blocking the angiotensin II receptor rather than inhibiting the enzyme, so they do not cause bradykinin accumulation and are used as an alternative when a patient develops cough or angioedema on an ACE inhibitor. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined with each other.
questions.question:
A. Describe ACE inhibitors under the following headings:
A(i) mechanism of action
A(ii) pharmacokinetics
A(iii) adverse effects
B. Explain the clinical basis of the dry cough and angioedema associated with this class of drug.
C. Distinguish between ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs).

Describe the pharmacology of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) and NSAIDs under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the chemical classification of salicylates, the stability of aspirin, and the more stable salicylates.
A(ii) Describe the mechanism of action of aspirin, including its effects on COX isoforms, prostaglandins, and platelet aggregation.
B(i) Describe the classification of NSAIDs into subclasses, giving specific examples under each subclass.
B(ii) Describe the common adverse effects of salicylates, including GI effects, the role of prostaglandins in GI protection, and salicylism.
B(iii) Describe the clinical uses of salicylates beyond pain relief.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Salicylates are derivatives of salicylic acid. The prototype drug is aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid), which hydrolyses easily, is unstable in aqueous media, and is affected by moisture. More stable salicylates include diflunisal (Dolobid) and the topical agent methyl salicylate. Other salicylates are salsalate, sodium thiosalicylate, and choline salicylate.
A(ii) Aspirin irreversibly and non-selectively inhibits the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), which converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2 (PGH2). PGH2 is converted by other enzymes to several other prostaglandins (which are mediators of pain, inflammation, and fever) and thromboxane. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2 but inhibits COX-1 more than COX-2. Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation and eventual thrombus formation. For antiplatelet activity, low dose of aspirin (75–100 mg) is usually given because the cyclooxygenase pathway within the platelet is more sensitive to low dose of aspirin. Inhibition of COX-2 is responsible for the analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory activities; inhibition of COX-1 is responsible for antiplatelet activity and GIT effects.
B(i) Classification of NSAIDs: Salicylates — salicylic acid, Na-salicylates, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), methyl salicylate (topical), benorylate, deflonisol. Indole derivatives — indomethacin, sulindac. Fenamates — mefenamic acid. Propionic acid derivatives — ibuprofen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen, fenoprofen, naproxane, oxaprozin. Oxicam derivatives — piroxicam. Phenylacetic acid derivatives — diclofenac (Voltaren). Pyrazolone derivatives — phenylbutazone (no longer used). Others — nabumatone, ketorolac, rofecoxib (COX-2 inhibitor).
B(ii) Adverse effects of salicylates:
(1) GI effects: nausea, vomiting, and gastric irritation → gastric bleeding → gastric ulceration → gastric perforation. Prostaglandin (PG) normally causes: increased mucus production, increased blood supply, increased HCO3 secretion, and decreased HCl secretion. Because aspirin inhibits PG, all these protective effects are reversed, causing irritation of the mucosa.
(2) Increased depth of respirations.
(3) Excessive bleeding associated with inhibition of thromboxane synthesis.
(4) Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, hyperglycaemia, and glycosuria.
(5) Delayed onset of labour.
(6) Low daily doses decrease renal urate excretion and increase serum uric acid levels; high daily doses have the opposite effect.
(7) Sulfasalazine has been shown to have male reproductive effects, causing infertility.
(8) Salicylism (salicylate toxicity): tinnitus, nausea, and vomiting; tinnitus and hearing loss are dose-related and usually completely reversible within 24–48 hours after dose reduction.
(9) Ingestion of 1 teaspoon of topical methyl salicylate can cause fatal intoxication.
B(iii) Clinical uses of salicylates beyond pain relief: aspirin is indicated for prophylaxis of myocardial infarction; methyl salicylate is used topically as a counter-irritant and anti-inflammatory; sulfasalazine, olsalazine, and mesalamine are used to reduce the inflammation associated with inflammatory bowel disease and Crohn disease.

(i) First-pass effect (first-pass metabolism). Drugs absorbed perorally are initially transported to the liver via the portal vein, where metabolism may occur in the gut wall, mesentery, and predominantly the liver before reaching systemic circulation, resulting in a reduction in bioavailability.
(ii) Liver disease reduces biotransformation of drugs and prolongs their duration of action. In this patient, cirrhosis diminishes the liver's enzymatic capacity, so even a standard oral dose causes drug accumulation and toxicity.
(iii) Three alternative routes: sublingual/buccal (the main advantage is that the liver is bypassed and drugs with high first-pass metabolism can be absorbed directly into systemic circulation); cutaneous/transdermal (the liver is also bypassed); and intravenous injection (the drug directly reaches the blood stream).
(iv) Two examples of drugs with extensive first-pass metabolism: nitroglycerin (and other nitrates), desipramine, morphine, lignocaine, or verapamil (any two accepted).
(v) Liver disease reduces biotransformation of drugs and prolongs their duration of action. The rate of occurrence of drug toxicity is therefore increased in patients with liver disease.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with liver cirrhosis is prescribed a drug that undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism. After receiving the standard oral dose, he develops signs of drug toxicity.
(i) Name the pharmacokinetic phenomenon responsible and explain its mechanism.
(ii) Explain why liver disease predisposes this patient to drug toxicity via this mechanism.
(iii) List three alternative routes by which this drug could be administered to avoid or reduce first-pass metabolism.
(iv) State two examples of drugs that undergo extensive first-pass metabolism.
(v) Explain what happens to biotransformation generally in liver disease and how this affects drug duration of action.

Describe the mechanism of drug action, focusing on drug-receptor interactions, under the following headings:
A(i) Define a receptor in the context of drug-receptor interaction.
A(ii) Describe the receptor occupation theory, its three tenets, and the later modification that introduced affinity and intrinsic activity.
B(i) Describe agonism (full and partial), antagonism (competitive, non-competitive), and physiological antagonism, giving one example of each.
B(ii) Describe synergism (additive and potentiation), giving one example of each.
B(iii) Describe pharmacokinetic antagonism and chemical antagonism, giving one example of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A receptor is that part of a cell directly involved in drug interaction; it is all specific molecules which bind the drug chemically to exert a pharmacological action. Drug-receptor interaction may initiate response by altering the membrane permeability, interfering with the transport mechanism, or modifying the template or action of enzymes.
A(ii) Receptor occupation theory: the interaction between a drug and a receptor is governed by the law of mass action; the effect produced is a direct function of the drug-receptor complex formed. The theory states: (1) the intensity of response is proportional to the fraction of the receptor occupied by the drug, and maximal response occurs when all the receptors are occupied; (2) drugs exert an all-or-none action on each receptor (no partial activation); (3) a drug and its receptor have complementary structural features (rigid lock and key relationship). Later it was found that not all receptors need to be occupied for a maximal response, so the concept of affinity (ability of the drug to combine with the receptor) and intrinsic activity/efficacy (ability to activate the receptor after occupation) was introduced.
B(i) Full agonism: all receptors are occupied and produce maximal pharmacological actions possible. Partial agonism: binds to receptors, activates them but unable to produce maximal pharmacological response; partial agonists have affinity and suboptimal intrinsic activity (AI 0 to 1). Competitive antagonism: binds to one receptor binding site at a time; the agonist is prevented from binding; effect is reversible/surmountable; e.g. atropine, propranolol. Non-competitive antagonism: binds tightly to a different site on the receptor but still blocks the response; e.g. hexamethonium. Physiological/functional antagonism: caused by two drugs acting at two independent sites and inducing independent but opposite effects; e.g. acetylcholine increases GIT motility while adrenaline decreases it.
B(ii) Additive synergism: when effect produced is the arithmetic sum of the individual effects; e.g. use of thiazide diuretic and a beta-adrenergic blocking drug in the treatment of hypertension. Potentiation: when the total effect is greater than the sum of individual effects; e.g. sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim (sequential blockade).
B(iii) Pharmacokinetic antagonism: the antagonist reduces the concentration of the active drug at the site of action by decreasing absorption, increasing metabolism, or increasing excretion; e.g. barbiturates (enzyme inducers in the liver) lead to increased metabolism and therefore reduce the effects of co-administered drugs. Chemical antagonism: interaction between agonist and antagonist outside of a receptor to form an inactive complex; no receptors involved; e.g. inactivation of metals - Fe and desferroxamine, Hg and succinyl, Ca and EDTA, Pb and dimercaprol.

questions.question:
Describe the principles of drug action as they relate to pharmacodynamics under the following headings:
A(i) Define pharmacodynamics and state the four principles of drug action.
A(ii) Describe the mechanism of action at enzyme-linked receptors and intracellular (nuclear) receptors, giving one example and the speed of response for each.
B(i) Describe ligand-gated ion channel receptors and G protein-coupled receptors, giving an example and the speed of response for each.
B(ii) Describe the functions of receptors.
B(iii) List the factors that affect drug response and explain the role of psychological factors including placebo effect.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pharmacodynamics is about drug action and consequent effects on body functions and/or dysfunctions, including dose-response relationships and factors that influence drug action. Four principles of drug action: (1) Stimulation: enhancement of existing bodily activities, e.g. adrenaline and tachycardia. (2) Depression: e.g. barbiturates and CNS function. (3) Replacement: e.g. L-Dopa in Parkinsonism. (4) Cytotoxic action: e.g. chemotherapeutic agents.
A(ii) Enzyme-linked (protein kinase-linked) receptors (e.g. receptors for insulin, growth factors, cytokines): possess intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity; are relatively slow; involved in cell growth and differentiation, release of inflammatory mediators. Example: insulin receptor. Intracellular (nuclear) receptors: very slow, usually hours; for thyroid, steroid hormones or related compounds.
B(i) Ligand-gated channels (ionotropic receptors): protein subunits that form a central pore; fastest response within milliseconds; most neurotransmitters; example: nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, GABA receptor. G protein-coupled receptors (metabotropic receptors): seven membrane-spanning alpha-helices, linked to a second messenger; effect observable within seconds; example: beta-adrenoceptor involving cAMP as second messenger.
B(ii) Functions of receptors: (1) to propagate regulatory signals from outside to the inside of the effector cell when the ligand cannot penetrate the cell membrane; (2) to amplify signals; (3) to integrate various extracellular and intracellular regulatory signals; (4) to adapt to short-term and long-term changes in the regulatory milieu and maintain homeostasis.
B(iii) Factors affecting drug response: age (peculiarities of the extremes of age); pathological state (e.g. liver disease, renal disease); other drugs and environmental factors; drug interactions; exposure to tobacco smoke; genetics (pharmacogenetics); psychological factors. Placebo effect: a psychological factor where the patient's belief in receiving treatment leads to a therapeutic response even in the absence of an active drug.

A(i) Drug addiction: a pattern of compulsive drug use characterized by overwhelming involvement with the use of a drug; using the drug takes precedence over other activities; even after promising to stop, most addicts relapse; there is compulsive drug-seeking behaviour. Examples: cocaine, cannabis, amphetamines. Drug habituation: a less intensive involvement with the drug, so that its withdrawal produces only a mild discomfort; no physical dependence. Examples: consumption of tea, coffee, tobacco, social drinking. Distinction: addiction involves compulsive drug-seeking and is much more intense; habituation causes only mild discomfort on withdrawal.
A(ii) Drug withdrawal reactions: sudden interruption of certain drugs used for treating other illnesses may cause adverse consequences such as worsening of the clinical condition. Mechanism: the body has adapted to the presence of the drug, and abrupt removal disrupts the adapted physiological state. Example 1: frequency of seizures is increased on sudden withdrawal of anti-epileptic drugs. Example 2: hypertension may worsen if certain antihypertensive drugs are stopped suddenly. These may be minimized by a gradual withdrawal of the drug.
B(i) Carcinogenicity is the capacity of a drug to cause cancer, and mutagenicity is the capacity to cause genetic defects. Mechanism: usually oxidation of such drugs results in production of reactive oxygen species that may damage genes or cause structural changes in chromosomes. Drug classes implicated: tobacco, radioisotopes, estrogens, some anticancer drugs.
B(ii) Photosensitivity is a cutaneous reaction resulting from drug-induced sensitization of the skin to UV radiation. Two types: Phototoxic: drugs or their metabolites accumulate in the skin, absorb light, and undergo a photochemical reaction followed by a photobiological reaction resulting in local tissue damage (sunburn-like symptoms); examples: blistering, erythema. Photoallergic: drugs or their metabolites induce a cell-mediated immune response which on exposure to light produces a papular or eczematous rash.
B(iii) Intolerance: the appearance of characteristic toxic effects of a drug in an individual at the therapeutic doses; example: a single dose of chloroquine may cause vomiting and abdominal pain in some individuals. Idiosyncrasy: genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a chemical; such adverse effects are restricted to individuals with a particular genotype; example: haemolytic anaemia due to G6PD deficiency in individuals with congenital G6PD enzyme abnormality.
questions.question:
Describe the adverse effects relating to drug dependence, withdrawal reactions, and carcinogenicity/mutagenicity under the following headings:
A(i) Define drug addiction and drug habituation and distinguish between them, giving two examples of each.
A(ii) Define drug withdrawal reactions, explain their mechanism, and give two clinical examples of the consequences of abrupt drug withdrawal.
B(i) Define carcinogenicity and mutagenicity, explain the biochemical mechanism by which drugs cause these, and list four drug classes implicated.
B(ii) Describe photosensitivity as an adverse drug reaction, distinguishing between phototoxic and photoallergic reactions with the mechanism of each.
B(iii) Explain idiosyncrasy and intolerance as types of unpredictable adverse drug reactions, giving one clinical example of each.

(i) A 60-year-old man with fatigue, weight loss, fever, night sweats and productive cough has a chest x-ray showing a right apical infiltrate, and a sputum smear showing many acid-fast bacilli. What is the diagnosis and what first-line drugs should be started?
(ii) Name the mechanism of action of one of these drugs (rifampicin).
(iii) What is a key adverse effect/monitoring parameter for rifampicin?
(iv) State a drug interaction/contraindication relevant to rifampicin.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pulmonary tuberculosis; the first-line antituberculosis drugs are isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol.
(ii) Rifampicin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA synthesis by binding to the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; it is bactericidal to M. tuberculosis and many other microorganisms (gram-positive, gram-negative, enteric bacteria, chlamydia), and acts on slow, intermittently dividing and many atypical mycobacteria.
(iii) Adverse effects: hepatitis, rashes, orange discolouration of body fluids, permanent staining of soft contact lenses, and a flu-like syndrome (chills, fever, myalgias, malaise) with GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps); liver function should be monitored given the hepatitis risk.
(iv) Rifampicin is a microsomal enzyme inducer, enhancing its own metabolism as well as that of other drugs — warfarin, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, sulphonylureas, digitoxin; co-administration with ketoconazole reduces the concentration of both rifampicin and ketoconazole, so these combinations require caution.

questions.question:
A(i) Classify the corticosteroids produced by the adrenal cortex into their two major groups.
A(ii) Describe the source, regulation, half-life, clearance and plasma protein binding of the major natural glucocorticoid.
A(iii) State the metabolic, catabolic, immunosuppressive, anti-inflammatory and renal actions of this hormone.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for using this class of drugs in adrenal and non-adrenal disorders, and state the toxicity that limits chronic use.
C(i) Distinguish glucocorticoids from mineralocorticoids in terms of their predominant physiological effect.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Corticosteroids are hormones produced by the adrenal cortex and comprise two groups: glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids.
A(ii) Cortisol is the major natural glucocorticoid; its secretion is regulated by ACTH, which peaks during the morning.
Its half-life is approximately 100 minutes, clearance is primarily by hepatic metabolism, and it is highly bound to plasma protein (corticosteroid-binding globulin, 95%); it binds cytosolic receptors that transport it to the nucleus to alter gene expression.
A(iii) Metabolic effects: stimulates gluconeogenesis (blood sugar rises) and stimulates muscle protein catabolism and fat cell lipolysis.
Catabolic effects: increases protein catabolism, causing general wasting of body tissue.
Immunosuppressive effects: depresses lymphocyte activity.
Anti-inflammatory effects: decreases the number of lymphocytes, eosinophils, basophils and monocytes.
Renal effects: cortisol is required for the normal excretion of water loads and also has a significant salt-retaining (mineralocorticoid) effect.
B(i) Clinical uses in adrenal disorders: chronic severe adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease), shock, trauma, adrenal hyperplasia.
Clinical uses in non-adrenal disorders: inflammatory disorders such as asthma, connective tissue diseases, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, drug reactions, hay fever.
Toxicity is predictable from the glucocorticoid effects: adrenal suppression (from suppression of ACTH), growth inhibition, diabetes, muscle wasting, salt retention, psychosis, and Cushing syndrome, which may result from excessive, chronic use.
C(i) Glucocorticoids have important effects on metabolism, catabolism and inflammation, whereas mineralocorticoids regulate sodium reabsorption in the collecting tubules of the kidney.

questions.question:
(i) A patient on a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) eats a meal containing a fermented food such as ripe cheese and subsequently develops a severe hypertensive crisis. What is the diagnosis/reaction?
(ii) Name the substance in the food responsible for this reaction.
(iii) Explain the mechanism by which this substance produces the reaction, and why it is exaggerated in a patient on an MAOI.
(iv) Name foods in which this substance is found in high concentration.
(v) State the drug treatment of this reaction.
questions.answerText:
(i) Tyramine reaction - a hypertensive crisis, a famous drug-food interaction.
(ii) Tyramine, a byproduct of tyrosine metabolism.
(iii) Tyramine is an indirect sympathomimetic that releases neurotransmitters (noradrenaline) from storage vesicles; in a patient on an MAOI, the released noradrenaline is not metabolised as it normally would be, so it accumulates and produces a severe hypertensive crisis.
(iv) Tyramine is found in high concentration in fermented foods such as ripe cheese, beer, wine, decayed animal tissues, and mistletoe.
(v) Treatment is with alpha blockers, e.g. phentolamine.

questions.question:
Describe the classification of sedative-hypnotic drugs under the following headings, and explain their clinical applications.
A(i) Define a sedative drug and a hypnotic drug, and state the pharmacological relationship between them.
A(ii) Classify benzodiazepines according to duration of action, giving examples in each class.
B(i) Describe the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines.
B(ii) State the therapeutic uses of benzodiazepines.
B(iii) State the advantages of benzodiazepines over barbiturates, and name the specific antagonist used in overdose.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A sedative drug is one which produces a calming effect and reduces anxiety and excitement without inducing sleep or affecting motor or mental functions; sedation is a minimum degree of CNS depression. A hypnotic drug produces drowsiness and facilitates onset and maintenance of sleep which resembles natural sleep (the patient can be easily aroused); hypnosis is a higher degree of CNS depression than sedation. Sedative-hypnotics produce dose-dependent CNS depression, i.e. increasing the dose leads to a higher degree of CNS depression.
A(ii) Classification by duration of action:
- Short-acting (3–5 hours): Triazolam
- Intermediate-acting (6–24 hours): Alprazolam, Lorazepam, Estazolam, Oxazepam, Temazepam
- Long-acting (24–72 hours): Chlorazepate, Diazepam, Quazepam, Nitrazepam, Chlordiazepoxide, Flurazepam, Prazepam
B(i) Benzodiazepines act very selectively on GABA-A receptors, which mediate the fast inhibitory synaptic response produced by activity in GABAergic neurons. The effect of benzodiazepines is to enhance the response to GABA by facilitating the opening of GABA-activated chloride channels. Entry of Cl- hyperpolarizes the cell, making it more difficult to depolarize, so neuronal excitability is reduced. Benzodiazepines bind specifically to a regulatory site on the receptor, distinct from the GABA binding site, and enhance receptor affinity for GABA.
B(ii) Therapeutic uses include: relief of anxiety (any benzodiazepine can be used; alprazolam has higher efficacy in anxiety associated with panic/phobic disorders); as sedatives for excitement, aggression, violence; as hypnotics in insomnia (triazolam for sleep induction, temazepam for sleep maintenance, flurazepam for early morning awakening); as anticonvulsants (IV diazepam in status epilepticus, clonazepam for other epilepsies); skeletal muscle spasm and alcohol withdrawal; and in anaesthesia (IV diazepam for minor surgical procedures; midazolam preferred for preanaesthetic medication).
B(iii) Advantages of benzodiazepines: wide safety margin (minor effect on respiratory and vasomotor centres); lower liability for drug abuse (less addictive); no effect on hepatic microsomal enzymes and therefore fewer drug interactions than barbiturates; no change in normal sleep pattern (no depression of REM sleep); no hangover effect. Flumazenil is a specific competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine receptor and can be used in benzodiazepine overdose.

questions.question:
Describe the pharmacology of the central nervous system divisions and neurotransmitters under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the divisions of the CNS and PNS.
A(ii) Describe the function of the major CNS regions: hypothalamus, limbic system, pons, medulla, cerebellum, and spinal cord.
B(i) Describe the autonomic nervous system — its two divisions and their opposing actions on key organ systems.
B(ii) Describe the structure of a neuron and the classification of nerves (sensory, motor, and mixed).
B(iii) State what is meant by the neurobiology of anxiety disorders, explaining the role of GABA and glutamate in CNS equilibrium.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord. The Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) consists of any nerves outside the brain and spinal cord; it includes cranial and spinal nerves. The Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) helps maintain balance in involuntary functions of the body and controls involuntary body functions. The CNS regions include: Cerebrum (frontal cortex, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, occipital lobe); subcortical region (thalamus, hypothalamus, mid brain); hind brain (pons, medulla, cerebellum); and spinal cord.
A(ii) Thalamus: acts as relay between incoming sensory pathways and the cortex. Hypothalamus: the principal integrating region for the autonomic nervous system; regulates body temperature, water balance, intermediary metabolism, blood pressure, sexual and circadian cycles, secretion from the adenohypophysis, sleep, and emotion. Limbic system: an assembly of brain regions (hippocampal formation, amygdaloid complex, olfactory nuclei, basal ganglia, and selected nuclei of the diencephalon) grouped around the subcortical borders of the underlying brain core. Pons: motor and sensory control, consciousness, and sleep. Medulla: breathing and heart rate. Cerebellum: maintaining the proper tone of antigravity musculature and providing continuous feedback during volitional movements of the trunk and extremities. Spinal cord: integrates sensory and motor reflexes and controls muscle tone.
B(i) The ANS has two divisions — sympathetic and parasympathetic. Their opposing actions:
- Heart rate: sympathetic increases, parasympathetic decreases.
- Respiratory rate: sympathetic increases, parasympathetic decreases.
- Blood pressure: sympathetic increases, parasympathetic decreases.
- Digestive system activity: sympathetic decreases, parasympathetic increases.
The sympathetic nervous system acts in emergency; the parasympathetic counteracts the sympathetic after the emergency.
B(ii) The neuron is the basic structural unit of the nervous system. It consists of: a nucleus, nerve fibres/dendrites, and an axon. Classification of nerves: Sensory nerves carry messages to the brain and spinal cord from the body. Motor nerves carry messages from the brain and spinal cord to the body. Connecting or mixed nerves carry both sensory and motor messages.
B(iii) CNS equilibrium is determined by a balance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. Excitation is mediated by glutamate; inhibition is mediated by GABA. Inhibition via GABA is primarily mediated by the ionotropic GABA-A receptor. GABA binding to GABA-A results in an increase in neuronal Cl- conductance and subsequent neuronal hyperpolarization. Disruption of this balance — with insufficient inhibitory GABAergic activity — underlies anxiety disorders and forms the basis for the pharmacological action of benzodiazepines and barbiturates.

questions.question:
A patient has episodes suggestive of catecholamine excess, and a clonidine suppression test is being considered.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing/diagnostic considerations for this condition?
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iv) Outline the pharmacological management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Phaeochromocytoma (a condition in which catecholamines are elevated).
(ii) Diagnosis can be supported by the clonidine suppression test: lack of suppression of plasma norepinephrine concentration to less than 500 pg/ml, 3 hours after an oral dose of 0.3 mg of clonidine, suggests the presence of phaeochromocytoma.
(iii) The tumour causes elevated circulating catecholamines; phentolamine and phenoxybenzamine (non-selective alpha blockers) are useful in diagnosis and treatment of conditions in which catecholamines are elevated, such as phaeochromocytoma.
Phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible alpha-adrenoceptor antagonist used to control hypertension caused by catecholamine released from phaeochromocytoma.
(iv) Labetalol lowers arterial pressure by reducing vascular resistance through blockade of alpha1-adrenergic receptors and can be used intravenously in hypertensive emergencies and phaeochromocytoma.
Phentolamine blocks both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic alpha-receptors and is useful in the diagnosis and treatment of phaeochromocytoma.
Clonidine can also be used in the diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma.
Alpha blockers reduce arterial pressure by dilating both resistance and capacitance vessels.

A(i) Drug metabolism is the process of converting compounds soluble in lipids and in the non-ionic state into compounds soluble in water and in ionic form so they can be excreted. Metabolism of drugs is an enzymatic process. The liver is the main organ of drug metabolism, although other tissues like the lungs, kidney, blood, intestinal mucosa, and placenta are also sites of drug metabolism.
A(ii) Phase I (non-synthetic phase) involves oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, and dehalogenation. Oxidation: oxygen is added to a compound or electron/hydrogen is removed; examples include aliphatic hydroxylation (hexobarbital hydroxylated to ketohexobarbital), aromatic hydroxylation (phenylbutazone to oxyphenbutazone), N-dealkylation (codeine to narcodeine), O-dealkylation (codeine to morphine). Reduction: hydrogen or electron added; example: chloral hydrate is reduced to trichloroethanol. Hydrolysis: water added; example: acetylsalicylic acid hydrolysed to salicylic acid and acetic acid. Dehalogenation: removal of a chlorine group from a compound.
B(i) Phase II requires functional groups such as hydroxyl, phenol, carboxyl, amine, or sulfhydryl groups before conjugation with endogenous materials. Conjugative processes include glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, and conjugation with glycine. The second phase reaction inactivates the parent compound/drug. If the parent drug already possesses a functional group, Phase I will be unnecessary.
B(ii) Enzyme induction: some drugs cause induction of liver enzymes (increased activity with continued use); this reduces the effectiveness of those drugs and other drugs metabolized by those enzymes. Example: barbiturates are enzyme inducers in the liver; co-administration leads to increased metabolism and therefore reduces the effects of other drugs. Enzyme inhibition: some drugs inhibit the activity of enzymes, which increases the effect of all drugs metabolized by that enzyme. Example: probenecid blocks the excretion of penicillins and cephalosporins via the same carrier transport system in the kidney, increasing their concentration.
B(iii) Self-induction is when a drug enhances its own metabolism when used for a prolonged time. This adaptive mechanism facilitates detoxification and elimination of foreign substances from the body. Self-induction is one cause of drug tolerance (decrease in drug action after prolonged use). Example of a drug that undergoes self-induction: tolbutamide.
questions.question:
Describe drug metabolism (biotransformation) under the following headings:

A(ii) Describe Phase I (non-synthetic) reactions, listing the types of reactions involved and give two examples of drugs that undergo oxidation.
B(i) Describe Phase II (synthetic/conjugation) reactions, listing the conjugative processes, and explain when Phase I can be bypassed.
B(ii) Explain what is meant by enzyme induction and enzyme inhibition and give one clinical example of each showing the effect on a co-administered drug.

questions.answerText:
(i) Lead poisoning (inorganic lead).
(ii) Lead affects mainly the haemopoietic system, the CNS, the kidney and the liver; varying degrees of demyelination of axons and nerve cell bodies may occur.
(iii) Common sources of lead are soil, dust, old paints, gasoline combustion engines, ceramic glazes, old lead water pipes and battery casings; it is absorbed through the GIT and respiratory tract, and to a lesser extent through the skin and mucous membrane, and is excreted into the bile, faeces and urine, with a half-life of 30 days.
Common symptoms of inorganic lead poisoning in adults include abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, vomiting and mental symptoms; organic lead poisoning results in sleep disturbances, nausea, anorexia, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, vertigo, headache, muscular weakness and tremor.
(iv) Treatment is CaNa2EDTA.
questions.question:
A patient with a history of exposure to old paints, contaminated soil/dust or lead water pipes presents with abdominal pain, constipation and mental symptoms.
(i) Identify the likely toxin.
(ii) Which organ systems are affected?

A. Describe the role of the liver's LDL-receptor pathway in cholesterol homeostasis.
B. State how disturbance of this pathway relates to the common pathology of hyperlipidaemia.
C. Explain how disease of this pathway leads to functional deficit in a distant organ system.
questions.answerText:
A. The liver expresses high-affinity LDL receptors that clear LDL and its precursor VLDL from the circulation. Statins competitively inhibit hepatic HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis; the resulting reduction in free intracellular cholesterol increases synthesis and reduces degradation of LDL receptors, increasing hepatic removal of LDL and VLDL from the blood and lowering plasma LDL while increasing HDL. Bile-acid sequestrants act similarly: by depleting the bile-acid pool they stimulate hepatic LDL-receptor production and increase LDL clearance.
B. Hyperlipidaemia (dyslipidaemia), including hypercholesterolaemia and low HDL-cholesterol, results from disturbance of this hepatic clearance pathway (as well as from genetic disorders and lifestyle factors such as sedentary behaviour and diets high in calories, saturated fat and cholesterol), and is the major cause of atherosclerosis.
C. Hyperlipidaemia is the major cause of atherosclerosis and atherosclerosis-associated conditions, so that a disturbance beginning in hepatic lipid handling produces distant functional deficits in the cardiovascular and cerebrovascular systems, namely coronary heart disease, ischaemic cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease, which account for most morbidity and mortality among middle-aged and older adults.

A(i) Antifungal drugs are classified as: inhibitor of fungal nucleic acid synthesis (flucytosine); inhibitor of fungal mitosis (griseofulvin); inhibitors of the ergosterol synthesis pathway — inhibitors of squalene epoxidase (allylamines and benzylamines) and inhibitors of 14-alpha-sterol demethylase (imidazoles and triazoles); inhibitors of fungal membrane stability (polyenes); inhibitors of fungal wall synthesis (echinocandins); and a chelator of polyvalent cations (ciclopirox).
A(ii) Amphotericin B is an amphoteric polyene macrolide produced by Streptomyces nodosus.
It is selective in its fungicidal effect because it exploits the difference in lipid composition of fungal and mammalian cell membranes: ergosterol is found in the fungal cell membrane, whereas the predominant sterol of human cells is cholesterol.
Amphotericin B binds to ergosterol and alters cell permeability by forming amphotericin B-associated pores in the membrane, allowing leakage of intracellular ions and macromolecules.
A(iii) Azole drugs are synthetic compounds, relatively nontoxic, with oral and parenteral formulations and broad spectrum of action; they comprise imidazoles (ketoconazole, miconazole, clotrimazole) and triazoles (itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole).
Their mechanism of action is inhibition of fungal cytochrome P450 enzymes, reducing ergosterol synthesis; triazoles have greater affinity for fungal cytochrome P450 enzymes and are more selectively toxic than imidazoles.
B(i) Amphotericin B has the broadest spectrum of action, covering Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, endemic mycoses and pathogenic molds, and is used for all life-threatening mycotic infections, including cryptococcal meningitis with altered mental status and immunosuppressed patients with severe fungal pneumonia.
It is also used as empiric therapy in cancer patients with neutropenia, as adjunctive therapy in fungal arthritis, and in candiduria.
Azole drugs are used for Cryptococcus neoformans and Candida species, blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, dermatophytes, and Aspergillus infections (itraconazole and voriconazole), being selected where a less toxic oral/parenteral option is clinically appropriate.
Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) inhibit synthesis of beta(1-3)-glucan, disrupting the fungal cell wall, and are used for candidal infections, being active against Candida and Aspergillus but not Cryptococcus neoformans.
C(i) Amphotericin B, as a polyene, is highly effective but quite toxic: infusion-related toxicity (fever, chills, muscle spasms, vomiting, headache, hypotension) and cumulative toxicity (renal damage, abnormal liver function tests).
Azole drugs, in contrast, are relatively nontoxic, with adverse reactions limited mainly to minor gastrointestinal upset and drug interactions, because triazoles in particular are more selectively toxic to fungal rather than human cytochrome P450 enzymes.

A(ii) Describe the mechanism of action of amphotericin B.

(i) A woman presents with galactorrhea, infertility and oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology?
(iv) What is the management?
questions.answerText:
(i) Hyperprolactinemia.
(ii) Drugs that block dopamine D2 receptors cause hyperprolactinemia by blocking the inhibitory effects of endogenous dopamine on the pituitary cells that release prolactin.
(iii) Prolactin is a peptide hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary whose primary function is to stimulate and maintain lactation; it also decreases sexual drive and reproductive function; its secretion is normally inhibited by dopamine acting at D2 receptors. Hyperprolactinemia causes hypogonadism, manifesting with infertility, oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea and galactorrhea in premenopausal women, and with loss of libido and erectile dysfunction in men.
(iv) Hyperprolactinemia is treated with D2 receptor agonists, such as bromocriptine and cabergoline.

A(i) Examples are troglitazone, pioglitazone and rosiglitazone.
A(ii) They are peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-gamma) agonists, found in adipose tissue, liver and muscle; they regulate transcription of genes for glucose/lipid metabolism, including FFA transport protein, insulin receptor substrate and GLUT-4, promoting uptake and storage of free fatty acids in adipose tissue, promoting expression and translocation of GLUT-4 in muscle and adipose tissue, and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis.
A(iii) Rosiglitazone reaches peak plasma levels 1 hour after administration, and pioglitazone reaches its peak in 2 hours; both are metabolised by hepatic CYP450 enzymes, and the effect on blood glucose is slow, with maximal effect achieved after 2 months.
A(iv) Troglitazone and ciglitazone caused serious hepatotoxicity and were withdrawn; weight gain and fluid retention are the commonest adverse effects (caused by up-regulating tubular transporters for sodium), and heart failure is a risk, likely caused by sodium retention and oedema; pioglitazone is associated with increased risk of bladder cancer on prolonged use, and TZDs inhibit osteoblasts, with higher fracture rates observed.
B(i) Pioglitazone is secreted in breast milk, so TZDs are not recommended for pregnant and breastfeeding women.
B(ii) The commonest adverse effects, weight gain and fluid retention, are caused by up-regulating tubular transporters for sodium, and heart failure is likely caused by this sodium retention and resultant oedema, directly linking the PPAR-gamma-mediated transcriptional mechanism to the cardiovascular adverse effect.

A(ii) Describe their mechanism of action.
A(iii) State their pharmacokinetics.
A(iv) List their adverse effects.
B(i) State the precaution regarding their use in pregnancy/breastfeeding and heart failure.

questions.answerText:
A(i) PTH is synthesised as pre-pro-PTH (115 amino acids), cleaved to pro-PTH (90 amino acids), and further cleaved before secretion of PTH (84 amino acids) from the chief cells of the parathyroid glands; intact PTH has a half-life of 3-4 minutes and normal levels are 1.3-6.8 pmol/L.
A(ii) The dominant regulator of PTH secretion is plasma Ca2+, to which secretion is inversely related; maximum secretion occurs at plasma Ca2+ below 3.5 mg/dL and secretion is maximally inhibited above 5.5 mg/dL. A calcium-sensing G-protein-coupled receptor on the parathyroid cell membrane senses extracellular Ca2+: when Ca2+ falls, cAMP rises and PTH is secreted. 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D also inhibits PTH gene expression as a further feedback control.
A(iii) PTH increases plasma calcium and decreases plasma phosphate by increasing osteoclastic resorption of bone, increasing renal tubular reabsorption of calcium while inhibiting reabsorption of phosphate, and increasing renal synthesis of 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D, which in turn increases intestinal absorption of calcium.
B. Teriparatide, the recombinant form of PTH(1-34), is used therapeutically because low, intermittent doses of PTH produce a net increase in bone formation, and it is used to treat osteoporosis by stimulating new bone formation.
C. In chronic excess of PTH (hyperparathyroidism), the sustained high concentration of PTH increases RANKL-mediated osteoclast activity, producing a net effect of increased bone resorption, hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia; this manifests clinically as fragility fractures and other skeletal manifestations of bone loss.

questions.answerText:
A(i) 5-ASA compounds (aminosalicylates) are topical anti-inflammatory drugs used in areas of diseased gastrointestinal mucosa; azo compounds contain 5-ASA connected by an azo bond (N=N) to a sulfapyridine moiety, another molecule of 5-ASA, or an inert compound - sulfasalazine (5-ASA + sulfapyridine), olsalazine (5-ASA + 5-ASA), and balsalazide (5-ASA + inert carrier, 4-aminobenzoyl-beta-alanine); mesalamine compounds (Pentasa, Asacol, Rowasa, Canasa) are also used.
A(ii) 5-ASA differs from salicylic acid only by addition of an amino group at the 5 (meta) position; it has anti-inflammatory action due to inhibition of prostaglandins and leukotrienes, decreased neutrophil chemotaxis, and antioxidant activity (scavenging free radical production).
B(i) The azo structure reduces absorption of the parent drug from the small intestine; in the terminal ileum and colon, resident bacteria cleave the azo bond (N=N) by means of an azoreductase enzyme, releasing the active 5-ASA; consequently, high concentrations of active drug are made available in the terminal ileum or colon.
B(ii) Because 5-ASA itself is absorbed from the small intestine, different formulations are used to overcome its rapid absorption from the proximal small intestine; sulfasalazine given orally has only a little amount absorbed (10%) as the intact pro-drug, so the azo-bond delivery mechanism allows the active 5-ASA to bypass absorption in the proximal gut and be released specifically at the terminal ileum and colon, the site of disease in ulcerative colitis and colonic Crohn's disease, distant from the site of oral administration.

questions.answerText:
(i) Irreversible anticholinesterase (organophosphate) poisoning, e.g. from parathion.
(ii) Organophosphorus anti-cholinesterase agents cause irreversible inhibition of cholinesterase by phosphorylating the active site of the enzyme; because the phosphorylated enzyme cannot be readily regenerated, acetylcholine accumulates at all cholinergic sites - muscarinic sites (glands, smooth muscle, heart), autonomic ganglia and the skeletal neuromuscular junction - producing widespread peripheral and central effects, including respiratory collapse from paralysis of the intercostal muscles.
(iii) The opposite picture is produced by atropine (anticholinergic/antimuscarinic) poisoning, which presents with dryness of the mouth, mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia, flushed dry skin and CNS excitation (restlessness, hallucination, delirium), in contrast to the excessive secretions, bradycardia and miosis of cholinergic excess seen in organophosphate poisoning.
(iv) Management includes supportive measures (removal from the site of exposure, washing contaminated skin, maintenance of the airway, oxygen, rehydration, and diazepam for convulsions); atropine, which blocks muscarinic receptor sites and is effective in toxicity due to both reversible and irreversible anticholinesterases; and an enzyme reactivator such as pralidoxime, which regenerates the cholinesterase enzyme and reverses the skeletal paralysing effect of irreversible anticholinesterases.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Sulfonamide is a generic name for derivatives of para-aminobenzenesulphonamide (sulfanilamide); classes include rapidly absorbed and eliminated sulfonamides, poorly absorbed sulfonamides (e.g. sulfasalazine), topical sulfonamides, and long-acting sulfonamides.
A(ii) Sulfonamides are structural analogs and competitive antagonists of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA).
They competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, the bacterial enzyme responsible for incorporating PABA into dihydropteroic acid, the immediate precursor of folic acid, thus preventing bacterial utilization of PABA for folic acid synthesis; bacteria that use preformed folate are not affected, and mammalian cells, which require preformed folic acid and cannot synthesize it, are also not affected.
A(iii) Sulfonamides are rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and are distributed throughout all tissues of the body, including fetal tissues.
They are metabolized in the liver, mainly to the N4-acetylated derivative (acetylation produces toxic metabolites with no antibacterial activity), and are eliminated mainly in the urine, partly unchanged and partly as metabolic products; sulfonamides can be found in urine within 30 minutes of ingestion, so their half-life depends on renal function.
B(i) The introduction in the mid-1970s of the combination of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole increased the use of sulphonamides for the prophylaxis and treatment of microbial infections.
Sulfonamide inhibits the incorporation of PABA into folic acid, and trimethoprim prevents the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate; the simultaneous administration of a sulfonamide and trimethoprim thus introduces sequential blocks in the pathway by which microorganisms synthesize tetrahydrofolate from precursor molecules, resulting in synergistic antimicrobial effects.
This combination is effective in the treatment of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections and for acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis caused by susceptible strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae, among other uses.
C(i) Sulphonamides act earlier in the folate synthesis pathway, by competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase and blocking incorporation of PABA into dihydropteroic acid.
Trimethoprim acts at a later step in the same pathway, preventing the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate.
Because the two drugs act at sequential, distinct steps of the same bacterial folate synthesis pathway, their combined use produces sequential blockade and a synergistic antimicrobial effect rather than simple additive action.
Bacteria that use preformed folate, and mammalian cells (which require preformed folic acid and cannot synthesize it), are not affected by the sulphonamide component of this pathway, which is the basis of its selective bacterial toxicity.

A(i) Describe the mechanism of action of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.
A(ii) State their indications/clinical uses.

questions.answerText:
A(i) ACE inhibitors inhibit the activity of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), the enzyme responsible for converting angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor; a reduction in angiotensin II level represents an advancement in hypertension treatment.
A(ii) They slow the development of diabetic glomerulopathy and glomerulosclerosis in hypertensive patients, and are preferred agents in the initial treatment of hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemic heart disease and myocardial infarction; they enhance the efficacy of diuretic drugs.
A(iii) The effect of ACE inhibitors on aldosterone influences K+ homeostasis and can lead to a rise in serum K+ (hyperkalaemia), which may arise when co-administered with potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone), NSAIDs, potassium supplements, or beta-blockers.
A(iv) ACE inhibitors should not be used in pregnancy, as they reduce glomerular filtration rate; angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) are also contraindicated in women who are or intend to become pregnant.
B(i) High doses of diuretic combined with ACE inhibitors can lead to excessive reduction in blood pressure and Na+ loss, so small diuretic doses are preferred; serum potassium should be monitored given the risk of hyperkalaemia, especially with concurrent potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, potassium supplements or beta-blockers.
B(ii) Angiotensin receptor blockers have an advantage over ACE inhibitors in that they prevent degradation of bradykinin and substance P and are devoid of the intractable cough associated with ACE inhibitors, indicating that ACE-inhibitor cough arises from accumulation of bradykinin (and substance P) due to inhibition of their breakdown by ACE.

(i) This patient is experiencing opioid withdrawal syndrome (physical dependence on opioids). Physical dependence develops as a result of tolerance produced by a resetting of homeostatic mechanisms in response to repeated drug use. Withdrawal signs and symptoms (WS) occur when drug administration in a physically dependent person is terminated abruptly. CNS depressants such as benzodiazepines and opioids exhibit physical dependence. The appearance of a withdrawal syndrome when administration of the drug is terminated is the only actual evidence of physical dependence. Patients who take medicine for appropriate medical indications and in correct dosages may still show tolerance, physical dependence, and withdrawal symptoms if the drug is stopped abruptly rather than gradually. Sweating, agitation, gooseflesh, and dilated pupils are consistent with opioid withdrawal.
(ii) Cannabis (also known as marijuana, pot, hashish, hash) is one of the most widely abused substances. Effects include heightened sensations, relaxation, and increased confidence. Risks include depression, impaired fertility, diminished immune responses, memory loss, difficulty learning, and psychotic symptoms. Withdrawal symptoms include insomnia, restlessness, and loss of appetite.
(iii) Stimulants include cocaine, amphetamine, Ritalin, etc. They are highly addictive and highly reinforcing with intense cravings and relatively mild physical withdrawal. Biology: stimulants directly enhance dopamine (DA) activity and also increase norepinephrine (NE), causing excitation; increased NE leads to being awake and alert. Some people self-medicate with stimulants. DA and NE down-regulation occurs with chronic use, resulting in depression/lethargy when the drug is not used; these symptoms increase craving and desire for the drug.
(iv) Types of drug abuse patterns: Abuse — pattern of use resulting in negative consequences or impairment; Dependence — pattern of continuing substance use despite symptoms; Misuse — taking a drug for a purpose or person other than the one intended, or not taking the recommended dose; Diversion — transfer of medication from the person it was prescribed to, to another person.
(v) Factors aiding drug abuse and misuse include: insufficient evaluation of patient by physician; overprescription of mood-altering drugs; patient factors (e.g. multiple prescriptions); peer pressure; desire to rebel against authority; affluence; boredom; genetic inheritance; and curiosity.
