Describe the pharmacokinetic parameter of bioavailability under the following headings:
A(i) Define bioavailability and state the bioavailability of an intravenously administered drug.
A(ii) Distinguish between absolute bioavailability and relative bioavailability, including their formulas.
B(i) Define the biological half-life (t1/2) and explain what it means for drug dosing frequency.
B(ii) List the factors that influence biological half-life.
B(iii) Define volume of distribution (Vd), provide its formula, and list five factors that determine Vd.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Bioavailability is the relative amount (fraction) of drug from the administered dosage form which enters systemic circulation; also, the rate and extent of drug absorption into systemic circulation. It indicates the extent to which the drug reaches its site of action or a biological fluid from which the drug has access to its site of action. For IV administration, bioavailability is 100% (f = 1).
A(ii) Absolute bioavailability: the extent or fraction of drug absorbed upon extravascular administration in comparison to the dose size administered, measured by comparing the respective AUCs after oral and IV administration; it is equal to the fraction of the drug absorbed (f). Relative bioavailability: the extent of drug absorbed upon extravascular administration in comparison to the dose size of a standard administered via the same route. % Relative bioavailability = (AUC of Drug A / AUC of standard) x 100.
B(i) Biological half-life (t1/2) is the time taken to reduce the drug concentration in blood, plasma, or serum to one-half after equilibrium is reached. It indicates the time required to attain 50% of steady state or time required to decay 50% from steady state after a change. A drug's half-life determines how often it must be taken and how long it takes for the drug to wear off. After 4 half-lives, 93.8% of the drug is eliminated (6.2% remains).
B(ii) Factors influencing t1/2: dose size; variation in urinary excretion (pH); intersubject variation; age; protein binding; presence of other drugs (enzyme inducers and enzyme inhibitors); type of disease (especially liver and kidney diseases).
B(iii) Volume of distribution (Vd) is a hypothetical volume of body fluid that would be required to dissolve the total amount of a drug at the same concentration as that found in the blood. Vd = Amount of drug in the body / Concentration of drug in blood/plasma. Vd is dependent on many factors: (1) blood flow rate in diffused tissues; (2) lipid solubility of drug; (3) partition coefficient of drug; (4) pH; (5) binding of drug to biological materials. Vd is often proportional to body weight, except in obesity (where Vd is lower than expected) and in oedema (where Vd is larger than expected).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the source, synthesis and structure of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).
A(ii) Describe the regulation of ACTH release and its actions on the zones of the adrenal cortex.
A(iii) State the extra-adrenal effects of ACTH.
B(i) State the therapeutic/diagnostic uses of ACTH and its site of action.
C(i) Explain the pharmacological basis by which excess ACTH secretion produces its clinical picture.
questions.answerText:
A(i) ACTH is processed from the precursor protein pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), from which alpha-MSH is also derived; human ACTH is a peptide of 39 amino acids, the first 13 of which are similar to those of alpha-MSH; it acts through melanocortin receptor 2 (MC-2) and much less through MC-1.
A(ii) Regulation of ACTH release: a diurnal (sleep-wake) rhythm of the hypothalamus acting through CRH and arginine vasopressin (AVP) on the corticotropes; negative feedback at multiple sites of the HPA axis and positive regulation by interleukins and alpha-TNF; the stress response overrides the negative feedback.
On the adrenal cortex: the outer zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); the middle zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol); the inner zona reticularis secretes androgens (DHEA and DHEA-S).
ACTH stimulates synthesis and release of adrenocortical hormones through MC2 (a G-protein coupled receptor); at the zona glomerulosa, stimulation is acutely mediated by ACTH but predominantly regulated by angiotensin II and K+ via CYP11B2; at the zona fasciculata, stimulation is mainly regulated by ACTH via CYP11B1 and CYP17; at the zona reticularis, ACTH acutely increases DHEA biosynthesis via CYP17.
A(iii) Extra-adrenal effects of ACTH include ketosis, lipolysis, hyperglycaemia (immediately after treatment) and insulin resistance (later after treatment); the mechanism of action of these is not clear.
B(i) ACTH preparations are used as replacement therapy for hormone deficiency states, as antagonists for diseases caused by excess pituitary hormone production, and as diagnostic tools for identifying endocrine abnormalities; ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex via melanocortin receptor 2.
C(i) In primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease), the adrenal cortex fails to respond to ACTH administration, so ACTH levels rise.
Because ACTH is derived from the same precursor (POMC) as alpha-MSH, the elevated ACTH stimulates melanocortin receptors in the skin.
This shared precursor origin is the pharmacological basis for the hyperpigmentation that characterizes Addison disease, alongside weakness, fatigue, weight loss and hypotension.
Conversely, in Cushing's disease, excess ACTH secretion by the anterior pituitary drives adrenocortical hyperplasia and hypercortisolism, producing the clinical picture of Cushing's syndrome.
Cortisol levels (urine, plasma, saliva) and the dexamethasone suppression test are used diagnostically; dexamethasone suppresses cortisol release in normal individuals but not in those with Cushing syndrome.
Thus the same hormone (ACTH), depending on whether it is deficient or in excess, produces opposite adrenal clinical pictures through its actions on the zones of the adrenal cortex.

A(i) Mycobacteria are dormant organisms with a lipid-rich mycobacterial cell wall that is impermeable to many agents; many of the organisms dwell intracellularly within macrophages, and they rapidly develop resistance to any single drug.
A(ii) First-line drugs are isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol.
Isoniazid (INH) is a prodrug activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG; the activated drug forms a covalent bond with an acyl carrier protein (AcpM) and KasA, blocking mycolic acid synthesis — mycolic acid being a unique component of the mycobacterial cell wall, which is the basis of its selectivity.
Rifampicin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA synthesis by binding to the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and acts on slow, intermittently dividing and many atypical mycobacteria.
Pyrazinamide is converted to pyrazinoic acid, the active drug, by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase, and is more active in an acidic medium, being highly lethal to intracellular organisms.
Ethambutol is tuberculostatic and clinically as active as streptomycin, with fast-multiplying bacilli and many atypical mycobacteria more susceptible.
Resistance to ethambutol results from mutation of the emb gene; rate of sputum conversion is faster when ethambutol is added to the triple regime of rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide, and this also helps prevent development of resistance.
B(i) Because the mycobacterial cell wall is impermeable and the organisms dwell intracellularly and rapidly develop resistance to a single drug, tuberculosis treatment requires a multidrug regimen (e.g. isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) to prevent development of resistance and achieve faster sputum conversion.
C(i) Isoniazid is structurally similar to pyridoxine (vitamin B6); its adverse effects include peripheral neuritis, which is pyridoxine-related, along with hepatitis, GI discomfort, and haematological effects including pyridoxine deficiency and anaemia.
Because isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) metabolism systemically, its local action of inhibiting mycolic acid synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall is accompanied by a distant, systemic vitamin-deficiency effect on peripheral nerves.
This illustrates why an antimycobacterial drug with a highly selective local mechanism of action (mycolic acid synthesis inhibition) can nonetheless produce a distant systemic toxicity (peripheral neuritis) through an unrelated pathway (pyridoxine interference).
Ethambutol similarly demonstrates a distant effect from a locally acting drug, producing retrobulbar/optic neuritis presenting as loss of visual acuity, colour vision defect (red-green) and visual field defect.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Drug distribution is the process by which a drug leaves the blood stream and enters the interstitial or intracellular fluid. Following drug absorption or systemic administration into the bloodstream, drug distribution depends on the physicochemical properties of the drug. Other factors that influence distribution include: cardiac output/blood flow (brain, kidney > skeletal muscle, fat tissues), capillary permeability, and tissue volume.
A(ii) Barriers that prevent some drugs from reaching target sites: (1) Blood-brain barrier; (2) Blood-testes barrier; (3) Blood-placenta barrier. NB: lipophilic drugs e.g. benzodiazepine readily cross the gut walls, capillary wall, and blood-brain barriers.
B(i) The binding of drugs to plasma proteins e.g. albumin tends to reduce the amount of free drug in circulation. Consequences of protein binding: (1) reduced pharmacological effect since only free drugs are available for drug-receptor interaction; (2) acts as storage sites for drugs; (3) increases t1/2e since bound drugs cannot be metabolized or eliminated; (4) decreases bioavailability; (5) displacement of drugs with less affinity during competition results in higher concentration of free drug which may result in toxicity, e.g. displacement of bilirubin by sulfonamides leading to kernicterus; displacement of warfarin by phenylbutazone leading to haemorrhage; (6) delayed urinary excretion since protein-bound drugs are not filtered through glomeruli.
B(ii) Depot storage: some drugs accumulate in storage sites, tending to either increase or decrease the amount of drug available for distribution. Example 1: Thiopental (a lipophilic drug) accumulates in fat and is released slowly; an obese person might be sedated for a greater period of time than a lean person given the same dose. Example 2: calcium-binding drugs e.g. tetracycline accumulate in bones and the teeth.
B(iii) Binding of drugs to biological materials occurs primarily to proteins, especially albumin and glycoprotein. It is reversible except for N-mustards and phosphorus-containing anticholinesterases. Binding is by weak bonds (van der Waals and ionic bonds). The binding has mostly unspecific capacity for many drugs. Competition occurs when another drug with higher affinity displaces a drug with lower affinity from its binding site, resulting in higher concentration of free drug and potential toxicity.

questions.answerText:
(i) The serotonin (5-HT3 receptor) pathway at the area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone, CTZ) is principally implicated in cancer chemotherapy-induced emesis; other relevant neurotransmitters/receptors include dopamine, acetylcholine, opioids, substance P (NK-1 receptor), and histamine.
(ii) Emesis is the involuntary forceful expulsion of stomach contents; coordination for emesis involves the emesis centre in the lateral reticular formation and the CTZ/area postrema in the medulla. The emesis centre receives afferent stimuli from parts of the body and via the CTZ; efferent pathways are the phrenic nerve (diaphragm), spinal nerves (intercostal, abdominal musculature), and the vagus nerve (larynx, oesophagus, stomach).
(iii) Vomiting may also be triggered by toxins, gastroenteritis, increased intracranial pressure, brain tumours, other drugs (opioids, digitalis), ionizing radiation, and, for motion sickness specifically, vestibular (histamine H1, muscarinic) pathways rather than the 5-HT3/CTZ pathway.
(iv) 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (e.g. ondansetron) and centrally acting dopamine (D2) receptor antagonists (e.g. metoclopramide) are indicated for cancer chemotherapy-induced emesis, as is the cannabinoid receptor agonist dronabinol and the neurokinin (NK-1) receptor antagonists (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, maropitant); by contrast, histamine H1 antagonists (cyclizine, promethazine) and muscarinic antagonists (hyoscine/scopolamine) are indicated for vestibular/motion sickness and have no role in cancer-induced emesis, so the choice of antiemetic is reasoned according to which receptor pathway is driving the vomiting in the given clinical setting.

A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He is in severe pain and is administered morphine intravenously. Shortly after, the nurse observes that his pupils are constricted, he becomes drowsy and his respiratory rate drops to 8 breaths per minute.
(i) What is the pharmacological basis for this clinical presentation?
(ii) What are the four broad classes of opioids, giving one example of each?
(iii) What are three distinguishing characteristics shared by all narcotic analgesics?
(iv) What receptor types mediate opioid actions and what are the cellular consequences of their activation?
(v) What agent can be used to reverse this patient's condition, and what is its mechanism?
questions.answerText:
(i) Morphine is a pure opioid agonist that binds to opioid receptors (particularly mu receptors) in the central and peripheral nervous system. By binding to CNS receptor sites, the perception of pain is reduced. Opioid receptors are coupled with inhibitory G-proteins; activation closes voltage-sensitive calcium channels, stimulates potassium efflux causing hyperpolarization, and reduces cyclic adenosine monophosphate production. Overall, the effect is a reduction in neuronal cell excitability, resulting in reduced transmission of nociceptive impulses. Constriction of pupils (miosis), drowsiness, and respiratory depression are recognised short-term effects of opioid analgesics.
(ii) The four broad classes of opioids are:
- Opium alkaloids (natural), e.g. morphine, codeine, thebaine
- Semi-synthetic opioids (opium derivatives), e.g. heroin, oxycodone, hydrocodone
- Fully synthetic opioids, e.g. pethidine (meperidine), methadone, fentanyl, pentazocine
- Endogenous opioid peptides (produced in the body), e.g. endorphins, dynorphins, enkephalins
(iii) All narcotic analgesics share three distinguishing characteristics: pain relief; production of withdrawal signs and symptoms when the drug is stopped after chronic administration; and their use will suppress the withdrawal signs and symptoms of chronic morphine administration (i.e. the various narcotic analgesics can be substituted for each other to relieve withdrawal symptoms).
(iv) Opioid receptors are: MOR – mu (μ) opioid peptide receptor; KOR – kappa (κ) opioid peptide receptor; DOR – delta (δ) opioid peptide receptor; NOR (nociceptin orphanin FQ peptide receptor); and ZOR (zeta receptor). They are distributed throughout the CNS with high concentrations in the nuclei of tractus solitarius, peri-aqueductal grey area, cerebral cortex, thalamus, and the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord. They have also been found on peripheral afferent nerve terminals and many other organs.
(v) Opioid antagonists such as naloxone have receptor affinity but no intrinsic activity. Naloxone (and naltrexone) are classified as opioid antagonists and can reverse opioid-induced CNS depression.

A(i) First-generation H1 blockers: alkylamines (e.g. chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine - strong antihistamine action, devoid of other side effects); ethanolamines (e.g. diphenhydramine - strong antihistamine, anticholinergic, sedative and antiemetic effects); ethylenediamines (tripelennamine, antazoline, chloropyramine, pyrilamine - strong antihistamine, mild anticholinergic and local anaesthetic effect); phenothiazines (e.g. promethazine - moderate antihistamine, strong anxiolytic and hypnotic effects); piperazines (e.g. thenylidine - antihistamine, anticholinergic, adrenolytic, anti-serotonin and spasmolytic actions); piperidines (e.g. cyproheptadine - used in allergy, migraine and as appetite stimulant).
A(ii) Second-generation: alkylamines (e.g. acrivastine); piperazines (e.g. cetirizine - has a mild anticholinergic effect, mild sedative effect, passes the blood-brain barrier); piperidines (e.g. loratadine, fexofenadine, terfenadine); phthalazinones (e.g. azelastine).
A(iii) H1 antagonists block histamine-mediated responses on smooth muscle of the blood capillaries, vessels, bronchioles and sensory nerve endings, and have no effect on H2-receptor-mediated responses; many H1-receptor blocking drugs have structural similarity to anticholinergic and local anaesthetic agents.
B(i) H1 antagonists have a valued place in treatment of hypersensitivity reactions such as hay fever, upper respiratory allergy (sneezing, rhinorrhoea, pruritus), acute urticaria, angioedema, conjunctivitis and dermatitis; the CNS effects are of therapeutic value for suppressing motion sickness and for sedation, and the antiemetic effect prevents and relieves nausea and vomiting of motion sickness, radiation sickness, post-operative emesis, vertigo and vomiting in later pregnancy; H1 antihistamines are ineffective in gastrointestinal allergies, bronchial asthma, hypersensitivity reactions to drugs, and anaphylactic shock.
B(ii) Ethanolamine-type first-generation agents (e.g. diphenhydramine) have strong sedative and anticholinergic effects, whereas the second-generation piperazine cetirizine, though passing the blood-brain barrier, has only a mild sedative and mild anticholinergic effect; cyproheptadine (first generation, piperidine) is used as an appetite stimulant, a use not stated for the second-generation piperidines (loratadine, fexofenadine, terfenadine).
