A. Describe the gross organization of bone as a dynamic organ, including the cells responsible for its formation and resorption.
B. State how disturbances in this organization relate to common bone pathologies.
C. Explain why disease of this organ may spread to affect a distant organ system, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A. Bone homeostasis is a dynamic balance between anabolic (bone formation) and catabolic (bone resorption) processes, referred to as remodeling. Osteoblasts are the cells responsible for anabolic activity, synthesising matrix proteins (type I collagen, osteocalcin) and mineralisation; osteoclasts, large multinucleated giant cells, are responsible for catabolic activity, degrading bone protein matrix and acidifying the bone surface. Osteoblasts express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their differentiation into active osteoclasts; when osteoblasts become encased in bone they become osteocytes.
B. Negative calcium balance (output exceeding intake) leads to osteoporosis, an abnormal loss of bone predisposing to fractures. At the high PTH concentrations seen in hyperparathyroidism, the net effect is increased bone resorption, hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia, whereas deficiency of active vitamin D metabolites causes defective mineralisation, producing rickets in the growing skeleton and osteomalacia in adults. Paget's disease is characterised by uncontrolled osteoclastic bone resorption with secondary disorganised bone formation.
C. In secondary hyperparathyroidism associated with chronic kidney disease, the skeletal disturbance is accompanied by extra-skeletal manifestations, including vascular calcifications, ischaemic cardiovascular events and cardiac failure, so that a disorder that begins in bone mineral regulation ultimately produces a functional deficit in the cardiovascular system.

(i) Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning.
(ii) CO binds haemoglobin (Hb) to form carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) in a reversible manner, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
Binding of CO to some Hb sites increases the affinity of the remaining sites for oxygen, severely impairing release of oxygen to tissues at low oxygen tension.
The affinity of CO for Hb is about 210-250 times greater than that of oxygen; CO may also directly bind cellular cytochromes such as respiratory enzymes.
Tissues most sensitive to oxygen deprivation (brain and heart) are most affected; severe poisoning can cause sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and ST-segment depression.
CO toxicity is associated with congestion and haemorrhages in most organs; the severe headache is believed to be related to cerebral oedema.
Anaemic individuals are more susceptible to CO toxicity, and death may occur when carboxyHb reaches about 60% of blood levels.
(iii) Remove the patient from the site of exposure and provide medical support, ensuring adequate pulmonary exchange; give artificial respiration with oxygen as needed.
(iv) Definitive treatment is administration of pure (100%) oxygen to promote displacement of CO from Hb molecules.
Raising inspired oxygen from 20% to 100% reduces the biological half-life of carboxyHb from about 250 minutes to about 40 minutes.
Blood transfusion is needed in severe poisoning to furnish an immediate supply of fresh Hb molecules.
Recovery is likely once the patient is removed from exposure and active respiration/oxygenation is carried out.
questions.question:
(i) A patient is brought in after exposure to smoke from incomplete combustion of organic material in an enclosed space, and is found with headache, sweating, mental confusion and coma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of the features seen in this condition.
(iii) Outline the initial (non-specific) resuscitative measures.
(iv) What is the definitive treatment, and what physiological effect does it achieve?

(i) A patient develops sudden hypotension, wheeze from bronchoconstriction, and congestion of the lung, heart and kidney shortly after exposure to an allergen. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Explain the pathological basis of this reaction and the receptor-mediated effects that produce the clinical picture.
(iii) Describe the immediate/resuscitative drug management of this condition.
(iv) Describe the definitive pharmacological treatment, including the receptors targeted and the effects produced at each receptor.
questions.answerText:
(i) Anaphylactic shock.
(ii) It is a type of shock in which there is congestion of the lung, heart and kidney due to vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability, with bronchoconstriction and hypotension as major features.
(iii) Give epinephrine (adrenaline) subcutaneously together with a steroid and an antihistamine to achieve bronchodilation, increase blood pressure and relieve decongestion. Appropriate fluid resuscitation should accompany or precede use of vasopressor drugs; a mean arterial pressure of about 60-65 mmHg is needed to perfuse organs, and vasopressors should be started if this is not achieved after fluid resuscitation.
(iv) Epinephrine acts on:
- alpha1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction, leading to increased blood pressure and relief of congestion.
- beta1 receptors to increase heart rate, leading to increased cardiac output and increased blood pressure.
- beta2 receptors to cause bronchodilation and relieve bronchospasm.

(i) Amitriptyline belongs to the class of classical tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs). TCAs are closely related in structure to the phenothiazines and were initially synthesised (in 1949) as potential antipsychotic drugs. The main immediate effect of TCAs is to block the uptake of amines by nerve terminals by competition for the binding site of the amine transporter. Most TCAs inhibit noradrenaline and 5-HT uptake but have much less effect on dopamine uptake. In addition to their effects on amine uptake, most TCAs affect other receptors including muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine receptors, and 5-HT receptors.
(ii) The initial effect of TCA overdosage is to cause excitement and delirium, which may be accompanied by convulsions. This is followed by coma and respiratory depression lasting for some days. Atropine-like effects are pronounced. Cardiac dysrhythmias are common, and sudden death (rare) may occur from ventricular fibrillation. TCAs are dangerous in overdose, and were at one time commonly used for suicide attempts — an important factor prompting the introduction of safer antidepressants.
(iii) TCAs bind strongly to plasma albumin, most being 90–95% bound at therapeutic plasma concentrations. They also bind to extravascular tissues, which accounts for their generally very large distribution volumes (usually 10–50 l/kg). Extravascular sequestration, together with strong binding to plasma albumin, means that haemodialysis is ineffective as a means of increasing drug elimination.
(iv) Atropine-like effects in TCA overdose include dry mouth and skin, mydriasis, and inhibition of gut and bladder. Anticholinesterase drugs have been used to counter atropine-like effects but are no longer recommended.
(v) In non-depressed human subjects, TCAs cause sedation, confusion, and motor incoordination. These effects occur also in depressed patients in the first few days of treatment but tend to wear off in 1–2 weeks. Atropine-like effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention — strong with amitriptyline and much weaker with desipramine. Postural hypotension occurs with TCAs. Sedation with long duration of action means daytime performance is often affected by drowsiness and difficulty in concentrating. TCAs, particularly in overdose, may cause ventricular dysrhythmias associated with prolongation of the QT interval. Usual therapeutic doses of TCAs increase, slightly but significantly, the risk of sudden cardiac death.
questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman is admitted following ingestion of a large number of amitriptyline tablets. She is initially agitated and delirious, then develops coma with a broad-complex tachycardia and prolonged QT on ECG.
(i) What class of drug is amitriptyline, and what is its mechanism of action?
(ii) What is the clinical progression of TCA overdose?
(iii) Why is haemodialysis not effective in managing TCA overdose?
(iv) What are the atropine-like (anticholinergic) effects of TCAs in overdose?
(v) What are the common adverse effects of TCAs at therapeutic doses, and what cardiac risk do they pose?

A patient presents with chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bleeding, anaemia and weight loss, along with joint pains and skin lesions.
(i) What is the most likely group of conditions?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors?
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology, including extra-intestinal features and complications.
(iv) Outline the drug management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) - Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis (UC), the major types of IBD.
(ii) IBD is a spectrum of chronic idiopathic inflammatory intestinal conditions and an autoimmune disorder.
(iii) IBD causes significant GI symptoms including diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bleeding, anaemia and weight loss, and is associated with a spectrum of extra-intestinal manifestations including arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, sclerosing cholangitis, uveitis, iritis, pyoderma gangrenosum and erythema nodosum.
Complications include anaemia, abdominal obstruction (in Crohn's disease), mega colon and colon cancer.
Therapy for IBD seeks to dampen the generalised inflammatory response; there is no cure, and treatment is restricted to controlling symptoms, maintaining remission, preventing relapse, and treating specific complications such as fistulas.
(iv) Drug classes used: 5-aminosalicylic acid compounds (azo compounds such as sulfasalazine, olsalazine, balsalazide; mesalamines such as Pentasa, Asacol, Rowasa, Canasa); glucocorticoids (prednisone, prednisolone, hydrocortisone, budesonide); immunomodulators (methotrexate; purine analogues such as azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine); TNF-alpha inhibitors/monoclonal antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab); and surgery in severe conditions.

questions.question:
A patient with a history of industrial exposure presents with anorexia, headache, nausea, vomiting and haemoglobinaemia.
(i) Identify the likely toxin.
(ii) Which organs are affected in chronic poisoning?
(iii) Explain the underlying biochemical mechanism.
(iv) Outline the treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Arsenic poisoning (arsenic exists in trivalent and pentavalent forms; arsine is the principal source of industrial arsenic poisoning and produces anaemia, haemolysis and renal failure).
(ii) Following chronic arsenic poisoning, the metal leaves the blood and is distributed to the liver, kidney, lung, intestinal wall and spleen; it is concentrated in the hair 4-6 times as much as in the liver.
(iii) In various tissues, arsenic is firmly bound to the sulfhydryl (SH) group of the protein fraction and released slowly; the sulfhydryl enzyme system, especially pyruvate oxidase, is inhibited, and arsenic also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in liver mitochondria. Trivalent compounds are more toxic and are converted to arsenoxide to act as a protoplasmic poison, while pentavalent compounds penetrate more readily from the intestine.
Inorganic arsenic is readily absorbed through intact skin, and soluble salts are well absorbed from the GIT, mucous membrane and lung; in red blood cells it binds to the globin of Hb, and in serum it is bound to protein.
(iv) Treatment includes supportive treatment such as gastric lavage and emesis, and chelation therapy with dimercaprol (BAL) and analogues (DMSA, DMPS) or d-penicillamine; dimercaprol binds arsenic as a chelating agent, reducing its distribution.

A(i) Systemic corticosteroids include hydrocortisone, prednisolone and others; inhalational corticosteroids include beclomethasone dipropionate, budesonide, fluticasone and flunisolide.
A(ii) Corticosteroids are not bronchodilators; they reduce bronchial hyperactivity, mucosal oedema, and suppress the inflammatory response, giving more complete and sustained symptomatic relief than bronchodilators; inhaled steroids suppress bronchial inflammation, increase peak expiratory flow rate, and prevent episodes of acute asthma, but have no role during acute attacks or status asthmaticus.
B(i) Side effects of inhaled steroids (hoarseness of voice, dysphonia, sore throat, oropharyngeal candidiasis) are local, and can be prevented by gargling after use; systemic effects (mood changes, osteoporosis, bruising, petechiae, hyperglycaemia, pituitary-adrenal suppression) are rare and occur only at very high doses, reflecting that inhaled steroids act mainly locally in the airway with low systemic activity, whereas systemic steroid therapy is used only in severe chronic asthma or status asthmaticus not responding to bronchodilators, with long-term use of systemic steroids discouraged because of adverse effects.
B(ii) Systemic effects such as pituitary-adrenal suppression occur only at very high doses because sufficient corticosteroid reaches the systemic circulation to act on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, a site distant from the bronchial airway that is the intended target of asthma therapy; inhaled steroids are noted to be safe in pregnancy, reflecting their predominantly local action at ordinary doses.
questions.question:
A(i) Classify corticosteroids used in bronchial asthma.
A(ii) Describe their mechanism/action in asthma.
B(i) Explain how the route of administration relates to their local versus systemic adverse effects.
B(ii) Explain why long-term systemic corticosteroid use produces effects on a distant system (the pituitary-adrenal axis).

questions.answerText:
(i) Primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison's disease).
(ii) Addison disease is caused by adrenal cortex dysfunction, diagnosed by the lack of response to ACTH administration; characteristic features are weakness, fatigue, weight loss, hypotension and hyperpigmentation.
(iii) Acute adrenal insufficiency usually occurs during abrupt withdrawal of chronic glucocorticoid administration; treatment is with intravenous hydrocortisone sodium succinate/phosphate.
(iv) Chronic replacement therapy: daily hydrocortisone, which is identical to natural cortisol, given to correct the deficiency (two-thirds of the daily dose in the morning, one-third in the afternoon), plus a salt-retaining hormone such as fludrocortisone (a potent synthetic mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid activity) to supplement mineralocorticoid deficiency.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents with weakness, fatigue, weight loss, hypotension and hyperpigmentation. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the pathologic basis of this presentation?
(iii) What is the treatment for an acute presentation (acute adrenal insufficiency)?
(iv) What is the definitive/chronic treatment?

(i) An immunosuppressed patient presents with altered mental status and is suspected to have a life-threatening fungal infection of the central nervous system. What are the risk factors for this class of infection?
(ii) What complications/severity markers are relevant?
(iii) State the antifungal treatment options and justify the use of one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Reasons for increased fungal infections include advances in surgery, cancer treatment, treatment of patients with solid organ and bone marrow transplantation, the HIV epidemic, and increasing use of broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy in critically ill patients.
(ii) The relevant severity marker in this presentation is cryptococcal meningitis with altered mental status; other severe presentations covered by the same treatment approach include sepsis syndrome due to fungal infection, severe fungal pneumonia in immunosuppressed patients, and empiric therapy in cancer patients with neutropenia.
(iii) Amphotericin B, a polyene antibiotic with the broadest spectrum of action (Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, endemic mycoses, and pathogenic molds), is used for all life-threatening mycotic infections including cryptococcal meningitis with altered mental status; it is justified as the choice here because it is highly effective as an induction regimen for serious fungal infections in immunosuppressed patients, despite toxicity that includes infusion-related effects (fever, chills, muscle spasms, vomiting, headache, hypotension) and cumulative renal damage. Azole drugs (e.g. fluconazole) are an alternative, being relatively nontoxic, but with a narrower/less broad spectrum than amphotericin B for the most severe presentations.

(i) The fundamental physiologic defect in heart failure is a decrease in cardiac output relative to the needs of the body, with dyspnoea and fatigue as the major manifestations.
(ii) This is best shown by the ventricular function (Frank-Starling) curve: in heart failure, output is reduced at all fibre lengths and the heart expands as the ejection fraction is decreased or filling pressure is increased, moving the heart from a normal point on the curve to a lower "heart failure" point; compensatory sympathetic discharge or effective treatment allows the heart to eject more blood, moving it to an intermediate point on the curve.
(iii) Acute heart failure/cardiogenic shock should be treated with a loop diuretic; if very severe, a prompt-acting positive inotropic agent such as a beta agonist (e.g. dobutamine) or a phosphodiesterase inhibitor; and vasodilators as required to optimise filling pressures and blood pressure. In cardiogenic shock, dopamine and dobutamine may be used together to increase heart rate, cardiac output and blood pressure.
(iv) Chronic failure is best treated with diuretics (often a loop agent plus spironolactone) plus an ACE inhibitor and, if tolerated, a beta blocker; digitalis glycosides may improve functional status but do not prolong life and are no longer first-line.
questions.question:
(i) A patient with a background of chronic hypertension presents with reduced cardiac output, dyspnoea and fatigue, consistent with heart failure, and subsequently deteriorates into cardiogenic shock. What is the pathophysiological defect underlying this presentation?
(ii) Explain the basis of this defect using the ventricular function relationship.
(iii) Describe the immediate/resuscitative drug management.
(iv) Describe the definitive/chronic management once the patient is stabilised.

(i) A patient on a statin for hyperlipidaemia, who is also taking gemfibrozil, develops muscle pain and weakness. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List the factors that predispose to this condition.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiological basis of the reaction.
(iv) Outline the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Statin-induced myopathy (with risk of rhabdomyolysis).
(ii) Predisposing factors include advanced age (especially over 80 years), hepatic or renal dysfunction, the perioperative period, multisystem disease (especially with diabetes mellitus), small body size, untreated hypothyroidism, and concomitant use of drugs that diminish statin catabolism - most notably fibrates (especially gemfibrozil), cyclosporine, digoxin, warfarin, macrolide antibiotics, azole antifungals, niacin, HIV protease inhibitors, amiodarone, and nefazodone.
(iii) The risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis increases in proportion to plasma statin concentration; factors and interacting drugs that inhibit statin catabolism raise plasma statin levels, and concomitant use of such drugs is associated with myopathy/rhabdomyolysis in about half of reported cases.
(iv) Management: the combination of statin with fibrate should be used cautiously, usually with a low-dose statin, since this combination increases the risk of myopathy; the interacting drug or the statin should be reviewed/discontinued, and liver enzymes should be monitored, particularly in patients on higher statin doses.

(i) Therapeutic index (TI) = TD50/ED50. Drug A: TI = 200/2 = 100. Drug B: TI = 15/5 = 3.
(ii) Drug A is safer because it has a higher therapeutic index (100 vs 3). A higher ratio (or larger difference) indicates better safety. Drug B has a low TI of 3, meaning the toxic dose is only 3 times the effective dose, leaving little margin between the therapeutic and toxic doses. This means a small increase in dose of Drug B could easily lead to toxicity.
(iii) The therapeutic index (TI) is a comparison of the amount of a therapeutic agent that causes the toxicity to the amount that has the desired therapeutic effect. It is the ratio of the toxic dose in 50% of subjects (TD50) divided by the dose that leads to the desired pharmacological effect in 50% of subjects (ED50). When a drug has a low therapeutic index, there is a narrow window between the therapeutic dose and the toxic dose; clinical monitoring and careful dose adjustment are required.
(iv) Three drugs with a low therapeutic index: digoxin, cocaine, vancomycin.
(v) The dose-response relationship is important because the concentration of a drug at its site of action controls its effect. The dose-response curve allows comparison of the efficacy curve (therapeutic effect) and the toxicity curve. A larger separation between the efficacy and toxicity curves represents a higher therapeutic index and greater safety. Drug dose-response involves the principles of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics and can be used to determine the required dose and frequency to achieve the desired response without toxicity.
questions.question:
A pharmacology class is asked to evaluate the safety of two drugs used for anxiety: Drug A (diazepam) and Drug B (a novel compound). Drug A has an ED50 of 2 mg and a TD50 of 200 mg. Drug B has an ED50 of 5 mg and a TD50 of 15 mg.
(i) Calculate the therapeutic index (TI) for both Drug A and Drug B.
(ii) State which drug is safer based on the TI and explain the clinical implication.
(iii) Explain what the therapeutic index means and what happens clinically when a drug has a low TI.
(iv) Name three drugs with a low therapeutic index.
(v) Explain the relationship between the therapeutic index and the dose-response curve, including what a larger separation between the efficacy and toxicity curves means.

A 35-year-old woman is scheduled for an elective laparotomy. She has a history of gastro-oesophageal reflux. She is brought to the operating room and is induced with propofol, maintained on sevoflurane, and given suxamethonium for intubation.
(i) What class of drug is propofol, and what is its mechanism of action?
(ii) What are the NPO (nil by mouth) requirements before general anaesthesia, according to the American Society of Anesthesiology guidelines?
(iii) What is premedication, and which drug is most commonly used? Why is it preferred?
(iv) What is the mechanism of action of suxamethonium, and what is the clinical significance of a phase II block?
(v) What are the stages of general anaesthesia?
questions.answerText:
(i) Propofol is a non-barbiturate intravenous anaesthetic (induction agent) and is the most common induction agent of anaesthesia in current use. Like most intravenous anaesthetics, propofol works by increasing GABA-mediated inhibitory tone in the CNS. Propofol decreases the rate of dissociation of GABA from the receptor, thereby increasing the duration of the GABA-activated opening of the chloride channel with resulting hyperpolarization of cell membranes. It is associated with less postoperative nausea and vomiting and a more rapid return of cognition.
(ii) NPO requirements per ASA guidelines:
- Clear liquids (e.g. apple juice, water — NOT orange juice): 2 hours
- Breast milk (unfortified): 4 hours
- Infant formula (unfortified): 6 hours
- Non-human milk (e.g. almond milk, soy milk, unfortified): 6 hours
- Light meal (e.g. tea and toast, no added fats): 6 hours
- Full meal (fatty meal): 8 hours. Unnecessarily long fasting times should be avoided to reduce dehydration, post-induction hypotension, and patient dissatisfaction.
(iii) Premedication is the administration of medication before anaesthesia. It is used to prepare the patient for anaesthesia and to help provide optimal conditions for surgery, including: reduction of anxiety and pain; promotion of amnesia; reduction of secretions; reduction of volume and pH of gastric contents; reduction of postoperative nausea and vomiting; enhancing the hypnotic effects of general anaesthesia; and prevention of infective endocarditis. The most commonly used premedication is midazolam, a short-acting benzodiazepine that has the benefit of providing anterograde amnesia. It is preferred because oral midazolam syrup can be given to children to facilitate calm separation from their parents prior to anaesthesia.
(iv) Suxamethonium is a widely used depolarizing muscle relaxant. It produces rapid, complete paralysis, which is very short-lasting in most patients, and is of particular value for laryngoscopy and intubation. Suxamethonium normally produces a phase I (depolarizing) neuromuscular block. After high doses or prolonged use, the nature of the block changes to a phase II (non-depolarizing) block; this phase II block (also known as dual block) is associated with prolonged neuromuscular blockade and apnoea.
(v) The four stages of general anaesthesia are:
- Stage 1 (Induction): Occurs between the administration of the drug and loss of consciousness; the patient moves from analgesia without loss of memory to analgesia with loss of memory.
- Stage 2 (Excitement): Period following loss of consciousness characterised by excited and delirious activity; breathing and heart rate become erratic; there is a danger of choking from irregular breathing and risk of vomiting.
- Stage 3 (Surgical stage): Muscles relax, vomiting stops, breathing is depressed; eye movements slow and then cease; the patient is ready to be operated on.
- Stage 4 (Overdose): Too much medication has been administered, leading to brain stem or medullary suppression, resulting in respiratory and cardiovascular collapse. The anaesthetist's priority is to take the patient to stage 3 as quickly as possible and keep them there for the duration of surgery.

(i) Digitalis (digoxin) toxicity.
(ii) Predisposing/precipitating factors: hypokalaemia, hypoxaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypothyroidism, and myocardial ischaemia.
(iii) Digoxin decreases sodium transport out of the cardiac cell by inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase (sodium pump); the resulting accumulation of sodium increases intracellular calcium via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, which is responsible for the positive inotropic effect but, in excess, produces early features such as anorexia, nausea and lethargy, and cardiac toxicity including ventricular and supraventricular dysrhythmias and all degrees of AV block.
(iv) Management: discontinue the drug at the first sign of toxicity; maintain serum potassium concentration between 4.0 and 5.0 mmol/L; treat bradyarrhythmias and AV block with atropine (0.6 mg IV), or a temporary pacemaker if there is no response; and give antidigoxin antibodies for massive overdose.
questions.question:
(i) A patient on a cardiac glycoside for heart failure develops anorexia, nausea and lethargy, followed by cardiac dysrhythmias and varying degrees of AV block. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) List the factors that predispose to this condition.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiological basis of the toxicity.
(iv) Outline the management of this condition.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Vasopressin (ADH) is synthesised in neuronal cell bodies in the hypothalamus and released from nerve terminals in the posterior pituitary; it acts through V2 receptors to increase insertion of aquaporin AQP2 water channels in the apical membranes of collecting duct cells, by activating adenylyl cyclase via Gs and increasing cyclic AMP. Vasopressin also contracts vascular smooth muscle by activating V1 receptors.
A(ii) ADH and desmopressin are useful in pituitary diabetes insipidus; desmopressin, a selective V2 agonist, is also used in patients with mild haemophilia A or von Willebrand disease; vasopressin, via V1 receptors, is sometimes used to treat bleeding from oesophageal varices or colon diverticula. They are of no value in nephrogenic DI, where salt restriction, water restriction, thiazides and loop diuretics may be used instead.
A(iii) In the presence of ADH or desmopressin, a large water load may cause dangerous hyponatraemia; large doses of either peptide may cause hypertension in some persons.
B(i) Because a large water load in the presence of these agents may cause dangerous hyponatraemia, fluid intake/water load should be limited and serum sodium observed during therapy.
B(ii) ADH and desmopressin act on V2 receptors to increase water reabsorption via aquaporin water channels in the collecting duct; if a large water load is given while this antidiuretic action is active, the retained free water dilutes serum sodium, producing dangerous hyponatraemia.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the mechanism of action of vasopressin/desmopressin.
A(ii) State their clinical uses.
A(iii) List their adverse effects/toxicity.
B(i) What monitoring precaution follows from their toxicity profile?
B(ii) Explain the pharmacologic basis of the hyponatraemia that can result from their use.

A 28-year-old woman is given phenobarbitone for epilepsy. She is also on warfarin for a mechanical heart valve. After two weeks, her INR drops and she develops a stroke.
(i) Name the pharmacokinetic mechanism responsible for this adverse drug interaction.
(ii) Identify the specific enzyme system involved and explain the mechanism in detail.
(iii) Explain why the effect on warfarin would not be immediate but takes 1-2 weeks to manifest.
(iv) Using the half-life concept, explain what happens to plasma warfarin concentration over time when phenobarbitone is started.
(v) List two other enzyme inducers in the same class and state two clinical consequences of enzyme induction in general.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pharmacokinetic mechanism is enzyme induction (pharmacokinetic antagonism). Phenobarbitone induces hepatic microsomal enzymes, increasing the metabolism of warfarin and reducing its plasma concentration, thereby reducing its anticoagulant effect.
(ii) Phenobarbitone is a microsomal enzyme inductor that enhances the activity of the cytochrome P450 enzyme system (particularly CYP2C9, which metabolizes warfarin). Drug metabolism occurs primarily in the liver through its enzymes, particularly the cytochrome P450 family. Increased enzymatic activity leads to faster biotransformation of warfarin, shortening its half-life and reducing its plasma level.
(iii) Enzyme induction requires time because it involves the synthesis of new enzyme protein; this takes days to weeks. As the drug is taken regularly, the inducing drug stimulates enzyme production progressively. Some microsomal enzyme inductors have self-inductive properties after prolonged use.
(iv) As phenobarbitone induces warfarin metabolism, warfarin's half-life is shortened. After each half-life, the plasma concentration falls to half its original value. With a shorter half-life due to induced metabolism, steady-state plasma warfarin concentration falls to a lower level and INR decreases.
(v) Two other enzyme inducers: rifampicin, carbamazepine (or phenytoin). Two general clinical consequences of enzyme induction: (a) drugs have a faster onset of action and shorter duration of action when used simultaneously with drugs that stimulate their metabolism; (b) self-induction is one cause of drug tolerance, where decreased drug action occurs after prolonged use.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with recurrent vomiting is brought to the emergency department. She cannot swallow tablets. The attending physician decides to administer a drug rectally.
(i) Identify the route of administration chosen and state how it is administered.
(ii) List three other systemic routes that bypass the oral route in similar circumstances.
(iii) State the pharmacokinetic advantage of the rectal route over the oral (peroral) route.
(iv) Explain why, despite this advantage, absorption by the rectal route may still be variable.
(v) State two additional clinical indications for preferring the rectal route.
questions.answerText:
(i) Rectal route. The drug is inserted into the anus as suppositories, from where it will be absorbed.
(ii) Three systemic routes that bypass the oral route: sublingual/buccal, cutaneous/transdermal, parenteral (intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intradermal, or inhalation).
(iii) Pharmacokinetic advantage: drugs absorbed rectally partly bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism, so some drugs with high first-pass metabolism can reach systemic circulation at higher concentrations than via peroral administration.
(iv) Despite this advantage, absorption by the rectal route may still be variable because absorption may be variable and the route is less reliable than other parenteral or enteral routes.
(v) Two additional clinical indications: (a) to administer drugs to unconscious patients or children; (b) to administer drugs that affect the bowel, such as laxatives.

A(i) Non-motor features of Parkinson's disease, by system:
- Autonomic: Postural hypotension (falling blood pressure on standing; may contribute to falls and blackouts later in the disease course, and is a leading cause of hospitalisation for patients with PD); constipation (pathology in the enteric nervous system).
- Psychiatric: Depression (affecting approximately 40% of patients); paranoia and hallucinations.
- Cognitive: Dementia (80% of PD patients).
- Sleep: Sleep disorders (especially the REM sleep behavioural disorder); restless leg syndrome and limb pain.
A(ii) The diagnosis of PD is a clinical one and should be based, preferably, upon validated criteria. Brain imaging by CT or MRI may be necessary to exclude hydrocephalus, cerebrovascular disease, or basal ganglia abnormalities suggestive of an underlying metabolic cause. There is no anatomical and pathological defect in the brain in functional psychosis; in PD, the diagnosis is clinical.
B(i) The treatment of PD at the current time is wholly symptomatic and no drug has proven to have significant disease-modifying or neuroprotective capabilities. There is no accepted algorithm for the treatment of PD, although guidance has been produced by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, 2017). Treatment options depend upon whether the motor symptoms impact on the patient's quality of life.
B(ii) After diagnosis, the provision of an explanation of the condition, education, and support are essential. Accurate adherence with the timing of therapy may be particularly important in patients beginning to experience long-term treatment complications. Patients can keep diaries when they begin to experience problems with either bradykinesia or dyskinesia so that symptoms can be related to drug and food intake. Other factors include the benefits of adequate sleep and rest at night; judicious use of hypnotic therapy may be appropriate; a tricyclic antidepressant may offer the dual benefit of sedation with antimuscarinic effects. Patients' relatives also need emotional and social support. The involvement of occupational therapists, social workers, and specialists in palliative care is important.
B(iii) Parkinson's disease is a progressive degenerative disorder of the central nervous system; loss of neurons from structures of the basal ganglia results in abnormalities in the control of movement. PD is caused mainly by the degeneration of nerve cells in the brain and its cause is unknown for most patients, rarely secondary to viral encephalitis. Parkinsonism, by contrast, has numerous causes ranging from the side effects of medications, chronic head traumas, metabolic diseases, toxins, and neurological diseases. Both genetic and environmental factors are likely to contribute to PD risk, with environmental factors precipitating the onset in a genetically susceptible individual.
questions.question:
Describe the non-motor features, diagnosis, and patient care in Parkinson's disease under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the full range of non-motor features of Parkinson's disease, organised by system.
A(ii) Describe the diagnostic approach and investigations used in Parkinson's disease.
B(i) Describe the overall general approach to PD treatment.
B(ii) Describe the general patient care principles for people living with Parkinson's disease.
B(iii) Distinguish between idiopathic Parkinson's disease and parkinsonism in terms of aetiology and causes.

questions.answerText:
(i) Atropine (antimuscarinic) toxicity.
(ii) Atropine, an alkaloid obtained from Atropa belladonna, is the prototype muscarinic antagonist.
(iii) Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic receptors (M1-M4) non-selectively; toxic doses cause dryness of the mouth and blurred vision, photophobia, confusion, headache, dizziness, tachycardia, palpitations, flushing, urinary hesitancy/retention, constipation, and loss of libido.
(iv) Toxic doses may lead to locomotor difficulties, disorientation, hallucinations, delirium, confusion, agitation, coma and central depression; severe atropine intoxication may progress to respiratory depression, coma, circulatory collapse and death.
(v) Physostigmine, a tertiary amine acting on the central and peripheral nervous system, is the drug of choice for atropine toxicity; it inhibits acetylcholinesterase, preventing hydrolysis of acetylcholine and thereby enhancing the effect of acetylcholine to overcome the competitive muscarinic blockade produced by atropine.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents with dry mouth, dilated pupils, flushed dry skin, tachycardia, hallucinations and delirium after exposure to an anticholinergic agent. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Name the prototype drug responsible for this toxic picture.
(iii) Explain the mechanism/receptor basis of this toxicity.
(iv) State the features of severe toxicity that may prove fatal.
(v) State the definitive antidote and explain why it is effective.

Describe the pharmacology of local and general anaesthesia under the following headings:
A(i) Define the three broad categories of anaesthesia, and state what local anaesthesia achieves.
A(ii) Describe the mechanism of action of local anaesthetics, and compare the dosage and duration of lidocaine with bupivacaine (with and without epinephrine).
B(i) State the advantages and disadvantages of general anaesthesia.
B(ii) Describe the role of epinephrine when combined with local anaesthetics, and state the maximum doses of plain lidocaine and lidocaine with epinephrine.
B(iii) Distinguish between spinal and epidural anaesthesia in terms of technique and uses.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The three broad categories of anaesthesia are: local anaesthesia, regional anaesthesia, and general anaesthesia. Local/conduction anaesthetics cause a reversible block to conduction along nerve fibres. Local anaesthesia blocks transmission of nerve impulses between a targeted part of the body and the CNS, leading to loss of sensation in the targeted body part. This reduces pain sensations in a small, focused area of the body, but the person receiving the treatment remains conscious. It is given before minor surgeries such as removal of a toenail or a tooth.
A(ii) Local anaesthetics produce anaesthesia by inhibiting excitation of nerve endings or by blocking conduction in peripheral nerves. This is achieved by anaesthetics reversibly binding to and inactivating sodium channels. Sodium influx through these channels is necessary for the depolarization of nerve cell membranes and subsequent propagation of impulses. When a nerve loses depolarization and capacity to propagate an impulse, the individual loses sensation. Lidocaine (the most widely used cocaine derivative): rapid onset; maximum dose 4.5 mg/kg (7 mg/kg with epinephrine); duration 120 min (240 min with epinephrine). Bupivacaine: slow onset; maximum dose 2.5 mg/kg (3 mg/kg with epinephrine); duration 4 hours (8 hours with epinephrine).
B(i) Advantages of general anaesthesia: reduces intraoperative patient awareness and recall; allows use of muscle relaxants; facilitates complete control of the airway, breathing, and circulation; can be used in cases of sensitivity to local anaesthetic agent; can be administered without moving the patient from supine position; can be adapted easily to procedures of unpredictable duration or extent; can be administered rapidly and is reversible. Disadvantages: requires preoperative patient preparation; requires increased complexity of care and associated costs; may induce physiologic fluctuations requiring active intervention; associated with malignant hyperthermia (an exceedingly rare, inherited muscular condition in which exposure to some general anaesthetic agents results in acute and potentially lethal temperature rise, hypercarbia, metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalaemia). More commonly encountered adverse events include vomiting, nausea, sore throat, incisional site pain, and emergence delirium in children.
B(ii) The local anaesthetic drug of choice is lidocaine 0.5% with or without epinephrine. The addition of epinephrine (adrenaline) diminishes local blood flow, slows the rate of absorption of the local anaesthetic, and prolongs its effect. No more than 4 mg/kg of plain lidocaine or 7 mg/kg of lidocaine with epinephrine should be administered on any one occasion.
B(iii) Spinal anaesthetic is used for surgeries of the lower limbs and abdomen. It is injected into the lower back and numbs the lower body, and is one of the most useful of all anaesthetic techniques for surgery of the abdomen and the lower limbs. Epidural anaesthesia is often used to reduce the pain of childbirth and lower limb surgery. It is administered to the area around the spinal cord through a small catheter instead of a needle injection; the catheter may remain in place for continuous infusion. Either lidocaine 1% or bupivacaine 0.5% is suitable; bupivacaine has the advantage of a longer duration of action. A patient under regional anaesthesia remains conscious.

questions.question:
(i) A female infant presents with virilization due to overproduction of adrenal androgens, in the setting of increased ACTH and accumulation of upstream steroidogenic metabolites. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology?
(iv) What is the management?
questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH).
(ii) CAH is a group of disorders resulting from defects in one of the enzymes in cortisol synthesis; it can present as classical (childhood) or nonclassical (after puberty) disease. Peripheral precocious puberty (in the nonclassical/late-onset form) can also arise from androgen secretion from a virilizing adrenal tumor.
(iii) CAH is a group of diseases resulting from an enzyme defect in the synthesis of one or more adrenal steroid hormones, with increased ACTH and accumulation of upstream metabolites in steroidogenesis; it may lead to virilization in females due to overproduction of adrenal androgens.
(iv) CAH is treated with hydrocortisone, while 'salt wasters' are treated with fludrocortisone; treatment requires administration of sufficient corticosteroids to normalize hormone levels by suppressing release of CRH and ACTH, which decreases production of adrenal androgens.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man with a known history of malignant hyperthermia in his family is listed for an elective inguinal hernia repair under general anaesthesia. The anaesthetist notes his history and plans the anaesthetic carefully.
(i) What is malignant hyperthermia, and what triggers it in the context of general anaesthesia?
(ii) What are the advantages of general anaesthesia that make it the preferred approach in certain surgical situations?
(iii) What induction agent would be appropriate for this patient, and what are its mechanism of action and side effects?
(iv) What traditional opioid analgesics are listed as adjuncts during the induction of anaesthesia?
(v) What post-operative monitoring is required, and what are the PACU discharge criteria?
questions.answerText:
(i) Malignant hyperthermia is an exceedingly rare, inherited muscular condition in which exposure to some (but not all) general anaesthetic agents results in acute and potentially lethal temperature rise, hypercarbia, metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalaemia. It is listed as one of the disadvantages associated with general anaesthesia and is a major consideration in pre-operative assessment, which requires attention to previous personal or familial adverse reactions to general anaesthetics.
(ii) Advantages of general anaesthesia: reduces intraoperative patient awareness and recall; allows use of muscle relaxants; facilitates complete control of the airway, breathing, and circulation; can be used in cases of sensitivity to local anaesthetic agent; can be administered without moving the patient from the supine position; can be adapted easily to procedures of unpredictable duration or extent; can be administered rapidly and is reversible.
(iii) Propofol (DIPRIVAN® Injectable Emulsion 10 mg/ml) is the most common induction agent of anaesthesia in current use. It is a non-barbiturate intravenous anaesthetic which has displaced barbiturates in many anaesthesia practices. Propofol works by increasing GABA-mediated inhibitory tone in the CNS — it decreases the rate of dissociation of GABA from the receptor, thereby increasing the duration of the GABA-activated opening of the chloride channel with resulting hyperpolarisation of cell membranes. The use of propofol is associated with less postoperative nausea and vomiting and a more rapid return of cognition. Side effects include: decrease in blood pressure; depression or cessation of breathing; and pain on injection. Because it is prepared in a lipid emulsion, it can be a medium for rapid bacterial growth if not handled using meticulous aseptic precautions.
(iv) Traditional opioid analgesics used as adjuncts during anaesthesia include: morphine, meperidine, and hydromorphone. Other short-acting opioids include fentanyl, sufentanil, and remifentanil. In addition to the induction drug, most patients receive an injection of an opioid analgesic. Induction agents and opioids work synergistically to induce anaesthesia.
(v) After awakening, patients typically recover in the Post Anaesthesia Care Unit (PACU). In more critically ill patients, recovery may occur directly in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Patients recover in the recovery unit until they have met PACU discharge criteria: adequate activity, circulation, consciousness, oxygen saturation, and maintenance of respiration. Final discharge is based on the ability to maintain appropriate surgical site dressings, adequate pain control, normothermia, ambulation ability, absence of nausea and vomiting, and stable vital signs.

(i) Central (neurogenic) diabetes insipidus (DI).
(ii) Central DI is due to a lack of the hormone vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone, ADH); this can be due to injury to the hypothalamus or pituitary gland, or genetics. (Other types include nephrogenic DI, where the kidneys do not respond properly to vasopressin; dipsogenic DI, from excessive fluid intake due to damage to the hypothalamic thirst mechanism; and gestational DI, occurring only during pregnancy.)
(iii) Vasopressin is synthesised in neuronal cell bodies in the hypothalamus and released from nerve terminals in the posterior pituitary; it acts through V2 receptors to increase insertion of water channels (aquaporin AQP2) in the apical membranes of collecting duct cells, by stimulating adenylyl cyclase via Gs and increasing cyclic AMP.
Deficiency of ADH in central DI therefore results in failure of water reabsorption from the collecting tubule, producing large amounts of dilute urine and increased thirst.
(iv) ADH and desmopressin are prototypical ADH agonists; desmopressin is a selective agonist of V2 receptors, administered orally, nasally, or parenterally, and is useful in pituitary (central) diabetes insipidus.
ADH and desmopressin reduce urine volume and increase its concentration; they are of no value in the nephrogenic form of the disease.
A large water load in the presence of ADH or desmopressin may cause dangerous hyponatraemia, and large doses of either peptide may cause hypertension in some persons.
questions.question:
A patient presents with large amounts of dilute urine (up to nearly 20 litres per day) and increased thirst, following injury to the hypothalamus or pituitary gland.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors/causes?
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iv) Outline the pharmacological management.

questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is typical absence seizures (Petit Mal Seizures). According to the classification, absence seizures are a type of generalized non-motor seizure. Typical absence seizures happen almost exclusively in childhood and early adolescence and are characterized by behavioural arrest for a few seconds. The child goes blank and stares; fluttering of the eyelids and flopping of the head may occur. The attacks last only a few seconds and afterwards normal activity is resumed as if nothing had happened. They are seen in developmentally normal people.
(ii) According to the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE), epilepsy is defined by any of the following conditions: at least two unprovoked (or reflex) seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart; one unprovoked seizure (or reflex) and a probability of further seizures similar to the general recurrence risk (at least 60%) after two unprovoked seizures, occurring over the next 10 years; or diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.
(iii) The drug of first choice for absence seizures is ethosuximide. It has no useful effect against any other seizure type. Its mechanism of action is through blockage of low-voltage activated calcium channels. Clobazam and lamotrigine are also listed as first-line options. Adjunctive AEDs include clonazepam, sodium valproate, levetiracetam, topiramate, and zonisamide.
(iv) A first-line AED suitable for the person's seizure type should be introduced slowly, starting with a small dose. A hasty introduction may induce side effects that may challenge the person's confidence. For most drugs, a gradual introduction will produce a therapeutic effect just as fast as a rapid introduction. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is indicated at the onset of therapy, if seizure control is poor or sudden changes in seizure control occur, if toxicity is suspected, if poor or non-adherence is suspected, to monitor the timescale of drug interactions, and when changing AED therapy.
(v) AEDs should not be withdrawn abruptly. Withdrawal of individual AEDs should be carried out in a slow, stepwise fashion to avoid precipitation of rebound seizures (e.g. over 2–3 months). This risk is particularly great with barbiturates (phenobarbital and primidone) and benzodiazepines (clobazam and clonazepam). If a drug needs to be withdrawn rapidly, for example if there are life-threatening side effects, a benzodiazepine can be used to cover the withdrawal phase. Example: Ethosuximide withdrawal is 125–250 mg every 2 weeks as part of a drug change, and 125–250 mg every 4 weeks for total withdrawal.
questions.question:
A 16-year-old girl with no prior medical history is brought to the clinic after her teacher witnessed her staring blankly for several seconds during class, with fluttering eyelids. She then resumed normal activity as if nothing had happened. Similar episodes occur multiple times daily. She is developmentally normal.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and seizure classification?
(ii) What are the ILAE criteria for diagnosing epilepsy?
(iii) What is the drug of first choice for this seizure type, and what adjunctive agents can be used?
(iv) How should antiepileptic drug (AED) therapy be initiated and monitored?
(v) What are the general principles for withdrawal of AEDs?

A 19-year-old male is brought to the emergency department unconscious. His friend states he had been taking oral diazepam prescribed to him for anxiety and then consumed alcohol at a party. His respiratory rate is 8 breaths per minute and GCS is 6.
(i) What is the mechanism of action of diazepam, and how does it interact with the CNS equilibrium of excitation and inhibition?
(ii) Why is the combination of diazepam and alcohol particularly dangerous?
(iii) What specific antagonist can be used for benzodiazepine overdose, and what are its pharmacokinetic properties and clinical uses?
(iv) What are the adverse effects of chronic benzodiazepine use, and how should they be discontinued?
(v) What are the differences between short-acting, intermediate-acting, and long-acting benzodiazepines, providing examples?
questions.answerText:
(i) Benzodiazepines act very selectively on GABA-A receptors, which mediate the fast inhibitory synaptic response produced by activity in GABAergic neurons. The effect of benzodiazepines is to enhance the response to GABA by facilitating the opening of GABA-activated chloride channels. Entry of Cl- hyperpolarizes the cell, making it more difficult to depolarize, so neuronal excitability is reduced. Benzodiazepines bind specifically to a regulatory site on the receptor, distinct from the GABA binding site, and enhance receptor affinity for GABA. CNS equilibrium is determined by a balance between excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) neurotransmission; inhibition via GABA is primarily mediated by the ionotropic GABA-A receptor.
(ii) Alcohol is classed as a CNS depressant because it produces sedation and sleep, acting on inhibitory systems. Alcohol produces cross-tolerance to other sedatives such as benzodiazepines. These may be relatively safe in overdose when given alone but potentially are lethal in combination with alcohol. Both substances enhance GABA-mediated inhibition; their combination produces additive or synergistic CNS and respiratory depression.
(iii) Flumazenil is a selective competitive antagonist of benzodiazepine receptors (Bz1). It blocks the action of benzodiazepines, zaleplon, and zolpidem but not other sedative/hypnotics. It blocks psychomotor, cognitive, and memory impairment of benzodiazepines. Pharmacokinetics: short duration of action, half-life of 1 hour; absorbed orally but undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism; no active metabolites; should be used IV (repeated doses are necessary). Therapeutic uses: acute benzodiazepine toxicity (comatose patients); and reversal of benzodiazepine sedation after endoscopy and dentistry. Side effects include nausea, dizziness, and it may precipitate withdrawal symptoms.
(iv) Adverse effects of chronic benzodiazepine use include: sedation, drowsiness, and confusion which reduce driving ability; anterograde amnesia which reduces learning ability; acquired tolerance after repeated use (due to down-regulation of benzodiazepine receptors); and drug dependence (addiction) after prolonged use — sudden stopping can produce withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, insomnia, convulsions), so gradual withdrawal is recommended after chronic use. Benzodiazepines in acute overdose are considerably less dangerous than other sedative-hypnotic drugs; they cause prolonged sleep without serious depression of respiration or cardiovascular centres. Recommended withdrawal: 25% dose reduction per week until 50% of dose is reached, then reduce by 1/8 every 4–7 days.
(v) Short-acting benzodiazepines: t½ less than 24 hours, metabolized to active metabolites which have shorter t½ (1–1.5 hours); examples: triazolam and midazolam. Intermediate-acting benzodiazepines: t½ of 5–20 hours, can be used once daily, have no active metabolites except alprazolam; examples: oxazepam, temazepam, lorazepam, and alprazolam. Long-acting benzodiazepines: t½ of about 60 hours, have active metabolites except nitrazepam; examples: diazepam, clonazepam, flurazepam, and nitrazepam.

(i) This presentation represents a mood (affective) disorder. Affective disorders are a set of psychiatric diseases also called mood disorders; the primary symptom is change in mood state. Types include: persistent depressive disorder (patients have depressed mood for at least two years); bipolar disorder (mood fluctuates from depression to mania); seasonal affective disorder (mood is affected by season with depression developing during winter); psychotic depression (patients exhibit signs of psychosis along with depression); and perinatal depression (women experience symptoms of major depression during pregnancy or after delivery).
(ii) Fluoxetine is an SSRI that inhibits 5-HT reuptake into nerve terminals. However, the increase in synaptic 5-HT levels has been observed to be less than expected because increased activation of 5-HT1A receptors on the soma and dendrites of 5-HT-containing raphe neurons inhibits these neurons and thus reduces 5-HT release, cancelling out to some extent the effect of inhibiting reuptake. On prolonged drug treatment, the elevated level of 5-HT in the somatodendritic region desensitises the 5-HT1A receptors, reducing their inhibitory effect on 5-HT release from the nerve terminals. This need to desensitise somatodendritic 5-HT1A receptors explains the slow onset of antidepressant action of 5-HT uptake inhibitors. The SSRIs have plasma half-lives of 18–24 hours (fluoxetine is longer acting: 24–96 h); the delay of 2–4 weeks before the therapeutic effect develops is similar to that seen with other antidepressants.
(iii) Common side effects include nausea, anorexia, insomnia, loss of libido, and failure of orgasm. Some of these unwanted effects result from the enhanced stimulation of postsynaptic 5-HT receptors. In combination with MAOIs, SSRIs can cause a 'serotonin syndrome' characterised by tremor, hyperthermia, and cardiovascular collapse, from which deaths have occurred.
(iv) The use of SSRIs is not recommended for treating depression in children under 18, in whom efficacy is doubtful and adverse effects — including excitement, insomnia, and aggression in the first few weeks of treatment — may occur. The possibility of increased suicidal ideation is a concern in this age group.
(v) Non-drug management options listed for depression include: electroconvulsive therapy; electromagnetic therapy; deep brain stimulation; and vagus stimulation. These more recent interventions have more rapid onset than drugs and are described as effective.
questions.question:
A 22-year-old university student presents reporting 3 weeks of persistent depressed mood, loss of interest in activities he previously enjoyed, poor sleep, and feelings of worthlessness. He is prescribed fluoxetine. Two weeks later, he feels little improvement and his family is concerned about possible suicidal ideation.
(i) What type of disorder does this presentation represent, and how are mood disorders classified?
(ii) What is the mechanism of action of fluoxetine, and why is there a delayed therapeutic effect of 2–4 weeks?
(iii) What are the common and serious unwanted effects of SSRIs?
(iv) Why is fluoxetine not recommended in patients under 18 years of age?
(v) What non-drug management options are available for depression?

questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors to evaluate: age, family history, lipids, obesity, microalbuminuria, inactivity, and smoking.
(ii) Target organ damage to evaluate: left ventricular hypertrophy or reduced ejection fraction, angina, stroke, dementia, kidney disease, peripheral arterial disease, and retinopathy. New-onset or uncontrolled hypertension should also raise suspicion of secondary hypertension.
(iii) This patient has Stage 2 hypertension (>160/>100). Guideline: Stage 1 hypertension is treated with a thiazide first unless there is a compelling indication; Stage 2 requires two drugs, one of which should be a diuretic or an ACE inhibitor/ARB. Drug classes include: ACE inhibitors, thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics, calcium channel blockers, and other classes with compelling indications for certain disease states.
(iv) Captopril (an ACE inhibitor) inhibits the enzyme ACE (kininase II), preventing conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, and is absorbed and eliminated rapidly; its adverse effects include a dry irritant cough (about 15%, from bradykinin accumulation), first-dose hypotension, hyperkalaemia, and rare angioedema. ACE inhibitors combine well with thiazide diuretics and calcium channel blockers for an additive antihypertensive effect. A thiazide diuretic is used first-line in Stage 1 hypertension unless there is a compelling indication for another class.
questions.question:
(i) A 35-year-old male undergraduate undergoing a routine medical examination is found to have a blood pressure of 160/105 mmHg and a BMI of 22 kg/m2. List the cardiovascular risk factors that should be evaluated in this patient.
(ii) List the evidence of target organ damage that should be sought.
(iii) Classify the drugs that may be used in the management of this individual.
(iv) Describe the clinical pharmacology of any two named examples, one from each of two different classes.

A. Describe the role of the kidney in calcium and phosphate homeostasis.
B. State how impairment of this role relates to a common bone pathology.
C. Explain how the resulting disorder produces a functional deficit in a distant organ system.
questions.answerText:
A. The kidney is one of the organ systems (with the skeleton and the GI tract) important in calcium metabolism: PTH acts on the kidney to stimulate calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule and to inhibit reabsorption of phosphate (stimulating its excretion); the kidney also performs the 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25(OH)-vitamin D to the active hormone 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D (calcitriol), a step increased by decreased serum calcium, increased PTH and decreased serum phosphate.
B. Failure of the kidney to excrete phosphate, as in chronic kidney disease, results in hyperphosphataemia; this leads to formation of calcium phosphate with a resultant reduction in ionised calcium, and induces FGF-23, which reduces active vitamin D synthesis. The reduction of active vitamin D reduces calcium mobilisation and disinhibits the parathyroid gland to release PTH, producing secondary hyperparathyroidism, with skeletal manifestations of bone loss and fractures.
C. Secondary hyperparathyroidism arising from renal impairment also produces extra-skeletal manifestations, including vascular calcification, ischaemic cardiovascular events, and cardiac failure, so that a disorder originating in the kidney's regulation of calcium and phosphate produces a distant functional deficit in the cardiovascular system; management includes dietary phosphorus restriction, phosphate binders, calcitriol or selective vitamin D analogues, and cinacalcet.

A(i) Absorption of drug is the transfer of a drug from the site of administration to the blood stream; it is the passage of drug from its site of administration into plasma. Bioavailability is the fractional extent to which a dose of drug reaches its site of action or systemic circulation in an unchanged form. The rate and efficiency of absorption depends on the route of administration; following the IV route, absorption is complete (100%), while with other routes, a fraction/percentage of the administered drug reaches the target organ.
A(ii) Mechanisms of drug transport across membranes: (1) Passive diffusion: no energy, no carrier; rapid for lipophilic, nonionic and small molecules; slow for hydrophilic, ionic and large molecules. (2) Facilitated diffusion: no energy required; carriers are required; drug binds to carrier by non-covalent mechanisms; chemically similar drugs compete for carrier. (3) Aqueous channels: no energy; no carrier; small hydrophilic drugs (<200 mw) diffuse along concentration gradient by passing through aqueous channels (pores). (4) Active transport: energy is required; carriers are required; identical to facilitated diffusion except that ATP powers drug transport against concentration gradient.
B(i) Drug-associated factors that influence absorption: (1) ionization state; (2) molecular weight; (3) solubility (lipophilic vs hydrophilic); (4) formulation (solution vs tablet). NB: small, non-ionized, lipid-soluble drugs permeate plasma membranes most readily.
B(ii) Patient-associated factors following oral route: blood flow to the GIT, GIT motility, stomach pH, presence of food in the GI tract, contact time at the absorption surface, total surface area available for absorption, and route of administration.
B(iii) Passive diffusion: no energy, no carrier, movement along concentration gradient. Active transport: energy (ATP) is required; carriers are required; it is identical to facilitated diffusion except that ATP powers drug transport against the concentration gradient.
questions.question:
Describe the process of drug absorption under the following headings:
A(i) Define drug absorption and bioavailability.
A(ii) List all mechanisms of drug transport across membranes, with the energy requirement and carrier requirement of each.
B(i) State the drug-associated factors that influence absorption.
B(ii) State the patient-associated factors that influence absorption following the oral route.
B(iii) Distinguish between passive diffusion and active transport in terms of their key characteristics.

(i) A patient in a hypertensive emergency is placed on sodium nitroprusside infusion. What are the risk factors/indications that lead to use of this agent?
(ii) What complication can arise from prolonged or high-dose use of this drug, and why?
(iii) What are the management options for this complication, and justify the agent of choice.
questions.answerText:
(i) Vasodilators such as sodium nitroprusside are only used in hypertensive emergencies (such as malignant hypertension or aortic dissection) or when other drugs have failed, and are rarely given alone; sodium nitroprusside is a very potent, short-acting vasodilator used for quick, temporary reduction of blood pressure in emergencies.
(ii) Toxicity is due to accumulation of thiocyanate, resulting in lactic acidosis. The metabolism of nitroprusside by smooth muscle involves its reduction to cyanide and release of nitric oxide; cyanide is further metabolised in the liver by rhodanase to thiocyanate, which is eliminated in the urine.
Sodium nitroprusside decomposes under strong alkaline conditions and when exposed to light, and must be given by continuous infusion, with onset of action within 2 minutes.
(iii) Concomitant administration of sodium thiosulfate can prevent accumulation of thiocyanate, especially in patients receiving high doses.
Thiosulphate is used to increase the conversion of cyanide into thiocyanate.
Sodium thiosulfate is justified as the agent of choice because it supplies the sulphur donor needed by the enzyme rhodanase to accelerate the transulphuration of cyanide to non-toxic thiocyanate, directly addressing the mechanism of the toxicity.
In patients with good renal function, thiocyanate is eliminated within 3 days once formed.

questions.question:
Describe the dose-response relationship in pharmacology under the following headings:
A(i) Define the dose-response relationship and its two components.
A(ii) Describe the construction and key features of a dose-response curve.
B(i) Explain the concept of potency and efficacy and how they are compared using dose-response curves.
B(ii) Define the therapeutic index and explain its clinical importance, including examples of drugs with low therapeutic index.
B(iii) List the multiple factors that can cause variation in dose-response curves.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The dose-response relationship describes the magnitude of the response of an organism, as a function of exposure (doses) to a drug after a certain exposure time. When a drug is administered into the system, the dose-response relationship has two components: (1) dose-plasma concentration relationship, and (2) plasma concentration-response relationship. The first is determined by pharmacokinetic considerations. Generally the intrinsic response increases with increase the dose.
A(ii) A dose-response curve is a coordinate graph relating the magnitude of a stimulus to the response of the receptor. The measured dose is generally plotted on the X axis and the response is plotted on the Y axis. In some cases, it is the logarithm of the dose that is plotted on the X axis, and in such cases the curve is typically sigmoidal, with the steepest portion in the middle. Drug dose-response involves the principles of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics and can be used to determine the required dose and frequency to achieve the desired response. The dose-response relationship is important because the concentration of a drug at its site of action controls its effect.
B(i) Potency is a measure of drug activity expressed in terms of the amount required to produce an effect of given intensity. A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations, while a drug of lower potency evokes the same response only at higher concentrations (e.g., Enalapril vs Captopril; Alprazolam vs Diazepam). Efficacy is the capacity to produce a desired effect; it is the maximum response achievable from a given agent regardless of dose. Dose-response curves allow comparison of potency (horizontal shift) and efficacy (height of curve).
B(ii) The therapeutic index (TI) is a comparison of the amount of a therapeutic agent that causes toxicity to the amount that has the desired therapeutic effect; it is the ratio TD50/ED50. In animals, it refers to LD50/ED50. A higher ratio (or larger difference) indicates better safety. Digoxin, cocaine, and vancomycin are examples of drugs with low therapeutic index.
B(iii) Multiple factors that can cause variation in dose-response curves: population differences, patient-related factors, and measurement methodologies. Repeated measurements carried out under identical conditions can help establish the pharmacologic profile of the drug being evaluated.

(i) The pharmacokinetic mechanism is enzyme induction. Rifampicin (an enzyme inducer) induces liver microsomal enzymes, which increases the metabolism of the co-administered antiretroviral drug, reducing its plasma concentration and efficacy.
(ii) The cytochrome P450 (CYP) family of enzymes is involved. These are heme-containing enzymes involved in Phase I drug metabolism (oxidation), found in great abundance in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of the liver. They are involved in the phase I metabolism of 70-80% of clinically used drugs.
(iii) Rifampicin is an inducer of CYP3A4/5 (and also CYP2B6). Antiretroviral drugs that are substrates of CYP3A4: ritonavir, efavirenz, atazanavir (any two accepted).
(iv) Competitive inhibition of drug metabolism: when two or more drugs are metabolized by the same enzyme, they may compete for the active site; the drug with higher affinity for the active site may competitively inhibit the metabolism of the other drug, causing it to accumulate. Induction is the opposite: it increases enzyme activity (faster metabolism, reduced effect and shorter duration), while inhibition reduces enzyme activity (slower metabolism, increased effect and possible toxicity).
(v) Enzyme inhibition increases the plasma concentration of the co-administered drug and prolongs its effect, which may cause toxicity. Example: cimetidine (a CYP3A4 inhibitor) increases plasma concentration of drugs like midazolam and felodipine, leading to enhanced or toxic effects.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old man who is HIV-positive and on antiretroviral therapy is started on rifampicin for tuberculosis. Two weeks later his HIV viral load rises dramatically.
(i) Name the pharmacokinetic mechanism responsible for this drug interaction.
(ii) Identify the enzyme family involved and explain its role in drug metabolism.
(iii) State the CYP subfamily induced by rifampicin and name two antiretroviral drugs that are substrates of this isoform.
(iv) Explain the concept of competitive inhibition of drug metabolism, contrasting it with induction.
(v) State the effect of enzyme inhibition on the plasma concentration and effect of a co-administered drug, giving one clinical example.

A. Describe noradrenaline under the following headings:
A(i) synthesis and storage
A(ii) release
A(iii) metabolism/fate after release
B. State a clinical/surgical procedure in which a drug affecting this pathway is used, and the purpose it serves.
C. Explain the basis of the effect that follows depletion of this transmitter by a drug that blocks its storage.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Tyrosine is transported into the noradrenergic nerve ending and converted to dopamine, which is transported into storage vesicles/granules; dopamine is converted to noradrenaline (NA) within the vesicle by dopamine-beta-hydroxylase. The conversion of tyrosine to dopa is the rate-limiting step, controlled by end-product feedback inhibition by NA. NA is stored as a complex with ATP adsorbed onto a protein called chromogranin; in the adrenal medulla, NA is methylated to adrenaline and stored in chromaffin cells.
A(ii) An action potential arriving at the nerve terminal triggers calcium influx, which causes storage vesicles to fuse with the cell membrane and release their contents (exocytosis) into the synapse; released NA binds to postsynaptic receptors on the effector organ or presynaptic receptors on the nerve terminal.
A(iii) NA leaking into the cytoplasm, or reuptaken by axonal uptake (Uptake 1, the most important mechanism terminating its action), is acted on by monoamine oxidase (MAO); NA diffusing into the circulation is acted on by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) in the liver and other tissues. Uptake 1 is inhibited by cocaine and imipramine; granular uptake is inhibited by reserpine.
B. Adrenaline is added to local anaesthetic during minor surgery to cause vasoconstriction at the site, which decreases bleeding and decreases the amount of local anaesthetic reaching the systemic circulation, thereby decreasing the cardiodepressant effect of the anaesthetic.
C. A drug such as reserpine blocks uptake of NA into storage vesicles and exposes the amine to MAO deamination, depleting NA stores; the resulting loss of sympathetic tone at blood vessels and the heart produces effects such as reduced blood pressure, which is the pharmacological basis exploited when NA-neuron blockers (e.g. guanethidine, bethanidine) are used to treat hypertension.

questions.question:
Describe the divisions of pharmacology and basic pharmacokinetic parameters under the following headings:
A(i) Define pharmacology and list its major divisions with a one-line definition of each.
A(ii) Define the following terms: biophase, receptor, drug-receptor interaction, and loading dose.
B(i) Define clearance, state its formula and unit, and list the factors affecting clearance.
B(ii) Explain first-pass effect in detail, including sites where it can occur, the routes by which it can be avoided, and give three examples of drugs with high first-pass metabolism.
B(iii) Explain accumulation and steady state, and state the clinical implication of accumulation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pharmacology is the study of drugs (agents that interact with living systems). Major divisions: Pharmacokinetics: fate of drug in the body (what the body does to the drug - ADME). Pharmacodynamics: effects of drug in the body (what the drug does to the body). Pharmacogenetics: study of inter-individual variations in DNA sequence related to drug response. Pharmacogenomics: study of the variability of the expression of individual genes relevant to disease susceptibility and drug response. Therapeutics: treatment of disease or disorder (prescription, dosage, side effects, indications). Toxicology: toxic effects of drugs; science of poisons and poisonings. Pharmacovigilance: science and activities relating to detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse reactions and other drug-related problems. Pharmacoeconomics: compares the value of one drug or drug therapy to another.
A(ii) Biophase: actual site of drug action in the body; drug-receptor interaction at the molecular level; may be surface of a cell or within the cell. Receptor: site in the biophase to which a drug molecule can be bound; usually a protein or proteinaceous material. Drug-receptor interaction: the combining of a drug molecule with the receptor for which it has affinity and the initiation of a pharmacological response by its intrinsic activity. Loading dose (DL): dose size used in initiating therapy so as to yield therapeutic concentration which will result in clinical effectiveness; LD = Cp (Target) x Vd.
B(i) Clearance: the hypothetical volume of distribution of the unmetabolized drug cleared from blood per unit time by any pathway. Clearance = Rate of elimination / Concentration of drug in blood/plasma. Unit = ml/min or ml/h. Total systemic clearance is additive: CLkidney + CLliver + CLothers. Factors affecting clearance: dose size, blood flow, intrinsic organ function. CL = Elimination rate constant x Volume of distribution (CL = kVd).
B(ii) First-pass effect: phenomenon where drugs may be metabolized following absorption but before reaching systemic circulation, due to passage through the liver prior to systemic absorption. Metabolism may occur in the gut wall, mesentery, and predominantly the liver. Hepatic first-pass may occur in peroral and deep rectal administration but not in IV. Routes to avoid first-pass: sublingual and buccal routes (liver is bypassed); cutaneous/transdermal route also bypasses the liver. Examples: nitroglycerin, desipramine, morphine, lignocaine, verapamil.
B(iii) Accumulation is the increase of drug concentration in blood or tissue upon multiple dosing until steady state is reached. Accumulation in tissue serves as a reservoir to prolong the effect of drugs. Steady state is the level of drug accumulation in blood and tissue upon multiple dosing when input and output are at equilibrium. Clinical implication: drugs that accumulate significantly (e.g. lipid-soluble drugs in fat) may produce prolonged or unexpected effects; dosage regimen must account for this, especially in obese or elderly patients.

(i) Status asthmaticus/refractory asthma (asthma attack not responding to intensive bronchodilator therapy).
(ii) Nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium bromide, with humidified oxygen inhalation; salbutamol or terbutaline IM or SC may be added.
(iii) Salbutamol is a selective beta2 agonist causing bronchodilatation through beta2 receptor stimulation; it has minimal cardiac effect and fast onset of action, especially when inhaled, and aborts asthma attacks.
Ipratropium bromide is an anticholinergic (atropinic) drug that causes bronchodilatation of the larger airways by blocking cholinergic constrictor stimulation of smooth muscle, though it is less efficacious than sympathomimetics.
(iv) IV steroids (glucocorticoids) are required, started at a high dose of a rapidly acting agent. Chest infections should be treated with antibiotics, and dehydration and acidosis corrected.
Side effects of salbutamol include palpitation, restlessness, throat irritation and nervousness.
questions.question:
(i) A patient with continuous asthma symptoms requiring hospitalisation is not responding to intensive bronchodilator therapy. What is this condition called?
(ii) Name the bronchodilator agents used by nebulisation in this condition.
