A(i) Describe the synthesis and regulation of antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
A(ii) Describe the receptor subtypes and mechanism of action of ADH at the renal collecting duct.
B(i) Explain how disorders of this system relate to SIADH and diabetes insipidus.
C(i) Explain why excess ADH secretion (SIADH) produces a distant systemic effect (dilutional hyponatraemia).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Human ADH is 8-arginine vasopressin (AVP), a nonapeptide secreted by the posterior pituitary along with oxytocin; it is synthesized in the hypothalamic (supraoptic and paraventricular) nerve cell bodies as a large precursor peptide along with its binding protein, neurophysin.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus and volume receptors in the left atrium, ventricles and pulmonary veins primarily regulate the rate of ADH release, governed by body hydration; the two main physiological stimuli for ADH release are a rise in plasma osmolarity and contraction of extracellular fluid.
A(ii) V1 and V2 receptor subtypes have been identified; V2 receptors are located primarily on the principal cells of the collecting ducts and regulate water permeability through cAMP production.
Activation of V2 receptors increases intracellular cAMP formation, activating cAMP-dependent protein kinase A, which promotes exocytosis of aquaporin-2 water channel-containing vesicles into the apical membrane, increasing water permeability; continued stimulation upregulates aquaporin-2 synthesis via the cAMP response element of its gene.
B(i) Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH) occurs when ADH is released in excessive, unregulated quantities, resulting in excess water reabsorption and dilutional hyponatraemia, with patients typically remaining euvolemic; settings include malignancies (autonomous ADH production by small cell lung cancer), CNS disturbances, drugs (carbamazepine) and surgery.
Central diabetes insipidus is a failure of ADH secretion, so ADH levels are low and collecting tubules are impermeable to water, causing excess water excretion; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus involves normal ADH secretion but a defect in the V receptor or signalling mediators, making the kidneys unresponsive to ADH.
In either form of diabetes insipidus, the net effect is increased water excretion, producing large volumes of dilute urine, hypernatraemia, hyperosmolarity, polyuria, polydipsia and possible electrolyte imbalance.
C(i) Because the V2 receptor mechanism at the collecting duct governs how much water is reabsorbed back into the circulation, unregulated excess ADH release in SIADH causes excess water reabsorption in quantities greater than the body's needs.
This dilutes the plasma sodium concentration, producing dilutional hyponatraemia even though the kidney itself is not diseased — the effect is systemic (on plasma sodium and cellular hydration) rather than confined to the kidney.
Symptoms of hyponatraemia are due to shift of water intracellularly, resulting in cerebral oedema producing headache, mental confusion, lassitude, nausea, vomiting and even seizures, with children more susceptible.
This is why the vasopressin antagonist tolvaptan, an orally active nonpeptide selective V2 receptor antagonist, is used to treat hyponatraemia due to SIADH: it increases free water clearance by the kidney (aquaretic effect) and helps correct the low plasma sodium, though too-rapid correction should be avoided because of the risk of thrombotic complications from haemoconcentration.
Mozavaptan (a V2-selective antagonist) and conivaptan (a V1a plus V2 antagonist) are other vasopressin antagonists in clinical use for this systemic, ADH-driven disturbance of plasma sodium.

questions.question:
Describe extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) associated with antipsychotic drugs under the following headings:
A(i) Define extrapyramidal symptoms and list the four main types.
A(ii) Describe the clinical features, onset, risk factors, and treatment of dystonia.
B(i) Describe the features of pseudoparkinsonism and its treatment.
B(ii) Describe tardive dyskinesia — its features, risk factors, and management.
B(iii) State the general procedures for managing adverse drug reactions (ADRs) to antipsychotic drugs.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) affect the extrapyramidal system and basal ganglia — the system that includes descending fibres reaching the medulla other than by the corticospinal tracts, which is important in maintenance of equilibrium and muscle tone. The four main types are: dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia, and pseudoparkinsonism.
A(ii) Dystonia is prolonged tonic muscle contractions occurring usually within 24–96 hours of dosage initiation or dosage increase; they may be life threatening (e.g. pharyngeal-laryngeal dystonia). Other dystonic presentations include trismus, glossospasm, tongue protrusion, blepharospasm, oculogyric crisis, torticollis, and retrocollis. They occur primarily with FGAs. Risk factors include younger patients (especially male) and use of high-potency agents and high doses. Treatment includes IM or IV anticholinergics or benzodiazepines: benztropine mesylate 2 mg, or diphenhydramine 50 mg may be given IM or IV, or diazepam 5–10 mg slow IV push, or lorazepam 1–2 mg IM. Relief usually occurs within 15–20 minutes of IM injection or 5 minutes of IV administration. Prophylactic anticholinergic medications are reasonable when using high-potency FGAs (e.g. haloperidol and fluphenazine), in young men, and in patients with a prior dystonia.
B(i) Pseudoparkinsonism may involve any of the four cardinal symptoms: akinesia, bradykinesia, or decreased motor activity including mask-like facial expression, micrographia, slowed speech, and decreased arm swing; tremor — predominantly at rest, decreasing with movement; rigidity — stiffness with cogwheel rigidity; and postural abnormalities — stooped, unstable posture and slow, shuffling, or festinating gait. Onset is usually 1–2 weeks after initiation or dose increase. The risk with SGAs is low except with risperidone in doses greater than 6 mg/day. Treatment: benztropine (1–2 mg twice daily, up to 8 mg daily); trihexyphenidyl (Benzhexol), diphenhydramine, and biperiden usually require three-times-daily dosing. Amantadine is as efficacious as anticholinergics with less effect on memory.
B(ii) Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is a chronic EPS characterised by abnormal involuntary movements of the tongue, lips, face, trunk, and extremities occurring with chronic antipsychotic therapy. The classic presentation is buccolingual-masticatory (BLM) or orofacial movements. Symptoms may become severe enough to interfere with chewing, wearing dentures, speech, respiration, or swallowing. Facial movements include frequent blinking, brow arching, grimacing, upward deviation of the eyes, and lip smacking. Restless choreiform and athetotic movements of the limbs occur in later stages. Risk factors: duration of antipsychotic therapy, higher dose, possibly cumulative dose, increasing age, occurrence of acute extrapyramidal symptoms, poor antipsychotic response, diagnosis of organic mental disorder, diabetes mellitus, mood disorders, and possibly female gender. Treatment includes discontinuing or tapering down the antipsychotic dose; botulinum toxin; deep brain stimulation; or medications such as deutetrabenazine and valbenazine.
B(iii) General procedures for managing ADRs: Lower the dose — initiate therapy with the lowest dose to achieve treatment goals. Switch to another antipsychotic drug — adopted when dosage adjustment cannot be proven beneficial and when addressing life-threatening or fatal cases. Prescribe a non-pharmacologic intervention — diet and exercise programmes are effective when weight gain and related lipid abnormality are addressed. Treat with a concomitant medication — used for reducing ADRs associated with antipsychotic drugs, though these concomitant medications have their own adverse effects.

A(i) Classification of muscarinic antagonists: natural alkaloids (atropine, hyoscine); semi-synthetics (homatropine, ipratropium bromide); synthetic mydriatics (cyclopentolate, tropicamide); antisecretory/antispasmodic quaternary ammonium compounds (pipenzolate, clidinium) and tertiary amines (oxybutynin, dicyclomine); antiparkinson drugs (benzhexol, biperiden); and miscellaneous agents (tricyclic antidepressants, antihistamines).
A(ii) CNS: stimulate medullary centres (vagal, respiratory, vasomotor), depress vestibular excitation (anti-motion-sickness effect), suppress parkinsonian tremor and rigidity, and at higher doses cause cortical excitation, restlessness, disorientation and hallucination. Eye: cause mydriasis, cycloplegia and photophobia, and increase intraocular pressure especially in narrow-angle glaucoma. Smooth muscle: reduce tone and contraction of the stomach and intestine (constipation), cause bronchial relaxation, and relax the urinary bladder sphincter. Glands: reduce sweating, salivary, tracheobronchial and lachrymal secretion (dry mouth and eyes). Cardiovascular system: cause bradycardia followed by tachycardia, and vasodilatation with hypotension at high dose.
A(iii) Uses include: pre-anaesthetic medication to reduce secretions; peptic ulcer disease; antispasmodic use in intestinal/renal colic and irritable colon; bronchial asthma; ophthalmology as a mydriatic/cycloplegic; mild parkinsonism; urological disorders (bladder spasm, urge incontinence, enuresis); counteracting bradycardia/partial heart block from vagal overactivity; motion sickness; and as an antidote to anticholinesterase (organophosphate) poisoning.
B. Antimuscarinic drugs increase intraocular pressure, which is dangerous in narrow-angle glaucoma where drainage of aqueous humour is already compromised; and they relax the bladder and can precipitate urinary retention, which is dangerous in prostatic hypertrophy where outflow is already obstructed - both are listed contraindications.
C. Antimuscarinic drugs selectively block muscarinic receptors at parasympathetic effector sites, with little or no action at the autonomic ganglia or skeletal neuromuscular junction; ganglion blockers instead block the nicotinic receptors at the autonomic ganglia, blocking transmission across both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia without selectivity, so their effect on any organ depends on which division normally predominates in that organ.

(i) A patient from an endemic region presents with weight loss, weakness, fever lasting weeks to months, enlarged spleen and liver, decreased blood cell production, bleeding and swollen lymph nodes, occurring two to eight months after a sandfly bite. What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the pathologic basis of this disease?
(iii) What supportive/general management is relevant?
(iv) What is the definitive drug treatment?
questions.answerText:
(i) Visceral leishmaniasis (also known as kala-azar, black fever, or Dumdum fever), mostly caused by Leishmania donovani in Asia and Eastern Africa and by Leishmania infantum in Latin America, Central Asia and the Mediterranean region, transmitted through the bite of the female phlebotomine sand fly.
(ii) In the human host, the parasites are obligate intracellular parasites of the reticuloendothelial system and survive and multiply in various macrophage populations; the disease damages internal organs such as the spleen and liver, and also affects the bone marrow and the immune system through damage to these organs; it is the most severe form of leishmaniasis and is almost always fatal if not treated, particularly in persons living with HIV and other chronic immunosuppressive diseases.
(iii) Visceral leishmaniasis always requires treatment, since without proper diagnosis and treatment it is associated with high fatality.
(iv) Commonly used medicines include sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam), amphotericin B, paromomycin, and miltefosine (Impavido).

A(i) Insulin was discovered in 1921; it is a 51-amino acid polypeptide made up of an alpha (21 amino acid) and a beta (30 amino acid) chain linked by disulphide bonds.
It has a half-life of about 5 minutes (3-5, 5-9 minutes); it is degraded in the GIT if given orally and is metabolized largely by the liver, kidney and muscle; during biotransformation, the disulphide bonds are reduced and the chains are broken down to constituent amino acids.
A(ii) Food intake, increased glucose and elevated ATP mediate insulin release through ATP-dependent potassium channels in the membrane of pancreatic beta cells; closure of these channels causes depolarization, calcium influx and subsequent insulin release.
Insulin receptors have 2 alpha- and 2 beta-subunits linked by disulphide bonds; alpha-subunits carry the insulin binding sites while beta-subunits have tyrosine protein kinase activity; insulin binds the extracellular alpha-subunits, the receptor is internalized, and autophosphorylation of the beta-subunit occurs, with subsequent phosphorylation of phospholipase C and release of diacylglycerol and inositol triphosphate.
A(iii) Insulin stimulates anabolic actions: controls uptake, utilization and storage of glucose, amino acids and fatty acids; lowers blood glucose concentration; increases uptake and metabolism of glucose by muscle and adipose tissue and hepatic glucose uptake.
It inhibits catabolic processes: inhibits breakdown of glycogen, fat and protein; inhibits hepatic glucose production; inhibits flow of gluconeogenic precursors (alanine, lactate, pyruvate) to the liver.
B(i) Insulin is required by all Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM) patients and many Non-IDDM patients; it is administered intramuscularly, intravenously or subcutaneously, with only regular insulin given IV or IM, and all preparations may be given subcutaneously for long-term use; its site of action is the insulin receptor on target tissues such as muscle, adipose tissue and liver.
C(i) Insulin and oral hypoglycaemic agents increase the risk of hypoglycaemia; ethanol, adrenergic receptor antagonists and salicylates may also induce hypoglycaemia.
Among the sulfonylureas, hypoglycaemia, including coma, occurs especially in renal and hepatic impairment and in the elderly taking long-acting drugs; the longer the half-life, the more likely the agent is to cause hypoglycaemia, and severe hypoglycaemia may present as an acute neurologic emergency mimicking a cerebrovascular accident in the elderly.
Because insulin and insulin secretagogues act by lowering blood glucose through the same mechanism used therapeutically to control hyperglycaemia, excessive dosing or impaired clearance (renal or hepatic impairment) shifts this same pharmacological action into the adverse effect of hypoglycaemia.
This is the basis for treating severe hypoglycaemia with glucagon, which enhances gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis to raise blood glucose, opposing the action of insulin.
Diazoxide, which has a potent hyperglycaemic action, is also used to treat hypoglycaemia, further illustrating that agents opposing insulin's glucose-lowering mechanism are the pharmacological basis for reversing insulin-related hypoglycaemia.

(i) A patient presents with features of cholinesterase enzyme inhibition following exposure to an insecticide, progressing to respiratory failure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) Name the first pharmacological agent used in treatment.
(iii) Explain its mechanism of action.
(iv) Name the enzyme that is inhibited by the toxin, and the agent used together with the first drug to reactivate it.
(v) Explain the mechanism of this second agent.
questions.answerText:
(i) Organophosphate (or carbamate) poisoning/toxicosis.
(ii) Atropine is the first pharmacological approach.
(iii) Atropine competes with acetylcholine for its receptor site, thus reducing the effects of the neurotransmitter.
(iv) The adverse effects of organophosphorus (and carbamate) pesticides are mediated through inhibition of the cholinesterase enzymes. N-methylpyridinium 2-aldoxime (2-PAM/pralidoxime), or obidoxime, is used together with atropine.
(v) Oximes such as pralidoxime and obidoxime act as an effective means to restore the covalently bound (cholinesterase) enzyme to a normal state.
Since organophosphate toxicosis results in respiratory failure, the treatment approach also includes maintenance of a patent airway, with artificial respiration employed as needed.

questions.question:
A(i) Classify the drugs used to suppress gastric acid secretion in peptic ulcer disease.
A(ii) Describe the mechanism of action of proton pump inhibitors.
A(iii) State their pharmacokinetics.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for the shift in preference from H2-receptor antagonists to proton pump inhibitors.
B(ii) Distinguish between H2-receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Agents used include proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole), H2-receptor antagonists (e.g. ranitidine, nizatidine), prostaglandin analogues (misoprostol, enoprostil, arbaprostil), anticholinergic agents (pirenzepine, telezepine), antacids (aluminium hydroxide, magnesium carbonate), and mucosal protectants (bismuth chelates, sucralfate, carbenoxolone).
A(ii) The parietal cell actively secretes acid in response to histamine, acetylcholine or gastrin; PPIs are weak bases that partition into the acidic secretory canaliculus, where they are protonated and transformed into active inhibitors (a thiophilic sulfonamide or sulfenic acid), which irreversibly bind the sulfhydryl group of cysteine on H+K+ ATPase, the final mediator of gastric acid secretion.
A(iii) PPIs are acid-labile and formulated as enteric-coated granules or tablets; absorption begins only after granules leave the stomach, is pH- and formulation-dependent, and they are highly protein bound and metabolised in the liver by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19; since binding to the proton pump is irreversible, inhibition of acid production lasts 24-48 hours or more, until new enzyme is synthesised.
B(i) The focus of antisecretory therapy has shifted from H2-receptor antagonists to proton pump inhibitors, which have gained widespread acceptance as antisecretory agents for gastrointestinal disorders; a PPI or H2RA significantly enhances the effectiveness of H. pylori regimens containing pH-dependent antibiotics such as amoxicillin or clarithromycin, because these antibiotics require bacterial growth to exert their lethal effect, and higher pH allows the growth necessary for eradication.
B(ii) H2-receptor antagonists block histamine-mediated acid secretion at the H2 receptor, whereas PPIs act further downstream by irreversibly inhibiting the H+K+ ATPase proton pump itself, the final common mediator of acid secretion regardless of the stimulus (histamine, acetylcholine or gastrin).

(i) In the sublingual route, the drug is placed under the tongue or crushed and placed in the buccal cavity. Only lipid-soluble drugs can be so administered. Absorption is rapid because the drug is absorbed directly from the highly vascular mucosal membrane into systemic circulation.
(ii) The main advantage of the sublingual route is that the liver is bypassed and drugs with high first-pass metabolism can be absorbed directly into systemic circulation, avoiding the first-pass effect that significantly reduces the bioavailability of nitroglycerin when swallowed.
(iii) Two limitations of the sublingual route: (a) inconvenient; (b) only small doses can be given; (c) unpleasant taste of some drugs (any two accepted).
(iv) The intravenous (IV) route produces onset within 30-60 seconds. The drug is injected into one of the superficial veins; it directly reaches the blood stream and the effects are produced immediately. The absorption phase is bypassed and bioavailability is 100%.
(v) Sublingual: 3-5 minutes (highly vascular mucosa, but drug still needs to cross membrane). Intramuscular: 10-20 minutes (drug injected into large skeletal muscles; absorption is fast, and it is less painful, but still requires absorption from muscle tissue). Subcutaneous: 5-30 minutes (drug is deposited in the loose subcutaneous tissue; absorption is slow because it is less vascular; should be avoided in shock patients due to vasoconstriction).

questions.answerText: The test was requested to rapidly assess for sickle haemoglobin, though the test is unreliable in early infancy due to high HbF. Principle: Red cells are lysed in a reducing solution of sodium dithionite/metabisulphite; deoxygenated HbS polymerises and scatters light, producing turbidity, whereas normal HbA solutions remain clear. Normal result: A clear solution through which printed text can be read, indicating a negative result; an equivocal result in a neonate should be confirmed later with electrophoresis once HbF has declined. Precautions: Confirm any positive screen with haemoglobin electrophoresis since the test cannot distinguish trait from disease, and avoid false negatives in severely anaemic patients by ensuring an adequate red cell concentration in the reagent.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for sickle haemoglobin as part of routine antenatal work-up. Principle: Red cells are lysed in a reducing solution of sodium dithionite/metabisulphite; deoxygenated HbS polymerises and scatters light, producing turbidity, whereas normal HbA solutions remain clear. Normal result: A clear solution through which printed text can be read, indicating a negative result; a positive result requires electrophoresis and partner testing to assess risk to the fetus. Precautions: Confirm any positive screen with haemoglobin electrophoresis since the test cannot distinguish trait from disease, and avoid false negatives in severely anaemic patients by ensuring an adequate red cell concentration in the reagent.

A 45-year-old man about to receive a blood transfusion for chronic anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Indirect Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Indirect Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test is requested to screen his serum for unexpected antibodies before crossmatching, to ensure the safest possible transfusion. Principle: Patient serum suspected of containing antibody is incubated with reagent red cells of known antigen composition, and antihuman globulin reagent is then added to detect antibody that has coated the cells without producing visible agglutination. Normal result and interpretation: A negative IAT means no clinically significant antibody was detected, while a positive result indicates the presence of an alloantibody, important in antenatal screening and pre-transfusion compatibility testing. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before adding AHG reagent to remove unbound globulin, incubation temperature and time must be strictly observed since many antibodies react best at 37°C, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with microcytic anaemia of uncertain cause. The attending doctor requests a Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity is requested to distinguish true iron deficiency anaemia from anaemia of chronic disease based on the pattern of iron and TIBC. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after its release from transferrin, while total iron binding capacity measures the maximum iron that transferrin can bind, together indicating percentage transferrin saturation. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum iron is about 10–30 micromol/L with TIBC around 45–70 micromol/L. Low iron with high TIBC indicates iron deficiency anaemia, while low iron with low or normal TIBC suggests anaemia of chronic disease. Precautions: the sample should be collected fasting in the morning to avoid diurnal variation, haemolysed samples must be rejected as they falsely raise the iron result, and all glassware used must be iron-free to avoid contamination.

The test was requested to confirm an enzyme deficiency predisposing him to oxidative haemolysis. Principle: A quantitative spectrophotometric or fluorescent-spot assay measures the activity of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that protects red cells from oxidative stress by generating NADPH. Normal result: Enzyme activity within the laboratory's established reference range (typically reported relative to a normal control); reduced activity confirms G6PD deficiency, and the family should be counselled on foods and drugs to avoid. Precautions: Avoid testing during or shortly after an acute haemolytic episode, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a true deficiency; retest several weeks later if an acute episode has just occurred.
questions.question: A 6-year-old boy develops acute jaundice and dark urine hours after eating fava beans, and is subsequently diagnosed with favism. The attending doctor refers the patient for G6PD Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to monitor the degree of anticoagulation and adjust the infusion rate. Principle: A phospholipid reagent, activator and calcium are added to citrated plasma to measure clotting time via the intrinsic and common pathways (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 25-35 seconds, depending on the reagent used; an APTT within the therapeutic range (usually 1.5-2.5 times control) confirms adequate anticoagulation. Precautions: Avoid drawing the sample from a line contaminated with heparin, which falsely prolongs results, and centrifuge promptly to obtain platelet-poor plasma for accurate testing.
questions.question: A patient on intravenous unfractionated heparin for a pulmonary embolism is reviewed, and is subsequently diagnosed with heparin monitoring. The attending doctor refers the patient for Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to calculate transferrin saturation, a sensitive early marker of iron overload. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after releasing iron from transferrin, while TIBC is determined by saturating transferrin with excess iron and measuring the total binding capacity, allowing calculation of transferrin saturation. Normal result: Serum iron 50-170 micrograms/dL, TIBC 250-450 micrograms/dL, transferrin saturation 20-50%; a transferrin saturation above 45% strongly supports hereditary haemochromatosis. Precautions: Collect the sample in the morning when iron levels are most stable, avoid haemolysis which falsely raises serum iron, and ensure the patient has not taken iron supplements in the preceding 24 hours.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with abnormal liver function and raised ferritin is further evaluated, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemochromatosis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess the leucocyte differential for a left-shifted myeloid series. Principle: A thin smear of blood is stained with Romanowsky stain (e.g. Leishman or Wright-Giemsa) and examined under the microscope to assess red cell, white cell and platelet morphology and number. Normal result: Red cells are normocytic and normochromic with normal white cell and platelet morphology and no abnormal cells; a full spectrum of granulocyte precursors with basophilia supports chronic myeloid leukaemia over a reactive leukocytosis. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood within one hour of collection to avoid crenation and morphological artefact, and use a clean grease-free slide with a smooth, even spreading technique to avoid a poorly feathered edge.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with abdominal fullness and unintentional weight loss, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Peripheral Blood Film. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A dialysis patient with declining haemoglobin requires transfusion, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic renal failure on dialysis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Crossmatching (Compatibility Testing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to ensure compatibility given his likely prior transfusion history and alloimmunisation risk. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and observed for agglutination or haemolysis across immediate spin, 37°C incubation and antiglobulin phases, confirming serological compatibility before transfusion. Normal result: No agglutination or haemolysis at any phase, indicating compatible blood; a positive crossmatch despite correct grouping indicates an antibody requiring extended phenotyping to find suitable units. Precautions: Confirm patient identity and sample labelling meticulously at both collection and issue, and complete the full antiglobulin phase rather than relying on immediate spin alone, since clinically significant antibodies may only react at this stage.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents with fatigue and massive splenomegaly and a raised white cell count, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukaemia diagnosis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Cytogenetic Analysis for Philadelphia Chromosome (BCR-ABL). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm the diagnosis by detecting the characteristic genetic abnormality. Principle: Metaphase chromosome preparation or fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) detects the t(9;22) translocation forming the Philadelphia chromosome, or the resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene product is quantified by RT-PCR. Normal result: Absence of the t(9;22) translocation or BCR-ABL fusion transcript; detection of the Philadelphia chromosome or BCR-ABL transcript confirms chronic myeloid leukaemia. Precautions: Ensure the marrow or blood sample is fresh and contains adequate dividing cells for metaphase analysis, and use molecular quantification (RT-PCR) rather than karyotyping alone for sensitive monitoring of minimal residual disease.

The Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity is requested to help distinguish anaemia of chronic disease, in which both iron and TIBC are typically reduced, from true iron deficiency. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after its release from transferrin, while total iron binding capacity measures the maximum iron that transferrin can bind, together indicating percentage transferrin saturation. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum iron is about 10–30 micromol/L with TIBC around 45–70 micromol/L. Low iron with high TIBC indicates iron deficiency anaemia, while low iron with low or normal TIBC suggests anaemia of chronic disease. Precautions: the sample should be collected fasting in the morning to avoid diurnal variation, haemolysed samples must be rejected as they falsely raise the iron result, and all glassware used must be iron-free to avoid contamination.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and mild anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess primary haemostatic (platelet-vessel wall) function. Principle: A standardised skin incision (Ivy method) is made and the time to cessation of bleeding is measured, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall in primary haemostasis. Normal result: Approximately 2-9 minutes, depending on the method used; a prolonged bleeding time with normal platelet count supports a qualitative platelet or von Willebrand factor defect. Precautions: Use a standardised, calibrated incision device and consistent incision depth, and avoid the test in patients taking aspirin or NSAIDs within the preceding week unless specifically assessing their effect.
questions.question: A 20-year-old woman with recurrent nosebleeds and heavy periods is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with von Willebrand disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bleeding Time. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 10-year-old boy with recurrent mild jaundice, splenomegaly and a family history of similar illness. The attending doctor requests a Osmotic Fragility Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Osmotic Fragility Test is requested to confirm hereditary spherocytosis by demonstrating increased red cell osmotic fragility. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; spherocytic cells with a reduced surface area to volume ratio lyse earlier than normal biconcave cells, and the percentage lysis at each concentration is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells begin to lyse at about 0.45% saline and are completely lysed by 0.30%. Increased fragility (lysis at higher saline concentration) suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while decreased fragility suggests thalassaemia or iron deficiency. Precautions: blood must be defibrinated or collected into heparin rather than EDTA, saline dilutions must be prepared accurately and freshly, and tubes must be mixed gently to avoid mechanical haemolysis that would give a false result.

questions.question: A Rhesus-negative woman presents after a car accident during pregnancy, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-anti-D prophylaxis assessment. The attending doctor refers the patient for Indirect Antiglobulin Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to check for existing anti-D before giving Rh immunoglobulin prophylaxis. Principle: Patient serum is incubated with reagent red cells of known antigen type; if antibody is present in the serum it binds the cells in vitro, and subsequent addition of antiglobulin reagent causes visible agglutination, detecting free circulating antibody. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination, indicating no clinically significant antibody in the serum; a negative result confirms she has not yet been sensitised and should receive prophylaxis promptly. Precautions: Incubate at 37°C for the correct time to allow antibody-antigen binding, and use a fresh antiglobulin reagent since a weakened reagent can give false-negative results.

The test was requested as a nonspecific marker to support ongoing chronic infection alongside sputum testing. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is left to stand vertically in a calibrated Westergren tube, and the distance red cells fall under gravity in one hour is measured; raised plasma fibrinogen and immunoglobulins promote rouleaux formation and faster sedimentation. Normal result: Below 15 mm/hr in men and below 20 mm/hr in women (age-adjusted); a markedly raised ESR is consistent with active tuberculosis, though it cannot confirm the diagnosis alone. Precautions: Keep the tube perfectly vertical and free of vibration, read exactly at 60 minutes, and perform the test within two hours of collection since delay alters sedimentation.
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with chronic cough, night sweats and weight loss, and is subsequently diagnosed with tuberculosis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

An elderly man with no prior bleeding history develops extensive spontaneous bruising and a prolonged APTT, and is subsequently diagnosed with acquired haemophilia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Mixing Study (Correction Test). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to distinguish a factor deficiency from an acquired inhibitor as the cause of the prolonged APTT. Principle: Patient plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma and the clotting time (PT or APTT) is repeated immediately and after incubation, distinguishing a factor deficiency (which corrects, since normal plasma supplies the missing factor) from an inhibitor (which does not fully correct). Normal result: Full correction of the prolonged clotting time into the normal range; failure to correct, especially after incubation, supports an inhibitor such as an acquired factor VIII autoantibody. Precautions: Repeat the test after incubation at 37°C for one to two hours, since some inhibitors (such as factor VIII autoantibodies) are time- and temperature-dependent and only become apparent on delayed testing.

questions.question: A 60-year-old diabetic on long-term metformin presents with new peripheral numbness, and is subsequently diagnosed with metformin-associated deficiency. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Vitamin B12 Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for drug-induced B12 malabsorption. Principle: An automated immunoassay (competitive binding or chemiluminescence) measures circulating cobalamin, which is required as a cofactor for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells including erythroid precursors. Normal result: Approximately 200-900 pg/mL; a low level supports metformin-related deficiency, warranting supplementation without necessarily stopping the drug. Precautions: Take the sample before any B12 injection is given, protect from prolonged light exposure which can degrade the vitamin, and interpret low-normal results cautiously alongside methylmalonic acid if pernicious anaemia is strongly suspected.

The Haemoglobin Electrophoresis is requested to distinguish sickle cell trait from sickle cell disease by quantifying the actual proportions of HbS and HbA present. Principle: A haemolysate of red cells is applied to a support medium such as cellulose acetate or agar gel and subjected to an electric field, separating haemoglobin variants according to their electrical charge at a given pH. Normal result and interpretation: The normal adult pattern shows predominantly HbA with small HbA2 (under 3.5%) and trace HbF. Abnormal bands or altered proportions identify HbS, HbC, HbE or a thalassaemia pattern. Precautions: a fresh, clot-free haemolysate must be used, voltage and running time must be standardised, and known control samples must be run alongside the patient sample to allow accurate identification of each band.
questions.question: A 18-year-old man with a positive sickling test whose parents want to know if he has trait or disease. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to support or help exclude a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism alongside clinical scoring. Principle: An immunoassay detects D-dimer, a specific breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin, whose presence indicates that both clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis have occurred. Normal result: Below the assay-specific cut-off, usually less than 0.5 micrograms/mL FEU; a raised level supports further imaging, while a normal level in a low-risk patient helps rule out the diagnosis. Precautions: Recognise that many conditions besides thrombosis (pregnancy, infection, malignancy, recent surgery) raise D-dimer, so a positive result is not diagnostic on its own; primarily use a negative result to help exclude thrombosis in low-probability patients.
questions.question: A 40-year-old presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, and is subsequently diagnosed with pulmonary embolism. The attending doctor refers the patient for D-Dimer Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm intravascular red cell destruction. Principle: An immunoturbidimetric assay measures haptoglobin, a plasma protein that binds free haemoglobin released from lysed red cells; because the haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex is rapidly cleared by the liver, intravascular haemolysis depletes circulating haptoglobin. Normal result: Approximately 30-200 mg/dL; a markedly reduced or undetectable level supports significant intravascular haemolysis. Precautions: Interpret with caution since haptoglobin is also an acute-phase reactant that can be falsely normal or raised in the presence of concurrent inflammation despite ongoing haemolysis.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden dark urine and back pain after a mismatched blood transfusion, and is subsequently diagnosed with intravascular haemolysis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Haptoglobin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Heinz Body Test is requested to look for Heinz bodies supporting a diagnosis of unstable haemoglobin disease. Principle: Denatured, precipitated haemoglobin within red cells (Heinz bodies) is demonstrated using a supravital stain such as methyl violet or new methylene blue, since Heinz bodies do not stain with routine Romanowsky stains. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of Heinz bodies is normal. Their presence indicates oxidative damage to haemoglobin, seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidant stress, unstable haemoglobin variants, or exposure to certain drugs and chemicals. Precautions: the stain must be fresh and the preparation examined promptly, since Heinz bodies may be removed rapidly by the spleen and disappear from circulation, and adequate numbers of cells must be examined to avoid missing a low percentage.
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with unexplained chronic haemolysis and a family history of an unstable haemoglobin variant. The attending doctor requests a Heinz Body Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to distinguish sickle cell disease (HbSS) from sickle cell trait. Principle: Hb variants are separated on cellulose acetate (alkaline pH) or citrate agar (acid pH) according to their electrical charge, allowing identification of HbA, HbS, HbC, HbF and other variants by their migration pattern. Normal result: Predominantly HbA (>95%), with HbA2 1.5-3.5% and HbF less than 1% in adults; a predominant HbS band with absent or reduced HbA confirms homozygous disease, while HbAS confirms trait. Precautions: Run both alkaline and acid media to resolve variants that co-migrate on one system alone, and include known controls on every run to validate migration positions.
questions.question: A 5-year-old with recurrent painful crises is being confirmed for definitive diagnosis, and is subsequently diagnosed with sickle cell disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for uraemia-related qualitative platelet dysfunction despite a normal platelet count. Principle: A standardised skin incision (Ivy method) is made and the time to cessation of bleeding is measured, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall in primary haemostasis. Normal result: Approximately 2-9 minutes, depending on the method used; a prolonged bleeding time with normal platelet numbers supports uraemic platelet dysfunction. Precautions: Use a standardised, calibrated incision device and consistent incision depth, and avoid the test in patients taking aspirin or NSAIDs within the preceding week unless specifically assessing their effect.
questions.question: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops mucosal bleeding, and is subsequently diagnosed with uraemic platelet dysfunction. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bleeding Time. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

An elderly patient with aortic stenosis presents with new gastrointestinal bleeding, and is subsequently diagnosed with acquired von Willebrand syndrome. The attending doctor refers the patient for von Willebrand Factor Assay (Antigen and Activity). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to detect an acquired reduction related to shear-stress destruction of the factor by the diseased valve. Principle: Immunoassay quantifies von Willebrand factor antigen, while a functional assay (such as ristocetin cofactor activity) measures its ability to mediate platelet binding, together characterising both the amount and function of the protein. Normal result: Approximately 50-200% of the reference standard for both antigen and activity; a reduced level supports acquired von Willebrand syndrome, which may improve after valve replacement. Precautions: Be aware that vWF is an acute-phase reactant and can be transiently raised by stress, exercise or inflammation, and that blood group O individuals have physiologically lower baseline levels.

questions.question: A leukaemia patient develops rapid deterioration shortly after starting chemotherapy, and is subsequently diagnosed with tumour lysis syndrome. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess the extent of malignant cell breakdown. Principle: A spectrophotometric enzymatic assay measures LDH activity by monitoring the conversion of NADH to NAD+ during the reduction of pyruvate to lactate; LDH is released from many tissues including red cells during cell breakdown or turnover. Normal result: Approximately 140-280 U/L (assay-dependent); a markedly raised level supports tumour lysis and correlates with the metabolic disturbances requiring urgent management. Precautions: Avoid any degree of haemolysis during sample collection or handling, since red cells contain very high LDH activity and even minor in vitro haemolysis will falsely raise the result.

The test was requested to detect the characteristic coagulopathy associated with this leukaemia subtype before starting treatment. Principle: A combined panel assesses the extrinsic pathway (PT), intrinsic pathway (APTT), platelet number and fibrinogen concentration together, since disseminated intravascular coagulation produces a characteristic pattern of simultaneous consumption across all these parameters. Normal result: PT and APTT within normal range, platelets above 150 x10^9/L and fibrinogen above 2.0 g/L, with a low D-dimer; a severe consumptive pattern, especially very low fibrinogen, confirms the expected coagulopathy requiring aggressive blood product support. Precautions: Collect and process the sample promptly and correctly (proper citrate ratio, prompt centrifugation) since delayed or incorrect handling can mimic or mask true consumptive coagulopathy, and repeat serially since DIC evolves rapidly.
questions.question: A patient newly diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukaemia develops spontaneous bleeding at diagnosis, and is subsequently diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Coagulation Screen (PT, APTT, Platelets, Fibrinogen) for DIC. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 5-year-old boy known to have sickle cell disease, being reviewed to distinguish it from sickle-thalassaemia. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Haemoglobin Electrophoresis is requested to differentiate homozygous sickle cell disease from sickle cell-thalassaemia, which have different clinical courses. Principle: A haemolysate of red cells is applied to a support medium such as cellulose acetate or agar gel and subjected to an electric field, separating haemoglobin variants according to their electrical charge at a given pH. Normal result and interpretation: The normal adult pattern shows predominantly HbA with small HbA2 (under 3.5%) and trace HbF. Abnormal bands or altered proportions identify HbS, HbC, HbE or a thalassaemia pattern. Precautions: a fresh, clot-free haemolysate must be used, voltage and running time must be standardised, and known control samples must be run alongside the patient sample to allow accurate identification of each band.

questions.question: A patient with known breast cancer develops unexplained pancytopenia, and is subsequently diagnosed with metastatic marrow infiltration. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Trephine Biopsy. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to look for metastatic tumour cells replacing normal marrow. Principle: A core of marrow tissue is removed with a trephine needle, processed histologically and examined intact, preserving marrow architecture in a way that aspiration alone cannot, allowing assessment of cellularity, fibrosis and focal lesions. Normal result: Normal marrow architecture with preserved trilineage haematopoiesis and no fibrosis or abnormal infiltrate; clusters of malignant epithelial cells confirm marrow metastasis. Precautions: Obtain an adequately long core (at least 1.5-2 cm) to allow representative assessment, and handle the specimen gently to avoid crush artefact that distorts cell morphology.

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman started on iron tablets two weeks ago for iron deficiency anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Reticulocyte Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Reticulocyte Count is requested to confirm an early marrow response to iron therapy before waiting for the haemoglobin itself to rise. Principle: Reticulocytes contain residual ribosomal RNA that precipitates as a network when stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, allowing them to be counted as a percentage of red cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult reticulocyte count is about 0.5–2.5%. A raised count indicates active bone marrow response to anaemia or haemorrhage, while a low count in an anaemic patient suggests bone marrow failure. Precautions: staining must be done on fresh blood mixed thoroughly with the stain and incubated for the correct time, and at least 1000 red cells should be counted, preferably with a Miller eyepiece, to minimise sampling error.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with recurrent wheeze, skin rash and a history of asthma. The attending doctor requests a White Cell Differential Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The White Cell Differential Count is requested to check for eosinophilia, which may support an allergic or parasitic cause of his symptoms. Principle: A well-made, Romanowsky-stained blood film is examined under oil immersion to identify and enumerate the different types of white cells, revealing shifts in proportion or the presence of abnormal cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal differential is roughly neutrophils 40–75%, lymphocytes 20–45%, monocytes 2–10%, eosinophils 1–6% and basophils 0–1%. Deviations indicate infection, allergy, parasitic disease or leukaemia depending on the cell type affected. Precautions: the film must be made from fresh blood spread thinly and evenly to avoid EDTA storage artefact, and counting must be performed in a representative area of the film where cells are well separated and not overlapping.

The Full Blood Count (FBC) is requested to evaluate the child for anaemia and rule out infection or an underlying haematological disorder as the cause of the pallor. Principle: An automated or manual count of red cells, white cells and platelets together with haemoglobin estimation and packed cell volume, giving a composite picture of the cellular elements of blood. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult ranges are approximately Hb 13–17 g/dl (male) or 12–15 g/dl (female), PCV 40–50%, WBC 4.0–11.0 x10^9/L and platelets 150–400 x10^9/L. Values outside these ranges point to anaemia, infection, leukaemia or a bleeding disorder depending on which parameter is deranged. Precautions: the sample must be collected into EDTA and mixed gently by inversion to prevent clotting or platelet clumping, analysed within a few hours of collection, and the counting chamber or analyser aperture kept free of debris that could give false counts.
questions.question: A 4-year-old boy brought in pale, irritable and with reduced appetite for two weeks. The attending doctor requests a Full Blood Count (FBC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Autohaemolysis Test is requested to further characterise a suspected hereditary spherocytosis when osmotic fragility results alone are equivocal. Principle: Defibrinated blood is incubated sterile at 37°C for 48 hours, with and without added glucose, and the percentage of red cells that lyse spontaneously is measured, reflecting intrinsic red cell membrane or metabolic fragility. Normal result and interpretation: Normal autohaemolysis is under about 4% without glucose and is corrected by added glucose. Markedly increased autohaemolysis that is corrected by glucose suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while increased autohaemolysis not corrected by glucose suggests an enzyme defect such as pyruvate kinase deficiency. Precautions: strict aseptic technique must be maintained throughout the 48-hour incubation to prevent bacterial contamination that would give a false result, and defibrination or an appropriate anticoagulant must be used correctly.
questions.question: A 15-year-old boy with chronic jaundice, splenomegaly and inconclusive osmotic fragility results. The attending doctor requests a Autohaemolysis Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Whole Blood Clotting Time is requested to demonstrate the markedly prolonged clotting time typical of severe factor deficiency. Principle: Whole blood is placed in a plain glass tube and tilted at intervals until a clot forms, giving a simple bedside measure of the overall intrinsic clotting pathway. Normal result and interpretation: Normal clotting time is about 5–10 minutes. Marked prolongation suggests a severe coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia. Precautions: glass tubes must be clean and dry, the tube must be tilted gently and consistently without excessive agitation, and the test must be performed at a constant temperature since cold significantly prolongs clotting.
questions.question: A 12-year-old boy with known severe haemophilia presenting with a swollen knee. The attending doctor requests a Whole Blood Clotting Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 8-year-old boy in a rural clinic with prolonged bleeding after a minor injury and no advanced laboratory available. The attending doctor requests a Whole Blood Clotting Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Whole Blood Clotting Time is requested to obtain a simple bedside estimate of his overall clotting ability where PT and APTT are not readily available. Principle: Whole blood is placed in a plain glass tube and tilted at intervals until a clot forms, giving a simple bedside measure of the overall intrinsic clotting pathway. Normal result and interpretation: Normal clotting time is about 5–10 minutes. Marked prolongation suggests a severe coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia. Precautions: glass tubes must be clean and dry, the tube must be tilted gently and consistently without excessive agitation, and the test must be performed at a constant temperature since cold significantly prolongs clotting.

questions.question: A child with severe diarrhoea and vomiting is brought to the emergency unit, and is subsequently diagnosed with dehydration. The attending doctor refers the patient for Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess haemoconcentration as a marker of fluid loss. Principle: A blood sample in a capillary or vacutainer tube is centrifuged so that red cells pack at the bottom, and the proportion of the column occupied by red cells is read as the packed cell volume. Normal result: 36-48% in women and 40-52% in men; a raised PCV out of keeping with the Hb pattern suggests haemoconcentration rather than true polycythaemia. Precautions: Fill capillary tubes fully without air bubbles, seal one end properly before centrifuging, and centrifuge for the standard validated time and speed to ensure complete red cell packing.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman of Mediterranean descent found incidentally to have mild anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC) is requested to check for a microcytic pattern with normal or near-normal red cell count, suggestive of thalassaemia trait rather than iron deficiency. Principle: Derived mathematically from the red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV to describe the average size and haemoglobin content of red cells, classifying anaemia as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic. Normal result and interpretation: Normal MCV is 80–100 fl, MCH 27–32 pg and MCHC 32–36%. Values below these indicate microcytic hypochromic anaemia while values above indicate macrocytosis. Precautions: an accurate red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV must first be obtained since the indices are only as reliable as the values used to calculate them, and lipaemic or haemolysed samples must be avoided as they distort the result.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with menorrhagia and microcytic anaemia is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with iron deficiency anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Ferritin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm depleted iron stores as the cause of her anaemia. Principle: An immunoassay (ELISA or chemiluminescence) measures serum ferritin, an acute-phase protein that reflects total body iron stores, since it correlates with the amount of iron sequestered within tissue macrophages and hepatocytes. Normal result: Approximately 15-150 ng/mL in women and 15-200 ng/mL in men; a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, while a normal or raised value should prompt consideration of coexisting inflammation. Precautions: Interpret cautiously in the presence of infection or inflammation, which raises ferritin independently of iron status as an acute-phase reactant, and avoid haemolysed samples which falsely elevate results.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with facial plethora, itching after a hot bath and a raised red cell count. The attending doctor requests a Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score is requested to support a diagnosis of polycythaemia vera, in which the LAP score is typically raised. Principle: Neutrophils on a blood film are stained for alkaline phosphatase activity and each cell is scored according to the intensity of staining, giving a total score reflecting neutrophil enzyme activity. Normal result and interpretation: A normal LAP score is roughly 20–100 depending on the scoring system used. A markedly low score is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia, while a high score is seen in leukaemoid reactions and polycythaemia vera. Precautions: the blood film must be fresh since LAP activity deteriorates on storage, staining must be carried out under standardised conditions, and at least 100 neutrophils should be scored to obtain a reliable result.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman attending antenatal booking clinic for the first time. The attending doctor requests a ABO Blood Grouping. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The ABO Blood Grouping is requested to determine her ABO group as part of standard antenatal blood grouping and screening. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed separately with known anti-A and anti-B antisera (forward grouping) and patient serum is mixed with known A and B cells (reverse grouping); agglutination identifies the ABO group present. Normal result and interpretation: Consistent forward and reverse grouping results confirm the patient's ABO group as A, B, AB or O. Discrepancies between forward and reverse results require further investigation before blood can be issued. Precautions: fresh antisera of adequate potency must be used, an adequate cell suspension concentration must be prepared, and both forward and reverse grouping must always be performed and cross-checked to avoid mistyping.

The Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing is requested to determine her Rh status, since Rh-negative mothers require monitoring and prophylaxis to prevent sensitisation. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with anti-D antiserum; agglutination indicates the presence of the D antigen (Rh positive) while absence of agglutination indicates Rh negative status, with a weak D test performed if the initial result is doubtful. Normal result and interpretation: A clear agglutination reaction confirms Rh positive status while no agglutination confirms Rh negative status. Correct Rh status is essential to prevent haemolytic disease of the newborn and haemolytic transfusion reactions. Precautions: a control tube without antiserum must always be run to exclude spontaneous autoagglutination, the correct incubation temperature must be maintained, and a weak D (antiglobulin) test should be performed on apparently negative results before confirming Rh negative status.
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman attending her first antenatal visit. The attending doctor requests a Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to quantify plasma cell infiltration supporting the diagnosis. Principle: A needle is inserted into the marrow cavity (usually posterior iliac crest or sternum) to aspirate a liquid marrow sample, which is smeared, stained and examined for cellularity, maturation and abnormal cell populations. Normal result: Normocellular marrow with an orderly maturation sequence of erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages and no abnormal infiltrate; plasma cells exceeding 10% of marrow cellularity support myeloma. Precautions: Prepare smears immediately before the sample clots, obtain particles for a representative trephine/clot section, and maintain strict asepsis at the puncture site to prevent infection.
questions.question: A 65-year-old presents with bone pain, anaemia and renal impairment, and is subsequently diagnosed with multiple myeloma. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Aspiration. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for marrow involvement, which upstages the disease. Principle: A core of marrow tissue is removed with a trephine needle, processed histologically and examined intact, preserving marrow architecture in a way that aspiration alone cannot, allowing assessment of cellularity, fibrosis and focal lesions. Normal result: Normal marrow architecture with preserved trilineage haematopoiesis and no fibrosis or abnormal infiltrate; presence of lymphomatous infiltrate confirms marrow involvement and affects treatment intensity. Precautions: Obtain an adequately long core (at least 1.5-2 cm) to allow representative assessment, and handle the specimen gently to avoid crush artefact that distorts cell morphology.
questions.question: A patient newly diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma is being staged, and is subsequently diagnosed with lymphoma staging. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Trephine Biopsy. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain is requested to determine whether the blast cells are of myeloid origin, confirming acute myeloid leukaemia. Principle: Myeloid cells contain peroxidase enzyme in their primary granules that reacts with hydrogen peroxide and a chromogen to give a coloured precipitate, positive in myeloblasts but negative in lymphoblasts. Normal result and interpretation: Peroxidase positivity in blast cells confirms myeloid lineage (acute myeloid leukaemia) while peroxidase-negative blasts suggest lymphoid lineage (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia). Precautions: fresh, well-fixed films must be used since old films lose enzyme activity, reagents must be prepared and used promptly as they deteriorate quickly, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included with every batch.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with fatigue, bleeding gums and blast cells seen on peripheral blood film. The attending doctor requests a Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient reporting excessive bleeding after dental extractions is assessed before surgery, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-operative screening in a bleeding history. The attending doctor refers the patient for Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for an underlying intrinsic pathway coagulation disorder. Principle: A phospholipid reagent, activator and calcium are added to citrated plasma to measure clotting time via the intrinsic and common pathways (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 25-35 seconds, depending on the reagent used; a prolonged result warrants factor assays before proceeding with elective surgery. Precautions: Avoid drawing the sample from a line contaminated with heparin, which falsely prolongs results, and centrifuge promptly to obtain platelet-poor plasma for accurate testing.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man donating blood for the first time at a blood bank. The attending doctor requests a ABO Blood Grouping. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The ABO Blood Grouping is requested to determine his ABO group so his donation can be correctly labelled and issued to compatible recipients. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed separately with known anti-A and anti-B antisera (forward grouping) and patient serum is mixed with known A and B cells (reverse grouping); agglutination identifies the ABO group present. Normal result and interpretation: Consistent forward and reverse grouping results confirm the patient's ABO group as A, B, AB or O. Discrepancies between forward and reverse results require further investigation before blood can be issued. Precautions: fresh antisera of adequate potency must be used, an adequate cell suspension concentration must be prepared, and both forward and reverse grouping must always be performed and cross-checked to avoid mistyping.

The Autohaemolysis Test is requested to look further at intrinsic red cell fragility as part of a comprehensive chronic haemolysis work-up. Principle: Defibrinated blood is incubated sterile at 37°C for 48 hours, with and without added glucose, and the percentage of red cells that lyse spontaneously is measured, reflecting intrinsic red cell membrane or metabolic fragility. Normal result and interpretation: Normal autohaemolysis is under about 4% without glucose and is corrected by added glucose. Markedly increased autohaemolysis that is corrected by glucose suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while increased autohaemolysis not corrected by glucose suggests an enzyme defect such as pyruvate kinase deficiency. Precautions: strict aseptic technique must be maintained throughout the 48-hour incubation to prevent bacterial contamination that would give a false result, and defibrination or an appropriate anticoagulant must be used correctly.
questions.question: A 25-year-old man with unexplained jaundice and negative haemolysis screening results so far. The attending doctor requests a Autohaemolysis Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient several years after total gastrectomy presents with fatigue and glossitis, and is subsequently diagnosed with post-gastrectomy anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Vitamin B12 Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm B12 deficiency resulting from loss of intrinsic factor-secreting cells. Principle: An automated immunoassay (competitive binding or chemiluminescence) measures circulating cobalamin, which is required as a cofactor for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells including erythroid precursors. Normal result: Approximately 200-900 pg/mL; a low level confirms the expected deficiency, requiring lifelong parenteral replacement. Precautions: Take the sample before any B12 injection is given, protect from prolonged light exposure which can degrade the vitamin, and interpret low-normal results cautiously alongside methylmalonic acid if pernicious anaemia is strongly suspected.

The Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit) is requested to quantify the exact severity of her anaemia and decide whether packed cell transfusion is indicated. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is centrifuged in a capillary or Wintrobe tube so that red cells pack down, and the height of the red cell column is expressed as a percentage of the total blood volume. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PCV is about 40–50% in men and 36–46% in women. A low PCV confirms anaemia while a raised PCV suggests polycythaemia, dehydration or haemoconcentration. Precautions: capillaries must be filled without air bubbles, sealed adequately, centrifuged at the correct speed and time, and read immediately after centrifugation before plasma and cells begin to remix.
questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with known anaemia, to assess how severe it is before deciding on transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 50-year-old man brought into the emergency department after a road traffic accident requiring urgent transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing is requested to rapidly determine his Rh status alongside ABO group before issuing emergency blood. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with anti-D antiserum; agglutination indicates the presence of the D antigen (Rh positive) while absence of agglutination indicates Rh negative status, with a weak D test performed if the initial result is doubtful. Normal result and interpretation: A clear agglutination reaction confirms Rh positive status while no agglutination confirms Rh negative status. Correct Rh status is essential to prevent haemolytic disease of the newborn and haemolytic transfusion reactions. Precautions: a control tube without antiserum must always be run to exclude spontaneous autoagglutination, the correct incubation temperature must be maintained, and a weak D (antiglobulin) test should be performed on apparently negative results before confirming Rh negative status.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with chronic microcytic anaemia and known chronic gastrointestinal bleeding. The attending doctor requests a Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
