questions.answerText: The Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity is requested to confirm ongoing iron deficiency from chronic blood loss and guide the need for continued iron replacement. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after its release from transferrin, while total iron binding capacity measures the maximum iron that transferrin can bind, together indicating percentage transferrin saturation. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum iron is about 10–30 micromol/L with TIBC around 45–70 micromol/L. Low iron with high TIBC indicates iron deficiency anaemia, while low iron with low or normal TIBC suggests anaemia of chronic disease. Precautions: the sample should be collected fasting in the morning to avoid diurnal variation, haemolysed samples must be rejected as they falsely raise the iron result, and all glassware used must be iron-free to avoid contamination.

questions.question: A 2-year-old month-old infant exclusively breastfed and presenting with unexplained bruising. The attending doctor requests a Prothrombin Time (PT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Prothrombin Time (PT) is requested to check for vitamin K deficiency bleeding, since factors II, VII, IX and X are vitamin K dependent. Principle: Calcium and tissue thromboplastin are added to citrated plasma to activate the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the time taken for a fibrin clot to form is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PT is approximately 11–15 seconds depending on the reagent used. Prolongation indicates deficiency of factors II, V, VII or X, seen in liver disease, warfarin therapy or vitamin K deficiency. Precautions: blood must be collected into the correct trisodium citrate ratio of 1:9, the test performed within a few hours of collection, and platelet-poor plasma obtained by adequate centrifugation to avoid interference from residual platelets.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with a very high platelet count found incidentally on routine testing. The attending doctor requests a Bleeding Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Bleeding Time is requested to assess whether her platelets, despite being numerous, are functioning normally. Principle: A standardised skin incision is made and the time taken for bleeding to stop spontaneously is timed, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall during primary haemostasis. Normal result and interpretation: Normal bleeding time is about 2–7 minutes depending on the method used. Prolongation suggests a platelet function disorder, von Willebrand disease or severe thrombocytopenia. Precautions: the incision must be of standardised depth and length, blood must be blotted gently every 30 seconds without touching the wound edge, and the test must be interpreted cautiously in patients on aspirin or with an obvious bleeding tendency.

questions.question: A 22-year-old presents with sudden jaundice and dark urine after eating fava beans, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemolytic anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Reticulocyte Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess bone marrow response to ongoing red cell destruction. Principle: Blood is stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, which precipitates residual ribosomal RNA in young red cells as a reticular network, allowing reticulocytes to be counted as a percentage or absolute count. Normal result: 0.5-2.5% of red cells, or an absolute count of 25-100 x10^9/L; a markedly raised count indicates appropriate marrow compensation for haemolysis, while a low count in this setting suggests marrow failure. Precautions: Use fresh, well-mixed EDTA blood and count at least 1000 red cells to reduce sampling error, and distinguish true reticular staining from Heinz bodies or artefactual staining.

The test was requested to help exclude venous thromboembolism in a patient with low clinical probability. Principle: An immunoassay detects D-dimer, a specific breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin, whose presence indicates that both clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis have occurred. Normal result: Below the assay-specific cut-off, usually less than 0.5 micrograms/mL FEU; a negative result in this context makes DVT unlikely, while a positive result requires confirmatory ultrasound. Precautions: Recognise that many conditions besides thrombosis (pregnancy, infection, malignancy, recent surgery) raise D-dimer, so a positive result is not diagnostic on its own; primarily use a negative result to help exclude thrombosis in low-probability patients.
questions.question: A 55-year-old presents with a swollen, tender calf after a long-haul flight, and is subsequently diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis. The attending doctor refers the patient for D-Dimer Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Plasma Fibrinogen Assay is requested to assess fibrinogen consumption as part of the work-up for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Principle: Plasma fibrinogen is quantified by measuring the clotting time after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to fibrinogen concentration, or by a direct chemical or immunological method. Normal result and interpretation: Normal plasma fibrinogen is about 2–4 g/L. Low levels are seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation and severe liver disease, while raised levels occur as an acute phase response to inflammation. Precautions: the standard fibrinogen curve must be freshly prepared, citrated plasma must be free of clots, and haemolysed samples must be avoided as they interfere with accurate detection of the clotting endpoint.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man in septic shock with widespread bruising and prolonged clotting times. The attending doctor requests a Plasma Fibrinogen Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Autohaemolysis Test is requested to assess her red cell fragility over time as part of confirming the same inherited condition in the family. Principle: Defibrinated blood is incubated sterile at 37°C for 48 hours, with and without added glucose, and the percentage of red cells that lyse spontaneously is measured, reflecting intrinsic red cell membrane or metabolic fragility. Normal result and interpretation: Normal autohaemolysis is under about 4% without glucose and is corrected by added glucose. Markedly increased autohaemolysis that is corrected by glucose suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while increased autohaemolysis not corrected by glucose suggests an enzyme defect such as pyruvate kinase deficiency. Precautions: strict aseptic technique must be maintained throughout the 48-hour incubation to prevent bacterial contamination that would give a false result, and defibrination or an appropriate anticoagulant must be used correctly.
questions.question: A 12-year-old girl whose sibling has confirmed hereditary spherocytosis, now under investigation herself. The attending doctor requests a Autohaemolysis Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain is requested to confirm that the blast cells are peroxidase-negative, supporting a diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Principle: Myeloid cells contain peroxidase enzyme in their primary granules that reacts with hydrogen peroxide and a chromogen to give a coloured precipitate, positive in myeloblasts but negative in lymphoblasts. Normal result and interpretation: Peroxidase positivity in blast cells confirms myeloid lineage (acute myeloid leukaemia) while peroxidase-negative blasts suggest lymphoid lineage (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia). Precautions: fresh, well-fixed films must be used since old films lose enzyme activity, reagents must be prepared and used promptly as they deteriorate quickly, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included with every batch.
questions.question: A 6-year-old girl with bone pain, bruising and lymphoblasts suspected on blood film. The attending doctor requests a Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 29-year-old woman with pallor, brittle nails and a craving to eat clay. The attending doctor requests a Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC) is requested to classify her anaemia and confirm the microcytic hypochromic pattern typical of iron deficiency. Principle: Derived mathematically from the red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV to describe the average size and haemoglobin content of red cells, classifying anaemia as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic. Normal result and interpretation: Normal MCV is 80–100 fl, MCH 27–32 pg and MCHC 32–36%. Values below these indicate microcytic hypochromic anaemia while values above indicate macrocytosis. Precautions: an accurate red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV must first be obtained since the indices are only as reliable as the values used to calculate them, and lipaemic or haemolysed samples must be avoided as they distort the result.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute leukaemia. The attending doctor requests a Platelet Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Platelet Count is requested to monitor for marrow-suppression-related thrombocytopenia, which determines the need for platelet transfusion support. Principle: Platelets are counted directly using a haemocytometer under phase contrast after appropriate dilution, or automatically by impedance/optical methods, based on their small size and characteristic light scatter. Normal result and interpretation: Normal platelet count is 150–400 x10^9/L. A count below this range indicates thrombocytopenia with bleeding risk while a count above suggests thrombocytosis. Precautions: blood must be collected into EDTA without clotting, the film must be checked for platelet clumps that cause spuriously low automated counts, and skin puncture blood should not be used since tissue fluid promotes platelet clumping.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with placenta praevia experiencing significant obstetric haemorrhage. The attending doctor requests a Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch) is requested to urgently confirm compatible blood units are available given her high risk of continued severe bleeding. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and recipient red cells with donor serum (minor crossmatch), incubated at 37°C and tested by the antiglobulin technique to detect incompatibility before transfusion. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of agglutination or haemolysis in the major crossmatch indicates compatibility and the unit is safe to transfuse; agglutination indicates incompatibility and that unit must not be given. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before the antiglobulin phase, correct incubation time and temperature must be observed, and patient identification on the sample and request form must be verified to prevent transfusion of the wrong unit.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman with jaundice and dark urine after starting a new medication. The attending doctor requests a Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC) is requested to help classify her anaemia, since a normocytic pattern with raised indices can accompany active haemolysis. Principle: Derived mathematically from the red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV to describe the average size and haemoglobin content of red cells, classifying anaemia as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic. Normal result and interpretation: Normal MCV is 80–100 fl, MCH 27–32 pg and MCHC 32–36%. Values below these indicate microcytic hypochromic anaemia while values above indicate macrocytosis. Precautions: an accurate red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV must first be obtained since the indices are only as reliable as the values used to calculate them, and lipaemic or haemolysed samples must be avoided as they distort the result.

The test was requested to detect a qualitative functional defect out of proportion to the antigen level. Principle: Immunoassay quantifies von Willebrand factor antigen, while a functional assay (such as ristocetin cofactor activity) measures its ability to mediate platelet binding, together characterising both the amount and function of the protein. Normal result: Approximately 50-200% of the reference standard for both antigen and activity; activity significantly lower than antigen level suggests a type 2 (qualitative) variant. Precautions: Be aware that vWF is an acute-phase reactant and can be transiently raised by stress, exercise or inflammation, and that blood group O individuals have physiologically lower baseline levels.
questions.question: A patient with a bleeding tendency disproportionate to a mildly reduced antigen level is assessed, and is subsequently diagnosed with type 2 von Willebrand disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for von Willebrand Factor Assay (Antigen and Activity). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 35-year-old presents with recurrent early-morning dark urine and unexplained thrombosis, and is subsequently diagnosed with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. The attending doctor refers the patient for Ham's Acid Haemolysis Test / Flow Cytometry for CD55 and CD59. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm complement-mediated destruction of an abnormal red cell clone. Principle: The historic Ham's test exposes red cells to acidified serum, which activates complement and lyses abnormally sensitive cells; modern flow cytometry directly detects the absence of the GPI-anchored surface proteins CD55 and CD59 that normally protect cells from complement. Normal result: Negative Ham's test, or normal expression of CD55 and CD59 on flow cytometry; a positive Ham's test or deficient CD55/CD59 expression confirms paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Precautions: Use fresh, unclotted blood and appropriate positive and negative controls, since flow cytometry has now largely replaced the technically demanding and less reproducible Ham's test.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman who lost a significant volume of blood after a road traffic accident three days ago. The attending doctor requests a Reticulocyte Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Reticulocyte Count is requested to assess whether the bone marrow is appropriately compensating for the acute blood loss. Principle: Reticulocytes contain residual ribosomal RNA that precipitates as a network when stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, allowing them to be counted as a percentage of red cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult reticulocyte count is about 0.5–2.5%. A raised count indicates active bone marrow response to anaemia or haemorrhage, while a low count in an anaemic patient suggests bone marrow failure. Precautions: staining must be done on fresh blood mixed thoroughly with the stain and incubated for the correct time, and at least 1000 red cells should be counted, preferably with a Miller eyepiece, to minimise sampling error.

The test was requested to assess synthetic liver function through clotting factor production. Principle: Tissue thromboplastin and calcium are added to citrated plasma, and the time taken to clot is measured, reflecting the integrity of the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways (factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 11-14 seconds, or an INR of approximately 0.8-1.2 in a person not on anticoagulants; a prolonged PT reflects reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and correlates with disease severity. Precautions: Fill the citrate tube exactly to the mark since an incorrect blood-to-citrate ratio distorts results, and process the sample within a few hours as factor V and VII activity decline on standing.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man with known cirrhosis presents with easy bruising, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic liver disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Prothrombin Time (PT/INR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm neonatal polycythaemia before considering partial exchange transfusion. Principle: A blood sample in a capillary or vacutainer tube is centrifuged so that red cells pack at the bottom, and the proportion of the column occupied by red cells is read as the packed cell volume. Normal result: 36-48% in women and 40-52% in men; a PCV above 65% confirms polycythaemia and correlates with hyperviscosity risk. Precautions: Fill capillary tubes fully without air bubbles, seal one end properly before centrifuging, and centrifuge for the standard validated time and speed to ensure complete red cell packing.
questions.question: A large-for-gestational-age newborn appears plethoric and lethargic on day one, and is subsequently diagnosed with neonatal polycythaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for a markedly raised sedimentation rate suggestive of a paraproteinaemia. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is left to stand vertically in a calibrated Westergren tube, and the distance red cells fall under gravity in one hour is measured; raised plasma fibrinogen and immunoglobulins promote rouleaux formation and faster sedimentation. Normal result: Below 15 mm/hr in men and below 20 mm/hr in women (age-adjusted); a very high ESR supports the presence of abnormal immunoglobulins and warrants serum protein electrophoresis. Precautions: Keep the tube perfectly vertical and free of vibration, read exactly at 60 minutes, and perform the test within two hours of collection since delay alters sedimentation.
questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with bone pain and unexplained renal impairment, and is subsequently diagnosed with multiple myeloma. The attending doctor refers the patient for Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A patient presents with a chronically discharging neck swelling and low-grade fever, and is subsequently diagnosed with tuberculous lymphadenitis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Lymph Node Biopsy (Histopathology). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to distinguish tuberculous lymphadenitis from malignancy as the cause of the lymphadenopathy. Principle: An excised lymph node is fixed, processed and stained (with immunohistochemistry as needed) to examine nodal architecture and identify malignant infiltration, distinguishing reactive hyperplasia from lymphoma or metastatic disease. Normal result: Preserved normal nodal architecture with reactive follicular hyperplasia and no malignant infiltrate; caseating granulomas confirm tuberculous lymphadenitis rather than a malignant process. Precautions: Excise an entire, representative node rather than a fine-needle sample where lymphoma is suspected, since architecture is essential for classification, and transport the fresh specimen promptly to avoid autolysis.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man with unexplained pancytopenia and no obvious cause. The attending doctor requests a Reticulocyte Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Reticulocyte Count is requested to check whether the marrow is responding, since a low count despite anaemia would support marrow failure rather than peripheral loss. Principle: Reticulocytes contain residual ribosomal RNA that precipitates as a network when stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, allowing them to be counted as a percentage of red cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult reticulocyte count is about 0.5–2.5%. A raised count indicates active bone marrow response to anaemia or haemorrhage, while a low count in an anaemic patient suggests bone marrow failure. Precautions: staining must be done on fresh blood mixed thoroughly with the stain and incubated for the correct time, and at least 1000 red cells should be counted, preferably with a Miller eyepiece, to minimise sampling error.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man with sickle cell-thalassaemia being characterised for genetic counselling purposes. The attending doctor requests a HbF Alkali Denaturation Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The HbF Alkali Denaturation Test is requested to quantify HbF levels to help distinguish this compound condition from simple sickle cell disease. Principle: Haemolysate is exposed briefly to strong alkali; adult haemoglobin (HbA) denatures rapidly and precipitates while fetal haemoglobin (HbF) resists denaturation, allowing the percentage of HbF to be estimated after filtration and colorimetric measurement. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult HbF is less than about 2%. Markedly elevated HbF is seen in beta-thalassaemia major, hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin, and some cases of sickle cell disease. Precautions: fresh reagents must be used since old alkali gives inaccurate denaturation times, the exact timing of alkali exposure must be strictly observed since it critically affects the result, and the haemolysate must be free of turbidity before measurement.

questions.question: A chronic myeloid leukaemia patient in molecular remission is reviewed at a routine follow-up, and is subsequently diagnosed with disease relapse surveillance. The attending doctor refers the patient for Cytogenetic Analysis for Philadelphia Chromosome (BCR-ABL). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to detect early molecular relapse before clinical or haematological relapse becomes apparent. Principle: Metaphase chromosome preparation or fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) detects the t(9;22) translocation forming the Philadelphia chromosome, or the resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene product is quantified by RT-PCR. Normal result: Absence of the t(9;22) translocation or BCR-ABL fusion transcript; a rising transcript level after previous undetectability signals molecular relapse requiring treatment review. Precautions: Ensure the marrow or blood sample is fresh and contains adequate dividing cells for metaphase analysis, and use molecular quantification (RT-PCR) rather than karyotyping alone for sensitive monitoring of minimal residual disease.

The Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) is requested to monitor the anticoagulant effect of heparin therapy and ensure it remains within the therapeutic range. Principle: A contact activator such as kaolin, together with phospholipid and calcium, is added to citrated plasma to activate the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the clotting time is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal APTT is approximately 30–40 seconds. Prolongation suggests deficiency of an intrinsic pathway factor such as VIII, IX, XI or XII, seen in haemophilia, or the presence of heparin or a lupus anticoagulant. Precautions: plasma must not contact glass surfaces as this prematurely activates factor XII, the phospholipid reagent must be incubated with plasma for the recommended time before calcium is added, and samples for factor assay must be kept frozen or on ice if not tested immediately.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man admitted with a deep vein thrombosis and started on intravenous heparin. The attending doctor requests a Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Coagulation Factor Assay is requested to quantify factor VIII activity and confirm the diagnosis and severity of haemophilia A. Principle: Patient plasma is diluted and mixed with plasma known to be deficient in the specific factor being tested, and correction of the clotting time is compared against a standard curve made from pooled normal plasma to calculate percentage factor activity. Normal result and interpretation: Normal factor activity is about 50–150% of the standard. Levels below 50%, and especially below 5%, indicate significant deficiency of that factor, as seen in haemophilia A (factor VIII), haemophilia B (factor IX) or other factor deficiencies. Precautions: the specific factor-deficient substrate plasma must be genuinely deficient only in that factor, samples must be kept frozen or on ice to preserve labile factors such as VIII, and a fresh standard curve must be prepared with each batch of tests.
questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with recurrent joint bleeding and a prolonged APTT already demonstrated. The attending doctor requests a Coagulation Factor Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The White Cell Differential Count is requested to look for the lymphocytosis with reactive lymphocytes typical of infectious mononucleosis. Principle: A well-made, Romanowsky-stained blood film is examined under oil immersion to identify and enumerate the different types of white cells, revealing shifts in proportion or the presence of abnormal cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal differential is roughly neutrophils 40–75%, lymphocytes 20–45%, monocytes 2–10%, eosinophils 1–6% and basophils 0–1%. Deviations indicate infection, allergy, parasitic disease or leukaemia depending on the cell type affected. Precautions: the film must be made from fresh blood spread thinly and evenly to avoid EDTA storage artefact, and counting must be performed in a representative area of the film where cells are well separated and not overlapping.
questions.question: A 9-year-old girl with fever, malaise and atypical lymphocytes suspected on history of glandular fever. The attending doctor requests a White Cell Differential Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 45-year-old man presents with marked leucocytosis and splenomegaly, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to help distinguish chronic myeloid leukaemia from a reactive leukaemoid reaction. Principle: Neutrophils are stained cytochemically for alkaline phosphatase activity, and a semi-quantitative score is generated by scoring 100 consecutive neutrophils for staining intensity. Normal result: A score within the laboratory's established normal range, generally moderate staining intensity; a low or absent score supports chronic myeloid leukaemia, while a high score favours a reactive process. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood without delay, since enzyme activity deteriorates on standing, and score consecutively without selecting only strongly-stained cells to avoid bias.

The test was requested to confirm true red cell excess before further work-up. Principle: A blood sample in a capillary or vacutainer tube is centrifuged so that red cells pack at the bottom, and the proportion of the column occupied by red cells is read as the packed cell volume. Normal result: 36-48% in women and 40-52% in men; a raised PCV supports polycythaemia, prompting erythropoietin and JAK2 mutation testing. Precautions: Fill capillary tubes fully without air bubbles, seal one end properly before centrifuging, and centrifuge for the standard validated time and speed to ensure complete red cell packing.
questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with facial plethora, headache and pruritus after a hot bath, and is subsequently diagnosed with polycythaemia vera. The attending doctor refers the patient for Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to determine the current factor level and calculate the replacement dose needed before the procedure. Principle: Patient plasma is added to factor VIII-deficient substrate plasma, and the correction of the clotting time in a modified APTT-based assay is compared against a standard curve to quantify factor VIII activity. Normal result: 50-150% of the standard reference activity; a low baseline level guides the clotting factor concentrate dose required to reach a safe surgical level. Precautions: Process the sample promptly since factor VIII activity declines on standing, and avoid interference from a lupus anticoagulant which can falsely lower apparent factor VIII levels.
questions.question: A known haemophilia A patient requires dental extraction, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-surgical replacement planning. The attending doctor refers the patient for Factor VIII Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Heinz Body Test is requested to demonstrate Heinz bodies confirming oxidative denaturation of haemoglobin during his acute haemolytic episode. Principle: Denatured, precipitated haemoglobin within red cells (Heinz bodies) is demonstrated using a supravital stain such as methyl violet or new methylene blue, since Heinz bodies do not stain with routine Romanowsky stains. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of Heinz bodies is normal. Their presence indicates oxidative damage to haemoglobin, seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidant stress, unstable haemoglobin variants, or exposure to certain drugs and chemicals. Precautions: the stain must be fresh and the preparation examined promptly, since Heinz bodies may be removed rapidly by the spleen and disappear from circulation, and adequate numbers of cells must be examined to avoid missing a low percentage.
questions.question: A 30-year-old man with known G6PD deficiency who develops jaundice after taking an antimalarial drug. The attending doctor requests a Heinz Body Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 12-year-old boy with severe combined immunodeficiency requiring urgent stem cell transplantation. The attending doctor requests a Mixed Lymphocyte Culture. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Mixed Lymphocyte Culture is requested to functionally confirm donor compatibility given the urgency and high stakes of his planned transplant. Principle: Recipient lymphocytes are cultured together with irradiated or mitomycin-treated donor lymphocytes, and the degree of recipient lymphocyte proliferation in response to donor Class II antigen differences is measured, usually by radioactive thymidine incorporation. Normal result and interpretation: Low proliferation indicates close Class II compatibility and lower rejection risk, while high proliferation indicates significant mismatch and a higher risk of graft rejection or graft-versus-host disease. Precautions: donor lymphocytes must be adequately irradiated or treated to prevent their own proliferation from confounding the result, sterile technique must be maintained throughout the culture period, and viable lymphocyte counts must be standardised between test wells.

questions.question: A 25-year-old presents with pancytopenia and no organomegaly, and is subsequently diagnosed with aplastic anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Aspiration. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm marrow hypoplasia as the cause of the pancytopenia. Principle: A needle is inserted into the marrow cavity (usually posterior iliac crest or sternum) to aspirate a liquid marrow sample, which is smeared, stained and examined for cellularity, maturation and abnormal cell populations. Normal result: Normocellular marrow with an orderly maturation sequence of erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages and no abnormal infiltrate; a hypocellular marrow with fatty replacement confirms aplasia rather than infiltrative disease. Precautions: Prepare smears immediately before the sample clots, obtain particles for a representative trephine/clot section, and maintain strict asepsis at the puncture site to prevent infection.

questions.question: A patient on high-dose penicillin develops new anaemia and jaundice, and is subsequently diagnosed with drug-induced haemolytic anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Direct Antiglobulin (Direct Coombs) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to establish an immune basis for the haemolysis related to the drug. Principle: Anti-human globulin reagent is added to washed patient red cells; if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement, the reagent cross-links adjacent cells to produce visible agglutination. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination; a positive result supports drug-induced immune haemolysis, and stopping the drug is expected to resolve it. Precautions: Wash the red cells thoroughly to remove all free unbound globulin before adding the antiglobulin reagent, since inadequate washing causes false-negative results through neutralisation.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with jaundice, ascites and known chronic liver disease. The attending doctor requests a Prothrombin Time (PT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Prothrombin Time (PT) is requested to assess synthetic liver function, since reduced clotting factor production prolongs the prothrombin time. Principle: Calcium and tissue thromboplastin are added to citrated plasma to activate the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the time taken for a fibrin clot to form is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PT is approximately 11–15 seconds depending on the reagent used. Prolongation indicates deficiency of factors II, V, VII or X, seen in liver disease, warfarin therapy or vitamin K deficiency. Precautions: blood must be collected into the correct trisodium citrate ratio of 1:9, the test performed within a few hours of collection, and platelet-poor plasma obtained by adequate centrifugation to avoid interference from residual platelets.

The test was requested to distinguish benign gestational thrombocytopenia from pre-eclampsia or HELLP syndrome. Principle: An automated haematology analyser counts platelets using impedance or optical light-scatter methods, distinguishing them from red and white cells by their smaller size. Normal result: 150-450 x10^9/L; a mild reduction alone favours gestational thrombocytopenia, while a very low count with hypertension raises concern for HELLP. Precautions: Confirm any very low automated count by examining a blood film to exclude EDTA-induced platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia), which can falsely lower the automated count.
questions.question: A pregnant woman in her third trimester is found to have a mildly low platelet count on routine antenatal bloods, and is subsequently diagnosed with pregnancy-associated thrombocytopenia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Platelet Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 35-year-old woman currently receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer, presenting for a routine visit. The attending doctor requests a Full Blood Count (FBC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Full Blood Count (FBC) is requested to monitor for chemotherapy-induced bone marrow suppression, particularly neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, which could necessitate treatment delay. Principle: An automated or manual count of red cells, white cells and platelets together with haemoglobin estimation and packed cell volume, giving a composite picture of the cellular elements of blood. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult ranges are approximately Hb 13–17 g/dl (male) or 12–15 g/dl (female), PCV 40–50%, WBC 4.0–11.0 x10^9/L and platelets 150–400 x10^9/L. Values outside these ranges point to anaemia, infection, leukaemia or a bleeding disorder depending on which parameter is deranged. Precautions: the sample must be collected into EDTA and mixed gently by inversion to prevent clotting or platelet clumping, analysed within a few hours of collection, and the counting chamber or analyser aperture kept free of debris that could give false counts.

The White Cell Differential Count is requested to characterise the white cell differential and look for circulating blast cells suggestive of leukaemia. Principle: A well-made, Romanowsky-stained blood film is examined under oil immersion to identify and enumerate the different types of white cells, revealing shifts in proportion or the presence of abnormal cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal differential is roughly neutrophils 40–75%, lymphocytes 20–45%, monocytes 2–10%, eosinophils 1–6% and basophils 0–1%. Deviations indicate infection, allergy, parasitic disease or leukaemia depending on the cell type affected. Precautions: the film must be made from fresh blood spread thinly and evenly to avoid EDTA storage artefact, and counting must be performed in a representative area of the film where cells are well separated and not overlapping.
questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with unexplained fatigue, bruising and a very high white cell count on initial screening. The attending doctor requests a White Cell Differential Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

An Rh-negative woman undergoes amniocentesis for genetic testing, and is subsequently diagnosed with post-amniocentesis assessment. The attending doctor refers the patient for Kleihauer-Betke Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to check for procedure-related fetomaternal haemorrhage requiring anti-D cover. Principle: A blood film is treated with acid elution, which removes adult haemoglobin from maternal red cells while fetal haemoglobin resists elution, allowing fetal cells to be counted and the volume of fetomaternal haemorrhage estimated. Normal result: Very few or no fetal cells detected in maternal blood (typically less than 0.1-0.3 mL fetal blood); detection of fetal cells confirms the need for anti-D administration after the procedure. Precautions: Prepare and stain the film promptly and consistently, and count an adequate number of fields to avoid underestimating a small haemorrhage, since the calculated anti-D dose depends directly on this count.

The Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing is requested to determine her Rh status for correct labelling of her donated unit. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with anti-D antiserum; agglutination indicates the presence of the D antigen (Rh positive) while absence of agglutination indicates Rh negative status, with a weak D test performed if the initial result is doubtful. Normal result and interpretation: A clear agglutination reaction confirms Rh positive status while no agglutination confirms Rh negative status. Correct Rh status is essential to prevent haemolytic disease of the newborn and haemolytic transfusion reactions. Precautions: a control tube without antiserum must always be run to exclude spontaneous autoagglutination, the correct incubation temperature must be maintained, and a weak D (antiglobulin) test should be performed on apparently negative results before confirming Rh negative status.
questions.question: A 22-year-old woman registering as a first-time blood donor. The attending doctor requests a Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The LE Cell Test is requested to assess for systemic involvement in a patient presenting primarily with discoid skin lesions. Principle: Leucocytes are damaged in vitro to release nuclear material which, in the presence of anti-nuclear antibody in the patient's serum, is opsonised and then phagocytosed by other neutrophils to form the characteristic LE cell. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of LE cells is normal. Presence of LE cells supports a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus or occasionally drug-induced lupus, though the test is less sensitive than modern ANA methods. Precautions: the preparation must be examined promptly since LE cells degenerate on standing, an adequate number of fields must be examined before a negative result is reported, and technique-related artefacts must be distinguished from true LE cells.
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with a discoid facial rash and mild joint symptoms. The attending doctor requests a LE Cell Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Heinz Body Test is requested to confirm oxidative red cell damage as the cause of his chemical-induced haemolysis. Principle: Denatured, precipitated haemoglobin within red cells (Heinz bodies) is demonstrated using a supravital stain such as methyl violet or new methylene blue, since Heinz bodies do not stain with routine Romanowsky stains. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of Heinz bodies is normal. Their presence indicates oxidative damage to haemoglobin, seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidant stress, unstable haemoglobin variants, or exposure to certain drugs and chemicals. Precautions: the stain must be fresh and the preparation examined promptly, since Heinz bodies may be removed rapidly by the spleen and disappear from circulation, and adequate numbers of cells must be examined to avoid missing a low percentage.
questions.question: A 25-year-old man exposed occupationally to industrial oxidant chemicals, now with jaundice. The attending doctor requests a Heinz Body Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A pregnant woman presents with leg swelling and calf tenderness, and is subsequently diagnosed with pregnancy-associated thrombosis assessment. The attending doctor refers the patient for D-Dimer Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to aid assessment of possible DVT, interpreted cautiously given pregnancy's physiological elevation of D-dimer. Principle: An immunoassay detects D-dimer, a specific breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin, whose presence indicates that both clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis have occurred. Normal result: Below the assay-specific cut-off, usually less than 0.5 micrograms/mL FEU; a normal result is reassuring, but a raised result (common in pregnancy) requires imaging rather than the assay alone. Precautions: Recognise that many conditions besides thrombosis (pregnancy, infection, malignancy, recent surgery) raise D-dimer, so a positive result is not diagnostic on its own; primarily use a negative result to help exclude thrombosis in low-probability patients.

questions.question: An asymptomatic 25-year-old is found to have microcytosis on a routine antenatal full blood count, and is subsequently diagnosed with beta-thalassaemia trait. The attending doctor refers the patient for Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to differentiate thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency as the cause of microcytosis. Principle: Hb variants are separated on cellulose acetate (alkaline pH) or citrate agar (acid pH) according to their electrical charge, allowing identification of HbA, HbS, HbC, HbF and other variants by their migration pattern. Normal result: Predominantly HbA (>95%), with HbA2 1.5-3.5% and HbF less than 1% in adults; a raised HbA2 (>3.5%) confirms beta-thalassaemia trait despite normal iron studies. Precautions: Run both alkaline and acid media to resolve variants that co-migrate on one system alone, and include known controls on every run to validate migration positions.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman with new severe headache and scalp tenderness. The attending doctor requests a Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) is requested to support a suspected diagnosis of temporal (giant cell) arteritis, an inflammatory vasculitis with characteristically elevated ESR. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is left to stand vertically in a calibrated tube and the rate at which red cells sediment under gravity, influenced mainly by plasma fibrinogen and globulin concentration, is measured after one hour. Normal result and interpretation: Normal ESR (Westergren) is roughly up to 10 mm/hr in men and 15 mm/hr in women. A markedly raised ESR indicates active inflammation, infection or malignancy, though the test is non-specific. Precautions: the tube must be perfectly vertical, free of air bubbles and vibration during the test, the test must be set up within two hours of collection, and the sample must be neither clotted nor haemolysed.

The test was requested to establish her Rh status and identify those at risk of Rhesus alloimmunisation. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with known anti-A, anti-B and anti-D antisera (forward grouping), and patient serum is mixed with known A and B reagent cells (reverse grouping); agglutination patterns identify the ABO and Rh(D) type. Normal result: A concordant result between forward and reverse grouping confirming one of the four ABO groups and Rh status; an Rh-negative result flags the need for anti-D prophylaxis and antibody monitoring throughout pregnancy. Precautions: Always perform both forward and reverse grouping to detect discrepancies, use correctly labelled samples with a second independent check to prevent patient misidentification, which is the leading cause of fatal transfusion errors.
questions.question: A pregnant woman attends her first antenatal visit, and is subsequently diagnosed with antenatal booking. The attending doctor refers the patient for Blood Grouping (ABO and Rh Typing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess consumption of clotting factors as part of a DIC screen. Principle: Tissue thromboplastin and calcium are added to citrated plasma, and the time taken to clot is measured, reflecting the integrity of the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways (factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 11-14 seconds, or an INR of approximately 0.8-1.2 in a person not on anticoagulants; marked prolongation supports factor consumption consistent with DIC. Precautions: Fill the citrate tube exactly to the mark since an incorrect blood-to-citrate ratio distorts results, and process the sample within a few hours as factor V and VII activity decline on standing.
questions.question: A patient with severe sepsis develops widespread bruising and oozing from cannula sites, and is subsequently diagnosed with disseminated intravascular coagulation. The attending doctor refers the patient for Prothrombin Time (PT/INR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The LE Cell Test is requested to investigate systemic lupus erythematosus as a cause of her multisystem inflammatory presentation. Principle: Leucocytes are damaged in vitro to release nuclear material which, in the presence of anti-nuclear antibody in the patient's serum, is opsonised and then phagocytosed by other neutrophils to form the characteristic LE cell. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of LE cells is normal. Presence of LE cells supports a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus or occasionally drug-induced lupus, though the test is less sensitive than modern ANA methods. Precautions: the preparation must be examined promptly since LE cells degenerate on standing, an adequate number of fields must be examined before a negative result is reported, and technique-related artefacts must be distinguished from true LE cells.
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with unexplained fever, pleuritic chest pain and multi-organ involvement. The attending doctor requests a LE Cell Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 24-year-old man presents with painless haematuria and normal renal imaging, and is subsequently diagnosed with unexplained haematuria. The attending doctor refers the patient for Sickling (Solubility) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for sickle cell trait, a recognised cause of renal papillary necrosis. Principle: Red cells are lysed in a reducing solution of sodium dithionite/metabisulphite; deoxygenated HbS polymerises and scatters light, producing turbidity, whereas normal HbA solutions remain clear. Normal result: A clear solution through which printed text can be read, indicating a negative result; a positive screen supports trait as a contributing cause and prompts confirmatory electrophoresis. Precautions: Confirm any positive screen with haemoglobin electrophoresis since the test cannot distinguish trait from disease, and avoid false negatives in severely anaemic patients by ensuring an adequate red cell concentration in the reagent.

questions.question: A West African child presents with mild chronic haemolytic anaemia and splenomegaly, and is subsequently diagnosed with HbC disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to identify an abnormal haemoglobin band distinct from HbS. Principle: Hb variants are separated on cellulose acetate (alkaline pH) or citrate agar (acid pH) according to their electrical charge, allowing identification of HbA, HbS, HbC, HbF and other variants by their migration pattern. Normal result: Predominantly HbA (>95%), with HbA2 1.5-3.5% and HbF less than 1% in adults; a discrete HbC band supports the diagnosis and differentiates it from sickle cell disease. Precautions: Run both alkaline and acid media to resolve variants that co-migrate on one system alone, and include known controls on every run to validate migration positions.

The test was requested to detect abnormal cell proportions or circulating blasts suggestive of leukaemia. Principle: An automated analyser counts total leucocytes and classifies them into neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils based on size and internal complexity (light scatter), a process that can be confirmed by microscopic differential count. Normal result: Total WBC 4-11 x10^9/L, with neutrophils 40-75%, lymphocytes 20-45%, monocytes 2-10%, eosinophils 1-6% and basophils 0-1%; circulating blasts on the differential strongly suggest leukaemia and warrant urgent marrow examination. Precautions: Confirm any abnormal automated differential (flagged result) by manual microscopic examination of a blood film, since automated counters cannot reliably distinguish blasts or atypical cells.
questions.question: A child with fatigue, fever and bone pain is screened before referral, and is subsequently diagnosed with acute leukaemia screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for Total White Blood Cell Count and Differential. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Serum Ferritin is requested to confirm whether her iron stores are adequate to support the increased demands of late pregnancy. Principle: Serum ferritin, an intracellular iron storage protein that leaks into blood in proportion to body iron stores, is measured immunologically, providing a sensitive indicator of iron deficiency or overload. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum ferritin is roughly 15–300 microgram/L depending on age and sex. Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency while very high ferritin suggests iron overload, though it may also be raised non-specifically as an acute phase reactant. Precautions: results must be interpreted with caution in the presence of infection or inflammation since ferritin is an acute phase protein that can be falsely elevated, and haemolysed samples must be avoided.
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman in the third trimester of pregnancy with borderline low haemoglobin. The attending doctor requests a Serum Ferritin. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 20-year-old woman with chronic non-immune haemolytic anaemia and normal osmotic fragility. The attending doctor requests a Autohaemolysis Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Autohaemolysis Test is requested to investigate for a red cell enzyme defect such as pyruvate kinase deficiency, in which autohaemolysis is not corrected by glucose. Principle: Defibrinated blood is incubated sterile at 37°C for 48 hours, with and without added glucose, and the percentage of red cells that lyse spontaneously is measured, reflecting intrinsic red cell membrane or metabolic fragility. Normal result and interpretation: Normal autohaemolysis is under about 4% without glucose and is corrected by added glucose. Markedly increased autohaemolysis that is corrected by glucose suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while increased autohaemolysis not corrected by glucose suggests an enzyme defect such as pyruvate kinase deficiency. Precautions: strict aseptic technique must be maintained throughout the 48-hour incubation to prevent bacterial contamination that would give a false result, and defibrination or an appropriate anticoagulant must be used correctly.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant with a low dietary folate intake. The attending doctor requests a Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay is requested to confirm adequate folate status in early pregnancy, since deficiency increases the risk of neural tube defects. Principle: Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels are measured, usually by immunoassay, to identify deficiency states that impair DNA synthesis in developing blood cells and cause megaloblastic change. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum B12 is about 200–900 ng/L and folate about 3–20 microgram/L. Levels below these ranges confirm the deficiency responsible for macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia. Precautions: the sample should be protected from prolonged light exposure where applicable, haemolysis must be avoided, and results should be interpreted alongside the full blood count and blood film since dietary and absorption factors affect the levels obtained.

The Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay is requested to confirm vitamin B12 deficiency as the cause of her combined haematological and neurological findings, suggesting pernicious anaemia. Principle: Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels are measured, usually by immunoassay, to identify deficiency states that impair DNA synthesis in developing blood cells and cause megaloblastic change. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum B12 is about 200–900 ng/L and folate about 3–20 microgram/L. Levels below these ranges confirm the deficiency responsible for macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia. Precautions: the sample should be protected from prolonged light exposure where applicable, haemolysis must be avoided, and results should be interpreted alongside the full blood count and blood film since dietary and absorption factors affect the levels obtained.
questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with numbness in her feet, a smooth sore tongue and macrocytic anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm the diagnosis urgently and quantify parasitaemia, which guides severity assessment. Principle: A thick film concentrates red cells to increase sensitivity for detecting parasites, while a thin film preserves red cell and parasite morphology for species identification, both examined microscopically after Giemsa staining. Normal result: No malaria parasites seen on thick or thin film; a very high parasitaemia percentage supports severe malaria requiring urgent parenteral treatment. Precautions: Prepare films from a fresh fingerprick or anticoagulated sample without delay, ensure correct Giemsa staining pH and time for accurate parasite morphology, and examine an adequate number of fields before reporting a film negative.
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with high fever, convulsions and altered consciousness, and is subsequently diagnosed with severe malaria in a child. The attending doctor refers the patient for Thick and Thin Blood Film for Malaria Parasites. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 22-year-old man volunteering to donate blood at a donation drive. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Estimation. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Haemoglobin Estimation is requested to confirm his haemoglobin meets the minimum safe threshold for blood donation before he is accepted as a donor. Principle: Haemoglobin is converted to a stable coloured compound (acid haematin or cyanmethaemoglobin) whose colour intensity, read colorimetrically, is proportional to haemoglobin concentration. Normal result and interpretation: Normal values are 13–17 g/dl in men and 12–15 g/dl in women. Values below this confirm anaemia while markedly elevated values suggest polycythaemia or dehydration. Precautions: reagents must be fresh and correctly diluted, the exact volume of blood must be drawn without air bubbles, and colour development must be allowed to reach completion before reading to avoid underestimation.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with decompensated liver cirrhosis and spontaneous bruising. The attending doctor requests a Plasma Fibrinogen Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Plasma Fibrinogen Assay is requested to assess hepatic synthetic function, since fibrinogen production is reduced in advanced liver disease. Principle: Plasma fibrinogen is quantified by measuring the clotting time after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to fibrinogen concentration, or by a direct chemical or immunological method. Normal result and interpretation: Normal plasma fibrinogen is about 2–4 g/L. Low levels are seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation and severe liver disease, while raised levels occur as an acute phase response to inflammation. Precautions: the standard fibrinogen curve must be freshly prepared, citrated plasma must be free of clots, and haemolysed samples must be avoided as they interfere with accurate detection of the clotting endpoint.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with unexplained chronic haemolysis, recurrent abdominal pain and thrombosis. The attending doctor requests a Ham's Acidified Serum Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Ham's Acidified Serum Test is requested to investigate for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria as a cause of her recurrent unexplained thrombotic episodes. Principle: Patient red cells are incubated in fresh, acidified normal serum, which activates complement via the alternate pathway; abnormally complement-sensitive cells characteristic of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria lyse under these acidic conditions. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no lysis, while a positive test, showing lysis in acidified serum but not in heat-inactivated serum, confirms paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Precautions: fresh serum must be used as a complement source since stored serum loses complement activity, appropriate control tubes with heat-inactivated serum and normal cells must be run in parallel, and the pH of the acidified serum must be accurately adjusted.

The test was requested to detect early trauma-induced coagulopathy and guide massive transfusion protocol activation. Principle: A combined panel assesses the extrinsic pathway (PT), intrinsic pathway (APTT), platelet number and fibrinogen concentration together, since disseminated intravascular coagulation produces a characteristic pattern of simultaneous consumption across all these parameters. Normal result: PT and APTT within normal range, platelets above 150 x10^9/L and fibrinogen above 2.0 g/L, with a low D-dimer; deranged results early after trauma predict a higher requirement for blood products and worse outcome if untreated. Precautions: Collect and process the sample promptly and correctly (proper citrate ratio, prompt centrifugation) since delayed or incorrect handling can mimic or mask true consumptive coagulopathy, and repeat serially since DIC evolves rapidly.
questions.question: A patient with major blunt trauma and ongoing haemorrhage is assessed in the trauma bay, and is subsequently diagnosed with trauma-associated coagulopathy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Coagulation Screen (PT, APTT, Platelets, Fibrinogen) for DIC. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Donath-Landsteiner Test is requested to establish a firm diagnosis before counselling the family on strict cold avoidance. Principle: Patient serum containing the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is incubated with red cells at 4°C, allowing antibody and complement to bind, then warmed to 37°C, which triggers complement-mediated haemolysis characteristic of paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no haemolysis. A positive biphasic haemolysis pattern confirms paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria, usually occurring after a viral infection. Precautions: the cold and warm incubation steps must be performed in strict sequence and at the correct temperatures since reversing or skipping a step gives a false negative result, and fresh complement-containing serum must be used.
questions.question: A 7-year-old girl with recurrent episodes of dark urine each time she is exposed to cold. The attending doctor requests a Donath-Landsteiner Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm inadequate erythropoietin production as the cause of the anaemia. Principle: An immunoassay measures circulating erythropoietin, the hormone produced predominantly by the kidney in response to tissue hypoxia, which stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow. Normal result: Approximately 4-27 mU/mL, though appropriately elevated in genuine anaemia due to physiological hypoxic drive; a level that is low or inappropriately normal for the degree of anaemia supports renal erythropoietin deficiency, guiding erythropoiesis-stimulating agent therapy. Precautions: Interpret the result in the context of the patient's haemoglobin level, since a normal or low erythropoietin in the presence of anaemia is inappropriately low and clinically significant.
questions.question: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops progressive anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with anaemia of chronic kidney disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Erythropoietin Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Sickling Test is requested to screen her own sickle cell status as part of pre-marital genetic counselling given her partner's carrier status. Principle: Red cells are mixed with a reducing agent such as sodium metabisulphite that lowers oxygen tension, causing hemoglobin S to polymerise and distort the cells into a sickle shape under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no sickling and excludes HbS, while a positive test confirms the presence of HbS but cannot distinguish sickle cell trait from sickle cell disease. Precautions: a freshly prepared reducing agent must be used since an old reagent gives false negatives, the preparation must be sealed with a coverslip and petroleum jelly to prevent drying, and it must be observed for the recommended time as delayed reading may miss early sickling.
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman planning to marry, whose partner is a known sickle cell carrier. The attending doctor requests a Sickling Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Full Blood Count (FBC) is requested to screen broadly for anaemia, occult malignancy-related marrow suppression, or infection as the cause of his constitutional symptoms. Principle: An automated or manual count of red cells, white cells and platelets together with haemoglobin estimation and packed cell volume, giving a composite picture of the cellular elements of blood. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult ranges are approximately Hb 13–17 g/dl (male) or 12–15 g/dl (female), PCV 40–50%, WBC 4.0–11.0 x10^9/L and platelets 150–400 x10^9/L. Values outside these ranges point to anaemia, infection, leukaemia or a bleeding disorder depending on which parameter is deranged. Precautions: the sample must be collected into EDTA and mixed gently by inversion to prevent clotting or platelet clumping, analysed within a few hours of collection, and the counting chamber or analyser aperture kept free of debris that could give false counts.
questions.question: A 68-year-old man with progressive fatigue, weight loss and pallor over three months. The attending doctor requests a Full Blood Count (FBC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 2-year-old day-old newborn noted to be plethoric and lethargic on the ward. The attending doctor requests a Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit) is requested to check for neonatal polycythaemia, which can cause hyperviscosity symptoms and requires prompt recognition. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is centrifuged in a capillary or Wintrobe tube so that red cells pack down, and the height of the red cell column is expressed as a percentage of the total blood volume. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PCV is about 40–50% in men and 36–46% in women. A low PCV confirms anaemia while a raised PCV suggests polycythaemia, dehydration or haemoconcentration. Precautions: capillaries must be filled without air bubbles, sealed adequately, centrifuged at the correct speed and time, and read immediately after centrifugation before plasma and cells begin to remix.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with marrow fibrosis and a leukoerythroblastic blood film. The attending doctor requests a Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score is requested to assess LAP activity as part of the work-up for a chronic myeloproliferative disorder such as myelofibrosis. Principle: Neutrophils on a blood film are stained for alkaline phosphatase activity and each cell is scored according to the intensity of staining, giving a total score reflecting neutrophil enzyme activity. Normal result and interpretation: A normal LAP score is roughly 20–100 depending on the scoring system used. A markedly low score is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia, while a high score is seen in leukaemoid reactions and polycythaemia vera. Precautions: the blood film must be fresh since LAP activity deteriorates on storage, staining must be carried out under standardised conditions, and at least 100 neutrophils should be scored to obtain a reliable result.

The test was requested to assess the degree of anaemia resulting from occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Principle: A blood sample in a capillary or vacutainer tube is centrifuged so that red cells pack at the bottom, and the proportion of the column occupied by red cells is read as the packed cell volume. Normal result: 36-48% in women and 40-52% in men; a reduced PCV correlates with the severity of chronic blood loss and guides transfusion decisions. Precautions: Fill capillary tubes fully without air bubbles, seal one end properly before centrifuging, and centrifuge for the standard validated time and speed to ensure complete red cell packing.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with long-standing peptic ulcer disease presents with fatigue, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic blood loss. The attending doctor refers the patient for Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A male neonate develops unexplained significant jaundice in the first week of life, and is subsequently diagnosed with neonatal jaundice screening.
