The attending doctor refers the patient for G6PD Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for G6PD deficiency as a cause of neonatal haemolysis and kernicterus risk. Principle: A quantitative spectrophotometric or fluorescent-spot assay measures the activity of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that protects red cells from oxidative stress by generating NADPH. Normal result: Enzyme activity within the laboratory's established reference range (typically reported relative to a normal control); reduced activity confirms the diagnosis and prompts closer bilirubin monitoring. Precautions: Avoid testing during or shortly after an acute haemolytic episode, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a true deficiency; retest several weeks later if an acute episode has just occurred.

The HbF Alkali Denaturation Test is requested to quantify the markedly elevated HbF that helps confirm the diagnosis of beta-thalassaemia major. Principle: Haemolysate is exposed briefly to strong alkali; adult haemoglobin (HbA) denatures rapidly and precipitates while fetal haemoglobin (HbF) resists denaturation, allowing the percentage of HbF to be estimated after filtration and colorimetric measurement. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult HbF is less than about 2%. Markedly elevated HbF is seen in beta-thalassaemia major, hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin, and some cases of sickle cell disease. Precautions: fresh reagents must be used since old alkali gives inaccurate denaturation times, the exact timing of alkali exposure must be strictly observed since it critically affects the result, and the haemolysate must be free of turbidity before measurement.
questions.question: A 10-year-old girl with confirmed beta-thalassaemia major awaiting quantification of her fetal haemoglobin level. The attending doctor requests a HbF Alkali Denaturation Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to demonstrate ineffective erythropoiesis with intramedullary destruction of abnormal red cell precursors. Principle: A spectrophotometric enzymatic assay measures LDH activity by monitoring the conversion of NADH to NAD+ during the reduction of pyruvate to lactate; LDH is released from many tissues including red cells during cell breakdown or turnover. Normal result: Approximately 140-280 U/L (assay-dependent); a markedly raised level, often very high, supports ineffective erythropoiesis typical of megaloblastic anaemia. Precautions: Avoid any degree of haemolysis during sample collection or handling, since red cells contain very high LDH activity and even minor in vitro haemolysis will falsely raise the result.
questions.question: A patient with severe macrocytic anaemia from B12 deficiency is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with megaloblastic anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 8-year-old girl who develops dark urine specifically after exposure to cold weather. The attending doctor requests a Donath-Landsteiner Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Donath-Landsteiner Test is requested to demonstrate the characteristic biphasic cold-reactive antibody responsible for her cold-triggered haemoglobinuria. Principle: Patient serum containing the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is incubated with red cells at 4°C, allowing antibody and complement to bind, then warmed to 37°C, which triggers complement-mediated haemolysis characteristic of paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no haemolysis. A positive biphasic haemolysis pattern confirms paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria, usually occurring after a viral infection. Precautions: the cold and warm incubation steps must be performed in strict sequence and at the correct temperatures since reversing or skipping a step gives a false negative result, and fresh complement-containing serum must be used.

The test was requested to screen the patient's serum for atypical red cell antibodies before crossmatching. Principle: Patient serum is incubated with reagent red cells of known antigen type; if antibody is present in the serum it binds the cells in vitro, and subsequent addition of antiglobulin reagent causes visible agglutination, detecting free circulating antibody. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination, indicating no clinically significant antibody in the serum; a positive screen requires antibody identification before compatible blood can be selected. Precautions: Incubate at 37°C for the correct time to allow antibody-antigen binding, and use a fresh antiglobulin reagent since a weakened reagent can give false-negative results.
questions.question: A patient scheduled for elective surgery requires blood to be reserved, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-transfusion compatibility testing. The attending doctor refers the patient for Indirect Antiglobulin Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Ham's Acidified Serum Test is requested to confirm complement-mediated red cell lysis characteristic of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Principle: Patient red cells are incubated in fresh, acidified normal serum, which activates complement via the alternate pathway; abnormally complement-sensitive cells characteristic of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria lyse under these acidic conditions. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no lysis, while a positive test, showing lysis in acidified serum but not in heat-inactivated serum, confirms paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Precautions: fresh serum must be used as a complement source since stored serum loses complement activity, appropriate control tubes with heat-inactivated serum and normal cells must be run in parallel, and the pH of the acidified serum must be accurately adjusted.
questions.question: A 30-year-old man with pancytopenia and evidence of ongoing intravascular haemolysis on other tests. The attending doctor requests a Ham's Acidified Serum Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 30-year-old woman who develops fever and back pain during a blood transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test is requested to check for antibody coating of red cells as part of an urgent transfusion reaction work-up. Principle: Antihuman globulin reagent is added directly to the patient's washed red cells; agglutination occurs if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement. Normal result and interpretation: A negative DAT indicates no in vivo sensitisation of red cells, while a positive DAT confirms antibody or complement coating, seen in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, haemolytic disease of the newborn, or drug-induced and transfusion-related haemolysis. Precautions: the red cells must be washed thoroughly, at least three times, with saline to remove all free globulin that would otherwise neutralise the antiglobulin reagent, and the tubes must be centrifuged at the recommended speed before reading.

The test was requested to evaluate marrow output before committing to a marrow biopsy. Principle: Blood is stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, which precipitates residual ribosomal RNA in young red cells as a reticular network, allowing reticulocytes to be counted as a percentage or absolute count. Normal result: 0.5-2.5% of red cells, or an absolute count of 25-100 x10^9/L; a low count despite anaemia confirms inadequate marrow production, consistent with aplasia. Precautions: Use fresh, well-mixed EDTA blood and count at least 1000 red cells to reduce sampling error, and distinguish true reticular staining from Heinz bodies or artefactual staining.
questions.question: A 19-year-old presents with pancytopenia and recurrent infections after chloramphenicol use, and is subsequently diagnosed with aplastic anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Reticulocyte Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 66-year-old woman on long-term warfarin for a mechanical heart valve, for routine monitoring. The attending doctor requests a Prothrombin Time (PT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Prothrombin Time (PT) is requested to monitor the anticoagulant effect of warfarin and guide dose adjustment to keep her within a safe therapeutic range. Principle: Calcium and tissue thromboplastin are added to citrated plasma to activate the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the time taken for a fibrin clot to form is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PT is approximately 11–15 seconds depending on the reagent used. Prolongation indicates deficiency of factors II, V, VII or X, seen in liver disease, warfarin therapy or vitamin K deficiency. Precautions: blood must be collected into the correct trisodium citrate ratio of 1:9, the test performed within a few hours of collection, and platelet-poor plasma obtained by adequate centrifugation to avoid interference from residual platelets.

The test was requested to check for folate depletion from chronically increased red cell turnover. Principle: An automated competitive immunoassay measures serum folate, a vitamin required together with B12 for thymidylate and DNA synthesis in dividing marrow cells. Normal result: Approximately 3-17 ng/mL (red cell folate is a more stable indicator of tissue stores); a low level indicates increased folate consumption, requiring maintenance supplementation. Precautions: Draw blood before any folic acid supplementation is started, avoid recent alcohol intake which can transiently lower levels, and pair with a B12 assay since folate replacement alone can mask B12 deficiency and worsen neurological damage.
questions.question: A patient with chronic hereditary spherocytosis develops worsening anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemolytic anaemia with increased turnover. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Folate Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A patient with splenomegaly and a leucoerythroblastic film is being classified, and is subsequently diagnosed with differentiating myelofibrosis from CML. The attending doctor refers the patient for Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to help differentiate primary myelofibrosis from chronic myeloid leukaemia. Principle: Neutrophils are stained cytochemically for alkaline phosphatase activity, and a semi-quantitative score is generated by scoring 100 consecutive neutrophils for staining intensity. Normal result: A score within the laboratory's established normal range, generally moderate staining intensity; a normal or raised score favours myelofibrosis, while a low score favours chronic myeloid leukaemia. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood without delay, since enzyme activity deteriorates on standing, and score consecutively without selecting only strongly-stained cells to avoid bias.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man on long-term warfarin for atrial fibrillation attends for routine review, and is subsequently diagnosed with warfarin monitoring. The attending doctor refers the patient for Prothrombin Time (PT/INR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to monitor his anticoagulation level and adjust his dose. Principle: Tissue thromboplastin and calcium are added to citrated plasma, and the time taken to clot is measured, reflecting the integrity of the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways (factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 11-14 seconds, or an INR of approximately 0.8-1.2 in a person not on anticoagulants; an INR within the therapeutic range confirms adequate anticoagulation, while values outside range signal bleeding or clotting risk. Precautions: Fill the citrate tube exactly to the mark since an incorrect blood-to-citrate ratio distorts results, and process the sample within a few hours as factor V and VII activity decline on standing.

The test was requested to monitor the level of systemic inflammatory activity. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is left to stand vertically in a calibrated Westergren tube, and the distance red cells fall under gravity in one hour is measured; raised plasma fibrinogen and immunoglobulins promote rouleaux formation and faster sedimentation. Normal result: Below 15 mm/hr in men and below 20 mm/hr in women (age-adjusted); a raised ESR supports active inflammation, and serial values help track response to treatment. Precautions: Keep the tube perfectly vertical and free of vibration, read exactly at 60 minutes, and perform the test within two hours of collection since delay alters sedimentation.
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents with symmetrical joint swelling and morning stiffness, and is subsequently diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Peripheral Blood Film Examination is requested to examine red cell morphology for spherocytes, fragments or other features that would indicate the type of haemolytic anaemia present. Principle: A thin film of blood is spread on a slide, fixed and stained with a Romanowsky stain so that red cell, white cell and platelet morphology can be examined directly under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells appear as uniform biconcave discs with central pallor, white cells show normal proportions and morphology, and platelets are adequate in number. Abnormal shapes, inclusions or immature cells point to specific haematological disease. Precautions: the film must be made promptly from fresh anticoagulated or capillary blood, spread with a smooth, even-angled stroke to avoid artefacts, and properly fixed before staining to prevent cell distortion.
questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with jaundice, dark urine and a falling haemoglobin. The attending doctor requests a Peripheral Blood Film Examination. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 4-year-old day-old newborn with unexplained haemolytic jaundice shortly after birth. The attending doctor requests a Heinz Body Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Heinz Body Test is requested to look for Heinz bodies as a clue to an underlying red cell enzyme or haemoglobin stability defect. Principle: Denatured, precipitated haemoglobin within red cells (Heinz bodies) is demonstrated using a supravital stain such as methyl violet or new methylene blue, since Heinz bodies do not stain with routine Romanowsky stains. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of Heinz bodies is normal. Their presence indicates oxidative damage to haemoglobin, seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidant stress, unstable haemoglobin variants, or exposure to certain drugs and chemicals. Precautions: the stain must be fresh and the preparation examined promptly, since Heinz bodies may be removed rapidly by the spleen and disappear from circulation, and adequate numbers of cells must be examined to avoid missing a low percentage.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease on erythropoietin therapy. The attending doctor requests a Serum Ferritin. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Serum Ferritin is requested to check her iron stores, since adequate ferritin is required for erythropoietin therapy to be effective. Principle: Serum ferritin, an intracellular iron storage protein that leaks into blood in proportion to body iron stores, is measured immunologically, providing a sensitive indicator of iron deficiency or overload. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum ferritin is roughly 15–300 microgram/L depending on age and sex. Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency while very high ferritin suggests iron overload, though it may also be raised non-specifically as an acute phase reactant. Precautions: results must be interpreted with caution in the presence of infection or inflammation since ferritin is an acute phase protein that can be falsely elevated, and haemolysed samples must be avoided.

questions.question: A leukaemia patient is due for the next cycle of chemotherapy, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-chemotherapy assessment. The attending doctor refers the patient for Platelet Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to ensure the platelet count is adequate before proceeding, given bleeding risk. Principle: An automated haematology analyser counts platelets using impedance or optical light-scatter methods, distinguishing them from red and white cells by their smaller size. Normal result: 150-450 x10^9/L; a count below the safe threshold may require platelet transfusion or delay of chemotherapy. Precautions: Confirm any very low automated count by examining a blood film to exclude EDTA-induced platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia), which can falsely lower the automated count.

questions.question: An 70-year-old woman presents with new headache, scalp tenderness and visual disturbance, and is subsequently diagnosed with temporal arteritis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to support urgent clinical suspicion before starting corticosteroids and awaiting biopsy. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is left to stand vertically in a calibrated Westergren tube, and the distance red cells fall under gravity in one hour is measured; raised plasma fibrinogen and immunoglobulins promote rouleaux formation and faster sedimentation. Normal result: Below 15 mm/hr in men and below 20 mm/hr in women (age-adjusted); a very high ESR strongly supports the diagnosis and, in this context, justifies immediate treatment. Precautions: Keep the tube perfectly vertical and free of vibration, read exactly at 60 minutes, and perform the test within two hours of collection since delay alters sedimentation.

The test was requested to rapidly screen for sickle haemoglobin before anaesthesia, which can precipitate crisis under hypoxia. Principle: Red cells are lysed in a reducing solution of sodium dithionite/metabisulphite; deoxygenated HbS polymerises and scatters light, producing turbidity, whereas normal HbA solutions remain clear. Normal result: A clear solution through which printed text can be read, indicating a negative result; a positive (turbid) result requires urgent electrophoresis to distinguish trait from disease before proceeding. Precautions: Confirm any positive screen with haemoglobin electrophoresis since the test cannot distinguish trait from disease, and avoid false negatives in severely anaemic patients by ensuring an adequate red cell concentration in the reagent.
questions.question: A 20-year-old Nigerian patient is scheduled for elective surgery under general anaesthesia, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-operative screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for Sickling (Solubility) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 6-year-old boy with fever and chills after returning from a rural malaria-endemic area. The attending doctor requests a Peripheral Blood Film Examination. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Peripheral Blood Film Examination is requested to look directly for malaria parasites and assess red cell and white cell morphology for other causes of his fever. Principle: A thin film of blood is spread on a slide, fixed and stained with a Romanowsky stain so that red cell, white cell and platelet morphology can be examined directly under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells appear as uniform biconcave discs with central pallor, white cells show normal proportions and morphology, and platelets are adequate in number. Abnormal shapes, inclusions or immature cells point to specific haematological disease. Precautions: the film must be made promptly from fresh anticoagulated or capillary blood, spread with a smooth, even-angled stroke to avoid artefacts, and properly fixed before staining to prevent cell distortion.

The Bleeding Time is requested to assess the effect of aspirin on platelet function before proceeding with the procedure. Principle: A standardised skin incision is made and the time taken for bleeding to stop spontaneously is timed, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall during primary haemostasis. Normal result and interpretation: Normal bleeding time is about 2–7 minutes depending on the method used. Prolongation suggests a platelet function disorder, von Willebrand disease or severe thrombocytopenia. Precautions: the incision must be of standardised depth and length, blood must be blotted gently every 30 seconds without touching the wound edge, and the test must be interpreted cautiously in patients on aspirin or with an obvious bleeding tendency.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man booked for minor surgery, on long-term aspirin therapy. The attending doctor requests a Bleeding Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity is requested to monitor whether iron stores are improving in response to his ongoing supplementation. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after its release from transferrin, while total iron binding capacity measures the maximum iron that transferrin can bind, together indicating percentage transferrin saturation. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum iron is about 10–30 micromol/L with TIBC around 45–70 micromol/L. Low iron with high TIBC indicates iron deficiency anaemia, while low iron with low or normal TIBC suggests anaemia of chronic disease. Precautions: the sample should be collected fasting in the morning to avoid diurnal variation, haemolysed samples must be rejected as they falsely raise the iron result, and all glassware used must be iron-free to avoid contamination.
questions.question: A 40-year-old man with anaemia of chronic disease already receiving oral iron therapy. The attending doctor requests a Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC) is requested to classify the anaemia, since a normocytic normochromic pattern would support anaemia of chronic disease. Principle: Derived mathematically from the red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV to describe the average size and haemoglobin content of red cells, classifying anaemia as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic. Normal result and interpretation: Normal MCV is 80–100 fl, MCH 27–32 pg and MCHC 32–36%. Values below these indicate microcytic hypochromic anaemia while values above indicate macrocytosis. Precautions: an accurate red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV must first be obtained since the indices are only as reliable as the values used to calculate them, and lipaemic or haemolysed samples must be avoided as they distort the result.
questions.question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and mild anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to help distinguish true coagulopathy from sample contamination with heparin. Principle: Patient plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma and the clotting time (PT or APTT) is repeated immediately and after incubation, distinguishing a factor deficiency (which corrects, since normal plasma supplies the missing factor) from an inhibitor (which does not fully correct). Normal result: Full correction of the prolonged clotting time into the normal range; correction with a heparin-neutralising reagent (or use of thrombin time) helps confirm heparin as the cause. Precautions: Repeat the test after incubation at 37°C for one to two hours, since some inhibitors (such as factor VIII autoantibodies) are time- and temperature-dependent and only become apparent on delayed testing.
questions.question: A hospitalised patient on a heparin infusion has an unexpectedly high APTT on a routine sample, and is subsequently diagnosed with heparin contamination check. The attending doctor refers the patient for Mixing Study (Correction Test). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Ham's Acidified Serum Test is requested to check for the development of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, a recognised complication of aplastic anaemia. Principle: Patient red cells are incubated in fresh, acidified normal serum, which activates complement via the alternate pathway; abnormally complement-sensitive cells characteristic of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria lyse under these acidic conditions. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no lysis, while a positive test, showing lysis in acidified serum but not in heat-inactivated serum, confirms paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Precautions: fresh serum must be used as a complement source since stored serum loses complement activity, appropriate control tubes with heat-inactivated serum and normal cells must be run in parallel, and the pH of the acidified serum must be accurately adjusted.
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman recovering from aplastic anaemia, now noted to have haemoglobinuria. The attending doctor requests a Ham's Acidified Serum Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit) is requested to monitor fluid shifts and haemoconcentration following the burn injury, which guides fluid resuscitation. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is centrifuged in a capillary or Wintrobe tube so that red cells pack down, and the height of the red cell column is expressed as a percentage of the total blood volume. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PCV is about 40–50% in men and 36–46% in women. A low PCV confirms anaemia while a raised PCV suggests polycythaemia, dehydration or haemoconcentration. Precautions: capillaries must be filled without air bubbles, sealed adequately, centrifuged at the correct speed and time, and read immediately after centrifugation before plasma and cells begin to remix.
questions.question: A 40-year-old man with extensive burns covering 30% of his body surface. The attending doctor requests a Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 26-year-old man with jaundice, dark urine and a falling haemoglobin. The attending doctor requests a Reticulocyte Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Reticulocyte Count is requested to assess the bone marrow's compensatory response to ongoing red cell destruction in suspected haemolytic anaemia. Principle: Reticulocytes contain residual ribosomal RNA that precipitates as a network when stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, allowing them to be counted as a percentage of red cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult reticulocyte count is about 0.5–2.5%. A raised count indicates active bone marrow response to anaemia or haemorrhage, while a low count in an anaemic patient suggests bone marrow failure. Precautions: staining must be done on fresh blood mixed thoroughly with the stain and incubated for the correct time, and at least 1000 red cells should be counted, preferably with a Miller eyepiece, to minimise sampling error.

questions.question: A 1-year-old month-old infant identified as having an abnormal result on newborn screening. The attending doctor requests a Sickling Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Sickling Test is requested to follow up the newborn screening result and confirm whether HbS is present before more definitive testing. Principle: Red cells are mixed with a reducing agent such as sodium metabisulphite that lowers oxygen tension, causing hemoglobin S to polymerise and distort the cells into a sickle shape under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no sickling and excludes HbS, while a positive test confirms the presence of HbS but cannot distinguish sickle cell trait from sickle cell disease. Precautions: a freshly prepared reducing agent must be used since an old reagent gives false negatives, the preparation must be sealed with a coverslip and petroleum jelly to prevent drying, and it must be observed for the recommended time as delayed reading may miss early sickling.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man who has received excessive heparin during a procedure. The attending doctor requests a Whole Blood Clotting Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Whole Blood Clotting Time is requested to detect gross prolongation of clotting time suggesting heparin overdose. Principle: Whole blood is placed in a plain glass tube and tilted at intervals until a clot forms, giving a simple bedside measure of the overall intrinsic clotting pathway. Normal result and interpretation: Normal clotting time is about 5–10 minutes. Marked prolongation suggests a severe coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia. Precautions: glass tubes must be clean and dry, the tube must be tilted gently and consistently without excessive agitation, and the test must be performed at a constant temperature since cold significantly prolongs clotting.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy with high fever, chills and vomiting in a malaria-endemic community. The attending doctor requests a Malaria Parasite Blood Film. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Malaria Parasite Blood Film is requested to directly identify malaria parasites, confirm the species, and quantify parasitaemia to guide treatment. Principle: Thick and thin blood films are stained with Giemsa or Field's stain; the thick film concentrates parasites for sensitive detection while the thin film preserves parasite and red cell morphology for species identification and parasitaemia quantification. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of parasites on a well-examined film excludes malaria at the time of testing. Presence of parasites confirms the diagnosis, with the species and percentage parasitaemia guiding severity assessment and treatment. Precautions: films must be made from fresh blood before antimalarial treatment reduces parasite counts, the staining buffer pH must be correctly maintained since incorrect pH affects parasite staining quality, and an adequate number of fields must be examined before a film is reported negative.

The HLA Typing is requested to determine her HLA type as part of assessing her suitability and compatibility as a living donor. Principle: Lymphocytes are separated and tested against panels of antisera of known HLA specificity in a microcytotoxicity assay, or by molecular methods, to determine the patient's HLA type for compatibility matching. Normal result and interpretation: A close match between donor and recipient HLA type reduces the risk of graft rejection and graft-versus-host disease; a significant mismatch increases the likelihood of rejection or complications following transplantation. Precautions: lymphocytes must be viable and adequately separated by density gradient centrifugation, trypan blue exclusion must confirm cell viability before testing, and the correct antisera panel and complement source must be used to avoid a false result.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman being evaluated as a potential kidney donor for a family member. The attending doctor requests a HLA Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Full Blood Count (FBC) is requested to assess for anaemia of pregnancy, which is common due to increased plasma volume and fetal iron demand, and to check white cell and platelet status before delivery. Principle: An automated or manual count of red cells, white cells and platelets together with haemoglobin estimation and packed cell volume, giving a composite picture of the cellular elements of blood. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult ranges are approximately Hb 13–17 g/dl (male) or 12–15 g/dl (female), PCV 40–50%, WBC 4.0–11.0 x10^9/L and platelets 150–400 x10^9/L. Values outside these ranges point to anaemia, infection, leukaemia or a bleeding disorder depending on which parameter is deranged. Precautions: the sample must be collected into EDTA and mixed gently by inversion to prevent clotting or platelet clumping, analysed within a few hours of collection, and the counting chamber or analyser aperture kept free of debris that could give false counts.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant and complains of tiredness and dizziness. The attending doctor requests a Full Blood Count (FBC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to detect a delayed antibody response to a previously transfused red cell antigen. Principle: Patient serum is incubated with reagent red cells of known antigen type; if antibody is present in the serum it binds the cells in vitro, and subsequent addition of antiglobulin reagent causes visible agglutination, detecting free circulating antibody. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination, indicating no clinically significant antibody in the serum; a newly positive screen supports a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction. Precautions: Incubate at 37°C for the correct time to allow antibody-antigen binding, and use a fresh antiglobulin reagent since a weakened reagent can give false-negative results.
questions.question: A patient develops unexplained falling haemoglobin one week after a transfusion, and is subsequently diagnosed with investigation of a delayed transfusion reaction. The attending doctor refers the patient for Indirect Antiglobulin Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm the presence of an inhibitor rather than a true factor deficiency. Principle: Patient plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma and the clotting time (PT or APTT) is repeated immediately and after incubation, distinguishing a factor deficiency (which corrects, since normal plasma supplies the missing factor) from an inhibitor (which does not fully correct). Normal result: Full correction of the prolonged clotting time into the normal range; failure to correct supports a lupus anticoagulant, prompting confirmatory phospholipid-based testing. Precautions: Repeat the test after incubation at 37°C for one to two hours, since some inhibitors (such as factor VIII autoantibodies) are time- and temperature-dependent and only become apparent on delayed testing.
questions.question: A woman with recurrent pregnancy loss and an unexplained prolonged APTT is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with lupus anticoagulant. The attending doctor refers the patient for Mixing Study (Correction Test). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Whole Blood Clotting Time is requested to quickly screen for a severe clotting abnormality before an emergency procedure in a resource-limited setting. Principle: Whole blood is placed in a plain glass tube and tilted at intervals until a clot forms, giving a simple bedside measure of the overall intrinsic clotting pathway. Normal result and interpretation: Normal clotting time is about 5–10 minutes. Marked prolongation suggests a severe coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia. Precautions: glass tubes must be clean and dry, the tube must be tilted gently and consistently without excessive agitation, and the test must be performed at a constant temperature since cold significantly prolongs clotting.
questions.question: A 30-year-old man in a peripheral health centre requiring urgent pre-operative screening. The attending doctor requests a Whole Blood Clotting Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to help distinguish haemolysis from hepatic or obstructive causes of jaundice. Principle: An immunoturbidimetric assay measures haptoglobin, a plasma protein that binds free haemoglobin released from lysed red cells; because the haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex is rapidly cleared by the liver, intravascular haemolysis depletes circulating haptoglobin. Normal result: Approximately 30-200 mg/dL; a low level supports a haemolytic cause, while a normal level favours hepatic or obstructive causes. Precautions: Interpret with caution since haptoglobin is also an acute-phase reactant that can be falsely normal or raised in the presence of concurrent inflammation despite ongoing haemolysis.
questions.question: A jaundiced patient without evidence of biliary obstruction is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with differentiating haemolytic from other causes of jaundice. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Haptoglobin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity is requested to investigate for haemochromatosis, in which iron is elevated and TIBC saturation is markedly increased. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after its release from transferrin, while total iron binding capacity measures the maximum iron that transferrin can bind, together indicating percentage transferrin saturation. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum iron is about 10–30 micromol/L with TIBC around 45–70 micromol/L. Low iron with high TIBC indicates iron deficiency anaemia, while low iron with low or normal TIBC suggests anaemia of chronic disease. Precautions: the sample should be collected fasting in the morning to avoid diurnal variation, haemolysed samples must be rejected as they falsely raise the iron result, and all glassware used must be iron-free to avoid contamination.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man with unexplained fatigue, bronzed skin and joint pain. The attending doctor requests a Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 25-year-old woman with fever, anaemia and jaundice of unclear cause in an endemic area. The attending doctor requests a Malaria Parasite Blood Film. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Malaria Parasite Blood Film is requested to investigate malaria as a cause of her anaemia and jaundice alongside other possible diagnoses. Principle: Thick and thin blood films are stained with Giemsa or Field's stain; the thick film concentrates parasites for sensitive detection while the thin film preserves parasite and red cell morphology for species identification and parasitaemia quantification. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of parasites on a well-examined film excludes malaria at the time of testing. Presence of parasites confirms the diagnosis, with the species and percentage parasitaemia guiding severity assessment and treatment. Precautions: films must be made from fresh blood before antimalarial treatment reduces parasite counts, the staining buffer pH must be correctly maintained since incorrect pH affects parasite staining quality, and an adequate number of fields must be examined before a film is reported negative.

questions.question: A patient with a history of easy bruising is scheduled for major surgery, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-operative coagulation screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for Prothrombin Time (PT/INR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to exclude an extrinsic pathway clotting defect before the procedure. Principle: Tissue thromboplastin and calcium are added to citrated plasma, and the time taken to clot is measured, reflecting the integrity of the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways (factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 11-14 seconds, or an INR of approximately 0.8-1.2 in a person not on anticoagulants; a normal PT reassures against a significant extrinsic pathway deficiency, while prolongation requires further work-up before surgery. Precautions: Fill the citrate tube exactly to the mark since an incorrect blood-to-citrate ratio distorts results, and process the sample within a few hours as factor V and VII activity decline on standing.

The Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) is requested to screen for a lupus anticoagulant, which characteristically prolongs the APTT without necessarily causing bleeding. Principle: A contact activator such as kaolin, together with phospholipid and calcium, is added to citrated plasma to activate the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the clotting time is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal APTT is approximately 30–40 seconds. Prolongation suggests deficiency of an intrinsic pathway factor such as VIII, IX, XI or XII, seen in haemophilia, or the presence of heparin or a lupus anticoagulant. Precautions: plasma must not contact glass surfaces as this prematurely activates factor XII, the phospholipid reagent must be incubated with plasma for the recommended time before calcium is added, and samples for factor assay must be kept frozen or on ice if not tested immediately.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman booked for surgery with a history of recurrent miscarriage and previous clot. The attending doctor requests a Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 68-year-old man with known chronic lymphocytic leukaemia develops new pallor and jaundice, and is subsequently diagnosed with lymphoproliferative disease-associated haemolysis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Direct Antiglobulin (Direct Coombs) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm secondary autoimmune haemolysis complicating his underlying malignancy. Principle: Anti-human globulin reagent is added to washed patient red cells; if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement, the reagent cross-links adjacent cells to produce visible agglutination. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination; a positive result supports an autoimmune process requiring corticosteroid therapy alongside management of the underlying leukaemia. Precautions: Wash the red cells thoroughly to remove all free unbound globulin before adding the antiglobulin reagent, since inadequate washing causes false-negative results through neutralisation.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with vomiting and diarrhoea for two days, appearing severely dehydrated. The attending doctor requests a Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit) is requested to check for haemoconcentration from dehydration, which can falsely raise other blood parameters and affect fluid management. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is centrifuged in a capillary or Wintrobe tube so that red cells pack down, and the height of the red cell column is expressed as a percentage of the total blood volume. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PCV is about 40–50% in men and 36–46% in women. A low PCV confirms anaemia while a raised PCV suggests polycythaemia, dehydration or haemoconcentration. Precautions: capillaries must be filled without air bubbles, sealed adequately, centrifuged at the correct speed and time, and read immediately after centrifugation before plasma and cells begin to remix.

questions.question: A chronic myeloid leukaemia patient is reviewed six months after starting imatinib, and is subsequently diagnosed with monitoring treatment response. The attending doctor refers the patient for Cytogenetic Analysis for Philadelphia Chromosome (BCR-ABL). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to quantify residual disease and assess molecular response to therapy. Principle: Metaphase chromosome preparation or fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) detects the t(9;22) translocation forming the Philadelphia chromosome, or the resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene product is quantified by RT-PCR. Normal result: Absence of the t(9;22) translocation or BCR-ABL fusion transcript; a falling BCR-ABL transcript level indicates a good treatment response, while a rising level suggests resistance. Precautions: Ensure the marrow or blood sample is fresh and contains adequate dividing cells for metaphase analysis, and use molecular quantification (RT-PCR) rather than karyotyping alone for sensitive monitoring of minimal residual disease.

The Platelet Count is requested to monitor for the thrombocytopenia characteristic of dengue fever, which guides admission and monitoring decisions. Principle: Platelets are counted directly using a haemocytometer under phase contrast after appropriate dilution, or automatically by impedance/optical methods, based on their small size and characteristic light scatter. Normal result and interpretation: Normal platelet count is 150–400 x10^9/L. A count below this range indicates thrombocytopenia with bleeding risk while a count above suggests thrombocytosis. Precautions: blood must be collected into EDTA without clotting, the film must be checked for platelet clumps that cause spuriously low automated counts, and skin puncture blood should not be used since tissue fluid promotes platelet clumping.
questions.question: A 25-year-old woman with high fever, headache and muscle pain in a dengue-endemic area. The attending doctor requests a Platelet Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient with fever of unknown origin and pancytopenia is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with granulomatous marrow disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Trephine Biopsy. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to look for granulomas suggesting tuberculosis or fungal infection of the marrow. Principle: A core of marrow tissue is removed with a trephine needle, processed histologically and examined intact, preserving marrow architecture in a way that aspiration alone cannot, allowing assessment of cellularity, fibrosis and focal lesions. Normal result: Normal marrow architecture with preserved trilineage haematopoiesis and no fibrosis or abnormal infiltrate; caseating granulomas support tuberculous marrow involvement, guiding anti-tuberculous therapy. Precautions: Obtain an adequately long core (at least 1.5-2 cm) to allow representative assessment, and handle the specimen gently to avoid crush artefact that distorts cell morphology.

The test was requested to identify other affected males in the family given its X-linked inheritance. Principle: A quantitative spectrophotometric or fluorescent-spot assay measures the activity of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that protects red cells from oxidative stress by generating NADPH. Normal result: Enzyme activity within the laboratory's established reference range (typically reported relative to a normal control); reduced activity confirms he shares the same deficiency and needs the same dietary and drug precautions. Precautions: Avoid testing during or shortly after an acute haemolytic episode, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a true deficiency; retest several weeks later if an acute episode has just occurred.
questions.question: The brother of a boy recently diagnosed with G6PD deficiency is brought for testing, and is subsequently diagnosed with family screening after index case. The attending doctor refers the patient for G6PD Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain is requested to provide additional cytochemical information to complement the peroxidase result in classifying his leukaemia. Principle: This reaction detects glycogen and other polysaccharides in cells; lymphoblasts, particularly in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, often show coarse block positivity while myeloblasts and normal erythroblasts are typically negative or weakly diffuse. Normal result and interpretation: A coarse granular or block PAS-positive pattern in blast cells supports acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while diffuse or negative staining is more typical of myeloid lineage; strong diffuse positivity in erythroid precursors suggests erythroleukaemia. Precautions: films must be well fixed before staining, the periodic acid and Schiff reagent must be fresh and correctly prepared, and controls must be run to confirm the reaction is working correctly.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a leukaemia of uncertain lineage after an inconclusive peroxidase stain. The attending doctor requests a Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Haemoglobin Estimation is requested to assess for nutritional anaemia arising from malnutrition, which is common in undernourished children. Principle: Haemoglobin is converted to a stable coloured compound (acid haematin or cyanmethaemoglobin) whose colour intensity, read colorimetrically, is proportional to haemoglobin concentration. Normal result and interpretation: Normal values are 13–17 g/dl in men and 12–15 g/dl in women. Values below this confirm anaemia while markedly elevated values suggest polycythaemia or dehydration. Precautions: reagents must be fresh and correctly diluted, the exact volume of blood must be drawn without air bubbles, and colour development must be allowed to reach completion before reading to avoid underestimation.
questions.question: A 2-year-old boy who is severely underweight with poor dietary intake. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Estimation. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm B12 deficiency as the cause of her megaloblastic anaemia. Principle: An automated immunoassay (competitive binding or chemiluminescence) measures circulating cobalamin, which is required as a cofactor for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells including erythroid precursors. Normal result: Approximately 200-900 pg/mL; a low level supports deficiency, which should prompt testing for intrinsic factor antibodies to confirm pernicious anaemia. Precautions: Take the sample before any B12 injection is given, protect from prolonged light exposure which can degrade the vitamin, and interpret low-normal results cautiously alongside methylmalonic acid if pernicious anaemia is strongly suspected.
questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with fatigue, glossitis and peripheral paraesthesia, and is subsequently diagnosed with pernicious anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Vitamin B12 Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Mixed Lymphocyte Culture is requested to assess donor lymphocyte reactivity as part of understanding and planning around her earlier complication. Principle: Recipient lymphocytes are cultured together with irradiated or mitomycin-treated donor lymphocytes, and the degree of recipient lymphocyte proliferation in response to donor Class II antigen differences is measured, usually by radioactive thymidine incorporation. Normal result and interpretation: Low proliferation indicates close Class II compatibility and lower rejection risk, while high proliferation indicates significant mismatch and a higher risk of graft rejection or graft-versus-host disease. Precautions: donor lymphocytes must be adequately irradiated or treated to prevent their own proliferation from confounding the result, sterile technique must be maintained throughout the culture period, and viable lymphocyte counts must be standardised between test wells.
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman being evaluated for a repeat transplant after graft-versus-host disease from a prior procedure. The attending doctor requests a Mixed Lymphocyte Culture. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Coagulation Factor Assay is requested to quantify factor IX activity and confirm the specific type of haemophilia present. Principle: Patient plasma is diluted and mixed with plasma known to be deficient in the specific factor being tested, and correction of the clotting time is compared against a standard curve made from pooled normal plasma to calculate percentage factor activity. Normal result and interpretation: Normal factor activity is about 50–150% of the standard. Levels below 50%, and especially below 5%, indicate significant deficiency of that factor, as seen in haemophilia A (factor VIII), haemophilia B (factor IX) or other factor deficiencies. Precautions: the specific factor-deficient substrate plasma must be genuinely deficient only in that factor, samples must be kept frozen or on ice to preserve labile factors such as VIII, and a fresh standard curve must be prepared with each batch of tests.
questions.question: A 10-year-old boy with a bleeding tendency and a family history suggestive of haemophilia B. The attending doctor requests a Coagulation Factor Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain is requested to help distinguish lymphoblasts from myeloblasts based on the characteristic PAS staining pattern. Principle: This reaction detects glycogen and other polysaccharides in cells; lymphoblasts, particularly in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, often show coarse block positivity while myeloblasts and normal erythroblasts are typically negative or weakly diffuse. Normal result and interpretation: A coarse granular or block PAS-positive pattern in blast cells supports acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while diffuse or negative staining is more typical of myeloid lineage; strong diffuse positivity in erythroid precursors suggests erythroleukaemia. Precautions: films must be well fixed before staining, the periodic acid and Schiff reagent must be fresh and correctly prepared, and controls must be run to confirm the reaction is working correctly.
questions.question: A 10-year-old girl with an acute leukaemia whose blast cells need further lineage characterisation. The attending doctor requests a Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Ham's Acidified Serum Test is requested to investigate for chronic intravascular haemolysis from paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria as the source of the iron loss. Principle: Patient red cells are incubated in fresh, acidified normal serum, which activates complement via the alternate pathway; abnormally complement-sensitive cells characteristic of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria lyse under these acidic conditions. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no lysis, while a positive test, showing lysis in acidified serum but not in heat-inactivated serum, confirms paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Precautions: fresh serum must be used as a complement source since stored serum loses complement activity, appropriate control tubes with heat-inactivated serum and normal cells must be run in parallel, and the pH of the acidified serum must be accurately adjusted.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with unexplained iron deficiency due to chronic urinary iron loss. The attending doctor requests a Ham's Acidified Serum Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit) is requested to establish his baseline red cell mass before surgery so any intra-operative blood loss can be accurately assessed. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is centrifuged in a capillary or Wintrobe tube so that red cells pack down, and the height of the red cell column is expressed as a percentage of the total blood volume. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PCV is about 40–50% in men and 36–46% in women. A low PCV confirms anaemia while a raised PCV suggests polycythaemia, dehydration or haemoconcentration. Precautions: capillaries must be filled without air bubbles, sealed adequately, centrifuged at the correct speed and time, and read immediately after centrifugation before plasma and cells begin to remix.
questions.question: A 34-year-old man booked for a caesarean-section blood loss backup transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 3-year-old boy of West African descent with recurrent painful swelling of the hands and feet. The attending doctor requests a Sickling Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Sickling Test is requested to screen for sickle cell disease as the underlying cause of his recurrent painful dactylitis episodes. Principle: Red cells are mixed with a reducing agent such as sodium metabisulphite that lowers oxygen tension, causing hemoglobin S to polymerise and distort the cells into a sickle shape under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no sickling and excludes HbS, while a positive test confirms the presence of HbS but cannot distinguish sickle cell trait from sickle cell disease. Precautions: a freshly prepared reducing agent must be used since an old reagent gives false negatives, the preparation must be sealed with a coverslip and petroleum jelly to prevent drying, and it must be observed for the recommended time as delayed reading may miss early sickling.

The Haemoglobin Estimation is requested to quantify blood loss from postpartum haemorrhage and determine whether transfusion is required. Principle: Haemoglobin is converted to a stable coloured compound (acid haematin or cyanmethaemoglobin) whose colour intensity, read colorimetrically, is proportional to haemoglobin concentration. Normal result and interpretation: Normal values are 13–17 g/dl in men and 12–15 g/dl in women. Values below this confirm anaemia while markedly elevated values suggest polycythaemia or dehydration. Precautions: reagents must be fresh and correctly diluted, the exact volume of blood must be drawn without air bubbles, and colour development must be allowed to reach completion before reading to avoid underestimation.
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman who delivered a baby six hours ago and is now bleeding heavily. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Estimation. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to demonstrate the functional effect of aspirin on platelet aggregation. Principle: A standardised skin incision (Ivy method) is made and the time to cessation of bleeding is measured, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall in primary haemostasis. Normal result: Approximately 2-9 minutes, depending on the method used; a prolonged bleeding time confirms impaired platelet function attributable to the drug. Precautions: Use a standardised, calibrated incision device and consistent incision depth, and avoid the test in patients taking aspirin or NSAIDs within the preceding week unless specifically assessing their effect.
questions.question: A patient on regular aspirin presents with excessive bruising, and is subsequently diagnosed with aspirin-induced platelet dysfunction. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bleeding Time. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm G6PD deficiency as the trigger for the drug-induced haemolysis. Principle: A quantitative spectrophotometric or fluorescent-spot assay measures the activity of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that protects red cells from oxidative stress by generating NADPH. Normal result: Enzyme activity within the laboratory's established reference range (typically reported relative to a normal control); reduced activity confirms the diagnosis, and the offending drug must be stopped and avoided in future. Precautions: Avoid testing during or shortly after an acute haemolytic episode, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a true deficiency; retest several weeks later if an acute episode has just occurred.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden haemolysis after starting primaquine for malaria treatment, and is subsequently diagnosed with antimalarial-induced haemolysis. The attending doctor refers the patient for G6PD Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm B12 deficiency as the underlying neurological cause. Principle: An automated immunoassay (competitive binding or chemiluminescence) measures circulating cobalamin, which is required as a cofactor for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells including erythroid precursors. Normal result: Approximately 200-900 pg/mL; a markedly low level supports the diagnosis, and urgent replacement is needed to prevent permanent neurological damage. Precautions: Take the sample before any B12 injection is given, protect from prolonged light exposure which can degrade the vitamin, and interpret low-normal results cautiously alongside methylmalonic acid if pernicious anaemia is strongly suspected.
questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with unsteady gait and loss of vibration sense in the legs, and is subsequently diagnosed with subacute combined degeneration. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Vitamin B12 Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to distinguish marrow infiltration (e.g. leukaemia) from marrow failure as the cause. Principle: A needle is inserted into the marrow cavity (usually posterior iliac crest or sternum) to aspirate a liquid marrow sample, which is smeared, stained and examined for cellularity, maturation and abnormal cell populations. Normal result: Normocellular marrow with an orderly maturation sequence of erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages and no abnormal infiltrate; a hypercellular marrow with abnormal cells suggests infiltration, while hypocellularity suggests aplasia. Precautions: Prepare smears immediately before the sample clots, obtain particles for a representative trephine/clot section, and maintain strict asepsis at the puncture site to prevent infection.
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with pallor, recurrent infections and easy bruising, and is subsequently diagnosed with unexplained pancytopenia in a child. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Aspiration. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to detect carrier status for sickle cell trait or thalassaemia before conception. Principle: Hb variants are separated on cellulose acetate (alkaline pH) or citrate agar (acid pH) according to their electrical charge, allowing identification of HbA, HbS, HbC, HbF and other variants by their migration pattern. Normal result: Predominantly HbA (>95%), with HbA2 1.5-3.5% and HbF less than 1% in adults; detection of HbAS or HbAC in both partners carries reproductive risk and warrants genetic counselling. Precautions: Run both alkaline and acid media to resolve variants that co-migrate on one system alone, and include known controls on every run to validate migration positions.
questions.question: A couple planning marriage requests screening for inherited haemoglobin disorders, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-marital genetic counselling. The attending doctor refers the patient for Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 35-year-old woman with severe symptomatic anaemia requiring packed red cell transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch) is requested to confirm that the selected donor units will not cause a haemolytic transfusion reaction before they are given. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and recipient red cells with donor serum (minor crossmatch), incubated at 37°C and tested by the antiglobulin technique to detect incompatibility before transfusion. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of agglutination or haemolysis in the major crossmatch indicates compatibility and the unit is safe to transfuse; agglutination indicates incompatibility and that unit must not be given. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before the antiglobulin phase, correct incubation time and temperature must be observed, and patient identification on the sample and request form must be verified to prevent transfusion of the wrong unit.

The Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score is requested to help distinguish chronic myeloid leukaemia, in which LAP is typically low, from a reactive leukaemoid reaction. Principle: Neutrophils on a blood film are stained for alkaline phosphatase activity and each cell is scored according to the intensity of staining, giving a total score reflecting neutrophil enzyme activity. Normal result and interpretation: A normal LAP score is roughly 20–100 depending on the scoring system used. A markedly low score is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia, while a high score is seen in leukaemoid reactions and polycythaemia vera. Precautions: the blood film must be fresh since LAP activity deteriorates on storage, staining must be carried out under standardised conditions, and at least 100 neutrophils should be scored to obtain a reliable result.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with marked splenomegaly and an extremely high white cell count of mixed maturity. The attending doctor requests a Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A neonate presents with unexpected bleeding from the umbilical stump, and is subsequently diagnosed with vitamin K deficiency. The attending doctor refers the patient for Prothrombin Time (PT/INR). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency causing haemorrhagic disease of the newborn. Principle: Tissue thromboplastin and calcium are added to citrated plasma, and the time taken to clot is measured, reflecting the integrity of the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways (factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 11-14 seconds, or an INR of approximately 0.8-1.2 in a person not on anticoagulants; a prolonged PT that corrects with vitamin K confirms the diagnosis. Precautions: Fill the citrate tube exactly to the mark since an incorrect blood-to-citrate ratio distorts results, and process the sample within a few hours as factor V and VII activity decline on standing.

The test was requested to assess the white cell count and differential as part of a septic screen. Principle: Whole blood is passed through an automated haematology analyser that uses electrical impedance and/or light-scatter to count and size red cells, white cells and platelets, and to compute derived indices such as MCV and MCH. Normal result: Hb 11.5-16.5 g/dL, WBC 4-11 x10^9/L, platelets 150-450 x10^9/L, with all indices within age/sex-adjusted ranges; marked neutrophilic leukocytosis supports bacterial infection, whereas a normal count makes it less likely. Precautions: Draw into a properly filled EDTA bottle, mix by gentle inversion (not shaking) to prevent clot or haemolysis, and analyse within 4-6 hours as prolonged storage causes cell swelling and falsely raised MCV.
questions.question: A febrile 6-year-old boy with a swollen, painful knee is seen in the children's emergency room, and is subsequently diagnosed with acute bacterial infection. The attending doctor refers the patient for Full Blood Count (FBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
