Increased fragility (lysis at higher saline concentration) suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while decreased fragility suggests thalassaemia or iron deficiency. Precautions: blood must be defibrinated or collected into heparin rather than EDTA, saline dilutions must be prepared accurately and freshly, and tubes must be mixed gently to avoid mechanical haemolysis that would give a false result.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman undergoing pre-operative coagulation screening before elective surgery. The attending doctor requests a Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) is requested to complete the routine coagulation screen alongside the prothrombin time before she proceeds to theatre. Principle: A contact activator such as kaolin, together with phospholipid and calcium, is added to citrated plasma to activate the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the clotting time is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal APTT is approximately 30–40 seconds. Prolongation suggests deficiency of an intrinsic pathway factor such as VIII, IX, XI or XII, seen in haemophilia, or the presence of heparin or a lupus anticoagulant. Precautions: plasma must not contact glass surfaces as this prematurely activates factor XII, the phospholipid reagent must be incubated with plasma for the recommended time before calcium is added, and samples for factor assay must be kept frozen or on ice if not tested immediately.

The test was requested to demonstrate ongoing fibrin formation and breakdown as part of a DIC screen. Principle: An immunoassay detects D-dimer, a specific breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin, whose presence indicates that both clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis have occurred. Normal result: Below the assay-specific cut-off, usually less than 0.5 micrograms/mL FEU; a markedly raised level supports active DIC alongside the other coagulation abnormalities. Precautions: Recognise that many conditions besides thrombosis (pregnancy, infection, malignancy, recent surgery) raise D-dimer, so a positive result is not diagnostic on its own; primarily use a negative result to help exclude thrombosis in low-probability patients.
questions.question: A septic patient develops widespread bruising and prolonged clotting times, and is subsequently diagnosed with disseminated intravascular coagulation. The attending doctor refers the patient for D-Dimer Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to obtain a rapid estimate of red cell mass while awaiting a full blood count. Principle: A blood sample in a capillary or vacutainer tube is centrifuged so that red cells pack at the bottom, and the proportion of the column occupied by red cells is read as the packed cell volume. Normal result: 36-48% in women and 40-52% in men; a low PCV supports the need for blood transfusion alongside clinical assessment. Precautions: Fill capillary tubes fully without air bubbles, seal one end properly before centrifuging, and centrifuge for the standard validated time and speed to ensure complete red cell packing.
questions.question: A trauma patient with ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding is being resuscitated, and is subsequently diagnosed with transfusion decision-making. The attending doctor refers the patient for Packed Cell Volume (Haematocrit). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to identify a subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with a distinct prognosis and treatment approach. Principle: Metaphase chromosome preparation or fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) detects the t(9;22) translocation forming the Philadelphia chromosome, or the resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene product is quantified by RT-PCR. Normal result: Absence of the t(9;22) translocation or BCR-ABL fusion transcript; detection of the translocation confirms Philadelphia-positive disease, warranting tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in addition to chemotherapy. Precautions: Ensure the marrow or blood sample is fresh and contains adequate dividing cells for metaphase analysis, and use molecular quantification (RT-PCR) rather than karyotyping alone for sensitive monitoring of minimal residual disease.
questions.question: An adult presents with a rapidly progressive pancytopenia and lymphoblasts on film, and is subsequently diagnosed with Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Cytogenetic Analysis for Philadelphia Chromosome (BCR-ABL). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 30-year-old woman in active labour with placenta praevia at risk of major haemorrhage. The attending doctor requests a ABO Blood Grouping. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The ABO Blood Grouping is requested to determine her ABO group urgently so compatible blood can be prepared in case of severe bleeding. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed separately with known anti-A and anti-B antisera (forward grouping) and patient serum is mixed with known A and B cells (reverse grouping); agglutination identifies the ABO group present. Normal result and interpretation: Consistent forward and reverse grouping results confirm the patient's ABO group as A, B, AB or O. Discrepancies between forward and reverse results require further investigation before blood can be issued. Precautions: fresh antisera of adequate potency must be used, an adequate cell suspension concentration must be prepared, and both forward and reverse grouping must always be performed and cross-checked to avoid mistyping.

questions.question: A 10-year-old girl with severe aplastic anaemia requiring a bone marrow transplant. The attending doctor requests a HLA Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The HLA Typing is requested to determine her HLA type so that a matched sibling or unrelated donor can be identified. Principle: Lymphocytes are separated and tested against panels of antisera of known HLA specificity in a microcytotoxicity assay, or by molecular methods, to determine the patient's HLA type for compatibility matching. Normal result and interpretation: A close match between donor and recipient HLA type reduces the risk of graft rejection and graft-versus-host disease; a significant mismatch increases the likelihood of rejection or complications following transplantation. Precautions: lymphocytes must be viable and adequately separated by density gradient centrifugation, trypan blue exclusion must confirm cell viability before testing, and the correct antisera panel and complement source must be used to avoid a false result.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy who developed acute jaundice and dark urine after eating fava beans. The attending doctor requests a G6PD Screening Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The G6PD Screening Test is requested to confirm favism secondary to G6PD deficiency as the cause of his acute haemolysis. Principle: Red cell lysate is incubated with glucose-6-phosphate and NADP; adequate G6PD enzyme generates NADPH, which fluoresces under ultraviolet light, whereas deficient samples show little or no fluorescence. Normal result and interpretation: A normal (fluorescent) result excludes significant deficiency, while absent or reduced fluorescence indicates G6PD deficiency, predisposing the patient to oxidative haemolysis after certain drugs, infections or fava beans. Precautions: the test should ideally be delayed until after an acute haemolytic episode has resolved, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a deficiency, and reagents must be protected from light and used fresh.

The Plasma Fibrinogen Assay is requested to check for the low fibrinogen characteristic of obstetric disseminated intravascular coagulation. Principle: Plasma fibrinogen is quantified by measuring the clotting time after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to fibrinogen concentration, or by a direct chemical or immunological method. Normal result and interpretation: Normal plasma fibrinogen is about 2–4 g/L. Low levels are seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation and severe liver disease, while raised levels occur as an acute phase response to inflammation. Precautions: the standard fibrinogen curve must be freshly prepared, citrated plasma must be free of clots, and haemolysed samples must be avoided as they interfere with accurate detection of the clotting endpoint.
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with placental abruption and heavy vaginal bleeding in late pregnancy. The attending doctor requests a Plasma Fibrinogen Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to help exclude iron deficiency as an alternative or coexisting cause of his microcytic anaemia. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after releasing iron from transferrin, while TIBC is determined by saturating transferrin with excess iron and measuring the total binding capacity, allowing calculation of transferrin saturation. Normal result: Serum iron 50-170 micrograms/dL, TIBC 250-450 micrograms/dL, transferrin saturation 20-50%; normal iron studies in a microcytic child should prompt consideration of lead toxicity or thalassaemia. Precautions: Collect the sample in the morning when iron levels are most stable, avoid haemolysis which falsely raises serum iron, and ensure the patient has not taken iron supplements in the preceding 24 hours.
questions.question: A 4-year-old with pica and developmental delay is investigated for anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with lead poisoning work-up. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 35-year-old woman with gum infiltration, bleeding and monocytic-appearing blast cells. The attending doctor requests a Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain is requested to assess peroxidase reactivity in suspected monocytic leukaemia, which is often only weakly positive. Principle: Myeloid cells contain peroxidase enzyme in their primary granules that reacts with hydrogen peroxide and a chromogen to give a coloured precipitate, positive in myeloblasts but negative in lymphoblasts. Normal result and interpretation: Peroxidase positivity in blast cells confirms myeloid lineage (acute myeloid leukaemia) while peroxidase-negative blasts suggest lymphoid lineage (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia). Precautions: fresh, well-fixed films must be used since old films lose enzyme activity, reagents must be prepared and used promptly as they deteriorate quickly, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included with every batch.

The test was requested to establish the severity of his anaemia of chronic disease before erythropoietin therapy is considered. Principle: Whole blood is passed through an automated haematology analyser that uses electrical impedance and/or light-scatter to count and size red cells, white cells and platelets, and to compute derived indices such as MCV and MCH. Normal result: Hb 11.5-16.5 g/dL, WBC 4-11 x10^9/L, platelets 150-450 x10^9/L, with all indices within age/sex-adjusted ranges; a normocytic normochromic anaemia is expected, and any microcytosis should prompt a search for coexisting iron deficiency. Precautions: Draw into a properly filled EDTA bottle, mix by gentle inversion (not shaking) to prevent clot or haemolysis, and analyse within 4-6 hours as prolonged storage causes cell swelling and falsely raised MCV.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man on long-term dialysis complains of increasing tiredness and breathlessness, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic kidney disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Full Blood Count (FBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 45-year-old man scheduled for elective hernia repair surgery next week. The attending doctor requests a Full Blood Count (FBC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Full Blood Count (FBC) is requested as part of routine pre-operative work-up to ensure haemoglobin, white cell and platelet levels are adequate for safe anaesthesia and surgery. Principle: An automated or manual count of red cells, white cells and platelets together with haemoglobin estimation and packed cell volume, giving a composite picture of the cellular elements of blood. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult ranges are approximately Hb 13–17 g/dl (male) or 12–15 g/dl (female), PCV 40–50%, WBC 4.0–11.0 x10^9/L and platelets 150–400 x10^9/L. Values outside these ranges point to anaemia, infection, leukaemia or a bleeding disorder depending on which parameter is deranged. Precautions: the sample must be collected into EDTA and mixed gently by inversion to prevent clotting or platelet clumping, analysed within a few hours of collection, and the counting chamber or analyser aperture kept free of debris that could give false counts.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man started on an antithyroid drug and now presenting with fever and sore throat. The attending doctor requests a White Cell Differential Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The White Cell Differential Count is requested to check for agranulocytosis, a recognised drug-induced complication that would require the drug to be stopped immediately. Principle: A well-made, Romanowsky-stained blood film is examined under oil immersion to identify and enumerate the different types of white cells, revealing shifts in proportion or the presence of abnormal cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal differential is roughly neutrophils 40–75%, lymphocytes 20–45%, monocytes 2–10%, eosinophils 1–6% and basophils 0–1%. Deviations indicate infection, allergy, parasitic disease or leukaemia depending on the cell type affected. Precautions: the film must be made from fresh blood spread thinly and evenly to avoid EDTA storage artefact, and counting must be performed in a representative area of the film where cells are well separated and not overlapping.

The test was requested to detect a significant fall suggestive of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Principle: An automated haematology analyser counts platelets using impedance or optical light-scatter methods, distinguishing them from red and white cells by their smaller size. Normal result: 150-450 x10^9/L; a fall of more than 50% from baseline supports the diagnosis, requiring immediate cessation of heparin. Precautions: Confirm any very low automated count by examining a blood film to exclude EDTA-induced platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia), which can falsely lower the automated count.
questions.question: A patient on heparin for five days develops a new falling platelet count and a leg swelling, and is subsequently diagnosed with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Platelet Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 55-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops mild anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with anaemia of chronic disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Ferritin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to distinguish true iron deficiency from anaemia of chronic disease, where iron is sequestered rather than depleted. Principle: An immunoassay (ELISA or chemiluminescence) measures serum ferritin, an acute-phase protein that reflects total body iron stores, since it correlates with the amount of iron sequestered within tissue macrophages and hepatocytes. Normal result: Approximately 15-150 ng/mL in women and 15-200 ng/mL in men; a normal or raised ferritin despite anaemia favours chronic disease over true iron deficiency. Precautions: Interpret cautiously in the presence of infection or inflammation, which raises ferritin independently of iron status as an acute-phase reactant, and avoid haemolysed samples which falsely elevate results.

The Plasma Fibrinogen Assay is requested to note whether fibrinogen is elevated as part of a general acute phase response to his infection. Principle: Plasma fibrinogen is quantified by measuring the clotting time after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to fibrinogen concentration, or by a direct chemical or immunological method. Normal result and interpretation: Normal plasma fibrinogen is about 2–4 g/L. Low levels are seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation and severe liver disease, while raised levels occur as an acute phase response to inflammation. Precautions: the standard fibrinogen curve must be freshly prepared, citrated plasma must be free of clots, and haemolysed samples must be avoided as they interfere with accurate detection of the clotting endpoint.
questions.question: A 40-year-old man with an active infection and generally raised inflammatory markers. The attending doctor requests a Plasma Fibrinogen Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to exclude malignancy when lymphadenopathy fails to resolve after antibiotics. Principle: An excised lymph node is fixed, processed and stained (with immunohistochemistry as needed) to examine nodal architecture and identify malignant infiltration, distinguishing reactive hyperplasia from lymphoma or metastatic disease. Normal result: Preserved normal nodal architecture with reactive follicular hyperplasia and no malignant infiltrate; preserved architecture with reactive follicular hyperplasia reassures against malignancy and supports an infective cause. Precautions: Excise an entire, representative node rather than a fine-needle sample where lymphoma is suspected, since architecture is essential for classification, and transport the fresh specimen promptly to avoid autolysis.
questions.question: A child presents with tender, enlarged cervical nodes following a recent throat infection, and is subsequently diagnosed with reactive lymphadenopathy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Lymph Node Biopsy (Histopathology). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A patient treated for malaria a week earlier returns with recurring fever, and is subsequently diagnosed with recurrent fever after apparent treatment. The attending doctor refers the patient for Thick and Thin Blood Film for Malaria Parasites. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to distinguish true treatment failure or relapse from a new infection or an unrelated cause of fever. Principle: A thick film concentrates red cells to increase sensitivity for detecting parasites, while a thin film preserves red cell and parasite morphology for species identification, both examined microscopically after Giemsa staining. Normal result: No malaria parasites seen on thick or thin film; persistent parasitaemia despite treatment suggests resistance or inadequate dosing, requiring second-line therapy. Precautions: Prepare films from a fresh fingerprick or anticoagulated sample without delay, ensure correct Giemsa staining pH and time for accurate parasite morphology, and examine an adequate number of fields before reporting a film negative.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with active rheumatoid arthritis develops mild anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with anaemia of chronic disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to differentiate chronic disease anaemia, where both iron and TIBC are typically low, from true deficiency. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after releasing iron from transferrin, while TIBC is determined by saturating transferrin with excess iron and measuring the total binding capacity, allowing calculation of transferrin saturation. Normal result: Serum iron 50-170 micrograms/dL, TIBC 250-450 micrograms/dL, transferrin saturation 20-50%; low iron with a low or normal TIBC favours chronic disease rather than deficiency. Precautions: Collect the sample in the morning when iron levels are most stable, avoid haemolysis which falsely raises serum iron, and ensure the patient has not taken iron supplements in the preceding 24 hours.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with anaemia and abnormal erythroid precursors suggestive of erythroleukaemia. The attending doctor requests a Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain is requested to check for strong diffuse PAS positivity in erythroid precursors, a recognised feature of erythroleukaemia. Principle: This reaction detects glycogen and other polysaccharides in cells; lymphoblasts, particularly in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, often show coarse block positivity while myeloblasts and normal erythroblasts are typically negative or weakly diffuse. Normal result and interpretation: A coarse granular or block PAS-positive pattern in blast cells supports acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while diffuse or negative staining is more typical of myeloid lineage; strong diffuse positivity in erythroid precursors suggests erythroleukaemia. Precautions: films must be well fixed before staining, the periodic acid and Schiff reagent must be fresh and correctly prepared, and controls must be run to confirm the reaction is working correctly.

The test was requested to reassess inhibitor strength before selecting the appropriate bypassing agent. Principle: Patient plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma and the clotting time (PT or APTT) is repeated immediately and after incubation, distinguishing a factor deficiency (which corrects, since normal plasma supplies the missing factor) from an inhibitor (which does not fully correct). Normal result: Full correction of the prolonged clotting time into the normal range; persistent non-correction confirms ongoing inhibitor activity, guiding the choice of treatment. Precautions: Repeat the test after incubation at 37°C for one to two hours, since some inhibitors (such as factor VIII autoantibodies) are time- and temperature-dependent and only become apparent on delayed testing.
questions.question: A known haemophilia patient with a previously identified inhibitor requires urgent surgery, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-transfusion planning in inhibitor patients. The attending doctor refers the patient for Mixing Study (Correction Test). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Haemoglobin Estimation is requested to monitor the degree of anaemia resulting from reduced erythropoietin production in chronic renal failure. Principle: Haemoglobin is converted to a stable coloured compound (acid haematin or cyanmethaemoglobin) whose colour intensity, read colorimetrically, is proportional to haemoglobin concentration. Normal result and interpretation: Normal values are 13–17 g/dl in men and 12–15 g/dl in women. Values below this confirm anaemia while markedly elevated values suggest polycythaemia or dehydration. Precautions: reagents must be fresh and correctly diluted, the exact volume of blood must be drawn without air bubbles, and colour development must be allowed to reach completion before reading to avoid underestimation.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man with known chronic kidney disease on routine follow-up. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Estimation. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient reports a lifelong bruising tendency before minor surgery, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-operative screening for a bleeding disorder. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bleeding Time. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for a primary haemostatic defect not detected by PT or APTT. Principle: A standardised skin incision (Ivy method) is made and the time to cessation of bleeding is measured, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall in primary haemostasis. Normal result: Approximately 2-9 minutes, depending on the method used; a prolonged result should prompt further platelet function testing before surgery. Precautions: Use a standardised, calibrated incision device and consistent incision depth, and avoid the test in patients taking aspirin or NSAIDs within the preceding week unless specifically assessing their effect.

The Haemoglobin Electrophoresis is requested to screen for a thalassaemia trait pattern before conception so that genetic counselling can be offered. Principle: A haemolysate of red cells is applied to a support medium such as cellulose acetate or agar gel and subjected to an electric field, separating haemoglobin variants according to their electrical charge at a given pH. Normal result and interpretation: The normal adult pattern shows predominantly HbA with small HbA2 (under 3.5%) and trace HbF. Abnormal bands or altered proportions identify HbS, HbC, HbE or a thalassaemia pattern. Precautions: a fresh, clot-free haemolysate must be used, voltage and running time must be standardised, and known control samples must be run alongside the patient sample to allow accurate identification of each band.
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with a family history of thalassaemia planning pregnancy. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score is requested to help differentiate a genuine chronic myeloproliferative disorder from a benign reactive leucocytosis. Principle: Neutrophils on a blood film are stained for alkaline phosphatase activity and each cell is scored according to the intensity of staining, giving a total score reflecting neutrophil enzyme activity. Normal result and interpretation: A normal LAP score is roughly 20–100 depending on the scoring system used. A markedly low score is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia, while a high score is seen in leukaemoid reactions and polycythaemia vera. Precautions: the blood film must be fresh since LAP activity deteriorates on storage, staining must be carried out under standardised conditions, and at least 100 neutrophils should be scored to obtain a reliable result.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with an elevated white cell count of uncertain chronic versus reactive cause. The attending doctor requests a Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to monitor platelet count as a marker of disease severity. Principle: An automated haematology analyser counts platelets using impedance or optical light-scatter methods, distinguishing them from red and white cells by their smaller size. Normal result: 150-450 x10^9/L; a progressively falling count supports severe dengue and the need for close monitoring for bleeding. Precautions: Confirm any very low automated count by examining a blood film to exclude EDTA-induced platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia), which can falsely lower the automated count.
questions.question: A 28-year-old presents with high fever, rash and bleeding gums after recent travel, and is subsequently diagnosed with dengue fever. The attending doctor refers the patient for Platelet Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Bone Marrow Aspiration is requested to obtain direct marrow tissue examination, since peripheral blood tests alone are insufficient to reach a diagnosis. Principle: Marrow tissue is aspirated, usually from the posterior iliac crest or sternum, smeared on slides and stained to examine the cellularity, myeloid:erythroid ratio and morphology of developing blood cell precursors. Normal result and interpretation: A normal marrow shows active trilineage haemopoiesis with a myeloid:erythroid ratio of about 2:1 to 4:1. Hypocellularity suggests aplastic anaemia, and infiltration by blast cells or other abnormal cells confirms leukaemia or another marrow disorder. Precautions: the aspirate must be smeared quickly before it clots, particle-rich areas of the smear must be selected for staining, and strict aseptic technique with local anaesthesia must be used to prevent infection and minimise patient discomfort.
questions.question: A 40-year-old man with unexplained cytopenias persisting despite adequate outpatient investigation. The attending doctor requests a Bone Marrow Aspiration. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for a lupus anticoagulant, which paradoxically prolongs the APTT in vitro despite causing thrombosis in vivo. Principle: A phospholipid reagent, activator and calcium are added to citrated plasma to measure clotting time via the intrinsic and common pathways (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen). Normal result: 25-35 seconds, depending on the reagent used; a prolonged APTT that fails to correct on mixing study supports the presence of an inhibitor such as lupus anticoagulant. Precautions: Avoid drawing the sample from a line contaminated with heparin, which falsely prolongs results, and centrifuge promptly to obtain platelet-poor plasma for accurate testing.
questions.question: A woman with recurrent miscarriages is investigated for an antiphospholipid syndrome, and is subsequently diagnosed with lupus anticoagulant screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Prothrombin Time (PT) is requested to screen the extrinsic coagulation pathway before surgery and identify any unsuspected bleeding risk. Principle: Calcium and tissue thromboplastin are added to citrated plasma to activate the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the time taken for a fibrin clot to form is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PT is approximately 11–15 seconds depending on the reagent used. Prolongation indicates deficiency of factors II, V, VII or X, seen in liver disease, warfarin therapy or vitamin K deficiency. Precautions: blood must be collected into the correct trisodium citrate ratio of 1:9, the test performed within a few hours of collection, and platelet-poor plasma obtained by adequate centrifugation to avoid interference from residual platelets.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man scheduled for major surgery with a history of easy bruising. The attending doctor requests a Prothrombin Time (PT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient newly diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma undergoes baseline staging investigations, and is subsequently diagnosed with lymphoma prognostication. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to provide prognostic information, since higher tumour burden is associated with higher levels. Principle: A spectrophotometric enzymatic assay measures LDH activity by monitoring the conversion of NADH to NAD+ during the reduction of pyruvate to lactate; LDH is released from many tissues including red cells during cell breakdown or turnover. Normal result: Approximately 140-280 U/L (assay-dependent); a markedly raised level at diagnosis is associated with a poorer prognosis and higher tumour burden. Precautions: Avoid any degree of haemolysis during sample collection or handling, since red cells contain very high LDH activity and even minor in vitro haemolysis will falsely raise the result.

questions.question: A 30-year-old presents with fatigue, bruising and a very high blast count on peripheral film, and is subsequently diagnosed with acute leukaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Aspiration. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm marrow infiltration by blasts and classify the leukaemia subtype. Principle: A needle is inserted into the marrow cavity (usually posterior iliac crest or sternum) to aspirate a liquid marrow sample, which is smeared, stained and examined for cellularity, maturation and abnormal cell populations. Normal result: Normocellular marrow with an orderly maturation sequence of erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages and no abnormal infiltrate; over 20% blasts confirms acute leukaemia, guiding immunophenotyping and treatment planning. Precautions: Prepare smears immediately before the sample clots, obtain particles for a representative trephine/clot section, and maintain strict asepsis at the puncture site to prevent infection.

questions.question: A pregnant woman in an endemic area presents with fever and anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with malaria in pregnancy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Thick and Thin Blood Film for Malaria Parasites. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm malaria infection, which carries increased risk to both mother and fetus in pregnancy. Principle: A thick film concentrates red cells to increase sensitivity for detecting parasites, while a thin film preserves red cell and parasite morphology for species identification, both examined microscopically after Giemsa staining. Normal result: No malaria parasites seen on thick or thin film; a positive film confirms the diagnosis and mandates prompt, pregnancy-safe antimalarial treatment. Precautions: Prepare films from a fresh fingerprick or anticoagulated sample without delay, ensure correct Giemsa staining pH and time for accurate parasite morphology, and examine an adequate number of fields before reporting a film negative.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy with recurrent jaundice and splenomegaly is investigated for a possible inherited haemolytic disorder, and is subsequently diagnosed with hereditary spherocytosis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Osmotic Fragility Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to demonstrate increased red cell fragility consistent with spherocytosis. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; cells with reduced surface-to-volume ratio (spherocytes) lyse at higher saline concentrations than normal biconcave cells. Normal result: Complete lysis begins around 0.45% saline and is complete by about 0.30% saline; increased fragility (lysis at higher saline concentrations) supports the diagnosis, while normal fragility argues against it. Precautions: Use fresh blood less than 24 hours old, ensure accurate serial dilution of the saline, and run a normal control in parallel to validate the test on each occasion.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man on antimalarial treatment being reviewed after three days for response. The attending doctor requests a Malaria Parasite Blood Film. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Malaria Parasite Blood Film is requested to assess parasite clearance and confirm the treatment is working as expected. Principle: Thick and thin blood films are stained with Giemsa or Field's stain; the thick film concentrates parasites for sensitive detection while the thin film preserves parasite and red cell morphology for species identification and parasitaemia quantification. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of parasites on a well-examined film excludes malaria at the time of testing. Presence of parasites confirms the diagnosis, with the species and percentage parasitaemia guiding severity assessment and treatment. Precautions: films must be made from fresh blood before antimalarial treatment reduces parasite counts, the staining buffer pH must be correctly maintained since incorrect pH affects parasite staining quality, and an adequate number of fields must be examined before a film is reported negative.

The Haemoglobin Electrophoresis is requested to confirm the specific haemoglobin pattern of beta-thalassaemia major, characterised by absent or reduced HbA. Principle: A haemolysate of red cells is applied to a support medium such as cellulose acetate or agar gel and subjected to an electric field, separating haemoglobin variants according to their electrical charge at a given pH. Normal result and interpretation: The normal adult pattern shows predominantly HbA with small HbA2 (under 3.5%) and trace HbF. Abnormal bands or altered proportions identify HbS, HbC, HbE or a thalassaemia pattern. Precautions: a fresh, clot-free haemolysate must be used, voltage and running time must be standardised, and known control samples must be run alongside the patient sample to allow accurate identification of each band.
questions.question: A 14-year-old boy with growth retardation, bone deformities and dependence on repeated blood transfusions. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Electrophoresis. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The HLA Typing is requested to investigate for HLA alloimmunisation as the cause of his platelet transfusion refractoriness. Principle: Lymphocytes are separated and tested against panels of antisera of known HLA specificity in a microcytotoxicity assay, or by molecular methods, to determine the patient's HLA type for compatibility matching. Normal result and interpretation: A close match between donor and recipient HLA type reduces the risk of graft rejection and graft-versus-host disease; a significant mismatch increases the likelihood of rejection or complications following transplantation. Precautions: lymphocytes must be viable and adequately separated by density gradient centrifugation, trypan blue exclusion must confirm cell viability before testing, and the correct antisera panel and complement source must be used to avoid a false result.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man who repeatedly fails to achieve adequate platelet increments after platelet transfusions. The attending doctor requests a HLA Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A child from a consanguineous family presents with severe mucosal and joint bleeding, and is subsequently diagnosed with type 3 von Willebrand disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for von Willebrand Factor Assay (Antigen and Activity). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm a severe, near-total deficiency of von Willebrand factor. Principle: Immunoassay quantifies von Willebrand factor antigen, while a functional assay (such as ristocetin cofactor activity) measures its ability to mediate platelet binding, together characterising both the amount and function of the protein. Normal result: Approximately 50-200% of the reference standard for both antigen and activity; very low or undetectable antigen and activity confirm the severe recessive form. Precautions: Be aware that vWF is an acute-phase reactant and can be transiently raised by stress, exercise or inflammation, and that blood group O individuals have physiologically lower baseline levels.

The Coagulation Factor Assay is requested to monitor his factor VIII level and confirm adequate replacement before a planned surgical procedure. Principle: Patient plasma is diluted and mixed with plasma known to be deficient in the specific factor being tested, and correction of the clotting time is compared against a standard curve made from pooled normal plasma to calculate percentage factor activity. Normal result and interpretation: Normal factor activity is about 50–150% of the standard. Levels below 50%, and especially below 5%, indicate significant deficiency of that factor, as seen in haemophilia A (factor VIII), haemophilia B (factor IX) or other factor deficiencies. Precautions: the specific factor-deficient substrate plasma must be genuinely deficient only in that factor, samples must be kept frozen or on ice to preserve labile factors such as VIII, and a fresh standard curve must be prepared with each batch of tests.
questions.question: A 8-year-old boy with known severe haemophilia A currently receiving factor replacement therapy. The attending doctor requests a Coagulation Factor Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with worsening fatigue, and is subsequently diagnosed with pregnancy-related anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Iron and Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm iron deficiency, common in pregnancy due to increased demand. Principle: Serum iron is measured colorimetrically after releasing iron from transferrin, while TIBC is determined by saturating transferrin with excess iron and measuring the total binding capacity, allowing calculation of transferrin saturation. Normal result: Serum iron 50-170 micrograms/dL, TIBC 250-450 micrograms/dL, transferrin saturation 20-50%; low serum iron with raised TIBC supports the need for iron supplementation before delivery. Precautions: Collect the sample in the morning when iron levels are most stable, avoid haemolysis which falsely raises serum iron, and ensure the patient has not taken iron supplements in the preceding 24 hours.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman who is Rh-negative, expecting her second child after an uneventful first pregnancy. The attending doctor requests a Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Rhesus (Rh-D) Typing is requested to confirm her Rh status and assess the need for anti-D prophylaxis given her risk of sensitisation from the first pregnancy. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with anti-D antiserum; agglutination indicates the presence of the D antigen (Rh positive) while absence of agglutination indicates Rh negative status, with a weak D test performed if the initial result is doubtful. Normal result and interpretation: A clear agglutination reaction confirms Rh positive status while no agglutination confirms Rh negative status. Correct Rh status is essential to prevent haemolytic disease of the newborn and haemolytic transfusion reactions. Precautions: a control tube without antiserum must always be run to exclude spontaneous autoagglutination, the correct incubation temperature must be maintained, and a weak D (antiglobulin) test should be performed on apparently negative results before confirming Rh negative status.

The Indirect Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test is requested to screen for alloantibodies she may have developed from earlier sensitising exposures. Principle: Patient serum suspected of containing antibody is incubated with reagent red cells of known antigen composition, and antihuman globulin reagent is then added to detect antibody that has coated the cells without producing visible agglutination. Normal result and interpretation: A negative IAT means no clinically significant antibody was detected, while a positive result indicates the presence of an alloantibody, important in antenatal screening and pre-transfusion compatibility testing. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before adding AHG reagent to remove unbound globulin, incubation temperature and time must be strictly observed since many antibodies react best at 37°C, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included.
questions.question: A 33-year-old woman who has had multiple pregnancies and previous transfusions, now needing another transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Indirect Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 30-year-old farmer with cyclical fever and chills returns from a rural trip, and is subsequently diagnosed with malaria. The attending doctor refers the patient for Peripheral Blood Film. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to identify malaria parasites within red cells and determine species and parasitaemia. Principle: A thin smear of blood is stained with Romanowsky stain (e.g. Leishman or Wright-Giemsa) and examined under the microscope to assess red cell, white cell and platelet morphology and number. Normal result: Red cells are normocytic and normochromic with normal white cell and platelet morphology and no abnormal cells; visualisation of ring forms or gametocytes confirms infection, while a negative film on three occasions excludes it. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood within one hour of collection to avoid crenation and morphological artefact, and use a clean grease-free slide with a smooth, even spreading technique to avoid a poorly feathered edge.

The Sickling Test is requested to confirm the presence of HbS as part of the diagnostic work-up for his recurrent vaso-occlusive crises. Principle: Red cells are mixed with a reducing agent such as sodium metabisulphite that lowers oxygen tension, causing hemoglobin S to polymerise and distort the cells into a sickle shape under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no sickling and excludes HbS, while a positive test confirms the presence of HbS but cannot distinguish sickle cell trait from sickle cell disease. Precautions: a freshly prepared reducing agent must be used since an old reagent gives false negatives, the preparation must be sealed with a coverslip and petroleum jelly to prevent drying, and it must be observed for the recommended time as delayed reading may miss early sickling.
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy with recurrent severe bone pain crises since early childhood. The attending doctor requests a Sickling Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 20-year-old man known to have sickle cell disease, presenting with severe bone pain. The attending doctor requests a Peripheral Blood Film Examination. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Peripheral Blood Film Examination is requested to look for sickle-shaped cells, target cells and features of hyposplenism such as Howell-Jolly bodies confirming a sickling crisis. Principle: A thin film of blood is spread on a slide, fixed and stained with a Romanowsky stain so that red cell, white cell and platelet morphology can be examined directly under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells appear as uniform biconcave discs with central pallor, white cells show normal proportions and morphology, and platelets are adequate in number. Abnormal shapes, inclusions or immature cells point to specific haematological disease. Precautions: the film must be made promptly from fresh anticoagulated or capillary blood, spread with a smooth, even-angled stroke to avoid artefacts, and properly fixed before staining to prevent cell distortion.

The Platelet Count is requested to confirm suspected immune thrombocytopenic purpura by demonstrating an isolated low platelet count. Principle: Platelets are counted directly using a haemocytometer under phase contrast after appropriate dilution, or automatically by impedance/optical methods, based on their small size and characteristic light scatter. Normal result and interpretation: Normal platelet count is 150–400 x10^9/L. A count below this range indicates thrombocytopenia with bleeding risk while a count above suggests thrombocytosis. Precautions: blood must be collected into EDTA without clotting, the film must be checked for platelet clumps that cause spuriously low automated counts, and skin puncture blood should not be used since tissue fluid promotes platelet clumping.
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman with easy bruising and small red spots on her legs but no other symptoms. The attending doctor requests a Platelet Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A young boy with a prolonged APTT and joint bleeding is being worked up, and is subsequently diagnosed with congenital factor deficiency confirmation. The attending doctor refers the patient for Mixing Study (Correction Test). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm that the prolongation is due to a simple factor deficiency rather than an inhibitor. Principle: Patient plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma and the clotting time (PT or APTT) is repeated immediately and after incubation, distinguishing a factor deficiency (which corrects, since normal plasma supplies the missing factor) from an inhibitor (which does not fully correct). Normal result: Full correction of the prolonged clotting time into the normal range; full correction supports an inherited factor deficiency such as haemophilia, prompting a specific factor assay. Precautions: Repeat the test after incubation at 37°C for one to two hours, since some inhibitors (such as factor VIII autoantibodies) are time- and temperature-dependent and only become apparent on delayed testing.

The test was requested to detect early evidence of marrow recovery before the full blood count normalises. Principle: Blood is stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, which precipitates residual ribosomal RNA in young red cells as a reticular network, allowing reticulocytes to be counted as a percentage or absolute count. Normal result: 0.5-2.5% of red cells, or an absolute count of 25-100 x10^9/L; a rising count signals marrow regeneration, while a persistently low count may indicate ongoing marrow suppression. Precautions: Use fresh, well-mixed EDTA blood and count at least 1000 red cells to reduce sampling error, and distinguish true reticular staining from Heinz bodies or artefactual staining.
questions.question: A 40-year-old leukaemia patient is monitored two weeks after induction chemotherapy, and is subsequently diagnosed with post-chemotherapy marrow recovery. The attending doctor refers the patient for Reticulocyte Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Serum Ferritin is requested to confirm depleted iron stores, since ferritin is the most sensitive marker of early iron deficiency. Principle: Serum ferritin, an intracellular iron storage protein that leaks into blood in proportion to body iron stores, is measured immunologically, providing a sensitive indicator of iron deficiency or overload. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum ferritin is roughly 15–300 microgram/L depending on age and sex. Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency while very high ferritin suggests iron overload, though it may also be raised non-specifically as an acute phase reactant. Precautions: results must be interpreted with caution in the presence of infection or inflammation since ferritin is an acute phase protein that can be falsely elevated, and haemolysed samples must be avoided.
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman with fatigue and mildly low haemoglobin but an inconclusive iron and TIBC result. The attending doctor requests a Serum Ferritin. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 48-year-old man presents with joint pain, bronzed skin and new-onset diabetes, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemochromatosis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Ferritin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for iron overload as part of a hereditary haemochromatosis work-up. Principle: An immunoassay (ELISA or chemiluminescence) measures serum ferritin, an acute-phase protein that reflects total body iron stores, since it correlates with the amount of iron sequestered within tissue macrophages and hepatocytes. Normal result: Approximately 15-150 ng/mL in women and 15-200 ng/mL in men; a markedly raised ferritin supports iron overload and warrants genetic testing and transferrin saturation. Precautions: Interpret cautiously in the presence of infection or inflammation, which raises ferritin independently of iron status as an acute-phase reactant, and avoid haemolysed samples which falsely elevate results.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman with lifelong easy bruising and heavy periods is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with type 1 von Willebrand disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for von Willebrand Factor Assay (Antigen and Activity). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm a partial quantitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor. Principle: Immunoassay quantifies von Willebrand factor antigen, while a functional assay (such as ristocetin cofactor activity) measures its ability to mediate platelet binding, together characterising both the amount and function of the protein. Normal result: Approximately 50-200% of the reference standard for both antigen and activity; proportionally reduced antigen and activity support type 1 disease, the mildest and most common form. Precautions: Be aware that vWF is an acute-phase reactant and can be transiently raised by stress, exercise or inflammation, and that blood group O individuals have physiologically lower baseline levels.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with recurrent spontaneous joint bleeding and a normal factor VIII level, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemophilia B diagnosis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Factor IX Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm the diagnosis and severity of haemophilia B (Christmas disease). Principle: Patient plasma is mixed with factor IX-deficient substrate plasma in an APTT-based clotting assay, and the degree of correction is compared against a reference curve to quantify factor IX activity. Normal result: 50-150% of the standard reference activity; activity below 1% indicates severe disease, guiding the intensity of prophylactic treatment. Precautions: Ensure correct sample handling and prompt processing, and be aware that vitamin K deficiency or warfarin therapy also lowers factor IX and can confound interpretation.

The test was requested to monitor for the coagulopathy characteristically associated with this leukaemia subtype. Principle: The Clauss method measures the clotting time of diluted plasma after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to the fibrinogen concentration, allowing quantification of this key clotting protein. Normal result: Approximately 2.0-4.0 g/L; a markedly low level supports an associated consumptive coagulopathy requiring urgent correction. Precautions: Ensure the correct citrate anticoagulation ratio and process promptly, since fibrinogen is an acute-phase protein and results must be interpreted alongside the clinical context of inflammation or infection.
questions.question: A patient newly diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukaemia develops spontaneous bruising, and is subsequently diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Fibrinogen Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The LE Cell Test is requested to support a suspected diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus based on demonstrable LE cell formation. Principle: Leucocytes are damaged in vitro to release nuclear material which, in the presence of anti-nuclear antibody in the patient's serum, is opsonised and then phagocytosed by other neutrophils to form the characteristic LE cell. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of LE cells is normal. Presence of LE cells supports a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus or occasionally drug-induced lupus, though the test is less sensitive than modern ANA methods. Precautions: the preparation must be examined promptly since LE cells degenerate on standing, an adequate number of fields must be examined before a negative result is reported, and technique-related artefacts must be distinguished from true LE cells.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with a butterfly facial rash, joint pain and unexplained fever. The attending doctor requests a LE Cell Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The HbF Alkali Denaturation Test is requested to quantify the infant's HbF proportion as part of confirming the specific haemoglobinopathy suspected. Principle: Haemolysate is exposed briefly to strong alkali; adult haemoglobin (HbA) denatures rapidly and precipitates while fetal haemoglobin (HbF) resists denaturation, allowing the percentage of HbF to be estimated after filtration and colorimetric measurement. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult HbF is less than about 2%. Markedly elevated HbF is seen in beta-thalassaemia major, hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin, and some cases of sickle cell disease. Precautions: fresh reagents must be used since old alkali gives inaccurate denaturation times, the exact timing of alkali exposure must be strictly observed since it critically affects the result, and the haemolysate must be free of turbidity before measurement.
questions.question: A 1-year-old month-old infant being investigated for a suspected haemoglobinopathy detected on newborn screening. The attending doctor requests a HbF Alkali Denaturation Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to investigate a suspected inherited deficiency of fibrinogen. Principle: The Clauss method measures the clotting time of diluted plasma after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to the fibrinogen concentration, allowing quantification of this key clotting protein. Normal result: Approximately 2.0-4.0 g/L; an undetectable or very low level confirms a congenital fibrinogen disorder. Precautions: Ensure the correct citrate anticoagulation ratio and process promptly, since fibrinogen is an acute-phase protein and results must be interpreted alongside the clinical context of inflammation or infection.
questions.question: An infant from a consanguineous family presents with umbilical stump bleeding, and is subsequently diagnosed with congenital afibrinogenaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Fibrinogen Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A patient develops fever, back pain and dark urine shortly after starting a blood transfusion, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemolytic transfusion reaction. The attending doctor refers the patient for Direct Antiglobulin (Direct Coombs) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm that the patient's own red cells are being attacked by incompatible antibody from the transfusion. Principle: Anti-human globulin reagent is added to washed patient red cells; if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement, the reagent cross-links adjacent cells to produce visible agglutination. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination; a positive result supports an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction, requiring immediate cessation of the transfusion. Precautions: Wash the red cells thoroughly to remove all free unbound globulin before adding the antiglobulin reagent, since inadequate washing causes false-negative results through neutralisation.

The HbF Alkali Denaturation Test is requested to quantify HbF and confirm hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin as opposed to thalassaemia. Principle: Haemolysate is exposed briefly to strong alkali; adult haemoglobin (HbA) denatures rapidly and precipitates while fetal haemoglobin (HbF) resists denaturation, allowing the percentage of HbF to be estimated after filtration and colorimetric measurement. Normal result and interpretation: Normal adult HbF is less than about 2%. Markedly elevated HbF is seen in beta-thalassaemia major, hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin, and some cases of sickle cell disease. Precautions: fresh reagents must be used since old alkali gives inaccurate denaturation times, the exact timing of alkali exposure must be strictly observed since it critically affects the result, and the haemolysate must be free of turbidity before measurement.
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy with anaemia and bone changes suspected of having a persistent fetal haemoglobin variant. The attending doctor requests a HbF Alkali Denaturation Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Osmotic Fragility Test is requested to investigate for hereditary spherocytosis as a cause of early and pathological neonatal jaundice. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; spherocytic cells with a reduced surface area to volume ratio lyse earlier than normal biconcave cells, and the percentage lysis at each concentration is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells begin to lyse at about 0.45% saline and are completely lysed by 0.30%. Increased fragility (lysis at higher saline concentration) suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while decreased fragility suggests thalassaemia or iron deficiency. Precautions: blood must be defibrinated or collected into heparin rather than EDTA, saline dilutions must be prepared accurately and freshly, and tubes must be mixed gently to avoid mechanical haemolysis that would give a false result.
questions.question: A 3-year-old day-old newborn with jaundice appearing earlier and more severely than typical physiological jaundice. The attending doctor requests a Osmotic Fragility Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient is scheduled for a caesarean section with anticipated blood loss, and is subsequently diagnosed with elective surgery blood reservation. The attending doctor refers the patient for Crossmatching (Compatibility Testing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm specific donor units are safe to transfuse if bleeding occurs during surgery. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and observed for agglutination or haemolysis across immediate spin, 37°C incubation and antiglobulin phases, confirming serological compatibility before transfusion. Normal result: No agglutination or haemolysis at any phase, indicating compatible blood; a compatible crossmatch allows the units to be released for use, while incompatibility requires selection of alternative units. Precautions: Confirm patient identity and sample labelling meticulously at both collection and issue, and complete the full antiglobulin phase rather than relying on immediate spin alone, since clinically significant antibodies may only react at this stage.

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve develops fatigue and mild jaundice, and is subsequently diagnosed with mechanical heart valve haemolysis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Haptoglobin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm mechanical (traumatic) intravascular destruction of red cells by the valve. Principle: An immunoturbidimetric assay measures haptoglobin, a plasma protein that binds free haemoglobin released from lysed red cells; because the haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex is rapidly cleared by the liver, intravascular haemolysis depletes circulating haptoglobin. Normal result: Approximately 30-200 mg/dL; a reduced level supports ongoing mechanical haemolysis, prompting valve function assessment. Precautions: Interpret with caution since haptoglobin is also an acute-phase reactant that can be falsely normal or raised in the presence of concurrent inflammation despite ongoing haemolysis.

The Sickling Test is requested to screen for sickle cell status before surgery and anaesthesia, since undiagnosed sickle cell disease increases peri-operative risk. Principle: Red cells are mixed with a reducing agent such as sodium metabisulphite that lowers oxygen tension, causing hemoglobin S to polymerise and distort the cells into a sickle shape under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no sickling and excludes HbS, while a positive test confirms the presence of HbS but cannot distinguish sickle cell trait from sickle cell disease. Precautions: a freshly prepared reducing agent must be used since an old reagent gives false negatives, the preparation must be sealed with a coverslip and petroleum jelly to prevent drying, and it must be observed for the recommended time as delayed reading may miss early sickling.
questions.question: A 24-year-old man undergoing pre-operative screening before a scheduled tonsillectomy. The attending doctor requests a Sickling Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 4-year-old day-old newborn with unexpectedly severe jaundice requiring phototherapy. The attending doctor requests a G6PD Screening Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The G6PD Screening Test is requested to check for G6PD deficiency as an underlying cause of the severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. Principle: Red cell lysate is incubated with glucose-6-phosphate and NADP; adequate G6PD enzyme generates NADPH, which fluoresces under ultraviolet light, whereas deficient samples show little or no fluorescence. Normal result and interpretation: A normal (fluorescent) result excludes significant deficiency, while absent or reduced fluorescence indicates G6PD deficiency, predisposing the patient to oxidative haemolysis after certain drugs, infections or fava beans. Precautions: the test should ideally be delayed until after an acute haemolytic episode has resolved, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a deficiency, and reagents must be protected from light and used fresh.

The test was requested to assess the adequacy of the administered dose alongside the haemoglobin response. Principle: An immunoassay measures circulating erythropoietin, the hormone produced predominantly by the kidney in response to tissue hypoxia, which stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow. Normal result: Approximately 4-27 mU/mL, though appropriately elevated in genuine anaemia due to physiological hypoxic drive; an inadequate haemoglobin rise despite therapy should prompt review of iron status and dosing. Precautions: Interpret the result in the context of the patient's haemoglobin level, since a normal or low erythropoietin in the presence of anaemia is inappropriately low and clinically significant.
questions.question: A dialysis patient started on erythropoietin-stimulating therapy is reviewed after several weeks, and is subsequently diagnosed with monitoring response to erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Erythropoietin Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 30-year-old woman with a markedly raised white cell count during a severe bacterial infection. The attending doctor requests a Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score is requested to confirm a reactive leukaemoid reaction, in which LAP is typically high, rather than a leukaemic process. Principle: Neutrophils on a blood film are stained for alkaline phosphatase activity and each cell is scored according to the intensity of staining, giving a total score reflecting neutrophil enzyme activity. Normal result and interpretation: A normal LAP score is roughly 20–100 depending on the scoring system used. A markedly low score is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia, while a high score is seen in leukaemoid reactions and polycythaemia vera. Precautions: the blood film must be fresh since LAP activity deteriorates on storage, staining must be carried out under standardised conditions, and at least 100 neutrophils should be scored to obtain a reliable result.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant with fever and headache in an endemic region. The attending doctor requests a Malaria Parasite Blood Film. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
