questions.answerText: The Malaria Parasite Blood Film is requested to promptly diagnose or exclude malaria in pregnancy, a condition associated with significant maternal and fetal risk. Principle: Thick and thin blood films are stained with Giemsa or Field's stain; the thick film concentrates parasites for sensitive detection while the thin film preserves parasite and red cell morphology for species identification and parasitaemia quantification. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of parasites on a well-examined film excludes malaria at the time of testing. Presence of parasites confirms the diagnosis, with the species and percentage parasitaemia guiding severity assessment and treatment. Precautions: films must be made from fresh blood before antimalarial treatment reduces parasite counts, the staining buffer pH must be correctly maintained since incorrect pH affects parasite staining quality, and an adequate number of fields must be examined before a film is reported negative.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man scheduled for major abdominal surgery next week. The attending doctor requests a Platelet Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Platelet Count is requested to assess his bleeding risk before surgery by confirming an adequate platelet count. Principle: Platelets are counted directly using a haemocytometer under phase contrast after appropriate dilution, or automatically by impedance/optical methods, based on their small size and characteristic light scatter. Normal result and interpretation: Normal platelet count is 150–400 x10^9/L. A count below this range indicates thrombocytopenia with bleeding risk while a count above suggests thrombocytosis. Precautions: blood must be collected into EDTA without clotting, the film must be checked for platelet clumps that cause spuriously low automated counts, and skin puncture blood should not be used since tissue fluid promotes platelet clumping.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man in septic shock with bleeding from venepuncture sites. The attending doctor requests a Platelet Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Platelet Count is requested to assess for consumptive thrombocytopenia as part of suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation. Principle: Platelets are counted directly using a haemocytometer under phase contrast after appropriate dilution, or automatically by impedance/optical methods, based on their small size and characteristic light scatter. Normal result and interpretation: Normal platelet count is 150–400 x10^9/L. A count below this range indicates thrombocytopenia with bleeding risk while a count above suggests thrombocytosis. Precautions: blood must be collected into EDTA without clotting, the film must be checked for platelet clumps that cause spuriously low automated counts, and skin puncture blood should not be used since tissue fluid promotes platelet clumping.

The test was requested to confirm replenishment of iron stores following treatment. Principle: An immunoassay (ELISA or chemiluminescence) measures serum ferritin, an acute-phase protein that reflects total body iron stores, since it correlates with the amount of iron sequestered within tissue macrophages and hepatocytes. Normal result: Approximately 15-150 ng/mL in women and 15-200 ng/mL in men; a rising ferritin toward the normal range confirms adequate repletion, guiding when to stop supplementation. Precautions: Interpret cautiously in the presence of infection or inflammation, which raises ferritin independently of iron status as an acute-phase reactant, and avoid haemolysed samples which falsely elevate results.
questions.question: A patient previously diagnosed with iron deficiency anaemia returns three months after starting oral iron, and is subsequently diagnosed with monitoring iron replacement therapy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Ferritin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A jaundiced neonate born to a Rhesus-negative, previously sensitised mother is assessed, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemolytic disease of the newborn. The attending doctor refers the patient for Direct Antiglobulin (Direct Coombs) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to demonstrate maternal antibody coating the infant's red cells. Principle: Anti-human globulin reagent is added to washed patient red cells; if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement, the reagent cross-links adjacent cells to produce visible agglutination. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination; a positive result on cord blood confirms alloimmune haemolysis and predicts the need for phototherapy or exchange transfusion. Precautions: Wash the red cells thoroughly to remove all free unbound globulin before adding the antiglobulin reagent, since inadequate washing causes false-negative results through neutralisation.

questions.question: An elderly smoker presents with a hard, fixed supraclavicular lymph node, and is subsequently diagnosed with metastatic carcinoma. The attending doctor refers the patient for Lymph Node Biopsy (Histopathology). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to identify metastatic malignant cells from a primary tumour elsewhere. Principle: An excised lymph node is fixed, processed and stained (with immunohistochemistry as needed) to examine nodal architecture and identify malignant infiltration, distinguishing reactive hyperplasia from lymphoma or metastatic disease. Normal result: Preserved normal nodal architecture with reactive follicular hyperplasia and no malignant infiltrate; clusters of epithelial malignant cells confirm nodal metastasis and prompt a search for the primary tumour. Precautions: Excise an entire, representative node rather than a fine-needle sample where lymphoma is suspected, since architecture is essential for classification, and transport the fresh specimen promptly to avoid autolysis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old presents with widespread lymphadenopathy and weight loss, and is subsequently diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The attending doctor refers the patient for Lymph Node Biopsy (Histopathology). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to characterise the malignant lymphocyte population and subtype the lymphoma. Principle: An excised lymph node is fixed, processed and stained (with immunohistochemistry as needed) to examine nodal architecture and identify malignant infiltration, distinguishing reactive hyperplasia from lymphoma or metastatic disease. Normal result: Preserved normal nodal architecture with reactive follicular hyperplasia and no malignant infiltrate; effacement of normal architecture by a monoclonal lymphocyte population confirms non-Hodgkin lymphoma and guides subtyping. Precautions: Excise an entire, representative node rather than a fine-needle sample where lymphoma is suspected, since architecture is essential for classification, and transport the fresh specimen promptly to avoid autolysis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man who developed acute haemolysis after taking dapsone for a skin condition. The attending doctor requests a Heinz Body Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Heinz Body Test is requested to confirm Heinz body formation as evidence of oxidative drug-induced haemolysis. Principle: Denatured, precipitated haemoglobin within red cells (Heinz bodies) is demonstrated using a supravital stain such as methyl violet or new methylene blue, since Heinz bodies do not stain with routine Romanowsky stains. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of Heinz bodies is normal. Their presence indicates oxidative damage to haemoglobin, seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidant stress, unstable haemoglobin variants, or exposure to certain drugs and chemicals. Precautions: the stain must be fresh and the preparation examined promptly, since Heinz bodies may be removed rapidly by the spleen and disappear from circulation, and adequate numbers of cells must be examined to avoid missing a low percentage.

The test was requested to look for macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils suggestive of B12 or folate deficiency. Principle: A thin smear of blood is stained with Romanowsky stain (e.g. Leishman or Wright-Giemsa) and examined under the microscope to assess red cell, white cell and platelet morphology and number. Normal result: Red cells are normocytic and normochromic with normal white cell and platelet morphology and no abnormal cells; oval macrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils support megaloblastic change, guiding further vitamin assays. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood within one hour of collection to avoid crenation and morphological artefact, and use a clean grease-free slide with a smooth, even spreading technique to avoid a poorly feathered edge.
questions.question: A 60-year-old vegan presents with glossitis and peripheral numbness, and is subsequently diagnosed with megaloblastic anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Peripheral Blood Film. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 25-year-old presents with fever, headache and chills after travelling to an endemic area, and is subsequently diagnosed with uncomplicated falciparum malaria. The attending doctor refers the patient for Thick and Thin Blood Film for Malaria Parasites. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm the presence and species of malaria parasites and quantify parasitaemia. Principle: A thick film concentrates red cells to increase sensitivity for detecting parasites, while a thin film preserves red cell and parasite morphology for species identification, both examined microscopically after Giemsa staining. Normal result: No malaria parasites seen on thick or thin film; ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum confirm the diagnosis and guide antimalarial treatment choice. Precautions: Prepare films from a fresh fingerprick or anticoagulated sample without delay, ensure correct Giemsa staining pH and time for accurate parasite morphology, and examine an adequate number of fields before reporting a film negative.

The Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain is requested to establish the myeloid versus lymphoid lineage of his leukaemia, which directly affects the choice of chemotherapy. Principle: Myeloid cells contain peroxidase enzyme in their primary granules that reacts with hydrogen peroxide and a chromogen to give a coloured precipitate, positive in myeloblasts but negative in lymphoblasts. Normal result and interpretation: Peroxidase positivity in blast cells confirms myeloid lineage (acute myeloid leukaemia) while peroxidase-negative blasts suggest lymphoid lineage (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia). Precautions: fresh, well-fixed films must be used since old films lose enzyme activity, reagents must be prepared and used promptly as they deteriorate quickly, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included with every batch.
questions.question: A 8-year-old boy newly diagnosed with acute leukaemia requiring lineage-specific treatment planning. The attending doctor requests a Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 50-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use and macrocytic anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay is requested to check for folate deficiency, which is common in chronic alcoholism due to poor diet and impaired absorption. Principle: Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels are measured, usually by immunoassay, to identify deficiency states that impair DNA synthesis in developing blood cells and cause megaloblastic change. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum B12 is about 200–900 ng/L and folate about 3–20 microgram/L. Levels below these ranges confirm the deficiency responsible for macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia. Precautions: the sample should be protected from prolonged light exposure where applicable, haemolysis must be avoided, and results should be interpreted alongside the full blood count and blood film since dietary and absorption factors affect the levels obtained.

questions.question: A jaundiced neonate born to a Rhesus-negative mother is assessed on day one of life, and is subsequently diagnosed with haemolytic disease of the newborn. The attending doctor refers the patient for Reticulocyte Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to demonstrate compensatory red cell production in response to immune haemolysis. Principle: Blood is stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, which precipitates residual ribosomal RNA in young red cells as a reticular network, allowing reticulocytes to be counted as a percentage or absolute count. Normal result: 0.5-2.5% of red cells, or an absolute count of 25-100 x10^9/L; an elevated count supports ongoing haemolysis and correlates with the severity of the disease. Precautions: Use fresh, well-mixed EDTA blood and count at least 1000 red cells to reduce sampling error, and distinguish true reticular staining from Heinz bodies or artefactual staining.

questions.question: A farmer presents with a snakebite and diffuse bleeding from the bite site and gums, and is subsequently diagnosed with snakebite-associated DIC. The attending doctor refers the patient for Coagulation Screen (PT, APTT, Platelets, Fibrinogen) for DIC. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy. Principle: A combined panel assesses the extrinsic pathway (PT), intrinsic pathway (APTT), platelet number and fibrinogen concentration together, since disseminated intravascular coagulation produces a characteristic pattern of simultaneous consumption across all these parameters. Normal result: PT and APTT within normal range, platelets above 150 x10^9/L and fibrinogen above 2.0 g/L, with a low D-dimer; markedly deranged results confirm systemic envenomation requiring antivenom and supportive blood product therapy. Precautions: Collect and process the sample promptly and correctly (proper citrate ratio, prompt centrifugation) since delayed or incorrect handling can mimic or mask true consumptive coagulopathy, and repeat serially since DIC evolves rapidly.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man who developed dark urine and jaundice two days after starting an antimalarial drug. The attending doctor requests a G6PD Screening Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The G6PD Screening Test is requested to confirm G6PD deficiency as the cause of his acute drug-induced haemolytic episode. Principle: Red cell lysate is incubated with glucose-6-phosphate and NADP; adequate G6PD enzyme generates NADPH, which fluoresces under ultraviolet light, whereas deficient samples show little or no fluorescence. Normal result and interpretation: A normal (fluorescent) result excludes significant deficiency, while absent or reduced fluorescence indicates G6PD deficiency, predisposing the patient to oxidative haemolysis after certain drugs, infections or fava beans. Precautions: the test should ideally be delayed until after an acute haemolytic episode has resolved, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a deficiency, and reagents must be protected from light and used fresh.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man scheduled for major elective surgery with anticipated significant blood loss. The attending doctor requests a Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch) is requested to ensure that specific donor units are fully compatible with his blood before they are reserved for surgery. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and recipient red cells with donor serum (minor crossmatch), incubated at 37°C and tested by the antiglobulin technique to detect incompatibility before transfusion. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of agglutination or haemolysis in the major crossmatch indicates compatibility and the unit is safe to transfuse; agglutination indicates incompatibility and that unit must not be given. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before the antiglobulin phase, correct incubation time and temperature must be observed, and patient identification on the sample and request form must be verified to prevent transfusion of the wrong unit.

questions.question: A jaundiced neonate with severe haemolytic disease requires exchange transfusion, and is subsequently diagnosed with exchange transfusion in neonatal jaundice. The attending doctor refers the patient for Crossmatching (Compatibility Testing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to ensure the donor blood is compatible with both the infant's and mother's serum. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and observed for agglutination or haemolysis across immediate spin, 37°C incubation and antiglobulin phases, confirming serological compatibility before transfusion. Normal result: No agglutination or haemolysis at any phase, indicating compatible blood; compatible units confirmed against maternal serum help avoid ongoing haemolysis during the exchange. Precautions: Confirm patient identity and sample labelling meticulously at both collection and issue, and complete the full antiglobulin phase rather than relying on immediate spin alone, since clinically significant antibodies may only react at this stage.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with a haematological malignancy being assessed for unrelated donor stem cell transplantation. The attending doctor requests a HLA Typing. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The HLA Typing is requested to determine his HLA type so it can be matched against an international donor registry. Principle: Lymphocytes are separated and tested against panels of antisera of known HLA specificity in a microcytotoxicity assay, or by molecular methods, to determine the patient's HLA type for compatibility matching. Normal result and interpretation: A close match between donor and recipient HLA type reduces the risk of graft rejection and graft-versus-host disease; a significant mismatch increases the likelihood of rejection or complications following transplantation. Precautions: lymphocytes must be viable and adequately separated by density gradient centrifugation, trypan blue exclusion must confirm cell viability before testing, and the correct antisera panel and complement source must be used to avoid a false result.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with fever, bone pain, bruising and blast cells seen on peripheral film. The attending doctor requests a Bone Marrow Aspiration. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Bone Marrow Aspiration is requested to confirm the diagnosis of acute leukaemia and determine its type from marrow blast morphology. Principle: Marrow tissue is aspirated, usually from the posterior iliac crest or sternum, smeared on slides and stained to examine the cellularity, myeloid:erythroid ratio and morphology of developing blood cell precursors. Normal result and interpretation: A normal marrow shows active trilineage haemopoiesis with a myeloid:erythroid ratio of about 2:1 to 4:1. Hypocellularity suggests aplastic anaemia, and infiltration by blast cells or other abnormal cells confirms leukaemia or another marrow disorder. Precautions: the aspirate must be smeared quickly before it clots, particle-rich areas of the smear must be selected for staining, and strict aseptic technique with local anaesthesia must be used to prevent infection and minimise patient discomfort.

The test was requested to observe normalisation of neutrophil enzyme activity as a marker of treatment response. Principle: Neutrophils are stained cytochemically for alkaline phosphatase activity, and a semi-quantitative score is generated by scoring 100 consecutive neutrophils for staining intensity. Normal result: A score within the laboratory's established normal range, generally moderate staining intensity; a rising score toward normal supports haematological response to therapy. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood without delay, since enzyme activity deteriorates on standing, and score consecutively without selecting only strongly-stained cells to avoid bias.
questions.question: A chronic myeloid leukaemia patient is reviewed after starting imatinib, and is subsequently diagnosed with monitoring response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A patient with severe macrocytic anaemia and low B12 is further evaluated before treatment, and is subsequently diagnosed with megaloblastic anaemia confirmation. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bone Marrow Aspiration. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm megaloblastic change and exclude a myelodysplastic process. Principle: A needle is inserted into the marrow cavity (usually posterior iliac crest or sternum) to aspirate a liquid marrow sample, which is smeared, stained and examined for cellularity, maturation and abnormal cell populations. Normal result: Normocellular marrow with an orderly maturation sequence of erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages and no abnormal infiltrate; large megaloblasts with nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony confirm megaloblastic erythropoiesis. Precautions: Prepare smears immediately before the sample clots, obtain particles for a representative trephine/clot section, and maintain strict asepsis at the puncture site to prevent infection.

The Prothrombin Time (PT) is requested to assess the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways as part of a suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation work-up. Principle: Calcium and tissue thromboplastin are added to citrated plasma to activate the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the time taken for a fibrin clot to form is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal PT is approximately 11–15 seconds depending on the reagent used. Prolongation indicates deficiency of factors II, V, VII or X, seen in liver disease, warfarin therapy or vitamin K deficiency. Precautions: blood must be collected into the correct trisodium citrate ratio of 1:9, the test performed within a few hours of collection, and platelet-poor plasma obtained by adequate centrifugation to avoid interference from residual platelets.
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman in septic shock with widespread bleeding and low platelets. The attending doctor requests a Prothrombin Time (PT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 15-year-old with beta-thalassaemia major on regular transfusions is reviewed, and is subsequently diagnosed with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Ferritin. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to monitor for transfusion-related iron overload. Principle: An immunoassay (ELISA or chemiluminescence) measures serum ferritin, an acute-phase protein that reflects total body iron stores, since it correlates with the amount of iron sequestered within tissue macrophages and hepatocytes. Normal result: Approximately 15-150 ng/mL in women and 15-200 ng/mL in men; a progressively rising ferritin indicates iron accumulation and the need for chelation therapy. Precautions: Interpret cautiously in the presence of infection or inflammation, which raises ferritin independently of iron status as an acute-phase reactant, and avoid haemolysed samples which falsely elevate results.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent episodes of dark urine and normal Coombs test is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with unexplained intravascular haemolysis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Ham's Acid Haemolysis Test / Flow Cytometry for CD55 and CD59. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to exclude an inherited complement-regulation defect as the cause of the haemolysis. Principle: The historic Ham's test exposes red cells to acidified serum, which activates complement and lyses abnormally sensitive cells; modern flow cytometry directly detects the absence of the GPI-anchored surface proteins CD55 and CD59 that normally protect cells from complement. Normal result: Negative Ham's test, or normal expression of CD55 and CD59 on flow cytometry; a positive result confirms a PNH-type mechanism, distinguishing it from immune haemolysis. Precautions: Use fresh, unclotted blood and appropriate positive and negative controls, since flow cytometry has now largely replaced the technically demanding and less reproducible Ham's test.

The Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay is requested to confirm vitamin B12 deficiency, since B12 is found almost exclusively in animal products. Principle: Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels are measured, usually by immunoassay, to identify deficiency states that impair DNA synthesis in developing blood cells and cause megaloblastic change. Normal result and interpretation: Normal serum B12 is about 200–900 ng/L and folate about 3–20 microgram/L. Levels below these ranges confirm the deficiency responsible for macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia. Precautions: the sample should be protected from prolonged light exposure where applicable, haemolysis must be avoided, and results should be interpreted alongside the full blood count and blood film since dietary and absorption factors affect the levels obtained.
questions.question: A 33-year-old man following a strict vegan diet for several years, now with mild macrocytic anaemia. The attending doctor requests a Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient with a raised PCV and pruritus after bathing is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with polycythaemia vera. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Erythropoietin Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to help distinguish a primary marrow disorder from a secondary cause of polycythaemia. Principle: An immunoassay measures circulating erythropoietin, the hormone produced predominantly by the kidney in response to tissue hypoxia, which stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow. Normal result: Approximately 4-27 mU/mL, though appropriately elevated in genuine anaemia due to physiological hypoxic drive; a low or suppressed level supports polycythaemia vera, while a raised level suggests a secondary cause. Precautions: Interpret the result in the context of the patient's haemoglobin level, since a normal or low erythropoietin in the presence of anaemia is inappropriately low and clinically significant.

The G6PD Screening Test is requested to screen for G6PD deficiency before prescribing an oxidant antimalarial drug that could otherwise trigger haemolysis. Principle: Red cell lysate is incubated with glucose-6-phosphate and NADP; adequate G6PD enzyme generates NADPH, which fluoresces under ultraviolet light, whereas deficient samples show little or no fluorescence. Normal result and interpretation: A normal (fluorescent) result excludes significant deficiency, while absent or reduced fluorescence indicates G6PD deficiency, predisposing the patient to oxidative haemolysis after certain drugs, infections or fava beans. Precautions: the test should ideally be delayed until after an acute haemolytic episode has resolved, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a deficiency, and reagents must be protected from light and used fresh.
questions.question: A 28-year-old man about to be started on antimalarial prophylaxis before travelling to an endemic region. The attending doctor requests a G6PD Screening Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to detect an unexpectedly low factor VIII level suggesting an acquired inhibitor. Principle: Patient plasma is added to factor VIII-deficient substrate plasma, and the correction of the clotting time in a modified APTT-based assay is compared against a standard curve to quantify factor VIII activity. Normal result: 50-150% of the standard reference activity; a low level that fails to correct on mixing study supports acquired haemophilia due to an autoantibody. Precautions: Process the sample promptly since factor VIII activity declines on standing, and avoid interference from a lupus anticoagulant which can falsely lower apparent factor VIII levels.
questions.question: An elderly patient with no bleeding history develops sudden extensive bruising, and is subsequently diagnosed with acquired haemophilia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Factor VIII Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Malaria Parasite Blood Film is requested to check for breakthrough infection or a resistant parasite species requiring a change in treatment. Principle: Thick and thin blood films are stained with Giemsa or Field's stain; the thick film concentrates parasites for sensitive detection while the thin film preserves parasite and red cell morphology for species identification and parasitaemia quantification. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of parasites on a well-examined film excludes malaria at the time of testing. Presence of parasites confirms the diagnosis, with the species and percentage parasitaemia guiding severity assessment and treatment. Precautions: films must be made from fresh blood before antimalarial treatment reduces parasite counts, the staining buffer pH must be correctly maintained since incorrect pH affects parasite staining quality, and an adequate number of fields must be examined before a film is reported negative.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman who is pregnant with recurrent fevers despite standard antimalarial prophylaxis. The attending doctor requests a Malaria Parasite Blood Film. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to support the diagnosis of a myeloproliferative disorder. Principle: Neutrophils are stained cytochemically for alkaline phosphatase activity, and a semi-quantitative score is generated by scoring 100 consecutive neutrophils for staining intensity. Normal result: A score within the laboratory's established normal range, generally moderate staining intensity; a raised score is typical of polycythaemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood without delay, since enzyme activity deteriorates on standing, and score consecutively without selecting only strongly-stained cells to avoid bias.
questions.question: A patient with confirmed raised PCV and splenomegaly is further characterised, and is subsequently diagnosed with polycythaemia vera. The attending doctor refers the patient for Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 40-year-old man with an acute leukaemia of uncertain lineage on routine morphology alone. The attending doctor requests a Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Myeloperoxidase Cytochemical Stain is requested to resolve the lineage of the blast population when morphology alone is insufficient for classification. Principle: Myeloid cells contain peroxidase enzyme in their primary granules that reacts with hydrogen peroxide and a chromogen to give a coloured precipitate, positive in myeloblasts but negative in lymphoblasts. Normal result and interpretation: Peroxidase positivity in blast cells confirms myeloid lineage (acute myeloid leukaemia) while peroxidase-negative blasts suggest lymphoid lineage (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia). Precautions: fresh, well-fixed films must be used since old films lose enzyme activity, reagents must be prepared and used promptly as they deteriorate quickly, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included with every batch.

The Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) is requested to screen the intrinsic coagulation pathway for an undiagnosed factor deficiency responsible for his bleeding tendency. Principle: A contact activator such as kaolin, together with phospholipid and calcium, is added to citrated plasma to activate the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the clotting time is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal APTT is approximately 30–40 seconds. Prolongation suggests deficiency of an intrinsic pathway factor such as VIII, IX, XI or XII, seen in haemophilia, or the presence of heparin or a lupus anticoagulant. Precautions: plasma must not contact glass surfaces as this prematurely activates factor XII, the phospholipid reagent must be incubated with plasma for the recommended time before calcium is added, and samples for factor assay must be kept frozen or on ice if not tested immediately.
questions.question: A 30-year-old man with unexplained excessive bleeding after a dental extraction. The attending doctor requests a Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A blood donor from a malaria-endemic area is being screened before donation, and is subsequently diagnosed with transfusion-transmitted malaria screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for Thick and Thin Blood Film for Malaria Parasites. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to exclude parasitaemia that could be transmitted to a transfusion recipient. Principle: A thick film concentrates red cells to increase sensitivity for detecting parasites, while a thin film preserves red cell and parasite morphology for species identification, both examined microscopically after Giemsa staining. Normal result: No malaria parasites seen on thick or thin film; a positive film defers the donor from donating until treated and cleared. Precautions: Prepare films from a fresh fingerprick or anticoagulated sample without delay, ensure correct Giemsa staining pH and time for accurate parasite morphology, and examine an adequate number of fields before reporting a film negative.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a very high white cell count and circulating immature cells noted on automated count. The attending doctor requests a Peripheral Blood Film Examination. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Peripheral Blood Film Examination is requested to examine cell morphology directly and identify blast cells confirming a diagnosis of leukaemia. Principle: A thin film of blood is spread on a slide, fixed and stained with a Romanowsky stain so that red cell, white cell and platelet morphology can be examined directly under the microscope. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells appear as uniform biconcave discs with central pallor, white cells show normal proportions and morphology, and platelets are adequate in number. Abnormal shapes, inclusions or immature cells point to specific haematological disease. Precautions: the film must be made promptly from fresh anticoagulated or capillary blood, spread with a smooth, even-angled stroke to avoid artefacts, and properly fixed before staining to prevent cell distortion.

The Osmotic Fragility Test is requested to investigate a chronic haemolytic process and check whether increased fragility supports a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; spherocytic cells with a reduced surface area to volume ratio lyse earlier than normal biconcave cells, and the percentage lysis at each concentration is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells begin to lyse at about 0.45% saline and are completely lysed by 0.30%. Increased fragility (lysis at higher saline concentration) suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while decreased fragility suggests thalassaemia or iron deficiency. Precautions: blood must be defibrinated or collected into heparin rather than EDTA, saline dilutions must be prepared accurately and freshly, and tubes must be mixed gently to avoid mechanical haemolysis that would give a false result.
questions.question: A 25-year-old woman with unexplained jaundice, gallstones and a palpable spleen. The attending doctor requests a Osmotic Fragility Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The LE Cell Test is requested to investigate for systemic lupus erythematosus as a possible unifying diagnosis for her multisystem symptoms. Principle: Leucocytes are damaged in vitro to release nuclear material which, in the presence of anti-nuclear antibody in the patient's serum, is opsonised and then phagocytosed by other neutrophils to form the characteristic LE cell. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of LE cells is normal. Presence of LE cells supports a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus or occasionally drug-induced lupus, though the test is less sensitive than modern ANA methods. Precautions: the preparation must be examined promptly since LE cells degenerate on standing, an adequate number of fields must be examined before a negative result is reported, and technique-related artefacts must be distinguished from true LE cells.
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman with fatigue, mouth ulcers and photosensitivity of unclear cause. The attending doctor requests a LE Cell Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient with coeliac disease presents with chronic diarrhoea and mild anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with malabsorption syndrome. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Folate Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for folate malabsorption secondary to small bowel disease. Principle: An automated competitive immunoassay measures serum folate, a vitamin required together with B12 for thymidylate and DNA synthesis in dividing marrow cells. Normal result: Approximately 3-17 ng/mL (red cell folate is a more stable indicator of tissue stores); a low level supports malabsorption and improves once the underlying bowel disease is treated. Precautions: Draw blood before any folic acid supplementation is started, avoid recent alcohol intake which can transiently lower levels, and pair with a B12 assay since folate replacement alone can mask B12 deficiency and worsen neurological damage.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with unexplained postpartum bleeding not controlled by usual measures. The attending doctor requests a Plasma Fibrinogen Assay. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Plasma Fibrinogen Assay is requested to check for hypofibrinogenaemia contributing to her ongoing postpartum haemorrhage. Principle: Plasma fibrinogen is quantified by measuring the clotting time after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to fibrinogen concentration, or by a direct chemical or immunological method. Normal result and interpretation: Normal plasma fibrinogen is about 2–4 g/L. Low levels are seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation and severe liver disease, while raised levels occur as an acute phase response to inflammation. Precautions: the standard fibrinogen curve must be freshly prepared, citrated plasma must be free of clots, and haemolysed samples must be avoided as they interfere with accurate detection of the clotting endpoint.

questions.question: A neonate born to a group O, Rh-negative mother is assessed, and is subsequently diagnosed with newborn blood grouping. The attending doctor refers the patient for Blood Grouping (ABO and Rh Typing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to determine the infant's own blood group and assess risk of ABO or Rh incompatibility. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with known anti-A, anti-B and anti-D antisera (forward grouping), and patient serum is mixed with known A and B reagent cells (reverse grouping); agglutination patterns identify the ABO and Rh(D) type. Normal result: A concordant result between forward and reverse grouping confirming one of the four ABO groups and Rh status; a group A or B infant of a group O mother is at risk of ABO haemolytic disease, requiring bilirubin monitoring. Precautions: Always perform both forward and reverse grouping to detect discrepancies, use correctly labelled samples with a second independent check to prevent patient misidentification, which is the leading cause of fatal transfusion errors.

questions.question: A woman one hour after vaginal delivery is noted to be pale, tachycardic and passing large clots, and is subsequently diagnosed with postpartum haemorrhage. The attending doctor refers the patient for Full Blood Count (FBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to determine her current haemoglobin and guide the decision on blood transfusion. Principle: Whole blood is passed through an automated haematology analyser that uses electrical impedance and/or light-scatter to count and size red cells, white cells and platelets, and to compute derived indices such as MCV and MCH. Normal result: Hb 11.5-16.5 g/dL, WBC 4-11 x10^9/L, platelets 150-450 x10^9/L, with all indices within age/sex-adjusted ranges; a sharply reduced Hb compared with her antenatal value confirms significant blood loss requiring transfusion. Precautions: Draw into a properly filled EDTA bottle, mix by gentle inversion (not shaking) to prevent clot or haemolysis, and analyse within 4-6 hours as prolonged storage causes cell swelling and falsely raised MCV.

The Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch) is requested to confirm compatibility of multiple donor units rapidly issued during his emergency resuscitation. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and recipient red cells with donor serum (minor crossmatch), incubated at 37°C and tested by the antiglobulin technique to detect incompatibility before transfusion. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of agglutination or haemolysis in the major crossmatch indicates compatibility and the unit is safe to transfuse; agglutination indicates incompatibility and that unit must not be given. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before the antiglobulin phase, correct incubation time and temperature must be observed, and patient identification on the sample and request form must be verified to prevent transfusion of the wrong unit.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man involved in a major road traffic accident requiring massive transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 65-year-old man with anaemia, renal impairment and bone pain suggestive of myeloma. The attending doctor requests a Bone Marrow Aspiration. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Bone Marrow Aspiration is requested to examine the marrow for plasma cell infiltration confirming a diagnosis of multiple myeloma. Principle: Marrow tissue is aspirated, usually from the posterior iliac crest or sternum, smeared on slides and stained to examine the cellularity, myeloid:erythroid ratio and morphology of developing blood cell precursors. Normal result and interpretation: A normal marrow shows active trilineage haemopoiesis with a myeloid:erythroid ratio of about 2:1 to 4:1. Hypocellularity suggests aplastic anaemia, and infiltration by blast cells or other abnormal cells confirms leukaemia or another marrow disorder. Precautions: the aspirate must be smeared quickly before it clots, particle-rich areas of the smear must be selected for staining, and strict aseptic technique with local anaesthesia must be used to prevent infection and minimise patient discomfort.

The test was requested to provide baseline information relevant to counselling and planning delivery. Principle: Patient plasma is mixed with factor IX-deficient substrate plasma in an APTT-based clotting assay, and the degree of correction is compared against a reference curve to quantify factor IX activity. Normal result: 50-150% of the standard reference activity; knowledge of maternal and fetal factor IX status helps plan safe delivery and neonatal precautions. Precautions: Ensure correct sample handling and prompt processing, and be aware that vitamin K deficiency or warfarin therapy also lowers factor IX and can confound interpretation.
questions.question: A pregnant carrier of haemophilia B undergoes prenatal work-up, and is subsequently diagnosed with genetic counselling for haemophilia B. The attending doctor refers the patient for Factor IX Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A patient with confirmed paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is started on eculizumab, and is subsequently diagnosed with monitoring response to complement-inhibitor therapy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Ham's Acid Haemolysis Test / Flow Cytometry for CD55 and CD59. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to monitor the proportion of the abnormal clone and haemolytic activity during treatment. Principle: The historic Ham's test exposes red cells to acidified serum, which activates complement and lyses abnormally sensitive cells; modern flow cytometry directly detects the absence of the GPI-anchored surface proteins CD55 and CD59 that normally protect cells from complement. Normal result: Negative Ham's test, or normal expression of CD55 and CD59 on flow cytometry; a reduction in overt haemolysis with therapy supports adequate complement blockade. Precautions: Use fresh, unclotted blood and appropriate positive and negative controls, since flow cytometry has now largely replaced the technically demanding and less reproducible Ham's test.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man who developed lupus-like symptoms after starting a new anti-arrhythmic drug. The attending doctor requests a LE Cell Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The LE Cell Test is requested to investigate for drug-induced lupus as the explanation for his new symptoms. Principle: Leucocytes are damaged in vitro to release nuclear material which, in the presence of anti-nuclear antibody in the patient's serum, is opsonised and then phagocytosed by other neutrophils to form the characteristic LE cell. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of LE cells is normal. Presence of LE cells supports a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus or occasionally drug-induced lupus, though the test is less sensitive than modern ANA methods. Precautions: the preparation must be examined promptly since LE cells degenerate on standing, an adequate number of fields must be examined before a negative result is reported, and technique-related artefacts must be distinguished from true LE cells.

questions.question: A jaundiced neonate with a family history of splenectomy in a parent is assessed, and is subsequently diagnosed with neonatal jaundice work-up. The attending doctor refers the patient for Osmotic Fragility Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to investigate a hereditary red cell membrane defect as the cause of neonatal haemolysis. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; cells with reduced surface-to-volume ratio (spherocytes) lyse at higher saline concentrations than normal biconcave cells. Normal result: Complete lysis begins around 0.45% saline and is complete by about 0.30% saline; increased osmotic fragility supports a hereditary spherocytic process contributing to the jaundice. Precautions: Use fresh blood less than 24 hours old, ensure accurate serial dilution of the saline, and run a normal control in parallel to validate the test on each occasion.

The Indirect Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test is requested to monitor for rising antibody titres that would indicate developing Rh sensitisation and fetal risk. Principle: Patient serum suspected of containing antibody is incubated with reagent red cells of known antigen composition, and antihuman globulin reagent is then added to detect antibody that has coated the cells without producing visible agglutination. Normal result and interpretation: A negative IAT means no clinically significant antibody was detected, while a positive result indicates the presence of an alloantibody, important in antenatal screening and pre-transfusion compatibility testing. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before adding AHG reagent to remove unbound globulin, incubation temperature and time must be strictly observed since many antibodies react best at 37°C, and appropriate positive and negative controls must be included.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman who is Rhesus-negative and married to a Rhesus-positive partner, in her second pregnancy. The attending doctor requests a Indirect Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to identify sickle trait, which carries a small risk of exertional sickling and sudden collapse. Principle: Red cells are lysed in a reducing solution of sodium dithionite/metabisulphite; deoxygenated HbS polymerises and scatters light, producing turbidity, whereas normal HbA solutions remain clear. Normal result: A clear solution through which printed text can be read, indicating a negative result; a positive test warrants counselling on hydration and exertion limits pending confirmatory testing. Precautions: Confirm any positive screen with haemoglobin electrophoresis since the test cannot distinguish trait from disease, and avoid false negatives in severely anaemic patients by ensuring an adequate red cell concentration in the reagent.
questions.question: A 17-year-old athlete undergoes routine screening before competitive sport, and is subsequently diagnosed with sports pre-participation screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for Sickling (Solubility) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to exclude G6PD deficiency before prescribing an oxidant drug. Principle: A quantitative spectrophotometric or fluorescent-spot assay measures the activity of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that protects red cells from oxidative stress by generating NADPH. Normal result: Enzyme activity within the laboratory's established reference range (typically reported relative to a normal control); reduced activity should prompt selection of an alternative regimen or careful monitoring. Precautions: Avoid testing during or shortly after an acute haemolytic episode, since young reticulocytes have relatively higher enzyme activity and can mask a true deficiency; retest several weeks later if an acute episode has just occurred.
questions.question: A leprosy patient is being started on dapsone therapy, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-dapsone therapy screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for G6PD Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Mixed Lymphocyte Culture is requested to functionally assess Class II compatibility between him and his sibling donor beyond simple HLA typing. Principle: Recipient lymphocytes are cultured together with irradiated or mitomycin-treated donor lymphocytes, and the degree of recipient lymphocyte proliferation in response to donor Class II antigen differences is measured, usually by radioactive thymidine incorporation. Normal result and interpretation: Low proliferation indicates close Class II compatibility and lower rejection risk, while high proliferation indicates significant mismatch and a higher risk of graft rejection or graft-versus-host disease. Precautions: donor lymphocytes must be adequately irradiated or treated to prevent their own proliferation from confounding the result, sterile technique must be maintained throughout the culture period, and viable lymphocyte counts must be standardised between test wells.
questions.question: A 30-year-old man being worked up for a bone marrow transplant from a haploidentical sibling. The attending doctor requests a Mixed Lymphocyte Culture. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

An Rh-negative woman experiences an unexplained stillbirth, and is subsequently diagnosed with stillbirth investigation. The attending doctor refers the patient for Kleihauer-Betke Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to investigate whether a large fetomaternal haemorrhage contributed to the fetal death. Principle: A blood film is treated with acid elution, which removes adult haemoglobin from maternal red cells while fetal haemoglobin resists elution, allowing fetal cells to be counted and the volume of fetomaternal haemorrhage estimated. Normal result: Very few or no fetal cells detected in maternal blood (typically less than 0.1-0.3 mL fetal blood); a substantial fetal cell count supports massive haemorrhage as a contributing cause. Precautions: Prepare and stain the film promptly and consistently, and count an adequate number of fields to avoid underestimating a small haemorrhage, since the calculated anti-D dose depends directly on this count.

questions.question: A patient with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops a raised haemoglobin, and is subsequently diagnosed with secondary polycythaemia from chronic hypoxia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Erythropoietin Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm an appropriate physiological drive for increased red cell production. Principle: An immunoassay measures circulating erythropoietin, the hormone produced predominantly by the kidney in response to tissue hypoxia, which stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow. Normal result: Approximately 4-27 mU/mL, though appropriately elevated in genuine anaemia due to physiological hypoxic drive; an appropriately raised level supports secondary polycythaemia due to chronic hypoxia. Precautions: Interpret the result in the context of the patient's haemoglobin level, since a normal or low erythropoietin in the presence of anaemia is inappropriately low and clinically significant.

questions.question: A sibling of a child recently diagnosed with hereditary spherocytosis is brought for evaluation, and is subsequently diagnosed with family screening. The attending doctor refers the patient for Osmotic Fragility Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen asymptomatic relatives for the same inherited membrane defect. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; cells with reduced surface-to-volume ratio (spherocytes) lyse at higher saline concentrations than normal biconcave cells. Normal result: Complete lysis begins around 0.45% saline and is complete by about 0.30% saline; increased fragility in an otherwise well relative suggests a mild or compensated form of the disease. Precautions: Use fresh blood less than 24 hours old, ensure accurate serial dilution of the saline, and run a normal control in parallel to validate the test on each occasion.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman with leukaemia in remission, evaluated for stem cell transplantation from an unrelated donor. The attending doctor requests a Mixed Lymphocyte Culture. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Mixed Lymphocyte Culture is requested to assess the functional degree of lymphocyte reactivity against her potential unrelated donor before proceeding. Principle: Recipient lymphocytes are cultured together with irradiated or mitomycin-treated donor lymphocytes, and the degree of recipient lymphocyte proliferation in response to donor Class II antigen differences is measured, usually by radioactive thymidine incorporation. Normal result and interpretation: Low proliferation indicates close Class II compatibility and lower rejection risk, while high proliferation indicates significant mismatch and a higher risk of graft rejection or graft-versus-host disease. Precautions: donor lymphocytes must be adequately irradiated or treated to prevent their own proliferation from confounding the result, sterile technique must be maintained throughout the culture period, and viable lymphocyte counts must be standardised between test wells.

The Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) is requested to support the diagnosis of an inflammatory arthropathy such as rheumatoid arthritis and to monitor disease activity. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is left to stand vertically in a calibrated tube and the rate at which red cells sediment under gravity, influenced mainly by plasma fibrinogen and globulin concentration, is measured after one hour. Normal result and interpretation: Normal ESR (Westergren) is roughly up to 10 mm/hr in men and 15 mm/hr in women. A markedly raised ESR indicates active inflammation, infection or malignancy, though the test is non-specific. Precautions: the tube must be perfectly vertical, free of air bubbles and vibration during the test, the test must be set up within two hours of collection, and the sample must be neither clotted nor haemolysed.
questions.question: A 38-year-old woman with symmetrical joint pain and swelling for six weeks. The attending doctor requests a Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Donath-Landsteiner Test is requested to confirm a post-infectious paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria as the explanation for his new haemolysis. Principle: Patient serum containing the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is incubated with red cells at 4°C, allowing antibody and complement to bind, then warmed to 37°C, which triggers complement-mediated haemolysis characteristic of paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria. Normal result and interpretation: A negative test shows no haemolysis. A positive biphasic haemolysis pattern confirms paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria, usually occurring after a viral infection. Precautions: the cold and warm incubation steps must be performed in strict sequence and at the correct temperatures since reversing or skipping a step gives a false negative result, and fresh complement-containing serum must be used.
questions.question: A 10-year-old boy recovering from measles, now noted to have sudden haemoglobinuria. The attending doctor requests a Donath-Landsteiner Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 60-year-old man with unexplained chronic anaemia and a positive cold agglutinin history. The attending doctor requests a Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test is requested to determine whether antibody or complement is bound to his red cells in vivo, supporting an autoimmune haemolytic process. Principle: Antihuman globulin reagent is added directly to the patient's washed red cells; agglutination occurs if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement. Normal result and interpretation: A negative DAT indicates no in vivo sensitisation of red cells, while a positive DAT confirms antibody or complement coating, seen in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, haemolytic disease of the newborn, or drug-induced and transfusion-related haemolysis. Precautions: the red cells must be washed thoroughly, at least three times, with saline to remove all free globulin that would otherwise neutralise the antiglobulin reagent, and the tubes must be centrifuged at the recommended speed before reading.

The Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC) is requested to classify his anaemia, since a macrocytic pattern would support megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 deficiency. Principle: Derived mathematically from the red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV to describe the average size and haemoglobin content of red cells, classifying anaemia as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic. Normal result and interpretation: Normal MCV is 80–100 fl, MCH 27–32 pg and MCHC 32–36%. Values below these indicate microcytic hypochromic anaemia while values above indicate macrocytosis. Precautions: an accurate red cell count, haemoglobin and PCV must first be obtained since the indices are only as reliable as the values used to calculate them, and lipaemic or haemolysed samples must be avoided as they distort the result.
questions.question: A 65-year-old man with a beefy red tongue and unsteady gait. The attending doctor requests a Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 40-year-old man with longstanding unexplained mild chronic anaemia and splenomegaly. The attending doctor requests a Osmotic Fragility Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Osmotic Fragility Test is requested to further characterise a chronic haemolytic anaemia by assessing red cell membrane fragility. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; spherocytic cells with a reduced surface area to volume ratio lyse earlier than normal biconcave cells, and the percentage lysis at each concentration is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal red cells begin to lyse at about 0.45% saline and are completely lysed by 0.30%. Increased fragility (lysis at higher saline concentration) suggests hereditary spherocytosis, while decreased fragility suggests thalassaemia or iron deficiency. Precautions: blood must be defibrinated or collected into heparin rather than EDTA, saline dilutions must be prepared accurately and freshly, and tubes must be mixed gently to avoid mechanical haemolysis that would give a false result.

The Bone Marrow Aspiration is requested to directly examine erythroid precursors for megaloblastic change and exclude a myelodysplastic process. Principle: Marrow tissue is aspirated, usually from the posterior iliac crest or sternum, smeared on slides and stained to examine the cellularity, myeloid:erythroid ratio and morphology of developing blood cell precursors. Normal result and interpretation: A normal marrow shows active trilineage haemopoiesis with a myeloid:erythroid ratio of about 2:1 to 4:1. Hypocellularity suggests aplastic anaemia, and infiltration by blast cells or other abnormal cells confirms leukaemia or another marrow disorder. Precautions: the aspirate must be smeared quickly before it clots, particle-rich areas of the smear must be selected for staining, and strict aseptic technique with local anaesthesia must be used to prevent infection and minimise patient discomfort.
questions.question: A 70-year-old woman with macrocytic anaemia not responding to simple vitamin replacement. The attending doctor requests a Bone Marrow Aspiration. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

The sister of a boy with severe haemophilia A wishes to know her carrier status before starting a family, and is subsequently diagnosed with carrier testing in haemophilia families. The attending doctor refers the patient for Factor VIII Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess her factor VIII level as part of carrier evaluation. Principle: Patient plasma is added to factor VIII-deficient substrate plasma, and the correction of the clotting time in a modified APTT-based assay is compared against a standard curve to quantify factor VIII activity. Normal result: 50-150% of the standard reference activity; a level around 50% is consistent with carrier status, though genetic testing gives a more definitive answer. Precautions: Process the sample promptly since factor VIII activity declines on standing, and avoid interference from a lupus anticoagulant which can falsely lower apparent factor VIII levels.

questions.question: A fetus shows unexplained signs of anaemia on antenatal ultrasound, and is subsequently diagnosed with unexplained fetal distress or anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Kleihauer-Betke Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess whether a significant fetomaternal haemorrhage might explain the fetal anaemia. Principle: A blood film is treated with acid elution, which removes adult haemoglobin from maternal red cells while fetal haemoglobin resists elution, allowing fetal cells to be counted and the volume of fetomaternal haemorrhage estimated. Normal result: Very few or no fetal cells detected in maternal blood (typically less than 0.1-0.3 mL fetal blood); a large fetal cell count in maternal blood supports haemorrhage as the cause. Precautions: Prepare and stain the film promptly and consistently, and count an adequate number of fields to avoid underestimating a small haemorrhage, since the calculated anti-D dose depends directly on this count.

The test was requested to have his group on record so blood can be rapidly crossmatched if needed intra-operatively. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with known anti-A, anti-B and anti-D antisera (forward grouping), and patient serum is mixed with known A and B reagent cells (reverse grouping); agglutination patterns identify the ABO and Rh(D) type. Normal result: A concordant result between forward and reverse grouping confirming one of the four ABO groups and Rh status; correct typing avoids delay in issuing compatible blood should unexpected bleeding occur. Precautions: Always perform both forward and reverse grouping to detect discrepancies, use correctly labelled samples with a second independent check to prevent patient misidentification, which is the leading cause of fatal transfusion errors.
questions.question: A patient is scheduled for elective orthopaedic surgery with anticipated blood loss, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-operative type and screen. The attending doctor refers the patient for Blood Grouping (ABO and Rh Typing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Haemoglobin Estimation is requested to quantify the degree of blood loss anaemia resulting from her menorrhagia and guide the urgency of iron replacement or referral. Principle: Haemoglobin is converted to a stable coloured compound (acid haematin or cyanmethaemoglobin) whose colour intensity, read colorimetrically, is proportional to haemoglobin concentration. Normal result and interpretation: Normal values are 13–17 g/dl in men and 12–15 g/dl in women. Values below this confirm anaemia while markedly elevated values suggest polycythaemia or dehydration. Precautions: reagents must be fresh and correctly diluted, the exact volume of blood must be drawn without air bubbles, and colour development must be allowed to reach completion before reading to avoid underestimation.
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding for six months. The attending doctor requests a Haemoglobin Estimation. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A child with chronic itching and abdominal discomfort is investigated, and is subsequently diagnosed with allergic reaction and helminthic infection. The attending doctor refers the patient for Total White Blood Cell Count and Differential. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to look for eosinophilia suggesting a parasitic or allergic cause. Principle: An automated analyser counts total leucocytes and classifies them into neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils based on size and internal complexity (light scatter), a process that can be confirmed by microscopic differential count.
