Normal result: Total WBC 4-11 x10^9/L, with neutrophils 40-75%, lymphocytes 20-45%, monocytes 2-10%, eosinophils 1-6% and basophils 0-1%; a raised eosinophil count supports helminthic infestation or an allergic process. Precautions: Confirm any abnormal automated differential (flagged result) by manual microscopic examination of a blood film, since automated counters cannot reliably distinguish blasts or atypical cells.

The Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch) is requested to ensure fully phenotype-matched compatible blood is selected, since sickle cell patients are prone to alloimmunisation from repeated transfusions. Principle: Donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum (major crossmatch) and recipient red cells with donor serum (minor crossmatch), incubated at 37°C and tested by the antiglobulin technique to detect incompatibility before transfusion. Normal result and interpretation: Absence of agglutination or haemolysis in the major crossmatch indicates compatibility and the unit is safe to transfuse; agglutination indicates incompatibility and that unit must not be given. Precautions: cells must be washed adequately before the antiglobulin phase, correct incubation time and temperature must be observed, and patient identification on the sample and request form must be verified to prevent transfusion of the wrong unit.
questions.question: A 18-year-old man known to have sickle cell disease, admitted in a painful crisis requiring transfusion. The attending doctor requests a Compatibility Testing (Crossmatch). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 45-year-old man with mucosal bleeding and known severe thrombocytopenia. The attending doctor requests a Bleeding Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Bleeding Time is requested to correlate his platelet count with actual bleeding tendency before a planned procedure. Principle: A standardised skin incision is made and the time taken for bleeding to stop spontaneously is timed, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall during primary haemostasis. Normal result and interpretation: Normal bleeding time is about 2–7 minutes depending on the method used. Prolongation suggests a platelet function disorder, von Willebrand disease or severe thrombocytopenia. Precautions: the incision must be of standardised depth and length, blood must be blotted gently every 30 seconds without touching the wound edge, and the test must be interpreted cautiously in patients on aspirin or with an obvious bleeding tendency.

questions.question: A teenager with confirmed spherocytosis is being assessed before elective splenectomy, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-splenectomy work-up. The attending doctor refers the patient for Osmotic Fragility Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to document baseline red cell fragility for comparison with post-operative improvement. Principle: Red cells are exposed to a graded series of hypotonic saline concentrations; cells with reduced surface-to-volume ratio (spherocytes) lyse at higher saline concentrations than normal biconcave cells. Normal result: Complete lysis begins around 0.45% saline and is complete by about 0.30% saline; markedly increased fragility supports ongoing haemolysis that splenectomy is expected to reduce. Precautions: Use fresh blood less than 24 hours old, ensure accurate serial dilution of the saline, and run a normal control in parallel to validate the test on each occasion.

questions.question: A patient completing six months of anticoagulation for an unprovoked DVT is reviewed, and is subsequently diagnosed with monitoring anticoagulation duration. The attending doctor refers the patient for D-Dimer Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to help assess residual thrombotic risk when deciding whether to stop anticoagulation. Principle: An immunoassay detects D-dimer, a specific breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin, whose presence indicates that both clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis have occurred. Normal result: Below the assay-specific cut-off, usually less than 0.5 micrograms/mL FEU; a persistently raised level after stopping anticoagulation is associated with higher recurrence risk. Precautions: Recognise that many conditions besides thrombosis (pregnancy, infection, malignancy, recent surgery) raise D-dimer, so a positive result is not diagnostic on its own; primarily use a negative result to help exclude thrombosis in low-probability patients.

The test was requested to establish ABO compatibility between donor and recipient before transplantation. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with known anti-A, anti-B and anti-D antisera (forward grouping), and patient serum is mixed with known A and B reagent cells (reverse grouping); agglutination patterns identify the ABO and Rh(D) type. Normal result: A concordant result between forward and reverse grouping confirming one of the four ABO groups and Rh status; ABO incompatibility between donor and recipient predicts hyperacute rejection unless specifically managed. Precautions: Always perform both forward and reverse grouping to detect discrepancies, use correctly labelled samples with a second independent check to prevent patient misidentification, which is the leading cause of fatal transfusion errors.
questions.question: A patient being assessed for kidney transplantation requires baseline typing, and is subsequently diagnosed with organ transplantation work-up. The attending doctor refers the patient for Blood Grouping (ABO and Rh Typing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm drug-induced folate deficiency. Principle: An automated competitive immunoassay measures serum folate, a vitamin required together with B12 for thymidylate and DNA synthesis in dividing marrow cells. Normal result: Approximately 3-17 ng/mL (red cell folate is a more stable indicator of tissue stores); a low level supports the drug interaction, and supplementation is given without stopping the anticonvulsant. Precautions: Draw blood before any folic acid supplementation is started, avoid recent alcohol intake which can transiently lower levels, and pair with a B12 assay since folate replacement alone can mask B12 deficiency and worsen neurological damage.
questions.question: An epileptic patient on long-term phenytoin presents with macrocytic anaemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with anticonvulsant therapy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Serum Folate Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The ABO Blood Grouping is requested to determine his ABO group as part of routine pre-operative preparation for possible transfusion. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed separately with known anti-A and anti-B antisera (forward grouping) and patient serum is mixed with known A and B cells (reverse grouping); agglutination identifies the ABO group present. Normal result and interpretation: Consistent forward and reverse grouping results confirm the patient's ABO group as A, B, AB or O. Discrepancies between forward and reverse results require further investigation before blood can be issued. Precautions: fresh antisera of adequate potency must be used, an adequate cell suspension concentration must be prepared, and both forward and reverse grouping must always be performed and cross-checked to avoid mistyping.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man scheduled for elective bowel surgery with anticipated blood loss. The attending doctor requests a ABO Blood Grouping. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A 5-year-old boy with high fever, sore throat and neck swelling for three days. The attending doctor requests a White Cell Differential Count. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The White Cell Differential Count is requested to look for a neutrophilia suggestive of acute bacterial infection guiding antibiotic decisions. Principle: A well-made, Romanowsky-stained blood film is examined under oil immersion to identify and enumerate the different types of white cells, revealing shifts in proportion or the presence of abnormal cells. Normal result and interpretation: Normal differential is roughly neutrophils 40–75%, lymphocytes 20–45%, monocytes 2–10%, eosinophils 1–6% and basophils 0–1%. Deviations indicate infection, allergy, parasitic disease or leukaemia depending on the cell type affected. Precautions: the film must be made from fresh blood spread thinly and evenly to avoid EDTA storage artefact, and counting must be performed in a representative area of the film where cells are well separated and not overlapping.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman being worked up for a planned kidney transplant. The attending doctor requests a ABO Blood Grouping. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The ABO Blood Grouping is requested to determine her ABO group, since ABO compatibility is essential for successful organ transplantation. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed separately with known anti-A and anti-B antisera (forward grouping) and patient serum is mixed with known A and B cells (reverse grouping); agglutination identifies the ABO group present. Normal result and interpretation: Consistent forward and reverse grouping results confirm the patient's ABO group as A, B, AB or O. Discrepancies between forward and reverse results require further investigation before blood can be issued. Precautions: fresh antisera of adequate potency must be used, an adequate cell suspension concentration must be prepared, and both forward and reverse grouping must always be performed and cross-checked to avoid mistyping.

The Whole Blood Clotting Time is requested to obtain a basic screening result for gross coagulation abnormality. Principle: Whole blood is placed in a plain glass tube and tilted at intervals until a clot forms, giving a simple bedside measure of the overall intrinsic clotting pathway. Normal result and interpretation: Normal clotting time is about 5–10 minutes. Marked prolongation suggests a severe coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia. Precautions: glass tubes must be clean and dry, the tube must be tilted gently and consistently without excessive agitation, and the test must be performed at a constant temperature since cold significantly prolongs clotting.
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with unexplained excessive bleeding and no access to specialised coagulation testing. The attending doctor requests a Whole Blood Clotting Time. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for DIC precipitated by placental abruption before and during emergency delivery. Principle: A combined panel assesses the extrinsic pathway (PT), intrinsic pathway (APTT), platelet number and fibrinogen concentration together, since disseminated intravascular coagulation produces a characteristic pattern of simultaneous consumption across all these parameters. Normal result: PT and APTT within normal range, platelets above 150 x10^9/L and fibrinogen above 2.0 g/L, with a low D-dimer; a consumptive pattern confirms DIC, requiring coordinated obstetric and haematological management. Precautions: Collect and process the sample promptly and correctly (proper citrate ratio, prompt centrifugation) since delayed or incorrect handling can mimic or mask true consumptive coagulopathy, and repeat serially since DIC evolves rapidly.
questions.question: A pregnant woman presents with sudden abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding and a tense uterus, and is subsequently diagnosed with obstetric DIC (placental abruption). The attending doctor refers the patient for Coagulation Screen (PT, APTT, Platelets, Fibrinogen) for DIC. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 55-year-old man with pancytopenia and no obvious peripheral cause identified. The attending doctor requests a Bone Marrow Aspiration. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?
questions.answerText: The Bone Marrow Aspiration is requested to directly examine marrow cellularity and morphology to distinguish aplastic anaemia from marrow infiltration. Principle: Marrow tissue is aspirated, usually from the posterior iliac crest or sternum, smeared on slides and stained to examine the cellularity, myeloid:erythroid ratio and morphology of developing blood cell precursors. Normal result and interpretation: A normal marrow shows active trilineage haemopoiesis with a myeloid:erythroid ratio of about 2:1 to 4:1. Hypocellularity suggests aplastic anaemia, and infiltration by blast cells or other abnormal cells confirms leukaemia or another marrow disorder. Precautions: the aspirate must be smeared quickly before it clots, particle-rich areas of the smear must be selected for staining, and strict aseptic technique with local anaesthesia must be used to prevent infection and minimise patient discomfort.

The test was requested to assess for a neutrophilic leucocytosis supporting an acute inflammatory process. Principle: An automated analyser counts total leucocytes and classifies them into neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils based on size and internal complexity (light scatter), a process that can be confirmed by microscopic differential count. Normal result: Total WBC 4-11 x10^9/L, with neutrophils 40-75%, lymphocytes 20-45%, monocytes 2-10%, eosinophils 1-6% and basophils 0-1%; a raised neutrophil count supports the diagnosis and the need for surgical review. Precautions: Confirm any abnormal automated differential (flagged result) by manual microscopic examination of a blood film, since automated counters cannot reliably distinguish blasts or atypical cells.
questions.question: A 15-year-old presents with right iliac fossa pain and fever, and is subsequently diagnosed with acute appendicitis. The attending doctor refers the patient for Total White Blood Cell Count and Differential. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to demonstrate impaired platelet aggregation in a rare inherited platelet disorder. Principle: A standardised skin incision (Ivy method) is made and the time to cessation of bleeding is measured, reflecting the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall in primary haemostasis. Normal result: Approximately 2-9 minutes, depending on the method used; a markedly prolonged bleeding time with a normal platelet count supports this inherited platelet function defect. Precautions: Use a standardised, calibrated incision device and consistent incision depth, and avoid the test in patients taking aspirin or NSAIDs within the preceding week unless specifically assessing their effect.
questions.question: A child from a consanguineous family presents with severe mucocutaneous bleeding since infancy, and is subsequently diagnosed with glanzmann thrombasthenia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Bleeding Time. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) is requested to monitor disease activity of his inflammatory bowel disease over time. Principle: Anticoagulated blood is left to stand vertically in a calibrated tube and the rate at which red cells sediment under gravity, influenced mainly by plasma fibrinogen and globulin concentration, is measured after one hour. Normal result and interpretation: Normal ESR (Westergren) is roughly up to 10 mm/hr in men and 15 mm/hr in women. A markedly raised ESR indicates active inflammation, infection or malignancy, though the test is non-specific. Precautions: the tube must be perfectly vertical, free of air bubbles and vibration during the test, the test must be set up within two hours of collection, and the sample must be neither clotted nor haemolysed.
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with known ulcerative colitis presenting with worsening abdominal symptoms. The attending doctor requests a Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test is requested to confirm whether her red cells are coated with antibody, supporting a diagnosis of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Principle: Antihuman globulin reagent is added directly to the patient's washed red cells; agglutination occurs if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement. Normal result and interpretation: A negative DAT indicates no in vivo sensitisation of red cells, while a positive DAT confirms antibody or complement coating, seen in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, haemolytic disease of the newborn, or drug-induced and transfusion-related haemolysis. Precautions: the red cells must be washed thoroughly, at least three times, with saline to remove all free globulin that would otherwise neutralise the antiglobulin reagent, and the tubes must be centrifuged at the recommended speed before reading.
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with rapidly progressive jaundice, dark urine and splenomegaly of unknown cause. The attending doctor requests a Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test. Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

A patient with severe anaemia from a gastrointestinal bleed requires urgent transfusion, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-transfusion work-up. The attending doctor refers the patient for Blood Grouping (ABO and Rh Typing). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to determine his ABO and Rh group before selecting compatible blood. Principle: Patient red cells are mixed with known anti-A, anti-B and anti-D antisera (forward grouping), and patient serum is mixed with known A and B reagent cells (reverse grouping); agglutination patterns identify the ABO and Rh(D) type. Normal result: A concordant result between forward and reverse grouping confirming one of the four ABO groups and Rh status; an accurately determined group ensures ABO-compatible blood is issued, preventing a fatal haemolytic transfusion reaction. Precautions: Always perform both forward and reverse grouping to detect discrepancies, use correctly labelled samples with a second independent check to prevent patient misidentification, which is the leading cause of fatal transfusion errors.

The test was requested to confirm a benign reactive leukaemoid reaction rather than a leukaemic process. Principle: Neutrophils are stained cytochemically for alkaline phosphatase activity, and a semi-quantitative score is generated by scoring 100 consecutive neutrophils for staining intensity. Normal result: A score within the laboratory's established normal range, generally moderate staining intensity; a high score supports a reactive leukaemoid reaction rather than chronic myeloid leukaemia. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood without delay, since enzyme activity deteriorates on standing, and score consecutively without selecting only strongly-stained cells to avoid bias.
questions.question: A patient with overwhelming sepsis has a very high white cell count, and is subsequently diagnosed with leukaemoid reaction from severe infection. The attending doctor refers the patient for Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) Score. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A patient with decompensated cirrhosis presents with bleeding gums, and is subsequently diagnosed with chronic liver disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Fibrinogen Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess hepatic synthetic function, since fibrinogen is produced in the liver. Principle: The Clauss method measures the clotting time of diluted plasma after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to the fibrinogen concentration, allowing quantification of this key clotting protein. Normal result: Approximately 2.0-4.0 g/L; a low level reflects impaired synthetic function and correlates with bleeding risk. Precautions: Ensure the correct citrate anticoagulation ratio and process promptly, since fibrinogen is an acute-phase protein and results must be interpreted alongside the clinical context of inflammation or infection.

The Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) is requested to investigate for haemophilia by assessing the intrinsic coagulation pathway responsible for factor VIII or IX deficiency. Principle: A contact activator such as kaolin, together with phospholipid and calcium, is added to citrated plasma to activate the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, and the clotting time is measured. Normal result and interpretation: Normal APTT is approximately 30–40 seconds. Prolongation suggests deficiency of an intrinsic pathway factor such as VIII, IX, XI or XII, seen in haemophilia, or the presence of heparin or a lupus anticoagulant. Precautions: plasma must not contact glass surfaces as this prematurely activates factor XII, the phospholipid reagent must be incubated with plasma for the recommended time before calcium is added, and samples for factor assay must be kept frozen or on ice if not tested immediately.
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy with prolonged bleeding after a minor cut and swollen painful joints. The attending doctor requests a Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT). Why was this test requested, what principle does it work on, what result is normally expected and what does a deviation mean, and what precautions must the laboratory scientist observe to avoid a false result?

questions.answerText: The test was requested to screen for abnormal white cell counts, blast forms and cytopenias suggestive of marrow infiltration. Principle: Whole blood is passed through an automated haematology analyser that uses electrical impedance and/or light-scatter to count and size red cells, white cells and platelets, and to compute derived indices such as MCV and MCH. Normal result: Hb 11.5-16.5 g/dL, WBC 4-11 x10^9/L, platelets 150-450 x10^9/L, with all indices within age/sex-adjusted ranges; a very high or very low WBC with anaemia and thrombocytopenia raises strong suspicion of acute leukaemia and warrants marrow examination. Precautions: Draw into a properly filled EDTA bottle, mix by gentle inversion (not shaking) to prevent clot or haemolysis, and analyse within 4-6 hours as prolonged storage causes cell swelling and falsely raised MCV.
questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with easy bruising, recurrent fevers and bone pain, and is subsequently diagnosed with suspected leukaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Full Blood Count (FBC). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 40-year-old woman presents with sudden jaundice, dark urine and splenomegaly, and is subsequently diagnosed with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. The attending doctor refers the patient for Direct Antiglobulin (Direct Coombs) Test. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm antibody-coated red cells as the cause of her haemolysis. Principle: Anti-human globulin reagent is added to washed patient red cells; if the cells are already coated in vivo with antibody or complement, the reagent cross-links adjacent cells to produce visible agglutination. Normal result: Negative - no agglutination; a positive result confirms an immune-mediated process, distinguishing it from hereditary haemolytic anaemias. Precautions: Wash the red cells thoroughly to remove all free unbound globulin before adding the antiglobulin reagent, since inadequate washing causes false-negative results through neutralisation.

questions.question: A farmer presents with a snakebite and gum bleeding several hours later, and is subsequently diagnosed with snakebite envenomation. The attending doctor refers the patient for Fibrinogen Assay. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to assess for venom-induced consumption coagulopathy. Principle: The Clauss method measures the clotting time of diluted plasma after adding excess thrombin, which is inversely proportional to the fibrinogen concentration, allowing quantification of this key clotting protein. Normal result: Approximately 2.0-4.0 g/L; an undetectable fibrinogen (consistent with a positive 20-minute whole blood clotting test) supports systemic envenomation requiring antivenom. Precautions: Ensure the correct citrate anticoagulation ratio and process promptly, since fibrinogen is an acute-phase protein and results must be interpreted alongside the clinical context of inflammation or infection.

The test was requested to confirm or exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia among the myeloproliferative disorders. Principle: Metaphase chromosome preparation or fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) detects the t(9;22) translocation forming the Philadelphia chromosome, or the resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene product is quantified by RT-PCR. Normal result: Absence of the t(9;22) translocation or BCR-ABL fusion transcript; absence of the translocation excludes chronic myeloid leukaemia, prompting evaluation for JAK2-related disorders instead. Precautions: Ensure the marrow or blood sample is fresh and contains adequate dividing cells for metaphase analysis, and use molecular quantification (RT-PCR) rather than karyotyping alone for sensitive monitoring of minimal residual disease.
questions.question: A patient with marked leucocytosis and splenomegaly is being classified, and is subsequently diagnosed with differentiating CML from other myeloproliferative disorders. The attending doctor refers the patient for Cytogenetic Analysis for Philadelphia Chromosome (BCR-ABL). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm the presence of sickle-shaped cells and assess disease severity. Principle: A thin smear of blood is stained with Romanowsky stain (e.g. Leishman or Wright-Giemsa) and examined under the microscope to assess red cell, white cell and platelet morphology and number. Normal result: Red cells are normocytic and normochromic with normal white cell and platelet morphology and no abnormal cells; sickle cells, target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies (from hyposplenism) support the diagnosis and its chronicity. Precautions: Prepare the smear from fresh blood within one hour of collection to avoid crenation and morphological artefact, and use a clean grease-free slide with a smooth, even spreading technique to avoid a poorly feathered edge.
questions.question: A 16-year-old known sickle cell patient presents with severe bone pain during a vaso-occlusive crisis, and is subsequently diagnosed with sickle cell disease. The attending doctor refers the patient for Peripheral Blood Film. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

A 33-year-old woman with iron deficiency anaemia returns for review 10 days after starting oral iron, and is subsequently diagnosed with response to iron therapy. The attending doctor refers the patient for Reticulocyte Count. Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.
questions.answerText: The test was requested to confirm an early erythropoietic response before waiting for the haemoglobin to rise. Principle: Blood is stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, which precipitates residual ribosomal RNA in young red cells as a reticular network, allowing reticulocytes to be counted as a percentage or absolute count. Normal result: 0.5-2.5% of red cells, or an absolute count of 25-100 x10^9/L; a reticulocyte rise (reticulocyte 'crisis') by day 7-10 confirms response, while a flat count suggests poor compliance or continued blood loss. Precautions: Use fresh, well-mixed EDTA blood and count at least 1000 red cells to reduce sampling error, and distinguish true reticular staining from Heinz bodies or artefactual staining.

The test was requested to identify an underlying von Willebrand defect before the procedure. Principle: Immunoassay quantifies von Willebrand factor antigen, while a functional assay (such as ristocetin cofactor activity) measures its ability to mediate platelet binding, together characterising both the amount and function of the protein. Normal result: Approximately 50-200% of the reference standard for both antigen and activity; reduced levels prompt pre-operative desmopressin or factor concentrate cover. Precautions: Be aware that vWF is an acute-phase reactant and can be transiently raised by stress, exercise or inflammation, and that blood group O individuals have physiologically lower baseline levels.
questions.question: A patient with a history of prolonged bleeding after tooth extraction requires elective surgery, and is subsequently diagnosed with pre-operative assessment in suspected mild bleeding disorder. The attending doctor refers the patient for von Willebrand Factor Assay (Antigen and Activity). Explain why this test was requested, the underlying principle of the test, the expected normal result and the implications of any deviation, and the precautions a laboratory scientist must observe to avoid a false result.

courses.title: Electrotherapy II

questions.question: A therapist is treating a patient recovering from recent radiotherapy to the thigh and considers Russian current for quadriceps strengthening. What is the correct clinical decision?
options: Avoid Russian current due to recent radiotherapy
Radiotherapy history is irrelevant to Russian current use
Increase treatment frequency to compensate for tissue changes
Apply treatment only over the irradiated skin
questions.explanation: Recent radiotherapy is listed as a specific contraindication to Russian current application, reflecting concerns about tissue vulnerability following irradiation. Proceeding despite this history risks further tissue compromise. An alternative strengthening approach should be considered until sufficient time has passed and medical clearance obtained.

Medium frequency currents, such as interferential and Russian current, are classified between 1 kHz and 100 kHz. Low frequency currents lie below 1 kHz, while high frequency currents exceed 100 kHz. This classification affects skin comfort and depth.
questions.question: According to standard classification, medium frequency currents fall within which range?

questions.explanation: Amplitude reflects current intensity, and greater intensity permits deeper tissue penetration and more muscle fibre recruitment. Frequency and duty cycle influence fatigue and comfort rather than depth. This relates to the Arndt-Schultz principle of stimulus-response.
questions.question: Which stimulation parameter is directly associated with the depth of current penetration into tissue?

questions.explanation: A cardiac pacemaker is an absolute contraindication because electrical stimulation may interfere with pacemaker function. Disuse weakness and healed scars are not contraindications and may even benefit from faradic stimulation. Active infection and thrombosis are similarly absolute contraindications.
questions.question: Which is an absolute contraindication to faradic stimulation?
A patient recovering from a fracture with delayed union is referred for interferential therapy. Which physiological effect is the therapist primarily targeting?
questions.explanation: Interferential therapy is used in delayed union to enhance fracture healing, likely through improved local circulation and tissue stimulation rather than any direct structural bony effect. This reflects its broader listed indication for enhancement of ossification. It complements rather than replaces standard orthopaedic management.
options: Permanent denervation of the fracture site
Enhancement of fracture healing through improved circulation

questions.question: What is the purpose of a vaginal electrode in faradic stimulation?
questions.explanation: A vaginal electrode allows targeted re-education of pelvic floor muscles, useful in early prolapse or stress incontinence, particularly after childbirth. A rectal electrode serves a similar purpose in male patients. Both apply the same principle of muscle re-education through electrical stimulation.

questions.question: A patient recently received botulinum toxin injections to the upper limb for spasticity management six weeks ago and is now referred for FES. What should the physiotherapist consider?
questions.explanation: Patients who have received botulinum toxin therapy within the last six months may not respond well to FES due to the toxin's effect on neuromuscular transmission. This is a recognised consideration rather than an absolute lifelong contraindication. The therapist should factor in timing and expected muscle responsiveness when planning treatment.
options: FES is absolutely contraindicated forever after botulinum toxin
Botulinum toxin history is irrelevant after any time period
FES will have no interaction with the botulinum toxin
FES should be applied at maximum intensity to overcome the toxin
The patient may not respond well to stimulation currently

questions.question: The recommended maximum current density at the negative cathode electrode during iontophoresis is approximately which value?
questions.explanation: A current density of no more than 0.5 mA per square centimetre is considered safe at the negative cathode electrode, compared to 1.0 mA per square centimetre at the positive anode. Exceeding these limits risks tissue damage and skin burns. This safety threshold guides electrode sizing relative to current intensity.

options: Apply electrodes directly over the numb area
Position electrodes proximally over intact sensation
questions.question: Diminished skin sensation under a proposed TENS electrode site should prompt which clinical action?
questions.explanation: When sensation is diminished or absent, electrodes should be placed proximal to the affected area over intact, normally innervated skin to safely stimulate the relevant afferent pathway. Placing electrodes directly over insensate skin risks unnoticed burns. This precaution ensures both safety and treatment effectiveness.

Making the electrode smaller than the pad, with rounded corners, reduces the risk of the metal electrode touching the skin directly and causing a burn. Sharp electrode corners can otherwise dig into the pad. This safety measure is standard in electrode preparation.
questions.question: Why should faradic electrodes be made approximately one centimetre smaller than their pads?
options: Improve visual appearance of the pad
Prevent electrode contacting the skin directly

questions.explanation: Reactive hyperaemia magnitude depends on current intensity, treatment time, and tissue resistance, with greater values of each producing a stronger local reaction. The colour of the electrode wire has no physiological bearing on this response. This distinction highlights which parameters clinicians must actually control.
questions.question: Which factor does NOT influence the magnitude of the local reactive hyperaemia seen during iontophoresis?

questions.explanation: Iontophoresis is contraindicated over recent scar tissue as well as damaged or denuded skin, due to altered current distribution and increased injury risk. An alternative treatment site or modality should be considered instead. This precaution protects vulnerable healing tissue from further compromise.
questions.question: A patient has recent scar tissue at the exact site planned for iontophoretic drug delivery. What is the appropriate clinical decision?
options: Increase treatment time to compensate for scarring
Apply the active electrode directly over the scar
Use smaller electrode over the scar
Avoid iontophoresis over the recent scar tissue

questions.explanation: A frequency range of 30 to 100 Hz produces a tetanic contraction suitable for muscle strengthening purposes with interferential current. Frequencies below 10 Hz instead produce coarse twitches rather than sustained tetany. Selecting the correct range ensures the treatment matches the intended physiological muscle response.
questions.question: A patient requires interferential stimulation aimed at producing a tetanic muscle contraction for strengthening purposes. Which frequency range should be selected?
A physiotherapist wants electrodes aligned correctly for optimal Russian current quadriceps stimulation. What orientation should be used?
options: Parallel to the muscle fibre direction
Only over the tendon insertion point
Perpendicular to the muscle fibre direction
Randomly placed without regard to fibre direction
questions.explanation: Electrodes for Russian current should be arranged parallel to the direction of the muscle fibres, aligned with the estimated line of pull of the muscle, to optimise the contraction produced. Incorrect orientation may reduce the efficiency and comfort of the stimulation. This principle applies broadly across muscle groups treated with Russian current.

questions.question: During a first-time TENS session, a patient reports the sensation feels uncomfortably strong shortly after intensity was increased. What is the correct immediate action?
options: Apply a second overlapping TENS unit
Reduce intensity to a strong but comfortable level
Remove electrodes and abandon TENS permanently
questions.explanation: Intensity should be increased slowly and adjusted until the sensation is described as strong but comfortable, not uncomfortable. Continuing to increase intensity despite discomfort risks reducing treatment benefit and patient tolerance. This gradual titration is a fundamental principle of safe TENS application.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is choosing an electrode site for a patient with hypersensitivity following a peripheral nerve injury at the exact painful site. What is the best approach?
options: Place electrodes proximal to the hypersensitive area
Increase intensity to override the hypersensitivity
Use acupuncture-like TENS directly on the site
Avoid TENS entirely for this presentation only
Place electrodes directly on the hypersensitive skin
questions.explanation: When the painful site itself is hypersensitive, it is more appropriate to place electrodes proximal to the area of hypersensitivity rather than directly upon it. This avoids aggravating the pain while still stimulating the relevant afferent pathway. Direct application in such cases would likely worsen the patient's discomfort.

Once axonal degeneration is complete, interrupted direct current with a long pulse duration is required to elicit contraction in denervated muscle. Faradic current cannot depolarise denervated fibres because its pulse is too brief. This principle guides electrodiagnostic and therapeutic decisions.
questions.question: Which current is preferred for stimulating a denervated muscle after nerve degeneration is complete?

questions.explanation: Using the formula of maximum safe current density multiplied by electrode area, 0.5 mA per square centimetre multiplied by 6 square centimetres equals a maximum safe current of 3 milliamps at the cathode. Exceeding this risks tissue damage. This calculation ensures treatment remains within established safety limits.
questions.question: A physiotherapist calculates that a 6 square centimetre active electrode will be used at the cathode for iontophoresis. What is the maximum current that can be safely applied?

questions.explanation: Active dermatological conditions such as eczema increase the risk of skin irritation and impaired current tolerance, making them a contraindication. Normal intact and healed skin present no such risk. This precaution protects compromised skin from further damage.
questions.question: Which skin condition is listed as a contraindication to faradic-type current application?

questions.explanation: Interrupted galvanic current, with its long duration impulses, produces a more marked stabbing or burning sensation compared to the mild prickling typically felt with faradic current. This reflects the differing pulse characteristics of the two current types. Recognising this distinction helps the therapist select an appropriately tolerable current.
questions.question: A patient reports a stabbing, burning sensation rather than mild prickling during electrical stimulation. Which current type is most likely responsible for this response?
Rebox current operates within which pulse frequency range?
questions.explanation: Rebox current uses specific impulses within a frequency range of 2 to 4 kHz, with a pulse width of 100 to 300 microseconds and weak currents of 100 to 200 microamps. These parameters distinguish it from lower frequency faradic-type currents. Its low current strength contributes to its gentle treatment profile.

questions.question: Which condition is listed as a contraindication specifically relevant to FES due to electromagnetic interference risk?
questions.explanation: A cardiac pacemaker is listed as a contraindication to FES because electrical stimulation may interact with and interfere with the pacemaker's normal electrical signalling. Muscle weakness and old healed injuries are, by contrast, common indications for FES use. This safety consideration is consistent across most electrotherapy modalities.

After tendon transplantation, the muscle must learn to perform a new action different from its original function, so faradic current is used for training a new pattern. The patient concentrates on the new movement while stimulation assists. This differs from reeducation, which restores a previously known movement.
options: Teach a completely new muscle action
questions.question: Following tendon transplantation surgery, faradic current is used mainly to achieve which outcome?
Russian current is theorised to produce muscle contraction stronger than voluntary effort because it recruits motor units in which manner?
options: Synchronously across nearly all motor units
Randomly with long delays between units
Exclusively in slow-twitch type I fibres
questions.explanation: Maximal electrical stimulation with Russian current causes nearly all motor units to contract synchronously, something not achievable during a normal voluntary contraction. Voluntary contractions instead recruit motor units asynchronously. This synchronous recruitment underlies the current's strengthening and hypertrophy effects.

questions.question: Maximum torque with Russian current stimulation is achieved at approximately which duty cycle?
questions.explanation: Maximum torque output with Russian current occurs at a duty cycle of approximately 10 percent. This differs from the 50 percent duty cycle commonly used in standard 10:10 on-off protocols. Selecting the correct duty cycle influences the balance between force generation and fatigue.

questions.question: A continuous unidirectional flow of charged particles lasting at least one second best describes which current type?
questions.explanation: Direct current flows continuously in one direction, causing charge build-up and a chemical effect at the electrodes. Alternating current reverses direction periodically, avoiding charge accumulation. Pulsed current stops periodically rather than flowing continuously.

Conventional TENS uses low intensity, high frequency stimulation of large diameter afferents to activate spinal segmental pain gate mechanisms. This produces rapid onset but relatively short-lasting analgesia. Acupuncture-like TENS instead relies more heavily on descending opioid pathways.
questions.question: Conventional TENS primarily achieves analgesia through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Since a simple sharp and blunt test confirms intact cutaneous innervation, TENS can proceed safely at this site despite the presence of a scar. Only genuinely absent or significantly diminished sensation would necessitate repositioning electrodes proximally. This demonstrates the importance of basic sensory testing before starting treatment.
questions.question: A patient reports their pain is close to a scar with intact but slightly altered sensation. Testing confirms sharp and blunt discrimination is present. What is the appropriate action regarding TENS?
options: Delay treatment until the scar fully fades
Avoid TENS entirely due to any scar presence
Proceed with TENS since cutaneous innervation is intact
Use TENS exclusively in acupuncture-like mode
Apply TENS only at maximum tolerable intensity

questions.question: A therapist wants to use interferential current to promote reabsorption of post-traumatic oedema in a patient's ankle. Which beat frequency is most appropriate?
options: Approximately 15 Hz with a 10-15 Hz sweep
questions.explanation: A beat frequency of approximately 15 Hz, with a sweep range of 10 to 15 Hz, is recommended for promoting reabsorption of oedema through combined muscle pumping and local vascular changes. Higher frequencies around 100 Hz are instead more associated with pain gate mechanisms. Suction electrodes may further enhance this effect.

questions.question: Faradic current is characterised by a pulse duration and frequency closest to which values?
questions.explanation: Classical faradic current has an unevenly alternating waveform with a pulse duration around 1 millisecond and a frequency near 50 Hz. This is followed by damped oscillation at 10 Hz. These parameters are optimal for stimulating innervated muscle.

questions.question: A therapist is planning FES for a patient with poor skin condition and epidermal breakdown over the intended electrode site. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Increase current intensity to compensate for poor contact
Select an alternative intact skin site for the electrodes
Proceed since skin condition is not clinically relevant
Apply electrodes directly over the compromised skin
Use only vacuum electrodes on the compromised area
questions.explanation: Poor skin condition is listed as a contraindication to FES, so an alternative intact site should be selected for electrode placement wherever possible. Applying electrodes over compromised skin risks further breakdown and poor current distribution. This precaution parallels similar skin-related contraindications seen across other electrotherapy modalities.

Muscle group stimulation covers the motor points or muscle bellies together, permitting many more contractions to be elicited efficiently. This suits large muscles with multiple nerve supplies. Motor point stimulation instead isolates individual muscle action but limits the number of contractions possible.
questions.question: Which advantage is associated with muscle group stimulation compared to individual motor point stimulation?
options: More contractions can be elicited per session

questions.explanation: Burst train TENS combines a low frequency baseline, typically 1 to 4 Hz, with internal high frequency trains around 100 Hz within each burst. This produces a more comfortable muscle contraction than pure acupuncture-like TENS. It merges features of both conventional and acupuncture-like modes.
questions.question: Burst train TENS is best described as a combination of which two parameter patterns?
options: Low frequency baseline with high frequency pulse trains
Continuous high intensity with zero frequency

questions.explanation: The classic triangular sweep pattern gradually varies the frequency from base to top over approximately six seconds, delivering all frequencies in equal proportion. Rectangular and trapezoidal sweeps follow different profiles. Sweeping helps prevent nerve accommodation to a constant stimulation frequency.
questions.question: Which frequency sweep pattern gradually changes from base to top frequency over roughly six seconds?

questions.explanation: It is good practice to trial both conventional and acupuncture-like TENS because often dramatic differences in the length and amount of analgesia are noted within the same patient. This individualised approach ensures the most effective mode is identified. Relying on a single mode risks missing a better clinical response.
questions.question: A patient wants to know why the therapist recommends trialling both conventional and acupuncture-like TENS during the treatment programme. What is the best explanation?
options: Both modes produce identical physiological effects
Acupuncture-like TENS is always more effective
Dramatic differences in relief are often seen between modes
Conventional TENS is required by law before other modes
Only one mode is ever effective for any given patient

questions.question: A patient with a known skin allergy to electrode gel requires interferential treatment. What is the most appropriate initial precaution?
questions.explanation: Given a known allergy, trialling an alternative electrode type or conducting gel is the most appropriate precaution before proceeding with treatment. Applying a known allergen risks an adverse skin reaction. This individualised approach allows treatment to proceed safely while avoiding the specific sensitivity.
options: Refuse treatment permanently for this patient
Increase current intensity to override sensitivity
Apply electrodes without any gel or conducting medium
Trial an alternative electrode type or gel
Apply the known allergen regardless of history

questions.explanation: Russian current causes a blockage in sensory nerve transmission through the pain gate mechanism, allowing higher amplitude motor stimulation to be tolerated comfortably. This permits stronger contractions than would otherwise be achievable. The prickling sensory effect remains moderate compared to the motor response.
questions.question: Why is Russian current stimulation generally described as relatively painless despite high amplitude use?
options: Sensory nerve fibres undergo pain gate blockade
It never stimulates sensory nerves at all
It only stimulates deep visceral nerves
Amplitude is always kept below sensory threshold
The current bypasses the skin entirely
Try various modes and electrode sites before concluding non-response
Apply electrodes over the eyes for stronger effect
Immediately abandon electrical stimulation for that patient permanently
Switch to a stronger prescription medication instead
questions.explanation: Before concluding a patient is a non-responder, various TENS modes and electrode placement sites should be tried systematically, comparing conventional and acupuncture-like approaches. Only after exhausting these options is TENS considered ineffective for that individual. This step-by-step approach maximises the chance of a successful outcome.
questions.question: What is the recommended course of action if a TENS trial produces no pain relief at all?

options: Avoid electrode placement on the neck or head
Apply electrodes freely across the entire neck
Refuse any TENS treatment for this patient outright
Apply TENS while patient is unsupervised
questions.explanation: Practitioners should be cautious with epileptic patients and avoid applying electrodes to the neck or head specifically, since TENS-induced seizures have been reported in vulnerable patients. Treatment elsewhere on the body may still be considered with appropriate caution. This reflects a site-specific rather than blanket restriction.
questions.question: A patient with epilepsy is being considered for TENS treatment of neck pain. What is the most appropriate clinical approach?

questions.explanation: Removing tape in the direction of hair growth minimises discomfort and reduces the possibility of skin irritation or infection from hair removal against the grain. This is a simple but important practical precaution. It has no bearing on electrical performance itself.
questions.question: Why is it recommended to remove TENS tape in the direction of hair growth?
The motor point used for faradic stimulation is best described as which anatomical feature?
options: Location farthest from the nerve trunk
Area of highest density of motor end plates
questions.explanation: The motor point is where the greatest concentration of motor end plates lies close to the skin surface, allowing optimal contraction with minimal current. Placing the active electrode here maximises efficiency. This concept underlies both faradic and electrodiagnostic testing.

options: Time of day treatment is given
questions.question: Which factor is described as a determinant of the physiological effects produced by interferential therapy?
questions.explanation: The physiological effects of interferential therapy depend on the magnitude of current, mode used, frequency range, and accuracy of electrode positioning. Incorrect placement may fail to direct the crossing point over the target tissue. This makes careful setup essential to achieving intended outcomes.

options: Completely random and unrelated in phase
Always at a ninety degree phase shift
Exactly out of phase by half a wavelength
Travelling in entirely opposite directions permanently
Exactly in phase or whole wavelengths apart
questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when two waves are exactly in phase, or offset by one, two, or three whole wavelengths, causing their amplitudes to supplement each other. Destructive interference instead occurs when peaks and troughs coincide and cancel. This wave interaction underlies the interferential beat effect.
questions.question: Constructive interference in interferential current occurs when two sinusoidal waves are related in which way?

options: One electrode each side at metatarsal shaft level
One electrode under the heel only
A single electrode on the foot dorsum
Both electrodes placed proximal to ankle
Both electrodes under the metatarsal heads together
questions.explanation: For plantar interossei stimulation in a faradic foot bath, one electrode is placed on each side of the foot at the level of the metatarsal shafts. Lumbricals instead use electrodes under the heel and metatarsal heads. Correct electrode placement targets the specific intrinsic muscle group intended for treatment.
questions.question: A therapist wants to treat the plantar interossei using a bipolar faradic foot bath. How should the electrodes be positioned?

questions.explanation: Adding salt to the soaking water increases ionic content, which reduces the resistance of the solution and improves current conduction. This lowers the intensity needed for effective stimulation. Plain tap water alone offers comparatively higher resistance.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of adding salt to the water used for soaking faradic electrode pads?
In iontophoresis, why is the indifferent electrode typically made larger than the active electrode?
questions.explanation: The indifferent, or dispersive, electrode is commonly made larger, often about twice the size of the active electrode, to reduce current density and avoid skin irritation at that site. The active electrode remains smaller to concentrate the therapeutic ion delivery. This size difference protects the non-treatment site from adverse effects.

questions.question: A pregnant patient in her first trimester requests TENS for lower back discomfort. What is the safest electrode placement approach?
questions.explanation: It is prudent to avoid placing TENS electrodes over the trunk or pelvis during the first trimester, and never directly over the pregnant uterus except specifically for labour pain management. This precaution reflects uncertainty about effects on fetal development. Alternative treatment sites or modalities should be considered instead.
options: Apply electrodes directly over the pregnant uterus
Avoid the trunk and pelvis during the first trimester
Use maximum intensity over the abdomen
Recommend TENS use while bathing for comfort
Apply bilateral electrodes across the lower trunk

questions.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to interferential therapy involving cardiac safety?
questions.explanation: A cardiac pacemaker is a recognised contraindication to interferential therapy due to potential electromagnetic interference with the device. Chronic low back pain and healed injuries are not contraindications and may benefit from treatment. Cardiac safety concerns take priority in contraindication screening.

In advanced cardiac disease, treatment over the heart, cervical ganglia, or vagus nerve should be avoided due to potential autonomic and cardiac effects. Shoulder pain away from these structures may still be treated with appropriate caution. This reflects a site-specific rather than blanket contraindication in cardiac patients.
questions.question: A patient with advanced cardiac disease requests interferential therapy for shoulder pain. Which precaution is most relevant to electrode placement?
options: Increase intensity substantially to overcome cardiac risk
Avoid treatment over the heart, cervical ganglia, or vagus nerve
Apply electrodes directly over the sternum for best effect
No precaution is needed if pain relief is the goal
Treat only using vacuum suction electrodes regardless of area
Switching to a stronger adhesive tape
Allowing the skin to heal before reapplication
Continuing treatment at the same site
Ignoring the irritation if pain relief occurs
questions.explanation: The skin should be allowed to heal before electrodes are reapplied to the same site, with an alternative site such as a peripheral nerve or spinal root used meanwhile. Determining the cause, whether allergy or prolonged wear, guides further management. Hypoallergenic electrodes may also help if allergy is suspected.
questions.question: Skin irritation beneath TENS electrodes after prolonged wear is best managed by which initial step?

options: Directly over the tendon insertion only
Randomly placed regardless of fibre direction
Parallel to the muscle fibre direction
Perpendicular to the muscle fibre direction
questions.explanation: Electrodes for Russian current are arranged parallel to the direction of muscle fibres, aligned with the estimated line of pull of the muscle. This orientation optimises the contraction produced. Correct alignment is essential for effective strengthening outcomes.
questions.question: Which electrode orientation is recommended for muscle strengthening protocols using Russian current?
A physiotherapist wants a patient to feel comfortable paraesthesia without any muscle contraction for postoperative wound pain. Which TENS mode should be selected?
questions.explanation: Conventional TENS uses low intensity and high frequency to produce comfortable paraesthesia without muscle contraction, ideal for postoperative pain management. Acupuncture-like TENS instead deliberately produces visible muscle contraction. This mode selection matches the patient's need for gentle, non-contractile analgesia.

options: Consult the patient's cardiologist before proceeding
Apply TENS directly over the chest immediately
Apply maximum intensity to compensate for pacemaker interference
Refuse to ever consider TENS for this patient
Use Russian current instead without further caution
questions.question: A patient using a demand-type cardiac pacemaker presents with shoulder pain and requests TENS. What is the most appropriate initial action?
questions.explanation: Because TENS can interfere with pacemaker function, consultation with the patient's cardiologist is recommended before proceeding, and if used, electrodes should be applied away from the chest area. Complete refusal is not always necessary given appropriate precautions. This reflects manufacturer guidance treating pacemakers as a serious contraindication requiring specialist input.

Vacuum electrodes rely on an airtight seal that cannot be achieved over hairy skin, making them unsuitable in this scenario. Plate electrodes, whether standard or with water-soaked sponges, remain appropriate for such an area. Electrode choice must account for skin surface characteristics to ensure effective treatment delivery.
questions.question: A patient has a hairy back requiring interferential treatment over a broad, flat area. Which electrode type is least appropriate?
Bipolar faradic foot baths are most commonly used in the treatment of which condition?
questions.explanation: Bipolar faradic foot baths stimulate the intrinsic foot muscles, particularly useful in flat foot to strengthen the arch-supporting musculature. Water provides even contact, reducing skin resistance. However, treatment cannot easily be localised to individual muscles.

questions.question: A therapist is treating a bony area, such as over the lateral malleolus, where little muscle tissue is present. Which TENS mode is least appropriate here?
questions.explanation: Acupuncture-like TENS requires visible muscle contraction to be effective, which is not achievable over a bony area devoid of muscle tissue. Conventional TENS instead only requires comfortable paraesthesia, making it more suitable here. Electrode placement should therefore match the physiological requirements of the chosen mode.

Severe hypertension requires avoiding the lower cervical ganglia, since blood pressure control partly occurs through this region and stimulation nearby could provoke further autonomic disturbance. This is a specific contraindicated site rather than a total prohibition on cervical treatment. Careful site selection allows safer symptom management elsewhere.
options: Apply maximum intensity to lower blood pressure
No precaution differs from a normotensive patient
Treat only in the standing position
Avoid the lower cervical ganglia region
Use suction electrodes exclusively regardless of risk
questions.question: A patient with severe hypertension is scheduled for interferential therapy of the cervical spine. What specific precaution should the therapist observe?
Which time delay switch mode for Russian current triggers both channels simultaneously?
questions.explanation: Synchronous mode triggers both channels at the same time, achieved by not setting any time delay. Reciprocal mode instead alternates channels, and overlapping mode allows partial overlap between channel activations. These settings allow flexible muscle group coordination during treatment.

questions.question: The typical depth of ionic penetration into tissue during iontophoresis is estimated to be which value?
questions.explanation: Ionic penetration during iontophoresis is generally considered to be less than 1 millimetre, with any additional depth effect attributed to local capillary circulation rather than direct ion migration. This shallow penetration still allows effective local drug delivery. Reactive hyperaemia observed under the electrodes confirms local vasodilation from this process.

questions.question: Which term describes the minimum stimulation intensity that produces a visible muscle contraction during FES?
questions.explanation: Motor threshold is defined as the minimum intensity producing a visible muscle contraction, even without functional movement. Sensory threshold instead is the lowest intensity perceivable by the patient without necessarily causing contraction. These thresholds guide safe and effective FES parameter selection.

questions.question: A therapist notices a patient has an active skin infection at the intended faradic treatment site. What is the appropriate clinical decision?
questions.explanation: Infection is listed as a contraindication to faradic stimulation, so treatment at the affected site should be avoided until it resolves. Proceeding despite active infection risks spreading the infection or causing further tissue damage. Alternative treatment sites or modalities should be considered if urgent intervention is needed elsewhere.
options: Proceed with treatment using a smaller electrode
Increase current intensity to sterilise the area
Apply electrodes directly over the infected skin
Switch only to Rebox current instead
Avoid faradic treatment at that site until resolved

questions.question: A self-contained iontophoresis patch delivering a small current is typically left in place for how long?
questions.explanation: Self-contained iontophoresis patches deliver a smaller current, typically around 0.1 mA, and are applied for 12 to 24 hours depending on the intended dose before disposal. They cannot be reused once removed. This differs from clinic-based iontophoresis, which uses higher currents over shorter, supervised sessions.

For muscle strengthening protocols with Russian current, a pulse rate or burst frequency of 50 to 70 Hz is used alongside tetanic contraction during volitional isometric or short arc movements. This range is distinct from that used for spasm reduction or oedema management. Matching parameters to the treatment goal ensures appropriate physiological response.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is designing a Russian current protocol to strengthen the quadriceps after knee ligament surgery. Which pulse rate range should be selected?
If two interferential currents of 4000 Hz and 3900 Hz interfere, what is the resulting beat frequency?
questions.explanation: The beat frequency equals the difference between the two carrier frequencies, so 4000 Hz minus 3900 Hz produces a 100 Hz beat frequency. The mean of the two frequencies, 3950 Hz, instead represents the carrier frequency. This beat frequency mimics low frequency nerve stimulation.

questions.question: Which faradic application method is described as the most comfortable way to stimulate facial muscles?
questions.explanation: In the nerve conduction method, the active electrode stimulates the nerve trunk at a superficial point, producing contraction of all muscles supplied distally. This is considered the most comfortable method for facial expression muscles. It avoids stimulating multiple individual motor points.

Faradism under pressure uses an elastic bandage over a thick wool layer to enhance the pumping effect of alternating muscle contraction and relaxation, aiding venous and lymphatic drainage. This is particularly effective for oedema and gravitational ulcers. Treatment typically lasts up to twenty minutes with rest periods due to fatigue.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with gravitational leg ulcers and chronic oedema using faradic current under an elastic bandage. What is this technique called?
A TENS unit's constant current output is measured using which unit?
questions.explanation: A constant current TENS unit measures intensity in milliamps, while a constant voltage unit measures intensity in volts. The device automatically adjusts the complementary parameter to maintain the chosen constant output as impedance changes. This distinction affects how comfort and consistency are experienced by the patient.

Russian current uses a carrier frequency of 2500 Hz, delivered in bursts at 50 Hz, making it a medium frequency burst-modulated current. The burst frequency, not the carrier frequency, produces the low frequency nerve stimulation effect. This combination allows comfortable, deep muscle stimulation.
questions.question: Russian current is delivered using which carrier frequency?
A standard TENS device typically delivers pulse durations within which range?
questions.explanation: Standard TENS devices deliver biphasic pulsed currents with durations of 50 to 250 microseconds and frequencies of 1 to 200 pulses per second. These short durations allow selective stimulation of sensory fibres without excessive discomfort. Longer durations are instead associated with muscle stimulation currents.

questions.question: The key difference between two-pole and four-pole interferential application lies in where interference is generated. Where does it occur with a two-pole system?
questions.explanation: In a two-pole application, the interference is pre-modulated and generated within the machine unit before reaching the patient. In four-pole application, interference instead occurs within the tissues where the two currents cross. No known physiological difference has been established between the two methods.

Bony prominences such as the malleoli produce uncomfortable sensations under conventional TENS, so electrodes are placed to avoid direct contact with the prominence itself. Acupuncture-like TENS is also unsuitable here since muscle contraction is not achievable. Alternative sites like peripheral nerve pathways may be preferred.
questions.question: Which TENS electrode site is chosen when treating pain over a bony prominence lacking muscle tissue?
A patient with scoliosis is being treated with faradic stimulation of the lateral trunk muscles. Where should the electrodes be positioned relative to the spinal curve?
options: Directly over the vertebral spinous processes
On the concavity of the curve only
On the convexity of the curve
questions.explanation: In scoliosis management with faradic stimulation, the lateral trunk muscles on the convexity of the curve are specifically targeted for electrical stimulation. This aims to strengthen the relatively weaker musculature on that side. Electrode placement follows the anatomical location of the muscles to be stimulated, guided by the curve's structure.

questions.question: Which condition is listed by TENS manufacturers as a contraindication primarily for legal and safety reasons?
questions.explanation: Manufacturers list cardiac pacemakers, pregnancy, and epilepsy as contraindications partly because excluding TENS as a causative factor for any adverse event can be legally difficult. Some specialists still use TENS cautiously in these groups with medical consultation. This reflects a precautionary rather than absolute restriction.

Because interferential current acts primarily on excitable nerve tissue, pain relief and muscle stimulation are considered its direct effects. Increased blood flow and oedema reduction are more likely secondary consequences of these primary actions. This hierarchy guides clinical reasoning about expected treatment outcomes.
questions.question: Which clinical application is considered a primary, direct effect of interferential current rather than a secondary consequence?
Intact motor nerve excitability is essential for which type of electrical stimulation to be effective?
options: Long duration current for denervated muscle
questions.explanation: NMES activates motor units by inducing action potentials in the motor nerve, requiring an intact and excitable nerve to function effectively. Denervated muscle instead requires long duration interrupted direct current applied directly to the muscle fibres. This distinction determines which modality is appropriate after nerve injury.

options: The time of day treatment is given
questions.explanation: The choice between faradic-type current and interrupted direct current for facial weakness depends on whether nerve degeneration has occurred; faradic current suits muscles with intact nerve supply, while interrupted direct current with a longer pulse duration is needed once degeneration is present. Electrodiagnostic testing typically confirms this status. This distinction directly determines the appropriate current selection for effective treatment.
questions.question: A therapist is considering electrical stimulation for a patient with facial muscle weakness secondary to Bell's palsy using galvanic current principles. What should guide the choice between faradic and interrupted direct current?
The term iontophoresis literally means which combination of concepts?
questions.explanation: Iontophoresis derives from 'ionto', meaning ion, and 'phoresis', meaning transfer, together describing the transfer of ions. It is a non-invasive method of propelling charged substances transdermally using electrical current. This etymology reflects its core mechanism of ionic drug delivery.

questions.question: Modulated TENS output automatically varies which parameters to reduce nerve accommodation?
questions.explanation: Modulated TENS cyclically varies pulse duration, frequency, or amplitude to prevent nerve fibres from accommodating to a constant signal. This maintains treatment comfort and effectiveness over time. Continuous unmodulated output is more prone to accommodation.

questions.question: A patient reports mild blistering beneath the iontophoresis electrode partway through treatment. What is the correct immediate action?
questions.explanation: If blistering occurs during iontophoresis, treatment should be discontinued immediately to prevent further skin damage. This reflects standard precaution guidance for adverse skin reactions during treatment. Continuing despite blistering risks a more serious burn or skin injury.
options: Ignore the blistering since almost complete
Increase current intensity to complete the session
Continue treatment but reduce time by half
Apply a second electrode over the blister

questions.question: Which beat frequency range is most associated with producing a tetanic muscle contraction using interferential current?
questions.explanation: Frequencies between 30 and 100 Hz produce a tetanic contraction, while lower frequencies around 5 to 20 Hz cause partial tetany and very low frequencies cause a simple twitch. This graded response allows tailored muscle stimulation. The choice depends on the desired therapeutic muscle response.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is setting the intensity for a new FES user and wants to identify the point of visible muscle contraction. Which threshold is being determined?
questions.explanation: Motor threshold is defined as the minimum stimulation intensity that produces a visible muscle contraction, distinct from sensory threshold which only requires perception without contraction. Establishing this threshold guides safe and effective parameter setting. Operational intensity is then set relative to this baseline for actual treatment use.

questions.question: A therapist notices the patient's machine offers triangular, rectangular, and trapezoidal sweep options. What is the primary clinical purpose of using a sweep pattern at all?
options: Converting the current into direct current
Preventing nerve accommodation to a constant frequency
Reducing the beat frequency to zero permanently
Eliminating the need for electrode placement accuracy
questions.explanation: Sweep patterns automatically and gradually vary the stimulation frequency to prevent nerves from accommodating to a constant, unchanging signal. This helps maintain the effectiveness of stimulation throughout the treatment session. Different sweep shapes, such as triangular or trapezoidal, offer varied patterns of frequency change over time.

questions.question: Which electrode arrangement is recommended for the labile method when stimulating small denervated muscles?
options: Both electrodes fixed over the tendon insertion
Active electrode placed over the joint capsule
Active electrode placed over the antagonist muscle
Active cathode on the muscle belly, inactive anode away from it
Both electrodes placed over the nerve trunk only
questions.explanation: For small muscles, the active cathode electrode is placed on the muscle belly slightly distally, while the inactive anode electrode is kept away from the muscle on the opposite side.
