Trichomoniasis treated with azithromycin 1 g single dose
Herpes simplex treated with cefixime 400 mg twice daily
questions.question: Which of the following STIs is correctly matched with its first-line treatment?

options: Antiphospholipid antibody testing and genetic karyotyping of both partners
Early anatomy scan at 8 weeks to confirm fetal cardiac activity
Serum beta-hCG serial measurements to track pregnancy viability
Full blood count to exclude anaemia as a cause of pregnancy loss
Cervical length measurement to predict preterm delivery risk
questions.question: A pregnant woman with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss presents at 8 weeks gestation. The most important investigation to guide her management is:
questions.explanation: Recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more consecutive miscarriages) requires investigation of the most common causes. Antiphospholipid syndrome (detected by antiphospholipid antibodies including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies) is the most treatable cause and can be managed with low-dose aspirin and low molecular weight heparin. Genetic karyotyping of both partners identifies chromosomal abnormalities contributing to repeated implantation failure or early pregnancy loss.

For women with active breast cancer or a history of breast cancer, hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated due to the hormone-sensitive nature of most breast cancers. The copper IUD is recommended as the first-line contraceptive option because it is highly effective, non-hormonal, and does not influence hormonal tumour activity. Barrier methods such as condoms are also encouraged during chemotherapy to prevent exposure to cytotoxic agents in bodily fluids.
options: Hormonal implant containing etonogestrel for long-term protection
Copper intrauterine device as a non-hormonal first-line option
Combined oestrogen-progestin vaginal ring for easy insertion
Combined oral contraceptive pill for its cycle-regulating effects
Progestin-only injectable for its convenience and effectiveness
questions.question: The most appropriate contraceptive method for a woman currently undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer is:

questions.explanation: Klumpke's palsy results from trauma to the C8 and T1 nerve roots. The shoulder and upper arm are typically unaffected, but the lower arm, wrist, and hand are paralysed, resulting in wrist drop, absent grasp reflex, and a characteristic claw-like appearance of the hand. If the cervical sympathetic nerves are also affected, Horner's syndrome presents with ipsilateral pupillary constriction, eyelid ptosis, and loss of sensation on the affected side.
options: C6-C7 with biceps weakness and impaired forearm supination
C4-C5 with phrenic nerve damage and respiratory difficulties
C5-T1 with total paralysis of the entire upper extremity
C8-T1 with wrist drop, absent grasp reflex, and claw hand
C5-C6 with shoulder and elbow weakness and internal rotation
questions.question: Klumpke's palsy in a neonate is caused by trauma to which nerve roots and presents with which clinical features?
Cleft lip and palate is described as the second most common congenital deformity after:
questions.explanation: Cleft lip and palate ranks as one of the most frequent congenital anomalies overall, generally cited as second in frequency after congenital cardiac defects, reflecting the relatively high combined incidence of craniofacial clefting worldwide. This ranking underscores the importance of routine screening and multidisciplinary management pathways for affected infants. Early recognition supports timely feeding support and surgical planning.

Long-acting reversible contraceptives including both copper and hormonal IUDs are safe and appropriate for nulliparous women. The historical concern that IUDs were only for parous women is no longer supported by evidence; modern IUD designs are suitable for nulliparous clients. IUDs provide greater than 99% efficacy and are reversible upon removal. Tubal ligation is permanent and inappropriate for a nulliparous woman who has not completed her family.
questions.question: A 32-year-old nulliparous woman presents for family planning counselling and requests a long-acting method. She has no medical comorbidities. The most appropriate recommendation is:
options: Copper or hormonal IUD, both of which are safe for nulliparous women
Tubal ligation as it provides permanent protection without daily effort
Barrier methods only as IUDs are contraindicated in nulliparous women
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate as the best option for young women
Combined oral contraceptive pills as the most effective option available

questions.question: The Pap smear screening interval recommended for women aged 21 to 29 years is:
questions.explanation: For women aged 21 to 29 years, cervical cancer screening is recommended every three years using Pap smear alone. HPV co-testing is not recommended in this age group because transient HPV infections are common and usually self-resolve without causing significant cervical pathology. Starting screening at age 21 — not earlier — prevents overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment of benign transient HPV infections in younger women.
options: Every five years using HPV testing alone without Pap smear
Only when clinically indicated by symptoms or risk factors
Annually due to higher HPV acquisition rates in this age group
Every three years using Pap smear alone without HPV testing
Every two years with both Pap smear and HPV co-testing

questions.question: The prognosis of puerperal psychosis in tropical countries compared to temperate climates is:
questions.explanation: The prognosis of puerperal psychosis is generally very good, with high rates of complete recovery. The prognosis is reported to be even better in tropical countries, where recovery rates exceed the 75 to 80 percent reported in temperate countries. Early diagnosis, prompt psychiatric intervention, antibiotic treatment where infection is the aetiology, and adequate nursing care contribute to favourable outcomes.
options: Variable based entirely on the severity of the initial presentation
Better in the tropics, with higher complete recovery rates reported
The same, with 75 to 80 percent recovering completely in both
Consistently poor regardless of geographical location globally
Significantly worse due to limited psychiatric services available
Genetic counsellor for chromosomal karyotyping and testing
Urologist or andrologist for gonadal endocrine assessment
Psychiatrist for emotional management of fertility challenges
Reproductive endocrinologist or gynaecologist for ovarian dysfunction
Oncologist in case ovarian cysts represent malignant tumours
questions.question: In counselling about the referral process for infertile couples, which type of specialist is most appropriate for a female partner with suspected polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and anovulation?
questions.explanation: PCOS with anovulation is a cause of female infertility requiring evaluation and management by a reproductive endocrinologist or gynaecologist with expertise in fertility. Management includes ovulation induction with clomiphene citrate or letrozole, metformin for insulin-resistant PCOS, lifestyle modification for obesity-related PCOS, and ovarian drilling for clomiphene-resistant cases. A urologist or andrologist is appropriate only for male factor infertility evaluation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised common cause of puerperal pyrexia?
questions.explanation: Congenital hip dysplasia is a musculoskeletal condition of the newborn and has no relationship to maternal puerperal fever, whereas endometritis, urinary tract infection, wound infection, and mastitis are all well-recognised maternal sources of postpartum pyrexia. Systematic assessment of the uterus, urinary tract, wound, and breasts is therefore essential when investigating a febrile postnatal woman. Identifying the correct source directs appropriate antibiotic selection.
options: Wound infection at the caesarean or episiotomy site
Urinary tract infection acquired during labour
Congenital hip dysplasia of the newborn
Mastitis developing during the breastfeeding period

questions.question: In the prevention strategies for HIV and STIs, hepatitis B vaccination is recommended in family planning settings primarily to:
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccination in family planning settings is offered to prevent new hepatitis B infection, which is sexually transmitted and can cause chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Vaccination before sexual exposure provides lasting protection. Family planning settings are an important point of contact for vaccination of at-risk individuals who may not otherwise access vaccination services. Hepatitis B vaccination has no therapeutic effect on existing infection.
options: Prevent sexual transmission of hepatitis B and its complications
Reduce the viral load of hepatitis B in already infected individuals
Provide cross-protection against hepatitis C viral infection
Treat existing hepatitis B infection before starting contraception
Screen high-risk populations for hepatitis B surface antigen

questions.explanation: Primary subarachnoid haemorrhage involves capillary or venous bleeding into the subarachnoid space. It is most common in preterm babies who suffer hypoxia at birth and in full-term babies who experience traumatic birth. Many cases may be undiagnosed as they can present with no signs. When signs are present, they include generalised convulsions from the second day of life and apnoeic episodes in preterm infants.
questions.question: Primary subarachnoid haemorrhage in newborns is most commonly seen in which group?
options: All newborns regardless of gestation or mode of delivery
Full-term babies born by elective caesarean section
Preterm babies with hypoxia at birth and those with traumatic birth
Full-term newborns with Rh incompatibility and haemolysis
Post-term babies with macrosomia and prolonged delivery

questions.question: Which of the following is the most significant long-term reproductive consequence of repeated episodes of PID?
questions.explanation: Recurrent pelvic inflammatory disease causes progressive scarring and adhesion formation within the fallopian tubes, damaging the ciliated epithelium needed for ovum transport and substantially increasing the risk of tubal factor infertility and ectopic pregnancy. The risk of infertility rises with each additional episode of infection. This makes prompt treatment of PID essential for preserving future fertility.
options: Complete resolution without any lasting effect
Permanent cessation of menstrual cycles entirely
Tubal factor infertility from scarring and adhesions

questions.question: Routine antenatal tetanus toxoid immunisation is primarily aimed at preventing which condition in the newborn?
questions.explanation: Maternal tetanus toxoid immunisation during pregnancy induces protective antibodies that cross the placenta, protecting the newborn against neonatal tetanus, a life-threatening infection that can occur through the umbilical stump if cord care is unhygienic, particularly in settings with low immunisation coverage. This vaccine has no direct effect on preventing rubella, hepatitis B, group B streptococcal disease, or syphilis, which require separate specific preventive measures. This is a key component of safe motherhood and newborn protection programmes.
options: Neonatal tetanus following unhygienic cord care
Neonatal hepatitis B infection at birth
Congenital syphilis at the time of delivery

questions.question: The evaluation for infertility referral requires documentation of ovulation, which is best assessed by which investigation?
questions.explanation: Ovulation is most practically assessed by mid-luteal serum progesterone measurement (typically on day 21 of a 28-day cycle), which should be elevated above 30 nmol/L if ovulation has occurred. Alternatively, LH detection kits measure the LH surge that precedes ovulation by approximately 24 to 36 hours, allowing prediction of the fertile window. Both methods provide objective evidence of ovulatory function as part of the infertility evaluation prior to referral.
options: Serum FSH and LH measurement on day 1 of the menstrual cycle
Basal body temperature charting over one menstrual cycle only
Endometrial biopsy to confirm secretory phase transformation
Mid-luteal serum progesterone or LH detection on ovulation kits
Pelvic ultrasound to visualise follicle development on day 2

questions.question: A woman with a family history of sickle cell disease requests family planning counselling. The most appropriate investigation to guide this counselling is:
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis identifies the specific haemoglobin genotype, distinguishing normal, carrier (trait), and disease states, which is essential information for genetic counselling and reproductive decision-making, particularly if her partner's genotype is also relevant to the risk of an affected child. The other listed tests do not provide information about haemoglobinopathy status. This investigation is a standard component of comprehensive preconception and family planning counselling in populations where sickle cell disease is prevalent.

Puerperal psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that most commonly has an acute onset within the first two weeks after delivery, often presenting suddenly with confusion, hallucinations, delusions, and mood disturbance. This early onset distinguishes it from postnatal depression, which may develop somewhat later and more gradually. Rapid recognition and psychiatric referral are essential given the risk of harm to the mother or infant.
questions.question: Puerperal psychosis typically has its onset within which time frame after delivery?
options: Within the first two weeks postpartum
Not until at least one year postpartum
Only immediately during the labour process
Only after six months have fully elapsed

questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) targets various stages of the HIV replication cycle using different drug classes, including NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors, and integrase inhibitors. The combined goal is to suppress HIV replication to undetectable levels in the blood, thereby restoring immune function, preventing disease progression to AIDS, and significantly reducing the risk of onward transmission.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of action of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in HIV management?
options: Suppressing viral replication to undetectable serum levels
Reversing damage already caused to the immune system
Eliminating HIV from the body completely and permanently
Stimulating CD4 cell production in the bone marrow
Preventing sexual transmission without affecting viral load

questions.question: The complete clinical assessment required before infertility referral should include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Semen analysis for the male partner within the last year
Cervical cancer screening history and current Pap smear status
Endometrial biopsy to assess endometrial receptivity for implantation
TSH and morning fasting prolactin levels for hormonal assessment
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to assess ovarian and uterine anatomy
questions.explanation: The standard pre-referral infertility evaluation includes: semen analysis, TSH and prolactin levels, documentation of ovulation (LH kits or day 21 progesterone), cervical cancer screening status, transvaginal ultrasound, nutrition consultation for BMI over 30, and optimisation of comorbidities. Endometrial biopsy is not part of the standard pre-referral assessment; it is an advanced investigation performed in specialist settings to assess endometrial histology in specific clinical scenarios.

Women with poorly controlled diabetes, especially those with complications such as nephropathy, retinopathy, or cardiovascular disease, should avoid oestrogen-containing contraceptives due to the increased risk of cardiovascular events. The levonorgestrel-releasing IUS is a highly effective non-oestrogen option that does not adversely affect glucose metabolism, making it a preferred choice for diabetic women.
questions.question: A family planning client with poorly controlled diabetes presents for contraceptive counselling. Which contraceptive method is most appropriate for her?
Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) is administered to a neonate with a duct-dependent congenital cardiac defect primarily in order to:
questions.explanation: In duct-dependent cardiac lesions, such as severe coarctation, pulmonary atresia, or transposition of the great arteries, systemic or pulmonary blood flow depends on continued patency of the ductus arteriosus, and prostaglandin E1 is administered to keep the ductus open, stabilising the infant until surgical or catheter-based correction can be performed. This is the opposite intent to drugs used for uncomplicated patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants. Close monitoring for apnoea, a known side effect, is required during infusion.
options: Maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus until definitive treatment
Accelerate spontaneous closure of the ductus arteriosus

questions.explanation: A hysterosalpingogram involves injecting contrast medium through the cervix under fluoroscopy to outline the uterine cavity and demonstrate whether the fallopian tubes are patent, an important step in evaluating tubal factor infertility. It does not assess ovarian reserve, sperm parameters, or cervical mucus, which require separate specific tests. Findings guide decisions about surgical correction or referral for assisted reproduction.
questions.question: A couple undergoing infertility investigation is scheduled for a hysterosalpingogram. The primary purpose of this test is to assess:
options: Patency of the fallopian tubes and uterine cavity shape
Endometrial thickness during the luteal phase
Cervical mucus quality around ovulation time
Ovarian reserve through hormone level measurement

questions.question: In a family planning clinic, a nurse identifies a woman at risk of venous thromboembolism. Which combination of factors most significantly increases VTE risk in a woman considering COCs?
options: Regular exercise, normal blood pressure, and healthy BMI
Multiparity, low BMI, and occasional social alcohol consumption
Obesity, smoking, and personal or family history of DVT
Age 35, no smoking, and normal coagulation studies
Age under 25, nulliparity, and a BMI of 22 kg/m²
questions.explanation: The combination of obesity, cigarette smoking, and a personal or family history of DVT significantly elevates VTE risk when oestrogen-containing contraceptives are used. Oestrogen increases coagulation factors II, VII, VIII, and X while reducing protein S, promoting a prothrombotic state. Obesity and smoking independently increase VTE risk and synergise with oestrogen to create substantial cumulative risk. This combination represents a strong relative or absolute contraindication to COC use.

Microcephaly is defined by a head circumference that falls significantly below the expected range for the infant's age, sex, and gestation, often reflecting underlying abnormal brain growth or development, and may result from genetic conditions, congenital infections, or teratogenic exposures. A head circumference at the average percentile would be entirely normal rather than microcephalic. Serial measurement and plotting on standardised growth charts are essential for accurate identification and monitoring.
options: Delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle only
Premature fusion of a single cranial suture only
Head circumference exactly at the fiftieth percentile
Head circumference significantly below the expected range for age and sex
Isolated widening of the sagittal suture alone
questions.question: A neonate presents with microcephaly, most accurately defined as:

options: Interventions and treatments already provided before referral
The waiting time experienced at the referring health facility
The financial arrangements made for the patient's inpatient care
The names of all family members accompanying the patient
The patient's religious preference and dietary requirements
questions.question: The referral letter for a pregnant woman being transferred to a higher level facility for complications must NOT omit which critical piece of information?
questions.explanation: The referral letter must include all interventions and treatments already provided, such as medications administered (oxytocics, antihypertensives, antibiotics, IV fluids), blood transfusions given, and procedures performed. This information is critical because it prevents duplication of treatments, informs the receiving team about the clinical course, and identifies what has been attempted and what remains to be done. Omission of this information risks patient safety through dangerous gaps in care.

options: Arranging transport before stabilising the patient
Obtaining written consent before any emergency stabilisation
Stabilising the patient then communicating with the receiving facility
Notifying the family before contacting the referral centre
Documenting findings before administering any treatment
questions.question: The referral process for a high-risk pregnant woman should begin with which priority action?
questions.explanation: The correct sequence in the referral process begins with stabilising the patient — administering medications, fluids, or oxygen as needed, controlling haemorrhage, managing seizures, and providing pain relief. Only after stabilisation should transport be arranged and communication established with the receiving facility. Notifying the referral centre in advance allows them to prepare for the patient's arrival and confirm capacity to manage the specific condition.

Active current PID is an absolute contraindication for IUD insertion because the device can act as a conduit for ascending infection, converting lower genital tract infection into more severe upper genital tract disease. Inserting an IUD in the presence of active PID risks worsening the infection, causing tubo-ovarian abscess or septicaemia. The infection must be fully treated and resolved before IUD insertion can be considered.
questions.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to IUD insertion in a family planning client?
options: History of a single episode of PID treated 3 years ago
A woman with a history of ectopic pregnancy two years ago
A nulliparous woman requesting long-acting contraception
A woman who delivered her last baby 10 weeks ago

questions.explanation: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants accelerate hepatic metabolism of oestrogen and progestin, substantially reducing the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives that rely on systemic hormone levels. The copper IUD works through a local mechanism unaffected by liver enzyme activity, making it the most reliable option. DMPA at standard dosing or the levonorgestrel IUD are also reasonable alternatives with adjusted dosing considerations.
questions.question: A woman with well-controlled epilepsy on enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants seeks contraceptive advice. The nurse should recommend which method as most reliable?
options: Contraceptive patch delivering standard hormone dose
Copper intrauterine device unaffected by enzyme induction
Combined oral contraceptive at the standard dose
Progestin-only pill at the standard dose
A reproductive endocrinologist for IVF planning
A urologist for male infertility evaluation
An oncologist for cancer screening and staging
A genetic counsellor for karyotyping and DNA analysis
questions.explanation: Clients with a personal or family history of chromosomal or genetic disorders such as sickle cell anaemia, cystic fibrosis, or Klinefelter syndrome require referral to a genetic counsellor. Genetic counselling, karyotyping, and DNA analysis provide information on the risk of passing genetic conditions to offspring, enabling informed reproductive decisions and family planning.
questions.question: For a client with a suspected chromosomal or genetic disorder seeking family planning advice, the most appropriate referral is to:

questions.explanation: The RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) and VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) tests are non-treponemal serological screening tests used for syphilis at the primary level. They detect reagin antibodies produced in response to treponemal infection and are used for screening and monitoring treatment response (titers fall with effective treatment). Positive results are confirmed with treponemal-specific tests such as TPHA or FTA-ABS. These tests are important in preconception and antenatal screening.
questions.question: The immunological test used to diagnose syphilis serologically at the primary level of care is:
options: ELISA for Treponema pallidum antibody detection
Dark field microscopy for visualising the spirochaete organism
PCR for direct detection of Treponema pallidum DNA
Western blot for treponemal-specific antibody confirmation
RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) or VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory)

questions.question: A newly delivered woman has been prescribed stilboestrol for lactation suppression in the context of puerperal psychosis management. The primary reason for suppressing lactation in this case is:
questions.explanation: In puerperal psychosis, the infant must be separated from the psychotic mother for safety, as she may have desires to harm the infant or be unable to care for it. Since breastfeeding cannot safely continue in this clinical scenario, lactation is suppressed to prevent breast engorgement, mastitis, and discomfort. Stilboestrol (a synthetic oestrogen) inhibits prolactin-mediated milk production. Modern practice may use cabergoline for lactation suppression as a safer alternative.
options: Stilboestrol prevents mastitis in mothers separated from their infants
Breast milk carries psychotropic medications that harm the newborn
The psychotic mother cannot safely breastfeed and the infant is separated
Lactation increases oxytocin levels worsening psychotic symptoms
Oestrogen suppresses prolactin release causing postpartum psychosis

questions.explanation: Facial nerve palsy in the newborn commonly results from pressure on the facial nerve during delivery, often related to forceps application, and is recognised by asymmetric facial movement that becomes most apparent during crying, with the affected side failing to wrinkle or move while the unaffected side functions normally. Brachial plexus injuries instead affect limb movement rather than facial expression. Most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks as nerve compression subsides.
questions.question: A neonate presents with facial asymmetry noted only when crying, with the affected side failing to move while the unaffected side wrinkles normally. This is most consistent with:
options: Klumpke's palsy affecting the lower limb
Erb's palsy affecting the upper limb
Facial nerve palsy from birth trauma

questions.explanation: The initial nursing management of a puerperal woman with pyrexia involves reducing the temperature through non-pharmacological measures such as tepid sponging or fanning if the temperature exceeds 37 to 39°C, while simultaneously initiating systematic investigations to identify the cause (genital swabs, MSU, blood film, blood culture). The patient should be made comfortable and barrier-nursed while results are awaited. Antibiotic treatment is specific to the identified cause once investigations reveal the diagnosis.
questions.question: The comprehensive management of a puerperal woman with documented pyrexia should begin with which initial nursing action?
options: Informing the patient's family before conducting any examination or treatment
Reducing temperature first by tepid sponging or fanning while initiating investigations
Transferring the patient to an isolation room without any immediate assessment
Administering empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics before any investigations
Documenting the vital signs and waiting 24 hours before starting treatment
Repeat testing is required only after menopause
Repeat co-testing may be deferred for approximately five years
Repeat testing must be performed every six months
Repeat testing must be performed within one month
No further screening is required for life
questions.explanation: When cytology and HPV co-testing are both negative, current guidelines allow extension of the screening interval to approximately every five years because the combined negative predictive value is very high, reducing unnecessary procedures while maintaining safety. Screening every six months or requiring lifelong cessation would either be excessive or unsafe. Screening continues at appropriate intervals until the recommended upper age limit is reached.
questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects current guidance on the interval for repeat Pap smear testing in a woman with a normal result and negative HPV co-test at age 35?
The primary advantage of using long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) in family planning is:
options: They are suitable for all women regardless of medical history
High efficacy with reduced user-dependent failure rates
They provide immediate return to fertility upon removal always
They provide protection against sexually transmitted infections
They are available without prescription at any pharmacy
questions.explanation: Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs), including IUDs and subdermal implants, have very high efficacy (greater than 99%) because they eliminate user-dependent failure — the most common cause of contraceptive failure with methods such as oral pills or condoms. Once inserted or implanted, LARCs provide consistent protection for several years without requiring daily action. They are particularly recommended for women seeking extended contraception, including those who are post-partum or who have difficulty adhering to daily regimens.

questions.question: The most common causative organism of bacterial vaginosis, associated with a fishy-smelling thin greyish discharge, is:
options: Treponema pallidum as a spirochaete bacterium
Candida albicans as a fungal pathogen
Trichomonas vaginalis as a protozoan pathogen
Neisseria gonorrhoeae as a gonococcal diplococcus
questions.explanation: Bacterial vaginosis results from a shift in vaginal flora with overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and other anaerobes replacing protective lactobacilli, producing a thin, greyish-white discharge with a characteristic fishy odour, especially after intercourse. It is not classified as a sexually transmitted infection in the traditional sense but is associated with sexual activity. Diagnosis uses Amsel's criteria or Gram stain scoring.

options: Review of laboratory and imaging findings from the specialist
Discussion of alternative family-building options if treatment fails
Monitoring response to ovulation induction therapy
Continued emotional support and counselling for the couple
Reassessment of ovarian reserve every 3 months during treatment
questions.explanation: Follow-up after infertility referral and treatment includes ongoing emotional support, monitoring treatment response (e.g., ultrasound follicle tracking during ovulation induction), review of specialist findings, and counselling on alternative family-building options such as donor gametes, adoption, or child-free living if primary treatment fails. Reassessment of ovarian reserve every 3 months is not a standard component of follow-up; AMH is typically measured once as a baseline marker, not as frequent monitoring.
questions.question: The follow-up after infertility treatment and referral should include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Doxycycline, a tetracycline-class antibiotic, is contraindicated in pregnancy because it binds to calcium in developing bone and teeth, causing permanent discolouration and potential effects on skeletal growth in the fetus. Azithromycin is therefore preferred for treating chlamydia during pregnancy. This teratogenic risk is specific to tetracyclines and does not apply to macrolide antibiotics.
options: Requires refrigeration unavailable in most clinics
Cannot be absorbed adequately in pregnancy
Increases the risk of neonatal conjunctivitis
Is completely ineffective against Chlamydia trachomatis
Can cause discolouration of the fetal teeth and bones
questions.question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with genital chlamydia at 32 weeks gestation. Doxycycline is avoided in her treatment primarily because it:

options: Septicaemia from ascending genital tract infection
Development of ovarian cysts requiring hormonal suppression
Scarring of fallopian tubes leading to infertility
Tubo-ovarian abscess requiring emergency surgical drainage
Chronic pelvic pain discouraging intimacy and sexual activity
questions.explanation: Untreated or recurrent PID causes scarring and adhesion formation in the fallopian tubes, permanently impairing tubal patency and function. This tubal factor infertility directly compromises a woman's ability to conceive naturally and may necessitate in vitro fertilisation (IVF). Additionally, tubal scarring increases the risk of ectopic pregnancy, another life-threatening consequence that directly affects reproductive outcomes and family planning goals.
questions.question: Which complication of untreated PID most directly affects future family planning goals?

questions.explanation: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) contain oestrogen, which can alter lipid metabolism by increasing triglycerides and LDL cholesterol while reducing HDL cholesterol, thereby increasing cardiovascular risk. A baseline lipid profile is therefore indicated before initiating COCs in clients with risk factors for cardiovascular disease. Dyslipidaemia is a relative contraindication for oestrogen-containing contraceptives.
questions.question: A lipid profile is most indicated in family planning for a client who intends to use which contraceptive method?

questions.explanation: The Gardasil HPV vaccine provides maximum protection when administered before any exposure to HPV through sexual activity. It is recommended for preadolescents and adolescents typically between ages 9 and 14 years. The vaccine protects against high-risk HPV strains (16 and 18) responsible for most cervical cancers and against low-risk strains (6 and 11) causing genital warts. It is not therapeutic and does not clear existing infection.
options: As a single lifetime dose to both partners simultaneously
After the first episode of sexual activity in young adults
To individuals already infected to clear the existing virus
Only to women over 40 years with abnormal Pap smears
Before the onset of sexual activity in preadolescents
questions.question: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination with Gardasil is most effective when administered:

questions.explanation: Azoospermia (complete absence of sperm) requires targeted investigation including Y-chromosome microdeletion testing to detect Azoospermia Factor (AZF) deletions on the Y chromosome, which account for 10 to 15% of non-obstructive azoospermia cases. Scrotal ultrasound assesses testicular size, echogenicity, presence of obstruction (epididymal dilation), and varicocele. Together, these investigations differentiate obstructive (correctable surgically) from non-obstructive (requires testicular sperm extraction for IVF-ICSI) azoospermia.
options: Hysterosalpingography to assess the female partner's tubal status
Serum testosterone level as the primary endocrine investigation
Y-chromosome microdeletion testing and scrotal ultrasound
Antisperm antibody testing in the female partner's blood
Prolactin level measurement to assess pituitary function
questions.question: Which investigation is most specifically indicated in assessing male infertility when the semen analysis reveals azoospermia?
A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with cervical cancer on a routine Pap smear. The next appropriate step in her management is:
options: Administering the HPV vaccine to eliminate the current infection
Referral to a gynaecologic oncologist for specialist management
Repeat Pap smear in 6 months to confirm the diagnosis
Immediate hysterectomy without further diagnostic workup
Initiating combined oral contraceptives to suppress HPV activity
questions.explanation: When screening reveals an abnormality suspicious for cervical cancer, immediate referral to a gynaecologic oncologist is essential for definitive diagnosis (colposcopy, biopsy, staging), treatment planning, and coordination of oncological care. The HPV vaccine is preventive and has no therapeutic effect on existing infection or malignancy. Combined oral contraceptives are not a treatment for cervical cancer and hormonal methods are contraindicated in active malignancy.

When maternal viral load is suppressed to undetectable levels near term, the risk of intrapartum transmission is very low, and vaginal delivery is generally considered safe rather than mandating routine caesarean section. Elective caesarean is instead reserved for women with detectable or unknown viral loads close to delivery. Antiretroviral therapy is continued throughout pregnancy, labour, and postpartum to maintain suppression.
options: Breastfeeding is automatically permitted without any precautions
Caesarean section is mandatory for every HIV-positive woman
Vaginal delivery is generally safe with an undetectable viral load
Formula feeding is required regardless of viral suppression
Antiretroviral therapy should be stopped before labour begins
questions.question: A pregnant woman living with HIV has an undetectable viral load on antiretroviral therapy near term. Regarding delivery mode, the nurse should advise that:

options: Symmetrical flattening of the medial longitudinal arch
Plantar flexion, inversion, and forefoot adduction
Isolated overgrowth of the fifth metatarsal bone
Dorsiflexion, eversion, and forefoot abduction only
Complete absence of all toes on the affected foot
questions.explanation: Talipes equinovarus involves a combination of plantar flexion of the ankle (equinus), inversion of the heel (varus), and adduction of the forefoot, giving the foot a characteristic turned-in appearance. This combination distinguishes it from other positional foot deformities that may involve opposite directions of deformity. Early splinting or serial casting, such as the Ponseti method, is the mainstay of management for this condition.
questions.question: Talipes equinovarus, or clubfoot, is characterised by which combination of foot deformities?
The cornerstone of management for puerperal psychosis secondary to severe puerperal sepsis is:
questions.explanation: When puerperal psychosis arises secondary to severe infection, treating the underlying sepsis with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care is the essential first step, since resolving the infective and metabolic disturbance often leads to significant improvement in the psychiatric symptoms. Psychiatric treatments may still be needed but should accompany, not replace, treatment of the causative infection. Multidisciplinary care involving obstetric, medical, and psychiatric teams gives the best outcome.
options: Immediate electroconvulsive therapy without any antibiotics
Prompt treatment of the underlying infection with antibiotics
Discharge planning with no further medical treatment
Permanent separation of mother and infant

questions.question: Which statement most accurately reflects the management of high-risk pregnancy at the primary care level before referral?
questions.explanation: At the primary care level, high-risk pregnancies should be closely monitored while managing pre-existing conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, or anaemia with appropriate medications. Antenatal care visits should be more frequent, and the threshold for referral should be low when conditions deteriorate or exceed primary care management capacity. Stabilisation before referral is essential, and timely communication with the receiving facility ensures safe transfer and continuity of care.
options: High-risk conditions should be monitored closely while managing pre-existing conditions
High-risk pregnancy should be immediately transferred to a tertiary hospital without stabilisation
Only obstetric emergencies require referral while stable conditions are managed locally
All high-risk conditions should be managed at primary care with extra monitoring
Primary care should initiate delivery before referring to higher-level facilities
Urine dipstick for protein and glucose
Full blood count with platelet estimation
Luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone
questions.explanation: Clients with a personal or family history of clotting disorders require a coagulation profile before initiating combined hormonal contraceptives because oestrogen increases the risk of venous thromboembolism. Tests including PT, aPTT, and D-dimer, alongside thrombophilia screening (e.g., factor V Leiden, protein C, protein S, antithrombin levels), help determine the degree of risk and guide contraceptive choice.
questions.question: Which laboratory investigation is most appropriate for a client with a history of clotting disorders who wishes to use a combined hormonal contraceptive?

options: Cryotherapy to freeze the affected columnar tissue
Cauterisation using chemical or thermal method
Immediate surgical hysterectomy of the uterus
questions.explanation: Cervical ectropion is a benign condition that does not warrant hysterectomy. Management depends on symptom severity and includes observation for asymptomatic cases, discontinuation of oestrogen-containing contraceptives, cryotherapy, laser therapy, or cauterisation to destroy the exposed columnar epithelium and promote squamous metaplasia. Hysterectomy is not an appropriate treatment for this condition.
questions.question: A client diagnosed with cervical erosion reports increased vaginal discharge and post-coital bleeding. Management options for this condition include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy is a minimally invasive diagnostic technique in which a fine needle is used to aspirate cells from a breast lump for cytological examination under microscopy. It is used to differentiate benign from malignant lesions, assess the nature of palpable or imaging-detected breast abnormalities, and guide further management including surgical biopsy or referral to oncology. Core needle biopsy provides histological samples and is used when FNA is inconclusive.
questions.question: The role of fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy in the diagnostic workup of a breast lump is to:
options: Drain the lump if it contains cystic fluid under pressure
Surgically remove the lump for complete histological analysis
Collect cells from the lump for cytological microscopic examination
Measure the lump's vascularity using Doppler flow estimation
Mark the lump's location before surgical excision under anaesthesia

questions.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot comprises four specific features: pulmonary stenosis obstructing right ventricular outflow, a ventricular septal defect, an aorta that overrides the septal defect, and compensatory right ventricular hypertrophy resulting from the increased workload. This combination produces the classic cyanotic presentation seen in affected infants, particularly during hypercyanotic spells. Surgical repair addressing all four components is required for definitive treatment.
options: Atrial septal defect, mitral stenosis, aortic coarctation, and left atrial enlargement
Transposition of great arteries, pulmonary atresia, mitral regurgitation, and biventricular hypertrophy
Truncus arteriosus, atrial septal defect, mitral valve prolapse, and right atrial enlargement
Patent ductus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, aortic stenosis, and left ventricular hypertrophy
Pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy
questions.question: Tetralogy of Fallot is characterised by which combination of four cardiac abnormalities?

options: It screens for cervical dysplasia and cancer
It detects chromosomal abnormalities in cells
It confirms ovulation by detecting LH surge
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the Pap smear in family planning consultations?
questions.explanation: The Pap smear (cervical cytology) is a screening tool for cervical dysplasia and carcinoma, collecting cells from the transformation zone of the cervix for microscopic examination. In family planning, it is used to identify precancerous changes or cancers that may influence the choice of contraceptive method and necessitate referral for colposcopy or further investigation.

options: Day 7, due to excessive prolactin causing milk overproduction
Day 1, due to insufficient oxytocin during the third stage
Day 5, due to bacterial colonisation of the breast ducts
Day 10, due to maternal exhaustion reducing milk ejection reflex
Day 3, due to venous and lymphatic congestion of the breasts
questions.question: Breast engorgement is most accurately described as occurring on which postnatal day and from which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Breast engorgement is a venous and lymphatic congestion of the breasts that typically occurs from around the third postnatal day as milk production transitions from colostrum to mature milk. It is more common in primiparous women and can range from mild discomfort to severe engorgement with stretched, shiny skin, flattened nipples, and low-grade pyrexia. Management includes frequent feeding, hot bathing before feeds, and gentle expression.

Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe hyperbilirubinaemia that fails to respond adequately to intensive phototherapy or when bilirubin levels approach thresholds associated with a high risk of kernicterus, since it rapidly removes bilirubin and antibody-coated red cells from the circulation. Mild elevation or jaundice confined to limited body areas without dangerous bilirubin levels does not warrant this invasive procedure. Careful monitoring of serial bilirubin levels guides the decision to proceed with exchange transfusion.
options: Jaundice is confined only to the face and chest
Bilirubin levels remain dangerously high despite intensive phototherapy
Bilirubin levels are only mildly elevated at birth
The infant is otherwise healthy and feeding well
Jaundice first appears after seventy-two hours of age
questions.question: Exchange transfusion in neonatal jaundice is most indicated when:

questions.explanation: Dual protection promotes the simultaneous use of condoms alongside another contraceptive method to achieve two distinct goals: prevention of sexually transmitted infections and prevention of unintended pregnancy. This is particularly important in family planning settings where clients may be at risk for both STIs and unintended pregnancy. No hormonal or intrauterine contraceptive method provides protection against STIs, making condom use essential for comprehensive sexual health protection.
options: A single method is always insufficient to prevent pregnancy
To reduce the cost of contraception per unit of protection
To improve convenience and ease of contraceptive compliance
To ensure protection during menstruation when other methods fail
To simultaneously prevent STIs and unintended pregnancy
questions.question: The most important reason why family planning services promote dual protection (condom plus another contraceptive method) is:

questions.explanation: Rubella IgG antibody measurement is used in preconception counselling to confirm whether the woman has protective immunity from previous infection or vaccination. Women found to be non-immune (IgG negative) should be vaccinated with the MMR vaccine before conception to prevent congenital rubella syndrome, which can cause severe fetal abnormalities including cataracts, deafness, and congenital heart defects if infection occurs in the first trimester.
questions.question: During preconception counselling for a woman planning pregnancy, which screening test is most important to determine rubella immunity status?
options: Rubella IgM antibody titre to detect current active infection
Lymphocyte stimulation test for cellular immunity to rubella
Live rubella virus challenge test to confirm immune protection
Throat swab culture for rubella virus isolation and identification
Rubella IgG antibody titre to confirm past immunity or vaccination

questions.explanation: Physical examination provides multiple data points that directly influence contraceptive selection. Elevated BMI combined with elevated blood pressure may contraindicate COCs due to combined cardiovascular risk. Pelvic examination identifies uterine abnormalities that may preclude IUD insertion or indicate underlying pathology. Breast examination detects masses that may contraindicate hormonal methods. Together, these findings, along with laboratory results, guide personalised contraceptive counselling.
questions.question: Which statement best describes how physical examination findings guide contraceptive selection in a family planning consultation?
options: Only the woman's personal preference should guide contraceptive selection
Physical examination is less important than laboratory results in guiding selection
Physical examination findings are relevant only for surgical contraceptive methods
A normal pelvic examination confirms all contraceptive methods are equally safe
BMI, blood pressure, and pelvic findings together guide personalised contraceptive choice
Using both male and female condoms during every sexual encounter
Combining ART with an IUD to prevent both HIV progression and pregnancy
Using condoms alongside another effective contraceptive method for both STI prevention and pregnancy prevention
Combining emergency contraception with routine contraception for dual safety
Using two hormonal contraceptive methods simultaneously for maximum efficacy
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the 'dual protection' approach recommended in family planning education for women with HIV?
questions.explanation: Dual protection for women living with HIV involves using condoms consistently alongside another highly effective contraceptive method such as an IUD, hormonal implant, or injectable. The condom prevents transmission of HIV and other STIs to sexual partners, while the additional contraceptive method provides highly effective pregnancy prevention. This approach addresses both the woman's contraceptive needs and the public health imperative to prevent HIV transmission.

Polydactyly refers to the presence of one or more supernumerary digits on the hand or foot, which may be an isolated finding or occur as part of a broader genetic syndrome. It is distinguished from syndactyly, in which digits are fused together rather than duplicated. Surgical removal of the extra digit is often performed for functional and cosmetic reasons depending on its structure and attachment.
options: An extra digit on the hand or foot
Webbing confined to the toes only
Fused digits on the hand or foot
questions.question: Polydactyly is defined as a congenital condition in which the infant has:

options: Androgens excess as found in polycystic ovary syndrome
Low FSH levels seen in premature ovarian failure
Elevated progesterone during the luteal phase
High oestrogen levels in pregnancy and OCP use
questions.explanation: Cervical ectropion occurs when the columnar epithelium of the cervical canal extends to the ectocervix, replacing the squamous epithelium. This is predominantly driven by elevated oestrogen levels, as seen during pregnancy, adolescence, and with the use of combined oral contraceptives. Oestrogen causes eversion of the endocervical canal, making the columnar epithelium visible on the ectocervix.
questions.question: Cervical ectropion (erosion) is most commonly associated with which hormonal condition?

options: Submucous cleft palate with bifid uvula identified at birth
Complete bilateral cleft lip and palate at six months of age
Bilateral cleft lip deformity requiring symmetrical reconstruction
Unilateral cleft lip deformity with nine anatomical landmarks
Cleft palate repair requiring Bardach two-flap technique
questions.explanation: The rotation-advancement method is the most commonly used surgical technique in the United States for repair of unilateral cleft lip deformity. The technique uses nine anatomical landmarks and involves rotation flap cuts made first, followed by advancement cuts, and finally cleft-side nasal ala cuts. Cleft lip repair is typically performed at around 10 weeks of age. Lip adhesion at 2 weeks may be performed as a temporising measure in severe cases.
questions.question: The rotation-advancement method is the most common surgical technique used in the United States for repair of which cleft type?
Which of the following is a fetal indication for emergency referral of a pregnant woman during antenatal care?
questions.explanation: Absent or markedly reduced fetal movements are an important fetal warning sign that may indicate fetal distress, placental insufficiency, or fetal compromise requiring urgent assessment with cardiotocography (CTG) and obstetric ultrasound. This is an acute fetal indication for emergency referral. Maternal indications for referral include severe preeclampsia, haemorrhage, obstructed labour, uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes, and severe anaemia unresponsive to initial treatment.
options: Blood pressure of 125/80 mmHg on routine antenatal measurement
Absent or markedly reduced fetal movements detected by the mother
Fundal height measuring 1 cm less than the gestational age in weeks
Mild ankle oedema appearing in the third trimester of pregnancy
Haemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL responding to oral iron supplementation

questions.question: Thalidomide, taken by pregnant women in the past, is most specifically associated with which congenital abnormality?
questions.explanation: Thalidomide is a well-documented teratogen historically associated with severe limb reduction defects, including phocomelia in which the limbs are markedly shortened or absent, following maternal use during critical periods of limb development in early pregnancy. This association led to major changes in drug safety testing during pregnancy worldwide. It remains a classic teaching example of a specific teratogen linked to a distinct pattern of malformation.
options: Isolated cleft lip without limb involvement
Neural tube defects without limb involvement
Isolated congenital cataracts without limb involvement
Limb reduction defects such as phocomelia

questions.explanation: Visual and auditory hallucinations, paranoid ideation, and expressed desire to harm the infant are severe manifestations of puerperal psychosis. The woman should be immediately referred to a psychiatrist without delay. The infant must be separated from the mother with adequate precautions to ensure its safety. The patient may require heavy sedation, psychiatric nursing in an isolated room, and antibiotic therapy if infection is a contributing cause.
options: Provide postnatal education and discharge home with family support
Administer haloperidol and allow her to remain with the baby
Reassure the family that this is normal postnatal adjustment
Document and review at the next scheduled postnatal visit
Refer to a psychiatrist without delay and separate from infant
questions.question: A postnatal woman is observed talking to herself, hearing voices, and expressing fear that family members want to harm her. She also shows a desire to injure her infant. The appropriate immediate nursing action is:

questions.explanation: A tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) that does not respond to intravenous antibiotic therapy requires surgical intervention. Options include ultrasound-guided or CT-guided percutaneous drainage of the abscess, laparoscopic drainage, or, in refractory cases, surgical salpingo-oophorectomy (removal of the affected tube and ovary). The choice of procedure depends on the size of the abscess, patient stability, desire for future fertility, and response to initial antibiotic therapy.
options: Increasing the antibiotic dose and extending the course to 28 days
Inserting a levonorgestrel IUS to reduce local inflammatory response
Prescribing oral corticosteroids to reduce the peri-tubal inflammation
Changing to an oral antibiotic and discharging with close follow-up
Surgical drainage, aspiration, or salpingo-oophorectomy as indicated
questions.question: In managing a woman with a tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) complicating PID, the definitive treatment when antibiotics fail is:
A 41-year-old woman with unexplained infertility for over two years has had normal ovulation, tubal patency, and semen analysis results. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Referral to a fertility specialist for assisted reproduction
Repeating identical investigations every six months
Reassurance with no further action required at all
Advising permanent discontinuation of conception attempts
questions.explanation: When standard investigations are all normal yet conception has not occurred, the diagnosis is unexplained infertility, and given the woman's age and duration of trying, prompt referral to a fertility specialist for consideration of assisted reproductive techniques such as IVF is appropriate rather than further repetition of the same normal tests. Reassurance alone would delay time-sensitive treatment given declining ovarian reserve with age. Empirical antibiotics have no established role in unexplained infertility.

questions.question: The Amsel criteria used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Positive whiff test with added potassium hydroxide
Presence of clue cells on microscopy
Presence of motile flagellated protozoa on wet mount
Vaginal pH greater than four point five
questions.explanation: Amsel's criteria for bacterial vaginosis require at least three of four features: characteristic discharge, vaginal pH above 4.5, a positive amine (whiff) test, and clue cells on microscopy. Motile flagellated protozoa are instead the diagnostic hallmark of trichomoniasis, not bacterial vaginosis. Distinguishing these two conditions is important because their first-line treatments and implications differ.

questions.question: Which of the following teratogens is correctly matched with its associated congenital defect?
questions.explanation: Congenital rubella syndrome results from maternal rubella infection, particularly in the first trimester, and classically causes the triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart defects. Rubella is a known teratogen that damages developing organ systems during critical periods of embryogenesis. Prevention through MMR vaccination before conception is the most effective strategy to prevent congenital rubella syndrome.
options: Tetracycline causing neural tube defects in the first trimester
Folic acid supplementation causing neural tube defects
Rubella virus causing congenital cataracts, deafness, and cardiac defects
Vitamin B12 deficiency causing chromosomal trisomy 21
Warfarin causing limb reduction defects like thalidomide

questions.question: In family planning counselling, which statement most accurately advises on the use of emergency contraception?
questions.explanation: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception (EC) pills are most effective when taken as soon as possible within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, with efficacy decreasing with time. They can be taken up to 120 hours (5 days) with reduced but still significant effectiveness. The copper IUD is the most effective form of emergency contraception (greater than 99%) when inserted within 5 days. EC pills are not appropriate for regular use and do not provide ongoing contraceptive protection.
options: Emergency contraceptive pills are effective if taken within 24 hours only
The copper IUD is less effective than oral EC pills for emergency use
Levonorgestrel EC is most effective within 72 hours but works up to 120 hours
Emergency contraception is an appropriate method for regular use monthly
Emergency contraception always works by preventing implantation only

questions.explanation: The comprehensive family planning approach integrates physical examination, targeted laboratory investigations based on individual history and risk, and timely referrals when conditions exceed primary care management capacity. This personalised assessment ensures contraceptive methods are matched to the client's health profile, contraindications are identified and respected, underlying conditions are addressed, and clients requiring specialist care are referred promptly. This holistic, client-centred model improves safety, efficacy, and satisfaction.
questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the comprehensive approach to family planning that integrates physical examination, laboratory investigations, and appropriate referrals?
options: Personalised assessment of health status guides safe contraceptive choice with referral when indicated
Referral is only required when laboratory investigations reveal an abnormal result
Family planning services focus only on contraceptive provision without addressing underlying conditions
Physical examination and laboratory tests are always mandatory for all family planning clients
One method of contraception should be recommended to all women of reproductive age
Insert only if symptoms are mild and patient is non-febrile
Decline insertion and treat the PID first
Insert IUD since copper IUDs have anti-infective properties
Insert IUD and begin antibiotics concurrently
Insert the IUD after administering a single antibiotic dose
questions.explanation: Active or current PID is an absolute contraindication for IUD insertion. Inserting a device in the presence of genital tract infection risks facilitating ascending infection, worsening PID, and increasing the risk of tubo-ovarian abscess and septicaemia. The appropriate management is to treat the infection completely with antibiotics before reconsidering IUD insertion once the infection has resolved.
questions.question: A woman with active PID is requesting insertion of a copper IUD for emergency contraception. The most appropriate response is to:

questions.explanation: Referral to a sexual health clinic or specialist is necessary when STIs are complicated, recurrent, or fail to respond to standard first-line antibiotic treatment. This allows for advanced diagnostic tests such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), antibiotic resistance testing, and assessment for complications including tubo-ovarian abscess or pelvic adhesions that require specialised management.
questions.question: A referral to a sexual health specialist for an STI patient is most urgently warranted when:
options: The patient has symptoms that resolved after a full course
The patient is asymptomatic but has a positive HPV test
The patient has one episode of chlamydia already treated
The STI is complicated, recurrent, or unresponsive to first-line therapy
The patient requests a repeat Pap smear after normal results

questions.question: A woman presents with a profuse, frothy, greenish-yellow vaginal discharge with a strawberry cervix on speculum examination. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: A frothy, malodorous, greenish-yellow discharge combined with punctate haemorrhages on the cervix, described as a strawberry cervix, is a classic presentation of trichomoniasis caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia more commonly present with mucopurulent cervical discharge without this frothy quality. Diagnosis is confirmed by wet mount microscopy or nucleic acid amplification testing.

Uncomplicated clavicular fractures in neonates typically heal well with conservative management, which involves gentle handling, avoiding traction on the affected arm, and sometimes pinning the sleeve to the clothing to limit movement and reduce discomfort while natural healing occurs. Surgical fixation, rigid casting, and prolonged traction are unnecessary and inappropriate for this generally self-limiting injury. Parents should be reassured that healing is usually complete within a few weeks.
options: Traction applied continuously for several weeks
Gentle handling with the arm supported against the chest
Immediate surgical fixation with metal plating
Complete immobilisation of the entire body
Application of a rigid full-arm plaster cast
questions.question: The most appropriate nursing management for a neonate with an uncomplicated fractured clavicle is:

options: Haemolytic disease such as Rhesus or ABO incompatibility
Physiological jaundice from normal bilirubin metabolism
Mild dehydration from insufficient early feeding
Delayed passage of meconium in a healthy infant
Breast milk jaundice from prolonged breastfeeding
questions.question: Neonatal jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is most likely caused by:
questions.explanation: Jaundice appearing within the first twenty-four hours of life is considered pathological and most commonly results from haemolytic conditions such as Rhesus or ABO blood group incompatibility, which cause rapid red cell breakdown and bilirubin release. Physiological and breast milk jaundice typically appear later, after the first day, and follow a more gradual course. Early-onset jaundice therefore warrants urgent investigation to identify and treat the underlying haemolytic process.

questions.question: Achondroplasia results from which genetic mechanism and typically presents with which combination of features?
questions.explanation: Achondroplasia is caused by a mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene, most often occurring sporadically, which disrupts normal cartilage growth at the growth plates and results in disproportionately short limbs relative to a near-normal trunk length, along with a large head and characteristic facial features. Intelligence in achondroplasia is typically normal, distinguishing it from other syndromes with cognitive impairment. Genetic counselling addresses the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern for future pregnancies.
options: A mitochondrial mutation causing muscle weakness
A chromosomal trisomy causing short-trunk stature
An X-linked mutation causing generalised short stature
An autosomal recessive mutation causing microcephaly
An FGFR3 gene mutation causing short-limb dwarfism

questions.explanation: Cervical ectropion during pregnancy is primarily caused by high oestrogen levels and is a benign physiological response. In most cases, no active treatment is required during pregnancy because the condition often resolves spontaneously after delivery when oestrogen levels fall. Observation and reassurance are appropriate unless there are features suggesting dysplasia on a Pap smear.
questions.question: In the management of cervical ectropion diagnosed during pregnancy, the most appropriate approach is:
options: Observation and reassurance since it may resolve after delivery
Surgical cauterisation to prevent postpartum complications
Starting broad-spectrum antibiotics for three weeks
Urgent referral for colposcopy and cervical biopsy
Immediate laser therapy to destroy exposed columnar cells

questions.question: The most common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage is:
questions.explanation: Subinvolution is the most common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage, which occurs after 24 hours up to 12 weeks following delivery. Subinvolution is most often caused by infection related to retained placental fragments or membranes, which prevent the normal physiological shrinkage of the uterus. Multiparity, prolonged labour, and premature delivery are additional contributing factors.
options: Uterine inversion following mismanagement of the third stage
Trauma to the cervix during precipitate labour and delivery
Coagulation disorder developing after the third stage of labour
Subinvolution of the uterus due to infection or retained products
Atonic uterus from prolonged oxytocin infusion during labour

questions.explanation: Progestin-containing implants are relatively contraindicated in a woman with a current, actively treated thromboembolic event because ongoing anticoagulation and vascular risk require careful joint specialist input before any hormonal method is started. The remaining listed features are actually reasons that favour, rather than exclude, implant use. Referral for haematology input should precede insertion in this scenario.
questions.question: Which finding would make the etonogestrel subdermal implant an INAPPROPRIATE first-line choice for a family planning client?
options: Desire for a method lasting several years
Difficulty remembering a daily pill schedule
Preference to avoid a permanent surgical method
Current active deep vein thrombosis under treatment
History of heavy but regular menstrual bleeding

questions.explanation: Foul-smelling lochia, uterine tenderness, and pyrexia in the early puerperium are hallmark features of genital tract infection (puerperal sepsis). Infection at the placental site or perineal wound is common and can ascend to involve the fallopian tubes, ovaries, and peritoneum. Prompt identification of the causative organism through high vaginal swab and blood culture is essential before initiating targeted antibiotic therapy.
options: Urinary tract infection with upper renal involvement
Genital tract infection causing puerperal sepsis
Breast engorgement with early mastitis formation
Deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism risk
questions.question: A woman on the 4th postnatal day presents with a temperature of 38.2°C, foul-smelling lochia, and uterine tenderness. The most likely diagnosis is:

options: A couple requiring preimplantation genetic testing for inherited disease
A couple where the woman has severe endometriosis with ovarian involvement
A couple where the male partner has azoospermia confirmed on semen analysis
A couple with mild male factor infertility or unexplained infertility
A couple where the woman has complete bilateral fallopian tube obstruction
questions.question: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) is most appropriate as an infertility treatment for which couple?
questions.explanation: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) is most appropriate for couples with mild male factor infertility (reduced motility or mild oligospermia), unexplained infertility, or cervical hostility. Processed sperm are deposited directly into the uterine cavity at the time of ovulation, bypassing cervical barriers and increasing the concentration of motile sperm available for fertilisation. IUI is contraindicated if the fallopian tubes are blocked, as sperm cannot reach the oocyte for fertilisation.

PrEP involves the use of antiretroviral medications, typically tenofovir-emtricitabine, taken daily by HIV-negative individuals who are at high risk of acquiring HIV infection. It is indicated for people with multiple sexual partners, men who have sex with men (MSM), and individuals in serodiscordant relationships. PrEP significantly reduces the risk of HIV acquisition when taken consistently.
questions.question: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in HIV prevention involves the use of:
options: A vaccine to generate HIV-specific antibodies before exposure
An antiretroviral drug taken by HIV-negative persons at high risk
A monthly injection to eliminate HIV in seropositive individuals
Post-exposure prophylaxis taken after confirmed HIV contact
A single antibiotic given immediately after suspected exposure
Genetic testing of embryos before ovarian stimulation begins
Fertilisation of oocytes in the laboratory before any ovarian stimulation
Ovarian stimulation to produce multiple mature follicles for oocyte retrieval
Retrieving the male partner's sperm for cryopreservation before stimulation
Transfer of embryos into the uterus before follicle development
questions.question: In counselling a couple about in vitro fertilisation (IVF), the nurse should explain that the first step in the IVF process involves:
questions.explanation: In vitro fertilisation begins with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation using gonadotrophin injections to stimulate the ovaries to produce multiple mature follicles. This is followed by oocyte retrieval (egg collection) using ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, fertilisation of retrieved oocytes with prepared sperm in the laboratory, embryo culture for 3 to 5 days, and finally embryo transfer into the uterine cavity. Genetic testing (PGT) may be performed on embryos before transfer if indicated.

questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates primary from secondary postpartum haemorrhage in terms of timing?
questions.explanation: Primary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more occurring within the first 24 hours after delivery. Secondary (or delayed) PPH occurs from 24 hours after delivery up to 12 weeks postpartum. The most common cause of secondary PPH is subinvolution of the uterus, often from retained placental fragments or membranes and associated infection. This distinction guides the midwife in identifying the cause and selecting appropriate management.
options: Secondary PPH specifically refers to haemorrhage occurring after caesarean section only
Primary PPH occurs in the third stage; secondary PPH occurs on the third postnatal day
Primary PPH occurs within 24 hours; secondary PPH occurs from 24 hours to 12 weeks
Both primary and secondary PPH occur within the first 48 hours after delivery
Primary PPH occurs after 24 hours; secondary PPH within 24 hours of delivery

questions.explanation: Tubal ligation is intended as a permanent method of contraception, and although reversal surgery exists, success rates are variable and the procedure is costly and not widely available. Counselling must therefore confirm that the woman is certain about future fertility intentions before the procedure. This distinguishes sterilisation from long-acting reversible methods.
options: Easily reversible through simple outpatient surgery
Temporary and effective for approximately five years
Irreversible and unsuitable if fertility may be desired later
Associated with immediate return of fertility on request
Equivalent in reversibility to a copper IUD
questions.question: A 29-year-old woman requests permanent contraception via bilateral tubal ligation. Counselling should emphasise that the method is most appropriately considered:

options: Risk of spreading to the intracranial space and causing meningitis
Higher risk of developing neonatal jaundice from haemolysis
Permanent skull deformity requiring cosmetic surgical repair
Predisposition to chronic subdural haemorrhage in childhood
Association with 25% mortality due to massive haemorrhage
questions.question: The most serious complication of subaponeurotic haemorrhage compared to cephalhaematoma is:
questions.explanation: Subaponeurotic haemorrhage (subgaleal haemorrhage) is an emergency because blood can accumulate extensively in the potential space beneath the epicranial aponeurosis across the entire cranial vault. It is associated with a 25% mortality rate due to the risk of massive haemorrhage causing hypovolaemic shock. The swelling crosses suture lines, is fluctuant, and can extend into the neck and eyelids. Immediate medical assistance, stabilisation, and blood transfusion may be required.

In a primigravida with mild preeclampsia at 36 weeks, primary care management before referral includes initiating antihypertensive therapy if blood pressure exceeds safe thresholds, monitoring fetal wellbeing, documenting all findings, and arranging urgent referral to a higher-level facility capable of managing preeclampsia and its complications (eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption). IV magnesium sulphate is given when there is imminent risk of eclampsia (severe headache, visual changes, clonus).
options: Reassurance and daily blood pressure monitoring at home alone
Starting antihypertensive therapy, foetal monitoring, and urgent referral
Immediate delivery by caesarean section at the primary care facility
Intravenous magnesium sulphate infusion and transfer without antihypertensives
Prescription of diuretics to reduce oedema and monitoring for 2 weeks
questions.question: In managing a primigravida at 36 weeks with mild preeclampsia (BP 145/95, no severe features), the most appropriate initial management at primary care level before referral includes:
Which statement about infertility investigation is most accurate according to established guidelines?
questions.explanation: The preliminary investigations for infertile couples focus on the three most common causes of infertility: semen analysis (to assess sperm count, motility, and morphology), ovarian function assessment through hormonal assays (FSH, LH, mid-luteal progesterone), and tubal patency evaluation by hysterosalpingography (HSG). Laparoscopy is reserved for suspected endometriosis or pelvic adhesions. Genetic testing is indicated when chromosomal abnormalities are suspected.
options: IVF should be offered to all couples after 6 months of trying to conceive
Semen analysis is not necessary if the female partner has ovulatory dysfunction
Semen analysis, hormonal assays, and HSG form the preliminary investigation panel
Genetic testing is mandatory for all couples before infertility treatment begins
Laparoscopy is the first investigation recommended for all infertile couples
Apply a new patch and use backup contraception for a week
Wait until the next scheduled change day only
Discard the entire pack and await her next period
Reapply the same detached patch immediately without concern
Continue the current cycle without any additional precaution
questions.question: A woman using the combined contraceptive patch reports it detached for more than 48 hours mid-cycle. The most appropriate advice is to:
questions.explanation: When a contraceptive patch has been detached for more than twenty-four hours, contraceptive protection cannot be assured, so a new patch should be applied promptly and additional barrier contraception used for seven days while hormone levels re-establish. Reapplying the same detached patch is unhygienic and unreliable since adhesion and hormone delivery may be compromised. Discarding the pack unnecessarily would not address the immediate risk of reduced protection.

options: Communicating hydrocephalus involves impaired CSF absorption without intraventricular obstruction
Non-communicating hydrocephalus is caused by impaired CSF absorption in the arachnoid
Both types present identically and cannot be distinguished by imaging studies
Non-communicating hydrocephalus results from overproduction of CSF by choroid plexus
Communicating hydrocephalus has no connection between ventricles and subarachnoid space
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the classification of hydrocephalus as 'communicating' versus 'non-communicating'?
questions.explanation: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when CSF can flow freely through the ventricular system but is impaired in its absorption at the level of the arachnoid granulations (subarachnoid space). Causes include meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and arachnoid cysts.
