questions.explanation: Bimanual palpation allows the clinician to assess the size, shape, and position of the uterus as well as identify ovarian or adnexal masses that may affect contraceptive choice or indicate pathology. This examination is essential before inserting an IUD or selecting any intrauterine contraceptive device. The other assessments listed require different diagnostic techniques.
options: Depth and integrity of the vaginal fornices
Uterine size, position, and adnexal masses
questions.question: A bimanual pelvic examination in family planning is primarily used to evaluate which of the following?

questions.explanation: Women who have experienced repeated episodes of PID are at significant risk of tubal damage, which can result in infertility or increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. These women require specialist follow-up with a reproductive gynaecologist to assess tubal patency (via HSG or laparoscopy), discuss fertility implications, and plan appropriate family planning strategies. Specialist input is essential to address long-term reproductive consequences of recurrent PID.
options: Complete resolution of symptoms within 72 hours of oral antibiotics
Mild residual lower abdominal discomfort one week after completing treatment
Patient requesting a repeat STI screen 6 months after treatment completion
A negative STI test result after completing the full course of treatment
Suspected tubal damage and infertility risk following repeated PID episodes
questions.question: A family planning nurse reviewing the indications for referral after PID treatment notes that which of the following outcomes most necessitates specialist follow-up?

options: Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli
Klebsiella species acquired postnatally in the nursery
Candida species acquired from hospital equipment
questions.question: Early-onset neonatal sepsis, occurring within the first seventy-two hours of life, is most commonly caused by:
questions.explanation: Early-onset neonatal sepsis most commonly results from vertical transmission of organisms colonising the maternal genital tract during labour and delivery, particularly Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli, reflecting exposure during passage through the birth canal. Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Candida, and Pseudomonas are instead more typical causes of late-onset, hospital-acquired sepsis. Maternal intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for identified Group B Streptococcus colonisation reduces this risk.

options: Between twenty-four hours and six weeks postpartum
Within the first six hours postpartum only
Between one week and twelve weeks postpartum
Within the first twenty-four hours postpartum
Within the first seventy-two hours postpartum
questions.question: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is defined as blood loss exceeding 500 mL occurring within which time frame after delivery?
questions.explanation: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is defined as excessive vaginal bleeding exceeding 500 mL occurring within the first twenty-four hours following delivery, most commonly due to uterine atony. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage, by contrast, occurs from twenty-four hours up to six weeks postpartum and is more often related to retained products of conception or infection. This time-based distinction guides the likely underlying cause and management approach.

options: Complete absence of the choroid plexus tissue
Excessive closure of the anterior fontanelle only
An imbalance between cerebrospinal fluid production and drainage
Reduced total blood volume within the brain
Premature ossification of the cranial sutures
questions.question: Hydrocephalus fundamentally results from which physiological disturbance?
questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus arises when there is an imbalance between the production of cerebrospinal fluid by the choroid plexus and its absorption or drainage, leading to accumulation of fluid within the ventricular system and progressive ventricular dilation. This imbalance may result from obstruction to flow, impaired absorption, or, rarely, overproduction. Recognising the underlying mechanism guides whether shunting or removing an obstruction is the appropriate treatment.

options: Full blood count to assess degree of leucocytosis
Blood culture and sensitivity for systemic bacteraemia
High vaginal swab for STI screening and culture
Chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia as the cause
Midstream urine specimen for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity
questions.question: Which investigation is most appropriate for a puerperal woman suspected to have a urinary tract infection causing pyrexia?
questions.explanation: Urinary tract infection is a common cause of puerperal pyrexia and may be pre-existing or acquired postpartum through catheterisation or urethral trauma. A midstream specimen of urine (MSSU) for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity identifies the causative organism, detects pus cells, and determines antibiotic sensitivity. The midwife should also test the urine for albumin as a routine step in investigating puerperal pyrexia.

options: Reduce the efficacy of chemotherapy agents being used
Suppress the immune system, worsening cancer prognosis
Interfere with surgical anaesthesia during tumour resection
Increase VTE risk and may exacerbate hormone-sensitive tumours
Cause direct tumour proliferation through oestrogen receptor binding
questions.question: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are contraindicated in women with active cancer primarily because they:
questions.explanation: Combined oral contraceptives carry a significantly increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) due to their oestrogen component. Women with active cancer already have elevated VTE risk from the malignancy itself, its treatment, and immobility. Furthermore, COCs may exacerbate hormone-sensitive cancers such as oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer or endometrial cancer by providing exogenous hormonal stimulation. These factors make COCs contraindicated in women with active cancer.

options: 500 cells/mm3 in the absence of symptoms
100 cells/mm3 only in the presence of tuberculosis
questions.explanation: AIDS is defined as the most advanced stage of HIV infection and is diagnosed when the CD4 T-cell count falls below 200 cells/mm3, regardless of whether opportunistic infections are present, or when the individual develops one or more AIDS-defining opportunistic infections (e.g., Pneumocystis pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma, tuberculosis). This threshold reflects severe immunosuppression that markedly increases susceptibility to opportunistic disease.
questions.question: AIDS is clinically diagnosed when the CD4 T-cell count falls below which threshold?
In a woman with history of ectopic pregnancy seeking future conception, the most appropriate investigation to assess risk before attempting pregnancy is:
questions.explanation: A history of ectopic pregnancy significantly increases the risk of recurrent ectopic implantation due to tubal damage or adhesions. Before attempting a new pregnancy, HSG assesses tubal patency and morphology, while pelvic MRI provides detailed information about tubal architecture and any peritubal adhesions. Identifying tubal pathology allows clinicians to counsel appropriately about recurrence risk and the potential need for IVF to bypass the damaged tube.
options: Transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness
Serum beta-hCG measurement to confirm current pregnancy status
Laparoscopy and dye test as the only reliable assessment method
Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) level to measure ovarian reserve
Hysterosalpingography (HSG) or pelvic MRI to assess tubal patency
Congenital underdevelopment of the uterus at birth
Delayed return of the uterus to its pre-pregnancy size
Complete absence of any uterine contraction postpartum
Rapid overcontraction of the uterus after birth
Normal expected uterine size throughout the puerperium
questions.question: Subinvolution of the uterus is best defined as:
questions.explanation: Subinvolution refers to a delay or failure of the uterus to return to its normal non-pregnant size and consistency during the puerperium, often due to retained placental tissue or infection, and is typically detected when the fundal height remains higher than expected for the postnatal day. It results in a larger, softer uterus with prolonged lochia and increased bleeding risk. Prompt evaluation and treatment of the underlying cause prevents ongoing haemorrhage.

questions.question: A pregnant woman tests positive for syphilis on routine antenatal screening. The most important reason to treat her immediately is to prevent:
options: Vertical transmission to the fetus causing congenital syphilis
Maternal pelvic inflammatory disease worsening in pregnancy
Development of cervical cancer due to Treponema pallidum
Maternal HIV co-infection from untreated syphilis
Maternal death from cardiovascular syphilitic complications
questions.explanation: Treponema pallidum can cross the placenta after approximately 18 weeks of gestation and infect the fetus. Untreated maternal syphilis can lead to congenital syphilis in the newborn, manifesting as hepatosplenomegaly, joint swelling, palmar rash, anaemia, jaundice, and snuffles. Early treatment with penicillin G in the antenatal period is highly effective in preventing vertical transmission and congenital syphilis.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management for superficial scalp abrasions in a newborn?
questions.explanation: Superficial scalp abrasions from forceps, vacuum extractor cups, or scalp electrodes should be kept clean and dry to promote healing and prevent secondary infection. Deeper lacerations may require closure with sutures or butterfly strips. Parents should be reassured and given explanations about the findings. If infection develops, medical advice and antibiotic therapy may be required. Fat necrosis typically heals rapidly without residual scarring and needs no specific treatment.
options: Covering with a pressure bandage to reduce haematoma formation
Immediate antibiotic prophylaxis for all scalp abrasions
Keeping the area clean and dry to prevent infection
Incision and drainage of the affected scalp tissue immediately
Application of topical corticosteroid cream to reduce inflammation

questions.question: Preconception screening for rubella immunity is important primarily because maternal rubella infection in early pregnancy can cause:
options: Congenital rubella syndrome with cardiac and ocular defects
Neonatal tetanus through umbilical cord contamination
Isolated maternal joint pain without any fetal effect
Congenital hip dysplasia specifically in the fetus
Isolated maternal skin rash with no lasting fetal risk
questions.explanation: Maternal rubella infection during early pregnancy can cross the placenta and cause congenital rubella syndrome in the fetus, characterised by a combination of cardiac defects such as patent ductus arteriosus, cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and other anomalies, making preconception screening and vaccination of non-immune women an important preventive strategy. It is not linked to neonatal tetanus or hip dysplasia, which have entirely different causes. Rubella vaccination should be given before conception rather than during pregnancy itself due to its live-attenuated nature.

Chlamydia trachomatis infection can be treated with azithromycin 1 gram as a single oral dose, which improves adherence and ensures complete treatment in a single healthcare encounter. Alternatively, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days is also a first-line option with equivalent efficacy. The single-dose azithromycin regimen is particularly advantageous in resource-limited settings or when adherence to a multi-day course cannot be guaranteed.
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly as single dose
Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
Erythromycin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Azithromycin 1 gram as a single oral dose
questions.question: Which of the following drugs used to treat Chlamydia trachomatis is given as a single oral dose?

questions.explanation: IUD insertion involves passing the device through the cervical canal into the uterine cavity. If lower genital tract STIs such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea are present at the time of insertion, the procedure can introduce these organisms into the uterus and fallopian tubes, causing endometritis, salpingitis, or pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Pre-insertion STI screening with cervical and high vaginal swabs ensures that infection is treated and resolved before the procedure, preventing iatrogenic PID.
questions.question: Which of the following best explains why STI screening is recommended before IUD insertion in a family planning setting?
options: STIs reduce the efficacy of IUDs by altering the uterine environment
STI screening is a legal requirement before any gynaecological procedure
IUD insertion can introduce lower genital tract organisms into the uterus
STI screening confirms ovulatory function required before IUD insertion
IUDs protect against STIs by maintaining cervical mucus thickness

questions.question: Petechiae on the face and head of a newborn, noted on examination, are most accurately attributed to:
options: Venous congestion during passage through the birth canal
Vitamin K deficiency causing reduced clotting factor production
Forceps-related compression causing deep tissue injury
Sepsis-related disseminated intravascular coagulation at birth
Thrombocytopenia from maternal antiplatelet antibody transfer
questions.explanation: Petechiae on the face and head of a newborn are small, non-raised haemorrhagic spots caused by a sudden increase and release of pressure during passage through the birth canal, resulting in transient venous congestion. This is a common and usually benign finding in normal newborns. However, petechiae can also indicate an underlying bleeding disorder or systemic infection, and should be evaluated in the context of the complete clinical picture.

options: Reassure her and discharge home with routine follow-up
Delay any intervention until the following week
Provide only written information about postnatal mood
Ensure continuous supervision and urgent psychiatric referral
Advise her to rest alone without any supervision
questions.explanation: Expressed intent to harm the infant alongside psychotic features such as hallucinations and paranoid delusions constitutes a psychiatric emergency requiring continuous close supervision of both mother and baby together with urgent psychiatric referral for assessment and likely admission. Discharging her home or delaying intervention would place both mother and infant at serious risk. Ensuring safety while arranging specialist care is the immediate priority.
questions.question: A postnatal woman exhibits auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions about family members, and expresses a wish to harm her baby. The most appropriate immediate nursing action is to:
A palpable, firm, irregular breast lump in a 45-year-old woman is being investigated. Which combination of tests constitutes the recommended triple assessment?
options: Clinical examination and blood tests only
Ultrasound alone repeated after three months
Clinical examination, imaging, and needle biopsy
Pap smear combined with pelvic examination
Mammography and complete blood count only
questions.explanation: Triple assessment for a suspicious breast lump combines clinical examination, appropriate imaging such as mammography or ultrasound, and tissue sampling by fine needle aspiration or core biopsy, providing complementary information that improves diagnostic accuracy. Relying on blood tests, imaging alone, or unrelated cervical tests would miss important diagnostic information. This structured approach is standard practice for suspected breast malignancy.

questions.question: Spina bifida occulta is distinguished from spina bifida aperta primarily by the fact that occulta:
options: Always presents with an open protruding sac
Involves protrusion of both cord and meninges
Requires emergency surgical closure at birth
Causes immediate paralysis of both lower limbs
Is covered by intact skin without any visible sac
questions.explanation: Spina bifida occulta is a mild, often asymptomatic form in which the vertebral arch fails to close but the spinal contents remain covered by intact skin, sometimes marked only by a tuft of hair or a dimple. Spina bifida aperta, encompassing meningocele and myelomeningocele, involves an open lesion with an exposed or thinly covered sac. This distinction determines whether urgent surgical intervention is required after birth.

options: Progesterone-only injectable administered every three months
A copper IUD as first-line despite the history of ectopic pregnancy
Natural family planning methods based on basal body temperature
Combined oral contraceptive pill for high contraceptive efficacy
A long-acting progestin implant or hormonal IUS to prevent ovulation
questions.question: In managing a client with a history of ectopic pregnancy who now desires contraception, which method is most strongly recommended?
questions.explanation: For women with a history of ectopic pregnancy, long-acting progestin-containing methods such as the subdermal implant or levonorgestrel-releasing IUS are strongly preferred because they suppress ovulation and prevent any fertilised oocyte from implanting in the fallopian tube. The copper IUD, while highly effective for contraception, does not suppress ovulation and carries a slightly higher proportional risk of ectopic implantation if contraceptive failure occurs.

Prevention of PID in family planning education focuses on consistent condom use, which reduces exposure to STI pathogens that cause PID, and regular STI screening for early detection and treatment of infections before they ascend to the upper genital tract. Douching is harmful as it disrupts the normal vaginal flora and increases susceptibility to infection. Dual protection — using condoms alongside another contraceptive method — is the recommended prevention strategy.
questions.question: Educational counselling in family planning should address which key message regarding PID prevention?
options: Consistent condom use and regular STI screening significantly reduce PID risk
Douching effectively removes pathogens causing PID from the vagina
Copper IUD insertion provides protection against ascending infection
Multiple sexual partners are permissible if regular antibiotic prophylaxis is used
Hormonal contraception provides complete protection against PID

questions.question: Which laboratory investigation is most useful for confirming a diagnosis of neonatal sepsis before starting empirical antibiotics?
options: Blood culture obtained prior to antibiotic administration
questions.explanation: Blood culture remains the gold standard investigation for confirming neonatal sepsis and identifying the causative organism along with its antibiotic sensitivities, and ideally should be obtained before starting empirical antibiotic therapy to maximise diagnostic yield. Other tests such as glucose, bilirubin, hearing screening, or urinalysis do not confirm bacterial sepsis directly. Empirical antibiotics should nonetheless be started promptly on clinical suspicion without waiting for culture results given the rapid deterioration risk.

questions.question: Genital warts caused by low-risk Human Papillomavirus types most commonly involve which HPV subtypes?
questions.explanation: HPV types six and eleven are classified as low-risk subtypes responsible for the majority of anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata) but carry minimal oncogenic potential. High-risk types such as sixteen and eighteen are instead strongly associated with cervical dysplasia and cancer. This distinction underlies why the quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines target both wart-causing and cancer-causing types.

questions.question: The ventriculoperitoneal shunt used to treat hydrocephalus is most at risk of which two major complications?
options: Spontaneous closure of the anterior fontanelle only
Mechanical blockage and infection of the shunt system
Complete resolution of ventricular dilation permanently
Excessive hair growth and skin pigmentation change
Improved cognitive outcome without further monitoring
questions.explanation: Ventriculoperitoneal shunts, while effective at diverting excess cerebrospinal fluid to the peritoneal cavity, carry significant long-term risks of mechanical malfunction such as blockage or disconnection, and of infection along the shunt tract, both of which can present with recurrence of raised intracranial pressure or systemic signs of sepsis. Ongoing surveillance for these complications is essential throughout the child's life. Shunt revision surgery is frequently required when either complication occurs.

questions.question: A woman presents for family planning with a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Which laboratory investigation should be prioritised?
questions.explanation: A history of DVT raises concern for inherited or acquired thrombophilia. A coagulation profile including prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and D-dimer helps assess clotting risk. Oestrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated in thrombophilia due to the significantly increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Thrombophilia screening guides the choice of a safe contraceptive method.
options: Coagulation profile including PT and aPTT
Liver function tests and serum albumin

questions.question: Polycystic ovary syndrome, a common cause of anovulatory infertility, is most accurately diagnosed using which set of criteria?
questions.explanation: The Rotterdam criteria diagnose polycystic ovary syndrome when at least two of three features are present: oligo-ovulation or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. A single test such as glucose or BMI alone cannot establish this diagnosis. Accurate diagnosis guides appropriate ovulation induction and metabolic management strategies.
options: A single fasting blood glucose measurement alone
Body mass index calculation without any other test
Cervical mucus ferning pattern observed alone
Rotterdam criteria combining clinical, biochemical, and ultrasound features
Endometrial biopsy findings exclusively used alone

questions.explanation: Because chlamydial infection is frequently asymptomatic yet can cause significant reproductive harm such as pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility, annual screening is recommended for all sexually active women under twenty-five regardless of symptoms. Waiting for symptoms to appear would miss the majority of infections and delay treatment. Regular screening allows early detection and treatment before complications develop.
options: Annual screening even without symptoms present
Screening only when pregnancy is being planned
One-time screening performed at age eighteen only
Screening only after three confirmed sexual partners
Screening only if visible symptoms develop
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the recommended screening interval for chlamydia in sexually active women under twenty-five years of age?
A client recently diagnosed with HIV asks about the window period for antibody-based testing. The nurse should explain that this refers to:
options: The period during which viral load is undetectable
The time before detectable antibodies appear after exposure
The interval between two doses of antiretroviral therapy
The time needed for CD4 count to normalise
The duration antiretroviral prophylaxis remains effective
questions.explanation: The window period is the interval following HIV exposure during which the virus is present but the body has not yet produced detectable antibody levels, potentially causing a false-negative antibody test result. Repeat testing after this period, or use of a fourth-generation combination antigen-antibody assay, improves detection reliability. Understanding this concept is essential for accurate counselling after a recent possible exposure.

A high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion carries a substantially higher risk of underlying cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade two or three and requires prompt colposcopic evaluation with biopsy, unlike lower-risk findings that may simply warrant repeat testing or HPV co-testing. Atypical cells of undetermined significance and low-grade lesions are typically managed with less urgent follow-up protocols. Timely referral for high-grade lesions reduces progression risk to invasive cancer.
options: Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance
Normal cytology with satisfactory sample adequacy
questions.question: Which cervical cytology finding on a Pap smear requires the MOST urgent referral for colposcopy?
A woman with a copper IUD in situ develops fever, cervical motion tenderness, and adnexal tenderness consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease. The most appropriate initial action is to:
options: Reassure her that the device cannot cause this presentation
Remove the device immediately before starting any antibiotics
Start appropriate antibiotics while the device remains in place
Replace the copper device with a hormonal device instead
Refer for immediate hysterectomy without antibiotic trial
questions.explanation: Current guidance generally recommends starting appropriate antibiotic therapy promptly while leaving the intrauterine device in place, since removal is not usually necessary for successful treatment of mild to moderate pelvic inflammatory disease and may be considered only if there is no clinical improvement within 48 to 72 hours. Immediate removal or drastic surgical measures without an antibiotic trial would be premature and unnecessarily invasive. Close follow-up ensures escalation of care if symptoms fail to resolve.

questions.question: Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between pelvic inflammatory disease and subsequent risk of ectopic pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Inflammation and subsequent scarring of the fallopian tubes caused by pelvic inflammatory disease can distort normal tubal anatomy and impair ciliary transport of the fertilised ovum, substantially increasing the risk of ectopic implantation in future pregnancies. This risk increases with the number and severity of PID episodes rather than being confined to a single occurrence. Women with a history of PID should be counselled about this risk and monitored closely in early subsequent pregnancies.
options: PID has no measurable effect on future ectopic pregnancy risk
PID reduces the risk of ectopic pregnancy occurring later
Ectopic pregnancy risk is unrelated to tubal damage entirely
Only a single episode of PID carries any measurable risk
Tubal scarring from PID substantially increases ectopic pregnancy risk

questions.question: The midwife's responsibility when discharging a woman with puerperal psychosis who has recovered includes counselling her on:
questions.explanation: Women who have experienced puerperal psychosis have a significant risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies — estimated at 25 to 50% for postpartum psychosis and higher for bipolar disorder. Discharge counselling must include education on this recurrence risk, the importance of early antenatal disclosure of the history to healthcare providers, and early referral to a perinatal mental health team in any future pregnancy for close monitoring and preventive intervention. This does not necessitate permanent sterilisation or indefinite medication.
options: Avoiding all breastfeeding in any future pregnancies due to psychosis risk
Permanent sterilisation to prevent future at-risk pregnancies
Risk of recurrence in future pregnancies and early antenatal mental health referral
Mandatory quarterly psychiatric review for the rest of her life
Taking antipsychotic medication continuously for the next 10 years

questions.question: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system differs from the copper IUD primarily in that it:
questions.explanation: The hormonal intrauterine system releases levonorgestrel locally, causing endometrial thinning that substantially reduces menstrual blood loss, an effect the copper IUD does not share since it works through a non-hormonal inflammatory mechanism. Both devices provide several years of protection once correctly sited. This added benefit makes the hormonal system particularly useful for women with heavy menstrual bleeding.
options: Also reduces menstrual blood loss through endometrial thinning
Requires daily oral supplementation to remain effective
Cannot be used by any nulliparous woman
Provides no protection against ectopic pregnancy
Must be replaced annually to remain effective
After a full 12 months, as for women under 35 years
After 18 months if initial workup at primary care is normal
Immediately, as all women over 35 should be referred at once
Only if an obvious cause of infertility is identified on examination
After 6 months, as the threshold is reduced for women over 35
questions.question: A 36-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 5 months. According to infertility referral guidelines, when should she be referred?
questions.explanation: Infertility referral guidelines recommend that women under 35 years be referred after 12 months of unsuccessful regular unprotected intercourse. For women aged 35 years and older, this threshold is reduced to 6 months due to the accelerated decline in ovarian reserve and fertility with advancing age. Immediate referral is warranted if obvious infertility factors are identified (e.g., amenorrhoea, imperforate hymen, known tubal disease) regardless of age.

Suppressive antiviral therapy, typically with daily acyclovir or valacyclovir, reduces the frequency and severity of recurrent herpes outbreaks and lowers the risk of viral shedding and transmission to partners, but it does not eradicate the latent virus residing in nerve ganglia. Safer sexual practices remain important even with suppressive treatment. This distinction should be clearly communicated during client counselling.
questions.question: A client with recurrent genital herpes outbreaks asks about suppressive therapy. The nurse should explain that long-term suppressive antiviral therapy is used primarily to:
options: Permanently eliminate the latent virus from the body
Replace the need for safer sexual practices entirely
Prevent all future pregnancies from being affected
Cure any active outbreak within twenty-four hours
Reduce the frequency of symptomatic recurrent outbreaks

questions.explanation: Migraine with aura is associated with an increased baseline risk of ischaemic stroke, and oestrogen-containing contraceptives further amplify this risk through effects on coagulation and vascular tone. Progestin-only and non-hormonal methods do not carry this same risk elevation. Current guidelines therefore classify combined oestrogen methods as unsuitable for this client group.
questions.question: A woman with a history of migraine with aura is requesting contraception. Which method should be AVOIDED because of increased stroke risk?

questions.explanation: Elevated prolactin levels (hyperprolactinaemia) can cause irregular or absent menstrual cycles, galactorrhoea, and infertility. Measuring serum prolactin is indicated when these symptoms are present, as hyperprolactinaemia may indicate a pituitary adenoma or hypothyroidism. Identifying this condition affects contraceptive choice and may require treatment before effective family planning can be achieved.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate indication for prolactin level measurement in a family planning setting?
options: Client requests emergency contraception after unprotected sex
Client uses barrier methods and wants STI screening
Client is a primigravida requesting postpartum contraception
Client has irregular cycles and galactorrhoea
Bilateral absence of the Moro reflex entirely
Hyperextension of both lower limbs bilaterally
Complete facial asymmetry when crying vigorously
Persistent bulging of the anterior fontanelle
Asymmetric or absent Moro reflex on the affected side
questions.explanation: A fractured clavicle typically causes pain on movement of the affected arm, leading to an asymmetric or absent Moro reflex on that side, along with possible crepitus or a palpable bony irregularity over the clavicle itself. Bilateral Moro absence, facial asymmetry, and fontanelle bulging suggest entirely different underlying pathologies. Clavicular fractures generally heal well with simple supportive measures such as gentle handling and pinning the sleeve to clothing.
questions.question: A newborn with a suspected fractured clavicle following a difficult vaginal delivery is most likely to present with which clinical finding?

questions.explanation: Ovulation induction refers to the use of pharmacological treatments to stimulate the ovary to produce and release one or more mature follicles in women with anovulation or oligo-ovulation. Common agents include clomiphene citrate, letrozole, gonadotrophins (FSH/LH), and metformin in insulin-resistant women. This is distinct from ovarian stimulation, which aims to produce multiple mature follicles for IVF, and from intrauterine insemination (IUI), which is a method of achieving fertilisation.
questions.question: Ovulation induction in infertility treatment refers specifically to:
options: Retrieval of oocytes directly from the ovary under ultrasound guidance
Intrauterine insemination timed to coincide with natural ovulation
Hormone replacement therapy to restore regular menstrual cycles
Surgical removal of ovarian cysts to restore normal ovulation
Use of pharmacological agents to stimulate follicle development and ovulation
Exclusive formula feeding regardless of her wishes
Discontinuation of all psychiatric follow-up immediately
Permanent avoidance of any future pregnancy entirely
Isolation from family support during recovery
Early warning signs and risk of recurrence in future pregnancies
questions.question: The community midwife providing follow-up for a woman who has recovered from puerperal psychosis should prioritise counselling on:
questions.explanation: Women who have experienced puerperal psychosis have a significantly increased risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies, so follow-up counselling should cover recognising early warning signs, the importance of continued psychiatric support, and preconception planning for any future pregnancy. Advising against all future pregnancy or withdrawing psychiatric follow-up would be inappropriate and unsupported by guidelines. Family involvement and support are generally encouraged rather than discouraged during recovery.

questions.question: The most important nursing measure to prevent mastitis from progressing to breast abscess is:
questions.explanation: Effective and frequent emptying of the affected breast, whether by continued breastfeeding, hand expression, or pumping, prevents milk stasis, which is the key factor allowing bacterial proliferation and progression from simple mastitis to abscess formation. Stopping breastfeeding altogether can worsen stasis and engorgement, increasing rather than decreasing the risk of abscess. Prompt antibiotic therapy alongside continued drainage gives the best outcome.
options: Application of a tight supportive binder continuously
Ensuring effective and frequent milk drainage from the breast
Restriction of maternal fluid intake during treatment
Complete cessation of breastfeeding on both breasts
Delaying antibiotic therapy until fever resolves

questions.question: Fracture of the clavicle in a newborn most commonly occurs in which clinical circumstance?
questions.explanation: Clavicle fracture in the neonate most commonly occurs during shoulder dystocia or during breech delivery. The affected bone is typically the one nearest the maternal symphysis pubis. On examination, a distortion in the bone with crepitus or callus formation may be palpated. Fractures of the clavicle generally require no specific treatment and achieve stable union within 7 to 10 days.
options: During a normal vertex delivery at full-term gestation
During shoulder dystocia or breech delivery
Following forceps application to deliver the fetal head
After vacuum extraction in a premature neonate
From maternal abdominal trauma in the third trimester

questions.question: During a speculum examination in a family planning clinic, the nurse observes a red, inflamed area on the ectocervix. The most appropriate immediate action is to:
questions.explanation: A red, inflamed appearance on the ectocervix may represent cervical erosion (ectropion), infection, or, rarely, a precancerous lesion. The appropriate step is to collect a Pap smear to rule out cervical dysplasia and a cervical swab to exclude infection, particularly STIs such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea. This ensures a systematic and evidence-based approach before initiating any treatment.
options: Immediately initiate antibiotic therapy for PID
Perform a Pap smear and cervical swab for investigation
Proceed with IUD insertion without further workup
Reassure the patient that this is always benign
Refer immediately to a gynaecological oncologist

questions.question: Persistent insomnia without apparent reason in a newly delivered woman is most importantly significant because it:
questions.explanation: Persistent insomnia without apparent reason in the postnatal woman is an important early warning sign of puerperal psychosis. Other early warning signs include refusing meals, loss of interest in the baby, and restlessness. Early recognition and prompt referral to psychiatric services are critical to prevent progression to more severe manifestations including hallucinations, suicidal ideation, and risk of harm to the infant.
options: Suggests the woman is experiencing anaemia from delivery
Indicates inadequate pain relief following perineal repair
Is expected and normal in the immediate postnatal period
Serves as an early warning sign of puerperal psychosis
Confirms postnatal depression has developed fully
Ensure the infant has stopped breastfeeding completely
Avoid any need for future orthodontic treatment entirely
Wait until all primary teeth have fully erupted
Allow adequate palatal growth while supporting early speech development
Allow complete closure of the anterior fontanelle first
questions.question: Surgical repair of cleft palate is typically delayed until 18 to 24 months of age primarily to:
questions.explanation: Delaying palate repair until around 18 to 24 months balances allowing sufficient palatal tissue growth to facilitate a technically successful repair against the need to complete surgery before critical periods of speech development, since an intact palate is important for normal speech sound production. Waiting significantly longer risks compromising speech outcomes, while operating too early may increase technical difficulty and growth disturbance. This timing reflects a careful balance established through clinical experience and outcome studies.

Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis, providing direct visualisation of endometriotic lesions, ovarian endometriomas, and pelvic adhesions, with the ability to biopsy lesions for histological confirmation. While pelvic ultrasound can detect ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) and MRI can assess deep infiltrating endometriosis, neither can diagnose peritoneal endometriosis — the most common form — without laparoscopy. Clients with suspected endometriosis should be referred for specialist evaluation.
options: MRI of the pelvis with contrast to visualise endometriotic deposits
Pelvic ultrasound as the definitive diagnostic investigation
Endometrial biopsy to confirm retrograde menstruation histologically
Serum CA-125 level as the sole diagnostic blood test needed
Referral for diagnostic laparoscopy as the gold standard
questions.question: The most appropriate investigation for a woman presenting with chronic pelvic pain and suspected endometriosis in a family planning setting is:

questions.explanation: Metronidazole given as a single two-gram oral dose is the standard first-line regimen for uncomplicated trichomoniasis in non-pregnant women, with a seven-day lower-dose course as an alternative. Azithromycin and doxycycline are used for chlamydia, while ceftriaxone and penicillin target gonorrhoea and syphilis respectively. Sexual partners should be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection.
options: Metronidazole two grams as a single dose
Benzathine penicillin as a single injection
Azithromycin one gram as a single dose
Doxycycline one hundred milligrams twice daily
Ceftriaxone two hundred and fifty milligrams intramuscularly
questions.question: Which of the following is the recommended first-line single-dose oral treatment for uncomplicated trichomoniasis?

questions.explanation: Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, and adnexal tenderness constitute the classic clinical triad of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). These minimum diagnostic criteria, as defined by the CDC, justify empirical treatment to prevent long-term sequelae such as infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and ectopic pregnancy. IUD insertion is absolutely contraindicated in the presence of active PID.
options: Cervical cancer at an advanced stage
Normal findings in a postmenstrual examination
questions.question: A nurse in a family planning clinic identifies a client with cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, and adnexal tenderness. These clinical findings most strongly suggest:
A client presents with unexplained vaginal bleeding. Which investigation is most urgently indicated to exclude endometrial pathology?
questions.explanation: Unexplained or abnormal uterine bleeding may indicate endometrial polyps, fibroids, hyperplasia, or carcinoma. Pelvic ultrasound provides initial imaging to assess the uterine cavity and endometrial thickness, while endometrial biopsy provides histological diagnosis. Together, they are the most appropriate initial investigations to exclude serious endometrial pathology before proceeding with family planning.
options: High vaginal swab and cervical culture
Hormonal assay for FSH and oestradiol
Complete blood count and coagulation profile
Thyroid function tests and prolactin level

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the primary contraceptive mechanism of the copper-bearing intrauterine device?
questions.explanation: Copper ions released from the device provoke a sterile inflammatory reaction within the endometrial cavity that is toxic to sperm and ova, preventing fertilisation. Unlike hormonal methods, the copper IUD does not suppress ovulation. This local inflammatory effect is the accepted primary mechanism of copper-based intrauterine contraception.
options: It suppresses ovulation via hormonal feedback
It thins the endometrium to prevent bleeding
It blocks the internal cervical os physically
It creates a spermicidal inflammatory reaction
It alters vaginal pH to immobilise sperm

questions.explanation: The nonavalent vaccine expands coverage beyond the original quadrivalent formulation to include additional high-risk oncogenic types such as thirty-one, thirty-three, forty-five, fifty-two, and fifty-eight, broadening protection against cervical cancer. Types six, eleven, sixteen, and eighteen were already covered in the earlier quadrivalent vaccine. This expanded coverage increases the proportion of cervical cancers potentially prevented by vaccination.
questions.question: Which of the following HPV types is included in the nonavalent HPV vaccine but NOT in the earlier quadrivalent vaccine?
options: Type eleven responsible for genital warts
Type fifty-two among additional high-risk strains
Type eighteen as the principal high-risk type
Type six responsible for genital warts
Type sixteen as the principal high-risk type

questions.explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia with warning signs such as severe headache, visual disturbance, or epigastric pain indicates impending eclampsia and requires urgent referral to a tertiary centre with facilities for intensive maternal and fetal monitoring, magnesium sulphate administration, and potential emergency delivery. Mild gestational hypertension and the other listed benign discomforts of pregnancy do not require this level of urgent escalation. Timely referral in severe pre-eclampsia significantly reduces the risk of maternal seizures and other serious complications.
questions.question: Which of the following maternal conditions during pregnancy most urgently requires referral to a tertiary centre?
options: Mild round ligament pain in the second trimester
Severe pre-eclampsia with signs of impending eclampsia
Uncomplicated physiological oedema of the ankles

questions.question: The primary reason progestin-only pills must be taken at the same time each day, with minimal flexibility, is that:
questions.explanation: Traditional progestin-only pills have a short duration of action on cervical mucus thickening, meaning a delay of more than three hours can allow mucus to thin and permit sperm penetration. This narrow window contrasts with combined pills, which allow a twelve-hour margin. Strict timing is therefore emphasised during counselling for this method.
options: Their contraceptive effect on mucus wanes quickly
They interact significantly with most antibiotics
They contain a much higher hormone dose
They cause irreversible changes if delayed
They require food for adequate gut absorption
Misoprostol given as the sole first-line agent
Ergometrine given routinely to every woman
Tranexamic acid given prophylactically to all
questions.question: Which uterotonic drug is recommended as first-line for the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage during active management of the third stage of labour?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is recommended as the first-line uterotonic for prophylaxis during active management of the third stage of labour because of its rapid onset, favourable safety profile, and proven effectiveness in reducing postpartum haemorrhage. Misoprostol is typically reserved for settings where oxytocin is unavailable, while ergometrine and carboprost carry more contraindications, such as hypertension, that limit routine first-line use. Tranexamic acid is used as treatment rather than routine prophylaxis.

options: Advise hormonal implant as it does not affect cervical cancer treatment
Insert a levonorgestrel IUS to manage menorrhagia related to tumour
Prioritise referral to oncology and use non-hormonal barrier methods
Recommend combined oral contraceptives to regulate the menstrual cycle
Recommend progesterone injections for long-term contraceptive protection
questions.explanation: In a woman with confirmed cervical cancer, the immediate priority is timely referral to a gynaecologic oncologist for staging, treatment planning, and management. Contraceptive counselling should emphasise non-hormonal methods — primarily barrier methods such as condoms — during cancer treatment. Condoms are additionally recommended to prevent exposure to cytotoxic agents in bodily fluids during chemotherapy. Hormonal methods are generally contraindicated in active malignancy.
questions.question: A woman with confirmed cervical cancer requests advice on family planning. The most appropriate contraceptive counselling would be to:

options: Monitoring recovery through communication with the receiving facility
Maintaining documentation of referred clients for future audit
Encouraging the patient to return for postnatal follow-up visits
Supporting ongoing family planning needs after treatment completion
Recording the referral in the health facility register for tracking
questions.explanation: Follow-up care after PID referral includes: recording the referral in the health facility register, maintaining communication with the receiving facility to track patient progress, encouraging the patient to return for subsequent follow-up visits specific to PID and family planning, and providing ongoing support for reproductive health needs. Encouraging postnatal follow-up visits is not relevant as PID is not a postnatal condition — this is an error that confuses obstetric and gynaecological follow-up protocols.
questions.question: The follow-up care required after referral of a PID patient to a specialist includes all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Adequate folic acid intake before conception and during early pregnancy supports proper closure of the neural tube during the first month of gestation, significantly reducing the risk of neural tube defects including spina bifida and anencephaly. While folate may have modest benefits for other anomalies, its strongest and best-established protective effect is specifically against neural tube defects. This is why preconception folic acid supplementation is a key public health recommendation.
questions.question: Folic acid supplementation before conception is recommended primarily to reduce the risk of which condition?
options: Neural tube defects such as spina bifida

questions.question: A continuous 'machinery-like' murmur heard at the left infraclavicular area in a neonate most likely indicates which congenital cardiac defect?
questions.explanation: The continuous machinery-like murmur, heard best at the left infraclavicular or upper sternal border area throughout both systole and diastole, is the classic auscultatory hallmark of patent ductus arteriosus, reflecting continuous flow from the higher-pressure aorta into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery. Other defects such as VSD or ASD produce murmurs confined to systole rather than being continuous. Confirmatory echocardiography establishes the diagnosis and guides management timing.

options: Routine well-baby discharge without any special support
Provision of compassionate, supportive, and palliative care
Immediate aggressive resuscitation regardless of prognosis
Transfer for emergency cardiac surgery immediately
Urgent neurosurgical shunt insertion at birth
questions.question: An infant born with anencephaly should be managed by the midwife with which primary approach?
questions.explanation: Anencephaly is a uniformly fatal neural tube defect involving absence of major portions of the brain and skull, and management focuses on compassionate, supportive, and palliative care for the infant along with emotional support and counselling for the grieving family, rather than invasive resuscitation or surgical intervention that would not alter the inevitable outcome. Routine well-baby care without acknowledgment of the situation would fail to meet the family's needs. Multidisciplinary bereavement support is an essential part of this care.

questions.question: The most common anatomical site for spina bifida lesions along the vertebral column is:
options: The upper cervical region of the spine
The mid-thoracic region of the spine
The coccygeal tip exclusively in isolation
The lumbosacral region of the spine
The base of the skull at the foramen magnum
questions.explanation: The lumbosacral region is the most frequent site for spina bifida because this area of the neural tube closes last during embryological development, making it particularly vulnerable to defective closure. Cervical and thoracic lesions occur far less commonly. The level of the lesion correlates with the extent of resulting motor and sensory impairment below that level.

In the presence of active or recurrent PID, the IUD should be removed to eliminate a potential source of ascending infection and allow adequate antibiotic treatment of the pelvic infection. History of recurrent PID is a relative contraindication for IUD use. After the infection has been fully treated and resolved, reinsertion may be considered, but only if adequate treatment has been confirmed and the patient understands the associated risks.
options: Copper IUDs should be replaced with hormonal IUDs for reduced infection risk
The IUD must be removed and the infection treated before reinsertion
History of recurrent PID is not a contraindication if properly treated before
IUD reinsertion should proceed six months after the last PID episode
The IUD can remain in place while antibiotics are administered concurrently
questions.question: A woman with recurrent PID who continues to use an intrauterine device should be advised that:

questions.explanation: Gonorrhoea is treated with ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly as a single dose combined with azithromycin 1 g orally to provide coverage for potential co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis and to reduce the risk of antibiotic resistance. Dual therapy is now recommended because of the increasing prevalence of antibiotic-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains. Doxycycline alone is the treatment for chlamydia, not gonorrhoea, and penicillin G is used for syphilis.
questions.question: Which of the following treatment regimens is correct for gonorrhoea according to current STI treatment guidelines?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days as sole therapy
Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days as first-line therapy
Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 7 to 10 days
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g orally simultaneously

questions.explanation: Contact tracing for gonorrhoea and other STIs focuses on notifying recent sexual partners within the relevant exposure window period, typically the past 60 days or the most recent partner if longer. This allows partners to be tested and treated to break the chain of transmission and prevent reinfection. The process should be conducted confidentially and sensitively.
questions.question: A nurse conducting contact tracing for a client diagnosed with gonorrhoea should prioritise notifying:
options: The client's employer and immediate family members
Healthcare providers who previously examined the client
Recent sexual partners within the exposure window period
The client's entire community for public health awareness
All previous sexual contacts from the past five years

questions.explanation: Breech presentation is a well-recognised risk factor for congenital hip dysplasia because of the abnormal intrauterine positioning of the hips and increased mechanical stress on the developing joint, making careful hip examination especially important in infants born by this route. Uncomplicated cephalic delivery does not carry the same increased risk. Additional risk factors include female sex, family history, and firstborn status, all of which should heighten clinical suspicion during newborn examination.
options: Multiple pregnancy with all fetuses in cephalic position
Breech presentation at the time of delivery
Delivery by elective caesarean section for maternal request
Post-term delivery beyond forty-two weeks in isolation
Uncomplicated cephalic vaginal delivery at term
questions.question: Congenital hip dysplasia occurs more commonly in which of the following clinical circumstances?

questions.explanation: Primary infertility refers to the inability to achieve pregnancy in a couple where the woman has never been pregnant before. In contrast, secondary infertility refers to difficulty conceiving after a previous successful pregnancy. The distinction is clinically important as it guides the differential diagnosis: primary infertility more often involves congenital or developmental causes, while secondary infertility may be related to post-pregnancy complications, adhesions, or newly acquired infections.
options: Infertility diagnosed within 6 months of attempting conception
Infertility caused exclusively by male factor sperm abnormalities
Inability to conceive after previous successful pregnancies
Inability to achieve pregnancy despite never having been pregnant before
Infertility associated with primary ovarian insufficiency at any age
questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with the definition of primary infertility?

questions.explanation: The secondary palate forms between the 6th and 9th weeks of gestation when the palatal shelves change from a vertical to a horizontal position and fuse in the midline. Importantly, the secondary palate closes one week later in female fetuses than in male fetuses. This difference in timing explains why females have a higher incidence of isolated cleft palate — if the fusion process is disturbed, the later closing timeline in females provides a longer window for disruption to occur.
options: Weeks 10 to 14; closes only after birth in response to suckling
Weeks 4 to 7; fuses simultaneously in both sexes at the same time
Weeks 6 to 9; closes one week later in females than in males
Weeks 9 to 12; closes two weeks earlier in females than males
Weeks 3 to 6; fuses earlier in females due to oestrogen effects
questions.question: The secondary palate forms between which weeks of gestation, and when does it fuse in female fetuses compared to males?

options: Amputation of the deformed foot in infancy
Prolonged bed rest without any physical intervention
A single injection of botulinum toxin only
Serial gentle manipulation and casting of the foot
Immediate surgical release of all foot tendons
questions.explanation: The Ponseti method corrects clubfoot through a series of gentle manipulations followed by application of a cast after each session, gradually repositioning the foot into a corrected alignment over several weeks, often followed by a minor tenotomy and subsequent bracing to maintain correction. This non-surgical approach has become the gold standard, largely replacing extensive surgical release as first-line treatment. Early initiation shortly after birth improves the likelihood of successful correction.
questions.question: The Ponseti method, used in the management of talipes equinovarus, primarily involves:
A family planning nurse notices a client has a persistently elevated prolactin level. Which contraceptive implication does this finding have?
options: Elevated prolactin may indicate a pituitary adenoma affecting fertility and contraception
High prolactin has no clinical significance in the family planning context
High prolactin is a contraindication specifically for progestin-only pills
High prolactin levels make combined oral contraceptives more effective
Elevated prolactin enhances the efficacy of the copper IUD intrauterine device
questions.explanation: Persistently elevated serum prolactin (hyperprolactinaemia) may indicate a pituitary prolactinoma, which causes anovulation, amenorrhoea, and infertility through suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. This finding has direct implications for contraceptive choice and fertility counselling: if the client desires pregnancy, treating the underlying prolactinoma (with dopamine agonists such as cabergoline or bromocriptine) may restore ovulation. If contraception is required, an appropriate non-hormonal or progestin-only method should be selected.

options: Semen analysis and testicular ultrasound only
Mammography and bone density scanning only
Ovulation assessment, tubal patency testing, and pelvic ultrasound
questions.question: A woman aged 34 has been trying to conceive for over a year without success. Baseline infertility investigations for the female partner should include which combination?
questions.explanation: Standard baseline female infertility workup includes confirming ovulation, typically via mid-luteal progesterone or ultrasound follicle tracking, assessing tubal patency, and performing a pelvic ultrasound to identify structural abnormalities such as fibroids or ovarian cysts. Semen analysis and testicular investigations pertain to the male partner rather than the female. This combination allows identification of the most common causes of female-factor infertility.

options: The infant is older than six months of age
Breastfeeding occurs on demand day and night
Menstruation has not yet returned after delivery
The mother is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding
The infant is younger than six months of age
questions.question: The lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) is effective as a contraceptive when all of the following criteria are met EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: LAM relies on suppression of ovulation by frequent suckling, which only reliably persists while the infant is under six months old, the mother is amenorrhoeic, and breastfeeding is exclusive or nearly exclusive. Once the infant passes six months, supplementary feeding reduces suckling frequency and ovulation risk rises. LAM effectiveness therefore declines sharply beyond this age.

options: Repeated ELISA using a different kit brand
Western blot or nucleic acid test (NAT)
questions.explanation: A positive ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) screening result must be confirmed using the Western blot test or a nucleic acid test (NAT). The Western blot detects antibodies to specific HIV proteins and provides high specificity. NAT directly detects HIV RNA in plasma, confirming infection and allowing viral load quantification. Repeating ELISA alone is insufficient for confirmatory diagnosis.
questions.question: The gold standard confirmatory test for HIV after a positive ELISA screening result is:

options: The dura mater overlying the cerebral hemispheres
The mature cerebral cortex directly beneath the skull
The fragile germinal matrix adjacent to the ventricles
The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle only
The subarachnoid space surrounding the brainstem
questions.explanation: The germinal matrix is a highly vascular, fragile structure present in the preterm brain that is particularly susceptible to haemorrhage because of its rich but poorly supported capillary network, especially in infants born before term. This vulnerability decreases as gestation advances and the germinal matrix involutes closer to term. Bleeding here can extend into the ventricular system, producing the graded severity seen in periventricular-intraventricular haemorrhage.
questions.question: Periventricular-intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm infants most commonly originates from bleeding within which structure?

questions.explanation: The elderly are more likely to complete suicide because they plan more carefully and use more lethal methods (e.g., firearms, hanging) compared to younger individuals who more often use impulsive, less lethal methods (e.g., overdose). Additionally, they are less likely to be discovered in time due to social isolation. This combination results in higher completion rates.
questions.question: According to suicide epidemiology, the elderly attempt suicide LESS often but are MORE successful. The primary reason for their higher completion rate is:
options: Better planning and more lethal methods
Higher rates of depression at all times

questions.question: A patient meets ICD-10 criteria for generalised anxiety disorder. How does the required symptom duration in ICD-10 compare with DSM criteria for the same diagnosis?
questions.explanation: ICD-10 traditionally requires a shorter minimum duration of symptoms, around six months in ICD-10, similar in fact to DSM's six-month requirement in more recent editions, but historically ICD-10's threshold has been considered more lenient in certain diagnostic nuances compared with stricter DSM criteria in earlier versions. Clinicians should be aware that classification system differences can affect diagnostic thresholds and cross-study comparability. Understanding these nuances is relevant when interpreting research literature using different diagnostic systems.
options: Both systems require an identical duration
ICD-10 requires no minimum duration at all
DSM requires a shorter duration than ICD-10
ICD-10 requires a shorter minimum duration than DSM
Duration is irrelevant to either system

questions.explanation: Dysthymia, now often classified as persistent depressive disorder, involves a chronic, low-grade depressive mood lasting at least two years in adults, with fewer or less severe symptoms than a full major depressive episode, though patients can experience a superimposed major depressive episode on top of this baseline, sometimes called double depression. This distinction is important because the chronic nature of dysthymia can make it easily overlooked or normalised by both patients and clinicians. Treatment often requires longer-term therapeutic engagement given the chronic course of the condition.
options: Dysthymia always involves more severe symptoms than major depression
Dysthymia has an identical symptom severity to major depression
Dysthymia lasts only a few days at most
Dysthymia involves fewer, less severe symptoms but a much longer chronic duration
Dysthymia always includes psychotic features unlike major depression
questions.question: A patient with dysthymia describes a chronic, low-grade depressed mood persisting for over two years, without ever meeting full criteria for a major depressive episode. How does this differ from major depressive disorder?
The hallmark feature that distinguishes delirium tremens from uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal is:
questions.explanation: Clouding of consciousness — a qualitative reduction in awareness — is the defining feature that distinguishes delirium tremens from uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal. Both share tremor, tachycardia, insomnia, and anxiety. DTs additionally involves disorientation, amnesia, psychomotor agitation, and hallucinations, all underpinned by the reduced conscious awareness.

questions.question: A patient with insulin-treated diabetes is found confused, sweating, and tremulous with a blood glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. Which psychiatric-like presentation is this metabolic derangement MOST likely to produce?
questions.explanation: Severe hypoglycaemia commonly produces acute confusion, agitation, and abnormal behaviour that can closely mimic a primary psychiatric emergency, but which resolves rapidly once blood glucose is corrected. Recognising the reversible metabolic cause avoids inappropriate psychiatric-only management. Blood glucose should always be checked in any patient presenting with acute confusion of unclear cause.
options: Isolated auditory hallucinations with clear sensorium
Gradual, insidious personality change over years
Selective memory loss for remote events only
Acute confusion with agitation and abnormal behaviour

questions.question: The concept that a psychiatric diagnosis should be made on positive evidence, rather than as a diagnosis of exclusion after failing to find physical causes, reflects which clinical principle?
questions.explanation: The principle that psychiatric diagnosis should be made on positive evidence — not merely as exclusion of organic causes — reflects the concept of diagnostic affirmation in psychiatry. A psychiatric diagnosis is not a failure to find a physical cause; it is a positive, evidence-based clinical conclusion. This principle combats diagnostic nihilism and promotes early, appropriate psychiatric treatment rather than prolonged medical investigation.

Depersonalisation is the subjective sense of detachment from one's own self or body while insight is retained. Derealisation instead refers to the surrounding environment feeling unreal. Retained insight distinguishes this neurotic phenomenon from a delusional passivity experience.
questions.question: A patient describes feeling detached from his own body, as though he is watching himself from outside during a stressful meeting, while remaining fully aware that this feeling is not real. This experience is best termed:

questions.explanation: Automatism is a defence based on involuntary action occurring without conscious control, such as during a seizure, rather than on impaired mental state per se. It differs from the insanity defence, which concerns mental disease affecting understanding of wrongdoing. Loss of voluntary control is the defining feature here.
questions.question: A man commits an assault during a confirmed complex partial seizure with no recollection of the event and no voluntary control over his actions. This defence, based on involuntary conduct, is best described as:

questions.explanation: A full manic episode is distinguished from hypomania by the presence of marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, need for hospitalisation, or psychotic features, whereas hypomania, though involving similar symptoms, does not reach this level of severity and does not require hospitalisation. This distinction is central to differentiating Bipolar I from Bipolar II disorder. Careful assessment of functional impact, not just symptom checklist matching, is essential for accurate diagnosis.
options: Mania and hypomania are identical in all diagnostic respects
Hypomania always lasts longer than a manic episode
Mania requires no impairment in functioning to diagnose
Presence of marked functional impairment or psychotic features
Hypomania always includes psychotic symptoms while mania does not
questions.question: A patient with a manic episode is noted to have decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, and risky spending, all persisting for over a week and causing significant impairment. What severity feature distinguishes this from hypomania?
In the context of gender identity, a condition formerly termed 'Gender Identity Disorder' has been reclassified in recent nomenclature. The reclassification reflects which principle?
questions.explanation: The reclassification of 'Gender Identity Disorder' to 'Gender Dysphoria' reflects the principle of destigmatization - separating pathological distress (dysphoria) from gender identity variation itself. The diagnosis now focuses on the distress caused by incongruence rather than the gender identity itself. ICD-11 further moved gender incongruence out of mental disorders entirely, reflecting evolving scientific and ethical understanding.
options: Destigmatization by separating distress from identity variation
Removal of the condition from all classification systems
The condition is now considered a personality disorder

questions.question: A patient in renal failure develops acute confusion, agitation, and visual hallucinations that fluctuate over the course of the day. This presentation exemplifies which category of psychiatric disturbance?
questions.explanation: Renal failure can produce delirium through accumulation of metabolic toxins affecting brain function, presenting with the fluctuating course and disturbed consciousness typical of an organic confusional state. This differs fundamentally from primary schizophrenia, where consciousness remains clear. Correcting the underlying metabolic derangement is central to resolving the delirium.
options: Organic delirium secondary to metabolic derangement

questions.question: A patient with schizophrenia is being transitioned from an oral antipsychotic to a long-acting injectable formulation. What is the primary clinical rationale for this change?
options: Improved medication adherence and reduced relapse risk
Long-acting injectables always work faster than oral forms
Injectable formulations have no risk of side effects
Oral antipsychotics are never effective for schizophrenia
Injectable formulations eliminate the need for any monitoring
questions.explanation: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics provide sustained medication delivery over weeks, significantly improving adherence in patients who struggle with daily oral medication, thereby reducing the risk of relapse associated with covert or inadvertent non-adherence, a common challenge in the long-term management of schizophrenia. This does not mean injectables act faster in acute crises, since therapeutic levels still build up gradually, and ongoing clinical monitoring remains essential regardless of formulation. Patient preference and shared decision-making are important when considering this treatment option.

questions.question: A patient describes a specific and sudden experience where an ongoing train of thought is felt to be forcibly removed from his mind by an outside influence, leaving his mind suddenly empty. This is termed:
questions.explanation: Thought withdrawal is the delusional experience that thoughts are being actively removed from the mind by an external force, distinguishing it from thought blocking, which is a non-delusional interruption of thought flow without attribution to an outside agency. Recognising the presence or absence of external attribution is key to differentiating these two phenomena. Thought withdrawal is classified among the first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia.

options: The patient's mental state specifically at the time the alleged offence occurred
The patient's current mental capacity to understand proceedings and assist in their own defence
Whether the patient is guilty or innocent of the charge
The patient's overall moral character and personal history
Whether the patient has ever had any psychiatric diagnosis
questions.question: A patient is being assessed for legal competency to stand trial following a criminal charge. What is the primary focus of this specific competency evaluation, distinct from an insanity defence assessment?
questions.explanation: Competency to stand trial evaluates the defendant's current mental state and functional ability to understand the nature of the legal proceedings and rationally assist their attorney in their defence, which is distinct from an insanity defence evaluation that focuses retrospectively on the defendant's mental state at the time the alleged offence was committed. This distinction is fundamental in forensic psychiatric practice, as a patient with a severe mental illness may be found incompetent to stand trial regardless of the ultimate question of criminal responsibility. Restoration of competency, often through treatment, may be pursued before proceedings can continue if a defendant is found incompetent.

questions.question: The desire phase of the sexual response cycle is primarily characterized as:
questions.explanation: The desire phase is primarily psychological — it represents the conscious desire to engage in sexual activity, driven by motivation and personality factors. Unlike the excitement phase (which has objective physiological components like vasocongestion and lubrication), desire is entirely psychological and may be suppressed by psychological factors like stress, depression, and relationship problems.

questions.question: Paranoid-type schizophrenia has a greater prevalence in late-onset schizophrenia (beginning after age 45). By age 65, what happens to psychopathology in established schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Psychopathology in schizophrenia generally decreases with age. Approximately 20% of people with schizophrenia show no active symptoms after age 65. The first episode of schizophrenia diagnosed after age 65 is extremely rare, and late-onset schizophrenia (after age 45) more commonly presents with paranoid features in women. Age appears to reduce the severity of positive symptoms over time.

questions.question: A researcher studying decision-making and emotional regulation identifies the anterior cingulate cortex as playing a key integrative role in psychiatric disorders. What is this region primarily thought to integrate?
questions.explanation: The anterior cingulate cortex serves as a key integrative hub linking cognitive processes, such as attention and conflict monitoring, with emotional processing, playing an important role in regulating behaviour and has been implicated in the neurobiology of conditions such as depression, anxiety, and OCD when its function is disrupted. This integrative role explains why ACC dysfunction is associated with such a broad range of psychiatric symptoms across different disorders. Neuroimaging studies of ACC activity are increasingly used to understand treatment response in various psychiatric conditions.
options: Cognitive and emotional information for regulation of behaviour

questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, incorporating sleep restriction, stimulus control, and cognitive restructuring around sleep-related anxiety, is recommended as first-line treatment for chronic primary insomnia, with evidence showing more durable benefit compared with pharmacological approaches, which are generally reserved for short-term use or when CBT-I is unavailable or insufficient. This approach addresses the behavioural and cognitive factors that often perpetuate chronic insomnia. Long-term reliance on hypnotic medication carries risks of tolerance, dependence, and rebound insomnia upon discontinuation.
questions.question: A patient reports chronic difficulty falling asleep and non-restorative sleep for several months, with significant daytime impairment, in the absence of any other identifiable psychiatric or medical cause. What is the recommended first-line non-pharmacological treatment for this presentation?
options: Long-term nightly benzodiazepine use as first-line therapy
Immediate polysomnography for all patients regardless of history
Permanent daytime napping to compensate for lost sleep
Long-term antipsychotic medication for sleep induction

questions.question: A patient presents with multiple physical complaints, such as headache and fatigue, but on careful history reveals underlying excessive worry about several life domains. What clinical clue in this presentation is characteristic of GAD?
questions.explanation: Patients with generalised anxiety disorder frequently present with somatic complaints such as headache, muscle tension, or fatigue rather than directly reporting excessive worry, making careful history-taking essential to uncover the underlying anxious cognitions and avoid misattributing symptoms solely to physical illness. This pattern can lead to delayed diagnosis if clinicians focus only on ruling out organic causes without exploring the psychological dimension. Recognising this clue allows more timely and appropriate treatment of the underlying anxiety disorder.
options: The patient always volunteers anxiety as the primary complaint
Physical symptoms are never seen in anxiety disorders
This presentation excludes any anxiety diagnosis entirely
Physical symptoms are the presenting complaint rather than the anxiety itself
Somatic symptoms always indicate a purely medical cause

questions.explanation: Resolution phase (return to a resting physiological state) is inherently longer in males than females and further lengthens with advancing age. The refractory period — the time after orgasm during which another orgasm is not possible — increases progressively with age in males. This physiological reality is clinically important in the assessment and management of male sexual dysfunction.
questions.question: Resolution phase of the sexual response cycle is LONGER in males compared to females. An additional factor that prolongs resolution is:
Sleep is described as essential for optimum intellectual functioning and creativity. Growth hormone production surges during which phase of sleep?
questions.explanation: Growth hormone production surges during NREM (non-REM) sleep, particularly during slow wave sleep (stages 3 and 4). NREM sleep serves restorative and homeostatic functions, maintains thermoregulation, energy conservation, and satisfies metabolic needs.
